->THE ARMS OF THE CITY OF STRASBOURG<-
<note>original: "INSIGNIA • CIVITATIS • ARGENTINE." Argentina is the Latin name for the city of Strasbourg.</note>

->IN THE YEAR 1593<-
<note>original: "ANNO • M • D • LXXXXIII"</note>

This sixteenth-century binding is a fine example of **blind-tooling**, a technique where decorative patterns are stamped into the pigskin leather using heated metal tools without the use of gold leaf. The cover is framed by multiple rectangular borders, some featuring delicate floral motifs and others containing a series of tiny portrait medallions.

In the central panel, we see the city's <term>heraldic achievement|the full display of a coat of arms, including the shield and its accessories</term>. The shield itself displays a <term>bend|a diagonal band</term>, which is the official emblem of Strasbourg. Above the shield rests a barred helmet with flowing, leafy <term>mantling|decorative drapery</term>, topped by a crest featuring a pair of wings.

The volume is held shut by two metal clasps with leather hinges on the fore-edge. The spine is reinforced with four prominent <term>raised bands|the ridges where the sewing cords pass under the leather</term>, ensuring the book remained sturdy for centuries of use.

# TO THE MOST DISTINGUISHED CONSULS
## AND ILLUSTRIOUS SENATORS
### OF THE REPUBLIC OF NUREMBERG
->Greeting<-

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'P' decorated with intricate floral and foliate scrolls.</image-desc>

It is a well-known saying of Plato, most distinguished Fathers, that Republics will only be happy if either philosophers rule or kings philosophize. <note>original: "Philosophi regnent, vel reges philosophentur." This is a famous quote from Plato’s *Republic*.</note> For since the correct administration of the State <note>Latin: *Politia*</note> depends entirely on the perfect use of reason, and according to the opinion of Aristotle, the one who most excels in virtue and wisdom is, by the silent consensus of all nature, the most worthy of ruling over all. While this honor belongs by its very nature only to God and to the Man-Christ, the Best and Greatest, it is also shared by a certain participation with those whom He willed to be His vicars on earth, honoring them with the name of "Gods." <note>This refers to Psalm 82:6, "I said, 'You are gods,'" a common biblical justification for the authority of civil magistrates in the early modern period.</note>

Just as He has been accustomed to stir up, call, and instruct these men for right governance by a certain special destiny—as the examples of Moses, Joshua, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson, the Maccabees, and similar figures teach us—so too, by a more general method, that good Author of a good nature is accustomed to unfold and illuminate the rules of right living inscribed on the minds of all men. He does this by the efficacy of the Spirit in certain people born to command, who possess "golden souls" <note>A reference to Plato’s *Republic*, where he suggests that those fit to lead are endowed by nature with "gold," while others are made of silver or bronze.</note> in Plato’s view. He makes them participants in truth and virtue, as much as is divinely permitted, just as they share in His own essence. 

Indeed, there are two norms of virtue and truth: **Sacred Authority**, consisting of eternal reason, and **Profane Reason**, relying on mortal authority. The former, enjoying the unpretentious name of **Theology**, is like a most brilliant sun that can dispel and illuminate all the shadows of the human mind by itself. However, this is granted only to those who, through the singular kindness of the Divine Power, have received the revelation of the divine oracles—first outlined in the **Mosaic Law**, and subsequently explained by the **Gospel Law**. 

The latter norm, which men have called **Philosophy** in imitation of the wise God, gathers the remnants of the "human shipwreck" <note>A common theological metaphor for the state of human nature after the Fall—the idea being that while the "ship" of perfect human nature was wrecked by sin, some fragments (reason) still float on the surface.</note> and investigates the law of uncorrupted nature. While it understands and deplores the accidental foulness of man, it strives to reach the idea of native beauty, if not by action, then at least by contemplation. But even in that effort it is frustrated; while it recognizes what it lacks, it remains ignorant of the cause of the disease and sees no way to dispel it. Thus, it turns entirely to the good Author of nature—whose goodness envies no one—so that, as it owes the beginnings of its birth to Him, it may also humbly and devoutly seek from Him the aid for its restoration and preservation. This goal of its philosophy...

The author distinguishes between Theology (divine revelation) and Philosophy (human reason) as the two paths to understanding virtue.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the preface addressed to the Senators of Nuremberg, moving from the divine right of rulers to the philosophical foundations of knowledge and the necessity of respecting traditional authority.</meta>

# PREFACE

Socrates, judged by the oracle of Apollo to be the wisest of all mortals, established this principle when he taught that all things should be referred to that "highest good and beautiful," and defined philosophy as a "preparation for death." <note>original: "philosophiā mortis commentationem esse." This is a classic Platonic definition found in the *Phaedo*.</note> Indeed, he did not hesitate to assert that philosophy holds the primary place among all things we have received from the Gods. In this one thing, however, he was deceived: through his ignorance of Divine Authority (even if he perhaps silently suggested that this authority was placed beyond the reach of human gifts), he assigned the first rank to reason—which, in truth, ought only to be numbered among the secondary gifts.

Now, indeed, human reason itself—for divine reason completely dims and obscures the eyes of men, much like the sun's brilliance blinds owls—deduces universal theory and contemplation from the history and observation of individual things. Yet, such observation cannot be performed in a short time, nor by a single person. Therefore, to provide the "equipment" of reason, so to speak, the constant order of nature persuades us that experience must serve as a handmaid and midwife. Consequently, we must place the highest value on the authority of those who have found things through observed reason, established what they found, and taught what they established. For this reason, that admirable initiate and interpreter of nature, Aristotle—who asserted that nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the senses—pronounced that "the learner must believe." <term>τὸν μανθάνοντα πιστεύειν <note>original Greek: "ton manthanonta pisteuein." A core pedagogical principle in Aristotelian thought: a student must first trust the teacher's authority to eventually reach independent understanding.</note></term>

For although the freedom of reason and speech, beholden to no authority and devoted to truth alone, is becoming of a philosopher, such a state can only be attained by those few whom "impartial Jupiter has loved" <note>A reference to Virgil's *Aeneid*, describing those rare individuals capable of heroic or divine insight.</note> and who have surpassed all authority through the piercing clarity of a divine mind. Meanwhile, for the average person—who makes up the largest part of humanity—it is much more advisable to serve the opinions of their predecessors than to seize the tyranny of <term>vainglory <note>original Greek: "κενοδοξίας" (kenodoxias), meaning empty pride or conceit.</note></term> through a reckless zeal for liberty that repudiates the authority of the elders.

We might set aside the "Sarmanes" <note>original: "Germanas." Likely referring to the Shramanas, ancient Indian ascetic practitioners.</note> and Brahmins of the Indians, the priests of the Egyptians, the Chaldeans of the Babylonians, the *Tarabosteseos* <note>A term for the noble, hat-wearing class of the Scythians or Getae.</note> of the Scythians, and the Druids of the Germans and Gauls. Certainly, the two most famous schools of the ancient Greek philosophers—the Ionic school, stretching from Thales to Epicurus, and the Italic school, from Pythagoras all the way to Socrates—granted a great deal to authority. While they followed the tracks of reason, they frequently turned into the "territories of authority." This is more than proved by that famous Pythagorean saying: "He himself said it." <term>ἀυτὸς ἔφα <note>original Greek: "autos epha." Known in Latin as *ipse dixit*; it refers to an assertion accepted as true simply because a master said it.</note></term>

Socrates, indeed, when he had determined to restore a mutilated philosophy to its wholeness—investigating not only the obscurity of nature but also the corruption of morals and seeking a way to repair them—brought forth various "colonies" of later philosophers from himself, thanks to his elegant method of philosophizing and the holiness of his life. These skillful disciples strove to either understand more rightly or cultivate more diligently the natural seeds of virtue and truth they had gathered from him.

<meta>This page continues the preface by tracing the lineage of philosophical schools from the foundations of Socrates and Plato through the development of the Academy and the Lyceum, leading eventually to the life and historical context of Plotinus in Rome.</meta>

# PREFACE

From this point, the sect of the Academic philosophers was established by **Plato**, and that of the **Cynics** by **Antisthenes**, which soon also produced the **Stoic** school from within itself. **Aristotle**, the disciple of **Plato**, led the **Peripatetic** colony into the Lyceum; a school by no means inferior to its "mother city" <note>Metropolis</note> due to the clarity of its order and method, which has continued in an unbroken succession for so many centuries. Meanwhile, **Speusippus** preserved the name and dignity of the Old Academy with his successors, while **Arcesilaus** introduced the Middle Academy, and **Lacydes** the New.

Later, after the constitution of the Athenian school was disturbed along with the fall of the empire, the Academy began to spread its branches before all other sects—first through all of Greece, and then even through Italy. Such was the kindness of the climate and the soil that these living roots grew into the widest forests. And after "captured Greece took captive her fierce conqueror," <note>original: "Græcia capta, ferū victorē cepit." A famous quote from the Roman poet Horace, referring to how Greek culture dominated Rome after the Roman military conquest of Greece.</note> as the saying goes, the harvest of **Platonic** philosophy was especially abundant in Rome. This was attested and celebrated wonderfully, not only through living tradition but also by the writings of most learned men.

This is best demonstrated by **Plotinus of Lycopolis**, whom we here bring forth onto a more refined and elegant literary stage. From the age of twenty-eight, when he first approached philosophy, he was a diligent pupil for eleven years under **Ammonius of Alexandria**, the greatest of philosophers, and a fellow student of **Origen** and **Erennius**. <note>The "Origen" mentioned here is the Neoplatonist philosopher, a contemporary of Plotinus, though early modern scholars often debated if this was the same person as the famous Christian Church Father.</note> It had long been agreed among them that they would not publish the <term>acroamatic <note>Oral teachings intended only for an inner circle of advanced students, rather than for the general public.</note></term> doctrines of their teacher, but would protect the authority of the school by communicating them only by word of mouth to legitimate listeners. 

But after **Erennius** first broke this faith, and then **Origen** followed suit—and also because the students of **Plotinus** (of whom he had many learned followers in Rome over twenty-six years) were following only a disorganized oral tradition without a written reading of the doctrines—**Plotinus** finally applied his mind to writing. This occurred when he was over forty years old, continuing until his sixty-sixth year, which was the second year of the Emperor **Claudius II**—a year that proved fatal to both. 

Since **Porphyry** has followed the details of his life diligently and at length, there is no reason for us to "do what has already been done." <note>original: "actū agamus."</note> But let us observe this one thing: **Plotinus** lived in those times when secular philosophy—provoked by the rivalry of the **Christian** religion, which was then emerging far and wide, and further compelled by the truth of its doctrines—could have most easily submitted to the yoke of Christ. This would have happened had it not been for the ambition and wickedness of those who practiced philosophy only as far as their beards and cloaks, <note>A reference to those who took on the outward appearance of a philosopher without the inward virtue.</note> and who, swollen with the reputation of their wisdom, thought it most disgraceful to obey those they considered unlearned and common. For while they strove to defend the authority of secular wisdom, they observed in the meantime that Christian piety relied not so much on the subtlety of arguments as on the holiness of character and the frequency of miracles. They did not hesitate to "stir up Hell itself," <note>original: "Acheronta mouere." A classical idiom meaning to resort to any means possible, even the most underworldly or forbidden, to achieve a goal.</note> that is, to call upon **Magic** for assistance under the pretext of human philosophy. Thus, after **Apollonius of Tyana** (whose wonderful illusions the most cunning <term>evil spirit <note>original: "cacodæmon."</note></term> used to mock the miracles of Christ the Best and Greatest)...

# PREFACE

...to undermine the authority [of the Apostles], and tried to set this man up as a kind of antagonist against him) <note>The author is likely referring to how critics tried to set up pagan "wonder-workers" as rivals to Christ or the Apostles.</note> Julian the Chaldean, called the Wonder-worker, Iamblichus of Chalcis, Maximus of Ephesus, Libanius the sophist, Amelius and Sopater of Apamea, Aedesius the Cappadocian, Chrysanthius the Lydian, and that impious **Porphyry** of Tyre, along with the blasphemous **Proclus** the Lycian, introduced impious magic under a philosophical mask. 

This state of affairs certainly caused the followers of the Christian religion in that age not only to condemn the philosophers (and rightly so), but also philosophy itself (though undeservedly) as impiety; this was especially so since Saint Paul seriously commands the godly to abstain from empty philosophy <note>original: "ab inani philosophia." A reference to Colossians 2:8, "See to it that no one takes you captive through hollow and deceptive philosophy."</note>. Matters reached the point where, out of hatred for magic, divine Theology was completely stripped of the service and ministry of pure Philosophy—a service that was as honorable as it was necessary. 

But since the more excellent a thing is, the worse its abuse tends to be, these things should have been carefully distinguished from one another, so that what was the fault of human morals was not attributed to the art itself. More rightly did those—among whom were Melito, Bishop of Sardis (a disciple of the philosopher Fronto), Pantaenus of Alexandria the Stoic, with his disciples Clement of Alexandria and Alexander, Bishop of Jerusalem, as well as Quadratus, Aristides of Athens, Justin Martyr, **Cyprian** of Carthage (who was a magician before becoming a bishop), and **Origen** the Egyptian, along with many others—who, having rejected philosophical vanity, forced philosophical truth to serve as a handmaid to revealed truth. Thus, they turned the otherwise forbidden use of "Egyptian gold" <note>A common metaphor in early Christian writing for taking the "wealth" of pagan learning and repurposing it for the worship of God, based on the Israelites taking gold from Egypt during the Exodus.</note> toward the worship of the true God. This was done with such success that **Julian the Apostate** <note>The Roman Emperor Julian (reigned 361–363 AD), who attempted to revive paganism and famously banned Christian teachers from using classical Greek texts.</note> thought the only way to uproot Christianity was to bar the godly from the literature of the heathens, because <note>original: "q," an abbreviation for "quia."</note> he realized that if they were instructed in these things, they would defend the truth with much greater probability and effectiveness, defeating the impious with their own weapons.

Indeed, although it seems absurd that men turned away from God and who are professed enemies of true piety could arrive at any knowledge of sincere (though profane) truth, yet great is the indulgence of that eternal Giver of all good things. Just as He shines His sun upon the impious as well as the godly, so too, by a wonderful counsel, He gave the prophets of the heathens much clearer revelations concerning the Messiah (as can be established from the Sibylline Oracles <note>A collection of ancient oracular utterances which many early Christians interpreted as pagan prophecies of the coming of Christ.</note>) than even to the prophets of the Jews themselves. 

Therefore, though **Plotinus** may have felt impiously regarding our revealed religion, and perhaps even attacked it with magical efforts (even if **Porphyry** trifles with the claim that it was a God, not a demon, who appeared to the Egyptian priest when summoning his guide), yet in that branch of philosophy which is consistent with human reason and nature—that is, the study and expression of God’s works in every kind of being—he was outstanding after **Plato**. Indeed, if it is true, as someone once said, that "Platonists can become Christians with only a few things changed," then **Plotinus** certainly...

# PREFACE

...certainly, [Plotinus], who investigated and interpreted Platonic teachings much more accurately and diligently, has earned the first place among these. When compared to others of the same profession, he seems no less worthy of being called **divine** than Plato once seemed when compared to the **daemonic** Aristotle. <note>The author uses "divine" (theos) and "daemonic" (daimonios) in the classical sense: "divine" as reaching the highest truths, and "daemonic" as possessing a brilliant, supernatural-like intellect.</note> 

But if—either because he did not wish to, or because, lacking divine favor, he could not reach the knowledge of eternal piety—he remained a pagan, we, upon whom the more generous grace of the divine spirit has shone, should compel his philosophy to serve as a handmaiden to Theology. For his thought is consistent with right nature and thus not foreign to divine authority. Let us learn to take these treasures of nature, unearthed from these inner shrines through both contemplation and action, and refer them to the glory of the one God. Let us find rest in the light of Him who illuminates every man, though in different ways. <note>A reference to John 1:9, "The true light that gives light to everyone."</note>

With this very intention, most distinguished gentlemen, we wished to present **Plotinus**—who was issued from our workshop some years ago in Marsilio Ficino’s translation—now speaking in his own language <note>The "own language" refers to the original Greek text, which was being printed alongside the Latin translation.</note>, both expanded and corrected. This was made possible through the literary generosity of four Greek manuscript copies: three from Italy, and a fourth by **Johannes Sambucus** of Trnava, the Imperial Historian, which is to be preferred above all private copies and even compared with those of many princes. 

Our goal was to provide students of both languages the opportunity to understand, judge, and apply Platonic philosophy (that is, the philosophy most akin to the Christian religion) to the practice of true piety. For the text flows with such a wealth of thought and brevity of words that it can sometimes be understood more correctly from the Greek than from the Latin—not through any fault of the translator, but because of the obscurity of the subject matter and the specific character of the language itself.

Indeed, most honorable Fathers, I wished to offer this same author especially to your Republic. Since similarity breeds friendship, it is fitting that this leading philosopher—and an outstanding teacher of truth and virtue in his own right—should come forth under the title and patronage of that Republic which:

> *Has raised its head among the cities of Germany as much*
> *As cypresses are wont to do among the pliant shrubs* <note>original: "Inter Teutoniæ tantum caput extulit urbes, / Quantum lenta solent inter uiburna cupressi." This is a clever adaptation of Virgil’s *Eclogues* (1.24-25), where the poet originally praised the city of Rome. Here, the author substitutes "Germany" to praise the city of Nuremberg.</note>

This city, through a steady succession of many years, has expressed both Corinthian wealth <note>referring to the city's commercial prosperity</note> and an excellent discipline (much holier than that of Sparta) in the heart of Germany. It has bravely preserved these through long-lasting kindness among so many who would plot against its liberty. 

But while these praises of your city are ancestral, what must now be said is personal to you, the noble descendants of such parents: that with a mind no less royal than philosophical, you have acted at a time when we see most people brooding over their states in either shameful or vain idleness. You have established the **Academy of Altdorf**, and invited the most learned...

<meta>This page serves as the formal opening of Marsilio Ficino’s preface to his translation of Plotinus. It continues the theme of using Platonic philosophy to support Christian theology, specifically tracing a lineage of "pious philosophy" and identifying the intellectual threats of the time, such as radical Aristotelianism.</meta>

# PREFACE

...are more easily passed down. Therefore, it was not without divine providence—which clearly wishes to wonderfully recall all people to itself according to their individual talents—that a certain pious philosophy was born long ago, appearing both among the Persians under **Zoroaster** <note>The legendary ancient Persian prophet, seen by Renaissance scholars as a source of primordial wisdom.</note> and among the Egyptians under **Mercury** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical Egyptian sage.</note>, consistent with itself in both places. It was then nurtured among the Thracians under **Orpheus** and **Aglaophemus**, and soon reached its youth under **Pythagoras** among the Greeks and Italians, until finally it was brought to perfection in Athens by the divine **Plato**. 

However, it was the ancient custom of these theologians to shroud divine mysteries in mathematical numbers and figures, as well as in poetic fables, so that they would not be easily accessible to just anyone. Finally, **Plotinus** stripped these theological veils; as **Porphyry** and **Proclus** testify, he was the first and only one to divinely penetrate the secrets of the ancients. Yet, because of his incredible brevity of speech, his abundance of thoughts, and the depth of his meaning, he requires not only a translation into another language but also commentaries. We have therefore worked on translating and explaining the earlier theologians found in Plato and Plotinus, so that as this theology comes to light, poets may cease to count the sacred deeds and mysteries of piety among their impious fables. 

Furthermore, many **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note>—that is, nearly all philosophers—should be warned that they must not think of our common religion as if it were a collection of old wives' tales. Indeed, almost the entire world is now occupied by the Peripatetics and divided into two main sects: the **Alexandrian** and the **Averroistic**. <note>The Alexandrians followed Alexander of Aphrodisias, believing the soul was mortal; the Averroists followed the Muslim philosopher Averroes, believing there was only one "intellect" shared by all humans. Both views were seen as threats to Christian doctrine on the individual soul.</note> The former think our intellect is mortal, while the latter contend it is one single entity for all. Both equally destroy all religion at its foundation, especially since they seem to deny divine providence regarding human affairs; in both cases, they have even abandoned their own teacher, Aristotle. Today, few interpret his mind with that same piety shown by the sublime **Pico**, our fellow Platonist <note>original: "Picum Complatonicū," referring to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note>, or as **Theophrastus**, **Themistius**, **Porphyry**, **Simplicius**, **Avicenna**, and recently **Plethon** once did.

If anyone thinks that such widespread impiety, protected by such sharp intellects, can be erased among men solely through a simple preaching of faith, he is straying far from the truth; he will undoubtedly be proven wrong by the reality of the situation. There is a need here for a much greater power: either through divine miracles appearing everywhere, or at least through a certain **philosophical religion** <note>Ficino's concept of a philosophy that leads the mind to religious truth through reason.</note> that will eventually persuade philosophers, who would listen to it more willingly. It pleases divine providence in these times to confirm the nature of its religion through philosophical authority and reason, until at a set time, it may confirm the true form of religion among all nations with manifest miracles, as it once did. 

Led therefore by divine providence, we have interpreted the divine Plato and the great Plotinus. We sent Plato to you long ago, so that in him **Cosimo** <note>Cosimo de' Medici, Lorenzo's grandfather and Ficino’s first patron.</note> might live again, in whom he did indeed live again, and, reborn, grew according to our wishes and now happily flourishes in his maturity. As for Plotinus, although we are now rightfully sending him to you, we do not so much "send" him as watch him hurrying toward your house of his own accord and with great eagerness. It is as if he were drawn from Plato himself, like iron by a **Herculean stone** <note>original: "lapide Herculeo," a classical term for a magnet.</note>, so that he may live most happily alongside his Plato in your care, O magnanimous **Lorenzo**, the unique patron of the learned. 

Listen happily, therefore, to Plotinus as he speaks with Plato in your home about all the mysteries of philosophy. But before you listen to him, you must listen to **Porphyry**, his pious disciple, who narrates the life, character, and deeds of his master both briefly and most truly. Our **Angelo Poliziano**, your protégé and a man of the sharpest judgment, considers this history to be as oratorical as it is philosophical; for that reason, it will please you greatly. Finally, not only listen happily, but live most happily. And as much as you love us, my dearest Lorenzo, I pray that you love our **Valori**—I mean **Filippo**, an excellent man, a student of Platonic wisdom, and one who loves you ardently.

<summary>Marsilio Ficino presents his translation of Plotinus to Lorenzo de' Medici, tracing a lineage of wisdom from Zoroaster to Plato. He argues that Platonic philosophy is a necessary tool to combat the "impious" Aristotelian sects of his day and defend the immortality of the soul.</summary>

# EXHORTATION OF MARSILIO FICINO THE FLORENTINE TO THOSE LISTENING TO AND READING PLOTINUS.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'P' at the beginning of the text, featuring ornate scrolls and botanical flourishes within a square frame.</image-desc>

FIRST, I advise all of you who come here to hear the divine Plotinus that you should consider yourselves as listening to Plato himself speaking through the mask of Plotinus. For either Plato once lived again in Plotinus (which the followers of Pythagoras will easily grant us), or the same Spirit <note>Original: *Dæmon*—in the Platonic sense, this refers to a guiding divine spirit or "genius" that inspires a philosopher, rather than a malevolent entity.</note> first inspired Plato and then Plotinus (which no Platonist will deny). Entirely the same inspirer breathes through both the Platonic and the Plotinian mouth. But in inspiring Plato, the spirit poured out a more abundant breath; in Plotinus, however, a narrower breath—or rather, let me not say narrower, but at least no less majestic, and sometimes even deeper. Thus the same divinity pours out divine oracles for the human race through both mouths, in both cases worthy of a most keen interpreter. For while in the former case [Plato] the divinity lingers in unfolding the covers of allegories, in the latter [Plotinus] he labors both in expressing the most sacred meanings everywhere and in explaining them with the briefest words. Remember, moreover, that you will penetrate the exalted mind of Plotinus not with the senses as a companion nor human reason as a guide, but with a certain more sublime mind. Indeed (to speak in the Platonic manner), we call other men "rational souls," but Plotinus we call not a soul, but an <term>Intellect</term> <note>Original: *intellectus*. In Neoplatonism, the Intellect is a higher stage of being than the Soul, representing pure, intuitive thought.</note>. This is what all philosophers of his age, especially the Platonists, called him. And would that the assistance of Porphyry, or Eustochius, or Proclus—who arranged and explained the books of Plotinus—were here for us in interpreting these mysteries. I hope, however, for that which is far more blessed: that divine help will not fail Marsilio Ficino in translating and explaining the divine books of Plotinus. But now, with heavenly omens, let us happily approach the task of translating the first book of Plotinus and briefly explaining its argument, and the rest in turn. And may you imagine Plato himself crying out thus toward Plotinus:

> He alone is wise; the rest flit about like shadows.
> <note>Original Greek: *Οἷος πέπνυται, τοὶ δ' ὡς σκιαὶ ἀΐσσουσι*. A quote from Homer's *Odyssey* describing the prophet Tiresias.</note>

->MARSILIO FICINO<-
->To the Great-Souled Piero de' Medici<-
->Greetings<-

*WHEN I was walking on the Ides of November in the countryside of Careggi <note>The location of the Medici villa where the Platonic Academy of Florence met.</note> together with the Great Lorenzo de' Medici, and we were interpreting many of Plato's mysteries back and forth, I happened to fall in our talk from wisdom into the subject of Fortune. I began to accuse her more sharply because she had resisted Plato for many centuries as he strove toward the light. Then he said, "Do not, Marsilio, call our Plato unfortunate, unless perhaps you think that I am to be unfortunate." We finished our conversation then with these words. But is it permitted to consider Lorenzo unfortunate because of the death that followed? And to think that the fortune of Plato has utterly collapsed at the same time? Far be it from me to think that soul less than happy, whom the joyful ether received with a new applause as he flew out from the shackles of the body—with a great star falling upon the roofs of Lorenzo, and wonderful flames from on high flashing for three days through the fields of Careggi. But two days before his death, Jupiter, hurling bolts from his glowing right hand at the sacred citadels, terrified the city—soon to be orphaned of such a father—and terrified the enemies, lest they might attempt something grave against the unconquered House of Medici. Therefore, neither the hero Lorenzo, nor the heroic Piero, son of Lorenzo, should be judged less happy hereafter for the things that have recently happened; nor for that reason is our Plato unfortunate. His head was until now comforted by the altogether healthy shadow of the Laurel <note>A pun on the name Lorenzo (*Laurentius*), which is derived from *Laurus* (Laurel).</note>; now his feet rest upon a most firm Rock <note>A pun on the name Piero (*Petrus*), which means Rock (*Petra*).</note>. Finally, Plotinus, now grasped by your hands, will meanwhile support the elder Plato on his pious shoulders, and with you as leader, will bring him forth into the light.*

<summary>In this preface, Ficino argues that Plotinus is the definitive interpreter of Plato, even suggesting they share the same divine inspiration. He concludes with a personal dedication to Piero de' Medici, framing the continued study of Neoplatonism as a legacy of his late father, Lorenzo the Magnificent.</summary>
<keywords>Marsilio Ficino, Plotinus, Plato, Lorenzo de' Medici, Piero de' Medici, Neoplatonism, Careggi, Intellect, divine inspiration, Laurel and Rock pun</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s introductory "Exhortation," moving from the spiritual nature of Plotinus’s inspiration to a historical lineage of "pious philosophy" (the *prisca theologia*). Ficino explains why he translated Plotinus: to combat contemporary secularism and heresy by using Platonic philosophy to defend the faith.</meta>

# P R E F A C E.

...are more easily transmitted. Thus, not without divine providence—wishing, clearly, to wonderfully recall all people to Himself according to the capacity of each individual—it happened that a certain pious philosophy was born long ago both among the Persians under Zoroaster and among the Egyptians under Mercury <note>Original: *Mercurio*. Ficino refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage thought to be a contemporary of Moses.</note>, in both cases consistent with itself. It was later nourished among the Thracians under Orpheus and Aglaophemus. It grew up soon after under Pythagoras among the Greeks and Italians, and was finally brought to perfection by the divine Plato in Athens. However, it was the ancient custom of the Theologians to cover divine mysteries with mathematical numbers and figures, as well as with poetic fictions, so that they would not be common to just anyone. Plotinus finally stripped Theology of these veils, and he was the first and only one, as Porphyry and Proclus testify, to penetrate the secrets of the ancients by divine inspiration. But because of his incredible brevity of words, his abundance of thoughts, and his depth of meaning, he requires not only a translation into another language but also commentaries. We have therefore labored in translating and explaining the higher Theologians—Plato and Plotinus—so that, as this Theology comes to light, the poets may cease to impiously count the deeds and mysteries of piety among their fables. Furthermore, the many Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, whose school was called the Peripatetic school.</note>—that is, nearly all philosophers—may be warned that one should not think of religion, at least the common sort, as if it were old wives’ tales. For almost the entire world is occupied by Peripatetics and divided into two main sects: the Alexandrian and the Averroist. The former think our intellect is mortal; the latter contend that there is only one single intellect [for all mankind]. Both equally destroy all religion from its foundations, especially because they seem to deny divine providence regarding human beings, and in both cases, they have even abandoned their own master, Aristotle. Today, few interpret his mind with that same piety with which Theophrastus, Themistius, Porphyry, Simplicius, Avicenna, and recently Pletho once did—except for our own sublime Pico, the fellow-Platonist <note>Count Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Ficino’s brilliant young colleague.</note>. If anyone thinks that such widespread impiety, fortified by such sharp wits, can be erased among men by a certain simple preaching of the faith alone, he is wandering far from the truth; he will undoubtedly be proven wrong by reality itself. Here, a much greater power is needed: either divine miracles appearing everywhere, or at least a certain philosophical religion that might eventually persuade philosophers, who would listen to it more willingly. It pleases divine providence in these times to confirm the very nature of its religion with philosophical authority and reason, until at a certain appointed time, as it once did, it may confirm the truest form of religion with manifest miracles throughout all nations.

Led, therefore, by divine providence, we have interpreted the divine Plato and the great Plotinus. We sent Plato himself to you long ago, so that in him he might one day live again—the one in whom Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici, Lorenzo’s grandfather and Ficino’s original patron.</note> lived again, and having been reborn, grew up according to our wishes and now flourishes happily as an adult. As for Plotinus, although we are now rightfully about to send him, we do not so much "send" him as we watch him hurrying toward your house of his own accord and with eagerness. He is as if drawn from Plato himself, like iron by a certain Herculean stone <note>A classical term for a magnet or lodestone.</note>, so that he may live most happily alongside his own Plato in your care, Magnanimous Lorenzo, the unique patron of men of letters. Hear then, happily, Plotinus speaking with you and with Plato about all the mysteries of philosophy; but before you listen to him, you must listen to his pious disciple Porphyry, who tells of the life, character, and deeds of his master both very briefly and very truly. Our Angelo Poliziano <note>A famous humanist poet and scholar in the Medici circle.</note>, your own student and a man of the sharpest judgment, deems this history to be as much oratorical as it is philosophical; therefore, it will please you greatly. Finally, not only hear him happily, but also live most happily. And as much as you love us, most beloved Lorenzo, I pray you love our Valori—I mean Filippo <note>Filippo Valori, the patron who funded the printing of this edition.</note>, an excellent man, a student of Platonic wisdom, and one who loves you ardently.

<summary>Ficino outlines the historical lineage of "pious philosophy" from Zoroaster to Plotinus and argues that Platonic philosophy is a necessary tool for defending Christian providence against the secularizing trends of contemporary Aristotelianism.</summary>
<keywords>Prisca Theologia, Zoroaster, Hermes Trismegistus, Peripatetics, Averroism, Alexandrism, Divine Providence, Lorenzo de' Medici, Pico della Mirandola, Filippo Valori</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s introduction, transitioning from his general theory of "pious philosophy" to a specific exhortation on how to read Plotinus. He frames Plotinus as the direct spiritual successor—or even the reincarnation—of Plato, and contextualizes the publication of this work within the transition of patronage from the late Lorenzo de' Medici to his son, Piero.</meta>

# THE EXHORTATION OF MARSILIO FICINO
### THE FLORENTINE, TO THOSE HEARING AND
### READING PLOTINUS.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a landscape with a building and a seated figure.</image-desc>

At the outset, I advise all of you who come here to listen to the divine Plotinus, that you should consider yourselves to be hearing Plato himself speaking through the person of Plotinus. For either Plato once lived again in Plotinus (which the followers of Pythagoras will easily grant us) or the same <term>Daemon</term> <note>In the Platonic tradition, a 'daemon' is not an evil spirit, but a guiding supernatural power or guardian spirit that mediates between the divine and the human.</note> who previously inspired Plato later inspired Plotinus, which no Platonist will deny. In every way, the same inspirer breathes through both the Platonic and the Plotinian mouth. But in breathing into Plato, he pours out a more abundant spirit; in Plotinus, however, he breathes a narrower breath—yet I would not say narrower, but at least no less majestic, and sometimes nearly more profound. Thus, the same divinity pours forth divine oracles to the human race through both mouths. In both cases, he is worthy of a most sharp-witted interpreter: for there [in Plato], the interpreter must labor to unroll the coverings of allegories, while here [in Plotinus], he must work both to express the most sacred meanings found everywhere and to explain his extremely brief words. Remember, moreover, that you will penetrate the lofty mind of Plotinus not by following your senses or by the guidance of human reason, but by a certain more sublime mind. Indeed (to speak in the Platonic manner), we call other men "rational souls," but we call Plotinus not a "soul," but "<term>Intellect</term>." <note>Ficino uses 'Intellectus' to denote the highest part of the soul that perceives truth directly and intuitively, rather than through step-by-step reasoning.</note> This is what all the philosophers of his age, especially the Platonists, called him. And I wish that, in interpreting these mysteries, we had the assistance of Porphyry, or Eustochius, or Proclus, who arranged and explained the books of Plotinus. Nevertheless, I hope for that which is far more fortunate: that divine aid will not fail Marsilio Ficino in translating and explaining the divine books of Plotinus. But now, with heavenly omens, let us happily proceed to the translation of the first book of Plotinus and to a brief explanation of its argument, and so on for the rest. And you should imagine Plato himself crying out thus toward Plotinus:

->He alone is wise, while the rest flit about like shadows.<-
<note>original Greek: "Οἷος πέπνυται, τοὶ δ' ὡς σκιαὶ ἀΐσσουσι" – original Latin: "Iste sapit solus, volitant reliqui sicut umbra." This is a quote from Homer’s Odyssey, describing the prophet Tiresias in the underworld.</note>

### MARSILIO FICINO
->To the Great-souled Piero de' Medici<-
->Greetings.<-

*On the Ides of November, while I was walking in the fields of Careggi <note>The location of a famous Medici villa where Ficino's Platonic Academy met.</note> together with the Great Lorenzo de' Medici, and while we were interpreting many of Plato’s mysteries back and forth, it happened by chance during our conversation that the topic shifted from wisdom to fortune. I began to accuse fortune quite sharply for having obstructed Plato—who sought the light—for so many centuries. Then Lorenzo said, "Marsilio, do not call our Plato unfortunate, unless perhaps you think that I am going to be unfortunate." We concluded our conversation then with those words. But is it permitted to consider Lorenzo unfortunate because of the death that followed? And that Plato’s fortune has utterly collapsed along with him? Far be it from me to think that soul less than happy, for as it flew from the shackles of the body, the joyful heavens received it with a new applause, while a great star fell over the house of the Medici and wondrous flames flashed from on high through the fields of Careggi for three days. But two days before his death, Jupiter, "with his red right hand striking the sacred towers," <note>A quotation from the Roman poet Horace, describing a divine omen.</note> terrified the city that was soon to be orphaned of such a father; he terrified his enemies, lest they might attempt something grave against the unconquered house of the Medici. Therefore, neither the hero Lorenzo, nor the heroic Piero, son of Lorenzo, should be judged any less fortunate hereafter because of what has recently happened; nor for that reason is our Plato unfortunate. His head, which until now was sheltered by the truly healing shade of the "laurel," <note>A pun on the name Laurentius (Lorenzo) and the 'laurus' (laurel tree).</note> now has its feet resting upon the firmest "rock." <note>A pun on the name Petrus (Piero/Peter) and 'petra' (rock).</note> Finally, Plotinus, now grasped by your hands, will meanwhile support the elder Plato upon his pious shoulders and, with you as his leader, will bring him forth into the light.*

<summary>Marsilio Ficino presents Plotinus as the "Intellect" of the Platonic tradition and recounts the death of Lorenzo the Magnificent, framing his son Piero as the new "rock" of support for Platonic philosophy.</summary>

<meta>This page begins the biography of the Neoplatonist philosopher Plotinus, written by his student Porphyry. The text is presented in parallel columns of the original Greek and the Latin translation by the Renaissance scholar Marsilio Ficino.</meta>

# THE LIFE OF PLOTINUS, AND THE ORDER OF HIS BOOKS, BY PORPHYRY,

->Translated by Marsilio Ficino of Florence.<-

->Porphyry on the life of Plotinus, and the order of his books.<-

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Historiated initial 'Π' showing a figure seated at a desk within a room, looking towards a window or doorway.</image-desc>
Plotinus, the philosopher who lived in our time, seemed like one ashamed of being in a body. Because of this disposition, he could not bear to speak about his lineage, his parents, or his homeland.
<margin>B</margin>
He so disdained to endure a painter or a sculptor that he even said to Amelius, who was begging for permission to have a portrait made of him: "Is it not enough to carry this image <note>The physical body</note> with which nature has clothed us? Do you truly think I should agree to leave behind a longer-lasting image of an image, as if it were some work worth seeing?" Therefore, because he forbade it and refused to sit for it, Amelius had a friend, Carterius—the best of the painters then living—come in and attend the lectures (for anyone who wished was allowed to attend). By paying close attention, Carterius grew accustomed to capturing more striking mental images from sight. Then, drawing from the likeness stored in his memory, he sketched the resemblance. As Amelius helped correct the lines to achieve a better likeness, nature provided a portrait of Plotinus through Carterius’s talent—without Plotinus even knowing—that was a perfect resemblance.
<margin>D</margin>
Often suffering from a stomach ailment, he would not endure a clyster <note>An enema</note>, saying that it was not fitting for an elderly man to undergo such treatments. Nor did he endure taking medicinal antidotes <note>original: "θηριακὰς ἀντιδότους" (theriac), a complex herbal concoction</note>, saying that he did not even accept food from the bodies of domestic animals. He abstained from baths, but used a massage at home every day. However, when the plague grew heavy and it happened that those who massaged him died, he neglected this treatment and gradually developed a severe roughness of the throat <note>original: "κυνάγχου" (kynanche), a sore throat or croup</note>. While I was present, no such symptom appeared; but after I sailed away, the disease became so fierce—as my companion Eustochius told me upon my return, he having remained with Plotinus until death—that the clear and melodic power of his resonant voice failed him as he grew hoarse. His vision became blurred, and his hands and feet became covered in sores. For this reason, his friends avoided meeting him, because he had the habit of greeting everyone personally by name.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Historiated initial 'P' showing a scholar or saint reading at a lectern with a book.</image-desc>
<margin>Plotinus despised luxuries, vain glory, and life: he died of a throat infection <note>original: "angina"</note>; a dragon appeared.</margin>
Plotinus the Philosopher in our age seemed to be affected by a singular shame that his soul was in a body. Since he was so affected, he would not recount with a calm mind where his lineage came from, nor from which parents he was born, nor even from which country he originated. He likewise so greatly disdained to surrender the likeness of his body to be expressed by painters and sculptors that when
<margin>B</margin>
Amelius begged him to allow his image to be portrayed, he said: "As if it were not enough to carry this image which nature surrounded us with from the beginning, do you also think that an image of this image should be left to posterity as
<margin>C</margin>
a work worthy of a spectacle?" When he therefore diligently denied this and refused to wait upon the work of a painter by sitting for it, Amelius ordered a friend named Carterius, the best painter of his time, to enter Plotinus's schools. For anyone was allowed to be present at the gatherings of those disputing there. Amelius therefore accustomed the painter through long attention to conceive in his mind more vivid images from his gazing. Then, while
<margin>D</margin>
Carterius rightly rendered the likeness from the image committed to memory, and Amelius simultaneously corrected the features to achieve the resemblance, the painter’s talent produced a portrait very similar to Plotinus without him knowing. Furthermore, though he was often vexed by a colicky disease, he always refused enemas, saying it did not befit an old man to undergo treatments
<margin>E</margin>
of that kind. Nor did he ever accept medicinal antidotes <note>original: "theriaca"</note>, as he said he would not even take food from the bodies of tame animals. He also abstained from baths; however, he used massages at home every day. But when the pestilence grew heavy beyond measure and those who were massaging him had already departed from life, and he himself had entirely neglected treatments of that sort, he gradually fell into a throat infection <note>original: "angina"</note>. Indeed, while I was present, this evil never gave any sign of itself. But when I had departed, the plague of this disease grew so strong (as my friend Eustochius later reported to me when I returned, who did not leave Plotinus until his death) that because of excessive hoarseness, all that clear and melodic vigor of his resonant voice departed. His sight also grew dim, and his hands and feet were covered in sores. For this reason, since his friends no longer greeted him—because he himself was accustomed to address everyone with his own voice—

<summary>This page introduces the Life of Plotinus, describing his extreme asceticism, his refusal to have his portrait painted (which was circumvented by his student Amelius), and the onset of the painful illness that eventually led to his death.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the biography of Plotinus by Porphyry, detailing the philosopher's final days, his death, his early education in Alexandria, and his travels to the East with the Roman army.</meta>

## PLOTINUS'S LIFE.

<margin>A</margin> [He] departed from the city and, having set out for Campania <note>A region in southern Italy</note>, he was brought to the estate of his old friend Zethus, who had already passed away. His needs were supplied from the estate and heirs of Zethus, and even brought from the fields of Castricius at Minturnae. Castricius, indeed, had properties at Minturnae <note>A coastal town between Rome and Naples</note>. But when Plotinus was approaching death—as Eustochius told us, who was living at Puteoli <note>Modern Pozzuoli</note> and arrived to see him somewhat late—he said: "I am still waiting for you, and indeed I am now striving to lead back the divine within us to the divine that flourishes in the universe." <note>original Latin: "quod in nobis diuinũ est, ad diuinũ ipfum quod viget in vniuerso redigere"</note> And with these words, he released his spirit.

<margin>B</margin> Meanwhile, a snake <note>original Latin: "draco," often signifying a protective or divine spirit in this context</note> that had been wandering under the bed in which he lay suddenly hid itself in a hole in the wall. Plotinus was then sixty-six years old (as Eustochius related), the second year of the Emperor Claudius's reign <note>Claudius II Gothicus, roughly 270 AD</note> having already been completed.

<margin>C</margin> At the time when Plotinus migrated from this life, I, Porphyry, was staying in Lilybaeum <note>Modern Marsala, Sicily</note>; Amelius was in Apamea in Syria; but Castricius was in Rome. Only Eustochius was present. Now, if we calculate backward sixty-six years from the second year of Emperor Claudius, the time of his birth coincides with the thirteenth year of Emperor Severus <note>Septimius Severus, roughly 205 AD</note>. He himself never declared to anyone in which month or on what day he was born, for he thought it was not at all proper that his birthday be celebrated with sacrifices and banquets.

<margin>D</margin> Yet he himself would perform the sacred rites on the traditional birthdays of Plato and Socrates and would host his friends at a banquet, where indeed all friends who were able were required to recite a properly composed oration before the entire gathering. The things he often told us about his own life during our conversations are as follows.

<margin>
Concerning the education of Plotinus, and his training under Ammonius and his fellow students, and at what time.
</margin>

<margin>E</margin> He used to relate that when he was in his eighth year of age, even though he was already attending a schoolmaster, he was still accustomed to visit his nurse and, in his eagerness for milk, would bare her breasts to suckle. When it was eventually pointed out to him that he was being a troublesome boy, he ceased out of shame. After this, when he was completing his twenty-eighth year, being vehemently inflamed with a love for philosophy, he was recommended to those who were then considered the most excellent in Alexandria. However, he eventually left their schools very sad and mournful, and declared the cause of his sorrow to a certain friend. This friend, fully understanding the desire of his mind, led him to Ammonius <note>Ammonius Saccas, the self-taught philosopher of Alexandria</note>, whom he had not yet tried. Then, when he had entered Ammonius’s school and heard him, he said to his friend: "This is the very one I was seeking."

<margin>F</margin> From that day, therefore, he diligently heard Ammonius for eleven years. He made such progress in that philosophy that he desired to gain experience in the philosophy practiced among the Persians, and he even determined to pursue the wisdom especially esteemed among the Indians.

<margin>G</margin> Therefore, when Emperor Gordian <note>Gordian III</note> was about to set out for Persia to bring war to those peoples, Plotinus joined the army, being about thirty-nine years of age. But after Gordian was killed near Mesopotamia, Plotinus, barely escaping, arrived safely in Antioch. Then, during the reign of Philip, he came to Rome, at forty...
<insert>fleeing with difficulty, he escaped safely to Antioch. And</insert> <note>original Greek: "μόλις φὐγων, εἰς τὴν ἀντιόχειαν διεσώθη. καὶ"</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> He departed from the city and, coming into Campania to the estate of an old friend of his who had died, he settled there. His necessities were provided for him from the property of Zethus and were brought from Minturnae from the lands of Castricius (for Castricius had his holdings in Minturnae). Being about to die, as Eustochius related to us—since Eustochius was living in Puteoli—

<margin>Β</margin> he arrived late to him, and Plotinus said, "I am still waiting for you," and said he was trying <gloss>* the divine in you</gloss> to lead the divine in you back to the divine in the universe. A snake having passed under the bed in which he lay and having crept into a hole existing in the wall, he released his spirit, being (as Eustochius said) sixty-six years old, the second year of the reign of Claudius being fulfilled.

<margin>Γ</margin> At his death, I, Porphyry, happened to be spending time in Lilybaeum, Amelius in Apamea of Syria, and Castricius in Rome. Only Eustochius was present. Counting back for us sixty-six years from the second year of the reign of Claudius, the time of his birth falls into the thirteenth year of the reign of Severus. He never revealed to anyone which month he was born, nor his birthday, since he did not think it worthy to sacrifice or feast

<margin>Δ</margin> on his own birthday. Although on the traditional birthdays of Plato and Socrates, he would sacrifice and feast his companions, and it was necessary for one of the companions who was able to read a discourse before those who had gathered. But what he himself often related to us about himself in our meetings was of this sort.

<margin>Ε</margin> He used to go to his nurse, even though he was going to the grammar-teachers, until the eighth year from his birth, and would bare her breasts, desiring to suck. But having heard once that he was a troublesome child, he refrained out of shame. In his twenty-eighth year, he was moved toward philosophy. Being introduced to those then having a good reputation in Alexandria, he came away from their lectures downcast and full of grief, so that he told one of his friends what he was suffering. The friend, understanding the wish of his soul, took him to Ammonius, whom he had not yet tried. Having entered and heard him,

<margin>Ϝ</margin> he said to his companion, "This is the one I was seeking." And from that day, remaining continuously with Ammonius, he acquired such a habit in philosophy that he requested to gain experience in that practiced among the Persians, and that achieved among the Indians. When Emperor Gordian was about to go against the Persians, giving himself to the camp, he went along. He was already in his thirty-ninth year. For eleven whole years he had remained studying with Ammonius. When Gordian was killed in Mesopotamia,

<margin>G</margin> and Philip had seized the throne, [he went] toward...

# PLOTINUS'S LIFE.

[Having] reached forty years of age, he went up to Rome. Since a pact had been made between Herennius, Origen <note>This is Origen the Platonist, a contemporary and fellow student of Plotinus, not to be confused with the famous Christian father of the same name.</note>, and Plotinus not to reveal any of the doctrines of Ammonius <note>Ammonius Saccas, the self-taught philosopher of Alexandria who was the teacher of Plotinus.</note> which had been clarified in his lectures, Plotinus also remained [silent], though he associated with some who came to him. He kept the doctrines received from Ammonius unrevealed. But when Herennius was the first to break the agreement, Origen followed the example of Herennius, who had acted first. Origen, however, wrote nothing except a treatise *On the Daemons*, and during the reign of Gallienus, a book stating that "the King is the only creator." <note>original Greek: ὅτι μόνος ποιητὴς ὁ βασιλεύς</note> Plotinus, for a long time, continued to write nothing, but drew from his association with Ammonius for his lectures. Thus he spent ten whole years associating with some students but writing nothing. His lectures were conducted in this way: they were full of disorder and much babble, as Amelius used to tell us, because some students would provoke him [with questions]. Amelius came to him in the third year of his stay in Rome, during the third year of the reign of Emperor Philip <note>roughly 246 AD</note>. Having stayed until the first year of the reign of Emperor Claudius, he was with Plotinus for twenty-four whole years. He possessed a certain habit [of mind] when he arrived, gained from his time with Lysimachus. In his love of labor, he surpassed all his contemporaries, because he had transcribed and collected almost all the works of Numenius <note>Numenius of Apamea, a Neopythagorean philosopher whose work heavily influenced Neoplatonism</note>, and had learned most of them by heart. Making notes from the lectures, he composed nearly one hundred books of notes, which he gave as a gift to his adopted son, Hesychius of Apamea. In the tenth year of the reign of Emperor Gallienus <note>roughly 263 AD</note>, I, Porphyry, arrived from Greece with Antonius of Rhodes. I found Amelius already in his eighteenth year of association with Plotinus, but he had not yet dared to write anything except the notes, which had not yet reached a hundred in number. In the tenth year of Gallienus’s reign, Plotinus was about fifty-nine years old, and I, Porphyry, first joined him when I was thirty years of age. From the first year of Gallienus's rule, Plotinus had been urged to write on whatever subjects arose; and in the tenth year of Gallienus's rule, when I, Porphyry, first became known to him, he was found to have written twenty-one books. These I have obtained, though they were issued to only a few. For the publication was not yet easy, nor was it done with general knowledge or simply at random, but only with great judgment by those who received them. These writings were of such a sort that, because he did not provide them with titles himself, different people gave different titles to each. However, the titles that prevailed are these:
*On Beauty*. *On the Immortality of the Soul*.
*On Fate*. *On the Essence of the Soul*.
*On Intellect, Ideas, and Being*.
*On the Descent of the Soul into Bodies*.
*How that which follows the First comes from the First, and on the One*.
*Whether all Souls are One*.
*On the Good, or the One*.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> [He was] already forty years of age. But when Herennius, Origen, and Plotinus had formerly agreed among themselves not to publish the doctrines of Ammonius, which they had heard from him and approved as especially purified, Plotinus indeed stood by his promises. He received some visitors familiarly but kept the secret teachings of Ammonius intact. <margin>B</margin> Herennius, however, was the first to dissolve the pact, and Origen followed Herennius’s lead afterward. He wrote nothing except a certain book *On Daemons*, and under Gallienus, a book in which he proved that "the King alone is the creator." <note>original Latin: "Regē solū effectorē esse"</note> Plotinus, meanwhile, restrained himself from the study of writing for a long time; he only brought into his own discussions what he had formerly received from his association with Ammonius. And so he persevered for ten whole years: admitting some to discussion, but writing nothing. But because he had allowed or invited his friends to question him at will, Amelius says that <margin>C</margin> those sessions were full of a certain "play of confusion" <note>original Latin: "Ludū illū cōfusionis"</note> and nonsense. This Amelius truly came to him in Rome when he was already in his third year there, in the third year of Emperor Philip. He persevered with him until the first year of Emperor Claudius, and so lived with him for twenty-four whole years. When he first brought himself to Plotinus, he was endowed only with the habit which he had conceived from his familiarity with Lysimachus. In endurance of labor, however, he surpassed all his fellow students, because he wrote down and brought together almost all the doctrines of Numenius, and committed many of them to memory. <margin>D</margin> From the very study of hearing him, he collected certain scholastic notes and composed nearly one hundred books from these, which he gave as a gift to a certain Hesychius of Apamea, his adopted son. In the tenth year of Emperor Gallienus, I, Porphyry, coming to Rome from Greece together with Antonius of Rhodes, found Amelius, who had already enjoyed eighteen years of familiarity with Plotinus, yet had not yet dared to write anything besides those notes I mentioned, <margin>E</margin> which had not yet grown to the number of one hundred. <u>Accordingly, in the tenth year of the Emperor Gallienus, Plotinus was already nearly fifty-nine years old; I, Porphyry, when I first joined him, had then completed thirty years.</u> Plotinus indeed, in the first year of the Emperor Gallienus, turned himself to writing whatever questions happened to arise; and in the tenth year of the same, when I, Porphyry, became known to Plotinus, he had already written twenty-one books. <margin>F</margin> These I found had been handed over to only a few. For publication was not yet easy, nor was anyone aware of it; for nothing was published easily or rashly, but only to those who were approved by a certain mature judgment. These things which I shall mention had already been written. Since he had not inscribed them with certain titles, different people inscribed the books differently. The titles, therefore, which more widely prevailed, are of this sort:

<margin>What Plotinus wrote, in what order, and at what time.</margin>
*On Beauty*. *On the Immortality of the Soul*.
*On Fate*. *On the Essence of the Soul*.
*On Intellect, Ideas, and Being*.
*On the Descent of the Soul into Bodies*.
*How that which follows the First comes from the First, and on the One*.
*Whether all Souls are One*.
*On the Good, or the One*.

He sent these books to me in the first year of the Emperor Claudius’s reign <note>Claudius II, who reigned from 268 to 270 AD</note>. At the beginning of the second year, shortly before he departed from this life, he also sent these:

<margin>B</margin>
What are Evils.
Whether the stars have any influence.
What is Man? What is the Living Being?
On the First Good, and other goods <note>often titled "On Happiness"</note>.

<margin>C</margin>
These books, together with the forty-five written in his earlier periods, bring the total to fifty-four. Just as they were written—some in his early years, others in his prime, and finally those written when his body was failing—so too do the books reflect his varying strength. The first twenty-one, if compared to those that follow, seem to have a gentler force, not yet possessing a sufficiently steady vigor. Those composed in the middle period, however, display the very peak of his power. These twenty-four books (with a few brief exceptions) are the most perfect. Finally, the last nine show a somewhat diminished capacity; this is more evident in the final four than in the five that preceded them.

<margin>D</margin> <margin>The students of Plotinus</margin> He had many listeners, but among his followers and those most devoted to the grace of philosophy were Amelius of Tuscany and others. To this Amelius, the personal name given was Gentilianus. However, he himself preferred to be called "Amerius" with an "R," saying it was more fitting for him to be named after <term>Ameria</term> <note>meaning "indivisibility"</note> rather than <term>Amelia</term> <note>which sounds like the Greek word for "neglect"</note>. There was also Paulinus of Scythopolis, a physician and a very diligent student, whom Amelius called "Miccalus" because he was so full of learning and lectures <note>original Latin: *auditionum*; referring to the oral teachings he had absorbed</note>. Furthermore, there was Eustochius of Alexandria, also a physician, who came to know Plotinus near the end of his life and remained devotedly attending to him until his death; by dedicating himself solely to Plotinus’s teachings, he took on the character of a true philosopher. Zothicus was also an associate, a critic and a poet who corrected the works of Antimachus <note>a Greek epic poet</note> and translated the story of Atlantis into verse with great poetic skill. Later, however, his sight failed him, and he died shortly before Plotinus.

<margin>E</margin> Paulinus also died before Plotinus. Another very close friend to Plotinus was Zethus, who was of Arabian descent; he married the daughter of Theodosius, a friend of Ammonius <note>Ammonius Saccas, Plotinus's own teacher</note>. Zethus was also skilled in medicine and very dear to Plotinus. Plotinus frequently tried to discourage him from his involvement in political affairs, to which he was inclined, and used to visit him at his country estates six miles before reaching Minturnae. These estates were owned by Castricius,

<column-break/>

<margin>F</margin> known as Firmus, a man who was certainly the most devoted of our age to all the fine arts. He was a great admirer of Plotinus and Amelius, serving them with the devotion of a faithful servant, and he treated me, Porphyry, in all matters as if I were his own brother. <margin>G</margin>

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s biography of Plotinus. The previous page ended with a list of his students, including Amelius. This page recounts anecdotes of Plotinus’s supernatural insight, his relationship with the Emperor, and his failed project to build a city for philosophers.</meta>

### THE LIFE OF PLOTINUS.

...of a higher order, he was a more powerful guardian spirit. It was said that at that time it was not permitted to ask any questions or to see the spirit for long; for a certain companion who was watching with them, who held birds in his hands for protection, suffocated them, either out of envy or because he was terrified with fear. Since Plotinus therefore possessed a <term>familiar daemon</term> <note>original: *familiarem daemonem*; in Neoplatonism, this refers to a personal guiding spirit or "genius," not an evil entity</note> from the order of the more divine beings, he himself always directed the divine eye of his mind toward it with great sublimity. For this reason, he later composed a book concerning the spirit allotted to each of us, in which he carefully attempts to provide the causes for the differences among these guiding spirits. Furthermore, when Amelius—who was a diligent observer of sacred rites and performed sacrifices on the <term>kalends</term> <note>the first day of the Roman month</note>—once asked Plotinus to join him, Plotinus replied: "It is for those gods to come to me, not for me to go to them." With what lofty mind he spoke such a thing, we could neither understand nor did we dare to ask. 

He was most shrewd in discerning character. Thus, when a valuable necklace was stolen from a woman named Chione—who lived with him along with her children and led a chaste life as a widow—and all the servants and members of the household were summoned into Plotinus's presence, Plotinus looked at each one and singled out a certain man, saying: "This one stole the necklace." Though the man was beaten and denied it for a long time, he finally confessed and returned the stolen item. Similarly, he would predict with wonderful accuracy what kind of men the boys living there would become. For instance, he predicted of Polemo: "This one will be prone to love and will not reach a mature age," and so it happened. I myself <note>the author, Porphyry</note> once contemplated ending my own life; he sensed this miraculously and, as I was walking at home, he stood before me and said: "Porphyry, this pursuit of yours is not that of a healthy mind, but rather of a soul raging with <term>black bile</term> <note>original: *atra bile*; a reference to the four humors of ancient medicine, where an excess of black bile was believed to cause melancholy or madness</note>." He therefore ordered me to leave Rome. Obeying him, I departed for Sicily, especially since I heard that a certain noble and elegant man was living near Lilybaeum. By this action, I was indeed freed from this mental disturbance, but in the meantime, I was prevented from leading my life alongside Plotinus until his death.

<margin>Plotinus wished to build Platonopolis:</margin>
Furthermore, the Emperor Gallienus and his wife Salonina honored Plotinus and held him in the highest esteem. Relying on their goodwill, he petitioned them to restore a certain ruined city in Campania that was once suitable for philosophers, and to grant the surrounding territory to the restored city. He promised that those who would inhabit the city would live there with all their friends. The Philosopher would easily have obtained this request, had not certain of the Emperor’s associates—driven by envy, indignation, or some other unfair reason—bitterly opposed it.

<margin>A sharp debater, handsome, lovable, negligent in speech but profound in sense:</margin>
He was vigorous in debate, clever in invention, and most prompt in perceiving the appropriate points, but perhaps he slipped in some of his speech: for he did not pronounce *meminisse* <note>Latin: "to remember"</note> but *menimisse*, and he misused certain other words in a similar fashion. This defect also followed him in his writing. Furthermore, while he was speaking, his mind would shine forth, and...

<margin>He abundantly joined Platonic and Peripatetic philosophy.</margin>

<column-break/>

...with a certain one of his kind, but it was not possible to ask the cause, nor to see him longer as he was present, because the friend watching with him, who was holding birds for the sake of protection, strangled them, whether through envy or through some fear. Having thus a companion from the more divine <term>daemons</term>, he himself continued to lift his own divine eye toward that one. For this reason, he even wrote a book 
<margin>B</margin>
**concerning the daemon who has been allotted to us**, where he tries to provide the reasons for the differences among these companions. Since Amelius was a lover of sacrifice and performed the rites according to the new moon and the festivals of the cycle, he once asked Plotinus to join him, but Plotinus said: "It is for those gods to come to me, not for me to go to those ones." What he meant by speaking so grandly, we ourselves were not able to understand, nor did we dare to ask him.
<margin>C</margin>
He possessed such an abundance of insight into character as to perceive human habits and discover stolen things. He would predict what kind of person each of the children would turn out to be. Once, when a very expensive necklace belonging to Chione—who lived with him and her children, conducting her widowhood with dignity—was stolen, he looked at all the servants gathered before Plotinus's eyes and 
<margin>D</margin>
said: "This is the one who has stolen it," pointing to a certain individual. Though the man was whipped and denied it at first, he later confessed, and bringing the stolen item, he returned it. He also predicted for each of the children living with him what they would become, just as he said of Polemo that he would be amorous and short-lived, which is exactly how it turned out. And once he perceived that I, Porphyry, was planning to take myself out of this 
<margin>E</margin>
life. Emperor Gallienus and his wife Salonina honored and revered Plotinus most of all. Taking advantage of their friendship, he requested that a certain city of philosophers said to have existed in Campania, but otherwise in ruins, be rebuilt. He asked that the surrounding land be granted to it, and that those who were to live there should use the laws of Plato and that the city be named **Platonopolis**. He promised to retire there himself with his companions; and this wish would have been easily granted to the philosopher, had not some of the king’s associates, out of envy or resentment or some other malicious reason, blocked it. In his compositions, he was capable of expressing himself and most powerful in finding and perceiving what was relevant, though he made mistakes in his words. For he would not say *anamimneskesthai* <note>Greek: "to remember"</note>, but *anamnemiskesthai*, and he kept other strange terms in his writing. And in his speaking, the manifestation of his mind...
