<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s biography of Plotinus, specifically focusing on his teaching style, his intellectual background, and anecdotes regarding his students and contemporaries. It follows the previous discussion of his character and spiritual nature.</meta>

### THE LIFE OF PLOTINUS.

While a light shone upon his face, he was lovely to behold. He appeared most beautiful at those times, and a slight sweat would break out upon him. His gentleness shone through, and he showed a kind disposition toward those who asked questions, as well as a great vigor. Indeed, when I, Porphyry, questioned him for three days on how the soul is joined to the body, he persisted in his demonstration. At one point, a man named Thaumasius 
<margin>B</margin> entered the school to hear him speak on general principles and said he wished to hear Plotinus’s views on written texts, but that he could not tolerate Porphyry’s constant questioning and answering. But Plotinus replied: "If we do not resolve the difficulties raised by Porphyry’s questions, we will be unable to say anything at all for the book." In his writing, he was concise and full of thought. He was brief, and more abundant in ideas than in words, often speaking with <term>enthusiasm</term> <note>original: *enthousiōn*; meaning divinely inspired or possessed by a god</note> and great passion. In his works, there is a blend of 
<margin>C</margin> hidden Stoic and Peripatetic doctrines. In particular, Aristotle’s *Metaphysics* is condensed within them. No theorem of geometry, arithmetic, mechanics, optics, or music escaped his notice, although he did not prepare himself to work at these subjects in a practical way. In his sessions, the commentaries of Severus, Cronius, Numenius, Gaius, or Atticus were read. Among the Peripatetics, the works of Aspasius, Alexander, and Adrastus were also read, as well as whatever else happened to be at hand. However, he never spoke simply from these texts, but was original and distinct in his contemplation, bringing the mind of Ammonius <note>Ammonius Saccas, Plotinus's teacher in Alexandria</note> to his investigations. He would quickly fill himself with understanding and, with a few words, 
<margin>E</margin> would arise having provided the insight of a deep theorem. When the works of Longinus *On Principles* and *The Lover of Antiquity* were read to him, he remarked: "Longinus is a philologist, but certainly not a philosopher." Once, when Origen <note>Origen the Platonist, a fellow student of Ammonius, not the famous Christian Father</note> came to his session, Plotinus was filled with a blush and wished to stand up. When Origen urged him to continue speaking, he replied that the desire to speak withers when the speaker knows he is addressing those who already know what he is about to say. And so, after speaking briefly, he stood up. 
<margin>F</margin> When I read a poem on "The Sacred Marriage" <note>original: *hieros gamos*; a mystical union</note> during the festival of Plato, someone present said that Porphyry was "mad" because much of it was spoken mystically and with hidden inspiration. But Plotinus said in the hearing of everyone: "You have shown yourself to be at once a poet, a philosopher, and a <term>hierophant</term> <note>original: *hierophantēn*; a priest who interprets sacred mysteries</note>." When the rhetorician Diophanes read a 
<margin>G</margin> defense of Alcibiades from Plato’s *Symposium*, arguing that for the sake of learning virtue, a student should submit himself to the sexual advances of his teacher, Plotinus rose up several times as if to leave the gathering. However, he restrained himself...

<column-break/>

An inner light spreading even to his face. He was indeed lovely in appearance, but while he disputed, he seemed far more beautiful: then truly a thin sweat, like dew, distilled from his face; then a kind gentleness shone forth; then a placid leniency appeared for receiving questions, and a very robust vigor was demonstrated in resolving them. Now indeed, when I, Porphyry, questioned him for three days as to what condition the soul is rather joined with the body, he persevered in demonstrating it. When even a certain man named Thaumasius 
<margin>B</margin> entered the school to treat common matters, he stated that he desired to hear Plotinus's opinions on the exposition of writings: but that he could by no means tolerate such a disputation of Porphyry questioning and responding. But Plotinus objected: "Unless we dissolve the doubts raised by Porphyry's questioning, we shall not be able to compose anything in a continuous discourse for any book." Moreover, he writes with a most intense 
<margin>C</margin> sharpness and a manifold intellect. He is very brief, but everywhere more abundant in sense than in words. He pours out many things inspired by a divine power: he often suffers wonderfully from the very matter of which he treats; nor does he speak with so simple a discipline as with a mind ardently affected by the thing itself. Inserted in his books are the hidden doctrines of the Stoics and likewise of the Peripatetics; especially, however, the opinions of Aristotle collected in his *Metaphysics* are more frequently present there. Nothing at all was hidden from him: whatever pertained to geometry, 
<margin>D</margin> arithmetic, mechanics, optics, and music: although he never rendered himself ready to execute these by hand. In the schools, the commentaries of Severus, Cronius, Numenius, Gaius, and Atticus, the Platonic philosophers, were read to him; likewise the Peripatetics Aspasius, Alexander, Adrastus, and whichever commentaries happened to fall in: but nothing from these was spoken in a continuous draw. For he was of his own law and right, and diverse from these in contemplation. But in discussing matters, he brought the intellect of Ammonius. 
<margin>E</margin> He would emerge from a reading as soon as he was imbued with it, and bringing the understanding of a deep contemplation in a few words, he would rise. When the book of Longinus and Phylarchaeus *On Principles* had been read: "Longinus is indeed a man studious of letters, but a philosopher by no means." When Origen had once come into the school, Plotinus, immediately suffused with a redness of the cheeks, wished to rise; but being asked by Origen to continue his discourse, he responded: "The zeal for speaking ceases when he who speaks perceives that he is about to address those who know the very same things." And so, when he had discussed a few things, he rose from there. 
<margin>He celebrates the birthday of Plato. He was the most modest of all.</margin>
<margin>F</margin> When I had recited a poem on the "Sacred Marriage" at the birthday feast of Plato, and a certain person present objected that Porphyry was insane—inasmuch as many things had been said there by a certain divine inspiration and secret mystery—Plotinus said openly in the hearing of all: "You have demonstrated yourself to be at once a poet, a philosopher, and a priest." When at some 
<margin>G</margin> point the orator Diophanes read a defense for Alcibiades, raving in Plato's *Symposium*, proving that for the sake of learning virtue, one ought to expose oneself to a lover; even if he should affect a venereal union. During the reading, Plotinus rose up several times, as if he were suddenly about to depart from that assembly; nevertheless, he restrained himself:

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s biography of his teacher, Plotinus. It highlights Plotinus’s encouragement of Porphyry’s own intellectual development, their shared defense of Platonic thought against Gnostic groups, and the refutation of claims that Plotinus’s work was unoriginal.</meta>

### THE LIFE OF PLOTINUS.

Soon, once the gathering had dispersed, he specifically commanded me to refute the orator. But since that man, Diophanes, refused to grant me his book to read, I recalled the arguments through the power of memory. I wrote a response against them and soon recited it back before the same audience. I filled Plotinus with such joy that, during the assembly itself, he would frequently repeat: "Strike thus, if indeed you will be a light to men." <note>original Latin: *Sic feri, siquidem ita viris lumen eris*; this is a quote from Homer’s *Iliad* (8.282), where Agamemnon encourages the archer Teucer to keep shooting true. Plotinus is likening Porphyry's intellectual refutation to a well-aimed arrow.</note> <gloss>Bubulus</gloss> <note>The Greek text identifies him as Eubulus, the Platonic successor in Athens.</note>, a follower of Plato, wrote from Athens and sent writings to Rome regarding certain Platonic questions. Plotinus, however, ordered these to be handed over to me, that I might consider each one and report back to him. He devoted effort to the rules of astronomy, though not in the manner of a professional mathematician; however, he applied himself more diligently to the judgments of the astrologers. When he discovered that their predictions were not worthy of trust, he did not hesitate to frequently refute their prophecies in his own writings.
<column-break/>
After the gathering was dismissed, he commanded me, Porphyry, to write a rebuttal. Since Diophanes was unwilling to give me the book, I recovered the arguments through memory and, having written the rebuttal, I read it aloud before the same listeners. I pleased Plotinus so much that in the meetings he would continually say: *"Strike thus, if you might become a light to men."* <note>original Greek: *Ball' houtōs, aiken ti phōs andressi genēai*</note> When Eubulus, the Platonic successor, wrote from Athens and sent treatises concerning certain Platonic questions, Plotinus saw to it that these were given to me, Porphyry, and he requested that I examine them and report the written contents back to him. He paid attention to the rules regarding the stars, though not strictly as a mathematician, but he studied the outcomes predicted by the casters of horoscopes more accurately. And having detected the unreliability of their promises, he did not shrink from refuting them in many places in his writings.
<column-break/>
<margin>He wrote against certain Christian heretics and commanded his followers to do the same.</margin>
There were many Christians at that time, as well as others—heretics who had strayed from ancient philosophy, such as the followers of Adelphius and Acylinus. These people possessed many books by Alexander the Libyan, Philocomus, Demostratus, and Lydus, and they openly displayed certain <term>revelations</term> <note>original: *apokalypseis*; claiming divine secret knowledge</note> of Zoroaster, Zostrianus, Nicotheus, Allogenes, Messos, and others of that kind. They deceived many, having been deceived themselves, by asserting that Plato had by no means penetrated the depths of the <term>intelligible essence</term> <note>The realm of pure, non-physical reality that can only be understood by the mind.</note>. For this reason, Plotinus introduced many arguments against them in his discussions. He wrote a book against them, which we have titled *Against the Gnostics*, and he left it to us to discuss and judge the remaining matters. Amelius, moreover, composed forty books against the *Book of Zostrianus*. I, Porphyry, showed through many arguments that the *Book of Zoroaster* titled by them was a forgery and a recent creation, concocted by those who established the heresy so that their teachings might be believed to belong to the ancient Zoroaster.
<column-break/>
There were also in his time many Christians, including others who were heretics derived from the ancient philosophy, those around Adelphius and Acylinus. They owned a great many works of Alexander the Libyan, Philocomus, Demostratus, and Lydus, and they produced "revelations" of Zoroaster, Zostrianus, Nicotheus, Allogenes, Messos, and other such figures. They deceived many, and were deceived themselves, claiming that Plato had not approached the depth of the intelligible substance. For this reason, Plotinus himself made many refutations in his sessions and wrote a book which we titled *Against the Gnostics*, leaving it to us to judge the rest. Amelius proceeded as far as forty books in writing against the *Book of Zostrianus*. And I, Porphyry, made numerous refutations against the *Book of Zoroaster*, demonstrating that the book was both spurious and modern, fashioned by those who founded the heresy to create the impression that the doctrines they chose to honor were the ancient teachings of Zoroaster.
<column-break/>
<margin>Very few truly understood Plotinus's thoughts. Testimonies of Amelius and Porphyry on the excellence of Plotinus's books.</margin>
Most of the Greeks falsely accused Plotinus of secretly usurping the discoveries of Numenius <note>Numenius of Apamea was a philosopher who preceded Plotinus and also combined Platonic and Pythagorean thought.</note>, a rumor that very few actually investigated. Because of this, Amelius wrote a book which we titled *On the Difference between the Doctrines of Plotinus and the Teachings of Numenius*. Amelius dedicated the book to me and, in the inscription itself, addressed me as <term>Basileus</term> <note>Greek for "King."</note>, for that was my name. In my native language, I was called Malchus, which was also my father's name. When "Malchus" is translated into the Greek tongue, it is called "King" (*Basileus*). Therefore, when Longinus dedicated his writings *On Impulse* to Cleodamus and myself, he began: "O Cleodamus and Malchus." But Amelius, interpreting the name itself—just as Numenius called Maximus "the Great"—addressed Malchus as "King." <note>original Latin: *Amelius Basileo, id est regi salutem*; "Amelius to Basileus (King), greetings."</note> "Be well assured," [Amelius wrote], "that I would never have spoken out on account of those famous men who, as you say has already been made public, attribute our friend's doctrines to Numenius of Apamea. For it is clear that this arises from their own boastful manner of speaking and their pride."
<column-break/>
Among those from Greece who said he was adopting the ideas of Numenius, and among those such as Trypho the Stoic and Platonist who reported such things, Amelius wrote a book which we titled *On the Difference between the Doctrines of Plotinus and Numenius*. He addressed it to me as "Basileus." The name Basileus belongs to me, Porphyry, for in my native tongue I was called Malchus, which was the same name my father was called. "Malchus," if one wished to translate it into the Greek tongue, would be interpreted as "King" (*Basileus*). Hence Longinus, addressing his work *On Impulse* to Cleodamus and me, Porphyry, wrote "O Cleodamus and Malchus" in the preface. But Amelius, translating the name just as Numenius translated "Maximus" as "the Great," wrote "Basileus" for "Malchus." Amelius to Basileus, greetings: "Know clearly that on account of those common men, whom you say have been noisily asserting that our companion's doctrines are traced back to Numenius of Apamea, I would not have uttered a word. For it is obvious that these claims proceed from their own vaunted 'eloquence' and talkativeness."

### THE LIFE OF PLOTINUS.

<margin>A</margin> ...now calling him a teller of empty tales, now a fraud, and thirdly, that he puts forward the most worthless of things, obviously intending to mock him through these claims. But since you thought it necessary to take advantage of this occasion—both so that we might have our own preferred views more readily available for memory, and so that, in the name of a friend, such as the great and admirable Plotinus, <margin>B</margin> mysteries long celebrated might be more fully understood—I have seen fit to obey you. I am now returning to you what was promised, having labored for three days, as you yourself know. It is only right to forgive these writings of ours, as they are not composed or selected with the careful arrangement of those formal treatises, but are recollected from our old associations. <margin>C</margin> And as each point first occurred to me, so they have been arranged here for the present. Therefore, I deserve a just pardon from you. Moreover, the intention of the man <note>Amelius is likely referring to Plotinus here.</note>, who has been brought into agreement with our judgment by some, is not easily grasped; for he speaks differently at different times about the same matters, just as it might please him. But I know well that you will kindly correct anything that has been recorded here by us that deviates from our familiar character of Plotinus. Indeed, I seem compelled, as it is said in the tragedies, like a busybody, and thus further removed from the very doctrine of our leader, to undergo the judgment of an editor and to revise it. Such was the power of my ardent desire to please you. Farewell.

<margin>D</margin> I was moved to include this letter not only to provide proof that some people at that time, even while Plotinus was still living, suspected that he took pride in the discoveries of Numenius <note>Numenius of Apamea was a 2nd-century philosopher who combined Platonic and Pythagorean thought; critics often accused Plotinus of merely copying him.</note>, but also because they considered him a great babbler and held him in contempt, for the simple reason that they did not understand what he was saying. Plotinus himself was a stranger to all sophisticated display and pride; in the very gatherings of disputants, he seemed to conduct himself no differently than in familiar conversations. He did not quickly reveal to anyone the necessary power of the arguments lying hidden in his discourse. <margin>E</margin> The same thing happened to me, Porphyry, when I first heard Plotinus. Therefore, I attempted to provoke him by writing against him, trying to show that the objects of thought exist outside the intellect <note>This was a major technical dispute: whether the "Forms" exist independently or are internal to the Divine Mind (the Intellect).</note>. But when he had commanded Amelius to read my writings, and Amelius had finished reading them, Plotinus said with a smile: "It would be your task, Amelius, to dissolve these doubts into which he has fallen through a certain ignorance of our opinion." <margin>F</margin> After Amelius had composed a book of no small size against my objections, and I had again contradicted his writings, and Amelius had written back to me once more—at this third stage, having finally and with difficulty suspected the mind of Plotinus, I changed my opinion. Therefore, writing a retraction <note>original Greek: *palinodia*; a formal "recantation" or "singing again" of one's views.</note>, I recited it in the assembly of everyone. From then on, I judged the books of Plotinus to be most worthy of faith, and I challenged the master himself with all zeal to distinguish his opinion point by point and to describe it more extensively. <margin>G</margin> Indeed, it was from this that he also made Amelius very inclined toward writing. <margin>A</margin> Now indeed calling him mere trifles, now truly a substitute: again, they accuse him as if he puts forward certain very cheap things: and they wrongly attack him with lying sarcasm. But since you think this opportunity should be used—namely, so that I might make what we believe more ready for recollection, and also for the glory of a friend, especially one like the great and admirable Plotinus—so that mysteries <margin>B</margin> long chanted might be more fully understood, I thought I should obey you, and now I return to you what was promised, labored over by us for three days, as you know. It is proper indeed to forgive our writings, as they are not composed or selected by comparison with those formal compositions, but are repeated from old meetings; and as each first occurred, so they have been arranged for the present. Therefore, pardon must be granted to me all the more, because the counsel of that man, who has been led by some into the agreement of our judgment, is not easily <margin>C</margin> grasped: because at other times he speaks differently about the same things, however it might please him. Clearly, the burning will to please you was so powerful in me. Farewell.

<margin>D</margin> I was moved to bring forward this letter, not only to give confirmation of the fact that some of that time, even while he was still living, suspected that Plotinus had been arrogant with the inventions of Numenius: but also because they thought him a great trifler and despised him: namely for that reason, because they in no way understood his words. The same happened to me, Porphyry, when I first heard Plotinus. Wherefore I tried to provoke him by writing against him, attempting to show that those things which are understood exist outside the intellect. <margin>A</margin> What I especially indicated when writing to him will be made clear by a part of the letter written to me in this manner. <margin>Testimonies of Longinus regarding the excellence of the books of Plotinus</margin>
<margin>B</margin> Send those works to us whenever it pleases you, or rather, bring them yourself. Indeed, I will not easily stop begging you to prefer the journey to us over every other journey. Even if for no other reason—for I do not know what new wisdom you might hope for by coming to us—at least come for our old friendship’s sake, and for the healthiness of the air, which would benefit that bodily weakness of which you complain. But if you think you might achieve something else, do not expect anything new from me, nor even the old works which you say have largely perished. Truly, there is such a shortage of transcribers <note>Scribes or copyists responsible for hand-copying manuscripts.</note> here that, by the gods, in all this time I have spent trying to restore the missing parts of Plotinus’s works, I have scarcely found a scribe to help, even though I have pulled him away from his usual duties and ordered him to focus on this one task alone. <margin>C</margin> Indeed, I have as many of those books as I seem able to have, now that I have received those sent by you; but I confess I do not have them in a perfect state. For these books are significantly full of errors. I had thought our friend Amelius <note>A student of Plotinus and close associate of Porphyry.</note> had corrected the mistakes left everywhere by the copyists, but other matters were of greater concern to him than the diligence of correcting texts. <margin>D</margin> For this reason, I have very little idea how to use these books, although I desire beyond measure to study what Plotinus wrote concerning the soul <note>original: "de anima"</note> and concerning being <note>original: "de ente"</note>. But these books especially have been corrupted by the faults of the transcribers. Therefore, I greatly desire to receive those same books from you, written with the highest diligence, so that I may read them through, correcting my own copies from them, and then quickly return them. <margin>E</margin> But again, I will repeat the same thing I said from the beginning: do not merely send them, but bring them with you yourself when you come here. And do not bring only these, but if there is anything else remaining that escaped Amelius. For I possess those things which he brought here, having sought them out with the greatest zeal. Why should I not seek with the utmost diligence the writings of that man, which are worthy of every honor and veneration? I have always indicated this to you, both when you were present and when you were far away, and when you lived in Tyre: namely, that I do not entirely grasp many of the arguments in Plotinus’s books, but I love and venerate beyond measure the very form of his writing, the density of his insights, and the highly philosophical arrangement of his inquiries. Indeed, I judge that those who seek the truth should bring the books of Plotinus into comparison only with the works of the most excellent authors.

<margin>Confirmation of the above.</margin>
<margin>F</margin> I have been rather lengthy in relating the above matters so that I might demonstrate what that man—who possessed the sharpest judgment of our age—thought of Plotinus. For he examined and critiqued almost all the works of the writers of his time. Even he, initially led by the ignorance of others, looked down on Plotinus for a long time. He thought that the works of Plotinus which he had received from Amelius were written in a common style, and he did not at all understand the man's manner of expression. <margin>B</margin> And you, on the one hand, send these things whenever it seems best to you, or rather bring them. For this I happen to have sent to you when you were present, and when you were far away, and while you were spending time in Tyre: that I have not happened to accept many of the underlying premises, but the style of the writing, and the density of the man’s thoughts, and the philosophical arrangement of his investigations, I admire and love exceedingly. And I would say that those who are investigative should rank those books among the most celebrated works.

<meta>This page continues the biography of Plotinus by his student Porphyry. The previous page included a letter from the critic Longinus to Porphyry requesting copies of Plotinus’s works. ### THE LIFE OF PLOTINUS.

By Amelius, they had been corrected, as if copied from the original autographs. Concerning the judgment of Longinus, it is necessary to set forth what he wrote in his own work about Plotinus, Amelius, and the philosophers who lived in his own time, so that a full judgment of them may be made, such as was formed by a man most eloquent and most skilled in critical examination. The book is inscribed: *Longinus to Plotinus and Gentilianus Amelius, On the End*. It begins with a kind of 

->preface.<-

Many philosophers have arisen in our time, O Marcellus <note>Likely Marcellus Orontius, a student of Plotinus.</note>, especially during the first years of our youth; for the present time is unusual for its scarcity of such men. But when we were boys, no small number of those who lead in philosophical discourse flourished. It was our fortune to see all of them, because from childhood we traveled through many cities with our parents. We associated with those who were still living, as we visited many nations and cities. Some of these men attempted to treat their doctrines in writing, leaving behind the benefit of their work for those who come after. Others, however, thought it sufficient to lead their associates toward an understanding of their favored views without writing. Of the first order, among the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato’s philosophy.</note>, were Euclides, Democritus, and Proclinus, who lived in the Troad <note>The region surrounding ancient Troy.</note>. Then there are those who until now teach publicly in Rome: Plotinus and Gentilianus Amelius, the latter being very well known at that time. Among the Stoics <note>Philosophers who emphasized virtue and logic as the path to happiness.</note> were Themistocles and Phoebion, and Annius and Medius, who flourished until recently. Of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school.</note>, there was Heliodorus the Alexandrian. In the second order were the Platonists Ammonius and Origen <note>Note original: "ὠριγένης". This is Origen the Platonist, not to be confused with the famous Christian theologian of the same name.</note>, with whom we studied for a very long time—men who far surpassed their contemporaries in understanding. There were also the successors at Athens, Theodotus and Eubulus. While some of them wrote small works—such as Origen’s *On Daimons* or Eubulus’s *On the Philebus* and *On the Gorgias*, and his replies to Aristotle’s objections to Plato’s *Republic*—these are not sufficient for one to count them among those who have fully worked out their doctrines in writing. They treated such efforts as a side-project <note>original: "πάρεργον"</note>, rather than making writing their primary impulse. Of the Stoics, there were Herminus and Lysimachus, and those who lived in the city of Athens, Athenaeus and Musonius. Of the Peripatetics, there were Ammonius and Ptolemaeus, both the most learned of their time, especially Ammonius, for there is no one who came close to him in vast knowledge. Yet they wrote nothing technical, only poems and exhibition speeches <note>Speeches intended to demonstrate rhetorical skill rather than technical philosophy.</note>, which I believe have been preserved against the authors' wishes; for I do not think they would have wanted to become known to posterity through such books, having neglected to store their deep thoughts in formal treatises.

<column-break/>

**A** By Amelius, they were most corrected; indeed, they had been transcribed from the very books written by Plotinus’s own hand. Therefore, it is worth the effort to report what Longinus wrote in that very work concerning Plotinus, Amelius, and the other philosophers of his time: so that it may be more certain to us what opinion that most elegant man, so prompt in testing intellects, held regarding them. The book is indeed titled *On the End, to Plotinus and Gentilianus, surnamed Amelius*: the preface of which is as follows.

**B** <margin>Testimonies</margin> Although many philosophers have existed in our times, O Marcellus, a greater number of them certainly existed in the first years of our age. <margin>Longinus on the same subject.</margin> For it is impossible to say how few the present time holds. But while we were youths, not a few excelled in the study of philosophy, all of whom it was our lot to see: since from our tender years we traveled through many regions together with our parents. There, truly, the opportunity was given to me to **C** meet them, because they were still surviving in life, as I often gathered in the same place with them among many nations and cities. But from their number, some indeed committed their opinions to letters, intending to be of use to posterity by writing; others, however, thought they had done enough if they made their present friends and associates partakers of their counsel. In the first class, therefore, were the Platonists Euclides, Democritus, and Proclinus, who lived in the Troad. Besides these, there are those who even now live in Rome, Plotinus and Gentilianus, **D** Amelius the friend of Plotinus; of the Stoics, Themistocles and Phoebion; and those who flourished until their final day, Annius and Medius. Of the Peripatetics, Heliodorus the Alexandrian. But in the second class, the Platonists were Ammonius and Origen, with whom we lived for a long time, men truly surpassing the philosophers of their century by no small interval in intelligence. Likewise, those who were successors at Athens, Theodotus and Eubulus. Now, if anything was written by any of them—as by Origen, a certain book *On **E** Daimons*; and by Eubulus, a certain exposition on the *Philebus* and the *Gorgias*; and concerning those things which Aristotle opposes to the *Republic* of Plato, and by what arguments these are refuted—these things are surely of little weight if you wish to compare them with the arguments which they were accustomed to assign more exactly by voice. For they do not seem to have written with any serious zeal, nor to have chosen the duty of writing as their chief office. Furthermore, from the number of the Stoics, Herminus and Lysimachus; and those who lived in Athens, Athenaeus and **F** Musonius. But among the Peripatetics, Ammonius and Ptolemaeus: both truly most full of all learning in their time, especially Ammonius; for no one seems to have approached nearly to the abundance of his learning. Nevertheless, they constructed nothing very technical, but only certain poems and demonstrative speeches. Which writings I judge were preserved for posterity against the **G** authors' will. For I do not think they desired to become known to posterity through books of that kind, since they neglected to commend their opinions to more exact writings.

<meta>This page continues Longinus’s critical survey of contemporary philosophers, as quoted in Porphyry's biography of Plotinus. He distinguishes between mere compilers and original thinkers like Plotinus and Amelius. Longinus also references his own scholarly debates with Amelius and Porphyry (here called Basilius) concerning the nature of Platonic "Ideas" or Forms.</meta>

### THE LIFE OF PLOTINUS.

**A** Of those who have written, some produced nothing more than a collection or transcription of things already composed by the ancients, such as Euclides, Democritus, and Proclinus. Others, recording only very small details from the history of the ancients based on the same topics, set out to compose books themselves, such as Annius, Medius, and Phoebion. This latter group clearly believed they should acquire glory more from the elegant arrangement of their speech than from the depth of their thought. Among these we might also count Heliodorus, who seems to have contributed nothing at all to the distinct structure of discourse beyond what he had heard from the elders.

**B** Plotinus, however, and Gentilianus Amelius <note>Amelius was Plotinus's most devoted student for nearly two decades before Porphyry arrived.</note> are filled with a wealth of propositions which they treat with great care. They chose the duty of writing with serious intent, employing their own particular method of contemplation. Plotinus, it seems, explained the principles of Pythagoras and Plato more clearly than those who came before him. Even the writings of Numenius, Cronius, Moderatus, and Thrasyllus <note>These were Middle Platonists and Neopythagoreans who lived before or during the time of Plotinus.</note> do not come close to his exact diligence when he writes on the same subjects.

**D** Amelius, for his part, chose to follow in Plotinus’s footsteps and pursues many of his discoveries; however, while he is more wordy in explaining matters and wanders through a broader scope of interpretation, he takes on a style opposite to Plotinus’s own density. We consider the books of these two men alone to be worthy of serious consideration.

**E** For why should anyone strive to follow the others, while neglecting to investigate those from whom these men received what they committed to writing? They added nothing of their own—not just regarding the main points of doctrine, but not even a single new argument. They cared for nothing more than gathering the opinions of the majority, or selecting the better parts through much discussion. We have achieved the same through other works: as when we argued against Gentilianus <note>Amelius</note> regarding the concept of justice in Plato, and when we examined Plotinus’s book treating the Ideas <note term="Ideas">The "Ideas" or "Forms" are the perfect, eternal patterns of all things in Platonic philosophy.</note>.

**F** I speak of our common friend, Basilius of Tyre <note>Basilius is the Greek version of "Malchus," the original name of Porphyry, the author of this biography.</note>, who himself treated many subjects in imitation of Plotinus. Favoring Plotinus more than our own path and school, he attempted in a certain book to show that the Platonic opinion on Ideas was truer than ours. I believe we have moderately refuted him in a counter-reply, as one who had not correctly recanted his views. We have certainly examined many of their opinions in these works, as also in a letter to Amelius which grew to the size of a book; this was in response to several things he had sent and written to us from Rome, which he titled according to the custom of Plotinian philosophy. We, however, were content with a common title for the book, simply addressing the volume as a "Reply to Amelius's Letter."

**G** <margin>Longinus prefers Plotinus and Amelius over the other wise men of his age, noting that they use a unique method of contemplation.</margin> <margin>Again, on the excellence of Plotinus.</margin> <margin>The wealth of propositions and questions.</margin> In these words, then, Longinus confessed that among all...

<column-break/>

**A** Of those who have written, some produced nothing more than a collection and transcription of what was composed by the elders, such as Euclides, Democritus, and Proclinus. Others, recording very small matters from the history of the ancients, attempted to compose books in the same style as them, such as Annius, Medius, and Phoebion. This last man sought to be known more for the construction of his phrasing than for the composition of his thought; among these one might also count Heliodorus.

**B** [Those who] contributed something more to the articulation of discourse beyond what was said by the elders in their lectures, and who handled a great number of problems, following their own art from its foundation and using their own method of contemplation, are Plotinus and Gentilianus Amelius. Plotinus, it seems, established an explanation of Pythagorean and Platonic principles more clearly than those before him.

**D** The [writings] of Numenius, Cronius, Moderatus, and Thrasyllus do not approach the accuracy of Plotinus’s writings on the same subjects. Amelius, choosing to walk in his footsteps and holding to most of the same doctrines, yet being expansive in his labor and led by the breadth of his interpretation toward an imitation of them—it is only their writings that we consider worthy of examination.

**E** Why should anyone think it necessary to disturb the others, while leaving aside the examination of those from whom these men received what they wrote? They added nothing from themselves—not only of the main points, but not even of the arguments—except for what they diligently gathered from the many, or chose by better judgment. Indeed, we have done this through other works, as when [we spoke] against Gentilianus...

**F** ...regarding justice in Plato, and when we examined Plotinus’s work on the Ideas. For I speak of our common companion Basileus of Tyre, who himself has written a few things in imitation of Plotinus. Having accepted him more than our own school, he attempted through a book to show that Plotinus held a better opinion on Ideas than the one we favor. We believe we have moderately discussed the matter with him in those writings where he recanted. Also in the letter to Amelius, which has the size of a book, answering everything sent to us by him from Rome. He himself [titled it] a letter concerning the philosophy of Plotinus. We, however, were satisfied only with the common title of the book, addressing it as "To the Letter of Amelius."

**G** In these things, then, he [Longinus] acknowledged that Plotinus and Amelius excelled all those of his time in the number of problems they solved, and that these men especially used their own unique method of contemplation.

<margin>A</margin> Regarding the works of Numenius, it is not merely that Plotinus did not "borrow" them or simply honor his doctrines; rather, we see that while Plotinus shared an interest in Pythagorean principles, the works of Numenius, Cronius, Moderatus, and Thrasyllus <note>These were influential Middle Platonist and Neopythagorean philosophers who preceded Plotinus.</note> do not even come close to the precision found in Plotinus’s writings on the same subjects. 

Longinus, having said of Amelius that he followed in Plotinus’s footsteps but was prone to excessive detail and a rambling style of interpretation <margin>B</margin>, then makes mention of me, Porphyry, who was then at the beginning of my association with Plotinus. He says: "And our common friend, Basileus of Tyre <note>original: "Basileus" (Greek) / "Basilius" (Latin). This is Porphyry himself; 'Basileus' is a Greek translation of his original Phoenician name, Malchus, meaning 'King.'</note>, who has himself composed no small number of works, has written in imitation of Plotinus." 

In these words, Longinus truly observes that I most diligently avoided the unphilosophical "roundabout ways" <note>original: "ambages" (Latin)</note> of Amelius and sought to embrace the concise style of Plotinus. It is enough that a man of such stature, the foremost in judgment, has given such testimony about Plotinus. 

<margin>C</margin> Indeed, if I had been able to go to him when he invited me, he certainly would never have written those criticisms which he ventured to write before he had accurately examined our doctrine. But why (to speak in the manner of Hesiod) should I speak "concerning the oak and the rock"? <note>A Greek idiom meaning to waste time on trivialities or things well-known.</note> For if one must use the testimony of the wise, who could be wiser than a God? Indeed, a God who truly said of himself:

Furthermore, when he had said that Amelius proceeded indeed in the footsteps of Plotinus, but was led by a certain excessive length of exposition <margin>B</margin> into the opposite of Plotinus, he soon made mention of me, who had recently gained the friendship of Plotinus, and says: "Our common friend, that Basilius of Tyre, has himself treated and composed no few things according to the model of Plotinus." 

In these words, Longinus surely indicates that he perceived that I most diligently avoided the Amelian "ambages" (ramblings), which are too foreign to a philosopher, and that in writing I had embraced the form of Plotinus. It is enough, therefore, that so great a man, and first in judgment, has thus far been brought forward as a testimony for us, writing such things about Plotinus. 

<margin>C</margin> Now truly, if I could have gone to him then when he called me, he certainly would never have written back those things which he first set out to write before he had diligently examined the doctrine itself. But what does it profit me now (to speak in the manner of Hesiod) to speak around the oak and the rock? Certainly, if it is necessary to use the testimonies of the wise, who can be wiser than a God? A God, I say, who truly said of himself: *I know indeed the number of the sand, and the measure of the sea. I understand the mute, I hear the one not speaking.*

### THE LIFE OF PLOTINUS.

But having shaken from your eyelids the heavy film
Of darkness, while you were tossed by the waves, with your eyes
You beheld many and beautiful things, which no man has easily seen
Of those who have been seekers after wisdom.
But now, since you are released from the shell and have left the tomb
Of the guardian soul, you hasten to the guardian
Council, which breathes among pleasant breezes:
Where friendship is, where Desire is gentle to the sight,
Full of pure joy and irrigated by the Deity
With eternal ambrosial streams: from where come the bonds
Of love, and the sweet breath, and the tranquil ether
Of the golden race of great Jove <note>original: "Iouis" (Jupiter/Zeus). This refers to the highest divine order.</note>: where the brothers 
Minos and Rhadamanthus <note>Traditional judges of the dead in Greek mythology, here representing divine justice.</note> dwell; where the just
Aeacus is; where the sacred power of Plato is; where the beautiful
Pythagoras is, and all who have established the choir of immortal
Love, all who have shared a common ancestry
With the most blessed spirits; where the soul among the banquets
Always grows cheerful with joy. O blessed one, who after many
Exhausting labors have departed to the holy spirits,
Advancing toward the most stable life.
Let us stop our song, and the spinning circle of the dance,
O Muses of Plotinus, in our rejoicing. These were the things my 
Golden lyre had to say for one who has lived his life well.

...but having armed himself with powerful life-forces...
to mingle with the joyful Plotinus. But for me,

<margin>A</margin> In this oracle, it is contained that Plotinus was
good, and mild, and especially gentle and sweet,
which we ourselves have confirmed through true experience.
Furthermore, it states that he was vigilant, and always with a 
pure soul directed upward toward the divine itself, which 
indeed he loved ardently with his whole soul. Likewise, that he
strove with all his strength to emerge entirely from the bitter
wave of this bloody life. Therefore, by this means, by this
<margin>B</margin> blessed light, when he often raised himself with his
whole mind to the first God through a higher intellect, and ascended
through all the steps arranged by Plato in the *Symposium* <note>The "Ladder of Love" from Plato's dialogue, describing the soul's ascent from physical beauty to the Idea of Beauty itself.</note>
toward divine things: that God suddenly shone upon him—the one
who has neither form nor any idea, but is above
the intellect and the whole intelligible world, establishing it in himself.
To this God I, Porphyry, once approached 
and was joined, when I was already completing my
sixty-eighth year of age. Therefore, that 
<margin>C</margin> end appeared very close to Plotinus. For the goal and 
the end for Plotinus was to reach and be joined 
to the God who is present everywhere to all. Four times, moreover,
while I was with him, he attained this
end; not merely in potential, I say, 
but attained it through a certain ineffable act. Furthermore, 
the oracle adds: the gods often directed Plotinus onto the 
right path when he was wandering, while they
kindly offered the most abundant rays of divine light to the
vision of his eyes: so that it might truly be said that Plotinus 
composed his books under the contemplation and the divinely 
glowing intuition. Now indeed, from this intuition,
<margin>E</margin> watching from within and without, he is said 
by the oracle to have seen many and most beautiful

professor of philosophy might easily have seen. For the 
contemplation of men may indeed be superior to other 
human contemplation; but compared to divine
knowledge, though it may be graceful, it still lacks the 
strength to penetrate the depths which the higher beings penetrate.
Thus far the oracle shows what things Plotinus performed while
he was enclosed in the body, and what he 
attained. After this, it prophesies that Plotinus,
<margin>F</margin> released from the body, reached the blessed assembly, where...

Wherein is Friendship, and wherein is Desire, sweet to the sight,

In these words it is said, on the one hand, that he became
good, and kind, and very gentle indeed, and mild,
which we also knew to be truly the case. And it is said
that he was vigilant, having a pure soul,

To Him, I Porphyry say I once

it might be graceful, and yet not so as to be able to grasp

<meta>This page concludes the mystical "Oracle of Apollo" regarding the fate of Plotinus's soul and begins Porphyry's explanation of his editorial work. It details how Porphyry organized Plotinus’s scattered writings into the systematic "Enneads."</meta>

### THE LIFE OF PLOTINUS.
<sig>γ 3</sig>

...assembly. There is a community there, with friendship, desire, and wisdom, and a kindled love; there is the vision of God <note>original: "θεόπτεσθαι" (theoptesthai), the act of beholding the divine</note> and the so-called judges of souls, the children of God: Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Aeacus. He goes toward them, not to be judged, but to converse. Following these are those whom the other best gods follow, and who are still preserved there: Plato and Pythagoras. And all the others who have established the choir of immortal love. There the blessed spirits have their home. They lead a life filled with festivities and joys, and they continue in this state, being blessed by the gods.

This then is the life of Plotinus as it has been recorded by us. Since he himself entrusted us with the arrangement and the correction of his books, and I promised him while he was still living and announced to the other companions that I would do this: first, I decided not to leave the books scattered in a messy chronological order. Instead, imitating Apollodorus of Athens <note>A famous scholar who organized the works of Epicharmus.</note> and Andronicus the Peripatetic <note>The scholar credited with organizing the "Corpus Aristotelicum."</note>—the former of whom collected the works of the comic writer Epicharmus into ten volumes, while the latter divided the works of Aristotle and Theophrastus into systematic treatises, gathering related subjects together—so I too, having fifty-four books by Plotinus, divided them into six Enneads <note>From the Greek "ennea," meaning nine. Each Ennead is a group of nine treatises.</note>. I was delighted by the perfection of the number six and the groups of nine. For each Ennead, I gathered and combined related topics, giving the first position to the easier problems.

The first Ennead contains these more ethical subjects:
- What is the living being, and what is man?
- On the virtues.
- On dialectic.
- On happiness.
- Whether happiness increases with the passage of time.
- On the beautiful.
- On the primary good and other goods.
- From where do evils come?
- On the rational departure from life <note>A discussion on the conditions under which a philosopher might choose to end their life.</note>.

Thus, the first Ennead contains these, encompassing ethical positions. The second, in turn, contains a collection of physical matters, embracing things concerning the world and what pertains to the world. They are these:
- On the world.
- On the circular motion.
- Whether the stars have an effect.
- On the two matters <note>Refers to intelligible (divine) matter and sensible (physical) matter.</note>.
- On potentiality and actuality.
- On quality and form.
- On total mixture.
- Why things seen from a distance appear small.
- Against those who say the creator of the world is evil and the world is evil <note>A famous polemic against the Gnostics.</note>.

The third Ennead, also containing things about the world, encompasses those things observed regarding the circumstances of the world, as follows:

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...charity, sweet desire, and joy, and a love joined to God. Furthermore, the judges of souls are established there: Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Aeacus, the sons of God. Plotinus goes to them, not indeed to be judged, but to live among them, as the other best gods also do. There also Plato and Pythagoras and the others lead their lives, whoever has firmly established the choir of immortal love. There the most happy spirits <note>original: "Dæmones," referring to tutelary spirits or divine beings, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note> have their offspring. Likewise, they lead a life there most full of festive vitality and joy, <margin>B</margin> and such a life continues, made blessed by divine generosity.

<margin>The arrangement of Plotinus's books digested by subject order.</margin>
Thus far, the story of Plotinus's life has been told in the historical manner. But since Plotinus committed to us the care of the order and correction of his books, and I promised him while he was living, and promised the others that I would perform it: I judged it first of all a worthwhile task not to permit the books to lie in a jumbled state, just as they were composed in the succession of time. But just as Apollodorus <margin>C</margin> the Athenian collected the comedies of Epicharmus into ten volumes, and Andronicus the Peripatetic distributed the books of Aristotle and Theophrastus into treatises, gathering related themes into one: so I also have divided the fifty-four books of Plotinus into six Enneads, rejoicing in the opportunity of the perfect number six, and indeed of the number nine. To each Ennead—that is, a group of nine—assigning its own subjects, I have gathered together related things, always setting in the numerical order <margin>D</margin> those subjects that are lighter.

*The first Ennead contains chiefly moral matters.*
- What is an animal: what is a man.
- On the virtues.
- On dialectic.
- On happiness.
- Whether happiness consists in the extension of time.
- On the beautiful.
- On the primary good and other goods.
- Where evils come from.
<margin>E</margin> - On the rational exit from this life.

The first Ennead, as I said, contains these, rather embracing moral positions. The second truly collects natural things, embracing what things belong to the world, or what pertain to the world: these indeed are:
- On the world.
- On circular motion.
- Whether the stars do anything.
<margin>F</margin> - On the two matters.
- On that which is in potentiality, and that which is in act.
- On quality and species.
- On mixture throughout.
- Why those things seen far off seem small.
- Against those thinking the maker of the world to be evil, and the world evil.

The third Ennead also, containing things which are of the world, encompasses those things which are considered around the world.

# MARSILIO FICINO THE FLORENTINE
## COMMENTARY ON THE FIRST BOOK OF THE FIRST ENNEAD.

### S U M M A R Y  O F  T H E  W H O L E  B O O K.

> *The rational soul is the midpoint between divine and natural forms; it is not "inside" the body, but rather "present" to it, and from itself it radiates the life that exists in the body, from which—and from the body itself—the single composite animal is made.*

->Chapter One.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap P showing a robed scholar sitting at a desk with an open book, inside a vaulted room with a window.</image-desc>
VERY OPPORTUNELY, this first of all books meets us, in which we may contemplate ourselves as if in a mirror, lest, like those who are overly curious, we seek out the affairs of others before our own. For it will teach us that the "true human"—that is, this very thing that we properly are—is not the body (because we use the body as an instrument), nor is it the life entirely proper and bound to the body (since we share this with the brute animals). And because the very reason through which we exist often opposes and commands this bodily life, we are not something composed of the body and its own life, for the very same reasons we have assigned here. For this "animal" is not ultimately joined from a rational soul and an irrational living thing, since one thing cannot be made from the indissoluble and the dissoluble. Rather, the human is the soul—that is, an incorporeal, rational substance, existing indeed from the divine intellect, but subsisting in itself, not <term>inhering: being stuck inside something like a property (like the color of an apple).</term> in the body, but rather <term>assisting: being present to govern and give life without being physically part of the material.</term> the body, and by its very presence producing this life in the body, from which and the body the composite "animal" is named.

That our soul is indeed present to the body, but not "in" it, we shall briefly show thus. There are three kinds of forms. The lowest forms are "natural," the highest are "divine," and the middle are "rational souls." Natural forms, such as those of the elements and mixtures, are said to be present to matter insofar as they affect it and produce something in it; they are also said to be "in" matter insofar as they suffer together with the matter. But divine forms—that is, the Divine Intellect, the architect of the world, and the "Ideas" of things (the first acts of divine intelligence and the patterns of things)—are not in matter; otherwise, one could not even imagine anything separated from matter. Furthermore, they are not even "present" to matter. I do not mean they are far from matter in terms of physical location, for they are undoubtedly everywhere; but they are not present according to any kinship of nature or any affection toward matter. For who would not notice that the divine intellect is secret from all commerce with matter? Since even the human intellect cannot carry out its own action of intelligence except by segregating and perfecting itself away from matter. Therefore, between natural forms (which are both present to and "in" matter) and entirely divine forms (which are neither "in" nor even "present" to it), there must exist a middle nature of form. This nature is not "in" matter—lest it suffer with matter, and by suffering, act imperfectly upon it, and by acting imperfectly, fail to form it to the vigor of life—but it is "present" to matter. That is, it favors it with natural providence and cherishes it with a certain love of affinity, and by cherishing it, it forms and vivifies it, and by vivifying it, it gives birth to the human animal, which is subject to the human (that is, the soul) that generates it. That the rational soul is such is clearly evident; it appears not to be "in" the body, where...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's commentary on the first book of Plotinus's first Ennead. Ficino is exploring the hierarchy of the soul, distinguishing between the higher rational soul and the lower animating principle that gives life to the physical body.</meta>

### THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

It resists and commands: it even appears to be present where it naturally loves the union with the body. It possesses something of its own when it reasons—that is, when it ascends by its own arguments through a certain movement and time from effect to cause, and descends again—and when, having proposed an end and discovered a variety of ways to reach it, it deliberates on the choice between them. Indeed, this entire faculty—reason, thought, deliberation—is most properly called the characteristic of man. Again, it has something in common, as it were, with the divine intellect: namely, the intellect that contemplates truth constantly, not by moving from point to point, but by direct intuition. By the stable intuition of this intellect, the wandering discourse of reason is governed, beginning from there and finally ending there. It also has something in common, as it were, with the brute animal: imagination—that is, the most internal and simple sense of the soul and the judge of the senses that follow.

Accordingly, the mediating power itself which moves discursively is called "thought" by the way it reasons, and simultaneously "reason" and "counsel." But where it takes its starting points from the intellect through discourse, it is called "intelligence," "wisdom," and "knowledge"; yet where it begins its course from the imagination, it is called "conjecture," "faith," and "opinion." This substance, endowed with these twice-three powers, is properly called the "soul" by the Platonists. Insofar as it is so disposed as to pour a certain life into the human body, it is also called "man." This is properly the soul. The life poured out from here, however, should properly be called "animation" and "vivification" <note>Ficino distinguishes between the soul's essence (anima) and the act of giving life to matter (animation).</note>; yet, relying on common usage, we shall call the former the "first soul" and the latter the "second soul." We shall say that the second soul and its powers arise from the first and its powers.

In the first soul, reason proceeds from the intellect, and imagination from reason. In the second soul, there are also three principal powers: imagination (that is, a certain common sense); then the exterior sense divided into five parts; and finally the generative power, which is also called "Nature," the origin of generation, growth, and nutrition. Imagination in the second and animal soul represents the intellect of the first soul (for from this second soul and the body, the human animal is made). The exterior sense represents reason. Finally, the "vegetable" nature reflects the imagination of the first soul. Again, the imagination which belongs to the prior soul is the lowest part, which dictates distinct "phantasy" <term>Phantasy (Phantasia): The mental faculty that forms or processes images of things not present to the senses.</term> and judges somewhat regarding particular substance; it follows reason more closely. But the imagination which holds the highest place of the following animal soul is usually called "confused phantasy"; it perceives only accidents <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are qualities (like color or size) that are not essential to a thing's fundamental nature.</note> and is mostly led by natural instinct.

Accordingly, every sense in this animal pertains to external sensible things and to the passions of the body brought on by external things, which it experiences most closely; and properly, it suffers along with the suffering body. But the sense—that is, the imagination of the higher soul—does not direct itself toward sensible things, but toward the senses of the subject animal. It does not feel the passions of the body directly but immediately notices the "compassions" <note>The shared feelings or reactions.</note> of the senses. It is entirely occupied with the images, actions, and passions of the inferior sense; yet it does not receive harmful passion from them, but is very often touched by a certain paternal affection toward it. This concludes the general form of the argument for the whole book.

->The division of the book into thirteen parts.<-

**I** We divide this whole book into thirteen chapters or small sections. Up to the seventh, he only inquires; in the seventh, he begins to define the questions; but thereafter, he investigates and defines equally. In the first chapter, therefore, he establishes that we must first track down where the disturbances (passions) are. Second, where the actions and effects that chiefly accompany them are. Third, where thought and opinion reside. Fourth, where intelligence is. Fifth, what this very thing is that considers these matters. Sixth—which he wishes to be first—where sense is. Now, seeking where these are and to whom they belong, he asks: do they belong to the simple soul, or to the soul used by the body, or to something composed of both, or perhaps to a mixture? This inquiry and those following tend toward this: that it may finally be found what "man" is and what the "living being" is. This, then, is the purpose and order of the book.

->The rational soul is the same as the rational nature of the soul itself; although it is separated from the body according to being, it nevertheless produces a life joined to the body in the single existence of the living being. Therefore, the opinion of Plotinus is the middle ground between the opinions of Alexander and Averroes.<-

**II** In the second chapter of the book, he begins thus: If the soul is a simple form consisting in itself, it receives neither any passions nor those things which precede or follow passions. But if it is either something composed of matter and form, or a certain form that is a proper part of a composite, it will easily receive such things. Here you will note what he says: "If the soul is one thing, and the very being of the soul another." This can be read not only as "the very being of the soul," but also "the very being as soul." For Plotinus, these mean exactly the same thing. "Soul" signifies this soul demonstrated in some way or known by its outcome, which, whatever it may be, is present somewhere or at some time. But "the very being of the soul," or "that which is to be soul," signifies the special nature of the soul itself (if I may put it that way). In this nature, nothing necessary for the complete essence of the soul is lacking, nor is anything superfluous present.

He intends them to be the same. He declares this in the book *On the Will of God*, saying: "The soul is the same as that which is the being of the soul." Since the soul is a simple form, it is not predicated of anything else. It is as if he were to say: it should not be said of a composite, nor of the proper form of a composite (which itself seems to be a certain composite in some way), that "this thing" is the same as "the being of the thing" or "the essence of this thing." For "this man" is one thing, and "human nature" itself is another; for human nature lacks nothing of human perfection, nor does anything superfluous happen to it. But in *this* man, there are some things not at all necessary to a human, and (to speak in a Platonic way) because there are certain things within him too foreign to a human, this man degenerates from the integrity of the ideal pattern.

Forms separated from matter, however, which are both simple and exist in themselves, admit nothing from the ideal pattern and undergo nothing foreign. He judges the substance of the rational soul to be such. He demonstrates this in the book *On the Immortality of the Soul*. And in the book *On Happiness*, he signifies this, saying: "That the soul is not part of the composite is witnessed by its very separation from the body." Now, understand this separation to be two-fold. One is through moral philosophy, by which it segregates itself from the disturbances serving the body; the other is through contemplative philosophy, by which it separates itself from the senses and imagination. Surely, because the soul is not a part of the composite, it can turn back into itself and toward the first causes, and rightly resolve any composite things down to their simple parts, and those again to the simple forms already existing in themselves.

It is well known that this opinion of Plotinus is the middle ground between Alexander and Averroes <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias (c. 200 AD) viewed the soul as a byproduct of the body; Averroes (1126–1198) viewed the human intellect as a single, separate entity shared by all humans. Plotinus offers a bridge: the soul is separate but still animates the individual.</note>. For Alexander confesses that the intellectual nature is the body's own passive quality. Averroes, however, neither grants that it is the life of the body, nor that it pours any life into the body. Finally, Plotinus denies that the intellectual nature is a life "familiar" to the body, yet he grants that it propagates a certain familiar life into bodies by its presence—from which life and the body the "human animal" (though not "man" in the highest sense) is fashioned. Now, remember to investigate what "man" is and what the "living being" is, not only in this book but also in the book *How the Multitude of Ideas Rightly Exists*. Where he says that sense receives either the species <note>The "form" or "appearance" of a thing without its physical matter.</note> or the body into the impassible, he embraces both opinions concerning sense. For some wish the sense to receive only incorporeal images; others, certain corporeal things, yet of such a kind that where they are received—

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's first Ennead, specifically focusing on the relationship between the rational soul and the physical body. Ficino is moving from a general description of the soul's faculties to a technical investigation of how a spiritual substance can interact with a material one without being corrupted.</meta>

### ON THE FIRST BOOK OF THE FIRST ENNEAD

->*The rational soul, although it exists in itself, nevertheless inclines in a certain way toward the body, which is a state that least of all suits a purely intellectual substance.*<-

**III.** Since he had indicated that the soul exists in itself, lest anyone think it does not differ at all from the Mind <note>original: "mens"; in Neoplatonism, the Mind or Intellect is the level of reality above the Soul</note>, he adds that the soul, although it exists in itself just as the Mind does, nevertheless fosters the body, and by fostering it, forms it and fills it with life—something that the Mind itself does not do. Next, he says the soul uses the already vivified body as a kind of natural and conjoined instrument. After this, he investigates whether, while the soul uses the body as an instrument, it receives the same sensations and "passions" <note>term: "passions" (passiones); in this context, it refers to any state where something is acted upon or "suffers" an external influence, rather than just emotions</note>. He gradually leans toward the view that it does *not* receive them, because it uses the body not by leaning upon it, but by ruling it. Then he signifies that the soul is separable from the body by its very nature, and that this is proven most effectively through the practice of philosophy. Finally, he asks: if it is joined to the body in some way, how is it joined? Is it like a certain "tempering" <note>original: "temperatio"; a blending of elements</note> of the body? Or is it because the soul propagates itself through the whole body? Or is it because it is a form "lying" within the body? Or a species presiding over it? Or is it partly separate, insofar as it acts as the user (like the rational soul), and partly conjoined, insofar as it is a living instrument subject to the user (that is, the life lacking reason, and the "animal" constituted from both this life and the body)? Indeed, the philosopher must turn this instrument toward the "user"—which is Reason—so that it obeys most willingly, and must also recall Reason itself from this use, as much as possible, toward contemplation.

->*A double reason shows that the soul is not mixed with the body.*<-

**IIII.** In the fourth chapter of the book, he follows up on these modes, saying: If the soul were a certain mixture or a form lying within the body, just as it would not truly be its own self (but rather the "composite" <note>the union of body and soul</note> itself would be), so too it would not feel, act, or suffer, but the composite would; the soul itself, so to speak, would only "co-suffer." But if it is an essence possessing its existence within itself—not mixed, not lying within, but merely unfolding itself through the body by its own abundance and vivifying by its presence alone—it will never admit any passions of the body. It is much like how light does not admit the "passions" of the air <note>a favorite Neoplatonic analogy: light passes through air without being changed by the air's qualities</note>. Now, he demonstrates that the soul is not mixed with the body, and therefore not "lying" within it, by a double reason. First: If the soul, which is the very principle of vivifying the body, were mixed with the body, it would be utterly infected by being mixed with something inferior, and it would fall away from life at the very moment it was meant to give life; therefore, it would not perfectly vivify and form the body. Indeed, life mixed into an already living body is not so much "life" as it is a certain "vivification" received in the body as a passion; however, in terms of action, it belongs to the separable life itself. Just as any form in matter is a certain "formation"—a passion of the matter depending on the effective action of a separate form—and as light in the air is an "illumination" rather than the source of light itself; therefore, to perfectly vivify and form the body is neither the task of an imperfect life lying within the body, nor of a purely detached Intellect. It is, therefore, the duty of the intellectual and rational soul. Second reason: Things do not mix into one unless they agree in a common matter and are compatible in their genus. The soul, however, especially the intellectual soul, is more distant from the body than a line is from the color white. But these two are not mixed at all; therefore, neither is the soul mixed with the body.

->*Unless it is known how the soul is joined to the body, it will not be known which actions or passions belong to the soul itself and which belong to the composite.*<-

**V.** Since he touched upon the Aristotelian opinion <note>Aristotle often viewed the soul as the "form" of the body, making the "animal" the primary subject of experience</note> which says that passions and affects belong not so much to the soul as to the "animal" (the living creature), he shows again that it is difficult to say how this "conjunction" or "commonality" belongs to the whole animal. For whether you say these things proceed through the senses from the body into the soul and into the whole, it is not yet clear what "sense" belongs to which part; or if they proceed from the soul through an opinion or a certain judgment into the whole body, it has not yet been established what "opinion" belongs to which part. Likewise, the desire for the common good, for knowledge, and for eternal glory can belong to the soul alone. Again, the opinion of an evil does not necessarily produce pain, specifically in such a living body. Thus, neither does an opinion or a feeling of contempt necessarily provoke anger or the desire for some good in such a body. Furthermore, if the "perturbations" <note>original: "perturbationes"; emotional disturbances or passions</note> are said to belong to the power of desiring and being angry, and these powers are founded in the composite, and thus the perturbations belong to the composite: Plotinus similarly challenges this. Finally, if the Peripatetics <note>term: "Peripatetics" (Peripatetici); the followers of Aristotle, who walked while they taught</note> claim that such affects belong both to the power of desiring/anger and to the composite, but in different ways: he brings this into doubt as well, signifying that such ambiguity happens to us mostly because we do not yet sufficiently understand how the soul is joined to the body, and how the composite "animal" is made.

->*If it is judged that the rational soul is a part of the composite animal, the doubts are not resolved.*<-

**VI.** In the sixth chapter, he brings forward the Peripatetic solution to the preceding doubts. For they say: Since in a living creature, "being" itself belongs not to a part but to the whole, actions and passions properly belong to the whole. Specifically, the soul and the power of the living creature are that *by which* the animal acts; but the animal itself is primarily that *which* acts and suffers. Plotinus will perhaps concede that this is manifest in actions and passions that pass into external matter; but regarding the sense that is internal, and regarding the life that is most inward, he says it must be questioned why the soul itself does not feel and live. This entire controversy, as I was saying, tends toward this: that we understand that these ambiguities cannot be cleared up unless it is first established how the soul relates to the body and the body to the soul—what remains simple, and what and how things are composed. Thus far, as I said at the beginning, he is only inquiring; nothing is defined in the meantime.

->*The rational soul consists in itself, has its own proper rational actions, and a certain sense free from passion; however, it produces an irrational life in the body, whose sense is occupied with the passions of the body.*<-

**VII.** In the seventh chapter, he begins gradually to define things and brings forward his own opinion. He wants it to be clear that his view is especially true because the doubts about the soul cannot be solved unless this view is accepted. And truly, unless one makes such a distinction, it will be very difficult to assign reasons for the part of us that is divine, and the part of those things in us which seem alien to divinity. This is not only the opinion of Plato and Pythagoras (as is clear from the *Timaeus*) and the Egyptians (as Iamblichus teaches), but even Themistius asserts that Aristotle felt this way. This, then, is the opinion: That there are two lives in us...

<summary>Ficino examines the complex relationship between the rational soul and the physical body, arguing against the idea that they are "mixed" like physical substances and instead proposing a hierarchy where the soul governs the body without being corrupted by it.</summary>
