### COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO

of which the second comes from the first and is its image. But while the first exists independently in itself, the second is inherent in the body. The first is a complete entity in itself; the second is a part of a composite—that is, of this living animal which is the primary subject of life. No one doubts that there is a certain life inherent in the body; but reason proves that another life presides over this one, existing in itself, for a life that lies within another <note>original: "vitam in alio iacentem"; referring to life dependent on a physical host</note> is imperfect and must depend on a perfect life. In the same way, the intellect situated in the soul flows from the Intellect flourishing in itself, and the good found in the intellect flows from the Good itself existing in its own right. Furthermore, the intellectual good is not only created by the "Good" itself, but is also preserved by it and never separated from it. Similarly, the intelligence infused into the soul is both created and preserved by the pure Intellect and is never uncoupled from it. By the same logic, the life or soul bound to the body is produced and preserved by the Life—that is, the Soul—that always remains within itself, staying in contact with it. Just as a ray of the sun is connected on one end to its sun, but on the other end touches and gives form to an object, so it is with the soul. Therefore, the "primary life" is, in a sense, the form of the living animal; but the "secondary life" is the form of the natural body equipped with organs <note>term: "natural instruments" (naturalibus instrumentis); Ficino is using Aristotle’s famous definition of the soul as the "act of a natural organic body."</note> adapted for the animal’s use. Aristotle also says this: after he called the soul a "form" or "act," he added that the intellectual soul is an act in one sense, and the other life is an act in another. But to return to our subject: with this distinction proposed, Plotinus attributes sensation accompanied by "passion" <note>term: "passion" (passio); here meaning a physical or emotional reaction where the subject is acted upon by an outside force</note> to the animal; but to the soul, he attributes a sensation free from passion. Again, he assigns the discursive movements of reason to this same soul, whether they incline toward the senses or rise toward the intellect. The remaining parts of this chapter will be clear to anyone who considers them carefully on their own.

->The rational soul is joined through its own intellect to the divine mind, and through that to God; thus, the irrational life is also subject to the rational soul. Moreover, the intellect is both personal and common.<-

**VIII.** The eighth chapter investigates how the soul relates to all things, both above and below it. First, it asks how it relates to the Divine Intellect—the father of rational souls—which presides over the soul almost as the soul presides over the animal. You should know that the "One" itself, or the "Good" itself, which is the Highest God, has no "respects" <note>term: "respects" (respectus); in this context, it means a relationship, perspective, or orientation toward something else. God is absolute and has no external dependencies.</note>. However, the Intellect (who is the "Son of the Good" in Plotinus's system) has two respects: first, insofar as it comes from the One, and thus is itself one; second, insofar as it exists in itself, and thus branches out into a multitude of "Ideas." Yet, it possesses and beholds all these Ideas at once in a single act. The Soul, then, has three respects. From the Intellect, it receives the power of knowing; but since this power depends directly on the Intellect, it is itself "intellect." It is always continuous with its father, and under his "form" and "act," it always understands all things simultaneously. However, insofar as it is taken according to the nature of the soul, it now moves through time, proceeding from potential to act in a sequence; this is called "reason" and "thought," and in this state, it seems to hold the species <note>term: "species"; the mental forms or categories of things</note> of things as distinct from one another. Finally, as it turns toward the animal, it descends from the level of universal reason to the level of imagination of particulars. 

But this "animal life" seems to undergo four respects. Insofar as it depends on the soul as an image depends on a substance, it possesses imagination. Insofar as it is something in itself, it branches out into a multitude of senses. Insofar as it rules the body, it exercises vital power. Insofar as it clings to the body and becomes part of the animal, it is rendered liable to passions. Therefore, this "life" is the form of the body; but the "soul" is rather the form of the animal; and the "Intellect" is the form of the soul. God, in a way, is the form of the Intellect itself. Each lower level always exists and acts under the "act" of the higher level as if it were its form. 

Furthermore, the Divine Intellect itself is called "common" insofar as it is indivisible and entirely present everywhere; but it is called "personal" <note>original: "proprius"; belonging to the individual</note> insofar as it is received by individual souls, each in its own way. From this, different ways of reasoning follow in different souls, as well as different ways of imagining. However, no one would say that the "intellect" which is already a form within the soul—not just presiding but implanted—is common. To be sure, many eyes reflect many souls; many visual rays naturally implanted in the eyes represent the various intellects naturally implanted in souls. But the one common light of the sun, present everywhere, represents the Divine Intellect, the father of souls and intellects. Finally, the one light of the sun staying within the sun itself shows us the Good itself, the father of the Mind. Therefore, the intellects innate to souls, even if they are not a single "one" intellect, are nevertheless "one thing"—that is, one according to their intellectual being, made understanding in act by that one light of the Mind. In that light, as if in a common form and object, they are one, even though they are many according to the multitude of souls. Just as visual rays or sights are numbered according to the number of eyes and are not one, they are nevertheless one as they converge in a single light; they would seem most of all to be "one" if they existed in themselves, freed from eyes, just as intellectual souls remain after being released from bodies. 

Themistius seems to adapt this opinion of Plato and Plotinus to Aristotle and Theophrastus; Avicenna and Al-Ghazali also follow it. Alexander <note>note: Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle</note>, however, agrees with Plotinus in that he attributes many intellects to us, but he differs in asserting that these many are mortal. But Averroes <note>note: A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose "monopsychism" argued that all humans share one single, eternal Intellect</note> agrees with Plotinus in asserting that every intellect is immortal, yet he differs by assigning us only a single one. You, however, should take the "number" of the human intellect from Alexander, and the "immortal gift" of all intelligence from Averroes, and you will have the complete opinion of our Plotinus. Furthermore, know that regarding the nature of the intellect, one should believe Plotinus above all others, for his life, deeds, and writings testify that he always lived by the intellect. I want to mention this now so that Alexander and Averroes do not disturb you. Finally, he concludes that "we"—that is, the human being—are properly the soul using rational discourse, whether it moves through universals or particulars. Those things above or below reason are "ours": the higher things because we always depend on them, and the lower because they depend on us. He adds, in the manner of Plato, that the intellectual nature (both presiding over us and dwelling within us) is indivisible, whereas the life diffused as far as the body is said to be divisible. This is because although it is one and whole in every limb, it is nonetheless affected by different things and gives life to different parts in different ways. In many limbs—or vehicles <note>term: "vehicles" (vehiculis); in Neoplatonism, the "astral body" or subtle spirit that carries the soul into the physical body</note>—the rational soul does not make a single thing out of itself and the body, but rather out of the body and a certain life granted to it as a kind of image of the soul itself. Finally, he teaches that one power of the soul depends on another in sequence.

->The cause of sin is in the irrational soul and our animal nature; however, in the [rational] soul, it lies in its consent. Likewise, the rational cycle is a middle point between rest and straight motion. Again, how intelligence and reason relate to each other and to the imagination. Also, the allegory of Adam and Eve.<-

**IX.** In the ninth chapter, he teaches us the distinctions mentioned above: that the beginning of sins is in the animal nature, but the "middle" is in the imagination of the higher soul. This is because the soul follows the promptings of the animal nature before reason has clearly judged whether something should be pursued or avoided. Hence the "inner man" complains about the "outer man":

### ON THE FIRST BOOK OF THE FIRST ENNEAD

I perceive another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind, and leading me captive. <note>original: "Sentio alia legem in membris meis..." — This is a direct reference to St. Paul in Romans 7:23, used here to describe the conflict between the lower animal nature and the higher rational mind.</note> But reason itself, since it is also occupied with things to be done, should have long ago trained its imagination to be less hastily impulsive and to tame the "animal." Reason ought to have first directed and shaped itself toward the intellect; for the intellect certainly does not involve itself in the specific details of actions, and therefore it is entirely free from blame. But we—defined here by our rational power and action—sometimes reach the intelligible and ideal principles <note>original: "rationes" — used here in the sense of 'Logoi' or formative principles</note> and the species of things, which exist first in the divine mind and then in our own; however, for the most part, we fail to rise toward them. Yet, in our reason, these principles are only occasionally in a state of power; but in both the Divine Mind and our higher mind, they are always in a state of act <note>original: "in actu" — a technical term meaning 'actually functioning' rather than just having the potential to function</note>. Plotinus said that discursive movements of reason are most characteristic of us—that is, of the soul—because the soul is the middle point between divine things that always remain the same and natural things which, by a certain fall and movement, drift away from themselves. Thus, the soul rightly possesses a circular, discursive movement as a middle ground between straight movement and a state of rest. 

Intelligence is also said to belong to the soul, not so much because it is the soul's primary nature, but because the soul can understand without the instrument of the body. Likewise, the soul performs discursive reasoning even without the body. But there is at least this difference: although discursive argumentation does not use a bodily instrument, it almost always has certain images of sensible things before its eyes. For its movement naturally slides toward such things. True intelligence, however, neither uses a bodily instrument nor looks at such images. Furthermore, when reason turns itself entirely toward the intellect, it perceives universals without the images of particulars. But we discuss these matters more extensively in our own *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his major work, *Platonic Theology*.</note>. While he uses the words of Aristotle here, he signifies that Aristotle does not differ from Plato on these points. He adds that the discourse of reason involves both the intellect and imagination, and does not touch the passions of the body, but rather deals with certain "images of passions" through its own sense—that is, the primary imagination. 

Likewise, reason (or thought) is a certain act of the intelligence. For true thought is a certain intelligence expanded more widely: at one moment, reaching toward the intellect, it perceives universal species; at another, turning toward the imagination and through it toward the "animal," it derives those universal species down into particulars. Sometimes, comparing these particulars with the universals to see where they agree or disagree, it discerns and judges. If it begins from the intellect and moves away from there, it descends from universals to individuals by "composition." But if it takes its occasion from the imagination and rises higher, it ascends from individuals to universals by "resolution." Finally, you should observe this order in the soul: remember that it holds species in the mind that are both universal and stable. In reason, the species are universal but in a way mobile; in the imagination, however, they are already particular and changeable. He concludes that passions, disturbances, and the causes of sins properly reside in the "animal" (the lower nature); but in the soul, there is an awareness of these things and often a certain consent to them. 

Now, notice in Plotinus's words a Mosaic allegory: namely, two personae—the man himself, like Adam; and the human soul drawn from him and declining, like Eve. Add to this the idea of the soul being drawn from a "sleeping" soul. For the soul propagates from itself when, sliding from its former wakefulness in God toward natural things and forgetting divine things, it now sleeps and dreams. Thus, it then generates the corporeal life, which is like Eve. Consider her as the first to sin, and then the man as consenting; but consider the intellect presiding over him like an angel, soon rebuking him, and God presiding over the angel. Finally, consider two things in the flesh—that is, two souls, as it were, in the same body. Since Plotinus, Origen, and Ammonius <note>Ammonius Saccas, the teacher of Plotinus and Origen.</note> understood Moses in this way, let us proceed to the rest.

->How the "animal" in us relates to the soul, and whether any life perishes.<-

<margin>Chapter 10</margin> The tenth chapter of the book teaches that those things proper to our "animal" nature also belong to us in a certain way. Likewise, in the rational soul, there are virtues acquired through reason; in the "animal," there are virtues acquired through habit. Furthermore, the life granted to the body by the rational soul is not extinguished when the body is dissolved, but follows its soul much as light is seen to follow its candle. Numenius <note>A Neopythagorean philosopher who influenced Plotinus.</note> had felt the same.

->How the soul relates to the intellect, through which it always understands, although reason does not always notice it. Also concerning children and brutes.<-

<margin>Chapter 11</margin> After he has dismantled in the previous sections how we relate to the "animal" below us, now in the eleventh chapter he discusses how we relate to the intellect—that is, our higher reason. He says, therefore, that our intellect always acts within itself concerning divine things, and through perpetual intellection, it always gazes upon all intelligible things. Iamblichus <note>A later Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> asserts that this was an Egyptian discovery. Therefore, the same act occurs even in children. I believe Plotinus accepted the idea that "the angels of the little ones always see the face of the heavenly Father" <note>A quote from Matthew 18:10; Ficino is linking Platonic "intellect" to Christian "guardian angels."</note>. For Ammonius and Origen were also accustomed to interpreting the Sacred Scriptures in the Platonic manner. 

However, he says that in children, the powers of the "animal" work most intensely due to the necessary labor of building and growing the body. Around these same powers and this same service, the imagination of the higher soul is mostly occupied; meanwhile, only the smallest sparks of reason flash out into these things, since they are turned toward opposite concerns. He adds that the act of reason, when free from these tasks, operates in the meantime around the intellect; for a power so effective cannot be entirely idle. Nevertheless, neither the act of the intellect regarding intelligible things, nor the act of reason regarding the intellect, is recognized by us at that time. This is because the imagination proper to the higher soul—by whose service awareness happens in us—is turned entirely toward the opposite direction. Therefore, it does not receive any "images of the intelligences" to reflect back to the eyes of reason like a mirror. It is only when they are so reflected that reason, and thus we ourselves, are accustomed to noticing the actions of intelligence and reason. 

They call this imagination in us "the medium." For it is the middle point between our rational and irrational parts, and like a medium, it receives images from both sides. Sometimes he also calls reason "the medium," for it is the middle of the soul. But the imagination is the medium of the "aggregate"—that is, when we form something joined from the human and the animal. Awareness usually happens through these two mediums. For the imagination reflects images, as it were, and reason sagaciously apprehends that reflection. 

Accordingly, after the question about children, he rightly inquires about "brutes" (animals), as if they were matters nearly similar in appearance. He argues that wherever life is so united to a body that a single common "animal" existence results from them, there must also be present a life remaining in itself. By the virtue of this higher life, the other life (the animation of the body) is supplied and continually preserved, just as motion is suggested by a mover and light is always supplied by a source of light; for in every genus, the imperfect continually depends on the perfect. In less clever animals, therefore, life is infused by the soul of the [celestial] sphere, just as the power of nature is infused into plants. But in more perfect beasts that display something of reason, life is supplied not only by the rational soul of the sphere, but by another rational soul that is even more closely related. When this soul has "departed" from the intelligible world and its logical thought and affection, and has thus declined and lost its wordless reason, it is said to be adapted now to the life of the animal...

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...of which the second is made from the first, and is its image: but the first subsists in itself, while the second is inherent in the body. The first is a certain whole within itself; the second becomes a part of a composite—namely, of this **living creature** <note>original: "animalis huius" — referring to the 'animal' or the composite of body and lower soul</note>—which is subject to that first life. No one doubts that there is a certain life inherent in the body; but reason proves that another life presides over this one, subsisting in itself, suggesting that life in a dependent thing, being imperfect, depends on a perfect life. In this same way, the intellect situated in the soul flows from the Intellect flourishing in itself, and the good in the intellect flows from the Good itself existing in itself. Furthermore, the intellectual good is not only created by the Good itself (which is simple), but is also preserved by it and is not separated from it. Similarly, the intelligence infused into the soul is both created and preserved by the Pure Intellect, and is not disjoined from it. By the same reasoning, the life or soul bound to the body is produced and preserved by the Life—that is, the soul—which always remains in itself and stays in contact with it. Just as a ray of the sun is continuous with its own sun at one end, but at the other end touches and gives form to a subject. For this reason, the first life is like a certain **form** of the living creature; but the second is the form of a natural body endowed with organs <note>original: "naturalis instrumentis præditi" — a reference to Aristotle's definition of the soul in *De Anima*</note> suited for the use of the living creature. Aristotle also says this: after he called the soul a form or **act** <note>original: "actum" — technical term for the realization or functioning of a potential</note>, he added that the intellectual soul is an act in one sense, and the other life is an act in another. But to return to our own points: Plotinus, having proposed this distinction, attributes sensation accompanied by passion <note>meaning physical or emotional suffering/reaction</note> to the living creature, but assigns to the soul a sensation free from passion; again, he assigns to that same soul the discourses of reason, whether they incline toward the senses or rise toward the intellect. The remaining points of this chapter will be clear to anyone who considers them diligently.

->*The rational soul is coupled through its intellect to the divine mind, and through that to God; thus, the irrational life is also linked to the rational soul. Moreover, the intellect is both personal and universal.*<-

**VIII** The eighth chapter investigates how the soul relates to all things, both those above it and those below it; but first, how it relates to the Divine Intellect, the father of rational souls, which presides over the soul almost as the soul presides over the living creature. Know, however, that the **One** itself, or the **Good** itself—which is the Highest God—has no "respect" <note>original: "respectum" — in this context, a relation or looking toward something else</note>. But the Intellect, which in Plotinus is the Son of the Good, has two "respects": the first insofar as it comes from the One, and thus is itself one; the second insofar as it exists in itself, and so it branches out into a multitude of **Ideas** <note>the divine archetypes or blueprints of all things</note>, all of which it nevertheless possesses and beholds simultaneously in a single act. The soul then has three respects. From the Intellect, it has the power of knowing, but this very power, as it depends most closely on the Intellect, is also itself an intellect; it is always continuous with its father and, under his form and act, always understands all things simultaneously. However, as it is understood according to the nature of the soul, it now moves through time and discourses in succession from potentiality to act; this is called **reason** and **thought**, and thus it seems to hold the species of things as separate from one another. Finally, as it turns toward the living creature, it descends from the reasoning of universals to the imagination of particulars. Yet this "animal" life seems to undergo four respects. Insofar as it depends on the soul, like an image from a substance, it possesses imagination; insofar as it is something in itself, it branches into a multitude of senses. Insofar as it governs the body, it exercises vital power; insofar as it adheres to the body and becomes part of the living creature, it is rendered subject to passions. Therefore, this life is the form of the body; but the soul is rather the form of the living creature; and the Intellect is the form of the soul. God, in a certain way, is the form of the Intellect itself, and each lower step always sits and acts under the "act" of the higher step as if under its form. Furthermore, the Divine Intellect itself is called "common" <note>universal</note> insofar as it is indivisible and entirely everywhere, and "personal" <note>own</note> insofar as it is received by individual souls, each in its own unique way. From this, different modes of reasoning follow in different souls, as well as different modes of imagining. But no one would say that the intellect which is already a certain form in the soul—not only presiding but also implanted—is common. Truly, many eyes reflect many souls; many visual rays naturally implanted in the eyes represent the various intellects naturally implanted in souls; but the one common light of the sun, present everywhere, represents the Divine Intellect, the father of souls and intellects. Finally, the one light of the sun existing in the Sun itself shows us the **Good** itself, the father of the Mind. Therefore, although the intellects inborn in souls are not one single intellect, they are nonetheless "one"—that is, one according to their intellectual being—rendered "actually understanding" by the one light of that Mind. In that light, as if in a common form and object, they are one, even though they are many according to the multitude of souls. Just as visual rays or sights are numbered according to the number of eyes and are not one, yet they are one as they run together in a single light; they would seem most of all to be one if they existed in themselves, freed from the eyes, just as intellectual souls remain independent when released from bodies. This opinion of Plato and Plotinus seems to be adapted to Aristotle and Theophrastus by Themistius; Avicenna and Algazel also follow it. Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle</note>, however, agrees with Plotinus in that he attributes many intellects to us; but he disagrees in asserting that these many are mortal. Averroes, on the other hand, agrees with Plotinus in asserting that every intellect is immortal, but disagrees by assigning only one single intellect to us all. You, however, should take the **number** of human intellects from Alexander, but from Averroes take the **immortal gift** of all intelligence, and you will have the complete opinion of our Plotinus. Furthermore, know that regarding the nature of the intellect, Plotinus is to be believed above all others; his life, deeds, and writings testify that he always lived by the intellect. I wish to advise you of this now, so that Alexander and Averroes do not disturb you. He finally concludes that **we**—that is, the human being—are properly the soul using rational discourse, whether it discourses through universals or through individuals. Those things which are above or below reason are "ours": the higher things because we always depend on them, and the lower things because they depend on us. He adds in the manner of Plato that the intellectual nature, both presiding over us and residing within us, is indivisible; but the life diffused as far as the body is said to be divisible. For although it is one and whole in every member, it is nonetheless directed toward different things and vivifies different parts in different ways. In many members, or in many "vehicles" <note>the 'spirit-body' that carries the soul between incarnations</note> at once, or in bodies to be vivified in succession, the rational soul does not create a single entity out of itself and the body, but rather out of the body and a certain life granted to it, which is like a certain image of the soul itself. Finally, he teaches that one power of the soul depends on another in succession.

->*The cause of sinning is in the irrational soul and in our animal nature; but in the soul, it is consent. Likewise, the rational circuit is a middle point between rest and straight motion. Again, how intelligence and reason relate to each other and to the imagination. Also, the allegory of Adam and Eve.*<-

**IX** The previous distinctions teach us in the ninth chapter that the beginning of sins is in the living creature, but the middle point is in the very imagination of the higher soul: namely, because it obeys the promptings of the living creature before reason has clearly judged whether something should be pursued or fled. Hence the **inner man** complains about the **outer man**:

# ON BOOK I OF THE FIRST ENNEAD

"I feel another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind, and leading me captive." <note>original: "Sentio aliam legem in membris meis..." — a reference to St. Paul's Letter to the Romans 7:23, illustrating the conflict between physical desires and spiritual reason</note> But even reason itself, since it is occupied with things to be done, should have long ago trained its imagination in such a way that it would hasten less rashly, and should have tamed the **animal** <term>animal: in this context, the "animal" refers to the composite of the physical body and the irrational soul, the part of us governed by instinct and sensation</term>. Reason should have first directed and formed itself toward the intellect; for that intellect certainly does not involve itself in the individual details of actions, and therefore it is entirely far from fault. But we—that is, those of us defined by rational power and action—sometimes reach the **intelligible and ideal species** <note>These are the "Forms" or "Ideas," the eternal blueprints of all things in the divine mind</note> of things, which exist first in the divine mind and then in our own; yet for the most part, we rarely rise up to them. At those times, they exist in our reason only as a potential, but in both the divine and our higher mind, they are always "in act" <note>meaning they are always being actively thought and realized</note>. He said that the "discussions of reason" <note>original: "rationis discursus" — discursive reasoning, the step-by-step process of logical thought</note> are most characteristic of us, that is, of the soul. This is because the soul is the middle point between divine things, which always remain still, and natural things, which move away from themselves in a straight line or "fall." Thus, the soul rightly possesses a circular, discursive motion, being the proper midpoint between straight motion and stillness.

Intelligence is also said to belong to the soul, not so much because it is its primary nature, but because the soul understands without the instrument of the body. In this way, the soul also reasons discursively without the body. But there is at least this difference: although discursive argument does not happen through a bodily instrument, it almost always holds some "images" of sensible things before its eyes. For motion naturally slides toward such things. **Intelligence**, however, uses neither the instruments of the body nor looks at such images. Indeed, when reason turns itself entirely toward the intellect, it gazes upon universals without the images of particulars. But we discuss these things more at length in our *Theology* <note>Marsilio Ficino's *Platonic Theology*, his major work harmonizing Plato with Christianity</note>. While he uses the words of Aristotle here, he signifies that Aristotle does not differ from Plato in these matters. He adds that the discourse of reason, the intellect, and the imagination are active and do not touch the "passions" <note>physical disturbances or emotions</note> of the body, but rather that certain images of those passions are handled by a sense of their own—that is, the "primary imagination."

Likewise, he says that reason, or thought, is a certain act of intelligence. For true thought is a certain intelligence explained more broadly: sometimes it touches the intellect and gazes upon universal species; sometimes, turning toward the imagination and through it toward the animal, it diverts universal species down to particulars; and sometimes, comparing the former with the latter, it discerns and judges where they agree or disagree. And if it begins from the intellect and departs from there, it then descends from universals to individuals by "composing." But if it takes its occasion from the imagination and rises higher, it ascends from individuals to universals by "resolving." Finally, you will observe this order in the soul: remember that it holds species in the **mind** that are both universal and stable; but in **reason**, the species are indeed universal, but in a way mobile; while in the **imagination**, they are already particular and changeable. He concludes that the passions, disturbances, and causes of sin properly reside in the **animal**; but in the **soul**, there is the observation of these things and often a certain consent to them.

Now, notice in Plotinus's words a **Mosaic allegory** <note>Ficino is linking Plotinus's philosophy to the story of Adam and Eve in the Book of Moses (Genesis)</note>: namely, two persons—the man himself, like **Adam**, and the human "animal" drawn from him and degenerating, like **Eve**. Add to this that she is drawn from the "sleeping soul." For the soul propagates this "animal" part from itself when it slides down toward natural things from its former watchfulness near God; forgetting divine things, it now sleeps and dreams. And so, it then generates the corporeal life as if it were Eve. Consider her as the one who sins first, and then the man as the one who consents; but the **intellect** is like an angel presiding over him, soon rebuking him and given over to the angel. And finally, consider "two in one flesh," that is, two souls, as it were, in the same body. This is how Plotinus, Origen, and Ammonius understood Moses; let us proceed to the rest.

## X
->How the "animal" in us relates to the soul, and whether any life perishes.<-

The tenth chapter of the book teaches that the things proper to our "animal" nature also belong to us in a certain way. Likewise, that in the rational soul there are virtues sought through reason, while in the animal there are virtues acquired through habit. Again, that the life granted to the body by the rational soul is not extinguished when the body is dissolved, but follows its own soul almost exactly as light is seen to follow its candle. Numenius <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who influenced Neoplatonism</note> had felt the same.

->How the soul relates to the intellect, through which it always understands, even if reason does not always notice it. Likewise concerning children and beasts.<-

## XI
After discussing in the previous sections how we relate to the animal which is below us, he now discusses in the eleventh chapter how we relate to the **intellect**, which is above our reason. He says, therefore, that our intellect always acts within itself regarding divine things, and by perpetual intellection always contemplates all "intelligibles" <note>things that can be understood by the mind rather than sensed</note>; Iamblichus asserts that this was an Egyptian discovery. For this reason, the same thing happens even in children. I believe Plotinus accepted the saying: "The angels of the little ones always see the face of the heavenly Father." <note>A reference to Matthew 18:10</note> For both Ammonius and Origen were accustomed to interpreting the sacred scriptures in the Platonic manner. 

However, he says: in children, the powers of the "animal" operate most intensely because of the necessary work of growing the body, and the imagination of the higher soul is very much occupied with these same powers and this service. Only the smallest sparks of reason flash out in them, as they are turned toward opposite things. He adds that the act of reason, when vacant from these things, meanwhile operates around the intellect; for a power so effective cannot be entirely idle. Nevertheless, neither the act of the intellect regarding intelligible things, nor the act of reason regarding the intellect, is recognized by us then. This is because the **imagination** proper to the higher soul—by whose service "noticing" occurs in us—is turned completely in the opposite direction; it does not receive any images of the intelligences to reflect them, like a mirror, to the eyes of reason. It is by these reflected images that reason is accustomed, and therefore we are accustomed, to notice the actions of the intelligence and reason. 

They call this imagination in us the "middle." For it is a middle between our rational and irrational parts, and as a middle, it receives images from both sides. Sometimes he also calls **reason** the "middle," for it is the midpoint of the soul. But imagination is the "middle of the composite" <note>the 'composite' of soul and body</note>, namely when we imagine something gathered from the human "animal." Through these two "middles," noticing usually occurs. For imagination, as it were, reflects the images, and reason shrewdly grasps those reflections. Consequently, after the question about children, he rightly inquires about beasts, as if about things that appear nearly similar. He certainly wants it to be that wherever there is life so united to a body that one common "animal existence" results from it and the body, there must also be present a life remaining in itself. By the power of this life, another life—a kind of "vivification"—is supplied and continually preserved, just as motion is suggested by a mover, and light is always suggested by a source of light; for in every kind, the imperfect continuously depends on the perfect. 

In the less "shrewd" beasts, therefore, life is infused from the sphere of the soul itself, just as plants are aided by nature. But in the "more perfect" beasts, which show some glimmer of reason, life is supplied not just from the rational sphere of the soul, but from another more nearby rational life. This soul, when it has departed from the "words" and thoughts of the intelligible world—as if it had failed and lost much of its reason—is then said to be adapted to a less rational animal life...

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

of which the second is made from the first and is its image; but the first is self-subsisting, while the second is inherent in the body. Let the first be a whole thing in itself, and the second be a part of a composite—namely, of this **living creature** <term>living creature: the 'animal,' the combination of the physical body and the lower soul</term> which is subject to that first life. No one doubts that there is a certain life inherent in the body; but reason proves that another life presides over this one, subsisting in itself, showing that a life lying in another thing depends upon a perfect life, just as an imperfect thing depends on a perfect one. In this way, the intellect situated in the soul flows from the intellect flourishing in itself, and the good in the intellect flows from the Good consisting in itself. Furthermore, the intellectual good is not only made by the Good itself, but is also preserved by it and not severed from it. Similarly, the intelligence infused into the soul is both made and preserved by the pure Intellect and is not disjoined from it. By the same reasoning, the life or soul enslaved to the body is produced and preserved by the life—that is, the soul—that always remains in itself, and it remains contiguous to it. Just as a ray of the sun is on one hand continuous with its own sun, and on the other hand touches and forms its subject. Therefore, the first life is like a certain form of the living creature; but the second is the form of a natural body endowed with instruments <note>original: "instrumentis præditi" — meaning organs or physical tools of the body</note> adapted for the use of the living creature. This is also what Aristotle says; and after he called the soul the "form" or **act** <term>act: 'entelechy' or actualization; the state of being fully realized</term>, he added that the intellectual soul is an "act" in one way, and another soul is an "act" in a different way. But to return to our own points: Plotinus, having proposed this distinction, attributes sensation accompanied by **passion** <term>passion: here meaning a physical reaction or being 'acted upon' by external stimuli</term> to the living creature; but he assigns to the soul a sensation that is free from passion. Again, he assigns the **discussions of reason** <note>discursive reasoning, the step-by-step logic used by humans</note> to the same soul, whether they incline toward sensation or rise toward the intellect. The remaining points of this chapter will be clear to anyone considering them diligently for themselves.

->*The rational soul is joined through its intellect to the divine mind, and through that to God; likewise, the irrational life is connected to the rational soul. The intellect is both personal and common.*<-

<margin>VIII</margin> The eighth chapter inquires how the soul relates to all things both above and below it. But first, it asks how it relates to the divine Intellect, the father of rational souls, which presides over the soul almost in the same way the soul presides over the living creature. Know, however, that the One itself, or the Good itself—which is the most high God—has no **respects** <note>original: "respectum" — in this philosophical context, a 'respect' is a relational perspective or way of looking at something. God is absolute and has no such relations</note>. However, the Intellect, which in Plotinus's view is the son of the Good, has two respects: first, insofar as it is from the One, and thus it is itself "one"; second, insofar as it exists in itself, and thus it is divided into a multitude of **Ideas** <note>The eternal archetypes or blueprints of all things</note>. Yet it possesses and contemplates all these simultaneously in a single act. The soul, then, has three respects. For from the Intellect it has the power of knowing; but this very power, as it depends most closely on the Intellect, is itself "intellect" and is always continuous with its father, and under his form and act, it always understands all things simultaneously. However, insofar as it is taken according to the nature of the soul, it now runs through a sequence from potentiality to act in a certain amount of time; and it is called "reason" and "thought," and thus it seems to have the species of things separated from one another. Finally, as it turns toward the living creature, it descends from the logic of universals to the imagination of particulars. 

But this life of the living creature seems to undergo four respects. For insofar as it depends on the soul, like an image from a substance, it has imagination; insofar as it is something in itself, it is derived into a multitude of senses. Insofar as it rules the body, it exercises vital power; insofar as it adheres to the body and becomes the passion of the living creature, it is rendered subject to passions. Therefore, this life is the form of the body; but the soul is rather the form of the living creature; and the Intellect is the form of the soul. God, in a certain way, is the form of the Intellect itself, and always in succession an inferior grade exists and acts under the act of a superior grade, as if under its form. Furthermore, the divine Intellect itself is called "common" insofar as it is itself indivisible and entirely everywhere, and "personal" insofar as it is received by individual souls in their own individual ways. From this, different ways of reasoning follow in different souls, and also different ways of imagining. 

But no one would say that the intellect which is already a certain form in the soul—not only presiding but also implanted—is "common." Truly, many eyes reflect many souls; moreover, many visual rays naturally implanted in the eyes represent the various intellects naturally implanted in souls. But the one common light of the sun, present everywhere, represents the divine Intellect, the father of souls and intellects. Finally, the one light of the Sun, consisting in the Sun itself, shows us the Good itself, the father of the mind. Therefore, although the intellects inborn in souls are not one intellect, they are nevertheless "one thing"—that is, one according to their intellectual being, rendered "understanding in act" by the one light of that higher mind. In that light, as if in a common form and object, they are one, even though they are many according to the multitude of souls. Just as visual rays or sights are numbered according to the number of eyes and are not one, yet they are one as they run together in one light; they would seem most of all to be one if they existed in themselves, released from eyes, just as intellectual souls remain when absolute from bodies. 

Themistius <note>A 4th-century commentator on Aristotle</note> seems to adapt this opinion of Plato and Plotinus to Aristotle and Theophrastus, and Avicenna and Algazeles follow it. Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle</note>, however, agrees with Plotinus in this: that he asserts these "many" are mortal. But Averroes agrees with Plotinus in asserting that every intellect is immortal; yet he disagrees when he assigns only a single one to us. But you should take the number of the human intellect from Alexander, and the immortal gift of all intelligence from Averroes, and you will have the complete opinion of our Plotinus. Furthermore, know that regarding the nature of the intellect, one must believe Plotinus most of all, whom his life, deeds, and writings testify to have always lived by the intellect. But I want to have warned you of this now, so that Alexander and Averroes do not disturb you. He concludes at last that "we"—that is, the human being—are properly the soul using rational discourse, whether it discourses through universals or through individuals; but those things which are above or below reason are "ours." The former because we always depend on them; the latter because they themselves depend on us. He adds, in the manner of Plato, that the intellectual nature—both the one presiding over us and the one residing within—is indivisible; but the life diffused as far as the body is said to be divisible. Because although it is one and whole in any member, it is nevertheless affected toward different things and vivifies different things in various ways; and in many things—whether members, or **vehicles** <note>original: "vehiculisne" — the 'astral body' or subtle spirit that carries the soul</note>, or bodies to be vivified in succession—the rational soul does not create one thing out of itself and the body, but out of the body and a certain life granted to it, as if by a certain image of the soul itself. Finally, he teaches that one power of the soul depends on another in succession.

->*The cause of sinning is in the irrational soul and our animal nature; but in the soul itself, it is consent. Likewise, the rational circuit is the middle point between rest and straight-line motion. Again, how intelligence and reason relate to each other, and to the imagination. Likewise, the allegory of Adam and Eve.*<-

### ON BOOK I OF THE FIRST ENNEAD

"I feel another law in my members resisting the law of my mind, and leading me captive." <note>original: "Sentio aliā lēge in mēbris meis repugnantē legi mētis meæ..." Ficino is quoting the Latin Vulgate translation of Romans 7:23, aligning Plotinus's philosophy with the words of St. Paul.</note> But even reason itself, since it is involved in practical affairs, should have trained its own imagination long ago to be less impulsive and to tame the "animal" part of us. Reason should have directed and formed itself toward the **intellect** first. This intellect does not involve itself in the specific details of what is done, and therefore it is entirely free from blame. But we—defined through our rational power and action—sometimes reach the intelligible and ideal principles and the "forms" of things, which exist first in the Divine Mind and then in our own. Most of the time, however, we do not rise up to them. In our reason, these forms exist as potential; but in both the Divine Mind and our higher mind, they are always "in act" <term>in act: a philosophical term meaning fully realized or currently functioning, rather than just being a dormant potential</term>. Plotinus said that discursive reasoning <term>discursive reasoning: the step-by-step process of logical thought, moving from one premise to another, rather than knowing something instantly</term> is most characteristic of us—that is, of the soul—because the soul sits in the middle between divine things (which always remain still) and natural things (which fall away from themselves in a straight motion). It is only right, then, that the soul has a circular movement of reasoning, which is the proper middle ground between straight motion and absolute stillness. **Intelligence** is also called characteristic of the soul, not so much because it belongs to its lower nature, but because the soul understands without using the body as a tool. In this way, the soul carries out its reasoning even without the body. But there is at least this difference: even if discursive reasoning and argumentation do not happen through a physical organ, they almost always keep images of sensory things before their eyes. For natural motion slips from one thing to another; but the intellect neither uses physical tools nor looks at such images. Indeed, when reason turns itself entirely toward the intellect, it gazes upon universals <note>original: "vniuersalia" — general concepts like 'Beauty' or 'Justice' rather than specific beautiful things</note> without any images of individual things. I discuss this more extensively in my own *Theology*. By using Aristotle's words here, Plotinus signifies that Aristotle does not differ from Plato on these points. He adds that the movement of reason, the intellect, and the imagination are all active here and do not touch the physical sufferings of the body, but rather deal with certain "images" of those sufferings through their own internal sense—that is, the primary imagination. Likewise, reason (or thought) is a certain act of intelligence. For true thought is simply intelligence expanded further: at one moment, reaching toward the intellect, it gazes at universal forms; at another, turning toward the imagination, it passes those universal forms down through the imagination to the "animal" level until they reach individual things. At other times, it compares the two, judging and discerning how they agree or disagree. If it begins from the intellect and moves outward, it descends from universals to individuals by "composing." But if it takes its start from the imagination and rises higher, it ascends from individuals to universals by "resolving." Finally, you should observe this order in the soul: remember that it holds forms in the higher Mind that are both universal and stable. In **reason**, however, the forms are universal but "mobile" (moving through logic). In the **imagination**, they are already individual and changeable. He concludes that passions, disturbances, and the causes of sin reside properly in the "animal" <term>animal: the 'living creature' composed of the body and the lower animating power</term>; but in the soul itself, there is only an awareness of these things and, often, a kind of consent.

Observe the **Mosaic allegory** <note>Ficino often sought to harmonize Plato and Plotinus with the Bible, here connecting Greek philosophy with the Book of Genesis</note> in Plotinus's words: specifically, the two personas, where the man himself is like **Adam**, and the human "animal" drawn from him and falling away is like **Eve**. Add to this that Eve is drawn from the soul while it "sleeps." For the soul propagates this lower life from itself when it falls from its original wakefulness in God toward natural things; forgetting divine things, it now sleeps and dreams. And so, it generates the corporeal life as "Eve." Consider her as the first to sin, and Adam as the one who luego consents; but the intellect is like a presiding angel, rebuking him and given to him as a guide. Finally, consider two things in the flesh—that is, as if there were two souls in the same body. This is how Plotinus, Origen, and Ammonius understood Moses. Let us proceed to the rest.

<margin>How the animal in us relates to the soul, and whether any life perishes.</margin>

->**Chapter ten** of the book teaches that the things belonging to our "animal" side also belong to us in a certain way. Also, that there are virtues in the rational soul sought through reason, and virtues in the animal side acquired through habit. Again, the life granted to the body by the rational soul is not extinguished when the body is dissolved, but follows its soul almost as light is seen to follow a candle. Numenius <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who influenced Neoplatonism</note> felt the same.<-

->**How the soul relates to the intellect, through which it always understands, even if reason does not always notice it. Also regarding children and brute animals.**<-

**XI.** After discussing in the previous sections how we relate to the "animal" below us, Plotinus now discusses in the eleventh chapter how we relate to the **intellect** above us—that is, superior to reason. He says that our intellect is always acting within itself concerning divine things, and through perpetual understanding, it always gazes at all intelligible things. Iamblichus <note>A later Neoplatonist who emphasized Egyptian wisdom</note> asserts that this was an Egyptian discovery. Therefore, it acts in children as well. I believe Plotinus accepted the idea: "The angels of the little ones always see the face of the heavenly Father." <note>A quote from Matthew 18:10, suggesting children have a direct spiritual connection</note> For Ammonius and Origen used to interpret Holy Scripture in the Platonic manner. He says, however, that in children, the powers of the "animal" work most intensely because of the necessary task of building and growing the physical body. Around these same powers, the imagination of the higher soul is very occupied with this service. Only tiny sparks of reason flash out in them, as they are turned toward opposite things. He adds that the act of reason, when free from these tasks, operates meanwhile around the intellect, since such an effective power cannot be completely idle. However, we do not recognize the act of the intellect regarding intelligible things, nor the act of reason regarding the intellect, because the **imagination**—which belongs to the higher soul and is the tool through which awareness happens in us—is turned entirely in the opposite direction. It does not receive any images from the intellect to reflect them, like a mirror, to the eyes of reason. When they are reflected, reason is accustomed to noticing them, and thus we notice the actions of intelligence and reason. They call this imagination in us the "middle." It is the bridge between our rational and irrational parts, and as a bridge, it receives images from both sides. Sometimes he calls reason the "middle" because it is the center of the soul. But imagination is the "middle of the composite" <note>the 'composite' is the human being viewed as a mix of body and soul</note>, specifically when we imagine something as a combination of man and animal. Awareness usually happens through these two "middles." For imagination reflects the images, and reason cleverly catches those reflections. Therefore, after the question about children, he rightly inquires about **brute animals**, as they are nearly similar cases. He maintains that wherever life is so united to a body that a single "common animal" results, there must also be a life remaining in itself, by whose power the other life is supplied as a kind of "living-force" <note>original: "viuificatio"</note> and is continually preserved. Just as motion is suggested by a motor, and light is always suggested by a source of light; for in every category, the imperfect continually depends on the perfect. In less clever animals, he thinks life is infused from the "sphere of the soul" <note>the World Soul</note>, just as in plants. But in more "perfect" beasts that show a bit of reason, life is supplied not just by the rational sphere, but by another rational soul that is closer. This soul, when it has moved away from the intelligible world and its logical thought and focus, and has thus fallen away and lost much of its reason, is then said to be adapted to the life of the animal...

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

<meta>catchword: PLO</meta>

...divine <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely continuing from "divine soul" on the previous page.</note>, although it must be provided to the rational part, it is said in the meantime to be present. Yet, it is not "present" in the sense that it merely provides life, nor is it "present" in the usual way: for it does not perform the customary duty of reason there <note>i.e., in the lower state</note>, even though it performs it in the higher realms of intelligence. Furthermore, the substance of the rational soul itself stands on its own and is not a part of the "composite" <term>composite: the human being understood as a mixture of soul and physical body</term>. This last point pleased Proclus, and before him Porphyry, who denied that the rational soul of a human becomes the specific soul of a beast, though he granted that the souls of clever animals have something of reason and live forever. Origen also attempted this same line of reasoning; namely, when he heard that demons frequently slip into humans and are sometimes sent into pigs, he dared to suggest that human souls are sent into animals, perhaps to be purified. But let those authors see to these matters themselves. One should notice, however, that Plotinus tempers his judgment here when he says: "If our souls are in beasts." Likewise where he says, "As it is said," specifically by the Egyptians. Again, when he adds, "Those which have sinned," as if to say the animal state is a place of purgatory. Finally, he denies that the soul becomes the specific "form" of the beast or a part of the composite. We will correct this opinion in the following sections. Indeed, we have declared how these Platonic sayings should be purified in the books of our *Theology* <note>original: "Theologiæ nostræ," referring to Ficino's major work, the *Platonic Theology*</note>, especially in the final volumes.

->In the rational soul there is strictly neither sin nor punishment; rather, these exist in the irrational life, which is the image of the soul. When the soul departs from here, although this life is no longer an image, it is still a certain vital activity rooted within the soul.<-

**Chapter XII** moves through doubts regarding these sayings and solves them by stating that in the soul’s own essence there is neither sin nor punishment, because it is a "simple form" standing in itself, never falling from its own state. Rather, these exist in the life flowing from the soul, and strictly in the "animal" <note>In this context, "animal" refers to the living creature formed by the union of body and the lower vital power</note>, which is composed of this life and the body. He says in one place that the soul "sins," and in another that it does not. It "sins" in the sense that the intention previously turned toward higher things is somewhat relaxed; it "does not sin" in the sense that it neither loses its natural qualities nor admits foreign ones within itself. Then he declares how the generation of the "animal" occurs: namely, when a certain life reflects from the soul into a body already prepared in a specific condition. This is a natural process, not a sin, and the soul does not strictly "fall" in this way, but rather gives its consent and nourishment. Furthermore, this life—which is both an activity and a certain image of the soul—does not perish when the soul departs, insofar as it is an activity of the soul; rather, it simply ceases to be an "image." It is just as if an image is formed in a mirror from a face; when the face departs, a certain activity remains in the face—a shining vigor capable of producing the image—but the image itself in the mirror does not remain. This activity of the soul stops being an "image" when the prepared body is missing for the image to result in, and the soul turns entirely toward the intelligible world. Yet such an activity does not cease insofar as it is the vigor of life, just as when a hand is cut off, the life-giving activity itself does not cease; it is the same activity that would rule the hand again if it were restored, as is seen in hair that grows back. Remember that Numenius and Plotinus thought that no life ever perishes, because life is a certain splendor of eternity—that is, of the Primary Intelligence—and the unbreakable bond of the universe.

->The rational soul reasons through itself, not through the instrument of the body. It also understands through its own intellect; yet it also understands through the "common" intellect, which is like a form for every individual intellect.<-

**Chapter XIII** explains what was nearly the last point proposed in the inquiry: namely, what it is that considers these matters in the present. He asserts that it is not some "composite" thing that considers these through the soul as if the soul were merely a part, but the soul itself, existing in itself, that meditates on such things. Therefore, the soul is not changed even when the body changes, but its motion is its own, an activity of its essential life, or a vital and perennial act of its essence. He adds: just as rational consideration is our own (belonging to the soul and not carried out through the body), so understanding is the soul's own. For the soul is "intellectual," so much so that intelligence in the soul is life, the very summit of the soul's life. This intelligence is a part of us and acts upon us—that is, upon the reason most characteristic of us—just as the "common intellect" <term>common intellect: the universal Divine Mind or Logos that illuminates all individual minds</term> acts upon our own intellect. Note here that life in all things is almost the final splendor of the Mind; but the highest Mind is the supreme degree of life. Hence that prophetic saying:
> "Give me understanding, and I shall live." <note>original: "Intellectum da mihi, & viuam." Ficino quotes Psalm 118:144 from the Latin Vulgate.</note>
He adds that the soul understands both through its own intellect and through the common and divine intellect. Reason strives toward our intellect, and our intellect strives toward the divine. Both are part of us, but in different ways. Our own intellect is part of us because it is, in a way, the "peak" of the soul. The divine intellect seems to be a part of us because our intellect is subject to the divine as matter is to form; through this form, which is common to all, individual intellects—though not literally one—are yet a certain "one." Thus, the divine seems to be a part of us as a "form"—a form, I say, providing to our intellects their very intellectual being and their actual power of understanding. To this point tends that prophetic saying:
> "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance." <note>original: "Dominus pars hereditatis meæ." From Psalm 15:5 in the Vulgate.</note>
Whatever we have omitted in this Commentary can be clear to one who considers it diligently; some parts will be explained more broadly in the following sections, and some we have already explained in our *Theology* and in our arguments on all of Plato's works. Furthermore, concerning how the intellect is "ours," and whether it is a part of us or not, you will learn in the third book of the fifth *Ennead*.

<summary>Ficino explains that the rational soul remains pure and separate from the body's sins, using the analogy of a face and its mirror image to show how life reflects into the body without the soul itself falling. He also discusses how the human mind is illuminated by a "common" divine intellect, linking Platonic philosophy with Biblical scripture.</summary>

### ON WHAT IS THE ANIMAL, AND WHAT IS MAN.
### What is the animal, what is the man.

---

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial letter 'H' used for the Greek text. The background of the letter features a landscape with a castle or fortress on a distant hill, a tree on the left, and a figure seated on a rock in the foreground.</image-desc>

<margin>A</margin> PLEASURES and pains, fears and boldness, desires and aversions and physical suffering—to whom would these belong? Would they belong to the soul, or to the soul making use of a body, or to some third thing composed of both? <note>original: "τρίτου τινὸς ἐξ ἀμφοῖν". Plotinus is investigating whether our emotions belong to our spiritual essence (soul) or our physical presence.</note>

<margin>B</margin> This third thing can be understood in two ways: either it is the mixture itself, <margin>* or another</margin> or it is something different arising from that mixture. In the same way, we must ask about the things that arise from these <term>passions: in ancient philosophy, "passions" (pathē) refer to any way the soul or body is "acted upon" by external forces, including emotions and sensations</term>—namely, our actions and our opinions. Furthermore, we must investigate whether thought and opinion <margin>* themselves</margin> belong to the same thing that experiences the passions, or if some belong to one and some to the other. We must also consider how and to whom intellectual perceptions belong. And indeed, what is this very thing that conducts the investigation, making the inquiry and the judgment concerning these matters? And before this: to what does "sensing" belong? For it is proper to begin from there, <margin>C</margin> since passions are either certain types of sensations or at least do not occur without sensation.

FIRST, we must consider the soul: whether the soul is one thing and "being a soul" <note>original: "ψυχῇ εἶναι" (the essence of the soul)</note> is another. For if this were so, the soul would be something composite. <margin>* even if</margin> And it would not then be strange to accept that the soul itself receives such passions—provided that the argument holds—and possesses habits and dispositions, both better and worse. But if "soul" and "being a soul" are the same, the soul would be a certain "form" <term>form: the essential nature or "blueprint" of a thing that gives it identity</term> that does not receive all these activities. Rather, it would provide these activities to something else, while having its own activity innate within itself, whatever the argument may reveal it to be. <margin>D</margin> In this way, it would be true to say that the soul is immortal, if indeed that which is immortal and incorruptible must also be "impassible" <note>original: "ἀπαθές" (incapable of being affected or suffering change from the outside)</note>—giving something of itself to another, but receiving nothing from elsewhere, or only as much as it possesses from the beings prior to it, from which it is not cut off. For what could such a thing fear, being closed off to everything from the outside? <margin>* that thing</margin> Let that thing feel fear <margin>* which</margin> which is capable of suffering. Nor can such a soul be "bold," for boldness belongs to those for whom fearsome things are not yet present.

<column-break/>

<margin>Whether the disturbances, senses, opinions, and intelligence belong to the soul alone, to intelligence, or to the composite, etc.</margin>

<margin>A</margin> PLEASURES and pains, fears also, and boldness, desires and aversions, and torture—whose are they? Are they of the soul alone? Or rather of the soul using a body? Or of some third thing composed of them? <margin>B</margin> This can be taken in two ways: For either it is the mixture itself, or the mixing; or it is something else proceeding from that very mixture. Likewise concerning those things which are made from these passions, and are acted upon, and are thought. Again, it must be asked concerning thought and opinion, whether they belong to the same things as the passions: or do some behave in this way, while others behave differently? Furthermore, one must investigate intelligence—to whom it belongs, and in what manner it behaves. And indeed, regarding this very thing which considers and carries out the inquiry and judgment about these matters, what might it be? And first of all, to whom does sensing <margin>C</margin> chiefly belong? For from here it seems we must begin: since the passions themselves are either certain senses, or at least they do not occur without sense.

<margin>If the soul is not a simple form existing in itself, it receives passions: if however it is such a form, it does not receive them.</margin>

FIRST, however, we must think about the soul, whether the soul is indeed one thing, and "being a soul" <note>In Latin: "animae esse," referring to its essential definition or essence.</note> is another. For if it is another thing, the soul is something composite: and it will not be absurd for it to receive forms and other things, and for such passions to exist as part of it, provided that reason permits it, along with habits and affections both better and worse. But if the soul and "being a soul" are the same, the soul will certainly be a certain "form" that does not receive such actions as it brings upon another: but in itself <margin>D</margin> it has an action related to itself, whichever one reason shall demonstrate. For thus it will be true to say that it is immortal. Indeed, it is necessary that what is immortal and incorruptible is also impassible—imparting something of itself to another, but receiving nothing from another, except as much as it may have received from higher things, from which more excellent things it is by no means separated. Why then should such a thing fear, since it receives nothing from external things? Let that certainly fear, which [is capable of suffering] and also boldness, for those for whom things they should fear were not yet [present]. <note>The Latin text cuts off mid-sentence at the bottom of the column, mirroring the Greek.</note>

<summary>Plotinus begins his inquiry into the nature of the human being by asking whether emotions, sensations, and thoughts belong to the pure soul, the body, or a combination of both. He introduces the concept that the soul’s essential nature might be 'impassible'—meaning it cannot be changed or harmed by the physical world.</summary>

occur. Moreover, those desires which are satisfied through the body—namely, when the body is emptied or filled—do not belong to this essence <note>The "essence" here refers to the soul's pure, spiritual nature.</note>, but to another thing that is capable of being emptied and filled. But in what way will the soul desire through a mixture, if that which is essential always remains unmixed? Again, in what way will it seek to introduce something else into itself? For in doing so, it would strive not to be what it is. Suffering is also far removed from it. Indeed, by what reason and for what cause could pain and sadness be there? For that which is simple in essence is self-sufficient, remaining as it is in its own nature. Does it take pleasure in something newly arriving? Certainly not, not even if a good thing arrives. For what it is, it is always. Furthermore, it will not even sense things. Again, there will be no thought or opinion concerning it. For sensation is the perception either of a form or of a body that does not suffer. Thought and opinion, however, lean toward sensation. We must consider, in some way, whether we should grant the soul intelligence, and concerning pure pleasure, whether it happens to the soul only insofar as it remains alone.

<margin>*III. The Soul both lives in itself and gives life to the body; the whole is called the animal. Using it as an instrument, it is not subject to the same passions.*</margin>
NEVERTHELESS, it is necessary to place the soul in the body, whether it is said to be "above" this or "in" this, from which together with the soul the whole is called the "animal" <term>animal: from the Latin 'anima' (soul), referring here to the 'living being'—the composite of body and soul</term>. Therefore, using the body as an instrument, the soul is not forced to receive the passions <term>passions: from the Greek 'pathē,' meaning things the soul 'undergoes' or 'suffers,' such as emotions, pains, or physical sensations</term> of the body, just as craftsmen do not feel the "passions" of their tools. However, it perhaps necessarily experiences sensation, if indeed it must use the body as an instrument to recognize external impressions through the senses—just as using the eyes is the act of seeing. But the injuries that happen concerning sight will also happen to the soul; therefore, so too will distresses and pains, and everything that happens to the body. Consequently, desires arise when the soul, of course, takes care of its own instrument. But in what way will these passions enter from the body into the soul? A body can indeed hand over something of itself to another body; but how can a body do so to a soul? This would be as if one thing suffered because another suffered. For as long as one is the user and the other is that which is used, each is separate. Thus, he who grants that the soul is the "user" separates it. But before it is separated through philosophy, how did it stand? Was it perhaps mixed? But if it was mixed, was it a kind of blending and tempering, or was it diffused and spread through the body, or like a form not at all separate, or like a form touching it, such as a pilot <note>original: "gubernator". This is a famous Platonic image: the soul relates to the body like a captain relates to a ship.</note>? Or is one part truly separate, which is the "user," while another part is mixed, which is within the order of that which is used? In this way, philosophy might turn the soul back toward its role as the user, and lead the user away from the body, except as far as extreme necessity forces it, so that as much as possible, it remains as if it does not always use the body.

<margin>*IIII. The Soul is not mixed, nor is it in the body, but in another, namely God, and therefore it does not receive passions; but the composite does.*</margin>
LET US SUPPOSE therefore that the soul is mixed. But if it were mixed, that which is worse—the body—would become better, and that which is better—the soul—would become worse. The body would become better by participating in life, but the soul would become worse by participating in death and an irrational condition. But how could that which is in any way deprived of life receive sensation as an addition? On the contrary, the body itself, having obtained life, will receive sensation and its passions. This, then, will also desire; for this will also enjoy the things it desires, and will fear for itself. This also sometimes...

<column-break/>

<margin>* and that which is being filled belongs to the thing being filled</margin>
A ...and those desires which are satisfied through the body, of that which is being emptied and filled, belong to another, namely the thing being emptied or filled. <note>original: "καὶ τὸ πληρούμενον εἶναι ἢ πληρούμενον ὄντος"</note> For how can there be a mixture, if the essential remains unmixed? And how can there be an introduction of one into another? For then it would go out of itself so as to not be what it is. As for suffering, it is far off. And how could it be grieved, or over what? For that which is simple in essence is self-sufficient, remaining as it is in its own essence. It is pleased, indeed, by nothing added, even if a good is present, for what it is, it is always. And truly, it will not perceive, nor will there be thought or B opinion about it. For sensation is either the reception of a form, or of a body that does not suffer. Thought, certainly, and opinion lead toward sensation. But concerning the act of the intellect <note>original: "νοήσεως" (noēseōs)</note>, we must investigate how we might leave this to the soul. And also concerning pure pleasure, if it happens to the soul when it is alone.

<margin>* to be forced</margin>
C BUT if we must take the soul to be in the body, whether it belongs to this, or is in this, or comes from it, the whole is called the "animal." Therefore, using the body as an instrument, it is not forced <note>original: "ἀναγκάζεται"</note> to receive the passions that come through the body, just as craftsmen do not receive the passions of their tools. But perhaps it necessarily has sensation, if indeed it must use the instrument, knowing external impressions through the senses. Since using the eyes is seeing. But there are also injuries regarding sight. Thus there are also griefs, and suffering, and generally whatever happens regarding the whole body. Thus there is also desire when the soul seeks the care of the instrument. But how will the passions come from the body into the soul? For a body D will share its own state with another body; but how will a body share with a soul? For this would be like one thing suffering when another suffers. For as long as one is the user and the other the thing used, each is separate. At least, he who gives the soul as the "user" separates them. But before separating it through philosophy, how did it hold, was it mixed? But if it was mixed, what was the blending? Either as if it were woven through, or as if it were a separate form, or a form touching it like a pilot. <margin>* of that</margin> E Or is one part really that very thing <note>original: "ἐκείνας"</note>—I mean, one part is separate, which is the user, and the other part is mixed in some way and is itself in the order of that which is used. So that Philosophy might turn even that part toward the user, and lead the user away from that which it uses—except for what is absolute necessity—so as not to always use it.

F LET US SUPPOSE then that it is mixed. But if it is mixed, the worse part, the body, will be better; and the better part, the soul, will be worse. And the body is better, having shared in life; but the soul is worse, sharing in death and irrationality. How could that which is in any way deprived of life receive sensation as an addition? On the contrary, the body, having received life, would be that which shares in sensation and the passions arising from sensation. This, then, will also desire; for this will also enjoy what it desires, and will fear for...

<summary>This page explores the relationship between the soul and the body, arguing that while the soul uses the body as an instrument, it remains an unmixed essence that does not inherently suffer physical passions. Plotinus introduces the "animal" as the living composite of both and discusses how philosophy serves to separate the soul's identity from its bodily functions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation into the relationship between the soul and the body. Having established that the soul is an "essence" that does not naturally suffer, he now explores the mechanism of the "mixture" (*mixis*) between the two. He questions whether the soul is like light in the air or a shape in an iron tool, eventually arguing that emotions like pain and desire belong to the "living being" (the composite of soul and body) rather than the soul in its pure state.</meta>
