Plotinus is exploring how a non-physical soul can connect with a physical body without being corrupted by it.</note>, lest it be impossible—just as if one were to say a line is mixed with whiteness, one nature with another entirely different one. 

As for the idea of being "interwoven": does it make the interwoven parts feel the same? It is possible for the thing interwoven to remain unaffected. The soul might be interwoven and yet not suffer the body’s passions, just as light <note>A classic Neoplatonic analogy: light permeates the air but remains pure and distinct from it.</note> does not—especially if it is spread through the whole. This refers to the "animal" or the composite of soul and body, as opposed to the pure, transcendent soul.</note> that does so.

<column-break/>

He will not obtain pleasant things, and he will be dissolved. We must inquire concerning the manner of mixture, lest perhaps it be impossible: just as if someone said a line is mixed with whiteness, a nature very different from another.

But if the soul is said to be diffused and unfolding itself through the body, it does not follow from this that the soul suffers along with the body. For that which is diffused through another can remain unaffected. It can happen that the soul, insinuating itself into the body, does not receive its passions—just as light does, especially if it is stretched and extended everywhere through the whole. Therefore, it will not receive the passions of the body from the fact that it is diffused and unfolded into the body.

But is it in the body as form is in matter? Yet it will be a separate form, since it is an essence, and rather like the "user." But if it is like the figure in an axe—the figure, he says, in the iron—and both joined together (the axe) do what the iron so figured does, then we should attribute the common passions to the body—I mean such a natural body, endowed with instruments, having life in potentiality. Indeed, he says it is absurd to say the soul weaves, and so also to desire and to grieve; rather, he thinks the *living being* should be said to suffer or act in these ways.

<margin>Why it is difficult to say how disturbances refer to the composite rather than the soul alone.</margin>
V.
BUT we must say it is either the LIVING BEING, or a body of such a kind, or a "common" thing, or some third thing composed of both. However it may be, one must either keep the soul unaffected, since it is itself the cause of passion in another, or say the soul itself suffers along with it. And if so, it either undergoes the same passion or something similar: as if the living being desires in one way, but the nature of concupiscence <note>The faculty or "power" of desire.</note> acts or suffers in another. 

The nature of such a body should be considered in what follows. But as for the "combined" entity, how does it happen to be affected by distress? Is it because the body is so disposed, and the passion progresses as far as the sense-perception, while the sense-perception ends in the soul? But it is not yet clear how sensation occurs. Or does pain take its beginning from an opinion and judgment—as if some evil were present, either to itself or to one of its own? Then from there, a distressing change propagates into the body, and generally into the whole living being. 

Nevertheless, it is not yet clear whose opinion this is—the soul's, or the combined entity's? Furthermore, an opinion about evil does not necessarily have the passion of pain; for it is possible that while the opinion of evil is present, pain does not follow, nor anger, nor (when the opinion of being slighted is present) any wrath, nor even (when the opinion of good is present) an impulse of desire. In what way then are these things "common"? Is it because desire belongs to the nature of desiring itself, and anger to the nature of being angry, and is every impulse simply the outward movement of the appetitive power? But even then, they would not be "common," but belong to the soul alone, or rather to the body—because blood and bile must boil, and the body, being disposed in a certain way, incites desire, as happens in sexual matters. But let the desire for the good not be a common passion, but belong to the soul, just as other things do; nor does reason permit all things to be given to the "common" entity. But when someone desires sexual things, it will be...

Here, he explores whether the soul itself feels desires and sensations, or if these belong solely to the "composite" entity formed by the union of soul and body.</meta>

Will the human provide the beginning of the desire, and will the power of lusting follow? But in what way would the human desire at all if the power of lusting were not first stirred? Or will the nature of desiring begin it? But how will it begin if the body has not been affected in such a way beforehand?

<margin>
VI
It is called into doubt: whether it is one and the same thing that perceives; and whether the "animal kind" is the part that suffers; and whether the thing that gives life is the same as that which perceives, acts, or suffers.
</margin>
BUT perhaps it is better to say generally that, because these powers are present, those things which possess them act through them, while the powers themselves remain immobile, simply providing the capacity for action. But if this is so, when the living animal suffers, the soul—which gives the cause of living to the composite—must itself be unaffected, since passions and actions belong to the one who possesses the powers <note>Plotinus is arguing for the "impassibility" of the soul; it provides the 'battery' for life but doesn't feel the 'shock' of physical pain itself.</note>. But if this is the case, then living itself will not belong to the soul at all, but to the composite; or rather, the living of the composite will not belong to the soul. Likewise, the power of perceiving will not perceive, but rather the thing that possesses that power will perceive. Yet if sensation, which is a movement through the body, reaches as far as the soul and ends there, how will the soul not perceive? But if the power itself is not moved, how can the composite perceive if neither the soul nor the power of the soul is counted toward this very act?

<margin>
VII
The rational soul presides over the animal kind; in that soul, sensation exists without suffering.
</margin>
BUT let the composite itself exist because of the soul, specifically because the soul is present there. The soul itself, being what it is, does not hand itself over into the composite or into its other part, but instead—from a body of such a kind and from a certain light given by the soul—it creates the nature of the animal as something else entirely. It is to this "something else" that sensing and the other animal passions we have described belong. But how do *we* perceive? Perhaps because we are not separated from such a living thing. And even if other, more excellent things are present to us in the whole essence of a human (which is constituted of many parts), the sensory power of the soul must perceive not the sensible things themselves, but rather the images of them impressed upon the animal through the senses. For these forms are, in a way, intelligible. Therefore, the exterior sense is a mere image of this interior sense; the interior sense is truer in its essence, since it is a perception of images alone, without suffering <note>original: "absque passione" / "ἀπαθῶς". Plotinus makes a distinction between the body being physically 'hit' by a sensation and the soul 'observing' that sensation without being harmed.</note>. From these forms—from which the soul alone receives the command of the living being—come opinions, thoughts, and intellectual acts, and this is where "we" most truly reside. The things that come before these are ours, but we are what follows, presiding over the animal from above. Nothing, however, prevents us from calling this whole thing "the animal," but we should say the lower part is "mixed," while the remainder is the "true human." The lower part is partly lion-like and partly brute, and is called "altogether manifold" <note>A reference to Plato's *Republic* (Book IX, 588c), where the soul is described as a composite of a multi-headed beast, a lion (the spirited part), and a human (the rational part).</note>. For when the human concurs with the rational soul, whenever we reason, it is certainly "we" who reason, because the discourses of reason are the actions of the soul.

<margin>
VIII
How the rational soul is joined to the divine intellect, and through this to God. Likewise, how it is joined to its animal nature, and through that, to the body. Indeed, even if all souls are reduced to a common mind, and each receives in its own way, they carry back from there other intellects peculiar to themselves.
</margin>
BUT how do we relate to the Intellect? I mean the Intellect not as a certain habit or state which the soul might have from the Intellect, but the Intellect itself. Perhaps we have this above us. We have it either as something common or as something our own. Common, indeed, because it is indivisible and one...

<column-break/>

the human who desires; or will it be otherwise, with the desiring part also desiring? Or how? Will the human start the desire, and the desiring part follow? But how did the human desire at all, if the desiring part was not moved? Or will the desiring part start it? But if the body has not been disposed in a certain way beforehand, from where will it start?

BUT perhaps it is better to say generally that by the powers being present, those things that have them exist and act according to them, while the powers themselves are immobile, supplying the "being able" to those that have them. But if this is so, when the living being suffers, it is necessary that the soul—having given the cause of living to the composite—be unaffected, the passions and the actions belonging to the possessor. But if this is so, living altogether will not belong to the soul, but to the composite; or the composite living being will not belong to the soul. And the sensory power will not sense, but the one having the power. But sensation is a movement through the body, ending in the soul. How then will the soul not sense? Or, with the sensory power being present, will the composite sense the sensible thing by the fact that this power is present? But if the power will not be moved, how is it still the composite,

if the soul is not numbered with it? Nor the power of the soul, or the composite.

And the sensory power of the soul must not be of the sensible things themselves, but must rather be perceptive of the types arising from sensation in the animal. the part from that point is the true human, or nearly so. Those other parts are the lion-like part, and the altogether manifold beast. For the human being concurrent with the rational soul, whenever we reason, "we" reason, because the reasonings are activities of the soul.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation into the relationship between the higher soul and the "living being" (the composite of soul and body). Previously, he asked whether it is the soul itself that perceives and feels, or if these experiences belong only to the composite. Here, he explores how the soul remains "everywhere the same" while appearing divided among bodies, and why the higher soul remains sinless even when a person does evil.</meta>

# BOOK ONE.

<column-break/>

A and everywhere it is the same, yet it is unique because each individual possesses it entirely within the primary soul. We therefore possess the **Forms** <note>original: εἴδη (eide) / species. In Neoplatonism, these are the eternal blueprints or archetypes of all things.</note> in two ways: in the soul, they are, as it were, unfolded and separated; but in the **Intellect** <note>original: νῷ (no) / intellectu. The 'Nous' is the second principle in Plotinus's system, the realm of pure thought.</note>, they are all together. But how do we possess God? Perhaps as one who hovers over the intelligible nature and true essence. We humans come third from there—from that "indivisible nature," as Plato says, which is above, and from the nature that is "divisible" regarding bodies. 

B We must understand this "divisible" nature as that which gives itself to the dimensions of the body, insofar as each thing becomes a living being, even while it exists as one in the whole and the universe. Furthermore, it appears to be present to bodies by shining upon them, making them alive—not, I say, out of itself and the body combined, but while remaining itself, it provides **images** <note>original: εἴδωλα (eidola) / simulachra.</note> of itself, just as a face reflects an image in many mirrors. 

C The first of these images is **sensation** <note>original: αἴσθησις / sensus.</note>, which flourishes in the "common part" <note>The 'common part' refers to the composite of body and soul, the 'living animal' as opposed to the pure soul.</note>. From this, in turn, every other form of soul is named, one following another, reaching down to the nature of reproduction and growth, and even to the performance of another work beyond the power that performs it, with that performing power turned toward the work being completed.

D **IT WILL** therefore be the case for us that the nature of that [higher] soul is free from the cause of the evils that a human does and suffers. For these things pertain to the "common animal" itself—the "common part," as has been said. 

<margin>IX The causes of sins, and the soul’s consent: its own property is intelligence, which is called thought, by which we do not act through the body's instruments.</margin>

But if opinion and **thought** <note>original: διάνοια (dianoia) / cogitatio.</note> belong to the soul, how can it be beyond the fault of sin? For false opinion is frequent, and many evils are done because of it. Perhaps these evils are done by us because we are overcome by our "worse part." For we are often accustomed to yield to desire, or to anger, or to a "bad image." 

E Thus, what is called the "thought of falsehoods"—which is also the **imagination** <note>original: φαντασία (phantasia).</note>—often does not wait for the judgment of the deliberating mind. Instead, we follow after, obeying the worse parts, just as happens in sensation: before you can discern by the power of consideration, you see falsely through the "common sense." 

F Has the Intellect touched this? Perhaps not; therefore it remains innocent. Or perhaps it must be said that we either "touched" the intelligible itself (which is in the Intellect) or we did not; or perhaps we touched that which is within us. For it is possible to possess something without having it "ready and at hand." 

<margin>X What is proper to our animal nature also pertains to us, and animal life does not exist unless it follows the soul as its cause. Likewise, intellectual virtues are in the soul, while moral virtues are in the animal.</margin>

We have distinguished between "common" and "private" things by the fact that some are corporeal and do not occur without the body, while others do not need the body for their action; these latter we judge to be private to the soul. And **thought** <note>Plotinus uses 'dianoia' here to mean the discursive reasoning process.</note>, which carries out the selection and judgment of images coming from the senses, already looks toward the Forms and perceives them with a kind of internal sense. 

G True thought is the activity of **intellections** <note>original: νοήσεων / intellectionum.</note>, and it is often a likeness and communion of external things with internal ones, which remains unshaken. However, the changes and disturbances in us arise from those things which are joined to us, and from those passions which belong to the "common part"—whatever that may be, as has been said.

**BUT** if we are the soul itself, and we suffer these things, then surely the soul suffers; and again, it will do what we do. Perhaps we said that the "common part" is "ours" especially before we are separated [from the body]...

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK I.

<column-break/>

->A<-

...whatever our body suffers, we say that we are suffering. Therefore, the word "we" is used in two ways: either including the brute <note>The animal nature or the lower part of the soul-body union.</note> within us, or referring to that which stands above it. The brute is the body enlivened by the soul. But the true human is distinct from these things; he is pure, possessing the virtues found in the Intellect, which are established in the separate soul itself—separate, I say, and separable even while it is here. Indeed, when the soul departs entirely, that which shines out from it also goes away, following its source.

->B<-

However, those virtues which come not from wisdom <note>original: prudentia / φρονήσει</note>, but from habit and practice, seem to belong to the "common part" <note>The composite of soul and body.</note>. For the vices belong to this part as well, such as envy, emulation, and pity. But to whom does friendship belong? Perhaps partly to the common part, and partly to the inner human.

<margin>XI. In children, the animal nature and the imagination of the soul reign supreme. The intellect and reason are occupied with higher things. Likewise, the specific path of brutes depends on the rational soul, whether our own or another's.</margin>

->C<-

**XI** As long as we are children, the faculties of the composite are active, but only a few things from the higher realms shine down into it. When these higher parts are at rest regarding us, they are meanwhile active toward the realms above; they act upon us only when they proceed as far as the "middle" part of our being. What then? Are we not also that which exists before this? Indeed, but a "turning" <note>original: aduersionem / ἀντίληψιν. This refers to the soul's conscious attention or awareness.</note> must occur. For we do not constantly use everything we possess, but only when we turn the middle part either toward the higher things or toward their opposites—that is, whenever we bring something from potentiality or habit into actual practice.

->D<-

But how do brute animals possess the "living being"? Perhaps if human souls are in them (as is said) because they have sinned, the separable part of the soul is not "theirs," even though it is present to them. Instead, their consciousness—the image of the soul—is joined with the body; I mean a body such as is made by that image of the soul. But if a human soul has not entered, then such a living being is produced by an illumination from the Universal Soul.

<margin>XII. In the essence of the soul there is neither sin nor punishment, but these occur in the animal nature generated by it, and in the manner of its generation.</margin>

->E<-

**XII** But if the soul is sinless, how can there be judgments and punishments? This statement seems to disagree with every tradition that says the soul sins, is purified, pays the penalty in the underworld, and transmigrates through bodies. We must, therefore, consider which account to follow. Perhaps someone might find a way they do not contradict one another. For the one who claims the soul does not sin posits that the soul is something entirely simple and one, taking "soul" and "the essence of soul" to be the same thing.

->F<-

But the one who says the soul sins joins to it another "species" of soul that possesses heavy passions. Thus, the soul itself becomes a sort of composite made of all these parts, and it suffers as a whole, and it is the composite that sins. It is this composite that receives the punishment, not the other [the higher soul]. Hence Plato says: "For we see the soul as those who look upon the sea-god Glaucus." <note>A reference to Plato's Republic 10.611d. Glaucus was a sea-god whose true form was hidden by shells, seaweed, and stones that had grown onto him over time; Plotinus uses this as a metaphor for the soul encrusted with earthly passions.</note> If anyone wishes to behold its true nature, they must strip away the additions and look toward its "philosophy"—to what it touches and to what it is related, which makes it what it truly is.

->G<-

Therefore, there is one life and one set of actions for the higher soul, and another for that which is punished. The withdrawal and separation must be not only from this body, but from every added part. For in the process of birth, an addition occurs—or rather, the whole of birth seems to belong to that other species of soul. But as for how this generation occurs, the answer would be that the soul descends...

<column-break/>

->A<-

...and whatever our body suffers, we say we suffer. Thus, "we" is twofold, either including the beast <note>original: θηρίῳ (therio)</note> or that which is already above this. The beast is the body made alive. But the true human is another, pure of these things, having the virtues in thought which are indeed seated in the soul as it is separated—separated and separable even while it is here. For when the soul stands away entirely, the light shone from it also departs, following along.

->B<-

For that is where the vices are, since envy, jealousy, and pity are there too. But friendships—to whom do they belong? Perhaps some to this part, and others to the inner human?

->C<-

While we are children, the activities are from the composite, and little shines from the things above into it. But when the higher part is idle toward us, it is active toward the realm above.

For we do not always use all the things we have; but only when we station the middle part either toward the things above or toward their opposites,
<margin>* whenever</margin>

->D<-

<margin>* through</margin>

<margin>* or</margin>
The body *is such a kind as is made by the image of the soul. But if the human soul did not enter, then such a living being is produced by an illumination from the Whole [Soul].

->E<-

But if the soul is sinless, how are there punishments? Truly this word disagrees with every word which says that the soul itself both sins and is purified, and pays penalties in Hades, and is reincarnated. One must try, in whatever way one wishes, to see how these do not fight with one another. For the word that gives sinlessness to the soul poses it as entirely simple, saying "soul" and "being soul" are the same.

->F<-

<margin>* according to</margin>

Therefore, there is another life, and other activities, and the thing being punished is another. The retreat and the separation are not only from this body, but from everything that has been added. <meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the "we" and the soul's relationship to the body, specifically addressing whether the soul's "downward" inclination constitutes a sin and how the higher and lower aspects of a person can exist in different realms simultaneously, using the mythological example of Hercules.</meta>

<page-num>7</page-num>
<header>BOOK ONE. 7</header>

<margin>*thought by it, another produced*</margin>
<margin>*upon it*</margin> ...produced upon the soul itself, resulting from its descent in the "inclination" <note>The Greek term *neusis* refers to a "lean" or "nod" of the soul toward the material world.</note>. Does the soul then abandon its "image" <note>The *eidolon*, or the lower reflection of the soul that animates the body.</note>, and if this inclination occurs, how is it not a sin? But if this inclination is merely an illumination of what is below, it is not a sin, just as a shadow is not a sin. Rather, the cause is the object being illuminated. For if that object did not exist, the soul would have nowhere to shine.
B Therefore, the soul is said to "descend" and "incline" because the thing it illuminates becomes connected to it. It lets go of the image only if there is nothing nearby to receive it. It lets go not by being torn apart, but by the image simply ceasing to be. And the image ceases to be when the soul looks entirely toward the higher realm. The poet <note>Homer, in the Odyssey (Book 11).</note> seems to separate these two parts in the case of Hercules, placing his image in the underworld while he himself is among the gods. Held by both accounts, the poet observes both that Hercules is among the gods and that he dwells in
<margin>*similarly then*</margin> the underworld. Thus, he divided him. Perhaps this account would be persuasive in this way: that Hercules possessed active virtue, and having been deemed worthy of being a
C god because of his noble goodness <note>original: *kalokagathian* / *probitatem*</note>, he was deified because he was active, but not entirely contemplative.
<margin>*he was wholly*</margin> For if he had been contemplative, he would have been entirely in the higher realm. As it is, while he is there, a part of him remains below.

The one who examines these things—is it "us," or the soul? It is "us," but through the soul. And how is it "through the soul"? Is it because we possess it that it examines, or is it the soul itself? If it is the soul, it will not be moved; or rather, we must grant it a motion that is not of bodies, but is its own 
D life. Furthermore, thought belongs to us because 
<margin>*of us*</margin> the soul is intellectual. Thought is a better form of life, both when the soul thinks and when the Intellect acts upon us. For a part of us is also there, and to that part we ascend.
For this is a part of us, and we ascend to it.

<column-break/>

...descending, and then something else is produced by the soul, occurring in the soul’s very inclination toward the body, like a kind of nod. Does it then stop illuminating that which is lower? Surely not. And how is this "nod" not a sin? But if to "incline" is to illuminate that which is lower, it is certainly not a sin, any more than a shadow is. The cause, truly, is the thing being illuminated; for if this did not exist, the soul would have no way to shine.
B To descend and to incline, or "to nod," is therefore said because that which is illuminated by the soul is connected to it. It lets go of the image, then, unless there is something close by to receive it. It lets go not because it is being cut away, but because the image is no longer there. It is no longer there if the soul looks back entirely toward the heights. The poet seems to separate this in Hercules, sending his image to the underworld, but counting the hero himself among the gods. He observes both in his words: that he stays among the gods, and that he dwells among the dead. Thus, he divided him. Perhaps
C the argument will be plausible in this way: Since Hercules possessed active virtue and was judged to be a god because of his uprightness—since he was active, but not contemplative—otherwise he would surely have been entirely among the celestial beings. Thus, he is indeed among the celestials, yet something of him meanwhile remains in the underworld.

<margin>XIII. It is not the composite being, but the soul itself that reasons and understands, through the primary intellect, and indeed through the common intellect.</margin>
D As for the one who considers these matters: is it "us," or the soul? Perhaps it is us, but through the soul. But how through the soul? Did someone consider it merely by possessing a soul? Or was it the soul itself? It will not, therefore, be moved; or we must allow such a motion which is not of bodies, but is the soul's own life. Moreover, intelligence is ours because the soul is intellectual; and this intelligence itself stands forth as a better life: both when the soul understands, and when the intellect acts within us.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON
# THE BOOK OF VIRTUES
### ARGUMENT.

### SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

->We must strive to become like God by fleeing from here through virtue.<-

<margin>Chapter one begins from that golden sentence of our Plato, found in the book *On Knowledge* (that is, the *Theaetetus*): "To escape evils, we must flee from here immediately." To flee from here is to become like God; and the soul becomes like God through virtue. But lest anyone err regarding the knowledge of the goal, he argues that the soul becomes like God through virtue not because there is virtue in God in the same way there is in the soul, but because God is the principle, the exemplar, and virtue itself. By "God," I mean the Divine Mind, the architect of the world, presiding over the world and its soul. And although in the beginning of the debate he grants that the soul becomes like the World Soul and its Mind through virtue (which is true), as the discussion progresses, he asserts that the goal of this likeness extends higher: to the Divine Intellect itself. To this goal, as if to a fourth level where the archetypes of the virtues reside, the soul arrives through three stages: first, through civil virtues; second, through purifying virtues; and third, through the virtues of the already purified soul. This is the summary of the entire book.</margin>
The goal of this book is for the soul to become like God. Its subject matter is virtue, through which such a likeness is attained. Finally, the form of the book is its distribution into seven chapters: in the first, there is a certain exercise to find virtue; in the following, its discovery, definition, and distribution.

Although the soul becomes like God through virtues, God does not "have" virtue; rather, He is the exemplar of virtue. What is a quality in the soul is essence in God. Likewise, the existence of the Ideas <note>The Platonic Archetypes or Forms.</note> is confirmed here.

Marsilio Ficino provides a preface to the next section, defining virtue as the means by which the soul achieves likeness to God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's inquiry into the dual nature of the human person. The previous page concluded with the mythological example of Hercules, whose "image" dwells in the underworld while his true self resides with the gods. This page expands on that distinction, defining the "true man" versus the "animal" or "brute" and addressing the problem of how a "pure" soul can be said to sin or undergo punishment.</meta>

<page-num>6</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS, ENNEAD I.</header>

...that which our body suffers, we say that "we" suffer. There are, therefore, two ways in which "we" are spoken of: either including the brute <note>original: *bruto* / *θηρίῳ*. Referring to the animalistic or purely biological nature of a human.</note> within ourselves, or that which stands above it. The "brute" is the body brought to life. The true man, however, is distinct from these—he is pure, possessing the virtues found in the intellect, which are rooted in the soul that is separate; separate, I say, and separable even while it remains here. For indeed, even when the soul departs entirely, that which shines out from it <note>The "illumination" or reflection of the soul that animates the body.</note> departs as well, following it. But the virtues that come not from wisdom <note>original: *prudentia* / *φρονήσει*</note>, but from a certain habit and exercise, seem to belong to the "common" part <note>The "common" or composite part refers to the mixture of soul and body.</note>. For to this part belong the vices, such as envies, rivalries, and pities. But to whom do friendships belong? Perhaps some belong to the common part, while others belong to the inner man.

<margin>XI
In children, the animal nature and the imagination of the soul rule. The intellect and reason are occupied with higher things. Likewise, the path of brutes belongs to the rational animal, or to our own related parts.</margin>
AS LONG AS we are children, the powers in the composite being are active, but only a few things from the higher realms shine down upon it. When these higher powers are idle in relation to us, they are active within the higher realm; they act upon us only when they reach as far as the "middle" part. What then? Are we not also that which exists before this? Nevertheless, a turning <note>original: *adversio* / *ἀντίληψιν*. A conscious awareness or "taking hold" of the higher self.</note> must occur. For we do not always use everything we have, but only when we turn the middle part toward the higher things or toward their opposites—or when we bring something from potentiality or habit into actual activity. How do the brutes possess the "animal"? Perhaps, if human souls that have sinned are in them (as is said), this "separable" part of the soul does not belong to the brute, but though present, it is not truly "there" for them. Rather, their sensory awareness has an "image" of the soul <note>original: *simulachrum* / *εἴδωλον*</note> together with the body—a body that is formed, as it were, by the soul's image. But if a human soul has not entered, such an animal is produced by an illumination from the Soul of the All.

<margin>XII
In the essence of the soul there is neither sin nor punishment, but these things exist in the "animal" nature, along with how it is generated.</margin>
BUT IF the soul is not a sinner, how can there be judgments and punishments? This discourse seems to disagree with every teaching that says the soul sins, is purified, pays penalties in the underworld, and migrates through bodies. We must adhere to whichever of these views one prefers. Yet perhaps someone might find a way that they do not conflict. For the one who teaches that the soul does not sin posits a single, entirely simple thing, taking "soul" and "the essence of soul" to be the same. But the one who says it sins joins to it another form of soul that possesses terrible passions <gloss>of the mind</gloss>. Let the soul itself, then, be a composite of all these things; it suffers as a whole, and the composite sins—and it is this composite that pays the penalty, not the higher soul. Hence Plato says: "For we see it as those who look upon the sea-god Glaucus." <note>In Plato’s *Republic* (Book 10), the soul is compared to the sea-god Glaucus, whose original form is obscured by shells and seaweed; Plotinus argues we must "scrape off" these additions to see the soul's true nature.</note> But if someone wishes to see its true nature, they must strip away what has been added and look toward its "philosophy"—what it touches and what it is related to, which makes it what it is. Therefore, its life is one thing, its actions another, and that which is punished is something else entirely. The withdrawal and separation must be not only from this body, but from every added part. For in the process of birth, there is an addition <margin>*addition*</margin>, or rather, the whole process of birth seems to belong to that other form of soul. As for how this "generation" occurs, the answer is that the soul descends...

<column-break/>

...and what our body suffers, we say that we suffer. There are two "we's," either the one counted with the beast, or that which is already above it. The "beast" is the body made alive. But the true man is another, pure of these things, having the virtues in the intellect which are established in the soul that is separate—separate, I say, and separable while still being here. For when the soul itself departs entirely, the illumination from it also departs, following it. But the virtues which come not from wisdom, but from habits and exercises, belong to the <gloss>mind</gloss> <note>original: *νῦ* (abbreviation for *νοῦ* or *κοινοῦ* - the "common" or composite being).</note>. To this part also belong the vices, such as envies, jealousies, and pities. But friendships, to whom do they belong? Perhaps some to this part, and others to the inner man?

WHEN WE ARE CHILDREN, the activities are those of the composite being, and little of the illumination from above reaches it. But when that illumination is idle toward us, it is active toward the higher realm. It acts toward us when it comes as far as the middle part. What then? Are "we" not also that <gloss>and the thing before this</gloss>? But a perception <note>original: *antilepsin*</note> must occur. For we do not always use all that we have, but only when we arrange the middle part either toward the higher things or toward their opposites, or toward <gloss>whatever</gloss> we lead from potentiality or habit into activity. How do the brutes have the "animal"? If there are not human souls in them, as they say, which have sinned, this "separable" part does not belong to the brutes, but though present, it is not there for them. But their perception has the image of the soul together with the body. And the body <gloss>indeed</gloss> is such as it is, having been made by the image of the soul. But if the soul of a man has not entered, such an animal is produced by an illumination from the whole <note>The World-Soul.</note>.

BUT IF the soul is sinless, how are there punishments? But this discourse disagrees with every discourse that says the soul both sins and does right, and pays penalties in Hades, and is reincarnated. One must accept whichever discourse one wishes. For perhaps one might find a way in which they do not fight. For the discourse that gives sinlessness to the soul makes it entirely one and simple, saying that "soul" and "to be soul" are the same. But the one that allows it to sin, entwines and adds to it another kind of soul which has the terrible passions. The soul itself then becomes a composite of all these, and it suffers <gloss>according to</gloss> the whole, and the composite sins. And it is this which pays the penalty, not that higher one. Whence Plato says: "For we have seen it as those who see the sea-god Glaucus." He says that if anyone wants to see its nature, they must look at its "philosophy," what it touches and to what it is related, being what it is. There is therefore another life, and other activities, and the thing punished is different. The withdrawal and the separation are not only from this body, but from everything that has been added. For in generation, there is an <margin>*addition*</margin> addition, or a total decline into another kind of soul. As for how the generation happens, it has been said that the soul descends...

<summary>This page explores the duality of the human self, distinguishing between the "true man" (the intellectual soul) and the "animal" (the living body). Plotinus argues that while the composite person may sin and suffer, the higher soul remains pure and separable, like the god Glaucus hidden beneath the sea's debris.</summary>

# BOOK ONE.

<margin>by herself *from her</margin> ...of thought, but of another thing *produced from her*, that which descends into the lower nature. Does she then let go of her **image** <note>original: *eidolon* / εἴδωλον. In Neoplatonism, the "image" is the lower reflection of the soul that animates the body, while the higher soul remains above.</note>, and if intellection <unclear>remains</unclear>, how is it not a sin? But if intellection is an illumination directed toward what is below, it is not a sin, just as a shadow is not; rather, the cause lies in that which is illuminated. For if that thing were not there, the soul would have no place to cast its light. Therefore, the soul is said to "descend" and to "incline" <note>original: *neuein* / νέυειν. A technical term for the soul's "nod" or leaning toward the material world.</note> because of its coexistence with that which is illuminated by it. It lets go of the image, then, unless there is something nearby to receive it. It lets it go, however, not by being torn away, but by the image simply no longer existing. And it no longer exists if the soul looks entirely toward the higher realm. The poet <note>Referring to Homer in the *Odyssey* (Book 11).</note> seems to separate this in the case of **Hercules**, placing his **image** in the underworld while he himself is among the gods. Held by both accounts, he is both among the gods and in <margin>our own</margin> Hades. This is our condition as well. Perhaps the explanation is persuasive in this way: because Hercules possessed **practical virtue** and was deemed a god due to his excellence in action—for he was active rather than **contemplative** <note>Plotinus distinguishes between the "active" life of social/heroic virtue and the "contemplative" life of the philosopher.</note>—he was not *entirely* <margin>was whole</margin> there. So that the word might be true, he is both in the higher realm and also exists partly in the realm below.

BUT concerning the investigation of these things: is it "we" who investigate, or the "soul"? It is "we," but by means of the soul. But how is it by means of the soul? Is it because the soul *possesses* the power to investigate, or is it the soul itself? In that case, will it not be moved? Or must we grant it a motion that is not of bodies, but is the soul's own **life**? And <margin>ours</margin> intellection is ours in this way: because the soul is intellectual, and intellection is a higher form of life, both when the soul thinks and when the **Intellect** acts upon us. For this too is a part of us, and to it we ascend.

> For this too is a part of us, and to it we ascend.

<column-break/>

...descending, and then another thing being made by the soul, and descending into the very inclination of the soul toward the body, as if by a certain "nod." Does she then let go of the **image**? Likewise, how is that very inclination or "nod" not a sin? But if to "nod" is to illuminate that which is lower, it is certainly not a sin, just as a shadow is not. The cause, truly, is that which is illuminated; for unless this existed, the soul would have no way to shine. <margin>B</margin> Therefore, it is said to "descend" and "incline" or "nod" because that which is illuminated by it is connected to it. It lets go of the image, then, unless there is something close by to receive it. It lets it go, however, not because it is torn away, but because the image is no longer here. And it is no longer here if the soul looks back entirely toward that which is above. The poet seems to separate this in the case of **Hercules**, sending his image to the lower world, but counting the man himself among the gods. Thus he observes both in his words: that he dwells among the gods, and that he is among those below. Thus he divided him. <margin>C</margin> Perhaps, indeed, the discourse will be persuasive in this way: since Hercules possessed **active virtue** and was considered a god on account of his uprightness—inasmuch as he was active, but not **contemplative**—otherwise he would surely have been entirely among the celestial beings. And so he is indeed among the celestial beings, yet a part of him remains meanwhile among those below.

<margin>XIII</margin>
<margin>XIIII It is not the mind that he composes, but the soul in a true way: Does someone consider the soul by possessing it, or is it rather the soul itself? It will not, therefore, be moved; or one must grant a motion such as does not belong to bodies, but is the soul’s own life. Furthermore, intellection is ours, since the soul is intellectual; and this intellection itself stands as a better life: both when the soul understands, and when the intellect acts within us, even through what is common.</margin>
<margin>D</margin> BUT concerning the one who considers these things: is it not we, or the soul? Perhaps it is we, but through the soul. Through the soul, but in what way? Does someone consider it by possessing it, or is it the soul itself? It will not, therefore, be moved. Or one must grant a motion of such a kind as does not belong to bodies, but is its own **life**. Furthermore, intellection is ours, since the soul is intellectual: and this intellection itself stands as a better life, both when the soul understands and when the **Intellect** acts within us.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON
## THE BOOK OF VIRTUES
### ARGUMENT.
#### SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

->We must strive to become like God by fleeing from here through virtue.<-

The purpose of this book is for the soul to become like God. The **matter** <note>In the Aristotelian sense of "subject matter."</note> is virtue, through which such likeness is obtained. Finally, the **form** or structure of the book consists of its distribution into seven chapters: in the first, a certain exercise to find virtue; in the following ones, its discovery, definition, and distribution. The first chapter begins with that golden sentence of our **Plato**, found in the book *On Knowledge* (that is, the *Theaetetus*): *In order to avoid evils, we must flee from here immediately.* But to flee from here is to become like God. The soul becomes like God through virtue. But lest anyone err concerning the knowledge of the goal, he argues that the soul will be like God through virtue—not because you might see virtue in God just as it is in the soul, but because God is the principle and **exemplar** of virtue, and virtue itself. By "God," I mean the **Divine Mind**, the craftsman of the world, presiding over the world and its soul. And although in the beginning of the debate he allows that the soul becomes like the **World Soul** and its mind through virtue (which is true), as the discussion progresses he asserts that the goal of this likeness extends to the **Divine Intellect** itself. The soul reaches this goal, as if it were a fourth step where the exemplars of the virtues reside, through three stages: first by the **civil virtues**, second by the **purgatory virtues**, and third by those of the soul already **purified**. And this is the summary of the whole book.

---

Although the soul becomes like God through virtues, God does not have virtue: but is the exemplar of virtue. And that which is a quality in the soul is essence in God; likewise, the **Ideas** <note>Platonic Forms.</note> are confirmed here.

# SUMMARY BY MARSILIO FICINO
<meta>catchword: [to] be</meta>

<margin>I</margin>
*In the first chapter, he first states: if any of the human virtues exist within God, it is more probable that prudence and justice are present rather than the others, which are concerned with emotional disturbances <note>original: "perturbationes" — referring to the passions or "passions of the soul" like fear or anger</note>. Next, he argues that no human or civil virtues exist in God; meanwhile, he introduces the definitions of these virtues as set down by Plato in the books of the Republic. Nevertheless, he admits that through these virtues, we achieve a certain divine likeness. However, he rejects the logical conclusion that some might lean upon—namely, that because the soul becomes like God through virtues, God must therefore possess virtue. He also rejects the distinction where one might say God has virtues, but in some "superior" form. For he objects: if the soul is granted to be like God, and if the virtues in God are not similar but vastly different, then one could also grant that the soul is similar to a God who possesses no virtues at all. Indeed, although the air receives heat from the presence of light, the sun—from which the light flows—receives no new heat; nor does fire become hot simply because something else is heated by it. And yet, these things become like those sources. In this way, the soul receives virtue from God, through which it becomes like God, and yet God does not possess virtue. Nor should anyone object: just as heat is "adventitious" <note>external or added</note> in water but "native" in fire, so virtue is foreign in the soul but naturally implanted in God, so that virtue exists in both, but is more excellent in God. For virtue is necessarily both "of someone" and "in someone," existing in a subject like a "form" <note>term: form — in Aristotelian/Platonic thought, the shape or essence that gives a thing its character</note> within a substance; however, nothing of this kind exists in God. Truly, the gift the soul receives from God retains nothing of the same nature in the soul as it has in God: for there, it is the very essence of God; here, however, it is like a quality within an essence. There, it is the exemplar <note>term: exemplar — the perfect original model or archetype</note> and principle; here, it is a certain "imaginary" effect. For an image, although it performs the duty of representing, seems to preserve nothing of the same nature. Here, virtue is a certain arrangement and composition, but there, nothing is such; rather, by a certain arrangement, the soul reflects the Idea <note>original: "Idea" — the perfect, eternal blueprint in the Divine Mind</note>, just as a house reflects the intelligence of the architect. Indeed, it is the opinion of many philosophers: qualities that are "accidents" <note>term: accident — a non-essential quality, like being "hot" or "cold"</note> in the order of bodies can nowhere be "substances" within that same corporal order. Therefore, heat and light, which are accidents in water, are not substances in the sphere of fire or in the heavens; rather, here they are qualities that happen changeably, while there they are (so to speak) essential and entirely immobile qualities. From this, the Platonists will argue: things that proceed from the imperfect are finally perfected into something more perfect by the same power by which they proceeded, reaching the "most perfect" being. By its power, whatever is not "most perfect" is guided as if in need, and is fully completed. Therefore, the condition of forms—which has been led from a changeable quality to an immobile quality and an entirely essential property—is finally led to forms that are now "essences" themselves rather than existing "in" an essence. Truly, such a thing can only exist in an incorporeal reality—indeed, can only *be* an incorporeal reality—and nothing else exists but the Ideas of natural forms. There, heat, light, and the remaining forms are essences; and being themselves the "acts of essence," the Idea of the soul is there, and the perfect Idea of a perfect soul. Therefore, the Idea of the virtues by which the soul is perfected is also there, by the power of that which is both naturally implanted and continuously preserved—though the Ideas of the virtues are there in another way, as will appear in what follows. Furthermore, the "exemplar" of virtue is in God—namely, God himself—while a certain "form" of virtue is in the substance of the rational soul itself, and an "image" of virtue is in the irrational part of the soul. Additionally, in our soul, virtue is an adventitious quality; in the superior souls <note>referring to celestial or angelic beings</note>, it is an inborn and immobile quality; in the Divine Mind, virtue is the very essence of the Mind and the act of being.*

---

->How the soul through virtue becomes like God. And how virtue is civil, purifying, and of the purified soul.<-
->The exemplars are distinguished among themselves. And concerning the first and second movements of the soul.<-

---

<margin>II</margin>
*The second chapter of the book approaches the definitions of virtue and the virtues, specifically toward the same end we mentioned: so that we may know the reason for our likeness to God and, once known, compare ourselves to it. In the beginning, he brings forward two primary ways of likeness in this manner: When two things established under one principle both receive a quality from it, agreeing in species or genus <note>original: "species vel genere" — biological or logical categories</note>—as two white things or at least colored things—then just as this one is like that one, so in turn that one is said to be like this one. But when two things are different in genus (or more than genus), and this one is from that one and under it—like an image from a substance, or as if one were made in a mirror—then the image is indeed like the exemplar without any sharing of the same nature; yet the exemplar is not in turn said to be like the image. By this condition, the soul becomes like God through virtue, insofar as it receives virtue from there, which is the image of the divine exemplar. After this, he distinguishes the definition of the virtues. To understand these, understand which movements in us are "first" and which are "second": for the "first movements" are certain sudden impulses in our animal nature, stirred by external impacts through the animal's senses and the natural instinct of its imagination, before the rational soul consults with reason or perhaps notices with imagination whether it should be pursued or rather fled—whether these be terrors or certain incitements. The "second movements," however, placed in either pursuing or declining, follow either the observation of the higher imagination or even the counsel of reason, whether it be reckless or mature. Therefore, the virtue that cuts away the "second movements" which decline toward sensible things is called "civil" <note>original: "ciuilis" — also known as social or political virtues</note>, whether it be courage, or temperance, or prudence consulting thus far, or justice conducting itself so. For we think enough has been done by a citizen up to this point. However, the virtues that not only cut away the second movements but uproot them are called "purifying" <note>original: "purgatoriæ"</note>. Finally, the virtues that have already mastered the second disturbances and, moreover, either eradicate the "first impulses" (if that can even be done by a human) or at least moderate them by some reason and habit, belong to the "purified soul" <note>original: "purgati animi"</note>. Of these virtues which are in a threefold category, the exemplars are in God—but the virtues themselves are not. For there are no movements or business there in which our virtues are engaged. Through these three steps, then, together with Paul, being drawn "from glory to glory" <note>original: "à claritate in claritatem" — a reference to 2 Corinthians 3:18</note> by the Spirit of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image; that is, we apply our virtues like images to the divine exemplar and are reformed. Plotinus, as if imitating Paul, will declare this in what follows. In this second chapter of the book, he carries out the duty of only the "civil virtues," which he calls certain moderations and measures—both as far as it regards the emotions and as far as it regards right opinion, which is established in the place of knowledge for the sake of prudence. He adds that matter, since it is by its own nature void of all measure and moderation, is most unlike God, but appears similar to the extent that it receives measures and "species" <note>forms/appearances</note> from Him. And since matter, though naturally most remote from God, can appear somewhat like God by this condition, he wants the soul (naturally closer to God) much more to acquire a certain divine likeness through civil virtues, which determine and moderate it like matter—even though God has neither measure nor species. You should understand "nor species" to mean that the Father himself <note>The "One" or First Principle</note> exists above species and forms. Concerning the "Intellect" <note>The "Nous" or Second Principle</note>, his Son, understand that he does not have a species distinct from his essence, but that he is the Species itself, and the fullness of the form of all things; from which we all receive, insofar as we progress toward the virtue infused into us when we are turned toward Him. Through this, He gave us the power to become the sons of God. From God truly...*

<summary>This page features Marsilio Ficino's commentary on how the human soul achieves likeness to God through different levels of virtue (civil, purifying, and purified). It clarifies that while we become like God, God does not possess "virtue" in the human sense, as He is the perfect Archetype from which all virtues flow.</summary>

# ON BOOK II OF THE FIRST ENNEAD
<meta>catchword: to [be]</meta>

...in this way, the soul is like God, so that if one were to look deeply into the soul, they would believe they immediately see God. But you, in this chapter, where you read "for our Better" <note>original: "Meliori nostro" — referring to the rational part of the soul</note>, that is, for reason: you can also read "by a certain better way," that is, by introducing a better opinion, or by making progress through the power of what is superior. Likewise where Plotinus says: "Let this be entirely of God," he means either such a constitution of the soul, or that the soul becomes entirely divine and vice-versa, or that it belongs entirely to God. The same discourse in Plotinus often (as his student Porphyry admits) allows for multiple equal meanings.

->*Understanding is spoken of according to a certain analogy regarding both the divine intellect and the soul. Likewise, the text treats the discourse, or the "word," as it exists in the voice, in the soul, and in the mind.*<-

<margin>III</margin>After discussing the "civil virtues" <note>social and political virtues like justice or temperance in daily life</note> in the third chapter of the book, he approaches the higher ones. He defines the "purifying virtues" <note>original: "purgatorias" — virtues that cleanse the soul from bodily attachments</note> in their proper sense, and along with these, the virtues of the soul that has already been purified. Meanwhile, he shows that civil virtues should rather be called "dispositions toward virtue" than actual virtues; similarly, through them we are prepared and disposed for a divine likeness rather than being made truly similar. Furthermore, he maintains that even these virtues do not exist in God, because they are affections and qualities, or certain restorations of the soul, which cannot exist in the divine. 

Again, he argues that "prudence," the quality by which these virtues are guided, is a type of intelligence situated in temporal reasoning <note>thinking that happens step-by-step over time</note>, which is a type of intelligence that cannot exist in God. However, we say both God and the soul "understand" by a certain common name. This is not just a vague or accidental name, nor is it a "univocal" term where the definition of both intelligences is exactly the same in species or genus. Rather, it is an "analogical" condition: this intelligence in the soul is like a secondary reflection or image, and it is sustained by the intelligence of God as an "exemplar" <note>a perfect original pattern</note> placed far above it. 

He then compares them through this analogy: Just as speech in the spoken voice relates to "speech" in the soul, so also speech in the soul relates to the "speech" in the mind. Note that where we say "speech," you can also say "reason" or "word" <note>original: "sermo," "ratio," and "verbum" — all translating the Greek concept of "Logos"</note>. The spoken word is an image and interpreter of the word in the soul; the word of the soul is an image and interpreter of the word in the mind. Finally, Plotinus says elsewhere that the mind is an image and word of God, whom he also calls the father of mind and intelligence. 

Here, Origen and, as I believe, their teacher Ammonius, thought that the divine intellect (the Son) relates to the Father God (the Good itself) just as light relates to brightness. They also held that the Spirit (the life of the world) relates to the intellect as heat relates to light. Now, even though they seem to suggest a certain essential difference between these three, they prove such a great unity among them in other respects that no greater oneness could be imagined. Thus far have the minds of the philosophers proceeded, especially in that era; but their judgment must then be referred to the councils of the Holy Fathers. 

But let us conclude the chapter thus: Speech in the voice requires air, which the soul's speech does not. Spoken speech is divided into many parts and takes more time than the soul's speech; however, the soul's speech itself is still conducted within time. But the mind's speech, or reason, or word, is not stretched out by any time at all. Likewise, this "reason" or notion of the mind often fulfills through a single form and a single act what the soul's reasoning is forced to perform through many forms and acts. Finally, the Good itself towers over all limits of forms and intelligences; from this it appears that one proceeds step-by-step from multiplicity and need toward unity and a greater and greater self-sufficiency.

->*The soul is neither the Good itself nor that which is properly called "Good-formed." Also, the steps by which the Ideas are participated in. Again, proof of the Ideas, and concerning the divinity of the soul. And how the forms of things exist in the divine mind, how they exist in ours, and how they exist in reason and imagination.*<-

---

<margin>IIII</margin>Moving now from the virtues that are still "purifying" to those that are "purified" within the soul, he says that the result of purity itself is the goal of purification. These virtues are like more excellent ends—the highest grade of human virtue and the primary vessel for divine likeness. For this purity, restored through the labor of purification, is not the soul's "Good" itself; the soul is not content with itself as its own final goal, since it received its beginning from elsewhere. Indeed, this nature, which has been liberated from foreign and evil things through purification, cannot be the Good itself; otherwise, it would never have been subject to evil in the first place. 

Furthermore, the soul is not even what the Platonists call "Good-formed" <note>original: "Boniforme" — having the shape or character of the Good</note>; for that term refers to something that is always and equally a participant in the Good from the very beginning. A nature in need of purification does not always participate equally, and therefore is not the primary participant in the Good. For the order of goods necessarily rises from things that participate in the Good only occasionally or unequally, toward that which always participates equally, and from there finally to the "Good in itself," which is good by its own nature and not by participating in anything else. 

Thus, one ascends from the soul to the intellect, and from the intellect to the Good itself. This is like ascending from the fleeting forms found in physical matter (which are participated in unequally) to the forms in the "heavenly matter" (which are always participated in equally), and finally to the forms in the "intellectual heaven." These last forms do not exist "inside" something else through participation; they *are* the intellectual heaven itself—simple, uniform, and yet containing all forms <term>omniforme: containing all potential shapes or ideas</term>. This intellectual level is the "Good-formed" splendor of the Good itself. 

Since an effect is more similar to its cause at first and then gradually becomes more dissimilar as it moves away, it rightly depends first upon the simple and eternal Good. He then points out the divinity of the soul when he says: the "evil" of the soul is to cling to foreign, fleeting things, but its "good" is to cling to its own domestic and kindred things. Therefore, since the Good—which is life free from passions, complete truth, solid vigor, and full joy—only happens to the soul when it clings to divine things, it is clear the soul was born from them. Hence the saying: "But for me, to cling to God is good" <note>original: "Mihi verò adhærere deo bonum est" — a quotation from Psalm 73:28</note>. 

Now, since the soul is suddenly turned toward the Good by purification alone (which is a restoration to its own nature), and suddenly possesses it by that turning alone, it is clear that its nature is divine. Indeed, our soul is moved more strongly toward the Good than toward the Truth: for it desires the Truth only because it is a "good," and the Good itself is more powerful than the Truth. Since the soul sometimes attains the Truth suddenly when the causes of error are removed, it follows that once purified from evils, it continuously attains the Good. After this, he says that the very "turning" of the pure soul toward the Good is a virtue—the third grade of virtue belonging to the purified soul. He adds that what the soul attains from this turning is much more a virtue: he is now referring to the "exemplary" virtue...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains Plotinus’s hierarchy of virtues, moving from social "civil" virtues to "purifying" virtues that distance the soul from the body. He uses the analogy of speech and light to explain how the human mind reflects the divine mind and eventually the "Good itself."</summary>

# 10 COMMENTARIES OF MARSILIO FICINO

By which the soul ascends through the three steps already mentioned, it must now be formed from that point. And indeed, just as there are three steps, so there are three types of exemplary virtues. The first is when the soul turns its imagination toward its own reason to be better formed there or from that source. The second is when it transfers the formulas of reason to the forms innate to its own intellect, so that it may know better there. The third is when it perfectly adapts its own intellect to the divine mind and conforms its own intelligence to the ideas of the divine mind. This, however, it achieves through a certain eternal contact. From this it happens that they are able, in time, to conform both reason to their intellect and imagination to their own reason. That the primary forms of all things exist in one intellect—namely, the creator of all—is signified by the gathering of natural forms in one matter subject to all. That they are also distinct there in some way is shown by the formal difference of natural forms among themselves; this difference is neither from formless matter, nor by chance (since it is always most ordered), nor from one specific type of form among these, since it is ordered toward the one most common to all. Therefore, since the formal distinction of all forms proceeds from one form that is the creator of all, it is necessary that the principle of distinction exists there, through which the forms are present there, distinct from one another by a certain principle. That intellect is, therefore, both uniform and "omniform" <note>original: "omniformis" — containing all forms or shapes</note> at the same time. But since there is also the greatest union there, the essence of all the forms is certainly one, while the principles <note>original: "rationes"</note> are diverse. 

However, in any intellect after that one, the forms are certain eternal and deeply intimate "essential contacts" with the Ideas. From this contact, thereafter in the soul—that is, in the rational faculty—the "formulas of the Ideas" <note>original: "formulæ idearum" — the soul's internal concepts derived from the higher Ideas</note> are conceived from that union. These are indeed always innate, but they pass from a state of habit into action, and vice versa, over time. These are both universal formulas and they designate what each thing is and why it is. Furthermore, from these formulas, other formulas flow into the imagination, now declining closer to individual things; these show "what kind" a thing is rather than "what" it is, and if they reveal what kind of thing it is, they do not reveal "why" it exists. 

But you, where Plotinus denies elsewhere that the figures of things are received by the soul, understand this so that he does not contradict himself in this book: the figures are not imprinted on the soul by lower things, arriving recently and then receding and being completely erased. For these forms, which the soul draws from an intimate fountain, are like the very nature of the soul, or the natural power of the soul, and not something brought in from outside or added. For the soul proceeds from the author of its nature, and one of its powers always issues from another natural power, endowed with its own duty. Remember, Plotinus is acting here specifically concerning the intellectual good of the soul, and considers the end of the virtues to be that the soul should emerge as an entire "intellectual world," the end of which world is the "Simple Good" itself. For just as the soul itself is, so to speak, "corporeal" <note>Ficino means the soul acts as the "body" or vessel for higher things</note> compared to what is above the soul, so also the Intellect itself is above animal intelligence; and the "Good itself" stands simply above the intellectual good. 

In explaining the words where he says that the figures or "impressed forms" ought to be adapted to their exemplars once they are brought into action and subjected to the "illuminating power," understand that the formulas of the imagination are to be subjected to the forms of reason and to reason itself. Likewise, the formulas of reason are to be applied to one's own intellect and its forms, or rather its "formations." For this is always formed by the divine mind. Where he says that the intellect is not foreign to the soul, understand this because the soul has its own intellect innate to itself, and its own intellect is always joined to the divine mind, and joined in its own specific way. Indeed, we have sufficiently proved in our *Theology* <note>Referring to Ficino's *Platonic Theology*</note> that forms are naturally innate to the soul and that our intellect is always conformed to the divine.

->In the specific imagination of the rational soul, images are often stirred up according to the "first movements" of the imagination, which exist in the animal before it deliberates or notices.<-

<margin>V</margin>He defines the virtues of the purified soul in a sufficiently manifest order. What he calls "prefigured phantasy" <note>original: "phantasiam... præfiguratam"</note> here, understand as the fact that through first impulses, certain images are often stirred up even in our imagination that are inclined toward the senses before reason notices enough.

->Wisdom in the divine mind is like a touch; in our mind, it is like a contact; in reason, it is like a visible figure.<-

<margin>VI</margin>He confirms that the goal of the soul is not mere innocence, but to "become a god" <note>A core Neoplatonic concept: *theosis* or deification</note>. He says that the person in whom only the "first movements" <note>initial reflexive impulses</note> now remain is both a certain god and a "daemon" <note>original: "dæmonem" — here meaning a guiding spirit or intermediary being, not an evil spirit</note>. For some daemons are touched by passions, but the person in whom even the first movements now seem to be put to sleep is simply a god—that is, a completely intellectual soul of the number of those who properly accompany the divine mind. He adds that the soul, when it is entirely turned toward itself (following a preceding purification), is such as it had proceeded from the divine mind; and suddenly in that same place, it is completely restored. For even when it set out for this world long ago, it did not entirely depart from there. Indeed, reason clings to its own intellect by its own choice, and the intellect is naturally coupled with the divine mind. After this, he defines the "exemplary virtues" insofar as they are adapted to us in a certain way. For insofar as they are in the divine mind, they are indeed exemplars, but not "virtues." 

Where he says that wisdom in the soul is an "inspection" of those things which the intellect possesses, but that the intellect possesses wisdom by a certain "touch," understand "intellect" here as twofold: namely, our own and the divine. Wisdom in the divine is called a "touch" <note>original: "tactus"</note>, that is, the possession of the thing itself and rather its very existence, not just an image. In our intellect, however, it is rather called "contact" <note>original: "contactus"</note>, that is, a real (so to speak) coupling, not an imaginary notion. For in the rational nature which is properly called "soul," possession is more imaginary; but in the intellect, it is (so to speak) substantial. But this possession is first in the divine mind, and then it is transferred into ours.

->The divine intellect is primarily the very things which it possesses; our intellect is secondarily the very things which it possesses; reason is not similarly the things which it possesses. Likewise, a comparison is made here of the virtues, and several precepts are handed down.<-

<margin>VII</margin>He fits the exemplary virtues adapted to the soul into a certain corresponding order with the divine exemplars. He declares what the exemplar of each virtue is in God, and in what way the exemplary virtues in the soul rightly respond to the divine exemplars of the virtues. And where he says that the soul is not, like the intellect, the very things which it possesses, understand "soul" as the "discursive power" <note>the faculty of thinking through things step-by-step</note> in which essence is one thing, forms or images are another, and habits and acts are yet another. But in the divine mind, essence is reduced to act from eternity; and the essential act itself fills all those things which are carried out in the soul through certain additions. Furthermore, our intellect is, in a way, what it possesses, to speak according to the mind of Plotinus.

# ON BOOK I OF THE FIRST ENNEAD

For he is brought into action regarding all ideas by an eternal and intimate contact: into whose action the divine mind came forth from eternity. After this, he compares the virtues with each other in a certain way, and hands down specific precepts or solves doubts. He says, therefore: Those things which precede the complete purity of the soul are ways to virtue rather than virtue itself. Likewise, neither should purity be considered virtue unless it is referred to God, both to be imitated and attained according to one’s strength. Again, in the lower levels of virtue, the higher levels exist only through an image <note>original: "per imaginem" — the lower levels of human behavior reflect the higher spiritual realities like a mirror</note>. In the higher levels, however, the lower levels exist through the exemplar <note>original: "per exemplar" — the higher divine forms contain the blueprint for the lower versions</note>, and virtue is contained there. Likewise, where the principles change, the species of virtues also change. By principles, I mean two things: the end <note>purpose or goal</note> proper to each virtue, and its own rules and laws to which it is formed; especially where the principles of prudence change, which is judged the rule of other virtues. From this it happens that <term>civil temperance</term> <note>social moderation used in daily life</note> is of one species, <term>purgatory</term> <note>purifying virtues used to detach the soul from the body</note> of another, <term>purified</term> of another, and <term>exemplary</term> <note>the perfect divine form of the virtue</note> of another, and the other virtues similarly. Finally, he concludes that the entire common and chief end of virtues is not in external things, nor in virtue itself, nor in the soul, but in God. Nothing more holy can be said than this conclusion, which also testifies to the divine mind of our Plotinus.
