### COMMENTARIES OF MARSILIO FICINO

Once the soul has ascended through the three levels already mentioned, it must then be formed from that point. And indeed, just as there are three levels, so there are three kinds of <term>exemplary virtues</term> <note>the perfect, divine patterns of behavior and thought that exist in the mind of God</note>. The first is when the soul turns its imagination toward its reason to be better formed there or from that source. The second is when it transfers the <term>patterns of reason</term> <note>original: "rationis formulas" — the logical blueprints the mind uses to understand the world</note> to the forms innate in its own intellect, so that it may know better there. The third is where it fits its own intellect entirely to the divine mind, and conforms its own intelligence to the <term>Ideas</term> of the divine mind. Moreover, it achieves this through a certain eternal contact. From this, it becomes possible for the soul to conform its reason to its intellect in time, and its imagination to its own reason. That the primary forms of all things exist in one source—namely, in the single Intellect that produces all things—is signified by the gathering of natural forms into one matter that is subject to them all. That these forms are distinct there in some way is shown by the formal difference between natural forms; this difference does not come from formless matter, nor from chance (since it is always perfectly ordered), nor from any one specific kind of form among these, since all are ordered toward the one thing most common to all. Since, therefore, the formal distinction of all forms proceeds from the one form that produces all, it is necessary that the principle of distinction exists there, through which forms exist there distinct from one another by some principle. That Intellect, therefore, is at once uniform and "all-form." But since there is also the greatest union there, the essence of all forms is surely one, even if their principles are diverse.

However, in any intellect after that one, the forms are certain essential contacts with the eternal and deeply intimate Ideas. From this contact, in turn, there are in the soul—that is, in the rational faculty—certain "formulas" of the Ideas, as if conceived from that union; these are always innate, but they pass from a state of potential to a state of action and back again through time. These are universal formulas, designating what each thing is and for what purpose it exists. Beyond these, other formulas flow into the imagination, now declining closer to individual things; these show "what sort" of thing a matter is rather than "what" it is fundamentally, and if they reveal "what sort," they do not reveal "why" it exists.

But you, where Plotinus denies elsewhere that the figures of things are received by the soul—lest he seem to contradict himself in this book—must understand that the figures are not "impressed" into the soul by lower objects, arriving recently and then departing or being entirely erased. For these forms, which the soul draws from its innermost fountain, are like the very nature of the soul, or the soul's natural power, and not something foreign or added on. For the soul proceeds from the author of its nature, and its various powers come forth from one another, always endowed with their own natural duty. Remember that Plotinus is dealing here specifically with the intellectual "good" of the soul, and considers the end of the virtues to be that the soul should emerge as an entire "intellectual world," the end of which is **The Good** itself in its simplicity. For just as the soul itself is above the body, so the Intellect itself is above the soul's intelligence; and above the intellectual good stands **The Good** itself in its simplicity. 

In explaining the words where he says that figures or impressed forms (once brought into action) ought to be fitted to their exemplars and subjected to that which illuminates them, you should understand this to mean the formulas of the imagination must be subjected to reason, and those of reason to the soul's own intellect and its forms—or rather, its "formations." For the intellect is always formed by the divine mind. Where he says that the intellect is not foreign to the soul, understand that the soul has an intellect proper to itself and innate to it; its own intellect is always joined to the divine, and joined in a way unique to itself. That forms are naturally innate in the soul, and that our intellect is always conformed to the divine, we have sufficiently proven in our *Theology*.

->In the imagination belonging to the rational soul, images are often stirred according to the first movements of the imagination, which exists in an animal before it deliberates or takes notice.<-

<margin>V</margin> He defines the virtues of the purified soul in a clearly manifest order. Regarding what he calls "prefigured fantasy" here, understand that through the first impulses, certain images are often stirred even in our own imagination that are inclined toward the senses, before reason fully takes notice.

->Wisdom in the divine mind is like a touch; in our mind, it is like a contact; in reason, it is like a visible figure.<-

<margin>VI</margin> He confirms that the soul's goal is not merely innocence, but to become a god. He says that the person in whom only the "first movements" <note>initial reflexive impulses or emotions</note> still remain is a certain kind of "god and daemon" <note>original: "deum... & dæmonem" — a daemon in Platonic thought is a mediating spirit, higher than humans but lower than the supreme gods</note> at once. For daemons are touched by some affections; but he in whom even the first movements seem to be put to sleep is purely a god—that is, a completely intellectual soul of the number of those who properly accompany the divine mind. He adds that when the soul is turned toward itself (namely, after the preceding purification), it is such as it had proceeded from the divine mind, and it is suddenly and entirely restored in that same place. For even when it set out for this world long ago, it did not entirely depart from there. Indeed, reason clings to its own intellect and guide at will, and the intellect is naturally joined with the divine mind. 

After this, he defines the exemplary virtues insofar as they are suited to us in some way. For insofar as they are in the divine mind, they are indeed exemplars, but not "virtues" <note>because God is already perfect and does not need the "effort" of virtue</note>. Where he says that wisdom in the soul is a "bending" of those things which the intellect possesses, but that the intellect possesses wisdom through a certain "touch," understand here a twofold intellect—namely, our own and the divine. Wisdom in the divine is called a "touch," meaning the possession (or rather the existence) not of an image, but of the thing itself. In our intellect, however, it is better called "contact"—that is, a real union (if I may say so) and not an imaginary notion. For in the rational nature which is properly called "soul," possession is more imaginary; but in the intellect, it is (so to speak) substantial. But this possession exists first in the divine mind, and is then transferred into our own.

->The divine intellect is, in a primary way, the very things it possesses; our intellect is, in a secondary way, the very things it possesses; reason is not similarly the things it possesses. Likewise, a comparison is made here between virtues, and several precepts are handed down.<-

<margin>VII</margin> He fits the exemplary virtues suited to the soul into a certain order corresponding to the divine exemplars; he declares what the exemplar of each virtue is in God, and in what way the exemplary virtues in the soul rightly correspond to the divine exemplars of those virtues. And where he says that the soul is not "these very things which it possesses" in the same way the intellect is, understand the soul as a <term>discursive power</term> <note>original: "potentiam discurrentem" — a mind that moves from one thought to another rather than holding all truth at once</note>, in which the essence is one thing, the forms or images another, and the habits and actions yet another. But in the divine mind, the essence has been reduced into action from eternity; and that very essential action fulfills all those things which are performed in the soul through various additions. Moreover, our intellect is, in a certain way, what it possesses, to speak according to the mind of Plotinus.

# ON THE FIRST BOOK OF THE FIRST ENNEAD

For the soul is brought into actualization by an eternal and intimate contact with all the <term>Ideas</term> <note>the divine archetypes or perfect patterns of all things</note>: the very Ideas into whose action the divine mind has come forth from eternity. After this, he compares the virtues to one another in a certain way, and hand down certain precepts or resolves doubts. He says, therefore: those things which precede the complete purity of the soul are paths toward virtue, rather than virtue itself. Likewise, even purity is not considered virtue unless it is directed toward God—both to be imitated and to be pursued according to one’s strength. Furthermore, in the lower levels of the virtues, the higher ones do not exist except as an image. In the higher levels, however, the lower virtues are contained as an <term>exemplar</term> <note>an original model or pattern</note>. Likewise, where the principles change, the species of virtues also change. I mean two principles: namely, the specific end of each virtue, and its own rules and laws according to which it is formed; especially where the principles of <term>prudence</term> <note>original: "prudentia" — practical wisdom or the ability to govern oneself by reason</note> change, which is judged to be the rule of the other virtues. From this it follows that <term>temperance</term> <note>self-control and moderation</note> is of one species at the "civil" level, another at the "purifying" level, another at the "purified" level, and yet another at the "exemplary" level; and the other virtues follow a similar pattern. Finally, he concludes that the common and primary goal of all virtues is not found in external things, nor in virtue itself, nor in the soul, but in God. Indeed, nothing holier than this conclusion can be said. It testifies to the divine mind of our Plotinus.

#### ENNEAD I
#### BOOK II

->On the Virtues<-

<margin>A</margin>

Since evils exist here, and of necessity revolve around this place, and because the soul desires to flee from evils, we must undoubtedly flee from here. What then is this flight? It is, says Plato, to become "like unto God." And how is this done? It happens if we become just and holy with <term>prudence</term>, and live entirely according to virtue. If, therefore, we are made like Him through virtue, does it follow that we become like a God who possesses virtue? And indeed, to which God? Is it perhaps to the one who seems most likely to possess these things—namely, the <term>Soul of the World</term> <note>the "Anima Mundi," the mediating spirit between the divine intellect and the physical universe</note> and its inner leader, in whom there is a wonderful prudence? For it is reasonable that we, living here, should become like this being.
<margin>B</margin>
But perhaps it is first a matter of doubt whether all virtues belong to that being—for instance, being temperate and brave. For one who faces nothing terrifying has no need of bravery. Nothing from the outside happens to it, nor does any pleasure approach it whose desire might provoke it in its absence, so that it would need to possess or seize it.

Does that being itself then possess these virtues? <meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the hierarchy of virtues. Having established that the "civil" or social virtues are the first step, Plotinus now investigates how these virtues actually create a "likeness" to the Divine, despite the fact that the Divine Mind does not need to practice "virtue" in the way humans do.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD I.

<margin>A</margin>
...reasoning: furthermore, justice is the proper action of each of these parts [of the soul], agreeing in the matter of leading and being led. Perhaps we are not made like the Divine according to the <term>civil virtues</term> <note>original: "civiles virtutes" — the practical social virtues like justice, courage, and temperance that govern human life in society</note>, but according to greater virtues that share the same name? But if according to others, are we in no way made like Him according to the civil ones? Or perhaps it is contrary to reason to say we are in no way made like Him through these. For tradition also declares these virtues to be divine: and it must be said that we are made like Him in some way; but it is through the greater virtues that the true likeness occurs. In both ways, however, it seems to happen that God possesses virtues, even if they are not of the same kind as ours. If someone should grant that, although they are not the same, it is still possible to be made like Him—since we relate to some virtues in one way and He to others in another—nothing prevents us from being made like Him through our virtues, even though He does not possess virtue, with the likeness being of a kind that does not strictly involve "virtue" in the source. But how? In this way: If something becomes hot by the presence of heat, is it necessary that the source from which the heat comes is also "heated"? And if something is hot by the presence of fire, is it necessary that the fire itself be "heated" by the presence of fire? But to the first point, someone might say that there is indeed heat in the fire, but it is innate, so that the <term>reason</term> <note>original: "ratio" / "logos" — the underlying principle or logic of a thing</note> is drawn following an analogy: namely, that virtue is something added to the soul, but in that source from which the soul possesses it through imitation, it is innate. To the argument drawn from fire, someone will answer that virtue is present there, but it is a "virtue" greater than our virtue. But if that which the soul participates in were the same as the source from which it receives it, then one ought to speak in that way; but as it is, the source is one thing, and the participation is another. For the sensible house is not the same as the <term>intelligible house</term> <note>the perfect, non-physical idea or blueprint of a house existing in the divine mind</note>, although it is like it; for the sensible house receives order and ornament, but in the "reason" or idea itself there is no order, nor ornament, nor proportion in a physical sense. Thus, since we participate in ornament, order, and <term>harmony</term> <note>original: "consensionem" / Greek: "homologias"</note> from that source, and these things belong to virtue here below, but the things that are there do not require harmony, ornament, or order: then surely there will be no need for virtue there. Nevertheless, we become like those divine things through the presence of virtue. Let these things be said, then, primarily to show that it is not necessary for virtue to exist there just because we are made like them through virtue. However, one must not only compel the mind by logic, but also persuade it.

<margin>II The soul, through the civil virtues, as if by its measure and form, approaches more closely to divine likeness than matter does by receiving natural forms.</margin>

### FIRST, therefore, we must examine the virtues through which we say the likeness is made: so that we may find that very same thing which, being an imitation in us, is virtue, but there exists as a kind of <term>exemplar</term> <note>an original model or archetype</note> and is not virtue, signifying that the likeness is twofold. One kind of likeness requires the same nature in similar things, as happens when things are made similar by the same source in an equal or mutual proportion. But in cases where one thing is made like another, but the other is primary and does not turn back toward the imitation, nor is it said to be "like" it—here the likeness must be understood in another way, not requiring the same form, but rather a different one, since the likeness is formed according to a different principle. What then is virtue, both as a whole and in each part? The discourse will be clearer if we look at each part. For in this way, the common element itself, according to which all are virtues, will appear more easily. The civil virtues which we were just mentioning truly adorn us and make us better,

<note>The following Greek text is the original version of the Latin passage translated above.</note>

...reasoning, and justice as the proper action of each of them regarding being ruled. Are we then made like Him according to the civil virtues, or according to the greater ones using the same name? But if according to others, is it not at all according to the civil ones? Or is it unreasonable to not be made like Him in any way according to these? For fame also calls these "divine." And it must be said that we are made like Him in some way, but according to the <margin>B</margin> greater ones there is a [true] likeness. But in both ways it happens that he has virtues, and yet not such as ours. If therefore someone <gloss>*</gloss> <margin><gloss>*</gloss> agreement</note> concedes that even if they are not such, it is possible to be made like Him—we having some and He having others—nothing prevents <margin><gloss>*</gloss> us</margin> from being made like Him through our virtues, even if we are not made like Him according to civil virtues, but are made like Him who does not possess virtue. And how? <margin>C</margin> Thus: if by the presence of heat a thing is heated, is it necessary that the source from which the heat came is also heated? And if by the presence of fire a thing is hot, is it necessary that the fire itself be heated by the presence of fire? But to the former, one might say that in fire there is heat, but it is innate. So that the reasoning follows the analogy: virtue is adventitious [added from outside] to the soul, but to that <margin>D</margin> from which the soul has it by imitation, it is innate. To the argument from fire, [one would say] that the quality there is "virtue," but a virtue greater than what we deem virtue. Yes. But if that which the soul partakes in were the same as the source, then one should speak thus. But now that is one thing, and this is another. For the sensible house is not <gloss>*</gloss> <margin><gloss>*</gloss> itself</margin> the intelligible one, even if it has been made like it. <margin>E</margin> And the sensible house partakes of order and ornament; but there, in the "reason," there is no order, nor ornament, nor proportion. Thus then, partaking <gloss>*</gloss> <margin><gloss>*</gloss> partaking</margin> from there of ornament and order and agreement, and these things being virtue here, since those things there do not need agreement, nor ornament, nor order, there will be no need of virtues. And we are made like those things there no less through the presence of virtue. Regarding the fact that it is not necessary for virtue to be there, even though we are made like it by virtue, these [are the arguments]; but it is necessary to bring <gloss>*</gloss> <margin><gloss>*</gloss> the argument</margin> persuasion to the <margin>F</margin> argument, not remaining only <gloss>*</gloss> <margin><gloss>*</gloss> the argument</margin> upon force [of logic].

### FIRST then, we must take up the virtues according to which we say we are made like Him, so that we may find that same thing, which in us being an imitation is virtue, but there, being as it were an archetype, is not virtue. We should note that likeness is twofold: one as of the things that require the same in similar things, such as are equally made similar <margin>G</margin> by the same [source]. But in those things where one is made like another, and the other is primary—not being referred back to the former, nor being called "similar" to it—here the likeness must be taken in another way; not requiring the same form, but rather another, since it has been made like it in the other way. What then is virtue, both the whole and each part?

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of virtue. Having previously distinguished between social or "civil" virtues and higher virtues, Plotinus now explores how these virtues act as "measures" that bring the soul into harmony with the Divine.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD I. 13

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
They affect the soul by moderating desires and all other disturbances, and by removing false opinions in a better way. They do this because they define the soul and keep it outside the immeasurable and the indefinite. By being defined according to the measures that exist in the higher realm, they become similar to that measure and preserve a trace of the best thing which is there. For that which is entirely immeasurable, being matter itself, is entirely dissimilar to the Divine. But insofar as it 
<margin>B</margin>
receives form, it becomes similar to that which has no form <note>In Neoplatonic thought, the highest principle (The One) is "formless" because it is the source of all forms; thus, receiving a pure form makes one more like the Formless source than remaining as chaotic matter.</note>. Those things which are near to it participate more. The soul is closer and more related to the Divine than the body is, and therefore becomes a greater participant in it—to the extent that it can deceive us, appearing as a god and leading to the suspicion that it is entirely divine. This, then, is how these people become similar to God.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Definitions of purificatory virtue, and the common traits of a soul already purified.</margin>
<margin>Plato makes the comparison to God in such a way that our intelligence is far surpassed by the divine intelligence.</margin>
<margin>III</margin>
BUT since he <note>Referring to Plato</note> indicates that there is another kind of likeness which belongs to the greater virtue, we must speak of that. In this discussion, it will become clearer what the essence of <term>civil virtue</term> <note>The virtues of a good citizen (justice, temperance, etc.) as applied to social life.</note> is, and what the nature of the virtue that is more excellent in its essence is. It will also be established that there is another virtue entirely beyond the civil one. Plato says that likeness to God is a "flight from lower things" <note>A famous reference to Plato's *Theaetetus* 176b: "flee from here to there as quickly as possible."</note>. Furthermore, when he speaks of the virtues suitable for citizens, he does not call them simply "virtues," but assigns them the name "civil virtues." Elsewhere, he calls all virtues "purifications." It is clearly seen that he posits two types of virtue, and that 
<margin>D</margin>
the likeness to God is not fully achieved through civil virtue alone. How then do we call these "purifications"? And how, once purified, are we thoroughly made like Him? Perhaps it is because the soul is evil when it is mixed with the body, suffering along with it and agreeing with it in opinion through all things. Conversely, the soul will be good and endowed with virtue if it does not agree with the body, but acts alone—which is what "to think" and "to be wise" really mean. In this state, the soul is not "co-passionate" (which is to be temperate); it does not fear the departure from the body (which is to be courageous); and it allows reason and intellect to lead while the other parts do not resist (which is to be just). If someone calls this state of the soul—in which it understands and lives far from disturbance—a "likeness to God," they would not be mistaken. For the Divine is pure, and its activity is such that whatever imitates it possesses wisdom. What then? 
<margin>F</margin>
Is the Divine itself affected in this way? Perhaps it is not even "affected" at all. A disposition or state belongs to the soul; the soul thinks in a different way than God does. Of the things that are said to exist there in the divine realm, some exist differently than they do here, and others do not exist there at all. Is the term "to think," then, being used equivocally? Not at all. Rather, that thinking exists primarily, while our thinking proceeds from it and exists in a different manner. For as the spoken word is an imitation of the word in the soul, so the word in the soul is an imitation of that 
<margin>IIII</margin>
<margin>The soul must be rendered pure so that the purified mind may turn toward its own proper intellect, and from there to the divine: so that the models of the virtues may be brought back from that source.</margin>
which remains in the higher realm. Just as the spoken word is "divided" (uttered in parts) when compared to the word in the soul, so the word in the soul is an interpreter of the higher word, and is divided compared to what came before it. Virtue, however, belongs to the soul; it does not belong to the Intellect, nor to that which is beyond Intellect <note>Original: "mens" and "mente superius" referring to the *Nous* and *The One*.</note>.

WE MUST INQUIRE whether purification is the same thing as this kind of virtue, or does purification come first and virtue follow? And does virtue consist in the process of being purified, or in the purification already completed? Surely the virtue still laboring in the process of purifying is less perfect; for the goal of that labor is the virtue of one who has already been purified. But to have been purified is the removal of everything alien...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of virtue, moving from the "civil virtues" discussed previously to the higher "purificatory virtues." It examines how the soul, by stripping away the material and the alien, returns to its true intellectual nature.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD I. 14

<margin>
V
The virtues of the purified soul are defined, and their duties are set forth.
</margin>
...to have been purified <note>The Latin text begins mid-word with "rificatum," likely completing "purificatum."</note> is the removal of everything alien. But the Good seems to be something other than this purification itself. Perhaps if the soul was good before it lost its purity, the purification itself might suffice; but even then, while the purification is sufficient, the Good is what remains, not the purification itself. Then we must ask what that which remains actually is. For perhaps the underlying nature left behind is not the Good; otherwise, it would never have fallen into evil. Should we then say it is "good-form" <note>original: "boniformem"; having the shape or appearance of the good</note>? Or rather that it is not sufficient to remain in that which is truly Good? For its nature leans in both directions. Therefore, its good is to cling to its kindred, and its evil is to cling to its opposites. It is necessary, then, for the soul, once purified, to cling; and it will cling by being converted.

Does it then convert after the purification? Or is it already converted by the very act of purification? This, then, is its virtue: or rather, is it that which follows from the conversion? What then is this? It is a vision, an impression of the thing seen, imprinted and active within, just as sight acts concerning the visible. Therefore, the soul did not previously possess these things, nor does it remember them; or perhaps it did possess them, but not as active things, lying instead dormant and obscured. But so that they may be illuminated, and the soul may then recognize them as being within, it must move toward that which illuminates it. It possessed not the things themselves, but their figures <note>original: "figuras"; images or representations</note>. It is necessary, therefore, to perfectly accommodate the figures to the true things of which they are the shapes. Perhaps in this way the soul is thought to possess them from above; for the Intellect is not alien, and it is most especially not alien when the soul looks toward it. Otherwise, even when present, the Intellect is alien; just as sciences are alien to us if we do not use them at all.

MOREOVER, we must state how far the purification should proceed. For in this way it will be clear to which god the soul becomes similar and identical. This is primarily to ask to what extent it is possible to purify the soul from anger, desire, pleasure, and pain, and similar things, and to separate the soul from the body. To separate it from the body means, perhaps, for the soul to collect itself as if from diverse places, remaining entirely segregated from disturbances, and ensuring that necessary pleasures are merely sensations and some kind of remedies or quietings of labors or weariness, so that no interruption occurs. It should remove pains; and if it cannot, it should bear them moderately and diminish them by not suffering along with the body. It should remove anger as much as possible, even entirely if it can; but if not, at least the soul itself should not join in the anger. It will see to it that the "unpremeditated" <note>original: "inconsulto"; an involuntary or sudden impulse</note> and sudden movement belongs to another part, and that this suddenness is very small and weak. Furthermore, it will expel fear entirely, for it will fear nothing; though sudden movement may occur here too, unless it serves as a warning. As for desire for shameful things, it will clearly have none; nor will the soul itself have a desire for food and drink for the sake of easing pain, nor for sexual pleasures. If it does have them, I think they will be only natural, and even then without an unpremeditated impulse. But if it should have them, they will extend only as far as the imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note> and even then will be unpremeditated. In short, the soul itself will be pure of all these things, and it will wish to make the irrational part pure as well, so that it is not even shaken; or if it is, that the shocks be minimal and immediately calmed by the soul's proximity. Just as if someone living near a wise man were to benefit from that very proximity

<column-break/>

**A** ...to strip away everything [alien], but the Good is something other than it. Or, if it was good before the impurity, purification is enough. But though purification is sufficient, the thing left behind will be the Good, not the purification. And we must seek what it is that is left behind. For perhaps the nature remaining was not the Good; for otherwise it would not have been in evil. Should we then say it is "of the form of good"? Or
**B** is it not sufficiently able to remain in that which is truly good? For its nature is inclined toward both. Its good, then, consists in being with its kin, and its evil in being with its opposites. It must, therefore, be with its kin once purified; and it will be so by being converted <note>original: "ἐπιστραφεῖσα" (epistrapheisa); turned back toward the source</note>. Does it then convert after the purification? Or is it already converted after the purification? Is this then its virtue, or that which happens to it from the conversion? What then is this? A vision and a type <note>original: "τύπος" (typos); an impression or stamp</note> of the thing seen, placed within and 
**C** active, as sight is regarding the object seen. Did it not then possess them, nor does it remember them? Or did it possess them not as active, but as underlying things unlit? But so that they may be lit, and that it may then know them as being within, it must apply itself to that which illuminates. It possessed not the things themselves, but types. It must, then, fit the type to the true things of which they are the types. Perhaps
**D** it is said to have them in this way, because the Intellect is not alien, and most especially not alien when the soul looks toward it. Otherwise, even when present it is alien; since even sciences, if we do not act according to them at all, are alien.

**E** BUT we must say to what extent the purification goes. For thus it will be clear to what [divinity] the likeness belongs and with which god it is identical. This is especially to seek how far it is possible to dissolve anger and desire and all other things, such as grief and its kin, and to separate from the body. From the body, perhaps, by gathering itself toward itself as if from certain places, being entirely unaffected, and making the sensations of necessary pleasures only, as well as healings and releases from pains, so that it is not troubled; and removing pains, or if it is not possible, bearing them mildly and 
**F** making them less by not suffering with them; and removing anger as much as possible, and if possible, entirely; but if not, at least not joining in the anger itself, but letting the "unpremeditated" <note>original: "ἀπροαίρετον" (aproaireton); involuntary or without choice</note> belong to another; and that the unpremeditated be small and weak. And as for fear, [it will remove it] entirely (for what should it fear? It will fear nothing). And the unpremeditated is here too, unless it be for warning. As for desire, it is clear there will be none for anything base. Of food and drink for relaxation, the soul itself will not have it, nor of sexual matters. If it should, they would be natural, I think, and not even 
**G** having the unpremeditated. Or if so, only as far as the imagination, and even the imagination would be unpremeditated. In short, the soul itself will be pure of all these things, and it will wish to make the irrational part pure also, so that it is not even struck; or if so, that its strikes be few and small, and immediately dissolved by the proximity [of the soul], just as if someone living near a wise man were to benefit...

He details how a purified person should manage physical passions like anger, fear, and desire, reducing them to minimal, involuntary impulses.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the "purificatory virtues." Having established that the soul must be cleansed of material attachments, Plotinus now discusses how the soul transitions from a human state of "civic virtue" to a divine state of "paradigmatic virtue," where the soul no longer struggles against its lower nature but is entirely ruled by the Intellect.</meta>

# BOOK THE SECOND

...perceiving the neighborhood of the Wise One: either having become like him, or out of reverence, so that it dares to do nothing of which the good man would not approve. <note>original: "τοῦ δεσπότου"; here "the master" refers to the higher Reason or Intellect that should rule the soul.</note> There will therefore be no battle. For the presence of reason is sufficient, which the lower part will revere to such an extent that it is even displeased with itself if it is moved at all—because it did not keep quiet while the master was present—and it will reproach its own weakness.

**It is** therefore not a sin for such things to occur <note>referring to the movements of the lower soul</note>, but rather a correction for a man, and his duty. For the aim is not simply to be without sin, but to be a god. <note>This is a central Neoplatonic goal: "deification" or "likeness to God" (homoiosis theo).</note> If, therefore, any of these things should happen involuntarily, such a man would be both a god and a <term>daemon</term> <note>In this context, a "daemon" is a tutelary spirit or a secondary divine being, not an evil spirit.</note>, being double; or rather, having another with him who possesses a different virtue. But if nothing of the sort happens, he is a god alone—a god of those who follow the First. For he himself is the one who came from there. And if he should live by himself as he was when he came, he is there <note>i.e., in the intelligible realm</note>. But now that he has come to live here, he has seen he has this <note>the lower soul</note>, and he has made it like himself and strengthened it, so that, if possible, it might be unswayed, or at least perform nothing that is not pleasing to the master. 

What, then, is each specific virtue for such a person? Wisdom is the contemplation of what the Intellect <note>original: "νοῦς" (Nous)</note> possesses; but the Intellect possesses these by a kind of "touch." <note>original: "ἐπαφῇ"; Plotinus uses the metaphor of touch to describe the direct, non-discursive way the Intellect knows truth.</note> Each of these is twofold: one being in the Intellect, the other in the soul. And in the Intellect, it is not "virtue" as such, but in the soul, it is virtue. What is it there, then? It is the activity of the Intellect and its very essence; but here, as it exists in another, it is virtue derived from there. For neither Justice itself <note>original: "αὐτοδικαιοσύνη"</note> nor any of the other virtues in the Intellect are virtues in the human sense, but are like models or archetypes. That which comes from them into the soul is virtue, for virtue belongs to someone. But the archetype itself belongs to itself and not to another. 

If Justice is "doing one's own work" <note>original: "οἰκειοπραγία"; a Platonic definition of justice where every part of the soul performs its proper function.</note>, does it always require a multitude of parts? Justice exists in a multitude when there are many parts; but it is simply the act of doing one's own work even if it belongs to only one thing. True Justice, then, is the relationship of the one toward itself, in which there is no "one thing and another." <margin>D</margin> Thus, for the soul, the greater Justice is to direct its activity toward the Intellect. Temperance <note>original: "σωφρονεῖν"</note> is the internal turning toward the Intellect. Courage <note>original: "ἀνδρία"</note> is the state of being free from passion, patterned after that toward which it looks, which is by nature impassive. <margin>* d'</margin> This comes from virtue, so that the soul does not suffer along with its inferior companion <note>the body or the lower soul</note>.

<margin>E</margin> **These virtues** follow one another in the soul, just as the models in the Intellect exist before virtue. For there, thinking is knowledge and wisdom; turning toward itself is temperance; its own proper work is "doing one's own business" and justice; and that which is like courage is immateriality and remaining pure within itself. In the soul, therefore, the vision directed toward the Intellect is wisdom and prudence, which are its virtues. For the soul is not these things themselves, as the Intellect is. And the other virtues follow in the same way. So too with purification, <margin>G</margin> since all virtues are kinds of purification, they must all exist in a completed state of being purified, or none of them would be perfect. And he who possesses the greater virtues necessarily possesses the lesser ones potentially; but he who has the lesser does not necessarily have the greater. This, then, is the primary life of the virtuous man. But whether he possesses the lesser virtues in actuality...

<column-break/>

...perceives: either having been made like him, or having revered him, so that he dares to do nothing of which the good man does not approve. There will therefore be no battle. For the present reason is sufficient: which that lower part will revere: so much so that it is angry with itself if it is moved in any way, and does not keep quiet in the presence of the master, and it reproaches its own inconstancy.

<margin>VI. He confirms that the end of virtue is to enjoy the gods: and the exemplary virtues are finally defined as being acquired by us.</margin>
**There is** therefore no sin in such things, but rather a correction for a man, and his duty. But the very pursuit and desire is not to be without sin, but to be a god. If, therefore, any such thing should happen only inadvertently, such a person will be a god and a <term>daemon</term>, existing as a double being: or rather, having another with him endowed with a different virtue; but if nothing [inadvertent occurs], he is a god alone. A god, I say, from the number of those who follow the First. For he himself is the one who proceeded from there. And if he lives according to himself, as he came, he is there: but he clings to the intellect having set out for here: and his power will furthermore assimilate this [lower part] to him: so that if it were possible, it would neither be <margin>D</margin> moved, nor do anything from those things which are least pleasing to the master. 

What then is any virtue to such a one? Wisdom is indeed the inspection of those things which the intellect possesses. But the intellect possesses them by a certain touch. Moreover, each is twofold: one existing in the intellect, the other in the soul. And there it is not virtue, but in the soul it is virtue. There, then, what is it? It is the action of [the intellect] and that which it is; but here it is what is in another, and is virtue from there. For neither is justice itself, nor temperance itself, <margin>E</margin> nor anything similar, a virtue of its own essence, but like an exemplar. That which is produced by it in the soul is already virtue, for it is the virtue of someone. But each thing itself belongs to itself, and not to someone else. 

If justice is indeed the action of one's own duty, is it then always in a multitude of parts? Rather, it is in a multitude whenever there are many parts. But simply, it is the action of one's own duty, even if it exists in one alone. True justice itself, therefore, is of the one toward himself, in which there is not "one thing and another." For which reason, the greater justice for the soul itself is to direct its activity toward the intellect. Temperance is the inward conversion toward the intellect. Fortitude is a habit free from passion, by the likeness of that at which it looks, which is naturally constituted outside of passion. But the soul through virtue overcomes passion, so that it does not suffer together with its inferior companion.

<margin>VII. He accommodates the exemplary virtues to us in a certain order, and fits them to the divine exemplar: then he compares the virtues among themselves: he resolves doubts: and proves the divine end of virtue.</margin>
**These virtues** follow each other in turn in the soul, just as in the intellect those things which come before virtue are exemplars. For indeed, intellection there is science and wisdom; but to be converted toward itself is temperance. Its own work is called the action of its own parts, and justice. Finally, in place of fortitude is that separation from matter and pure remaining in itself. In the soul, therefore, the intuition into the intellect is wisdom and prudence, its virtues. For the soul is not these things which it has, in the same way as the intellect. The other virtues likewise follow in a similar way, and purification likewise. 

It is necessary, indeed, if all virtues <margin>G</margin> are certain purifications, that they consist in a certain completed purification; otherwise none would be perfect. Furthermore, whoever has the greater must necessarily have the lesser in potential; conversely, he who has the lesser does not necessarily have the greater. This is the principal life of a man endowed with virtue. But whether he has the lesser in act...

<summary>This page defines the "paradigmatic" or higher virtues, arguing that the soul's ultimate goal is not just human morality but becoming like a god by aligning itself with the Intellect. Plotinus reinterprets the four cardinal virtues (Wisdom, Justice, Temperance, and Courage) as internal states of the soul's relationship to its higher source.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the "purificatory virtues" of the soul. On page 15, Plotinus established that a person seeking the divine must transcend mere "civic virtue" (good citizenship) to reach a state where the lower soul is entirely silent in the presence of the Intellect. Here, he begins to examine whether these higher virtues differ in kind from the lower ones and how the soul models itself after the divine archetype.</meta>

<page-num>16</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS, ENNEAD I.</header>

<margin>A</margin> Whether these things <note>original: "res"; referring to the virtues</note> are greater, or whether one should consider them individually in another way, such as prudence <note>original: "prudentiam" / "φρόνησιν" (phronesis)</note>. For if it uses other principles, how does it still remain the same virtue? And what if it is not even active? Likewise, if the nature of the lower virtue proceeds only this far, while the higher proceeds that far: and if that temperance <note>original: "temperantia" / "σωφροσύνη" (sophrosyne)</note> merely moderates, while the higher virtue removes the passions entirely. The same applies to the others, once prudence has been moved altogether. Perhaps the soul will see how much it holds within itself. And perhaps at some time, under certain circumstances, it will act according to some of those lower virtues.

<margin>B</margin> But ascending to greater principles and acting through other measures according to them, the soul will operate by such rules: for example, placing temperance not in that former measure, but separating itself entirely as far as possible, and living not the life of a "good man" such as civic virtue <note>original: "ciuilis probaret virtus"</note> would approve, but leaving this behind and choosing another—namely, the divine life. For the likeness proposed to us is toward the gods, not toward good men. Our likeness to good men is as if one image were likened to another image, since both are produced from the same source.

<margin>C</margin> But that other likeness <note>the divine one</note> is perfected toward another thing, as if toward an exemplar <note>original: "exemplar" / "παράδειγμα" (paradeigma) or archetype</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Whether these virtues are smaller or greater, or in another way, must be considered in each case, such as prudence. For if it will use other principles, how does that virtue still remain? And what if it is not even acting? Or if the nature of one is of such a degree, and the other of such a degree? And if that temperance is a moderating force, but the other is a total removal. The same holds for the others, once prudence is entirely shifted. Or perhaps the soul will know them, or how much it will have of them from its own resources. And perhaps at some time, it will act through some of them according to circumstances.

<margin>B</margin> But having come to greater principles, it will perform other measures according to those. For instance, in practicing temperance, it does not place it in that former measure, but separates it entirely as much as possible; and living altogether not the life of a good man which civic virtue requires, but leaving this one behind, choosing that other life of the gods. For the likeness is toward these, not toward good men. For likeness toward the latter is as one image is made like another image when both come from the same source; but the likeness toward the former is as if toward a model <note>original: "παράδειγμα" (paradeigma)</note>.

# MARSILIO FICINO’S ARGUMENT ON THE BOOK CONCERNING THE TRIPLE RETURN OF THE SOUL, AS A DIVINE PRELUDE.

->In which he treats the Trinity that produces, restores, and perfects, and the ninefold number in divine matters.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'V' featuring a man's face and leafy flourishes.</image-desc>Where others have titled this book *On Dialectic*, they judged it should be named after its more excellent part. Although (as I think) they would have titled it much more correctly if they had called it *On the Return of Souls to the Divine*. For this is the greatest, indeed the entire wish of the book. This is the first thing proposed to be investigated; this is treated in every part of the discussion. Because Plotinus here delights in the number three, leading us to God by a triple path, it is helpful as a sort of prelude to wander a little more freely through the number three. The higher principles of the universe produce those things which follow; they lead back <note>original: "reducunt"</note> what has been produced; and they perfect what has been led back. While they produce, they grant "being"; while they convert, they preserve "being"; when they perfect, they reform it into a "better being." From these effects, which are counted as a composite trinity, we ascend to the absolute and threefold Trinity: namely, the Productive, the Restorative <note>original: "conuersoniam"; referring to the soul turning back toward God</note>, and the Perfecting.

In the Productive Trinity, the first is the Good itself; the second is the Intellect, the son of the Good; the third is the Soul and the life of the world, acting as the spirit of the divine Intelligence. How these three produce all things with one single consent will be discussed often elsewhere. Next follows the Restorative Trinity, or the one that leads back to the higher realms: in which Mercury <note>The god associated with Reason and communication.</note> holds the first rank, recalling souls to sublime things through reason; the second is Venus, alluring them to the supernal through sight; the third is Phoebus <note>Apollo, the god of light and music.</note>, effecting the same through hearing. And even if each of the three calls us back to all higher things, Mercury does so especially to the Good itself; Venus to the Intellect in which the first beauty shines; and Phoebus to the Soul, to which harmony most belongs—as we have treated more widely in the compendium of the *Timaeus* and in our *Theology*. 

Indeed, each of these three planets acts through its own intellect upon our reason, through its animal power upon our imagination, and through its body upon our body, to allure us toward the same goal. Finally, all three lead first to the planet Saturn, the leader of intelligence; then to the higher Saturn, the father of intelligence and the first Intellect; and at last to the Good itself, the father of Saturn. Moreover, Mercurial, Venereal, and Phoebean <term>daemons</term> <note>Spiritual intermediaries associated with these planetary influences.</note>, and finally Saturnian daemons, similarly assist in this same office. 

There remains the Perfecting Trinity, similarly distributed into a ninefold <note>original: "nouenarium"</note> structure. For whether the soul is led back to the Soul of the World itself, or higher to the Mind, the queen of the world, or more loftily to the Good itself, the father of intelligence, it surely recognizes the Father as the beginning, middle, and end of all—which is opened more clearly in the fourth book of the *Laws*. It recognizes the Divine Mind as essence, as life, and as intellect; and finally the Soul as life, as motion, and as reason—describing that life as a "mobile reason." Again, everything it finds in the lower things, it adapts by a certain proportion to the individual things present in the higher ones. Thus, it refers the reason in the soul to the Intellect reigning in the Mind, and to the end considered concerning the Good. Similarly, it refers the motion of the soul to the life of the Mind and to the "middle" in the Good; and finally, it refers the life of the soul to the essence of the Mind and to the very principle of the universe. 

But let us set aside these other trinities for the present. For in this book, the discussion is primarily about the Restorative Trinity, and especially the way in which the soul is recalled to the Divine Mind, insofar as it is thought of as both intellect and something intelligible. For from there, one suddenly arrives at the Good itself. In this Intellect, the Ideas are comprehended, which Plotinus elsewhere also calls certain "numbers." Therefore, the soul, called toward these, considers a trinity in each one. For it contemplates them as truth, as concord (or proportion), and as beauty—which Plato discusses in the *Philebus*: Mercury leading to truth, Apollo to concord...

Ficino explains how the soul is produced, returned, and perfected through a series of divine Trinities linked to planetary influences and Platonic philosophy.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page transitions from the specific virtues discussed on page 16 to the metaphysical framework of how the soul ascends to the "Good." It explores the three paths to the divine (philosopher, lover, musician) and the nature of the "Absolute Good."</meta>

<header>ON BOOK II OF THE FIRST ENNEAD.</header>

Venus leads the soul toward beauty. In truth, the mind recognizes the perpetual firmness of nature, as well as a purity that admits nothing foreign, and an integrity that never loses what is its own. It also contemplates Concord in a similar three-fold pattern, insofar as any given "idea" <note>An "idea" in Platonic thought is a perfect, divine blueprint for something in the physical world.</note> agrees with itself, harmonizes with those above it, and fits with those below it. It likewise views Beauty as a trinity; for a true, harmonious idea appears to us as a beautiful Venus surrounded by the three Graces. It approaches the soul to be admired, joins it to be loved, and enters it to be enjoyed. Thus, the "ideal trinity" is properly expanded into a "nonary" <note>original: "nonarium"; a group of nine.</note>. In the same way, the trinity that turns the soul back toward the divine ideas is derived into a nonary, because Mercury does not only turn the soul back by his own power, but in this duty he joins partly with Venus and partly with Apollo. By the same logic, Venus both calls the soul back by her own nature and harmonizes differently with Mercury and with Apollo. Finally, Apollo acts by his own power, agreeing here with Mercury and there with Venus.

### That the goal of the soul is beyond intellectual nature, toward the Good itself.

The book is divided into three chapters, just as there are three paths to divinity. The third chapter, being the most important, is divided again into three parts. In the first part, the author describes the goal that must finally be reached: he suggests that the soul does not find rest in some "intellectual" or "intelligible" good—which are nearly the same thing—but rather in the "Absolute Good" and the highest principle itself. For the appetite for the good proceeds only as far as the discovery of the good proceeds. But just as the most keen-scented hounds find by the power of smell what they do not yet see with their eyes, and perhaps may never see, so the soul, by a wonderful sagacity of nature and intellect, prophesies that the Good exists, towering above all eyes of the intelligence. Just as we find nothing above the "sensible" <note>Capable of being perceived by the senses.</note> through the senses, so we find nothing above the "intelligible" through the intellect. But just as we find the intelligible above the sensible by using an intellect superior to the senses, so by a certain power of the soul superior to the intellect, we both guess at and desire the "Absolute Good" itself, which is above any intellectual or intelligible good. Once you have spoken of "the Good" itself, to immediately add the word "intellectual" or "intelligible" is nothing other than to describe a "partial good"—something good that is either lying within the intellect, or at least confined to the limits of intelligence, or marked by some intellectual quality. Above this, however—as if above something imperfect, narrow, and dependent—is the Absolute Good itself, without limit. By its most ample power, both the intellectual good and the non-intellectual good are made; both the non-sensible good and the sensible good are created. For toward these opposites, the Absolute Good spreads itself everywhere. This is what the soul desires as its ultimate end; it enjoys this not through some imaginary perception of the intelligence, but through a true understanding of a superior power and a "substantial contact." Here, the soul does not only see, but also tastes and touches "how sweet the Lord is" <note>original: "quàm suauis sit dominus"; a reference to Psalm 34:8.</note>. This is what David (as I believe) calls the "great multitude of sweetness" hidden with God, entirely concealed from the intelligence. Since the Absolute Good is above knowledge and above the "knowable" good, the natural affection of the soul drives it toward knowledge, yet not as its highest end. Otherwise, the end would be a mere "accident" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a non-essential quality, unlike "substance" or "essence."</note> of our being, and no knowledge would ever fail us, and some imaginary shadow of the good offering itself to our knowledge would satisfy the desire of our nature. Nature, therefore, desires knowledge not for the sake of knowledge alone, but so that through it, it may seek, find, and apprehend the Good in whatever way possible. It is not the nature of this Good to be "known" or to be "knowledge," but rather to truly harmonize, to provide, to sweetly refresh, and to help. In this state—which is far more excellent than the intellect or the intelligible—the soul finally rests as if in its ultimate natural end, through a power superior to the intellect. The Apostle Paul calls this kind of affection a "love" that is higher than the limits of sense and intelligence. Let this suffice for now regarding the goal.

### On the intelligible and sensible worlds: and on the triple path and nature toward the intelligible.

Let us now proceed to the "paths," and to those people who, through these paths, might more easily progress toward this goal or be led there. The Platonists propose two main worlds: First, the "Intelligible World," which is the Divine Mind, the principle and model of this world. Second, the "Sensible World," which is this world manifest to the senses, the image of the divine model. Plotinus thinks our soul is always in the first world through the intellect, but always in the second world through its "vegetative" nature—just as a ray of the sun touches both the earth at one end and the sun at the other. Through its "middle nature" <note>The rational soul, situated between the high intellect and the lower bodily functions.</note> placed in the first motion (which is perpetual and circular), the soul undergoes perpetual cycles: it lives for one age in the intelligible world, and for another in the sensible world. This does not happen through a literal change of place; rather, when the imagination turns toward reason, and reason turns entirely toward the mind, then the soul is said to have "ascended" to the intelligible world. But when reason bends toward its imagination, and the imagination toward the lower "animal" imagination (whether of something already born or about to be born), then the soul is judged to have "fallen" into the sensible world. He teaches that souls are of three kinds: Some are always in the higher world, such as the souls of the celestial spheres, the stars, and the higher spirits <note>original: "dæmonum"; in the Neoplatonic sense, these are intermediary divine beings, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note>. Others are only in the lower world, such as those dedicated only to growth and the passions of the senses. But the "middle" souls—the rational ones, whether they are ours or those of the lower spirits—pass back and forth in eternal cycles. Accordingly, our souls contemplate or are affected by the higher world, some more intently and others more loosely, just as in this world we see some people more affected by these things than others. Now, those souls that work more readily there contemplate either all or many divine things. Therefore, when such souls (having finished certain cycles of time) gradually slide back toward sensible things, they remain ready for a longer time to remember divine things. Those who are the most ready of all are judged to be endowed with a "philosophical nature." Those who are ready in the second degree have an "amorous nature" <note>original: "ingenio potissimum amatorio"; the nature of a lover of beauty.</note>. Finally, those in the third degree are more suited to "music." For those who are enslaved to physical things through touch, taste, and smell are judged to be the most distant from that incorporeal world; they seem not to have recently descended from it, but to have migrated here from somewhere else entirely. But the philosophical nature, while it investigates the "reasons" of natural things through reason—reasons which are derived primarily from the "ideas"—begins to see the divine ideas. Therefore, the eyes are rightly judged to be the closest and most attentive servants of our reason. This is because they are less "physical" and seem to deal with things that are somewhat less physical; moreover, the things offered to the eyes and ears more clearly show a certain most exact order. For this reason, we are more easily provoked by these two senses than by the others toward the intellect and the intellectual "reasons" from which all order is arranged. Thus, while reason hastens toward the wisdom of divine things, the sight meanwhile provides the mind with discoveries as best it can, and hearing suggests "discipline" <note>original: "disciplinam"; often referring to formal learning or mathematical study.</note>. Therefore, by a triple...

<header>PLOTINUS ENNEAD I.</header>

...the other path, however, is for those who have already reached the higher realms. 
->A<-
The first path indeed ascends from lower things; but the second belongs to those who are already in the intelligible <note>The "intelligible" (Latin: *intelligibilis*; Greek: *noētos*) refers to the realm of pure ideas and divine intellect, which Plotinus considers more real than the physical world.</note> place, and have set their footsteps there. They must proceed further until they have reached the very summit. This represents the end of the journey, which occurs when one reaches the peak of the intelligible world. But let this second process wait for now. Regarding the ascent and the "leading back," we must first attempt to speak.
->B<-
First, we must distinguish between these men, beginning with the **musician**, by describing what his nature is. We must define him as one who is easily moved and awestruck by beauty, but who is not sufficiently able to be moved by himself. However, he is easily stirred by whatever chance forms he encounters. Just as the timid are startled by a noise, so is he stirred by harmonious sounds. He is naturally inclined toward the beauty that appears in sounds, and he flees from dissonance everywhere. He seeks that which is "one" <note>Plotinus emphasizes "The One" as the ultimate source; here, the musician finds a reflection of that unity in the harmony of a song.</note> in songs and rhythms, and follows what is well-proportioned and graceful.
->C<-
Therefore, after these sensible <note>Meaning things perceived by the senses.</note> sounds, rhythms, and forms, one must lead him in this way: namely, by separating out the matter in which the proportions and their comparisons reside, and leading him back to the beauty that is within them. Furthermore, he must be taught that the things he was so vehemently awestruck by are not these physical sounds, but rather an *intelligible harmony*, and the beauty within it—and indeed, Beauty itself, not just some beautiful thing. 
->D<-
Finally, one must apply the principles of philosophy to him, through which he may be led to a firm belief in the things he possesses but does not yet know. What these principles are, we shall declare in what follows.

<margin>
II
The amorous nature must be recalled from the beauty of the body, then to the beauty of the sciences, and finally to the beauty of the mind.
</margin>

# II
The **LOVER**, into whose character the musician might perhaps fall—and having fallen, either stays there or passes through—remembers beauty in a certain way. But because he is separate from Beauty itself, he cannot perceive it clearly. 
->E<-
Struck by the beauties that are open to his sight, he is vehemently stirred by them. Therefore, one must teach him not to fall forward and revolve around a single body, but he should be properly guided by reason to all beautiful bodies. He should consider that the same beauty is in all of them, and realize that beauty is something different from the bodies themselves—that it proceeds from elsewhere and exists more fully in other things, such as beautiful pursuits and beautiful laws. For in these things, the lover's interest already becomes accustomed to loving incorporeal things.

->F<-
It must be shown, furthermore, that beauty exists also in the arts, the sciences, and the virtues, and that there is one beauty in all of them; and in what manner this beauty comes to be. Finally, from the virtues one must reach the Intellect and Being itself, and there complete the journey to the heights.

<margin>
III
The philosophical nature is by nature released from matter and only requires a guide to divine beauty through certain stages of discipline.
</margin>

# III
The **PHILOSOPHER** is naturally ready and, as it were, "winged." He does not require the same process of separation as those we mentioned a little while ago, for he is already stirred toward the higher things; however, being uncertain, he only requires someone to show the way. 
->G<-
Therefore, it is worthwhile to demonstrate the path and lead the man who is willing to be led by nature and who has long been released from bonds. Mathematical studies should therefore be employed, so that he may become accustomed to thinking of and believing in the incorporeal. For he will perceive them easily, since he is greedy for learning; and his nature, being noble by its natural virtue, must be led toward the perfection of the virtues:

<column-break/>

...or for those who have returned.
->A<-
The first path is from the things below, while the second is for those who have already reached the intelligible realm and have, as it were, set a footprint there. They must necessarily travel there until they arrive at the furthest point of the place. This happens to be the end of the journey, when one reaches the top of the intelligible. But let that path wait; regarding the "leading up," we must try to speak a second time.
->B<-
First, then, we must distinguish these men for ourselves, beginning with the **musician**, by describing his nature. We must define him as someone easily moved and excited by beauty, but less able to be moved by himself. He is ready to be cast out, as it were, by whatever he encounters; just as the cowardly are toward noises, so is he toward sounds and the beauty found in them. He always flees from the discordant and that which is not "one" in songs and rhythms, and he pursues the well-ordered and the well-formed.
->C<-
After these sensible sounds and rhythms and forms, he must be led in this way: by separating the matter on which the proportions and ratios <note>original: "λόγοι" (logoi)</note> depend, he must be led to the beauty that is upon them. And he must be taught that those things about which he was excited were the *intelligible harmony* and the beauty in it—and Beauty in general, toward Beauty alone. One must instill the reasonings of philosophy, from which he is led to a firm grasp of what he possesses without knowing. What those reasonings are, we must say later.
->D<-
The **LOVER**—into which the musician might change, and having changed, might either stay there or move beyond—is in some way mindful of beauty. But being apart from it, he is unable to fully understand it. Struck by the beauties in his sight, he is excited by them. 
->E<-
He must therefore be taught not to be so affected as to be excited by one body, but he must be led by reason to all bodies, showing him that which is the same in all, and that it is different from the bodies; and it must be said that it comes from elsewhere, and that it exists more in other things—such as beautiful practices and beautiful laws. The habit of loving the incorporeal is already shown in these things, and that it exists in the arts, the sciences, and the virtues. Then these must be made "one," and he must be taught how they come to be. From the virtues he now ascends to Intellect, to Being, and there he must travel the upward path.

<margin>F</margin>
->G<-
The **PHILOSOPHER** is by nature ready and, as it were, "winged," and not in need of separation like those others, having been moved toward the things above. But being in doubt of one to show the way, he needs only that. One must therefore show him and release him, for he is willing. Mathematical lessons should be given to him for the sake of habituating him to the understanding of and belief in the incorporeal. For he receives them easily, being a lover of learning; and his naturally virtuous character must be led toward the perfection of the virtues.

# BOOK THREE.

...should be taught <note>Original Greek: *...τέον*, the suffix of a verb indicating necessity, likely "must be educated" or "must be taught."</note>, or whether after mathematical studies one should provide dialectical discourses, or simply make them skilled in dialectic.

<column-break/>

and after mathematical reasoning, to hand down dialectic, and to make one thoroughly a dialectician.

->A<-

<margin>Dialectic, that is, metaphysics; for it contemplates the whole breadth [of reality], and proceeds beyond, and uses logic as a single instrument.</margin>
What is this "dialectic" which must also be granted to those who have come before? It is certainly a state of mind <note>Greek: *hexis*; Latin: *habitus*. A settled disposition or skill.</note> capable of saying in speech what each thing is: how it differs from others, and in what way it is the same. Furthermore, it determines how and where each thing is, and if it truly exists, and how many real beings there are, and conversely, what things are "non-beings" <note>Plotinus uses "non-being" to refer to things that are not permanent or fundamental, like physical matter, compared to eternal ideas.</note>—which are distinct from true beings. This same science also discusses the Good itself, and
->B<-
that which is not good, and those things that fall under the Good, and those that fall under its opposite. Likewise, it discusses what is eternal and what is not. I say it treats all things not by mere opinion, but by certain knowledge. Free from the error that occurs around the world of the senses, it adheres entirely to the intelligible <note>The realm of pure thought and divine mind.</note> world. It acts diligently around that realm, setting aside what is false, nourishing the soul in what is called the "field of truth" <note>Greek: *alētheias pedion*. A poetic reference to the place where the soul finds its ultimate satisfaction.</note>. It relies on the Platonic method of "division" <note>Greek: *diairesis*. The process of categorizing things by dividing them into their natural components.</note> to distinguish ideas and species, and to define each thing. It reaches toward the primary "genera" <note>The "Greatest Kinds" from Plato's *Sophist*: Being, Rest, Motion, Sameness, and Difference.</note>, and weaving together the things that
->C<-
come from them by intellectual means, it proceeds until it has traversed the entire intelligible world. Then, it reverses the process, analyzing back to the very beginning. Finally, it rests in stillness, for as long as it is in that higher place, it attains peace. No longer busying itself with many things, but having been reduced to unity, it looks out upon what is called "logical business"—the study of propositions and syllogisms. It treats these like the art of writing; it grants them to another craft, considering some of them
->D<-
necessary and preparatory to the art itself. It judges these logical rules just as it judges everything else, deeming some useful and others superfluous, belonging merely to the faculty that desires such things.

->E<-

<margin>The Metaphysician receives principles from the intellect, and through the rules of truth, refutes sophisms, including those contained within logical rules.</margin>
But from where does this science obtain its principles? Perhaps the Intellect <note>Greek: *Nous*. The divine Mind or the second level of reality in Neoplatonism.</note> gives clear principles, if the soul is able to receive them. Then, the soul composes, joins together, and divides these principles until it arrives at a perfect understanding. For this, as he says <note>Likely referring to Plato's *Philebus* or *Republic*.</note>, is the purest part of intelligence and wisdom. It is necessary, therefore, since it is the most excellent state among those within us, that it deals with "Being" <note>Latin: *ens*; Greek: *on*. Reality itself.</note> and the most excellent things. Wisdom <note>Latin: *prudentia*; Greek: *phronēsis*.</note> concerns Being, and the Intellect concerns that which is *beyond* Being <note>The "One" or the absolute source, which Plotinus famously places above even the level of Being.</note>. What then is philosophy? It is undoubtedly the most excellent thing. But is philosophy the same as dialectic? Indeed, dialectic seems to be the most excellent part of philosophy. For we must not think that this is merely a "tool" for the philosopher;
->F<-
it does not consist of naked propositions and rules, but it is concerned with things themselves, and it has "Beings" as its subject matter. However, it proceeds toward these beings by a path, possessing the things themselves along with their concepts. It recognizes falsehood and "sophistry" <note>Arguments intended to deceive.</note> only incidentally. That is, when someone else introduces a falsehood, dialectic judges it as something foreign, recognizing the lie through the truths it already possesses, whenever someone brings forward something that is outside the rule of truth. Therefore, it does not properly concern itself with the "proposition"—for these are just letters. But by knowing the truth, it knows
->G<-
that which they call a proposition. More generally, it knows the movements of the soul: what it affirms and what it denies, and whether it denies the same thing it affirmed, or something else. Likewise, it knows whether things are different or the same when they are brought together, grasping them much like the way our senses touch objects. But it leaves the technical details to another faculty that makes much of such things.

<summary>This page defines "Dialectic" not as mere logic or debate, but as the supreme metaphysical science that allows the philosopher to categorize reality and ascend to the "field of truth." Plotinus argues that while logic deals with words and propositions, Dialectic deals with true Being and the divine Intellect.</summary>
