<header>PLOTINUS ENNEAD I</header>

<margin>A</margin>...bestowing exact diligence in these matters; for it gives [this] to those who love it.

### PART 1 <note>This marks the concluding section of the treatise on Dialectic.</note>
Therefore, this science is to be honored. For philosophy also possesses other faculties: indeed, it contemplates nature, taking assistance from dialectic, just as the other arts make use of arithmetic. However, philosophy itself draws its principles more closely from dialectic. The faculty concerning ethics <note>original: "περὶ ἠθῶν" / "de moribus"</note> likewise contemplates from that source; but it adds habits and exercises, from which the habits themselves proceed. <margin>B</margin>The rational virtues also have habits, and they now regard the things derived from dialectic as their own. For most of these are involved with matter. And while other virtues exercise their reasonings within their own specific passions and actions, Prudence <note>term: "Prudence" (Phronesis). In this context, it refers to practical wisdom or the ability to apply universal truths to specific, material situations.</note> is a certain superior reasoning, and it deals more with the universal. It considers whether one should restrain and abstain in the present, or wait for the future, or if something else is entirely better. It also notices what follows in turn and what does not. <margin>C</margin>Dialectic, however, and Wisdom <note>term: "Wisdom" (Sophia). Here, the theoretical grasp of eternal, immaterial truths.</note> also bring everything to the use of Prudence by means of universal and immaterial reasoning. <margin>D</margin>But it may be asked whether the lower [virtues] can exist without dialectic and wisdom? Perhaps they are quite imperfect; yet it is possible to be wise and dialectical without them. Or rather, they do not happen in that way, but either arise earlier or grow together at the same time. And perhaps one possesses certain natural virtues, from which the perfect ones are formed when wisdom is applied. After the natural ones, therefore, wisdom comes forth: then it perfects the character, or rather, while the natural ones exist, both now grow together and are finally perfected at the same time. Or perhaps one, anticipating the other, perfects it. For altogether, natural virtue has an imperfect eye and character: and the principles for both occur mostly from what we already possess.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...bestowing exact diligence in these matters.

<margin>VI</margin>
<margin>Metaphysics provides rules to the other faculties, both speculative and moral: and without it, sciences do not exist, and morals are imperfect.</margin>

### PART
Therefore, this [science] is to be honored. For philosophy has other faculties besides: namely, it even speculates on nature, taking aid from dialectic, just as the other arts make use of arithmetic: but philosophy itself draws its principles more closely from dialectic. The faculty also concerning morals similarly contemplates from there: but it joins to it habits and exercises, from which the habits themselves proceed. <margin>B</margin>The rational virtues also have habits, and as if they were already their own, they take what is led from there. For they have many things in common with matter. And other virtues indeed have their ratiocinations in their own passions and also in actions. But Prudence is a certain primary ratiocination, and it is occupied with the more universal. It considers whether something should be restrained or abstained from in the present: or in the future? Or is something else better altogether? And it observes which things follow in turn, and which do not. <margin>C</margin>Dialectic, truly, and also wisdom, brings forward all things for the use of prudence by universal and immaterial reason. <margin>D</margin>But it can be asked whether the lower things can exist without dialectic and wisdom? Perhaps in a very imperfect way: but it can happen that one is wise and dialectical without them. Or it does not happen quite like that, but either they grow together earlier, or at the same time. And perhaps someone has natural virtues, from which also perfect ones are made, namely when wisdom is applied. Therefore, after the natural ones, wisdom comes forth: then it perfects the character, or rather, with the natural ones existing, both now grow together, and at last are perfected together. Or perhaps one, coming before, perfects the other. For altogether, natural virtue has an imperfect eye and character: and the principles occur for both mostly from those things which we have.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON THE
## BOOK CONCERNING HAPPINESS,
->ARGUMENT.<-

### SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK,
->He is blessed who lives by the mind alone.<-

<image-desc>A decorative drop-cap initial 'L' showing a seated scholar or figure in profile, possibly holding a book or gesturing during a discourse.</image-desc> THE BOOK on happiness begins from that opinion in which all agree. *Truly, everyone proclaims that happiness is to live well. But since they are utterly ignorant of what life is, and what the good is: therefore, as often as they define living well, they are forced to err. Plotinus detects their errors in the first and second chapters of the book: namely, admonishing us that we should make the beginning of our disputation from the definition itself. And so, in the third chapter of the book, he describes life, and the good, and happiness. In the fourth, he raises and solves doubts: asking whether a blessed life is suitable for a human being. Likewise, by what reasoning it might again be hindered: meanwhile signifying that it cannot be hindered. In the following chapters, he then brings forward similar questions and finally solves them: proving from all of them that he alone is blessed, who, living by the mind alone, is now entirely intellect, depending on no other thing than the divine intellect, and the Good itself, the principle and end of all things. This is the purpose of the entire book.*

->Various opinions on what it is to live well.<-

I *The first chapter, therefore, through indirect paths, deals with those who, being ignorant of what life itself is and what the good itself is, meanwhile strive to define living well, saying namely: "To live well is to pass through life without hindrance"; likewise "to be in a good state"; again "to perform one's own proper work"; furthermore "to attain the end naturally desired by appetite"; then "to live tranquilly"; finally "to live according to nature." In all these things, he leads those ignorant of the true definition to the point where they are compelled to grant the divine gift of blessedness to even the most dejected little beasts, and even to plants, and to attribute happiness—that is, the highest point of life—to those in whom the least of life exists.*

II *Just as in the first, so in the second chapter he agitates false opinions and chooses something of the truth from them: in which take note concerning sensation in animals and plants.*

# ON BOOK III. ENNEAD I.

### II
In the second chapter of the book, while he achieves nearly the same goal as in the first, Plotinus meanwhile attempts to gather various conjectures from the errors or doubts of others to find true happiness. Now, some had said that happiness <term>felicitas; the state of flourishing or "well-being"</term> is a certain affection of nature, according to which someone is usually said to be doing well. After this, some among them deny that happiness exists in plants, even though they attribute it to all animals.

From this, Plotinus says: those who deny happiness to plants because they do not "feel" seem likely to deny it to certain animals as well—that is, to oysters and similar creatures which scarcely seem to have sensation. Indeed, the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, known for believing that all living things, including plants, possess a soul and a degree of consciousness.</note> thought that plants perceive perfections in almost the same way, so that the highest grade in plants matches the lowest in animals. Furthermore, there is a distinction of sex in plants: plants situated near their "spouses" sprout more fruitfully; and by some unknown sense, they turn toward moisture and heat, and when they are pruned or handled too violently, they dry up.

We consider sensation to be twofold: a **Lower** kind, by which neither the nature of a thing nor any quality is discerned, but only a certain affection brought upon it is felt; this is a dull sensation, like that in sleepers, and is suited to plants. Then there is a **Higher** kind, which perceives both nature and quality and is proper only to animals. 

But to return to those who said that happiness was a certain affection or habit suited especially to a bodily nature: they certainly were not right to take happiness away from plants just because they lacked sensation, since a habit of that kind exists similarly even before sensation. But if they say that the "highest good" consists not in such a habit but in sensation and knowledge, they are immediately refuted from that point. For if the very definition of the "good" is contained within sensation, then surely whatever is felt, and in whatever way it is felt, would be proven to be "good." 

The opposite, however, happens: for we often reject the action of sensation and this kind of knowledge when we notice it is—or fear it will be—troublesome to us. Furthermore, if they then add that the highest good is a mixture of the habit and the perception of it, they are again convicted. For if something indifferent to the good is joined with another thing equally indifferent to it, the "good itself" will not be produced from the two. Therefore, if they concede that both are indifferent to the good, the highest good will by no means result from them.

Perhaps they will say that a certain habit is the highest good, but only when it is known to be present. To this, Plotinus argues: "Living well" is appropriate to someone not solely because they know such a thing is present, but primarily because they truly judge it to be good. For only in this way will they truly enjoy it as a good. 

To judge the nature and reason of the good is no longer the duty of sensation, but of **reason** and **mind**. Therefore, neither a pleasurable habit nor the sensation of it, but reason and the mind are the cause of living well and happily. Indeed, an affection agreeable to the bodily nature, or a pleasure of that sort, is something devoid of reason. By this very fact, both reason and the mind are superior, acting as a judge and a charioteer <note>original: "auriga"; a reference to Plato’s Phaedrus, where the soul is depicted as a charioteer guiding the horses of passion and spirit.</note>. If the mind is superior, then its natural and principal action is directed toward a superior end. 

Even those who attribute "living well" to all animals, or even plants, certainly seem to be prophesying when they add that these live well when they are affected in a certain way and live more perfectly. It is as if they mean that sensual and vegetative life—not insofar as it is simply such, but by the logic through which it sometimes lives better—is "living well." It is as if above such a life (which is not always perfect, and indeed is always imperfect) there is another certain life that is always most perfect. 

Those, therefore, who place happiness around that which lives more perfectly—namely, the rational being—judge more correctly. But rational virtue itself is not necessary for making people happy simply because it provides the things necessary for the first impulses of the physical nature; for these things can be provided or be present even without virtue. Likewise, in that case, the rational nature would only serve the inferior nature, which is absurd. For it is necessary that the superior nature also has a superior duty and a goal of its own, leading properly to a superior end. 

And just as the bodily and sensual nature sometimes attains its own end, so must the rational nature attain its own; its perfection does not consist in being occupied with imperfect things, but in a perfection that is even above reason itself. For whatever is to be perfected by virtue and the attainment of perfection can only be perfected by that very perfection. Finally, since the rational nature can never be filled by things agreeable to the body, nor ever rest in the possession of such things, it is clear that it is placed in another and more excellent order, and is perfected and made happy from elsewhere—namely, from on high.

->One life is supreme, namely the supreme intellect; others depend on it through many degrees.<-

### III
The third chapter of the book now defines this, asserting that if the same reason and an equal condition of life were in all things said to "live," then all things would equally arrive at a happy life at some point. But since the case is not so—indeed, true life is the **Intellect** <term>intellectus; the highest faculty of the soul, beyond discursive reasoning</term>, while others are merely images of life—a happy life exists only in the Intellect. In other things, certain images of happiness are seen. Reason also is an image of the intellect. 

Therefore, those who place happiness in reason think more correctly than the rest (since reason is closest to the mind), yet they do not judge most correctly. Since reason is occupied in motion <note>Discursive reasoning "moves" from one thought to another, unlike the Intellect which perceives truth all at once in stillness.</note>, the ultimate end does not properly belong to it; for the ultimate end, like a supreme rest, is quite distinct from motion. 

Furthermore, the happy life is life itself, and life in its most absolute form. But those who say that happiness is not simply "life," but a certain habit of rational life, first deny that the happy life is life itself; then they place it in a certain accidental quality; and again, they place it in "discourse" <note>discursione; the step-by-step process of logical thinking.</note>, which, while it is always occupied in motion, is never a life that is entirely absolute. 

Plotinus concludes, therefore, that the **Happy Life** must be placed in another species of life: one different from the sensual, and different also from the rational. But meanwhile, he corrects himself for having said "species." For he does not want the Intellect itself to be counted in the same category with plants, or sensation, or reason, as if it were one species distributed equally with them through specific differences. Rather, he wants the Intellect itself to be **Life Itself**, the principle and archetype of all living things. 

The other living things flow from it through various degrees: first the rational, then the sensual, and finally the vegetative. Yet they are connected in such a way that in the rational animal there is also something of the intellectual; in the sensual there is something of the rational; and in the vegetative there is something of the sensual. Finally, in mixed bodies, there is something vital and vegetative. In this way, the fruitfulness of the Principle is declared, the condition of the following things is preserved, and the universe is perfectly connected on all sides. But now let us ascend by these arranged steps to life, the mind, and the happy life itself.

->The first essence, the first life, and the first intellect are the same.<-

In the very order of things, we see that **essence** strives toward **life**, insofar as whatever exists is inclined toward motion and generation. Now, motion and generation display something vital. Likewise, life strives toward **knowledge**, insofar as that which lives generates forms within itself; in this matter, it imitates the knowing nature, which conceives forms in itself by knowing. From this, it is clear that life is the perfection of essence, while knowledge is the perfection of life. Although all this is under the logic of...

<meta>catchword: life (vitæ)</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that happiness is not a physical state or mere sensation, but is found only in the highest form of life—the Intellect—which serves as the archetype for all lower degrees of existence (rational, sensual, and vegetative).</summary>

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

### ON BOOK III. ENNEAD I.

Life can be considered in various stages. For it seems that **Essence** <term>essentia; the fundamental "being" or "what-ness" of a thing</term> is like life being born, while knowledge—especially intellectual knowledge—is life that is fully adult. Furthermore, we see certain traces of these three—Essence, Life, and Intellect—extended through all things that exist. Everywhere, under the aspect of **form**, a trace of essence is found, since every individual thing seems to "be" through its form. Likewise, under that same aspect, a trace of **life** is found, since through form, inclination, motion, and generation occur. Again, by the same logic, a trace of **intelligence** appears, because through form, there is order everywhere, which is the specific sign of intelligence. Therefore, since through one thing—namely, form—these three are spread through all things, it is necessary that there be one primary form of all things, which is itself the first essence, and similarly the first life, and the first intelligence. For this reason, these three are extended through all things by the single gift of form: because one form exists above all things, embracing these three within itself.

Now, it is clear that the first form is the first essence because essence and "being" are produced everywhere through form, and where there is more form, there is a greater gift of being. Likewise, we gather that this same first form is both the most perfect life and the most perfect intellect, because life is the perfection of essence, and intellect is the perfection of life. Therefore, with the highest perfection of essence, the highest perfection of life and intellect concur. This is especially true since the most perfect essence possesses its own most perfect attribute: life is the act of essence, and the most absolute life is moved most perfectly. Indeed, that motion is nothing other than to be turned back into oneself through intelligence. 

Hence, just as in the sensible world—which is the image of the intelligible world—essence is formed by life as if it were matter, and life is similarly formed by intellect (or whatever kind of cognition represents intelligence), so in the intelligible world, intellect is a certain act of life, and life is the act of essence. Because these three are distinguished among us by a certain formal order, they are also distinguished by a certain reason—even there, where the first form is the principle, the model, and the end of the entire formal order. 

We suspect these are distinguished there in some way because among us, although traces of all three are everywhere, in things that most people say only "exist," the evidence of essence appears more clearly than that of life or mind. In those things that are only said to "live," we find a surer trace of life than of mind. And since essence there also appears as something unformed if compared to life, and life similarly if compared to mind—and the unformed cannot form itself—therefore, above **Being** <term>ens; the realm where these three are thought of together</term> itself reigns the **One** and the **Good** itself. By its power, essence advances toward the better when it proceeds into life, and life toward the better when it is fully perfected in mind. 

Thus, this mind is the "blessed life"—that is, a life brought to the summit of its nature and desire by the vigor of the Good itself, reflected back into itself, converted toward the Good, and filled with the overflowing goodness from that source. The Good itself, being simply the **One**, is not Essence, Life, or Intellect by way of form, but in a far more excellent way: by way of being their **Cause**. That these three are placed immediately below the Good is due to their form. The **Soul** then possesses these three through true participation. Finally, that which is subject to the rational soul is judged to possess these three through a kind of "imaginary" participation—just as light, illumination, and splendor are in the invisible heaven by way of cause, in the visible heaven by way of form, in the ether by true participation, and thereafter by a purely imaginary condition. 

As for Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a later Neoplatonist who often divided the divine realm into many distinct layers; Ficino here defends a more unified view.</note>, who wanted these three to be three separate substances—essence being higher than life, and life more excellent than mind—we do not easily agree with him. For if that were so, their traces would have to follow the same order: namely, that which only "is" would be more excellent than that which "lives," and that which "lives" would be more excellent than that which "understands." We, therefore, say that the more noble gifts of this substance belong to the few, while the less noble gifts fall to the many. For a great and perfect preparation is required in things to receive the more excellent gift.

->Intellect itself is the summit of life.<-

We describe **Life** in a general sense first as a certain emergence of essence into its own act, and as its first act, and as its intimate and perennial internal motion—the principle of all motions. Because of this, where there is a trace of life, there is act and motion; and a more perfect motion and act is a clearer sign of a more perfect life. Since the highest grade of life is that toward which every motion of the universe strives as its end, we conclude that intellect itself is the highest life. We see this because the entire motion of the world finally results in an intellectual form: beginning with the generation of the forms of elements, then the forms of mixtures, then plants, then animals, and finally arriving at the very form of man, which already participates in intelligence. 

Similarly, in the generation of a man in the womb, there is a process from the form of a mixture to a certain plant-like form, from this to a sensory form, and from this to an intellectual form. I pass over the fact that the entire motion of the world and all generation proceed toward the common order and beauty of the whole, which is a certain image of intellect in things. The arts also try to imitate this, starting the work from tools and matter, and finally finishing in an artistic form, which is an image of intellectual art. 

Since, therefore, intellect appears as the ultimate end in the order of motions (as if of lives), who would not see that the highest life is the highest intelligence? And that Mind itself is the efficient and exemplary cause of the universe? For by the power of Mind itself, all things are brought back to the likeness of Mind as their end, according to their capacity. This, therefore, is life itself. There is no life "simply" except this one; rather, other lives are participations in it. Rational life is a certain image of it; the life called "sensual" is an image of rational life; the "vegetative" life appears as a likeness of this; and finally, a trace of vegetative life is found in any form in matter—when it is inclined toward motion, when it generates in the manner of a living thing, or when it thins or thickens, in which the conditions of growth and decay appear. 

Thus, there is a descent from the substance of Life to one image after another, and to traces of life. It is as if a living artist were to craft a very similar statue of himself, then represent it in a painting, and then hold the painted image up to a mirror, from which a final "mirror-image" appears. Only this artist is the human; none of the images will be the human. Similarly, only Intellect is life; those things that come after it are considered images of life rather than life itself. This is not only because they degenerate from life by a long interval, but because they seem to have something similar to death mixed in, as they fail at some grade of life and undergo a certain privation as they pass from potentiality to act—changing through time and suffering ignorance and forgetting. 

Hence, the more external the motion, the weaker the life is shown to be, as if departing from its own source. Elements and mixtures move externally and generate only in separate matter. Plants, however, already move internally and give birth in joined matter. Next, the sensory power of animals, beyond such birth, conceives forms within itself by imagining. Then the rational power does not borrow the beginnings of its conception from the senses (as imagination does), but draws from an internal seed; and it embraces its own conception by noticing it. Finally, Intellect itself generates within itself in such a way,

<meta>catchword: that it [ut se]</meta>

<summary>Ficino defines the metaphysical triad of Essence, Life, and Intellect, arguing that Intellect is the "adult" and highest form of life. He uses the analogy of an artist and their reflections to explain how life "descends" and weakens as it moves from the divine Mind down to physical matter.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Ficino’s commentary on Ennead I, Book 4, following the discussion of how Essence, Life, and Intellect are unified in the highest reality. He now explores how the human soul participates in this divine life.</meta>

# ON BOOK IIII. ENNEAD I.

...so that it appears, in a way, to have begotten itself. For in that realm where being, living, and understanding are in reality one, while it understands itself, it simultaneously seems to beget, or unfold, or preserve something essential and vital within itself. From all this we can gather that the most intimate and perfect motion and generation flourish in the mind; therefore, it is the most perfect life. I mean this primarily and through itself in the divine mind, but in our mind, it exists proximately and through that divine one. Thus we consider the blessed life to be not just any life, as if it were in need of some addition, but life itself flourishing at the highest degree of living. This life, I say, is the act of the primary **essence** <term>essentia; the fundamental being of a thing</term> naturally directed toward the **Good** <note>In Neoplatonism, "the Good" is the ultimate source of all reality, synonymous with "the One."</note> itself, and thus perfect. And in this very degree of perfection, we think that the intellect is simultaneously formed, and that life itself is fully completed by that very intellect.

In this intellect, living, understanding, and willing are the same thing, although in a **rational nature** <term>rationalis natura; the human level of soul that reasons step-by-step</term> living is one thing, thinking another, and choosing yet another. Just as in celestial light, to shine, to sparkle, and to warm are the same thing, although in this light of our air, to glow is one thing, to reflect another, and to burn another. For those things which a lower nature is forced to do through diverse parts, a higher nature fulfills through one. Just as the **imagination** <term>imaginatio; the faculty that processes sensory images</term> performs through one power what the five external senses do with five instruments. And what the imagination contrives through many individual forms, **reason** <term>ratio; the discursive faculty of the soul</term> collects into a single universal species. Finally, what reason runs through in a multiple act, the **intellect** <term>intellectus; the faculty of direct, non-discursive spiritual intuition</term> attains in a single stable act—or rather, possesses in a perpetual act.

Therefore, for the intellect, to live is to understand; to understand is to will. Or if there is perhaps some distinction in the will, it is nevertheless called "willing" by the same instinct of its nature (so to speak) while it strives toward the good; it is said to "understand" while it attains the good; and again, it is judged to "will" when it embraces the good it has attained. This primary life and primary mind, always enjoying the paternal good, is judged to be the blessed life. From this, any mind becomes perpetually blessed by clinging to the primary mind, and through it, to the Good forever. Hence, reason also turns out to be happy as often as it is joined to its own mind, and through its own, to the divine Mind.

->Rational nature can attain the blessed life: namely, when it is formed and acts by the intellect.<-

### IIII
Since, therefore, the blessed life is the perfect life, and the perfect life is the true and actually perfect intellect, it is next asked: whether man—that is, the rational soul—can attain this mind and this life by its own rational power. To this question, an answer is given in the fourth chapter of the book, stating that it can be attained at some point; a matter which we open up more widely in our *Theology* and in the book *On the Mind*. This rational power has two principal acts: namely, **intuition** and **argumentation**. Through intuition, it resolves and abstracts forms from the conditions of matter, and withdraws itself from the individual forms of the imagination to universal forms; and again to more universal ones, until it reaches the most common forms proper to intelligence itself. There it seems to find its end in the Mind, from which it also derives the power of argumentation, while it prescribes to itself the principal rules of the sciences naturally implanted in the intellect as principles for arguing.

Thus, by intuiting, it fixes its end in the Mind; and by arguing, it draws its beginning from the Mind; and rightly so, since as something "later" it naturally depends upon it. Therefore, the end of reason is to possess the Mind to the best of its ability. From this, it strives daily—as much as it is not hindered—to be formed more and more, step by step, by the Mind. Since this power is not in vain (as it is natural to this species), it can eventually attain the Mind, and finally be perfected by that virtue through which it daily makes progress. When the rational power has proceeded to the ideal forms and rules of intelligence, then, like a kind of matter, it will be formed by the Mind itself as if by a form, and it will now act under the act of the Mind. And so, at last, it will live that Mind's life, and live blessedly. But if it cannot acquire this in this life, occupied as it is by diverse things, it will obtain it in the next; and he will attain it more quickly who has prepared himself for it more readily.

In Plotinus’s words, you will note that a certain intellect is the innermost and proper part of the soul itself. Before the whole reason is turned toward the Mind, the intellect and reason are still in the soul as two parts of the soul. But after it has been turned, the intellect is no longer a "part," but the soul itself is then the intellect—which soul is certainly not happy until it becomes entirely intellect in act. It is much like how the high air beneath the sphere of fire is fiery and acts as fire. Furthermore, a being is not even a "man" unless he has at least the intellect in potential. I believe this was said because of the brute animals: if there is any power of argumentation in their imaginations, it still cannot be formed by the Mind. For since the forms of the proper Mind are entirely stable and most universal, the imagination of a brute—through its forms which are only particular and mobile—can never be formed by the Mind. Reason, however, through its own forms (which, although somewhat mobile, are nevertheless universal), can eventually be led to the forms of intelligence.

After this, he argues that such happiness is not at all disturbed by the care of the animal body or its inconveniences; for the soul affected in this way does not consider the animal body to be a part of itself, but rather something made from it or commended to its providence. Plotinus asserts, moreover, that the soul thus affected exists as a good for itself, namely through the intellectual form which the rational soul has recently put on—put on, I say, under its own intellect, just as its own intellect is clothed from the beginning by the divine intellect. And entirely through the intellect, both its own and the divine, the soul enjoys the Good itself. This is simply "the Good" in itself, but in the intellect, it is an essential, vital, intellectual, and intelligible good.

->What the Peripatetics might object.<-

### V
The fifth chapter of the book summarizes what a **Peripatetic** <term>Peripateticus; a follower of Aristotle</term> would object to this definition of happiness, and what things he would count as necessary for happiness. Among these, you will note that **magical sorceries** <term>magica veneficia; the belief that external spiritual influences could harm the soul</term> can have some effect on the body and soul, as **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was Plotinus's student and biographer.</note> also asserts: especially in souls that are somewhat weak—that is, those addicted to the imagination and not fortified by the intellect as if by the shield and spear of Pallas Athena. But concerning sorceries and fascinations, we treat these sufficiently in our *Theology* and *Commentary on the Symposium (On Love)*.

->The ultimate end is the one Good: namely the highest, intelligible or more than intelligible.<-

### VI
To these things, he responds in the sixth chapter of the book: if we placed happiness in the prosperity and tranquility of human affairs, then the objections of the Peripatetics would follow—namely, that a person to whom adversities happen is not happy. But since we place the blessed life in the possession of the primary and divine Good itself, he does not think the remaining things called "goods" should be counted alongside this; nor does he think their opposites take happiness away from us, provided that in the meantime [we are not separated] from divinity itself...

<summary>Ficino explains how the human soul ascends from sensory imagination to reason, and finally to the divine Intellect to achieve true happiness. He defends the Neoplatonic view that this internal spiritual state is the only true "blessed life," which remains unaffected by external misfortunes or Aristotelian objections.</summary>
<keywords>Intellect, Reason, Blessed Life, Marsilio Ficino, Plotinus, Neoplatonism, Peripatetics, Porphyry, The Good, Imagination, Human Soul</keywords>

Having established their unity in the divine, he now examines how these three "vestiges" or traces are distributed throughout the created world, moving from the highest forms of existence down to the physical realm.</meta>

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

->on the life<- of the soul can be considered. For it seems that **essence** <term>essentia; the fundamental "whatness" or being of a thing</term> is like life just being born, while **knowledge**, especially the intellectual kind, is life fully adult. We see, moreover, certain traces of these three extended through all things that exist. For everywhere a trace of essence is found under the rationale of **form** <note>In Platonic thought, "form" is the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is.</note>: since every single thing seems to exist through its form. Likewise, a trace of life is found under the same rationale: since through form comes inclination, movement, and generation. Again, by the same rationale, a trace of intelligence appears: because through form there is order everywhere, which is the proper sign of intelligence. Since, therefore, through one thing—that is, through form—these three are extended through all things, it is necessary that there be one primary form of all things: which is itself the primary essence, and similarly the primary life, and the primary intelligence. For this reason, these three are extended through all things by the single gift of form: because the primary form contains these three within itself.

Now, indeed, it is clear that the primary form is the primary essence from the fact that essence and being are produced everywhere through form, and wherever the power of form is, there the function of being is greater. Likewise, we conceive that this same primary form is both the most perfect life and the most perfect intellect from this: that life is the perfection of essence, and intellect is the perfection of life. Therefore, with the highest perfection of essence, the highest perfection of life and intellect concurs. Especially since the most perfect essence has the most perfect proper act; but life is the act of essence. Likewise, the most absolute life is moved most perfectly; but that is nothing other than to be revolved into itself through intelligence. 

Hence, just as in the **sensible world** <note>The physical world we perceive with our five senses.</note>, which is the image of the **intelligible world** <note>The higher reality of pure ideas and divine mind.</note>, essence is formed as if it were matter through life, and life similarly through intellect (or whatever kind of cognition represents intelligence); so in the intelligible world, the intellect is indeed a certain act of life, and life is the act of essence. Since, however, these three are distinguished among us by a certain formal order, they are therefore distinguished by a certain reason; and there, where the primary form is the principle, exemplar, and end of the entire formal order. We conjecture that these are also distinguished there in some way from the fact that among us, although the traces of those three are everywhere, yet in things which most say only "exist," the evidence of essence appears more expressly than that of mind or life. But in those things which are said only "to live," a more certain trace of life meets us than a trace of mind. 

And since essence also seems like something unformed there if it is compared to life, and life similarly if compared to mind—and the unformed cannot form itself—therefore above **being** <term>ens; that which exists</term> itself, in which these three are contemplated, reigns the **One and the Good** <note>The "One" or "the Good" is the absolute source in Neoplatonism, standing above even Being and Intellect.</note> itself: by whose power essence profits into something better while it goes forth into life; and life into something better while it is fully perfected in the mind. This mind, therefore, is the **blessed life**, that is, life brought to the summit of its nature and appetite by the vigor of the Good itself, reflected into itself, turned toward the Good itself, and filled with the overflowing goodness from there. But the Good itself, and the simply One, is not essence. It is the One of the intellect by way of form, but in a much more excellent way, that is, by the rationale of a **cause**. However, that these three are immediately beneath the Good is through form. 

The **Soul** thereafter is these three by true participation. But that which is subjected to the **rational soul** <note>The human level of soul that uses logic and discourse.</note> is judged to be these three by a certain imaginary participation: just as light, radiance, and splendor are in the invisible heaven by the rationale of cause, in the visible heaven by the mode of form, in the **ether** <note>The "fifth element" or celestial substance.</note> by true participation, and thereafter by a purely imaginary condition. 

We do not easily approve of **Proclus** <note>A later Neoplatonic philosopher (5th century AD) who tended to multiply divine categories more than Ficino preferred.</note> wanting these three to be three separate substances, and essence indeed superior to life, and life more excellent than mind. For thus it would be necessary for their traces to behave similarly—namely, that what only *is* would be more excellent than what *lives*; and again, that what *is and lives* would be more excellent than what only *understands*. We shall say, therefore, that the more noble gifts of this substance belong to the few; but the less noble suit the many. For a great and perfect preparation is required in things to receive a more excellent gift.

### Intellect itself is the highest peak of life.

We describe Life in a general sense as a certain first outgoing of essence and of being itself into its act, and as its first act itself, and as if it were an intimate and perennial movement, the principle of all motions. By this it is brought about that acts and movements are the trace of life; and a more perfect movement and act is a more express sign of the perfection of life. But since that is the highest grade of life toward which, as if toward an end, every movement of the universe strives, we conjecture that the intellect itself is the highest life from this: that the entire movement of the world finally ends in an intellectual form. It begins generation with the forms of the elements, then the forms of mixed things; thereafter plants, then animals, finally proceeding to the form of man itself, which is already a participant in intelligence. 

Similarly, in the generation of a human in the womb, there is a process from the form of a mixture to a certain plant-like form, from this to a sensory one, and from this to an intellectual one. I omit the fact that the entire movement of the world and all generation proceeds toward the common order and beauty of the whole: which is certainly a fixed image of the intellect in things. The arts also try to imitate the same, beginning the work from tools and matter, and finally ending in an artistic form, an image of the intellectual art. Since, therefore, the ultimate end in the order of motions appears as the universal intellect, who does not see that the highest life is the highest intelligence? And that the Mind itself is the **efficient and exemplar cause** <note>The "efficient" cause is the builder; the "exemplar" is the blueprint or model.</note> of the universe? Especially since by the power of the Mind itself all things are reduced, as if to an end, to the likeness of the Mind according to their strength. 

This, therefore, is life itself. But besides this, there is no life simply, but rather a certain participation in life: of which rational life is a certain image; and the image of rational life is the life which is called sensory; and the likeness of this seems to be vegetative life; finally, any form in matter is a trace of life, while it is inclined and inclines toward movement, while it generates as if in the manner of a living thing, while it rarefies and condenses, in which the condition of growth and decrease appears. 

There is, therefore, a descent from the substance of life to images, one after another, and traces of life: just as if a living craftsman himself should fashion a statue most like himself, and then represent this in a painting, and again place the painted image before a mirror, from which a certain final mirror-image would appear. Only this craftsman is a man; but none of the images will be a man. Similarly, only the intellect is life; but those things which happen later, and later again, are judged to be images of life rather than life itself. Not only because they degenerate from life itself by a long interval, but because they seem to have something similar to death mixed in, while they both fail in some degree of life and undergo a certain privation from potentiality into act, and passing through time, they suffer ignorance and forgetfulness. 

Hence, the more external a movement is, the more it indicates that life has already become weaker, as if departing from its very source. The elements and mixtures are moved externally, and generate leaves in separate matter. But plants are already moved internally and beget in joined matter. Thereafter, the sensory power of animals, besides generation of this kind, conceives forms in itself by imagining. Then the rational power does not borrow the beginnings of its conception from the senses as the imagination does, but contracts it from an already intimate seed; and it embraces its own concept by observing it. Finally, the intellect itself now begets in itself in such a way that it...

<summary>Ficino argues that Essence, Life, and Intellect are a unified triad derived from the One, manifesting as "traces" throughout the hierarchy of existence from the divine Mind down to physical elements. He defines Intellect as the highest form of life and illustrates the descent of reality through the analogy of a craftsman, his statue, a painting, and a reflection.</summary>

# ON BOOK IV OF THE FIRST ENNEAD.

II ...so that it appears to have generated itself in some way. For in that state where being, living, and understanding are in reality one, while it understands itself, it seems meanwhile to generate, or unfold, or preserve something essential and vital within itself. From all these points we can gather that the most intimate and most perfect motion and generation flourish in the mind: and therefore it is the most perfect life. I am speaking of the divine mind, where this is found primarily and of itself, but in our mind, it is found secondarily and through the divine. Therefore, we think the "blessed life" <term>beata vita; the state of supreme happiness or eudaimonia</term> is not just any kind of life, as if it were in need of some addition, but life itself flourishing at the highest degree of living. It is life, I say—that is, the act of the primary essence <term>essentia; the fundamental being of a thing</term> naturally directed toward the **Good** itself, and thus made perfect. And at this very degree of perfection, we think that the intellect is simultaneously created, and that life itself is completely perfected by that very intellect. In this intellect, living, understanding, and willing are the same thing, although in a rational nature <note>original: "natura rationali"; referring to humans who must reason through steps, unlike the divine which knows instantly</note> living is one thing, thinking another, and choosing another. It is just as in celestial light, where shining, sparkling, and warming are the same; although in this light of our air, glowing is one thing, reflecting another, and burning another. For what an inferior nature is forced to do through many different ways, a superior nature completes through one. Just as the imagination performs through one power what the external sense does through five instruments; and what the imagination contrives with many individual forms, reason collects into one universal species. Finally, what reason runs through in a manifold act, the intellect attains in a single, stable act—indeed, it possesses it in a perpetual act. Therefore, for the intellect, to live is to understand: for the intellect, to understand is to will. Or if perhaps some distinction is made in the will, nevertheless, by the same instinct of its own nature (so to speak), while it strives for the good, it is naturally said to "will"; when it attains the good, it is said to "understand"; and again, when it embraces the good it has attained, it is judged to "will" once more. This primary life and primary mind, always enjoying the paternal good, is judged to be the blessed life. Hence also any mind becomes perpetually blessed by clinging always to the primary mind and to the Good through it. From this, reason also turns out to be happy as often as it is joined to its own mind, and through its own, to the divine mind.

->The rational nature can attain the blessed life: namely when<-
->it is formed and acts through the intellect.<-

IIII Since, therefore, the blessed life is the perfect life, and the perfect life is the true intellect, perfect in its act, the next question is: Whether man—that is, the rational soul—can attain this mind and this life through his own rational power. To this question, an answer is given in the fourth chapter of the book: that it can sometimes be attained. We have opened this up more widely in our *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his major work, the *Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls*</note> and in the book *On the Mind*. This rational power has two principal acts: namely, **intuition** and **argument**. Through intuition, it releases and abstracts forms from the conditions of matter, and from the individual forms of the imagination, it retreats to universal forms. From there, it moves toward even more universal ones, until it arrives at the most common forms, which are proper to the intelligence itself. Here it seems to find its end in the mind, from which it also draws the power of argument, while it prescribes to itself the principal rules of the sciences and arts—naturally implanted in the intellect—as the principles of its reasoning. Thus, by intuiting, it establishes its end in the mind; and by arguing, it draws its beginning from the mind. This is rightly so, since like a follower, it naturally depends upon it. The end of reason, therefore, is to take possession of the mind as much as its strength allows. From this, it strives daily, as much as it is not hindered, to be formed more and more, step by step, by the mind. Since this power is not in vain, as it is natural to this species, it can eventually attain the mind; and finally be perfected by the same virtue through which it makes progress daily. When the rational power has proceeded to the ideal forms and rules of the intelligence, then, like a kind of matter, it will be formed by the mind as if by a "form," and it will act under the mind's impulse. And thus, at last, it will live by that mind's life, and live blessedly. But if in this life it cannot acquire this, occupied as it is by various things, it will obtain it in the other life; and he will attain it more quickly who has prepared himself more readily for it. In Plotinus’s words, you will notice that a certain "intellect" is the most intimate and proper part of the soul itself. And before the whole reason is turned toward the mind, there are still intellect and reason in the soul, like two parts of the soul. But after it has been turned, the intellect is no longer a part, but the soul itself is then the intellect. Certainly, the soul is not happy before it turns entirely into the intellect by its act. It is almost as the high air under the sphere of fire is fiery and acts like fire. Indeed, a man is not even a man unless he has at least the potential for intellect. I think this was said on account of the brute animals; for if there is any power of arguing in their imaginations, it still cannot be formed by the mind. For since the forms of the mind itself are entirely stable and most universal, the imagination of a brute, through its forms—which are only particular and mobile—can never be formed by the mind. Reason, however, through its forms—though they are in a way mobile—can nevertheless eventually be led to the universal forms of intelligence. After this, he argues that this kind of happiness is not at all disturbed by the care of the animal body or its discomforts. For the soul affected in this way does not think the animal body is a part of itself, but rather something either made from it or commended to its providence. Plotinus affirms, however, that the soul affected in this way exists as a good for itself, namely through the intellectual form which the rational soul has recently put on. It has "put it on," I say, under its own intellect, just as the proper intellect from the beginning "puts on" the divine intellect. And entirely through the intellect, both its own and the divine, the soul enjoys the Good itself. This Good is simply good in itself, but in the intellect, it is the essential, vital, intellectual, and intelligible Good.

->What the Peripatetics might object.<-

V The fifth chapter of the book briefly lists what a **Peripatetic** <note>A follower of Aristotle's school, often seen as focusing more on external goods and logic than on mystical ascent</note> might object to this definition of happiness, and what things he would count as necessary for happiness. Among these things, you will note that magical sorceries <note>original: "magica veneficia"</note> can do something to the body and soul, as Porphyry <note>A student of Plotinus and a major Neoplatonist philosopher</note> also asserts—especially in souls that are in some way weak, that is, addicted to the imagination and not fortified by the intellect as if by Pallas’s shield and spear <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom; her armor represents the protective power of the intellect against base influences</note>. But we deal enough with sorceries and fascinations in our *Theology* and in the *Commentary on the Symposium* <note>original: "Conuiuio de amore"</note>.

->The ultimate end is the One Good, namely the highest,<-
->intelligible or more than intelligible.<-

VI To these things, he responds in the sixth chapter of the book: If we placed happiness in the prosperity and tranquility of human affairs, the things objected to by the Peripatetics would follow—namely, that he to whom adversities happen is not happy. But since we place the blessed life in the possession of the primary and divine Good, he does not think the rest of what are called "goods" should be numbered with it; nor does he think the opposites of these take away our happiness, as long as from that divinity...

# THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...let us not depart from this at all. As long as the soul is joined to [the Divine Mind], Plotinus says it is equally blessed, even if the body is meanwhile racked with pains. I believe Plotinus learned this not so much from the words of the Stoics <note>The Stoics were famous for teaching that virtue is the only good and that a wise person can be happy even while being tortured.</note> as from the examples of the Christian martyrs who were so numerous in his own century. Then, indeed, he denies that happiness should be placed in an accumulation of greater and lesser goods; indeed, he calls those so-called "lesser goods" "necessities" <term>necessaria; things required for physical survival but not for the soul's ultimate fulfillment</term> instead. Surely God, the author of nature, willed that our animal nature—that is, the living body—be subject to the soul as something less perfect. 

Consequently, within the soul, He subjects the imagination to reason, reason to the mind <term>mens; the highest, intuitive part of the soul</term>, and finally the mind to Himself. By this same logic, He established that the "good" and the specific goal of the animal body should serve the goal and good of the soul. Within the soul, He commanded that the goal of the imagination serve the goal of reason, and likewise that the familiar goal of reason serve the goal of the mind. Just as the goal of the intelligence is its own proper end, so it is the common end for everything that follows it—the "end of ends." 

For this reason, the goal of the rational soul is not composed of various diverse goods, but is the single good of the intelligence itself. All subsequent goods are referred to this as their final goal. This is especially true since the soul is considered blessed only when it is no longer distracted by many things, but—having dismissed or at least greatly relaxed its other powers and duties—it has been entirely transported into the mind. Therefore, the entire good of the soul is that one single good of the intelligence. At that point, if the soul chooses other things which are called "goods," it chooses them not for their own sake, but as certain remedies, so that all discomforts might be avoided as much as possible. Such discomforts might otherwise seem to pull the soul down to care for lower things, making it act more slackly regarding the divine good. 

Furthermore, he says that the ultimate goal, which is to be desired above all else, must not only be the greatest good in itself, but also most intimate <note>original: "intimum"; meaning most deeply internal or essential to one's own being</note> to the soul. For a good is most profitable if it is most deeply internal; and thus it is the greatest good for the soul. Conversely, that which is the greatest good in itself becomes the most intimate to our soul if only our soul senses it; this is both because that good most effectively seizes and penetrates the soul, and because the soul is most vehemently moved toward it. Only the "intelligible" <term>intelligibile; things known by the mind rather than the senses</term> and the "more-than-intelligible" good is of such a kind. For other things called "goods" are either outside our animal nature—such as wealth, honors, and power—or they are within our animal nature, like the pleasures of the senses. Or, if they are in the soul, they look toward external things, such as the delights of the imagination, hopes, and the reason when it is occupied with worldly business. Even if they do not look toward external things, they are still (so to speak) imaginary and are perpetually in motion, like the wandering discussions and concepts of speculative reason. But only that good which stands above the motion of reason is deeply intimate to the mind, and is (so to speak) solid, stable, and a complete whole. Therefore, it is both the greatest good in itself and the greatest good for the soul.

->*The happy man wants a single good; he chooses others for its sake.*<-

VII & VIII. In the seventh chapter of the book, he admits that the happy man chooses comforts rather than their opposites; but he chooses comforts not for themselves, but so that discomforts may be avoided. Indeed, he prefers discomforts to be far away, not because their presence would take away his happiness, but because they might take away his very existence (though he considers this of no importance hereafter) and because they tend to interrupt his zeal for contemplation. He concludes that the blessed man, being full of divinity, considers all other things as nothing; therefore, he cannot be turned away from his state by them in any direction. He pursues this same point in the eighth chapter.

->*Eternal wisdom is in the mind; when reason reaches it, the soul is blessed.*<-

IX. In the ninth chapter, a doubt is raised again: will he who has been defined as "blessed" remain so if he suffers from a most heavy disease or some harm that causes madness <term>phrenesim; a state of delirium or mental disturbance</term>? The answer is: he remains blessed. It is as if he were sleeping and dreaming in his imagination, yet he is awake and acting perfectly in his mind (as has been said of every soul), and in the higher power of reason, which is called "contemplative reason" and is a sort of intelligence. This reason is already formed by the mind in the blessed man and operates as the mind does. This occurs according to universal forms of things and acts of reason. For it is not so perfectly formed according to individual things, which are further distant from the mind. Even the remaining power of reason, which is more focused on action, if it should be distracted or idle during madness, is nevertheless most ready—after the onset of madness—to be reflected back toward the higher power of reason and the mind. 

After this, he distinguishes eternal knowledge from temporal knowledge; a point which we think should be examined more deeply here. Since in the primary essence, "living" is acting inwardly, and "understanding" is acting upon itself and being reflected back into itself by knowledge of itself—an act which in no way leans toward the body—we rightly think that intellectual nature extends as far as the knowledge of oneself and a certain separation from matter. Therefore, although in a rational nature a certain "image of the mind" is sometimes called by that name, an intellectual nature appears there in some way. For reason both notices itself and often separates forms from the conditions of matter. 

Thus, there are three grades of intellectual nature: namely, the **Common Intellect** <note>The Universal or Divine Mind</note>; the **Soul’s own Intellect**; and **Reason**. There are also three images of intellectual nature: first, the **Senses**; second, the **Vegetative power** <note>The faculty responsible for growth and nutrition</note>; and third, the **Form of the body**. But we shall speak of the images elsewhere. Now, in the First Intellect, "to understand" is "to be" itself. In the second, "to understand" is as if "to be" or (so to speak) "to exist." For it is to act: to act remarkably by a certain essential, intimate, and perpetual act, almost as "to shine" or "to sparkle" is in light. Finally, in the third, "to understand" is "to argue" or "to reason"; that is to operate through motion, almost as "to reflect" is in light. 

Rightly, then, between understanding which is "being" simply and without participation (being entirely through essence), and understanding which is "acting through motion," there is a middle understanding which is "acting entirely without motion." The first intelligence is by essence; the second is by participation, yet entirely immobile; the third is by a mobile participation. It is just as the essence of the sphere of fire is hot; the upper air is hot from there by perpetual participation; but the lower air is hot by a changeable participation. 

This reasoning not only shows us that there is a proper intellect in the soul that operates stably, but it is further confirmed by this: that the power of rational nature is in some way "passive" while it is being formed by motion and comes out of rest into action. Most people would call this the "passible" or "formable" intellect. It is necessary, therefore, that this intellect—being imperfect—be led from potentiality into a state of perpetual change by something else more perfect that is always in "act" <note>In Aristotelian and Platonic thought, "act" or "actuality" is the state of being fully realized, whereas "potency" is the capacity to become something.</note>. And it is not only necessary for the Common Intellect to be always in act here, but also the soul’s own proper intellect. This is so that rational nature does not lack an effective, intimate, and sufficient principle of its own intelligence, just as vegetative nature does not lack the "seminal reason" <term>ratio seminalis; an internal "seed-logic" that directs growth</term> of its own generation, which is its intimate, effective, and continuous principle of procreation. 

Therefore, just as universal nature (that is, the total "seed-logic" of the universe) presides over particular nature (the "seed-logic" of each living thing), and the latter perpetually presides over the mobile duty of generation; so the Common and Active Intellect presides over the soul's own Active Intellect; and this in turn over the Reason, which is now as if "passive." Thus, between the common active power and the soul's own passive power, the soul's own active power holds the middle place. From this it happens that the soul, when called back to the highest part of itself, immediately finds things it has not yet sought.

<summary>Ficino explains how the soul achieves happiness by focusing on the "Mind" and "Intelligence" rather than external goods or bodily states. He argues that the soul remains blessed even in madness because its highest intellectual part is perpetually active and connected to the Divine.</summary>

[Header: ON BOOK 4. ENNEAD I.]

...and it often prophesies, and performs works to be wondered at by all: since it suddenly returns into its own mind, which flourishes with a certain divine power to which all things lie open. But of these things we dispute most widely in [our] *Theology* <note>Ficino refers here to his own major work, the *Platonic Theology on the Immortality of the Soul*.</note>. To this intellect especially—as if to a third heaven, that is, an intellectual heaven above the imaginal and rational heaven—Plotinus would perhaps say Paul ascended <note>original: "Paulum ascendisse"; a reference to the Apostle Paul’s vision of the "third heaven" in 2 Corinthians 12:2</note>; and Moses onto this mountain <note>original: "Moysen in hunc montem"; referring to Moses ascending Mount Sinai to receive the Law</note>; and an angel of this kind announced many things to the prophets. For it is not fitting for the deities to descend to us; nor is it necessary for the soul that is to see divine things to change its physical location: for it is enough for the soul to be turned toward the mind and toward divine things. But let Plotinus see to these matters.

## The previous points are confirmed: that eternal wisdom is in every mind, and how the rational nature ascends to it.

The soul often considers many things, either by intuiting them or by arguing about them—not only that they are eternal, but also by what reasoning they are eternal: and it conceives a proper reasoning of eternity itself, so to speak. Indeed, the reasoning itself is of greater importance for eternity than the "mode" or manner of it. Since, therefore, there is such power in the soul that it thinks of eternal things and of eternity itself through an eternal reasoning, there is much more power in the soul to consider eternal things in an eternal way—that is, eternally and always. 

Thus, above the act of the **imagination** (which is "mobile" or shifting around shifting things), there stands the act of **reason** (which is "mobile" around things that are "immobile" or unchanging). Above this is the act of the **intelligence** (which is entirely "immobile" or steady around unchanging things). Thus, just as the action of the soul advances toward the better, so it may be perfected in the "best." 

Tell me, then: from where does our reason get its power? For while it gathers itself from individual forms to universal ones, it simultaneously releases those forms from this or that place, motion, or time. How could it do this unless by a certain virtue implanted within it and presiding over it—a power whose own action is released not only from place, but also from motion and time? Otherwise, reason itself, while it acts in a shifting and temporal way, could never release forms from motion and time through its own act. I called this an "implanted virtue": for if someone objects that reason achieves this under the "common intellect" <term>intellectus communis; the universal divine mind that illuminates all humans</term>, they will nonetheless be forced to confess that a specific act cannot be provided without a specific power. Since such an action follows such a faculty, it follows that a certain power, operating stably, is placed over reason by the common intellect. Through this power, even if reason moves, it nevertheless turns itself toward the unchanging. 

This stable power we call our "own intellect" <term>intellectus proprius; the individual human mind’s capacity for direct insight</term>. It is necessary that the most universal and certain principles of the sciences and arts reside within it, as well as the "exemplars" or blueprints of things. There, reason can pour out its discussions of arguing, and rightly discern true and good things or opinions from their opposites. And through the power of that intellect, which always perceives everything suddenly, reason also sometimes perceives something suddenly. 

When we say that "intelligible things" <note>original: "intelligibilia"; things that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses</note> are in the intellect, understand it this way: that the intellect *is* the intelligible thing itself. For this is the order of things: **Sense** is not the thing itself, nor does it possess the object of sense; it merely turns itself outward toward it. **Thought**, although it is not the object of thought, possesses it internally. Finally, the **Intellect**, being superior to reason, does not merely "possess" the intelligible object, but *exists* as it. Where Plotinus says that "the wisdom of the happy soul is located in a certain essence, or rather in Essence itself," he means that the act of understanding is the very act of being—both in one’s own intellect (which is a specific essence) and in the Common Intellect (which is Essence itself). He added "or rather," because the act of one’s own intellect is created and preserved by the act of the Common Intellect. 

Therefore, just as in light it is the same thing to *be* light as it is to *shine* (even if it is not the same thing to be light as it is to reflect or to be warm), so in the intellectual soul, it is the same thing to be intellectual as it is to understand—even though it is not the same to be, to reason, and to imagine. But remember, according to Plotinus’s mind, a twin species of reason must be placed between the intellect and the imagination: one is **speculative**, rising toward the intellect; the other is **active**, leaning rather toward the imagination. Otherwise, since one person cannot be more blessed than another through the intellect alone (since the intellect acts similarly and always in everyone), no one would be happier than another—unless it is because in this person, the speculative reason (which is naturally closest to the intellect) is turned entirely toward the mind. However, the same cannot be said of the active reason, because it is both more remote from the mind and is occupied with labor, serving external things in a certain way. It is clear that these types of reason differ in species, not only because the speculative nature thinks of its own works and the active nature thinks of the works of men, but also because the natural dexterity for both rarely, and perhaps never, occurs in the same talent.

## Neither does everyone notice that their mind is always acting upon the divine; nor does the blessed person always notice that their superior reason is acting upon the mind.

<margin>X</margin> Even if, in the blessed person, speculative reason acts under the form and action of the mind, it does not always notice that it is acting in this way—just as others do not always recognize that our mind is acting upon the divine mind. For just as in our animal nature, "to live" according to the **vegetative power** is almost the same as "to vegetate" (that is, to nourish, grow, generate, and preserve), yet we do not recognize that this power is doing these things, nor how it performs them. This is because no image of this action reaches the imagination of the animal, or our own. In the same way, in our mind, "to live" is the same as "to understand," yet we do not notice its eternal action unless a certain image of it is conceived in our imagination. 

Indeed, the blessed person does not always recognize that the speculative reason within them is already acting together with their intellect toward the divine mind. This is because an image of such an action is not always formed in their imagination—the tool through which the soul is usually warned about what a power, either lower or higher than itself, is doing. 

Here note: it belongs to our **intellect** to always know in "act" <term>actu; currently and fully performing the function</term>. It belongs to our **reason** to recall things known, in a way, as it passes from "habit" <term>habitu; possessing knowledge without currently thinking about it</term> into act while thinking through forms. Finally, it belongs to the **imagination** to learn new things. For if the imagination, turning away from reason, turns toward the "animal" (the body), it immediately notices what the animal sees or hears; but it does not recognize what reason or the intellect is doing in the meantime. Conversely, if it ever turns entirely toward reason while being free from the animal body, then the soul, through this very imagination, feels that reason is doing something. But if reason is turned toward the mind (as happens in the blessed person), then the soul immediately notices both that reason is awake around the mind, and that our mind is awake around the divine. Because our imagination is free from the animal body and is not fabricating anything corporeal, certain images appear from the very act of the mind and reason, through which the soul is warned—whether in speculative or active reason—that both the intellect and the speculative reason are acting. 

But you, remember: In the intellect itself, just as "to live" is the same as "to know," so "to know" and "to acknowledge" (that is, to notice that one knows) are entirely the same. But in reason, because "to live" and "to know" are not entirely the same—since the former is eternal while the latter is perpetually changeable—it is rightly the case that "to know" is not the same as "to acknowledge" that one knows or acts.

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

what follows is that recognition <note>original: "agnitio"</note> here follows cognition <note>original: "cognitionem"</note> as something subsequent, and perhaps as a certain consequence and accompaniment; it often happens that, due to a certain distraction of the soul, the prior action is somewhat diminished. Therefore, it is not without reason that Plotinus says that such recognition and awareness <note>original: "animaduersionémque"</note> are carried out through a subsequent and following faculty and form. We do not doubt that this faculty, which follows later as a companion, is the imagination itself. Similarly, we call the form that accompanies the prior form an "image." Let there be, therefore, natural forms in the mind or in the reason: although in the mind they are eternal, while in the reason they are perpetual. Let there be, then, adventitious forms in the imagination—images of the natural forms—through which the soul, as if in wonder, attends to and notices what is being done in the reason and the mind, as if they were new things. Indeed, just as the eye is contained within the face, so reason is contained in the mind. And just as the eye neither sees the face nor notices its movement except when the linear rays of the face are directed into a mirror <term>speculum</term> <note>Ficino uses the mirror as a classic metaphor for the imagination, which reflects the higher activity of the mind so that our lower consciousness can "see" it.</note> placed before us in a certain way, and are reflected from there at similar angles to the eye—and the mirror thus displays the image, if it has any image—in a similar way, the reason, like an eye, neither sees the mind nor notices that it is acting (even though it is always acting) unless its act performs something upon the imagination, which is distinct from it but turned toward it. By this act, an image of the higher action is reflected from the imagination into the reason.

Here you will note, first, where Plotinus says that we are not the act of the vegetative faculty <note>The lowest part of the soul responsible for basic biological growth and nutrition.</note>, but are rather the act of intelligence: this is especially true in the blessed state, and true also in every soul, which Plotinus considers more closely joined to the intellect than to the animal nature. Next, where he says that the act of understanding is then without phantasy <note>original: "phantasia"; the capacity to form mental images.</note> when no image is formed or reflected from it: pure intelligence does not depend on phantasy, but rather phantasy depends on intelligence. Nevertheless, rational intelligence—that is, thought and mobile reason—is often stirred by phantasy, especially the "active reason." Aristotle says that this active reason always requires phantasy, as Themistius <note>A 4th-century Byzantine philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> and Simplicius <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist known for his extensive commentaries on Aristotle.</note> wisely interpret. Finally, know that Plotinus agrees, while reviewing certain words of Aristotle, that this was his opinion concerning the mind: where in the third book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's *De Anima*.</note> he writes that the intellect always understands, and that intelligence is its very substance and exists as truly immortal. For immortality is not so true in the lower powers; for even if some are perpetual, they are nevertheless involved in motion. As for the fact that he denies that we—that is, the rational power—remember after death, Plotinus will examine this diligently elsewhere.

Finally, remember that Averroes <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher (Ibn Rushd) whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Medieval and Renaissance thought.</note>, even if not saying the exact same thing, introduced something similar when he says that our intellect has a double intelligence within it: one eternal, the other temporal. The former is exercised through its own being, the latter through our images. He says we never notice the former because it communicates nothing with our imagination, but we recognize the latter because its forms agree with the images of our imagination. And since he places a twin intellect in the same substance—namely, the "form-giver" <note>original: "formatorem"</note> and the "formable" <note>original: "formabilem"</note>—he says that this formable intellect does not recognize what the form-giver is doing through us until it has been perfectly formed by that agent through us. Only then, and simultaneously with it, will it be happy within us. But let us set aside Averroes; for Porphyry <note>Plotinus's student and editor.</note> and Proclus <note>A later, highly influential Neoplatonic philosopher.</note> also left Plotinus behind in this regard, not approving of the idea that the intellect of our soul is always acting in the way Plotinus says. We have set this out in the preceding sections, not so much approving it as interpreting it. Indeed, we must believe there is enough stability and excellence in our mind if the essence and forms of things are implanted there and the principles of the sciences remain.

### ON HAPPINESS
### On Blessedness <note>The Greek term is *Eudaimonia*, often translated as happiness, flourishing, or "having a good guardian spirit."</note>
