<image-desc>Decorative initial 'T' in a woodcut square, showing a figure in a classical landscape looking towards a distant building.</image-desc>
<margin>A</margin> If one identifies living and being happy <note>original: "εὐδαιμονεῖν" (eudaimonein)</note> as the same thing, must we then grant these to other animals too? For if it is their nature to lead their lives without hindrance, what prevents us from saying that they, too, are in a state of living well? For whether one places "living well" in a state of being unaffected by suffering <note>original: "ἀπαθείᾳ" (apatheia)</note> or in the fulfillment of a proper function, both would belong to other animals. For it is possible for them to be free from suffering and to be engaged in their natural work; for example, musical animals and all others who have what is proper to them—even those that sing according to their nature—have a life that is desirable to them for this reason. Furthermore, if we establish happiness as a certain end <term>telos</term> <note>The goal or final purpose toward which a thing naturally develops.</note>, which is the ultimate point of natural desire, we would have to grant happiness to them in this way too, as they reach that ultimate point. Once they arrive there, their internal nature stops its movement, having traversed their entire life and fulfilled it from beginning to end. But if someone is annoyed at the idea of bringing happiness down to the level of other animals—for in this way he would grant it even to the most humble of them, and even to plants, which also live and have a life that unfolds toward an end—first of all, he will seem to be in an absurd position if he denies that other animals live well simply because <margin>D</margin> he does not think they are of much value. As for plants, he would not be forced to grant them what he grants to all animals, on the grounds that they lack sensation. Yet perhaps there might even be someone who grants happiness to plants, since life is present in them as well. For life can be well-constituted, or the opposite; just as with plants, it is possible for them to be in a good state, to bear fruit, or not to bear fruit. If, then, pleasure is the end, and living well consists in this, <margin>E</margin> it is absurd for anyone to take living well away from other animals. The same would happen if the end were tranquility <note>original: "ἀταραξία" (ataraxia)</note>. It would also follow if living according to nature were said to be living well.
HOWEVER, to plants, because they do not perceive—

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'C' in a woodcut square, depicting a seated scholar in a library or study setting.</image-desc>
<margin>
8
Various opinions on what it means to live well, and to whom it applies.
</margin>
Since we establish living well and being happy as the same thing, should we grant this to the other living creatures as well? For if it is granted to them to pass through life without hindrance in the way they were born to do, what prohibits them from also living well—that is, living happily? For whether one defines living well as being in a good state, <margin>B</margin> or as the perfection of one's own proper work, both will apply to the other animals as well. For it will be possible for them both to be in a good state and to perform their natural work: just as musical animals, and any others who are in a good state in other respects, sing as they are naturally suited to do; and in this way it seems possible for them to achieve a desirable life. Furthermore, if we define happiness as a certain end—which is indeed the ultimate goal in the appetite of nature—in this way too we shall confess that they are happy, namely when they have arrived at the ultimate point. When they have progressed to that point, nature halts its motion within them: for it has already completed their entire life, and fulfilled it entirely from the beginning even to the end. But if anyone should find it troublesome for happiness to be transferred to beasts, asserting that it would thus apply to even the lowliest things, and to plants besides (which are themselves living, and bring their life to its own proper end), such a person might indeed seem absurd, saying that other animals cannot live well because they do not seem to him to be of much value. He will not be compelled to grant to plants what he grants to all animals on the grounds that they lack sensation. And perhaps there will not be wanting someone who grants happiness to plants as well, since <margin>
11
False opinions discussed; through them, some truth is extracted by inquiring whether living well applies to those lacking reason, and to plants.
</margin> living is present in them. For living happens partly well, and partly the opposite; just as it is given to plants to be in a good state, and to bear fruit, or not to bear fruit. Therefore, if pleasure is the end, and living well consists in this, the person who takes living well away from the brutes will be absurd. If tranquility <note>original: "tranquillitas"</note> is the end, the same will happen. Likewise, if "living according to nature" is said to be living well itself, the same result will seem to follow.
WHOEVER denies that happiness is present in plants because they do not perceive, seems—

# PLOTINUS ON THE ENNEADS I.
## BOOK IV: ON HAPPINESS

<margin>A</margin>
...they are in danger of not even granting it to all animals. For if they say that "to perceive" means that an affection <note>An "affection" (*pathos*) refers to a state or feeling experienced by the soul or body.</note> does not go unnoticed, then the affection itself must be good before it is noticed. For instance, being in a natural state is good even if it is unnoticed; and it is one's own, even if one does not yet know it is one's own. Furthermore, it must be sweet; for a thing must be sweet before you perceive it as sweet. Therefore, since the good is present and possessed, the one who has it is already faring well.

<margin>B</margin>
So, why is it necessary to add sensation? Unless, perhaps, they do not place the good in a present affection or state, but rather in the knowledge and sensation of it. But if so, they will be saying that sensation itself, or the activity of the sensory life, is the good; and thus they must admit that the good is present to those perceiving anything at all. But if they say the good is composed of both—namely, the perception of a certain specific thing or affection—how can they claim that the result of both is good, when each part is indifferent on its own?

<margin>C</margin>
But if they say the good is the affection, and that "living well" is such a state where someone knows the good is present to them, we must ask them: Does the person live well because they know this present thing *is* present? Or is it not enough to know it is sweet, but they must also know it is the good? Indeed, if one must know it is the good, that is no longer the work of the senses themselves, but of some virtue superior to the senses. Therefore, living well will not belong to those who are merely drenched in pleasure, but to the one who is able to know that pleasure is the good. Thus, the cause of living well will not be pleasure, but rather the faculty capable of judging that pleasure is good.

<margin>D</margin>
And that which judges is certainly superior to the affection and the passion; for it is reason, or intellect, while pleasure is a passion. In no way is the irrational superior to reason. How then could reason, abandoning itself, place something else belonging to an opposite class as being superior to itself? But it seems that those who do not grant happiness to plants, and those who place it in a certain kind of sensation, are unaware that they are seeking "living well" as something greater; they are placing that which is called "better" in a more complete form of life.

<margin>E</margin>
Again, those who say happiness lies in the rational life, rather than in life simply—even if it were sensory—might perhaps be speaking correctly. But we must ask them why they place happiness only around the rational animal: "Do you add 'rational' because reason is more skillful and sagacious, and can more easily investigate and acquire the primary things according to nature?" <note>The "primary things according to nature" (*prota kata physin*) is a technical Stoic term for basic needs like health, strength, and survival.</note>

<margin>F</margin>
What if reason were not able to investigate sagaciously nor to achieve those things? If reason is mentioned only because of its power to find things, then happiness would also belong to those lacking reason, provided they could naturally attain the primary things of nature without it. In that case, reason would be a mere servant, and not in any way choice-worthy for its own sake, nor would its perfection (which we call virtue) be choice-worthy.

<margin>G</margin>
But if you say that reason does not have its dignity because of the primary things of nature, but is to be cherished for itself, you must then state what its other work is, what its nature is, and what makes it perfect. For it must become perfect, not because of its inspection of these physical things, but its perfection must consist in something else, and a different nature must belong to it; it is not in the number of these primary things of nature, nor from those things which are the primary...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...they are in danger of not even granting it to all animals. For if they say that "to perceive" <note>original: "αἰσθάνεσθαι" (aisthanesthai)</note> is this—namely, that the affection does not go unnoticed—then the affection itself must be good before it is noticed; just as being in a natural state is good even if it is unnoticed; and it is one's own, even if one does not yet know it is one's own. And it must be sweet; for it must be sweet before [perception]. Thus, since this good is present, the one who has it is already living well. So why is it necessary to add sensation? Unless...

<margin>B</margin>
...perhaps they do not place the good in the occurring affection or state, but in the knowledge and sensation. But in this way, they will say that sensation itself is the good, or the activity of the sensory life; thus, to those perceiving anything at all, [the good is present]. But if they say the good is from both, as in a sensation occurring, how, when each is indifferent, can they say that which is from both is good?

<margin>C</margin>
If the affection is the good, and living well is such a state when someone knows the good is present to him, they must be asked whether one must know that this present thing is what is present, or not? Or only that it is sweet? Or rather that this is the good? But if this is the good, this is no longer the work of sensation, but of another power greater than sensation; so living well does not belong to those taking pleasure, but to the one able to know that pleasure is the good. The cause of living well is not pleasure, but the ability to judge that pleasure is good.

<margin>D</margin>
Since that which judges is better than the affection. For it is reason <note>original: "λόγος" (logos)</note> or intellect <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous)</note>, but pleasure is an affection; and nowhere is the irrational better than reason. How then could reason, letting itself go, place something else lying in the opposite camp as being better than itself? But it seems that those who do not grant it to plants, and as many as [place it] in such sensation, are unaware of themselves seeking "living well" as something more, and placing the "better" in a higher life.

<margin>E</margin>
And as many as say it is in the rational life, but not simply in life, nor even in the sensory, might perhaps be speaking well; but why they place being happy <note>original: "εὐδαιμονεῖν" (eudaimonein)</note> thus only concerning the rational animal, it is proper to ask them: "Do you add 'the rational' because reason is more resourceful, and can easily track down and provide the primary things according to nature, or even if it were not able to track them down or obtain them?"

<margin>F</margin>
But if it is because of being more able to find them, then happiness will also belong to those not having reason, if they should happen upon the primary things of nature by their nature in a way proportional [to reason]. And reason would be an under-servant, and would not be choice-worthy for its own sake, nor would its own perfection, which we say is virtue, be so either.

<margin>G</margin>
But if you will say that it does not have its honor because of the primary things of nature, but is to be embraced for itself, it must be stated what its other work is, and what its nature is, and what makes it perfect. For one must make it perfect, and the contemplation concerning these things, but it must be some other thing that is its perfection, and another nature must be its own. And it must not be from the primary things according to nature, nor from those which are the primary...

He asserts that if reason is the defining characteristic of a happy life, it must be because reason has its own intrinsic value and higher purpose beyond being a tool for survival.</summary>

...by the gods: and that it is not at all of this kind, but is the most excellent of all these things: otherwise, I do not think they can assign how it is to be venerated. But indeed, as long as they find a nature better than these things upon which they now dwell, they must be permitted to delay there wherever they please, doubting what "living well" actually is, in whom it can exist, how, and in which of these things it might be found.

<margin>
III
If all things lived with the same reason and degree of perfection, all would be able to live well: happiness itself is the intellect, but in other beings, "living" is distant from the intellect—that is, from life itself—more than by mere genus.
</margin>

**B** But let us resume from the beginning, considering what we suppose <term>happiness</term><note>The Greek term is *eudaimonia*, often translated as flourishing or well-being.</note> to be. Indeed, since we place happiness in "life," if we were to think that "living" meant the same thing for everyone, we would grant the capacity for happiness to all animals. We would then think that "living well" was an activity belonging to those in whom one and the same thing was present, of which all animals are naturally capable. Nor would we divide the matter in such a way as to grant this capacity to a rational being while denying it to an irrational one. For "life" would be the common element, which ought to be capable of attaining <term>blessedness</term><note>Latin: *beatitudinem*; a state of supreme happiness.</note> if indeed happiness consisted in a certain kind of life. Therefore, those who say that happiness occurs in the rational life, by not placing it in life in general, do not, I think, sufficiently notice that they are defining happiness as something other than life. They are compelled to say that a "rational quality" or "power" is that around which happiness consists. But for them, the subject is the "rational life": for happiness itself revolves around this whole, and for that reason, it seems it must be placed in a specific *kind* of life. **C** I say this not as if different kinds of life are distinguished as equals against reason, but as we are accustomed to say: one is prior, and the other is posterior. Since life is spoken of in many ways, having differences according to first, second, and so on; and since "living" is used equivocally—differently in plants, and differently in irrational animals—and has differences in its fullness and its scarcity, certainly both "living" and "living well" are spoken of by a certain analogical proportion among all these things. **D** And if one living thing is the image of another living thing, then similarly, one habit of "living well" must be judged as the image of another "living well." But if "living" is sufficiently present to anyone—that is, if it lacks nothing in any part of life—then happiness belongs to that one. Certainly, happiness will belong only to the one who lives sufficiently. For to this one, the "best" is also present: if indeed in the very order of beings, the best is that which truly exists in life, and that is the **perfect life**. **E** Thus, the good will not be something added from the outside: nor will anything else coming from elsewhere make it so that **F** the subject is placed in the good. For what must be added to the perfect life for it to be the best? If someone says the nature of the "good" itself must be added, our argument will be more precise; however, we are not seeking the cause, but what is inherent within us. It has often been said that the perfect and true life flourishes in that **intellectual nature**: while other lives are imperfect, being mere images of life, neither living perfectly nor purely; indeed, they are no more "lives" than they are "non-lives." And let it be said briefly now: insofar as all living things live from one principle, and others do not live equally, it necessarily follows that the principle of living itself is the **first life** and **perfection**.

<margin>
IIII
Man can follow the blessed life insofar as he attains the intellect, because then the whole soul becomes intellect.
</margin>

**G** If, therefore, man is able to have the perfect life, certainly the man having this is happy: otherwise, we would attribute happiness only to the gods, if we say that happiness can also exist in men...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of happiness (*eudaimonia*), transitioning from a general definition to a defense of the Stoic-Platonic view that the "perfect life" is internal and intellectual, independent of external suffering or bodily health.</meta>

-># PLOTINUS ENNEAD. I<-

A
We must consider in what way this is so. I say it this way: it is clear from other arguments that a man has a perfect life, not if he possesses the sensory life alone, but reason also and true intellect. But does he, existing as one person, hold this as something else? Or surely he is not a man at all, unless he possesses this either potentially or actually—the kind of man we call happy. B But shall we place this as a part of him, and say it is the perfect species of life? Or shall we say another man has this as a part, possessing it by some potential; but that the happy man is he who already exists as this in actuality, and has arrived at the point where he is one and the same with it. All other things already surround him: which indeed someone might not consider his parts, being surrounding things against his will; they would belong to him only if he wished to be connected to them. C What, then, is "good" for this man? Perhaps he is his own good through what he possesses. That which stands above is the cause of the good that flourishes in him. And that thing is good in itself in one way, but is present to another in another way. Evidence for this can be taken from the fact that one who is thus affected desires nothing further. For what would he seek? Certainly nothing of the inferior things; for he is joined to the best. D Therefore, he who lives thus has a sufficient life. And if he is endowed with virtue, he will be sufficient for happiness and for the possession of the good. For there is no good that he does not have. But what he seeks as "necessary," he seeks not for himself, but for something belonging to him: he seeks it for the body attached to him. And if he seeks it for the living body, it is certainly those things which pertain to the body, not those which are the property of the "inner man." E Truly he knows these things plainly, and gives what he grants in such a way that he never departs from his own life. For this reason, in adverse fortunes, he will nonetheless be blessed; for such a life remains just as it is. # BOOK FOUR.

A And [if he is] encompassed by misfortunes and pains, will he be happy, even if he is a good man? <note>original: "εὐδαίμων εἴη... ὄντι γίγνοιτο" / "felix erit... etiam si bonus sit"</note> Indeed, for the gods, the perfect disposition of the mind alone is happy and self-sufficient. But for men, whose souls have a lower part <note>the body and sensory desires</note> joined to them, happiness must be sought in the whole composite <note>the human being as a union of soul and body</note>, and not just in one part, even if that part is the more excellent one. Otherwise, as long as the other part is in a bad state, the better part is necessarily hindered in its duties. Unless, of course, one ought to cast aside the body, or at least the perception of the body, and in that way seek the self-sufficiency required for happiness.

B But if reason placed happiness in the absence of pain, disease, danger, or falling into great adversities, then no one could be happy when the opposites of these things were imminent. However, if happiness is placed in the possession of the True Good <note>the "True Good" refers to the intellectual and divine realm in Plotinus's system</note>, why should we pass over this and judge a man's happiness by looking at things that happen to him, which are not counted as part of happiness at all? C But if the End <note>original: "τέλος" / "finis" — the ultimate goal or purpose of life</note> must be one thing and not many—otherwise a person would be seeking "ends" rather than "The End"—then one must pursue only that which is ultimate and most excellent, which the soul seeks to fold into itself. He responds to objections: that the ultimate end is a simple good, namely the intelligible <note>that which is known by the mind</note>; other things are not the end, but lead to the end.</margin>

To have "necessities" <note>such as food, health, or safety</note> present is not a matter of the "will," if you use the word strictly and not loosely. We think these things should be present because we avoid evils as much as we can; yet this act of avoiding is not what we primarily desire. A But how this is so, we must consider. We shall put it this way: It is clear from other arguments that a human being possesses a **perfect life** <note>original: "τελείαν ζωὴν" / "perfectam vitam"</note> not merely by having sensory life, but by possessing **reason** and **true intellect**. But does he possess this as something separate from himself, as if he were one thing and the intellect another? No, a person is not a human being at all unless he possesses this either potentially or actually—and we say the one who is <term>happy</term> <note>original: "εὐδαίμονα" / "felicem" — refers to the state of "Eudaimonia," a flourishing life guided by a divine spirit or "daimon."</note> is the one who has it actually. But shall we say this perfect form of life is merely a *part* of him? B Or rather, shall we say that another sort of man has this only as a potential part, while the happy man is he who *actually* exists as this intellect, and has transformed himself so as to be identical with it? All other things now merely "surround" him; he would not even count them as parts of himself, for they surround him against his will. They would only be truly "his" if he chose to be joined to them. To such a man, then, what is his "Good"? C Perhaps it is simply himself, by virtue of what he possesses. That which exists above him <note>The One or the Absolute Good</note> is the cause of the good that flourishes within him. That higher Good is good in one way to itself, but is present to the man in another way. Proof of this can be found in the fact that someone in this state desires nothing further. For what would he seek? He seeks nothing of inferior things, for he is joined to the best. The life of one who lives thus is therefore **self-sufficient**. If he is endowed with <term>virtue</term> <note>original: "virtute" / "σπουδαῖος" — specifically the moral and intellectual excellence of the "sage."</note>, he will be sufficient for happiness and the possession of the Good. For there is no good that he does not have. D What he seeks as "necessary," he does not seek for himself, but for something that belongs to him: he seeks it for the **body** that is annexed to him. And if he seeks it for the living body, it is for the needs of the body's life, not for the things proper to the **inner man**. He surely knows these needs, and he gives what he gives without in any way departing from his own life. For this reason, in the face of adverse fortunes, he will be no less happy; for his life remains as it is. Furthermore, in the death of family and friends, he is not ignorant of what death is. Those who suffer such things, if they themselves are virtuous, also clearly know this. E As for relatives and close associates who suffer, if their suffering brings any distress, it does not affect the man himself, but rather that part of him which is <term>lacking mind</term> <note>original: "mente captum" / "νοοῦν οὐκ ἔχον" — refers to the non-rational, sensitive part of the soul.</note>, whose specific distresses the happy soul will not take upon itself.

# BOOK FOUR

A If one who is beset by sorrows through fortune and pain should be happy, provided he were a virtuous man, how could this be? To the gods, such a state is indeed happy and self-sufficient. But for a human being, who has received an addition of the "inferior" <note>Referring to the physical body and its sensory demands.</note>, one must seek for <term>happiness</term> <note>original: "εὐδαίμον" / "felicitas" — a state of flourishing and well-being.</note> in the whole of their being, not merely in one part. For if one part is in a bad state, would it not necessarily follow that the other, better part, is hindered in its own activities? Either one must cast off the body, or the senses of the body, and only then seek self-sufficiency for the sake of being happy.

B BUT if our reasoning placed happiness in the absence of pain, or in not being sick, or in not falling into great misfortunes, then no one could be happy when the opposites of these things were present. However, if happiness is placed in the possession of the **true good**, then why should we look at these other things and judge a man’s happiness by them, seeking things that are not counted toward happiness? C For if happiness were a mere accumulation of goods and "necessities"—or even things not strictly necessary but still called "goods"—then we would require these to be present as well. But if the <term>End</term> <note>original: "τέλος" / "finis" — the ultimate goal or purpose of life.</note> is not found in many things, but in one (otherwise it would not be "an end" but "ends"), then one must lay hold only of that which is ultimate and most precious, which the soul seeks to establish within itself. Is this search and this will <margin>* within her own nature</margin> D not directed toward this? For reasoning does not choose to avoid troubles because of a primary wish of nature, but rather it avoids them by a process of calculation <margin>* looking away / managing</margin>, or seeks to add comforts. But the primary desire itself is directed toward what is best; when that is present, the soul is fulfilled and at rest. And this is the life that is truly willed. E As for the presence of "necessities," this would not be a matter of "will" if one uses the term strictly, though one might use the word loosely, since we do think these things ought to be present. This is proven by these very things when they are present, such as health and the absence of pain. F For which of these is truly seductive to the soul? <meta>This page continues the discussion of Plotinus’s Ennead I, Tractate 4 (On Happiness). Having established that happiness belongs to the soul’s intellectual life, Plotinus now argues that external tragedies—loss of family, property, or even physical torture—cannot diminish the inner light of a truly virtuous person.</meta>

->### PLOTINUS, ENNEADS I.<-

A He enjoys the Good, and desires to have it alone, and nothing else along with it. Indeed, even if something else occurs, it does not take away the <term>End</term> <note>original: "finis" / "τέλος" — the ultimate goal of life, which is union with the Good.</note>, which is present even when these other things are there. In general, if something happens to the happy man that he does not wish for, he does not for that reason fall away from his <term>blessedness</term> <note>original: "beatitudo" / "εὐδαιμονία" — a state of flourishing independent of external luck.</note> in any part. Otherwise, he would be changed and fall out of happiness every single day; for instance, if he were to lose a son, or suffer the loss of some household goods. Surely there are countless things that, happening contrary to his desire, subtract nothing from the presence of the End.

B But they say that "great adversities" can change happiness. Yet what human thing is so great that it cannot be looked down upon by one who has raised himself to things higher than all these, and no longer depends on any inferior things? For when he considers even great prosperities—such as kingdoms, empires over cities and nations, or the founding of cities—to be of little account, even if he himself achieved them, why should he consider the loss of power or his fatherland a grave evil? 

C Indeed, if he were to think such a thing a great evil, or an evil at all, he would be ridiculous. He would no longer be a man of <term>virtue</term> <note>original: "probus" / "σπουδαῖος" — the excellent or serious person who lives according to reason.</note> if he considered wood and stones and—by Jupiter!—the deaths of mortals to be something great. We hold that such a man ought to consider death to be better than a life joined to a body.

D If he himself were to be sacrificed, would he think death an evil to him simply because he was being slaughtered near an altar? And unless it is granted otherwise, will the body not be dissolved anyway, whether above or below the earth? Would he make much of the fact that he is buried with little expense and without fame, judged unworthy of a high monument? It is the mark of a small-minded man to make much of such things. Furthermore, if he is led away as a captive, there remains a way to free himself <note>A reference to the Stoic and Platonic acceptance of "rational departure" or suicide as a final escape from unbearable conditions.</note> if it is not possible to be happy there. But if his family members are led away as captives, such as granddaughters or daughters being dragged off, will he be any less happy?

E What shall we say then? If he dies without having seen such things, does he leave life with an opinion that these things could not happen? To think so would be absurd. Will he not then think it possible that his people might fall into such fortunes? Would he then, because of this very opinion of what *might* happen, fail to be happy? On the contrary, even holding such an opinion, he can still be happy.

F Therefore, even if it happens in his presence, he will reflect that such is the nature of the universe—that it brings such things—and that they must be followed. Many who are led into captivity may even fare better. Furthermore, it is in the power of those who are bound to free themselves. If they remain, they remain for some reason, and so it is not truly grave; or if they remain without reason, it is not fitting that he should be the cause of his own disturbance. Truly, a virtuous man will never be weighed down by evil because of the ignorance of his kin, nor will he be moved by the fortunes of others, whether they be adverse or prosperous.

The blessed man
preserves the 
**intelligible good**
whole in any 
turn of
fortune.
</margin>
G When his pains are fierce, he will bear them as long as he can; but if they exceed his strength, the pains will carry him out of life. He will not be pitiable even when placed in pain; but his own light will shine steadily in his inner sanctuary, like a small torch in a beacon, even while the winds blow outside, raging with whirlwinds and storms. But if he should be less consistent with himself, or if perhaps—

<column-break/>

<margin>* [Reading: It is established] </margin>
A **It is established** that the one who possesses the Best wants to have that alone, and not anything else with it; or if something else is present, it does not take that away, but it is there nevertheless. In general, it is not the case that if something the happy man does not want is present, it already takes away something from his happiness. Otherwise, he would shift every single day and fall out of happiness; for example, if he lost a child or any of his possessions. There would be ten thousand things that turn out not according to his will, but none of them will make the present End vanish from him.

B But they say it is "great things" that do this, not just anything. Yet what of human affairs could be "great" so as not to be despised by one who has ascended to what is higher than all these, and is no longer attached to anything below? For why does he think even great successes—however large they may be, such as kingdoms, and the rule over cities and nations, and the settling and founding of cities—not to be great, even if they were from him and through him? Why then would he consider the loss of power and the razing of his city a terrible and great thing?

C If he truly thought it a great evil, or an evil at all, he would be ridiculous in his doctrine, and no longer an excellent man, if he thought wood and stones and—by Zeus!—the deaths of mortals were great. We say his doctrine must be that death is better than life with a body.

<margin>* [Reading: it is placed] </margin>
D And he himself, if he should be sacrificed, will he think death is an evil for him because he died at an altar? But even if he were not buried, the body, whether placed above the earth or below it, would still rot. And if he is buried without great expense or anonymously, not being deemed worthy of a high tomb, that is mere pettiness of mind. But if he were led away as a captive, there is a path to depart if it is not possible to be happy. If his own people are captives, for example, daughters and daughters-in-law being dragged away, what then?

E We shall say: if he died without seeing such a thing, would he depart with a different opinion, as if these things were not going to happen? He would be strange indeed. Would he not then think that his family could fall into such fortunes? Would he then, because he thinks they *might* happen, not be happy? Or rather, even thinking they might happen, he is happy, and even if they *are* happening.

F For he reflects again that the nature of this universe is such that it brings these things, and they must be followed. Many, having become captives, will even do better; and it is in the power of those who choose it to depart. If they stay, they stay because of themselves, and it is not terrible; or if they stay irrationally, they should not be the cause of trouble to him. For he will not be in a bad state through the folly of others who are his kin, nor will he be dependent on the good or bad fortunes of others.

G Regarding the pains within him, when they are intense, he will bear them as long as he is able; if they exceed his power, they will carry him out, and he will not be pitiable in his pain. But the light within him shines—like the light in a lantern—even when much is blowing from outside in a great surge of winds and storm. But if he is not at least— <margin>is called</margin>

# BOOK FOUR.

A If pain should be extended so far that it is so intense that it almost kills us, what shall we say? Truly, if it is prolonged, he <note>The virtuous person.</note> will deliberate on what must be done; for in these matters, his free will <note>original: "liberum arbitrium" / "αὐτεξούσιον"</note> is not taken away.
One must know that things do not appear to the man of excellent virtue as they do to others; nor do they reach his innermost self—neither tortures, nor pains, nor the distresses that weigh down others when they are oppressed by narrow circumstances. B To think otherwise would be a certain weakness of our soul. This is clearly seen when we think it is better for these things to be hidden from us, or if we think it better that imminent death remains unknown. Furthermore, when we desire to avoid the misfortunes of those close to us, we are no longer looking out for them, but for ourselves, so that we are not affected by any trouble. C That is entirely the fault of our own weakness, which we must drive far away; we should not yield to weakness by fearing that some trouble might happen. 
If someone objects that we are naturally built to grieve for the misfortunes of our kin, let him understand first that not everyone is so affected. Second, it is the duty of <term>virtue</term> <note>Virtue (arete) here is the power of the soul to maintain its rational state despite physical or emotional pressure.</note> to lead the common condition of nature toward what is better, and toward something more honorable than the common opinion. D It is more honorable not to give in to things that seem heavy to our common nature. One should not behave like a novice, but like a strong contestant <note>original: "strenuum certatorem" / "ἀθλητὴν μέγαν"</note> manfully repelling the blows of fortune. For he knows that while such things are displeasing to common nature, they are to be endured by his own character—not as truly terrible things, but as "terrors for children." <margin>* children</margin> Did he then wish for these things? Perhaps he did not; but when they happen, he opposes them with virtue, through which the soul is not easily changed or made to suffer. <margin>* therefore these things</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>
**IX**
The happy man, with the higher eye of his reason already fixed on eternal intelligence—from which he is happy—even if the lower eye of reason looks upon other things.
</margin>
But when he is not himself, perhaps overwhelmed by disease or the arts of magicians, what then shall we say? E If they concede that he retains his own virtue in that state, even if he is like one who is sleeping, what prevents him from being happy? For they do not take away his <term>happiness</term> <note>original: "felicitatem" / "εὐδαιμονία"</note> in sleep, nor do they consider that moment of time as counting against him being happy throughout his whole life. If they say he is no longer a man of integrity, then they are no longer talking about the virtuous man. We, however, assuming he is virtuous, ask whether he is always happy insofar as he is virtuous. F But if he is endowed with virtue, they say, yet does not perceive it, nor act according to virtue—how then will he be happy?
Truly, even if he does not feel himself to be healthy, he will nonetheless be healthy; again, if he does not notice that he is beautiful, he will be no less beautiful. If he does not feel himself to be wise, will he be any less wise? But perhaps someone might say that <term>wisdom</term> requires a sense of itself and an awareness, for happiness is located in the very act of wisdom. G However, if wisdom and its action were something added from the outside <note>original: "adventitia" — something not essential to the soul's nature.</note>, such an argument might perhaps be convincing. But if the substance <note>original: "substantia" / "ὑπόστασις"</note> of wisdom is situated in a certain essence—or rather, is essence itself—and if this essence does not perish in the sleeper, or in the one who is said to be unaware of himself; and if the act of the essence is within itself, and such an act is perpetually awake <note>Plotinus believes the highest part of the soul is always "thinking" even when our conscious mind is distracted or asleep.</note>; then surely the virtuous man, as a virtuous man, will still act, even if he is sleeping or in a weakened state. It will be hidden...

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD I.

...however, such an activity does not involve the whole of us, but rather only some part: just as when the <term>vegetative activity</term> <note>original: "vegetali actu" / "Φυτικῆς ἐνεργείας". This refers to the basic biological functions like growth and nutrition which happen without our conscious thought.</note> is in full force, the awareness of such action does not pass into the rest of the person through the nature of sensation itself. For if we were entirely the same as our vegetative power, we would undoubtedly be "acting" whenever it acted. But in truth we are not that, but rather we are the activity of the <term>Intellect</term> <note>The "Intellect" (Nous) is considered the highest part of the human soul in Neoplatonism, the seat of eternal truths.</note> itself; therefore, when that acts, we act.

<margin>
X
Why the eternal act of intelligence is hidden from man, and how it can be perceived.
</margin>

**B** But it is hidden, perhaps, because it does not reach a certain perceiving power. For it is necessary for an activity to work through a certain medium—like a sense—to reach us. But why should the Intellect itself not act? And again, why should the soul not act around the Intellect, preceding both sensation and awareness? For there must be some activity before there is awareness, if indeed "to think" and "to be" are the same thing. It seems that awareness occurs and comes into being when the act of intelligence is reflected: and when that which acts according to the life of the soul is, as it were, struck back again, like something in a <term>mirror</term> <note>Plotinus uses the mirror as a metaphor for the "imagination" (phantasia). If the "mirror" of the mind is calm, we are conscious of our thoughts; if it is disturbed by the body, the thoughts continue but we lose conscious awareness of them.</note> that rests upon a smooth and bright surface. For as in such objects, when a mirror is present, an image is produced; but when it is not present, or is not in the right condition, the activity that would have produced the image is still present, but the image itself is absent. So it is regarding the soul: when that which is within us—wherein the images or certain marks of thought and intellect shine—is in a state of quiet, then such images are seen. In this way, it is recognized through a quasi-sensible manner that the intellect and thought are acting, alongside the prior knowledge. But when this "mirror" is confounded because the harmony of the body is disturbed, then the thought and the intellect continue to think without an image, and the act of understanding then takes place without <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "phantasia" / "φαντασίας". In this context, it refers to the mental faculty that produces images of thoughts.</note>. Therefore, one can consider that intelligence occurs alongside imagination in a certain way, even though intelligence is by no means the same as imagination. Indeed, one will find many noble speculations and actions even among those who are awake, in which we do not notice ourselves speculating or acting. For it is not necessary for one who reads to be consciously aware that they are reading, especially when they read with the greatest attention; nor does one who acts bravely necessarily know they are acting bravely. There are many other similar cases, so much so that conscious awareness seems to make the actions they accompany weaker. But when actions are alone, they are then pure, and seem to possess more of action and life. Now, when virtuous men live in that state, it is certain that they live more fully; for at that time, life is not diffused into the senses, but is gathered into itself in the same consistent tenor.

<margin>
XI
The blessed man lives most of all: and by what reason.
</margin>

**G** And if anyone should object that such a man does not even "live," we shall certainly affirm that he does live: but his happiness remains hidden from them, just as his life does. But if they will not believe it, we shall deem it fair that, while granting that he lives and is virtuous, they should then inquire whether he is happy in this way; they should not perhaps strip him of life while inquiring whether he lives well. Nor, again, should they remove the man from the discussion entirely while deliberating on the happiness of a man. Finally, when they have conceded that the virtuous man has turned toward his innermost self,

<column-break/>

<margin>* Vegetative</margin>
...But this activity would not be his whole self, but some part of him, just as when the **vegetative** activity is active, the perception of such activity does not reach the rest of the man through the sensory faculty. And if indeed we were our **vegetative** part, we would be the ones acting. But now we are not that, for we are the activity of the thinking principle. Thus, when that acts, we would be the ones acting.

**B** But it is hidden, perhaps, by not being concerned with the whole of sensible things. For through sensation, as if through a medium, it seems to **act** <note>original: "ἐνεργεῖν" (energein)</note> concerning these things and about these things.
<margin>* surely to act</margin>
Should not then the intellect itself act? And the soul around it, or before sensation? And generally before perception? For there must be an activity concerning perception, if indeed thinking and being are the same. And it seems that perception exists and comes to be when the thought reflects back, and when the activity according to the life of the soul is, as it were, pushed back again, as in a mirror around a smooth and bright stillness. Just as in such things, when the mirror is present, the image is produced, but when it is not present or not in such a state, the **activity** is present by which the image would have been; so also regarding the soul: when that which is within us is at rest—that in which the images of thought and intellect are reflected—then these things are seen, and are known as if sensibly, along with the primary knowledge that the intellect and thought are active. But when this is shattered because the harmony of the body is lost, the thought and the intellect think without an image, and the thinking then happens without imagination. Thus one might consider that thinking happens with imagination, though thinking is not imagination. And one might find many noble activities and contemplations even of those awake, and actions which we contemplate, and yet when we act, we do not have the "following along" <note>original: "παρακολουθεῖν" (parakolouthein) - this refers to self-conscious awareness or monitoring of one's own actions.</note> with them. For is it necessary for the reader to **be aware** that he is reading?
<margin>* to follow along / be aware</margin>

**E** Or that the one acting bravely is aware that he is acting bravely, and acts according to bravery in all he does? And a myriad of other things, so that these "followings-along" <note>self-conscious reflections</note> run the risk of making the very activities they follow more obscure. But when they are alone, they are then pure, and act more, and live more. And indeed, when the virtuous are in such a state, there is more "living," not poured out toward sensation, but gathered together in the same place within itself.

**G** But if some should say that such a one does not even live, we shall say he lives; but his happiness is hidden from them, just as his life is. And if they are not persuaded, let us ask them to assume he is living and virtuous, and then seek if he is happy—not diminishing his life, and then seeking if life is present; nor taking away the "man" and then seeking the happiness of the man; nor, having conceded the virtuous man has turned toward the inner...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of the "sage" or the "perfectly happy person" (eudaimon) from the previous section. Having established that happiness is found in the life of the Intellect, Plotinus now addresses whether external misfortunes or a lack of physical pleasure can diminish this state.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR.

<column-break/>

**A** ...but rather to note that if he were to seek external activities, his will would be placed entirely in outward things. Otherwise, there would be no actual substance to happiness if you were to place his will in external matters, or say that the virtuous man desires such things. To be sure, he wishes that all men live well and that no one be afflicted by any evils. Nevertheless, if these things do not turn out according to his wish, he will be no less happy. If someone should say that he would be deceived or stray from reason if he were to wish for such things (since it is **B** impossible for evils not to exist), that person will surely grant us that the sage turns his will toward the inward things of the soul.

<margin>XII *The happy man does not lack any external pleasure; why is the mind satisfied?*</margin>

**B** But if people demand pleasure in this kind of life, they will surely not demand the pleasures of the intemperate, nor those of the body at all. For it is impossible for these to be present without contaminating happiness. Nor, again, do they require the overflow of exuberant joy. For why would they require such things? Rather, they possess those pleasures that necessarily accompany the presence of the Good: these are not found in **C** motion <note>Plotinus distinguishes between "motion" (kinesis), which is a process toward a goal, and "activity" (energeia), which is the state of being at the goal.</note>, nor are they newly arrived. For his goods are already present; he is present to himself, and his pleasure and serenity remain constant. The virtuous man is always serene, his state is quiet, and his disposition is self-sufficient: a state which no "evils" (as they are called) can disturb, provided he is truly virtuous. If someone seeks another kind of pleasure in the life of the virtuous man, it is no longer the virtuous life they are looking for.

<margin>XIII *The eternal act of the mind and reason is not hindered by externals.*</margin>

**Δ** Nor, indeed, are his actions entirely hindered by fortune; rather, different actions will arise according to different fortunes. All of them are equally noble, and perhaps those are even nobler which correctly manage difficult circumstances. The activities found in contemplation, if they concern specific matters, will perhaps be such as he brings forth after he has sought and considered them. But the greatest learning is always ready at his command: and even more so if he were placed in the so-called **bull of Phalaris** <note>The "Bull of Phalaris" was a famous ancient Greek torture device where a victim was locked inside a bronze bull and roasted over a fire. Stoic and Platonist philosophers often used this extreme example to argue that a sage could remain happy through internal contemplation even while being tortured.</note>. That which is said to be "sweet" in such a case is said foolishly, though it is repeated twice or many times. For there, the part that utters such a cry is the very part that is in torment. But here, the part that feels pain is one thing, and the part that dwells within itself is another; as long as he necessarily dwells with himself in this way, he will never fail in his contemplation of the universal Good.

<margin>XIIII *What a man is; that the happy man is not hindered by the external.*</margin>

**G** That a man—especially a virtuous one—is not merely a composite of soul and body is witnessed by the very separation from the body and the contempt for those things called "bodily goods." It would be ridiculous if someone were to say that happiness belongs also to the "animal" part within us <note>The "animal" (zoon) refers to the biological union of body and lower soul.</note>. For since happiness is a "good life," it surely consists in the soul itself. This good life is an activity, yet not an activity of the whole soul—not, for instance, of the vegetative part, which reaches down even to the body. For happiness is not placed in physical size or a good bodily condition; nor, again, is it in the sharpness of the senses. Indeed, an excess of physical health and sensory prosperity can weigh down the soul and turn the man toward itself. On the contrary, it is fitting to "thin out" the body through a certain compensation and diversion, turning instead toward the Best, so that it may be shown that the real man is different from external things. Nevertheless, let that man among us be both handsome and great and wealthy, and the lord of all men, as one who is considered a citizen of this lower region; yet he is not to be envied for these things. **G**

<column-break/>

<summary>Plotinus argues that the sage's happiness is internal and independent of external fortune, even in extreme pain like the Bull of Phalaris. He emphasizes that the "true man" is the higher soul, not the body-soul composite.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "sage" (the wise and virtuous person) and how their inner happiness relates to physical suffering or external circumstances. Plotinus is arguing that true happiness (eudaimonia) belongs to the soul and the intellect, and is therefore invulnerable to the "blows of fortune."</meta>

### PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS: BOOK I.

**A** ...one deceived by such things is to be pitied. Concerning the sage <term>sage: (Latin: *sapiens*, Greek: *sophos*) a person who has achieved perfect wisdom and virtue, a central figure in ancient philosophy</term> himself, such things perhaps do not exist from the start; and if they are present, he will diminish them himself, provided he cultivates his own self. He will wear away the luxury and the gifts of the body through neglect, and he will set aside positions of worldly power. Furthermore, he will care for the health of his body in such a way that he does not desire to be altogether inexperienced in disease, nor similarly in pains. Rather, if they have not occurred, he will wish to learn of them in his youth; but in old age, he will wish to be disturbed neither by these nor even by pleasures—nor by any bodily thing, whether pleasant or **B** troublesome—lest he be forced to incline toward the physical body. When placed in the midst of pains, he will oppose them with the virtue that is present and sufficient for these things. He will so prepare himself that he does not judge himself to be happier in pleasures, health, and rest from labors, nor consider himself less happy in their opposites. For since the former do not increase his happiness, certainly their contraries do not diminish it.

<margin>
XV. 
Nothing can be added to or taken away from the happy man.
</margin>

**C** What if there were two wise men? Suppose one has everything considered to be in accordance with nature, while the other has the opposite. Shall we say they are equally happy? We shall indeed say so, provided they are equally wise. Truly, if one has a beautiful body and possesses all other things that contribute neither to wisdom, nor to virtue in general, nor to the contemplation of what is best, nor to the best life, I do not see what more weight he gains from these. For even he who possesses such things will not boast as if he were **D** happier than the one who does not. Indeed, such an abundance would not even contribute to the flute-player's own goal <note>original: *tibicinis finē*. Plotinus uses the analogy of a musician to show that external luxuries do not improve the quality of a person's inner "art" or virtue.</note>. But we, out of our own weakness, consider a man happy by judging as heavy and horrible things which the happy man himself does not judge so. Otherwise, he will not yet be wise, nor yet happy, unless he has first driven away all such delusions of the imagination. Having become as if entirely another person, he trusts in himself that he will suffer no evil. In this way, he will live without fear in all things. But if he fears anything, he is not yet **E** perfect in virtue, but will seem to possess only half of it. As for those unforeseen fears that occur before judgment can be made, if they happen while he is intent on other things, the sage will try to repel them. He will restrain the physical sensation joined to him—like a child moved by pain—either with threats or with reason. I say "threats" in a way that is not disturbing, just as a child might be immediately restrained by the look of a person of great authority. Yet such a man will not be a stranger to friendship and **F** gratitude for these reasons; for he is such toward himself and toward his own. Since, therefore, he attributes to his friends the same things he attributes to himself, he will be a friend above all, and simultaneously live according to the mind.

<margin>
XVI. 
The wise man, happy in his own affairs, turns only toward the mind: he hangs upon God; other things he either despises or governs without being disturbed.
</margin>

**G** If anyone does not establish the virtuous man in this lofty mind, but instead subjects him to the blows of fortune and fears these things for him, then surely he is not describing the virtuous man as we think he ought to be. Instead, he brings forward a mediocre man, a mixture of good and evil, leading a mediocre life composed of both. Such a person is not easy to find, nor if he were found, would he be worthy of the name "happy," since he would possess nothing great, neither in the excellence of wisdom nor in the purity of the good. Therefore, happiness is not found in a "mixed life." For Plato rightly judges that the highest good must be sought from above.

<column-break/>

**A** ...for the one deceived by such things. Concerning the sage, these things perhaps would not happen in the first place, but if they are present, he will diminish them himself, if indeed he cares for himself. He will diminish and wither the advantages of the body through neglect. He will lay aside offices of power. While guarding the health of the body, he will not wish to be entirely inexperienced in disease, nor indeed inexperienced in pains. Rather, even if they happen, he will wish to learn of them while young; but being already in old age, he will not want these or pleasures to disturb him, nor any of the things here, such as attachments or their opposites, so that he does not look toward the body. When he is in the midst of pains, he will oppose them with the power he has prepared for this. He does not take pleasures, health, and the absence of pain as an addition to his happiness, nor does he see their opposites as a subtraction or a lessening of it. For if he does not add the opposites to the same state, how could the contrary take anything away?

**C** But if there were two wise men, and one had all things that are said to be according to nature, while the other had the opposite: shall we say that happiness is present to them equally? We shall say so, if indeed they are equally wise. For if the one has a beautiful body, and all other things that do not lead to wisdom, nor at all to virtue or the best vision and being best, what would this be? Since he himself, possessing these things, will not pride himself as being more happy than those **D** who do not have them. For an abundance of these things would not even contribute to the goal of the flutes <note>A marginal note here suggests the word "self-will" (*authadeia*) instead of "flutes" (*auliskōn*), a scholarly debate over whether Plotinus meant the goal of a musician or a state of character.</note>. But we look at the happy man through our own weakness, thinking things are frightening and terrible which the happy man would not think so. Otherwise, let him not yet be wise, nor happy, if he has not changed all his imaginations about these things, and become altogether another person, having trusted in himself that he will never have any evil. For when he stands toward virtue, he is fearless about everything. But if he is afraid, **E** he is not perfect in virtue, but will be a kind of half-measure. The fear that happens without choice and comes readily, if it should approach him while he is occupied with other things, he will push away. And the movement within him, as if toward pains, he will stop with a threat or with reason—with a threat that is impassive, as if a child were struck with awe merely by the dignified look of a superior. Truly, such a man is not a friendless or unfeeling person; for he is such toward himself and among his own **F** people. Giving therefore to his friends what he gives to himself, he would be a friend most of all, along with possessing intellect.

**G** But if one does not count the virtuous man in this Intellect <note>original: *agathotēti* (goodness) is suggested as a marginal correction for *arithmēsei* (count/number).</note>, but brings him down to fortunes, and fears that these things might happen to him, one is not keeping the virtuous man as we think he should be. Instead, you are giving us an average man, a mixture of good and evil, and you will give such a person a mixed life of some good and some evil. It is not easy for such a person to exist, and if he did, he would not be called happy or worthy, for he does not possess greatness, either in the value of wisdom or in the purity of the good. Therefore, happiness does not exist in the common life. For Plato rightly says that one should take the good from above.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the "sage" finds happiness solely in the life of the mind/intellect, making him indifferent to physical pain, illness, or loss of external status. He concludes that true happiness is not a "mixture" of pleasure and virtue but is found by looking toward the higher, divine Good.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Enneads, Happiness, Sage, Virtue, Stoic indifference, Plato, Intellect, Eudaimonia, Physical pain, Ancient Philosophy</keywords>

Marsilio Ficino provides both the translation of Plotinus and his own introductory commentary.</meta>

### BOOK FOUR.

And toward that <note>the One or the Good</note> the one who is to be wise and happy must look, and to that be made similar, and live according to that. This alone, therefore, must be held toward the end <note>original: *télos*</note>. As for other things, such as when he changes locations, he does not receive an increase in his happiness from those places, but rather considers them as things surrounding him—just as if he were to lie down in this way or that—giving to the body whatever necessity requires and what is within his power. But he himself is something else, not hindered from letting the body go, and he will let it go at nature's proper time. And he himself is the master of his will regarding this, so that his works—those which contribute to happiness—he possesses, but others are not for the sake of the end, and not at all for himself, but for that which is attached to him <note>the physical body</note>, which he will care for and choose as long as possible. Just as a musician uses his lyre as long as it is possible to use it; but if not, he will change it for another, or he will let go of the use of every lyre, and will abstain from the activity involving the lyre, having another task without the lyre. He will look down upon the lyre lying nearby, singing himself without instruments. And yet the instrument was not given to him from the beginning in vain; for indeed he has used it many times already.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> And he who is wise and is to be happy must look toward that same thing: he must strive to approach its likeness and live by its life. That alone, therefore, is to be held for the perfection of the end itself. Other things, truly, the wise man will regard as certain changes of place, receiving no increase toward happiness from those locations, but rather weighing those other things which stand around him: as if they were arranged here and in this way, or there and in another. He grants to this <note>the body</note> whatever necessity <margin>B</margin> demands and ability provides; but he himself, living as another, is not prevented from releasing himself. He will yield to nature at its own time, and will easily let it go; he can also deliberate on this according to his own judgment. For this reason, his duties partly lead to happiness; but partly they are undertaken neither for the sake of the end, nor at all for his own sake, but only for the sake of that which is joined to him. This he will care for as long <margin>C</margin> as he can and as long as he can endure it; just as a musician cares for his lyre as long as he is able to use it. But when it becomes useless, he either changes it or lets go of the use of the lyre altogether, and completely abstains from actions involving the lyre, having another duty himself without the lyre. Thus he looks down upon the lyre lying nearby, singing himself without the assistance of the instrument. Nor, however, was the instrument granted to him from the beginning in vain, since he has already used it often.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON
## BOOK V: WHETHER HAPPINESS
## IS INCREASED BY TIME.

->*What eternity is; what beatitude is; how all minds enjoy eternity*
*forever, but rational natures only at certain times: and as long as*
*they enjoy it, they act with stability.*<-

<margin>I</margin>
**T**he Platonists place the Principle of Being <term>the One: (Latin: *vnum*) the supreme, simple principle from which all reality emanates in Neoplatonism</term> above Being itself; and they name it the One and the Good. Within Being, however, they conceive of the first essence, the first life, and the first mind. We can name that life both "eternal" and "blessed" <term>beatitude: (Latin: *beatitudo*) a state of supreme happiness or blessedness, often linked to the contemplation of the divine</term>, but for different reasons. For life is the first, most inward, and perpetual act of essence. Therefore, insofar as an act of this kind is attached to its own essence all at once, and the essence always rests upon it as one, it is called "eternal life," or rather, "eternity" itself. But insofar as the same act, departing as if from its source, is reflected toward internal things, it is called "Mind" <note>Intellect</note>; which, being thus immediately joined to the Good, is rightly called "blessed life" or rather "happiness." Because all minds enjoy this Mind, this eternity, and this happiness directly, they do so forever. But rational natures <note>human souls</note>, because they occupy the following rank, do indeed possess eternity and happiness of this kind, but (to speak in the Platonic, or rather Plotinian, manner) they do not enjoy it eternally. Thus, at some times they are happy, and at other times they are not happy. Nevertheless, while they are happy, they no longer act in a shifting way, but with stability. Since first eternity and happiness are in reality one, rational natures follow eternity to the same extent they attain happiness. Since stability is the most proper characteristic of eternity, it follows that as long as they possess eternity as happy beings, they act immovably, and embrace all the gifts of action at once in a single gaze. However, to speak my own opinion, the soul cannot enjoy eternity unless it enjoys it eternally. Therefore, as soon as it touches the state of eternity, being placed there beyond time and motion, it acts so stably that it can no longer be moved from there in any part. Our own opinion having been stated once, let us follow the Plotinian interpretation.

->*A rational nature lives happily in the sublime spheres for much longer*
*ages than it lives unhappily near the earth.*<-

<margin>II</margin>
Furthermore, they judge that the souls of men living on the earth, or for the most part in the thicker air, are not happy but miserable, being established in a place of sin and purgatorial punishment. But they believe all will be happy when they have ascended from here to the pure spheres with a pure body—either to the higher air, or the ether, and the heavens. For then, on account of the prosperity of the body and the location, and the easy care for the body, they think they live a life there far different from the one here; and therefore they are happy for much longer than they are miserable. Plato testifies to this in the *Phaedo*, where he discusses the long-lived; and Olympiodorus confirms it. Added to this: just as the mind, which lifts one to sublime things, is more powerful than the animal imagination, which turns toward opposites, so the life of the rational soul is longer when raised to the heights through the mind than its life through the imagination toward the lower...

# COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO

...turned toward lower things. Furthermore, the **Mind** consists only of identity <note>original: *identitate*, the state of being the same or unchanging</note> and stability; therefore, it always acts steadily in the same way. **Imagination** consists of opposites; for that reason, it always fashions varied images. However, the **rational faculty** is composed of all these: for in it, identity concurs with diversity, and stability with motion. Therefore, it operates both with mobility and stability; it revolves through various things and, in turn, reflects on the same ones. 

The more excellent the nature of identity and stability is compared to the nature of diversity and motion, the longer the soul lives in eternity when it has turned toward it, rather than in time, having occasionally fallen into time. But since this is fulfilled less in this life, it is necessarily compensated for in the next. Certainly, if the pure intellect in no way declines toward the body, but a life entirely devoid of intelligence declines completely, they <note>the Platonists</note> think it follows that the intellectual soul—in that part where it is intellectual—never inclines toward the body; however, in that part where it does not share in natural intelligence, it is bent toward bodies. 

Likewise, if the rational soul is the true medium between eternal and temporal things, and the <term>indissoluble bond of the universe</term> <note>original: *indissolubile vinculum universi*. A central concept in Ficino's philosophy where the soul acts as the "knot" or "center" connecting the spiritual and material worlds</note>—which we often prove in Theology—they want it to follow that it never entirely departs from either this side or that. Instead, holding both at once, it reconciles both within itself in a fitting proportion. For this reason, through the intellect, it is always awake in eternity; through the life-giving power, it always acts in time in some way; through the imagination, which is closest to the life-giving nature, it is mostly occupied in time; through reason, being near to the mind, it lives as much as possible in eternity; and through the other imagination, which is directly subject to reason, it alternates between both equally, offering us images now of eternal things, now of temporal ones. 

Truly, as long as reason leads a happy life, so too does the imagination; and if it occasionally brings forth images of temporal things, it still brings those images into the midst of happiness. Finally (to speak briefly), if from the circuit of the whole world—which some think is completed in thirty-six thousand years <note>The "Platonic Year" or "Great Year," the time it takes for all the stars to return to their original positions</note>—the soul lives here as an exile for three hundred years (though at different times), they think it dwells in its ancestral seats for at least three thousand years in return. Those souls dwell here for an even shorter time and there for a longer time who were either adapted to more excellent stars and entrusted to <term>daemons</term> <note>original: *daemonibus*. In the Platonic sense, these are guardian spirits or higher mediating beings, not "demons" in the modern sense</note> from the beginning, or who, fortified by a more effective virtue, have despised perishing things and cherished the eternal. 

Nor do they think only human souls change bodies and degrees of happiness, but many "daemonic" souls do as well—both those of the air and those of the ether. However, those only descend as far as the thick air, while our souls descend as far as the earthly body. Both types of souls lead a happier and much longer life in the higher regions. But more on these matters elsewhere.

->How the rational nature is formed by its own mind, and how<-
->the individual mind is formed by the universal mind.<-

### III
It is also possible that reason in this life, by separating itself from matter and the lowest imagination more than others and calling itself back to the mind, may in some way taste the happiness of that other life. And certainly, insofar as it possesses it—since it is already formed by the intellect—it enjoys this happiness of its own by a certain eternal pact: that is, by a stable and simultaneous total act. That this can and ought to happen at some point, we prove by tracing the matter back to its source. 

The reason why two things are with difficulty fused into one is either because of dimensions that are too solid on both sides, or because of dimensions of any kind, or because of opposing forms on both sides. Iron is fused into fire, even if both the solidity of the iron and its coldness seem to hinder it; and it is fused in such a way that the iron, now formed by the fire, acts as fire rather than as iron—that is, it grows hot and shines, it heats and illuminates. Air, however, is ignited more easily, where neither density nor such great diversity of quality hinders it any longer. That same air becomes luminous under the sun even more easily, since no dimension in the light retards the union of both. Even more easily and more closely is a naturally prepared body formed by a soul, and through that soul, it already acts as a living thing. Finally, the soul is most easily formed by the mind and most closely joined to it. 

For since it is the property of form to shape and perfect, and the property of matter to bind itself to its own form, surely the more excellent a form is, the more easily and closely it shapes and binds the matter that is subject and adapted to it. Therefore, the soul is more absolutely formed by the mind than the body is by the soul—just as the mind is a more perfect form than the soul, and the soul is a more perfect subject than the body. Since the divine Mind is everywhere, and the essence of the rational soul is perpetually created and preserved by an outflow from there, and is therefore perpetually turned toward the Mind by the instinct of its own essence, nothing prevents the soul, thus hanging and thus turned, from being always formed from there. 

Since this formation is effected both through the essential instinct of the soul and through the essential act of the mind, it is rightly an essential formation on all sides. Just as in the Mind, essence is the same as the intellect, and being is the same as understanding; so in the soul, the intellect becomes the same as its essence, and understanding becomes the same as being. This is especially true because the divine intellect itself forms the soul by the very act of intelligence. To be formed by the act of understanding is nothing other than to understand; just as to be formed by the act of seeing is already to see. Or at least, just as in the air, to become luminous and to shine happen entirely at once; and in the body under the soul, to become alive and to live happen at once; so in the soul, by essential reason, to become intellectual and to understand happen at once. For there is nothing else for the soul to be perfectly formed by the intellect than to be under the form of the intellect and to act under the act of the intellect. 

In the intellect itself, its form is the same as its act. Therefore, as soon as the soul exists under the form of the intellect, it already acts under the act of the intellect and thoroughly understands. Hence that saying of Iamblichus <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> according to the mind of the Egyptians: "For the intellectual soul, to be is to understand God and divine things." For just as we perceive temporal things by a certain temporary act, so we steadily contemplate eternal and truly existing things by a similarly eternal and essential act. These are his words. But enough and more than enough concerning the intellect.

->The rational nature both can and ought to be formed at some point<-
->by the mind, and then by a single act it<-
->possesses all things.<-

### IIII
The same reasons indicate to us that the rational faculty can also be formed by the intellect in a similar way at some point, especially since it is in the same essence as the intellect. We have shown elsewhere that it *ought* to be, lest natural appetite be in vain. And since in every rational nature there is an everlasting appetite for intelligence, the Platonists want everyone to arrive eventually at happy intelligence. And if one departs from there, one can return again; and in that age, as long as one acts as a mind and lives blessedly, one imitates the eternal intelligence of the mind—so that one beholds all things at once in a single act, whether one tastes this in this life or rather feeds upon it in the next. The intellect itself truly gazes upon the whole circuit of things at once, just as the eye sees a small sphere...
