...produces the whole <term>reason</term> <note>original: *rationem*; here referring to a logical or structural plan</note> all at once. However, **reason** that has not yet been turned toward the **intellect** approaches things part by part, one after the other. It is like the touch of a blind man’s finger, which, by feeling the same sphere bit by bit, judges it to be a sphere—something the eye judged instantly. Finally, we believe that when reason is turned toward the mind, it embraces all things together with the mind, just as the hand of a sighted man, guided by the eye and grasping a small ball in his whole fist, immediately perceives it to be a sphere. Now, a soul affected in this way knows and possesses in a single moment as much as another would over a long period. This is similar to that prophetic saying: *One day in your courts, O Lord, is better than a thousand years of others.* <note>A reference to Psalm 84:10, illustrating that spiritual experience transcends linear time.</note>

## Who is blessed: and how happiness consists in a certain possession of a present good: to which the extension of time adds nothing by reason of the past or future, but only by reason of the present.

*¶ We consider a person to be supremely happy when they already behold all true things and possess all goods. But they see all true things together in a single form of truth—that is, in the **divine mind**—and similarly enjoy all goods in a single fountain of goods—that is, in **Goodness** itself. Since, therefore, through one form and one fountain they both behold truths and draw in goods, they undoubtedly contemplate all truths with a single intuition and drink in all goods with a single draught. Whoever has not yet arrived here is not yet supremely happy. But whoever has arrived this far can no longer be happier simply because of the length of time.* 

*But suppose that in one soul such happiness lasts a year, while in another it lasts a day: is the former more blessed than the latter? Certainly not on that very day when the latter is also blessed. For both then possess all things equally. On the remaining days, one is not "happier" than the other; rather, one is indeed blessed, while the other is no longer blessed. Let us then compare a year’s happiness with a day’s. Is the annual version considered greater or "more" of a happiness than the daily one? It is certainly more lasting, or longer in time, but not greater in its degree of intensity—just as a certain heat can last a year, yet not be hotter in degree than a heat that lasts a day. But should we not desire annual happiness more than daily happiness? Without a doubt. Yet that long duration of time is not to be desired for its own sake; otherwise, we would choose a long fever over a short one. Rather, it is desired for the sake of the happiness itself, and not the other way around: for the **Good** itself seems to pertain to quality rather than quantity.* 

*Indeed, the soul desires quantity for the sake of the good: if it is joined with the good, the greater the quantity, the more the soul desires it; if joined with evil, the greater the quantity, the less it chooses it. Why, then, do we think we should choose a life of a year with happiness rather than a day? Certainly not because of the temporal succession itself, which is longer in a year; for even in a day’s happiness, we do not prefer to be happy for a whole day rather than an hour because of such succession. For we fundamentally desire the **present** itself in happiness. This is all we seek, and we seek to "be" while we seek to be happy. We primarily desire this same "present" to be fixed and to remain entirely, which is the property of <term>eternity</term>, in the enjoyment of which we are blessed. We enjoy this continually through the intellect, and sometimes through reason when it is formed by the intellect. But if we distrust that this same present can remain firm for us, we then choose in the second degree another present moment, and then another and another to succeed it—always directing our affection and gaze toward the "present" rather than the succession. For in succession there is always some mixture of privation and evil. This shows us that as long as we live in this motion, we cannot truly be blessed, although we may taste something of <term>beatitude</term> <note>A state of supreme, divine happiness or "blessedness."</note> to the extent that we approach eternity. Plotinus deals with this in the ten questions of this book.*

### First Question.

*Whether happiness increases with time? He concludes that happiness consists in a certain affection or disposition of life through which someone is actually well-off: this state is present, and the memory of the past adds nothing to it.*

### Second Question.

*Since every man desires to live forever: whether attaining this perpetual perseverance is the chief happiness. He concludes that happiness is not increased by this perpetual succession; otherwise, time, not virtue, would measure happiness. Nor would happiness ever be absolute even among the gods, because it would always be increasing in this way. He confirms the same point: because natural desire specifically wishes for what it can actually attain. It only attains what is present, whenever it attains it; therefore, it does not desire what is not, but only what is. Only the present exists: the past no longer is, and the future is not yet. Therefore, it only desires the present, and prefers this very present to be fixed entirely and remain the same rather than having another succeed it.*

### Third Question.

*Whether one who has contemplated longer is happier? He concludes that if they always saw the same things with equal clarity, they have gained nothing in happiness from the duration; if, however, they finally knew more things better, they were not happy before, but only then.*

### Fourth Question.

*Whether longer pleasure increases bliss? He concludes that if "pleasure" here signifies a certain motion or act distinct from the act of intelligence itself, it should not be counted with happiness. But if it signifies the very act of intelligence, free from all hindrance, and thus unhampered, absolute, and pleasing to us, then the soul is happy only when the intelligence is of such a kind, and nothing greater can be brought to it by time—especially since it is now in eternity rather than in time. The motion of pleasure is also desired only because of what is present within it.*

### Fifth Question.

*Whether one who is happy for their whole life is happier than one who is happy only for a part of life? He concludes that if they are compared according to the same part of life, they are equally happy; if according to different parts, one is blessed, and the other is not.*

### Sixth Question.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's *Enneads*, specifically discussing the nature of happiness (*felicitas*) and its relationship to time and eternity. Ficino argues that while misery might seem to increase over time, true happiness—rooted in the eternal—does not change or increase by duration, as it is already complete.</meta>

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO
### ON PLOTINUS

Since a miserable person seems to become more miserable over a longer period of time, why is a happy person not also made happier by the same logic? He concludes that evil itself—because it happens to a <term>subject</term> <note>The "subject" here is the human soul or body which "undergoes" the experience.</note> that is by nature weak and liable to suffering—continually infects that subject more and more. If this subject were to always remain the same, and no greater harm occurred, only the present evil would be weighed in one's judgment. However, if the subject continues in such distress that the evil within it actually increases, then the misery is judged to be heavier—not so much because the time is longer, but because a greater degree of evil has been added. 

**Happiness** <note>original: *Felicitas*</note>, on the other hand, possesses a certain fixed limit; that is, the highest degree of the good. Likewise, it always maintains that same limit—namely, the highest itself—being neither greater nor lesser than it was at the start or for as long as it remains happiness. Otherwise, it would not be the "highest" happiness. Finally, the condition of evil exists in time and in a temporary subject, which is subject to change; but happiness exists in its own eternal subject, to which <term>identity</term> <note>original: *identitas*; meaning a state of remaining perfectly the same.</note> and stability properly belong. This eternal state also belongs to the rational part of the soul once it has been made happy; otherwise, it would neither have truly been made happy, nor would it live securely, if it thought it might ever fall away from that state.

### Seventh Question.

Since in **time** we count the past and the future together with the present, and thus call it a "longer space of time," why do we not do the same with **happiness**? He concludes that in the length of time, we are permitted to count "non-being" along with "being," since the very nature of time consists in a certain number and flow. Things that no longer exist, but passed away long ago, are still counted. Likewise, in every flow, "being" is joined as if with "non-being"; for the present moment, which is in a sense called "being," falls in the middle between the past (which is no longer) and the future (which is not yet). 

He denies, however, that the same thing happens in the nature of happiness itself. For its essence consists in a present life and a stable act that has already obtained, in a way, the gift of **eternity**. Otherwise, if it were still running through some motion or time, it would not yet be an absolute condition; the soul would not yet have reached its goal. Since the nature of happiness includes the "present" itself and a state of stability, it naturally excludes temporal calculation from itself. 

Indeed, since eternity belongs to the First Essence and is the very life of **Being** <note>original: *entis*; referring to the ultimate reality or God.</note>—whether it resides in the Divine Mind or is communicated to some other mind—it in no way admits anything of "non-being." Therefore, it utterly expels temporal flow from itself. In eternal life, therefore, there is a single, stable act. But in time—whether in the soul or thereafter in the body—acts are many, succeeding one another in a certain flow. It is like a circle: in the center, the point is one and stable; from it, various moving points are produced along the length of lines toward the circumference. There, the "one" is seen dispersed into "many," and stability has progressed into motion. 

In short, he concludes that the **blessed life** is the best life. This is the life of Being itself—whether it exists through itself in the Universal Mind, or is forever communicated from there into each individual mind, or is eventually communicated further into the rational faculty. Everywhere, it preserves its eternal condition, especially since the highest degree of life (which serves as our Goal) is no longer placed in motion, but in stability. Finally, the "present" of eternity is not the same as the "present" of time. In time, there are many present and individual moments, one outside the other. But in eternity, the present is a single "Now," including all the "presents" of time at once—just as a single point in the center of a circle contains all the points of the lines coming from the circumference.

### Three Questions.

->The remaining three questions are easily understood and solved, both on their<-
->own and through the previous points. From all of this, it is finally<-
->gathered that the perfectly blessed life is a life not occupied<-
->with external actions, but collected within the mind itself.<-
->It is not gathered from many acts of intelligence, whether<-
->past or present, but is focused entirely into one<-
->present, stable act of its own mind: an act, I say,<-
->formed by the divine mind, and through the<-
->divine mind, enjoying the Good which<-
->is above the mind.<-

->Concerning whether happiness increases with time.<-

A
<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'E' containing a bust of a woman in profile, with the text 'AGRIPP' on the left and 'INA' on the right.</image-desc> Whether happiness <note>The Greek term is *eudaimonein*, meaning to live well or flourish.</note> increases with time, or not. Is happiness always to be understood as existing in the present? For indeed, the memory of having been happy does not make one so now; <margin>Happiness is found in the eternal itself. Or is it a state not of being present, but an activity of life?</margin> as we say, happiness is found in the eternal. Or is it a state not defined by its presence, but by the very activity <note>original: *energeia*; the active expression of life.</note> of life?

B
But if someone says that because we always desire to live and to act, then attaining what we strive for should be called happiness: first, in this way, tomorrow’s happiness would always be greater than today’s. And the next would always be greater than the one before, and happiness would no longer be measured by virtue <note>original: *arete*.</note>.
<margin>* if they are happy</margin>
Furthermore, the gods would be happier now than they were before, and never fully complete, never perfectly so.
<margin>* to be a state/habit</margin>
Then, when desire achieves its * goal, it has grasped the present—always the present—and it seeks to have happiness for as long as it exists. But the desire for life, in seeking "to be," is clearly seeking the present; for "to be" is found in the present. If it desires the future and what follows, it desires what it already has; it desires that which *is*, not what has passed, nor what is to come, but what already exists: it seeks not a perpetual stretching out, but to be in the "now" which is already present.

D
What then? Does someone who has been happy for a longer time, and has looked upon the same object with their eyes for a longer time, gain more? If, in that longer time, they saw more accurately, then time would have accomplished something more for them. But if they saw the same thing equally throughout, then the one who has gazed upon it only once possesses just as much.

E
But what if one person felt pleasure <note>original: *hēsthē*.</note> for a longer time? This should not be calculated into the definition of happiness. If by "pleasure" you mean an unimpeded activity, you are saying the same thing we are investigating.
<margin>the greater [pleasure]</margin>
And * the greater pleasure always possesses only the present. Its past has already vanished.
What if one person was happy from the beginning to the end,

<column-break/>

A
<margin>Question 1.</margin>
<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'Q' containing a figure (possibly a deity or shepherd) in a rural landscape.</image-desc> WE MUST ASK whether happiness <note>original: *felicitas*.</note> takes on an increase through time, since being blessed <note>original: *beatum esse*.</note> is always understood according to the present? Truly, neither the memory of past happiness has any weight; for happiness consists not in the speaking of it, but in a certain disposition <note>original: *affectione*; a state of being or soul-condition.</note>. This disposition is placed in the present quality, as is the action of life.

B
<margin>Question 2.</margin>
BUT if someone should say—from the fact that we always desire to live and to act—that to attain this is rather what happiness is, we must respond as follows. First, if it were so, tomorrow’s happiness will be greater, and those following always greater than the predecessor; and virtue <note>original: *virtus*.</note> itself would no longer be the measure of happiness. Next, the gods would also be happier now than they used to be; and happiness would neither be perfect now, nor could it ever be perfect. Furthermore, when desire reaches its goal, it is rather something present that is attained, and it always strives toward the present itself: and as long as it exists, it requires that it always be thus in happiness. But the appetite for living, seeking "to be," undoubtedly seeks something present; since "to be" is the opposite of [non-existence] in the present. But if it desires the future, and that which follows next, it desires what it already has, or what it is: it desires neither what has passed, nor what is future, but rather what already is, to exist: seeking not a sempiternal <note>original: *sempiternam*; everlasting in a linear sense.</note> extension or progression, but that what is already present be present.

D
<margin>Question 3.</margin>
WHAT then shall we say of him who has lived happy for the longest time? And has looked upon the same sight for the greatest duration? Surely if in the longer time he saw more piercingly, the length of time brought him something more; but if he saw similarly throughout the whole time, certainly he gains nothing, and he who has looked but once carries away an equal amount.

E
<margin>Question 4.</margin>
BUT someone might say that the other person was delighted for a longer duration. But this it is not permitted to count toward happiness; unless perhaps someone names "pleasure" as the unimpeded action of the intelligence <note>original: *actionem intelligentiae*.</note>. Here, indeed, he would be saying the same thing we are seeking. Accordingly, a longer pleasure always possesses the present alone: for that which is said to be from the past has now utterly vanished.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the start of Book V of Plotinus's first Ennead. Having established that happiness is found in the "activity of life," Plotinus now investigates whether the duration of time adds anything to the quality of that happiness, or if misery is compounded by its length.</meta>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK I.

<margin>A</margin> ...but another only for the future; and another, finally, who was once happy, has now ceased to be happy? Would they be equally happy? Certainly, a comparison of this kind is not made between those who are all happy. But indeed, those not happy—that is, when they are not happy—are compared with someone who is happy. If, therefore, he possesses anything more, he certainly possesses as much as a happy man does against those who are not happy: for it happens to him that he surpasses others by a certain present state.

<margin>Question 6.</margin>
<margin>B</margin> WHAT then? Is not the miserable man more miserable through a longer time? And do not all other troublesome things bring a greater calamity over a longer time: such as distress, long-lasting anxieties, and other things of the same kind? Now, if these things increase evil through time, why do their opposites not also increase happiness? But perhaps regarding troubles and distresses, one might say that an increase happens through time: as in diseases. For a disease 
<margin>C</margin> becomes a habit <note>original: *habitus*; a settled state or condition of the body or soul.</note>: and the body itself is more infected by time. Otherwise, if it remained the same, and no greater harm occurred, here too the present itself would always be what is troublesome, unless one counted the past: by looking back, evidently, at what has been done and what remains. So it is that even in the habit of a miserable man, the evil is increased over a more extended time, because depravity is brought into that which remains, insofar as it remains. Therefore, a greater misery seems to come about not by a more extended time, but rather by the addition of a greater degree of suffering. 
<margin>D</margin> However, that "more" perhaps does not exist all at once: nor should we say "more" at all when that which is not <note>the past</note> is counted together with that which is <note>the present</note>. Truly, the very nature of happiness possesses a certain and always identical limit <note>original: *terminum*.</note>. Now if improvements also come from the length of time itself, so that by progressing in virtue, one also progresses in happiness, we do not approve of happiness as if it were a long duration numbered through many years, but rather that which is said to be "more" at that time when it exists more fully.

<margin>Question 7.</margin>
<margin>E</margin> FURTHERMORE, why is it that, if we should look only at the present and not count it together with the past, we do not do the same regarding time itself, but instead, counting the past together with the present, we call it a greater span of time? Why then do we not say that happiness is as great as the time it lasts? For perhaps it is possible to divide blessedness according to the divisions of time itself. For if we measure by the present alone, we shall make it indivisible. But perhaps it would not be absurd to count time even for those things which have passed. Indeed, we calculate the number even of those things which have passed and are no longer, such as the number of the dead. 
<margin>F</margin> But as for a happiness that is already past and no longer exists, if someone were to say it is "more" than the present happiness by adding it to the present, he would be in error: for he would be comparing the fact of having attained blessedness. Moreover, a longer time beyond the present is nothing else than what must be said "not yet to be." 
<margin>G</margin> In general, a length of time that is drawn out longer somehow contrives a dispersion <note>original: *dispersio*; the scattering of a single point into a line.</note> of that single thing which is in the present. Therefore, time is rightly called the image of eternity <note>original: *aeternitatis imago*; a famous Platonic concept where time mimics the stillness of eternity through movement.</note>, desiring to destroy through its own dispersion that which is permanent in eternity. And so, if that which is permanent is taken away from eternity and becomes part of time, it will immediately vanish, insofar as...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...and another for the later time, and another who was happy <note>original: *eudaimonēsas*; having flourished.</note> before and then changed—do they have an equal share? Or has a state of well-being resulted from both not being happy at all, rather than from those being most happy, at the time they were not happy, compared to the one who is happy? So that he would not have more, he has as much as the happy man has compared to the unhappy ones, by which it happens that he has an advantage over them in the present.

<margin>B</margin> WHAT then? Is the miserable man <note>original: *kakodaimon*; literally "one with an evil spirit."</note> more miserable by having more time? If other things, or as many as are troublesome, give a greater calamity in a longer time—such as long-lasting pains, or griefs, and all such things? Or is it by the "more"? But if these things increase the evil through time, why not also the opposites, like being happy, in the same way? Or regarding griefs and pains, one might say that time gives an addition; as the persistence of a disease 
<margin>C</margin> becomes a state <note>original: *hexis*; a stable disposition.</note>, and the body is more corrupted by time. Since if it remained the same, and the damage did not become greater, even here the present would always be the painful thing: unless one were to add the past, considering the flow into what is happening and remaining. And in the state of misery, the evil is intensified by more time, as the vice increases by its persistence. At least by the addition of the "more" in the longer time 
<margin>D</margin> perhaps, one becomes more miserable. But the "more" is not equal or all at once; thus "more" should not be said at all of that which is no longer counted among what exists. But the nature of happiness has a boundary and a limit <note>original: *peras*.</note>, and is always the same. And if there is any increase here through a longer time, so that one is more happy by increasing in greater virtue, then one praises the happiness not for the number of many years, but for that which is becoming more at the time when it exists more.

<margin>E</margin> BUT why, if we must consider the present alone, and not count it with what has happened, do we not do the same with time, but instead count the past with the present and speak of "more"? Why should we not say that happiness is as great as the time? Or shall we divide happiness according to the divisions of time? For indeed, <margin><gloss>*by it</gloss></margin> 
<margin>F</margin> by measuring it by the present, we shall make it indivisible. Or is it not absurd to count time which is no longer, since we make a count of things that happened but are no longer, such as the dead. But to say that happiness which is no longer is "more" than the presence of the present is absurd. For being happy requires being a property <note>original: *symbebekenai*; an attribute or accident of the person.</note>, but more time beyond the present is that which no longer is. In general, the "more" in time seeks a scattering <note>original: *skedasin*; a spreading out.</note> of some form existing in the present. 
<margin>G</margin> Therefore it is also reasonably called an image of eternity <note>original: *eikon aionos*.</note>, wishing to vanish by its own scattering that which is permanent in the other. Whence, even if it takes away from eternity that which would not have remained with it, and makes it its own, it has lost it, while saving...

<summary>Plotinus argues that happiness (eudaimonia) is a complete state that does not increase with duration, whereas misery may seem to increase over time as it becomes a corrupted habit. He concludes that time is a "dispersion" or a moving image of eternity, and that true well-being is found in the present activity of the soul.</summary>

# BOOK FOUR.

<column-break/>

->**THE FOURTH BOOK.**<-

<margin>\* preserved</margin> ...is \*preserved, insofar as it is in some way kept within that [eternity]; but it vanishes if it were to happen entirely within time. If, therefore, to be happy consists in a good life, then clearly one must place this life in the life of Being itself <note>original: *tēn tou ontos autēn zōēn*. Plotinus refers to "True Being" or the spiritual realm where things do not change.</note>. This life is defined not by numbered time, but by eternity <note>original: *aiōn*. In Neoplatonism, eternity is not an infinite amount of time, but a state of existence entirely outside of time.</note>. This eternity is neither more nor less, nor does it consist of any length; rather, it is the "now," the non-extended, and the timeless. Therefore, one should not join Being with non-being, nor time with eternity, nor the temporal "always" <note>original: *to chronikon aei*. The "always" of time is just a sequence of "befores" and "afters," unlike the "now" of eternity.</note> with eternity, nor stretch out the non-extended into different parts. Instead, if you ever grasp it, you must take it as a whole; you must grasp the life of eternity as something indivisible, not gathered from many intervals of time, but whole and all at once from the entirety of the age.

**Question 8.**
<margin>C</margin> IF, HOWEVER, someone should say that the memory of past things remaining in the present brings something more to that man who has lived a longer time in happiness, we must ask: what does he actually mean by "memory"? Does he mean the memory of wisdom already past? If so, he would be calling the man wiser [today because of yesterday's wisdom], which would not hold to his premise <note>Plotinus argues that if the man is wise *now*, the past wisdom is redundant; if he isn't wise now, the memory doesn't make him happy.</note>. Or does he mean the memory of pleasure, as if the happy man required many delights and were not content with his present joy? <margin>D</margin> Furthermore, what sweetness does the memory of a past pleasure bring? It would be as if someone remembered that he tasted a fine delicacy yesterday; if he remembered it from ten years ago, it would be even more ridiculous. The same applies if he remembered that he possessed wisdom last year.

**Question 9.**
BUT if the memory is of noble and virtuous things, why would that not contribute something? Yet that is the behavior of a man who lacks noble things in the present; because he has nothing now, he seeks the memory of things that have passed away.

<margin>E</margin> BUT it is argued that a long time provides the opportunity for many noble actions, which a man who is happy for only a short time would be deprived of. To this we must say: happiness is not based on many noble actions. Otherwise, whoever says happiness is accumulated from many times and actions is building happiness out of things that no longer exist—the past—leaving only one present moment. This is why we placed happiness in the present. We then asked whether "more" happiness consists in a longer duration. <margin>F</margin> We must ask: does the happiness of a long time excel only because it abounds in many actions? First, it is possible for one who is not occupied with any actions to be happy—and indeed, no less happy, but even more so than the one who has been busy. <margin>G</margin> Furthermore, actions do not provide "the good" from themselves; rather, it is the internal dispositions <note>original: *diatheseis*. The character or state of the soul.</note> that make the actions good. The wise man reaps the fruit of the good even while acting, not because he acts, nor from the external results, but from what he possesses within himself. For even the safety of the fatherland could be achieved by a wicked person; and the joy found in saving the fatherland can be felt even by someone doing something else. Therefore, this is not what creates the happy man’s pleasure; rather, it is the joy that comes from himself and through himself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...saved, insofar as it is preserved in a certain way in eternity; but it vanishes if it becomes entirely subject to time. If therefore happiness consists in a good life, certainly the good life itself must be placed in the life of the existing one, or of Being itself. For this life is the best. It is not, therefore, to be numbered by time, but measured by eternity. This eternity is neither more nor less: nor does it consist of a certain length, but in that which is both this very thing, and non-extended, and existing beyond time. For which reason, one should not join that which exists <margin>B</margin> with that which does not exist, nor time with eternity, nor that which is "forever" in time with eternity, nor stretch out that which is non-extended into different parts. Rather, if you ever receive it, it must be received as a whole. When, I say, you receive it, you receive not some individual piece proper to time, but the life of eternity—not piled up from many times, but all at once from the whole age.

**Question 8.**
<margin>C</margin> IF ANYONE, however, should say that the memory of the past remaining in the present brings something more to that man who has lived longer in happiness: he must be asked what he means by memory itself? For either the memory of wisdom already past is meant here: for which reason he would call this man wiser, and yet would not keep to his premise? Or he means the memory of pleasure, as if the happy man were in need of many delights, and were not content with present joy. <margin>D</margin> Besides, what pleasantness does the memory of a past pleasure bring? As if someone should remember that he tasted a delicacy yesterday with pleasure: or if from ten years ago, he would be even more to be laughed at. Similarly also if he should remember that he had wisdom in the previous year.

**Question 9.**
BUT if it should be the record of good and noble things, why would it not contribute something? But that is the mark of a man lacking in good or noble things in the present: and because he has very little now, he seeks the memory of those things which have passed away. <margin>E</margin> FOR a long time provides the occasion for many noble actions: of which he will be deprived who has lived happily for only a short time. To these things it must certainly be said that one is not entirely happy because of noble actions, even many of them. Otherwise, whoever says happiness is to be accumulated from many times as well as actions, would be heaping up happiness from things which are no longer, but from things passed, and from only one present thing. Therefore we have placed happiness in a certain present. Then we asked whether that which is called "more" consists in <margin>F</margin> a certain "more" of time: and thus a greater happiness also happens? This therefore must be asked: whether the happiness of a long time excels only in this, that it abounds in many actions? First, indeed, it can happen that he who is occupied with no actions is happy, and not less so, but indeed more so than he who has been <margin>G</margin> busy with actions: then, actions do not bring the good from themselves, but the dispositions themselves make the actions good. Now indeed, the wise man possesses the good even while acting, not because he acts, obviously, nor from these things which happen, but from that which he possesses. Since even the safety of the fatherland can proceed from some wicked person. Even the very joy in preserving the fatherland can be perceived by another who is acting. Therefore, this is not what effects the pleasure of the happy man; rather...

<summary>Plotinus argues that happiness is a state of timeless eternity rather than a sum of past pleasures or actions. He concludes that wisdom and "the good" are internal dispositions of the soul that exist in the present, meaning duration of time adds nothing to the quality of true happiness.</summary>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD I.

<margin>A</margin> ...but if another is happy only for the future, or another who was once happy has now ceased to be so, do they have an equal share? Certainly, this kind of comparison is not made between those who are all happy [at the same time]. Instead, it involves those who are currently *not* happy—that is, when they are no longer in that state—being compared to someone who is happy. If, therefore, one man possesses more, he possesses it in the same way a happy man does compared to those who are not: he happens to surpass others by means of a certain present reality.

<margin>Question 6.</margin> <margin>B</margin> ### WHAT THEN?
Is a miserable man not more miserable over a longer period of time? And do not all other troublesome things bring a greater calamity over a longer duration—such as long-lasting distress, grief, and other things of that kind? If these things increase the evil through time, why does the opposite not also increase happiness? Perhaps regarding pain and distress, one might say an increase happens over time, as in diseases. For a disease becomes a "habit" <note>original: *habitus* / *hexis*. In ancient philosophy, a "habit" or "disposition" is a stable, long-term state of being, like a permanent health condition or a character trait.</note>, and the body itself is <margin>C</margin> more infected over time. Otherwise, if it remained exactly the same and no greater harm occurred, the present moment would always be the only thing that is painful—unless someone counts the past as well, looking back at what has happened and what remains. Thus, in the "habit" of the miserable man, the evil is stretched out into a longer time, with wickedness being added to that which remains, insofar as it remains. Therefore, a greater misery seems to come not from a longer duration, but from the addition of a greater degree [of suffering]. <margin>D</margin> However, the "more" itself perhaps does not exist all at once; nor should we speak of "more" at all when that which no longer exists is counted alongside that which currently is. But the nature of happiness itself possesses a certain fixed and always identical limit. Now, if an advancement comes here from the length of time itself—so that by progressing in virtue, one also progresses in happiness—we do not praise happiness as something "long-lasting" as if counting many years; rather, we call it "greater" then because it exists more fully. <margin>E</margin>

<margin>Question 7.</margin> ### BUT WHY,
if we ought to look only at the present and not count what has passed, do we not do the same with time itself? Instead, we count the past together with the present and speak of a "longer span of time." Why then do we not say that happiness is as great as the duration of time? For perhaps one could divide blessedness <note>original: *beatitudinem* / *eudaimonian*. This is the ultimate flourishing of the soul, distinct from mere temporary pleasure.</note> according to the divisions of time itself. If we measured it by the present alone, we would make it indivisible. Perhaps, indeed, it would not be absurd to count time that does not yet exist. We certainly calculate the number of things that have passed and are no more, such as the number of the dead. But to say that happiness which is already past and no longer exists is "more" than a present happiness is an error; for "to be happy" <note>original: *beatus* / *eudaimonein*</note> requires that the state actually be present. A longer time beyond the present is nothing other than "not yet being." <margin>G</margin> In general, a longer interval of time is a sort of device that scatters that single "one" which exists in the present. Therefore, time is rightly called the "image of eternity" <note>original: *aeternitatis imago* / *eikōn aiōnos*. This is a famous Platonic concept: time mimics the stillness of eternity through constant, orderly motion.</note>, desiring to scatter through its own extension that which remains permanent in eternity. And so, if that which remains is taken away from eternity and becomes part of time, it immediately vanishes, insofar as...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...but if one is happy in the later time, and another who was happy in the earlier time has changed, do they have an equal amount? Or is the comparison here not between those who are all happy, but between those who are not happy—when they are no longer happy—compared to one who is? If, then, one should have more, he has it insofar as a happy man is compared to those who are not, where it happens that he surpasses them in the present.

<margin>B</margin> What then? Is the miserable man more miserable in a longer time? And do not all other troublesome things give a greater calamity in a longer time, such as long-lasting pains, and griefs, and all such things? But if all things increase the evil through time, why not also the opposite—happiness—in the same way? Perhaps regarding griefs and pains one could say that time always adds to the magnitude; for example, the staying of a disease <margin>C</margin> becomes a "habit," and the body is more harmed by time. Since if it remained the same, where the damage did not become greater, even there the present would always be the painful thing—unless the past were counted together, looking at what is happening and remaining, and in the "habit" of misery, the evil is intensified into the longer time, with the vice also increasing by its remaining. At least by the addition of the "more" in the longer time <margin>D</margin> perhaps, the state of being more miserable comes about. But the "more" is not all at once; thus "more" should not be said at all when one counts that which is no longer with that which is. But the matter of happiness has a boundary and a limit, and is always the same. And if there is some increase here by a longer time, so that one is more happy by advancing toward a greater virtue, one praises the many-yeared happiness in number, but rather that which <margin>E</margin> becomes "more" then, because it *is* more.

<margin>F</margin> BUT why, if we must consider the present only, and not count it with what has happened, do we not do the same regarding time, but also counting the past with the present, we say "more"? Why do we not say that happiness is as great as the time? Or we might divide happiness by the divisions of time itself. For even measuring by the present itself, we shall make it indivisible. Or it is not strange to count time even when it is no longer, since we make a count of things that have happened but are no longer, such as the dead. But to say that happiness which is no longer is more than the present presence is strange; for "to be happy" claims to be a present occurrence. But the longer time compared to the present is "no longer <margin>G</margin> being." In general, the "more" of time is called a scattering of something existing in the present, which is why it is reasonably called the "image of eternity," wishing to destroy that which remains in that [eternity] by its own extension. Whence even if it takes away from eternity that which remains in it, and makes it its own, it destroys it, <meta>catchword: the, sav-</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that true happiness (eudaimonia) is found in the timeless "now" of eternity rather than the accumulation of years. He distinguishes between misery, which can worsen over time through the decay of the body or habit, and happiness, which is a perfect and complete state that does not grow "larger" simply by lasting longer.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of happiness (eudaimonia). Having previously established that happiness is a quality of life rather than a quantity of time, he now addresses whether the memory of past happiness or the accumulation of many virtuous deeds increases one's total well-being.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR.

<margin>preserved</margin> ...that which is somehow preserved <note>original: σωζόμενόν</note> in that [eternal] way, or within it, if it were to become a whole. If, therefore, happiness <note>Greek: εὐδαιμονεῖν. Plotinus uses this to mean "living well" or "flourishing" in accordance with the highest part of the soul.</note> consists in life, it is clearly to be found in the life of Being <note>The "life of Being" refers to the intelligible realm, which is perfect and unchanging.</note>. For this is the best life; and it is not measured by the number of moments in time, but by eternity <note>Greek: αἰῶνι. Unlike time, which flows, eternity is an "ever-present now."</note>. For this is something more—not less, nor of any specific length, but that which is without extension and outside of time. Therefore, one must not join Being with non-being, nor time with eternity, nor the "everlasting" of time with the eternity of the timeless. One must not stretch out that which has no extension, but rather grasp it as a whole, if you are to grasp it at all. When you grasp it, you are not grasping a segment of time, but the life of eternity—not a life gathered from many moments of time, but a life that is entirely present all at once from the whole of time.
<margin>B</margin>
But if someone should say that the memory of past events remaining in the present provides something more to the man who has spent a longer time in happiness, what would you say of this memory? For either it is a memory of wisdom that occurred in the past—in which case he would simply be saying the man is wiser, and thus he would not be sticking to the original premise—or it is a memory of pleasure, as if the happy man required a great deal of "rejoicing" <note>original: πειχαρείας (likely περιχαρείας, excessive joy)</note> and were not satisfied with what is present. And what if the memory itself is not pleasant? For example, if someone remembers that yesterday he enjoyed a fine meal <note>original: ὄψῳ. Usually refers to a seasoned dish or "relish" eaten with bread.</note>. If he remembers a meal from fifteen years ago, he would be even more ridiculous. The same applies to a memory of wisdom: that "last year I was wise."
<margin>C</margin>
Even if the memory were of beautiful things, a person is not happy because of this; rather, this is the talk of a man who lacks beautiful things in the present and, because he does not have them now, seeks the memory of things that have passed away.
<margin>D</margin>
"But," one might argue, "the man who lives a long time performs many beautiful actions, which the man who is happy for only a short time does not share." If such a person says that a man is happy as a whole because of many beautiful deeds—or if he says happiness is made of many times and actions—he is saying it is made of things that no longer exist, but have passed away. Or he is saying that happiness is composed of one thing: the present. Therefore, we have established that happiness exists according to the present. Then we asked whether being happy over a longer period is "more" happiness. On this point we must ask: do many actions cause the happiness of a long time to be superior? First, it is possible to be happy without being involved in actions; such a state is not less, but rather more happy than that of one who has acted. Secondly, actions do not provide "the good" of themselves; rather, it is the internal dispositions <note>term: disposition (διάθεσις). The stable internal state of the soul, which Plotinus argues is the true source of happiness, rather than external events.</note> that make the actions beautiful. The wise man reaps the fruit of the good even while acting—not because he acts, nor because of the outcomes, but because of what he possesses within. For the safety of the fatherland might even be brought about by a wicked man, and the pleasure of the fatherland being saved might be felt by another who also acted. Therefore, this is not what creates the pleasure of the happy man, but rather...
<meta>catchword: but rather</meta>

<column-break/>

...is false, insofar as it is preserved in a certain way in eternity; but it vanishes if it all occurs in time. If, therefore, happiness consists in the good life, certainly that good life must be placed in the life of the existent, or of Being itself. For this is the best life. It is not, then, to be numbered by time, but to be judged by eternity. That, indeed, is neither more nor less, nor does it consist in any length, but in the fact that it is both itself and without extension, and exists outside of time. Wherefore, it is not fitting to join Being
<margin>B</margin>
with non-being, nor time with eternity, nor that which is everlasting in time with eternity, nor to stretch out that which is without extension into different parts. Rather, if you ever grasp it, it must be grasped as a whole. When, I say, you grasp it, it is not as some individual piece of time, but as the life of eternity; not heaped up from many times, but as a whole simultaneously from the entire age.
<margin>C</margin> <margin>Question 8.</margin> BUT IF ANYONE should say that the memory of past things remaining in the present brings something more to that man who has lived longer in happiness, he must be asked: what exactly does he mean by this "memory"? For either he means a memory of wisdom that is now past—in which case he would call this man "wiser," and would not be keeping to the proposition—or he means a memory of pleasure, as if the happy man required many delights and were not content with present joy.
<margin>D</margin> Furthermore, does the memory of past pleasure bring some sort of joy? It is as if someone remembered that he tasted a fine meal with pleasure yesterday; but if he remembered it from ten years ago, he would be even more to be laughed at. It is similar if he remembers that he possessed wisdom in a year that has passed.
<margin>E</margin> <margin>Question 9.</margin> BUT IF it is the record of good or honorable things, why should it not contribute something? Yet that is the behavior of a man who lacks good or honorable things in the present; and <insert>therefore</insert> because he currently has very little, he seeks the memory of those things which have passed away.
<margin>F</margin> <margin>Question 10.</margin> BUT INDEED a long time provides the occasion for many noble and famous actions, of which a man who has lived happily for only a short time will be deprived. To this it must surely be said: a man is not happy at all because of famous and numerous actions. Otherwise, whoever says happiness is to be accumulated from many times and actions would be heaping up happiness from things that are no longer present, but from things passed, and from one certain present moment. For this reason, we have placed happiness in a certain present. Then we asked whether that which is called "more" consists in a "greater number," and whether thus a greater happiness might occur? This, then, must be asked: does the happiness of a long time excel only in this—that it abounds in many actions? First, indeed, it can happen that he who applies himself to no actions may be happy—and indeed no less
<margin>G</margin>
so, but rather more so than he who has been occupied with actions. Secondly, actions do not bring about "the good" from themselves, but the internal dispositions themselves make the actions good. Now, the wise man possesses the good even while acting, not because he acts (evidently), nor from those things which happen to him, but from that which he possesses. For even the safety of the fatherland can proceed from some wicked man. The pleasure in the safety of the fatherland itself can be perceived even by one doing something else. Therefore, this is not what produces the pleasure of the happy man; rather...
<meta>catchword: not this</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that true happiness (eudaimonia) belongs to the timeless realm of eternity rather than the duration of time. He concludes that neither the memory of past joys nor the quantity of one's virtuous actions increases the quality of a wise person's present state of being.</summary>

PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK I.

Indeed, the habit itself produces a pleasure of this kind and provides happiness. And if anything pleasant happens, it makes it so by its own power. However, to place happiness in external actions is nothing other than to place it in things which are outside of virtue and outside the soul. For the soul's own proper action consists in wisdom: so that it acts within itself; and this is to act happily.

<column-break/>

For happiness is not placed in how one shall act, but is not for those who have placed it in things outside of virtue and the soul. For the activity of the soul is in wisdom, and in itself it shall act thus. And this is to live happily.

## MARSILIO FICINO’S
## ARGUMENT ON THE
### BOOK OF BEAUTY.

->From the first essence, life, and mind, influences emanate through all things, like rays, voices, and words through six levels.<-

<image-desc>A large decorative drop-cap "I" containing intricate floral and vine-like woodcut patterns.</image-desc>

Certain influences <note>original: "Influxus"</note> flow from Being itself through all beings everywhere: but insofar as essence exists in Being, they flow out chiefly in the manner of a solar ray; insofar as life exists there, they break forth in the manner of sound and voice; finally, insofar as intellect exists there, they are carried in the manner of a meaningful word. Insofar as they are like certain rays, they are seen to move the sight; as voices or sounds, they strike the ears; as words, they especially provoke the soul. Everywhere, truly, they encounter things as certain beauties or "fairnesses," for they proceed from the very form of Beauty itself. When we name Beauty itself, we wish "Being" <note>Ficino uses "Being" (Ens) to refer to the first level of reality below the One.</note> to be understood properly through the mode of form—that is, as formal beauty. But through the mode of cause—that is, as the cause of beauty itself—we wish the "Good" to be considered. For we think the Good is the light itself, the fountain of sparkling beauty that flows from it. Beauty, however, we think is the splendor emanating from that light of the Good; that is, Being itself depending on the One and the Good. From Being itself, as I was saying, we do not doubt that influences proceed through all things like rays, voices, and words. 

These influences are first in the idea of the divine mind; secondly, they are received in any mind thereafter; through universal providence, they are in the mind of the world-soul; thirdly, in the reason of that same soul; fourthly, in its primary imagination; fifthly, in the secondary imagination; sixthly, in the vegetative power, which is also called "universal nature." Thus far, they retain a certain <term>ideal reason</term> <note>These are "logos-structures" or blueprints within the mind.</note> within themselves. For thus far they are living, effective, fertile, and eternal. For in this last level of divine things are the <term>seed-reasons</term> <note>Latin: "seminariæ rationes." These are the internal "seeds" or blueprints that allow nature to grow specific forms.</note> of all things, by which the species of things themselves are propagated. Since the first life and the first formal reason of all things exists in that first essence as the principle of every essence—in which principle both reason and life were present—it is right that, insofar as the influences emanating from there preserve life and formal reason together (pure, whole, and effective), they are called "essential," "ideal," and "divine." They preserve this great office even in nature—that is, the vegetative power of the soul. Therefore, on this "sixth day" <note>A reference to the Biblical creation, signifying the completion of the divine structural work before the physical results manifest.</note> the proper works of God reach their end. 

Thereafter, those influences strike the matter subjected to the soul. But since they can neither progress further, nor retain the nature of true essence and life within matter (which is next to nothingness), they now escape from "forms" into "images." Images, I say, which are likenesses of the true and divine forms. These images—falling under the generative nature of the soul acting upon matter—result from that patient matter. They are like a ray reflected from a mirror, like a voice echoing from a vault, or like a word returned from a flat wall, just like an Echo. To this lowest level of formal outflow, the Moon seems to favor, as the mistress of final generation. To the seed-reasons flourishing in nature and nourishing matter, Venus favors. To those same reasons in the lower imagination hastening toward motion, Mars favors. To those same reasons reigning in the higher imagination, the Sun. To those flourishing in reason, Mercury. To those dominating in the mind of the soul, Jupiter. Finally, to those resting in the divine mind, Saturn. In this seventh level, as if on the day of Saturn, the maker of the world rests—that is, the Idea itself is entirely inward-looking. For the maker does not refer this Idea to other things made from it, but refers other things to it as a model.

->Formal beauty itself is the mind itself: with whose allurements are mixed wonder, power, diffusion, and pleasure.<-

Because this model is the "all-formed" reason of all forms, it is therefore judged to be the first and universal form and species. And for that reason, it is the first "formal beauty." Hence, we are accustomed to call beauty everywhere both "form" and "species," and the beautiful we call "shapely" <note>original: "formosos"</note>; the opposite of which we call "deformity" and "deformed." From this, it is clear that matter—which is by its nature entirely formless—must rightly be judged as deformity itself. But more on this elsewhere. Truly, formal beauty itself arises with the first essence; it matures while essence goes forth into life; and it is finally judged adult when life is completed into mind. For through the very act of the mind, the beauty of essential life is perfectly formed and becomes an "all-formed" form. For this reason, in the order of things, there is the most beauty where there is the most mind—whether it be a certain nature of the mind, or its own proper craftsmanship, or its footprint or sign. And everything there moves more vehemently where it encounters us more vividly. For the true form of beauty itself is life itself, made entirely absolute through the act of the mind. The proper quality of beauty is to allure and snatch away at the same time. Whence in Greek it is called <term>Calon</term> <note>Greek: καλόν. Ficino connects this to the verb "kalein" (καλεῖν), meaning "to call" or "provoke."</note>, as if it were "the provoker." And because beauty exists as an intellectual gift, it allures only those who know—those who know, I say, either by some intellectual reason, or by sight or hearing, which are the chief servants of reason. Moreover, wonder is mixed with the allurements of beauty,

<meta>catchword: power (Latin: vis)</meta>

<summary>This page concludes Plotinus's thoughts on internal happiness and introduces Marsilio Ficino's commentary on Beauty. Ficino explains Beauty as an emanation from the Good that descends through six levels of reality, associated with the planets, before becoming physical "images" in matter.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Marsilio Ficino, Neoplatonism, Beauty, emanations, seed-reasons, planetary influence, Saturn, Jupiter, Venus, Calon, formal beauty, matter, deformity</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "Ennead I, Book 6" (On Beauty). Having established the cosmic hierarchy on the previous page, Ficino now distinguishes between the "Good" and the "Beautiful," arguing that while all things instinctively seek the Good for survival, only higher souls are drawn to Beauty. He begins a systematic critique of the common definition of beauty as mere physical proportion.</meta>

ON BOOK VI OF ENNEAD I.

...a certain sharper force, diffusing a longing. You must remember, therefore, what we prove in Theology <note>Ficino refers to his own "Platonic Theology," where he harmonizes Platonic philosophy with Christian doctrine</note>: that all things indeed seek the good, but not all things seek the beautiful. Only those who possess a certain judgment of beauty seek it. Furthermore, these individuals always seek the good, yet they do not always strive after beauty. Since the appetite and draw toward the good is the most universal and perpetual, it follows that the good itself is the most universal and most powerful principle of all; and the form of beauty itself is closest to the good. 

And because the provocation from beauty and toward beauty is, as it were, something new—occurring only to certain beings, and only at certain times, and following after nature and knowledge—a certain wonder <note>original: "admiratio"</note> is rightly mixed into the allurements of beauty. Likewise, there is a certain violence (so to speak); for although the appetite for the good, which is universal and perpetual, is most intimate to nature and draws from our innermost depths, the appetite for the beautiful seizes us as if from the outside, necessarily following upon knowledge. Therefore, since it is less "natural" <note>in the sense of a basic biological instinct</note>, it seems to possess something violent. Finally, it diffuses the lover in a certain way. For once it has snatched the lover away from himself, it does not immediately restore or reintegrate him into one, since it pulls from the outside and seizes through the mode of knowledge (which deals with distinctions), and thereby scatters him. 

Ultimately, the lover's affection, whether it be gentle or sharp, always moves with pleasure: just as there is delight not only in a sweet flavor or a deep sound, but even in a certain sharp flavor and in high-pitched voices. We have found that one is affected by pleasure whenever one is touched by something congruent to oneself and is led toward the good. But Beauty, wherever it meets us, approaches as something congruent, and for that reason it pleases and is approved: because it responds to the Idea of beauty innate within us and fits it in every way. Again, by its own nature, beauty always leads the soul to the good: for the participation in beauty here among us calls us to its intellectual form, and through that form, leads us finally to the good itself—just as a brightness leads to a light, and light leads to the source of radiance. But let it suffice for now to have run through Plotinus’s most beautiful book on beauty with "freer feet" <note>an idiom meaning to discuss the topic broadly or poetically rather than strictly</note>. Next, we must repeat the chapters of this new book in order, and these too cursorily, for we discuss these matters more extensively in our *Commentary on the Symposium* <note>original: "Conuiuio de amore"</note>.

->*Beauty is a certain grace, which is found more in things seen than in things heard, and even more in things thought, and it is not a matter of proportion.*<-

<margin>I</margin> We conceive by a common notion that Beauty is something "gracious," or a certain grace alluring us through sight, or hearing, or reason. Indeed, insofar as this exists in things seen, heard, and thought, it is called beauty, and represents for us the "Three Graces." But insofar as it consists in the act of sight, hearing, and reason, it is named delight and pleasure: a "becoming" <note>decorous or fitting</note> pleasure, I say. For a becoming pleasure properly follows a becoming thing of its own accord. A becoming appetite also follows this: namely, love itself. Foul disturbance, however, happens perhaps for other causes. 

The first chapter, therefore, inquires into what this grace and beauty is most of all, and assigns what it is not. It signifies, meanwhile, that beauty pertains more to sight than to hearing, because sight and light-forms are more akin to intelligence than hearing and sound. Furthermore, the habits of the soul are more beautiful than bodies which are called "shapely," and voices too, because they are similarly more related to the mind. Even the habits of the soul—both in morals and in learning—can rightly be called not only "beautiful" but "beauties" themselves. For they are forms: forms, I say, close to the mind. Voices and bodies, however, cannot truly be called "beauties." For although beauty itself ought not to be called "beautiful" at one moment and "not beautiful" the next, the same body is beautiful today, but tomorrow, once its lightness is gone, it is not beautiful. Similarly, the matter of a voice remains nearly the same, but once the proportion is changed, it turns from beautiful to foul. 

Nevertheless, although beauty pertains more to those things which are looked at than those heard, and again more to those which are thought, we must investigate whether there is something common to all these, and what that very thing is by which all these are called beautiful. But first, he investigates this in bodies that are seen, as if it will be more manifest that way. At the outset, he refutes the common opinion concerning these things, which says that the beauty of a body is a certain proportion of the parts among themselves and to the whole, together with a charm of color. He refutes this with four arguments. 

First, if beauty is proportion itself, or a certain symmetry, then certainly only a composite thing can be beautiful; therefore, no simple thing, however gracious it may be <note>such as light or gold</note>, will be called beautiful. Second, again, if only the composite is beautiful, none of the parts (especially simple ones) will be beautiful; indeed, none of the parts at all, since beauty is placed only in the proportion measured against another. From this it would follow that the beautiful is created from things that are not beautiful; yet we have found that nothing gracious is ever made from things entirely lacking in grace. Third, the same face, often while the same proportion of its figure remains, appears beautiful to us at one moment and not beautiful at another—as if symmetry were one thing and beauty another. Fourth, it is necessary that beauty in bodies refers us to a higher beauty. It is therefore necessary to accommodate this lower beauty to that higher one as much as possible, yet in such a way that it exists in the higher things in a much more excellent manner than in bodies. However, in what way there might be a certain "symmetry" there—namely, in the soul or the intellect—cannot easily be assigned. And in the soul, we cannot understand how morals and sciences are "symmetries" or proportions, if we follow Plotinus. For he does not want habits of morals or science to be built up in the soul from many related shapes, but rather that the simple act of moral virtue shines out as soon as the clouds of contingent vices are shaken off, and the simple form of science glows once false opinions are finally expelled. For the soul is, in a certain way, all things; and it knows the thing itself most of all when, stirred by arguments, it is now in "act" <note>term: act - the state of being fully realized or active, as opposed to "potentiality"</note> the very thing which it was before, but previously it was so only by a certain fertile power. But these things will be discussed more opportunely elsewhere.

->*Beauty in bodies is absolute perfection and the grace of form especially, which dominates both matter and the other forms within it; it reports the unimpeded victory of divine art and reason over matter, and clearly represents the Idea itself.*<-

<margin>II</margin> The second chapter examines what beauty itself is in bodies. He asserts that it is something readily offering itself at first sight. For since beauty is the "form of intelligible forms" in the intelligible world, and is similarly the "form of forms" in the body, it rightly moves the intellect there and the sight here, primarily and most promptly—as Plato testifies in the *Phaedrus*. Plotinus adds that the soul shrinks vehemently from the foul and is affected by the beautiful, and not without reason: for ugliness is a certain grim face of evil, while beauty is the charming face of the good. Furthermore, the rational soul hangs most closely from the divine mind and keeps the Idea of beauty impressed within itself from that source; it is congruent to this Idea, as if it were a kinsman of its own fatherland...

<summary>In this page, Ficino introduces Plotinus's theory of Beauty, arguing that Beauty is a divine "grace" that draws the soul toward the Good. He systematically refutes the Stoic idea that beauty consists solely of physical proportion, suggesting instead that it is an internal "Idea" that reflects divine reason.</summary>
<keywords>Beauty, The Good, Proportion, Symmetry, Soul, Plotinus, Plato, Intellectual Form, Three Graces, Neoplatonism</keywords>

# MARSILIO FICINO ON THE
# BOOK ON BEAUTY,
### AN ARGUMENT.

->From the first essence, life, and mind, influences emanate through all things, like rays, voices, and words, through six levels.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial letter 'I' featuring a landscape with a human figure and foliage.</image-desc> Certain *INFLUENCES* flow from Being itself through all beings everywhere. But in the way that essence exists in Being, they flow forth chiefly in the manner of a solar ray; in the way that life exists there, they break forth in the manner of sound and voice; and finally, in the way that intellect exists there, they are carried in the manner of a signifying word. Insofar as they are like rays, they seem to move the sight; as voices or sounds, they strike the ears; and as words, they especially provoke the soul. Everywhere, however, they encounter us as beautiful things, or as various beauties, for they proceed from the very form of beauty itself. 

When we name beauty itself, we wish "Being" itself to be properly understood in the manner of a form—that is, as formal beauty. But in the manner of a cause—that is, as the cause of beauty itself—we wish "the Good" itself to be considered. For we believe the Good to be the light itself or the source of sparkling beauty flowing from it. Beauty, then, is the splendor emanating from that light of the Good—that is, Being itself depending on the One and the Good. 

From Being itself, as I was saying, we do not doubt that influences proceed through all things like rays, voices, and words. Influences of this kind are first in the Idea of the divine mind; secondly, they are perceived in any mind thereafter; then, through universal providence, in the mind of the world-soul itself; thirdly, in the reason of that same soul; fourthly, in its primary imagination; fifthly, in the following imagination; and sixthly, in the vegetative power, which is also called "universal nature." 

Thus far, they retain a certain ideal character <note>original: "idealem... rationem"</note> within themselves. For up to this point, they are living, effective, fertile, and eternal. In this last level of divine things are the "seminal reasons" <term>seminal reasons: the underlying blueprints or "seeds" in nature that dictate the form and growth of physical things</term> of all things, by which the species of things themselves are propagated. Since the first life and the first formal reason of all things exist in the first Essence as the principle of every essence—in which principle both reason and life were present—it is right that insofar as the influences emanating from there preserve life and formal reason together, pure, whole, and effective, they are called essential, ideal, and divine. They preserve such a great gift even in nature, that is, the vegetative power of the soul; therefore, on this "sixth day" <note>a reference to the Biblical creation narrative</note>, the proper works of God reach their end. 

Immediately afterward, however, those influences strike the underlying matter of the soul. But since they can neither progress further, nor retain the nature of true essence and life in that matter (which is next to nothingness), they pass from being forms into being images. Images, I say, which are likenesses of the true and divine forms. These, under the generative nature of the soul acting upon matter, result from the matter itself which receives them. They are reflected from the matter like a ray from a mirror, or echoed back like a voice from a vault, or returned like a word from a flat wall, as if an Echo. 

This lowest level of formal outflow seems to be favored by the Moon, the mistress of final generation; the seminal reasons flourishing in nature and nourishing matter are favored by Venus; those same reasons in the lower imagination hastening toward motion, by Mars; those same reasons reigning in the imagination, by the Sun; those flourishing in reason, by Mercury; those ruling in the mind of the soul, by Jupiter; and finally, those resting in the divine mind, by Saturn. In this seventh level, as if on the day of Saturn, the maker of the world rests—that is, the Idea itself is deeply internal to him. For he does not refer this Idea to other things that are made from it, but refers other things to it as a model.

->Formal beauty itself is the mind itself: with whose allurements are mixed<-
->wonder, power, diffusion, and pleasure.<-

*Because this model is the all-forming reason of all forms, it is therefore considered the first and universal form and species. For this reason, it is the first "formal beauty." Hence, we are accustomed to call beauty everywhere "form" or "species," and the beautiful "shapely" <note>original: "formosos"</note>; the opposite of which we call deformity and the deformed. From this, it is clear that matter, which by its nature is entirely formless, must rightly be considered deformity itself. But of this, more elsewhere.* 

*Formal beauty itself truly arises with the first essence; it grows as essence proceeds into life; and it is finally judged to be adult when life is completed in the mind. For through the very act of the mind, the beauty of essential life is perfectly formed and becomes an all-forming shape. Therefore, in the order of things, there is the most beauty where there is the most mind—whether there is some nature of the mind present, or its own craftsmanship, or a trace or sign of it. And all of it moves us more vehemently there, where these things encounter us more vividly. For the true form of beauty itself is life itself, completely perfected through the act of the mind. The property of beauty is to allure and to seize at the same time. Hence in Greek it is called "Calon," as if it were "calling" or provoking <note>original: "Calon, quasi prouocans"</note>. And since beauty exists as an intellectual gift, it allures only those who know—I mean, whether by some other intellectual way, or by sight or hearing, which are the chief servants of reason. Moreover, wonder is mixed into the allurements of beauty,*

<summary>This page concludes Plotinus's thoughts on internal wisdom as true happiness and begins Ficino's commentary on Beauty. Ficino describes beauty as a divine radiation that descends through six levels of existence, from the Divine Mind down to physical nature, shaped by planetary influences.</summary>
