<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s Ennead I, Book 6, specifically focusing on the transition from the general desire for the Good to the specific experience of Beauty, and beginning a systematic critique of the classical definition of beauty as mere proportion.</meta>

<header>ON BOOK VI OF ENNEAD I.</header>

A certain sharper force, diffusing desire. You must remember, therefore, what we prove in <term>Theology</term> <note>Ficino refers to Neoplatonic theology, the study of divine principles.</note>: that while all things indeed seek the **Good**, not all things seek the **Beautiful**, but only those that possess a certain judgment of beauty. Furthermore, these beings always seek the Good, yet they do not always strive for Beauty. Since the appetite and draw toward the Good is most universal and perpetual, it follows that the Good itself is the most universal principle of all, and the most powerful; the very form of Beauty is closest to the Good. And because the provocation from and toward beauty is, as it were, something new—since it happens only to certain beings, only at certain times, and follows after nature and knowledge—a certain wonder is deservedly mixed with the charms of beauty. 

Likewise, there is a certain "violence" (so to speak): for although the appetite for the Good, which is universal and perpetual, is most inward to nature and draws from the innermost depths, the seeking of the beautiful seizes us as if from the outside, necessarily following upon knowledge. Therefore, because it is less "natural" <note>In the sense of being a basic biological instinct for survival/good.</note>, it seems to possess something somewhat violent. Finally, it diffuses the lover in a certain way. For once beauty has snatched the lover away from himself, it does not immediately restore him whole and unified; since it draws from the outside and seizes through the mode of knowledge (which deals with distinctions), it thereby scatters or "diffuses" him. 

Ultimately, the affect of love, whether it be gentle or sharp, always moves with pleasure: just as there is a certain delight not only in sweet flavors and deep sounds, but also in a certain sharp flavor and in high-pitched voices. We know for certain that the soul is affected by pleasure when it is touched by something congruent to itself and is led toward the Good. Indeed, wherever Beauty meets us, it approaches as something congruent, and for that reason, it pleases and is approved; this is because it responds to the <term>Idea</term> <note>The divine archetype or perfect pattern of beauty.</note> of beauty innate within us and agrees with it in every way. Again, by its own nature, it always leads the soul to the Good: for the participation in beauty among us calls us to its intellectual form, and through that form finally to the Good itself; just as splendor leads to light, and light leads to the source of radiance. 

But let it suffice for now to have run through Plotinus’s most beautiful book on beauty with "freer feet" <note>meaning: in a general or summary fashion.</note>, so to speak. Next, we must repeat the chapters of this new book in order, and these also briefly; for we discuss these matters more extensively in our *Commentary on the Symposium* <note>original: "Conuiuio de amore"</note>.

->Beauty is a certain grace, which exists more in things that are seen than those that are heard,<-
->and even more in things that are thought, and it is not merely proportion.<-

**I**  We conceive by a common notion that **Beauty** is something gracious, or a certain grace alluring us through sight, or hearing, or reason. Indeed, insofar as it exists in things that are seen, heard, or thought, it is called "Beauty," and it represents to us three **Graces**. Insofar as it consists in sight, hearing, and reason, it is called "delight" and "pleasure"—a decent pleasure, I say. For a decent pleasure properly follows a thing that is decent in itself; and a decent appetite, namely **Love** itself, follows this pleasure. A foul disturbance, perhaps, happens for other reasons. 

Thus, the first chapter inquires into what this grace and beauty chiefly is, and assigns what it is not. It signifies, meanwhile, that beauty pertains even more to sight than to hearing: because, evidently, sight and light are more similar to the <term>Intellect</term> than hearing and sound. Furthermore, the habits of the soul are more beautiful than the bodies that are called "handsome," and more than voices, because they are more closely related to the Mind. Even the habits of the soul, both in morals and in learning, can rightly be called not only "beautiful," but "beauties" themselves. For they are forms, I say, close to the Mind. 

Voices and bodies, however, cannot truly be called "beauties." For while Beauty itself ought not to be called "beautiful" at one moment and "not beautiful" at another, the same body is beautiful today, but tomorrow—with a slight change—it is not. Similarly, the matter of a voice remains nearly the same, but once the proportion is changed, it becomes ugly. Nevertheless, although beauty pertains more to those things that are looked upon than those that are heard, and again more to those that are thought, we must nonetheless investigate whether there is something common to all these, and what that very thing is by which all these are called "beautiful." 

But first, he investigates this in the bodies that are seen, as this will be more manifest. To begin with, he refutes the common opinion concerning these, which says that the beauty of a body is a certain <term>proportion</term> <note>original: "commensuratio", often translated as symmetry.</note> of the parts to each other and to the whole, together with a harmony of color. He refutes this with four arguments:
1. **First**, if beauty is itself proportion or a certain measuring, then certainly only a composite thing can be beautiful; therefore, no simple thing, even if it is most gracious, will be called beautiful.
2. **Second**, if only the composite is beautiful, none of the parts (especially simple ones) will be beautiful; indeed, none of the parts at all, since beauty would be placed only in the proportion relative to another. From this it would follow that beauty is created out of non-beautiful things; yet we have certain knowledge that nothing gracious is ever made from things entirely lacking in grace.
3. **Third**, the same face, often with the same proportion of features remaining, appears to us at one moment beautiful and at another not beautiful—as if proportion were one thing, and beauty another.
4. **Fourth**, it is necessary that beauty in bodies should represent the beauty of higher things to us. We must therefore, as far as possible, accommodate the former to the latter; yet in such a way that beauty exists in those higher things in a far more excellent manner than in bodies. 

However, in what way a certain "proportion" could exist there—namely in the soul or the intellect—cannot easily be assigned. And in the soul, we cannot understand how morals and sciences are "proportions" if we follow Plotinus. For he does not wish for habits to be heaped up in the soul from many figures and acts (which would be called habits of morals or sciences), but rather that the simple moral act of virtue shines forth as soon as the clouds of incidental vices are shaken off, and the simple form of science glows once false opinions are finally expelled. For the soul is, in a way, all things; and it knows a thing most especially when, excited by arguments, it becomes in act that very thing which it was before, but by a certain fruitful potentiality. But these things will be discussed more opportunely elsewhere.

->Beauty in bodies is the absolute perfection of form chiefly,<-
->which dominates both matter and other forms within it, and brings back a clear<-
->victory of divine art and reason over matter,<-
->and clearly represents the Idea itself.<-

**II**  The second chapter examines what beauty itself is in bodies. It asserts that it is something offering itself readily at first sight. For since Beauty is the form of intelligible forms in the **Intelligible World**, and is similarly the "form of forms" in the body, it deservedly moves the intellect there, and the sight here, first and most readily—as Plato testifies in the *Phaedrus*. Plotinus adds that the soul vehemently rejects the ugly and adopts the beautiful, and not without cause: for ugliness is a certain foul face of evil, but beauty is the charming face of the good. Furthermore, the rational soul depends most closely on the **Divine Mind**, and keeps the <term>Idea</term> of beauty impressed upon itself from there: with which indeed it agrees, as if with its own fatherland and kin...

**Vocabulary:** Beauty, Plotinus, Plato, Phaedrus, soul, good, form, grace, proportion, intellect, Theology.

He argues that beauty is a "form" that dominates matter and resonates with the innate Ideas already present within the human soul.</summary>

<header>THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...gladly embraces. Moreover, that form in bodies is fitting which is composed according to the very norm and rule of the <term>Idea</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, an "Idea" is the perfect, eternal blueprint of a thing existing in the Divine Mind.</note>; provided that the <term>seminal reason</term> <note>Original: *ratio seminalis*. These are the formative principles or "seeds" within nature that guide the growth and shaping of physical matter.</note>, which exists in nature as the former of bodies, dominates the matter as much as possible, rendering the form within it not at all material, but maximally formal. Indeed, as we learn from the *Timaeus*: the Intellect itself is divinely the father of forms, and matter is the mother. But the reason and the kindling of forms flourishing in nature can rightly be called the paternal and effective seed; the form born from it is the offspring. Beauty <note>Original: *formositas*, literally "shapeliness" or "having good form."</note>, however, is nothing other than the very disposition of this offspring, more expressly reflecting the image of the father. Deformity, by contrast, is both a certain lack of likeness in the failing form to the father's form, and the matter itself which is the origin of this failure—especially when, by some impeding chance, the subject is not at all overcome by the forming reason; that is, it either does not sustain the act of the forming agent, or receives it most awkwardly. Furthermore, although there are many accidental forms in any element, there is nonetheless one substantial and chief form. Similarly, in mixed things, such as stones and metals, if there are many substantial forms in potential, there is nonetheless one principal form in act, which is common to all. So it is in plants and animals: if many substantial forms are present in each through some act, there is nonetheless one form in chief act ruling over the many. Everywhere, however, beauty is a certain absolute perfection, or grace, and as it were a certain flower of the form itself, chiefly dominating other forms. It is therefore something divine and imperial: because it signifies both the empire of the reigning form, and represents the victory of divine art and reason over matter, and clearly represents the Idea itself.

->*Beauty in bodies is a more expressive likeness; and if matter is subtracted, it is the Idea itself. Likewise, the beauty of any species is judged by the soul through a formula of that Idea implanted within itself, according to which the species was instituted.*<-

III. Who then is a beautiful man? Or a beautiful lion? Or a beautiful horse? Surely he who is chiefly so formed, so born, as the divine mind instituted through his Idea, and as universal nature thereafter conceived through its seminal power. Now indeed, our soul possesses the formula of that Idea in its mind, and similarly possesses the seminal reason in its own nature. Therefore, by a certain natural judgment, it is accustomed to judge concerning a man, or a lion, or a horse, and the rest, that this one is not beautiful, but that one is beautiful: because, clearly, the former disagrees entirely with the formula and reason, while the latter agrees; and among the beautiful, that this one is more beautiful than that one, because this one agrees more with the formula and reason than the other. And indeed, since both judgments regarding these things are natural, they cannot be more conveniently explained than through the formulas and reasons innate to us; it is probable that divine providence, disposing all things as well as possible, impressed such characters upon us from the beginning as if they were marks. When we judge concerning beauty, we approve as beautiful above all others that which is animate and rational, and so formed that it satisfies the formula of beauty which we have in our mind through the soul, and corresponds through the body to the seminal reason of beauty which we possess in our nature and fruitful soul. 

The form in a beautiful body is as similar to its Idea as the shape of a building in matter is similar to the model in the architect’s mind, and as a speech in the voice is similar to the speech which is in the soul. Therefore, if you take away the matter from a man but leave the form, this very form which remains to you is that very Idea according to which the man was formed. Just as if you take away its matter from a building, while the shape remains; or if you take away the broken air <note>A classical way of describing sound waves or articulated speech.</note> from a speech, while the meaning is preserved: surely the remaining shape there is nothing other than the model itself residing in the architect, and the preserved meaning here is nothing other than the thought of the speaker himself. Whence he who gathers such a meaning is said to have the mind of the speaker and to "commentate" upon it. 

Thus we also ought to hold matter as secondary in beautiful things, but loving the forms and order, we should suspect the Ideas within these things, and contemplate the divine art and mind. He [Plotinus] considers that the beauty of a body composed of forms consists in this: that both the individual forms within it overcome the formlessness of matter, and the common form entirely excels the individual forms. However, he considers the beauty of a simple body in which there is a single substantial form in act—such as gold, or silver, and the like—to be situated in the greatest portion of light. Indeed, he holds that light is fire, that is, the form of heaven, which is a certain image of the life of heaven; so much so, that what is intellectual in the celestial life is luminous in the celestial body. Likewise, he holds light beneath the moon to be an act and (so to speak) an image of the form, that is, of the celestial light. From this it is clear how great the power of heaven is, since the image of its form produces and preserves all things among us. He also considers the fire beneath the moon to be a fiery or ignited body, rather than pure fire. Nevertheless, because it is more similar to heaven to exist as something lucid and, as it were, the form of other bodies, and close to the incorporeal, it is therefore most beautiful; and by participation in it, other things become most beautiful, especially those that carry light from it. Such things are those that have either the least of earth, or a most tempered nature. For that which is either most earthy or least tempered, being as it were far different from heaven, is most unsuited for light and lucid color, as if incapable of receiving something celestial. What has been said regarding bodies that appear beautiful holds similarly in those things that are heard as beautiful, whether it be a single voice or a certain pleasing composition of voices. And just as the beauty of a visible form proceeds from its ideal and seminal reason, so the beauty of a voice and its harmony is perfected both by the spirit itself and by the harmonic conception of the mind. And everywhere beauty is the empire of form over the subject; and corporeal form proceeds from incorporeal form.

->*Beauty that is seen represents the beauty of the mind; beauty that is heard reflects the beauty of the soul. Likewise, no one ought to or can speak of the beauty of the mind and soul unless he himself possesses it.*<-

IIII. Beauty is twofold: namely, incorporeal and corporeal. And just as corporeal beauty is again twofold—one indeed in those things that are seen, the other in those that are heard—so also incorporeal beauty is twofold: one in the intellect, the other in the soul. The beauty of intellectual light is represented to us chiefly by that which is seen in light as its image. Again, the beauty of the soul, constituted in a certain way in harmony, is rightly reflected by that beauty of harmony which is heard, as if by an image. Altogether, however, just as no one can speak of corporeal beauty unless he has known it by sense, so neither can one speak of incorporeal beauty unless he has perceived it with the soul. But in knowing the corporeal, one is carried outside of oneself; yet to perceive the incorporeal, it is necessary to be brought back within oneself. Having been recalled to himself, however, he will not perceive it unless he possesses it. Be, therefore, beautiful in both intellect and soul before you dare to dispute concerning incorporeal beauty. Remember, if you are delighted by sensible beauty, which is the image of insensible beauty, you will perceive a much greater pleasure...

He distinguishes between corporeal beauty (seen and heard) and incorporeal beauty (intellectual and spiritual), noting that one must be internally beautiful to truly understand the latter.</summary>

It establishes a hierarchy where beauty descends from the "First Form" (the Intellect) down through the soul and finally into matter.</meta>

<header>ON BOOK VI OF ENNEAD I.</header>

You will know pleasure when you recognize the beauty of the soul and mind themselves; even more so, when you possess it.

-> Matter indeed possesses a natural deformity, while its beauty is foreign. But the soul <-
-> possesses an accidental ugliness, while its beauty is innate. Likewise, <-
-> the beauty of the divine mind is like light. The beauty of the human mind— <-
-> specifically in intellectual virtue—is like a most <-
-> brilliant color. The beauty of the soul—specifically in <-
-> moral virtue—is like a figure. <-

<margin>V</margin> Since beauty—that is, <term>shapeliness</term> <note>Original: *formositas*. In this context, it refers to the state of having a "good form" or being well-ordered.</note>—is the very flower, vigor, and grace of form, surely matter, just as it is formlessness itself, is also deformity itself. To matter, therefore, deformity is natural, while beauty becomes something foreign, insofar as matter receives form from elsewhere. But for the soul, by contrast, beauty is innate; for by its own nature it is a true form—that is, an activity existing within itself. For the remaining forms below the soul are "formings" rather than "forms"—that is, they are the actions of the soul upon matter, and in turn, they are the "passions" <note>In the philosophical sense, a "passion" is something acted upon or received by a subject.</note> of matter.

Therefore, the soul’s beauty is natural, and its deformity is accidental. For just as matter seems to become beautiful when it borrows something formal from the soul, so in turn the soul becomes deformed when it receives something formless from matter. It receives this insofar as it yields to the body through its affections and concedes through its cognition. Thus, the soul does not become beautiful by the acquisition of some new gift, but by <term>purgation</term> <note>Original: *purgatio*. The Neoplatonic process of "cleansing" the soul of material distractions to return it to its divine state.</note> alone, through which it is restored to its original nature. In that nature, its own <term>Idea</term> <note>The eternal blueprint of the soul in the divine mind.</note> and the divine intellect formed it. The beauty of that divine intellect is like light; the beauty of our intellect flowing from there, called intellectual virtue, is like a most brilliant color; but moral beauty, proceeding from both, is like a figure or shape.

-> Virtue and beauty are natural to the soul; and its own purity is restored to the soul: thus <-
-> it is immediately radiant with the beauty of the divine mind, and most happily <-
-> enjoys the Good itself. Likewise, the first form, the first mind, and the first being are the same. <-

<margin>VI</margin> An ancient oracle, cited both by Plato in the *Phaedo* and by Plotinus here, teaches that all virtue, whether intellectual or moral, is a certain purification and purity. Consider this also said of beauty under the name of virtue: as if virtue and beauty were innate to the soul, while ugliness and depravity were foreign. *Thus, the soul purged of bodily filth not only becomes beautiful, but becomes beauty itself—that is, a form existing through itself, a certain "ideal reason," and an expression of the divine face. This occurs when the soul evolves from a rational soul into an intellectual one, and then into Intellect itself. For the "First Beauty" exists according to form, where the "First Form" resides; and the First Form is the Intellect. For the First Form must be uniform and all-forming, the origin of all other forms. Just as primary matter is entirely formless and a receptacle for forms, only the First Intellect can be such a principle; and it is also Being itself. For if being exists everywhere through form, surely the Primary Being coincides with the First Form.*

Furthermore, just as in matter natural evil coincides with natural deformity, so in the Primary Being and the Primary Mind, innate Good (that is, "good-formedness") coincides with innate beauty. But regarding the Good itself, which is above Being and Mind: if it is ever called "beauty," it is understood as the *source* of beauty, from which the Intellect flows as the first form of beauty. From the Intellect, the soul is born as the first "participation" in beauty; other things below the soul obtain a second and then a third degree of beauty through their participation in the soul. Finally, we gather that the soul itself is beautiful and divine by nature from this: that in bodies, beauty shines out chiefly where the "seed-like virtue" <note>Original: *seminaria virtus*. The formative power inherent in the soul that "seeds" order into physical things.</note> of the soul—whether in universal nature or in any individual nature—finds a strongly obedient subject.

-> How the Gods are distinguished from daemons, and how their bodies are seen. Likewise, six <-
-> differences between the sight of gods and the spectacles of daemons. Con- <-
-> clude: if you desire to contemplate divine beauty, <-
-> be beautiful and divine yourself. <-

<margin>VII</margin> There is no need to interpret Plotinus’s mind at greater length, for he speaks as clearly as he does divinely. He speaks most divinely, striving everywhere not so much to lead the soul toward *looking* at beauty as toward *possessing* it. As for what he briefly hints regarding the appearance of gods and <term>daemons</term> <note>Original: *dæmones*. In Neoplatonism, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits or guardian beings between humans and the higher gods.</note>, understand it thus: *He signifies the sublunary gods, and daemons likewise, who naturally have invisible bodies and are beneficent; and sometimes, by a certain kindness toward us, they reveal themselves to our eyes.*

Distinguish the gods from the daemons here in this way: In the "God of gods" <note>The One or the Supreme Principle.</note>, providence is entirely universal, for he provides for and grants all things to everyone. Providence is also universal in a certain way in the Divine Mind and the Soul of the World. In the following gods, whether they be invisible or visible, providence is also universal in a way, but under a particular condition. For they either give certain gifts to all things, or they give all things to certain things. In daemons, however, providence is both particular and under a particular condition. For they distribute only certain specific gifts to certain kinds of things and regions. Nor are they, like the gods, entirely separated from all passion, worry, or affection; for they seem to incline somewhat toward the very things they care for. Add, moreover, that many daemons follow each of the gods—whether celestial or sub-celestial—as their leader.

But in what way are those who are invisible by nature seen? For I do not think a god or daemon, in order to be grasped by your eyes, must necessarily compress its too-thin and rare body into a narrow space, and thus reflect the rays of your eyes back to you, or terminate them in a false way. They do not wish to be seen by you through their own "suffering" <note>That is, by undergoing a physical change to their own essence.</note>; but perhaps by a certain powerful virtue of movement, they repel the visual rays of your eyes back to you, or terminate them in themselves, and thus make themselves known to you. But we shall discuss sight according to the mind of Plotinus elsewhere. You can also perceive them in another way, not from external sight, but from a certain internal and celestial sight, if you ever collect yourself toward this from every side.

Regarding the differences between the forms of gods and daemons—whether both are ethereal, or igneous, or aerial—Iamblichus, following the thinking of the Egyptians, briefly reveals them thus: The appearance of any god is offered to us as a simple figure and measure; that of a daemon is manifold. Again, the appearance of a god is stable; that of a daemon is changeable with swift variety. Likewise, the form of a god is venerable and at the same time propitious and entirely benign; that of a daemon is not only to be revered but to be feared. Furthermore, the divine spectacle seems to suddenly fill the whole world; the daemonic shows itself in a certain place. Again, a divine flash (so to speak) occurs even at the strike of the intelligence...

<header>COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...willingly embraces <note>The text continues from the previous page: "The soul willingly embraces beauty."</note>. Moreover, that form is fitting in bodies which is composed according to the very norm and rule of the <term>Idea</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, an "Idea" or "Form" is the perfect, eternal blueprint of a thing that exists in the Divine Mind.</note>. This occurs when the <term>seminal reason</term> <note>Original: *ratio seminalis*. These are the "seed-logics" or formative powers within nature that direct the growth and shape of living things.</note>—which resides in the nature that forms bodies—largely dominates the matter, rendering the form within it not material at all, but rather highly formal. Indeed, as we learn from the *Timaeus* <note>Plato's dialogue on the creation of the universe.</note>: the Intellect itself is the divine father of forms, while matter is the mother. But the "reason" and "kindling" of forms flourishing in nature can rightly be called the paternal and effective seed, while the form born from it is the offspring. <term>Shapeliness</term> <note>Original: *formositas*. This refers to the quality of being well-formed or beautiful.</note>, then, is nothing other than the very character of this offspring, reflecting the father’s image more clearly. By contrast, deformity is both a certain lack of resemblance to the father’s form and the very origin of this defect in the matter—especially when some hindering chance prevents the subject from being overcome by the "forming reason"; that is, it either cannot sustain the act of the forming power or receives it most poorly. Accordingly, although there are many accidental forms in any element, there is one <term>substantial form</term> <note>The essential nature that makes a thing what it is.</note> that is primary. Similarly, in mixed things like stones and metals, even if there are several substantial forms in action, there is one principal and common form. This is also true in plants and animals: though many substantial forms may be active in each, there is one principal act ruling the others. Everywhere, beauty is a certain absolute perfection or grace—a kind of flower of that form which dominates the other forms. Thus, beauty is something divine and commanding, for it signifies the empire of the ruling form, represents the victory of divine art and reason over matter, and clearly mirrors the Idea itself.

-> Beauty in bodies is a more expressive likeness of the Idea; indeed, if matter is taken away, it is the Idea itself. Likewise, the beauty of any species is judged by the soul through a formula of that Idea implanted within itself, according to which that species was established. <-

### III. Who then is a beautiful man? Or a beautiful lion? Or a beautiful horse? 

Certainly, it is the one who is so formed and born as the Divine Mind established through its Idea, and as universal nature conceived through its "seminal virtue." Now, our soul possesses the formula of that Idea inborn in its mind; it also possesses a similar seminal reason in its own nature. Therefore, by a certain natural judgment, the soul is accustomed to judge a man, a lion, or a horse, and all other things, deciding that this one is not beautiful, while that one is. This is because the former disagrees with the formula and reason, while the latter agrees. Furthermore, among beautiful things, one is more beautiful than another because it agrees with the formula and reason more than the other does. And since this judgment cannot be more conveniently explained than through the formulas and reasons innate to us, it is probable that Divine Providence, disposing all things for the best, impressed these "characters" <note>Imprints or hallmarks.</note> upon us from the beginning.

When we judge beauty, we approve above all else that which is animated and rational, and so formed that it satisfies the formula of beauty we hold in our mind (through the soul) and corresponds to the seminal reason of beauty we possess in our fertile soul (through the body). Indeed, the form in a beautiful body is as similar to its Idea as the shape of a building in matter is similar to the model in the architect's mind, or as a spoken speech is similar to the speech held in the mind. Therefore, if you strip the matter from a man but leave the form, this remaining form is the very Idea according to which the man was formed. Just as if you took away the material from a building while leaving the shape, or if you removed the vibrating air from a speech while preserving the meaning: certainly, the remaining shape is nothing but the model existing in the architect, and the preserved meaning is nothing but the thought of the speaker. Thus, one who grasps such a meaning is said to hold the speaker's mind and to "interpret" it. 

In the same way, we ought to look past the matter in beautiful things; selecting their forms and order, we should catch sight of the "Ideas" within them and "interpret" the divine art and mind. He <note>Plotinus.</note> considers the beauty of a body composed of many forms to consist in each form overcoming the formlessness of matter, and the common form excelling every individual form. However, he considers the beauty of a "simple body" (in which a single substantial form is active, like gold, silver, and the like) to be located in the greatest portion of light. Indeed, he holds light to be the form of the heavens—an image of celestial life—such that what is intellectual in celestial life is luminous in the celestial body. Likewise, light beneath the moon <note>The terrestrial realm.</note> is an activity and (so to speak) an image of celestial light. From this, it is clear how great the power of heaven is, since the image of its form creates and preserves all things among us. He also considers that fire beneath the moon is a "fiery" or "ignited" body rather than pure fire. Nevertheless, because it is more similar to heaven, it exists as something more lucid—the "form" of other bodies, as it were—and is close to the incorporeal. It is most beautiful, and other things become most beautiful through participation in it, especially those that carry light back from it. Such things are those that have the least "earth" or a most temperate nature. For whatever is most earthy or least temperate is, as it were, far removed from heaven and most unsuited to receive light and lucid color, which are celestial qualities. 

What has been said regarding bodies that appear beautiful also applies to things heard as beautiful, whether it be a single voice or a pleasing composition of voices. Just as the beauty of a visible form proceeds from its ideal and seminal reason, so the beauty of a voice and its harmony is perfected both by the spirit and by the harmonic conception of the mind. Everywhere, beauty is the empire of form over its subject, and corporeal form proceeds from incorporeal form.

-> Beauty that is seen represents the beauty of the mind; beauty that is heard reflects the beauty of the soul. Likewise, no one ought to or can speak of the beauty of the mind and soul unless they possess it themselves. <-

### IIII. There are two kinds of beauty: incorporeal and corporeal. 

And just as corporeal beauty is twofold—one in things seen and the other in things heard—so incorporeal beauty is twofold: one in the intellect and the other in the soul. The beauty of intellectual light is represented to us chiefly by those things seen in light, as if by an image. Again, the beauty of the soul, which is constituted in a certain harmony, is rightly reflected by that harmonic beauty which is heard, as if by an image. Altogether, just as no one can speak of the beauty of the body unless they have known it through the senses, so no one can speak of incorporeal beauty unless they have perceived it with the mind. But to know corporeal beauty, one is carried outside of oneself; to perceive incorporeal beauty, one must be brought back within. Yet, having been called back to oneself, one will not perceive it unless one possesses it. Therefore, be beautiful in both intellect and soul before you dare to dispute concerning incorporeal beauty. Remember: if you take delight in sensible beauty, which is an image of insensible beauty, you will receive a much greater pleasure from the perception of the latter.

Here, Ficino explores the ontological status of beauty—how it moves from the Divine Mind down into human virtue and physical matter—and begins a discussion on the hierarchy of spiritual beings.</meta>

# ON BOOK VI OF ENNEAD I.

->You will know true pleasure when you have recognized the beauty of the soul and mind itself; or rather, when you have come to possess it.<-

->Matter possesses a natural deformity, but a foreign beauty. The soul, however, has an external ugliness, but a native beauty. Likewise, the beauty of the divine mind is like light. The beauty of the human mind—specifically in intellectual virtue—is like a most brilliant color. The beauty of the soul—specifically in moral virtue—is like a shape.<-

*V. Since beauty—that is, shapeliness—is the very flower, vigor, and grace of form, certainly matter, just as it is formlessness itself, is also deformity itself. For matter, deformity is natural; beauty is something "foreign" <note>Original: *peregrina*. In Neoplatonism, matter is considered a void or "non-being" that only becomes beautiful when a higher form is "loaned" to it.</note>, insofar as matter receives form from elsewhere. But for the soul, the opposite is true: beauty is native to it, because by its very nature the soul is a true form—that is, an active force existing in itself. For the other forms below the soul are "formations" rather than true forms; they are the actions of the soul upon matter, and in turn, they are the "passions" <note>Here, "passions" refers to the way matter is acted upon or "suffers" the impression of a form.</note> of matter. Therefore, for the soul, shapeliness is natural, while deformity is external. Just as matter seems to become beautiful when it borrows something formal from the soul, so the soul becomes deformed when it takes on something formless from matter. It takes this on whenever it yields to the passions of the body or concedes to its limited way of knowing. Thus, the soul does not become beautiful by acquiring some new gift, but through <term>purification</term> <note>Original: *purgatione*. This refers to the process of stripping away material attachments to reveal the soul's original divine state.</note> alone, by which it is restored to its original nature. In that state, its own <term>Idea</term> <note>The eternal blueprint of the soul in the divine mind.</note> and the Divine Intellect shaped it. The beauty of that Divine Intellect is like light; the beauty of our own intellect, which flows from it and is called "intellectual virtue," is like a most brilliant color; but moral beauty, which proceeds from both, is like a shape.*

->Virtue and beauty are natural to the soul: its very purity restored to it. Thus, it immediately shines with the beauty of the divine mind and most happily enjoys the Good itself. Likewise, the first form, the first mind, and the first being are one and the same.<-

*VI. An ancient oracle—cited both by Plato in the *Phaedo* and by Plotinus here—teaches that all virtue, whether intellectual or moral, is a certain purification and purity. Consider this said also of beauty under the name of virtue: as if virtue and beauty were native to the soul, while ugliness and depravity were foreign. Thus, a soul purged of bodily filth becomes not only beautiful but Beauty itself—that is, a form existing by itself, a certain "ideal reason," and an expression of the divine face. This happens when the soul transitions from being merely rational to being intellectual, and finally becomes Intellect itself. For the "First Beauty" exists according to form, where the "First Form" is; and the First Form is the Intellect. The First Form must be "uniform" <note>Meaning simple or singular in its essence.</note> yet "omni-form" <note>Containing the seeds or patterns of all things.</note>, and the origin of all other forms—just as Prime Matter is utterly formless and the receptacle of all forms. Only the First Intellect can be such a thing; it is also "Being" itself. If "to be" is everywhere achieved through "form," then surely the First Being coincides with the First Form. Furthermore, just as in matter natural evil coincides with natural deformity, so in the First Being and First Mind, native Goodness—that is, the "Good-form"—meets with native beauty. But above Being and Mind is the Good itself; if the Good is ever called "Beauty," it is understood as the **Source of Beauty**, from which the Intellect flows as the "First Form of Beauty." From the Intellect, the soul is born as the "first participation" in beauty; all other things below the soul gain their beauty through a second or third level of participation. Finally, we infer that the soul is beautiful and divine by nature because, in bodies, beauty shines most brightly where the <term>seed-power</term> <note>Original: *seminaria virtus*. The formative power within the soul that directs the growth and beauty of physical organisms.</note> of the soul finds a subject that is strongly obedient to it, whether in universal nature or in any specific nature.*

->How the gods are distinguished from demons, and how their bodies are seen. Also, that there are six differences between the appearance of gods and the spectacles of demons. Conclude: if you wish to contemplate divine beauty, be beautiful and divine yourself.<-

*VII. However, there is no need to interpret Plotinus’s mind at greater length, because he speaks as clearly as he does divinely. He strives everywhere not so much to lead the soul to *look at* beauty, as to *possess* it. As for what he briefly hints at regarding the appearance of gods and <term>demons</term> <note>Original: *daemones*. In Greek philosophy, these are not "evil spirits" but intermediary beings between humans and gods.</note>, understand it thus: he means the sublunary gods and demons alike, who naturally have invisible bodies and are benevolent, and who sometimes reveal themselves to our eyes as a favor to us. Distinguish the gods from the demons in this way: in the "God of gods" <note>The Absolute One.</note>, providence is entirely universal; He provides all things for everyone. Providence is also universal, in a sense, in the Divine Mind and the Soul of the World. In the lower gods, whether invisible or visible, providence is still somewhat universal but under a "particular condition"—either they give certain gifts to all things, or they give all things to certain people. In demons, however, providence is both particular and under a particular condition, for they distribute only specific gifts to specific types of things and regions. Nor are they, like the gods, entirely separated from all passion, worry, or emotion; for they seem to "lean down," so to speak, toward the very things they care for. Furthermore, many demons follow each god (celestial or sub-celestial) as their leader. But how are those who are invisible by nature seen? I do not think a god or demon must necessarily compress their thin and rare body into a smaller space to be caught by your eyes, reflecting your visual rays back to you or creating a false boundary. They do not wish to be seen through some change in themselves; rather, perhaps by a powerful virtue of moving your visual rays, they repel those rays back to you or terminate them in themselves, making themselves known to you. But we shall discuss vision according to Plotinus elsewhere. You can also perceive them another way—not with external sight, but with a certain innermost and celestial sight, if you ever collect yourself from all sides into that center. As for the differences between the forms of gods and demons—whether they are both ethereal, or fiery, or airy—Iamblichus <note>A later Neoplatonic philosopher who wrote extensively on theurgy and spiritual hierarchies.</note> briefly explains them according to the Egyptian view: The appearance of any god is offered to us as a simple figure and measure; that of a demon is manifold. A god's appearance is unchanging; a demon's changes with rapid variety. Likewise, the form of a god is at once venerable, propitious, and entirely benign; a demon's is not just revered but to be feared. Furthermore, a divine spectacle seems to suddenly fill the whole world; a demonic one shows itself in a specific place. Again, divine radiance (if I may say so) flashes even with a strike of the intelligence...*

COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

is swifter and acts more quickly: the demonic <note>In Neoplatonism, "daemons" are intermediate spirits between humans and gods, possessing greater speed and clarity of mind than mortals.</note> is indeed swift, but it does not sufficiently surpass the speed of the human mind. Become intellectual <note>original: *intellectualis*. Here meaning "existing in the realm of pure Mind or Intellect," above mere logic.</note>—first your own intellect, and then the Divine. Then at last, just as an eagle’s eye is lifted by flying into the sky and gazes upon the solar and celestial splendor surrounding the innermost light of the sun as a single beauty together with that light, so you too—having progressed through your own intellect to the Divine Intellect—will see it flashing with a wondrous series of Ideas. Flowing from the paternal light of the Good itself, you will see at first glance an intellectual splendor continuous with that paternal light, as if they were one and the same. Soon, however, you will notice that the light is entirely uniform, while the splendor is in some way multiform; likewise, that the light pours forth, while the splendor is poured out. Indeed, you will discern (to speak in the Platonic manner) the Mind itself as the very form of beauty, but the Good itself as the father of the Mind and the progenitor of beauty. Thus, you will admire the Son in the Father, and you will love the Father in the Son, and you will rejoice in the mutual love of both.

BEAUTY exists mostly in the sense of sight. It is also in hearing, according to the composition of words and in all music, for songs and rhythmic harmonies are beautiful. Furthermore, if we ascend from the senses to that which is above the senses, we find that studies, duties, actions, and habits are beautiful, as are the sciences and the beauty of the virtues. Whether there is any beauty even above these, the investigation itself will declare as we proceed. What is it, then, that causes bodies to appear beautiful, and the hearing to approve of voices as beautiful, and so on with everything pertaining to the soul? In what way, then, do all these things become beautiful? Are all things beautiful by one and the same principle of beauty, or is beauty one thing in a body and another thing in something else? Again, what are these things if there are two? Or what is it if there is only one? For some things are undoubtedly not beautiful by the very nature of their subjects—such as bodies—but rather by some participation <note>original: *participatione*. The Platonic idea that physical things are not "Beauty" itself, but "participate" in or reflect the perfect Form of Beauty.</note>. Others, however, are beautiful in themselves, such as the nature of virtue itself. Indeed, the same bodies appear beautiful at one time and not beautiful at another, as if being a body were one thing and being beautiful were another. What, then, is this thing that makes bodies beautiful by its presence? For this is the first thing we must consider. Tell me: what is it that most attracts the eyes of beholders, turns them toward itself, seizes them, and delights the observer? For if we find this, perhaps we can use it as a ladder to reach the rest. For almost everyone teaches that a certain symmetry of parts, both in relation to each other and to the whole, together with the charm of color, constitutes beauty...

### [ON BEAUTY]

...to create beauty for the eyes, and they claim that the beauty of all things is situated in this: that they are moderated and <term>commensurate</term> <note>original: *commensurata*. The Stoic theory that beauty consists solely in the "symmetry" or proportion of parts to one another and to the whole.</note>. But for those who hold this opinion, nothing simple can be beautiful; only a composite will necessarily be beautiful, and the whole itself will be lovely. However, the individual parts will have no beauty of their own; they will only be called beautiful insofar as they contribute to the whole. And yet, if the whole is beautiful, the parts must also be lovely; for beauty does not consist of ugly things. It is necessary for all the parts to have received beauty. Furthermore, colors—just like the light of the sun itself—since they are simple and do not derive beauty from <term>commensuration</term> <note>original: *symmetria*. Plotinus argues that if beauty requires parts in proportion, then a single color or a single flash of light (which have no "parts") could not be beautiful, which is clearly false.</note>, would be excluded from beauty according to their view. In what way will gold be beautiful to them? Or the flashing of lightning at night, or the sight of the stars? Similarly in voices, that which is a simple tone will be alienated from beauty. And yet, every single note in those songs which are entirely beautiful is itself beautiful. Consequently, when the same proportion remains but the same face appears beautiful at one time and not beautiful at another, must we not say that beauty is something else beyond that which is commensurate, and that the <term>commensuration</term> is one thing, but the beauty is another? And that the commensurate thing is beautiful because of something else? If they then turn to beautiful pursuits and beautiful speeches, and assign the cause of beauty in these also to a proportion of measure, what proportion would be called commensurate in beautiful pursuits, or laws, or disciplines, or sciences? Moreover, how are the <term>speculations</term> <note>original: *theorema*. Mathematical or philosophical contemplations.</note> themselves said to be commensurate with one another? If someone should claim they are so because they are in harmony, we shall certainly say that there is also a certain agreement and harmony among evil things. For these two things agree with one another (as it is said): namely, that "temperance is foolishness" and "justice is noble ignorance." Therefore, the beauty of the soul is all virtue, and this species is much truer than the ones mentioned before. But in what way will there be commensuration here? For it is neither like that of magnitude, nor like that in number. And since there are many parts of the soul, in what ratio would the composition or the tempering of the parts or the speculations be situated? Finally, what would the beauty of the <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: *Nous*. The divine, intuitive mind that exists above discursive reason.</note> itself be—the beauty of that which is segregated and exists only according to itself?

<margin>Beauty in bodies is the flower of form overcoming matter because of the imparting of ideal reason upon matter.</margin> LET US REPEAT again from the beginning, asking what is this beauty in bodies? In the first place, it is something that makes itself known to the sense at the first glance; the soul, apprehending it and recognizing it as something familiar, welcomes it and, as it were, approves and embraces it as most suitable. But when it falls upon the ugly, it recoils; <margin>* The soul recoils, or rather, the opposite [of harmony].</margin> and as if abhorring it, rejects it as alien because of the discord. For the soul, being by nature what it is, and being most excellent in the order of things according to its essence, whenever it sees something kindred to itself, or a trace of its kindred, it rejoices and is struck with awe; it refers the sight back to itself and remembers itself and its own. What then is the similarity between these things which appear beautiful to us and those beautiful things above us? Indeed, if there is a similarity, it is thus...

[The divine intellect] is swifter and acts more quickly; the demonic is indeed swift, but does not quite surpass the speed of the mind. ...even if there are thousands of them. But in what way are **A** both these and those beautiful at the same time? We say that these things are beautiful by participation in a <term>Form</term> <note>original: "species" (Latin) / "εἶδος" (Greek). In Platonic philosophy, this refers to the ideal archetype or 'essence' that gives a thing its character.</note>. For everything that is formless, though naturally fit to receive shape and form, is ugly and removed from divine <term>Reason</term> <note>original: "ratio" / "λόγος". This refers to the formative principle or 'blueprint' of the universe.</note> as long as it lacks reason and Form. Indeed, that which is entirely removed from it is entirely ugly. A thing is also ugly when it is not fully mastered by shape and reason, because the matter does not fully support the complete formation. **B** Therefore, when Form approaches, it organizes and reconciles those things which are to become one through composition; it produces unity through this very agreement. Since the Form itself was one, it was necessary that the thing being formed also become one, as far as a thing composed of many parts can be made one. Beauty, then, is established in the object when it has been reduced to unity, and it imparts itself to both the parts and the whole. But when the Form finds something that is already one and composed of similar parts, it gives itself and that same beauty to the whole. **C** Sometimes, for example, it communicates itself to a whole building along with its parts, and other times to a single stone; in the former case it is done by art, but in others it is done by nature. In this way, a beautiful body is created through communion with a Reason that comes down from the divine.

<margin>
III
The soul, through an innate formula of beauty within itself, recognizes beauty in bodies: this would be the Idea itself if matter were removed. This arises from the victory of divine art over matter.
</margin>

**D** But a certain power appointed for this purpose recognizes beauty; nothing is more capable of judging its own affairs, especially when the rest of the soul joins in the judgment. Perhaps this power speaks by adapting the object to the Form within itself, using that internal Form for judgment just as one uses a ruler to judge what is straight. But how does that which is in the body agree with that which is above the body? Tell us: how does an architect, by matching the external building to the Form of the building in his mind, judge it to be beautiful? Perhaps it is because, if you were to remove the stones, the external building is nothing other than the internal Form, though divided by the external mass of matter; it remains indivisible in essence, even if it appears in many parts. **E** Therefore, when the sense-perception sees the Form in bodies—binding together and overcoming the contrary nature of formless matter, and seeing a shape shining out elegantly upon other shapes—it collects that which appeared dispersed, brings it together as a whole, and introduces it to the indivisible Form within. It then renders it harmonious, congruent, and friendly to that internal Form. Just as the appearance of a virtuous nature in a young man is pleasing to a good man, because it harmonizes with the true virtue within him. **F** The beauty of color arises simply where the darkness of matter is formed and overcome by the presence of light, which is itself incorporeal and a kind of Reason and Form. **G** For this reason, fire itself is beautiful beyond all other bodies; for when compared to the other elements, it holds the rank of Form. It is more eminent than the others and the most subtle of all bodies, being already close to an incorporeal nature. It alone does not receive other things into itself, though other things receive it. For other things are heated by it, but fire itself does not receive cold. Furthermore, it possesses color primarily;

<column-break/>

...even if they are similar within. But how are both those and these beautiful? **A** We say these things are beautiful by participation in a Form. For everything formless, which is by nature capable of receiving shape and Form, is ugly and outside of divine Reason as long as it has no share in Reason or Form. This is what is entirely ugly. That which is not mastered by shape and Reason is also ugly, because the matter has not endured being fully shaped according to the Form. Therefore, when the Form approaches, it arranges that which is to be made of many parts into a synthesis, brings it into a single completion, and makes it one by agreement; since the Form itself was one, that which is shaped must also be one, as far as possible for something made of many parts. Beauty, then, is settled upon it **B** once it has been <margin>* arranged together</margin> <gloss>*</gloss> into a unity, and it gives itself to both the parts and the whole. But when it takes hold of something that is already one and uniform, it gives that same beauty to the whole. **C** Just as sometimes nature gives beauty to a whole house with its parts, and sometimes to a single stone, while in other cases it is art. Thus, a beautiful body comes into being by communion with a Reason that comes from the divine.

**D** But the power appointed for this purpose recognizes it, and nothing is more authoritative in judging its own things, especially when the rest of the soul judges with it. Perhaps that power speaks by harmonizing the object with the Form within itself, using that Form for the judgment as a rule for straightness. But how does that which concerns the body harmonize with that which is before the body? How does the architect, sensing the house outside as harmonized with the house within, say it is beautiful? Is it not because the house outside, if you could separate it from the stones, is the internal Form, divided by the external mass of matter, yet being indivisible, though it is manifested in many? **E** When, therefore, sense-perception sees the Form in bodies, binding together and mastering the contrary nature (which is formless), and sees a shape riding prominently upon other shapes, it brings <margin>* having come together</margin> <gloss>*</gloss> that which was scattered everywhere into a single whole, carries it back, and brings it into the indivisible part within, giving it as something harmonious, congruent, and dear to the inner Form. Just as a trace of virtue appearing in a young man is pleasing to a good man, harmonizing with the truth within him. **F** The beauty of color is simple, created by Form and the mastering of the darkness in matter by the presence of light, which is incorporeal and is Reason and Form. **G** Hence fire itself is beautiful above all other bodies, because it holds the rank of Form in relation to the other elements; it is placed in the heavens and is the most subtle of other bodies, being near to the incorporeal. It alone does not admit other things into itself, while other things admit it. For they are heated, but it is not cooled. It is colored primarily,

# PLOTINUS ENNEADS. I.
## PAGE 54

<column-break/>

...splendor: whenever you look upon it within yourselves, or <margin>A</margin> contemplate in another the greatness of soul, the just character, pure temperance, and fortitude with its noble and venerable countenance; and finally, modesty and honorable dignity, walking with a certain fearless, tranquil, and serene step, as if a divine mind were shining down upon these things from above. Why then, loving these things, do we call them beautiful? For they exist and are apparent; and no one who looks upon them would ever say they are anything other than truly existing things. But what are "truly existing" things? Perhaps they are beautiful. Yet reason still desires to know what makes these existing things so that the soul is lovable. What is the grace in all these virtues, like a light?* On the contrary, <margin>B</margin> shall we compare those things which are ugly in the soul? For perhaps if we know what ugliness is and why it exists, it will help us find what we seek. Let the soul be ugly, then, which is <margin>C</margin> intemperate and unjust, overflowing with many desires, and vexed by a great deal of disturbance due to fears—laboring under envy because of its own narrowness of spirit and greed—thinking of nothing but what is mortal and base, always twisting its thoughts, enslaved to impure pleasures, living a life proper to whatever it suffers through the body, and undergoing its own ugliness as if it were pleasant. And shall we not say that this very ugliness <margin>D</margin> comes to the soul as an added evil, like a mask over its natural beauty? It renders the soul impure with heavy loss, mixed with much wickedness, no longer possessing a pure life or sense, but using a meager life because of the mixture of evil, wasted by much death, no longer seeing what ought to be seen, no longer allowed to dwell within itself because it is always snatched away toward external, lower, and dark things. <margin>E</margin> Truly becoming impure in this way, snatched here and there by things that strike the senses, full of the stain of the body—certainly when it has given itself over to matter and drawn material nature into itself—sinking into a worse state because of such a mixture, it has now almost changed its own form into another. It is just as if someone, having rolled in mud and filth, no longer displays their natural beauty. Instead, what is seen is only what they have contracted from the mud and filth. Indeed, <margin>F</margin> ugliness seems to have happened to it through the addition of a foreign nature. If the soul desires to recover its former beauty, it will be worth the effort to wash away the stains and, through purification itself, be again what it once was. Therefore, if we say the soul becomes ugly through mixture, confusion, and commerce with the body and matter, we shall (I believe) be speaking correctly. For this is the ugliness of the soul: not to be pure and sincere. Just as <margin>G</margin> ugliness happens to gold if it is covered with earthy clods; if someone shakes these off, pure gold suddenly remains. And it is then beautiful, when it has been separated from foreign things, content with its own purity for its beauty. In the same way, the soul, once separated from those desires which it conceived within itself from too much commerce with the body, and from other disturbances...

<column-break/>

...the light of the virtues, whenever you see it in yourselves, or <margin>A</margin> behold in another the greatness of soul and the just character, pure temperance, and courage with its stern countenance, and dignity, and modesty shining upon a calm, unruffled, and impassive disposition, and upon all these, the god-like mind shining. Why then, admiring and loving these, do we call them beautiful? For they exist, and they are manifest, and never would he who sees them say anything other than that these are the truly existing things. <note>original: "τὰ ὄντως ὄντα" (Greek). A Platonic term for ultimate realities or Forms.</note> <margin>* such things</margin> What then are these truly existing things? They are beautiful. But reason still yearns to know: what is it that makes the soul lovable? What is that which shines forth upon all the virtues, like a light? Do you wish, then, by taking the opposites, <margin>B</margin> to compare the ugly things that happen to the soul? For perhaps it would contribute to what we seek, to see what the ugly is, and why <margin>C</margin> we call it so. Let the soul be ugly, then—unrestrained and unjust, full of many desires, and full of much turmoil in fears: because of cowardice, in envies, because of small-mindedness, thinking only those things which it thinks: mortal and base: crooked everywhere: a lover of impure pleasures: living the life of whatever it might suffer through the body: taking the ugly as something sweet. This very ugliness in it, shall <margin>D</margin> we not say it has come to it as an added evil, which has outraged it and made it impure, and thoroughly mixed it with much evil, no longer having a pure life, nor a pure sense, but by the mixture of evil, using a dim life, and mixed with much death, no longer seeing what a soul ought to see, no longer being permitted to remain in itself, by being dragged always toward the outside, and the downward, <margin>E</margin> and the dark? Being impure, I suppose, and being carried everywhere by attractions toward the things that fall upon the senses, having much of the body mixed in, being with much matter, and receiving it into itself, it has changed to another form by the mixture with the worse. Just as if someone were to fall into mud or filth, the beauty they had they no longer <margin>F</margin> *show forth; <margin>* show forth / display</margin> but they are seen as that very thing which they *received <margin>* wiped off / took on</margin> from the mud or filth. To this person, ugliness has come as an addition of a foreign nature, and it is a task for them, if they are to be beautiful again, to wash and cleanse themselves to be what they were. We would be speaking correctly, then, in calling a soul ugly by its mixture and blending and its leaning toward the body and matter. And this is ugliness for a soul: to be not pure, and not unmixed. Just as <margin>G</margin> gold is filled with earthy matter, which if someone takes away, gold is left behind, and it is beautiful, being isolated from other things, and being alone with itself. In the same way also the soul: being isolated from desires, which it has because of the body with which it associated too much, and being rid of the other passions...

<summary>Plotinus explores the nature of "intellectual beauty," arguing that virtues like justice and temperance are beautiful because they represent the soul's true, divine form. Ugliness is described not as an inherent trait, but as a pollutant caused by the soul's entanglement with the material body and base desires, comparable to gold being obscured by mud.</summary>

# BOOK SIX.
<note>original: LIBER SEXTVS. In early editions of the Enneads, this tractate was often numbered differently, though it is famously known today as Ennead I, Tractate 6, "On Beauty."</note>

...freed from its lower states: with those stains deleted which a familiarity with the body had previously imprinted: and thus left alone to itself, it has undoubtedly purged away all the ugliness absorbed from a nature foreign to its own.

<margin>
VI
How the soul, when it possesses virtue and beauty, becomes most like God.
</margin>

INDEED, as the ancient oracle <note>likely a reference to Plato's *Phaedo* or Orphic traditions</note> relates, temperance, courage, and even prudence itself, and altogether every virtue, is a certain purification. For this reason, the sacred mysteries rightly, though somewhat obscurely, prophesy that the unpurified soul lies in the mire among the dead in the underworld. For the impure soul, on account of its depravity, is a friend to filth; just as pigs, being dirty in body, delight in filth. For what else is true temperance <term>temperance|the Greek *sophrosyne*, meaning self-restraint or sound-mindedness</term> but to not indulge in corporeal pleasures, but to flee them as things that are neither pure nor belong to the pure?

Courage, moreover, is the lack of fear regarding death. For death is merely a certain separation of the soul from the body. But he does not fear this who desires to be alone <note>meaning the soul existing in its own pure state, independent of matter</note>. Furthermore, magnanimity <term>magnanimity|literally "greatness of soul," the virtue of being worthy of great things</term> is the contempt for mortal things. Finally, prudence is intelligence turning away from lower things and raising the soul to the things above. Therefore, the soul, once purified, becomes a Form <term>Form|an eternal, intellectual blueprint of reality</term>, and a Reason <term>Reason|the Greek *logos*, the ordering principle of the universe</term>, and is entirely incorporeal, intellectual, and wholly divine: from whence the fountain of beauty flows, and all such kindred things. Wherefore, the soul, being brought back into the intellect, progresses wonderfully in beauty. But the intellect and whatever flows from the intellect becomes the soul's own beauty, not something foreign; since only then is it truly a soul.

It is rightly said, then, that the good and the beautiful for the soul consist in becoming like God: because from Him comes the soul's beauty and the shared lot of all truly existing things. Or rather, that which is called both Being and beings is beauty itself. But the nature that is different is ugliness, the primary evil; and therefore that same thing is the Good and the Beautiful. Perhaps, indeed, the Good and Beauty are the same thing. Therefore, the beautiful and the good should be sought by a similar path, as should the ugly and the evil.

At the first level, beauty itself must be placed, which is clearly the same as the Good itself; from which the Intellect flows immediately as something beautiful. The soul, however, is beautiful through the Intellect; but other things are beautiful because they are formed by the soul, whether they are found in actions or in studies and duties. Now, whatever bodies are called beautiful are made so by the soul, which, being a divine thing and a portion of beauty itself, makes whatever it touches and overcomes beautiful, according to the capacity of their nature.

<margin>
VII
The soul, having driven away its passions like clouds, turns toward the light of intellectual beauty and is filled with an inexpressible pleasure.
</margin>

WE MUST ASCEND, therefore, back to the Good itself, which every soul desires. If anyone has known it, they know what I mean, and in what way it is beautiful. For it is desirable as the Good, and our desire tends toward it. But those reach it who climb to the higher realms and turn toward it, stripping off the garments we put on as we descended. Just as those who enter the inner sanctum of the temples are first purified, and strip off their clothes, and proceed naked, until someone, moving forward and leaving behind all that is foreign to God, might see with himself alone the Divine itself—sincere, simple, and pure, upon which all things depend: toward which they look, and are, and live, and think. For He is the cause of life, and mind, and being.

<summary>Plotinus defines the classical virtues as forms of spiritual purification that allow the soul to strip away material "filth" and return to its divine origin. He concludes by describing the soul's ascent to the "Good," a journey compared to entering a sacred temple where one must be stripped of everything non-divine to see the One.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s discourse on Beauty from Ennead I, Book 6. Having previously discussed how the soul must be purified through virtue to see its own internal light, Plotinus now describes the ecstatic experience of encountering the "Source" of all beauty and warns against the trap of physical reflections, famously alluding to the myth of Narcissus.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK I

<column-break/>

->A<- Therefore, whoever has seen this—by Jupiter! <note>original: "proh Iupiter"; a Latin exclamation of amazement</note>—with what love are they inflamed, with what longing do they burn, desiring vehemently to be united in one with it: how wonderfully do they mingle pleasure with awe. For it is so ordained by nature that he who does not yet see it desires it as a "Good," but he who already sees it delights in it as "Beautiful," and is filled equally with admiration and pleasure. He is struck by a certain healing wonder, affected by a true and supreme love, and laughs at those sharp passions and other loves he once felt, despising what were previously considered beautiful things. ->B<- This indeed almost happens to those who, when they have encountered the forms of gods or spirits <term>spirits|the Latin "daemonum" refers to Greek "daimones," intermediary divine beings, not "demons" in the modern sense</term>, no longer value the forms of other bodies. What then do we think he will do who has contemplated Beauty itself? That Beauty, I say, which is pure in itself: not weighed down by flesh or any other body: not confined by earth or heaven: so that it exists purely as itself. ->C<- For indeed, all these other things are additions and mixtures, and therefore not primary, but proceeding from it. If someone, therefore, should ever behold that which provides gifts to all things, yet remains meanwhile within itself while it gives, receiving nothing from any other, and should remain fixed in that intuition—and enjoy it so much as to become like it—what further beauty could they possibly need? For since that is the chief and primary Beauty itself, it makes its lovers beautiful and lovely. ->D<- Here indeed is the greatest and ultimate contest proposed for souls, for the sake of which we must labor entirely, lest we be left without a share of that best contemplation. Whoever attains it is blessed with a happy vision; on the contrary, he who does not follow it is unhappy. For a man is not wretched because he does not possess beautiful colors or handsome bodies, nor because he fails to achieve power or a kingdom; he is wretched only if he lacks the possession of this one thing, for the sake of which alone it is right to cast away kingdoms and empires ->E<- of the whole earth, the sea, and the heavens: if, leaving all these behind and despising them, one turns and looks upon it.

<margin>
VIII
How the soul may see Beauty.
</margin>
What then is the way? What "machine" or method is there? By what reasoning may one contemplate this inestimable Beauty—a Beauty, I say, established in the sacred inner sanctuaries <note>original: "sacris adytis"; the "adyton" was the innermost chamber of a Greek temple where only priests could enter</note>, not coming outside lest some profane person behold it? ->F<- Let him, therefore, who is able, enter and proceed into the inner depths, leaving behind the sight of the eyes and not looking back at the accustomed spectacles of the senses. For he who looks upon this must not look at corporeal beauty any longer, but recognizing these bodily things as mere images, traces, and shadows, he must flee entirely to that of which these are the likenesses. ->G<- For if anyone rushes toward these physical things as if grasping for the truth—things which appear as beautiful images in water—he will undoubtedly suffer what (as the fable tells) that man suffered who, striving to catch a shadow, plunged into the water and perished <note>This is a clear reference to the myth of Narcissus, used here as an allegory for the soul drowning in the material world</note>. For in the same way, he who embraces the forms of bodies and does not depart from them is cast down—not so much in body as in soul—into the dark depths, horrible to the mind: where, remaining blind both among the dead in the underworld and here on earth, he will dwell among shadows. Here, therefore, it is more true to say: "Let us flee to our beloved fatherland." <note>Plotinus is quoting Homer's *Iliad* (2.140), interpreting the "fatherland" as the divine realm from which the soul originated</note>

<column-break/>

->A<- If someone should see this, what loves would they have, what longings, wishing to be *mingled with it <margin>*To be mingled.</margin>, and how would they be struck with pleasure! For it is not that he who has not yet seen it reaches for it as the Good; rather, he who has seen it rejoices in it as the Beautiful, and is filled with wonder together with pleasure, and is struck without harm, and loves with a true love and sharp longings, and laughs at other loves, and ->B<- despises those things previously thought beautiful. This is what those experience who, having met with the forms of gods or spirits, would no longer accept the beauties of other bodies in the same way. What then do we think if someone should behold Beauty itself, pure by itself, not full of flesh or body, not on earth, nor in heaven, but pure? ->C<- For all these things are accidental and mixed, and not primary, but from that. If then one should see that which supplies to all, but remaining in itself gives and receives nothing, and remaining in the vision of such a thing, and enjoying it, being made like it, <unclear>what would</unclear> he still need of beauty? For this itself, being especially Beauty and the First, makes its lovers beautiful and makes them lovely. There also ->D<- the greatest and ultimate struggle lies before souls; indeed, all their labor is for this: not to be without a share of the best vision, which he who attains is blessed, having seen a blessed sight; but he is unfortunate who does not attain it. For he is not unfortunate who does not attain beautiful colors or bodies, nor power, nor office, nor he who does not attain a kingdom, but he who misses this and this alone—for the sake of the attainment of which one must not spare kingdoms and ->E<- offices of the whole earth, and sea, and heaven, if by leaving these behind and looking over them, one might turn toward it and see.

What then is the way? What the device? How shall one behold the "un-device-able" beauty <note>original: "kallos amēchanon" - a play on words; "amēchanon" means "ineffable" or "beyond reach," but shares a root with "mēchanē" (device/machine)</note> which remains within the holy sanctuaries and does not proceed outside, so that even the profane may see? Let him who can, go and ->F<- follow into the interior, leaving outside the sight of the eyes, not turning himself back to the former splendors of bodies. For seeing the beauties in bodies, one must not run toward them, but knowing they are images and traces and shadows, flee to that of which these are images. For if one runs to them, wishing to seize them as true—as if they were a beautiful image riding on water, which someone wishing to seize (as a certain ->G<- myth, I think, enigmatically tells) sank into the bottom of the stream and disappeared—in the same way, he who holds onto beautiful bodies and does not let go will sink, not in body but in soul, into dark and unpleasant depths for the mind, where remaining blind in Hades, he will be with shadows both here and there. Let us flee then to our "dear fatherland," as one might more truly exhort.
