<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of Beauty in Ennead I, Book 6. Following the previous page's warning about being trapped by physical reflections (the Narcissus myth), Plotinus now shifts to the practical "ascent" of the soul, using the journey of Odysseus and the metaphor of the sculptor to explain how one must purify the self to see the Divine.</meta>

# BOOK SIX

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> What then is this flight? And how shall we ascend, just as Odysseus is said to have escaped from the sorceress Circe or from Calypso <note>original: "μάγου κίρκης, ἢ καλύψους"; Plotinus uses these figures from Homer's Odyssey as symbols of the soul being trapped by worldly or sensual charms</note>? He was not content to stay, even though he had pleasures for his eyes and lived with great sensory beauty. Our fatherland is the place from which we came, and our Father is there. What then is this journey and this flight? We do not need to travel it on foot, for feet only carry us from one place on earth to another. <margin>B</margin> Nor do you need to prepare a chariot of horses or a vessel for the sea; rather, you must let all these things go. Do not look with your physical eyes, but instead, as if closing them, exchange your vision for another kind and awaken it—a vision which everyone possesses, but which few actually use.

What then does that inner eye see? When it is newly awakened, it is not yet able to look upon very bright objects. Therefore, the soul must be trained. First, look at beautiful pursuits; then at beautiful works <margin>C</margin>—not the works produced by the arts, but those performed by men who are called "good." Next, look into the soul of those who perform these beautiful works. How then can you see the kind of beauty a good soul possesses? <margin>* and therefore</margin> Return into yourself and look. If you do not yet see yourself as beautiful, then act like a sculptor of a statue that must be made beautiful: he cuts away one part, polishes another, makes this line smooth and that one pure, until he has revealed a beautiful face upon the statue. In the same way, you must cut away whatever is excessive, straighten whatever is crooked, and purify whatever is dark to make it bright. Do not stop "carving" your own statue until the <margin>D</margin> god-like splendor of virtue shines out upon you, and until you see Temperance <term>Temperance|In Greek, 'sophrosyne'; a state of self-control and inner harmony</term> standing firmly upon its holy pedestal.

If you have become this, and have seen it, and have communed purely with yourself—having no obstacle <margin>E</margin> toward becoming one in this way, and having nothing else mixed within you, but being entirely yourself, a true and solitary light, not measured by magnitude or limited by a shape that diminishes it, nor expanded into a vastness through lack of limit, but everywhere unmeasurable, as being greater than all measure and superior to all quantity— <margin>F</margin> <margin>* if it has become</margin> if you see that you have become this, you have now become Sight itself. Take courage in yourself; you have already ascended and no longer need a guide. Look intently, for only this eye can behold the Great Beauty. But if the eye goes to the vision clouded by vices, and not <margin>* cowardice</margin> purified, or weak <note>original: "ἀνανδρίᾳ"; literally "unmanliness" or lack of courage/strength</note> through its inability to see very bright things, it sees nothing, even if someone else points out a spectacle that is present and capable of being seen. For <margin>G</margin> that which sees must be made kindred and similar to that which is seen before it can apply itself to the vision. An eye would never see the sun unless it had first become sun-like <note>original: "ἡλιοειδὴς"; a famous Plotinian concept that "like knows like"</note>; nor can a soul see Beauty unless it has become beautiful. Therefore, let everyone first become god-like and beautiful if they intend to behold God and Beauty. For first, in his ascent, he will come to the Intellect.

<column-break/>

Fleeing to our sweet fatherland. What then is the manner of flight? And by what way shall we avoid the enchantments of Circe and Calypso? This is indeed what the story of Odysseus signifies, albeit through a clouded myth: it depicts him as unwilling to remain, even though spectacles pleasing to the eyes were before him, and other things which delight the senses were promised. But our Fatherland is there, from whence we came, and our Father is in that same place. What then is this fleet, and what is this flight? Truly, we must not flee on foot. For feet carry us only from one land to another. Nor again should we prepare horses for carrying us, nor ships for sailing for this purpose; rather, we must dismiss all these things and not even look toward them. Instead, with the eyes of the body closed, we must assume and awaken another vision in its place. This is a vision which all men have, but very few use.

<margin>IX. How the soul may reach true beauty, and what that beauty is.</margin> WHAT THEN does that innermost eye behold? Truly, having just been awakened, it cannot at first look upon very bright things. The soul must therefore be accustomed first to consider beautiful studies, then beautiful works—works, I say, not those made by the manual arts, but those performed by upright men. After these, you must inspect the soul of those who perform such things. By what means then shall you inspect the beauty of a good soul? Come, call yourself back into yourself and contemplate. And if you do not yet recognize yourself as beautiful, imitate the sculptor. For he, when he desires a beautiful statue, cuts away part, straightens another, and by polishing scrapes away, and by smoothing wipes clean, until he expresses a fair face in the statue. In this way, you also: take away what is superfluous, straighten the crooked, purify the dark to make it shine; and do not cease working on your statue until the divine glow of virtue shines forth upon you, until you discern Temperance sitting firmly in pure and holy majesty.

If you have emerged as this very thing, and have seen it and yourself together, and now dwell purely within yourself, having no impediment to being thus made one: nor again having anything else mixed within you, but being yourself entirely a true and solitary light—a light, I say, not measured by magnitude, nor circumscribed by some confining shape, nor swollen in magnitude (though immense), but immeasurable everywhere, as being greater than every measure and superior to every quantity—if, I say, you see yourself having become this, having now become Sight itself, and being confident in yourself, and having progressed so far that you no longer need a leader or a pointer: fix your gaze now directly. For only this eye beholds the vast beauty. But if perchance the eye is infected with filth and not yet purged, or is weak through sloth when it is directed toward the most lucid spectacle, it will immediately grow dim and discern nothing, even if someone should point out a spectacle that is otherwise able to be seen. For it is necessary that the one who is to see be first made kindred and similar to the thing seen, before he may be applied to the beholding. Neither indeed would the eye ever see the sun, unless it had become solar in nature. Nor again will the soul behold Beauty itself, unless it has been made beautiful. Therefore, let everyone become divine, or god-like and beautiful, if he is to behold God and Beauty. For thus, first, he will ascend into the Mind.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus, specifically expanding on the nature of the Good, the One, and the soul's relationship to life and death. It follows the discussion of how the soul must transcend physical beauty to find the source of all beauty.</meta>

### COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...of evil, yet evil itself (if it is even right to speak of "evil" itself) is forced under the immense empire of the Good to desire the good <note>original: "consuepiscere bonum"; literally to grow accustomed to or seek the good</note> and to be named "good." The third gift of the Good is *form* <note>original: "species"; referring to the specific intelligible shape or "look" of a thing</note>. For this is a certain determination, or distinction, or the actual expression of essence. But when you hear here that the gift of the One and the Good is spread more widely than the gift of "being" and "essence," conclude that the One and the Good themselves are higher than being. Furthermore, as unity, essence, and form are found in things, so too is their participation in the Good. Truly, in the **First Mind** <note>the Divine Intellect</note>, in other minds, and in animals endowed with reason, there is a true participation in the Good because there is true unity, essence, and form. For though unity in these higher beings allows for a certain multitude, it nevertheless creates a true "one" there because it overcomes that multitude and renders the result an indissoluble unity. Therefore, there is also true essence there, since it can never "not be." There is also true form, since the form there cannot be dissolved into something formless. However, in lower things, the soul and its unity are often overcome by multitude, and therefore they can mostly be dissolved; in their essence there is a certain deprivation and a slide toward "not-being." Here, form is mixed with a subject that is utterly formless <note>referring to prime matter</note> and sinks into it. For this reason, there is no true "one" in these things, no true essence, and no true form; therefore, there is no true portion of the Good, but only an imaginary one.

->Just as life is not simply a good in itself, but is good if it is directed toward the highest principle,<-
->and evil if toward matter: so death is not simply and purely<-
->an evil; indeed, if it separates the soul from evil (that is, from matter), it is a good.<-

III **The third chapter brings three questions to the center.** The first is this: If life is a good, is living a good for anyone and everyone, regardless of how they live? Certainly not. For life itself is not the "first good" simply in its own right, but only insofar as it powerfully and directly rises toward the First Good itself does it emerge as a "perfect life." But wherever it limps or wanders, falling away from the Good, it simultaneously degenerates from the perfection of life. Hence that saying of **Democritus**: *To live without wisdom, without self-control, and without piety is not so much a "bad life" as it is a "long death."* 

The second question: Since life, insofar as it is mixed with what is mortal and thereby disturbed, becomes a kind of evil for the soul (even if it is a "good" for the body and the universe), is not death an evil, given that what is mortal makes life evil by its proximity? In responding, we must ask: For whom is death an evil? Certainly, since evil is either an "accident" <note>a non-essential property</note> or even weaker than an accident, it cannot exist by itself and must happen to someone. But it does not happen to that which does not exist at all, or to that which can by its nature exist without life. Again, it does not happen to the soul if the soul is immortal; and in whatever other way it might happen, it will benefit the soul to perform its own specific actions more perfectly and eternally without the hindrance of the body. But if the soul, after the death of the body, performs not only its own specific actions but also shared actions—acting as a colleague of the universal life <note>original: "universa vita"</note>—then even less could any evil happen to it there. On the contrary, for a soul that is gravely ill with "disturbances" <note>original: "perturbationibus"; the passions or emotional storms of the mind</note>, whether here or in the underworld, death is actually to be wished for, and life is the evil. This solves the question of whether those who are utterly miserable would prefer to die rather than live. Nature undoubtedly teaches this: those who are severely tormented, as nature warns, prefer to lose their senses rather than feel such dire pains. Finally, since the soul has its own life and is, through its essence, a kind of life living in itself, it neither borrows life from elsewhere nor undergoes death. If, however, one defines "living" as being joined to the body and "dying" as being separated from it, then both happen to the soul in that sense, but neither will properly change its substance. 

The third question: If life is good, why is death not evil? He responds that death is not simply an evil because life is not simply a good. For life is judged to be like a kind of "motion"; and any motion, whatever it may be, must be named after the end-point toward which it properly tends. Therefore, insofar as this vital motion happens to fall toward evil—that is, toward matter—it is judged to be evil. But insofar as it directs itself toward the Good—that is, toward the highest principle of the universe—it is judged to be a good.

<meta>catchword: PLOTINUS</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains that life's value is not intrinsic but depends on whether the soul is oriented toward the Divine Good or toward material decay. He argues that death is not an inherent evil, especially if it liberates a virtuous or suffering soul from the limitations and "disturbances" of the physical body.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the general discussion of the soul’s ascent to a specific investigation of the nature of the "Primary Good." It translates the beginning of Ennead I, Book 7, where Plotinus defines the Good in relation to life, activity, and the source of all things.</meta>

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD I
### BOOK VII

->**On the Primary Good and Other Goods.**<-

Can anyone say that the "good" for each individual being is anything other than the activity of its life according to its nature? Furthermore, if a being is composed of many parts, its good would be the activity of its better part—an activity that is its own, always in harmony with its nature, and never failing in any way. Thus, the activity of the **Soul** <note>the vital, animating principle of a person</note> according to its own nature is its good. But if the soul should act toward that which is "best" (since the soul itself is of the highest rank), then this is not only its own personal good, but it exists as Good in an absolute sense. Therefore, if there is something that does not act toward any other thing—because it is itself the most excellent of all beings, and indeed beyond all beings—while all other things act toward it, it is clear that this must be the Good itself. It is through the power of this Good that all other things are participants in goodness. These other things possess goodness in two primary ways: first, because they are made in its likeness; and second, because their activities are directed toward it. 
<margin>in this way</margin>
Consequently, if desire and action are directed toward the "best" as their goal, it follows that the Good itself does not look toward anything else, nor does it desire anything else. Rather, it is the still, quiet source and the origin of all actions that happen according to nature; it is what makes other things "good-like" <note>original: "agathoide" (Greek) / "bona" (Latin); sharing the character of the Good</note> through their activity toward it. For it does not make them good by any action of its own toward them, but rather because they act toward it. Thus it is clear that the Good exists as such neither by intelligence nor by any action at all, but simply by its very self. For since it stands above essence <note>original: "epekeina ousias"; a famous Platonic phrase meaning "beyond being" or "beyond substance"</note>, it likewise exists above action, and above intellect and thought. Furthermore, one must assert that the Good is that upon which all things depend, while it depends on nothing else. In this way, the saying is true: "The Good is that which all things desire." It must, therefore, remain fixed in itself, while turning all things back toward itself, just as a circle revolves around a center from which every line is drawn. We can use the Sun as an example: it is like a center for the light that depends upon it and is joined to it. For this reason, the light exists everywhere along with the sun and is never cut off from it. Even if you tried to cut it off on one side, the light remains held by the sun.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>The proper good for each is desire, and by acting they are turned toward it; the good of the universe is good not by any action, but by its very self.</margin>

Can anyone say that the good for each being is anything other than the natural activity of its life? And if a thing is composed of many parts, is its good not the activity of its better part—an activity that is proper, natural, and never failing? Thus, the
<margin>B</margin>
activity of the Soul according to its nature is its good. But if it acts toward the "best," being itself the best of things, then that is not only a good for the soul, but it is Good in the absolute sense. If, then, there is something that does not act toward anything else—because it is the most excellent of all things and beyond all things—while all other things act toward it, it is certain that this is the Good, by whose virtue all other things are
<margin>C</margin>
partakers in goodness. Other things possess the good in two main ways: by being made similar to it, and by acting toward it. Therefore, if desire and action are toward the "best," it follows that the Good itself does not look toward another, nor does it wish for anything else. It is the source, the quiet and still principle of all natural actions; it is that which makes other things "good-like" <note>sharing the form of the Good</note>. It does this, I say, not by any action toward them, but because
<margin>D</margin>
they act toward it. It is therefore clear that the Good exists as such neither by intelligence nor by any action whatsoever, but by itself alone. For because it stands above essence, it also exists above action, intellect, and intelligence. Furthermore, we must call the Good that to which all things are referred, while it is referred to nothing else. Thus the saying is true: "The Good is what all things desire." It must, therefore, remain firmly in place and
<margin>E</margin>
turn all things toward itself, just as a circle revolves around a center from which each line is produced. The Sun can serve as an example for us: it is like a center for the light that depends on it and is joined to it; therefore, the light exists everywhere with the sun and is nowhere separated from it. Even if you wanted to separate it on one side, the light meanwhile remains powerful within the sun.

<summary>In this opening of Ennead I.7, Plotinus defines the "Supreme Good" not as an active or thinking being, but as a static, perfect source (the One) toward which all life naturally gravitates. He uses the metaphors of a circle's center and the sun's light to explain how all things depend on the Good without the Good needing to act upon them.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Ennead I, Book 7, specifically moving from the definition of the Primary Good to how all other things participate in it, and whether life or death can be considered "good" or "evil" for the soul.</meta>

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD I
### BOOK VII

<margin>
II. In all things there is something of the Good itself: unity, essence, and form; and where these three are truly present, there too is the true Good.
</margin>

->A<-
But in what way do all other things relate to the Good? Inanimate things are certainly traced back to the **Soul** <note>the animating principle of life</note>, and the Soul is traced back to the **Good** itself through the **Intellect** <note>original: "intellectum" / "νοῦ" (nous); the divine mind or pure reason</note>. Indeed, everything possesses something of the Good, insofar as each thing is in some way "one" and "a being," and shares in a **Form** <note>original: "species" / "εἴδους"; the eternal blueprint or ideal shape of a thing</note>. Therefore, by the same logic that things participate in these qualities, they also participate in the Good; however, they participate only as an **image** <note>original: "simulachri" / "εἴδωλα"; a reflection or shadow of the true reality</note>. For those things which participate in it are considered mere images of Being and Unity, and their Forms are the same.

->B<-
But in the primary soul, which is closest to the Intellect, to live is closer to the truth; it attains the character of the Good through the Intellect. It attains it, I say, if it receives the Good itself; for the Intellect holds its seat immediately after the Good. For this reason, life is the "good" to be achieved by those to whom living is granted; similarly, intellect is the good for those to whom intelligence belongs. Thus, wherever life flourishes together with intellect, the Good is present in a twofold way.

<margin>
III. Three questions concerning life and death, and the solution showing that neither is simply good or evil in itself.
</margin>

->C<-
Now, if life is a good, does it perhaps belong to every living thing? On the contrary, it does not: for life is "lame" in the wicked, just as it is in an eye that does not see clearly, since it by no means performs its proper work. Furthermore, if life is a "good" for us only insofar as it is a mixture of good and evil, why should death not be an evil? But to whom would it be an evil? For evil must happen to someone who exists. But that which is called "dead" no longer exists; or if it does exist, it lacks life, and thus is no more an evil to it than it is to a stone. 

->D<-
But if life and the soul continue after death, then death would surely be a good, especially since the soul performs its actions without the body. And if the soul joins the **Universal Soul** <note>the soul of the cosmos</note>, what evil could possibly happen to a living being there? Just as the Good exists among the gods without any mixture of evils, so nothing is evil for the soul, provided it preserves its purity. If it does not preserve it, then it is not death that is an evil for the soul, but rather life itself. Furthermore, if punishments are paid in the underworld, life there is again an evil for the soul, because it is not merely life <note>original: "non vita solùm"; implying it is a life of suffering</note>.

->E<-
Truly, if life is the coupling of the soul and the body, and death is their dissolution, the soul is capable of undergoing both. But if life is good, why is death not an evil? Certainly, life is good for those in whom the Good is present—not because of the coupling itself, but because it drives away evil through **Virtue** <note>original: "virtutem" / "ἀρετῆς"</note>. Death is, in fact, the greater good. In summary, one must say that life in the body is itself an evil; however, the soul is established in the Good through virtue—not by preserving and animating the composite <note>the human combination of body and soul</note>, but by already separating itself from commerce with the body.

<column-break/>

->Α<-
But how do all other things relate to it? Either inanimate things relate to the soul, and the soul to it [the Good] through the mind. Each thing has something of it, by being in a way one and in a way a being, and it also participates in form. As it participates in these, so it does in the Good, being therefore images—of which it participates—being images of the one and of the form likewise.

->Β<-
For the soul, living—at least for the primary soul after the mind—is closer to truth and through the mind; this soul is good-form <note>original: "ἀγαθοειδὲς" (agathoeides); having the form of the Good</note>. It would have the Good if it looks toward that; for mind is after the Good. Life, therefore, is the good for that to which life belongs, and likewise for that which participates in mind. Thus, for that which has life with mind, the Good is present in a double way.

->Γ<-
If life is a good, does this belong to every living thing? Or is life "lame" for the wicked, just as for an eye not seeing clearly. For if it does its own work [it is good], but if life for us is a mixed evil and good, how is death not an evil? Or to whom? For evil must be an attribute of a being. But that which is not a cause of being, or if it is deprived of life, like a stone. <margin>* it is</margin> * Is evil for the stone? But if there is life and soul after death, it would already be a good, insofar as it acts more in its own ways without a body.

->Δ<-
But if it becomes part of the whole, what evil could be there? And in general, just as there is good for the gods, but no evil, so it is for the soul that preserves its own purity. But if it should not preserve it, death would not be an evil for it, but life, because it is not [true] life. And if there are judgments in Hades, again this life there is an evil, not just the lack of life.

->Ε<-
But if life <gloss>is</gloss> the meeting of soul and body, and death is the dissolution of these, the soul is receptive of both. But if life is good, how is death not evil? Or <margin>* what kind</margin> * life is good such as it is good, not according to the meeting, but because it wards off evil through virtue. But death is more of a good. Or it must be said, that life in the body is an evil by itself; but by virtue the soul comes to be in the good <margin>* or the one living</margin> * not by saving the composite, but by already separating itself.

<summary>Plotinus argues that everything participates in the Good through unity and form, though life in the body is often a "lame" or diluted version of true Good. He concludes that death is not an evil, but rather a potential good that allows the soul to operate in its pure state, free from bodily corruption.</summary>

# MARSILIO FICINO
## ARGUMENT ON BOOK VIII: WHAT EVILS ARE, AND WHENCE THEY COME.
### Four questions concerning good and evil.

This entire book seems to be concerned with how we might avoid evils to the best of our strength and pursue goods: that is, how we may flee from **matter** <term>materia; in Neoplatonism, the physical world or "stuff" that lacks form and is the furthest point from the divine</term> and follow divine things separated from matter. It teaches us to recognize that the very principle of the universe is the Good itself, but the lowest point of the universe—that is, matter—is evil itself. It explores how evil affects us and by what means we might finally avoid it. The first chapter of the book raises these questions: What things are evil, and from where do they proceed? To find this, the author inquires into what things are good; and to find this in turn, he sets out to track down what the Good itself is, or what evil is. He asks how we can know evil, since, because of its weakness, it is entirely foreign to the very **form** <note>original: "forma"; the internal structure or essence that gives a thing its identity</note> of the knowing soul. He teaches that the "formlessness" of evil is discerned through the form and light of the Good itself. Finally, he asks in what way evil is the contrary of good—whether, perhaps, as the ultimate end of the universe is to the first, or as a total lack is to the greatest abundance. Regarding his statement that <note>original: "vim cognituram esse rei cognoscendæ persimilem"</note> "the power of knowing is very similar to the thing to be known," understand this to mean a similarity both in its nature and in a certain effect. For there is no reason why sight should hunger for and recognize light rather than a voice, except because it naturally agrees with light more than with sound, and conforms itself to light more than to the other. Truly, because the senses in perceiving things seem only to touch the external aspects, while the **intellect** <note>the higher, divine part of the mind</note> penetrates even to the innermost parts, it is clear that the intellect agrees with the intelligible and divine more than the senses agree with the sensible and fleeting. From this, a more certain argument can be held by us: that the intellect is divine, just as the senses are fleeting. Furthermore, regarding his claim that the perfect necessarily precedes the imperfect, and that form is prior to privation, take care not to understand this in our physical order of generation—where things are first begun and imperfect, then gradually acquire the perfection of form—but rather accept it in the universal order of things, causes, and degrees. There, whatever is imperfect, since it cannot exist or be preserved by itself, depends on a higher and more perfect thing which exists and is preserved by itself. Indeed, since that higher cause is **act** <term>actus; the state of being fully realized or active</term> and form and species in itself, it rightly leads the formless subject (which is powerless to form itself) through appropriate stages toward its forms. Since an agent acts through its own nature, it renders its effect similar to itself; and as the subject itself is led to form and act by higher agents, we conclude that higher causes exist as forms and acts within themselves.

->The universe has a beginning and an end, and that end is the Good itself; likewise, the intellect, both human and<-
->divine, is always in act; although human reason<-
->proceeds from potentiality into act.<-

**II** In the second chapter, he signifies what the Good itself is, and designates how far the "parts" of the Good proceed. He says that the Good is the principle and the end of the universe: where the Good depends on nothing, but all things depend on it; likewise, it is the measure and the limit of all things. You, however, must remember that whenever the parts achieve their end—that is, their natural perfection—the whole which the parts serve also achieves its end. When the eyes see clearly, when the hands promptly grasp something, when the feet walk with the greatest speed, they possess their own purpose. Much more so does the whole body eventually enjoy its natural perfection. Just as these parts of the body relate to the whole body, so do the parts of human life relate to the whole of life. By "parts of life," we mean for the moment our choices, faculties, and all the arts. Individual choices and arts have a certain "extreme" or ultimate point by which they are rightly perfected, beyond which they require nothing more. Thus, medicine has health as its extreme, and military affairs have victory. Just as the parts of life achieve their own ends, so much more does the whole of life look toward a certain final common good, by which it is at last perfected, so that the whole life is more perfect than its parts. Similarly, as in man, one may argue in other species of animals and all things. For natural appetite is a certain necessary inclination of nature, striving from a state of indigence toward fullness; and "fullness" and the "ultimate end" are the same thing. If no ultimate end were prescribed for our seeking, but nature progressed from end to end without a final stop, it could never be sufficiently filled. Therefore, it would strive to be filled in vain—indeed, it would not even strive at all. For no species of thing is moved toward that which is entirely impossible. To be moved naturally is to progress gradually from a natural **potential** <note>original: "potentia"; the capacity to become something</note> into **act**. This natural progression, by whatever faculty it advances step by step, is eventually perfected when it reaches the final end. Otherwise, nature would everywhere struggle in vain, and the Author of nature himself would move it rashly and fruitlessly. Accordingly, if the species of things, which are parts of the universe, are not cheated of their own perfection, much less will fortune frustrate the striving of the universe itself. For the universe also strives toward a common end, since it constantly leads the parts toward their own ends (which serve the common end) and attains the ultimate end, lest the whole be more imperfect than its parts—whether the world is to reach such an ultimate end at some point, or is said to have already reached it in its present state. If, however, there were no "best" end, but it were imagined to proceed toward the "better" without any limit, certainly, since it cannot pass through infinite degrees, it could never arrive at the best. Therefore (and it is a sin even to say this), this universe, constructed undoubtedly with the best form, would strive toward the best end in vain. The end and the best state of the universe consists in this: that it be conformed in every way to its Principle and Author. For the fact that this collection of things in the world, so diverse and conflicting among themselves, both meets in one common form of the whole and leads rightly to one common good, does not proceed from the nature of the diverse things themselves, but rather from the single form and will of the higher Craftsman. Just as the world is formed under the "form" of its Author as its principle, so it is always being reformed and conformed to the same as its end. Plotinus names this Author of all things "the Good itself," because by Him this universe is both affected and perfected. From this, the measure of all things...

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...regards even the limit: just as Plato mentions in the *Philebus*. God measures all things as the beginning; he likewise limits all things as the end. If God is the measure of all things, then certainly the order of things does not ascend from a beginning to a beginning without some first principle of all. To think otherwise would be to wander through principles at random without any logic of a "beginning"; for the very logic of a **beginning** <note>original: "principium"</note> is that it must be first. By using God as our measure, we perceive that the intellect is better than the soul, and the soul better than the body: because the former is closer to God (as the highest good) than the latter. But if a first and highest goodness did not exist anywhere, and one were to imagine it proceeding through degrees into infinity, there would certainly never be any logic or rule of measurement by which one thing could be preferred over another; for things would not be closer or more in harmony with a measure. Therefore, let God be the beginning and the measure. Furthermore, let Him be the limit of all things, because He is the end. I say "limit" in the sense that He limits subjects by their forms, and limits the motions of forms by their proper ends, so that nature does not perhaps wander from end to end without a final stop. That would be nothing other than wandering through ends without any logic of an "end." The chief logic of an **end** <note>original: "finis"</note> is that it be the last and ultimate point.

After this, in the second degree of goods, he places **Essence** <term>essentia; the fundamental "being" or "is-ness" of a thing</term>, and within essence, the **Mind**. In the third degree, he places the **Soul**, and within the soul, **Life**. He says all these things are good because they are from the Good itself, and because they act around the Good by the power of the Good. In the fourth place of goods, he wishes to count only those forms of bodies which never depart from the soul, which itself never departs from God. Such things are the celestial bodies, or things similar to the celestial. To these he adds a difference between the divine intellect and the rational intellect: namely, that the divine is itself the fullness of all things, while the rational intellect strives to be filled from that source.

Therefore, when you hear here that our intellect is called "empty," do not take this to mean our simple intellect which is always filled by the divine; rather, take it to mean our rational intellect—that is, the power of the soul running through **universal species** <note>general concepts or categories</note>. This power is, in a way, the potentiality of the intellect and the "intelligible in potentiality"; it comes into "act" <note>the state of being fully realized or functioning</note> by the power of the superior intellect which always exists in act. I say this happens by the power of both the divine intellect and our own. For just as that which is all things simply in potentiality becomes all things in act through that which is simply all things in act (or as matter becomes through the divine mind), so too must this power, which is the human intellect in potentiality, become the human intellect in act through the human intellect that is always flourishing in act. This is much like how a human living in act is generated not only by universal nature (which holds the **seminal reasons** <term>rationes seminales; the "seeds" or formative principles that guide the growth of living things</term> of all animals reigning in act), but also by its own specific human nature, which possesses the seminal reason of "man" already flourishing in act. For the generation of perfect things requires this; and this is Plotinus’s opinion everywhere.

He adds that the divine intellect possesses all things in itself in such a way that it *is* all things. You may understand this by the following example: if all sorts of vessels of different shapes are submerged in the sea, the water will immediately fill them all, and in filling them, it will assume as many similar shapes as there are vessels to fill. Such shapes, however, will be nothing other than the water of the sea, adapting itself in different ways. Thus, the intellect is all the species it is thought to possess; and it is its own species much more truly than the sea water is those shapes. This is because no novelty, no dimension, and no distance hinders their union there; and also because it does not take on or produce these species from another or in another (as water does), but from itself and in itself, or rather, it exists as them. In what way the species are distinguished from one another in the mind, and yet all are in each one, we will discuss often elsewhere.

He adds that that which becomes a participant in the divine mind does not have all species flourishing in act at once; understand this to refer to the rational power, which is accustomed to becoming a participant in the divine mind at certain times. For the intellectual nature itself, even in us, does not become a participant only occasionally (as Plotinus maintains), but is always in possession of the divine mind. Furthermore, he calls the divine mind the "first act" of the Good itself and the "first essence." He does not want there to be any act in God through which God does something; otherwise, we would distinguish such an act from the very substance of God at least by some logic. Yet from the **Primary Unity** <note>the "One," the source of all things in Neoplatonism</note>, every difference and every number must be absent. He thinks, therefore, that the "act of God" itself is outside of God, just as light is outside a lamp. He believes God is of such great power that His act is not some motion or accident, but the first substance and essence. There, the "act" and the "thing acted upon" are the same—that is, the most full fountain of the essence of all things. Thus, while one thing seems to be made by the divine unity, all things are made together in that One. For rightly from the Unity which is above all things and regards all things equally and most closely, this One is made which is equally all things. Finally, he wants the act of essence itself around God to be His "Life," and the completion of life to be the "Mind."

He joins to this that the pure soul—through its own mind acting as an eye, and the divine mind acting as light—beholds the light of the Good itself; and up to this point, no evil occurs. If either the soul or nature itself stopped at this stage of descent, there would be no evil. However, the very fecundity of nature ensures that there are many further degrees of things below the soul and nature itself. Because the portion of good gradually diminishes as one descends step by step (for effects cannot equal their causes), one eventually arrives from a "lesser good" into evil.

As for his statement that all things are "around God," this means they are equally from God and toward God. Likewise, the first orders of things (the **Ideas**) are "around God," from whom they come into the mind and into whom they are reflected by the mind. The second orders (**rational notions**) are "around the second," that is, the intellect, from which they flow into the soul and flow back similarly. Further, the third orders (**seminal reasons**) are "around the third," that is, the soul, from which they flow into nature and flow back again into the soul. Finally, he wants the fourth orders to be understood as "around the fourth," that is, the **natural forms** around nature, from which they fall into matter, and into which they fall back according to their strength. All of this, I say, we have spoken of and will speak of more fully elsewhere.

->What is above being; what is true being; what is not true being; how far<-
->goods extend; where evils first appear; and in how many ways things are called evil;<-
->and many reasons why<-
->matter exists.<-

### Chapter 3 discusses what evil is, how many evils there are, and where they are. 

He denies that evil exists in that which surpasses all beings. For that is the Good itself. This is recognized to be "above beings" because the very nature of desiring and choosing does not only wish to exist in many ways, but also chooses many things *not* to be, *not* to have been, or *not* to be in the future; yet it always chooses under the reasoning of "the good." From this, it is clear that the "desirable"—that is, the Good—perhaps pertains not only to "being," but also to "non-being," and therefore the Good itself exists as something more common and higher than "being." However, because **Essence** is the first recipient of the Good, and thus the Good is derived through it into other things, it follows that as far as the true participation in essence extends, so far does a true portion of the good proceed. Up to this point, there are no evils; just as where true heat flourishes, cold is absent. But a true portion of essence extends all the way to the very substances of the spheres of the world, in whose essences no **privation** <note>the lack of a quality that should naturally be present</note> is found. In these, therefore, evils cannot exist.

# ON BOOK VIII. ENNEAD I.

Whatever is eventually dissolved among composite things <note>things made of multiple parts, such as physical bodies</note> is not called "truly being." This is because a long period of **privation** <note>original: "privatio"; a lack or absence of a quality that should naturally be present</note> preceded its existence, and a similar state follows it. Furthermore, the very path of its existence, as it passes through motion and time, possesses only a fleeting "present" moment of being; as far as "non-being" is concerned, it suffers a long past and a long future. Therefore, a composite of this kind, in which much privation of being is mixed, is called "not truly being," just as something is called "not truly hot" if a tiny amount of heat is mixed with a vast amount of cold.

Thus, evil befalls these things because that which is "not truly being" falls too far from the **First Essence** <term>essentia prima; the highest level of pure existence, often identified with God or the Divine Mind</term>. While it slips away from the lot of the Good, it is meanwhile cast headlong into evil. Truly, **evil itself** is that which is most distant from the Good: namely, the formless **matter** <note>original: "materia"</note> of the world itself. In the second place, evil is experienced as form or quality lying within matter, which is called a certain "passion" or "affection" of matter stirred up from the outside. In the third place, the **soul** admits evil insofar as it is inclined toward matter by a sharper affection. But there is this difference: matter can, in a sense, be called the "substance" of evil; composite things (made of matter and falling form) "suffer" evil within their substance; finally, the soul receives evil not in its substance, but as a certain quality or **accident** <note>original: "accidente"; a non-essential property that can change without destroying the subject</note>.

Among these points, Plotinus understands that which is called "non-being" in three ways. First, as **absolute non-being**, which is "nothing." Second, as **truly non-being**, which is the primary matter of the world. Third, as **not truly being**, which refers to form inherent in matter, the falling composite, and its properties and accidents. Furthermore, when he calls the "sensible universe" <note>the physical world perceived by the senses</note> "not true being," he refers primarily to everything **below the moon** <note>original: "sub luna"; the realm of change and decay in ancient cosmology</note>. He intends for **form**—which depends on and reflects the **Idea**—to be the "image" of being; but he considers **matter** to be the "shadow" of being. Matter does not depend on the Idea insofar as it is an Idea, but rather insofar as it is an essence capable of being formed through Ideas; likewise, matter does not represent the Idea. For no one looking closely into matter will ever suspect the specific "face" of any Idea there.

He says that matter must be judged as "non-being"—not indeed as "nothing," but as a "not-nothing" most distant from the First Being. He also says that form and the composite are distant from the First Being not only by that space occupied by "rest" and "motion" (which are placed in the First Being), but by a much greater distance. In what manner those five—**essence, motion, rest, the same, and the other**—exist in Being itself, we shall discuss elsewhere. Certainly, there, motion is not Being itself; otherwise, there would be no rest in things. Nor is rest Being itself; otherwise, nothing would ever move. Rather, they are different properties and acts of Being.

But for the present, he sets aside the properties of Being itself and approaches certain properties of "non-being," that is, of matter. These are opposed to those he numbered as properties of the Good. Therefore, he judges that matter should be named "evil itself," as it is most distantly at odds with the Good. The **Good** itself is **measure**; but matter (to use his words) is called **lack of measure**. Likewise, the Good is **limit**; matter is the **infinite** <note>original: "infinitum"; in this context, it means "unlimited" or "unbounded," which was viewed negatively as a lack of definition</note>. Furthermore, matter is formless, while the Good is the giver of form; matter is needy, while the Good is self-sufficient; and so on.

Yet, just as those properties of the Good are one and the same as the Good itself insofar as they are within the Good (though they seem to differ when compared to what follows them), so too the properties of matter are one with matter itself insofar as they are in matter. But when they are compared to higher things, they are judged as diverse—just as the points of lines are one at the center but many at the circumference. Then, in things composed between God and matter, there is a certain infinity and limit, a formlessness and a beauty. A composite thing is not identical to either of these opposites; otherwise, the thing would either lack one of them, or at least one would be the same as the other. For if this thing were "limit" itself, it would not have infinity; if it were "infinity," it would not have limit. Finally, if this thing were both this and that by itself, then both would remain the same. But the nature of things does not allow "limit and form" to be the same as their opposites, "infinity and formlessness."

Since all things mixed from opposites are not "perfectly" such things, they must be traced back to "simple" things that are most perfectly such. Therefore, above the form and limit which are mixed in "another," we must ascend to the **Form** and **Limit** which exist in themselves and are most pure. Conversely, beyond the formlessness and infinity which are joined to opposites in "another," we must descend to **Formlessness** and **Infinity** subsisting simply in themselves. Accordingly, when Plotinus says, "That which happens to others must first exist as something itself before it happens," he did not mean that it exists "in itself" or "by itself" before it happens so that you might believe an accident is a substance. But remember this: the heat which sometimes happens to water is reduced to the heat of fire (because it exists in another and belongs to it by accident). Although the heat of fire is also in "another," it is not said to be present by chance, but by nature. Finally, this heat is traced back to the **Idea of Heat** itself, which exists by itself and through itself. Thus, just as that which exists by accident is referred to that which exists according to nature, so that which lies in "another" is referred to that which consists in itself.

Finally, remember that evils happen to the forms of things, and not merely by chance; for they come in a continuous and perpetual series. Nor do they come from the nature of the **Form** itself (which ultimately proceeds from the First Form, the Divine Mind, in the way that the Mind is turned toward the Good). Therefore, know that evils flow from the outside, and indeed from a certain determined principle—certainly not a principle like a form or any sort of form. Therefore, they come from **matter**. Thus, matter is the **first evil**, just as goods come from the First Principle; therefore, that Principle is **the Good itself**.

The points above are confirmed again as follows: we see in the order of things that individual items are composed of a certain **potential** and **act**—that is, they are constituted from a "formable nature" and a "formal act." Those things which hold the middle ground of reality are duly mixed with an equal portion of both opposites. But above the middle of the universal order, the "formable potential" is gradually more and more exceeded by the "formal act." Conversely, toward the middle, the act decreases, and the potential for suffering and a "deformed nature" increases. For this reason, the increase of "act" through the most orderly degrees finally reaches the **highest and pure Act**. Its decrease descends gradually to the **minimum act of form**. This is soon succeeded by a certain "highest formlessness" and "suffering infinity," a nature entirely exposed to forms coming from above as measures and limits.

But meanwhile, notice this: just as the descent of this order passes beyond the minimum form into matter, so the ascent passes beyond the highest form (that is, Essence and the First Mind) to the **Good itself**. Conversely, just as something exists above Being (the Good itself), so something subsists at the very bottom—the **evil itself**, the medium between Being and nothing, which is entirely opposite to the Good. For the Platonists place matter as the middle between Being and nothing (or non-being); it is called "non-being" and yet "not-nothing." This matter, like a **common potential**, precedes the active universe in its origin and order of generation, just as the "potential to suffer" and the "act" itself similarly precede their own specific actions.

Since, however, matter always lacks support due to an extreme defect of power, and cannot rest on any lower foundation (for nothing is lower than it), it has obtained a support from above on which it hangs: namely, **Nature**. Similarly, Nature hangs from the Soul. Matter depends on the essence of Nature and from the very essence of the Mind. Forms generated in matter depend on the "seeds" of Nature and the "Ideas" of the Mind. Specifically, matter is like a shadow of the intellectual essence...

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...of nature; moreover, forms [act] as images of the mind itself and of the "seeds" <note>original: "seminum"; in Neoplatonism, "seminal reasons" are the formative principles that organize the physical world</note>. Indeed, matter seems to be held up from above, almost in the manner of a small hanging weight, just as iron is suspended by a magnet from above.

->Three levels of evils: how evil is in the soul, and how matter possesses nothing of the good.<-

IIII In the fourth chapter, Plotinus pursues the levels of evils. He places **matter** in the first level; in the second, he places the **corporeal form** of matter. Plotinus briefly indicates here—and we demonstrate more extensively in our *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his own major work, the *Platonic Theology*</note>—that this corporeal form is not a "true form." In the third level, he establishes the **evil of the soul**, saying: the soul itself is not evil by its own nature; otherwise, every soul would be evil, and it would be evil from the beginning and forever. He believes that the "secondary soul"—that is, the life occasionally granted to the body by the "primary soul"—becomes depraved immediately at the very beginning of this granting. For since it is so bound to the body that a single living creature is composed from it and the body, it is naturally infected by matter. Consequently, it becomes liable to passions and undergoes immoderate movements in both excess and deficiency, after the manner of the body.

The Platonists <note>The "Platonici" usually refers to the lineage of thinkers following Plato, especially Plotinus himself</note> believe that every such life becomes this way, though it might finally, with difficulty, be tempered at some point. However, before that moderation takes effect, they judge those passions to be involuntary, because they are clearly natural. They also believe the "higher soul"—because it willingly consents with the lower—receives false opinions from it. By these opinions, it judges without enough consideration that whatever the lower soul pursues or flees with a certain natural impulse will, in truth, be "good" or "evil" for itself as well. Just as the lower soul becomes evil by natural impulse, so the higher soul becomes evil through love, consent, and opinion.

But there is this difference between this lower life and the corporeal form: this form is a certain "passion" <note>In this context, a "passion" is something that happens to a subject, an impression received rather than an action performed</note> of matter, whereas "life" is rather an action or an act of the soul. Therefore, the evil of the form is incurable, but the evil of life is curable. 

Now, when he says that matter possesses "nothing of the good," understand this to mean nothing of a formal, intrinsic, or absolute good. Since the first effect of the Good itself is something **formal** <term>formalis; having to do with "Form," the divine blueprint or essence of a thing</term>—namely, the Divine Mind, the "Form of forms"—it follows that where the formal nature is absent, the intrinsic nature of the Good is also absent. But because matter is the "prime subject," equally exposed to all forms, it claims no form as its own, and thus nothing formal. To this matter, therefore, nothing of formal, intrinsic, or absolute good is proper. 

Yet, matter does not lack a "desire" for the good. For the "indigence" <note>a state of extreme lack or poverty</note> of matter is naturally most ready to receive formal abundance; therefore, it naturally desires this, and thus it yearns for the good. This desire can, in a certain way, be called "good"—not absolutely, but because it looks toward and leads to the good; to an **extrinsic** <note>originating from the outside</note> good, I mean. For that which is received never truly becomes the "property" of matter. Consequently, the effective principle from which the appetite and motion of matter toward the good is produced is not in matter itself (for there is no efficacy where there is no form), but in Nature, acting as the instrument of God. 

Nevertheless, such appetite and motion are not called "violent." For matter does not resist this pull; rather, it is most ready, suffers it most willingly, and is most easily formed. Finally, matter itself is evil because it is formless—or rather, because it is "formlessness" itself, it is Evil Itself. Yet, it can be called "good" in a certain way insofar as it is "formable" by the Good. 

Furthermore, because he often calls form a **limit** <note>original: "terminum"</note> and a **measure**, know that he calls it a "limit" because it terminates the nature of matter—which is equally indifferent to any shape—within certain boundaries of a species. For instance, through the "form of a man," it receives the species of a man; through the "form of a horse," it is narrowed to the species of a horse. He calls it a "measure" because matter, by its own nature, has no proper size or figure; but while a certain form limits it to a certain species, it imprints a certain proper size and figure. 

Just as the corporeal form is the measure and limit of matter, so the **intellectual form** is the measure and limit of the soul; and the Good itself is the measure and limit of the Mind and of all things. Finally, the soul which is turned toward the Mind through all its powers is composed by the Mind's measure and limit, and it receives or foresees nothing of evil. But the soul which departs from the Mind and proceeds with an inclination toward matter already foresees evil and is, as it were, "bewitched" <note>original: "fascinatur"</note> by a certain gaze. After it pours out the "seminal power" of its nature—as if it were an image of the higher soul—entirely into matter, it is then said to have "touched" evil. When it finally conceives a habit through which it sympathizes and consents with the suffering material body, it then seems to wither from a poisonous touch.

->In what defect evil consists: how matter is evil itself: how evil comes to be in the soul.<-

V The fifth chapter introduces and solves two questions. The first question is of this kind: It has been said that the rational power is an "imperfection" of the Mind and its image; similarly, the natural power is more imperfect than the rational, and its image. Is, then, such a defect—either here or there—evil? By no means. For evil does not consist in just any defect of the good, such as when something is found to be surpassed by an external and superior good and yields to it. For these are certain levels of goods arranged by Divine Providence. 

Rather, evil resides in a **proper defect**: when something is seen to be robbed of some good belonging to its own species or its unique gift. The "Supreme Evil" is measured by a **universal defect**, which by its own nature lacks the good of every species and is inwardly deprived of every formal gift. He says matter is of this kind, having no portion of the good—that is, no internal or proper portion. 

Since "Being" <term>ens; that which exists</term> receives the Good internally first, as if it were closest to the Good itself, an **intrinsic good** is rightly granted to things through the gifts of Being—namely, through **Essence** and **Existence** <term>essentiam et esse</term>. Matter, however, has no "existence" <note>original: "esse"</note> of its own, since it is not a form; nor does it have its own form. It exists, therefore, through the existence of a "substantial form," just as an "accidental form" <note>a secondary quality, like color</note> exists through the existence of a substance. Nor, again, does it have an "essence." For since the "First Essence" is something formal in itself (especially when compared to other essences), matter, which is nothing formal, is rightly said not even to be an essence. Nevertheless, it is in some way similar to essence, although it has nothing similar to "existence." 

Therefore, that in which there is some defect, of whatever kind, is not the Good itself. Where there is a defect falling away from a certain "proper good," there is already some evil. Where there is a total defect, there is **Evil Itself**, and that is matter. 

However, a defect degenerating from one's proper good—in which there is a potential and a proclivity that eventually falls into evil—is a worse defect than a simple lack of some good. For the latter constitutes a "lesser good," but the former constitutes "evil." For that proclivity, especially when already leaning, verges toward Evil Itself (which is already evil before the proclivity). And that proclivity in the soul, having become more prone at some point, is already evil even before the habit of "falling headlong" is confirmed. Now, the "first evil" of the soul is not this or that vicious habit, but the very proclivity that is too inclined toward matter, and the matter itself with which it is occupied—either by touching it with certain of its parts (namely, nature and the powers serving nature) or by being affected by it, namely by a certain...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, Book I, Book 8. Having previously discussed the levels of evil, Ficino now addresses the soul’s relationship to matter and explains why evil is a necessary consequence of the existence of the Good, drawing on Plato’s "Theaetetus" and "Timaeus."</meta>

...sometimes by the rational counsel choosing matter, sometimes by the command of the higher imagination; or by falling into matter—that is, through the affection of the lower imagination—or finally by suffering through the lowest sense. Indeed, since all things are judged to be of a certain kind according to something similar, insofar as they are referred simply to that "kind" itself, Plotinus rightly considers all things to be evil through some relation to matter (which is evil itself). This is true both in the soul, as has already been said, and in the body and external fortunes, which he shows next where he raises and solves the second question. He concludes from these points that the soul is not an evil principle, because it is not itself evil by nature; for it is an intellectual nature, and the intellect itself is closest to the Good. Indeed, the intellect turns toward the Good directly, and the soul turns toward it through the intellect.

Here he suggests that souls do not fall away from God through a deliberate purpose, as if they were rebels, but rather as a result of a contingent consequence—insofar as they are affected by matter and things that are material. Because of this, the soul is secretly turned away from God while it willingly turns toward the opposite. For if, in this wretched place of ours, the soul does not depart from a greater good into evil by some specific purpose, but rather under the appearance of a good, much less would a soul living outside this body choose an obvious evil over an obvious good. Therefore, he wants the beginning of the soul's evil to be "by accident" <note>original: "per accidens"; a philosophical term meaning something that happens as a side effect rather than by essence or direct intent</note>, insofar as it is inclined more favorably toward something of lesser good—that is, toward the service of generating life. Meanwhile, evil creeps in secretly, and sometimes it detains the soul against its will, both because the soul is struck by the unavoidable impulse of fate and is shut up in a prison for a long time, and because it does not know from the start what or how much damage follows from its affection for and habituation toward the body.

Plotinus thinks that only those souls will avoid evil in some way who, before the bodily habit is confirmed, recognize the danger and withdraw themselves entirely into the mind. Since not everyone is wicked, and since even some wicked people can eventually be reformed, it is clear that wickedness is not inherent in nature, nor should it be considered evil itself. Finally, he concludes that the soul avoids, repels, and overcomes the wickedness sprouting from matter (or rushing toward matter) only by that nature which is in the soul separate from matter, and which is therefore divine. Even though it is divine, because it is close to natural things, it gradually admits evil. However, it does not do so like a bodily form, which falls from its own good because it is both inherent in matter and mixed with a contrary form; thus, evil and destruction follow it. Instead, the soul seems to degenerate from its own specific good and admit evil because it enters into too much commerce with a lower nature. From this kind of companionship, worry and the hindrance of higher duties follow, rather than total destruction.

### How something may be contrary to the Good, namely matter; and how forms separated from matter are contrary.

VI The sixth chapter explains what Plato intends when he says in the book *On Knowledge* <note>Plato’s dialogue, the *Theaetetus*</note> that evils cannot be entirely destroyed. For there must necessarily be something "sub-contrary" to the Good, and evils themselves must dwell in mortal nature. Among these things, understand that there is no "contrary" to the Good in the proper sense, as if it were divided from the Good as an opposite within the same category. For the Principle of all things <note>God or the One</note> cannot belong to the same category as anything else, nor can it be distinguished from anything else by added differences. Rather, something is called "sub-contrary" to the Good because it is placed under the Good's command, being most distant from it and utterly unlike it—namely, the lowest matter of the world.

Furthermore, he teaches that among other contraries, it is not necessary that if one exists, the other must immediately exist. However, if the Good itself exists, its sub-contrary necessarily follows; that is, if the first principle of the universe exists, a certain lowest level of the universe is necessarily given. In this context, he accepts "contrariety" differently than most people, who define it as a conflict between two qualities in the same category (which would imply that substances are not contrary to one another and that contraries must be in the same category). Here, he wants contrariety to be the greatest possible distance between things everywhere, creating opposites and bearing opposites. Thus, matter will be sub-contrary to God. For matter is not "essence" <note>original: "essentia"</note>, while God is the principle of being. Matter is the origin of evils; He is the origin of goods. Matter is the cause of formlessness and deformity; He is the principle of forms. These two are much more contrary to each other than heat and cold or similar things. For these [God and matter] agree in nothing, while other contraries agree in category and matter. He adds that if fire and water preserved their "form" <note>their essential identity</note> after matter was removed from them, they would still be contrary to each other—specifically, the essence of water to the essence of fire. In that case, heat and cold would not only be essential properties but would also, in a way, be essences or acts of essence, most distant from each other and the causes of contraries in the universe. Likewise, no portion of one would then be present in the other, since the common matter would be lacking. Again, these two would differ by their whole selves and would be distant by their very "otherness," so to speak.

### How if the Good exists, it is necessary for evil to exist, and how the universe consists of matter and form, from mind and necessity.

VII After these things, in the seventh chapter, he shows why it is necessary that if the Good exists, evil will exist. Surely the work of the world made by God himself would never have been made into a present effect or act unless it had been possible for it to be made. Two things are therefore considered: the power (potency) and the act of being. These are contrary, or rather opposite, to each other. For by the reason that something already exists in act, it cannot be made further; and by the reason that it was able to be made, it was not yet in act. Likewise, potency is a kind of "starting point" from which the creation of the world proceeds, while act is the "end point" toward which it goes. Act already exists in the potency of the world, but potency is not in the act; rather, it is "under" the act. Thus, potency precedes act in a certain order and in the discourse of reason—just as in any birth of things among us, the potency for being born precedes the act of birth in time and proceeds into the act within time.

If you ask what that first potency of the world was before it was born, I will answer: it was not entirely "something" (for then it would have been in act), nor was it entirely "nothing" (for nothing is founded on nothing). I will say, therefore, that it was "not-nothing"—namely, the very potency and matter of existing. This was not founded in God (for nothing accidental happens to God), nor was it founded in nothing, but was itself rather the foundation. It was not the first thing in the intention of the divine Architect, but rather the last. For the first thing—the most important—in God's thought is the form of the world; the later thing is the matter hiding under the world’s form. Conversely, in the execution of the work, matter is first, and form follows. Therefore, the universe consists, as Plato says <note>in the *Timaeus*</note>, of Mind—that is, the formal act, which is the chief object of the divine mind’s will and the mind’s image—and of Necessity—that is, matter, which is taken into this work not so much by its own intention as by a certain necessary condition. If, therefore, the Good itself is most effective...

He further argues that matter is the "sub-contrary" to the Good and that the existence of evil is a philosophical necessity for a world created through both Mind and Necessity.</summary>
