<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, Book I, Chapter 8. Ficino is explaining the metaphysical necessity of evil as a consequence of the "overflow" of the Good, transitioning into Chapter 8 which investigates how matter corrupts the soul and body.</meta>

of all things, Plotinus necessarily maintains that the work of the world follows from it. If the world exists, matter necessarily exists, and matter is evil. Therefore, if the Good exists, evil necessarily follows. Furthermore, since the Good itself possesses an inestimable efficacy, it diffuses its power and effect as far and as wide as possible. If it stretches out to the furthest distance, it certainly produces a series of innumerable successive steps, so that the final step is, as it were, most distant from the first—that is, contrary to the Good, or entirely diverse and most dissimilar to it. This, then, will be evil: evil, I say, in a simple and general sense. Likewise, if it diffuses its power as widely as possible, the many degrees across the breadth of things ensure that one thing is most different from another, and often truly contrary. Such a thing is not evil in a simple sense, but rather evil in relation to something else. If, therefore, the Good exists, it follows that evil eventually creeps in, both at the far end of the chain and in the lateral conflicts between things. From the inestimable fertility of the Good itself, there necessarily follows another most fertile good. And from the fertility of this one, another follows in turn, and then another. But since the effect always falls short of the goodness of its cause, a diminishing of the good continually arises; and finally, evil follows this. Thus, the effect of the Good is both good, because it comes from the Good, and "less good," because it is outside and below the Good; and finally, it suffers evil after a very long loss of goodness. 

Because matter is evil itself, and the entire world is composed of it, evil lies hidden in every small part of the world, even though the usual effects of evil do not happen in the higher spheres of the heavens. In those heights, the deficiency of matter is completely overcome by the perfection of the <term>form</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, 'Form' refers to the perfect, non-physical essence of a thing, while matter is the physical substance that tries to imitate it.</note>. Nevertheless, the continuous privation brought about by the world's perpetual motion into the past and future seems to present something similar to evil. Because the matter of the heavens is indifferent to all forms, it might perhaps change its fundamental substance at some point, were it not restrained by a wonderful power of its present form, as if by a bridle. Having been tamed, it yields to this bridle—perhaps not so much because it is matter in a simple sense, but because it is the matter of such a high form. For this reason, Plato says in the *Timaeus* that the spheres and stars of the world could be dissolved—specifically because of the nature of matter—unless they were bound together by divine power, that is, by the wonderful goodness of their form. 

Therefore, <term>separated forms</term> <note>These are pure intellectual realities that exist without being joined to physical matter.</note> cannot be dissolved. For even if these are preserved by the gift of the Good, this very gift is itself a form. While any form separated from matter is preserved by this gift, it seems meanwhile to be preserved by itself, since it is truly a form. If anyone wonders why the human body is not kept indissoluble by its form—that is, the soul, which is divine—let him hear Moses teaching that the body could also be kept indestructible, provided that the soul preserves its own divinity. The Persian Magi <note>Original: "Persarum Magi"; referring to the followers of Zoroaster, whom Renaissance philosophers like Ficino viewed as ancient keepers of divine wisdom.</note> followed this same idea, promising perpetual health of the body to the soul that recovers its original health.

->How matter is the cause of evil, first in its forms, then in the soul; likewise, that all good things are referred back to one Good, and all evil things are finally referred back to one Evil.<-

VIII. In the eighth chapter of the book, he wonders whether matter is the cause in the soul of both ignorance and depravity, or whether it is rather a certain form or combination of forms. He soon answers: If any kind of bodily form is said to be the cause of evil in the soul, that form is a cause of evil only because it is bound to matter; it is entirely a material effect. It is not a "true" form, but a mere image of a form and an affection of matter. 

Since the region below the heavens is mobile and wavering unsteadily by its own nature, it must be ruled and led by the celestial region, which is mobile but "steadily mobile"—that is, revolving always with a perpetual and constant tenor. Again, because the celestial region is subject to motion and is not yet perfect, it is governed by a higher region that is entirely immobile. We rightly trace the lower forms in our world of matter back to the forms in the heavens, and we refer the celestial forms back to those which exist in the Maker and Leader of the heavens. There, these forms are nothing other than the intelligence of the Maker and Leader themselves; therefore, they are judged to exist in themselves. 

The forms beneath the heavens degenerate far from the celestial ones. In the heavens, forms are pure, whole, effective, free from suffering, and not combative. Here, however, they are defiled by some mixture, crippled, ineffective, subjected to countless sufferings, and if they do act, they fight among themselves unto destruction. Nevertheless, these forms agree with the celestial ones both in the general type of body and in matter and motion. Therefore, they degenerate far more from the forms that are entirely non-bodily and far from matter—those consisting within themselves without any motion—than they do from the celestial forms. It reaches the point where those sublime ones are the true forms, while these lower ones are merely "deformed" marks or very small and uncertain traces of forms in a matter that is otherwise formless. Matter, I say, now overcomes the forms, just as in the heavens the forms overcome the matter joined to them, and as forms above the heavens eliminate all matter far from themselves. 

Consider light in itself once more, and in it all the powers and degrees of colors; yet in the light itself, these are nothing other than the light itself. Notice then the colors transferred into plants: you will immediately recognize how far the colors in these materials fall away from those that exist in light, or rather in themselves. I will even say that these colors are now shadowed and polluted by a nature contrary both to light and to each other. Do you not see that they have become so ineffective that when the light leaves, they do nothing, and perhaps are nothing? So much so, that while they seem to exist when light is present, this very "being" perhaps belongs to the light itself; certainly, their "acting" and moving the eyes is the work of the light acting within them. Remember that such is the comparison between our forms and the divine ones. 

For matter infects all the forms lying within it with its own formlessness far more than a cold object receives a weak, approaching heat. For there is a greater diversity between a form and an entirely formless subject than between any form and a subject that is already shaped in some way. If, therefore, heat mixed with cold is not "true" heat, certainly a form immersed in an entirely formless subject—or, to speak more truly, in formlessness itself—is not a true form. Take four colors: white, saffron, green, and red. Mix any of these with any other; you will not defile them by mutual mixing as much as if you mixed any of them with black. Blackness, compared to the other colors, represents matter compared to forms. 

Remember, furthermore, that forms in matter become needy and subject to dangers because they have become material; therefore, they struggle against each other unto destruction, so that they may be nourished by another’s loss however they can, and be safer once their opposite is extinguished. But forms separated from matter, although very different from each other, do not fight in any way. They do, however, generate contraries in the universe: the Idea of fire generates fire, and the Idea of water generates water. Because each property remains unconfused among the different Ideas, here in the material world, that difference becomes a hostile repugnance. 

Conclude finally that forms entirely shadowed in matter become so weak that, being sickened by the "favor" of matter, they are in a way poisonous to a soul that approaches them too closely. In our *Theology* <note>Ficino refers here to his own major work, *Platonic Theology*.</note>, we often dispute the reason why different temperaments and characters of men exist according to the diversity of the <term>humors</term> <note>The "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) were believed in ancient medicine to determine a person's health and personality.</note>, and whether and how these inconveniences can be overcome or tempered; there we also frequently assert that forms in matter are not "true" forms. # ON BOOK VIII. OF ENNEAD I.

To hold in summary what Plotinus brings forward here and in the preceding sections regarding the good, the evil, and the degrees of both, consider it in this way. We call various goods by the common name "good," in whatever category of things they may be. We are led to do this not by chance, but by a certain defined condition. Thus, we divine <note>original: "vaticinamur"; Ficino uses this to mean an intuitive grasp or an "inkling" of a higher truth that precedes formal logic.</note> one common lot in all things, though not one in species or genus. For in all genera, however diverse, we perceive and name a "good." Therefore, this naming is unified because of a certain union of order toward the same thing—namely, because they originate from the same principle, possess something of it, and are carried toward and contribute to the same end. Similarly, we find some evil across all genera; we mark all evils with the same name of "evil," not by chance, but for a specific reason. This cannot be done more truly than if we refer all things to one supreme evil—specifically because they either happen to come from there, or possess something of it, whether by resemblance, inclination, or nature, or because they are carried toward it and bring others there. That which is the Good itself is the highest degree of the universe; therefore, Evil itself would be the final degree of all things. Truly, it is not fitting to judge evils solely by their departure and distance from the Good itself; rather, it is much more correct to judge them by their approach to Evil itself. For we do not immediately judge as evil whatever is distant from the first principle, but we only detect evils after a long interval—those which, through their proximity to the ultimate <term>ultimate: in this context, the furthest point from God, which is pure matter</term>, are already deformed and ruinous. For it is very probable that those things closer to the Good than to Evil are reckoned as good; conversely, those closer to Evil are thought of as evil. But if one were to descend without any end, there would never be a "lowest" point most distant from the Good itself. This being established, let it be permitted to consider one thing closer to this end than to the Good, and to weigh one thing as closer than another by any reasoning. To refer the judgment of evils solely to a certain distance from the Good would be the same as if someone referred the entire judgment of goods solely to their distance from Evil.

### How that which is formless can be known by the soul, which is form, and usually knows through forms.

**IX** In Chapter 9, he asks how that which is formless <note>original: "informe"; in Neoplatonism, matter is "formless" because it lacks the defining structures given by the Divine Mind.</note> can be known, since the power of knowing is itself a form, and the soul acts through form, and the object must meet the power through a form. He responds that darkness is known through light—that is, by imagining all light to be absent, one thinks of "ultimate darkness." Or, by imagining a part of light to be missing here, which we see elsewhere, something "dark" is recognized. Similarly, by taking away every form, the soul divines matter; but by taking away only some forms, something "deformed" is thought of. But something marvelous happens here. For just as we see nothing without light, nor do we see darkness in the light, so too we understand nothing without form, nor do we understand matter through form or within form. Finally, just as the soul knows the Good itself *above* the intellectual light, it imagines matter *below* such light. Both types of knowledge seem better called "divination" rather than "reason."

### That matter is evil, not because of what quality it has, but because it lacks quality; likewise, God is good without quality; also, that matter is entirely formless, and what form is.

**X** After this, in the remaining chapters of the book, he raises and solves questions. The first question in Chapter 10 is: Whether matter, if it possesses no quality, can be evil. For virtue and vice, goodness and malignancy, usually belong to the category of "quality." He responds: things that are mixed from a certain subject and a form are usually judged as either good or evil in that way. But those things which are most simple are not judged so, but differently. Thus, the Principle of things, when it is called "goodness," is not a quality; or when it is called "the Good," it is not "of a certain quality." For it is Goodness itself, superior not only in quality, but in substance and essence. Thus the ultimate of things, that is, matter, when it is called "malignancy," is not a quality; otherwise it would exist in another subject, and thus would not be the "ultimate," and through a formal nature it would possess something of formal good. Likewise, when it is named "evil," it is not so named because it is something composed of a subject and a quality; otherwise it would not be the ultimate, for it could be resolved into simpler parts and a subject. Furthermore, its quality would not necessarily be compatible with certain other qualities; otherwise matter would not be equally ready to receive any quality whatsoever. Nor would it be a quality equally indifferent to all qualities; for in that case, even the quality itself would be drawn toward the nature and lot of matter. And if it were judged to be something formal, it would at least follow that what is called the "subject of all things" would still be composed of form and subject. However, so that there is no process into infinity, one must arrive at a subject that is entirely simple and formless. Matter, therefore, is considered evil not because it *has* a quality, but because it *does not have* one. If, then, a quality is sometimes called good, it is not because it is "of a certain quality," but because it *is* a quality <note>In Ficino's thought, any "Form" or "Quality" is a reflection of divine order, and therefore inherently good.</note>; thus matter is evil, not because it is of a certain quality, but because it is matter, possessing no quality in itself. For quality and form in a subject are nothing other than the measure and determination of the subject, and a certain expression from the Good itself, impressed through the primary Form (that is, through the Mind) as if by its own seal, reflecting the Good itself. We can imagine matter as something also hanging from the Good itself, through a mode of "procession" rather than "conversion" <note>Procession refers to the flow of existence away from God; Conversion is the turning back of a soul toward God. Matter is the point where the flow stops before it can turn back.</note>, not yet having looked back toward the Good, nor yet sealed by the seal as something specific. In this way, whatever follows is ruled by the common power of the celestial nature, hanging from it all the way to the center of the earth. But the common nature of heaven expresses nothing further beyond the surface of the earth through light (which is like its seal, similar and proper to itself); it forms nothing similar to itself there. Therefore, what follows is similar to formless matter; but what stands above is similar to forms and the beautiful. Let that light represent the divine Intellect to you; but let the simple, prior nature of heaven represent the Good itself.

### Whether evil is the ultimate privation: and whether it can exist by itself and in itself? The answer is given by making a distinction.

**XI** The second question in Chapter 11 asks: Since a "privation" <term>privation: the absence or lack of something that ought to be present</term> cannot exist in itself due to its own defect, it follows that the *ultimate* privation, due to its *ultimate* defect, can least of all exist by itself or in itself. In what way, then, is evil itself the ultimate privation, or if it is such, how does it consist by itself or in itself? We respond to this: the ultimate privation—that is, the total emptiness of all forms—cannot exist in another, for otherwise there would not be ultimate emptiness there. Nor, in truth, does it exist in itself in the sense that it depends on nothing, but rather because it is not sustained by anything as if by a subject. Therefore, let no one say that the primary evil is either the soul or within the soul; otherwise, there would be no intellect in the soul, no life, no essence, nor would the soul itself be a soul any longer.

<summary>Ficino explains Plotinus’s view that Good and Evil are the two poles of existence, with matter being "formless" and the ultimate "privation" of Good. He argues that matter is not evil because of a bad quality, but because it lacks any form or quality from the Divine Mind.</summary>

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

### Whether evil itself is not pure evil, and whether it is in the soul? It is answered that it is pure, and not in the soul.

XII. The third question in chapter 12 examines whether it is permissible to judge the first evil <note>The "first evil" refers to the primary source of all badness, which Neoplatonists identified as matter itself.</note> as being not purely evil in every respect, and thus to place it within the soul. I respond: for Plotinus, the first and highest evil is understood as the extreme void of forms. Insofar as it relates to forms, it is a pure emptiness and "prime matter." Indeed, if this matter had anything formal <note>In this philosophy, "form" is what gives a thing its identity and reality; matter is the "stuff" that lacks identity until form is applied.</note> within it, it would not be true matter, just as a form that admits something material into itself is not a true form. Conversely, if it turns out to have a form within, it is not true matter; likewise, any form that becomes material is no longer a true form. This is especially true because if matter ceases to be "true" matter when it is shaped toward the better (that is, when it is given a form), then much more does a true form cease to exist as a form when it is transferred toward the worse (that is, into matter). Therefore, to move from the non-true to the true, we must both ascend to pure forms above matter and descend to pure matter below forms. For this reason, matter is always a pure void: even when it seems to possess all forms, it has none. This is because these forms are not truly forms in that state, and because matter neither takes on any form as its own nor keeps a trace of them; perhaps, like a mirror, it shows what it does not actually possess.

### Whether evil itself is an impediment in the soul? It is answered that the first evil and the first good are outside the soul, and that the soul descends into evil—namely matter—through four degrees.

XIII. The fourth question in chapter 13: Whether the first evil should be placed in the soul in such a way that this evil is not so much a privation as an impediment to achieving one's own good. He [Plotinus] denies that such an impediment—namely vice <note>original: "vitium"</note>—is the first evil. First, because it is called evil only because, by hindering the good, it leads one toward evil; therefore, it is not the *first* evil. Likewise, just as virtue is not the highest good, wickedness is not the highest evil. It is clear that virtue is not the first and highest in goodness, both because it involves labor and does not fully satisfy the natural appetite, and because it proceeds from a quiet potential into an actual effect, and its course in time moves from lesser to greater. Furthermore, virtue can admit some level of composition. These characteristics cannot apply to the Good itself, which is entirely simple. Therefore, just as the Good itself is more excellent than virtue, so Evil itself is lower than vice and far worse. Certainly, the evil of the soul is to turn away toward matter, which Plato in the *Theaetetus* <note>A famous dialogue by Plato; the "region of dissimilarity" refers to the material world's distance from the divine perfection.</note> calls the "region of dissimilarity," that is, a place utterly unlike the divinity in every way. The soul slides down into this deep abyss <note>original: "lethum"; literally death or the underworld.</note> through four stages, like four rivers <note>Ficino is referencing the four rivers of the classical Underworld, used here as a metaphor for the soul's degradation.</note>. In the first stage, it imagines this bodily structure too intently; in the second, it desires it too ardently; in the third, now joined to it, it builds the body; in the fourth, it turns the pleasure of such a union into a habit. Thus far, the soul seems to be cast headlong through four rivers into the underworld. Once cast down, it is revolved there through four stages again: first, when judgment is totally blinded by imagination; second, when human affection becomes beast-like; third, when the union with the body makes the soul "corporeal" [flesh-like]; and finally, when the habit of staying in the commerce of the body becomes indelible, unless perhaps it is wiped away by divine power. In this final stage, the soul is said by Plato to "slumber" after it has fallen into the underworld.

### How evil in the soul is a weakness, what kind of weakness it is, and how it comes from matter; how the soul is joined to the body and how it is separate; how matter depends on the soul and also from above.

XIIII. The fifth question in chapter 14 investigates whether the evil in the soul—that is, vice—is a weakness <term>imbecillitas (weakness): in this context, it refers to the soul's loss of its natural power and its inability to resist material influences.</term>? He grants this, saying a similar weakness occurs in the soul and body, though they are not the same. Each is called weak when it easily suffers from outside influences and performs its own functions with difficulty. But bodily weakness is two-fold: it occurs either when the body loses what is its own, or when it is weighed down by something foreign. In the soul, however, weakness happens only from a "foreign weight." The soul is said to take in the foreign insofar as it admits matter, which is always present to it as if from outside. I say "present" because wherever the soul is, matter is there; "outside," I say, because matter hangs from the soul from without, while the soul resides only in itself, even while matter depends upon it. This matter—because it stands outside, is utterly needy, and is drawn toward the soul like iron to a magnet—seems to seek to penetrate the soul to be perfected by forms. It is as if a cloud, by its own movement, subjects itself to light and receives a reddish glow <note>original: "ruborem"</note> as its "form." In that case, the light truly exists in itself rather than in the cloud, while the red glow exists in the cloud. The light is not divided there so that one part is in itself and another in the cloud; rather, the light exists entirely in itself. Its power and action in the cloud become the red glow. Because this glow is received by a nature lower than ours, it is much weaker than the light itself, and the gift of the light seems to be obscured from our perspective. The cloud in this metaphor is matter; the light is the soul; and the red glow is the appearance or form infused into matter. This "life," because it is received not according to the soul's own vastness but according to the narrow capacity of matter, turns out to be a small and weak life—ineffective in action and liable to suffering—even though the intellect shines above in the soul, just as the light shines from above while its glow in the cloud falls away from that brilliance, and the cloud hides the sight of the true light from us. Remember that Plotinus hints here and elsewhere that matter is generated by Nature—that is, by the lowest power of the soul. I say by the soul either "suffering" [undergoing change], as some texts say, or "presenting itself," which I think is the better reading. For the soul suffers nothing while matter is not yet born, unless one understands the soul "suffering" in the sense of being affected by the desire to generate something. Since natural things are subject to divine ones, it is probable that the subject of generation itself—that is, matter—depends on the last of the divine things: namely Nature, the mother of natural things. And just as specific natures create specific subjects for their works (that is, subjects prepared in a certain way), so universal Nature creates a universal subject. It is like an architect who both lays the foundation and builds the house. If you argue that matter comes from even higher than Nature, we will concede it, but only on this condition: that this subject, which is most universal to all forms, depends most closely on Nature (insofar as Nature is thought of as not yet formed but as a potential to be shaped), then from the essence of Mind (insofar as that essence is formable), and finally it is derived from the highest Principle of all things—though not strictly by that reason which is the Good...

<summary>This page discusses the nature of evil as a "void" of form (matter) and explains how the soul's descent into the material world through four stages leads to spiritual weakness and "slumber." Ficino uses the metaphor of light hitting a cloud to explain how the soul provides life to matter without being divided or inherently corrupted by it.</summary>

# ON BOOK VIII. OF ENNEAD I.

The [Good] is that which communicates itself abundantly, but rather insofar as it is the One itself, it is wonderfully segregated <note>original: "segregatum"; here meaning set apart or transcendent.</note> from all things. Thus, matter ends up being utterly destitute and unarmed, set apart from all gifts. In this way, matter is called "a certain one" rather than "good"; it possesses unity as an internal trait, but goodness appears only from the outside. Since all effects of the highest principle [the One] are both from it and yet compelled to exist outside and below it, they certainly receive forms and activities from that source. However, insofar as they are outside it and inferior, they suffer a "material lot" (if I may call it that) admitted into themselves, and a condition of lesser good. Finally, they end in matter, the extreme and lowest subject of all, and the origin of evils. Now, when the soul generates matter, it is not yet evil, nor is it yet weak; rather, it is fertile, and thus it is able to generate. But when it clings too closely to the matter it has made, it becomes weaker, as if under a heavy burden, and grows worse. Two things cause the soul to embrace matter: the destitution and appetite of matter itself, and the fertile nature of the soul. Therefore, this very connection, insofar as it arises from the soul’s fertility, is in some way good and produces good things—namely, life and forms. But insofar as it is stirred up by a certain wantonness <note>original: "procacitate"; referring to matter's aggressive tendency to draw the soul toward it.</note> of matter, it is evil and gives birth to evils: the weakness of life, obstacles to knowledge, and countless passions of the mind.

---

->Proof that matter is indeed utterly formless; likewise that evil exists in the world, as does<-
->the good; how evil arises in the soul; how matter is inwardly<-
->evil, but is covered by good on the outside.<-

---

**XV** The sixth question in chapter XV asks whether, in this kingdom of the highest good—so good and so beautiful—there can exist matter that is utterly formless and evil that is entirely deformed. That matter *must* exist, we prove in our earlier writings and in our *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his major work, the *Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls*.</note>, and we confirm it again here with Plotinus; thus we briefly affirm it for the present. The forms of individual works, whether made by art or by nature, are always resolved into their own proper materials. These materials are formless in relation to the forms they are meant to receive, even if they might already possess some other form. Therefore, the form of the entire work of the world <note>The "universal world-work" refers to the cosmos as a divine creation.</note> is reduced to an utterly formless matter. If one imagines that this matter from which the universe is made still possesses some form other than the "worldly" one, that form would eventually be traced back to a matter that lacks all form in itself. This must be so, unless one imagines an infinite sequence of forms within forms without end—which cannot happen. First, because every subsequent form acting as matter would be a "worse" or lower form, and this process of declining into the worse cannot last forever. Second, if there were no "first form" and no "prime matter," the work [of creation] would have no starting point; indeed, an infinite crowd of materials and forms would be contrary to the principle, end, order, and union of the work to be built. Third, since matter cannot form itself due to its own defect, and must therefore be formed by another, it receives its limit of forms—both the first and the last—from a higher former. Finally, when one arrives at the first principle and the ultimate end of the universe, it is not permitted to proceed without a beginning and an end through materials and forms which are usually led from an efficient cause to a certain goal. 

Therefore, an utterly formless matter underlies the entire order of forms. Thus, evil underlies good things, which necessarily follows from a defect of the good. A defect of the good follows by necessity from a lower "degree" of good. Finally, a "lesser good" undoubtedly accompanies the effect of the Good itself. Just as evil necessarily follows from the Good itself by a necessity of nature, so conversely, if you take away evil, you will necessarily—by a necessity of consequence—take away the good. If nothing were ever encountered by us as "good" or "evil," but all things were indifferent (as some dream), the appetite <note>The "appetite" here refers to the soul's natural drive to seek or avoid things.</note> would never be moved toward seeking or fleeing. Senses, which were granted by nature for the sake of this service, would cease; and the intellect would cease as well. For just as the sense serves the sensible good, so the intellect serves the intelligible good. From this, it is also clear that the Good itself is superior to the intellect, since the "intelligible good" is in some way higher than the intellect. Therefore, since we see many things in the order of reality that are partly good and partly evil—some of which you might approve and others not—it is necessary to correctly resolve these composite things into a simple, first Good and a simple, first Evil. After this, Plotinus confirms again that the evil of the soul happens from elsewhere, namely from matter. Since the soul suffers only for the sake of the body, it fears for the body, desires for the body, grieves because of the body, and is disturbed in its imagination by the impulse of the body. While it is disturbed by imagining, it drinks in false opinions. Finally, evil comes to the soul from the outside, just as good comes to matter from the outside. Conversely, the soul's good arises from within, from the soul's own intellectual form; just as the evil of matter hides within, arising from its very lack of intellectual form and image.

<summary>Ficino explains that matter is the "ultimate void" and the origin of evil, arguing that a "prime matter" must exist to prevent an infinite regress of forms. He posits that evil is a necessary consequence of the existence of the Good, as without the distinction between them, human desire, sensation, and intellect would have no purpose.</summary>

# THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

-> Whether evil itself is not pure evil, and whether it resides in the soul? The answer is that it is pure [evil], and it is not in the soul. <-

<margin>XII</margin> The third question in chapter twelve examines whether it is permitted to judge that "primary evil" <note>In Neoplatonic thought, "primary evil" is not a personified force but the absolute absence of form and goodness.</note> is not entirely pure evil, and thus to place it within the soul. The answer is as follows: for Plotinus, the primary and highest evil is understood as the extreme emptiness of forms. Insofar as it pertains to forms, it is a pure void and "primary matter." If this matter possessed anything formal within itself, it would not be true matter, just as a form that admits something material into itself is not a "true form." Conversely, if it were to turn out to be formal within, it is not true matter; likewise, whatever turns out to be material is not a true form. This is especially true because if matter ceases to be "true" [matter] when it is imagined to be improved—that is, when it is transferred into a formal state—then much more does a true form cease to exist as a form when it is transferred into something worse, namely into matter. Therefore, so that we may arrive at the true from the non-true, we must both ascend to the pure forms above matter and descend to the pure matter below the forms. For this reason, matter is always a pure void; for even when it seems to possess all forms, it possesses none. This is partly because such forms are not "true" in that state, and partly because matter neither takes any form as its own nor preserves a trace of them afterward; perhaps, in the manner of a mirror, it shows what it does not actually have.

---

-> Whether evil itself is an impediment in the soul? The answer is that primary evil and primary good are outside the soul, and the soul descends into evil—that is, matter—through four stages. <-

<margin>XIII</margin> The fourth question in chapter thirteen asks whether primary evil should be placed in the soul in such a way that this evil is not so much a privation <note>A "privation" is the lack of a quality that should naturally be present, like blindness is a privation of sight.</note> as it is an impediment to achieving one's own good. [Plotinus] denies that such an impediment—namely, vice—is the primary evil. First, because vice is called evil precisely because it leads toward evil by hindering the good. Therefore, it is not the *primary* evil. Likewise, just as virtue is not the *highest* good, so too vice is not the *highest* evil. That virtue is not the primary and highest state of goodness is evident: first, because it involves labor and does not fully satisfy the appetite of nature; second, because it proceeds from a certain inactive potential into an effect, and its course moves through time from the lesser to the greater; and finally, because it can admit some degree of composition within itself. These traits cannot apply to the "Good Itself" in its simplicity. Therefore, just as the Good itself is more excellent than virtue, so evil itself is lower than vice and far worse. Indeed, the soul's evil is to turn itself toward matter, which Plato in the *Theaetetus* calls the "region of dissimilarity" <note>original: "dissimilitudinis regionem"; a famous Platonic metaphor for the material world, which is unlike the divine realm.</note>—that is, entirely unlike the divine in every way. The soul falls into this depth of Lethe <note>original: "letheum hoc profundum"; Lethe was the mythological river of forgetfulness in the underworld.</note> through four stages, like four rivers. In the first stage, it imagines this bodily structure too intently; in the second, it desires it too ardently; in the third, now joined to it, it builds it; in the fourth, it turns the pleasure of such a union into a habit. Thus far, the soul seems to be cast headlong into the lower regions through four rivers. Having been so cast down, it is further rolled through four [additional stages] in that same place: namely, when judgment is totally blinded by imagination. Likewise, its affection changes from human to beastly; hence, from a union of this kind, it renders the soul corporeal along with the body. Finally, the habit that detains the soul in its commerce with the body becomes entirely indelible, unless perhaps it is cleansed by divine power. In this stage, Plato says that the soul "sleeps" after it has fallen to the lower regions.

---

-> How evil in the soul is a weakness, and what kind of weakness, and how it comes from matter; how the soul is joined to the body and how it is separated; how matter depends on the soul, and how it also depends from above. <-

<margin>XIIII</margin> The fifth question in chapter fourteen investigates whether the evil that is in the soul—that is, vice—is a form of weakness? He grants this, saying that a similar kind of debility occurs in the soul as in the body, but they are not the same. For both of these are called "weak" when they are easily affected by external things and perform their own functions with difficulty. But weakness in the body is twofold: it occurs either when it loses its own [strength] or when it is burdened by something foreign. In the soul, however, weakness happens only from a foreign weight, so to speak. Now, the soul is said to receive something "foreign" insofar as it occasionally admits matter, which is always present to it externally. I say "present" because wherever the soul is, matter is also there. I say "externally" because matter hangs, as it were, outside the soul, and the soul in no way resides in matter, but rather in itself, while matter hangs from it. This matter—partly because it stands out from the soul, partly because it is utterly destitute, and partly because it is drawn to the soul like iron to a magnet—seems to desire to penetrate the soul to be perfected by forms. It is as if a cloud, either by its own movement or drawn by light, submits itself to the light and receives a "redness" from it, as if it were a form. In that case, the light does not seem to exist in the cloud so much as in itself, but the redness is in the cloud. Nor is the light divided there, as if one part were in itself and another in the cloud; rather, the light exists entirely within itself. Its power and act, however, become "redness" in the cloud. Because this redness is received by a nature lower than ours, it is much weaker than the light itself, and it seems to obscure the gift of light as far as our sight is concerned. In this analogy, the cloud is matter, the light is the soul, and the redness is a certain life or form already infused into matter. Because this life is not received according to the soul's own vastness but rather according to the narrow capacity of matter, it turns out to be a meager and weak life, ineffective in action and subject to passions. Meanwhile, the intellect shines in the soul from above, just as light shines from above, even while its redness in the cloud degenerates from that splendor, and the cloud takes away from us the sight of the true light. Remember that Plotinus hints to us here and elsewhere that matter is generated by "nature"—that is, by the lowest power of the soul—either from the soul while it "suffers" [is affected], as some texts read, or while it is "present," which I think is the more correct reading. For the soul suffers nothing before matter is born, unless perhaps one understands the soul to "suffer" in the sense that it is affected in some way toward generating something. Since natural things are subject to divine things, it is probable that the subject of generation itself—that is, matter—depends on the last of the divine things, which is "Nature," the natural mother. And just as the specific subjects of any particular nature produce specific works (disposed in a certain way), so too the "common subject" [matter] is produced by the "common nature"; just as the same architect who constructs a building also lays the foundation. If you should be convinced that matter originates even higher than from Nature, we shall concede it, but only on this condition: that this subject, which is most common to all forms, depends most closely on Nature (insofar as Nature is thought of as not yet formed but as a subject to be formed by rational principles); next, that it comes from the essence of the Mind itself, insofar as that essence is "formable"; and finally, that it is derived from the highest principle of all things, though not properly by the same reason that the principle is the Good itself...

<summary>Ficino explains Plotinus’s view that primary evil is identical to primary matter (the absolute absence of form) and details how the soul "falls" into this material state through four stages of psychological and habitual attachment. He uses the analogy of a cloud being colored by light to explain how life and form enter matter without the soul itself being divided or diminished.</summary>

### ON BOOK VIII OF ENNEAD I.

It is "the thing itself," that is, communicating itself abundantly, or rather insofar as it is the "One itself," it is wonderfully set apart from all things. Thus, matter ends up being utterly needy and formless, set apart from all gifts whatsoever. In this way, matter is called "a kind of unity" rather than "the good"; it possesses an internal unity but an external appearance of goodness. Generally, since all effects of the highest principle proceed from it and are compelled to exist outside and beneath it, they certainly receive forms and actions insofar as they are from it. Yet, insofar as they are outside and inferior to it, they suffer an admission of a "material lot" (so to speak) within themselves, and the condition of a lesser good. Finally, they terminate in matter—the extreme and lowest subject of all things, and the origin of evils. Now, when the soul generates matter, it is not yet evil, but good; it is not yet weak, but fertile, and therefore it is able to generate. However, when it embraces the already-created matter too much, it becomes weaker and worse, as if from a heavy burden. Both the soul's own fertility and the poverty and longing of matter cause the soul to embrace matter. Therefore, this very embrace—insofar as it happens because of the soul’s fertility—is in a certain way good and produces good things, namely a kind of life and forms. But insofar as it is fused with a certain wantonness <note>original: "procacitate"; referring to matter's insolent or demanding nature that draws the soul down.</note> of matter, it is evil and gives birth to evils: that is, the weakness of life, obstacles to knowledge, and the innumerable passions of the mind.

---

-> It is proven that matter is indeed entirely formless; likewise that evil exists in the world, as does <-
-> the good: How evil is made in the soul: How matter is internally <-
-> evil, but externally covered by the good. <-

---

<margin>XV</margin>
The sixth question in chapter XV wonders whether, in this kingdom of the highest good—so good and so beautiful—there can exist matter that is utterly formless and an evil that is entirely deformed. It is necessary that matter exists; we have proven this in previous sections and in our *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his own major work, *Platonic Theology*.</note>, and we prove it again elsewhere with Plotinus. Thus, we briefly confirm it for the present. The forms of individual works, whether they are made by art or by nature, are everywhere resolved into their own appropriate matters. These matters, insofar as they relate to forms to be acquired later, are formless, even though they might possess some other form. Therefore, the form of the entire work of the universe—which is the universal form—is reduced to matter that is entirely formless. If one imagines that this matter from which the universe is made still possesses some form besides the mundane one, that form would eventually be led down into a matter that is, by itself, lacking all form. This must be so unless one imagines that beneath one form lies another, and another again without end. This, however, cannot happen: first, because since any subsequent form taking the place of matter is a worse form than the last, this progression, failing bit by bit into the worse, cannot last into infinity. Second, if there were no primary form or primary matter given anywhere, there would be no beginning for the work. Indeed, an innumerable crowd of matters and forms would utterly oppose the beginning, end, order, and union of the work to be constructed. Furthermore, since matter cannot form itself due to its own defect and is therefore formed by another, it receives the limit of forms on both sides—the first and the last—from a higher former <note>term: "former" (formator) — the divine agent or intellect that imposes shape on formless void.</note>. Finally, when one comes to the first principle and the ultimate end of the universe, it is rightly not permitted to proceed without beginning or end through matters and forms, which are usually led from an efficient principle to a certain end.

Therefore, beneath the entire order of forms lies matter, which is by itself entirely formless. Thus, evil lies beneath good things, which necessarily follows the defect of the good. A defect of the good necessarily follows from a lower grade of the good. Finally, a "lesser good" undoubtedly accompanies the effect of the Good itself. Just as evil finally follows from the Good itself by a necessity of nature, so conversely, if you take away evil, you necessarily—that is, by the necessity of consequence—take away the Good. If nothing ever occurred to us as good or evil, but all things were "indifferent" as some dreamers imagine, the appetite would never be moved to either pursue or flee; the senses, which were granted by nature for the sake of this service, would cease; and the intellect would cease as well. For just as the sense serves the sensible good, so the intellect serves the intelligible good. From this, it is also clear that the "Good itself" is more excellent than the intellect, since even the "intelligible good" <note>In Platonism, the "Good" is the sun that illuminates the "Intelligible" (the realm of Ideas), making it visible to the "Intellect."</note> is in some way higher than the intellect. Since, therefore, we see many things in the order of reality that are partly good and partly evil—which you might approve of in one respect and disapprove of in another—and likewise some things better and others worse, it is necessary to rightly resolve these composite things into a simple, primary good and a simple, primary evil.

After this, he confirms again that the evil of the soul happens from elsewhere, namely from matter. For since the mind suffers only for the sake of the body, it fears for the body, it lusts for the body, it grieves because of the body, and it is disturbed in its imagination by the impulse of the body. While it is disturbed by imagining, it drinks in false opinions. Finally, evil approaches the soul from the outside, just as the good approaches matter from the outside. Conversely, the good of the soul arises from within, from the intellectual form of the soul, just as the evil of matter hides within, proceeding from its very emptiness of intellectual form and image.

<summary>This page argues that matter is the "lowest limit" of existence and the necessary origin of evil due to its total lack of form. Ficino explains that while the soul is naturally good and fertile, it becomes weakened and "evil" only when it becomes overly preoccupied with the material body and its physical passions.</summary>

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD I
### BOOK VIII.
---
# PLOTINUS
## THE FIRST ENNEAD
### BOOK VIII.

### On what evils are, and from where they come.

<margin>
Four questions concerning good and evil.
</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial Q featuring a figure seated on a stone plinth within a landscape of foliage.</image-desc>
WHOEVER seeks to discover from where evils have fallen, whether among existing things or concerning a certain class of things, will make a proper beginning to their investigation if they first propose what evil itself is and the nature of evil. <margin>A</margin> For in this way, it will become apparent from where it has come, where it is grounded, and to whom it happens; and it will be established altogether whether it even exists within the nature of things. However, there is a doubt: by which of the powers within us <margin>B</margin> do we chiefly perceive the nature of evil? For the knowledge of individual things is achieved through a certain similarity. Indeed, since the Intellect and the Soul are certain "species" <note>original: "species" or "eide"; in Neoplatonism, these are the formal, ideal patterns of things.</note>, they also know species and naturally desire species. But in truth, no one can form an image of evil under the logic of a species, since it is conceived as a total absence of the good. But if—because the knowledge of opposites is the same, and evil is the opposite of good—there will therefore be the same <margin>C</margin> knowledge of both good and evil, then it is certainly necessary for those who would know evils to first discern the Good. This is because superior things properly precede inferior ones, and species precede those things which are not judged to be species, but rather privations <note>term: "privation" (sterēsis); the absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present.</note>. It is also worth questioning in what way the good is the opposite of evil. Perhaps it is because the former is the "first" and the latter is the "last"; or certainly the former is like a species, and the latter like a privation. But we shall speak of these <margin>D</margin> more opportunely in what follows.

<margin>
II. 
A description of the good: to what extent goods are pure: and how the intellects were nearest to the good, but the soul is so through the intellect.
</margin>
In the present moment, however, we must state what the nature of the good is, so far as the current discussion requires. It is this upon which all things depend, and which all things desire, receiving their principle from it and being entirely in need of it. But the Good itself is in need of nothing; it is sufficient unto itself, desiring nothing at all, the measure and the limit of all things. Out of itself, it produces intellect, essence, soul, and life; and in turn, the activity concerning the intellect. Up to this point, all things are beautiful, and the Beautiful itself, which is above all the best things, reigns in the intelligible world. This is indeed the Intellect—an intellect, I say, not of the sort one might perhaps think, imagining it to be like those which are called "intellects" among us, which are completed by

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative initial T featuring a figure seated beneath an ornamental canopy or archway.</image-desc>
THOSE seeking from where evils come—whether they have entered into the realm of being or are merely concerning beings—would make a proper beginning of their inquiry if they first established what evil is and the nature of evil. For in this way, its origin, its foundation, and the subject it happens to would be known, and it would be agreed upon whether it exists at all among beings. But it might be a difficulty to know by what power among those in us we might know the nature of evil, since the knowledge of each thing occurs through similarity. For Intellect and Soul, being forms <note>original: "eide"</note>, would produce knowledge of forms and have a desire for them. But how could one imagine evil as a form, appearing as it does in the absence of all good? But if the knowledge of opposites is considered to be the same, and evil is some kind of opposite to the good, then the knowledge of the good would also be the knowledge of evil. Thus, it is necessary to look clearly at the good so that <margin>* evil things</margin> <note>original: "kakà"; the margin corrects the main text's "kalà" (beautiful things), indicating that to know evil, one must first know the good.</note> may be known through their members. For the better things precede the worse, and forms precede those things which are not forms, but rather privations. Yet there is still a question: in what way is evil the opposite of the good? Unless perhaps it is because the one is the beginning and the other is the extreme; or the one is as a form, and the other as a privation. But these things we will discuss later.

NOW, however, let it be said what the nature of the good is, as far as is fitting for the present arguments. It is that upon which all things are suspended, and which all beings desire, having it as their principle and needing it. But it is without need, sufficient for itself, needing nothing, the measure and limit of all things, giving from itself intellect, essence, soul, and life, and the activity concerning intellect. And up to this point, all things are beautiful; for it is itself "super-beautiful" and beyond the best things, reigning in the intelligible world. That world is the realm of Intellect—not an intellect such as one might suppose by looking at those called "intellects" among us, which are filled out from premises...

<summary>Plotinus begins his investigation into the nature of evil, arguing that evil is not a positive 'form' but a 'privation' or total absence of the Good. He defines the Good as the self-sufficient source of all being, intellect, and life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous chapter of Plotinus’s First Ennead, Book Eight. While the previous page established that the Soul knows evil by its absence of good, this page moves into a formal definition of the Divine Intellect (Nous) and explores why Evil cannot exist within the higher realms of Being, locating it instead in the "non-being" of the material world.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...those who are capable of understanding what is said, who can reason and engage in contemplation through logical sequence, as if truly beholding the things that exist—as if they did not possess these truths before, but were empty before learning, even though they are essentially minds. Is the <term>Intellect (Nous)</term> <note>original: "ho nous"; the second level of reality in Plotinus's system, containing the archetypes of all things.</note> truly like this? No, it possesses all things; it dwells with itself and is entirely united with itself. It has all things without "having" them as if they were external; for it is not one thing and its contents another, <margin>B</margin> nor is each thing within it separated from the others. For each part is the whole, and the whole is everywhere. They are not confused together, yet they are distinct. That which participates in this Intellect does not participate in everything at once, but only as much as it is able. This Intellect is the "first activity" and the "first essence" <note>original: "prote ousia"</note>, while the One remains within itself. Yet the Intellect acts around the One, as a life centered upon it. The Soul, dancing on the outside around the Intellect, looking toward it and contemplating its inner depths, sees God through it. <margin>C</margin> This is the painless and blessed life of the gods, where evil is nowhere to be found. If nature stopped at this level, evil would not exist at all. But there are first, second, and third ranks of things around the King of all; He is the cause of all beautiful things, and all those things are for His sake. Thus, the second rank of things relates to the second, and the third rank to the third.

<margin>III
Evil is not in those things which truly exist, but in those things which either do not truly exist, or which incline toward those things that do not truly exist.</margin>

<margin>D</margin> If these are the "beings" <note>the higher spiritual realities</note>, and there is that which is "beyond being," then evil cannot exist within being, much less in that which is beyond being. For all these things are good. It remains then that if evil exists at all, it must be found in "non-being" <note>original: "me on"</note>—as a certain "form" of non-being, or among things mixed with non-being, or which share in it in some way. By "non-being," I do not mean that which is absolutely non-existent, but rather that which is merely "other" than being. This non-being is not like the concepts of "motion" or "rest" which are related to being, but rather like an image of being, or something even further removed from being. This is the entire sensible universe <note>the world perceived by the senses</note> and all the passions associated with it—or perhaps something that follows these, like an accident, or their principle, or one of the elements that completes this state of existence. <margin>E</margin> For one can already conceive of this state as a lack of measure <note>original: "ameteria"</note> compared to measure, as the infinite compared to a limit, as the formless compared to a forming principle, and as that which is always in need compared to that which is self-sufficient. It is always indeterminate, never at rest, affected by everything from all sides, insatiable, and an absolute poverty. These are not merely accidental qualities of it, but rather they seem to be its very essence. Whatever part of it you look at, you will find all these qualities present. Other things that participate in it or are made like it become evil, <margin>G</margin> yet they are not "Evil itself." Therefore, these qualities belong to a certain underlying subject, not as something different from it, but as the subject itself. Just as there is "Good itself" and then that which is good by accident, so there is "Evil itself," and then that which is evil by association with it.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...propositions are usually filled, and what is gathered by reasoning they can perceive: likewise they reason, and they think out what follows from what, and they behold things through their consequences: as those who previously did not have it, but before they learned they were empty, although even then they existed as intellects. That Intellect, I say, is not such, but has all things, is all things, dwells with itself, is completely united to itself, and possesses all things while not "having" them: for it does not possess them as other than itself, nor <margin>B</margin> does it exist as something different from them. Nor are the things that are in it separated one from another: indeed, any part you choose is the universe, and is the whole everywhere; yet all things are not confused, but rather each is distinct. Therefore, that which becomes a participant in this does not participate in all things at once, but participates as much as it can. It is likewise the first act of that One, and the first essence, while the One remains indeed within itself. It acts surely around the One, living as if around it. Accordingly, the soul moving on the outside around this Intellect <margin>C</margin> looks around it; indeed, inspecting its innermost parts, through the Intellect it sees God as well: and this is the unhurt and happy life of the gods, entirely removed from evils. If nature stopped its steps here, evil would be nowhere. But truly there are first goods, and there are second goods: there are also third goods: and all are around the King of the universe: and the King himself is the cause of all goods, and for his sake are all things. Finally, around the second are the second things, and the third around the third.

<margin>III
Evil is not in those things which truly are, but in those which either are not truly, or are inclined to those which are not truly.</margin>

<margin>D</margin> If these are the beings, and this is that which is "above being," then evil certainly will be nowhere in the beings: and much less in that which over-tops the beings. For all these are good things. It remains, therefore: if evil is anywhere, it is found in those things which "are not," as if a certain species of non-being: and around some of those things which are mixed with non-being, or in whatever way they have commerce with non-being. "Non-being," I say, is by no means altogether non-existent, but only different from being. Not indeed "non-being" in the way that motion and rest are said to be around being, but as an image of being, or even further removed from being. But that is the entire sensible universe, and as many passions as are around the sensible: or something posterior to these, and as if an accident to them, or the principle of these, or one of those things which complete it, such a thing as I shall now describe. For it is permitted to think of it as a certain immoderation if it is referred to measure, <margin>F</margin> also as the infinite compared to a limit, as the formless again to a former: likewise as always needy compared to the sufficient, always indeterminate, nowhere at all resting, suffering all things from every side, insatiable, an altogether extreme poverty. Nor are such things accidental to it, but they seem to be its very essence. Moreover, whatever portion of it you see, you will find in any part all these things in summary: but other things which participate in it, and are made like it, become evil indeed, <margin>G</margin> yet they are not Evil itself. And so these things are in a certain foundation, not as some other things from itself, but as itself. For if evil happens to another, it is necessary that it be something prior itself, even if it be no essence. For as the good exists as one thing which is Good itself, and another which happens to others, so also is evil: this indeed is Evil itself, but that is according to the other.

<summary>Plotinus distinguishes the Divine Intellect—a realm of unity and goodness—from the material world, arguing that Evil is not a positive existence but a "non-being" characterized by lack of form, measure, and limit.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of evil. While the previous page established that the Divine Intellect is a realm of pure goodness and light, Plotinus now turns to define "Evil" itself as a lack of measure, identifying it primarily with Matter and secondarily with the bodies and souls that become entangled with it.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. BOOK I.

<margin>
IV
The three degrees of evil: how they exist in the soul, and why matter possesses nothing of the good.
</margin>

**A** ...this happens to another. Someone might ask: what is <term>immoderation</term> <note>original: "amētria" (Greek) / "immoderatio" (Latin); literally "un-measurement" or the lack of a defined limit or proportion.</note> if it does not exist in that which is unmeasured? Conversely, what is measure, except in a thing that participates in measurement? But just as there is a "measure" that is not contained within any measured thing, so too is there an "immoderation" that exists outside of any unmeasured subject. For if it were in something else, it would either be in the unmeasured—but the unmeasured does not need immoderation, since it is already immoderation itself—or it would be in a measured thing; yet it is impossible for that which is measured, insofar as it is measured, to undergo immoderation. **B** Truly, there must be something that is infinite <note>original: "apeiron"</note> in itself, and by its very nature formless, possessing all the characteristics we previously used to describe the nature of evil. Furthermore, if anything else is "evil" besides that primary nature, it is because it is either mixed with it, or because it looks toward it and thus becomes such, or because it is the cause of such a thing. Therefore, we speak of a nature that is subjected to figures, species, forms, measures, and boundaries, yet is adorned with a beauty that is not its own, possessing no good of itself; **C** it is a mere <term>image</term> <note>original: "eidōlon"; a shadow or phantom of true reality.</note> when compared to true beings. This nature is the very "essence of evil"—if such a thing as an "essence of evil" can even exist. Our reasoning rightly concludes that this is the primary evil, evil in and of itself.

**D** The NATURE of bodies, insofar as it participates in <term>matter</term> <note>original: "hylē"; the underlying "stuff" of the universe which Plotinus views as the ultimate source of lack and limitation.</note>, is indeed an evil, though not the primary one. For a body possesses a certain form (though not a true one) and yet is deprived of life. Bodies bring about mutual corruption among themselves and undergo a chaotic, disordered motion. They act as obstacles to the soul’s own activity. Furthermore, they are in a state of perpetual flux, fleeing from true essence; for this reason, they hold the second rank of evil. **E** The Soul itself is not evil by its own nature, nor is every soul wicked. But which soul is wicked? It is that one which, as Plato says, serves that which is naturally prone to wickedness; it is as if the irrational part of the soul undergoes evil, receiving immoderation, excess, and defect. From these spring licentiousness, cowardice, and the rest of the soul's vices—involuntary passions which produce false opinions, leading one to think things are "good" or "evil" when they are merely things to be pursued or avoided. **F** But what brings about this wickedness? And how can you trace its cause back to that first principle? First, it must be said that such a soul is not outside of matter, nor is it like this by itself. It is mixed with immoderation and becomes devoid of the form that beautifies and brings things into measure. It is, in a sense, submerged in the body that possesses matter. Furthermore, if the rational power is damaged, it is prevented from seeing, being darkened by passions and buried in the shadows of matter. It stoops toward matter, looking not toward true essence but toward <term>generation</term> <note>original: "genesis"; the world of change, birth, and decay.</note>. The origin of this is the nature of matter, which is so evil that even that which is not yet within it, but merely looks toward it, becomes filled with its evil. **G** For being entirely devoid of good—a privation of it and a pure defect—it makes everything that touches it in any way similar to itself. Therefore, the perfect soul, which inclines toward the <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "nous"</note>, is always pure; it turns away from matter and excludes everything that is indeterminate, unmeasured, and evil. It neither approaches these things nor looks toward them; thus, it remains pure and centered in the intellect...

<column-break/>

**A** ...and to that. What then is unmeasure, if not in the unmeasured? And what is measure, if not in the measured? But just as there is measure not in the measured, so there is unmeasure not in the unmeasured: for if it is in another, it is either in the unmeasured, but the unmeasured does not need unmeasure, being itself unmeasured: or it is in the measured, but it is not possible for the measured to have unmeasure, according to which it is measured. **B** And still there must be something both infinite in itself, and formless in itself, and the other things, those before, which characterized the nature of evil. And if anything after that is such, it either has it mixed, or is such by looking towards it, or is productive of such. Of the things indeed underlying shapes, and species, and forms, and measures, and limits, and adorned with an external ornament, having nothing good from itself, **C** an image indeed as towards beings, the essence of evil, if anyone can say an essence of evil exists, this reason will choose to be the first evil, and evil in itself.

**D** The nature of BODIES indeed, insofar as it participates in matter, would be an evil not the first: for it has a certain species not true, and it is deprived of life, destroying each other, and a motion from them disordered, and obstacles of the soul, towards its own activity, and it flees essence always flowing, a second evil. **E** But Soul in itself is not evil, nor indeed every soul evil. But which is the evil one? Such as, he says, having enslaved itself, in which it is natural for the vice of the soul to arise, as the irrational form of the soul, receiving the evil, unmeasure, and excess, and defect, from which also licentiousness, and cowardice, and the rest of the soul's vice, involuntary passions, producing false opinions, to think things are evil and good, which it flees and pursues. **F** But what is the thing having made this vice? And how will you lead it back to that principle or cause? Or first indeed such a soul is not outside matter, nor is it such in itself. It is mixed then with unmeasure, and without a share of the form that adorns and leads into measure. For it is mixed in the body, having matter. And then also the reasoning part, if it should be harmed, is hindered from seeing, both by the passions, and by being darkened by matter, and having leaned towards matter, and looking not at all towards essence, but towards generation, of which the principle is the nature of matter being so evil, as even that not yet in it, but only having looked into it, to fill itself with its evil. **G** For being entirely without a share of good, and a privation of this, and unmixed defect, it makes like to itself everything whatsoever that should touch it in any way. The soul indeed being perfect and leaning towards intellect, is always pure, and has turned away from matter, and everything indeterminate, and the unmeasured and evil, it neither sees, nor approaches. It remains therefore pure...

<summary>This page defines Evil as a lack of measure ("immoderatio") and identifies Matter as the primary source of evil because it is formless and devoid of the Good. It also explains how bodies and souls become secondary evils when they lose their connection to the Divine Intellect and sink into material existence.</summary>

While the previous page established that the Divine Intellect is a realm of pure goodness and light, Plotinus now turns to define "Evil" itself as a lack of measure, identifying it primarily with Matter and secondarily with the bodies and souls that become entangled with it.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

<column-break/>

...sees, and already possesses matter, looking toward that which it does not see, as we are said to see even the darkness.

->A<-

But if the lack of the Good is the cause of seeing and dwelling with darkness, then evil would consist **B** in that lack. Or rather, in the darkness that affects the soul—first, and then secondly within—the darkness and the nature of evil exist not just in matter, but even before matter. Or perhaps evil is not found in just any lack, but only in total and universal lack. For that which lacks the Good only slightly is not yet evil; it can still be perfect according to its own nature. But when it lacks it entirely—which is the very nature of matter—this is the "truly evil," possessing no share of the Good. **C** For Matter does not even possess true "being" <note>original: "esse" (Latin) / "einai" (Greek); Plotinus argues that because Matter has no form or quality of its own, it cannot be said to truly exist in the way that divine or intellectual things do.</note> through which it might share in the Good; rather, "being" is said of it only equivocally—as we might say that "truly being" for matter is actually "non-being." Thus, a simple lack is merely the state of "not being good," but a total lack is "Evil itself." A partial lack is the capacity to fall into evil, or is already a degree of it. What then should we conceive Evil to be? Not this or that specific evil, like injustice or some other vice, but that primary Evil which is not **D** yet any of these; these specific vices are like species of that primary Evil, distinguished by certain additions. <margin>* mentō <note>A textual variant or correction in the Greek margin.</note></margin> For instance, in the soul, there is wickedness and its various kinds, which depend on the matter the soul deals with, or the parts of the soul—as when one part "sees" <margin>* to urge <note>original: "horman"; a marginal correction replacing "to see" (horan) in the main text.</note></margin> while another part "urges" or "suffers." If someone were to suggest that external things are also evils—such as disease, poverty, or ugliness—we must ask how they relate to the primary nature of evil. Perhaps disease is a lack or excess in bodies made of matter, where order and measure are not maintained; **E** ugliness is matter that has not been conquered by Form; and poverty is the lack and deprivation of those things we need because of the matter to which we are bound—for matter has a nature that is essentially "neediness." If these things are said correctly, we should not say that we are the original source of evils, as if we were evil by our own nature, but rather that these things exist before us. As for the vices that seize men, they are held by them unwillingly; yet an escape from the evils of the soul is possible for those who have the strength, though not all are able. Because matter is present in the world of the senses, the "evil" which is human wickedness is present, though not in all men (for they have the power to overcome it). Those whom it does not affect are better, and they overcome it by that part of themselves which is not immersed in matter.

->**G**<-

WE MUST INVESTIGATE how it is said <note>referring to Plato's *Theaetetus* 176a</note> that "evils cannot be destroyed, but exist by necessity," and that they are not among the gods, but always haunt the mortal nature and this lower region. Was it said this way because the heavens are always...

<column-break/>

...entirely determined. But that which does not maintain this office, but proceeds from itself, existing in a certain grade that is neither perfect nor primary—like an image of the former—falls into a certain lack; it is filled with indefiniteness and looks toward the shadows. Now it possesses matter, looking into that which it does not discern; and as is commonly said, it looks at the darkness.

<margin>V
In what defect evil consists; how matter is the evil itself; how evil is made in the soul.</margin>
MOREOVER, if the lack of the Good is the cause for the soul seeing darkness and being submerged in it, the evil of the soul will be situated in the lack and the darkness, and that will be the primary evil. The secondary evil will be the darkness itself and the nature of evil—not first in matter, but even before matter. Or certainly, evil consists not in any lack, but in a universal lack. That which lacks the Good by a small amount is not yet evil; for it can be perfect according to its own nature. Indeed, that which lacks it utterly, which is Matter, is truly evil, possessing no portion of the Good. Matter surely does not even have "Being" (by the gift of which it might have possessed Good), but "being" is said of it only equivocally. Therefore, it is the lot of a defect not to be good; but a universal defect is the lot of Evil itself. A middle defect is the capacity to fall into evil, which is already a type of evil. Hence it is necessary to think of Evil not as this specific evil, like injustice or some other depravity, but as that which is not yet any of these; these are as it were species of that [primary evil], distinguished by certain additions. Just as in the soul there is depravity; and again, species of this, either according to the matter it concerns, or according to certain parts of the soul—as from the fact that it partly sees, partly is incited by desiring, and partly suffers. If anyone should place evils also outside the soul, it must be asked how they can be reduced to that nature of evil, such as disease, ugliness, and poverty? Perhaps they will say disease is a defect or excess in bodies composed of matter, which do not maintain order and measure. Ugliness is matter not at all overcome by form. Poverty, finally, is the want and privation of those things we need, because of the matter to which we are joined, which is so instituted by nature as to be indigence itself. Therefore, if these things are said rightly, it must not be said that we are the principle of evils, as if we were evil from our own nature, but that these exist before us. As for the vices that occupy men, they are held by them unwillingly. Nevertheless, a flight from the evils of the soul is provided for souls capable of it, though not all are able. The position of matter in bodies is the evil of the present nature; for the wickedness of men is not Evil itself, since it is not in all men (for the power to overcome it is given). Those to whom it does not happen are certainly more excellent. They overcome it, finally, by that which in them is segregated from matter.

<margin>VI
How something is contrary to the good; how forms separated from matter are contrary.</margin>
IT IS WORTH THE EFFORT to understand by what reasoning it was chiefly said by Plato that "All evils cannot be destroyed, but come by necessity. Nor are they among the gods, but they revolve assidously around the mortal nature and this lower place." Was it then said because the heavens are always free...

<meta>catchword: assiduously</meta>

<summary>Plotinus defines Evil as a total privation or "universal lack" of the Good, identifying it fundamentally with Matter. He argues that human vices and physical ailments like disease are secondary evils resulting from the soul's entanglement with the inherent "neediness" of matter.</summary>
