<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of evil, specifically moving from the definition of evil as "matter" or "lack of measure" to its role in the physical world and its logical necessity as a contrary to the Good.</meta>

### PLOTINUS' ENNEADS, BOOK I

<margin>A</margin> Does evil arise from the heavenly bodies? Surely not, since they move in a perpetual order and are carried along in beauty; neither injustice nor any other unfairness exists there, nor do the celestial beings cause injury to one another, guided as they are by an orderly moderation. But on the earth, there is injustice and an unfairness that lacks all order. For this is the nature of mortality and this lower place. But when Plato says that we must "flee from here," <note>original: "hinc aufugiendum esse" (Latin) / "ἐνθένθεν φεύγειν" (Greek). This refers to a famous passage in Plato's *Theaetetus* (176a-b) where Socrates discusses escaping the world's evils.</note> it is by no means spoken of earthly locations. For "fleeing," he says, is not to depart from the earth, but rather for a person even <margin>B</margin> while living on earth to become just and holy along with wisdom. This is the same as saying one must flee from wickedness, as if both wickedness and the things born from it are the "evils" belonging to man. 

Then, when Theodorus argued that evils could be removed from our midst if only men could be persuaded by what he said, Socrates denied that this was possible. For he says that evils happen by necessity, since it is necessary that something exist as a sub-contrary to the Good. <margin>C</margin> But by what reasoning can human evil—that is, wickedness <note>original: "prauitas" (Latin) / "κακία" (Greek); the moral corruption of the soul.</note>—be contrary to the Good itself? Truly, this wickedness is contrary to virtue. Virtue, however, is not the Good itself, but a certain kind of good which enables one to dominate matter. 

But how will anything be contrary to the Good itself? For the Good is not a "quality" <note>In Aristotelian logic, contraries usually exist within the same category, like "black" and "white" in the category of color. Plotinus argues that since the Good is above all categories, it shouldn't have a contrary.</note>. Furthermore, does the existence of one contrary everywhere necessitate that the other must also exist? Perhaps it could be so, provided that its contrary already exists— <margin>D</margin> just as where health exists, disease can also exist, yet disease does not arise by necessity. Perhaps Plato does not think this kind of necessity applies to every order of contraries, but only to the contrary of the Good itself. 

Yet, if the Good itself is essence, or rather "beyond essence," <note>original: "super essentiam" (Latin) / "ἐπέκεινα οὐσίας" (Greek). A central Neoplatonic concept: the ultimate Source (the One/the Good) is so transcendent that it is "beyond being" or "beyond essence."</note> what can possibly be contrary to it? That nothing is contrary to a specific essence is made clear enough through the study of individual things. Whether there is anything <margin>E</margin> contrary to Essence in a simple or absolute sense has not yet been demonstrated. But what could be contrary to universal Essence, or to the first principles of the universe? 

Perhaps non-essence will be the contrary to Essence; and to the nature of the Good, there will be a contrary if there exists a nature and principle of Evil. For both would be principles: the one of good things, the other <margin>F</margin> of evil things. All things that exist in either nature are contrary to one another, and therefore the two wholes are themselves contrary—indeed, more contrary than any other things. For other contraries are placed either in the same species or the same genus, and they share something in common in whatever they are found. But things that are separate, and which are constituted as the fulfillment of one nature or the other, must be contraries. What prevents them from being the most extreme contraries? Especially if contraries are defined as things that stand at the greatest possible distance from each other. 

<margin>G</margin> Truly, to Limit and Measure, and to all other things that are proper to the divine nature, the contraries are Infinitude, Lack of Measure, and all the other things that are said to belong to the nature of evil. Therefore, the whole of one is contrary to the whole of the other. The one [Evil] possesses an existence that is utterly false—the primary and true falsehood and lie—while the existence of the other [the Good] is "true being." Therefore, the falsity of the one is repugnant to the truth of the other. Again, that which exists according to the essence of the one is opposed to that which exists according to the essence of the other. For these reasons, it is well established—

<column-break/>

...of those things that are purely evil, always moving in order and carried along in beauty; neither is there injustice there, nor any other vice, nor do they do wrong to one another, but are carried along in beauty. But on the earth, there is injustice and disorder, for this is the mortal nature and this [lower] place. But the command that "one must flee from here" <margin>* things happening</margin> is not spoken of things upon the earth. For fleeing, he says, is not to depart from the earth, but even while being on the earth, to be just and holy with wisdom; this is what is meant. One must flee wickedness, so that "evils" to a person are wickedness itself and all that comes from it. 

And when the one talking with him [Theodorus] said that there would be a removal of evils if he could persuade men of what he said, Socrates replied that this could not happen, for there is a necessity for evils to exist: since there must be something contrary to the Good. But how is it possible for the wickedness concerning man to be contrary to that Good? For this [wickedness] is contrary to virtue; yet virtue is not the Good, but "a good" that makes one master matter. But to that Absolute Good, how could this wickedness be contrary? For the Good is surely not a "quality." 

And what necessity is there that everywhere, if there is one of two contraries, there must be the other? For though they may be connected, let it be granted that a contrary exists only if its opposite is already there—just as when health exists, it is possible for disease to exist, but not out of necessity. Or perhaps it is not necessary to say this is true of *every* contrary, but it was said specifically regarding the Good. But if the Good is essence, how can there be a contrary to it, or to that which is "beyond essence"? That nothing is contrary to essence is a point trusted regarding individual essences, as demonstrated by induction. But it has not yet been demonstrated regarding Essence as a whole. 

What, then, shall be contrary to universal Essence and to the Firsts? Perhaps to Essence, the contrary is Non-essence; and to the nature of the Good, it is that which is the nature and principle of Evil. For both are principles—one of evils, the other of goods—and all things in the nature <margin>* and the</margin> of each are contrary. Thus the wholes are contrary, and more contrary than other things. For other contraries are either in the same species or the same genus, and they share something in common in those things in which they exist. But where things exist apart—where those things that make up the one are the natural contraries of those that make up the other—how could they not be the most extreme contraries, since contraries are defined as things most distant from each other? 

To Limit and Measure, and the other things which exist in the divine nature, are contrary: Infinitude and Lack of Measure, and the other things which the evil nature possesses. Thus the whole is contrary to the whole. And its "being" is a lie—the primary and true lie—while the other has "being" that is the Truth. Thus, that which is truly according to the lie is contrary to the Truth, and that which is according to its essence is contrary to the essence of the other; thus, it has been revealed to us.

<summary>Plotinus explores why evil exists, arguing that while the heavens are perfect, the mortal realm requires "evil" as a logical contrary to the "Good." He identifies the absolute nature of evil as a lack of measure and a form of "non-being" or "falsehood" that stands in total opposition to the divine Truth and Essence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical inquiry into whether evil is a "substance" and why it must exist in a universe created by a "Good" first principle. It transitions from a general definition of evil to the specific logical and cosmic necessity of its existence.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

It is not everywhere true that nothing is contrary to substance <note>original: "οὐσίαν" (Greek) / "essentiæ" (Latin). In classical logic, substances like "man" or "horse" were thought to have no opposites, unlike qualities like "hot" or "cold."</note>. For instance, we would admit that fire and water are contraries, even if they did not share a common **A** matter in which their heat, coldness, moisture, and dryness exist as accidents. If, however, they existed only as themselves, completing their own substance without a common subject, then even there, substance would be contrary to substance. Therefore, things that are entirely separated, having nothing in common and maintaining the greatest possible distance, are contrary in their very nature. For contrariety is not defined by what *kind* of thing they are, or by any specific category of being, but by the fact that they are most distant from one another, consist of opposites, and produce contrary effects. **B**

---

<margin>VII
How, if there is Good, is it necessary for there to be Evil? Is it because matter is necessary for the universe? For this universe consists necessarily of contraries; something would not exist if matter did not exist. The nature of this world is thus a mixture of Necessity and Mind.</margin>
BUT how is it necessary that if the Good exists, Evil must also exist? Is it because matter must exist in the universe? For this **C** universe necessarily consists of contraries. Indeed, it would not exist at all if matter did not exist. For the nature of this world is "mixed" <note>This refers to Plato’s *Timaeus*, where the world is described as a mixture of "Intellect" (Mind) and "Necessity."</note> from both mind and necessity. And whatever comes into it from God is good; but the evils come from the "ancient nature," by which Plato means the underlying matter not yet set in order. But how can he call it a "mortal nature"? For when he says that evils revolve around this place, he is indicating the universe as a whole. Or perhaps it is confirmed by what he says in the *Timaeus*: "But since you have been born, you are not indeed immortal; yet you shall **D** never be dissolved, being preserved by my will." <note>original: "δι᾽ ἐμέ" (Greek) / "mea virtute" (Latin). In Plato's dialogue, the Creator speaks to the lesser gods, explaining that though they are created (and thus naturally mortal), his power will keep them from ever perishing.</note> If this is so, it is rightly said that evils cannot be destroyed.

How then shall one escape them? Not by fleeing to another place, he says, but by acquiring virtue and separating oneself from the body; for in this way, one also separates from matter. Indeed, whoever is joined to the body is also joined to matter. He makes it clear how one "separates" or does not: to be "among the gods" means to be in the intelligible world <note>The "Intelligible World" is the realm of pure thought and forms, above the physical world.</note>, for there they are immortal. 

We may also consider the necessity of evil in this way: **E** Since the Good does not remain alone, it is necessary that by the "outflow" <note>original: "ἐκβάσει" (Greek). Plotinus uses the metaphor of light or water flowing out from a source; as it gets further away, it grows weaker and darker.</note> from it, or if one prefers to say, by the perpetual descent and distance from it, something "last" must eventually come forth, beyond which nothing more can be produced. This "last thing" is Evil. It exists by necessity because there must be something after the First, and therefore also something Last. This Last thing is Matter, which possesses nothing more of the First. And this is the necessity of evil.

---

<margin>VIII
How matter is the cause of evil: first through its forms, then through the soul. Although all good things lead to one Good, all evil things lead to and are referred to one Evil.</margin>
PERHAPS someone will object that we do not become evil because of matter, and that neither ignorance nor wicked desires arise because of it. For if a composition of the body causes wickedness, it is not the **F** matter but the *form* of the affection that acts as the principle—such as heat, cold, bitterness, saltiness, and all the various types of humors; furthermore, states of being "full" or "empty." And not just any fullness, but fullness of such-and-such a kind, and generally being "of a certain quality," which creates the difference in our desires and, if you like, the discrepancy in our false opinions. Thus, it would seem that *form* rather than matter is the evil. Nevertheless, such a person would still be compelled to admit that matter is evil <column-break/> and that it does not appear true everywhere that nothing is contrary to essence. For we would admit fire and water to be contraries even if no common matter lay beneath them, in which heat, cold, moisture, and dryness are mere accidents. If they were alone in themselves, completing their own essence without a common subject, then they would also be contraries: essence against essence. Things that are entirely segregated from each other, share nothing, and have the greatest distance between them, are contrary in their very nature. Contrariety does not happen because of what *sort* of thing they are, nor according to any genus of things, but because they are most distant from each other, and because they are constituted from opposites and produce contrary results.

He addresses the counter-argument that evil comes from physical qualities (like heat or cold) rather than matter itself, maintaining that matter is the ultimate root of lack and opposition.</summary>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD I

...be forced to admit. For whatever a quality produces while embedded in matter, it does not act as something existing separately, just as the shape of an axe does not cut without the iron. Furthermore, the forms that are in matter are not the same as they would be if they existed by themselves; rather, they are material organizing principles <note>original: "rationes" (Latin) / "λόγοι" (Greek) — these are the rational "blueprints" or structures that shape physical things.</note> already corrupted in matter and filled with a material nature. For neither does fire itself—that is, fire separated from matter—burn; nor does any other thing that exists in its own right perform the actions that forms, once established in matter, are said to do. Indeed, since matter is the mistress of that which appears within it, it depraves and dissolves the form, applying its own nature which is contrary to it. I do not mean that it brings cold to heat, but rather it opposes its own formlessness to the species of heat, and its own lack of shape to the form. It opposes excess and defect to a nature that is measured, until at last it makes the form no longer its own master, but belonging entirely to matter. 

Just as in the nourishment of animals, that which is taken in does not remain as it was when it entered; but in a dog it becomes blood and entirely dog-like, and all the fluids turn out according to the nature of the recipient. Therefore, if the body is the cause of evils, for this reason also matter is judged to be the cause of evils. Perhaps someone might say that one ought to overcome such things; but it is no small task to overcome them, unless one flees. Now, more violent desires arise from a certain bodily composition <note>original: "complexione" (Latin) / "κρασίᾳ" (Greek) — the specific balance of "humors" or fluids in the body believed to determine temperament.</note>; different people have different desires, so that it is not easy for just anyone to overcome them. What of the fact that some are more dull and unfit for judgment? This is because they are naturally "cold" and sluggish in movement; others, by contrast, are carried away by an unbridled lightness. 

Our own changing states according to the times testify to this: for when we are full, we desire and think in one way; when we are empty, in another; and indeed, when we are replenished, we are accustomed to being affected differently. Finally, to sum up: in the first place, that which is entirely devoid of measure is evil; but that which exists in a nature devoid of measure—whether by likeness or participation—is evil in the second degree, because it has happened to be associated with it. Again, darkness is evil in the first degree, while that which is darkened is evil in the following degree. Thus, vice—being ignorance and a lack of measure in the soul—occupies the second place of evil, and is not evil itself <note>Plotinus distinguishes between the "source" of evil (Matter/Measurelessness) and the "result" of evil (Vice in the soul).</note>; for neither is virtue the primary Good, but it is considered good only insofar as it becomes similar to or a participant in the Good itself.

<margin>
IX
How that which is formless can be known by the soul, which is form and is accustomed to knowing through forms.
</margin>

How then do we know these things? And first, how do we know vice? We know virtue, certainly, through the mind and through prudence, for it knows itself. But how do we know vice? Is it perhaps like a rule by which we discern the straight from the crooked—is vice known by its lack of harmony with virtue? Truly, we do not perceive "total vice" by looking at it directly, for it is infinite <note>original: "infinitum" / "ἄπειρον" — meaning "unbounded" or "limitless," referring to the chaotic nature of evil.</note>. Therefore, we perceive it by a kind of removal <note>original: "ablatione" / "ἀφαιρέσει" — the process of defining something by what it is *not*.</note>, when we say it has absolutely nothing of virtue. We judge that vice is not a whole, but a deficiency of virtue. Thus, seeing a part, and assuming what is absent from what is present—that which is contained in the whole form but missing here—by this reasoning we judge vice to be in that which is deprived...

<column-break/>

**A** ...will be forced to), that it is evil. But if matter produces quality, it does not produce it separately, just as the shape of the axe does not cut, but the iron does. Furthermore, the forms in matter are not the same as they were when they existed by themselves, but are material principles corrupted in matter and filled with that nature. For fire itself does not burn, nor does any of the other things that exist by themselves perform these tasks which forms <margin>* produced</margin> produced in matter are said to do. **B** For the matter that is produced is the mistress of the phantom appearing in it; it destroys and dissolves it, imposing its own nature which is a contrary nature: not by bringing cold to the hot, but by wrapping its own formlessness around the form of the heat, and its shapelessness around the shape, and excess and defect around the measured, until it makes it its own, and no longer belonging to the form itself. **C** Just as in an animal, that which is brought in is no longer what it was when it entered, but becomes dog’s blood and everything dog-like, and all the humors are changed for the sake of that which received them. 

If indeed the body is the cause of evils, then matter would also be the cause of evils in this way. But someone else might say one ought to master it. Yet that which is able to master it is not pure unless it flees. And more intense desires come from a certain blending of bodies, and different ones from different bodies, **D** so that the thing in each person does not master them. Some are unpracticed and weighed down by bodies toward judgment, being cooled and hindered by the opposites, being light and unstable. These things are witnessed by the changes in our circumstances. For when some people have come, their desires and thoughts change; when they are empty, they are different, and when they are filled, they are altered. 

Let it be then that, **E** in the first place, the unmeasured is evil; and that which is in unmeasure—either by likeness or by participation—is evil in the second degree by its coincidence with it. And in the first place darkness is evil, and in the second degree that which is darkened is evil in the same way. Thus vice, being ignorance and lack of measure regarding the soul, is evil in the second degree, and is not <margin>* not the thing itself</margin> the thing itself which is evil. For neither is virtue the primary good, but it is good because it has been made like it or participates in it.

**F** BY WHAT then do we recognize these things? And first, by what do we recognize vice? For virtue we recognize by the mind itself and by prudence; for it recognizes itself. But vice? Just as we know the straight and the not-straight by a rule, do we also know vice as that which does not harmonize with virtue? Do we see it then or not see it—I mean vice? **G** Or do we not see complete vice, for it is infinite? By removal <note>Taking away all qualities to see what is left.</note>, we say it is nothing of this; but the vice that is not complete, we know by its deficiency compared to the parts. Even if we do not see it, by taking the part that is absent from the part that is present—that which is in the whole form, but is absent there—thus we speak of vice, leaving that which is deprived in the indeterminate...

# BOOK EIGHT.

...leaving behind that which is limited and deprived.
And indeed, looking upon matter itself as if at a deformed face, because reason does not rule there, nor can it cover the foulness of matter, we surely conceive of deformity as arising from a certain defect of form <note>original: "speciei" (Latin) / "εἴδους" (Greek) — the 'form' or 'species' that gives a thing its intelligible identity.</note>. But truly, how do we come to know that which has obtained no part of form? Perhaps by removing form entirely, we call all that remains—which lacks any form—'matter'; and in doing so, we admit a certain formlessness into ourselves while we strip away every form, if we are indeed to inspect matter. 
Therefore, this intellect becomes something else, almost a non-intellect: for it dares to look upon things that are not its own. Just as an eye, turning away from the light so that it may see the darkness (and thus it does not truly 'see'), because it leaves the light behind in order to see the darkness; for it cannot see darkness along with light. Nor, on the other hand, can it see anything without light, by which it might happen to see; thus, it 'sees' as much as it is possible to see nothing. 
Similarly, the intellect <note>original: "intellectus" (Latin) / "νοῦς" (Greek) — the higher, divine mind or intuitive reason.</note>, hiding its own light within its inner chambers and proceeding as if outside itself, goes into those things which are alien to it, not bringing its own light with it. Therefore, it undergoes a condition contrary to its own nature, so that it may look upon that which is contrary to itself.

<column-break/>

<margin>That matter is evil, not because it is of a certain quality; just as God is the Good without quality; also that matter is completely formless; and what form is.</margin>
Enough has been said on these matters for now. But since matter is entirely devoid of quality, by what condition is it said to be evil? Perhaps it is called 'without quality' <note>original: "ἄποιος" (Greek) — literally 'without suchness,' meaning it has no defining characteristics.</note> because it possesses no quality of its own among those it is about to receive, which will exist within it as in a subject. Yet, it is not said to be 'without quality' as if it has no nature at all. If it does have a certain nature, what prevents us from saying this nature is evil? I do not mean 'evil' as if it were endowed with a specific quality; for 'quality' is that by which something else is named as being of a certain kind. 
Quality, therefore, is an accident <note>A 'property' that is not essential to the thing's core being.</note> and lies within another; but matter is not in another, but is the subject around which every accident turns. Since, therefore, that which is called a 'quality' has the nature of an accident, surely matter—not having obtained such a thing—is said to be 'without quality.' Furthermore, if quality itself is 'without quality,' how can matter, which has not obtained a quality, be said to have one? It is rightly called both 'without quality' and 'evil' at the same time. 
For it is not judged evil because it has a quality, but rather because it has *no* quality; otherwise, if it were a form, it might perhaps be evil in a certain way, but it would not be a nature contrary to form.

<margin>Whether evil is the ultimate privation: and whether it can exist by itself and in itself: Answered by making a distinction.</margin>
But the nature contrary to all form is privation <note>original: "privatio" (Latin) / "στέρησις" (Greek) — the total absence or lack of a quality that should be present.</note>. Privation, however, is always found in another; in itself, it is not a substance. Therefore, if evil is situated in privation, it will certainly be evil in that which is deprived of form. Thus, it cannot exist by itself. If, then, evil is in the soul, privation will be the evil and the depravity within it, and it will not be necessary to receive anything from the outside to make it evil. For other arguments entirely do away with matter; while these thinkers do not believe matter is evil, even though it exists. Nothing, therefore, is to be sought from elsewhere as if it were evil; rather, he who places evil in the soul should place it there so that it is simply the absence of good. But if privation is of a certain form that belongs to being...

He uses the analogy of the eye looking at darkness to describe how the intellect must temporarily 'blind' itself to its own light to perceive the formlessness of matter.</summary>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS. BOOK I

...to confess. Truly, whatever quality lies within matter does not produce its effect by existing separately, just as the shape of an axe does not cut without the iron. Furthermore, the forms that exist within matter are not the same as they would be if they existed by themselves; rather, they are "material ratios" <note>original: "rationes materiales" (Latin) / "λόγοι ἔνυλοι" (Greek) — the formative principles or 'blueprints' of things as they exist concretely in the physical world.</note> already corrupted in matter and filled with its material nature. For neither does fire itself—that is, fire separated from matter—burn, nor does any other thing of those which are said to act when they are made in matter.

->B<-

Since matter is the mistress of what appears within it, it depraves and dissolves that appearance, by applying its own nature which is contrary to the form. I do not mean that it opposes cold to heat, but rather that it opposes its own "formlessness" <note>original: "orbitatem" (Latin) / "ἀνείδεον" (Greek)</note> to the species of heat, and its own lack of shape to the form. It opposes excess and defect to a measured nature, until it finally brings it about that the form is no longer its own master, but belongs entirely to matter.

->C<-

Just as in the nourishment of animals, that which is taken in does not remain as it was when it entered, but in a dog it becomes blood and everything "canine" <note>original: "caninum" (Latin) / "κύνειον" (Greek) — meaning the food is transformed into the specific substance of the dog.</note>, and all the humors turn out according to the nature of the recipient. Therefore, if the body is the cause of evils, for this reason also matter is judged to be the cause of evils. Perhaps someone might say that one ought to overcome such things; but that which could overcome is not pure, unless it flees.

->D<-

Now indeed, the more violent desires arise from a certain temperament of bodies; different desires belong to different people, so that not everyone can be easily overcome. What of the fact that some are more dull and unfit for judgment, as those who are cold by nature and unfit for motion? Others, on the contrary, are carried away by a certain unbridled lightness. Our various habits at different times testify to this: for when we are full, we desire and think in one way; but when we are empty, in another. Indeed, when we are replenished in one way, we are accustomed to be affected in another.

->E<-

Finally, to speak briefly: first, that which is entirely devoid of measure is evil. Secondly, that which exists in a nature entirely devoid of measure—whether by likeness or participation—becomes evil because of what has happened to it. Again, primary evil is "darkness," and in the following degree, that which is "shadowed" likewise becomes evil. Then, since vice is a type of ignorance and lack of measure in the soul, it holds the second place of evil; it is not "Evil itself," just as virtue is not the "Primary Good," but is considered good insofar as it becomes either like or a participant in the Good itself.

<margin>IX. How that which is formless can be known by the soul, which is form, and is accustomed to know through forms.</margin>

->F<-

By what means, then, do we know these things? And first, by what do we know vice? We know virtue, certainly, by the mind and by "prudence" <note>original: "prudentia" (Latin) / "φρονήσει" (Greek) — practical wisdom or the ability of the soul to see the truth.</note>, for it knows itself. But how do we know vice? Is it perhaps as we discern the straight from the crooked by a certain rule, and thus know vice as that which does not harmonize with virtue? But do we know vice by looking at it itself? Certainly, we do not perceive "total vice" by looking at it, for it is infinite <note>original: "infinitum" (Latin) / "ἄπειρον" (Greek) — in the sense of being unlimited, boundless, or lacking any defining form.</note>.

->G<-

Therefore, we know it by a certain "ablation" <note>original: "ablatione" (Latin) / "ἀφαιρέσει" (Greek) — the process of taking away or stripping characteristics to see what is left.</note>, namely when we say that it has nothing of virtue at all. We weigh vice—though not in its entirety—by the fact that it falls short of virtue. Seeing a part, and from the part present suspecting the rest which is absent—which is contained in the whole form, but is absent here—by this reasoning we judge vice in that which is deprived of—

He explains that we recognize vice not as a positive entity, but through the "ablation" or subtraction of virtue, seeing it as a deficiency of form.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's metaphysical inquiry into the nature of evil. Having previously discussed how matter corrupts the forms that enter it, he now explores how the human mind can perceive matter—which is essentially "nothingness" or "darkness"—and whether evil is a quality matter possesses or simply the absence of all quality.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

...terminating, leaving behind that which is deprived. And indeed, looking upon matter as if it were a foul face, since the Reason <note>original: "logos" (Greek) — the organizing principle or rational structure of the universe.</note> does not master it so as to hide the foulness of matter, we imagine foulness through the lack of form. But how do we know that which has attained no form at all? Perhaps by removing every form entirely, we say that whatever remains, which possesses no forms, is matter; we ourselves take on a certain formlessness in the act of removing all form, if we are to behold matter.

**B** Therefore, this is a "different" intellect, or rather a "non-intellect," having dared to look upon things that are not its own. It is like an eye turning away from the light in order to see the darkness; in doing so, it does not truly see, for it leaves the light behind to see the darkness, and without light, it cannot see. It does not see in the absolute sense, but rather "fails to see," so that it may experience darkness as far as is possible.

**C** In the same way, the intellect, hiding its own light within itself and proceeding as if outside of itself, goes toward things that do not belong to it. By not bringing its own light with it, it experiences a condition contrary to its own nature, so that it may look upon that which is its opposite.

### ->SO MUCH for these matters.<-

**ΚΑΙ** <note>This marks the beginning of a new section in the Greek text.</note> And being infinite, how is matter evil? Or is it called "without quality" <note>original: "apoios" (Greek) / "non qualis" (Latin) — Plotinus argues that matter has no properties of its own; it is a blank slate.</note> because it possesses nothing in itself of the qualities it will receive and which will exist in it as a substrate?

**D** Yet it is not said to be without quality as if it had no nature at all. If it has some nature, what prevents this nature from being evil? It is not evil in the sense of having a "bad quality"; for "quality" is that by which something else is called "qualified." Quality is therefore an accident and exists in something else.

**E** But matter does not exist in something else; rather, it is the substrate, and the accidents exist around it. Since the nature of "quality" belongs to an accident, matter—having no such thing—is called "without quality." Furthermore, if quality itself is "without quality" <note>A logical paradox: the concept of 'redness' isn't itself 'red'.</note>, how could matter be called "qualified" before it has received a quality? Therefore, it is rightly called both "without quality" and "evil."

**F** For it is not judged to be evil because it *has* a quality, but rather because it *lacks* quality. If it were a form <note>original: "eidos" (Greek) / "species" (Latin) — the ideal shape or essence of a thing.</note>, it might perhaps be evil in some way, but it would not be a nature contrary to form.

**Ἀλλ᾿** <note>New section: "But..."</note> The nature contrary to every form is "privation" <note>original: "sterēsis" (Greek) / "privatio" (Latin) — a technical term meaning the lack or absence of something that ought to be there, like blindness is the privation of sight.</note>. Now, privation is always in something else and does not have a substance of its own.

**G** If evil is situated in privation, it will be the evil of that which is deprived of form; thus, it cannot exist by itself. If, then, evil exists in the soul, this privation in the soul will be the evil and the vice, and nothing from the outside will be necessary. For this reason, some other theories would do away with matter entirely. Others say that the soul itself is the essence of vice. Therefore, one should not seek evil from elsewhere, but place it in the soul, defining it as the absence of good. But this privation, when it is imposed, is the presence of some form...

<column-break/>

**A** ...bounded, leaving behind that which is deprived. Yet, beholding in matter as it were a deformed face, because reason does not rule there, nor can it cover the baseness of matter, we surely conceive of deformity from a certain defect of species <note>original: "species" (Latin) — here used to translate the Greek 'eidos' (form/essence).</note>. But truly, how do we recognize that which has in no part obtained a species? Perhaps by taking away species altogether, we assert that the whole of what is left, in which species do not exist, is matter.

**B** Meanwhile, we admit a certain formlessness within ourselves while we remove every species, if we are to inspect matter. For this reason, this intellect is something else, almost a non-intellect: while it dares to look upon things that are not its own. It is like an eye turning away from light so that it may see shadows, and yet it does not see: because it leaves the light to see the shadows. For it cannot see shadows along with light; nor again can it see anything without light, by which it might happen that it sees as much as is possible.

**C** Similarly, the intellect, hiding its own light in its inner chambers and proceeding as if outside of itself, goes away into those things that are foreign to it; nor does it bring its own light with it. Therefore, it subjects itself to a condition contrary to its nature, so that it may look upon that which is contrary to itself.

### ->SO FAR enough has been said of these things.<-

<margin>x That matter is evil, not because it is of a certain quality, but because it lacks quality: just as God is good without quality, being formless: and what form is.</margin>

**D** Since matter is entirely devoid of quality, by what condition is it said to be evil? Perhaps it is called empty of quality because it possesses no quality of its own from those which it is to receive, which will exist in it as in a substrate; and yet it is not said to be "not qualified" as if it had no nature at all.

But if it has some nature, what prohibits us from saying that this nature is evil? I do not say it is evil in such a way as if it were endowed with some quality; for that very thing which is a "quality" is that by whose presence something else is also called "qualified."

**E** A quality, therefore, is an accident <note>original: "accidens" (Latin) — a philosophical term for a property that a thing has, which is not essential to its nature (e.g., being painted green is an accident of a table).</note>, and it lies in another. Matter, however, is not in another, but is the substrate around which every accident turns. Since, therefore, that which is called a quality has the nature of an accident, matter—having obtained no such thing—is called "not qualified."

Furthermore, if quality itself is "not qualified," in what way can matter, not having obtained a quality, be called "qualified"? Correcty, therefore, shall it be called both "not qualified" and at the same time **F** "evil." For it is not judged to be evil because it has a quality, but rather from the fact that it has no quality; lest if it were a species, it might perhaps be evil in some way, but it would not be a nature contrary to species.

<margin>xx Whether evil is the supreme privation: and whether it can exist through itself and in itself: It is answered by making a distinction.</margin>

**G** BUT the nature contrary to every species is privation: and privation is always in another, but in itself it is not a substance. If evil, therefore, is located in privation, it will certainly be evil in that which is deprived of species. Thus, it will not be able to exist through itself. If, therefore, evil is in the soul, privation in it will be evil and wickedness, and it will not be necessary to receive anything from the outside from which evil is made in it. For other theories do away with matter entirely; but these others do not think that [matter] itself, though it exists, is evil. Nothing, therefore, is to be sought from elsewhere as evil: but he who places evil in the soul...

<sig>g 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: places,</meta>

<summary>This page explores Plotinus's definition of matter as a "privation" or "formlessness" that the intellect can only perceive by turning away from its own light. It argues that matter is essentially evil not because it possesses a bad quality, but because it is the total absence of form and quality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation into the origin of evil. He has just established that matter is a form of "non-being" or "darkness." Now, he explores whether evil can truly exist within the soul itself, or if the soul is merely affected by an external evil (matter).</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD I

->A<- If the privation of the good exists in the soul, and if the soul produces wickedness within itself by its own reason, it would follow that the soul possesses nothing of the good. In that case, it would no longer have life, even while it remains a soul. But if it lacked life, the soul would be inanimate; thus, even while being a soul, it would not be a soul. Therefore, by its own reason, it must possess life. For this reason, it does not possess the privation of the good from within itself. It is, therefore, "good-like" <note>original: "boniformis" (Latin) / "agathoeidēs" (Greek) — having the form or nature of the Good.</note>, insofar as it possesses a certain trace of the Good—which is the Intellect—and it is not evil of its own accord. Therefore, the soul is not "primary evil," nor is that which is primary evil an "accident" <note>original: "accidens" — in philosophy, a property that is not essential to a thing’s nature.</note> of the soul, since the soul is never entirely devoid of the good.

<margin>
XII
Whether evil itself is not "pure" evil, and thus exists in the soul. The answer is that it is pure, and not in the soul.
</margin>

->C<- What then if one were to say that wickedness and evil in the soul are not the total privation of the good, but only a certain partial privation? Truly, if the matter stood thus—partially possessing and partially lacking—the soul would have a mixed perception, not "pure" evil; thus, we would not yet have found the "first" and "pure" evil. Furthermore, the good of the soul would reside in its very essence, while evil would be considered merely a temporary accident.

<margin>
XIII
Whether evil itself is an impediment in the soul: and how the soul descends into evil, namely matter.
</margin>

->D<- Unless, perhaps, evil is said to be an impediment to the soul, just as an obstruction is to the eye's vision. If this is so, then evil would be the *cause* of evil, and thus the cause would be something else entirely from evil itself. If vice is an impediment to the soul, then vice is certainly not "evil itself," but the cause of evil. For virtue is not the Good itself, but rather something that contributes to it. If virtue is not the Good, then vice is not Evil. Furthermore, just as virtue is neither Beauty itself nor the Good itself, so vice is neither Ugliness itself nor Evil itself. We have said that virtue is not Beauty itself nor the Good itself because the Absolute Beauty and Absolute Good exist before and above it. Therefore, virtue is judged to be good and beautiful only through a certain "participation." 

->E<- Just as the soul, ascending from virtue, encounters Absolute Beauty and the Good, so too, descending from wickedness, it encounters Evil itself. When the soul begins its descent into wickedness, it begins to "behold" evil—if indeed any such intuition of evil itself is possible. Finally, when it has fully descended, it undergoes evil; it enters completely into the "region of dissimilarity" <note>original: "regio dissimilitudinis" — a famous Platonic concept used by Plotinus and later St. Augustine to describe the soul's alienation from God.</note>, where, having been submerged, it is said to have fallen into "shadowy mud." 

->F<- Indeed, if the soul were to fall into total and utter wickedness, it would no longer possess wickedness as a quality, but would instead take on a different, inferior nature. For "wickedness" is still something human, being mixed with its contrary. Thus, the vicious man "dies" in the only way a soul can die. The "death" of the soul occurs while it is still plunged in the body—it is the act of sinking into matter and being filled by it. Even after it has laid aside the body, it remains rolled in that same filth <margin> * Behold </margin> until it finally returns to the higher realms and lifts its gaze up from the mud. Otherwise, this state is exactly what is meant by the saying that the soul "falls into Hades and falls asleep there."

<margin>
XIV
How evil in the soul is a "weakness." How the soul is joined to the body, and how it is separated.
</margin>

->G<- Perhaps someone might say that wickedness is a "weakness" of the soul. For an evil soul is easily affected and moved by anything, being carried away into every kind of evil, toward lusts... 

<column-break/>

->A<- If there is a privation of the good in the soul, and if the soul produces vice within itself by its own inner principle, the soul would possess nothing of the good. It would therefore not even have life, though it is a soul. The soul would thus be lifeless, if it did not even have life. So, while being a soul, it would not be a soul. It must, therefore, have life by its own principle. Consequently, it does not have the privation of the good from itself. Being "good-like," it has a certain trace of the Good from the Intellect, and evil does not belong to it. Therefore, it is neither primarily evil, nor is primary evil an accident of it, because all good has not fallen away from it.

->C<- What then if one says that vice and evil in the soul are not a complete privation, but a certain privation of the good? But if this were so, possessing some part and being deprived of another, it would have a mixed perception, and not "unmixed" evil. Thus, the first and unmixed evil would not yet be found. The good for the soul would be in its essence, and evil would be an accident.

->D<- Unless, perhaps, evil is an impediment to it, just as an obstruction is to the eye's seeing. But in this way, its evil would be "productive" of evil, and not "evil itself," just as the cause is different from the effect. If, then, vice is an impediment to the soul, it is productive of evil, but vice itself will not be Evil. Likewise, virtue is not the Good, but a "co-worker" with it. So, if virtue is not the Good, vice is not Evil. Furthermore, virtue is not Absolute Beauty, nor is vice Absolute Ugliness or Absolute Evil. We said that virtue is not Absolute Beauty or Absolute Good because Absolute Beauty and Absolute Good are before it and beyond it. Virtue is good and beautiful by participation. 

->E<- As one who ascends from virtue meets Beauty and the Good, so one who descends from vice meets Evil itself. Starting from vice, one contemplates it; the contemplation is already of Evil itself, and as one becomes part of it, one participates in it. One comes to be entirely in the "place of dissimilarity," and then, sinking into it, one falls into "dark mud." 

->F<- For if the soul were to fall into complete vice, it would no longer have vice, but would have exchanged it for another, worse nature. For vice is still something human, mixed with a certain opposite. The soul dies, then, as a soul might die. And death for it, while still submerged in the body, is to sink into matter and be filled with it. And upon leaving the body, to lie there until it runs back up and somehow removes its vision from the mud. And this is what it means "to go to Hades and fall asleep there."

->G<- But if someone should say that vice is a "weakness" of the soul—that the soul is passive and unmoving, or rather carried from anything into every evil, being moved toward lusts...

<summary>Plotinus argues that evil is not inherent to the soul's essence but is a result of the soul "descending" into matter, which he describes as a "region of dissimilarity" or "dark mud." He defines the "death of the soul" not as cessation of existence, but as being completely overwhelmed and filled by the influence of matter.</summary>

# BOOK EIGHT <note>Note: While the header reads "Book Eight," this text is actually from the First Ennead, the eighth treatise, in the standard arrangement of Plotinus's works.</note>

...immovable, indeed, towards desires, but it might provoke to anger, headlong into assents <note>original: "synkatatheseis" — a philosophical term for the mind's agreement to an impression.</note>, and easily yielding to dim fantasies, just like the weakest of things made by art or nature, which are easily destroyed by winds or by scorching heat. It would therefore be worthwhile to investigate, 
<margin>and the soul</margin>
what is this weakness of the soul and where does it come from? For surely the weakness in the soul is not like that found in bodies; rather, just as in the body weakness is an inability to perform a task and a susceptibility to harm, so here in the soul, it receives the designation of "weakness" by a certain analogy—unless, perhaps, matter is the cause of weakness for both. But let us approach the argument more closely: what is the cause of that which is called the "weakness" of the soul? For it is not density or rareness, nor dryness or thickness, nor a disease like a fever that makes a soul weak. It is necessary that such a weakness of the soul exists either in those souls entirely separated from matter, or in those joined to matter, or in both. If it is not in the souls without matter—for they are all pure and, as the saying goes, "winged" <note>original: "epterōmenai" — a reference to Plato’s *Phaedrus*, where the soul is described as having wings to soar in the divine realm.</note> and perfect, and their work is unhindered—then it remains that the weakness must be in the fallen souls, those that are not pure nor purified. In these, weakness would not be the removal of something, but the presence of something foreign, just as phlegm or bile exists in the body. The cause of the "fall" for the soul is more clearly grasped, and when we understand how it is born to fall, that which we seek—the weakness of the soul—will be manifest. It exists, then, in things that are matter; and there is a soul, and as it were, one place for both. For the place of matter is not in one spot and the place of the soul in another—as if the place of matter were in the earth and the soul in the air—but rather, the "place" for the soul that is said to be "apart" from matter signifies that the soul is not *in* matter. This means it is not united with matter. This means it does not become a single thing arising from itself and matter. This means it does not exist in matter as if in a "subject" <note>original: "hypokeimenō" — the underlying substance in which properties reside.</note>. And this is what it means to be "apart." But the powers of the soul are many; the soul has a beginning, a middle, and an end. Matter, being present, begs and, as it were, bothers the soul, wishing to penetrate within; but the whole place is sacred, and nothing is without a share of soul. Matter is therefore illuminated by the soul, subjecting itself to it, yet it cannot grasp that by which it is illuminated. For the soul does not endure matter, even though it is present, because the soul does not "see" it due to its own evil <note>original: "kakēn" — referring to the inherent badness or lack in matter.</note>. But the soul darkens that illumination and the light coming from the divine by mixing with matter, and makes it weak; matter provides the soul with the generation and the cause for entering into it—for the soul would not have come to that which was not present. And this is the "fall" of the soul: to enter into matter in this way and to become weak. Because all the powers of the soul are not present for action, matter hinders them from being present by occupying the "place" which the soul should hold, and as it were, it makes the soul "compressed" <note>original: "symprathēnai" (blended/compressed).</note>. That which the soul takes from matter, as if by theft, it turns into evil until it is able to run back up to the heights.

* to be mixed together
</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...prone to actions, headlong toward anger and truces <note>original: "inducias" — here implying a temporary cessation or yielding to impulse.</note>, inconsiderately yielding to the faintest judgments of the imagination, not otherwise than those things which are made very weak either by nature or by art. For these are easily corrupted by winds and whirlwinds. It is truly worthwhile to ask of the one who speaks thus, what is the weakness of the soul and where does it come from? For the weakness in the soul is not entirely the same as that in bodies; but just as there, debility is the inability to execute one’s own proper work and also to suffer very easily, so nearly here, a certain similarity of proportion has brought about the name of "weakness," unless perhaps matter is the same cause of weakness for both. But we must approach more closely by reason, and examine what is the cause of this which has received the name of "infirmity" in the soul. For neither a certain nature, whether dense or rare, or thinned out or fat, nor some disease like a fever, renders the soul weak. Furthermore, it is necessary that such a weakness of the soul be either in souls entirely segregated from matter, or in those joined to it, or in both. But if there is no weakness in those segregated—for they are all pure, and (as is said) "winged" and perfect, and they carry out their action unhindered—it remains that the weakness is in the souls that have fallen, since they are neither pure nor expiated. Their weakness is not the taking away of something, but the presence of something foreign: just as phlegm or bile in the body. Therefore, if we rightly and clearly comprehend the cause for which the soul falls, what we seek will already be discovered by us: namely, what the weakness of the soul is. Truly, there is matter in the order of things, and there is soul: and as it were, one "place" for both. For the place of matter is not separate, and the place of the soul separate in addition—as if the place of matter were in the earth and the soul’s in the air—but the place of the soul which is said to be "separated from matter" signifies that the soul is not *in* matter. This indicates that it is not united to matter; that again shows that one single thing does not come to be from the soul and matter together. Finally, this implies that the soul is not in matter as if in a material subject; and that is the very thing which is meant by saying the soul is separated from matter. But the powers of the soul are many: for the soul has within itself a beginning, and again a middle and the last things. But matter, being present, affects it, and as if a bold beggar, it demands to penetrate within; but the whole place is sacred, and nothing is void of soul. Matter is therefore illustrated <note>original: "illustratur" — lit. "lighted up" or "illuminated."</note> by subjecting itself to the soul; and yet it is not able to comprehend that by which it is illustrated. For that [the soul] does not sustain it, even though it is present, since it does not even see it on account of its depravity. But matter obscures that illustration and the light proceeding from there by a sort of permission, and renders it weak; because matter itself provides the "generation" and the occasion for the entry into itself. For the soul would never approach unless matter were present. And that is the "fall" of the soul, to slip thus into matter and to become weak: because all the powers of the soul are not present for acting, since matter prohibits them from being present, because matter occupies the place which the soul itself contains, and as it were, makes it [the soul] be contracted. That which the soul snatches from there, as if by theft, it renders evil, until it is able to flee away from there. Matter, therefore, is the cause of both the weakness...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 81 regarding the source of evil in the soul. Plotinus argues that matter is the "primary evil" and that the soul's contact with it results in passions like fear and desire. # PLOTINUS, ENNEAD I.

...and is the cause of the soul’s depravity. For this reason, matter itself is **A** first evil, and the primary evil. For even if the soul itself generated matter by being affected, or if it were present and shared in it, and thus became evil, matter is certainly the cause by its presence: for the soul would not have approached it unless it had taken on its generation through its presence.

<margin>
XV
It is proven that matter is indeed altogether formless. Also how evil is made in the soul: how matter is itself evil.
</margin>

But if anyone should deny that matter exists, it must be shown to him from the discussions concerning matter <note>Plotinus refers here to his other treatises specifically on the nature of matter, such as Ennead II.4.</note> how necessary its existence <note>original: "hypostaseōs" — a term referring to the underlying reality or substance of a thing.</note> is. For many things are brought forward there in support of this view. Furthermore, if anyone should altogether deny that evil exists in the order **B** of things, he will also be compelled to do away with the good: and whatever is to be desired anywhere, and desire itself, and likewise avoidance, and again intelligence. For desire is of the good, but avoidance is of evil. Finally, intelligence and prudence deal simultaneously with the good and the evil: and intelligence itself is placed in the number of the good things. It is necessary, therefore, that there be the good; and again, the pure good; and also that which is mixed from good and **C** evil. Likewise, that which participates in more evil already declines toward that which is total evil; but that which has less evil, in that very respect where it has less, looks toward the good. Now indeed, what will be the evil of the soul? And for what soul, unless it touches upon an inferior nature? Otherwise, neither desires, nor pains, nor angers, nor fears will arise. For those who fear, do so because of the composite <note>original: "synthetō" — Plotinus refers to the human person as a "composite" of soul and physical body.</note>, lest it be dissolved. Again, pains and torments **D** arise when the composite is dissolved. Furthermore, lusts grow when something disturbs the composition itself; or they arise to prevent something from disturbing it, as if consulting a remedy. Fantasy <note>original: "phantasia" — the faculty of imagination or the way we receive mental impressions.</note> indeed is a certain impulse of the irrational living being brought in from external things; it receives the impulse through that which is not impassible. Finally, false opinions happen to the soul when it is placed outside of the truth itself. It is placed outside because it is not pure. But the instinct turning toward the intellect is something else **E** entirely. For it is necessary to cling only to the intellect, and for the soul situated in it to remain firm, and never to decline toward that which is inferior. But evil is not only evil on account of the power and nature of the good: since it occurs by necessity, bound and covered by certain beautiful bonds, like those who are bound with golden chains: lest it come openly into the sight of the gods, or men always have naked evil before their eyes: and if ever they should see it in any way, they might then be recalled to the memory of the good by the beautiful images of that same good. **F**

<column-break/>

...and is the cause of vice. Therefore, it [matter] is evil first, and the primary evil; for even if the soul itself generated matter by being affected, and even if it shared in it and became evil, matter is the cause by being present: for the soul would not have come into it, had it not received its generation through its [matter's] presence.

<margin>* of substance</margin>
If anyone says that matter does not exist, it must be shown to him from the accounts of matter the necessity of its * substance, through the many things said about it there. But if someone should say that evil does not exist at all among the things that are, it is necessary for him to do away with the good as well, and not even to have a desire for anything, nor avoidance, nor thought; for desire is of the good, but avoidance is of the evil; and thought and prudence are of the good and the evil. And this [prudence] is one of the good things. There must, therefore, be both the good, and the unmixed good, and that which is already mixed from evil and good, and that which participates in more evil, which itself already contributes to that [evil] in being totally evil; and that which is less [evil] in the degree it is diminished by the good. For indeed, what would be evil for the soul? Or for which [soul], if it did not touch the inferior nature? For otherwise, there would be no desires, nor pains, nor angers, nor fears; for fears are for the composite, lest it be dissolved; and pains and sufferings occur as it is being dissolved. And desires [occur] when something bothers the constitution, or they are working a cure so that it may not be bothered. Fantasy is a blow of the irrational [part] from without, and it receives the blow through the part that is not indivisible. And false opinion arises from outside the truth itself. It arises from outside because it is not pure. But the desire toward the intellect is of another kind. For it [the soul] must be alone, and established in it [the intellect], not leaning toward the worse. But evil is not

<margin>* or leaning</margin>
only evil because of the power of the good and its nature, since it appeared out of necessity, enveloped in certain evil <note>The Greek OCR says "kakoïs" (evil) but the Latin says "pulchris" (beautiful). In standard editions of Plotinus, this word is "kaloïs" (beautiful), matching the "golden chains" metaphor that follows.</note> bonds, like certain prisoners in golden [chains], it is hidden by these, so that while it exists, it might not be seen by the gods, and men might not always see evil, but when they do see it, they are accompanied by images of the beautiful into remembrance.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON
## BOOK IX, CONCERNING THE WITHDRAWAL
### OF THE SOUL FROM THE BODY,
### THE ARGUMENT.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial V featuring an ornate floral and vine pattern.</image-desc>
Whether it is ever permitted to forcibly release the soul from the body or not is a matter of dispute among certain Platonists; both sides bring forward patrons for their cause, namely Plato and Plotinus. Specifically, two authors, Olympiodorus and Macrobius <note>Olympiodorus the Younger was a 6th-century Neoplatonist; Macrobius was a 5th-century Roman provincial. Both wrote influential commentaries on Plato's works.</note>, seem to disagree. Macrobius’s side is favored by certain arguments of Socrates in the *Phaedo*, and by many arguments of Plotinus. Socrates's argument rests primarily on Orphic authority <note>References to Orpheus, the legendary musician and prophet whose mythical teachings formed the basis of "Orphism."</note>. Orpheus, under the universal providence of Jupiter (that is, the world-soul), places the providence of Dionysus (that is, nature). To him, the Titans (that is, Daemons) provide service; these, persuaded by Juno (that is, the care for progression and generation), are imagined to tear Dionysus <note>original: "Dionysium"—the god Dionysus. In Neoplatonic allegory, the "tearing of Dionysus" represents the fragmentation of the One into the Many (the physical world).</note> apart. This is because they divide his common duty—which is to generate and move all things equally—among themselves into specific portions, leading the species of things down to individual acts of generation. 

Furthermore, Orpheus imagines that because the Titans devoured the torn Dionysus, they were struck by lightning—that is, turned toward higher things by Jupiter—and that human beings were born from their fire <note>The "incendio" or fire refers to the soot/ash left behind by the Titans after Jupiter struck them; from this ash, humanity was created.</note>, meaning they are fortified by the divine gifts of those who were restored. And because humans were born from the Titans, who had been nourished by the body of Dionysus, he therefore calls them "Dionysiac," as if they were certain members of Dionysus sprouting anew from the germinating Titans. Thus, the human body is a part of the Dionysiac (that is, the mundane or cosmic) body, and human nature and life are a certain portion of that nature and life. If there is anything of a specific form or gift within us that exists fundamentally, it ought to comply with the whole. For this reason, we who are guarded by the providence of Dionysus (that is, universal nature) must remain in this custody, and not depart from here before God commands it. Likewise, we must preserve what we have received from that source for as long as we were given it to be preserved; we must not dissolve what God himself has bound, nor inflict violence upon the members of God himself. 

Socrates first introduces this Orphic opinion in the *Phaedo*, and then confirms it by the authority of Philolaus the Pythagorean <note>A 5th-century BCE Greek philosopher who was one of the first to write down Pythagorean doctrines.</note>. For Philolaus says, "Do not split wood on the path," that is, do not divide the body from the soul in the very span of life while the path still leads toward the end. Again, "When you have arrived at the sacred place, do not look back," that is, once you have attained the height of contemplation, do not turn back again to lower things. In the first precept, he commands that just as nature has bound the body to the soul, so you should allow nature to be the one to release the body from the soul. In the second, he instructs that just as our will has bound the focus of the soul to the body, so the will should release this focus from the body, and once released, not allow it to be bound further. 

Plotinus follows these Pythagorean and Platonic mysteries, weaving the first clause with a verse of Zoroaster, and confirms it thus: The soul, as something divine, ought to retain its own dignity in the manner of divine things; and meanwhile, with no envy or other disturbance, it should not prevent that which is subject to it—the body—from receiving some gift from it, namely life, as much as it can. Therefore, let the soul remain in itself, and never through any disturbance let it disjoin its companion, the body, from itself. For by that same disturbance, it would soon be revolved back either toward the same body or toward something similar; for movement itself draws one toward bodies, and a disturbed movement precipitates one toward lower bodies. But if the soul dwells within itself according to its strength, and meanwhile does not begrudge the body whatever life it has, and waits until the body itself fails—at least until it can no longer preserve the life received from above—then truly, with no movement distracted within itself and snatched by no downward impulse, it will exist entirely within itself outside the body, no longer wandering from this body into that one, but already translated from a soulish nature into an intellectual nature. 

After this, Plotinus asks: how does the body fail the soul? He answers in this way: When the body loses a certain <term>proportion</term> <note>original: "proportionem"—referring to the vital balance of humors and qualities that sustain life.</note> through which it won life for itself under the soul, it then fails the soul. It is like a piece of solid, green wood upon which a certain flame was applied via oil by the sun's rays through a concave mirror; eventually, when the oil is consumed, it soon loses the flame as well, but the light of the sun remains in itself just as before. Certainly, universal nature acts more, earlier, and longer upon the seminal matter of the man to be generated, in the manner of a universal cause, than does this particular human nature. For this specific nature—the human power—acts within the power of common nature. And in turn, universal nature is directed toward the specific character of this human body by the specific nature of the man. Therefore, in the fetus of this man about to be born, universal nature, directed through the specific nature of the parents, stirs and forms the seminal matter. It affects it with a certain proportion of humors and vital qualities, by which the fetus, as if by <term>bait</term> <note>original: "esca"—literally food or bait; here, the material conditions that attract the soul.</note>, wins for itself a certain life from the rational soul already present; through these things, it retains that same power. However, the ability to retain it for a fixed span is firmly given from the beginning, insofar as that conciliatory power flourishes in the body. Indeed, this power was inserted by universal nature so that the life of that man might be extended for a course of time suitable to the universe. 

If someone, while this power is still reigning of its own accord and still preserving life in the body, violently breaks this bond, he frustrates the counsel of universal nature as much as he can, intercepting the middle of nature's course which was meant to run through to a certain order. He sins, therefore, against the god Dionysus—that is, against the very nature of the universe; and against Jupiter—the common soul of the world and the ruler of common nature; he sins also against Saturn—that is, the divine mind, which commands our soul to be tranquil. This man, on the contrary, stirred by some disturbance, rages against the body; or at least, while he is occupied with such a task, he is distracted from simple and exalted contemplation. He sins again against Coelius <note>The Roman name for Uranus, the sky-god and father of Saturn.</note>, the father of Saturn—that is, the Good itself—while he begrudges the body entrusted to him its bodily good. Finally, he sins against himself: both because the soul had fashioned this animal and then destroys its own workmanship (which would not have fallen yet by its own fault), and because we need a long time to purge from the soul the stains of vices infused from our tender years, so that it may depart pure from the body and thus attain a pure state of life thereafter. Therefore, no one ought to take away the span of time from himself in which he might be able to purge his soul and prove himself more and more, and profit in moral virtue and discipline. For the ancient theologians hand down in their secrets concerning the return of the soul that souls sinning in this life are very much like those who have fallen upon level ground: to whom the ability to rise is again readily granted without difficulty;

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains the Neoplatonic argument against suicide, using the Orphic myth of Dionysus and the Titans to illustrate that the human soul is part of a divine order and must remain in the body until naturally released. He argues that violently ending one's life is a sin against the gods, universal nature, and the soul’s own purification process.</summary>
<keywords>suicide, Dionysus, Orphic myth, Titans, providence, Philolaus, Pythagoras, world-soul, purification, ethics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus (specifically Ennead I.9), focusing on the ethical debate regarding whether a philosopher may ever take their own life. It contrasts the strict prohibition supported by Macrobius and Porphyry with the more flexible interpretations of Olympiodorus.</meta>

HEADER: MARSILIO FICINO'S COMMENTARY.

souls, however, who depart from this life weighed down by the filth of their transgressions, are rather to be compared to those who have fallen from a great height into an abyss; having plunged headlong, they lack the power to rise again. They therefore warn us to use the granted span of life so that the opportunity for a perfect purgation is not lost. Macrobius, persuaded by these arguments of Plato and Plotinus, interprets the mind of both in such a way that under no condition is it permitted for anyone to lay hands upon themselves. Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was Plotinus’s student and editor of the Enneads.</note> seems to feel the same in his book *On Abstinence*. Olympiodorus understands and approves of these same arguments, yet from the words of these same authors, both here and elsewhere, he maintains that this may sometimes be permitted. To prove this point, he brings forward certain words of Socrates in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the soul and the death of Socrates.</note>. First, indeed, where he says: *A philosopher will perhaps not bring violence upon himself.* Since he said *perhaps*, he seems to have left a suspicion that it is sometimes lawful. Then, because he added the following: *Philosophers ought not to inflict death upon themselves, unless God brings about some great necessity, such as he has brought upon me at present.* <note>original: "nisi Deus ingentem necessitatem inuexerit qualem mihi in præsentia intulit." Socrates refers to his own legal execution as a divine necessity.</note> It is as if he were saying: *A philosopher placed in a similar necessity may rightfully release himself from life by death.* He further brings forward the testimony of Plato in the *Republic*, where he seems to permit a man utterly overwhelmed by a long and incurable disease to release himself from here, because he is useless to the city. For he says that citizens ought to live not for themselves, but for the city. Likewise, he adds the testimony of Plato in the *Laws*, saying: *a man gripped by an incurable crime, such as lust for his mother, or a desire for sacrilege, or a similar impulse which he sees he cannot restrain, it is fitting for him to remove himself from the midst.* Similarly, Olympiodorus seems to have understood certain words of Plotinus; first, where Plotinus says: *If someone perceives imminent madness, he will choose this very thing [death] then, not as something to be sought for its own sake, but to be chosen as a necessary condition.* Olympiodorus seems to have taken this to mean that one should rather drive the soul away from here than live with madness; for while madness persists, a man does not live as a man, but as a brute, and no opportunity for making progress is given. Someone might further confirm these things by what Plotinus says in the book *On Happiness* in this manner: *If a happy man should happen to be led captive, the path to his exit is ready; if not, he is permitted to live happily there.* <note>This refers to the "open door" policy of the Stoics and some Platonists regarding suicide as a final escape from unbearable circumstances.</note> 

To these points, Macrobius might respond thus: first, that Plato used that word *perhaps* (as is his custom) for the sake of modesty; second, regarding what he says about *unless God brings about a necessity*, he would say that it is then lawful for the philosopher not to kill himself, but to choose from the many conditions placed in his own choice which one he prefers. Furthermore, he would explain Plato’s words in the *Republic* and the *Laws* in this way: that Plato does not so much wish to permit anyone to kill themselves as he wishes to provoke a great love for one's country and to sharply call them back from impious crime. He would also take Plotinus’s words in the book *On Happiness* to mean that he releases the happy man from his shackles by calling the mind away from the senses rather than life from the body. Finally, regarding what he says in this book about choosing it as a necessity, someone might explain it as enduring the madness as a thing that must necessarily be borne, rather than bringing violence upon nature. This opinion is confirmed again by Plotinus’s words at the end of the disputation *Against the Gnostics*, where he forbids departing from here before the natural time. 

Against these points, Olympiodorus would argue in return that the words of Plato and Plotinus are being too twisted; on the contrary, it is fitting to undergo certain death, even by one’s own hand, for the safety of one's country, for honor, or for the preservation of truth. Likewise, one should sometimes separate the soul from the body by starvation <note>original: "inedia"—fasting or starvation, a common method of "philosophical" suicide in antiquity.</note> rather than permit it to live uselessly through long madness or an entirely incurable disease—or rather, live to the detriment of oneself and others, and far from every duty of reason. For in this way, even if one does not follow the order of a lower nature, one will follow the order of a higher nature, and the more perfect is always to be preferred to the imperfect; and this should be chosen not by impulse, but by deliberation. *These things they bring back and forth, and the dispute is still before the judge.* <note>original: "Hæc illi vltro citroq; afferunt, & adhuc sub iudice lis est." This is a reference to Horace’s Ars Poetica, indicating the matter is still undecided.</note>

<summary>Ficino presents a debate between Neoplatonic commentators on whether suicide is ever permissible. While Macrobius argues for a total prohibition, Olympiodorus suggests exceptions for cases of incurable disease, madness, or extreme moral failure.</summary>
