# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD I
### BOOK IX

# PLOTINUS
## THE FIRST ENNEAD
### BOOK IX

#### ON THE WITHDRAWAL.
#### On the leading out of the soul from the body. <note>original: "De eductione animae a corpore." The term "eduction" or "leading out" was a common philosophical euphemism for suicide.</note>

---

<margin>* He will not lead it out</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'O' featuring a philosopher or scholar seated in an armchair within a rural landscape.</image-desc>
One does not lead the soul out, so that it might not depart [burdened]. For if it were pulled out, it would carry something with it as it goes. Indeed, to "go out" is to move from one place to another. But the body must be allowed <margin>* it will all depart from her</margin> to depart entirely from the soul, until there is no longer any part of it shared, and the soul is completely outside. How, then, does the body depart? It departs when no bond of the soul is any longer tied to it—when the body is unable to bind the soul because its <term>harmony</term> <note>The "harmony" refers to the specific proportion of elements or vital forces that allow a body to host a soul.</note> is gone, which, while it possessed it, held the soul. But what if someone should devise a way for the body to be dissolved? In that case, he has used violence; he himself has departed, rather than letting the body release him. And when he dissolves the bond, he is not free from passion, but is driven by resentment, or grief, or anger. But one must do no such thing. If at the beginning of the process one perceives a coming [of madness], perhaps then—wherever the soul's eternity is concerned—one might act. Yet even if this happens, what must be done? It is not to be chosen as a root [principle], but as one of those things that are necessary by circumstance, not <margin>* application / introduction</margin> simply desirable. Indeed, the application of drugs to force the exit of the soul is perhaps not beneficial to the soul. And if a fated time is given to each person, to go before that time is not fortunate, unless (as we said) it is considered a necessity. Furthermore, if each person retains the same rank in the hereafter as that which they had when they exited, one must not extract the soul, while there is still the possibility of making progress.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' featuring a standing figure with a staff, possibly a traveler or shepherd, in a landscape.</image-desc>
Let no one thrust the soul out from the body by force, lest perhaps it should go out only to migrate into a similar place [of materiality]. Otherwise, it will depart carrying something of the corporeal with it, by which it will travel toward similar things. For to "emigrate" is to pass from one place to another. Instead, one must wait until the body itself fails the soul; for when the soul does not require a migration, it is then entirely outside. <margin>B</margin> In what way, then, does the body fail the soul? When, clearly, no power of the soul is tied within it any longer. This happens when the body can no longer bind the soul, having lost its harmony, which, when it formerly held it, held the soul as well. What, then, if someone takes care to ensure the body is dissolved from the soul? In truth, he would be applying force; the body would not then be dismissing the soul, but rather the soul would be deserting the body. It must be added <margin>C</margin> that when someone dissolves the body, he is not free from passion, but is compelled by anguish, or pain, or anger. But nothing of this sort should be done. And if someone feels a looming insanity, what shall he do? Perhaps, in truth, such a thing will not happen to a virtuous man. But if it should happen, it must be placed in that category of things called "necessary"—chosen because of the surrounding circumstances, but not chosen for its own sake. Truly, the devising of poisons to compel the exit of the soul is perhaps not expedient for the soul. And even if a fated time is given to

---

each person, it will hardly be done happily before that time, unless (as we have said) it is held to be a necessity. Finally, if each person retains the same rank there as that with which they exited, the soul is not to be extracted from the body while there is still a possibility of making further progress.

<summary>In this brief but influential text, Plotinus argues that a philosopher should not commit suicide, as a forced death causes the soul to depart while still attached to the passions and material residue of the body. He suggests that death should be a natural "falling away" of the body when its internal harmony fails, rather than an act of violence by the soul.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Enneads, soul, death, suicide, ethics, harmony, fate, poisons, philosophy of mind</keywords>

# MARSILIO FICINO’S
## COMMENTARY ON THE FIRST BOOK OF THE SECOND ENNEAD,
## ON THE HEAVEN,

### SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter D</image-desc>Plotinus’s dispute concerning the heaven consists of eight chapters. In the first and second chapters, he raises several doubts and, in the meantime, introduces certain points that contribute to solving these questions. In the third, resuming his doubts, he begins to untie the knots little by little, doing the same in the remaining chapters. He concludes summarily from all of these that the heaven is fire, and specifically a fire that is pure and solitary. Its form for our senses is light, and then a harmless and vital heat. However, he maintains that this twin form proceeds from the insensible <note>original: "insensibili"—referring to that which cannot be perceived by the physical senses, but only by the intellect.</note> form of that same heaven: he holds that the heat comes from life, while the light comes from the intellect, which is its everlasting substance. He further maintains that this intellectual life—that is, its soul, which never departs from divinity—is the cause of this immortality and perpetual motion. As for the corporeal nature of the heaven itself, although it is not strictly the cause of immortality, it nevertheless contributes to perpetual endurance through a certain suitability, as it aptly, opportunely, and willingly obeys its ever-preserving cause. Let this serve as the summary of the whole book thus far.

---

->Since the world is corporeal, it is neither from itself, nor through itself<-
->eternal, but through a cause that is entirely<-
->incorporeal.<-

<margin>1</margin>In the beginning, therefore, he seems to wonder how the world, since it is a body, is able to be eternal, just as many of the wise have agreed. For a universal body cannot be perpetual through itself, since it cannot even exist through itself—a point we have sufficiently proven in our *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his own major work, *Platonic Theology*.</note>. Nor is it easily demonstrated how it might be eternal through another cause, especially under the singularity of its own substance. Because it consists of dimension and motion, it seems likely to undergo division and change of substance. Furthermore, there is one matter for the whole world, for the work of a single Creator is one. One, I say, through one matter and form, being everywhere in agreement and sympathy with itself. This unity of form and matter creates that communion of acting and being acted upon among all things. Finally, since the nature of matter itself is utterly formless, and distinction usually occurs through forms, there seems to be no reason why matter should be distinguished from matter anywhere. Since matter is the lowest subject of all, entirely formless and equally greedy for all forms (even those that conflict with one another), it is perpetually changeable. For this reason, just as it is below the moon, so too in the heaven a certain potential for the change of form always lies hidden in matter, since the matter is the same everywhere. We mark this as follows: since the motion that flourishes in the soul is the "first motion" and therefore an action, while the motion in the body is "secondary" and therefore a "passion" <note>In this context, "passion" refers to being acted upon or undergoing change from an external force.</note>, this passion undoubtedly threatens the body with destruction. This is especially true because motion in the soul, as in an indivisible thing, does not tend toward dissolution, whereas in the body, as something divisible, it does tend that way in a certain manner. 

Nor is anyone permitted, in the manner of Averroes <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was a medieval Islamic philosopher who argued that the heavens were made of a unique substance where "quantity" or "dimension" could exist without traditional matter.</note>, to place dimensions in the heaven without matter. For if the first forms of all things (that is, the Ideas) have something material-like joined to them—namely, the "formable" essence of the mind—how much more do the lowest forms (dimensions) have something material, or rather something entirely material, with them everywhere. And if substantial forms are placed in a subject, how much more does dimension require a subject, being accidental and entirely ineffective on its own. Now, indeed, any corporeal form is nothing other than a "passion" of matter while that matter is being affected from elsewhere; nor is dimension anything other than the extension of matter itself while it is being extended by the same force that forms it, so that it may be formed more distinctly and abundantly. Therefore, the foundation of the world is matter and dimension together: changeable because of matter, divisible because of dimension, and from both, ineffective and passive, necessarily depending on something else. 

The world, therefore, is not eternal by the power of its own body, but rather by the soul as an external cause of immortality, and by the divine will as an external principle and end. If one considers the nature of God as existing always in the same act and being utterly immutable, the world seems to have been always and will always be from that source. Hence Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius"—referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage.</note> and Plotinus, because the "being" and "acting" of divine things are the same and the effect immediately follows that action, judge the world to be entirely eternal. If, however, one considers the free will in God and judges this to be the beginning of the world—which Hermes, Plato, and Plotinus also believe—it seems that the world can be made "new" by God without any novelty in the divine nature and without a new will. In this way, Plutarch, Severus, and Atticus <note>Platonist philosophers who argued for a literal beginning of the universe in time.</note> believe in a new world, taking the saying of Timaeus of Locri <note>The protagonist of Plato’s *Timaeus*, though Ficino treats the text attributed to him as an older Pythagorean source.</note> in this sense where he says: "God created the soul of the world, prior to its body both in power and in time." Whence Plato also says in the *Timaeus*: "the soul of the world was created prior to its body, both in virtue and in generation." 

Nevertheless, Plotinus, Porphyry, Proclus, and others explain these words of Timaeus and Plato as follows: that the "time" and "generation" by which the soul precedes the body are not an external interval, but a certain succession in the soul—within the discourse of the forms themselves—that precedes the motion of the world's origin. Thus, this motion comes from that one, and that one is the "age of ages" <note>original: "seculum seculorum."</note>. I pass over for now the opinion of Heraclitus, that every body of the world, even of the spheres and stars, is always flowing out and flowing back, and therefore either ceasing or being perpetually renewed. Plato also touched on this when he said the world is "always becoming, but never is"; as did Plotinus here, and Proclus in his commentary on the *Timaeus*. Even Plethon <note>Gemistus Plethon, the Byzantine scholar who inspired the revival of Platonism in Florence.</note> does not deny this is probable, and we ourselves prove in our *Theology* that the same can happen. If the entire body of the world always flows out and flows back in this way, while the substance of the soul remains, then the soul will not undeservedly be prior in time and generation to any "new" body of the world, if the world is always being made new from the old. Perhaps this is why the Prophets and the Evangelists say: "I saw a new heaven and a new earth." Likewise the Evangelist: "the world indeed passes away." But let us return now to Plotinus. Since the matter in the heaven is the same as that below the heaven, Plotinus asks whether celestial things are changed just as others are, and whether the species <note>The "species" here refers to the formal identity or "type" of a star or sphere, which remains even if the underlying material changes.</note> of any sphere or star always remains while the singular nature of each is changed little by little and renewed in a way, just as happens below the moon? To this, if someone should answer that the universe is perpetual because nothing can flow out of it or into it, since...

<summary>Ficino introduces Plotinus's work on the heavens, arguing that the physical universe is not eternal by its own nature (which is passive and material) but is sustained by the divine will and the world soul. He reconciles various philosophical views on whether the world had a beginning in time or is in a state of perpetual "becoming" and renewal.</summary>
<keywords>Cosmology, Eternity of the World, Matter and Form, World Soul, Timaeus, Heraclitus, Plethon, Celestial Bodies, Divine Will</keywords>

--- Page 143 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "On the Heaven" (Ennead II.1). In the preceding text, Ficino established that while the world is corporeal and thus not eternal by its own nature, it achieves immortality through the influence of the World Soul. Here, he explores the physical mechanics of this eternity, the nature of the four elements, and the role of the celestial "spirit."</meta>

...since it embraces all things. He has not yet sufficiently discovered why any sphere and the everlasting stars are so; for not every sphere and star contains all things. Neither has he attributed sufficient eternity to the whole world. For perhaps the world can still be changed, if not outside itself, then within itself, so that, just like our own animals, it often changes its individual substance while retaining the everlasting nature of its species. Finally, a doubt remains: whether this whole world, or at least the celestial part, is everlasting, and for what cause; and why in heaven the species and the individual <note>original: "indiuiduum"—referring to a specific, single existing thing as opposed to the general category or "species."</note> remain together, while under heaven <note>The sublunary realm, or Earthly sphere.</note> only the species itself remains while individual things are exchanged.

### *The Soul is indeed the cause for the heaven being immortal, but the heaven does not resist the soul in this.*

II. In the second chapter, therefore, he raises the same doubt, hinting everywhere that nothing mundane can remain perpetual by its own nature; so that you may remember all these things are made and preserved from elsewhere. As for what the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching.</note> say—that the heaven is everlasting because it is a "fifth body" <term>fifth body: also known as the quintessence or aether, a celestial element distinct from the four earthly elements.</term> besides the four elements—he passes over this negligently here. For by the very fact that it is a body, since it is not simply from itself, it certainly is not always through itself; especially since its nature is divisible and changeable. Finally, he signifies that the soul itself is the cause of the immortality of life for the heaven, which is also simply the cause of life. Yet, he holds that the celestial body and the universe are naturally prepared, if not to produce immortal life, at least to receive it; or at least that it does not in the least resist receiving it.

### *The causes by which the world becomes everlasting, and the distribution of the four elements.*

III. But in the third chapter he asks: how does this body contribute to a state of stability, when it is naturally inclined to motion? He answers that it is because it does not flow outward, but flows back inward. Therefore, it does not resist continuing perpetually in such motion; indeed, it contributes to it. If any animal, as long as it lives, is said to be the same because almost the same nature and form are preserved under the same soul—even though an "outflow" <note>Metabolic change or the shedding of matter.</note> occurs daily—how much more can the world be said to remain the same in substance as long as the same form continues under the same soul? For nothing flows outside of it, even if one imagines that in any part of the world the proper substance is exchanged by turns of outflow and reflux. Since nothing flows out of the whole, nor flows in from elsewhere, the entire body of the world seems to contribute to everlasting perseverance. 

The parts also seem to contribute to the same end. For even these spheres of the elements remain, at least in their mass and forms. The four seats of the elements themselves, disposed separately in the world, contribute to the same; things flee to these seats under the guidance of nature. Thus, the elements, although they are contraries, are so sequestered that they never destroy or confound one another. We treat abundantly the fact that there are four elements of the world, that the heaven is pure fire, and what kind of fire is there, in our *Compendium of the Timaeus*, in the fourth book of our *Theology*, and again in the fourteenth. 

Since fire differs from earth in most qualities, it is rightly distant from it in place as much as possible. Just as in the sphere of the world the earth is driven into the middle, so fire is extended into the outermost circuit of the whole. And if the earth is always stable, that which is most distant from it is surely most mobile; but no straight motion is everlasting. Therefore, fire by its nature is always mobile in a circle. Finally, if the greatest distance from the earth, perpetual circuit, and light are proper to fire, then the heaven is undoubtedly fire. Furthermore, just as the nature and power of the world itself are bounded by a certain higher cause, so too are its amplitude and figure; which, compelled by the invisible circle of the mind and soul, is similarly formed into a circle. Thus the figure is more equal and similar to itself, as well as more capacious and more fit for motion. 

Therefore, while fire seems to ascend—or rather, while it stretches itself out in every direction from the center—it is compelled to stop its step somewhere "upward," that is, at the circuit, and there to be extended and revolved in a circle, so that its figure and motion may reflect the circuit of its cause. The figure reflects the circuit consisting in the essence of the cause; the motion reflects the circuit performed in the action of the cause. Fire contributes to making the circuits of the world because of its expandable nature. The power of fire claims this expandable faculty for itself as something very effective, naturally rare, bright, mobile, and quite foreign to resisting and restraining solidity. 

The greatest solidity, which is proper to the earth, hinders expansion as much as possible. Hence the earth contributes to making the middle of the world; while air and water, being by nature intermediate, have filled the space between. Let no one distrust that fire, because it yields most easily and thus seems most easily to suffer, composes a heaven subject to no "passions" <note>In this context, "passions" refers to being acted upon or changed by external forces.</note>. For that which by wonderful agility seems to yield to being taken—while it seems to be divided—actually penetrates and divides, and immediately escapes every blow. 

Remember, finally, that the Divine Mind willed many forms in its work: both because it is itself "all-form," and so that from many materials (I mean forms), one supremely formal work might be summarily composed. It willed forms in this work that were far distant from each other in nature, so that from their blending, very diverse and formal grades of things might coalesce over a long span. Think, therefore, that these things were made together from the beginning, differing both in rarity and quality. These things, then, suddenly chase and flee from one another. Then all the most subtle things flee first and most quickly, both because they are more agile for motion and penetration, and because liquid things can float more conveniently upon solid things than the reverse. Thus the distinction of things was immediately made, with matter obeying the counsel of the Author. But meanwhile, a spiritual portion of the subtler things was preserved everywhere within the densest things—not so much by the density restraining it, as by the soul of the whole itself containing its own spirit everywhere, with the other souls conspiring toward that same office of breathing.

### *The heaven is the spirit, the breath, and the word of the world soul, and it is everywhere, though hidden.*

Such a spirit carries us further here. In the beginning, the celestial soul is not joined to a heaven already made; rather, by its own fecundity—which is both superior and most proximate to the heaven yet to be—it begets the heaven everywhere, while it, being supremely living, breathes everywhere. But what does it breathe? A vital breath, surely, and a sensory one; not one that must necessarily be felt by others, but one by which it both gives life and perceives other things. Since a breath <note>original: "flatus"—breath or blowing.</note> of this kind proceeds from the soul, it imitates the soul’s penetrating power, insofar as the breath itself, penetrating the universe, is infused into all things. Hence that saying: "The spirit nourishes from within." <note>original: "Spiritus intus alit"—a famous line from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (VI.726) describing the world-soul.</note> It also imitates the soul’s containing power, insofar as it—by its own "glue," so to speak—floats and encompasses other things like oil. To this, perhaps, that other saying tends: "The Spirit of God was moved over the waters," or brooded over them...

<summary>Ficino explains that the heaven's immortality is granted by the World Soul, while its circular motion and physical structure are determined by the nature of fire and the soul's "vital breath." He reconciles Platonic and Aristotelian views by arguing that the heaven's material—pure fire—is uniquely suited to obey the soul's eternal preservation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "On the Heaven" (Ennead II.1). Ficino is currently explaining the nature of the celestial "spirit" (spiritus) and how the World Soul generates the physical heavens through various stages of expression.</meta>

-># COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO<-

...waters, clearly nourishing materials that are cold in themselves, which yet grow warm through his vital—though hidden—power; and from this, they obtain the power of heating, as much as is hidden within. By this breath, by this "word" of the first soul (to speak in the Platonic manner), the heaven was made; indeed, such a spirit *is* the heaven itself. This spirit is a fire, at least as much more subtle and effective than our fire here as our fire is sharper and more powerful than air. This spirit is like a sight that is already a touch and a part of nature, having no proportion to our own sight or touch. It is also the "word" of the soul itself, now brought forth externally. For the first word of the soul is in the mind, entirely simple; the second is in the reason, already distinct there; the third is in the imagination and nature, now receiving motion and emotion <note>original: "affectum"—refers to a state of being moved or influenced, often translated as "affection" or "disposition."</note>; the fourth is in the "prolation" <note>original: "prolatione"—the act of bringing something forth or uttering it.</note>, that is, the heaven, now admitting dimension along with motion. 

Indeed, the magnitude of power in the soul, within its forces that are far distant from one another, creates the magnitude of dimension in the heaven. The motion of the soul creates motion in the heaven. Its "affect" creates the efficacy toward an effect. The rational power produces other forms in the heaven, while intellectual clarity provides light. Therefore, the heaven is like a spirit breathed out from the mouth of the more divine soul; and for that reason, it vivifies and nourishes all things. Again, it is like a certain eye and the sight of the soul, by which the affect and counsel of the soul are often indicated to us; by its rays and gaze, all things grow together. Light in the heaven, as far as it is transparent, represents the intellect of the soul; as far as it is in motion, it represents joy. Light alone is the image of intelligence itself; but the other forms, whether they are in the heaven or in other things through the heaven, reflect other "Ideas" <term>Ideas: In Platonic philosophy, these are the eternal, perfect archetypes of all things.</term> conceived in the intellect itself, which are conceived and discerned there through intelligence, just as other qualities are discerned here through light. And just as through the whole intelligible <note>the realm of pure thought/forms</note> world there is the same act of intelligence, so through this whole world, a certain transparent and lucid spirit is the image of that intelligence, producing and discerning forms everywhere just as the intelligence does. 

Hence Julian the Platonist <note>Likely referring to the Emperor Julian or a specific Neoplatonic commentator.</note> says, from the theology of the Phoenicians, that a certain translucent nature—shining in itself, as if tempered from transparency and light—is diffused through the universe and implanted in all things. It is never subject to foreign mixture nor to any passions; it is surely a certain act of pure intelligence—pure indeed, but proceeding outward in a way—and it possesses an invisible and incorporeal light, which is the cause of this visible but incorporeal light. So he says. In almost the same way, the Soul of the World, having conceived it in its own mind under the act of the first Mind, gives birth to this light in its nature, and there joins it with motion and affect; from there, it breathes it forth like a spirit, and now extends it with dimension. Yet it does not disperse it, but contains it within itself by its own circuit in a sphere; and as far as the soul pours itself out, so far does it surround the heaven, and it brings forth from the first origin a continuous spirit, as if it were the single breath of a single breather. 

But other souls, following this soul from time to time, also breathing by their own spiritual power into this spirit now flourishing everywhere, each reduces and shapes it into the form of its own intimate circuit. For this reason, different spheres are distinguished from one another in different places; they are arranged in position almost exactly as the breathing souls are arranged by nature. But all souls always "conspire" <note>literally "breathe together"</note> in the common and perpetual breathing of the first soul. Such spiritual orbs, however, become denser near the center of the world due to the narrowness of the location, and in turn generate denser things around themselves. And the Earth remains infused as the orb that is most dense. But if compared to the Earth, the heaven will be judged as very thin, agile in motion, and vivifying that which is dense. Do not ask, therefore, for what reason dense things descend to the middle. For these things are dense precisely because they were allotted the middle from the beginning. 

Again, consider how much rarefaction and condensation avail in the mutual generation of elements, lest perhaps you deny that, according to the varying density of the first spirit, various elements occur besides the spirit itself. But in the meantime, remember that rarity and density serve the actions and formations of the Ideas in things to be generated. Conclude, then, that a certain animal spirit always sprouts from the World Soul like an offshoot of inner life, and that this spirit is fiery; it is, as it were, the animal light itself now stretched out into dimensions—a spirit active in light, potential in heat, and the fuel for generation everywhere. I mean the heaven, which is not only surrounding everything, but also infused into all things, a "heaven of colors" <note>original: "caelumque colorum"—perhaps referring to the variety of appearances in the physical world.</note>. It is the breath of the more divine soul, flying out under a form closest to the soul—that is, celestial, fiery, translucent, and immediately warm—soon swelling into air (which is somewhat more unlike the soul), and then compacted into water and earth. 

Within these three elements, however, the celestial spirit is present everywhere as the maker and preserver of all things; it is the closest thing to a flame and the "veil" of the soul, and the nourishment of all. Wherever other things are, therefore, the celestial spirit is present beneath them; yet wherever this spirit is, other things are not immediately present. Thus, all things are governed most closely by the heaven—I say by the very substance of the heaven, not just by celestial power, which necessarily requires its own substance everywhere. Thus even under the earth, certain things are generated as if they were celestial. Thus all things live by heat alone, and they live by a certain hidden heat, even those things which manifest heat seems to have abandoned. Thus where extreme cold appears, fire is kindled; and it is procreated in the mutual collision of cold things, with the heaven, clearly, doing the procreating. 

Similarly, in any animal, the soul continually produces a spirit infused into all the members, but in some places it exists alone, while in others it is involved with humors <note>bodily fluids</note>, and in others with the limbs as well. But particular souls produce this spirit (which is the vapor of the blood and by which they rule the body) from heated blood; however, rational souls receive the celestial spirit—with which they wrap themselves most closely—from the substance of the heaven itself, which is present everywhere. Plotinus confesses elsewhere that this spirit is also received from the souls of the earth; Plutarch, Johannes Grammaticus <note>John Philoponus</note>, Proclus, and Plethon bear witness that Aristotle also thought our souls were wrapped in this spirit here. From this, it is clear that the heaven is everywhere, so that both the whole and the individual parts are governed perfectly and with wonderful ease by the heaven in a continuous series; and rational souls, wherever they receive or possess a celestial body, have and possess it in a place natural to celestial things. 

Truly, this celestial fire, of which the poet says: "Fiery is the vigor of those seeds, and celestial their origin" <note>original: "Igneus est ollis vigor: & cælestis origo"—a quote from Virgil's Aeneid, Book 6.</note>; although it is infused in all things, it is mixed with none; for neither does the visible light proceeding from it mix anywhere, nor does manifest fire easily allow for mixture. Moreover, celestial fire is the only pure fire, neither suffering force nor inflicting it; it shines wonderfully, but is most sweetly warm if it is touched in any way, beyond any "affect." Manifest and burning fire, however, is not pure fire, but rather an "ignited element." Because it is generated more easily than other things, and because it generates and amplifies itself, shines the furthest, draws all things to itself, and is born everywhere, it has all of this from the heaven, which flourishes everywhere. Hence Theophrastus, in an entire book, admires the power of fire. 

Perhaps from this comes that "spirit" which the Egyptians say is infused into all things as the parent of natural things. Most truly, however, the nature of this spirit will appear if one imagines (which is perhaps permitted) that there are not many spheres of heat, but only one, both filling all things and surrounding them, which has that motion which they say belongs to the "first mover." All the stars would then be led by the motion of this sphere, and would also run through their own progression, with the heaven yielding everywhere without any offense, if indeed yielding is necessary. In this way, the stars will seem most of all to have lives, if they progress in the manner of animals, and are not simply fixed like planets. Thus, besides the souls of the stars, there will be a single soul for the entire sphere. I would perhaps defend these things as probable, if the authority of great men did not restrain me.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "On the Heaven" (Ennead II.1). In the previous section, Ficino described the heaven as a "spirit" breathed out by the World Soul, possessing dimension and motion derived from the soul's own powers. He now moves to a detailed comparison between the soul and the physical celestial body.</meta>

# ON THE BOOKS OF ENNEAD II.

->*The heaven is the image of the soul, and the individual things in the heaven correspond to the individual things in the soul.*<-

But let us repeat the whole matter from another principle. If you consider the heaven—which fills the entire world in its form and motion—to be far removed from extended matter, you will undoubtedly be thinking of the World Soul itself. Of this soul, the heaven is indeed the image, while everything else is merely a shadow. That soul is, therefore, an indivisible heaven; but the heaven is a soul already extended in space. Therefore, match each part to its counterpart, as one moves from an image to its archetype <note>The "archetype" or "exemplar" is the perfect, original pattern in the divine realm that physical things imitate.</note>. The soul is a simple form; the heaven is likewise a simple body. The soul has no parts; the heaven is never separated into parts. The soul completes its primary duty by a single act—that is, by its own self-awareness; the heaven performs all its tasks through a perpetual turning back upon itself. Furthermore, the soul is an unchanging essence, although it is mutable in a certain way through a formal change of "spherical discourse" <note>original: "discursionis sphæricæ mutatione." This refers to the soul’s logical movement, which Ficino compares to a circle because it always returns to its starting point in God.</note>. Similarly, the heaven does not change in its substance, even as it revolves in its activity. The soul always acts in the same way; and even within the diversity of its forms, it restores similar cycles of revolution. The heaven also moves without changing, and while it seems to change certain configurations and external states, it meanwhile preserves its center and circumference; and through the same circuits of time, it both repeats the same things and recreates similar ones. In the soul, the light of intelligence comes first; then follows the "affect" of the will, which is like heat. In the heaven, light everywhere precedes heat. And just as there the will is, as it were, the very limit of the intellect (to will what is understood), so here heat is, as it were, the limit of light—to shine and to be warm. But just as purely and broadly as it shines, so harmlessly does it warm. Hence it happens that in materials similar to heaven—that is, the diaphanous and translucent—illumination precedes heating; but in opaque things, it is the reverse. For these must first be heated, purged by heat, and made translucent, before they can become bright. Now, the acts of this hidden celestial fire, which thrives everywhere, are the manifest rays of the stars; and its image is the ether—that is, that sublime air closest to the moon, an "fiery air," I say. For the heaven alone is pure fire; the rest are called "ignited." But the heaven and the air—especially that sublime air where there is little or no solid resistance but a great deal of breadth—shine more purely and warm more gently. Water and earth, and terrestrial things, being heated more violently, also heat violently. Because the fire kindled among us is still more similar to heaven than the other elements, it has become a participant in light (which is something incorporeal) and is the most powerful of all things. It is as if it were alive with perpetual motion, dividing all things while remaining undivided, drawing all things into itself, and fleeing any foreign mixture. And suddenly, when it is released, it flees back into the celestial fire that hides everywhere. Perhaps this is why the ancients were afraid to extinguish fire, lest they seem to do violence to the power of a living celestial nature. Therefore, just as ignited matter is suddenly converted into the very act and form of fire, so too this fire flees from here into the form of heaven; and the form of heaven is considered to be always converted into the form and act of life. Indeed, the matter of heaven seems entirely converted into form. Truly, just as in a glowing vapor such as a comet, the very matter of the vapor is so reduced to the proper act of fire that no condition or action appears there except a fiery one; so the celestial form so far surpasses and absorbs its matter that no manifest condition of matter can be seen. This is what many mean when they say the heaven lacks "matter"—that is, it lacks the manifest passions and conditions of matter. Similarly, those who say that the vehicle <note>The "vehicle of the soul" (ochema) is a Neoplatonic concept of a subtle, quasi-material body that carries the soul down from the heavens into the physical body.</note> of our celestial soul is free from matter. This is what *Iamblichus* and *Proculus* <note>Proclus (412–485 AD), a major Neoplatonic philosopher.</note> believe. Now, since the nature of form is ultimately more powerful than matter, it is rightly the case that just as the lowest of forms—quantity—is so absorbed into matter that it seems to be matter itself, acting not at all and suffering infinite division (being nothing else than a passive extension of matter itself), so the most excellent of bodily forms—the celestial form—occupies and hides its matter entirely. Everything that results there is form; a bodily form, I say, but so bodily that it is almost "not-body." It is a kind of flashing-forth of an incorporeal life and a more hidden virtue, shining outward especially through the eyes of heaven—that is, the stars. Therefore, not without reason does *Iamblichus* say the celestial body has been so reduced into life that it *is* life itself, and its nature is now in a certain way incorporeal, having only this much of "body": that its parts are perceived to be distant from one another. Surely, just as in us this tangible body differs greatly from the soul, but the spirit itself (which many call the most subtle vapor of the blood) is like a kind of soul—so much so that the *Epicureans* and others, deceived by its proximity, judged this spirit to be the soul—so the rest of the body of the world differs more manifestly from the World Soul itself. But the celestial nature thriving everywhere—that "nurturing spirit" <note>original: "spiritus almus"—a phrase often associated with the life-giving force of nature or the divine.</note> fostering all things—deceived the *Stoics* and *Strato* by its proximity, so that they thought it was the divine soul and God. That Platonic poet, *Maro* <note>Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro). Ficino often treated Virgil as a philosopher-poet who hid Platonic truths in his verse.</note>, seems to have judged more correctly. For when he said, *“The spirit nourishes all things from within,”* <note>original: "Omnia spiritus intus alit" — from Virgil’s Aeneid, Book VI.</note> so that the spirit (which is by itself dissipable and accidental) might be ruled by a stable and organizing nature, he added: *“Mind, infused through the limbs, moves the whole mass.”* <note>original: "Totámq; infusa per artus mens agitat molem" — also from Aeneid VI. Ficino uses this to show that "Mind" (Mens) is superior to "Spirit" (Spiritus).</note> And when he named "limbs" and "members," he signified that the world is one single animal, living by a certain single spirit everywhere, and ruled similarly by a single intelligence. Ruled, I say, most easily and always. For the more that spirit is near to the soul through its purity, the more easily and longer it obeys the soul toward perseverance and order. And the rest of the body, easily penetrated by the spirit, is supported by it, and does not know how to deviate from its natural place, while the soul, being far more powerful, arranges and contains everything in its proper places; and by its own motion, it anticipates all motions, and revolves each thing in certain places and times according to the rule of its own revolution.

->*Although the world is said to be infinite in its endurance, it is not infinite in power, magnitude, or number.*<-

The universe, therefore, remains through infinite time, although it is not infinite in magnitude. For if it is very close to the eternity of the World Soul—that is, the Divine Mind—and is therefore eternal and vivified by essential life, it certainly always suggests life, and its body continually draws eternal life from there. Furthermore, if the soul always conforms this world to the ideas of the Divine Mind, then just as it preserves all species of things as motionless as the ideas themselves (while individual things are continually changed), so it contains this entire work as an indissoluble image of the whole Archetype. For just as any species of things in the universe is referred back to its ideas, so this whole is referred to this whole Exemplar. However, individual things here under a species change because of the succession of certain "seminal reasons" <note>The "seminal reasons" (rationes seminales) are formative forces or "seeds" within nature that direct the growth and development of physical things.</note>, which is carried out in nature and a certain "imagination" joined to nature within the World Soul, with the celestial motion meanwhile constantly contributing to the same end. Nevertheless, the same species is preserved everywhere because of the eternal perseverance of the ideas in the Mind, and of similar forms thriving in the soul, with the similar celestial restoration always assisting in the same. Truly, the world, although infinite in time, is not so...

He cites classical authorities like Virgil and Iamblichus to define the "spirit" that connects the divine mind to the physical world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Ennead II.1. The text begins mid-sentence, likely completing the word "mundum" (the world) from the previous page, as it transitions into a discussion on whether the universe is infinite in number or size.</meta>

...the world, whether in number or in size, is infinite, we briefly conjecture thus. We conceive of a fourfold infinity. The first is of power as well as perseverance, found especially in the supreme God. The second is of perseverance at least in divine works, which remain perpetually permanent because of Him. The third is of number; the fourth, finally, is of mass <note>original: "molis." In this context, Ficino uses this term to refer to physical bulk or the three-dimensional volume of the universe.</note>. An infinity of number seems to arise gradually through a certain perpetual succession of individual things, yet it never exists as a completed act all at once. For it is limited by the unity of the species as its boundary, and an uncountable multitude in actuality admits no order. Yet all things are defined under the First [God] by a certain order that is both common to all and specific to some. If a crowd devoid of order is not found even in the lowest things, much less is it found in the highest, where the highest order exists. For this reason, neither are there innumerable worlds, nor are there innumerable parts of a single world. Furthermore, infinite mass is farther removed from the divine mind than infinite number. Since the divine mind does not at all desire an uncountable number, much less will it tolerate an immense mass; otherwise, this mass would have received no order or limit from God. Nor is it permitted to imagine that a corporeal mass exists entirely of itself, or from many causes completely different from one another. This is a point we frequently refute in our Theology <note>original: "Theologia." This refers to Ficino's own major work, *Platonic Theology on the Immortality of the Soul*.</note>. Nor is it necessary that under one cause of all things there be more than one work; nor multiple worlds, one disjointed from the other. Indeed, we refute that in the Timaeus <note>original: "Timæo." Plato’s dialogue *Timaeus*, for which Ficino wrote an extensive and influential commentary.</note>. Nor, again, can the mass of a single world be entirely immense; otherwise, it would either be divided into many members or exist as a single mass everywhere. If it were cut into an infinite number of parts, there would be no infinity of mass anywhere, but only of number; nor would it be a single or ordered work, but something entirely scattered and accidental. But if there were a single immense mass, no variety of things would remain at all, and this mass itself would receive neither order nor shape. And if such a machine were imagined to grow through the immense void everywhere beyond its circumference—at least toward the middle—if any middle could be imagined, it would be gradually reduced into a narrow space. Therefore, if it were moved, the circles marked in that mass would be so arranged that near the center one would always revolve more slowly than another, while toward the circumference, in turn, one would be driven continually faster than another. Thus, the motion would range from infinite slowness on one side to a similar infinite speed on the other. From this, the circuit of an immense mass would be completed in a single moment. From the other side, it would not move at all; indeed, there would be no motion. For infinite speed and infinite slowness both seem finally to meet in a state of rest. Another might object differently: there would be an immense space everywhere, both of the whole and of the parts relative to parts, which, through lines extended in length from the center, would become continually wider and more distant. Thus, the space of either the parts or the whole could never be traversed. Therefore, it would move in vain—or rather, it would not move at all. What more? The manifest difference of forms, the repugnance of qualities, and the obvious opposition of motions declare that the worldly mass possesses a distinction of members within itself. That this machine is not immense is shown both by the limit of every revolution and by the defined order of the whole. That it is spherical at its summit is demonstrated by its interior spheres, which clearly imitate the widest one. That all are connected to one another by a single cause is proved by the wondrous harmony of discordant things. Finally, we learn that it lives by a single life and is breathed upon by a single spirit from a certain mutual communion of acting and suffering, through which lower things easily receive gifts from higher things everywhere, and higher things seem to hear the prayers of lower ones and look out for their vows; and from any part of the world, however distant, a motion often results in any part that is rightly prepared.

## *It is confirmed that the heaven is everlasting, first by the benefit of the soul, then by that of the body.*

IIII In the fourth chapter of the book, pushing doubts aside for what follows, he proves the immortality of the heaven both by the reason of the soul and by the reason of the body. Truly, the summit of the corporeal order—that is, the heaven—conspires with the last of the incorporeal nature of divine things—that is, the soul—in such a way that it cannot be dissolved. Just as the highest air touching fire is always ignited, the life of the soul itself, since it hangs most closely from eternity and does not depart from it, is eternal. And since the soul itself, because of its natural proximity, is the bond of temporal things (as we show in our Theology), it is right that it should eternally reach those things which it has bound together. Likewise, since for so many ages it has not grown weary in ruling and moving this mass—as shown by the same steady pace of its acting—it will never be weary. This is especially true since the soul does not drive the body by force (the body being naturally balanced for such motion), nor can violence be brought here from elsewhere, nor are the parts of the world worn away, but rather they are changed into one another. Finally, if the soul, through its own eternal life (the nature of which is always to give life), has always provided life to the world, it will provide it always. Nor will that most divine soul ever repent of having benefited the world, as if it had either sinned when it began to do good, or were about to sin when it stops—a notion he refuted in the book against the Gnostic heretics <note>The Gnostics were early thinkers who believed the material world was a flawed creation of a lesser deity; Plotinus wrote a famous treatise (Ennead II.9) against them.</note>. As for what he says about fire, partly following Aristotle’s opinion and partly his own, understand it thus. This fire of ours, by a certain greediness, devours all sudden matter, and then, luxuriating from it, vomits out flame like a heat; by this, it consumes even distant objects. For since fire, because of its thin, expandable, and mobile nature, is easily dispersed when placed and mixed among foreign things, nature has granted it the ability to easily devour things nearby lest it perish soon. On the other hand, lest it destroy all things like a most powerful tyrant, it was granted in turn that it be more quickly extinguished. But truly, lest so noble a nature be lacking to the world, it was arranged so that it is recreated most easily of all things everywhere, and quickly grows from the smallest spark into something large. But celestial fire consumes nothing because it is not itself consumed; it is not dissipated because it never changes its place, nor is it ever abandoned by life.

## *Why celestial things remain everlasting both in species and as individuals. Composite things, however, only according to species; likewise concerning the twin souls.*

V The fifth chapter indicates that we should judge the maker <note>term: "opifice" (Demiurge). The craftsman or divine architect of the cosmos.</note> of the world or its parts to be not only the first Intellect, but also the World Soul, and the souls of the spheres, insofar as they are entirely intellectual and always agree as colleagues with the first Intellect in this work. It indicates again that if composite bodies were made directly from the substance of any celestial soul itself, they would be indissoluble. For there, both substance and action—that is, intelligence—remain; and from an entirely stable cause, there should be a stable effect. But because every such soul brings forth another from itself as a sort of [lower] soul, and pours out an image of itself and instills it into matter—from which that kind of life is now weak—therefore, this life keeps the celestial and simple bodies always undissolved, as they seem not at all to resist the conciliation of perseverance. However, it cannot restrain composite bodies against the attacks of conflicting elements. Here you will note that the celestial spheres remain both as a whole and in their parts; other simple spheres [the elements], however, no longer remain in all their parts everywhere, but remain as a whole; finally, composite things must remain neither as a whole nor in their parts. Nor should anyone object to anything in...

<summary>Ficino argues against an infinite universe, asserting that divine order requires limits in size and number. He explains that the heavens are eternal because they are uniquely bound to the World Soul and composed of a non-consuming celestial fire.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Ennead II, Book 1, specifically addressing the composition of the heavens and the relationship between the soul and the physical body.</meta>

### ON BOOK I OF ENNEAD II.

...especially in rational animals, with the soul remaining after death, and matter existing before, the view of the parts of an animal among the Plotinians is refuted. For this soul is not so much a part as it is the cause of the animal, and the subject of "prime matter" <note>Prime matter refers to the most basic, formless substance that underlies all physical things.</note> is rather that by which an animal is made. It is made, I say, properly from its own specific matter, which is already entirely adapted to its specific form. But when he says that the things within the heavens are not parts of the heavens, understand this to mean "below," not so much in physical location as in rank. For the heavens, although they flourish everywhere, are never separated from themselves. Where he says the heavens extend as far as the Moon, understand this as reaching the "lunar condition." For the lunar lot is the last in the ranks of celestial dignity. Indeed, the ancients call the entire region above the Moon "solar," and the following region "lunar." Finally, he declares that in the human fetus, once it is already shaped in the womb, life is infused by the powers of the free animals and the Soul of the All <note>The "Soul of the All" or World Soul is the animating principle of the entire universe.</note> toward that same end; meanwhile, the soul of the mother, together with the father’s power, contributes in the interim. Through this, life—like bait—draws the rational soul to the body, and in a way, the rational soul contracts that life to itself, preserves it under its own action, and leads it, should the generative process ever cease. In that state, the lower soul provides the state of being an animal simply as a form; but the superior soul bestows the state of being a rational animal, contributing a very small amount in the manner of a form toward its existence. And that indeed comes from rational power or action, since it seems to contribute not to the simple "being" of the form, but to being "such a kind." And it contributes to being "such a kind" to the same extent that the other soul contributes to "being" simply. Perhaps it can be said to contribute to existence in the manner of an "efficient cause" <note>An efficient cause is the primary agent that brings something into being, like a carpenter making a table.</note>.

---

->Individual elements are pure in themselves. Heaven is only fire.<-
->Likewise regarding metals and demons.<-

---

In the sixth chapter, Plotinus again brings up two doubts: whether there is only fire in heaven, and whether anything flows down from there. He solves the first in both this sixth and the seventh chapters, and the other in the eighth. I say that there is fire in it, and at the same time no earth—or rather, Timaeus <note>A character in Plato’s dialogue of the same name who describes the creation of the universe.</note> thinks there is a certain solidity or resistance, a sort of earthy consistency, so that it can be seen through fiery clarity and touched through earthy solidity. But by whom is it so perceived? Not primarily by others. For the whole world was not established for the sake of individual parts, since it is the most perfect of all these and their final end; rather, it was established so that it might first be perceived by itself. For when the body was joined to the World Soul (which was in a sense born first) as its own proper body, it was probable that it would be such a thing as would be most akin and most known to the soul. Now, the soul properly knows its own body, and under the condition of the body, this is nothing other than being perceived. Thus, the body of heaven obtained light from fire so that it could be perceived by its soul in the manner of intelligence—which is "to be seen." It also had a certain resistance from solidity or an earthy-like consistency, so that it could again be perceived in the manner of essential life—which is "to be touched," first by itself, and consequently by others. For it could neither be seen through light unless solidity were also present, reflecting the visual rays in some way, nor could it be touched through solidity unless fire again gave it life.

Between these points, Plotinus indicates that if heaven is touched, whether by itself or another, a gentle heat is felt; but he conjectures that the earthy-like solidity is present more by reason. Finally, he insists that the nature of earth itself—which is both opaque (and thus opposite to light) and extremely dense (and therefore most unsuited for such motion)—is in no way present in the most bright and swift heavens. Likewise, neither is water, which is contrary to heaven because of its coldness, since heaven is the "primary heat"; nor again is air. For nothing is changed more easily than air into something else. Thus, if it approached so powerful a heaven, it would suddenly be transformed into the form of heaven. While he strives to agree that there is nothing in heaven besides fire, he brings into doubt that opinion of Timaeus: namely, that two solids and extremes always require two means <note>In Platonic physics, the elements are linked by geometric proportions; between the "solids" of Earth and Fire, two "means" (Air and Water) are needed to bind them.</note>. For perhaps that is more manifest in the numbers and dimensions of mathematical solids, as we have already explained in the argument on the *Timaeus*. In the elements, however, it is not so manifest, except perhaps in the composition of the whole world as it is arranged and distinguished by places.

Plotinus indicates, however, that fire or air can penetrate the earth without water, and water can penetrate the earth and glide into it without the benefit of fire and air. But if someone argues that the other two elements are always present in both earth and water, Plotinus responds that these two would not be necessary for joining them. But while Plotinus "plays" in this way, we must remember that water, far from the warmth of air and fire, freezes into ice and becomes crystal; therefore, it cannot easily penetrate the earth without them. But these points matter little to Plotinus, whose intention is to refute the common saying that "everything is in everything"—as if following the mind of Anaxagoras <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who taught that every substance contains a portion of every other substance.</note>—so that nowhere is anything pure in itself, nor can the essence of any thing be established or stand on its own without the essence of another. To this, someone might say that there is no earth unless it is glued together by the moisture of water; no water unless it is liquid through air; no air unless it is thin and light through internal fire; and conversely, fire never lives unless it is fed by moisture, nor does moisture stand unless it is held in by earth. But surely the formal "reason" of each thing—that very thing which makes it what it is—can be seen to stand without the addition of an alien nature. Since it can and should be understood correctly even without this; otherwise, if things were not something in themselves, they consequently would not be anything in others, nor would anything be composed of multiple things. 

Furthermore, since imperfect things (because they do not exist by themselves) depend on perfect things (which do exist by themselves), and the form of the whole is more perfect than the forms of the parts, it is right that above the elements which exist as parts in mixtures, there are elements in themselves as wholes set apart. They are, I say, as whole elements, though not as the "whole body" [of the universe]. There, again, the form of the whole body precedes as something more perfect; even if it does not precede in the physical work, it does at least in the Mind of the Maker. In Him, the intention of the whole form more generally precedes the intention of the parts toward that consequence, just as is evident in art. Finally, just as in the "Exemplar of the World" <note>The divine blueprint or the world of Forms.</note> the "reason" for the form of each species is distinct from another, so things are distinguished from one another in the work itself. They are distinguished, I say, both in their reason and their existence simultaneously, especially since the diversity is greater here than there. This is also evident to the senses, since contraries flee from one another insofar as they flourish as contraries. Therefore, just as composite bodies are composed internally of simple elements, so they are governed externally by simple ones. Many simple things—that is, ether, air, water, and earth—are governed by one thing: the celestial fire, which is the simplest of all. This "One" is governed most closely by the Soul; and through this fire, as if through a spirit, the remaining bodies (whether simple or subsequently composite) are governed by the Soul. For it is necessary that many bodies—which are indeed more unlike the soul—be inspired and moved by the one Soul of the world through a single body that is more like it. But to return to our purpose, every element must be something in itself, even without the mixture of another. For either there is some tiny portion of earth that is properly what "earth" is, or there is none. If some is granted, it is possible for earth to stand without water...

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

Whether the world is infinite in number or in size, we briefly speculate as follows. We conceive of a fourfold infinity: First, of power and perseverance in God, especially the Supreme Being; Second, of perseverance at least in divine works, which remain forever; Third, of number; and Fourth, of bulk <note>original: "moles," referring to physical mass or volume</note>. Indeed, an infinity of number seems to arise gradually through a certain perpetual succession of individual things, yet it never actually exists all at once. For it is defined by the Unity of the species as its limit, and an "innumerable multitude" cannot, in reality, sustain any order. Yet all things are defined under a certain order—partly common to all, partly specific to some. If a crowd devoid of order is not found even in the lowest things, much less is it found in the highest, where the supreme order resides. For this reason, neither are the worlds innumerable, nor are the parts of one world innumerable. Furthermore, an infinite bulk is even further removed from the Divine Mind than an infinite number. Since the Divine Mind by no means wills an uncountable number, it will much less tolerate an immense bulk; otherwise, this bulk would have received no order or limit from God. Nor is it permitted to imagine that a corporeal mass exists entirely of itself, or from several causes completely diverse from one another—a point we frequently refute in our *Platonic Theology*. Nor is it necessary that under one cause of all things, the work should not be one; nor that there be several worlds, one disjointed from another. This we refute in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation and structure of the universe.</note>. Nor, again, can the mass of one world be entirely immense; otherwise, it would either be divided into several members or exist as a single mass everywhere. If it were cut into innumerable parts, there would be no infinity of bulk anywhere, but of number; and the work would not be one or ordered, but entirely scattered and accidental. If, however, it were a single mass of immense size, no variety of things would remain at all, and this mass itself would receive no order or shape. And if such a machine were imagined to grow outward through an immense circuit on all sides—or at least toward the center—if a center could even be imagined, it would gradually be reduced into a narrow space. Therefore, if it were moved, the innumerable circles marked in that mass would be such that, near the center, one would always revolve more slowly than the other; toward the circumference, conversely, one would be driven continually faster than the other. Thus, the motion would range from infinite slowness on one side to infinite velocity on the other. Consequently, the circuit of the immense mass would be completed in a single moment. On the other side, it would not move at all; indeed, there would be no motion. For both infinite velocity and infinite slowness seem finally to meet in a state of rest. Another might object differently: the space would be immense everywhere, both of the whole and of the parts relative to other parts, which, through lines drawn lengthwise from the center, become continually wider and more distant. Therefore, the space of either the parts or the whole could never be traversed. Thus, it would move in vain—or rather, not move at all. What more? The very difference of forms, the conflict of qualities, and the manifest opposition of motions clearly declare that the worldly mass possesses a distinction of members within itself. That this machine is not immense is shown both by the limit of every revolution and by the defined order of the whole. That it is spherical at its summit is demonstrated by its interior spheres, which evidently imitate the most ample one. That all parts are connected by one cause is proved by the wonderful harmony of discordant things. Finally, we learn that it lives with one life and is breathed upon by one spirit from a certain mutual communion of acting and suffering, through which the lower things easily receive gifts from the superior everywhere, and the superior seem to hear the prayers of the inferior and provide for their vows; and from any part of the world, however distant, a motion often rebounds toward any part that is rightly prepared.

->It is confirmed that the heaven is everlasting, first by the benefit of the soul, then by that of the body.<-

**IIII** In the fourth chapter of the book, setting aside doubts for later, he proves the immortality of the heaven both by reason of the soul and by reason of the body. Namely, the summit of the corporeal order—that is, the heaven—conspires with the last of the incorporeal divine natures—that is, the soul—in such a way that it cannot be dissolved. Just as the highest ether touching the fire is always "ignitive" <note>having the quality of fire or being able to ignite</note>, so the life of the soul itself, since it hangs most closely from eternity and does not depart from it, is eternal. And since the soul itself, due to its natural proximity, is the "bond of temporal things" <note>original: "vinculum temporalium"</note>—as we show in the *Theology*—it deservedly continues eternally those things which it binds. Likewise, since it has not become exhausted in ruling and moving this mass for so many ages (which is shown by the same steady tenor of its action), it will never be exhausted. This is especially true since the soul does not drive the body through violence—the body being naturally balanced for such motion—nor can violence be brought in from elsewhere, nor are the parts of the world worn away, but rather they are exchanged with one another. Finally, if the soul, through its own eternal life (whose nature is always to give life), has always provided life to the world, it will provide it forever. Nor will the most divine soul ever repent of having benefited the world, as if it had either sinned when it began to do good, or were about to sin when it stopped—a point which Plotinus refuted in the book against the Gnostic heretics <note>Referring to Ennead II.9, "Against the Gnostics."</note>. As for what he says about fire, partly following Aristotelian and partly his own opinion, understand it thus: This fire of ours devours all nearby matter with a certain greed, and soon, luxuriating therefrom, vomits forth flame like a heat, which consumes objects even further away. For since fire, because of its thin, expansive, and mobile nature, is easily dispersed when placed and mixed among foreign things, it was granted by nature the ability to easily devour things nearby so that it might not immediately perish. On the other hand, lest it destroy all things like an all-powerful force, it was granted in turn that it might be more quickly extinguished. But so that a nature so noble should not be lacking to the world, it was arranged that it might be recreated most easily everywhere and from all things, and quickly grow from the smallest bits into something large. But celestial fire consumes nothing because it is not itself consumed; it is not dissipated because it never changes its place, nor is it ever abandoned by life.

->Why celestial things remain everlasting both according to species and according to the individual, while composite things remain so only according to species; likewise concerning twin souls.<-

**V** The fifth chapter signifies that for the sake of the Maker of the world and its parts, we must judge not only the first Intellect but also the Soul of the World, and the souls of the spheres, insofar as they are entirely intellectual and always agree as colleagues in this work together with the first Intellect. It signifies, again, that if composite bodies <note>Bodies made of multiple elements, like plants or animals.</note> were made directly from the substance of any celestial soul, they would be indissoluble. For there, both substance and action (that is, intelligence) remain; and from an entirely stable cause, a stable effect should arise. But since any such soul pours forth from itself another "instated" soul, as it were, and an image of itself, and instills it into matter—wherefrom such life is already weak—this life therefore preserves the celestial and simple bodies forever undissolved, as they seem not to resist reconciliation and perseverance. However, it cannot restrain composite bodies against the impulses of conflicting qualities. Here you will note that the celestial spheres remain permanent both as a whole and in their parts; other simple spheres <note>The elements of fire, air, water, and earth in their pure states.</note> no longer remain in all their parts everywhere, but remain as a whole; finally, composite things ought to remain neither as a whole nor in their parts. Nor should anyone object regarding
