<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s Ennead II, Book 1, focusing on the composition of the heavens and the nature of the elements.</meta>

# ON BOOK I OF ENNEAD II.

In the case of rational animals especially, where the soul remains after death, Plotinus intends to refute those who claim the parts of an animal are merely portions of primary matter <note>Primary matter refers to the formless "stuff" that underlies all physical reality before it is shaped by an essence or "form."</note>. For this soul is not so much a part as it is the cause of the living being, and the subject of primary matter is rather that by which the animal is made. It is made, I say, properly from a specific matter already entirely adapted to a specific form. When he says that those things which are "within the heaven" are not "parts of the heaven," you should understand "within" to mean lower not so much in physical location as in the hierarchy of order. For the heaven, although it flourishes everywhere, is never separated from itself. Where he says the heaven extends as far as the moon, understand this as reaching down to the moon's condition. For the "lunar lot" is the last among the grades of celestial dignity. Indeed, the ancients call the entire region above the moon "solar," and the region following it "lunar." Finally, he explains that in the human fetus, once it is formed in the womb, life is infused by the "animals of plants" <note>This refers to the vegetative soul, the most basic level of life responsible for growth.</note> and the soul of the whole toward that same end. Meanwhile, the mother's own soul, together with the father's power, contributes so that the rational soul may be drawn to the body as if by a bait <note>original: "velut escam," meaning food or bait</note>, and in a sense may bind and contract the body to itself, preserving it under its own action and leading it, should the generative process ever cease. In that state, the lower soul provides the simple state of being an "animal" by way of form; but the higher soul itself grants the state of being a "rational" animal, contributing just a little to its existence by way of form. And it does this from a rational power or act, since it seems to contribute not to simple existence by reason of form, but to "such an existence" <note>i.e., a specific kind of existence—rational rather than merely biological</note>. And it contributes to "such an existence" insofar as the other soul contributes to simple existence. It can perhaps be said to contribute to existence by way of an efficient cause.

->Individual elements are pure in themselves. Heaven is fire alone.<-
->Also concerning metals and demons.<-

<margin>VI</margin> The sixth chapter introduces two further doubts: whether fire alone is in the heaven, and whether anything flows down from there. He solves the first in both this sixth and the seventh chapters, and the second in the eighth. I say that fire is in it, and at the same time I say there is no "earth"—or rather, Timaeus <note>The narrator of Plato's dialogue on the creation of the world.</note> thinks there is a certain solidity, or resistance, or a sort of "earthy" consistency, so that through the clarity of fire it might be seen, and through the earthy solidity it might be touched. But by whom is it so perceived? Not primarily by others. For the whole world was not constituted for the sake of its individual parts, since it is the most perfect of all these and their final end; rather, it was made so that it could first be perceived by itself. For when a body was joined to the world-soul <term>World-Soul (Anima Mundi)</term> as its own proper instrument, it was probable that it would be such as to be most related and known to that soul. For a body to be known properly and relatedly, under the very condition of being a body, is nothing other than for it to be sensed. Thus, the body of the heaven obtained light from fire so that it might be perceived by its soul by way of intelligence (which is "to be seen"); it also had resistance from solidity or an earthy consistency so that it might be perceived again by way of essential life (which is "to be touched"). This sensing happens first by itself, and subsequently by others. Furthermore, it could not be seen through light unless solidity were also present, reflecting the visual rays in some way; nor could it be touched through solidity unless fire revivified it.

Plotinus indicates among these points that if the heaven is touched, whether by itself or another, a "gentle heat" is felt. He suggests that the earthy solidity is present more by a reasoning of conjecture. Finally, he maintains that the nature of earth itself—which is both opaque (and thus opposite to light) and extremely dense (and thus most unsuitable for the celestial motion)—is in no way present in the most lucid and swift heaven. Likewise, neither is water, which is contrary to the heaven because of its coldness (since the heaven is the "primary heat"); nor is air. For nothing is more easily changed into something else than air. Therefore, if it approached so powerful a heaven, it would be suddenly changed into the form of the heaven. 

While he strives to prove that nothing is in the heaven besides fire, he brings up that opinion of Timaeus: namely, that two solids and extremes always require two means <note>In Platonic geometry, to join two cubic numbers, two mean proportions are needed; here, air and water are the "means" between fire and earth.</note>. For perhaps that is obvious in the numbers and dimensions of mathematical solids, as we have already explained in the argument on the *Timaeus*. In the elements, however, it is not so obvious, except perhaps in the composition of the whole world as it is arranged and distinguished by places. Nevertheless, Plotinus indicates that fire or air can penetrate the earth without water, and water can penetrate the earth and flow into it without the benefit of fire and air. But if someone argues that the other two elements are always present in both earth and water, Plotinus responds that these two would not be necessary for the sake of "uniting" them. 

But while Plotinus "plays" in this way <note>original: "quasi ludit," suggesting a dialectical or lighthearted philosophical exercise</note>, we must remember that water, far from the warmth of air and fire, freezes into ice and becomes crystal; thus, it cannot easily penetrate the earth without them. But these points are nothing to Plotinus, whose plan is to refute the common saying—derived from the mind of Anaxagoras <note>A philosopher who taught that "everything is in everything."</note>—that anything is in anything, such that nothing is ever pure in itself, and the essence of any thing cannot be established or exist without the essence of another. To this, someone might say that there is no earth unless it is glued together by the moisture of water; no water unless it is made liquid by air; no air unless it is made thin and light by internal fire; and conversely, that fire never lives unless nourished by moisture, nor does moisture exist unless held together within earth. 

But surely it seems that the formal principle of each thing—that which makes it what it is—can exist without the addition of an alien nature. Since it can and should be understood correctly without this addition, otherwise if things were not something in themselves, they would consequently be nothing in others; nor would anything be constituted from multiple things. Furthermore, since imperfect things (which do not exist through themselves) depend on perfect things (which do exist through themselves), and the form of the whole is more perfect than the forms of the parts, it follows that above the elements which exist as parts in mixtures, there are elements existing in themselves as wholes and arranged separately. They exist, I say, as whole elements, though not as the "whole body" of the universe. There, the form of the whole body, being more perfect, takes precedence. Even if it does not come first in the physical work, it does in the mind of the Craftsman; in Him, the intention for the form of the whole precedes the intention for the parts that follow from it, just as is evident in art. Finally, just as in the "Model of the World" <note>The divine realm of Ideas or Forms.</note> the principle of each species is distinct from the others, so are things in the physical work distinguished from each other. They are distinguished, I say, by both reason and existence simultaneously, especially since the diversity is greater here than there. This is also evident to the senses, as contraries flee from one another insofar as they flourish as contraries. Therefore, just as composite bodies are made of simple elements internally, they are ruled by simple things externally. Also, many simple things—that is, ether, air, water, earth—are ruled by one thing, the simplest of all: the celestial fire. This "One" is ruled directly by the Soul; and through this fire, as if through a spirit, the remaining bodies—whether the primary simple ones or the composite ones that follow—are ruled by the Soul. For it is necessary that many bodies, which are quite unlike the Soul, be inspired and moved by the one World-Soul through a single body that is more like it. But to return to the subject: any element, even without the mixture of another, must be something within itself. For either some small portion of earth is granted which is properly "earth" itself, or none is. If some is granted, it is possible for earth to exist without water.

--- Page 150 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s Ennead II, Book 1. The previous page discussed how the soul acts as a binding agent for the body and the hierarchical nature of the heavens reaching down to the "lunar lot."</meta>

->### COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO<-

If there were nothing, then the earth would be nowhere, and water would not be able to bind together an earth that is found nowhere. Furthermore, the nature of air is one thing, and the nature of earth is another; indeed, their natures are quite diverse. If anyone were to say that the earth, in order to be earth, requires air within it, he would be saying that coldness, dryness, density, and weight require their opposites in order to be what they are. Moreover, air is something in itself before it is poured into the earth; similarly, earth is something in itself before it draws in air. Truly, air exists first in its own rarity before it is condensed into earth, and earth consists in itself before it is condensed. As for air: if it were condensed by another—namely, water—it would pass into water. For this reason, *Timaeus* <note>Referring to Plato's dialogue, the *Timaeus*, which describes the creation of the universe.</note> did not say that the earth requires fire in order to be earth; otherwise, coldness and weight would be ridiculously said to require heat and lightness in order to be coldness and weight. Rather, he said it requires fire so that it may be **visible**. For it is through light that both the eyes see and things themselves are seen, which are also colored by a certain participation in light. 

Light, however, is proper to fire. Since the earth is naturally opaque and neither shines by itself nor receives light within itself—while water and air, being **diaphanous** <term>diaphanous: transparent or translucent, allowing light to pass through</term> (that is, translucent and permeable to light), do not possess light themselves but receive it suddenly—it follows that fire possesses light through itself. This is especially true since other things clearly receive light from it, and fire leaves the light itself, as if its own, in nothing when it departs, even though it may leave behind heat for a time. From this it is established that fire is the heaven. 

Since fire projects light—as if its primary quality—sooner, faster, and further than it projects heat, it can certainly apply this action of its own (which is light) and the passion resulting from it (which is color, especially a clear color) to other things through which they may be seen, even though it does not mix itself into them. It grants light and brilliance to moister things as if they were more similar to the heaven, but to drier things it grants heat, and this heat is consuming, made so by dryness, confinement, and violence. Thus far we have shown that the earth is this very thing that it is without an intimate mixing of fire, air, and water. 

Again, it is evident through similar arguments that water can be water without the participation of earth. Indeed, when water is forced into an earthy density, it ceases to be water and becomes **crystal** <note>original: "chrystallum"; in ancient science, rock crystal or quartz was often thought to be water frozen so intensely it could never melt.</note>—specifically, after it has received a new and **substantial form** <term>substantial form: the essential nature that makes a thing what it is according to its species</term>, for before that it becomes ice. Therefore, earth does not make it be water, but rather makes it *not* be water. Furthermore, anyone who considers that nothing is softer, more yielding, or more penetrable than air—and nothing is more unsuited to these qualities than earth—will realize that air does not participate in earth. Therefore, earth does not make air be air, since it possesses a contrary property. 

If inferior things are something by themselves apart from others, how much more so is fire, which is intolerant of mixing and the most excellent of all things—that is, the heaven. Nor does it need earth to acquire dimensions and continuity; for because of its nature, which is most effective in matter, it expands its own matter into dimensions in a wonderful way. Likewise, since it suffers mixing least of all, it preserves its own continuity for itself. It possesses a certain resistance and consistency, which they call **solidity** in it, neither because of earth nor simply because of triple dimension, but through a certain density proper to itself in certain places. By this density, it not only reflects the rays of the eyes but also adapts the powers of higher things to lower things in a more kindred way. 

It is clear that nothing earthy underlies the celestial lights, because nowhere in the heaven is seen the kind of redness found in the color of clouds, which contain something earthy. Instead, the color is such as either a frequent flame or a gathered paleness of saffron is accustomed to produce. Certainly, *Plotinus* <note>The founding philosopher of Neoplatonism (c. 204–270 AD), whose work Ficino is translating and explaining here.</note> maintains that **solidity**, which resists in whatever way, exists differently in the earth than in other things. In the earth, it exists along with a certain rough and dry hardness proper to the earth, insofar as it is furthest distant from the heaven, which is the smoothest and most agile of all things. Elsewhere, it exists in its own proper way: in fire, its solidity is not through earth but through a density proper to itself in certain places. Just as in water, often not through earth but through a proper coherence and union, **crystal** is formed, as well as metal—namely, **gold**. 

He seems to believe that gold does not participate in earth but is made from water alone in the manner of crystal, but more tightly compressed within itself, in which there is a certain appearance similar to oil. From this it happens that **gold** is indissoluble because of its very tight concretion; it flows and liquefies at fire because of a viscous moisture; and because it does not participate in earth, it does not produce rust. It obtains its brilliance from the solar species and **Idea**. **Silver** behaves almost similarly, except that it follows the **Moon** instead. For the authors of **alchemy** <term>alchemy: the medieval forerunner of chemistry, concerned with the transformation of matter and the influence of planets on metals</term> attribute **gold** to the **Sun**, **silver** to the **Moon**, **lead** to **Saturn**, **tin** to **Jupiter**, **iron** to **Mars**, **copper** to **Venus**, and the silver they call "**living**" <note>original: "argentum vivum," meaning quicksilver or mercury</note> to **Mercury**. I approve of this distribution at present more than the one I followed in the compendium of the *Critias*. 

It seems that *Plotinus* accepted this opinion about metals primarily from the *Timaeus*, where metals are called "compacted and fusible waters" <note>original: "concreta fusilesque aquae"</note>; and **gold**, compacted from water between adamantine veins, is said to emerge like a flower. Copper is added because, since it participates in earth, it is consumed into rust by age as the earth reveals itself. Therefore, although *Plato* seems to place nothing of earth in gold and similarly in silver, he can probably be understood according to the opinion of others in this way: that whatever is earthy in gold is so tempered and exactly mixed with the other elements that it can never be separated from them. 

Let it be said that **gold** and every metal is called "water" because of a certain glutinous moisture from which all metals are made as if from a mother. This they call the first and hidden **quicksilver**, which they think is cooked and formed by **sulfur**, as if by the father of metals. From this, all metals are made, and they are diverse insofar as there is more of one or the other in that union, and according to whether this or that of the two is purer or more impure there, and according to whether the "cooking" is lesser or greater. These two elements in gold are considered most pure, most equal, and most highly mixed; it is almost the same in silver, but in the others, these things behave far differently. All metals are indeed liquefied at fire because their "mother" is a great, oily, and viscous moisture. Rocks, however, do not liquefy because they have a great deal of earth, yet they do not have a moisture that is so fatty or glutinous like oil. Thus we can interpret *Plato*. 

And where *Plotinus* says: "**Gold**, since it is water, is compressed into itself without earth," it can be understood thus: that is, when it is melted at fire like water, and then removed from the fire, it grows together again into itself without the addition of earth. But let anyone accept these things however they wish. Finally, let us return to the intended subject. If, in moisture, condensation alone either completes the form of crystal or restores the form of metal, why should the soul not, like a glue, continue the fire, connect it to itself, and preserve it under the form of life? 

Now, there are also the **igneous bodies of demons** <note>In Ficino's worldview, "demons" (daemones) are not necessarily evil but are spiritual beings or mediators inhabiting the upper elements.</note>, not joined through earth nor forced together through concretion like frost, but held together by the connecting power of the soul into their own proper form and reduced to a spherical figure. For there are demons above us in each of their spheres, like stars; although they are mostly hidden from us, they express a naturally orbicular figure in their bodies through the interior orb of the mind, with their disposition and place contributing to the same effect. Although they often show us whatever figures they please—while they either easily transform the agile matter of their body into various modes and then very easily re-form it into the previous shape, or through the affections and vehemence of the imagination (like pregnant women) they fashion any forms they like in a softer body. I set aside the fact that they often do not change their own body as much as they stir up various images in our imagination. Although demons are properly aerial animals, they are often named as both igneous and aqueous. For there are properly three...

# ON BOOK 1 OF ENNEAD II.

These are properly the orders of **daemons** <term>daemons: in the Platonic tradition, these are intermediary spirits or "guides" that inhabit the spaces between the divine heavens and the earthly realm</term> assigned to the three regions of the air. The first group inhabits the high air closest to the Moon, which is heated and illuminated by the warmth and motion of the heavens; they call this region "fire" and "ether." The second group inhabits the middle air, and the third group the lowest region. The highest air is called "fiery," the middle is "airy," and the lowest is "watery"—and the daemons are named similarly. Furthermore, this triply divided air is ruled (as they say) by a certain "airy triplicity" <note>An astrological classification referring to the three signs associated with the element of air</note>. Gemini rules the highest air, Libra the middle, and Aquarius the lowest; the same applies to the daemons. The ancients sometimes called these beings "gods"—not simply so, but "divine daemons." Just as some call similar living beings in heaven "daemons"—not simply, but "daemonic gods." I believe that celestial daemons are not in the region of the fixed stars, but in the region of the planets, like stars accompanying the planets. Maintaining a certain proportion, they follow the movements of the stars and planets; likewise, daemons in the pure air complete a "celestial dance" through appropriate progression. For perhaps one might think that just as with daemons, the stars and planets walk through the heavens with their own movements, after the manner of living animals.

->Heaven is fire alone. Likewise, any element is pure in itself somewhere, although in any element there are also certain qualities of the others. Likewise, heaven is everywhere. Likewise, of what sort that celestial Jerusalem <note>A reference to the spiritual or "perfect" city, often used by Ficino to describe the ideal state of the heavens</note> might be.<-

<margin>VII</margin>The seventh chapter confirms the response to the previous doubt using Platonic authority: namely, that Heaven is pure fire, and that any element is pure somewhere—meaning that it exists as itself even without the others, although they borrow and lend their gifts to one another as if from the outside. Furthermore, in any element there exists—I do not say the nature of the others, for then everything would be utterly confused—but a certain quality somewhat similar to the qualities of the other elements. Since the world is a single "animal" <note>original: "animal vnum" — Plotinus and Ficino view the entire universe as a single, living, breathing organism</note>, living primarily through one soul everywhere and made of one matter, every member necessarily has something in common with the others due to this union, and participates in the qualities of the others. This is just as physicians have discovered in the human body. Thus, celestial fire possesses not earth, air, or water, but a consistency or resistance somewhat similar to earth; likewise, a fluid liquidity and agility suited to air; and finally, a smooth, mild, and slippery equality very similar to water. It possesses something of the remaining elements in a similar way, yet they are not confused in that kind of mixing where the whole is blended with the whole, nor are the qualities and the natures of the matter themselves fused together. Thus, where Plato says in the *Timaeus*: "God kindled a light around the second sphere from the earth," he declared that in the heavens there is only fire, and from the qualities of fire, only light. I say "only light"—that is, the first and principal quality. For beneath this are all other qualities present there, namely a vital and mild heat, which contains the moving and forming action of all things. When Plato says "light," he understands the body of the sun itself, shining of itself—by a manifest light, through an inward light which is of a different kind from the light that flows from there through all things like an image of the sun. But its inward light again shines forth from the incorporeal light most closely; otherwise, it would not be incorporeal, nor could the light flowing from it be incorporeal. For what is incorporeal in a body, or exists around a body like light, comes from the incorporeal which exists in itself. It is clear that light is not corporeal, because it illuminates the whole suddenly and fills the whole without obstruction; many lights join into one immediately without resistance, nor are they stained by filth. Likewise, the sun's light is not the property of any subject; it does not remain in anything for a time, nor does it require a specific elemental quality in the subject to be present, but rather a purity very similar to heaven and the soul. This same light, without collision, condensation, rarefaction, or delay, pours itself through the widest space as easily as it immediately draws itself back into a narrow one. Thus, one ascends from a coal to a flame, which is already departing from thicker matter; from the flame, one arrives again at light, which leaves even thin matter behind. For it is no longer poured *into* matter, but rather poured *through* matter. Finally, from this visible light, one proceeds to the light of the celestial soul; by its vigor and motion, matter is extended in dimension, and light is poured out through that dimension, just as if a shining orb suddenly flashed forth from the rotation of a spark. But enough of this in the *Theology* <note>Referring to Ficino's own massive work, the *Platonic Theology*</note>. As for placing the globe of the sun next above the moon, this is not only Plato's opinion, but that of Aristotle, the Egyptians, and many other philosophers, both ancient and more recent. That there is a great distance between Saturn and Jupiter, and between Jupiter and Mars, is clear from the fact that Saturn completes its circle in thirty years, Jupiter in twelve, and Mars in two. It is also manifest that there is a great interval from Mars to the planets that similarly run their course in a year. Finally, we clearly find a great gap between these and the moon, which completes its course in a month. Since, therefore, the Sun, Mercury, and Venus revolve in a one-year period, and are thus close to each other, the question is: which of these three is closer to the Moon? It is probable that it is the sphere of the Sun, so that it may be better accommodated to the larger planet. But what mathematical reasoning says about these things has been sufficiently treated by others. Physical reasoning certainly seems to demand that the source of heat and the source of moisture—namely, the Sun and the Moon—be joined closely above this region of the world dedicated to generation, which primarily requires moisture as matter and heat as nourishment. Furthermore, the Sun and Moon possess contiguous "houses" <note>In astrology, a "house" or "domicile" is a zodiac sign where a planet is particularly at home</note>: the Moon has Cancer, and the Sun has Leo. They also have contiguous "exaltations" <term>exaltation: a specific zodiac sign where a planet's influence is considered to be at its most powerful</term>: the Moon has Taurus, and the Sun has Aries. Rightly, therefore, they also have contiguous spheres. Finally, in this order, Mercury will hold the middle position among the planets like a wise man; and deservedly so, since it must turn toward all equally and easily conform, so as to more quickly facilitate the actions of all. If, moreover, anything were to be believed by the eyes, I would say the sun and moon appear the largest because they are both closest to us. Practical experience seems to declare their proximity because they manifestly act upon us the most—so much so that the others, compared to these, seem to do almost nothing. Finally, the Moon, which is the lowest of the stars and alone does not possess manifest light, is deservedly alone beneath the sun and closest to the sun, so that it may more conveniently borrow manifest light from the most luminous body. It borrows it in the manner of a mirror, and similarly reflects the image of light. They call the celestial body "white," meaning luminous; and when they say "white," they mean "most shining." For what whiteness is among colors, brightness is clearly there.

By these things he implies that the form of paleness or redness is not actually in the stars, but appears so to us because of certain vapors. For we know that the purer the light of fire is, the brighter it is. Conversely, it grows red in thick matter, and pale in middle matter; but in the thinnest matter, it shines. He adds that the burning flame is neither in the celestial regions nor does it reach up to heaven; instead, it is either extinguished by the wind, or if it is in drier and more tenacious matter, it is reflected downward as lightning. Or if it flies up higher, it creates comets; but if the flame remains there longer, it is amplified through the ether and becomes milder,

### COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

and receive light from heaven. After these things, he says the entire heaven is light, although invisible to our eyes due to its thinness, yet the lights of the stars appear within it because of a certain density. Certainly, pure light cannot be seen at all, but only when mixed: either beneath the heaven with foreign matter, or within the heaven with a certain solidity and resistance that is, so to speak, "earth-like." I do not mean a solidity in heaven in the manner of some who say it resists touch (for this is truly a property of earth), but rather a solidity that either gathers or reflects rays. Indeed, this light—even the invisible part—is stretched throughout the entire universe, as is taught in the tenth book of the *Republic* <note>Plato’s *Republic*, Book X, describes the "Spindle of Necessity" and the light that binds the heavens</note>, like the sight of the World Soul, through which it perceives, touches, and nourishes its whole self. The Platonists think the sphere of the Sun is the sight of its own soul, and likewise, the other spheres and globes are the sights of other celestial souls. Whence we see that in the eyes of all creatures, "sight" is nothing other than a ray, and the shapes and qualities of the eyes are most similar to heaven—namely, that which is seen to be light, or a primary participant in light, which is color. But the stars and planets are eyes that are not only seeing, but visible: by which they may see living beings and govern them from above. For through denser rays, their powers are more easily accommodated to us. The remaining spheres are truly invisible eyes—invisible, I mean, to earthly eyes—for they can be perceived by ethereal eyes, that is, by the sense that flourishes in our own ethereal body <term>ethereal body: in Neoplatonic thought, a subtle "vehicle" of the soul that mediates between the physical body and the immortal spirit</term>. Plato proves in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the physical world</note> that this hidden light, or vital fire and spirit, is diffused through the universe. He says that the circuit of all nature, having embraced the remaining kinds of things in its circular path, and striving to meet itself within itself, constrains all things and allows no empty place to be left anywhere. Therefore, fire penetrates most greatly through all things; then air, since it is closest to fire in thinness; and others by a similar logic in succession. Here he seems to think that the first nature of this hidden fire proceeded from a certain "breathing" of the World Soul, and flowed into a circle from the soul's innermost circuit, by whose power the remaining elements coalesced. These were soon encompassed by the circuit of fire itself, and, as if restrained, left no vacuum within themselves. Likewise, since that fire desired to be amplified into an orb, it both met itself everywhere within and left no vacuum anywhere, penetrating all things deeply while being itself penetrated the least. Subsequently, it penetrated the air, and similarly the water, and finally the water penetrated the earth. Thus, if you ascend by degrees from the center through the middle orbs, where the earth is, you will find the three remaining elements present to each other rather than separated by matter; they preserve themselves for use by a most careful guardianship, as they are compared among themselves so that the terrestrial orb is the narrowest; the watery is wider, both filling the earth from within and rising above its surface; the airy is likewise wider than the earth and water; and finally, the fiery, by similar logic, is the widest of all, both nourishing everything from without and sustaining it from within. Arnaldus and Raymond <note>Referring to Arnaldus de Villa Nova and Raymond Lull, two famous medieval figures associated with alchemy and medicine</note>, thinking this fiery and vital spirit is implanted in all things, call it the **fifth essence** <term>fifth essence: or "quintessence," the pure celestial element distinct from earth, air, fire, and water</term>. They investigate most diligently by what machines they might separate it from foreign matter and, once separated, by what guardianship they might best preserve it for the most healthful uses. I omit what they hope for: that if they carefully obtain this from wine (as if it were something highly celestial), they will apply it to "celestial gold" <note>original: "auro caelesti"</note> as much as possible; the gold would soon drink this up as something most kindred to it, retain it forever, and become "potable gold" <term>potable gold: a legendary alchemical elixir made of liquid gold, believed to grant eternal youth or cure all diseases</term>. But let them see to those things. For my part, I know for certain that unless a spirit of this kind is in all things, many cannot perform what they promise; nor would that Platonic saying be true: that fire could be the "navel" or center of the world. It is indeed probable that the center and hinge of the universe is not an earthly torch, but rather fire. Again, what is written in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the immortality of the soul</note>, where he discusses mountains rising above the clouds—namely, that the "pure earth" lies in "pure heaven" in which the stars are—cannot be true unless either the heaven there is mingled with pure air, or only heaven is there, as if there were a single orb above the clouds. But let us set aside the unity of the orb for the present. Perhaps that most excellent **Theologian** <note>Ficino likely refers to St. John the Evangelist, describing the New Jerusalem in the Book of Revelation</note>, when he says the celestial city has twelve foundations, understands the city to be this vital spirit reigning everywhere. The twelve foundations are the twelve spheres of the world: namely, eight heavens above the ether, and again four heavens spread through the ether, namely air, water, and earth. He also describes twelve gates: three from the East, three from the West, three from the South, and three from the North, to show the four **triplicities** <term>triplicities: in astrology, groups of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element</term> of the signs. One is Eastern, that is, fiery: containing Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius. Another is Western, that is, airy: comprising Libra, Gemini, and Aquarius. Another is Southern, earthy: having Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn. Finally, another is Northern, embracing Pisces, Cancer, and Scorpio. Furthermore, when he says the whole city is made of pure gold, he means this fiery splendor is diffused through all things. He adds that this gold is like pure and transparent glass, that is, both translucent and shining at the same time. For if you were to apply a light (as if its own) to the transparency of glass, or if you added transparency to the natural splendor of gold, you would then have the substance of heaven; which is indeed everywhere translucent and bright at once, even if it does not appear so to us everywhere. Where the theologian adds a variety of precious stones, he signifies the lights of the stars, whether appearing to us or not. For in any sphere of the world above us, there are certain stars of wonderful size and power, even if not everywhere visible. It is necessary for the whole to shine in itself, if heaven is everywhere, if light is proper to heaven, and if light is the most excellent quality and the origin of other forms. However, that it shines differently in different stars does not happen because of different mixtures (as usually happens in our colors), but by certain specific degrees of rarity, density, and distance. Thus, the color of saffron looks red when gathered together, pale when diffused, and shines when most scattered. I omit how much our sight is deceived in these matters from a distance and through different media. But besides the lights, add to the celestial bodies various powers, from which various colors and actions proceed; not the kind that come from elements, but by a certain more hidden property, specifically a "formal" one, such as that by which iron is drawn by a magnet. For things among us that act in this way are said to act by celestial power.

->It is confirmed that heaven is eternal, both from its soul and from its body: and although it is fire, it is moved by nature in a circle.<-

**VIII** The eighth chapter responds to a doubt asking: Does anything flow out from or into heaven? It responds that nothing flows out. For the soul can contain its own spirit everywhere, and the spirit willingly obeys the soul; nor can any violence be brought from elsewhere into this most powerful thing. All things are first preserved in themselves before being converted into another. Since, therefore, nothing flows out from there, it is rightly necessary that nothing flows in to preserve it. Nor is it permitted to imagine that heaven is anything other than fire, so that its circular motion is natural. For circular motion is natural to every spherical body placed in its own location whenever it is moved; whereas straight motion is either a certain violent disturbance from a natural place or a sudden return to a natural place. In the midst of this, where he says the chief action of fire is heating, understand this to be the action of elemental and mixed fire. For the principal action of celestial fire is that which [is] principal...

COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

and to be allotted light from heaven. After these things, he says that the entire heaven is light, although invisible to our eyes due to its thinness <note>original: "tenuitatem"—referring to the subtle, non-material quality of celestial substance</note>, yet in it the lights of the stars appear because of a certain density. Certainly, pure light cannot be seen at all, but only when mixed: either beneath the heaven with foreign materials, or within a certain solidity and resistance in the heaven that is almost like earth. I do not mean a solidity in the heaven in the manner of some thinkers, which would resist touch (for this is truly the property of earth), but rather a solidity that either gathers or reflects rays. Indeed, this invisible light is extended, as is taught in Book 10 of the *Republic* <note>Plato’s "Myth of Er" describes the spindle of Necessity and the structure of the celestial spheres</note>, throughout the entire universe, like the sight of the World Soul, by which it sees, touches, and nourishes its whole self. The Platonists think that the sphere of the Sun is also the sight of its own soul, and likewise the other spheres and globes are the sights of other celestial souls. Whence we see in the eyes of all living things that sight is nothing other than a ray, and the shapes and qualities of the eyes are most similar to heaven, or to what is seen to be light, or that which partakes of light most excellently—that is, colors. But the stars and planets are eyes that are not only seeing [visual], but also visible: by which they may see animals, and from which animals may be guided. For through denser rays, their powers are more easily adapted to us. Truly, the remaining spheres are invisible eyes—I mean to earthly eyes—for they can be perceived by ethereal eyes, that is, by the sense which thrives in our own ethereal body. Plato proves in the *Timaeus* that this hidden light, or vital fire and spirit, is diffused through the universe. He says that the entire circuit of nature, since it has embraced the remaining kinds of things in its circular path and strives to meet with itself within itself, constrains all things and allows a vacuum to be left nowhere. Therefore, fire has penetrated most of all through everything; then air, as it is closest to fire in thinness; and the others in a similar sequence. Here he seems to think that the very first nature of hidden fire proceeded from a certain breathing [aspiration] of the World Soul, and flowed into a circle from the innermost circuit of the soul, by whose power the remaining elements coalesced. These elements, soon encompassed by the circuit of fire itself and as if restrained, left no vacuum within themselves. Likewise, since that fire, expanded into a sphere, desired both to meet itself within itself and to leave no vacuum anywhere, it penetrated everything deeply while being itself least penetrated: thereafter it penetrated the air, and similarly the water, and finally the earth. Thus, if you ascend step by step from the center through the middle spheres, where the earth is, you will find the other three present to each other rather than confused. Then where there is water, there are the other two; where there is air, there is also fire. Thus the spheres of the four elements are compared among themselves, so that the narrowest sphere is the earthly one; the watery is wider, both filling the earth from within and overhanging the surface of the earth. The airy sphere is similarly wider than both earth and water; finally, the fiery sphere, by a similar reasoning, is the widest of all, both nourishing everything from without and feeding it from within. Arnald <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist</note> and Raymond <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a polymath and mystic often associated with alchemy</note>, thinking this fire and vital spirit to be implanted in all things and calling it the "fifth essence" <term>quintessence: the fifth element, thought to be the pure substance of the heavens</term>, investigate most diligently by what machines it may be separated from foreign matter, and once segregated, by what guardianship they may best preserve it for uses they hope will be most healthy for everyone. I pass over the fact that they hope if they diligently obtain this from wine—as if from something highly celestial—they will apply it to "celestial gold" <note>An alchemical term for a purified or spiritualized state of gold</note> as much as possible; which the gold would then drink up as something most kindred to it, and retain it forever, and thus become "potable gold" <note>Aurum Potabile: a legendary alchemical medicine thought to grant eternal youth</note>. But let them see to those things. For my part, I know for certain that unless a spirit of this kind is present in all things, many cannot perform what they promise; nor would that Platonic saying be true, namely, that fire can be the navel <note>original: "umbilicum"—the center or focal point</note> of the world. It is indeed probable that the center and axis of the universe is not an earthly face, but rather fire. Again, what is written in the *Phaedo*, where he discusses mountains rising above the clouds—namely, that the "pure earth" lies in the "pure heaven" in which the stars are—cannot be true unless either the heaven there is infused with pure air, or only the heaven is there, as if there were a single sphere above the clouds. But let us set aside the unity of the sphere for the present. Perhaps that greatest Theologian <note>Likely referring to the author of the Book of Revelation</note>, when he says the celestial city has twelve foundations, understands the city to be this vital spirit reigning everywhere. The twelve foundations are truly the twelve spheres of the world: namely, the eight heavens above the ether, and again the four "heavens" spread through the ether, namely air, water, and earth. He also describes twelve gates: three from the East, three from the West, three from the South, and three again from the North, to show the four triplicities of the signs <note>In astrology, the twelve signs are divided into four groups of three based on the elements</note>: of which one is Eastern, that is, fiery, containing Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius. Another is Western, that is, airy, comprising Libra, Gemini, and Aquarius. Another is Southern, of the earth, having Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn. Finally, the Northern one, completing Pisces, Cancer, and Scorpio. Furthermore, when he says the entire city is made of pure gold, he means this fiery splendor is diffused through all things. He adds that this gold is like pure and transparent glass, that is, both translucent and shining at the same time. For if you were to add light, as if it were its own, to the pervasive transparency of glass, or if you were to join transparency to the natural splendor of gold as if it were its own, you would then have the substance of heaven: which is indeed everywhere translucent and shining at once, even if it does not appear so to us everywhere. But when the theologian adds a variety of precious stones, he signifies the lights of the stars, whether appearing to us or not appearing. For in any sphere above us and in certain parts of the world, there are stars of wonderful magnitude and power, although they are not visible everywhere. It is necessary for the whole to shine in itself, if heaven is everywhere, if light is proper to heaven, and if light is the most excellent quality and the origin of the remaining forms. However, the fact that it shines differently in different stars does not happen by one or another mixture, as usually happens in our colors, but by certain proper degrees of rarity, density, and distance. Thus, the color of saffron, when gathered, appears red, but when spread out it is pale, and finally, when most widely diffused, it glitters. I pass over how much our sight is deceived in these things from a distance and through different media. But besides the lights, add to the celestial things diverse powers as well, from which various colors and actions may proceed—not such as come from the elements, but by a certain more hidden property, almost a specific one, such as that by which iron is drawn by a magnet. For things among us that act in this way are said to act by celestial power.

-> It is confirmed that the heaven is eternal, consisting of both soul and body: and although it is fire, it is nevertheless moved in a circle by nature. <-

## VIII. The eighth chapter responds to a doubt asking: Does anything flow out of or into the heaven? It responds that nothing flows out. For the soul can contain its own spirit everywhere, and the spirit willingly obeys the soul; nor can any violence be brought in from elsewhere to conquer it, as if it were most powerful: and it would sooner turn all things into itself than be turned itself into another. Since, therefore, nothing flows out from there, it is rightly the case that nothing needs to flow in to preserve it. Nor is it permitted to imagine that the heaven is anything other than fire, so that its circuit is natural to it. For a natural circuit belongs to every spherical body placed in its own location whenever it is moved; whereas straight motion is either a certain violent disturbance from a natural place, or a sudden return into a natural place. Among these things, when he says the most powerful action of fire is heating, understand this as the action of elemental and mixed fire. For the chief action of celestial fire is that which is the chief action

For only the intellectual nature <note>the realm of pure Mind or 'Nous'</note> drives all motion far away from itself.

For he says: by what means, since they are bodies and are visible, can they prevail in conserving an immutable nature that is always the same? In Aristotle's view, this would not be very difficult, if one has already granted his suppositions regarding the fifth body. But among those who do not posit this, by what reasoning can the celestial body be everlasting under a singular property of substance? Especially since, according to them, the heaven is composed of the same elements from which the animals here on earth are made. Moreover, this must be doubted much more concerning the sun and the other parts in the heaven. Surely, since every animal is composed of a soul and a nature of body, it is necessary that the heaven—if indeed it has always been the same in number—has it either according to both, or according to one or the other of the things within it: namely, either through the body or through the soul. Whoever, therefore, attributes incorruptibility to the body will need the soul for nothing in this regard, except perhaps for this one thing: that the soul is always with the body to constitute the animal itself. But for him who posits that the body is of itself corruptible, and attributes the cause of eternal safety to the soul, he must strive to show that the nature of the body is by no means repugnant to such a constitution and perseverance. <margin>
III
He replies that the heaven is eternal, through the benefit of both the soul and the body.
</margin>

In what way, then, will the matter and the body of the universe contribute to the immortality of the world, given that it is in a perpetual state of flux? <note>original: "fluat" / "ῥέον" — Plotinus is addressing the ancient philosophical problem that physical matter is never stable, like a flowing river.</note> Or perhaps we should say it contributes because it does not flow *outward*? If, therefore, it flows within itself, but not away from itself, it surely remains the same, neither increasing nor diminishing; therefore, it does not grow old. It is worthwhile to observe the earth, remaining always in the same shape and mass, and the air, which never fails, and the water likewise. Yet, that which changes within these elements does not alter the nature of the whole living being. For even in us, while the parts are constantly changing and flowing outward, each of us lives for a long time in the interval. But where nothing "exhales" outward, the nature of the body does not disagree with the soul, so that one living being <note>original: "animal" / "ζῶον" — Plotinus views the entire universe as a single, living organism.</note> is composed of both and remains forever. B Fire contributes to this very thing; it is sharp and swift, insofar as it does not rest upon the earth, just as the earth does not rest upon anything else. But after the fire has ascended to the heights, where its passage must stop, it certainly ought not to become sluggish. C For one must not think that fire, when placed in its own proper seat, seeks its own expansion in every direction any less than other things do. It cannot ascend higher (for nothing higher exists) and its nature does not allow it to be carried downward. D Therefore, what remains is that it is easily led into a wide space, and by a natural pull is led by the soul toward life; and so, in a truly beautiful region—namely, in the soul itself—it is moved. But if someone perhaps fears that the fire might fall, he will find reason for confidence if he considers how the soul's rotation there prevents every downward inclination, driving it around forcefully and sustaining it. But if it has no natural weight pushing it toward a descent, certainly nothing prevents it from remaining there. E The parts within us, which are shaped into our form, cannot maintain their own constitution; they seek to borrow parts from others to preserve themselves in their habit. But if nothing flows out from heaven, there is no need at all for nourishment. If, however, something flows out into something else and is extinguished, then another fire must be lit there in turn. And if it receives something from another source that falls away from there, that too must be replaced in its turn. But for that reason, the whole living being would not remain the same, if the matter truly stood in that way.

# BOOK ONE.

A ...that the Flame is a certain boiling heat and a fire that, as if through excess, is violent and luxurious. But the fire found there [in the heavens] is even and quiet, and suited to the nature of the stars. But what is most important is that the soul, being ranked next to the highest things and endowed with a wonderful power, how can it allow itself—or any of the things once placed within it—to slip away into non-existence? One should not think that any bond is stronger than the one ordained by God, for He is the cause that holds all things together. B For it is absurd to think that a soul which was able to hold the heavens together for any length of time would not do so forever; as if this preservation happened by force, or as if there were some other natural state for the universe than this one, which is situated in the nature of the whole and in those things which are most beautifully arranged. It is as if there were something that could bring violence and dissolve the world's essence, or some other power from the beginning that could overthrow the natural kingdom of the soul. C For this very fact—that the world never had a beginning (otherwise it would be absurd)—gives us faith in its future persistence. For what could be the cause for the world to ever cease? The elements of the world are not worn away like wood and such things. Since the elements always remain, the whole surely remains as well. Even if it changes continually, the whole remains nonetheless, D because the cause of the change persists. We have demonstrated elsewhere that the idea of the world eventually changing due to some "repentance" <note>original: "pœnitentiā" / "μετάνοια" — the idea that the World Soul might change its mind or regret its creation.</note> of the soul is empty, especially since the governance of the world is positioned far from all labor and harm. <margin>* cause</margin> Furthermore, even if the entire body could ever be destroyed, nothing of this would happen to the soul that would be foreign to its nature.

E But why do the parts in heaven remain, while the elements and animals here with us do not? Perhaps, as Plato says, it is because those heavenly things were made by God himself, but the animals here were produced by the gods who were themselves generated by Him. <note>original: "diis genitis" / "γινομένων... θεῶν" — A reference to Plato's Timaeus, where the supreme Demiurge creates the stars/gods, and those lesser gods then create mortal humans.</note> It is not lawful for things made by God himself to perish. This is the same as saying that the heavenly soul is next in line after the Architect of the world, and our souls are similar; but from the heavenly soul, a certain "image" <note>original: "indalmam" / "ἴνδαλμα" — a reflection or lower-tier representation of a higher reality.</note> is produced, flowing down from the higher realms to create the earthly animals. Since this secondary soul mimics the higher one as much as it can, yet cannot fully succeed because it uses F inferior bodies for its work and exists in an inferior place—trying to unite things that are unwilling to stay together—these animals cannot live forever. These earthly bodies are not held with the same power, since a different, more immediate soul governs them. If the whole heaven must endure, then its parts (the stars) must also endure; otherwise, how could the whole remain if the parts did not likewise persist? G For the things below the heaven are no longer parts of the heaven; otherwise, the heaven would not extend only as far as the moon. We, however, are formed by the soul given by the celestial gods and are joined to earthly bodies according to the heaven itself. For that other soul through which we exist is the cause not of our existence, but of our well-being. And...

<column-break/>

A ...that the flame is a certain boiling heat, and a fire that is, as it were, injurious and luxurious due to its fullness. However, the celestial fire is even and quiet, and adapted to the nature of the stars. But what is of greatest importance is that since the soul is neighbor to the best things and endowed with a marvelous power, by what path could any of the things once placed within it escape from it toward destruction? If anyone does not judge the soul flowing from God B to be stronger than any bond, he will surely seem to be ignorant of the cause that contains all things. It is certainly absurd to suppose that the soul, which can contain the heaven for a time, cannot also do this forever—as if it held it together by violence, or as if what is natural were anything other than this very thing, which is placed in the nature of the universe and consists of those things which are most beautifully arranged. It is also as if anything could, by a certain brought-in force, dissolve the constitution of the world C and, as it were, weaken the kingdom and sovereignty of the soul's nature. Therefore, this very fact—that the world never began (otherwise it would be absurd)—creates faith in its future perseverance. For what can be the cause for the world to at some time cease? For the elements of the world are not worn down like wood and other such things. Since, therefore, they always remain, the universe undoubtedly remains. It remains even if it is continually changed; nevertheless, the universe persists, D since the cause of the change perseveres. We have demonstrated elsewhere that it is vain to think there will be some future change of the world due to a certain repentance of the soul; especially since the government of the world is placed far from all labor and detriment. Furthermore, if the whole body could ever be dispersed, nothing from this would happen that is alien to the soul.

<margin>Solution to the doubt of why celestial things remain rather than sub-celestial things.</margin>
E But why do the parts in heaven persist, while the elements among us, and the animals, do not? Perhaps, as Plato says: because those celestial things were indeed made by God himself, but these animals among us were produced by the generated gods. It is a sin for things made by God himself to perish. This is the same as if it were said that the celestial soul is next after the Architect of the world, and our souls are similar; but from that celestial soul, a certain image is produced, and as if flowing from the higher beings, it makes the terrestrial animals. Since, therefore, this imaginary soul imitates the superior soul according to its strength, and yet cannot entirely achieve it because it uses F inferior bodies for its work and is in an inferior place, and contends to reconcile into one those things which hardly meet, and which, having met, remain together against their will—undoubtedly these animals cannot live forever. And these bodies are not held by a similarly valid power, because another soul governs them more closely. Therefore, if the whole heaven must persevere, it is necessary that its parts, namely the stars, persevere; otherwise, in what way G would it remain, unless they similarly endured? For those things which are below the heaven are no longer parts of the heaven; otherwise, the heaven would not extend only as far as the moon. We, however, are formed by the soul which is handed down by the celestial gods, and we cling to bodies according to that heaven itself. For the other soul through which we are is not the cause of our being, but of our well-being. And...

### PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK II.

<margin>
VI. A demonstration that only fire is in the heavens, and that its qualities exist in a pure state within itself or within whatever it inhabits.
</margin>
...for it yields once the body is formed, since reason contributes little to its being present at the same time.

A Next, it remains to be considered whether only fire exists in the heavens, and whether anything flows out from there, such that it would require nourishment? Since Timaeus <note>In Plato’s dialogue "Timaeus," the character Timaeus explains the creation of the physical world.</note> composes the body of the world primarily from fire and earth—so that it might be visible through fire and solid and tangible through earth—B it seems consistent that the stars are not entirely fire, but consist mostly of it, seeing as the stars appear to possess solidity. Perhaps this view is correct, since Plato confirms this opinion with probable and apparent reasoning. Indeed, to our senses, both through sight and touch, the heavens appear to be composed mostly or entirely of fire; but to those considering the matter through reason, they will be thought to possess earth as well, since solidity cannot exist without earth. C But why would it need water and air? For it might seem absurd for there to be water in such a great amount of fire. As for air, if it were present there, it would immediately be transformed into the nature of fire. D However, if two solids require two means <note>term: means (mathematical proportion). In Pythagorean and Platonic physics, two "solid" numbers require two geometric means to be linked in a proportion.</note> to be joined, one might wonder whether this is also the case in natural things. For could someone not mix earth with water without needing any intermediate "mean" to reconcile them? If we say that the remaining elements are already present in earth and water, we might seem to contribute nothing; another might object that those remaining elements are not at all inclined to reconcile the two. E Nevertheless, we shall say they are now bound together because each possesses all the elements. Furthermore, we must consider whether earth cannot be seen without fire, and conversely, whether fire cannot be solid without earth. For if nature were so established, perhaps nothing would have its own essence within itself, but all things would be a confusion. F Each thing is named according to what prevails within it; for they say that earth cannot hold itself together without moisture, as the moisture of water is the "glue" <note>original: "glutinum" (Latin) / "κόλλαν" (Greek). Plotinus is discussing the physical property that allows dry particles to adhere.</note> for the earth. But even if we grant this, it would be absurd to say that while each thing is a specific "something," it does not provide its own constitution to itself, but only does so together with the others—at which point nothing would exist as a distinct thing in itself. For in what way will there be a nature of earth, or an actual essence of earth, if no portion of earth is that which is earth unless water is present there as glue? Besides, what would do the gluing there where there is no magnitude <note>term: magnitude. Here referring to physical extension or size in space.</note> to connect one part to the next in a continuous line? For if there is any magnitude of earth at all, it will be possible for earth to exist by its own nature without water; otherwise, there will be nothing left for the water to glue together. Likewise, why would a mass of earth need air in order to be earth, while the air remains air before it is transformed? It has not been said that earth needs fire to be earth, but it is granted that it needs fire so that it and these other things may be seen. G For it is consistent with reason to grant that sight occurs because of light. One should not say that darkness is seen, but rather that it is *not* seen, just as silence is not "heard." However, it is by no means necessary for fire to be in the earth; light is sufficient. Indeed, snow and many very cold things are bright without fire.

<margin>* being taken together</margin>
A ...body, it comes into being, contributing <note>original: "συλλαμβανομένη" (Greek). To assist or participate in the process of being.</note> a small amount from reasoning toward existence.
NOW we must consider whether there is only fire, and whether it flows away from there and requires nourishment. To Timaeus, who made the body of the universe first from earth and fire—so that it might be visible through fire and solid through earth—it seemed to follow that he should also make the stars, not entirely, but B having the greatest part consist of fire, since the stars appear to have solidity. And perhaps this would be correct, judging alongside Plato and his opinion entirely. For to the perception of sense, both through sight and the grasp of touch, the heavens appear to possess fire for the most part, or even entirely. But to those looking through reason, it would not become solid without earth, and thus it would possess earth. But of water and air, what C would it need? For would it not seem that water exists in so much fire? And the air, if it were in there, would change into the nature of fire. But if two solids D having the ratio of extremes require two means, one might wonder if it is so in natural things as well. For could one mix earth with water, needing no mean? If we should say then that the others are already present in the earth and the water, we shall perhaps seem to be saying something. If in some way they are not, how will the two be bound together? E But nevertheless we shall say they have already been bound together by each having all things. But it must be examined if earth is visible without fire, and again, if fire is not solid without earth. For if fire [is so], perhaps nothing would have its own essence by itself, but all things are mixed. And each is named according to that which F prevails, since they say that earth cannot hold together without the moist; for the moisture of water is a glue for the earth. But even if we grant it so, it is absurd for someone saying each thing is something, not to give it a constitution by itself, but only together with the others, when no individual thing exists. For how could there be a nature of earth, and the "what it was to be" <note>term: what it was to be. A translation of the Aristotelian "τὸ τὶ ἦν εἶναι," referring to the essential nature or definition of a thing.</note> for earth, if no part of earth exists which is earth, unless water were in it for gluing? What then would prevent there being no magnitude at all to join continuously to another part? For if there is to be any magnitude of earth itself, there will be a nature of earth which exists without water; or if not this, there will be nothing which will be glued by the water. And of air, why would a mass of earth have need in order to be, while air still remains, before changing? And concerning fire, it has not been said that it is for the sake of being earth. But for the sake of being visible, and * it <margin>* itself</margin> G with the other things. For it is unreasonable to grant that being seen happens through light. For indeed darkness is not seen, but one must say it is not seen; just as silence is not heard. But fire at least must be present in it. For it seems to be light. Snow, at any rate, and many very cold things, are bright without fire.

# BOOK ONE.

A But, someone will say, it has been stated that fire was present there and gave color before departing. Furthermore, regarding water, it must be questioned whether it is possible for it to be water if it does not partake of earth? And how can air be said to partake of earth, <margin>* to be excluded</margin> being unbreakable? Fire would also need earth if it lacks continuity from itself, or three-dimensional extension. Its B solidity, then, is evidently not according to its three-dimensional growth, but according to its resistance. Why is it not a natural body? Hardness belongs to earth alone; since even the density found in gold—which is essentially water <note>Ancient philosophers often classified metals like gold as a "liquid" element (water) that had become extremely dense or "frozen."</note>—occurs not because earth was added, but through density or solidification. And as for fire itself, why—if a soul is present—will it not establish its own power without earth? Indeed, there are even fiery living beings among the demons <note>term: demons (daimones). In Neoplatonism, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, often thought to be composed of a more refined "airy" or "fiery" element.</note>. But should we argue that the entire living universe has its composition from all the elements? Or should one argue that earthly things C are fixed to the ground, while to raise earth into the heaven <margin>* ancient</margin> is a false nature and contrary to the order assigned to them? It is not plausible that the celestial motions would carry along the thickness of * dead bodies. Finally, earth would be an obstacle to the brightness and the white fire found there.

D PERHAPS, then, it will be better to hear Plato saying that in the whole world there must be something solid of this kind, which is resistant, so that the earth, being established in the middle, might be a foundation and a firm base for those walking upon it. All living beings upon it must of necessity have this kind of solidity. The earth would have its continuity from itself, but would be illuminated by fire and partake of water so as not to be excessively dry; and how parts are joined to parts should not be hindered by their collection. Air would settle mingled within the masses of the earth. E But the earth is mixed with the celestial fire, not in the sense that it is counted within the composition of the stars, but because in the world, as each thing is produced, fire will enjoy something of earth just as earth enjoys something of fire. Each partakes of each, not as if our own bodies were constituted from both—that is, from itself and that in which it partakes—but according to the F fellowship existing in the world. It takes not the thing itself, but something of it; for example, not air itself, but its <margin>not</margin> softness, and from earth not its mass, but from fire its brilliance. This mixture, <margin>* entirely</margin> entirely given, makes the body both things at once, not just earth and the nature of fire, but this solidity and density. Plato himself bears witness to these things, saying: "God kindled a light in the second orbit from the earth," referring to the sun; elsewhere he calls the sun the G brightest fire, and in the same way the most brilliant, leading us away from thinking it is anything other than fire. But it is neither of the other two species of fire, but light, which he says is different from flame. It is only appropriately warm. And light-fire is a body. From it shines that light of the same name <margin>* of it</margin> which we say is incorporeal. This indeed...

<column-break/>

A Although someone might say that fire was present there and colored those things before it departed. Furthermore, one must doubt concerning water, whether it can be water unless it is a partaker of earth? Likewise, by what reasoning shall air be called a partaker of earth, since it is most soft and yields most easily to those penetrating it? B Regarding fire, however, it is doubted whether it has need of earth, as if it did not have continuity from itself, nor three-fold dimension insofar as it is a natural body. Solidity in fire will perhaps be placed not through three-fold dimension, but through a certain resistance. Rough hardness, however, belongs only to earth; for density belongs to gold (which is water), not indeed because of earth, but because of density and a congealed glue-like bond. Accordingly, why should fire in itself, when a soul is present, not be connected with its own power? For there are also fiery animals of the demons. But shall we thus C change the saying that the "universal animal" <note>A Platonic concept describing the universe as a single, living, rational organism.</note> is composed of all things? Perhaps someone might grant that earthly animals are thus composed, but will say that to lift earth into heaven is against nature and contrary to those things which are arranged in the order of nature. Now, it seems in no way probable that the swiftest course of the celestial bodies would carry earthly bodies within itself. Finally, earth would be a future hindrance to the splendor and brightness of the celestial fire.

<margin>VII. He confirms the same by Platonic authority.</margin>
D PERHAPS it is worthwhile to hear Plato saying that it is necessary in the universe for there to be such a solid thing, which is evidently resistant, so that the earth, being placed in the middle, may be a most stable foundation for all things walking through it; and earthly animals necessarily have a certain solidity of this kind. The earth possesses this very fact of being continuous from itself, but it is illuminated by fire and also becomes a partaker of water to avoid excessive dryness. It has, moreover, a faculty by which its parts are not prohibited from conspiring with other parts; finally, air supports the mass of the earth with a certain lightness. E One must remember, however, that earth is not so mixed with the sublime fire that it is numbered within the very composition of the stars; but since individual things are placed in the one body of the world, fire surely has something of the earthly, just as earth has something of the fiery. And in short, individual things have something of the other individuals, not so much that what is said to possess others is constituted from both (namely, from itself and from that in which it partakes); F rather, in the very communion of the world, it is rightly situated so that it receives not so much the other thing as a little something of the other. Just as it receives not air itself, but the liquidity of air itself; so also the earth receives not so much fire as a fiery clarity. This mixture itself brings all things together, and both consist as one—not earth alone and the nature of fire, or fire alone and the nature of earth—namely, a certain solidity and density of that kind. Plato himself provides testimony to these things, saying: "God kindled a light around the second sphere from the earth," certainly signifying the sun, which elsewhere he calls G most splendid and most bright. In these words, he drives away from us every opinion suspecting that there is anything else there besides fire. He also signifies that no other quality of fire is present except light, which he says is different from flame; the heat is only mild, and this light is a body; and from it shines...
