# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS, BOOK II.

...poreal: which indeed depends on that light, shining from it like its flower <note>original: *flos* / *anthos*. Plotinus often uses "flower" to mean the finest or most radiant peak of a substance's power.</note> and brightness, which is truly said to be an *actually* white body. We, however, are accustomed to interpret what is called "earthy" in a negative sense; for whereas Plato takes "earth" to mean a kind of solidity, we tend to call just one specific thing "earth," even though he considers different qualities within earth. Since, therefore, such fire provides the purest light, and resides itself in a sublime seat, dwelling there naturally, we must not suppose that this flame of our world is mixed with the higher things. Rather, after traveling a certain distance, it is utterly extinguished, since so much air stands in its way. When it does proceed, it is often cast down with earth, since it cannot transcend to the heights but settles below the moon, where it thins the nearby air. If a flame remains there, it certainly becomes more subtle and gentle; it possesses a splendor not in terms of heat, but insofar as it is illuminated by the light from above. Celestial light, however, is partly distributed in various proportions among the stars—in which the difference is seen both in their appearance and their magnitude—and partly flourishes in the rest of the heaven outside the stars in a similar way. And if it does not appear to our eyes because of the thinness and transparency of its body, which offers no resistance to the sight (just as happens in pure air), there is also the factor of the great distance involved.

<margin>
VII
That nothing flows out from or into heaven.
</margin>

SINCE, therefore, such light thrives on high, where it is naturally established—pure, clearly, in the purest seat—by what path could any outflow occur from there? For such a sublime nature does not flow down of its own accord, nor is there anything there to drive it headlong downward. Add to this that every body behaves very differently when it is joined to a soul than it would if it were separated from the soul; and the celestial body is by no means destitute of a soul. Likewise, whatever approaches the heaven is either air or fire. First, if it is air, I do not see how it could act upon the heaven. Second, if it is fire, it is in no way compatible with it, nor does it touch the heaven so as to act upon it. Furthermore, it is suddenly transformed into the celestial nature before the heaven can suffer anything from it. It is also much smaller in size and far inferior in strength. Moreover, the primary action of fire is heating. But that which is to be heated must not be hot of itself. If anything is dissolved by fire, it must first be heated entirely, and in that heating, be moved from its natural state. For this reason, the heaven has no need of any other body to preserve its nature, nor again to ensure its natural circuit, although this has not yet been demonstrated. Nor does the natural motion of the heaven tend in a straight line; indeed, their own nature commands celestial things either to remain at rest or to revolve. Other motions belong to violence. Therefore, celestial things do not require nutrition. Consequently, it is not fitting to judge sublime things by the condition of our own affairs; for they have neither the same soul containing them, nor a similar region, nor is there that cause there which forces inferior composite things, being in a state of continuous flux <note>term: flux (*rhoē*). The idea that physical bodies are constantly losing and gaining matter, like a flowing river, and thus need food to replace what is lost.</note>, to require nourishment. Far be it

<column-break/>

...to be provided from that light, shining out from it like a flower and its radiance, which indeed is that <margin>* actually</margin> white body. We, however, taking the "earthy" toward the worse sense—while Plato took earth according to its solidity—at least call the earth one thing, while he posits differences of earth. Since such fire provides the purest light, being situated in the upper place and established there according to nature, one must not suppose that this [earthly] flame mixes with the things there. Instead, reaching only to a certain point, it is extinguished, meeting with much air. Having departed with earth, it is thrown downward, being unable to transcend toward the heights, but standing below the moon, so that it even makes the air there thinner. And the flame, if it should remain, withers and becomes milder, and does not have splendor in terms of burning, but only insofar as it is illuminated by the light from above. The light there is varied in its principles among the stars, producing a difference in colors just as in magnitudes; and the rest of the heaven is also <margin>* such</margin> a light. It is not visible, however, due to the thinness of the body and a transparency that does not resist the sight, just like pure air. Added to these factors is the distance.

<margin>* actually</margin>
<margin>* such</margin>

SINCE such light remains above in that pure place, in the purest state, what way could there be for an outflow from it? For it is not its nature to flow toward the bottom, nor is such its nature; nor is there anything there of those things that use force to push it toward the bottom. For every body with a soul is different, and not the same as a body alone. Such is the thing there, not like a body alone. As for that which neighbors it, whether it be air or fire: if it were air, what could it do? If it were fire, if it were bound to act upon it, it would not even touch it so as to act. For by <margin>* strength</margin> and change, it would be altered before that [heaven] could suffer. This [earthly fire] is smaller and weaker, not equal to the things there. Then also, to "act" is to heat. That which is to be heated must not be hot in itself. If anything is to be destroyed by fire, it must first be heated, and become contrary to its nature in the process of being heated. But the heaven has no need of another body in order to remain, nor that its revolution be according to nature; for it has not yet been shown whether its motion is <margin>* impassibility</margin> or according to nature. For it is natural for them either to stay still or to be carried in a circle. Other motions are the result of those being forced. If, then, those things there do not even need nutrition, we should not declare things about them based on the things here. For they do not have the same soul among those things that hold them together, nor the same <margin>* in some</margin> manner, since the cause is there by which the things here are composed and flow and need to be nourished. <margin>...bodies changing from themselves, another nature commanding them, or because of weakness, I know not if they maintain their being. But it imitates, in its becoming or living, the nature before it. It has been said that it is not in the same way entirely as the intelligible things. <note>original Greek: σωμάτων ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῶν μεταβάλλειν... Therefore, change from those higher things disturbs those things which are masters in these bodies from their natural habit; since another certain nature presides over these, which on account of weakness it cannot contain in its own very being. Nevertheless, in that which is to be generated and to generate, it imitates the superior nature as much as it can: concerning which it has been said elsewhere, that it itself cannot remain in exactly the same way in which intelligible things always maintain themselves.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON
## BOOK II OF THE SECOND ENNEAD,
### ON THE MOTION OF THE HEAVEN,
### COMMENTARY.

---

#### SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

->The heaven is moved by its own soul, which is rational and intellectual, and is driven in a circle: because the soul and intellect perform circuits within themselves.<-

That the heaven is moved not by some nature such as an elemental or similar force, but by life: not indeed by an external life, but an internal one, through which the heaven may live—I say, a rational and even an intellectual life. Likewise, why it is moved in a circle, and in what manner, both Plotinus disputes in the present work, and we treat more extensively in our *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his own major work, the *Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls*.</note>. It shall be enough now, therefore, to have touched upon it briefly. That the heaven lives is demonstrated by its matter and form, which are the most excellent of all living things: its motion is most natural and intimate to itself, never deserting itself; its perpetual action naturally gives life to all things. Likewise, that the heaven lives with a rational life is indicated by the marvelous order in the motions and in all things produced from it. Again, that it flourishes with intellectual power is declared by its constancy in producing such diverse things and motions while always remaining immobile itself. 

Therefore, you should not think that a work disposed with such admirable and perpetual reason is driven and moved by some headlong chance; nor perhaps that it is driven by a royal reason, but one that is, as it were, blind and merely the bare reason of nature, in the same way that members in an animal or parts in a plant are formed by a vegetative power through "seed-reasons" <note>term: <term>seminarias rationes</term> (seminal reasons). These are the latent creative blueprints within nature that allow things to grow into their specific shapes.</note>. For a natural reason of that kind is only "irrational" (if I may say so) and blind, since it has no awareness of itself, nor does it ever possess itself by noticing itself. Therefore, as something imperfect, it is ruled by a more perfect reason which flourishes in the power of the soul, discoursing rationally if need be; and this soul in turn, being mobile, is ruled by the most perfect reason which reigns immobile in the Mind (Intellect). 

That final reason is the Word of God, by which, as if by a primary hinge, the heaven is at once moved and made firm. But let us now return to the soul. The Soul of the World is the mother, made pregnant from the Divine Intellect (the father of the world) through understanding; she conceives the world through reason in nature. Finally, from this natural offspring, while a certain imagination and affection together contribute to the birth, the world is born: an image of the Mind, an expression of reason, an offspring of life that is necessarily alive. Hence Orpheus calls Jupiter, the maker of the world, both male and female. Plato also in places understands the architect of the world to be Mind and Soul together, as if at once the father and mother of the world. 

That the soul is constituted of five genera of things <note>These are the "Five Greatest Kinds" from Plato's *Sophist*: Being, Sameness, Difference, Motion, and Rest.</note>, and by what logic, we have said and shall say in our *Theology* and commentary on the *Timaeus*: namely, by Essence, Sameness, Difference, Rest, and Motion. The essence of the world, therefore, reflects the essence of the soul; likewise, the common matter and form in the world reflect the "Sameness" of the soul. Again, the extension of this matter and the distinction of forms represent the "Difference" of the soul. Similarly, the motion of the world represents the motion of the soul; and the "Rest" of the soul is represented by the stability of the world within its motion. For since the motion of the world must "stand" in such a way that it neither changes its substance nor leaves its natural place, it deservedly revolves around the same center. Thus, even while it moves, it does not depart from a state of rest, and it represents the revolution of the soul. 

For the soul, beginning from the Good and the Intellect together, revolves back to the same through intellect and will; and as it discourses by reason, it returns through the same forms from which it began to discourse. The imagination of the generative nature, the companion of nature, also brings forth the seeds of things and motions to be generated from potentiality into act in such a way that both a most orderly and perpetual succession occurs, and finally a return to the same or similar things is made in certain circuits of time. The revolution of the world follows this revolution of the soul at least as easily as the motion and formation in our own spirit follows the effective instinct of a presiding nature and the affection of a similar imagination. This, then, is the summary of the entire book.

->While the heaven moves in a circle, as much as possible it becomes the whole in any of its parts, and thus attains the whole soul everywhere. However, it remains through an indivisible center, just as the soul remains through intellect and substance.<-

For this first circuit is turned back from the Good into the Good through the light of the Good itself, and from the intellect into the same intellect through...

<margin>A</margin>
[...corporeal] <note>The Latin text begins mid-word with "-poreum," likely "corporeum" (corporeal).</note>: which indeed depends on that light, gleaming from it like its bloom and brilliance, which is truly said to exist as a "white body." We, however, have become accustomed to take what is called "earthy" in a negative sense; for while Plato <note>Referring to Plato's *Timaeus*, where he discusses the four elements.</note> accepts "earth" to mean a kind of solidity, we are usually accustomed to call only one specific thing "earth," even though he considers different qualities within the earth. Since, therefore, such a fire provides the purest 
<margin>B</margin>
light, and resides in that sublime seat, and dwells there naturally, we must not think that our local flame is mixed with those superior things. Instead, our flame, running through a certain space, is utterly extinguished, clearly because it encounters so much air. But as it proceeds, it is often cast down toward the earth, since it cannot transcend the upper limit, but settles below the moon, where it thins out the nearest air. And if a flame remains there, it certainly becomes thinner and milder; it possesses a splendor not in terms of heat, but insofar as it is 
<margin>C</margin>
illuminated by the superior light. Indeed, the celestial light is partly distributed in various ways among the stars, in which a difference is perceived both in their appearance and their magnitude; and partly it flourishes in the rest of the heaven beyond the stars in a similar manner. And if it is not apparent to our eyes on account of the thinness and transparency of the body, which offers minimal resistance to our sight—just as happens in pure air—the great length of the distance also contributes to this.
<margin>VIII That nothing flows out of or into the heaven.</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
Since, therefore, such light flourishes on high, where it is naturally established—pure, clearly, in a most pure seat—by what way can any "out-flow" <note>original Latin: "defluxus"; Plotinus is arguing against the idea that the heavens lose matter or "leak" energy like earthly things do.</note> happen from there? For such a sublime nature does not flow down of its own accord; nor, again, is there anything there which might precipitate it downward by force. Add to this that every body 
<margin>E</margin>
behaves very differently when it is joined to a soul than if it were separated from a soul; and the celestial body is by no means destitute of a soul. Likewise, whatever approaches the heaven is either air or fire. First, if it is air, I do not see how it could act upon the heaven; second, if it is fire, it by no means matches or touches the heaven in such a way as to act upon it. Furthermore, it is suddenly transformed into the celestial nature before the heaven can suffer anything from it. Also, it is much smaller in magnitude and far inferior in strength. Besides, the primary action of fire is heating. But 
<margin>F</margin>
that which is to be heated must not be hot of itself. If anything is to be dissolved by fire, it must first be entirely heated, and in that very heating, be moved out of its natural habit. Therefore, the heaven has absolutely no need of any other body to preserve its nature; nor, again, is its circuit anything but natural, even if this has not yet been demonstrated. The natural motion of the heaven does not tend in a straight line; for their own nature commands celestial things either to rest or to revolve; other motions would pertain to violence. Therefore, the celestial things do not even require nourishment. Thus, it is not fitting to judge sublime things by the conditions of our own affairs; since they neither have the same containing soul, nor a similar region, nor is there any cause there for which inferior composite things are forced to require nourishment due to a constant flowing out. Far be it...

<column-break/>

...provided from that light, shining out from it like a radiance and brightness, which is indeed to be the <margin>*truly</margin> <note>original Greek: "ontos" (truly)</note> white body. But we take the "earthy" toward the worse sense, whereas Plato takes earth according to its solidity; we, at least, call it one thing, "earth," whereas he posits differences of earth. Since such a fire provides the purest light, lying in the upper place and established there according to nature, one must not suppose that the flame here mixes with the things there, but reaching up to a certain point, it is extinguished, meeting with more air. Nor, again, is there anything there of those things that force it to be pushed downward. Every body is different with a soul, and not the same as it is when being alone. And the body there is such, not like a body alone. And that which is neighboring, whether it be air or fire—if it is air, what can it do? And if it is fire, if it were to make itself into bonds, it could not even touch it so as to 
<margin>*strength</margin>

If anything is to be destroyed by fire, it must first be heated, and become contrary to nature in the process of being heated. For neither do they have the same soul of those things holding them together, nor in the same <margin>*disease</margin> <note>The marginal note "nosou" (disease) suggests a variant or correction for the word "tropon" (manner/way) in the text.</note> manner, because there is a cause there [on earth] why the things here are nourished: because they are confused and flowing. # MARSILIO FICINO ON
## BOOK II OF THE SECOND ENNEAD,
## ON THE MOTION OF THE HEAVENS,
## COMMENTARY.

### SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

->The heaven is moved by its own soul, which is rational and intellectual, and it is driven in a circle: since the soul and intellect perform circular movements within themselves.<-

That the heaven is moved not by some elemental or similar nature, but by life: and not by an external life, but an internal one, through which the heaven lives—a life, I say, that is rational, and indeed even intellectual. Likewise, why it is moved in a circle, and in what manner, both Plotinus discusses in the present work, and we treat more extensively in our *Theology* <note>Referring to Ficino's own major work, *Theologia Platonica* (Platonic Theology).</note>. It will suffice for now, therefore, to have touched upon it briefly. The matter and form of the heaven, being the most excellent of all living things, demonstrate that it lives: its motion is most natural and intimate to itself, never deserting itself: a perpetual action naturally giving life to all things. Likewise, the wonderful order in its motions and in all things born from it indicates that the heaven lives with a rational life. Again, its constancy in producing such diverse things and motions, while remaining itself always immovable in its essence, declares that it flourishes with intellectual power. Therefore, you will not think that a work disposed with such marvelous and perpetual reason is driven and moved by some rash chance; nor perhaps that it is driven and ruled by reason, but only by a kind of blind and bare "reason of nature," in the way that members in an animal or parts in a plant are formed from a vegetative power through <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>original: "seminarias rationes" — the Stoic and Neoplatonic concept of formative, seed-like principles that govern the growth of physical things.</note>. For that kind of natural reason is merely irrational (if I may put it that way) and blind, since it has no knowledge of itself, nor does it ever possess itself by noticing itself. Therefore, as something imperfect, it is ruled by a more perfect reason, which flourishes in the power of the soul—discursively reasoning, if need be. And this in turn, being mobile, is ruled by the most perfect reason, which reigns immovable in the Mind. That, finally, is the Reason and the Word of God, by which, as if by a primary hinge, the heaven is both moved and made firm at the same time. 

But let us now return to the soul. The <term>World Soul</term> <note>Anima Mundi; the spiritual principle that animates the entire universe.</note>, as a mother, becoming pregnant through the divine Intellect (the father of the world) by means of her own intellect, conceives the world through reason in her nature. Finally, from this natural offspring, while a certain imagination and emotion contribute to the birth, the world is born: an image of the Mind, an expression of Reason, a sprout of Life that is necessarily living. Hence Orpheus calls Jove the craftsman of the world both male and female <note>Ficino often references the Orphic Hymns to show that the Divine contains all creative and receptive powers.</note>. Plato also in some places understands the architect of the world to be both Mind and Soul together, as if both father and mother of the world. We have said, and shall say, in our *Theology* and commentary on the *Timaeus*, that the soul is constituted by five genera of things: namely Essence, Sameness, Difference, Rest, and Motion. Therefore, the essence of the heaven reflects the essence of the World Soul; the "Sameness" of the soul is reflected by the common matter and form in the world. Again, the "Difference" of the soul is represented here by the extension of this matter and the distinction of forms. The motion of the soul is reflected by the motion of the world; likewise, the "Rest" of the soul is reflected by the stability of the world within its motion. For since the motion of the world must remain so stable that it neither changes its substance nor leaves its natural place, it deservedly revolves around the same point. Thus, precisely while it is moved, it least of all departs from its state of rest, and it represents the revolution of the soul. For the soul, beginning from the Good and from the Intellect, revolves back to the same through intellect and will; and though it may run discursively through reason, it returns through the same forms to those from which it began to run. The generative nature, and the imagination which is the companion of nature, also bring forth the seeds of things and motions from potentiality into act within themselves, so that both a most orderly and perpetual succession occurs, and finally a return to the same or similar things is made in certain cycles of time. The revolution of the world follows this mental revolution at least as easily as the motion and formation in our own spirit follows the effective instinct of a powerful nature and the impulse of a similar imagination. This is the summary of the whole book.

->While the heaven moves in a circle, it is as much as possible whole in any<-
->part of itself, and thus attains the whole soul everywhere. However, it remains<-
->fixed through an indivisible center, just as the soul remains through the<-
->intellect and substance.<-

1 Plotinus teaches in the first chapter of the book, according to the opinion of our Plato, that the heaven is moved in a circle because it imitates intelligence: most closely the intelligence of the celestial soul, and even higher, the intelligence of the divine Mind. For that first circuit is one turned back from the Good into the Good through the light of the Good itself, and then from the intellect into the same intellect through...

<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...returned to its own proper forms. Therefore, the circuit occurs in the soul by the power of the mind, and in the heaven it is carried out in imitation of the mind. But in the mind and in any intelligence, this happens in an eternal moment; however, in the <term>discursive reasoning</term> <note>The process of the soul moving step-by-step from one thought to another, unlike the mind which perceives all at once.</note> of the soul, it happens at least in a particular time. Finally, in the heaven, it is forced to require not only a body, but also a place, whatever that place may be. 

One asks, however: what produces such motion? Not the body of the heaven itself, for a body, insofar as it is a body, does nothing. The soul, therefore, produces motion from itself into the body; yet the motion in the soul and the body is not of the same *kind*. For even in our own body, a dilation occurs in the <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritu". In this context, 'spirit' refers to the subtle, breath-like substance that acts as a bridge between the immaterial soul and the material body.</note> through pleasure, and a contraction through pain, responding to a certain motion of the soul; yet that motion in the soul—as it is indivisible—can be neither a dilation nor a contraction. There is, however, a "second" soul, as it were, from which motion is most closely produced; it is so continuous with the body that from the soul and the *body*, a single *living being* is formed: namely, the *heaven*. And while the soul itself revolves by a certain *formal* motion (that is, from one act of its form to another act and state of its form), the heaven meanwhile is *figured differently and differently* by a motion that is essentially local. 

If, therefore, the soul stood still, the body would also stand still, even though the body is moved in a different way than the soul's own motion. Now, because it is a body, insofar as it is extended through different dimensions of space, it has happened that it is also led through different parts of that body. It would even have the tendency to be pulled in a straight line, and thus perhaps be scattered, had it not been reduced to a *spherical* shape by the intellectual soul; from this, it was made naturally inclined toward a circuit. 

Therefore, imagine the body of the heaven as a *spirit* <note>Again, the 'spiritus' or vital breath.</note> rushing forth from the breathing soul as if in a straight line, and thus entirely liable to dispersion, but in turn immediately restrained by the soul *breathing back in*. And since it cannot rest while the soul is active, it is necessarily twisted back into a circle around the soul, or rather, within the soul. *Remember*, therefore, that its motion is not entirely local. For it never changes the place it obtained from the beginning; nor does the whole pass from here to there as if traveling. Instead, while the parts are in a certain way passing through, the whole meanwhile remains at rest. Thus, the circular motion of the heaven is local "by accident"—that is, it passes through parts of space according to its own parts incidentally, rather than as the soul's primary purpose. 

What is the primary purpose of the soul, and at the same time, the chief instinct of this body? Certainly, motion in the soul is a constant transition from one thing to another. For since its lower mind is not so powerful that (like the higher mind) it can be all things at once in its activity, yet it wishes to bring all its own things into action, it does through perpetual succession what it cannot achieve all at once. Since the types of its acts are limited, it eventually exhausts them all; but still desiring them all equally, it repeats them all in turn. It performs this as quickly as possible, so that by the very speed of repeating, it seems as if it has recovered what it just lost. 

By the same logic and similarity, the heaven changes all its configurations in a perpetual succession and cycle. In this effort of both the soul and the heaven, the chief wish is not to "pass through," but to embrace all things at once in act as much as possible; and if they must pass through, to recover what has passed as quickly as possible and to continue the activity of all things. Therefore, the motion of the soul is vital, sensing, and thinking; but it is such that it affects all acts of living, sensing, and thinking at once, to have all forms simultaneously, and to observe all of them absolutely. Likewise, it lives through the whole of itself at once, feeling all its mutual parts from every side at once, and knowing them at once: so that everywhere there is the life, sense, and consciousness of the whole, proceeding not outward but inward. 

The motion of the heaven is similar to this. Imagine a certain space equal to the heaven in which it rotates—whether this space is something other than the heaven, or rather the very nature of the heaven itself. Divide that space, just like the heaven, into a hundred portions, drawn from the circumference to the middle, defined by lines from the wide part narrowing down in order. The heaven desires to possess this space as its foundation and nature with the whole of itself—with the whole of itself, I say, meaning that all its parts from every side should touch every single part of that space. But it cannot touch them all at once, for the extension of space prevents it. Therefore, it hurries by succeeding quickly through all its own parts to soon touch every single part of the space, so that the whole may enjoy the whole natural space—indeed, its whole nature—equally everywhere. And this is like a common and mutual "conspiracy" of life everywhere, and a certain intimate communion of sense and knowledge. 

Now, indeed, the soul (which through this very space is whole and simultaneous everywhere) seems to be imitated in this way: while the heaven also becomes present everywhere as quickly as possible, the whole and every part of it thus follows the soul everywhere—namely, by a certain motion following the soul that moves. The soul, I say, moves not only by a formal and intimate motion as I have said, but in a certain way even by local motion, insofar as it does not reside in a narrow corner but diffuses itself through the whole space in every direction. For it could not form a body that is both extended and mobile with life in any other way than by a certain diffusion and motion of itself. For the life of the body is a certain motion: for even a solid body lives insofar as the spirit diffuses itself through it and acts; and the spirit itself lives insofar as the soul similarly propagates itself through it. 

Therefore, that which is primary in a living being (whether a specific one or the world-animal), which is the soul, connects the rest—that is, its most proximate spirit, the heaven. It connects, I say, the heaven both to the soul itself and to the heaven's own self. Through the heaven, as if through a spirit, it similarly connects the remaining elements and mixtures as well. 

Plotinus, however, maintains that circular motion belongs to fire by the necessity of nature's providence. For the Divine Mind, foreseeing that fire would be a body, and because a body is extended through its substance into parts outside of parts, it would therefore proceed through action in moments according to "before" and "after"—which is indeed to be moved, and that indeed from the primary nature of a body, to be moved in a straight line. Thus, knowing that the fiery body would be liable to dissipate, in order to prevent its destruction, God deservedly added a sort of "second nature" to the primary nature of the body (that is, to its naturally mobile dimension); this second nature is the spherical shape of its dimension. 

The whole nature of fire was therefore granted by providence through the first nature: whenever it is placed outside its natural location, it seeks its own proper seat by a straight, shorter path. Then, through the second and first nature together, after it has returned to its proper seat, it rests most willingly. But since it remains in its own place, it also remains in its nature, which is to be moved; thus, it deservedly rests there *in motion*. This is surely nothing other than to be revolved around the same center and circumference, with both this very nature (which is to be moved and to rest in motion in its own place) and the circular shape contributing to this. 

Furthermore, necessity itself, following nature and providence, contributes to the same end: namely, since it naturally desires to be moved there as well—or even if it perhaps wished to move in a straight line by its primary nature—yet because it cannot move in a straight line, it falls back by the same necessity. I say it cannot move in a straight line because no such infinite space is given. For in such a space, scattered in a straight line through parts, the power of the natural space, gradually weakened through the immense distance, could not remain vigorous. Nor should one think that the celestial body repeats its turns back and forth through a certain space produced in a straight line. For those motions would be opposite to one another, and therefore a middle point of rest would intervene between them everywhere. Thus, the first motion would not be uniform and perpetual, but immediately deformed and interrupted. Therefore, celestial fire, placed in its own proper location, is always and perfectly rotated in a perpetual orb; especially since for it to be moved in this place is nothing other than to be moved within itself. For the parts of the universal body are in a place other than themselves; but the universal body, especially through its outermost circumference, is the universal place; just as...

<meta>catchword: each [singuli]</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains that celestial motion is the physical imitation of the soul's internal intellectual cycles. He argues that circular motion is a "rest in motion" designed by providence to prevent the heaven's fiery body from dissipating into infinite space.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Ennead II.2, focusing on the relationship between the physical motion of the celestial spheres and the inner life of the soul, specifically how the center of a circle represents the indivisible power of the divine.</meta>

# ON BOOK II. ENNEAD II.

Individual movements are certainly carried out in fixed times, but the first and universal movement is almost the same as time itself, just as the first "state" or condition is eternity. Furthermore, because something within this perfect and continuous orb—which is moved perfectly in a circle—remains still, it is clear that it has nothing outside of its motion, nor does the whole itself change its location from elsewhere. Likewise, it is established that no part of this circular and solid dimension which possesses magnitude can remain still while the whole is moved; this is because it is not broken by the motion, but remains everywhere whole as well as continuous. Therefore, this very thing which remains still in the orb while it is shaken is **indivisible** <note>original: "indiuiduum". In Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to a point or entity that cannot be divided into smaller parts, representing a higher state of unity.</note>. And that indeed is the center of the orb. For since slowness increases little by little toward the center, it is established that the center itself is entirely at rest. But if you imagine some dimension placed in the middle to be the center, certainly this, when it is grasped, will be shaped as a sphere. Then I would ask: does this entire sphere remain still or not? If you say the whole remains, the universal orb is now broken; but if it is turned by the circumference yet rests at the center, I will ask again about the center. If you say it is divisible, the previous question will return, and you will be forced to wander infinitely and will never find the center. But if you confess it is indivisible, you must admit that only something indivisible in a continuous sphere is at rest. And that is not so much a physical mark or a point as it is the very heart of the sphere and the power of the soul—or rather, the soul itself. When, however, the sphere hastens with natural desire toward this indivisible point, as if toward the life-giving foundation of the whole orb, yet does not wish to be compressed into an indivisible point lest it lose its natural shape, it is deservedly revolved around it. For in this way, through every point and line marked in the sphere, the whole sphere inserts itself little by little, so that in this way at least it may seem to become indivisible, and be whole everywhere just like the soul, and from every side as a whole behold the whole soul. Now indeed you will not deny, I think, that this whole world lives, when you consider that in its "womb" and by its power, even the smallest things live. But if the whole lives, the heaven—which is the greatest part of the whole, and indeed a "whole" in itself—lives most of all. If you say the heaven is an instrument of a more divine life for generating living things, you will still confess that this natural and nearest instrument of the divine life (its "genital" instrument, so to speak) lives by its own proper life. By the nourishment of this life, and in its womb, all things grow together into life. Indeed, the benefit of living is translated into the rest only through this which has already been made living from that source. This life proper to the heaven is the nature of the heaven and the universe itself, through which the motion of the heaven (as the first leader of natural motions) is most natural and intimate, and most voluntary; the heaven wishes to be moved so freely, just as zealously as either the higher life or the heaven's own life (consenting with the higher) decrees to move it. Hence it happens that this motion is most easy and perpetual: both because in a sphere and its motion, whatever you mark as an end will be just like a beginning; and because the power and act of moving in the soul is the very natural life of the soul. Therefore, this life—this soul which is everywhere whole and as if it were moved—renders itself present everywhere and creates **light**. The heaven also, wherever it can through revolution alone, is everywhere a whole, and through motion it enjoys the mobile soul; nor will it ever reach the soul it follows in any other way than by reaching it at every single moment. Thus, perpetually revolved toward the soul (or rather, within the soul) by its own pact, the heaven is also revolved eternally in its own way. Thus the whole orb, through any of its parts, enjoys any of the natures and parts of its space; and every smaller sphere, through its entire convex surface, constantly enjoys the concave of the higher sphere, while by perpetual revolution it applies all its parts to each part of the larger sphere; and it always does this out of **love**. Thus also the larger orbs, through all their regions, look upon and cherish any regions of the lower ones. Thus finally, with the figures varied from above by motion, the forms are also varied among us, and individual things are multiplied; and through similar returns of revolutions, with similar things returning among us, all species of things are preserved.

---

-> The **rational soul** <note>The human soul, capable of logic and free choice.</note> is moved by free motion; the **irrational** <note>The animal or vegetative soul, which lacks reason.</note> follows the universe. Likewise, in the universe, the circumference desires the center and enjoys it through a circuit. <-

-> Likewise, from the circuit of the soul and mind around **God**, the circuit in the heaven arises. <-

---

**II** — In the second chapter, he raises and solves questions concerning the things mentioned above. In the **first question**, it is notable that the heaven is indeed diffused through all things, and all bodies are either proper parts of the heaven or attached to its parts, and therefore are moved by the pull of the heaven. In the **second question**, you will consider that every rational soul exists as something whole in itself, and is not merely a part of the universal soul; this is especially clear from three points: First, because no part continuous with a whole is reflected back into itself by its own motion; second, no part can equal the whole; third, no part fights against the whole. But the rational soul is turned back into itself by its own self-awareness; it measures the order of the universe and proceeds to the cause of the universe which transcends it; it often leads itself differently than the nature of the whole might pull it, whether it rises toward the better or falls toward the worse. But that which is in us—whether the body or the life proper to the body—is a certain part of the world-body and world-life; therefore, it follows the pull of the universe for the most part. In the **third question**, it is discussed that the body of the world wanders perpetually so that, according to its strength, it may be whole everywhere, just as the soul is everywhere whole at once, and may enjoy the soul everywhere in like manner. From here, certain conclusions are brought forward: The **first** is of this kind: Since the power of the soul (namely the vital power) flourishes most in the center of the world as if in the heart of an animal, and spreads itself from there everywhere through the whole, this world-body, desirous of life, rightly turns itself around the center, being led to the same by the soul. For by bringing its whole self toward the center through any lines drawn from the circumference, it seems to touch the center from every side. Nor indeed is the extension of mass or the propagation of life from the center done without cause. For this is necessarily first, since it is indivisible and entirely immobile. Every "first" thing is thought to be in itself in that very thing which it is, before it is extended; and that which is indivisible and stable precedes all things that are divisible and mobile. The **second conclusion**: just as the center is that from which the rest of the world and the medium from which others hang, so in the soul the center is the intellectual substance itself; from which all other power and the "second life" <note>Probably referring to the lower, animating functions of the soul as opposed to its higher intellectual essence.</note> proceed. And just as what remains in the soul is turned back toward its principal part as if toward a center, so the whole machine revolves around the center. Here you will note that the substance of the heaven itself is to be placed no less (indeed more) in the center and near it than in the circumference. The **third conclusion**: Just as the body revolves around the soul, so the soul revolves around **God**. It revolves, I say, both by a certain perpetual and natural instinct (hidden though it be from us), and by the zeal of meditation and love; and even if it cannot behold God in a single gaze or touch Him in one touch, it at least turns itself toward God through a multiple gaze and touch in turn. After these things, it is asked: Do all rational souls do the same? He responds immediately: All always do so.

He argues that the soul is an independent whole that governs the body, just as the World Soul governs the universe from its central "heart."</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Ennead II.2. The previous page established that the center of the celestial sphere represents an indivisible point of rest (the divine), while the circumference represents perpetual motion. This page explores how human and world souls "revolve" around God through intelligence and desire, and how the celestial bodies follow this spiritual impulse.</meta>

->### COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO<-

For everyone, through a certain perpetual act of intelligence—though it remains hidden from us—enjoys the divine mind and God. Everyone, through a certain rational discourse, either performs the same action or strives to perform it. You will notice here that every act proceeding from one endpoint to another, even if it happens suddenly and without an intermediate step, can be called "motion." Thus, you might name the intelligence proceeding from the divine mind into God itself a "motion" and, in a sense, a "circuit." 

However, an act that proceeds from one thing to another suddenly, yet through a medium, you may call "motion" in a more proper sense; by this motion, I mean the intellect of the soul is turned around God using the divine intellect as a kind of medium. Finally, an act that passes from one thing to another both through a medium and over time, you will rightly call "motion" in the most proper sense of the word. Through this circuit of rational nature, the soul is both turned within itself around the "forms" <note>original: "formas". In Platonic thought, these are the eternal archetypes or ideas of all things.</note> and turned out of itself toward its own intellect, and through the divine, it turns toward God.

Next, the question is asked: Do our bodies revolve according to the revolution of our soul, just as the body of the world revolves according to the circuit of its own soul? The answer is: A solid and composite body does not do this at all. Rather, it moves in a straight line, both because the things within it are placed outside their natural location, and because it is drawn toward external things due to its own lack or need. 

However, the "celestial body" <note>original: "Corpus... cæleste". Ficino refers here to the "spirit" or "astral vehicle," a subtle, luminous body that mediates between the immortal soul and the physical flesh.</note> which is hidden within us, reduced its spherical shape from the beginning to match the shape of the earthly body into which it was introduced; yet when it departs from here, it will suddenly regain that shape. In the meantime, its circular motion can be hindered in some way—it is even strained and driven to the extent that the shape of the earthly body is strong. But as soon as the soul leaves the earthly body, that subtle body is agitated with similar agility at every nod of the soul. There is also, as it were, a certain "eye of the soul," but it is rotated by the soul's whim more easily than our physical eye is moved by the influence of the visual power. 

Suddenly, God is present in all things as their center; like a lure, He attracts minds and souls entirely to Himself. These souls turn themselves around God not so much by knowledge as by "affect" <note>original: "affectu". This refers to the soul's disposition, desire, or love toward an object.</note>, and by that same affect, they turn the body toward the same goal as much as they are able. For it is not knowledge, but affect that is the principle of movement. Knowledge seems to be somewhat imaginary, while affect is instead substantial; knowledge rests within itself, while affect is transferred toward another. 

Among these points, if you ask about the motion of the stars, Plotinus (along with Plato) responds: they are not only moved by their sphere, but they also turn with their own motion around their own center. Since those things which possess their own substance and life—as if set apart—they must also have their own motion. Indeed, the globe of a star is moved according to the motion of its soul: so that just as the soul circuits around God, so the globe revolves around its own soul. When he says that the soul, enjoying God, immediately leaps with joy, he signifies that the celestial globe is turned there not so much by the soul's "appetite" or craving, but by its joy—just as in our own souls, the spirits are expanded and the limbs exult with joy. 

Furthermore, when he says that the circuit there happens not by deliberation but by the "necessity of nature," he means both that the souls who gaze upon the Good find it by a certain necessary attraction (since the Good itself, which is all good and contains every reason for willing, cannot be "un-willed"), and because souls gazing upon it do not stop to deliberate. Then, whether they choose or not, and whether they move the body in this way or that, they primarily and suddenly desire the infinite, and they rejoice, and they are moved, and they move others. This is especially true since in any mind, its natural "being" and its "understanding" are the same; and understanding is almost the same as "willing." Similarly, in the "vegetative nature" <note>original: "vegetali natura". The lowest part of the soul responsible for growth and nutrition.</note> which follows the mind there, to live, to give life, and to move are the same thing. And these three necessarily accompany those three.

### That there are powers in the soul of the world, and how the lower orbs are moved toward the orb of the higher ones, and finally the lowest heaven circles toward the circuit.

III. The third chapter of the book confirms the previous points in this manner: The "First Soul" <note>original: "Anima prima". The World Soul (Anima Mundi) which animates the entire universe.</note> reigning in the world as if in its own living creature, seems to propagate vital power from the center (as if from a heart) through the whole. However, it communicates sensory and motive power beginning from the superior spheres (as if from a head) to the rest. It exercises reason within itself, and its mind within the divine mind. This mystery seems to have been received from Orpheus <note>Ficino often credited the mythical poet Orpheus as a source of "ancient theology" that preceded Plato.</note>. 

Now, just as we see a higher sphere contain and move a lower one, so the substance of the World Soul encompasses and leads the life communicated to its body. Similarly, powers within that substance revolve the powers in this life. In the substance itself, there is intellect, reason, and "primary imagination"—which is the first, common, and universal sense. When joined to reason, it is often called "opinion," just as reason joined to imagination is, in turn, called "opinion." 

These imaginations, by their own nature, are such that they perform their duties by discoursing through time, unless they are governed and strengthened by the mind. Nevertheless, they perform their circuits at every moment, just as a visual ray flashes out and is reflected back almost in the same instant. Therefore, from this substance of the World Soul—which by its nature and dignity is separate from the body—the world’s body is nourished and fed in no other way than through that "life" (as we said) which is entirely devoted to the body. Indeed, that life, by the power of the superior substance (insofar as it is substance), has the ability to nourish and move by nourishing. Insofar as that substance is "knowing," it has the ability to know through imagining. 

Thus, in this life, the duty of "procreation" <note>original: "genituræ". The generative or formative power of nature.</note> concurs with imagination in such a way that they move each other. Just as it is prepared for procreation, so it imagines; and as it imagines in turn, it becomes more ready for procreating. In us, indeed, a power of this kind is not open to our superior power, and it remains hidden from it while acting, since it depends not so much on us as on the nature of the world. This is both because when our soul first descends into the body, the body is already living by another life, and because this life of the body—even if it depends on our soul—becomes the body's own. Since our body becomes a part of the universal body, it rightly follows the life of the universe. 

But in the life and nature of the world, it accompanies the imagination joined to it, and vice versa. This life, along with both powers, proceeds from the soul's substance, flashes from the soul's powers, and is moved from there. But since this life is to generate individual things, it imagines individual things; and so that it may rightly imagine the order of the universe, it is led by a "prior imagination" that thinks of individual things rationally, being most closely joined to reason. Universal reason, in turn, considers both the whole and the individuals; finally, the intellect comprehends individuals within the universal. 

For this reason, the motion of heaven in a circle follows the motion of its own life, insofar as such a life is encompassed by a superior power and substance (as if by an orb) and is bent back into a circle. Indeed, in any corporeal sphere, whatever part is moved continuously with the whole draws the whole with it, while it pushes the parts in front of it and draws the parts behind it. Thus, the superior sphere surely makes the inferior one vibrate by its own motion. 

Finally, just as when our soul rejoices and is moved in its own way by a sudden "opinion of the good," the body (and especially the spirit) is moved in its own way (though through local motion), so too the "generative life" in the world—enjoying the good through its imagination (which is guided by the higher imagination)—rejoices and exults, suddenly inciting its body and leading it in a dance. The superior imagination, too, both guided by reason toward the good and itself rejoicing in the good already found...

Similarly, the reason directed toward the good intellect acts; similarly, the intellect moved by the Good is stirred. But since it is closest to the Good, and while it acts toward it, it does not need any formal medium, much less a temporal medium, therefore while it is moved—that is, acts around the Good—it is said and perceived to be at rest.

It is the circumference indeed, insofar as the superior part undoubtedly exceeds the inferior power by many degrees. By this excess, as if by a broader circuit, it stands above that lower, narrower power, and embraces, preserves, leads, and brings it back alike.

### ON THE MOTION OF THE HEAVEN.
### On the motion of the heaven.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Ennead II, Chapter 2, where Plotinus explores the physics and metaphysics of celestial motion. Having previously established the center as a point of divine rest, he now addresses why the heavens move in circles rather than straight lines, harmonizing the physical tendencies of elements like fire with the governing power of the Soul.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS BOOK II.

Since a body, by its own nature, is carried in a straight line, but the soul contains and restrains it, a certain motion is produced from both, in which the body is moved and yet remains in place at the same time. If circular motion is said to be a property of the body, how can this be rightly stated, since every body—even fire itself—is moved in a straight line? Indeed, we must say that it proceeds in a straight line until it reaches the place where it has been naturally established. For as it has been ordained by order, it appears both to remain according to its nature and to be moved toward that for which it was ordained. 

Why then does fire not rest after it has attained its proper seat? Is it because the very nature of fire is to be constantly in motion? Therefore, unless it revolves, it would surely be scattered in a straight line and immediately dissipated. Does it remain, then, so that it may be moved in a circle? But is this already the task of <term>Providence</term><note>Latin: "prouidentia"; Plotinus views Providence not just as foresight, but as the ordering principle that ensures the universe reflects the perfection of the Divine Intellect.</note>? Let it be so: for fire itself is placed within itself by Providence. For this reason, if it occurs there, it will revolve circularly of its own accord. Or perhaps, if it desires straight motion but has no further place to move toward, it necessarily revolves, as if circling back, in those places where it is able. For no place lies open to it beyond itself; this is the extreme limit. 

Thus, it runs around in the seat which it possesses; indeed, it is its own place, naturally established, not for the purpose of staying still, but to be moved. Accordingly, in a circle, the center naturally rests; but if the outer circumference were to rest, the center would become immense. Rather, the movement will exist around the center, specifically for a living body that is naturally disposed. For in this way, it will conspire toward the middle with a continuous inclination—not by settling down (for otherwise it would lose its orbit), but when it cannot do that, at least by wandering around it. Only by this means will it completely fulfill its desire. 

If the soul leads it around, it never grows weary; for the soul does not "pull" it, nor is the body moved against its nature. For that very thing is "nature" which has been ordained by the <term>Soul of the Universe</term><note>Also known as the "Anima Mundi," the third hypostasis in Plotinus's system, which gives life and order to the physical world.</note>. Furthermore, the Soul of the World, existing everywhere and not divided into parts but whole everywhere, grants to the heaven that it also, as much as it can, may be everywhere. But it can only do so by traversing and proceeding through all things. 

The heaven would surely rest if the soul rested anywhere, for it would have finally reached the soul. But now, since the soul itself, which the heaven desires, pours itself whole through the whole, the heaven follows the soul everywhere. What then, will it never catch up to the soul? Perhaps it always catches up to it in this way—indeed, the soul rather leads the heaven to itself always, and by always leading it, moves it forever. It does not move it elsewhere, but toward itself and in the same place, not indeed in a straight line but leading it in a circle; therefore, it grants to the heaven that wherever it arrives, it finds the soul there. If the soul were to rest, as if staying only in one place where anything might rest, the heaven would also rest. If, therefore, the soul is not in only one place but everywhere, the heaven is surely moved through all things. and since it is not carried outside, it is rightly turned back into an orbit.

<margin>
II.
The questions are resolved:
How the soul and human body move.
Again, how the heaven moves in a circle.
</margin>

But in what way are other things moved? Each is contained in its own place; but the heaven [contains all things], for it is the universe itself. By what logic then do they depend on the whole, of which each is a part? In what way does the body find the soul, and what is it compelled to do?

<column-break/>

For while the nature of the body is to be moved in a straight line, the soul holds it back; from both together comes a motion that is both moving and staying. If circular motion were said to be of the body, how could that be, when every body, even fire, moves in a straight line until it reaches the place where it is ordained? For as it is ordained, so it seems it will be according to nature, both to be moved toward what was ordained and to remain there. Why then does it not stay when it arrives? Is it because the nature of fire is in motion? If, then, it cannot move in a circle, it will be scattered in a straight line; is it therefore moved in a circle? But this is a work of Providence—yet it is within that very thing which belongs to Providence: so that if it should be there, it moves in a circle by its own nature. Or, desiring to run but having no more place to go, it turns back upon itself in the places where it can. For it has no place beyond itself; for this is the extreme limit. It runs therefore in the place it has, and is its own place, not so that it might stay still in nakedness, but so that it might be moved. And in a circle, the center remains according to nature, but if the outer circumference were to stay still, the center would be a great thing. Rather, it stands around the center, for a living body that is naturally disposed. For thus it tends toward the center, not by collapsing—which the circle prevents—but since it cannot do that, it moves around it. For in this way alone will it fulfill its impulse. <margin>* if the soul leads around</margin> If the soul leads it around, it does not tire: for it does not drag it, nor is it against nature; for nature is that which is ordained by the whole soul. Since the soul of the universe is everywhere whole, and not divided into parts, it gives to the heaven the power to be everywhere as much as it can. It is able to do this by passing through and traversing all things. Indeed, it would stay still if the soul stayed still anywhere, having arrived there. But now, since <margin>* in all things</margin> the soul is whole in all, the heaven desires the whole. Or will it never attain it? Or does it always attain it in this way, or rather, the soul always leads the heaven toward herself, and in leading it, moves it, and not moving it elsewhere, but toward herself in the same place, leading it not in a straight line but in a circle, she gives to it, wherever it may come, to have her there. But if she stayed as if she were only in one place, where each thing stays, it would stop. If <margin>* it will be placed</margin> then she is not only there but anywhere, it will be placed everywhere, and not being outside, it moves therefore in a circle.

How then are other things? Or is not each thing a whole, but a part, and also held in a partial place? But that other thing is the whole, and like a place, and nothing hinders the whole itself. How then are men? Or is it that they are as much a part as they receive from the whole? But as much as they are themselves, each is its own whole. If it is not everywhere, and does not have the soul where it is, why must it wander further? Or is it because the soul does not flourish only there, if it were...

Truly, not every thing is a whole, but each is a part. The whole is like a place, and nothing hinders it. How then are men moved? Perhaps by the same reasoning as the whole, each of us is a certain part; but insofar as we are ourselves, each is a proper whole. Likewise, if the soul does not only flourish alicubi [somewhere]...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of circular motion in the heavens from Ennead II, Chapter 2. Having established that the celestial spheres move because of the soul's influence, Plotinus now investigates the nature of the "center" around which they revolve and why the soul's orientation toward the Divine necessitates a circular path.</meta>

# BOOK SECOND.

Its power is around the center, and in this way also, the center is in a circle. <margin>Matter is not in it</margin> and likewise for the body. The nature of the soul must be understood similarly; but there the center is that from which <margin>Matter</margin> arises, while in a body, it is spatial. Therefore, one must consider the center by analogy. For as it is there, so also here there must be a center, which is the center of the body alone; and since that other center is spherical around it, so too is this one. If indeed it is the soul’s nature to revolve around God, she loves Him with all her being, and as much as possible, she holds herself around Him. For all things depend upon her. But since she does not remain directly with Him, she moves around Him. Why then do not all things act thus? Or rather, does each thing act according to where it is? Why then do our bodies not do the same? Because the <term>Aetherial</term><note>The "Aether" was considered the fifth element, pure and celestial, making up the stars and heavens.</note> path is joined to wisdom and <margin>the Sun</margin> their impulses are toward one another. Our own spherical part cannot be easily turned in a circle, for it has become <term>earthly</term><note>Meaning weighted down by physical, heavy matter compared to the "light" celestial bodies.</note>; for there, that which is subtle and easily moved follows along. For I do not see why it should rest, by whatever motion the soul is moved. Perhaps in us also the <margin>not in the soul, not in all</margin> spiritual body which is diffused around the soul produces a fire. For if God is in all things, it is necessary for the soul, desiring to be with Him, to pour herself around Him. For He is not merely in one place. Therefore, Plato attributes to the stars not only a circular motion together with the whole, but also gives to each a motion around its own center. For each globe, wherever it is, embracing God in a certain way, exults; not by any deliberate counsel, but moved by a natural necessity.

<column-break/>

The soul does not merely affect the body in some specific place. If, however, the power of the soul flourishes around the center, for this reason also motion occurs in a circle. But the center is not to be placed in the soul in the same way as it is in the body. For this reason, there must be a center here by a certain proportion: for as it is there, so also here there must be a center: which is indeed only the center of the body, and specifically of this spherical one; for just as that is, so also this is around itself. If this is so, the soul again revolves around God and desires to embrace Him, and behaves toward Him in whatever way she can, for all things depend upon God. But since she does not remain fixed within Him, she at least moves around Him. Why then do not all things achieve this? Indeed, every thing does so from wherever it is. But why do our bodies not do the same? Because, clearly, that which proceeds in a straight motion is joined to them, and furthermore, their impulses turn toward other things. That which is spherical in us cannot easily be twisted back into a circle: for it has already become earthly; but there, that which is subtle and easily moved finds rest. For I do not see how it could rest, by whatever motion the soul may be moved. Perhaps in us even the spiritual body, which is spread around the soul, performs the same. For if God is in all things, it is necessary for the soul, desiring to meet with Him, to pour herself around Him. For He is not merely in some one place. Accordingly, Plato attributes to the stars not only a circular motion along with the whole, but also to each a motion around its own proper center. For every sphere, wherever it is, in some way embracing God, exults—not indeed by any plan, but moved by a natural necessity.

<margin>III. The points above are confirmed: the soul turns the world in a circle through its higher power, and through its lower power rotates the heavens.</margin>

Let this same matter be considered in this way. The last power of the soul, starting from the earth, pours itself through the universe; but the power of the sensory soul, and that which possesses the reasoning of opinion, flourishes among the higher spheres, brooding over the lower power and extending from itself a more vital and life-giving force to it. This lower power is therefore moved by the higher one, which embraces it in a circle and sits upon the whole, as much as it reaches up into the spheres. Therefore, since the higher power encompasses the lower in a circle, the lower is rightly reflected back into itself. This reflection of the soul twists the body into which it has been infused. For in a sphere, no matter how small a part is moved, if it is moved while remaining in place, it necessarily shakes the sphere in which it exists, from which the motion of the sphere proceeds. For in our own bodies, when the mind is moved—even if it is moved in a far different way, such as rejoicing with joy at the thought of something good—a local motion of the body is also produced from it. From there, therefore, the soul emerging near the Good, and having become more sharp in its perception, moves around the Good, and the body, according to its nature, is stirred to local motion. The sensory power, stirred again by the higher, and perceiving its own good and congratulating itself, follows after it; and since it is everywhere, it rightly brings all things together through itself. The <term>Intellect</term><note>Greek: "Nous." In Plotinus's system, the Intellect is the realm of pure being and thought that eternally contemplates the One (the Good).</note> also performs a certain action: thus it certainly moves. For it remains still and moves at the same time, for it is reflected into itself. In a similar way, the universe moves in a circle and remains still at once.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON
## BOOK III OF THE SECOND ENNEAD,
## WHETHER THE STARS DO ANYTHING.
### COMMENTARY.

### SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

*Species and individuals within species are generated primarily from the <term>seminal reasons</term><note>Latin: "rationes seminales." In Neoplatonism, these are the formative, creative powers or blueprints inherent in nature that direct the growth and development of physical things.</note> in species and individuals; however, celestial things dispose matter in one way or another.*

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial P featuring floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>Porphyry writes in his *Life of Plotinus* that Plotinus, although he had applied diligent effort to astrology, discovered that the judgments of astrologers were not to be trusted. He frequently refuted them, both in speech and in writing. This he did indeed in his book *On Fate*, and in his books *On Providence*. But finally, in this book, *Whether the stars do anything*, he seems to have carried this out more diligently. In this work, Plotinus’s purpose is primarily to assert that whatever things are generated and moved by nature are chiefly produced and guided both by the <term>seminal reasons</term> of universal nature and by the specific reasons and seeds that are in no way discordant with universal nature. Therefore, he argues that neither the natural influences of the stars (insofar as they are merely general) nor the present configurations of the celestial bodies among themselves (being highly changeable and common to all) produce these individual things specifically. Instead, they perhaps sometimes serve as "signs." Even then, he argues that conjecture is deceptive and judgment happens to be uncertain because it is based on very general and confused indications. It is certainly necessary that common things be distinguished by specific ones, and that changeable things be governed and guided by firm things—or at least by somewhat firmer things—lest things happen by chance everywhere. He admits, however, through the daily concurrence of celestial and lower causes, that while things exist, they are changed in quality but not in species; likewise, they are changed through art and practice. As for the causes of our affairs, he refers them partly to higher things, partly to those things around us, and partly to counsel, practice, and opportunity. He believes, moreover, that just as the body is ruled by the soul, so the soul is ruled by the intellect, and that the soul can be liberated from the common impulses of fate and fortune through the gift of intelligence.

-> The nature of the planets is not malevolent, nor is it changeable by a change of <-
-> location; nor are natural things primarily generated from their <-
-> rays and motions, but from their own internal <-
-> natures everywhere, and from universal nature. <-

<margin>1</margin> In the first chapter, therefore, he relates how astrologers—not all of them, I say, but many—think that individual things are both signified and produced by the powers and motions of the stars. This applies to external things, to the body, and even to the soul and the actions of the soul, whether they be good and honorable or, conversely, evil and base. But you must remember that the principal authors of astrology do not hand down these views; rather, certain "common" astrologers, utterly ignorant of astronomy, divulge such things. He notes, furthermore, that Plotinus, right from the beginning, perhaps for the sake of argument, concedes that certain things are signified by celestial motion, but not all; and that many things are produced from it, but not all; and that those things which are signified can hardly be discerned. While relating these points, he mocks the astrologers for two things. First, because they say that the stars change their natures according to the change of their locations and <term>aspects</term><note>The relative positions and angles between planets (like square, trine, or opposition) which astrologers believe alter their influence.</note>. Certainly, such a change does not happen even in earthly things, which are most changeable, from a mere change of location or a difference in how they are viewed. Second, because they say that even the best stars are made evil, and that those which perform the beneficent duty of providence often harm innocent men. He especially detests the idea that all stars are animate and endowed with intelligence and obey God at his nod—which Ptolemy himself admits—yet these people do not hesitate to call some of them good and others evil. Likewise, he mocks them because they assert that even the planets they call "evil" often bestow good things. For example, they say Saturn may stabilize the good things granted by others, and that when he is placed in his own "temple" or "exaltation," he—the Saturnian influence—is beneficial. They say Mars provides greatness of soul and fortitude, and though he harms others, he spares his own. He mocks them again because they admit the planets they call "good" sometimes do harm—specifically, that Venus mixed with Mercury hinders prudence, and Jupiter joined with Mars establishes tyranny. Then they say the planets are changed in this way—either by looking at one another or by not looking—such that it is a marvel that eternal things are changed so greatly by such a small action. Thus they believe that the Moon, if she looks at Mercury, provides a desire obedient to reason; if she does not look at him, she provides unbridled lust, especially if she looks at Venus or Mars in the meantime. He mocks them for saying that Mercury, while he looks at Saturn or Mars, becomes "Mars-like" or "Saturn-like," but then by looking at Jupiter he becomes "Jupiter-like"—as if, like a chameleon, he has no constant nature of his own, even though nothing among us is so uncertain and utterly changeable. Furthermore, he wonders how it can be true, as they teach, that the "gaze" of the planets among themselves is so unstable that every time they behold each other in a different configuration, that gaze is forced to change its nature. Certainly, such a great change does not occur even in our own gaze when we behold one another now from one position and then from another. He seems, however, willing to concede that because of the various aspects of the stars, some natural variety can occur—if less in the stars themselves, then at least in physical things; a point we investigate in our book *On Life*. Finally, regarding their claim that from the combination of all celestial rays, a new form and virtue is produced within the rays themselves when joined together—a form that differs in various ways according to the diversity of times and places, just as one form is made from different liquids mixed together—Plotinus seems to condemn this for the reason that rays are neither bodies, like liquids, nor qualities in bodies, like the natures of liquids. Rather, they are certain vital and sensory acts of the stars, like "visual rays" flashing out from the stars as if from the eyes of a celestial <term>Argus</term><note>In Greek mythology, Argus Panoptes was a giant with a hundred eyes, making him an all-seeing watchman. Ficino uses this as a metaphor for the stars' watchful and active influence.</note>, and wonderfully completing all things. These rays are not perceived in any external subject in the manner of qualities; therefore, they are not "stained" by it, nor are they changed from their prior condition, nor do they change into another form common to all. This is just as the visual rays of many animals that see at night are neither made specific to some subject nor do many rays confuse themselves into one form. But although Plotinus has not approved of the astrologers up to this point, he will perhaps approve if they say that from rays scattered everywhere—even if they are not specific to any subject—nevertheless specific qualities are now produced (just as heat is produced from light), and these qualities are reduced into one form in a subject. And just as in the mixing of liquids a new form is made all the more quickly the more powerful the cause that mixes them, so qualities are suddenly granted to subjects from the common gathering of rays, and these rays reconcile those qualities into one.
