# ON BOOK III OF THE SECOND ENNEAD.
<sig>k 2</sig>

...because the causes are both vast and powerful, and the movement is most effective and swift. Plotinus will indeed concede that qualities converging into such a form are brought forth by a certain stable cause that is entirely and everywhere active—namely, the **seminal power** that flourishes in the life of the world—lest things reach a unity merely by chance or instability. He admits that rays flowing together in one way or another might affect matter differently, or provoke the acting cause (that is, the <term>seminal reason</term><note>The "ratio seminalis" is a formative blueprint in nature that directs growth.</note>) toward its proper effect. 

However, he argues that a new form, which requires a specific amount of time to be initiated and perfected, cannot be produced solely from a confluence of rays (which changes from one moment to the next). Such a form is determined not just by that immediate confluence, but by the preceding disposition of the matter, and finally by what the **seminal reason** of both specific and universal nature decrees for such a condition. Ultimately, however the matter stands, it is extremely difficult to judge the future. For if it is hidden from us what new thing might arise from the mixture of natural elements that we handle every day, it will be far more hidden what new fellowship or form is forged by the casting of celestial rays. 

Indeed, since astrologers admit that the union of two celestial rays produces something different than the casting of a single ray, and undoubtedly something else is produced by a coupling of all the planets than by just two, it follows that something far different occurs from the confluence of all the stars. But the more causes that flow together to act, the more difficult the judgment becomes: because not all causes are grasped, nor, if they were grasped, is it immediately weighed what new thing is produced from the whole. This is especially true since, to judge, one must look around at the confluence not only of celestial causes, but also of elemental causes and contingent things, as **Ptolemy**<note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and geographer of antiquity.</note> himself admits and instructs.

### How celestial things signify even those things they do not cause: the celestial bodies are animate. Many things cannot be brought about by celestial bodies and motions.

II In the second chapter, he treats the idea that not all things are caused by the heavens: for if they are inanimate, they cannot do those things which properly belong to the soul; and if they are animate—possessing, namely, a divine soul—they do not do evil. The authors of astronomy concede to us that the celestial bodies are animate, especially **Ptolemy**, **Abu Ma’shar**, and **Sahl ibn Bishr**<note>Abu Ma’shar (Latinized as Abumasar) and Sahl ibn Bishr (Zaeles) were prominent medieval Arabic astrologers whose works were central to Renaissance science.</note>. This is also confirmed by **Hali**<note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an Egyptian physician and astrologer.</note>, who, following Ptolemy’s opinion, mocks those who doubt that the heavens are alive simply because they do not wander about in the manner of our animals. He says, along with Ptolemy, that the celestial animals perpetually preserve the one best course of motion they have chosen once and for all. **Aratus** and **Manilius**<note>Roman poets who wrote on the stars and constellations.</note> think similarly. 

I believe they understood that if the heavens act upon the soul, they cannot act upon it except through a soul, and a superior one at that. Furthermore, if they signify things to us that cannot be referred to a bodily cause, this can only happen if the series of future events is inscribed in the celestial souls; the stars then explain this to us at times, as if by the **nods of eyes**. Plotinus believes that this explanation, when it occurs, happens in many things for which not the stars, but we ourselves and our own causes, will be responsible. Truly, where there are signs, there are not immediately causes—just as a father’s favorable nod toward his son is not the *cause* of a future benefit, but a *sign* of it. 

Thus, when astrologers predict that a person will be wise because **Mercury** is positioned in a certain way, the body of the planet itself is not the cause of that wisdom. For that which does not create a soul cannot create the wisdom proper to a soul. Rather, the sign indicates to us that the body of the newborn will be tempered to be obedient to wisdom. And as a sign, it portends that the soul descending into the body (to speak in a Platonic way) at that time is a "familiar" of the Mercurial soul and divinity, and is governed by a certain **Mercurial daemon**<note>In this context, a "daemon" is a guiding spirit or guardian assigned to a person at birth based on their astrological profile.</note> or something similar. 

**Porphyry**<note>Plotinus's student and biographer.</note> indeed says: "Anyone will know what sort of daemon they have obtained if they recognize the figure of their birth and who stood as the ruler within it." However, although some have claimed to know who the principal lord in a birth chart is, Porphyry says in his *Questions to Anebo*—on the testimony of **Chaemon** and other astronomers—that this matter is uncertain. 

If some were to deny that the celestial bodies are alive, they would be forced to admit that their bodily natures produce nothing among us except by the ministry of elemental bodies. Therefore, they would bring only the qualities of bodies, and nothing beyond that. But they would not even bring all the qualities of bodies. Just as in art, the form of a crafted work, even if it seems to be made by a tool, is actually produced by the form of the craftsman’s intelligence, which alone it imitates; so too the forms of natural things, arranged by a logic greater than any art, do not so much imitate the mass or qualities of celestial bodies as they follow the **concepts** of celestial souls. 

Furthermore, the heat in an animal does not transform food into the form of life simply because it is heat (the job of which is to dissolve), but insofar as it is guided by life. Nor do heat and moisture in the world, or any other quality, perform a work toward a most chosen end in a certain order because they are drawn by their own nature or the impulse of the celestial mass, but insofar as they are tempered within themselves and among each other by the **reason** of the celestial movers and are conveniently directed to a prescribed end. 

For this reason, Plotinus says: "The outflow of each celestial body is the same—namely, that in the respect that they are bodies, they are everywhere bodily; and insofar as they are fiery, they heat; and by their own reason which moistens or thins, they always moisten or thin." Although whatever comes from there, whether by common or specific reason, happens more or less in one place than another, no other variety arises from there except in certain accidental qualities of matter and the degrees of those accidents. 

However, the variety of specific shapes and special forms and virtues will not be primarily from the natural intention of the celestial bodies; rather, as far as they are concerned, it happens by chance, or at least is given from elsewhere. For that which is done by artistic reason comes only from art and living reason—especially if the thing itself is alive. We will not concede to astrologers if they say that the bodies of the **fixed stars** provide the specific differences of things, while the daily configurations of the **planets** provide individual differences, even if the heavens had no soul. For the bodies of the fixed stars can indeed bestow various bodily qualities everywhere, being uniform just as they themselves are uniform. But they can only attribute proper shapes to species and an order toward an end if they possess soul and mind—especially since in many species of foreign stones and precious gems there are certain singular powers by which they act wonderfully upon the **spirit** and, through the spirit, seem to bring wondrous gifts to the soul. 

Yet these bodies could not have received such a gift from celestial bodies alone, but from their souls. Indeed, the bodies of the stars themselves can much less inflict upon us those differences that pertain to arts, fortunes, and necessities. Just as there is nothing in the nature of your body—and likewise nothing in the nature of a celestial body—to make you a **theologian** rather than an **orator**, or to designate you as a **Praetor**<note>A high-ranking judicial official in Ancient Rome.</note> at a certain time, or to give you such a father or brother; we are compelled to investigate the causes of these things elsewhere immediately. Finally, all the stars...

<meta>This page transitions from the general introduction of Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Enneads to a specific critique of deterministic astrology. It establishes the central argument: that while stars may be signs, the true power of generation lies within the "seminal reasons" of nature itself.</meta>

MARSILIO FICINO'S COMMENTARY ON THE THIRD BOOK OF THE SECOND ENNEAD: WHETHER THE STARS ACT UPON ANYTHING.

## SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

->Species and individuals within species are generated primarily by the **seminal virtues** <note>Ficino uses "virtues" here to mean inherent powers or capacities.</note> within those species and individuals; however, celestial bodies dispose matter in various ways.<-

Porphyry writes in his *Life of Plotinus* that although Plotinus had devoted diligent effort to the study of astrology, he eventually concluded that the judgments of astrologers are not to be trusted. He frequently refuted them, both in speech and in writing—most notably in his book *On Fate* and his books *On Providence*. But in this final book, *Whether the Stars Act*, he seems to have accomplished this task even more thoroughly. In this work, Plotinus’s primary aim is to assert that whatever is born or moved by nature is chiefly created and guided by two things: the **universal seminal reasons** <term>seminal reasons</term><note>Latin: *rationes seminariae*. In Neoplatonic thought, these are the invisible, formative blueprints that exist within nature to direct the growth of specific living things.</note> of nature as a whole, and the specific reasons and seeds of individual things that are in harmony with that nature.

Therefore, he argues that the influence and nature of the stars are too universal to be the sole cause of specific events. Nor can the fleeting "aspects" <note>The relative positions and angles between planets.</note> of the heavenly bodies be the cause, as they are too common and changeable to produce specific individual effects. Instead, he suggests that stars might sometimes **signify** (rather than cause) events. Even then, because the signs are so general and confused, any conjecture based on them is often fallacious and judgment remains uncertain. It is necessary for general influences to be specified by the individual's own nature, and for moving things to be guided by what is firm—or at least firmer—lest things happen by mere chance. 

He does admit, however, that through the daily meeting of celestial and earthly causes, things are changed in their qualities and appearance while they exist; this also happens through art and human practice. As for our own affairs, he attributes their causes partly to higher things, partly to our surroundings, and partly to human counsel, practice, and opportunity. He believes, moreover, that just as the body is ruled by the soul, so the soul is ruled by the intellect; through the gift of intelligence, the soul can be freed from the common impulses of **fate** and **fortune**.

->The nature of the planets is not malicious, nor is it changeable by a change of location; nor are natural things primarily generated from their rays and motions, but from their own internal natures and universal nature.<-

<margin>1</margin> In the first chapter, then, he recounts how astrologers—not all of them, mind you, but many—think that every single thing is both signified and caused by the powers and motions of the stars. This includes external events, the state of the body, and the actions and character of the soul, whether they be good and honorable or evil and base. But you should remember that it is not the leading authors of astrology who teach this, but certain "common" astrologers, utterly ignorant of true astronomy, who spread such ideas.

Notice, furthermore, that right from the start, Plotinus concedes for the sake of argument that *some* things are signified by celestial motion (though not all), and many things are caused by it (though not all), and that what is signified can hardly be discerned. While recounting these things, he mocks astrologers for two reasons. First, because they say the stars change their very natures based on their change of location and aspect. Such a change does not even happen to earthly things (which are the most changeable of all) merely because they move or because someone looks at them differently.

Second, he mocks them because they claim that even the "best" stars can be evil, and that those which perform a beneficial duty of providence often harm innocent people. He finds it especially detestable that they dare to call some stars "good" and others "bad," when all stars are animate, endowed with intelligence, and obey God’s command—a fact that Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the most influential astronomer and geographer of antiquity.</note> himself admits.

Furthermore, he points out their inconsistency: they claim that planets they call "bad" (like Saturn) can often bestow "good" things, such as stabilizing the benefits given by others or helping those born under Saturn's influence when the planet is in its "exaltation." They say Mars provides greatness of soul and fortitude, and though he may harm others, he spares his own. Conversely, he laughs at how they admit "good" planets can sometimes cause harm: for instance, that Venus mixed with Mercury might hinder prudence, or Jupiter joined with Mars might establish a tyranny.

Then there is the claim that planets change simply by "looking" or not "looking" at one another. It is absurd that eternal things could be so completely altered by such a minor interaction. They believe that the Moon, if it "looks" at Mercury, provides a desire that obeys the laws of reason; but if it does not look at him, it provides unbridled lust—especially if it looks at Venus or Mars in the meantime. He mocks them for saying that Mercury, when looking at Saturn or Mars, *becomes* Saturnian or Martial, and then Jovial when looking at Jupiter—as if he were a **chameleon** <note>The original text uses the comparison to a chameleon to emphasize Mercury's supposed lack of a stable nature in astrology.</note> with no constant nature of his own, when even among us, nothing is so utterly unstable.

He wonders, moreover, how it can be true that the "gaze" of the planets between themselves is so unstable that every time they see each other in a different geometric figure, that gaze is forced to change its very nature. Such a massive change does not even occur in our own sight when we look at one another from different positions. He seems willing to concede, however, that due to various celestial aspects, some natural variation might occur in earthly things (a topic we investigate in our book *On Life*).

Finally, he addresses the idea that a new form and power is created from the total convergence of all celestial rays, which varies by time and place—much like a single liquid created from a mixture of different ingredients. Plotinus seems to condemn this idea because rays are not physical bodies like liquids, nor are they qualities *within* bodies like the properties of liquids. Instead, they are the **vital and sensory acts** of the stars—like "visual rays" flashing out from the stars as if from the eyes of a "celestial Argus" <note>Argus Panoptes, the hundred-eyed giant of myth; here, a metaphor for the many-eyed heavens.</note> and wonderfully affecting all things. These rays are not absorbed like qualities into a physical subject; therefore, they are not stained by it, nor changed from their prior state, nor do they combine into a single "common" form. Just as the visual rays of many animals that see at night do not become the property of the object they see, nor do they blur together into one form.

But although Plotinus has not approved of astrologers thus far, he might approve if they were to say that from these scattered rays, qualities are indeed produced in the subjects—just as heat is produced from light—and that these qualities are reduced to a single form within the subject. And just as in a mixture of liquids a new form is created all the more quickly the more powerful the mixing cause is, so from the common convergence of rays, qualities are suddenly bestowed upon subjects and reconciled into one...

The true cause of generation lies in internal "seminal reasons" rather than shifting planetary aspects.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of Plotinus’s skepticism regarding traditional astrology. On the previous page, Ficino introduced the idea that natural growth is driven by internal "seminal reasons" rather than external celestial forces. Here, he deepens the argument by questioning whether the stars are causes or merely signs, and whether they possess souls capable of directing human affairs.</meta>

### ON THE THIRD BOOK OF THE SECOND ENNEAD

...because the causes are immense and powerful, and their motion is most effective and swift. Plotinus will certainly grant that the qualities merging into such a form are brought about by a single cause that is entirely stable and flourishing everywhere—namely, by the **seminal virtue** <note>Latin: *virtute seminaria*. These are the vital, formative powers inherent in the life of the world that ensure nature follows a consistent pattern rather than acting randomly.</note> that thrives in the life of the world, so that unity is achieved neither by chance nor instability. However, he argues that rays converging in one way or another might affect matter differently, or provoke the active cause—that is, the seminal reason—to produce its specific effect. Yet, a new form cannot be produced from a mere confluence of rays, which is always changing from one moment to the next; a form requires a certain amount of time to be initiated and perfected. Such a form is not merely the result of that confluence, but also depends on the preceding disposition of the matter and, finally, on what the seminal reason decrees for that condition, both within its own nature and in the nature of the universe. 

In short, however things may stand, it is extremely difficult to judge the future. For if it is hidden from us what new thing might arise from the mixing of natural elements which we handle daily, it will be much more hidden to see what new communion and form is produced by the casting of rays. It is admitted that something different is produced from a conjunction of all the planets than from just two; and therefore, something vastly different occurs from the confluence of all the stars. But the more causes that flow together to act, the more difficult the judgment becomes. This is because not all causes are grasped, and even if they were, one cannot immediately weigh what new result might be produced from them all together—especially since a judge must look around at the confluence not only of celestial causes, but also of elemental causes and contingent events, as **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century mathematician and astronomer whose works *Almagest* and *Tetrabiblos* defined the field for over a millennium.</note> himself admits and commands.

->How celestial things signify even those things they do not cause. Celestial things are ensouled. There are many things<-
->which cannot be brought about by celestial bodies and motions.<-

<margin>II</margin> In the second chapter, he argues that not everything is caused by celestial things. For if they are inanimate, they cannot do those things which properly belong to the soul; and if they are animate—possessing a divine soul—they do not do evil. The authors of astronomy grant us that the celestial bodies are indeed animate, especially Ptolemy, **Abu Ma'shar**, and **Zielen** <note>original: *Abumasar & Zielen*. Abu Ma'shar was a leading Persian astrologer; 'Zielen' likely refers to Arzachel (Al-Zarqali) or another medieval authority.</note>. **Hali** <note>Haly Abenragel or Ali ibn Ridwan, prominent Arabic commentators on Ptolemy.</note> confirms this, mocking those who, following Ptolemy’s opinion, disagree that the heavens are alive simply because they do not wander about aimlessly like our animals. For he says, along with Ptolemy, that celestial animals perpetually preserve the best course of motion once it has been chosen. **Aratus** and **Manilius** think similarly. I believe they understood that if the stars act upon the soul, they can only do so through a soul, and a superior one at that. 

Furthermore, if through them something is signified to us that cannot be referred to a bodily cause, this can only happen if the series of future events is inscribed in the celestial souls. These souls then explain these events to us at certain times through the stars, as if by the "nods" of eyes. Plotinus believes that this explanation, whenever it happens, also occurs in many things for which not the stars, but we ourselves and our own actions, will be the cause. 

Where there are signs, there are not immediately causes. Just as a father’s favorable glance toward his son is not the *cause* of a future benefit, but a *sign* of it. Thus, when astrologers predict that a person will be wise because **Mercury** <note>The planet Mercury was traditionally associated with intelligence, eloquence, and calculation.</note> is positioned in a certain way, the physical body of the planet is not the cause of that wisdom. For that which does not create the soul cannot create the wisdom proper to the soul. Rather, the body of the newborn indicates to us—acting as both a cause and a sign—that the person will be tempered in a way that is obedient to wisdom. And as a sign, it portends that the soul descending into the body at that time (to speak in a **Platonic** manner) is kindred to the Mercurial soul and divinity, and is governed by a certain Mercurial or similar **daemon** <term>daemon</term><note>A guiding spirit or intermediary being, not to be confused with the modern "demon." In Neoplatonism, it is a personal guardian that directs a person's destiny.</note>. 

Indeed, **Porphyry** says: "A person will know what kind of daemon he has obtained if he recognizes the figure of his birth and who was the ruler within it." However, while some claim they can know who the principal lord in the birth chart is, Porphyry, in his *Letter to Anebo*, says that the testimony of **Chaeremon** and other astronomers shows this is uncertain. 

Even if some deny that the celestial bodies are alive, they are forced to admit that their physical natures cannot achieve anything here among us except through the service of elemental bodies. Therefore, they would only bring about the qualities of bodies and nothing further. But they do not even bring about all the qualities of bodies. For just as in art, the form of a crafted work—though it seems to be made by a tool—is actually produced by the intelligence of the form, which it alone imitates; so too the forms of natural things, arranged with more than artificial reason, do not so much imitate or follow the bulk or qualities of celestial bodies as they do the **notions** <note>Divine ideas or mental blueprints.</note> of celestial souls. 

Furthermore, the heat in an animal does not transform food into the form of life simply because it is a physical body, but because its duty is to dissolve matter insofar as it is guided by life. Similarly, heat and moisture in the world, or any other quality, do not complete their work toward a most chosen end in a certain order because they are drawn by their own nature or the impulse of the celestial mass, but because they are tempered within themselves and among each other by the **reason** of the celestial movers, and are directed conveniently to a prescribed end. 

For this reason, Plotinus says: "The outflow of each celestial body is the same," meaning that in their capacity as bodies, they are everywhere corporeal; and in their capacity as fiery things, they nourish with heat. This is true even though some stars bring moisture along with heat, others bring rarity, others density, others speed, others firmness, and so on. Thus, by a common condition, all stars heat in some way, and by their own specific reason (which may moisten or rarefy), they always moisten or rarefy. However, whatever is produced there by common or specific reason happens more or less in one place than another. No other variety arises from this than in certain accidental qualities of matter and the degrees of those accidents. 

But the variety of special shapes, forms, and virtues will not arise primarily from the natural intention of the celestial bodies; rather, as far as the stars are concerned, it will happen by chance, or at least be granted from elsewhere. For whatever exists by artificial reason is made only by art and by a living reason—especially if it is alive itself. 

Nor shall we concede to the astrologers if they say that the bodies of the **fixed stars** <note>The stars that do not move relative to each other, as opposed to the "wandering stars" or planets.</note> provide the species of things, and the daily positions of the planets provide individual differences, even if the heavens had no soul. For while the bodies of the fixed stars can indeed bestow various physical qualities uniformly (just as they themselves are uniform), they can only grant specific shapes to species and an order toward an end if they possess a soul and a mind. This is especially true because in many kinds of foreign stones and precious gems, there are certain singular powers that act wonderfully upon the **spirit**; through that spirit, they seem to bring marvelous gifts to the soul. Such a great gift cannot have been received from the celestial bodies alone, but must come from their souls. 

Furthermore, the physical bodies of the stars can even less bring about those differences among us that pertain to skills, fortunes, and necessities. For just as there is no nature in your body—and no nature in a celestial body—that makes you a **Theologian** rather than an **Orator**, or designates you as a **Praetor** <note>A high-ranking government official or judge in ancient Rome.</note> at a certain time, or determines that you have a certain father or brother; we are compelled to investigate the causes of these things elsewhere immediately. Finally, all the stars...

<summary>Ficino argues that the stars act more as signs than as physical causes for human traits like wisdom or social status, asserting that celestial influence requires the presence of a "soul" rather than mere material force. He critiques the limits of physical astrology, suggesting that complex human destinies cannot be explained by the simple movement of planetary bodies alone.</summary>

<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

[The celestial causes] are far removed from the lowliest things and are very different from one another; and whatever is diffused from there down to here seems to be an <term>accident</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist, unlike its "substance."</note>. However, since a substantial cause is needed to generate a substance among us, and a proximate cause is needed for perfect generation, and a living cause for a living thing, we must also consider the need for a common leader to reconcile diverse agents into a unity. We certainly believe that one life reigns everywhere, primarily creating all things and using celestial and earthly instruments for that purpose.

### Chapter III

The third chapter continues the same arguments as follows: Astrologers will perhaps admit that planets are indeed living beings and are not evil by nature, but that they are made <term>malefic</term> <note>Latin: *maleficos*. In astrology, "malefic" refers to planets like Saturn and Mars, traditionally thought to bring hardship.</note> by a certain degree of a sign or by a certain geometric figure formed while looking at each other, and thus they change their nature along with their location. However, this is disproved for five reasons. 

**First:** because that degree of the signs—or at least the degree that is so affected—would have to be evil by nature if a planet placed in it or affecting it were to turn out evil. Yet they admit that no part of the heavens is naturally evil. 

**Second:** if degrees and figures of this sort possessed an evil nature in themselves, all planets placed in that degree and figure would similarly be rendered evil. This, however, the astrologers will not concede. 

**Third:** one must ask how this or that planet can become different in different degrees—so different, in fact, that it becomes harm-doing. First of all, no planet is actually *in* a degree of the Zodiac, but is at a vast distance from it; so even if that degree happened to be harmful, the planet could not be so infected from there. Furthermore, wherever it may be, it is in heaven. Heaven is the most excellent body, closest to divinity; therefore, every single part of heaven is utterly excellent and divine. 

**Fourth:** since heaven is largely uniform and its motion is local—and local motion does not necessarily cause an earthly moveable object to change its nature—it is ridiculous to suggest that a planet assumes a different nature in one region of heaven after another. This is especially true since it is a powerful and eternal substance, and since it must be "at home" in a living divinity wherever it is. 

**Fifth:** it is also absurd to say, as they do, that a planet has one nature when it is in an <term>angle</term> <note>Latin: *angulo*. The "angles" are the four most powerful points in a horoscope: the Ascendant (East), Descendant (West), Midheaven (Zenith), and Imum Coeli (Nadir).</note> and another when it declines from an angle. For at the same time, the same planet is at an angle for us, but for distant nations, it is declining, and vice versa. It would therefore have different natures at the very same time. 

Astrologers invent four "angles" in the celestial figure: in the East, in the West, in the Midheaven above, and the Midheaven below. They say a planet is "angular" when it holds an angle within five or at least three degrees of a sign on either side: namely, the very point of the East, the West, or the Midheaven. But as soon as it moves from there, they say it "falls" from the angle. They dread Mars above all others in the angles, especially in the West. They also do not choose Saturn to be angular. Since they consider these planets harmful, they do not think they should be placed in the angles lest they be more powerful—unless perhaps Saturn is in Aquarius, his own <term>house</term>, or in Libra, his <term>exaltation</term>, especially in a daytime birth. 

They therefore place Saturn in the <term>twelfth house</term> of the figure, and Mars in the sixth. They call the twelfth region of heaven that which precedes the Eastern part, and they claim this twelfth house is "falling" <note>Latin: *cadentem*. Cadent houses were traditionally considered weak.</note>, even though in reality it is rising upward. They name the "sixth" house that which seems to fall from the angle of the West. I will pass over other points for now, but in placing Saturn in the twelfth and Mars in the sixth, they seem to contradict themselves. For in this way, they set them opposite to one another, an opposition which they usually sharply detest. Add to this that they so infest the sixth house (by which diseases are signified) both with the opposition of Saturn and the presence of Mars, that all diseases would be incurable. 

In general, since reason does not permit a transition from the strongest to the weakest without a middle point, no one would dare say that if a planet is strongest in an angle, it will suddenly be weakest after the angle. Furthermore, since a star acts more completely upon us the longer it remains, and the sign they call the twelfth lingers longer over us than the angular portion of the Ascendant, they are forced to admit that it acts more upon us than the Ascendant. Yet they do not usually admit this. Again, while Ptolemy usually says a planet or sign in the Midheaven is most powerful, how can the teaching of <term>Zael</term> <note>Latin: *Zaelis*. Referring to Sahl ibn Bishr, a 9th-century astrologer whose works were standard textbooks in Ficino's time.</note> be true—namely, that the Ascendant is strongest, which is far from the Midheaven? Rather, the twelfth and eleventh regions of heaven, which are midway between the Ascendant and the Midheaven, would perhaps seem more powerful the closer they are to the Midheaven, if indeed the Midheaven is strongest. 

Furthermore, they say that the lights <note>The Sun and Moon.</note> in the twelfth and eighth houses are obscured by the vapors of the earth and water together, and are therefore weakened (for the eighth is nearly as close to the West as the twelfth is to the East). If so, they are also compelled to say that they are much more darkened in the angles of the East and West, and are hindered everywhere by earthly obstacles. But they can never assign a reason why they make so much of any "angle"—which are fleeting and seem hardly to pertain to us—while other parts stay with us longer. For any part occupies thirty degrees. 

And what of this? While they admire the angles, they meanwhile assert that the planets they consider beneficial "rejoice" elsewhere than in the angles? The Sun in the ninth, the Moon in the third, Jupiter in the eleventh, and finally Venus in the fifth. They call "ninth" the house that slightly precedes the Midheaven above the earth toward the west; the "eleventh" follows the Midheaven toward the east; the "third" precedes the Midheaven under the earth toward the east; and the "fifth" follows that point and is closer to the west than the Midheaven. They call the ninth the "house of great religion," the third the "house of lesser religion" (or of "God" and "Goddess"), yet they are not angular. They call the eleventh the "foundation of hope and friendship," and the fifth the "seat of joy and children." 

I pass over the fact that while they want the Sun to rejoice in the ninth and the Moon in the third, they meanwhile make them opposite—and they are accustomed to fear opposition. I pass over how they say Mercury rejoices in the rising rather than the setting, while Venus in turn delights in the setting rather than the rising; they will be forced to admit that these planets rejoice and grieve equally at the same time. For while a planet is rising for some people, it is setting for others. Since they consider the Eastern angle to be the angle of beginning life, and death is the opposite of life, why do they not assign the Western angle (opposite the East) to death? To this they assign the eighth seat near the west and commit it to Saturn. But why do they also entrust the first house and the origin of life to Saturn? As if both death and life were in his hand. 

But I see where they will flee. They attribute the first house to Saturn, the first of the planets; the second house to Jupiter, the second of the planets (following the sign rising in the east); the third to Mars; the fourth to the Sun; the fifth to Venus; the sixth to Mercury; and finally the seventh to the Moon—that is, the sign located in the West. Thus they repeat the sequence of the planets starting again from Saturn in the eighth...

<summary>Ficino presents a rigorous logical critique of traditional astrology, arguing that the heavens are uniformly divine and that planetary influences cannot be "malefic" or change based on arbitrary geometric "angles" or "houses." He points out the contradictions in how astrologers assign power and "joy" to different celestial locations.</summary>

<header>ON BOOK III OF ENNEAD II</header>

But when they assign a new house to **Jupiter** after **Saturn**, the tenth to **Mars**, the eleventh to the **Sun**, and the twelfth to **Venus**, nothing remains to dedicate to **Mercury** and the **Moon** in a similar sequence. Yet the effects of these two appear most clearly to us of all, after the **Sun**. Unless, perhaps, they accommodate the rising path to **Mercury** and the **Moon** just as they do to **Saturn**—which belongs more to someone making things up than to someone teaching. Furthermore, why do they not designate the ages of a person already born in that same order? Indeed, in a reversed order, they destine the first age to the **Moon**, the second to **Mercury**, and so on. But in truth, all these things are quite "pretty" and entirely arbitrary, confirmed by no reasons at all. It is similarly arbitrary that they place **Mercury**—whom they think can easily be turned to evil just as to good—in the "place of life" at its beginning, as if in "joy." Why not the **Sun** instead, or **Venus**, or **Jupiter**? Why do they also consider **Mercury** both the author of reason and yet so slippery toward evil? But I seek a reason in vain from those who never rely on any reason, but most often on some imaginary likeness and empty comparison. Who does not see that they compare things too foolishly? For when they assign **Saturn** to the ascending sign <note>The "Ascendant," or the sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note> because he is the highest of the planets and signifies darkness and absence: surely because of his height, the midheaven <note>The *Medium Coeli*, the highest point in the sky.</note> would suit him better than the ascendant; and because of darkness and absence, the signs below the earth <note>The houses of the chart that are below the horizon.</note> agree with **Saturn** better than a sign rising from the earth. Truly, it is too childish to say that **Saturn** portends the absence of something for us because he himself is distant—as if the **Moon**, by similar folly, should signify something present because she is near, and a middle planet signify middle things. It is no less insane to assign darkness to **Saturn**, who is closest to the immense and vast stars <note>Referring to the "Fixed Stars" in the highest sphere above Saturn.</note> and necessarily flashes with the wonderful light of them all; rather, one must admit that the eye is deceived in judging his light, rather than **Saturn** shining less brightly. In short, in all things (as I was saying), they immediately flee to some empty likeness, having no regard for actual causes. Why does a star rising from the East signify the beginning of life? "Because," they say, "the star emerges from the darkness of the earth at the same time the newborn comes out from the darkness of the womb." O, what an utterly hollow invention! Similarly, someone might say: "A boy now leaving the city signifies a son leaving the house at the same time, and moreover, it helps the son who is leaving." But if anything were to be signified this way, the position that was rising when the fetus first began to live in the womb should signify life and the beginning of life; but they neither observe this, nor can they observe it by any logic. Why, likewise, does the region of the midheaven portend dignity for those being born? "Is it because the highest seat signifies height of status?" Thus the fourth house, because it is the subterranean angle, dreams of signifying treasures hidden under the earth. If they are so delighted by this fictional likeness, they should have described marriage through the sign joined to the ascendant. Yet they announce it through the seventh house, far removed from the ascendant. But what does the West have to do with the marriage of the East? "Because," they say, "rays are joined from both sides from that region." Let it be so, then. But why does this seventh house also signify manifest enemies? "The planets closer to the ascendant," they say, "rule the youthful age, and the more remote ones rule old age." Truly, this is too childish: as if this local transition, like a dance of players, suddenly brings about through actions that some should dominate first, while others wait, and only then act when they are furthest from their original position. Let them say further, since they are so fond of likeness, why the twelfth region—into which the ascendant comes toward the light—signifies a prison and hidden things, rather than the second house, from which one must emerge as if from darkness? In short, they rave similarly in all things, and they force others—either believing them or disputing with them too long—to rave in nearly the same way, as <term>Abumafar</term> <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a highly influential Persian astrologer whose works were standard textbooks in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> shows even against his will. For when he struggles to assign the reasons why the twelve houses are distributed with their duties, he says that astrologers disagree among themselves, and some designate them far differently. Then, in assigning reasons for why certain signs are the houses of certain planets, they differ greatly among themselves: for the ancients say one thing, **Ptolemy** another, **Hermes** another, and **Abumafar** assigns them differently still—because, clearly, they are fictions rather than reasons. **Abumafar** hands down that **Jupiter** signifies riches and **Mercury** wisdom. Since the desires for these things are opposites, he says that both the houses of **Jupiter** and **Mercury** are opposite: namely **Pisces** to **Virgo**, and **Gemini** to **Sagittarius**. O **Abumafar**, if it pleases you to distribute them thus, why do you not also oppose the houses of **Venus** and **Mercury**? For Venereal lust and Mercurial contemplation are much more opposed than what we have said; yet you admit they are in harmony with each other: **Libra** with **Gemini**, and **Virgo** with **Taurus**. Likewise, since Jove-like equity and violent **Martial** fury are most opposed to each other, why do you not grant that their seats should fight? Instead, you say **Aries** entirely agrees with **Sagittarius**, and **Scorpio** with **Pisces**? Furthermore, when they ascribe other regions of the earth to other signs, they are carried along by uncertain opinion. For they do not distribute them because a sign passes perpendicularly over such a region; for if that were so, **Cancer** would signify nothing in **Europe**, since all of Europe exists beyond **Cancer**, leaning toward the North; nor is it because of any harmonious property. For they say **Virgo** is a cold sign, yet they judge it to rule over **Spain**, a hot region. With similar rashness, they place signs over parts of the body: for they often prefer hot things for cold parts, and cold things for hot. They also join together meanings for the same planets that are too repugnant to one another. They want **Saturn** to signify the worship of the one God and also gluttony; **Jupiter** to signify piety and also intemperance in intercourse; **Mercury** wisdom and the oracles of prophets, and moreover, superfluous amusements. I pass over the many things spread about with equal rashness: as for instance, that **Saturn** designates rain, whom they nevertheless admit is dry. Likewise, they call him masculine, though they say he is cold. Finally, they say he portends slowness because he himself is slow—though he is certainly the fastest in terms of the length of the space he travels. And what of the fact that they dream of the <term>Head and Tail of the Dragon</term>? <note>The lunar nodes (where the moon's path crosses the ecliptic). Ficino argues these are mathematical points, not physical entities.</note> For these are only imaginary. The Head is thought of as a certain imaginary line left in our mind from the motion of the **Moon** from the South to the North, which can be imagined in any degree of the **Zodiac**. And where the head is now imagined, there at some point the tail will also be imagined. What power could that imaginary line have? When the **Moon** has departed from there, why is the tail worse than the head? Why is the tail cold and feminine, when the northern region is colder than the southern? Thus the head, where the **Moon** declines toward the North, should be cold rather than hot; and the tail the opposite. They call a planet <term>retrograde</term> <note>When a planet appears to move backward in the sky from Earth's perspective.</note> when it proceeds toward the East in the lower part of its epicycle. From this likeness, they dream that the business of men is retarded, and then again accelerated, as if both motions were not equally natural to the planets. Furthermore, they are accustomed to say: because the **Bull** (Taurus) or the **Lion** (Leo) have such powers in themselves, therefore those born under these signs obtain a similar nature. And yet these animals are falsely fashioned in the heavens; neither is there any figure or nature there similar to our **Bulls** and **Lions**. The ancients placed the **Bull** among the stars in honor of **Jupiter**, because he was fabulously turned into a bull. **Hercules** killed a huge **Lion**; they placed him (as it is said) among the signs. They designated the **Ram** (Aries) as the head of the signs because of **Jupiter Ammon**, on whose head the ancients fashioned the horns of a **Ram**. After the **Ram**, they say the **Bull** was soon fashioned because the earth was then arable and fit for cultivation. The **Twins** (Gemini)...

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...because then everything is budding and "doubled" <note>Ficino is likely playing on the etymology of Gemini/geminando (budding).</note>. They named **Cancer** [the Crab] because from that point the Sun returns backward in the manner of a crab. **Leo** [the Lion], because the Sun is most intensely hot there. **Virgo** [the Virgin], because the earth, then scorched by the Sun's heat, brings forth nothing. **Libra** [the Scales], because the Sun then makes nights equal to days. **Scorpio** [the Scorpion], because then the air stings with the first cold. **Sagittarius** [the Archer], because of the "stings" of the more vehement cold and winds, and the rest similarly. What, therefore, is more foolish than to attribute specific natures of animals and their particular outcomes to people born or acting under this sign or that? For there is nothing of that sort in the heavens, but it is established by a far different reasoning. You will not, therefore, give medicine when **Taurus** or **Capricorn** is rising: because since these animals "ruminate" <note>original: *ruminent* — to chew the cud.</note>, the potion will provoke vomiting. As if, truly, there were a ruminating goat in the sky, and not rather that **Capricorn** was fashioned there because the Sun begins to ascend again from there in the manner of a climbing goat. And after these, **Aquarius** [the Water-Bearer] and **Pisces** [the Fish], because then more abundant rains are poured out, and then fish are most greatly produced. Someone, therefore, will fashion an image of a **Fish** in silver, when the Moon is under the rising Pisces, intending to catch fish as he wishes—relying, evidently, on the false figure and fabricated nature of the "Fish" in the sky.

But to return at last to **Plotinus**: he maintains that celestial bodies are led by a soul, and that the soul lives entirely by divine intellect, having no affection toward lower things; for indeed, those bodies are neither in need of, nor disturbed by, lower things. Therefore, they are never touched by pain or new joy, nor do they do harm to anyone out of hatred, nor do they do harm simply, nor do they signify things to us by choice—if they signify anything at all. Rather, perhaps, we occasionally grasp a significance from them while they are content within themselves. For if birds, which are closer to us in nature and place, signify nothing to us by their own choice (if perhaps there is any truth in augury), but while they are doing their own business, we happen upon a significance in their flight and chatter: much less do the stars deliberate to portend our affairs. Certainly, unless vain parents taught augury in fruitlessly, these things—auspices, auguries, and divinations from entrails—will stand only by the worship of demons. For demons, the rulers of the dark air, once held their worshippers by this divination, or rather, by this deception.

But if any conjecture of future things happens through the movement of the stars, where are those future things "prescribed," by which such or such a constitution of the sky follows or accompanies them? Certainly, they are prescribed in the celestial minds, which move the celestial "face" (that is, their own), and by their expressions indicate their thoughts in different ways. But these things are not eternal in their minds—not only those things which they themselves will do, either by themselves or through the heavens, but also those things which elemental causes will follow and do by their own nature; and moreover, those things which rational souls will do by a nature, fate, or counsel common to the celestial souls. I say "common" because these things are not designated in them sign by sign or distributed down to the smallest detail according to the condition of lower things; rather, they are arranged summarily by the "heads" of things according to their common providence. These are then further divided through specific natures, affections, occasions, and counsels, and are brought down into a somewhat different quality. For this reason, individual things cannot be known for certain from there, but for the most part only certain common things—which **Ptolemy** also asserts. One must look into the natures and imaginations of individuals for their specific conditions. Thus, for such prophecies to be occupied both from "there" [the heavens] and from "here" [the earth] daily (if we believe **Origen** and **Porphyry**), is the work not of men, but of demons—and I mean the more sagacious demons. For they think that most demons are often deceived by conjecture regarding these things and lie to us.

Ancient astrologers, therefore, doubted by what means significance is made to us from the sky. Thus **Abū Maʿshar** <note>original: *Abumafar* — a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note>, where he treats judgments, says some astrologers think the planets provide signs only for universal things, namely for the elements and the species of natural things. But regarding individuals and the parts and acts of individuals—namely, whether they move, rest, and nothing of that sort—they demonstrate nothing at all. Others, however, think the stars show only things that are "necessary"—for instance, that fire is hot and water is cold—but not things that are "contingent"—for instance, whether a man speaks or is silent. Finally, others think the planets only portend changes of the seasons and how far they affect bodies. **Abū Maʿshar** adds that all later astrologers follow the ancients, and that none of the sayings of the ancients lead to this intention of "judgment" [horoscopic prediction]; for they would say it is impossible even for wise astronomers to find anything in the science of judgments. In this, **Abū Maʿshar** admits that the causes and rules of judgments had not yet been found; he lived long after **Ptolemy**, and in his judgments, he himself offers no reasoning, but only childish similarities. **Ptolemy** also, in his book *On Judgments* <note>The *Tetrabiblos*.</note>, hints that there is very little truth in judgments, saying: "Even if it happens that the prediction deceives us for the most part, it would still be worthwhile to investigate these things subtly, because some bit of truth is in them."

### On the five aspects of the planets, and how astrologers err in these, and are deceived in the qualities and actions of the celestial bodies.

**IIII.** After this, he descends to the "loves" and "hatreds" of the planets, and their "aspects" and effects. It would be long and too absurd to narrate the loves and hatreds of the planets among themselves, and what is more disgraceful, to recount how this one loves that one, but that one does not love him back, but rather hates him. As if they were not all kindred, and the best, placed as they are in a uniform and divine region! Certainly, since a mutual likeness in our affairs creates mutual love by an equal reasoning on both sides, much more does it create mutual charity in the heavens, where a closer likeness and union flourish.

However, so that we may more clearly understand what he says about the "aspects," we must remember that astrologers cite five aspects:
1. **Conjunction** is when a planet comes almost to a perpendicular line under another planet.
2. **Opposition** is when they are at their maximum distance: as if one were in **Aries** and the other in **Libra**, the seventh sign from Aries.
3. **Sextile aspect** is when a sixth portion of the twelve signs falls between one and the other, that is, a measure of two signs. For example, if the Sun is seen in the middle of Aries and the Moon in the middle of **Gemini**, or the former is at the beginning of Aries and the latter at the beginning of Gemini. For the whole of **Taurus** falls between them, plus parts of Aries and Gemini.
4. **Quartile aspect** <note>The "Square" aspect.</note> is where a fourth part of the Zodiac falls between them, that is, three signs: as when the Sun is in the middle of Aries and the Moon in the middle of **Cancer**, as we said. For three signs are seen between the Sun and Moon: the whole of Taurus, plus Gemini, and parts of Aries and Cancer. Three signs possess a fourth portion of the twelve signs.
5. **Trine aspect** is when similarly four signs are between them: which is the third part of the Zodiac, as if the Sun were under Aries and the Moon similarly under **Leo**.

**Ptolemy** says the reason there are only this many aspects is this: because from the twelve signs a figure can be made having six angles [a hexagon], so that in any side there are two signs; where the aspect of one angle to the other will be sextile, containing a sixth part of the figure. A quadrangular figure [a square] can also be described; likewise a triangular one. In the former, the **Quartile** aspect arises; in the latter, the **Trine**.

<meta>catchword: Not</meta>

<summary>Ficino mocks the "puerile" logic of naming Zodiac signs based on earthly seasons and behaviors, arguing that celestial bodies signify through divine providence rather than emotional "choices." He also explains the geometric basis of the five planetary aspects—Conjunction, Opposition, Sextile, Square, and Trine—while questioning their reliability in prediction.</summary>
<keywords>astrological aspects, Zodiac signs, Ptolemy, Abū Maʿshar, Plotinus, divination, planetary houses, geometry of the heavens, celestial providence</keywords>

He transitions from mocking the naming of signs to a more sophisticated argument based on Pythagorean harmony and the physical properties of light.</meta>

# ON BOOK III OF THE ENNEADS, CHAPTER II

A figure having five angles <note>a pentagon</note> cannot be formed from twelve whole signs. However, it seems that <term>aspects</term><note>The geometric angles—like 60, 90, or 120 degrees—formed between planets which astrologers believe influence human affairs.</note> can be formed in another way. For there are three hundred and sixty degrees in the Zodiac, which, when divided into five parts, create a figure possessing five angles; in this same way, angle will behold angle, just as occurs in the <term>trine</term><note>A 120-degree aspect, generally considered harmonious.</note> and <term>square</term><note>A 90-degree aspect, generally considered tense or challenging.</note> aspects. Therefore, a pentagonal aspect can be considered there. Again, from all the degrees of the Zodiac, a figure of eight angles can be made, or nine, or ten; and thus there would be an eighth, ninth, and tenth aspect. For this reason, to assert only five aspects is the work of a storyteller rather than a true mathematician. The circle of the Zodiac is indeed continuous; stars are everywhere, and signs are woven into other signs, so that we can create aspects not only through the twelve signs—as if they were separated from each other—but through every degree of the Zodiac.

Accordingly, if we speak truly, we do not say this star beholds that one, or planet beholds planet, for any other reason than because one casts its rays upon the other. Any star casts its rays upon any other; therefore, any star, wherever it may be, gazes upon any other. And from this kind of "gaze" of rays, it reaches and beholds a neighbor more than a distant one, which is evident in the case of lit candles. Let no one say, therefore, that this sign does not behold its neighbor, but only one removed by a certain distance; or that a star does not behold what is near, but only what is far. For this opinion—or rather, this error—arises because some people measure (or rather, lie about) the celestial bodies based on our own limitations. A man in a dance usually finds it more difficult to look at the person right at his side than someone further away, because his head does not have eyes on every side with which to see everywhere with equal ease. But in the celestial countenance, whatever exists are eyes; and as for these eyes, each one is entirely an eye, entirely vision on every side.

They say that the <term>sextile</term><note>A 60-degree aspect.</note> aspect indicates moderate love, but the trine indicates perfect love. Again, they say the square aspect indicates moderate hatred, but the <term>opposition</term><note>A 180-degree aspect.</note> indicates the highest. A conjunction with good planets is good, but with bad planets it is bad. And yet, they cannot assign a cause for why one aspect differs from another in being "good" or "bad" solely based on shape or number. For good and evil do not pertain to quantity, but to quality. Furthermore, action and passion <note>In the philosophical sense of "acting" and "being acted upon."</note> do not pertain to shape or number, but to forms and qualities. Certain shapes or numbers either follow or accompany these qualities.

Nor, again, is it permitted to say that **Aries** is contrary to **Cancer** in some quality, and therefore the square gaze of planets from one to the other is contrary and hostile. For there are no contraries in heaven, where there is no battle, no transgression, and no destruction. Indeed, if the figures in a work of art are in some way clashing with each other, they do not clash in the mind of the artist; if natural forms fight amongst themselves, they do not disagree in the mind of the observer; if opposing limbs do not oppose one another in the seed, then certainly the powers of these effective forms do not disagree in heaven. These forms only struggle when in lower matter, which is clearly incapable of reconciling what it receives.

Indeed, not only does **Cancer** not disagree with **Aries**, but it harmonizes with it. For both are parts of a body that is largely uniform and which, by its own nature, harmonically tempers those things which disagree among us. Everything harmonizes in heaven no less than in a musical song. Thus, perhaps we may be allowed to devise a human music from the celestial harmony; for the **Pythagoreans** called the heaven the "Lyre of God."

Therefore, let the conjunction of planets represent the harmony of the <term>octave</term><note>original: *octavæ vocis* — the eighth voice.</note> for us, for this seems to unite with the first note. But the opposition of celestial bodies, which occurs in the seventh sign, is similarly represented by the "seventh voice" among us, which is the most dissonant of all. The sextile aspect, which occurs in the third sign, corresponds to the "third voice"; the square to the "fourth"; the trine, which occurs in the fifth, to the "fifth." Just as in our own harmony (which depends on the celestial), the fourth voice or sometimes the seventh, which are dissonant by themselves, nevertheless contribute to the grace of the harmony when combined with the others; so, and much more so, in the celestial harmony, all aspects are judged necessary for absolute concord.

From this it happens that the wiser astronomers do not dread a fourth aspect added to either a sextile or a trine, but rather desire it. It also happens that through cycles of seven—whether of days in illness or years in life—at which the squares of either the Moon or Saturn soon arrive, the changes in us do not always result in the worse, but sometimes in the better. Meanwhile, it is fun to laugh at the astrologers who, while saying **Cancer** is more contrary to **Aries** in quality than **Libra** is, are nevertheless accustomed to loathe the opposite aspect (such as results from **Libra** to **Aries**) more than the square.

But why do they babble that **Cancer** is "cold and wet," when the Sun positioned there increases the heat for us? Why is **Sagittarius** "hot," under which the Sun does not protect the lands from cold or rain? From this it is clear that heat and cold are intensified or relaxed in turn by the approach and departure of the Sun, rather than by the inherent quality of the stars. Nor should they object that the Moon or Mercury changes the air’s quality by being in one sign or another, on the grounds that there is a different quality there; for first of all, they do not produce this everywhere—summer never arises from this for the Scythians <note>An ancient people living in the cold regions of modern-day Ukraine and Russia.</note>, nor do cold and humidity arise for the Indians. Secondly, even if they did happen to change things, it is not immediately proven that such qualities exist there, fighting equally among themselves; for these things proceed from there by another power, far different from our own.

Sometimes, from various affections of the soul, and then from a certain contraction or dilation of the spirit, contrary qualities immediately arise in the body—qualities which are not in the soul or the spirit, neither as contraries nor as qualities themselves. From light reflected too much comes heat, which does not exist in the light itself. From light comes both liquidity in wax and dryness in clay; yet there is no "dry" or "liquid" passion in the light. Likewise, by a certain position or impulse of the stars, vapors and winds are raised on the earth, yet neither do winds blow there, nor do vapors cloud things over there.

That the virtues in heaven are very foreign to those which fight in the elements, we can guess from the fact that in all things mixed from the qualities of the elements, there are certain marvelous powers—both beyond and above the natures of the elements—which they call "special properties," attributed to these species from heaven. I pass over the rest, for they are innumerable. Thus the magnet follows its Arctic pole, and iron follows the magnet; thus straws follow amber. This [amber] perhaps follows the Antarctic pole.

Therefore, through such virtues as these—and such as those in scammony <note>A plant used as a powerful laxative.</note> that purge bile, or in hellebore <note>A medicinal herb used for mental illness or "black bile."</note> that purge black bile—**Abumafar** <note>The Latinized name for the Persian astrologer Abu Ma'shar.</note> proves that the principal actions of the heavens are fulfilled. Whether such virtues are fixed in the stars, or whether they are prepared for themselves from their daily aspects with each other and then sent down to lower things.

Rightly, therefore, **Abumafar** and **Albius** <note>Likely referring to the scholar Al-Bīrūnī.</note> everywhere rebuke **Ptolemy**, because he often attributed elemental and mutually-repelling qualities to the stars, and they prove that such natures are not in heaven. I pass over now the fact that not only those I mentioned disagree with **Ptolemy**, but **Ptolemy** himself disagrees with others when he speaks of the "terms" <note>Subdivisions of a Zodiac sign ruled by different planets.</note> of the planets, and he recounts that others disagree among themselves. For he says the Egyptians were most accustomed to receiving terms from the lords of the houses, but the Chaldeans from the lords of the triplicities, and he refutes this at great length. I pass over the fact that they disagree in aspects and exaltations. For **Ptolemy** measures simply from sign to sign; certain others measure from degree to degree. **Ptolemy** thinks the exaltations of the planets should be accepted in a whole sign; but several others from a certain specific space in the sign. Similarly, they disagree about the "significator of life" and the "giver of years."

I return for a moment to the qualities. Since they think **Mars** is "fiery," why do they not teach that it falls in **Pisces** rather than in **Libra**? Is it because **Libra** is most distant from **Aries**, the home of **Mars**? But surely the distance of nature is greater than the distance of position; therefore, **Pisces** (which they call "watery") differs more from **Aries** than the "airy" **Libra** does.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "Enneads," specifically the section addressing astrological influences. # COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

Why, then, in <term>Libra</term><note>The zodiac sign of the Scales.</note> do they wish Saturn to be <term>exalted</term><note>In astrology, "exaltation" is a specific sign where a planet’s influence is thought to be most powerful and harmonious.</note>, even though they consider Saturn to be "earthy" in nature? It would be a long task to review other examples of this kind. Let us now return to Plotinus's conclusion. He reports first that astrologers believe each star performs something on its own, but from all of them conspiring together, something new is additionally produced. From this, it is clear that no one can clearly judge what will ultimately result from these combinations. Next, he indicates that astrologers have no explanation for the *way* in which planets act to produce whatever they are said to effect. For they do not need either their own individual plan or a collective counsel to act: indeed, natural causes below the Moon are sufficient in their own nature for acting, and they do not require any counsel beyond nature. Furthermore, since the stars perform these things by way of nature, they do not act differently, or do other things, than what can be done through the course of nature—though they may act more excellently and produce more excellent things, clearly because they possess a more excellent nature. Therefore, the stars do not produce prophets, nor miracles (which must happen by divinity), nor theologians, nor geometers (who are made by mind and art), nor the wealthy, nor kings—nor their opposites, who are made by prudence, opportunity, and favor, or are hindered by their opposites.

### The Errors of Astrologers concerning Saturn, Mars, and the Moon.

V. In the beginning of the fifth chapter, he pursues and attacks the errors of astrologers more extensively. They teach that Saturn, because it is cold, is harmful to nature, and for that reason, they separate it from the <term>ascendant</term><note>The degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth, considered the "starting point of life."</note> (as they call the beginning of life). And so that they might separate it as much as possible, they foolishly place it in the <term>twelfth house</term><note>In astrology, the 12th house is often associated with hidden enemies and misfortune; Ficino argues this placement is geometrically illogical.</note>. This position, although it seems furthest from the first house according to some of their methods of calculation, is in reality the closest. For it is continuous with the East, moving upward, and because it hastens into the twelfth house from the ascendant; thus, they would have more probably placed Saturn in the seventh house as being the most distant of all. But they do not even want that, lest it be "opposed" to those being born; but in both cases, they seem to contradict themselves. For they usually assign the beginning of the first conception to Saturn and the ascendant for a different reason. Furthermore, they say that Saturn and Mars harm us when they are either joined together or opposite each other. It might have been more correctly said that in this way, Saturn’s coldness is tempered by the heat of Mars, and the latter's fervor by the former's cold. They add that if Saturn is above the earth for those born during the day, or near the East, it becomes favorable to us because it is tempered by the day's heat. And also, if it rises in this way, especially in <term>Aquarius</term>, it does not harm nature. But they say Mars, being fiery, should be placed in the night, or beneath the earth, so it does not burn too fiercely with the sun's heat; and in this, as often, they rave. For since the shadow of the earth—from which night comes—scarcely reaches even to the moon, all the lights of all the stars above the moon are continuously touching each other with nothing intervening; they are similarly always "in the day" and never "under the night." Saturn, most of all, exists separated from shadow and coldness, which are two properties of the earth; so that nothing seems more absurd than to call this planet "dark" and "cold." Furthermore, they are accustomed to disparage the conjunction of the Moon with Saturn or Mars. However, if she approaches Saturn while full of light, or Mars while empty, they do not dare to condemn it. For if she joins with Saturn while full, they say she then nourishes him with her light and that he does not chill her while she is full. On the other hand, if she submits to Mars while full, she is scorched and burned by him at the same time; if she is empty, she is tempered by him and tempers him in turn. Here too, as elsewhere, they err more boldly. First, the celestial bodies, being always in harmony, never burn or chill each other; second, if that were perhaps granted, the opposite should be done. For when the Moon is "full" in the semicircle facing us, she is meanwhile "empty" in the other, and vice versa. Therefore, to avoid that disadvantage, she ought rather to be subjected to Saturn when she is empty to us, for then she offers herself as "full" to him; but to Mars when she is full to us, for then she shows herself as "empty" to him. 

Amidst these things, it is useful to warn that many clauses in the Greek <term>codex</term><note>A handwritten manuscript book.</note> seem to be transposed, and words are frequently swapped; I have diligently corrected these to the best of my ability, relying on the office of a <note>original: "vatis"</note> <term>prophet</term><note>Ficino uses "vatis" (prophet or inspired poet) to describe his role in interpreting these difficult ancient texts, suggesting he is more than just a literal translator.</note> rather than a mere interpreter. Therefore, what follows next in the text can admit a double meaning. For either they signify that Saturn sometimes does not help us much because he is far away, and therefore the Moon at least ought to be full toward us then, so that she at least may help us; or rather they signify that Saturn does not help the Moon because he is far from the Moon, nor does she help him in turn if she ever becomes "empty" toward him; and therefore she ought to extend herself to him as "full"; and that she does enough for us then with her half-circle toward us, even though it is empty toward us. Likewise, even though Saturn is far from us. The first sense seems to follow the words more clearly, but I fear it is perverse. For it seems to agree neither with the preceding nor following statements and opinions of Plotinus, but rather to contradict them.

### That in heaven there is only light, heat, and moisture; but cold and dryness are around the center; nor does anything celestial by itself bring cold, or dryness, or anything harmful to life.

VI. Since heaven is closest to life, and therefore most living and most life-giving, it must be thought to heat and moisten by itself and primarily. For these two things specifically lead to life; but it never by itself chills or dries, which are by their very nature contrary to life. And if they do contribute, they contribute in a way by "accident": cold, indeed, so that excessive heat does not suddenly dissolve the moisture; and dryness, so that the moisture does not flow away too much. These two, however, are sufficiently supplied to us by the earth. Furthermore, this will be confirmed if what most people think is true: just as death is nothing other than the privation of life, so the deadly qualities of cold and dryness are nothing other than the privations of heat and moisture—which Plotinus himself indicates elsewhere. It is also probable that just as darkness occurs only as a privation of light at the greatest distance from heaven, so cold and dryness perhaps occur from an excessive distance from heaven due to the absence of heat and moisture. 

That the whole heaven is hot is clear, because the whole is fire; again, that the whole is fire is shown by its height, mobility, light, and heat (either hidden or nourishing all things). Moreover, heat that is most ample in space, suffering no violence, has a familiar moisture. Surely in the soul of heaven there are three most important things: life, intellect, and motion. For the soul is a certain life that is both intellectual and mobile, and all of this is one. Therefore, what is "life" in the soul exists as "heat" in the heaven. What again is "intellect" there, is "light" here. What finally is "vital motion" there, is "vital moisture" here. Thus, moisture is nothing other than an agility (if I may speak thus) for motion. Celestial fire, therefore, can not only be called hot, but additionally moist—that is, liquid, fluid, agile, and slippery, and smooth, and mild; since in dryness we understand a rough rigidity, such as even a more vehement coldness brings. Wherefore, nothing else in heaven is in any way similar to our qualities except heat, moisture, and light. Light, I say, is there in the place of intelligence; heat is there the efficacy of life; moisture is the motion and food of life. Nor is that heat felt there otherwise than as favor, warmth, recreation, and vigor; nor is moisture felt otherwise than as growth, and amplification, and a sweet agility. From this, these things...
