<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "Enneads," specifically the section addressing astrological influences. Having previously discussed the geometry of planetary aspects, Ficino now shifts to a physical and metaphysical critique of celestial qualities, arguing that the "coldness" or "dryness" traditionally attributed to planets like Saturn are relative terms rather than absolute physical properties of the heavens.</meta>

### ON BOOK III. ENNEAD II.

There are certain things among us similar to these. In turn, that moist heat and moderately warming moisture of the heavens is somewhat similar to the spirit and vital heat and moisture found either clearly in animals or hidden in plants, implanted everywhere by the heavens—by the heavens, I say, which are implanted in all things. However, dryness and cold happen to our things from here on Earth, certainly not from there in the heavens. Dryness occurs because of the very narrowness of this place and its dense, rough, resistant nature, which strikes against and is unsuited for formation and motion. Cold, however, occurs because of the greatest possible distance, both by nature from the whole of heaven and by position from the stars. Therefore, as far as cold is concerned, we strongly approve of **Averroes** <note>A 12th-century Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> when he says: nothing celestial brings cold, but all bring heat; those things which are said to bring cold are simply those which heat less. This is his opinion in his book *On the Heavens*, based on **Aristotle**. 

<margin>Abraham Ibn Ezra</margin> **Abraham Ibn Ezra** <note>A celebrated 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note> calls Saturn "cold" because it brings a heat that is more faint to us. Therefore, the whole of heaven is a luminous, moist heat; that is, a kind of effective life that can be expanded with favor, agile and capable of being formed. It is capable of being formed, I say, easily through moisture, rendered translucent by the **archetype** <note>The original "blueprint" or ideal form in the divine mind.</note>; and in turn, through its luminous heat, it easily forms the lower things. But in some places in heaven there is a little more heat than moisture, and in others the reverse; in some places the portion of light is equal on both sides. And because of the different proportions of these three things, different things exist there, just as here various things coalesce everywhere under the rays of heaven from the varying mixture of heat and moisture—while dryness and cold perhaps hinder or even assist somewhat, more or less. 

One must remember, however, that celestial heat and moisture are of a vastly different kind from ours; even more so than the natural heat in a living being differs from the glow of a furnace, or the Sun's own warmth in the open air differs from this very flame. Yet, when that solar warmth is sometimes gathered into a hollow space <note>Likely referring to a burning mirror or concave lens.</note> upon hard or dry matter, a flame is indeed ignited. Finally, the moisture in celestial things does not drip, nor is the heat consuming. This moisture differs from the moisture of the air at least as much as the moisture of the air differs from that of water. Therefore, cold and dryness, or hard solidity, are rashly imagined to exist in heaven. Indeed, as one ascends upward from the Earth, dryness is fled, as is cold and the hardness of all things; and one soon arrives at moisture and softness, and at the same time at the beginning of a gentle heat from light. 

Therefore, the cold, the dry, and the hard arise from the natural and extreme distance from heaven; meanwhile, the things that are in the middle are moist, translucent, and easily moved, in imitation of heaven. In the most mobile heaven, however, there is nothing of cold or dryness, nothing hard that hinders motion and light. If, therefore, anything beneath the heaven can be imagined similar to the substance of heaven—tangible to the hands and visible to the eyes—it seems to be **quicksilver** <note>Mercury, the metal.</note>, in which a vigorous heat with much moisture (though tenacious) produces a restless motion. If you then applied a more subtle, translucent, and luminous nature to this, you would have heaven itself. That heaven is not hard seems to be confirmed by the fact that among the physicists and astronomers who assert its hardness, a complex and insoluble controversy arises when they dispute about circles, centers, distances, and motions. The physicists accuse the astronomers of imagining impossible things, while the astronomers accuse the physicists of being unable to assign reasons for these phenomena. 

I pass over how the **Theologians** insert "glorious bodies" into the heavens unless they yield. I pass over the "vehicles of souls" among the ancients <note>The Neoplatonic concept of a subtle, ethereal "body" that carries the soul down from the stars.</note>. It is not right to call "evil" that happiness of suddenly yielding, joined with a return, where no disturbance of natural substance, quality, or order follows. But let us now return to other qualities of celestial things. Even if nothing there is cold or dry, we nevertheless call a star "cold" which heats less: perhaps also because while that star opens our passages <note>Our pores or internal channels.</note> with its tepid rays, earthly cold enters more easily. We can also call a star "dry" which moistens less: perhaps also because by moistening little, it often provides fuel for fire, which will thereafter dry the matter more fervently. 

However, all stars everywhere heat, not only by motion but also by their very nature—chiefly by the nature of light. 

<margin>Avicenna</margin> This is also proven by **Avicenna** <note>An 11th-century Persian philosopher and physician.</note>, who says: where there is more light, there is also more heat. 

<margin>Hippocrates</margin> Hence **Hippocrates** says: the night air becomes thinner and somewhat warm from the lights of the stars, made suited for generation and life. 

<margin>Aristotle</margin> **Aristotle**, too, where he wonders about the *Parts of Animals*, says: nights at the full moon are warmer because of the Moon's light. 

The Moon is indeed the least hot and very moist. If she were said not to heat for the sole reason that she moves more slowly than the Sun, she ought perhaps to compensate for her slowness of motion with her proximity to us, and thus, in a way, heat by motion just as the Sun does. Likewise, if the fixed stars, although they move most rapidly, were said not to heat by motion because they are most distant, they ought perhaps to compensate for their distance with their very swift motion, and thus heat in a similar way. But if motion itself were simply the cause of heat, then no motion would extinguish heat or flame; at least a faster motion would be the source of a more vehement heat, and a slower one of a more tepid heat. Again, if it is not motion itself that simply begets heat, but a certain velocity, I truly do not see at first what distance or proximity would matter, provided the motion itself is swift. 

Therefore, it is clear enough here that the effect of heat must be referred to another cause besides motion. And rightly so, because motion—whether it comes from the will—requires before it a form of the imagination and nature; or whether it is of a natural inclination, it requires a preceding form of nature. Motion itself, therefore, does not generate heat or any other form; but form sometimes does so through motion, and such a form produces such an effect, although the form is prior and more excellent by nature. Finally, who would assert that local motion—which is inferior to every form and pertains to external things—by its own nature generates heat, which is often latent? Or that by the collision of hard bodies it breaks the middle air and only thins it? The air, thus thinned to the proper condition of fire, is clothed by the **seminal idea** <note>A formative power or "seed" in nature that directs growth and change.</note>—the rational principle of fire—with the form of fire, as if with tinder. 

The Moon, therefore, heats less than the Sun because she is less hot. The higher stars also heat less than the Sun because they are either less hot, or smaller than the Sun, or much more distant, or quite separated from one another. It seems, however, that the Sun dries by accident: not because there is a dry nature in it or some other power of desiccating (otherwise it would not naturally increase all things, but rather decrease them in the manner of fire), but because the Sun's rays are either too constricted in very hard hollows, or, striking directly, are reflected more strongly toward us. For then a new force occurs through that kind of violence. In truth, because the rays are, as it were, immaterial, most liquid, and immaculate, they do not properly gather, nor break, nor are they broken; but they are either collected or returned from a region. It appears that heat is in them by nature, which is intensified by their own gathering and acts more vehemently. 

The Moon also seems to bring cold by accident, because her light opens our passages and meanwhile thins the nocturnal cold, whereby it happens that the cold thereafter enters more freely and subtly through the opened entries. Indeed, the nature of cold is to kill and compress; but the light of the Moon entirely generates and increases, insofar as it possesses heat with moisture. Similarly, the light of the Sun is sometimes the cause of cold by accident: whether it calls the natural heat of our body outward, or if you expose a body that has been warmed and softened by the Sun’s heat to a sudden change. Furthermore, it is a sin to call Saturn "cold" in any way, and therefore "death-bringing." For in such great and vital fire, nothing can be cold or lethal in any way. It is enough to say that in Saturn, heat is overcome by moisture. And since he is such, and moreover most remote from us, he brings very little heat, and not much moisture; because besides these two, there is a power in him naturally of contracting, halting, containing, and compelling. Whence, although he never effects...

<summary>Ficino argues that the heavens are essentially composed of vital heat and moisture, and that astrological qualities like "cold" or "dry" are relative terms describing a planet's lack of heat or its indirect effects on Earth's atmosphere.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s defense of Saturn. On the previous page, he argued that "cold" in the heavens is merely a lower degree of heat. Here, he explains Saturn's specific role in the formation of life and the soul, challenging the common medieval view of Saturn as a purely malevolent or "deadly" planet.</meta>

<page-num>118</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO</header>

just as the Moon also seems to dry things out in a way when it draws moisture into itself, as it does when its light wanes or when it descends. Truly, it is difficult for people to deny that Saturn is "moist" when they claim it often increases rainfall and moves the bowels. Nor is it right to call this planet "deadly" <note>original: "pestiferum"</note>; for Providence, which disposes all things, has honored Saturn with such a vast orbital sphere and willed it to be closest to the rays of the countless stars. I will set aside the fact that the ancient Theologians attributed **Mind** itself to Saturn, and dedicated the **first life** and **eternity** to that very Mind. Do not Astrologers, when calculating the "Ascendant," consider it the beginning of life? Do they not entrust the first month of conception to Saturn? Would it be fitting to begin life under a deadly influence?

What then? They entrust the first month to Saturn so that, with its "dry cold," it may constrain the seed and stop it from flowing away. It certainly stops it and constrains it, not through a cold, dry power—otherwise the beginning of life would be sought from the opposite of life—but by a certain wonderful virtue of contracting, collecting, and containing. For there are many things that cause milk and other liquids to thicken by a power other than cold. Therefore, Saturn does not bind things together through chill or dryness—otherwise it would render the seed entirely unfit for generation and life from the very start—but rather by a power that leads everything from the circumference back to the center. This is not just the action of cold, but more like the action of a hand or a fist, or the nature of **rennet** <note>original: "coaguli"; an enzyme used to curdle milk, here used as a metaphor for how Saturn "sets" the biological material of the embryo</note> pressing things tightly together, just as Mars, in turn, pushes outward from the center to the circumference.

As for the claim that a child born in the eighth month does not live—if indeed that always happens (for it happens otherwise in Egypt and in parts of Greece)—the cause is not the coldness or dryness of Saturn, but a certain violence brought from elsewhere at that time, which compels the child to be born while Saturn was still holding it within the womb. For while Saturn is "retaining," no one is born unless expelled from the belly by an excessively violent cause. Indeed, the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</note> and physicians assign reasons for this from sources other than Saturn; and astrologers report that in the regions of India subject to Saturn, lives are the longest of all. 

But shall we not say that a dry or cold nature sometimes results from Saturn, at least by accident? This might seem to happen if Saturn’s ray is caught in matter that is already cold and dry; for Saturn can slightly warm or moisten such matter, but if it stays too long, the matter is constrained into frost. Yet it seems to contribute most of all to both moister and especially hotter conditions. For with its own moisture it tempers the excess of heat, and by its very power of binding, it restrains the flowing away of moisture. **Mars**, on the other hand, moderates the effect in colder or moister matter; but in hotter matter it accelerates it, not so much by an excess of heat as by the vigor of its motion.

Since we have mentioned the matter of the seed, it is worthwhile to point out that the influence of the **Sun** and **Moon** in the fetus is universal, directed toward heat and vital moisture. **Saturn’s** power is to collect and firmly establish the seminal matter deep within. **Jupiter’s** office is to move it thereafter and nourish it from within. **Mars’s** action is to move toward the external parts. **Mercury’s** task is to shape the spirit, senses, and limbs. **Venus’s** ministry is to conform everything toward affection and the continuation of the line. These are the gifts pertaining chiefly to the body, coming from the bodies of the planets and signs.

From their souls, in turn, certain qualities are increased in our own souls: from **Saturn**, contemplation, caution, and diligent preservation; from **Jupiter**, primarily civil and prudent governance; from **Mars**, a magnanimity that drives out evils and injuries; from **Mercury**, every kind of investigation and expression; from **Venus**, charity and humanity; from **Sun**, goodness, <unclear>truth</unclear>, care, modesty, and the pursuit of true glory; and finally from the **Moon**, the diligent care and providence for the necessities of life.

But lest anyone condemn us for arranging the planets in the **Platonic order** <note>Ficino refers to the specific sequence of planets used in Plato’s cosmology, which differed from other systems like the Chaldean or Egyptian</note>, remember that divine providence decreed that the Sun should wander very little across the width of the Zodiac; its entire deviation falls under the estimation of a single degree. Because the Sun would perhaps confound the planets that come too close to it in height or width, and would entirely occupy them with the excellence of its power, it was decreed that the **Moon** and **Venus**, between which the Sun travels, should wander more widely; for the ancients held that they wander nearly twelve degrees. **Mercury**, being further from the Sun than Venus, protects itself with a narrower wandering; for it runs through nearly eight degrees, while Mars and Jupiter run through five. **Saturn**, being the most remote, runs out to three degrees in width. Thus, the opinion of those who place Mercury before Venus is confirmed; although those who do the opposite defend themselves by the order of the signs. For they want the planets to be arranged just as the "houses" proceed. Thus, **Cancer** places the Moon first; **Leo**, the Sun second; **Virgo**, Mercury third; **Libra**, Venus fourth; **Scorpio**, Mars fifth; **Sagittarius**, Jupiter sixth; and **Capricorn**, Saturn seventh. Then they are placed in reverse order. But let them look to those matters.

---

### Compositions in the natures of the planets, and their various powers and actions: and the wonderful tempering of the heavens from all of them.

But I return to **Plotinus**. Since he asserts that everything in the heavens is hot and nothing is cold, and yet that heat is tempered more or less in certain things, he seems to join moisture there with heat; by the mixing of which, tempering occurs. For there, heat is not repressed by coldness, nor is it restrained by itself, nor does pure heat reign there alone; otherwise it would not dominate more in one place than another. Therefore, there is "moisture" there—that is, a certain smooth and agile tenderness, a kind of unified liquidity and nourishing fertility. Moisture of this kind, I say, both feeds the heat there like **nectar** (just as heat feeds the light like **ambrosia**) and restrains the fire, lest the heat itself be destroyed by its own burning. Furthermore, it prevents the mutual collision of the spheres, which would otherwise happen from their most rapid motion and would immediately burn up the spheres and everything else. Finally, it softens and soothes the motions and rays, so that they may touch the lower things more mildly.

Moisture performs all these things: a moisture, I say, so necessary to its familiar heat that it never drips away or flows off, nor does it dull or suffocate the heat itself. Indeed, just as vital motion in the soul depends on animal life, and life depends on the intellect, and they are preserved in turn; so in heaven, liquidity depends on heat, and heat on light. Thus, for example, you may compose the celestial bodies: in **Saturn**, moisture greatly exceeds heat; in **Mars**, heat far exceeds moisture; **Jupiter**, being the middle between these, tempers heat almost equally with moisture. After Mars, to arrange it in the Platonic manner, follows **Mercury**, reflecting the nature of Saturn. To this follows **Venus**, representing a Jovian mixture. I say "as if," because of the opinion of those who think that Jupiter indeed inclines a little toward heat, while Venus inclines rather toward moisture, but from both of them the most perfect temperament is created. The **Sun**, then, like Mars, greatly overcomes moisture with heat; the **Moon**, finally, like Saturn and Mercury, possesses much more moisture than heat. But the moisture of these three seems to relate to each other in this way: Saturn’s moisture always returns to the center; the Moon’s moisture, however, expands rather toward the circumference as its light increases; Mercury's...

<summary>Ficino explains that Saturn is a vital, binding force rather than a "deadly" one, outlining the specific physical and spiritual gifts each planet provides to humans. He also describes the celestial "moisture" that tempers the heat of the stars, preventing the universe from burning itself out.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s second book of the third Ennead. Having previously argued that Saturn is not inherently "deadly" but rather a principle of contraction and focus, Ficino now expands on how the celestial spheres balance heat and moisture to sustain life across the universe.</meta>

<page-num>119</page-num>
<header>ON BOOK III OF ENNEAD II</header>

Of which, finally, each does so moderately. But to return to the Moon: more learned astrologers say that when she wanes in light, she does not actually diminish the substance of her moisture, but rather draws it back toward her center. Conversely, when waxing, she expands it, which is visible in the sea, whose breadth expands while the Moon seeks the middle of the sky from the East; but while she tends from the middle toward the West, the sea flows back into a narrower space. Meanwhile, it is not likely that celestial substance increases or decreases so easily and suddenly. Furthermore, the heat of the Sun and of Mars move and are moved under different conditions: that of Mars moves, as it were, in the shape of a pyramid <note>The pyramid shape implies a sharp, piercing heat</note>, while the Sun's moves in a sphere. In two of them, therefore—that is, Jupiter and Venus together—there is an almost equal portion of moisture and heat. But since in two others—the Sun and Mars—heat far exceeds moisture, why then are there three—Saturn, Mercury, and the Moon—in which moisture exceeds heat? Because heat is more effective than moisture, and the combined mass of the Sun and Mars is immense. Therefore, these two joined together are rightly tempered by the works of the three from the opposite region. Indeed, so great is the effectiveness of heat upon moisture that the craftsman of the world himself <note>A reference to the Demiurge or God as the architect of the cosmos</note> willed that in the very masses of the spheres which contain the stars, moisture should exceed heat in a balanced portion; so that by portion, as if by weight, moisture might equal its own nature to the effectiveness of heat. For this reason, all the spheres above the earth are called "waters," and just as the sea is water and liquid in relation to the earth, so the air is moisture in relation to the sea; likewise, the Moon’s circuit is liquid in relation to the air. Thus, the higher spheres seem to relate to the lower and to each other in sequence, so that the higher things always cherish and fortunately nourish the lower. There are, therefore, waters below the firmament; there are also waters in the firmament, both in the very temperament of the firmament and in the stars shining within it, composed in the same proportion as the planets. There are even waters above the firmament itself, which astronomers have posited so that a completely simple motion might rule and lead the double and opposite motion of the firmament. Above these waters, theologians have placed fire, that is, the empyrean heaven, which is more expansive than the crystalline heaven. And this is perhaps the light which, according to Moses, God kindled before the Sun, the Moon, and the stars. This heaven is judged to precede the crystalline for the same reason that rest precedes motion, and heat precedes moisture. But does moisture accompany heat in the empyrean? It does indeed, but it is absorbed into it. Conversely, does heat accompany moisture in the crystalline? It certainly does, but it is drawn toward it. And so, thereafter, moisture gradually increases in the spheres, until finally, below the middle region of the air, moisture—as if superfluous and now foreign to heat—flows away and scatters. Above, however, one is so necessary and familiar to the other that moisture nourishes and moderates heat, and heat cherishes and preserves moisture. By both, light is also guarded. But where there is more heat, there the light is more effective and much more manifest to the eyes; where moisture abounds, the light is both less effective and, like a spreading whiteness, offers itself less to the sight. Meanwhile, I want you to remember that light and heat in the more "moist" stars—even if it affects them no less as far as the individual star is concerned—nevertheless affects them most and for a longer time gradually thereafter, unless perhaps superfluous moisture or cold flows in from elsewhere at the start. This is both because a quick resolution does not happen in such matter, and especially because when such a star is of nearly the same temperament as the sphere it rules, it naturally draws to us the influx of the entire sphere more abundantly along with its own particular gift. Thus, as much as other stars are powerful by their own virtue, these are prepotent by a collective virtue—especially the stars located in the larger spheres. For the common and leading influence around the ancient things is always more excellent, and it inserts a wonderful but hidden virtue into its star. But to return to Plotinus: Mars does not harm by the sharpness of its heat, but tempers more moist matter. Nor is Saturn harmful, but because it is the most remote, its influx is like a stranger to us; why does it not easily harmonize with us, especially with the young? Unless it is either rightly mixed with the other lights, or the planet itself, sitting in a "human" sign <note>Signs of the Zodiac represented by human figures, like Aquarius or Gemini</note> in which it either has its home or is "exalted," acts as the author of the work. Nor is Mercury ever bad, but since it is the middle of all things, it easily becomes very similar to all. Finally, just as in an animal individual members, however diverse in quality, contribute to the good both of each other and the whole; so in heaven, which also lives by a common life, the Sun holds the place of the heart, Mars of the gall <note>The gallbladder, associated with anger and choler</note>, Jupiter of the liver, Venus and the Moon of the genital members (so to speak), Mercury of the tongue and face, Saturn of the head, spleen, and stomach. The fixed stars represent the eyes, and things that seem diverse contribute to the overall temperament. Indeed, I have said that the universe flourishes by a certain common life through which all members of the world share passions in turn—that is, influence is easily transferred from one to another, a hidden sense is excited everywhere, and an impulse is incited. When I say "common life," I mean, along with Plotinus, the irrational life <note>The basic biological or animating force</note> bestowed upon the universe by the <term>World Soul</term> <note>original: "anima mundi"</note>; in whose communion a certain consensus of action and passion is born in all things. But to this life we wish to see joined (not confused) the similar lives of stars, demons, and men—like the various lives of limbs conspiring thoroughly with the common life of the whole animal. So it is no wonder that these things become signs of one another through a certain proportion—that is, from some members of the mundane animal, through a similar proportion, certain indications are provided for judging the effects of others.

->Five signs that the stars do not do everything.<-

VI Chapter six confirms with five signs that the stars do not do everything. First, it is certainly established by the dignity of their nature, the sublimity of their location, and the amplitude of their power, that any star—even the least "good" one—must be considered altogether better than even the best man. Therefore, the stars do not perpetrate crimes that even a good man would not commit—especially since all celestial things are the living instruments of the divine craftsman. This is asserted by both Ptolemy and reason: first, because through them individual things here are formed with such skillful reason that all human art imitates these to the best of its ability, but none can ever equal them; second, because although celestial things are endowed with such great power, they never seem to wander freely, but like instruments, they are led by a certain path and limit to a prescribed end, always through the same movements, and similarly led back. Whatever, therefore, is carried out through the celestial instruments of the divine craftsman proceeds chiefly from God himself. Since evil, falling away from order, cannot come from the highest good, then certainly what some astrologers prattle—that adulteries are committed here because Mars and Venus meet in Aries or Taurus—is false. The second sign: Since divine things above the heaven change neither in nature nor in manner, while things below the heaven change in both, it follows that the celestial things, acting as intermediaries, never change in nature, even if they always seem to change in a certain manner. He is raving, therefore, who says that the planets at this hour, from this very aspect, obtain such a nature, but in the following hour undergo another nature from another aspect, and so on; and that they have no limit proper to their nature or to others in time, but like a Chameleon always change according to the objects before them. Third: the stars are quite separate from our affairs, they are most general causes, and they are limited in nature and number...

<summary>Ficino describes the universe as a "World Animal" where planets act as vital organs, arguing that celestial bodies are inherently good instruments of God and do not cause human immorality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus, specifically addressing Ennead II.3. Having previously discussed the physical properties of the planets (heat and moisture), Ficino now transitions into a philosophical argument: do the stars actually cause human events, or are they merely signs of a higher providential order?</meta>

<page-num>120</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO</header>

The influx of the stars, in whatever constitution of celestial movements they are sent to us, reaches us in a general and defined way. Therefore, the resulting multitude of effects is uncertain, and an infinite diversity cannot be carried out from those stars without a medium. Instead, between the celestial bodies and the inferior effects, there must fall middle causes and occasions, which are both more diverse in nature and perhaps vary daily, through which the stars are led down to even the smallest and innumerable effects. Therefore, the stars do not arrange every tiny detail on earth by deliberate counsel—otherwise, they would be miserable with such great anxiety—nor do they descend by a natural condition directly from their most general nature to every most distinct thing. Fourthly, astrologers are accustomed to say that a planet placed in a certain <term>term</term> <note>A "term" (Latin: *terminus*) is a specific subdivision of a zodiacal sign, usually five per sign, each ruled by a different planet.</note> of a sign promises certain things which it does not provide until it either returns to that same term, or as many years pass as the degrees it had ascended. Likewise, they say it does not fulfill what it promised until that same sign ascends for us again in a <term>natal revolution</term> <note>A "natal revolution" or solar return is the moment the Sun returns to the exact position it held at an individual's birth.</note>; and as many degrees as it had ascended for us from the beginning, it ascends again for that many years in the natal revolution. Furthermore, they say that as individual planets and other stars loom over those being born in various places, the effect differs more or less. All of this is the talk of a man counting according to his own will, and inventing rather than teaching. Even if one may more probably imagine that a planet does something similar when it returns to the same spot, nevertheless, what it could not do the first time, it will not be able to effect the second; nor do I clearly perceive why it should not act from its first position, which is much stronger in us than the second. What is said simply regarding the delay of action is entirely fabricated; for if the cause itself does not act while it is present, much less does it carry it out while absent. They will perhaps claim that a certain power of this cause is preserved until that time; I, however, will ask where it is preserved. For it is preserved either in the causes closer to us, or in the matter, or in both. Grant, then, that it is so preserved. It is certainly preserved according to the condition of those things that preserve it, and is drawn gradually toward their nature, and is distinguished according to their distinction. Therefore, what finally happens will occur under our own specific property rather than a general celestial one. Fifth: as we have proved in Theology, and will repeat elsewhere: the whole crowd of causes depends on one first cause, so that it originates from there, is preserved, and is led; otherwise, the diversity of causes would not lead to a single end unless it were also derived from one. Therefore, whatever things happen from above, hanging as if from the highest good, are both most ornately made and come as the best. Let no one, therefore, dare to confess that the stars alone do everything, or even that they do evil.

### Five indications that the stars signify our affairs rather than act upon them.

**VIII** Plotinus and Origen <note>Origen (c. 185–253 AD) was an early Christian theologian; Ficino highlights his shared education with the Neoplatonist Plotinus to show a consensus between Christian and Platonic thought.</note>, fellow students under Ammonius of Alexandria <note>Ammonius Saccas, the mysterious teacher of both Plotinus and Origen in Alexandria.</note> and always friends, agree on this matter as in most others: that the stars neither do everything, nor, where they do act, do they carry it out entirely. Likewise, they signify many things which they do not themselves do; I say they do not do everything, lest if they did evil, either God would not be providing, or He would be unjust, and the stars would be unjust at the same time. Nor again do they do everything, lest if they themselves carried out every single thing to the most exact detail, the action of natural things would be empty, and free will would cease. By a similar consensus, they therefore willingly grant frequent signification to the stars even where they do not act: because by this, divine providence is most greatly confirmed. For indications of past and future things could not be presented in this present face of the universe unless things were connected to things, and times to times, everywhere in a certain and consequent order. From this it is clearly evident that all things do not wander by uncertain chance, but are ruled by a certain reason and providence. If you consider the perpetual lights of the stars, and their approaches toward us and withdrawals, Plotinus and Origen will grant that only as much is effected among us from these as proceeds by natural order, and pertains to the affections of bodies; and that indeed by a general condition, which may be changed through things close to us. If you look again at the daily positions of the stars and their mutual aspects, know that according to these philosophers, our affairs are signified by these rather than enacted. This indeed Origen argues in his commentaries on Genesis, where it is said that the stars were made for signs; and Plotinus argues both here and in his book *On Fate*, primarily by five indications. First: That which is later cannot exist as the efficient cause of what preceded it. But astrologers promise to judge from the hour of birth not only what will happen to the one born, but what has already happened: whether it is male or female, whether maimed or whole. Indeed, they even profess to reveal many past things to us from today's position of the stars, which preceded not only the birth but even the conception of the one born: the natures and fortunes of parents and grandfathers, and also of older brothers and others joined to us by necessity. However, the later configuration of the heaven cannot be the cause of these prior things; but let it be a sign, if it declares anything at all. But if anyone grants that past things are only represented by these, while future things are additionally effected, he will be compelled to show us the difference and assign the cause of this distinction. Why, if the present configuration is not the cause of past things, should it be the cause of future things? And if the position of Mars in the fourth <note>The "fourth house" in astrology relates to ancestors, parents, and hidden things.</note> demonstrates both that the parents will die soon and that the patrimony of the one born will be dissipated: just as this position does not kill the parents, so it does not squander the patrimony. Now indeed, astrologers also promise to predict certain future things through this, of which this configuration cannot be the cause: namely, the fates of a wife, brothers, and friends, which have their own causes not in this configuration, but elsewhere. Finally, through the present disposition of the heavens, things which will happen after thirty years, if they can indeed be portended, certainly cannot be perfected. Rightly, therefore, they often say: this person being born will himself be the cause of his own disadvantages, and another of his advantages. The second judgment: If they say someone will die on a gallows, they think this can be understood not only from his own birth, but also from that of his parents, brothers, sons, and other relatives; indeed, even from the birth of his killers. But if there is any cause of this gallows, it is either one, or if many, they are certainly joined, and in the person himself; but where these are dispersed in different people, they are seen not as causes, but as signs. Finally, if through the configuration of the heaven at birth the fate of the boy is predicted as having been made long ago, this configuration itself does not effect the fate, but declares it; just as the boy is not then made, but the effects are declared. But even before conception, the Platonists will say the fate was conceived, namely when the soul chose the body. The third indication: Since many methods of foreseeing are thought to exist—oracle, augury, soothsaying, interpretation of dreams, the presages of doctors and farmers, omen, physiognomy—in all of which signs are weighed, not the causes of future things; why do they think that in the inspection of the celestial configuration alone there is not just an indication, but a cause? Is it because that configuration is superior to us? But the flights of birds and thunders are also superior, yet we are not accustomed to catch the future through these as through causes, but as if through indications. Finally, what and how much of an efficient cause for these things is in the heaven, has already been established. Are not God and the divine minds also superior? Yet oracles and the words of prophets pronounced or written by divine inspiration are prodigies of future things...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino argues that stars are primary signs of Divine Providence rather than direct causes of human events, citing the agreement of Plotinus and Origen. He provides logical proofs, such as the fact that stars can "predict" the past, which they could not have caused.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s Ennead II.3. In the previous section, Ficino discussed how celestial influences are general rather than specific. Here, he deepens the argument that stars act as signs or "letters" in a divine book rather than as direct physical causes of specific human choices or accidental events.</meta>

# ON THE THIRD BOOK OF THE SECOND ENNEAD

**...portents are not judged as causes.** Similarly, the face of the heaven can be a book in which figures written by the divine display things to come, but do not enact them; especially if through the consideration of celestial bodies those things are foreknown which cannot happen by the physical flow of that corporal nature: namely, specific honors and depressions of men at certain times, the discovery of treasures, the thoughts of our counsels, and changes of fortune, both our own and those of our people.

**Fourth Indication:** If by the present constitution of the stars either monstrous crimes or works proper to the divine are portended, it will be said far more probably that the stars declare both, rather than that they—being most excellent—perpetrate the worst things, or that they—being bodies—perform incorporeal acts, or bring about things that are either against or above corporal nature.

**Fifth Indication:** Interrogations <note>Latin: *Interrogationes*. This refers to "horary astrology," where an astrologer answers a specific question based on the moment the question is received.</note> which are made daily among astrologers—whether concerning the past (did such deeds happen?), the future (will they happen?), or the present (are they happening?) regarding matters both foreign to us and far distant—confirm that whatever is answered from the present hour of the interrogation is answered not through a cause, but a sign. From this, the previous points are confirmed: that for everything which happens to us that does not come from ourselves, we find manifest and sufficient causes among us—in the specific nature of our kind, in habit, affection, counsel, action, and the gathering of surrounding causes. Nor does anything ever happen from heaven without these causes, so there is no need to scrutinize the causes of these things in heaven when they are often plain on earth and yet are not found in heaven. 

And yet, if we concede that the figures of heaven always acting upon the present hours do something in us, we shall say they pertain only to the affections of bodies and their first impulses. And even that is of little weight, since it is acted upon through a momentary cause; it is then taken up according to our own nature and changed into our own more stable conditions. Furthermore, from the fact that the constitution of the stars does not "effect" everything it "signifies," the action proper to divinity, nature, and art is confirmed. Therefore, whether a conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn portends a new religion, a true religion can nonetheless be perfected by God in the meantime, or a false one fashioned by man. Or if through celestial motions those things which happen to the nature below the Moon are sometimes designated, nature nonetheless does and effects such things by the flow of nature. Or if through those same motions human actions are portended, they nevertheless proceed by human counsel and according to our will. And signs sometimes become empty when the efficient cause changes the cause within itself while the signifier remains.

Accordingly, what Plotinus and Origen say—that the letters of future things were either written in heaven from the beginning and are gradually unfolded, or are perpetually written—they understand as the stars and the figures composed of stars, as well as imaginary ones. Likewise, they mean the degrees and minute parts of the signs, and finally the aspects and motions of the planets, and those things which follow or accompany them wherever they please. But you should understand "heaven" here as the universe. For heaven is everywhere; and the *Timaeus* <note>A famous dialogue by Plato concerning the creation of the world.</note> names the universe "heaven." 

Above the Moon, just as through the force of inferior things the causes are common, so too are the signs common. But below the Moon there are specific causes; once these are known, the common signs are channeled into specific indications, and this whole world exists like the body of a single living animal. It is necessary, therefore, in this mundane animal, to look around at all things both above the Moon and below, and to weigh them against each other. For just as there are diverse things acting among themselves—both above and below, and sometimes superior things toward inferior ones—so too signs are often diverse among themselves everywhere. Just as in any animal there are natures contrary to each other, and diverse members, and signs in some parts repugnant to others. 

Therefore, Rasis <note>The Latinized name for Al-Razi (865–925 AD), a Persian polymath and physician.</note> commands the <term>physiognomist</term> <note>Someone who judges a person’s character or future from their physical features, especially the face.</note> not to trust a single sign, but to comprehend all of them and balance them against each other; and where there are contraries, to follow the majority and the more certain ones together. He who would divine from the world ought to observe the same in the world. Aristotle, in his book *On Sleep and Waking*, twice warns with these words that one must be cautious in judging: "There are often signs even in bodies from heaven, such as of rains and winds, and yet the signified event does not happen when another more vehement motion occurs." 

For this reason, Origen and Porphyry took such divination away from men and granted it to <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, *daemones* are not "demons" but intermediary spirits or guardian beings that bridge the gap between gods and humans.</note>, to whom that celestial book lies open to be read. Not to all spirits equally, I say: for Porphyry, in his book *On Oracles*, after he proved that whatever the gods announce as fated they predict by observation of the stars, adds that the gods also often lie, and that the exquisite knowledge of future things is utterly uncertain not only to men, but even to many of the gods; and to those gods to whom it can become known, it is not fully perceived at every hour. 

Thus, regarding the present, it is pleasing to arrange the spirits in this way: **Ethereal spirits**, dwelling in the higher air, contemplate celestial omens more than terrestrial ones. **Aqueous spirits**, inhabiting the lowest air, hunt for arguments of things from our affairs more than from celestial ones. Finally, the **Middle spirits** behold signs more conveniently in both places; therefore, they are much more suited for prophecy among us. From these, Origen says, men have sometimes received forewarnings; nevertheless, whether they received them from these spirits or learned them by observation, they see things confusedly and hallucinate as if in a certain darkness.

-> For many reasons, judgment about the future is most difficult. <-

But that neither man nor spirit can perceive every tiny detail among us by the sole inspection of celestial things, we argue in this manner: Just as any celestial nature is more common than any terrestrial nature, so any celestial motion is more common than any terrestrial motion. Individual things, therefore, cannot be rendered one-for-one from heaven to earth down to the smallest detail; nor can every smallest thing here be clearly discerned from there. For celestial motion is always, as it were, more "common," and is indifferent to many motions here. Thus, unless you have looked upon these things of ours in addition to heaven, you cannot weigh by what specific condition this celestial motion is received, or toward which part it is more likely to be defined. 

Take, if you please, the figure of heaven at your birth: you will see in it certain defined marks, few in number, by which you can note from there certain common and few effects in yourself. Thus, you can never perceive from there all your motions—which are innumerable not only in your whole life, but in every year and month—not even if you unfold the <term>revolution</term> <note>The "solar return," a chart calculated for the exact moment the Sun returns to its birth position each year.</note> of your nativity every year, nor again if you observe diligently every day. I leave aside for now what spirits can do; certainly, men cannot. No wise person will deny that all the stars, which are innumerable to us, contribute something to every effect, and from their confluence something common is fashioned, and that indeed according to the nature of the place and the matter. But astrologers observe only one thousand and twenty-two stars, or at most, just over one thousand four hundred and seventy-six. 

The result is that since they hold a smaller number of causes, and do not yet know those perfectly, they cannot judge the absolute condition of the effect—especially since there are very many stars above the planets, marvelous both in magnitude and splendor. There are also innumerable stars in the Milky Way entirely hidden from our eyes; and they cannot deny, based on their own doctrine, that the planets are affected in one way or another by the aspects of the stars. I pass over the fact that the philosopher Favorinus argues not only that other stars exist besides the known ones, but even that other planets could exist, unknown either because of the abundance of their splendor or because of their exceeding height; without the observation of which a perfect knowledge of things perhaps cannot be had. To this, if someone objects that the stars of our hemisphere act upon a man born under this very horizon, and others upon others: I respond—

# COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO
<meta>catchword: who</meta>

...let us grant this: that the stars, wherever they may be, all cast their rays upon one another—with the shadow of the earth never hindering this—and transmit them from every direction all the way to us. Likewise, let us grant that only a very few stars in the hemisphere have been recorded by men. Indeed, individual motions have not yet been fully grasped, neither by the eye, nor by instrument, nor by a lifespan sufficient to observe them all. Furthermore—and this is very difficult to believe—is it possible that the magnitude, height, and motion of Mercury have been perceived with perfect accuracy? <note>Latin: *ad unguem*, literally "to the fingernail," meaning with precise perfection.</note> For it is seen only very rarely, and even then it presents itself obscurely and almost in an instant, not waiting for sufficient diligence of observation. Since, therefore, what *is* or what *happens* in the heavens has not yet been fully perceived, much less can we perceive what happens *because* of the heavens. Furthermore, astrologers rely not on reason, but on experience and practice; yet experience, unless all surrounding circumstances on both sides are similar, very often fails. Was it truly because Mars held the angle of the East in Aries <note>Aries is the "house" or sign where Mars was traditionally thought to be most powerful.</note> at the birth of Romulus that he performed such great deeds? This assumes that the stars known to human wit were converging in almost that exact way at that time. If, therefore, such a Romulus existed under such a heaven once upon a time, would Hannibal—for whom Mars also ascended in Aries—necessarily follow the exact same outcome? Not at all. For even if you imagine all the planets were additionally disposed in the same way for both men, the other stars of the firmament do not hold their parts in the same alignment as they once did. For the signs that are somewhat manifest to our eyes have already changed their position toward the east from the time of Romulus to Hannibal, while those moving under the more stable "hidden signs" complete one degree every hundred years. <note>Ficino is describing "precession," the slow shift of the earth's axis which causes the constellations to move out of alignment with the calendar dates of the Zodiac signs over long periods of time.</note> In such a time, the position of the signs is changed, and the visible constellation, relating differently and in various ways to the hidden signs, undoubtedly produces different effects.

<margin>For even astronomers</margin>
confess that all things must be referred back to the "invisible sign." For perhaps the manifest Aries, which then coincided with the hidden Aries, now corresponds with Taurus, or at least with another degree or minute of that Aries. Thus, the other signs correspond to signs in a different following order. Whence, if the signs change their powers through other signs, the planets also change through the signs. But how long the world will have run, and in what alignment these apparent signs stand in relation to those hidden ones, man cannot even begin to guess. We can see how much the diversity regarding the eighth sphere <note>In the ancient model, the "eighth sphere" was the shell of the fixed stars, surrounding the seven spheres of the planets.</note> matters from the fact that, although for many thousands of years the planets have frequently returned to the same positions relative to each other, nevertheless perfectly similar effects do not return. The ancient face of the world is not yet renewed; the same empires do not return in the same places, nor do similar laws and customs. By the "diversity of the eighth sphere," we mean not only that which occurs from west to east, but also its "access and recess," <note>A reference to the theory of "trepidation," a supposed oscillation of the equinoxes once believed to exist by medieval astronomers.</note> through which the images approach the north in some ages and the south in others. Therefore, astrologers could not have established certain rules for confirming experience while they imagined similar effects for men born at different times, even if they had a somewhat similar positioning of certain stars. For the exact same face of the total universe will not return until thirty-six thousand years have been consumed. <note>This is the "Platonic Year" or "Great Year," the time it was thought to take for all the stars and planets to return to a starting configuration.</note> Added to this is the fact that, just as the rules of doctors must be observed differently in different places if they are to be life-saving, so too the rules of astrologers admit change under different regions. For the system of observation used by the Chaldeans <note>The Chaldeans were famous ancient Babylonian astronomers/astrologers.</note> cannot hold if one wishes to use the same system under different regions of the sky. For the same stars do not provoke frosts everywhere, nor similarly heat, winds, and rains, but they change and vary, moving calm weather in one place and violent storms in another at the exact same time—or none at all. Why then would they not effect some human events for the Chaldeans and others for the Getae and Scythians? <note>The Getae and Scythians were ancient tribes from the regions around the Black Sea, representing "foreign" or "northern" climates compared to the Middle East.</note> Certainly, just as the habit of the body is different under a different curve of the sky, so in all other human affairs you cannot conclude the exact same thing if you view the stars from a different land. But let it be: let astrologers observe in individual regions what is most likely to happen from the heavens in certain ages—which to this day no one has properly observed—they certainly cannot explore to the highest degree the celestial figure which they are accustomed to destining as "fetal" or "fatal" for each person. First, indeed, they concede that the fate of one being born depends not only on their own specific figure, but simultaneously on the figure of their parents, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, and from the very time of the marriage itself. It is not possible to explore so many configurations, nor is it given to us to collect the "fatal" causes of the newborn which are so widely dispersed and signs so distracted. Nor, even if they turned their attention to these things, could they weigh the more serious moments of affairs; and even if someone could comprehend all that, they still would not see every event in the life of the newborn from these things alone. For they say that universal causes often come which are so powerful that they change the specific qualities of each individual, clearly for better or for worse. But let us return to the figures pertaining in some way to the newborn.

<margin>Ptolemy says in the *Tetrabiblos*:</margin>
Ptolemy says in the *Tetrabiblos*: <note>The *Tetrabiblos* (Four Books) was the foundational text of Western astrology, written by Claudius Ptolemy in the 2nd century AD.</note> A brief time makes a very great change in the matter itself, and therefore judgment is exceedingly difficult.

<margin>Hence also Abu Ma'shar in the *Book of Judgments*.</margin>
Hence also Abu Ma'shar <note>Latin: *Abumaxar*. A famous 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note> in the *Book of Judgments* says: It is necessary for judgment to know most excellently the courses of the planets at any hour, and to hold the degrees and minutes of the signs most certainly. Indeed, the six signs starting from Cancer, because they proceed straight, take two hours or a little more in ascending; the remaining six which begin from Capricorn, because they rise obliquely, ascend in less than two hours. Therefore, the hour must be divided on both sides and parts of the hour must be distributed to parts of the sign. In the "straight" signs, five degrees of the signs require almost a fifteenth part of an hour; in the "oblique" ones, almost a twentieth. But just as there are thirty degrees in the signs, and sixty minutes in any degree, and sixty seconds in any minute, so in the part of the hour on both sides—either the fifteenth or the twentieth—it is necessary to distribute it into sixty parts, and again similarly into sixty, and to accommodate each part to each precisely.

<margin>For Origen also says.</margin>

<margin>Nigidius showed this with the turning of a potter’s wheel.</margin>
which Nigidius <note>Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero. He famously used the "potter's wheel" analogy: if you touch a spinning wheel twice, even in quick succession, the marks are far apart. This illustrates how fast the sky turns.</note> showed with the turning of a potter's wheel), who can possibly grasp such small details? Now truly, since for the most part half a sign occupies one hour in ascending, by what means will you find the minute of the ascendant, when you cannot observe such a minute division of time? For it is necessary to know not only what hour, but even at what minute of the hour the child was poured out from the womb. In Pisces and Aries, however, because of their oblique ascension (for they seem to ascend in almost an hour and a third of an hour), they do not doubt that the smallest part of time brings a great change, so that even a twentieth part of one hour changes the degree of the ascendant. Since, therefore, they claim that even a tiny amount of time—whether occurring between births, or of twins, or of any two men born from different parents but in almost the same part of time—brings a diversity which is perceived in the effect between them:

<margin>Augustine asks.</margin>
Therefore Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo, whose *City of God* contains famous arguments against astrology using the example of twins.</note> asks them this: does that tiny interval bring a tiny discrepancy between them, or a great one? If they say "tiny," we will point out that the twins Jacob and Esau, born without an interval of time, were greatly dissimilar. If they say "great," then since those minute details—namely seconds, thirds, fourths—cannot be grasped by any instrument, they certainly cannot judge. I have experienced that time brings a great difference among my own relatives: twin sisters were born in our family without an interval. Disease killed one after seven weeks; the other was suffocated by a negligent nurse after seven months. Twins were also born similarly: fire killed one within a few days; water suffocated the other after fourteen years. Twins were also born in my neighborhood without intermission,

<meta>This page continues Ficino’s systematic deconstruction of astrological determinism. Having previously argued that stars are signs rather than causes, he now addresses the technical impossibility of pinpointing the "exact moment" of birth or conception, which astrologers claim is necessary for an accurate horoscope. He introduces the perspectives of ancient authorities like Favorinus, Iamblichus, and Porphyry to highlight the internal contradictions and uncertainties within the astrological tradition.</meta>

# ON BOOK III. ENNEAD II.

...who are already adults, and are very diverse in their bodies, characters, and fortunes. I pass over how diverse is the lot of many animals born together, especially when they are warmed together in eggs. Surely, if the moment of time in which a human being receives their fate when being born is so small and fleeting that in that same point, under the exact same circle of heaven, several can hardly be born at the same time to the same fitness; and if, for that reason, twins also do not have the same lot in life because they were not born at the same moment, let them answer, I pray, as I ask with Favorinus <note>Favorinus of Arelate (c. 80–160 AD), a Skeptic philosopher known for his arguments against the validity of astrology.</note>: that course of fleeting time, which can hardly be grasped by the thought of the mind—in what way do they catch it, since they say that even the smallest moments in the headlong whirling of the heaven bring about massive changes? 

Now, truly, there is a greater delay in the birth of one individual than between twins succeeding each other soon in birth. If, therefore, in a certain blink of an eye the celestial constitution and fate are changed, it will now be necessary for them to state as many fates as there are limbs being born. Here too it is very opportunely asked: is the sequence of fate unfolded at the first moment the child begins to come out of the womb? Or rather when he is halfway out? Or perhaps when he is entirely out? For they even disagree among themselves on this. But the matter seems to be repeated from a deeper origin, the beginning of the fetus. Even if some profess that they will find the figure of the heaven at that time, and indeed from the figure of birth, yet since they have this one as uncertain, then surely that one is much more uncertain. But let us grant them that they have this discovered; by what rules, finally, will they be able to catch the one from the other? 

Some will perhaps say that the degree of the Moon rising at birth was the degree at conception, and conversely, the degree of the ascendant at birth was the degree of the Moon when the fetus was conceived in the womb; but neither can this be firmly established; rather, it is entirely arbitrary. Now others seek from elsewhere, and as Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who integrated theurgical and astrological traditions.</note> reports, some are accustomed to use five laws for it, others fewer, and others truly more. But Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD), the student of Plotinus; he was often critical of the deterministic claims of Egyptian and Chaldean astrology.</note> says, even with astronomers conceding it, that it is altogether uncertain. 

But suppose someone perhaps finds the beginnings of the fetus: we ask whether that first tempering of the heaven, when the human work is first begun, alone contributes to the work, or also the subsequent celestial harmonies which, just like the first was momentary, are varied in individual moments? If the first alone is said to be effective, it is a wonder that a momentary figure of heaven completes a long-lasting work—and when it is no longer present, continues to act. But they will bring forward from the first figure a certain power left in the fetus, as if surviving and acting. Let it be so, truly, although it is so marvelous; but surely the figures that follow continuously thereafter—do they act not at all on the fetus? Indeed, these also act and brand their marks upon it. And although they are received according to the nature of the previous one, they nevertheless flow in also according to their own nature, and gradually change the previous things, confound the signs, and deceive the judgments. 

But the greatest change of the preceding things and the beginning of the following ones occurs when the soul first flows into the small body of the fetus already prepared for the soul. This moment is surely uncertain even to daemons <note>original: *demonibus*. In Ficino's Neoplatonism, these are spiritual intermediaries, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note>. Iamblichus, following the mind of Plato, proves that the lot and the leader of life and the daemon are assigned to the soul even before conception by the universal disposition of the whole world: just as the soul is related to the universe when it first desires a body, and vice versa. Therefore, that time must first be known and weighed, which he thinks can only be grasped by divine inspiration. 

Beyond these things, moreover, if any times are to be observed in judging the effects on men, five seem to be observed. 

**First**, indeed, the time of bearing, when the seed is cast into the matrix <note>the womb</note>: the condition of this casting follows the voluntary movement of the parents, and the present nature of both of them, and the accompanying imagination, rather than the present constitution of the heaven. For the beginning of the movement was the will of both; truly, chance in a movement of this kind happens most of all according to their nature and imagination, while the heaven favors it somewhat in the meantime. How much imagination can do appears from the greed of pregnant women, and in animals that are born white from parents imagining white things, as is said of peacocks. 

**Second**: the time when, with the aforesaid movement now ceasing, the seed collected and firm in the matrix now begins to be changed from what it was, and perhaps first to be bound together. The origin and source of such binding and action follows the condition of the seed and the parents more than the heaven, because what is produced is very material, and that indeed was and becomes a part of the parents. But a part follows its own near and proper whole. Whence we see such a species and individual, and such a species and individual of seed, coalesce. Meanwhile, however, the heaven contributes. 

**Third**: the time when the fetus is first formed into life. And they say this happens in the second month, in which Jupiter acts most of all. But it is uncertain whether life is present as soon as it has filled the middle of its month, or some days after, when it has reached the forty-ninth day from conception, because nature frequently rejoices in the number seven in our affairs. And altogether, whether it happens otherwise is obscure. For perhaps it happens in the ninth month, which they attribute to Jupiter again; not every infant is brought forth into the light in the same way, so neither does everyone receive life equally in the second month. For they say it has been found that females do not receive it in the same way as males: thus it is probable that males among themselves and females do not receive it at the same intervals. What? That some will perhaps say the rational soul descends not in the month of Jupiter, in which they say the vegetative power is assigned, nor in the month of Mars, in which they say the sensory power is assigned, but in the month of the Sun, or perhaps of Mercury. 

But leaving these opinions aside, let us consider simply the principle of one’s own life. The beginning of life is most of all drawn from this day and hour. For from conception there was rather the beginning of essence and mass; until now it lived no other life than that of the parents, and existed as a part of another; but now it claims its own life for itself. And let it now be a whole, and soon use its own motion. Therefore, life of this kind seems to see the exterior life—that is, the second life of the universe—or the divine mind. The lot of life, in the body I mean, follows most of all the present constitution of the heaven. Then also the habit of the body; I mean the present habit, for it is already different than it was in conception. And rightly, just as that which was more material followed a more material cause, so that which is and becomes most formal follows first of all a formal cause—that is, the celestial and especially the super-celestial. 

**Fourth**: the time when the grown infant in the womb strives with all its force to release itself from maternal bonds. The chance of such a release follows, first indeed, the present strength of the child and the condition of the mother; then the habit of the heaven contributing more or less to it. 

**Fifth**: the time when the child, entirely released, breaks out from the womb. The condition of the one breaking out follows the preceding condition of the one striving. But what the future condition of this one will be, who has now come forth from the womb—if indeed it is judged from the celestial constitution in which he came forth—is weighed not as from a cause, but as from a sign. For they will say it is probable that the preceding prosperity of the heaven led to the subsequent prosperity of the heaven. 

But remember: perhaps it cannot be weighed at all, both because the times are unknown, and because the causes are unknown (how many or of what kind they are), and because it is not known what is most of all fused from the gathering of all things. By "gathering," I mean both of the present things among themselves, and of the following causes with the preceding ones. For the army of the stars <note>original: *stellarum agmen*</note> was one thing at the time when a man was first conceived, another afterwards when the soul was infused, and another when he was brought forth into the light. If different positions and paths of the stars promise different fortunes, who then will choose the lot in judging especially from these? Who in any tempering...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s Enneads, specifically refuting the technical claims of astrologers. On the previous page, Ficino argued that the precise moment of birth is impossible to capture.
