# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...let us grant: the stars, wherever they may be, all cast their rays upon one another, with the shadow of the earth never hindering this, and they transmit those rays from every direction all the way to us. Likewise, only a very few stars of the hemisphere have been noted by men. Indeed, even if the number of stars were calculated at the absolute minimum, their power is certainly not yet all known. Furthermore, their individual motions have not yet been fully grasped, neither by the eye, nor by instrument, nor by a lifespan sufficient for them all. What of the fact that it is most difficult to believe that the magnitude, height, and motion of **Mercury** have been perceived "to the fingernail" <note>original: "ad vnguem"—a Latin idiom meaning "to perfection" or "with extreme precision."</note>, since it is seen very rarely, and even then presents itself obscurely and almost in an instant, not waiting for sufficient diligent observation? Since, therefore, what exists and what happens in heaven is not yet fully perceived, much less is it perceived what happens *from* heaven. Moreover, astrologers rely not on reason, but on experience and practice; yet experience very often fails unless all the surrounding "families" <note>Here, "families" refers to the complex groupings of celestial bodies and their relationships.</note> on both sides are familiar. 

Was it truly because **Mars** held the corner of the East in **Aries** when **Romulus** <note>The legendary founder of Rome.</note> was being born that he performed such great deeds? Simply because the stars known to human ingenuity happened to coincide in that way at that time? Since, then, such a Romulus existed once under such a heaven, will **Hannibal** <note>The Carthaginian general and rival of Rome.</note>—for whom Mars also ascended in Aries—necessarily follow exactly the same outcome? Not at all. For even if you imagine all the planets were additionally disposed in a similar way for both, the other stars and parts of the firmament do not hold themselves in the same state they once did. For the signs that are in some way manifest to our eyes have already changed their position at the rising point from the time of Romulus to Hannibal; while running beneath the hidden and more stable signs, they complete one degree every hundred years. In this span of time, the position of the signs is permuted, and the visible firmament, relating itself differently and yet differently to the hidden signs, undoubtedly produces different effects. For even astronomers confess that everything must be referred to the "invisible sign." 

For perhaps the visible Aries, which then coincided with the hidden Aries, now coincides with **Taurus**, or at least with another degree or minute of that Aries. Thus also the other signs correspond to signs in a different following order. Whence, if signs permute their powers through other signs, the planets also commute through the signs. Truly, for as long as the world has run, and in what state these apparent signs relate to those hidden ones, man is not even permitted to guess. Indeed, we perceive how much diversity exists regarding the **eighth sphere** <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, which sits above the spheres of the seven planets.</note> from the fact that, although for many thousands of years now the planets have frequently returned among themselves to the same spot, they do not yet return with entirely similar effects; the ancient face of the world is not yet renewed; the same empires do not return in the same place; nor do similar laws and customs. 

We speak of the diversity of the eighth sphere not only regarding that which happens from the west to the east, but also its **accession and recession** <term>Trepidation</term> <note>A now-obsolete theory that the equinoxes oscillated or "shook" back and forth rather than moving in a steady precession.</note>, through which the constellations approach the north in some ages and the south in others. Therefore, astrologers could not have established certain rules for confirming their experience while they supposed similar effects for men born at different times, yet having in some way a similar position of certain stars. For the exact same face of the universe will not return until thirty-six thousand years <note>The "Great Year" or Platonic Year, after which the stars were thought to return to their original positions.</note> have been consumed. 

Added to this is the fact that, just as the rules of physicians are to be observed differently in different places if they are to be health-giving, so too the rules of astrologers admit change under different regions. For the system of observation of the **Chaldeans** <note>A common term for ancient Babylonian astrologers.</note> cannot stand if someone wishes to use the same system under different regions of the sky. For the same stars do not stir up frost everywhere, nor similarly heat, winds, and rains, but they change and vary, moving calm weather in one place and violent storms in another at the same time, and in another place none at all. Why then, in the outcome of human affairs, should they not effect one thing for the Chaldeans and another for the **Getulae** and **Scythians**? <note>Peoples of North Africa and Central Asia/Eastern Europe, respectively, used here to represent geographical extremes.</note> Truly, just as under a different curvature of the heaven there is a different habit of the body, so in all other human affairs you cannot infer exactly the same thing if you view the stars from any different land. 

But so be it: let astrologers observe in individual regions what is most fitting to happen from heaven in certain ages—which to this day no one has rightly observed—certainly they cannot explore to the highest degree the celestial figure which they are accustomed to destine as "fatal" <note>In the sense of "ordained by fate."</note> for each person. First, indeed, since I would concede that the fate of one being born depends not only on their own figure, but also on the figure of their parents, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, and from the very time of the marriage; it is not permitted to explore so many configurations, nor is it given to collect the "fatal" causes of the newborn which are so widely dispersed and signs so distracted; nor, if they have ever appeared to themselves, to weigh the weightier moments of things. And even if someone were to comprehend those things, they will not see every outcome in the newborn from these alone. For they say that "universal causes" often come which are so powerful that they change what is proper to each individual, namely for the worse or the better. 

But let us return to the figures pertaining in some way to the newborn. <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer and astrologer of antiquity.</note> says in the <term>Tetrabiblos</term> <note>The primary ancient textbook on astrology; original title "Quadripartitum."</note>: "A short time makes the greatest change in the matter itself, and therefore judgment is extremely difficult." Hence also <term>Abumazar</term> <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a famous Persian astrologer.</note> in his *Book of Judgments* says: "It is necessary for judgment to know the courses of the planets perfectly at any hour, and to hold the degrees and minutes of the signs most certainly." 

Truly, the six signs starting from **Cancer**, because they proceed directly, occupy two hours or a little more in ascending; the remaining six which begin from **Capricorn**, because they rise obliquely, ascend in less than two hours. Therefore, the hour must be divided in both cases and the parts of the hour distributed to the parts of the sign. In the "straight" signs, five degrees of the signs require almost a fifteenth part of an hour; in the "oblique" ones, almost a twentieth. But just as there are thirty degrees in the signs, and sixty minutes in any degree, and sixty seconds in any minute: so in the part of the hour in both cases, whether the fifteenth or the twentieth, it is necessary to distribute it into sixty parts, and again similarly into sixty, and to accommodate each one to each. 

Since, therefore, astrologers assert (as <term>Origen</term> <note>The early Christian theologian Origen of Alexandria.</note> also says) that not only degrees, but also minutes and minutes of minutes must necessarily be known—in which the planets are, and which are ascending or descending (for in the smallest there is the greatest difference; which <term>Nigidius</term> <note>Publius Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero, who used the analogy of a potter's wheel to show how fast the heavens move.</note> also showed in the turning of a potter’s wheel)—who indeed can catch such minutiae? Now truly, since for the most part half a sign occupies one hour in ascending, in what way will you find the minute of the ascendant, when you cannot observe such a minute division of time? For it is useful to know not only which hour, but also at which minutes of the hour the child was poured forth from the womb. In **Pisces** and **Aries**, indeed, on account of the oblique ascension of the hours (for they seem to ascend in almost an hour and a third of an hour), they do not doubt that the smallest part of time brings a great change, so that even the twentieth part of one hour changes the degree of the ascendant. 

Since, therefore, they assert that even a tiny time, which falls between the birth either of twins or of any two men, born indeed from different parents but in almost the same part of time, brings the diversity which is perceived in the effect between them: therefore **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo, who famously argued against astrology in "The City of God."</note> asks them: does that tiny interval bring a tiny discrepancy between them, or a great one? If they say tiny, we will object that the twins **Jacob and Esau**, brought forth without an interval of time, were different in great ways. If they say a great one—since those minutiae, namely seconds, thirds, fourths, can be perceived by no instrument—certainly they cannot judge. 

That it brings a great difference, I have experienced among my own relatives: twin sisters were born in our family without an interval; a specific disease seized one after seven weeks; the other, after seven months, an ignorant nurse smothered. Twins were also born in my neighborhood without intermission,

## ON THE THIRD BOOK OF THE SECOND ENNEAD

...who are already adults, and are most diverse in their bodies, talents, and fortunes. I pass over how different is the lot of many brute animals born at the same time, especially those fostered together in eggs. Surely, if the moment of time in which a human being receives their fate is so small and fleeting that in that same point, under the exact same circle of heaven, several can hardly be born at the same time to the same destiny; and if, for that reason, twins also do not have the same lot in life because they were not born at the same moment—then let them answer, I pray, so that I may ask with **Favorinus** <note>A Roman philosopher and orator (c. 80 – c. 160 AD) known for his skeptical arguments against astrology.</note>: by what means do they capture that course of flying time, which can hardly be grasped by the thought of the mind, when they say that even the smallest moments in such a headlong whirling of the heaven bring about enormous changes? Now, truly, there is a greater delay in the birth of one individual than there is between twins succeeding each other in labor. If, therefore, the celestial constitution and fate are transformed in the blink of an eye, it will now be necessary for them to declare as many fates as there are limbs being born. Here also it is very opportunely asked: is the series of fate unfolded at the first moment the boy begins to emerge from the womb? Or rather when he is halfway out? Or perhaps when he is entirely out? For 
<margin>&</margin> & even on this point they disagree among themselves. But it seems the matter must be traced deeper, from the very beginning of the fetus. Even if some profess themselves to be the "discoverers" of the very figure of the heavens at that time <note>i.e., at the moment of conception.</note>, and indeed derive it from the figure of the birth, yet since they hold the latter to be uncertain, the former is surely much more uncertain. But let us grant them that they have found this out; by what rules, finally, will they be able to hunt for the one from the other? Some will perhaps say that the degree of the **Moon** ascending at birth was the degree at conception, and conversely, that the degree of the **Ascendant** <note>The sign of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note> at birth was the degree of the Moon when the fetus was conceived in the womb; but neither can this be firmly established; indeed, it is entirely arbitrary. Now others also seek answers from elsewhere, and as **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who integrated theurgy and astrology into Platonic thought.</note> reports, some are accustomed to using five laws for this, others fewer, and others more. **Porphyry** <note>A student of Plotinus; he wrote extensively on astrology and the soul's descent.</note>, however, says that even astronomers concede this is utterly uncertain. But suppose someone should by chance find the beginnings of the fetus: we ask, does that first tempering of the heaven, when the human work is first begun, alone contribute to the work, or do the remaining celestial harmonies thereafter also contribute—which, just like the first, were momentary and vary from moment to moment? If the first is said to be the only one to act, it is a wonder that a momentary figure of heaven completes a long-lasting work; and when it is no longer present, it continues to act. But they will assert that from the first figure a certain power is left in the fetus, surviving and acting as it were. Let it be so, although it is indeed quite a wonder; but surely the figures that follow immediately after, do they act not at all upon the fetus? On the contrary, these also act, and brand it with their own marks. And although they are received according to the nature of the prior one, they nevertheless flow in according to their own nature, and gradually transform the prior ones, confuse the signs, and deceive the judgments. But the greatest transformation of preceding things and the beginning of subsequent ones occurs when the soul first flows into the small body of the fetus already prepared for the soul; which moment, surely, is uncertain even to the **daemons** <note>term: *daemon* — In Neoplatonism, these are intermediary spirits or guiding geniuses, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note>. Iamblichus, following the mind of **Plato**, proves that the lot and the leader of life and the daemon are assigned to the soul even before conception by the universal disposition of the whole world: just as the soul, when it first desires a body, relates itself to the universe, and vice versa. Therefore, one ought first to know and weigh that time, which he thinks can only be understood by divine inspiration. Beyond these things, moreover, if any times are to be observed in judging the effects of men, five seem to be observed. First, indeed, the time of bearing, when the seed is cast into the womb: the condition of this casting follows the voluntary movement of the parents, and the present nature of each, and the accompanying imagination, rather than the present constitution of the heaven. For the principle of the movement was the will of both; but the "chance" in such a movement happens chiefly according to their nature and imagination, while in the meantime the heaven favors them somewhat. How much imagination can do is apparent from the greediness of pregnant women, and in animals that are born white from parents imagining white things, as is said of peacocks. Second, the time when, the aforementioned movement now ceasing, the seed is collected and firm in the womb, and now begins to be transformed from what it was, and perhaps first to conglutinate. The beginning and source of such conglutination and action follows the condition of the seed and the parents more than the heaven, because what is being made is very material, and indeed it was and becomes a part of the parents. But the part follows its own near and proper whole. Whence we see such a species and individual, and a seed of that kind, coalesce from such a species and individual. Nevertheless, the heaven contributes in the meantime. Third: the time when the fetus is first formed into life. And they say this happens in the second month, in which **Jupiter** chiefly acts. But it is uncertain whether life is present as soon as it has filled the middle of its month, or some days after, when it has reached the forty-ninth day from conception, because nature frequently rejoices in the number seven in our affairs; and altogether whether it happens otherwise is obscure. For perhaps it happens in the ninth month, which they attribute again to Jupiter; not every infant is brought forth into the light in the same way, so neither does everyone receive life equally in the second month: for they say it has been found that females do not receive it in the same way as males: thus it is probable that males among themselves and females among themselves do not receive it at the same intervals. What of the fact that others will perhaps say the rational soul descends not in the month of Jupiter, in which they say the vegetative power is granted, nor in the month of **Mars**, in which the sensual power is granted, but in the month of the **Sun**, or perhaps of **Mercury**? But setting aside these opinions, let us simply consider the beginning of one's own life. The auspice of life is chiefly drawn from this day and hour: for from conception, the auspice was rather of essence and mass; thus far it lived no other life than that of the parents, and existed as a part of another: but now it claims its own life for itself, and becomes a whole, and soon uses its own motion. Therefore, such a life now sees the exterior life—that is, the secondary life of the universe or the divine mind. The lot of life also, in the body I mean, follows most of all the present constitution of heaven. Then also the habit of the body: the present habit, I say: for it is already different from what it was at conception. And rightly, just as what was more material followed a more material cause, so that which is most formal—and becomes so—follows a cause that is primarily formal, that is, celestial, and especially super-celestial. Fourth: the time when the adult infant in the womb strives with all its might to release itself from the maternal bonds. The lot of such a release follows, first indeed, the present strength of the child and the condition of the mother; then the habit of the heaven, contributing more or less to that end. Fifth: the time when the entirely released child breaks forth from the womb. The condition of the one breaking forth follows the preceding condition of the one striving. But of what sort the future condition of this one will be, who has now come forth from the womb—if indeed it is judged from the celestial constitution in which he came forth—it is weighed not as from a cause, but as if from a sign: for they will say it is probable that the preceding prosperity of heaven led to the subsequent prosperity of heaven. But remember, perhaps it cannot be weighed at all, both because the times are unknown, and because the causes are unknown (how many or of what sort they are), and because it is not known what is chiefly forged from the concourse of them all. A concourse, I say, both of present causes among themselves, and of subsequent causes with preceding ones. For there was one array of stars when the human was first conceived, another later when the soul was infused, another when he was brought forth into the light. If different positions and paths of the stars promise different fortunes, who then will choose the lot in judging chiefly from these? Who then [will judge] the tempering in any [alignment]?

## COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...let us grant: that the stars, wherever they are, all cast their rays upon each other in turn, with the shadow of the earth never hindering this, and that they transmit them from all sides down to us. Likewise, let us grant that only a very few stars have been noted by men. Indeed, even if the number of stars were calculated to the minimum, certainly not every power of theirs is yet known; in fact, not even their individual motions have yet been grasped, for neither the eye, nor any instrument, nor a single lifetime is sufficient for them all. What of the fact—which is most difficult to believe—that the magnitude, height, and motion of Mercury have been perceived to a hair's breadth? For it is seen very rarely, and then it presents itself obscurely and almost in a moment, not waiting for sufficient diligence. Since, therefore, what exists and what happens in the heaven has not yet been fully perceived, it follows that what happens *from* the heaven is also not understood. Furthermore, astrologers rely not on reason, but on experience and practice; yet experience, unless all surrounding circumstances are similar on both sides, very often fails. 

Is it truly because Mars was in Aries at the corner of the East <note>The "Ascendant" or Eastern Horizon in a birth chart.</note> when Romulus was born that he performed such great deeds? This was because stars known to human wit happened to be running together in that way at that time. Since, therefore, such a man as Romulus once existed under such a heaven, will Hannibal—for whom Mars also ascended in Aries—altogether follow the same outcome? Not at all. For even if you imagine all the other planets were similarly disposed in both cases, nevertheless, the other stars and parts of the firmament do not hold themselves in the same habit as they once did. For the signs that are in some way manifest to our eyes have already changed their position toward the east from the time of Romulus to Hannibal, while running under more stable, hidden signs at a rate of one degree every hundred years. In this time, the position of the signs is permuted, and the visible constellation, relating itself differently and still more differently to the hidden signs, certainly produces different and still more different effects. 

For even astronomers confess that all things must be referred to the invisible sign <note>The "invisible sign" refers to the abstract mathematical divisions of the zodiac (tropical zodiac), as opposed to the visible constellations (sidereal zodiac) which shift due to the precession of the equinoxes.</note>. For perhaps the manifest Aries, which then ran together with the hidden Aries, now corresponds with Taurus, or at least with another degree or minute of that Aries. Thus, the other signs correspond to the signs in a different following order. Whence, if the signs change their powers through other signs, the planets also change through the signs. Indeed, how long the world has run, and in what habit these signs appear in relation to those, man is not even permitted to suspect. How much weight this diversity around the eighth sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, believed to be the outermost part of the visible universe in the Ptolemaic system.</note> carries, we perceive from the fact that although the planets have frequently returned to the same position among themselves over many thousands of years, nevertheless, identical effects do not yet return. The ancient face of the world is not yet renewed; the same empires do not return in the same place; similar laws and customs do not return. Moreover, we speak of the diversity of the eighth sphere not only regarding its motion from west to east, but also its "access and recess" <note>A reference to the theory of "trepidation," an ancient astronomical theory that the equinoxes oscillated back and forth.</note>, through which the images approach the north in some centuries and the south in others. 

Astrologers, therefore, cannot have established certain rules for confirming experience while they imagine similar effects for men born at different times who nevertheless have a somewhat similar posture of certain stars. For the exact same face of the universe will not return before thirty-six thousand years are consumed <note>The duration of the "Great Year," the time it takes for the fixed stars to complete one full revolution.</note>. Added to this is the fact that, just as the rules of doctors must be observed differently in different places if they are to be healthy, so the rules of astrologers admit change under different regions. For the system of observation used by the Chaldaeans <note>The ancient Babylonians, often cited as the founders of astrology.</note> cannot hold if someone wishes to use the same system under different regions of the sky. For the same stars do not provoke frosts everywhere, nor similarly heat, winds, and rains; but they change and vary, and at the same time they stir up calm weather in one place, violent in another, and none at all in another. Why then should they not also produce some human events for the Chaldaeans and others for the Getulians and Scythians <note>Getulians were from North Africa; Scythians from Central Eurasia—Ficino is highlighting extreme geographic differences.</note>? Surely, just as the habit of the body is different under a different curvature of the heaven, so in all other human affairs you cannot infer the exact same thing if you view the stars from any different land. 

But let it be: let astrologers observe in individual regions what is most likely to happen from the heaven in certain centuries—which to this day no one observes properly—they certainly cannot explore to the highest degree the celestial figure which they are accustomed to assign as "fetal" to each person. First, indeed, they concede that the fate of one being born depends not only on their own figure <note>The "figure" or "chart" of the heavens at the moment of birth.</note>, but simultaneously on the figure of the parents, grandparents, and great-grandparents, and from the very time of the wedding. It is not possible to explore so many configurations, nor is it given to collect the fatal causes of the child which are so widely dispersed and the signs so distracted; nor, if they should contradict each other anywhere, is it possible to weigh the more serious moments of affairs. And if someone should comprehend those things, he will still not see every outcome in the child from these alone. For they say that universal causes often come which are so powerful that they change the individual causes of each person, namely for the worse or the better. 

But let us return to the figures pertaining in some way to the newborn. **Ptolemy** in the *Quadripartitum* <note>Also known as the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology.</note> says: a brief time makes the greatest change in the situation itself, and therefore judgment is extremely difficult. Hence **Abu Ma'shar** <note>A Persian astronomer and astrologer (787–886 AD), known in the West as Abumasar.</note> in his *Book of Judgments* says: it is necessary for judgment to know perfectly the courses of the planets at any hour, and to hold the degrees and minutes of the signs most certainly. Indeed, the six signs starting from Cancer, because they proceed straight, occupy two hours or a little more in ascending; the six remaining signs which begin from Capricorn, because they rise obliquely, ascend in less than two hours. Therefore, the hour must be divided in both cases, and the parts of the hour distributed to the parts of the sign. In the straight signs, five degrees of the signs require almost a fifteenth part of an hour; in the oblique, almost a twentieth. But just as there are thirty degrees in the signs, and sixty minutes in any degree, and sixty seconds in any minute, so in the part of the hour in both cases—either the fifteenth or the twentieth—it is necessary to distribute it into sixty parts, and again into sixty similarly, and to accommodate each one to each other exactly. 

Since, therefore, astrologers assert (as **Origen** <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 185 – c. 253 AD) who often argued against deterministic astrology.</note> also says) that not only degrees, but also minutes and minutes of minutes <note>i.e., seconds of arc.</note> must necessarily be known—in which the planets are, and which are ascending or descending (for in the smallest thing is the greatest difference, which **Nigidius** <note>Publius Nigidius Figulus (98–45 BC), a Roman scholar and occultist. Legend says he proved how much the sky moves in an instant by throwing a glob of ink at a spinning potter’s wheel.</note> also demonstrated with the turning wheel of a potter)—who, I ask, can grasp such minutiae? Now truly, since for the most part one half-degree of a sign occupies an hour in ascending, in what way will you find the minute of the one ascending when you cannot observe such a minute division of time? For it is useful to know not only which hour, but also at which minutes of the hour the boy was poured out from the womb. In Pisces and Aries, because of their oblique ascension (for they seem to ascend in almost an hour and a third of an hour), they do not doubt that the smallest part of time brings a great change, so that even a twentieth part of one hour changes the degree of the ascendant. 

Since, therefore, they assert that even a tiny time—which falls between the birth of twins, or any two men born from different parents but at almost the same part of time—brings about the diversity which is perceived in their effects, **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), who famously used the "argument of the twins" to debunk astrology.</note> thus interrogates them: does that tiny interval bring about a tiny discrepancy between them, or a great one? If they say a tiny one, we object that the twins **Jacob and Esau**, brought forth without an interval of time, were dissimilar in great ways. If they say a great one—since those minutiae, namely seconds, thirds, fourths, can be grasped by no instrument—certainly they cannot judge. 

Indeed, I have experienced this myself among those close to me: twin sisters were born in our family without an interval; one was killed after seven weeks by a specific disease, the other after seven months was smothered by an ignorant nurse. Twins were also born similarly: fire killed one within a few days, water drowned the other after fourteen years. And in my neighborhood, twins were born without intermission,

He argues that if even the smallest moment changes a person's fate, the process of being born is too long and complex for any astrologer to capture accurately.</meta>

# ON BOOK III. ENNEAD II.

...who are already adults, and who are most diverse in their bodies, characters, and fortunes. I pass over how different is the lot of many animals born at once, especially when they are warmed together in eggs. Surely if the moment of time in which a human being receives their fate when being born is so small and fleeting that in that same point, under the very same circle of the heaven, several could scarcely be born at the same time to the same fitness; and if for that reason even twins do not have the same lot in life, because they were not born at the same moment, let them answer, I pray, so that I may question them with <term>Favorinus</term> <note>Favorinus of Arelate was a Roman-era philosopher whose skeptical arguments against astrology were preserved by Aulus Gellius.</note>: how can they catch that flight of passing time, which can scarcely be grasped by the mind's thought, when they say that even the smallest moments in the headlong spinning of the heaven bring about massive changes? Indeed, the delay of birth in one individual is greater than the delay between twins following one another in delivery. If, therefore, the celestial constitution and fate are transformed in the blink of an eye, it will now be necessary for them to say there are as many fates as there are limbs being born. Here too, it is very opportunely asked: Whether the sequence of fate unfolds at the first moment the child begins to emerge from the womb? Or rather when he is halfway out? Or perhaps when he is entirely out? For <margin>and on this they disagree</margin> <note>referring to the internal debates among astrologers about what constitutes the "exact" moment of birth.</note>.

But it seems the matter must be traced deeper, from the very beginning of the fetus. Even if some profess that they will find the configuration of the heaven at that time [conception] from the configuration of the birth, yet since they have the latter as uncertain, surely the former is much more uncertain. But let us grant them that they have this discovered; by what rules, finally, can they hunt for the one from the other? Some will perhaps say that the degree of the Moon rising at birth was the degree of the <term>Ascendant</term> <note>The point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note> at conception, and conversely, the degree of the Ascendant at birth was the degree of the Moon when the fetus was conceived in the womb; but even this cannot be firmly established—indeed, it is entirely arbitrary. Now others seek it from other sources, and as <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who integrated theurgy and astrology into his system.</note> reports, some are accustomed to use five laws for it, others fewer, and others more. Moreover, <term>Porphyry</term> <note>A student of Plotinus who also wrote on astrology and the "Master of the Geniture."</note> says that even with the astronomers conceding it, the matter is utterly uncertain.

But suppose someone does happen to find the beginnings of the fetus: we ask, does that first tempering of the heaven, when the human work is first begun, alone contribute to the work? Or do the remaining celestial harmonies that follow likewise vary at every moment, just as the first one was momentary? If the first is said to be the only one that acts, it is a marvel that a momentary configuration of the heaven completes a long-lasting work—and continues to act when it is no longer there. But they will claim that a certain force is left in the fetus from the first configuration, surviving and acting as it were. Let it be so, even though it is quite a marvel; but surely the configurations that follow immediately after, do they act not at all upon the fetus? On the contrary, these also act and brand it with their own marks. And although they are received according to the nature of the first, they still flow in according to their own nature, and gradually transform the previous ones, confound the signs, and deceive the judgments. 

Indeed, the greatest transformation of what went before, and the beginning of what follows, happens when the soul first flows into the small body of the fetus, which has already been prepared for the soul. That moment is uncertain even to the <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Neoplatonic sense, these are intermediary spirits or guiding intelligences, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note>. Iamblichus, according to the mind of Plato, proves that the lot and the daemon that guides life are assigned to the soul even before conception by the universal disposition of the whole world; just as the soul is related to the universe when it first desires a body, and vice-versa. Therefore, one would first need to know and weigh that time, which he thinks can only be grasped by divine inspiration. 

Besides these things, if any times are to be observed in judging the effects of men, five seem to be observed. 
**First**, the time of sowing, when the seed is cast into the matrix: the condition of this casting follows the voluntary motion of the parents, and the present nature of both of them, and the accompanying imagination, rather than the present constitution of the heaven. For the principle of the motion was the will of both; and in such a motion, chance happens mostly according to their nature and imagination, while the heaven favors it a little in the meantime. How much imagination can do is apparent from the cravings of pregnant women, and in animals that are born white from parents imagining white things, as is said of peacocks. 
**Second**, the time when, the aforementioned motion having ceased, the seed is collected and firm in the matrix; now it begins to be transformed from what it was, and perhaps first to be bound together. The beginning and source of such bonding and action follow the condition of the seed and the parents more than the heaven, because what is being produced is quite material, and it was, and is becoming, a part of the parents. A part, moreover, follows its own nearby whole. From this we see that from such a species and individual, such a species and individual and such a seed grow together; yet the heaven contributes in the meantime. 
**Third**: the time when the fetus is first formed into life. And they say this happens in the second month, in which Jupiter especially acts. But it is uncertain whether life is present as soon as it has filled the middle of its month, or some days after, when it has reached the forty-ninth day from conception, because nature frequently delights in the number seven in our affairs. And altogether, whether it happens otherwise is obscure. For perhaps it happens in the ninth month, which they attribute to Jupiter again; just as not every infant is brought forth into the light in the same way, so not everyone receives life in the second month. For they say it has been found that females do not receive it in the same way as males; thus it is probable that males among themselves, and females among themselves, do not receive it at the same intervals. What of the fact that others will perhaps say the rational soul descends not in the month of Jupiter (in which they say the vegetative power is given), nor in the month of Mars (in which the sensory power is given), but in the month of the Sun, or perhaps of Mercury? 

But setting aside these opinions, let us consider simply the principle of one’s own life. The auspicious beginning of life is mostly drawn from this day and hour: for from conception, the beginning was rather of essence and mass; thus far it has lived no other life than that of the parents, and existed as a part of another. But now it claims its own life for itself. It becomes a whole now, and soon uses its own motion. Therefore, such a life seems to see the exterior life—that is, the second life of the universe, or the divine mind. The lot of life, in the body I mean, follows especially the present constitution of the heaven. Then also the habit of the body—I mean the present habit, for it is already different than it was at conception. And rightly so: just as what was more material followed a more material cause, so what is most formal, and is becoming so, follows a cause that is primarily formal—that is, the celestial and especially the super-celestial. 
**Fourth**: the time when the adult infant in the womb strives with all its might to release itself from its maternal bonds. The chance of such a release follows, first indeed, the present strength of the child and the condition of the mother; then the habit of the heaven contributing more or less to it. 
**Fifth**: the time when the child, entirely released, breaks out from the womb. The condition of the one breaking out follows the preceding condition of the one striving. But what the future condition of this person will be, having now come forth from the womb—if indeed it is judged from the celestial constitution in which he came forth—it is weighed not as from a cause, but as from a sign. For they will say it is probable that the preceding prosperity of the heaven led to the subsequent prosperity of the heaven. 

But remember: perhaps it cannot be weighed at all, partly because the times are unknown, partly because the causes are unknown (how many and of what sort they are), and partly because it is not known what is most especially forged from the concurrence of all things. By "concurrence," I mean both of the present causes among themselves, and of the following causes with the preceding ones. For the array of stars was one thing at the time the man was first conceived, another later when the soul was infused, and another when he was brought forth into the light. But if one stellar position and another, and different pathways, promise different fortunes, who, in judging, will choose the lot from these especially? Who, in any tempering...

    *   Ficino's Commentary on Plotinus (specifically Ennead III, Book 2 or 3, though the text says "COMMENT. MARSIL. FICINI" and seems to be about astrology/divination).
    *   Language: Latin.
    *   Page: 124.
    *   Themes: Skepticism of astrology, divination vs. nature/demon/divine, the interconnectedness of the universe (microcosm/macrocosm), physiognomy, medical cycles.

    *   *Paragraph 1:* The difficulty of synthesis (astrological mixture). Even dissonant things create harmony when mixed. Not just stars, but material and location matter. Only God knows all (Isaiah, Plato, Ptolemy, Avicenna quotes). Humans lack the ability to grasp all causes. Experience is fallible. Signs are ambiguous. Medical examples (7-day cycles) vs. human aging (7-year cycles). Divination happens by chance, art, nature, demons, or God. Porphyry on Plotinus. Even astrologers like Ptolemy admit the soul's power is greater than art. <header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...of the heaven, he will perceive how much good or evil is brought, taken away, increased, or diminished from one side or the other by the comparison of diverse factors. Finally, he will see what new thing is forged from the mixture of all these, in which they do not doubt the greatest power resides. For even emotions which perhaps are thought to be dissonant on their own, when joined with consonant ones, produce a more pleasing harmony. When I speak of the mixture of all things, I think not only the celestial lights, but also the powers of lower things, their matter, and their location contribute very much to such a mixture. To certainly embrace all these things is a property of divinity alone. Hence <term>Isaiah</term> says: "Tell me the things that are to come, and I will say you are gods." <note>original: "Dicite mihi ventura atque ego vos deos dicam" — Isaiah 41:23. Ficino uses the Bible to show that true prophecy is a divine, not human, attribute.</note> Hence Plato attributes knowledge to God, but opinion to us. Hence <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the most famous astronomer/astrologer of antiquity, whom Ficino cites here as a cautious scientist rather than a certain prophet.</note> says that judgments about the future fall in the middle between the necessary and the contingent, and nothing should be affirmed as certain or uniquely discovered. Hence <term>Avicenna</term> <note>A famous Persian polymath and physician (980–1037 AD) whose works were foundational to European medicine and philosophy.</note> in his *Metaphysics* denies that astrologers should be believed, because they do not grasp all the celestial things, nor the natures of lower things necessary for judgment, nor do they rely on demonstration, but on a certain experience, or prophecy, and on the proofs of the orator and the poet. For the number and quality of causes lie hidden from the human intellect; experience fails, and signs deceive. Indeed, since many causes can often concur toward the same result, it is scarcely discerned from which cause primarily such an effect has proceeded. Furthermore, an experiment is not similar unless in entirely similar matters and times. 

The fallacy in judging also increases because there are frequently many and dissimilar signs of the same effect due to different causes; and conversely, a dissimilar outcome sometimes follows somewhat similar signs. Finally, the judgments of things vary at different times; thus the astrologer is forced to observe the revolution of each year to avoid error; thus the physician must look around at the symptoms of the sick person at every hour to predict the future outcome. Similarly, the <term>auspex</term> and <term>haruspex</term> <note>Ancient Roman diviners who read the future in the flight of birds (auspex) or the entrails of animals (haruspex).</note>—if there is any truth in this—must catch at omens everywhere and all things at every single moment. Similarly, the <term>physiognomist</term> <note>One who judges a person’s character or future by their facial features and body.</note>—if only there is any truth in this—must perceive the arguments for health and character in every seven-year cycle of human life. For just as in the sick, new indications are primarily captured every seventh day, so every seventh year certain new accidents and features, new shapes, new colors, and gestures either arise in us or are at least more clearly demonstrated. 

But remember that in whatever way or rite things are said about the future, or however they are said to be hidden from men, it often happens by chance—especially for those who say a great deal. Often also something similar to this occurs because many things in life are common to almost everyone, and happen daily in many ways from every side. Sometimes what seems to have been perceived by chance or art was instead brought forth by a natural, or <term>daimonic</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, "daemons" are not necessarily evil demons but intermediary spirits or guiding geniuses that bridge the gap between gods and humans.</note>, or divine instinct. I say by natural instinct when nature in us is so tempered that it is easily moved by universal nature. By daimonic, when the imagination is so affected that it is opportunely struck by a daemon. By divine, when the reason or intelligence is so disposed that it is then most suitably subjected to the divine mind, even if this is hidden from us. 

There are therefore five modes of predicting: by art, chance, nature, daemon, or God. From this it follows that many who are either lazy or less learned in the arts excel the learned in prescience. Hence <term>Porphyry</term> <note>The student and biographer of Plotinus.</note>, before he recounted that <term>Plotinus</term> possessed a wonderful prophetic power like that of Socrates, says that he had something wonderful by nature itself beyond other men, and had not only a daemon but even God as his teacher. Hence that astrological judgment from the stars is made not only through their inspection, but also from the nature of the one who judges. Hence Ptolemy: "Judgments of this are ambiguous to him who considers the natures of things and the stars; but those who know the future from a better part are closer to the truth because of the power of the soul ruling in them, even though they may not have much skill in this art." Conclude finally: if farmers and doctors are very often deceived in predicting more certain matters, other predictors are deceived most often of all. Detecting this fallacy, all the most learned astronomers have neglected judgments. I pass over others known to me. <term>Paolo of Florence</term> <note>Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli (1397–1482), a famous mathematician, astronomer, and friend of Ficino. He is famous for providing the map that supposedly influenced Columbus.</note>, a singular astronomer, used to laugh at this; though he fulfilled eighty-five years of life, having contemplated his own birth chart most diligently, he could find nothing in it contributing to such a long age.

### How great is the communion of things in the universe: and how there are
### certain indications of hidden things in objects.

Although the judgment of future and hidden things is most fallible—and if it is ever truthful, it proceeds more often from a natural, daimonic, or divine instinct than from art—nevertheless, certain indications of things are implanted in things. A mind more sagacious by nature, having been warned by these, explains by its own or a higher faculty what the indications lightly suggest. Plotinus wants there to be signs placed in things by the very communion of the nature of all things; from which one thing signifies another event, and one thing mutually signifies another, similarly in the world and similarly in us. Surely if in perfectly mixed things, every element is in any part; much more so in an animal, which is composed of limbs just as a mixture is forged from elements, all things are in any limb. For a composite that is better by nature is undoubtedly also joined by a better reason. But no composite is perfectly connected by nature unless, just as the parts are in the whole, so conversely the whole is in the parts. However, the whole is not in the parts if it is in other parts only through one or a few parts; rather, it is in any part through absolutely all the parts: that is, if all are in any part. 

Added to this is that in the generative faculty of the soul, the whole human is present at once, such that he is whole in any limb. Similarly in the formative power of the seed, wherever any limb receives a somewhat similar form from it. For this reason, even if there is some distinction of place among the limbs, it is a distinction of reason. Therefore, since the animal visible to the eyes springs from both the soul and the seed under this condition of union, it follows that it receives a somewhat similar union from there. Therefore, even if the head seems to be in one place, and the hands and feet in another, yet perhaps by a certain common participation all things are in all: thus in the brain there is something of the heart and liver; thus in the heart some of the liver and head; thus let it be in the liver in turn: in the face, hands and feet; in the hands perhaps both face and feet; in the feet perhaps face and hands. And so in any limb, just as there is naturally something of the others, so besides its own indications, the indications of others also sometimes lie hidden. 

You, therefore, after you have especially contemplated the forehead and the eyes, look around at all signs everywhere. For what either lies hidden from you elsewhere, or has not come forth at all because of an impediment, you will perhaps find elsewhere. By a similar reason, the mundane animal [the universe] has sprouted from its own soul and its own seed, namely by that reason that the whole is in any of its members: thus in any sphere, in its own way, all spheres are present. All stars are in any star, living things in living things, all mixed things lie hidden in mixed things: so much so that an influx easily happens from all into all, and in almost every single thing, besides its own signs, certain indications for the rest lie hidden. I pass over the fact that in Saturn there is not only a certain nature of Mercury and the Moon, but also of the others. In Jupiter, not only the nature of Venus, but additionally that of the others. In the Sun, the nature of Mars and of all things. I pass over how similarly in us the lungs and stomach are referred to the head, and the rest in turn; to the heart, the spirit and bile, and the rest; to the liver, the blood and genital organs, and the others consequently. Gather finally, that just as in our body...

### ON BOOK III. ENNEAD II.

parts obey other parts for a specific duty, and perhaps for a logical purpose: thus the whole world, of which the human body is a part, contributes everywhere through its own signs to our own affairs. For just as in us all members follow one generative and formative power <note>original: "virtutem unam genitalem atque formatricem"</note>, which is also preserved within them: so all bodies, together with powers of this kind, accompany the body of the universe itself and its similar power in the same way, so that it is perhaps not surprising that signs adapted to us can be perceived from the universe. But while those signs provided from there seem more general, in us they approach a human specificity. For from there they pertain in some way to all things, while in us they are drawn toward the human being. 

Truly, just as things designated in the heavens do not always come to pass because a different cause or opposing matter sometimes stands in the way: so the signs implanted in us are cheated of their outcome <note>original: "fraudantur euentu"</note>, hindered obviously by other causes, either openly or secretly repugnant. For although the causes and indications in us are more specific to the human being, they are nevertheless often most uncertain—partly because they have become too manifold and confused by their own internal crowd and opposition; partly because our matter is not only subject to very many things, but is more often unstable, hindered, and deceptive; partly because the likenesses and imaginings of our own minds often confuse the rest; and finally because the power of the soul, both natural and acquired, often changes many things. 

But since we have come quite opportunely to the soul—that is, our own—we ought to note in the words of Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism; Ficino's life work was translating and commenting on his "Enneads."</note> that all things do not live by one single soul alone. Indeed, he says: If our individual members have their own powers and actions, even though they are not "wholes" but only parts, how much more do the rational animals in the world have them? For they are both greater, and are not only parts, but are moreover "wholes" themselves. From this it is clear that, besides a common fate, certain gifts belong to them either within the fatal dispensation or beyond fate. Finally, he confirms that there is no mere chaotic heap or wandering in the universe, but a perpetual series of things and motions arranged by a certain natural and divine art: because individual things are directed toward a certain end, and all contribute to the common end, and the consequent order of succession is always conducted and repeated in a similar way everywhere.

### IX
There are three most powerful principles of the world: the Good, the Intellect, and the Soul. The world, therefore, established under the Good and for the sake of the Good, is led by both intellectual and vital providence. Furthermore, all souls—which through intelligence and reason not only produce orbits within themselves, but also both imitate and follow the orbits of the mundane soul <note>The "Anima Mundi" or World Soul, which animates the entire universe in Neoplatonic thought.</note>—are themselves thought to have the nature of a principle: especially because they are received as "colleagues" <note>original: "college"</note> in the very management of the world. Although the duty which the soul of the world performs in a single revolution, the remaining rational souls fulfill through many revolutions as far as they are able. 

Therefore, the rational soul is not only led in the cosmic dance <term>chorea: a metaphor for the harmonious, choreographed movement of the stars and souls in the universe</term>, but it also leads. For it begins its own work as an agent when, from itself, it proceeds rightly both to contemplate the intelligible and to govern the sensible. It proceeds "rightly" to the sensible, I say, when it conducts itself toward it in such a way that it does not permit the intelligible to be abandoned for the sake of the sensible. This is to proceed correctly, for thus it tends properly toward that end where providence fully intends; but it prevaricates through crooked paths <note>original: "per obliqua"</note> whenever it prefers a sensible good too much over an intelligible one. 

Plotinus seems here, in the manner of Plato, to touch upon the power of "rectitude" in measurements through the names of the "straight" and the "oblique." A straight column supports great weights; one that is not straight breaks or falls. Rays of light that are straight in their perpendicularity are seen to be reflected; they do not slide away through different paths but return to themselves. And when they are submerged from the easy air into the difficulty of water, they are not broken, but proceed straight and are not twisted from the course they began. But oblique rays both depart from themselves in solid bodies where they are forced to be reflected, and are "broken" <note>A reference to refraction, which in Latin is often described as a "breaking" of the light ray.</note> when descending from air into liquids or vice versa. You can quite rightly transfer each of these points to the rectitude or obliquity of the soul. 

I return now to the beginning: namely, that the judgment of divine providence justly transforms a soul that conforms itself to something worse into a worse state. Providence had intended this step in the order—if not primarily, then consequently—so that whoever departs from the first step rightly proceeds into the second. And the soul, which had been free in a certain way until then, thereafter follows as if a slave and unhappy those things which it more ardently loved, until it releases itself from the heat of that love. 

Truly, divine judgment is never either absent or escaped. For by the law of that same all-powerful providence, by which its own nature is everywhere adapted to things, things which are agreeable and appropriate are also rendered to each soul. Moreover, the stars seem to serve this law of providence in three main ways:
1. First, they make this universe almost as beautiful as the divine mind previously devised beauty with the "ideal" stars <note>The "ideal" or archetypal stars existing in the Divine Intellect, of which the physical stars are copies.</note>.
2. Second, they contribute to natural effects, which we see are clearly fostered by the rays of the stars.
3. Third, they provide to demons and to men signs of future things and indications of hidden ones. 

If they are said to portend all things that arise in the sensible world, understand "all things" in a general sense, especially all things that proceed by sensible reason. Finally, "all things" for demons rather than for men: for God seems to have set forth the celestial volume for them to read. But if anything is transferred from there to us, either by instinct or by argument and portents, it is clear that this too was done by divine institution. And if we are not warned from there in vain, it is established that we can often avoid evils and also follow the good things that are shown beforehand through our own industry. 

Hence Abumazar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a highly influential Persian astrologer known in the West as Abumazar.</note>, against those who say the science of the future is useless, says: "He will perhaps be able to take precautions for himself by changing the place in which a future plague is to be; he will even sometimes be able to repel the whole thing from himself, and by foreseeing a future infirmity, or an invasion of enemies and similar things, avoid them." Hence also Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most famous astronomer/astrologer of antiquity.</note> says: "The wise man will rule the stars," insofar as being warned he can decline an imminent danger. Likewise, the wise man will aid the work of the stars, just as a prudent farmer aids the natural power of the earth, insofar as he himself accomplishes by his own industry the good things sometimes indicated from heaven. For as a prudent farmer is to the earth and the sky, so is the physician and the prudent man to both. Just as the farmer perfects what nature began, and in turn heaven completes what the farmer starts. Likewise, the farmer changes many things regardless of the nature of the sky and the sun: he defends certain things by watering them more often out of greed, by protecting them from the cold, or by propping them up against a fall. In the same way, the physician and the wise man can conduct themselves specifically toward the heavens and our body. 

How much the diligence of medicine is worth in these matters, I have learned by experience, both often elsewhere and in the case of a boy: who was born in the eighth month of conception, at night, under Saturn while it was stationary in its station...

He defends the utility of astrology and medicine, arguing that a wise person can use celestial signs to mitigate fate, much like a farmer works with the seasons.</summary>

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

*...of the heaven will accomplish, how much good or evil is brought here or there from a comparison of diverse things, how much is taken away, increased, or diminished? Finally, what new thing is forged from the mixture of all things, in which they do not doubt the greatest power exists? For even aspects which perhaps are thought to be dissonant by themselves, when joined with consonant ones, create a more pleasing harmony. But when I speak of the mixture of all things, I consider not only the celestial lights, but also the forces, matter, and location of inferior things to contribute very much to such a mixture. To certainly encompass all these things is surely the property of divinity alone. Hence Isaiah says: "Tell me the things to come and I will call you gods." <note>original: "Dicite mihi ventura atque ego vos deos dicam" — Isaiah 41:23.</note> Hence Plato attributes knowledge to God, but opinion to us. Hence Ptolemy says that judgments about the future fall in the middle between the necessary and the contingent, and nothing ought to be affirmed as certain or as a personally discovered fact. Hence Avicenna, in his Metaphysics, denies that astrologers should be believed, because they do not grasp all the celestial things, nor the natures of inferior things necessary for judgment; nor do they rely on demonstration, but on a certain experience, or on prophecy and rhetorical or poetic proofs. For the human genius is hidden from both the number and quality of causes, experience is deceptive, and signs fail. Indeed, since many causes can often concur toward the same result, it is scarcely discerned from which cause such-and-all effects chiefly arise. Furthermore, an experiment is not similar unless in entirely similar materials and times.*

*Moreover, the fallacy in judging increases because there are often many and dissimilar signs of the same effect due to different causes; and conversely, sometimes dissimilar outcomes result from somewhat similar signs. Furthermore, the indications of things vary in different times; thus the astrologer is compelled to observe the revolution of every single year; thus the physician must look around at the accidents of the sick person at every hour to predict the future outcome. Similarly, the augur and the soothsayer—if there is any truth in this—must hunt for portents everywhere and all things at every single moment. Similarly the physiognomist <note>One who judges character or future health from physical features.</note>—if only there is any truth in this—is able to perceive the proofs of health and character in every seven-year cycle <term>septennariis</term> <note>Ficino refers to the "Ages of Man," believed to change every seven years.</note> of human age. For just as in the sick, new indications are chiefly caught every seventh day, so every seventh year certain new accidents and features, new figures, new colors, and gestures either arise in us, or at least are more clearly demonstrated. But remember that in whatever way or rite concerning the future, or in whatever way things hidden from men are brought forth, it often happens by chance—especially among those who speak many things. It also often happens (and this is similar) because there are many things in life common to almost everyone, and many things happening daily in many ways from every side. Sometimes what seems to be perfected by chance or art was actually brought forth by the instinct of Socrates's spirit—whether daemonic <note>In the Platonic tradition, a "daemon" is an intermediary spirit or guiding "genius," not an evil demon.</note> or divine. By natural instinct, I mean, when nature in us is so tempered that it is easily moved by universal nature. By daemonic, when the imagination is so affected that it is opportunely struck by a daemon. By divine, when reason or intelligence is so disposed that it is then most suitably subjected to the divine mind, even if this is hidden from us.*

*There are, therefore, five modes of predicting: by art, chance, nature, a daemon, or God. From this it happens that many who are either lazy or less learned in the arts excel those more learned in foreknowledge. Hence Porphyry, before he related that Plotinus wonderfully possessed a power of prophecy like that of Socrates, says that he had something wonderful in his nature itself beyond other men, and had not only a daemon but also God as his teacher. Hence that astrological judgment from the stars is made not only through the inspection of them, but also from the nature of the one who judges. Hence Ptolemy says: "Judgments of this kind are ambiguous to him who considers the natures of things luckily; but those who know the future from a better part are closer to the truth because of the power of the soul dominating in them, even if they do not have much skill in this art." Conclude finally: if farmers and doctors are very often deceived in predicting more certain matters, the other predictors are most often deceived. Discerning this fallacy, all the most learned astronomers neglected judgments; I pass over the others known to me. Paulus Florentinus <note>Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli (1397–1482), a famous Florentine mathematician and astronomer.</note>, a singular astronomer, used to laugh at these things; he completed eighty-five years of life, yet having contemplated his own birth chart <term>genesim</term> most diligently, he could find nothing that contributed to such a long age.*

### How Great is the Communion of Things in the Universe: and How Certain Signs of Hidden Things Exist within Things.

*However, although the judgment of future and hidden things is most fallible—and if it is ever truthful, it proceeds more often from a natural, daemonic, or divine instinct than from art—nevertheless, there are certain signs of things within things, by which a more sagacious mind, having been naturally warned, explains by its own or a higher faculty what the signs lightly suggest. Plotinus wants there to be signs placed in things by things in turn from the communion of nature itself. From this communion, one thing signifies another event, and one thing mutually signifies another, similarly in the world and similarly in us. Truly, if in perfectly mixed things an element is in anything, much more so in an animal—which is composed of members almost as a mixture is forged from elements—are all things present in any member. For a composite that is better by nature is surely compacted by a better reason. But no composite is perfectly connected by nature unless, just as parts are in the whole, so in turn the whole is in the parts. But the whole is not in the parts if it is present in other parts only through one or some parts; rather, if through all parts entirely it is in any part: that is, if in any part all are present. Added to this is the fact that in the generative faculty of the soul, the whole man is present at once, such that he is whole in any member. Similarly, in the formative power of the seed, wherever any member is driven, the rest follow at the same time; thus far there is no distinction of place between members, but only of reason. Therefore, since the animal visible to the eyes sprouts from both the soul and the seed under this condition of union, it follows that it receives a similar union in some way. For this reason, even if the head seems to be in one place and the hands and feet in another, yet by a certain common participation perhaps all things are in all: thus in the brain there is something of the heart and liver; thus in the heart some of the liver and head; thus in the liver it is so in turn. In the face, there are hands and feet; in the hands perhaps both face and feet; in the feet perhaps both face and hands. Therefore, in any member, just as something of the others is naturally present, so besides its own signs, the indications of others sometimes lie hidden. You, therefore, after you have contemplated the forehead first and the eyes especially, look around at all signs everywhere. For what is hidden from you somewhere, or has come forth least because of some impediment, perhaps you will find elsewhere. For the same reason, the worldly animal <note>The Macrocosm or the Universe conceived as a living being.</note> once sprouted from its soul and its seed, clearly by that reason so that the whole is in any of its members. Thus, in any sphere, in its own way, all spheres are present. All stars are in any star; living beings in living beings; all mixed things lie hidden in mixed things. This is so that an influx from all things into all things easily occurs, and almost in individual things, besides their own signs, certain indications of the rest lie hidden. I pass over that in Saturn there is not only a certain nature of Mercury and the Moon, but also of the rest. In Jupiter, not only the nature of Venus, but above that of others. In the Sun, that of Mars and of all. I pass over that similarly in us, the lungs and stomach and the rest in succession are referred to the head; the spirit and bile and the rest to the heart; the blood and reproductive members and the rest consequently to the liver. Gather finally, that just as in our body...*

# ON BOOK III. ENNEAD II.

parts comply with other parts for a specific duty and perhaps for a logical proof: thus the whole world, of which the human body is a part, leads to our advantage through its signs scattered everywhere. For just as in us all members follow a single generative and formative power <note>original: "virtutem genitalem atque formatricem" — the biological force that shapes the body</note> which is preserved within them, so all bodies, together with powers of this kind, similarly accompany the body of the universe itself and its like power, so that it is perhaps not surprising that signs adapted for us can be perceived from the universe. But while those signs are provided from that source, they seem more general; in us, however, they approach a specifically human quality. For what pertains in some way to all things there is drawn toward the individual human being here. But just as things designated in the heavens do not always come to pass—sometimes because a different cause stands in the way, or because of adverse matter—so the signs implanted in us are cheated of their outcome, hindered by other causes that resist them either openly or secretly. For although the causes and indications in us are more specific to a human being, they are nevertheless often extremely uncertain: partly because they have now turned out to be too manifold and confused by their own crowd and opposition; partly because our matter is not only subjected to many things, but is more often unstable, hindered, and deceptive; partly because the likenesses and imaginations of our own minds often confound the rest; and finally, because the power of the soul, both natural and acquired, often changes many things. But since we have arrived most opportunely at the soul—that is, our own soul—we ought to note in the words of Plotinus that all things do not live by one soul alone. Indeed, he says: "If our individual members have their own powers and actions, even though they are not whole things but parts, how much more must the animals that are rational in the world have them: since they are both greater, and are not only parts, but are also wholes besides." <note>Plotinus argues that individual souls have a degree of autonomy even within the World Soul.</note> From this it is clear that, beyond a common fate, certain gifts fall to them either within the fatal dispensation or even beyond fate. Finally, he confirms that in the universe there is not a chance heap or wandering, but a perpetual series of things and motions arranged by a certain natural and divine art: because individual things are directed toward a certain end, and all things contribute to a common one, and a consistent order of succession is always conducted and repeated in the same way everywhere.

->What the principles of things are, and how our soul also has the character of a principle:<-
->how it overcomes fate, yields to fate, and is punished by divine law. Also how it can<-
->perform wonders, and in some way free the body from fate.<-

---

IX. There are three most powerful principles of the world: the Good, the Intellect, and the Soul. <note>These are the three "Hypostases" or primary levels of reality in Neoplatonic philosophy.</note> Thus the world, established under the Good and directed toward the Good, is led toward it by intellectual and animate providence. Again, all souls—which through intelligence and reason both create orbits within themselves and both imitate and follow the orbits of the World Soul—are themselves also thought to have the character of a "principle" <note>A "principle" or *principium* here means a starting point or cause of action, implying free will.</note>: especially because they are received as colleagues into the very administration of the world, even though the other rational souls fulfill through many revolutions as much as they can the duty which the World Soul accomplishes in a single revolution. Therefore, the rational soul is not only led in the cosmic dance, but also leads. For it begins its own work as an agent whenever it proceeds rightly from itself both to contemplate the intelligible and to govern the sensible. I say it proceeds "rightly" to the sensible when it conducts itself toward it in such a way that it does not at all abandon the intelligible for its sake. This is to proceed "straightly," for thus it tends properly toward that end where providence directly intends; but it wanders through "oblique" <note>crooked or indirect</note> paths whenever it prefers a sensible good too much over an intelligible one. Here Plotinus, in the manner of Plato, seems to touch upon the power of "rectitude" <note>straightness/moral uprightness</note> in measurements through the names of the "straight" and the "oblique." Straight columns can sustain great weights; but that which is not straight is broken or falls. Rays that are straight to the perpendicular, when they are seen to be reflected, do not glide away through different paths but return to themselves; and when they are submerged from the easy air into the difficulty of water, they are not broken, but proceed straightly and are not twisted from the course they began. But oblique rays, in solids, depart from themselves where they are forced to be reflected, and in liquids, descending from the air or vice versa, they are broken. You can quite rightly transfer each of these points to the rectitude or obliquity of the soul. Now I return to what I began: namely, that in the meantime the judgment of divine providence transforms the soul that conforms itself to something worse into a worse condition. Providence had intended this step in the order—if not primarily, then as a consequence—so that whoever departs from the first step may rightfully proceed into the second. And the soul, which had been in some way free until then, thereafter follows as a slave and an unhappy thing those things which it loved too ardently, until it releases itself from the heat of that love. But divine judgment is never absent, nor is it ever escaped. For by the law of that same all-powerful providence by which their own things are fitted to each natural object everywhere, things that are suitable and their own are also rendered to each soul. Now, the stars seem to serve this law of providence in three main ways. First, they make this universe almost as beautiful as the Divine Mind previously thought out beauty through the "Ideal" stars <note>The archetypal forms of the stars in the Mind of God.</note>. Second, they contribute to natural effects, which we see clearly fostered by the rays of the stars. Third, they provide signs of future things and indications of hidden ones to daemons and "daemon-like" humans <note>original: "demoniciscis" — humans who possess a spirit or intellect similar to the intermediary daemons.</note>. If they are said to portend all things that arise in the sensible world, understand "all things" in a general sense, especially all things that proceed by sensible reason. Finally, all things rather for daemons than for humans; for God seems to have set forth the celestial volume for them to read. But if anything from there is transferred to us either through instinct or through logic and omens, it is clear that this also happened by divine institution. And if we are not warned from there in vain, it is certain that we can for the most part avoid evils and also follow the good things that are shown in advance by our own industry. Hence Abumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note>, against those who say the science of the future is useless, says: "He will perhaps be able to take precautions for himself by changing the place in which a future plague is to be; he will also sometimes be able to repel the whole thing from himself, and by foreseeing a future infirmity, or an invasion of enemies and the like, avoid it." Hence also Ptolemy says: "The wise man will rule the stars," <note>original: "Sapiens dominabitur astris" — a common medieval/Renaissance astrological maxim.</note> insofar as he, being warned, can decline an imminent danger. Likewise, he will help the work of the stars, just as a prudent farmer helps the natural power of the earth, insofar as he himself accomplishes by his own industry the good things sometimes indicated from heaven. For as a prudent farmer is to the earth and the sky, so a doctor and a prudent man are to both. Just as the farmer completes what nature began, and the heaven in turn completes what the farmer starts, so the farmer changes many things regardless of the nature of the sky and the Sun: and he defends certain things, sometimes by irrigating more often in drought, sometimes by protecting them from the cold, and sometimes by supporting them against falling. In the same way, the doctor and the prudent man can conduct themselves specifically toward the heaven and our body. Indeed, how much the diligence of medicine is worth in these matters I have discovered, both often elsewhere and in a boy: who was born in the eighth month of conception at night under Saturn, stationary in its station...
