# COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO

When the first degree of Sagittarius was rising, a child was born, indeed half-dead and, as it seemed, unlikely to live for three days; nevertheless, having been most diligently cared for by us, he gradually recovered his strength and has now completed many years. I pass over the many ways I nurtured the heart, brain, liver, and stomach of the newborn, applying things both to the child himself and to the nurse, both externally and internally, observing the more favorable days and hours of nature for their application. Plotinus indeed thinks that the rational soul not only frequently defends its own body (which is entrusted to it) from a common fate by such arts, but also, like the celestial souls, can sometimes exercise command over the lower matters of the world. This is because the soul is a sibling of the celestial souls, and thus acts in all things as if possessing a certain principle of governance. When it is able to do this, and how it is able, we discuss more extensively in our *Theology* <note>original: "Theologia" — referring to Ficino’s major work, "Platonic Theology on the Immortality of the Soul."</note>. I also pass over what it is capable of through astronomical and physical magic simultaneously: how it draws the marvelous powers of the stars through certain images, just as it gathers the rays of the Sun in a concave mirror. From there, it reflects them onto wood placed in the region, burning it, and sometimes blinding those looking on. So, in certain materials prepared by nature and then by art for the stars, it may conceive certain stellar rays and influences, which it can both keep for itself and hurl back at others, which Porphyry relates that Olympus of Alexandria <note>A 4th-century philosopher and rival of Plotinus.</note> was accustomed to do. There, Porphyry says that the soul of Plotinus possessed such great power that it was able to turn back the stings of the stars cast against him onto others. Indeed, the Jews confess through Kabbalistic wisdom and the inward spirit of the sacred letters that a fatal lot looming from the heavens can often be broken; Iamblichus says the same through the effective worship of the sublime gods; and Porphyry through magical wisdom, as the oracle of Apollo testifies. For he says in his book *On Oracles*: when someone asked why he had been judged by Apollo as unfit for some matter, or what should be done so that he might be accepted as fit, the oracle replied: he was hindered by the force of the Fates, which he was able to escape by magical arts. From this it is clearly evident that the magical art was granted to men by divine gift, so that they might in some way repel fate. These are the words of Porphyry. Furthermore, Plato indicates in the *Charmides* that health of mind and body can be cured through magic, and finally immortality can be obtained, especially through temperance acquired by the virtue of wisdom: for they prove by the testimony of the Magi that the health of the body proceeds from the health of the soul. But let us hear Zoroaster <note>The legendary founder of the Magi, whom Ficino regarded as a primary source of ancient wisdom.</note> singing divinely: "If you direct your mind, burning for the duties of piety, you will also preserve your fleeting body." Hence it has been handed down that the Pythagoreans were accustomed to expel diseases of mind and body with sacred songs. If the mind has such great power, what wonder is it that it is naturally free from fatal servitude, until it itself embraces the body with excessive love beyond the measure of providence? For thereafter the mind follows the body, and the body serves the law of fate, until the mind again turns its love away from the body toward the Intellect. Whence it first exempts itself from fate by fleeing; then it defends the body (since the mind is now strengthened by the Intellect) for the most part from fate, both by a certain hidden power related to the celestials and sometimes by art revealed divinely.

Conclusion of the chapter: the stars signify many things; they do not cause them. <note>original: "stellas plurima significare, non facere" — a cornerstone of Ficino's astrology: stars are signs in a cosmic language, not physical causes of human choice.</note> Therefore, they do not make riches or poverty, which happen to us from the concurrence and occasion of various causes among us; they do not make virtues, which in the senses arise from reason, and in reason are perfected from the Intellect; nor do they make vices, for which there is no properly efficient cause, but perhaps a deficient one—namely, insofar as the sensual life falls away from reason, and reason degenerates from the Intellect. To be sure, some incentive for vices can happen from the stars through a certain defect of matter in the living body; however, the love of the higher soul for the animal nature provides the occasion for conceiving a vice from this. Indeed, that soul otherwise lives free from fate insofar as, dedicated to the Intellect, it agrees through its own intellect with the primary law of the Divine Mind. Hence the prophecy <note>original: "prophetiæ" — referring to the Psalms.</note> says: "My soul is in my hands always, because I have not forgotten your law." <note>Psalm 119:109. Ficino interprets "having the soul in one's hands" as having self-mastery through divine law.</note>

->How the rational soul is not subject to fate, while the irrational is; how the life proper to our body depends on the life of the celestials and on our soul. Likewise, that there are twin souls in all celestial bodies. Likewise concerning demons, and from where evils happen.<-

**IX** Regarding the previous points where it is asserted that the stars do all things for us—although they may signify many things—someone might perhaps object to the words of Plato, especially in the *Republic* and the *Timaeus*. For he says in the *Republic*: souls proceed into bodies under the fatal revolutions of the goddess Necessity and her daughters, the Fates. He also says in the *Timaeus*: a corporeal life is infused into us—by which words he seems to subject us to the heavens. It is answered to the first point: the souls themselves chose this form of living by their own will before they came into the body under the fatal revolution. Therefore, they have not so much lost their pristine virtue and self-governing authority as they have interrupted it for a time; which, finally, they can receive back, partly because they themselves decreed it, partly because they were aided divinely, and partly because they were warned by laws. It is also answered to the second point: just as in the *Timaeus*, corporeal life is given to us by the stars, from which perturbations arise; so from the divine Intellect an intellectual soul is procreated as the ruler of this life. While this soul loves this life excessively in this world, it loses itself along with this life in fate; but by loving it as little as possible, it meanwhile recovers itself above fate in eternity. That the rational soul can enslave itself to fate and, in turn, emancipate itself, is taught by the sentence of Zoroaster, which commands: "Do not increase your fate." Where Plotinus says: "We"—that is, the human being himself—are the rational soul itself, which by natural law should preside over the animal nature; he adds: "we must beware lest we perhaps become this animal." For he thinks that through the perfected affections of the imagination, a consensus can occur, making one living thing out of the soul and the animal nature together: namely, when each imagines the same thing in a similar way, and is affected toward the same thing similarly, almost as one thing is made from fire and wood by the communion of light and heat. He adds again that in the animal—that is, the animated body—the nature of the body prevails. For there the body is truly body, because it is formal to the highest degree and brought to the peak of corporeal form; but its own life is not true soul, not true life, because it is very corporeal, holding almost the last place in the order of life. Therefore, just as this life acts upon the body naturally by forming it, or rather is acted upon in the body while the body is formed by it from on high, so also the body in some way acts upon the life while it conforms this life to itself. For which reason, just as four alterations especially seem to be in the body through heat and cold, moisture and dryness; so in corporeal life four perturbations chiefly arise. Likewise, what is expansion and contraction in the body, is pleasure and pain in the life of the body. Truly, just as the rational soul, joined with the animal through imagination and affection, is touched by its passions and struck by the fatal lot, so when it has finally subjugated this animal to itself by the laws of reason, it first resolves itself from perturbations and fate, while it recognizes itself as one thing and the animal as another, and therefore that fate pertains to the other. Then, it defends this animal (entrusted to it naturally) from the most atrocious wounds of fate or fortune. Where Plotinus...

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Marsilio Ficino on Plotinus's Enneads, Book III, focusing on the dual nature of the human soul and its relationship to celestial influences and fate. ### ON BOOK III. ENNEAD II.

He [Plotinus] says that of the **twin souls** of humans, the higher one is indeed sent from the divine intellect, but the lower one is infused by the gods who are carried along; understand here that these "gods" are the souls of the spheres and the stars, which act in harmony with the **Soul of the World**. For all things are said to be moved, whether they are carried by a certain local motion or a formal one. But in what way does life overflow into the body from the conspiracy of all these things? Is it like a single harmony echoing under a hollow vault from many voices singing together? Or again, like a certain common splendor in a hall produced by many lamps? Not quite in that way. For here, both the harmony and the splendor are more of a union through a certain gathering than a single form. But the soul, whatever kind it may be, is simply a substance, and the form of a single living being is one—even if, when compared to a more excellent soul, it is judged as if it were an accidental quality. In what way, then, does this happen? Perhaps just as a single voice with a distinct meaning comes forth from one imagination through the many vocal instruments within us; or again, as a single light from one sun, penetrating through glass stained with various colors, does not thereafter split into many lights, but remains one, although shaped by the power of the various colors. In almost the same way, a single form of life, manifold in its power, results in the body; specifically, one life from the life of the world, but also manifold in power from the communion of many souls besides this one, all breathing life together.

The **character** <note>original: "Character" — here meaning a distinctive stamp or spiritual imprint</note> most proper to the animal is imprinted mostly in the spirit by the soul of the parent. By the property of this character, either the breath of all things is reduced to a familiar soul, or at least the body becomes "animatable" by such a specific soul above all others. Someone might guess that life can be infused into us by the soul and the common souls without the benefit of our own individual soul, observing those living creatures that are born spontaneously, or those from eggs without the warmth of their own parent. On the contrary, however, reason seems to dictate that our soul—that is, the superior one—must conspire together with the superior powers to breathe life into the soul. This is both because the human being is the most perfect creature and obeys reason, and because, just as common natures are usually defined by specific natures to achieve specific effects in nature, so too for a specific life (provided the form is perfect and distinct according to its strengths), the work of a superior soul seems to be necessary in a specific capacity, beyond the common souls.

Therefore, someone might perhaps be able to say that in some cases, a specific influence arrives in addition to the common influx, but in other cases, not at all. And in the former case, the human animal is more perfect and more obedient to reason, but in the latter, it is less so—specifically where the body of the rational soul finds itself already alive from another source. I pass over the fact that if perhaps the rational soul does not approach a body living in this way, a "brute animal" is born in the shape of a human, and that soul will be a monster, just as sometimes monsters are born in the body. Therefore, when Plotinus says in one place that the second life flows from the first and from our own, and in another place from elsewhere, you can understand it as we have said.

Remember indeed that what Plotinus discusses concerning the **twin souls** is confirmed by Iamblichus according to the mind of Hermes <note>original: "Mercurij" — referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage</note>, where he adds that the superior soul in us, since it is made by the highest Intelligible, possesses a world-making power within the mundane force, as well as a power by which it may transcend the world, release itself from fate, and help its own people, especially with the aid of the gods. And this "release," insofar as it seems to transcend the fatal order, is to that extent contained within the order of **Providence**.

Accordingly, where Plotinus distinguishes one soul from the other, he says: Whatever are the ministries of the inferior soul are corporeal; for all the passions and motions of this soul are incited by the body, serve the body, and accompany the motion of the body, and vice versa. But the duty of the other soul, which stands outside, is to raise itself higher. In this place, take note that Plotinus interprets that Aristotelian saying in its legitimate sense: **The intellect comes from without.** <note>original: "Intellectus venit forinfecus" — a famous and debated phrase from Aristotle's "On the Generation of Animals."</note> "Intellect," that is, the superior soul—not the single intellect of Averroes's interpretation <note>Averroes argued for a single, universal human intellect; Ficino, as a Christian Platonist, insists on individual immortal souls.</note>, but each individual intellectual soul. "From without" likewise means not from the seminal spirit or heat, nor from this life in the depths of the world, but from the divine mind, which, as if exterior—that is, not joined like a physical form—rules over all things. From this it follows that the intellectual soul, both by thought and also by will, can seek those things that are above the body, nature, and corporeal life according to its own judgment, and can overcome the body, nature, and fate whenever it has fully resolved to do so. For insofar as it is segregated from temporal things, to that extent it is joined to eternal things, and in a certain way rules over these temporal things along with them.

Both occur through thought, but especially through the **will**. For just as we are joined to temporal things, so we are joined to eternal things not so much by considering them as by loving them; and rightly so, since consideration stays rather within, but love turns the lover into the beloved. In the same way, any matter reaches the nature of fire by undergoing its heat rather than its light. It is from this, therefore, that the soul becomes most capable of eternal things and a mistress over temporal things alongside them: because it both loves them ardently and, by loving, imitates them in life as much as it can; and having imitated them, it attains them by living; and having attained them, it in turn imitates them by the authority of its work. From this, finally, amazing works sometimes proceed in the body beyond the accustomed tenor of fate. In this state, the soul is counted within fate as an agent; it does not so much break the fatal chain as claim it for itself. For you may find this also designated in the laws of providence, from which fate depends. Therefore, if by the benefit of an artificial intelligence through art—namely, through images and medicine—the mind is sometimes received as a colleague in the fatal cohort, much more can it achieve this through the fire of a more divine intelligence, or most importantly, of the **will**.

For the act of the will is more effective than knowledge, and freer; it is the principle, the middle, and the end of action. Thus, by mere thought nothing happens; but by mere affection, even if hidden and natural, many things occur. There is, however, a natural appetite joined to the will which can seem to emulate it, constant and prior to imagination, and more natural, and closer to substance. We have touched upon the efficacy of art within fate in the sections above, but we shall demonstrate it elsewhere.

But to return now to the previous points: the souls live in providence above fate in that respect where the animal is formed by reason, reason by the mind, and the mind finally by God. But where, in turn, the formation occurs, it lives under the judgment of providence within fate; not as an agent, but it is counted among the number of fatal things as a passive subject. If, therefore, anything is portended to this subject from the stars, it can simply happen as it is portended, with the mind not resisting these things at all. And if evil things happen, they are not sent as evils from on high, but they result as evils in the lowest realm. Plotinus says, however, that the inferior soul in us is in a certain way a part of the universe, since it both depends on the universal soul and follows its common instinct—almost as our body is in a certain way a member of the universal body. Thus our "animal" is connected to the mundane animal, and is completed in you.

Nevertheless, the superior soul in us concurs mostly with the mundane soul and the other mundane powers to produce the inferior life in us. For just as the maternal seed cannot produce the body of the one to be born, so neither can the eternal soul likewise procreate the [lower] soul. Nor again is the soul of the one to be born made by the soul of the father who is then far absent, nor does it proceed from the power of the seed itself, which is both inferior and accidental. It remains, therefore, that it is procreated by the Soul of the World with the celestial souls concurring—and with the superior soul of the human birth also concurring for the most part, if indeed it is already present in the vivifying of the fetus. But where Plotinus says that the rational soul does not contribute to the "being" of the animal itself, or does so very little, he is denying it the status of a "form" [in the physical sense], not its status as an efficient cause. For although it is the cause of life for the animal, it is not the proper form of the body—even if it is sometimes called the form of the animal contributing to the animal's well-being. Furthermore, those things that are in us from the twin souls and the body...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, Book III. It expands on the previous page's discussion of how the Soul of the World and individual souls (like those of stars) interact. Ficino is specifically addressing the mechanism by which higher, intellectual realities govern the physical world through "lower" versions of themselves, and how this relates to the concepts of fate and celestial influence.</meta>

COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

there is a harmonious agreement, <note>original: "conspiratio," meaning a "breathing together" or cosmic sympathy</note> he judges such a thing to be in the world itself, in the spheres, and in the stars. For everywhere, an intellectual soul rules a body through a life flowing from the soul that is closer to the body. For insofar as it is intellectual, separate, and reaching toward higher things, it is too distant from the body; but it approaches the body through something within itself, or something that has already degenerated from the intellect out of itself. I say "out of itself" because if elemental nature—such as fire—approaches a subject, it not only moves its own substance toward it but also inserts some quality similar to itself. Much more does the soul, as a more powerful nature, infuse a certain vital faculty into the body by the presence of its vital substance.

Let there be, therefore, twin souls throughout the world, the spheres, and the stars. Let the first ones everywhere hold the place of good angels and gods; but let the following ones be judged to take the place of the angels who fell into bodies, and of the <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, daemons are intermediary spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense of being purely evil.</note>. All such "first" angels follow the angel of the mundane soul <note>The "Soul of the World"</note> which always clings to God. Similarly, all such "first" daemons follow the daemon of the mundane soul which departs further from God and weighs down entirely upon the body everywhere. Again, angels turn mostly toward incorporeal things, while daemons turn toward corporeal things and allure souls. Therefore, angels release souls from fate, but daemons bind them to fate. In the daemons is placed the immediate empire of this corporeal world. From this, it follows that if a comparison is made from here to the angels, this world may rightly be said to be "placed in the power of the evil one." <note>A reference to 1 John 5:19, showing Ficino's synthesis of Platonic and Christian thought.</note> From this also the error of the **Manichaeans** <note>A dualistic religious movement that viewed the physical world as inherently evil.</note> easily arose.

Furthermore, just as he asserts that our intellect always dwells upon divine things, even though the reason is meanwhile occupied with human affairs, so he affirms that the whole reason and the higher soul in the celestial regions enjoy the perpetual contemplation of divine things, while the inferior souls of the celestial beings rule the bodies and imagine the bodies. In these, therefore, he thinks there are "demonic" affects. The divine affects are in the first ones; human affects are in ours, and often bestial ones; but truly, of what sort are those demonic ones there? Imagine a wise man constantly occupied with divine contemplations, but in him meanwhile, in his vegetative nature, an affect for the nourishment of the body flourishes; a "generalized itch" of hunger sometimes creeps into the stomach, or the natural libido for procreating titillates him. But the reason of the wise mind, dedicated meanwhile to separate things, by no means notices such affects; the imagination also feels them barely or stupidly—almost as it usually happens to someone in whom these things are incited during sleep without dreams. Such, then, are the demonic affects toward these things in heaven.

Therefore, nothing of evil or vileness proceeds from the prior souls; but from the following souls, not indeed evils in reality, but certain vile and "less good" things follow. Insofar as from those souls, changes sometimes occur less orderly in bodies, and incitements frequently arise in souls bonded by nature to the body. Through these, even if the souls do not necessarily become wicked, they nonetheless indulge more freely in the incitements of the body, or at least they cherish the body more propensively and care for it more accurately every day. Moreover, he says that the superior souls of the stars are not "parts" of this universe. For since they are turned entirely toward the intellectual world, they seem more likely to be called parts of *that* world. But he calls the inferior souls of the stars parts of this universe, because they are bonded to the bodies of the world which, since they are of the same matter among themselves and under the same common form of the whole, are thought to be parts of the universe. In this common matter and form of the world, all such souls harmonize together into one body, both among themselves and with the Soul of the World everywhere; and they communicate with each other through a common sense, however occult, and a certain latent compassion.

While indeed whatever works are done by them exist as individual parts of the world, or pertain to the parts and the whole. Truly, nothing proceeds from them anywhere that is separate from the natural condition of this world; they do whatever they do almost by a nature that is animated, just as elemental nature moves the elements, and plants and animals move by a vegetative nature, with absolutely no **choice** <note>original: "electio," meaning conscious or deliberative choice.</note>. For since choice is something other than life, and is posterior to life, if the life of inferior things performs its tasks by itself without the duty of choice, much more does the life of superior things complete its own tasks by itself. If there is any intellectual and rational choice there, it is not this "ministry" <note>low-level service</note> that is chosen, but a superior duty. And yet, even before that choice, perhaps something proceeds from within from the prior life without choice. Indeed, it is established entirely without any necessity, even if some imagination accompanies the work; and from the first soul there proceeds the second, and from the second likewise a singular power in the body, and from the body a light, and in the light a power generating and governing lower things.

Thus, the things that are generated and happen daily in this world are distant from the intelligible world by many degrees, so that it should not seem a wonder that these affairs of ours do not turn out most orderly or most happy. For such things would follow if they were made directly by the divine intellect, or at least by the intellectual souls; but now they are driven by bodies living by an irrational soul, and through powers emanating from those bodies. If, therefore, anything occurs in the world that is troublesome, or laborious, or which you do not approve of, remember that all of it happens to us from the **female** <note>In the philosophical tradition Ficino follows, the "female" principle is associated with matter, receptivity, and the lower, wandering part of the soul, whereas the "male" is associated with form, intellect, and stability.</note>—that is, from the soul bonded to the body, from the matter of the body, and again from the contrariety of elemental qualities.

---

->### *What things are done by the stars, what are not, and how signification occurs. By what instinct the soul enters the body, by what fate, and how it loves the body before fate.*<-

**X** The tenth chapter of the book, with the world, spheres, and stars כך composed, follows the lot of signifying and acting, teaching that those things which are naturally generated are made by the stars and their motions, insofar as in them only corporeal life and the body are considered. Nor are these things properly made by the primary souls of the stars, which tend entirely toward separate things; nor are all things here made by the stars. For those things which surpass corporeal life cannot be produced by the body of the stars or by corporeal life. Again, those things which are done by us through counsel and art, or by fortuitous occasion, are not performed from there, from whence whatever is done is done through corporeal qualities and is led by the course of nature. Finally, nothing truly evil is committed through the instruments of the divine beings.

Therefore, let the stars do not all things, but only those which are the passions and motions of the mundane body, and those which are necessarily generated from these. Moreover, let them do these things by a common condition: for a specific condition seems to pertain to the specific causes of things. Let them also signify many things, but not equally all things. For it is probable that, if most things surpass or escape the efficiency of the stars, some things even surpass their significance. It is probable, again, that those things which are portended through common causes are portended only by a common condition.

Plotinus thinks that the soul approaches this body not because it is forced by a certain fixed constitution of the stars; for before any new configuration of the sky, it is in the ancient nature of the soul itself to animate a body, and to transcend corporeal and temporal fate. For every soul which, by the duty of its own natural reason, can resolve the whole corporeal nature into an incorporeal essence, and all of time into eternity as if into a beginning and an end, can undoubtedly exist both before and after any body and time, and any corporeal and temporal motion. Therefore, the position of the stars does not impel the soul 

<meta>catchword: toward the body</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains the dual nature of celestial souls, where higher souls remain in divine contemplation while lower souls govern the physical world through natural instinct rather than choice. He argues that the soul is not forced into the body by astrology but enters it by its own inherent nature, which predates and transcends fate.</summary>

ON BOOK III OF THE ENNEADS, TRACTATE II.

*...toward the body: but first, a certain natural care of the soul leads it toward this; then, a certain disposition acquired from preceding actions; and finally, a choice of reason which eventually agrees with that nature and disposition. Nature and disposition incline toward the body most strongly when they harmonize most opportunely with universal nature, yet they are not forced to harmonize by power. Just as those dancing in a sacred procession* <note>original: "tripudio," a rhythmic ritual dance</note> *harmonize with the song and the sound, yet they are not bound by necessity, but are in accord by their own will. To take up this or that form of life consists in the soul's own choice; but however it happens, the great passion or affection by which the soul is inclined toward the body is not provoked by the stars, but originates from the soul itself. At the time it enters a new body, it is thought to obtain this or that fortune from the present position of the stars, which falls upon the already chosen life in various ways as it can. Then, therefore, the present harmony of the stars effects something in us, contributing by its own ministry to the fulfillment of that kind of life which best fits the universe. For every daily configuration of the heaven is a part of the total harmony, and as a part, it complies with the nature of the universe, with which every individual nature—both bodily and animal—agrees. For this reason, individual things are carried out by the nature of the world itself together with the specific nature of each person; they are disposed in one way or another by the motion and figure of the heavenly bodies, and are foretold through a certain concord with nature. Yet, because a thing's own specific nature and the universal nature run together toward any effect, the specific character of an outcome is judged only very obscurely through signs.*

## The evils that happen here are not sent from heaven as evils.

<margin>Chapter XI</margin> *The eleventh chapter defends the dignity of heaven in all things which are said to be done or signified from there, based on the fact that the things that happen here are not the same there, nor do they arrive here in the same state as they eventually turn out. You might say our fire here is procreated in some way by celestial fire. Yet this earthly fire is so different from that one that nothing is more persistent than the former, and nothing more combustible than the latter, which hardly lasts a moment without foreign fuel. Nothing is more health-giving than that celestial fire; nothing more pestilential than this earthly fire, which devours all things most greedily. I omit the fact that the celestial is almost entirely light, while this is almost entirely smoke. Indeed, as far as the name "fire" is concerned, you might perhaps understand that whatever is given from celestial fire is something fiery in itself, but it turns out meager and degenerate among us. It can also make people lustful in another way: when the fire within us—a nature degenerating from the celestial—is combined with our own affection for loving, it falls far short of the celestial principle of benevolence and often rouses a less honorable lust, specifically regarding the nature of desiring. Next, he brings an example pertaining to the nature of anger; then to the reason placed in action; and finally to reason in its contemplative state, to show that what is granted from heaven is received differently in us. Thus Venus, while supplying or increasing necessary* <term>charity</term> <note>In this context, "charity" refers to divine or brotherly love (caritas), rather than just almsgiving.</note>, *is often accused of making people lustful, when in fact the charity offered through her turns into lust among those of us who are more lecherous. So too Mars is blamed for making the unsubdued more ferocious, or the tamed more timid; so too the Sun and Jupiter for making people ambitious and vain; so too Mercury for making them too crafty and seductive; so too Saturn for making them more reclusive and slow. Yet Mars wished to provide magnanimity; Jupiter and the Sun, a zeal for honesty; Mercury, industry; and Saturn, contemplation and gravity. But we have contaminated these things through a nature or custom that has been corrupted. Meanwhile, remember that the gifts of the mind are not given, increased, or nourished by the motions or bodies of the planets, but by their souls. Truly, evils are brought upon us neither by the souls nor the bodies of the celestial beings. For it is wicked to say that any stars harm us with their disposition like a "king-serpent"* <note>original: "reguli serpentis," referring to the basilisk, a mythical serpent whose gaze or presence was fatal</note>; *but it is pious to believe that all stars naturally nourish all things with the gaze of their rays, in the manner of an ostrich* <note>Renaissance natural history claimed ostriches hatched their eggs by simply staring at them, a metaphor for pure, non-physical influence</note>. *This is just as in a living animal, the life of the principal members nourishes and helps all the other members of the whole. Thus the light of the Sun by its own nature contributes to life and sense, although sometimes, due to the weakness of the subject or a defect of the "humors,"* <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health and temperament</note> *it may seem to be harmful. Just as the heat of the liver naturally helps the stomach, but it might perhaps weaken a stomach in which there is too little moisture or very little liquid nourishment. It seems, therefore, that Mars falsely brings about fury, or Saturn brings about stupor or fear. Indeed, take away an excess of bile or a surplus of black bile, and neither the aspect of Mars nor of Saturn will make one furious, or stupid and fearful. Again, that slander against Mars and Saturn—that they make people unfortunate—happens because Saturnine people, since they are contemplators, neglect external things or are slower to action, especially if they received that influx in colder matter; thus they do not attempt anything at the right time. Martian people, on the contrary, if they received the instinct of Mars in hotter matter, disturb everything with headlong motion. Perhaps even the Saturnine "daemons,"* <note>Intermediary spirits associated with the planet Saturn</note> *as contemplators, act more negligently regarding our affairs if we are commended to them; but Martian daemons urge the minds of their followers more importunely. Just as the lower nature differs from the superior nature, so does the condition of what is received differ. Thus the lower matter, when it is forsaken by heat, often receives the containing and halting power of Saturn in a condition that is too compact or congealed by frost. So too a somewhat hotter subject receives the moving power of Mars with a rush of inflammatory excitement. What more? Who does not understand that even the mild heat of heaven turns into a devouring heat among us, and the nourishing moisture from heaven becomes a suffocating and instantly diluting force here? To speak briefly: as the heaven visible to us relates to the intellectual heaven, so does our tangible region relate to the visible heaven. The forms of things in the intelligible heaven are free from matter, dimension, and motion; but in the visible heaven, these three necessarily occur. Yet there, matter is far from suffering; dimension is without division; and motion is similarly separate from the violation of order or the transmutation of substance. Finally, in our region, things naturally suffer these three. Therefore, what is a perfect good on all sides through complete participation in the first heaven, becomes less good in the second heaven, and in our region, it is already evil. Let no one, therefore, impute evil to the celestial beings. For just as when you speak or walk, you have the power from your soul and its motive faculty, but if you speak or walk ineptly, it is from a defect of the tongue or the foot; so whatever is sent down to you from the celestial soul and body proceeds in the right order, but is often compelled to "limp" within you. We conclude this whole matter, along with Plotinus and Iamblichus, in this way. The gifts attributed from heaven degenerate for five reasons. First, because what comes from a cause—especially a higher one—necessarily falls away from that cause by the very fact that it exits it. Second, because when it is received in more base matter, it is taken according to the capacity of the matter. Third, since the nature of the receiver is far different, it rightly renders what it receives not only worse, but excessively different in character. Fourth, while the subject receives various other things from elsewhere besides the celestial gift—things that are both repugnant to each other and different from heaven—it deservedly not only infects the celestial gift, but greatly confuses it and renders it frequently subject to passions. Fifth, because a new thing results from all these things confused together, very unlike its original source; the weakness of the lower nature, being subject to passion, often cannot sustain the celestial good, and lacking a fitting proportion to it, suffers poorly even under that which acts healthfully.*

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains that celestial influences are inherently good and virtuous, but they become "evil" or "unfortunate" when they are received by the corruptible matter and imbalanced humors of human beings. He provides five Neoplatonic reasons for why divine gifts degenerate as they descend into the physical world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, Book III, Tractate II. ### COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO
#### Things generated here possess their specific nature more from their own causes than from celestial ones.

# XII

The twelfth chapter shows that various influences coming from the heavens converge into a single point here among us, though they do so differently in different places; from this convergence, whatever is born under that influence carries away some specific trait. *Indeed, that which is born is aided in its birth by the general favor of the heavens. However, that a human or a horse is born is not obtained from a general influence—which favors all things equally—nor is it determined solely by this or that celestial flow. For under any given celestial sign, humans and horses are born alike. Therefore, a human comes forth because they are born from a human, and a horse because it comes from a horse. But as to whether a human is of a certain type—perhaps "sanguine" or "choleric" <note>These terms refer to the "four humors" or bodily fluids thought to determine temperament in Renaissance medicine.</note>, more or less beautiful, tall or short, and so on—they seem to derive this partly from the heavens, but certainly most of all from their parents. Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and astrologer whose "Tetrabiblos" was the standard textbook for Ficino’s era.</note> admits this, compelled by the evidence. Hence, he forbids judging a newborn solely by looking at the stars; instead, he commands us to diligently consider the nature of the parents, the nutrition, the location, and the local customs. I will set aside for now how much variety the imagination of the parents brings to their children. Certainly, the nature of both the species and the individual parent is far more powerful in determining the specific substance and natural quality of the offspring than any celestial influence. Manifest experience teaches this in all things, especially through the likeness by which the offspring reflects both the species and the specific person of the parent. Therefore, universal and celestial causes have the most authority over the most general conditions, but near and specific causes are undoubtedly more powerful regarding specific traits. This is especially true because what is brought down from higher causes is received according to the nature of the subject and the location, and according to the determination of the nearer causes, and is thus transformed into another form. Hence Ptolemy says, with Aristotle also testifying, that celestial effects can be changed due to the nature of the lower matter and thus do not happen inevitably. Therefore, a human exists as if from a cause from the human <term>seminal reason</term> <note>Original: "seminaria ratione." In Neoplatonism, these are formative, "seed-like" powers or blueprints within nature that direct the growth of specific things.</note>, which is in the soul and its own nature, and is ruled under the "Ideal Human Reason," which flourishes in the common nature and soul and is ultimately ruled by the Idea in the Divine Mind itself. While a human is being conceived by the power of the seed, an obstacle or an aid can be brought in—either from the heavens or from the nearby surrounding matter—by which the one to be born receives either a worse or a more perfect quality. Yet, they usually come forth similar to the parent, always in species and often in personal likeness. While an impediment can happen from the heavens or the matter, that which happens from the matter is far greater, for it often produces defective things. But the greatest impediment is that which happens through the imagination, for this is known to produce "monsters" <note>In this historical context, a "monster" (monstrum) referred to any biological birth that deviated from the natural norm, often blamed on the mother's intense thoughts or fears during pregnancy.</note>. If, therefore, the greater impediment comes from matter, place, and the causes standing near us, then surely the greatest help comes from here as well. Ultimately, no celestial influence, but rather the seminal reason, possesses the authority of generation. For even where animals seem to arise spontaneously under the Sun and moisture, they necessarily arise from the seminal power which the Life of the World possesses, as we declare more fully in our Theology.*

->All things are generated from the common life of the world and its seminal reasons, and simultaneously from the specific reasons of each thing. Likewise, beyond the common action of the World Soul, there are specific actions in most things; the influences of celestial motions seem to approach as if from the outside.<-

# XIII

Since he had already descended to the causes of things—both common and specific—he duly follows the principles of things in the thirteenth chapter of the book. Just as in every living thing, so in the world (as the greatest possible animal), the entire body is formed under the "form of the whole" by the seminal reason, which exists in the vegetative power of the soul and the natural and vital spirit. *The members are also formed by the specific forms of those members, and each is shaped both by mutual communion with one another and by their relationship to the form and goal of the whole. Since all things are formally contained within the form of the whole, while in the forms of individuals other things are not formally included (though they seem to be present by a certain participation), it is right that whatever is done, acts, or suffers in the world—acting as something familiar and specific to it—leads to its own good. However, not everything that comes from one part to another part arrives as equally "domestic." For what comes from one part of the world to another part distant in location or nature seems to offend it like a stranger; what comes otherwise seems to help. But all things, whatever they do to one another, always conspire everywhere toward the common spirit of the total life, in addition to existing in themselves and acting by their own faculty. Therefore, distinguish between agents in this way: Those things in this living body of the world which possess no life of their own (beyond a tiny trace of the common life) are not properly "agents," but rather instruments of the agents—namely, instruments of the world itself and the principles of the mundane parts. And this is not without reason: for natural action depends on motion, and the principle of motion is life. For just as life is the first, innermost, and perpetual motion of essence, so it is the principle of every motion and the origin of natural action. Therefore, those things lacking their own life also lack their own motion and action; where they seem to act, they are being "acted upon." Thus, heavy and light things, heating things, and the like are drawn to motions and actions by the Life of the World itself, no differently than iron is drawn by a magnet, or heat and moisture in an animal are led and drawn by the vital power. But those things born with some gift of their own life beyond the common life of the world seem to possess something of their own motion and action. But distinguish these living things: since the principle of motion is in all living things, it is either determined by another toward a certain condition of motion (indifferent to motions differing among themselves), or rather it is determined by itself. It is determined by another in the case of plants, namely by universal nature and a certain daily need, opportunity, occasion, and the concurrence of surrounding causes. It is determined by another again in the case of brute animals, namely by the encounter with things that are sensed, which drive the imagination this way or that, while also serving the necessity of nature. But the rational animal <note>A standard term for human beings, who share "animality" with beasts but "reason" with higher beings.</note> often defines the internal principle of its motion toward certain movements by its own notion and choice conceived through itself. The more its intelligence advances, the more it is counted in the order of "agents" and separated from "patients" <note>In philosophy, an "agent" is one who acts; a "patient" is one who is acted upon or receives an action.</note>. Both types of animals—those with reason and those without—lead to the beauty of the world as parts of the world. Again, distinguish animals thus: Celestial and ethereal animals are said to act simply rather than to suffer. Brute animals have the least action and the most passion. But aerial <term>daemons</term> <note>In Ficino’s Neoplatonism, "daemons" are not evil spirits but intermediate beings inhabiting the air, possessing more intelligence than humans but less than the celestial gods.</note> and humans occupy a middle ground between action and passion. From these three kinds of animals, the beauty and duty of the mundane animal is fulfilled. The highest genus is in the world just as intelligence is in us; the middle is like reason (whether universal or particular) in us; finally the lowest...*

<summary>Ficino explains that while the stars provide a general influence, the specific nature of a living thing is determined primarily by its "seminal reasons" and parental heredity. He categorizes the hierarchy of the world-organism, placing humans and daemons as intermediate agents between celestial beings and instinctive animals.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's *Enneads*, specifically Book III, Tractate II, which discusses Providence. On the previous page, Ficino argued that while the heavens provide a general influence, the specific nature of a living being—such as whether it is a human or a horse—is determined by its own biological lineage and "seminal reasons." Here, he further explains how the World Soul organizes these life-forces and how human agency and local causes often outweigh the remote influence of the stars.</meta>

### ON BOOK III. ENNEAD II.

Just as that which is lowest exists within us, so too throughout the universe: the higher souls of the spheres and stars provide more excellent things to the whole than their lower souls. These higher souls are called by Plato the "colleagues of Jupiter"—that is, the mundane intelligences. <note>In Ficino’s Neoplatonism, "Jupiter" often represents the World Soul or the ordering intelligence of the cosmos.</note> Indeed, everything that exists anywhere in the world lives in some way, whether by its own specific life or by a shared life, no less than every part within any animal lives. I say they live, and all things become living according to a life—I mean a bodily life—principally through the benefit of the **World Soul**, in whose **seminal reasons** <note>original: "seminaria ratione." These are the formative, "seed-like" spiritual blueprints that govern the development of physical forms.</note> all the reasons of living things are contained. Everywhere, the seminal reason flourishing in the soul—both in the universal Soul and in any individual one—is the primary principle of motion, generation, and formation.

The fact that specific powers exist in things which cannot be traced back to the elemental qualities (like heat or cold) happens simply because of the influx of many factors; otherwise, they would occur by chance or would not be stable. Therefore, these powers arise from the seminal reason of the living being. Thus:
*   **Peony** hung around the neck helps those suffering from the "falling sickness" <note>Epilepsy.</note>;
*   **Polypodium** <note>A type of fern.</note> purges black bile;
*   **Coral** drives away fear;
*   **Laurel** wards off lightning;
*   The **Torpedo fish** numbs a person even when they touch it only with a rod;
*   The little **suckerfish** <note>original: "echinus." While this usually means sea urchin, the context of "stopping a ship" refers to the legendary *echeneis* or remora.</note> brings a ship to a halt.

Now, such special powers exist from the same source as the species themselves. The various species of natural things are referred not only to different *daemons* <note>In the Greek sense: guiding spirits or intermediary entities, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note> and stars, but also to their own seminal reasons reigning everywhere in the life of the world. For many agents everywhere concur to produce the effect of any given species; these would never rightly lead to a single result in a common form and order unless they were directed by a single leader present everywhere. 

Just as the species of many things are reduced to certain genera, and these finally to one universal genus, so too many agents are necessarily reduced step-by-step to one universal agent. I mean agents either as instruments—such as lower bodies relating to higher ones, and those perhaps to the **Sun** by the benefit of its everywhere-present light—or as principal agents, such as rational souls of a lower order relating to rational souls of a higher order, and those finally to the one Soul ruling everywhere equally. Plotinus wishes there to be such great power in the nature of a living being and its seminal reasons that he thinks no part or motion of the world, however huge, can utterly disturb them from their order. Thus, certain species and properties of things proceed from specific reasons just as the order of all animal nature prescribes, and as every attendant nature duly follows.

What then do the **stars** do? What will their daily motion effect? Certainly, it will not create species, nor change them, nor twist their outcomes away from their species. Rather, the stars may affect things with certain qualities for better or worse, whether regarding the body, or regarding a soul deeply immersed in the body, or regarding certain actions for which the higher soul requires physical instruments. All of that celestial influx is said to act "by accident" <note>In philosophy, an "accidental" cause is secondary or incidental, rather than essential.</note>: partly because it acts by the opportunity it finds from the meeting of lower things, and because it does not produce deformities by its own intent, and because it does not move the soul—unless perhaps the soul is moved accidentally by the body's motion through the heavens, or if the soul consents to the motion. 

If anyone should doubt whether seminal reasons or species are changed because of the occasional birth of monsters, let them notice that the principal part and the "root" of the species is always properly preserved in them, even if something has been added or taken away. I say "added or taken away" not so much by celestial influence, but by a defect of the matter, the location, or the imagination, or by some fortuitous encounter of different things. The principal part is always preserved, or at least as much as possible, because the principal and continuous agent there is the seminal reason; if this were removed, things would happen by chance rather than by nature. We prove in *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his own major work, *Platonic Theology*.</note> that this reason is necessary even in things that seem to be born spontaneously. Since these are formed so skillfully and endowed with life and sense just like those born through propagation, they must certainly be formed, just like the others, by the living reason of a hidden seed. This reason, reigning everywhere in the life of the world, forms matter that is prepared opportunely, acting both most skillfully and most swiftly. As one possessing the most excellent and divine power, it creates the most beautiful things in a moment from the lowliest materials, while it directs diverse agents toward a single end and distinguishes general influences into specific effects according to the disposition of the matter.

---

### In the individual events that happen to humans, we find sufficient causes within ourselves besides the celestial motions.

# XIII

So far, he has argued that celestial influxes do not have much authority over things pertaining to the body and soul; next, he declares that they have even less power over what are called "external things." In all matters, he brings to light the highest causes beneath the heavens which are sufficient and manifest: whether they be the determined causes of things, or certain occasions happening from the meeting of many factors, or human arts and choices. 

Among these, note that the nature of the parents and the quality of the location and nutrition have much more power over the health of the body than the common, remote, and momentary motions of the heavens. Therefore, those things which are sufficiently acted upon by nearby causes are sometimes only *signified* by the stars rather than *effected* by them. He says, moreover, that there is a "mutual consequence" in things, through which they can provide signs for one another—provide them, I say, in regards to the connection of the universe itself. These signs are meaningful at least to one who, looking around at everything, perceives the consequence of all things. 

Furthermore, in the generation of a human, he says the seminal reason and power is the principal cause—indeed, the entire cause from a nearby perspective. That certain species arise from certain seeds in their own proper ways, without confusion or transgression, depends entirely on the seminal natures. He declares that they possess the total authority of generation; where nothing hinders it, the offspring is duly formed according to the norm of the seminal reason. Something is said to "hinder" when it does not allow the absolute image of the seminal power to be expressed. He indicates that such an impediment proceeds not so much from the motions of the planets (which are remote and momentary) but rather from a defect in the mother or from the quality of the air affecting the conception.

---

## On fate and the fates: and how the soul, before it is touched by fate, is touched by the love of the body. On the daemon as the guide of life. On the liberation from fate. On the principles of beings. How our soul also possesses the nature of a principle.

# VI

After explaining what a "part of fate" is—that is, merely the daily revolution of the heavens—he now explains what "total fate" is. Universal **fate** is the entire series of all moving causes, whether they be animal causes or bodily, higher or lower. Since, therefore, the subsequent connection of moving causes is fate, it follows that the rational soul, to the extent that it departs from intellectual stability and is spread out further in motion, is to that extent entangled in the snares of fate. On the contrary, while the whole mind lives by a strictly stable intelligence, it is entangled in no nets of fate. Think, therefore...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus, moving from the general governance of the world to the specific way the human soul descends into a body. Ficino explains how our "daemon" (a guiding spirit) and our "fate" are determined by the choices the soul makes before it is even born.</meta>

### COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO

The rational faculty in the soul, after it has lived for a long time within the **Mind** <note>In Neoplatonic thought, the "Mind" or *Intellectus* is the realm of eternal truths above the realm of change.</note>, eventually turns toward the vegetative nature beneath it through a new kind of movement. Its imagination becomes linked to nature in such a way that its desire for a noble, corporeal life grows more intense. Then the soul, by a new motion of its own, leans toward things that change; choosing this "mutable life," it falls into **Fate**. This happens even before it enters an earthly body and before it is conceived in the womb. For perhaps it suddenly enters an **aerial body** <note>A subtle, "spirit-like" body that the soul was thought to inhabit as it descended from the stars toward the earth.</note> by a certain fatal lot—a lot which the soul itself partly chose shortly before, and which the harmony of the whole universe accommodated to it.

The soul first receives a **daemon** <note>term: **Daemon** (original: *dæmon*). In this context, it is not an evil spirit, but a personal "guardian angel" or "guiding spirit" that oversees a person's specific destiny.</note> as the leader of its life at the moment it first desires and chooses that kind of life. Similarly, when it later desires and chooses an earthly body, it is thought to receive the form of its life partly through its own choice and partly through the harmony of the heavens. In these matters, it is guided by its daemon. 

The **Egyptians** hold that a daemon is given to us by God himself (the ruler of daemons) according to the pattern of the life we have already chosen, and according to the universal harmony at the time of that choice. This daemon is not given by a specific star or planet—as **Porphyry** <note>An earlier Neoplatonist philosopher who often emphasized the role of astrology more than Ficino preferred.</note> thought—but is assigned to accommodate the soul to Fate. However, because it is given by God and corresponds to the soul's own choice, it is more divine than Fate itself; in a way, it can liberate the soul, leading it back toward the daemon, and through the daemon, back to God. For this reason, **Pythagoras** in his songs prays to **Jove** <note>Jupiter/God</note> either to release us from these evils or to show us which daemon we should follow. Finally, he suggests that the solution is to be hoped for through a certain "divinity" implanted within us, which will suggest remedies for our ills.

You should especially commit these points to memory:
1. First, the lot and form of one's life do not begin with Fate, but with the soul's own affection and choice; only afterward is it managed by the daemon it has received.
2. Second, as I said, the lot and form of life are governed or fulfilled by the entire disposition of the world, which converges from all sides—both when the soul desires a body and when it enters it.
3. Third, the disposition of life will not be exactly what the heavenly bodies alone might decree; rather, it is shaped by the preparation of lower matter, the location, the nature of the parents, the imagination, and all other surrounding circumstances joined with the heavens.
4. Fourth, from all this it follows that many people born under the exact same alignment of the stars turn out differently. This is because the beginnings of Fate are drawn from deeper sources before birth (or even before conception), and the conditions of Fate are fulfilled by the meeting of lower, earthly factors.
5. Fifth, no one can perfectly know these things—neither the higher causes, nor how they combine with lower ones, nor what follows from their complexity.
6. Sixth, judgment based on signs (astrology) is therefore completely confused, because so many conflicting indications are drawn from the different origins and causes of our lot. Indeed, traces of one thing are blurred by others, so that judging one’s lot truly is more a matter of "luck" than of "science."

After this, Plotinus says that the name **Lachesis** signifies the lots and forms of living; the name **Clotho** shows their spinning and unfolding through the universe; and **Atropos** represents the necessary effect of this—necessary, I say, insofar as it exists in the nature of Fate and as much as the soul yields to it. <note>Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos are the Three Fates of Greek mythology. Ficino is interpreting them as stages of cosmic law.</note> I say "in Fate" because Plato places the kingdom of the Fates specifically in the heavens; therefore, among the celestial spheres, the outcome is always necessary. But if the confluence of lower things perfectly matched the assembly of heavenly things, then the decree of Fate would also result in necessity here on earth. But perhaps they do not match. It may happen that lower things clash among themselves or with the heavens. Here, then, someone might mix **Fortune** with Fate.

Furthermore, even if the heavens and lower bodies conspire toward the same event—making it seem inevitable—nevertheless, where the **Mind** has authority (where movement is primary and free), that which the necessity of the world intended for a person does not necessarily happen. Just as many place the kingdom of Fate in the heavens and the power of Fortune below the heavens, so they place the "choice of counsel and election" in the **Reason**, which can move between opposites. Thus, Plato confesses that the virtue of the soul is always free, even within Fate. Even **Ptolemy** <note>A famous ancient astronomer and astrologer.</note> admits that a celestial decree can be changed by the meeting of Fortune and wise counsel. 

Regarding **Necessity** and the **Three Fates**, we have said enough in our commentary on the tenth book of the *Republic*. Now we must consider what Plotinus brings up: some men become such that they are dragged away by the charms of the universe (either by nature, habit, or both), while others are such that they can withdraw themselves from those charms. They become this way by nature—partly through the soul's prior choice and life, and partly through the body's natural causes—and they also become this way through habit. 

When Plotinus says that most people are "fascinated" by the world in a "magical way," he means the soul is caught by no other hook than **Love** (either natural or new) and the bait of pleasure. He explains that the nature of the universe has bestowed upon all bodies not only a beautiful form but also a certain life. Because this form is like an "Idea" and this life is "kindred" to the soul, the soul is lured by it like bait and, once enticed, begins to provide for lower things. 

Meanwhile, he signifies that souls—because their intellectual nature is superior to the whole body and corporeal life—can sometimes release themselves from Fate by despising the charms of this world. The soul detaches itself when it loves the higher world; by loving that, the soul returns to its original and primary nature—that is, into the **Mind**, or into **Reason** shaped by the Mind. 

Indeed, since all natural things have their own nature and action (besides the conditions they receive from outside), the soul possesses this gift even more so, as it is the "principle" of things. I say it is the principle of natural and moving things: for nature and motion depend on the soul—specifically, the **intellectual soul**. For the "efficient principle" under the **Good** is the **Intellect**; and under the Intellect, the principle of the soul is the efficient and forming power. The **World Soul** is the principle of all natural things in general, while other souls are principles in particular. The World Soul is the principle of the form of the entire universe; others are principles of the forms of the parts of the universe. 

Therefore, every rational soul, insofar as it acts as a principle, forms its body; it can also do other things in other ways. Just as the soul as a principle forms and leads that body (and only that one), so it can do not only other things, but greater things, provided it is similarly disposed toward them. For example, a soul that gives life to a small body could similarly give life to one three times as large. But we explain these things more broadly in our *Theology*. 

As far as the "principle" is concerned, we must note that the nature of **Being** is considered either as it is in the "first act" through **Form**, or as it is in the "second act" through **Motion**. <note>"First act" refers to the mere existence or potential of a thing; "second act" refers to its actual operation or movement.</note> Where motion (as a second act or action) is not strictly found, the "being of the form" takes the place of action, and is called motion in a certain way. But let us consider Being either in "act through form" simply, or in "act through motion." In the first way, the principle of beings is the **Intellect**; in the second way, the soul is judged to be their principle. Therefore, the Intellect is the principle of Being insofar as...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus, specifically focusing on Ennead III, Book 2. It transitions from the soul’s descent and its guiding "daemon" to the philosophical nature of the soul as a principle of motion and its relationship to the "World Soul."</meta>

# ON BOOK III OF THE ENNEADS, DISCOURSE II.

By its very nature, **being** is something actual—so to speak—and formal; the **soul**, however, is the principle of being insofar as it is capable of movement. If the soul is the principle of forms, it is primarily the origin of those forms that arise through motion. If it is the principle of other forms, it possesses that quality not so much as a living thing, but as an intellectual existence. The **One** and the **Good** itself <note>In Neoplatonic thought, "The One" is the ultimate source of everything, existing above even the Mind or Intellect.</note>, which is higher than the intellect, is the principle and end of all beings, however "being" itself is understood—whether as potential, as act, as a first or second act, as something not yet moved, or as something already in motion. It is especially the principle and end of being insofar as being is one and good. Most powerfully, it is the principle of being because both it and being are one; it is the end of being because both it and being are good. But we discuss this elsewhere. 

Let us return to the soul. We are accustomed to arguing that the rational soul is an essence—that is, a form and species <note>term: **Species** (original: *species*). In this philosophical context, it refers to the "essential form" or "blueprint" of a thing that makes it what it is.</note> consisting firmly in itself, having its own "to be" and "to exist" entirely within itself—because it possesses certain desires and actions proper to it, which are both separate from the body and frequently opposed to the body. Plotinus, in turn, takes it as a settled fact here that the soul exists as such an essence; through this, he argues that the soul possesses certain duties of its own. 

But from where does he take this as settled? Perhaps from the fact that it is the principle of a "moved being" that moves in an orderly and perpetual way. It is, therefore, a fixed essence; even if it moves, it moves from itself, living its own proper life, just as it moves by its own internal and intimate motion. For life is an internal motion and act. Therefore, if the soul is occasionally moved or shaped by external things, this happens because the soul has already voluntarily yielded—and continues to yield—to bodies. Meanwhile, however, the soul possesses its own form and holds its "being" firmly within its essence. Indeed, from the beginning, it approached the body naturally—not as something moved or passive, but as a mover and an active agent. How our soul is also a principle of motion and, in its capacity as a principle, a partner to the **World Soul** <note>term: **World Soul** (original: *anima mundana*). The vital principle that animates the entire universe, just as a human soul animates a human body.</note>, we prove in our *Theology*. 

For now, let us concede that the soul, in its duty of movement, agrees almost equally with the celestial bodies; it also agrees with them in a higher duty—that is, the task of contemplation. In this, it transcends motion by seeking refuge in eternal things. Finally, Plotinus concludes that our "animal nature" <note>The "animal" part of a human refers to the biological and sensory life shared with other living creatures.</note> depends on the "World Animal"—specifically from the beginning, as I have explained elsewhere, and for the most part daily. But just as it depends daily on our soul, so from the beginning it also depended on our soul; and conversely, as it was in the beginning, so it is day by day. Therefore, this "animal" within us is much like the "World Animal"—namely, it has a soul that naturally looks after the needs of the body, acts together with the body, and (in us at least) suffers in some way. 

Likewise, certain wonderful "world instincts" result daily in our animal nature according to the various dispositions of the world, both while we sleep and while we are awake. This animal nature often consents and suffers along with the World Animal, except insofar as the higher soul within us—the mistress of this nature, and thus separable and a sibling to the World Soul—moves and stops this animal in a different way. For this higher soul is separate from the beginning by its essence and being, and it can be even further separated by study through opposing its affections and its acts. It has its own proper actions; and as if it were taming an animal entrusted to it, it can turn that animal toward itself. As Plotinus says elsewhere, the soul can sometimes, by a miraculous virtue, rescue this animal from evils, just as it rescues itself, while it occasionally considers the things pertaining to the animal as alien and of no value.

### XVI

After demonstrating in the preceding sections what the true causes of things are *not*, and having pointed out in some way what they *are*, Plotinus now defines the true causes in the three following chapters of this book. First, where he says that the soul is inseparable when it is in the body, *note that perhaps Plotinus intends to say that the life dedicated to the body—which he often calls the "second soul"—is inseparable from the body. That is, it acts inseparably (performing every action together with this body) as long as it is within it. Nevertheless, it might eventually depart from here along with the higher soul. For it depends on the higher soul like an "assisting act," even though this act is joined to the body through the act of the World Soul—just as a visual ray filters into the air through the act of a solar ray. And just as neither ray vanishes, according to Plotinus, but both are folded back into their own source, so too both vital acts—the common one from the World Soul and the proper one from our own—return to their source.* 

Nor, perhaps, does this duality of life prevent the union of life or the unity of the animal; for while one is common and the other is proper, that which is proper naturally conspires with the common one toward the same end. It determines the common life toward specific things, and is in turn aided by it toward its own work, which is consistent with the common work of the whole. But we discuss this more diligently elsewhere. 

He wants the primary causes of natural things to be the **seminal reasons** <note>term: **Seminal Reasons** (original: *seminales rationes*). These are the divine "blueprints" or "seeds" of logic and form that exist within the World Soul, governing how every physical thing grows and develops.</note> within the vegetative nature of the World Soul; the seminal reasons in individual species always respond to these in a certain order. But he investigates through many questions how all things sprout from the entire "seedbed of the world" (*seminarium mundi*).

**First**, he asks whether the World Soul makes individual things through a sort of direct succession—that is, in an order of steps and temporal opportunities—creating the elements first according to their origin, then the things composed of them; likewise, creating man first according to dignity, then the beasts. He asks, I say, whether it does these things and provides for them only as far as the species of things and their offspring, but does not attend to the things that happen to individuals daily. 

**Second question:** Whether the soul of individuals is also the cause of what happens to individuals daily, because the things generated by it then act, and those that follow also act; as if the World Soul were said to act in any contingency whatsoever—not through itself, but through intermediate causes everywhere. 

**Third question:** Whether the soul has prescribed within itself, in its seminal reasons, the individual actions and passions of every single thing, so that nothing happens by chance, but all things are led by fatal necessity. 

**Fourth question:** If the soul contains individuals in itself this way, do the seminal reasons of the soul *effect* these things, or do they only *know* them? Or does the soul itself know through them? Do they thus look around daily not only at individual things (which are in some way generated by the soul), but also at their actions, passions, and all outcomes? This would mean it understands all present things and concludes whatever follows from them by a kind of reasoning. Does it contemplate many things in the past as if they were present? Or does it never contemplate things following in a summary way, but is instead compelled to follow individual things hour by hour? 

**Fifth question:** Whether it is entirely wrong to imagine the World Soul as being so anxious; rather, should we think that all these things were foreknown once and for all in its reasons, or even destined in the seminal reasons? 

**Sixth question:** Whether the vices and defects of nature can be destined and created from the seminal reasons of nature. For perhaps even those things that seem evil individually contribute to the good of the whole. 

Finally, he solves these questions by denying that anything "in act" contrary to the order of nature is contained in the seminal reasons of natural things; just as in the "reasons of an art" <note>He is comparing Nature's blueprints to an architect's plans; an architect's plan for a house doesn't include the "mistake" of a wall falling down.</note>, insofar as they are such, nothing is contained besides the art itself. Whatever, therefore, is formal in things...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the soul relates to the material world, specifically addressing why things in the physical world are often "deformed" or "deficient" compared to their perfect spiritual patterns.
