### COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

and beauty is contained within the formative principles <note>term: **Formative principles** (original: *rationibus*). Also called "reasons" or "logoi," these are the divine blueprints or seeds that dictate the shape and function of everything in the natural world.</note> by themselves and proceeds properly from them. Whatever deformity occurs, however, seems to happen first from formless matter, or consequently from those things that have been infected by it. But what does he mean when he says that the deficiency of things is contained in these principles not in actuality, but in potentiality? Certainly not in actuality, because deficiencies are not produced from that source; there is no proper "form of deficiency" there. Rather, it is said to be there at least in potentiality, because from the perfect form—as if from a model—one can infer in what way or to what degree something might fall short of it. Therefore, things that are evil or less than good can indeed be foreknown there, but they cannot be predestined. For whatever is determined from that source is defined by form; but what is actually made from it does not turn out in matter exactly as it is possessed by the soul. Because it is made "outside" <note>That is, outside the purely spiritual realm of the soul and inside the physical world.</note>, it degenerates; and because it is made in formless matter, it becomes deformed, and is further confused by the mixing of different elements.

<margin>1</margin> The soul, therefore, acts through these formative principles as long as things match those principles in their beauty. However, the soul can go further and infer deformity as well—generally through intelligence, but specifically through reason or a kind of imagination joined to nature. Yet, even in that state, it does not do so by wandering through every single detail, but rather in summary. Here Plotinus also says that forms in matter fall away from the forms of nature due to a certain "clash" <note>original: *concussione*. Ficino uses this to describe the inherent instability and friction of the material world compared to the stillness of the divine.</note>. This is partly because they seem to depart from their principles, partly because they turn out deformed due to formless matter, partly because they are mixed with opposites, and partly because they gradually degenerate from their original dignity. Plotinus says in earlier passages that natural things degenerate gradually through the ages, as do Plato in the *Statesman*, *Protagoras*, *Critias*, and *Menexenus*. We assigned the causes in those places, and here we assign them briefly as well. There is a kind of long-term degeneration of things, stretching from the beginning of the world's circuit to its very end; and another long-term one, persisting from one great flood of the earth to the next.

Consider, then, the twelve signs <note>The twelve constellations of the Zodiac.</note> that are seen in the firmament to lie beneath the twelve signs marked in the ninth sphere. Plato thought this sphere could exist, even if he could not prove it clearly, since he does not deny that it is possible. Thus, once upon a time, the signs corresponded to the signs everywhere: the Ram to the Ram, the Bull to the Bull, the Twins to the Twins, the Crab to the Crab, the Lion to the Lion, the Virgin to the Virgin, the Scales to the Scales, the Scorpion to the Scorpion, the Archer to the Archer, the Goat to the Goat, the Water-bearer to the Water-bearer, and finally the Fish to the Fish. Then was the happy omen of the "age of ages," happy for as long as the same things matched the same. But then, through motion toward the east, the Ram passed beyond the Ram, and the remaining signs followed in sequence. Meanwhile, natural things began to degenerate by a similar degree. Nevertheless, in certain ages, they seem to be able to recover some of their original vigor for a time, when these signs come—if not to those exact same ones—at least to similar ones. The Ram to the Lion, or at least to the Twins; or the Lion to the Archer, or to the Scales; the Twins to the Scales, or the Scales to the Water-bearer, and others similarly; or at least when those relationships arise which astronomers teach are more harmonious. Meanwhile, certain great conjunctions of the planets contribute to this, although sometimes they happen to cause harm in turn. Similarly, the movement of the images <note>Referring to the constellations or astrological "images."</note> through their approach toward the south and their retreat, restored over many centuries, leads to changes in things; but things will not recover their original happiness until the same things return to the same places. Indeed, the motion of the signs visible to us, turning toward the east, passes one degree of the higher signs every hundred years. Therefore, the "age of ages" will be completed in thirty-six thousand years <note>term: **Platonic Year** (original: *seculum seculorum*). The time it takes for the constellations to return to their original positions relative to the equinoxes.</note>. 

Meanwhile, another kind of change in the age occurs when the earth is either washed away by a flood of waters or devastated by a conflagration of flames. Whether a powerful heat of the sun falls upon the moisture after the waters, or an overflowing rain follows the fires in turn, the earth soon becomes more fertile in both cases from the heat and moisture and brings forth the most beautiful things—until, becoming more sterile every day due to dryness, it gives birth to less beautiful things, and finally a similar flood or fire returns for the sake of a remedy. Remember, however, that the motions and positions of the celestial bodies do not pertain so much to the generation of forms themselves (which properly happens through the seminal principles), but rather to the disposing of matter in one way or another. 

A third cause of degeneration pertains especially to human affairs: in the very newness of the world—whether it is made new through creation or appears new after a prior destruction—humans are governed by the diligent providence of the higher powers as if by "shepherds." For being weak and naked by nature, and unskilled in art, they completely lack the guidance of the higher powers. But providence never deserts its own in necessary things. Hence it happens that nature also does not fail in necessary things. For this reason, nature works harder in the body of an animal for a member that has a greater necessity. Therefore, human affairs once proceeded entirely rightly by divine means—more divinely, in fact—for a long time. But as soon as the human mind, sharpened by time and fate, seemed to need the constant care of spirits <note>term: **Daemons** (original: *dæmonum*). In the Platonic sense, these are intermediary spirits or "guardian angels," not "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note> less, it began to be governed more negligently by those spirits (or angels, if you prefer). From this, human affairs slip daily into a worse state, until the human disease, incurable by itself, provokes the necessary care of divine beings toward it. But by what reasoning the world is continually made more beautiful—either through various degrees of degenerating things or from the deformity of some of its parts—we have said enough elsewhere and will say more.

### XVII.
The seminal principles <note>term: **Seminal principles** (original: *rationes seminales*). These are the "seed-reasons" or internal powers that cause a thing to grow according to its specific form.</note> in any soul are not "notions" (concepts); otherwise, they would generate continuously by knowing, and they would know by generating. This is also true in the Soul of the Universe, whose life is more effective than any other life, and which therefore can generate by the simple power of life without the help of a concept. First, such principles do not exist in the Intellect; for the Intellect separates both itself and, if necessary, the thing to be understood from matter. But an effective power, such as that of a natural seed, since it is meant to give birth only in matter, approaches matter first and enters it deeply. Second, they are not "reasonings" either; for these are almost accidental and imaginary, and therefore they cannot produce things that are substantial and vital. They are accustomed to produce things in the manner of "Art," from the outside and with the help of external instruments, and they produce things that are somewhat imaginary. But seminal principles act from within, through themselves and through joined instruments in the manner of any nature, and they produce substances. Furthermore, they are not "imaginations"; for these, as is apparent in us, produce nothing in the body without the power of an "affection" (an emotion or drive). In fact, even affection is not sufficient for the imagination to generate forms, but perhaps only for local motion. For from an imagination strengthened by affection, local motion immediately occurs in the spirit <note>term: **Spirit** (original: *spiritu*). A thin, vaporous substance that Platonists believed connected the soul to the physical body.</note> and the heart. From this motion, in turn, qualities that have long been in the body...

### COMMENTARY ON BOOK III, ENNEAD II.

...are now aroused, from which they produce either an additional quality on top or a passion. Similarly, in the Soul of the World <note>term: **Soul of the World** (original: *anima mundi*). In Neoplatonic thought, this is the mediating spirit that connects the divine Intellect to the physical universe, giving life and movement to the stars and elements.</note>, imagination does not primarily generate the forms of things—for imagination itself seems to be a sort of "imaginary" thing even more than reasoning is. Rather, when joined with an emotional state, it leads to the local motion of the world. Before this motion occurs, the forms of things already exist in the world, having been generated there long ago by the world's generative power through what we call **seminal reasons** <note>term: **Seminal reasons** (original: *seminales rationes*). These are the "spiritual seeds" or blueprints within nature that dictate how a plant, animal, or object will grow and take shape.</note>. Therefore, from these types of reasons infused into nature, the primary forms of things are procreated in the world. 

Subsequently, however, from the "imaginations" that look upon individual things to be generated, daily and individual motions occur through specific movements. By these motions, the forms of things are stirred toward mutual alteration. Through this perpetual alteration, matter everywhere is properly prepared to receive new daily forms from the "reasons." Thus, in the soul, imagination and nature are companions; similarly, in the universe, alteration and generation are constant companions. Nor is it wrong that nature—the mother of individuals—accompanies imagination (and vice versa), which distracts itself through individual things. Yet, nature does not directly accompany Reason, which ultimately takes refuge in universals, nor Intelligence, which always persists in universals. Even if Intelligence or Reason perceives individual things, it does so as a consequence; its primary devotion remains meanwhile to the universals. 

Generation, therefore, or alteration and motion—which belong only to individual things—seems to exist just after nature, close to the imagination, which concerns itself solely and primarily with individuals. In short, since generation is entirely concerned with matter, if we are to find the power that generates most directly, we are forced to descend below any cognitive power. For any power of "knowing" possesses a form and an action by which it knows that is separate from matter. Just as that which is light at its highest point and splendor in the middle becomes heat at its lowest point—and it is as *heat* that it generates, not as splendor or light—so too in the soul: it exists as intellectual at its peak, discursive <note>term: **Discursive** (original: *discurrens*). This refers to step-by-step logical reasoning, moving from one thought to another, as opposed to the "intellectual" power which understands things instantly and as a whole.</note> in the middle, and finally only vital and life-giving at its lowest point. It generates and gives life not as an intellectual or discursive power, but as a vital one. And if it happens to "know" while it is making things, it does not make them *because* it knows, but because it is constituted that way and is naturally disposed to act; therefore, it makes such things in such a way. 

I said it does not make them because it "knows"—meaning by some knowledge separate from its essence. For at its highest point, "to understand" is the same as "to be." Therefore, through this essential and vital intelligence, it naturally produces forms (that is, seminal reasons) in nature through essential and ideal notions, just as nature shapes forms in matter through those reasons. 

Therefore, just as a circle arises in water from the tossing of a pebble, and soon another circle arises, and so on, so too from a certain "ideal circle" of the Divine Mind there hangs a nearly identical circle in the mind of the World Soul; from here it moves into nature, and from nature into matter. Therefore, for the formulas impressed by the soul's intelligence into the soul's generative nature to be essential and effective, and to create substantial things, the forms must exist essentially in both the Divine Mind and the soul's mind. In those realms, to understand is the same as to be; and to understand is also to "form nature" through the act of understanding. This is just as in nature, "to be" is the same as "to live," and in a way, "to give life to matter" is the same as "to live." 

But one might ask: Does the animal intelligence <note>referring to the soul as it governs the "world-animal"</note> form nature through some rational or imaginary discourse, like a craftsman often shapes matter? Not at all. For even the most perfect art does not deliberate further, but acts in the manner of the nature it has already mastered, having imitated it as far as it could. Furthermore, if it decided to form nature through some discourse of thought, it would have already referred the forms to be made to others as a firm model and spectacle—something for the gaze of "wandering reason" to intend toward, something stable around which the discourse could be performed and against which discoveries could be compared. 

The question then is: Does it look upon some external spectacles, or does it possess such firm forms within? Certainly not external and corporeal ones (for these do not yet exist, being still to be generated by nature—that is, still to be formed by the intellect through nature). Therefore, it possesses the forms within. But that which is possessed intrinsically and naturally does not need to be sought through persuasion. If nature, therefore, continually forms matter without any ministry of counsel <note>i.e., without having to stop and think about it or plan it out</note>, much more so does the Mind form the nature joined to it without counsel, and vice versa. 

Conclude, then, that discourse itself (through momentary acts) is everywhere something "beyond essence"—an accidental thing like a flash of lightning. Since it appears in parts and suddenly vanishes, it cannot by itself make firm and substantial things. For such an effect, one needs the firm and essential efficacy of another nature. Thus, not through anxiety or labor, but with untiring ease, natural things will spring from nature itself, and the seeds of nature will spring from intelligence. 

Conclude again: just as in the heavens the native light and heat remain most stable while the configurations are changed by the circuit, so too in the life of the world, intelligence and nature remain in their "reasons" and work stably through them, even if some universal or particular discourse is occurring there. 

But since the "secondary" World Soul—that is, a life that is essentially irrational—has been granted to the worldly body by the intellectual World Soul as the final "trace" of the divine, and since it possesses seeds that are like the final traces of the Ideas, it is no wonder that the world composed of this life and body degenerates far from divinity. Often its "seeds" seem to be hindered in their work, and such an "animal" <note>The physical universe viewed as a single living organism.</note> will seem imperfect when compared to higher things. For although this "world-animal" can be called gentle and blessed by the perpetual presence of its intellectual soul, nevertheless, because this animal is something else and something posterior to the intellectual soul, one can imagine the soul itself separated from the animal. This is what Plato considered in the *Statesman* <note>original: *Politicus*</note>, the *Timaeus*, and the *Laws*. 

Tell me, then: what would this vast and most robust animal soon become if the "reins of intelligence" were removed? We can call iron "naturally cold" even if it is currently glowing hot, and air "naturally dark" even if it is currently luminous. For the iron soon declares its coldness, and the air soon clearly shows its darkness. By such a condition, Plotinus seems to portray this world-animal as if it were "ferocious" <note>original: *ferox*. Meaning wild, untamed, or prone to chaos without divine order.</note>. 

Imagine also, if you please, a wise man with a body that is excessively choleric or melancholic. Look into the habit of his body: you will see this "animal" held back as if by reins under the wise mind, acting quietly and appearing gentle. But meanwhile, it is most ready for outbursts of anger and grief; or if it is of a sanguine nature, for lust—an affection which it barely shows while awake, but more easily reveals in dreams. Imagine the world-animal in much the same way: prone to wrath and pride from fire (as if from yellow bile); prone to grief from earth (as if from black bile); prone to wantonness and lust from air (as if from blood); prone to sluggishness from water (as if from phlegm); and from **primary matter** <note>term: **Primary matter** (original: *materia prima*). The formless, underlying "stuff" of the universe that has no qualities of its own but receives all forms.</note>, which is like a sort of dregs or lees settling beneath natural things, you will encounter something equally bitter and sharp. For these "dregs" are thought of as both bitter and acidic due to their dryness and coldness. 

Therefore, this animal will appear most ferocious because of its grander powers, yet too destitute, small-souled, envious, and complaining about its own vileness and mutability because of its matter. Finally, you will cease to wonder why, in an animal so affected, not everything goes according to its wish, and many things even happen to others contrary to their wish.

# COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO.

And what is beautiful is contained within the **formative principles** <note>term: **Formative principles** (original: *rationibus*). Also called "reasons," these are the divine blueprints or patterns that give shape to physical things.</note> in themselves and proceeds properly from them. Whatever deformity occurs, however, seems to happen primarily because of formless matter, or consequently from those things that have followed after this matter. But what does he mean when he says that "defects in things are contained in the principles not according to act, but according to potential"? Certainly not according to act, since defects are not produced from those principles; for there is no proper "form of a defect" there. Instead, they are said to be there at least according to potential, because from a perfect form, as if from a model, one can guess in what way or to what degree something might fall short of it. Therefore, things that are evil or less than good can be foreknown there, but they cannot be predestined. For whatever is determined from that source is defined by form; but that which comes from there into matter does not turn out the same way it is possessed by the soul. Not only because it exists outside the soul does it degenerate, but also because it exists in formless matter it becomes deformed, and is further confused by the mixing of diverse elements. The Soul, therefore, acts through these principles only so far as things correspond to them in beauty, although it can perceive even further—that is, it can recognize deformity—generally through intelligence, but specifically through reason or a certain imagination joined to nature. Even in that, it does not act by running through every single detail, but rather summarily. 

Here he also says that the forms in matter fall short of the forms of nature by a certain "shaking"—that is, partly because they seem to depart from the principles, partly because they become deformed in formless matter, partly because they are mixed with opposites, and partly because they gradually degenerate from their pristine dignity. Plotinus says in earlier passages that natural things degenerate gradually through the ages, as do Plato in *The Statesman*, *Protagoras*, *Critias*, and *Menexenus*. We assigned the causes there, and here we assign them briefly. One type of degeneration in things is more lasting, stretching from the beginning of the world’s circuit to its very end; another is long-lasting but less so, persisting from one great flood of the earth to another. 

Consider, then, the twelve signs that are seen in the firmament <note>original: *firmamento*. The sphere of the fixed stars.</note> to be positioned beneath the twelve signs marked in the ninth sphere. Even if Plato did not explicitly establish this sphere, he thought it could exist, since he does not deny the possibility. Thus, once upon a time, the signs corresponded to the signs in every way: Aries to Aries, Taurus to Taurus, Gemini to Gemini, Cancer to Cancer, Leo to Leo, Virgo to Virgo, Libra to Libra, Scorpio to Scorpio, Sagittarius to Sagittarius, Capricorn to Capricorn, Aquarius to Aquarius, and finally Pisces to Pisces. Then there was a happy omen for the "age of ages," which remained happy as long as the same things corresponded to the same signs. But afterward, through movement toward the east, Aries crossed over Aries, and the remaining signs followed in turn. Meanwhile, natural things began to degenerate at a similar pace. 

Nevertheless, in certain ages, they seem to be able to recover some of their pristine vigor for a time, when these signs—even if not reaching those exact same ones—at least come to similar ones: Aries to Leo, or at least to Gemini; or Leo to Sagittarius, or to Libra; Gemini to Libra, or Libra to Aquarius, and others similarly. Or at least, certain influences arise there which astronomers teach are more harmonious. Meanwhile, certain great conjunctions of the planets contribute to this, although sometimes they happen to do harm instead. Similarly, the movement of the images through their approach to the south and their withdrawal, restored over many centuries, contributes to the changes in things. But things will not recover their pristine happiness until the same signs return to the same positions. The movement of the signs manifest to us, veering toward the east, passes one degree of the higher signs every hundred years. Thus, the "age of ages" will be completed in thirty-six thousand years <note>note: This refers to the "Platonic Year" or "Great Year," the time it takes for the stars to complete a full cycle and return to their original positions.</note>. 

Meanwhile, there is another kind of change in an age, when the earth is either washed away by a flood of waters or devastated by a fire of flames. Whether a powerful solar heat weighs upon the moisture after the waters, or an exuberant rain follows the fires, the earth soon becomes more fertile in both cases due to heat and moisture and produces beautiful things—until, becoming more sterile day by day due to dryness, it gives birth to less beautiful things, and finally a similar flood or fire returns for the sake of a remedy. Remember, however, that the motions and positions of the celestial bodies pertain not so much to the actual generation of forms (which occurs properly through the **seminal reasons**), but rather to the different ways in which matter is disposed. 

The third cause of degeneration pertains especially to human affairs: in the very newness of the world—whether it is made new through creation or appears new after a prior destruction—humans are governed by the diligent providence of the higher powers as if by shepherds <note>note: This is an allusion to the "Age of Saturn" described in Plato's *Statesman*, where gods personally tended to humanity.</note>. For being weak and naked by nature, and unskilled in art, they stand in total need of the governance of those above. Providence never deserts its own in necessary things. Whence it happens that nature also does not fail in necessary things. For this reason, in an animal body, nature works harder according to the greater necessity of any given limb. Therefore, human affairs once proceeded entirely rightly for a long time by divine power—indeed, by divine beings. But as soon as the human mind was sufficiently cultivated by time and seemed to need the constant care of spirits <note>term: **spirits** (original: *daemonum*). In the Platonic sense, these are intermediary beings between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note> less, it began to be governed more negligently by those spirits (or angels, if you prefer). From this, human affairs slip into a worse state daily, until the human illness, incurable by itself, provokes the necessary care of the divine beings back to it. By what means the world is continuously made more beautiful—either through the various degrees of degenerating things or from the deformity of some of its parts—we have said enough elsewhere and will say more.

**XVII** Now, the **seminal reasons** <note>term: **Seminal reasons** (original: *rationes seminales*). The active, internal biological and metaphysical powers that cause a thing to grow according to its species.</note>, just as they are in any given soul, are not certain "notions" or abstract concepts. Otherwise, they would generate continuously by the act of knowing, and they would know by the act of generating. Nor are they such in the Soul of the Universe, whose life is more effective than any other life, and therefore can generate by a simple power of life without the help of a concept. First, reasons of this kind do not exist in the Intelligence <note>original: *Intelligentia*. The higher divine Mind above the Soul.</note>; for the Intelligence separates both itself and, if necessary, the thing to be understood from matter. But an effective power, such as the natural power of a seed, since it is only meant to generate in matter, approaches matter first and enters it deeply. 

Second, they are not "reasonings" either; for reasonings are as if accidental and imaginary, and therefore they cannot produce substantial and vital things. They are accustomed to produce things in the manner of an art—from the outside, with the help of external instruments, and producing certain imaginary things. But the seminal reasons act from within, through themselves and through joined instruments in the manner of any nature, and they produce substances. 

Furthermore, they are not "imaginations" either; for these, as is apparent in us, produce nothing in the body without the effectiveness of an emotion. Indeed, even emotion is not sufficient for the imagination to generate forms, but perhaps only for local motion. For from an imagination strengthened by emotion, a local motion immediately occurs in the spirit and the heart. From this motion, in turn, those qualities which have long been in the body...

### ON BOOK III. ENNEAD II.

...are now awakened, from which they produce either a further quality or a passion. Similarly, in the **Soul of the World**, <note>original: *anima mundi*</note> imagination does not primarily generate the forms of things—since imagination itself seems to be something imaginary even more than reasoning is—but when joined with an impulse, it leads to the local motion of the world. Before this motion, the forms of things already exist in the world, having been generated there long ago by the procreative power of the world through **seminal reasons**. <note>term: **Seminal reasons** (original: *seminales rationes*). These are the active, life-giving principles or "seeds" within the Soul that contain the patterns for all physical things.</note> Wherefore, from such principles infused into this nature, the primary forms of things are procreated in the world. Subsequently, from imaginations regarding the individual things to be generated, through individual movements as it were, daily and individual motions occur, by which the forms of things are stirred to mutual alteration. By this perpetual alteration, matter is everywhere duly prepared to receive new daily forms from the principles.

Therefore, imagination and nature are companions in the soul; similarly, alteration and generation are always companions in the universe. Nor is it wrong that nature, the mother of individual things, accompanies imagination, and vice versa—that which distracts itself through individual things, and yet does not immediately reach reason (which ultimately flees to universals), nor intelligence (which always persists in universals). For if intelligence or reason perceives individual things, it does so as a consequence; meanwhile, it has its chief devotion to universals. Therefore, generation or alteration and motion, which pertain only to individuals, seem to exist just after nature, which is close to imagination and occupies itself solely and chiefly with individual things.

But entirely, since generation is concerned with matter, if we are to find the power that most closely generates, we are forced to descend below any cognitive power. For any cognitive power possesses the form and the action by which it knows as something separate from matter. Therefore, just as that which is light at its summit and splendor in its middle becomes heat at its lowest point—and just as it generates as heat, not as splendor nor as light—so in the soul, which exists as intellectual at its summit, as discursive in its middle, and finally as merely vital and life-giving at its lowest point, it generates and gives life not as intellectual, nor as discursive, but as vital. And if it also knows while it acts, it does not act because it knows, but because it is constituted so and is naturally affected so; therefore it acts in such a way and produces such things.

Indeed, I said "not because it knows," meaning knowledge as something external to its essence; for in its very summit, to understand is the same as to be. Therefore, by this essential and vital intelligence, through essential and ideal principles, it naturally produces forms—that is, seminal reasons—in nature, just as nature through them fashions forms in matter. Just as from a circle made by the cast of a pebble in water another circle soon arises, and so on in succession, so from the sphere of the divine ideal mind there hangs a nearly similar sphere in the mind of the **World Soul**; from here it soon passes into nature, and from nature similarly into matter.

Therefore, for the formulas impressed by the soul's intelligence into the soul's procreative nature to be essential and effective, and to produce substantial things, it is necessary that forms exist both in the divine mind and in the soul's mind as so essential that "to understand" is the same as "to be." And also, that to understand is the same as to form nature through understanding, just as in nature "to be" is the same as "to live," and in a certain way "to give life to matter" is the same as "to live."

But it is asked: does the soul’s intelligence form nature through some rational or imaginative discourse, as a craftsman often treats matter? Not at all. For even the most perfect art does not deliberate further, but acts now in the manner of the nature it pursues, having imitated it as far as it could. Furthermore, if it were determined to form nature by some discourse of thought, it would have already referred the forms to be made to others as a firm exemplar and spectacle, toward which it might direct the gaze of wandering reason, around which stable point its discourse might be performed, and to which it could compare its findings. It is asked, then: does it look toward certain external spectacles, or does it possess such firm forms within? Not external and corporeal ones (for these do not yet exist, being still to be generated through nature, still to be formed by the intellect); therefore, it possesses the forms within.

But what is possessed intrinsically and naturally is not to be sought through wandering. If, therefore, nature continually forms matter without any deliberation or mystery, much more does the mind form the nature joined to it without deliberation, and vice versa. Conclude, then, that discourse itself, through its momentary acts, is everywhere something beyond essence and a certain accidental thing, like flashes of lightning; it vanishes suddenly or by parts, and thus cannot by itself make firm and substantial things. Instead, for such an effect, there is need for the firm and essential efficacy of another nature. Thus, not by worry, not by labor, but with untiring ease, both natural things will sprout from nature itself, and nature from intelligence.

Conclude again: just as in the heavens native light and heat remain most stable while configurations change daily in their circuit, so in the life of the world, intelligence and nature remain in their principles, and through them they act stably, even if some universal or particular discourse is conducted there. But since the "secondary" part of the World Soul—that is, a certain life irrational in itself—is granted to the worldly body by the intellectual Soul of the World as the ultimate trace of the divine, and similarly possesses as if the ultimate traces of the **Ideas**, <note>term: **Ideas**. In Platonic philosophy, these are the perfect, eternal forms of which all physical things are mere shadows.</note> undoubtedly the world composed of this life and body degenerates far from divinity. Often its "seeds" seem to be hindered in their work, and such an animal, compared to higher things, will seem imperfect. For although by a certain perpetual presence of its intellectual soul this world-animal could be called tame and blessed, nevertheless, because this animal is something else and posterior to the intellectual soul, one may imagine the soul itself separated from the animal—as **Plato** imagined in the *Politicus*, the *Timaeus*, and the *Laws*.

Come, tell me: what would this vast and robust animal soon become if the reins of intelligence were removed? We can call it cold and dark by nature, even if it is now fiery and airy, even if it is now luminous. For iron manifests its coldness shortly after being heated, and air manifest its darkness shortly after the light is gone. Under such a condition, Plotinus seems to depict this world-animal as if it were a wild beast. Imagine, if you please, a wise man with a body that is too choleric or melancholic; look inside at the condition of the body, and you will see this animal acting quietly under the mind of the wise man as if held by reins, and appearing tame. But meanwhile, it is most ready for anger and sorrow; and if it were sanguine, for lust—an affection which, though it barely shows while awake, it indicates more easily in dreams.

Imagine the world-animal to be much like this: from fire, as if from bile, it is prone to wrath and pride; from earth, as if from black bile, more prone to sorrow; from air, as if from blood, to wantonness and lust; from water, as if from phlegm, more prone to torpor. From **prime matter**, <note>term: **Prime matter** (original: *materia prima*). The formless "stuff" that exists before any qualities are added to it.</note> which is like a kind of dregs settling beneath natural things, there will appear to you an animal that is at once most fierce from its grander powers, and from its matter, destitute, overly small-minded, envious, and complaining about its own utility and changeability. Finally, you will cease to wonder that in an animal so affected, in which not all things go according to its wish, many things also happen to others contrary to their wish.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s Ennead III, Book 2. # COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

Next, he encompasses the causes of the universe. The cause of evils, however, is considered in one way by the logic of consequence, and in another by the logic of the end. For just as a lesser good follows a greater good, and in turn the smallest good follows the lesser in a long sequence, so too do evils happen at the very lowest level. Furthermore, just as in a musical harmony the fourth, or even the second and seventh notes—which do not harmonize when played alone—create a more pleasing consonance when combined with the harmonious notes: so in the order of things, lesser goods with greater ones, the smallest with the lesser, and even evils with the smallest, make the common good of the whole more admirable. What then? You may find that those things which seem evil in this or toward that, are good in another thing or toward another end; ultimately, everything leads to the common good of the universe.

After this, he posits three craftsmen of the world. The first is the divine intellect; the second is the living intellect and the intellectual soul; the third is the image of this soul—that is, the life dedicated thereafter to the body. In this matter, as Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major Neoplatonist philosopher who succeeded Plato's Academy.</note> testifies, Porphyry <note>Porphyry was the student of Plotinus and the editor of his works.</note> agrees with Plotinus. But why does he not call the **Good** itself the craftsman? Because the patterns of works are within the craftsman. But in the **Good** itself, since it is the most simple unity, he does not dare to place the pattern of the world, which is manifold. Instead, Plato and Plotinus call the **Good** itself both the father of the worldly craftsman and the end of the worldly work; as if the son, pregnant with the love of the paternal good, procreates the world for the sake of the good and shapes it according to the good.

Therefore, the **Good** itself generates the intellectual world; this in turn procreates the living world; this similarly produces the natural world; and the natural produces the corporeal. One flows from the other much like a ripple in water depends on a previous ripple, or as light comes from brilliance, splendor from light, heat from splendor, and generation proceeds from heat. The intellect, in procreating the intellectual soul, in no way departs from the Father; rather, through its union with the Father, it possesses the power and act of creation. Similarly, the intellectual soul, insofar as it leans upon the highest intellect, abounds from there and overflows into another. The other in turn—that is, the corporeal life—insofar as it depends on the soul of which it is the image, is filled with seeds, and likewise fills the matter of this world with forms.

The **Good** itself exceeds "state" <note>term: **State** (original: *status*). In Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to a fixed, stable, or unchanging condition of being.</note>; for "state" exists in the good and for the sake of the good. The intellect itself exists as the "state"; the intellectual soul is judged to be the first stable thing. But the life that is the image of this soul is indeed stable insofar as it exists from there, but mobile by accident, insofar as it is coupled to a body that is inherently mobile. Plotinus calls such life the **seminary world** <note>term: **Seminary world** (original: *mundum seminarium*). A realm acting as a "nursery" or source of seeds/principles for physical growth.</note> properly speaking, which the ancients called the image, which is always engaged in assimilation. For this is called not so much the soul as the image of the soul. For as much as it approaches matter—which is foreign to the intellectual source—so much does it degenerate from the intellectual soul. The seeds in it are also not so much **reasons** as they are images of reasons. For if "reason" properly exists according to form in the intellectual soul, then in the lower life it is rightly only an image of reason. For who would call that "true reason" which, being ignorant of itself, has no account of itself?

This life, therefore, is a certain image, full only of images; this image has always attained the likeness of the pattern and always attains it. Again, it is always being fashioned and is perpetually fashioned, by which logic the acts of the seeds themselves seem to flourish at different times; yet they always correspond to the pattern. Thus, life revolves as if one with the body of the world; by this, finally, along with the celestial revolution, the mind is affected and imagines in different ways, and outwardly it is somehow always clothed in other figures. Perhaps Plotinus also touches upon the opinions of Heraclitus <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher known for the idea that "everything flows" (*panta rhei*).</note> and the *Timaeus* <note>Plato's dialogue on the creation of the universe.</note> with these words, saying that this world manifest to the eyes never truly "is," but is perpetually "becoming." 

Indeed, just as water is shaped under a seal, but the shape does not remain once the seal is removed—and therefore the shape seems not so much to be made once as to be always being made, especially if the water flows continuously beneath it—so matter relates to nature, and nature in turn to the soul fertile with intellect. Plotinus wants this world to "become" or "be" to the extent that the image of the soul flows from the soul, the soul proceeds from the mind, and the mind is generated from the good—and finally, the good as long as it is that which is good, and the intellect thereafter as long as it exists as that which is intellect. Since these remain so, the following things either always remain or flow from them naturally, just as light flows from the sun, and subsequently light from light. We, however, regarding these things can say for the sake of religion: If we consider eternity in divine matters, then the procession of the world from there rightly seems eternal; but if we consider the **Will**, the world proceeds from that limit which the divine will has decreed, by whose judgment, just as there is a limit of power and magnitude in the world, so too there is a beginning and an end.

<meta>catchword: PLOTINI</meta>

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains the Neoplatonic hierarchy of creation, arguing that the world is a continuous "becoming" generated by the Intellect and Soul under the influence of the Good. He uses analogies of light and water to describe emanation and concludes by reconciling this eternal procession with the Christian concept of Divine Will.</summary>

# P L O T I N V S
## E N N E A D  T W O
### B O O K  I I I.

->Whether the stars have an effect.<-
<note>original Greek: "ΠΕΡΙ τοῦ εἰ ποιεῖ τὰ ἄστρα"; original Latin: "Vtrum stellæ aliquid agant."</note>

<column-break/>

**R**egarding the motion of the stars, each one signifies the things that will be, but the stars do not themselves produce everything, as is believed by the masses. I have spoken about this elsewhere, and provided certain proofs, but it must be discussed more accurately and with more arguments now. For it is no small matter to hold a belief in this way or that. People say that the wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" or <term>planets</term> (from the Greek *planētai*) refer to the five known planets plus the Sun and Moon.</note> in their travels cause not only other things, such as poverty, wealth, health, and disease, but also ugliness and beauty, and—most importantly—vices and virtues. They even say that our individual actions at every moment arise from these stars, as if the stars were angry with humans <margin>*on whom</margin> <note>original: "ἐφ' οἷς"</note> *under whom* <note>original: "ὑφ' οἷς"</note> —even though humans have done them no wrong—and that humans are thus scattered by the stars' influence according to how they are positioned. They say the stars grant what are called "goods" not because they love the <margin>*those being harmed according to the places</margin> <note>original: "κακουμένοις κατὰ τὰς τό-πους"</note> recipients, but because they themselves are either *harmed according to the manner of their movement, or again, are not affected. And they say that the stars' intentions change in another way: whenever they are at the "centers" <note><term>centers</term> (Greek: *kentra*): The four pivotal points of an astrological chart—the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.</note> and when they are declining, it is different. Most significantly, while saying some of them are bad and others are good, they nevertheless claim that those called bad often grant goods, and those called good sometimes become foul. Furthermore, they say that when the stars "see" <note><term>aspect</term>: The geometric relationship or "gaze" between planets in the sky.</note> one another, they produce certain effects, but if they do not see one another, they produce others; as if they were not their own masters, but become one thing by looking, and another by not looking. And they say a star is good when looking at a certain one, but if it should look at another, it becomes different. It sees in one way if the "view" is in this configuration, and in another way if it is in that. Moreover, they say the mixture of all of them together becomes something different, just as a mixture made from different liquids is different from the individual parts that were mixed. Regarding how those who hold such beliefs should be answered, it is proper to speak by examining each point. This storehouse of arguments may be set aside.

<column-break/>

<margin>He recounts the opinions of astrologers regarding the motions and powers of the planets.</margin>
<margin>A</margin> **W**E have said elsewhere, bringing forward other arguments, that the movement of the stars signifies each future event, but does not cause everything, as many think. However, we must speak at present with more exact and more numerous arguments. For it matters not a little <margin>B</margin> to think of these things in this or that way. Many astrologers hand down the tradition that the planets, by their motions, cause not only other things such as poverty and wealth, and favorable or adverse health, but indeed even the shameful and the beautiful, and what is greatest: vices as well as virtues. Likewise, they say individual actions at individual times arise from these, just as if the stars are angry against men—in those cases, clearly, in which the men themselves have brought no injury upon them. They are as they are because they have been so established by the <margin>C</margin> planets. They add, furthermore, that those stars bring what are called "goods," not because they love those who are to receive them, but because they themselves, through the diversity of their motion and place, are affected either entirely well or badly. Again, they are said to change their minds according to the change of their course, and they turn out different from themselves when they are either in the "angles" <note>The Latin *angulis* refers to the same pivotal astrological points as the Greek *kentra*.</note> or when they decline. But what is most significant is that, while they say some among them <margin>D</margin> are bad and others are good, nonetheless, the bad ones often bestow goods, and the good ones sometimes turn out bad. They add that the planets do some things when they mutually behold one another, and other things when they do not behold one another, as if they are not at all in their own right, but become one thing by looking, and another by not looking. Finally, when a planet gazes upon a certain other one, it turns out good; but when it gazes upon another, it is suddenly changed. They also claim that they look differently if the gaze is made in a certain <margin>E</margin> figure, and differently if the figure of the gazing is changed. Then, from all of them breathing together at once, another mixture is fashioned, just as from various liquids a certain different mixture is produced besides the individual mixed elements. Since, therefore, these and other things are argued in this manner...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Enneads. In the previous section, the discussion focused on the celestial movements as signs. Here, Ficino explores the metaphysical hierarchy of the universe—from the "Good" down to the physical body—and explains how "evil" is actually a necessary part of the cosmic harmony.</meta>

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...he then grasps the causes of the universe. The cause of evils, however, is considered in two ways: one by the logic of consequence, the other by the logic of the end. For just as a lesser good follows from a greater good, and again the smallest follows the lesser in a long sequence, so also evils happen at the level of the smallest things. Furthermore, just as in a musical harmony the fourth note—or indeed the second and seventh, which would not harmonize on their own—together with the consonant notes create a more pleasing harmony; so in the order of things, lesser goods with greater ones, the smallest with the lesser, and evils with the smallest, make the common good of the whole more admirable. What then? You may find that those things which seem evil in this instance or toward this purpose, are found to be good in that instance or toward that purpose; in short, all things lead toward the common good of the universe. After this, he posits three "craftsmen" <note>The <term>artifices</term> or "craftsmen" refer to the creative principles in Neoplatonic thought, often called the Three Hypostases.</note> of the world. First, indeed, the divine intellect; second, the animate intellect and intellectual soul; and third, the image of this soul, which is life, thence dedicated to the body. In this matter, as Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a major Neoplatonist who systematized these hierarchies.</note> testifies, Porphyry agrees with Plotinus. But why does he not call "the Good" itself a craftsman? Because the patterns of works exist within the craftsman. But since in the Good itself there is the simplest unity, he does not dare to place the pattern of the world—which is multiple—therein; rather, Plato and Plotinus call the Good both the father of the worldly craftsman and the end [goal] of the worldly work. It is as if the son, pregnant with the love of the paternal Good, creates the world for the sake of the Good and conforms it to the Good. Thus, the Good itself generates the intellectual world; this world indeed procreates the animate world; this, similarly, the natural world; and the natural world, the corporeal world. One flows from another almost as one circle in water depends upon another; and just as light comes from light, splendor from light, heat from splendor, and generation proceeds from heat. The Intellect, in procreating the intellectual soul, in no way departs from the father; rather, through its union with the father, it possesses the power and act of creation. Similarly, the intellectual soul, insofar as it leans upon the highest Intellect, overflows from there and pours out into the other. This other, in turn—that is, the corporeal life—insofar as it depends upon the soul of which it is an image, is filled with "seeds" <note>Ficino uses <term>semina</term> (seeds) to describe the "Logoi" or formative principles that organize physical matter.</note> and fills the matter of this world with similar forms. The Good itself exceeds any "state"; for if a state exists within the Good and by the grace of the Good, then the Intellect itself exists as a state; the intellectual soul is judged to be the first stable thing. But "Life," the image of this soul, is indeed stable insofar as it exists from it, but mobile by accident, insofar as it is coupled with the body, which is properly mobile. Plotinus calls this kind of life the "seminary" <note>original: "seminarium"</note> of the world, which the ancients called an "image" that is always engaged in assimilation. For this is called not so much a "soul" as an "image of the soul." For as much as it approaches matter—which is alien to the intellectual source—so much does it degenerate from the intellectual soul. The seeds in it are also not so much "reasons" as they are "images of reasons." For if reason, according to its form, properly consists in the intellectual soul, then in the lower life it is rightly only an image of reason. For who would call that "true reason" which, being ignorant of itself, has no account <note>original: "rationem"; a pun on "reason" and "account/reckoning."</note> of itself? This life, therefore, is a certain image, full only of images; this image has always attained the likeness of its pattern, and always attains it. Again, it is always being fashioned and is perpetually formed; by this reasoning, the very act of the seeds seems to flourish at different times; yet they always correspond to the pattern. Thus, the life is rolled along, as it were, together with the body of the world; and finally, together with the celestial revolution, both the mind is affected and imagines in various ways, and outwardly it is always clothed in other figures. Perhaps Plotinus, with these words, touches upon the opinion of Heraclitus and Timaeus, who say that this world manifest to our eyes never "is," but is perpetually "becoming." <note>Heraclitus famously argued that all things are in flux (Panta Rhei).</note> In every way, just as water is shaped under a seal, but the shape does not remain once the seal is removed—and therefore the shape seems not so much to be made "once" as to be "always being made," especially if the water flows continually beneath it—so it is with matter in relation to nature, and nature in turn to the fertile intellectual soul. To that extent, Plotinus wishes this world to "become," or to "be," insofar as the image of the soul flows from the soul, and the soul proceeds from the mind, and the mind is generated from the Good, and finally, the Good lasts as long as it is itself "the Good," and the intellect as long as it exists as "the intellect." While these things remain so, the things following from them naturally always either remain or flow forth, just as light comes from the sun, and subsequently light from light.

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. II.

<margin>
If the stars are inanimate, they only produce bodily effects; if they are animate, they do not cause evils.
</margin>

->A<-

**IN THE FIRST PLACE**, we must consider whether the celestial bodies are animate—that is, possessing a soul—or the opposite. For if those bodies which are carried through the heavens lack a soul, they will be able to bring about nothing other than heat and cold and similar physical states, provided we even grant that those stars can be cold. Thus, they will only propagate their actions and functions as far as the nature of our own bodies; for in that case, only a bodily impulse could reach us from them. This would mean that not even much diversity of bodies would happen because of them, 

->B<-

since the outflow from each would be the same, and they would be mixed together into one on the earth. In such a scenario, diversity would only arise according to the variety of locations—a diversity born from the fact that something is exposed either closer to or further from the influx, and thus receives it differently. The same logic would apply if cold were admitted among these influences. But how these stars could produce wise men and ignorant ones, or make some men grammarians, others orators, and others musicians, or cause them to differ in the other arts, I do not see at all. 

->C<-

Similarly, there are other things that can in no way have the cause of their occurrence from a mere mixture of bodies: for instance, why you have such a brother, such a father, or such a son and wife; or finally, why prosperous things sometimes succeed for you, and you are now designated a leader of an army or obtain a kingdom. 

->D<-

But if the celestial bodies are animate and act by deliberation, tell me, I pray, what injury have they received from us that would cause them to harm us daily of their own accord? This is especially difficult to believe since they are placed in a divine seat and are divine themselves. For those things that cause men to become evil do not happen to them; nor does any good or evil happen to them at all as a result of human prosperity or adversity.

<margin>
Stars do not change their nature by character, locations, or emotions.
</margin>

->E<-

**THEY WILL PERHAPS SAY** that the stars do not do such things of their own will, but are compelled by their positions and configurations. But if they are compelled, it would be necessary for all stars to do the same things whenever they are in the same locations and configurations. Yet now, what difference does this planet experience while it passes through this degree or that degree of the <term>zodiac<note>The 'zodiac' refers to the belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs, which ancient astrologers believed influenced human fate.</note></term>? Or what difference does that one experience? For a planet is not actually *in* the zodiac itself, but is far distant beneath it; in whatever portion it passes through, it remains similarly in the heavens. 

->F<-

For it is ridiculous that a planet should become of one nature and then another according to every tiny portion of the sky it traverses, and exhibit different effects one after another. Likewise, it is absurd to claim it has one nature when it rises and is in an <term>angle<note>In ancient astrology, an 'angle' refers to the four most powerful points in a chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.</note></term>, and another when it <term>declines<note>To 'decline' or 'cadence' means the planet is moving away from a powerful angle, traditionally interpreted as a weakening of its influence.</note></term>. It does not feel joy when it is in an angle, nor does it feel pain or torment when it declines. Nor again does it grow fierce when another planet rises, or become gentle when it sinks. Yet they say one among them becomes better when it declines. Indeed, any star is always "angular" to some people and "falling" to others at the exact same time; 

->G<-

likewise, it is falling for some and in turn angular for others. Surely it does not feel delight and sorrow, or anger and calmness, at the same moment. Furthermore, their claim that some stars rejoice in their setting while others rejoice in their rising seems absurd. For it would happen that the same star would be delighted and sorrowful at once. Moreover, why should their sorrow bring evil to us? In truth, we must not concede that they feel pain or temporary delight; rather, they are always

->D<-

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's critique of astrological determinism. On the previous page, he questioned how physical bodies like stars could produce complex human traits. ### BOOK THREE.

<column-break/>

...tranquil, rejoicing in the good things they have and see. Indeed, the life of each star exists within itself, and its excellence is found in its own activity. This excellence is not directed toward us; it does not belong to us, especially since we do not share a common life with those celestial beings. Nor is their work directed toward us at all, except perhaps by coincidence, just as birds signify things to us <note>original: "σημαίνειν" — to signify or give a sign through augury</note> by mere chance.

<margin>
**IV.**
Astrologers do not truly assign the natures of planets based on their aspects.
</margin>

**FURTHERMORE**, it seems absurd to say that one planet rejoices at the sight of another, while another is offended by a specific view. What kind of discord can exist between them, and over what? Moreover, why do they behave one way when they view each other in a **trine aspect** <note>original: "aspectu trino" — an astrological position where planets are 120 degrees apart, usually considered harmonious</note>, but differently when they look at each other from an opposing or **quadrate aspect** <note>original: "quadrato" — a 90-degree angle between planets, often considered a sign of conflict</note>? And why does a planet "see" another when configured in one way, yet when it moves to the next sign and is actually closer, it is said not to "see" it at all?

In general, how could they possibly bring about the effects attributed to them? How does each act individually, and how do they all act together to produce something entirely different? They certainly do not meet in council to deliberate on what they will do to us, with each one relaxing its duty a little, nor does one violently prevent the work of another, nor does one yield to another, having been persuaded to hand over its office. Finally, to say that one planet is delighted to be in the "house" of another, while another is "offended" by being received in such a place, seems as if one were to grant that two people are friends, but then assert that one loves the other while the other hates him in return.

<margin>
**V.**
They are mistaken about the natures of the planets.
</margin>

**THEY CLAIM** <note>original: "TRADVNT" — they hand down (referring to the teachings of astrologers)</note> that one of the planets is *extremely cold* <note>original: "ψυχρότατα" — very cold; likely referring to Saturn</note>, yet even when it is far from us, it is more beneficial to us, placing its "evil" cold in opposition to us. Yet, it ought to be that its goodness toward us exists when it is in the opposite signs of the zodiac. Furthermore, they say that when a cold planet is opposite a hot one, both become oppressive, even though a temperate balance <note>original: "temperantiā"</note> should result from this mixture.

Moreover, they say one planet delights in the day and becomes favorable through the sun's heat, while another, being fiery, rejoices in the night—as if it were not perpetually day (that is, light) up there, or as if one were "occupied" by the night, even though it is very far removed from the shadow of the earth.

As for what they say about the Moon—that she is good when full of light and bad when "empty" or waning—if we were to grant such a thing, the opposite should be said. For when she is full toward us, she is "empty" of light on her upper side facing the stars. Conversely, when she wanes for us, she is full on that other side. Therefore, she ought to produce the opposite effects when diminished, since she is then looking at the higher heavens with her light. Thus, for the Moon herself, it makes no difference how she appears to us, as she is always half-full of light; perhaps it matters to the one who is said to be "heated" by her. But she would provide heat even when her light is not visible to us. While she is good toward the other planet, being full on that side, she is "empty" toward us. Therefore, when that planet does not help because it is far away, the situation seems worse; but when she is full, it suffices because she is lower, even if that planet is far. When she is "empty" toward the fiery planet, she appears good toward us. For her own power is sufficient in itself...

<column-break/>

<summary>Plotinus critiques astrological logic, questioning why planets would "rejoice" or "hate" based on their geometric positions (aspects) and pointing out the logical flaws in attributing human-like moods to celestial bodies.</summary>

# 140 PLOTINUS, ENNEAD II.

<column-break/>

**A** ...as it is more fiery when compared to the other. The bodies of living beings flowing from that source are more or less hot among themselves, but none is truly cold; the very region [of the heavens] bears witness to this. Furthermore, the one they call Jupiter is well-tempered with fire, as is the morning star <note>original: "lucifer" — the planet Venus when appearing in the morning</note>; therefore, they seem to be in harmony through a certain similarity. As for the one called "the fiery one" <note>original: "pyroenta" / Mars</note>, it should be thought of as contributing to a specific tempering.

**B** Finally, it must be said that Saturn, because it is far away, behaves as a stranger. Lastly, what they say of Mercury—that it is indifferent to all—must be understood as meaning it easily becomes similar to all. Yet all these contribute to the whole; thus, they relate to one another as is expedient for the entirety, just as individual parts are arranged within a single living being. For it is for the sake of the whole that they are primarily positioned, just as bile <note>In ancient medicine, yellow bile was one of the four humors; here Plotinus argues even "negative" elements serve a cosmic purpose</note> contributes both to the whole and to its neighboring part. For it was necessary to stir the soul, and not allow either the whole or the nearby part to be affected by injuries; indeed, even in the universe such a thing was necessary, and another element besides was added for a more pleasant temperament.

**C** Other parts are like eyes; and all things in the irrational life of those parts suffer together in turn. For in this way, the whole is one, and the harmony of the whole is one. How, then, will these things not be certain signs considered through a specific proportion?

<margin>
**VI**
They err regarding the actions of the planets.
</margin>

**D** **FURTHERMORE**, what they say—that Mars or Venus, when arranged in a certain way, produce adulteries—is greatly at odds with reason. For that would be nothing other than those planets ardently satisfying their own mutual greed and need in the manner of human intemperance. Accordingly, what they say—that when they look upon each other in a certain condition, the sight is pleasing, but otherwise there is no limit for them—seems by no means grantable by reason. Likewise, since there are continually countless thousands of animals being born, in what way 

**E** do they always perform individual tasks for each one? Do they bring both glory and riches? Do they make people poor and incontinent? And do they effect the individual actions of every single person? What kind of life would those planets have? Or how can they accomplish so many and such diverse things? It is also said quite absurdly that they wait for the "ascensions" <term>ascension: the rising of a zodiac sign over the horizon</term> and returns of the signs again, and only then complete their appointed duty; and that however many degrees each one ascends, there are just as many years of ascension or return—counting on their fingers, as it were, when they are going to act, and not being permitted to act before that time.

**F** Finally, they ascribe the authority of government to no single one at all, but attribute everything to these planets, as if there were not one presiding Prince <note>Referring to the Platonic "One" or "Demiurge"</note> upon whom the universe depends, who distributes to each their own proper duties to be performed naturally, in which all things are subsequently coordinated in a similar way. This is surely the mark of a man who both dissolves the order in which he himself is numbered, and who is ignorant of the nature of the universe, which has a Principle and a First Cause propagating its power thoroughly through all things.

<margin>
**VII**
The meanings of the stars occur because of the wonderful connection of things in the world.
</margin>

**G** **MOREOVER**, if the stars portend future things, just as we are accustomed to observe many other signs of the future, what is it that makes all this happen? And in what way is the order maintained? For unless they proceeded in a certain fixed order, individual things could not be signified. Therefore, let them be like letters in the sky, which are either being written continuously, or having already been written, move—performing their own work and another...

<column-break/>

**A** ...more fiery, or being in relation to that. The bodies of living creatures coming from there, some are more or less hot than others, but none is cold. The place bears witness. Regarding the one they call <gloss>well-tempered</gloss>, it is unmixed with fire, and this is the morning star. Thus they seem harmonious by similarity. Regarding the one called "the fiery," by its mixture; regarding Saturn, it is alien because of its distance. Mercury is indifferent, appearing to liken itself to all.

**B** All are useful to the whole; so they are toward one another as is useful to the whole; as in a single animal each of the parts is seen, especially for the sake of this—such as bile—both to the whole and to what follows; and it was necessary to rouse spirit, both for the whole and so as not to allow the neighbor to be insulted. And indeed in the perfect whole, there was need of such a thing, and one for another for the sake of the pleasantness of the mixture.

**C** ...one part is the eye. All things are sympathetic to their irrational part. For thus there is one [whole] and one harmony. How then could these not be signs by analogy?

**D** But to suggest that Mars or Venus, if they are in such a position, cause adulteries—as if they were satisfying themselves from the licentiousness of men, as if <gloss>they desire one another</gloss> they have need of each other—how is that not much more irrational? And that for these gods, the sight of each other, if they are so positioned, is pleasant; but that there is no limit for them—how could anyone accept this? While countless myriads of animals are being born and existing, <gloss>to each</gloss> to perform for each, and to give something with them—making some rich, some poor, some licentious—and that they themselves perform the activities of each: what kind of life is that for them? Or how is it possible to do so many things? And as for waiting for the "ascensions" of the zodiac signs and then acting, and how-

**E** <gloss>it extends</gloss> -ever many degrees; that each should extend for so many years of ascension, and to set it out as if on one's fingers when they will act, and that it is not permitted for them to act before these times. And generally to give the authority of administration to no single one, but to give everything to these, as if there were not one Overseer from whom the whole is suspended, giving to each

**F** the completion of its own task according to nature and the carrying out of its own activities. To suggest that things are coordinated with him [the One] while [the astrologers] dissolve and ignore the nature of the world—which has a beginning and a first cause going through all things.

**G** But if these signify what is to be, just as we say many other things are significant of the future, what would be the cause? And how is the order? For <gloss>it signified in an orderly way</gloss> it would not signify in an orderly way if each thing were not happening. Let them be, then, like letters being written in the heaven always, or written and moving, doing their own work and another...

# BOOK THREE.

<column-break/>

...something else, and let the following follow from it: the meaning provided by them <note>The stars and celestial bodies</note>, as if from a single principle in one living being, is found in another part. Furthermore, one might learn of a person's character or even the dangers and paths to safety they face by looking into their eyes or some other part of the body. For those parts are not merely isolated pieces, nor are we; rather, all things are full of signs, and a wise person is one who learns one thing from another. Many things that occur through habit are already known to everyone. What, then, is this single coordination? It is the same as the logic found in the flight of birds and other animals from which we receive signs for various things. Indeed, all things must be linked to one another. And this is not only true in the way individual things are connected—a **single shared breath** <note>original: "sympnoia mia" — a Stoic term Plotinus uses to describe the "sympathy" or interconnectedness of all parts of the universe</note>—but it is much more and primarily true in the context of the whole. And from one principle, do not imagine many living things, but a single one that is not one of all. Just as in each individual the parts exist—not each for a different task—so too in the whole, each thing has its own task, and even more so than these. For they are not only parts, but also wholes and greater things. Indeed, each thing proceeds from one principle, performing its own task, and everything contributes to one another; nothing is ever truly separated from the whole. It both acts and is acted upon by others; one thing approaches and causes pain or pleasure, and it does not act randomly or by chance. For something else comes from these, and another follows sequentially according to nature.

<margin>* he might decline / again</margin>
And indeed the **Soul**, having been set in motion to perform its own work—for the soul performs everything, possessing the principle of reason—proceeds to wherever it may go. Furthermore, there is justice for what is done in the universe, which will not be dissolved but remains forever. The whole is kept upright in order and by the power of the one who rules it. The stars also work together, as they are significant parts of the heavens contributing to the whole, both for its beauty and for the purpose of giving signs. Therefore, they signify all things that occur to those with senses, and they clearly perform other actions. We, however, perform the works of the soul according to nature, as long as we do not stumble within the vastness of the universe. If we do stumble, we face justice, and the error itself leads to a worse fate in the future. Now, wealth and poverty are matters of external chance; but virtues and vices—virtues exist because of the ancient nature of the soul, while vices are accidents resulting from the soul’s contact with external things. But concerning these matters, it has been discussed elsewhere.

<margin>he might follow</margin>
Now, however, we must call to mind that **spindle** <note>original: "atrakton" — the Spindle of Necessity from the Myth of Er in Plato’s Republic, which represents the mechanism of the cosmos and fate</note> which the Fates of old spin. For Plato, the spindle represents both the wandering <note>the planets</note> and the non-wandering <note>the fixed stars</note> parts of the cosmic revolution; and the Fates, and Necessity who is their mother, turn it, and it does not follow the will of each individual.

<column-break/>

...let them be explained openly, performing some other work: from which follows the significance of things produced by them. Just as in a single living being, can one not judge one thing from another member based on a single principle? For indeed, who can guess a person's character by rightly considering the eyes or another part of the body? Or even the dangers and the avoiding of those dangers? These are parts of our body, and we are parts of the world. Therefore, some things serve others. Truly, **all things are full of signs**, and a wise person argues one thing from another. Many things, indeed, are known to all through daily habit. What, then, is the mutual order of all things? It is in this way that it is consistent for omens to have power in augury <note>The practice of interpreting signs from nature, like the flight of birds</note>; and indeed in other animals from which we predict individual events. It is necessary, therefore, that all things be ordered together and depend upon one another. For not only does a single harmony thrive in any of those things which are best connected, but much more so, and primarily, in the universe. There, it is necessary that from one principle the manifold animal itself becomes one—one, I say, constituted of all. And just as in each individual part any part has its own work, so too in the universe individual works are assigned to individual things; and much more so because these are not only parts, but are also wholes and greater things. Each thing, therefore, proceeds from one principle, performing its own task, and some things are useful to others everywhere. For nothing is anywhere separated from the form of the whole: they act and suffer in turn, and something approaches each thing, by which it is either helped or offended. They proceed, however, not randomly, nor however it happens to fall: for something else is produced from these, and another thing naturally in sequence, and another follows.

<margin>VIII. The Soul of the world is the principle of natural things. All rational souls have freedom of choice.</margin>
Now indeed, the **soul**, while it acts by beginning its own task—for the soul does all things, having reason as its principle—proceeds for the most part rightly. But if, being led elsewhere, it should prevaricate, it follows the course of those things produced in the world by a certain judgment, unless perhaps it is released. For the judgment itself always remains: since the universe is ruled and directed by the order and power of the ruler. The stars serve and contribute to this, like no small parts of heaven: both for the beautiful form of the whole, and also for the duty of signification. Thus they portend all things that arise in the sensible world, and they clearly do whatever else they do. We, however, perform the works of the soul according to nature, as long as we do not wander and slip in that multitude of the whole. When we wander, however, we pay the penalty to judgment, namely both the error itself and a certain worse lot that will come to us in the future. Riches, therefore, and poverty happen by the meeting of external things; but what of virtues and vices? Virtues indeed exist because of that which is more ancient and excellent in the soul; but vices come from a certain commerce of the soul with external things. But concerning these, it has been said elsewhere.

<margin>IX. The soul which dwells in us depends on heaven and is subject to fate; but that which is given to us by God is free from fate and is all-powerful.</margin>
In the present, however, it is worthwhile to recall that **spindle** which the Fates twist among the ancients, by which Plato signifies that which is called "wandering" or "not wandering" in the circuit of the world. This, according to him, the Fates and **Necessity**, the mother of the Fates, twist and roll together in the generation of each person, and...
