He argues that while our souls are subject to cosmic order and "fate" when entangled with external things, they possess an inherent virtue from an ancient, divine source.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the influence of the heavens. Having established that the universe is a single living organism where all parts act as signs for one another, he now addresses a challenge from Plato’s Timaeus: if the "wandering gods" (the planets) shape our lower nature and passions, is there any part of the human soul that remains free from the stars and the grip of Fate?</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD II. I.

<column-break/>

**A** From this circuit and revolution, all things that are born come forth into generation. In the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the cosmos</note>, the **Craftsman of the world** <note>The Demiurge or creator god</note> also hands down the principle of the soul itself; but the "traveling gods" <note>the planets</note> bring to it grave and necessary **passions** <note>original: *passiones* / *pathê* — in this context, these are "undergoings" or external influences rather than just emotions</note>: angers, lusts, pleasures, pains, and another species of soul from which such disturbances arise. These words of Plato certainly seem to bind us to the stars, implying that we receive our souls from them. Likewise, they seem to subject us to necessity as we fall into this realm. He says that from these same stars we possess our **B** characters, and according to those characters, even our actions and passions proceed from a certain passive habit. Therefore, we must inquire: what else are we besides this? Perhaps what remains is what we truly are: those to whom nature gave the power to master these passions. For besides the fact that we are surrounded by these evils due to the nature of the body, God has granted a **virtue** <note>original: *virtutem* / *aretê*</note> that is entirely free from servitude. We do not need virtue when we are placed in a safe state, but rather when a crisis of evil looms in its absence. **C** For this reason, we must flee from here and segregate ourselves from those things which are joined to us in generation. We must take care lest we happen to be that very thing which is **composed**—namely, the animated body—in which the nature of the body prevails, having caught a certain trace of the soul, so that this common life belongs primarily to the body. For whatever belongs to this life is corporeal. But to the other soul, which exists externally, belongs the ascent to the sublime—that is, to the beautiful and the divine, over which **D** nothing anywhere holds dominion. Indeed, the mind uses its power so that it might escape to that very place, and it lives according to this when it receives itself back into itself. But whoever is devoid of the soul thus established now lives in **Fate** <note>original: *fatum* / *heimarmenê*</note>. In this habit of life, the stars do not only signify things for a man, but he himself becomes like a part of the universe, and he serves the whole of which he is a part, not without injury. **E** For every person is **double**: partly comprising both <note>The body and the lower soul</note> within himself, and partly existing as his true self. The whole world is also this way: partly a composite of a body and a soul enslaved to that body, and partly the Soul of the All itself, which is not *in* the body, but rather imprints certain traces upon the soul that lies within the body. The Sun and the rest of the stars are similarly double. And while that other soul which is pure brings nothing evil or base, **F** those things which are done through the universe by them—insofar as they are parts of the universe (namely because they are both a body and an animated body)—proceed as parts. Meanwhile, by its own choice, the star and its true soul look toward that which is best. Other things follow from this; or rather, not so much from the soul itself as from the things around it, just as many things are produced from a fire by the heat **G** diffused everywhere from it, or if something flows from one soul into another kindred soul. Troublesome or difficult and adverse things are born in the world because of a certain mixture; for the nature of this world is mixed. And if one were to separate the soul from it, the remainder would be seen as nothing great.

<column-break/>

**A** ...of it into generation are the things that are produced. As in the *Timaeus*: God who made the world gives the beginning of the soul; but the traveling gods give the terrible and necessary passions—angers and desires, pleasures and pains again—and another form of soul from which these passions come. For these words seem to bind us to the stars, as we receive a soul from them and fall under **Necessity** <note>original: *anangkê*</note> when coming here; and thus we have characters from them, **B** and according to these characters our actions and passions come from a passionate habit. So what is left for us to be, or rather, who are we in truth? We are those to whom nature gave the power to rule over the passions. For even though we are involved in foul evils because of the body, God gave us **undominated virtue** <note>original: *adespoton aretên* — virtue that has no master and is inherently free</note>. For we do not need virtue when in a quiet state, but when there is danger of being in evils, virtue not being present. <margin>* hence indeed</margin> **C** Therefore one must flee *from here, and separate oneself from the things attached to us, lest we be the **composite** <margin>* animated</margin> **animated body** in which the nature of the body rather rules, having taken a certain trace of soul, so that the shared life is more of the body. For all things are corporeal, as many as belong to this. But of the other soul, the one outside, the movement is toward the heights, the beautiful, and the divine, which no one masters, **D** but it is nearby, so that it may live according to that, having withdrawn. But he who is deserted by this soul lives in **Fate**. And here the stars do not only signify to him, but he himself becomes as a part, and follows the whole of which he is a part. <margin>* the composite something</margin> For each is **double**: one, *the composite; the other, the self. And the whole world too: one is the thing from body and a certain soul **E** bound to the body; the other is the Soul of the All, which is not in the body, but shines traces upon the soul in the body. And the sun and the others are double in this way. And to the one, the pure soul, they give nothing base; but the things that happen in the whole from them, insofar as they are parts of the whole—body, and <margin>* animated</margin> **animated body**—give parts according to the choice of the star, and its **F** soul which truly looks toward the best. But other things follow it; or rather not it, but the things around it; just as from fire <margin>* and it supervenes</margin> comes heat going into the whole, *and it supervenes upon another soul, into another soul that is kindred. But the difficult things are because of the mixture; for the nature of the whole is indeed mixed; and if one should separate the separable soul from it, the remainder is not great. God indeed is that soul **G** being joined together. But the remainder, he says, is a **part-daemon**; and the passions in it are daemonic.

If anyone should separate its soul in some way...
For the World is only a god if that separable soul is numbered in its substance. For the remainder is a **daemon**, which Plato called the **Great Daemon** <note>A reference to the *Symposium*, where a daemon is an intermediary between gods and men</note>; the affections in it are likewise daemonic.

<summary>Plotinus argues that while our physical bodies and lower impulses are influenced by the stars and Fate, the "true self" is a higher, separable soul that possesses inherent freedom and virtue. He characterizes the physical world without this higher soul as a "Great Daemon" rather than a true God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the influence of the heavens on human life. Having previously discussed the stars as "signs," he now shifts to whether they are "causes" of our behavior and whether the "evils" of the world originate in the celestial spheres.</meta>

### SECOND BOOK.

<column-break/>

**A** If this is how things are, we must now grant that the stars provide signs. As for their actual effects, we should not grant them entirely, nor to all of them, but only to the extent of the passions of the whole <note>The physical universe</note>, and whatever remains of them. We must also grant that the soul, even before entering into **becoming** <note>original: *genesis* — the process of being born into the physical world</note>, arrives by its own nature from itself; for it would not come into a body unless it already possessed something capable of being affected. We must also grant that its fortunes come from there, in the sense that it enters at the moment of the universe's movement. Finally, we must grant that the movement of the universe itself acts as a co-worker and fulfills from itself what the whole must complete, since each of the parts within it has received its own rank and order.

It is necessary to keep this in mind: that which comes from the stars is not the same when it reaches those who receive it as it was when it left the stars. For instance, if there is fire there, it becomes dim here; if there is a feminine disposition <note>Associated with receptivity or softness in ancient thought</note> that becomes weak, **B** it was not made that way for the receiver by some friendly act. Similarly, a certain anger, which if measured might have suited a brave man, instead produces irritability or despondency. Even the desire for boldness, if it possesses beauty in a lesser way, produces a craving for things that only *seem* beautiful. And the "outflowing" of mind produces cunning; for cunning wants to be "intellect," but it is unable to achieve what it desires. Thus, each of these becomes "evil" in us here, even if they were **Δ** lights there; and yet, they are not those same lights. Nor do they remain the same once they have arrived, being mixed with bodies, matter, and one another.

<margin>to make one</margin>
**Ε** Furthermore, the things that come down fall into a single mixture, and each thing that is born carries away something from this blend. Thus, the celestial influence is harmonized to "make one" <note>To contribute to the unity of the organism</note>; for it does not "make" the horse, but gives something *to* the horse. For a horse comes from a horse, and a man from a man, while the Sun acts as a helper in the shaping. The man himself comes from the **reason-principle** <note>original: *logos* — the formative, logical blueprint of a species</note> of man; but external factors sometimes hinder or help. Likewise, a son is usually similar to his father, but often it turns out for the better, and sometimes for the worse, though it never departs entirely from the underlying subject. Sometimes **matter** <note>The raw, chaotic "stuff" of the universe</note> prevails rather than nature, so that the result is not perfect, or is a defect of the form.

<margin>thus through</margin>
**F** Therefore, since some things happen because of the celestial movement and others do not, we must distinguish and decide where each thing comes from. The starting principle is this: the Soul governs this entire universe according to reason, just as in any individual animal, the principle of life within it shapes each part and coordinates them toward the whole. All things are in the whole; but in the parts, there is only as much as belongs to each part. As for things approaching from the outside, some are contrary to the will of nature, while others are suitable. But for the whole, all things are coordinated as parts **G** of it. They possess the nature they have received and fulfill their own impulses, yet they contribute to the total life of the universe...

<column-break/>

<margin>The stars produce only corporeal things, but the soul by itself enters into fate and fortune.</margin>
If the matter stands thus, we must now also concede that the stars have significance. However, their "effects" should not be granted entirely, nor to all of them, but only insofar as they concern the remainder of their physical nature. Again, we must admit that the soul, even before it reaches the state of being born, descends while carrying something from itself; for it would not come down into a body unless it possessed a passive quality, and a great one at that. We must admit that "fortunes" happen to the one entering a body because of this very fact: that it enters according to the course of the universe. Finally, we must admit that the course of the world acts in such a way that it assists in the work and fulfills from itself those things which are to be performed by the whole; for those things which are in the course of the universe itself obtain the order of parts.

<margin>XI. The evils that happen here are not sent as evils from heaven.</margin>
**C** Nor indeed should it escape us that what proceeds from the heavenly bodies does not turn out exactly the same in those who receive it as it was when it departed from the higher powers. For example, if there is a fire in us that has degenerated far from the celestial fire, or an affection inclined toward loving that has become weaker in us, it produces a love that is not honorable. Likewise, when spiritedness happens to exceed the measure necessary for courage, it procreates irritability, fury, or sluggishness. Thus, the study of true honor and honesty can become a craving for things that merely *appear* beautiful and honest. Thus, a "downflow" of mind begets cunning; for cunning emulates the mind because it wishes to obtain what it is not powerful enough to reach. Therefore, while these individual things are not "evils" among the higher powers, they happen to be evils among us. For the things that come from there are neither the same as those higher things, nor do they remain as they were when they first arrived, being mixed as they are with bodies, matter, and one another.

<margin>XII. Things are generated primarily by the feminine reason-principles of nature; celestial influx arranges the matter.</margin>
Furthermore, the things that come from there converge into a unity, and from this mixture, whatever is born contracts something of it. From this, that which "is" exists, and turns out to be such a thing. For the celestial influx does not "make" the horse, but gives something to the horse; for a horse is generated from a horse, and a man from a man. The Sun, however, approaches this formation as a helper. A man is made from the **seminary reason-principle** <note>The "seed-logic" or biological blueprint</note> of a man; yet in such a way that what is external either hinders or assists. For a son usually turns out like his parent, but often for the better, and sometimes it happens to be for the worse, yet he is never led away from the subject itself. Sometimes matter prevails rather than nature, to the point that the effect does not come out perfect—specifically when the **Form** <note>The ideal "species" or essence</note> is overcome by the matter.

<margin>XIII. Concerning the common life and action of the world: they also live their own lives and have their own actions.</margin>
Next, since some things are done by the movement of the world and others are not at all, it is necessary to distinguish, judge, and explain from where each thing truly originates. The principle, therefore, shall be this: the Soul governs this whole by reason, just as in any animal the principle of life itself is that from which the individual limbs of the living being are formed and ordered toward the whole of which they are parts. In the whole, indeed, are all things; but in the parts, there is only as much as belongs to each one. Those things which approach from the outside are partly contrary to the natural appetite and partly in agreement with it; yet all things harmonize with the whole itself as if they were its members on every side, having obtained the nature they possess and simultaneously filling the whole life of the universe with their own impulse.

# 144 PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. BOOK II.

<margin>
14. He assigns the causes of human affairs apart from the stars, even in those cases where such things are signified by the stars.
</margin>

**A** Therefore, those things in the world which are inanimate are entirely the instruments of others, and are, so to speak, driven to action from the outside. Those which are animate, if they lack reason, possess an indeterminate motion, much like horses pulling a chariot before the charioteer has prescribed their course, seeing as they are driven, as it were, by a whip. However, the nature of a rational living being has a charioteer within itself; if it possesses a skilled one, it is carried straight forward for the most part and does not wander by chance, as often happens. **B** Both types of beings are within the world and contribute to the whole. Those which are greater and more excellent in their rank perform many great deeds and contribute from every side to the very life of the whole; they are allotted a role of acting rather than being acted upon. Many others, however, are occupied with being acted upon, possessing very little power for action. Those in the middle are indeed acted upon by others, but they frequently act upon other things themselves, as they possess the principle of action and doing within themselves.

**C** For this reason, the whole world becomes a universal and perfect life, while the best parts perform the best actions, insofar as there is something "best" in each. This "best" part must be considered a colleague to the leader of the whole, just like the fellow-soldiers to a general, who are said by Plato <note>A reference to Plato's *Phaedrus* 246e, where a "mighty leader in heaven, Zeus, driving a winged chariot" is followed by an army of gods and souls.</note> to follow Jove <note>original: *Iouem* — the Roman name for the Greek god Zeus</note> as he advances into the intelligible nature. But those things which are established in a lower grade of nature occupy a secondary place in the universe, and are much like the secondary powers of the soul within us; **D** all other things likewise behave like our lowest parts. For not everything within us is equal. Therefore, all living things exist or come to be according to the total <term>reason</term> <note>original: *rationem* / *logon* — here meaning the "formative principle" or blueprint of the universe</note> of the universe—both those in heaven and whatever is distributed throughout the whole. No part, even a great one, has the power to disturb the <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>original: *rationes seminarias* / *logoi spermatikoi* — the active spiritual germs or blueprints that direct the growth of the physical world</note> of the world from their order, nor to change those things which proceed according to such reasons out of their own species.

And although it may bring about a certain change, sometimes for the better and sometimes for the worse, it cannot push a thing out of its own proper nature. **F** It makes things worse either by bringing weakness to the body, or to the soul—insofar as a cause of depravity arises by accident in that soul which is "co-suffering" <note>original: *compatiente* — meaning the soul is influenced by the physical conditions it is linked to</note> and handed down from the higher to the lower—or when a body is poorly composed, an obstacle is brought to the action of the soul being fulfilled through the body. This is as if a lyre were not so composed and tuned that it could sustain a perfect harmony to produce musical tones.

**E** But what should be said concerning poverty and wealth, glory and power? Perhaps if wealth proceeded from parents, the heavenly bodies signified that the person would be wealthy, just as they merely declared one to be high-born who derives glory from his lineage. **G** Where, however, wealth is acquired by the excellence of virtue, if the body supplied the strength for it, then surely those who provided strength to the body contributed to the accumulation of wealth. First, the parents, and then if any region has a propitious sky; to this is added the fertility of a healthy land. But if virtue increased one's money without the benefit of the body, then in this matter, the credit must be given chiefly to virtue alone. And whatever divine rewards are paid back, they have occurred. Where, however, men have given...

<column-break/>

<margin>* in it</margin>
Therefore, the inanimate things *in it* <note>original: *en autēi* — referring to the world/universe</note> are all instruments, and are, as it were, pushed from the outside to act. But of the animate, some have an indeterminate motion, like horses under a chariot before the charioteer has defined their course for them, being driven by the lash. But the nature of a rational animal has the charioteer from itself. And if it has a knowledgeable one, it is carried straight; if not, often just as it happens. Both are inside the whole and contribute to the whole; and those of them that are greater and of higher worth do many great things, and contribute to the life of the whole, having a rank that is active rather than passive. But those that are passive continue having little power for acting. Those between these are acted upon by others, but do many things among many, having the principle for their deeds and actions from themselves. And the whole becomes a complete life, with the best parts performing the best things, insofar as the best is in each. This must be ranked with the leading principle, just as soldiers with a general, who are also said to follow Zeus as he goes toward the intelligible nature. But those that employ a lesser nature have a second place in the whole, like the secondary parts of the soul in us. And the others are analogous to the parts in us; for among us, not all things are equal. All living things, then, are according to the <term>reason</term> <note>original: *logon*</note> of the whole, both all those in heaven and the others as many as are partitioned into the whole. And none of the parts, not even a great one, has the power to work a change in the reasons, nor in the things that happen according to the reasons. It can work an alteration toward both the worse and the better, but it cannot displace a thing from its own nature. It works for the worse, either like a weakness in the body, or in the soul through the sympathy given to it as it descends by accident, becoming a cause of baseness, or when the body is badly put together, it goes as an obstacle to the soul's performing its own activity in it.
<margin>* having tuned</margin>
For instance, a lyre might not be *tuned* <note>original: *harmosasēs* — correcting the text's *harpasasthai* (to seize)</note> so as to receive the accuracy of harmony, in order to produce musical sounds.

Regarding poverty and wealth, and glory and power, how is it? Either if the wealth was signaled from parents, it [the sign] signaled the wealth; just as it only showed the well-born man among such people because of his famous lineage. But if it has come from manly excellence with the body as a co-worker, those who granted strength to the body would contribute—parents first, then if perhaps any of the places had the heavenly bodies [favorably], and the earth. But if virtue [attained it] without the body, one must grant the creation of it to virtue itself, as many things as were contributed by those who repay it; we would be the good people who have given...

### BOOK THREE.

**A** Similarly, the cause of these things <note>referring to wealth and status discussed on the previous page</note> must be assigned. If people are wicked, yet they have given justly, we must consider that this benefit arose from something "best" within them that acts. But if the person who gathered wealth is evil, we must judge that their primary cause was their own wickedness, along with whatever caused that wickedness. Furthermore, those who contributed to that wealth should be included in the order of causes. Likewise, if an abundance of goods comes from labor, as happens in agriculture, the cause should be attributed to the farmer, as well as the fertility of the soil and the mercy of the heavens. But if one finds a treasure, it must be thought that something from the whole universe concurred to that end; nor is it strange if these things are indicated by certain signs. For all things follow one another entirely, and therefore can be signified everywhere. If someone throws away their wealth, they themselves are

**B** the cause; if it is stolen, the thief is the cause. If the loss occurs through a shipwreck, many factors flowing together provided the cause of the damage. Reputation is held either justly or unjustly: if justly, it is gained both by one's duties and the fairness of those who judge; if unjustly, it proceeds from the injustice of those who grant the honor. The same

**C** reasoning applies to power <note>original: "imperio" / "ἀρχῆς"</note>: for it is possessed either honorably or the opposite. One case has its cause in the fairness of those who chose the leader, or pertains to the one who attained it through the gathering of others and the favor of friends, or however else it may stand. Marriage is brought about either by choice, or by chance, or a confluence of all

**D** these factors. The generation of children follows these things, and the fetus is formed according to the "seminal reason" <note>term: seminal reason (ratio seminaria/λόγος); the Stoic and Neoplatonic concept of a formative "blueprint" or "seed-logic" that directs growth</note> provided there is no hindrance; or it turns out poorly if some internal obstacle interferes, or through a defect in the one conceiving, or by a disposition of the environment <note>original: "continentis" / "περιέχοντος"</note> that is adverse to this particular conception.

**E** When PLATO, before the circuit of the world-spindle <note>referring to the "Spindle of Necessity" in the Myth of Er from Plato's Republic</note>, brought forward certain "Lots" and choices as helping factors, he then described the powers or Lots upon the spindle itself, by which those things that were chosen are fulfilled; since a "daemon" <note>term: daemon (δαίμων); not an evil spirit, but a personal guiding spirit or guardian assigned to a soul</note> also approaches as a confirmer to fulfill these same things. But what are these "Lots"? Perhaps by "Lots" is signified the disposition of the universe as it was at the moment the souls set out to enter a body. Likewise, it signifies entering *this* specific kind of body, and under *such* parents. Furthermore, being born in such a region, or what I was saying in summary: the confluence of external things. **G** For it must not be thought that the soul is such that it merely carries back a nature exactly like whatever passion it received from external things, as if it possessed no nature of its own. <margin>B</margin>
Furthermore, we must next seek—making a new beginning—what the "mixture" is, what is not, what is separable, and what is inseparable when it is in the body, and in general, what a "living being" is. <margin>C</margin>
But first, does it see fire and earth, and then all these things running together, either destroying or helping one another, and only see the complication made from all these, and the accidents merely in summary? Truly, it does not notice or act upon those things which are accustomed to happen to these one by one in succession, but only regenerates the primary animals again: and it leaves those which are born subject to the passions they inflict upon one another.

<margin>D</margin>
Or shall we say that the soul is also the cause of the effects that arise in this way, because the things that follow are produced and act from the soul itself? Is it possible that the seminal reason of the soul also contains within itself something of this kind: to do such individual things and to suffer such things? And so, none of these things happen by chance or by accident, but occur by necessity. If this is so, do the "reasons" themselves do these things? Or rather, are the reasons not like agents, but like knowers?

<margin>E</margin>
On the contrary, does the soul, containing such generative reasons, know whatever proceeds from all its works? For when the same circumstances coincide and surround them, it is entirely consistent that the same effects should occur. The soul, grasping or foreseeing these, determines and connects those things which follow in them. It therefore notices and cares for the preceding and following things entirely, and again looks upon those which follow the preceding ones, as if from the things that came before: from which, perhaps, the things that follow become continually worse; as some men lived once, but now others live, while meanwhile the reasons yield to the passions of matter through a certain perpetual necessity of distance and degeneration.

<margin>F</margin>
Does the soul, therefore, always look at different things, and continuously follow the individual passions of its works, and lead such a life? Is its care never free from the instant demands of its individual works, nor does it impose a prescribed end on its work—as if it had not thought out once and for all by what method its handiwork might always proceed rightly? Is it instead like a farmer, who not only sows and plants, but continuously corrects and restores what the winter rains, or the cold, or the whirlwinds of the winds have devastated?

<margin>G</margin>

# THIRD BOOK.

**A** All things <note>original: "πάντα"</note> are contained within the Rational Principles <note>original: "λόγοις" / "rationibus". These are the formative blueprints of the universe.</note>, including destruction and the effects that proceed from vice. But truly, if things are so, we might say that even vices arise from these Principles; yet, in the arts and the principles of the arts, there is no error, nor is there anything contrary to the art, nor is there a destruction of the thing crafted according to that art. To this, someone will respond that nothing happens to the universe that is evil or contrary to nature; rather, that which seems worse must be conceded as being for the better. What then, if even that which is worse serves the whole, **B** and it is not necessary for all things to be beautiful? Since even opposites contribute to the perfection of the universe, the world cannot exist without them. Indeed, nature behaves similarly in individual living beings. Certainly, the Rational Principle necessarily brings forth and forms those things which are better; but those things which are less good lie within the Principles according to a certain potential <note>original: "δυνάμει" / "potentia"</note>, whereas they exist in actuality <note>original: "ἐνεργείᾳ" / "actu"</note> within the things that are born. Therefore, it is no longer necessary for the soul to do anything further, or to stir up the Principles: since matter, **C** through a certain concussion of the Principles coming from preceding things—which are in its possession—renders things worse; and yet, it is nonetheless overcome by the Principles so as to conceive better things. Therefore, one single beauty is produced from all, while individual things result one way from matter itself, and are contained and created another way within the Principles themselves.

<margin>* All things</margin>
<margin>* in</margin>
<margin>* of the physical [power]</margin>
<margin>* it is nourished, not by her reasoning</margin>
<margin>* being present</margin>
<margin>* as concerning herself and those things from such [a soul]</margin>

<margin>XVII Whether these seminal reasons, which are in the soul, are thoughts. Whether seminal reasons are thoughts, or any kind of motions.</margin>

**D** WE MUST ASK, whether these seminal reasons <note>original: "rationes seminales" / "λόγοι σπερματικοί". These are the biological and metaphysical "seeds" that contain the plan for a living thing's development.</note> which are in the soul are actually thoughts. But in what way would the soul act through thoughts? For the Principle acts in matter: and that which it effects naturally is neither an act of intellect, nor a vision, but a certain force that agitates matter. It does not truly "know," but only acts, like a stamp or a figure in water; just as a second circle flows from a circle made elsewhere. For it is the duty of the natural and generative power to act, provided that the chief power of the soul leads to it, insofar as it moves and forms the material and generative soul.
**E** But does it move and form it by a certain discourse of reason? If it acted by rational discourse, it would be referred elsewhere. Is it then directed toward some other thing? Or rather toward those things which are in itself? But if it is toward those things within, there is no need for a discourse of reason. For it will not form these by moving them, but because it contains the Principles within itself: for that is more powerful and more effective for acting in the soul; therefore, it acts according to the species <note>original: "species" / "εἶδος". Here meaning the formal essence or "blueprints" of things.</note>. It is necessary, therefore, that the soul itself, receiving the species from the Intellect, should pass them on.
**F** For the Intellect grants these to the Soul of the Universe: and the soul closest to the Intellect passes them from itself to the soul that follows after it, illuminating and forming it. This latter soul, led as if by the order of the higher one, creates the species; but it creates some without hindrance, and others while hindered, and these latter are therefore worse. Since, therefore, it has received the power to act, and was not previously imbued with the Principles, it does not only act according to what it received, but something else arises from itself, and that is undoubtedly worse. And it will indeed be a living thing, but a living thing that is now **G** imperfect, bearing its own life heavily, as if it were the lowest, and difficult, and wild: composed of worse matter, like a certain dreg of preceding things settling at the bottom. This matter is indeed bitter, and it makes things bitter: and such things will the soul itself also bring into the universe.

<margin>XVIII Whence evil, and what are the causes for the universe, and how.</margin>

ARE THE EVILS, therefore, which happen in the world, necessary because they follow from preceding things? Or because...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the cosmic order, specifically addressing how seemingly negative elements like vice and poison contribute to the perfection of the whole. It transitions into Marsilio Ficino's commentary on the nature of "Matter" in both the physical and divine realms.</meta>

<page-num>148</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS, ENNEAD II.</header>
<meta>catchword: Because</meta>

<margin>A</margin> ...do these things follow? Perhaps it is because if these were not present, the whole would be imperfect. For many evils—or rather, almost all of them—provide a certain utility to the whole; just like poisonous things, although the use and underlying reason for most of them remains hidden. Indeed, it is well established that even wickedness itself contains many useful things and produces many beautiful things, much like the skillful artistry found in beauty. It often rouses men to <margin>B</margin> prudence <note>The Greek term is "phronesis," a practical wisdom or mindfulness.</note> and does not allow them to grow numb in a state of careless freedom. If these things have been rightly stated, it is necessary for the soul of the whole to constantly contemplate the best things, rising toward the intelligible nature <note>The realm of pure thought and divine ideas.</note> and God. And when the soul itself is filled and has become full, it then overflows into its own image, which is the final and lowest level: this is a certain "ultimate maker" <note>This refers to the "Demiurge" or the generative power that shapes the physical world.</note>. Therefore, this is the final effector; but presiding over this is that which is first filled in the soul by the Intellect. Finally, the Intellect presides over all things as the artisan of the universe, who indeed pours forms into the soul closest to himself, the traces of which are imprinted <margin>C</margin> upon the third nature. Therefore, this world is rightly called an image, which is always in a state of being made like its original. The first and second <note>The Intellect and the Soul.</note> certainly stand firm; the third also stands firm, but in matter; and therefore it is mobile as if by accident. For as long as the Intellect and the soul exist, so long do the seminal reasons <note>term: "seminales rationes" (Logoi Spermatikoi). These are the formative blueprints or "seeds" that determine the structure of physical things.</note> flow out into this image of the soul. Just as as long as the sun itself shines, all lights flow forth from it.

<column-break/>

...if these things were not, the whole would simply be incomplete. For many of them, or even all, provide <margin>* to the whole</margin> a service to the Reason <note>original: "logoi"</note>, just as do poisonous creatures. Most of these uses are hidden. For these very reasons, it is possible for vice itself to have many useful aspects and to be <margin>* productive</margin> productive of many beautiful things, just as beauty is produced by the art of the whole; or it moves one toward prudence, not allowing one to sleep in a state of impunity. If these things are said correctly, the soul of the whole must always contemplate the best things, striving toward the intelligible nature and God. Being filled by this and having been fulfilled, as if it were becoming the middle-ground, it makes from itself a certain final image toward the downward direction, which brings about existence. Being the final maker <margin>* and over it...</margin> since that part of the soul which is first filled stands over all things. The Creator <note>original: "demiurgos"</note> is over all, who also gives to the soul that comes after him the things whose traces are in the third nature. Thus the world is rightly said <gloss>to be</gloss> an image, always being imaged. While the first <gloss>and the</gloss> second stand firm; <gloss>but in</gloss> the third, though it stands firm in itself, it is in matter. <gloss>And</gloss> it moves by accident. For as long as the soul looks toward it, the reasons <note>original: "logoi"</note> flow into this form <gloss>of the</gloss> soul. Just as as long as the sun exists, so do all the lights from it.

## ->MARSILIO FICINO ON THE<-
## ->FOURTH BOOK OF THE SECOND ENNEAD,<-
## ->CONCERNING MATTER<-
## ->COMMENTARY.<-

### ->SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.<-

Since Plotinus never speaks more beautifully, nor more clearly, nor more distinctly than when he disputes concerning the formless, the obscure, and the indistinct substrate of things: therefore, this book disputing about matter seems not so much to demand an exact commentary from us, as it does to be content with certain reminders. He will prove, therefore, that in both worlds—the intellectual as well as the corporeal—there is a certain matter of its own, and in both places, it is one thing underlying all; and that this matter here differs from that there as much as the form of this world differs from that one. He will refute false opinions about matter; he will most diligently confirm the true ones; he will conclude that matter in both places is a certain infinity—that is, a nature without power, enclosing no boundary of form within its own vitals, but terminable only from elsewhere, and formable only from elsewhere. He will show that matter in the divine world is indeed a "being," but formable by an intellectual act. Matter in the sensible world, however, is judged not to be truly "being," but a shadow of that being, perpetually subjected to receiving natural forms as images of that true being.

*Different opinions of philosophers concerning matter, and that a certain matter exists even in incorporeal things.*

I In the first chapter, he provides a very general description of matter through its relationship to forms: in which all have agreed that matter is the "receptacle of forms." But others have explained the details differently. The **Stoics**, **Cynics**, and **Cyrenaics**, imagining nothing above the body, wanted matter to be merely substance: and they held that forms are nothing other than certain passions of matter, and that matter itself is a body stretched out in three dimensions. We refute these thinkers at great length in our first books of *Theology*. The **Pythagoreans**, **Platonists**, and **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note>, however, thinking of something above the body, were able to conceive that matter too is not a body; and therefore they understood a certain matter to exist even in incorporeal things. For just as they place something formal and divine in bodies, so they in some way concede something material in divine things, so that they may more aptly accommodate the former to the latter, and so that this lower order may exist from their higher order. For we conceive that the corporeal nature is derived from the animal nature, and the animal from the intellectual, and is composed by a certain similar proportion. We have found that the most perfect composition in bodies is that which is made from matter and form. For in this alone is there the greatest union: since matter is something belonging to form, and form in turn is something belonging to matter; indeed, matter is like form in potentiality, and form is like matter in actuality. Thus, this union is similar to the harmony in the **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason", the musical interval where two notes blend into one sound.</note> arising from a double proportion: where the high voice joins with the low, like form with matter, into one. If, therefore, there is any composition in the animal and intellectual nature—which there certainly is, since they exist after the "One" itself—it is certainly a composition of the kind in which there is both form and, moreover, something like matter. Concerning this matter, we dispute more extensively in the seventeenth book of our *Theology* and in our commentaries on the *Philebus* <note>A dialogue by Plato.</note>.

### That there are not several equally first principles, and that matter is from God.

II In the second chapter, he <note>Plotinus</note> asks whether there is any matter within the intellectual nature <note>The "intellectual nature" refers to the realm of pure thought and divine forms, which precedes the physical world.</note>; and he brings forward five reasons why it might seem that there is no matter there, which he will refute in the following sections. You, however, will note among these points that there cannot be several principles of all things that are equally supreme. We have sufficiently demonstrated this, insofar as it generally pertains to principles, in our *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his own major work, the *Platonic Theology*.</note>. But as it pertains to God and matter—specifically that they cannot be equal principles—pay attention here. Atticus <note>A 2nd-century Platonist who argued for the literal creation of the world in time.</note> and his followers, and in a certain way even Plutarch, posited that matter existed from eternity of its own accord, no differently than God the artisan of the world; they held that matter was indeed alive, but void of reason, and therefore tossed about inordinately by itself. They believed it finally received reason from the divine, from which it was formed, moved, and grasped by reason. Thus, they thought the world was established at a certain time, having existed even before it was reduced to chaos, and that it would in turn one day return to chaos, having been once reformed by God and destined to be reformed by Him again. Surely those who fell into this opinion seem to have taken the words of Plato in the *Timaeus* and the *Statesman* exactly as they sound to the ears <note>Ficino implies they took Plato's metaphorical language about "chaos" too literally.</note>. Porphyrius <note>Porphyry, the student and editor of Plotinus.</note> abundantly refutes these men in his commentary on the *Timaeus*. From the many arguments he brings forward, only three need be mentioned at present to refute the idea that matter exists entirely of itself like God, as if these two were equal principles of all things meeting each other from opposite sides. He says: If neither God comes from matter, nor matter exists from God, but both are equally principles, we ask: what is the cause of the difference between them, by which they differ so much? That is, why is God good and active, while matter is evil and passive? Certainly, the cause of this difference does not come from one to the other (since neither is said to be made by the other), nor again from some third thing to both (since nothing is placed above them). Since they differ entirely between themselves, and there is no reason or cause for the difference, they differ by chance; and the meeting of such principles happens by an irrational lot. It certainly happened by chance that there are two; it happened by chance that they are principles. For their meeting for this very purpose—that they should be equal principles—has no cause determined either from one to the other or from some third thing. Therefore, they meet by chance, and consequently, all things thereafter will meet by chance. Furthermore, if God is fit to adorn matter, and matter is fit to be adorned by God, we ask: From where does this mutual fitness between them come? For there ought to be something that rightly reconciles them; since these things are so greatly discordant and opposite, they are never made fit for a meeting of their own accord. You will not say they are reconciled by a "nothing"; and I do not admit "Fortune" as a reconciler. Finally, since matter is not sufficient of itself for "well-being" <note>original: "bene esse" – a philosophical term meaning not just existing, but existing in a state of goodness or perfection.</note> but entirely needs God for this, while God is sufficient for Himself both for being and for well-being, who does not see that God is superior to matter, and that matter in no way supplies itself with existence? Otherwise, it would also supply itself with well-being. Therefore, it is produced by the same God by whom it is admitted to be perfected.

---

### How God is infinite: and how there is a certain infinity in all things after God, like matter: and how composition is different in incorporeal and corporeal things.

III In the third chapter, he solves the reasons for denying that there is matter in the incorporeal world. The Good itself is often called "infinite" because it is not constituted of parts (where one would be bounded by another), nor is it surpassed from above, nor is it constrained by the limits of any subject, nor does it admit a limit to its power; hence it does not suffer a limit to its endurance. Matter is also called "infinite," not indeed like God who surpasses limits, but as something needing limits and demanding them from another. Again, the Good itself is called infinite because it is "Form" in the highest degree; matter is called infinite because it is "formless" <note>original: "informis"</note>, being inferior to form, yet not altogether nothing. For just as the order of forms does not end in nothingness at the top, but in an entirely pure act <note>original: "actum ... purum" – pure actuality, a state of being with no unfulfilled potential.</note> and the effector of forms; so at the bottom it does not end in nothing, but in a similarly pure potentiality capable of forms. We conceive of such a potentiality underlying not only the forms of bodies in the physical world, but also underlying the incorporeal forms in the incorporeal world. There, we call this "indefinite" of itself, and we do not shudder at that name there, since it is most obedient to the shaper and is always entirely formed. Similarly, we are accustomed to praise the affection of the irrational soul when it offers itself to be rightly formed by the rational soul. We also praise the rational soul when it is similarly formed by the mind. Composition is also judged to be different there than it is among us. Here, a form often becomes material <note>meaning it is limited and divided by the matter it inhabits</note>; there, on the contrary, matter always becomes formal. Furthermore, we would rightly condemn any composition there in which a certain form arose from parts *after* those parts—as usually happens in bodies. But it is not right to condemn the fact that there are many things there that do not so much "make one" as "follow the one." Matter and form there do not create a third thing, nor is form compared to matter there in the strict sense of a "habit" to a "potentiality" or a "quality" to a "subject"; but rather as an "act" to a "habit," and again "action" to a "quality." The Ideas there do not constitute the mind as if they were parts, but they exist as certain acts of the mind, into which the mind itself has proceeded from eternity. There, therefore, form does not so much happen to matter as matter itself is eternally proceeding into act. Just as the form of a whole living being is one, in which many forms of the parts are contained; so too the seminal power <note>The "virtus seminalis" is the life-force or "seed-logic" that directs growth and development.</note> of the whole is one, but within it are many powers that form the various limbs. Meanwhile, a body is composed in one way, and the seminal power in another: for in a body, a common form is made from particular forms; but in the generative power, the form of the whole is propagated into the forms of the parts. Here, then, it is not so much that one is made from many, but rather that many are propagated from one; otherwise, many things in a body would never be reasonably led back to one, unless the "one" preceded the "many" in the seminal reason, and similarly in the mind. We ought not to reject such a composition in the soul or in the mind. Meanwhile, when Plotinus speaks of such composition, look to his meaning, not his words. He hints that the Mind is above the generative power and is composed in a nearly similar way. For since such a power does not so much conceive within itself as it gives birth in matter, and does not so much exist and act in itself as in and around matter, it is clear that it depends on something else—namely, it depends on some higher thing, which is the Intellect. From there, it not only exists once in the manner of a substance, but is constantly preserved in the manner of an image, borrowing its manifold rational form and power from that manifold intelligence—though borrowing it as something mobile from the immobile. Finally, he concludes that that which holds the place of matter in the divine world never changes its forms for this reason: because it possesses them all at once. At once, I say, both in the same moment of eternity and in the same (so to speak) sign of itself; by which it happens that it is entirely and everywhere in the quiet possession of all things. Furthermore, since it...

<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

Matter, on account of its extreme poverty and insatiable appetite for change among us, is rightly described as it is here, where material forms pass away. However, it is not described that way there <note>In the "intelligible world" or divine realm.</note>, where matter is entirely "formal" <note>Meaning it is fully actualized and shaped by divine essence, rather than being a chaotic void.</note>. Nor indeed, because matter and form exist there simultaneously in time, is there any less of an "order of origin" (so to speak), by which matter may be thought to precede form. For order is something different from time, and is prior to time; for time requires order in motion from a "before" to an "after." There can therefore be an order in the higher realms where this "original" thing relates to that, as a kind of matter to a form—just as in the sun there is an order of substance to its inner light, with no interval of time intervening. Again, you should not shudder at the name "matter" among the higher beings simply because matter among us appears corporeal; for even in physical bodies, since matter precedes both the forms of bodies and their dimensions in its origin, it is neither a body itself, nor is it truly judged to be corporeal.

### In the intelligible world there is something similar to matter, and concerning the ideas.

IIII In the fourth chapter, he <note>Plotinus</note> proves that in the intellectual world there is something in a certain way similar to matter. He wishes it to be held as a certainty that Ideas exist there, which we have abundantly proved in our *Theology*. Truly, from the fact that there are many species <note>original: "species"</note> in the Mind, it is established that the essence of the Mind—which is one for the one Mind—exists as something else besides the Ideas, and therefore stands under the ideal forms like a kind of matter. It is clear that there are different formal reasons <note>Principles or blueprints</note> there, because from that source—that is, from the first origin of forms—comes the formal distinction in the order of things, and not from the matter of the lowest realm. Nor does it come from chance in any part of the order, nor finally from various agents, unless they are directed toward the One by a certain single guiding force. In that very Guide, as in a Mind that is simultaneously uniform and "all-form," there is both a destined union and a described distinction of all things pertaining to the necessary order of the universe. But in what way? This has been said elsewhere and must be said again. For now, notice that Plotinus does not ascribe Ideas to the Mind as pictures on a tablet, but as species within a genus; otherwise, there would not be a union there so much as a gathering and a pile. Therefore, there is one intellectual nature there, which someone might call "intellectuality" <note>original: "intellectualitatem"</note>, in which all species—that is, the Ideas—meet as if in a general nature. Yet they differ among themselves through various modes of intellectuality, or intelligence—modes which are not merely (so to speak) conceptual, but also effective, like a seminal power. Such formal modes of difference approach the general nature of intelligence as particular forms for the sake of conceiving the ideal species. But Dialectic <note>The art of logical division and synthesis</note>, which distributes that "genus" into species, is not external but internal; not sought after, but natural. For there, that which is distributed is a vital essence, like a living being. The things into which it is distributed are the Ideas, like certain living creatures. That which distributes is the very power of intelligence, strengthened by the Good, like the power of a living being to conceive. If various properties are there, because they distinguish and bring things into the most absolute act, they are like forms; certainly, the common nature itself stands in relation to these like matter. Thus, the corporeal world is an image of the higher world, reflecting the incorporeal world as its model: if the multiform is compared to the multiform, and if this matter is compared to that. But in this world, the parts are in the whole, but the whole is not in the parts. There, however, that entire intellectual nature is contained in any Idea you choose, but in different ways, as will be explained elsewhere. Then truly, if you were to cut that world into parts that were afterwards distinct from one another, it would have the same matter as ours. For "sectioning" is a passion of our matter. But note: matter properly admits sectioning when it has quantity; matter does not admit it if it lacks quantity; nor again will quantity suffer it if it is far removed from a matter that is primarily passive. Thus, "quantified matter" is cut, rather than quantity or matter alone. But if any of those things conceived there embraces the rest within itself by a great force, so that the whole itself never appears to have been disjoined by sectioning, you will deny that our kind of matter is there. But meanwhile, you will find something there like matter; since, having contemplated many things at first glance, you soon find the One beneath the many. It first offers itself to you as manifold and multiform. For the "formal" comes into our notice first as the thing that moves us, even though in a certain origin the "material" itself is prior there. Prior even to that material is the Good, its own act, by which this material becomes actual. Now, since "being" simply precedes "being this" or "being such," "being" is rightly considered there before being "manifold" and "formal."

### Confirmation of the above regarding the penetrative and resolutive power of the mind: the similarity and dissimilarity of lower matter to higher matter, and how it is constituted from otherness and motion.

V In the fifth chapter, he resolves what might be objected to these statements, and at the same time confirms what has been said: warning that you should not deny that there is some matter in the higher realms just because the essence there always has its forms and is simultaneously one, since even among us, matter is always formed and makes a "one" with its form. It is no wonder that matter is hidden there, if matter is always hidden here as well. The intellect thinks this out there; the intellect finds it here by resolving things <note>Breaking them down into their fundamental components.</note>. Truly, the power of intelligence, since it is most effective, naturally penetrates and resolves all things like fire; and because it is likewise most simple, it never rests until it has arrived at the simplest things through resolution. When resolving natural things, it conjectures that what lies hidden beneath the formal reasons of things—as the "least being"—is matter, like a "depth" <note>original: "profundum"</note>; but it says the formal reason is "height" <note>original: "sublimitas"</note>; and the things that stand around it, it places as if between the height and the depth. If ever you see the formal reasons of things entirely segregated from matter, yet turning their efficacy toward matter, you will see those very things in nature, and nature itself. If, moreover, you think of such formal reasons as not only segregated but turning their efficacy toward themselves, you will immediately contemplate the Mind. For the Divine Mind is the exemplary reason of the universe, knowing all things simultaneously and making them through its conversion to itself. Then truly, every mind born from that source is full of formal reasons, and it affects the forms in things, and the formal reasons—like certain rays of the divine intelligence—corresponding to its own reasons. Just as the eye, created by the sun and being solar in nature, looks everywhere at solar colors in the solar light, and warns us to call what lies beneath them "dark," so any intellect created by the divine mind and imbued with the lights of the Ideas always hunts for and gladly recognizes the ideal similarities in the formal reasons of things; and beneath the lights of divine intelligence, it intuits <note>original: "vaticinatur"</note> that matter lies hidden as the lowest thing in objects; and because it is by itself devoid of forms (which are like ideal rays), it is therefore "dark." Remember, however, that the matter of bodies does not agree in "genus" with the matter of the incorporeal world, but in a certain relationship. For both relate similarly to their forms and to the One itself...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, Book II, Treatise 4. Ficino is contrasting "Intelligible Matter" (the divine potentiality in the realm of Ideas) with "Sensible Matter" (the physical substrate of our world).</meta>

<page-num>151</page-num>
<header>ON BOOK IV. ENNEAD II.</header>

...it seems. Both [types of matter] are defined into <term>act<gloss>actual existence or completion</gloss></term> in almost the same way through their forms: both are referred back to the One in nearly the same manner. Indeed, they depend on the One in the same way: namely, through a pure <term>mode of procession<gloss>the way things flow or emanate from the divine source</gloss></term> immediately over nothingness, by way of a certain indeterminate and determinable state. 

Again, these two matters—the higher and the lower—exchange certain qualities with each other. For just as this lower matter receives certain incorporeal gifts of nature, so too that higher matter, in its turn, possesses within the Mind the <term>ideal reasons<gloss>the divine blueprints or archetypes</gloss></term> of bodies. Then, in the Soul, it undergoes (beyond such reasons) certain motions and affections, acting toward this lower matter like <term>passions<gloss>passive undergoings or responses</gloss></term>. Those things which hold the place of forms both here and there similarly look toward their own matters and toward the One. For they depend on the One by a single mode of conversion, gaze, and limit, and they are seen to terminate their own matters in both realms. 

However, the forms of this world differ from those: for these physical forms are produced immediately by the Soul, while those higher ones are produced by the Intellect, or God. This lower matter also differs from that higher one: for this is a "depth of images," while that is a "depth of forms," of which these lower ones are merely reflections. Therefore, just as the form there is a true thing, so too is that matter a true <term>essence<gloss>being or substance</gloss></term>. Just as the form here is an image of a form, so this matter is an image of essence. Indeed, Plotinus is so far from calling this physical matter "essence" that he scarcely dares to call even that higher matter "essence," at least if it is compared to the subsequent perfection of Being. 

After this, you will observe that the <term>intelligible world<gloss>the realm of pure thought and divine ideas</gloss></term> always is, but it exists always from the Good—almost like the light joined to the sun is immovably from the sun. But the <term>sensible world<gloss>the physical world of the senses</gloss></term> does not so much "be" or "exist" as it is "always becoming" from that higher world, like the light in the air is (as they say) mobile from the sun. Those things which occur below the moon "become" only at certain times. Thus, that higher world fills all eternity, while this world fills all time; those things subject to the moon fill only a part of time. 

Let us consider essence in the intelligible world as "formable," preceding itself as "formed"—I mean by a certain order of logic, not by time—and let us consider its form to be the fullness and series of the Ideas. We also consider the Father of that world as both the One and the Good: in Unity, we see the most eminent simplicity; in Goodness, a fertility that is utterly communicable. From Unity, which is wonderfully set apart from all things, we think there hangs that which in the intelligible world takes the place of matter—solitary and as yet undefined, and set apart from the subsequent forms. But from Goodness comes that which is now formal and fertile through that overflowing communication. In the Father of that world, we distinguish Unity and Goodness only by relationship; but in his "Son" (the intelligible world), we distinguish the "formable essence" from the "ideal form," and we distinguish the ideal forms from one another by a formal principle. 

In the sensible world, however, to the formal distinction coming from above, there is added a material, local, and temporal distinction. Matter in this world follows the matter of that world; form follows form. But let us return again to that higher matter. After we have established the One itself, we are accustomed to think that something hangs from it which is not the One itself. Therefore, because it hangs from it, it is not the One; and because it is not the One itself, it in turn depends upon the One. To "hang" from the source seems to be a certain motion; but "not to be the source itself" seems to be <term>alterity<gloss>otherness or difference</gloss></term> and diversity. These two things, then, follow each other, although the reason for each is not the same. For it is not the case everywhere that whatever is not a certain thing immediately depends upon it. 

Furthermore, matter has no formal or ideal reason, but only a material one. This reason is chiefly thought to be this: namely, to hang from the source, and not to be that source, and vice versa. For this reason, the **Pythagoreans** called matter the **Binary** <note>The number two, representing the first departure from unity.</note>. For just as the binary is the first process away from natural unity, so the first matter of the higher world is the procession from divine unity. It also consists in a way of twin elements—whatever they may be—namely, dependence and negation at once, like a first motion and alterity. Whatever you add to these is already formal, and matter is seen to bring this back through an "appetite" turning back toward the source from which it proceeded; this appetite indeed seems to fulfill the **Triad** <note>The number three, representing return and completion.</note>. 

Although matter by itself lacks the efficacy of form, it does not lack "conversion" <note>Turning back toward the source.</note>, provided that conversion is itself a longing or appetite; for appetite follows the poverty proper to matter. That which is acquired through this appetite now fulfills the **Quaternary** <note>The number four</note>, which properly belongs to form. After this follows the **Quinary** <note>The number five</note>, pertaining chiefly to action; the **Senary** <note>The number six</note>, to the internal end of action; and the **Septenary** <note>The number seven</note>, to the external end which is superior to action. By these numbers, certainly, the higher world is perfected and rests in the agent; by the same numbers, the lower world is also completed and finds its rest in the higher. 

But lest these words disturb you, remember that where something exists in act, its formal and ideal reason is considered—that by which it is this very thing it is judged to be—before considering how it is from another or is not another. But because matter lacks formal and ideal reason, it is thought of first as hanging from elsewhere and as "not being that from which it hangs," rather than under any absolute reason. For this is its very reason: namely, dependence itself and negation itself; therefore, it is considered the most lowly of all things. Thus, you can understand what Plotinus means when he says that matter is "conflated" of motion and alterity, as we have said. You can also understand it another way: namely, from the fact that there is motion in any thing, it is known that its condition exists as not yet determined and perfect, otherwise it would require nothing further. 

An indeterminate and imperfect condition properly belongs to matter. Furthermore, from the fact that there is alterity and diversity in any thing—provided there is a true union there—one part takes the place of act and form, and the other the place of potency and matter. Indeed, to be "other" than that source is to "not be" that source. This very thing which is called "not being that" pertains to matter, as it verges toward a negative and indeterminate condition.

---

->**It is proven that matter exists in bodies.**<-

**VI** Chapter six shows by four arguments that matter exists in bodies. 
1. The first is from the **mutual change of elements**, which neither makes something out of nothing, nor leads anything into nothing; therefore, it is necessary that matter underlies the change of forms on both sides. 
2. The second is from a certain **dissolution of the composite**. 
3. The third is from **resolution** reduced to the very extreme. 
4. The fourth confirms the same from the **nature of the elements**. 

Certainly, when air is made from water, certain forms are changed there; yet not everything that was in the water perishes, lest something be led into nothingness (since nature's intention is not toward evil), nor otherwise would air be forced to be made from nothing. For since not just anything is made from anything else, much less does anything naturally come from nothing. It remains, therefore, that there is something which, casting off the form of water, in turn puts on the form of air. It is thus continually subject to motion, which neither that which departs nor that which approaches can sustain; and yet change, as the weakest sort of accident, requires a foundation. 

But lest you deny that matter underlies natural forms, remember that form, since it is the principle of action, is rightly judged to be a certain "act." But "act," by the very reason that it is act—since it properly acts—cannot "suffer" <note>Meaning it cannot be passive or be acted upon.</note>. Since, therefore, natural things suffer from one another, it is clear that besides the forms by which they act...

Ficino is exploring the paradoxical concept of "Intelligible Matter"—the idea that even in the divine realm of pure thought, there must be a "substrate" or "potential" that allows for the existence of many different Ideas.</meta>

<page-num>150</page-num>
<header>THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...it seems <note>original: *videtur*</note> that matter, because of its extreme poverty and unquenchable hunger for change here among us, is rightly called the origin of mutability where material forms escape. But in that higher realm, it is not so, for there matter is entirely <term>formal<gloss>shaped or perfected by a divine blueprint</gloss></term>. Nor should you think that because matter and form exist there at the same moment in time, there is no "order of origin" (so to speak), by which matter might be thought to precede form. For order is something different from time, and it is prior to time; for time requires order in motion from a "before" to an "after." Therefore, in the celestial realms, there can be a certain original order of one thing to another—as of a certain matter to a form—just as in the sun there is an order of substance to its inner light, with no intervening gap of time. Furthermore, just because matter among us appears corporeal, you should not shudder at the name of "matter" among the celestial beings. For even in physical bodies, since matter precedes the forms and dimensions of those bodies in its origin, it is neither a body itself, nor is it truly judged to be corporeal.

### That there is something similar to matter in the intelligible world, and concerning the Ideas.

IIII In the fourth chapter, he proves that in the intellectual world there is something in some way similar to matter. He wants it held as certain that the <term>Ideas<gloss>the eternal, divine archetypes of all things</gloss></term> exist there, a point which we have proved abundantly in our *Theology*. Indeed, from the fact that there are many species in the mind, it is clear that the essence of the mind—which is one essence for one mind—is something that exists beyond the Ideas themselves; therefore, it underlies the ideal forms like a kind of matter. It is clear that there are different <term>formal reasons<gloss>logical blueprints or definitions</gloss></term> there, because from that source—that is, from the first origin of forms—comes the formal distinction in the order of things. This distinction does not come from formless matter, nor by chance on the part of the whole order, nor finally from diverse agents, unless they are directed toward a single goal by one single leader. In that leader, as a mind that is both uniform and "all-form" at once, there is both a destined union and a described distinction of all things pertaining to the necessary order of the universe. But in what way? This has been discussed elsewhere and will be discussed again. For now, notice that Plotinus does not attribute Ideas to the mind like paintings on a tablet, but applies them like <term>species<gloss>sub-categories</gloss></term> to a <term>genus<gloss>a general category</gloss></term>; otherwise, there would not be a union there so much as a mere gathering or heap. Therefore, there is one nature of "intellectuality" there (if I may call it that), in which all species—that is, the Ideas—meet as if in a general nature. Yet they differ among themselves through various modes of intellectuality or intelligence; these are not merely "notional" (as I might say), but are also effective, like a <term>seminal power<gloss>the life-force within a seed</gloss></term>. Formal differences of this kind, like particular forms, approach the general nature of intelligence itself to conceive the ideal species. But <term>Dialectic<gloss>the art of logical division and synthesis</gloss></term>, which sorts that general "genus" into species, is not something external, but internal; it is not sought out, but natural. For there, that which is distributed is a vital essence, like a living being. That into which it is distributed are the Ideas, which are like certain living creatures. That which performs the distribution is the very power of intelligence, strengthened by the Good, like a power of conceiving in a living way. But if the various properties there act as forms because they distinguish and bring things into the most absolute act, then certainly the common nature itself relates to these as matter. In this way, the corporeal world is the image of the higher world, reflecting the incorporeal world as its <term>exemplar<gloss>the original model or pattern</gloss></term>: if the multiform is compared to the multiform, and if this matter is compared to that. But in our world, the parts are in the whole, yet the whole is not in the parts. There, however, that entire intellectual nature is contained in every single Idea, but in different ways, as will be explained elsewhere. Furthermore, if you were to cut that world into parts that were afterwards distinct from one another, it would have the same matter as our world. For "cutting" is a passive experience of our kind of matter. But note: "matter-with-quantity" properly allows for cutting; matter cannot allow it if it lacks quantity; nor can quantity undergo it if it is far removed from a matter that is capable of being acted upon first. Thus, it is matter-with-quantity that is cut, rather than quantity or matter alone. But if any of those things conceived there embrace the rest within themselves as "many," so that the whole itself never appears to have been disjoined by cutting, you will deny that our kind of matter is there. Yet in the meantime, you will find something there *like* matter. When you have contemplated many things at first glance, you will soon find the "One" beneath the "many." It offers itself to you at first as manifold and multiform. For the formal aspect comes into our notice first as the thing that moves us, although by a certain origin the material aspect is prior. Again, prior to that material aspect is the good act of the thing itself, by which this material aspect exists in reality. Now, since "being simply" precedes "being this" or "being such," being is rightly considered prior there as well, before it is considered manifold and formal.

### Confirmation of the above concerning the penetrating and resolving power of the mind: what the similarity is between lower and higher matter, what the dissimilarity is, and how it is constituted from "otherness" and motion.

V In the fifth chapter, he resolves objections that might be raised against these statements and confirms them at the same time. He warns you not to deny that there is some matter in the higher realms simply because the essence there always possesses its forms and is simultaneously "One," since even among us, matter is always "formed" and makes a unity with its form. It is no wonder that matter lies hidden there, if even here matter always lies hidden. The intellect thinks this out there; the intellect finds it here by <term>resolving<gloss>breaking a complex thing down into its simplest components</gloss></term> things. Truly, the power of intelligence, because it is most effective, naturally penetrates and resolves all things like fire. And because it is similarly most simple, it never rests until it reaches the simplest parts through resolution. In resolving natural things, the intellect guesses that what lies hidden beneath the formal reasons of things (as the thing with the "least" being) is matter, which it calls a "depth." It calls the formal reason "sublimity," and the things that stand around it, it places as if between the sublime and the depth. If you ever see the formal reasons of things entirely segregated from matter, yet still turning their effectiveness toward matter, you will see these very things in Nature, and Nature herself. If, moreover, you imagine such formal reasons not only segregated but turning their effectiveness back toward themselves, you will immediately contemplate the Mind. For the Divine Mind is the <term>exemplary reason<gloss>the master blueprint</gloss></term> of the universe, and through its "turning back toward itself," it knows all things and creates them all at once. Then, every mind born from that source is full of formal reasons; it affects the forms in things and the formal reasons (like certain rays of divine intelligence) that correspond to its own reasons. Therefore, just as an eye created by the sun and being "solar" in nature sees solar colors everywhere in solar light, and is warned to call what lies hidden beneath them "darkness," so every intellect created by the divine mind and imbued with the lights of the Ideas always hunts for and gladly recognizes the ideal similarities in the formal reasons of things. Beneath the forms—which are like the lights of divine intelligence—it prophesies that matter lies hidden as the lowest thing in objects; and because it is itself devoid of forms (the "ideal rays"), it is therefore "dark." Remember that the matter of bodies does not agree with the matter of the incorporeal world in its <term>genus<gloss>its basic category of being</gloss></term>, but in a certain "relationship." For both seem to relate similarly both to their own forms and to the One itself...
