# ON BOOK IV, ENNEAD II.
<note>original: "IN LIBR. IIII. ENNEAD. II." Note: Although the header says Book 4, the content corresponds to Ennead II, Treatise 4, concerning the nature of matter.</note>

It seems that both are defined into act in a nearly similar way according to their own boundaries: both are referred back to the One in a nearly similar way. In this same way, each depends on the source—namely, through a process of proceeding as a trace <note>original: *euestigiō*</note> above nothingness, as a kind of indeterminate or determinable thing. Again, these two types of matter—the physical and the divine—exchange certain qualities with one another. For just as this physical matter receives certain gifts from incorporeal nature, so too that divine matter possesses the <term>ideal ratios<gloss>the formal blueprints or mathematical patterns</gloss></term> of bodies within the mind. Furthermore, in the soul, beyond such ratios, it undergoes certain motions and affections relative to this physical matter, much like passions. These qualities, which hold the place of forms both here and there, look toward their respective matters and toward the One in a nearly identical way. For they depend on the One through a single mode of conversion, gaze, and limit, and they appear to terminate their own matters in both realms.

However, the forms of this world differ from those: for these physical forms are produced immediately by the soul, while those divine ones are produced by the Intellect, or God. This physical matter also differs from that divine matter: for this is a "depth" or abyss of images, while that is a depth of forms, of which these physical ones are merely images. Therefore, just as the form in that higher realm is a true thing, so too is its matter a true <term>essence<gloss>being or substance</gloss></term>. And just as form here is but an image of a form, so too is this physical matter merely an image of essence. Indeed, Plotinus is so far from calling this physical matter "essence" that he hardly dares to call even that higher matter "essence" when it is compared to the following perfection of true being.

After this, you should observe that the **intelligible world** <note>the realm of divine ideas</note> exists always, but it exists always from the **Good**, much like that light which, joined to the sun, exists immovably from the sun. The **sensible world** <note>the physical world of the senses</note>, however, does not so much "be" or "exist" as it is always "becoming" from the higher world—just as, they say, light in the air is a mobile thing from the sun. Furthermore, those things that happen "below the moon" <note>the terrestrial realm of change and decay</note> only happen at certain times. Thus, that higher world fills the whole of eternity, while this world fills the whole of time; but the things subject to the moon fulfill only a part of time.

In the intelligible world, let us consider essence as "formable," preceding itself as "formed"—I speak here of an order of origin, not an order of time. Its "form" is the fullness and series of the Ideas. We also consider the Father of that world as both the **One** and the **Good**: in His unity, He is most eminent simplicity; in His goodness, He is a fruitfulness that is entirely communicable. From the Unity, which is wonderfully set apart from all things, we think of that which is in the place of matter in the intelligible world as being solitary and still undefined, set apart from the forms that follow. From the Goodness, however, we think of that which is already formal and fruitful through that overflowing communication. In the Father of that world, we distinguish Unity and Goodness by relation alone; but in the Son of that world <note>referring to the Divine Intellect</note>, we distinguish "formable essence" from "ideal form," and we distinguish the individual ideal forms from one another by their formal nature. In the sensible world, however, to the formal distinction coming from above, there is added a material, local, and temporal distinction. In this, physical matter follows divine matter, and physical form follows divine form.

But let us return to that higher matter. After we have established the One itself, we usually think that something depends on it which is not the One itself. Therefore, because it depends on the One, it is not the One; and because it is not the One itself, it depends in turn on the One. To "depend" from the source seems to be a kind of motion; but to "not be the source itself" seems to be **alterity** <note>original: *alteritas*; the state of being "other" or different</note> and diversity. These two, therefore, follow one another, although the reason for each is not the same. For it is not the case everywhere that whatever is "not something" immediately depends on it. 

Furthermore, matter has no formal or ideal reason, but only a material one. This material reason is primarily thought of as this very thing: namely, depending on the source and not being that source, and vice versa. For this reason, the **Pythagoreans** called matter the **dyad** <note>original: *binarium*; the number two</note>. Just as the dyad is the first procession from natural unity, so the first matter of the higher world is the first procession from divine unity. It even consists, in a way, of twin elements (whatever they may be)—namely, dependence and negation together, acting as the first motion and alterity. 

Whatever you add "twice" <note>to the dyad</note> is already formal; and matter seems to bring this back through an "appetite" or desire that turns it back toward the place from which it proceeded. This appetite seems to fulfill the **triad** <note>the number three</note>. Although matter in itself lacks the efficacy of form, it does not lack this "conversion" or turning back, provided that this conversion is itself the appetite; for appetite both feels a need and follows the nature of matter. That which is acquired through this appetite fulfills the **quaternary** <note>the number four</note>, which properly pertains to form. After this follows the **quinary** <note>five</note>, pertaining chiefly to action; the **senary** <note>six</note> to the internal end of action; and the **septenary** <note>seven</note> to the higher external end of action. By these numbers, the superior world is completed; and in the agent, it knows itself. By these same numbers, the lower world is finished, and it finds its rest in the superior world.

But lest these words disturb you, remember that where something exists in act, its formal and ideal reason is considered—which is the very thing it is judged to be—before considering how it is made by another or is not another. But because matter lacks formal and ideal reason, it must be thought of as "depending from elsewhere" and as "not that from which it depends" before it is thought of under any absolute reason. For this is its very nature: dependence itself and negation itself; and therefore it is considered the most lowly of all things. Thus, you can understand what Plotinus says: that matter is "blown together" <note>composed</note> by motion and alterity, as we have said. 

You can also understand it another way: namely, from the fact that because there is motion in a thing, its condition is known to exist as not yet determined and perfect; otherwise, it would require nothing further. An indeterminate and imperfect condition belongs properly to matter. Furthermore, because there is alterity and diversity in a thing (provided there is a true union there), one part is in the place of act and form, and the other in the place of potentiality and matter. Indeed, to be "other" than that source is to "not be" that source. This very thing which is called "not being that" pertains to matter, as it verges toward a negative and indeterminate condition.

---

->**It is proven that matter exists in bodies.**<-

<margin>VI</margin> **Chapter Six** shows that matter exists in bodies by four arguments. The **first** is from the mutual change of the elements, which neither makes something out of nothing, nor leads anything into nothing; therefore, it is necessary that matter underlies the change of forms in both directions. The **second** is from a certain dissolution of the composite; the **third** from a resolution reduced to the very extreme; the **fourth** confirms the same from the nature of the elements. 

Surely, when air is made from water, certain forms are changed there; and not everything that was in the water perishes (lest something be reduced to nothingness, since nature’s intention is not toward evil), nor is the air otherwise forced to be made from nothing. For since not just anything is made from anything else, much less does anything naturally come from nothing. There remains, therefore, something of the water which, stripping off the form of water, in turn puts on the form of air. This thing is continually subject to motion, since it can sustain neither that which leaves nor that which approaches; and yet change, as the weakest kind of accident, requires a foundation. But lest you deny that matter underlies natural forms, remember that form, since it is the principle of action, is rightly judged to be a certain "act"; but an act, by the reason that it is an act, cannot "suffer" or be acted upon. Since, therefore, natural things suffer from one another, it is clear that besides the forms by which they act...

<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

And yet, the very <term>formal principle<gloss>the essential definition or blueprint</gloss></term> of quantity is neither large (otherwise it would not be compatible with small things) nor, on the other hand, is it small (otherwise it could not accommodate itself to large things). Similarly, matter itself is neither of a specific size, properly speaking, nor of another specific size, so that it remains equally indifferent to undergoing all modes of quantity. Nor is it "quantity" in a simple sense, lest it possess something formal within itself and thus be a composite thing.

### How matter may be known, since it is without form.

<margin>X</margin> A doubt therefore arises as to how matter can be known, since it lacks all forms. For it is necessary both that the thing to be known moves the knowers through a form, and that the knowers act upon the thing to be known through a form that is harmonious with the thing itself. Since, therefore, cognition occurs through forms, it seems we would consequently only think of things with form, not things without form—unless perhaps we strive in our minds, by setting aside all forms from the soul, to guess at something in things that is similarly set aside from all forms. But meanwhile, while we strive, we certainly strive by means of some form; and therefore, we unwillingly produce a form, even though we think it is formless—specifically, while we think of something indefinite to the best of our ability, and under such a form we suspect an indefinite matter also exists. Thus, by a certain indefiniteness of our own conception, we think of the indefiniteness of matter. A certain indefiniteness, like a material state lying hidden under the natural act of the soul's form, leads to the same conclusion. If an infinite circle is imagined, the principle and definition of the circle will be finite and certain; but the cast of the eye, or of a similar imagination through an infinite circle, will wander infinitely. Similarly, if someone, having removed all forms, directs the sharp edge of the mind toward matter—just as an eye would look—he will see nothing at all, just as the eye sees nothing when light and colors are everywhere removed. But in this state, while the light is withdrawn, the mind meanwhile guesses at an underlying dark body. Does it not also guess, once forms are taken away, that a formless thing lies beneath? It guesses indeed as best it can; but such a guess is neither <term>legitimate reasoning<gloss>logical deduction based on clear principles</gloss></term>, which is accustomed to conceiving forms through the guidance of the mind and the <term>ideal reason<gloss>the divine patterns in the Intellect</gloss></term>, nor is it a legitimate imagination, which is accustomed to perceiving forms from the mind or the senses. Therefore, this guesswork is created from a <note>original: "furia ratione & adulterina rursus imaginatione," a reference to Plato's *Timaeus* 52b, where matter is known by a "bastard reasoning."</note> frantic reason mixed with a "bastard" imagination. Yet this indefiniteness of the soul regarding the suspicion of the indefiniteness of matter nonetheless possesses something definite, insofar as it acts through forms and defines something about matter by negation; it does not, however, understand it properly. For understanding is the contemplation of <term>Ideas<gloss>the eternal, divine archetypes</gloss></term>, or at least of things related to the Ideas. Nor, again, does it "reason" properly. For reasoning is a kind of gathering or collection. But here, the mind does not so much gather as scatter, while it negates all things concerning matter—and if it affirms anything in the meantime, it confirms the things negated. For while it affirms that matter is the recipient of all forms, it confirms meanwhile that matter is entirely formless in itself. And since the soul, being a species and a true essence, recoils from formless things and hates the "fall" from essence, while it negates forms, essence, and being from matter, it nonetheless refers back to all these things; and just as it knows first by negating, so it knows then by referring. In this regard, the cognition of the lowest of things and the cognition of the highest seems similar: both are known, so to speak, by "unknowing." But when Plotinus says, <note>original: "Simile cognosci simile"</note> "Like is known by like," you should understand that a power about to know something is first, before the act of knowing, in some way kin to it, and then in the act of cognition itself, it either brings forth the form of that thing or undergoes its condition. Conclude further that where cognition is more effective, there the likeness is greater. And since intelligence and reason do not merely touch a thing from the outside like the senses do, but also penetrate it most effectively, for this reason, they exist as more akin to the eternal reasons than the senses are to the body.

### Matter is neither quantity, nor has its own quantity; Also, the reception of forms is not by reason of quantity but by reason of matter. Also, form precedes quantity.

<margin>XI</margin> Furthermore, Plotinus confirms that matter is not "something quantified" <note>original: "quantum aliquid"</note> against those who say there is no other matter in things besides dimension subjected to qualities—as <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was a medieval Islamic philosopher who argued that "prime matter" was essentially "indeterminate quantity." Ficino, following Plotinus, disagrees.</note> Averroes seems to posit in the heavens. Many people, considering that dimension is both ineffective and suited for receiving (which is how we judge matter to be), have thought that dimension itself is matter. Plotinus responds to these people, proving that dimension is not necessary for the effect of receiving itself, since the mind and the soul receive things without dimension. Moreover, since "being" simply precedes "being quantified," quantity rightly arrives at being later; thus it happens that matter receives quantity without a prior quantity already being there. Similarly, matter without preceding quantity sustains quantity; therefore, the fact that it receives other things is not because it is quantified, but because it is matter—inasmuch as matter itself was the first recipient. It happens, however, that matter receives forms within dimension, because it receives dimension just as it receives forms; and as space is produced, quality is extended within it at the same time, and when it is contracted, the quality is contracted. Now, in the very intention of nature, the <term>species<gloss>the specific form or essence</gloss></term> and the property of the first species seem to be prior to its quantity or figure. Therefore, matter is so naturally established that its most powerful preparation is for a species rather than for some quantity. I am speaking of simple and primary matter; for secondary matter, already prepared in a certain way for some species, is already capable of receiving a magnitude suitable to it. But even before magnitude, it certainly underwent a certain quality congruent with the future species; the power of this quality gradually adapts magnitude and figure to the species. Therefore, a certain form precedes a certain quantity in a way; and if you imagine a determined quantity preceding certain forms, we shall similarly imagine an indeterminate quantity preceded by an indeterminate form, by whose efficacy the matter is extended into quantity. Thus, following the command and action of the separate form upon the matter, the antecedent form will soon follow in the matter—namely, quantity, which is more distant from the separate form. Then, since acting and moving is the property of quality, not quantity, it is rightly the case that quantity does not act upon quality, but on the contrary, quality acts upon quantity, moves it, and draws it along with itself. Thus, it is not magnitude that makes something hot, but heat that extends it into something large. It is not smallness that renders something cold, but cold that forces it into something small. What more? The powers of seeds, without having their own magnitude, certainly destine specific magnitudes for the things to be born, to which their own species is immediately present and always the same—though the due magnitude or figure is not immediately present. For these, through the power of the species, proceed gradually from the potentiality of the species into act at certain times. For this reason, matter sustains form for this very reason: because matter is subject to natural art, and it sustains form primarily from the acting form. Therefore, it does not receive form because it becomes a <term>mass<gloss>moles, meaning physical bulk or weight</gloss></term>, but because matter becomes "formable." It sustains form in a corporeal way because matter becomes a mass in the meantime, while by the power and grace of form it receives a quantity suitable to that form. Yet even if it did not have mass, it would still sustain quality, though not yet a corporeal one.

<summary>This page discusses the nature of matter as a formless substrate and how the human mind can "know" it through a process of negation and "bastard reasoning." Ficino also argues against Averroes, asserting that matter is not synonymous with quantity or dimension, but rather that quality and form precede and determine physical size.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s treatise "On Matter" (Ennead II, Book 4). Ficino is currently exploring the relationship between matter, space, and the "seminal reasons" (formative seeds) that bridge the gap between the divine mind and the physical world.</meta>

<header>ON BOOK 4 OF ENNEAD 2</header>

Just as many qualities exist within the same space without that space distracting or separating them from one another, so too—even if space did not exist—could they exist together, and all the more so could they exist together within matter. Most people think of matter as if it were space, and indeed as something empty and immense. This is because when the mind directs its gaze toward matter, it is unable to fix itself upon any specific sign or limit; otherwise, it would be thinking of some form there. Consequently, the mind's intuition finds nowhere to stop; wandering here and there, distracted, it seems to travel through an empty interval, and once again through something immense. For if it were to designate a center, a circumference, or lines in any other way, it would be forced to devise forms. In reality, just as space itself is the capacity for other things without being any other space, so matter is the capacity for space without having a space of its own. And although matter itself lacks magnitude in its own right—just as the <term>ideal species<gloss>the perfect, non-physical blueprints of things in the divine mind</gloss></term> do—nevertheless, no species appears to one contemplating space, because the species defines its own proper form and preserves it as indivisible. Matter, however, seems like space because it underlies space and defines no sign for itself; it never rests within itself, but as it puts on various species, it successively casts them off. Indeed, it usually seems to us to "run" along with the course of forms, just as the shore itself seems to move to sailors as their ship moves. But he who, under the long procession of various forms, perceives the stretching out of matter in the meantime, is rightly compelled to think of matter as if it were space, and a mobile space at that.

### Confirmation of the preceding points

XII You have now heard quite often that all the forms of natural things exist according to <term>seminal reasons<gloss>Latin: *seminales rationes*; the active, formative powers or "seeds" within the World Soul that generate physical life</gloss></term> in the very nature of the World Soul. And because there is no division there, any one exists in any other, and all exist everywhere together; such a series is called the "seminal," "animal," and "incorporeal" world. Imagine, therefore, that dimension at some point arises there. Suddenly, nature, amplified in length, breadth, and depth, will be stretched out; the forms which were previously corporeal in nature without space, having then obtained space in that same nature, now turn out to be corporeal and separated from one another by locations. Think of such an incorporeal world as having propagated from the incorporeal, perhaps having accepted only dimension. Subtract dimension, if you please, and the seminal forms will still remain, which had once preceded dimension in nature. But in the meantime, the world will have turned from corporeal back to incorporeal, perhaps by the removal of dimension alone.

But I wish to remind you that what is already "nature" in the seminal world becomes <term>matter<gloss>the underlying "stuff" that receives form</gloss></term> in this corporeal world. For in this way, that world seems to be able to be propagated into this one: if matter sprouts immediately out of nature, in which dimension can arise solely by the command of a prepotent nature. We think that this dimension is bestowed upon bodies—not because it is itself the matter of bodies, for the matter of bodies is certainly that which remains matter even under dimension and yet is devoid of dimension. Nor, again, is dimension necessary simply for forms to exist, even if they eventually become corporeal. For they possess the fact that they are forms because they come from the seminal world into matter. But they obtain the fact that they are corporeal from the fact that they are extended in matter. Plotinus's point tends toward this: *Forms do not arise properly around magnitude, but around matter.* For even if magnitude is taken away, forms can remain—perhaps in the seminal reasons, perhaps even in matter itself, though not in a corporeal way.

Furthermore, this is confirmed by the opinion of those who argue that upon the arrival of a <term>substantial form<gloss>the essential nature that makes a thing what it is, like "human-ness" or "gold-ness"</gloss></term>, everything there is resolved down to the <term>prime matter<gloss>the most basic, formless substrate of reality</gloss></term>, so that the substantial form, as a simple act, comes to be in that which is substantial and simple potential. Thus, they wish for the form to adhere to matter before <term>quantity<gloss>an "accident" or non-essential property describing how much there is of something</gloss></term> (which is an accident) does. And if quantity preceded it there, then at least the substantial form would cross the boundary of quantity and insinuate itself deeply into the naked bosom of matter. For this reason, perhaps, some judge substantial forms to be indivisible: because, with no quantity intervening, they pour themselves entirely into matter, though dimension may accompany them and precede accidental forms. Thus, dimension would only make these accidental forms divisible.

Plotinus seems to have touched on this when he says: if the substantial form were necessarily in dimension, it would utterly perish if dimension were subtracted. Yet form can remain there, however indivisible, whether it is founded properly in matter or in nature. But perhaps it can also remain indivisible in matter, for it is thought to exist before it is stretched out. I omit the fact that even when quantity is changed for a long time, the form remains the same; yet matter does not remain the same when it is changed. From this, it is clear that form is not made around quantity, but around matter. Moreover, many bodies are easily mixed into one body because they agree in the same matter, being equally prepared for all things and equally greedy for all, and not having by their own nature a dimension through which they would be forced to stand apart from one another. 

Now, since dimension in a certain way hinders the union of bodies while matter reconciles it, it is established that dimension is one thing and matter is another. Matter itself by its nature neither has dimension, nor does it receive forms through dimension, but rather through itself—especially since the primary reason for receiving consists in that which is the primary receptacle of all. That indeed seems to be most capable of all which can receive all things together everywhere. Dimension, however, causes all things to be unable to be taken in together; rather, it causes individual things to be disposed separately. Hence, we confirm again that matter is not dimension. If dimension were matter itself, it would be the foundation of all things and would be <term>substance<gloss>the underlying reality or "being" of a thing</gloss></term>. Since quantity is everywhere an <term>accident<gloss>a property that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist</gloss></term>, quantity cannot be substance at the lowest level of things, even if those things which are accidents for us are in some way indicated as substances in higher realms. 

Furthermore, just as with a change of quality, so too with a change of quantity, the substance is not necessarily changed; from this, it is clear that both are equally accidents. For this reason, when you define a thing, you do not usually determine "how much" it is in the definition, as if quantity does not belong to the formal reason as a part, but is added as an accident. Nor indeed does quantity seem to be less "contingent" than quality; in fact, it seems more so, since quality seems to agree more with the formal reason through efficacy, act, and property. Therefore, if quantity is not substance, it is certainly not matter itself—which, since it is the subject of all things, is rightly judged as substance. But who does not see that quantity is not matter? Let him only think of matter as utterly indefinite, and it is immediately determined by quantity just as by quality—namely, exactly how much and of what sort it is. 

But if you take dimension as determined in itself, it still determines matter—at least to the extent that it is not only matter simply, but also so that it is stretched out in length and depth and breadth, so that it occupies a place, so that it is divisible, so that it has so many parts within it, so that part is different from part, and part is bounded by part, and the parts are bounded toward the whole, and so that there is a relationship among the parts and to the whole. Finally, to give indeterminate dimension to matter is nothing other than to confess that matter relates to any dimension indifferently, just as it does to any quality. Therefore, just as it is conceded that matter lacks quality, you will concede that it lacks dimension. Nor should anyone deny that matter exists simply because it is described by us as invisible and indivisible. For even quantity, if it is considered in itself without quality, will be invisible. And quality, in turn, if taken apart from quantity, will immediately be indivisible. Yet they are something, even though they are accidents. Matter, therefore, which sustains such things in the manner of a substance, [remains...].

<summary>Ficino distinguishes matter from space and quantity, arguing that matter is a formless "receptacle" that receives dimension as an accidental property rather than as its essential nature. He uses the Neoplatonic concept of "seminal reasons" to explain how incorporeal forms eventually manifest as extended, physical bodies.</summary>

He now moves into the paradox of how we can "know" something that has no defining characteristics.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

And yet, the very formal principle of quantity is neither large—otherwise, it would not fit small things—nor is it small, for then it could not accommodate large things to itself. Similarly, matter is not "of a certain size" in a proper sense, nor "of such a size," so that it may remain equally indifferent to undergoing all modes of quantity. Nor, again, is it "quantity" in a simple sense, lest it possess something formal within itself and thus become a composite thing <note>If matter had its own inherent size, it would be a "thing" (a composite of matter and the form of size) rather than the pure, underlying "stuff" that receives forms.</note>.

### ->How matter is known, since it is formless.<-

<margin>X</margin>
A doubt therefore arises: how can matter be known, since it lacks all forms? It is usually necessary both for the thing being known to move the knower through its form, and for the knower to act upon the thing through a form that matches the thing being known. Since knowledge occurs through forms, it follows that we seem destined to think of things that have form, not things that are formless—unless, perhaps, we strive in our minds to set aside all forms, attempting to glimpse something in things that is similarly set apart from all forms. Yet, while we are striving, we are certainly striving by means of some form; therefore, against our will, we create a form, even if we think it is "formless." That is to say, we think of it as "indefinite" to the best of our ability, and under such a form, we suspect there is an indefinite matter. Thus, through a certain indefiniteness of our own conception, we think of the indefiniteness of matter. A certain indefiniteness—hidden naturally and in actuality beneath the form of the mind, as if it were a "material" part of the soul—contributes to this. If one imagines an infinite circle, the principle and definition of the circle will be finite and certain, but the cast of the eye (or a similar act of the imagination) through that infinite circle will wander infinitely. Similarly, if one removes all forms and, like the eye of the mind, focuses the sharp gaze of the soul as much as possible upon matter, one will see nothing at all—just as the physical eye sees nothing when light and colors are everywhere removed. But in that case, once light is withdrawn, the mind suspects an underlying dark body. Does it not also, once forms are taken away, suspect that a formless thing lies beneath? It suspects it as best it can; yet such a suspicion is neither "legitimate reasoning" (which is accustomed to conceiving forms from other forms under the guidance of the mind and <term>Ideal Reason<gloss>the divine logic that structures the universe</gloss></term>), nor is it "legitimate imagination" (which is accustomed to looking at forms from either the mind or the senses). This suspicion regarding matter is therefore a mixture of <note>original: "spuria ratione & adulterina imaginatione"</note> spurious reasoning and a corrupt imagination. Yet this indefiniteness of the mind, while suspecting the indefiniteness of matter, still possesses something definite, insofar as it acts through forms and defines something about matter. However, it does not "understand" it in the proper sense. For understanding is the contemplation of Ideas, or at least of things related to Ideas. Nor, again, does it "reason" in the proper sense. For reasoning is a kind of gathering or collection of thoughts. Here, however, the mind does not so much gather as scatter, while it denies all things of matter; and if it affirms anything in the meantime, it confirms what it has denied. For while it affirms that matter is the "receptacle of all forms," it confirms that matter is, in itself, entirely formless. And since the soul—being a <term>species<gloss>here meaning a formal, spiritual essence</gloss></term> and a true essence—shudders at formless things and hates the "fall" from essence, it denies forms, essence, and being to matter while simultaneously relating matter to all these things. Just as it first knows by denying, so it then knows by relating. In this regard, the knowledge of the lowest of things <note>Matter</note> and the knowledge of the highest of things <note>God or the One</note> seem similar: both are known (if I may say so) by *not knowing*. When Plotinus says, "Like is known by like," you should understand this to mean that the power intending to know something must first be somehow akin to it before the act of knowing, and then, in the act of knowing itself, it must produce the form of that thing or undergo its condition. Conclude, further, that where knowledge is more effective, there the likeness is greater. And since intelligence and reason do not merely touch a thing from the outside (as the senses do), but also penetrate it most effectively, reason is more akin to the eternal principles than the senses are to the body.

### ->Matter is neither quantity, nor does it have its own quantity; also, the reception of forms is not by reason of quantity, but by reason of matter. Furthermore, form precedes quantity.<-

<margin>XI</margin>
Furthermore, Plotinus confirms that matter is not "something quantitative" against those who argue that there is no other matter in things except for "dimension" subjected to qualities—a view <note>original: "Auerrois"</note> Averroes seems to hold regarding the heavens. Many people, observing that dimension is both inactive and suited for receiving things (which is how we think of matter), have believed that dimension itself is matter. Plotinus responds to them, proving that dimension is not necessary for the effect of receiving, since the mind and soul receive things without any dimension. Moreover, since "being" simply precedes "being quantitative," quantity naturally arrives at "being" later; thus, matter receives quantity without needing a prior quantity to do so. Similarly, matter undergoes quantity without a preceding quantity; therefore, it receives other things not because it is "quantified," but because it is matter—since matter itself was the first receptacle. It happens, however, that matter receives forms within dimension, because it receives dimension just as it receives forms; as space is produced, quality is extended within it, and when it is contracted, the quality is contracted. Now, in the very intent of nature, the <term>species<gloss>the specific form or nature of a thing</gloss></term> and the property of the primary species seem to exist prior to its quantity or shape. Therefore, matter is naturally designed so that its most powerful preparation is for the species rather than for any particular quantity. I am speaking here of "first matter" (simple and primary); for "second matter," already prepared in a certain way for some species, is already capable of receiving a magnitude suitable to it. But even before magnitude, it certainly underwent a quality congruent with the future species—the power of which quality gradually accommodates the magnitude and shape to the species. Thus, a certain form in a way precedes a certain quantity. And if you imagine that even a limited quantity precedes certain forms, we will similarly imagine that an "unlimited quantity" is preceded by a certain "unlimited form," by whose efficacy matter is stretched out into quantity. Thus, the command and action of a "separate form" <note>A non-physical idea</note> over matter will soon be followed by a form within the matter, preceding the quantity which stands at a further distance from the separate form. Then, since acting and moving are proper to quality, not quantity, it is rightly not quantity that acts upon quality, but rather quality that acts upon, moves, and draws quantity along with it. Thus, it is not "largeness" that makes something hot, but heat that extends it into something large. It is not "smallness" that makes something cold, but cold that forces it into something small. What more? The powers within seeds, without having their own "greatness," destine certain magnitudes for the things about to be born; their own species is immediately present to them, always the same, but the due magnitude or shape is not immediately there. For these latter things proceed gradually into actuality through the power of the species at certain times, coming out from the potentiality of the species. For this reason, matter receives form for the very reason that matter is subject to natural art, and it receives form primarily from an "acting form." Therefore, it does not receive form because it becomes a "bulk," but because it is "formable" matter. It receives form in a bodily way because matter becomes a "bulk" in the meantime, while through the power and grace of the form, it receives the quantity suitable for that form. And yet, even if it did not have bulk, it would still receive quality, though not yet a bodily one.

# ON BOOK IV OF ENNEAD II.

### THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

Just as many qualities exist together in the same space without the space itself pulling them apart, so too, if space were not there, they could exist together, and much more so together in matter. Most people think of matter as if it were space—and indeed a vacuum and an immense one—because when the mind directs its gaze toward matter, it cannot direct itself toward any specific sign; otherwise, it would be thinking of some form there. Therefore, the gaze never stops; thus, distracted and wandering here and there, it seems to travel through a vacuum-like interval, and an immense one at that. For if the mind were to designate a center, a circumference, or even lines, it would be forced to think of forms. In reality, just as space itself is a capacity for other things without being any other space, so matter is a capacity for space without having its own space. And although matter itself lacks magnitude, just as the <term>ideal species</term><note>The perfect, non-physical blueprints of things in the divine mind.</note> do, no species appears to one contemplating space, because the species defines its own proper form and preserves it as indivisible. Matter, however, appears to be space because it underlies space and defines no sign for itself; it never rests within itself, but while it puts on various species, it always casts them off in turn. Indeed, it usually seems to us to "run" along with the course of forms, just as the shore itself seems to move to sailors as a ship moves. But whoever thinks of the stretch of matter beneath a long sequence of various forms is rightly compelled to think of matter as a kind of space, and a mobile one at that.

->The above points are confirmed<-

**XII** You have heard quite often now that all forms of natural things exist according to <term>seminal reasons</term><note>Latin: *seminarias rationes*. These are the formative principles or "seeds" of all physical things, held within the World Soul.</note> within the very nature of the World Soul. And since there is no division there, any one form exists in any other, and all exist everywhere at once; such a series is called the "seminal world," and it is living and incorporeal. Imagine, then, that dimension <note>extension in space—length, width, and depth</note> occasionally arises there. Suddenly, nature is amplified in length, breadth, and depth, and is stretched out; the forms that were previously incorporeal in nature without space, then, having found space in that same nature, now emerge as corporeal and separated from one another by location. Think of this corporeal world as propagated from the incorporeal, perhaps having received only dimension. Remove dimension, if you please, and the seminal forms will still remain, which had preceded a certain dimension in nature; but in the meantime, the world will have turned from corporeal back to incorporeal, with perhaps only dimension removed.

But I wish to remind you that what is "nature" in the seminal world becomes "matter" in this corporeal world. For the former seems able to be propagated into the latter if matter sprouts immediately from nature, in which dimension can only arise by the command of the most powerful nature. We think that this dimension provides for bodies, not because it is the actual matter of bodies, for the matter of bodies is certainly that which remains even beneath dimension while being itself devoid of dimension. Nor, again, is dimension necessary for forms simply to exist or even to become corporeal. For they possess their existence as forms because they are in matter derived from the seminal world. But they obtain their corporeality from the fact that they are extended in matter. This is Plotinus’s point: Forms do not originate around magnitude properly, but around matter; for even if magnitude is taken away, the forms can remain—perhaps in the seminal reasons, perhaps even in matter itself, insofar as it is not in a corporeal mode.

Furthermore, this is confirmed by the opinion of those who argue that upon the arrival of a <term>substantial form</term><note>The essential nature that makes a thing what it is (e.g., the "human-ness" of a human).</note>, everything down to <term>prime matter</term><note>The most basic, formless reality underlying all physical things.</note> is resolved there, so that the substantial form and its activity become potential within that substantial simplicity. They want such a form to cling to matter before <term>quantity</term> (which is an <term>accident</term><note>A non-essential property, like being "six feet tall" or "red."</note>) arrives; or if quantity has preceded it there, then at least the substantial form crosses the boundary of quantity and embeds itself again in the bare lap of matter. For this reason, perhaps, some think substantial forms are indivisible; because no quantity of matter intervenes, they infuse themselves deeply, though they are accompanied by dimension, which precedes accidental forms. Thus, dimension only makes these accidental forms divisible. Plotinus seems to have touched on this when he says: If the substantial form were necessarily in dimension, it would perish entirely if dimension were removed; yet a form can remain there even if it is indivisible, whether it is founded in matter properly or in nature. But perhaps it can also remain indivisible in matter, for it is thought of even before it is stretched out. Not to mention that the form remains the same even when quantity is changed for a long time, but it does not remain the same if the matter is changed; from this, it is clear that form is not created around quantity, but around matter.

Many bodies easily mix into one body because they come together in the same matter, which is equally prepared for all things and equally greedy for all, and which does not have dimension by its own nature—through which they would be forced to stay distant from one another. Now, since dimension in some way hinders the union of bodies, while matter reconciles it, it is established that dimension is one thing and matter is another. Matter itself neither has dimension by its own nature nor receives forms through dimension, but rather into itself. This is especially true because the primary reason for "receiving" consists in that which is the first receptacle of all; that which can receive everything everywhere at once certainly seems to be the most capable of all. Dimension, however, makes it so that not everything can be taken in at once—rather, individual things are arranged separately.

Therefore, we confirm again that matter is not dimension. If dimension were matter itself, it would be the foundation of all things and would be a <term>substance</term>. Since quantity is everywhere an "accident," quantity cannot be a substance at the lowest level of things, even though things that are accidents for us are in some way indicated as substances in higher realms. Furthermore, just as with a change in quality, so too with a change in quantity, the substance is not necessarily changed; from this, it is clear that both are equally accidents. For this reason, when you define a thing, you do not usually determine "how much" it is in the definition; it is as if quantity does not belong to the formal definition as a part, but is added as an accident. Nor does quantity seem to be any less contingent than quality—indeed, it seems more so—since quality seems to agree more with the formal definition through efficacy, activity, and property. Therefore, if quantity is not substance, it is certainly not matter itself, which is judged as substance since it is the subject of all things.

But who does not see that quantity is not matter? One only needs to think of matter as completely indefinite, then immediately determined by quantity (just as by quality)—namely, how much and what kind it is specifically. But if you take dimension as determined in itself, it still determines matter; at least to the point that it is not only matter simply, but also that it stretches out in length, depth, and width, that it occupies a place, that it is divisible, that it has so many parts within it, that part is different from part, and part is terminated by part, and parts are terminated at the whole, and that there is a relationship among the parts and toward the whole. Finally, to give indeterminate dimension to matter is nothing other than to confess that matter relates to any dimension whatsoever indifferently, just as it does to any quality. Therefore, just as it is granted that matter lacks quality, you will grant that it lacks dimension. Nor should anyone deny that matter exists just because it is described by us as invisible and indivisible. For even quantity, if considered in itself without quality, will be invisible. And quality, in turn, if taken far from quantity, will immediately be indivisible. Yet they are something, even though they are accidents. Matter, therefore, which supports such things in the manner of a substance,

# THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

And yet, the very formal nature of quantity is neither large—otherwise it would not fit small things—nor, on the other hand, is it small—otherwise it would not be able to accommodate itself to large things. Similarly, matter is not properly of this or that size, so that it remains equally indifferent to undergoing all modes of quantity; nor, again, is it "quantity" simply, lest it possess something formal within itself and thus be a composite thing.

### How matter may be known, since it is formless.

X It is therefore questioned how matter can be known, since it lacks all forms. For it is necessary both that the thing to be known move the knowers through its form, and that the knowers act upon the thing to be known through a form that matches it. Since knowledge occurs through forms, we would seem to logically think of formal things, not formless ones—unless perhaps we strive in our minds to set aside all forms, guessing at something in things that is similarly set apart from all forms. But while we are striving, we are certainly striving by means of some form; therefore, we unwillingly strive for a form as well, even if it is, as we think, formless—namely, while we think of it as indefinite to the best of our ability. Under such a form, we suspect there is also an indefinite matter. Thus, by a certain indefiniteness of our own conception, we think of the indefiniteness of matter. A certain indefiniteness, like a material quality lurking naturally and actively under the mind's form, contributes to this same end. If an infinite circle were imagined, the logic and definition of the circle would be finite and certain; however, the glance of the eye, or a similar movement of the imagination through an infinite circle, will wander infinitely. Similarly, if one were to sharpen the focus of the mind toward matter, like an eye peering at dull shapes, one would perceive nothing at all—just as the eye perceives nothing when light and colors are everywhere removed. But in this case, the mind meanwhile guesses at an obscure body of a subject once the light has been withdrawn. Does it not also guess, once forms are taken away, that a formless thing lies beneath? It guesses as best it can; however, such a guess is neither legitimate reasoning (which usually conceives forms from forms by the guidance of the mind and the <term>ideal reason</term><note>The divine patterns or archetypes used by the intellect to understand the world.</note>), nor is it a legitimate imagination (which usually looks at forms from either the mind or the senses). Therefore, this guess is created from a <term>frenzied reason</term><note>Latin: *furiata ratione*. A state of intellectual agitation where the mind tries to grasp something beyond its normal capacity; Plotinus calls this "spurious reasoning."</note> mixed with a <term>bastard imagination</term><note>Latin: *adulterina imaginatione*. An imagination that operates outside its proper bounds, used by Plato and Plotinus to describe how we "see" the formless.</note>. But this sort of indefiniteness of the mind regarding the suspicion of matter's indefiniteness meanwhile holds something definite, in so far as it acts through forms and defines something about matter—even if it understands it through negation. For understanding is the contemplation of <term>Ideas</term><note>The eternal, unchanging forms in the divine mind.</note> or at least of things related to Ideas. Nor, on the other hand, does it "reason" in the proper sense. For reasoning is a kind of gathering or collection. Here, however, it does not so much gather as scatter, while it denies all things of matter; and if it affirms anything in the meantime, it confirms what has been denied. For while it affirms that matter is the <term>receptacle</term><note>The "space" or container that allows forms to manifest in the physical world.</note> of all forms, it meanwhile confirms that matter is, in itself, entirely formless. And because the soul—since it is a species and a true essence—shudders at formless things and hates the fall from essence, it refers back to all these things while it denies forms, essence, and being to matter. Just as it first knew by denying, it then knows by referring back. In this, the knowledge of the lowest of things seems similar to the knowledge of the highest; both (if I may say so) are known by "not-knowing." But you, where Plotinus says, <note>original: "Simile cognosci simile"</note> "Like is known by like," understand the power that is to know something: first, before the act of knowing, it is in some way related to it; then, in the act of knowing itself, it either produces its form or undergoes its condition. Conclude again that where knowledge is more effective, there the likeness is greater. And since intelligence and reason do not merely touch a thing from the outside like the senses do, but also penetrate most effectively, for this reason, they exist as more closely related to the eternal reasons than the senses are to the body.

->Matter is neither quantity, nor does it have its own quantity: Likewise, the receiving of forms<-
->is not by reason of quantity, but by reason of matter. Likewise, form<-
->precedes quantity.<-

XI Furthermore, he confirms that matter is not something "quantitative" against those who say there is no other matter in things besides dimension subjected to qualities—as <term>Averroes</term><note>Ibn Rushd, a medieval Islamic philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> seems to posit regarding the heavens. Most people, considering dimension to be both ineffective and suited for receiving (which is how we judge matter to be), have thought that dimension itself is matter. But Plotinus answers them, proving that dimension is not necessary for the very effect of receiving, since the mind and soul receive things without dimension. Moreover, since "being" simply precedes "being quantitative," quantity deservedly approaches being later; thus it happens that it receives quantity without a prior quantity. Similarly, matter takes on quantity without a preceding quantity; therefore, the fact that it receives other things is not because it is quantitative, but because it is matter—since matter itself was the first receptacle. It happens, however, that matter receives forms within dimension, because it takes on dimension just as it takes on forms; as space is produced, quality is extended within it at the same time, and when space is contracted, quality is contracted. Now, in the very intention of nature, the species and the primary property of the species seem to be prior to its quantity or shape. Therefore, matter is so naturally established that its most powerful preparation is for species rather than for any quantity. I speak of simple and primary matter; for secondary matter, already prepared in a certain way for some species, now begins to receive the magnitude suitable to it. But even before magnitude, it certainly undergoes a certain quality agreeable to the future species; the power of this quality gradually fits the magnitude and shape to the species. Therefore, a certain form in a certain way precedes quantity. And if you imagine that at least an indeterminate quantity precedes certain forms, we will similarly imagine that an indeterminate quantity is preceded by a certain indeterminate form, by whose efficacy matter is stretched out into quantity. Thus, surely, the command and action of the <term>separate form</term><note>A form that exists independently of matter, like a soul or a divine idea.</note> upon matter will soon be followed in matter by a form preceding quantity—which is more distant from the separate form. Then truly, since acting and moving is the property of quality, not of quantity, deservedly quantity does not act upon quality, but on the contrary, quality acts upon quantity, and moves and pulls it with itself. Thus, it is not magnitude that makes something hot, but heat that extends it into something large. It is not smallness that makes something cold, but cold that forces it into something small. Why say more? Indeed, the powers of seeds, without their own magnitude, destine certain magnitudes for things to be born; for these things, the power is immediately present in its own species, and is always the same, but the due magnitude or shape is not immediately present. For these things proceed gradually into actuality through the power of the species at certain times from the potentiality of the species. For this reason, matter receives form for this very reason: because it is matter subjected to natural art, and it receives form primarily from the acting form. It does not receive form because it becomes a mass, but because it becomes formable matter. It receives form in a bodily way because matter meanwhile becomes a mass, while by the power and grace of the form it takes on the quantity suitable to the form; and yet, even if it did not have mass, it would still receive quality, though not yet a bodily one.

# ON BOOK 4 OF THE SECOND ENNEAD

Just as many qualities exist together in the same space without the space pulling them apart, so too, if space were absent, could they exist together—and much more so—within matter. Most people think of matter as if it were space, and indeed a space that is empty and immense. This is because when the mind directs its sharp focus toward matter, it cannot direct itself toward any particular "sign" <note>original: "signum," meaning a defining mark or form</note>; otherwise, it would be thinking of some specific form there. Therefore, the mind's gaze finds nowhere to stop; being thus wandering and pulled this way and that, it seems to travel through an empty interval, and moreover, an immense one. For if the mind were to designate a center, a circumference, or even lines, it would be forced to devise forms. In truth, just as space itself (without anything else) is the capacity for other things, so matter (without its own space) is the capacity for space. And although matter by itself lacks magnitude <note>size or extension</note>, just as the <term>ideal species</term> <note>the perfect, spiritual archetypes of things</note> do, no such species appears to one contemplating space. This is because a species defines its own proper form for itself and preserves it as something indivisible. Matter, however, appears to be space because it underlies space and defines no "sign" for itself. It never rests within itself, but while it puts on various species, it always casts them off in turn. Indeed, it usually seems to us that matter "runs" according to the course of the forms, just as the shore itself seems to move to sailors due to the motion of the ship. But someone who, beneath the long succession of various forms, considers the stretching out of matter in the meantime, is rightly compelled to think of matter as space—and a mobile space at that.

->The things said above are confirmed<-

XII You have now heard quite often that all the forms of natural things exist according to <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>the spiritual "seeds" or blueprints of nature</note> within the very nature of the World Soul. And since there is no division there, any one of them exists in any other, and all exist everywhere at once; such a series is called the "seminal," "animal," <note>meaning "living" or "ensouled"</note> and "incorporeal" world. Imagine, then, that dimension <note>physical extension in space</note> occasionally arises there. Suddenly, nature—amplified into length, width, and depth—will be stretched out; and the forms, which previously had been incorporeal within nature without space, then having obtained space in that same nature, now emerge as corporeal and separated from one another by locations. Think of this corporeal world as being propagated from the incorporeal in such a way, perhaps only by the addition of dimension. If you like, subtract dimension: the seminal forms will still remain, which once preceded dimension in nature; but meanwhile, the world will have changed from corporeal back into incorporeal, perhaps by the removal of dimension alone. 

But I wish to remind you that what is already "nature" in the seminal world becomes "matter" in this corporeal world. For the former seems able to be propagated into the latter if matter sprouts immediately from nature, in which dimension alone can arise by the command of the all-powerful nature. We think of this dimension as contributing to bodies, not because it is the "matter" of bodies, but because the matter of those bodies is certainly that which remains even under dimension, though it is itself devoid of dimension. Nor, again, is dimension necessary simply for forms to exist; it is only necessary for them to become corporeal. For they possess the fact that they are "forms" because they come from the "seminal" into matter; but they obtain the fact that they are "corporeal" from the fact that they are extended in matter. 

This is what Plotinus is driving at: Forms do not arise around their own magnitude, but around matter. For even if magnitude is taken away, the forms can remain—perhaps in the seminal reasons, perhaps even in matter itself, though not in a corporeal way. This is further confirmed by the opinion of those who argue that, upon the arrival of a <term>substantial form</term> <note>the essential nature that makes a thing what it is</note>, everything right down to <term>primary matter</term> <note>pure potentiality without any qualities</note> is resolved, so that the substantial form (which is "act" in a simple sense) comes to be in the substantial matter (which is "potency" in a simple sense). Thus, he wanted the form to adhere to matter before quantity—which is an <term>accident</term> <note>a non-essential property, like color or size</note>. And even if quantity precedes it there, then at least the substantial form transcends the limit of quantity and curls itself again into the bare bosom of matter. 

For this reason, perhaps, some judge substantial forms to be indivisible: because, with no quantity intervening, they pour themselves completely into matter; yet dimension accompanies them, preceding the <term>accidental forms</term> <note>forms that define secondary traits like "being hot" or "being blue"</note>. Thus, it makes only those accidental forms divisible. Plotinus seems to have touched on this when he says: If the substantial form were necessarily in dimension, it would perish entirely if dimension were subtracted; yet the form can remain there as something indivisible, whether it is grounded in its own matter or in nature. But perhaps it can also remain indivisible in matter, for it is thought to exist even before it is stretched out. I might also mention that while quantity is frequently changed, the form remains the same; however, the form would not remain the same if the matter were changed. From this it is clear that form is not created around quantity, but around matter. 

Furthermore, many bodies are easily mixed into a single body because they agree in the same matter, being equally prepared for all things and equally greedy for all things; matter, by its own nature, does not have dimension, through which things would be forced to stay distant from one another. Now, since dimension in a certain way hinders the union of bodies, while matter reconciles it, it is clear that dimension is one thing and matter is another. Matter itself neither has dimension by its own nature, nor does it receive forms by means of dimension, but rather into itself. This is especially true because the primary reason for "receiving" consists in the fact that it is the "first receptacle" <note>original: "primum susceptaculum"</note> of all things; surely that seems most capable of all which can receive all things everywhere at once. Dimension, however, makes it so that all things cannot be taken in at once; rather, it causes individual things to be arranged separately. 

Hence, we confirm again that matter is not dimension. If dimension were matter itself, it would be the foundation of all things, and it would be "substance." But since quantity is everywhere an "accident," quantity cannot be "substance" at the lowest level of things—even though those things which are accidents for us are, in a certain way, indicated as substances in higher realms. Moreover, just as substance is not necessarily changed by a change of quality, so it is not changed by a change of quantity; from this it is clear that both are equally accidents. For this reason, when you define a thing itself, you do not usually determine "how much" it is in the definition; it is as if quantity does not belong to the formal definition as a part, but is added as an accident. Indeed, quantity seems to be no less contingent than quality—infact, more so—since quality seems to agree more with the formal definition through efficacy, act, and property. 

Therefore, if quantity is not substance, it is certainly not matter itself; for matter, being the subject of all things, is rightly judged as substance. But who cannot see that quantity is not matter? One need only consider that matter is entirely undefined, while it is immediately determined by quantity just as it is by quality—namely, "how much" it specifically is and "of what kind." But if you take dimension as something determined in itself, it still determines matter; at the very least, it makes it so that it is not just "matter" simply, but that it is stretched out into length and depth and breadth, so that it occupies a place, so that it is divisible, so that it has so many parts within it, so that part is different from part, part is bounded by part, and parts are bounded by the whole, so that there is a relationship among the parts and to the whole. Finally, to give "undetermined dimension" to matter is nothing other than to confess that matter relates to any dimension indifferently, just as it does to any quality. Therefore, just as it is granted that matter lacks quality, you must grant that it lacks dimension. Nor should anyone deny that matter exists simply because we describe it as invisible and indivisible. For even quantity, if considered in itself without quality, will be invisible. And quality, in turn, if taken apart from quantity, will immediately be indivisible. They are nonetheless "something," even though they are accidents. Matter, therefore, which sustains such things in the manner of a substance...

<summary>Ficino distinguishes matter from space and physical dimension, arguing that while matter provides the "capacity" for things to exist, it is itself an indivisible, incorporeal substance that precedes size and shape.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "On Matter" (Ennead II, Book 4). Ficino continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of matter, arguing that it is a substrate entirely devoid of form, size, or quality.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

*...it is not entirely a figment of the imagination. Then truly, although it is perceived by no sense, it nonetheless must be posited as something. For we affirm that nature itself and the mind are something, even though they cannot be felt. We know matter, however, if not by sense, then by reason. And yet, it is not known by the kind of reasoning full of intelligence—that is, founded on <term>ideal forms</term> <note>the perfect archetypes or "blueprints" of reality in the divine mind</note>—but by an argumentation that partly denies forms and partly relates matter to forms. Furthermore, the words of Plotinus can be understood here as follows: that matter is known by a certain reasoning, not a reasoning of the vacuum itself, but in a "vacuous" manner <note>original: "vacuo modo"</note>; it is as if he forbids matter from being called the vacuum itself, or nothingness and vanity. Yet he allows that it is known in a certain vacuous way—that is, by conceiving of it as empty of forms. Since it has been proved that matter is neither quantity, nor has quantity by its own nature, nor quality, it is clear that it is neither a body nor, again (so to speak), "corporeity"—if <term>corporeity</term> <note>the state or quality of being a physical body</note> is taken as a certain form mixed with dimension. Otherwise, matter would be a body. Nor again if corporeity itself is taken as the ideal or seminal reason that produces a body, for this is far different from matter. Indeed, that resides in the soul and the mind. No one, truly, ought to say that a body can exist without matter simply because the action of a body seems to exist without matter. For actions are not composed in the manner of bodies, nor are some generated from others like bodies; instead, the substance of the agent or the patient itself, which is composed of matter, takes the place of matter for those actions.*

### Matter is neither quality, nor does it have its own quality.

*XIII Just as he showed in the previous sections that matter is neither quantity nor "quantified" <note>possessing size or extension</note>, so now he shows it is neither quality nor "qualified" <note>possessing properties like color or heat</note>. For it is absurd to say that the subject is entirely a quality, since being "in a subject" is the defining property of qualities. Moreover, if that subject is called a certain definite and certain nature, matter—which is necessarily indefinite—cannot be it; if it is an uncertain and indefinite nature, then it will indeed be matter, but by no means a quality. For it is the property of quality to determine and distinguish something. Someone might object that matter either is or has a quality because it lacks the qualities of all other things—as if this very <term>privation</term> <note>the absence or lack of a quality that would normally be present</note> were the property and quality of matter, through which it is thought to differ from the rest. We will concede that this very absence of qualities is a property of matter. But meanwhile, we will deny that it is a quality. For the privation of quality is more different from quality than quantity or substance is. Therefore, if the privation of qualities were called a "quality," substance or quantity could be named "quality" with much more probability. Furthermore, it is foolish to say that something becomes "qualified" not by the nature of quality itself, but by the opposite of quality—that is, by the privation of qualities. Certainly, when he says that matter is "other" (and thus "qualified") because it is different from the qualities of others, do they then want matter to be "otherness" <note>original: "alteritas"</note> itself? If they think so, it will not be "qualified," since it is not even considered a quality. Or perhaps they want matter then to be "something else"? If they think so, certainly just as otherness is "other," so also it would be "qualified" by a quality—I mean, by a nature other than itself. But just as there is something proper to affirmation and quality, so there is something proper to negation and privation that is the quality of matter. Then truly, just as the privation of any particular quality is not that quality, so the bereavement of all qualities must be judged as no quality at all; nor again is it "qualified," since it is void of qualities on all sides. Likewise, just as negation is not affirmation, so privation is not quality. For privation consists in denying, just as quality consists in affirming. Again, not every property should be judged a quality. For just as privation is opposed to quality, so also their properties are opposed to each other. Yet just as something is proper to affirmation and quality, so something is proper to negation and privation; however, that will not be a quality, but rather the opposite to quality. It is added, moreover, that just as the property of quality is not matter, so the property of matter is not quality, but rather the privation of quality. Through this privation, if someone should say that matter is "qualified," he would be no more careful than one who says matter is "great" because of the privation of magnitude. Now, if the property of matter were something absolutely opposite to matter itself, it would surely behave as a quality. But in fact, the property of matter itself is judged to be matter itself, just as we are accustomed to think regarding the first principle of things. Therefore, matter is judged to be different from others not through another property, but through itself. Matter is therefore, in a way, diversity itself, or if you prefer, "otherness." Otherwise, it would not be different by itself, but different by a diversity outside of itself. This "diversity" seems to signify two things especially: namely, both the common negation of other things (through which it agrees with them in no general reason) and the universal power of receiving, referring itself by a certain natural habit to other things. From both sides, matter is surely weighed as being diversity: both because other things are excessively denied of it, and because it is naturally referred to others. For in this way it is necessarily "other" than those things, and is opposed to them as power is opposed to acts. Conclude, therefore, for the present, that matter itself is the property of itself; and that this property is namely that it is "other" than other things—that is, that it is neither those other things nor anything similar to them. For other things agree among themselves either by communion or similarity. Matter, however, is entirely segregated, just as the first principle <note>the One or God</note> is also segregated. Again, other things, besides being different among themselves or from matter, exist as something according to a species within themselves. Matter, however, is not "through another" thing; nor is it different "through another"; rather, it is diversity itself—or, if you prefer, something entirely secret from the communion of others. Because Plotinus feared that by speaking of matter in the singular number—either as "diversity" or "the other"—matter might appear to us as something defined and formal, he therefore advises that it should be spoken of in the plural number: that matter is "others" or "diversities," so that through this we may better conceive of its infinity.*

### Matter is entirely the same as the privation of all forms, if privation signifies a certain infinity and formal potentiality.

*XIIII Thus far we have treated how matter relates especially to those things that are more remote from it, namely to quality and quantity. Next, we must compare how it relates to those things that are closer to it, namely to privation and the infinite. But concerning privation first: He discusses that <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>the school of Aristotle</note> saying: "matter and privation are indeed one in subject or reality, but two in reason." Since the Peripatetic said these two are distinct in reason, he ought first to have assigned two reasons—that is, two definitions: one proper to privation and the other to matter. Unless this is done, it cannot be proven that they are "two in reason." But if two definitions are brought into the open, we shall ask whether they are such that neither of the two is placed in the definition of the other. If it happens so, they will not be one in subject or reality*
