<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "On Matter" (Ennead II, Book 4). Having previously established that matter is a formless substrate, Ficino now investigates the relationship between matter, privation (the absence of form), and the concept of infinity.</meta>

<header>ON BOOK IV OF ENNEAD II</header>

...one: Or is it rather that each is placed within the definition of the other, as is commonly said regarding a "snub nose" and "snubness" itself? <note>original: "naso simo ... simitas". This is a classic Aristotelian example: you cannot define "snub" without mentioning "nose," but they are conceptually distinct.</note> If that is the case, there are still two distinct things: namely, the nose and the snubness. Or perhaps one of them is in the definition of the other, but not vice-versa—much like heat is in the definition of fire, but fire is not in the definition of heat. Even if it were said this way, there are still two things: the subject and the quality. After this, he discusses whether matter and <term>privation</term> <note>the lack or absence of a quality that a thing could naturally possess</note> are called one and the same thing: because privation adds no actual thing to matter, but merely denies all other things of it. In this case, however, it remains ambiguous how there can be two "reasons" <note>the logical accounts or definitions of a thing</note>: one pertaining to the subject (that is, matter), and the other pertaining to the relationship that exists through privation toward all other things. It is certainly probable that not only the definition of privation, but also the definition of the subject, is rightly referred to other things. Those things that are "above" matter are not only referred to an "end" <note>a goal or final purpose</note>, but they also possess the quality of being the ends for other things. However, since matter alone is the end of nothing—no one serves it in the natural order, but it instead serves all things—and since everything it is remains empty of the role of an "end," it is always naturally directed toward an end and is needy and "desirous" of one. Therefore, it is rightly said that its nature is referred to other things in its very definition. Just as in the highest of all things, the entire nature is that of an "end" but is not directed *toward* any further end; so conversely, in the lowest thing, there is no nature of an "end" at all, but everything about it is directed *toward* an end. In the meantime, do not dream of logical hair-splitting here. For we wish the "reason" <note>the governing principle</note> of nature itself to be understood here as divine providence. Indeed, nothing is more foreign to matter than a logical relationship. For such a relationship is founded either in an opinion or in some actual thing, such as a subject. Matter, on the contrary, is merely the subject and the foundation. Furthermore, it is probable that here, by the name of "privation," a certain relationship is signified: that is, the <term>indefiniteness</term> of this subject, and its neediness, naturally established and leaning toward other things with desire. Thus, one cannot easily discern how there can be two separate definitions: one for privation and another for matter. For they are one not only in reality, but also in definition. No one, truly, would say that matter is a privation in the same way we usually speak of other privations—that is, as specific defects in subjects. For matter itself is the subject of all things. Again, let no one think of matter as privation in the sense of "nothingness." For when bodies are either composed from matter or resolved back into matter, it is far from being the case that they either come from nothing or are reduced to nothing.

## Infinity is not an accident of matter, but is matter itself.

<margin>XV</margin> This privation, which is called <term>infinitude</term> or infinity—that is, a capacity that is merely "formable" by itself, possessing no formal limits within itself—this infinitude, I say, does not merely "happen" to matter as an accident; it *is* matter itself. Consider the "reasons" and the "numbers." I speak of the formal <term>reasons</term> <note>the "logoi" or formative blueprints of things</note> which depend on the "seed-like" and "ideal" principles. I speak of the numbers of these kinds of reasons: both the properties within them, the grades of their power, and the differences between them. Reasons indeed set limits; they bring order by limiting. Numbers truly order, and they limit by ordering. Likewise, the reasons and powers of forms terminate "genera" (acting as matter) into "species"; they also limit the wandering appetite of matter toward a specific effect. Numbers also order and limit the series of things and the matter subject to them; likewise, powers and motions define quality, and through these, they seem to terminate matter as well. Since, therefore, such reasons and numbers provide the limit, there must certainly be a subject that is limited by them. That primary subject is matter itself. For even composite things possess, through matter, the need to be limited from elsewhere; and nature, or the soul, or the mind, possess through their own "matter" a need for the boundaries of forms. Since matter is this very thing which is limited from elsewhere, it is surely by its own nature "the infinite" <note>meaning the "unlimited" or "boundless"</note>. Just as that which is illuminated from elsewhere is, by itself, dark. Somewhere, therefore, an infinite nature truly—nay, everywhere—lies beneath; indeed, it is infinity itself. For just as an infinite thing corresponds to a finite one, so also does "infinitude" correspond to "limit" <note>original: "fini", the end or boundary</note>. I mean a substantial infinitude that corresponds to a substantial limit, and one that is not a fiction. I mean an infinitude that is not "in another" [as an accident], just as the first limit or boundary is not "in another." If anyone were to say that this infinity is not matter itself, but merely happens to it, they would be forced to admit that infinity has something "formal" within itself; for if it were in a subject, it would determine that subject under a certain condition—which is surely contrary to the nature of infinity. Now, infinity itself is not any formal reason. For it is the "extreme of formability." If there were anything uniquely "formal" in it, it would not be formable in that part. Yet, in order for it to look toward the Supreme Creator to provide all forms, it is necessary for the subject corresponding to Him to have no form at all. Furthermore, if matter is infinite by itself, it is not necessary for infinity to happen to it as an accident. If it were said to be "terminated" or "limited" [by itself], then it is not <term>primary matter</term>. Finally, if matter is imagined as some kind of formal limit, and infinity (that is, merely the capacity to be formed) happens to it, then whatever is imagined as formal in matter would immediately be lost. For nothing actually "formal" is left under the condition of "extreme formability." That the matter of the corporeal world is infinity is confirmed by the fact that the matter of the incorporeal world is also infinity. For infinitude does not "happen" to that [incorporeal matter]; for whatever is in it exists as a "limit." From that [higher matter], this [lower matter] depends through a similar mode of infinity. Think, therefore, of that "Simply One" which is higher than "the One that Is" <note>the Neoplatonic hierarchy: The One, then Being/Mind</note>. Consider in "the One that Is" an infinity—that is, a power capable of being formed by the One itself. Insofar as it is extended into formal limits there, it is called power and infinity. Insofar as it is led into perseverance beyond the limits of duration, it is called <term>eternity</term>. That infinitude, named so because of a certain "defect," follows the infinity of the One, which is conceived according to a "super-eminent excess." And insofar as the one exceeds, the other succeeds to form; the latter is, as it were, opposed to the first through a relationship. Subsequently, from the infinity that is "formable" there [in the higher world], the infinity of mundane matter itself takes its beginning: it is under a "formable" nature just as that higher one is under "the Good." The two infinities introduced here do not belong to the same genus, under which they might be distinguished by specific differences. And yet, each is most simple: and while this lower one depends on that higher one, it seems to agree with it by referring back to it; yet because it is not that one, nor is it established for similar forms, it is judged to differ from it immensely. It does not differ through some added "difference," but by itself; or further, because it was not born for similar forms—but this also is to differ "by itself." Because that "formable power" [in the higher world] is like matter toward the Ideas, yet in itself and in relation to our view it is considered a "form," it is therefore not judged to be as indefinite as the matter of bodies. Especially because that higher formable nature is always reduced to the "act" of form through its likeness [to the One]. This lower matter, however, is reduced only little by little, and the "act" is far apart. Also, that higher matter becomes "formal." Here, conversely, the form becomes "material." Therefore, the indefinite condition is found more in this lower world than in that one. The condition of the "limit" <note>original: "termini"</note> excels there; here it necessarily fails. Accordingly, if you consider the composite of matter and form, you will say this is in a certain way "infinite"—namely, by reason of its matter. However, you will not say that this infinite thing is the "nature of infinity" itself. That nature is said to belong to "the infinite" by the reason that it is infinite: for this pertains to matter. When you consider this matter by itself and call it "this infinite," then this "infinite" is truly the same as "infinity" itself, which we were just calling the...

<summary>Ficino argues that infinity is not a secondary quality of matter, but constitutes its very essence as a "formless capacity" or "extreme formability." He distinguishes between the divine infinity of the One (which is infinite by excess) and the material infinity of the physical world (which is infinite by lack or defect).</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "On Matter" (Ennead II, Book 4). Ficino is currently examining the paradoxical nature of matter as an infinite, formless substrate that exists at the very edge of being.</meta>

<header>THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...to be finite, insofar as it is infinite. You, however, when you speak of matter and say "this is the very nature of infinity," stop there; do not add, "this is the very <term>reason</term> <note>original: "ratio". In this context, it refers to the logical definition or the formative principle of a thing.</note> of infinity." For "reason" signifies either form or definition; and therefore a limit is not suited to formless and undefined matter. Likewise, when you say this is infinite and that this is the very nature of the infinite, be careful not to understand under this name of "being" some limit or act or mode of that undefined essence. For these three—limit, act, and mode—pertain to "reason"; that is, to the rational, ideal, seminal, and formal principles. No such "reason" fits the nature of the infinite itself. If you try to define it, you will try in vain: for you will lose it by the very act of defining it; and you will be forced to define infinity only by its relationship to limits which it does not yet have. In this case, infinity does not have a "reason" pertaining to itself internally, but rather externally to other species: which is indeed truly what it means to be infinite. If you place anything in this as its own, so that it is not referred to something else, then this very thing which is not "to an end" <note>limitless</note> will itself be the "end" <note>the limit</note>. But an end is contrary to infinity. We shall therefore consider matter to be infinity: defining it not from within, but referring it from the outside to "reason" itself. To "reason," I say (as we have often said), the ideal, seminal, and formal reasons. To these, we oppose matter as if to an end and a limiter—matter being that which is toward an end, undefined, and needing to be defined. We oppose, I say, this to that: the simplest to the simplest. Whence we rightly conclude: just as reason itself is reason, end, and form not by some other gift but by its very self; so matter is completely undefined not by something added, but by its own nature. Whatever you produce from it will be an added end, and it defines it.

->Four questions about matter are resolved regarding otherness,<-
->privation, the infinite, and evil.<-

**XVI** Chapter XVI, the last of the book, moves and solves four questions about matter: concerning otherness, privation, the infinite, and evil. Among these, note that "otherness" itself, or diversity, is common to both formal things and matter alike. For it exists in both and between both. Matter, therefore, is the same as "otherness"—not simply, but an otherness from those things which truly are (that is, it is most distant from the ideal reasons). If it is sometimes called "non-being" because it is most distant from the first Being, it can meanwhile be called a "certain being"—that is, something most separated from the first. Similarly, <term>privation</term> <note>the lack of a quality or form</note> is not spoken of simply as if it were "nothing," but as the extreme opposition to the first Being and to the ideal reasons within it. Therefore, this kind of privation is not destroyed (that is, this nature of matter which can be formed from elsewhere) when it receives form; rather, this nature remains always as the underlying subject, and it perpetually alternates forms or the modes of forms, being formed in turn. If matter were infinite in quantity, it would lose its nature entirely when it accepted a limit. But since it is infinite through its "formability" [capacity to receive form]: the more it is formed, the more it seems to exercise its formability and perform the proper office of a formable subject. Furthermore, since after receiving "goods" (that is, forms) it still remains formless—because it acquires none of them as its own property and is prone to the loss of forms—it is still rightly called "evil." Finally, you will consider three levels here. First, the One itself, which is above being. Second, Being itself, in which the "matter of being" <note>often called "intelligible matter"</note> is placed; which nothing prevents from being judged as "being." Third, the matter of the corporeal world: which, since it is lower than being by the final degree, is usually called "non-being" on this condition. I do not say it is "nothing," but as if it were non-being, if compared to the beauty of true Being itself. For from the first Being down to Nature, all things are indicated as "true beings." But the forms of bodies, which are made by Nature in matter, are not "true beings." Finally, matter is "true non-being." Because, clearly, it falls away not only from the nature of Being itself, but even from its image—such an image as is found in natural forms. For matter is neither a true being, nor does it represent Being anywhere in the manner of an image.

->Although matter is not properly called "being," "essence," or "to be,"<-
->it should not be called nothing, but something, and that<-
->in the manner of a substance.<-

**XVII** Among the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>, if someone called matter "non-being," they would mean it is completely "nothing." But among the Platonists—who extend the nature of the "One" wider than the nature of "Being," stretching it further up and down—even if you call matter "non-being," you do not take it for "nothing." Just as you do not take the "Good" itself for nothing, even though it is judged to be "non-being" <note>because it is beyond and above the category of Being</note>. But the Good is "non-being" in such a way that it is above Being; while matter is "non-being" in such a way that it is below Being. Just as the highest God is said by most to be "pure act," under whom there is no proper and formable potentiality, but rather the potentiality of all other things corresponds to that act; so, since matter is "pure potency" <note>the capacity to become something</note>, to which no proper "act" corresponds within it, at least the acts of other things seem to correspond in place of this very act. Although we do not grant a proper "act" to matter when we use the name "act" in its strict sense (because it signifies formal power), nevertheless, where "act" would signify "something present and firm in its own dependent nature," we will not fear to attribute the firm truth of this nature or presence to matter as a kind of "act"; and we shall call it, in a certain way, the "being" of matter. Indeed, this "act" or "being" does not prevent matter from being called "pure potency." For the present and firm truth of material potency makes it more truly, purely, and firmly be "potency." Nor should you weigh this potency by the condition of others. For other potencies are in subjects; but this is the subject of all natural things. Therefore, this is (so to speak) a "subject-based" and "substantial" potency. I will add "essential"—if only "essence" can be named below the limits of Being. For thus we would call matter either a "potential essence" or, in turn, an "essential potency." Rightly, however, since potencies and acts in things are accidental and lie in something else, just as they are reduced to a pre-existing "first act," so are they reduced to a subsisting "first potency," whose "to be" is perhaps "to be beneath," just as the "to be" of a material form is perhaps "to be within." But here, some theologians will say that "to be" simply precedes naturally (or by a certain reason and order) "to be thus or otherwise" or "here or there." Therefore, neither can form be "within" unless it first "is" simply in itself; nor can matter be rightly understood as being "beneath" unless it is understood in some way first to "is" simply. This they call the "being of essence" <note>original: "esse essentiae"</note>; to which they soon add the "being of existence" <note>original: "esse existentiae"</note>. By the first, they say a thing is in its essence and from it. By the second, they say a thing is in effect and in the order of things, and depends on something else. Therefore, they will grant to matter the first "to be" through itself, but the second through form. Perhaps some Platonists even the first...

<summary>Ficino explains the nature of matter as an infinite, formless substrate that exists as "non-being" because it is most distant from God, yet remains a necessary foundation for the physical world. He distinguishes the Platonic view of matter as "pure potency" from the Aristotelian view that might equate non-being with absolute nothingness.</summary>

...they will take away "being" from the first existence of matter: especially when they hear Plotinus forbidding that "being" itself be assigned to matter. Just as many theologians place "being" <note>original: *esse*. In medieval and Renaissance philosophy, *esse* refers to the act of existing, whereas *essentia* refers to what a thing is.</note> at the beginning of things without "essence": so these thinkers will consider matter as a kind of essence without being; yet they will not call it nothing, but will name it "something." For Plotinus also calls matter the "image of essence." Just as other things have their own images—which, although they are not the things themselves, are nonetheless something—so we shall name this "image of essence." Although it is not a true essence, it is nonetheless "not-nothing" and "something." However, although matter can be called "one," and "not-nothing," and "something," they are usually accustomed to deny that it is properly "something" <note>original: *aliquid*. Philosophers often reserved "something" for things with a specific form or definition.</note>: lest perhaps the mind, when it hears "something," suspects there is something formal about it, as it is very much accustomed to do. Indeed, since the mind is itself a form, and is incited to think by forms, it thinks through forms. In truth, however, matter is judged by the thing itself to be "not-nothing" and something like a substantial foundation. Hence Plotinus says in the preceding sections that matter is necessary for bodies. Nor is it a hollow name, existing for bodies beyond our concepts and relations. The Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> also confirm this: where it does not merely "subsist" <note>exist on its own</note>, but is a certain substrate, however hidden; and this substrate subsists much more than quantities and qualities do. This is also indicated by the *Timaeus* <note>Plato's dialogue on the creation of the universe.</note> where it says that before the world there was the architect of the world as a father, and matter as a mother; and it calls matter the "substrate," the "receptacle," and the "place." From these words, it appears that matter is a thing beyond forms and motion: in which those forms exist as if in a body. And so they seem to arrive at this, which they distribute as "substance" into matter, form, and the composite. Although we may name matter a "substance" because it stands under bodies and does not lie in another, we nevertheless think that it depends perpetually from above: so much so that there is no vigor in it to preserve itself. It depends, therefore, on nature itself, as if bound to it by a certain nerve. Furthermore, it is continually gathered together through forms cast into matter by nature, as if by nerves assiduously bound. Matter itself sustains form in the manner of a depth. And while it falls away from "Being"—that is, from Nature, which is the lowest of the true beings—it meanwhile stands under as a foundation for the images of Being, namely, natural forms. For this reason, even if among some thinkers matter is said to have a kind of "being" in itself proper to its essence—which indeed precedes formal "being" and "existence" in it—nevertheless, that first "being" attributed to it is preserved for it by Nature itself once and for all, just as the "secondary being" and "existence" is preserved by the forms of bodies: but by turns, one after another; as if Nature applies various nerves hour by hour, in turns, to bind matter more closely to herself. But let us now put an end to this discussion. For in the book where Plotinus discusses how incorporeal things suffer nothing, and elsewhere, many things concerning matter will be treated.

<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

to be limited, insofar as it is infinite. But when you speak of matter, and say this is the very nature of infinity, stop right there: do not add, "this is the very principle <note>original: *ratio*. In this context, *ratio* refers to a defining principle or formal definition.</note> of infinity." For if "principle" signifies either a form or a definition, then it is not appropriate to apply a limit to formless and undefined matter. Likewise, when you say this "infinite" is the very natural state of the infinite, be careful that under this name you do not understand some limit, or act, or mode of that undefined essence. For these three—limit, act, and mode—belong to the "principle," that is, to the rational, ideal, seminal, and formal principle and to form itself. Indeed, no such principle fits the nature of the infinite itself. If you try to define it, you will try in vain: for you will lose it by defining it. You will be forced to define infinity only by its relationship to limits which it does not yet have; in this case, infinity does not have a principle pertaining to itself and internally, but rather looking externally toward other things: which is truly what it means to be infinite. For if you were to place something in this matter as its own, so that it was not referred to something else, this very thing which would not lead to an end would itself be an end. However, an "end" <note>original: *finis*, meaning both an ending and a purpose or limit.</note> is repugnant to infinity. Therefore, we shall consider matter as infinity when defining it internally, but referring it externally to the "principle" itself. I say "principle" (as we have often said) in the ideal, seminal, and formal sense. We oppose matter to this principle as if to an end and a "limiter," as something toward an end, both infinite and needing to be limited. I say we oppose this to that, the most simple to the most simple. From this we rightly conclude: just as the principle itself is a principle, an end, and a form not by any other gift but by itself; so matter, by its own nature and without anything else added, is utterly undefined: for whatever you add to it will be a limit, and will define it.

## Four questions about matter are solved regarding otherness, privation, the infinite, and evil.

### XVI
The last chapter of the book moves and solves four questions about matter: regarding otherness, privation, the infinite, and evil. But among these, note that "otherness" itself, or diversity, is common to both formal things and to matter. For it exists in both and between both. Therefore, matter is the same as <term>otherness</term> <note>original: *alteritas*. A Neoplatonic concept describing the distance or "otherness" of material things from the divine Unity.</note>, not indeed simply, but as an otherness from those things which truly exist—that is, being most distantly removed from the ideal principles. If, for this reason, it is sometimes called "non-being" because it stands at the greatest distance from the First Being, it can meanwhile be called a certain "being"—that is, something separated at the greatest distance from the First. Similarly, <term>privation</term> <note>original: *privatio*. The lack or absence of a quality or form that should naturally be present.</note> is not spoken of simply as if it were "nothing," but as the extreme opposition to the First Being and to the ideal principles which are within it. Therefore, this kind of privation is not destroyed (that is, the nature of matter, which is capable of being formed from elsewhere, is not lost) when it receives a form; rather, such a subject nature always remains, perpetually alternating or receiving forms or the modes of forms, and is formed in turn. If matter were infinite in quantity, it would utterly lose its nature when it received a limit. But since it is infinite through its "formability" <note>original: *formabilitatem*. The capacity or potential to receive a form.</note>: the more it is formed, the more it seems to exercise its formability and perform its proper duty as a formable subject. Furthermore, since after receiving "goods" (that is, forms) it still remains formless—because it contracts nothing as its own through itself and is prone to the loss of forms—it is still rightly called "evil." Finally, you will consider three grades here. First, the <term>One</term> itself, which is superior to being. Second, <term>being</term> itself, in which the "matter of being" is placed, which nothing prevents from being judged as being. Third, the matter of the corporeal world: since this is lower than being by the extreme degree, it is usually called "non-being" by this condition—I do not say "nothing," but as if "non-being," if it is compared to the beauty of true being itself. For from the First Being down to nature, all things are judged as "true beings." But the forms of bodies, which are produced by nature into matter, are not "true beings." Finally, matter is "true non-being." This is because it falls away not only from the nature of being itself, but even from its image—the sort of image that is certainly found in natural forms. For matter is neither true being, nor does it represent being anywhere in the manner of an image.

## Although matter is not properly called being, or essence, or "to be," yet it should not be called nothing, but something, and that indeed in the manner of substance.

### XVII
Among the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note>, if anyone were to call matter "non-being," they would mean it is entirely nothing. But among the <term>Platonists</term>, who extend the nature of the "One" more widely than the nature of "being," and stretch it further upwards and downwards: although you call matter "non-being," you do not hold it for "nothing"—just as you do not hold the "Good" itself for nothing, although it is judged as "non-being" <note>In Neoplatonism, God or the "Good" is "beyond being," and therefore can be called non-being in a superior sense.</note>. But the Good is "non-being" such that it is superior to being, while matter is "non-being" such that it is inferior to being. Just as the highest God is said by most to be "pure act," under whom there is no formable potency <note>original: *potentia*. The capacity or power to become something else.</note> within God, but rather the acts of the potency of all other things correspond to Him in place of such potency; so, since matter is <term>pure potency</term>, to which no proper act in it corresponds, at least in place of this very act, the acts of other things seem to correspond to it. However, where we use the name "act" in its proper sense—because it signifies formal vigor—we do not grant it as belonging to matter. Yet, where "act" would signify "not-nothing" present and firm in some way in its dependent nature, we will not fear to attribute the firm truth of this nature (or its "presence," as it were) to matter as if it were a certain act; and we shall call it, in a certain way, the "being" <note>original: *esse*.</note> of matter. Surely this "act" or "being" does not prevent matter from being called "pure potency." For the present and firm truth of material potency makes it more truly, purely, and firmly be "potency." Nor should you weigh this potency by the condition of others. For other potencies are in subjects; this is the subject of all natural things. Therefore, this potency is (so to speak) "subject-like" and "substantial." I will add "essential"—if only "essence" can be named below the limits of being. For thus we would call it either the "potential essence" of matter, or conversely its "essential potency." For it is right that the potencies and acts that are accidental in things and lie in another, just as they are reduced into a pre-existing first act, so they are reduced into a subsisting first potency—whose "to be" is perhaps "to stand under," just as the "to be" of a material form is perhaps "to be within." But here, moreover, some theologians will say that "to be" simply precedes naturally (or by a certain reason and order) "to be" in this or that way, or here, or there. Therefore, they deny that form can "be within" unless it first "is" simply in itself; nor can matter be rightly understood to "stand under" unless it is understood in some way first simply "to be"—which "to be" they call the "being of essence" <note>original: *esse essentiae*. The reality of a thing's definition.</note>, to which they soon add the "being of existence" <note>original: *esse existentiae*. The actual fact of a thing's presence in the world.</note>. By the first, they say a thing is in its essence and from it. By the second, they say a thing is in effect and in the order of things, and depends on something else. For which reason, they will grant to matter the first "to be" through itself, but the second through form. Perhaps, indeed, certain Platonists also...

They will take away the primary being of matter; especially when they hear Plotinus forbidding "being" itself to be assigned to matter. Therefore, just as many theologians place "being" without "essence" in the first principle of all things <note>Referring to God as pure being (Esse) without a limiting essence.</note>: so these thinkers will consider matter as "essence" without "being." Yet they will not call it "nothing," but rather "something." For Plotinus also calls matter the "image of essence." Just as other things have their own images—which, although they are not the things themselves, are still something—so too we shall name the image of essence; though it is not true essence, it is nevertheless not "nothing," but "something." However, although matter can be called "one," and "not-nothing," and "something," they usually deny that it is "something" in a proper sense. This is done so that the mind, upon hearing the word "something," does not perhaps suspect it to be something formal <note>original: *formale*. In this system, "form" implies a specific identity or limit, which matter lacks.</note>, as is most common. For the mind itself is a form, and is moved to think by forms, and thinks through forms. In truth, however, matter is indicated by the thing itself to be "not-nothing" and a "something" that is, in a way, substantial. Hence Plotinus says in the preceding sections that matter is necessary for bodies, and that it is not a vain name, but something subsisting in bodies beyond our concepts and relations. The Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> also confirm this: that there is some subject, however hidden, and that this subject subsists much more than quantities and qualities do. Timaeus <note>The narrator of Plato's *Timaeus*, a dialogue about the creation of the universe.</note> also indicates this when he says that before the world, there was the architect of the world as a father, and matter as a mother; he calls matter the "subject," the "receptacle," and the "place." The Peripatetics also confirm this when they divide substance into matter, form, and the composite. Although we call matter a "substance" because it stands under bodies and does not lie in another, we nevertheless think of it as perpetually depending from above, to such an extent that there is no strength in it to preserve itself. It depends, therefore, on nature itself, as if bound to it by a certain nerve <note>original: *nervus*. Ficino uses this to mean a connecting bond or vital tension.</note>. Indeed, it is continually gathered together by forms cast from nature into matter, as if by nerves constantly drawing it. Matter itself will substitute for form in the manner of a depth. And while it falls away from "being"—that is, from nature, which is the lowest of true beings—in the meantime, it stands beneath as a foundation for the images of being, namely, the natural forms. For this reason, even if among some thinkers matter is said to have a kind of being in itself proper to its own essence—which indeed in matter precedes "formal being" and "existence"—nevertheless, that primary being attributed to it is preserved by nature itself once and for all, just as "secondary being" and "existence" are preserved by the forms of bodies. But this happens in turn by one form after another, as if nature applies various "nerves" hour by hour, in succession, to bind matter more closely to itself. But let us now put an end to this discussion. For in the book where Plotinus disputes that incorporeal things suffer nothing, and elsewhere, many things concerning matter will be treated.

<header>PLOTINUS, ENNEAD II.</header>

...stretching even to the gods. Finally, they claim that the supreme God himself is this very matter, existing in a certain specific way. Furthermore, they hand down that matter is a body, calling it a "body without quality" <note>This refers to the Stoic view, which held that the fundamental principle of the universe was a type of material substance.</note>; they also attribute magnitude to it. However, among those who admit an incorporeal essence <note>referring to Platonists and Aristotelians who believe in non-physical reality</note>, some do not posit only one kind of matter. Instead, they say that one kind is subject to bodies—the same matter the earlier thinkers spoke of—but that there is another, prior matter found in the "intelligible" things <note>The "intelligible world" is the realm of pure thought and divine Forms, existing beyond the physical senses.</note>, which serves as the substrate for the forms and incorporeal essences that exist there.

II
<margin>II. Reasons for those proving there is no matter in the intelligible world.</margin>
FOR THIS REASON, we must first inquire about this latter kind of matter: whether it exists, what it is, and in what manner it subsists. If matter must be something indefinite and formless, and if in those "best things" (the incorporeal ones) nothing is indefinite and nothing is formless, then there would be no matter there. Furthermore, if each of those divine things is "simple" <note>In ancient philosophy, "simple" means not made of parts; a single, pure essence.</note>, it would have no need for matter, from which—with something else added to it—a "composite" thing would be manufactured. Again, in things that are born and among those things that produce one another, there is a need for matter; however, in those things that are not "generated" <note>original: *non gignuntur*. These are eternal beings that were never born and will never die.</note>, there is no such need. Indeed, in sensible things, matter seems to have been discovered only because of the process of birth and the mutual transformation of elements. Finally, from where would matter in that higher realm proceed and subsist? For if it was made, it was surely made by someone; but if it is eternal, then there are multiple first principles. And if a "form" <note>original: *species* / *εἶδος*</note> were to be added to it there, the resulting composite would be a body. Thus, there would be bodies in the higher realm as well.

III
<margin>III. He resolves the arguments proving there is no matter in the intelligible mode.</margin>
FIRST, it must be said that what is "indefinite" is not to be utterly despised everywhere, nor is that which is "formless" in its own concept, provided it offers itself to the things above it and the "best" things. In the same way, the soul is related by its own nature to the intellect and to reason; the soul is formed by these and is led toward a better form. Added to this is the fact that in the intelligible world, what is called a "composite" is of a different nature; it is certainly not like physical bodies. Since the "reasons" <note>original: *rationes* / *λόγοι*. These are the formative principles or blueprints of reality.</note> themselves are composites, they create a certain composite through their activity—namely, the very nature that acts toward a form. If a thing is directed toward another, it surely depends on that other, and even more so in the divine realm. Likewise, the matter of things that are born always takes on one form after another. But the matter of eternal things always possesses the same form. Indeed, the matter here in our world behaves almost the opposite of the matter there. For our matter becomes all things through parts and alternation, being one thing at one time and another at another; therefore, nothing remains permanently, as some things are pushed out by others. For this reason, nothing here is always the same. In the higher realms, however, matter is all things simultaneously. And since it already possesses all things, it has nothing into which it could possibly change. Therefore, matter there is never truly formless, just as our own matter is never actually formless. But in this regard, the two kinds of matter differ. Furthermore, as to whether it is eternal or generated, that will finally be clear to us once we have shown what it actually is.

IIII
<margin>IIII. He proves there is matter in the intelligible world.</margin>
TO BEGIN, since it has been demonstrated elsewhere that the "Ideas" <note>The eternal archetypes or Forms of all things.</note> exist, let us proceed with our plan, accepting for now that the Ideas are real. Surely, if there are many different forms there, it is necessary that there be something common within them, and again, something "proper" or unique by which one is distinguished from the other. This unique quality and the difference that separates them is their own specific form.

<column-break/>

...bringing it [matter] even to the gods. And finally, they say that the supreme God himself is this matter, being in a certain state. They also grant it a body, calling it a "quality-less body" and a magnitude. But those who say it is incorporeal—and some of them say it is not just one thing—claim that this matter is subject to bodies, about which the earlier thinkers spoke. However, they say there is another, prior matter in the intelligible things, which is subject to the forms there and to the incorporeal essences.

WHEREFORE we must first seek concerning this: whether it is, and what it happens to be, and how it is. If indeed the nature of matter must be something indefinite and formless, and in the best things there, nothing is indefinite nor formless, then matter would not be there. And if each thing is simple, it would not need matter, so that a composite would be made from itself and another <margin>* from them</margin>. And for things that are generated, there is a need for matter, and things produced one after another, from which the matter of sensible things was conceived; but for things not generated, how and from where must it have come and subsisted? If it was generated, it was by someone. But if it is eternal, then there are many principles. And the first things would exist by chance. And if a form approaches it, the composite would be a body, so that there would be body there as well.

FIRST, then, it must be said that not everywhere is the indefinite to be dishonored; nor the formless in its own concept, if it is to provide itself to the things before it and the best things; just as the soul is by nature disposed toward intellect and reason, being formed by these, and led toward a better form. And in the intelligible things, the composite is otherwise, not like bodies. Since even the "reasons" <note>original: *logoi*</note> are composite, and by their activity they make a composite—the nature that acts toward a form. If it follows another, and is with another, then even more so. The matter of generated things always holds one form and then another. But the matter of eternal things holds the same form forever. Matter there is the opposite of matter here. For here, it is all parts, and in each [part a different thing]. Therefore nothing remains, but one thing is pushed out by another. Therefore it is not all things at once. But there, all things are together; therefore you have nothing into which it could change, for it already has all things. Therefore it is never formless, neither the matter there; since even the matter here is not, but each is formless in a different way. But whether it is eternal or generated, it will be clear once we grasp what it is.

OUR argument now, having hypothesized that the forms exist—for it has been shown in other places—let it proceed. If then the forms are many, it is necessary that there be something common in them; and indeed something proper, by which one differs from another. This proper thing and the difference that separates them is the peculiar form. <margin>which [is] the</margin>

But if there is a form <note>Greek: *morphē*</note>, there is also that which is being formed, around which the difference exists. There is, therefore, also a matter which receives the form, and there is always a substrate <note>The underlying "stuff" or potentiality that supports the qualities of a thing.</note>. Furthermore, if an intelligible world exists there, and this physical world is an imitation of that one, and this world is composite and made of matter, then there must be matter in that world as well. Or how could one arrange a world <note>Greek: *kosmos*, which implies order and beauty.</note> without matter coming into form? And how could there be form, if there were not something upon which the form was received? For that which is entirely indivisible is completely the same. But that which is divisible in any way—and if the parts are separated from one another—that cutting and * difference belongs to matter; it is an affection of matter. For it is matter itself that is divided. But if, being many, the "many" are indivisible and exist within a single thing, then that one thing is the matter for the many, as they are its forms. For the manifold nature within this consists of manifold and multiform thought; yet this thought is not formless before its * manifoldness. For if you were to strip away the variety, the forms, the rational principles, and the thoughts through your mind, that which remains before these is formless and indefinite; and this is none of the things that exist upon it or within it.

But if one says that because the intelligible world always possesses these forms, and both exist together as one, that there is no matter there, then it would follow that there is no matter for bodies here either. For here, matter is never found without form, but is always a whole body—nonetheless, it remains a composite. And how could the intellect distinguish the duality? For the intellect divides until it reaches that which is simple, which can no longer be resolved further. As long as it can be resolved, it proceeds into the "depth" <note>The inner core or fundamental nature of a thing.</note> of the object. And the depth of each thing is its matter. Therefore, all matter is "darkness," because the rational principle <note>Greek: *logos*</note> is light. And the intellect is also a rational principle. Thus, when the intellect sees the rational principle in each thing, it considers that which is beneath it—as if under the light—to be dark; just as an eye, being light-like itself, when it directs its gaze toward light and colors (which are themselves types of light), says that what lies beneath the colors is dark and material, hidden by the colors. Yet there is a great difference between the dark substrate in intelligible things and that in sensible things. The difference in the matter is as great as the difference between the forms placed upon them. For divine matter, receiving that which limits it, possesses a life that is defined and intellectual; but the matter here, though it becomes something defined, is * indeed not living or thinking, but is a "decorated corpse" <note>A famous Plotinian image: physical matter is inherently "dead" or non-being, only made to look like something by the "decoration" of form.</note>. And the form there is a true form, so the substrate is also a true essence <note>Greek: *ousia*</note>. Therefore, those who say that matter is "being" or "essence" would be understood to speak correctly if they were speaking of that intelligible matter. For the substrate there is essence; or rather, when conceived along with what is in it, it is a "be-lighted" essence. Whether intelligible matter is eternal or not must be investigated in the same way one asks if the Ideas <note>The eternal archetypes of all things.</note> are eternal. They are "generated" in the sense that they have a * beginning, but "un-generated" because they do not have a beginning in time...

<column-break/>

A. But if there is form in that realm, there is also that which is formed, concerning which the difference exists. Therefore, there is a substrate which receives that form, and it is a perpetual subject. Furthermore, if an intelligible world exists there, and this world of ours is an imitation of that one and is composed of matter, then it is necessary for matter to be there as well. Otherwise, by what reasoning will you call it a "world" and an "ornament" unless it is by its species <note>Latin: *species*, equivalent to the Greek *eidos* or form.</note>, or if you consider the species themselves? In what way will you behold a species, unless you also behold that in which you may grasp the species? Indeed, the superior world itself is entirely indivisible everywhere, yet by a certain condition, it is also divisible. And if its parts were dispersed among themselves, that very cutting and dispersion would be a certain "affection" of matter: for it is matter itself which is properly said to suffer division. But if those things which are "many" there are a single indivisible being, then surely those many things existing in one are in that one as if in matter, and they are the forms of that matter. For that one thing itself which is varied must be considered primarily as varied and multiform. It must be considered again as "inform" <note>Without form; formless.</note> before it is varied. For if by thought you were to take away the variety, the forms, the rational principles, and the intelligences, undoubtedly that which precedes these occurs as something formless and indefinite; and nothing appears of those things which are in its power or within itself.

<margin>He resolves the objections that could be made to the above: and confirms the teaching.</margin>
But if it were said that because such an essence always possesses these things, and both are one at the same time, that there is no matter there, it would follow that neither is there matter for bodies here. For this matter is never without form, but is always a whole body: nevertheless, it is a composite. And the intellect finds a duality. For it divides until it reaches that which is simple: namely, that which cannot be further resolved. But as far as it can be referred to another, the intellect proceeds by penetrating into its depth. Finally, the depth of each thing is matter. For this reason, all matter is darkness, since the rational principle itself is light, and the intellect itself is reason. Therefore, perceiving the reason in each thing, the intellect conjectures that which is lower—as if under the light—to be obscure. Just as the eye, since it is light-bearing, when looking into light and simultaneously into colors (which are certain lights), brings itself to say that those things which lie hidden under the colors remain obscure and material, covered by the colors. Nevertheless, there is a wide gap between that which we conjecture to be dark in intelligible things and that in sensible things; and that matter differs from this one as much as the species inherent in that one differs from the species inherent in this one. For divine matter, receiving that which terminates it, obtains a life that is determined and intellectual. This matter here, however, becomes something determined; yet it is neither living nor in any way intellectual, but something void of life, however much it may be "decorated." Furthermore, this form is imaginary; and therefore the substrate is imaginary. In that realm, however, both the form is a true thing and the substrate is consequently a true essence. Therefore, those who say that matter is essence—if only they are speaking of that matter—must be thought to judge correctly. For that which is the substrate there is essence: or rather, it is considered together with that which is in it. For that whole is now truly a luminous essence.

...they have a beginning, but are always derived from another; they are not as things that are always coming into being, like this world, but as things existing always, just as that world [the intelligible world] does. For the Otherness <note>Greek: *heterotēs*. The principle of difference or being "other" than the One, which allows for multiplicity.</note> which is there always produces matter. For this is the principle of matter, the primary motion. For this reason, it is also called Otherness: because motion and Otherness arose there together. But both motion and Otherness, which depend on the First [the One], are indeterminate and need that First to be defined. They are defined when they turn back toward it. But before they turn, that which is indeterminate—that is, matter and the "other"—is not yet good, but is something void of the light of the Good. For if light shines out from the Good, then surely that which receives the light, before it receives it, does not have light; and insofar as it has it, it possesses it as something else, if indeed the light itself proceeds from another. Thus far concerning the matter of the intelligible world; perhaps it has been discussed further than this inquiry required.

<margin>VI. He proves that there is a primary matter in bodies.</margin>
### Concerning the receptacle of bodies, let us next speak in this way. In the first place, that there must be something underlying bodies—which is something else besides the bodies themselves—is shown to us by the mutual transformation of the elements. For that which is transformed is not entirely destroyed; otherwise, a certain essence would vanish into non-being. Nor, on the other hand, is that which is created made from that which in no way exists. Rather, a certain change occurs from one form into another. But that which takes on the form of the created thing remains, while it casts off the other form. This is further evident from decay. For decay pertains to the composite. If this is so, then everything that is perishable is made of matter and form. Induction <note>The logical process of drawing a general conclusion from specific observations.</note> also testifies that what is dissolved is a composite. Analysis, in turn, shows us the same thing. For example, if a bowl is resolved into gold, and gold is resolved into water; and finally water, when it perishes, requires something proportional [as a substrate]. Furthermore, it is necessary that the elements are either form, or primary matter, or consist of both matter and form. It is impossible for them to be form alone. For how could they have bulk and magnitude if they were without matter? But neither are they primary matter, since they are dissolved. Therefore, they are composed of both matter and form. And while form looks toward quality and shape, matter pertains to the substrate. And because matter is not form, it is indeterminate.

<margin>VII. He refutes false opinions concerning matter.</margin>
### ACCORDINGLY, against Empedocles <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who argued that the world was made of four permanent elements: earth, air, fire, and water.</note>, who posits the elements as matter, the very destruction of those elements cries out in protest. And Anaxagoras <note>A philosopher who proposed that all things were originally mixed together and then separated by "Mind" (Nous).</note>, who introduces a certain mixture (like water) and says that this does not merely have an aptitude for all things but actually contains all things in reality, effectively does away with the Intellect <note>Greek: *Nous*. The divine Mind.</note> he had introduced. For he does not say that the Intellect provides the shape and form, nor that it is prior to matter, but that it exists together with matter. It is indeed impossible for them to be together. For if the mixture participates in being, then Being itself is older. But if Being itself is also a certain mixture, these would require some third thing. Therefore, if it is necessary for the Craftsman of things to be prior, why was it necessary for the forms to exist in matter as tiny fragments? And why then should the Intellect distinguish what was confused through an inexplicable labor? Since it is possible for the Intellect to impress quality and form upon matter, provided that matter is without quality...

<column-break/>

**A** It has a beginning, but always from another; not as things that are always becoming, like the world, but as things existing always, like the world there. For the otherness there always produces matter. For this is the principle of matter: the first motion. Therefore, this was also called otherness, because motion and otherness grew out together. But both motion and otherness which come from the first are indeterminate, and need that [first] in order to be defined. It is defined when it turns back toward it. **B** But before then, both matter and the "other" are indeterminate, and not yet good, but unlit by that [Good]. For if the light is from that [Good], then that which receives the light, before receiving the light, does not have it always, but has it as another thing, if indeed the light is from another. And regarding intelligible matter, more <margin>*among the intelligibles</margin> has been said than was fitting for a brief account, in this way.

### Regarding the receptacle of bodies, **C** let it be said thus. That there must be something underlying the bodies, being different from them, is shown by the change of elements into one another. For change is not total. Either the destruction from which the essence was would perish into non-being, or what is becoming has come into being from total non-existence; but instead, there is a change of form, from one to another. That which receives the form of what has become remains, **D** even after casting off the other. This is shown by destruction in general, for it belongs to a composite. If this is so, each thing is from matter and form. Induction also bears witness, showing the thing destroyed to be a composite. And so does analysis. For example, if a bowl is reduced to gold, and the gold to water; and the water being destroyed, requires something proportional. It is necessary for the elements to be either form, **E** or primary matter, or from matter and form. But as form, it is not possible. For how, without matter, could there be bulk and magnitude? But they are not primary matter either, for they are destroyed. Therefore, they are from matter and form. And the form is according to the quality and the shape, while the matter is according to the substrate <margin>*indeterminate</margin> which is indeterminate because it is not form.

### **F** But Empedocles, having placed the elements as matter, has their very destruction as a witness against him. And Anaxagoras, making the mixture [like] water, saying it has not [just] an aptitude for all things, but contains all things in actuality, does away with the Intellect he introduces; for he does not make it the giver of shape and form, nor prior to matter, but together with it. But it is impossible to be together. For if the mixture partakes of being, Being is prior. **G** And if Being itself is also the mixture, that would require a third thing above them. If then it is necessary for the Craftsman to exist, why was it necessary for the forms to be in matter in small parts? And then for the Intellect to distinguish them through impossible difficulties? When it was possible, matter being without quality, [to give] the quality and the form...

# BOOK FOUR. 163

...to extend to the whole. And as for "all being in all," <note>original: *to, te pān en panti einai* — a reference to the Pre-Socratic philosopher Anaxagoras, who taught that every substance contains a portion of every other substance.</note> how is this not impossible? Let him who posits the infinite as a starting point say what this truly is. And if it is infinite in the way we have analyzed—as something that is not a quality among unequal things, nor the infinite itself, nor existing in some other nature as an accident of a body—this must be explained. The infinite itself is problematic because a part of it would necessarily be infinite. As for being an accident, that which it is an accident to would not be infinite in itself, nor simple, nor matter; this is clear. Furthermore, atoms will not hold the rank of matter, since they are not truly infinite. For every body is divisible, as is every whole and every continuous thing. This is also true of the fluidity of bodies; it is impossible for things to be composed of atoms, which lack a unifying nature and soul, for one cannot create a single continuous thing out of atoms, just as a craftsman cannot create something from matter that is not continuous. Many other things could correctly be said against this hypothesis, and have been said, so there is no need to dwell longer on these arguments.

What, then, is this thing which is said to be one, continuous, and devoid of quality? That it is not a body—if it is indeed without quality—is clear; otherwise, it would possess quality. When we say it is the matter of all sensible things, we do not mean it is the matter for some and the form for others (as we say clay is matter for the potter, but in an absolute sense, it is not "matter"). We do not speak of it in that way, but rather in relation to all things; we should attribute nothing to its own nature that is seen in the realm of sensible things. If this is so, then besides other qualities—such as colors, heat, and cold—we must not attribute to it lightness, weight, density, rarity, or even shape. Consequently, it has no magnitude. For magnitude is one thing, and to be "magnified" is another; shape is one thing, and to be "shaped" is another. It must not be composite, but simple and one in its own nature. In this way, it is destitute of all things. And the one who gives it form will also give it a form that is distinct from its own nature. He brings magnitude and everything else from the things that exist; it does not follow its own magnitude, nor does the creator make it as large as he wishes, but as large as the matter is willing to receive. To say that matter "runs along" with its own magnitude is a mere fiction. But if the producing cause precedes the matter, then matter will be exactly as the producer wants it, easily led into all things, and thus into magnitude. If it already had magnitude, it would also have shape, and would therefore be more difficult for the craftsman to work with. Form, therefore, enters into matter bringing all things with it; every form contains magnitude and the measure of quantity along with reason <note>Greek: *logos* — here meaning the rational principle or "blueprint" of a thing.</note> and under reason. Therefore, in each individual thing, quantity is defined along with its form. For the quantity prescribed for a human is different...

<column-break/>

...to extend through the whole. Lastly, by what reason it could happen that "all things are in any thing," <note>original: "vt in quolibet omnia sint"</note> I certainly do not see. Moreover, he who puts the infinite in the place of matter ought to explain what this itself is. And if it is infinite in such a way that one cannot traverse it, one must remember that such a thing cannot exist in reality, neither if it is infinite in and of itself, nor if it exists in another nature as an accident of some body. Truly, it cannot be **B** immense in itself, because a part of it would also necessarily be immense. Nor can the infinite be an accident to another, because that to which it happened would not be infinite by its own nature; nor would it be simple; and certainly it would not be matter. Furthermore, atoms will not obtain the rank of matter, which indeed are nothing at all. For every body is divisible through all its parts. The same is refuted by the very continuity and fluidity of bodies. Again, it is refuted because individual things cannot exist without mind and soul, **C** which nature does not allow to be composed of atoms. Likewise, because no nature discovered besides atoms can fabricate anything out of atoms: since no craftsman is able to fashion anything from matter that is not continuous. Many other things besides these could be said against this opinion, and have been said; therefore, it is superfluous to linger on them any longer.

<margin>VIII. What matter is not; namely, that it has no forms; and how it relates to forms.</margin> **D** WHAT, then, is this which is said to be one, continuous, and devoid of quality? To begin with, it is manifest that this is not a body, if indeed it is devoid of quality; otherwise, it would possess quality. When we say that this itself is the matter of all sensible things, we do not mean that it is the matter of some things and the form of others—as we are accustomed to say that clay is the matter in the hands of the potter, but simply speaking, it is not "matter." When, I say, we do not distinguish it in that way from the matter of the world, but refer it to all things simply: then surely we shall attribute to it **E** nothing at all of those things which are perceived in the sensible genus according to its own nature. If this is so, then besides other qualities such as colors, heat, and cold, we must not ascribe lightness, weight, density, rarity, or shape to matter. Therefore, we should not even ascribe magnitude to it. For magnitude itself is one thing, but that which is "large" is another. Again, shape is one thing, but that which is "shaped" is another. It is necessary that matter itself be nothing composite, but something simple and one in its own nature. For only in this way will it be the vessel <note>original: *vas* — Plotinus uses the Platonic concept of matter as a "receptacle" or container that holds the forms.</note> **F** of all things, existing as something else besides matter. It will grant magnitude and all things from those which exist, as if offering and bringing them; otherwise, it would serve the magnitude of matter itself, and the craftsman would produce work not as much as he himself decides, but as much as the matter itself can take. That which some suggest—that the will of the craftsman coincides with the magnitude of the matter—seems to be a fiction. But if the efficient cause precedes the matter, then matter will behave exactly as the efficient cause wishes, being easily led to all things, and therefore even to **G** magnitude. If, however, it already possessed magnitude, it would also have shape; for that reason, it would be even more difficult to be worked upon by the craftsman. Therefore, the form <note>original: *species* — used here as the Latin equivalent of the Greek *eidos* (Form/Idea).</note> enters the matter bringing all things with it: and every form contains magnitude, and every mode of quantity, together with reason and under reason. Therefore, in each individual genus of things, quantity is designated together with the form. For one quantity is prescribed for a human...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of matter. Having previously argued that matter is not a body or a collection of qualities, he now examines whether matter possesses "quantity" (size or magnitude) and how the human soul can possibly perceive something that is, by definition, formless and "nothing."</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEADS II.
### PAGE 164

<columns>
...magnitude, and another for a bird. It would certainly be absurd to claim that it is one thing to bring a specific quantity to matter, but quite another to impress upon it a specific quality. We should not say that while quality is a certain "reason-principle," <note>original: *rationem quandam*. In Plotinian philosophy, a *ratio* (or Greek *logos*) is a formative power that gives shape and definition to chaotic matter.</note> quantity is not a form, especially since it exists as a specific measure and number.

<margin>That matter possesses no quantity of its own.</margin> But by what reasoning can one grasp a thing that has no magnitude at all? Perhaps because "being" is not the same thing as "being a certain size." For "being" and "quantity" are not identical; there are many other things besides quantity. We must assume that every incorporeal nature is removed from quantity. Matter is also incorporeal. Furthermore, quantity itself is not a "quantified" thing; rather, it is that which participates in quantity that becomes a "quantified" thing. From this, it is clear that quantity is a type of form. Just as the presence of whiteness makes something white, that which produces color and various hues in a living being is not itself a variegated color, but a variegated reason-principle. Likewise, that which produces a specific size is not itself a specific size, but magnitude itself, or quantity itself, or the reason-principle that effects quantity. When this quantity approaches matter, does it unfold and extend matter into a wide space? Not at all. Matter was not previously squeezed into a narrow space; rather, quantity brings a magnitude that did not exist before, just as it brings a quality that was not there before.

<margin>Whether, and in what way, matter can be thought of since it lacks quantity and all form.</margin> What then? Shall I perceive this "lack of magnitude" in matter? How? Will you perceive it as something somehow formless? What kind of understanding or mental intuition would that be? Perhaps it is an intuition of "indefiniteness." <note>original: *indefinitas* / *aoristia*. This refers to a state of being undefined or boundless.</note> For if like is known by like, then the indefinite is perceived by the indefinite. A reason-principle can indeed be "defined" when it concerns the indefinite, but the intuition directed toward it becomes indefinite. If everything is known by reason and intelligence, and here reason says whatever it has to say about matter, then the "intellection" that strives to see matter is not truly intellection, but rather a sort of "absence of intellection." It is a "spurious" or "illegitimate" imagination, <note>original: *imaginatio non legitima* / *nothos logismos*. Plotinus is quoting Plato's *Timaeus*, where matter is said to be grasped by a "bastard reasoning" because it doesn't fit into the normal categories of being.</note> composed partly of a lack of truth and partly of a different kind of reasoning. Perhaps looking at this, Plato said that matter is perceived by a "bastard reasoning." What then is this "indefiniteness" of the soul? Is it total ignorance, like an absence? Perhaps rather, the "infinite" <note>original: *infinitum*</note> consists of a certain negation combined with an affirmation. Just as the eye perceives the "obscurity" of darkness—which is the matter of every invisible color—so the soul, by stripping away everything in the sensible world that acts like light, and being unable to define what remains, becomes like an eye stationed in the dark. At that moment, the soul becomes somewhat identical to that which it "sees." Does it then see? Perhaps it sees as if seeing a lack of shape, a lack of color, a lack of light. Furthermore, it sees something having no magnitude; otherwise, it would already be reduced to a form. Therefore, when the soul understands nothing at all, is that not the same experience? Not quite. When it understands nothing, it says nothing—or rather, it undergoes no change. But when it thinks of matter, it undergoes an experience similar to receiving a "stamp" of a formless thing. For even when it thinks of things that are formed and have magnitude...

<column-break/>

...and another [quantity] for a bird. And it would be even more marvelous if we brought one [quantity] to matter and another [quality] to it, as if quality were a reason-principle <note>Greek: *logos*</note> but quantity were not a form <note>Greek: *eidos*</note>, despite being measure and number.

How then shall any of the things that exist be grasped if they have no magnitude? Or perhaps everything that is not in <gloss>* quantity</gloss> is not the same as being and quantity. There are many other things different from quantity. Generally, every incorporeal nature must be placed outside of quantity. Matter is incorporeal; since even quantity <gloss>* itself</gloss> <note>original: *autē* (itself) vs *autēs* (of itself)</note> is not "quantified," but rather that which participates in it is. Thus it is clear from this that quantity is a form. Just as something becomes white by the presence of whiteness, that which produced the white <gloss>* body</gloss> <note>original: *sōma* (body) vs *chroma* (color)</note> in a living thing, and other various colors, is not itself a variegated color, but a variegated or "multi-colored" reason-principle. When this quantity approaches, does it unroll matter into a magnitude? By no means. For it was not <gloss>* contracted</gloss> <note>original: *synestalto* (contracted) vs *syneschēto* (held together)</note> in a small space, but quantity gave it a magnitude that did not exist before, just as it gave quality which was not previously there.

What then is this "sizelessness" of matter in our thought? And what is this intellection <note>Greek: *noēsis*</note> or application of the mind? It is indefiniteness. For if like is known by like, then the indefinite is known by the indefinite. A reason-principle might be gathered as something "defined" concerning the indefinite, but the application of the mind toward it is indefinite. If each thing is known by reason and intellection, but here reason says what it must say about it, yet the "intellection" that wishes to be there is not intellection, but a kind of "privation" <note>Greek: *apoia*</note>, then its phantom would be "bastard" and not legitimate, composed of the "not-true" and the other reason-principle. Perhaps it was with this in mind that Plato said it is "graspable by a bastard reasoning." What then is this indefiniteness of the soul? Is it a complete ignorance like an absence? Or rather, is the indefinite a kind of "non-assertion," like darkness to the eye, which is the matter of all invisible color? Thus the soul, having removed all things that are in the sensible realm—like light—and no longer having anything to define, becomes like sight in the dark, becoming in a way identical to what it "sees." Does it then see? Or does it see as a kind of "poverty," a "colorlessness," and a "lack of light," and moreover as having no magnitude? If it were not so, it would <gloss>* already</gloss> <note>original: *ēdē* (already) vs *eidē* (forms)</note> be informed. When it thinks nothing, is this the same state of the soul? No; when it thinks nothing, it says nothing, or rather <gloss>* it undergoes nothing</gloss> <note>original: *paschei mēden*</note>. But when it thinks matter, it undergoes an experience like the "imprint" of the formless. Since, even when it thinks of things that have been formed and given magnitude...

<summary>Plotinus explains that matter has no inherent size or quality, but receives these as "forms" from a higher "reason-principle." He explores the paradox of how the soul perceives matter, concluding that we "see" it through a "bastard reasoning" or a deliberate mental blurring, similar to the eye trying to see darkness.</summary>

...thinks of it as a certain composite. For the mind considers things as if they were distinct or colored and distinguished by qualities. However, the perception of the **formless subject** <note>original: "subiecti," referring to the underlying matter</note> becomes merely a shadowy suspicion, for matter itself is not a "form" or "species." 

Therefore, when the mind receives the subject within the whole and the composite along with those things that are within it, if it should analyze and separate the consequences, then that which the reason-principle leaves behind—the residue—is perceived as a kind of thinness; it is suspected thinly, darkly by the dark, and the mind **understands it without understanding.** <note>original Greek: "νοεῖ οὐ νοοῦσα"; Latin: "intelligit non intelligens." It is as if the soul fears it might fall outside the order of real beings and cannot tolerate staying for long in that which "is not." <margin>* ideally</margin>

**BUT** why is there a need for some other thing for the composition of bodies besides magnitude <margin>XI. That matter is not a quantity.</margin> and all the qualities? For if it were a bulk, it would also be a magnitude. But if it is devoid of magnitude, how will it have a place to receive the rest? Indeed, wherever matter is, it seems to happen to bodies through matter itself. In every way, just as actions, effects, <margin>* all</margin> times, and <margin>* and movements</margin> movements—though they have no "suspicion" of matter within themselves—are nonetheless within the order of things; so too it is not necessary for the primary bodies to "have" matter as a separate component. Thus, the name of "matter" for that which is said to lack magnitude seems to be an empty term. 

Furthermore, it is by no means necessary that the thing receiving a form must be a bulk or a dimension, unless perhaps magnitude is already present; for the soul, in receiving all things, possesses them all simultaneously. If magnitude were a property of the soul, it would rightfully hold each thing within that magnitude. However, **matter** receives what it takes in within a certain space precisely because it is *receptive* to distance. Just as animals and plants receive an increase in quality while they are extended in magnitude—and where the quantity is contracted, the quality is also contracted—so too does matter function.
