...magnitude, or something else: certainly it would be absurd to apply a quantity specific to itself, while impressing a quality also specific to itself. For it should not be said that quality is a certain reason-principle <note>original: "rationem," the formative logic or "logos" that gives shape to reality</note>, but quantity is not a form <note>original: "speciem," the intelligible structure</note>, since it exists as a certain measure and number.

<margin>That matter possesses no quantity.</margin>
**BUT** by what reasoning can one grasp something that has absolutely no magnitude? Perhaps it is because whatever exists is not the same as "quantity" <note>original: "quantum," a thing with physical size</note>. For "being" and "quantity" are not the same thing; many other things exist besides quantity. In general, we must define every incorporeal nature as being removed from quantity; and matter is incorporeal. Furthermore, quantity itself is not "quantified." For the "quantified" is that which participates in quantity; therefore, it is clear from this that quantity is a kind of form. Just as the presence of whiteness makes a thing white—but the principle that creates whiteness in a living creature and various colors is not itself a variegated color, but a certain variegated reason-principle—so that which makes a thing "of a certain size" is not itself that size, but size itself, or quantity itself, or the reason-principle that produces quantity. Therefore, when quantity itself enters into matter, does it unfold and extend matter into a physical size? Not at all. For matter had not been compressed into a narrow space; rather, quantity brings a magnitude that did not previously exist, just as it brings a quality that was not there before.

<margin>Whether, and in what way, matter can be thought of, given it lacks quantity and all form.</margin>
**WHAT** then? Shall I understand the lack of magnitude itself within matter? And what? How will you understand that which is formless? What kind of intellection is this, or what gaze of the mind? Perhaps it is an indefinite one. For if "like is grasped by like," then the indefinite is perceived by indefiniteness. A reason-principle can indeed be definite when dealing with the indefinite, but the mind’s gaze upon the indefinite becomes infinite. But if everything is known through the logic of intelligence: what does that logic say here about the matter itself? That which strives to be intelligence is by no means intelligence, but is like a certain "orbit" of intelligence: truly, the imagination regarding matter is not legitimate, but spurious <note>original: "spuria," echoing the Greek "nothos." Just as the eye perceives the obscurity of darkness, which is the "matter" of every invisible color; so too the soul, by removing everything that belongs to the sensible world like light, and being unable to define what remains, becomes like an eye situated in the dark. It becomes, in a way, the same as the thing it "sees." Does it then see? Perhaps it "sees" as if something were devoid of shape, color, and light. Furthermore, it sees it as having no magnitude, otherwise it would already be reduced to a form. For when it understands nothing, it says "nothing," or rather, it experiences nothing. ...magnitude, and another bird: surely it would be absurd to suggest that providing the specific quantity of a certain bird is different from impressing its specific quality. # BOOK FOUR.

...thinks of it as if it were a composite. For because it perceives things as separate, and entirely colored, it does not think of the whole [matter] as such. The perception or thought of the inherent qualities is clear, but the perception of the formless substrate is dim. Since it is not a "form," when the soul takes the substrate within the whole composite along with its inherent qualities, it analyzes and separates those qualities. What reason leaves behind, the soul perceives dimly as something dim, and darkly as something dark, and it "thinks" while not truly thinking <note>original: "νοεῖ οὐ νοοῦν," describing the paradoxical attempt to mentally grasp something that lacks any defining characteristics</note>. And because matter itself did not remain formless, but is constantly given form in actual things, the soul <margin>specifically</margin> imposes the form of things upon it, for the soul finds it difficult to bear the indefinite—as if fearing to be outside the realm of beings—and does not endure staying in "non-being" for long.

<margin>according to itself</margin> **AND** why is there a need for some other thing to exist for the composition of bodies, besides magnitude <note>physical size or extension</note> and all the various qualities? Or is there a need for that which receives all things? If so, this would not be a mass <note>original: "moles," meaning physical bulk</note>. For if it were mass, it would also be magnitude. But if it is devoid of magnitude, <margin>from</margin> perhaps it will have no place to receive other things. Indeed, if it lacks magnitude, what would it contribute, if it contributes neither to <margin>and motion</margin> form and quality, nor to extension and magnitude? For wherever magnitude is, it seems to come to bodies from matter itself. In general, just as actions, effects, times, <margin>and a common creation</margin> and motions—even though they have no substrate of matter within them—exist among things that are: so also it is not necessary for the primary bodies to have matter, but for each whole thing to exist as it is, being more complex through a mixture of many forms that make up its constitution. Thus, this name "matter," which is said to lack magnitude, would seem to be a hollow term. First, it is by no means necessary for that which receives something to be its own mass, unless it were already magnitude. Matter is present to itself; for just as the soul, while receiving all things, holds them all together, if it happened to possess magnitude, it would hold each thing within that magnitude. Matter, however, receives things within a space for this very reason: because it is receptive to space. Just as animals and plants, along with their growth in size, also receive their quality <margin>and contracted, and perceived</margin> in proportion to their quantity, and if they were contracted, the quality would contract as well. If anyone says that because in such things a certain magnitude precedes the formation of the substrate, magnitude is simply required, they would not be speaking correctly. For in the making of these things, it is not "matter simply," but the matter of a specific plant that is considered. But matter simply <note>pure matter without any attributes</note> must receive its magnitude from something else. Therefore, it is not necessary for that which is to receive form to be a mass; <margin>to receive</margin> rather, at the same moment it becomes a mass, it receives other qualities. It has the phantom of a mass <margin>just as from the new things</margin> as a kind of suitability for it; whence some have said that matter is the same as the void.

->they have handed down that it is the same as the vacuum.<-

<column-break/>

The soul thinks of it as a kind of composite. For it considers things as if they were distinct or colored, and infinite in their qualities. Therefore, it understands a certain whole, and both aspects at once; and the understanding or sense of the inherent qualities is indeed clear. But the suspicion of the formless substrate becomes shadowy: for it is not a "form." When, therefore, in the whole and the composite, the soul accepts the substrate along with those things which are in it, and if it should resolve and separate the consequences, then that residue which reason leaves behind, it suspects as something thin—like a thin thing—and obscurely as something obscure, and it understands without understanding. And since matter itself does not remain formless, but is formed assiduously in things, the soul suddenly applies to it the form of things, poorly enduring the indefinite, just as if it feared it might fall outside the order of things, and could not tolerate lingering longer in that which is not.

**BUT** why is there a need for some other thing <margin>XI. That matter is not quantity</margin> for the composition of bodies besides magnitude and all the qualities? Is there perhaps a need for that which might receive all things? Therefore, it will not be a mass. For if it were mass, it would also be magnitude. But if it is devoid of magnitude, perhaps it will not have a place where it may receive the rest: since, if it lacks magnitude, what will it contribute, if it contributes neither to form and quality nor to distance and magnitude? For wherever magnitude may be, it seems to happen to bodies from matter itself. In every way, just as actions, effects, times, and motions—although they have no substrate of matter—are nonetheless in the order of things: so too it is not necessary for the primary bodies to have matter, but for each whole individually to exist as that which it is; things which exist are indeed more various, having their constitution from a mixture of several forms. Therefore, the name of matter which is said to lack magnitude seems to be empty. Moreover, it is by no means necessary for anything that receives to be a mass or dimension, unless perhaps magnitude is already present: since even the soul, while taking in all things, possesses all things at once. But if magnitude happened to it, it would rightly have each thing within that magnitude. Matter truly receives those things which it accepts within a certain space for this very reason. Just as animals and plants, while they are extended by magnitude, receive in the meantime the production of quality: where also, if the quantity is contracted, the quality is also contracted. But if anyone, because in things of this kind some magnitude precedes the substrate to be formed, should say that magnitude is simply required, he will certainly not speak correctly. For in the finishing of these things, not the matter itself simply, but the matter of such a thing is thought of. But that which is matter simply ought to receive magnitude also from something else. And so it is not necessary for that which is about to receive form to be a mass; indeed, while it becomes a mass, it receives another quality: and it has a vision and an image of mass, seeing as it is the first [substrate], it is a certain suitability for it. Moreover, it is limited as if it were a certain mass or empty dimension: for this reason, some have said that matter is the imagination of dimension.

<summary>Plotinus argues that matter is a formless substrate that lacks inherent magnitude or mass, comparing the soul's difficulty in perceiving it to looking into a dark void. He concludes that matter is not a physical "bulk" but rather a receptive "suitability" or space that allows forms and dimensions to manifest.</summary>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD II.

...magnitude, another for a bird <note>original: "auis/ὄρνιθι," referring to the specific proportions or "ratios" that define different living things</note>. Indeed, it would be truly absurd if it were necessary to apply a specific <term>quantity</term><note>physical size or number</note> to a bird, but not to impress it with its own specific <term>quality</term>. For we should not say that while quality is a certain <term>rational principle</term><note>original: "ratio/λόγος," the formative logic that gives a thing its nature</note>, quantity is not a <term>form</term><note>original: "species/εἶδος," the intelligible shape or idea</note>, seeing as quantity exists as a type of measure and number.

<margin>That matter has no quantity.</margin>
But by what reasoning can one grasp something that has no magnitude at all? Perhaps it is because whatever exists is not the same as "the quantified." For "Being" and "Quantity" are not the same thing; many other things exist besides the quantified. In general, we must place the entire nature of the body far away from quantity, since matter itself is incorporeal. Furthermore, quantity itself is not "quantified" <note>The abstract concept of "three-feet-long" does not itself have length</note>. For the "quantified" is that which participates in quantity. Therefore, it is manifest from this that quantity is a certain Form. Just as the presence of "whiteness" makes something white, that which produces color and various hues in a living <margin>* color</margin> * body <note>original: "σῶμα," a marginal correction for "χρῶμα" (color) in the Greek text</note> is not itself a varied color, but a varied formative principle. In the same way, that which produces a certain magnitude is not itself a magnitude of that size, but is Magnitude itself, or "Quantity-in-itself," or the formative principle that effects quantity. When Quantity itself approaches matter, does it then unfold and extend the matter into a broad magnitude? By no means. For matter had not been <margin>* contracted</margin> compressed into a narrow space; rather, Magnitude brings a size that was not there before, just as Quality brings a characteristic that was previously absent.

<margin>Whether, and in what way, matter can be thought of since it lacks all form.</margin>
What then? Shall I understand matter in itself as something lacking magnitude? And how will you understand it as something without any quality? What kind of intellection or mental intuition would that be? Perhaps it is <term>indefiniteness</term> itself. For if like is grasped by like, then the "indefinite" is perceived by the "indefinite" part of ourselves. A rational principle can certainly be defined when it concerns the indefinite, but the intuition directed toward the indefinite becomes indefinite itself. Yet if every thing is known through reason and intelligence, and here reason says whatever it can say about it—while that which strives to be "intelligence" of matter is not intelligence at all, but a sort of "un-intelligence"—then the image of matter in the soul is not a legitimate one. It is a <term>spurious</term> image <note>original: "notha/νόθον," meaning bastard or illegitimate. This references Plato's Timaeus 52b, where matter is said to be grasped by a "bastard reasoning"</note>, composed partly of that which is not true and partly of a different kind of reasoning. Perhaps looking at this, Plato said that matter is perceived by "adulterine" or "spurious" reasoning. What then is this "indefiniteness" of the soul? Is it total ignorance, like an absence? Perhaps rather, the indefinite consists of a certain negation combined with a certain affirmation. Just as the eye perceives the "obscurity" of darkness, which is the "matter" of every invisible color, so the soul, by stripping away all that is in the sensible realm like a light, and being unable to define what remains, becomes like an eye stationed in the dark. In a way, it then becomes the same as that which it "sees." Does it then "see"? Perhaps it sees it as a lack of shape, a lack of color, and a lack of light. 

<column-break/>

Furthermore, it sees it as having no magnitude, for otherwise it would already be reduced to a Form <margin>* already</margin>. When the soul understands nothing at all, is that state of the soul the same as this perception of matter? Not at all. For when it understands nothing, it says "nothing," or rather, it <margin>* would experience nothing</margin> experiences nothing. But when it thinks of matter, it undergoes an experience <note>original: "passio/πάθος," an impression or suffering</note> such as if it were receiving the "form" of a formless thing. For even when it understands things that are formed and have magnitude,

He explains that we can only perceive this "indefinite" matter through a kind of "spurious reasoning" or mental darkness, stripping away all definitions to grasp the formless substrate.</summary>

# BOOK FOUR.

...thinks of it as if it were a composite thing. For the mind considers things as if they were distinct or colored, and marked out by qualities. And since matter itself does not remain formless, but is constantly being shaped in real things, the soul immediately applies to it the "form" of things, bearing its indefiniteness with difficulty, as if it feared <margin>* image</margin> <note>original: "ἰνδαλμα" (indalma), an apparition or phantom</note> that it might fall outside the order of things, and could not tolerate staying too long in that which "is not."

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of "Prime Matter." Having established that matter is not "bulk" or "magnitude" in itself, he now explains how the soul perceives this formless substrate and why matter is a necessary foundation for physical bodies, distinct from their mathematical dimensions.</meta>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK II

A Since the soul <note>In Neoplatonism, "soul" often refers to the higher mind or the animating principle of the universe.</note> is unable to define anything when it looks upon matter, it pours itself out into a state of indefiniteness <note>original: "indefinitatem," or in Greek, "aoristia" (ἀοριστία)—a lack of boundaries or limits</note>. It cannot circumscribe it or point to a specific mark, for if it did, it would already be defining something. For this reason, we should not say that this underlying subject is "large" on its own, nor "small"; rather, it is both large and small. It is thus a "bulk" <note>original: "moles," meaning a mass or volume without specific shape</note> and yet devoid of magnitude, because it serves as the matter for bulk. If it is contracted into a narrow point, or conversely stretched out from the narrow into the wide, it traverses bulk, so to speak. This kind of bulk belongs to its very indefiniteness; it is, I say, the capacity for magnitude within itself. B In our imagination, however, it appears in the way we have described. For other things that lack magnitude—that is, the "Forms" or "Species"—are each defined, so that no suspicion of "bulk" falls upon them. But matter, because it is indefinite and never rests within itself but is shifted here and there into every possible Form, and flows with a wonderful slipperiness into anything at all, naturally becomes "many" through this process of being led through all things and through "becoming" <note>The process of change in the physical world</note>. By this condition, it seems to have acquired the nature of bulk and dimension.

<margin>
XII. 
The reception of forms does not occur by reason of quantity, but by reason of matter, which differs from quantity.
</margin>

### Thus, spaces are provided for bodies,
for the "Forms" <term>Species/Forms</term><note>The essential blueprints that make a thing what it is (e.g., "tree-ness" or "roundness")</note> of bodies exist within dimensions. By this reasoning, they are not created around magnitude itself as if it were the subject, but rather around that which *becomes* a certain size. For if they arose around magnitude itself rather than around matter, they would similarly lack magnitude and substance, or they would be nothing but "reasons" <note>abstract definitions</note>. But such things belong to the soul, and therefore they would not be physical bodies. D It is necessary, then, that many things here revolve around a single thing—a "one" that becomes a certain size. This must be something other than magnitude itself. Since whatever things are mixed together come into the same space because they possess matter, they do not need anything else to exist within. For each of the things being mixed comes to the meeting bringing its own identical matter with it; nevertheless, there is a simultaneous need for a certain "receptacle"—that is, a vessel or a place. E Place, however, comes *after* matter and bodies; therefore, bodies need matter first. Nor is it proven that bodies exist without matter simply because actions and effects are immaterial. For bodies are composite <note>made of multiple parts</note>, whereas actions are not. Matter itself offers the substrate for the agents when they act, remaining within them. F Yet it does not offer itself *as* the action; for the agents themselves do not seek that. Nor is one action transformed into another so that matter would need to be inside them; rather, the agent himself passes from one action to another, so that it is consistent to say he is the "matter" for the actions. Matter is therefore necessary for both quality and magnitude, and thus for bodies. It is not an empty name, but an underlying subject, G even if it is invisible and devoid of size. Otherwise, by similar logic, we would have to deny that qualities and magnitude exist at all. For if each of these were taken only by itself, it would be said to be nothing. But if these things exist—even if each exists only faintly—then much more so will matter exist, even if it is not clear to us, since it cannot be grasped by the senses. For it cannot be seen by the eyes (being colorless), nor by the ears (lacking sound), nor even by...

<column-break/>

A Because the soul, having nothing to define, when it comes into contact with matter, holds itself in a state of indefiniteness <margin>* and</margin>. It is unable to draw a boundary or reach a specific point, for that would already be to define it. Therefore, one must not speak of it as "large" on its own, nor again as "small," but as both "large and small." And in this way, it is "bulk," and yet without magnitude, like the matter of bulk; and when it is contracted from the large to the small, or from the small to the large, it runs through bulk, as it were. And its indefiniteness is this kind of bulk: the reception of magnitude within itself. But it is not in the imagination in that [other] way. For each of the other form-species that lack magnitude is defined, so that nowhere is there a hint of bulk. But matter, being indefinite and not yet entirely of itself <margin>* nature</margin>, being carried toward every form, here and there, and being led in every direction, becomes "much" by being led toward all things and by "becoming." And in this way, it possesses a nature—the nature of bulk.

### BUT the greatest things contribute to
bodies; for the Forms of bodies do not exist in magnitudes. These things would not happen around magnitude, but rather around that which is "made-large" <note>having had size applied to it</note>. For if they were around magnitude and not around matter, they would likewise be without magnitude and without substance, or they would be "reasons" <term>logoi</term><note>The Greek word "logoi" (λόγοι) here refers to the formative principles or definitions that exist in the mind.</note> alone. These would belong to the soul, and there would be no bodies. It is necessary here, then, to have something around which the many things exist; and this is what is "made-large." This is something other than magnitude; since even now, whatever things are mixed because they have matter come into the same thing, and they do not need <margin>* but of that around which</margin> another thing to be "around," because each of the mixed things arrives bringing its own matter. Nevertheless, they still need a "receptacle," <margin>* of some kind, that which will receive</margin> something that receives them, or a vessel, or a place. But place is later than matter and bodies; so bodies would need matter first. Nor because actions and deeds are immaterial are bodies also [immaterial]; for bodies are composite, but actions are not. And to those who act, matter—whenever they act—provides the underlying subject, remaining in them; it gives itself for the acting. For neither do the actors change [it], nor does one action change into another so that there would be matter for them, but the actor changes from one action to another, so that he is the matter for the actions. <margin>* there is</margin> There is, then, a necessity for matter both in qualities and in magnitude, and thus also in bodies. And it is not a hollow name, but there is some underlying subject <margin>* and existing as invisible and without magnitude</margin>, which is both invisible and without magnitude. Otherwise, we shall say that neither qualities nor magnitude exist by the same reasoning; for each of these might be said to be nothing if taken by itself <margin>* in itself</margin> alone. But if these things are, even though each exists obscurely, much more so would matter be, even if it does not exist clearly, being perceptible, though not to all the senses; for not to the eyes, for it is colorless; nor to the hearing, for it is not a sound.

<summary>Plotinus argues that "Prime Matter" is a necessary but formless substrate that serves as the "receptacle" for physical bodies. He explains that while matter itself has no size or quality, it is the capacity through which size and quality become manifest in the physical world.</summary>

--- Page 253 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of matter (hyle). Having previously discussed matter as a formless "bulk" without magnitude, Plotinus now argues why it cannot be perceived by the senses and why it must be distinguished from the "qualities" of the objects it underlies.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR

A Matter has no flavors, therefore it has no need for noses or a tongue. Could it be grasped by touch? No, because it is not a body. Touch perceives bodies, sensing whether they are dense or rare, soft or hard, moist or dry. None of these belong to the nature of matter. Matter, therefore, is not grasped by the senses, but can only be inferred by reason—not by a reason full of intellect, but by a "void" or "empty" reason. For this reason, this kind of reasoning is called "bastard" <note>original: νόθος (nothos) / adulterina. Plotinus follows Plato’s *Timaeus* in calling the grasp of matter "bastard reasoning" because matter is formless and cannot be known directly by the mind or the senses.</note>. Furthermore, corporeity itself is not a property of matter. B If corporeity is a certain rational principle <note>original: λόγος (logos)</note> distinct from matter, then matter is something other than it; if, however, it is already mixed with matter in the act of creation, then it is clearly a body and no longer matter alone.

<margin>
XIII
Matter is neither a quality, nor does it possess its own quality.
</margin>

->IF MATTER IS A SUBJECTIVE QUALITY<-

If matter were said to be a certain quality that is the underlying subject—one that is common to each of the elements—we must first explain what kind of quality this is. Then, we must ask how a quality can be a substrate. How can something be perceived as "qualified" when it lacks magnitude, possessing neither matter nor size? C Furthermore, if this quality is defined, how can it be matter? If it is indefinite, it is not a quality, but rather the substrate and the very matter we are seeking. Perhaps someone will object that nothing prevents matter from being "without quality" <note>original: ἄποιον (apoion)—lacking any specific property or characteristic</note> insofar as its own nature does not participate in any of the other qualities, but that because it participates in none of them, it effectively possesses a "quality" or "property" <note>original: ἰδιότητα (idiotēta)</note> that distinguishes it from others, like a certain privation of them. D Indeed, one who is deprived of something is in a sense "qualified," just as a blind person is. If, therefore, there is a privation of these qualities around matter, why is it not "qualified"? If there is a total privation around it, this follows even more strongly: for privation is a type of quality. But whoever says this makes everything into "qualities" and "qualified things." E In that case, quantity would be a quality, and so would essence <note>original: οὐσία (ousia) / essentia—the fundamental being of a thing</note>. If everything is a quality, then the concept of quality itself vanishes. It is ridiculous to say that something is made "qualified" by something that is not qualified, or by something that is merely "different" from a quality. If it is argued that it is "different," is it "Difference" itself? If so, it is not "qualified," just as Quality itself is not "qualified." F If it is only "other," it is made "other" not by itself, but by "otherness," just as the "same" is made so by "identity." Moreover, privation is not a quality or a qualified thing, but rather the absence of a quality, or the "emptiness" of something else—just as silence is the absence of sound, or the absence of something visible. For privation is a negation, whereas a quality consists in an affirmation. Furthermore, the property of matter is not a "Form" <note>original: μορφή (morphē)</note>; for its unique nature is to be neither qualified nor to possess a species. It is absurd to call it "qualified" precisely because it is "not qualified." G This is like saying that because it has no magnitude, it therefore possesses a magnitude. Therefore, its property is nothing other than what it is itself. This property is not something added to it, but rather this property is considered in its relationship to other things—namely, that matter is "other" than them. Other things are not only "other," but each of them is also "something" as a species. Matter, however, may be appropriately called "only other." Perhaps it is more fitting to use the plural and call it "Others," so that you do not define it too narrowly with the singular "Other," but rather show its indefinite nature by naming it "Others" <note>original: Alia / τὰ ἄλλα. By using the plural, Plotinus emphasizes that matter is not a single defined entity but an infinite, indefinite potentiality.</note>.

<column-break/>

A Matter cannot be known by touch or taste, for it has neither moisture nor vapor. But could it be known by touch? Not even that: because it is not a body. For touch reaches a body, perceiving it as either dense or rare, soft or hard, moist or dry. None of these are properties of matter. Matter, therefore, cannot be reached by sense, but can be inferred by reason: I do not mean by a reason full of intellect, but one that is empty. And so this reason is called "bastard." Consequently, corporeity itself is not a property of matter. B For if corporeity were a certain rational principle, surely differing from matter, then matter is clearly something other than it; but if it is already mixed in the act of making, it will undoubtedly be a body, and no longer matter alone.

<margin>
XIII
Matter is neither quality nor has its own quality.
</margin>

IF, however, a certain quality were said to be the substrate of things—one that is common to all elements—it must first be explained what sort of quality it is. Then, how a quality C can be a substrate: likewise, in what way something that lacks magnitude can be perceived as "qualified," possessing neither matter nor magnitude. Finally, if this quality is defined, how can it be matter? If it is a certain indefinite thing, it will by no means be a quality, but rather a substrate, and the very matter we seek. But perhaps someone will object that nothing prevents matter from being free of quality, insofar as by its own nature it participates in no quality of others, but for that very reason D that it participates in none of the others, it is already "qualified," possessing a property of such a kind through which it differs from others, like a certain privation of them. For he who is deprived is in a way said to be "qualified," just as the blind man is. If, therefore, the privation of these is around matter, what prevents it from being "qualified"? And if there is an absolute privation around it, this follows even more so: since privation is a certain "qualified" thing. But he who says such things, what else does he do but make everything "qualified" and "qualities": so that E quantity would be a quality, and likewise essence. But if each of these is "qualified," then quality is present. It is truly ridiculous to admit that something becomes "qualified" not so much by a "qualified" thing as by something that becomes "other" than a "qualified" thing. If it is said that this can happen because that which is called "other" becomes "qualified," it must be asked whether that which is called "other" is "Otherness" itself. If that is so, it will not be as a "qualified" thing, since even quality itself does not become "qualified." But if it is said to be only "other," the response will be that it does not become "other" by itself, F but by "Otherness," just as the "same" becomes so by "Identity." But neither is privation a quality or "qualified"; rather, it is either a quality or the loss of something else: just as silence is the loss of voice, or the vacancy of any other thing. For privation is a negation: but "qualified" consists in an affirmation. Added to this is the fact that the property of matter is not a Form: for it is its own property neither to be "qualified" nor to possess a species. It is absurd, however, to name it "qualified" for the very reason that it is not "qualified": for that is the same as if you said that G by the same reason that it has no magnitude, it therefore possesses a magnitude. Therefore, its property is nothing other than what it itself is: nor is the property something added to it; rather, this property is judged in a certain relationship to other things: because matter is clearly something other than them. And other things are not only "other," but also each of them is something like a species: matter, truly, will be quite appropriately said to be "only other." Perhaps, indeed, it will more conveniently be said to be "Others" in the plural number, lest by pronouncing it "Other" in the singular you already define the matter; but rather by naming it "Others" in the plural, you may show its indefinite nature.

<summary>Plotinus explains that prime matter is fundamentally non-sensory and formless, reachable only through "bastard reasoning." He argues that matter cannot be a "quality" or "privation," defining it instead as the "Other" or "Others" to emphasize its total lack of definition.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's metaphysical investigation into the nature of matter (hyle). Having established that matter is formless, the text now examines the relationship between matter and "privation" (the absence of form) and why matter must be considered inherently "infinite" or "limitless" before it receives order from a higher principle.</meta>

# PLOTINUS' ENNEADS II.

<margin>
XIII
Whether matter is privation itself, or whether privation is predicated of matter.
</margin>
**B**ut now we must truly investigate whether matter is privation itself <note>original: *privatio* / στέρησις (sterēsis). In this context, privation refers to the total absence of form or quality.</note>, or if instead privation is merely something said of matter. If someone says that matter and privation are the same in their underlying subject, but different in their definition, they ought to explain which specific definition should be assigned to each. They should provide a definition for matter that touches upon nothing of privation, and a definition for privation that does the same. For either neither definition is contained within the other, or each is in both, or one is only in the other, whichever that may be. If, therefore, each is defined separately and neither requires the other, they will be two distinct things; and matter will be something other than privation, even if privation happens to be present in it. In such a case, it should be possible to see the definition of one without even a potential glimpse of the other. But if they are related as a "nose" is to "snubness" <note>Plotinus uses a classic Aristotelian example: a "snub nose" requires both the subject (the nose) and the quality (the curvature). He is testing if matter can exist without the "quality" of being empty or deprived of form.</note>, then each is a double entity and they are two. However, if the relationship is like that of "fire" and "heat"—where heat is in the fire, but fire is not necessarily included in the concept of heat—and matter is privation in the same way fire is hot, then privation would be a kind of form of matter, while the underlying subject would be something else, which ought to be the matter itself. Thus, in this way, they would not be one. Furthermore, could they be one in subject but two in definition because privation does not designate the presence of anything, but rather an absence? In this way, privation would be a negation of beings, as if one were to say "non-being." For a negation adds nothing, but simply states "it is not"; and thus privation would be like non-being. If it is called "non-being" because it is not "Being" but something else, would there then be two definitions? One regarding the subject, and the other regarding the privation, signifying its relationship to other things? Or rather, does the definition of matter look toward other things, just as the definition of the subject does? If the definition of privation shows its indefiniteness, it perhaps touches upon its very nature—except for the claim that they are one in subject but two in definition. But if, because it is something indeterminate, indefinite, and formless, it is the same as matter, how then can there still be two definitions?

<margin>
XV
How matter is called infinite, or even privation.
</margin>
**O**nce again we must examine whether the "infinite" and the "indeterminate" exist as an accidental property in some other nature, and how they are accidental, and whether privation is also accidental. Truly, if all order descends from higher principles into other things, and these principles order that which is not yet ordered—not ordering "orders," but something else besides the one who orders—and if limit, end, and Reason <note>original: *ratio* / λόγος (logos)</note> provide the order, then it is necessary that what is being ordered and limited is, by its own nature, infinite. Matter is what is ordered, or anything that is not matter but participates in it or takes on the condition of matter. Therefore, it is necessary that the infinite itself is matter. Yet, we must not call it "infinite" as if it were an accidental property <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist (like a person being tan). Plotinus argues that being "infinite" or "limitless" is not an accident of matter, but its very essence.</note>, or as if the infinite "happens" to matter. For first, whatever happens to something must itself be a kind of rational principle, but the infinite is not a rational principle. Secondly, to what existing thing would the infinite happen? Would it happen to a limit or to something already limited?

<column-break/>

**B**ut that which must be investigated is whether privation is the subject, or whether privation is *about* the subject. The person who says that both are one in their underlying substance <margin>hypostasis</margin> but two in definition, should be expected to teach us the definition of each. What is the definition of matter that includes none of the privation, and what is the definition of privation that includes none of the matter? For either neither is in the definition of the other, or each is in each, or one is in the other alone. If, then, each is separate and neither seeks out the other, both would be two things, and matter would be different from privation, even if privation happened to it. But it must be that in the definition of one, the other is not <gloss>is seen</gloss> seen even potentially. If they are like a "snub nose" and "snubness," then each is double and they are two. If they are like "fire" and "heat," where heat is in the fire, but fire is not necessarily taken along with the definition of heat, and matter is thus privation as fire is hot, then privation will be a kind of <gloss>form</gloss> form of it, and the subject will be something else, which must be the matter. And not even in this way are they one. Is it perhaps that they are not even one in the underlying subject, but two in definition, because privation does not signify that something is present, but that it is not present? Thus, privation is a negation of things that are, just as if one were to say "non-being." For negation does not add anything, but says it is not. If privation is "non-being" in this way—if it is non-being because it is not the "Being" but some other thing—are there two definitions? One touching the subject, the other showing the relationship of the privation to other things? Or perhaps the definition of matter is in relation to other things, and the definition of the subject is also in relation to other things. But the definition of privation reveals its indefiniteness, and perhaps it touches the matter itself. How then are they one in the subject but two in definition? If being "indeterminate" and being "infinite" are the same thing as being "matter," how are there still two definitions?

**A**gain, we must inquire whether the "infinite" and the "indeterminate" are accidental to some other nature; and how they are accidental; and whether privation is accidental. If all things that are numbers and rational principles are outside of "infinitude"—for they are limits and order and <margin>ordered</margin> <gloss>from*</gloss> that which is ordered—and these things give order, then it is not the thing already ordered, nor the "order of the mind," but something else being ordered <margin>from</margin> that which orders. Since limit, boundary, and Reason give order, it is necessary that the thing being ordered and defined is itself "the infinite." Matter is what is ordered, as are all things that are not matter but have the quality of matter through participation. It is therefore necessary for matter to be the infinite itself. It is not infinite in an accidental way, as if the infinite were merely a property that happened to it. First, because that which happens to something must be a rational principle, but the infinite is not a rational principle. Second, to what existing thing would the infinite happen? To a limit or a thing that is limited?

<summary>This page explores the metaphysical identity of matter, arguing that it is essentially synonymous with 'privation' (the absence of form) and 'the infinite' (the absence of limit). Plotinus concludes that matter must be inherently limitless so that it can receive form and order from the higher realm of Intellect.</summary>

# BOOK FOUR.

...to the finite? But insofar as it is finite, matter is not a limit, nor is the infinite something that, by approaching the finite, will destroy its nature. This "infinite," then, is an accident <note>original: συμβεβηκός (*symbebēkos*) / *accidens*. In Aristotelian logic, an accident is a property that isn't essential to a thing's definition, but here Plotinus is debating if infinity is essential to matter.</note> of matter. Thus, matter itself is the infinite. For even in the Intelligible world, matter is the infinite, having been generated from the infinity of the One, or from its power, or because the infinity was not already in that higher realm, but was produced by it. How then is it both there and here? Or rather, is the infinite twofold?

**B** What then is the difference? It is as an archetype and an image. Is the infinite among us "less" infinite? Or rather, is it more so? For insofar as an image has fled from true being, it is more infinite. For infinity is "less" when it is defined within life. But what is "less" in the Good is "more" in the Evil. Therefore, that which is there [in the Intelligible realm], being more truly a being, is infinite only as an image <note>original: *velut imaginariè*. Plotinus argues that higher "Intelligible matter" is more "real" and thus less chaotic/infinite than physical matter.</note>. But the matter here, insofar as it falls away from being and truth and sinks into the nature of an image, is more truly infinite.
<margin>As it descends into an immaterial nature, it is more truly infinite.</margin>
<margin>The Infinite-itself.</margin>
<margin>Concerning Matter.</margin>
*As it descends into an immaterial nature, it is more truly infinite. Is the infinite, then, the same as the "essence of the infinite"? Or are they different, as reason and matter are different, and must we say that matter is only "matter," or must we say both? Or rather—which is better—that the "essence of the infinite" does not exist here at all? For that essence would be a "reason" or "form," which does not exist in the infinite, insofar as it is infinite. Matter here must be called infinite in its very self, by its very opposition to reason. For just as reason, being nothing else, is reason, so too matter, being opposed to reason according to its infinity, must be said to be infinite in such a way that it is nothing else besides being matter itself.

<margin>Concerning Matter.</margin>
**A** But is matter the same as "otherness," or just "otherness"? Perhaps it is not otherness simply, but a part of otherness, namely that which is opposed to the things which truly exist—which are the "reasons" <note>original: *logoi*. These are the formative principles or "blueprints" that shape the world.</note>. For this reason, matter can be called a "non-being," and is the same as privation <note>original: στέρησις (*sterēsis*) / *privatio*. The state of lacking something that should naturally be present.</note>, if indeed privation is a certain opposition to those things which consist in reason itself. Will privation then be destroyed when that thing arrives of which it is the privation? Not at all. For the recipient of a habit <note>original: *habitus* / ἕξις (*hexis*). Here meaning a "positive state" or "possession" of form.</note> is not the habit itself, but the privation. Likewise, the recipient of a limit is neither a limited thing nor a limit, but the infinite, insofar as it is infinite. But how can it be that the arriving limit does not destroy the very nature of the infinite? Especially since this infinite is not said to be an "accident"? Perhaps if this infinite were infinite in quantity, it would be destroyed; but now that is not the case, but on the contrary, the limit preserves it in being. For that which nature had intended, the limit brings into act and perfection. It is like that which was not yet sown when it is planted, or like the female when she is possessed by the male. For then the nature of the female is not lost, but rather she becomes "more female"—that is, she becomes more fully that which she is. But has matter, having obtained the Good, become evil? Perhaps because it was already in need; for it did not possess the Good. For that which lacks something and obtains it [might be considered] evil, if it stood equally between both. But that which possesses nothing, as if pressed by poverty—or rather, since it is poverty itself—must necessarily be evil.

<column-break/>

**A** But indeed matter is neither something limited, nor is it a limit. Likewise, the infinite, when it approaches the limited, does not lose its nature: therefore, the infinite is not an accident of matter. Matter itself is therefore the infinite: seeing that even in the Intelligible world, matter is the infinite itself. This was perhaps generated from the infinity of the One itself, whether by its power or its eternity; so that in the One itself there is no infinity, but the One is the author of infinity. By what reason, then, is the infinite both there and here?

**B** Perhaps the infinite is twofold. But how do they differ? Specifically, as archetype and image. Is it therefore the case that the one with us is "less" of an infinite? Perhaps, in truth, it is "more." For insofar as a likeness fails to reach existence and truth, it is to that extent more infinite. For infinity is less when it is more limited. But what is "less" in the Good is "more" in the Evil. That which is there, therefore, being a more existing being, is infinite as if in an image.

**C** But the being here, being "less," insofar as it falls away from being and truth and slides into the nature of an image, is more truly infinite. Accordingly, is "the infinite" the same as "to be infinite"? Perhaps where there is both reason and matter, each is different; but where there is matter alone, we must either say they are the same, or—which is more correct—we should not assign "to be itself" to the infinite there. Otherwise, it would be a "reason" <note>original: *ratio*. A translation of the Greek *logos*, representing the rational structure or form.</note>, which is not present in the infinite at all, if it is to be truly infinite.

**D** We must say, therefore, that matter is infinite of itself through a certain opposition to reason. For just as reason is reason without being anything else, so also matter, opposed to reason according to its infinity, must be said to be infinite in such a way that it is nothing other than matter itself.

<margin>XVI. Questions concerning matter regarding otherness, privation, the infinite, and evil.</margin>

**A** But is matter never the same as otherness? Perhaps it is not the same as otherness simply, but a part of otherness—specifically the part opposed to those things which primarily exist, which are the existing reasons. For this reason, that which is "non-being" can be called a "certain something." It is also the same as privation, if indeed privation is a certain opposition to those things which consist in reason itself. Will privation then be destroyed when that arrives of which it is said to be the privation? Not at all.

**E** For the recipient of a habit is not the habit itself, but the privation. Likewise, the recipient of a limit is neither a limited thing nor a limit, but the infinite, insofar as it is infinite. But by what means can it happen that the arriving limit does not destroy the very nature of the infinite?

**F** Especially since this infinite is not spoken of as an "accident"? Perhaps if this infinite were infinite in quantity, the limit would destroy it; but as it stands, that is not so, but on the contrary, it preserves it in being. For that which nature had established, it leads into act and perfection: just as that which had not yet been sown is perfected when it is sown, and as a female when she is joined with a male. For then the nature of the female is not lost, but rather she is "more feminized"—that is, that which she is becomes more fully realized.

**G** But has matter become evil because it has found the Good? Perhaps because it was already in want, for it did not have it. For that which needs something and obtains it is evil, if it stands equally toward both [good and evil]. But that which has nothing, as if pressed by poverty—or rather, since it is poverty itself—must necessarily be evil.

<summary>Plotinus argues that matter is essentially "the infinite" (apeiron) and "poverty" (penia), acting as the shadowy mirror of the divine. He concludes that when matter receives form or limit, it is not destroyed but rather fulfilled in its natural role as a recipient, much like a field being sown with seed.</summary>

<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

For this is not a lack of riches or physical strength, but a lack of wisdom, a lack of virtue, of beauty, of value, of shape, of form, and of quality. What then prevents this from being deformed, and altogether foul, and altogether evil? Yet matter among the higher beings <note>original: *superos*. Referring to the Intelligible or Divine realm.</note> ought to be called "being." For that which exists above it is considered "superior to being," while among us, that which is above matter exists as "being." Therefore, when "non-being" is said of this higher matter, it is understood as a different kind of being in relation to the beauty of being itself.

<column-break/>

For the poverty of the whole is not of strength, but a poverty of wisdom, a poverty of virtue, of beauty, of strength, of shape, of form, of quality. How then is it not misshapen? How is it not altogether foul? How is it not altogether evil? But that matter there <note>original: ἐκείνη δὲ ἡ ὕλη (*ekeinē de hē hylē*). Plotinus distinguishes between lower physical matter and the "Intelligible matter" that exists in the realm of Forms.</note> is being; for that which is before it is "beyond being." But here, what is around it is being. Therefore, that [higher matter] is a different being in relation to the beauty of being.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON
# BOOK I: ON THAT WHICH IS IN ACT,
# AND THAT WHICH IS IN POTENTIALITY,
# A COMMENTARY.

## SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

->Also concerning act and potentiality. Also concerning metals and stones.<-

<margin>I</margin> THE BOOK on potentiality and *act* <note>In Aristotelian and Neoplatonic philosophy, "potentiality" (*potentia*) is the capacity to become something, while "act" (*actus*) is the state of being real or fulfilled.</note> summarizes and confirms those things said in the book on matter, and through these, they are more clearly understood. It is divided into five chapters. In the first, you will note after certain doubts that whatever is said to be "in potentiality" is necessarily referred to something else—namely, to that which is made from it, or that which is "in act." Likewise, potentiality is properly referred to act. Furthermore, in that which is in potentiality for something, the substance sometimes remains when something new arrives, and sometimes it is changed, whether the change is for the better or the worse. You will consider, moreover, that there is no potentiality in the intelligible world <note>The realm of pure thought and divine forms, which is eternal and unchanging.</note> for a new act to be produced or acquired; otherwise, if it never reached that act, it would be judged to be in potentiality in vain, or if it did eventually reach it, there would be a temporal change within eternal things. Therefore, lest these absurdities follow, all potentiality there has been reduced to its total act from eternity. Subsequently, you will observe that the "power of doing" should not be said to be "in potentiality," but the "power of being acted upon" can be said to be "in potentiality." Finally, you will observe here what Plotinus has already revealed twice elsewhere: he thinks that metal is "congealed water," whether he thinks it is simply water in the manner of crystal, or mostly water. For it is the opinion of the physicists that in composing mixtures, heat and cold act as agents rather than as matter; for because of their intensity, they could not easily be mixed. But you should establish that the "dry" and the "moist" are beneath these. Where indeed the dry prevails over the moist, stone congeals; but where the moisture exceeds the dryness, metal is fashioned, which, because of the abundance of moisture, liquefies in fire—a liquefaction that the dryness in stone prevents.

->Concerning the two matters, and act, and potentiality, both in bodies and in the soul.<-

<margin>II</margin> IN the second chapter, you will observe a twofold matter. First is "composite natural matter," taken for the form of art, such as when a statue is made from bronze. Second is "simple natural matter," taken for a natural form, such as when air is made from water. In the first case, that which is said to be a "statue in potentiality" is the bronze itself; to this is opposed what is called the "statue in act," which is neither the bronze nor the figure fashioned in the bronze, but a certain composite of both. This composite, as existing "in act," is opposed to the bronze insofar as it was "in potentiality," and it is not predicated of the bronze in that way. Therefore, the bronze does not "become" the statue, but the statue "is made from" the bronze. Here, certainly, although the same matter—that is, the substance of the bronze—remains under the figure, yet it is something other than the figure and the composite. Much more, therefore, is the matter different from the form and the composite when, upon the arrival of a new form and for the generation of a new composite, the substance of the prior composite is necessarily changed, as when air is made from water. For there, "primary matter" <note>original: *materia prima*. The most basic, formless substrate of all physical things.</note> lies beneath, in which there is no form, so that it may rightly be said to be "nothing in act." But "secondary matters," as composites, possess something of form, so much so that while they are "in potentiality" for one thing, they are "in act" according to another. In higher things, therefore, because something else (that is, a composite) is made from preceding matter and arriving form, and that is not the same as the matter or even the form, it is rightly said that one thing is "in potentiality" (the matter) and another exists "in act" (the composite). But indeed, in the soul, it seems it should not be said so. For when the soul acquires a habit <note>original: *habitum*. A stable disposition or quality, like knowledge or virtue.</note>, a third composite essence does not emerge from the soul and the habit. Therefore, the same soul which was called "knowing in potentiality" is soon called "knowing in act." It becomes "knowing in act," however, not by the logic by which it was ignorant, but by that which makes it rational and teachable. Indeed, when it is already "taught in act," it still preserves the aptitude for knowledge, but it does not preserve the ignorance. But it is "in potentiality" in one way for acquiring a habit, and in another way "in potentiality" for the act once the habit is acquired. That it does not become learned by the same logic by which it is ignorant is clear, since not just any ignorant person is easily made learned, but only one who is apt. Neither does "privation" contribute to the habit, but "potentiality" does.

Conclude everywhere that what is called "in potentiality" is the subject, while what is "in act" is the composite or quasi-composite. Note that form in a subject is called "act," not simply, but the act of the subject. Finally, besides form or habit (which is a certain form), the action itself which proceeds from the form or habit is also called "act." Action is most especially called "act" because it is both more manifest, and for its sake the form or habit is acquired, and the whole...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's *Ennead* II.5, specifically focusing on the distinction between potentiality (the capacity to be or do something) and actuality (the state of being or doing something) across the different levels of reality—from the physical world to the divine mind.</meta>

<header>ON BOOK V. ENNEAD II.</header>

the power of form or state as it relates to the produced effectiveness of an action. Observe here again, that the act which is form—or stands in the place of form—requires the benefit of some external cause because it approaches a subject that is as of yet unformed and powerless. However, the act which is "action" proceeds from the very power of the form or state itself.

->How potentiality and act differ below the heavens, in the heavens,<-
->and again in the intelligible world.<-

<margin>III</margin> After these things, however, he <note>Plotinus.</note> forbids us from saying that anything in the intelligible world <note>The realm of the Forms or the Divine Mind, as opposed to the physical world.</note> is "in potentiality"—meaning a potentiality that sinks down toward a new act, or is some thing and nature other than the act itself. He says that whatever potentiality is imagined there, the thing itself is not only always "in act," but exists as "act" itself. This is both because what is placed there as a kind of "material potentiality" is a certain form (and therefore an act), and because this potentiality and the act it affects are not two natures, but one. 

We should not, however, say that exactly the same thing exists just because that matter always holds the same form. For even if God were to continue the form in the matter of a body for eternity, the form would still be something other than the matter—just as we believe happens in the celestial bodies. Again, just as the potentiality for learning does not perish in someone who has already learned (for the capacity to be taught is not removed by instruction, but perfected), so in the intellectual world, a certain potentiality lies hidden together with the formal act. Yet, nothing there is said to be "in potentiality" because of this, nor is this a different substance from the act; they differ only by reason <note>original: *ratione*. Meaning they are conceptually distinct but the same in reality.</note>. 

Certainly, just as Aristotle wanted matter and form under the Moon <note>The "sub-lunary" realm: the Earth and its atmosphere where things are subject to change and decay.</note> to be two natures and two substances; and in the heavens perhaps there is one nature of that body which stands in the place of matter or a subject for its own light (which light is not some other nature besides the nature of that body, but is the property and act of that nature); so Plotinus thinks concerning matter and form in the corporeal and incorporeal world. For here <note>On Earth.</note> there are two natures, but there <note>In the higher realms.</note> one. And here they differ just as light diffused through the air (as a form) differs from the airy matter. But there, it is either like a glimmer from light, or shining from light, or at least like light from a flame. For light in the air is a different nature than the air; but in a flame, light adds no other nature, but is a certain property and act of the perennial flame. 

Therefore, just as this light is to the flame as form and act are to potentiality, so almost exactly does the formal seem to relate to what is placed as material in the intelligible world. Such a distinction between the concave and the convex will immediately appear if you consider a spherical surface to which no depth is added. For then the concave and convex conditions would differ neither by location in a subject nor by nature, but perhaps by reason alone. For the single nature of the surface will seem convex to those things outside the circle, but to those inside, it will be indicated as concave—just as intellect and will differ in the soul. 

But to summarize, in this entire corporeal world, matter and form are two natures. But beyond the heavens, form stands for the nature of matter; in the heavens, matter in turn stands for the nature of form. In the incorporeal world, however, whatever matter exists is the essence and nature of form; while form is the being and act of matter. Again, matter there is not "in potentiality" toward form, nor is it a potentiality for form; rather, it is the very potentiality *of* the form. Form, meanwhile, is not some act *in* matter or in potentiality, but is the act of the potentiality itself. 

Since, however, when he names the "intelligible world," he does not wish only the divine intellect to be understood, but additionally all intellects and souls capable of intelligence, he therefore also denies that the intellectual soul is "in potentiality" toward anything new. Rather, it is the procreatress of the animal through its vegetative power, and the producer of science through its rational power. Then he adds that anything—whether an Idea or a thing separated from the body—is entirely whatever it is in act, and is itself an "act," because the whole is a species and a form entirely absolute from time. 

Here you will also note that not only is a superior being required when something is in potentiality (to possess the whole in the present and apply what is missing to the needy thing), but also wherever potentiality and act are two natures, a superior being is needed even if the potentiality is perpetually under the act. For a nature that is in itself "formable" <note>Capable of receiving form.</note> would not be led to a formal nature except by the benefit of some one and simple nature. For above what is composed of two natures stands a simple nature, performing a perpetual act; which, because it always emits its own act from itself, is rightly called "Act." 

Furthermore, where he says that the intellectual soul is in the intelligible world, while the irrational soul is in matter, you will notice that the former is distinct from the intelligible world by nature (though joined by action), just as the latter is a different nature from matter (though meeting it in affection and effect). Indeed, it is not the act of matter, but rather the act of the superior soul into matter, acting as a kind of form for matter. The first soul is especially called "act" because not only does nothing new approach or recede from its nature, but it also exerts its own act within itself; through the intellect it enjoys eternal action, and through its discursive power it conceives nothing from external things, but rather gives birth within itself. 

The second soul also, even if it seems to exchange various actions, nevertheless, as far as it is in itself, it shapes what flows in and out with a single act (or at least a vigor of vivifying matter). Just as fire burns different things with the same heat, it is as if someone were to figure flowing waves in diligent succession with the same seal. I pass over the fact that some argue the soul always perceives and wills these or those things through one continuous act of cognition and will, as they fall into this act of the soul—just as if someone, with eyes not blinking at all, were to see many things in their sight at the same time, not only those continuing at once but also those proceeding step by step. 

The things he signifies afterward concerning the Ideas, saying all are lives and acts, will be treated elsewhere. Certainly remember that the first essence in which the Ideas reside is this very thing: Life. For life does not approach that essence from the outside like a form (as it does to a corporeal essence), but proceeds from within like an act. Therefore, that essence is perfect, and life is perfect; thus it is in act in a perfect manner. Therefore, what is in act there also exists as "act." Just as life is the innermost act of essence, so intellect is the innermost act of life. From that life, the true soul proceeds; and from that intellect, intellect flashes forth into the soul.

->Matter is not anything in act.<-

<margin>IIII</margin> He asks in the fourth chapter whether primary matter is anything in act. Yet it is necessary first that it not be any of those things which are entirely above it (which are true beings), nor again any of those things which are generated in it (which are not true beings). He wonders in the meantime: could it be something else lower than itself in act? Certainly not. For since it falls away from the entire nature and name of "being," and therefore does not have being, it certainly does not have being "in act."

<sig>P 2</sig>

<summary>Ficino explains the Neoplatonic view that in the higher realms, potentiality and actuality are one single nature, unlike in the physical world where they are separate. He concludes by arguing that primary matter lacks all actuality because it lacks true being.</summary>

For this lack is not found in wealth or strength, but rather in a poverty of wisdom, a poverty of virtue, beauty, value, form, appearance, and quality. For this is not a lack of riches or of physical strength, but a poverty indeed of wisdom, a poverty of virtue, of beauty, of value, of form, of appearance, and of quality. What then prevents this from being deformed, and entirely shameful, and entirely evil? Truly, "matter" among the celestial beings is called "being." For that which stands above it is considered superior to being; but among us, that which is above matter exists as "being." Wherefore, when it is said that this <term>matter is "non-being,"</term><note>In Neoplatonism, "non-being" does not mean "nothingness," but rather something that lacks the defined form and reality of the higher spiritual world.</note> it is understood as a "different kind of being" in relation to the beauty of Being itself.

# MARSILIO FICINO’S COMMENTARY ON THE FIRST BOOK CONCERNING THAT WHICH IS IN ACT AND THAT WHICH IS IN POTENTIALITY.

## SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

->Also concerning act and potentiality; also concerning metals and stones.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial L decorated with floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>The book on potentiality and act summarizes and confirms those things which were said in the book on matter, and through them it is more clearly understood. It is divided into five chapters. In the first, you will note—after certain doubts—that whatever is said to be "in potentiality" is necessarily referred to something else: namely, to that which is made from it, or that which is "in act." Likewise, potentiality is properly referred to act. Furthermore, in that which is in potentiality toward something, sometimes the substance remains while something new arrives, and sometimes it is changed; this change may be for the better or for the worse. 

You will consider, moreover, that in the <term>intelligible world</term><note>The realm of divine ideas or the Mind of God, which is eternal and unchanging.</note> there is no potentiality for a new act to be produced or acquired. Otherwise, if it never reaches the act, the potentiality will be judged to be in vain; or if it eventually reaches it, there would be temporal change within eternal things. Therefore, lest these absurdities follow, <margin>||</margin> all potentiality there has been reduced to its total act from eternity. Next, you will observe that the "power of doing" should not be said to be "in potentiality," but the "power of being acted upon" can be said to be "in potentiality." Finally, you will observe that Plotinus here—as he has already revealed twice elsewhere—thinks that **metals are condensed water**, whether he thinks they are simply water in the manner of crystal, or mostly water. 

For it is the opinion of the Natural Philosophers that in composing mixtures, heat and cold approach more as active agents than as matter; for they cannot easily be mixed because of their intensity. But "the dry" and "the moist" are the matter beneath these. Where the dry prevails over the moist, **stone** hardens; but where the moisture exceeds the dryness, **metal** is formed, which melts in fire because of the abundance of moisture—a liquefaction that the dryness in stone prevents.

->On the two matters, and act, and potentiality, both in bodies and in the soul.<-

I I IN the second chapter, you will observe a twofold matter. First, there is "composite natural matter," taken up for the form of art, such as when a **statue** is made from bronze. Second, there is "simple natural matter," taken up for a natural form, such as when **air** is made from water. In the first case, that which is said to be a "statue in potentiality" is the bronze itself. This is opposed to what is called the "statue in act," which is neither the bronze alone nor the figure carved into the bronze, but a certain composite of both. This composite, existing "in act," is opposed to the bronze insofar as it was "in potentiality"; nor is it predicated of the bronze in that way. Therefore, the bronze does not *become* the statue, but the statue is made *from* the bronze. Here, certainly, although the same matter (that is, the substance of the bronze itself) remains under the figure, yet it is something other than the figure and the composite. 

How much more, therefore, is the matter different from the form and the composite in cases where, upon the arrival of a new form and for the generation of a new composite, the substance of the previous composite is necessarily changed, as when air is made from water. For there "primary matter" lies beneath, in which there is nothing of form, so that it can deservedly be said to be "nothing in act." But "secondary matters," being already composites, possess something of form, so much so that while they are one thing in potentiality, they are another thing in act. 

In higher things, therefore, because something else is made from the preceding matter and the incoming form (that is, the composite), and that is not the same as the matter or even the form, it is rightly said that one thing is "in potentiality" (the matter) and another exists "in act" (the composite). But in the **soul**, it seems we should not speak this way. For when the soul acquires a <term>habit</term><note>A "habit" (habitus) here refers to an acquired skill or state of knowledge.</note>, no third composite essence results from the soul and the habit. Therefore, the same soul which was called "knowing in potentiality" is soon called "knowing in act." 

It becomes "knowing in act," however, not by the same reasoning that it was "ignorant," but by the reasoning that it was "rational and teachable." Indeed, when it is already "learned in act," it still preserves its aptitude for knowledge, but it does not preserve its ignorance. It is "in potentiality" in one way for acquiring a habit, and in another way "in potentiality" for action once the habit is acquired. That it does not become "learned" by the same reasoning that it is "ignorant" is clear, because not every ignorant person is easily made learned, but only he who is apt. And it is not "privation" (the lack of knowledge) that contributes to the habit, but "potentiality."

Conclude everywhere that what is called "in potentiality" is the **subject**, while what is "in act" is the **composite** or quasi-composite. The form in the subject is called "act," not simply, but the act *of the subject*. Finally, besides the form or habit (which is a kind of form), the **action itself** which proceeds from the form or habit is also called "act." Action is most especially called "act," since it is both more manifest and it is for the sake of this that the form or habit is acquired, and the whole power of the form...

<summary>Ficino explains Plotinus’s definitions of potentiality and actuality, distinguishing between how they operate in physical substances (like the formation of metals from "moist" matter) and in the human soul (the transition from ignorance to learned action).</summary>
