->IN BOOK 5 OF THE SECOND ENNEAD<-
P 2

...the power of form or habit is brought forth to the effectiveness of action. Again, observe here that the act which is a form, or stands in place of a form—since it approaches a subject that is as yet unformed and powerless—requires the benefit of some external cause. However, the act which is an "action" proceeds from the power of the form or habit itself.

### How potentiality and actuality differ below the heavens, in the heavens, and again in the intelligible world.

III After this, he forbids the judgment that anything in the <term>intelligible world</term><note>The "intelligible world" (mundus intelligibilis) in Neoplatonism refers to the realm of pure thought and divine ideas, which is more real than the physical world.</note> exists in "potentiality"—I mean a potentiality that moves toward a new act, where a thing's nature would be one thing and its act another. He says that whatever potentiality is imagined there, the thing itself is not only always in act, but it exists as the act itself. This is because, firstly, whatever is placed there as "material potentiality" is actually a certain form, and therefore an act; and secondly, because this potentiality and the act it regards are not two in nature, but one. Nevertheless, we should not say that they are exactly the same just because that "matter" always possesses the same form; for even if God were to continue the form in the matter of a body for eternity, the form would still be something other than the matter, as we believe happens in the celestial bodies. 

Again, just as in someone who has already learned, the potential for learning itself does not perish—for the teachable potential is not taken away by instruction but is perfected—so too in the intellectual world, a certain potential lies hidden together with the formal act. However, one cannot say there is anything "in potential" there because of this, nor is this potential a different substance from the act; they differ only in reason. Indeed, just as Aristotle maintained that matter and form are two natures and two substances "beneath the Moon," but perhaps in the heavens the nature of that celestial body is a single thing acting as the matter or subject for its own light—which light is not some other nature besides the nature of that body, but is the property and act of that nature—so Plotinus thinks regarding matter and form in the corporeal and incorporeal worlds. 

For here [on earth] there are two natures, but there [in the intelligible world] there is one. Here they differ as light diffused through the air (as form) differs from the airy matter. But there, it is like the redness within light, or shining within light, or at least like light within a flame. For light in the air is a different nature than the air; but in a flame, it does not add a different nature, but is a certain property and act of the eternal flame. Therefore, just as this light is like the form and act to the flame (which is like the potentiality), so roughly does the "formal" relate to the "material" in the intelligible world. This is almost like the distinction between the concave and the convex that would appear immediately if you considered a spherical surface that had no depth beneath it. In that case, the convex and concave conditions differ neither in subject nor in nature, but perhaps only in reason. For the single nature of the surface would be judged "convex" toward those things outside the circumference, but "concave" toward the interior; just as the intellect differs from the will in the soul. 

But to speak briefly: in this whole corporeal world, matter and form are two natures. But beyond the heavens, form stands for the nature of matter; in the heavens, matter in turn stands for the nature of form. In the incorporeal world, however, matter is the essence and nature of form, while form is the being and act of matter. Again, matter there is neither "in potentiality" toward form, nor is it a potentiality for form; rather, it is the very potentiality *of* the form. Form, meanwhile, is not some act *in* matter or potentiality, but rather the act *of* the potentiality itself. 

Since, however, when he names the intelligible world, he does not wish only the divine intellect to be understood, but also all intellects and understanding souls, he therefore denies that the intellectual soul is "in potentiality" toward anything new. Instead, he says that on its vegetative side, it is the procreative power of the animal, while on its rational side, it is the productive power of knowledge. Then he adds that anything—whether an Idea or a thing separated from the body—is entirely whatever it is in act, and is an "act," because the whole is a species and a form entirely absolute from time. 

Here you will also note: not only that where something is "in potential," it requires a superior being to possess the whole at once and thus provide what is missing to the needy thing; but also that wherever potentiality and act are two natures, a superior being is required even if the potentiality is perpetually under the act. For a nature that is "formable" in itself is only led to a "formal" nature by the benefit of some nature that is one and simple. For above a composite made of two natures stands a simple nature, performing a perpetual act; because it always brings forth its own act from itself, it is deservedly called "Act" itself. 

Therefore, where he says that the intellectual soul is in the intelligible world, but the irrational soul is in matter, notice that the latter is as distinct in nature from the intelligible world as it is joined to it in action—just as this lower nature is different from matter, though it meets it in affection and effect. This [lower soul] is not the act of matter, but rather the act of the higher soul *into* matter, serving as a kind of form for matter. The first soul is chiefly called "act" because not only does nothing new come to its nature, nor leave it, but it also exerts its own act within itself. Through the intellect, it enjoys eternal action; but through its discursive power, it conceives nothing from external things, but rather gives birth within itself. The second soul as well, even if it seems to exchange various actions, nevertheless, as far as it is in itself, it shapes the inflowing and outflowing matter by a single act, or at least by the vigor of vivifying matter. It is like a fire that burns different things with the same heat, or as if someone were to shape flowing waves in diligent succession with the same seal. I pass over the fact that some argue that the soul, by a certain continuous and single act of cognition and will, perceives and wills now these things and now those, as they fall into this act of the soul—as if someone, with eyes not blinking for a time, were to see several things in their view, not only continuous at once but also proceeding one after another in their tracks. 

What he signifies after this regarding the Ideas—saying they are all "lives and acts"—will be treated elsewhere. Certainly, remember that the "First Essence" in which the Ideas reside is this very thing: Life. For life does not come to that essence from the outside as a form (as it does to a corporeal essence), but it proceeds from within as an act. Therefore, that essence is perfect, and its life is perfect; thus it is "in act" in a perfect way. What is there "in act," exists also as an "act." Just as essence is the innermost act of life, so intellect is the innermost act of life. From that life, the true soul proceeds; from that intellect, in turn, the intellect shines forth into the soul.

### Matter is not anything in act.

IIII He asks in the fourth chapter whether primary matter is anything "in act" [actually existing]. And yet, it is first necessary that it not be any of those things that are entirely above it, which are "true beings"; nor again any of those things generated within it, which are "untrue beings." Meanwhile, he doubts: could it be some other kind of act? Certainly not anything "above being"; again, not "true being"; nor again "apparent being." What then? Will matter be something else even lower in act? Certainly nothing. For since it falls away from the whole nature and name of Being, and therefore does not have "being," it surely does not have "being in act."

<summary>Ficino explains Plotinus's view that in the higher intelligible realm, potentiality and actuality are identical, unlike in the physical world where they are distinct. He concludes that "primary matter" cannot be considered an "act" or a "being" because it lacks the formal reality found in higher substances.</summary>

<keywords>potentiality, actuality, intelligible world, matter, form, Plotinus, Aristotle, soul, intellectual soul, primary matter, being, non-being</keywords>

--- Page 260 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Ennead II.5. On the previous page, Ficino discussed how potentiality and actuality function differently across the hierarchy of existence—from the physical world to the celestial spheres and finally to the intelligible realm of divine ideas. Here, he focuses on the nature of "prime matter" as pure potentiality and begins the translation of the Ennead itself.</meta>

-> He confirms the preceding points. <-

He wonders again in the fifth chapter: If matter is nothing in actuality, how can we speak of this very thing? And he confirms what has been said through argument. Now, matter is indeed called the "matter of beings" because it is in **potentiality** <term>potentia</term><note>Latin: *potentia*; Greek: *dynamis*. This refers to the capacity or power to become something, as opposed to already being it.</note> toward those beings, or toward receiving their images; or rather, it is the very **formability** <note>Ficino uses the term *formabilis potentia* to describe matter's core nature: the pure capacity to be shaped by form without having any form of its own.</note> that can be shaped from elsewhere. Indeed, in any art, to name "matter" as subject to the artisan is nothing other than to introduce something that possesses nothing of the craft itself, but is capable of receiving all things. In nature, however, to place matter under the Architect of all things is not so much to bring forward something that is "in potentiality" toward forms, as it is to bring forward a completely formable potentiality. Although this sort of potentiality is thought to precede the effect of form in a certain order, nevertheless, because the very reason for this potentiality is nothing other than "formability," it necessarily depends on the **act** <term>actus</term><note>Latin: *actus*; Greek: *energeia*. The state of being fully realized, completed, or "in action."</note> of the form. Where, even if the potentiality seems present while the form is still seen as future—awaiting, of course, the effect of the form—nevertheless, that which is called the "presence" of the potentiality itself is nothing other than the possibility (if I may put it this way) of the future form: as if one were to imagine a certain confused beginning of a form. Now, if you compare the form to its efficient cause, that which is future for the form depends on the presence of the cause; but if you compare the matter to the nature of the form itself, whatever presence you imagine in the matter depends on the future form, or rather, even on the present form. Indeed, form seems to be included in the very definition of matter, insofar as matter is defined as "formability."

Likewise, if you relate this lowest level to the highest point of the universe, and you say that just as the highest is **pure act**, the shaper of all things, so this lowest is **pure potentiality**, capable of being formed only under all other things; then, surely, if you attribute any formable potentiality to that Supreme being, you have immediately destroyed its nature; and conversely, whatever "act" you dedicate to this lowest thing as its own, you have suddenly lost its nature as well. If anything is said to "belong" to this matter, it is properly the formability of this act. Its presence is nothing other than the futurity of form. Matter is so separated from the nature of being that it does not adhere to being as its property or attribute, nor does it represent being like an image, nor is it so impressed under the image of being that it is affected by it, contracts a footprint from it, or preserves it. It is always naturally stripping off any acts, while preserving its possibility. It only comes to aid where the grade of true beings is at its lowest—that is, nature itself—and there it subsists by the images of beings, without carrying away anything familiar to itself from them. Nothing can be said of it regarding beings, except that it is a **shadow of nature**. And since it is further removed from being than the image of being is, it should in no way be considered either a "being" or "to be."

Now we must judge regarding "non-being" just the opposite of how we judge "being." A being in act has more "being" than a being in potentiality; conversely, therefore, what is called "non-being in act" has less being (or more non-being) than what is named "non-being in potentiality." Since, therefore, matter is more distant from the first essence and truth than can be thought, and is therefore **falsity** itself and a true "non-being," if you imagine this in its own act, you will assert it to be more of a non-being. And as much as it is truer to call matter "possibility," so much will it be falser to think of it as "act," and vice-versa. Conclude the book with this sentiment: Truth itself lends its power even to the false; otherwise, unless it were true that it is false, it would not be false. And the more truly it is false (or the truer it is that "this is false"), the more undoubtedly false it is. So, therefore, the more matter is "true matter"—that is, the more it is a true possibility toward beings—the more it is a "false act," and vice-versa.

-> ON THAT WHICH IS IN POTENTIALITY AND THAT WHICH IS IN ACTUALITY. <-
-> On that which is in potentiality, and that which is in actuality. <-

<margin>1. What has been said: to be in potentiality refers to that which is in act: potentiality itself refers to the act.</margin>
It is customary to say that something is in **potentiality** <note>original: "in potentia"</note>, and something else again is in **actuality** <note>original: "in actu"</note>, and that something in the order of things is an **act** <note>original: "actus"</note>. We must therefore consider what exactly "in potentiality" is, and what "in actuality" is; and whether "to be in actuality" is entirely the same thing as "the act" itself. Likewise, if something is an "act," is it also "in actuality"? Or is each of them different, so that it is not necessary for that which is "in actuality" to also exist as "an act"?

<column-break/>

It is said that one thing is in **potentiality** <note>original: "δυνάμει" (dynamei)</note> and another is in **actuality** <note>original: "ἐνεργείᾳ" (energeia)</note>. It is also said that there is such a thing as **actuality** among beings. We must examine, then, what is "in potentiality" and what is "in actuality." Is "actuality" the same as "being in actuality"? And if there is an "actuality," is this also "in actuality"? Or is each distinct? And for that which is "in actuality," is it not necessary for it to also be an "actuality"?

The page also begins Plotinus's formal investigation into the definitions and differences between potentiality (dynamis) and actuality (energeia).</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s translation and commentary on Plotinus’s Enneads, specifically Book II.5, "On Potentiality and Actuality." While the previous page established that prime matter is a "formable potentiality" that depends on the act of form, this page begins a systematic investigation into how these concepts apply to both the physical (sensible) world and the divine (intelligible) world.</meta>

# BOOK FIVE.

<margin>A</margin> That there is, therefore, something in **potentiality** <term>potentiality</term><note>Greek: *dynamei*; Latin: *in potentia*. The capacity to become something else.</note> among sensible things is clear; but whether there is something in potentiality among intelligible things must be considered. Is it perhaps the case that there is only that which is in **actuality** <term>actuality</term><note>Greek: *energeia*; Latin: *in actu*. The state of being fully realized or active.</note> there? And if there is anything there in potentiality, is it always merely in potentiality, since that realm is eternal? Would it ever proceed into actuality, given that it is not governed by the passage of time? But first, we must explain what it means to be "in potentiality." For "being in potentiality" is not said in a single, simple sense. For it cannot be that what is said to be in potentiality is not referred to anything else; <margin>B</margin> just as bronze is called a statue in potentiality. But if nothing were to be made out of it or in it, and nothing was going to exist beyond what it already was, and it was not possible for anything further to happen, it would simply be what it was. And what it was, was already present; nothing further was going to happen. What else, then, could it be besides that which is currently present? <margin>C</margin> Therefore, it could not be said to be "in potentiality." It is necessary, then, that whatever is something in potentiality—and is already something in actuality—is said to be in potentiality because something else can happen besides it, either with the prior state remaining in some way while producing the next, or by offering itself to that which can be made from it, so that what it was before perishes. For bronze is a statue in potentiality in one way, but water is bronze in potentiality in another, and air is similarly fire in potentiality <note>Ancient physics, following Aristotle, suggested that the elements (earth, water, air, fire) could transform into one another.</note>. Regarding these things which are thus in potentiality, can they also be said to be a certain "power" <margin>D</margin> toward the future? For instance, if bronze is called a certain power of the statue? Perhaps if "power" is taken in the sense of bringing something about <note>Original: *secundum effectionem*. This refers to active power or agency.</note>, it should not be said so at all. For power considered in the sense of bringing something about is not said to be "in potentiality." But if that which is "in potentiality" is referred not only to that which is "in actuality," but also to the activity itself, then "power" would also be "in potentiality." It is more correct and clearer, however, to refer that which is "in potentiality" to that which is "in actuality," and "power" <margin>E</margin> similarly to "activity." Indeed, that which is in potentiality is of such a kind as to be a certain subject for passions, forms, and species, which it is suited by its own nature to receive, or which it even hastens to attain; and some of these lead toward the better, while others lead toward the worse and the destruction of those things, each of which is also something else in actuality.

---

<margin>* only.</margin>
<margin>F</margin> Regarding **matter** <term>matter</term><note>Greek: *hyle*; Latin: *materia*. The underlying "stuff" of the universe that lacks its own form.</note>, we must investigate whether it—being something else in actuality—is additionally in potentiality toward those things by which it is formed, or whether it is nothing in actuality at all. And in general, do the other things we call "in potentiality"—namely those that receive a form while remaining the same—become "in actuality"? Perhaps that which is "in actuality" will be said of the statue: in such a way, clearly, that "the statue in actuality" is opposed to "the statue in potentiality"; however, "that which is in actuality" is not predicated of the thing that was called "the statue in potentiality." If it is so, then that which is in potentiality does not become that which is in actuality, but from that which was in potentiality first, there comes to be that which is later in actuality. <margin>G</margin> For that which is said to exist "in actuality" is the **composite** <term>composite</term><note>Latin: *compositum*; Greek: *synamphoteron*. A thing made of both matter and form, like a bronze statue.</note> itself, and not the matter; what remains is the form within it. And that is indeed the case if a different essence is made, such as a statue from bronze; for the statue is a different essence, like a joined thing. But in those things that do not remain at all, it is manifest that what was in potentiality was something entirely different...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It is evident, therefore, that in the realm of the senses there is something in potentiality; but whether there is anything in potentiality in the realm of the mind <note>Original: *in genere intelligibili*. Referring to the divine realm of Ideas.</note> at all must be inquired. Or is it perhaps that only what is in actuality exists there? And if there should be anything there in potentiality, is it perhaps always in potentiality, if indeed it exists there eternally? And does it never proceed into act because it is not completed through time? But first, we must set forth what that is which is said to be "in potentiality." For that which is in potentiality is not said in a simple way. For it cannot be that what is called "in potentiality" is not referred to any other thing: just as <margin>B</margin> potentiality is spoken of in relation to the making of a statue. Otherwise, if nothing were to be made from it, nor in it, nor was there to be anything beyond that which it was, nor was it possible for anything further to be made, it would certainly be only what it was. But what it was already existed and was present, and nothing was going to be. What, then, could be anything else besides that very present thing? <margin>C</margin> Therefore, it could not be said to be in potentiality. It is necessary, then, that what is something in potentiality—and already something in actuality—is said to be in potentiality from this: that something else can further be made, either with the prior thing remaining in some way, or by offering itself to that which can be made from it, so that what had been before perishes. For in one way bronze is a statue in potentiality, but in another way water is bronze in potentiality, and air similarly is fire. That which is thus in potentiality, is it not also said to be a certain power <margin>D</margin> toward the future? As if bronze were called a certain power of the statue? Perhaps if power is accepted according to the "bringing about" <note>Original: *effectionem*. The act of making or producing.</note>, it should by no means be said so. For power considered according to bringing about is not said to be "in potentiality." But if that which is in potentiality is referred not only to that which is in actuality, but also to the act itself, there will certainly be power in potentiality. One can more correctly and clearly refer that which is in potentiality to that which is in actuality, and similarly <margin>E</margin> power itself to the act itself. Surely that which is in potentiality is of such a kind, like a certain subject for passions and shapes and species, which it is going to receive by its own nature, or even hastens to follow, and partly indeed toward the better, but partly toward the worse and the destruction of those things, any of which is also another thing in actuality.

---

<margin>II. Where a third composite thing is made from potentiality and act, the subject is indeed said to be in potentiality, but the composite is in act. But form is called "act" not simply, but the act of the subject. Where, however, a third thing is not made, that which was called "in potentiality" is soon said to be existing "in act."</margin>
<margin>F</margin> Concerning matter, however, it must be investigated whether—being something else existing in actuality—it is additionally in potentiality toward those things by which it is formed, or rather nothing in actuality. And entirely, those other things we say are in potentiality—namely, receiving a species and remaining the same—become "in act." Perhaps, however, that which is in actuality will be said of the statue: in this way, namely, that what is a statue in actuality is opposed to what is a statue in potentiality; yet that which is in actuality is not predicated of that of which the "statue in potentiality" was said. If it is so, then that which is in potentiality does not become that which is in actuality, but from that which was in potentiality first, that which is later in actuality is made. <margin>G</margin> For that which is said to exist in actuality is the composite itself, not the matter; the remainder is the species <note>Original: *species*. Here meaning the "form" or "design" that defines the thing.</note> within it. And that indeed holds true if another essence is made, such as a statue from bronze; for the statue is another essence, like a joined thing. In those things, however, in which what is called "in potentiality" does not remain at all, it is manifest that it was entirely another thing...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 171 regarding the nature of prime matter. On the previous page, Ficino explored how matter exists as a "non-being" that nonetheless underlies all physical transformations. Here, he moves into the formal commentary on Plotinus's Ennead II, Book 5, focusing specifically on the definitions of "potentiality" and "actuality."</meta>

### COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO

### Confirmation of the preceding points.

He raises a question again in the fifth chapter: If matter is nothing in actuality, in what way can we speak of it? He confirms what has been said through further debate. Now, matter is called the "matter of beings" precisely because it exists in **potentiality** <term>potentiality</term><note>Latin: *potentia*. The inherent capacity for something to become something else, like a seed being a tree in potentiality.</note> to receive them or their images; or rather, it is the very "formable potentiality" itself. Indeed, in any art, to name "matter" under the hand of a craftsman is nothing other than to introduce something that possesses nothing of the craft itself but is capable of receiving all its designs. In nature, however, to subject matter to the "Architect of all things" <note>A Neoplatonic reference to the Divine Mind or Demiurge who shapes the universe.</note> is not so much to provide something that is in potentiality for forms, as it is to provide a completely formable potentiality. 

Even if this kind of potentiality is thought to precede the effect of a **form** <term>form</term><note>Latin: *forma*. The defining characteristic or essence that makes a thing what it is.</note> in a certain logical order, nevertheless, because the very logic of this potentiality is nothing other than "formability," it necessarily depends upon the **actuality** <term>actuality</term><note>Latin: *actus*. The state of being fully realized or functional.</note> of the form. While the form still seems to be in the future, the potentiality already appears present, waiting for the form's effect. Yet, what is called the "presence" of that potentiality is nothing other than the possibility—or, if I may put it this way—the "futurity" of the form; a kind of confused beginning of the form, as someone might imagine it. Now, if you compare the form to its efficient cause, the form's future depends on the presence of that cause. But if you compare the matter to the nature of the form itself, whatever "presence" is imagined in the matter depends on the future—or even the current presence—of the form itself. Indeed, the form seems to be included in the very definition of matter, insofar as matter is defined as "formability." 

Furthermore, if you relate this lowest level to the highest point of the universe, you might say that just as the highest is "pure act," the shaper of all, so this lowest is "pure potentiality," formable only beneath all forms. If you were to attribute any "actuality" to that supreme formable potentiality, you would immediately destroy its nature; likewise, if you dedicated any specific "act" to this lowest level as its own, you would suddenly lose its nature as well. For the "being" of this matter is defined as being in potentiality; its specific act is "formability." Its presence is nothing other than the "futurity" of form. Matter is so separated from the nature of **Being** <term>Being</term><note>Latin: *ens*. In this context, true reality or existence associated with the divine and the formal.</note> that it does not cling to Being as a property or an attribute, nor does it represent Being like an image, nor is it so impressed under its image that it is truly affected by it, or retains a footprint or trace. It is always naturally shedding any acts, yet preserving the possibility for them. It serves only as the very last step in the hierarchy of true beings—that is, nature itself—and it is there that its existence must be considered to reside. 

Now, we must judge non-being in the opposite way we judge Being. A "being in act" has more "being" than a "being in potentiality." Conversely, then, what is called "non-being in act" has less being (or more non-being) than what is called "non-being in potentiality." Since matter is more remote from the primary essence and truth than can be imagined, and is therefore "falsity" itself and truly "non-being," if you imagine it in its own "act," you would assert all the more that it is "non-being." It will be a reversal to call matter "possibility"; it would be as false to consider it an "act" as it would be to consider the reverse. Conclude the book with this sentiment: Truth itself grants power even to the false; otherwise, unless it were true that it is false, it would not be false. And the more "truly" it is false—or the more truly it is what it is, namely false—the more false it undoubtedly is. Thus, the "truer" matter is as matter (that is, the more it is a true possibility for beings), the "falser" it is as an act, and vice versa.

# PLOTINUS
# ENNEAD II
# BOOK V.

# PLOTINUS
# THE FIFTH BOOK
# OF THE SECOND ENNEAD.

-> ON THAT WHICH IS IN POTENTIALITY, AND THAT WHICH IS IN ACTUALITY. <-

<column-break/>

<margin>
1. That which is said to be in potentiality is referred to that which is in actuality: Potentiality itself is referred to the act.
</margin>
It is common to say that something exists in **potentiality**, something else again in **actuality**, and that something in the order of things is an **act**. We must therefore consider what that which is "in potentiality" is, and what that which is "in actuality" is, and whether "being in actuality" is entirely the same as the "act" itself. Likewise, if something is an act, is it also "in actuality," or are the two different, such that what is "in actuality" does not necessarily exist as an "act"?

<column-break/>

<note>original: "Λεγεται τι μὲν δυνάμει..."</note>
<note>This right-hand column contains the original Greek text of the passage translated in the left-hand column.</note>

It is said that one thing exists in potentiality, and another in actuality; and among existing things, something is also called an "actuality" or "activity" <note>Greek: *energeia*</note>. We must therefore examine what is meant by "in potentiality" and what by "in actuality." Is "being in actuality" the same thing as the "actuality" itself? Or is "actuality" one thing and "being in actuality" another? Or is each of them something different? And is it not necessary that that which "is in actuality" is also an "actuality"?

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the original page is "ὅτι μὲν," which begins the next sentence of the Greek text: "That it exists..."</meta>

The text then transitions to Plotinus’s formal investigation into the definitions and relationships between potentiality, actuality, and the "act" itself.</summary>

### BOOK FIVE.

<margin>A</margin> That something exists in **potentiality** <term>potentiality</term><note>The capacity or possibility for something to happen or change; the state of being "able to be."</note> in the realm of the senses is clear; but whether there is something in potentiality in the **intelligible realm** <note>The non-physical world of pure thought and divine forms, which Neoplatonists believe is more real than the physical world.</note> must be investigated. Or is it perhaps only what exists in **actuality** <term>actuality</term><note>The state of being fully realized, completed, or active.</note> there? And if anything is there in potentiality, is it always in potentiality only, since it exists forever? Would it never proceed into actuality because it is not completed in time? But first, it must be explained
<margin>B</margin> what is meant by saying something exists in potentiality. For that which is in potentiality should not be spoken of simply. It is not possible for that which is called "in potentiality" to not refer to something else; just as bronze is said to be a statue in potentiality. Otherwise, if nothing were to be made out of it, nor in it, nor would anything further exist beyond what it was, nor would it be possible for anything more to be made, it would only be what it was. But that which already was and was present would not be anything in the future. What else, then, could it be besides that present thing? Therefore, it could not be said to be in 
<margin>C</margin> potentiality. It is necessary, therefore, that what is something in potentiality—and already something in actuality—is said to be in potentiality because something else can be made beyond it, either by the prior thing remaining in some way, or by offering itself up to that which can be made from it, so that what had been before perishes. For bronze is a statue in potentiality in one way, but water is bronze in potentiality in another, and air is similarly fire in potentiality. Therefore, as for that which is thus in potentiality,
<margin>D</margin> might it also be called a certain "power" toward the future? For example, if bronze is called a certain power of the statue? Perhaps if "power" is taken in the sense of **effecting** <note>The active ability to produce a result.</note>, it should by no means be said this way. For power considered in terms of effecting is not said to be "in potentiality." But if that which is in potentiality is not only referred to that which is in actuality, but also to the act itself, there will certainly be both a power and a potentiality. It is more correct and clear for someone to refer what is in potentiality to that which is in actuality, and to refer the power itself similarly to the act. Indeed, that which is in potentiality is of
<margin>E</margin> such a kind, like a certain subject for **passions** <note>In philosophy, "passions" refer to things that happen to an object or changes it undergoes, rather than its own actions.</note> and forms and species, which it is meant to receive by its own nature, or even hastens to attain; and partly toward the better, but partly toward the worse and the destruction of those things, each of which is also something else in actuality.

# <margin>F</margin> Concerning **matter**, however, we must investigate whether, being something else existing in actuality, it is additionally in potentiality for those things by which it is formed, or rather nothing in actuality. And entirely so for other things which we say are in potentiality—namely, those receiving a species and remaining the same—they exist in actuality. Perhaps, indeed, the term "in actuality" will be said of the statue: in such a way, clearly, that the thing which is actually a statue is opposed to that which is a statue in potentiality; yet the thing which is in actuality is not
<margin>G</margin> predicated of that which was called a statue in potentiality. If this is so, that which is in potentiality does not become that which is in actuality, but from that which was previously in potentiality comes that which is later in actuality. For that which is said to exist in actuality is the **composite** <term>composite</term><note>A single object made of both matter (the stuff) and form (the design or essence).</note> itself, not the matter: the remainder is that which is the species within it. And this is indeed how it stands if another essence is made, just as a statue from bronze: for the statue is another essence, like a joined thing. But in those things that do not remain at all, it is manifest that the thing said to be in potentiality is entirely something else.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> That something exists in potentiality in the sensible realm is clear; but whether there is something in potentiality in the intelligible realm must be investigated. Or is it perhaps only what exists in actuality there? And if anything is there in potentiality, is it always in potentiality only, since it exists forever? Would it never proceed into actuality because it is not completed in time? But first, it must be explained
<margin>B</margin> what is meant by saying something exists in potentiality. For that which is in potentiality should not be spoken of simply. It is not possible for that which is called "in potentiality" to not refer to something else; just as bronze is said to be a statue in potentiality. Otherwise, if nothing were to be made out of it, nor in it, nor would anything further exist beyond what it was, nor would it be possible for anything more to be made, it would only be what it was. But that which already was and was present would not be anything in the future. What else, then, could it be besides that present thing? Therefore, it could not be said to be in 
<margin>C</margin> potentiality. It is necessary, therefore, that what is something in potentiality—and already something in actuality—is said to be in potentiality because something else can be made beyond it, either by the prior thing remaining in some way, or by offering itself up to that which can be made from it, so that what had been before perishes. For bronze is a statue in potentiality in one way, but water is bronze in potentiality in another, and air is similarly fire in potentiality. Therefore, as for that which is thus in potentiality,
<margin>D</margin> might it also be called a certain "power" toward the future? For example, if bronze is called a certain power of the statue? Perhaps if "power" is taken in the sense of effecting, it should by no means be said this way. For power considered in terms of effecting is not said to be "in potentiality." But if that which is in potentiality is not only referred to that which is in actuality, but also to the act itself, there will certainly be both a power and a potentiality. It is more correct and clear for someone to refer what is in potentiality to that which is in actuality, and to refer the power itself similarly to the act. Indeed, that which is in potentiality is of
<margin>E</margin> such a kind, like a certain subject for passions and forms and species, which it is meant to receive by its own nature, or even hastens to attain; and partly toward the better, but partly toward the worse and the destruction of those things, each of which is also something else in actuality.

II
Where potentiality and actuality are combined, the subject is said to be in potentiality, but the composite is in actuality. But the form is said to be in actuality not simply, but of the subject. Where, however, a third thing is not made, that which was said to be in potentiality is soon said to exist in actuality.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of potentiality and actuality in Plotinus's Enneads, Book II, Tractate 5. While the previous page discussed how physical objects (like bronze) contain potentiality, this page transitions into the psychological and metaphysical realms, asking how these concepts apply to the human soul and the divine, intelligible world of Forms.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEADS II.

But when one who is a **grammarian in potentiality** <note>In ancient philosophy, a "grammarian" is a standard example of someone possessing a specific branch of knowledge or technical skill.</note> becomes a grammarian in **actuality** <term>actuality</term><note>The state of fully realizing or practicing a capacity.</note>, why is that which exists in potentiality not the same as that which exists in actuality? For it is the same Socrates who is both wise in potentiality and wise in actuality. Is it then the case that he who is ignorant is also knowing? For he was knowing in potentiality. On the contrary, a man becomes knowing from being ignorant only by **accident** <note>original: "secundum accidens" / "κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς". In philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that isn't essential to what a thing is; Socrates is still Socrates whether he knows grammar or not.</note>. For it is not by reason of being ignorant that he is potentially knowing; rather, it just happens to him that he was ignorant. But the soul, existing according to itself and having certain capacities, remains in **potentiality** <term>potentiality</term><note>The inherent power or capacity to do or become something.</note> even insofar as it is knowing, and it still retains what is called potentiality: so much so that he who is already a grammarian does not cease to be a grammarian in potentiality. Perhaps nothing prevents a thing from being one way and then another. For in one case, it is said to be "in potentiality" only; but in the other, it is "in potentiality" while already possessing the **form** <note>In this context, "form" refers to the specific nature or essence that makes a thing what it is.</note>. If, therefore, that which is called "in potentiality" is the **subject** <note>The underlying material or substance.</note>, while that which is "in actuality" is the composite whole—like a statue—how shall the form or species that exists in the bronze be named? Perhaps it is not out of place to name the "act" according to which the subject is in actuality (and not merely in potentiality); I mean to name the form and species not simply as an "act," but rather as the act *of this specific thing*. For we can also name another kind of act in a more primary sense: namely, the act that is the opposite of the potentiality which leads into action. For that which is called "in potentiality" receives from another the very thing that makes it actual; but that potentiality through which something is able to act produces from itself an act that is in some way its opposite—such as a **habit** <note>original: "habitus" / "ἕξις". A stable disposition or trained faculty, like the virtue of courage.</note>, and the act named according to it, such as courage and acting courageously. But enough on these matters for now.

<margin>
III.
In the intelligible world, nothing exists in potentiality relative to another, although there is a certain power there; but it is always so much in actuality that the whole is said to exist in actuality.
</margin>

->C<-

Now we must explain the purpose for which these things were said. All these points tended toward this: that we might clearly consider in what way, in the **intelligible world** <note>The realm of pure intellect and eternal truths, which Plotinus contrasts with the physical world of change.</note>, that which is "in actuality" is to be spoken of; and whether only that which is called "being in actuality" is there, or whether every single thing there is itself an "act." And if all things there are acts, in what way can that which is named "being in potentiality" exist there? Surely, if there is no **matter** <note>In Neoplatonism, matter is the principle of change and limitation; since the divine realm is perfect and eternal, the presence of matter there is a complex philosophical problem.</note> there in which potentiality consists, nor is anything there going to be something that it is not already, nor does it change into another, nor does it generate another while remaining itself, nor does it depart from itself to hand over its place to another—then certainly that which is called "being in potentiality" will not be there, where the kingdom of beings is not of temporal things, but of eternal ones.

->D<-

If someone, therefore, were to ask those who place "matter" in the intelligible world how matter can be there if there is no "potentiality" associated with that matter (for even if matter is there in another way, there will still be in each thing one part as matter, another as form, and another as the composite), what will they answer?

->E<-

Perhaps they will say that what is called matter there is actually a form, since the soul itself is a form in its own right, yet relative to another thing it acts as matter. Is it therefore in potentiality relative to that thing? By no means. For it is already the form of that thing; it is not a form "in the future," nor is it distinguished from it except by reason. In this way, it "has matter" in the same sense that **Aristotle** <note>Plotinus often debates or adapts Aristotle's theories. Here he refers to Aristotle's "fifth element" (aether) as an immaterial body.</note> asserted that the "fifth body" is an immaterial body.

->F<-

But what shall we say of the soul? For it is a "living being" in potentiality when the living being is not yet born, but is about to be born. Likewise, it is music in potentiality, and other such things that come into being at some time and do not exist always.

->G<-

<meta>catchword: Wherefore (Quapropter)</meta>

<column-break/>

But when one who is a grammarian in potentiality becomes so in actuality, how is that which was in potentiality not the same as that which is in actuality? For the same Socrates is both wise in potentiality and wise in actuality. Is it then the case that the ignorant person is also a knowing person? For he was knowing in potentiality. Or is the unlearned person knowing only by accident? For it is not the unlearned state that is potentially knowing; rather, it happens to him to be unlearned. But the soul, having its own nature, was in potentiality insofar as it is knowing, still being in a state of potentiality; and it is a grammarian in potentiality even while being a grammarian. Or does nothing prevent it from being so in another way—in the former case being potentiality alone, but in the latter case the potentiality possesses the form. Or is it not the case that the "potential" is the substrate, while the "actual" is the composite—for instance, the statue? Should the form upon the bronze be called an "act"? Or is it not strange that we should call only the "act" by which a thing is actual, and call the shape or form "potential" as a simple act, but rather call it "the actual"? Since we might also more properly speak of another act: the one opposite to the potentiality that leads to an act. For that which is "in potentiality" has its "being in act" from another; but that "potentiality" which is able to act from itself is an act—like a habit—and the act spoken of according to it, such as courage and the act of being courageous. These things, then, are so.

->C<-

We must now state the reason why these things were said. For in those intelligible things, how is "being in actuality" ever said? Is it only act,
<margin>* in actuality</margin>
* or is each thing an act? And are all things acts? And is the "potential" there as well? Truly, there is neither matter there in which the potential exists, nor is there anything among the things there that is "going to be" which is not yet, nor does it change into another, nor does it stay and produce something else, nor does it depart from itself and give itself to another to be in its place. The "potential" would not exist there, in that which is of real beings and of things that are eternal.

->D<-

If someone, therefore, were to ask those who wrongly posit matter even among the intelligibles, whether the "potential" is not there according to the matter that is there (for even if matter is there in another way, there will be in each case that which is as matter, that which is as form, and the composite), what will they say?

->E<-

Either that what is there as matter is actually form, since the soul, being a form, would be matter relative to another. Is it not therefore in potentiality relative to that? Or was it
<margin>* was</margin>
* immediately its form, and its form is not something that comes later; or perhaps I should say it is the "reason" <note>original: "logos". Here meaning the formative principle or rational structure.</note> that has matter in such a way that both are understood as one nature—as Aristotle says the fifth body is immaterial.

->F<-

But concerning the soul, how shall we speak? For it is a living being in potentiality when it is not yet, but is about to be. And it is music in potentiality and all other things that come to be and are not always.

->G<-

Plotinus argues that in the divine realm, things exist in a state of pure actuality without the need for material change or "becoming."</summary>

-># BOOK FIVE.<-

So too in the **intelligible realm** <term>intelligible realm</term><note>The world of "Forms" or divine ideas, accessible only to the mind, not the senses.</note>, is there that which exists in **potentiality** <term>potentiality</term><note>The capacity to become something; Greek: *dynamis*.</note>? Or in what way are these things in potentiality? Are the souls the "powers" of these? And as for that which is in **actuality** <term>actuality</term><note>The state of being fully realized; Greek: *energeia*.</note>, how does it exist there? Is it as a statue is the composite whole in actuality because it has received its specific form? Or is it because each thing there is a Form, and is perfect in what it is? For the **Intellect** <term>Intellect</term><note>Greek: *Nous*; the divine mind containing the archetypes of all things.</note> does not proceed from a potentiality of being able to think into an actuality of thinking; otherwise, it would require something prior to itself to move it from potentiality. Rather, it possesses the whole already in itself.

<margin>original: "ὅθ' αὑτό" — by itself.</margin>
**B** For that which exists in potentiality seeks to be led into actuality by another, so that through that cooperation something may come to be. * Therefore, whatever possesses its state eternally by itself must be Actuality. Thus, all "First Things" are Actuality; for they possess what they ought to possess, both from themselves and eternally. And so too the soul exists in this way—specifically the soul that is not in matter, but in the intelligible world. And even the soul that is in matter is another kind of actuality, such as <margin>original: "φυσική" — the natural/vegetative power.</margin> * the **natural** power; for it too is an actuality. But if all things are in actuality, and in this way, <margin>original: "ἐνεργείᾳ δὲ πάντα, καὶ ὅτως" — but all things are in actuality, and in this way.</margin> * are all things then "Actuality" itself? Or how should we say it?

**C** If it has been rightly said that the Intelligible Nature is the **archetype** <note>The original pattern or model from which all things are copied.</note>, and is Life, and the most excellent Life, then the activities there must be the most excellent. Therefore, all things there are both "in actuality" and are themselves "Activities," and all things are Lives. That place is truly the principle and fountain of Life, of the Soul, and of the Intellect.

**D** All other things that are something in potentiality have it so that they are also something else in actuality; which, being already one thing, is said to be in potentiality toward something else. But regarding that which is called **Matter** <term>Matter</term><note>Greek: *hyle*; the underlying "stuff" of the universe which has no form of its own.</note>, of which we say all existing things are made in potentiality: how can we say it is any of the existing things in actuality? For if it were, then all existing things would not be in potentiality. If it is none of the existing things, it must necessarily not even be a "being." How then can it be any "actuality," if it is none of the beings? Perhaps it is none of these things that are produced from it. But what prevents it from being something else? If indeed not all beings are dependent on matter. Truly, if matter is none of the things that exist upon it, and these things are "beings," then matter would be "non-being." Since it is always conceived as something formless, 

<margin>original: "πλάνως" — deceptively or wanderingly.</margin>
it is not a Form; therefore, it will not be numbered among those things as a "being." Thus, it will be "non-being" in this way too. * It is "non-being" in a deceptive and wandering sense. If it flees the nature of truly existing things, and yet <margin>original: "ὑφίστασθαι" — to subsist or exist underneath.</margin> * it is able to **subsist**, yet it is of the nature of those things falsely called "beings"—since it is not even an image of reason <note>original: "ἰνδάλμα λόγῳ"; an image or reflection of the rational principle.</note> as those are said to be—in what kind of existence can it be caught? If it is caught in no kind of existence, how can it be anything in actuality?

**G** How then do we speak of it? And in what condition is it judged to be the matter of beings? Perhaps because it is "in potentiality." Is it not therefore already "in potentiality," and thus already exists, in the sense that it is that which is promised to be in the future? For its very being 

is considered in that which is to come? For its being is referred to and deferred to that which it will become. Therefore, that which is in potentiality is not indeed anything—

<column-break/>

**A** Wherefore in the intelligible genus it will be so: that which is commonly called "in potentiality." But the soul is not these things in potentiality; rather, the soul is the **power** <note>original: "potestas"; here used to distinguish a "productive power" from a mere "potential to be changed."</note> of these things. However, regarding that which is commonly named "in actuality," by what reason can it exist among the higher beings? Does it possess a form, or rather, just as each thing like a statue is a composite in actuality, is it the same there? For every intelligible thing possesses its own form; or rather, every thing is a Form, and that which it is, is a perfect Form. For the Intellect by no means proceeds from 

**B** a potentiality of being able to understand into an act of understanding: otherwise, it would have need of some other prior thing so that it might not break forth from potentiality into act: but it already possesses the whole in itself. For that which is in potentiality requires another thing, by whose approach it may be led to act, so that something may finally become actual. But that which is of itself always in such a state, is Actuality. Therefore, all first things exist as Actuality: for they have whatever they ought to have, and that indeed both from themselves and eternally. Now truly the soul 

**C** is in this same state, especially that which is not in matter, but in the intelligible world. And yet, even that which is in matter is another actuality, namely the **vegetative** <note>original: "vegetalis"; the basic level of life responsible for growth and nutrition.</note>; for it too is an actuality by the very fact that it exists. But if all things are in actuality, and in this way, are all things also "Acts," and by what reason? Surely if it is rightly said that the intelligible nature is ever-wakeful and Life, and the best Life: then without doubt the best activities are there. And therefore, all things there consist both "in actuality" and as "Acts," and they are all Lives. And that place is the place of Life, the principle and fountain of the true soul and of the mind.

**D** <margin>Prime Matter is not anything in actuality.</margin> All other things, whatever they are in potentiality, have it so that they are also something else in actuality. Which, since it already exists and inclines toward another, is judged to be "in potentiality." But as for **Matter** itself, which we judge all beings to be in potentiality: by what condition can we affirm it to be anything of beings in act? Otherwise, all beings would not already be in potentiality. If therefore it is none of the beings, it is necessary that it is not even a "being" itself. Therefore, since it is none of the beings, how can it be anything in act? Perhaps it is none of these things which are made in it. Yet what prevents this from being something else? If indeed not all beings are in matter. Certainly, if it is nothing of those things which are in it, and these are beings, matter will be called "non-being." Also, insofar as it is thought of as something formless, 

**F** it is not a Form: therefore, it will not be numbered among those things as a being. Therefore, by this reason as well, it will be judged "non-being." When therefore, compared to both, it is not a being, it is clearly considered "non-being" all the more. If then it flees the nature of true beings, and yet it cannot achieve being among the number of those things which are falsely said to be—since it is not even an image of reason, as those are said to be—in what kind of being can it be apprehended? But if in none, what will it be able to be in act?

**G** <margin>He confirms the above and concludes that matter should be called nothing other than being in potentiality.</margin> BUT if it is so, how do we speak of it? And by what condition is matter judged among beings? Perhaps because it is "in potentiality." Is it not therefore, because it is already in potentiality, already existing, in the way that it is that very thing which is promised to be in the future? Since indeed being... That which is therefore in potentiality, is not indeed anything...

<summary>Plotinus argues that while divine beings (Soul and Intellect) are pure Actuality because they are perfect and eternal, Prime Matter is unique in being pure Potentiality, existing only as a "non-being" or a shadow that waits to receive form.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's metaphysical investigation into the nature of "matter" (hyle). Having previously discussed potentiality in the soul and intellect, he now descends to the lowest level of reality to define prime matter—the substrate that lacks all form.</meta>

<page-num>176</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS ENNEAD II.</header>

Indeed, all things: since it is not any kind of being by its own self, but is exactly what matter is, it is rightly said not to be in **actuality** <term>actuality</term><note>Latin: *actus*; Greek: *energeia*. The state of being fully realized or "at work."</note>. For if it were something in actuality, that very thing which is in actuality would not be matter: therefore it would not be matter at all, but would behave as a "being." Thus, it will be judged as **non-being** <term>non-being</term><note>Latin: *non ens*; Greek: *me on*. Not "nothingness," but a lack of substantial reality.</note>, not as something different from "being" in the way that **motion** is. For motion clings to being, inasmuch as it comes from being and exists within it. But matter is, as it were, cast out and utterly segregated, nor is it able to transform itself: but what it was from the beginning—which was non-being—so it always remains. Nor was it anything in actuality from the beginning, seeing as it falls so far short of all beings; nor has it ever become anything. For those things which it perpetually seeks to put on, it can never be colored by them: rather, it remains constantly leaning toward something else, existing in **potentiality** <term>potentiality</term><note>Latin: *potentia*; Greek: *dynamis*. The capacity or power to become something else.</note> continually toward those things that follow. And since it appears where the order of beings ends and is constrained by those things that come into existence after it, it surely stands at the very extremity of both; and being constrained by both, it is in actuality toward neither: it remains only in potentiality, left as a certain weak and shadowy **image** <term>image</term><note>Latin: *simulachrum*; Greek: *eidolon*. A phantom or reflection that has no substance of its own.</note> incapable of being formed. Is it not therefore an image in actuality? Is it not therefore a **falsehood** in actuality? This is the same as saying "truly a falsehood," and "really non-being." If therefore it is non-being in actuality, it is all the more non-being: and thus, really non-being. It is far, then, from being any of the things that exist in actuality, for it retains its truth in being "non-being" itself. Wherefore if it must exist, it must not exist in actuality, so that it may have its "being" in "non-being" itself, having avoided the state of "truly being." Since if you take away falsehood from things that are false, you have suddenly taken away whatever essence they had. Likewise, if you introduce actuality into those things whose essence and being consist in potentiality, you have at once destroyed the cause of their substance: because their "being" was to be in potentiality. Therefore, if it is necessary to keep matter incorruptible, it is necessary to keep it as matter. It is necessary then, as it seems, to say it exists only in potentiality, so that it remains that which it is—or else one must accurately debate these arguments.

<column-break/>

That which is not "one being" by itself, but is that which is matter, exists outside of **actuality**. For if it is to be something in actuality, that which is in actuality is not the matter; or it is not matter entirely, but something like bronze. Therefore, "non-being" would exist, not as something different from being (such as motion); for motion depends upon being, as if coming from it and being in it. But matter is like something cast out and entirely separated, and unable to change itself, but remaining always as it was from the beginning: non-being. For it was not anything in actuality from the beginning among all beings, because it was generated. For those things it wished to go under, or to be colored by, it was not able to be; but remaining toward another, it exists in potentiality toward the things that follow. Since those beings have already stopped, it appeared, and being caught by the things coming after it, it stood as the last of them. Caught therefore by both, it would not be in actuality toward either. But to be only in potentiality is to have been left behind as a weak and dim **image** <term>image</term><note>Greek: *eidolon*. A phantom or ghost of a thing.</note>, unable to be shaped. Is it not then an image in actuality? <margin>* by the truth</margin> Is it not then a falsehood in actuality? And this is the same as a *true falsehood. That is, the "really non-being." If then it is non-being in actuality, it is more "non-being"; and therefore "really non-being." It is far then from being any of the things that are in actuality, having its truth in non-being. If indeed it is to be itself, it must be "not being" in actuality, so that having departed from "truly being," it may have its "being" in "not being." Since for things that exist falsely, if you take away their falsehood, you take away the very substance they had. In those things that have their being and substance in potentiality, by introducing actuality, you have destroyed the cause of their existence, because their being was in potentiality. If then it is necessary to keep matter indestructible, one must keep it as matter. It is necessary therefore, as it seems, to say it exists only in potentiality, so that it may be what it is, or these arguments must be refuted.

# MARSILIO FICINO'S COMMENTARY ON BOOK VI OF THE SECOND ENNEAD, CONCERNING ESSENCE AND QUALITY.

## SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

->Concerning essence, how it is constituted from being, motion, rest, the same, and the other; what distinction exists there; and concerning substantial form, formal reason, and accidents.<-

<image-desc>A large decorative initial letter D, depicting a landscape with a building and figures, possibly classical in theme.</image-desc>

WE rightly begin the DISPUTATION concerning essence and quality from the first **essence** <term>essence</term><note>Latin: *essentia*; the fundamental nature or "whatness" of a thing.</note>. There, then, from the "One" simply, proceeds a "one" that is not simple, but a "one being": "one" insofar as it comes from the One, but "being" insofar as it is under the One. But since the origin of being itself is a certain **procession** <term>procession</term><note>Latin: *processio*; the Neoplatonic idea that all reality flows or emanates out from a single source.</note>, having been born, it is now engaged in a certain perpetual procession—an internal procession, I say. For internal progression there signifies fertility; but external progression would signify need. We are accustomed to call such a procession a certain "motion," which we do not call local, but as it were, "vital." If any motion is there, there is also **diversity** <term>diversity</term><note>Latin: *diuersitas*; the quality of being different or "other."</note>, which for the sake of argument you may allow to be called "otherness." For in every motion, one passes from one boundary to another boundary. Already, therefore, we have applied motion and otherness to being itself. But because its procession does not depart from its own land, and therefore is not transmuted into another nature, **rest** and **identity** are rightly recognized there: for since it does not depart, it remains; and since it is not transmuted into another thing, it remains the same.

<summary>This page explores the paradoxical "existence" of Prime Matter as a "true falsehood" that exists only in potentiality, followed by Ficino's introduction to the five Platonic categories—Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Otherness—which constitute Essence.</summary>
<keywords>Matter, Potentiality, Actuality, Non-being, Image, Essence, Procession, Motion, Rest, Identity, Marsilio Ficino, Plotinus</keywords>

--- Page 267 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of prime matter as "non-being" to an analysis of the "First Essence" and the five Great Kinds (Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Otherness) that structure reality. It explains how definitions are formed through genus and difference, and why sensory qualities are not the same as a thing's true essence.</meta>

<page-num>177</page-num>
<header>ON BOOK V. ENNEAD II.</header>

Indeed, we call this entire progression of being itself, along with its stable identity within that progression, **essence** <term>essence</term><note>Latin: *essentia*. The fundamental nature or "whatness" of a thing.</note>, properly named after "being." In a similar way, these five are found in any subsequent essence: **being**, **motion**, **otherness**, **stability** (if I may call it that), and **identity**. For any essence that proceeds outward also proceeds inward in a similar way before its external progression. We can again designate these five within the formal principle <term>formal principle</term><note>Latin: *ratio formalis*. The logical structure or definition that makes a thing what it is.</note> of any thing, which is grasped by its definition; for in that definition, we place **genus** and **difference**. Through the **genus**, the defined thing is in some way the "same" as others, insofar as it agrees with them; but through the **difference**, it is "other" than them, insofar as it disagrees with them, while remaining the "same" as itself. In this principal essence of the thing, designated by genus and difference, there remains its natural and proper power, through which the thing itself endures in time and continues its effectiveness in acting. In this stability, not only does **rest** <term>rest</term><note>Latin: *status*. Often translated as "stability" or "permanence" in this context.</note> shine forth, but **motion** also flashes out—specifically, the natural inclination or dexterity toward acting. All these things seem to be included in the definition, although perhaps some are more manifest than others. Furthermore, the five we have listed agree much more with "essence" than they do with one another. For they spring from essence itself rather than from each other. First, indeed, **motion** and **otherness** differ from being itself in the way a process differs from the starting point from which it proceeds. **Stability** and **identity**, since they are opposed to motion and otherness, are something other than "being," which is not opposed to them in the same way. No one doubts that **motion** is something other than **stability**, or that **identity** is something other than **otherness**, since they are opposites. It is also clear that motion differs from otherness because stability is also something other than identity. For someone can remain in diversity just as they can remain in identity; yet these do not differ so greatly from essence. For essence belongs to them: it "is" that which is motion and otherwise—especially if they are considered at their foundation. For in the same foundation, they differ from one another by their formal reasons. However, although **motion** may in some way be called essence, essence itself does not exist as motion in reverse; otherwise, it would not suit stability at all. Nor, again, is essence stability, for then it would not fit with motion. One may argue similarly regarding the "other" and the "same." Let there be, therefore, one essence, and in it let there be many things—which are not so much "many essences" as they are (if I may say) many **essential things** <term>essential things</term><note>Latin: *essentialia*. Qualities that belong to the very core of a thing's being.</note>. I mean essential principles, properties, and acts, much like light, heat, and lightness are in fire. And yet (as some think), neither these nor those are "qualities" as if in a subject <term>subject</term><note>Latin: *subiecto*. In logic, the underlying thing that possesses traits; here, Plotinus argues these traits are the thing itself, not just "tacked on."</note>, but are rather certain **acts** in an acting principle, proceeding entirely from the same source. Truly, since the first essence is most effective as the primary cause, doubtless nearly innumerable essential powers and acts spring from it and into it, differing from one another in their formal principle and efficacy. There, they are all like certain differences which seem to constitute essences under one single essence, while they establish essential species there. Nor will you wonder that there are many things there which are formally diverse from each other, though they are one in their foundation, if you consider how varied the **germinal principles** <term>germinal principles</term><note>Latin: *rationes seminariae*. The "seeds" or blueprints in nature that direct growth and development.</note> of the limbs are in the single power of a seed, and how varied the powers in the soul are, germinating from the soul and all existing at once. Likewise, consider how much lines distant from the center are separated from each other, yet they are not distant at the center. You shall certainly think of a circle as one thing, in whose center (as if in an essence and foundation) the lines are one, but through the circumference (as if through the form) they are many and distant. In a similar way, you shall imagine the first essence. Indeed, no one doubts that things which are joined in the cause are discrete in the effect. For things that in the cause are not only together in place and time, but are furthermore one in essence, are in their effects distinguished by essences, in addition to the distance of places and intervals of time. For an essence that is weaker than the first cannot supply the same many powers at once to many forms, nor suffice for many actions which proceed variously from the forms. Remember, however, that what is said here about essence and those five kinds is an **attempt** rather than a final conclusion. For these matters will be treated more diligently in the books *On the Genera of Being*. Remember, moreover, that no "qualities" in a strict sense should be placed in divine things. For what appear to be qualities there are both **special differences** <term>special differences</term><note>Latin: *differentiae speciales*. The specific characteristics that distinguish one species from another within a genus.</note> by which the species themselves are necessarily constituted and discerned, and the most intimate and perpetual acts of essence. Among us, too, special differences and similar acts should not be called qualities. For **qualities** are those things which happen to a specific nature that is already complete in itself, whether they come inseparably, like certain properties accompanying a species or individual, or whether they arrive separably, as they are called "common accidents" <term>common accidents</term><note>Latin: *accidentia communia*. Traits that can change without the thing's nature changing (e.g., being tanned or pale).</note>. And this is indeed the correct naming, although it is sometimes allowed that those primary differences and intimate properties be called certain "essential qualities." But where we use names correctly, we call the heat in water a quality and a "passion" <term>passion</term><note>Latin: *passio*. Here meaning an external influence or a state of being acted upon, not an emotion.</note>. Likewise, the heat manifest to the senses in the mass of fire is also a proper quality and an act. But the **heating power**, or the mother of heat, which is included in the substantial nature of fire and in some way in its definition, we call not a quality, but the producer of quality. It must be thought, therefore, that whatever is grasped in the rational principle itself exists entirely as something substantial or essential. We understand this rational principle here as threefold: First, the **ideal** in the mind; second, the **seminal** in nature; third, the **formal** wherever it may be, which is weighed by definition. To this, in natural things, corresponds the **substantial form**, specific in its own matter, in whose power the origin of proper qualities consists. Effects manifest to the senses are received as "qualities," which in the rational principles themselves are "substantial." Hence Plato says in his *Epistles* that we fail in defining whenever, intending to define what is substantial in things, we look at and use those things which occur to our senses. For all these are accidents. For substance is not perceived by the sense so much as it is sought out by reason; and since substantial form does not necessarily rely on physical dimension, many think it is indivisible and reduce it to the intelligible genus. Plotinus says that what the senses openly touch are not essences, but "passions of matter," proceeding from the efficacy of the essential form, and thus the sense is in a way "affected" by them, while reason argues from them. Therefore, no one ought to insert "this coldness" or "liquid manifest to the senses" into the definition of water: both because "cold" and "liquid" designate *what kind* of body this is, but do not define *what* it is; and because even if it is heated, it is still water; and if it appears solid as ice and not liquid, it is still water. Furthermore, that which is gathered from many qualities is not to be thought of as a substance, or essence, or essential principle. For there is one form of one thing, and one formal principle, preceding the heap of accidents. It is absurd to assemble the proper nature of a thing from many qualities at once, especially when any of them taken separately is common; otherwise, an essence would be composed of things that are neither essence nor are they even close to essence. But if someone asks how that first essence of all things is composed, first it is answered that it is not necessary for the thing that is constituted to be exactly the same as those things from which it is said to be constituted. Then, that essence is not wrongly named which is made from "being," which is there first and simple...
