<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...itself: <note>original: "cius"</note> while its various acts are joined to it, through which certain internal differences arise, the essence is completed—not indeed as something more perfect than Being <term>Being</term><note>Latin: *ens*. The most basic category of existence.</note> itself, specifically insofar as it is essence. This is because it is a kind of procession of Being, or a temporary departure from its own primary unity (which chiefly represents the **One** itself), and it requires the parts of which it is composed—if indeed composition can properly be spoken of in that realm. Thus far, we have spoken of **essence** <term>essence</term><note>Latin: *essentia*. The fundamental nature or "whatness" of a thing.</note> in relation to Being and the One. How it is compared to **Life** and **Mind** must be sought elsewhere.

### What Essence properly is in things. Moreover, what Quality is.

**II.** In the second chapter of the book, he inquires what **quality** is, and whether it pertains in any way to the essential definition. He admits, however, that it does not pertain to essence accepted simply, but to *such* an essence. For if you define the essence of fire as "heat-giving," you will rightly include heat there; but perhaps heat will then cease to be properly named a "quality." If, however, you define the absolute **substance** <term>substance</term><note>Latin: *substantia*. That which exists in itself rather than in another.</note> of fire, which precedes such a substance, you do not clearly interpose heat there. 

Indeed, he intends the substance of fire to be not merely a body, but a body placed in a certain species. In its essence, the primary element is the **substantial form** <term>substantial form</term><note>Latin: *substantialis forma*. The internal blueprint or power that makes a thing what it is (e.g., "fireness").</note>, which is hidden from the senses and endowed with hidden powers; the secondary element is its **matter**. Form holds the first place because it places the thing in its species and gives being to matter. Here and elsewhere, he often calls the substantial form the **principle** <term>principle/reason</term><note>Latin: *ratio*. Also translated as 'formula' or 'definition.' In Neoplatonism, it refers to the formative power derived from the divine Mind.</note>, because it primarily corresponds to the ideal and seminal principle, and through it, the thing itself is both understood and primarily defined, and because it is properly known by reason. 

Meanwhile, he touches upon the opinion of some who say that the qualities we encounter through the senses are not something firm in themselves, but are mostly certain **passions** <term>passions</term><note>Latin: *passiones*. Not emotions, but "undergoings" or "affections" caused by an external force.</note> of the underlying subjects or their opposites, brought about by the actions of substantial forms lurking everywhere. Whatever shines forth steadily from these forms into their own matter are the acts and actions of such forms—such as heat, light, and lightness in fire. Whatever passes from there into a "foreign" matter, however, exists as a passion, such as heat passing from fire into water. 

Among these things, he repeats that those which necessarily complete the essence of the thing itself ought not to be called "qualities" there—whether they complete such an "essential" quality (like heat completing the "heat-giving" essence) or the essence simply (like the **specific difference** <term>specific difference</term><note>The characteristic that distinguishes one species from another within the same genus.</note> or the primary power in fire that also precedes heat). He adds that neither the triangle nor the "triangularity" itself in a triangle is a quality (that is, an accident), but for wax or paper to *become* triangular happens in the manner of a quality. 

He concludes that **quality**, accepted by its proper name, happens after the simple essence is already complete, whether the quality is separable from it or, conversely, inseparable. These points seem to be confirmed by the fact that some theologians dispute concerning essence or nature, which they call **quiddity** <term>quiddity</term><note>Latin: *quidditas*. The "what-ness" of a thing; its definition.</note> or the **formal principle**. For they establish four "signs" or stages concerning it: 

1. In the **first sign**, man is an "earthly rational animal"; this is the formal principle of man. 
2. In the **second**, they apply to this principle the negations of everything else, even of the proper consequences. I mean negations resting on formal principles: such as that "man is neither capable of laughter nor not capable of laughter," "neither capable of being taught nor not capable of being taught." <note>This refers to considering the definition in its purest state, before its logical properties are even considered.</note> 
3. In the **third sign**, his **properties** <term>properties</term><note>Latin: *proprietates*. Characteristics that always belong to a species but are not part of its core definition (e.g., humans are the only animals that laugh).</note> are joined to the man: such as "man is capable of being taught and capable of laughter." 
4. In the **fourth sign**, common **accidents** <term>accidents</term><note>Latin: *accidentia*. Non-essential traits that can change, like being tall or sitting down.</note> flow together. 

It is clear that "proper" traits must exist before "common" ones, because movable things necessarily lean upon firm ones. Furthermore, if there are many "proper" traits, they are reduced to the one most proper trait. This, again, if it provides "being such-and-forth" in the manner of a quality (even if it does so constantly), is resolved back into the substantial form, which, as something more perfect, provides "being" simply. This "being" precedes "being such," just as power itself simply precedes a specific power. Thus far is the resolution of accompanying traits into essence. Within the essence itself, the essential power naturally implanted is resolved into the essence, which one may mentally place before the power; from this power, the proper passions arise. After these, common accidents mostly happen from elsewhere.

### Confirming the previous points.

**III.** The third chapter confirms the above and concludes that quality, wherever it may be, is a certain "passion" of the subject depending on a certain hidden efficacy of the essence and the essential power. In the essences and formal principles of things themselves, the "specific differences" and (so to speak) "essential properties" take the place of qualities; through these, the species of things are both established in themselves and distinguished from others. These are indeed certain essential acts, especially in essences separated from matter. 

He adds that the principle itself—that is, both the "seminal" principle and the efficacy of the substantial form—propagates the qualities manifest to the senses on the surface from that which is "proper" and hidden from us within them. And where he says that the heat innate to fire is not a quality, but a species and act of fire, one should primarily understand "heat" to mean the substantial form of fire and its property, from which the manifest heat arises. This manifest heat is not received so much in the form of the fire itself as in some subject. 

In the midst of this, where he says that in the "exemplary principles" <note>The ideal blueprints or Platonic Forms.</note> of qualities there are certain "acts" in place of the qualities that appear openly in subjects, you can also read it this way: *The exemplary principles of qualities are the acts of those things in which they primarily reside.* Nor would it be absurd where he says that the implanted essence of nature is its species or act, but the "affection" passing into another is called a quality instead. Such a statement can be understood in two ways: 

1. First (as we said), that the property lurking in the species itself is its "difference" and "act," but the quality appearing in matter is a "quality." 
2. Second, the affection proper to this species, flourishing constantly in its own matter (like heat in fire), should be considered not so much a quality as an "act" of fire; but it is especially a quality when it passes into water.

<summary>Ficino distinguishes between a thing's true "essence" (its hidden substantial form) and its "qualities" (the outward effects or accidents), using the example of fire's heat to show how a trait can be an essential "act" within the thing itself but a "quality" when it affects something else.</summary>

<keywords>essence, quality, substantial form, accident, quiddity, formal principle, specific difference, seminal reasons, fire, Marsilio Ficino, Plotinus</keywords>

### ON essence and quality.
### On essence and quality.

<margin>A</margin> Is "Being" <term>Being</term><note>Greek: *to on*; Latin: *ens*. The most fundamental category of existence.</note> something different from "Essence" <term>Essence</term><note>Greek: *ousia*; Latin: *essentia*. The fundamental nature or "whatness" of a thing.</note>? Is Being spoken of even when other things are excluded? Essence, however, is Being along with other things joined to it: namely movement, rest, identity, and difference. These are the elements of Essence. Therefore, the whole is Essence. But each of those parts is one thing as Being, another as movement, and another similarly.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, is movement "Being" by accident? Or is it perhaps a component that completes Essence? Rather, it is Essence itself, and all things that exist in the divine realm are Essence. Why then is it not the same with us? Perhaps it is so there because all things are one; here, however, since the images <term>images</term><note>Greek: *eidōla*. Refers to the physical reflections or shadows of the true Forms.</note> are already distinct, this thing is one thing, and that thing is another. Just as in a seed, all things are present together—each part is everything. A hand or a head is not separate within the seed; but in the actual result, they are distinguished from each other. For they are not true realities, but images.

<margin>C</margin> Shall we say then that qualities in that higher realm are essences? Are these the "differences" regarding Essence or Being? Shall we say these differences are what make essences distinct from one another, and are entirely essences? Perhaps that is not absurd to say. But it would be absurd to say this of the qualities found here among us. Some of these are differences of essences, like "two-footed" or "four-footed."

<margin>D</margin> Others are not differences at all, and for that reason alone are called "qualities." Yet the same thing can be seen as a "difference" when it completes an essence, but not as a difference when it does not fulfill the essence in another thing. For example, whiteness completes the nature of a swan or white lead <term>white lead</term><note>Greek: *psimythion*; Latin: *cerussa*. A white pigment used in antiquity.</note>, but in a human, it is merely an accident <term>accident</term><note>Latin: *accidens*. A property that is not essential to the nature of a thing (e.g., a person remains a person whether they are tan or pale).</note>. Or perhaps whiteness, insofar as it exists in the definition <term>definition</term><note>Greek: *logos*; Latin: *ratio*. Here referring to the formal structure or concept of a thing.</note>, is not a quality but a completing factor; but insofar as it exists on the surface, it is a quality.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <margin>He raises doubts concerning essence and quality and provides their solution.</margin> Is Being something different from essence, and is Being spoken of even when others are excluded? Essence, however, is Being along with other things simultaneously joined to it: namely movement, rest, identity, and difference. These are the elements of essence. Therefore, the whole is essence. But each of those parts is one thing as Being, another as movement, and others similarly.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, is movement Being by accident? But is it also essence by accident? Or perhaps it completes essence? Rather, it is itself essence, and all things that are in the divine realm are essence. Why then does the matter not stand the same way among us? Perhaps it is so there because all things are one; here, however, since the images are already distinct, this is one thing, and that is another. Just as in a seed, all things are together, and anything is everything. Neither is a hand separate, nor a head separate; but in the effect, they are distinguished from one another. For they are not true things, but images.

<margin>C</margin> Shall we say then that qualities there are essences? Which indeed are differences around essence or around Being. Shall we say, I ask, that these differences are efficient causes, so that essences are distinct from one another, and are entirely essences? Perhaps that is not absurd to say; but it would be said absurdly regarding the qualities that are among us, of which some are indeed differences of essences, such as "two-footed" and "four-footed." Others truly are in no way differences, and for this very reason alone are they said to be qualities. Although the same thing can seen as a difference where it completes an essence, and in no way a difference in another where it does not fulfill the essence: just as whiteness in a swan or white lead completes the nature, but in a man it is merely an accident.

<margin>D</margin> Or whiteness, insofar as it is in the definition, is not a quality, but a completing factor; insofar as it is on the surface, however, it is a quality. Perhaps, indeed, that which is called "of a certain sort" <term>quality</term><note>Latin: *quale*. The category of "quality" or "suchness."</note> must be distinguished, so that one kind is essential, being a certain property of the essence; the other, however, is only a quality, according to which an essence is named as being of a certain sort. In this case, this very quality does not induce a diversity or change of the essence, nor does it remove it from its essence. But since the essence is already there, and is full, it applies something of an addition after the essence of the thing, or brings a certain disposition from the outside, and after...

...whether this is produced regarding the soul or regarding the body. Therefore, as someone might say, the visible whiteness in a swan does not complete its essence <term>essence</term><note>Latin: *essentia*; Greek: *ousia*. The fundamental "what-it-is" of a thing.</note>: for a swan can exist and not be white. But in white lead <term>ceruse</term><note>A white pigment made from lead, where whiteness is an intrinsic property rather than an accidental one.</note>, whiteness is said to complete its essence; and similarly, heat in fire.

If someone further says that "fire-ness" (to use such a term) is the essence, and says the same of white lead, nonetheless the "fire-ness" of this visible fire is a heat that completes its essence, and similarly with the whiteness in white lead. Therefore, these same things will both complete the essence and yet not be qualities; or again, they will not complete it and will be qualities. And it is absurd to say that where they complete the essence they are one thing, and where they do not complete it they are another, even though the nature of the property is the same.

Perhaps it should be said that the formative principles <term>formative principles</term><note>Latin: *rationes*; Greek: *logoi*. The internal "blueprints" or rational structures that shape matter.</note> themselves, which produce these things, exist as entirely essential. These effects, however, carry over those things which are substantial in the principles themselves—not as substantial things anymore, but as qualities. Hence it happens that we always err in assigning what a thing is, straying in our inquiry into substance and sliding into quality.

For we should not think that fire is this very thing we call "fire" when we look at its quality; rather, we should think that the essence itself is what fire truly is. But what we see now, and what we pronounce while looking at it, leads us a little away from the "whatness" <note>original: *quid est* / *to ti*</note>, and "what sort of thing" <note>original: *quale quiddam* / *poion ti*</note> is correctly designated in the realm of the senses. For none of these sensible things are essence, but are rather the passions <term>passions</term><note>Latin: *passiones*; Greek: *pathē*. From this arises the question: how can essence be composed of non-essences? We have already said that the thing produced need not be the same as those things from which it is composed. But now we must say that even that which is produced is not essence. Yet how do we say that the essence we named in the higher realm is constituted from non-essence? We shall say that essence there possesses "Being" <term>Being</term><note>Latin: *ens*; Greek: *on*. The most pure, unmixed state of existence.</note> more primarily and purely, being constituted, as it were, in the differences of Being itself; or rather, we shall consider it to be named essence with the addition of activities, which seems to be the perfection of Being. But perhaps, due to this addition, it should be judged as more deficient; for it departs from simplicity and declines from Being itself.

Therefore, in such an essence, the "essence" and the "whatness" <note>original: *quid est*</note> must exist before it becomes "of such a kind." What then? In fire, is there an essence simply, before it becomes a specific kind of essence? Perhaps it follows from this that it is "body." <margin>A</margin> ...whether it occurs regarding the soul or regarding the body. That essence seems to be more, but perhaps it is more deficient by the addition, and by not being simple, but already standing apart from it then.

<margin>F</margin> BUT concerning quality, it must be considered what it is in general. For perhaps if it is known what it is, it will rather stop the difficulties. How then is it to be sought? ...is essence. But is the species <term>species</term><note>Latin: *species*; Greek: *eidos*. In this context, it refers to the "form" or "type" that makes a thing what it is.</note> a quality? Perhaps it is not a quality, but the species itself is the formative principle <term>formative principle</term><note>Latin: *ratio*; Greek: *logos*. The rational structure or "blueprint" that governs the development and nature of a being.</note>. What then is the thing that consists of the formative principle and the substrate <term>substrate</term><note>Latin: *subiecto*; Greek: *hypokeimenon*. The underlying "stuff" or matter that receives a form.</note>? For that which presents itself as visible and burning—what kind of thing is that? A dynamic expression of a thing’s nature; an "activity" or "actualization."</note> flowing from the formative principle. In this way, one might affirm that heating, whitening, and other things of this kind are actions.

If this is so, we will find no place to put "quality." Perhaps, indeed, we should not call those things qualities which are said to "complete the essence"—since these are activities or acts arising from the formative principles and essential powers. Instead, we should only call those things "qualities" which are outside the total essence. These are things that do not appear as qualities in one place and not in another, but seem to bring something extra to the essence after it already exists: such as virtues and vices, beauty and ugliness, health, and the disposition of shape or position.

A triangle or a square, in and of itself, is not a "quality." Rather, it is the fact of *becoming* triangular—insofar as it is formed that way—that should be called a quality. We cannot call "triangularity" a quality, but rather the formation of the whole. We can also call the arts and the aptitudes for studies qualities. Therefore, a quality will be a certain disposition in an essence that already exists, whether this disposition is added later or accompanies it from the beginning. If it had not accompanied the essence, would the essence have been any less complete? One might say that this quality is partly <margin>To square.</margin> easily changeable and partly difficult to change, so that its species appears twofold: one stable, the other mobile.

<margin>III. Quality is manifest by a "passion" <note>An effect received from an outside source.</note> from an entirely hidden action. In what way, then, does the quality found there differ from our own? For those are also acts. <margin>F</margin> But when the reason <term>reason</term><note>Latin: *ratio*; Greek: *logos*. If this is so, nothing prevents the heat innate in fire from being a certain species and an act of fire, rather than a quality of fire. But it becomes a quality only when it is received in something else, where it is no longer the "form" of the essence, but only a "trace" <term>trace</term><note>Latin: *vestigium*; Greek: *ichnos*. <margin>G</margin> Therefore, whatever things are "accidents" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that is not essential to the thing (e.g., the color of a shirt is an accident; being a garment is its essence).</note> and are neither acts nor species of essences, but merely provide certain forms through which they make the subjects "of a certain kind"—such as habits, dispositions, or other affections—these should be called qualities. In the principles and archetypes <margin>It has remained.</margin> of these things, there are acts, which in these subjects are merely named qualities.

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS II.

...whether that process is produced in relation to the soul or the body. Therefore, as one might say, the visible whiteness in a swan does not complete its essence <term>essence</term><note>Latin: *essentia*; Greek: *ousia*. The fundamental nature or "being" of a thing that makes it what it is.</note>; for a swan can exist without being white. But in white lead <note>Latin: *cerussa*; a white pigment used in antiquity, where whiteness is a defining characteristic rather than an accident.</note>, whiteness is said to complete the essence; and similarly, heat completes the essence in fire. Furthermore, if someone were to say that "fire-ness" (if I may use such a term) is the essence, and say the same of white lead: nevertheless, the fire-ness of this visible fire is the heat that completes its essence, just as whiteness does in white lead. Therefore, these same things will both complete the essence and not be qualities; and again, they will not complete it and will be qualities. And yet, it is absurd to say they are one thing when they complete the essence, and another thing when they do not, since the nature remains the same. Perhaps, indeed, it should be said that the formative principles <term>formative principles</term><note>Latin: *rationes*; Greek: *logoi*. The rational structures or "blueprints" that organize matter into specific things.</note> which produce these things are entirely essential; however, these effects—which are substantial within the principles themselves—report back to us no longer as substantial things, but as qualities. Thus it happens that we always err in assigning "what a thing is," <note>Referring to the "quiddity" or definition of a thing.</note> deviating in our investigation of substance and slipping into quality. For we must not think that fire is merely this thing we call "fire" when we look at its quality; rather, fire itself is an essence. But the things we now look upon, and looking upon them make our pronouncements, lead us far away from "what a thing is," so that a "certain quality" is correctly designated in the sensible genus. For none of these sensible things is an essence, but rather they are the passions <note>Latin: *passiones*; Greek: *pathē*. Here meaning the "affections" or ways an essence is acted upon or appears to the senses.</note> of essence. Hence the question is asked: how is essence fashioned out of non-essences? We have said, therefore, that what a thing is need not be the same as the things from which it is fashioned; but now we must say that even that which is produced is not essence. But how do we say that what we called "essence" there <note>Plotinus often uses "there" to refer to the higher, intelligible realm of true Being.</note> is constituted from non-essence? We shall say that essence exists there in a more primary and pure way, as if constituted in the differences of Being itself; or rather, we shall think that it was named "essence" with the addition of activities <term>activities</term><note>Latin: *actionum*; Greek: *energeiai*. The dynamic expression or "working" of a thing's nature.</note>, which seems to be the perfection of Being. Perhaps, indeed, because of this addition, it should be judged more deficient, since it falls away from simplicity and declines from Being itself.

<margin>
II
*What quality is, and whether it pertains to the essential reason in any way.*
</margin>

BUT we must consider altogether what quality is. For perhaps when we have learned what it is, we shall push away doubts of this kind. First, we must inquire whether it should be thought that the same thing is sometimes merely a quality and at other times also completes an essence—so that we do not struggle too harshly to prove that quality simply completes essence, but rather a "certain kind" of essence. It is necessary, therefore, in such an essence, for the essence (the "what it is") to exist before it becomes "such a kind." What then? In fire, before it is such an essence, is it simply an essence? Perhaps it follows from this that it is a body. Therefore, the genus itself, which is body, will be the essence; but fire will be a "hot body," and the whole will not be the essence. Instead, heat will be in it just as a snub-nosed shape <note>Plotinus uses the classic Aristotelian example of "snub-nosedness" (simitas), a quality that cannot be defined without the substance (a nose) it belongs to.</note> is in you. For this reason, if the heat, the brightness, and the lightness (which seem to be qualities) were taken away, and the resistance were removed, and that which is called the three-fold dimension and matter were left behind, that remainder itself would be the essence. But that does not seem likely. For the species <note>Latin: *species*; Greek: *eidos*. The "form" or "type" that defines the thing.</note> is more...

<column-break/>

Α ...whether it happens in relation to the soul or in relation to the body. But even if the visible white in white lead <note>Greek: *psimythio*; the same as Latin *cerussa*.</note> were to be completing its nature. For in a swan, it is not completing, for it could also become not white; but in white lead, [it is] like the heat of fire. But if someone were to say that "fire-ness" is the essence, and the same by analogy for white lead; nevertheless, the visible aspect of fire—whether fire-ness or heat—is completing [the essence]. And the whiteness likewise in the other. These same things become both completions and qualities, and both not completions and qualities. And it is absurd to say they are one thing in those cases where they complete, and another where they do not, when the nature is the same. But perhaps the formative principles <note>Greek: *logoi*.</note> that made them are entirely essential, while the results already possess something from that "there" <note>The intelligible realm.</note> as "qualities" here; and for this reason, we always err concerning the "what" <note>The essence.</note>, slipping away in our inquiries into them and being carried down into the "of what kind" <note>The quality.</note>. For fire is not what we say it is when we look toward the "of what kind," but rather it is an essence. But the things we now see, and looking at them speak, lead us away from the "what" and we define the "of what kind," even in sensible things, irrationally. For none of them is essence, but rather the passions <note>Greek: *pathē*.</note> of essence. From this comes that other question: how then is essence made from non-essences? <margin>+ It was said</margin> *It was said, therefore, that the thing produced is not the same as the things from which it is made. But now it must be said that even the thing produced is not essence. But how do we say that what we called essence there is not from non-essence? For we shall say that essence there possesses Being more primarily and purely, being essence as if in the differences of true Being—or rather, it is called essence with the addition of activities <note>Greek: *energeiōn*.</note>. While that [higher realm] seems to be a plurality, perhaps it is [actually] more deficient in its distance [from the One], as it is not simple but already departing [from unity] then.

BUT concerning quality, we must consider it as a whole; for perhaps by knowing what it is, we will better handle the difficulties. First, then, we must seek this: whether the same thing is required to be at one time only a quality and at another time a completion of essence—or, being uneasy that a quality should be a completion of essence, we should rather call them "qualified essences." It is necessary for a qualified essence that the essence exists before the "quality," just as fire is. What then was the essence of fire before it was a qualified essence? The essence, therefore, is the body. For the qualified essence will be the body. Thus fire is a "hot body." The whole is not the essence. But let the heat be in it as the "snub-ness" <note>Greek: *simon*; referring to the shape of a nose.</note> is in you. <margin>to square.</margin>

<margin>the quality.</margin>

But regarding what is only called "quality," it is likewise an activity; when it belongs to the peculiarity of an essence, it is clearly not a quality. When the rational principle separates the peculiarity in them—not by removing it, but rather by receiving it and generating another thing—it has generated a "quality," as if taking a part of the essence that appeared on the surface. If we look at fire, nothing prevents heat from being innate to fire, being a form and an activity of the fire rather than a quality; but it is then a "quality" only when it is received in something else, where it is no longer the form of an essence, but only a trace, a shadow, and an image, leaving behind the essence whose activity it is. <margin>B</margin>

<margin>C</margin>

Therefore, a quality will be a certain disposition in essences which already exist, whether this be an added thing or something accompanying them from the start.

<margin>D</margin>

Therefore, when it has the property of essence, it follows that it is not properly a quality: but when the rational principle makes what is proper in these—not taking away or cutting off from there, but rather receiving and generating—it procreates another "quality," as if taking a part of the essence appearing on the surface. If this is so, nothing prevents heat from being innate to fire as a certain form and act of fire, and not a quality of fire. It would be absurd to say that a thing is one thing when it completes an essence, and something else entirely when it does not, even though the nature of the thing remains the same. What we perceive now, and what we refer to when we speak, leads us away from the "whatness" of a thing; thus, a "quality" is correctly designated within the realm of the sensible. 

For none of these sensible things are essence, but are rather the passions <note>affections or outward effects</note> of essence. Hence the question: how can an essence be composed of non-essences? <meta>This page continues the investigation into the Aristotelian category of "Quality" (*poiotēs*) from a Neoplatonic perspective. Plotinus is specifically distinguishing between "essential differences" (the things that make a substance what it is, like heat in fire) and "accidental qualities" (things that can change without destroying the substance, like a person's health or virtue). This page concludes that true qualities are mere "shadows" or "traces" of the higher Activities (*energeiai*) that constitute Essence.</meta>

<summary>Plotinus distinguishes between essential "activities" that make a thing what it is (like heat in fire) and "qualities" which are mere accidental surface features or shadows of those higher powers. He concludes that true quality only exists when an essential act is viewed as separate from the substance it belongs to.</summary>

COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

<columns>

Nor should the same thing be a quality in one instance but not a quality in another; rather, that which is separated from essence <term>essence</term><note>Latin: *essentia*; Greek: *ousia*. The fundamental reality of a thing.</note> turns into quality. However, that which remains with the essence exists as essence, or species <term>species</term><note>Latin: *species*; Greek: *eidos*. Often translated as "form," the intelligible look or nature of a thing.</note>, or activity <term>activity</term><note>Latin: *actus*; Greek: *energeia*. The active expression of a thing's being.</note>. For no nature is the same when it is in its own source as it is when it is in another thing; in the latter case, being removed from its origin, it no longer retains the dignity of species and activity. Nevertheless, that which is never the species of anything but is always an accident <term>accident</term><note>Latin: *accidens*. A property that is not essential to a thing’s nature, such as hair color or location.</note> is now purely quality, and quality alone.

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the original Greek text for the passage in the left column: "At least those before them are as to the firsts, their activities, and qualities do not arise there, or non-quality. But that which has been stripped of essence is quality; while that which has it is essence, or form, or activity. For nothing is the same in itself and in another, having fallen away from being form and activity; but that which is never the form of another, but always an accident, is purely quality and this alone."</note>

</columns>

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO ON BOOK SEVEN OF THE SECOND ENNEAD.

## SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

->How composition and mixture occur in numbers and in nature: Also concerning the three opinions on mixing.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial Q depicting a detailed classical building or temple in a rural landscape with mountains in the background.</image-desc>JUST AS in numbers it is one thing to be added and another to multiply, so in natural things it is one thing to compose <term>compose</term><note>Latin: *componere*. Putting things side-by-side without them losing their individual boundaries, like a pile of stones.</note> and another to mix <term>mix</term><note>Latin: *commiscere*. A thorough blending where the components interpenetrate.</note>. Indeed, by a certain similar proportion, just as in the order of numbers unity is added to unity and becomes the number two, so in nature form is added to matter and becomes a body. There, again, unity is added to a number to produce the number three; here, similarly, power is joined to a body to effect motion, and it becomes a "movable body." There, once more, a number is applied to a number—as two to two, from which comes four, or even three moved toward four to compose seven. In a similar way in nature, a body already made movable joins itself to another equally movable body, and vice versa; thus bodies are composed of bodies just as numbers are composed of numbers. Furthermore, just as in numbers multiplication occurs beyond simple addition, so in nature mixture occurs beyond composition or apposition. You see the number four created by addition when you say "two and two"; you see mixture in the same when you say "twice two" makes four. Again, you see the number nine created by addition when four is added to five. You find mixture in the same when you say "three times three is nine." Similarly, either a body is moved toward and in a way even poured into another body, or they are thoroughly confounded into one. In this state of "confusion" <term>confusion</term><note>Latin: *confusio*. Here used in the technical sense of "pouring together" or blending completely, not mental muddle.</note>, it is not possible to discern one thing here and another there in the parts of the mixed body, but all things are contained in each individual part; and thus the whole is enclosed in any part you choose. Just as when you multiply a number—for instance, three into each unit—you grasp the whole three in any part of the three; otherwise, you could not calculate three times three. Then indeed, just as in numbers, whatever is produced by multiplication is also produced by addition, but not vice versa; so in nature, wherever an exact mixture of things occurs, composition also happens, but not the other way around. Therefore, just as in numbers you cannot deny that a "fusing together" occurs in which the whole is contained in any of its parts to produce a new form of number (as the whole three multiplied in any of its parts leads to the form of nine), so you should not deny a similar mixture in nature. For such a fusing occurs in both nature and numbers because such is the mutual harmony of the seminal or ideal reasons <term>reasons</term><note>Latin: *rationes*. The formative principles or "blueprints" in nature that guide development.</note> in vital nature and in ideal life itself. Plotinus, therefore, about to treat this subject at present, brings forward three opinions: first, the opinion of those who, in reconciling bodies with one another, did not mix the matters or the qualities at all, but simply placed matters next to matters and qualities next to qualities. This opinion he immediately rejects. The second is of those who, although they did not mix the matters but rather placed them together, nonetheless confounded the qualities with one another. He declares their sentiment to be more probable. Third and finally, he admits as also probable the view that both matters can be fused with matters and qualities with qualities in the most exact way. In the beginning, we mix vinegar with honey in oxymel <note>A traditional medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar.</note> to such an extent that no tiny portion is left in this composite that does not have the taste of both. By this, those people are refuted who believe in a simple "placing together," as if whole grains of panic-grass were gathered together with whole grains of millet. Others will crush individual grains from both sides equally, but they say the matters are not entirely confounded, even though the qualities are mixed. For they say that in any tiny bit of millet there is a certain taste of the panic-grass, and vice versa. Others indeed, having added wine to these, will grind them more diligently; therefore they will mix them more exactly, so that the matters—now not only crushed but even liquefied—are no longer merely placed next to each other but, with nothing preventing it, are thoroughly confounded. In that state, henceforth, there are not only the qualities of each of the three everywhere (as the senses themselves declare), but also the fused matters. Such people will conclude that things of this kind can be fused by nature much more perfectly than by art—matters that are not foreign but their own, not occasionally but always from the start, tempered not from the outside but from within. Plotinus, however, brings forward no reason for the first opinion, but three for the second opinion. The first reason is of this kind: Two bodies cannot be made entirely equal to each other in the same place; for if they ought to be entirely in the same place, it is necessary that they first be divided into parts, and then that they apply their parts to the other parts in turn. If these parts are indivisible, then those bodies have been resolved into atoms. And since they were composed of the same things into which they are dissolved, it follows that the magnitude of the bodies grew out of certain indivisible points; but this could never happen, because indivisible points gathered together produce no magnitude. But if those parts of the bodies are divi-

# ON BOOK VII. ENNEAD II.

...[if they] were divisible, each would be a body standing by itself and would have its own existence apart from others. Therefore, two bodies will not be in exactly the same place; rather, many small bodies will be in many small places. **The second reason:** When two bodies are mixed, they almost always occupy a larger space together than either one did alone; from this, it appears that the dimensions were not fully penetrated on both sides to the highest degree. **The third reason:** When a much smaller body is introduced into a much larger one, the smaller itself cannot be made entirely equal to the larger. If someone objects that sometimes the space occupied after the mixing of two things is not larger, they will respond that air exits that space as the new body enters.

After these points, it is argued in favor of the **third opinion** <note>This refers to the Stoic view that bodies can completely interpenetrate.</note> that sweat drips from the entire body from deep within, and no breakage occurs there. But if the adversaries say that passages were established there by nature through which the sweat might flow without a tearing of the flesh, others will respond: oil penetrates and completely fills even very thin plates of horn or ivory made by art, and even very dense membranes, without increasing their bulk or cutting them apart. Then they will prove that materials are completely equalized with each other by the fact that often, after their mixing, the bulk does not seem to grow at all. 

The adversaries will object again that two bodies cannot penetrate each other to the highest degree without cutting; and if they were to cut each other exactly by penetrating each other exactly, they would be entirely destroyed. Often, however, the original space is not increased because an exhalation of more subtle parts occurs at the same time. The authors of the third opinion will respond: even where a larger space is required after mixing, they defend that there was an exact mixture there. For why should it be a wonder that the magnitude increases there, where many powers have coalesced from the bringing together of many things? For perhaps the previous dimension does not perish fundamentally, but from many qualities another coalesces, and from many dimensions another finished magnitude is formed. 

To this they will object: no increase can happen if materials are not placed next to materials, like lines added to lines along their length; but they are inserted into each other, and a line is completely infused into a line, whether you imagine it being poured in fundamentally from the end or joined from the side. Likewise, where it is established that the mixing was complete, it cannot be understood how the smallest body matches the quantity of the largest. They will respond: either the smallest body is mixed with the largest as far as it can be, or it can even diffuse itself through the whole, namely when the prior quantity is extended. For they say that usual extension is not properly quantity itself, but a passion <term>passion</term><note>In a philosophical sense, a "passion" is an effect or a way a thing is acted upon, rather than an action it performs.</note> and mode of quantity. Therefore, the same quantity, like matter, receives various modes through extension. Plotinus says such a response is not "safe" where it is assigned by those who say that several bodies, while being mixed, preserve the form and quality of their prior substance. For then the smallest body, while it preserved its prior form, perhaps could not be stretched out fundamentally in quantity to the measure of the largest; but if it received another form, it is no wonder if it receives another quantity, just as when air is made from water.

### Discussion of opinions on blending, in which it seems to be approved that in perfect blending the whole body on both sides is mixed throughout the whole.

II. In the second chapter, he tests what should especially be said in these doubts. First, indeed, he seems to grant that a liquid body enters completely through another, both in matter and in quality, just as water through silk <note>original: "bombice"</note>. And after such a mixing, the magnitude there can be equal to what it was before, especially where air was displaced by the entering liquid; magnitude can also be increased where one is thoroughly mixed into the other. For what wonder is it if this thing receives new qualities from that one, and meanwhile receives a new magnitude? And just as it receives quality throughout the whole, so it admits the dimension of that thing completely, and thus they grow together? 

But since quality is opposed to quality rather than quality to quantity, or quantity to quantity, in mixing, some prior quality rightly either passes into a new one or is obscured; quantity, however, seems to remain more so. Indeed, the more exact the permission of entry is, the more the prior forms yield to the succeeding form; this is perfected both by art and by nature. Perhaps, indeed, dimension can enter dimension without cutting, just as quality enters quality, and often matter enters matter. For nothing prohibits this from entering completely, since by its own nature it is incorporeal <note>Ficino is exploring the idea that "extension" or "dimension" as a concept isn't a hard physical barrier.</note>. 

Where, however, entry is hindered, it is not hindered by the reason that dimension is there, but by the reason that density, resisting with hardness, is there. For it is this which properly does not know how to yield, and therefore does not know how to admit or enter. No one is ignorant that hardness is one thing and dimension is another. Entry is usually hindered not only by a hard quality, but also by a hostile quality; where neither occurs, entry is not usually hindered. Let it suffice to have tested these things along with Plotinus rather than to have exhausted them. For someone might perhaps say, when this body is poured completely into that one and an alteration occurs in the meantime, if the magnitude does not grow, the prior dimension ceases along with its own form, while both become new. For dimension itself is the cause of distance in things; and therefore, insofar as two certain dimensions exist in something, there is a distance between them and the bulk is extended. 

And indeed Plotinus perhaps signified it thus, saying that matter by its own nature does not reject mixing, especially when it has neither its own quantity nor rejects any quantity; and when he repeats that one body penetrates through another, he does not repeat dimensions, but qualities and matter. Nevertheless, he does not seem to think it impossible for dimension to penetrate dimension without breakage among very liquid bodies, since breakage usually happens among hard things. He will perhaps also grant that a flame similarly penetrates iron and is simultaneously made entirely equal to it.

### What body is, what corporeity is, and regarding the ideal, seminal, and formal reason.

III. He defines the natural body in the third chapter as a substance affected by three dimensions and qualities; but "corporeity" as a certain productive reason <term>reason</term><note>Latin: *ratio*; Greek: *logos*. Here it means a formative principle or blueprint.</note> of dimensions and qualities. He certainly accepts "reason" here both as the seminal principle in nature and as the substantial form in matter, in whose specific power the dimensions and qualities familiar to its species are contained. He wished these to be contained in it when he says: "Body is composed of matter and reason." 

Among these things, he says that in the definition of natural substance, matter is included; but in the definition of substantial form, matter is not included, since it does not sprout from matter, but is impressed by a seminal reason. He also touches upon a triple reason: the **highest and ideal** in the intellect, which is the intellect itself, whose being and action do not occur in matter. The **second, the seminal**, in the soul of nature itself, whose action, rather than its being, occurs in matter. The **third, the formal**, that is, the substantial form of the body, whose being and action are simultaneously in matter. It can be understood, however, how it exists without the joining of matter; since it does not proceed from matter, but rather from a separate cause, it seems in that first step of proceeding to have some formal reason in itself, in which it can be thought of before it applies itself to matter. From this, perhaps, what many argue can be confirmed: that the distinctions and grades of forms do not proceed from matter at all, but all these, as formal things, are reduced to the power of the form, just as material conditions are reduced to matter.

COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

Nor should it be that a thing is a quality in one place but not a quality in another; rather, that which is deserted by essence becomes a quality. However, that which remains with essence surely exists as essence, or species, or act <note>original: *actus*. In Neoplatonic philosophy, "act" or "actuality" refers to the completed reality of a thing's nature.</note>. For no nature is the same when it is in its own source as it is when it is in another; where it is already separated from its origin, it does not retain the dignity of species and act. Nevertheless, that which is never the species of anything else, but is always an accident <note>A property that is not essential to a thing's core identity, like color or temperature.</note>, is now purely quality, and quality alone.

<column-break/>

The archetypes of those things in which they primarily exist are the activities <note>original: ἐνεργείας (*energeias*)</note> of those things, and they do not become qualities or non-qualities; but that which is detached from substance <note>original: οὐσίαν (*ousian*)</note> is a certain quality, while that which is with it is substance, or form, or activity. For nothing is the same in itself as it is in another, having fallen away from being form and activity. However, that which is never the form of another, but always an accident, is purely quality and only this. <note>This column contains the original Greek text of Plotinus that Ficino translated in the first column.</note>

## COMMENTARY.
### *SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.*

->How composition and mixture occur in numbers and in nature:<-
->Also concerning the three opinions on mixture.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental initial Q showing a landscape with a building, trees, and clouds within a decorative frame.</image-desc>

Just as in numbers it is one thing to be added and another to be multiplied, so in natural things it is one thing to compose and another to mix. Indeed, by a similar proportion, just as in the order of numbers unity is added to unity and becomes the number two, so in nature form is added to matter and becomes a body. There again, unity is added to a number to create the number three; here, similarly, a power is joined to a body to produce motion, and it becomes a "mobile body." There again, a number is added to a number, as two to two, from which comes four, or even three is moved toward four to compose seven. In a similar way in nature, a body already made mobile moves toward another equally mobile body, and vice versa; thus bodies are composed with bodies just as numbers are with numbers.

Furthermore, just as in numbers multiplication occurs beyond simple addition, so in nature mixture occurs beyond composition or "apposition" <note>Putting things side-by-side without them merging.</note>. You see the number four created by addition when you say "two and two"; you see a mixture in the same number when you say "twice two makes four." Again, you see the number nine created by addition when four is added to five. You find a mixture in the same when you say "three times three is nine." Similarly, a body is either moved toward—and in a way even poured into—another body, or it is confused <note>In the sense of "fused together" (Latin: *confunditur*).</note> thoroughly into one. In such a fusion, it is not possible to discern one thing here and another there in the parts of the mixed body, but everything is contained in each individual part; and thus the whole is concluded in any part you choose. Just as when you multiply a number—for instance, three—within any single unit, you grasp the whole three in the parts of the three; otherwise, you could not calculate three times three.

Then, just as in numbers, whatever is produced by multiplication is also produced by addition, but not vice versa; so in nature, wherever an exact mixture of things occurs, a composition also happens, but the reverse is not true. Therefore, just as you cannot deny that in numbers a fusion occurs in which the whole is contained in any part of itself to produce a new form of number (as the whole three multiplied in any of its parts leads to the form of nine), so you should not deny a similar mixture in nature. For such a fusion occurs in both nature and numbers because such is the mutual harmony of seminal or ideal reasons <note><term>seminal reasons</term>: *rationes seminales*, the hidden "seeds" or formative principles that govern how physical things grow and develop.</note> in vital nature and in ideal life itself. 

Plotinus, therefore, being about to treat this matter at present, brings forward three opinions: 
**The first** is of those who, in reconciling bodies with one another, did not mix the matters or the qualities thoroughly, but placed matters next to matters and qualities next to qualities; he immediately rejects this opinion. 
**The second** is of those who, although they did not mix the matters but rather moved them close together, nevertheless confused the qualities with one another. He declares their sentiment to be more probable. 
**The third** and last, which thinks that both matters can be fused with matters and qualities with qualities most exactly, he also admits as probable. 

In the beginning, we mix vinegar with honey in *oxymel* <note>A medicinal drink made of vinegar and honey.</note> to such an extent that no tiny portion is left in this composite which does not have particles of both their natures now crushed together. They will say that the grains of each side are close to each other, like the taste of millet; and vice versa. Others, however, when wine is added to these, will crush them more diligently, and therefore mix them more exactly, so that the matters are not only crushed but even liquefied, and are no longer merely placed side-by-side but are thoroughly fused, with nothing preventing it. Thereafter, in every part of the three, there are not only the qualities (which the senses themselves declare) but also the fused matters. They conclude that such things can be fused by nature much more perfectly than by art—not using foreign matters, but their own; not occasionally, but always from the start; tempered not from the outside, but from within. Plotinus, however, brings forward no reason for the first opinion, but three for the second. 

The first reason is of this kind: Two bodies cannot be made entirely equal to one another in the same place; for if they must be entirely in the same place, they must first be divided into parts, and then those parts must be applied to the other parts in turn. If these parts are indivisible, then those bodies have been resolved into "indivisibles" <note>Atoms.</note>. And since they were composed of the same things into which they are dissolved, it follows that the very magnitude of bodies grew from certain indivisibles; this could never happen, because indivisibles gathered together produce no magnitude <note>If an atom has zero size, adding zero to zero never creates a physical object with height or width.</note>. But if those parts of bodies are divi-

...if they were [indivisible], each would be a standing body by itself and would have its own space separate from the others. Thus, two bodies would not be in exactly the same place, but rather many little bodies in many little places. Second reason: When two bodies are mixed, they almost always occupy a larger space together than either one did alone; from this it appears that the dimensions were not fully penetrated to the highest degree. Third reason: When a much smaller body is introduced into a much larger one, the smaller itself cannot be made exactly equal to the larger. But if someone should object that sometimes after the mixing of two things a larger space is not occupied, they will answer that air departs from that place before the new body enters. After these points, it is argued for the third opinion that sweat exudes from the entire body deep within, and yet no break or fracture occurs there. But if the adversaries say that passages were established there by nature through which the sweat might flow without a tearing of the flesh, others will answer: oil penetrates and completely fills even thin plates of horn or ivory made by art, and even very dense membranes, without increasing their mass or splitting them. Then they will prove that materials are indeed made completely equal to one another by the fact that often after their mixing the mass does not seem to grow at all. The adversaries will object again that two bodies cannot penetrate each other to the highest degree without incision; and if by penetrating each other most exactly they should cut each other most exactly, they would be entirely destroyed. Often, however, the original space is not increased because an exhalation of more subtle parts accompanies the process in the meantime. The authors of the third opinion will answer: even where a larger space is required after mixing, they defend that there was a most exact mixture there. For why should it be a wonder that the magnitude is increased there, where from the blending of many things, many powers have also grown together? For perhaps the former dimension does not perish fundamentally, but from many qualities another quality grows together, and from several dimensions another magnitude is completed. Furthermore, they will object: no increase can occur if materials are not placed next to materials, as lines added to lines along their length; but instead they are inserted into each other, and a line is completely infused into a line, whether you imagine it being poured in from the end or brought together from the side. Likewise, where it is clear that the mixing was complete, it cannot be understood how the smallest body can there equal the quantity of the largest. They will answer: either the smallest body is mixed with the largest to the extent that it can, or it can even diffuse itself through the whole, specifically when the prior quantity is extended. For they will perhaps say that extension is not properly quantity itself, but a passion and mode of quantity; thus the same quantity, as if it were matter, receives various modes of extension. Plotinus says that such a response is not safe when assigned by those who say that several bodies, while they are mixed, preserve the form and quality of their prior substance. For then the smallest body, while it preserves its prior form, perhaps cannot be stretched out in quantity to the measure of the largest; but if it should receive another form, it is no wonder if it receives another quantity, just as when air is made from water <note>original: "ex aqua fit aer". This refers to the Aristotelian idea of elements transforming into one another, where a small amount of liquid becomes a large volume of gas/vapor.</note>.

->*A discussion of opinions on mixture, in which he seems to approve that in a perfect mixture the entire body on both sides is confused throughout the whole.*<-

II. In the second chapter he tries to determine what should most especially be said in these doubts. First, indeed, he seems to concede that the body of liquids enters completely through another both in matter and in quality, just as water passes through cotton. And he suggests that after such a mixture the magnitude there can be equal to what it was before, especially where air was displaced as the liquid entered; it is also possible for the magnitude to be increased where one thing is completely mixed with the other. For what is the wonder if this thing receives new qualities from that one, and in the meantime receives a new magnitude? And just as it receives quality through the whole, so it introduces the dimension of that thing deep within, and grows together from there? But since quality is more opposed to quality than either quality to quality or quantity to quantity, it is right that in a mixture some prior quality either passes into a new one or is obscured, while quantity seems to remain more stable. Indeed, the more exact the permitted mixture, the more the prior forms yield to the following form; which is indeed perfected by both art and nature. Perhaps, truly, dimension can enter dimension without a cutting, just as quality enters quality, and matter often enters matter. For nothing prohibits this from entering completely, since by its own nature it is incorporeal <note>In Neoplatonic thought, "dimension" is considered an incorporeal principle that organizes matter, rather than a physical thing itself.</note>. But where entry is hindered, it is not hindered by the reason of dimension, but by the density and hardness which resists. For this is what properly does not know how to yield, and therefore does not know how to admit or enter. No one is ignorant of the fact that hardness is one thing and dimension is another. However, entry is usually hindered not only by a hard quality, but also by a hostile quality; but where neither is present, entry is not usually hindered. Let it suffice to have held these things together with Plotinus rather than to have fully resolved them. For if someone should perhaps say, when this body is completely infused into that one and there is an alteration in the meantime, that if the magnitude does not grow, the prior dimension ceases along with its own form; while both are new, for that dimension itself is the cause of distance in things: and therefore to the extent that two dimensions exist in something, there is a distance between these and those and the mass is extended. This is indeed what Plotinus perhaps signified here when saying that matter by its own nature does not reject mixture, especially when it has neither its own quantity nor rejects any quantity: and when he repeats that one body penetrates through another, he does not repeat dimensions, but qualities and matter. Nevertheless, he does not seem to think it impossible for dimension to penetrate dimension without a breaking between very liquid bodies: especially since breaking usually occurs among hard things. He will perhaps also concede that flame similarly penetrates iron, and at the same time is made completely equal to it.

->*What a body is, what corporeity is, and concerning the ideal, seminal, and formal reason.*<-

III. In the third chapter, he defines a natural body as a substance affected by three dimensions and qualities; and corporeity <term>corporeitas: the essential nature that makes a body a body</term> as a certain "reason" <note>original: "rationem". In this context, it refers to the Greek *logos*, a formative, creative principle or blueprint.</note> that effects dimensions and qualities. He certainly accepts "reason" here both as the seminal principle in nature and as the substantial form in matter, in whose specific power the dimensions and qualities familiar to its species are contained. He wished for these to be contained in it when he said: A body is composed of matter and reason. Among these things, he says that in the definition of natural substance, matter is included; but in the definition of substantial form, matter is not included, since it does not sprout from matter, but is impressed by a seminal reason. He also touches upon a triple reason: the highest and ideal reason in the intellect, which is the intellect itself; whose neither being nor action occurs in matter. The second is the seminal reason in the nature of the soul itself; whose action, rather than its being, is in matter. The third is the formal reason, that is, the substantial form of the body; whose being and action are simultaneously in matter. It can be understood, however, how it exists without the joining of matter; since it does not proceed from matter, but rather from a separate cause, it seems in that first grade of proceeding to have some formal reason in itself, in which it can be thought of before it applies itself to matter. From here perhaps can be confirmed what many argue, that the distinctions and grades of forms do not at all proceed from matter: but all these things, as formal elements, are traced back to the power of the form, just as material conditions are traced back to matter.

# OF PLOTINUS

->ON THE COMPLETE MIXTURE OF BODIES.<-
<note>original Greek: ΠΕΡῚ τῆς δι' ὁλων κράσεως; Latin: De permixtione per tota. This refers to the Stoic theory of "total blending" where two substances interpenetrate completely.</note>
---

<margin>An account of the opinions of both sides regarding the mixing, and their reasons.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial C depicting two figures in classical attire; one is seated on a stone block, and the other stands before them, extending an arm in a rhetorical or teaching gesture.</image-desc>
A. WE MUST CONSIDER that mixing of bodies which is said to happen "through the whole" <note>per tota</note>. Is it possible for one liquid to be so mixed with another liquid that the whole is poured through the whole—whether both pass through each other, or only one penetrates the other? It makes no difference in which way it occurs. 

B. To begin with, those who define mixture as a kind of juxtaposition <note>appositione; placing things side-by-side</note>, as if they were merely adding things together rather than truly mixing them, should be dismissed. Indeed, a true mixture ought to make the whole as similar as possible in every individual part, so that even the smallest possible particle is composed of those things which are said to be mixed. However, those who believe that only the qualities are completely mixed, while the materials <note>materias</note> of both bodies are merely placed side-by-side—carrying the qualities of each through both—might perhaps be persuasive, because one could then argue against the idea of a mixture that happens "through the whole."

C. Likewise, it would otherwise follow that the sizes of the masses would pass entirely into infinite divisions <note>sectiones</note> if no space at all were left in either of the bodies; for the division would be continuous because one body would insinuate itself entirely into the other. Furthermore, they would argue that mixed things often occupy a larger space together than either one did alone—occupying as much space as if they were joined together. Yet, if the whole entered entirely through the whole, they say the space of the first body should remain the same as it was before the second was cast into it.

D. In cases where the space containing the two mixed things does not become larger, they blame certain "exhalations of air," whose place the second body has taken. Finally, they bring forward cases where a smaller body enters a larger one. They ask how it is possible for this smaller body to be so extended that it pours itself through the entire larger body. They are accustomed to bringing many other similar arguments into the discussion. However, those who advocate for the mixture of both bodies "through the whole" seem to be able to say that bodies are indeed distributed, but they are not consumed into infinite divisions, even when a mixture through the whole is completed.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative initial Π (Pi) set against an ornamental background of vines, leaves, and blooming flowers.</image-desc>
WE MUST EXAMINE the so-called mixture of bodies "through the whole." <note>original: ΠΕΡῚ τῆς δι' ὅλων λεγομένης τῶν σωμάτων κράσεως</note>. Is it possible for a liquid mixed with a liquid to pass whole through whole, either both through each other, or one through the other? For it makes no difference which way it happens. Those who grant mixture by "juxtaposition" <note>original: παραθέσει; placing side-by-side</note>, as if they were mixing rather than <margin>* blending</margin> blending, should be left aside. For if there is to be a mixture, it must make the whole "uniform in its parts" <note>term: homoiomerous; a substance where every part is the same as the whole</note>, and every part, even the smallest, must be made of the things said to be mixed. Those who <margin>* blend</margin> blend only the qualities, while placing the matter <note>hyle</note> of each body side-by-side and bringing the qualities from each over them, might be persuasive in their criticism of "mixture through the whole." This is because the magnitudes of the masses would result in infinite divisions if no gap were left for either of the bodies, and the division would be continuous. Indeed, the whole happens by the penetration of one into the other. And when the mixed things occupy a larger space than one of them, it is as much as both spaces together. Yet, if the whole had passed through the whole, they say the space of the one ought to have remained the same as when the other was thrown in. In cases where the space does not become larger, they blame certain "outlets of air" <note>original: ἀέρος τινὰς ἐξόδους</note>, which the other body entered. They also ask: how could the small be extended in the large so as to pass through the whole? They say many other things as well. But those who introduce "mixture through the whole" could say that the bodies are cut and spent into divisions, even as the mixture through the whole is occurring. For they will say that sweats <note>original: ἱδρῶτας</note> do not create visible cuts when they pass out of the body. And as for what some say, nothing prevents nature from having made it so for the sake of letting sweat pass through, but...

C. D. But here perhaps others would say against them: if matter is adjacent to matter, and bulk to bulk—which magnitude accompanies—you are bringing this up according to our opinion. But if matter, together with the magnitude that was previously in it, should enter through the whole of the other bulk, it will happen thus: not as if lines were joined one after another at their endpoints by points—where growth can happen—but rather, I say, it will happen in that way, as if a line were so applied to a line that no increase results. E. Finally, it was argued against these: it seems impossible for a smaller body to extend itself through the whole of a body larger than itself, especially the smallest through the largest, where it is certain that a mixture has been performed. Indeed, where it is not sufficiently examined whether such things are entirely confused together, one may object that the smallest does not run through the whole of the largest. But where that is clearly found to happen, certain extensions of the bulks themselves can be assigned: although those who attempt to extend the smallest bulk into the largest bulk do not speak with sufficient probability, especially when they attribute a larger magnitude to the body, and yet do not transform it in the same way as when air is made from water.

Or even when it does not flow out, in what way shall we join matter to matter, and bulk to bulk? Shall we concede that only the qualities are mixed with one another? SINCE we have made mention of corporeity <note>original: "corporeitas" (Latin), "σωματότης" (Greek)</note>, we must examine whether corporeity itself is something composed of all things, or rather a certain species and formative principle <note>original: "ratio" (Latin), "λόγος" (Greek)</note> which, when infused into matter, creates a body. Truly, if a body is this very thing gathered from all qualities together with matter, then that will be corporeity. And yet if it is a formative principle which, by its arrival, creates a body, then clearly that principle, embracing all things, contains all the qualities. It is necessary, moreover, that such a principle—if it is not simply a defining reason stating what each thing is, but a principle that actually *makes* the thing—should by no means embrace the matter within itself, but rather that the principle exists around the matter, and when infused, makes the body.
