# MARSILIO FICINO’S COMMENTARY ON THE EIGHTH BOOK [OF THE SECOND ENNEAD], CONCERNING VISION, AND WHY THINGS WHICH ARE FAR AWAY SEEM SMALL.

## SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

### Two reasons from others, and two from Plotinus: why more distant things appear smaller.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial Q featuring floral scrolls and a small seated figure.</image-desc>
TWO THINGS ARE SOUGHT in this book: First, why objects usually seem smaller when they are further from the eyes. Second: For what reason two very distant sights, separated from each other by a certain distance—say, a stadium <note>a Greek unit of length, roughly 600 feet</note>—seem to be separated from each other by a smaller space than a stadium; likewise, why they seem closer to us than they actually are. To these questions, some respond: the very light by which we see, as it comes from the object and approaches the eye, adapts itself more and more to the eye and the pupil, just as liquid bodies adapt themselves to their containers. This response is only properly valid if the light spoken of is a <term>visual ray</term> <note>original: "radius visualis"</note> sent from the eye and then reflected back from the object to the eye; for in this way, perhaps by a certain natural vigor, it gradually returns to the size of its origin. For there are those who say that this light proceeding from the eye reaches the thing to be seen in a <term>pyramidal figure</term> <note>an ancient theory of perspective where vision is imagined as a cone or pyramid with the eye at the tip</note>, and suddenly expands through it: and from there, as if from a base, it reforms a pyramidal figure toward the eye, and touches the pupil of the eye with its point, the eye being similarly pyramidal by nature. According to their opinion, therefore, such a response will perhaps be properly valid. Indeed, some might say it is generally valid: because the primary luminous body, that is, the sun, pours out light from its entire circumference, but this light gathers itself into a point <note>original: "conum" (cone/point)</note> from all sides so that it does not vanish by flowing outside its source; in this way, it will also act more powerfully, and the whole will be more easily present everywhere. Thus, while the entire base is narrowed into a point, the whole sun and all its power will be present through that angle and will act everywhere; and so its entire magnitude can be seen in that angle. Thus also, since the center and the circumference are in the sun, its light itself, insofar as it flows from the whole circuit of the sun, imitates the circumference; but insofar as it is gathered into a narrow space, it also imitates the center. From this they will say it happens that from any illuminated body, the light gathers itself toward other things and toward the eyes in almost the same figure. So much for the first response. They respond again with another reason: that the form of the thing to be seen has a material nature in the thing itself; but when taken up by the spiritual light, it suddenly casts off its matter and travels by a certain spiritual reason, although for a long distance it seems to keep a certain proportion to its own matter. But as soon as it begins to lose this proportion as well, it appears smaller; and finally, when all proportion to its own matter is consumed, it no longer appears to the eyes at all: just as the <term>formal reasons</term> <note>original: "rationes formales"; the underlying blueprints or formative principles of things</note>, the seeds, and the ideas of natural forms are not seen by the eyes. These are the responses from the opinions of others. How much truth this opinion or these responses might have will be discovered elsewhere.

After this follows Plotinus's own response to the same question. Indeed, we clearly measure how great the dimension of a thing is when we more piercingly gaze at its individual parts one by one. Therefore, when a thing is placed far away and many of its very small parts are hidden from us, the measurement of the whole naturally escapes us, and it seems smaller. This is especially true because the quality of light—inasmuch as it is more effective than quantity and is specific to sight—presents itself to the eyes more effectively or sooner than quantity does. Therefore, we first see what the thing is <note>its quality/nature</note>, and second, how big it is, specifically while we perceive the quality. Therefore, when the visual ray is poured out from us onto the thing, and is finally weakened by a longer progression, it discerns the quality—that is, the color and the luminous nature—less clearly; naturally, it also measures the quantity in a confused way. Now, that which is "more perfect" and "less perfect" in <term>substantial form</term> <note>the essence of a thing</note> is "more intense" and "more relaxed" in <term>accidental form</term> <note>properties like color or heat</note>; the same is "greater" and "smaller" in quantity, "faster" and "slower" in motion, and "longer" and "shorter" in time. Therefore, since "greater" and "smaller" (which are proper to quantity) have a certain proportion to "more intense" and "more relaxed" (which belong to quality), and since quantity follows quality in the order of our knowledge, it is no wonder that when the sight perceives a quality at a more "relaxed" or weaker degree, it meanwhile perceives the quantity as a smaller measure. Amidst these things, remember that color is the proper object of sight, just as voice is the proper object of hearing; likewise, the intensity and power of color belong properly to sight, and the vigor of the voice similarly to hearing. Magnitude <note>size</note>, however, is perceived by several senses, and it is not so much the effectiveness of the sensible thing itself as a certain diffusion of it through multiplicity and space; and this is known to us not primarily, but through the quality and effectiveness of the thing. Thus it happens that where quality is less evident, quantity meanwhile lies hidden. These points are confirmed chiefly by three proofs. The first is of this sort: If you look at hills full of the forms of various things, and you clearly see those forms there, you will measure the magnitude of that region more correctly than if you did not look at such forms at all, as if magnitude becomes clear through forms. Second: Look at a tablet placed nearby impressed with various figures; if you look at the figures one by one, you will not judge the magnitude of the tablet to be as great as if you clearly saw all of them both individually and as a whole. Third: If on a wall decorated only with a green color...

ON BOOK VIII. ENNEAD II.

But the form <note>original: εἶδος (eidos)</note> itself is seen as being without matter, viewed as bare. Even if it is as inseparable as possible... <gloss>The written variant: another is separate, the one in the Mind <note>In Plotinus's philosophy, "Mind" or "Intellect" (Nous) is the realm of pure forms</note>. If it is in the Mind, it is because it is itself Mind; but also other things because of it.</gloss>

<column-break/>

Indeed, the rational principle <note>original: "ipsam verò rationem"; Ficino uses 'ratio' to translate the Greek 'logos', the formative power of a thing</note> itself, since it is a form, can be considered bare without matter, even if it is as inseparable from matter as possible. Truly, the separate rational principle is different from that in the mind: in the mind, I say, because it is also the mind itself. But concerning these things, elsewhere.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON 
## THE EIGHTH BOOK CONCERNING VISION, AND 
## WHY THOSE THINGS WHICH ARE FAR OFF 
### APPEAR SMALL, 
### A COMMENTARY.

### SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK.

->*Two reasons from others, and two from Plotinus: why more remote things appear smaller.*<-

Two things are investigated in this book: First, why objects more remote from the eyes are accustomed to appear smaller. Second: For what cause two very distant sights, though separated from each other by a great distance—say, a stadium <note>An ancient Greek unit of length, roughly 600 feet</note>—appear to be separated by a smaller space than a stadium; likewise, why they seem closer to us than they actually are. To these questions some respond: that the light itself by which we see, as it approaches the eye from the object, accommodates itself to the eye and the pupil, just as liquid bodies accommodate themselves to their containers. This response is only properly valid if the light spoken of is a visual ray <note>Many ancient thinkers believed the eye emitted "rays" to perceive objects</note> sent from the eye and reflected back from the object to the eye; for in this way, perhaps by a certain natural vigor, it would gradually return to the size of its origin. For there are those who say that this light proceeding from the eye reaches the thing to be seen in a pyramidal shape, and is suddenly dilated through it; and from that object, as if from a base, it reforms a pyramidal shape toward the eye, and touches the pupil of the eye with its tip, which is similarly pyramidal in nature. Therefore, in their opinion, such a response will perhaps be properly valid. 

Indeed, some might say it is commonly valid: because the primary light-source, that is, the sun, pours out light from its entire circumference, but this light collects itself from all sides into a cone <note>Ficino is describing the "Visual Cone," a standard concept in ancient and Renaissance optics</note>, lest it vanish as it flows out beyond its source. In this way it will also act more powerfully, and the whole will be easier everywhere. And while the entire base is narrowed into a cone, the whole sun and all its power will be present through the angle, and will act everywhere; and thus its entire magnitude can be seen in that angle. Thus, since there is a center and a circumference in the sun, its light itself, insofar as it comes from the whole circuit of the sun, imitates the circumference; but insofar as it is collected into a narrow space, it also imitates the center. From this, they say, it happens that from any illuminated body, the light collects itself toward other things and toward the eyes in essentially the same shape. Thus far is the first response. 

Others respond with another reason: that the form of the thing to be seen has a material nature in the thing itself; but when it is taken up from there by spiritual light, it suddenly sheds its matter and travels by a certain spiritual rational principle, although it seems to preserve a certain proportion to its own matter for a long distance. But as soon as it begins to lose this proportion as well, it appears smaller; and finally, when all proportion to its own matter is consumed, it no longer appears to the eyes at all—just as the formal, seminal, and ideal rational principles <note>These are the "blueprints" of nature that Ficino believes exist in a non-physical state</note> of natural forms are not seen by the eyes. These are the responses according to the opinions of others. Truly, how much truth these opinions or responses contain will be discovered elsewhere.

After these follows Plotinus's own response to the same matter. Assuredly, we plainly measure how great the total dimension of a thing is when we look more keenly at its individual parts step by step. Therefore, when a thing is placed far away, and many very small parts are hidden from us, the measure of the whole deservedly escapes us, and it seems smaller. This is especially true because the luminous quality—inasmuch as it is both more effective than quantity and proper to the sense of sight—presents itself to the eyes more effectively before quantity does. Therefore, we first see what sort of thing it is <note>its quality</note>, and secondly how great it is <note>its quantity</note>, namely while we are perceiving the quality. Since, therefore, the visual ray poured out from us onto the object is finally weakened by a longer progression, it discerns the quality (that is, the color and the luminous nature) less; deservedly, it also measures the quantity confusedly. 

Now, indeed, what is "more perfect" and "less perfect" in substantial form is the same as "more intense" and "less intense" in accidental form, and "greater" and "smaller" in quantity, and "faster" and "slower" in motion, and "longer" and "shorter" in time. Since, therefore, "greater" and "smaller" (which are proper to quantity) have a certain proportion to "more intense" and "less intense" (which are qualities), and since quantity follows quality in the order of our knowledge, it is no wonder that where the sight perceives a quality at a weaker degree, it meanwhile perceives the quantity at a smaller measure. Amidst these things, remember that color is the proper object of sight, just as voice is the proper object of hearing; likewise, the intensity and power of color belong properly to sight, and the vigor of the voice to hearing. But magnitude is perceived by many senses, and it is not so much the effectiveness of the sensible thing itself as a certain diffusion of it through multitude and space; and this becomes known to us not primarily, but through quality and effectiveness itself. Thus it happens that where quality is less evident, quantity meanwhile lies hidden. 

These things are confirmed by three principal proofs. The first is of this kind: If you look at hills full of the forms of various things, by clearly seeing those forms there, you will measure the magnitude of the region more correctly than if you do not look at such forms at all, as if magnitude were made evident through forms. Second: Look at a tablet placed nearby impressed with various figures; unless you look at the figures one by one, you will not judge the magnitude of the tablet to be as great as you would if you clearly saw them all individually and as a whole. Third: If on a wall of vivid color alone... <note>The text ends mid-sentence</note>

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains Plotinus's theories on optics, arguing that we perceive the size of distant objects through their qualities (like color) and the visibility of their parts; when these qualities fade at a distance, the object appears smaller.</summary>

<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...if you turn the sharpness of your sight <note>original: "aciem verteris"</note> through the clear air, such a wall will not encounter you to the extent that it has been marked with many colors. For you can hardly discern the parts of dimension among themselves where the variety of forms does not distinguish them; instead, you slip away from any part of the dimension suddenly, unless a difference in quality halts the gaze. Through these points, the second question can be answered: namely, for what reason two buildings situated on an opposite hill, very remote from us and separated from each other by the distance of a stadium <note>A Greek unit of length, roughly 600 feet</note>, also appear to be less distant than a stadium. Likewise, why if they are separated from us by a hundred stadia, they seem to be away from us by an even shorter interval. For where we perceive the variety of forms more confusedly, we surely do not discern the quantity of the interval.

### That things which are more remote do not appear smaller because of smaller angles.

In the second chapter, he refutes the response of those who think a pyramidal figure <note>A cone-shaped field of vision with the base at the object and the point at the eye</note> is stretched from the visible object through lines of rays to the eye, touching the pupil with a certain cone: and that the further the object is, the more the cone is made gradually sharper. They argue that while we perceive the thing by a gradually smaller angle, we also conjecture a smaller magnitude—especially when it has proceeded so far that the angle is already smaller than the pupil. What should be said regarding other matters, we shall dispute elsewhere together with Plotinus. 

For the present, however, this is especially rejected: their claim that a body appears smaller for the reason that the angle has now become smaller than the pupil. For this reasoning would allow that some other things would then be seen by the pupil besides that object, since one thing could not fill the pupil with its angle. But indeed, where the object is so huge that nothing further can be perceived in a single glance, it then also appears smaller than it is, although the angle by which it is said to be seen has not become smaller than the pupil. For the whole hemisphere <note>The visible dome of the sky</note> is perceived by the entire sight, which fills the pupil to such an extent that it can perceive nothing besides. Therefore, that it is thought to be smaller than it is does not happen because it is seen through an angle narrower than the pupil. 

Among these things, you will notice a proof by which you may confirm that, according to Plotinus, the form of the object does not reach the eyes, but the ray of the eye reaches the object. For vision is performed like a certain action according to the very mode of the visual form. If, therefore, the object conformed itself to the narrowness of the pupil (as they say), it would never be judged to be larger than the pupil. But as it is, it is judged to be far larger, because the visual ray, stretched outward, spreads itself through the magnitude of the thing itself. 

But certainly we cannot deny that rays from luminous bodies reach the eyes in a certain pyramidal figure, and with this very figure they carry a spiritual quality <note>In this context, 'spiritual' refers to the non-material transmission of an object's image or "species"</note> of the thing, or its power, or act, all the way to us. Conversely, the radial nature of sight testifies that rays are also emitted from the eyes, especially in animals that see at night. Some see things from nearby, others from afar; we do not see very thin things, nor clouds that are very close, because they do not terminate the still-powerful rays of the eyes. I pass over the fact that men and certain animals affect things outside themselves by the gaze of their eyes. Finally, more light is necessary near the object than near the eye: for where our ray is emitted, it is strong. Furthermore, it is not expedient for it to be scattered here with more abundant light, but near the object where it is already weak, it is nurtured by much light, to be spread straight through the object by the same light. For it seems probable that the visual ray of the eye is stretched out through the pyramidal breadth of the encountering light, with the help of that same light toward the breadth of the thing to be seen, insofar as Plato in the *Timaeus*, and Galen and Calcidius <note>Calcidius was a 4th-century commentator whose Latin translation of the Timaeus was the primary source of Plato for the Middle Ages</note> in the same place, teach that vision is produced by a certain commerce <note>An interaction or exchange</note> of the visual ray and the more abundant light, and those skilled in perspective <note>Scientists of optics</note> confirm this. Truly, the said light is either innate to the visual ray or applied from without.

The intensity <note>original: "vehementia"</note> of each thing's nature is, in fact, the same as the nature itself. However, the progression into a multitude is considered according to the extension into every place that is filled. But are colors not small? Rather, they are weak; magnitudes, however, are small. Perhaps it is common to both that they are said to be "less" than what they truly are. Color has that which is called "less" in that it is weak and fleeting. B Magnitude, however—that is, dimension—has that which is called "less" in that it is small. Truly, magnitude, following color, is diminished by a certain consequent proportion. This kind of experience <term>passio; the way the senses are affected</term> becomes more manifest in sights that are varied: as in the sight of mountains having many dwellings and a multitude of trees and many other things. If any of these is clearly seen, it allows the observer to measure the whole from each of the things inspected. But when C the distinct form <note>original: "species"; Greek: "εἴδους"</note> of the individual parts does not reach the eye, the eye has no way to know how great the whole is, namely by measuring the underlying magnitude according to each presented form. Since even things that are nearby, when they are varied but the gaze suddenly turns toward them all at once so that not all forms are discerned, they tend to appear smaller in a proportional ratio, to the extent that each form defrauds the viewer. But when individual forms are clearly discerned, then the measure of magnitude is correctly judged. D
Whatever magnitudes occur that are uniform and of a single color, these most greatly deceive the judgment of quantity. Indeed, since the sight cannot easily measure them discretely by parts, it suddenly slips beyond in its measuring of a part, not having a way of differentiation by which it can stop its progress in individual parts. Moreover, that which is far removed appears to be situated nearby. This is because the intervening space is usually compressed <note>literally "collected" or "shrunk"</note> for the same reason that its quantity is judged. For that which is near does not hide how great it is, for the same reasons. But where the sight does not travel through the length of the distance as it is according to its form, it certainly cannot measure how great it is in magnitude.

As for what is said by some—that things E far distant appear smaller for the reason that they are seen through smaller visual angles—this is a laughable claim. Surely he who says that an object is seen through a smaller angle leaves the rest of the vision—either the angle or something outside the viewer—to be either some other visible thing or at least something external like the air. Therefore, when nothing is left over because the mountain is immense, but it either equals the vision or nothing else can be perceived by the sight—since the space of the vision is matched to the object, or even the object exceeds the visual gaze on both sides—what will anyone respond here? G For the object itself appears much smaller than it is, even though it is seen by the whole sight. Indeed, if one looks up at the sky, anyone will understand this without a doubt. For otherwise, no one would be able to behold the entire hemisphere in a single glance.

Color, then, being "less," is faint. Magnitude, being "less," is small; and the magnitude, remaining upon the color, is diminished proportionally. This experience <note>original: "πάθος" (pathos)</note> becomes clearer in the case of variegated things. For example, in the case of mountains having many dwellings and a multitude of trees, and many other things, of which each, if it were seen, would allow the whole to be measured by the equality of each of the things seen. But when the form of each does not arrive, it is deprived of the ability to measure the underlying magnitude by each individual form, or to know the whole as much as it is. Since even things that are nearby, when they are variegated, if the application of the sight to them is sudden and the forms are not seen in every part, they would appear smaller according to the proportion by which each thing is stolen <note>original: "κλαπῇ" (klape); meaning omitted from the visual calculation</note> from the view. And in measuring the parts, it does not have the difference of the parts as a sign for each. # MARSILIO FICINO’S
## COMMENTARY ON BOOK IX OF THE 
## SECOND ENNEAD AGAINST THE GNOSTICS.

### SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

->The One and the Good are the same and the first of all things. Likewise, there are three principles: The Good itself, Mind, and Soul.<-

We can infer that the mind of Plotinus was not entirely foreign to the Christian law <note>original: "à Christiana lege"</note> from the fact that, since he was a disciple of Ammonius [Saccas]—who was always a Christian—and always a friend of the very Christian Origen, it is said that he agreed together with Origen and Herennius that he would never depart from the teachings of Ammonius: and this, just as he had promised, he preserved. Furthermore, his own disciple Porphyry is witness that Plotinus at one time profoundly despised the cult of the pagans when Amelius exhorted him to it. Finally, though frequently provoked by many heretics who were partly corrupting and partly even despising his beloved Plato, he responded at great length: yet in responding, he introduced nothing in common with the Christians, but only what was specific to the heresy. This was despite the fact that it was permitted to attack Christians with impunity at that time, and the occasion was offered. Porphyry, in his biography of Plotinus, lists who the authors of this heresy were and which heretics professed it—those who are called Gnostics, who are similar to the Manicheans. Certainly, from their opinions, it is clear that their heresy, although they honored Christ, nevertheless disagreed no less with the common opinion of Christians than they did with the Platonists.

But as far as the present work is concerned, these are their primary errors: Above the One and the Good themselves, they dreamed of some unknown thing. Furthermore, they foolishly distinguished between separate Intellects <term>Intellectus; the divine Mind or realm of forms</term>. They inserted something intermediate between the Intellect and the Soul. They thought a "depraved" soul had made the world—an evil thing from an evil principle. 

That there is nothing higher or prior in goodness than the Good itself, or higher in unity than the One itself, is shown thus: First, it must be remembered that what is not first is not simple <term>simplex; meaning uncomposed or not made of parts</term>; and conversely, what is not simple is not first. For if any thing were not the first of all, it would certainly depend on another; and therefore there would be two things in it: namely, something of its cause, and something of its own nature differing from the cause. Therefore, while it is not first, it deservedly cannot be simple. Again, if any thing is not simple, it will necessarily have in itself "this" and "that." We ask, therefore, whether "this" comes from "that" alone, or whether both come equally from each other; or neither from neither; or whether both come from some third thing. If you answer that "this" depends on "that," then "that" will certainly be first, and "this" second; nor will it be permitted to say that a composite thing is the first here. Nor, again, will it be permitted to say that both are made equally from each other; otherwise the same thing, compared to itself, will be both cause and effect, both prior and posterior. But if you say that both are made by some third thing, then not this composite, but that third thing will be the first and the principle. 

Furthermore, it is a sacrilege to place two things in the highest realms of which neither is from the other, nor both from a third; otherwise they would come together by no determined cause or reason, but by mere chance. But reckless chance cannot exist in the highest realms; otherwise there would be no order in the things that follow. Wherefore, as we said, that which is not first is not simple; so also we say that what is not simple is not first. Therefore, the more prior something is, the simpler it is, and vice versa. Thus, what is first is most simple, and vice versa. For this reason, primariness itself (if I may say so) is simplicity itself, and vice versa. Since, therefore, Unity and Goodness hold the highest place in simplicity, both are certainly the same, and the first of all things and the principle. 

Goodness is surely most simple; otherwise it would be composed of many things. Therefore, it would lack parts and a composer, and thus it would be least sufficient in itself. Yet it is necessary that Goodness itself be not only the most sufficient, but be sufficiency itself. For this is desired as the good. Thus the Good itself, since it is most sufficient, is also most simple. It is therefore first; especially because if it were not first, that which would be higher than the Good itself would also be better than Goodness—even though nothing better than Goodness can be imagined, for by Goodness alone is whatever is better made better. 

Then we ask whether the Good itself desires that which is perhaps placed before it, or not. If it does not desire it, it is a wonder that an effect does not desire the cause by which it is perfected. If it does desire it, again it is marvelous that the Good itself should long for something outside itself, since all desire ends in the Good. Furthermore, we inquire similarly regarding other things: whether they desire what is imagined to be above the Good, beyond the limits of the Good, or not. It is indeed a sacrilege if all things do not desire the first principle. It is again a sacrilege to desire anything beyond the Good. From all this, it is gathered that the Good itself is the most simple of all things, and the first. Truly, that Unity (or the One itself) is the most simple, no one doubts. For in every essence, composition or number can either exist or be imagined: In Unity alone it cannot; otherwise it would not be Unity itself, but "one certain thing" and a multitude. Division, furthermore...

Ficino is moving from the discussion of physical optics into the metaphysical core of Neoplatonism: the nature of the One, the hierarchy of the three divine principles (the One, Mind, and Soul), and a critique of those who introduce unnecessary divisions within the divine realm.</meta>

COMMNETARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...cannot happen to unity. For if someone should strive to divide this, he will not indeed divide it, but will instead repeat the unity. You certainly cut one piece of wood, and a larger piece of wood becomes smaller pieces of wood. But that unity which was conceived in the wood you could not divide into any parts of unity—otherwise, they would be smaller than unity—but you have multiplied that unity, or rather propagated it, so that what was previously in one would thereafter be the same whole in two. Since, therefore, unity is the most simple and the first, it is rightly the same as goodness: lest perhaps there be two first principles of things that happen upon one another by chance, and lest a "twoness" <note>original: "binarius"; the dyad, which in Neoplatonism represents the first step away from perfect unity into multiplicity.</note> exist before unity.

When, however, we say that goodness and unity are utterly simple, we do not mean a certain simple thing that exists in something else, or from which something else is composed. For if it were in another and could not sustain itself, it would certainly depend on that other. If, again, another thing were composed from it, it would by no means be a perfect thing, but would strive further and be reduced into the form and act of the composite. Therefore, the Good itself, or the One itself, is altogether the same: both most simple and first, not residing in anything else, nor considered in such a way that anything else in itself is prior to it. For if it were first a thing and *then* became good and one, then in that case one thing would be added to another, there would be something prior that was imperfect, and a composition would occur. Therefore, with the first and simplest intuition of the mind, we ought to contemplate goodness itself or unity, not predicating one thing of another, but perceiving simplicity itself with the first and total strike of the mind.

Since, however, after these things Plotinus treats the three principles of the world—namely the Good itself, the First Mind, and the First Soul <note>These are the three "Hypostases" of Neoplatonism: The One (the Good), the Nous (Mind/Intellect), and the Psyche (Soul).</note>—we ought to remember that when we investigate the common principles of the world, we must first contemplate those which are most common above all others in the world. Now, the most common of all things everywhere is unity and the bond to the Good. For that office extends even to things not yet formed. In the second degree of commonality or origin, there is "form" in the formal order; finally, in the third degree is placed vital motion itself. 

Since a function belongs to a prior cause the more common it is, the first cause of all is rightly the Good itself, or the One: from which and by which unity and the striving toward the Good depend. The second cause of things is the First Mind, to which the formal order pertains. The third is the First Soul, by which every vital motion everywhere is returned. Therefore, when we behold the universe—most beautiful in its order of forms and most effective everywhere in its vital motions—we rightly think that Mind governs everywhere and Soul breathes everywhere. And since both the order of forms conspires into one for the sake of the Good, and vital motion strives toward the Good, it is not without reason that we wish both the Mind, which thus orders all things, and the Soul, which thus moves all things, to depend on the One and the Good itself. 

Thus, then, this entire universe of bodies, which is movable by another, will first be reduced to the Soul, which is movable through itself and moves all things by its own motion. This, in turn, leads to the Mind, which is entirely stable and directs all things by its own state. But both—namely, Mind and Soul—are referred back to the Good: for the sake of which the Mind is seen to move stably and the Soul to move with mobility; in which the Mind itself rests, and around which the Soul revolves. Surely, whether the Soul is moved and moves, it is moved and moves toward the Good. Whether the Mind rests and makes firm, it certainly rests and stays in the Good. Hence, it is a gift of nature to all things that, just as they are moved toward the Good, so they also rest in the Good. 

And indeed, just as the Good itself is something other than those things which are moved toward it, and other than the motion itself; so also it is something other than those things which stand in it, and other than the state of standing: otherwise they would have rested in themselves from the beginning. After the Good itself, the Mind follows most closely; the Soul accompanies the Mind most closely. For since every agent acts toward the Good, the Mind—which while it acts, acts stably toward the Good and is revolved into itself by acting—is judged to be closest to the Good. But the Soul—which both remains through its essence and again is moved out of itself by acting, and completes its circle after its progression—is closest to the Mind, which is entirely stable and entirely turned into itself. 

But who does not see that the Soul, being always and truly a sharer in intelligence, is first and foremost closest to the Intellect? Therefore, that there is in the world any motion and action contributing at last to life, proceeds from the Soul. However, that such motion is ordered and stable, and is restored into a circle and expresses forms, is allotted from the Mind. Finally, that a certain end is prescribed everywhere for motion, and that forms here and there are conducive to others, is a gift from the Good itself. In the heavens indeed, essence, light, mobility, and the good represent the Mind and the Soul. Beneath the heavens, the final cause seems to refer to the Good, the formal cause to the Mind, and the efficient cause to the Soul. 

Since, however, we dispute more extensively concerning the three principles of all things both here and there in our arguments on Plato and in our theology, let it suffice to have touched upon these things briefly. After this, however, he [Plotinus] refutes those who distinguish divine things among themselves, either because some are in potentiality and others in act <note>term: <term>potentiality and act</term> (Latin: *potentia* and *actus*); Aristotelian concepts where potentiality is the capacity to be something and act is its realization. Ficino argues divine things are purely realized "act."</note>. For nothing in eternal things is in potentiality. Or because one intellect remains while another is moved. For in the intellect there is no motion, but the first motion is in the soul. Or because this intellect understands a certain substance, whether its own or even another's, while that one understands only the action of another intellect, which that other—whose action it is—does not understand. 

Truly, a distinction of this kind in the nature of souls divides the substances of souls. Indeed, the same soul that understands either itself or anything else often understands that it is understanding. Therefore, much less are the substances of minds thus divided: and much more can the same mind fulfill both. Now, however, we concede that "to understand" simply differs by a certain reason from "conscious perception" <note>original: "intelligentia animaduersione"; the difference between basic cognition and reflexive awareness of that cognition.</note>. For the former has some essence as its object, while the latter seems to look upon the action as its object. And in us, he who knows does not always also acknowledge that he knows. Nevertheless, any mind separated from commerce with the body understands so readily that, insofar as it understands anything, it thoroughly acknowledges that it understands itself. Especially since the condition of understanding there is such that the mind looks to its own essence in order to understand. For if perfect intelligence is there, it has the most intimate and certain intelligible [object] and is least dependent. This happens most fully if it looks to its own essence as the object. 

While it gazes upon its own essence, placed in its intellectual being and in a perpetual act of intelligence, it knows itself to be an intellectual and always-understanding essence. Insofar as it understands itself, it understands that it is understanding. Especially since, just as in light to shine is the same as to be, so in the intellect itself to be is the same as to understand. Therefore, while it knows that it exists, it also thoroughly acknowledges that it understands. Wherefore any absolute intellect, just as it always understands, so it always perceives what it understands: especially since no exterior occupation diverts it from this perception of itself. Moreover, there is one and the same act of intelligence: by which it both understands something simply, and by which it always acknowledges that it understands it. For if you were to distinguish such acts there, we would then say that a third act and similarly a fourth, and so on infinitely, are distinguished there; insofar as through the following act it is imagined to understand the preceding one innumerably. Philosophers think it a sin to place infinite acts, and these indeed superfluous ones, in that presence: especially if through them infinite substances are said to be multiplied there. Among these things you will note yourself that Plotinus places in minds a blessed and perpetual awareness of their essence and action; and by the same act, both the intelligence...

ON BOOK VIII OF ENNEAD II.

...knowledge and recognition are filled by the intelligent essence. If he <note>Referring to Plotinus.</note> should say anywhere that the simple and primary act of intelligence is distracted by attention, explain it this way: namely, when attention is an action that differs in reality from intelligence, and when attention occurs through the service of a certain imagination which differs too much from the intellect and meanwhile distracts it toward external things. He immediately refutes what they say: that there is a certain middle substance between the mind itself and the soul, which they call "intellectual reason" itself; they say the soul receives reason from this substance. If this were so, the soul would have no true and perpetual intelligence. For true and perpetual intelligence exists either in the mind itself, or in that which is most closely a participant in the mind. According to their opinion, the soul would receive some small part of intelligence not in the first degree, but in the second—an image of intelligence rather than its nature. And thus, it would neither notice itself—which is the duty of an intellectual nature—nor could it contemplate the substance of any intellect separate from subsequent natures, nor grasp the formal reason of any thing, nor embrace the definition of truth itself. For such things belong properly to the mind.

## Different modes of Providence, namely in the three principles: Then in the stars: Thirdly in daemons: Fourthly in humans.

II In the second chapter, therefore, he gathers the three principles of things: namely, the Good itself, and its son, the Intellect, flowing from the paternal light in the manner of a beam of light; and furthermore, the Soul of the World <term>Anima Mundi; the soul that animates the entire universe</term> flowing forth from the divine intellect like a spirit through all things. But it provides for lower things on the condition that, meanwhile, it does not turn away from divine things in any part. Rather, he says that the more closely it clings to divine things, the more powerful and fruitful it is rendered toward the things that follow, and as if already pregnant from that source, it gives birth to what follows. Universal providence pertains to these three principles, which provide both for all things and for everything. A less universal providence belongs to the souls of the spheres and the stars; for any of these provides indeed for all things, but not for everything <note>Ficino distinguishes between "providing for all" (omni) and "providing all aspects" (omnia). A star might influence every person, but only regarding specific qualities like heat or timing.</note>. For each one bestows its own properties, though upon all. Providence in daemons <term>daemones; intermediary spirits in Neoplatonism, not necessarily evil</term> is even less universal. For each cares for certain specific kinds of things, to which they also bestow certain properties. There is also a particular providence in our souls toward lower things. This is with an even more intensive anxiety than that with which daemons care for their own things; thus it is foolish to compare human providence with the providence of the World Soul. For since the primary soul is most powerful, and its providence is universal—outside of which there is nothing that might resist its duty—Plotinus says, not without justice, that while it provides, it neither labors nor is it less blessed. But our soul is so occupied with governing bodies that it sometimes departs from higher things. It departs, I say, through its lowest part first—that is, through the imagination and its affect—leaning more toward lower things. These indeed might thereafter drag with them the middle part of the soul, whose property it is to move through reason. Yet he confirms (as he often does) that the Intellect—which he names a "part" of the soul—never ceases from divine intelligence. This opinion regarding the intellect seems to have been not only Plotinus's, but also that of his teacher, Ammonius of Alexandria. Plotinus is said to have followed him in all things. We have heard that certain other students of Ammonius remained in the same opinion, which Iamblichus also seems to count among the dogmas of the Egyptians. You will note meanwhile that our soul, although it is called a "particular soul" because it has a particular providence, is in no way a part of the World Soul. Again, our soul is anxious and labors in governing the body because it neither holds the highest rank of soul—which the World Soul obtained—nor does it remain entirely in the highest state when it provides for lower things. He certainly thinks it is the condition of particular souls that they do this or that by turns: namely, as far as reason and imagination are concerned; but as far as the intellect is concerned, they take no turns. For any intellect is established entirely within eternity. Since indeed, in the property of the soul that follows immediately, there is the first movement and the first time.

## The world was not at some time "new" from some new depravity of the soul: nor will it ever perish.

III In vain, therefore, did the heretics <note>original: "heretici"; Ficino refers here to the Gnostics, whom Plotinus criticized for believing the physical world was an evil creation of a fallen soul.</note> imagine that the primary soul at some point fell from divine bliss, and thus, degenerating into worse things, fabricated the world. Too rashly they gave a beginning to the world on the grounds that its maker had recently been changed into evil. It was much better to say that the world was produced from the soul always by a certain natural necessity, just as the form of a body is produced by the vegetative power, and heat and light by fire. For we see that all the most perfect things always act in natural bounty, not from the evil of poverty but rather from the good of abundance. But if those things whose power and action are determined only toward certain things—like any element or composite—always act, much more do those three principles of things, whose power is common to all, always act. It is better, therefore, to say that the maker of the world, from an eternal abundance of goodness, begot the world from eternity, rather than as something "new" from a new depravity. Certainly, if we consider the nature of the principles as always absolute in act, and we compare the work here to it, an eternal work seems to follow from there. Although if you look at the very will of the divine goodnesses or intelligence, you could conceive of a "new" world without a new depravity of the maker, and without a novelty of divine counsel. Truly, since in divinity nature is the same as will, neither does the will take away from nature what is proper to nature, nor does nature take away what is proper to the will. Then indeed he refutes those who thought the world would at some time perish. For only those things that can be resolved into something else seem able to perish. For the very goodness of nature does not allow anything to vanish into nothingness, just as it does not allow a vacuum anywhere. Into what, then, can the world be resolved? Perhaps into matter? Let it be so, certainly. But then we ask: does that matter have a form or not? If it has one, it will still be a composite resolvable into matter. Then it can neither vanish into nothingness, nor persist in forms. For existence is given everywhere through form. And if you imagine that it remains without form, then matter will be in one place, and divine things in another, as if separated by boundaries; since nothing from those divine things would shine forth into the matter. Therefore, divine things would not be everywhere. We have proved in *Theology* <note>Referring to Ficino's own work, *Platonic Theology*.</note> that saying this is a sacrilege, and we will prove it elsewhere. Nor is it permitted to imagine that matter can be resolved into nothing. Indeed, no agent strives to resolve simply for the sake of resolving, but rather to increase or propagate itself. But that can only happen from something and into something. Furthermore, if matter were reduced to nothing, it would certainly be established that matter from the beginning had no necessity from any preceding subject from which it was made; since in this way no some-

*...when the subject has preceded, just as "none" follows at last. It existed, therefore, from the beginning by a certain necessity of consequence from a higher and efficient cause. By the same necessity of consequence, it will always exist.*

## The Architect of the world made the world not through a downward inclination, but through constancy.

*IV. He <note>Referring to Plotinus, whom Ficino is interpreting.</note> again rejects what they say: that the primary soul created the world not because it remained in its own dignity, but because it degenerated. But before I pursue the refutations of Plotinus, it is helpful to review the words of Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was the student and biographer of Plotinus who edited his works.</note> on the same subject, from his book demonstrating the ways to the intelligible. Thus he says: "None of the substances that are universal and perfect turn back toward their own offspring. Rather, all perfect substances are led back toward their generators, even as far as the mundane body <note>The "mundane body" refers to the entire physical universe.</note>. Since this body is indeed perfect, it is led back to the soul—I mean the intellectual soul—and therefore it moves in a circle. But the Soul of the World is raised up toward the Intellect, and the Intellect is raised toward the Principle <note>The "Principle" refers to the One or the Good, the source of all existence.</note>." He adds a little later: "In particular substances, however, which are capable of falling into many things, there is a downward leaning toward their offspring; therefore, in these, a 'fault' is said to have occurred, and in these, 'unfaithfulness' is condemned. Matter itself contaminates these things because they can lean toward it, even though they are meanwhile able to turn themselves toward the divine. For this reason, perfection stands secondary to the prior things, preserving them as they are turned toward the prior. Elsewhere, a defect also causes certain prior things to lean toward posterior things, and it makes these very things love while meanwhile turning away from the higher." So says Porphyry. In these words, he confirms that certain <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, "daemons" are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note> or human souls produce bodies by degenerating from divine things. But the world was constructed by a certain divine soul that persists in divine things. For to produce such a great, such a beautiful, and such a long-lasting work—and to guide it without transgression, and to move it with such wonderful reason—is not the power of something that occasionally leans downward, but of something that always stands firm in the best state. It creates this structure not so much so that it might *appear* best, but because it *is* naturally best itself. But if that power is best and, as is apparent from its motion, untiring, it will never destroy what it makes so excellently out of regret, nor will it cease to preserve it out of exhaustion. To say that worldly things are established poorly, and to argue from this that the nature of the world is evil and its author is evil, is the mark of men who are either wicked or utterly ignorant. It is also the mark of fools to imagine that this power needs deliberation in order to act. For if it was in its nature to generate, it needed no deliberation whatsoever for this. If there were need for deliberation, that first power was not naturally sufficient for the effect of generation. Therefore, no nature and no power would be able to generate or make anything of itself.*

## Neither is the soul corporeal, nor was the world established by an evil principle.

*V. He furthermore refutes what they <note>The Gnostics, whom Plotinus and Ficino are criticizing.</note> were saying: that the Soul that is the architect of the world, by which the world lives and moves, was composed of the elements of the world, and that it is corporeal, irrational, and mortal. First, it is a sacrilege to suggest that the Universe has a soul worse than ours. Second, it is wrong for the soul to be composed of elements as if it were subsequent to them; for the soul, as the power that joins together clashing things, must be prior, simpler, and more constant. Finally, a nature composed of elements produces nothing except a single body, nor can it turn back into itself. He mocks them further for thinking they will be happy when they enjoy the "Model of the World," while they do not shrink from detesting this very workmanship <note>The physical universe.</note> which was established according to that model—especially since they say that the Architect of the world first thought of the world's model only when he turned toward worse things. They added that he had fabricated the world to keep souls under guard, which was an attempt in vain. As for their belief that he has such a care for the world, it is asked: did he care for it before the world existed, or did he begin to care after the world was already made? If before, he cared in vain, as we said. If after the world, then perhaps he received the arrangement of the world from the "form" of the world itself by separating it from matter, or from souls. If he perceived the condition of caring from the form of the world itself, souls could have perceived it similarly by themselves. If from souls, it is ridiculous to say—indeed, both options are ridiculous. But where it is said that souls must be restrained, an opinion is touched upon—which Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD), an early Christian theologian who famously taught the pre-existence of souls.</note> also touched upon—namely, that all spirits were equal from the beginning. But because of diverse movements of the will, being more or less turned toward God or away from Him, they then received various ranks among themselves. Thus, the bodies of the world were established in different ranks, and finally, some spirits were assigned to some bodies and others to others. The error of this opinion is proven by the fact that the entire arrangement of the world consists in the very distinction of ranks; since this is the highest formal and final goal and the best thing in the universe, it is rightly the first thing in the intention of the first Agent <note>The "first Agent" refers to God or the Creator.</note>. It does not, therefore, happen because of a diversity of merits—especially since if rational natures were equal from the beginning, one did not depend on the other. Thus, the meeting of various wills would have happened by chance, and the order among spirits and in the world would have followed by chance. Likewise, since specific differences and species are natural and essential in lower things, it is sacrilege to say they are accidental in higher things. They would be accidental if they had not existed from the beginning but happened afterward through free movements of wills. Although it is very difficult to explain why spirits who were so equal were moved in such different ways. Certainly, if they were many before the moments of their wills, and yet not distinct through the division of quantity, nor differing as of yet by any accident, then they differed from one another through certain formal and essential things, insofar as something was in one that was not in the other. Such a distinction cannot exist without a diversity of ranks, since it is reduced to "privation" and "form." Therefore, before the variety of movements, there was an inherent variety of natural characteristics. But we shall speak of these more opportunely elsewhere.*

## The Creator of the world is the primary Intellect acting through the soul; likewise there are three principles: the Good, the Mind, and the Soul. Likewise, the first Intellect and the first Intelligible are the same.

*VI. It was an ancient opinion that forms in matter result from a certain impression made by divine forms, while matter reflects the influence of the "Ideas" <note>The "Ideas" or "Forms" are the eternal patterns of all things in the mind of God.</note> much like a mirror. Therefore, it reports or renders or simulates things that look like the true forms of the Ideas. Thus, they say souls are deceived after falling from the supernal world, until they are finally moved by repentance and return to their homeland from this colony or exile. The heretics, usurping this ancient sentiment, foolishly covered such passions of the soul with certain names of substances. After this, you will observe that among the ancient Christians, the heretics <note>Likely referring to the Gnostics or Manichaeans.</note> accepted the <term>transcorporation</term> <note>Original: *transcorporationem*; the transmigration of souls or reincarnation.</note> of souls from the ancients; but I believe they held it only from human into human...*

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s second Ennead, specifically the ninth book, which is a polemic against the Gnostics. Ficino is explaining how the higher principles (the One and the Intellect) generate the world without suffering or "falling" into matter.</meta>

ON BOOK VIII <note>Though the header says Book VIII, the content corresponds to Ennead II.9, which Ficino and others sometimes grouped differently in early editions.</note> OF ENNEAD II.
r 2
<meta>catchword: body</meta>

...whether earthly or airy, but he did not believe that the human soul was transferred into beasts. Indeed, the doctors of the Hebrews <note>Ficino often refers to the "Hebrew doctors" when discussing the Kabbalah or Jewish Platonic traditions that he believed aligned with his own "Ancient Theology."</note> are said to have understood it in this way. Plotinus also judges that these people <note>The Gnostics.</note> have perverted the words concerning the "craftsmanship of the world" <note>A reference to Plato’s *Timaeus*, the primary Greek text on the creation of the physical universe.</note>. For they take three words from the *Timaeus* as if they represent three distinct substances. However, according to Plotinus, these three words signify three properties of the same substance: namely, that the same God, the craftsman of the world, devised it; that is, he decreed it, and by naturally decreeing it, he completed as many species of things in the world as his own intellect contemplated as Ideas within its own living self—that is, within its living essence. 

But the heretics <note>The Gnostics, whom Plotinus and Ficino viewed as deviating from true Platonic philosophy.</note> used to say that the "Living Being" itself is Intelligible Being itself, the first thing superior to every intellect. They claimed that the one who contemplates the Ideas within it is the "first formal intellect." Furthermore, they said the one who devised the making of the world is the "primary soul," and that this soul acts by a certain deliberation—and poorly at that—after it has degenerated from the higher realms. 

Plotinus, however, will prove that the first Intelligible and the first Intellect are the same thing. Since the first Intellect understands in a perfect manner, it possesses the Intelligible within itself. Therefore, it is understood by itself, as if it were the Intelligible itself, just as it is the Intellect. Likewise, because it is the first and perfect Intelligible, it must be understood in a perfect way. It is understood by a perfect reason if it is understood by itself. Therefore, whether you look at the Intellect, the internal Intelligible immediately follows; or if you perceive the Intelligible, the internal Intellect immediately accompanies it. And rightly so, since there is a far greater proportion between the Intelligible and the Intellect (and vice versa) than there is between the visible and sight. For the Intellect penetrates, divides, and defines the very thing to be understood; no sense does this regarding a sensible object. Therefore, since there is a marvelous proportion between the Intelligible and the Intellect, it rightly follows that by whatever path something reaches the point of being the highest Intelligible, by that same path it follows that it is the highest Intellect, and vice versa. 

Plotinus believes this to be the primary craftsman of the world. However, he does not wish the primary Soul to be excluded from the office of the craftsman; rather, he denies that she makes the world through deliberation or conducts it with anxiety. Otherwise, neither the substance of the mundane work could stand, nor could its order persevere, if it were made and moved by some shifting action of a craftsman—especially a laborious one. He detests even more the claim that the "craftsman soul" is void of mind and subject to perturbation, even worse than our own souls; for in this craftsmanship, nothing is done foolishly, and nothing appears disturbed. 

Accordingly, he distributes the order of principles in this manner. The most absolute Unity of God, or His simplicity, so greatly towers above all things that He has no similarity or respect toward anything else. Therefore, He does not look at this before that; certainly, He either produces nothing, or He produces all things at once. But indeed, the highest Goodness above all things rightly produces all things immediately; the highest Unity immediately produces the One. Therefore, that which flows most closely from there—namely, from the Unity which is above all—is surely the "One-All": that is, one Being, which is all beings. This is the Intelligible itself, which is all intelligible things. This is the primary Intellect, which is also every intellect—the absolute Intellect, I say, and all the Ideas. This is the Intelligible World, generated by the One who is above all: the One-All generated. 

From here is born the primary Soul, already "one and all," which you may see unfolding internally (albeit in a mobile way) what the primary Intellect embraces in a stable way. Since the world then proceeds from the Intellect through the Soul, it is not so much "one and all" as it is "one out of all." Certainly, in both the Mind and the Soul, their own unity precedes the multitude. But in the corporeal world, the unity of forms follows the multitude in a certain way. Yet you can gather it thus: all the members of the world and the natures of those members are led toward the single nature of the World-Soul as their leader; all souls are led toward the one World-Soul as their principle; all intellects that are within souls are led toward the one Intellect existing above souls, like eyes toward the light of the sun. Finally, the pure Intellect is led toward the paternal light and goodness. 

Among these things, you will observe that while many philosophers posit intellects that are absolute and separate from bodies, Plotinus posits intellects only within souls, which he calls "animal intellects" and "intellectual souls." These intellects can surely be judged free from bodies because, although they are in souls, they are not in bodies; since souls are not truly "in" bodies, and intellects of this kind have no commerce with the body. And as Plotinus often confirms, they are always joined in active thought with the Divine Mind. The opinion of the Christian theologians among the Greeks <note>Referring to the Greek Church Fathers like Origen or Dionysius the Areopagite.</note>—which attributes bodies to angels—seems hardly to differ from this view. 

Where Plotinus concedes that things may be multiplied as much as possible in the lower realms, he forbids introducing a similar multiplication in the higher realms. Understand that the multiplication forbidden there is that which happens through tiny, superfluous, or disjointed parts, as usually happens among us; he does not forbid that which happens into species or necessary things, or that which is gathered summarily into one. Specifically, he forbids multiplying the principles or "heads" of things. That he wishes there to be multiple intellects, however, he shows where he says that intellects are the highest parts of rational souls, and that the souls themselves differ from one another in their passions and natures.

## ->The World-Soul binds its own body to itself, and through this, as it were, other souls. Also, how the individual soul gives life to the body.<-

VII. He rejects again the idea that the soul who generates the world labors in this construction in the manner of our own soul, and is distracted from the duty of contemplation itself. For he says: Since the whole machine <note>A common term for the structured physical universe.</note> is subject to the World-Soul, nothing there resists it, nothing of its own flows away, and nothing foreign affects it. Likewise, he says the entire mass of bodies, having had life infused into it from the earth itself, is both bound together and tied to the Soul, and is entirely subject to it. 

Our soul, however, approaches the body as if it were a certain member of the world, and even then as something living in the lap of the whole Soul, bound to it much like a fetus in the womb. Thus, the soul coming from the outside is bound to an animal that is already, as it were, made, and does not rule it completely. But the World-Soul generates the animal for itself, and binds it to herself, rather than herself to it; therefore, she never suffers along with the passions of the animal. For that which is inferior, being connected to that which is superior, is accustomed to suffer if the superior suffers; but it does not happen the other way around. 

You, however, should remember that although our soul obtains a body that is already living, nothing prevents our soul from also applying life to the body, like light to light. For here, the prior life is easily drawn toward the action and property of the life that comes after. The latter is more powerful in its own body, and if it is compared to the other, it seems to stand as something substantial compared to something accidental. He concludes, finally, that the universe is well-disposed everywhere, having been led toward the common good. If, meanwhile, some inconvenience happens to certain parts, it occurs because of their own weakness—they either cannot properly follow the order of the whole, or cannot withstand its force, or they deviate. 

Take note, however, that in Plotinus’s comparison, the intellectual soul can either escape the fatal order <note>The order of Fate or physical necessity.</note> because it hangs from a superior principle, or it can willingly and diligently comply with this order; and finally, it can so conform the body commended to it with the order that it sometimes avoids inconveniences.

<summary>Ficino explains the Neoplatonic hierarchy of being, arguing that the World-Soul and the Intellect govern the universe effortlessly and without the "fall" or labor described by Gnostic heretics. He distinguishes the transcendent World-Soul from individual human souls, which are subject to physical necessity but can rise above it through their intellectual nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "Against the Gnostics" (Ennead II.9). Ficino is defending the goodness of the physical world and its creator against Gnostic claims that the material universe is a mistake or a prison created by a fallen, arrogant deity. He reconciles Platonic philosophy with Christian scripture, specifically citing Genesis and the Psalms to support the dignity of the cosmos.</meta>

## The craftsman of the world made the world not by a change in himself, but by the abundance of his natural power, as if it were a statue of God.

VIII When the heretics <note>The Gnostics.</note> are asked why the craftsman of the world constructed it, they respond: because he fell from contemplation and, being ambitious, turned himself toward action and commanding. However, it was better to assign this to a natural fecundity rather than an iniquity of the will, and to respond to those asking in this way: just as heat, by the very reason that it is heat, naturally heats, and light, as light, naturally illuminates and similarly gives life, so that most powerful agent makes things through the presence of his natural power. Indeed, it seems entirely contrary to all religion and philosophy, as the heretics said, that the craftsman of the world was first formally changed within himself before he made the world, or that the craftsmanship—which is eternal, or rather, is the same thing as eternity—experienced a beginning at some point; namely, when that craftsman became less powerful due to a "fall" from better things.

It is also against religion to revile the world as if it were evil. For in Genesis, Moses says both that the individual things in the world were good, and that the creator of the world made all things "very good." To this also belongs that saying: "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands" <note>original: "Cœli enarrant gloriam Dei, & opera manuum eius annuntiat firmamentũ" — Psalm 19:1.</note>. Thus the magnitude, power, and motion of the universe show us the marvelous power of divinity; the wondrous order, especially preserved in such a variety of things, shows his wisdom; and the usefulness which everywhere leads to the best result undoubtedly declares his goodness. I mean power, wisdom, and goodness not only as they exist in the craftsman, but as they are also communicated to the craftsmanship; otherwise, we could not judge such things about the maker by contemplating this work. For this reason, it would be much better, in the Platonic manner, to honor this universe as if it were a <term>statue of God</term> <note>Ficino uses the Platonic concept of the world as an "agalma" or living statue/shrine that reflects the divine beauty.</note>, and to honor those things in it which are more excellent as more certain "statues" of the Ideas, rather than to revile them in the manner of the heretics. For the Platonists judge it impious to despise, let alone accuse, the living statues of God manufactured by him and placed in the worldly temple to demonstrate the legitimate worship of all things. Nor should we neglect the meaning of: "He placed his tabernacle in the sun" <note>Psalm 19:4.</note>.

Therefore, the world not only imitates the divine mind "dissimilarly," as the heretics claim, but also imitates it "similarly." Dissimilar imitation is understood where a comparison is made through opposites: just as that [the divine] is immaterial, indivisible, and immobile, so this [the world] is in turn material, divisible, and mobile. Therefore, if that is good, this would be evil. However, there is additionally a certain imitation of the divine mind through similarities in the world: insofar as this work represents that essence, life, intelligence, and the Ideas; indeed, even unity itself and goodness. Therefore, this too is good, as an imitation of the Good. Plotinus thinks that this actually emanates from there by a certain natural exuberance of that goodness, but that the cause cannot be equaled by the effect.

After this, he says that the earth is full of immortal animals, and similarly the space all the way to heaven, and much more so heaven itself. There are immortal living beings on earth—beyond the soul of the earth itself, there are at least our own souls, which are joined here to celestial bodies. I will pass over the fact that the followers of Orpheus even introduce <term>demons</term> <note>original: "dæmones" — in the Platonic sense, these are intermediary spirits or guardians, not "demons" in the modern sense of evil spirits.</note> who preside over the earth. There are immortal demons in the air as well as in the ether, at least as far as their celestial bodies are concerned. In all the spheres of the heavens, there are immortal and divine animals—namely, the stars themselves. There are also those who place demons in the orbits of the planets, beyond the planets themselves, like stars subjected under a planet, just as in the firmament the smaller stars are ruled by the greater ones. I omit the fact that all the Ideas are everywhere, which they are accustomed to call "intelligible animals." Finally, we have discussed in our *Theology* <note>Ficino's major work, the "Platonic Theology."</note>, and will discuss elsewhere, how any intellectual substance can be everywhere in a similar way.

But if someone argues that the souls of men and even of demons can at some point lay down their "celestial vehicle" <note>The "astral body" or subtle spirit that carries the soul.</note>—from which it would follow that such an animal is not immortal—we say first that this is not easily admitted. Second, if it were admitted, the laying down of such a body should hardly be called "death," because it happens neither by the natural course of fate, nor by violence brought from without or within, but by a certain easy "laying down," like a garment, and by will. Finally, if they grant that earthly things live but perhaps deny that celestial things live, let them hear Theophrastus saying that he is no philosopher who denies that celestial things live. But if they deprive the celestial things of reason—which always move in a marvelous way—let them realize that they themselves are sometimes devoid of either eyes or reason. If they deny that the world is from the Good, let them hear the world crying out twice: "Since I constantly provoke you by my order to divine wisdom and life, know that I depend upon divinity."

### The errors of the Gnostics are no less opposed to Christians than they are to Platonists.

IX In the following parts, while he refutes the foolish accusations of the heretics against the world, notice that there are three primary levels in the world. In the first are placed the movers of the spheres and stars. In the second, the spheres. In the third, the composite things below the moon. Without the distinction of these levels, the world would not be beautiful. Similarly, there are three levels of human life. For there are divine men, there are human men, and there are, in a way, brute men. Similarly, diversity appears by reason even in a city most rightly constituted. Remember that beauty, both in life and in the city, consists in such distinction and order.

You will note, meanwhile, that the celestial gods provide for individual things among the inferiors, and that below the moon there are many good demons, better than men—though it is conceded that some demons are evil. Furthermore, consider how foolish was the arrogance among the Gnostic heretics, such that they said no form of virtue could exist except in those who followed their same heresy. Likewise, they claimed all demons and angels here are evil; that the rulers of the celestial spheres are wicked; and so is the life of the whole world itself. Finally, they claimed that no divinity anywhere was to be honored in any way or invoked, but only the First was to be prayed to without a mediator; and to obtain what they asked for, only the profession of their heresy and certain words and rituals sufficed, and that an exact purity of life and morals was not necessary for this. Finally, they judged even the worst follower of their heresy to be better than the entire universe. So it is no wonder that Plotinus is twice as sharply indignant.

Finally, you will note that just as the greatest power of the sun shines forth to us if we are convinced that there are many "solar" things from it (that is, the lights of all things everywhere), so the wondrous power of God shines if many gods are made by and depend upon the One. After this, he says the gods inspire men with things that please both the higher God and themselves. Take "gods" here to mean both the souls of the stars and the good demons. For the souls of the stars inspire the demons with what has been decreed by the mind of the World Soul and the Divine Mind, and these demons inspire us. 

But you, while Plotinus inveighs more broadly against the heretics, remember that neither the legitimate kind of Christians is being touched here, nor the person of Christ himself. Because the errors of the Gnostics are no less foreign to Christ than they are to the Platonists. And indeed, if Porphyry—who took up the cause against the Christians—judged Christ to be wise, pious, and blessed through the testimony of oracles, then Plotinus, who only acts against certain heretics, rightly judges that Christ should be excluded from these curses. Nor does he unjustly pursue those who asserted the world...

He emphasizes that Plotinus's attacks on "heretics" target Gnostics, not mainstream Christianity or Christ, whom even the pagan Porphyry respected.</summary>
