<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's work against the Gnostics. Ficino is specifically addressing the Gnostic claims that the material world is inherently evil and that salvation is achieved through secret knowledge rather than moral effort. He contrasts these views with both Platonic philosophy and Christian scripture.</meta>

...that the world is evil by nature, and comes from an evil source. They claim that our souls are better than the soul of the world, and even become better than the angels. They say this happens without any labor or duty of purification, but solely through the confession of that heresy, through certain rituals, and the pronunciation of specific words; they claim it is not permitted for anyone to become good in any other way. Finally, they believe that God Himself cares only for the human race, and that there is no divine providence for the whole world or for worldly things. 

These ideas are no less opposed to the Christian law than they are to Platonic teachings. For if you listen to Paul's letter to the Romans, you will learn that God is the God not of one nation only, but of all nations. Or, if you listen to the Gospel, you will recognize that God provides for the entire universe, even down to the smallest things. Likewise, that Prophetic saying is confirmed: namely, that all can be called "gods" and "sons of the Most High" <note>original: "omnes videlicet posse dici deos, ac filios excelsi omnes" — a reference to Psalm 82:6.</note>. And together with the Prophet, the angels are placed above souls. Above all else, arrogance is to be rooted out. God must be worshiped in spirit and truth alone. Favor must be earned through purity of character alone; and indeed, this gift is obtained only with the greatest labor.

->Confirmation of the arguments above.<-

**XII** In the twelfth chapter, you will see even more clearly: it is not the Christian law that is being rejected in any part, but the most arrogant heresy of the <term>Gnostics</term> <note>A diverse group of early religious movements that emphasized secret knowledge (gnosis) over faith or works.</note>, who forge false books of Zoroaster, profess the highest philosophy, and arrogantly place themselves above Plato in wisdom. Many of those practicing philosophy among the associates of Plotinus were deceived by these people before they became close to Plotinus. 

But what shall I say? Here he ridicules that most foolish heretical notion: they call the very craftsman of the world both "Wisdom" and "Soul"—"Wisdom" <note>original: "sapientia" (Sophia)</note> insofar as he previously lived in the intellect, but "Soul" <note>original: "anima" (Psyche)</note> insofar as he inclined toward the making of the world. They further debate whether his power first declined toward the making of the world. They add that other souls consequently descended to bodies after him, as if bound to him by a fatal law, and at the same time the "members of Wisdom"—that is, the <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note>—assented to the bodies. Then they say the craftsman infused matter with something imaginary, and subsequently, from this material imaginary thing, another even vainer imaginary thing resulted, as if further removed from substance; and perhaps yet another, which is the final world. All this is done to "prove" that the whole thing is utterly empty.

->The life that depends on the soul within the body is immortal, as it is an act of the soul.<-

**XIII** You will observe in the thirteenth chapter that irrational life, which depends on rational substance like its image and act, is in no way sustained by matter, nor does it become a quality of any subject. Instead, it exists from the soul alone and, as it were, shines out from it—just as a visual ray shines from the eye of an animal that sees at night. Even if it happens that this ray is not extinguished, it may still occasionally not shine out, or it may shine out while depending solely on the eye.

->According to the intention of nature itself, the whole exists before the parts of the work; and the whole is begun all at once.<-

**XIIII** In the fourteenth chapter you will note: since nature acts through "form," and acts with the full force of the entire form to propagate the whole, the form of the whole is first and complete within the very intention of the natural agent. Thus, the whole, along with almost all its parts, is begun fundamentally at once from the vigor of that agent. This is how the species of plants and animals are begun; this is how the entire world flowed out from the divine cause all at once.

->The heavens are indeed warm and provide heat, but they do not burn, nor do they cause harm.<-

**XV** In the fifteenth chapter, remember that the heaven is indeed warm and provides heat, but it does not burn—a claim the heretics added. If in every living body heat is born together with life, then surely a body that is primarily living is primarily warm, and by heating it gives life to all things; and while it increases and nourishes all things, it burns nothing. That it provides heat not only by motion but by its nature is evident: for it heats through rays diffused through all things without motion. Even if those rays are gathered together and collide, they will heat more intensely, but they do not naturally burn. Otherwise, both by its great size and the speed of its motion, it would suddenly consume everything else. 

As for the fact that fires are ignited on high, this comes not from the heat of the heaven, but perhaps from the confinement of the air there. In that place, heat—at first lightly ignited by the heat and motion of the heaven—becomes a little sharper due to the narrowness of the space. When a subtle, dry, and sulfurous vapor applies itself to this, the heat becomes far more intense in the vapor, where the heat is also increased by the shaking motion of the vapors. Nevertheless, there is still more light there than heat. Lightning, however, is sent down from a lower region for a more violent cause. 

After this, you will note that since the nature of the celestial bodies generates, gives life to, and preserves all things, it is naturally good. Furthermore, those things that are judged to be "unjust" are signified by the heavens, not caused by them. Finally, those things that happen among us under the common influence of the celestial bodies are produced differently among themselves, both because of the different species and because of the various fortunes occurring to individuals. "Various," I say, as they pertain to the seasons of the year, different places, and the dispositions of minds. Therefore, these differences do not exist because of the heaven; rather, what is given from heaven by a common influx is received differently because of these factors. 

It is a sin to disparage the degrees of good things—which proceed from the greater to the lesser through the very breadth of the Good—as if they were "evil," and thus to reject the nature of the universe itself. It is also ridiculous to introduce a "principle of malice" just because something evil occasionally creeps in while things proceed in order. It is as if evil were an efficient cause rather than a deficient one, or as if things happened by a set purpose rather than by chance. Indeed, while certain forms are generated by the intention of nature proceeding from the very principle of things (and are therefore made good), other forms consequently give way—which appears to be an "evil." 

Since, therefore, evil occurs by accident through the same motion by which good is made through itself, no one ought to propose contrary principles because of the difference between goods and evils, nor introduce "Evil" alongside the principle of Good. Much less should one introduce something that is evil by its "first nature" and "essence"; otherwise, essence and being itself would be evil. Yet being is sought as a good, and its opposite is rejected as an evil. Furthermore, a principle acts upon what follows it insofar as it is effective and in "act," and it acts through form. These things are good. Therefore, the principle itself is not evil, nor does it produce evil things through itself, but rather things like itself—that is, formal things, and therefore good things. Evil, however, pertains to the privation of form, which happens but is not intended. By these arguments, therefore, the error of both the Gnostics and the <term>Manichæans</term> <note>Followers of Mani who believed the universe was a struggle between two equal powers: Light (Good) and Darkness (Evil).</note> is refuted.

->Prayer does not change the God or deity being worshiped, but the one who worships.<-

**XVI** The sixteenth chapter ridicules the heretics for thinking that celestial bodies, the souls of the heavens, and the deities above the heavens can be turned from their own state by human words and rituals. Likewise, they think all the power of prayer lies in the melodies of voices...

<summary>Ficino refutes Gnostic and Manichaean dualism, arguing that the physical world and its celestial bodies are naturally good and that "evil" is merely a deficiency of form rather than a competing creative principle.</summary>

In the previous section, Ficino emphasized that salvation requires moral purification and "spirit and truth," rather than just secret rituals. He continues here by contrasting Gnostic dismissals of the physical world with the Platonic and Christian view of a divinely ordered cosmos.</meta>

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...with scents and ritual characters. Furthermore, they insist that all diseases are nothing other than demons <note>The Gnostics often attributed physical illness to demonic possession rather than natural causes</note>. But the evangelical doctrine commands that God be worshiped in spirit and truth; it does not wish for God to be changed by us, but for the worshiper to be changed. Moreover, it heals many sick people who are not possessed by a demon.

->Not ritual worship, but virtue obtains the divine gift from God.<-

### XVII
The specific gift of providence shines forth in the excellent arrangement of the universe and in the perfect state of the worldly Craftsman. The heretics <note>meaning the Gnostics</note> foolishly tried to strip all of this away when, in their criticism of the world's arrangement, they accused the Lord and author of providence. Now, in order to prove there is nothing good in the world, they used to say that no laws—whether of nature or of men—are good, and that what are called "virtues" are nothing. They themselves said nothing about the virtues, nor did they care at all about purifying their souls. For they preached that if someone merely thought about God and invoked Him with certain prayers of theirs, they would obtain everything, even if they did not expel the disturbances of the senses. Certainly, nothing is more alien to the evangelical doctrine than this. For it is "not he who says Lord, Lord," and so on <note>A reference to Matthew 7:21: "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven."</note>. Remember, however, what he says: absolute virtue shows God to us. For just as the perception of fiery heat, when brought to its peak, immediately fills matter with light and creates fire, so too the imitation of God through virtue eventually makes the soul divine and "a god." Thus, the soul, by seeing itself, also sees God.

->Platonists more easily accept Christian dogmas than Gnostic ones.<-

### XVIII
Suppose Plotinus had heard from Greek Christians—especially from John of Damascus—that a certain final order of angels had fallen away from God and were thereafter enclosed in bodies made of thick air; he would not reject these ideas, but would adapt them entirely to Plato. Indeed, Egidius of Rome <note>A 13th-century theologian and philosopher</note> teaches that this does not conflict with the Christian law. However, Plotinus cannot help but be sharply indignant when he hears that the entire world was created as something "worst" by an "evil angel" <note>The Gnostic concept of the Demiurge</note>. Likewise, he is outraged that these heretics profess to be most acceptable to the deities above the heavens, while they bitterly detest the rulers of the heavens who depend on those deities and are most like them. They curse the whole world, which is arranged in a most divine order, as if it were evil, and they preach that God has care for the human race alone. Yet they claim He does not even look upon the whole world in which man exists and to whose order human affairs are connected. These ideas are so ridiculous that they are sufficiently refuted by their own absurdity.

->Concerning the living world, demons, and beauty: and that beauty proceeds from goodness and is a sign of goodness.<-

### XIX
Separate, if you can, the dimension and matter from the world; leave the rest, and you will have an intelligible sphere—that is, a living and manifold one <note>original: "sphæram intelligibile, id est, animale & multiplicem"</note>. In this sphere, the first soul, which is harmonized with the universe, will be a wider orb according to its virtue. Thereafter, like orbs narrower in power, come the remaining intellectual souls in order, so that one power almost always encompasses another, just as in visible things one sphere encompasses another. But in the living world, because no physical dimension pulls things apart, any part is found everywhere as a whole within every other part. There is motion and rotation there, such as suits an intellectual soul; dimension exists not in actual fact, but as a certain potential very close to action. For the outward appearance <term>species<gloss>the formal or visible appearance that reflects an inner essence</gloss></term> of the body is destined to proceed immediately from the power of the soul, demanding from the soul a certain quantity and shape within matter. And as far as the soul’s proceeding power extends, so far is quantity extended in the body according to its strength.

Truly, if one inspects the intimate motion of the soul, one will see both a formal diversity there and, because of temporal motion, a certain interval from one act to another. In this diversity, and in this interval of the living circuit, the soul of the future body will already begin to suspect a dimension—just as someone suspects a continuous circle from the rapid vibration of a spark. Moreover, that entire spherical assembly of souls is stable because of its intellectual faculties (as if certain centers were fixed), but mobile because of the powers that follow. From the vigor of that state and motion, the corporeal world is made, and it consists and moves. From its clear and wonderful beauty, it is right to judge its natural and intimate goodness; and from these two, one can conjecture the beauty and goodness of the soul.

Therefore, where he says that demons can be perceived and are most beautiful, understand that they can indeed be perceived, as we said in the book *On Beauty*. Furthermore, they are most beautiful—those whom Basil the Great calls "good angels"—having bodies that are partly fiery and partly airy, most bright and most beautiful, just as David indicated when saying that the angels are God’s ministers in "spirit and flame" <note>A reference to Psalm 104:4</note>. Thus Basil thinks that it is easier for angels to change place, to rest, to minister, and to offer themselves to the senses without deception. Psellus asserts that this was also the opinion of the Apostle Paul. Therefore, by this reasoning, whether you prefer to call them "good demons" or "angels," they are beneficial deities in bodies, worthy of some honor and worship, according to the opinion of both the Platonists and the Christians, and contrary to the opinion of the Gnostics. 

For while the Gnostics remove these beneficial deities from the world, they subvert the order of the universe; they take away from themselves the very means through which they could be properly reconciled to the highest things. In short, whatever things are truly beautiful on the outside are also naturally good on the inside; for external beauty arises from the perfection and victory of the "seed-reason" <term>rationis seminariæ<gloss>Stoic and Neoplatonic term for the formative inner principles that shape matter</gloss></term> over matter. But if the inner form is lacking, then the thing itself is both diminished in its better parts (that is, the internal parts) and falls away from the better things (that is, from those things higher in rank). It is not absolutely beautiful, but mutilated in its beauty. Hence Porphyry says that demons whose minds are wicked also have deformed bodies, while those whose minds are upright have beautiful bodies. 

And Origen argues from the light and order of the heavenly bodies that spirits are present in them which are closer to God and possess bright intelligence. Together with the Apostle Paul, he includes spirits that have degenerated far from God in bodies composed of murky air. Truly, if the body depends on the soul, then surely such a disposition of the body arises from such an affection of the soul—whether natural, or contracted through habit, or conceived through a sudden inclination, especially when the beginnings and the growth of the body are given. Therefore, a beautiful body is a sign of a beautiful soul—that is, one that is thoroughly harmonious, shining, and entirely well-composed, both in terms of thought and imagination, and in terms of affection and its "seed-like" nature. A base body, however, is a sign of an uncomposed soul, one that has already collapsed into a discordant habit or affection. Since, therefore, the world is most beautiful, the Soul of the World is simultaneously most beautiful and best, and similarly the souls of all the spheres and stars. Among us, it can perhaps happen—though rarely—that a non-beautiful soul is currently in a beautiful body, because a soul that was unformed from the beginning of conception later gradually became deformed...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino defends the goodness and beauty of the physical world against Gnostic claims of its evil nature. He argues that external beauty is an indicator of inner moral goodness and that the cosmos is a divine hierarchy of souls and beneficial spirits.</summary>

BOOK NINE.

...but she was once entirely beautiful, when she chose to fashion a beautiful body for her head, under a beautiful star and a guiding spirit <note>original: "demone," referring to the *daimon* or tutelary spirit that Platonists believed guided an individual's destiny</note>. Moreover, the soul can sometimes be beautiful within an unattractive body: either because what was once not beautiful eventually became so, or because often, when a beautiful soul strives to fashion a beautiful body, some impediment from surrounding circumstances and influences occurs or is occurring. But to the World Soul, nothing is added, nothing recedes, and no impediment stands in its way. For nothing of the sort can happen to the universe.

->Our soul, because it is the sister of the World Soul, is able to overcome the decrees of fate and<-
->reach its state of blessedness.<-

**XX** Where he says that our soul is the sister of the World Soul and of the celestial souls, remember: the intellectual soul is neither a part nor an offspring of the World Soul or the celestial souls. Likewise, it can eventually reach their state of blessedness and become, in a sense, their colleague in the governance of the world. Furthermore, we can never—when the soul withdraws into itself—either diminish or avoid the blows of fate <note>Ficino is clarifying the limits of human agency versus cosmic destiny</note>. Finally, it is not permitted to depart from this worldly prison by forcibly breaking its bonds <note>A classic Platonic prohibition against suicide</note>, and it is even less lawful to accuse the celestial spheres or souls.

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...they establish [remedies] by odors and signs <note>original: "characteribus," referring to talismanic symbols or occult scripts used in Gnostic rituals</note>. Moreover, they want all diseases to be nothing other than <term>demons</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, *daimones* are intermediary spirits, but the Gnostics viewed them as malevolent entities inhabiting the body to cause illness</note>. But the Gospel doctrine commands that God be adored in spirit and in truth; it does not wish for God to be changed, but for the one adoring Him to be changed. Furthermore, it heals many who are sick who are not possessed by a demon.

->Not [mere] adoration, but virtue obtains the divine gift from God.<-

**XVII** The proper office of providence shines forth in the excellent arrangement of the universe and in the most perfect disposition of the worldly Creator. The heretics <note>The Gnostics</note> foolishly took all this away when they found fault with the arrangement of the world and accused the Lord and author of providence. Now, indeed, so that they might convince others that there is nothing of good in the world, they said that no laws—either of nature or of men—are good; and they claimed that what are called virtues are nothing. Nor did they themselves speak of the virtues, nor did they have any concern for the purification of souls. For they preached that if someone merely thought of God and invoked Him with certain prayers used among them, they would obtain absolutely everything, even if they expelled none of the disturbances of the senses. Certainly, nothing is more foreign to Gospel doctrine than this. For it is not "he who says, Lord, Lord," and so forth <note>A reference to Matthew 7:21: "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father."</note>. Remember, however, what he says: absolute virtue shows God to us. For just as the perception of fiery heat, when brought to its peak, immediately fills the matter with light and creates fire, so also the very imitation of God through virtue finally makes the soul divine and even a god; and the soul, by seeing itself in this way, also sees God.

->Platonists more easily admit the dogmas of Christians than those of the Gnostics.<-

**XVIII** Suppose Plotinus had heard from the Greek Christians—especially from John Damascene <note>Ficino is speaking anachronistically here to make a point, as Damascene lived centuries after Plotinus</note>—that a certain final order of angels fell away from God and were afterwards enclosed in bodies made of thicker air; he would not reject these things, but would adapt them entirely to the teachings of Plato. Indeed, Egidius the Roman <note>Giles of Rome (c. 1243–1316), a medieval theologian</note> records that this does not conflict with Christian law. However, Plotinus cannot help but be sharply indignant when he hears that the whole world was created as something most evil by some "most evil angel." Likewise, he is outraged that the heretics profess themselves to be most acceptable to the divinities above the heavens, while they sharply detest the rulers of the heavens <note>the planetary spirits or celestial bodies</note> who depend on those divinities and are most like them, as if they were evil. They curse the whole world, arranged in a most divine order, as something evil, and they preach that God has care for the human race alone. Yet they claim He does not even look upon the whole world in which man exists, to whose order human affairs are connected. These things are so ridiculous that they are sufficiently refuted by their own absurdity.

->Concerning the animate world, demons, and beauty: and that beauty<-
->proceeds from goodness and is a sign of goodness.<-

**XIX** Separate, if you can, dimension and matter from the world; leave the rest: you will have an <term>intelligible sphere</term> <note>The realm of pure Forms or Ideas, which Plotinus describes as a sphere where every part contains the whole</note>, that is, a sphere that is animate and manifold. In this sphere, the first soul, being congruent with the universe, will be a wider orb according to its power. The remaining intellectual souls follow in order as orbs narrower in power, so that one power almost embraces another, just as in the visible world one sphere embraces another. But in the animate world, because no dimension pulls things apart, any part is found everywhere as a whole in every other part. Movement and rotation exist there, of the kind that suits an intellectual soul, but dimension exists not in act, but in a certain potentiality very close to act. For from the proceeding power of the soul, the species of the body will immediately emerge, demanding a certain quantity and figure from the soul into the matter. And as far as the soul's proceeding power extends itself, to that extent the quantity in the body is extended according to its strength.

Surely, if one inspects the innermost motion of the soul, one will see both a formal diversity there and, because of the temporal motion, an interval from one act to another. Therefore, in this diversity, in this interval of the animate circuit, one will begin to suspect the dimension of the future body and sphere, just as someone suspects a continuous circle from the frequent vibration of a spark. Moreover, that universal sphere of souls is stable because of its intellectual faculties, as if by certain centers and poles, but it is mobile because of the powers that follow. From the vigor of that state and motion, the corporeal world is made, and it stands and is moved. From its clear and wonderful beauty, it is proper to judge its natural and inward goodness; and from these two—beauty and goodness—to conjecture the beauty and goodness of the soul.

Therefore, when he says that <term>demons</term> <note>intermediary spirits</note> can be perceived and are most beautiful, understand that they can indeed be perceived, just as we said in the book *On Beauty*. Furthermore, they are most beautiful, whom Basil the Great <note>St. Basil of Caesarea, a 4th-century Church Father</note> names "good angels," having bodies partly fiery and partly airy, most lucid and most beautiful, as David indicated when saying, "God makes His angels spirits and His ministers a flame" <note>Psalm 104:4</note>. Thus Basil thinks that the Angels more easily change location, rest, minister, and offer themselves to the senses without deception. Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine philosopher</note> asserts that this was also the opinion of the Apostle Paul. For this reason, whether you prefer to call them good demons or angels, they are beneficial divinities in bodies, worthy of some honor and worship, according to the opinion of both the Platonists and the Christians, against the opinion of the Gnostics. The Gnostics, while they could easily be reconciled to the Highest [God], instead take away the Highest, pervert the order of the universe, and destroy those means through which they could be comfortably reconciled to the Highest.

In summary, whatever things are truly beautiful on the outside are naturally good on the inside; for external beauty proceeds from the perfection of the internal form and the victory of the <term>seminary reason</term> <note>the formative rational principles or "seeds" within nature</note> over matter. But if the internal species is lacking, then the thing itself is both diminished in its better parts (that is, its internal ones) and falls away from the better things (that is, those things higher in rank). It is not absolutely beautiful, but mutilated in its beauty. Hence Porphyry says that demons whose minds are wicked also have deformed bodies, while those whose minds are upright also have beautiful bodies. And Origen argues from the light and order of the heavenly bodies that spirits more near to God dwell within them, possessing lucid intelligence; and along with the Apostle Paul, he concludes that spirits that degenerate far from God are enclosed in bodies compacted from dark air. 

Certainly, if the body depends on the soul, then such a disposition of the body proceeds from such an affection of the soul—whether natural, or contracted through habit in the manner of nature, or conceived at some time by affection and inclination, especially when the beginnings of the body are given and as long as it grows. Therefore, a beautiful body is a sign of a beautiful soul—that is, a soul that is inwardly harmonious and shining, and altogether well-ordered within itself, as much as pertains to thought and imagination, as well as to affection and its formative nature. Conversely, an ugly body is a sign of an uncomposed soul, which has already fallen into a dissonant habit or affection. Since the world is most beautiful, the Soul of the World is simultaneously most beautiful and best, and similarly the souls of all the spheres and stars. Among us, it can perhaps happen, though rarely, that a soul in a beautiful body is not currently beautiful, because a soul that was beautiful at the beginning of conception later gradually became deformed...

<summary>Ficino argues against Gnostic pessimism by asserting that the physical world's beauty is a direct reflection of divine goodness and that virtue, not just ritual, is the path to God. He aligns Platonic views on intermediary spirits (demons/angels) and the "World Soul" with Christian authorities like St. Basil and Origen.</summary>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD II.

Now, however, we must investigate in the present context whether there are more than these three natures, or if there are others besides them. Indeed, since the principle of the universe itself stands as we were just saying, no one can find any principle simpler or more exalted. For one would not dare to posit one principle in potential <note>original: "in potētia" — the capacity to do or be something, not yet realized</note> and another in act <note>original: "in actu" — the fully realized state of being</note>. For it is ridiculous to introduce multiple natures among those things which are in act and without matter <margin>B</margin> by means of a distinction distributed between potential and act. Furthermore, one must not imagine in the subsequent levels one intellect placed in a certain rest and another as if in motion. For what is the rest of the intellect? What is its motion, its progression, or its utterance? Again, what would be the leisure of the one, and what the work of the other? For the Intellect <note>original: "intellectus" / "νοῦς" — the second highest level of reality in this system, representing divine thought</note> always remains in the same way, established in stable activity. Motion toward it or around it is already the function of the Soul.

Indeed, the rational principle <note>original: "ratio" / "λόγος"</note> proceeding from the Intellect into the Soul <margin>C</margin> makes the soul intellectual, but it does not introduce some other nature intermediate between the Intellect and the Soul. Furthermore, it is not fitting to introduce multiple intellects for the reason that one might think, while another thinks that it thinks. For even if in these things simply "to think" were one thing and "to think that one thinks" were another, there nonetheless thrives a single intuition in those beings, where their own actions are by no means hidden from them. For it is absurd to think otherwise regarding the true Intellect. Rather, the one who thinks and the one who understands that he thinks will be precisely the same. <margin>D</margin> Otherwise, let this one be only thinking, while the other is noticing that this one thinks; in that case, someone else would be the one who understands rather than the one who merely notices.

If they say these two differ from one another by a certain conceptual distinction, they first will not be able to introduce multiple substances there. Secondly, it is worthwhile to consider whether any conceptual distinction or invention can admit an intellect that is only thinking, yet not <margin>E</margin> noticing that it thinks. If this were to happen to us—we who are always intent upon impulses and deliberations—even if we were only moderately studious and upright, it would bring upon us a charge and crime of foolishness.

Now, truly, since that true Intellect in its thinking understands itself, and the object of thought is not placed outside the thinker, but the thinker is himself the object of thought, it necessarily possesses itself in the act of thinking and sees itself. In seeing itself, it certainly sees itself not as ignorant, but as thinking. Therefore, in the very first act of thinking <margin>F</margin> it possesses both that which it thinks and that it thinks that it thinks, existing as one and the same. Not by any figment of imagination can what is one there be made double. And if it always thinks that which it is, what place is given there for the invention that separates "simply thinking" from "noticing that it thinks"?

But if someone should bring in a third invention besides that which said "thinking that it thinks"—now claiming <margin>G</margin> "thinking that it thinks that it thinks"—then the absurdity of this opinion will appear even more clearly, nor would anything prevent us from wandering thus into infinity. When they bring forward a certain rational principle flowing from the Intellect, from which another rational principle is then made in the Soul, so that

<column-break/>

But now to examine as in the present, if there are more than these three, any natures besides them; since the stated principle is thus, no one could find another simpler or higher than it. For one would have to say that one is in potential and the other in act. For it is ridiculous among those things in act and immaterial to make more natures by dividing them into potential and act. But neither in the things after these should one imagine that there is one certain intellect in a kind of stillness and another as if moved. For what would be the stillness of the intellect, and what its motion and utterance? Again, what would be the idleness of one and the work of the other toward something else? For it is as it is, and always in the same way, situated in activity; it is standing. But motion toward it and around it is already the work of the soul. And the rational principle from it into the soul, making the soul intellectual, is not some other nature between the intellect and the soul.

One should not, therefore, make more for this reason—if one thinks and the other thinks that he thinks. For even if to think in these cases were different from thinking that one thinks, yet <margin>* approach/intuition</margin> the intuition of its own activities is not one * without perception. For it is ridiculous to assume this regarding the true intellect. But in every way the one who thinks is the same as the one who thinks that he thinks. But if not, the one would be thinking only, and the other thinking that he thinks. But there being * [two]. But <margin>* and that</margin> that [awareness] is not away from the thinking itself. But if they say it is by a conceptual distinction, first they will be positing a substance of more [than one]. Then they must examine if the conceptual distinction could find a place for an intellect thinking only but not following itself in that it thinks. Which, if it happened to us—who always command our impulses and thoughts—even if they were moderately serious, they would have a cause for folly.

But when the true intellect thinks in its thoughts * by itself, and <margin>* by itself</margin> the object of thought is not from outside it, but it is itself also the object of thought, it necessarily holds itself in the act of thinking and sees itself; and seeing itself, it sees itself not as unthinking but as thinking. So that in the primary act of thinking, it would also have the "thinking that it thinks," as being one. And it is not torn apart there even by a conceptual distinction. If, then, the thinking being is one with what it is, what place is there for a conceptual distinction which separates thinking from thinking that one thinks? And if someone should introduce yet another third conceptual distinction over the second one which says "thinking that it thinks," the one saying "thinking that it thinks that it thinks," the absurdity would be even more manifest. And why <margin>* it is <br/> * of this</margin> * does this * not go on to infinity? <meta>This page continues the argument of Ennead II, Book IX, specifically targeting the Gnostic belief that the soul's creation of the material world was a "fall" or a mistake. Plotinus argues instead that the world is an eternal, necessary, and beautiful radiation of the divine.</meta>

### BOOK NINE.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...becomes a middle-ground, it forces the soul to lack intelligence. For if it does not receive its rational principle <note>original: "ratio" / "λόγος" — the formative power or logic that shapes reality</note> from the Intellect itself, but from some other intermediary, then it will not possess the rational principle itself, but only a certain image of that principle. Consequently, it would neither know the Intellect itself, nor would it understand anything at all.

<margin>II. He confirms the previous points. Also, that the Soul of the World and our own soul provide for things in a divine manner.</margin> THEREFORE, it is not proper to posit more than these levels in the intelligible world, nor to place superfluous inventions there which those realities do not admit. Instead, one should posit one Intellect that always remains in the same state, entirely <margin>B</margin> unchanging, and which imitates its Father <note>The "Father" refers to The One, the ultimate source of all existence in Plotinus's system</note> to the best of its power. Our soul, however, has one part of itself living among those higher things, another part verging toward these things of ours, and finally a part situated in the middle. For since its nature is one but possesses many powers, sometimes the whole soul joins with its best part—with Being itself. At other times, however, the lower part in it is dragged down toward inferior things, pulling the middle part along with it. Yet it is not permitted for the soul’s entirety to be plunged into the depths. This "suffering" <margin>C</margin> happens to the soul only because it did not remain in the most beautiful part of the universe. In that state, the Soul remains—that which is not a "part," and of which we are not parts either—and it has granted to the entire body of the world the gifts of its power to the extent that the world can receive them. Meanwhile, the Soul itself lives far from all anxiety, governing without any deliberation <note>original: "consultationē" — Plotinus argues that the World-Soul doesn't have to "think through" or "worry" about management; it happens naturally</note> and correcting nothing with fussy effort. Rather, by its own contemplation of the things above, it adorns the whole world with wonderful power. For the more it fixes itself in its own contemplation, the more beautiful and powerful it becomes; and drawing from <margin>D</margin> above, it pours its light into the lower things, and as if eternally illuminated from a divine source, it shines through them.

<margin>III. The world is made not by an accident of the soul, but by its power remaining in divine things; therefore, it remains one and eternal.</margin> ALWAYS illuminated, therefore, and possessing a perpetual light, the Soul passes it down to the things that follow. These lower things are always held together and flourish by this light, and they receive life from it according to each thing's capacity—just as if they were being warmed by a fire placed in the middle, provided they are capable of being warmed, even if that fire is limited in its measure. But when the powers <margin>E</margin> are not limited by measure, and are not absent from the universe, by what logic could it be possible for these powers to exist, yet nothing anywhere participate in them? Surely it is necessary for each thing to give something of its own to others. Otherwise, the Good itself would not be good, nor would the Intellect itself be Intellect, nor would the Soul be Soul, unless after that which has life in the primary sense <note>The Intellect</note>, there also lives a second thing <note>The Soul and the World</note> that follows as long as the primary thing exists. For this reason, it is necessary for all things to exist after the First, one after another and forever. Some things are involved <margin>F</margin> in "becoming" because they depend on something else. Therefore, they were not "made" at a single point in time, but they were always being made and will be made—all those things which are said to be in a state of generation. Nor will they ever be destroyed, except for those things that have something they can dissolve back into. But that which has nothing into which it can be resolved will never be able to perish. Now, if someone says that a thing must be resolved into matter, let them answer: why should they not also concede that matter itself is resolvable? And if they claim that matter can also be resolved, we will ask what necessity was there for it to be made in the first place? If they say it was necessary for it to follow as a consequence, we will assert <margin>G</margin> that it is similarly necessary for it to exist now. But if matter were left alone, it would follow that divine things are not everywhere, but are restricted to a certain determined place, as if separated by some boundary. But if that cannot be the case, it follows that matter is perpetually illuminated.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the material world is not a mistake or a fall, but a necessary and eternal radiation of light and life from the Intellect and the World-Soul, which remains untroubled while it governs.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Enneads, World-Soul, Intellect, Matter, Emanation, Divine Providence, Eternity, Contemplation</keywords>

--- Page 302 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s "Against the Gnostics" (Ennead II.9). The previous page established that the soul is a bridge between the divine Intellect and the material world. Here, Plotinus argues against the idea that the soul "fell" or made a mistake in creating the world.</meta>

### PLOTINUS: ENNEAD II.

<column-break/>

<margin>
IIII.
He confirms the previous points, proving the world is neither evil nor from an evil source.
</margin>
If, however, they <note>Plotinus is likely referring to Gnostic sects who believed the material world was a flawed creation of a fallen soul (Sophia).</note> say that the soul created the world because its wings were broken and it fell <note>This is a reference to Plato’s *Phaedrus*, where the soul is described as having wings that fail when it focuses too much on the material.</note>, we will object that the Soul of the World itself cannot suffer such a thing. But if they bring forward the idea that the soul once strayed, they must be compelled to explain the cause of that error and straying. Furthermore, at what time did it wander? For if it was from eternity, then by that same logic, it surely remains in error even now; if it began at some specific time, we must ask why it did not wander before that time. We, however, do not believe that the "inclination" or "turning away" of the soul was the maker of the world; rather, we believe the world was made by a state that is not inclined toward the lower at all. If the soul had "turned away" [from the divine], it would surely be because it had already forgotten the things that are in the higher realm. And if it has forgotten them, by what power does it craft the universe? Where and from what does it build? Does it perhaps build from the things it once saw there? But if it builds while remembering those things, then it has not completely turned away from them; for its memory is not weak. Indeed, if it does not turn away, does it not see there clearly? Why would it not wish to return immediately, keeping the memory of those things? Furthermore, what did it imagine would come to it from the making of the world? It is absurd to say that it produced the world in order to be honored; this is the opinion of those who transfer the emotions of our own sculptors to the gods. Since, even if the soul made the world through thought, and it was not in its nature to simply produce it, but rather it pertained to its power to effect it—how exactly did it establish this world? Moreover, when would the soul destroy it? For if it has already repented for having made it, what is it waiting for? If it has not yet repented, and will never be touched by repentance (seeing as it has now grown accustomed to it, and has become more indulgent toward the work it made through the length of time), then why the delay? But if it is waiting for the souls of individuals, it should have been that long ago souls ceased to come into generation, as they would not be ignorant of the evils they suffered in their previous generation; because of this, they would have long since ceased to descend. Furthermore, when they say the world was poorly established, and that because of this many adverse and troublesome things happen in it, this must not be admitted. For this opinion attributes more dignity to the world than they intend, provided they judge this world and the intelligible <note>original: "intelligibilis" / "νοητῷ" — the world of pure ideas or forms that exists before the material world.</note> world to be the same, as if this world were not an image of that one. Indeed, what more beautiful image of that realm could have been made? What other fire could be a better image of the "Intelligible Fire" than our fire here? What other earth besides this one, after that higher Earth? And what sphere could be more perfect and venerable, or more orderly in its movements, than this one which follows the embrace of the Intelligible World within itself? Finally, what other Sun could be imagined after that one, beyond this visible Sun?

<margin>
V.
Neither is the soul corporeal, nor was the world constituted by an evil principle.
</margin>
Truly, it is altogether absurd that while they themselves possess a body, just as men do, and experience desire, pain, and anger, they do not think little of their own power; instead, they assert that it is possible for them to possess a soul more excellent than ours—we who were born only recently and are hindered by countless deceptions from attaining the truth. Nor is it fitting to assert that only our soul is immortal and divine (even the souls of the most worthless men), while the entire heaven and the stars lack the immortality of life, even though they are made of things far more beautiful and pure...

<column-break/>

If they say the soul created the world because it shed its wings, they cannot mean the soul of the whole universe. If they say it failed in its nature, let them tell the cause of the failure. When did it fail? For if from eternity, it remains in that failure by the same logic. But if it began, why not before then? We say the creation was not by a "downward turn" <note>original: "νεύσει" — a leaning or inclination, often used to describe the soul's fall toward matter.</note>, but rather by a "non-turning." If it had turned downward, it is clear that this was because it forgot the things there. If it forgot, how does it act as a craftsman? For from where does it create, if not from what it saw there? But if it creates while remembering those things, it did not turn downward at all. <margin>* For it does not have it dimly, in that it has [the memory] of those things most of all.</margin> For it did not conceive of it dimly, nor does it hold it so; or rather, it turns there so that it might not see dimly. Why would it not have wished to return, having whatever memory it had? For what would it calculate would happen to itself from the world-making? For it is ridiculous to say it was "so that it might be honored," thus transferring the motives of sculptors here to the divine. Since if it created by deliberate thought, and it was not in its nature to create, and the power was that which creates, how did it not make this world? And when will it destroy it? If it changed its mind, what is it waiting for? If it is still the same and will not change its mind anymore, it is already habituated, and through time has become more favorably disposed toward its work. If it is waiting for individual souls, they should have already ceased to come into birth, having experienced the evils of this place in their prior birth. So they should have already left off coming. Or must it be granted that this world was badly made because there are many difficulties in it? But this claim is greater than what is persuasive of itself, if one demands that it be the same <margin>* The same [thing] or some [other].</margin> as the Intelligible world, and not merely an image of it. For what other more beautiful image of that realm could have come into being? What fire is better, than the fire there, or than the fire of this place? What other earth after that earth there? What sphere is more accurate and venerable, or more orderly in its movement, after the world there which contains the Intelligible within itself? What other Sun is there after that one, compared to this visible one? Who?

But it is absurd that they who have bodies, such as men have, and desires and pains and rages, do not dishonor the power within themselves, but say they are able to touch the Intelligible; yet they say that the Sun has no soul more impassive than ours, even though it exists in a greater order and not in change. Or that they have a wisdom better than ours—we who were recently born and are blocked by the deceptions of the senses from coming to the truth. Or to say that their own soul is immortal and divine, even the souls of the most base men, but that the entire heaven and the stars there have no share in the immortal, though they are from much more beautiful and pure things...

<summary>Plotinus defends the beauty and divinity of the physical cosmos against Gnostic detractors, arguing that the world is a perfect "image" of the divine realm rather than a mistake or a fall.</summary>
<keywords>Soul of the World, Intelligible World, Gnosticism, divine image, cosmology, Plato, immortality, celestial bodies, Sun, creation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s critique of the Gnostic worldview. Having previously discussed the nature of the soul, he now focuses on the Gnostic claim that the material world is an evil or accidental creation, contrasting their "novel" terminology with the established wisdom of Greek philosophers like Plato.</meta>

### BOOK NINE.

->A<-

...seeing there that which is ordered, graceful, and **equitable** <term>epieikes: a Greek term for what is fitting, reasonable, or fair in a moral sense</term>, and especially those who do not blame its disorder on anyone, as if the immortal soul had deliberately chosen the inferior place so that it might **yield** <term>egchōrēsē: to give way or make room for a higher purpose</term> to a better one.

chosen for the mortal soul; but it is irrational * 
<margin>* and their introduction of it.</margin> 
and even their own introduction of this other soul, which they construct from the elements. 

->B<-

For how could a living thing have what belongs to the **spirit** <term>pneuma: the vital breath or animating force</term>, if it is a composition of the elements? For a mixture of these produces either heat, or cold, or a blend of dry and moist, or some mixture of these. Furthermore, how can the connection of the four elements be a later result of them, if the soul is the power that connects them? But when they are persuaded that it possesses perception, will, and a thousand other things, why do they assign these to it?

->C<-

But those who honor this craftsmanship, yet say it was produced by the soul and the mind as a cause, have reached a point where they do not...

->D<-

...that the Reason (*Logos*) is in the world. And indeed, if it exists there in a paradigm <note>original: "paradeigmati" - a model or blueprint in the divine mind</note> of the world, why do they hate it? From where does this paradigm come? For it shines forth among them when the one who conceives this paradigm has already declined toward these earthly things. If, therefore, the creator had great concern for the world—to make another world in its form beyond the intelligible one he already possesses—why was that necessary for him? And if he cared for it before the world existed, for whose sake did he decree it? Perhaps so the souls themselves would be guarded? How then were they not guarded? Thus the world was made in vain. But if, after the world was made, he took from the world to explain the form of matter, the skill was sufficient for the protection of experienced souls. But if they think the form of the world is to be received in the souls, what is this novelty of speech?

->E<-

<margin>* This is a novelty of speech, for the sake of their sect.</margin>
What more should I say of the other substances they bring in, giving them names such as "neighborings," "counter-types," and "repentances"? <note>These are technical terms used in Gnostic cosmology: "Paroikēseis" (neighborings), "Antitypoi" (reflections/echoes), and "Metanoia" (repentance of the soul).</note> For if they wish to say these are passions of the soul when it is affected by repentance, and "counter-types" when it contemplates the images of beings but not the beings themselves, then truly...

->F<-

...this is all empty talk introduced for the sake of confirming their own sect. Since they do not grasp the ancient Greek wisdom, they pile up these fictions. The Greeks knew clearly and described without vanity or boastfulness certain "ascents from a cave," <note>A reference to Plato’s famous Allegory of the Cave in the *Republic*.</note> and souls proceeding from there little by little into a truer contemplation. We have found that they have snatched most of their ideas from Plato, and whatever they innovate—in order to put forward a philosophy of their own—falls far from the truth. 

->G<-

Indeed, the judgments, the punishments in the underworld, the rivers of Hades, and the transmigrations into various bodies are all taken from Plato. Likewise, they have usurped the idea of a multitude in the intelligible world—namely, Being itself, then the Intellect, and after these another Creator—deriving this from the words of the *Timaeus*. <note>The *Timaeus* is Plato's dialogue concerning the creation of the universe by a divine Craftsman (Demiurge).</note> For thus it is written by Plato in the *Timaeus*: "Insofar as therefore..."

<column-break/>

...they admit: especially since we suspect whatever is there to be most orderly and beautiful; especially since they themselves complain of the confusion surrounding earthly things, as if the immortal soul studiously chose this inferior place—chose, I say, to serve that more excellent mortal soul. Furthermore, the introduction of this other soul, which they think is composed of elements, is absurd. For in what way can any composition of elements have any life? For a mixture of these produces either heat or cold, or a blend of dry or moist, or some composition from these. Moreover, how is the soul the power connecting the elements, if indeed it consists of them and comes after them? Finally, when they join perception and counsel to the soul, and many other things, anyone could ask by what reason such things can be assigned to the soul. Furthermore, since they do not venerate this worldly workmanship, nor honor this earth, they claim a new earth is reserved for them, into which they are finally to ascend: and that this is the very Reason (*Ratio*) and pattern (*Exemplar*) of the world. Truly, why would it be worthwhile for them to live there in the pattern of a world which they hate? Also, from where does this pattern come? For it shines forth among them only when the one who conceives this pattern has already declined toward these our things. If therefore in the creator himself there is much care for the world—namely, to produce another world, beyond the intelligible one which he possesses—why was that advantageous to him? And if before the world he already cared for it, for whose sake did he decree it? Perhaps so that the souls themselves might be guarded? In what way then were they not guarded? Thus the world was made in vain. But if after the world, taking from the world as if explaining the form of matter, skill was sufficient for the guard of experienced souls. But if they think the form of the world is to be received in the souls, what is this novelty of speaking?

<margin>
VI
The World Soul binds its body to itself, and through this, as if other souls. Also, how the individual soul gives life to the body.
</margin>

What more shall I say of the other substances they introduce, naming them sometimes "transmigrations," sometimes "reflected images," sometimes "repentances"? If they want such things to be passions of the soul, namely when it is affected by repentance; likewise "reflected images," when it contemplates as it were the images of beings, but not yet the beings themselves: surely this is all empty talk introduced for the sake of confirming their sect. And yet, since they have not reached the ancient wisdom of the Greeks, they devise fictions of this kind. Certainly the ancient Greeks both knew correctly and described without swelling and boasting certain ascents from a certain cave, and souls proceeding from there by degrees into a truer contemplation. We have found that they have snatched most things from Plato, and whatever they innovate, in order to put forward a philosophy of their own, they err far from the truth: namely, the judgments, the punishments in the underworld, the rivers, the transmigrations into various bodies are taken from Plato. Likewise, because they place a multitude in the intelligible world—namely Being itself, and then the Intellect, and after these another creator—they have usurped this for themselves from the words of the *Timaeus*. For thus it is written in the *Timaeus* by Plato: "Insofar as therefore..."

<summary>Plotinus critiques Gnostic cosmology, arguing that their concepts of a "fallen" soul and a secondary "elemental" soul are irrational innovations. He asserts that the Gnostics have distorted Plato's philosophy, such as the Allegory of the Cave and the Timaeus, to create a "new" but flawed belief system.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s "Against the Gnostics" (Ennead II.9). In the previous sections, Plotinus argued that the soul does not "fall" into the world through a mistake or sin, but rather governs it as part of a divine order. Here, he specifically critiques the Gnostic tendency to over-complicate the divine hierarchy with "new" names while disrespecting the foundational wisdom of Plato and the Greek tradition.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEADS II.

->**THE NINE VOLUMES OF PLOTINUS**<-

<margin>A</margin> The Intellect beholds the Ideas existing within that which is truly Alive <note>The "Living Being" or *Animal* in the Platonic sense refers to the archetypal Form of all living things in the divine mind</note>. Insofar as the architect of the world <term>Demiurge: the divine craftsman who shapes the material world based on eternal patterns</term> conceived them, he intended for them to be contained within the world. But they <note>Plotinus refers here to Gnostic groups who were members of his circle</note>, by no means understanding Plato, imagined a certain deity containing all things within itself in a kind of quietude; then they suspect a second intellect that looks upon what is in that deity; then they devise yet another to do the thinking. Often, in their system, that which is said to "think" is the Soul, the artisan of the universe. They <margin>B</margin> believe such a figure to be the world-craftsman described by Plato, entirely failing to understand who the world's maker is, or the purpose of his work. Furthermore, they are found to lie in their interpretation of Plato, distorting his opinions for the worse. It is as if they alone have attained an understanding of the intelligible nature <term>intelligible: things known by the mind/intellect rather than the physical senses</term>, while Plato and other blessed men of old were unable to reach it. Then, because they name a multitude of intelligibles, they confidently hope to appear to have reached the summit of wisdom, yet <margin>C</margin> by this very multitude, they drag the intelligible nature down into a likeness of the sensible <note>original: "sensibilis" — the world of physical matter and senses</note> and inferior nature. 

It is truly proper to gather the intelligible nature into the smallest possible number, as far as can be done. One should attribute all things to that which follows the First <note>In Plotinus's system, the "First" is the One; the "Second" is the Intellect/Nous</note>, and not count the levels of reality beyond what is necessary. For that Intellect is all things: it is the primary intellect, the primary essence, and contains all the beautiful things that are considered after the first nature. One should place the Soul as the third rank. <margin>D</margin> Furthermore, one should investigate the differences between souls based on their experiences or their nature, and not mock divine men in any way. Instead, one should kindly interpret the mysteries of the ancients, accepting what they say correctly: the immortality of the soul, the intelligible world, and the first God. Likewise, we should accept that the soul must flee the constraints of the body, and that the separation of the soul from the body is nothing other than turning away from the world of "becoming" toward true Being. If they speak of these things as clearly as Plato did, they do well. <margin>E</margin> Those who wish to disagree may do so without malice, but it is a sacrilege to confirm their own dogmas through mockery and insults against the Greeks. Rather, they should demonstrate that their own views are correct—whatever original ideas they have found beyond the opinions of the ancients—and they should bring forward those opinions with kindness and philosophical integrity. Where they oppose the ancients, they should look justly at the truth; <margin>F</margin> they should not seek popular approval by disparaging those men who have been approved for many centuries by men of great merit. It is altogether ridiculous to profess that they are superior to them; for what was handed down by the ancients concerning the intelligible order is stated much better and more learnedly. This will be easily recognized by those who have not been deceived by the fallacies that invade men everywhere. <margin>G</margin> Truly, in the things they have received from the ancients, one finds certain additions attached that do not fit at all. Indeed, where they strive to oppose the ancients, they assert multiple "generations" and "corruptions." Moreover, they accuse this universe and criminalize the soul's commerce with the body; they blame the one who disposes the whole world...

<column-break/>

Properly, the craftsman beholds the Ideas in the "Living Being itself," and thus he intended for this universe to contain as many. But they, not understanding, took one deity as having all things in quietude, and <margin>* opinions</margin> another as an intellect that beholds the first, and another as the one that thinks—often for them, the "thinking" principle is the Soul that creates. And they think this is the craftsman according to Plato, being ignorant of who the craftsman truly is and the general manner of creation. They tell many other lies against him and drag the man's opinions toward the worse, as if they themselves had understood the intelligible nature, while those others and the rest of the blessed men had not. Even if they name a multitude of intelligibles, they think they will seem to have discovered something great; yet by this very multitude, they bring the intelligible nature into a likeness with the sensible and lower nature. One ought to seek to reduce the number there as much as possible, and by attributing all to the one after the First, be done with it—since that one is all things: the primary intellect, the essences, and all that follows the first nature. 

One should place the Soul as a third kind, and track the differences of souls in their passions or nature, without mocking divine men. Rather, we should kindly receive their teachings as being older, taking from them what they said well: the immortality of the soul, the intelligible world, and the first God. And that the <margin>* it is necessary * to allow</margin> soul must flee from association with the body, and that the separation from it is a flight from "becoming" toward "being." For these things are laid down by Plato, and when they say them clearly like this, they do well. Where they wish to differ, let them speak without envy. But the way they insult the Greek schools in their own teachings is not fit for hearing. They should show their own views to be correct where they choose to speak differently from the ancients, setting out those opinions kindly and philosophically. Or, in those things where they disagree, they should look justly toward the truth rather than hunting for reputation by attacking men who have been judged well from of old. When they say they are better than those men, they speak as base men; for the things said by the ancients about the intelligibles are said much better and more educationally. This will be easily known by those who are not deceived by the "education" that has spread among all men. What they have taken from the ancients later, <margin>* becoming</margin> they have added things that do not belong, so that where they wish to oppose them, they introduce total "generations" and "destructions," and they find fault with the soul, blaming it and the one who administers this whole...

<summary>Plotinus critiques the Gnostics for over-complicating the divine hierarchy and disrespecting the Greek philosophical tradition, particularly Plato's concept of the Demiurge and the Soul. He argues that the ancients expressed the truth about the intelligible world more clearly and with greater integrity than these "modern" detractors.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Plato, Gnosticism, Demiurge, Intellect, Soul, Intelligible World, Sensible World, Greek philosophy, Marsilio Ficino</keywords>

--- Page 305 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s "Against the Gnostics" (Ennead II.9). Having previously discussed the nature of the Intellect and the Soul, Plotinus now addresses the Gnostic error of projecting human suffering and "passions" onto the divine creator and the soul of the universe.</meta>

# BOOK NINE.

...those who find fault, and who reduce the Creator to the same status as the soul, attributing to him the same passions <note>original: "πάθη" (pathe) — here meaning emotional disturbances or sufferings</note> as those found in individual parts. ->A<-

<margin>But it is indivisible.</margin>
It has already been stated that this world, since it began, will never cease to be, but exists forever as long as those higher realities exist. Furthermore, regarding the communion of our soul with the body, it has been said that this is not "better" for the soul <note>Plotinus agrees with the Gnostics that being in a human body is a struggle, but he disagrees that this applies to the World Soul</note>. But to judge the nature of the whole based on our own experience is similar ->B<- to a person who, seeing the district of potters or blacksmiths in a well-ordered city, would then find fault with the entire city. One must observe the differences in how the whole is governed; <margin>It is not possible.</margin> it is not the same method. * For the differences are vast, as has been said elsewhere; our soul is bound in the spirited part <term>thymoeides: the "spirited" or emotional part of the soul in Platonic psychology</term> as if by a chain, whereas we are bound by the body <gloss>indeed</gloss> as if by a visible shackle already formed. ->C<- But in the Soul of the All, the nature of the body is itself bound, and it binds whatever it touches; yet the Soul of the All itself is by no means bound by the things it binds. It rules them. Therefore, it is impassive <term>impassive: incapable of being affected by external suffering or change</term> in relation to them. We are merely the cycles of these things, but as much of the soul as is divine and belongs to what is above remains pure, and is not hindered. That portion of the soul which gives life to the body receives nothing back from it. For generally, that which is in another ->D<- <margin>Not even that through which it gives to the same.</margin> necessarily receives the passion of that in which it exists. * But this [Universal Soul] does not give any part of itself to that which already possesses its own life. It is like something inserted: if that into which it is inserted suffers <gloss>something</gloss>, it suffers with it; but if it should dry up, it allows that thing to keep its own life. Just as if the fire within you were extinguished, the "Total Fire" <note>The cosmic element of fire</note> is not extinguished. Even if the entire element of fire were to perish, the Soul there would not suffer, but rather the physical constitution of the body would. ->E<- And if it were possible for some other world to exist through the remaining elements, that Soul would have no concern for it; for its constitution is not like that of an individual living being. There [in the heavens], the Soul remains by commanding [the body] to stay, but here [in the material realm], as if the elements were slipping away, they must be bound by a second bond to return to their order. In the heavens, they have nowhere to flee. Therefore, it is not necessary to hold them in, nor to push them back from the outside * ->F<- <margin>Pressing.</margin> by squeezing, as if pushing them inward. Rather, each remains naturally where its nature willed from the beginning. If any of them move naturally, they suffer whose natures do not agree with such motion. The things that move naturally are carried along rightly, as members of the whole; but some things here are destroyed because they cannot sustain or follow the order of the whole. It is as if a great chorus <term>chorea: a circular dance accompanied by singing</term> were moving in order, and in the middle of its path a tortoise were caught and trampled, being unable to escape the order of the ->G<- chorus. If, however, the tortoise could adapt itself to that order, it would suffer nothing from them.

But as to the question of what made the world, it is the same as asking...

<column-break/>

They criticize [the world]. And they reduce the architect of the world and the soul to the same status. To him, they attribute the same passions that they assign to individual living beings.

<margin>VII
How the world is more easily ruled by the World Soul than our body by our soul. And that the world is well-arranged.</margin>
It has been said elsewhere that this world never began, nor will it ever end, but exists as long as divine things exist. Furthermore, it has been stated before them that the commerce of our soul with the body does not happen for the "betterment" of the soul. But to judge the soul of the whole by our own ->B<- is just as if someone, noticing the class of potters or blacksmiths in a well-governed city, should then criticize the whole city. It is worthwhile to consider by how different a principle the World Soul governs: for it is not the same method. Nor does it govern as if it were shackled. For besides the other differences which are numerous and listed elsewhere, one ought to consider this: we are bound by the body, as if by a bond already made. ->C<- But in the universe, the soul has already bound the nature of the body, and binds whatever it has taken hold of: yet the Soul of the Total is in no way bound by those things which it itself binds. For she herself provides the starting point like a mistress: therefore, she suffers neither from them nor with them. We, however, are [subjects] of these things. But as much of her as is raised toward the divine which is above remains whole and simple and is not hindered: but as much of her as hands over life to the body receives nothing back from it. ->D<- For commonly, that which is in another necessarily receives the passion of that in which it is. This, however, hands over nothing further of itself to that which possesses its own life. Just as if something were inserted into another, it suffers with it if that in which it is suffers; but if it should ever dry out, it permits that thing to have its own life. Since not even when this fire which is in you is extinguished is the "total fire" extinguished; indeed, not even if the whole fire were extinguished would that Soul suffer anything, but only the constitution of the body. And even if some world could exist through the remaining things, ->E<- there would be no care for that soul concerning this; since its constitution is not similar to the world and to any living being. But there, she looms over it, as it were, bidding it to stand firm; here, however, the elements, as if slipping away, are reduced to the prior order by a certain second bond. But there they have nowhere they might flee. It is not necessary, therefore, to keep them inside, nor to push them back to the interior by restraining them from the outside: but wherever its nature willed from the beginning, there the individual things remain naturally. ->F<- If any of them should be moved naturally, those things meanwhile suffer whose natures do not at all fit such motions. But those things which are moved by nature are carried along rightly, as members of the universe. Some things, however, are destroyed here, since they cannot sustain or follow the order of the whole: ->G<- as if a huge dance were performed in order, and in the middle of its movement a tortoise, caught somewhere, is trampled down because it cannot escape the order of the dance: yet if it had joined itself to the order of the dance, it would not have suffered anything from them.

<margin>VIII
The world was made not by error, but by natural power: out of good things; because it is similar to divinity, although not equal.</margin>
As to what is usually asked—for what reason did he make the world—it is the same as asking: why is there...

<margin>A</margin> ...of the soul? And why did the Craftsman himself make it? First of all, this question comes from those who attempt to grasp a beginning for eternity itself. Next, they imagine that the Craftsman of the world turned or changed from one state to another, thus becoming the cause of the world’s creation. They must therefore be taught (if only they show themselves willing to learn) what the nature of these things truly is, so that they may eventually stop disparaging those things that are venerable—which they detest all too readily, even though it is greatly appropriate to revere them. And who could <margin>B</margin> rightly find fault with the arrangement of the world, which above all demonstrates the magnitude of the intelligible <term>intelligible: the realm of pure thought and divine forms, which Plotinus considers more real than the physical world</term> nature? For if it has proceeded into life in such a way that it does not possess a life that is indistinct and confused—like the tiniest things within the world, which are generated in abundance by the world's life day and night—but is instead a continuous, clear, manifold, and ubiquitous life displaying an inestimable wisdom, how can one deny that this is a manifest and beautiful <margin>C</margin> statue of the intelligible gods? If this worldly statue, while imitating its heavenly exemplar, is not identical to it, that is exactly what its nature requires; otherwise, it would not be an "imitation" at all. As for their objection that it is a "dissimilar" imitation, that is false. For nothing has been omitted of those things that a beautiful and natural image could possibly possess. Indeed, it was necessary for this imitation to exist, yet not as the result of a specific deliberation or artificial effort. For it was not possible for the <margin>D</margin> intelligible itself to be the final thing in the universe; rather, it was necessary for its activity to be twofold: one part remaining within itself, and the other proceeding forth into another thing. It was necessary, then, for something else to exist after it. For only that which is the weakest of all things is so constituted that nothing of itself descends to lower levels; yet in the higher realm, a miraculous power flourishes. Therefore, a work has always shone forth from there. And if there is another world better than this one, what is it? But if it is necessary for a world to exist, and yet there is no other, then this is the only one which preserves the image of the higher realm by imitating it. The whole earth is indeed full of various <margin>E</margin> animals, and even immortal ones, and all things are full of these all the way to the heavens. As for the stars and those things in the lower spheres, and those that shine in the highest, it is unthinkable that they are not gods—seeing as they are carried along in a miraculous order and run their courses with such exceptional beauty. What reason could there be that they should not possess virtue? Or what could be an impediment to them attaining virtue? For those things which make <margin>F</margin> earthly men evil are not found there; nor is there any vice in those bodies, such as the kind here that is disturbed and causes disturbance. Furthermore, what forbids those heavenly beings, who live in perpetual leisure, from understanding? And from receiving God and the other intelligible gods into their minds? Perhaps we possess a wisdom superior to theirs? No one but a madman would ever admit this. For since souls, if they were driven here, descended from the Soul of the World, how can they be superior while they are suffering such force? Surely in souls, that which overcomes is superior and <margin>G</margin> better. But if they came here voluntarily, why do you disparage this region into which you came by your own choice? Especially since it permits one to leave, if anyone is not pleased to dwell here. Now indeed, if this universe is such...
