<margin>A</margin> ...of the soul? And why did the Demiurge <note>original: "δημιουργὸς" (demiourgos) — the divine craftsman</note> make it? First, one must not assume a beginning for that which is eternal; second, they think that he, having turned from one thing to another and having changed, became the cause of the creation. They must be taught, then—if they are well-disposed—what the nature of these things is, so that they may cease their slandering of honorable things, which they do so easily, instead of showing the great and <margin>B</margin> appropriate reverence they ought to have. Since regarding the governance of the whole, who could rightly find fault? First, because it demonstrates the magnitude of the intelligible nature. For it was necessary <margin>D</margin> for it to exist, though the imitation was not from deliberation or technical artifice. # BOOK NINE.

<columns>
...of the verses, so that it is possible to acquire wisdom in it, and for those living here to live according to the likeness of the things above, this undoubtedly bears witness that the world depends on the realm above.

<margin>IX. All things are justly dispensed in the world; there are good spirits within it, and it is good itself, for God has care for it.</margin> **I**f someone should complain about the lot assigned in this world, blaming the existence of wealth and poverty—specifically because an equal distribution does not occur in these matters—such a person is completely ignorant. A man of excellence <note>original Greek: spoudaios; refers to the morally and intellectually serious person</note> does not demand equality in these external things. <margin>In these things.</margin> He does not believe that those possessing more money have a greater share of the "Good," nor does he judge that those in power possess more than private citizens. Instead, he intentionally leaves the pursuit of such things to others. For the man of excellence knows that life here is twofold: one for the virtuous, and another for the many. The life of the virtuous is raised toward the highest degree and the nature above, while the life of those who are more earthly is likewise twofold. One part, being mindful of virtue, shares in some measure of the good; the other is like a base and mechanical crowd <note>Plotinus uses "mechanical" (mechanica) to describe those preoccupied only with physical labor and survival</note> providing for the needs of more honorable men. But if a murder is committed, or if the soul is overcome by pleasures <margin>Overcome by pleasures.</margin> due to weakness, it should not seem surprising that sins exist here. These sins are not found in the pure Mind, but in souls—just as they are found in children or youths who have not yet reached maturity. If this lot is a kind of training ground for winners and losers, then in this way too, the order is correct. If you suffer an injustice, it is nothing grave to that which is immortal. Again, if you are killed, you have what you desired <note>This likely refers to the philosopher’s desire for the soul to be released from the body</note>. But if you still condemn such things, nothing forces you to linger in this city <note>Plotinus often uses the "city" or "house" as a metaphor for the physical body or the world; if one finds life unbearable, one can leave it, though he generally discouraged suicide</note>. It is well established, moreover, that there are judgments and punishments here <margin>Judgments.</margin>. Therefore, it is unjust to accuse this "city" when it distributes to each according to their worth; in this city, virtue is honored, and wickedness receives its fitting disgrace. Nor are there only statues of the gods here, but the gods themselves look down from on high. They easily avoid and escape the faults of men (as the saying goes), leading all things from the beginning to the end in an orderly way. They assign to each a fitting lot according to the shifts of their lives—a lot, I say, that follows from their preceding actions. Anyone who is ignorant of this lot becomes the most reckless and unrefined of all in matters of the divine. One ought to strive with all one's strength to finally become the best version of oneself. Yet, do not think that you alone can become the best; otherwise, you would not yet be the best. Rather, believe that other men can be the best too, and that there are good spirits <term>demons: from the Greek 'daimones', these are intermediate beings between humans and gods, often acting as guardians or cosmic administrators</term>. Much more should one believe in the gods, who, while inhabiting this world, look up to the superior world. Most of all among these is the Soul of the whole world, a most blessed guide. From this point, one should also worship the intelligible gods <note>The "intelligible gods" are the pure divine intellects existing in the higher realm of Forms</note>, and finally, above all and within all, one must venerate the great King of that realm. Indeed, we should judge that He demonstrates His excellence most especially through the multitude of gods. For the duty of those who have known the power of God is not to shrink the divine into a single point, but to reveal that vast divine abundance which God Himself has displayed. By this, I mean that He, while remaining one as He is, makes many who all depend upon Him, existing through Him and from Him. Indeed, this world exists through Him, and the whole world looks toward Him.

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD II.

<columns>
<margin>A</margin>The whole company of the gods, and each one individually, looks upward; they announce the divine decrees to men and declare through their oracles and responses what is pleasing to them. But if these secondary gods <note>Plotinus refers to the celestial bodies—the stars and planets—which he considers divine, living beings.</note> are not the same as the first God, then surely this very fact is in accordance with nature. But if you wish to despise the higher things and make yourself important as if you were not inferior, remember first that the better a person is, the more kindly and modest they are toward both other men and the gods.
<margin>B</margin>Furthermore, it is necessary to maintain one's dignity with moderation, far removed from all bitter rudeness, raising oneself only as far as our nature is able to progress. One should believe that the path to God is open to others as well, and not fly about as if in a dream, imagining that they alone are placed next to God. Above all, one must take care not to deprive themselves of that very faculty—however much has been given to our soul for this purpose—to become like a god. One can do this only as far as the Mind <note>original: *mens* / *nous*; the highest part of the soul that perceives divine truth.</note> leads.
<margin>C</margin>Truly, to try to transcend the Mind is nothing other than to fall away from the Mind itself. Yet foolish men believe words of this kind the moment they hear them: "You shall be more excellent than all others, not only men but the gods as well." For a great deal of arrogance reigns among men; and one who was previously modest, humble, and simple is now carried away with confidence when he hears: "You indeed are a son of God, but the others whom you used to admire are not sons of God."
<margin>D</margin>They claim that even the things these others worship according to the customs of their ancestors are not sons of God, but that "You, without controversy or labor, are more excellent than the very heavens." To this is added what others likewise shout out: it is as if someone who does not know how to count were to hear from some source, amidst a crowd of others who also cannot count, that his own height fills exactly a thousand cubits. What then, if he should believe himself to be a thousand cubits tall? And if he hears that others do not exceed five cubits, he might not know how much those numbers are, yet he would
<margin>E</margin>imagine from this that the number by which he exceeds them is vast. Furthermore, they confess that God has a care for human affairs, but no care for the whole world in which humans live. But why does He neglect the world? If He neglects it because He does not have enough leisure to look after the universe, then surely it would be forbidden for Him to care for the inferior parts either. Likewise, while He looks after men, why does He not also see the things that surround them in the meantime, and thus the world in which men exist?
<margin>F</margin>If He does not look outside Himself, lest He see the world, then He does not see men either. But they will say that men have no need of that, yet the world needs it. Indeed, He knows the order of the world, and who is in it, under what condition they are there, and in what manner. Accordingly, those among men who are friends of God bear with a calm mind the things that happen from the world, and they rightly endure whatever necessarily comes from the movement of the whole.
<margin>G</margin>And this is not done with a sense of injury: for it is fitting to look not to each person's own wish, but to the whole itself, honoring each according to their worth. Therefore, they strive by nature according to their strength, thinking again that there are many things—or rather, that all things which strive toward that goal and follow it are blessed, while some, as far as their nature allows, attain a lot that is suitable for them. Truly, a man of integrity does not claim for himself alone the power of attaining happiness. For not from...

<column-break/>

<margin>* always</margin>and each of the gods. And those things there, as he says, [are announced] to men, and they proclaim what is dear to those [divine ones]. But if <insert>this</insert> * is not what I am, this very thing is according to nature. But if you wish to look down upon them,

Then, one must be dignified within measure, without rudeness, going as far as our nature is able to go, and considering that there is a place with God for others too. And one should not station himself alone after Him, as if flying in dreams, depriving himself of as much as is possible for a human soul to become a god. It is possible as far as the Mind leads; but that which is beyond Mind is already to fall outside of Mind. Foolish men are toyed with by such talk, suddenly hearing: "You will be better than all, not only men but also gods." For there is much self-will <note>original: *authadeia*; stubbornness or arrogance.</note> among men. And the man who was previously humble
<margin>* they hear</margin>and moderate, and a private man, * [is puffed up]. "You are a child of God, but the others whom you admired
<margin>* for not to all, taking them collectively.</margin>are not children *..." [They take this] dishonorably toward each side... not even better than the heavens, nor in... making. Then they also join in shouting with * others, as if someone who does not know how to count, among many who do not know how to count, hears that he is a thousand cubits tall.
<margin>* others</margin>
<margin>* or a thousand</margin>Why would he * think himself to be a thousand cubits tall? You hear that the others are five cubits tall. He would only imagine that being a thousand times larger is great. Concerning us, God thinks; but of the whole world, he does not? And why does he neglect it? For if he has no leisure to look toward it, it is not lawful for him to look downward and toward us. Why does he not look outward? He also looks toward the world, if [humans] are in it. But if he does not look out, so that he does not oversee the world, why does he look toward us? But they [men] have no need of those things. But the world has need, and he knows its order and those in it, how they are in it, and how they are there. For one must look not to each person's whim, but to the whole, honoring each according to merit. Instead of... * always all... those things which are able. ### BOOK NINE.

<columns>

<margin>He claims to have what he says he has; but many, even knowing they do not have it, say they have it and think they have it, when they do not; or they think they alone have what they alone lack.</margin>

**A** Many other things, or rather everything, could be examined by someone, and he would have an abundance of evidence, showing in each argument how the matter stands. A certain shame <note>original: *aidōs*; a sense of respect or modesty.</note> holds us regarding some of our friends who happened upon <margin>first.</margin> these arguments first, or rather, met with them before meeting us.

**B** Friends, we thought—I know not how—who persist in these views. And yet they themselves do not hesitate to make their own views appear true, with an air of reliability, or perhaps they even think their own views are correct as they say what they say. But as for us, if we spoke to their actual opinions, nothing more would come of it in terms of persuading them, lest they be troubled by their own side. They do not bring demonstrations <note>original: *apodeixeis*; logical or mathematical proofs.</note> here; rather, from everywhere we have spoken, there is a way in which they defend themselves, mocking the words of the ancient and divine men <note>Plotinus is defending the classical Greek philosophical tradition, particularly Plato, against Gnostic reinterpretations.</note>—words beautifully spoken and held fast to the truth—daring to do so. We must, therefore, leave them to be examined. For to those who have accurately grasped what has now been said, it is possible to know how it stands regarding all other things. Having said that, we must leave the argument. For it has surpassed all absurdity.

**C** If there is an absurdity in the telling—for they say the Soul <note>original: *psyche*</note> and a certain Wisdom <note>original: *sophia*</note> inclined toward what is below, whether the Soul began the <margin>unspeakable.</margin> unspeakable inclination or Wisdom was the cause of it, or whether they want both to be the same. They say the other souls descended together and are "members" of Wisdom, and they say these souls enter bodies, such as those of humans. But for the sake of which they themselves descended, they say that she <note>Sophia/Wisdom</note> again did not descend. As if she did not perceive it! But only shone into the darkness. Then, from that, an image was born in Matter. Then, they fashion an image for the image, somewhere here through matter or "materiality"—or whatever they wish to name it, calling it first one thing and then another, and inventing many other names which they use to obscure the one they call the "world-maker" <note>original: *demiurge*; the craftsman of the physical world.</note> here. And having made him revolt from his Mother, they say the world comes from him. At the very edge of images, so that the one who crafted these things might be even more harshly insulted.

**D** First, then, if she did not descend but only shone into the darkness, how could it be rightly said that she "inclined"? For if something like light flowed out from her, it is not proper to say she has already inclined. Unless perhaps one part is there and another part is below. But they say she came locally toward it, and having become near <margin>into the...</margin>, she shone. But if she remained in herself and shone, she performed nothing specifically toward the work.

<column-break/>

...because he professes to possess something, he now possesses it: indeed, many, knowing they do not have it, boast that they do, and even though they do not have it, they think they have it, and that they alone possess it, when they are the only ones who do not possess it.

<margin>How much they err who say the world was made by a creator’s error and is evil.</margin>

**A** Many other things besides, or rather all things, anyone discussing them will find easily and abundantly how to show, point by point, the nature of their speech. I cannot help but be affected by shame for the sake of certain friends who, before they entered into friendship with us, fell into speeches of this kind, in which they still somehow persevere; although they are not ashamed,

**B** but they study more intensely so that their opinions may undoubtedly seem true: or they even think the matter is so. We, however, speak only to those we know, and not at all to the many who listen to them; for we would gain nothing by persuasion, trying to convince them not to allow themselves to be perverted by those men, who bring no demonstrations into the open—for by what reason would they prevail?—but boast most stubbornly. Since there is another way in which someone writing might refute them,

**C** who do not fear to mock the most excellent and truest mysteries of the ancient and divine men. Therefore, let us set aside that mode of discussion for the present. For those who have perfectly understood what has just been said will be able to judge clearly what the rest are like. I also set aside for the present that saying which surpasses all in absurdity—if indeed it is appropriate to call this an absurdity: for they say that the Soul and a certain Wisdom inclined to that which is lower, whether the Soul began this inclination <note>original: *nutum*; a nod or downward movement.</note> or Wisdom was the cause of the inclining, or whether they want both to be the same: they say that other souls

**D** descended together, as members of Wisdom, and that they enter bodies like human ones. But they say that she, for whose sake the souls collapsed, did not herself fall, as if she did not incline, but only illuminated the darkness. Then from this, an image resulted in matter: next, they form an image of the image here through matter, or through "materiality," or however they wish to name it, calling this one thing and that another, and devising many other names for the sake of obscurity, since the one who is called the "creator of the world" among them is made in this way. And imagining him revolting from his Mother, they derive the world from him to the extremes of images: so that he who wrote these things might even more bitingly hurl insults.

<margin>XI. He refutes the claim that the illumination from the soul into matter made another soul, and that this soul built the world.</margin>

**F** But indeed, if that Soul did not fall, but illuminated the darkness, how will it be rightly said to have inclined downward? For it is not because something like light flowed out from her that she must now be said to have inclined: unless one thing is positioned below in one way, while she, as if moved from place to place, descended toward it and, having become nearer, illuminated it. If, however, remaining in herself, she poured out

**G** light, she performed nothing more intimately in this: why...

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD II.

<columns>

For why did the soul alone shine forth, and not also those things that are more powerful than the soul in the universal order? If they say that the soul, because it grasped the rational concept of the world within itself, was able to illuminate from that rational discourse: what prevented it from creating the world at the same moment it first illuminated it? Why did it wait any longer for the birth of "images" <note>original: *simulachrorum*; referring to the Gnostic idea that the material world is a mere shadowy reflection of the divine.</note>? Furthermore, this rational concept of the world, which they call the "hospitable and foreign land" <note>original: *terra peregrina hospitalisque*; likely referring to a Gnostic term for a spiritual realm intermediate between the divine and the material</note>—supposedly made by greater beings—hardly forced the creators of the gods to agree. Besides, what is the reason that matter, once illuminated, produces the images of souls rather than the nature of bodies? In truth, an image of the soul seems to need neither darkness nor matter; but if anything is made, the thing made will immediately follow its creator and remain attached to it. Likewise, that which is first infused into matter—is it an essence, or rather (to use their words) an "excogitation" <note>original: *excogitamen*; a mental construct or thought-product</note>? For if it is an essence, what will be the difference between this and that from which it flowed? But if it is another species of soul—if the higher one is rational—perhaps this one is vegetative and generative. If that were so, how could it be true that it was honored for making the world? And how did it create through "audacity" <note>original: *audaciam* / Greek: *tolma*; a technical term in Gnosticism for the 'boldness' or 'presumption' that led to the fall of Wisdom and the creation of the material world</note> and pride? Indeed, the claim that it created through imagination, and even more so through reasoning, is utterly refuted. Why was it necessary for the creator to work from within matter and the image? But if it is said that what is first infused is an "excogitation," one must first explain where such a name comes from; then by what reason it exists, unless it gave the power of creating to this very thought. But how can the power of creation reside in a mere figment? They will surely say that this thing is made first, and another follows. But they say this by their own whim. Why was fire made first, and then the rest?

<margin>
XII.
He refutes the same points and proves the world was made all at once.
</margin>

SIMILARLY, it must be asked by what reason that newly-born image attempts creation through a certain memory of the things it knew before. For there was nothing at all through which it could have known them; nor was that "image" what they call its mother. To this we add that they [the Gnostics] did not descend into this world as mere images of souls, but as true souls; and yet, barely one or at most two of them, moved by the world and recalling themselves to memory, finally recover some small part of what they had seen through contemplation. Is it not, therefore, beyond all wonder that this image—even if, as they say, it does so dimly—nonetheless immediately upon being born "excogitates" the things above? Or even that its mother suspects the same things, she who is a purely material image? And not only does she consider those things and receive a notion of this world and that one, but she even understands from what materials it should be made? From where did she first think to make fire, judging that it must be made first? Why not something else? But if she was able to create from the fact that her notion was marked by "fire," why was it not marked by the "world"? For it was necessary to be marked by the whole first: she made the whole world at once. For in the very thought, the mark of the whole—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But why did she alone shine out, and not the things among beings more powerful than her? And if she was able to shine out from the reasoning process by receiving the rational concept of the world, why did she not make the world at the same time she shone out, but instead waited for the generation of images? Furthermore, the rational concept of the world—which they call the "foreign land," having been made by the greater ones as they <margin>B</margin> themselves say—brought it down into the mind along with the creators. Then how does matter, having been illuminated, produce the images of souls but not the nature of bodies? An image of a soul would have no need of darkness or matter; rather, having been made (if it were made), it would follow the creator itself and remain joined to it. Furthermore, is this an essence, or as they say, an "excogitation" <note>original: *ennōēma*; a thought or conception.</note>? If <margin>C</margin> it is an essence, what is the difference from that from which it came? But if it is another kind of soul—if that one is rational—perhaps this one is vegetative and generative. If this is so, how could it still be honored, or how does it create through "audacity" <note>original: *tolma*</note> and "recklessness"? And in general, the idea of creation through imagination—and still more through reasoning—is <margin>* refuted</margin> refuted. For what does it mean to say the creator produced it out of matter and images? And if it is an "excogitation," first, where does the name come from? Then, how does it exist, unless one gives the power of creating to the thought? But <margin>D</margin> how does the creation belong to the figment? They will say that one thing is first, and another after that. But they speak as if they have the authority to decide. Why was fire first?

**K** How does that which was just born attempt creation by an imitation of what it saw? For it did not exist at all to have seen anything. Furthermore, he himself [the creator], or the mother they give him—if they did not come here into this world as images of souls, <margin>E</margin> but as true souls—yet barely and with difficulty can one or two of them, moved by the world, come into remembrance and barely grasp a perception of what they once saw. But this image—even if dimly, as they say—nonetheless, having just been born, remembers those things? Or even its mother, a material image, not only remembers those things and <margin>* world</margin> gains a concept of that world, but even learns from what it should be made? <margin>F</margin> From where did it think to make fire first, thinking this must be first? Why not another thing? But if it was able to create by thinking of fire, why not by thinking of the world? For it was necessary first to think of the whole world all at once...

</columns>

# BOOK NINE

<sig>S 4</sig>

<margin>
* in fortune and life. <note>original Greek: ἐν τῇ τύχῃ καὶ ζωῇ</note>
</margin>

<columns>

...those things were also sealed within that thought. In this way, it will certainly be judged that the world was produced more naturally. We must not think that it was fabricated in the manner of human craftsmen, since the **arts** are later than both **nature** and the **world**. Indeed, those things which are generated naturally in individual species every day are not produced by first making fire, then the other elements one by one, and finally a mixture of them all. Rather, the entire configuration of the living being—embracing the necessary connection of the members to the whole—comes together in the womb. <note>original: *in menstruis coalescit*; referring to the ancient biological theory that a fetus forms from the union of formative principles and maternal blood.</note> What, then, prevents the matter from being marked with the figure of the entire world within the very order of things? In this figure, earth, fire, and the rest would necessarily have been connected. Perhaps they <note>The Gnostics.</note> would have fathered the world in such a way because they possessed a "better" soul. But the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The "Craftsman" or creator of the physical world.</note> of the world did not know how to make the world in that way—even though he foresaw the great size of the heavens, their certain measure, the slanted arrangement of the zodiac signs, the movements carried out beneath them, and the earth. To foresee all these things so that the <term>rational principle</term> <note>original: *ratio*; the underlying logic or blueprint of a thing.</note> of each part is maintained is not the task of a mere phantom, but rather of some power that proceeds from the highest beings. This is something they themselves will admit, even if unwillingly. For that illumination diffused through the darkness, if carefully examined, will force them to admit the true causes of the world. Why was it necessary to illuminate at all, if it was not entirely necessary? For that necessity was either according to nature or against nature. If it was according to nature, then it was certainly always so; but if it was against nature, and something contrary to nature happened to those higher beings, then undoubtedly **evil** existed before this world. Therefore, this world is not the cause of evils, but the higher realms are the cause of evil to this world; nor does the evil of the soul happen because of this world. Rather, it happens to this world because of the soul. Thus, a rightly running argument will lead this world back to the highest principles. But if they say that **matter** is also the cause of evil, from where did matter come? For the soul, leaning toward the lower realms, saw and illuminated the darkness (as they say) which already existed. From where, then, shall we say the darkness came? If they say the soul brought it forth by leaning downward, it follows that before the soul leaned down, the darkness did not exist; thus the cause of the "leaning" is not in the darkness, but consists in the very nature of the soul. That is nothing other than assigning a cause from preceding necessities; therefore, such a cause is referred back to the very first principles of things.

<column-break/>

<margin>
XIII. Evil does not occur in heaven: and all worldly things are naturally good, although not equally good among themselves; nor are they equal to divine things.
</margin>

WHOEVER, therefore, disparages the nature of the world does not understand what he is doing, nor does he realize where his rash arrogance leads him. Most people err in this because they do not know the perpetual **order** descending from the first things, through the middle, to the third, and so on always down to the extremes. They do not consider that it is improper for the lower to accuse the supreme, or for the supreme to reject those that follow them. Instead, one ought to always obey the nature of the universe with a calm mind and raise oneself toward the higher things, utterly despising those <term>tragic terrors</term> <note>Plotinus is likely mocking the Gnostic fear of the "Archons" or planetary rulers who were thought to imprison the soul.</note> which some people believe are inflicted on mortals from the spheres of the world...

</columns>

<summary>Plotinus argues that the cosmos is a natural, organic byproduct of divine order rather than a botched creation, refuting Gnostic claims that the material world and its creator are inherently evil.</summary>

--- Page 314 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s systematic refutation of the Gnostic cosmogony. In the preceding section, he challenged the idea that the soul "fell" or was "dragged down" to create the world. Here, he examines the logical contradictions in the Gnostic claim that a "simulacrum" or an inferior reflection of the Soul (the Demiurge) created the physical universe through a process of trial, error, or fragmented memory.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD II.

<margin>
XII.
He refutes the same arguments and proves that the world was made all at once.
</margin>

<columns>

For it <note>The soul.</note> only illuminated with soul, but not those things which in the very order of reality are more powerful than the soul. If they <note>The Gnostics.</note> say that the soul, because it contained the rational notion of the world within itself, was able to provide illumination out of that same rational discourse: why then, when it first provided light, did it not simultaneously create the world? Why did it wait for the birth of "images" <note>original: *simulachrorum*; referring to the Gnostic concept of inferior reflections of divine reality.</note> to occur first? Furthermore, this rational notion of the world itself—which they call the "foreign and hospitable land" <note>original: *terra peregrina hospitalisque*; a Gnostic technical term for a middle realm.</note> and say was made by the greater beings—by no means forced the creators to look downward. Moreover, what logic is there by which matter, once illuminated, produces not the nature of physical bodies, but rather the "images" of souls? Indeed, the image of a soul seems to require neither darkness nor matter; but if anything is created, that which is made will immediately follow the creator and remain attached to it. 

Likewise, regarding that which is first infused into matter: is it an essence, or rather—to use their own terminology—a "deliberation" <note>original: *excogitamen*; a thought or mental construct.</note>? For if it is an essence, what will be the difference between this and the source from which it flowed? But if it is another species of soul, then if the higher soul is rational, perhaps this lower one is merely "vegetative and generative" <note>original: *vegetalis atque genitalis*; the lowest level of soul responsible for growth and reproduction.</note>. If this is so, how can it be true that it was honored for having made the world? And how could it have created through "audacity and pride" <note>Gnostic terms for the Demiurge’s motivation.</note>, or through what they call "imagination"—and much more so, how is the claim that it created through "reasoning" thus refuted? Why, again, did the creator need to work from within matter and the image? But if they say that what is first infused is a "deliberation," they must first explain where such a name was derived from, and then by what logic it exists, unless one grants the power of creation to this "deliberation" itself. But how will the power of making reside in such a fiction <note>original: *figmentum*</note>? They will surely say that one thing happens first, and another follows next. Yet they say this by their own whim. Why should fire be created first, and then the rest?

### SIMILARLY, 

it must be asked by what reasoning that recently born "image" approaches the work of creation through a memory of those things it knew before. For it did not exist at all in a state where it could have known them; nor indeed was it that being whom they call its "mother" <note>Sophia, in Gnostic myth.</note>. Add to this the fact that these Gnostics did not descend into this world as mere "images" of souls, but as true souls; and yet scarcely one or at most two of them, moved by the world and calling themselves back into memory, can finally recover some notice of what they had once seen. Is it not therefore beyond measure wonderful that either this "image"—even if, as they say, it is a dim one—nevertheless thinks of heavenly things immediately upon being born; or even that its mother, who is an entirely material image, suspects the same things? Not only to consider those things and receive a notion of this world and that one, but even to comprehend the elements from which the world is made? From where did it first conceive that fire must be made, thinking it necessary to make that first? Why not something else? But if it could create fire because its notion was marked with the form of fire, why was it not marked with the form of the world? For it ought to have been marked with the whole first; it made the whole world at once. For within the deliberation itself, the seal <note>original: *signaculo*; the divine blueprint or impression.</note> of the whole...

<column-break/>

As if she alone shone in; but not those things more powerful than them among the beings. And if, by receiving the reasoning of the world, she was able to illuminate from that reasoning, why did she not create the world at the same time as she illuminated, but instead waited for the generation of the images? Then also the reasoning of the world—what they call the "strange land"—having been made by the greater ones (as they themselves say), did not bring the creators down into the mind. Then how does matter, once enlightened, produce "soul-like images" rather than the nature of bodies? An image of the soul would have no need of darkness or matter. But having come to be, if it were to come to be, it would follow the creative principle, being joined to it. Next, is the <unclear>infused thing</unclear> an essence, or as they say, a "deliberation" <note>original Greek: ἐννόημα (*ennoēma*)</note>? For if it is an essence, what is the difference from that which it came from? But if it is another kind of soul—if that one is rational—perhaps this one is vegetative and generative. If this is so, how could it still be for the sake of being honored, and how could it produce "arrogance and audacity," and in general, that which is through "imagination"? And even more, "reasoning" <margin>*</margin> is ruled out. Why then did the creator still need to produce from matter and images? If it is a "deliberation," first the name must be noted, where it comes from. Then how does it exist, unless one gives "deliberation" the power to create? But how does creation belong to the fiction? That one thing is first, and another after that. But they speak as if they have the authority to say so. Why then is fire first?

AND how does it, having just come to be, attempt [creation]? By memory of what it saw? But it did not exist at all, so that it could see anything. Furthermore, he himself, and the mother they give to him; how can they say this? It is a marvel that not "images" of souls have come here into this world, but true souls, and yet with difficulty and only as a rare blessing can one or two of them be moved by the world, and coming into remembrance, barely receive a perception of what they once saw. But that the "image"—then and dimly, as they say, but even so having just been born—should think of those things! Or even the mother, or that she is those things! And <margin>*</margin> to take a liking for this world because of that world. But also to learn the things from which it would come to be. From where indeed did he first make fire, thinking that this must be first? For why not another? But if he was able to create by thinking of fire, why not by thinking of the world? For he ought first to have thought of the whole, not the world all at once...

<margin>
* in fortune and life <note>original: ἐν τῇ τύχῃ καὶ ζωῇ</note>
</margin>

</columns>

<summary>Plotinus critiques the Gnostic creation myth, arguing that a fragmented or "ignorant" creator could not have fashioned the world element-by-element; instead, the universe must have been created as a complete, rational whole by a higher intelligence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s argument against the Gnostic view of the physical world. In the previous section, he questioned why the soul would create through "images" rather than direct action. Here, he argues that the creation of the world is a natural, unified process—more like a biological development than a craftsman's assembly—and that those who despise the physical world fail to understand its place in the necessary order of existence.</meta>

### BOOK NINE.

->S 4<-

A
it <note>The Soul</note> acted. For those things were also included within the desire. Indeed, it acted in a more natural way <note>original: Φυσικώτερον</note>, and not as the arts do; for the arts are subsequent to Nature and the world. Even now, things that come into being through individual natures do not happen such that first there is fire, and then each thing in succession, and finally a mixing of them all. Rather, there is a sketching and an outlining of the whole living creature, forming it according to what has been grasped.
B
Why then is matter not carved out in a mold? <margin>* in the mold</margin> Within the mold <note>original: τύπῳ</note> is the world—within the mold are the earth, the fire, and all the rest. Perhaps they <note>The Gnostics</note> themselves would have made the world differently, as if they possessed a truer soul than the one that made it! Yet they claim the Maker was ignorant of how to create: ignorant of the rotation and the magnitude, or perhaps even why the zodiac is tilted <margin>* the motion</margin> and why there is a difference <note>original: τὴν διαφορὰν</note> in the movements beneath them.
C
And why the earth is as it is. Yet the causes of why things are so did not come from a mere "image" <note>original: εἰδώλου</note>. Rather, the power absolutely came from those things above, which they <note>The Gnostics</note> themselves admit, even if against their will. For that illumination <note>original: ἔλλαμψις</note> into the darkness, if examined, will force one to admit the true causes of the world. For why did it shine forth an image <margin>* the illumination from below.</margin> if it were not entirely as it ought to be?
D
This necessity was either according to Nature, or toward Nature, or by force. But if it is according to Nature, it is always so. And if it is according to Nature, then that which is "Nature" here also exists among the things there. Therefore, the evils are about this world, and the world itself is not the cause of the evils; rather, the evils belong to it <note>Matter</note>. And they do not come to the soul from here, but are brought here from the soul itself. Thus, reason will lead the way by referring the world back to the first principles. 
E
But if they say matter is also the cause of evil, where does it appear from? If the soul is the one that is "sick," and the darkness already existed, they say <margin>* the illumination is from that [Soul].</margin> that it "shone through" <note>original: μετέλαμψε</note> there. From where, then, did this come? If the soul itself, they say, will make a house for the Intellect <note>original: νοῦ οἶκον</note>, then it is clear that she has looked upward. But if darkness itself is the cause of perception, that is the very nature of the soul. This is the same as the preceding necessities, which refer the cause back to the first principles.

F
**The person who finds fault with the nature of the world does not know what they are doing**, nor where their own boldness is leading them. This happens because they do not know the order of succession: the first, the second, and the third, and so on down to the last. They think they must revile the lower things in favor of the first.
G
Instead, one should gently yield to the nature of all things, while personally hastening toward the first principles, and cease from the "tragedy" of terrors—as they imagine them to be—within the spheres of the world, which indeed...

<column-break/>

A
in that [soul] those things were also sealed. In this way, it will certainly be judged to have acted more naturally. One must not think that it fabricated things in the manner of craftsmen <note>original: artificum more</note>; for the arts are posterior both to Nature and to the world. For those things which are generated naturally in individual species every day do not happen such that fire is made first, then the rest one by one, and finally a mixture of all. Rather, the configuration of the whole living being is formed simultaneously, embracing the necessary connection of members to the whole, coalescing within the womb.
B
What then prevents matter, in the very order of things, from being marked at once with the figure of the whole world? In which figure the earth, fire, and other things were necessarily connected. Perhaps those [Gnostics] would have procreated the world so, as they might have happened upon a better soul. But the Maker of the world <note>original: Faber mundi</note> did not know how to make the world so, even though he foresaw the magnitude of heaven, its certain measure, the oblique texture of the zodiac, and the motions acted under them. He foresaw the earth and all these things so that the reason of each—
C
by which they are so constituted—might be maintained. This is not the task of an "image" <note>original: simulachrum</note>, but rather of some power that proceeds from the best things. Which [the Gnostics] themselves will admit, even if unwillingly. For that illumination diffused through the shadows, if diligently examined, will make them confess the true causes of the world. For why was it necessary to illuminate, if it was not necessary at all?
D
For that necessity was either according to nature or beyond nature. But if it were according to nature, it would certainly be so always. If, however, it were beyond nature, and something beyond nature happened to those higher things, then without a doubt there were evils before this world. Neither is this world the cause of evils, but the higher things are the cause of evil for this world; nor does the evil of the soul happen because of this world, but rather to this world because of the soul. And so, reason running its course rightly will lead this world back to the supreme things.
E
But if they say that matter is also the cause of evil, where did matter come from? For the soul, turning toward the lower things, saw and illuminated the shadows (as they say) which already existed. From where, then, shall we say the shadows came? If they say the soul, by turning toward the lower things, brought them into the open, it follows that before the soul inclined, there were no shadows; and thus the cause of the inclination is not in the shadows, but consists in the very nature of the soul. But that is nothing else than assigning a cause from preceding necessities; therefore, such a cause will be referred back to the very principles of things.

F
<margin>XIII. Evils do not come from heaven: and all worldly things are naturally good, even if they are not equally good among themselves, nor equal to divine things.</margin>
**Therefore, he who disparages the nature of the world is utterly ignorant of what he does**, nor does he understand where his rash arrogance leads him. In this, most people err, because they do not know the perpetual order from the first things through the middle to the third;
G
and so always descending by necessity to the extremes. Nor do they consider that it is not fitting for the lower to accuse the supreme, or to disapprove of what follows the supreme. Rather, one ought to obey the nature of the universe always with an equal mind, and betake oneself to the higher things, utterly scorning the tragic terrors which some [attribute] to mortals from the spheres of the world, in which...

He refutes the Gnostic claim that the world is inherently evil, suggesting instead that any perceived evil arises from the soul's own nature or the necessary descent of being.</summary>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD II.

...strike. Yet these [the celestial bodies] bring all things that are beneficial to mankind. For what do these contain in themselves to be feared, that most men who are unskilled in reason and devoid of instruction and right knowledge should be so terrified? For although the bodies of the spheres <note>The concentric circles carrying the planets and stars in ancient cosmology.</note> are fiery, they are not to be feared, since they are most perfectly suited to the good of the universe and the earth. It is proper, however, to consider their souls; it is by these souls that the stars think themselves to be of great value. Even if their bodies far surpass ours in magnitude and beauty, they contribute to the production and preservation of all things that are born according to nature. Otherwise, as long as these primary things exist, these subsequent things would not be made. Indeed, they fulfill the universe and are the vast members of the whole. 

But if humans are to be honored above other living creatures, how much more so those stars, which are in the world not for the sake of exercising tyranny, but to produce beauty and order. As for the things said to be done by them, one must judge that they are *signified* by them <note>Plotinus argues that stars are like an alphabet—they reveal the future but do not "cause" our misfortunes through malice.</note> rather than *caused* by them. Moreover, the things that happen proceed from differing fortunes. For it is impossible for the same things to happen to everyone, given the differences in the times of birth, the diversity of places, and the vastly different dispositions of their souls. 

Again, it should not be expected that everyone in the world be good; nor, if that is impossible, is it right to suddenly blame the order of the world. Nor should one require that these inferior things differ in no way from the superior ones, nor judge that to be "evil" which is merely less suited to prudence and less good, and so on as we proceed always toward the lesser. It is as if someone were to claim that Nature is "evil" because it is not sensation; and similarly that the sensory world is "evil" because it is not Reason. Otherwise, they would be forced to admit that there are evils among the higher beings as well. For even there, the Soul is inferior to the Mind <note>original: mens / νοῦς (nous)</note>, and the Mind is inferior to another <note>The One, the ultimate source.</note>.

<margin>
**XIIII**
He refutes those who say that higher beings are swayed by a certain sound of words; and that diseases are demons; and that these are expelled by certain words and rituals without virtue.
</margin>

BUT they especially act from this position again: they make the higher beings appear not to be inviolable, because they compose certain chants to move them at will—not only bodies and souls, but even those things superior to them. But what do they actually achieve through these? They will answer that they compose spells <note>original: fascinationes</note>, charms, and persuasions, so that the higher beings might hear the words and be drawn down. This assumes one of us knows how to pronounce such things with great art, and to produce songs and sounds in a certain way, along with breathings of the voice, and whistlings <note>original: sibila</note>, and whatever else they have written that supposedly contains magical power. 

But if they do not wish to say this, but rather that their voices signify certain incorporeal things, it follows that while they wish to make their art seem more honorable, they meanwhile—though they may not notice—strip away their own glory. Furthermore, they boast that they expel diseases. If they promised to do this through temperance and a right rule of life, they would certainly speak rightly and in the manner of philosophers. But now, when they say that diseases are demons <note>original: dæmones / δαιμόνια (daimonia)</note>, and claim to expel them with words, and broadcast this profession, they might appear impressive to the common...

<column-break/>

...do <note>The Greek text here mirrors the Latin defense of the cosmos.</note> most of all those things which they have, or which they possess that is fearsome, so that those unskilled in logic and uneducated in hearing and harmonious knowledge are afraid. And even if their bodies are fiery, they should not be feared, for they are in proportion to the whole and to the earth. But if one looks <margin>* to look.</margin> at their souls, by which they themselves are surely worthy of honor. Yet even their bodies differ in magnitude and beauty, cooperating and working together with things that come to be according to nature. These things would never happen if the primary things were not there, which fulfill the whole and are great parts of the total universe. 

If humans are honorable (for why else mention other animals?), how much more so these stars? They do not exist in the universe for the sake of tyranny, but provide beauty and order. Those things said to happen by them should be considered signs of what is to be; for things happen by differing fortunes. It is not possible for the same things to happen to each person, both because of the times of birth, and places far removed, and the dispositions of souls. <margin>* unrequested / necessary.</margin> And <margin>* ceases.</margin> one must not demand <margin>* shines forth.</margin> that all things be good; for since this is not possible, it is fitting to find fault, again demanding that those things [below] differ in no way from those [above]. And one should not consider "evil" to be anything other than that which is more deficient in wisdom, and a lesser good. And always moving toward the smaller. Just as if one were to say Nature is "evil" because it is not sensation; or the sensory is evil because it is not reason. If not, they will be forced to say there are evils even there [above]. For even there, Soul is worse than Mind. And in the other, it is less.

BUT they do this especially in another way, making the things there [the heavens] not pure. For when they write incantations, speaking as if to those beings—not only to the soul, but to the things above—what are they doing? They speak of sorceries and charms and persuasions; that the beings obey a word and are led, as if one of us were more skilled in speaking these things or those, or in a certain tone and sound, and in breathings and <margin>* hissings of the voice.</margin> whistlings of the voice, and all the other things written there to work magic. 

But if they do not wish to say it is by the speaking, then how do voices affect the incorporeal? In their attempt to make their words appear more solemn, they have unknowingly stripped those beings of their dignity. And next, speaking of disease <margin>* diseases</margin>, they say they can expel them. If they said they did this by temperance and a disciplined life, they would speak correctly, just as the philosophers speak. But now, having posited that diseases are demons, and claiming to be able to remove them by a word, and announcing this, they might seem to be solemn-faced...

### THAT which especially must not escape our notice is what these words do to the souls of those who hear them, teaching them to despise the world and the things within it.

For there are two choices regarding the attainment of the "end" <note>The *telos* or ultimate goal of life.</note>: one which places the end in the pleasure of the body, and another which chooses beauty and virtue, which must be said to come from God and lead back to God.

<margin>\* as if by which desire is suspended.</margin>

A are held as more excellent. For the common sort are accustomed to admire the powers of magicians too much; however, to prudent men they would never persuade that human diseases do not have causes: namely, proceeding from labor, or satiety, or indigence, or a certain putrefaction, and in short, arising from certain changes either internal or external. The very cures of these diseases declare this to us; for by a flux of the belly and by medicines, the disease is usually led out through the lower parts.

B Furthermore, by bloodletting and fasting, a person is often cured. Perhaps the demon is then hungry, and the medicine so acts that the demon liquefies and wastes away. If, however, it has gone out, what was the cause? For what did the demon itself suffer? Was it perhaps because it was being nourished by the disease? Therefore, the disease was something other than the demon itself.

C Moreover, if the demon enters even when no cause exists, why is the person not always sick? But if it enters only when a cause is present: why is a demon needed for the sickness? For the cause itself is sufficient to kindle a fever. Truly, it is ridiculous that when a cause first happens, a demon is suddenly present as if diligently prepared for it. However, in what way and for whose sake such things are boasted by them, we have sufficiently understood. For no less than for the sake of the other, we have just made

It does not follow empty boasting, but the dignity of elegance. Furthermore, it contains spiritedness with reason, safe caution, and circumspect providence. But with religion prepared for this, it appears conversely that the other [doctrines] are entirely contrary in every part. For nothing further can be said. It seems fitting for us to speak of them in this way.

### E IN the first place, however, it must not be hidden from us what their speeches produce in the minds of those who hear them, persuading them to despise the world and the things that are in it.

<margin>XV. How harmful to morals is the opinion that disparages the whole nature of the world, and life, and whatever is produced in the world or even done by men.</margin>
There is indeed a double choice and sect concerning the "end": one indeed places the end in the pleasure of the body, the other truly prefers honesty and virtue—the desire for which depends upon God and is referred back to God. And in what way

F that may be done must be contemplated elsewhere. Epicurus indeed, when he had taken away providence, commanded to follow pleasure and delights, which is what remained. But the speech of the Gnostics <note>original: "Gnosticorum"; followers of a diverse religious movement that often viewed the material world as evil.</note>, even more insolently, blames the lordship and authority proper to providence, and providence itself. And stripping of honor all the laws which are here, and virtue which has been approved for many ages,

G and thinking temperance to be ridiculous, so that nothing of the good may appear to be among us, it extirpates temperance, and the justice implanted in our morals which is to be acquired by reason and exercise.

...and absolutely every path by which one might attain virtue: so much so that nothing else remains for them but to pursue pleasure <note>Plotinus accuses the Gnostics of hedonism because their philosophy rejected the "goodness" of the physical world’s laws.</note>, to attend only to their own affairs, and, having abandoned the fellowship of the human race, to study only their own advantage—unless, perhaps, someone is by his own nature better than such teachings. For of those things which are judged good and honorable among us, nothing is considered good among them, but rather something else, whatever it is they may occasionally pursue. Yet it was proper for those who have already known [the divine] to pursue it from this point forward, and as they follow, to first set right these matters of ours, approaching them from their divine nature. For it belongs only to that nature which neglects the pleasure of the body to understand what is truly good and honorable. Those who are entirely devoid of virtue can in no way approach the things above. This is further evidenced by the fact that they make no mention of virtue, and they entirely omit all discourse regarding those things that pertain to virtue. They do not strive to define what virtue or the "good" is, or how many types there are, nor any of the many noble things contained in the discussions of the ancients <note>Referring to Plato and the Stoics, who emphasized the cultivation of character.</note>. Nor, again, do they discuss the means by which the good is acquired and possessed, nor how the soul is cultivated and purified. For to simply say, "Look toward God," is of no use at all, unless they clearly teach the manner in which one is to look. For someone might say that nothing prevents a person from looking, yet abstaining from no pleasure, nor restraining his anger—mentioning only the name of God while remaining a slave to all passions and making no effort to repel them. Virtue, certainly, when acquired through wisdom and progressed to the highest point, reveals God to us; but if someone speaks of God without true virtue, he possesses nothing but a name.

XVI
Those who say that no [good] rules in the bodies of the world, and say "look to God," they overturn the order of the universe and deprive themselves of the means by which they could more easily reach higher things.
</margin>

**LET NO ONE** think he has become good from the mere fact that he despises the world, and the gods who rule in the world, and the other good and noble things of the world. Indeed, every evil man possesses this trait first of all: he despises the gods. No one is ever fully evil until he despises those above. And if he is not yet evil in all other things, he becomes excessively evil through this one thing alone. Therefore, their claim that they worship the "intelligible gods" <note>original: "deos intelligibiles"; in Neoplatonism, these are the pure forms or divine intellects existing above the physical world.</note> has nothing consistent or kindred about it. For he who loves anything also pursues with affection whatever is kindred to that which he loves. For you also love the children if you love the father. Every soul, indeed, is a daughter of that Father. And the souls in the spheres of the world are intellectual and good, and far more kindred to the things above than our own souls are. For how could this world be separated from that one, or how could the gods who are in the world be separated? But we have spoken of these things in earlier sections. Now, however, it must be affirmed that those who despise the kindred of the higher powers do not even know those powers themselves, but only grasp them in words. Furthermore, when they say that providence does not reach to all these things, or even to anything at all, how can this be pious? Likewise, how is it consistent with their own views? <summary>Plotinus argues that the Gnostics' rejection of physical world ethics and their claim to "look to God" without practicing virtue is hypocritical and logically inconsistent. He asserts that true divinity is found through cultivating virtue and respecting the cosmic order, which is a "child" of the divine Father.</summary>

the land of the living? <note>Original: terra viuentiū. This refers to the Gnostic "New Earth" or spiritual realm.</note> If there, how did they descend? But if they are also here, how are they still in that land? Again, why would God not be here as well? For from where will he know that they are here? And how has he found it to be true that those living here, failing and departing from him, have become evil? For if he knows minds not yet evil, he surely also perceives those already made evil, so that he may be able to discern these from those. Therefore, he will be present to all things: and he will be in this world, in whatever way he may be present. For this reason, the world will be a participant in him. But if he is absent from the world, he will also be absent from you: and you will be able to speak nothing either of him or of those things which are after him. But whether some providence favors you from that place, or whatever you wish, certainly this world also possesses it from there in like manner, and it is neither forsaken by God, nor will it ever be forsaken. For God has care for the whole much more than for the parts: and the whole is a participant in divinity more than a part of the world. And indeed, the soul of the universe is cared for and adorned by God even more. This demonstrates that the world is, and that it exists wisely. And who among those who are foolishly proud is as orderly and wise as the universe? Indeed, it is altogether ridiculous: it is an absurdity to bring these into comparison. And whoever compares them otherwise than for the sake of argument cannot be free from impiety. Truly, to doubt these things is by no means the mark of a prudent man, but rather of one who is blind, and who possesses neither sense nor mind, and is removed far from the knowledge of the intelligible world itself, since he does not see this world at all. For what man will be a musician, who, when he has grasped the intelligible harmony, is not then moved when he perceives harmony resonating in voices? Or who is skilled in geometry and numbers, who, when he beholds a spectacle composed with fitting proportion, is not greatly delighted? For they by no means look upon the same things in the same way, even in the descriptions and pictures themselves, as those who look through artistic eyes. But they perceive a certain imitation in that which is sensed of that which is placed in the intelligence. Therefore, they are as if stunned, and are called back to the memory of the truth. From which affection, moreover, loves arise. But truly, he who perceives beauty shining more fitly in a face is elevated to the intelligible. That man, therefore, would be of a completely sluggish mind: nor would he ever be incited toward anything else. Whoever, seeing all the magnificent spectacles in this world, and the absolute order composed from the perfect proportion of measures, and the species wonderfully shining in the stars however far remote, would not behold them here with the most intent admiration, and worship them, admiring what kind of things proceed from what kind of [sources]. Otherwise, he has neither considered these things, nor known those.

**XVII**
Above the corporeal world is the world of the soul, which is mobile in a certain way, possessing the dimensions of bodies by the magnitude of its power: and producing this world by the very stability of its power, and being most beautiful itself, it produces the beautiful.

He mocks the Gnostics for their contempt of the universe, pointing out that a true sage recognizes divine harmony in music, geometry, and the stars.</summary>

...should not be imagined through opinions that lead to a separation from the intelligible realm <note>original: "κατὰ τὸ νοητὸν εἰς διάστασιν"</note>, as if the magnitude produced here could ever be equal in power to the indivisible realm there through our ignorance. For greatness in the divine realm consists of power, but here it consists of physical bulk. And whether they wish to conceive of this celestial sphere as moving—being led around by the power of God, who holds the beginning, middle, and end of the whole—or as standing still as some say, while governing something else, it would be well for their understanding. As for this universe being governed by a Soul, those who do not yet recognize its body <note>meaning the physical universe as the "body" of the World Soul</note>—which suffers nothing itself but grants existence to others—should realize it is not lawful for envy to exist among the gods. Thus, the Soul can hold and receive each part of the world. Let one consider the world itself: it was made equal throughout by the power of the World Soul, which made the nature of the body as beautiful as it was capable of being. It participates in beauty, and this beauty moves souls that are divine. Unless, of course, they were to claim their souls are not moved by it, and that they do not see any difference between ugly and beautiful bodies. But if that were true, they would also see no difference between ugly and beautiful behaviors, or between beautiful studies and theories. And they would not know God. For if they do not know these lower beauties, they cannot know the higher ones. For these earthly beauties exist after the divine ones. But when they say they despise the beauty found here, they would do well to despise only the beauty in boys and women, so as not to fall into lack of self-control. One must realize, however, that they should not be proud of despising what is ugly, but rather they show their pride by claiming to despise what they previously admitted was beautiful. And how can they turn away from it?

<margin>In part vs. the whole, and in each vs. the all.</margin>
Furthermore, beauty exists within the thing itself. <margin>already parts and wholly and in each and in each and in the all.</margin> If there are such beauties even in sensible things, and in those things that are not merely parts—such as the nature of spirits <note>original: "δαιμόνων" (daemons)</note>—how can they not admire the one who made them? How can they deny these things come from there? It is impossible to speak of the beauty there if you are completely detached from these things. Rather, one must go from these beauties to those. One should not insult the physical world. And if the internal forms are beautiful, we should say they are in harmony with one another.

<margin>Plotinus <note>original: "πλατῖ@"</note></margin>
But if the internal things are foul, how could the external things be better? <note>In Plotinian thought, the external is a reflection of the internal; a beautiful body must reflect a beautiful source.</note> It is never the case that the external is truly beautiful while the internal is ugly. For the external is beautiful only because the internal form has mastered the matter. Those who are called beautiful in appearance but are foul within have only a false external beauty. If someone claims to have seen a person who was truly beautiful in body but ugly within, I believe that person did not truly see <margin>himself <note>original: "αὐτὸς"</note></margin> but only thought the other was beautiful. Or if they truly were beautiful, then the foulness must have been an added corruption to a nature that was originally beautiful. For there are many obstacles here that prevent us from reaching our goal, both for individuals and the whole...

<column-break/>

->A<- ...giving [the soul] a distance under the intelligible reason <note>original: "ratione intelligibili"</note>, and leading it into extension: so that from the magnitude of that which is produced, an equalization to the indivisible reason of the exemplar might be made according to its strength. For that which is great there in power, here comes forth great in physical bulk. And whether they wish to consider this very sphere as being in motion—being led around by divine power, which contains the beginning, middle, and end of the whole sphere—or as standing still, as if governing something else like a central knot, they will certainly approach rightly ->B<- to the understanding of the Soul which governs the world. And if they then connect a body to the Soul—not in such a way that the Soul suffers anything, but rather that it bestows something upon another—they will be judged to think quite rightly about the world; for it is a sin to believe envy exists among the gods. This allows individual things to receive from that source according to their capacity. One should contemplate the immense power in the ->C<- World Soul, because it makes the nature of the body (which is not beautiful by itself) a participant in beauty according to the body's capacity. This beauty indeed draws souls to itself as if they were divine. Unless perhaps they say their own minds are not at all stirred by this, nor do they look upon ugly and beautiful bodies with any different reasoning. But if that is admitted, it follows also that they are not differently affected toward foul or honorable actions. They would not prefer beautiful doctrines to others, nor contemplation itself, nor even God himself. For these things are good or beautiful because of the primary things. ->D<- If therefore these earthly things are not good or beautiful, we must conclude that the divine things are not good or beautiful either, since these are judged to be good or beautiful because they follow those. Accordingly, whenever they say they care nothing for this beauty, if they mean they despise the form in boys and women so as not to obey lust, they do indeed act rightly. Nevertheless, it should not escape us that they are by no means to be praised for merely despising something ugly. Rather, they take pride in this very thing: that they scorn what they had previously conceded to be beautiful, and which they were once affected by. Furthermore, the beauty in the part is not the same as in the whole, or in the universe. Finally, many things are so beautiful even in the things we sense—in specific parts and objects, such as in the order of spirits <note>original: "dæmonum"</note>—that we often greatly admire the Author from these, and easily believe these were made by him. And from here ->F<- we can praise the inestimable beauty of the Author. If only we are not ensnared by these things, but fly from these to those, and do not disparage these works of his. Indeed, if the interior things are beautiful like the exterior, we must affirm that they agree with each other. But if the internal things are evil, then the beauty must have been diminished by better things. But certainly it cannot happen that what is truly beautiful on the outside is deformed on the inside. For what is entirely beautiful on the outside is made so by the interior form ->G<- overcoming the material. Those who are said to be beautiful in appearance, yet foul within, possess only a false external beauty. But if anyone objects that they have seen people beautiful in body but foul in soul, I truly think they have not seen [true beauty], but only imagined others to be beautiful. Or if they did see it, I maintain that the foulness was something added later to those who were beautiful by nature. For there are many impediments among us to attaining our goal. But for the whole world...

<summary>Plotinus argues that physical beauty is a reflection of divine power and that the Gnostics' rejection of the world's beauty is logically inconsistent with their claim to love divine beauty. He explains that "size" in the divine realm is power, whereas in the material world it is physical bulk.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s critique of the Gnostic worldview. Having previously established that the physical world is a reflection of the divine, he now argues that the universe was created perfect from the start and that true wisdom lies in respecting the "World Soul" rather than despising the material "house" we inhabit.</meta>

# BOOK NINE.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Since the world is most beautiful to behold, what could have possibly hindered it from being beautiful on the inside as well? Indeed, for those to whom nature did not grant perfection from the beginning, it might happen that they never reach their end, and thus they could be found to be base or flawed. But for the Universe, it was never like a child—imperfect or incomplete. As it progressed and its body was formed, where would any new addition come from? For it already possessed all things. Nor can one imagine anything being added to its soul later. Even if one were to grant the Gnostics <note>The "Gnostics" were a religious-philosophical group Plotinus critiqued for believing the material world was evil or a mistake.</note> this point, they cannot allow for any evil to be admitted into it.

<margin>B</margin> **XVIII**
<margin>It is not right to disparage the worldly craftsmanship and its creator; nor should one flee from here. It is possible both to preserve such things and also to remain moderate. It is also given to reach the worldly life of the soul and its own happiness.</margin>

<margin>C</margin> Perhaps they will say that their teachings cause one to flee from association with the body and to hold it in utter hatred, while our teachings hold the soul down within the body. This is much like two people living in the same beautiful house: one of them disparages the structure, the equipment, and the builder <note>original: "vituperet... domicilij fabrum"</note>, yet remains living there nonetheless; the other does not disparage it at all, but says the builder has constructed it with the greatest skill. This second person waits for the time to come when he shall depart, as he will no longer need a dwelling. The first person might think himself wiser and more ready to leave because he knows how to say that the building is made only of lifeless stones and timber, and that he is far removed from the true dwelling—yet he ignores the fact that the real difference lies in bearing necessities with grace rather than complaining. As long as we have bodies, we must remain in these dwellings built for us by our "sister," the good Soul <note>Plotinus refers to the World Soul (Anima Mundi) as a "sister" to the individual human soul, as both originate from the same divine source.</note>, who possesses the great power to create without labor. 

<margin>D</margin> But is it not strange that these men deign to call even the most wicked people "brothers," yet they utterly refuse to call the Sun and the other heavenly bodies their brothers? <note>original: "Solem verò... fratres penitus dedignantur"</note> With an insane mouth, they even exclude the Soul of the entire world from their "fraternal" fellowship. 

<margin>E</margin> Surely, as long as we are base, it is a sacrilege to claim kinship with the divine beings above. But when we become good, we are no longer merely bodies, but souls dwelling in bodies—and we are able to dwell in them in a way that closely approaches how the World Soul inhabits the entire body of the universe. This means not being cast down from one’s own rank, not indulging in external allurements, and not being broken by hardships. 

<margin>F</margin> That World Soul is never struck, for there is nothing from which she can be struck. But we, living here, can use virtue to repel the blows. Through greatness of mind and strength, some blows become lighter, while others do not touch us at all. When we have come close to that which cannot be struck, we then imitate the Soul of the world and of the stars. 

<margin>G</margin> Once we have achieved this close resemblance, we shall finally move in harmony with the divine. Then the same sights will be offered to us that have been present to the higher beings from the beginning, and which are not lacking for us, provided we are well-ordered by nature and prepared by study. If any boast that they alone—

<summary>In this passage, Plotinus argues that the physical world's beauty is a reflection of divine power and that the World Soul governs the universe without being corrupted. He critiques the Gnostics for claiming to love God while despising the beauty of His creation, asserting that true external beauty must reflect an internal, spiritual order.</summary>
