<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s polemic against the Gnostics (a group he viewed as overly pessimistic about the physical world). On the previous page, he argued that the beauty of the universe reflects a divine origin; here, he contrasts the Gnostic "hatred" of the body with a more balanced, philosophical approach to living in the material world.</meta>

# BOOK NINE.

<column-break/>

A Since it is a thing of beauty, what could have hindered it from being beautiful within as well as without? Furthermore, for those things to whom nature did not grant perfection from the beginning, it might happen that they never reach their end. Thus, they might become base. But for the Universe, it was never a "child" or incomplete; nor did anything new grow into it as it progressed, nor was anything added to its body. For from where could it come? It already possessed all things. B Nor could anyone imagine anything being added to its soul. Even if one were to grant this to the Gnostics <note>The "Gnostics" (from the Greek *gnosis*, meaning knowledge) were a diverse group of early thinkers who often taught that the material world was a flawed or evil creation of a lesser god.</note>, it would certainly not be anything evil.

<margin>* That one</margin> **B**UT perhaps they will say that *that* argument [their own] flees the body, which they view with long-standing hatred, while our arguments hold the soul down to it. This is very much as if two people were living in the same beautiful house. One of them might C criticize the construction and the builder, yet remain in it nonetheless. The other does not criticize, but says the builder of the residence has constructed it with the greatest skill; he simply waits for the time to come when he may depart and no longer require a house. The former might think himself wiser and readier to leave because he knows how to say that the walls consist of soulless stones and wood, and that he is far removed from the true D dwelling. He ignores the fact that the difference lies in whether one bears the necessary things with grace or not; for he does not choose to be bothered by the building, as he moderately loves the beauty of the stones. We must surely remain in our dwellings while we have a body, which was built by a sister Soul—a good one—who possesses great power to create without labor. Or do those men [the Gnostics] deign to call even the basest of people "brothers," yet E disdain to call the Sun and the other heavenly bodies "brothers"? Do they, with a truly insane mouth, separate the Soul of the whole world <note>term: World Soul (Anima Mundi). In Neoplatonism, this is the animating principle of the entire universe, connecting the divine realm to the physical one.</term> from their brotherly fellowship? Indeed, as long as we are base, it is a sacrilege to join ourselves in kinship with the higher beings; but once we become good, we are no longer merely bodies, but souls dwelling in bodies, able to inhabit them in a way that F <margin>* The small thing</margin> comes as close as possible to the way the World Soul inhabits the whole body. This means not being cast down from one’s rank, nor indulging in external allurements, nor being broken by hardships. That Soul [the World Soul] is not struck by such things, for there is nothing to strike her. We, however, living here, can repel blows through virtue, so that by greatness of mind and strength, some blows become lighter and others do not touch us at all. When we have come close to that which cannot be struck, we shall finally imitate G the Soul of the universe and of the stars. Likewise, when we have attained a close likeness, we shall finally move in harmony with it. Then, the same spectacles will be offered to us which are present to the higher beings from the start, and which are not lacking for us, provided we are well-ordered by nature and prepared by study. But if some men boast that they alone—

<column-break/>

A Since the appearance is most beautiful, what hindrance could there have been for it to be beautiful on the inside as well? Then truly, for those things to whom nature did not give perfection from the beginning, it perhaps happens that they do not reach the end at all: and therefore they can become depraved. But it did not happen to the world that it was at some time a boy, as it were, and not yet perfect: nor did anything new coalesce into the world as it progressed further, nor was anything added to its body. For from whence could that have happened? Since it already B possessed all things. Nor is it permitted to imagine anything added to its soul. And if perhaps someone grants this to the Gnostics, it will still not be permitted to admit it into anything [evil].

<margin>XVIII
It is not fitting to blame the worldly craftsmanship and its maker; nor to depart from here. One must bear the usual things and, moreover, be moderate. It is granted also to reach the life of the World Soul and its blessedness.</margin> **T**HEY will say perhaps in their speeches that it is brought about that the commerce of the body is to be fled, and held in utter hatred: while our speeches detain the soul in the body. But this is very similar to two people inhabiting the same beautiful house: and one indeed C blames the constitution and the apparatus of the house and its author, but nevertheless remains there; while the other by no means blames it, but says the builder of the domicile constructed it most skillfully. He waits for the time as long as he inhabits it, when he is to depart from there: as one who then no longer requires the dwelling. The latter seems wiser and readier for the exit D for this reason, that he knows how to say the building is constructed from inanimate stones and wood, and that he is far from the building. He is ignorant that it matters most whether one tolerates necessary things, or bears them not at all: since he will not depart with trouble from the building which he thinks beautiful, if he loves the beauty of the stones moderately. One must surely remain while we have a body in the domiciles which were fabricated by our sister Soul, a good one, having the greatest power through which she fabricates without labor. Or do those men deign to call even the most wicked men brothers daily, but E utterly disdain to call the Sun and the other heavenly bodies brothers? Indeed, with a truly insane mouth, they segregate the Soul of the whole world from brotherly fellowship. And surely as long as we are base, it is a crime for us to join in affinity with the higher beings: but then finally when we are good, we are not bodies, but souls in bodies, and thus able to dwell in them so that we come as close as possible to that manner of dwelling by which the World Soul inhabits the whole body. That is, not to be F cast down from one’s step, nor to indulge in external allurements, nor to be broken by hardships. That Soul indeed is not struck, nor is there anything from which she might be struck. We, however, dwelling here, can repel blows by virtue, so that by greatness of soul and strength, some blows become lighter, others truly do not touch us at all. But when we have come close to that which cannot be struck, then finally we shall imitate the Soul of the G world and of the stars. Likewise, when we have attained the closest likeness, we shall finally harmonize in the same thing. Then indeed the same spectacles will be offered to us, which are present to the higher beings from the beginning, and are not lacking to us, namely, to those well-instituted by nature and prepared by study. But if some boast that they alone—

...they might be able to contemplate divine things, they possess no greater capacity for contemplation because of this. Nor should they boast that they will depart from their bodies at death, while claiming that the souls governing the world forever are never permitted to do so. For they say these things out of a certain ignorance, not knowing what is meant by "outside" <note>Plotinus is refuting the Gnostic idea that the soul is "trapped" inside the world; he argues the soul contains the world, rather than being contained by it</note>, and being unaware of how the total Soul of the universe governs that which is inanimate. Therefore, a faculty has been given to us so that we might not indulge the body, but instead become pure at some point. Let us despise death: let us understand higher things and follow the objects of the intellect. Let us never envy others who are able to follow, and who do follow always, nor should we disparage them as if they were unable. Let us never suffer the same delusion as those who think the stars do not move simply because their senses report them to be at rest. For this reason, they themselves do not believe the nature of the stars looks upon things "outside," because they do not see the soul of the stars existing externally.

<column-break/>

...easier to contemplate, they would have a greater power of contemplation. But as for their claim that it is possible for them to depart when they die, but not for those souls who will always adorn the world—this is because they are ignorant of what the "outside" truly is. Or rather, they do not understand the manner in which the Soul of the whole cares for it, or how it governs the inanimate as a whole. It is not for us to be lovers of the body, but to become pure, to despise death, to know better things, and to pursue them. And we should not envy those others who are able to pursue them and do so always, as if they were not pursuing them. Nor should we fall into the same trap as those who think the stars do not run their course because their senses tell them they are standing still. For this reason, they do not think the nature of the stars sees what is outside, because they do not see the soul of the stars being on the outside.

# MARSILIO FICINO’S COMMENTARY ON THE FIRST BOOK OF THE THIRD ENNEAD, CONCERNING FATE.

## SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

### Concerning eternal things and their action: Concerning the causes of things that happen: Concerning four opinions regarding fate.

<margin>✳</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring classical scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>
**I**n the order of things, some things merely *are*, while others *become*. Likewise, those things which only *are* are either principles themselves or derived from principles. Furthermore, of the things that exist, they either happen always or at a specific time. Those things which are primary, insofar as they are primary, cannot be referred back to other causes. For that which is simply first simply has no cause. But that which is first within a certain category has no cause within that category. Thus, in the category of moving things, that which is moved by itself, since it is the primary mover, has no higher cause for its being mobile; however, it does have a cause for its being intellectual. Similarly, the primary Intellect <term>Intellectus: the second hypostasis in Neoplatonism, representing the realm of pure thought and Forms</term> does not properly have its intellect through a higher cause, but it possesses its existence as a "One" and a "Good" from a higher cause. The Good itself, however, possesses nothing from any cause.

Therefore, those things which exist among the eternal by means of a cause have their essence from that cause, and their action accompanies that being perpetually. This action (to speak according to Plotinus's view) is the same there as "being." To be sure, where action passes outside of the thing, it is undoubtedly different from "being." Likewise, where an action that remains inside proceeds from an "added form" <note>original: "aduentitia forma" - a quality or characteristic that is not part of the thing's basic definition</note>, it is also different from "being." But where it is both internal and perpetual, and arises solely from the essential form, it is certainly the same as "being," or at least what we call "existing." For the same form comes from it and resides in it; thus, that from which it comes and in which it stays is the same as "being."

So, the act of heating proceeding from fire into water is undoubtedly different from the "being" of fire. Again, the heat in glowing iron is different from the "being" of iron, because it comes from an added form. But in fire, being hot is nothing other than being fire. Since, therefore, in purely eternal substances there is no added form, the "acting" arises from the same natural form as the "being," and so closely that acting is rightly the same as being. For we say that "being" is the act of essence and of essential form. This act is internal, and an entirely internal action. For this reason, since life in the soul is not an added form, living is the being of the soul. Similarly, in the Intellect itself, "understanding"—shining naturally from the intellectual form—is the very being of the Intellect; especially since intellection is the primary action. Therefore, since it is most perfect and internal, it does not differ from being.

The Platonists <note>The "Platonists" here refers to the Neoplatonic school, which followed Plotinus’s interpretations of Plato</note> certainly place this first; they do not place "action" properly within the Good itself, since all action is directed *toward* the Good. So much for those things which properly *are*, which we wish to be neither under fate nor in fate. But those things which *become*, if they become at a specific time, we consider subject to fate. If they happen always—that is, if they revolve perpetually—we place them not so much *under* fate as *in* fate. In short, we must refer every action situated in any kind of motion, as something not entirely perfect, back to a cause, and ultimately to a cause that is permanent. Regarding that which is moved by another, there is no doubt that its motion and action proceed from another. Furthermore, that which is moved by itself (that is, by its own nature), has its mobile action by its own nature; but it receives the fact that it acts simply and that it *is* from elsewhere. For a mobile action, being more imperfect than a stable one, signifies that the essence in which it exists proceeds from another. And an action of this kind is governed by a certain stable power of that same essence. Indeed, since motion is like a certain indeterminate and unworthy accident, suffering an admixture of deprivation and dispersion, it is rightly dependent [on a cause]. Therefore, from the subject in which it exists, and the efficient power from which it is produced, and the end for the sake of which it happens, and a certain occasion*

<summary>Plotinus concludes his critique of Gnostic pessimism by defending the Soul's governance of the world, while Ficino introduces a new book on Fate, distinguishing between eternal "Being" and temporal "Becoming."</summary>

The previous page concluded the polemic against the Gnostics; here, Ficino transitions into a systematic analysis of causality, necessity, and the various philosophical schools' views on fate.</meta>

[page 219]

->ON BOOK I. ENNEAD III.<-

...depends on what incites it. Therefore, let no one dream of some sort of "swerve" or incursion of atoms, or a sudden motion of any body, or a similar inclination of the soul that depends on no cause as having given a beginning to things. Instead, one should consider every action or passion of this kind to be produced by some higher cause, or even incited by surrounding circumstances. Since, therefore, whatever happens at any time happens because of causes, we possess near and manifest causes in most cases. But where the near causes are not clear enough, or are not sufficient to produce the effect, we rightly investigate more remote causes—especially when, under the same imminent near cause, an effect follows in one person but not in another, or when similar outcomes do not result from similar human works. Likewise, we look further when fortune and the coincidence of events favor someone beyond the merit of their actions, or the opposite. Finally, the great diversity of talents, characters, and fortunes—which cannot be so vast based only on causes known to us—compels us to track down more hidden and superior causes. In the investigation of these hidden causes, the "opinion of fate" arose among philosophers. They define fate, by a certain common notion, as a certain necessity brought upon things from above. Since there are four primary opinions regarding the principles of things, there are likewise four opinions concerning fate. For some have found that necessity is brought upon things by certain bodies which they take to be the principles of all things: whether it be from the collisions of atoms, as Democritus held, or whether it is brought in from the natures and motions of certain other bodies, as they say was pleasing to Thales, Anaximenes, and Anaximander. Others think a principle of life has been infused into all things, by which individual things are moved everywhere by the necessity of fate; this is what some Stoics <note>The Stoics believed in a "World Soul" or *pneuma* that dictated the deterministic chain of events.</note> maintained. There are also those who think the principle and fate of things lie within the celestial revolution of the stars. Nor is there a lack of physicists and metaphysicians who think that individual events happen daily because of a certain series and connection of all causes with one another—whether celestial, superior, or again, inferior. From this, they believe fate hangs over all things, whether such a heap of causes has a single beginning or not.

### *That not all things are forced or made by bodies; and that there is neither fate nor perhaps any foreknowledge if the principles of things were contingent.*

III. We have sufficiently shown in our *Theology* <note>original: "Theologia"; referring to Ficino's own work, *Platonic Theology*.</note> that the nature of bodies proceeds from an incorporeal cause, and ultimately all things from one cause that provides for everything. Again, we proved in our *Book on Love* <note>Ficino's *De Amore*, a commentary on Plato's *Symposium*.</note> that the common beauty of bodies consists in order, proportion, and appearance, and that these three, along with beauty itself, are something non-physical. Democritus himself admits that the motion of atoms lacks order. Thus, he cannot easily produce the supreme order of the universe from things that are themselves inferior to order, nor could he keep it going forever. Furthermore, it is clear that the mass of all bodies, insofar as it is physical, does not preserve order by itself, because order, proportion, appearance, and beauty in the very mass of the world are more excellent than the mass itself, and are, moreover, non-physical. For this reason, they are propagated into the body by a more excellent, non-physical, rational, and living nature. And that which is closest is the Soul, the mover of bodies, as well as the Mind and the Good itself, which is the beginning and end of the universe. Therefore, order itself and the Reason <note>original: "ratio"; can also mean "rational principle" or "plan."</note> from which it comes, and the Soul in which Reason exists, do not follow bodies but precede them. Now, whoever deduces all things from the disordered motion of bodies cannot bring a fatal necessity to things. Indeed, to introduce a contingency devoid of order into the principles of things is nothing other than to exclude fate from things entirely. For in that case, no thing at all will come forth in a determined or necessary way if there is no order from which one thing follows another in sequence. But as it stands, what fate is, we confess after it has been done <note>Ficino is playing on the Latin *fatum* (fate) and *factum* (a thing done).</note>; it is called "necessary fate" because, clearly, while it was happening in the present, it happened by a certain necessity. And all this conditional necessity—whether regarding the past or the present—proceeds from a certain higher nature which is Necessity itself in a simple sense. From this, it is established that we should not posit "chance" in the principles of things, but rather "necessity." I will pass over the fact that if there were no order in things, in which one thing properly follows from another, there could be no correct prediction of the future, whether it be done by art, by some natural instinct, or by some divine inspiration. Furthermore, that power and motion cannot come into the soul from atoms or other bodies by which it moves itself and other things with vital and sensory vigor; by which it suddenly imagines such varied things as if by craft; by which it transcends the physical realm through contemplation and love; by which it opposes the disturbances of the body; by which some souls are more suited than others to different disciplines (and non-physical ones at that); and by which, finally, they act as if free and in their own right, discerning liberty from necessity. We discuss the soul's possession of some degree of liberty more extensively in our *Theology*.

### *That there is not only one agent in the universe.*

IIII. Again, one must not think that the world is only "one animal" in such a way that there is only one soul and one unique body in it, and that all motions and effects everywhere are necessarily only the proceeding works of that same soul, with no other cause besides it and no other agent. For in that way, the order of causes (in which fate is commonly thought to consist) is destroyed, and the highest dignity is taken away from the world if there is only one mover and agent in it while all other things only suffer and are moved. For the perfection of the world consists chiefly in this: that this universe be maximally formal <note>meaning "full of forms" or "shaping principles."</note> and active, and that there be within it the greatest possible order of forms and agents. Furthermore, since the entire nature of the first agent is an utterly immense efficacy, it propagates many effective things—and therefore agents—from itself, just as an active fire generates an active fire. Likewise, whatever the first mover alone acts upon and moves, it performs perfectly. Yet many things seem to happen here and there that are outside the most exact and best order, relative to individual natures. From this, it is clear that subsequent natures do not lack their own duty to act. Finally, when the intellectual soul turns toward itself; when it distracts itself by deliberating between opposing conjectures; when it imitates, corrects, and restores the works of nature; when it progresses rightly in some things and errs in others; and when it transcends the order of both bodies and souls—it surely declares that it is neither a mere part of the universal "animal" nor necessarily subject to it.

### *That we are neither forced by the heavens, nor are other things made by the heavens alone and of necessity.*

V. The third group of those who assert fate are the astrologers—not all of them, I say, but many—and they say that fate is that which the configuration of the stars at one's birth decrees by necessity. They confirm that each person's lot is destined from that source because

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...through the observation of the stars, things to come are foretold to individuals. Furthermore, many changes occur in physical bodies due to the approach, departure, and relative positions of the celestial lights <note>The "lights" refers to the sun, moon, and planets</note>. Plotinus, however, can in no way endure the idea that a human being is necessarily driven in every single motion by the confluence of celestial rays. This is because the human body is not a continuous part of the world’s physical mass, nor is the human soul a part of the World Soul <note>The *Anima Mundi*, or World Soul, was thought by some philosophers to be a spirit that animated the entire universe</note>, nor is it created by the World Soul. Therefore, the human body possesses, besides its own shape, its own internal motion and its own progression; it has, I say, an intellectual mover <note>The rational soul</note> which, by its intellectual nature, transcends the body and the life of the world, seeing as it is not merely a part of the universe, but is itself a kind of "universe" within itself. And since every motion is for the sake of the Good, and our soul holds a general notion of the total Good in its simplicity—within which all individual goods are contained—it follows that the motion of the soul is not necessarily destined toward this or that specific thing as if it were the only good. Instead, it can apply itself equally to any choice based on the variety of its judgments. Indeed, the long consultation we engage in over individual matters, the diligent weighing of opposites, the exactness of our choice, and our frequent retraction in favor of other judgments, all declare that the soul is not carried along by a certain blind nature, habit, or natural instinct, but rather by a universal and free power of moving and acting. Since, therefore, we possess our own nature and efficacy, and consequently our own power of action, we do not merely suffer under celestial action; rather, we receive celestial influence according to our own effective properties, and we do something of our own with it. Likewise, we perform some things through our mere independent property.

The celestial influence also changes around us according to the nature of the places we inhabit. For even under a tiny portion of a specific climate, where the influence of the stars is identical, different things are born and happen at the same moment and always, due to the diversity of the site—the earth, air, water, winds, vapors, and even the local customs and laws. Furthermore, children are usually similar to their parents and nurses regardless of the hour in which they are born or raised, as they receive much more from their own lineage than from the astrological hour. Even if they are similar in form due to a shared nature of place, generation, and nutrition, they often differ greatly in character and talent, since the diversity of minds—differing in both genius and morals—arises from sources other than bodily causes. Finally, when the soul opposes the incitements of the body for the sake of tranquility and understanding, it declares that it both operates freely and does not depend on its own body, and therefore not on the celestial bodies either; for it seems the stars can only act upon us through our physical bodies. We can, however, resist our body through both the virtue and grace of the mind, and choose a life agreeable to the mind even if it is harmful to the body. Often, while the nature and incitement of the body remain the same, we choose different things at different times based solely on the variety of our judgments. Even when the nature of the body has become different, we are nonetheless accustomed to choosing similar things if similar reasoning persuades us, as we then depend not so much on bodily influence as on the abundance of intelligence and reason. As for what some claim—that these actions of ours are *caused* by the stars because they are *signified* by the stars—this has been more diligently refuted elsewhere. You should conclude this: at any given moment, and even in the same location, many different things can be born at once, differing not only in their individual accidents but even in species and genus. These things also meet very different fates, as if the nature and fortune of things were not drawn solely from the astrological hour. This is also confirmed by the fact that many people often perish together in the same common destruction, and yet they were not born at the same hour, nor did they arrive at the place of their death at the same time.

->How individual things are generated by their own specific natures with the heavens contributing. How celestial things signify, and how demons <note>The word *daemones* here refers to intermediary spirits or "daemons" in the Platonic sense, which could be good or bad, rather than just "demons" in the modern sense</note> know and execute these things.<-

**VI** Therefore, as we have argued elsewhere, in the specific generation of things, lower causes <note>Earthly causes like biological parents</note> are extremely powerful as the most immediate and "proper" causes. Thus, this person is born a human, and that one a horse—not because of the time of birth, but because the former comes from a human and the latter from a horse. Similarly, that this human is born with a certain disposition proceeds from the specific disposition of the parents rather than from some external, common, accidental, and momentarily fleeting arrangement of the heavens. Nevertheless, celestial influence contributes to this, either toward the efficacy or the quality applied to the parents and the offspring; but this influence is entirely corporeal, since it comes from physical bodies acting upon physical bodies, and it is received according to the condition of the recipient and the place. However, the gifts of the soul—which do not obey the body, nor follow from the body, but look toward incorporeal things—cannot proceed from the body of the heavens into the soul, neither through our body, nor much less without it. Therefore, human industry, sagaciously investigating the incorporeal reasons of things, does not follow the body of the heaven, but the incorporeal nature of the human mind, which perhaps is aided in these matters by the souls of the stars themselves and their minds, through the ministry of contemplative demons. 

That the stars, which are divine by nature, should change their nature daily due to local motion and sometimes turn toward evil, is a wicked thing to say, as we have demonstrated elsewhere. We have also said that when evils, troubles, and disorders are portended by the observation of the heavens, these things are not *caused* by those stars (which are good and orderly), but are merely *signified* by them, just as many things are said to be signified (but not caused) by the flight and chatter of birds or other omens. This faculty of signifying consists in a certain mutual connection of things; neither men, but rather the demons themselves, are able to know these signs and this connection. This is what Origen <note>An early Christian theologian</note> argues, and what Plotinus hints at here when he speaks of those who "know the writings of such a kind." Plato signifies this in the *Timaeus* with these words: to attempt to know what happens or is signified by the celestial arrangement is vain without a diligent inspection of those "images" <note>simulachrorum</note>. To perceive all those things is not our task, but that of the demons; for we have neither the lifespan, the eye, nor the talent for it. 

Just as it is the special office of demons to hold the celestial signs and suggest them to us—whether we are sleeping or awake—so it is also their task to frequently execute, at certain times, what the heavens have portended: the better demons performing better things, and the worse performing worse things. Thus, through these spirits, after long cycles of time, those things can be fulfilled which that celestial arrangement (which has long since vanished) once signified would happen. Yet, demons do not move us in such a way that they compel us by necessity—as Plato says—for they act more often through the imagination than the body alone. Although they act upon us not only by choice but also by a certain property of nature, just as the stars appearing to our eyes do. Furthermore, they act upon lower things through their own motions and affections, insofar as they accompany the dances <note>The rhythmic, circular orbits</note> of the stars <gloss>stellarum</gloss>. But because they apply something of their own office, the action and judgment of the heavens are combined within us. In this way, what the visible stars portended, the invisible stars—that is, the demons—subsequently partly suggest to us and partly execute according to their powers. Hence that saying of Plato: "The souls falling into generation are led by <meta>catchword: demons</meta>

### ON BOOK I. ENNEAD III.

daemons <note>original: "demones." In this context, these are not evil spirits, but intermediary beings or guardian spirits assigned to guide souls</note>, having already chosen their lot in life, are the executors of destiny. Indeed, Saturnian daemons rule Saturnian souls and carry out the gifts of Saturn; similarly, Jovian spirits rule Jovian souls and carry out Jovian works, and so on for the others. And just as there are humans in every region who are partly Saturnian and partly Jovian, so too do various daemons dwell in every sphere of the world. The better ones among the Saturnians perform the better tasks of Saturn, while the lesser ones among them tend to carry out the more difficult or unfavorable outcomes under that same influence; the same is true for the spirits of Mars and all the others. When Plotinus says that the daily motions of the heavenly bodies are not only for the general health of the world but are also useful for signifying the future to those capable of understanding them, he shows that the things signified can be avoided if they are bad, or aided if they are good. This is much like how a doctor can assist health based on the signs he finds in us; otherwise, the observation of signs in both astrology and medicine would be useless, and God, who established the signs in the heavens to look after the safety of those below, would have provided warnings in vain.

> *Those who introduce a necessary series of things, with each detail being carried out inevitably, take away*
> *both contingency from the lowest things and freedom from the power of counsel.*

VII The fourth opinion on fate, which we are taking up for examination, agrees with the second opinion in this: it believes that all individual things are generated through "seminal reasons" <note>original: "rationes seminales." These are the internal blueprints or natural "seeds" that determine how a living thing grows and acts</note> from a single vital principle infused into all things, a view primarily championed by Strato. However, it differs in that its followers believe not only that such a vital principle is effective, but that many other things beneath it possess some power of acting—provided they act only as they are drawn by the first principle. They add that other causes follow one after another in a sequence, so tightly connected that those following are necessarily drawn and led by those preceding them. Consequently, they claim that whatever they do, they do by necessity; whatever results, happens by necessity; and every outcome everywhere is linked to all others, though conspiring differently in different places. This seems to have been primarily the opinion of Chrysippus <note>A famous Stoic philosopher who argued for a deterministic universe where everything is linked by cause and effect</note>. For now, I will set aside the fact that this opinion robs things of contingency <note>The quality of being able to happen or not happen; things that are not strictly determined</note>, which all the most learned men believe occurs at least in the lowest parts of the world. Plotinus seems especially to detest this view because it undoubtedly strips the rational soul of its freedom of choice and its authority over its own actions—if indeed it were true, as they say, that every action of the soul proceeds necessarily from a certain impulse, and that impulse from the imagination, and the imagination from the present series of things acting either within us or around us. We have already shown enough in our *Theology* how shameful it is to subject the intellectual soul—which separates the incorporeal from the corporeal and places the former above the latter—to the necessity of bodies. Furthermore, Zael and Mesahach <note>Sahl ibn Bishr and Masha'allah, influential Arabic astrologers whose works were widely read in the Renaissance</note> and others show that not every movement of the mind is stirred by the heavens when they speak of "interrogation" <note>A branch of astrology where a chart is cast to answer a specific question</note>. For they say that a question and its judgment only have an effect when the person asking seeks with a certain intense anxiety, as if only then is the mind seen to be moved by the heavens. But when the question is not anxious, the answer is most deceptive, as if the questioner is not then being moved by the heavens. What more? The zeal and industry we use to struggle against fate are not given to us by fate. The worship of the God who is above the heavens finally resolves into a cause higher than the heavens.

->How the soul is above fate, in fate, and under fate.<-

VIII The common opinion of philosophers regarding fate is that it is a certain necessity brought upon things by the conspiracy of physical causes. But since the motion of bodies comes from the soul, and the order of physical forms comes from the Intellect, we rightly believe that the intellectual soul is naturally free from the necessity usually imposed by physical motion or sequence. So far is the soul from being subject to fate that it is actually the principle of fate itself—provided that fate is a physical series, for this series depends on the intellectual soul. I say the entire universal series depends on the World Soul, while other series here and there depend on other souls endowed with similar intelligence. Therefore, there are two kinds of causes in fate: I call them "soul-causes," which are the principles of fate (that is, souls accommodating themselves to ruling bodies), and physical causes, which are like the things that complete fate. Furthermore, there is a triple order: first, of all bodies to the first body; second, of all souls to the first soul; and third, of bodies to souls, and through those souls to the first soul, and through that intellectual soul to the first Intellect. Thus, the entire series of fates is ultimately brought back to divine providence. If, therefore, the soul is entirely outside the body, it is likewise outside of fate; if it is in the body, to the extent that it indulges the body which naturally suffers under fate, the soul also suffers in fate to that extent. But if it separates itself from the body as much as it can and only grants its vegetative power <note>The basic biological functions of growth and nutrition</note> to the body, it is counted in fate only as an "agent" (one who acts). Yet it acts according to the condition of fortune: some things it changes through its natural faculty, others it amends and corrects through art, or endures most easily through greatness of soul. Timaeus shows that the soul undergoes fate only insofar as it immerses itself in the body, saying that souls first learned the laws of fate when they were joined to their "vehicles" <note>The "astral body" or subtle casing that allows the soul to interact with the physical world</note>; for from this the beginnings of fate are drawn. But meanwhile, Plato declares in both the *Timaeus* and the tenth book of the *Republic* that the soul approaches fate by its own free motion and can eventually free itself. He says God revealed to souls both the laws of fate and the principles of divine and human law, so that God would remain without blame <note>A reference to the famous line "The blame is his who chooses; God is blameless"</note>, and he adds that virtue and reason are free.

->How the soul is in fate as one who acts; how as one who suffers; also<-
->concerning the contingency of things.<-

IX To those who say that whatever happens occurs necessarily and inevitably because all causes are linked together—and that once all causes are in place, the effect necessarily follows—we now object as follows: Even if we grant you that point, the mind can still retain its own authority. For the mind itself is in the order of causes—both natural causes (insofar as it acts on the body through the vegetative power rather than just suffering) and those causes which act by will and therefore move freely from within themselves. Thus, when the mind decides to move the tongue or an arm, the motion in the limb occurs necessarily, provided that all causes concur—namely, the choice and purpose of the mind, and the surrounding circumstances (that is, everything besides the mind, the meeting of which is here called "fortune"), such as the limbs being fit and nothing standing in the way. Also numbered among the external causes designated by the name of "fortune" is anything from the motion of the universe which, along with subsequent causes, contributes to the work. Therefore, the work proceeds by necessity at that moment, yet the mind is not like...

<summary>Ficino explains that while physical bodies are subject to fate and celestial influence, the rational human soul remains free because it is a "cause" in its own right and can choose to transcend physical necessity.</summary>

<meta>The previous page concluded with a discussion on how signs in the heavens can be read to avoid misfortune, comparing the astrologer to a doctor. This page continues the exploration of how the rational soul maintains its agency despite external influences and the role of "daemons" (spirits) in human behavior and mental health.</meta>

[page 222]

<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...is compelled and moved to work, if it follows neither an incentive creeping in from the body by choice, nor thinks about external bodily advantage or disadvantage. It does not look at external things at all, nor is it deceived by false opinion, but it holds intellect and certain reason, void of passion, as its guide, and directs all things toward its own best state as if toward an end. From the fact that the wise soul directs its actions toward itself as an end, it is certain that the soul possesses an internal, not an external, principle of action. To this extent, the soul is judged to "act," because it operates through its own proper, intimate, and principal form, and for its own sake. But when it—either first degenerating of its own accord, or through ignorance, or incited and instigated from the outside by the body—undertakes something while looking elsewhere than toward the soul, it is judged not so much to "act" as to "suffer" <note>original: "pati." In philosophical Latin, this means to be passive or to be acted upon by an external force.</note>. It acts most of all when it operates not only from itself and for its own sake, but also within itself, by itself alone, without instruments—that is, when it exercises the duty of contemplation. But where it lives a life of pleasure without moderation, or follows an active life without prudence, it serves and suffers most gravely. Yet as often as it leads an active life with prudence, it partly acts itself, and is partly acted upon, insofar as it is incited to motion by external things and carries out its service according to the condition of its surroundings. Remember, however, that Plotinus here considers this "concourse of things" which surrounds us—which he calls "fortune"—not necessarily to be reduced in every case to celestial fates, as if everything were tuned to a hair's breadth in the same way the heavens arrange themselves. For the order in these lower things is not as exact as in those higher ones, nor is their stability equal, nor their harmony similar. Hence that saying of Plotinus: "The effects of the celestial bodies among us happen according to the condition of the lower causes"; likewise, "natural effects have a far greater similarity with nearby causes than with remote ones." Again, the dispositions of the celestial bodies are often not so much causes as signs; therefore he speaks with a certain condition when he says: *And if anything further from the motion of the heavens contributes to the work.* Finally, he thinks that the order may perhaps be changed from there to here by human diligence and the virtue of the soul.

---

### Intellectual nature acts freely, but its effect is sometimes hindered in the reason.

X He concludes, therefore, neither that things are moved by chance, but that there is an order in things following from causes, from which things can be skillfully made and signified; nor, on the other hand, that all things are carried along and struck by external necessity. Indeed, it is necessary that we be moved not only by what is external, but also by what is internal. And those things which are internal are moved partly by a certain determined instinct of nature, and partly by an absolute, ample, and free principle; otherwise, the order of movable things will either be nonexistent or will not be reduced to the highest level. And those things which are movable through another would not be referred back to that which is movable by itself, which nonetheless must exist. For that which is moved solely by the instinct of nature does not move itself, but is either impelled by the one impressing that nature (in the manner of an arrow) or is drawn by something related to it (as iron is by a magnet). For this reason, when the intellectual soul does all things with a certain excellent—that is, intellectual—reason (reason, I say, which is entirely universal and absolute), whatever it brings forth, it acts from an intellectual principle and does not "suffer." For intellectual wisdom, according to Plotinus and most great philosophers, does not have an external cause (such as an inciting cause from things encountered), but shines from within out of eternity <note>original: "ab æuo." Referring to the 'Aion' or eternal realm beyond linear time.</note>, and glimmers internally, with nothing at all hindering it. This intelligence also flashes into the nearby reason, using that reason as long as it is not hindered. It is hindered, however, both commonly due to a certain distraction of the soul toward many things, and specifically in certain people who are either born insane or become so. And this happens in three main ways: for they are either dull, or forgetful, or stupid, or furious. The cause of this insanity is partly the unfitness of the sensory instruments, partly the rising of vapors, partly a more vehement intensity of the imagination which slackens the act of reason, partly the excessive preoccupation of nature with the cure of a disease, and finally a certain demonic occupation <note>The term "demonica" here refers to influence by spirits, a common explanation for mental illness in the Renaissance.</note>. Perhaps, just as monstrous actions in our morals usually proceed from us by the instigation of the lowest daemons, so insanity often happens through a certain marvelous machinery of daemons. Just as they stir up the vapors of the humors and sensory images as incentives for vices, so they sometimes provoke vapors in the body and images in the phantasy to incite and thoroughly strengthen insanity, so that from there, reason is either slackened or mocked. That insanity is caused by daemons wonderfully irritating the humors is not denied by Serapio <note>A 9th-century Christian physician from Damascus.</note> and Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the famous Persian physician and philosopher.</note> and the elders, and the Gospel testifies to it everywhere: where those seized by a daemon are healed, the insane are cured. For it is not likely that the soul, which participates in divinity, would either sin so wickedly or be so insane unless a demonic nature were additionally engineering it. Perhaps this is why he said in the second chapter that the immense diversity of talents and characters is not from manifest and nearby causes alone. For this reason, Paul the Apostle <note>Ephesians 6:12.</note> says that our struggle is not merely against the body, but against the daemons assigned to this dark air. Therefore, a favorable disposition of the humors and limbs, or the position of the stars, does not *create* wisdom, but signifies that the *use* of wisdom is not hindered by an opposing disposition or position. Once this hindrance is removed from us, the light of wisdom flashes forth of its own accord. What we have said about daemons is confirmed by Porphyry <note>Plotinus' student and biographer.</note> in his book *On Oracles*: "The bodies of men," he says, "are full of evil daemons, especially those who live on more delicate feasts. For while we are eating, they arrive and cling to the body; therefore fasting and chastity are greatly praised—not because they specifically please a good God in that way, but so that those who rejoice in blood and impurity might depart, lest they also enjoy these things by entering the bodies of the voluptuous." For it is certain that a vehement desire for falling things and the impulse of a lustful spirit grow excessively strong from no other source than the presence of evil daemons. Therefore, when the appetite is more vehemently inflamed, and the heat of pleasure so agitates the soul that every thought wanders to external things, know then that daemons of this kind are present, whose presence causes the naturally greedy spirit within us to grow. These are his words there, which he confirms in almost the same words in his book *On Abstinence*.

<summary>Ficino explains that the soul truly "acts" only when following its own internal reason and wisdom, while it "suffers" or becomes passive when led by bodily desires. He also discusses the causes of insanity, attributing it to a mix of physical humors and the influence of malevolent spirits (daemons) who are attracted to luxury and vice.</summary>

<header>ON BOOK I OF THE THIRD ENNEAD</header>

# THE MARSILIAN SUMMARY

## That not all things occur by fatal necessity.

<insert>1.</insert>

Since you desire, Lorenzo <note>Likely Lorenzo de' Medici, Ficino's patron.</note>, to understand separately what Marsilio thinks about these matters, I shall take up the matter itself again from a deeper beginning. It is well established that the Good itself provides for all things, arising from the order of all things which is marvelously established toward a certain end. In this order, indeed, individual things are everywhere directed toward their own specific good, and all things together contribute to the common good. And if it can seem a wonder that the Good itself, in the order of its providence, permits evil, it is nevertheless well known by the fates that it often permits this, namely for the sake of the good: while it permits the destruction of present things, it does so so that infinite faces of new forms may thereafter be generated. Neither the conflict between forms nor the limitations of space would allow these forms to exist all at once. Since, however, God is goodness itself in a simple sense, but is not "necessity" in that same simple sense—but rather, so far as the good is concerned, evil seems (if I may say so) more opposed to God than contingency <note>term: contingency. In philosophy, this refers to things that happen by chance or could have happened differently, as opposed to things that "must" happen (necessity).</note> does—it follows that if He permits evil, he surely permits contingency as well. Nevertheless, just as He everywhere leads evil back into good, so He everywhere reduces the contingent into the necessary. For whatever was able to happen or not happen while it was still in the future, all of that is "necessary" both while it currently exists and "necessary" to have passed once it is in the past. When all circumstances are collected together through specific conditions, what was contingent usually seems to emerge as necessary.

Therefore, one should not think that the opposite of necessity, according to formal reason, is that which is called "impossible." For in the formal opposite of necessity, no necessity ought to be included; yet necessity is included in that which is impossible. For the "impossible" is that which cannot be. But that which cannot be is "necessarily" not. Likewise, the "impossible" seems to be included in the "necessary" itself: for that which is necessary to exist is "impossible" not to be. Therefore, the true opposite of the necessary is the contingent. For just as the very definition of the necessary is restricted only to "being" or only to "not being," so conversely the definition of the contingent leans toward "being" just as much as "not being."

However, between the necessary and that which happens equally either way, there seems to be a middle ground: the "contingent for the most part" <note>original: "contingens ut plurimum." A technical term for things that usually happen in a certain way but are not strictly guaranteed by logic.</note>, the opposite of which happens only rarely. Thus, it is "necessary" for the human species to exist; but it happens "equally" <note>meaning by chance or choice</note> whether this or that specific man moves or rests. It is contingent "for the most part" that a man’s hand has five fingers, but it is rare for it to have six or four. The order of things requires that "being" itself applies equally to both possibilities of the contingent; for if the necessary is given, its opposite must also be given. In this proper opposition, the distinction of that which is called "being" is found. So, if an opposite is to be given to the necessary by formal reason, there must exist that which is equally contingent in either direction.

Again, if an opposite is to be given to the same by reason of matter, we shall say that the "necessary to be" is opposed by the "impossible to exist." Between these, we shall place the "possible" as a middle ground. This "possible" is the contingent: sometimes it is the "more frequent," which approaches closer to the necessary; sometimes it is the "rarer," which seems to decline toward the impossible; and sometimes it is the "indifferent" contingent (to be or not to be), which must certainly be granted as true and equidistant, being by this reasoning the middle between "necessary to be" and "impossible to happen."

Contingency is born through the order of things itself, descending through many continuous levels. In this order, those things that are closer to the source are at first entirely immobile—namely, to the Intellect itself. Next, the Souls, being a little more remote, are moved only by "formal" motion, without their substance changing. Then the celestial substances <note>the stars and planets</note>, while they themselves remain permanent, are meanwhile rolled by a certain local motion; they also move "formally" insofar as they change their configurations in their spheres. But they move (if I may say so) immovably, insofar as they are always revolved in the same necessary order.

Following this, however, it is necessary that those things which are beneath the heavens <note>on Earth</note> are moved "movably" (changeably). In this wandering chance of motions, contingency is born, since things moved in this way sometimes seem to depart and deviate from their own usual order, even though they cannot transcend the common order of the universe. For when the effective power is diminished through many successive levels of agents, and finally a great multitude of conflicting forms flows together, it surely follows that each specific nature sometimes fails in its duty. Its power, gradually weakened, is eventually more easily hindered by the encounter of diverse things. Thus, the seeds of a plant or animal do not always produce their natural offspring, nor do they produce it everywhere at the right time, nor in a perfect state. Therefore, although—so far as it pertains to the celestial nature—it is a thing undoubtedly necessary and absolute that the offspring of this plant or animal would come forth at certain times, it nevertheless happens occasionally that it does not occur, or does not come forth perfect, specifically when the generator's own nature fails internally or is hindered externally.

Often, the present disposition of the heaven seems about to produce a certain quality in this matter; but a different quality of the matter, contracted from nearby causes and conditions, changes the effect of the heaven in one way or another. And let no one object to us that this quality of matter also happened because of the celestial bodies, on the grounds that nearby causes are moved by the celestials. Let it be that they are indeed moved, but "according to their own nature" <note>original: "pro natura sua."</note>. For God, while he acts through the heaven upon lower things, does not take away his gifts from the heaven; nor does the heaven, when it acts through lower causes upon our affairs, meanwhile subtract the proper and natural powers and actions from these causes. Therefore, since the effect, form, and condition of each thing usually emerge according to the "affection" <note>the state or disposition</note> of the matter, and since this affection of the matter is caused by the celestial bodies in a more general way, but by nearby causes in a more intimate and specific way, it follows that the specific condition of an earthly effect emerges as such as the nearby cause requires by affecting the matter, rather than as the remote cause seems to attempt or begin. For it does not follow that if a remote cause is necessary, every event arising from it is immediately necessary, unless the nearby cause was also necessary.

Now it is manifest (as we often say) that individual effects turn out more similar to their own specific causes everywhere than to remote ones. For example, any plants and animals are judged not so much similar to the celestial bodies as to their own parents and the seeds from which they are born. From this it is clear that the nature and form of such effects follow their own seeds rather than the celestial ones, and they occur changeably according to the condition of familiar causes and all surrounding circumstances (which are entirely changeable), not necessarily according to the condition of the celestial bodies. And rightly so: for those things whose nature does not necessarily retain its being, but can fail from it, their power also does not act necessarily, but sometimes falls away from action. Therefore, things which might perhaps have been necessary...

He argues that earthly events are governed more by "proximate causes" (like seeds or local materials) which are imperfect and changeable, rather than "remote causes" (like the stars), which are necessary and fixed.</summary>

<page-num>224</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

judged from the heavens, these same things among us are governed by this matter and occur contingently <note>term: contingently. Happening by chance or subject to change, rather than being fixed by absolute necessity.</note>. By matter, I mean that which is always greedy for all forms equally. By region, I mean that here, innumerable and conflicting qualities flow together. Therefore, although the celestial influence proceeds toward a certain goal in its own specific order, it is easily confused with other things and lost—both because this matter is greedy for other forms, being easily receptive and mixed, and because this region is full of discordant qualities that immediately mix and transform it. Thus, it is rare for something certain to arise here from the heavens, and you can hardly guess what sort of thing will be born unless you have perhaps looked around at the whole universe: to see how many and what kind of conditions of causes flow together at any moment, whether from on high, from the middle, or from the lowest depths—and how you might weigh what kind of thing arises again from them all. Furthermore, if corporeal nature—which is more obviously subject to the celestial body and seems determined toward one thing above all—does not necessarily admit celestial influences (I mean exactly as they are sent from heaven), then much less does the **rational soul** necessarily follow celestial instinct. The soul's understanding and movement are both internal and incredibly broad; it often transcends the physical realm and resists the body. Surely, nature would have given the soul the power of daily deliberation in vain—allowing it to propose many opposing options based on different guesses—unless the soul could lead itself by choosing between them. It could not turn toward whichever it pleased if it were compelled to a specific path every day by a fixed constitution of the heavens. Added to this is the fact that while divine providence allows for a certain contingency in natural things (arising from their defects), it allows it much more in voluntary agents, where this contingency arises from *perfection*. This is certainly more appropriate to them, since natural things move and act only from an impressed form, while voluntary agents act from a conceived notion as well.

Add to this that every celestial instinct, insofar as it comes from heaven as the nearest instrument of divine providence and is thus wonderfully ordered, always leads toward the best in a certain order. Therefore, that we often wander without order and stray from the best is not due to the heavens, and much less to the mover of the heavens, but happens because of the condition of our own species, or our character, or our fortune. Now, if the particularity of our species and character can pervert the celestial influence from an ordered good into its opposite, it can much more easily turn itself from any other quality into another. Common nature granted to heavy things that they should descend through gravity. All heavy things will therefore descend by a certain impulse of common nature, unless they are perhaps hindered. They can undoubtedly be hindered from moving, or even incited to be cast down more greedily than nature allows. Then, according to the diversity of their shape—whether natural or artificial—they descend down slopes in different ways. For a sphere falls in one way, a cylinder in another, and an angular shape in another; even **Chrysippus** <note>original: "Chrysippus". A Stoic philosopher who famously used the analogy of a rolling cylinder to explain how external fate and internal nature cooperate.</note> himself admits this, though he was a great defender of celestial fate. Therefore, a given constitution of the heavens at this hour seems likely to bring heat to the body and vehemence to the soul of those being born; but in one person, the cold and moist nature of the parents, the place, the time, and the nourishment tempers the looming force of heaven and perhaps turns it to the opposite. In another person, the hot and dry nature of those same factors pushes a moderate quality coming from the heavens into an excess. Again, both the specific and varied natures of the parents and those being born, as well as diverse laws and customs, perhaps distinguish such an impulse of the soul and body descending from heaven through various degrees and modes. This is why, as we have often said, effects usually arise not so much from the nature of the distant agent <note>The "distant agent" refers to the stars or planets.</note> as from the condition of nearby agents, and finally from the affection of the matter and the disposition of the place. Why say more? The same ray of the Sun acts differently if it strikes directly versus obliquely; or if it passes through clear air versus foggy air. For celestial things make the air foggy just as much as terrestrial things do. Likewise, the ray acts differently if it attacks wax than if it attacks mud: for it liquefies the former and dries out the latter. Again, it acts differently on ice than on crystal: it eventually melts the ice, but never the crystal. If it falls upon snow on the mountain peak versus snow in a hollow of the mountain, it melts the latter much faster than the former. You can often see here on the same peak that snow which fell at the same time melts away much faster on the part facing south, while on the part facing north, it lasts longer, even though one part is barely a cubit’s distance from the other; such is the effect of even a small difference in location. Finally, if the ray acts for a short time, it often gathers fogs; if for a long time, it scatters them. It acts differently in open spaces than in hollows; and at the same time, it helps some while harming others, even in the same place. The powers of superior things are changed so much by place and matter that, although waters generally rise and fall with the motion of the Moon, they do not all do so equally: for the sea does not experience this everywhere or in the same way, and where it seems to observe this most, it is often hindered from rising by a contrary wind. There are qualities specific to places under every star: some belonging to marshlands, others to pure plains, others to inhabited hills, and others to forests. Likewise, there are far different qualities according to the variety of heat, cold, dryness, moisture, winds, vapors, rivers, and valleys, whatever star may hang over them; from these come different lifespans, various body types, and different capacities of intellect. Many born at the same moment do not fall ill at the same time because they live in different places; many not born at the same time fall ill together due to a similar wind, cloud, or vapor. Regardless of when they were born or what age they are, those who have converged in a contagious region fall into sickness at the same time. Truly, although universal and superior causes have an ample, intimate, and lasting power over effects, the **middle causes** <note>The "middle" or "proximate" causes refer to local environment, biology, and human choice.</note>—those nearby—are most powerful and can do almost everything regarding the specific qualities of events; thus, the effect turns out much more similar to them. For the most common influences of distant causes are determined and distinguished step by step as they follow through the causes. Thus the life-giving power of heaven, favoring all things to be born in common, is narrowed down to those specific species in the various types of plants and animals; in individuals within a species, it is further contracted to singular properties. Then, the natural actions and passions of things follow the individual principles of individuals first, and then the special principles, rather than the most common ones everywhere—especially when the most common principles are "equivocal" <note>term: equivocal. In this context, meaning a cause that is of a different nature or "category" than its effect, like the sun (a celestial body) causing growth (a biological process).</note> and very different in kind from their effects; no one denies that celestial things are such. But let no one object that whatever is in the secondary causes is present from the first, and whatever is found in the third is attributed entirely to the second—and thus nothing comes from the following causes that does not similarly come from the superior ones. Remember that the nature of a following cause is not only similar to the superior one because it receives from it, but

He uses analogies like the sun melting wax but drying mud to show how the same heavenly cause produces different effects based on the recipient.</summary>

On the previous page, Ficino argued that while the heavens exert influence, the material world and the human soul possess their own distinct powers that can modify or resist these celestial "inputs."</meta>

It even becomes dissimilar insofar as it has proceeded outward; not only has it degenerated from its source, but it has additionally turned into something else, differing now by its own specific quality. It is like a ray of light which is soothing in the heavens but devouring on the earth; or shining in the sky, yet turning red in a cloud. Thus, it is no wonder that something occurs here or there in such a way that it did not originally arise that way from its source. Therefore, many things are produced by causes lower than the heavens—things of such a nature that they are not produced by the heavens themselves. 

Remember again that these causes below the Moon <note>The "sublunary" realm: in ancient cosmology, the region between Earth and the Moon where things are subject to change and decay.</note> receive their powers from the life of the world, not only through celestial power but also directly through the vegetative power of the soul which flourishes everywhere. Just as the life of an animal gives many things to the feet and hands through the primary limbs, it also gives many things through itself; and the things it gives through the primary limbs are also transformed within them. Finally, remember that from the gathering of all causes there arises a power that is properly found in none of them individually—just as from a confluence of materials and qualities, a certain new material or quality results. 

Truly, that legitimate follower of Plato <note>referring to Plotinus or the ideal Platonist</note>—who rightly contemplates the multitude under unity and motion under stability—will not entirely deny that **contingencies** <note>term: contingencies. Events that happen by chance or could happen otherwise, rather than being strictly determined.</note> exist under the realm of the necessary. He sees that things themselves, though starting under a simple unity and state of rest, eventually reach an almost innumerable number and uncertain mobility through a long stretch of degrees, through a specific multitude and movement. Indeed, the beauty and goodness of the universe consist in this most ample order of differing degrees. 

For this reason, the individual motions and passions of single things—which vary within an infinitely manifold multitude and mobility—cannot be properly distributed or directed solely by celestial powers. Celestial powers are defined by a certain number and proceed in a fixed order, whereas these earthly things vary continually. One would have to be quite mad to assign every single movement of a delirious person or a playing child to a specific celestial influence at every moment—as if the hands, feet, fingers, lips, eyes, senses, and imagination could not move in any way at any given moment except as that celestial influence decreed. According to such a rule, one would have to map out the leaps of innumerable locusts, the flight of flies, and every random stumble of anyone at all. 

But surely not all things are entirely made and compelled by the heavens. On the contrary, the heavens do not produce the works and actions of the elements, mixtures, plants, and animals without the participation of those things themselves. Fire heats and generates fire by its own natural property under any star whatsoever; it does not cool or generate water under any particular star, and the same applies to other things. Therefore, regardless of how the heavens are positioned, all natural things—whether living or non-living—continually act according to their own nature, impulse, occasion, indulgence, or imagination; they are clearly carried toward this or that. Because all these things exist and live in common, and can act and be moved in common, they possess celestial favor. However, that they exist in such a specific form and with singular properties, they receive from their progenitors and their location, and because such things act in such a way. 

That there are so many and such kinds of species in the universe comes partly from the **Ideal Forms** <note>term: Ideal Forms. The perfect, eternal blueprints of things existing in the Divine Mind.</note> of the Divine Mind and partly from the **seminal reasons** <note>term: seminal reasons (rationes seminales). Internal formative "seeds" or principles within the soul/nature that direct growth and development.</note> of the soul. For the specific distinction of things does not happen by chance, since it is always most orderly. Nor does it come from entirely formless matter, since form itself is a marvelous beauty superior to the formed subject. Nor does it come from the shifting habit of the heavens, for form itself is immobile and entirely eternal; nor even from celestial forms and figures alone, since species cannot be described that way in the heavens, and many species of things are incorporeal. Their formal order, skillfully directed toward an end, must proceed from an intelligence that prescribes that end.

## Confirmation against celestial fate through Alexander, Oenomaus, Diogenianus, and Ptolemy.

**II** Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A famous 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle who defended human free will.</note>, in his book *On Fate* dedicated to Antoninus, refutes the opinion of Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher who argued for a deterministic view of the universe.</note> regarding fate. With many arguments, he shows that fate or "the fated" is nothing other than what nature is. He demonstrates that some things even happen "contrary to nature" when nature is sometimes hindered by an impediment. Since some things happen contrary to nature, it follows that if acting by nature is acting by fate, then things also happen contrary to fate. He adds: 

*We see that human bodies are subject to various diseases, each according to their particular nature. We also know that the condition of such bodies can be turned for the better through a diligent rule of living, the art of physicians, and the counsel of the gods. The same happens similarly to the soul: for despite the natural inclination it has from the complexion of the body, it often becomes better through exercise and teaching.* 

This is why, when the physiognomist Zopyrus had said certain shameful things about Socrates that were foreign to his virtue—for which Zopyrus was mocked by many—Socrates responded: 

*Zopyrus is not wrong. For I would have been such by nature, had I not overcome nature through philosophy.* <note>original: "Non errat Zopyrus. Talis enim natura forem, nisi naturam philosophia superauissem."</note> 

Therefore, such are the things over which nature presides; these natural things differ in no way from fated things. 

However, those things happen by **fortune** <note>term: fortune (fortuna). Random chance or luck.</note> which are in no way intended. When some things are done for the sake of one thing, and something else happens that was not even hoped for from the start—such as if someone digging a field finds a treasure, even though he was not digging for that purpose—these things are certainly not done by fate. There are also certain causes entirely unknown to men. For some things hung around the neck are said to cure certain diseases, for which we have no certain cause. It is also uncertain what cause the arts of wicked incantations might have. 

But besides these, there are some things called **contingencies** that can go either way, which we entirely deny happen by fate: such as moving a foot, raising the eyebrows, keeping silent, speaking, and innumerable other things of this sort which can in no way be said to happen by the fates. For that which is fated cannot admit the opposite. Furthermore, human counsel ought not to be entirely in vain. It would be in vain if we did by necessity whatever we do. Without a doubt, man possesses this above other animals: he does not follow his **imagination** <note>term: imagination (phantasia). Here, the raw mental impressions or impulses common to animals.</note> everywhere in the same way they do, but he possesses **reason**, by which he judges what ought to be done. By the use of this reason, he examines the things that have fallen into his imagination. If he approves by examining, he yields to the imagination and is then moved to act. But if he disapproves, he rejects and expels them, obeying reason. 

Thus, we are accustomed to deliberate only about those things which we can do or not do. If ever we commit something not by mature counsel but by headlong desire, we later accuse ourselves of the crime of rashness and of having despised counsel; we blame all who act rashly and exhort them to use counsel, as if the power of acting were within us. That the opinion held about fate is utterly false is evident from this: even the authors of such an opinion teach, learn, exhort, and give counsel; they even rebuke and punish their own people as if they were sinning by their own will. Therefore, even according to them, there is no such necessity of fate. 

Freedom, therefore, is naturally present in our nature for everyone. However, we concede that many things are not in our power, such as things that happen by nature or fortune, which no one would ever *dare* to say are subject to the fates. 

*Thus says Alexander. The philosopher Oenomaus relates almost similar things against Chrysippus, concluding that brute animals...*
