at any moment, things move by a certain appetite of their own as it happens, rather than by some necessary series of causes. This is much more the case for humans, who live by their own counsel; they can even use their own industry to change many causes to prevent them from combining to produce a certain effect. The philosopher Diogenianus <note>A 2nd-century Peripatetic philosopher known for his critiques of Stoic determinism.</note> confirms these same points in his book against Chrysippus <note>Chrysippus was a major Stoic philosopher who argued for a strict chain of fate.</note>. He proves that not everything happens by a necessary series of inevitably concurrent causes; rather, some things happen by a specific and singular nature, others by fortune, others by our own counsel, and others by the will of the gods. Ptolemy confirms this often elsewhere and in the *Quadripartitum* <note>original: "Quadripartito"; also known as the *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology.</note>, saying that effects proceed from God into the heavens and from the heavens among themselves in an indissoluble series; however, from the heavens toward inferior things, they do not always proceed inevitably or in the order begun in the sky. For they can be changed and hindered, sometimes by the resistance of inferior natures, and sometimes by human art and counsel together. Furthermore, in his book *On Judgments*, he says that humans do not always follow the general instincts established by the heavens because of the particular natures of locations and parents, and because of various customs and the opportunities of regions which specifically provoke or assist certain outcomes.

### Confirmation of the above by Bardesanes the Syrian, by others, and by Marsilio himself.

<margin>III</margin> Bardesanes the Syrian <note>A 2nd-century Gnostic and scientist often cited in the early church for his defense of free will against astrology.</note>, who they say was the wisest of all the Chaldeans in astronomy, disputes this in a long dialogue. He argues that while brute animals are driven individually to certain specific things by the instinct of nature, humans possess a mind in addition to natural instinct, and speech which is produced by the mind. By the gift of this mind, they are not entirely driven by nature; hence, the lives of men are varied. There is not just one way of eating as there is for beasts, nor the same clothing, nor similar customs and laws, nor a single simple desire for things; rather, by their own judgment, they make different choices and follow various ways of life. From this, he proves that man is not driven everywhere by nature, since nature is one in all people, yet their pursuits are diverse. He then recounts in a long list how different the laws of nations are, by which certain actions are prohibited or even permitted. These institutions are kept by them regardless of what hour they were born or to what region they have migrated; nor are they compelled to act otherwise by any position of the stars, either in their birth chart <note>original: "genesi"</note> or in the ruling place. It is as if the authority of laws and customs is firmer for the norm of living than the authority in the stars. After much more, he adds this: "All Jews, according to the Mosaic law, circumcise boys on the eighth day; they are not compelled to such a thing by the force of any star, nor forced by the nature of their region, nor are they ever led away by foreign customs to do otherwise. Indeed, wherever they are, they keep their law. This can in no way happen by the necessity of birth. For it is not possible for all Jews to have the same birth chart, such that being born at the same time they would similarly shed blood on the eighth day, or likewise rest on every seventh day." What shall we say about the sect of the Christians, who are found in every part of the world—indeed, in every city? Wherever they are, they cannot be forced to live by foreign laws and customs; nor will they follow the necessity of birth charts <note>original: "genethriaca necessitate"</note> or the command of some prince so that they think they should do what their Master judged unspeakable. Instead, they endure poverty, labors, ignominy, and intolerable tortures. Therefore, if everything were in our power, we would be the universe; but if we could do nothing, we would be the instruments of others and would do nothing by our own will. But by the will of God, nothing can be hindered; for all things are then subject to His power, He who granted something excellent to every nature. To man, He gave that exceptional gift: to use the freedom of will and judgment. Amidst this, he shows it is vain to divide the globe into seven climates <note>A traditional geographic division of the world into seven zones, each ruled by a planet.</note> and say one planet dominates in one climate and another in another, since laws are established everywhere by human virtue. For even if the world is divided into seven parts, in each part many laws are found—not just seven, like the seven planets; nor twelve, following the number of signs; nor thirty-six, following the number of the thirty-six "faces" <note>A 10-degree division of the zodiac in astrology.</note>; but he asserts that innumerable differences of laws are found, by whose institutions some live one way and others another, to whatever region they have migrated. Clement, a follower of the Apostles <note>Likely referring to Clement of Alexandria or the Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions.</note>, confirms the same things in almost the same words; the experience of morals confirms it as well. For where it is permitted to sin with impunity, people even sin with moderation; but where and when those who sin are more sharply punished, even those who are naturally instigated toward crimes are restrained. Often, also, because of greater or lesser opportunity and convenience, people sin more or less, or even act rightly. Aristotle and Plutarch confirm the same, especially by the authority of Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note>, whom they say wished to show how much law, custom, and education prevail over other things. He raised twin puppies from the same litter; to the extent that they were raised differently by Lycurgus, they turned out differently from one another. If education in brute animals overcomes the equality of birth and parents, much more can it overcome them in humans. Now, Plutarch shows in a long narrative how much custom and diligence can do, writing that many who were always weak by nature fulfilled their old age by diligence alone. I skip what he wrote about the poet Philetas, and Maecenas, and many others. Aristotle certainly writes that a certain Herodicus, a man of letters but very sickly, reached a hundred years of age by diligence in diet alone. Plato is also a witness to this in the *Republic*. But what need is there for witnesses? We ourselves have known similar things, and have often experienced the wonderful fruits of medicine and diligence, and how a great diversity in bodies, morals, and talents proceeds from different customs, education, and discipline. And what all Physicists <note>Natural philosophers or doctors.</note> approve, we have found to be true in many cases: that custom itself is a "second nature." We know that custom does not consist of such a natural necessity, but comes from public laws, morals, or private example and discipline, or from some fortune and opportunity, or from one's own counsel and opinion—or even from a gathering of all these. Often, moreover, the custom of a region and time and the example of someone excellent makes many musicians and poets, or orators and painters, or even hunters, rather than a certain birth chart. And when a birth chart begins something, it is nonetheless not completed except according to the capacity of those being born, and of the region and time. Often a military or royal house produces soldiers and kings rather than the birth chart doing so. By the imitation of good men, many daily become good; but by the imitation of the wicked, they become wicked, by whatever star they were born. Just as by contagion from one person many soon fall ill, infected not so much by the stars as by the poison of the contagion. What more? How much the capacity of a region and the instruction of men can do is declared by the fact that no star makes fishermen and hunters where there is no capacity or custom for fishing and hunting; and conversely, almost everyone born under any star fishes and hunts where opportunity, use, and need provide for it, and when and where people have become accustomed to eating animals—indeed, countless animals daily before the institution of na—

In the meantime, they are destroyed; on the contrary, the same animals grow old, regardless of the star under which they are said to be born. One may argue that similar things happen regarding the destruction of crops and fruits, at whatever time they grew together, according to human custom and desire, rather than a fated series. I myself observe the boundaries and aspects <note>The angular relationships between planets in an astrological chart.</note> of the planets daily and diligently explore what they portend. I pass over the fact that on a so-called "unfortunate" day, prosperity comes to many, and on a "fortunate" day, adversity happens to many. At any given moment, those who are struggling—some indeed overcome, while others are overcome. Certainly, the "unhappy" days of astrologers are often the clearest and most peaceful, while "happy" days are often the opposite. 

Indeed, I have experienced that the qualities of both bodies and souls are affected differently by variations in the air rather than by different aspects of the stars. Finally, I have found that the noted effects of the planets turn out very differently depending on the diversity of regions and people. If rain is promised, it rains much in one place, little in another, and not at all in yet another, according to regional differences. If discord or lusts are indicated, some are incited to these more vehemently, others more mildly, and others not at all. I see this happening differently not only because of the natural variety of bodies but also due to the diversity of ages, and indeed even the difference in education, discipline, habit, and opportunity. 

Finally, I am certain that daily events from the sky are not fulfilled exactly as if destined by celestial law, but happen differently here and there. If anything is of such importance for the distinction, it is from the very moment of birth, in which a certain quality from the sky is said to be infused into us. I similarly assert that this quality cannot be perfectly expressed in us according to the exact celestial rule, since many things below the sky—both from the beginning and daily—apply their own efficacy or passion to confuse this expression. Just as individual things have a nature far different from celestial things, so do all their meetings and progressions not entirely agree with celestial orders. 

Therefore, many things beneath the sky flow together in a way that is often different from what the celestial order would arrange, just as rational souls often act differently than what the supreme reason of God dictates. Many things also occur contingently, such as beauty and eloquence in a man at the same time. These two have no mutual order between them, from which it is clear they never flow together from a single determined cause. Yet from this concurrence, a greater public persuasion often arises. That a man is beautiful can happen from a certain cause. Likewise, that he is eloquent from a certain cause, albeit another. But that both exist at once, from whose meeting easy persuasion is born, seems to happen from no determined cause; otherwise, they would have a necessary mutual order. In reality, it happens by chance that a beautiful man is eloquent, and vice versa; and not because he is beautiful or white is he necessarily eloquent, nor the other way around. 

You cannot refer this and similar concurrences, as if they were fortuitous, to a determined cause. It is therefore false that everything proceeds from a certain determined cause. It is also false that, once a certain cause is established, the effect must necessarily follow immediately. For impediments fall from various quarters among inferior things, both because they conflict with each other and because they resist the celestial order, yielding more harshly and causing confusion, or flowing together by chance. To change natural things, there is added the movement of the living being as well as the counsel of rational nature—whether of one or many, and whether they agree or disagree. 

Therefore, since those two points on which the supporters of fate mostly rely are false, it is clear that not all things happen by fate—that is, by a necessary series of causes depending on the heavens. It is helpful to conclude the present dispute with a certain prophetic and royal authority. In the works of Synesius the Platonist <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a philosopher and bishop who wrote on the myth of Osiris.</note>, the King of the Egyptians—who was also, as he says, a prophet and highly skilled in divine matters—admonished his son Osiris as he handed over the empire. He told him to remove his brother Typhon <note>In this context, Typhon represents chaos or an "unjust fate."</note>, saying: "Take care to remove your brother as a kind of plague and unjust fate, if you think rightly; so that you may confront your unfavorable fate and that of all Egyptians, and by counsel prevent him from invading:

-> Concerning fate. <- <note>The Greek term is *heimarmene* (εἱμαρμένη), referring to the string of causes that determine destiny.</note>

Some things exist, others come to be. Those things that come to be, do so by a cause; and beyond immediate causes, we are often compelled to investigate more remote ones.
</margin>

**A** The order of those things which exist <note>The eternal, unchanging realities.</note> and those which come to be <note>The temporal, physical world.</note> must be of such a kind that either both exist and come to be through a cause, or both occur without a cause, or in both cases some things happen without cause and others from a cause. Or, perhaps all things that come to be **B** arise from a cause, while those that truly exist partly have a cause and partly do not. Or, perhaps nothing among existing things is traced back to a cause, or conversely, all existing things are from a cause. As for those things which come to be, perhaps some happen one way and some another, or none of them arise from a cause. In the first place, in the order of eternal things, those which are primary, by the very fact that they are primary, cannot be referred back to other causes; but those which depend on the first things receive their existence from them. You will also rightly distribute actions to individuals if you refer them back to their essences. For **C** their being consists in this: namely, producing an action of such a kind. But in the category of those things which come to be, or those which are indeed always but do not always produce the same action, it must be affirmed that everything happens according to causes. We must in no way admit that anything happens without a cause. To do so would clearly open the door to empty inclinations and accidents, or to the sudden motion of bodies proceeding with no preceding leader, **D** or to a rash and sudden impulse of the soul with nothing inciting the soul to do something it was not doing before. Perhaps from this very fact a greater necessity would constrain the soul—the fact that it is not in control of itself, but is carried along by such motions occurring without its will and without its own cause. For either something incited the soul to will something, whether it be from without or from within, or it provoked something to be desired; otherwise, if nothing to be pursued had moved it, **E** it would not have been moved at all in any way. But since all things happen according to causes, we can easily find the immediate causes for each thing and reduce the effects to them: for example, the immediate cause of going to the marketplace is

All things that come to be and that exist—either those things which come to be do so according to causes, and those that exist are also according to causes, or both are without cause; or some are without cause and some are with cause in both categories. Or all things coming to be are with cause, while of those that exist, some are with cause and some without cause. Or, they are not with cause; or conversely, all existing things are with cause, while of those coming to be, some are one way and some the other; or none of them are with cause. Now, regarding eternal things, one cannot lead the primary things back to other causes, precisely because they are primary. But as many things as depend on the first things, let them have their being from those. And if one assigns the activities of each, let him lead them back to their essences; for this is what "to be" is for it: to provide such an activity. But regarding things that are always coming to be, or things that always exist but do not always perform the same activity, one must say that all happen according to causes. <meta>This page continues the investigation into "Fate" (Heimarmene) from Ennead III, Book 1. The previous page established the philosophical problem: whether all things, some things, or no things are driven by a cause. Here, Plotinus explores the hierarchy of causes, moving from immediate human actions to universal theories like Atomism and Stoic Providentialism.</meta>

# BOOK ONE.

<column-break/>

**A** If one wishes to see what should be understood, it is generally the choice of this or that and the impulse to act. Then, there is the appearance to each person that they ought to do certain things. Furthermore, there are things that we do not attribute to the technical arts <term>arts (technai): refers here to specialized knowledge or skills like medicine or finance</term> such as the restoration of health being attributed to medicine or the doctor; or the acquisition of wealth to a found treasure, or a gift from someone, or earning money through labor or a craft. Similarly, a father is the cause of a child.
<margin>one thing coming after another <note>original: ἄλλο παρ' ἄλλο ἥκον</note></margin>
And there is the external cooperation toward procreation, **B** such as specific foods, or perhaps things older than life itself <note>referring to ancestral or cosmic influences</note>. Or generally, for the sake of procreation, a woman who is well-suited for childbirth. And we refer all these things to Nature.

<margin>II. Because immediate causes are not sufficient, higher causes are sought. From this arises the opinion concerning Fate, distributed into four viewpoints.</margin>
**C** To have progressed this far and then suddenly rest, not wishing to proceed toward higher causes, would perhaps be the mark of a lazy man, or one who has not lent his ears to those who ascend to sublime causes. For what is the cause, when the same conditions arise—such as the appearance of the moon—that one man should commit a robbery while another does not? Or when similar conditions come from the surrounding heavens or the air, one man falls ill while another does not? Indeed, from the same activities, one man becomes rich while another remains poor. Furthermore, various types of character, differing habits, and diverse fortunes warn us to investigate more remote causes.

**D** Therefore, since philosophers never wished to rest in immediate causes, those who posited corporeal principles <note>referring to the Atomists like Democritus and Epicurus</note>—such as atoms—making individual things through their motion, impacts, and mutual entanglements, said that things happen and exist in whatever condition those principles happen to combine, act, and suffer. They argue that our own impulses and dispositions are also such as those atoms produce.

**E** These thinkers, therefore, introduce this necessity into the principles themselves and into all things that arise from them. And whatever others say that bodies are principles and that all things are made from them, they undoubtedly believe that all things serve a certain necessity founded in these bodies.

**F** Others, however, ascending to the very principle of the universe, derive all things from it. They think that this first cause diffuses itself through all things and not only moves them but also creates each individual thing. This they call Fate <term>Fatum: the Latin translation of the Greek "Heimarmene," implying a string or chain of events</term>, considering Fate to be the most powerful cause moving all things. They believe not only that all other things happen because of it, but that our very thoughts proceed from its motions, just as in a living creature <note>original: *animal*</note> the individual parts are moved, not by themselves, but by that which holds the governing principle <term>principatum: the "hegemonikon" or ruling part of the soul in Stoic philosophy</term> in any animal. Others, furthermore, judge Fate to be the circuit of the whole world encompassing all things, creating each thing by its motion and by the mutual positions and configurations of the stars, both wandering <note>the planets</note> and fixed. Relying on predictions made through these celestial bodies, they believe that each thing arises from them.

**G** Someone might additionally describe Fate in another way, saying that it is a mutual embrace of causes, a connected series emanating from above, through which later things always obey prior things. These later things are reflected back into the preceding ones, as they are made through them and cannot be produced without them. Thus it is brought about that the following things are always tied to the preceding...

<column-break/>

**A** Judgment <note>original: *existimatio*</note> is that through which we decide that something must be found, or a debt must be collected, and generally to choose these or those things and pursue them. Finally, the cause is clearly the opinion in which it seems to someone that such things ought to be done. And we refer some things to the arts as causes, just as we refer recovery to medicine and the doctor. And we refer the cause of recently accumulated riches to a treasure found by chance, or a gift made by someone, or labors, or a money-making craft. Similarly, a father is the cause of a son, and whatever else contributes from the outside to procreating children: while clearly one thing proceeds from another;

**B** or things somewhat prior and more remote that contribute to generating sons, such as a woman being more suited for conception and birth. And we refer all this to nature.

PLOTINUS, ENNEADS BOOK III.

...serves. If someone distinguishes these in two ways, they will perhaps not wander from the truth. Some will think all things depend on one principle; others, however, will not. These views will be discussed in the following sections. For now, we must first debate with the primary theories, and then consider the statements of others in succession.

### It is certainly IMPOSSIBLE and absurd

<margin>
III
Neither are all things forced nor do they happen by way of bodies: neither Fate nor prophecy would exist if the principles of things were merely accidental.
</margin>
to entrust everything to bodily causes, whether to atoms <note>Refers to the Epicurean theory that the universe is made of tiny, indivisible particles.</note>, or to elements, or to subject order, reason, and the leading soul to the unorganized motion of bodies. It is especially impossible to subject things to atoms; many true arguments have been handed down to refute them. Even if someone were to propose such principles, it does not necessarily follow that Fate—either by some total necessity or by any other means—would result from them. Suppose first that atoms exist: these will move, some downwards (if indeed there is any "downward"), and others crosswise, wherever they happen to fall. There would be no order at all, since no order exists in them. The event itself, whenever it happens, would be entirely random. Therefore, there would be no prediction, no prophecy, nor any technical foresight. For how can there be any art <term>art (ars/techne): refers to any specialized branch of knowledge or skill based on rules, like medicine or navigation</term> in things that have no order? Nor could there be prophecy from divine inspiration or mental instinct. In these cases, too, the future must already be determined. Bodies would merely suffer whatever the atoms happen to strike them with by necessity. As for the actions of the soul—whether they happen through the descent or any incidental collision of atoms—to what atomic motions could you possibly attribute its passions? What kind of impulse in the soul could produce such rational discourses or such drives? Or how could rational sequences, impulses, or movements necessarily arise, or arise in any way at all from atoms? Furthermore, when the mind opposes the disturbances of the body, how do atoms contribute to that? Tell me again, by what differences in atoms are men compelled so that some become geometers, others arithmeticians and astronomers, and others wise? Entirely, the freedom of our will <note>original: "libertas arbitrij"</note> and our own work would be abolished, and along with it, the very essence of being a living creature. We would be carried wherever our bodies drag us, just like inanimate objects being pushed. The same arguments can be applied to those who believe other bodies are the causes of all things: such things might be able to heat us, cool us, or dissolve us—and anything else weaker than themselves—but the kinds of actions the soul produces cannot be done by them; these must come from another principle.

<margin>
IIII
There is not one single agent in the universe.
</margin>
BUT does a single soul running through all things perform every individual thing? So that any given thing is carried along as a part to wherever the whole leads? Do the subsequent causes then follow by necessity? And should we call this continuous connection of all things "Fate"? Just as in a plant that has its principle in the root, someone might call "Fate" the disposition spread from the root through all parts of the plant, governing them as it were, creating a mutual conspiracy and extension, even over the internal parts...

<meta>catchword: ...under the rule</meta>

<column-break/>

**A** ...he will appear to be speaking, and he has harmonized the truth again. And in this way, he would not miss the truth. For some suspend all things from one principle; others do not. This shall be discussed as follows. But now we must go to the first theories in our discourse; then we must examine the views of the others in order.

**B** To entrust everything to bodies—whether to atoms or to the so-called elements—and to give the leadership of order, reason, and the soul to their unordered movement, is in both ways absurd and impossible. It is even more impossible to speak of that which comes from atoms. Many true arguments have been spoken concerning these things. But even if one were to suppose such principles, it is not necessary that necessity follows for all things, nor that any kind of Fate follows. **C** Come now, first: let there be atoms. These, then, will move, some downwards (for downward exists), and some from the sides, as it happens, but according to others. Nothing would be consistent, as there is no order. And what happens then, happens entirely by chance. So there would be neither prediction, nor any prophecy at all, nor any art <margin> * either movement or bending back </margin> from chance. For how can there be art in disordered things? **D** Neither is there any art from divine inspiration and thought. For there, too, the future must be determined. And it will happen to bodies to suffer the impact of atoms, whatever those atoms carry by necessity. But as for the works of the soul, or its passions, to what movements of the atoms shall one attribute them? **E** For what kind of blow, whether from an atom falling downwards or from wherever it strikes, results in such reasonings or impulses, or in reasonings or impulses at all, * or in thoughts or in necessary actions, that are as they are? And what when the soul opposes the passions of the body? According to what movements of atoms will one man sit down to be a geometer, another an arithmetician, or another study astronomy? Or another be wise? For entirely, our own work and our being a living creature is destroyed, if we are carried along by bodies that lead us like soulless objects. **F** These same things apply to those who set other bodies as the causes of all things. Further, these things can heat us and cool us, and destroy things that are weaker. But no work of the soul—as many as the soul performs—could happen through these. But these must come from another principle.

**G** BUT does some one soul dwelling through the whole finish all things? Does it lead each thing by its movement as a part, or does it lead the whole? And do the causes follow from there by necessity? Is this Fate? Just as in a plant having its principle from a root, the internal management of all its parts, and their intertwining with one another, and the making...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s critique of determinism. On the previous page, he dismissed the idea that random atoms could create an ordered universe. Now, he addresses the "Chain of Causes"—the idea that everything is a single, interconnected web of necessity—and begins to examine the influence of astrology on human behavior.</meta>

BOOK ONE.

<margin>A</margin> ...both action and passion <note>original: *poiesin te kai pasan dioikesin mian*. In this context, Plotinus refers to the cosmic balance of "doing" and "undergoing."</note> contained within a single administration. Indeed, this excessive reliance on necessity and such a constitution of fate would utterly destroy fate itself, along with the sequence and interweaving of causes. Just as it is absurd to say that the movements within our own body parts are driven by a "fatal sequence" when they are moved by our **governing part** <term>governing part (hegemonikon): the highest, directing faculty of the soul or mind</term>, for it is not as if one thing hands over the motion and another receives it, having its own unique impulse; rather, it is that primary part which moves the leg. In the same way, if the "All" is one single thing, both acting and undergoing, and not one thing following another according to a chain of causes leading from one to the next, then it certainly would not be true that "all things happen according to causes," for all things would simply be **One**. Because of this, we ourselves would not truly be "us," nor would any work be ours. We would not be the ones reasoning; rather, our reasoning and our counsel would belong to something else. We would not be the ones acting, any more than our feet are said to "kick" by themselves; rather, we are said to kick *through* our feet as our parts. <margin>C</margin> However, it is necessary that each of us exists as a distinct individual, and that our actions and thoughts are truly our own. Each person's honorable or shameful deeds must proceed from that individual; it is not right to attribute shameful actions to the Universe.

<margin>D</margin> **PERHAPS**, however, individual things are not carried out in this way. <margin>Neither are we ruled by heaven, nor do other things happen only and necessarily by heaven.</margin> Rather, it is the celestial circuit that governs all things, and the movement of the stars that disposes each thing according to their mutual relations—their positions relative to the meridian, their rising, their setting, and their conjunctions. From these signs, those who practice divination predict what will happen to the universe and to every individual, not only regarding their fortune but even their very thoughts. We can see that other animals and plants are increased or diminished by the "sympathy" <note>original: *sympatheias*. The Stoic idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected and affect one another.</note> of these stars, and that they undergo all other things through them. Furthermore, different regions of the earth vary according to their relationship to the whole, and especially by their orientation to the sun. It appears that the nature of a place influences not only plants and brute animals, but also the physical appearance, size, color, temperament, desires, pursuits, and characters of human beings. Therefore, it seems that the authority over all things lies with the circuit of the universe. In response to these claims, we must first say that this argument, though in a different way, also subjects all our affairs—wills, passions, vices, and impulses—to external factors. <margin>F</margin> It assigns nothing to us, but considers us to be moved like **stones**, rather than as humans who possess a specific function of our own arising from our own nature. Yet, it is proper to grant what is ours to ourselves. We should recognize that while certain influences reach us from the universe, we are already distinct entities with our own nature. We must distinguish between what we ourselves do and <margin>G</margin> what we undergo by necessity; we must not grant everything to the heavens. We should believe that something is sent to us from the regions of the air and the diversity of the surrounding atmosphere, but these cosmic influences act upon things that already exist in their own right. They do not merely create the things themselves, nor do they impose qualities that are entirely contrary to the underlying nature of those things.

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK III.

<margin>
VI
Individual things here arise from their own natures more than from the heavens—whether a horse or a man—since they receive their quality from themselves during generation, even if they are signified by the heaven.
</margin>

...necessity that many things happen to us: for instance, in the **complexion** <term>complexion (krasis): the specific "mixture" of hot, cold, wet, and dry qualities in the body that was believed to determine health and temperament</term> of the body, heat and cold occur, and things also happen because of the condition of those who are being born. Is it not true that children are mostly born similar to their parents, both in form and figure, and also in certain passions of the irrational soul? Indeed, they are often similar in form because of the common nature of their location; yet we see a very great difference in their manners and thoughts, as if these things arise from some other principle.

B -> Furthermore, the resistance of reason against the bodily complexion and against lusts serves to similarly refute these astrological claims. But if they believe that because they can predict the future for individuals by looking at the positions of the stars, then the stars must be the *causes* of those events, they are mistaken. It would be just as if birds were said to be the causes of the things they signify <note>original: "aves eorum quae significant, causae forent." Plotinus refers to augury, where the flight of birds acts as a sign from the gods, but the birds themselves don't cause the events they predict.</note>; similarly, if everything that prophets foresee through their observations were said to be *caused* by the objects they look at. We can consider these same points more perfectly:

C -> the astrologer predicts things for a newborn, looking at the arrangement of the stars as it was established at the moment of birth. If they say these things are not merely *signified* by the present arrangement, but actually *caused* by it, they will often be proven wrong. For example, when they judge a noble lineage, saying the child is born of noble fathers or mothers: how can they say these qualities are caused by the stars when those qualities existed in the parents long before that specific arrangement of stars occurred? Indeed, the fortunes of the parents are often declared by the birth of their children. Again, they portend the future conditions and fortunes of children from the parents themselves, regarding those who are not yet born.

D -> From the horoscopes of brothers, they often predict the deaths of brothers; likewise, from women, they judge the fates of husbands, and vice versa. By what reasoning, then, does the star-arrangement belonging to one individual "make" those things which are already said to be certain to happen because of the condition of the parents? For either those prior conditions are the efficient causes, or if they are not the causes, then these stars will not be the causes either. Furthermore, the fact that a child's form is similar to their parents' proves that beauty and deformity proceed from the lineage itself, not from the motions of the stars. It is probable, moreover, that at the same time, all kinds of animals and humans are born together; in all of these, the exact same things ought to happen if they are under the same arrangement of stars. In what way, then, do humans and all other creatures arise differently through the same celestial figures?

F -> **BUT** surely, each thing happens according to its own nature. A horse is born because it comes from a horse, and a man because he comes from a man; moreover, a *certain type* of horse or man is born because he comes from a *certain type* of parent. The parent contributes something of its own to the offspring, even while conceding much to the generators and the generated. Let us grant that the celestial bodies provide much regarding the body, and these things are indeed of a bodily condition—heats, colds, and the resulting complexions of bodies. But in what way could they cause manners and studies, especially those which do not seem to obey the body's complexion? Such as someone being a grammarian, or a geometer, or a gambler, or the inventor of this or that thing?

G -> Now, how can the wickedness of character be given to humans by the celestial beings, who are gods? And if they teach <note>original: "κράτει σωμάτων δουλεύειν" (kratei somaton douleuein)</note> that we are "slaves to the temperament of our bodies"—for example, that one is a grammarian, another a geometer, another a gambler, or someone possesses a certain virtue—whence could a vice of character be given, seeing as the stars are gods? And in general...

<column-break/>

...having an effect on us, such as heat or cold in the mixture <note>original: "en te krasei"</note>. And there is also something regarding those being born. Certainly, children are born similar in form to their parents for the most part, and even in some of the passions of the irrational soul. And yet, while being similar in form, they differ greatly in their manners <margin>* from all things</margin>. This suggests that such qualities come from another principle. Furthermore, the change that is seen in thoughts, as they oppose the mixtures of the bodies or the desires, would be rightly mentioned here. But if, by looking at the relation of the stars <margin>* going to</margin>, they speak of the events concerning each person, and they claim these things are *made* by the stars, then in the same way, birds would be the makers of what they signify, as would all the things that seers look at when they make predictions. Therefore, one should examine these things more accurately: whether those things which someone attributes to the relation of the stars as it was when each was born, happen naturally because of the stars—as if the stars were not only signifying but also *acting*. Whenever they speak of nobility, as being from famous fathers or mothers, how is it possible to say that the stars "make" these things which already existed in the parents before this specific arrangement of stars occurred? Indeed, they even predict the fortunes of parents from the birth of children; and they speak of the freedom of children—what kind it will be and what fortunes they will encounter—from the fathers, concerning those yet to be born. And from brothers, the deaths of brothers; and from wives, things concerning husbands. And again, from these, those things. How then does each person's relation to the stars *make* these things, which are said to come from parents or those next in line? For either those things prior to the stars were the makers, or if those did not make them, neither did these. Furthermore, the similarity in form to the parents suggests that beauty or ugliness comes from home, from the lineage. But if all things come from the movement of the stars, it is irrational that at the same times and simultaneously, all sorts of animals and humans are born together <margin>* others</margin>. To all of these, the same things ought to happen, since they have the same star-relation. How then is one a human, and others something else, through the same celestial configurations?

**BUT** indeed, each thing is born according to its own nature: for a horse comes from a horse, and a man from humans; and a certain kind comes from a certain kind. Let the movement of the whole be a co-worker, or something that yields much to the things being born. And let the stars give many things to the bodies in a bodily way: heats and colds, and the resulting mixtures of bodies. How then do they instill manners and pursuits, especially those that do not seem to be slaves to the mixture of the body: such as being a grammarian, or a geometer, or a gambler, or possessing a certain virtue? But as for wickedness of character, <unclear>from where</unclear> could it be given, since the stars are gods? And in general...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into whether the stars are causes of human events or merely signs. On the previous page, he suggested that while astrology can predict the future, the heavenly bodies themselves are not "evil" or "good" in their intent toward us. He now expands on the idea of the universe as a readable text and moves into a critique of absolute determinism.</meta>

# BOOK ONE.

**A** In general, wherever the stars are said to "give" evil—specifically when they are said to be "made evil" because they are setting or passing beneath the earth—it is as if they themselves were suffering some change. But if they set in relation to us, they are nevertheless always being carried through the celestial sphere, and as far as they are concerned, they look upon the earth in the same unchanging way. Nor should it be said that one of the gods <note>Plotinus, like many of his time, refers to the planets as "gods," viewing them as divine, ensouled beings.</note> becomes better or worse simply because he looks at another god from a different position. It is wrong to think they only do us good when they are "well-disposed" and harm us when "ill-disposed." It is better to say that the heavenly bodies run their courses for the safety of the whole universe, but in the meantime, they provide another use: those who look upon them as if they were **letters**—provided they know this kind of "literacy"—may read the future. Using these celestial figures, they can track meanings through a certain logical analogy. **B** It is just as if one were to say that a bird flying high in the air signifies certain "high" or noble actions.

<margin>
VII
Those who introduce Fate as a necessary path for things, leading inevitably to every single act; and whether there is any room for chance or freedom in their plan.
</margin>
<margin>
How he says the future is revealed through configurations. <note>original Greek: ὅπως λέγει τὰ μέλλοντα δηλοῦσθαι διὰ τῶν σχηματισμῶν</note>
</margin>

**C** IT REMAINS for us to consider the opinion which claims that all things are intertwined and connected, from which a specific condition is assigned to every individual. This view posits a single Principle from which all things are generated through **seminal reasons** <term>seminal reasons (rationes seminales / σπερματικοὶ λόγοι): In Stoic and Neoplatonic thought, these are the "rational seeds" or formative blueprints that exist within the soul of the world, directing the growth and destiny of all material things.</term>. This opinion is very similar to the one that says every habit and motion—both our own and that of the universe—proceeds from the Soul of the World. **D** Even if someone wishes to grant us individuals some credit so that we might effect something by ourselves, this view still holds an absolute necessity for all things. Indeed, once all causes are grasped together, it becomes impossible for any single thing not to happen. For there is nothing else remaining that could either prohibit it or compel it to happen differently, if indeed all things are encompassed by Fate. When things are such that they flow from a single Principle, nothing else remains for us but to be carried wherever those causes drive us. For even our **imaginations** will follow antecedent causes, and our **impulses** will follow those imaginations. Then, "freedom of will" becomes an empty name. **E** For we will not have more "will" simply because we ourselves approach something with an impulse, since every impulse is stirred up by what came before it. Our "agency" would be the same as that of other animals, infants, or the insane, who run about driven by certain blind stings. **F** For even in these, there are impulses. And by Jupiter <note>A common classical exclamation, here translating "per Iouem."</note>, there is a nearly identical impulse in fire, and in all things which, serving their own condition, are hurried along by its instinct. All who look clearly at this see no doubt in it; but those seeking other causes for this impulse do not rest at this as a starting point.

<margin>
VIII
How the soul is above fate, in fate, and under fate.
</margin>
<margin>
* seminal reasons (Greek: σπερματικοὶ)
* motion (Greek: κίνησιν)
* becoming (Greek: γενομένης)
</margin>

**G** WHAT other cause then remains besides these? One which, by its arrival, leaves nothing without a cause, preserves the sequence and order of things, yet allows us to be something ourselves, and does not destroy the validity of predictions and oracles. It is necessary, then, to introduce the **Soul** as this other principle into the order of things. Not only the Soul of the Universe, but also the soul of each individual along with the Soul of the All. This is no small principle for weaving all things together. For the soul does not arise from "seeds" like other things, but is ranked as a **primary cause** in the generation of effects. Therefore, when it lives apart from the body, it is most truly mistress of itself—free and outside the power of the **cosmic cause** <note>original Greek: κοσμικῆς αἰτίας. Plotinus argues that while our bodies are part of the physical machine of the universe, our higher soul remains independent.</note>.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of human agency versus the influence of the stars and Fate. On the previous page, he discussed how celestial bodies serve as signs. ### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III.

power: but when it is infused into the body, it no longer has the authority to dominate or its liberty in all things: because it has now been arranged together with other things. Regarding **Fortune**—namely, those surrounding circumstances into which the soul falls when it enters the midst of the world—these can do quite a lot, even to the point that the soul does many things because of the circumstances. Some things, however, it may do by its own command, according to whatever it has decreed. Indeed, the soul dominates in more matters if it is better, and in fewer if it is worse. For it is either compelled to desire or be angry by obeying the temperament <term>complexio: the physical makeup or balance of humors in the body</term> of the body, or it becomes humble by succumbing to poverty, or it swells with pride by admiring riches, or it exercises tyranny while exulting in power. But a soul relying on the goodness of its own nature, if it falls into these same conditions, resists and dominates them; it changes them rather than being changed by them: and partly it alters things, and partly it permits them without blame.

<margin>
IX
How the soul exists within Fate and how it acts; also concerning the contingency of things.
</margin>

Therefore, those things are **NECESSARY** which are accomplished through a combination of purpose and fortune. For what else could exist besides these? When all causes are taken together, they determine everything completely. Among those causes that are external, we count whatever the motion of the universe contributes to the work along with the following causes. Therefore, whenever the soul acts or approaches something having already been changed by external factors, using a kind of **blind motion**, we ought not to call such an action or affection voluntary and free. Similarly, this is true when the soul, becoming worse through its own nature, does not use right or primary principles for its motions. But whenever it approaches a task having **pure reason**—free from passion—as its own guide, we must judge this approach alone to be within our own judgment and truly free. This is our own work, which is not drawn from elsewhere but from within, from the pure soul: a soul, I say, proceeding from a first, primary, and proper principle, not wandering because of ignorance, nor overcome by the violence of lusts. For when lusts occupy the soul too vehemently, they lead and drag it; they no longer permit actions to be in our power, but rather turn them into passions <note>In this context, "passions" (passiones) refers to things that happen to us or that we suffer, rather than things we actively do.</note>.

<margin>
X
The intellectual nature acts freely: but its effect is sometimes hindered in reason.
</margin>

**REASON** finally concludes in summary that all things are signified and occur according to causes. However, these causes are twofold: partly pertaining to the soul and partly to the surrounding circumstances. Furthermore, when souls act according to right reason, they do everything from themselves; in other cases, they are hindered from executing their own work and thus "suffer" or are acted upon rather than acting. For this reason, when a soul lacks prudence, one must think there are other causes at play, and it might be said correctly that such actions happen according to **Fate**—especially by those who think Fate is an external cause. But we should believe that all the best things are done by ourselves: for we are of the highest nature when we are alone <note>Plotinus refers to the "solitude" of the soul when it is detached from bodily distractions and focused on the divine.</note>. Finally, it is fitting to judge that the virtuous act and do honorable things freely from themselves; others, however, act freely and honorably only insofar as they have "caught their breath" and been liberated from external pressure. Nor do they obtain wisdom from elsewhere whenever they are wise, but rather they use it as soon as they are no longer hindered from using it.

<column-break/>

<margin>* authority <note>original Greek: ἐξουσία (*exousia*)</note></margin>
* ...once they have been brought into a body, the soul is no longer entirely sovereign, as it has been ranked with other things. **Fortune** refers to all the things in the surroundings which the soul encounters when it comes into the center of the world; these surroundings lead it in many ways, so that it does some things because of them, but other things it does by mastering them, leading them wherever it wishes. It masters more things if it is better, and fewer if it is worse. For either by the temperament of the body it is taught to desire or be angry, or it is enslaved by necessities, or made humble by poverty, or vain by riches, or a tyrant by power. But the soul, from its own nature, resists these things if it is good by nature, and it changes them rather than being changed itself. Thus, it alters some things and concedes to others, but not out of wickedness.

Necessary things, therefore, are all those that occur when choice <note>original Greek: προαιρέσει (*proairesei*)</note> and fortunes are mixed. For what else could one say exists? When all causes are taken, all things happen by all means. Among external things, some result from the movement of the universe. Therefore, when the soul is altered by external things and acts or moves as if using a **blind impulse**, the action and the disposition should not be called voluntary. This is also true when the soul is worse by its own doing and does not use right or leading impulses everywhere. But when it moves having **Reason** as its own pure and dispassionate leader, we must say that this impulse alone is "up to us" and voluntary; this is our own work, which does not come from elsewhere but from within, from the pure soul, from a first and sovereign principle. It is not an error born of ignorance, nor is it overcome by the force of desires, which approach and drag the soul. Such things no longer allow for "actions," but are rather our "passions" <note>things we undergo rather than things we do.</note>.

**FINALLY**, Reason says that all things are signified and happen according to causes, but these causes are twofold: some by the soul, others by external causes in the surroundings. When souls act, whenever they act according to right reason, they act of themselves. <margin>* whatever they do</margin> * when they act. But in other matters, they are hindered from doing their own work. They are acted upon rather than acting. Thus, a lack of wisdom is caused by other factors. In such cases, it is perhaps correct to say they act according to **Fate**—at least for those who believe Fate is an external cause. But the best things come from us. For we are of this nature when we are alone, or when we do virtuous things, and honorable acts are within our power. <margin>* but for others</margin> * but for others, they act honorably only insofar as they can breathe and are permitted. They do not receive wisdom from elsewhere when they are wise, but only uncover it.

ON BOOK II OF ENNEAD III.

# MARSILIO FICINO’S
# COMMENTARY ON THE SECOND BOOK OF THE THIRD ENNEAD, ON PROVIDENCE.

->SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.<-

---

->Order in the world does not happen by chance.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing a figure surrounded by scrolling foliage.</image-desc>
We are accustomed to attribute **chance** only to those things which are able to be other than they are. However, the possibility for things to be "otherwise" arises solely from the indeterminate nature of **matter**, which is always sliding from one thing to another, and not from the nature of **form**, which always determines a thing toward something certain. But in the order of the universe, there is both primary matter—which does not come from other matter—and forms that exist naturally in themselves; these forms cannot arise from matter either. Therefore, neither these substances nor the distinction between them can occur by chance. For perhaps the distinction of certain individuals, separated from one another only by the division of their physical bulk, might happen by some accident. But the distinction of the species themselves, which is a **formal** distinction <note>original: "formalis" — referring to the essential 'Form' or blueprint of a species in Platonic thought</note>, cannot possibly have happened by any stroke of luck.

It is necessary that things were produced from the beginning along with their specific distinctions; indeed, there are many things in the universe that are neither generated from each other nor from some common source, since they do not share the same matter. Therefore, neither this formal distinction nor the production of things could have happened by any chance—especially since a cause that exists **through itself** <term>per se: a cause that acts by its own nature rather than by accident</term> is prior to one that exists **by accident**. Since, therefore, later things proceed mostly from a cause determined "through itself," it is wrong to say that the primary things arose from a fortuitous cause, or that a most unstable "luck" was the principle of stable things. On the contrary, it is necessary that the unstable is always ruled and led by the stable, and organized in its movements.

Furthermore, since it has been proven elsewhere that the universe is made by the **Divine Intellect**—which is evident from the highly skillful order of things characteristic of intelligence—it is necessary that the common form of the universe was already devised by the intelligence of God and then established by His will, which no outcome can frustrate. Since, therefore, the form of the world is not outside the intention of the agent <note>The "agent" here is the Creator or Divine Intellect</note>, it rightly does not happen by chance. Moreover, since the form of the whole consists in the distinction and order of its parts, that very distinction of things could not be fortuitous. Finally, that which is best in a work must rightly be judged as the end <note>The "end" or *telis* refers to the ultimate purpose or goal</note> of the work. The "best" of the entire world is located in the mutual order of its parts. But order cannot exist without distinction; through such order, the world is established in its integrity, which is its greatest good. Thus, the order of the parts of the universe and their distinction is the "best" end of its production; for this reason, the order and distinction of things cannot have happened by chance.

->Worldly order does not proceed from matter.<-

If the distinction of species does not result from chance, it follows that it does not result from matter either. Since matter is naturally indeterminate toward many things, if anything were to come from it, it would flow out by chance—especially if no intention of a higher agent were introduced. If you say that materials are diverse and therefore various forms proceed from them, you are forced to admit that materials—having the most imperfect condition of being—rightly depend not on themselves, but on a higher principle. Therefore, they receive both their existence and their distinction from elsewhere. Thus, matter is not the primary cause of distinction in the world: especially because many things are distinct from each other that do not consist of matter at all. Even matter itself is separated from immaterial things not by other matter, but by nature. Added to this is the fact that since any agent acts through **form**, it intends the form as its goal. Therefore, forms were not introduced into the universe for the sake of matter; rather, matter exists so that natural forms may exist, and materials are affected here and there so that such forms may come to be.

The distinction of things according to species is through forms. This distinction, therefore, should not be referred to matter as the primary cause, but matter should be referred entirely to forms. Matter is moved in various ways by a cause that acts through form and intends form; and rightly so, since matter is of lower value than form. Forms are not referred to matter as an end, but conversely, matter is referred to forms, while it is both made and moved and affected in certain ways by the form of the supreme agent. Therefore, formal distinction in the universe proceeds not primarily from the condition of matter, but from the intention of the Author. Whatever follows matter declines toward the "deformed" rather than the "formal," or if it follows the division of physical quantity, it does not change the specific form of the species.

->Worldly order is not from a diversity of principles.<-

If someone, marveling at the diversity of things, should therefore introduce a diversity of "primary agents" as the cause, they must consider whether those diverse agents have an order between themselves or not. If they share a common order, they possess this from a single higher source. From that source they exist, they are distinct, and they are united; to which the distinction of all things is finally reduced as to a cause. But if those agents are said to have no order and to meet by chance, then no perpetual order would be preserved in things.

->The order of things does not happen only from the succession of things, but from the intention of the One.<-

There are those who cannot derive the diversity of multiple things from one immediate cause, but think that the multitude grows step by step: from one into two, from two into three or four. They believe that because the **First Cause** is entirely simple and absolutely one, it makes only one thing, which—being unable to equal the parity of its cause—slides into potentiality and action. But while this opinion assigns determined causes to individual effects, it cannot assign one cause to the entire universe of things; instead, it imagines the whole results from a gathering of all causes, and thus happens by a kind of fortuitous luck. Accordingly, that which is best in the universe—namely, the common...

u 4

<summary>Marsilio Ficino argues that the universe's complex order and the distinction between species cannot be attributed to chance or matter, but must originate from a single, intelligent Divine Architect. He refutes the idea that physical matter or multiple competing principles could produce the stable, purposeful harmony observed in the cosmos.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on the second book of Plotinus’s third Ennead, focusing on Divine Providence. The previous page established that the formal distinctions between species cannot arise by chance; this page extends that argument to the purposeful design found throughout the natural world.</meta>

COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

the highest good, consisting in the order of all parts and their distinction, must be referred back to the best cause of those things that exist. Thus, the distinction and arrangement of things proceeds not merely from the subsequent levels of causes, but from the providence of the <term>Primary Cause</term> <note>original: "prima causa" — In Neoplatonic thought, this refers to the One or God, the ultimate source from which all reality flows.</note>. For who would not see it as an impiety to reduce this very thing, which is the best in all things, to a certain defect of causes? Namely, to suggest that a following cause degenerates from the simplicity of the prior cause. Now indeed, if the complete arrangement of the world, which is placed in the order of all its parts—just as order consists in distinction—if, I say, such an arrangement, as the ultimate form of the world, its greatest and most formal gift, and the end of all things, rightly corresponds to the Primary Cause, then it is only right that the causes following after God serve this arrangement. Therefore, this does not result, as if by chance, from the gradual action of subsequent causes; rather, to establish or preserve this arrangement, the subsequent causes do whatever they do as if toward an end prescribed for them by the mind of the Primary Cause. Indeed, if the arrangement of things is designed in that mind, then certainly all things are necessarily described there. And if that intelligence is most effective, many things can proceed from it simultaneously: especially because divine power can both act upon many things through a single act, and, being immense, is not limited to one thing. The simpler it is, the more (so to speak) it is united and stronger, and more powerful for procreating many things. Finally, since there are many things which, because of the wondrous simplicity and perfection of their essence, cannot proceed from anywhere else but directly from the Primary Cause, it is necessary that the arrangement of distinct things follows from the providence of the Primary Cause. Since His intelligence is capable of many things, and understands what it can do, it produces a work most like itself only if it creates something manifold and varied. The work itself represents the immense abundance of the cause in its many parts, which it cannot represent in only one or a few. And since in God there is both goodness and the diffusion of goodness, God is most aptly reflected in the divine work: if it is good, and exists in substance, and is spread out widely into other things. This diffusion, indeed, cannot happen unless a diversity and inequality of things exists—inequality, I say, according to species. For in this way, there will be a most perfect and most formal multitude in the world if there are as many species as possible.

### The ends of things and their motions declare that they are made, arranged, and moved by divine providence.

Furthermore, it is well established among physicians and other natural philosophers that if the assignment of an "end" or purpose is removed, the causes of natural arrangements and motions cannot be assigned in anything. Therefore, the entire arrangement of nature and the logic of science will perish if a certain end is not destined for natural effects. Many things are surely found in any given thing which would be both superfluous and burdensome—indeed, they could not even come to be—unless they were moved by the intention of a certain end, by which the parts in any thing serve each other in turn, and all parts comply with the form itself and the good of the whole. Tell me, please, why do vines not grow on the harder plants, but sprout on the more tender ones? Is it not because these latter ones alone need a support to which they may be bound by the vines? Thus nature neither allows for the superfluous nor lacks the necessary in any place. Thus the vine is stretched out like a hand, especially in that part where a support is perceived; as long as no support is offered, the vine is extended in length; as soon as one is given, the vine immediately entangles itself with it. Does nature not seem here to have a mind, and hands, and eyes? Tell me then, since the end itself moves the other causes and therefore in a way precedes them all (as appears in art and deliberate planning), where does the end precede in nature, toward which natural things are destined? Surely, since it does not precede in matter, it precedes in the mover of matter; for to set an end before those things which are directed toward that end, and to preserve a perpetual order, is the proper characteristic of reason. Therefore, there is a supreme reason of natural things in the mover of matter. If this reason commands the parts in any whole to serve each other and recalls them to the good of the whole as to an end, how much more does it accommodate various wholes to each other everywhere and lead them, as parts of the universe, toward the good of the universe, never allowing a vacuum to occur anywhere. And for the sake of this deity, as if by the intention of an end, it performs wonders everywhere; it moves and stops natural impulses beyond the measure of nature, like a leader far superior to nature. I pass over for now how wonderfully it transfers light things downward and heavy things upward, contrary to the condition of the elements, for the good of a living creature; and with what marvelous art it shapes everything. I pass over with what great caution it restrains the water, which by the proper order of the elements seems likely to overwhelm the whole earth, from completely covering the land, for this very reason alone: that many species of things may be generated on the earth. I pass over how opportunely members and instruments and all necessary things are provided everywhere for all things that are born, and how they are protected by divine power in various and diverse ways, and even how wonderfully they are adorned beyond necessity. In summary, however, since in art and planning the "end" is nothing other than some limit toward which the intention of the agent is chiefly moved and in which it finally rests, certainly a similar end is prescribed for natural motions. For things do not come to be from just anything, nor are they moved toward just anything, nor do they come to be in just any way; but all things happen in certain ways, always and in like manner, as things that are neither heaped together rashly nor wander by fortune. Thus heat, by the supreme reason of its mover, seeks a place suitable for itself where it may be preserved, flees what is unsuitable, and flees cold—sometimes even beyond the measure of its own nature—lest it be extinguished by opposites. Since, therefore, the motions of natural things everywhere seek a certain limit in which they may rest, and similarly the compositions of natural things, from which certain motions are produced, are arranged for the sake of certain limits, it follows that natural things are made and moved by an art more excellent than human crafts, just as they are directed toward an end more skillfully than crafts. And just as the most perfected art in us no longer deliberates but acts as if by the mode of nature, so the natural and divine art, although it acts by reason and for the sake of an end, nevertheless requires no discourses of reason, which a consummate art does not need; especially if human art were imagined not to handle matter from the outside (as it is now said to do), but to be stirred and shaped within, in the manner of divine art.

### How this world is made from the higher world, and how it descends; the nature of the intelligible world.

<margin>I</margin>
I. What is said in the first chapter: "If God at some time made the world anew, therefore He previously deliberated whether and how He should make it," does not follow. It only follows that we are able to think that God deliberated in this way; which is not allowed to be thought if it is posited that the world never had a beginning in time. Secondly, note that the first essence, life, and mind—which are the same—is the cause of the world, namely the efficient and <term>exemplary cause</term> <note>original: "exemplarem" — the blueprint or ideal pattern after which a thing is modeled.</note>, while the final cause is the Good. The world is made from that source because the world is that source itself, just as fire is made from fire. In the corporeal world, the formal order is one thing, and dimension and motion are another. If, therefore, you take away dimension and motion but leave the order, you are contemplating the Mind that is the craftsman of this world; in which, indeed, are the levels of all forms,

<meta>catchword: since indeed (siquidem)</meta>

He compares nature to a supreme form of art that operates from within matter, reflecting the perfect patterns found in the Divine Mind.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's *Enneads*, specifically Book II of the Third Ennead.
