since indeed it is a formal order. But because there is neither motion nor time there, nothing has passed into the past for a present form, nor is anything missing in the future. Furthermore, because there is no dimension—through which one part is usually distant from another—all things are present in every part. Therefore, every form is "omniform" <note>original: "omniformis" — the Neoplatonic idea that in the divine mind, every individual idea contains the essence of all other ideas simultaneously.</note>, though in different ways. For formal distinction itself is not removed, even if dimension and time are taken away. For even where there is dimension and motion, many quite different qualities exist together in the same thing, and all are present in any part of it. Since, therefore, in the intellectual world all things are in each thing, and thus nothing is lacking to anyone, there is rightly no motion there, no impulse from one thing to another, and no injury or new generation. For it does not allow some things to be contrary to others within the one containing whole. Indeed, even if they were contraries, one would not make an impulse against the other, since nothing is lacking to anyone, and each thing is entirely in <term>act</term> <note>original: "in actu" — a state of full realization or completion, as opposed to "potential."</note>, so that nothing further can be produced from it. In short, because motion is proper to the corporeal heaven, while stillness is proper to the incorporeal, it follows that just as this physical heaven acts and generates more on earth the more it moves, so that higher realm creates this whole world more truly the more it remains still, and in this stillness, it accomplishes all things.

### How this world arises from the higher world and how it descends.

11 In what way, then, does this world proceed from that one? Indeed, just as from any simpler seed a manifold sprout naturally blossoms everywhere, the fertility of that higher world results in a vast progression in this one. Its immense power becomes ample dimension here; that vigorous act passes into motion, and eternity into time. Therefore, from the distance of both form and position, discord arises; from division comes lack; from both come appetite, motion, and impulse. Since all of nature comes from the Good, and therefore its intention is never toward evil but toward good, natural things certainly do not act against each other out of hatred to destroy what is foreign, but out of need and love of themselves, so that they may form and refresh themselves from elsewhere. Since the primary nature in every genus produces by itself the things that follow in that genus (being most fertile), much more does the <term>Primary Essence</term> <note>God or the One</note> require no help beyond its own essential life to generate the essences and lives of things; rather, by that very life by which it lives, all other things receive their essence and life. If it is said to create through intelligence and will, nothing is added from outside for that reason. For there, intelligence and will are nature itself. Therefore, insofar as nature acts, it acts by necessity; but insofar as nature there is intelligence, it also acts by will. Since it acts both through a voluntary nature and a natural will, it certainly does not need inquiry or counsel to act. 

Thus, if you distinguish essence and intelligence by reason, you will see the matter of this world flowing from Essence, and form flowing from Intelligence. And just as essence is thought to precede intelligence in a certain order there, so here you will think of matter preceding form. But before that Intelligence provides a corporeal form to the world—which is distant from it—it presents an incorporeal form close to itself: namely, its own life, procreating the <term>World Soul</term> <note>original: "anima mundi" — the mediating spirit that connects the divine mind to the physical universe.</note> as a medium between essence and intelligence. This creates a vegetative life capable of intelligence, also acting as a medium between corporeal matter and form, just as life there holds the middle ground between essence and intelligence. And this very thing is the <term>Seminal Reason</term> <note>original: "ratio seminaria" — the formative "blueprints" or "seeds" of logic that organize matter.</note> of the world, and like a certain "word" of divine intelligence, by which matter, having been struck, receives its worldly adornment. When you read, "Intellect infuses reason into matter," interpret it to mean not just the simple Intellect itself, but also the <term>Animal Intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus animalis" — the intellect as it functions within the World Soul.</note>, which is formed by the first Intellect. For from the first, through the second, and by the power of the first, a genital power blossoms into matter, depending on the essence of both. Similarly, it is often said: "The Sun generates natural things," yet it does this with the light flowing from it. There, the solar light and the radiance together effect these things through heat. He compares both Intellects to the male, for he generates as one separate from the offspring. But the seminal nature of the world he compares to the power of the male's seed, for both act from within. He compares the world to the generated offspring. For everywhere the members are now distributed among themselves, and parts are now clashing, which in the seed were together and did not fight. The world indeed consists of "necessity"—that is, matter and the defect occurring from matter. Likewise, it consists of "intelligence"—that is, the formal order reflecting intelligence. It is resolved into its innermost parts, namely, into matter and the seminal and formal reason. But the essence of the intellectual soul itself is not an innermost part of the world, but presides over it.

### Four worlds after the Good: Intellectual, Animal, Seminary, and Sensible; and how progression and judgment occur.

III If anything offends you while considering the world, do not accuse God, as if He did not consult well or choose rightly regarding the world's construction. For He does not need counsel; nature itself acts sufficiently. Again, do not accuse nature in the first principle of things. For it is goodness itself, and by its goodness, it performs a work that is simply the best: namely, the intellectual world. And it does this by its primary purpose. For if it acts by goodness, it also acts by will. For in the first principle, will concurs with goodness. Therefore, the First wills the intelligible world by (so to speak) a primary will. But the <term>Animal World</term> <note>The world of the Soul/Living things</note> which follows next from the intelligible, He wills in a way by necessity—by the <term>necessity of consequence</term> <note>meaning it follows naturally and logically from the first act, like a shadow follows a body.</note>. For it is not hidden from Him that the second work follows the first, nor does He reject it, yet He does not approve it in the same way as the first. Similarly, that intellectual world generates the animal world not by counsel, but by nature. Since its nature is intelligence, and intelligence is will, while nature acts, intelligence and will also act. I say it wills the animal world primarily, and consequently also the <term>Seminary World</term> <note>The realm of biological growth and natural laws</note> within nature, which it knows must necessarily follow the animal. By the same reasoning, the animal world—that is, the intellectual soul—generates life and genital nature through a certain natural intelligence and will: namely, the seminary world, the final vestige of the divine. By the necessity of consequence, it also generates the <term>Sensible World</term> <note>The physical world we see and touch</note> following the seminary; following, I say, from the seminary world using only life itself to effect this, but not the intelligence or will which it lacks. For it acts by living, just as the intellectual soul and the first intellect act by understanding. And in turn, the intellect naturally creates by understanding in the manner of nature, just as nature generates by living and builds by the order of intelligence. Therefore, do not attempt to estimate or weigh the dignity of the marvelous Good itself, or of the pure Intellect, or of the Animal Intellect solely from this sensible world. Instead, from the sensible world, infer the dignity of the Seminary; from this, the nature of the Soul; from the Soul, the excellence of the Mind; and finally, from the Mind, the Good. Then, in contemplating the sensible world, do not fix your gaze on the parts, but behold the whole. Do not refer the whole to the parts, but the parts to the whole. Do not demand that this work be simply the "best," but the best as...

Ficino is transitioning from discussing the intellectual realm to the physical world and the role of souls and "demons" (mediating spirits) in the cosmic order.</meta>

...as far as it takes its steps, and the nature of the fourth world after the Good <note>The "Good" refers to the Platonic "One," the ultimate source of all existence.</note>. You will note, meanwhile, where the world is represented as speaking: since in the lowest globe of the world there are many kinds of living things, there are also many above throughout the whole, vast and immense in power and magnitude according to the dignity and width of the space. The first of these he calls gods, the second demons, and the third particular souls, which are transformed into demons. And where he places "peoples of demons," he shows that throughout the whole world above us, flocks of demons are distributed, having their own leaders who follow the stars like kings. For the bodies of demons everywhere above us follow the motions of the stars with their own motion, performing a dance everywhere. They also imitate the stars in power, size, shape, and manner of acting; and just as the stars act by the gaze of their rays, they follow an effective imagination. You will note, moreover, that ether is "ignited air" <note>original: "aerem ignitum" — Ficino follows the ancient view that the upper atmosphere (ether) was a finer, more fiery version of air.</note>. Likewise, you will note that all things hang upon the Good, since all things desire the Good. Finally, life itself is simply mind itself; he says that the intellectual nature alone possesses the whole of life. Thus you will conclude that any degree of things participates in life to the extent that it possesses something intellectual. 

That the world is made by God not through deliberation, but through nature, Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher and student of Plotinus who edited his works.</note> confirms in his commentary on the *Timaeus*: "Human arts indeed require instruments, because they do not preside over all matter, nor do they dominate it entirely, and they work from the outside. But natural powers, because they are both more perfect and internal, perform whatever they do merely by their very <term>being</term> <note>original: "esse" — the state of existence or essence. In Neoplatonism, the higher the being, the more it creates simply by existing rather than by 'working.'</note>. Thus it is for all things, and thus the soul, being always essential life, nourishes, increases, generates, breathes, feels, and so on. Even the imagination, being very powerful, immediately affects the body with various qualities and motions by a certain act of its own. Furthermore (as the theologians relate), demons do wonders everywhere by their imaginations without instrument or act, suddenly as they wish, emitting most effective rays from there, and often showing wonderful forms outside themselves through the motions of their imagination to those who are able to look upon such things. Much more does the Maker of the world, by His very being—that is, by His very understanding—provide substance to the universe: the indivisible One providing for the divisible world. For who should wonder that the corporeal is propagated from the incorporeal? Indeed, from a very small seed a vast animal often sprouts, composed of so many, so great, and so diverse limbs. Yet even in a small seed, the <term>seminal reason</term> <note>original: "ratio seminalis" — the latent "blueprint" or formative power within matter that guides its development.</note> itself is not small while it produces great things; nor is it large, since it flourishes whole in every particle of the seed. But while the seminal reason requires matter, the divine reason requires nothing, but crafts all things; and while it remains in its own nature, it produces and moves all things." Thus far Porphyry.

---

### Whatever things seem evil, whether regarding bodies or souls, are reformed into good.

IIII While this element <note>The physical world or the basic material reality.</note> lends its parts here and there to other elements, it meanwhile borrows parts from elsewhere; therefore, the globes of the elements seem to undergo no evil. Similarly, in the dissolution of composite things, the world itself suffers no loss. For the elements then return to their own spheres, or another composite is generated; and while this generation takes from the parts of elements, it adorns them with new forms. Indeed, this perpetual cycle of generation is necessary for the world. For since worldly matter both can and ought to receive innumerable forms of composite things for its own perfection, and yet cannot hold them all at the same time—because the matter from which they are made does not suffice for innumerable composites at once, nor does the space hold them, nor do diverse things concur—it has been arranged that it receives them through perpetual change. 

In the same way, the heaven takes on innumerable figures through motion and acquires new powers, which it cannot admit all at once or while remaining still, as they would be conflicting; and meanwhile, by its motion, it contributes to transforming the lower matter naturally. By this reasoning, therefore, transformation—both in location and in form, both in the heavens and below the heavens—contributes to the best state of the universe, and is therefore judged to be good. This is especially true because the order of the whole world is a kind of rule of the "best universe," by which we ought to judge individual things as good insofar as they are seen to contribute to that order. 

Order indeed seems to require that things constructed by another, and constructed through the destruction of others, should eventually be destroyed by another in turn for the construction of still other things. Whatever is born or happens that is harmful and evil toward some specific thing is not permitted to happen except as it contributes to other and more <insert>†</insert> beneficial things, and unless it rightly completes the order of the universe. Furthermore, the order of the whole requires that from the marvelous, overflowing power of the first things, many levels of following things should arise. From the unity and stability of the first things, stable things soon arise; then, as the procession and dependence grow, stability itself is mixed with motion, and an essence becomes mobile by itself before descending to things that are moved by another. Since motion is derived from stability, motion itself is rightly distinguished by the distinction of that stability. Therefore, just as many things that are stable through another are reduced to things that are stable in some way through themselves, so also those things moved by others are eventually resolved into those things that have motion from themselves. 

Then, indeed, in the very order of things that move themselves, there must be higher things established in a certain common power, and lower things succeeding them that have obtained a particular power through many parts. Since the procession of things ought to be continuous, and nothing left empty in this succession, it is right that after the universal things that move themselves, before descending to their opposites—namely particular things moved by another—some things are interposed that are indeed particular (having obtained a particular power) but have a nature that moves itself. And such things, because of the particular condition of their nature, can sometimes be contracted into a certain state; but because of that very faculty of self-motion, they can sometimes be released from every particular state. The condition of a particular nature also brings about a certain alternating cycle of life that reaches through parts, with free motion meanwhile contributing to this, so that sometimes they retain their own state, sometimes a higher, and sometimes a lower state. They can easily incline to either side, holding a middle nature, and they fulfill in alternating turns what higher and common things embrace in a single, continuous stretch. 

Meanwhile, the nature of the universe enjoys this circular change of motions. In this genus of particular and self-moving substances are placed souls, which Plotinus says change bodies in turn—that is, the souls of lower men, of demons, inhabiting this turbulent air. Indeed, it was necessary for rational souls to inhabit here as well; yet it was not necessary for intellectual natures to always inhabit this region individually, on account of a mission and discord of life that is repugnant to intelligence and happiness. Hence, the Platonists confirm the cycle of souls. And since a harder province has fallen to such souls, and one even more prone to worse things, it has been wisely compensated so that they can eventually transcend not only to the next higher degrees, but even to others still higher—that is, even to heaven. They believe that such souls, having laid aside the body of both the earth and the turbulent air, to the tem-

<meta>catchword: ad tem- (continuing to "ad templa" or "ad temperiem", likely "to the temples" or "to the tempered regions")</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains the Neoplatonic hierarchy of the universe, arguing that creation happens naturally from God’s being rather than by labored planning. He justifies the existence of "evil" and change as necessary components of a perfect, ordered cosmic system where souls cycle through different states of being.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's *Enneads*, Book II, specifically addressing the soul's relationship with the celestial spheres, the nature of evil as a "defect" or "asymmetry," and how Divine Providence coordinates the universe toward the Good.</meta>

# ON THE SECOND BOOK OF THE THIRD ENNEAD

<header>ON THE SECOND BOOK OF THE THIRD ENNEAD</header>

...for a time, in a body of purer air, to be counted among the ethereal spirits <note>original: "dæmones." In the Platonic tradition, "demons" are not evil entities but mediating spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humans.</note>, and even with a celestial body—which Plotinus says is placed beyond the reach of generation <note>original: "extra generationem." In this context, "generation" refers to the cycle of birth, decay, and death in the physical world.</note>—they become colleagues of the universal soul, that is, of the celestial souls. Finally, if they should furthermore lay aside the celestial body, they live not so much with a celestial soul as with the very Idea of souls, which they call the Soul of All.

Here Plotinus calls the **immobile life** the entirely intellectual life, whether of the primary Mind or of those that follow. But he calls **mobile life** the common animal effects, whether they are placed in rational and imaginary discourse or in the service of generation. Strictly speaking, he calls the generative power "mobile life" here, which flows continually from the stability of that higher life, just like its breath; much like the movement in a vital pulse comes from our soul. 

This generative faculty—poured into matter first from the soul of the world and simultaneously from the souls of all the worldly spheres, and dominating it—he calls the **worldly reason** <note>original: "rationem mundanam." This is the *Logos* or the structural plan of the universe.</note>, the mother of transient animals. He says that the forms of these animals consist in the higher heaven, that is, the intellectual realm. From there, through "seminal reasons" <term>seminal reasons: "rationem seminariam." These are the formative blueprints or spiritual "seeds" that translate divine ideas into physical matter.</term>, they come into matter in this way: just as many say that the forms of earthly things proceed from celestial forms through lights flashing from there to here. For we must not think that forms come from this formless matter, nor order from disordered chance, nor stable endurance from an entirely unstable nature.

But to return to the order of the universe—to which anything that harmonizes in any way is to be judged good—such an order requires that particular souls, being mobile by themselves, free in their motion, and kin not only to intelligence but also to generation, should be able to choose alternately both the intellectual good and the sensible good. And this very alternating choice is good for the universe: in which both ministries are fulfilled at once, and natural works proceed, while souls set before themselves the sensible good by choosing it over the intellectual. 

When the soul chooses anything, it chooses it by reason of the "good"; and if it is bad for the chooser to prefer a lesser good to a greater, it is nevertheless good for the universe. This is especially so because a fitting consequence is immediately repaid for such a choice: as the soul that turns toward worse things also becomes worse and undergoes a worse life. This state is certainly judged good, and good for the universe, because it harmonizes with the order of natural justice. It even turns out to be a good for the soul, insofar as the distress of a failing mind sometimes leads it to repentance for a depraved choice. 

Thus, the goodness of divine providence transforms suddenly arising evil into good; it effects this wonderfully both in the motions of bodies and of souls. It happens by chance that air is made from this water, or water from this air; but after either the matter of that water has received lightness, or the matter of air has received heaviness, it does not happen by chance that the former matter now ascends to the place of air, or the latter descends to the location of water. Rather, the form now naturally implanted, they necessarily seek the congruent places by the law of nature and the divine law, which the law of nature perpetually follows. 

Similarly, it happens that souls, by the faculty of their own free will, first lean toward such or such things; then they follow the inclination toward the same; finally, once a habit is formed, they are carried toward them as if by nature and by natural as well as divine law, and thus they eventually obtain such or such a life. 

But he who ordains the law of nature is not led to ordain the law and establish order by consulting the transgression of law and order, as men usually are. For before the first law itself—which is the first order—there is no transgression of law; nor can the first order be produced from the privation of order, under that condition by which the makers of laws among us are prompted by the transgression of natural law to write laws for the people. Rather, the essential form itself, first of the divine mind and then of nature, is the law and order of all things. 

Whatever, therefore, fails from this best order due to weakness, immediately falls by that same order from the good into evil—evil, I say, for itself, but good for the world; insofar as it eventually falls there, just as the order of the whole requires. And the evil proper to each thing is nothing other than a defect of this kind. In this way **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>, following (as I believe) **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher often blended with Neoplatonism by Ficino.</note>, explains it. 

**Evil is not in intellectual things**, for they are closest to the Good itself; **nor is it in universal souls and bodies**, for universal form and authority are proper to the Good. It remains, therefore, that evil exists in particular souls and bodies. Yet it is not in their essences, which are born from God; nor again in their natural powers, for these too depend on God. Evil, therefore, happens only in their actions. 

But as far as it concerns souls, it is not in their rational actions—for all desire the good—nor again in their actions lacking reason—for these are carried by nature—but in a certain incongruity between them, which they call **asymmetry** <term>asymmetry: "asymmetriam." In this philosophical context, evil is seen as a lack of proportion or harmony, rather than a positive force in itself.</term>, that is, incommensurability. As far as it then concerns bodies, evil is not in the form, for form wishes to dominate matter; nor again in the matter, for it desires to be adorned; but in the unsuitability of matter for the form. 

From this he concludes that all evil is "beyond subsistence" [without independent existence], and whatever suddenly creeps in is divinely "colored" under the condition of the good. Since generation exists, it is necessary that this defect also be present, contributing to worldly perfection; but with divine providence surpassing all things and willing good things, it is wonderfully shaped into the good. And if He uses the destruction of some as a kind of evil for the construction of others as a kind of good, and for the restoration of the world as something best, He uses the defect of the soul much more wonderfully toward perfection. 

At the end of this chapter, you will note three causes of the habit of evil being contracted: 
1. That **inclination** which began to lean toward such a life even before the present life, and gradually became more prone. 
2. The **body** being so affected that it provokes the soul toward such things—the soul being unwary at the start and gradually becoming accustomed. 
3. The **sudden encounter of sensible things** through the senses into the soul, affecting it in this or that way, before reason either notices or matures in deliberation, and the general negligence of the mind in consulting itself. 

Punishment necessarily follows. For the choice itself and the perverse movement is both the sin and the punishment, sharply afflicting the soul until providence, in the manner of a physician, heals the soul through the stings of such affliction, while it thus provokes a hatred for the perverse habit and a repentance for the unjust choice, and in turn a love for the contrary choice. Similarly, a right choice is both the reward and the beginning of virtue. Proclus says that both are the work of divine providence acting within, delighting the healthy mind but wonderfully afflicting the insane one.

¶ He confirms the same things. Note here the steps to happiness and **Synesius's** <note>Synesius of Cyrene, a Neoplatonist philosopher-bishop.</note> opinion on providence.

¶ It is fitting for intellects, as stable things close to the Good, to be happy. But for souls, as mobile and more remote things, they must *become* happy. But since they are mobile by themselves, they become so by their own effort. However, for the more common souls, happiness is gained by a short effort. For particular souls...

<summary>Ficino explains the soul's relationship to the material and intellectual worlds, arguing that evil is not a positive force but a lack of proportion (asymmetry) or a defect that Divine Providence ultimately uses to maintain the order and perfection of the universe.</summary>

# COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO

<header>COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...laborious happiness has fallen to them: they indeed make themselves blessed, but only through a long period of time and effort. Since everyone can eventually attain this, it is a crime to complain about our condition, nor is it right to distrust divine providence because of adversities. Hear Synesius the Platonist <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD) was a philosopher-bishop who combined Neoplatonism with Christianity.</note> speaking divinely on this matter: "Adversities, even those which seem to happen to us beyond what we deserve, contribute greatly to rooting out that harmful affection by which we are moved toward fleeting things. Certainly, for those who possess a mind, providence is confirmed by fortunes of this kind, which usually cause those who have lost their minds to distrust providence. For no place is left for the soul to flee from matter and return thus to its fatherland if it encountered no evil here." For this reason, one must think that the governors of the lower province <note>Likely referring to lesser spirits or natural forces governing the material world.</note> devised common prosperities as if to lay snares for souls: and so another might say that a "drink of forgetfulness" <note>original: "obliuioſum... potum." A reference to the river Lethe in Greek mythology, where souls drink to forget their past lives.</note> happens to souls departing from here. Certainly, as the soul enters this life, a certain lot of sweet and charming life brings a drink of forgetfulness. Thus he spoke. Accordingly, as the order of things runs its course, it is necessary that adversities happen to many in no other way than a certain dissonance happens in a musical harmony; but just as that which seems to be out of tune in one part of the harmony actually accords with the whole, so it is deep within the order of the world. In this order, besides the other things we have mentioned, adversity—whether in the body or in fortune—is an exercise and progress for the good, but for the wicked, it is punishment and purging. Furthermore, even wickedness itself contributes to the order, insofar as it is not only punished in an orderly way but also provides the material for justice and an example of the law. And while it is finally pressed by heavy misery, it then deters others from vices and declares, by comparison, how much happiness there is in virtue. After this, observe that evils have no "Idea" <note>In Platonic philosophy, "Ideas" or "Forms" are the perfect blueprints of all good things; evil, being a lack of good, has no perfect blueprint.</note> among the celestial rulers of the world, nor do they proceed from any intention of theirs, but they happen at the very end of the longest chain of good things, where the good finally fails. However, although these things happen as if by chance, it was nevertheless in the intention of the rulers and in the Power of nature from the beginning to use well whatever evils might occur, and to reshape the formless everywhere.

->**It confirms the same points and raises doubts.**<-

VI. Since everything is received according to the nature of the recipient, it is established that whatever happens to the good eventually turns out good, but for the wicked, it turns out bad. Likewise, since the man himself is the soul, and the whole good of the soul consists in virtue, while the whole evil consists in wickedness, it follows that for a man who is blessed through absolute virtue, the subsequent comforts or discomforts outside the soul add or take away nothing from his good. Similarly, for a man—that is, a soul—who is already made miserable by confirmed vices, subsequent events bring nothing of the good and take away nothing of the evil. Yet it will seem more fitting to most people that prosperous things happen to the good and adverse things to the wicked, so that at least the noble works of the good may be increased and the public crimes of the wicked suppressed. But before these things are answered, you will consider that the universe, down to the smallest details, depends on Intelligence in such a way that the power and action of intellectual providence spreads itself down to the minimum, leaving nothing unordered.

->**He gives the principles for responding.**<-

VII. Do not desire the absolute beauty of the first world in this world, which is not the first world, but the fourth, and degenerates far from the first. <note>Ficino refers to the Neoplatonic hierarchy: 1. The One, 2. Intellect, 3. Soul, 4. The Material World.</note> Again, in the actions of rational souls—which, as if movable by themselves, are the principles of their own actions (namely of such or such a kind)—do not accuse God as if He were properly the cause of such actions. Do not think either that souls are compelled by the very nature of the world to choose one action or another. For since the essence of souls is superior to and prior to the worldly nature, it happens not from the world, but from themselves, that they live in the world and are more or less affected by the world. Finally, do not demand the perfection of sublime souls from souls that are already too closely bound to the nature of bodies. Beware lest, because the human race seems less ordered, you deny that divine providence reaches down to humans; for it is fitting that the most skillful disposition and simultaneous motion of the good of all things descends even below man to the smallest details. This cannot be achieved otherwise than by the vital "reason of seeds" <note>original: "seminaria vitalis ratione." These are the 'Logoi Spermatikoi' or formative forces in nature.</note> through the breath of the divine mind; just as in an animal, by a similar principle of nature, not only the higher and middle parts but even the lowest members are made and governed.

->**He responds to the above doubts and touches on new opinions.**<-

VIII. In responding to the doubts, so that no one wonders why there is not the same most absolute order among us on earth as there is in the highest things, he says that the human race is not the highest of animals, but the middle between beasts and gods—that is, demons <note>Ficino uses "demons" in the Platonic sense of mediating spirits.</note>—and therefore it errs. Yet even this belongs to the order of the universe: that a middle nature, mixed from both sides and movable by itself, sometimes keeps to the middle and sometimes turns itself toward the extremes on either side. Among these things, to express the insignificance of our affairs, he says the earth is to the universe like a point, or like a certain tiny star compared to the others. Perhaps he touches here on the opinion of certain Pythagoreans <note>The Pythagoreans were ancient Greek philosophers who suggested the Earth was not the center of the universe and might be in motion.</note> who thought the globe of the earth, surrounded by water, appears like a moon struck by the sun's rays if viewed from the wider heaven. They thought that although it moves continually like a star, it is not perceived by us because the heaven and the stars move together consequently. Thus, in any star, there is something solid, and again something liquid and transparent, just as in the "earthly star," and perhaps something dark, just as in the moon, but from a distance it appears very small. They believed the whole space is similar to air, and the globe is one on all sides, filled everywhere with stars like worlds; the stars move by their own progression, as befits such animals, and are full of inhabitants just like the earthly star, though some are more excellent than others and are inhabited by more excellent beings. After this, you will observe the new response of Plotinus: that among the goods of the soul one should not count only those pertaining to contemplation, temperance, and justice, but also those consisting in all skill through talent, habit, and dexterity. Therefore, those who are more excellent in this kind of good, it is just that in those things which are properly acquired by this skill, they surpass others who are inferior in this very thing and thus carry away something more. And conversely, those who are more excellent in contemplation, temperance, and justice, it is fair that they similarly surpass in carrying away the rewards proper to their virtue. The rewards of the latter are divine, while those of the former are fleeting. Meanwhile, both their unbridled will and the more idle life of the others (often neglecting necessary things) are justly punished. Finally, providence and justice cannot be defended to the highest degree through these and similar points if we consider only this present life; nor can things that are frequently missing here in the present—whether reward or punishment—be compensated for except in another life, or from another life, or elsewhere.

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the page is "Quod" (Which/That).</meta>

He also explores Pythagorean ideas of the Earth as a moving "star" among many inhabited worlds.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's *Enneads*, specifically Book III, Ennead III, where he explores how divine providence operates through a hierarchy of causes without overriding the independent actions of individual things or human free will.</meta>

# ON BOOK III OF ENNEAD III.

### That divine power in its acting does not prevent other things from acting as well, especially rational beings.

---

IX Some people imagine that all effects—by whatever things they seem to be produced, whether inanimate or animate and rational—are so usurped by the First Cause <note>The "First Cause" refers to God or the "One" in Neoplatonic philosophy, the ultimate source of all existence.</note> that they are done only by this cause acting. In this view, all other things are merely passive (undergoing the action), and no proper action of the things themselves intervenes. Thus, if the proper actions of things are taken away, their own inherent powers will be empty, or rather, they will not exist at all. Similarly, individual essences will be removed from the midst, and there will remain only a totally common and confused essence, or rather, nothing would exist after the First. In this way, any events—even the vilest ones, those initially devoid of order, and even evil ones—would be produced directly by the Supreme Good alone. Thus, finally, after the immense act of the first agent, no subsequent act or action would remain, but only a most common and extreme passivity. Indeed, following that act, the things nearest to it would be as if from an immense light or heat, no brightness or warmth came forth—nothing which, by illuminating or heating, imitates its origin, but instead a completely dark work. It would certainly be a work of God, but in no way divine; it would be utterly abject if it were composed only of slaves and those who merely undergo action. Nor will God be rightly called the "First Cause" or the "First Agent" if there were no causes after Him and no other agents. He who acts with a most effective act would not be acting upon something that also acts, but would only produce a passive thing and a state of passivity. Finally, just as we now see specific effects produced everywhere through specific things, we would then see these resulting everywhere and immediately from God without the work of things—as if the sun, without the cooperation of the mixed elements, plants, or animals, were to complete all their outcomes by itself. This would be especially true if the action of the First (as it is said) required no "subject" <note>In this philosophical context, a "subject" is the underlying material or entity that receives an action or form.</note> and was not varied simply because it acts within various things.

But in truth, God gave natures to things and granted them actions from those natures. This is fitting, since it belongs to the First—who is "Pure Act" <note>original: "simpliciter actus." A scholastic term meaning God is fully realized being without any unrealized potential.</note>—to act simply; other things have from Him the ability to consist in a certain act, and they are allotted the power to act in some way. And while they receive from the Immense Good the capacity to be as good as possible, they diffuse their own good into other things by operating. So also the Good itself, while it communicated its likeness to things regarding their existence, also communicated it regarding their being causes for others. For the Good, as a Cause, gave them the ability to be. The effect of any thing proceeds—if not as "properly" (specifically), yet just as nearly—from God as from its own specific cause. Just as the power of the sun is as near to the grape as the vine is, though the sun's power is not as "proper" (specific) to the grape, nor is it a part of the work from the specific cause; it is a part from the common cause, yet the whole belongs to both. They relate differently, however, as if from a principal agent and an instrument simultaneously.

We consider, therefore, in any agent, both essence and power <note>original: "essentiam & virtutē." Here, "virtue" refers to a thing's inherent capability or power to produce an effect.</note>, and we see that this power depends on the power of a superior agent, insofar as it is given from there, or preserved, or moved toward its work. And just as an effect is made equally by the essence of the lower cause and its power, so it is made by this power and the power of the superior cause at the same time. This continues further to the superior causes and finally to the power of the First, with equal proximity always, insofar as the subsequent thing always acts by the power of the preceding one. By these reasons especially, we affirm that after the one most common Agent, there are many things which act by themselves in addition, and fulfill certain specific tasks by their own proper powers, insofar as they are led by the common power and action of the First Agent—just as agents under the moon act both by themselves and through the sun.

If this gift (or tribute) is given even to things below man, it is much more given to man: to act through a soul that is self-moving, to do something from itself, and to act differently and more often than if it were merely being pulled from on high. And just as in natural works, whatever is found to be more common and better is often attributed to superior causes, while whatever is more specific or less good is added from the proximate causes; so in human actions and works, the common, effective, and right act comes to us from divine things. But the "proper" (specific) condition of acting this way or that—the inferior condition—happens because of us and our circumstances. It is no different than how, in a lame person, the crookedness of the stride comes from the curvature of the leg, but the faculty of walking comes from the soul.

Since, therefore, divine providence does not take away from things their own natures and actions (which it both gave and preserves), and since from these failing gradually over a long sequence, defect and evil happen in the work, evil is deservedly not so much removed by providence as it is suddenly transferred into good. Just as a dissonant voice is not entirely removed from music, nor is the frequent silence in the middle, but both are applied as necessary to the harmony of consummate grace and perfection. Therefore, if providence does not remove evil from the world, it deservedly does not remove "fortune" (chance) <note>original: "fortunam." Ficino is arguing that chance events are part of the complex order and do not contradict God's goodness.</note> unless it were to be very contrary to the goodness of providence. For by the very fact that providence established a long order of causes under itself, superior causes endowed with greater power act further and wider than inferior ones. As far as natural power extends, so far does the intention of nature reach. Many things, therefore, happen in effects far distant from the First Cause through the power, action, and intention of the superior causes, to which the intention of the intermediate causes does not extend, since their power does not reach that far. Such things, since they happen beyond the intention of the inferior causes, yet from the intention of the superior ones, are indeed accidental to the former, but not so much to the latter—even those things called "prodigies" (monstrosities or wonders), as they occur beyond the intention and order of a particular nature, meanwhile follow the order and purpose of the superior causes.

Providence, therefore, does not remove chance, lest it lose the long order of causes; it does not remove evil, lest it take away the magnitude of good things, or rather lest it break the order of varied species. While these species are distinguished by their own differences, they are also separated by grades of goodness. He who would take away the diverse grades of goodness would take away the wondrous abundance of varied species. From the long production of mutable grades, evil finally arises where something either falls away from its own proper good or has the potential to fail.

If the goodness of divine providence does not remove evil, and if its reason does not destroy chance, certainly its freedom does not take away our freedom. Indeed, if providence rules fate, it does not want souls to be compelled by fates to sin, lest providence itself be the cause of sins. If God were to compel everything in some way by His immense power, He would impel the powers of things so that, acted upon divinely, they would act divinely everywhere. But because the divine power, while it acts upon all things, does not in its own way prevent them from acting also in the meantime and in their own way, certainly divine science, while it considers the proper natures of things, will not deprive a thing of its own property. For this science, together with the power—which is one and the same—is the cause of all things in such a way that they are endowed with their own natures. He is the cause that intellectual and rational natures lead themselves toward divine likeness in acting, rather than being dragged. He is the cause that inferior natures, more dissimilar to God, are instead led from elsewhere in acting, but are led according to their own property, so that under the order of God (the Institutor of Natures), a thing is not dragged everywhere against its nature. This ensures there is no perpetual violence, where all things are wonderfully disposed by the will of the Good itself, and they desire the good not by force, but naturally. Providence recalls souls to God: the ingenious ones to wonder at the beauty and order of things; the slower ones at least to love the miraculous convenience. All of them He treats like a doctor and a father, caring for and correcting them.

<summary>Ficino explains that divine providence does not negate the independent actions of individual things or human free will, but rather works through a hierarchy of causes to turn even defects and chance into a greater cosmic harmony.</summary>
<keywords>divine providence, hierarchy of causes, free will, problem of evil, Neoplatonism, First Cause, natural law, chance and fortune</keywords>

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

### Rational souls are not at all compelled to shameful actions either by higher or lower beings.

X Since he stated in the previous sections that humans are free under providence, he next wonders how one should understand what is often said by Plato: *that no one is evil voluntarily.* <note>original: "homines non sponte fieri malos." This is a famous Platonic paradox from the *Timaeus* and *Laws*, suggesting that evil is a result of ignorance or bodily disease rather than a healthy will.</note> For if this is the case, they seem to be compelled to sin, whether by the heavens, by some other fatal and internal instinct, or by <term>seminal reason</term> <note>The "seminal reason" (*ratio seminalis*) is a Neoplatonic concept referring to the hidden "seeds" or formative blueprints within matter that direct the growth and development of physical things.</note>. The answer is that when people sin, they move voluntarily toward the action they have chosen, even though they do not voluntarily fall into the perverse habit that grows secretly and gradually from frequent actions. Thus, they begin their movement from the will; but as they proceed far enough in that direction, they slide by necessity into a habit of that kind, and from such a habit, they are necessarily delivered into a corresponding punishment. That humans are not everywhere dragged into action by lower bodies <note>i.e., physical urges or environmental factors.</note> is clear when they choose and carry out things that reason proves to be beyond or even contrary to the condition of those lower things. Again, that they are not compelled by higher beings—either celestial bodies or their governors—is evident from the fact that they often act perversely against the dignity and order of those higher beings. Similarly, humans perform the movement toward virtues from their own proper rational principle. And if ever several principles of action are counted together, the rational faculty itself is always held to be among the number of those acting principles.

### Beyond the qualities of bodies, there is everywhere an incorporeal life ruling all things rationally; and this universal nature dominates particular natures.

XI In the eleventh chapter, the question is asked whether the individual outcomes of things arise solely from a certain "fatal" connection of bodily causes, and whether there is no other providence besides this. However, we have shown sufficiently elsewhere and in our *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his major work, *Platonic Theology*.</note> that besides bodily causes, there is a certain life infused everywhere into things, naturally crafting all things according to certain reasons. For this life imposes certain limits on bodily qualities that would otherwise break out with their full force (as they say); it reconciles conflicting elements; it carves certain forms and figures into materials that are wandering by nature; and it makes living things out of non-living ones. And just as art crafts from the outside, so this life acts like a "natural art"; therefore, it crafts from within more easily and successfully. It also moves from within the plants—which are dull by themselves—and all the most sluggish animals at appointed times and in marvelous ways to propagate their species. It also instructs from within the roots of plants to sagely choose moisture, and the fruits and leaves to choose heat. It also moves heavy and light objects according to straight lines geometrically, and it directs even the most lowly animals opportunely toward necessary things through "prophecies," sagacity, and natural arts, often by reasons that surpass human reason. For they are led divinely. For this is a certain "breath" and word of the <term>World Soul</term> <note>The *Anima Mundi*, or World Soul, is the animating spirit that connects the divine Intellect to the physical universe.</note>, vibrantly and rationally striking and shaping matter, and it has two boundaries. For it both hangs from the intellectual substance of the soul itself and ends in matter. Therefore, insofar as it ends in matter, it is simply called "seminal reason"; however, insofar as it proceeds from the Intellect (either the soul's own or through this from the First Intellect), it is called "intellectual and law-giving reason." Again, insofar as it is seminal, it creates bodily things; insofar as it is law-giving, it adapts certain degrees of change to the movements of souls. Certainly, insofar as it is both seminal and law-giving at once, it disposes the entire order of the universe in its own degrees—in as many degrees, I say, as it was itself first impressed by the intellectual principle, of which it is like a seal, imprinting matter exactly. This is "universal nature," from whose intention many things occur that often happen outside the intention of a "particular nature." Thus, while the generative power in any animal, as a male, strives everywhere to procreate a male (as the most perfect in its kind), meanwhile universal nature sometimes wants a female, so that from the propagated male and female animals, the universe may be more perfect. Thus, where any single thing intends only to continue itself and its own, universal nature meanwhile intends to compose one thing after another from this dissolved thing, consulting the good of the universe. Thus, while individuals under any species would look out for themselves rather than the species by their own nature, this [universal nature] secretly impels them to look out for the species as much as or more than themselves, and to provide more diligently for their offspring than for themselves, inasmuch as they are led not so much by their own quality as by universal providence. Thus, where only specific species would naturally be born from their own species, this [nature] procreates the species of the mule from the horse and donkey species; and she herself prohibits propagation from occurring from mules, even though particular nature arms the mules with generative instruments. Finally, she wants both any composite thing and the entire universal composite to be filled with vastly different and dissimilar things, enriching them with a marvelous abundance of various forms. From all of which it seems to admit "evil"—that is, a "lesser good" in some places—for the sake of the greater, universal good, arranged by degrees.

### Universal nature, because it is all-formed, makes the universe all-formed; and it does not compel souls.

XII If craftsmen who act through external qualities (and the qualities act similarly) are nevertheless accustomed to "make themselves" in a way—inasmuch as the craftsman’s imagination and imaginary spirit are formed into the image of a horse before he makes a horse; and if, again, natural things which act through natural qualities also "make themselves" while propagating their form outward; and if, furthermore, the heaven, acting through the quality of light and motion, acts upon the elements, gifting elemental things with celestial endowments—surely then this nature, ruling all these things, since she does not act with such qualities but is herself "Nature" in the making of the world, makes herself. She therefore makes it "all-formed," because she herself is <term>all-formed</term> <note>original: "omniformis." This means containing the patterns or archetypes of all possible shapes and species.</note>. All-formed, I say, flowing from an all-formed Intelligence—specifically on the condition that the forms of things in this nature are more widely separated from each other than they are in the Mind. This is both because nature departs much further from unity (and therefore is not able, like the Mind, to reconcile her own parts), and because, since she is inferior in power, she requires more aids from many forms for acting; and finally, because she is to adapt herself to matter, in which innumerable things are to be restored in place of the innumerable things that perish. Therefore, even nature, I say, is very much distracted under the intelligence of her duties. Many things, therefore, result in the matter of the world from the proper condition of nature herself rather than from the property of the Mind itself, in which things it is a sin to accuse the divine Mind as if it were the immediate craftsman. You will note that rational souls are not compelled by this seminal reason of the world to fall into a worse lot; for they themselves, as if colleagues of the World Soul, possess their own part—that is, their own authority and duty in the worldly office. They move up and down on their own hinge,

# ON BOOK II OF ENNEAD III

They are not indeed compelled by the nature of the world, but rather nature itself conspires opportunely. For to souls that adapt themselves in this way or that to the world, nature itself duly fits such seats and lots.

->*In what order providence punishes, and how it acts.*<-

### XIII
After this, he descends to the Platonic, Pythagorean, and Egyptian opinion that there is a cycle of all things. Therefore, those crimes which providence does not punish in one life, it punishes in another life by the penalty of retaliation <note>original: "talionis pœna." The *lex talionis* is the principle of "an eye for an eye."</note>. It was in this sense that Origen <note>An influential early Christian theologian (c. 184 – c. 253 AD) who was later controversial for his views on the pre-existence of souls.</note> understood that Gospel saying: *He who strikes with the sword, perishes by the sword* <note>original: "Qui ferit gladio, gladio perit." cf. Matthew 26:52.</note>. But let him see to that. The <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Referring to the practitioners of Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition.</note>, the teachers of the Hebrews, also approve of such a condition of punishment, believing that the souls of men often return to this life in human form; thus curable sins are purged, but they can return here only three times. For they believe this suffices for testing: a soul that has been purged twice or thrice deserves to become more blessed than it was before its descent; but one that has utterly cast away reason remains forever in a certain rank lower than reason, that is, in the imagination and brutal affection itself. They add, lest anyone excuse their own sin, that all souls were present at the time when God gave the Law to Moses. However, they do not fully approve of a perpetual cycle. For they judge that a transformation of this kind can occur until the end of the world’s movement, which is followed by the rest of the eternal Sabbath and the eternal happiness of the good. They judge that saying of David to tend toward this: *The inheritance of the blameless shall be forever* <note>original: "Immaculatorum hereditas in æternum." cf. Psalm 37:18.</note>. Likewise: *The holy shall be preserved forever* <note>original: "sancti in æternum conseruabuntur." cf. Psalm 37:28.</note>. 

But let us return to Plotinus. He confirms that all human actions and habits are observed by providence and arranged in a certain order according to merit, based on the fact that providence cares most diligently for things far inferior to us—indeed, even the lowest things—and disposes them most orderly. For if anything ought to have been neglected by the highest providence, it certainly should have been the most worthless things. Yet in these, a skill appears no less admirable than in the most precious things, looking both to necessity and also to ornament. Indeed, the power and diligence of the craftsman are so much greater as this matter and place seem to resist order. He judges that order in the universal matter of the world and the actions of worldly things is always established and restored by the divinity, not through some consultation by which order is sought, but through its very essence, which is order itself. 

By "divinity" here he understands not only the divine intellect, but also the intellectual soul of the world, and moreover, the intellectual and seminal <term>breath</term> <note>original: "spiraculum." A term for the life-giving or formative spirit that animates matter.</note> within the matter of the world. As for what was said about the cycle of things, nature seems to warn us in a way in the case of the viper, when the newborn children kill the mother, who had killed their father while mating. From this, perhaps, it is signified in what sense the ancient laws suffocate parricides <note>Those who kill their parents.</note> shut in a sack with a viper. And certainly, just as it is provided that the harmless genus of animals, being easily devoured by others, also multiplies most easily, so it is that the pestiferous genus has a more difficult increase.

->*The skillful works of nature are from providence acting in the manner of art and nature. Also, minds are not properly parts of this world.*<-

### XIIII
We are accustomed to guess the qualities of virtues in agents from the qualities of their works and actions. By this reasoning, we detect the heat-giving and moisture-giving power in the sun or moon, just as we do in fire and water through their works and actions. Since, therefore, the work of nature both as a whole and in every part is always such, and is done in such a way, as is usually done and governed by art and providence, we rightly conjecture that there is within nature, and presiding over it, a skillful and provident power—one that does not hesitate, does not grow weary, and does not waver. For the work is carried out correctly without ceasing, nothing is ever retracted, and the accustomed order is never deserted. 

And truly, since no discourse of human reason, however great, can fully grasp the absolute craftsmanship of natural things either in deed or in thought, we have a sign here that the work is not attempted by the wandering of thought, but is completed by the intellect. By "intellect" I mean one superior to the wandering of reason, at least as much as that work stands above the work of human art. This intellect, again, does not seek, but rather acts by the tenor of nature; for it acts in no other way than anything acting naturally is accustomed to do. It is undoubtedly a stable intellect; otherwise there would be no stability in things, no union, and no perpetual order of things and actions would be preserved. Finally, it is an intellect that understands all things at once more easily and happily than natural intelligences, and by understanding, it acts, just as the sun beholds and acts upon the universe and individual things at once with its rays. 

The nature of this intelligence, both the absolute and the animal spirit, is a "word" <note>original: "verbum." Here used in the sense of the *Logos*, the formative principle.</note>, generating and moving individual things by its striking, and in turn interpreting the notions of the craftsman intelligence to those who understand by its own significance. It is brought forth under this condition: that in this "voice," individual things are separated from one another by a greater distance than they are in the notion of the speaker. For there, because of a marvelous unity in any given notion, all are also comprehended; but here, because of a wider discrepancy, all are not equally and fully in any one part. Therefore, both here and in the world, the perfection of the whole is not to be sought in the parts, nor is the property of one part to be desired in another; rather, the power and wisdom of nature should be admired, because it has propagated itself so orderly through so many steps and so many disparate things. 

After this, understand the obscure end of this chapter thus: Men and demons, according to their corporeal life, are parts of the universe. Again, according to rational action, they are in a way something particular; because while discourse is distracted by movement through many things, earlier or later, at other times it determines itself properly to one thing or another. But according to the **mind**, they are the universe all at once; because the mind possesses all things at once, and is not defined toward one thing rather than another, nor does it have an affection contiguous to the world. Finally, just as stars shine in the heavens, so minds shine in demons and men; they have a more excellent function than merely acting as parts. Nevertheless, the minds of these beings, even if considered as parts, do not detract from the universe. For they are considered excellent to the extent that they are judged similar to the mind of the whole and to the intellectual order of the whole.

->*The seminal reason of the universe itself, which belongs to universal nature, has pre-marked within it even those things called evils, and confirms these for the good of the universe. Also, all worldly things are empty in the manner of games.*<-

### XV
He considers that the defect and destruction of things, brought upon things by each other, happens not only from matter and the condition of material things—for they have a perpetual order—but even from the very intention of universal nature. It is from its purpose that things fail by degrees, while it establishes disparate ranks. It is either by their own accord, or by others, that they perish; while...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's *Enneads*, Book III, regarding Providence. On the previous page, Ficino discussed the cycle of souls and the justice of reincarnation. Here, he explores the "seminal reasons"—the underlying blueprints of nature—and how the divine order descends through various levels of reality, from pure intellect down to the fragmented material world.</meta>

...from the present it wishes to form the future, so that it may successively achieve an infinite number of things which it cannot do all at once. Concerning this **seminal reason** <term>seminal reason: in Latin, *ratio seminalis*. These are the formative principles or "blueprints" within nature that direct the growth and development of living things, much like a seed contains the plan for a tree.</term>, which is to say, concerning universal nature, you will note four points. First, that this is the efficient principle of all things that can be generated. Second, that it is all these things insofar as it encompasses the seeds of all. Third, that individual things which are born are made through it one by one—namely, according to its own effective and exemplary power. Fourth, that the entire disposition and mutual change of natural things is prescribed within it; thus, it is expressed outwardly just as it is impressed within, so that nothing is left outside of **Providence**. For even that which happens by chance in a work is not "by chance" to the Reason itself, but is already pre-marked and wonderfully ordered.

Among these points, he touches upon the opinion of those who think the souls of all living creatures can be separated from their present bodies and not be dissolved back into the **World Soul**, but rather subsist in their own property and return again to bodies. He also touches on the opinion of those saying that the souls of brute animals, which flow out from the Soul of the universe, also flow back into the same. Truly, he thinks that a great deal of life exists in the universe—"much," I say, meaning powerful and manifold according to the various substances of rational souls. These souls propagate bodily lives from themselves everywhere, and by that very propagation, they make animals like playthings. Otherwise, if no animals were made from that source, then all matter would lack life, and life—residing in something other than matter, namely in its own source—would seem as if sterile and powerless.

Indeed, the settled opinion of Plotinus is that irrational life, of whatever kind and wherever it may be, proceeds from rational life (of whatever kind and however it is made) just as the imperfect necessarily depends upon the perfect. Certainly, just as you consider three things in a naturally luminous body: first, the form itself, which is light; second, its act within itself while it sparkles; and third, the action proceeding outside itself while it illuminates something (where "to illuminate" depends on "to sparkle," and this likewise on "being light"), so you should think that sensual life depends on rational life, and rational life on intellectual life. For **Reason** is a certain motion from the intellectual substance, like light turned back into itself, sparkling from the light. **Sensation**, however, is like a certain proceeding of light outward. Therefore, just as images—which are like bodies—flow from bodies, so from souls—which are more effective than bodies—flow "animal images," which are like souls. From these images, combined with the bodies suited to them, animals are made. And since these things are playthings, whatever benefit or disadvantage pertains to them has no more weight for good or evil than what an opinion brings that deceives and disturbs us.

### *What the seminal reason of the world is, and how it acts; likewise concerning the four stages of fullness; likewise how the reasons of things are contrary within the common reason.*

**XVI** If all things are, in a certain way, from the intention of a universal and natural reason, all things seem to happen naturally and rationally; therefore, nothing happens against nature, nor is any sin committed. To resolve these things, one must consider it thus: just as at night, two solar lights are not derived from the sun and the moon, but one light flashes out—not a little solar, but more lunar—and as it descends from there to our level, it turns out worse than the lunar; so from the **Intellect** itself and from the intellectual soul made there, the **seminal reason** and universal nature proceed. Now, it is indeed worse than both, being surely more "animal" than intellectual, and degenerating again from both within matter, by which natural things coalesce as if by moonlight. 

Because this nature depends on an animal substance, it is a kind of life; because it depends on an intellectual substance that does not wander <note>original: "nō discurrente," referring to non-discursive thought, which is immediate and intuitive rather than step-by-step reasoning.</note>, it is a reason that does not wander. Because it is an essential reason, it acts rationally—namely, through its essence—even if it does not feel what it does, although an "imagination" of the work accompanies it. Because its action penetrates from itself into matter, it is called "motion"; truly, it acts upon and moves all things. It does not act, I say, like a fire with a determined object and total impetus, but first with variety and a certain moderation, toward a certain end, limit, figure, and time, and in various ways. It varies first, I say, not like fire, which might also make various things by accident or consequence and through something else. It also moves not simply in space like something pushing, which usually moves without forming. Its "moving," however, is "forming"—not only by alteration, but even more by the tighter tension of reason. For there, art is Reason itself; there, Reason is Nature itself. 

Hence a natural body is moved just as a dancer is moved by the very art of dancing implanted in his mind—especially if this art were imagined not as something sought at some time, but as so naturally implanted that it is nature itself. Indeed, as many modes and forms as the art encompasses within itself, in so many modes and figures does it move the dancer from within. But is this reason, which forms natural things by moving them and moves them by forming them, a form and a kind of quality, or a kind of motion and action? It is certainly like both: for it is an act possessing the essential stability of form and the efficacy of motion. It is like a quality without accident; it is motion without passage; it is life—that is, a substantial vigor from the soul into matter, a perennial act performing all things vibrantly and rationally. 

It performs many things, indeed, and even contraries at first; for it does many and nearly contrary things simultaneously. Here you must understand a fourfold multitude or **fullness** <term>plenitudo: a Neoplatonic concept describing the "fullness of being" at different levels of reality.</term>: 
1. **Pure Intellect**
2. **Animal Intellect** (or Intellectual Soul)
3. **Natural Soul**
4. **Material Nature**

**Pure Intellect**, standing immediately under **Unity** itself, turns out so united to itself that, while it formally consists of all things, it is whole in any part of itself. Therefore, all its things are comprehended in any part of itself. Thus, in its presence, all parts are in any part, not only by potential, but by act. They differ formally, however, because they are through one act and another, in one way and another, or even more and less. 

**Animal Intellect** (or the intellectual soul) is indeed a fullness and an entirely universal multitude, although not entirely united; therefore, even if all its parts are comprehended in any part, they are nevertheless contained not so much by act as by potential. 

**Natural Soul**, which is universal reason and pure nature, is moreover a total fullness and multitude, but departing further from unity, it is no longer contained whole in any part of itself, neither by act, I say, nor by potential. From this it happens that certain parts are contrary to others, since one cannot now admit the other. 

Finally, **Material Nature**—that is, the bodily machine—is seen to be distracted into such great multitude and contrariety that one thing not only does not admit another, but even destroys it by its approach. This destruction would certainly not happen in the parts of the higher nature; returning to which, let us say that nature itself, by its own diversity, is already in a certain way the origin of the diversity and battle arising among the parts of the world. Thus this world is said to be "set in malice" <note>original: "in maligno." A reference to 1 John 5:19, *mundus totus in maligno positus est* (the whole world lies in the power of the evil one).</note>, and to neither have peace nor give peace to anyone; and that the powerful prince of this world is very near to the demons. Let us conclude, therefore, that since in universal nature unity now degenerates further from the unity of higher things, and at the same time fullness degenerates, the parts now so disagree with parts and fail,
