# ON THE SECOND BOOK OF ENNEAD III.

* 3

So that what is present to some is meanwhile absent from others: thus they now seem to fight among themselves, as they claim from elsewhere what they lack, while each individual part desires to become the whole. Yet the whole itself is not so powerful as to utterly expel contrariety from itself. Hence it happens that the corporeal world can never expel either contrariety or the mutual destruction of things. Meanwhile, however, universal nature itself—just like a word <note>original: *verbum*</note> of a higher intelligence uttered through musical reason—renders its opposing voices friendly through the power of proportions. Thus, the whole is "one" in the same way a complete musical piece or a complete tragedy is reconciled into a single harmony and beauty out of contrary elements. 

Moreover, this **World Reason** <term>World Reason: *ratio mundi*, the governing logic of the universe</term> is more similar to the logic of music than to the logic of poetry. For the poetic art accepts things and characters made elsewhere and is not necessarily composed of opposites. But music itself produces tones, which are necessarily contrary; for there is no harmony unless it is composed of deep and high notes, of tense and relaxed, of ascending and descending, and even of discordant and concordant sounds. Therefore, the logic of harmony itself is not a common thing unless it consists of the logic of these opposites being themselves opposed to one another in a similar way. In the same way, understand that the **seminal reason** <term>seminal reason: *ratio seminaria*, the formative seeds or blueprints of nature</term> of the world is constituted from contrary principles, through which it produces contrary forms in the world. Since the formal discrepancy between these things arises neither from each other, nor from matter, nor by chance, it is clearly expressed exactly from formulas that are contrary in their logic. 

To be sure, the **ideal forms** <term>ideal forms: the perfect, unchanging archetypes in the Divine Mind</term> of contraries in the Mind are not themselves contrary—indeed, opposites are often known through their opposites. However, the seminal formulas in nature that produce contraries *are* contrary. For in a seed, the "seed of fire" cannot be the "seed of water," just as fire cannot be in water. Remember that in the Divine Mind, there is the idea of **Identity** <note>original: *identitas*, or "Sameness"</note> and the idea of **Alterity** <note>original: *alteritas*, or "Otherness"</note>, and of rest and motion. You should refer intellectual substances primarily to identity and rest, rather than to opposites; but refer the rational powers instead to the idea of otherness and motion, especially the final reason which is contiguous with matter. 

Thus, the office of the Mind consists more in union, while the office of Reason is more concerned with description <note>meaning the "mapping out" or "unfolding" of details</note>. Reason could not exist unless it were quite manifold and contrary within its own parts—I mean the seminal reason of the world and the lowest of divine things, in which as much discrepancy of parts is found as can possibly occur in the divine genus. And since there is an extreme divergence there within the divine category, it rightly receives the name of "contrariety." Furthermore, since identity and rest belong more to the perfect, while otherness and motion lead toward the imperfect, it is right that the further one descends from the idea of identity and rest, the less the things participating in those ideas possess identity and rest. On the contrary, the further one descends from the idea of otherness or motion, the more do the participating things admit otherness—that is, diversity within themselves—and mobility. Therefore, otherness and diversity, divinely inserted into the seminal reason of the world, make it the most "other" and diverse among all divine things. 

Since the condition of this Reason looks especially toward the idea of Otherness, and its power prevails far more in this realm—while that idea or power propagates such a reason into extreme diversity—it seems that this reason propagates itself no differently than a plant's root into the trunk, branches, and the rest, which it does by a certain vigor of vegetal life. Indeed, things that lack life seem to act not within, but to produce effects outside themselves; but living things act also within themselves, and life acts much more interiorly, propagating itself from a single point into many things step by step. Thus, the seminal reason of the world is indeed life, but the last of the universal divine things; it seems, under the very idea of diversity, to diffuse itself within itself through diverse, articulated, and contrary parts.

->As virtue decreases from higher to lower things, it is supplemented by number: Also, how<-
->human affairs are noted and ordered in intellectual and natural providence.<-

XVII Nature contains more seeds within itself than the Mind contains ideas. For since the power of nature and the seed is weaker, it cannot encompass in one seed—or do through one seed—whatever a single idea possesses and can do. Therefore, the vigor of a single idea is distributed through many seeds, and the weakness of power is compensated for by number. By the same reasoning, matter is led into more forms under each seed. To the innumerable multitude of this world is added **dimension**, which is always subject to division, and **motion**, which varies every single thing, and the manifold mixing of things among themselves, and the heap of powers and gifts proceeding by necessity from each of the higher causes. Finally, lest the species of mutable things should ever perish, the number of individuals in these substances is divinely increased, both by succession and by the simultaneous multitude of those that remain. 

Therefore, in such a crowd of things, because of the greatest discrepancy and dissonance, some things become harmful to others; and because of their need, they try to protect, preserve, and recreate themselves through the destruction of others. Meanwhile, against such great multitude and dissension, **Providence** inserts a vehement love into each thing, both for itself and for the whole, so that individual things, being drawn together here and there, may be united with one another and, finally, with the whole. 

After this, it is questioned whether men are marked as good or evil by the very form of the universal reason, and how. This is answered by a long example of **comedies**: just as actors bring their own figures, voices, gestures, and natural talents with them besides those things which the poet commands—who wisely distributes the appropriate duties and places to each according to their properties—so rational souls, even before these bodies, become "such and such" through certain inclinations of their own. Subsequently, the World Reason accommodates such bodies to them, and as long as they persevere and follow through, it also assigns such fortunes and finally such seats. From this disparity on both sides, and the mutual harmony of proportions in the meantime, the world is most beautiful and most just. We have this entire finding similarly from the beginning; and many speak of "families" of angels, either those who do not fall, or those who fall more or less. 

But when "World Reason" is named, you should often understand the intelligence of the **World Soul** <term>World Soul: *Anima Mundi*, the spirit that animates the entire universe</term> joined with the seminal power, upon which seminal nature continually depends and is ruled according to the pattern. Therefore, the proper and antecedent motions of souls are not prescribed in the "seminal book," but rather in the "intellectual book"; yet they are not forced from there. For they are written there such as they themselves are—that is, arising from their own sources. Likewise, their lots, fortunes, and seats are foreknown from there at the same time and destined according to their merits. In the "seminal book," however, with the exception of the antecedent motions of souls, the remaining things that follow in order are impressed not intellectually, but naturally and effectively. Therefore, just as the seminal power corresponds to the intellectual, so do the effective formulas in the seed correspond to the notions that are there. Thus, the seminal power always adapts subsequent things to the antecedent motions of the souls, although it does so not for its own sake, but for the sake of the patterns of intelligence; just as in art, the motor power executes to a hair <note>original: *ad unguem*, literally "to the fingernail"</note> those things which it does not itself know, but which the imagination knows. In the antecedent things, the soul always acts properly <note>original: *propriè*, meaning "on its own/specifically"</note>; but God acts commonly. In the consequent things, the soul in turn operates commonly, but...

# COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO

<page-num>244</page-num>

From present things, nature wishes to form future ones, so that it may successively achieve that infinite number of things which it cannot produce all at once. Regarding this **seminal reason** <term>seminal reason: *ratio seminalis*, a Stoic and Neoplatonic concept of a "seed-logic" or formative power that governs the growth and development of the natural world</term>—which is to say, universal nature—you should note four points. First, that this is the efficient principle of all things that can be generated. Second, that it is all these things insofar as it encompasses the "seeds" of all. Third, that individual things are produced through it one by one, according to its own effective and exemplary power. Fourth, that the entire disposition and mutual alternation of natural things is prescribed within it; thus, it is expressed outwardly just as it is impressed within, so that nothing is left outside of **providence** <note>Ficino emphasizes that even what seems like chance is part of a divine plan.</note>. For even what appears as "contingent" in a finished work is not contingent to the Reason itself, but is already pre-signed and wonderfully ordered. 

Amidst these points, Plotinus touches upon the opinion of those who think the souls of all living creatures can be separated from their current bodies, and rather than being dissolved back into the Soul of the Universe, they subsist in their own individual properties and return again to bodies. He also touches upon the opinion of those who say that the souls of "brute" animals <note>meaning non-human animals lacking higher reason</note>, which flow out from the Soul of the Universe, flow back into it again. In truth, he believes that much life exists within the universe—powerful and manifold life, corresponding to the various substances of **rational souls**. These souls propagate corporeal lives everywhere from themselves, and through that propagation, they create animals as if they were playthings. Otherwise, if no animals were created from that source, then all matter would lack life, and the life which exists in its source (rather than in matter) would appear sterile and powerless.

Indeed, the settled opinion of Plotinus is that **irrational life** <note>original: *irrationalem vitam*</note>, whatever and wherever it may be, proceeds from **rational life** in the same way that the imperfect necessarily depends upon the perfect. Truly, just as you consider three things in a naturally luminous body—first, the form itself (the light); second, its internal act (the shimmering or twinkling within); third, the action proceeding outward (the illumination of something else, where "to illuminate" depends on "to shimmer," and "to shimmer" depends on "to be light")—so you should consider that sensory life depends on rational life, and rational life depends on **intellectual life** <term>intellectual life: the highest level of being, associated with pure divine thought</term>. For Reason is a kind of motion from the intellectual substance, like a light turned inward upon itself, as if shimmering. Sensation, however, is like a beam—a certain proceeding outward. Therefore, just as images (which are like bodies) flow out from physical bodies, so from souls (which are more effective than bodies) flow out "animal images," which are like souls. From these, as soon as they are joined to suitable bodies, living animals are made. And because these are merely playthings, whatever benefit or disadvantage pertains to them holds no more weight for good or evil than an opinion that deceives and disturbs us.

### What the seminal reason of the world is and how it acts; also regarding the four levels of fullness; also how the reasons of things are contrary within the common Reason.

**XVI** If all things exist according to the intention of the universal and natural Reason, it would seem that all things happen naturally and rationally; therefore, nothing would happen against nature, nor would there be any sin. To resolve this, one must consider: just as at night the sun and moon do not produce two separate solar lights, but a single light shines forth—not a little solar, but mostly lunar—and as it descends to our level, it becomes even weaker than the lunar; so from the **Intellect** itself, and from the **Intellectual Soul** formed therefrom, proceeds the universal seminal reason, which is **Nature**. This nature is indeed lower than both, being more "animal" than intellectual, and it degenerates further when it enters matter, where natural things coalesce as if by moonlight. 

Because this nature depends on an animal substance, it is a kind of life; because it depends on an unchanging intellect, it is a **non-discursive reason** <note>original: *ratio non discurrens*; it acts instinctively and perfectly without having to "think through" steps or deliberate</note>. Because it is an essential reason, it acts rationally—that is, through its very essence—even if it does not "feel" what it does, though a certain imagination accompanies its work. Because its action penetrates from itself into matter, it is called "motion." It acts upon and moves all things. I say it does not act like fire, which is determined to one specific thing and acts with total blind force; rather, nature acts with variety, under a certain governance, toward a specific end, limit, shape, and time. It moves things not simply in space like something pushing, which usually moves things without shaping them. Its "moving" is actually "forming," not only through physical alteration but even more through the power of reason and art. 

In that realm, art is the Reason itself, and Reason is Nature itself. Thus, a natural body is moved just as a dancer is moved by the **art of the dance** <note>original: *tripudiandi arte*</note> implanted in their mind—especially if we imagine this art was never "learned," but was naturally implanted so that the art is the nature itself. However many modes and forms the art encompasses within itself, it moves the dancer from within in just as many ways and figures. Is this reason—which forms by moving and moves by forming—a form and quality, or a motion and action? It is surely both: it is an act possessing the stability of an essential form and the efficacy of motion. It is like a quality without being an accidental property; it is a motion without a transition through space. It is life—that is, a substantial vigor flowing from the soul into matter, a perennial act working all things vivaciously and rationally. It produces many things, even contrary things, simultaneously. 

Here you must understand a four-fold "fullness" or hierarchy:
1. **Pure Intellect:** Positioned immediately under Unity, it is so unified with itself that, while formally existing as all things, it is "whole" in every part of itself. Thus, everything in it is comprehended in every part of it, not just by potential but by act.
2. **Animal Intellect (or Intellectual Soul):** This is a universal fullness and multitude, though not entirely unified; therefore, while all its parts are comprehended in every other part, they are held more by potential than by act.
3. **Natural Soul (Universal Reason and Pure Nature):** This is the total fullness and multitude, but departing further from Unity. It is no longer contained as a whole in every part of itself, neither in act nor in potential. From this it follows that certain parts are contrary to others, since one can no longer admit the other.
4. **Material Nature (the Corporeal Machine):** This is distracted into such a great multitude and contrariety that one thing not only refuses to admit another, but destroys the other by its very approach. 

Such destruction would not happen in the parts of the higher nature. Returning to that higher nature, let us say that through its own diversity, it is already in some way the origin of the diversity and conflict arising among the parts of the world. Thus, this world is "positioned in evil" <note>An allusion to 1 John 5:19, "the whole world lies in wickedness" or "under the power of the evil one."</note> and can neither have peace nor give peace to anyone; and the powerful **Prince of this world** <note>the devil or the material impulse</note> is very close at hand. Let us conclude, then, that as unity in universal nature degenerates further from the unity of higher things, and as fullness likewise degenerates, its parts begin to disagree with one another and to fail.

# ON BOOK II OF THE THIRD ENNEAD
<page-num>245</page-num>

*Just as what is present in some is, meanwhile, lacking in others: and so they almost seem to fight among themselves, as if they were claiming from elsewhere what they lack, while each individual part desires to become the whole. Yet the whole itself is not so powerful as to utterly expel contrariety from itself. From this it follows that the corporeal world can neither expel contrariety nor mutual destruction from among its things. Meanwhile, however, universal nature itself—like the **Word** <note>original: "Verbum"; here referring to the Logos or the divine expression of the higher Mind</note> of a superior intelligence uttered in a musical manner—renders its opposing voices friendly through the power of proportions. Thus the whole is a "one" in the same way that a complete musical piece or a complete tragedy is reconciled from contraries into a single harmony and beauty. This "reason" <note>original: "ratio"; here meaning the governing logic or blueprint</note> of the world is more like a queen of musical logic than of poetic logic. For the poetic art takes its characters and things from elsewhere as ready-made, and is not necessarily composed of opposites. But music itself brings forth tones, which are necessarily contrary; for there is no harmony unless it is composed of deep and high notes, of tense and relaxed, of ascending and descending, and indeed even of discordant and concordant sounds. Therefore, the logic of the harmony itself is not a common thing unless it consists of the logics of these opposites, which are similarly opposed to one another. In the same way, understand that the **seminal reason** <term>seminal reason: *ratio seminaria*, the "seed-logic" or formative power that directs natural growth</term> of the world is constituted from contrary logics, through which it produces contrary forms in the world. For the formal discrepancy between these things—since it arises neither from one another, nor from matter, nor by chance—is undoubtedly expressed precisely from the formulas that are contrary within that Reason. To be sure, the "Ideal Forms" in the mind are not contrary to their opposites; in fact, opposites are often known through their opposites. But the "seminal formulas" in nature, which effect opposites, are indeed contrary. For in the seed of fire there cannot be the seed of water, just as there is no fire in water. Remember that in the divine mind there exists the Idea of **Identity** <note>original: "identitas"; the principle of sameness and stability</note> and the Idea of **Alterity** <note>original: "alteritas"; the principle of "otherness," difference, and change</note>, as well as Rest and Motion. You should relate intellectual substances to Identity and Rest rather than to opposites; but relate the rational powers to the Idea of Alterity and Motion—especially the "final reason" which is already contiguous with matter. Thus, the duty of the Mind consists more in union, while the duty of Reason is more occupied with description. Nor could Reason exist unless it were quite manifold and contrary within its own parts: I speak of the seminal reason of the world, the lowest of divine things, in which as much discrepancy of parts is found as can possibly happen to divine things. Therefore, since there is extreme distinction there within the genus of divine things, it has deservedly received the name of "contrariety." Furthermore, since Identity and Rest belong more to the perfect, while Alterity and Motion act toward the imperfect: it is rightly so that the further one descends from the Idea of Identity and Rest, the less the things participating in those Ideas possess identity and rest. On the contrary, the further one descends from the Idea of Alterity or Motion, the more the things participating in them admit of alterity—that is, diversity within themselves—and mobility. Therefore, Alterity and Diversity, inserted divinely into the seminal reason of the world, make it the most "other" within itself and the most diverse of divine things. Since the condition of this Reason looks especially toward the Idea of Alterity, and its power prevails far and wide in this realm, while that Idea or power propagates this Reason into extreme diversity, it seems that this Reason propagates itself no differently than the root of a plant into the trunk and branches and the rest; yet it does this by a certain vigor of vegetal life. And indeed, those things which lack life seem to act not within, but to effect things outside themselves. But living things act also within themselves, and much more so does Life act internally, propagating itself from a certain "one" into many things step by step. And so the seminal reason of the world—which is indeed a life, but the last of the universal divine lives—seems, under the Idea of Diversity, to spread itself within itself through diverse, articulated, and contrary parts.*

->As virtue decreases from higher to lower things, it is compensated for by number: Likewise, how human<-
->affairs are noted and ordered in intellectual and natural providence.<-

XVII *Nature contains more seeds of things within itself than the Mind contains Ideas. For since the power of nature and the seed is weaker, it cannot encompass in one seed, nor do through one, whatever a single Idea possesses and can do. Therefore, the vigor of a single Idea is distributed through many seeds, and the weakness of its power is compensated for by number. By the same logic, matter is led into more forms under each individual seed. Added to the innumerable multitude of this world is dimension (which is always subject to division), motion (which varies individual things), and the manifold mixing of things, as well as the heap of virtues and gifts proceeding by necessity from each of the higher causes everywhere. Finally, lest the species of mutable things should ever perish, the number of individuals is divinely increased among substances, both by succession and by a multitude remaining beyond them at once. Therefore, in such a crowd of things, because of the greatest discrepancy and dissonance, some things become harmful to others; and because of their neediness, they try to protect, preserve, and recreate themselves through the destruction of others. Meanwhile, against such great multitude and dissension, Providence inserts in each thing a vehement love both for itself and for the whole, so that individual things, being insinuated everywhere, may be united to one another and, finally, to the whole. After this, it is questioned whether good or evil men are pre-marked by the very form of Universal Reason, and how. It is answered by the long example of comedies: just as actors bring with them their own shapes, voices, gestures, and dispositions besides those which the poet mandates—who prudently distributes appropriate duties and places to each according to their own properties—so rational souls, even before these bodies, become "such" or "such" by certain inclinations of their own. Then, the Reason of the world accommodates such bodies to them; and insofar as they persevere and follow through, it also accommodates such fortunes and, finally, seats. From this disparity on both sides, and the mutual agreement of proportions in the meantime, the world is most beautiful and most just. We have this entire discovery similarly from the origin; and similar things are said by many concerning angels—either those who do not fall, or those who fall more or less. But you, whenever "Worldly Reason" is named, should often understand the intelligence of the **World Soul** <note>original: "anima mundana"; the soul that animates the entire universe</note> joined with its seminal power, upon which seminal nature continually depends and is ruled according to a standard. Therefore, the proper and antecedent motions of souls are prescribed not in the "seminal book," but rather in the "intellectual book," yet they are not compelled from there. For they are written as being "such" everywhere as they themselves are—that is, arising from their own sources. Strong fortunes and seats are likewise foreknown and destined from there according to merits. But in the "seminal book," with the exception of the antecedent motions of souls, the remaining things which follow in due order are impressed not intellectually but naturally and effectively. Therefore, just as the seminal book agrees with the intellectual, so do the effective formulas in the seminal book agree with the notions that are there; thus, the seminal book always fits the consequences to the antecedent motions of souls, though not for its own sake, but for the sake of the signs of Intelligence: just as in art, the motive power executes to a hair's breadth what the imagination knows, even if the motive power itself does not know it. In antecedent things, the soul always acts specifically, while God acts generally; in consequent things, however, the soul in turn operates generally, while God acts specifically...*

...but indeed God and nature. It is necessary, however, that some proper action be inherent in souls beyond the influence <note>original: "tractum"; referring to the drawing or pull of the cosmic whole</note> depending on the universe. Otherwise, if they had no action of their own, they could not attain the reason of the principle of the universe, which is without form, nor of things more excellent than this world. Indeed, even all things in the very movement of the universe must have some property of their own. For in this way, they assert their own natures; and the principle that makes all things thus most effectively makes things similar to itself if it makes things that are themselves "makers" <note>Meaning the Creator makes beings that are also creative agents</note>. For the principle itself makes things by its own effect. If, therefore, action itself is the origin of all things, it is probable that the things arising from it will be agents; and so that they may have something to act upon, they will also be "patients" <note>In the philosophical sense: those who receive or undergo action</note>; and there will also be matter as the primary foundation of these experiences.

### On the orders, species, and differences of souls, and how individuals are designated in divine providence.

XVIII. Plato in the *Timaeus*, distributing the orders of souls, extended them to three principal levels; he did this, I believe, for the reason that in the soul we consider either the elements from which it is composed, its power, or its action. By reason of the elements, we conveniently distribute them into three levels: In the first order of souls, the "Same" and "Stability" overcome "Difference" and "Motion" <note>These are the fundamental metaphysical ingredients Plato uses in the Timaeus to describe the soul's composition</note>. In the second, they are equalized. In the third, a turning back toward the first occurs. Similarly, essence and being run through them in three degrees. Again, as far as powers are concerned: in the first, the intellect prevails; in the second, reason; and finally in the third, imagination. As far as actions are concerned: in the first level, there is an action that is entirely and universally providing—namely, "all things for all." In the second, it is universal in a certain way—namely, either "certain things for all" or "all things for certain." In the third, it is particular—namely, "certain things for certain [recipients]." In the first degree, we place the souls of the celestial spheres; in the second, the souls of the stars; in the third, the souls of <term>daemons</term> <note>Intermediary spirits or guardian beings, not to be confused with the modern concept of "demons"</note> and of men. 

Furthermore, in the souls of daemons and men themselves, the *Timaeus* posits as many species as there are stars in the sky, each differing from one another in species. To these stars, an equal number of species of demonic and human souls correspond in their respective spheres. But perhaps it will be thought that there is this difference: in the species of a star, any star is unique; but in the species of subsequent souls, there are more individuals in each. Likewise, there are more individuals in any species of human souls than in any species of daemons. For a lesser power is always compensated for by a greater number. Think of any nature in an <term>Idea</term> <note>A perfect, divine blueprint</note> in whose power there are a thousand "gifts" (so to speak) or effects pertaining to the multiple order and goodness of the universe. 

Furthermore, the stellar species, being most perfect, has within itself a single most perfect individual; therefore, it contains the whole species and Idea within itself, fulfilling all the actions of that species and Idea. But the demonic species, being less perfect, has individuals that are also less perfect, which cannot alone fulfill the various gifts of the Idea and species. Therefore, through many individuals here, the various effects of the species and Idea are fulfilled. Finally, in the human species, there must be even more individuals than in the demonic, through which the various gifts of the Idea or species are distributed, and very many souls accomplish what neither one nor a few could fulfill. 

The Platonist further conjectures that there are several species of human souls because there is such discrepancy among men that some seem divine, others brutish, and others human. Neither such diversity concerning the soul nor the body is found in any other species of animals. Nor do the Platonists think it safe to attribute this incredible diversity of souls solely to the diversity of earthly bodies as a cause; especially because those who are most similar in body are often most dissimilar in talent and character, and often vice versa. Moreover, that one person is somewhat faster or slower in talent, or angrier or milder, and the like—someone could somehow attribute these to bodily qualities. But that some are naturally more inclined and much more fit for certain sciences and arts, no one will be able to assert from the differences of bodies. For such arts and sciences often seem to pertain not so much to a corporeal nature as to an incorporeal one. I pass over mathematical and physical disciplines, and the prudence of governing, and the marvelous subtleties of the arts, in which some differ most widely from others by nature. Certainly, that this person seems to be by nature a theologian, that one a prophet, another an author of miracles and a founder of eternal laws—while others are not so at all, though they do not differ much in body—this cannot have its cause assigned to bodies, neither to their own nor to common ones, which would seem to instruct our souls only through their own structures. 

Therefore, the Platonists group the souls of men under a subordinate species, in which there are many (so to speak) "most specific" species; and many individuals under each species, so that certain souls are naturally most similar and friendly to one another, while others are the opposite. In general, every single species of soul is referred back to the congruent species of their daemons and to similar species of stars: thus "solar" souls to solar daemons and the Sun; "Venereal" <note>related to the planet Venus</note> souls to Venereal daemons and Venus, and others similarly. 

Thus far we have treated the differences of souls which Plotinus asserted as primary: namely, those which are from nature itself, either according to a special or according to a singular property under its species. Secondly, he thinks some souls differ from others after they have begun to rise or incline differently by free motion, perhaps even before entering the body. In this case, it happens that the same soul may act and live through various powers of itself at different times, so that it turns out dissimilar not only to others but even to itself. 

Thirdly, he thinks diversity in souls happens from bodies. First from the spiritual <note>ethereal or subtle</note> body, then from the solid one. For it matters a great deal from which part of the worldly sphere the soul has obtained its familiar spiritual "veil," whether it obtains a celestial, ethereal, or aerial one; where it also matters very much under what course and configuration of stars it received it. For many and varied things flow from the higher realms into such bodies, and the soul flows through them. This difference is increased by the various daemons then accepted as leaders of the souls, who lead them in different ways. Nor do these solid bodies, birth, time, and place bring a small weight to certain differences of souls. 

Finally, he wants a fourth difference to happen to souls from various education, custom, and discipline. He maintains that the entire distribution of such differing souls through unequal levels and parts is described in the very <term>intellectual reason</term> <note>The divine logic or blueprint of the Mind</note> of the world. Moreover, he thinks the whole distribution of various bodies, fortunes, and boundaries is marked in a certain congruent proportion to the differences of souls in the <term>seminal reason</term> <note>The "seed-logics" or formative principles within nature</note>, and that individual things are fittingly adapted to individuals in this way. He adds that Providence could not render appropriate duties, rewards, and punishments to the properties of souls unless it also fully embraced these within itself. Just as a poet cannot assign fitting roles and gestures to individual actors unless he grasps their natural and proper faculties. Therefore, in both cases, both the antecedents and the consequences are parts of Providence—both human and divine. But the first antecedents especially are not so much in the semi-

IN THE SECOND BOOK OF THE THIRD ENNEAD.

...as in the seminal book, so too in the intellectual archetype, there are parts of the book of divine providence where even those things are read which are not entirely brought about from there—just as is the custom with human providence. In truth, the consequent parts are also often in the "seminal" book of providence <note>Referring to the *rationes seminales* or "seed-reasons," the formative forces in nature</note>, where those things understood in the other book are imprinted and expressed from it. Indeed, individual things are always so rightly ordered through antecedents and consequences that when adultery is committed out of disordered lust: immediately, both in the book of nature, an ordered propagation of offspring follows from the coitus, and in the book of intelligence itself, a disturbed life and a worsened condition for the adulterer follow from the disturbed concupiscence—and ultimately from the bad choice—in the proper order. Thus, both nature and the various intelligences involve whatever seems to happen—whether badly or by chance—within their own orders by a certain common consensus. In this way, the unjust character of souls and evil works are called parts of the "worldly reason" <note>The *Logos* or rational structure of the physical universe</note>: and the reason itself is said to have communion with these evils. This is not because they are properly drawn from it, but because they are noted there as things to be done by others, and the deeds are punished. Therefore, since providence is considered as both the model of all things and the craftsman, sins are indeed parts of it insofar as it is the model, rather than as the craftsman; however, the punishments of the sinners are parts under both conditions. But whether evils have their own proper model there insofar as they are evil, or whether they are instead judged from the model of good things, is more conveniently treated elsewhere. Conclude now that providence—not only in the "vegetative" manner of a plant, but also in the intellectual manner of art and foresight, yet a natural one—diffuses itself even unto the smallest things.

### *Confirmation of the first book and the second: that God makes, understands, and cares for individual things.*

XIX It is worthwhile to briefly confirm the things transacted in both this and the following book concerning providence. Since "to be" is everywhere through form, and to the extent that a form is possessed, to that extent "being" is also possessed, and vice versa, we rightly conjecture that the First Essence is also the First Form. We think it necessary that the First Form be at once the simplest and the most common <note>Meaning "universal," covering all things</note>: insofar as it surpasses all beings, and conceives and gives birth to them. Truly, it possesses uniform simplicity and all-forming commonality only if it is "Intellect," especially since it belongs to intelligence both to resolve composite things entirely into simple ones and to comprehend individual things under the most universal form. Therefore, the First Essence is the First Form; the First Form is the First Intellect. But if essence there <note>In the divine realm</note> is in reality the same as intellect: then surely "to be" and "to understand" are there likewise the same. Then indeed, just as such an essence—everywhere, or the first of its kind—makes subsequent things with nothing else added, but only by the fact that it is such (as the sun illuminates by shining, or fire heats everywhere by being hot): so Essence itself, simply by being, procreates all beings. And if it is the cause so that all things have "being" simply, it is furthermore in the cause that all things have "being" as "this" or "that": for this specific being depends upon "being" simply, and the very common distinction of various types in formed things proceeds not from matter, but from that first uniform and simultaneously all-forming Form of all things. Therefore, insofar as this Form effects all things by being, it makes them by understanding; for within it, understanding is nothing other than being. Because it makes all things by understanding, it surely understands all things by making them. It understands, I say, not only certain things common to all, but even those proper to each one, by which each thing is perfected in its own being and act. Otherwise, it would surely understand confusedly and possess the least intelligence; it would know things in "potentiality"—and a remote and confused one at that—rather than in "actuality." Additionally, if its own action is intelligence—as the most eminent, most ample, and simultaneously most intimate action—as far as it acts, so far it utterly understands, and conversely. But it acts in the carrying out of individual and even the smallest things: since the influx of the First Being is most ample through individual beings following in certain orders, and those things which act after it are moved and act everywhere by its power. Truly, it is not the "species" of things (which are eternal and are God Himself) that are acted upon everywhere, but the "individuals." Either, therefore, God understands and acts upon nothing outside Himself (which is false), or by acting upon individual things, He understands the same, which would never happen unless they were first understood by God—just as nothing happens from the sun except what is foreseen by the sun. Therefore, God Himself understands individual things, not distracted into many, but collected into Himself: by gazing at Himself as the model of the whole and the cause of causes, He also gazes upon all things through the causes of all, and by gazing, He cares for and provides, insofar as He directs individual things toward their end and the good; for He procreated all things for the good under the very form of the Good itself. Moreover, it is proven that He cares for all things as easily as He does diligently from this: that from God himself, things have it not only that they *are*, but also that they are *causes*. For they have it from Him that they are, insofar as He is the cause. If, therefore, they have it from there that they are causes, they also possess from there the office proper to a cause. This, however, is to preserve and care for what it makes to the best of its power. For which reason, if all causes have this property from the First Cause, insofar as they are certain causes, that First Cause rightly has this most of all: to care for all and each, insofar as it is the greatest cause, and the cause of individuals. Indeed, unless they are guarded individually, common things (which are preserved in individuals) will never be guarded; the whole (which necessarily consists of parts) will not be preserved; and the universal order of the whole (which necessarily consists in degrees descending even to the smallest things) will not be destroyed. Surely this order and this distinction, since it has a certain and perpetual arrangement and therefore cannot be by chance, must proceed from the intention of some agent—yet not from the intention of an agent by necessity of nature, whose intention is determined toward one thing rather than many insofar as they are distinct. Rightly, then, it proceeds from a certain intention of an intelligence, and not of some particular intelligence or cause. For all such are counted in the number of distinct works. Therefore, from the intention of the first and most universal Intelligence proceeds the universal distinction of things. For that Intelligence is distinguished from others by itself, and it distinguishes other things among themselves by the norm of its own notion: and insofar as it knows most distinctly, it cares most distinctly. Finally, if providing proceeds from the abundant goodness of the provider and leads the governed things to the good, it rightly belongs to the best cause of causes to provide most exactly for individual things.

### *Confirmation of the same. Also that God certainly knows even contingent things, yet free will is not taken away by this.*

XX We do not doubt that God provides for things especially as they are His own, as far as He sees them. We also assert that God sees things insofar as they follow from certain orders of causes—either acting in succession or necessarily concurring out of sight: since even philosophers sometimes see many things far in the future as if they were present. They see these, I say, in causes which they themselves neither drive nor connect. How much more, then, does God foresee what results from...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Third Ennead, specifically addressing the transition between the discussions on Providence in Books 2 and 3. Ficino is reconciling the apparent conflict between God's total foreknowledge and the reality of human free will.</meta>

...causes, what comes from the properties of causes, and what arises from their conspiracy; for He Himself, by seeing the causes, brings them into being, grants them their properties, and connects them into one. And if philosophers, the more sagacious they are, the more quickly they gather absent things from present causes or judgments—and although they rely on a certain temporal discourse of reason, they nevertheless bring future things back to the present almost instantly—surely that indivisible, stable, and entirely simultaneous gaze of the eternal mind embraces the whole distance of things, whether local or temporal, in a certain indivisible and present-making strike, so that those things which are distant from one another and in the future are, to Him, intimately close and present. Thus, He does not gaze upon effects so much in their causes as in themselves. Now, from this very fact that He regards events not only in their causes, nor merely as future things, but follows them as present, it follows that while philosophers hesitate when they hunt for contingent <note>In philosophy, "contingent" refers to events that happen by choice or chance, rather than by absolute physical necessity.</note> events in the future, God Himself does not hesitate. For those things we call contingencies, as long as they are still in the future, have the possibility of not emerging from their causes; but as soon as they are present, they cannot "not emerge"; nor can they "not be" while they actually are. Nor is it granted to contingent things, insofar as they exist in the present, to be and not be at the same time, but only to be—even though in the future they might not be. Therefore, they seem to have already attained the condition of necessary things. God, therefore, holds contingent things as firmly as those that are naturally necessary, since He sees them as present. For anyone is certain that these contingent things exist and are happening when gazing at them in the present, even when they were uncertain whether they would be in the future. Furthermore, just as an effect can be known with certainty to follow from a necessary cause, so it is known from contingent causes whenever all of them are understood, and it is known whether they are hindered from elsewhere or not. But since God, as the model, the maker, and the mover of all, understands all things, He is as certain of the outcome following from contingencies as from necessities—indeed, that it is already following. 

Nor does He understand changeable things in a changeable way, nor does He discern divisible things divisibly; rather, He holds firmly and simultaneously the things that are scattered and wandering within themselves through His own indivisible and immobile nature. Just as the sight often perceives many moving things in a single glance, so things that are naturally changeable are not made fixed simply because He understands them firmly; just as material things do not become immaterial simply because He embraces them immaterially (so to speak). For He Himself, by His own intelligence—that is, by His own action—imposes the lot of contingency upon contingent things just as He exhibits the law of necessity to necessary things. Moreover, He holds most firmly any movements of our intellect and will, however free they may be. I say He understands them: for as the First Essence is the cause of being for all things in whatever way they exist, so He is the cause of rightly understanding and willing for intellectual beings. Thus, He understands direct movements as the one who moves them, but oblique <note>Refers to "crooked" or sinful actions that turn away from the right path.</note> movements as being from the opposite side of one who falls away from the right. He also understands certain movements which in themselves seem uncertain, since He sees them already happening rather than about to be. For all of time is present at once to eternity, just as the entire stretch of a circumference is equally present to its center. And although one who is now moved by the will in this way might afterwards be moved differently or in another way, He nevertheless does not judge this differently or in another way. For, anticipating each movement and its mode from the beginning, He stabilizes the changeable progression with an indivisible hinge within Himself. 

However, many are accustomed to argue this way: "If God is certain the soul will do that, the soul will necessarily do it." This does not follow. Indeed, He is certain the soul will do it *freely*—or rather, is doing it freely. For He discerns in Himself as present those things which are future to the world. Since He therefore discerns the events as already present, it is not permitted to ask again whether the soul can meanwhile change its choice after God has seen that the soul would so choose. For no "meanwhile" of time falls there; where He saw the soul would choose, He instead sees the soul choosing. Nor should you object again: "If God firmly sees the choice, therefore the soul chooses by compulsion." For what prevents the soul from doing by its own will in the meantime that which God, by His own nature, firmly discerns the soul is doing? And God Himself, by His own will, has always ordained that the soul should act by free will. Finally, as for what some have been accustomed to argue—that "it is necessary for the soul to do it, if God knows it will so will to do it"—we could similarly argue if a human were said to know the same thing. In both cases, the necessity is placed not so much in the consequence as in the relationship of the argument; it is detected not in the thing itself, but in the person arguing. This is a certain conditional necessity, not an absolute one; and conditional necessity is not at all accustomed to drag absolute necessity along with it.

THROUGH these points we solve the doubts that are raised at the end of this book, and we approach the second book on providence. Indeed, rational souls are designated as parts in providence—not, I say, as parts of nature or of the bodily machine, but as "parts" in the sense of participants in providence, and colleagues in governing. Hence, even inferior movements are permitted, once a certain authority has been granted to lesser beings. Since he says that the <term>seminal nature</term> <note>Latin: *naturam seminariam*. In Neoplatonism, these are the formative, "seed-like" powers that bridge the gap between pure intellect and physical matter.</note> of the universe is a certain soul, remember that just as vocal speech, which signifies distinctly, proceeds not only from an intellectual notion but is also itself a certain notion, so the living and all-formed "seed-bed" of the world, budding from the world-soul itself, is a certain soul. And if it is called an instrument of either pure intelligence or of the soul's intelligence, it is certainly such that its own mover provides it not only with motion but also with the form of the workmanship. For it is a most closely related instrument, and is subject to its craftsman, not...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Third Ennead, specifically addressing the transition between the discussions on Providence in Books 2 and 3. Ficino is reconciling the apparent conflict between God's total foreknowledge and the reality of human free will.</meta>

*...fixed, not like a pair of hands, but like an imagination or an imaginary spirit serving practical reason. He adds in the second book that a reason of this kind encompasses both good and evil things together. For if the habits <note>In this context, "habits" refers to the established conditions or essential qualities of things.</note> of things were first designated in this reason, then privations <note>The absence or lack of a quality that should normally be present.</note> were also consequently recorded. If the better things were described, then the worse were as well; and proceeding further, the very worst things were also written down—not in such a way that entirely worse things are carried out from there, but so that, as if begun or designed, they might finally be fulfilled in the world through physical causes or conditions. Indeed, all the levels and orders of this universe are so written in the worldly reason that the reason itself did not first construct them within itself; rather, the whole, along with its parts of this kind, was expressed from an intellectual seal <note>original: "intellectuali sigillo"; this refers to the divine blueprints or archetypes in the Divine Mind.</note>, even while it occasionally became inferior.*

*For many things in this very order of worldly reason are fitted precisely <note>original: "ad vnguem", literally "to the fingernail," a Roman idiom for perfect craftsmanship.</note> to the movements of souls. This congruity seems to be foreknown and predestined not only from this reason itself, which is subject to souls, but also—and much more so—from a certain intelligence superior to souls. Just as in the nursery of the world the whole does not generate the parts, nor does a part generate another part from the beginning, so too the physical machine of the world germinates as a whole from its nursery; it does not generate the parts of which it is composed, nor does one of its necessary parts procreate another. Thus, a star does not make a star, nor did fire make the earth from the beginning, nor a man a lion. From this it follows that no part of the world is entirely subject to others, but rather the whole corresponds to itself. Indeed, the generation of plants and animals similarly testifies that the world came forth as a whole along with its parts from its own seed, and the seed from the mind. There, a part does not make a part, but the parts, together with the whole, sprout little by little from the seed. From this it is also clear that the reasons <note>original: "rationes"; these are the formative, organizing principles or "logoi" that govern growth and structure.</note> for all the parts and the whole are contained in the seed; similarly, the reasons for the whole world are in nature, those of nature in the soul, and those of the soul are found entirely in the mind.*

*Accordingly, he says that the entire nursery of the machine is the "act" and, as it were, the spirit of the entire World-Soul; similarly, the parts within it are certain acts and, as it were, certain "breathing-vents" of the parts proper to the soul. In a similar order, this entire world is the act of the seed of the whole, and its parts are the acts of the parts. Since the nursery of the machine is congruent in every way with the soul of the world, and this soul with the mind, it follows that all things in the machine are dispensed at the nod of the mind. It is also probable that individual souls, like sisters and colleagues of the World-Soul, harmonize entirely with the World-Soul according to their own movements and circuits; so much so that the turns of choices and actions which the souls perform are adapted everywhere to the turns of the World-Soul in carrying out natural things. Indeed, by this connection to the specific choices, actions, and lives of souls, certain lots of fortune in the universe, certain bodies, and similar outcomes duly correspond.*

*Lest anyone think that the care of the whole world is difficult for God because there are innumerable and contrary things within it, he adds that all things, however diverse, converge into one form, through which they most easily obey one author. If, in mixed things, contrary elements end in a single form; if, in plants and animals, the contrary qualities of the limbs admit one form of a living being; and if this happens in both by the duty of a particular nature—why should it seem strange to anyone that the contrary parts of the world come together into one form, even if it is hidden from us? I say they come together through the works of universal nature, which particular natures follow everywhere. Therefore, if you trace individual works back to individual natures everywhere, and subject those to universal nature, and connect this to intelligence, and intelligence to unity, you will clearly recognize that intelligence moves all the subsequent "hinges" of things from the one single hinge with a single nod, and does so with marvelous ease. I say it moves them by understanding them, and thus provides for each.*

*The examples that Plotinus brings forward from the order of the categories <note>original: "praedicamentorum"; referring to the Aristotelian categories of being.</note> to reduce the multitude generally into one are clear. Among these, you will note this argument: that the One itself is the principle of all things; that all things in the universe are reduced into one through contraries—specifically, they are forced into one from unity, even beyond their own nature. You will note by what reasoning you may resolve "being" into a higher cause. For whether you say "a being," it consists of the essence of a body and its existence <note>original: "esse"; literally "to be."</note>; therefore you are forced to resolve it into simpler elements. Or if you say "existence" is an act, you reduce it to essence as its foundation. Or if you say "essence," you see this is first imperfect unless it receives an act. Thus, above this, you recognize that there is the One itself—that is, ineffable simplicity—upon which essence and the act of essence depend.*

*He says that the One itself is both diffused through all things and collects all things, just as a nerve does through the limbs; which, while it seems to be pulled apart, actually pulls things together. For the One itself, insofar as it is simply everywhere, collects all things into one; but insofar as it is such a "One" from that source, it appears to be diffused. Yet, in the meantime, it is necessarily bound back to the simply One itself. Nor is the One found in all things like a single species made of individuals, or one genus in species; but according to "prior and posterior," "more and less"—almost exactly like numerical unity throughout numbers. Hence, Plotinus derives the "simply One" next as a "one being": namely, the one Intellect, the proper author and ruler of the world, who produces the world from the manifold multitude conceived within himself, and from the unity in himself that surpasses his own multitude, collects the many members of the world into one living being. In this being, whatever exists is both a certain part of the whole from its common nature, and is also some "whole" from its own proper nature, and it exerts its own proper action, in addition to the common passion <note>In philosophy, "passion" refers to what is acted upon or received from outside, as opposed to "action."</note> inflicted on all from the universe. From this it appears that God, by the marvelous power of His action, does not take away from things their own proper actions—I say from even the smallest things, like fire or a horse—and much less does He take them from more excellent things, namely from souls, which are not determined to one thing by the condition of nature, but turn themselves toward many and opposite things in turn. And they do this according to their own nature, which is mobile through diverse things; but in the meantime, God orders it so that whatever kind of souls they have made themselves to be, such events are always rendered back to them.*

### *Nothing happens by chance. For Providence orders even the smallest things.*

*II. Consider first that the entire machine of the world surrounding the lands is always most orderly in every disposition and movement. Second, that all earthly things are mostly born and proceed in a most orderly fashion. Third, that the earth is like a point compared to the rest of the world. Through these points, fourth, you will conclude: that in this point of immense mass, enclosed by that very mass and wonderfully ordered, nothing can be left unordered. Thus, even those things which sometimes seem to float by some chance, you may know for certain do not lack their own order according to the order of the universe—I mean according to the Intellect that is the orderer of the entire world. For order has always been accustomed to be born from intelligence. By its simple and entirely immobile nod, the machine, gathered from such diverse and mobile things, conspires and is ruled in a most orderly way. Furthermore, since in any governance, the greater the intelligence and power in the governor, the less anything happens there by chance; surely, if a supreme power and intelligence governs the world, and the whole is entirely subject to it, nothing anywhere...*

# THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

### I I I

...no room is left for rashness. For an unexpected or foreign accident often happens to a human pilot <note>original: "gubernatori"; Ficino uses the metaphor of a ship's captain to contrast human management with divine governance.</note>, because he either does not see everything or does not rule over everything, and such chance events usually fall upon him from external sources. But the Universe is contained under the command and sight of a single Divine Mind, so that nothing can escape or transgress it. This is especially true because, just as the life of the world is whole in every part, so too is intelligence whole and everywhere at once in this living body of the world. Nor does it handle foreign materials from the outside, nor is it distracted by many things; rather, it moves its own matter from within, and governs the whole from a single hinge. It rules as easily through understanding as life gives life through living, or as a body acts by existing. For that which is "being" in the body through the form received from life and intelligence, is indeed "living" in life; and that, in turn, is "understanding" in the intellect. 

Indeed, the whole of life flows from the whole of intelligence; similarly, from the universal life, the common form of the entire universal body shines forth. By a certain similar proportion, the diverse forms in the cosmic machine leap forth from various seeds in life. These different seeds are sown from different notions <note>original: "notionibus"; in Platonic thought, these are the divine archetypes or ideas in the mind of God.</note> in the intelligence. Therefore, the notions of the intellect itself reach down to the individual forms of things through these "seeds of things." Just as a single seed, while it generates many forms of individual things, acts not confusedly but distinctly in each—otherwise it would not form each thing perfectly—so too the single notion of intelligence, where it expresses many forms in individuals through the many seeds of life, acts not indefinitely but determinately in each. Otherwise, it would act imperfectly, and its action and power would not reach down to the natural actions themselves. Nevertheless, it is necessary that the power and action of a higher and broader cause always proceed far and wide beyond the services of an inferior cause. 

The result is that the power and action of the First Essence itself, which is intelligence, extends through every individual thing. Furthermore, if you were to say that individual effects happen here and there in things solely from their own specific forms and powers, you must remember that these specific powers and forms—which belong to the formal order of the universe—proceed from the first Ordainer of things, and are inwardly preserved and moved by Him. Since, therefore, individual outcomes are contained within these forms and powers, it is necessary that every individual effect everywhere pertains deeply to the Giver, Preserver, and Mover of all powers and forms—I mean these powers and forms, whether they be general species or even individual ones. For even in individuals, physicists have found miraculous gifts <note>original: "dotes mirabiles"; these are unique properties or "occult virtues" found in specific herbs, stones, or people that aren't shared by their whole species.</note> which are often not granted to others under the same species. 

Finally, if what the Platonists believe is true—and which astrologers somehow acknowledge—that light in the heavens is a sense, and that stretching forth rays from that light is to perceive individual things, and by perceiving to act, and by acting to perceive; and if nothing lies hidden even under the earth that is not sensed from there by rays hidden everywhere (otherwise celestial things would not be generated even under the earth); then surely the rays of the First Intelligence also extend through all things. Insofar as they derive themselves down to individual things, they procreate individuals everywhere, and they perfect them by procreating, since they procreate by gazing upon them. It is as if you were to say that the stars create things by their "aspects" <note>An astrological term referring to the geometric angles between planets.</note>, or that the ostrich miraculously warms its eggs and forms its chicks simply by looking at them. 

Since, therefore, nothing anywhere is hidden from the divine intellect, and order is the proper quality of intelligence, nothing can happen anywhere in this workshop of intelligence that was not ordained by the Ordainer of the whole, even before it happens. Even a sudden event is linked consequently to the rest and brought back into the order of the universe. This order is only truly most absolute if even the smallest things are ordained with the greatest providence. It is likewise most excellent if it is completed not only by those things that are ordained, but also by the "ordainers" themselves. Therefore, many "ordainers" <note>Ficino refers here to a hierarchy of mediating spirits or angels who help manage the world.</note> under the First Governor distribute things according to the power and laws of the First. The power and action of this First Governor, as the most powerful, amplifies itself through all the governors beneath Him, even beyond their own duties. 

Thus, just as many things that are accidental to us are foreseen by those governors, so too some things come about outside the intention of those subordinate governors which are nonetheless from the providence of the First, to whom nothing ever happens unforeseen. For the most consummate providence belongs to the most perfect and best intellect. That providence is such that it ignores nothing and permits nothing to be unforeseen. Truly, what we call "unexpected chance," which happens from the clashing of diverse causes among themselves, is governed by some cause if it is ordained at all, and is not merely ruled by a cause acting only by the habit of nature. For a purely natural cause, since it acts through a single form, is determined toward a single result; it cannot by itself bring several scattered causes of an unexpected event into one effect, nor can it restrain multiform causes into one. Only a cause performing the duty of cognition <note>A cause with intelligence or "knowing" power.</note> can do this: having conceived many forms within itself, it is rightfully the principle of multiform things, and it miraculously gathers diverse causes into a single form of an event that was unexpected by others. Hence Proclus, in his commentary on the *Timaeus*, defining Fortune, says: "It is not rash or blind, but is a divine or demonic power, gathering diverse causes into one outcome."

<margin>//</margin> Therefore Plato, where he treats a certain accidental event in his *Letters*, suddenly introduced the name of a "daemon" <note>In the Platonic tradition, a "daemon" is a mediating spirit between gods and humans, not necessarily an evil entity.</note> after the name of Fortune. And so, daemons often, by a certain hidden persuasion, send this man by this way and that man by another to the same place, so that meeting each other there, they may produce an event that was unforeseen to them, but foreseen by the higher beings. Sometimes, too, the higher beings do not so much move different people toward one thing, but rather they use those people, who were already moving toward something else on their own, for a different purpose—unexpected indeed to the humans, but foreseen by the superiors. 

Therefore, whether the higher beings first move our minds, or whether they use us when we are already moved: the superior daemons act upon our reason through reason, by persuading simply and calmly; but the lower daemons act mostly through imagination and spirit <note>original: "spiritu"; the "spiritus" was thought to be a subtle bodily vapor that linked the soul to the physical body.</note>, stirring up certain disturbances in our spirit and imagination. Consequently, both act upon the will, but God acts directly upon the will. Finally, in whatever way and from wherever we fall into unexpected accidents, whether prosperous or adverse, the things that happen to us are always in accord with our merits—either present, past, or future. These events benefit us sometimes, but they always benefit the Universe. For in this way God tempers the harmony of the universe: so that if someone could behold the entire space of the world, and every individual thing in it, and all of time in one single gaze, he would see that just rewards are paid to each person; and that various things sound together with others in such a way that all things harmonize perfectly with the whole.

Thus, just as the souls are from the beginning, so are the bodies; and again, whatever each soul makes of itself, such are the lots to be repaid to them according to their merits. Therefore, all things—what they do, how they do it, what they suffer, and in what manner—are contained in that very order of providence. # ON THE SECOND BOOK OF THE THIRD ENNEAD

### III

...proceeds, the cause is simply that it began at some time in this or that way. That it began in such a way is merely because it was capable of beginning in various ways; but truly, you cannot resolve the fact that it was capable of both into any other cause. For this is its very nature—namely, a life that is freely mobile and rational. If anyone were to search further for the cause of why the soul is such from the beginning, he would be no less ridiculous than if he were to search for why the soul itself is soul, or why fire itself is fire. Certainly, you can assign a cause for why fire rises, penetrates, and dissolves: because it is light, subtle, and hot. But to scrutinize what the thing itself is, is nothing other than to inquire why fire is fire. Every species of things is defined from eternity by certain internal limits. 

Thus, all species, determined within themselves from age to age, seem to be nothing other than certain determinations by which the <term>First Intelligence</term> <note>In Neoplatonic thought, this is the 'Nous' or Divine Mind, the first emanation from the One.</note> primarily consists, and is distinguished within itself as if into parts; so much so that the Mind itself is these types of definitions by an intellectual necessity of nature. A similar arrangement of things follows in the nature of plants; a similar "machine of the world" <note>original: "machina mundi"; a common Renaissance term for the organized, clockwork-like structure of the universe.</note> results from a cause that does not deliberate or choose through counsel, but is so naturally disposed within itself and so naturally germinating. An arrangement of species of this kind in nature is nature itself; in the machine, it is likewise the machine of the world itself. To ask, therefore, why the world consists of so many and such diverse levels of things is to ask for what reason the world itself is the world. 

It is as if someone were to ask why a plant has life and not sensation, and has roots and branches; why an animal has sensation but not reason, or feet and a head; or why a human has human intelligence and not divine. To wish for a plant to be an animal, an animal to be a man, and a man to be God, is nothing other than to leave God alone and destroy the world. It is just as if someone wanted the foot to be a hand, or the hand to be an eye; in this way, he would destroy the members one by one, and finally the whole body.

But to descend to the condition more proper to us: man ought not to complain that he was not made more excellent from the beginning. Since he has enough as it is, and as some prove, he can in a certain way make himself more excellent—something that beings lower than man cannot do. Therefore, he has a certain principle of origin within himself: he can add good to the good he had from the beginning. That he is able to do so, we gather from the fact that he can also sometimes fall into worse states, which lower beings cannot do. God would not have made the human species (which is better than plants and brutes) such that it could fall into worse, unless He had also made it such that it could proceed into better, especially since it is closer to the <term>Primary Good</term>.

Among these things, however, when he says that the "model of the universe" and the universe itself are all things arranged by degrees, remember that in the first and pure form, many things cannot exist unless they differ, nor can they differ except formally. There, they are distinguished from each other in two ways: both by various modes of forms (as if by width) and by different degrees of forms (as if by length). Clearly, because the Mind received its form from the Good through a certain procession, it also takes on various degrees of its own form, like faces, by proceeding similarly within itself. From this, it follows that in the world, a procession also occurs through unequal degrees, and some things consequently make others, or are propagated into others. 

In the arrangement of plants and animals, the parts are sorted by unequal degrees; but such an arrangement in the world is said not to be simply "the best" because it is furthest distant from the Good, to which the first <term>World-Maker</term> <note>original: "mundi faber"; the Demiurge or craftsman of the universe.</note> is nearest, and to whom the <term>World Soul</term> <note>original: "anima mundi"</note> is subject. To this is submitted the <term>Seminal Reason</term> <note>original: "ratio seminalis"; the formative power or "seeds" that contain the blueprints for physical life.</note> of the world, from which, as soon as the worldly animal is made with a world-body, the form of the world's body is subjected to reason. Truly, a reason of this kind is not called "animated" (that is, living) in the same way the World Soul is; rather, the vigor of the soul itself ends in this reason as heat ends in lukewarmness, or light ends in paleness. By a certain similar proportion, certain lives dedicated to bodies degenerate from the lives that remain everywhere within themselves, whether this is considered in the spheres and stars, or in demons and men. Everywhere, however, the higher naturally provides for the lower in nature, and the higher it is, the more it provides; and by providing, it remains more firmly within itself. For from this very firmness of its own, the perpetual course of providence proceeds, while it is clearly not affected or inclined toward other things, but overflows.

->On the intellect, reason, and imagination. Why humans do not always use reason.<-
->Why the soul becomes worse. That it does not pass into beasts.<-

### IIII

In the following chapter, you will consider again that there is a twofold "reason" of the common world. The first is present to the world as an artisan; the second is within it as a form through which (as if kin to the artisan) the artisan also seems joined to the world. The presiding artisan is the intellectual substance itself; the residing form is the seminal reason, through which the intellect seems to unite with the matter of the world and generate. 

Collect the rest of Plotinus's opinion briefly as follows: There are two principles of free actions in our soul—Intellect and Reason—by whose work the soul can proceed beyond that which it had from the beginning. But through the Intellect, it profits suddenly, and the mind is immediately made divine from human. Through Reason, it profits over time, and similarly fails; so that it may be human, divine, or become demonic and beast-like. 

Intellect and Reason are indeed always present to all souls of men, but not all live by reason; and very few indeed live by intellect. For many live rather by imagination and sense; in their imagination, the sparks of reason themselves either rarely flicker, or sometimes do not flicker at all. Since the imagination is turned rather toward opposites—just as the intellect commonly seems to hardly flicker into human reason except in the blessed. That intelligence and one's own reason are present even to human souls not using them will not be doubted by anyone who knows that common intelligence and reason flourish everywhere and are present to even the smallest things. 

Meanwhile, you will note that the intellect is not so separate that it is not a part of the soul; likewise, just as fire is always hot, so the intellect is always understanding, and the power of the soul placed in discourse is always discoursing in whatever way it discourses: whether through reasons or through images, even in the manner of one dreaming. Similarly, the vegetative power is constantly vegetating. Furthermore, while the soul lives in a human, both the mind and reason are something belonging to humans, although both do not always overflow into humans in action, and the mind shines much more rarely than reason. 

If ever the soul should be in brutes, he does not want there to be anything of mind or reason in the brutes, but only imagination and vegetation can be shared with them. However, that the flash of not only common intelligence but even sometimes of reason seems to flicker very little in souls is caused either by a too perverse composition of the body (often unsuitable for talent and ready for disturbance) or perhaps the seminal reason of the soul itself has long since turned into a brutal habit, and thereafter [shapes] the body in matter as it <meta>catchword: brings forth/carries (fert)</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains the hierarchical nature of the soul and the universe, arguing that everything follows its inherent nature and that humans have a unique ability to improve their spiritual state through intellect and reason. He distinguishes between the artisan (the higher mind) and seminal reason (the formative force in matter), noting that while higher faculties are always present, they are often obscured by the physical body.</summary>
