...opportunity brings along, conforming it to something brutal: if indeed the <term>genital power</term> <note>The "potentia genitalis" refers to the soul's lower, life-giving faculty that animates the physical body.</note> brings the first quality to the body, so that the soul does not then turn out entirely as the body is born, but rather fashions for itself such a body as nature itself has already conceived for it; thus, having deservedly become worse in itself, it is transferred into a worse life and lot. After this, you will observe four causes by which our soul can at times become worse. The first is because it was placed from the beginning after the second order of souls. The second is because a tiny momentum from the beginning becomes greatest by falling gradually over a long time. The third is because while the soul happens to collide with some other soul or thing, or rather while a prior affection in the soul clashes with a later one, a new force results from such a clash and produces a new effect therefrom, just as is found in the mixing of other things. The fourth is because preceding actions in a past life initiated such a habit for the present life. But where Plotinus seems to want the "seed-like" reason of the soul to degenerate from antecedent actions to such an extent that the very genital power, which was in the proper species of man, now becomes the species of some brute—and thus conceives or receives such a brute—understand this as said conditionally: that is, *if* ever that natural power could change its species in itself, it would consequently be transferred to such a beastly species. However, reason shows us that this is certainly not possible. First, because since the proper essence and essential power of no thing, as long as it exists, can take on the being proper to another species and undergo its essential act, surely the soul of man—far more excellent than many things—cannot fall so far from its own species as to put on the species of others, and sometimes even inferior ones. Second, because since Plotinus says elsewhere that the act of understanding and the act of growing are entirely substantial, and that intelligence is not changed by the actions of the soul, it follows that he must admit that the <term>vegetal power</term> <note>The "potentia vegetalis" is the faculty responsible for growth and nutrition.</note> is not changed by any actions, as is evident from experience. For it does not become wicked through a habit of wicked morals, nor good through good; and reason itself demonstrates that accidents do not change the permanent substance of the moving thing, especially if it originates from within. Therefore, the vegetal essence itself will never be transmuted from its own species into the species of a brute through accidental imaginations (which are in some way similar to those of brutes), nor will it of itself abandon its proper species, since it is eternal. Rather, a certain beastly habit is contracted within the acts and affections of the imagination—a habit, I say, affecting the rational power as well, which often consents to the imagination. This habit, being too alien, surely twists the soul away from the contemplation of divine things, and from their life and place, for a long time. Third, since they think the soul is transferred into a worse life and lot for the sake of purgation—so that, led by repentance, it might retract the misdeeds of the past—every path to repentance is closed if the rational species itself is cast down into a beastly one. Added to this is the fact that in our own genus there are such diverse degrees that it is not necessary to change the figure of the body for the sake of justice or congruence, since under this very human figure men become humane, or brutal (so to speak), or even demonic. If Plotinus feels this way, he will not dissent from <term>Timaeus the Pythagorean</term> <note>Refers to the character in Plato's dialogue "Timaeus," whom Ficino considers a source of ancient wisdom.</note>, and perhaps he will not disagree with Aristotle, nor be disapproved of by the Hebrews <note>Ficino likely refers to Jewish Kabbalists or thinkers like Philo of Alexandria who shared similar views on the soul.</note>. For all these will easily concede that our soul can revolve only through the bodies of men, but can in no way be accommodated to brutes; yet it can be accommodated to demonic figures, for from the beginning it has a spiritual body very similar to the bodies of demons.

### *That there must be different degrees of things; that providence dispenses each thing with the equality of geometric proportion; that fate serves providence; concerning free will.*

Just as the Divine Mind has within itself the formal reasons of things, distinct by species and degrees (for distinction cannot exist in pure form except formally), so in configuring such a distinction in the world, it does not maintain an equal number everywhere—as if this thing should have as many and such powers as that one has. Otherwise, one thing might perhaps have sufficed, and the rest would be superfluous, adding nothing new, appearing to be many more by a division of dimension or some accident rather than by an essential difference of form. Therefore, those things which God does not make equal to one another in number and weight, He at least makes equal by the congruence of proportion. For instance, if you proceed in length, you might see the first creature surpass the second by a double proportion; furthermore, just as the second is surpassed by the first by double, it similarly surpasses the third by double, and so on for the third and fourth. By similar proportions by which natures surpass natures, you will recognize that the actions and passions of those natures in turn exceed the actions and passions of others. If again you diverge in breadth, you will see if the things accompanying or surrounding the first creature are exceeded by it by a sesquialter <note>A ratio of 3:2.</note> ratio, or rather a sesquitertiar <note>A ratio of 4:3.</note> one; by a similar proportion, those things surrounding the subsequent creatures are surpassed. Therefore, Providence delights not in arithmetic, but rather in <term>geometric equality</term> <note>In arithmetic equality, everyone gets the same amount (e.g., 2 and 2). In geometric equality, things are distributed according to the merit or nature of the recipient (e.g., 4 to a master, 2 to a servant), which Ficino identifies with true Justice.</note>. This is proper to Justice, which, as civil prudence, governs the home, the city, and the kingdom—to which prudence Plotinus compared divine Providence. Likewise, he compared it to poetry and music simultaneously, and even more often and more willingly to the vegetal nature governing an animal or a plant. For Nature is the instrument of Providence. Thus, by this comparison, he teaches that just as every single animal is dispensed by a single nature everywhere—present as much in the lowest members as in the highest—so too is this world-animal ruled by a single Providence present everywhere to each part. Among these things, you will observe that individual parts in the world, just as members in an animal, possess certain powers and proper actions beyond the common condition. Likewise, as easily as parts in any animal immediately communicate through sense and passion with other parts because of their common nature, so easily do individual things in this world-animal (as members) suffer and consent with one another because of the communion of one nature—not only those which are close in position, but even those which are very far apart. For just as motion and affection leap from the head to the feet, so they leap from the highest parts of the world to the lowest. Truly, the "seed-like" life of the world, by which this whole is one animal like a form, he calls **Fate**, the explanation of which is a certain series of celestial causes and motions. In this explanation, **Atropos** is sometimes named the firmament; **Clotho** the truly revolving region of the planets; and **Lachesis** that which is translated from there into the sublunary realm by lots. Therefore, this entire distribution and arrangement of things everywhere is simply **Providence**, but because it depends on the Mind and is carried out everywhere by the nod of the Mind, it is called Providence. Truly, because it proceeds through the vegetal nature of the soul, and subsequently through the celestial bodies, it is also called **Fate**. Whatever things, therefore, happen by Fate, happen by Providence; although Providence does many things besides which are not enclosed within the limits of Fate—namely, whatever pertains to intellectual things, and what intellectual substances themselves likewise do. Not otherwise...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, shifting from the specific descent of the soul into the body to the broader relationship between divine Providence, Fate, and the presence of "evil" or "defects" in the material world.</meta>

# ON BOOK II OF ENNEAD III.

Indeed, Fate depends upon Providence just as heat depends upon light. In this relationship, wherever heat acts, light also acts, but the reverse is not true. For there are wondrous virtues hidden in light that are not found in heat; similarly, the spirit depends on the soul, doing nothing without the soul, though the soul may do something without the spirit. Thus far, he has established Providence and Fate as the common principles of things and actions. However, the specific principles of motions are the effective "natures" found everywhere: especially the rational soul, which is not merely uniform or entirely determined to a single path, but is multiform and directs itself toward diverse ends through deliberation. 

Therefore, whatever comes from Fate comes equally and properly from Providence. Yet, what happens properly from the rational nature does not happen "properly" from Providence—even if it occurs through a certain common influx. If a person's deliberation proceeds toward the best end via the most choice-worthy path, then, while it is being done by the soul, it proceeds according to the order that Providence itself preserves. Otherwise, it is neither done by Providence nor according to the primary rules of Providence. Nevertheless, however our affairs may turn out, they are neither hidden from Providence nor neglected by it; rather, they are brought under that same providential order. Through the very rules of Providence, they are always disposed into a condition and place appropriate to their merits. 

Righteous movements are directed by the *primary* rules of Providence, while wandering or "oblique" movements are managed by the *secondary* rules. This is no different from how nature acts in a living body: while it maintains the health of the limbs, it also restores lost health through healing, accommodating and purging each of the <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed in pre-modern medicine to determine health and temperament.</note> in their proper places. That we occasionally transgress the order of Providence happens either solely from our ignorance (occurring due to negligence while we deliberate carelessly) or from a leaning of the senses and nature that grants too much to external pleasures. 

Even so, things offered to us from the outside move us not so much by their own nature as by our own quality. Nevertheless, from the meeting of a specific man with another specific man or thing, something new and hidden often occurs—in both or at least one of them—for a cause unknown to us but known to Providence. This might happen because of our own properties flashing outward and generating a "third property" by their confluence, or by the power of our <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Platonic tradition, a "daemon" is a guiding spirit or intermediary between gods and men, not necessarily an evil entity.</note>, or by the influences of the stars flowing together within and from us in various ways. Plato testifies in the *Theages* <note>A dialogue attributed to Plato concerning the "divine sign" of Socrates.</note> that this happened in a wondrous and happy way regarding Socrates.

### By what sequence of consequence can evils be foreseen from good things? How signs of future things are in present ones.

**VI** If evils are not according to the order of Providence, they seem to lack order; therefore, it seems they cannot be foreseen. Yet, they *are* foreseen by many. How then can they be predicted? Because they eventually follow the order of Providence itself, or, if they happen in a fractured way, they are wondrously inserted into the established order of Providence. 

Furthermore, since division and multiplicity increase step-by-step from the first to the last, and the extreme division occurs in the corporeal world, it is necessary that what exists in the higher worlds—not as actual <term>matter</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, "matter" is the lowest level of reality, often equated with "non-being" or the "source of evil" because it is the furthest point from God/The One.</note> but as something "material" compared to its most absolute act (distinguished not in reality but by reason)—exists in the corporeal world as actual matter. Here, it is separated both in reality and by the greatest distance from the nature of Form; thus, it remains formless in itself and "evil." You see, then, by what order of consequence the mind is able to see and foresee matter from form, and finally, evil from good.

Moreover, the order of Providence establishes various conditions of qualities in the world, which proceed through long propagation by natural fertility. From this order of progression, many things are forced to stand further away from their source, and thus they hold themselves in a worse state. Again, you see by what series of Providence the <term>privations</term> <note>A "privation" is the absence of a quality that should naturally be present (e.g., blindness is a privation of sight).</note> and defects can be foreknown from the "habits" or positive qualities. 

Just as the world itself and the things within it consist of both the beautiful and the deformed, and the perfections of natures gradually fade into defects, so too do the actions of all things. Therefore, from the very vigor of upright actions descending further, their own obliquity and defect can be sensed in advance. But such a prediction, looking from principles toward the extremes, belongs to God and divine beings. Others foresee future things in the present not through hidden causes, but through the signs that openly accompany those causes—just as one who has been made certain of what a friend will do in the future by reading his letters. For the present causes of things, in which future effects are contained, act everywhere as if "writing" something in a way that corresponds to what is coming; from this, wise men sense the future by "reading" it. 

Since all these things are members of a single "world-animal," the movements of the higher members frequently move, follow, or are imitated by the lower members. Signs of lower things are displayed in the higher, by which future events are known through a certain comparison of proportion rather than through the efficacy of reason. Thus the <term>auspex</term> <note>A priest in ancient Rome who interpreted the flight of birds to determine the will of the gods.</note> predicts: "A bird flew high for this man, but the opposite for that one; therefore, this one shall be exalted, and that one cast down." Similarly, the <term>augur</term> promises happier things from the joyful chirping of birds and threatens sad things from the somber. Similarly, astrologers are accustomed to designate height of dignity through the altitude of the planets. 

After this, you will note that—just as the <term>seed-like reason</term> <note>Original: "ratio seminaria." The formative blueprints or creative forces that unfold in the material world.</note> of the world is a single life gathered from many seeds, which does not make the seeds itself but proceeds from them so affected; and there one thing does not generate another, but they breathe together—so this world, together with its members, sprouts from there as if from a single animal. It does not make its own members, but is itself "made"; these members do not make those, but move and are moved in turn. Each individual part suffers or acts according to its own nature, signaling to others by a certain agreement and being signaled to by others in the same way.

### That in the Providence of God, artistic and natural action are the same, governing the world like life governs a plant.

**VII** We should not listen to those who quibble: "If there is Providence, then there is no evil; if there is evil, then there is no Providence." On the contrary, it is from this very fact—that the Best itself acts by providing, and provides by acting—that it acts upon and cares for something "less good." Step by step, through the "less and less good," one arrives at evil. Remove evil, and you would remove Providence. 

Do you desire to see Providence? Remember that the gifts distributed among the lower things are collected in the higher. Thus, astronomers recognize that the heat and moisture dispersed separately through Mars and the Moon are joined together in Jupiter. You believe the divine Mind to be superior to Nature and Art; for you do not deny that Nature is its instrument, and you think Art is the emulator of both. You recognize that Art understands what it fabricates, since it acts by understanding, but it fabricates from the outside. You admit that Nature acts from within, but does so without its own intelligence. 

You perceive, therefore, that both are imperfect. Thus, you are forced to trace them back to a perfect principle, which both fabricates from within by understanding and understands by fabricating. In this way, you grasp divine Providence, where those things which...

COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

In things, there are two powers—nature and art—which are separate. However, in the Divine, they are gathered into one and the same power, whereas in your soul they are divided into two powers. Through one power, you understand and arrange things; meanwhile, through the other, you nourish the body and generate and distribute individual parts within it. For this reason, you do not generate the things you understand, nor do you understand the things you generate. But consider the Divine Mind: by the very same act through which it understands, it also generates, and vice versa. Just as light and heat, which exist in fire as two distinct qualities, exist in the sun as one, so understanding and generating are two acts in you through two different powers. In God, they are a single act, which governs both the "intelligence" of the <term>World Soul</term> <note>original: "anima mundi"</note>—acting like art—and the power of the <term>vegetative soul</term> <note>original: "vegetalis animae"</note>—acting in the place of nature. Beneath these is the body of the world, so animated and so governed that it is like the body of an animal or a plant. For these three breathe together in harmony: the Divine Mind, the World Soul, and Nature. In them, all worldly things exist in such a way that the whole is contained within each part. This harmony <note>original: "conspiratio," a breathing-together</note> of these three is called the root of the "World Tree," or the radical vigor diffused everywhere throughout the tree. In this worldly tree, things are as different as the trunk is from the root, or the many branches from the trunk, or the twigs from the branches, or the many leaves and fruits from the twigs. Even in these furthest extremities, the vigor of the root itself is preserved, ready for propagation. In these things, one may consider first that all worldly things, however separate they seem from one another, are nonetheless interconnected and dependent on the same principle; and second, that they can easily communicate with one another in action and passion. Furthermore, everything is most easily governed by that same principle which remains everywhere and connects everything from within, articulately, in the manner of a nerve.

The arrangement of the world happens through divine providence, not by chance, nor by a process of deliberation preceding it in time, but by the priority of the order of cause and the expression of a mind that acts like a natural and firm seal.

**A** That it would be irrational to commit the essence and composition of the universe to accident and chance—the mark of a man possessing neither intellect nor sense—is clear even before any formal reasoning; although many sufficient arguments have already been brought forward on this very point. We must, however, taking up the discussion from the beginning, consider the manner itself

**B** in which all these things happen and have been made. This is especially necessary since, because some things seem not to happen rightly, it occurs that some doubt the providence of the whole. From this, it has happened that some deny providence altogether, while others assert that the world was established by an evil craftsman. For the moment, let us set aside that specific providence which is a kind of plan before the work in individual actions, describing how something ought to be done or not done among those things which it is not expedient to do; also how something may or may not

**C** be present for us. Instead, let us now assume that which we call the providence of the universe, and let us connect what follows in an orderly way. If, therefore, we were to think that the world was made at some specific point in time, when previously it had not existed, we would apply the same logic...

<column-break/>

That it would be irrational to attribute the essence and composition of the universe to spontaneity and chance—the mark of a man who possesses neither mind nor perception—is surely clear even before reasoning. Indeed, many sufficient arguments have been laid down demonstrating this. But regarding the manner in which each of these things comes to be and has been made: because of the way some things seem to happen incorrectly, it happens that people have doubts about the providence of the whole. To some, it occurs to say that providence does not even exist. To others, they say that the world has been produced by an evil craftsman. <note>The Greek text here has a marginal correction "gennemene" for "gegenemene," both relating to the world being "born" or "created."</note>

It is fitting to investigate this from above and from the beginning, taking up the argument. Let us, for now, set aside that providence which concerns individual things—where there is a plan regarding works, how they ought or ought not to happen among the things that must be done, or how something might or might not be for us. Instead, having hypothesized that which we call the providence of the whole, let us join together the points that follow. If, then, we were to say that the world had come into being at a certain time, as if it had not existed before that time, we would apply the same reasoning...

BOOK THE SECOND

<column-break/>

...if we were to establish a <term>providence</term> <note>The concept of God's foresight and care for the universe.</note> similar to the one we spoke of regarding individual things. This would be a certain foresight and reasoning of God, considering how this universe might come into being, and how it might be as excellent as possible. But since we say that eternity and the "all" are present in this world, we should correctly and logically assign providence to the whole.
<margin>* itself</margin>
This providence is the fact that the world exists according to the <term>Intellect</term> <note>original Greek: "nous," referring to the Divine Mind or the realm of pure forms</note>, and that the Intellect exists before it. Not that the Intellect is prior in time, but because the world comes from the Intellect. The Intellect is prior by nature, so to speak, and is the cause—it is the <term>archetype</term> <note>A primal pattern or blueprint from which all things are copied.</note> and the pattern of the world, being the "true whole." Or as they say, it exists in the manner of eternity. These are the things of the Intellect and of Being. Nature is the true and first world. It is not divided from itself, and it is not weakened by partition. It is not lacking in its parts, because no part is torn away from the whole. Rather, it is the entirety of life and the entirety of Intellect, living and thinking all at once. Even the part provides the whole. Everything is a friend to itself, and nothing is separated from another or made to be alone or estranged from the rest. Therefore, there is no injustice 
<margin>* the opposite</margin>
there, nor is one thing against another, even if <insert>opposites</insert> were to exist. Everywhere is one "good." It is perfect in every way; it stands still and admits no change. For one thing does not act upon another there. For what reason would it act, since nothing is missing or in need? What <term>Logos</term> <note>The guiding "reason" or "word" that shapes reality.</note> or what Mind would produce another now? It would only do so if it lacked the power it already possesses. But it does not lack; it is in a state of silent movement, wherein it rejoices. For those who are blessed in this way, it is enough to simply be what they are. To be "busy" with many affairs is not safe, for it draws one out from oneself. 
<margin>* out from themselves</margin>
But let that world be blessed, for in "not doing," it performs the greatest benefits, and by remaining within itself, it accomplishes no small things.

# HOW THE WORLD SUBSISTS
<note>original Greek: "Τ’ ὝΦΙΣΤΑΤΑΙ"</note>

Indeed, from that true world, this world here depends—a world that is not truly "one." It is many, divided into a multitude, where one thing stands apart from another and has become foreign. No longer is there only friendship, but also enmities born of distance and lack; by necessity, one thing becomes hostile to another. For no part is sufficient unto itself, but while it seeks to be saved 
<margin>* the whole</margin>
by another, it becomes an enemy to that which preserves it. This world came to be, and it must be concluded that the "whole" was made not by a process of reasoning, but by the necessity of a "second nature." For the realm of Being was not such that it could be the final limit of things. It was the first, and it possessed great power—indeed, all power—and this included the power to create something else. It did not need to "seek" to create, for if it had to seek, it would not have possessed the power within itself. It did not create as if from its essence <insert>through effort</insert>, but rather like a craftsman who has the power to create not from himself, but as something acquired through learning.

<column-break/>

-> A <-
...if we were to establish a providence, as we have established in the production of individual things—namely, a certain foresight and reasoning of a deliberating God, deciding by what condition the universe might best be made, and by what method it might be constructed as perfectly as possible. But because we believe that this world always exists, and never "is not," we must rightly and consequently assign providence to the world: this very fact that it exists according to the Mind, and that the Mind is before it—not as if preceding it in time, but because this world comes from the Mind. The Mind is prior to the world by nature, and the Mind exists as the cause of this world—this world being an image existing through that archetype, and in the same way, subsisting from it perpetually.

-> B <-
The manner of it is this: The nature of the Mind and of Being is the "true and first world," not distant from itself, nor weakened by any divisible condition, nor lacking even in its parts due to any defect. Indeed, no part is severed from the whole, but its entire life and entire Mind live in one and simultaneously understand. It even renders a part as the whole, and everything is a friend to itself, where one thing is not segregated from another, nor is anything solitary or destitute of the rest. Thus, one thing does not harm another, even if it were a contrary thing.

-> C <-
Since it is everywhere, and surely remains perfect everywhere, it admits no change at all: for there, one thing does not act upon another.

-> D <-
For for whose sake would it act upon another, since nothing is missing at all? Why should a "reason" there produce a "reason," or one intellect another intellect? Is it because it has the power to make something of itself? But then it would not have been entirely well beforehand; it would only attempt to "make" and be moved insofar as there was something inferior within itself. Truly, for the blessed ones, it is enough to consist in themselves and simply to exist as what they are. To be "busy" with business is not safe; business forces them to depart from themselves.

-> E <-
To such an extent is that archetype of this world blessed, that by "not doing," it does the greatest things, and by remaining within itself, it perfects no small things.

<margin>
II
This world is born from the intelligible world and differs from it; it is "one" named after the "One." It is necessary for the world to be made. The earth receives its "seed-like reason" <note>original Latin: "rationem seminalem," a formative power.</note> from the first Intellect and the living soul together.
</margin>

-> F <-
Therefore, from that world which is truly and uniquely "one," this world depends, which is now not truly one. It is therefore manifold and divided into a multitude, in which one thing, being distant from another, comes forth as a stranger. No longer does friendship alone thrive here, but because of the distance, discord is born, and in their very deficiency, some things are now necessarily opposed to others. For no part is sufficient for itself; but while it seeks safety for itself from elsewhere, it brings war to that by which it is preserved.

-> G <-
It was made, however, not by some concluding reasoning, but by a certain necessity of "making," so that a second nature might follow the first. For the intelligible world was not of such a kind that it could be the end of all things. For it was the first, and it had the greatest power—indeed, the whole power—and this was directed toward making something else, far from any care that seeks to act. Otherwise, it would not have had that power by its own nature, if it had to seek it. Nor would it be from its own essence, but it would be like a craftsman not having the power to make from himself, but acquiring it as an external thing through learning.

<summary>Plotinus explains that the physical world is a secondary copy of a perfect, unified "Intellectual World." While the divine realm is self-sufficient and peaceful, the physical world is characterized by division, lack, and necessary conflict among its parts.</summary>

### PLOTINUS: ENNEAD III

<columns>
A The **Intellect**, therefore, by pouring something of itself into matter, while remaining itself unmoved and at rest, has crafted all things. This "something" is the **Reason-Principle** <note>original Latin: "ratio"; Greek: "logos." In Neoplatonism, this is the formative power that acts as a bridge between the divine mind and the physical world.</note> flowing out from the Intellect. Indeed, that which flows from the Intellect is Reason, and it flows continuously for as long as the Intellect itself remains within the order of reality. Just as

B in the **Reason-Principle** implanted within a seed, all things exist together and in the same place—where nothing fights with another, nor disagrees, nor stands in the way—and yet, something eventually arises in a physical mass, where one part is in one place and another elsewhere, and one thing is hindered or harmed by another: so too, from the one Intellect and the Reason flowing from it, this universe has blossomed, now standing apart from itself. And by necessity, some things were born friendly to each other and healthy, while others were hostile and destructive. Some things, whether willing or unwilling, destroy one another, and through their very destruction, they work together to create a mutual rebirth. At the same time, the **Artisan** <note>Plotinus refers to the "demiurge" or the organizing force of the universe.</note> has established a single harmony among these things that suffer and act, while each individual part sounds its own unique note. But the **Reason-Principle** within them establishes a single

C concord and tempering of order throughout the whole. For this universe is not like the Intellect and Reason "yonder" <note>Plotinus uses "there" or "yonder" to refer to the higher, spiritual realm of forms.</note>, but is a participant in that Intellect and Reason. For this reason, it required a harmony, specifically because **Intellect** and **Necessity** <note>original: "necessitas." In Platonic thought, Necessity represents the stubborn properties of matter that Reason must persuade or organize.</note> concur here: with Necessity pulling toward what is worse and deviating into a deprivation of Reason (since it lacks reason itself), while the Intellect meanwhile dominates Necessity. Thus, it came forth as a mixture. And indeed, where the world ends, there is matter and Reason; but where it begins and is governed, there is the **Soul** <note>The "World Soul" that animates the physical universe.</note> which has been perfected by the mixture. We must not think that the Soul labors, for it governs the whole most easily, as if by its mere presence.

First, because the world exists out of necessity, not constructed by the deliberation of logic, but by a superior nature generating a work like itself according to its own nature. Second, even if deliberation were the cause, the world would not be a disgrace to its author. For he

F made the whole as something entirely beautiful and sufficient, and a friend to itself—moreover, fitting equally for its parts, both the greater and the lesser. Therefore, whoever finds fault with the whole based on its parts finds fault foolishly. For it is proper to consider the parts in relation to the whole to see if they are in concord and adapted to the whole; but when considering the whole itself, one should by no means look at every tiny little particle. Otherwise, that would not be the act of a man criticizing the world, but of one who takes certain parts of the world in isolation from the others.

For all things are within me: plants and animals, the nature of all generated bodies, many gods, and throngs of spirits <note>original Greek: "daimonon"; in Neoplatonism, these are intermediary beings between gods and men, not necessarily evil.</note>, and good souls, and men made divine by virtue." 

*The earth is adorned with all plants and animals of every kind; the power of the soul has reached even unto the sea. Is then the whole air, and the ether, and the entire heaven void of soul? No, for there all souls are good, providing life to the stars and to the well-ordered, eternal revolution of the heaven. Indeed, in imitation of the Mind <note>original Greek: "nous"; the divine intellect.</note>, the heaven is moved wisely in a circle forever, for it seeks nothing outside itself. All things within me strive toward the **Good**, and each attains it according to its own power. For the entire heaven depends upon the Good, as does my entire soul, and the gods who rule in my parts, and all animals and plants, and even whatever seems to be inanimate. For within me, some things seem to participate only in being, others in living, others more so in sensation, others possess reason, and some possess the fullness of life. One should not demand equal things for things that are not equal; for it is not assigned to the finger to see, but to the eye. To the finger belongs another way of being, I think—to be a finger and to possess its own nature.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Just as if someone, omitting all other living creatures entirely, should take the most abject, or—dismissing a whole genus like the human race—should bring forward Thersites into the center. But because that which has been made is the world as a whole, if it pleases you to turn the ears of the mind toward it, perhaps you will hear it crying out thus: "Without a doubt God made me, and from Him I was made perfect, constituted from all living things, sufficient to myself, deeply satisfying to myself, and in want of nothing. For all things are in me: animals as well as plants, the nature of all general things, many gods, populations of spirits, armies of good souls, <margin>B</margin> and men made happy by virtue." 

For the earth alone is not merely adorned with all plants and every kind of living creature, nor has the power of the soul spread itself only as far as the sea; rather, is the whole air and ether and the entire heaven lacking soul and life? On the contrary, souls are there also, all of them good, supplying life to the stars and to the <margin>C</margin> heavenly revolution most orderly and eternally. Add to this that, in imitation of the Mind, it is moved wisely in a circuit always around the same center; for it seeks nothing from the outside. 

Furthermore, whatever things are in me, they all indeed desire the **Good**, but each attains it according to its own faculty. For the whole heaven depends upon that Good, and even my entire soul. Moreover, there are the gods who reign in my parts; likewise all animals and plants; and finally, if anything <margin>D</margin> in me appears to be inanimate. Then indeed, some things seem to be participants only in being, others in living, others more in sensing, others already possess reason, and others, finally, the whole of life. For it is not proper to demand equal things everywhere in things that are not equal: nor is it assigned to the finger to see—that little thing—but that is to be assigned to the eye; to the finger, truly, something else is to be desired. And I judge that to be this: that it be a finger and perform its own proper duty.

### IIII.
<margin>E</margin> **NO ONE** ought to wonder that fire is extinguished by water, and that fire itself often consumes other things; for something else brought this fire into its own state of being. It is no injustice that, since it was not produced by itself, it is also destroyed by another. Indeed, it proceeded into its own being from the destruction of another, and thus death brings nothing unfair to it when it is in such a state.
<margin>Evil is never pure: for it exists around bodies and, in the case of souls, is mixed with good.</margin>
<margin>F</margin> Likewise, in place of the extinguished fire, another fire sometimes flourishes. Certainly, in the incorporeal heaven <note>The intelligible realm or the World of Ideas.</note>, each thing remains. But in this visible heaven, the whole indeed lives always, and whatever parts are honorable and sovereign remain. 

Souls, however, changing bodies in turn, become now one species, now another; and whenever a soul is able, being placed outside of generation <note>The cycle of birth and death.</note>, it lives together with the Universal Soul. Bodies, truly, exist according to their species and as individual wholes, provided that from them animals shall both exist and be nourished. For life here is mobile, but there it is immobile. It was surely necessary for motion to proceed from an immobile nature, and for another life to flow from the life flourishing in itself—like a certain breath of life, somewhat unstable, which <margin>G</margin> becomes a kind of expiration of the quiet life. Furthermore, there are the mutual attacks and slaughters of animals...

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD III.

<columns>
...necessarily happen. For these things were not born to be eternal. But they were born because Reason <note>original: "ratio" / "logos"; the guiding principle or divine logic that shapes the material world.</note> has occupied all matter, possessing in itself all things which indeed exist in the heaven above: for from where else would they have come, if they did not exist there? Furthermore, the mutual injuries men inflict upon one another perhaps proceed from the very appetite for the Good; specifically, when they are unable to attain the Good, they wander astray and attack others. But truly, those who have acted unjustly pay the penalty, both because they carry away a depraved soul from their wicked actions, and because they are transmitted by a certain fixed order into a worse place: for nothing can ever escape what has been ordained in the law of the universe. 

Order is not, however, as some think, instituted because of the violation of order, nor is the law established because of the transgression of the law—as if those things were made for the sake of the worse elements, so that they might be visible to us. On the contrary, it is because this order is inherent; and because there is order, the transgression of order has a place. Because of the law and Reason, and because Reason exists, the transgression of the law and Reason occurs. This does not mean that the better things have made the worse; rather, it is because those things which are in need, and which ought to look up to the better things, are often unable to receive them—either by their own nature, or by chance, or by some impediment brought from elsewhere. 

For when a thing uses an inherent order, it perhaps fails to achieve it either through an internal fault or because of something else happening from another source; it also suffers many things from others, sometimes even when those acting do not wish it and are striving toward something else. Truly, those living beings which possess a spontaneous motion of their own <note>original Latin: "spontaneum motum"; Greek: "kinesin autexousion" - referring to free will or self-determined action.</note> sometimes strive toward the better, and at other times slide toward the worse. It is perhaps not right to seek the cause of this inclination or fall toward the worse from anything outside itself; for a small momentum given toward falling at the beginning, proceeding along the same path, makes the error constantly greater and more significant. The body is also present, and desire exists therein by necessity. Furthermore, that which occurs suddenly at first, and is not immediately noticed and caught, creates a choice toward that which one was first inclined. Yet, punishment follows under divine judgment; nor is it unjust for a soul that has become such as it is to suffer things consistent with its own disposition. Nor should it be demanded that those be happy who have done nothing worthy of happiness. Only the good are happy; for by that very fact, even the gods are blessed.

If, therefore, the power to attain happiness is given to souls even in this world, no one is permitted to complain about this region because some are not happy. Rather, one should blame their own weakness, because they are not able to struggle vigorously where the rewards of virtue are set forth. For who could justly complain that those who have not yet been made divine do not possess a divine life? Consequently, poverty and disease are of no importance to good men, but are useful to the wicked. Moreover, it is sometimes necessary to be sick, since we possess bodies. Nor are these things entirely useless to the common order and the fullness of the universe; for indeed, just as when certain things are destroyed, the Reason of the universe...

As for those things which became eternal, they became so because Reason <note>original: "logos"</note> took hold of all matter and held all things in itself, they being there in the upper heaven. For from where else could they come, if they were not there? Regarding the injustices of men against one another, they might have their cause in the striving for the Good. But being frustrated by the inability to attain it, they turn toward other things and act unjustly. Some pay the penalty by being harmed in their souls—the activities of wickedness—and are led into a worse place; for it is impossible to escape in any way that which is ordained in the law of the universe. 

Order does not exist because of disorder, nor law because of lawlessness, as someone might think—as if those better things existed so that the worse might be known and made manifest. Rather, it is because of the order that follows; and because there is order, there is disorder through the law and Reason; and because there is Reason, there are lawlessness and folly. It is not that the better things have made the worse, but that those needing to receive the better things [fail to do so] through their own nature, or by coincidence, or by the prevention of others from receiving what they were able to. That which uses an inherent order may happen to do so through itself, or through its own nature, or through something else from elsewhere; it suffers many things from others, even against the will of those who act, who are striving for something else. 

Those living beings that have self-determined motion <note>original: "autexousion"; the power of self-governance or free choice.</note> might lean at one time toward the better, and at another toward the worse. Perhaps it is not worth seeking the turning toward the worse itself. For a small turn occurring at the beginning, <margin>* putting forward</margin> <margin>* making</margin> proceeding in this way, makes the error always more and greater. The body is also present, and there is desire by necessity. That which is first seen and sudden, if not immediately checked, works a choice toward that which one has fallen into. Judgment follows, which is not unjust for such a person, to suffer things following from their disposition. It should not be demanded for happiness to belong to those who have not worked for things worthy of happiness. Only the good are happy; for because of this, the gods are also happy.

If, then, it is possible for souls in this universe to be happy, those who are not happy should not blame the place, but rather their own inability, or their failure to struggle well where the prizes of virtue are laid out. What is so strange if one who has not become just does not have a divine life? Poverty and sickness are nothing to the good, but to the wicked, they are a misfortune. It is also a necessity to be sick for those having bodies. These things are also useful altogether for the arrangement and completion of the whole; for as some things are destroyed, the Reason of the universe...

<summary>Plotinus explains that evil and injustice are not products of Divine Reason but are "misses" or failures of individual beings to grasp the Good. He maintains that the universe is perfectly ordered because even the "disordered" actions of men result in just consequences and contribute to the cosmic whole.</summary>

# BOOK TWO.

<columns>
He uses those things which have perished for the generation of others; for just as nothing anywhere escapes being caught up by the Whole, so it is with a corrupted body or a soul made weak by such passions. Those things seized by disease or vice are subjected to another sequence and another order. Some of these things even benefit those who suffer them, such as poverty and disease. Even vice <note>original: "kakia"; moral badness or failure of the soul.</note> produces something useful for the whole, by becoming an example of justice and providing many useful things from itself. For instance, it makes people vigilant and rouses the mind and understanding as they set themselves against the paths of wickedness. It also teaches us what a great good virtue is by comparison with the evils that the wicked endure. Even if evils have come to be, it is not because they were sought out for their own sake; rather, as has been said, it belongs to the greatest power to be able to use even evils well, and to be capable of using things that have become formless to generate other forms. Generally, we must define evil as a lack of good. It is necessary for a lack of good to occur here because the good is present in "another" <note>This refers to the Platonic idea that when the Good is reflected in matter, it is no longer the "Pure Good" but a secondary, diminished version.</note>. For that "other" in which the good resides, being different from the Good, creates the deficiency; for it was not the Good itself. Therefore, as Plato says, it is impossible for evils to be entirely rooted out, both because some things are inferior to others in relation to the nature of the Good, and because others are different from the Good, having received the cause of their existence from there, yet becoming what they are because they have proceeded so far away from it.

<margin>* takes away</margin>
**AS** for that which seems to happen contrary to merit—for instance, when the good suffer evils and the base experience the opposite—it is rightly said that no evil happens to the good man. But as for why what is good for the base man happens as it does, we must ask: why are some things arranged this way by nature, while others happen according to the nature of the wicked man? How can this be a fair distribution? But if what is "according to nature" neither adds to happiness nor * takes away the evil of the wicked, what difference does it make whether things are this way or that? It is like a good man having an ugly body, or a base man a beautiful one. Instead, we should speak of what is fitting, proportional, or according to merit; yet currently, it does not seem to be so. Perhaps that point would demonstrate Providence. Truly, if the wicked were masters and rulers of cities while the decent were slaves, would that be fitting? Or would these things not contribute at all to the possession of good or evil? And yet, a wicked ruler might perform the most shameful deeds. And the wicked prevail in wars, or commit shameful acts against captives. How can such actions be part of Providence? Should we look to the Whole? That is what one should do. But we must also ask if the parts are correctly arranged for everyone as they should be, especially when they are living beings.

<column-break/>

**A** **H**e uses [the perished] for the birth of others (for nothing can ever escape without being encompassed by this very whole); thus, even with a depraved body and a soul weakened by passions of this kind, those things occupied by diseases and wickedness are soon encompassed under another series and order. Some things indeed benefit the sufferers themselves, such as **B** poverty and disease. Wickedness, however, brings something useful to the universe, becoming a visible example of justice itself, and produces many useful things from itself: for it makes souls vigilant and causes them to think diligently about how they might best decline from the precipice of depravity. Again, it makes us recognize how great a good virtue is by comparison with the evils afflicting vicious souls. Nor were evils made for their own sake: but it has been said that the world-crafting Reason <note>original: "ratio" / "logos".</note> itself is accustomed to using evils appropriately after they have been made. **C** It is a mark of the greatest power to be able to use even evils well. Furthermore, it is possible to use things that have already become formless to generate other forms. Truly, we ought to consider evil entirely as a defect of the good. It is necessary, moreover, that a defect of the good happens here, because it exists in another. Therefore, that "other" in which the good is, since it is diverse from the good, introduces a **D** defect of the good; for that thing was not the Good. Wherefore, as Plato says, it is impossible for evils to be utterly extirpated, since some things are inferior to others regarding the nature of the good itself, and others are diverse from the good, having obtained the cause of their existence from there, and they turned out as such because they proceeded most remotely from the good.

---

<margin>
VI
Confirmation, and he moves a doubt.
</margin>

**E** **TO** that which seems to happen often contrary to dignity, when either the good report evils or the wicked report goods, it will be rightly answered that nothing evil happens to the good, nor does anything good happen to the wicked. But it can be asked: why do many things contrary to nature happen to a good man, while many things consistent with nature happen to the depraved? By what reason can this be a right distribution? Truly, if that which is according to nature neither adds anything to the happiness of the good, nor takes away any evil from the depraved, and that which is contrary to nature does not take anything away from the good, what does it matter whether it behaves this way or that? **F** Just as it matters not if a wicked man has a beautiful body and a good man a deformed one. Nevertheless, it would be most fitting and consistent—what could be said to be according to dignity—if it happened in that way which it now least seems to; it would be the best part of providence to have instituted it so. Furthermore, it was least fitting for the wicked to be masters and princes of cities, and the upright to be slaves. Even if these things add nothing to good or evil, surely an unjust prince perpetrates the most unjust crimes. What of the fact that the wicked overcome in battle and commit the most foul things against captives? **G** All these things compel one to doubt by what reason they happen while Providence reigns. And if he who is about to effect anything ought to look to the whole itself, nevertheless the parts also ought to attain what is expedient for them, especially where they are animated with life.

<sig>Y 4</sig>
</columns>

<summary>Plotinus argues that "evil" is a necessary lack of good that arises as reality moves further from the divine source, yet Divine Providence uses these imperfections—like disease and social injustice—to highlight virtue and maintain cosmic balance. He begins to address the problem of why the wicked often prosper while the good suffer, suggesting that external status does not affect true internal happiness.</summary>

...they possess, especially if they possess reason. Finally, it is probable that providence extends itself through all things, and that this is its duty: that it neglects absolutely nothing anywhere. Therefore, if we concede that this whole world depends upon the Intellect <note>original: "intellectu"; the *Nous*, the second principle in Plotinus's system, representing divine mind and the realm of Ideas.</note>, and that the power of the mind pours itself through all things, we must try in every way to demonstrate how these individual things are well-ordered.

<margin>VII. Two principles are answered. He also treats the condition of this world as it degenerates from the first; and concerning the free choice of souls.</margin> <margin>A</margin> FROM THE BEGINNING it must not escape our notice, when we seek beauty in a mixture, that we must not demand "as much beauty" <note>original: "ὅσον τὸ καλῶς"</note> as is contained in a nature that is unmixed, nor should we look for the primary things in those that follow after them. But since <margin>B</margin> the world possesses a body, we must concede that something happens to the whole from the very nature of that body; likewise, we must seek for reason only so far as a mixture can receive it, as if enough has been done if nothing is lacking from those things which it is capable of receiving. Once these things are granted, we must proceed to the questions at hand. For perhaps in these things we can find the wonderful gift of providence and the marvelous power of the craftsman of this world. Indeed, regarding those actions of souls which are situated within the souls themselves—when they act for the worse, such as when <margin>D</margin> wicked souls harm others, or when the wicked harm the wicked—unless someone wants providence to be the cause of their depravity, it is not proper to demand from providence itself a reason for the deed or its correction. Rather, one should refer the cause to the one choosing <note>original: "eligente"; Plotinus emphasizes that moral evil comes from the soul's individual will or "choice" (prohairesis).</note>. For it has been said that souls also must have their own motions. Likewise, they are not only souls now, but already living beings <margin>E</margin>; furthermore, it is not to be wondered at that when they are such things, they also have a life that follows consistently. For they did not come here because the world existed, but they existed before the world so that they might one day belong to the world, care for mundane things, be the causes of its standing, govern it, and act in whatever way they might do so—whether by presiding and bestowing something from themselves, <margin>F</margin> or by immersing themselves and surrendering, or if some act in one way and others in another. For that is not the issue at present, but rather that however the matter stands, providence is not to be blamed.

But when someone considers the comparison of evils to their opposites—namely, that the good are poor while the wicked are rich, and that the worse people often possess far more of those things necessary for human nature; likewise, that they rule and occupy cities and nations—what shall he say? Perhaps that providence <margin>G</margin> does not reach as far as the earth? Nevertheless, since all other things happen according to reason, this itself is a testimony that it descends even to the earth: for animals and plants participate in reason, soul, and life. Perhaps it reaches this far, but does not dominate. But since this universe is one living...

<column-break/>

...possess [reason], or even are rational, and that providence reaches to all things. Its one work, by its very being, is to have neglected nothing. If indeed we say that this whole world is suspended from the Mind, and that its power has come into all things, I must try to show how each of these things is well-ordered.

FIRST, then, it must be understood that those who seek the "well-ordered" in the mixture <note>original: "μικτῷ"; the physical world where form and matter are mixed.</note> must not demand it in every way, as much as beauty exists in the unmixed, nor look for the first things in the second. But since it also has a body, we must allow that something comes into the whole from this [body], but meet it with the things of reason, as much as the mixture was able to receive, if nothing is lacking to it. For example, as in an image of the most beautiful "perceptible man" <note>The man we can see with our senses, as opposed to the "intelligible man" known by the mind.</note>. Having assumed these things, one must travel from there to the things being sought. For perhaps in these we might find the wonder of providence and its power: how from such things this whole exists.

As many works of souls as there are—which indeed will be in the souls themselves that work the worse things—such as whenever wicked souls have harmed others, and as many as the wicked do to each other: unless one were to blame them for being wicked at all, it would be proper to demand a reason or a reckoning concerning them, to the cause that chose them. For it has been said that it was necessary for souls also to have their own motions; and that they are not only souls, but already living beings. And indeed, it will be nothing to wonder at, if they are such, that they have a following life. For it was not because they were in the world that they came, but before the world they had their being of the world, and to care for it and to establish it, and to manage it, and to act in whatever way, either by standing over it and giving something from themselves, or by sitting upon it; whether some in this way and others in another. For we are not now concerned with these things, but that however it may be, providence is not to be blamed for these things.

But while other things happen according to reason, this is testimony that it goes even as far as the earth. For even animals and plants partake of reason and soul and life; but having reached here, does it [providence] not dominate? But since this universe is one...

He provides the principles for his response. He also treats the condition of this world as it descends from the First Principle, and the free will of souls.

**IN THE BEGINNING**, it must not escape our notice that when we seek beauty in a mixed thing <note>original: "in mixto." This refers to the physical world, which Plotinus views as a "mixture" of pure spiritual form and messy material matter.</note>, we must not demand all the qualities that beauty contains in a non-mixed nature; nor should we look for the primary qualities in secondary things. Rather, since the world possesses a body, we must concede that some things happen to the universe because of the very nature of that body. Likewise, we should expect reason from it only insofar as a "mixture" is capable of receiving it. It should be considered sufficient if nothing is lacking from those things which it is capable of receiving. 

Just as if someone on earth contemplates a most beautiful man: he should not think it necessary for this man to be the same as the "Ideal Man" who exists in the mind <note>Plotinus refers to the Platonic Idea or Form of Humanity, which is perfect and unchanging.</note>. Instead, he should think the creator has done enough if, even though this man consists of flesh, nerves, and bones, he has nevertheless embraced him with reason—to such an extent that he has rendered even these physical parts beautiful, and caused reason to spread itself over the matter. Having conceded these points, we must then proceed to the questions at hand. For perhaps in these matters we can find the wonderful gift of providence and the marvelous power of the craftsman of this world. 

Indeed, regarding those actions of souls which are situated within the souls themselves—when they perform worse deeds, such as when wicked souls harm others, or when the wicked harm the wicked—unless someone wishes to claim that providence itself is the cause of their depravity, one should not demand a calculation of fate or a retraction from providence itself. Rather, one should refer the cause back to the one making the choice. For it has been said that souls also ought to have their own proper motions. Furthermore, they are not just souls now, but already "living beings" <note>original: "animalia." In Latin and Greek, this refers to any being with a "soul" (anima/psyche), including humans and plants.</note>. Moreover, it is not surprising that since they are such beings, they have a life that follows accordingly. For they did not come here because the world existed, but they existed before the world so that they might one day belong to the world, care for worldly things, be causes of existence, govern, and act—in whatever way they might do so, whether by presiding over it and contributing something from themselves, or by immersing themselves in it, or in some other way. This is not the current issue; rather, however the case may be, providence is not to be blamed.

For animals and plants participate in both reason and soul and life: perhaps it reaches this far, but does not

...possess, or are even rational, or that providence reaches over all things. For its work is to have neglected nothing. <margin>A</margin> **FIRST**, then, it must be understood that those who seek the "well-ordered" in the mixture <note>original: "ἐν τῷ μικτῷ" (en tō miktō)</note> must not demand the same degree of beauty as is found in the unmixed, nor seek in secondary things the qualities of the primary. <margin>B</margin> But since it also has a body, one must allow things to come into the whole from this source as well; and one must demand from the Reason-Principle <note>original: "λόγου" (Logos)</note> only as much as the mixture was able to receive, provided that nothing is lacking in this regard. ...not those who merely pray, but those who cultivate the land gather the fruits; nor are they healthy who neglect the care of their health. Furthermore, it is ridiculous to do everything else pertaining to life according to one's own judgment—even if one's actions do not please the gods—and yet demand only safety from the gods, especially when one has not done those things through which the gods command humans to be saved. Indeed, death is better for such people than a life of that kind, which the laws of the universe themselves do not wish them to lead. If, while folly and wickedness persist, divine peace were given as a guardian for these contrary deeds, then Providence could be accused of negligence, as if it permitted the inferior to overcome the better. In truth, the wicked rule because of the cowardice of their subjects; for this is more just than the alternative <note>Plotinus argues that "justice" in the natural world involves cause and effect: if a population is too cowardly to defend itself, it is "justly" ruled by the strong, even if the strong are wicked.</note>.

<margin>
IX.
Besides the action of God, others also act, especially humans, who meanwhile are provoked in every way by providence toward God.
</margin>
**IT IS NOT** right, however, for Providence to be such that we ourselves become nothing; otherwise, if Providence were everything and existed alone, it would no longer be Providence. For whose providence would it be? It would surely be the divinity alone. But as it stands, the divinity exists and directs itself toward another, yet not so as to take that other away. For instance, when approaching a human being, it preserves in him the very fact of being human. To preserve someone is to have them live by the law of Providence, which means performing whatever that law prescribes. Now, it prescribes that those who have become good shall hereafter have a good life established, even after death, while the wicked shall have the contrary. It is a sin to think that those who have turned out evil should be guarded by other saviors while they themselves, being idle, trust only in prayers. Therefore, it is neither right for the gods to manage every single business while their own divine life is interrupted, nor is it fitting for upright men—who lead a life better than the human standard—to be burdened with governing the worse. After all, these wicked people never concerned themselves with how they might become good leaders for others, but rather they are envious if anyone happens to be born good; for many more would have become good if they had appointed these virtuous men as their leaders.

The human race, therefore, was made as a living creature—not the most excellent of all things, but one holding and choosing a middle rank. Yet, at the same time, because of its position, it is by no means permitted to perish by the benefit of Providence, but is continually called back to the heights. Divinity uses every kind of "machine" <note>original: "machinis." Plotinus uses the metaphor of stage machinery (*mēchanē*) to describe the various ways—hardships, lessons, and natural laws—that Providence uses to guide souls back to the divine.</note> to continually restore virtue as the prevailing power. By this means, the human race has never lost its rational faculty; rather, it participates—even if not in the highest degree—in wisdom, mind, art, and justice, which individuals exercise among themselves. Even when they do injury to others, they believe they are acting justly; for they judge those others to be worthy of receiving such injury. Indeed, the human being is as beautiful a workmanship as can possibly be, and is so placed in the world that he has a better lot than all other animals upon the earth.

<note>original: "ναι γὰρ * ἀξία..." This Greek fragment mirrors the Latin conclusion: "For the human being is so beautiful a work, as much as can be... he has a better portion than the other animals on earth; since for the others which are lesser..."</note>

<column-break/>

**A** ...to gather fruits [not by] praying, but by caring for the earth. Nor [can they] be healthy who do not care for their health. One should not be indignant if certain foul men get more fruits, or if it is generally better for those who farm. Then it is laughable to do all other things in life by one's own judgment—and not do them in a way dear to the gods—yet seek to be saved only by **B** the gods. Especially having not done those things through which the gods command us to be saved. And so, deaths are better for them than to live in such a way, which the laws in the universe do not themselves wish. Thus, if the opposite happened, and peace were guarded <margin>*and in abuse</margin> in the midst of abuse and all kinds of vice, then Providence would be negligent, as the **C** worse would be conquering in this way. The wicked rule when the subjects are cowardly. For this was just, and not that [the opposite].

**FOR** Providence must not be such that we are nothing. For if all things are Providence, it alone exists. If it were so, of whom would it be? It would only be the Divine. But it exists now and points toward another, not **D** that it should take away that other. But approaching, for example, a man, it will preserve him as being a man. This is to live by the law of Providence: that is, doing whatever the law itself says. And it says that to those who have become good, there will be a good life, both there and afterward; but to the wicked, the opposite. It is not right for those who have become evil to expect others to be their saviors while they have abandoned themselves, nor is it lawful for those who make light of it. It would not be right for the gods to rule every detail **E** by abandoning their own life. Nor is it fitting for good men who live another life—one better than human rule—to be the rulers of these [wicked] men. Since these [wicked] men never cared how they might become good rulers of others, nor how they might be cared for; but they are envious if anyone among them is born good. For many more would have become good if they had **F** appointed <margin>*becoming</margin> these men as leaders. Therefore, since man is a living being—not the best, but having been assigned a middle rank—and has chosen it, yet in the place where he is situated, he is not permitted to perish by Providence, but is always led back toward the things above by all kinds of machines which the Divine uses, making virtue more powerful. He has not lost the rational state of being the human **G** race, but participates, even if not in the highest degree, in wisdom, mind, art, and justice—at least toward one another. And even those whom they wrong, they think they do so justly.

For [the work] is <margin>*ordered</margin> worthy <margin>*that also</margin>. For the human being is so beautiful a workmanship, as far as it is possible <margin>*connecting</margin>...

<summary>Plotinus explains that Providence does not override human agency or natural law; instead, it rewards effort and virtue while punishing laziness and cowardice. He asserts that humans, though "middle" beings, are divinely guided back to higher realms through their inherent rational and moral faculties.</summary>
