<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s defense of the world’s design. Having previously discussed how human suffering often results from our own choices or the natural hierarchy, he now addresses the existence of "harmful" animals and the nature of human evil, arguing that variety is necessary for a complete universe.</meta>

### BOOK TWO. ###

<margin>* <note>original: "δάκνοι" (daknoi)</note> might bite</margin>
No wise person blames the animals that bring beauty to the earth as its ornament. For it would be truly absurd if someone were to find fault with the nature of animals because they might bite a person, as if it were necessary for humans to live in a state of total, carefree idleness. It is necessary, however, that these creatures also exist. The benefits that can come from them are partly self-evident; but even if they are less obvious, the passage of time demonstrates them, so that nothing among them exists in vain, either regarding themselves or regarding mankind. It is likewise laughable to complain because many animals are wild; for after all, many humans are also wild. If many creatures do not obey man, but resist out of distrust, it should not be seen as a wonder.

But if humans are evil against their will, and are such without choosing to be, one might argue that no one should blame those who commit an injustice, nor should one blame those who suffer it, as if they brought it upon themselves. To be sure, if it is necessary for them to become evil—whether by the movement of the stars <note>Plotinus often debates the extent to which astrology determines human character.</note> or by some first principle that mandates what follows in sequence—then that is simply the natural way of things. But if <term>Reason</term> <note>original: "ratio" / "λόγος" (logos). In Neoplatonism, this refers to the governing intelligence or blueprint of the universe.</note> itself brings this about, how can it be said that it does not cause injustice? Perhaps they are said to sin "involuntarily" because the sin itself is not something they truly desire. Yet, this does not prevent them from acting of their own accord. Because they are the ones performing the action, they are the ones who sin; otherwise, they would not have sinned at all if they were not the authors of such deeds. 

As for the claim that they become evil by "necessity," this should not be understood as coming solely from the outside; rather, it is because they sin according to a certain common condition. Similarly, regarding the influence of the heavens, it should not be taken as if nothing remains in our own power. For if everything were driven solely by external forces, things would happen exactly as those external authors willed. Consequently, humans would never do anything contrary to the will of the gods; nor would humans be impious if the gods themselves performed all these deeds. In reality, these actions proceed from the humans themselves. Once a first principle is set, what follows is carried out to its completion—specifically, everything that acts as a starting point is included in that sequence. And humans, too, are "starting points" or principles. A person is moved toward what is honorable by their own nature, which is a spontaneous principle within them.

Whether each thing happens by certain natural necessities and consequences, and in whatever way it can happen, it happens rightly. Or perhaps it is not exactly like that, but the dominant <term>Reason</term> itself makes all these things and wills them so. Even the things called "evil" are acted out rationally by Reason, though it does not wish for everything to be equally good. For just as a craftsman does not make every part of an animal into an eye, so too Reason did not make everything into gods. Instead, it decreed that some things should be gods, others should be <term>daimons</term> <note>original: "dæmones". In this context, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note> of a secondary nature, then humans, and then animals in succession. This was not done out of envy, but according to a logic that possesses intellectual variety. We, however, are like those who are ignorant of the art of painting and criticize the artist for not putting beautiful colors everywhere; but the painter has attributed to each part exactly what was appropriate for it. Even well-ordered cities do not have the same rank or arrangement for every citizen. Furthermore...

<column-break/>

No wise person blames the animals that represent the ornament of the earth. For it would be ridiculous if someone were to detract from the nature of animals because they bite a human, as if it were fitting for humans to live in a state of completely secure laziness. It is necessary, however, that these creatures also exist; and the utilities that can proceed from them are partly most evident in themselves, and partly—if they are less manifest—the long span of time demonstrates them, so much so that nothing in them is in vain, whether in regard to themselves or even in regard to humans. It is indeed worthy of laughter if someone disapproves on the grounds that most animals are wild: since even humans are wild. But if many do not obey man, but struggle out of distrust, it ought to seem no wonder.

<margin>X Although evil habits are not voluntary, actions are nevertheless voluntary.</margin>
But indeed, if men are evil against their will, and are such while not wishing it, no one will either criminalize those who inflict injury, or those who suffer it, as if they suffered such things through themselves. Certainly, if it is necessary for them to be made evil in this way, whether by celestial motion or by a certain principle asserting in turn what follows, then it naturally holds itself so: and yet, if Reason itself effects these things, in what way does it not thus do unjust things? Perhaps indeed they are said to sin "not of their own accord" because the sin itself is not voluntary. That, however, does not prohibit them from acting out of themselves: but because they themselves act, for that reason they also sin: otherwise, they would not even have sinned if they themselves were not the authors of such actions. As to what is said, that they become evil by necessity, it must not be understood as coming only from the outside, but because they sin by a certain common condition. Also, what is said about celestial motion is not to be taken as if nothing were placed in our power: for if all things happened only from the outside, they would certainly happen just as the authors themselves willed: wherefore men would by no means have perpetrated things contrary to them. And yet, men would not be impious if the gods had perpetrated all these things; as it is, it proceeds from the men themselves. But once a principle is given, that which follows is carried out from there, with all those things which are principles also being included in the consequence. And men are principles. Therefore, one is moved toward honest things by one's own nature, which is indeed a spontaneous principle.

<margin>XI The creative Reason of the world willed unequal ranks for the world's perfection.</margin>
But do individual things happen thus by certain natural necessities and consequences? And in whatever way it can happen, does it happen rightly? Perhaps indeed it is not so, but the dominant Reason itself makes all these things, and wills them so: and those things which are called "evil," Reason itself acts out rationally, not wishing all things to be equally good. For just as a craftsman does not make all parts that are in an animal into eyes, so neither did Reason make all things gods: but it established some things to be gods, others to be spirits of a following nature: after these, however, humans, and animals in sequence. Nor indeed was that done out of envy, but by a Reason possessing intellectual variety. We, however, are affected just like those who are unskilled in painting, who damn the painter because he has not placed equally beautiful colors everywhere; but the painter attributed to each part that which was fitting for it. Well-instituted cities also are not disposed equally in all things. Furthermore...

<meta>catchword: Præterea (Furthermore)</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that "harmful" animals and human "evil" are necessary parts of a diverse and complete universe. He explains that while human character may be influenced by external forces, actions remain the responsibility of the individual, and the variety of the world—from gods to animals—is like the varied colors of a painting.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s argument from Ennead III, Book 2, regarding Divine Providence. Having just discussed how the presence of "wildness" in animals and humans doesn't invalidate the beauty of the whole, he now uses the metaphor of a theatrical play to explain how diversity—even "lower" roles—is necessary for a perfect universe.</meta>

-> ### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III. ### <-

Who would find fault with a comedy or a tragedy because not everyone in it is a hero, but there is also a servant, or a peasant who speaks with a coarse voice? A poem would not be beautiful if one were to remove the lower characters, for it is fulfilled by the assembly of all.

<margin>XII. The seminal reasons <note>original: "Ratio seminaria" / "λόγος" (logos). These are the formative principles or "blueprints" that shape the physical world.</note> of the world shine forth from the all-forming intellectual nature, and they do not force souls to drown themselves in the world.</margin>

**XII.** If, therefore, Reason itself—adapting itself entirely to matter—has made all these things, existing as a specific kind of thing composed of dissimilar parts, then surely that which has been made cannot be more beautiful than it is, because it arises from what exists before it. Reason certainly ought not to be made from parts that are all entirely similar and identical; and in this way, the Author is not to be blamed, since this Reason, the craftsman of things, is indeed all things, but differs in each of its parts. But if Reason had introduced other things from outside itself into the world, such as souls, and had forced them against their nature to fit into the worldly craftsmanship—even pushing many into a worse state—what justification would there be for such an act? But we must surely believe that souls also exist as parts of Reason itself; Reason does not make them worse when adapting them to the world, but rather disposes them according to their merit <note>original: "dignitate" / "ἀξίαν" (axian). Plotinus argues that the soul’s placement in life is a reflection of its previous choices and inherent character.</note> where it is fitting and advantageous for them.

<margin>XIII. There is a change of all things.</margin>

**XIII.** Furthermore, we should not reject the common saying that it is not right to always look only at present circumstances, but also at past and future cycles. For from those cycles, a just repayment is given according to merit: a change occurs from being masters in one life to a private life, or to being servants in the following life, provided they were wicked masters; and indeed, it is beneficial for humans to be changed in this way. Moreover, if they have abused riches, they are transferred into the rank of the poor—where being poor is not without use for those who are good. Likewise, those who have unjustly killed someone will similarly be killed unjustly. It is "unjust" regarding the person who commits the murder, but "just" regarding the one who is killed. Indeed, the one who suffers will be brought together with the one who is ready to perpetrate such deeds, so that he suffers what was fitting for him to endure. Let no one think that anyone ever becomes a slave by reckless chance, nor that one becomes a captive by accident, nor that the body is violated without reason: rather, that person once perpetrated in the past what he suffers in the present. He who once killed his mother will, in the future, be killed by his son, having been born as a woman. And he who had violated a woman will later be born as a woman and be violated himself. Hence comes that oracle concerning <term>Adrasteia</term> <note>original: "ἀδράστεια". In Greek mythology and Neoplatonism, this is the "Inevitable" personification of justice and fate from which no one can escape.</note>, that is, the inevitable power of divine laws. For the institution of such an order is undoubtedly Adrasteia: it is truly judgment, justice, and wonderful wisdom. One can infer that such an order always exists in the universe from those things that are seen daily in the world: where certainly such an order runs through all things, even the smallest; and a wonderful art appears everywhere, not only in divine things but even in those which one might easily judge to be neglected by providence because of their smallness. Such is the artistic and amazing variety in even the lowliest little animals; indeed, such art propagates itself even to the fruits and leaves of plants. In these, one may marvel at how beautiful the forms are, how easily and opportunely they bloom, and how the varied and beautiful parts sprout without labor from nature—nor were they made this way only once, and then immediately...

<column-break/>

**A** ...or if someone should blame a drama because not all the characters in it are heroes, but there is also a servant and some <margin>peasant or low person</margin> peasant, speaking in a low manner; yet the play is beautiful, even if one were to take out the lower parts, and the whole is completed from these.

**B** If, then, Reason itself, having harmonized itself into matter, worked these things, being what it is—dissimilar in its parts—from itself, then that which is produced, being produced in this way, *could not have another version of itself that is more beautiful. <margin>but it [Reason] is not</margin> Reason would not come into being from parts that are all similar and indistinguishable. And this manner of creation is not to be blamed, for all things exist, each being different in its part. But if Reason introduced other things from outside itself, such as souls, and forced many of them against their own nature **C** to harmonize with the creation toward the worse, how could that be right? But we must say that the souls are also like parts of Reason; and it does not make them lower when harmonizing them, but assigns them to where they belong, according to their merit.

**D** Since we must not reject that argument which says we should not look only at the present state of each person, but at their previous cycles and the future, so as to arrange their merit from those. And so it changes them from being masters at first into being servants, if they were evil masters. And this is not to their disadvantage. And if they used wealth badly, they become poor; and for good men, it is the same, as being poor is a necessity for those who have unjustly murdered, that they should be murdered—unjustly on the part of the one who does it, but justly for the one who suffers it. **E** And the one who is to suffer is brought together with the one who is fit to do the deed. For it is clear it is not by chance, nor is one a captive as it happens, nor is the body outraged randomly. But he was once doing these things which he is now suffering. And if someone kills his mother, he will be killed by a child, having become a woman. And having violated a woman, he will be a woman in order to be violated. From this comes the divine rumor, Adrasteia. For this arrangement is truly Adrasteia. And truly it is justice and **F** wonderful wisdom. One must judge that there is such an order through the whole from the things seen in the universe, as it <margin>from eternity</margin> extends to all things, even the smallest. And the art is wonderful, not only in divine things, but also in those where one might suspect providence is to be looked down upon because of their **G** smallness. Such as in any ordinary animals, the varied wonder-working. And it reaches even to the things within plants, the fruits, and even the leaves; the simplicity, the ease of blooming, the smoothness and variety, and that it is not made just once...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the universe is a perfectly ordered "drama" where every role, including the lowly or suffering, is necessary for the whole's beauty. He explains suffering and social status through reincarnation and the law of Adrasteia (inevitable justice), suggesting that our current hardships are the just results of actions in previous lives.</summary>

### SECOND BOOK. ###

...did not happen just once and then cease; rather, it is always being done, for those things which are carried along eternally are done in this same way. Therefore, the things that are being changed are not changed at random, nor do they take on other forms * <margin>* for one who takes</margin> by chance. Instead, they act as it is beautiful and fitting for divine powers to perform. For the entire divine nature acts according to how it is born to act; and it is born to act according to its own essence. Its essence brings forth beauty and justice in its activities. For if these things did not exist there, where else could they be?

**T**HIS arrangement, therefore, is established according to the Mind <note>original: "νοῦν" (nous), the second hypostasis in Plotinus's system, representing pure Intellect.</note> in such a way that it exists without the need for logical reasoning. Let it be so, as if one were to use reasoning in the most perfect way, one would be astonished that Reason could not have made the sequence of things differently. This is known in the making of things, or in the individual natures * <margin>* being made</margin> that are created forever. It is more intellectual than an arrangement made through a tallying of logic. Therefore, in every kind of thing * <margin>* being made</margin> that is always being generated, one cannot find fault with the Reason behind it. This would be like a man who does not think it right that each thing happened as it should, as if things that did not happen were miserable—both in the intelligible world and in the world of the senses. There are those who, regarding mortal things, demand more for themselves than is good, or think that what seems sufficient for each person is to be healthy. For instance, someone might ask why humans do not have horns, not considering that it was impossible for Reason not to reach out to all things, and that it was necessary for smaller things to be contained in the greater, and for parts to be in the whole. Or that they could not be equal, otherwise they would not be parts. For the whole is indeed "all things," but the lower things are not each "all things." And a human, insofar as each is a part, or if I place any other thing as a part, is not the whole. But the individual part should not be required to be the ultimate end or the peak of virtue. For then it would no longer be a part. Yet a part is not decorated with a greater worth if it takes away from the whole through envy; for it makes the whole more beautiful precisely by excelling in its own proper worth. For it becomes such as it is by being made similar to the whole. And it is, as it were, permitted to be such, and arranged in silence, so that in the * <margin>* type</margin> human manner, something shines out in it. Just as among the divine works the stars shine, so * <margin>* so indeed</margin> there is a perception here, as if of a great and beautiful statue—whether it be alive or made by the art of Hephaestus <note>Vulcani / Ἡφαίστου: the Greek god of craftsmanship and fire.</note>—which might have stars shining in its face, and others in its breast. And thus the positions of the stars were placed where they were meant to be fitting.

**I**NDIVIDUAL things, therefore, seen in themselves in this way, show how their connection—both of things that have been made and things that are continually being made—carries with it a certain difficulty regarding the mutual devouring of other animals, or the attacks of humans against one another. And that there is always war, which perhaps never has a pause and cannot be taken lightly.

<column-break/>

...and they did not immediately cease to be; on the contrary, they are always made so; while the higher things are not carried along in an entirely similar way. Therefore, whatever things are brought across through various turns are not changed at random, nor do they take on other forms by chance: rather, they act as the beauty of the world requires and as it befits divine powers to act. For every divinity acts as its own nature carries it: and the divine nature acts according to its own essence alone. Its essence explains beauty and justice together in its actions: for if these were not there, they could exist nowhere.

<margin>XIV. Although natural works are younger <note>meaning "lower" or "subsequent"</note> than rational arrangements; they are as much more excellent than ours as those are. Likewise, the perfection of the whole is not to be sought in the parts themselves, nor should the property of one part be demanded of another.</margin>
**T**HE order is therefore established according to the Mind in such a way that it stands without the discourse of reason; and thus it stands, that if anyone were able to reason most perfectly, he would be astonished beyond measure that the whole was so arranged that reason would not have found or made it otherwise. This is always observed to happen in every individual nature: I say it always possesses more of the intellectual form than the order of reason could either conceive or produce. Therefore, in any genus of those things that are made, it is not permitted to accuse the creative Reason, unless someone thinks that every single thing ought to have been made like those things which were not made but are eternal—both in the intelligible and the sensible genus, in which some things are also eternal. Such a person seeks a heap of as much good as possible, not thinking that the species attributed to each thing is sufficient for itself. It is as if he blamed nature in man because she did not give him horns, not considering that it could not be otherwise than that Reason diffused itself through all things. However, it was necessary that the smaller be contained in the greater, and parts in the whole, and they could not be equal; otherwise, they would not be parts. The supreme world is indeed all things: but the inferior things are not each "all things." And a man, insofar as each is a certain part, is not all. But if somewhere in certain parts something else is also made, which indeed does not become a part, through this, that too is the whole. Nor is it to be demanded that any individual, insofar as it is specifically that thing, should have attained the summit of virtue, otherwise it would no longer be a part. Yet a part is not adorned more excellently in dignity than if it detracts from the whole through envy: for it makes the whole more beautiful, insofar as it excels in dignity. For it becomes such, insofar as it becomes similar to the whole, and it is as if granted to be such, and thus ordered together, so that according to the place of man something shines out in him, not otherwise than how the stars flash through the divine heaven. From this, indeed, such a thought arises, as if a certain huge and beautiful statue, whether living or fashioned by the art of Vulcan <note>Hephaestus.</note>, had indeed glittering stars in its face, and others besides in its breast, and were so arranged that they properly create beauty.

<margin>XV. In the universal nature, necessary evils are made for the sake of the good of the whole; and therefore the whole is good. Likewise, in this world all things are subject to vanity.</margin>
**I**NDIVIDUAL things, therefore, considered in themselves, seem to be so: but the connection of these things, both those which have been made and those which are perpetually being made, suffers from an objection and a doubt: both concerning the mutual voracity of brute animals, and concerning the attacks of men against men. Likewise, because of the perpetual war, which indeed can neither be calmed, nor easily endured,

<summary>Plotinus argues that the diversity and apparent imperfections of the world (like humans lacking horns or the existence of conflict) are necessary parts of a rational, beautiful whole, comparing the cosmos to a divine statue where every star is placed with purpose.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of Divine Providence. Having previously established that the universe is guided by a higher intelligence, he now addresses the presence of conflict, predation, and death, arguing that these are necessary parts of a larger, harmonious "play" directed by the Reason-Principle.</meta>

### PLOTINUS ENNEAD III ###

...especially if the world's very Reason-Principle <note>original: "ratio", translating the Greek "logos"</note> has brought it about that things are this way, and so it is said to be well-ordered. For that Reason-Principle does not support those who speak otherwise, saying that these things are as good as they can possibly be, and that matter is the cause <note>The author suggests that matter is not an accidental flaw, but a necessary component for the lower levels of existence.</note>, so that those things which are held in this way have an inferior condition, nor can evils be totally rooted out. Indeed, it was necessary for it to be so, and thus it is well. Nor does the encroaching matter conquer, but it was introduced so that it might be so; indeed, the Reason-Principle was the cause even of matter itself in this arrangement. Therefore, the Reason-Principle is the beginning, and all things are Reason; and the things that happen, happen through it. And the things which are organized together in the process of generation are thoroughly held in this way. What, then, is the necessity of the perpetual and natural war among animals and men? The mutual devouring of animals is necessary because there are certain successions of animals, which, even if no one killed them, could not remain as they are forever. But if it is necessary to die at some time, then it was right to die in such a way that a benefit might also come to others from them; why should one begrudge this? What if those which are devoured are born again as something else? It is as if, on a stage, a character who is faked to be killed soon changes their appearance, and putting on the mask of another person, returns to the stage. Perhaps someone might say that this person has not truly died. But if dying is merely changing the body, no different than changing a garment on a stage; or if death is to lay aside the body altogether, just as the final exit from the play in a comedy—where, however, one is to return to the play again in the future—what evil does such a mutual exchange of animals bring with it? Such are the works of a human being, who knows how to live only in the lower and external realms, and does not realize that even in his serious moments of weeping, he is, in a way, playing a part. ### PLOTINUS ENNEAD III ###

<margin>A</margin> Especially if the world-reason <note>original: "mundi ratio"; the Greek "Logos", the guiding principle of the universe</note> itself brought it about that things should be this way, and so it is said to be well-ordered. For that Reason-Principle does not support those who speak otherwise, saying that these things are as good as they can possibly be, and that matter is the cause <note>original: "materia"; the physical stuff of the world which Plotinus often views as a source of limitation</note> for things being in this inferior condition. Nor can evils be completely rooted out, since it was necessary for things to be this way, and thus it is good. Matter does not overcome the Reason-Principle by invading it; rather, it was brought in so that the world could exist in this way. Indeed, the Reason-Principle was the cause of matter itself in this arrangement. Therefore, the Principle is Reason, and <margin>B</margin> all is Reason. The things that are made are made through it, and the things that are organized together in the process of becoming are thoroughly governed by it. What necessity, then, is there for the perpetual and natural war among animals and men? Perhaps the mutual devouring of animals is necessary because there are certain successions <note>The idea that life must give way to new life</note> of animals which, even if no one killed them, could not remain as they are forever. ### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III. II. ###

...just as it is hostile through its parts, so also it is something unified and friendly, exactly as if the <term>ratio</term> <note>Latin: "ratio"; Greek: "logos." The underlying rational principle or "blueprint" of the universe.</note> of a tragic or comic play were one single whole, containing many battles within itself. The play itself reduces all those who disagree into one harmonious temperament, as if completing the entire arrangement of those fighting; however, in that instance, the battle of those who are distant and disagreeing is derived from a single principle. Therefore, one might better compare it to the harmony resulting from those who fight, and one should ask why conflict is included within the rational principles themselves.

A -> If, therefore, even here high and low notes are produced by the principles themselves, and they breathe together into one because they are the principles of harmony—for clearly they are for the sake of the harmony itself, which is a different, greater principle, while they themselves are smaller and mere parts—then we surely see opposites in the universe in a similar way: white and black, hot and cold; likewise the winged and the wingless, those with feet and those without, the rational and the irrational. Indeed, these individual things are parts of the one universal living being.

B -> Now, truly, the whole agrees with itself, even while the parts are fighting here and there among themselves, yet the whole exists according to <term>reason</term>. Thus it is necessary that this single reason be one composed of contrary reasons: to such an extent that such opposition brings about its very constitution and, as it were, its essence. For unless it were manifold, it would not be a "whole," nor would it be a "reason." But a reason, being what it is, is different from itself; and the greatest difference seems to be contrariety.

C -> Therefore, if one thing is entirely "other," and that "other" does something, it does not produce something less "other," but rather something more "other." It follows that if something produces an "other" to the extreme, it must necessarily create opposites. The reason will be perfect if it produces itself not only as a certain difference, but also as many opposites.

D -> <margin>17. In divine providence, those things which we do and those which we subsequently suffer are prescribed.</margin>
**SINCE** therefore the principle is such as it renders itself entirely through all things, it creates the things that happen as opposites to a much greater degree, the more they are now compelled to stand apart. Truly, the sensible world is less "one" than its own reason; and therefore it is more manifold and filled with contraries. Furthermore, the appetite for living is more vehement in individuals, and the love that sweeps things toward the "one" is more ardent; yet those things which love often destroy the things they love because of their greed for their own good—specifically when they are subject to corruption. Even the love of the part for the whole draws toward itself whatever it can.

E -> Thus, both the good and the bad are led through opposites, as if by the dance-steps of the same art; one part of which we shall call good, the other bad. And in this way, it maintains its beauty. But indeed, it will seem that none are "bad" anymore;

F -> Perhaps even the bad will be granted pardon here, unless they are those to whom pardon is not to be given, and for whom the reason itself does not act. Yet the reason acts so that such people are not forgiven; otherwise, if one part of it is a good man and another a bad man, the bad man occupies more parts in it.

G -> But certainly, it happens just as in a play: where the poet assigns some things to the actors, while for others...

<column-break/>

...hostile to itself in its parts, so also it is friendly, just as if the <term>logos</term> <note>original: "λόγος"; the Word or governing Principle of the universe</note> of a drama, being one, were the drama itself, having in itself many battles. Now the drama brings the things that have fought together, as if into one concordant harmony, as if it were the entire narrative of those fighting. <margin>* poem</margin> * For it makes these very things from a single reason, or from those things that support the battle. ...uses, as it already does. For he himself is the lead actor, the second, and the third; but by teaching to each the fitting speeches, he has now assigned to each where they ought to be stationed. Thus it is in every place. One is assigned to the good and another to the evil <note>original Greek: "πρῶτον," perhaps implying a primary rank</note>, each to their place, not contrary to nature or reason, but proceeding to that which is fitting, holding the place which they chose. Then, the actor speaks and acts: one performing impious words and deeds, and another the opposite. For there were already certain kinds of actors in the drama, giving themselves over to the play. 

Now, in human plays, the poet gives the words, but the actors possess from themselves—and out of themselves—the ability to perform each part well or poorly. For they have work to do beyond the mere speeches. But in this truer poem <note>The "truer poem" refers to the Universe itself.</note>, which humans imitate <note>original Greek: "κατὰ μέρ@" – in part</note> individually, having a creative nature, the Soul acts its part. It performs its role, having received from the Poet (just as actors here do) its destined circumstances—its wealth or its rags. So too this Soul takes its fortunes, and another takes others. 

According to reason, the souls harmonize themselves to these fortunes, becoming concordant and arranging themselves with the drama and the entire <term>Logos</term> <note>The rational principle or "script" of the universe.</note>. Then, the soul speaks its actions and all other things that it would do according to its own character, like a kind of song. And just as the sound and the gesture from the actor may be beautiful or shameful—and the voice might add a beauty to the poem or introduce a flaw through a poor voice—this does not make the drama itself different from what it was, though the actor appears ungraceful. 

The Poet of the drama, acting as a good judge, dismisses the actor according to his merit, dishonoring him or leading him to greater honors if he has performed a good work, perhaps even moving him to more beautiful dramas. But the other actor is sent to worse and more shameful roles. In this way, the soul entering into this whole "poem" of the world, making itself a part of the dramatic performance, brings from itself its own good or bad acting. At its entrance, it is woven into the order, and receiving all other things aside from its own works, it receives its punishments or honors. 

The choice belongs to the actors, who are placed in a larger arena than the measure of a stage; and it is the Master of the whole who does this, having a greater power to arrange many forms of character. For us, he shows another way of singing. And by including them in honors or dishonors, he fits the speeches to each place so that they harmonize with the <term>Logos</term> of the whole. There, each part is fitted according to justice into the places that will receive them, just as each string on a lyre is assigned to its own appropriate place, sounding according to the reason of that place. Such is the nature of the Whole.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...nature uses them. For he does not himself make one first in virtue in the play, another second, and another third; but granting to each their own reasons, he thereafter assigns an order thoroughly suited to each. So it is that a place is destined for every person, whether good or bad, according to what is most fitting. And so each person proceeds toward either end according to nature and reason as is appropriate, obtaining the place they had chosen. 

Then he speaks and acts: one <margin>B</margin> indeed performs profane words and deeds, while another performs the opposite. For the actors were already inclined one way or another even before the play, thereby inserting their own characters into the stories. In the stage-plays of men, the poet distributes the scripts to individuals; but they have within themselves, and from themselves, the power to act rightly or not rightly. For they have a duty beyond the words of the poet. 

But in the truer poem <note>The Cosmos.</note>, which men represent in part, having a creative nature, the soul is equipped for its role. And just as <margin>C</margin> actors are equipped by the poet—receiving their characters, robes, saffron-colored cloaks, or torn rags—so the soul, masked under the "Worldly Poet" <note>Latin: "mundanus poeta," referring to God or Providence as the writer of the world's story.</note>, undergoes its fortunes not by chance. For these fortunes are according to reason, and by undergoing them at the right time, the soul becomes concordant with the worldly tragedy or comedy. It inserts itself into the actions and the universal reason, agreeing with it. Then it speaks its actions and everything else that a soul would do by its own <margin>D</margin> innate character, like a certain melody. 

And just as the voice and the appearance are beautiful or ugly in themselves, and seem either to add grace to the poem or to mix in a flaw of the voice (which does not make the play different than it was, though the actor appears discordant), so it is here. The Poet, the author of the play, rejects this actor according to his merit, censuring him by performing the duty of an excellent judge. Another he promotes to greater honors and, if possible, to more excellent deeds; but the other he moves to worse things if he can. 

By this same <margin>E</margin> reasoning, the soul, entering into this universal poem of the world and making itself a part of the stage-play, brings with it the ability to portray its gestures well or poorly. Likewise, at the very entrance, being joined to the order of the rest and having obtained all other things separate from itself and its own duties, it carries away punishments or honors according to its merit. 

Furthermore, there is something more to such actors, as they are equipped in a much larger place than the small measure of a stage; especially since the Author of the universe has endowed them with authority and a <margin>F</margin> greater power to prepare many species of characters, gestures, and places. They therefore define the measure of honor and ignominy by that which they themselves communicate in the performance of honor or disgrace. 

There, indeed, individual dwellings are suited to individual characters, so that they agree with the reason of the universe itself. Every person is fitted according to the judgment of justice to their own lot; just as any string in a <margin>G</margin> lyre is stretched in its own proper and convenient place and order according to the logic of the sound, for such is the faculty given to each for this very purpose.

### PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS III. I. ###

...and as a part it is an enemy, yet so it is a single thing and a friend, just as if the logic of a tragic or comic drama were a single whole, containing many battles within itself. The play itself brings all those things that disagree into a single harmonious temperament, as if arranging all the combatants; there, however, the struggle of those who stand apart and disagree is derived from a single <term>Reason</term> <note>original Latin: "ratio," translating the Greek "logos"—the governing principle of the universe</note>. Therefore, one might better compare it to a harmony resulting from clashing elements, and ask why conflict is included within these principles themselves. If, therefore, even here the high and low pitches are produced by the principles themselves and combine into one—since they are principles of harmony within harmony itself—this is a larger principle of which the others are smaller parts. Indeed, we see opposites similarly in the universe: white and black, hot and cold; likewise, the winged and the wingless, the footed and the footless, the rational and the irrational. Truly, these are individual parts of the one universal living being; yet the whole agrees with itself, even while the parts struggle against each other in various places, for the whole follows Reason. And so it is necessary that this single Reason be one formed from contrary principles: so much so that such opposition brings about its very constitution and essence. For if it were not manifold, it would not be all-encompassing, nor would it be Reason. But being Reason, it is different from itself, and the greatest difference seems to be contrariety. Therefore, if it is something entirely other, and that "other" performs an action—not performing it as something less, but as something more "other"—it follows that in performing something to the extreme, it must necessarily create opposites. Reason will be perfect if it produces not only certain differences, but also many opposites within itself.

Since, therefore, Reason is such as it has rendered itself throughout the universe, it produces even more opposites in the things it makes, the further they are forced to be apart. To be sure, the <term>sensible world</term> <note>The physical world we perceive with our senses, as opposed to the intellectual world of forms.</note> is less unified than its own Reason; therefore, it is more manifold and filled with opposites. Furthermore, the desire for living is more vehement in individuals, and the love that sweeps them toward unity is more burning; yet those who love often destroy the things they love out of greed for their own good, especially when they are subject to corruption. Even the love of a part for the whole draws toward itself whatever it can. Thus, both the good and the bad are led through opposites, as if by the same art of a certain dancer’s rhythmic movement: one part of which we shall call "good" and the other "bad." And in this way, it is beautiful. But then it might seem that no one is truly evil anymore. Perhaps, however, nothing here prevents some from being evil; but perhaps it follows that they do not become evil from themselves. Perhaps even the evil will be granted pardon, unless there are those to whom pardon should not be given, and for whom Reason itself does not grant it. Indeed, Reason may bring it about that such people are not forgiven; but if one part of it is a good man and another part an evil man, the evil man occupies more parts within it. But certainly, it happens just as in a play: where the poet assigns some things to the actors, while for others...

<margin>A</margin> ...to itself in its parts an enemy, so it is one and a friend, just as if the logic of a drama were one—the drama <unclear>rs</unclear>—having in itself many battles. Thus, one might again rather liken it to the harmony <margin>B</margin> arising from combatants, and seek to know why the combatants are in the Reasons. If, therefore, even here the high and low pitches produce the Reasons, and they come together into one, being Reasons of harmony, it [the harmony] is itself another greater Reason, while they are smaller and parts. We see also in the universe opposites, such as white, black, hot, cold, and indeed winged, wingless; footed, footless, rational, irrational; all living things are forms <margin>C</margin> and parts of the whole. And the whole is in agreement with itself, while its parts <gloss>\* everywhere</gloss> <margin>\* in every place</margin> are fighting, yet the whole is according to Reason. It is necessary then that the one Reason <gloss>\* from</gloss> <margin>\* be a reason</margin> of opposites, being a reason <gloss>\* of the reasons or of each</gloss> <margin>\* to be of opposites or</margin> of them and as it were an essence, since such opposition carries it. For if it were not many, which it was as a whole, it would not even be Reason. But being Reason <margin>D</margin> it is different toward itself, and the greatest difference is opposition. So that if it makes something entirely "other," then that which is most "other"—but it will make from the "other"—so that in making the extremely "other," it will also make opposites of necessity. And it will be perfect, not if it makes only difference, but if it also makes itself to be opposites.

SINCE these things are so, <gloss>\* as it is</gloss> <margin>\* as</margin> it makes entirely, it will much more make the things being made opposite, <margin>E</margin> by as much as they stand further apart. For the world—not the sensible one, but the Reason—is so to itself entirely more, and the opposition more. And the desire for life is more in each. <gloss>\* and love</gloss> <margin>\* and love is more the one.</margin> The only thing toward the one is more, but the things loving often destroy the things loved, hastening toward the same good, when they are corruptible, but the desire of the parts toward the whole draws to itself. <margin>F</margin> But the whole, thus then both the good and the bad just as again from the same art <gloss>\* of dances</gloss> <margin>\* of dances</margin> are opposites, and we shall say that the part itself is indeed good, and the other bad. And so it is well. And yet are they still bad? Either the being bad is not taken away, but only that they are placed thus. | It is sufficient. | As even in a panpipe <note>original: "fistula" or "syrinx," an ancient musical instrument made of pipes of graduated lengths</note> a single voice does not suffice, but a smaller and weaker one is also required to complete the full consonance of the pipe: since the harmony is divided into unequal parts, and each of the tones is unequal to the others; yet one perfect consonance is made out of them all. For the Universal Reason <note>original: "ratio" / "logos," the governing principle of the universe</note> is one, but it is distributed into things that are not equal: hence there are different places in the whole, some better, some worse; and souls, being unequal, fit into these unequal places. | and more incomplete. For indeed, the whole Reason is one, but it is divided—or rather, not into equal parts—whence also the places of the universe are different, better and worse. And unequal souls fit thus into the unequal parts. |
| From this it follows that the places are dissimilar, and that unequal and dissimilar souls obtain these dissimilar places: as if according to certain differences in a panpipe or another instrument. They also inhabit different places according to the variety of souls among themselves, singing their own songs in whatever place they are, which may be discordant both with the individual places and with the whole: yet that which is sung poorly by any soul for itself, is sung well for the whole. Likewise, that which happens to them against their own nature happens according to the nature of the whole. | And so it happens here, that both the places and the souls are dissimilar, or rather, they are not the same; but being unequal, they occupy dissimilar places, as if according to the inequalities of a panpipe or some other wind instrument. They are in places that differ from one another, <margin>* the same things harmoniously</margin> sounding out the same things harmoniously in their places within the whole, so that what is bad D for them, will sound well according to the whole. Or that which is <margin>* of the</margin> against [their] nature, is according to the nature of the whole. |
| Nor does a minor tone harmonize less with the whole than a major one, nor does a person singing ineptly for himself render the whole more inept because of this: just as a certain wicked commoner does not make a city established with just laws worse, if it is useful to use this other example now. For the use of even a wicked man is sometimes necessary in a city when affairs so demand, and such a man is rightly placed. | The lesser sound is no less a sound, but the worse sound has made the whole [complete] when it sounds, just as if the executioner, being wicked, has not made the well-ordered city worse—if one must use this image. For there is a need even for such a person in a city; there is often a need for such a man, and he is <margin>* thus</margin> thus rightly placed. |

One must consider in the mind the second and third orders of souls: and again, that the same soul does not always act according to the same parts of itself: but this must be spoken of again in this way: for the present dispute requires much for the sake of explanation. | WORSE and better souls exist, some through other causes, and some, as it were, because from the beginning they were not all equal. For it is proportional if they are divided into unequal parts by the Reason itself, since they stand apart. One must also consider the second or the third [ranks], and that the same souls do not always act with the same parts; but again, it must be stated thus. For the argument requires much for the sake of clarity. |

BOOK SECOND.

...are generated, and sometimes perhaps more excellent men: and when cities are overturned by the works of evil men, other more excellent cities are established. If then that introduction of "supplementary souls" <note>Plotinus is debating a theory that new souls are constantly added to the world to explain new life, rather than being part of a pre-existing cosmic order</note> is absurd, while some souls do evil and others do good—for we would strip Reason <note>original: "ratio" / "logos," the governing principle of the universe</note> of the authority to produce good things if we take away from it all connection to evil—what prevents us from saying that the deeds of actors are parts [of the whole]? Just as in the stories within a comedy, so too are those within the Reason that exists in the universe. Here, both that which is done honorably and that which is done basely are included. Thus, the progression toward individual actors comes from Reason itself, so that the more perfect this worldly craftsmanship is, the more everything is encompassed by it and its Reason. But for what purpose is the effect of evil conceded from this source? And divine souls will seem to be nothing more in the universe, but all will be parts of Reason: and either all Reasons will themselves be souls, or why will some Reasons be souls while others are only Reasons, when the universal Reason is itself a certain Soul?

<column-break/>

...perhaps better men, and other better cities than those destroyed by wicked men. If then the introduction of souls is absurd, some will work evil, and others good; for we shall deprive the Reason of even the good things if we take away the evil from it. What prevents us from making the deeds of the actors parts [of the play], just as in the drama there, so also in the Reason of the universe? Here, both the bad and its opposite [are included]. So that just as it is with each of the actors, so it is with Reason itself; the more magnificent this drama is, the more everything comes from it. But why should it even produce evil? And as for the souls, the more divine ones will be nothing more in the whole. Rather, all are parts of Reason, and either all the Reasons are souls, or why are some souls, and others only Reasons, since the whole is of a certain Soul?

<margin>
1
What the universal nature is like, and how easy providence is where many things are reduced into one.
</margin>

**W**hat then do we think should be said about these things? Perhaps the universal Reason <note>original: "ratio" / "logos"</note> encompasses both evil and good together, of which these things are also parts. For this universal Reason does not create these things [as something external], but the whole exists together with them. For the "Reasons" <note>original: "rationes" / "logoi"; here meaning the formative principles or "blueprints" for things</note> are the activities of the universal Soul itself, and the parts [of the Reasons] are activities of the parts [of the Soul]. But since one Soul has different parts, the Reasons are distributed in a similar proportion: wherefore the works which are of the final generation are arranged in the same way. The souls are indeed in harmony with one another, and their works are also harmonious; harmonious, I say, in such a way that one single thing is constructed out of them, even out of opposites. For all things, flowing from a certain single source, also flow together into one by the necessity of nature. Therefore, various seeds or even contrary things having been made, because they sprout from one, they are finally drawn together into one order. For although in individual animals, as in the race of horses, they may fight one another; although they may bite, although they may strive...

<column-break/>

**W**hat then seems right concerning these things? Either the Reason which is the whole has encompassed both the evil and the good, and these are parts of it. For the whole Reason does not generate these, but the whole exists with them. For the Reasons are the activity of some universal Soul. And the parts [of the Reasons] are the parts of the parts; for there are differences of each part of the one [Soul], and the Reasons are analogous, so that the works are the final offspring. And the souls are in harmony with one another and the works; and they are harmonious in such a way that they are not [merely] from themselves. But if they are from opposites: for all things having started from one, [they flow] into a necessity of Nature. So that even differences having sprouted and become opposites, they are drawn together by being from one; <margin>* nevertheless</margin> *nevertheless*, into one arrangement. For just as in each of the animals, in the race of horses, even if they fight, even if they bite each other, even if...

The leading principle <note>The Logos or Universal Reason</note> weaves all things together, with the actions of each side converging according to nature, just as in military campaigns. The leadership belongs to the general, but the soldiers also act in unison in their assigned ranks. The whole is arranged by the general's foresight <note>original: "προνοίᾳ" (pronoia) – Providence</note>, regarding both actions and passions, as well as the provisions and drinks for the spirits, and indeed all weapons and machines. And thus, from all these things being woven and converging together, there follows the result of what happens from them, and each thing is placed in its proper ground. And everything has come about, in a certain way, through the skill of the general, even if they were from external sources, such as what the enemies were going to do. But if it were possible for the commander to rule over both camps—and indeed if there were a Great Leader <note>God or the Supreme Intellect</note> to whom all things were subject—what could still be disordered? What would not be harmonized?

<column-break/>

...they act, and are angry in their rivalry, and humans act similarly: nevertheless, all these species must be gathered into one genus of living beings. Then non-living things again according to their species; then into one "non-living" thing; after these, if it pleases you, gather them into Being itself; and finally, to that which grants being to each thing. But again, unfolding from here, descend by dividing, and contemplate that "one" as if it were distributed. This is because it runs through all things and, at the same time, embraces all things in a certain single order, so much so that it is like one living being, both manifold and distinct. Each one of those things which are in it performs what is proper to its own nature, yet exists within the universe—just as fire indeed burns, and a horse performs the works of a horse. Humans, however, just as they are established by nature, each execute their own proper duties, differing as they are different. Moreover, actions follow according to their natures: and again, living either well or poorly.

<margin>II Divine Providence is present to all things; it leaves nothing in the world to chance.</margin>
Therefore, accidents and fortune do not have authority over the good life; however, these also follow insofar as it is consistent with what preceded them, and then the ordered consequences of things proceed. Indeed, the principal part connects all things and leads all things, with those things which incline to either side according to nature contributing to the same end. This occurs just as it does in an army led by a commander, with those who fight together in a certain order acting in harmony. For the entire world is established by a certain "commander-like" providence, discerning actions and passions, and what nourishment, weapons, and machines ought to be present. And certainly, whatever follows from these things—connected and harmonized among themselves—is foreseen; so that whatever happens from these finds a place where it is well-situated. All things proceed from the leader of the army by a certain wise and skillful reason, even if they are external and foreign to him, such as the things the enemies are about to inflict. But if he were able to command both that army and this one similarly—indeed, if he were the Greatest Commander to whom all things are subject—what further could lack order? Or what would be void of connection?

<margin>III Although individual things are in the mind of God's providence, the soul acts freely. Likewise, living things must have different ranks.</margin>
And if I am the master of choosing these or those things rather than others, nevertheless in that very choice our affairs are ordered with the universe, since our nature is not an accidental addition to the universe, but is numbered in its order as being "such-a-one" or "such-a-one." But from where does such a nature come? There are two things required at present, one of which is: whether it is necessary to refer the cause to the Maker (whoever he may be), through whom each person is affected by such characters, or to the one born; or perhaps no cause is to be assigned. Just as in the generation of plants, we do not ask for a cause as to why they do not feel, nor in other animals why they do not behave as humans do. For that would be the same as asking why humans are not gods, especially since in these [animals] the human species is not present. Perhaps someone will blame nature because a human could have been something more excellent. But if, by itself, it provides something in addition...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of Divine Providence. Having previously established that the world is like a grand drama where everyone plays a part, Plotinus now addresses why some beings are "better" or "worse" than others, arguing that the variety and hierarchy of life are necessary features of a complete and rational universe.</meta>

# BOOK TWO <note>original: "LIBER SECVNDVS" — though these chapters are traditionally part of Ennead III, the volume is labeled Book 2 here.</note>

If a man is able to achieve a better state, he himself is the cause of it; if he does not, he who failed to act is his own cause of failure. But if he argues that the cause is not within himself, but that he desired the Creator to add good qualities to him from the outside, then he is foolish to demand more than what was given to him. This is just as if one were to demand more from other animals or from plants than their nature allows. For we should not ask if a thing has less than another, but rather if it has enough to be self-sufficient according to its own kind. Nor was it necessary for all things to be equal. Does this mean that the unequal distribution of things was made by a Reason <note>original: "Logos," the governing principle or rational plan of the universe.</note> that chose, by some preference, that not all things should be equal? Not at all; rather, it was necessary for things to happen this way according to nature. For it was a consequence of the Universal Reason being what it is, that there should be a Soul, and that the Soul should follow after the Intellect <note>original: "Nous," the divine, eternal mind.</note>. The Intellect, however, is not just one of these things, but all things; and because these things are many, they are not the same. It was necessary, therefore, that some should be first, others second, and others third in dignity. 

Furthermore, the animals that are created are not merely souls, but "decrements" of souls <note>original: "ψυχῶν ἐλαττώσεις" (psychon elattoseis), meaning a soul that has diminished or faded as it moves further from its divine source.</note>, as if they were something fading as they proceed into exile. For even if the "reason-principle" of an animal is animate, that soul is different from the soul from which the reason-principle flows. Indeed, this entire Reason-Principle decreases as it inclines toward matter, and that which is born from it is more imperfect. Consider, I pray, how great a distance there is between the finished product and its origin, and yet how much there is still to be admired. Nor should we think that if the thing created is such as it is, then the source before it is exactly the same. For the source is far superior to every effect, standing outside of the chain of cause and effect; it is more to be wondered at that it produced something after itself, and that the "traces" it left behind are so significant. If it gave more than things could actually hold, that is even more reason to approve of it, showing that any fault must be laid upon the created thing, while the gift of Providence is more than abundant.

<column-break/>

**A** If one judges that he could follow this path, he ought to blame the man, not the author. But if he desires that something be added from the outside by the maker, he is a fool for demanding more than was given, just as if he desired something beyond the measure of nature in other animals or plants. For one must not ask whether this thing has less than that, but whether it has enough of what it naturally needs. For it was not required that all things be equal. Was there then an unequal distribution of things made by Reason through a choice that decreed not all things should be equal? Not at all; rather, it had to happen this way naturally. **B** The Soul itself follows the Intellect. The Intellect is not just one of these things, but all things. And because all things are many, and since they are not the same, it was necessary for some to be first, some second, and others third in dignity. **C** Furthermore, the animals that are created are not just souls, but certain "decreases" of souls, as if they were something now proceeding into exile. For although the reason of an animal is animate, it is said to be animate through another soul, not through the one from which the reason flows. Indeed, this whole Reason already decreases as it is tilted toward matter, and what is born from it comes forth more imperfectly. Consider, I pray, by how great an interval the thing made now stands from its origin, and yet **D** how much is still to be admired. However, if the thing created is such, one must not think that what came before it is entirely the same. Truly, the source is far more excellent than every effect; it exists outside of the cause, and it is more wonderful that it produced something after itself, and that its traces are such as they are. If it gave more than the things could receive, that is all the more to be approved, from which it appears that all blame should be cast upon the effects, but the gift of Providence is more abundant.

<margin>IIII</margin>
<margin>*On intellect, reason, and imagination.*</margin>
<margin>*Why men are always rational by nature. Why the soul becomes worse, which does not happen to beasts.*</margin>

**IF** man were a simple being—simple, I mean, if he were only that which he was from the beginning, and acted and was acted upon according to that alone—then without a doubt every occasion for complaint would be far removed, just as we find in other animals. **E** But now, blame has a place only in the "bad man," and perhaps not without reason. For he is not only what he was made to be, but he has another free principle <note>original: "ἀρχὴν ἄλλων ἐλευθέραν" (archēn allon eleutheran), a second, autonomous starting point for action.</note>, though even this does not wander outside the limits of Providence and the Universal Reason. **F** For those superior things do not depend on our lower affairs, but rather Providence joins the better things to those that are being made. The order of the higher things is a Providence acting from above, but there is also a Providence derived from the higher one—a second Reason connected to the first—and from both a single "weaving" is completed, which is the total Providence. Men, therefore, possess another principle; however, not all men use everything they have. Rather, some use one principle, others use another, or they use several, and even the worse ones. Those higher principles are also present, **G** though they do not operate in everyone; yet they themselves are not sluggishly far from action in their own nature. Perhaps someone will ask...
<margin>* in themselves</margin>
<margin>* by an cause</margin>

<summary>This page argues that inequality in nature is a necessary result of the hierarchy of existence, where things "fade" as they move further from the divine Intellect. It introduces the idea that humans are unique because they possess a "free principle" that allows them to be judged for their actions, unlike simple animals.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of Divine Providence and the Universal Reason (Logos). Having previously discussed how individuals contribute to the cosmic drama, Plotinus now explores why the higher rational principle does not seem to exert equal influence over every person or creature, and how the soul’s previous lives and its relationship with matter affect its current state.</meta>

->### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III.<-

<margin>That there must be different grades of things. That providence dispenses individual things with proportional equality. That fate serves providence. On free will.</margin>

If these principles are present, why do they not act? Or is it perhaps that they are not present? Although we certainly admit they are present everywhere, and that nothing is destitute of them. Perhaps we should say they are not present in those upon whom they do not act. Why then do they not act upon everyone? If indeed these individuals are parts of them—I am speaking of such a principle as Reason. In other animals, this principle does not belong to them; in humans, however, it is by no means present in all. Is it then not in all, or is it not only that principle? But why not alone? In those where it is alone, it is appropriate to live according to it; but according to other things insofar as necessity compels.

For whether the composition of the person is such that it is plunged, as it were, into turbulence, or whether the desires overcome, it is similarly necessary to cast the cause back upon the subject itself. At first, it will seem that the cause is no longer in Reason <note>original: "ratio," translating the Greek "logos," the rational blueprint of the universe</note>, but rather in matter; and thus matter, not reason, will dominate. Then, the subject exists as it was formed, or rather, Reason is the subject for the principle, and that which is made from Reason exists according to Reason. Therefore, it is not matter that will dominate, with the formation following after; rather, because a person is as they are, one could refer the cause to a preceding life, as if the Reason had become weak due to antecedent events, if compared with a superior Reason. 

Indeed, since the soul has become weaker and then shines forth, the Reason itself must be said to have within itself the plan <note>original: "rationem"</note> of matter: for it will work upon matter for itself according to its own nature, either fashioning the matter or finding it to be in accord. For the seminal reason <term>seminal reason: translated from "ratio seminaria" or "logos spermatikos," the formative power or "seed" that determines the physical development and nature of a living thing</term> of a bull is not in any matter other than that of a bull. Hence, as it is said, a soul is destined for other animals, since the soul has become different and the Reason has already turned into something else, so that it becomes the soul of a bull whereas it was previously a man; wherefore, by the judgment of Justice <note>original: "Iustitia" / "Dike," the personification of cosmic justice and order</note> itself, it becomes worse. 

But why the soul became worse from the beginning and how it went astray has often been said: that not all things are primary, but those which are second or third have a nature inferior to the things above them. Likewise, a small momentum of inclination <note>original: "inclinationis momentum" / "ροπὴ," referring to the soul's "tilt" or leaning toward the material world</note> is enough to make us stray from the right path. Furthermore, the connection of one thing with another is like a certain mixing intended to produce a third thing from both. Nor is that which was here diminished, but that which is less was made less from the beginning, and that which was made was less according to its own nature; and if that which follows suffers, it suffers according to its worth. To this is added that the comparison must be referred to the preceding life: for from those things which were done and conceived in that life, the subsequent things are deduced.

PROVIDENCE therefore proceeds from the beginning to the end, spreading itself from above: not in an equal portion according to number, but according to a certain proportional comparison, it distributes differently in different places. Just as in a single animal, which is rightly connected from the beginning to its furthest parts, every limb possesses its own function; the better part has a more excellent action, while the worse part has an inferior one appropriate to it. It also undergoes its own experiences, which are suitable both to itself and to the order directed toward the other parts.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> If these [Reason-principles] are present, why do they not act? Or are they not present? Although we say they are present everywhere, and nothing is empty of them, or they are not present to those in whom they do not act. Why then do they not act upon all? If indeed these too are parts of it—I mean such a principle. For in other animals, this principle does not belong to them. In humans, it is not in all. Is it then not in all? Or is it only this one, but why only this? In those where it is alone, life is according to it. Other things follow as far as necessity requires. For whether the composition is such as to cast one into a murky state, or if the desires dominate, it is nevertheless necessary to say that the cause lies in the subject. 

But first, it will seem to be no longer in the Reason <note>original: "logos"</note>, but rather in the matter. And the matter holds what the Reason is, having dominated it, since the subject is like a thing molded; or the Reason is the subject for the principle, and that which is produced from the Reason, and that which exists according to the Reason. <margin>C</margin> So it is not matter that will dominate, but the molding. And for it to be of such a kind, one might refer it to the former life, as if it were produced from the dimness of preceding things, compared to the Reason before it. Just as when a soul has become weaker, and later there is an illumination, the Reason itself must be able to become [weak], and the Reason <margin>D</margin> has within itself the matter which it will work for itself, making the matter according to itself, or finding it in harmony. For the Reason of a bull is not in other matter than the matter of a bull; whence he says [the soul] is thrust into other animals, as if the soul had become something else. The Reason having been altered so that it becomes the soul of a bull, though it was formerly a man. <margin>E</margin> Thus, by Justice, it becomes worse. 

But why it became worse from the beginning, and how it went astray, has often been said: that not all things are first; but whatever things are second or third have a nature less than those before them. And a small tilt is enough for a departure from the right. And the weaving together of one thing with another is like a certain mixture of another thing produced from both. And it did not truly diminish [the whole]; but there is that which was made less according to its own nature. <margin>F</margin> And if the consequence suffers, it suffers according to its merit. And one must send the reasoning back to the things lived before, as the things following are hung from there.

<margin>G</margin> PROVIDENCE then comes to be, descending from the beginning to the end, from above, as if not by number but by analogy, different in different places. Just as in a single animal, it is hung from the beginning to the end. Each part has its own [role]. The better part has the better of the activity. The lower part [has its own]. Whether it acts or suffers, these are the experiences proper to it, both toward itself and toward the arrangement with others.

<summary>Plotinus explains that the variation in human virtue and nature is not a failure of Providence, but a result of the soul’s pre-existence and its necessary descent into different grades of being. He uses the analogy of a single organism to show how every part, whether high or low, has a specific and proportional role within the cosmic order.</summary>

And indeed, being struck in such a way, the vocal parts uttered sounds, while others remained silent in their experience, and the subsequent parts were moved. From all these sounds, experiences, and actions, there arises one single "voice" for all living beings, as it were, a single life and a single existence. For even though the parts are different and have different functions—feet do one thing, eyes another, the mind another, and the intellect <note>original: "νᾶς" (nous), the highest level of divine or human mind</note> another—from all of them comes a single Providence <note>original: "πρόνοια" (pronoia), the divine foresight or plan</note>. Fate <note>original: "εἱμαρμένη" (heimarmene), the causal chain of events</note> begins from the lower elements; but that which is above is Providence alone. For all things in the intelligible world are Reason <note>original: "λόγος" (logos)</note>, and even beyond Reason; for there is also the Pure Soul. From that point onward, as much as comes from that source is Providence, both in the Pure Soul and in how it extends here into living beings. From the earth, we also make divisions. The Reason, then, is equal, and from it, it creates equal things, just as in each individual animal. But from that point on, the things done are consequences and follow Providence, <margin>* which</margin> *which* does things dear to the gods. For the Reason of Providence is dear to the gods. Therefore, such works are woven together; but Providence has made some things happen differently than those produced by humans, or by irrational creatures, or by inanimate life. If it follows that one uses things twice, then again all these things are under Providence, so that virtue prevails everywhere; even when things are shifted, the errors find correction, just as those who care for bodies provide health. These are the animals under Providence, even when audacity or sin occurs. Again, in succession, the Reason that governs joins and brings things together, and so corrects what has suffered, so that evil follows by necessity. For among us, things happen according to causes and not strictly by the compulsion of Providence; but they are joined by us to the works of Providence and from the works of Providence. What follows is woven together according to the will of that higher power, not merely by the will of those who acted, but by something else in the universe, <margin>* nor even by itself</margin> where *nor even by itself* acting according to Providence, or having fallen into some passion within us. For the same thing does not always produce the same effect when meeting any other thing; rather, the same thing acts differently toward different things. <margin>paradoxical</margin> For example, the beauty of Helen produced one effect on Paris—he was struck with love—while Idomeneus <note>a Greek king and suitor of Helen who remained a hero in the Trojan War</note> was affected differently. Now, the actions of the intemperate are neither by Providence nor according to Providence. But the work of the temperate man is not strictly "by" Providence (since it is done by himself), yet it is "according to" Providence, for it is in harmony with the Reason. Just as if someone were to perform actions conducive to health, he acts himself, yet he acts according to the reason of the physician. They are according to causes among us, not indeed compelled by Providence, but arising from us while we join our works to the works of Providence and to those things set forth by Providence. For not everything approaching everything else produces the same effect; but that which is the same produces one thing toward one and another toward another. VI
In what order consequences of evil are foreseen from the good.
How signs of future things exist in the present.
