**FROM WHERE, then,** do the prophets also predict worse things? And why do astrologers, among their other prophecies, also announce these misfortunes? Surely it is from this: that all opposites are woven together simultaneously, whether as form and matter, or as in a composite living being <note>original: "animali composito"</note> such as the world itself is. Therefore, he who contemplates the form and the reason <note>original: "λόγον" (logos)</note> in present things also contemplates that which has been formed.
<margin>B</margin>
For he does not look upon the intelligible living being in the same way he looks upon the composite living being; rather, he sees the reason <note>original: "rationem" / "λόγον"</note> of the living being forming the lesser parts within the composite. Since, therefore, this universe is a living being, he who sees the things happening within it also sees those things from which they arise: and he sees the providence reigning within it, which indeed proceeds in order through all things that are and that are coming to be. These are living things whose actions and passions are both mastered by reason and permitted by necessity; thus, he contemplates them as mixed, and as things that are continually being mingled. And he himself cannot distinguish providence apart from that which happens according to providence, nor again can he distinguish what the subject provides from itself to that which happens within it. Indeed, it is not within the power of an ordinary man to do this, nor even a wise or divine one; rather, one might say this is a gift of God alone. For it is not the prophet’s duty to know the *reason why* something happens, but only to announce *that it will be so*. And the art of foretelling is a kind of "reading" of natural letters <note>Plotinus treats the movements of stars and events in nature as a language or script written by the universe.</note> which indicate the order of things and never decline toward disorder. Rather, this is especially testified by the movement of the world, which brings things to light even before it appears in the things themselves what kind they are, or how much they might suffer. For these things coincide with those, and those in turn with these, simultaneously contributing to the constitution and eternity of the world. And according to a certain analogy—that is, a comparison of proportion—they signify the rest to those who diligently observe such things, since other prophecies are also brought about through a certain analogy. For it was not necessary for all things to depend on one another in turn; but they ought to have been made like one another in some way. And this, perhaps, is what is commonly said: that all things are contained by analogy. Moreover, analogy is something like this: just as the better relates to the better, so in turn the worse relates to the worse; just as an eye is compared to an eye, so is a foot compared to a foot, as one corresponds to the other. Likewise, if you please, as virtue is to justice, so is vice to injustice. If, therefore, analogy reigns in the universe, it is certainly possible to prophesy. And if those things act upon these, they act in such a way that the parts in every living being work upon one another—not because one generates the other (for they are born together), but because each is endowed with its own nature, and thus suffers in a way that is consistent with its own natural property. And because this is such a thing, and that is such a thing similarly:
<margin>G</margin>
for thus the reason <note>original: "ratio" / "λόγος"</note> is also one.

That in the providence of God, artificial and natural action is the same, which governs the world like the life of a plant.

**FURTHERMORE**, since there are better things in the world, there are also, for that reason, worse things. In what way could there be anything "worse" in a multi-faceted work unless there were also a "better"? Or, in turn, how could there be a "better" without a "worse"? Just as...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...makes him healthy, he does it himself, and it was worked by the physician despite the patient's ignorance. <note>This column provides the original Greek text corresponding to the Latin on the left.</note>

**FROM WHERE, then,** do prophets predict worse things, and seeing the movements of all other things, predict these alongside other prophecies? Is it not clear that it is because all opposites are interwoven, such as form and matter, as in a composite living being? He who beholds its form and reason also beholds that which is formed. For he does not behold the intelligible living being and the composite living being in the same way, but <margin>* reason</margin> *the reason* of the living being, forming the lesser parts within the composite. Since the universe is a living being, he who beholds the things happening in it beholds at the same time both the things from which they exist and the providence over it. <margin>* it extends</margin> *It extends* through all things that happen. These are also living beings whose actions and dispositions are mastered by reason and mixed with necessity; he beholds them as mixed, and as things being continually mixed. He cannot distinguish the providence itself from that which is according to providence, nor again the substrate and how much it gives to the substrate from itself. But it is not for a man to do this, nor for any wise man or god; or as one might say, this is a divine privilege. It is the task of the prophet to say not the *why*, but only the *that*. And the art is a reading of natural letters indicating things in order. They are departures leaning toward the disordered, or rather you were testified to by the movement, which leads into the light even before the events through them appear, <margin>* such as</margin> *such as* each kind and how many. These things concur with those, and those with these, contributing together toward the constitution and eternity of the world. <margin>* analogous</margin> And other things signify by *analogy* to the one who has observed them, since other forms of divination also work by analogy. In this way, all things had to be hung from one another, and to be made like one another in some way. And this is perhaps what is meant when it is said that analogy holds all things together: as the worse is to the worse, so the better is to the better; as eye is to eye, and foot to foot, the one to the other. And if you wish, as virtue is to justice, so vice is to injustice. If then there is analogy in the universe, it is also in each one, and if those things act upon these, they act just as the parts in every living being act upon each other; not as one generates the other, for they come into being together; but as each is by nature, so it also suffers what is appropriate to its own nature. And because this is such, and that is such, they are one in Reason.

**AND** since there are better things, there are also worse things; for how could there be anything worse in a multiform thing if there were not a better? Or how could there be a better without a worse? So that...

<margin>A</margin>
Therefore, we must not blame the worse elements for being present in the better, but rather we should approve of that which is better: for it imparts something of itself to the worse. Indeed, those who think the worse should be entirely removed from the universe would also remove Providence itself. For whom would Providence be for? It would not be for itself, nor for that which is better; for when we speak of "heavenly Providence," we refer to its relation to that which is lower. For the very Principle <note>original: "principium" / "ἀρχὴ" (archē), referring to the One or the Source.</note> into which all things are reduced is that in which all things exist

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>* in all things.</margin>
simultaneously, and all things are a whole. Now, all things proceed from this Principle while it remains within itself; just as from a single root resting in itself, many things sprout into a divided multitude, each bearing a likeness to that root. But here, one thing is made within another. Some things are close to the root, while others, proceeding further, are divided as if into branches, twigs, fruit, and leaves; and some things remain always, while others, like fruit

<margin>C</margin>
and leaves, are always coming into being. And those things which are always coming into being possess within themselves the "reasons" <note>original: "rationes" / "λόγους" (logoi), the formative principles or blueprints of life.</note> of the higher things, as if they wished to be tiny little trees. And if they should generate before they decay, they would only generate what is close to them; but the empty spaces of the branches are filled again by the root itself, even if they have a different nature. From these, the furthest ends of the branches are affected, so that it seems as if the suffering comes only from what is nearby. But that which follows the Principle, one part

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>* immovable.</margin>
suffers, while another part acts. Yet the Principle itself is also connected <note>original: "ἀκίνητος" (immovable) / "connexa" (connected).</note>. For as things progress far away, they begin to act upon one another; yet from the Principle, they come from the same source: just as if brothers acted upon one another because they were made similar, having sprung from the same parents.

->MARSILIO FICINO’S<-
->COMMENTARY ON BOOK FOUR OF THE THIRD<-
->ENNEAD, CONCERNING DAEMONS.<-

->SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.<-
->A summary of the book, likewise concerning daemons and one's own personal daemon.<-

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a floral motif.</image-desc>
THE SUMMARY of this book concerning one's own daemon <note>In Neoplatonism, a "daemon" is not an evil spirit, but a guiding spirit or a higher level of the soul that "watches over" the individual's current life.</note> is more "daemonic" than divine in this way: Since the soul is all things and has naturally free motion, it can certainly form itself within its own likenesses into all things, and subsequently conform itself to the bodies of animals or plants. If, therefore, it has lived in the manner of a plant, it forms the body of a plant after this life, in which only the vegetative power acts; however, the sense-power presides over such a life like a daemon—not as an actor, but as an attending observer. Similarly, if the soul lives as a beast, it finally becomes a beast exercising only sense and vegetative power; in this case, the rational power hangs over it idly, like a daemon observer. But he who lives by reason along with sense has the Mind <note>original: "mentem" / "νοῦς" (nous)</note> as an attending daemon; and finally, he who lives by the Mind seems to have God as his presiding daemon. In this matter, Plotinus partly followed the *Timaeus* <note>A dialogue by Plato.</note> which says the more excellent power of the soul is the leader and daemon of man. He also followed the *Pythagorean Verses*, which pray to God to show us what "Daemon" we should use; they then declare that within each person there is a certain divinity of their own nature as a daemon, which can reveal hidden things to us. Hence Plotinus and Iamblichus, following the opinion of the Egyptians, place each person's own Intellect over them, like a daemon of reason always observing all things. Plotinus was led to compose this book, as Porphyry relates, by the magical works of an Egyptian priest, who claimed he could show each man his own daemon to his eyes; he demonstrated this to Plotinus in the presence of several others, and it was not the daemon of Plotinus that appeared, but a God—for Plotinus lived not merely by reason, but by the divine.

-> ### COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO ### <-

...rather than to live by intelligence, striving obviously by intuition much more than by discourse <note>In Neoplatonic thought, "discourse" (discursus) is step-by-step reasoning, whereas "intelligence" or "intuition" is immediate, direct understanding.</note>, and not merely pruning away disturbances but pulling them out by the roots. For this reason, in this book he not only teaches what kind of <term>daemon</term> <note>original: "daemon" / "δαίμων" (daimōn). In this context, a daemon is not an evil spirit, but a protective guiding spirit or "genius" assigned to a person.</note> belongs to each person, but also exhorts us toward God so that we may obtain a divine daemon. This is the summary of the book thus far. 

Plato often declares—as do all the Platonists—that besides the parts of the soul, there are other external daemons, both very many in number and acting as leaders of men; Plotinus himself says this elsewhere, and most especially in the book *On Love*. In this book, however, he primarily introduces daemons as being "parts of the soul." He does this because this topic had not yet been discussed by others, and because according to the various levels of these [inner] daemons, we are assigned different levels of external daemons. 

For where a life is arranged according to the imagination, our external daemon is "aerial," specifically in the lowest part of the air, and it moves us through its own imagination acting upon ours. But where one lives according to reason, a daemon from the middle air turns our human reason by its own reason. Finally, where the life is intellectual, a daemon from the highest air breathes into our intelligence through its own intelligence; and they do this not so much by choice as by the way of nature. For even within us, the thinking of the intellectual light naturally moves the imagination to imagine sensible light, and the imagination in sleep moves the senses, and in waking it frequently moves the emotions by way of nature. Conversely, passion moves the sense, the sense moves the imagination, and this naturally moves the reason. 

In the same way, the daemons constantly strike our powers with theirs; but the more excellent order of daemons acts quite hiddenly and calmly, constantly recalling us to the intelligence. Such a daemon is seen to have led Plotinus; therefore, it was called a God, just as the daemon of Socrates was. For the most outstanding daemons are often called by the name of "Gods," just as the lowest "Gods" are designated by the name of daemons. 

We have asserted enough in our *Theology* that there are daemons in the air; so that there may be rational animals everywhere, and in the air rather than just on the earth. These are as much more excellent and larger as the globe of the air itself is vaster and more excellent than the earth, and especially more akin to the rational life. For that which lives first and most eminently within us and obeys our thought is an "aerial spirit" <note>Ficino refers to the "pneuma" or medical spirit, a fine substance that connects the soul to the body.</note>. Therefore, immense and rational animals live in the air, possessing a round shape, as the shape of the air demands. Their sense is whole throughout their whole body, and it is extremely sharp according to the nature of the air. Their motion is similarly very fast due to their reason; the order of their motion is almost like that of the stars. 

Therefore, daemons are the "stars" of the aerial heaven, imitating the circuits of the celestial stars to the best of their power, moving from east to west and back again, progressing and regressing at fixed times, moving toward the north and then toward the south, and even ascending to their peak and descending again in a certain order—especially those daemons above the turbulent air. Nor do they act upon us by choice alone, as we have said, but mostly by their very nature, like stars, and by their rays, which though hidden are nevertheless very effective. A <term>Magus</term> <note>A practitioner of "natural magic" or "theurgy," who understands the hidden connections in nature.</note> who knows how to gather these rays will be able to see them and show them to others. 

Just as the rays of the sun, which cannot be discerned by themselves in a hidden corner, are sometimes gathered by certain vapors and are immediately seen in the form of redness or paleness; and just as a flame lit at midday cannot be seen from afar in linen, but appears once wood is added. Thus, it seems the Egyptian priest gathered the rays of Plotinus’s daemon and—as Porphyry testifies—displayed them to the eyes of those present <note>Referring to an event in Porphyry's *Life of Plotinus* (Ch. 10) where an Egyptian priest conjured Plotinus’s guardian spirit in the Temple of Isis, only to find it was a "God" rather than a lower daemon.</note>. Whether he obtained this through the gift of the daemons by worshiping them, or whether he infused the air with a certain vapor akin to the daemons, by which the gathered rays of the daemon became visible in a specific way. 

But by what form did the Magus conclude that Plotinus’s daemon was of the highest rank? Clearly because it did not come in a deformed brightness like a rainbow (as the lowest daemons in the mixed air usually do), nor in paleness or redness (as the middle ones sometimes do), but in a light that was utterly pure and most clear, which is the property only of the ethereal and celestial daemons. 

But if Plotinus’s daemon is so high, how does it lead him familiarly? How does that magus reach its rays? A daemon dwelling far off can strike something by the casting of "sensual rays" and words that signify meaning; by striking, it can see the innermost spirit of a man, and by seeing, it can signify and affect something as if by speaking. Remember, however, that "chains" <note>original: "catenae." The Neoplatonic concept of "Seirai" or series, linking the highest gods down to the lowest physical objects.</note> are extended everywhere from the highest things to the lowest. Thus, from individual stars, certain orders of daemons follow those stars and are affected in certain ways; and similarly, souls are affected by daemons—each soul by its own. 

There are, therefore, many in any given sphere, both below the moon and above the moon: Saturnian daemons under Saturn, Jovian daemons under Jupiter, and others likewise. And among the Saturnian daemons in that same sphere, some are more excellent than others, and similarly for the Jovian ones, just as happens among men. Therefore, a most excellent daemon among the aerial ones leads Plotinus and Socrates; this daemon is led by one of the most excellent among the ethereal ones, which is similarly led by one of the best among the celestial daemons. Thus, Socrates and Plotinus are moved from the highest level in a continuous series. 

But is each person moved by only one daemon in the same sphere? Perhaps not by one. For although any daemon might fill a very wide region, and therefore even if it does not change its place, it can observe a wandering man in many places and reach him everywhere with rays like a star; nevertheless, it is not probable that when someone travels from the east to the western region, a daemon (being far superior in nature) should follow the footsteps of a traveling man like a tutor bound to him. 

What then? Either there is a single daemon who is everywhere according to Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized theurgy and the omnipresence of divine powers.</note>, and so it is not forced to change place; or if it is not everywhere at once, it is not just one daemon—that is, one in number—but one in species that presides over each person. Thus, "solar" daemons preside over a solar man; wherever he goes, he comes specifically into the domain of solar daemons—he himself, I mean, and every solar person. Similarly, "Venereal" people <note>People born under the influence of the planet Venus.</note> fall into the hands of Venereal daemons everywhere. 

Yet there are certain differences among solar daemons: for all the gifts of the sun, which the one sun possesses, are distributed separately among many solar daemons. There are also many similar differences among solar men; so that a common man, though he finds his own leaders (that is, common daemons) wherever he goes, may find them less suitable in one place and more suitable in another. But he obtains the most perfectly suitable one, which is unique, in a certain region. From this it follows that a man is more fortunate in one place than another, and similarly in one task rather than another: namely, where his daemon is more powerful and more effective than in others. 

It follows, furthermore, that those who are singularly born for a certain work devise and perform many wonderful things beyond their age without teachers or assistants, being instructed by their own daemons. Then indeed, beyond their own hope and the opinion of others, they happen upon the right times, regions, persons, materials, instruments, and resources. When these are duly supplied, they naturally fulfill the work for which they were destined. The confluence of these diverse factors is connected into one outcome not by a natural cause, but by a daemonic one, directing each detail to an end foreknown to it. Meanwhile, it serves and supplies the heavens equally: I say it "serves" by providing the means toward the end foreknown by the celestial intelligence, and it "supplies" its own efficacy to carry out that which the celestial motion often does not do, but only signifies. Whence sometimes an astrologer, from a certain disposition of the heavens as if from a sign, will pronounce what a certain daemon, suited to such a disposition, is doing...

<meta>The catchword at the bottom "vticunq" (uticunque) indicates the next page begins with "howsoever" or "in whatever way."</meta>

He describes daemons as rational, aerial beings that influence human life and talent, citing the miraculous appearance of Plotinus's own divine daemon.</summary>

-> ON THE FOURTH BOOK OF THE THIRD ENNEAD <-

A 3
<meta>catchword: -tus (completing "intemperatus")</meta>

*In whatever way it is possible within us, and in whatever way we are able, we effect it. Clearly, after that celestial influence <note>original: "affectus," here referring to an astrological or spiritual state</note> vanished over many years, even if it did not return to the same state: from which it appears that it signified our affairs rather than caused them. But let us now proceed to the words of Plotinus.*

### How the intellect produces the soul, the soul produces nature, and nature produces matter.

I All bodies are always doing something, and by acting they emit something outward; simple bodies do so without any internal change to themselves. For since they are uniform, and one part holds to another, and they have nothing foreign within them, rightfully nothing of their substance flows out. In this way, fire provides heat and light without being diminished. Similarly, water, by providing coldness and its specific quality, generates substance in turn. Composite bodies, however, act by a contrary logic, because they emit things outward to their own detriment <note>Ficino means that complex, physical things wear out when they produce effects, whereas divine things do not.</note>. Much more do the intellect and the soul always propagate something from themselves: the intellect produces the soul, and the soul produces the sensory and vegetative life, which we can call **nature**.

But the intellect, in the manner of a simple body, procreates the soul without being changed; the soul, however, like a composite body, produces nature while being changed. Entirely, the intellect, the soul, and nature first generate substance, and then they generate quality within that substance. For it is the property of a more excellent agent to first generate a substance, and then to preserve it toward its generator, as if by gazing upon it in wonderful ways.

But in what way does the soul, while moved, produce nature? Certainly not by a movement of discourse <note>Discourse (discursus) refers to step-by-step logical reasoning.</note>. For it does not beget its essential part from its accidental part; rather, with "otherness" reigning within itself, it passes from its own intellectual power into a sensory and natural faculty far different from the intellect. Just as in a composite body, its own vapor, spreading itself to the outer circumference, weakens the substance which has been altered to some extent; and as that vapor, flying further outward, seems to represent—with some loss of substance—that passion of the soul, by which the soul sometimes promotes the vegetative power beyond itself, beyond the <term>spiritual body</term> <note>original: "spiritalem corpus," the "astral body" or subtle vehicle that connects the soul to the physical body</note> most familiar to it, toward composite bodies. For then, it is not merely moved in a certain way, but truly changed—that is, with some loss of its own dignity, it approaches the work of the lowest generation. And just as it is changed within itself, it co-creates such a body for itself out of matter, according to its strength.

Remember during these points that the World Soul itself, if compared with the Divine Mind, generates while being "moved" in a certain way, as we have explained; but if compared with our soul, it completes its generation "unchanged"—that is, in no way distracted from its principal actions. Where it is said that matter is procreated by nature, understand this as the **universal nature** that accompanies the World Soul. Nevertheless, any intellectual soul (as Plotinus wishes), unless it finds matter already procreated, seems destined to procreate it. He calls **matter** here the "last thing of the universe," subject to nature itself, which is the last of the divine things, which fashions bodies out of utterly indefinite matter, applying forms from above. Just as nature, the soul, and the mind were previously indefinite in a certain way before they arrived at their own form—though they were never *entirely* indefinite—they are only thought of as such insofar as they are compared to the most absolute Act <note>Pure Act or "actus purissimus" refers to God or the ultimate reality which is fully realized and lacks no potential.</note>.

### On the transmigration of the soul: and that it does not pass into beasts.

II What Plotinus himself once thought about the transmigration of the soul <note>reincarnation</note> is declared to those reading his writings—unless perhaps he is being poetic like Plato. We, however, wish that (as philosophers are often accustomed to doing upon more diligent meditation) if he did think this, he at least changed his opinion in this way—an opinion he seems to have held not so much by the necessity of reason as by the custom of his people and age. 

Although the human soul may be changed within itself in some way, it is never transformed beyond the certain limits of the human species. This also seems to have pleased <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A later Neoplatonist who argued against humans reincarnating as animals.</note>, who says that the soul preserves its own species in any transformation, since the beginning of its motion comes from itself and is acted out within itself. Where the soul is said to be "all things," it must be understood to be all things in whatever way, but in its own way—that is, in a way proper to its own species. Do not say, therefore: "If the soul is all things through its natural power, therefore it eventually becomes all things." For the soul itself never becomes a corporeal form or a body, because the soul is not such a form or body in every sense, but specifically according to the mode of life itself.

Thus, it does not become a beast, because the soul is not simply an animal, but an animal only in the human mode. Furthermore, since we see that certain effects arise not from just any causes, but from specific ones—heat from things that are hot, grapes from the vine, a lion from a lion—and therefore, in turn, specific species of things do not procreate just any effects, but their own; surely we ought not to hope that from the generative nature of a human, which is a certain specific species and human from the beginning, an ox could ever be made. Unless perhaps nature itself changes its species and a human nature eventually becomes a bovine one, which indeed cannot be done. For since it is said to be self-moving and eternal, it is never transformed by another; nor will it willingly desert its own species, since individual things always strive to preserve this for themselves. 

Now, for this very reason—that human generative nature cannot be bovine—it happens that neither a man procreates an ox, nor an ox a man. For nature is further distant from nature than the effect of this nature is from that one. Entirely, the species of things are not accustomed to degenerate into others unless they both lose their internal qualities and admit external ones, coming into a mixture; thus, they gradually cease to be what they were. A Platonist will not concede that this happens to our soul. He will concede, however, that the generative property of a human differs in species from the generative property of brutes, just as the human species differs from the wild. 

Add to this that when the soul is said to "become" such a thing—such and such, according to Plotinus—it is through its choices and actions; if these are its own, they are human. Therefore, it does not cross the human species through them. Finally, it is vain to say that a soul enslaved to wicked actions turns into a beast "deprived of reason," since the soul itself uses no reason at all. For the sharpness of reason does not lie entirely idle in the wicked; rather, it is busily occupied, although it dwells mostly upon the spectacles of the senses and the objects of the imagination, either to obtain or avoid them. What else is the cause for why the wicked often seem sharper and more effective in their works than the good, if not the sharpness and effect of the rational power? 

For this reason, if an unjust soul is to be transferred again into an earthly body after this life, it will return not into a brute, but into a human who similarly misuses the skill of reason. For the necessity of similarity itself seems to lead to this. For Plotinus himself clearly confesses that a human acts not according to one power alone, but according to all the powers of the soul. It will be purified eventually, for by the dispensing of providence, it will eventually fall into such calamities because of its crimes that it will repent of a life basely led, with common discipline and its **daemon** <note>the guiding spirit</note> meanwhile urging it on. Finally, the voluptuous man will not eventually become a plant destitute of senses. For how could a voluptuous man neglect the actions of the senses and in this way turn into a tree robbed of senses? On the contrary, no one uses the senses more than the intempera-

<summary>Ficino explains the Neoplatonic hierarchy of creation (Mind to Matter) and argues that human souls remain human even in reincarnation, as they cannot lose their essential rational species to become animals or plants.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on the fate of the soul after death, specifically addressing whether a human soul can truly descend into the body of an animal (metempsychosis). Ficino attempts to reconcile Plato’s writings with a more rational and humane interpretation.</meta>

-> COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO <-

If, therefore, the soul must be turned back again toward earthly bodies, it will return not into a plant, but into a human being. The violent command of its own senses may so disturb, vex, torture, and ruin it that it finally grows weary of a life of pleasure; meanwhile, laws and divine powers <note>original: "numinibus"</note> call it back to a better life. I pass over the fact that the souls of the wicked and the soft are sent here and there by God, so that those who committed crimes through perverse pleasure may at some point be punished by cares and pains. Yet, he who takes away all act of reason from those being punished also takes away immense and innumerable cares; for he who removes sensation takes away pain along with that sensation. Remember, however, that souls are purged not only in earthly bodies, but in **aerial** ones <note>The "aerial body" is a Neoplatonic concept of a "spirit-vehicle" that the soul inhabits between physical incarnations.</note>; a punishment which we have explained more clearly in our *Theology*. 

Furthermore, do not let what Plato says move you: that every soul has care for all that is inanimate. For it does not follow from this that any soul may be inserted into any body, which Plato himself would deny could happen. Surely, if the rational soul not only rules and moves the earthly body, but also the aerial and the celestial; if it sometimes lives in higher dwellings; if it performs various duties similar to the providence of the celestial beings; then it seems to have care for the state of the whole inanimate world in this way. It puts on various forms <note>original: "species"</note> within itself, not by changing its own nature, but by claiming for itself the likenesses of others, provided its essence remains eternal. 

Rightly, therefore, **Timaeus of Locri** <note>A Pythagorean philosopher whom Plato uses as a character; Ficino treats him as a historical authority.</note> denies that human souls pass over into beasts. He also denies that they migrate immediately from one human to another. Rather, he thinks that they live meanwhile in aerial bodies and are thus purged by the vexation of the mind. He says that sensory tortures—whether they occur in a living body, or in water, or in fire—are **fictions** <note>original: "confictos"</note>, intended to terrify those who are not led to virtue by persuasion. Indeed, men affected in this way do not understand spiritual punishments—namely, the sorrow of a soul recognizing it is deprived of the Highest Good, and the Narrowness <note>original: "angustiam," implying a state of mental constriction or anxiety</note> of the imagination accompanying the soul's own repentance, when the sins of this life are atoned for in the aerial body. 

Timaeus himself would not deny that these punishments are assigned to sinners. For he thinks our souls are distinct from one another and immortal. He is a Pythagorean, after all, and highly esteemed by Plato. He even says that God fashioned our souls from the same powers and principles as the World Soul, and sent some down under the moon from different stars; again, that the supreme nature of the soul consists of "Identity" <note>A technical term from Plato’s *Timaeus* regarding the composition of the soul.</note>. 

It is necessary, therefore, to say according to the opinion of Timaeus: the human soul which has fallen into perverse reason and a vehement imagination by sinning is, immediately after death, tortured in that same aerial body (which it possesses even now) by that very same perversity and vehemence of thought. It is held among the lowest **daemons** <note>In the Platonic sense, "daemons" are intermediary spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense.</note> who bind it to similar conditions, until, recognizing that the cause of such great distress was its aversion from the Intellect, it gradually returns to it. At that time, being less distracted by fewer things, it can perceive this more clearly than it can now. Thus, it is raised step by step into the order of the higher daemons, and finally to the stars themselves, together with the celestial body it has possessed from the beginning—each soul to that star whose order it was allotted at the start, or to which it made itself similar by its way of living. Everywhere, however, it preserves its human property. 

For there is the earthly human, the aerial human, and the celestial human; there is, moreover, the solar and the Martian human. Everywhere, the "human" is the very power of the rational soul, vivifying a body in a certain way: celestial in heaven, aerial in the air through the celestial, and earthly on earth through both. Finally, perhaps Timaeus will think that after certain ages, through a relaxation of contemplation and an intention toward generation, the soul subsequently slides back down through the same grades of daemons and aerial humans, and lastly descends to an earthly human. But after a man's death, this soul—a sibling to the World Soul and a partaker of celestial things—is not plunged headlong into beasts, nor does it immediately return to an equally earthly man. For it is more appropriate to be purged in an aerial body, and more fit to be called back to higher things. It always returns to a body and a habit of life most similar to itself, whether it revolves among us or above us, until it returns entirely to the same point. For not just anything proceeds to anything else. 

Meanwhile, on earth we truly "slumber," and do not easily remember higher things; but above the earth we "awaken" and perceive our pristine state. Thus, through all the ages, the person of the rational mind remains the same, as if through the stages of a single life. This is what I guess Timaeus felt, which seems to me more probable among the opinions of the Platonists. 

In the second place, I would approve among the Platonic views those I brought up earlier: namely, that a human soul is more rightly transmitted from an earthly human into an earthly human than into a beast. Some report that this finally pleased **Porphyry**. Nevertheless, from this opinion it is likely that one also spends a life in an aerial body between earthly lives. **Proclus**, moreover, along with the common school of Platonists, denies that an intellectual soul can be so fitted to a savage body—which is quite foreign to it—that it might at any time communicate life to it. They think, however, that it communicates with brutes at times through a certain "likeness of life," and that Plato felt this way. I pass over for now whether, from this very opinion, it should be said that a soul made similar to brutes dwells among them for a time for the sake of punishment; and also that through such imagination of its own, it is perhaps so inserted into the imaginations of such beasts, just as many report that lower spirits entering human bodies insert things into our imaginations and move them. 

This is almost like how **Averroes** <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose "monopsychism" theory was highly controversial in Ficino's time.</note> taught that the Intellect is infused into souls, or however else he holds it. For where the **Prophet Daniel** relates that the King of Babylon <note>Nebuchadnezzar, who according to the Bible lived like an ox for seven years.</note> was translated by divine power among the oxen on account of his gravest crimes until he was purged and came to his senses, the Hebrews interpret this as the King's imagination having been divinely perverted to such an extent that he believed himself to have become an ox, and grieved heavily—just as a sorcerer or a person suffering from "black bile" <note>Melancholy, believed to cause hallucinations.</note> is accustomed to do. 

What if such is also the "passage of souls" in Plato? And such in Timaeus? When I was just expounding his opinion, I expounded it as ambiguous. For he even seems to have denied all return of souls into an earthly body, unless perhaps it be the final return. He seems to have posited that various sins are variously purged through the affliction of the spirit, spurred on by the "scout-daemons" under the judgment of **Nemesis**. Finally, Plato himself warned us not to rashly join any soul to any body when he says in the *Phaedrus* that a soul which is the proper form of a brute, and which has never perceived divine things, cannot enter into a human. This is as if to signify that the soul of a man cannot descend into the very form of a brute, even though it may perhaps descend into a certain likeness and merit of one. 

Since we have frequently mentioned the souls of brutes here, it is opportunely asked: If all life is immortal and does not accept its opposite but flees death (as pleases **Numenius** and **Plotinus**); and if, again, the souls of moving animals are both immortal and in some way rational (as **Porphyry** wishes, and almost similarly **Iamblichus**), what then should be said of these? We shall perhaps say, according to their opinion, or we shall imagine: that the souls of beasts possessing imagination—and therefore possessing their own motion—subsist in themselves separated from the body, and have a certain fixed number from the beginning? And that each is inserted from body into body within its own species, but never confuses species? And that meanwhile, until they obtain a body more suited to their species, they live in their own aerial body? For it has its own...

### ON THE THIRD BOOK OF THE FOURTH ENNEAD
#### PAGE 281
<sig>A 3</sig>

... its own spirit, in which Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note> believes there is something of the art and gift of prophecy from the daemons <note>original: "daemonum"; refers to tutelary spirits or "genii" rather than evil spirits.</note> to whom they are dedicated. However, he considers those souls lacking their own movement and devoid of imagination—specifically the vivifications of marine shells <note>original: "cochærum scilicet marinarum"; likely referring to mollusks or simple sea life.</note> and plants—to be "reflections" from the World Soul <note>original: "anima mundi"</note> rather than individual souls. Just as it happens that the hairs of animals are nourished by the soul of the whole, these life forms are ultimately resolved back into the life of the universe.

When Plato calls our inferior souls "mortal," those I just mentioned explain that they are not mortal in the sense that they perish, but because they depend entirely on something else, and seem to have affection and action only toward mortal things. After this, when he says that the soul is a "universe" both intelligible and sensible, and that it always acts through the intellect in the eternal intelligible world by a certain intuition of ideas, such great divinity of the soul seems to clash with the idea that it could be confined within a beast or a plant. 

Yet, he tempers this statement in a way: he does not wish for the animal or the tree to coalesce from this very substance, but rather from a certain influence <note>original: "influxu"</note> of it and a specific body. Meanwhile, the intellect does not cease its own proper work, even if the rational act, habit, and faculty cease—a point we do not easily admit. For the rational faculty itself is the most proper characteristic of our soul; therefore, as it is most natural, it remains above all else. Finally, you will notice that the "generative nature" is a certain limit of intelligence: so that what is intellectual at its highest point is generative at its lowest. This is like light in smoke, which becomes heat at its lowest point; or a visual ray flashing from a bird, which becomes generative within the egg. 

And just as such a visual ray does not depend on anything external but only on the eye—and thus is not extinguished when it does not shine outward, but simply stops acting externally—so too is the generative nature. Does it not shine both within and without the intellectual substance? It remains in the intellectual substance itself, not shining outward, when the whole soul is turned toward the opposite; just as a visual ray is retracted rather than extinguished when the eye is turned away.

->*Our soul rules the body and senses through attention; the world soul rules without attention.*<-

III. Proclus <note>A later Neoplatonic philosopher who headed the Academy in Athens.</note> says that the soul, through its very being (which is "to live" and is eternal), always vivifies a body—at least a celestial one most akin to the soul. Plotinus, however, thinks the soul will eventually cease even from this act, as he declares here and often elsewhere. He argues this happens when the rational power, along with the imagination, is entirely converted toward pure intelligence. 

For often in us, an excessive intensity of speculation weakens the effect of the generative nature, and vice versa. This does not happen to the World Soul; its power is naturally broader and far more effective, and it has obtained a body that is entirely obedient and placed in safety. The world body lives by the life of the soul as easily as air is ignited by the presence of fire. Perhaps it belongs to providence to occasionally compensate the soul with a period of supreme rest after it has been so long fatigued among us. Let this be granted to Plotinus, provided he also grants this: that a soul capable of being raised so far above matter, transcending the whole sky and the duty of the celestial soul, can never be confined to a brute or a tree. 

But since in the World Soul there is no "attention" directed toward the body, is there any sensation there? There certainly is, but it feels nothing external. For the things it senses are within itself, and it is not distracted by the act of sensing. Sensation there is unique and inward, and it does not "perceive that it perceives." Nothing foreign happens to it, nothing new. It is entirely necessary that the body, which is most closely joined and akin to the soul, be felt by the soul. But just as it nourishes its body, so it senses it, without having a conscious "noticing" attached to the action.

->*How various souls are allotted daemons, how they change them, and how they enter into generation with them.*<-

IIII. In the following chapter, remember that the soul is allotted such-and-and-such a daemon because of its specific choice and movement. I do not mean because of individual choices, but the *type* of choice that directs it toward a specific *species* of life. It does not change its daemon as long as it does not change its species of life entirely. 

Therefore, as long as it leads a "Venusian" <note>Life governed by desire, beauty, or the planet Venus.</note> life, it holds a Venusian daemon. Even if it occasionally abstains from wanton loves, as long as it is prone to love (even if honorably), it does not change the species of its daemon; it still has a Venusian one, but of a more excellent order. Similarly, if one moves from commerce to letters, he keeps a "Mercurial" <note>Related to Mercury: trade, communication, or intellect.</note> daemon, though a higher one. If one moves from religion to military service, he changes the daemonic genus and order. For he passes from a "Jovial" <note>Related to Jupiter: law, religion, or statecraft.</note> daemon to a "Martial" <note>Related to Mars: war or conflict.</note> one, which is when the soul first becomes "unfortunate" <note>In an astrological sense; Mars was considered a "lesser malefic."</note>. 

Conversely, if one comes from the military to religion, he passes from a Martial to a Jovial daemon, unless he continues to be contentious there too, in which case he is not particularly fortunate. Most people, however much they seem to change their way of life in this body, retain something of their old condition; therefore, they have not yet entirely cast off their old daemon. 

Thus, from what follows, it appears that the soul's primary affection—whether natural or from different choices—preserves the "ancient character" <note>original: "mos animæ speciem seruat antiquam"</note> of the soul. When this is changed to the complete opposite, the daemon is also changed, and with the daemon, fortune itself changes; for the daemon disposes "chance" events for us. Ultimately, the highest authority lies in the quality of the soul: for according to the difference in the soul's quality, we put on or cast off a certain daemon, and through these daemons, chance events are mostly dispensed. 

Even if Porphyry says the daemon is distributed according to the dominant star in the birth chart <note>original: "figura genesis"</note>, or Iamblichus says it is according to the whole reigning "harmony of the world," understand that the celestial movement and its aspect are not so much the *cause* of such distribution as they are the *sign*. For the souls of men and daemons exist in their specific nature before the movements of the heavens, just as they are already "such" in themselves before such movements. Therefore, Timaeus <note>The narrator of Plato's dialogue *Timaeus*.</note> says that souls, through their own affections, first chose their lots and the forms of life set before them; then they received daemons, and thirdly, they reached their "fated movements." They reached these through their "vehicles"—that is, their celestial bodies—which are contiguous with celestial influences and motions. 

Imagine, then, the Celestial Lyre, which, as Phoebus <note>Apollo, god of the sun and music.</note> strikes it, produces various harmonies at different hours. All souls, along with the common Soul <note>The World Soul</note>, are in such accord that, being what they already are in themselves, they are moved by certain harmonies rather than others, and come to dance in one chorus rather than another. Thus, from such celestial harmony, by which the soul is touched and especially soothed, we know what the soul is like, what daemon it has been allotted by its own nature, what it will do in the dance, and how it will dance. While much proceeds from the soul itself, a significant portion also happens due to the condition of the celestial harmony. In this whole discussion, remember that neither the condition of our affairs nor the order of Plato’s words can be rightly maintained unless, besides external daemons, [the soul itself is considered]...

He argues that the soul’s character and choices determine its assigned daemon and its "fate," using the metaphor of a celestial lyre to explain how individuals resonate with different cosmic harmonies.</summary>

On the previous page, Ficino discussed the soul’s descent and its presence in lower forms of life like plants and mollusks.</meta>

<header>THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...some are internal, and in turn, others are appropriately fitted to one another. Likewise, he says that the power and affection of the soul—which is situated most closely beneath the innermost daemon <note>In Neoplatonism, a "daemon" is a tutelary spirit or a higher part of the soul that acts as a guardian or guide, rather than a malevolent entity.</note>—is occupied among the works of the present life and is the proper producer of these works. The daemon, however, acts as the charioteer and governor of this producer. This very productive and busy power does nothing above the daemon's strength, nor, on the other hand, does it act as an equal to the daemon’s dignity.

### On the best man and daemon, how the daemon leads the soul to judgment; and that souls can reach the stars.

After this, he says that he is especially upright in whom the powers of imagination and reason are shaped entirely by the intellect, so that his whole life is conducted according to intelligence. In such a person, it is not some daemon that presides over life, but God himself—namely, the divine intellect, the intellectual unity (which is the head of intelligence, the charioteer), and finally, Unity itself, the God of gods. 

Then he says that our soul is not always formed by intelligence; for from the very beginning, due to the laborious construction of generation <note>The process of being born into a physical body.</note>, the act of the vegetative power <note>original: "potentiæ vegetalis"; the biological functions of growth and nutrition.</note> is stretched beyond measure. The imagination is hurried toward this and similar things, and reason is occupied with them as well. These things are indeed opposite to intelligence. Nevertheless, even before we use the discourses of reason, we naturally desire the true and the good through the power of knowing itself. Since this power does not desire something entirely unknown, there is at least a form of the true and the good naturally implanted in the mind. 

The daemon rules the soul, not simply in the best way possible, but in the best way for the soul's present quality. After this life in the earthly body, the daemon—now more internal than external—leads the soul to judgment, specifically while the soul is established in its "aerial body" <note>A subtle, non-physical body made of "spirit" or "air" that Neoplatonists believed the soul inhabited between incarnations.</note> before it returns to an earthly body. I say "another" daemon insofar as there is a different mode of living in the soul at that time; otherwise, the daemon is the same. The state in the aerial body is most suited for purgatorial judgment. For there, the spirit suffers affliction for its sins, and due to having fewer distractions, there is a easier opportunity for repentance. A certain progress in the soul and a choice for its future state are expected. Therefore, to pass the soul into beasts where the imagination becomes dull is nothing other, as we have said, than to close off the place of its power.

In the midst of this, I warn you again: it is ridiculous to think that the soul—if it can exempt itself from the whole world—could be confined within the narrow limits of a beast or a plant. He might have spoken more probably with Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who argued that human souls never truly inhabit animal bodies, but only "overshadow" them.</note> that the soul neither descends below the human form nor goes outside a celestial body, but holds onto this constantly. I say "celestial" not to claim any random body for it, but that it has its own from the beginning. Plotinus thinks it is at least possible for the soul to be liberated from the universe at some point; he might also have suspected it could live there perpetually. They say Porphyry once held this opinion, which you can also suspect in the *Phaedo* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the immortality of the soul.</note> when you hear that they "live without bodies forever." For if it ever reaches beyond the mutable condition of this world, it does not seem likely to change its life further; but if you say it will change, do not say it exists outside a celestial body at the same time. 

For it is a marvel that a soul in heaven, contemplating the stars—indeed, contemplating all things—should desire our world, unless perhaps it happens then just as lust often secretly goads a person who is observing something. That can only happen to the soul insofar as it is connected to the world, for the sake of which generation exists. It is connected, at least, through the celestial body which is always given life by it; otherwise, the soul already placed above the moon would not at some point desire mundane generation below the moon. 

That the soul can reach the celestial bodies is proved by this: if all intellectual souls are expressed directly from the Divine Intellect (the exemplar of the world), and are expressed from the whole—for that Intellect is not divided—then they surely proceed impressed by the whole exemplar. They are, therefore, both that world and this one; not in just any way, I say, but rather in the manner of a living being. In our soul, therefore, there are certain powers conforming to the World Soul, and thus in some way corresponding to the stars which surround it. So it is no wonder that those who flourish in profound contemplation finally depart to Saturn; those in civic life to Jupiter; those in magnanimity <note>original: "magnanimitate"; Greatness of soul or courage.</note> to Mars, and the rest similarly, especially if they were such from the beginning.

You will note that the generative nature is eternal along with the essence of the soul, even if its effect is interrupted. It is also indivisible in itself, although it seems to be diffused through the body, just as indivisible light is through the air. That it is indivisible is apparent because the entire seminal power flourishes in every drop of seed, where many things are generated from one casting of seed. And the whole of life is in every part of a plant, where a cut-off part, preserving life, grows together again while the universal nature contributes in the meantime. 

Remember again that the soul’s own quality and the daemon domestic to it enter into Fate when it enters a mutable body. Besides the common condition of suffering, it also possesses its own efficacy, so that it does not only suffer in Fate, but acts. For external chance often turns out similarly or dissimilarly depending on the different character of the person it happens to; and conversely, similar fates turn out very different for souls that are different from one another. The soul is in Fate by reason of the body; it is celestial as an actor, but in other things, it is more of a sufferer. The already mobile body is placed by the fatal revolution of the heaven into a certain condition of fortune, according to a certain order of choice—namely, of conception, infusion, and birth.

While the fundamental realities <term>hypostases</term> <note>original: "ὑποστάσεις"; In Neoplatonic philosophy, these are the levels of reality—the One, the Intellect, and the Soul—that "stand under" and support all existence.</note> are motionless while they remain in their state, the soul, through its motion, comes to generate both sense-perception and nature, reaching even to the level of plants. For the soul contains this nature within us when it dominates, but it is only a part of us. However, when the soul enters into plants, this vegetative nature dominates, as if it were left alone. In this state, the soul itself generates nothing further; rather, it becomes everything that is distinct from itself. For there is no life after this level; instead, that which is produced is without life <note>Referring to inorganic matter or the final product of the soul's creative descent.</note>. What then? If everything created before this was created without form, it was shaped by turning back toward its creator—as if it were being nourished. So too here, that which is generated is an extension of the soul. But this extension is an absolute indefiniteness. For if there was indefiniteness in the earlier stages, it was still within a form; it was not entirely indefinite, but only in relation to its own perfection. But that which is here is entirely indefinite; when it is perfected, it becomes a body, taking a form suited to its power—a receptacle for that which generated and nourished it. This is the last of the higher things in the body, and the last of the lower things within itself.

It wanders through the entire heaven, sometimes in one form and sometimes in another—either in a form perceived by the senses, or a rational form, or even a vegetative <note>original: "φυσικῶ"; relating to the "nature" or the biological growth of a plant.</note> form. For the dominant part of the soul performs the task suited to itself, while the other parts remain idle. Outside of man, the lower parts do not dominate, but they coexist. And yet, the better part does not always dominate, for these lower parts also have their own place. Therefore, souls live as sensing beings, for they possess organs of sense; and many live as plants. For the body grows and reproduces like a plant, so that all parts work together. But according to the better part, the entire form is a Man.

There are those realities which produce their own active existence while remaining still. But the soul is said to generate through movement, producing sensation in an active existence, and nature, and proceeding even as far as the plants. For it holds this subsisting nature even while it is within us, but it dominates as a part. However, when it is grafted into plants, this nature itself prevails as if it were left alone. Therefore, it generates nothing further; or rather, it generates, but something entirely different from itself. For life does not flourish further after this point, but what is made is now lacking life. What then? Perhaps just as everything generated before this was generated without form, and was formed by a certain turning back toward its creator—as if nourished from there—similarly here, that which is born is no longer a species of soul. For it does not live further; it is something entirely indefinite, or a certain indefiniteness. In higher things, nature is indeed undetermined, but it consists within a certain form. For it is not entirely indefinite, but only insofar as it is referred to its own perfection. But what is called "indetermined" here is entirely indefinite, and is indefiniteness itself. When this is perfected, it becomes a body, receiving a form adapted to its power—namely, a participation in that which generates and nourishes it. This is only the extreme limit of the higher things within the body, and it exists in the extreme limit of the lower thing itself.

<margin>D</margin>
Hence, what is said by Plato—that every soul has care for all that is inanimate—finds its place especially in this soul. Others, however, behave differently. It revolves through the whole heaven, sometimes in one species and sometimes in another—whether in the species of the senses, the rational, or even the vegetative. For its dominant part performs the duty suitable to it; the rest, however, are sluggish. For they seem left on the outside. In man, however, those things that are worse do not overcome, but they exist together. And yet, that which is better does not always overcome; for these lower parts also have their place in him. For this reason, they live as sensory beings; for the instruments of sense are present. Many things are also done by men as if they were plants; for the body is increased and reproduced from within like a plant. But according to that which is better, the whole species is Man.

...is considered a human. The soul, finally migrating from the body, becomes that very thing which it possessed in abundance. Therefore, we must flee to higher things, so that we do not fall into a mere sensory appearance by following sensible images <note>original: "simulachris videlicet sensibilibus"; referring to the fleeting shadows of the physical world rather than eternal truths</note>; nor should we be cast headlong into a vegetative life, enslaved to the desire for procreation and ensnared by the sweetness of flavors. Instead, we must rise with all our strength toward the intellectual, toward the Intellect, and toward God. Whoever, therefore, has preserved their human character is born again as a human. Those who have lived by the senses alone return as brute animals. Specifically, those who lived by sense-perception joined with anger are born as wild beasts, and the differences among those beasts reflect the differences in their anger. Those who lived by sense-perception joined with desire and pleasure return as deceptive and gluttonous animals. However, if they did not even live by the senses in this way, but rather through a degeneration of the senses, they sprout again as plants. For in these people, the vegetative power <note>original: "vegetale"; the basic biological functions of growth and nutrition</note> was the only thing—or the strongest thing—active, and their whole care was to be transformed into plants. Furthermore, those who lived too much charmed by musical melodies, but were not otherwise depraved, are reborn as musical animals. And those who ruled without reason become eagles, unless they were infected by some other wickedness. Those who confidently treat of sublime matters without wisdom, often looking up toward the heavens, are changed into birds that always seek the heights in their flight. He who has attained "civil virtue" <note>original: "civilem uirtutem"; the social and political ethics of a good citizen</note> returns as a human; but he who has not sufficiently attained even civil virtue is transformed into a social animal, like a bee or similar creatures.

<margin>
Our daemons are a part of the soul itself presiding over us—specifically, the power of the soul by which we live. Therefore, according to the different ways of life, there are different daemons within us.
</margin>

WHO, then, shall be called the "daemon" <note>In Neoplatonism, a "daemon" is not an evil spirit, but a guiding spirit or a "higher self" that represents the level of reality immediately above where the individual is currently functioning.</note> in these cases? Who, likewise, is God? Is it the one who primarily operates in these things? For that which operates leads each individual as if it were the principal part. Is it then the daemon who has been allotted the living being? Perhaps not. Rather, it is that which is *above* the person: that which presides as if in quietude. But that which comes *after* it acts, and we are most truly that which acts. If we act and live as sensory beings, then Reason is our daemon; but if we live by Reason, then the daemon is that which is superior to Reason—a presiding daemon that yields the busy office of living to another. Rightly, therefore, it is said in Plato: "You shall choose your daemon." <note>A reference to the Myth of Er in Plato’s *Republic*, where souls choose their next life and its accompanying spirit.</note> For we choose the one who is set over us according to our kind of life. Why, then, does the daemon lead? Perhaps it is not granted to lead once life is finished; but it was able to do so before, while the person lived. Once life is over, it is necessary to yield the action to another, as one who has already laid down his actual life. Here, then, the daemon wishes to lead, and that which has surpassed the previous state lives itself, having another daemon of its own. But if a soul grows heavy—that is, if a worse character outweighs the better—it pays the penalty. In this way, the wicked person falls into a worse state, as the active part of the human declines through a similarity of life into the life of a beast. But if the soul could obey its superior daemon, it would become superior, living that daemon's life and appointing for itself a presiding guide—the more excellent part of itself by which it is led—and beyond that another, until it reaches the highest point. For the soul is many things—indeed, it is all things, both the higher and the lower, extending through every grade of life. Truly, each one of us is an "intelligible world," <term>kosmos noētos</term> <note>The realm of pure ideas and forms that exists beyond the physical world.</note> and through our lower parts we are joined to this world, but through...

<column-break/>

...human, having departed <gloss>lives as that which it was most full of</gloss> it becomes something; therefore one must flee toward the upward path, so that we do not follow sensory things into sensory images, nor follow the vegetative path through the desire for procreation and the greed for food; but rather toward the intellectual, and intellect, and God. Those who have kept their humanity are humans again; those who lived by sense alone are animals. If they lived by sense with anger, they become wild beasts—and the difference among these creates the variety of such beasts. Those who lived with desire and pleasure become the desiring and gluttonous animals. If they did not even live by the senses with these traits, but with a dullness of sense, they become plants; for only the vegetative part was active in them, and their study was to become trees. Those who loved music <margin>* of irrational animals</margin> but were pure in other things become songbirds; <margin>* foolish</margin> kings without reason become eagles, unless some other vice is present. Those who studied the heavens without wisdom, always lifting themselves toward the sky, become birds that fly high. He who practiced civil virtue is a human. He who shared less in civil virtue becomes <margin>* foolish</margin> a social animal, especially a bee or such things.

WHO, then, is the daemon even here? Who is either God, or the one who is here? That which has acted leads each person, as it was the leader *there* <margin>* in this world</margin>. Is this then the daemon, as if it had been allotted to the living being? Or is it not? Rather, it is the one *before* it. For while that one stands over it being idle, the one *after* it acts. <margin>* power</margin> And if the acting part is the sensory, then the daemon is the rational part. But if one lives according to the rational part, the daemon is that which stands over this beginning, yielding to the one who works. It is rightly said, then, that we shall choose. For we choose the one who lies above us according to our life. Why does it not lead itself? Or is it that one cannot lead the one who has finished living? But regarding the leading, it was while one lived; having ceased to live, one yields the activity to another, having died to that specific life of activity. The one part wishes to lead, and having prevailed, it lives itself, <margin>* to his own self</margin> having another daemon itself. If it should be weighed down by the strength of a worse character, that part pays the penalty. In this way, the evil person goes toward the worse, because the likeness of the acting part has weighed him down. In that life, he goes into the life of a beast. But if he was able to follow the daemon <margin>* to his own self</margin> who is the man above, he himself becomes upwardly focused, living that daemon’s life. And he is led by the better part of himself, being seated in that presidency. And after that, another, until the top. For the soul is many things, and all things, both the things above and the things below again, through every life. And each of us is an intelligible world. To those things below, we are joined...

# BOOK FOUR.

Through those things which belong to the higher, intelligible world, we reach that intelligible realm; we remain in the heights through that which is entirely intelligible within us. However, by the soul’s lowest part, we are bound to the world below—as if we were releasing an outflow <note>original: "apôrrhoian"</note> from the higher realm into the lower, or rather an activity <note>original: "energeian"</note>, while the higher part itself remains undiminished.

<sig>A</sig>

Is this activity of the soul, sent down to lower things, always in a body? Not at all. For if we turn ourselves toward the heights, that activity is turned upward along with us. What then shall we say of such an activity, or of this part of the World Soul? <sig>B</sig> When it is turned toward the higher, does it also turn away from here? Certainly, the World Soul does not fully descend to its lowest part; it did not "go out" or "come down" in a literal sense. Rather, while the Soul remains in its place, the body of the world is attached to it, as if the body were lit up and pervaded by its light. And because the world is placed in safety and is not disturbed, the Soul is likewise not troubled. <sig>C</sig> What then? Does the world perceive nothing? Plato says in the *Timaeus* <note>A famous dialogue by Plato describing the creation of the universe</note> that the world has no sight because it has no eyes, nor hearing because it has no ears, nor nostrils, nor a tongue. Does it then have a kind of inner awareness of the things within itself, such as we experience? Perhaps, since everything in the world remains in a constant state according to nature, there is a stillness regarding sensation, and no pleasure is felt. Thus, the vegetative <term>nature<note>original: "vegetale"; the basic life-force responsible for growth and nutrition</note></term> is present as if it were not present, and the sensory power is the same. However, we have spoken of the world elsewhere; for now, let this be said regarding the current doubt.

<column-break/>

Truly, we touch the intelligible world through the higher things that belong to it, and we remain in the sublime through that which is in us entirely intelligible. But through its final part, we are bound to the lower: as if sending down a certain outflow from itself to the lower, or rather its act, without itself being diminished in the least.

<sig>A</sig>

<margin>
IV
*The vegetative nature is eternal.*
*The World Soul rules the body and sound without focused effort.*
</margin>
But is the act of the soul that is sent down to lower things always in the body? Not at all. For if we are turned toward the heavenly things, that act is likewise <sig>B</sig> turned. What then shall we say of such an act or part of the World Soul? When it is turned toward higher things, is this part also turned away from here? Indeed, this Soul did not consent entirely to its lowest part, nor did it proceed or descend; but while it remains, the body of the world is joined to it, and as it were, it is approached and bathed in light. And since the world is placed in safety, and therefore is not disturbed, it rightly does not disturb the Soul. <sig>C</sig> What then? Does it feel nothing at all? The world indeed has no sight, says Timaeus, because it has no eyes; it has no hearing, and therefore no ears, nor nostrils, nor a tongue. Does it therefore have a certain shared feeling <note>original: "consensionem"; a sense of internal harmony or sympathy</note> perceiving what is in itself, such as we experience in ourselves? But perhaps, since all things in it always stay the same according to nature, there is a rest in it as far as sensing is concerned, nor is there pleasure within. Therefore, the vegetative power is present as if it were not, and the sensory power similarly. But concerning the world, it is discussed elsewhere; for the present, as far as the doubt reached, let it have been said.

<sig>D</sig> <margin>
V
*The soul, according to its changes, changes its daemon (guardian spirit), which holds the primary position over the power next in line.*
</margin>
Accordingly, if the soul chooses its <term>daemon<note>original: "dæmonem"; in Neoplatonism, this is not an evil spirit, but a guiding "genius" or higher self that oversees a person’s destiny</note></term> and its life there, are we in some way the masters of our future actions? Perhaps what is called an "election" there darkly indicates the soul's choice and <sig>D</sig> disposition <note>original: "proairesin"; the moral character or internal will</note> universally and everywhere. But if the soul’s choice is the master, and that part prevails which it has ready from the acts of its previous life, the body is no longer to be called the cause of any evil for the soul. <sig>E</sig> For if the character of the soul itself precedes the body by a certain prerogative, and it possesses what it chose, and (as Plato says) it does not change its guardian spirit, then it follows that it is not made good or evil here for the first time. Perhaps each is there in potential, but becomes so in actuality. What then should be said if a person with honest character happens upon a bad body? Or conversely, if one imbued with bad character should obtain a good body? Perhaps the things belonging to each soul can affect each body more or less; since other external fortunes <sig>F</sig> by no means override the total choice of the soul. When it is said that first the lots are drawn, then the examples of lives are proposed, and after these, fortunes follow—and again, that lives are chosen from the present options according to character—all these things, I say, grant authority rather to the souls as they assemble what is given according to their own character. <sig>G</sig> Therefore, this guardian spirit is not entirely from the outside, but is such that it is neither bound to us nor, on the other hand, strictly acting on its own. It becomes ours because it can be said to be of the soul or something belonging to the soul; yet it is not "ours" in the sense that we are these particular men living the lives we have under us. The matters treated in the *Timaeus* <note>original: "Timæo"</note> can serve as evidence for us; which indeed, if they are understood in this way...
