# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. BOOK III.

**A** A person is judged by their life. The soul, finally migrating from the body, becomes exactly that which it most fully practiced. Therefore, one must flee to the higher realms, lest we slide down into a merely sensible form <note>The world as perceived by the senses rather than the mind</note> by following after sensory images. We must also avoid being cast down into a vegetative life, enslaved to the lust for procreation and ensnared by the sweetness of physical flavors. Instead, we must rise with all our strength toward the intellectual realm, toward the Intellect <note>original: "intellectum"; the Divine Mind</note>, and toward God. Those who have preserved their human character are born again as humans. **B** However, those who lived by the senses alone return as brute animals. Among these, those who lived by the senses combined with a quickness to anger are reborn as wild beasts; the specific differences in their character determine the type of beast they become. Those who lived by the senses combined with lust and a desire for pleasure return as lascivious and gluttonous animals. But if they did not even live by the senses properly, but rather by a degeneration of the senses, they sprout again as plants. For in such people, only the vegetative power was active, and their whole care was to become trees. Furthermore, those who lived too much delighted by **C** musical melodies, but were not otherwise depraved, are reborn as musical animals <note>such as songbirds</note>. And those who ruled without reason become eagles, unless they were infected by some other vice. Those who, without wisdom, confidently handled lofty matters and frequently looked up to the sky, are changed into birds that always seek the heights in their flight. He who has achieved civic virtue <note>The practical virtues of a good citizen</note> returns as a human; but he who has not quite mastered civic virtue transforms into a social animal, such as a bee or something similar.

<margin>
III
Our Daemons: or is it something of the soul itself presiding, namely, the power to act <note>original: ποιῆσαι (poiesai)</note>? Or the soul by which we live? Therefore, according to the differences in our lives, there are different daemons within us.
</margin>

**D** Who then among these shall be called a "daemon" <note>A guiding spirit or guardian angel in the Platonic tradition</note>? And who is a God? Is it the one who is primarily active in these states? For that which is active leads each person, as if that part were the ruler. Is the daemon then the one who has been allotted to the living being? Perhaps not. Rather, it is that which is *above* the person: that which presides, as it were, in stillness. That which comes after it acts, and we are most truly that which acts. If we live and act as sensory beings, then Reason is our daemon. But if we live by reason, then our daemon is that which is higher than reason—**E** a presiding daemon that leaves the busywork to the other part. Thus it is rightly said in Plato: "You shall choose your daemon" <note>A reference to the Myth of Er in Plato’s *Republic*, where souls choose their next life and guardian spirit</note>. For we choose the presiding spirit over us according to the kind of life we choose. Why then does the daemon lead? Perhaps the daemon does not lead the person who has finished their life; but it could do so before, while the person was living. Once the life is finished, the daemon must concede the action to another, since the person has already laid down their active life. Here the soul wants to lead, and whatever it has mastered, it lives by that, having another daemon for itself. If the soul sinks down, with a worse character prevailing, it pays the penalty. In this way, the wicked person falls into a lower state, as that which acts in the person declines through a similarity of life into the life of a beast. But if the soul could obey its superior daemon, it would become superior, living that daemon's life and prescribing for itself a presiding power—namely, that more excellent part of itself by which it is led. **G** And beyond that, it might reach even another daemon, until it progresses to the Supreme. For the soul is many things—indeed, it is all things, both the higher and the lower, reaching through every grade of life. Truly, each one of us is an intellectual world <note>original: "cosmos noetos"</note>; by our lower parts we are joined to this world, but by

<column-break/>

If a person has gone out [from life], they become whatever part of themselves they made most prominent. Therefore, one must flee to the things above, so that we do not follow after sensible images and fall into the sensory life, nor follow the vegetative life through the desire for procreation and the greed for food. Instead, we must flee toward the intellectual, the Intellect, and God. Those who have kept their humanity are humans again. Those who lived by sense alone are animals. If they lived by sense combined with spirit <note>thumos; meaning anger or passion</note>, they become wild beasts; and the differences among them create the variety of such creatures. Those who lived with desire and the pleasure of the appetites become undisciplined and gluttonous animals. If they did not even live by the senses, but by a corruption of the senses, they become plants. For only this, or mostly this vegetative power, was active in them, and their practice was to become trees. Those who loved music but were pure in other things become songbirds. <margin>* others</margin> Irrational kings become eagles, unless some other vice is present. Stargazers who lacked wisdom, always lifting themselves toward the sky, turn into birds that fly high. He who practiced civic virtue is a human; he who shared less in civic virtue becomes a social animal, <margin>* especially, or * a bee</margin> such as a bee or similar creatures.

**W**ho then is the daemon here? Who is the God here? That which was active leads each person, and <margin>* he chose</margin> he chose his leader. Is this then the daemon that we have been allotted as living beings? No, it is the part prior to that. For the daemon stands over a person but does not act; it is the part after it that acts. And <margin>* we know</margin> we know the "seed" <note>the formative principle</note> or the sensory part, and the daemon is the rational part. But if we live according to the rational part, the daemon is that which stands above it, presiding and granting the active role to the worker. It is rightly said, therefore, that we shall choose; for we choose the one who is superior to us according to our life. Why then does the daemon lead? Either it is not possible to lead one who has finished living, but the daemon leads because the person lived; and once the life has ceased, the daemon yields the activity to another, as the person has died to their own active life. But the soul wants to lead, or having prevailed, it lives itself, having another daemon of its own. <margin>* by its own</margin> By the strength of a worse character, that person receives justice. In this way, the evil person goes toward the worse, because their likeness has sunk toward that which was active in them. If they lived a certain life, they go into the life of a beast. But if they were able to follow the daemon <margin>* the same</margin> in that same human, they become higher by living that daemon's life. And that toward which they are led is the better part of themselves, from which we were previously separated, and after that another daemon, until we reach the top. For the soul is many things, even all things: the things above and the things below, throughout all life. And each soul is an intellectual world. By the lower things, we are joined...

# BOOK FOUR.

<note>original: "LIBER QVARTVS"; This refers to the fourth treatise of the Third Ennead, titled "On Our Allotted Guardian Spirit."</note>

...attaining this, or those others, both above and in the intelligible world <note>The realm of pure thought and divine forms, existing beyond the physical world</note>. And we remain, in that other entirely intelligible human, above; but by the lowest part, we are shackled to what is below—as if providing an outflow from that higher realm to the lower, or rather an activity of it, while that higher part is not at all diminished.

**A** Indeed, regarding those superior things which belong to the intelligible world, we reach that world and remain on high through that part of us which is entirely intellectual. But through the lowest part of the soul, we are bound to the inferior: as if sending down a certain outflow from the higher to the lower—or rather, its activity—while the source itself is not at all diminished.

<column-break/>

**A** Those superior things indeed which belong to the intelligible world, we reach the intelligible world, and we remain on high through that which is in us entirely intelligible. But through that which is its lowest part, we are bound to the inferior: as if sending down a certain outflow from itself to the lower, or rather its activity, while it itself is not at all diminished.

<margin>
IV.
*The vegetative nature is everlasting. The soul of the world rules the external body without distraction.*
</margin>

**B** **BUT** is the activity of the soul sent down to lower things always in a body? Not at all. For if we turn toward the higher realms, that activity is turned upward along with us. What then shall we say of such an activity or part of the World Soul <note>The "Anima Mundi," the soul that animates the entire universe</note>? When it is turned toward higher things, does this part also turn away from here? Certainly, this soul does not entirely conform to its lowest part; it neither proceeded out nor descended. Instead, while that higher part remains still, the body of the world is attached to it, as if ignited or drenched in light. Because the world is situated in safety and is therefore not at all disturbed, it rightly follows that it does not disturb the soul. **C** What then? Does it feel nothing at all? The world has no sight, as the *Timaeus* <note>A famous dialogue by Plato concerning the creation of the physical world</note> says, because it has no eyes; it has no hearing, and therefore no ears, nor nostrils, nor a tongue. Does it then have a certain shared perception that senses things within itself, such as we experience in ourselves? Perhaps, since all things in it are always consistently in accordance with nature, there is a stillness in it regarding sensation, and no pleasure or pain is present. Thus, the vegetative part <note>The lowest level of soul responsible for growth and nutrition</note> is present as if it were not present, and the sensory part likewise. But concerning the world, we have spoken elsewhere; for now, let this be said as far as the current doubt is concerned.

<margin>
*The soul, according to its changes, changes its daemon (guardian spirit), which it possesses as its primary internal power; that is, it is able to preside over the soul’s next concern or power.*
</margin>

**D** **ACCORDINGLY**, if the soul chooses its daemon and its life in that higher realm, in what way are we masters of any further action? Perhaps what is called "election" or "choice" there obscurely indicates the disposition and affection of the soul universally and everywhere. But if the soul’s choice is the master, and that part of the soul prevails which it has made more ready through the acts of its former life, then it must no longer be said that the body is the cause of any evil for the soul. **E** For if the character of the soul itself precedes the body by a certain prerogative, and it possesses what it has chosen, and does not change its daemon (as Plato says), then surely this daemon is neither good nor bad by chance. Perhaps each is a daemon in potential, but becomes so in actuality. What then should be said if a person with honest character falls into an evil body? Or conversely, if someone imbued with evil character should eventually obtain a good body? **F** Perhaps the things belonging to either soul can affect either body to a greater or lesser degree, since other external fortunes do not entirely overpower the whole of one’s choice. But when it is said that first the "lots" are drawn, then the "examples of lives" are proposed, and after these "fortunes" follow; and again, that lives are chosen from the available options according to character—all these things, I say, grant authority rather to the souls to arrange what is given according to their own character. **G** Therefore, this daemon is not entirely external, but is such that it is neither bound to us, nor again is it operating as our own characteristic function. It is ours because it can be called "something of the soul," yet it is not ours insofar as we are particular men leading a particular life under it. If these things are understood in this way, the things in the *Timaeus* can serve as testimony for us...

...judged to be a human. Finally, when the soul departs from the body, it becomes that very thing which it allowed to dominate it. Therefore, we must flee toward the higher realms, lest we fall into the world of mere sense-perception by following sensible images; nor should we be cast down into the vegetal life <note>The most basic level of existence, focused only on growth and nutrition</note>, enslaved by the lust for procreation and entangled by the sweetness of flavors. Instead, we must rise with all our strength toward the intellectual, toward the Mind, and toward God. Whoever, then, has preserved their human character is born again as a human. But whoever
->B<-
has lived by sense alone returns as a brute animal. If they lived by sense alongside a tendency toward anger, they emerge as wild beasts; the specific differences in their character produce the differences in the species. Those who lived by sense combined with the desire for pleasure and appetite return as undisciplined and gluttonous animals. However, if they did not even live by the senses in a human way, but lived with a dulling of the senses, they sprout again as plants. For in these people, the vegetal power alone—or at least primarily—was active, and their only care was to become like trees. Furthermore, those who lived too much enchanted by musical
->C<-
melodies, but were not otherwise depraved, are reborn as musical animals <note>original: "animalia musica"; likely referring to songbirds</note>. And those who ruled as kings without reason become eagles, unless they were infected by some other vice. Those who, without wisdom, dealt with lofty matters with too much confidence—often looking up at the sky—are changed into birds that always seek the heights in their flight. He who achieved civic virtue <note>The practical virtues of a good citizen, like justice and moderation</note> returns as a human. But he who did not quite attain civic virtue is transformed into a social animal, such as a bee or similar creatures.

<margin>
777
Our guardian spirits <note>original: "Dæmones"</note> are a certain presiding part of the soul itself—namely, the power of the soul by which we live. Therefore, according to the differences in our lives, different guardian spirits are within us.

->D<-
**WHO**, then, among these shall be called a guardian spirit? And who is a God? For who is it that acts primarily in these cases? Whatever part of us is active leads each person, since it is the presiding principle there. Is this, then, the guardian spirit which has been allotted to the living being? Perhaps not. Rather, it is that which is *above* the active part. For that which is above presides as if at rest; while that which is below it acts. We ourselves are primarily that which acts. And if we act and live as sensual beings, then Reason is our guardian spirit. But if we live by Reason,
->E<-
the guardian spirit is that which is superior to Reason—a presiding spirit that grants the active duty to another part. Thus, it is rightly said in Plato: *You shall choose your guardian spirit.* <note>A reference to the Myth of Er in Plato's "Republic", where souls choose their next life and its accompanying spirit.</note> For we choose our overseer according to our kind of life. Why then does the spirit lead us? Perhaps it is not permitted for the spirit to lead one who has finished their life; but it could do so before, while the person lived. Once life is finished, it is necessary to yield the action to another, as one who has already laid down their active life. Here, then, the part that remains wants to lead, and whatever has prevailed lives by itself, having another
->F<-
guardian spirit of its own. But if the soul grows heavy—that is, when a worse character weighs it down—it pays the penalty. In this way, the wicked man falls into a worse state; that which is active in the human declines into the life of a beast through a likeness of lifestyle. But if the soul could obey its superior guardian spirit, it would become superior, living the life of that spirit and setting its own presiding principle as the most excellent part of itself, by which it is led—and beyond that spirit, yet another, until it reaches the highest point. For the soul is many things—indeed, it is all things,
->G<-
both the higher things and the lower things, down to every level of life. Indeed, each one of us is an intellectual world <note>original: "intelligibilis mundus"; a microcosm of the divine realm of forms</note>; through our lower parts, we are joined to this physical world, but through...

...was a human when they departed, they become whatever dominated them. For this reason, one must flee to the heights, so that we do not follow the images of the senses into the world of perception, nor follow the urge for procreation and the gluttony of food into the vegetal state. Instead, we must flee to the intellectual, to the Mind, and to God. Those who have kept the human standard are humans again. Those who lived by sense alone are animals. If they lived by sense accompanied by spirit <note>original: "θυμοῦ" (thymos); meaning anger or spiritedness</note>, they become wild beasts; the difference among these behaviors creates the variety of such animals. Those who lived with desire and pleasure in accordance with their appetites become undisciplined and gluttonous animals. But if they did not even live with the senses, but with a corruption of the senses alongside those desires, they become plants. For only the vegetal power, or primarily that, was active, and their practice was to become trees. Those who loved music but were pure in other respects become songbirds. <margin>* irrationally</margin> Irrational kings become eagles, unless some other vice was present. Those who studied the heavens <note>original: "μετεωρολόγους" (meteorologos); those who study things above, like stars</note> without wisdom, always lifting themselves toward the sky, are changed into birds that are lofty in their flight. He who practiced civic virtue is a human. But he who shared less in civic virtue <margin>* especially</margin> becomes an *especially* social animal, or something of that kind.

**WHO** then is the guardian spirit <note>original: "δαίμων" (daemon)</note> even here? Who is a god, even here? That which was active leads each person, since it was the presiding part. Was this, then, the guardian spirit which was allotted to the living person, or not? No, it is the part *before* it. For that which presides is the part that does not act; but that which follows it is the part that acts. <margin>* we know</margin> And if the active part is the sensual, then the guardian spirit is the rational. But if one lives according to the rational, the guardian spirit is that which is above it. It stands over the living person, while allowing the active part to work. Thus it is rightly said that we shall choose. For we choose that which is superior according to our life. Why then does the spirit lead? Perhaps it is not the case that it leads the one who has lived, but that it led while they were living. When one has ceased to live, one must yield the activity to another, having died to one's own active life. That which one did not wish to lead, and which prevailed, now lives itself, having its own guardian spirit. If the soul is weighed down by a life of a worse character, it has that as its penalty. In this way, the evil man goes toward the worse, because his active part has made him like that. If he lived a beastly life, he goes to that life. But if he could follow the guardian spirit <margin>eternity</margin> *of the man above*, he becomes that which is above, living that life. And that toward which he is led is the better part of him, if it was the presiding part. And after that, another, until the heights. For the soul is many things, even all things—both those above and those below—until every stage of life. And each of us is an intellectual world. To the lower things, we join...

# BOOK FOUR. 285

<note>original Greek: "πίοντες τῷδε..."</note> ...we reach toward the higher things belonging to the intelligible world, and we remain in that sublime state through what is entirely intelligible within us. However, through the lowest part of the soul, we are bound to the inferior world; it is as if we send out a certain outflow from the higher to the lower, or rather an activity, though the higher part itself is not diminished.

Is this activity of the soul, which is sent down to lower things, always in a body? Not at all. For if we turn back toward the higher realms, that activity is turned back along with us. What then shall we say of such an activity, or this part of the world-soul? When it turns toward the higher, does it also turn away from here? Certainly, this soul does not entirely descend or go forth to its lowest part; rather, while the soul remains still, the body of the world is attached to it, as if it were approaching and being bathed in light. And since the world is placed in safety and is not disturbed, the soul, in turn, is not troubled. What then? Does it perceive nothing at all?

<note>original Greek: "ὅρασιν οὐκ ἔχει..."</note> The world has no sight, as Timaeus <note>referring to Plato's dialogue, the *Timaeus*</note> says, because it has no eyes; it has no hearing, and therefore no ears, nor nostrils, nor a tongue. Does it then have a certain shared perception of what is within itself, such as we experience in ourselves? Perhaps, since everything within it always remains the same according to nature, there is a stillness in it regarding sensation, and no pleasure is present. Thus, the vegetal power is present as if it were not, and the sensory power likewise. But concerning the world, we have spoken elsewhere; for now, regarding the doubt raised, let this suffice.

But if the soul chooses its dæmon <term>dæmon: in Neoplatonism, a "spirit guide" representing the level of consciousness just above the one currently active in the individual</term> and its life there <note>in the realm of souls before birth</note>, how are we masters of our actions? Perhaps what is called "choice" there suggests the overall disposition and character of the soul everywhere. If the soul's choice is sovereign, and that part of it dominates which it has made more ready by the acts of its previous life, then the body is no longer the cause of evil for the soul.

For if the character of the soul itself precedes the body by a certain prerogative, and it possesses what it chose, and it does not change its dæmon (as Plato says), then it is certainly not the body that makes a person good or evil.

Perhaps each person is good or evil in potential, and becomes so in actuality. What then should we say if someone with good character falls into a "bad" body? Or conversely, someone imbued with bad character happens upon a "good" body? Perhaps the conditions belonging to each can affect each body to a greater or lesser degree; for external fortunes do not entirely force the soul's fundamental choice <term>proairesis: the moral character or "will" that defines an individual's choices</term>. When it is said that "lots" <note>The "Lot of Destiny" from the Myth of Er in Plato's Republic</note> come first, then examples of lives are proposed, and then fortunes follow, and that lives are chosen from the present options according to character—all these things attribute authority to the souls, which arrange what is given to them according to their own characters.

Therefore, this dæmon is not entirely outside of us, but is positioned as if it were neither bound to us nor, on the other hand, acting strictly on its own. It becomes "ours" because something of the soul can be said to belong to the dæmon, yet it is not "ours" in the sense that we are specifically these humans who have a certain life under us, as the matters discussed in the *Timaeus* can testify; which indeed, if they are understood in this way...

<column-break/>

A But as for the higher things which belong to the intelligible world <term>intelligible world: the divine realm of pure forms and intellect, beyond the physical world</term>, we reach the intelligible world and remain in the sublime through that which is entirely intelligible within us. Through that which is its lowest part, however, we are bound to the inferior; as if sending down a certain "outflow" from itself to the lower, or rather an activity of it, while the soul itself is in no way diminished.

<margin>IIII. The vegetal nature is eternal. The World Soul governs the body without focused attention and feels through it.</margin>

B BUT is the activity of the soul, sent down to lower things, always in a body? By no means. For if we are turned back toward the higher, that activity is turned back at the same time. What then shall we say of such an activity or part of the World Soul? When it is turned toward higher things, is this part also turned away from here? Truly, this soul does not consent entirely to its lowest part, nor did it proceed or descend: but while that soul remains, the body of the world is joined to it, and as it were, approaches it, and is flooded with light. And since the world is placed in safety, and therefore is not disturbed, it rightfully does not disturb the soul. What then? Does it feel nothing at all?

Does it therefore have a shared perception, in some manner, of the things that are within itself, such as we experience in ourselves? But perhaps, since all things in it always stay the same according to nature, there is a stillness in it regarding sensation, and no pleasure is present. Therefore, the vegetal part is present as if it were not, and the sensory part likewise. But concerning the world, we have spoken elsewhere: for the present, as far as the doubt touched upon it, let this be said.

<margin>V. The Soul, according to its changes, changes its dæmon, which it has as its chief internal guide, that is, presiding over the nearest power or business.</margin>

Perhaps what is there called "choice" dimly indicates the choice and affection of the soul commonly and everywhere. But if the soul’s choice is the master, and that part prevails which it has more ready from the acts of its former life, then the body is no longer to be called the cause of any evil for the soul.

E For if the very habit of the soul precedes the body by a certain prerogative, and it has that which it chose, and it does not change its dæmon (as Plato says), then surely it does not become good or evil here for the first time.

F Perhaps each is such by a certain potential, and becomes so in act. What then is to be said, if one who has honest habits should fall into an evil body? And conversely, one imbued with bad habits should sometimes obtain a good body? Perhaps the things which belong to each can affect each body more or less, this way or that: since even other external fortunes by no means overpower the entire choice. When, however, it is said that first the "lots" appear, then the examples of lives are proposed, and after these, fortunes follow: and again, that lives are chosen from the present and proposed options according to character: all these things, I say, attribute authority rather to the souls, which compose what is given to them according to their own habits.

G Therefore, this dæmon is not entirely outside us, but so behaves as if it were neither bound to us, nor again properly acting on its own: it becomes ours, since something of the soul may be said of it; yet it is not ours, in the sense that we are such-and-such men having such a life under us. # PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III

<margin>
**VI**
The living soul possesses the intelligence of God as its guardian spirit <term>daemon: a guiding spirit or higher principle of the soul, not an evil "demon"</term>; the spirit does not force the soul. Likewise, it can change as the soul changes. Also concerning the judgment of souls. Also how they return to the stars, and in turn fall back into fate, in which they do not only suffer, but also perform actions.

...no dissonance will follow; but if the guardian spirit is understood in any other way, a certain dissonance results. Again, where he says that the spirit is the "fulfiller of those things which one has chosen," <note>This refers to Plato’s *Republic*, where the soul chooses its lot before birth.</note> this also agrees: for presiding over us, it does not allow us to slip too far down into what is worse; but it only activates that which is directly below it, neither what is above it nor what is equal to it: for it cannot become anything other than the reason for which it exists.

**W**HO, then, is the upright man, and what does he do? Perhaps the upright man is he in whom the better part is active; otherwise, he would not be upright if he did not have a guardian spirit cooperating with him. For the Intellect acts in him; therefore, either the guardian spirit is the Intellect itself, or it acts according to the spirit, and the spirit is a god to him. Is it then even above the Intellect? If indeed that which is above the Intellect exists as his guardian spirit. But why does one not enjoy this gift immediately from the beginning? Perhaps because of the violent disturbance brought about by the very process of generation <term>generation: the process of being born into a physical body</term>. Yet, even before the use of reason, a certain internal movement is present, seeking those things which are suitable to itself. Does it then entirely correct and direct one toward the best? Perhaps not entirely; for if the soul is so affected that it exists as such among such things, it holds this life, this choice, and this purpose. Furthermore, this guardian spirit of which we speak is said to lead the soul to the lower regions; it does not remain entirely the same, unless the soul chooses the same things again. But how does it behave before that? It is said to bring the soul to judgment, and to arrive after the end of birth into the same form it once held before birth. Then, as if from another beginning, during the middle span of time that flows between the preceding and following birth, the spirit hangs over the souls paying their penalties; and perhaps life for them then is not so much "living" as it is judgment and punishment. 

What then? When souls of beasts enter bodies, is there something less than a guardian spirit present? Perhaps a "bad" spirit, or one that is foolish and idle. But for souls that have progressed to higher things, what kind of divinity is present? Certainly, from their number, some still lead a life in the sensible world <term>sensible world: the physical world we perceive with our senses</term>, while others are already outside the world. And of those in the sensible world, some are near the Sun, or any other of the planets, while others are in the firmament <note>the sphere of the fixed stars</note>: each, evidently, according to how they directed their actions by reason here on earth. For we must believe that within our soul there is not only an "intelligible world," but also a certain disposition conforming to the Soul of the World itself. Since the World-Soul is distributed into the fixed sphere and the wandering spheres <note>the planets</note> according to different powers, it follows that powers conformable to those are also within us, and that proper actions emanate from each of these powers. Then, truly, the souls that depart from here to go there reach the star most suitable to the character and power they most used in their acting and living, consistent with such a god and guardian spirit: where the soul will either use this same power, or something presiding over this power. But we must consider which is the better path. For souls that have traveled outside the sensible world, we must believe they have transcended the nature of the guardian spirit, every fate of birth, and every necessity of this world. Furthermore, such a soul would have drawn back with itself that essence which is desirous of procreating: which, if anyone should say is that essence which Timaeus <note>Referencing Plato's *Timaeus* regarding the soul being "divided around bodies."</note> says becomes divided...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...straightly pouring out to the invincible [soul], if there is any dissonance, if the guardian spirit is taken otherwise; but as for the fulfillment of what one chose, this <margin>* itself</margin> also agrees. For if it were much lower, it would have been situated above it to go toward the worse; but it activates only that which is under it, and even if it is above it, it does not go toward the equal. For it cannot become anything else than what it is.

<margin>B</margin> WHAT then is the serious man, or <margin>* the better [one].</margin> he who acts by the better part? He would not be serious unless he had the guardian spirit cooperating with him. For the Intellect acts in this man. Either, then, the guardian spirit is the Intellect itself, or it is according to the spirit, and the spirit is a god to him. Is it then also above the Intellect? If that which is above the Intellect is a spirit to him. Why then not from the beginning? Either because of the turmoil from the birth. But nevertheless, even before reason, there is either a movement or an internal longing for its own <margin>C</margin> things. Does it then altogether set things right, or altogether? If the soul is in such a state as to be among such things, it has this life and this choice. However, this spirit of which we speak is said to lead to Hades; it no longer remains the same, unless it chooses the same things again. But how was it before? To lead to the judgment, to come into the same form <margin>D</margin> after the end of birth which it had before birth. But for those above, or of the things above, some are in the sensible world, others outside. Those in the sensible world are either with the Sun or in another of the wandering stars; those in the <margin>E</margin> fixed sphere, each <margin>* universally well-acting</margin> as it acted well universally in these things. For one must think there is a world in our soul, not only an intelligible one, but also a disposition of the soul similar to the world. For that [world-soul] being distributed into the fixed sphere and the wandering ones according to different powers, it is likely that powers similar to these are also in us, and that there is an activity from each. And for those <margin>F</margin> set free, they go there to the star consistent with the character and power that acted and lived; and they will use such a god, or guardian spirit, or this very thing, or that which is above this power. But the better thing must be considered. For those that have come to be outside, they have transcended the spirit-like nature and all fate of birth. And generally, they are not in the visible world while they are there. But the procreative <margin>G</margin> essence having been drawn back in her, which if one were to say this is the partible essence which comes to be around bodies, * multiply...

We must also consider that the power flowing from the universe contributes to the same thing, existing here in the same way. As the mundane revolution carries it around like a wind, the soul sits or even walks in the ship; many and various sights occur, as well as transformations and accidents. For not everyone is tossed, or wills, or acts in the same way in the same circumstances. Therefore, different things happen to different people, either from the same or from different events occurring, or the same things happen to others, even though the events that occur are different. For such a thing is Fate, and so it acts.

# A COMMENTARY.

-> SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK. <-

> Every power, whether of knowing or of generating, rejects the ugly and strives toward the beautiful; since every power proceeds from and is moved by the primary beauty.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring floral patterns and scrollwork, used to begin the commentary.</image-desc>

I BELIEVE indeed, Magnanimous Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, Ficino's patron</note>, that you will not now require a long dispute about love from your Marsilio: both because we have discussed much about this in the *Symposium* <note>Ficino's own work, *De Amore*, written as a commentary on Plato's Symposium</note>, and especially since you have discovered many things about love through divine inspiration and have sung them in elegant poems. Therefore, I shall follow the highest peaks of the matter. Every power of the soul, whether rational or natural, strives with perpetual love to reach and generate the beautiful, because such power proceeds from Beauty itself; and therefore it retains within itself the indwelling form of beauty, and a perpetual instinct toward it as if toward the end-goal of love. Whoever is ignorant of this cause cannot express the natures of loves and the passions of lovers. Truly, the divine intellect is the *first form, entirely pure and all-forming*. The animal intellect is indeed a second form, but similarly all-forming. Nature is a third form, likewise all-forming; led by its own principles, it looks constantly toward covering the formlessness of matter with forms, wonderfully adorning it. If anything deformed happens within nature, it occurs contrary to the primary intention of God and nature, just as a deformity in a craft occurs contrary to every intention of the art. Therefore, just as the natural power does, so too the rational power everywhere derives its origin from the primary beauty; it rejects the ugly as something dissonant, but adopts the beautiful with all its might as something consonant, striving to generate a beautiful form and to preserve its own nature perpetually within it. But the rational power brings forth in the...

## The dual soul of the world. Two Venuses. Two Loves: which are not passions, but certain modes of existence.

II. Since we see that intelligence in us is perfected only insofar as the act of understanding and the thing to be understood are separated from matter and the conditions of matter, we may conclude that the first Intellect itself is entirely alien to matter. Furthermore, the intellectual soul, which is born directly from that Intellect and is therefore supremely intellectual, cannot join with matter to form a single combined substance. For this soul is both a certain intellect and, simply put, a soul. However, the "life" which is then born from this—a kind of soul and nature in its simplest form—can indeed merge into one with matter. 

Therefore, we call that first intellectual soul in the world the **First Venus**; but the life that is subsequently infused into the world from there, we call the **Second Venus**. In both, a perpetual love thrives, incited by the beauty of the divine mind: in the first, to generate a similar beauty within itself; in the second, to express beauty in matter according to its strength. 

Plotinus believes, following the mind of Plato, that while the intellectual soul of the world acts inwardly toward God by understanding Him and wishing to conceive Him, it produces within itself not a mere imaginary thing, but something natural and subsisting. <note>original: "non imaginarium quiddam, sed naturale aliquid & subsistens"</note> In this, I believe he imitates the mystery of the Christian Trinity. He considers that just as shining and heating are two different things in a fire, but are ultimately one in the sun, so knowing and loving are different in the rational power, but exist as a single act in the intellectual substance. 

Since this kind of act in the soul of the world is most internal, directed toward the most internal reality, and most effective, it produces within itself an offspring consistent with this act. Because this offspring is born from intelligence, it is something intelligible; because it proceeds from love, it is something beloved—indeed, it is love itself subsisting, produced from a certain act of loving. For there, to exist and to act are exactly the same thing. Surely, by acting inwardly in this way, a certain "existence" is produced within; in this produced thing, the essence is the same as that of the producer, differing only in this: that in the one it is propagating, and in the other it is propagated from there. It differs further by a certain relationship: for this "loving existence" belongs both to the lover and the beloved. It differs also because in the propagating existence, the vision of beauty is primary, while in the propagated existence, it is the pleasure taken in that beauty.

### Confirmation of the previous points.

III. If a pregnant woman often affects the fetus with a certain natural quality because of the wonderful intensity of her imagination and feelings—simply because the fetus is connected to the mother—and if, likewise, the reason of the soul expresses sudden qualities in its own body, is it any wonder that something "substantial" is born in the soul itself from a similar intensity? This is especially true in the intellectual soul, where action, intensity, and affection are not accidental or fleeting, but entirely natural and firm. The one who sees, rejoices, and desires is most effective, and his object is most powerful and flows in potently. 

These points are confirmed by the fact that if everywhere "accidental" things <note>Accidents in philosophy are non-essential properties, like the color of a shirt versus the shirt itself.</note> are reduced to certain "substantial" things that correspond to them in proportion, then it is necessary that those loves which are merely fleeting passions must be traced back to "substantial" loves. 

After this, you will note again that it is necessary for the world to have two souls: one somewhat separate, presiding over the body like an artisan; the other joined to it, which is within the body from that source, like a form. It must have a separate soul because such a soul shines out from the nearby Intellect, and because an artisan who is "mixed" into his work cannot command his craft with absolute power. Furthermore, a soul must be joined within the world, both because the first soul is fertile enough to generate this second self, and because it is necessary for the world to be a most perfect composite. Thus, it is necessary to have a most perfect form for its matter—that is, a living and sensing form. 

However, a single thing is not made in the world from the intellectual soul and matter properly speaking (as Plotinus wishes), because the intelligence, through its action and affection, tends toward the opposite of matter. Just so, he thinks a single thing is not formed in us; for in us, the intellectual soul does not share in the passions proper to the body, nor does the body share with such a soul in the actions properly belonging to it. We may say, however, that the intellectual soul is "mundane" in the world and "human" in us; from it and the animal nature, a single thing is created, because from its influence and matter, one sensing animal is made, into which that soul always inspires life, which would perish without its continuous spirit. 

Remember that these twin souls in the world are the twin Venuses, accompanied by twin similar Loves. Remember also that love in this fertile soul of the world not only generates all beauty in the world’s matter through its reproductive power, but also, through its effective power of imagination, it looks up to the divine form and calls both the world and all things in the world toward that same form as much as possible.

## Two loves naturally implanted in every soul are like two daemons.

IIII. He <note>Plotinus</note> briefly touches upon those loves which are incited in us daily like new movements of the soul by things brought from the outside; but he pursues more diligently the "substantial loves"—that is, the essential and perpetual instincts toward beauty naturally implanted in the soul. These draw us toward beauty continually, even if you do not choose it or notice it. One of these is naturally inserted into the power of knowing, and the other into the power of generating. 

And because it leads the soul like a prefect and rules it in the manner of providence, it is called a <term>daemon: a guiding spirit or guardian, not to be confused with a malevolent demon</term>, although the more excellent love is called a god. It is said that these generate souls—not daily, but from the beginning—when, according to its nature (partly handed down from eternity and partly contracted by the choice of a life), the soul conceives such instincts that will reign throughout the age. 

By the secret nod of these instincts, many more affections and concepts are aroused in us daily, which are not provided solely by external sights, nor by the present state of the body, nor by new deliberation. Truly, a certain perpetual tenor of life, directed mostly toward one thing—especially regarding the type of life, the sciences, the arts, and the natural faculties proper to each person—is ruled by such a "daemon," while it is guided in the meantime by an external daemon that is suitable to it. All rational souls also harmonize with the loves of the world-soul through their own similar loves, insofar as they are sisters of the world-soul. They and their loves depend upon the soul of the world and its love...

->On Daemons <note>Latin: *De Dæmonibus*. In this context, daemons are intermediate spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note><-

We have sufficiently shown in our *Theology* that it is necessary for daemons to exist as intermediaries between the stars and humans, so that every sphere above us, being far more excellent and ample than our own, might have rational inhabitants conforming to the nature of their sphere, just as our sphere has. For **Apuleius** also confirms that there are certain fiery animals by citing this testimony of **Aristotle**: that in burning furnaces, certain unique animals have been seen to fly with small wings, which spend their entire lives in the fire; they arise with it and are extinguished along with it. Indeed, that which first receives life from the life-giving substance itself (that is, the soul) is fire alone. For fire is the element closest to the soul among bodies, since it is the most excellent, most effective, and most mobile. From this it follows that while heat fosters them, individual things live; when it does not foster them, they do not live. Secondly, the air closest to fire seems to receive life through the fire, and serves as fuel for the heat; through these two, the subtle water is then closer to the air; through this, similarly, is the subtle earth. Through these four gathered together, a body is composed and becomes solid—made not just of vapors, but of thicker materials. It is possible, however, everywhere to resolve what is prior and simpler from the subsequent and composite. There are, therefore, five kinds of rational animals: The first are those whose bodies are made of fire alone. If they are of visible fire, they are those whom the ancients called gods; if of invisible fire, **Orpheus** calls them fiery or celestial daemons, who hold the place of stars in the planetary circles under a leading planet. For it is not fitting to descend immediately from the innumerable animals in the firmament to the single one below. The second are those whose bodies are a perfect mixture of fire and air; these he calls etheric or aerial daemons. There are also third animals in which fire and air are combined with a certain subtle water, which he now calls aqueous daemons; these, when they become a little denser, can sometimes be seen. Nor are the fourth lacking, which add subtle earth to the three already mentioned, like a certain vapor of the earth. These are called terrestrial daemons by **Orpheus**; these, when condensed a little further, can even be touched. He also calls these subterranean, whenever they enter the caverns of the earth. The fifth are the bodies of humans, who are like weak daemons, in whom, besides that daemonic mixture of the four subtle elements which we are as daemons—which is the <term>spirit</term> <note>Ficino refers to the "spiritus," a subtle substance in Renaissance medicine that bridges the gap between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</note> within us, and which first lives and feels—a mixture of more solid things is added. That the spirit first lives and feels is evident from the fact that once the spirit is withdrawn from the limbs, sensation and motion immediately desert the limbs, and therefore so does life. Since that which is received first and is more akin is held more firmly, it seems probable that souls of this kind shed the later bodies gradually, while the prior ones are meanwhile reserved longer. Thus, those who were in a solid body are afterwards in a thin one for a longer time, in which they were equally present before, and in which they felt most strongly; this thin body easily yields to the connecting soul because of their kinship. The more sublime and simple a body is, the more slowly it seems to be abandoned by the soul; the celestial body, indeed, is never abandoned. For in every genus, that which first becomes a participant is always a participant. And rightly so: eternal life, where it has once naturally animated an eternal body by its very being, never ceases to animate it. It is granted only to the souls of humans and lower daemons to change their decaying bodies, because they are composed of clashing elements and are therefore dissolvable, and also because they are distracted from beatitude <note>Supreme blessedness or happiness.</note> on account of such a body, place, and service. Moreover, it is a crime for rational souls, which are naturally established for absolute contemplation, to be deprived of it for too long. Therefore, when they reach the end, they live for many ages in an etheric and celestial body. For that which comes from the intention of the species, and especially from their principle, is the most abundant and the most long-lasting. It is likely that celestial and etheric daemons are both eternal and free from <term>perturbation</term> <note>Violent mental agitation or passions.</note> because of the simplicity of their nature and the purity of their location. The aqueous and terrestrial ones, however, are indeed long-lived but not indissoluble; they also have disturbances of the soul much like those we have. For proximity of region and the nature of habits brings about similarity. From the first two types, nothing ever flows out; therefore, they have no need of nourishment, but are delighted only by songs, patterns, and lights; they are worshipped and thus reconciled to us, especially at those times when those stars which they follow are dominant. Since something flows out from the next two, it must be restored; but in those where there is nothing earthly, scent and the exhalation of spices, flowers, and liquids are sufficient and reconcile them. The last daemons need thicker odors and vapors, such as are sent forth from blood and flesh, especially when cooked and consumed by us. Therefore, if you believe **Porphyry**, you will say that these spirits led us to devour animals so that they might draw and suck from our very vitals the often-digested nourishment from animals that is suitable to them. Moreover, there is implanted in them a certain power of attracting and fleeing, such as exists in the limbs of animals and the roots of plants. We allure them to us by such a smell; whence, as **Porphyry** says, men given over to the belly become vessels for impure daemons. For although daemons, if they need any nourishment, can supply it to themselves everywhere without our help (as **Iamblichus** says), it is nevertheless probable that certain allurements can be offered to them by man, and that incontinent daemons mingle with incontinent men. Truly, the proud are agitated by the higher daemons. For **Porphyry** says that pride is primary in them, so much so that they desire nothing more vehemently than to be thought by us to be the highest gods and to be worshipped above all others; and their prince especially strives for this, so that he may be held as the first god of all. They incite us to the pleasures of this body, in which they themselves take pleasure within us in almost the same way. They provoke us to contentions and battles, by which they themselves also sometimes conflict with one another, disturbing the air with their conflict, and they rejoice in constant lying. We, however, cannot resist them except insofar as we diligently expose our minds to the inspiration of the higher daemons, live soberly and chastely, and humbly commend ourselves to God. For by purity, sanctity, and piety alone is the human race defended from the powerful incursion of evil daemons. Hence **Democritus** used to pray that he might encounter good daemons; as one who, as **Plutarch** says, thought many daemons were evil; indeed, he calls them all "images" <note>Original: *Idola*.</note> large in the air, emitting voices among themselves, long-lived and difficult to dissolve. **Iamblichus** asserts that many daemons are evil and deceive men under the pretext of being good; but they suddenly flee the presence of good divine powers, and thus a legitimate, religious person cannot be deceived. These things are from the Egyptians and Chaldeans. Accordingly, **Plotinus** says that daemonic souls exist as more prone to bodies for the reason that a certain "intelligible matter" reigns in them. This is not only a nature capable of being formed (for this is in the higher ones too), but an intimate disposition of essence, in which neither identity...

<meta>Catchword: OF PLOTINUS</meta>

...surpasses otherness <term>alteritas: a Platonic term for the principle of difference or diversity</term>, nor does rest surpass motion, nor does the common nature surpass the particular, nor does the faculty of acting surpass the power of being acted upon. It is through this very arrangement that such an essence seems accommodated both to the fleeting body and to the disturbances of the soul. For this reason, as **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who emphasized theurgy and the hierarchy of spirits.</note> also asserts, daemons do not possess providence in a general sense as the Gods do, but rather individually, assigned to their own specific actions and provinces.

### On the origin of daemons.

**VI** As for what **Plotinus** says in the sixth chapter—that daemons are generated from the soul as a whole—and what **Porphyry** says in his book *On Abstinence*—that daemons sprout from the whole soul—you should not understand this to mean that the very substances of the souls within daemons are created from the World Soul. Rather, take "the whole soul" here to mean that "mixing bowl," <note>original: "pateram." A reference to the mixing bowl in Plato's *Timaeus* where the Creator mixed the soul of the universe and individual souls.</note> or goddess, and the common Idea from which **Timaeus** asserts that, besides the World Soul, the souls of the spheres were produced separately, and again the souls of daemons or humans. For **Proclus** also says in his commentary on the *Alcibiades* that daemons are generated by the life-giving goddess, from whom souls are also generated. 

Plotinus also maintains that from the World Soul itself, and from any rational soul, a certain irrational soul of its own emanates, which he names a "daemon." Although such daemons follow their own souls, they are nevertheless produced by them under a certain common influence of the World Soul; for it is chiefly within the providence of the World Soul that they serve nature itself, and the whole of nature, to complete the arrangement of the universe. Generally, whatever kind of daemons they may be, they are said to depend on the World Soul because the World Soul itself binds their souls to their bodies through vital powers infused into matter, acting as a kind of bait. 

Among these, he places the "intelligible gods"—that is, the Ideas and the intellectual souls of the heavens. Likewise, he mentions "sensible gods," namely the stars. After these come the daemons, who are invisible, whether they are in heaven or below heaven; although he properly applies the name "daemon" to those who are below the moon. We have described the bodies of daemons in the preceding sections with a somewhat freer reasoning, by which we did not depart far from most of the Platonists. However, we can perhaps say, by a more physical reasoning, that the bodies of sub-lunary daemons are mostly composite. For the elements are mixed together everywhere into a single globe; therefore, there must necessarily be fire in them. For through fire, life and motion flourish. There will also be air as fuel for the fire; yet not air alone with fire alone, lest they suddenly dissolve. Let there also be thin water, and not without subtle earth; otherwise, it will have very little stability under the fire. 

Indeed, the spiritual bodies of daemons, just like our own spirit, must be very well-tempered <note>In the medical sense of "balanced" or "proportioned."</note> so that they may be vessels for that noble life. It is necessary, therefore, for the tyrannical greed of fire to be so tamed within them that the rapacity of one tyrant is restrained by the other three in number, and by a greater quantity of them. However, there cannot be much earth there, nor even a great deal of water. Let there be, then, as much air as possible; in the second place, the thinnest moisture of water; in the third, fire, but of a very rare sort, lest it be consuming; and let the subtlest earth hold the fourth place. And although almost all daemons are well-tempered, some are the most tempered of all; in others, however, this or that element excels slightly more. Their complexions <note>The physical and humoral makeup of a being.</note> will therefore be roughly five, just like our own: namely, the tempered one, and the four that are not as tempered. These are indeed subject to similar stars and preside over humans of the same complexion by a certain natural instinct.

### On subsisting love, and on the eternal intelligence within us.

**VII** In the seventh chapter, where he says, "Reason therefore..." and so on: understand "Reason" to mean the seminal power flowing from the animal intellect into the soul, like a father into a mother, in which he begets love—a mixture born both from his own abundance and from a certain neediness of the soul. Likewise, he posits that love is perpetual: both in the animal intellect for the purpose of contemplating intelligible beauty, and in nature for the purpose of generating beauty. He considers both types of love to be something essential and "subsisting" <note>Existing as a real, independent substance rather than just a fleeting feeling.</note> because they exist from the soul through its very essence. 

However, those "loves" that are usually aroused recently—since they do not come from the soul simply as an actor, but happen to it as a sufferer from external things and the body—he does not call "subsisting" or "daemons," but rather "passions." After this, you will notice that the universal intellect common to all, and the intellect proper to each individual, differ greatly from one another. Again, the power of knowing that does not possess within its own essence the very thing to be known according to its essence, but only a certain image of it, is deceptive. But that power is certain which holds the object itself within itself; for if such a power does not hold it merely as something imaginary, it is the object itself. 

Therefore, the most perfect knowledge, such as that of the Intellect, is the very things themselves which are called objects. The most imperfect knowledge, such as sense-perception, is neither the things that are to be felt, nor does it possess them, but it merely turns itself toward them. Thought, however, even if it is not the thing it thinks about, nevertheless "possesses" it—that is, it possesses the notions of things, whether it draws them from itself properly or from its own intellect at its own will. If, while you contemplate the intelligible, the mind is there, then not only is the universal intellect the universal intelligible, but also in any specific Idea, a specific intellect is a specific intelligible. Furthermore, the intellect proper to each soul is its own intelligible object. 

Yet it also differs in this from the simply common intellect: for it is not itself the simply universal intelligible, but is so in its own particular way. Our intellect, therefore, has an understanding of universal things and a love of similar things, because it both possesses and exists as the universal intelligible itself. But since it exists as this thing not so much simply as in its own particular way—that is, not in the most completely effective manner—therefore, in any specific notion, it does not comprehend every single thing distinctly as the divine mind comprehends them. For the intellect must turn toward reason or imagination in order to know particulars distinctly. 

That there are other intellects besides the common intellect—not only those that know through discourse <note>Step-by-step logical reasoning.</note> but those that know by a perpetual state, distinct from the first—seems to be confirmed in this way: since the first Intellect is the "first multitude," it is rightly capable of being propagated naturally into several intellects. In it is the Idea of diversity, but the Idea of identity is also there, and is much more powerful. Therefore, since under diversity it is distributed into several discursive intellects, it is also rightly derived under identity into several intellects that know stably. But in those intellects naturally propagated from it, discursive reason is connected to stable intelligence in the same way that in the first Mind, diversity or "otherness" is connected to identity. To proceed into an infinite multitude by understanding—that is, to understand individual things—is granted to our intelligence through the service of joined reason and imagination. As for the other matters discussed regarding love and the gods, we believe we have sufficiently confirmed them in our book *On Love*.

CONCERNING love: is it a god, a certain spirit <term>daemon: in Neoplatonism, a spirit that acts as an intermediary between the divine and human realms</term>, or a passion of the soul? Or is it perhaps a god or spirit in one sense, but in another way a passion? It is worth investigating this, surveying the thoughts of all other men and especially those that have arisen in philosophy, and most of all those held by the divine Plato, <margin>*himself</margin> * who indeed wrote about love in many ways throughout his many works. He did not only say that love is a passion arising in souls, but he also called it a spirit and discussed its generation—how and from what it was born. Regarding the passion for which we hold love responsible—how it arises in souls that desire to be joined with something beautiful—and how this desire is either temperate for those who have become familiar with beauty itself, or how it wishes to end in a shameful act; no one, surely, is ignorant of this. However, it is proper to examine the origin of each through philosophy from the start. For the beginning of the impulse is the soul’s desire for beauty itself, its kinship with it, and its irrational <note>The word "irrational" here suggests an intuitive or innate recognition that precedes logical reasoning.</note> perception of its own affinity; this, I believe, would be the true cause. For what is ugly is contrary both to nature and to God. For nature acts by looking toward the beautiful and looking toward that which is defined, which is in the category of the good. But the indefinite is ugly and belongs to the other category. <note>In the Pythagorean and Platonic "columns" or categories, Limit and Good were paired against the Unlimited/Indefinite and Evil.</note> For nature’s origin is from there—from the good and, clearly, from the beautiful. Furthermore, a person <margin>*is drawn</margin> * is drawn to and is kin to their own kind, even toward images of it. If someone were to remove this cause—how the passion arises and for what reasons—they would not be able to explain it, even in the case of those loves that seek physical union. For these, too, wish to procreate in the beautiful;

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' (Latin initial 'O' in the original) depicting two figures reclining and gesturing towards each other, possibly in philosophical discourse or a domestic scene.</image-desc>
<margin>1 Concerning love: whether it is a passion; what it is, where it comes from, and how many species it has.</margin>
IT IS A WORTHWHILE TASK to consider concerning love, whether it be a certain God, or a spirit, or some passion of the soul; or rather, whether it is partly a certain God or spirit, and partly a passion. Moreover, it is worth asking what each of these should be called. It is also expedient to run through the opinions of other men on this matter, especially those of philosophers, and then most especially the opinion of the divine Plato, who wrote much about love in many places. He did not only say it was a certain passion flowing into souls, but he also called love a spirit, and discussed its generation—how and from where it was born. In the first place, almost no one is ignorant that the amorous passion flows into souls that desire to mingle themselves with someone beautiful, and that such an appetite is partly the property of the temperate, who have already become familiar with beauty itself, and partly ends in a shameful action. But from where either affection arises, we must next contemplate philosophically. If one, therefore, establishes its beginning as the soul's ancient, innate desire for beauty itself—its notion, kinship, and a certain perception of kinship that occurs without the act of reason—he will (as I judge) deviate very little from the truth of the cause. Truly, that which is ugly is contrary to nature and to God. For nature acts by looking toward the beautiful; it looks toward the defined, which is placed in the order of the good, while the undefined is ugly and belongs to the contrary order. But the origin of nature depends upon the good and the beautiful. Furthermore, whoever is delighted by something as if it were kin is also affected by images of it as if they were related. But if someone removes this cause, he will not be able to explain by what logic or for what causes amorous passions arise; not even in those loves that seek sexual union. For these too greatly desire to procreate in a certain beauty,

...since it is quite absurd to say that one wishing to create something beautiful by nature would want to procreate in something ugly. Indeed, for those who are incited to procreate here on earth, it is enough to attain the beauty found here. This beauty is lacking in images and bodies, because the primary archetype <term>archetype: the original, divine form or idea from which all physical things are copied</term> is not present in them—the very thing that is the cause for their loving even this earthly beauty. Therefore, among those who are called back from this beauty to the remembrance of heavenly beauty, this earthly beauty is loved as an image. But among those who, through ignorance of their own passion, do not remember the higher world, this beauty of ours is judged to be the true beauty. If they are temperate <term>temperate: showing self-restraint or moderation, especially in physical desires</term>, their familiarity with this beauty is without fault. But the fall of the intemperate into the mingling of sexual union is a sin. 

Therefore, he who is affected by a pure love of the beautiful is content with beauty alone, whether he remembers the higher world or not. He who admits another longing—the desire for immortality within a mortal thing—seeks the beautiful here through perpetual generation and eternal preservation to the best of his ability. While he proceeds according to nature, he strikes and procreates in the beautiful; he does so for the sake of eternity, and in the beautiful because of a certain kinship with beauty itself. For eternity is also akin to the beautiful, and eternal nature is the primary beauty, and all things that come from it are beautiful. 

Therefore, the one who does not desire generation seems more self-sufficient and content with beauty itself. But the one who desires to procreate strives to give birth to something beautiful because of a certain indigence <note>original: "indigentiam"; Plotinus uses this term to suggest that desire stems from a sense of lack or incompleteness</note>. From this, it appears that he is by no means self-sufficient. He thinks that in his making, he will only then create something beautiful if he procreates in the presence of beauty. But those who strive to procreate against the law and against nature start from a natural impulse; however, having strayed from the natural path, they slip down a lubricious slope and lie where they have fallen, ignorant of where love was leading them, what the desire for generation aims at, and how to use the image of beauty—ignorant, finally, of beauty itself. 

Truly, those who love beautiful bodies not for the sake of sexual union love them for the very reason that they are beautiful. Again, those who follow a "mixed" love—I mean toward women—so that perpetuity may be preserved through generation, and do not wander away from this goal, these desire both beauty and perpetuity at once. Both groups are temperate, though some are more excellent than others. The more excellent either honor this beauty of ours as sufficient for them, or they also honor beauty itself because they remember it—yet they do not despise this earthly beauty, as they consider it a certain effect and a plaything of the divine beauty. These people live within beauty without shame. Others, however, fall through beauty into what is shameful; for the appetite for the good often slips into evil. And these are the passions of the soul.

A ...to reach that greatness, or at least to increase the impulse already born toward it, we must especially philosophize at this point using everything said in Plato's *Symposium*. There, it is described how Love was not born on the birthday of Venus, but from Poverty and 

<margin>* Plenty <note>original: "poros"</note></margin>

Plenty. It seems this discussion will also require us to say something about Venus—whether Love is said to have been born from her, or perhaps alongside her. First, we must ask: who is this Venus?

B And how is Love related to her? Is he from her, or with her, or does he possess a nature that is both from her and with her at once? We say that there are two Venuses. One is the "Celestial Venus" <note>Greek: Aphrodite Urania</note>, whom we call the offspring of Heaven. The other is born of Jupiter and Dione; she is the overseer of the marriages seen here on earth. Both, however, are related to that higher realm, even those beyond marriage. Since marriages do not exist in heaven, the one called "Celestial," born from Kronos <note>Saturn, representing the Divine Intellect</note>—who is her current source—must be the most divine Soul.

C She was born immediately from him, pure and remaining pure in the higher realms. She neither wished nor was able to descend to the things here below, because it was not her nature to travel toward the lower depths. She is a separate substance <term>substance: in Neoplatonism, a "hypostasis" or a distinct, fundamental reality</term> and an essence entirely without a share in matter. This is why the ancients hinted at her origin by calling her "motherless"; one might also rightly call her a divinity <note>Greek: daimona</note> rather than a god.

D She is unmixed and pure, remaining within herself. For that which is born directly from Mind <term>Mind: the "Nous" or Divine Intellect, the first emanation from the One</term> is itself pure. 

<margin>* and herself</margin>

She is powerful in her own right through her closeness to that Mind, and she possesses an innate desire to stay fixed toward her progenitor, who is capable of holding her in the upper realms. Thus, that Soul never falls away; she hangs closely from the Mind, much more so than the light surrounding the sun proceeds from it and is reflected back into it. Following Saturn—or if you prefer, the Father of Saturn, Heaven—she directed her activity toward him and became joined to him; in her loving, she gave birth to Love. After this, she looks toward him, and her activity produced a substance and essence. Both look there: the mother who gave birth, and the beautiful Love who was born. Love is a substance always directed toward another beauty, holding his existence in the middle,

F as the eye of the desirer looking toward the desired. This eye provides the lover with the ability to see the beloved through itself; but the eye itself runs ahead and, even before it provides the power of seeing through an instrument, 

<margin>* previously indeed</margin>

it is itself filled with the spectacle. Indeed, it contemplates first, though not in the same way, by fixing the vision for the lover while it itself enjoys the vision of beauty that wonderfully surrounds it.

G We must not deny that Love is a substance and an essence emanating from an essence—lesser than the one who created it, but existing alongside it. For even that Soul was an essence born from an activity higher than herself; she is a living essence derived from the essence of all beings.

<column-break/>

A ...to reach that height, or at least to increase the instinct toward it already born. Here we must bring in all that is treated in Plato's *Symposium*, where it is written that at the birth of Venus, Love was fathered by Poverty and Plenty. It seems, moreover, that the present dispute requires something to be said of Venus: whether Love is said to be born from Venus, or rather together with Venus. And first, who is Venus? Then, how

B does she behave? Is Love from her, or together with her, or rather does she have Love from herself, produced at the same time and together with her? We say, therefore, that there are two Venuses: the first we affirm is the "Celestial," the daughter of Heaven; the other is born from Jupiter and Dione, the leader of human marriages. This second Venus does not reach as high. But the first is without a mother and exists before marriages, since weddings do not occur in heaven. That Celestial Venus, who they say was born from Saturn—that is, from the Intellect—must

C be a most divine soul, born pure and inviolable directly from that inviolable Intellect, and remaining above. She is one who neither wishes nor is able to descend to these mundane things, because she is endowed with a nature that does not incline toward lower things. It is necessary that she be a separate substance and an essence in no way participating in matter. For this reason, they spoke obscurely when they said she was "without a mother." 

D We ought to call her a God rather than a spirit <term>spirit: "Daemon," a middle-being between gods and men</term>, since she is sincere, pure, and consistent in herself. For that which is born directly from the Mind is also pure, being most powerful in itself by its proximity to the Intellect. It has an inborn appetite to stabilize itself within its parent—a parent, I say, who is capable of keeping it sufficiently among the heavenly beings. Thus it happens that the soul never falls, as it hangs immediately from the Mind. It possesses this gift much more than the light poured around the sun perpetually proceeds from it and is referred back to it. Following Saturn—and if you wish, even the father of Saturn, Heaven—she reflected her act toward him and reconciled herself to him. In loving, she produced Love; and with this very love, she looks up to him, and the act of this soul produces a substance and essence. Then both look there: both the mother who bore him and the beautiful Love who was born. Love is a substance always intent on another beauty, having its existence in the middle, namely

F between the one who desires and the thing desired. And indeed, Love is the eye of the one desiring, providing the lover the means to discern the beloved through him. He himself runs ahead, and before he provides the faculty of seeing through an instrument, he is already full of the sight, or the spectacle. He is the prior one, I say, yet he does not contemplate in the same way; he provides the spectacle for the lover, while he himself feeds on the vision of beauty marvelously poured around him.

<margin>III Confirmation of the above.</margin>

G It cannot be denied that this is a substance and an essence emanating from an essence—lesser indeed than the generator, but existing at the same time. For that Soul is an essence born from the activity that is above her; she is a living essence, derived from the very essence of beings.
