# PLOTINUS'S ENNEAD III

294

...depending on essence, and looking up at that which is the first essence <note>Referring to the Divine Intellect or the "Firsts" in Plotinus’s hierarchy</note>, looking up most intensely. Indeed, the first sight or spectacle of the Soul is this very thing. It looks upon this as its own good and rejoices in the seeing; and the sight itself is such that the Soul does not look upon what it gazes at in a negligent way. Thus, through a kind of pleasure and intense focus, and by the very vehemence of the vision, something is generated by the Soul that is worthy both of the Soul itself and of the spectacle it beholds. Therefore, both from the Soul’s most intense action toward the spectacle, and from what flows down from the spectacle itself—as an eye filled with sight and born with a reflected image—Love <note>original: "eros"</note> is born. It is perhaps called *Eros* because it derives its substance from vision <note>original: "horaseos"</note>. In this way, even the love that is a passion <note>Human emotional love</note> takes its impulse from this higher source. If indeed the Love that is an essence precedes the love that is not an essence, then the passion is called "to love" <note>original: "eran"</note> because it possesses the nature of Love, though it is not called Love in the absolute sense. Therefore, the Love of the heavenly soul exists in this way: it also looks upward to the heights as an attendant and a follower, generated from that soul and existing alongside it, satisfied by the contemplation of the gods. Since we say that this higher soul is "separate" <term>separate: existing independently of matter or a physical body</term>—I mean the soul that first illuminates the heavens—we must also admit that this Love is likewise separate. And even if we said that this soul is essentially celestial, just as we assert that our own best part is within us, we nevertheless affirm it is also separate. Therefore, that Love exists only there, where the inviolable soul resides. But since it was necessary for there to be a soul for this world also, a second Love now accompanies it, which is the "eye" of this lower soul, born from its desire. Since this Venus <note>The "Worldly Venus" or Aphrodite Pandemos</note> belongs to this world, and is not merely the soul in its simplest form, she rightly generated another Love who reigns in this world, and who now concerns himself with marriages and weddings. Yet, insofar as this Love also retains a touch of heavenly desire, he provokes the souls of the young to look upward, and turns the soul to which he is a companion toward higher things, as much as that soul can naturally be provoked into the memory of them. For every soul desires the Good, even the soul that is mixed with matter and has become part of a specific thing; for such a soul follows after the higher one and flows from it.

<margin>
IV.
Two loves
are naturally
implanted in
every soul,
acting as two
guardian spirits.
<note>original: "daemones"</note>
</margin>

One might ask whether every soul possesses such a Love within its essence and substance. Perhaps, since the Universal Soul <note>The soul of the entire cosmos</note> possesses and constitutes this Love, there is nothing to prevent the souls of humans from possessing and constituting it similarly, and indeed the souls of all other living beings. Perhaps this Love is the guardian spirit <note>original: "daemon"</note> that they say accompanies each person—specifically, the essential Love of each individual. This Love would easily be the one that introduces natural desires, insofar as every soul naturally feels appetite; for each soul, according to its own nature, generates a Love consistent with its own dignity and essence. Therefore, let the Universal Soul have the Universal Love, and let each particular soul have its own. However, insofar as each soul is related to the Universal Soul—not being cut off from it, but rather contained within it so that all are one—so too does each individual Love relate to the Universal Love.

<column-break/>

A ...and looking toward that which was the first substance, looking intensely, and seeing the spectacle before her, she is drawn to it as her own good, and she rejoices while looking. And the sight was of such a kind that it was not a side-task for her to perform this gazing. Rather, through a kind of pleasure and a mixing <note>original: "krasis"</note> with it, and by the vehemence of the sight, she generated something from herself, worthy of her and of the sight. From this action toward the seen object, and from what flows as if from the object seen, the eye is filled; thus a vision joined with an image—Love <note>original: "eros"</note>—was born. It has its name because it has its existence from vision <note>original: "horaseos"</note>. For the passion of desire takes its name from this, since the Love that is a substance precedes the love that is not a substance. Indeed, the passion is called "to love" <note>original: "eran"</note>, because Love possesses this state, but it is not called Love simply. The Love of the higher soul is of such a kind, looking upward itself, as an attendant of that soul, born from it and satisfied by the sight of the gods. And calling that soul "separate," which first shines upon the heavens, we shall also place this Love as "separate." Even if we say that the soul is most celestial, just as we say the best part in us is celestial, we nevertheless consider it separate. It remains only there, where the soul is pure. But since it was necessary for there to be a soul of this universe, there arose with her another Love, an "eye" for her too, born from her desire. In this world, there is this Venus—not only a soul, nor simply a soul—who generated the love in this world that oversees marriages. Insofar as this Love touches upon higher desire, it moves the souls of the young upward, and turns the soul with which it is joined toward the higher realm, insofar as that soul is naturally fit to enter into the memory of those things. For every soul seeks the Good, even the soul that is mixed, since it follows from the higher soul and is derived from it.

It may be asked: does not every soul have such a Love in its essence and substance? Just as the whole soul has it, and constitutes the Love of the universe, so each of our souls has it, and even the souls in all other living things. Is this Love then the guardian spirit <note>original: "daemon"</note> which they say follows each person, being the Love specific to each? For this would be the one that produces the desires according to the nature of each soul, generating a Love proportional to its own nature, according to its worth and substance. Let the whole soul have the whole Love, and each partial soul have its own. Insofar as each soul is toward the whole, and not cut off, each Love is toward the whole.

# BOOK FIVE.
B 4

<margin>* themselves</margin>
A **In the same way**, the particular love is present with the particular soul and with matter. This universal Love is present in the whole, and is everywhere throughout the whole. Once again, this single Love becomes many, appearing everywhere it wishes, taking the shape of its own parts and manifesting itself in images if it so chooses. Therefore, one must believe that there are many "Venuses" <note>Aphrodites</note> in the universe, acting as spirits <term>daemons: intermediary beings between the divine and the mortal</term> born alongside love, flowing out from a certain universal Venus. These depend on her individually along with their own specific loves. Since the Soul is the mother of Love, and Venus is the Soul, then Love is the energy <note>original: "energeia"</note> of a Soul that desires the Good. Since this Love leads each soul toward the nature of the Good, the Love belonging to the higher soul would be a god, who always joins the soul to that Good; however, the Love belonging to the mixed soul is to be called a spirit.

B **But** what is the nature of this spirit, or the nature of spirits in general, about which Plato speaks in the *Symposium* <note>The "Banquet," a dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of Love</note>? He speaks of how Love was born from Need <note>original: "Penia"</note> and Resource <note>original: "Poros"</note> at the birth of Venus. Anyone who thinks that this world <note>the physical cosmos</note> is what Plato calls Love—rather than Love being something born within the world—will face many contradictions. First, Plato calls the world a "blessed god" and self-sufficient, but he describes Love as neither a god nor self-sufficient, but always in need. Furthermore, it is necessary—if the world is composed of soul and body, and the Soul of the world is its Venus—that the primary part of Love is Venus herself. Or, if the world is the Soul itself (just as a human is the human soul), then Love must be Venus. Moreover, why would Love be a spirit and the world itself, while the other spirits who share the same essence are not also the world? Then the world would be nothing but a collection of spirits. Also, when Love is called the "leader of beautiful boys," how would that fit the world? Finally, he says Love is "unsheltered, shoeless, and homeless"; these descriptions cannot be applied to the world except in a very dry and inept way.

F **But** what must be said about Love and its so-called generation? Surely we must explain who "Need" <note>Poverty</note> is, and who "Resource" <note>Plenty</note> is, and how such parents are suited to him. It is clear that these parents must also suit the other spirits, if indeed there is to be one single nature and essence for all spirits by which they are spirits—unless they only share the name in common. Let us consider, then, how we distinguish gods from spirits. Although we often call spirits "gods," for now let us distinguish them as two different classes. We say and believe the class of gods is free from passion, but we assign passions to the spirits, saying they are eternal but in the rank immediately following the gods, and already close to us.

<column-break/>

A **The particular love** again imitates the particular soul, and that great Love imitates the universal soul. That which is in the whole flourishes everywhere throughout the universe. Again, this one love turns into many, and appears everywhere at will, shaped by its own parts and showing itself in a certain image if it pleases. Indeed, it must be thought that there are many Venuses in the world, like spirits being born together with love, flowing out from a certain universal Venus; these depend on her individually along with their own proper loves. For if the soul is the mother of love, and Venus is the soul, then love is the act of the soul desiring the good. Since, therefore, such a love always leads to the very nature of the good, the love of the higher soul is a god, who always joins the soul with that good; but the love of the soul already mixed with matter must be called a spirit.

<margin>He refutes those who said that love itself, which is called the "Great Spirit" by Plato, is the world.</margin>
C **MOREOVER**, what is the nature of the spirit <term>daemon</term> and of spirits in common? About which Plato writes in the *Symposium*: I ask about the nature of other spirits and of love itself—how, for instance, love was born from need and resource through a plan at the birth of Venus. Whoever thinks this world was named "Love" by Plato, rather than Love being something of the world and born in the world, will be convinced by many arguments. First, Plato calls the world a blessed god and self-sufficient in itself, while he says this Love is neither a god nor self-sufficient, but always

D needy. Then it is necessary, if the world is composed of soul and body, and the soul of the world is its own Venus, that the principal part of love is Venus. Or if the world is the very soul of the world, just as a human is the soul of a human, it is necessary that Love be Venus. Furthermore, why should Love, existing as a spirit, be the world, while other spirits who are of the same essence are not also the world? And the world will be this very

E constitution of spirits. Likewise, where Love is said to be the "leader of beautiful boys," in what way will that suit the world? Finally, he says Love wanders without a bed or covering, without shoes, and without a home: these things can in no way be attributed to the world except in an extremely dry and inept fashion.

<margin>VI On the origin of love, and on spirits.</margin>
F **TRULY**, what must be said about love and its generation? Certainly, it must be explained what the mother of love, *Penia* (that is, Need), is; and what the father, *Porus* (that is, Resource), is. And by what reasoning such parents are suited to love. It is established, however, that such parents must also suit the other spirits: if indeed it is necessary that the nature and essence of all spirits, by which they are spirits, be one, unless perhaps they are said to have only a name in common. Let us consider, therefore, how we distinguish gods from spirits: for although we often say spirits are also gods, for the present let us accept it as when we distinguish the race of spirits and the race of gods

G as being different from one another. Thus, we say and believe the race of gods is free from passion: but we join passions to the spirits, saying also that they are eternal, in the rank following after the Gods, and already close to the human race.

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK III

Hanging from essence, and looking up to that which is the first essence, the soul looks with intensity. Indeed, the first sight the soul has is that very essence. It looks upon it as its own good and rejoices in the seeing; and the vision itself is of such a kind that it does not look upon what it contemplates carelessly. Indeed, from its own pleasure and the intensity of the vision, something is generated by the soul, worthy of both the soul itself and the spectacle it beholds. Therefore, both from the fact that the soul acts most intensely regarding the spectacle, and from what flows out, as it were, from the spectacle itself, the eye of the soul is filled. Thus, like a vision born with an image, **Love** (*Eros*) was born. Perhaps for this reason it was called *eros*, because it takes its substance from *horaseos* <note>original: "horaseos," meaning "from vision"</note>, that is, from vision. 

Even the love that is a passion <note>human emotion or "suffering" of the soul</note> takes its impulse from this; for the Love that is an essence precedes the love that is not an essence. Yet it is also called "to love" as a passion, if Love itself already possesses it, though it is not simply called Love. Therefore, the Love of the heavenly soul exists in such a way, itself also looking up to sublime things, as a follower of that soul, born from her and remaining with her, content in the contemplation of the gods. 

Since we say that the soul is separate <note>transcendental or independent of the body</note>—I mean the soul that first illuminates the heavens—we shall rightly admit that this Love is also separate. And if we have said that this soul is most celestial, just as we assert that our own best part is within us, yet we also affirm it to be separate. Let that Love, then, be only there, where the inviolable soul is. 

But since it was necessary for there to be a soul of this world as well, there follows it now another Love, who is also the "eye" of this soul, born from its desire. Since this **Venus** <note>original: "Venus," the Roman name for Aphrodite, often used by the translator Ficino to represent the Soul's beauty</note> belongs to this world, and is not only soul, nor simply soul, she rightly generated a Love reigning in this world, who now concerns himself with the unions and marriages of this world. Yet, insofar as this Love also attains a heavenly desire, he in turn provokes the souls of the young, and turns the soul itself, of which he is a companion, toward higher things, as much as that soul can naturally be provoked into the memory of them. For every soul seeks the Good, even the soul that is mixed and belongs to something else, since this soul follows the higher one and flows from it.

IV
Two loves 
naturally 
implanted in 
every soul,

loves.
</margin>

**IT MAY BE ASKED** whether every soul possesses such a love in its essence and substance. Perhaps, since the soul of the universe possesses and constitutes this love, there is nothing to prevent the souls of men from possessing and constituting it similarly, as well as the souls of all other living beings. Perhaps this Love is the **spirit** <term>daemon: a guardian spirit or guiding force in Neoplatonism</term> that they say accompanies everyone—that is, the essential love of each individual. This spirit would certainly be the one that brings about natural desires, insofar as every soul naturally seeks what is appropriate for it, and each generates a love according to its own nature, dignity, and essence. Let the universal Soul, therefore, have a universal Love, and each particular soul have its own particular love. Insofar as each particular soul relates to the universal Soul—not being cut off from it but contained within it, so that they are all one—so too does each individual love relate to the universal Love.

<column-break/>

Or also looking toward that, which was the first essence, and looking intensely, the first sight she perceived was that which she saw as her own good; and she rejoiced in seeing, and the vision was such that she did not make the sight a secondary matter. <margin>* he loves</margin> By this pleasure and by her union <margin>* by this</margin> with it, and by the intensity of the sight, she generated something from herself, worthy of her and of the sight. From this acting upon the thing seen, and from that which flows, as it were, from the thing seen, the eye was filled. Thus, like a vision with an image, **Love** was born. Perhaps he also had his name from this, because he has his existence from vision (*horaseos*). 

Since even the love that is a passion would have its desire from this, a prior essence precedes the non-essence. And yet one is said "to love" as a passion, even if Love already possesses him, but it would not simply be called Love. The Love of the higher soul, being such, also looks upward, being the child of that soul, and having been born from her and toward her, to behold the gods. Or, by calling that soul separate—the one which first shone upon the heaven—we shall also place this Love as separate. Even if we said the soul was most heavenly; for while we say that the best in us is in us, we nevertheless place it as separate. Let him be only there, where the pure soul is. 

But since it was necessary for a soul to be here in this whole [world], there arose with her now also another Love, an eye for her also, born from her own desire. But **Aphrodite** herself in the world, being not only soul but simply soul, generated the Love in this world, who himself also touches upon the laws of marriage. And sometimes he himself touches upon the upward desire, leading the souls of the young toward the master <note>the Higher Good</note>, and leading the soul with which he exists back upward, insofar as it is in her nature to go toward the memory of those higher things. For every soul seeks the Good, even the mixed soul, and the one belonging to something, since even this one is next in order after that higher soul and comes from it.

Is it then the case that every soul has such a love in its essence and substance? Or if the whole soul has it, and the soul of the universe constituted Love, does the soul in each of us not have it? And how is it in all other living things? Is this Love the spirit <term>daemon</term> which they say follows each person—the Love belonging to each individual? For this would be the one that implants desires, as each soul reaches out according to its nature, each generating a love according to its nature, its worth, and its essence. Let the whole soul have the whole Love, and the particular souls have their own individual loves. Insofar as each soul relates to the whole soul, not being cut off but included so that all are one, each love would also relate to the whole Love.

...those who are intermediaries between the race of gods and humans. It is therefore worthy of consideration by what reasoning spirits <term>Daemons: intermediary spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense, but beings that bridge the gap between the divine and the mortal</term> did not remain free from passion, but descended in their nature toward the worse. We must also ask whether any spirit exists in the intelligible world <term>Intelligible world: the realm of pure ideas and divine intellect, as opposed to the physical world</term>, and again, whether spirits exist only in this world, while God exists only in the intelligible world. Perhaps there are gods here as well, and the world (as is commonly said) is a "third god"; and every being as far as the moon is a god. It is certainly better to call no one in the intelligible world a "spirit," but even if a spirit is placed there, to consider it a god; and to call those in the sensible world as far as the moon "visible gods," or second gods: coming after and according to the intelligible gods, depending on them just as radiance depends on the stars. 

But what shall we say spirits are? Perhaps since the soul is infused into the world, we shall call the spirit of each soul a "trace" <note>original: "vestigium" / "ίχνος"; a footprint or lingering impression of the higher soul in the lower realm</note> of that individual soul. I say "soul infused into the world," because the purer soul generates a god, and we have already said that its love is a god. But we must ask, first, why not all spirits are "loves": then, in what way these too are not free from matter. Perhaps those spirits are "loves" which are generated from a soul desiring the good and the beautiful; indeed, all souls in this world generate this love here. But the remaining spirits are themselves also generated by the soul—I mean by the soul of the entire universe—but are generated by certain other powers of it for the use of the universe, filling and administering individual parts for the sake of the whole. For it was necessary that the soul of the whole should sufficiently preside over and be enough for the entire world, generating powers of spirits suitable and contributing to its own whole. 

But in what way and of what matter do spirits participate? For they do not participate in a corporeal one <note>a physical body</note>, otherwise they would be sensible animals. For even if they receive "airy" or "fiery" bodies, it is still necessary that their nature be different beforehand, so that it may also become a participant in a body. For that which is entirely pure does not suddenly mingle with a body, even though many believe the essence of a spirit, insofar as it is a spirit, exists together with some airy or fiery body. But why does the essence of spirits have commerce with the body, while the essence of gods has none, unless there is some cause in the soul that mingles, contributing to the mixture? What then is the cause? One must posit an "intelligible matter," so that what participates in that matter may, through it, also come into this matter of bodies.

# ON BOOK 5. ENNEAD III.

Reason, therefore, having come into being within that <term>Logos: the Greek word for "Reason," "Word," or the ordering principle of the universe</term>, yet in an indefinite 
<margin>descent / lowering</margin>
descent and a dim subsistence, produced that which was born not as a perfect thing, but as something merely capable. It was lacking, however, because it was generated from an indefinite desire and a capable reason. * Not all reason is pure, since it contains within itself an indefinite, irrational, and infinite desire; for it will never be fulfilled so long as it possesses the nature of the indeterminate within itself. It depends 
on the soul, using the soul as its starting point, yet it is a mixture—not a mixture of Reason staying within itself, but mixed with indefiniteness. It is not 
<margin>blending / tempering</margin>
Reason itself that is blended with that indefiniteness, but that which emanates from Reason is sufficient for the mixture. Love <term>Eros: the Greek personification of Love and Desire</term> is thus like a stinging gadfly <note>original: "oistros" / "οἶστρος"; a gadfly whose sting causes frenzy or madness, often used to describe the pangs of love</note>, needy by its own nature because of its origin; even when it attains its goal, it becomes needy again. For it can never be truly filled, because the mixture itself lacks the capacity for fullness. Only that which is full by its own nature is truly fulfilled. But Love, because of the poverty <note>original: "penia" / "πενίαν"; in Platonic thought, Poverty is the mother of Love</note> within it, feels desire, and even if it should <unclear>be bereft</unclear> or fulfilled, it cannot contain it. Its demonic nature arises from this, as its essence is the power of acquisition <note>original: "poristikon" / "ποριστικόν"; the ability to find resources, a trait inherited from its father Poros (Plenty)</note> due to the nature of Reason. One must also believe the entire genus of spirits <term>Daemons: intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humans</term> to be of this kind and not common; for each one is assigned to be a provider for that which it oversees, and a desirer of that same thing. Or it is either related to this Love, or is itself full, yet desiring to exist not as a part but as a whole of the Good. From this, the love which the good possess—of the simple and true Good—is an essence in itself, not just a certain love. Those who are ordered according to other spirits are arranged by one spirit or another, having dismissed the simple Love they once held. They act according to the spirit they have chosen, in harmony with the part of the soul that is active within them. But those who desire evil things have bound all the loves within them to the wicked desires they have conceived, just as they have overwhelmed their innate right reason with the wicked opinions that have come upon them. Therefore, the loves that are natural are, by nature, beautiful. The loves of the lower soul 
<margin>as is worthy / according to merit</margin>
are lesser in dignity and power. Those of the higher soul are all superior, situated within the true essence. But those loves which occur contrary to nature are the passions of those who have gone astray. These have no essence at all, nor any essential subsistence; they are not produced by the soul itself but accompany a vice of the soul, which generates things similar to its own 
<margin>already / now</margin>
state and current habit. For if it is true that real goods belong to the essence of a soul acting according to its nature in a world of determined reason, then other things are not actions of the soul itself, but are merely passions—just like false perceptions that do not have real essences beneath them, unlike true, eternal, and determined perceptions, which are identical with the act of thinking itself.

<column-break/>

A Reason, therefore, not remaining as pure reason, but having been formed in an indefinite appetite and a weak subsistence, rendered that which was born from it neither perfect nor sufficient, but rather needy, inasmuch as it was born from a certain indefinite appetite and a sufficient reason. This reason is by no means pure: for it contains within itself an unlimited, irrational, and indefinite appetite. It will never be filled so long as it contains the nature of the indeterminate within itself. It depends, B however, upon the soul, since it proceeds from the soul as its starting point. It is a certain mixture, not indeed of reason remaining in itself, but of reason mixed with infinity; for reason itself is not mixed, but that which radiates from it is mixed with infinity. Love is thus like a certain needy sting of its own nature; even after it has attained its object, it is needy once more. For it does not have a nature that can be filled, since it is a mixture; and it is such a mixture because it does not possess, and therefore is not filled. C For only that which is already full by its own nature can truly be filled. Because it desires due to an inherent indigence, even if it is suddenly filled, it by no means retains it—for the resourceful industry of Love proceeds from indigence. The faculty of providing or supplying seems to be present because of the very nature of reason. It is necessary to believe that the entire race of daemons is constituted from such things. Any of these D has the nature of providing, supplying, and desiring that to which it is assigned; and by this logic, it is kindred to Love. It is not full itself, but is greedy for some particular good. The result is that those who are good in this world possess a love for the simply true Good itself, rather than just a certain kind of love. But those who are ordered according to other spirits are disposed according to one daemon or another; the simple love they had, they now let go as idle. E They work according to the other spirit they have chosen, in accordance with the part of the soul that is in harmony with what is operating within them. Those who desire evil things, because of the wicked desires they have already conceived, seem to have hindered and bound all the loves within themselves—just as they are accustomed to occupy right reason, if any was innate, with the evil opinions they have contracted over time. Therefore, the loves that are inherent by nature and are good according to nature—those of the inferior soul—are lower in dignity F and power; but those of the superior soul are higher. All, finally, are placed within the essence. Those loves, however, which happen contrary to nature, are certain passions of those who wander; they have no essence in any way, nor any essential subsistence. Indeed, they were not made by the soul itself, but they accompany a vice of the soul, which generates certain things similar to the affect and habit it has contracted. It is entirely probable that true G goods—which the soul acts upon whenever it acts according to nature in things determined by reason—are the true essence. Other things, however, the soul does not act upon from itself, and therefore they are nothing other than passions. Just so, false intelligences possess no essence beneath them, whereas true, eternal, and determined intelligences possess reality.

<summary>Plotinus explores how Love (Eros) is born from a mixture of Reason (Logos) and Poverty (Indigence), explaining its perpetual state of desire. He classifies "daemons" as intermediary spirits that reflect the soul's orientation toward either higher virtues or lower passions.</summary>

-> ### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III ### <-

...possessing at once both the act of understanding and the object of thought. The <term>intelligible: that which can be known by the mind alone, rather than the senses</term> exists not only in that which is simple, but also in every truly intelligible thing surrounding it. Indeed, intellect exists within every <term>species: a specific form or kind of being</term>. Furthermore, it is established that pure intelligence and the intelligible reside within each of us. These are not merely our own, but exist in a simple and universal way; this is why we possess a love that tends toward simple and universal truths, for such intelligences are present within us. If the intelligence of a specific individual is present, it seems to be there by accident. For example, when someone understands that a specific triangle has two right angles, they understand this only insofar as they understand the "Triangle itself" <note>This refers to the Platonic Form of a triangle, the perfect conceptual version of the shape</note> simply has two right angles.

<margin>
VIII.
Concerning Jupiter, his gardens, Venus, Porus, Penia, and Love.
</margin>

**BUT MOREOVER**, who is this Jupiter <note>original: "Iupiter"; the Roman name for the Greek god Zeus</note> into whose gardens Plato says Porus entered? And what are these gardens? We have already agreed that Venus <note>original: "Venus"; the Roman name for Aphrodite</note> is the Soul, and Porus <note>original: "Porus"; meaning "Resource" or "Plenty"</note> is the <term>Reason: the Greek "Logos," the ordering principle of all things</term>. It remains for us to reveal what he intends to signify by Jupiter and Jupiter's gardens. Certainly, we must not say that Jupiter is the Soul, since we have already conceded that Venus is the Soul. Rather, we must accept that the Jupiter named here by Plato is that "great leader" described in the *Phaedrus*, whom he elsewhere places as the third god. But he speaks more clearly in the *Philebus*, saying that in Jupiter there is a "royal soul" and a "royal intellect." If, therefore, Jupiter is the Great Intellect and Soul, and is ranked among the causes, he must be ranked according to that which is most excellent—both for many other reasons and because he is the cause, a royal and leading cause. If this is so, Jupiter represents the Intellect <note>original: "Intellectus"; the divine Mind or "Nous"</note>. Venus, who belongs to him, comes from him, and is with him, shall be placed in the rank of the Soul—specifically according to that which is beautiful and splendid, and according to the sincere, harmless, and delicate nature of the soul. From all these qualities, the soul is called "Venus." Indeed, if we judge the males among the gods according to the Intellect, we are accustomed to name their souls as females. Since a soul is joined to every intellect, it is for this reason that the Soul of Jupiter is Venus. This is especially true since the testimonies of priests and <term>theologians: those who study the nature of the divine</term> support this reasoning; for they identify Venus and Juno <note>original: "Iuno"; the queen of the gods</note> as the same deity, and they call the star of Venus in the heavens the "star of Juno."

<margin>
IX.
Confirmation of the above.
</margin>

**PORUS**, therefore, being a certain reason of those things which exist in the intelligible world and the intellect—a reason, I say, now more widely unfolded—comes to be around the soul and within the soul. For that which is gathered in the intellect and does not flow from another into it, is signified by Porus being "drunk with nectar," which represents an acquired fullness. But what is it there that fills Porus with nectar? It is surely the Reason flowing down from a higher principle to a lower one. Therefore, this reason is conceived by the soul from the intellect when Venus is said to be born, and while it is being conceived, it is judged to flow into the gardens of Jupiter. For every garden is a place of splendor and the beauty of abundance. Indeed, the gardens of Jupiter shine with Reason, and the "ornaments of Jupiter" are the splendors flashing from his own intellect into the soul.

<meta>catchword: What</meta>

<column-break/>

...and the intelligible, having existence not only in the simple, but also in each thing truly surrounding the intelligible. And intellect is in each form, and in each of us pure thought and the intelligible are placed. This is not only ours but also simple, which is why love for simple things is in us. For thoughts are the cause of particular things by accident, just as if one contemplates that *this* triangle has two right angles, it is because the "Triangle itself" simply has them.

<margin>
* But how Jupiter, etc. According to Reason.
</margin>

* **BUT** how is Jupiter said to be the one into whom Porus entered? And what is the garden? For if Venus is the Soul, as we say, then Porus is the Reason (*Logos*) of all things. In these matters, what must we take Jupiter and his garden to be? If we take Jupiter to be the Soul, we must make Venus a fire <note>original: "πῦρ" (pyr); here perhaps a reference to the warmth or vitality of the soul</note>. We must take Jupiter here, as in Plato, from the *Phaedrus*, where he calls him the "great leader" of the gods; or in other places where he is the third. Come then, in the *Philebus*, he says that in Jupiter there is a royal soul and a royal intellect. If then Jupiter is a great intellect and soul, and is ranked among the causes, he should be ranked according to the superior principle, both for other reasons and because he is the cause, both royal and leading. He, then, exists according to the Intellect (*Nous*); and his Venus, being from him and with him, is ranked according to the Soul, according to the beauty, the brilliance, the innocence, and the delicacy of the soul, which is why she is called Aphrodite <note>original: "Αφροδίτη"; Venus</note>. For if we rank the males of the gods according to the Intellect, and we speak of their souls as females—as a soul is present with each—then the Soul of Jupiter would be Venus. Again, this reasoning is witnessed by priests and theologians, who treat Hera <note>original: "Ἥρα"; Juno</note> and Aphrodite as the same. And they say the star of Aphrodite in heaven is the star of Hera.

Porus, then, being the Reason of the things in the intelligible and the intellect, and being more diffused, as if unfolded, would come to be around the soul and in the soul. For that which is compressed in the intellect and not unfolded is the same, but in this one [Porus] being drunk, the fullness is external. And that which fills him there being nectar, what would it be but a Reason falling from a superior principle into an inferior one? In the soul, then, the Reason is from the Intellect, which is what Venus is said to have become when it flowed into his garden. Every garden is a thing of beauty, a wealth of ornament. Jupiter’s things are made beautiful by Reason. And his ornaments are the beauties that come from him into the soul.

# BOOK SIX #

<column-break/>

**OR WHAT MIGHT** the garden of Zeus <note>original: "Διὸς"; Jupiter in the Latin text</note> be, or his statues, and his splendors? What then are his splendors and ornaments, if not the <term>Reasons: the "Logoi," or the formative divine principles</term> flowing from him, all at once? These Reasons are Poros <note>original: "πόρος"; meaning Resource or Plenty</note>, or the absence of want, and the lover of beauty, now in manifestation; and this is to be drunk on nectar. For what is nectar to the gods, except that which the divine receives? That which is subordinate <margin>* with Intellect</margin> receives <term>Intellect: "Nous," the higher divine mind</term> and Reason. It possesses the outflow from Intellect without satiety. He who is "drunk" possesses this, for he has something brought into him from outside; but it is a Reason, not a mere offspring. It is a <term>subsistence: a distinct way of existing</term> * with Intellect, and would not exist on its own but in another, which is why it is said to lie in the "garden of Zeus." This "lying down" occurs when Aphrodite <note>The Soul</note> is said to exist as a subsistence. We must understand these myths by dividing the things they describe by <margin>* of Reason</margin> time, even if they are eternal, and by separating many things that exist together, though they differ in order or power. This is why these accounts and stories create "births" for things that were never born. And they even divide things that are united in me. Once they have taught us as much as they can, they allow the one who understands to bring these things back together. This gathering together, as the Soul lives with Intellect and takes its <margin>* outflow</margin> subsistence from it, is filled with * Reason and beautifully adorned. Being filled with the vision of many splendors and images of all beautiful things, she is the "all-encompassing Venus." All the Reasons within her are called Porus and Resource, flowing from the nectar above. The splendors within her, as they reside in life, are called the "Garden of Zeus." There, Poros is nothing other than the manifestation of life, burdened by the things with which he was filled, and who exists forever among the beings called gods. Thus, as these beings exist in blessedness, and always exist in those things that have subsisted, they do so of necessity. From the <margin>* downward flow</margin> downward flow of the Soul toward what is better and good—and which always exists from above and from the Soul—is Love (Eros). This is a mixed fullness: participating in need, because it wishes to be filled, yet not without resource, because it seeks that which it lacks. For that which is entirely without a share of the good will never seek the good. He is said to be born of Resource <margin>* Poverty</margin> and Poverty, or rather, the lack and the desire, and the memory of the Reasons, coming together with the Soul, generated that activity directed toward the good, which is this Love. His mother is Poverty, because desire belongs to one who is in need. Poverty is like <term>Matter: the underlying "stuff" of the universe which has no form of its own</term>, because matter is in want of all things. And the indefinite nature of the desire for the good—for it is neither a specific form nor a Reason—is associated with this desiring subject. That which desires is more "material" insofar as it desires to create. It is only the Form of itself remaining in itself; and desiring to receive...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **FOR WHAT ELSE** can the gardens of Jupiter <note>original: "Iovis"; the Roman name for the Greek Zeus</note> signify, except his images and splendors? What, again, are the splendors and ornaments of Jupiter, if not the Reasons flowing from him? At the same time, these Reasons are called Porus, that is, a happy affluence, and a treasury of beautiful riches already shining forth openly and clearly. Now, this very thing is to "become drunk on nectar." For what else among the gods is nectar, except that which a god drinks? But that which is below the Mind drinks in <margin>B</margin> <term>Reason: the "ratio" or logical principle</term> from the Mind. The Mind itself, being what it will be, rests in peace; and since it already possesses everything, it does not, strictly speaking, become "drunk," because it has nothing foreign within it. But Reason is the offspring of the Mind, subsisting after the Mind, no longer existing within the Mind itself but "lying in another," in the garden of Jupiter (as it is said), and specifically at the time when the "birthday of Venus" is celebrated—that is, when Venus is born. It is necessary for myths, if they are truly to be myths and not far from the truth, to divide into different times the things they narrate, and to segregate many things from one another which <margin>C</margin> actually exist simultaneously in time. They differ, however, in rank and power. Since Reasons and discourses are accustomed to introduce "generations" (births) for things that are unbegotten, they also distinguish things that exist together; and after they have taught these things to the best of their ability, they usually allow those who will understand to reconnect what they had previously divided. Our highest connection at present is of this kind: the Soul, existing together with the Mind and subsisting from the Mind itself, is in turn imbued with Reasons from there. She is herself beautiful, <margin>D</margin> adorned with beautiful things, and luxuriating in affluence, so that in her one may behold various splendors and the images of all beautiful things: and in that whole state, she is considered Venus herself. All the Reasons in her are called Porus, that is, happy affluence, flowing forth from the celestial nectar. But the splendors in her, insofar as they shine in life itself, are called the gardens of Jupiter. There, Porus is also said to lie down, already heavy with those things with which he is said to be imbued.
<margin>E</margin> When, however, life shines in the order of things—or rather, since it is always shining—the gods are judged to be reclining at a banquet, inasmuch as they enjoy a happiness of this kind. But Love (Amor) necessarily exists always as long as the soul does, having proceeded from the appetite of the soul toward the more excellent Good. It is, however, a certain mixed thing: a participant in indigence, insofar as it affects to be filled, yet not without a share of plenty, insofar as it demands the remainder of what it already has. For if it were entirely without the good, it would never seek the good. For this reason, it is said to have arisen from affluence <margin>F</margin> and poverty together. Furthermore, the defect and the appetite, together with the memory of the Reasons conspiring in the soul, generated that act toward the good which is called Love. Its mother is Poverty (Penuria), because appetite is always that of one who is in need. Matter is this very Poverty, because matter is in need of all things. Furthermore, the indeterminate nature of the appetite turning toward the <margin>G</margin> good declares that this very thing which it desires—insofar as it desires it—has more of the character of Matter. For neither Form nor Reason yet appears to be in that which desires the good, in the very respect that it desires it. Insofar as it looks to itself, it is only a Species, remaining in itself, and at the same time affecting to receive its own nature, which is yet to receive the good...

He explains that Love is a "mixed" being born from Resource (Porus) and Poverty (Penia), representing the Soul's constant desire to be filled by the Good.</summary>

# MARSILIO FICINO ON THE
# SIXTH BOOK OF THE THIRD ENNEAD, CONCERNING THE FACT THAT INCORPOREAL THINGS DO NOT SUFFER [PASSION],
# COMMENTARY.

### SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

The summary of this book is to assert that an incorporeal thing cannot suffer <note>original: "pati"; in Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to "passion," or being passively changed or acted upon by an external force</note>. He defines an incorporeal thing as something that either includes no quantity in its own definition (even if it can receive it from the outside), which is what "matter" is; or something that entirely excludes quantity, which is "mind" and "soul." Furthermore, he defines "passion" <note>suffering/undergoing change</note> as a mutation that can destroy a substance, whether it happens through division—which occurs to quantity and to things that necessarily possess quantity—or whether it happens through alteration, such as what occurs between contrary qualities, and additionally to the forms that such qualities necessarily accompany. Therefore, both primary matter and the soul are incorporeal things; neither claims quantity nor that specific type of quality as its own, and thus they are separated from passion—the soul even more so than matter. For the soul not only refuses to admit destructive forms, but it does not even allow new qualities of any kind to take hold, though it may seem to receive forms. Therefore, many things are disputed in the following pages regarding the immutable essence of the rational soul and its parts, as well as some things concerning the primary essence, and many things concerning its opposite—that is, primary matter—to finally confirm that an incorporeal thing is devoid of passion.

*The Soul neither suffers, nor receives forms or qualities. Likewise concerning the twofold imagination.*

In the first part of the book, which contains five chapters, he shows that the soul is not subject to passion; in the second part, he will subsequently show something similar regarding matter. As far as the first part is concerned, he observes that no impulse or quality from bodies falls upon the cognitive power of the soul. For if it were to fall in a certain natural—and, so to speak, material—way, cognition and discernment would be immediately confounded. If it were to happen at least by some condition of the imagination, so that bodies "form" the soul, that would be a wicked thing to say: for it belongs to the soul, as the superior, to form bodies, not to be formed by them. Indeed, all cognition and affection of the soul, even when turning toward corporeal things, is a certain action of the soul regarding such things, and meanwhile, it does not suffer <note>undergo passive change</note> from them. For it does not share matter with bodies, which is the kind of communion that usually allows a reciprocal exchange of passion in the agent. What then is "to perceive"? It is indeed this very thing in the soul: namely, to apply itself and to deploy its power toward those things for which it has a harmonious and naturally fit essence. Similarly, "to remember" is to perform this same action most readily. Therefore, no power of knowing is formed through new images; rather, the intellect is always in "act" <note>fully realized or active</note> regarding those things which it knows. The reason and the phantasy <note>imagination</note>, starting from a state in which they possess those things potentially, eventually become in "act" those things which are always in "act" within the intellect. The external sense perceives things to be sensed, but it does not receive them <note>as a passive vessel</note>. The vegetative power nourishes and moves, yet it is not nourished or moved in the process. Porphyry <note>a student of Plotinus</note> confirms all these things, showing that when the soul is said to "suffer," this passion is not any alteration in its nature or some quality, but a certain accommodation and affection of the soul toward this or that thing; it is an action of the soul regarding external things, but a narrow one, specifically when it contracts the amplitude of its own powers and affections into a narrow space. Porphyry concludes that all the "movements" attributed to the soul are not properly movements in the soul, but in the body; in the soul they are actions, while in the body those same things become passions. He adds that the acts of growth, sensation, and memory are not imaginary but are in a way "natural," just as heating, being hot, illuminating, and shining are; Plotinus holds the same view. Meanwhile, you will note that virtue in the soul is generally twofold: one kind is "private," belonging to a specific part of the soul (this is when any part performs its duty rightly); the other is "public," namely, when all parts harmonize together rightly, when reason is ruled by the mind, and the irrational powers then obey reason, among which desire is subject to boldness. Neither virtue is like a quality "impressed" upon the soul as if on a subject—likewise neither is vice—but it is rather like movement and action, or the absence thereof. If there is any quality in us, whether impressed from elsewhere by way of a natural image or acquired through actions, such a thing is not in the soul, but rather in the body—either in the body itself or in the way it is affected—in which formations and passions occur while the soul gives life, senses, is affected, and judges. Finally, no change occurs in the soul except a progression from a certain potentiality into act; and this is not from another mover, but from the soul itself. Nor is it a move into an act that arrives like a quality, but one that proceeds like an action. If any part of the soul is called "passive," it is not understood as a subject for corporeal passions, but as a principle <note>source</note> of passions. Note again that there is a twofold imagination in us: the first is in the rational soul, capable of discourse and judgment, somewhat similar to reason; the second is impressed by this into the soul or "life" within us that lacks reason, which imagination does not use discourse so much as it is carried along by some inner instinct; but this concerns the passions of the body, which as if in common...

<meta>catchword: common</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains Plotinus’s argument that the soul and matter are "impassible," meaning they cannot be fundamentally changed or harmed by physical forces. He argues that perception and memory are active powers of the soul rather than passive receptions of external data.</summary>

--- Page 421 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Book 6 of Plotinus’s Third Ennead. The previous page introduced the concept of "impassibility"—the idea that higher realities like the soul and primary matter are not changed or "harmed" by physical interactions. This page moves into the specific relationship between essence, life, and the intellect, and contrasts "true being" with the physical world of matter.</meta>

<header>ON BOOK VI OF THE THIRD ENNEAD</header>

Common sense is the principle of the remaining senses. Sometimes, by a certain metaphor, Plotinus places imagination even in the vegetative part of the soul <note>The "vegetative soul" is the level of the soul responsible for basic biological growth and nutrition.</note>. This is neither a discursive reasoning through forms, like the first type of imagination, nor an intuition of form, like the second; rather, it is an expression of a form flourishing within itself, and through this, an impression into matter. In this process, the natural action is like a kind of "substantial imagination" that acts without actually imagining. Here you will also note that from the vegetative faculty of the soul sprout the faculties of desire and anger—just as reason naturally flows from the intellect, and then the first imagination, from which the second also flows.

### That life and intellect are contained in true essence: Also on the One which is above essence, and on the One which is below it.

In the sixth chapter, you will note that "true being" is that which is entirely being—that is, something which lacks nothing necessary for the perfection of its essence. Perfect essence includes an internal and perennial act of itself, which is life; and it requires this act to be most intimate. Such is the case if it is intelligence, for intelligence is the reflection of life back into essence. Therefore, from the first essence, as if from a root, life and intellect sprout into itself simultaneously. But such a germ is born from essence only insofar as it possesses fertility from the Good itself—I mean a shared fertility, just as a vine receives it from the sun. However, the way this fertility is distinguished into specific life and intellect comes from the essence itself; just as it is the nature of the vine that determines the power of the sun into a grape. 

Therefore, the gifts of living, understanding, and the like, flow from the Good itself as the most common principle and end, but they flow from the first essence itself as their own root and a certain formal power. Accordingly, Plotinus here accepts "true being" and "true essence" not only as Being itself—the head of all beings—but also as every form that possesses its own being and exists in its own essence. Such a form is separable from matter, and because of this, there is no potentiality or inclination toward non-being within it, and no foreign nature is mixed in. Nothing is missing for its necessary existence; the potential of the species is always realized in act. In this state, life and intellect are included equally with essence. All intellects and intellectual souls are numbered in this class of "true being." For sensible forms, which are inseparable from matter, are called "untrue beings" for the opposite reasons to those we have stated here. 

Since matter stands much further away from the first form of things than sensible forms do, and since these forms are called "true beings," matter itself is customarily called "non-being" by Plotinus and Porphyry <note>Porphyry was Plotinus's student and the editor of the Enneads.</note>, because it includes nothing formal in itself but excludes it entirely. To "be" is the function of form; for the first essence is the same as the first form, which is naturally all-form. 

To this discussion, we must bring what is both denied and then affirmed about the "One" in the *Parmenides*, and similarly what is said about "being" and "non-being" in the *Sophist* <note>Referring to Plato's dialogues *Parmenides* and *Sophist*, which were central to Neoplatonic metaphysics.</note>. You should understand "the One" in three primary ways: 
1. That which is seen as equal to being.
2. That which is superior to being. 
3. That which is inferior to it. 
Regarding the "One" that is equal to being—specifically the "first being"—all species and properties of things are affirmed equally. For it is the source and archetype of all beings. Of this it is usually said: it is the same and the other, stable and mobile, equal and unequal, great and small, and so on. For all ideal "reasons" <note>original: "rationes"; here meaning the divine blueprints or Forms</note> are present here. Regarding the "Supreme One," all these things are similarly denied: for that is not the form of these things, but their cause. Finally, regarding the "lowest One"—that is, matter—all these things are equally denied: for it has nothing formal within itself.

### That natural things are not true beings, and that matter is called non-being, and like a mirror appears to have forms which it does not truly possess.

Among these points, where he says that natural things do not so much "exist" in reality as they "seem to exist," he introduces an Epicurean <note>The Epicureans were materialists who believed only physical atoms and the void were real.</note> objection. This objection contends that corporeal things alone possess true essence, and that this is evident for two main reasons: first, because they resist anyone trying to divide them with their solidity; and second, because they strike objects with great force. 

He responds to the first point: when such hard bodies seem to resist, they are simply exposed to the one striking them for a longer time and await the blow because they are completely inept at fleeing. Because of this same ineptitude for motion and their ineffective nature, once they are divided into parts, they cannot return to their prior form. But subtler bodies, when they are struck, escape the "passion" <note>original: "passionem"; meaning the experience of being acted upon or changed</note> very quickly because of their wonderful efficacy, and due to that same efficacy, they suddenly return to themselves. 

Finally, since motion in things is a certain action and a sign of the most interior life—and since the "vestige" of life is everywhere—those things which are the least corporeal are the most ready for motion. Consequently, to the extent that things approach an incorporeal nature, they approach a life capable of motion and efficacy, and therefore approach true essence. Corporeal things, however, fall away from essence. 

In this section, he responds similarly to the second point: that corporeal things hurt more severely when they fall on something not because they are firmer, but because they are utterly weak—so much so that they cannot sustain themselves, and thus they hurt nearby things by their own ruin and fall. For those who are most inept at horsemanship are the ones who press upon and exhaust the horses most; and weak bodies are usually the most burdensome to those carrying them. 

After this, remember that matter is an empty shadow of the first essence, while material forms are various images of the Ideas contained in the first essence. These images have no similarity in nature with the Ideas, although they seem to have some similarity in their effect of representing them. And thus matter is like a mirror: while it either receives only images, or perhaps does not even receive those but only "seems" to receive them, it truly suffers nothing. This is especially true because matter cannot be resolved into anything else since it is the ultimate point, and therefore it cannot "suffer" change. Indeed, no form is contrary to matter, since it is equally and naturally exposed to all of them. Therefore, it can suffer from none of them; for the things that occur in matter do not suffer from just anything, but from their contraries. 

Likewise, matter contracts no quality or virtue of its own from the presence of a form, and therefore it does not suffer change. Otherwise, it would have long ago become "form-like" through familiarity, and thus would no longer be the most common subject, equally formable by all. Now, if it is necessary for the substance of the subject to remain in any alteration while the qualities are changed in the meantime, it is much more necessary for matter to remain throughout mundane transmutation. 

Finally, since the very goodness of nature would never allow something substantial to be resolved into nothingness, and simple substances can never be resolved into something else, it is rightly the case that neither simple forms subsisting in themselves nor simple matter can ever perish. Matter, since it is "evil"—that is, at the greatest distance from the Good itself—does not desire the Good so as to claim something natural from it for itself, but rather to put on a kind of imaginary garment from it and thus deceive. The more it remains in its formlessness, the more it is evil, or "the Evil." Matter itself does not become hot; rather, the composite object does. Matter itself sustains the heat, soon to set the heat aside like a garment, with its nature not being changed in the least. Again, when something is divided, it is the quantity and what follows from it that is divided, not the matter, which precedes quantity in nature.

# MARSILIO FICINO'S 
# COMMENTARY ON THE SIXTH BOOK, OF THE THIRD EN-
# NEAD, CONCERNING THE FACT THAT INCORPO-
# REAL THINGS DO NOT SUFFER,

### SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring floral and geometric patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

The summary of this book is to assert that an incorporeal thing cannot suffer. <note>In this context, "suffer" (Latin: *pati*) means to be acted upon or changed by an external force—the philosophical opposite of "action."</note> He calls "incorporeal" that which either includes no quantity in its own definition (even if it can receive it from the outside—this is matter), or that which excludes quantity entirely—which is the mind and the soul. Furthermore, he intends "passion" to be a change that is capable of destroying substance, whether it happens by division (which occurs to quantity and things that necessarily have quantity) or whether it happens by alteration (which occurs among contrary qualities, and also to the forms that such qualities necessarily accompany). Therefore, both primary matter and the soul are incorporeal things, claiming neither quantity nor such quality as their own; thus, they are separated from passion—the soul even more so than matter. For the soul not only does not admit destructive forms, but at times it seems not to receive any new forms at all, of whatever kind they may be. Therefore, many things are disputed in the following sections concerning the immutable essence of the rational soul and its parts; moreover, some things concerning the first essence, and many things concerning its opposite (that is, primary matter), so that it may finally be confirmed that an incorporeal thing is exempt from passion.

*The soul neither suffers, nor receives forms or qualities. Likewise concerning the double imagination.*

*In the first part of the book, then, which contains five chapters, he shows that the soul is not subject to passion; in the second part, he will thereafter show something similar regarding matter. As far as the first part is concerned, he observes that no impulse or quality from bodies falls upon the cognitive power of the soul. For whether it fell in a natural and, so to speak, material way, cognition and discernment would immediately be confused; or whether it happened at least through some imagistic condition—so that bodies would "form" the soul—this would be a wicked thing to say. For it belongs to the soul, as the superior, to form bodies, not to be formed by them. Indeed, every cognition and affect of the soul, even when turning toward bodily things, is a certain action of the soul concerning such things, and meanwhile it does not suffer therefrom. Nor does it share a common matter with bodies, the kind of communion that usually permits a mutual exchange of passion in the agent. What, then, is to perceive? It is indeed this very thing in the soul: namely, to apply itself and to exert its power toward those things to which it has a harmonious and naturally suitable essence. To remember is likewise to perform this very thing most readily. No power of knowing, therefore, is formed through new images, but the intellect is indeed always in act those very things which it knows. Reason and imagination, however, from that state in which they are potentially those things which they must think out, sometimes become in act those things which are always in act in the intellect. External sense perceives things to be sensed, but does not "receive" them. The vegetative power nourishes and moves, yet is not meanwhile nourished or moved. Porphyry <note>A student of Plotinus and a key Neoplatonic philosopher who edited the Enneads.</note> confirms all these things, showing that when the soul is said to "suffer," this passion itself is not any alteration in its nature or any quality, but a certain accommodation and affection of the soul toward this or that thing; it is a certain action of the soul regarding external things, but a "narrow" one—namely, when the soul itself contracts the amplitude of its powers and affections to a narrow point. Porphyry concludes that all which are called "movements" of the soul are not properly movements in the soul, but in the body; in the soul, they are actions, but in the body, these same things become passions. He adds that the acts of vegetation, sense, and memory are not imagistic, but in a certain way natural—just as heating, being hot, illuminating, and shining—and Plotinus thinks the same. Meanwhile, you will note that virtue in the soul is generally twofold: one kind is, as it were, "private," namely proper to one of the parts of the soul, and this consists in each part rightly performing its own duty; the other is, as it were, "public," namely that all parts harmonize rightly with one another: that reason be ruled by the mind, and the irrational powers then obey reason, among which desire should be subject to boldness. Neither virtue is like a quality impressed upon the soul as a subject (similarly neither is vice), but it is rather like movement and act, or the vacation of these. If there is indeed any quality in us, whether impressed from elsewhere by way of nature or image, or acquired by actions, such a thing is not in the soul, but rather in the body—either properly so, or so affected—in which formations and passions occur while the soul vegetates, senses, is affected, and judges. Finally, no change occurs in the soul except a progression from a certain potentiality into act; and this is not from another mover, but from the soul itself; nor, again, into an act that arrives like a quality, but one that proceeds like an action. If any part of the soul is called "passive," it is not understood as a subject for bodily passions, but as a principle of passions. You will notice again a double imagination in us: the first in the rational soul, capable of discourse and judgment, somewhat similar to reason; the second, however, impressed by the first upon the soul or life in us that lacks reason, which imagination does not use discourse so much as it is carried by an instinct, however intimate; but concerning the passions of the body, which as if*

Ficino explains that even emotions and sensory perceptions are active functions of the soul rather than passive impressions made by the body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, specifically moving into the details of Book VI of the Third Ennead. It explores the Neoplatonic hierarchy of being, from the "One" down to "prime matter," and argues that true reality resides in the incorporeal realm of intellect and life, while the physical world is merely a shadow or a reflection.</meta>

<header>ON BOOK VI OF THE THIRD ENNEAD</header>

Common sense <note>original: "communis sensus"; the internal faculty that integrates information from the five external senses</note> is the principle of the remaining senses. Plotinus sometimes uses a metaphor to place a kind of "imagination" even in the vegetative part of the soul. This is not a discursive process through forms (like the first type of imagination), nor an intuition of form (like the second); rather, it is the expression of a form flourishing within itself, and through this, an impression is made upon matter. In this state, natural action functions as a kind of substantial imagination that acts without actually "imagining." You should also note here that the faculties of desire and anger sprout from the vegetative power of the soul, just as reason flows naturally from the intellect; from reason, the first imagination flows, and from that, the second.

### That life and intellect are contained in true essence: Likewise concerning the One which is above essence, and the One which is below it.

In the sixth chapter, you will note that "true being" is that which is entirely being—that is, something which lacks nothing necessary for the perfection of its essence. Perfect essence includes an intimate and eternal act of itself, which is "life," and indeed it requires this act to be most intimate. Such is the case if it is "intelligence," for this is the reflection of life back into essence. Therefore, from the first essence, as if from a root, both life and intellect sprout into themselves. Yet a "shoot" of this kind is born from essence only insofar as essence possesses fertility from the Good itself—a shared fertility, I say, like that of a vine from the sun. However, for this fertility to be distinguished into life and intellect proper, it must come from the essence itself, just as a vine causes the power of the sun to be determined into a grape. <note>original: "vuã" / "uvam"</note> 

Therefore, the gifts of living and understanding flow from the Good itself as the most universal principle and end, but they flow from the first essence as their own root and a kind of formal power. Accordingly, Plotinus here accepts "true being" and "true essence" not only as Being itself (the head of all beings), but also as every form that possesses its own being and exists in its own essence. Such things are separable from matter, and thus contain no potentiality or inclination toward "non-being"; no foreign nature is mixed into them. Nothing is missing for their necessary existence, and their potential is always fully realized in act. In these, life and intellect are included equally with essence. All intellects and intellectual souls are of this kind, counted within the genus of true being. For sensible forms, which are inseparable from matter, are called "non-true beings" for the opposite reasons to those stated here. 

Since matter stands much further away from the first form of things than sensible forms do, and since those forms are not called true beings, it is no wonder that matter itself is customarily called "non-being" by Plotinus and Porphyry. <note>Porphyry was Plotinus's student and editor of the Enneads.</note> This is because matter includes no forms in itself, but utterly excludes them. To "be" is the gift of form, since the first essence is the same as the first form, which is naturally "all-formed." 

Here we must bring in those things said about the "One" in Plato’s *Parmenides*, which are sometimes denied and sometimes affirmed; and similarly what is said in the *Sophist* <note>Two of Plato's most complex logical dialogues.</note> concerning being and non-being. You should understand "The One" in three primary ways: either that which is seen as equal to being; or that which is higher than being; or that which is lower. Regarding the "One" that is equal to being—specifically the "first being"—all species and properties of things are equally affirmed of it. For it is the fountain and exemplar of all beings. Of this, it is usually said: it is the same and the different, stable and mobile, equal and unequal, great and small, and so on. For all the "ideal reasons" <note>The Platonic Ideas or Blueprints of reality.</note> are here. However, regarding the "supreme One," all these things are denied; for there, the One is not the *form* of these things, but their *cause*. Finally, regarding the "lowest One"—that is, matter—all these things are equally denied, for it has nothing formal within itself.

### That natural things are not true beings, and that matter is called non-being, and like a mirror it seems to have forms which it does not truly possess.

Among these points, where he says that natural things do not so much *exist* in reality as they *appear* to exist, he introduces a certain Epicurean <note>The Epicureans were materialist philosophers who believed only physical atoms and void were real.</note> objection. This objection contends that only corporeal things possess true essence, which is evident from two main points: first, because they resist something dividing them with their solidity; and second, because they strike objects forcefully. 

It is answered to the first point that such hard bodies, while they seem to resist, are merely exposed to the striker for a longer time and "wait" for the blow because they are totally unfit for flight. Because of this same unfitness for motion and their ineffective nature, once they are divided into parts, they cannot return to their prior form. But subtler bodies, when they seem to be struck, escape the "suffering" <note>original: "passionem"; here meaning the state of being acted upon or changed.</note> very quickly due to their marvelous efficacy, and because of that same efficacy, they suddenly return to themselves. Finally, since motion in things is a certain action and a sign of interior life, and since the trace of life is everywhere, those things which are least corporeal are most ready for motion. It follows that the more things approach an incorporeal nature, the more they approach a life capable of motion and efficacy, and thus they approach true essence. 

Corporeal things, however, fall away from essence. In this part, the second point is answered similarly: corporeal things, when they fall into something, hurt it more severely not because they are firmer, but because they are utterly weak—so much so that they cannot sustain themselves, and thus they hurt everything nearby by their own ruin and fall. For those who are least fit for horsemanship are the ones who press upon and exhaust the horses most; and weak bodies are usually the most burdensome to those carrying them. 

After this, remember that matter is an empty shadow of the first essence, while material forms are various images of the Ideas contained in the first essence. These images have no similarity in nature to the Ideas, even if they seem to have some similarity in their effect of representation. Therefore, matter is like a mirror: while it receives only images—or perhaps does not even receive those, but only *appears* to receive them—it truly suffers <note>In the sense of being changed or affected.</note> nothing. This is especially true because matter, being the ultimate thing, cannot be resolved into anything else, and therefore cannot suffer. Truly, no form is "contrary" to matter, since matter is naturally exposed to all forms equally. It can suffer from none of them; for even the things that occur in matter do not suffer from just anything, but from their contraries. 

Likewise, matter contracts no quality or virtue of its own from the presence of a form, and therefore does not suffer; otherwise, it would have long ago become "familiarly multiform," and would no longer be the most universal subject, equally capable of being formed by everything. If the substance of a subject must remain through any alteration while the qualities are changed, then it is much more necessary for matter to remain through the transformations of the world. Finally, since the very goodness of nature does not allow something substantial to be resolved into nothing, and simple substances cannot be resolved into anything else, it is right that neither self-subsisting simple forms nor simple matter can ever perish or suffer. 

Matter, since it is "evil"—that is, at the greatest distance from the Good itself—does not desire the Good in order to claim something natural for itself, but rather to put on a kind of imaginary garment from it and to deceive. The more it remains in its own formlessness, the more it is evil. Matter itself is not heated; rather, the "composite" <note>The combination of matter and form.</note> is. Matter sustains the heat, soon to put it aside like a garment, without its nature being changed in the least. Again, when something is divided, it is the quantity and what follows quantity that is divided, not the matter, which precedes quantity in nature.
