--- Page 424 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus, specifically examining the nature of prime matter and its relationship to the divine and the soul. Ficino uses metaphors of light, mirrors, and color to explain how the physical world is a mere reflection of a higher, intellectual reality.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO</header>

Just as in the progression of colors, the last—which is blackness—possesses nothing of the first—which is whiteness: so too **matter**, the final point in the descent of beings, possesses nothing within itself similar to the **First**, nor does it behold anything of the nature of the First in its appearance, but only certain empty imitations. And because of its extreme difference from the First, it claims for itself no flavor or scent of "being" from the presence of those images, so that it might remain equally ready to receive any forms that may arrive in the future, no matter how much they might conflict with previous ones. But above all, you should observe what Plotinus says: that natural things, if compared with divine things, have no greater substance than the images of bodies appearing in mirrors. These natural things depend perpetually on the divine in the same way that images depend on objects. This is the point of Solomon’s saying: *All is vanity* <note>original: "Omnia vanitas"; from Ecclesiastes 1:2</note>. This is also the point of Paul’s saying: *We see now through a mirror, darkly* <note>original: "Videmus nunc per speculum in ænigmate"; from 1 Corinthians 13:12</note>. But because we now see both the bodies and the mirror—upon which the images entirely depend—we therefore perceive the vanity of the images themselves. Otherwise, if we did not see the objects, we could not refute this vanity; instead, we would judge the images to be true things. In the same way, we now suppose the things called "natural" to be true substances, because we can see neither the divine things nor the matter from which and into which they leap and rebound like likenesses from objects into a mirror. Indeed, either as the physicists think, the images of things are actually in the mirrors, or as the "Perfectivists" <note>likely referring to a school of optical theory or higher Platonists</note> teach, there are no images in the mirrors at all, but the rays of things fall upon the mirror and are reflected back to the eye. This happens when they are reflected at equal angles; then the things themselves are returned to the eyes through their own rays in such a way that the sense is deceived, thinking it sees the things in a different place than it actually does. However the matter may stand, Plotinus and Porphyry maintain that the relationship of the mirror to visible things and sight is the same as the relationship of **matter** to divine things and sense. They consider this matter to be utterly opposite to Being itself; they believe it does not admit the rays of the act of the First Being and Mind into itself, but rather, like something dense and impassable because of its difference, it immediately strikes back their acts. By this very "reverberation," things appear to the senses as if they were "sensible" <note>physical things perceived by the senses</note>, which in themselves are actually "intelligible" <note>spiritual things understood by the mind</note>. This is so much the case that we think we are looking into matter at things which are actually in the First Being and Intellect, and which from there move the soul so that it may know. Finally, since these beings or **Ideas**, while they act upon matter, lose nothing of their nature, nor are they moved from their state, nor do they agree with matter in any proportion of true affection: therefore, that which seems to be given from them—as if something empty and very weak—always requires this material seat. And meanwhile, because this matter never receives anything true, nor does it truly receive what it *seems* to receive on account of its natural falsity, it is never filled; instead, it always affects a state of perpetual change.

### How much the soul towers over matter, and how a certain quantity of matter follows the mode of whatever species enters into matter.

When this wood is said to be "outside" that wood, they are separated from each other only slightly, since they are apart only by their external boundaries, while in their **species** <note>the "form" or "type" of thing they are, i.e., "woodness"</note> they are joined together. Fire is more "outside" water, for they are separated not only by external boundaries but by contrary qualities. However, since they agree in **genus** <note>the broader category, such as "element"</note> and matter, they can sometimes be mixed. But the **soul** is separated from matter by its entire genus; therefore, even though it penetrates matter, it is nonetheless further "outside" matter. For this reason, the forms which the **Soul of the World** obtains from the Divine Intellect and strives to translate everywhere into matter through its seminal power, cannot be reconciled with matter, nor can they mix with it, even though those forms may mix with each other. Furthermore, just as matter is by its own nature devoid of all forms, so too is it devoid of **quantity**; for quantity is itself a kind of form. And since quantity is the last of the forms, a certain specific quantity and shape is destined for things by the Mind and Soul according to the mode of the species’ form. Therefore, in the **formal ratios** <note>the "blueprints" or defining principles of things</note> of the species existing in the mind and soul, a certain defined quantity and shape is included which accompanies each species. In the formal ratio of a human or a horse, the quantity of the human or the horse is decreed. This quantity is released into effect because of the efficacy of the formal ratio everywhere, and its particular motion in action, and because of the "procession" <note>the flowing out of divine power into the world</note> of the natural form emanating from it. Thus, by this efficacy, motion, and procession, matter itself is produced into a "mass" upon its surface—a mass as large as the form itself requires: a worldly mass for the world, a human one for a human, a leonine one for a lion. And just as a specific quantity comes into matter along with any species, so it departs with the species; and upon the subsequent arrival of a new species, a new quantity is made, just as the quality proper to the species is made. Quantity is produced in matter according to the "distance" from the quantity of the acting power and its formal motion. Matter, on account of its own weakness, cannot avoid such motion, nor can it receive forms without such a "distraction" or stretching. But the **Soul**, because it is itself a kind of form and a subsisting species, embraces all the species of things as if in a single center. For this "form" (the Soul) receives those forms in the "manner of a form": and the manner of forms is that each one, as if simple, is collected whole within any part of itself, and all are most easily concluded within each one. From this it follows that our reason can comprehend forms both without numerical multitude (in the unity of the species itself) and can separate them from the dimension of quantity. But matter always receives forms with a certain extension, because it is dragged everywhere to the motion of the form proceeding divinely over it; meanwhile, its nature willingly yields to this dragging, prepared for any mass anywhere, since it possesses no mass of its own. And while it is extended into dimension through the entire space of the world, it is not divided into many "matters," but remains unique and continuous—both because it is not subject to suffering <note>it does not "feel" or get hurt by being stretched</note>, and because it follows the extending power not in life, but willingly, being extended by a single ratio toward the one form of the universe. This matter is, as it were, the **mother of the world**, and is even less than a mother. The **Father**, however, is that ancient **Mercury** <note>Ficino identifies the Greek god Hermes/Mercury with the Logos or Divine Reason</note> whom they wish to be both the "seminal ratio" of the world within the nature of the World Soul, and also the "ideal ratio" of all things in the Divine Mind. And in truth, the "ideal ratio" is the Father of the universe; the "seminal ratio" is the Mother, insofar as it has some commerce with matter and is filled from above. Matter, however, is the "matrix" <note>the womb or mold</note> and the place of generation and reception. But you should remember that in the planet Mercury there is both the gift of **contemplation** from the Divine Mind and of **action** from the nature of the world; hence from him is given a genius suited either for contemplations, or for actions and arts, or sometimes vigorous in both. If Mercury regards **Saturn** in a trine or sextile aspect <note>astrological alignments thought to be harmonious</note>, or occupies Saturn’s house, he favors contemplation most of all. If he regards **Mars**, he breathes rather toward action. If he regards **Jupiter**, he breathes successfully upon both offices. If he looks upon **Venus**, he designates a sweetness of genius together with eloquence and ornament.

# P L O T I N U S
## ENNEAD THREE
### BOOK VI.

# P L O T I N U S
## THIRD ENNEAD
### BOOK VI.

->On the impassibility of incorporeal beings.<-
<note>original Greek: "ΠΕΡΙ ἀπαθείας τῶν ἀσωμάτων"; Latin: "De impassibilitate incorporeorum"</note>

---

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>Regarding the kind of judgment... that the judgment occurs.</margin>
If we say that senses are not passions <note>The word "passion" (Greek: *pathos*) here refers to a state of being acted upon or suffering a change, rather than just an emotion.</note>, but rather activities concerning passions and judgments—where the passions occur in something else, such as the body receiving the influence, while the judgment belongs to the soul—then the judgment itself is not a passion. If it were, we would need another judgment to judge that one, and so on to infinity. Nevertheless, a difficulty
<margin>B</margin>
arises here: whether the judgment itself, in the act of judging, contains nothing of the thing being judged; for if it possesses a "form" or "impression" of it, it would seem to have been "affected" <note>suffered a passion</note>. Even if we speak of so-called
<margin>* called impressions.</margin>
"impressions" <note>original: "τυπώσεων" (typōseōn)</note>, the manner of this is entirely different, similar to how the intellect receives thoughts. These are activities that are capable of knowing passions without themselves being subject to them. Indeed, our entire
<margin>C</margin>
reasoning and our will aim to ensure that the soul is not subject to such turnings and alterations as the heating or cooling of bodies. We must also carefully examine the part of the soul called "passible" <note>the part capable of feeling or being affected</note> to see whether we should grant it immutability, or concede that it alone suffers passion. But we shall discuss this later; for now, let us address the primary doubts. For how can that which is
<margin>D</margin>
prior to the passible part and the senses—indeed, the soul as a whole—be immutable, especially when
<margin>* occurring.</margin>
vice occurs within it, along with false opinions, ignorance, and the soul’s becoming familiar or alienated, feeling pleasure or pain, being angry, envious, jealous, or desiring—never at rest, but moved and transformed
<margin>E</margin>
<margin>* has magnitude, or something.</margin>
by everything that happens to it? If the soul were a body or possessed magnitude, it would be difficult—indeed, entirely impossible—to show that it is impassive and immutable in any of these things said to happen to it. But if it is an essence without magnitude, and it must be...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>I / The soul, by sensing and giving life, does not itself suffer the passions of the body.</margin>
If we say that the senses are not passions, but actions and judgments concerning passions—which passions occur in something else, perhaps in a body of a certain kind, while the judgment is in the soul—then the judgment does not become a passion itself. Otherwise, there would have to be another judgment, and so one would proceed to infinity. If, I say, we speak this way, it will nonetheless
<margin>B</margin>
be possible to doubt whether the judgment itself, by the very reason it is a judgment, has nothing within itself of that which is judged; or whether it has some "form" of it, by having which it would seem to have already suffered a passion. One may indeed speak of those things which are called "formations" of the senses or of the intellect itself, but they occur in a far different way than most people think. This is especially apparent in the acts of the intellect themselves, which are also actions, capable of knowing something without passion. Truly, our
<margin>C</margin>
reason and our will desire that the soul not be subjected to such conversions and mutations as are the heatings and coolings of bodies. It is also necessary to consider diligently the part of the soul which is called "passible," whether we should confess this part also to be immutable, or grant some passion to this alone. But of this in what follows. Now, however, let us discuss the doubts of the earlier points. It is certainly doubted in what way that can be immutable which is
<margin>D</margin>

Again, there is conformity and disconformity when it rejoices, grieves, is angry, envies, emulates, and affects; it never rests, but at every incident, it is moved and changed. But if the soul
<margin>E</margin>
is a body and has magnitude, it is difficult, or even impossible, to show it to be impassive and immutable in any of those things which are said to happen to it. But if it is an essence devoid of magnitude, it must...

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD III.
### PAGE 304

If we are to grant that the soul is incorruptible, we must be careful not to grant it such passions <note>original Latin: "passiones"; Greek: "πάθη" (pathe). In this context, "passion" refers to any state of being acted upon or undergoing a physical change, not just an emotion.</note>, lest we unknowingly admit that it is corruptible. Furthermore, if its essence is either number or reason <note>original Latin: "ratio"; Greek: "λόγος" (logos)</note> (as we are accustomed to say), in what way could any passion happen to a number or a reason? Instead, we should think that irrational reasons and impassible passions occur within it; these are transferred from bodies into the soul and must be understood as opposites, translated as if by an analogical proportion. Thus, the soul "has" these things without truly possessing them, and "suffers" them without truly being affected, and we must consider what the nature of such a mode of being is.

<margin>II. What virtue is, what vice is, and that they are not qualities in the soul, but acts.</margin>
First, we must speak regarding virtue and vice, and what occurs when vice is said to be present in the soul. Indeed, we often say that it is necessary to "remove" something from the wicked person, as if there were some evil within them; likewise, we speak of "applying" virtue and "adorning" them, bringing forth beauty to replace ugliness. Now, if we say that virtue is a certain harmony <note>original: "consonantiam"; Greek: "ἁρμονίαν" (harmonian)</note> and vice is a certain dissonance, are we not bringing forward an opinion consistent with the ancients? Moreover, this will lead us toward what we are seeking. For if virtue is this very thing—namely, that the parts of the soul are in concord with one another according to nature—and vice is their discord, then nothing external or adventitious comes to us. Instead, each part will enter into a harmony just as it is in itself. Nor would it enter into dissonance while remaining as it is, much like dancers leaping and singing together in harmony; even if they are not the same, or if one sings alone while others are silent, or each sings by himself. For it is not only necessary to sing together, but for each to sing his own music rightly according to his own part, so that there is a harmony in the soul when each part performs what is agreeable to itself. Indeed, before this harmony itself, there must be another virtue of each individual part, or another depravity before their mutual dissonance. By the presence of what, then, is any part evil? Perhaps by the presence of vice. By what is it good? By the presence of virtue. In the rational part, if one admits that ignorance is its vice—ignorance, I say, defined as the negation of knowledge—this would not imply the presence of anything "added." But when false opinions are also present, which are the primary cause of vice, what prevents something from happening "inside" there? And thus that part of the soul would have already been changed into some quality. Furthermore, is not the nature of anger affected differently when it is cowardly than when it is brave? Likewise, the power of desire is disposed one way when it is intemperate, and another when it is temperate. Perhaps, however, when anything is judged to be endowed with virtue, it then acts according to that essence by which it exists; and we say this is to obey reason. The rational faculty is governed by the intellect, and the others by reason. Perhaps "obeying reason" is like "seeing," where that which obeys and sees is not shaped into a new form, but simply looks, and exists in activity while it sees.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> To be present to it as incorruptible, one must be cautious of giving it such passions, lest we forgetfully grant it to be corruptible. And indeed, whether its essence is number or reason, as we say, how could a passion arise in number or reason? But rather, <gloss>reason</gloss> * irrational reasons and impassible passions must be thought to occur in it. And these things, transferred from bodies, must be taken as opposites, and <margin>B</margin> transferred according to analogy; they have them without having them, and suffer them <note>The Greek "πάσχουσιν" (paschousin) implies undergoing an experience.</note>, and the manner of such things must be examined.

<margin>C</margin> FIRST, one must speak about vice and virtue, what happens then, when vice is said to be present. For we say it is necessary to "take away," * <gloss>as if there were still</gloss> as if there were some evil in it, and to "put in" virtue and to adorn it, and <gloss>evil in it</gloss> to instill beauty * instead of ugliness or in place of what was there before. If then we say virtue is harmony, and vice is dissonance, would we be stating an opinion that seemed right to the ancients? And yet, for the question at hand, the argument will be of no small help. For if the parts of the soul being harmonized with one another according to nature is virtue, and not being harmonized is vice, <margin>D</margin> then nothing would be brought in from the outside. But each part would be as it is in relation to the harmony; and it would not be unknown if it were a discordant thing, just as strings sounding * <gloss>and sounding</gloss> and harmonizing with one another. Even if they are not the same, <gloss>one</gloss> or if someone is singing alone, the others not singing, and each singing by himself. And not only must they sing together, but each must sing his own part well with his own music, so that <margin>E</margin> there is harmony in the soul when each part does what is fitting for itself. It is necessary then, before * <gloss>this</gloss> this harmony, that there be another virtue for each part, and a vice for each, before their mutual dissonance. By the presence of what, then, is each part evil, or by vice, and good for it, by virtue? In the rational part, perhaps someone saying that ignorance is vice—and ignorance <margin>F</margin> by way of negation—would not be speaking of a presence of something. But when false opinions are within, which especially makes for vice, how will he say it does not arise there, * <gloss>and there</gloss> and just as <gloss>in this way by the part becoming</gloss> in this way by the part becoming [something]? And the spirited part <note>original: "θυμοειδές" (thymoeides), the part of the soul associated with anger and courage.</note>, is it not one way being cowardly, and another way being brave? And the desiring part, being intemperate, is it not one way; and being temperate, another way than what it has suffered? Or when each is in virtue, it <margin>G</margin> acts according to the essence which each is? * <gloss>it will be</gloss> We shall say it is according to reason. And the rational part, <gloss>it will be</gloss> <unclear>intellect</unclear>; and the others, as if from this, or being affected in reason as if seeing—not being shaped, but seeing; and being in activity, when it sees.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul's essence is reason and number, making it fundamentally impassible (unable to be changed by physical forces). He redefines virtue not as an added quality, but as the internal harmony of the soul's parts acting according to their true nature and reason.</summary>

# BOOK SIX.
### C i
<meta>catchword: iii</meta>

Just as sight exists both as a power and in act, it remains one and the same in its underlying substance. Its activity is not an "alteration" <note>Greek: ἀλλοίωσις (alloiosis); Latin: alteratio. In ancient philosophy, this refers to a change in quality, like turning from cold to hot.</note>, but rather it applies itself all at once to that for which its essence is suited; it sees and knows without being affected <note>original: "ἀπαθῶς" (apathes); Latin: "procul à passione". Plotinus argues that knowing something doesn't "hurt" or change the soul the way heat changes wax.</note>. Furthermore, the reasoning faculty relates to the intellect in this same way: it sees. This power of intellection is like this—not that it receives impressions within itself as if from a seal, but it possesses what it sees, and yet, in another sense, it does not. It possesses it through the act of knowing, but does not possess it in the sense of being shaped by the vision, as happens in wax. We must remember that memory is not a preservation of impressed forms, but a certain power of the soul awakening itself so that it "has" what it previously did not have. What then? Was the soul one thing before it remembered, and another when it remembers? You may call it "different" if you like, but do not call it altered, unless perhaps one uses "alteration" to describe the progression from power into act. Indeed, nothing is added there; the soul simply brings about what it is naturally able to do. In general, the actions of immaterial things do not occur by the acting powers themselves being altered—otherwise, they would perish—but rather they perform their work by remaining as they are. It is the condition of things joined with matter that the agent is affected while acting. But for that which is immaterial to be affected <note>original: "πάσχειν" (paschein). To "suffer" or be "passive" to an outside influence.</note>, it has no way to remain itself. Just as in the act of looking, the vision is the agent, but the eye is what is affected. Opinions are like certain visions.

But in what way is the spirited nature <note>original: "τὸ θυμοειδὲς" (to thymoeides). This refers to the part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and "spirit."</note> cowardly? And in what way is it brave? Perhaps it is cowardly because it either does not look toward reason, or it looks toward a reason that is already corrupted, or because of a defect in its instruments—such as a lack or a weakness in its bodily "weapons"—or because it is prevented from acting, or not stirred to action. It is brave, however, if the opposite occurs. In these cases, there is no alteration or passion. Again, the power of desire itself, whenever it acts alone, brings about what we call "excess." For sometimes it acts alone, and the other parts are not present which, when they are present, can take turns mastering it and giving it orders. The faculty involved in seeing sometimes does something else; for it does not do everything at once, but is at leisure in some respects, because it observes other things as much as it can. Perhaps, indeed, a poor habit of the body is the "depravity" of this part, while virtue is the opposite habit. Therefore, no addition is made to the soul from either side.

<margin>The soul is not the subject of bodily passions, but the source.</margin>
It was asked, however, how similarities, differences, pains, angers, pleasures, desires, and fears are not permutations and passions that move the inner parts. Surely we must distinguish these things also: to deny that alterations and the violent sensations of these things happen to us would be to deny the obvious. Therefore, while conceding that these things happen, we must investigate *what* it is that is being changed. For if we grant such things to the soul, we risk admitting something similar to saying the soul itself becomes red or pale, failing to consider that it is *because* of the soul...

<column-break/>

Just as vision exists both in potential and in act, it is one and the same essence. The act, however, is not an alteration, but rather it applies itself at once to that for which it has an accommodated essence, and it discerns and knows far removed from any "passion" <note>original Latin: "passione". In this context, it means being acted upon by an external force.</note>. Furthermore, the faculty of reasoning stands in this relation to the intellect and sees; the power of understanding is such a thing, not because it receives impressions inside as if from a signet-ring, but it holds what it sees, and again, it does not hold it. For it holds it by the fact that it knows, but it does not B hold it because nothing of the spectacle is imprinted upon it there, as a shape is usually made in wax. One must truly remember that memory is also not a kind of guardianship over imprinted forms, but a certain faculty of the soul exciting itself, so that it holds even what it does not "possess." What then? Was it not one thing before it remembered, and another again when it now remembers? If it pleases you to call it another thing, do not however say it is C altered, unless perhaps someone names a certain progression from power into act "alteration." Yet nothing is added there; rather, it effects what it is able to do by nature. Generally, the actions of immaterial things do not happen in such a way that the very powers which act are meanwhile altered—otherwise they would also perish—but rather they act by remaining. That an agent should be affected by acting is a condition of things that are with matter. But that which is solely immaterial should be affected, D it has no way to remain [as it was]; just as in sight, while the vision is acting, it is the eye that is affected. Opinions, however, are like certain visions. But in what way is the nature of anger <note>original Latin: "irascendi natura". Translating the Greek 'thymoeides'.</note> timid? And in what way is it brave? Perhaps it is timid because it either does not look at reason, or it looks at a reason that is already bad, or by a vice of the instruments as if by a defect, or by a shakiness of the bodily weapons, or it is prohibited from acting, or not incited. It is brave, however, if the opposite happens: in which there is no alteration, there is no E passion. Again, the very power of desiring, as often as it acts alone, brings about intemperance. For sometimes it acts all alone, and then the rest are not present, which are permitted (when they are sometimes present) to overcome in turn and to command it. That which is occupied in seeing meanwhile does something else; for it does not do everything, but is at leisure elsewhere, because it gazes upon certain other things as much as it can. Perhaps, indeed, a very bad condition of the body is the "depravity" of this, while virtue is the F contrary condition: wherefore no addition is made to the soul from either side.

<margin>The soul is not the subject of bodily passions, but the principle.</margin>
G It was asked, however, how conformities, disconformities, pains, angers, pleasures, desires, and fears are not permutations and passions moving the internal things. Surely it is necessary to distinguish concerning these things also: to deny indeed that alterations and their vehement senses happen to us is to deny what is manifest to all. It is necessary, therefore, while granting that, to inquire what it is that is transmuted. Surely if we grant such things regarding the soul, we will seem to admit something similar: just as if we granted that the soul is red or pale, by no means noticing that it is *because* of the soul...

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK III.

Indeed, such passions <note>Greek: πάθη (pathe); Latin: passiones. In this context, "passions" refers to anything the soul "undergoes" or suffers, including emotions and physical sensations.</note> do occur, but they take place in something else—namely, the composite [of soul and body]. Indeed, shame itself exists in the soul as an opinion <note>original: "δόξα" (doxa); Latin: "opinio". For Plotinus, this is a cognitive judgment rather than a physical feeling.</note> regarding something disgraceful. However, because the soul contains the body—to ensure we do not wander in our definitions—we must say that the body is within the containing soul; it is not the same as an inanimate body. This body, I say, undergoes a change in its blood due to the soul's shame, especially if it is easily moved. Furthermore, the beginning of fear is in the soul, while paleness is in the body as the blood retreats to the interior. Likewise, in the case of sensible pleasure, the obvious diffusion and expansion happens in the body. But what then occurs in the soul is not a "passion." We must say the same regarding grief. Even in the impulse of desire, the beginning of the longing exists in the soul, hidden at the start, as it were; but what proceeds from there is then perceived by the senses. Now, when we say the soul is "moved" by lusts, by the wanderings of reason, or by opinions, we by no means understand that the soul is being tossed about in these things, but rather that the motions arise *from* the soul itself. Since we say that "to live" is to be moved, we do not mean that life is an alteration <note>original: "ἀλλοίωσις" (alloiosis). A qualitative change, like a cold object becoming hot.</note>; rather, the natural action of each part is a life that does not depart from itself. In short, the following summary will suffice: if we do not admit that actions, lives, and desires are alterations, and if we do not grant that memories are forms impressed upon the mind, nor that imaginations are configurations shaped as if in wax, then it follows—without controversy—that in all things called actions and motions, the soul remains the same in its underlying subject and essence. Therefore, virtue and vice do not arise in the soul in the same way that "white" and "black," or "hot" and "cold," occur in the body; rather, the soul relates to both virtue and vice in the way we have described—through entirely opposite dispositions.

<margin>IIII. Confirmation of the above, and regarding the double imagination.</margin>
## WE MUST NOW CONSIDER that part
of the soul which is usually called "passive" <note>original: "παθητικός" (pathetikos); Latin: "passiua". This refers to the part of the soul capable of being affected by external things.</note>. Although something has already been said of this where we discussed all the passions that arise in the nature of "spiritedness" or "desire" and how they occur, something more must nevertheless be said on this subject. First, we must define what exactly this "passive" element in the soul is called. That is said to be "passible" <note>capable of undergoing a change or suffering</note> around which the passions seem to revolve; these are the things followed by pleasure or pain. Some passions arise from opinions: for instance, when someone fears because they believe they are about to die, or rejoices because they believe a good thing is coming to them. In such cases, the opinion is in one part [of the soul], while the disturbance is incited in another. Other passions are of such a kind that, arising unexpectedly, they produce an opinion in that part which is naturally capable of forming opinions. We have already said that while an opinion is being formed, the one forming the opinion remains, in the meantime, unmoved. However, when an unexpected fear approaches, if it is traced higher up, it takes its beginning again from an opinion, providing a sort of perception to the fearing part of the soul. What, then, does this fear itself do? <meta>catchword: pers- (perhaps)</meta>

<column-break/>

->A<- These are the passions, but concerning the others, they do not occur as mere states. ->B<- inward. And in pleasure, the diffusion reaches the senses and concerns the body; but what concerns the soul is no longer a passion. The same applies to grief, and also to desire: while the beginning of the desiring is in the soul, it is hidden; but the sense-perception knows what has come from there. And when we say the soul is moved in desires, in reasonings, and in opinions, we do not say that she is diminished
->C<- in doing these things, but that the motions come from her. For even in calling life a "motion," we do not mean it is an alteration; the activity of each part according to its nature is a life that does not depart from itself. In summary, it is sufficient that we do not concede that activities, lives, and desires are alterations, nor that memories are seals stamped in, nor that imaginations <note>original: "φαντασίας" (phantasias)</note> are impressions as if in wax.
->D<- It must be conceded everywhere that in all the so-called passions and motions, the soul remains the same in its substrate and essence. And virtue and vice do not occur like black and white in the body, or hot and cold; but rather in the way it has been said concerning both, they occur regarding all opposites generally.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the "impassibility" of the soul. Having previously argued that intellectual functions are not physical changes, he now examines "Phantasia" (Imagination) and how bodily reactions like trembling or paleness relate to the soul's higher functions.</meta>

# BOOK SIX.

<column-break/>

<margin>They say that shock is a state of consternation at an expected evil.</margin>
Disturbances, and the manifestations of evils, or what they call the "stumbles" of things perceived. It is clear that Imagination <note>original: "Φαντασία" (Phantasia). In Neoplatonism, this is the faculty that bridges the gap between raw sensory data and pure intellectual thought.</note> resides in the soul—both the primary sort, which we call "opinion," and that which arises from it, which is not exactly an opinion but a dim, lower shadow, like an uncritical representation. This lower imagination exists in what we call "nature," and it performs each of its actions, as they say, without conscious representation. This can be understood by the fact that the resulting sensory disturbance occurs in the body—the trembling, the shaking of the frame, the paleness, and the inability to speak. These things belong to the physical part. Should we say the soul itself is bodily, since it undergoes these things? Or rather, that these effects reach the body because the soul sends out the impulse for them to happen, while the soul itself is "overcome" <note>original: "κατέχεσθαι" (katechesthai). Suggesting the soul is gripped by the experience without its essence being altered.</note> by the passion and stands outside itself? Yet, the "passive" part of the soul is either a body or a "form" <note>original: "εἶδος" (eidos). Here meaning the organizing principle or blueprint of the body.</note> within matter. The "matter" belongs to the spirit <note>original: "θυμοῦ" (thymou); Latin: "concupifcēdi". The irascible or desiring part of the soul.</note>, as well as the nutritive, augmentative, and generative powers, which are the root and principle of the desiring and passive form. But no disturbance or "passion" should be present in the form itself. Instead, the form remains empty of passion, while the matter enters a state of passion whenever it occurs through the presence of that which moves it. For the "vegetative" <margin>* The vegetative part</margin> or "natural" power does not itself "grow" when it causes growth, nor is it increased when it increases something else. In general, when it moves something, it is not moved by the same motion it imparts. Rather, it moves either not at all, or by some other mode of motion or activity. It is necessary, therefore, that the nature of the "form" be an activity, and that it acts by its mere presence, just as if a "harmony" <note>Plotinus uses the analogy of music to show that the governing principle (the harmony) remains perfect and unchanged even when the physical strings are struck and vibrate.</note> moved the strings by itself. Therefore, the "passive" part of the soul will be the cause of the passion—whether the motion of the passion arises from the sensory imagination, or even without imagination. We must consider this: if "opinion" starts from above, while the soul itself remains in the state of "harmony," the causes of the motion would be analogous to a musician, while the parts struck through the passion would be like the strings. For even there, the harmony does not "suffer," but the string does. <margin>* or if</margin> Even if the musician wished it, the string would not be moved correctly unless the harmony dictated it.

### WHY then must we strive through philosophy to make the soul "impassible," if it does not suffer passion from the beginning?
Perhaps it is because what is called the "passive part" casts a kind of "phantasm" or image into the soul; the subsequent passion causes disturbance, and this disturbance is joined to the expectation of an unwanted evil. <margin>* This refers to what is so-called</margin> Philosophy thinks it right to totally remove such a passion. We do not say that passion "comes to be" in the soul as if the soul were not already healthy; rather, the soul is "sane" when the imagination—which is the cause of the passion—is not allowed to take root or produce a "vision" within it. It is like someone wishing to drive away the images of a dream while awake...

<meta>catchword: impassible</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> They say that a disturbance and a stirring up occur in the estimation and expectation of evil. It is certain that Imagination truly exists in the soul—both the first sort, which we call opinion, and that which is born from it. This latter is not further "opinion," but is concerned with that which is lower; it is like a thin and obscure opinion, an undiscriminating imagination. Such a thing exists in nature as a kind of action, insofar as it does each thing, as is commonly said, without the office of imagination. <margin>B</margin> It is clear that the resulting sensory disturbance happens in the body, such as trembling, shaking, paleness, and the impediment of the voice. For such things do not occur in any part of the soul; otherwise, we would call that part "bodily." If any part of the soul "suffered" such things, they would not also reach the body. Indeed, the very thing whose office it is to "send" these signals would no longer perform the sending, because it would be already oppressed by the passions and distracted from itself. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, that which is called "passive" in the soul is not a body, but some "form" <note>term: Species/Form. In this context, it refers to the non-physical 'shape' or 'logic' that gives the body its life and functions.</note> existing within matter. It includes the faculty of desiring, as well as the power of nourishing, increasing, and generating—which is indeed the root and principle of the desiring and passive form. But no disturbance or passion ought to happen to the "form"; it should remain as it is. Its matter, however, undergoes the passion whenever the passion creeps in through the presence of that mover. For the "vegetative" principle does not "vegetate" <note>i.e., it does not undergo the process of growth itself; it is the *cause* of growth in the plant.</note> when it causes growth, nor is it increased when it increases another. In general, when it moves something, it is not moved by that motion with which it moves; it is said to be moved either not at all, or by some other reason of motion or action. <margin>D</margin> It is necessary, therefore, that the nature of the "form" itself be an "act," and that it acts by its presence—as if harmony moved the strings by itself. Therefore, that which is called "passive" in the soul will be the cause of passion—whether the motion of the passion is made by the soul itself from the sensory imagination, or even apart from imagination. Furthermore, it must be considered whether, while "opinion" begins from above, <margin>E</margin> the soul remains in the state of "harmony," while the causes of the moving are compared to a musician, and then those things which are struck through passion represent the strings. For there, it is not the harmony that "suffers," but the string; nor is the string moved rightly—even if the musician wills it—unless the harmony has dictated it.

<margin>V
To purge the soul is not to remove a quality, but to direct the affection.</margin>
### WHY, therefore, must we contend that we should make the soul free from passion through the study of philosophy?
Indeed, the soul does not "suffer" even from the beginning. <margin>F</margin> Perhaps it is because from that which is called "passive," a certain imagination falls into the soul, which then follows and brings in passion and disturbance. To this disturbance is joined the "opinionated image" of an evil. Philosophical reason commands us to extirpate such a passion and not permit it to sprout anywhere—as if, wherever it is born, the soul is not yet prospering, but where it does not germinate, the soul is healthy. This is because the imagination, which is the cause of the passion, has not yet fallen into it—just as if someone, desiring to shake off the troublesome visions of dreams...

<summary>This page explores how the soul remains essentially unchanged ("impassible") even when the body experiences strong emotions like fear or shame. Plotinus uses the metaphor of musical harmony to explain that the soul is the governing principle that causes physical reactions without itself being physically altered.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the "impassibility" (the inability to be affected or changed by external forces) of the soul. Following the discussion on how sensory shocks affect the body but perhaps not the soul's essence, he now examines whether "virtue" and "vice" are actual changes in the soul or merely states of harmony and discord.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD III.

<margin>A</margin>
Since we must maintain that the soul is incorruptible, we must be careful not to grant it such "passions" <note>original: "passiones" / "πάθη" (pathe). In this context, "passions" are not just emotions, but any way in which an external force "acts upon" or changes a subject.</note> that we might accidentally admit it is subject to decay. Indeed, if its essence is "number" or "reason" <note>original: "λόγος" (logos). Plotinus considers the soul as a rational structure or a mathematical-like principle of order.</note>, as we often say, how could any passion happen to a number or a reason? Rather, we should think that "irrational reasons" and "impassible passions" arise within it. These are transferred from the body to the soul and must be understood through a kind of opposition or analogy. Thus, the soul "has" these things without truly possessing them, and "suffers" them without truly being affected. We must consider how such a mode of existence is possible.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>II
What virtue is, what vice is, and that they are not like qualities in the soul, but like dispositions <note>original: "πείσεις" (peiseis). This suggests a state of being or a "way of holding oneself" rather than a physical change in substance.</note>.</margin>
FIRST, we must speak of virtue and vice: what exactly happens when vice is said to be present in the soul? For we often say that one ought to "remove" something from a wicked person, as if there were some actual "evil" inside them. Likewise, we speak of "applying" virtue, "adorning" the soul, and bringing "beauty" to replace a previous ugliness. Should we then follow the ancient opinion and say that virtue is a kind of harmony <note>original: "consonantiam" / "ἁρμονίαν" (harmonian). A reference to the Pythagorean and Platonic idea that a good soul is one where the parts "sing" together in tune.</note>, while vice is a dissonance? This would certainly help our inquiry. <margin>C</margin> For if virtue consists in this—that the parts of the soul are in accord with one another according to nature—and vice consists in their being discordant, then nothing "extra" comes to us from the outside. Instead, each part simply enters into a state of agreement according to what it already is. A soul would not fall into discord by having its parts change their nature, just as dancers <margin>D</margin> who sing together do not change who they are. Even if they are not all the same, and even if one sings while others are silent, or if each sings his own part, they must do more than just sing together; each must sing his own part well, with his own proper music. Thus, in the soul, harmony exists when each part performs what is appropriate to itself. It follows that before this harmony can exist, there must be another <margin>E</margin> virtue for each individual part, or another depravity for each part before they fall into mutual discord. What, then, is present when a part is "bad"? Perhaps it is vice. And when it is "good"? Virtue. In the rational part, if one admits that "ignorance" is its vice—meaning ignorance as a simple lack of knowledge—then no actual "thing" is present there. But when "false opinions" are present (which are the primary cause of vice), what prevents something from actually forming inside the soul? If so, that part of the soul would have been <margin>F</margin> transformed into a different "quality." Furthermore, is the nature of anger not affected differently when it is cowardly versus when it is brave? Likewise, is the faculty of desire not disposed differently when it is intemperate compared to when it is temperate? Perhaps, however, whenever a part is judged to possess virtue, it is simply acting according to its "essence" <note>original: "essentiam" / "οὐσίαν" (ousian). Its true, fundamental nature.</note>, which is what it truly is. We say this is "obeying reason." The rational faculty is ruled by the Intellect, while the other parts are ruled by Reason. <margin>G</margin> Perhaps "obeying reason" is like the act of seeing: while the part obeys and sees, it is not physically reshaped or "figured," but simply looks, and exists in a state of "actuality" <note>original: "actu" / "ἐνεργείᾳ" (energeia). Active expression as opposed to passive change.</note> when it sees.

<column-break/>

We must be careful to preserve its incorruptibility, ensuring we do not grant it passions of such a kind that we unthinkingly grant it to be corruptible. Indeed, if its essence is number or reason, as we say, how could a passion occur in a number or a reason? Rather, we must think that "reasons to irrationalities" <margin>reasons and reasons</margin> and impassible passions must supervene upon it. These are things transferred from bodies; each must be taken in an opposite sense and transferred by analogy, such that they possess without possessing and suffer without suffering. We must examine what the manner of such things is.

FIRST, we must speak about vice and virtue, and what occurs when vice is said to be present. For we say it is necessary to "remove" it, <margin>as if something evil were existing in it as a cause. And</margin> and to "place" virtue in it and to "adorn" it, and to produce "beauty" in place of the former "ugliness." Now, by saying that virtue is a harmony and vice is a lack of harmony, would we be stating an opinion held by the ancients? Certainly, this argument would contribute significantly to our inquiry. For if virtue is the parts of the soul being harmonized with one another according to nature, and vice is their not being harmonized, then virtue would be something added, and would not arise from elsewhere. Rather, each part is wherever it is, being what it is in relation to the harmony. Dissonance would not arise from "neighbors" (as strings <margin>and the use for some</margin> harmonizing with strings), even if they are not the same, or if one sings alone while others do not, or each sings by itself. It is not only necessary to sing together, but for each to sing his own part well with his own music, so that there too in the soul there is a harmony when each part does what is fitting for it. But before this harmony <margin>itself</margin> there must be another virtue of each part, and a vice of each, before their mutual dissonance. By the presence of what, then, is each part evil? Perhaps by the presence of vice or virtue. In the rational part, if one says that ignorance is its vice—ignorance in the sense of a negation—he would not be speaking of a "presence" of something. But when false opinions are also present, which especially produce vice, how will he say that they do not "enter into" it? <margin>and entirely by this, that the part becomes</margin> And that by this, the part is changed into something else, like heights. But the spirited part is not in one state when cowardly and another when brave. And the desiring part is not one way when intemperate and another when temperate, as if it has "suffered" something. Or, when each part is in a state of virtue, it acts according to its essence, which is what each part is. <margin>to speak</margin> We shall say this is "according to reason." And the reasoning part acts like the others; or rather, to be "affected" by reason is like "seeing"—it is not being stamped with a shape, but it is seeing and being in a state of "activity" when it sees.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul’s essence as "Reason" or "Number" makes it impossible for it to be physically altered by "passions." He explores the idea that virtue is a state of internal harmony (where each part performs its own nature) rather than a physical quality added to the soul's substance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the "impassibility" of the soul—the idea that the soul's essence is never actually changed or damaged by external experiences. He is currently arguing that mental activities like "seeing," "thinking," and "remembering" are not physical impressions (like a seal in wax) but are "actualities" that leave the soul’s substance untouched.</meta>

# BOOK SIX.

Just as sight is both a potentiality and an actuality, it is one and the same in its underlying essence. This "actuality" is not an alteration <note>original: "ἀλλοίωσις" (alloiôsis). In Greek philosophy, this refers to a change in quality (like turning red), which Plotinus argues does not happen to the soul's essence.</note>, but rather a simultaneous grasping of that which defines its essence; it is a state of knowing, and it knows without being affected. The reasoning faculty relates to the intellect in this same way: it "sees." This power of thinking is not like a seal being pressed into wax; rather, the soul "has" what it sees and yet does not have it. It "has" it through the act of knowing, but does not "have" it in the sense of being reshaped by the vision, as a form is shaped in wax. 

We must remember that we do not say memories exist within a physical substrate <note>original: "ὑποκειμένῳ" (hypokeimenô). A philosophical term for a "subject" or "underlying matter" that receives qualities.</note>. Instead, memory is a power of the soul that holds onto things so firmly that it "has" even what it does not physically possess. If the soul is no different before remembering and after remembering—except for the act of remembering itself—then it has not been "altered" in the physical sense, unless one calls the transition from potentiality to actuality an "alteration." But in truth, this is simply the soul doing what it was naturally born to do. 

<margin>* a traveler or someone</margin> 
Generally, the activities of immaterial things do not occur through their being altered; if they were, they would be corrupted. Rather, they act while remaining exactly as they are. To "suffer" or "be affected" while acting is a condition of things made of matter. But if something immaterial were to "suffer," it would have no way to remain itself. Just as in the case of sight: while the vision is the active force, it is the eye that is the "suffering" or affected organ. 

Opinions, however, are like the visions themselves. How then can the spirited part <note>original: "θυμοειδὲς" (thymoeides). Plato's term for the part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and social standing.</note> of the soul be cowardly or brave? Perhaps it is cowardly because it does not look toward reason, or because it looks toward a corrupted reason, or because of a failure of its instruments—such as a weakness or frailty in the bodily "weapons," or being blocked from acting, or not being stirred to action. It is brave if the opposite occurs. In these cases, there is no internal alteration or "passion." 

As for desire: when it acts alone, it results in what we call intemperance. 
<margin>* alone</margin> 
Does it act alone, or are other faculties present which might take turns in ruling and giving orders? 
<margin>* but to see</margin> 
The act of "seeing" involves moving toward one thing while acting on everything else, yet in some way it also involves 
<margin>* to be at leisure</margin> 
"leisure" <note>original: "σχολάζειν" (scholazein). This implies a state of contemplative rest or freedom from worldly distraction.</note>, in that it contemplates other things as much as possible. Perhaps what we call "vice" is largely due to a poor condition of the body, whereas virtue is the opposite condition. Thus, 
<margin>* in each thing</margin> 
there is no addition made to the soul in either case.

<column-break/>

Just as sight is both potential and actual, it is one and the same essence. The act is not an alteration, but a movement toward that for which its essence is suited; it sees and knows without being affected <note>original: "procul à passione" (far from passion/affection).</note>. Furthermore, the faculty of reasoning relates to the intellect in this way: it sees, and the power of understanding is such that it does not receive internal impressions as if from a seal. Rather, it "has" what it sees, and yet does not have it. It has it because it knows it, but it does not have it in the sense that anything from the sight is impressed upon it, as a shape is formed in wax.

One must remember that memory is not a storage house of impressed forms, but a power of the soul that rouses itself so that it "has" even that which it does not possess. What then? Is the soul one thing before it remembers and another when it is remembering? If you wish to call it "other," do not call it "altered," unless perhaps someone names the progression from potentiality to actuality an "alteration." Yet nothing is added there; the soul simply effects what it is naturally capable of doing. Generally, the actions of immaterial things do not happen in a way that the acting powers are altered—otherwise they would perish—but rather they perform while remaining stable.

That the "agent" should "suffer" while acting is a condition of things involving matter. But if an immaterial thing were to "suffer," it would have no foundation to remain as it is. Just as in the act of seeing: while vision is the agent, it is the eye that undergoes the "passion." Opinions are like visions. 

But how is the nature of anger <note>original: "irascendi natura". Equivalent to the Greek "thymos".</note> cowardly, and how is it brave? Perhaps it is cowardly because it either does not look at reason, or looks at bad reason, or because of a defect in its instruments, or a weakening of the "bodily weapons," or because it is prohibited from acting or not incited. It is brave if the opposite happens. In these things, there is no alteration or passion. Again, the power of desire, whenever it acts alone, brings about intemperance. Sometimes it acts alone when the other parts are not present to take their turn in overcoming it and taking command. Regarding "seeing": the soul acts on something else while it is seeing; it does not do everything at once, but is "at leisure" in some respects so that it may contemplate other things as far as it can. Perhaps what is called "vice" is mostly a bad habit of the body, while virtue is the opposite habit. Therefore, no addition is made to the soul from either side.

<margin>The soul is not the subject of bodily passions, but the principle.</margin>

THE QUESTION WAS ASKED how affinities, alienations, pains, angers, pleasures, desires, and fears are not internal "permutations" and "passions" that move the soul. We must distinguish these things: to deny that alterations and intense sensations happen to us would be to deny the obvious. Therefore, while conceding this, we must inquire: what is it that is actually being "transformed"? Truly, if we grant such things to the soul itself, we would seem to admit something similar: as if we were to grant that the soul itself turns red or pale, failing to notice that it is *because* of the soul...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul’s activities, such as memory and reason, are not physical changes (alterations) but are the soul’s natural "actualities" that leave its essence unchanged. He suggests that emotions like cowardice or anger are often results of bodily conditions or the soul's failure to look toward reason, rather than changes in the soul's substance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s discussion in Ennead III, Book 6 (On the Impassibility of Incorporeal Things). Having established that the soul’s essence remains unchanged by memories, he now addresses what "purification" of the soul actually means if the soul cannot truly be "stained" or "damaged" by the body.</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III

...should it recall the soul to wakefulness? Or, if one says that passions <note>The term "passions" (pathê) refers to any external influence or emotion that "acts upon" a person, potentially disturbing their inner peace.</note> arise from external sensations, he would be saying those passions belong to the soul. But what kind of purification will there be for the soul, if the soul is in no way stained? Or what does it mean to "separate" the soul from the body? Perhaps purification is simply leaving the soul alone, not permitting it to have commerce with other things, nor to look toward anything else, nor to hold "alien opinions"—whatever the condition of those opinions and passions may be (as has been said)—nor to gaze upon mere images <note>original: "simulachra". These are the fleeting, deceptive appearances of the physical world compared to the eternal truths of the mind.</note>, nor to produce passions from them. But if the soul is turned toward higher things from lower ones, what prevents this from being its purification and even its separation? This would apply to a soul not yet so enslaved to the body that it has become part of it—a soul that is like a light not immersed in a murky medium, even though the light is present within that murkiness without being affected by it. Regarding that which is called "passible" <note>The "passible" part is the part of us capable of feeling and being affected by the world.</note>, its purification is a kind of awakening from the intuition of absurd, scattered images. Its separation, truly, is to not be cast down at all, nor to let the imagination be twisted toward the lowest things. Again, to separate the soul is to remove those things from the middle; once they are taken away, the soul is in a sense set apart—specifically when it is not permitted to lie in a spirit made turbulent by a whirlpool, lest it be suffocated by the flesh, but rather that in which it dwells is properly refined so as not to kick back against it.

<margin>VI Forms that are separated or can be separated from matter are called "true beings," while those joined to matter are necessarily called "not true beings." Finally, matter is called "truly non-being."</margin>

**I BELIEVE** enough has been said now regarding how the intelligible essence itself—which is entirely situated in form and order—must be thought to be devoid of all passions. But since matter is also something incorporeal, although in a different way from the soul, we must look at this again to see how it behaves: whether it is passive (as is commonly said) and changeable through everything, or whether it too must be considered free from passion, and how it can be called "separated from passion." To begin, once we have been led to this point and must decide what the nature of matter is, we must assert: the nature and essence of "being" does not behave as many people think. For "Being" is what one could call "truly being"—or to put it another way, "being-ly being" <note>original: "enter ens". A technical term used by translators of Plotinus to express the Greek *ontôs on*, implying that this thing doesn't just "exist," it possesses the very quality of "Being" itself.</note>. This is that which is entirely "being," and which lacks nothing in its own existence. Since it is perfectly "being," it needs nothing to preserve its existence; rather, it is the cause for other things—which only *seem* to be—to appear as though they exist. If these things are true, it is necessary that Being exists in life, and in a perfect life; otherwise, if it failed in this regard, it would no longer be "being." This "Being" is the Intellect and perfect wisdom. Therefore, it is determined, defined, and completely absolute. Nothing there exists merely as a potential; rather, everything exists in such a Great Power that it could never suffer any defect. For this reason, it is eternal; it always behaves in the same way; it never receives anything into itself, nor is anything ever brought into it. For if it received anything, it would be accepting something from outside itself, which would be "non-being." But it must...

<column-break/>

**A** Does he then make the soul through the imaginative faculty, or would he say it has produced the passions—those sights from outside—calling them passions of the soul itself? But what would the purification of the soul itself be, since it is in no way defiled? Or what is it to "separate" it from the body? Perhaps purification would be to leave it alone, and not with others, nor looking toward another, nor again having alien opinions—whatever the manner **B** of those opinions or passions may be (as has been said)—neither to see images, nor to work passions out of them. But if it turns to the other side, to the things above from those below, how is this purification and separation? This belongs to the soul that is no longer becoming "in the body" so as to belong to it <margin>* or manifest and hard to stain?</margin>, and these things are like **C** light that is not in a murky medium. And yet, the light is entirely unaffected <margin>* or nevertheless</margin> even when in the murky medium. But for the "passible" part, purification is the awakening from absurd images and not seeing them. Separation is not being multiplied, and not having imagination concerning things below. And it would also be "separating it" to take away those things from which it is separated—when the things of the flesh are not upon a murky spirit, as if in a multitude <margin>* or even a multitude of flesh.</margin> * or of pure things or of flesh; but the trace of that in which it is, so as to be carried upon it **D** quietly.

I have already said that the essence of the Intelligibles <note>The "Intelligibles" are the eternal Forms or Ideas that can only be grasped by the mind, not the senses.</note>—which is entirely ordered by Form—must be thought of as being devoid of passion. But since matter is also a kind of incorporeal thing, even if in a different way, we must also examine this matter to see what its manner is: whether it is passive, as is said, and **E** changeable in every way, or if we should think that this too must be "without passion," and what the manner of that "passionlessness" is. First, we must take up the nature of these things and say what kind of thing it is—how "truly being" and "essence" and "existence" behave, or if they are the same as what most people believe. For there is Being, which one might truly **F** call "being," or "truly being." And this is that which possesses Being. And this is that which lacks nothing of existence. Being perfectly, it lacks nothing in order to be saved and to exist, but it is the cause for other things—which only *seem* to be—to appear to exist. If these things are said correctly, it is necessary for it to be in life, and in **G** a perfect life. If it were lacking in this, <margin>* or rather perhaps: since the Being</margin> * it would be no more "being" than "not-being." And this is Intellect and all Wisdom; it is therefore determined and limited, and in its power there is nothing that is not already there; it does not lack anything. Because of this, it is eternal and always the same. It is "un-receiving" <margin>* in every way</margin> * in every way. And nothing enters into it. For if it were to receive anything, it would in turn be receiving something else. And this would be "not-being," but it must...

<summary>Plotinus explores the nature of the soul's purification, arguing it is not a literal washing away of "stains" but a turning of the mind away from physical images toward eternal truth. He then begins an investigation into "Matter," questioning if it, like the higher Intellect, might also be fundamentally "impassible" or unchanging.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the nature of Being and its relationship to the physical world, specifically in Ennead VI, Book 5. He is addressing how "Being" can be everywhere and why physical matter, despite its apparent solidity, is actually a form of "non-being" compared to the Intellect and Soul.</meta>

### BOOK SIX. 390

->A<- Being must exist everywhere. Therefore, it is necessary for it to come into existence possessing all things within itself, and all things together as one; all things, that is, if we define "being" by these characteristics. For it must be so; otherwise, intellect and life would not emanate from Being itself, but these things would be merely accidental to Being, and yet they could not come from non-being. Thus, Being itself would be devoid of life and mind. But that which is not truly being <note>Plotinus refers here to the physical, material world which "becomes" but never truly "is" in an eternal sense.</note> will possess these qualities only as they must exist in inferior things, which are posterior to Being itself. For that which ->B<- exists above Being <note>The "One" or the "Good," the highest principle in Plotinus's hierarchy, which is beyond even existence itself.</note> grants these things to Being, yet does not itself stand in need of them. If, then, Being is of such a nature, it is necessary that it is neither a body, nor that which is a substrate for bodies <note>meaning: prime matter</note>; rather, it must be the substrate of bodies. To "be" a body is to dwell in "non-being." And yet, in what way is the nature of bodies—and in what way is matter <note>original: "hyle"</note>—not being? These mountains and stones, the whole solid earth, and whatever things can resist others—surely those things that are struck and forced by impacts confess their own essence <margin>* If anyone should say... how things that do not strike or use force do not exist at all.</margin> ->C<- by that very force? If someone were to ask: "In what way, then, are those things which neither collide, nor use force, nor suffer it, nor resist, nor are seen at all—namely, the soul and the intellect—truly beings?" We shall answer to the contrary: among those things which are corporeal, the earth remains still, but that which is less heavy is more mobile, and that which is more sublime is also more mobile. Indeed, fire is the most mobile of all, as it already begins to flee from the corporeal nature. But (as I believe), those things which are more self-sufficient ->D<- disturb other things less and bring less trouble to them. However, those things which are more heavy and earthy, the more they fail and fall and are unable to lift themselves up, these things, because of their weakness, falling in their own ruin and, as it were, through inertia, seem to bring collision to others. For bodies which lack life fall more heavily upon whatever is near them, striking and hurting them more violently. Living things, however, ->E<- as they participate more in Being: the more they possess "to be," the more they tend to be harmless to those near them. Accordingly, motion—which is a kind of life in bodies, or a mimicry of life—is more present in things where there is less "corpulence," as if the defect of Being <note>meaning: becoming more material/physical</note> makes that which it happens to more of a "body." Again, from those things which are called "passions" <term>passiones: external influences or emotions that act upon a thing</term>, it can be more clearly known that what is more corporeal is more "passible" <note>capable of being affected or suffering change from the outside</note>; namely, that earth is more so than the others, and the rest in a similar fashion. For other things, when they are divided, suddenly return to unity ->F<- with nothing prohibiting it. But when that which is earthy is split, the portions remain always separated from one another, as if they lack natural strength; they remain as they were struck by a small impulse and are destroyed. So also, that which has become "most body," as if it had fallen furthest into "non-being," is least able to recall itself into unity. Heavy and violent collisions, then, are a kind of ruin ->G<- by which some things, in falling, act upon others in turn. But when the weak runs into the weak, it is strong against that, and non-being runs into non-being. These things are said against those who place Being only in the category of bodies.

<column-break/>

<summary>Plotinus argues that true Being is found in the immaterial (Intellect and Soul) rather than the physical. He contends that the "solidity" and "resistance" of physical matter like earth and stone are actually signs of weakness and a lack of true existence, whereas higher forms of life are more unified and less disruptive.</summary>
<keywords>Metaphysics, Ontology, Being vs Non-being, Matter, Body, Soul, Intellect, Plotinus, Enneads, Materialism, Solidity, Impassibility</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Ennead III, Book 6, where Plotinus investigates the impassibility of incorporeal things. The previous page ended with a reflection on how physical objects seem real through their resistance and impact, but here Plotinus argues that this "reality" is merely a sensory illusion—a dream of the soul.</meta>

### PLOTINUS ENNEAD III.

...they are led, evidently, by the impulse and testimony of confusion; likewise, they testify to the truth of imaginations created through the senses, affected just as those who dream, who believe the things they see are real when they are actually dreams. For **sensation is the function of the sleeping soul**: for as much of the soul as is in the body, that part surely sleeps. True awakening and vigilance, however, is a true resurrection *away* from the body, not *with* the body. For the migration that happens with the body is merely a passage from sleep to sleep, as if one were being moved from bed to bed; but the truly real awakening is that which rises entirely away from bodies. Since bodies possess a nature that is repugnant to the soul, they also possess an essence that is the opposite of the soul's essence. This is further testified by their generation, their flux, and their destruction, all of which are utterly foreign to the nature of true Being.

---

<margin>
VII
Wonderful conditions of matter which I found also in Porphyry <note>Porphyry was Plotinus's student and editor; the translator here notes a thematic overlap.</note>: and concerning the vanity of matter, and of the forms appearing in matter.
</margin>

**BUT** we must return again, first to the underlying matter <note>original: "subiectam materiam"</note>, and then to those things which are said to be "in" matter, so that it may be clearly understood both that matter is exempt from "passion" <note>In this context, "passion" means the ability to be affected or changed by external forces.</note> and that neither matter nor those forms truly exist. 

Matter is therefore incorporeal, since the body is a later, composite thing, and matter itself completes the body by joining with something else. It has obtained this name according to the "incorporeal" genus because both true Being and matter are different from bodies. Since matter is neither soul, nor mind, nor life, nor species <note>original: "species" / "eidos", referring to the formal structure of a thing</note>, nor reason, nor even a limit—for it is a certain indefiniteness—it is also not a power. For what could it do? 

But since it escapes all these definitions, it certainly should not obtain the name of "being," but is deservedly called "non-being." Yet it is not called "non-being" in the same way that motion or rest are sometimes called non-being <note>Plotinus distinguishes between things that lack existence because they are categories of change, and matter, which lacks existence because it has no substance of its own.</note>; rather, it is truly non-being: a **simulacrum** <note>original: "simulachrum", an image or phantom</note> and an imagination of bulk, a reaching after substance or subsistence, standing yet not in a state of rest; invisible in itself, and fleeing from anyone who wishes to see it. When one does not look, it is in a way present, but when one looks intently, it is not seen. Again, it always appears in itself as opposites: the small and the great, the less and the more, the deficient and the exceeding. It is an image that can neither remain nor flee; for it does not even have the power to do this, since it received no power from the intellect, but was made in the defect of all Being. 

Therefore, in every name given to it, it lies and deceives; for if it is thought of as "great," it is meanwhile "small," and if "more," it is "less." The "being" that occurs in its imagination is actually "non-being," like a fleeing plaything. Thus, the things that seem to happen within it are themselves playthings—images within an image—exactly as in a **mirror**, where the object is located in one place, but appears in another. It seems to be full, yet has nothing, appearing to be all things. Those things that enter and exit are imitations of real beings and images around a formless image; and because it is formless, they are seen there. They seem to perform some action upon the underlying matter, but they actually do nothing, for they are weak and fleeting, possessing no solidity or any power of resistance...

<column-break/>

<margin>* These things are chimeras <note>original: "ταῦτα χιμαιρή"</note>.</margin>

...by the testimony of impacts; taking the truth from phantoms through the senses, like those who are in a stupor, who believe what they dream. *They think they are acting upon what they see, which are merely dreams. For that of sensation belongs to the soul while it sleeps. For as much as the soul is in the body, it sleeps. But true awakening is a true resurrection from the body, not with the body. For that which is with the body is a migration from one sleep to another, as if from different beds. But the true one is entirely away from bodies, which, being of a nature contrary to the soul, have an essence contrary to it. This is testified to by their generation, their flow, and their destruction, *all things which are far from true Being.

---

<margin>* subsistence: of nature.</margin>

**BUT** we must return to the underlying matter, and then to the things said to be in it, from which it will be known that matter is impassible. It is, then, incorporeal, since the body is later and composite, and matter itself with another makes a body. For it has obtained this name according to the incorporeal, because both Being and matter are different from bodies. But since matter is not soul, nor mind, nor life, nor form, nor reason, nor limit—for it is an infinity <note>original: "ἀπειρία"</note>... 

<margin>* stands</margin>

...under powers. For it is common, but it will fall away from all these. It might correctly receive the name of "not-being." Not as motion is "not-being," or rest is "not-being," but it is truly "not-being"—an image and a phantom of bulk, a falling away from subsistence. And *it stands without standing, and is invisible in itself, fleeing from the one who wants to see, and when one does not see, it is there, but to the one who stares it is not seen. And it always presents opposites within itself: the small and the great, the less and the more, the lacking and the exceeding—an image, neither able to stay nor to flee. For it has no strength for this, having received no strength from the mind, but having come to be in the lack of all Being. 

Therefore, whatever it may announce, it lies; if it is imagined as great, it is small; if as more, it is less. And "being" itself in its appearance is "not-being," like a fleeing plaything. Whence also the things that seem to happen in it are playthings—images in an image—altogether as in a mirror, where the object is established elsewhere, but appears elsewhere; and appearing to be filled, it has nothing, though receiving all things. Those things that enter and exit are imitations of beings and images into a formless image; and because of its formlessness they are seen there. They seem to act upon it, but they do nothing. For they are faint and weak, having no power of resistance; but the infusion of that...

<summary>Plotinus argues that physical matter is a deceptive "non-being" and that sensory life is a form of sleep; true reality is found only when the soul wakes and rises above the material body.</summary>
