<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s argument from Ennead III, Book 6 regarding the nature of matter (hyle). Having established that matter is a "formless" substrate, he now argues that it is "impassible"—meaning it cannot be changed, harmed, or truly affected by the forms that appear to enter it. He compares this to images in a mirror or water, which seem to be "in" the medium without actually altering the medium's nature.</meta>

# BOOK SIX.

<column-break/>

<margin>* acting</margin>
<margin>* from which</margin>
<margin>A</margin>
...it passes through without cutting. For instance, as through water, or as if one were to send shapes into what is called the "void." And again, if those things which are observed—which are * unseen <note>The Greek text here is slightly fragmented, suggesting a corruption in the original manuscript or a very technical distinction about the invisibility of the archetypes.</note>—came into it, and if they were to follow after those who sent them, one might say that matter is affected by them. But as it stands, those things which are manifested are one thing, while those that are woven into it are another. <margin>B</margin> From these things, one may learn that "passion" <note>In philosophy, "passion" (from the Greek *pathos*) refers to the state of being acted upon or changed by an external force.</note> is a falsehood. Since these images are false and possess only a likeness to that which created them—being weak and false, and falling into a false medium as if in a dream, or water, or a mirror—they necessarily leave matter unaffected. For in these examples, the relationship between the thing seen and the thing reflected is the same as the relationship between these forms and matter.

<margin>C</margin>
**GENERALLY**, that which is "affected" must be such that it exists within contrary powers and actions, which approach it and produce the affection. For that which is hot, there is either * alteration or destruction by that which cools. And for that which is wet, <margin>* or alteration</margin> there is either alteration or destruction by that which dries. * And we speak of the underlying subject <note>The "subject" or *hypokeimenon* is the underlying substance that remains through change.</note> undergoing alteration when, <margin>* it becomes,</margin> <margin>D</margin> from cold it * becomes hot, or from dry it becomes wet. This is also testified by what is called the "destruction of fire," when a change occurs into another element. For we say the fire was destroyed, not the matter; so that we must assign these "passions" to that which also experiences destruction. For alteration is the road to destruction, as are the "passions." And it is then the thing about to be destroyed that is the "patient" <note>The one who undergoes an action.</note>. But it is not possible for matter to be destroyed; for into what could it resolve, and how? How then can it be affected, having received within itself countless heats and colds and every quality, being defined by them and having them as if they were innate and mixed with one another? If each thing is separate, and matter itself is caught in the middle while the qualities <margin>* from others</margin> <margin>F</margin> are affected * by one another through mixing, is it not the case that the whole—including matter—is affected? Or will someone place matter entirely outside of these? Yet everything in a subject is present "inside" the subject, so that the whole gives something to it. <margin>G</margin>

**IT MUST BE UNDERSTOOD**, then, that "being present to another" and "being one thing in another" should not be taken in only one way, according to how they exist; but sometimes one thing is present so as to make that other thing better or worse by its presence, along with a certain turning or changing. This is seen in bodies, and especially in living animals. But there is another kind of presence where something becomes better or worse without "suffering" <note>Meaning it is not changed in its essence.</note>, just as was said regarding the soul. And there is another kind, such as when one applies a shape to wax. Is there then a "passion," such as to make the wax become something else when the shape is present?

<column-break/>

Since matter also has no solidity, the forms penetrate into it without dividing it, just as images enter water: or perhaps just as if someone were to send forms into what is called the "void." Now, if those things which are observed were the same as those from which they come into matter, perhaps anyone who attributed to them a certain power truly reaching into the matter from the things that sent them would not be wrong to suspect that matter is affected by them. But since those things which are represented are one thing, and those which are seen "inside" are another, one may also understand from this that the "passion" of matter is false: for it is false that what appears to occur "inside" happens, nor does the appearance have any true likeness to the agent that made it. Being weak and false, and falling into a false medium—like a sort of dream, or water, or a mirror—it undoubtedly allows matter to remain "impassible" <note>Incapable of suffering or change.</note>, even though in these examples I just mentioned, there is a certain likeness between the things that appear and those things to which they are referred.

->VIII<-

<margin>VIII
What kind of thing it is to which passion belongs, and that it does not belong to matter.</margin>
**ALTOGETHER**, that which is affected must be such that it contains contrary powers and qualities to those things which approach it and bring about the "passion": for that which is already hot, an alteration occurs from that which makes it cold. Again, in the presence of the wet, an alteration occurs from a drying agent, and we say the subject is "altered" when from hot it becomes cold, or from dry it becomes wet. <margin>Doubts.</margin> This is also proven by what is called the "corruption of fire," where a change into another element occurs. For we do not say the matter is corrupted, but the fire: therefore, the "passions" are centered around the same thing that experiences destruction. For the path to destruction is the receiving of "passions," and it is the nature of this thing to perish just as it is its nature to "suffer." But for matter to be corrupted is impossible: for we cannot even conceive into what it would resolve, or how. But truly, since matter receives into itself heats, colds, and very many qualities—altogether innumerable ones—and is distinguished by them, and holds them as if they were innate and mixed together (for these things are not separate up above), how can it be that when the qualities are mutually affecting one another in the mixture, matter itself does not also "suffer" with them? Unless, perhaps, someone were to place it entirely outside of them. And yet, whatever is in a subject is present to the subject in such a way that it passes something of itself to the subject.

->IX<-

<margin>IX
Response: That matter neither truly receives, nor receives true things, nor does it suffer: and what that thing is that suffers.</margin>
**IT MUST BE NOTED** that when it is said that "one thing is present to another," or that "one thing is in another," it should not be understood by us in only one way. Sometimes it is such that the thing, by its very presence, makes the other better or worse through a certain change: this is certainly manifest in bodies, especially in living ones. But sometimes something becomes better or worse by the presence of another without any reception of "passion": separately from "suffering," in the way we spoke regarding the soul. Sometimes it is also like when one applies a shape to wax, where there is no "passion" by which the wax becomes something else when the shape is present...

<summary>Plotinus argues that matter (hyle) is "impassible," meaning it cannot be truly changed or harmed by the qualities (like heat or cold) that appear to inhabit it. He compares matter to a mirror or a void that holds images without being altered by them, distinguishing between the destruction of elements (like fire) and the eternal, unchanging nature of the underlying substrate.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s argument in Ennead III, Book 6, specifically exploring the concept of the "impassibility" of matter—the idea that while matter receives forms and qualities (like heat, color, or shape), it is not fundamentally changed or "affected" by them, much like a mirror is not changed by the images it reflects.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III.

...its figure. Nor again does any defect happen to the wax when the figure is erased; and in truth, light does not change anything of the illuminated object with its figure. Even a stone made cold receives something from the cooling agent, yet it remains nonetheless a stone in the meantime, having acquired nothing except the coldness. Furthermore, what does a line suffer under a color? Or what does a plane suffer? Perhaps the underlying body will be said to "suffer" <note>In this context, "suffer" (Latin: *pati*; Greek: *paschein*) is a technical term meaning to be acted upon or to undergo a change of state.</note>, although it will be specifically pointed out what it suffers from the color. For it must not be said that "to suffer" is merely for something to be present, or to be adorned by a form.

If someone were to say that mirrors and all transparent things suffer nothing from the images that appear in them, he would certainly bring forth a fitting example. For the things that are in matter are also images, and matter itself is even more alien to "passions" <note>Emotional or physical changes</note> than mirrors are. Therefore, heat and cold occur in matter, yet heats do not truly warm the matter itself. For to be warmed or to be cooled consists in this: that a quality leads the subject from one quality into another.

Among these things, however, it would be worthy of consideration whether perhaps cold is nothing other than a certain absence and privation of heat. As for the qualities gathering in matter, many of them act upon one another—specifically those which are contrary to each other. For what would a scent do to sweetness? Or a color to a shape? Or what would that which is in one genus <note>A "genus" is a general category or class of things.</note> do to another genus? From this, one might most strongly believe that it is possible for one thing and another to be in the same place, or one within another, without its very presence harming that to which or in which it is present. Therefore, just as that which is harmed is not harmed by just anything, so too it is not changed or "suffers" change from just anything.

But indeed, only contraries suffer from contraries, while other things are not changed by the rest; certainly, those in which there is no contrariety suffer from no contrary. For this reason, if anything "suffers," it is necessary that it is not matter, but some composite thing, or that many things exist together. But that which is alone, and by nature separated from others, and entirely simple, can suffer from nothing. Instead, it can stand underneath as a medium while all things act upon each other; just as in the same house, when some people are striking one another, the house itself suffers nothing, and perhaps not even the air that is within it. Therefore, let the things that are in matter, which come together among themselves, do whatever they are naturally able to do to each other; but let matter itself be much further removed from "passion" than any qualities within it, which, because they are not contraries, suffer very little from each other.

<margin>
Confirmation of the previous points, that matter is moved from its state as little as possible.
</margin>
**IT IS ADDED** to these points that if matter were to suffer, it would be necessary for it to carry away something from that "passion"—either the passion itself or a different state than it had before the passion occurred in it. Therefore, when another quality enters after that one, the matter would no longer be that which receives it, but rather a "qualified matter." But if the quality itself were to cease, leaving something of itself behind because it had already affected the matter, the subject would become even more of something else; and proceeding under this condition, the subject would be something other than mere matter—namely, something varied and multiform.

<column-break/>

...the shape, upon the departure of that thing [the former shape]. But light, and the shape resulting from color, produce an alteration regarding the thing being illuminated. And indeed, the stone having become cold, what does it have of the coldness while remaining a stone? And what do the lines suffer from the color? I think it is the surface, or perhaps rather the underlying body; but what would it suffer from color? Either one must not say that "to suffer" <margin>A</margin> is merely to be present or to be clothed in a form.

If anyone should speak of mirrors or transparent things in general, saying they suffer nothing from the images seen in them, he would bring a very similar example. For the things in matter are also images; and matter itself is even more impassive than mirrors. Indeed, heat and cold arise in it, but it is not itself warmed. For to warm <margin>B</margin> and to cool is to lead the substrate from one quality to another.

One must consider regarding coldness whether it is perhaps an absence and privation. When qualities come together into matter, many of them would act upon each other, <margin>C</margin> namely those which are of a certain kind [contraries]. For what would a fragrance work upon sweetness? Or a color upon a shape? Or how would that which belongs to another genus affect or alter another? One might best believe that one thing and another can be in the same place, or one in another, without causing distress by that presence to the thing in which it is present. <margin>D</margin>

Just as a thing is not harmed by any random thing, so too a thing that is turned or "suffers" would not suffer from just anything; rather, for contraries, the "suffering" is from contraries, but other things are not turned by the rest. For those things in which no contrariety exists, they would not suffer anything from any [contrary]. It is necessary then, if something "suffers," that it is not matter, but the composite <note>The "composite" (*synamphoteron*) refers to the combination of matter and form.</note>, or generally that many things are together. <margin>E</margin> But that which is alone and deserted by the others, and altogether simple, would be impassive to all things, even when caught in the middle of all things, or among those acting upon each other; just as in the same house when people strike one another, the house is impassive, as is the air within it.

Therefore, let the things upon the matter, which come together, do whatever they are naturally suited to do; but let matter itself be impassive—much more so <margin>F</margin> than those qualities in it which, by not being contraries, are impassive to one another.

<margin>* no longer</margin>
**FURTHERMORE**, if matter were to suffer, it must have something * from the passion, either the passion itself, or be differently disposed than before the passion entered into it. If another quality then comes upon it after the first, the recipient will * no longer be matter, but a "qualified matter." <margin>* might become</margin> But if the quality itself departs, having left something of itself behind by its action, the substrate * might become <margin>G</margin> even more of something else; and in this way, matter as the substrate will be something different—something changeable and multiform.

<summary>Plotinus argues that "matter" is a neutral substrate that remains unaffected by the qualities (like heat or color) that pass through it. He uses the analogy of a mirror reflecting an image or a house containing a fight to show how a medium can host activity without being changed by it.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the "impassibility" of matter in Ennead III, Book 6. Having previously compared matter to a mirror that reflects images without being changed by them, he now argues that if matter were fundamentally altered by the forms it receives, it would cease to be the universal "receptacle" required for the existence of the physical world.</meta>

# BOOK SIX.

<columns>

<margin>* as it happens</margin>
A Therefore, matter would no longer be the common receptacle <note>original: "susceptaculum"; the "container" or "womb" of all physical things</note> for all things, since it would have already conceived within itself an impediment to the many things that might come into it later. Thus, the matter itself would no longer remain; it would no longer be incorruptible. For this reason, if it is necessary for matter to be as it was from the beginning, it must always remain the same. To say that it has been changed <note>original: "permutatam"</note> is to fail to preserve it as matter. Furthermore, if everything that is altered must remain in the same species while being changed in its accidents <term>accidents: qualities that can change without changing what a thing fundamentally is, like a person’s hair color</term>, B yet without the substance being transformed—if, I say, it is necessary for that which is altered to remain, and that which undergoes "passion" <note>the state of being acted upon</note> within it is not that which remains, then one of two things must happen: either the altered matter departs from its own nature, or, by not departing from its nature, it is not altered at all. If someone should say that it is indeed altered, but not in its capacity *as* matter, first, he will not be able to explain in what respect it *is* altered; and second, he will be forced to admit that the matter itself is thus not altered. C For just as in other things which are species <note>original: "formae" or "species"; the essential patterns of things</note>, it is impossible for them to be altered according to their essence—since their essence consists in this very thing—so also, because the "being" of matter is to be matter, it is not permitted for it to be altered insofar as it is matter; rather, it must necessarily remain. And just as the form itself is immutable there <note>in the intellectual realm</note>, so also here it is necessary for matter to be immutable.

<margin>XI
How forms come into matter according to the Timaeus by way of images in a mirror.</margin>
D HENCE, I believe the divine Plato, thinking in this way, spoke rightly when he said that the "imitations of beings" <note>original: "imitamina... entium"; the physical qualities we see are only shadows of true, eternal realities</note> enter and exit the matter. For he did not say they "enter and exit" pointlessly, but wished to make us cautious in our explanation of how matter is able to participate in the forms. From this it appears that the famous Platonic <margin>* the infinite</margin> doubt—which asks in what way matter becomes a participant in the forms—does not tend toward what many before us thought, namely, "how" a form comes into matter, <margin>* but how it is</margin> but rather *how* they are present within it. For it truly seems to be a wonder E how, while these forms are present to the matter, it remains the same, receiving no "passion" <note>no lasting change or suffering</note> from them, especially since the things that enter into it act upon one another. <margin>* substance</margin> But indeed, according to the Platonic view, we must think that those things which enter matter expel the prior ones, and that the "passion" exists in the composite <note>the combination of matter and form</note>. Nor does it exist in every composite, but only in that which requires a preceding form to be present or receding, and which F suffers through the absence or defect of something in its own constitution, but is perfected through its presence. Matter, however, has nothing more in its own nature when anything is added; for it is not then "made" into what it is by that addition. Nor again does it have anything less when something recedes; for it remains what it was from the beginning. To those things which lack order, decoration <note>original: "exornatio"</note> is indeed useful and necessary, and an ornament can be added without a total transformation, just as when we place jewelry around someone. But if something were decorated in such a way that the ornament became innate, G it would be necessary for that which is decorated to be changed from its previous "ugliness," <note>original: "turpe"; in Neoplatonism, "ugliness" often refers to the lack of form or order</note> becoming something different, and thus turning from ugly to beautiful. If, therefore, matter, being ugly, were made beautiful, that which was previously ugly would no longer exist.

</columns>

<summary>Plotinus argues that matter must remain fundamentally unchanged (impassible) despite the forms that enter and leave it. If matter were transformed by these forms, it would lose its identity as the universal receptacle of all things.</summary>

--- Page 438 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s argument from the previous section, where he established that matter must remain fundamentally unchanged to serve as the foundation for the physical world. Here, he specifically addresses why matter can "participate" in goodness or beauty without losing its essential nature as "evil" or "ugly" (in a philosophical sense), and he invokes Plato’s authority to support this view.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD. III.

<columns>

Therefore, while it is adorned in this way, it loses its status as matter—especially if its ugliness is not considered merely accidental. But if it were so ugly that it was ugliness itself, it could never participate in ornament; likewise, if it were so evil as to be evil itself, it would never receive any part of the good. For this reason, "participation" <note>original: "participatio"; the way physical things share in the perfect qualities of divine Forms</note> does not happen through "passion" <term>passion: from the Greek *pathos*, meaning the state of being acted upon or changed by an external force</term>, as many people think, as if the matter itself were suffering a change. Rather, it is a different kind of relationship—namely, a matter of *appearance*. 

Perhaps in this way we can also resolve the puzzle of how matter, if it is evil, can desire the good, seeing as it does not cease to be what it was through this participation. For if participation occurs on the condition that matter remains the same and entirely unaltered—just as we have been saying—then it should no longer seem strange that even if it is evil, it can participate in the good. It does not depart from its own nature. But since it is necessary for it to participate, it participates in a certain way for as long as it exists. By remaining exactly what it is, it preserves itself through the mode of participation, and its essence is not harmed by that which is passed into it. Indeed, it seems no less evil for this very reason: because it always remains exactly what it is. For if it were truly a participant and were truly changed by the good, it would not be evil by nature. Therefore, if anyone says that matter is evil, they speak the truth—provided they deny that it "suffers" or is changed by the good. This is the same as asserting that it is entirely impassible <term>impassible: incapable of being affected, hurt, or altered by outside influences</term>.

<margin>
XII
Confirmation of the previous points, showing that matter is not affected by things mixed with it, nor changed in its nature by forms, nor does it suffer, nor is it divided.
</margin>

PLATO, thinking the same thing about matter and judging that participation in it does not happen as if a "species" or "form" were placed into a subject to create a composite <note>original: "compositum"; a thing made of both matter and form, like a bronze statue</note>—where the parts are transformed, mixed, and "suffer" together—sought to explain how matter remains impassible while still possessing these forms. He searched for an example of "impassible participation." Without such an example, it would not be easy to show what kinds of things allow a subject to remain exactly the same by their presence. He raised many difficult questions in his attempt to reach this point. Furthermore, he sought to assert that in sensible things <note>objects we can perceive with our senses</note> there is a lack of true substance, and that the physical world is primarily a place of "likelihood" and images. 

Proposing then that matter, under various "figures" <note>shapes or geometric forms</note>, brings "passions" <note>physical sensations or changes</note> to living bodies while matter itself possesses none of these passions, he signaled its stability in this way. He challenged us to argue that matter itself is in no way affected or changed by these figures. In the case of physical bodies that change from one figure to another, someone might say an "alteration" occurs—meaning the change of the figure itself—though such an "alteration" is only a change in name. But since matter has neither figure nor any magnitude, how could anyone call the arrival of a figure—in whatever way it happens—an "alteration," even in a loose sense? Therefore, if anyone reads the texts here and considers the details, declaring that the underlying nature (matter) possesses nothing in the way people usually think, they will not stray from the truth. But then, in what way *does* it possess these things? If it does not possess them as figures, but rather as the Platonic proposition suggests as far as possible: that the nature of matter is devoid of "passion." 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
<gloss>as it is so adorned, it loses its being as matter</gloss>
If it were adorned in this way, it would lose its status as matter; especially if its "ugliness" were not merely an accident. If it were so ugly as to be ugliness itself, it could not <margin>* so that also</margin> share in order or beauty. And if it were so evil as to be evil itself, how could it share in the good? Thus, "participation" is not the same as "suffering" <note>original: *pathēsis*; being affected</note>; it is another mode, like a ghost or an appearance. Perhaps in this way the puzzle is solved: how can that which is evil strive for the good? If it were destroyed by participation, it would no longer be what it was. But if the so-called participation is of this kind—where the thing remains the same and <margin>* image</margin> unaltered, always being what it is—it is no longer a marvel how it can be evil and yet participate. For it does not <margin>C</margin> <margin>* nurse</margin> depart from itself. Because it is necessary for it to participate, it does so in some way as long as it exists. By being what it is, it preserves itself in the mode of participation, and its being is not harmed by that which is given to it. It remains in danger of "not being" <note>referring to matter's status as a shadow of reality</note> because it always remains what it is. If it were truly participating and truly altered by the good, it would not be evil by nature. Thus, if one calls matter evil, <margin>* because</margin> they are correct only if they mean it is impassible—which is the same as saying it is entirely unaffected.

<margin>D</margin>
Plato, considering these things, did not see participation as a form entering a subject or giving it a shape so as to become a composite, as if they were mixed or "suffering" together. He did not wish to say that; rather, <margin>* nurse</margin> he wanted to show how matter remains impassible while holding the forms. He sought an example of this "impassible participation," which is not easy to teach: how something can be present and yet leave the subject exactly the same. He faced many difficulties in trying to explain the "void of substance" in sensible things and the "place" of the image. By proposing that matter receives figures <margin>F</margin> and produces "passions" in living bodies, while it itself has none of these passions, he demonstrated its permanence. Thus we can reason that matter does not "suffer" or change through these figures. In bodies that receive one figure after another, one might speak of "alteration" because of the change of shape, using the word "alteration" in a general sense. But for matter, which has no shape or size, how could the presence of a figure be called "alteration"? If anyone says the underlying nature has nothing in the way people think, they are right. How then does it have it? If not as receiving shapes, then the theory teaches us, as far as possible, it is a state of impassibility. <margin>* he seeks</margin> <margin>* he desires</margin>

</columns>

<summary>Plotinus argues that matter is "impassible," meaning it acts as a permanent, unchanging mirror for forms and qualities without being transformed by them. He reconciles matter's "evil" nature with its "participation" in the good by explaining that this participation is an appearance rather than a physical change, citing Plato's concept of the "receptacle."</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion on the nature of matter, Plotinus now examines the "impassibility" of matter—the idea that while matter appears to change when it takes on different forms, it remains fundamentally unaffected and unchanged in its own essence.</meta>

# BOOK SIX.

<columns>

<margin>* providing</margin>
...the presence of forms within matter is merely apparent, like the presence of images or phantoms. Perhaps, however, we should first discuss the impassibility <note>original: "impassibilitas"; the state of being unable to be changed or affected by external forces</note> of matter itself. We must teach how it is necessary to use common names to describe its "passion" <note>original: "πάθος" (pathos); here meaning a state of being acted upon or modified</note> in a certain way: for instance, when we imagine it being dried, or set on fire, or moistened (as Plato says), and so on, as it receives the forms of air and water.

<margin>B</margin>
For when Plato adds that matter receives the forms of air and water, he both tempers and diminishes what had been said—that matter is "fired" or "moistened." He shows that in the act of receiving forms, matter is not itself formed, but rather the forms exist within it just as they entered. Likewise, when it is said to be "fired" <note>original: "ignitam" or "πυρωμένην"</note>, this was not spoken strictly, but rather signifies that it has *become* fire. For becoming fire is not entirely the same as being "fired" (in the sense of being changed by fire). To be "fired" implies something else is happening in which a "passion" occurs; but that which is a part of fire cannot be "fired" itself. Otherwise, it would be as if one said that a statue proceeded through the bronze itself, or that fire progressed through the matter and entered it.

<margin>C</margin>
And yet, even if the rational principle <note>original: "ratio" / "λόγος"</note> approaching matter is said to act upon it, in what way will matter be said to be "fired"? Perhaps into a shape? But that which is "fired" already consists of two things <note>matter and the form of fire</note>. How then can it come from both, if one thing is not made from the two? Or perhaps, even if one thing is made, it is not from two things having mutual "passions" (changes), but acting upon other things. Are both acting then? Or rather, is one effecting something so that the other does not flee from it?

<margin>D</margin>
But when a body is divided, how can it be that the matter itself is not divided? And when the body suffers in being divided, how does matter not sustain the same passion? Perhaps nothing prevents us from saying that matter is "corrupted" (destroyed) by the same logic, explaining how matter is not destroyed when the body is destroyed. Indeed, one would have to say that what "suffers" and is "divided" must be something that possesses size and magnitude.

<margin>E</margin>
But to that which is not a magnitude, the passions of magnitude cannot belong; and generally, the passions of a body cannot happen to that which is not a body. Therefore, whoever admits that matter can "suffer" or be changed is forced to admit that matter is also a body.

<margin>* encompassing</margin>
<margin>* itself</margin>
<margin>* departing from them</margin>
<margin>* the receptacle holds, and</margin>
<margin>* to become</margin>
<margin>XIII. It is confirmed and proved that matter relates to forms and to the divine mind just as a mirror relates to images and spectacles.</margin>
<margin>F</margin>
Furthermore, those people ought to prove by what reason they say matter "flees" from the form. For in what way could stones and other solid things that encompass matter "flee" it? They surely will not say it flees at some times and not at others. For if it flees by its own will, why does it not flee always? But if it remains by necessity, there is no time in which it is not in some form. Rather, the cause why the same form does not always contain any given piece of matter must be sought in the things that enter it. In what way, then, is it said to "flee"? Is it by its very nature and always?

<margin>G</margin>
And what else would that be, other than that matter, never departing from itself, holds the form as if it never held it at all? Otherwise, they will have no way to probably defend what they have said. Furthermore, Plato calls matter the "receptacle" <note>original: "ὑποδοχὴ" (hypodoche)</note> of all generation and the "nurse" <note>original: "τιθήνη" (tithene)</note>. Certainly, a receptacle and a nurse...

</columns>

<summary>Plotinus argues that matter is "impassible," meaning it does not actually change or suffer when it takes on physical forms like fire or water. He compares matter to a mirror or a "nurse" that holds forms without being altered by them, concluding that if matter were capable of "passion" (change), it would have to be a physical body rather than an underlying substrate.</summary>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III.

<columns>

<margin>A</margin> ...is something other than generation. That which is **Altered**, however, is involved in generation. And since the **receptacle** <note>original: "susceptaculum" / "ὑποδοχὴ" (hypodoche); Plato's term for matter in the Timaeus</note> and the **nurse** <note>original: "nutrix" / "τιθήνη" (tithene); another Platonic metaphor for matter as a provider of space for growth</note> of generation precedes generation itself, it also precedes alteration. Surely, that which is called the receptacle and nurse preserves matter as **impassible** <note>original: "impatibilem" / "ἀπαθῆ"; meaning it cannot be affected or modified by external forces</note>: it similarly preserves what is written: that matter is that in which each thing is seen to come into being, and from which it again departs. Likewise, because he calls it a **place** and a **seat**: finally, because he says with right reason that it is <margin>B</margin> as it were a **place of forms**, he is not describing a "passion" <note>original: "passionem" / "πάθος" (pathos); a state of being acted upon or changed</note> concerning matter, but is seeking some other mode of existence. What then is this mode? Certainly, since it is necessary that no such nature should be among the things that truly **Be** <note>original: "entium" / "ὄντων"; referring to the eternal, unchanging Forms</note>, but rather should have escaped every image of beings and be entirely different—for the **Ratios** <note>original: "rationes" / "λόγοι" (logoi); the formative principles or blueprints of things</note> are beings truly existing—it is necessary that matter, by this very "otherness," preserve the safety it has obtained. Therefore, it is not only unable to truly grasp beings, but even if <margin>C</margin> there be some **imitation** of beings, matter is also devoid of any intimacy with it. For in this way only is it entirely different from beings; otherwise, if it contracted any intimate familiarity with a **species** <note>original: "specie" / "εἶδος"; a form or kind</note>, it would certainly become something else along with it and lose that "otherness," and would no longer be the **place of all things**: or rather, it would no longer be a receptacle for anything, though it is said to be equally a receptacle for everything. It is necessary, then, that while forms enter, the same <margin>D</margin> matter remains, and while they depart, it remains **impassible**, so that something may always enter and exit. But that which enters will enter as a **simulacrum** <note>original: "simulachrum" / "εἴδωλον"; a phantom or ghost-like image</note>, and into something that is by no means true: and therefore, the entering thing itself will not be true. But will it be truly received? Yet how shall it be truly received by that which is in no way permitted to participate in truth, because it is **falsehood itself**? Perhaps, therefore, it proceeds falsely into the false, and <margin>E</margin> behaves similarly to the **images of objects** appearing in a **mirror**, so long as those objects remain in sight. For if you were to remove beings from the universe, nothing at all would ever appear, not even for a moment, of those things which are now seen in the world. Now, a mirror among us is itself also seen, for it is itself some kind of species or form. But that which is in the world, acting like a mirror, because it is no species, is itself in no way seen; otherwise, it would have to be <margin>F</margin> discerned first according to itself. But it suffers such a thing as **illuminated air**, which even then is hidden from the eyes, because without illumination it could not be seen. For this reason, those things which appear in mirrors are believed to either not exist at all, or to exist less: because that in which they are is clearly discerned, and it remains while they depart. But matter is not discerned at all, <margin>G</margin> whether it holds forms or does not; but if it happened that those things from which mirrors are filled remained, and the mirrors themselves were not seen, no one would doubt that the things seen in the mirrors were true. Whether, therefore, there is something in mirrors, let there be **sensible things** similarly in matter; or if there is nothing in mirrors but merely an appearance. Similarly, one must say that it "appears" in matter: the cause of which appearance is to be assigned to the **substance of the beings themselves**, which beings always participate in truly, but non-beings participate in not truly...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <margin><unclear>if it were opposed</unclear></margin> ...but generation is something else from it. That which is altered is in generation, so that she is the host of generation, without alteration, both the **receptacle**, and furthermore the **nurse**, keeping that in which it is impassible. And that in which each thing that is <gloss>produced</gloss> appears, and from there again goes out, and is a **place** and a **seat**. And that which is said and <gloss>solidified</gloss> * as if the whole <margin>* Should anything be said?</margin> were an **image**, as he says, or a **passion** is spoken of regarding that thing, <margin>for them</margin> but it seeks another way. How then is this? Since <margin>B</margin> <margin>* thus then and</margin> indeed it is necessary that this so-called nature be none of the beings, * but rather has escaped all the **substance of beings**, or is entirely other. For those are **Ratios**, and truly being; it is necessary then that she be guarded by this "otherness," which safety she has obtained. It is necessary that she not only be unreceptive of beings, but even if there is some **imitation** of them, even then she must be without any kinship to them. For in this way, being entirely other, the way that is settled in it, becoming something else after those things, would lose the quality of being <margin>C</margin> **other**, and being the **place of all**, and a receptacle of no such thing; but it is necessary that while things enter, she remains the same, and while they exit, she is **impassible**, so that things may always enter into her, and exiting things are indeed that which enters, being **unclear**, and into the **not-true**, it is **not true**. Is it then truly? And how is it permitted to that which in no way shares in truth, because it is a **lie**? * <margin>* I deem</margin> Is it then that it comes falsely into a lie, and becomes very similar to what is seen in **mirrors**, the **images** of the things looked at, and <margin>D</margin> as long as one looks at them. For even if these things—the beings—were removed, nothing would appear for any time of the things now seen in the **sensible world**. Now the mirror here is itself also seen, since it is also a certain form; but that in the world is not itself seen; for it would have been necessary for it to be seen first by itself according to itself; but it suffers something such as **air when lit up**, it is invisible even then, * <margin>* I do not deem</margin> when it was not seen by being lit up. In this way <margin>E</margin> therefore, things in mirrors are either believed to **be**, or not, because that in which they are is seen, and it remains, while they depart; but in **matter**, she is not seen, neither when she has [forms], nor from those things. If indeed it were possible for the things from which the mirrors are filled to remain, and the mirrors themselves were not seen, they would not be thought not to be true * and trusted when seen. <margin>* or to the faithful</margin> <margin>F</margin> If therefore there is something in the mirrors, let there be **sensible things** * in matter also. <meta>This page continues Plotinus's argument from the previous page regarding the "impassibility" of matter—the idea that matter provides a stage for the physical world without being changed by the forms that appear upon it. Here, he uses the famous Platonic myth of Poverty (Penia) and Plenty (Porus) to illustrate the "destitute" nature of matter.</meta>

# BOOK SIX. 317

<columns>

Since it must be this way, the things that exist would have been just as they are, even if matter <note>original: "αὐτᾷ" / "materia"; the underlying "stuff" of the universe</note> did not exist.

What then? If matter did not exist, would nothing at all subsist? Nothing at all except for the **Beings** <note>the eternal, unchanging Forms or Ideas</note>; just as an image would not exist if the mirror or a similar object were removed. For that which is naturally inclined to come into being in another thing cannot exist if that other thing is absent. For this is the very nature of an **Image** <note>original: "εἰκών" / "imago"</note>: to exist within another. If it could depart from its causes, it could certainly exist even if it were not in another.

But since those Beings remain, if something from them appears elsewhere, there must be something else providing a "seat" <note>original: "ἕδραν" / "sedem"; a place for the form to rest</note> for that which does not truly arrive. This other thing, by its very presence and **audacity** <note>original: "τόλμη" / "audacia"; a Neo-Platonic term for the "daring" of matter to exist apart from the One</note>, and as if by its procacity and **poverty** <note>original: "πενία" / "Penia"</note>, is driven as if by force to take what it can. Yet it is deceived by not truly taking it, so that its poverty remains, forever compelling it to beg. For once it

subsists (as the myth tells us), it always desires. In this way, its nature is shown to be devoid of **The Good** <note>original: "ἀγαθᾶ" / "boni"</note>. It desires to receive not the things that the giver possesses, but it seems satisfied if it receives anything at all, however slight. From this, it is shown that what appears in matter is different from matter itself. The name **Poverty** <note>original: "Πενία"; personified lack</note> declares that matter is never truly filled. When it is said that Poverty joins with **Plenty** <note>original: "Πόρος" / "Poro"; the source of resource and abundance</note>, it does not mean she joins with Being itself or with fullness,

but with a certain clever and marvelous thing—namely, with a certain cunning of the self-displaying image. For since it is impossible for anything that exists outside of Being to be entirely devoid of it—for it is the nature of Being to create beings—and since "Non-Being" <note>meaning matter, which has no form of its own</note> cannot be mixed with Being, a marvel occurs: matter participates without participating. By its very proximity, it gains something, even though by its own nature it is unable to be glued to it. What it receives

slips away as if from a foreign nature, like an **Echo** <note>original: "Echo"</note> from smooth and flat places. That which does not remain there nevertheless appears there and seems to come from there. If matter participated and received in the way some might think, that which approached it would surely penetrate it as if absorbed. But now it appears that nothing was absorbed, but that matter remained entirely the same, having gained nothing, but rather acting like a

seat that repels the process. It is a receptacle for things that run together in the same place and are mixed there. It is like when people, wishing to catch fire from the sun, hold up certain smooth and solid objects, or fill vessels with water; the flame is hindered by the contrary element within and does not pass through, but stays on the outside. In this way, matter becomes the cause of **generation** <note>original: "γενέσεως" / "generationis"; the process of physical things coming into being</note>, and the things composed within it are constituted in this manner.

<column-break/>

Since it is not fitting for these things to behave as they would have if they existed while Being itself did not exist.

<margin>XIII These same things are confirmed: that matter is never filled, but is always affected by something new, because it does not receive true things, nor does it truly receive what it seems to receive.</margin>
What then? If matter were not there, would nothing at all subsist? Nothing at all except the Beings: just as an image vanishes if the mirror or suchlike is taken away. For that which is so constituted by nature as to be in another will never exist if that other is not there; for this is the very nature of an image: to be in another. If it could indeed separate from its causes, it could surely exist even if it were not in another.

But since the Beings themselves remain, if anything from them appears elsewhere, there must be something else providing a seat for that which does not truly come: which indeed, by its presence and audacity—and as if by its procacity and poverty—is urged, and urges itself, to take; yet it is deceived by not truly taking, so that its poverty, persevering, always compels it to demand. For after it once

subsists (as the myth relates), it always desires: in which matter its nature is shown to be devoid of good. It desires to receive not those things which the giver has, but it seems satisfied if it receives a little of whatever kind, so that from this it is shown that what appears to us in matter is diverse from it: the name Poverty itself, that is, lack, declares that matter is not filled. When it is said that Poverty meets with Plenty, it does not mean she meets with Being itself or with satiety,

but with a certain crafty and wonderful thing. That, however, is with a certain cunning of the image showing itself. For since it is impossible to be entirely devoid of Being—whatever and however a thing may be outside of Being itself (for this is the nature of Being: to make beings)—and since "non-being" cannot be mixed with Being, surely something marvelous happens: namely, it participates while not participating, and by its very proximity it obtains something, although by its own nature it cannot be joined together.

What it has received slips away as if from a foreign nature, like an Echo from smooth and level places: because it does not stay there, it both appears there and seems to come from there. But if matter participated and received in such a way as someone might perhaps think, surely that which comes to it would penetrate it as if soaked in. But now it appears it was not soaked in, but that matter remained altogether the same, having acquired nothing, but like a

certain seat that strikes back, it has inhibited the process, being a receptacle of things running together into the same place and there mixed with one another: not otherwise than occurs here when some people, desiring to catch fire from the sun, oppose certain smooth and solid things, which they also fill with water, so that the flame, being restrained by that which is contrary within, does not pass through, but stands outside. In this way, therefore, matter turns out to be the cause of generation, and those things which are composed in it are constituted in this way.

<margin>XV Concerning the seminal reason, which is in the soul, that it is not mixed with matter, and that matter takes on form out of its own readiness.</margin>
In those things that gather fire from the sun around themselves, inasmuch as they receive flame from sensible fire, they also have the quality of being perceived by the senses. Therefore they appear, since the things fashioned there are extrinsic, placed in succession and nearby, and they touch each other, and there are undoubtedly two boundaries there. But the **Seminal Reason** <note>original: "Ratio veraria" / "λόγος σπερματικός"; the formative "blueprint" or soul-principle that gives shape to matter</note> in matter...

</columns>

<summary>Plotinus explains that matter acts as a "mirror" or "receptacle" that reflects forms without being altered by them, using the myth of Poverty and Plenty to describe matter's perpetual state of "want" and "lack." He compares the formation of physical objects to the way a lens or water-filled vessel focuses light to create heat without the light ever becoming part of the water itself.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the nature of Matter. Having previously established Matter as a "destitute" receptacle (Penia), he now explains its "otherness"—how it remains separate from the forms (like size and shape) that appear to inhabit it, much like a mirror remains separate from the reflections on its surface.</meta>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS. III.

<columns>

...it is in another way "outside" <note>original: "extra"</note>. For the "otherness" <note>original: "alteritas"</note> of its nature is sufficient; it does not need a double boundary. Much more than any foreign boundary, it retains a power that resists mixing because its essence is entirely different and lacks any kinship with the forms. This very fact is the cause of it standing by itself: neither does that which enters enjoy it, nor does it in turn enjoy that which comes in. 

Just as opinions and imaginations in the soul are not mixed with the soul's substance, but each departs again as it was, existing alone, dragging nothing with it and leaving nothing of itself behind because it had not been mixed; so too Matter is said to be "outside." This is not because it lies nearby in a physical place, nor is it distinguished from its foundation by sight like different objects are, but it is distinguished by Reason <note>original: "ratione" / "λόγος"</note>. 

In this case, the imagination <note>original: "imaginatio" / "φαντασία"</note> occupies the place of a certain image <note>original: "simulachri"</note>. Even though the soul is not naturally an image—though in many things it seems to lead, and to lead according to its own will—imagination is compared to the soul in a certain proportion, just as form is to matter. Although I say this is so, imagination does not obscure or hide the soul, since it is frequently shaken off by the soul's own proper actions. Nor does it ever cause the soul to be entirely hidden, even if it spreads itself through the whole, though sometimes it appears to be so. For the soul has within itself actions and opposing reasons through which these "accidents" <note>non-essential qualities</note> are repelled. 

But Matter, being far weaker than the soul, possesses nothing of the things that truly exist—neither truth nor even its own falsehood. Nor does it have anything through which it might appear, since it has been cast out into the solitude of all things. Yet it becomes the cause for other things to appear; but it cannot even say this much: "Here I am," though it is seen least of all. But if at some point a deeper reason finds it, affected by other existing things, it cries out that it is something destitute of all existing things. And since those things which come after the "True Beings" seem to exist, Matter is dragged through all these so that it appears to follow them, and yet again it does not follow.

<margin>
XVI
How the formal and seminal reason <note>original: "ratio formalis atq; seminalis" / "λόγος"</note>, which Mind <note>original: "nus" / "νοῦς"</note> provides to matter as forms, the same Mind also applies quantities and figures as companions to those forms.
</margin>

**But a certain** Reason <note>original: "ratio" / "λόγος"</note> approaching and extending Matter as far as it wishes, makes it "so much" <note>i.e., gives it size or quantity</note>. It applies quantity from itself to Matter, which does not have quantity by itself—nor does it even possess it after it is made, otherwise quantity would be inherent within it. If someone were to take away this form <note>the form of quantity</note>, the subject itself will no longer be "so much," nor will it even appear to have size. 

But if that which has become "so much" is a man or a horse, the magnitude of the horse comes along with the horse; and when the horse departs, the magnitude also departs. But if someone says that the horse is made in a certain large mass of such size, and that the magnitude remains, we shall say that it is not the magnitude of the horse, but the magnitude of the mass that remains there. If, however, this mass is fire or earth, then when the fire or earth departs, the magnitude of the fire or the earth also departs. Therefore, Matter enjoys neither figure nor magnitude; otherwise, it would not become something else from fire, but that magnitude of fire remaining, it would never cease being fire.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It is "outside" in another way. For the otherness of its nature is sufficient; it needs no double boundary. But much more than any boundary, being estranged <gloss>and from the good</gloss> from everything else, by the otherness of its essence <gloss>kinship</gloss> and having no kinship anywhere, it possesses an unmixed quality; and the cause of its remaining <gloss>unmixed</gloss> within <gloss>within itself</gloss> itself is this: that neither does that which enters enjoy it, nor does it <gloss>it does not</gloss> enjoy that which enters. But just as <margin>B</margin> opinions and imaginations in the soul are not mixed, but each comes in again as being only what it is, having dragged in nothing and being left behind by nothing, because it did not mix. And so "outside" means that it is beyond; and that upon which it exists is not seen as different by sight, but Reason says so. Therefore, in this case, the imagination <gloss>this</gloss> being an image, though the soul is not an image by nature <margin>C</margin>—even though it seems to lead many things and lead where it wishes. It uses it nonetheless as matter or something proportional. It does not, however, hide it, being frequently pushed out by the soul's own activities; nor did it make the soul such that it would be hidden even if it came with its full force, though the soul itself seems to be imagined. For it has within itself activities and opposing reasons, by which it pushes away those things that fall upon it. <margin>D</margin> For Matter is weaker than the whole power of the soul. And it possesses nothing of existing things, neither truth nor even its own falsehood yet. It has nothing by which it may appear, being a desert of all such things, but it becomes the cause for others to appear. Nor can it say even this: "I am here," but Reason finds it out <margin>E</margin> as something deep from other existing things, showing that it is indeed abandoned by all existing things; and of those <margin>F</margin> things thought to exist later, it is dragged into all of them, following them as they appear, and yet again not following.

**And** indeed, the Reason <note>Logos</note> having come and led it as far as it wished, made it great, just as if the "great" itself were in Matter, though it was not. For the "great" upon it was magnitude. If someone takes away the form, the subject is no longer great, nor does it appear so. But if that which has become great is a man or a horse, and with the horse the magnitude of the horse arrives, when the horse departs, the magnitude also departs. If someone says the horse exists in a certain large mass and size, and the magnitude remains, we will say it is not the magnitude of the horse, but the magnitude of the mass <margin>G</margin> that remains there. If this mass is fire or earth, when the fire departs, the magnitude of the fire departs, or that of the earth. Therefore, it <note>Matter</note> enjoys neither the shape nor the magnitude; otherwise it would not become something else from fire; but remaining as fire, it would not become fire <note>i.e., it would be stuck in one form</note>.

</columns>

<summary>This page argues that Matter is fundamentally "other" and unmixed with the forms it hosts. Using the analogies of imagination in the soul and reflections in a mirror, Plotinus explains that qualities like size (magnitude) and shape belong to the Forms/Reason (Logos) and depart when the Form departs, leaving Matter as a characterless, destitute receptacle.</summary>

--- Page 443 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Matter's relationship with Form. The previous page established that Matter remains "outside" of the forms it receives, acting as an unaffected mirror. This page explores how Matter—which has no size or quality of its own—can appear to possess "Magnitude" (size) and other physical properties without truly changing its own nature.</meta>

->### BOOK SIXTH.<-

<columns>

Since even now, having become as great as it seems—as great as this entire universe—if the heavens were to cease to exist, along with everything within them, then all **magnitude** <note>The Greek term is *megethos*, referring to physical size or extension.</note> would likewise depart from Matter. All other **qualities** would clearly vanish as well. Matter would then be left as it was, preserving absolutely nothing of those things that were previously around it. In those things that are capable of "suffering" <note>In philosophy, "to suffer" (passive) means to be affected or changed by an external force.</note> by the presence of certain qualities, something of what they received remains even after those qualities depart. 

But in things that do not truly "suffer" change, nothing remains. This is like the **air**, which is filled with light; when the light departs, the air retains nothing of it. If anyone wonders how something that has no magnitude can become "great," or how something without heat can become "hot," we answer that it is not the same thing for Matter to *be* Matter as it is for it to be Magnitude. For Magnitude itself is **immaterial**, just as Shape is immaterial. If we maintain the nature of Matter as a receptacle, we say it acquires all things through **participation**. 

Magnitude is one of these things. In composite bodies <note>Physical objects made of both matter and form.</note>, magnitude exists alongside other qualities, though it is not strictly defined. Because Magnitude is included in the very definition of a "body," it is present there. But in Matter itself, not even an undefined magnitude is present, because Matter is not a body.

<column-break/>

Since indeed even now, having been made as great as it seems—as great as this world is—if the heavens and all that are in them should cease to be, then all **magnitude** would likewise recede from Matter. At the same time, all other qualities would depart, and then that which was would be left behind, preserving nothing at all of those things that were formerly around it. However, for whatever things happen to "suffer" the presence of others, it is permitted for them to retain something of what was received after those things depart; but those which do not "suffer" retain nothing. This is just as the air, having obtained light, retains nothing of that light once it departs. But if anyone should marvel at how it is possible for that which has no magnitude to become "great," we shall likewise object: in what way does that which has no heat become "hot"? For being Matter is not the same as being Magnitude, since **magnitude is immaterial**, just as **figure** <note>Geometric shape or form.</note> is also immaterial. If we preserve the nature of Matter, we shall say that it obtains all things through a certain **participation**. 

Magnitude is one thing among all: in bodies, which are composite, magnitude is present together with other things, yet it is not determined. Since magnitude is included in the very "reason" <note>original: *ratione* / *logos*—the forming principle or blueprint.</note> of a body, it is present there; but in Matter itself, not even an indeterminate magnitude is included, since Matter is not a body.

<margin>XVII. Matter does not possess quantity from itself, but extends toward it under the effective entry of form.</margin>
But neither will it be Magnitude itself, for Magnitude is a **Form** <note>original: *species* / *eidos*</note>, and Matter is not prepared to take it on as its own essence. Indeed, Magnitude exists according to itself; and if Matter cannot even familiarly reconcile itself to the imitations of beings, then certainly it is not Magnitude in this way either. But because the **Intellect** or the **Soul** <note>The higher spiritual realities in Plotinus's system.</note> desires that which is situated within it to be "great," it has handed down to those things that wish to imitate it (by a desire for it or a movement toward it) a certain capacity for their "passion" to be imprinted in another. Therefore, "Greatness" running into the fullness of the **imagination** or **appearance**, making the "smallness" of Matter itself run toward this very greatness, causes it to appear great, even though it is not filled by that co-extension. For this "greatness" is false; since Matter does not possess the quality of being great, it is, as it were, "co-amplified" by extending toward that form. For since all beings act upon others, and each of the agents is of a similar nature, it makes a "great" thing in the same way as the whole. The "greatness" of each individual definition <note>original: *rationis* / *logos*</note> follows after it, such as that of a horse or any other thing. Furthermore, the phantom reflection itself, or the universal appearance, becomes "great," shining forth toward "Greatness" itself. Every part becomes something "great," and all things appeared together from the universal form, to which "Greatness" belongs. From each part, a kind of extension was made, everything toward everything, forced to be in that form; and it produced as much in **bulk** as it carried in **power**. From this, it happened that what is "nothing" <note>Plotinus often describes Matter as "non-being" or "nothing" because it lacks any defining characteristics.</note> becomes "all things" in appearance. For this reason, even **color** proceeds from what is not color, and **quality**—as it occurs among us—proceeds from what is not quality, receiving its name from them.

</columns>

<summary>Plotinus explains that Matter has no inherent size (magnitude) but appears large because it reflects the "Greatness" of the Forms/Intellect, much like a mirror reflects an object without becoming the object itself.</summary>

# PLOTINUS ENNEADS III.

<column-break/>

## Left Column

...they obtained an equivocal <note>original: *æquivocâ*; meaning things that share a name but have different definitions—like a "real" man and a "painted" man.</note> nature from those [forms], and magnitude arose from non-magnitude, or a magnitude in name only.

A Where these things are certainly considered as a middle ground between Matter itself and the Form itself. They indeed appear because they somehow shine out from that source; yet they deceive because the medium in which they appear does not truly exist. Each thing is stretched out into magnitude, evidently drawn by the power of those things which appear here, and they create a place for themselves. This drawing happens through all things, not by violence, because Matter is the "everything" <note>The underlying substrate of the whole universe.</note>.

B Each thing draws according to the power it possesses, which it holds from that source. Because it makes Matter "great," it seems to act by an image of that which is Great appearing here; and that which is called "appearing" is that which is great in this place. Matter, having been forced to concur—or being that in which these things are forced to concur—offers itself as a whole and everywhere at once. For it is Matter, the material of this universe, and it is not any specific thing.

C That which of itself is not anything can, through another, become its own opposite; and after it has become that opposite, it is not even that, for otherwise it would consist only in that very thing.

<margin>
XVIII
Just as Matter has no true form, so it has no true magnitude: and how it is produced into dimension for the effective movement of the form coming into it, yet is not pulled apart, but remains continuous.
</margin>

D **I**f anyone should possess the intelligence of the "Great" <note>The conceptual form of Magnitude or Greatness.</note>, which has a power through which it exists not only in itself but is also able to go forth as if outside itself, and should find a certain nature that does not exist in the intellect—neither having a form, nor any vestige of the Great, nor of anything at all—what would he do with such a power? Not a horse, nor an ox; for other causes will produce these. Perhaps since it comes from the "Great Father" <note>A reference to the higher Intellectual Principle or the One.</note>, no other thing can grasp that magnitude; this [Matter], however, will hold it only as an image. To this [Matter], which has by no means attained the Great such that it becomes great in its own nature, it remains only to appear as great as it can.

E This consists in not falling short; and if it is propagated everywhere, it does not proceed as if divided into many parts, but holds related parts within itself, and is nowhere entirely absent. For it was not possible that in a small mass there could be an equal image of the Great, since it is an image of Greatness itself. But insofar as it desired that form, it approached it; and running as far as it could along with its concurrent partner <note>The Form of Magnitude</note>, it made that which was not great into something "great"—not so that it *is* great, but so that it appears great, and is seen as magnitude in a mass.

F Matter meanwhile preserves its own nature, using this magnitude like a garment <note>A favorite Neoplatonic metaphor: physical properties are "clothes" that do not change the essence of the wearer.</note> with which it was clothed when it concurred with it, specifically while that running Form was leading it. If it should ever strip this off, it remains again the same as it was before within itself—that is, only as much as the present form makes it. Accordingly, the soul, possessing the forms of beings—since it is itself a form—possesses them all at once. Since every form is also whole and at once with itself, and seeing the forms of sensible things as if reflected and approaching it, the soul does not endure to grasp them along with their multitude, but discerns them once their mass is removed.

G For it cannot become anything other than what it is.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Matter (Hyle) from the previous section. Having established that Matter is a formless "mirror" for magnitude, Plotinus now explores its passivity—how it receives forms without being changed by them, much like a mirror remains unchanged by the images it reflects.</meta>

# BOOK SIX.

<column-break/>

Matter, having nothing within it to "cut off" or resist the incoming forms—for that which possesses active power is perhaps merely a shadow—remains waiting to be affected by whatever the Maker <note>The "Maker" refers to the *Demiurge* or the formative principle (Logos) that shapes the universe.</note> desires. That which proceeds from the shadow, directed by reason, already bears a "trace" of what is to be. For just as a movement within a pictorial imagination <note>original: *phantasia*; the faculty of the soul that produces mental images.</note>, the reason—or the movement originating from it—is a division; otherwise, if it were entirely one and the same, no motion would occur, but it would remain still. Matter is able to receive all things at once, just as the soul can, either into its own nature or into whatever those forms may be. But when Matter receives all things as its own, it does not receive them in an undivided way; therefore, it must proceed through every <margin>* place.</margin> manner. Since all things must come to it, it meets them all, and it runs through every interval <note>Plotinus uses "interval" to mean spatial distance or extension.</note> because it is not itself constrained by spatial dimensions, but lies exposed to whatever is to come. How then can it be that one thing entering does not block others? Perhaps those things which are unable to exist together were not one "first" thing; but if they were, then that was the Form of the whole, so that all parts remain together. For life is Matter divided alongside the division of life; otherwise, nothing would have happened according to reason.

The things that enter into Matter, as if into a mother, do it no harm, nor do they bring it any benefit. The "blows" <note>The "blows" (plēgai) represent the impact of forms or qualities acting upon the substrate.</note> that occur are not between the forms and the Matter, but between the forms themselves; for their powers are directed at their opposites, not at the underlying subject—unless one considers the subject as being bound up with the things that approach it. Heat ceases when it meets cold, or blackness when it meets white; or, if they are mixed, they create another quality from themselves. Thus, it is the things being mixed that "suffer" or are affected. To "suffer," for them, is to no longer be what they were. In living beings, these passions or affections occur in the bodies, as alterations happen according to qualities or inherent powers. When the physical structures are dissolved, or brought together, or pressed out of their natural state, the "passions" reside in the bodies, while in the souls there are "cognitions" of the more violent passions. If the soul does not perceive them, the Matter simply remains as it was. For Matter suffers nothing when cold departs or when heat arrives. Neither of these is truly "friendly" or "alien" to it. Therefore, its most appropriate name is "receptacle" or "nurse." But why has it also been called "mother"? For it generates nothing. It seems they call it "mother" because they believe a mother holds the place of Matter toward her offspring, as if she only receives <margin>* as far as the body of that which is being born.</margin> but gives nothing to the child; for whatever body the child has comes from nourishment. If the mother does give something to the child, it is not in her capacity as "matter," but because she possesses "form." For only Form is fertile; the other nature <note>i.e., Matter.</note> is sterile. From this, I believe, the ancient sages hinted at this through mysteries and rites when they depicted the ancient Hermes <note>original: *Hermēn*; Mercury.</note> as always possessing the organ of generation, to represent...

<meta>catchword: to represent...</meta>

<column-break/>

But Matter, since it has no power of rejecting <note>original: *excutiendi*; to shake off or cast out.</note>, for it has no action, and since it is a shadow, undergoes whatever the cause acting upon it wishes. Furthermore, that which proceeds from the reason (Logos) that is there already possesses a trace of what is to be done. For as if in a certain imagination or imaginary appearance, the reason being moved—or a motion depending on reason—is a partition. Otherwise, if it were entirely one and the same, no motion would occur there, but it would remain still. Yet Matter cannot receive all forms <note>original: *species*.</note> at once as the soul does within itself; otherwise, it would be one of them. Since it must receive all things, and yet not receive them individually/undividedly, it is necessary for it to be a place for all existing things, to move through all, to meet all, and to suffice for every interval everywhere, since it is not itself confined by any space, but is exposed to the future. In what way, then, is it possible that one thing entering does not prohibit others? For those things which cannot concur at once, perhaps there was not one "first" thing; but if there was, that was the Form of the universe itself. Wherefore all things are indeed together, but in part, whatever you will. For the matter of a living thing is distributed at the same time as the partition of the living thing itself; otherwise, nothing would have been produced according to reason.

<margin>XIX
How matter, from the quality of forms, does not become quantity; and how in the conception of forms it has even less power than a female.</margin> Therefore, the things that enter Matter, as if into a mother, do not hurt it at all, nor do they bring any utility. For the impulses of these things do not pertain to it, but rather to each other. For their powers are directed toward their opposites, not toward their subjects—unless one perhaps considers the subjects together with those things that are collected within them. For heat settles cold, and blackness obscures white; or if they are mixed together, they produce some other quality from themselves. Therefore, those things which are mixed "suffer." But to "suffer" in their case means to be no longer what they were. Then indeed, in animals, the passions <note>original: *passiones*; physical affections or sufferings.</note> are around the bodies, while an alteration occurs according to qualities and inherent powers. When the constitutions themselves are dissolved, or meet, or are transposed beyond their natural state, the passions are in the bodies, but in the souls, there are cognitions—the souls perceiving the more violent passions. Otherwise, they do not know them; but Matter remains. For it suffers nothing when cold departs and heat arrives. For neither of these is properly "friendly" or "hostile" to it. Therefore, its most proper name is the "receptacle" and "nurse." But truly, for what reason was it also called "mother"? For it generates nothing. They seem to call it "mother," whoever think that a mother also holds the place of matter toward those who are born, as if she only receives, but gives nothing to the offspring; since as much body as is in the newborn is held to come from nourishment. If the mother gives anything to the offspring, she does so not by the reason of being matter, but by the reason of being form. For only Form is fertile, while the other nature is sterile. Hence the ancient sages, I believe, signifying this obscurely in sacred mysteries, introduce the ancient Mercury <note>Hermes.</note> as always having the instrument of generation ready for the effect of the work...

PLOTINUS: ENNEAD III.

<margin>A</margin>
...declaring that the generator in the world of sense is the intelligible <term>reason</term> <note>original: *rationem/logon*; the formative principle that organizes matter</note>. By showing the sterility of matter, which always remains the same, they represent it through those things which are arranged around it as sterile. For they introduce the "mother of all," as they call her, taking this principle according to its role as a subject <note>The "subject" or *hypokeimenon* is that which underlies all changes.</note>, and they impose a name of this kind so that they may more clearly indicate what they mean: namely, that matter is not entirely like a mother. This is understood by those who study more deeply the mode in which these things exist, and who are not content merely with the surface of things. To these people, I say, they have demonstrated—from a distance, yet as far as they were able—that matter is sterile. It is not entirely "female," but is female only in the sense that it properly receives. As far as generating is concerned, it does so in no way; for that which has reached this point is neither female in a generative sense, nor is it able to give birth. Rather, it is separated from all power of birthing; for such power belongs only to that which remains "masculine" <note>In ancient philosophical metaphors, the "masculine" is the active, form-giving principle, while the "feminine" is the passive, receptive principle.</note>.

<column-break/>

...the work of the generator in the realm of sense, showing that it is the intelligible reason. The sterility of matter remains always the same, and because of this, they always assign it sterility <note>original Greek: *didontes*</note>, making it the mother of all, which they indeed proclaim in this way, taking the principle according to the underlying subject. And they give it this name so that it may show itself as a foundation <note>original Greek: *ballon*; Plotinus is playing with the etymological roots of the word for "mother" or "material foundation."</note>, wishing to show that it is not similar to a mother in every form. For those who wish to grasp the manner of these things more accurately and do not seek among the many: from afar, yet as they were able, they indicated that such a thing is both sterile and female; but it is female only insofar as it receives, but no longer insofar as it generates. By being separated from that which is joined to it, it is neither female [in a generative sense] nor able to generate, being cut off from all power of generating, which belongs only to that which remains male.
