# MARSILIO FICINO ON THE 
# SEVENTH BOOK OF THE THIRD 
# ENNEAD, CONCERNING ETERNITY 
# AND TIME, 
# A COMMENTARY.
## SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

->What eternity is, and where it is. What sempiternity is. What perpetuity is. How eternity relates to time.<-

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' showing a figure amidst foliage.</image-desc>
The Platonists first place ETERNITY in the "First Mind" <note>The Divine Intellect or *Nous*.</note>; then in other minds; thirdly in bodies, insofar as something stable is preserved within them. Similarly, they place Time first in the "First Soul" <note>The World Soul.</note>, then in other souls, and thirdly in bodies, insofar as motion is found in them. One asks what exactly eternity is in the First Mind and the First Being. Certainly, there are five <term>genera of being</term> <note>These are the five "Great Kinds" from Plato's *Sophist*: Essence, Motion, Rest, Identity, and Diversity.</note> or elements there: namely, essence, motion, rest, identity, and diversity. There are also the species of things which are called Ideas, such as "Humanity" and the like. These genera of being are by no means predicated of one another; for rest itself is neither motion, nor is it movable. Identity is neither diversity, nor is it diverse, for these are opposites. Essence itself also, in its first character, seems to have none of these opposites. Furthermore, the Ideas are not predicated of one another. For the Idea of a lion is neither the Idea of a man, nor is it human. 

Eternity, however, is predicated of all things that are there in such a way that every one of them is eternal. Therefore, eternity is neither a specific genus of being there, nor a specific Idea. It is a gift common to all, whereas the other things there are distinguished from one another either by incommunicable and (so to speak) singular properties, such as the Ideas, or by a certain opposition, such as motion and rest, or identity and diversity. Indeed, although eternity is a gift common to all—so much so that it applies even to motion itself, and to diversity and the multitude existing there, for all these are eternal—nevertheless, it is designated chiefly according to rest, identity, and unity, from which the other things there possess it. 

Yet one should not think that eternity is properly "rest" itself. For in the formal definition of eternity, three things are chiefly contained: namely, rest, <term>sempiternity</term> <note>original: *sempiternitas*; used here to mean "always-being" without beginning or end.</note> (as if you were to say "always" itself), and identity or unity or (so to speak) "indistancy" <note>The state of having no distance or separation between parts; total simultaneity.</note>. But rest itself does not necessarily include these in its definition. It does not include the "always." For we can imagine something standing still, but not always. It does not necessarily embrace unity or the "One," for it can persist within a multitude. Likewise, motion is opposed to rest, but it is not opposed to sempiternity. For what prevents that which is moved from being moved always? And yet sempiternity itself, even if it is not the whole definition of eternity alone, is nevertheless the most important part of its definition. Since, therefore, motion is most opposed to rest, yet does not conflict with sempiternity (which is the most important part of eternity), it is clear that eternity and rest are not entirely the same thing, as rest is in some way distinct from the other things there. 

Eternity, however, is equally common to all. For eternity is a certain vigor of the essential and intellectual life itself, always vigorous in the same way, possessing all its aspects at once, neither losing anything of itself nor acquiring any new gift at any time. Whatever things are there seem to claim this vigor for themselves equally. Meanwhile, you ought to remember that "sempiternity" is simply like a genus signifying perseverance or life that lacks a beginning and an end. Under this genus there are two species: the first is eternity, which is infinite life or perseverance, remaining entirely "at once." The second is <term>perpetuity</term> <note>original: *perpetuitas*</note> or Time itself: namely, infinite perseverance proceeding through parts in succession. Hence, as <term>Proclus</term> <note>A later Neoplatonist philosopher who heavily influenced Ficino's interpretations of Plotinus.</note> says, both are a certain measure: time is the measure of temporal and movable things, while eternity is the measure of eternal things. But time measures by frequent repetition and (as it were) by numbering; whereas eternity, being applied once and fitted to the thing, measures it. The proper definition and name of eternity is not so much...

<summary>This page concludes a discussion on the sterile and receptive nature of Matter before beginning Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Eternity and Time. Ficino defines eternity as a simultaneous, unchanging vigor of life that belongs to the Divine Mind, distinguishing it from both "rest" and "time."</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, specifically Book 7 of the Third Ennead, "On Eternity and Time." On the previous page, the text concluded a discussion on the sterility of matter and began the transition into the nature of the intelligible realm. Here, Ficino explores the distinction between the "ever-present" nature of eternity and the "successive" nature of time.</meta>

# ON BOOK VII OF ENNEAD III.

...essence or intelligence is as much as life. It is therefore life: but of what kind? Surely infinite: so that it differs from any part of time. Again, what kind? Certainly all at once, so that it differs from total time. Therefore, eternity <note>original: *ævum*; often used by Ficino to denote the "everlasting" duration of the intelligible world, distinct from the "eternity" (*æternitas*) of the One.</note> is infinite life, all at once; and to embrace it more briefly, it is life already infinite: while time is life proceeding through infinity. The very being of eternity is entirely fixed in the present, like a center; therefore, one is sufficient. Since it never passes away, there is no need for anything succeeding it. But what is called "present" in time, since it passes away suddenly, needs another successor in the present, lest the whole nature of time be lost—which is gradually piled up from infinite moments succeeding each other in turn. Therefore, if it has any essence, it is mixed from being and non-being, while the present intervenes between the past and the future, which do not exist; and however it can, it emulates the present of eternity through some continuous present of its own, applying itself to the stable presence of eternity, yet it is not stabilized. Therefore, what it cannot attain by remaining, it attains at least by succeeding: so that by proceeding infinitely through many moments, it matches itself to the fixed and simple infinity of eternity as much as it can. Meanwhile, the one remaining (so to speak) moment of eternity, like a center, contemplates and embraces the innumerable moments of time—like points on a circumference perpetually running through—as equally present to its view. Lines and points are indeed distant from each other outside the center, but in the center, they are gathered into one. Similarly, the moments of time and the progressions of temporal things are distant from each other, but in eternity—the principle of time and temporal things—they are so reduced to one that there is one presence of all, one and the same life, and one single vision. 

Among these things, where Plotinus speaks of the "perfect whole," remember that every whole or totality found in art and nature is a certain common form following the individual parts and resulting from the parts. Therefore, such a whole is not a whole through itself, but through its parts, and through that which gathered the parts together; nor is it, therefore, primarily a whole. Thus, that which is primarily a whole is a form and a certain simple substance generating within itself whatever parts it might have. And because it generates them, it somehow precedes them; and by the sign that it precedes the parts, it is entirely indivisible. Now, since it is indivisible, when it inserts itself into individual parts, it inserts itself everywhere as a whole: and this is the "absolute whole," which is recovered as a whole in any part of itself. Such is the divine mind toward the <term>Ideas</term> <note>The eternal, perfect archetypes or blueprints of all things in the mind of God.</note>; such is the universal vital nature toward the <term>seeds</term> <note>original: *semina*; the "seminal reasons" or formative principles that guide biological development.</note> of things; such is the eternity of the mind’s first life toward its entire presence, remaining always in the one and toward the one. In the one present act of itself: likewise toward the "One" which is the Good above essence, conferring itself by loving and acting. Remaining, I say, because whatever it is beneficial to have, it already has; remaining likewise through infinity, yet that infinity there is not some quantity besides life. For since the very life of the first being—which is its first and innermost act—precedes any quantity: if any quantity of duration and perseverance is placed in it, you should understand nothing as added to the simplicity of that indivisible, present life.

---

## On the conformity of the intellect to eternity. Also, what time is not: namely, that it is not duration in bodily motion, or a similar measure; or number, or a consequence and companion of bodily motion.

Where Plotinus, after a profound discussion on eternity, descends to time, you will consider by what reason he proves the eternity of the mind: because it touches eternal things by understanding, since understanding is, in a way, touching. For since all senses perceive the thing to be sensed by a certain touch, much more do the supreme powers of the soul—reason and intelligence—touch by knowing: especially because they penetrate the innermost parts of things by discerning, which the sense does not do. And yet their objects come more effectively to be touched; indeed, it is not even necessary for them to "come," since they are never absent. Therefore, the kinship of the intellect to its own eternal objects is greater than the kinship of the sense to things to be sensed—the kinship, I say, of mutual intelligence: for as much as it touches, it is touched in turn. 

Just as the sense is and acts in time, so the intellect is in eternity. But reason is like a middle between both: for it touches both eternal and temporal things. Such a middle can indeed exist. For the heaven is in both: through its substance in eternity, through its motion and action in time. Such a middle ought not to be lacking to the universe, so that between supernal things (which are eternal in both action and essence) and lower things (which are temporal in both), there are rational souls—through essence in eternity, but through action and motion in time. Accordingly, you will note that it greatly pleases the Platonists that the rational soul accommodates itself to various levels of the universe—eternal, temporal, or middle—insofar as it expresses within itself those same levels naturally implanted in it, just as our body adapts itself in various ways to any place, as it composes itself in various figures and modes. 

Time is either motion itself, or something proper to motion—namely, the innermost space of motion, or its measure, or its companion. It is clear that time is not motion, from the fact that all motion is completed in time: as if time were something else in which motion is performed, and motion itself were another. Furthermore, if a body that is now moving should cease to move a little later, and then be moved again, the motion will indeed be interrupted, but time is not interrupted. For just as we think of "how long it moved," so also "how long it rested": and by the same continuity of time, both the successions of motions and the intermediate rests can be measured. And even if a body ceases to be moved by another, we can think that time at least still remains in the mover that is mobile through itself, as if we should seek the nature of time above the motion of the body. Likewise, in the fastest motion, there is the most of motion but the least of time; in the slowest motion, it is the other way around. Finally, the properties of time are brevity and length; but the properties of motion are intensity and relaxation <note>That is, acceleration and deceleration.</note>, which are declared by swiftness and slowness. 

Those things whose properties differ are themselves different. It is more probable, therefore, that time is something properly pertaining to motion than motion itself. You will perhaps say it is a space—not of place, which is outside motion, but of duration and perseverance, which is internal to motion: like a proper interval and progression of motion. To these, two things can be objected. First, that there would be as many such internal intervals as there are motions; but time ought to be one common measure. Second, that such duration seems to be nothing other than motion itself—namely, the continuity of motion. And certainly, this is the nature of motion: just as dimension extended through space is either the body itself or most proper to the body.

<summary>Ficino explains the Neoplatonic distinction between eternity, which is a fixed "now" containing all life simultaneously, and time, which is a fragmented succession of moments. He argues that the human soul acts as a bridge between these two realms, possessing an eternal essence while acting within the temporal world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's *Enneads*, specifically Book 7 of the Third Ennead, "On Eternity and Time." ### THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO.

However, duration itself is not intrinsic to motions everywhere, but is preserved in this motion and that. We think of Time, however, as being everywhere, and we are accustomed to measure any duration and perseverance of motion by time. From this it appears that time is a certain "mensural interval" <note>original: *interuallum mensurale*; a gap or span that serves as a standard for measurement</note>, beyond the specific interval of the motion itself, yet not belonging to a spatial interval. Therefore, we shall ask concerning an external interval or "conduit" <note>original: *ductu*</note> of this kind: what is it naturally in itself, before this effect of measuring? For it must exist in itself as what it is before it can measure anything. We shall likewise ask whether it measures rest, and in what way. For a thing rests only insofar as something else is moved. Three propositions regarding time have been put forward by those who say time is "something of motion": first, that it is the space and duration of motion (about which enough has been said); second, that it is a certain measure of such duration; third, that it is something accompanying or following motion. But let us now return to the concept of "measure," to which we have just gradually descended, and we are compelled to answer: what is it in itself before it measures? Is it an external measure or an internal one? And whatever it may be, how does it measure motion and rest alike? We add, moreover, how it can be called a "numerical measure," as if it were gathered from units. Yet it is more probable to call time a certain measure simply because of its continuity, rather than a "number." And if it is a certain measure, then it is a certain quantity of whatever kind—a certain magnitude measuring motion, insofar as it runs alongside motion. Here, therefore, it will be asked under what condition it runs with motion, and why it measures motion rather than being measured *by* motion. For we are accustomed to measure "so much time" from "so much motion," and to perceive time from action no less than the other way around. In short, it is doubted again whether time is motion itself measured by a certain magnitude, or rather a certain magnitude measuring motion, or some third thing. Since it uses magnitude to measure motion, one might doubt this very "mensural magnitude." For it is as great in itself as the motion is great. Does it then exist as "so great" through something higher, just as motion is judged to be "so great" through it? Finally, it will be permitted to investigate what it is before it measures (as we have said). Certain similar doubts arise if the third opinion on motion is admitted, saying that time is something that accompanies motion. We are compelled, however, to posit that time itself is something, even if no mind using choice were to measure motion by time. For the Soul of the World <term>Anima Mundi; in Neoplatonic thought, the "soul" that animates the entire physical universe</term> generates time by its own natural and internal motion, using no choice for this purpose.

->Eternity is in the Divine Mind; Time is in the Soul of the World, by which<-
->the motion of the world is driven and measured.<-

In the Divine Mind, time is not present in its proper sense, but rather as a certain "idea" of time, like an archetype conceived there according to a certain likeness—imitating eternity <note>original: *ævum*</note> indeed, but meanwhile falling away from it through diversity. Time, however, is properly in the Soul of the World: in its very vegetative nature, and again in its natural "imagination," which constantly accompanies nature. In this dual faculty of the Soul, I say, the action of generating and imagining worldly things is not performed all at once because of "weakness" <note>original: *debilitatem*; the Soul is "weaker" than the Divine Mind because it must act through succession rather than simultaneous intuition</note>, but arises gradually—now one thing, now another—ordered indeed, but dissimilar, turning now to these things and now to those, proceeding according to "before" and "after." This succession according to such steps is "motion"; however, the continuity and length of this succession is "time." Now, if the length of a body differs from the body itself for any reason, by that same reason time differs from motion—that is, the "length" of the movement differs from the movement itself. Moreover, this very length relates to eternity just as a line relates to a point; especially if we may imagine that a line proceeds from the movement of a point, and the point is extended. Indeed, Plotinus thinks that just as the proper body sprouts from the power of any soul implanted in its seed, so the worldly body sprouts from the natural power of the World Soul breathing into matter. This body is contained, ruled, and moved within the Soul as if in a "place" for the world, following the motion of the Soul itself. It is moved temporally and through certain intervals of time, corresponding to the time of the motion that exists in the Soul and to the certain intervals of that time. For that Soul, through its internal motion, created time within itself, and together with this motion and time, it produced the world, which is movable *in* time. The "place" of the world is one: the Soul of the World. Time is also one and everywhere, since this Soul exercises its vital motion everywhere. Meanwhile, the worldly motion is ruled by the motion of its own Soul; this, in turn, is ruled by its own eternal Intellect; and that, finally, by the Divine Intellect and its primary eternity.

### ON ETERNITY AND TIME.
->On eternity and time.<-
->Introduction to eternity and to time.<-

WHEN we say that eternity and time are different from one another, and that the former concerns the everlasting nature, while the latter—time—concerns the realm of things that come into being: and this whole universe, we think immediately, as if by certain more collective applications of our concepts, that we possess in our souls a clear experience regarding these things. We speak of them constantly <margin>\* and all and everything</margin> and we name them in all circumstances. However, when we attempt to focus our attention upon them and, as it were, to approach them closely, we find ourselves again in difficulty in our thoughts. We take up the various declarations of the ancients concerning them—or perhaps different interpretations of the same declarations—and resting upon these, we consider it sufficient if, when asked, we can state what seemed true to those men; content with this, we abandon the search for ourselves. One must believe, then, that some of the ancient and blessed philosophers <note>Plotinus refers here to figures like Plato and Pythagoras</note> found the truth. It is proper, therefore, to investigate which of them reached it most successfully, and how we might gain an understanding of these matters. And first, we must seek concerning eternity: what exactly do they think it is, those who posit it as something different from time? For once the model—which stands firm—is known, perhaps its image <note>original: "εἰκόνος" / "imago"; Plotinus follows Plato's *Timaeus* in calling time a "moving image of eternity"</note>, which they call time, might become clear. But if someone, before beholding eternity, should form an image of what time is, it might happen that by a certain recollection <note>the Platonic concept of *anamnesis*, or soul-memory</note> he might pass from the latter to the former, to which time is likened, if indeed it possesses some similarity to it.

WHAT then should one say eternity is? Is it perhaps the "intelligible essence" itself <note>the world of Divine Forms or Ideas</note>, just as if one were to say that time is the whole of the heavens and the cosmos? For indeed, some have held such an opinion <margin>† most venerable</margin> concerning time. Since we imagine and understand eternity to be something of the highest majesty <margin>† most venerable</margin>, and

<column-break/>

AS WE say that eternity and time are different from one another, and that the former is concerned with the sempiternal nature, but the latter with that which is becoming: we think we possess, as if spontaneously, from a natural talent and by a sudden intuition of intelligence, a certain manifest instinct regarding these things deep within our minds, speaking of them always in the same way and naming them everywhere. But truly, when we strive to approach these things more closely and to explain them more absolutely, we fall into doubts; and accepting the opinions of the ancients—some one way, some another, or perhaps different views of the same things—we finally dwell upon these, thinking ourselves satisfied if, when questioned, we are able to report the opinion of the ancients, and thus we cease from further investigation. Truly, it must be thought that certain of the ancient and blessed philosophers discovered the truth. It is worthwhile, therefore, to inquire next which of them especially attained the truth, and by what means we also might chiefly know these same things. But first, we must inquire concerning eternity: what they think it is, those who judge it to be different from time. For once that which is held as the "exemplar" <note>the archetype or original pattern</note> is known, perhaps its image, which they call time, will be more clearly understood. If, however, anyone, before he contemplates eternity, should imagine what time is: it will perhaps happen to him that, through a certain reminiscence, he may proceed from here to there, and recognize that to which time is assimilated, if indeed this has a likeness to eternity.

<margin>A</margin> Perhaps one might rightly take the intelligible nature and eternity to be the same thing: for we are able to describe that which is above these things only by such names. Again, both the intelligible world and eternity encompass the same contents within themselves. Yet, when we speak of one being in the other, and we place intelligible things within eternity—and when we declare any intelligible thing to be eternal, as it is written in the *Timaeus* <note>original: "in Timaeo"; Plotinus refers to Plato’s dialogue regarding the creation of the universe</note> where it says: "if the nature of the model is eternal"—in these instances, I say, we are affirming that eternity is something other than the intelligible nature itself. Nevertheless, we admit it exists around that nature, or in it, or is present to it. But the fact that both are judged to be venerable <note>or "august/sacred"</note> does not necessarily demonstrate that they are the same as each other. <margin>B</margin> For perhaps one of these holds its claim to being venerable from the other. Furthermore, regarding the point that both contain the same things: it must be explained that while the intelligible nature contains each of its own parts as parts, eternity embraces the whole together at once—not as a part, but because all such things are called "eternal" by means of it. <margin>C</margin> But should we judge eternity according to the state <note>term: status; here meaning a condition of rest or unchanging stability</note> existing there, just as people are accustomed to thinking of time here according to motion? To begin with, one might rightly ask about eternity: should we say it is the same as "rest"? Perhaps not simply, but as the rest that is perceived to exist around essence <note>term: essentia/ousia; the fundamental reality or "being" of a thing</note>. For if it is the same as rest, we would first of all not call rest "eternal," just as we do not call eternity itself "eternal." For that which is eternal is that which participates in eternity. <margin>D</margin> Furthermore, in what way would motion be eternal? For in that case, it would also be "stable." Besides, how will the notion of rest itself contain the concept of "always"? I do not mean "always" in terms of time, but rather the kind of "always" we understand when we say "everlasting." If this "always" is contained within the very rest of essence, we shall surely separate the remaining "kinds" of being <note>Plotinus refers to the five "Great Kinds" from Plato's *Sophist*: Being, Rest, Motion, Sameness, and Difference</note> from eternity. <margin>E</margin> Added to this is the fact that eternity must be understood not only in rest, but also in the One. Moreover, the quality of "lack of extension" <note>term: indistantia; the state of being without parts or spatial/temporal spread</note> must be preserved for eternity, lest it be the same as time. Rest, by its nature as rest, contains in itself the concept neither of the One nor of the non-extended. Therefore, we preach that eternity "abides in the One." It participates in rest, therefore, but it is not rest itself.

<margin>II. Eternity exists in the first essence by way of life and rest and identity, and is truly the total and simultaneous and perfect possession of an unending life.</margin>

<margin>F</margin> WHAT, then, will that thing be most of all, through which we say the whole divine world is eternal and everlasting? And what is "everlastingness"? Is it the same as eternity, or is eternity something that exists according to it? Perhaps it is a single intelligence or nature—whether it follows those things that are there, or exists simultaneously with them, or is seen within them. All these things, I say, are reduced into that one nature which exists, which is also many and is capable of many things. Indeed, one who contemplates this manifold power names it "essence" <note>ousia</note> insofar as it serves as a subject; but insofar as he beholds its life, he names it "motion"; and then "rest," insofar as it maintains itself in exactly the same way. <margin>G</margin> Then "difference" and "sameness" insofar as these many things are at the same time one. Thus, by composing them again into one, I say into one

Regarding their containment: for the one [intelligible nature], it will be as of parts; but for eternity, it sees the whole not as a part; but because all such things are eternal according to it. <margin>\* But then</margin> <margin>C</margin> must it be said that the "rest" <margin>\* but then</margin> there is eternity, just as they say time here is according to motion? <margin>\* they say; reading?</margin> But reasonably one might seek time again, whether we speak of it as rest, or not simply, but as the rest concerning essence. If it is in the rest of essence, then the other things must again be excluded from eternity. <gloss>let us fall back</gloss> Then must we think of eternity only in rest, or also in the One? Then also as without extension, so that it is not the same as time. It would therefore partake of rest, but it would not be rest itself.

<margin>F</margin> WHAT then would this be, by which we say the whole world there [the intelligible world] is eternal and everlasting? And what is everlastingness? Is it the same thing, and is it the same as eternity, or is eternity according to it? For must it be according to some one thing? But it is a certain concept or nature gathered from many things, whether following the things there, or being with them, or being seen in them. I say that all these things there have a unity, but are capable of being many and will be many; and when one has gathered that manifold power, <margin>\* that essence is spoken of alone</margin> as if gathering the subject, one calls it "essence." <summary>Plotinus distinguishes eternity from the "intelligible world," arguing that while they are related, eternity is the unifying principle that allows the divine realm to possess its life all at once. He concludes that eternity is not merely "rest" or "stability," but a participation in the One that transcends spatial or temporal extension.</summary>

### BOOK SEVEN

<column-break/>

->[In that vision, one sees] life as a single whole,<- contracting <note>or "drawing together"</note> all otherness within it, and beholding the unending identity of its activity. This life never shifts from one thing to another, nor does its thought or life move from this to that; rather, it remains always the same, standing far apart from any distance <note>meaning spatial or temporal separation</note>. Beholding all these things, one beholds eternity. One sees life remaining in the same state, always present, possessing the whole at once—not "this thing now" and "that thing later," but all things together. 
<margin>B</margin> Nor are there different things at different times, but rather an indivisible end. It is as if all things were together in a single point, not yet flowing out into a stream, but remaining there in the same place—that is, in itself—and never changing. 
<margin>*by nature</margin>
It stands always in the present, for nothing of it has passed away, nor will anything new come to be in it. 
<margin>*truly</margin>
Rather, what it is, it always is. Thus, eternity is not a underlying subject, but that which shines forth from the subject <note>the "subject" here refers to the True Being or Essence</note> according to its own identity. Through this identity, it declares itself concerning things that are not "about to be," but are "already present." It promises to remain just as it is, and never otherwise. 
<margin>C</margin> For what could happen to it later that is not already with it now? Nor will it be anything later that it is not already. For there is nothing from which it could move into its present state. That Being was never anything else, and it will never be anything that it does not already possess by necessity. 
<margin>D</margin>
<margin>*then</margin>
Therefore, it does not have that which is called "it was." For what could have passed away from it? Nor does that which is called "it will be" happen to it. For what will it become? What remains, then, is for it to "be" in its very being. Thus, that which neither "was" nor "will be," but only "is"—having its being stably, because it neither changes into the future nor has been changed by the past—is eternity. 
<margin>*then</margin>
Therefore, eternity is the life that exists around Being, in its very act of being, a life that is whole, full, and everywhere entirely without interval. This is the very eternity we are seeking. 
<margin>E</margin>
<margin>*this</margin>

WE must certainly not think that eternity is something that happens to that divine nature from the outside; rather, it is from that nature, with that nature, and in that nature. It is seen as being deeply indwelling within it. 
<margin>III
Eternity exists in the first essence, not as an accident <note>a temporary or external quality</note>, but as an essential property of it. That essence is truly the Whole and the All. Likewise, it is shown how the being of eternal things differs from the being of temporal things.</margin>
For just as we say all other things are present there, looking at them as if they were internal, we say they all proceed from and exist together with the Essence. For those things which are "first" 
<margin>F</margin> must exist with the first principles and be within them, since truth is in them. And in one sense, the Whole is in the part, while in another, the parts are in the Whole. In truth, this "All" is not a collection gathered from parts, but is the very thing that generates the parts, so that for this reason it is truly the All. Furthermore, the truth found there is not a harmony with something else, but is the specific property of each thing that possesses it. 
<margin>G</margin> Truly, this whole must be real: if it is to be truly the All, it must not only be the All insofar as it is "all things," but it must possess the Whole in such a way that nothing is lacking. If this is so, nothing will "become" for it <note>nothing will be added to it in the future</note>. For if something were yet to be, it would have been lacking in that respect previously. It would not, therefore, have been the All before that point. But nothing can happen to this nature that is contrary to its nature.

<meta>Catchword: therefore (ἄρα / igitur)</meta>

<summary>Plotinus defines eternity not as a duration of time, but as the unchanging, "ever-present" life of the intelligible realm, where there is no past or future, only a total and perfect "is." He argues that eternity is an essential property of divine Being, rather than an external quality added to it.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s metaphysical inquiry into the nature of eternity. Following the previous discussion of eternity as a "total life" that exists all at once, Plotinus now explains why true Being cannot have a future or a past, contrasting it with the "becoming" of the physical world.</meta>

### PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK III.

<margin>A</margin> For it <note>the eternal Being</note> undergoes nothing. Therefore, if nothing happens to it, certainly nothing will be in the future, nor will it be, nor was it becoming, nor has it been made. If you were to take away the "will be" from objects that are subject to change <note>literally "general things," referring to the physical world of becoming</note>, since they exist in a state of perpetual acquisition, they would suddenly cease to exist. However, for things that are not of that nature, if you add a "will be" to them, they happen to fall away from the very seat of Being. From this, it is clear that "to be" is not innate to them if their existence depends on what is in the future, or what was in the past, or what is yet to be done. 

<margin>B</margin> Indeed, in generated things, essence <term>essentia; the fundamental nature of a thing</term> seems to be primarily a certain progression from the beginning of its generation until it reaches the end of its time, when it exists no longer. This progression is what is called their "existence." If someone were to cut anything away from this progression, their life would be diminished, and thus their "being" would also be diminished. The universe must be of this nature as long as it exists in this way. For this reason, nature hurries toward the future and does not wish to stand still, since it draws its "being" to itself by doing one thing after another, <margin>C</margin> moving in a circle because of a certain desire for essence. 

Thus, we have discovered what "being" is for these things. We have also found the cause of their motion: they hurry toward a "always being" by the aid of the future. But for the primary and blessed things, there is no desire for the future. For they are already the whole, and they already possess the entirety of the life they ought to have. Therefore, they seek nothing, because there is no future for them. Nor, then, does that condition in which the "future" exists apply to them. 

<margin>D</margin> Therefore, the absolute and total essence of Being is that which is not dissected into parts, but is whole in all its parts, failing in nothing and lacking nothing. To it, nothing that is called "non-being" can happen. For not only must all beings be present to the whole, but nothing of non-being should ever occur. This property and nature is eternity <term>æternitas; from the Latin "aeternus," meaning without beginning or end</term>, which is also called *aeuum* <note>original: "aeuum." A Latin term for a long age or eternity</note>. For *aeuum* is named from that which is "always" <note>original: "semper." This refers to the etymology of the Greek word "aion" from "aei on," meaning "always being"</note>.

Is it not already everlasting <term>sempiternum; lasting forever</term> unless its nature is such that one can believe without doubt that it will never be otherwise? So that, if you look at it again, you will find it the same. 

<margin>F</margin> What if someone never ceased from this contemplation, but persevered continually, admiring this nature and being able to persist with an untiring spirit? It possesses the whole life it has already; it has not received anything, nor is it receiving, nor <margin>G</margin> will it receive anything. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Ennead III, Book 7, where Plotinus explores the nature of eternity. Having defined eternity as the "total life" of the divine intellect, he now examines the linguistic origins of the word "Aeon" and begins the transition into an investigation of Time.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III.

<column-break/>

...for the sake of clarity, the word "always" is added. For "being" is not one thing and "always being" another, just as a "philosopher" is not one thing and a "true philosopher" another. However, because some people merely pretend to practice philosophy, the addition of "true" was made. In this same way, "always" is added to "being," and "being" to "always," so that it is called *Aion* <note>original: "aiõn" / "αἰῶν"</note>, which means "always being." This is why it is called *Aeon* <note>original: "æon" / "ævũ"</note>, that is, Eternity. Therefore, "always" must be understood with "being" so that it signifies "true being" to us. Truly, "always" must be gathered into an indistinguishable power which, besides what it already possesses, needs nothing else—for it possesses everything. Everything, therefore, is both "being" and, through being everything, is in need of nothing. A nature of this kind is not full in one part and empty in another. For that which exists in time, even if it seems perfect—like a body sufficient for a soul—is only perfect through the soul, and it lacks something of a future yet to come, since it lacks the very time it requires. Consequently, even if that future should happen to be present and coincide with it, being imperfect, it would only be called "perfect" in an ambiguous sense. But that which is such that it neither needs a future, nor is reduced into another measured time, nor is an infinite and infinitely-coming future—but already possesses whatever it is necessary to be—that is exactly what our intellect desires. For its existence does not come from a certain quantity, but is present even before any quantity. It is fitting that since it is not any quantity, it should not touch anything of a specific quantity or magnitude, lest its life, if divided, should lose its purely indivisible nature; rather, it should be individual both in its life and in its essence. As for what is said in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the universe</note>—that "the world’s maker was good"—this refers to the universal intellect, signifying that in placing something above the universe, he did not mean this in the sense of a specific time. For this reason, the world did not obtain a temporal beginning, since the very cause of its existence applies the word "was" beforehand. Nevertheless, after saying this for the sake of explanation, he later corrects this expression—that is, the word "was"—as if it were not correctly applied to eternal things.

The soul, through something eternal in itself, attains eternity; likewise, through its temporal part, it attains time. Also, he concludes the opinions concerning time.

But how can we be, since we exist in time? Yet, under what condition it is possible to be primarily in time, and under what condition in eternity, will be more clearly known once we have added a description of what time is. Truly, we must descend from eternity to the investigation of time. <meta>This page transitions from the definition of Eternity (Aeon) to the investigation of Time (Chronos). Having established Eternity as the life of the Divine Intellect, Plotinus now surveys the classical definitions of Time provided by earlier philosophers like Plato, Aristotle, and the Stoics to see how they align with his own emerging theory.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN.

<column-break/>

A ...to apply our own stated opinion to the very conception of it [Time] that we possess. But now it is necessary first to take up those things most worthily said by others, considering whether our account might harmonize with any of them. We should perhaps divide the accounts given about it into three: for it might be called either **motion**, or **that which is moved**, or **something belonging to motion**. To say that it is rest, or that which stands still, or something belonging to rest, would be altogether far from our conception of time, or it would not be time at all. B Of those who call it motion, some say it is *all* motion, while others say it is the motion of the universe. Of those who call it the thing moved, they say it is the sphere of the universe <note>Plotinus refers here to the Pythagorean or Platonic view of the celestial spheres.</note>. C Others say it is something belonging to motion: some an interval <note>original: "diastēma" / "διάστημα"</note> of motion, others a measure, others something that generally follows it, whether it be rest or ordered motion.

### MOTION
Indeed, it is not possible [that time is motion], whether one takes all motions together—making one out of them all—or only ordered motion. For both of these types of motion occur *in* time. D If there were a motion that was not in time, it would be even further from being time itself; it would be as if that in which the motion occurs were one thing, while the motion itself were something else. Though other things have been and could be said, this is sufficient: motion can cease and be intermittent, but time cannot. Even if someone says the motion of the universe does not cease, if this motion refers to the celestial circuit, it would still occur within a certain time, and it eventually returns to the same point. It does not return in the same space that half of the circuit completes; this motion is half, while the other is double, even though both are motions of the universe—the one returning from the same to the same, and the one only reaching the halfway point. E <margin>* outside this</margin> Furthermore, the common saying that the motion of the outermost sphere is the swiftest and most vehement confirms this account: namely, that the motion of the sphere is one thing, and time is another. For the swiftest of all is clearly that which, in a shorter time, covers the greatest and largest interval; F <margin>* slower</margin> while other things are slower because they cover the same distance in a longer time, or only a part of it. If, therefore, the motion of the sphere is not time, then the sphere itself—which was thought to be time because it moves—is certainly not time either. So then, is it "something of motion"? If it is an interval, first of all, is it the same interval for every motion, or only for uniform motion? For motion in space can be faster or slower, and if both intervals are measured by some third thing, that third thing would more rightly be called time. G <margin>* of a certain [motion]</margin> Of which of these is the interval time? Or rather, which of them, since they are infinite? If it belongs to ordered motion, will the interval be time? A ...to adapt our own opinion to the very notion of it. Now, however, it is necessary in the first place to receive those things which have been said with greater reason, considering whether our sentiment harmonizes with any of them. Before all else, perhaps we ought to distinguish the opinions of others concerning time into three members. For time is either **motion itself**, or **that which is moved**, or **something of motion**. To say, however, that time is rest, or the stable itself, or something of standing still, would be very far removed from the very notion of time; since it least allows for identity <note>Here, "identity" refers to static sameness; time is characterized by flow and change.</note>, and therefore cannot agree with rest and the stable. B Of those who think time is motion, some say it is all motion, others the motion of the universe. Those who affirm that the thing moved is time bring the sphere of the whole into the discussion. C Consequently, those who say time is "something of motion" call it partly an interval, or space, or the duration of motion; partly a measure, or partly something accompanying motion, whether all motion or rather ordered motion.

### TIME
Indeed, it is impossible for time to be motion: not even if you take all motions together, making as if one out of all, nor if you take only ordered motion; for both motions occur in time. D If any motion were said not to occur in time, it would be much further from this besides, that it should be time; as if one thing were that in which the motion is acted out, while another were the motion itself. Since there are other things which are and have been said, this is sufficient: motion can certainly cease and be interrupted, but time not at all. If someone says the motion of the universe is not interrupted, yet even this motion—if he means the circuit—occurs in a certain time, and at some point returns to the same: it does not do so in the space where half of it is fulfilled. This motion is half, and that is double, while clearly both are motions of the universe—the one which returns from the same to the same, and the one which only reaches the half. E Moreover, what is usually said—that the motion of the outermost sphere is the most vehement and swiftest—confirms the same: namely, that the sphere's motion is one thing, and time is another. For the swiftest of all is that which, in a shorter time, completes a greater and maximum space; others are slower, which follow in a longer time, covering only part of the same space. F If therefore time is not the motion of the sphere, neither will it be the sphere itself; which indeed, because it moves, was thought to be time. But is time "something of motion"? Surely, if it is said to be the interval of motion, we will first object that the interval of just any motion is not the same, even if the motions are uniform. G For faster and slower motion is also carried out in space. And it can happen that both intervals are measured by a certain third thing, which one would much more rightly say is time. Of which of these motions will the interval be time? Rather, of which of them, since they are infinite? If indeed ordered motion...

<meta>The catchword "Si verò ordinati motus" (If indeed ordered motion) indicates the sentence continues on the next page, further exploring the Stoic and Aristotelian definitions of time as a measure or interval of the celestial movements.</meta>

<summary>Plotinus begins his investigation into the nature of Time by reviewing and critiquing the definitions of previous philosophers. He argues that Time cannot be motion itself, the celestial sphere, or a mere interval of motion, because motion occurs *within* time and varies in speed, whereas time remains a constant measure.</summary>

--- Page 456 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s dialectical investigation into the nature of Time. Having previously dismissed the idea that Time is simply "motion" itself, he now turns his attention to the theory that Time is an "interval" or "extension" (diastēma) of motion, a view often associated with the Stoics or certain interpretations of Plato. He argues that if time were merely the extension of a motion, it would be indistinguishable from the motion itself or from the physical space traversed.</meta>

-># PLOTINUS ON THE ENNEADS, BOOK III.<-

<column-break/>

If an interval <note>original: "spatium" / "διάστημα" (diastēma), meaning an extension or span</note> is thought to be time, it certainly cannot be the interval of every such motion; for these are many, which would result in many "times" existing simultaneously. But if it is the interval of the motion of the universe, what else would that interval be but the motion itself? If it is "so much" [a specific quantity], this "so much" will be measured by place, since it is the space it traverses; and that interval will be place, not time. 

Or perhaps motion is said to have an interval or extension because of its continuity, and because it does not cease suddenly but is perpetually prolonged. But this will be nothing other than the magnitude or amplitude of the motion. If someone, looking at the motion itself, pronounces it to be "much," as if one said heat was "much," time still does not appear or occur to us <note>original: "φαίνεται" (phainetai)</note> <gloss>nor a defined one</gloss>; rather, it is motion again and again, like water flowing again and again. 

And the interval perceived <gloss>within it</gloss> and the repeated flowing out will be a number, like a "two" or a "three," while the interval <note>original: "spatium" / "διάστημα"</note> will belong to the bulk <note>original: "mola" / "ὄγκος" (onkos), referring to the physical mass or volume of the movement</note>. Thus, the magnitude <gloss>or nothingness</gloss> of motion will be like the number ten, or like an interval seen in the bulk of the motion; this does not contain the concept of time, but is merely something of a certain size occurring *within* time. 

Otherwise, time will not be everywhere, but only in motion as if in a subject, and we would again fall into calling time "motion." For the interval or duration of motion is not outside the motion, but is the motion itself not completed all at once or in an instant. When it is said to happen "not suddenly"—if anything said to happen suddenly occurs in time—we must ask how that which does not happen suddenly differs from that which happens suddenly and in a moment. Perhaps the difference is that it acts in time; therefore, both the lasting motion and its duration or interval are not time itself, but are fulfilled *in* time. 

If someone asserts that the interval of motion is time—not as something proper to the motion itself, but according to the extension the motion has, running alongside it <note>Plotinus uses the image of two things running together in parallel</note>—it has still not been explained what this actually is. For it is clear that this is the time in which the motion happened. But this was what we were asking from the beginning: what is time in its existence? For this answer is just like someone who, when asked "What is time?", responds "The interval of motion in time." 

What then is this interval? The one who places it outside the specific interval of motion calls it time. Furthermore, the person who places a temporal interval within motion itself will wonder where to place the interval of rest. For as long as one thing is moved, another remains at rest; and you will say the time of both is the same, even though it regards one differently than the other. What then is this interval, and what is its nature? It cannot be local <note>related to physical place</note>, since that too is present from the outside.

<margin>
VIII.
Time is not a measure of bodily motion inherent in motion, nor a continuous measure for them, nor as a number.
</margin>

### WE MUST CONSIDER next how time can be a "number of motion" or a "measure" <note>This is a direct critique of Aristotle's famous definition of time in the *Physics*</note>; which might perhaps be more probable to say because of its continuity. First...

<column-break/>

...whether of every motion, or not even of such motion. For these are many, so that there will also be many times at once. But if it is the interval of the universe, if it is the interval in the motion itself, what else would it be but the motion again? So much indeed; but the "so much" flow will be measured by the place it has passed through. And the interval will be this [place]; and this is not time, but place. Or the motion itself, by its continuity, and by not stopping immediately but always continuing, will have the interval. But this would be the "muchness" of the motion. And if someone, looking at it, declares it to be much, as if someone said the heat was much, even here time does not <margin>* appear</margin> appear <gloss>* nor a defined one.</gloss> but motion again and again, like water flowing again and again, and the <gloss>* in it</gloss> interval being observed <margin>* or itself</margin>. And the "again and again" will be a number, like a "two" or a "three"; but the interval belongs to the bulk. Thus there would be a multitude <gloss>* or nothing</gloss> of motion, or a ten, or as the interval appearing to the bulk, as it were, of the motion, which does not have the concept of time: but this "so much" will be happening in time. Or time will not be everywhere, but in the motion as a substrate. And it happens again that we call time "motion." For if the interval is outside it, yet motion is not all at once, and the "not all at once" [is used], if the "all at once" is not in time. The "not all at once" will differ from the "all at once" by something, namely by being in time. So the passing motion and its interval are not time itself, but are in time. If someone says the interval of motion is time, not the interval of the motion itself: but alongside it the motion has its extension, as if running along with it. But what this is, has not been said. For it is clear that this is the time in which the motion happened. And this the argument did not seek from the beginning, what time is. Since, <margin>* something similar and the same happens</margin> something similar and the same happens, as if someone asked what time is and said it is the interval of motion in time. What then is this interval, which you call time, you who place the interval as an image of motion on the outside? For again, even placing the interval in the motion itself, where will one place the interval of rest? For as long as something is moved, another thing will be standing still. And you would say the time of each is the same, as being clearly different from both. What then is this interval still, and what nature does it have? Since a spatial one is not possible, since this too is from the outside.

NUMBER of motion or measure. For it would be better [to speak] of it as continuous, how it is to be considered. First...

# BOOK SEVEN

<column-break/>

And here, we must similarly raise a doubt, as we did concerning the interval <note>original: "διαστήματος" / "intervallo" — a span or extension</note> of motion: whether we should say that time is the number or measure of every motion equally. <margin>one might say</margin> For in what way would anyone count a motion that is disordered and irregular <note>original: "ἄτακτον καὶ ἀνώμαλον" / "inordinatum inaequalemque"</note>, or what would its number or measure be, or according to what would that measure be defined? 

<margin>A</margin> But if he <note>Likely referring to Aristotle</note> measures both motions with the same measure, <margin>each to it</margin> or joins every motion together, whether slow or fast, then the number and the measure will be such as if the number ten <note>original: "δεκὰς" / "denarius"</note> were used to measure both horses and oxen; <margin>B</margin> or as if there were the same measure for both liquids and solids. 

If, therefore, time is such a measure, it has already been stated what things time belongs to—namely, motions. But what time itself is has not yet been explained. Just as the number ten <note>original: "δεκάδ'"</note> can be understood as a number even without the horses, and a measure is a measure having a certain nature of its own even if it is not yet measuring anything, <margin>through measuring; let it be</margin> so also must time be, since it is a measure. 

<margin>C</margin> If such time exists in itself just as a number does, in what way will it differ from this number—the kind of number that is a "ten" or any other number composed of units <note>original: "μοναδικά" / "vnitatibus"</note>? But if it is a continuous measure, being a certain quantity, it will be a measure like a cubit-long magnitude <note>original: "πηχυαῖον μέγεθος" / "cubitalis magnitudo"</note>. It would therefore be a magnitude, like a line running along with the motion. 

Yet how will this line, running along with it, measure that which it runs alongside? For why should one measure the other rather than the reverse? <margin>D</margin> It would be more probable to suppose this not of every motion, but only of the one it runs alongside. That motion must be continuous, so that the measure running alongside it may maintain its continuity. One should not take the measure from the outside, nor separately, but the measured motion should be taken together. 

Thus, what is it that measures? Will the motion be the thing measured, and the magnitude be the thing measuring? And which of these will be time? <margin>E</margin> Will it be the measured motion, or rather the measuring magnitude? Indeed, time will either be the motion measured by the magnitude, or the magnitude that measures, or a third thing using the magnitude, like a cubit used to measure how great the motion is. 

But in all these cases, we must suppose what we previously said to be more probable: that the motion is uniform <note>original: "ὁμαλὴν κίνησιν" / "aequale motum"</note>. For without uniformity, and especially without the unity of the motion of the whole universe, that opinion which thinks time is a measure in any way whatsoever is quite shaky. 

<margin>F</margin> If, then, time is measured motion—measured, that is, by quantity—just as if it were necessary for motion to be measured, it ought not to have taken the measure from itself, but from something else. Thus, if the motion has another measure besides itself, and for this reason we needed a continuous measure for its measurement, then in the same way the magnitude itself will need a measure, so that the motion can be as much as has been measured. <margin>G</margin> That is, after the thing according to which it is measured has been so much or so much. 

And so time will be that number of the magnitude which accompanies the motion <note>original: "παρομαρτῶν" / "comitantis"</note>, but not the magnitude itself running alongside the motion. What kind of number would this be? Perhaps one made of units? And how <meta>does it measure...</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Here also it will be doubted in a similar way as with the interval, whether we ought to call time the number or measure of every motion similarly. For in what way will anyone count a disordered and unequal motion, or what indeed is the number or measure: or according to what is it most especially a measure? 

But if he counts with the same number, or measures each motion altogether, whether fast or slow, it will indeed be a number and measure, as if the number ten measured both horses and <margin>B</margin> oxen alike, or if there were the same measure for liquids and solids. If, therefore, time is such a measure, it has already been said of what things it is the time, namely of motions. 

But what it is itself has not yet been explained. For if, just as the number ten can be understood as a number even without the horses, and a measure in itself is a measure having its own nature even if it does not yet measure, so it is necessary for time to be, since it is a measure. 

<margin>C</margin> If, I say, such time is in itself the same as a number is, in what will it differ from this number, such as is the ten or any other number gathered from units? But if it is a certain continuous measure, certainly being some quantity, it will be a measure like some cubit-long magnitude. It will therefore be a magnitude, like a certain line running together with the motion. 

But how will that which runs together measure that with which it runs? Why should one measure the other rather than the reverse? <margin>D</margin> It would be more probably posed not in any motion, but in that which runs along with it. But that must be continuous, insofar as the concurrent motion will continue its tenor; it is not fitting to place the measure from the outside, nor apart, but the measured motion together. 

Therefore, it will be something that measures. Will the motion be measured, while the magnitude is measuring? And which of these will be time? Will it be the measured motion, or rather the measuring magnitude? <margin>E</margin> Surely time will be either the motion measured by magnitude, or the measuring magnitude, or some third thing using the magnitude, like a cubit measure for measuring how great the motion is. 

But in all these, as we said was more probable, it must be supposed that the motion is uniform; without uniformity, and also the unity of the motion of the universe itself, that opinion is certainly more vacillating which thinks time is a measure in whatever way. 

<margin>F</margin> If, however, time be measured motion—measured, that is, by a quantity—just as if it were necessary for motion to be measured, it ought not to take the measure from itself, but to receive it from some other; so it is necessary, if motion has another measure besides itself, and because of this we lacked a continuous measure to dimension it: so, I say, the magnitude itself will also need a measure, so that the motion may be as much as was measured: <margin>G</margin> after, clearly, that according to which it is measured was so much or so much. 

And thus time will be that number of the magnitude accompanying the motion, but not the magnitude itself running together with the motion. But what kind of number is this, whether constituted of units, and how it measures <meta>...</meta>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK III.

<page-num>334</page-num>

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>A</margin> ...it measures, it must necessarily be doubted: since if someone even discovers how, they will not find the time that measures, but only time properly <note>original: "tempus propriè tantùm" — referring to time as a specific quantity rather than the essence of Time itself</note>. That, however, is by no means the same as time itself. For it is one thing to speak of time, and another to speak of time only as a measurement: for before it is a "so much," it must be defined what this itself is, which is, and is "so much." But will time be a number measuring motion from the outside? Not taken in the way that the number ten is taken along with horses, but rather <margin>B</margin> like the number ten *in* the horses. What this number may be has not been said—which, even before it measures, is that which it is, just like the number ten itself. Is it this number which, running through the motion according to "prior" and "posterior," measures it? Yet this number, measuring according to prior and posterior <note>Aristotle defined time as the "number of motion in respect of the before and after."</note>, has not yet appeared to us in its true quality. Nevertheless, whatever measures according to prior and posterior, whether it measures by some sign like a point or by anything else, it will measure entirely according to time. Therefore, time will be that which measures motion through prior and <margin>C</margin> posterior, being connected to time and touching time so that it might be able to measure. For either one accepts "prior" and "posterior" according to place, as at the beginning of a race-track <note>original: "stadi j" / "σταδίῳ" — a stadium or running track</note> and those parts following it: or else, certainly, one must accept not a local prior and posterior, but a temporal one. For that which is called "prior" is altogether time ending at that which is "present"; while that which is "posterior" is similarly time beginning from the "present." Therefore, time is something other than the number which measures motion through prior <margin>D</margin> and posterior—not only any motion, but even ordered motion. Furthermore, why indeed, when a number is applied—whether according to the thing measured or according to the measurer (for perhaps the same thing can be both measurer and measured)—why, I ask, when the number is applied, will there be time? While motion is already active, and "prior" and "posterior" occur entirely around the motion, time will not yet exist: just as if someone were to say that magnitude, as great as it is, does not exist unless someone perceives how great the magnitude is. <margin>E</margin> Likewise, since time is said to be infinite, under what condition will number exist around it, unless perhaps someone, selecting some part of time, measures it? In which case it happens to exist even before it is measured. What, then, prevents time from existing before there is a soul <term>soul: in Greek "psyche," the animating principle that Plotinus argues is necessary to perceive or "generate" the flow of time</term> to measure it? Unless, perhaps, someone says its generation proceeds from the soul. Yet, by the act of measurement itself, it is in no way necessary that time be made by the soul. For it exists in its quantity even if no one measures it. <margin>F</margin> As for the suggestion that time is perhaps what uses magnitude as a measure: if anyone should argue that this is the soul, we shall object that this pertains nothing to the notion of time.

### IX. Time is not something following after the motion of a body. Also, a preface to treating what time is.

IX. To say that time is a certain consequence of motion <note>original: "motionis consecutionem" — a following-along or accompaniment</note> is not to teach what this thing itself is, nor is it even permitted to say this before explaining what that is which follows. For that might perhaps be time itself. We must consider this very "consequence," whether it <margin>G</margin> occurs "prior," "posterior," or "simultaneously"—if indeed there is such a consequence. for in whatever way it is spoken of, it is spoken of in time: and therefore, if that is time, time will be called the consequence of motion in <note>original: "ἂν λέγηται, ἐν χρόνῳ λέγεται. εἰ τοῦτο, ἔσται ὁ χρόνος." — if it is spoken of, it is spoken of in time. If this is so, time will be...</note>

<column-break/>

...it measures, it is necessary to seek. Tell me, even if one finds how, he has defined the time that measures: but the flow is time. This, however, is not the same as time. For it is one thing to say "time," and another to say the "flow of time." For regarding the "so much," one must say what that thing is which is "so much." Is it the number that has measured the motion from outside the motion that is time? Like the number ten applied to horses, not taken along with the horses. What then is this number? It has not been stated: which, before measuring, is what it is, just as the number ten or a year is, which, <gloss>running through</gloss> according to the prior and posterior of motion, measured it. But this, according to prior and posterior, is not yet clear as to what it is. But that which measures according to prior and posterior, whether by a point or by any other such thing, will measure entirely according to time. Therefore, this time will be that which measures motion by the prior and posterior, holding onto time and touching it in order to measure. For either one takes a local prior and posterior, as the beginning of a race-track takes it, or it is necessary to take a temporal one. For "prior" and "posterior" are altogether this: the one is time ending at the "now"; the other is that which starts from the "now." But by the "now" as a number <gloss>and altogether by that which follows in order</gloss> <margin>D</margin> for the one measuring the prior and posterior of motion, time is needed not only for it to be any motion, but an ordered one. Then, why is it that when a number is provided—whether by the thing measured or according to the measurer? For it is possible for the same thing to be both measurer and measured. But in that <gloss>it is</gloss> number, time will come to be, yet when motion exists and the "prior" is entirely present, and even the "posterior," there is no time. It is as if someone were to say that magnitude is not as large as it is unless someone takes the "how much" of it. And since time is infinite and called such, how could there be a number about it, unless someone, taking a part of it, measures it—in which case it happens to exist even before being measured? And why is it not there before there is a soul to measure it? Unless someone were to say its generation occurs from the soul. Since by the act of measuring, it is by no means necessary for it to be. For it exists in its quantity even if no one measures it. And as for that which uses magnitude for the purpose of measuring, if someone again says this is the soul: what would this be in relation to the concept of time?

THAT which is called the accompaniment <gloss>indeed</gloss> of motion—what this actually is, they no longer teach, nor have they said it before saying what the accompaniment is. For that would perhaps be time. We must examine this accompaniment, whether it is posterior, or simultaneous, or prior. For if there is such an accompaniment, in whatever way it is spoken of, it is spoken of in time. If this is so, time will be the accompaniment of motion in time.

<summary>Plotinus critiques the definition of time as a "number" or "measure" of motion, arguing that measuring requires a pre-existing concept of time and a soul to observe it. He questions how time could be infinite or exist independently if it were merely a result of human or soulful measurement.</summary>

# BOOK SEVEN.

<page-num>535</page-num>

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>A</margin> ...since we are by no means seeking what it is not, but rather what time truly *is*, and much has been said on this by many before us—if one were to run through every single opinion, he would be writing a history rather than an inquiry. However, as far as we have briefly covered these views, it is possible to refute the claim that time is the "measure of the motion of the universe" based on what has already been said, and to bring further points to the discussion regarding the measurement of motion. For, aside from the problem of irregularity <note>If time were just the measure of motion, and motion is irregular, time would be irregular; however, Plotinus argues time is a constant.</note>, <margin>B</margin> all other points can be raised which will apply specifically to these arguments. Since things stand this way, it remains to explain more clearly what time actually is.

<margin>B</margin> **W**e must now lead ourselves back once again to that disposition which we previously said was found in Eternity: that immutable, simultaneously whole, and already infinite life; a life that is entirely unwavering, existing in the One and directed toward the One. Time did not yet exist, or at least it did not exist for those eternal beings. Time was destined to follow, both by a certain logic and by its posterior nature. While those higher beings were maintaining a state of rest within themselves, if anyone should wish to understand how Time first fell away <note>The "fall" or "procession" of time from eternity is a central concept in Neoplatonism; time is seen as a lower, moving reflection of a perfect, static reality.</note>, perhaps it would not be fitting to call upon the Muses to explain it—since the Muses perhaps did not yet exist. Or perhaps it *is* fitting to call them, since the Muses were indeed there even then. And regardless of how it happened, one might perhaps discover how time itself, once created, became manifest and came into being. <margin>D</margin> One might speak of it in this way: Before this "before" had arisen, and before it had any need of an "after," Time rested along with and within Being itself; it was not yet time, but it too maintained rest within that Being. However, there was a certain restless Nature <note>Plotinus is referring here to the World Soul (Anima Mundi).</note> that was prone to many actions, desiring to be its own master and to rule itself, and choosing to seek something more than the present. Thus, this Nature began to move, <margin>E</margin> and time itself flowed out along with it, moving always toward the "next" and the "after," not remaining the same, but moving from one thing to another. And we, having conceived of a certain length of this progression resulting from this motion, fashioned Time as an image of eternity. For since there was a certain restless power in the Soul, which wished to always transfer what it saw in the eternal realm into something else, it did not want the whole to be present to it all at once. Just as a "seminal reason" <note>original: "λόγος" / "ratio seminalis" — a formative principle or "blueprint" that exists inside a seed and dictates how it will grow.</note> unfolding <margin>F</margin> itself from a quiet seed, creates a wide-ranging progression (as it thinks), meanwhile losing its original unity through division, and instead of the one that remains in itself, it spends and consumes its unity, proceeding into a weaker length: so too this nature of the soul, having fashioned the sensible world in imitation of that higher world, set it in motion—not with the motion that is there, but with one similar to it, <margin>G</margin> a motion that strives to represent the image of that higher rest. First, the Soul made itself temporal,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...time. But since we are in no way investigating what it is *not*, but rather what time *is*, and many things have been said about this before us by many authors: if one were to run through these individual opinions, he would be telling a history rather than an inquiry. To the extent that a brief survey allows, something has been said of these; and it is possible to refute the one who says time is the measure of the motion of the universe using the arguments already given, and to bring in other points for discussion which were just mentioned regarding the measure of motion. For beyond the issue of irregularity, <margin>B</margin> all other points can be brought forward which will be congruently applied to them: when, I say, the matter stands thus, it remains now to explain more clearly what time is.

<margin>C</margin> <margin>* What time is: namely, a certain perseverance in the character of the Soul of the World in imitation of eternity.</margin> **I**T IS WORTHWHILE to recall ourselves again to that nature which we said in the preceding sections was in Eternity <note>original: "æuo" — referring to Aion, the timeless state of true Being.</note>: a nature, I say, that is immutable and simultaneously whole, and a life already infinite, entirely unwavering, and consistent in the One and toward the One. But Time was not yet, or at least it was not in those things; it was to follow by a certain logic and by a posterior nature. Therefore, while the higher things were maintaining rest in themselves, if anyone should desire to understand how in the beginning Time fell away, he would perhaps not appropriately call upon the Muses—who perhaps were not yet—to explain this. Yet perhaps it *is* appropriate, if indeed the Muses were even then. And however it may be, someone might perhaps find the time itself that has now been made, <margin>D</margin> insofar as it has been made and is now manifest. Let him speak of this very thing in this manner: Before that "before" itself arose and stood in need of an "after," Time was resting, not yet existing, together with and in Being itself; but in that Being, Time itself also maintained rest. But a certain Nature <note>The Soul.</note>, prone to many actions and greatly desiring to be of its own right and to command itself, and choosing always to have something more than what is present, was itself already stirred, <margin>E</margin> and at the same time Time flowed out, always hereafter and into the future, not through the same, but into another and again another. And we, having thought out a certain length of progression produced by this motion, now fashion Time as an image of eternity. For since there was a certain restless power of the soul, wishing namely to always transfer what is inspected there into another thing, it did not sustain the whole being present to it, collected all at once: but just as a seminal reason <note>original: "ratio seminalis" — the blueprint within a seed.</note> unfolding <margin>F</margin> itself from a certain quiet seed, produces a progression into many parts (as it thinks), meanwhile losing the very thing which is called "the many" by a certain partitioning; and instead of the one that exists in itself, it spends and consumes the one that does not remain in itself, proceeding into a weaker length: thus also that nature of the soul which we were speaking of, having fabricated the sensible world in imitation of that higher world, set it in motion—not the motion which is there, but one rather similar to the motion which is there, <margin>G</margin> a motion, I say, affecting to represent the image of that one; first indeed it rendered itself temporal,

receiving this in exchange for that: then it also granted to the work it had made that it should now serve time: specifically, since it had compelled all this "being" to exist in time, embracing all the progressions of this world within time itself.

<summary>Plotinus describes the origin of Time as a "fall" from the perfect rest of Eternity, caused by the Soul's restless desire to create and experience things in succession rather than all at once. He famously defines Time as the "image of eternity," produced as the Soul unfolds itself like a seed into the physical world.</summary>
