<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the origin of Time. Having previously discussed Eternity as a state of "static life," he now transitions into his famous definition of Time as the "life of the Soul" in motion. This follows the previous page's discussion on how Time "fell" or proceeded from the eternal realm.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD III.

<columns>
A For it was stirred within that Soul; for there is no other place for the universe than the Soul. Indeed, it was stirred within the Soul's own time. By performing its actions one after another, and then another in succession, the Soul generated the "sequence" alongside its own action. It proceeds together with a thought that follows another thought—a sequence that did not exist before, since the Soul had not previously operated through such discursive thought. But since the present life is not entirely like the life that preceded it, this new life constitutes a different span, and insofar as it is different, it has acquired a different time. B Thus, the distance and extension of life resulted in Time, and the perpetual extension of life possesses eternal time, just as past life possesses past time. If one were to say, therefore, that Time is the activity of the Soul in a transitory motion, proceeding perpetually from one state of life to another, they would perhaps be saying something meaningful. C For if Eternity is life in a stable state—remaining in the same and similar condition, and already infinite—and if Time must be the image of Eternity (just as this physical world is the image of that higher world), then certainly, in place of the life that flourishes there, we must introduce another life here. This life belongs to a certain power of the World Soul, acting, as it were, as a namesake <note>original: "aequivocam" / "ὁμώνυμον". Plotinus means that "Life" in the physical world is called "Life" just like in the divine world, but they are different in quality.</note> to the higher life. Instead of intellectual motion, we have the motion of a part of the Soul. Instead of identity and a remaining, similar condition, we have that which does not remain the same, but always executes one thing after another. Again, instead of a property without distance and the "One" being present all at once, we have an image of that "One" possessing unity in a continuous succession. D Furthermore, in place of that which is already infinite and whole, we have that which perpetually propagates itself toward infinity according to what follows in sequence. Finally, instead of that which is whole all at once, we have that which will be future by parts, and will always be "becoming" a whole. For in this way, it will imitate that which already exists as a whole, gathered together and immense, if it wishes to obtain its own being through a continuous sequence of existing. For that is how it will best imitate the Being of the higher world. E One must by no means assume Time to be outside of the Soul, just as Eternity is not there outside of Being itself. Nor, again, is Time a mere consequence or something that comes after; just as Eternity is not outside, but is something seen within, existing in and with the Soul, just as Eternity is with Being.

<margin>
XI
Confirmation of the previous points.
</margin>
IT MUST BE CONSIDERED from what has been said, that Time is a nature of this kind: namely, the length of such a life proceeding through changes that are equal and similar, F advancing quietly and gently—a length, I say, possessing a continuity of action. But if we were to imagine this power being somehow drawn back and ceasing from this life which it now leads—a life that is currently unending and never to cease because the action of a certain soul is everlasting—and if we imagine it not directed toward itself or within itself, but occupied in producing and generating; if we imagine, I say, that it no longer operates, but that this kind of action ceases, and this part of the Soul is turned back toward the higher realms, toward Eternity and stable stillness, G what then will remain besides Eternity? What would still be "one thing after another" if all things remained in the One? What would be "before" or "after," or more...

<column-break/>

A For it was stirred in that Soul. For what place is there for this universe other than the Soul? It was stirred in the time of that Soul. Presenting its activity one after another, and then another again in succession, the "after" was born along with the activity. It moves forward with one thought after another, which did not exist before; for the thought was put into action. Now, the present life is not similar B to the one before it. At once, therefore, there is another life, and that "otherness" has another time. Thus, the extension of life had time. And the "always forward" of life has time always; and the past life has past time. If one were to say that time is the soul in a transitive motion, passing from one life to another, would he not seem to be saying something? For if Eternity is life in a state of rest and in the same way, C and already infinite; and if time must be the image of Eternity, just as this universe is to that one: then instead of the life there, one must speak of another life belonging to this power of the soul, as a namesake; and instead of intellectual motion, the motion of some part of the soul. Instead of the same and the "in the same way" and the remaining, one must speak of that which does not remain in the same, but does one thing and then another. Instead of that which is without distance and one, there is an image of the one, D which is one in continuity. Instead of that which is already infinite and whole, there is that which tends toward the infinite by being always in succession. Instead of the "all at once" whole, there is that which is to be a whole part by part, and always about to be a whole. For thus it will imitate that which is already a whole, all at once, and already infinite, if it desires to be always acquiring being in its existence; for in this way, its being will imitate that other being. E But one must not take time as being outside of the soul, just as eternity is not there outside of being; nor again as something following or after, just as it is not so there: but as something seen within, being within, and existing with it, just as eternity is there.

WE MUST UNDERSTAND what was said: that this nature of time is the length of such a life, proceeding in changes, equal and similar, F proceeding noiselessly, having continuity of activity. If then we should turn this power back in our reasoning, and cause it to cease from this life which it now has without ceasing, and which will never end because it is the activity of a soul that is always existing—an activity not directed toward itself, nor in itself, but in making and generating—if we should suppose it no longer acting, but G ceasing from this activity, or that this part of the soul is turned toward the things there, and toward eternity, remaining in stillness, what would still be after eternity? What would be "one thing and another" if all things remained in one? What would still be "before," and what would be "after," or...
</columns>

He argues that Time is internal to the Soul's activity and would vanish if the Soul returned to a state of pure, non-generative contemplation.</summary>

# SEVENTH BOOK.
<note>original: "LIBER SEPTIMVS" — This is the seventh treatise of the Third Ennead, titled "On Eternity and Time."</note>

<columns>
...or even further? Under what condition would the Soul cast itself into something else, unless it were into that in which it already exists? Indeed, it would not even be in this very place <gloss>place</gloss> unless it had departed first, so that it might be able to confer itself into it. For even the sphere itself would not exist before time exists. Indeed, this sphere is also within time and is moved. And even if the sphere were to stand still while the Soul was active, we would still measure how long its state of rest lasted, as long as that external state of eternity persists.

<margin>A</margin> If, therefore, the space and the silence of the whole universe were removed, and time were immediately abolished, it is clear that the beginning of this motion and this life is what produces time. <margin>B</margin> For this reason, it is stated in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the universe.</note> that time was made together with this universe, because the Soul generated time along with this universe. For in such an action, this universe was also brought into being; and while the Soul is time, the universe exists within time.

If someone should say that Plato also calls the movements of the stars "times," they <margin>C</margin> must remember that Plato said these were created for the manifestation and distinction of time, and so that the measure might be more manifest to us. Since it was not possible for the Soul to define time itself, or to measure the individual parts of invisible and incomprehensible time by its own power—especially among men who were entirely ignorant of counting—the Soul created day and night. Through these, it was possible to perceive two distinct things from this difference, from which the concept of number is said to have arisen.

<margin>D</margin> Then, by perceiving how much distance is covered from one sunrise to the next, we were able to have a specific span of time, provided the form of motion remains uniform. Insofar as we fix our gaze upon this very sight, we use such a thing as a measure—a measure, I say, of time.

<column-break/>

For time itself is not the measure. For in what way would it measure, and what would it say while measuring? Would it say of something, "this is as much as I am"? Who then is it that is spoken of, or who says "I"? <margin>E</margin> Is it according to whom the measurement occurs? Does something not exist in itself so that it can measure, and yet it is not the measure? Therefore, the motion of the universe will be measured according to time. Time will not be the measure of motion according to what it is in essence, but only by happenstance; that is, by being something else prior, it reveals how great the motion is.

Indeed, a single motion taken over a certain time and counted many times will lead us to the knowledge of how much time has passed. Therefore, if someone says that the motion and revolution <margin>F</margin> measure time in some way, showing how much time there is—since it cannot be grasped or understood otherwise—he will certainly not wander far from a proper explanation. That which is measured by the circuit, then—that is, what is revealed—will be time. It is not generated by the circuit itself, but is demonstrated by it.

And so, the measure of motion seems to be that which is measured by a determined motion, being measured by it as something different from itself. <margin>G</margin> For if the measuring thing and the measured thing were the same, it would be as if someone said that the thing measured by a cubit <note>An ancient unit of length.</note> is "magnitude," without saying what the magnitude itself actually is...

<sig>F</sig>
</columns>

**XII.** TIME, therefore, is revealed by the celestial revolution, specifically within that revolution itself. However, it is necessary that time itself no longer merely be that in which something is transacted, but even more fundamentally, it must be that very thing which exists <gloss>the essence of Time</gloss> in
**B** which all other things move, and rest equally and in an orderly fashion. Time shines forth into our knowledge from a certain ordered arrangement, yet it does not originate from there. Whether that arrangement is at rest or in motion—though more so when it is in motion—motion seems to contribute more to our knowledge and grasping of time than rest does. It is clearly easier to perceive how much something has moved than how long it has stood still. For this reason,
**C** some have been led to say that time is the "measure of motion" <note>original: "mensuram motus" — a reference to Aristotle's definition of time</note>, perhaps because they mean to say it is *measured by* motion. Therefore, one must add what it is in itself that is being measured by motion, rather than simply stating an accidental quality that happens to it. Perhaps those thinkers did not intend their words to be taken in a literal, reversed sense, but we have failed to understand them. When they clearly speak of a "measure" according to the "measured," we have not quite followed their meaning. The reason we have not understood
**D** is this: in their writings, they do not explain what time is in itself—whether it is called the measurer or the measured—as if they were writing for students who already clearly understood these things. Plato, however, said that the essence of time is neither something that measures nor something measured by another, but to make it known, he said that the revolution of the world was allotted a very small part <note>original Greek: "ἐλαχίστην" — the smallest or most basic unit</note>, relative to a very small portion of time, so that from this one could know what kind of thing time is and how much of it there is. Desiring
**E** to indicate its essence, he said it was born together with the heavens, and that it is a moving image of the eternal model <note>original: "imaginem mobilem exemplaris æterni" — a famous phrase from Plato's Timaeus</note>. Time does not remain still because life itself does not remain still, with which time runs and revolves. It is said to be "born together with the heavens" because a life of this kind creates the heavens; a single life produces both the heavens and time. Therefore, if such a life could be entirely
**F** turned back into one, the time that dwells in this life would immediately cease, and the heavens would cease, being deprived of that life. If someone, taking the "before" and "after" of this lower life and motion, should assert that this itself is time, but denies that the "before" and "after" of a truer nature <gloss>the Soul's motion</gloss> is anything at all, he would be quite ridiculous. He would grant "before" and "after" to an inanimate motion, and claim it possesses time, but would deny it to the motion through which this inanimate one is born as a mere imitation.
**G** Yet it is from the Soul's motion that "before" and "after" first flowed, since that motion is self-effective <note>original: "efficax per seipsū" / Greek: "αὐτουργὸς"</note>. Just as it generates its own individual actions, so it produces a continuous succession, creating a transition along with the act of generation.

...its progress. Why, then, do we trace this motion of the universe back to the soul’s circuit, and say that it exists in time, yet we do not say the same of the motion of the soul, which exists within the soul itself in a perpetual progression? Perhaps it is because that which stands above this motion is eternity, which neither runs alongside the motion nor extends with it. Therefore, the soul was the first to look toward time; it generated time, and possesses time along with its own activity. In what way, then, is time 
<margin>B</margin> everywhere? It is because the soul of life—that vital motion—is absent from no part of the world, just as the life within us leaves no part of our body. If anyone should object that time exists in something without substance or existence (that is, that we speak falsely about it, just as it is said of God when we use the terms "was" and "will be"), what shall we say? For we say "He was" and "He will be" in the same way we say He "will be" in the future. But for these matters, another method of discussion is required. However, we must notice for the present, regarding what has been said, that when someone considers a man in motion and observes how far he has proceeded, he recognizes how great the motion is. When he judges the motion as a progression, for example, by the legs, he simultaneously thinks of the motion itself—the movement within the man prior to this progress—as having been of a certain amount; for it was this inner motion that directed and continued the body's progression to such an extent. The 
<margin>D</margin> body moved for such a time, and this will be traced back to a motion of a specific magnitude. This is the cause; the body’s time is traced to its own motion, and this motion in turn is traced to the motion of the soul, which produced the intervals through equal measures. To what, then, shall we primarily refer the motion of the soul itself? Certainly, to whatever you wish to refer it, you will eventually stop at a primary point. This, therefore, is what exists first: it is that in which all other things are contained, but it is no longer contained in anything else. For it can have 
<margin>E</margin> nothing else to encompass it. Thus, this reigns first. The same holds true in the soul of the universe. Is there, then, time in us as well? Perhaps it is in every soul of this kind, and it exists uniformly in every soul, and all souls are in a way one. Therefore, time will not be dispersed, since even eternity—which exists according to another manner—is present in all things of a uniform nature.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON THE EIGHTH BOOK OF THE THIRD ENNEAD, CONCERNING NATURE, CONTEMPLATION, AND THE ONE.

## COMMENTARY.

### SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK.

> Natural things are created by a certain active life through reasons that are, as it were, contemplative, which are infused into it by the divine intellect.

Some philosophers of old, who were strictly naturalists <note>Ficino refers here to the Pre-Socratics or early materialists</note>, believed that all natural things were generated by a certain elemental quality and motion. They thought such things arose either by the power of the quality flourishing in the agent or by the force of the motion ending in the matter, and that no inner reason or art governed these processes. Plotinus, however, maintains that bodily qualities and motions are derived from an incorporeal form <note>Latin: "incorporea forma"</note> that is not subject to motions itself, but presides over them; this he calls "Universal and Primary Nature." I call this a "substantial and vital form" which is not a mere quality of bodies (so that it may produce all things equally) nor does it act by mere impulse of motion (so that it may arrange all things with a certain moderation). Rather, it acts by its own formal reason and a certain natural art. It is as if the skillful reason, which is an accidental trait in a human craftsman, were instead something that exists on its own, 

<sig>F 2</sig>

<summary>This page concludes Plotinus's thesis that Time is the life of the Soul in motion and begins Marsilio Ficino's commentary on the origins of nature. Ficino argues that nature is not merely material or mechanical but is directed by an incorporeal, "contemplative" vital force.</summary>

<keywords>Time, Soul, Eternity, Motion, Marsilio Ficino, Plotinus, Universal Nature, Contemplation, Formal Reason, Vital Form</keywords>

--- Page 464 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus, moving from the discussion of Time in the previous Ennead to the nature of "Contemplation" and "Nature" in Ennead III, Book 8. Ficino is explaining how Nature acts as a bridge between the higher Soul and the physical world.</meta>

# 340 COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

although within matter: and so by its own nature it acts skillfully, just as a craftsman acts skillfully by choice; rather, it acts skillfully by natural art, just as fire by natural heat naturally heats. To this living and natural reason <note>original: *rationi*—here meaning a rational principle or blueprint</note>, qualities and motions are subject as instruments. Even without bodily movement, it produces bodily movement; without the quality of fire, it generates fire; and it generates living things everywhere without manifest seed. This is because it possesses within itself the essential and living reasons of all things, as we have sufficiently proved in our *Theology*, and thus we confirm it briefly for the present. Above nutrition and growth, which are types of generation, is generation itself, which is preserved in all these things. Since these generations are the works of certain lives or living beings, surely generation in its simplest, primary, and common form is the work of life itself—the common life ruling the whole world. And since in the massive bulk of the world there are not manifest seeds of bodies everywhere, surely in the life of the whole there are seeds and the specific principles <note>original: *rationes*</note> of seeds and of the things appearing to the senses.

Nature, which acts without choice, acts by an indwelling form and by certain forms everywhere—that is, by **seminal reasons** <note>original: *rationibus seminales*—these are the "software" or hidden blueprints that Plotinus and Ficino believe guide the growth of all physical things</note>. By these, as if by principles and rules, Nature defines all movements (which are inherently undetermined) with a certain steady course. It leads the qualities, which act with their full force in whatever they do and are naturally constrained, toward their work with a balanced moderation. It carries this out in a multiform way, yet with a uniform order. Nor does it look toward a certain end in any other way than art and counsel are accustomed to do, even in those things that do not see the end themselves. This living and natural art contains within itself all natural forms according to their act, no differently than human art possesses its crafts. For matter, which is always potentially formable into all things, is led to the actuality of all things only through a life that presides over matter, yet is akin to it, comprehending all acts within itself.

Nature, this artisan of all things, needs neither specific matter nor matter itself for its own existence. For Nature daily renders matter into this or that form, and moves matter with a ready command. Furthermore, it does not need this or that quality of matter for its basic action. It can generate qualities without using qualities as tools, since it is the common principle for generating all things equally. And if it generates living things everywhere without manifest seeds, it is even more able to procreate elemental qualities through its own seeds alone, without the service of such elements. If it uses matter affected by certain qualities, it does not use them out of necessity, but by coincidence. This is confirmed by those who believe that in generation, a resolution occurs all the way back to primary matter.

Therefore, remember that Nature is the principle of the generation of things everywhere. Because the material form is the last of the forms, it generates nothing "formal" in its own right. For that which is last in any category produces nothing within that category. Therefore, material form is not so much the principle of generation as it is a certain "affection" of matter induced from above by an occult principle generating the species. That it generates nothing is confirmed by the fact that generation belongs to life, yet material form lacks life. It is clear that it lacks life because essence must proceed further than life, yet essence does not proceed all the way to matter, nor does form. Essence ends in quality, and that defines it inwardly; therefore, life ends in Nature in a similar way, above the quality of matter.

Nature is indeed incorporeal; for if something corporeal moves anything, it is moved itself in the process—I mean, it is moved even in its substance. But the **First Mover** <note>The primary cause of motion in the universe</note> is that which remains in its substance, so that it can maintain a perpetual course in motion. Yet if there is an inner and familiar motor like a certain form, such as Nature itself, it must, while it moves, also be moved in some way—rather through a change from one state to another, not through a decline in its essence. Finally, just as in any living creature, it is not an elemental quality but a certain vital principle that is the source of what happens in the body (acting above and against the way of such qualities), so in the living universe—that is, the world—not elemental quality or motion, but a certain living reason dispenses things so beautiful and diverse. Plotinus says this reason remains in itself through its essence, even though it changes from one state to another in its outward activity. It depends not on matter and soul equally (as corporeal quality does), but on the soul alone, as a perennial act of the soul leaning toward matter. For this reason, Plotinus calls corporeal quality an "accident" <note>a non-essential property that happens to a substance</note> because it depends on both sides; but the life communicated by the soul to the body he calls not an accident of the body, nor an accident of the soul, but an essential act of the soul—a middle ground between the "accidents" of things and true substance, which proceeds all the way to the intellectual soul. Indeed, it has a certain power by which it sustains and preserves itself in some way and progresses within itself; by this function, all intellectual essences are said to subsist through themselves and from themselves.

But to return to Nature—that is, the life depending on the soul—within it are all the "reasons" that produce natural forms. Any such reason within it is not a mere notion conceived at some point from an argument or investigation, but an essential property and an act of essence, not differing from being such and such. There is, therefore, in Nature a certain **seminal reason** for that which is born from it. Although this is an essential act of Nature itself and its very way of being, it is called a "vision" or "gaze" (*intuitus*) by a certain metaphor—not a vision acquired at some time, but one naturally fixed there. It does not seek anything, but possesses it from the beginning; it does not observe anything within itself, but is, as it were, "dazed" <note>original: *stupidus*—in the sense of being in a trance or state of awe, rather than "unintelligent"</note>, like those in a state of astonishment. Perhaps it is a sense like the one some attributed to plants. For the universe is a common plant, enjoying its life through a certain quiet and substantial sense, conceiving natural things. Orpheus attributes this soundless sense—that is, a sense without the distraction of itself toward another—to Nature in his *Hymn to Nature*.

In Nature, to "behold" or "contemplate" is nothing other than to *be* such a thing and to *make* such a thing. And because it makes things as if by a certain gaze and vision, that which is generated in matter can be called a "spectacle." It can furthermore be called a "vision" of Nature, just as we are accustomed to say of a child: "this mark born in him is a certain desire and imagination of the mother." Truly, in neither the intellect nor in Nature is there any knowledge, notion, or vision that differs from "being" in the way that the vision called "consideration" differs—which belongs to those who do not naturally possess the thing they are looking at. However, the Intellect and the Nature that depends on the intellectual substance possess things naturally; indeed, they *are* the very things they behold, and they make things by beholding them. This essential and effective vision is what he calls the **seminary reason**.

He places the first reason in the Intellect itself; the second in the intellectual Soul, which he calls the "First Soul"; the third in Nature, which he calls the "Second Soul"; and the fourth in matter, that is, the material form. The primary forms of things are in the Intellect itself, and there they are certain contemplations or "visions" (*spectamina*). We call them "visions" or "spectacles," the notions of all things, or concepts resulting there meanwhile,

He establishes a hierarchy of creation where "vision" or contemplation is the productive force at every level, from the Divine Intellect down to the physical form of matter.</summary>

# 341 ON BOOK VIII. ENNEAD III.

...while the Intellect contemplates and beholds itself. But secondary forms <note>these correspond to the level of the Soul</note> are naturally expressed by the contemplating intellect into the intellectual soul: and here too there are certain objects of contemplation <note>original: *contemplamenta*</note>. Tertiary forms are imprinted from there into Nature. Since these are expressed precisely from these contemplations, they are themselves contemplations, or I might say "acts of vision" <note>original: *contemplamina*</note>. Finally, fourthly, from those very contemplative concepts of nature, forms are conceived in the matter of the world. And because they follow the aforementioned contemplations in a certain order and imitate them perfectly, they can be called "contemplations" themselves. Indeed, artistic works intended for the eyes are often called the "ingenious understandings" of the craftsman; this is even more true of musical sounds, and even more so of song, since they carry with them a more expressive thought and a living emotion, especially words, whether spoken or written. Therefore, natural forms have this quality above all: that they are both called and are "understandings," expressed concepts of the intellectual soul itself, shaping matter—not a matter that is "alien" or external as in art, but its own; not from the outside like art, but from within; not by such a choice, but by such an essence, and without tools, and forever. Now, in this way Nature differs from a geometer who draws figures in the dust: for Nature works both from within and without tools or choice, just as a geometer, while he imagines figures intensely and with a certain emotion, moves and shapes his innermost spirit through that imagination.

Plotinus imagines these four—Intellect, Intellectual Soul, Nature, and Matter—as if they were four panes of glass arranged one after another. The "understandings" of the first Intellect pass through them like rays from the sun, moving through the soul, nature, and matter with a continuous conformity. Thus, in a way, one could say these are the same rays and the same understandings in the following and final stages as were in the preceding ones, but they gradually lose their original dignity as they descend. Since the contemplation of the first Intellect, and then a certain contemplation in the soul and in nature, is the principle <note>the starting point or source</note> of natural things, then surely the goal of all things is also contemplation. Intellectual beings possess this perpetually and rest happily in such a goal; rational beings seek it so that they might one day rest in it; sensible beings <note>animals and plants</note> imitate it according to their strength through the continuous act of sensing; and even things that generate others strive to reflect it, both in the order of their movement and in the beautiful form of their offspring. Finally, the contemplation of divine providence directs all things toward the most exact beauty, while in the entire arrangement of things, no less—indeed more—attention is paid to ornament than to necessity. From this wonderful ornament, God rouses minds to discover the very art of the divine mind and to contemplate its beauty.

### On the goal of intellectual nature, and that in true knowledge, the knower and the known are the same. Also on the levels of life and intelligence, and that the first intellect is all things, and a perfect whole.

In the fifth and sixth chapters of the book, you will note that the goal of intellectual life is not simply to "have" the good in any way at all, but to understand the good that is possessed; for here, to "possess" is exactly the same as to understand. This is the action proper to intellectual nature and the chief way of possessing. Likewise, for us, the highest good is not something sensible <note>perceived by the senses</note>, but something intelligible <note>grasped by the mind</note>; for this alone is most intimate to us and most peaceful, and it is ultimately identical with the power of knowing itself. Furthermore, remember that the power of knowing becomes, in the very act of knowing, one with its object. The more they become one, the more perfect the knowledge is, and vice versa. Where knowledge is most perfect—or indeed wherever it is true—the knowing power and the thing known are one and the same in reality.

Therefore, the Intellect and every intellectual essence, just as it is always all things in act <note>actually, not just potentially</note>, so also it always understands all things in act. The rational nature of the soul is indeed all things, but not always all things "in act." Insofar as it actively applies itself to some "reason" <note>a principle or idea</note> lying hidden within itself, it becomes that reason, and through it, it understands the things contained within the power of that reason, and by understanding, it becomes those things. In short, to truly know something is nothing else than to be or to become that very thing. Finally, since the divine Artisan makes all things by the contemplation of himself and calls the things he has made to imitate him according to their strength, surely all things desire and strive for something contemplative or something contemplatable, whether by understanding, by sensing, or even by acting and generating.

Furthermore, in chapter 7, you will learn again that every intellectual power is the same as the thing understood, and in that realm, "to understand" does not differ from "to be," because it is the highest form of knowledge. The rational power, however, becomes one with the thing known, but the gaze of the external senses and of nature tends toward the external. Likewise, the First Form, because of its supreme effectiveness toward movement, is the First Life; and because of its effectiveness, it is the innermost and self-possessed First Intelligence. Just as form proceeds through all levels of things from the first form (made by essence), so also life and intelligence proceed, so that any form can be called a certain "life" and "intelligence." Finally, just as the First Intellect is "uniform" <note>one-form</note> because it is the first of its kind, it also becomes "all-form" because, by contemplating itself, it conceives of itself under various forms due to the fertility of its intelligence. Nevertheless, in any form conceived within itself, the common form of the whole is recognized. Therefore, it is a "whole"—a whole by perfect reason—because the whole is preserved in the individual parts. It possesses this because it is most unified, being closest to the divine Unity from which it nonetheless descends. Since the formal reasons <note>the blueprints</note> of things within it differ from each other in their formal character and are derived by degrees from the higher to the lower, and from the better to the worse, it is concluded that in any genus, that which is first is perfectly "the whole." Therefore, it is the whole in any of its parts: so is Being itself, so is Life itself, so is the Intellect. That which is a "whole" in this way is not composed of its parts like something that borrows its essence from its parts; rather, its own essence gives being to the parts. Now, a whole of this kind, which propagates itself into its members and is preserved in each one, is called an "infinite whole." For whatever part of it you take, the rest follow infinitely.

->The first Intellect is also necessarily manifold, and is all things; therefore<-
->before it is the principle of all things, which is not<-
->all things, but above all things.<-

These matters seem to be considered in the eighth chapter. For the definition of the intellect is this: that it is moved, illuminated, and formed; but the properties of the "intelligible" <note>the object of thought</note> are the opposite. Likewise, it is not necessarily included in the definition of an intellect that it must be the "intelligible" object itself; for no necessity prevents an intellect from existing even if it is understood by no one. Conversely, it does not necessarily pertain to the definition of the "intelligible" that an intellect must exist. For the intellectual power, in the scope of its object, comprehends material and spiritual things together, and among these it contains what it understands...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus, specifically focusing on the transition from the "Intellect" (the second hypostasis) to the "One" or the "Good" (the first and highest principle). Ficino explains why the Intellect, though divine, cannot be the absolute first principle because it contains a subtle form of multiplicity.</meta>

<page-num>342</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...and things they do not understand. Therefore, the **Intellect** and the **intelligible** <note>the "intelligible" refers to the object being thought or understood</note> are distinguished from one another by a certain formal reason; indeed, this type of distinction is very close to what is called a "real" distinction <note>original: *secundum rem*</note>. This real distinction is the final step: therefore, that very form in which the intellect is joined with the intelligible is not the most simple unity. Consequently, it is not the first principle of the universe, which is simply one and most simple—just as whatever is first in any category must necessarily be simple.

That the intellect is, by some necessity, multiple and therefore not the first, is also confirmed in this way: if the intellect is the highest form of cognition, it has a "partnered" intelligible with it—identical in reality, though not identical in reason. Thus, that which is intelligible first and through itself also follows this rule: it is also an intellect. For such an intelligible is a "separate subsisting form," and therefore, by reflecting into itself, it brings back understanding. If a material thing is called "intelligible," it only becomes so insofar as it is transformed into something else, or is understood through something else as a consequence. Since, therefore, the intellect and the intelligible accompany one another so closely that what is one is also the other, yet they differ by formal reason, it follows necessarily that the first intellect is multiple, and not the supreme principle of the universe.

A doubt is then raised in this way: since the principle itself is outside the category <note>original: *genus*</note> of intelligence, it seems to be unknown to itself; and insofar as it stands above the intelligible category, it cannot be known in any way. The answer to this is: the principle enjoys itself by a certain more excellent means than "knowing"; and the soul enjoys it by a cognition perhaps more excellent than the intellectual, or rather by a certain more eminent way than by knowing. For it is not simply the intellect that is the highest form of cognition in us, but a **good-form unity** <note>original: *unitas boniformis*; this refers to a divine spark in the human soul that corresponds to the nature of the Good</note>, through which we enjoy the first unity and goodness simultaneously—just as we enjoy a visible thing through our light-filled sense of sight.

Therefore, just as one who strives intensely to imagine must cease from physical movement and sensation, and one who wishes to understand deeply must quiet the imagination, so too one who desires to reach that which exists above intellectual and intelligible nature must pass through everything intelligible, leave behind their own intellect, and impose a total silence upon the intelligence. One must be reduced, as it were, into their own "first part," through which they may enjoy the **First** of the universe.

The conclusion is that different things enjoy themselves in different ways. The body of a living creature enjoys itself through the senses; reason enjoys itself not through the senses, but through something better than itself; the intellect also gains mastery of itself not through some discourse of reason, but through something more eminent than itself. Likewise, the **One** itself and the **Good** enjoys itself through something more sublime than intelligence or cognition.

Accordingly, if we are to ascend step by step from imperfect things to perfect ones, we must certainly place above the **imagination** (which usually runs only through certain types of things and takes a long time) the **reason**, which runs through all things and requires a shorter time—and where it is most perfect, the shortest time possible. Above reason is the **intellect**, which has attained all things forever and without the passage of time. If the intellect holds and sees all things perfectly within itself, it does not hold them confusedly, but as distinct and pure; it does not gaze upon them as obscure, but discerns them as clear and distinct.

Therefore, above this intellect—which is necessarily multiple—is the first principle of the universe. This principle is not merely "one certain thing" among all others (otherwise it would not have power over all things, nor could it be the principle of all); nor is it "all things" in such a way that it is not one and simple, for this is the first requirement. Everywhere, unity is prior to multiplicity, and the simple is prior to the composite. Nor, again, is it "one" and "all things" equally. If anyone were to grant this, we would distinguish it thus: either it is all things collectively, or rather individually. If collectively, this means there is one form there along with a multitude. Either this one form exists before the multitude (and thus this form alone is the principle, and there is no need to add the multitude to it for it to be the principle); or this one form exists simultaneously with the multitude (and thus it is not the principle of all things, since it does not exist before all things); or this one form is placed after all things, which seems the most absurd thing to say.

But if the other part of the choice is taken—namely, that the principle is "all things" in such a way that if you pointed to each thing individually, it would be true to say "this is the principle"—then it would follow that any thing you like is the principle. Since, however, the principle must necessarily be unique, there would either be only one single thing in the entire universe, or conversely, there would be as many principles as there are things.

->**The Good itself is above essence, life, and intellect, and cannot be reached by the intellect.**<-

Since we see in the levels of living things that the most consummate level of life is ultimately the intellectual life, we can infer that the "first life" in the whole order of things is simply the **Intellect** itself. Whether you consider life as a force, it is a movement toward a goal (and therefore toward something else, like the Good); or if you take it as intellect, it is a movement toward the Truth (as the Good). In both ways, it is something dependent and not satisfied with its own essence (of which life and intellect consist), but it seeks something better than essence—that is, the **Good** itself. The Good requires neither life according to form nor intellect to strive toward the good, since it is the Good itself, which has no need for any action. Indeed, every action is toward some good with which it is concerned.

Because this Good exists entirely above the intellect and the intelligible, and because names are usually given based on the conceptions of the intellect, it has no proper name. However, it is called **"The Good"** because all things are created from it and perfected once they are made. It is also called **"The One"** because it stands above all things and does not move while they proceed (otherwise nothing would remain stable anywhere); nor is it divided into parts (otherwise the One itself would cease to be—and if it were removed, all things would immediately perish); nor is it multiplied into forms (otherwise, suffering admission or addition, it would no longer be true unity and immense simplicity).

If you proceed through trees, through animals, through the soul, and through the mind, you will find that what is simplest and most "one" in each of them is the most powerful part and the principle of the rest. Similarly, you will reduce the universe to a most powerful unity, about which you will predicate nothing further once you have conceived of Unity itself or Goodness. Otherwise, if you predicate anything else, you create a composite; you diminish it by composing it, making it needy and secondary. Do not, therefore, add "intellection" to this. For the nature of intelligence is one thing, and the nature of the Good is another. Both do not belong equally to everything.

Therefore, intelligence added to the Good creates a collection. You shall not apply **Ideas** <term>divine archetypes or blueprints of reality</term> there, which are conceived by intelligence and differ from one another absolutely by formal reason—especially the Ideas of contrary and opposite things, as is evident from the order of the universe generated from them according to essence and form. For those things which in this physical "workmanship" <note>the material world</note> differ in reality and subject, must differ in the "Craftsman" <note>the Divine Intellect</note> of all by an absolute and formal reason. Otherwise, this order of forms would either consist of some disordered chance or would proceed from entirely unformed matter.

The **Platonists** <note>referring to Plotinus and his followers</note> first forbid applying formal and absolute distinctions [to the One]; they also forbid applying "life" or "essence" after unity or goodness, for the striving of these things does not rest in itself but contends toward the Good. They command that one place that first principle above "essence" and "being," just as they indicate that **Matter**—which is the opposite extreme—should be placed below essence and being. Therefore, just as in reaching matter one must descend below all...

<header>ON BOOK VIII. ENNEAD III.</header>

from all concepts of intelligence which are formal <note>original: *formales*; refers to concepts that have a specific shape or definition in the mind</note>: so, to reach that Absolute, one must ascend above all such concepts. One must not think that that which exists wonderfully above motion, multiplicity, and form can be reached by any act of intelligence that is changeable, multiple, or restricted by form.

-> The Good itself is the father, whose son is the intellect, always filled by the father; <-
-> of this intellect, the world is the image. <-

Just as sight is one thing, but light (for which the eye was created to receive) is another—even if one imagines an eye filled with eternal light—so too the intellect is one thing, but Truth itself and the Good are another, toward which the intellect naturally strives. The intellect differs from the Good, even that very intellect which, because of its proximity to the Good, always enjoys the Good most fully. Therefore, the Good itself, like light, has no need for sight. Now, if anyone could behold the beauty of the entire visible world all at once in a single gaze, he would wonder beyond measure; from this image, he might more easily sense the **intelligible world** <note>the realm of pure ideas and forms that exists beyond the physical world</note>, its maker, but as something far more beautiful. Again, if someone contemplates that realm—in which nothing is formless, nothing is ugly, nothing is immoderate, and nothing is without life or intellect, where all splendor exists, and within that purest splendor the entire order of nature resides—he would more easily guess who its father is, and by what reason he generated such a great son. For the Father, existing above intellect and fullness, generated the pure intellect and the fullness of all things within himself from eternity.

### ON NATURE, CONTEMPLATION, AND THE ONE.

IF, before we act seriously, we speak as if in jest, saying that all things seek contemplation, and tend toward an end of this kind—not only rational animals, but also those lacking reason; and even the nature of plants, and finally the earth itself, which generates all these. Likewise, all things attain contemplation insofar as each one's natural state can grasp it; some truly contemplate and attain it, while others reach it through imitation and image. If we spoke in such a way, would anyone accept this as a new opinion brought forward by us? <meta>This page continues the translation of Plotinus’s "Ennead III, Book 8." The previous page concluded the commentary on the distinction between the Intellect and the Good, and now the text moves into Plotinus’s exploration of Nature's inner life.</meta>

<page-num>344</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK III.</header>

<margin>I. Nature, remaining within itself, shapes matter through **seminal reasons** <note>original: *rationes seminales*; these are the internal "blueprints" or generative principles that guide the growth and form of living things</note> without the need for choice or physical tools.</margin>
...should we say that nature possesses contemplation within itself? And if what it creates, it creates through a contemplation it does not have, then how exactly does it accomplish this?

A. Since there are neither hands here, nor feet, nor any external or innate instrument—yet matter is required upon which nature acts or into which it places a form—this is clear to almost everyone. Nor should we think that nature performs its work through some kind of pushing or levering. For what kind of pushing or pressure could produce such varied and diverse colors and shapes?

B. Even the molders of wax and figures (whom we call "doll-makers"), when they look at something and think their craft is very similar to nature’s own workmanship, cannot create colors unless they bring them from elsewhere into their works.

C. It is worth considering how, in the case of those who practice such manual arts, something must remain inside the artist, according to which they work through their hands. Similarly, there must be something of this kind in nature: a certain power that remains and works without the service of hands. It remains whole, I say; for it does not need some parts to stay still while others move. Matter is that which is moved there, but within the power itself, nothing moves. Otherwise, that which moves would not be the primary mover, nor would it be nature itself, but rather that which stays immobile within the whole.

D. Someone might object that while the **reason** <term>reason: *ratio* in Latin or *logos* in Greek; here it refers to a creative governing principle rather than human logic</term> remains immobile, nature is different from reason and is moved. But if they say nature is moved as a whole, then reason would be too; if some part of it is immobile, that part will be the reason. Indeed, this must be a **form** <note>original: *species*; the formal essence or "idea" of a thing</note>, not a composition of matter and form. Why would this need hot or cold matter? For if matter brings those qualities to the work, it is touched by reason even before it puts on a quality.

E. Fire does not need to approach for matter to become fire; rather, the "reason" must approach. This is a clear argument in animals and plants: the seminal reasons are the makers of all things, and nature exists as a reason that generates another reason, like its own offspring. While it hands something over to the underlying matter, it stays meanwhile within itself. Thus, the reason expressed externally according to the visible form is the final one and is without life; therefore, it cannot make another reason further on.

F. But the reason that possesses life belongs to the maker of the form; it is like a sister, possessing the same power, and it generates the final reason in the result.

<margin>II. Seminal reasons in nature are like contemplations. When they are impressed from above by intellectual contemplation, the things made by nature are also made through contemplation, and are themselves forms of contemplation.</margin>
G. In what way then does nature act? And in acting, how does it touch upon contemplation? Truly, if it acts while remaining still, and remaining within itself, and if it is "reason," then it is certainly contemplation. For action is usually done according to a reason, being clearly different from that reason; but the reason that stands by and presides over the action is not itself the action. If it is not action but reason, then it is surely a kind of contemplation. Now, in the universal reason, the final reason proceeds from contemplation and is thus called contemplation, as if it were conceived and shaped through contemplation itself.

<column-break/>

...to be, that it possesses contemplation in itself, and what it makes, it makes through contemplation, even if it does not seem to possess it, and how it does so.

That there are neither hands here, nor feet, nor any instrument, whether external or innate; but that matter is needed upon which it will act, and which it makes into a form, is clear to all. But one must also remove the idea of "levering" from natural creation. For what kind of pushing, or what kind of levering, creates varied and diverse colors and shapes? Since not even the molders of wax or the doll-makers—looking at whom people thought the workmanship of Nature was of such a kind—can create colors without bringing in colors from elsewhere for what they make. But it was necessary to understand, as with those who pursue such arts, that there is something remaining in them, according to which, while it remains, they will make through their hands the works that are theirs; so one must ascend to the reliability of Nature herself, and realize that there must remain here too a power which does not act through hands, but remains entirely still. For it needs some things to be remaining and others to be moved. Matter is that which is moved; but within Nature herself, there is that which is unmoved. Otherwise, that would not be the primary mover; nor indeed would it be Nature then, but rather the immobile part of the whole.

Someone might say that "reason" is immobile, but Nature is something else besides reason, and it is moved. But if he says the whole is moved, then reason is too; but if some part of it is immobile, this is the reason. And indeed, it must be a form, and not composed of matter and form. For what does it need of hot or cold matter? Either it is mixed with the underlying matter, or bringing it along, it becomes such, or not having quality, it is made into reason. For fire does not need to approach so that matter may become fire, but rather reason; a sign of this is that in animals and plants, the seminal reasons are the things that act. And Nature is a reason which creates another reason as its own offspring, giving something to the underlying matter while remaining itself. The one reason, according to the form being contemplated, is now final and dead, and can no longer make another. But the one having life, being a brother to the one that made the form, and having the same power in itself, acts in that which is being produced.

How then, in making, and in what it makes, would it touch upon contemplation? If it makes while remaining, and remaining with itself, and is reason, it would itself be a contemplation. For action would occur according to reason, being clearly different from the reason; but the reason itself which is with the action and presiding over it would not be the action. If it is not action, but reason, it is contemplation; and in every reason, the final part is not contemplation. And it is a contemplation in this way: as a thing having been contemplated.

<summary>Plotinus argues that Nature creates living things not through physical effort or tools, but through an internal, silent "contemplation" of formal principles called seminal reasons. He distinguishes between the active, living reason that shapes life and the final, visible form which is "dead" and cannot reproduce itself.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s "Ennead III, Book 8." Having previously discussed how Nature works without physical tools, the text now explores the internal "vision" or contemplation that drives Nature's creative power, comparing it to the way a geometer’s mind produces shapes.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT

Everything concerning this subject is addressed in various ways; one speaks of it not as Nature <note>original: *Physis*</note> but as Soul <note>original: *Psyche*</note>. But that which is in Nature, and Nature itself—does it also arise from contemplation? It certainly arises from contemplation. But does it contemplate itself, and if so, how? For it is the result of contemplation, and of someone's contemplating. How then does Nature possess contemplation? It does not possess the kind that comes from reasoning; by "from reasoning," I mean the process of investigating what is within itself. Why is this? Is it not a kind of life, as well as a reason <note>original: *logos*</note> and a productive power? Does it not follow that to investigate is to not yet possess? But if Nature already possesses these things, then by the very fact of possessing them, it acts. For Nature, its "being" is its "doing," and insofar as it exists, it acts. It is a contemplation and a spectacle <note>original: *theorema*</note>, for it is a reason; by not being a contemplation, a spectacle, and a reason, but rather by acting, it has been revealed to us as a form of contemplation. For it is the result of a contemplation that remains still—not doing something else, but creating simply by being contemplation.

AND if someone were to ask Nature why it creates, if it were willing to hear the questioner and speak, it would say: "You ought not to ask, but to understand in silence, just as I myself am silent and am not accustomed to speaking. What then should you understand? That what is produced is my vision, born of silence—a spectacle produced by nature. Because I am born of a contemplation of this kind, my nature is to be a lover of spectacles <note>original: *philotheamona*</note>. And that part of me which contemplates produces a spectacle, just as geometers, while contemplating, draw their diagrams. But I do not draw; rather, as I contemplate, the lines of bodies emanate as if falling out of me. I also preserve the disposition of my mother and those who begot me. For they too originate from contemplation, and my birth was from contemplation. While they did nothing, being greater reasons or those who contemplate them, I was born." What does all this mean? It means that what is called Nature is a Soul, the offspring of a prior, more powerful Soul, living peacefully and holding contemplation within itself, looking neither upward nor downward. Staying fixed in its own place—in its own stability and, as it were, its own self-consciousness—it knows what comes after it as much as its nature allows, without seeking further. Thus, it has perfected a splendid and graceful spectacle. And if someone wishes to grant it a kind of understanding or perception, it should not be the kind of "perception" or "understanding" we attribute to others, but rather something one might compare to the consciousness of a person in a wakeful sleep. For while it contemplates its own spectacle, it rests in the product that arises from within itself and stays beside it.

<column-break/>

**A** perceived. Indeed, all this higher reason is of a different sort. One part is not like nature, but like the soul; the other part is in nature and is nature itself. But does this also happen through contemplation? Entirely through contemplation: but only if nature itself has also contemplated itself in some way. For it is the effect of contemplation and of someone having contemplated. How, then, does nature possess speculation? It does not have speculation proceeding from **B** reason—and by "proceeding from reason," I mean the consideration of those things which are in itself. But why does it not consider its own things at all, since it is a certain life, a reason, and an efficient power? Is it perhaps because to consider is to not yet possess? But if nature possesses these things, then surely it acts out of what it has. Therefore, for nature, its very being is its doing; and as much as it exists, so much is it also an agent. It is a kind of contemplation and (as I might put it) a **C** spectacle <term>contemplamen</term> <note>Latin: *contemplamen*; a term for the object being looked at or the result of a vision</note>, for it is a reason. Therefore, insofar as it is contemplation, spectacle, and reason, it acts to the extent that it exists through this reason. It has now appeared to us that the act of making is a kind of contemplation: it is the result of contemplation while the speculation remains still, not acting in any other way, but making because the contemplation itself comes to be.

<margin>
III.
The fullness of the **seminal reasons** in nature is like a certain sense by which nature enjoys both itself and the species of things to be generated; these are like threads of nature itself depending on heavenly speculation.
</margin>

IF ANYONE should ask this nature for **D** what reason it acts, if only it were willing to hear the questioner and speak, it would respond: "You ought not to have asked me, but it was fitting for you to understand in silence, just as I am silent and am not accustomed to speaking. What, then, did you need to understand? This, I say, first of all: that what is born is my vision, while I remain silent, a spectacle born by nature. And since I was born from a certain contemplation of this kind, I naturally have a nature that desires a spectacle. Consequently, that **E** which holds the place of a contemplator in me produces a spectacle, just as geometers describe things by contemplating them. Yet, I do not write; rather, while I contemplate, the lines of bodies emanate from here as if falling out. Certainly, the affection of my mother and my parents is preserved in me, for they derive their origin from contemplation. My generation also is derived from speculation. For while they do nothing, but are greater reasons and contemplate themselves, I was born." **F** Where is this leading? To the point that nature is a soul, the offspring of a prior soul that lives more vigorously, possessing a quiet contemplation within itself, turning neither toward higher things nor toward lower things. This nature, standing in that in which it is—namely, in its own state and a kind of consensus—knows what is after it through this knowledge and consensus, as far as its nature allows. It does not search further, but has already perfected a splendid and graceful spectacle. And if anyone wishes to attribute some **G** knowledge or sense to it, they should not attribute the kind of sense or knowledge we speak of in others, but just as if one were to compare it to the knowledge of a person who is awake. For while contemplating its own spectacle, it finds rest: I say a spectacle made in it, which proceeds from that which is worked out in itself and with itself.

<summary>Plotinus describes Nature as a "silent" philosopher that creates the physical world not through labor or tools, but as a byproduct of its own internal contemplation, comparing its creative process to the way geometric shapes naturally follow from mathematical thought.</summary>
<keywords>Nature, Physis, Soul, Psyche, Contemplation, Reason, Geometry, Plotinus, Enneads, seminal reasons, vision, creation, silence</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s "Ennead III, Book 8," specifically moving from a discussion of Nature's "silent contemplation" to how human action and the higher Soul relate to this same visionary process. It maintains the argument that all "doing" is actually a byproduct of "seeing."</meta>

### 346 PLOTINUS ENNEAD III.

<margin>A</margin>...let it remain, and let the spectacle itself be a quiet insight, although somewhat more obscure and weaker. For the other kind <note>The "other kind" refers to the higher contemplation of the Soul or Intellect.</note> is more effective for intuition; this kind, however, is but an image of that other contemplation. In this way, that which is produced by Nature is born very weak, because a weakened insight produces a weak spectacle. Indeed, even among men, when they become too weak for contemplation, they usually resort to action, which is but a shadow of speculation and reason. For when the <margin>B</margin> capacity for contemplation is not at all sufficient—because they are unable to grasp the vision adequately due to the weakness of their soul, and are therefore not filled by it—yet they still desire to see it, they take refuge in action. They do this so that they might see there, in the physical world, what they were unable to discern with the mind. Thus, whenever they "do" or "make," they themselves wish to see the object, to contemplate and perceive it, and they want others to behold it with them. When action is set before them, they do as much as they are able, as they see fit. Truly, <margin>C</margin> we shall find everywhere that "making" and "acting" are either a weakness of contemplation or a consequence of it. It is a weakness when you have nothing left beyond the act itself; but it is a consequence if you have something else to contemplate that is better than the work you have produced. For who, when they are able to behold the Truth itself with a particular devotion, would turn instead to an image of the truth? This is proven by the dullest of children, who, being most unfit for learning and contemplation, sink down into manual arts and labors.

<margin>
VIII.
The intellectual soul of the world, always full from the contemplation of divine things, being pregnant from that source, gives birth to a Nature that is likewise fertile with reasons <note>original: *rationibus*, Greek *logoi*—the formative principles of life</note>, as if through speculation; and through such speculation, it generates all things.
</margin>

<margin>D</margin> **N**ow that we have spoken of Nature and how its generation is a kind of contemplation, let us next proceed to the Soul that is superior to it, saying this: Truly, the Soul’s own contemplation, its desire for learning and its studious inquiry—together with the "birth-pangs" <note>original: *parturiens*, Greek *odis*—referring to the labor of a mind full of ideas seeking expression</note> arising from what it has come to know—has created a full fertility. Thus, having itself become a complete object of contemplation, it produces another object of contemplation. Just as an art does when it is full, it procreates a sort of "minor art" in a child who is learning, who acquires an image of all things, yet holds them in a dull, obscure, and weak way—spectacles that are initially unable to support themselves. Therefore, the higher, rational part of the Soul, filled and illuminated by the things above, remains there; but the other part participates in that which the first participation has shared. For life always proceeds from life. Indeed, the "act" <note>original: *actus*, Greek *energeia*</note> runs through all things and is never absent. Yet, as it progresses, it allows its prior part to remain where it left it. For if it were to lose the first part entirely, it would no longer be everywhere, but only in that where it ended. However, the part that proceeds is not equal to the part that stays at rest. If, therefore, it must exist through all things, and no place should be left where this same "act" is not present, the prior is always different from the posterior. Now, action proceeds from contemplation or action, but ultimately from contemplation, since action did not yet exist; for it cannot exist before contemplation. If this is how things stand, it is necessary that one be weaker than the other...
<gloss>Greek: Action is of contemplation; but weaker, and not yet, or... <note>original: τῆς θεωρίας ἡ πρᾶξις: ἥττω δέ, ἔπω δέ, ἢ...</note></gloss>

<column-break/>

...to remain, and to be a spectacle, and a silent contemplation, though more obscure. For the other [contemplation] is clearer for seeing; but this one is an image of another contemplation. In this way, that which is generated by it is altogether weak, because a weak contemplation makes a weak spectacle. For even men, when they become weak in contemplating, turn to action, which is a shadow of contemplation and reason. Because the power of contemplation is not sufficient for them, they are unable to grasp the vision adequately due to the weakness of the soul. And because they are not filled, yet long to see it, they are carried toward action so that they might see what they did not see with the mind. Whenever they act, they themselves wish to see it, to contemplate and perceive it, and to have others do the same when their purpose is achieved through action as far as possible. Everywhere we shall find that making and acting are either a weakness of contemplation or a byproduct. A weakness, if one has nothing after the deed is done; a byproduct, if one has something else better than the thing made to contemplate. For who, being able to contemplate the true reality intensely, would go to the image of the true? The slower of children bear witness to this; being incapable of learning and contemplation, they are pulled down toward crafts and manual labors.

<margin>E</margin> **B**ut having spoken of Nature, and how its generation is contemplation, let us move to the Soul which is before it. We say that its contemplation, its love of learning and inquiry, and the birth-pangs from what it has known, and its fullness, have made it—having become an entire spectacle—to make another spectacle. Just as an art does, when each is full, it makes another small art, as it were, in a child, who has an image of all things; yet these are dull, as if obscure and unable to help themselves, being spectacles and objects of contemplation at first. <margin>F</margin> Therefore, the rational part of it above, always being filled and illuminated by the thing above, remains there; but the other part participates by the first participation of that which participated. For life always proceeds from life. For energy <note>original: *energeia*</note> reaches everywhere, and there is nowhere where it is absent. As it proceeds, it lets the prior part of itself—concerning which it is in part—remain where it left it. For if it left behind that which proceeds, it would no longer be everywhere, but only at the end. But the proceeding is not equal to the remaining. If it must be everywhere, and there must not be a place where its energy is not, the prior is always before the posterior. <margin>G</margin> But energy comes because action is of contemplation—or action is weaker, and not yet... it is necessary that it be weaker...

<summary>Plotinus explains that physical action is a secondary "shadow" of mental contemplation, occurring when the soul is too weak to hold a pure intellectual vision. He transitions from discussing the silent creation of Nature to the more fertile, "pregnant" contemplation of the Soul which generates all life.</summary>
<keywords>contemplation, action, nature, soul, intellect, Plotinus, generation, vision, weakness of soul</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s "Ennead III, Book 8," titled "On Nature, Contemplation, and the One." The previous page argued that all "making" in the natural world is actually a silent form of seeing. Here, Plotinus expands this to human soul and intellect, arguing that even our busy actions are just "weakened" attempts to reach a state of contemplation.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...is one thing, while all else is contemplation <note>original: "theoria"</note>. To the extent that even an action which seems to follow contemplation is nothing other than a certain very weak form of contemplation. For it is necessary that what is produced always remains within the same genus as its source, yet it becomes weaker as it is produced, becoming thinner as it gradually descends. Indeed, all things proceed sweetly and quietly, because they do not require an external display of contemplation or action. The Soul itself contemplates from its highest <margin>B</margin> watchtower <note>original: "specula," referring to the mind's highest vantage point</note>. And because that which it contemplates rises outwardly—not in the same way as that which existed before it—it certainly produces what follows it: contemplation surely gives birth to more contemplation. For contemplation itself, or the object of contemplation <note>original: "contemplamen"</note>, has no fixed limit; because of this, it proceeds and advances through all things. What indeed prevents it from spreading through everything? Since in every soul, the object of contemplation is the same. It is not <margin>C</margin> limited by physical size, yet it does not exist in the same way in all people; therefore, it is not present in the same way in every part of the soul. For this reason, in the works of Plato, the soul's charioteer <note>A reference to Plato’s *Phaedrus*, where the Charioteer represents Reason and the horses represent the different parts of the human spirit.</note> shares what he has seen with the horses. They, in turn, receive it, as they are those who long for what they have seen; for they did not receive the whole vision. But if they act out of longing, they will act for the sake of what they desire. And that desire is for the object of contemplation and contemplation itself.

<margin>That the end of contemplation is seen. Likewise, that the reasons for things are gathered in the soul, and when action brings them forth with the soul, then you truly know.</margin>
<margin>D</margin> **ACTION**, therefore, exists for the sake of contemplation and the object seen. For this reason, contemplation is the goal of those who act. Truly, what they could not achieve by the direct path, they strive to grasp as if by a winding road <note>original: "per ambages"</note>. The same thing happens when they attain what they desire—which they wanted to be present. They do not do this so that they might remain ignorant, but so that they may recognize what they have now acquired, and behold it present in the soul as something situated there <margin>E</margin> for the sake of being seen. For they always act for the sake of the Good. This is not so that the Good remains outside of them or so that they possess it not at all, but so that they themselves might possess the good that comes from the action. But where is this good held? Surely, in the soul. Therefore, action slides back again into contemplation itself. For that which one grasps with the soul—which is a kind of reason <note>original: "ratio"</note>—what else is it but a silent reason <note>original: "ratio silens"</note>? And the more it is truly reason, the more it is silent, and vice versa. For then it remains at rest, and being full, it requires nothing further. Contemplation, established in such a <margin>F</margin> state, rests within itself because of the confidence of possession. And the more certain this "faith" or conviction is, the quieter the contemplation becomes, for it draws the soul closer into a unity. And by this logic, you will know the thing itself insofar as the knower (for now we must speak seriously) becomes one with the thing known. For if they remain two, this will be one thing and that another. Therefore, it will seem to be something merely adjacent; and that <margin>G</margin> duality has not yet contracted a true familiarity—just as when the rational principles existing in the soul are not yet active. On this account, it is necessary for reason

<insert>not to be something external, but to be united to the mind of the learner, until it finally finds its own home. Therefore, when the Soul becomes familiar with reason and is influenced by it, it simultaneously brings it forth, and, having been set free, it now proceeds into action. For what it held previously, it now notices, and by its own readiness, it brings it into the open, as if...</insert>

<summary>Plotinus explains that human action is merely a "weakened" or indirect form of contemplation; we act only to see and possess the Good within our souls. Ultimately, true knowledge occurs when the "silent reason" of the soul becomes one with the object it contemplates.</summary>
