-># PLOTINUS'S ENNEAD III.<-

<insert>A</insert> ...one might be distinct from itself, and another is known to have come from it; and in thinking, it beholds another, as if it were itself something else. This is because it is also a rational principle <note>original: "ratio" / "logos"</note>, and like an intellect, but one that beholds something else. For it is not full, but falls short of that which is above it; yet it also beholds, in a quiet manner, the things it brings forth. For those things it has not yet brought forth, it does not yet display; but those it does bring forth, it produces from a certain deficiency, as it learns through observation what it possesses. <insert>B</insert> But in matters of action, which are already external, it adapts what it holds within. Because it possesses more than nature does, it possesses it more quietly; and because it has more, it is more given to contemplation. Conversely, because it does not possess perfectly, it desires more strongly to have a perception of the thing seen, and a contemplation arising from the wandering of its consideration. When it has left its former state and passed into other things, and then returns to contemplate again, it leaves a part of itself behind; but that part which remains within itself does this less. Wherefore the good soul is already <insert>C</insert> reason <note>original: "ratio"</note> in its effect, and it demonstrates to others what is within itself; but toward itself, it is vision. For it is already gathered toward the One and toward the quiet—not only regarding external things, but regarding itself, and finally, all things within.

<margin>VI. It is confirmed that all things are made by contemplation, and therefore they are certain forms of contemplation, and whatever they do, they do for the sake of contemplation.</margin>

<insert>D</insert> JUST AS therefore it partly stands by itself, and partly reason has shown: all things come from contemplation and are themselves contemplations, both those which truly exist and those generated from them. While these things are contemplating, the things made become themselves "objects of contemplation" <note>original: "contemplamina"</note>, offering themselves everywhere to sense, or to knowledge, or to opinion. Furthermore, actions are directed toward knowledge as their end; desire also seeks knowledge. Generations, moreover, taking their beginning from contemplation, end in a form <note>original: "species"</note>, and another specimen to be fabricated. And in every way, the individual imitations of efficient causes everywhere produce spectacles and forms. Even produced <insert>E</insert> substances, like imitations of beings, declare that the efficient causes look toward contemplation as their end—not toward the making, nor the actions, but the work itself—for the purpose that it might be a spectacle for those who behold it. Indeed, even thoughts desire to see this very thing; and even before them, the senses themselves, whose end is knowledge. Again, before these, nature itself, possessing a specimen and a reason within itself, generates another reason. Therefore it is clear, since the first of all things consist in contemplation, that all <insert>F</insert> other things necessarily desire contemplation itself; since the end proposed for all is also the beginning. And now, even when animals generate, the seminal reasons <note>original: "rationes seminales" / "logoi"</note> within them stimulate them to give birth; and that whole act is an operation of contemplation, a stimulus desiring to produce many forms and various spectacles, to fill all things with reasons, and as it were, to behold them perpetually. For to make something exist is to produce a certain form, and that is to fill all things entirely with contemplation. Furthermore, <insert>G</insert> errors both in those things which are generated and in those which are done seem to be nothing other than "slips" of the contemplators and a certain diversion from the object of contemplation itself. Even an unskilled craftsman is judged similar to one who makes ugly forms.

<column-break/>

...one becomes different from itself; and in thinking, it beholds as one thing beholding another. For indeed, it is itself a reason <note>original: "logos"</note>, and like an intellect, but seeing another. For it is not full, but lacks that which is around it; yet it too beholds quietly the things it brings forth. For the things it has already produced, it no longer brings forth; but what it does bring forth, it brings forth through deficiency, learning through inspection what it possesses. In practical matters, it applies what it possesses to external things. And by possessing more than nature, it is quieter; and by having more, it is more contemplative. But by not possessing perfectly, it desires more strongly to have the learning and contemplation of that which is beheld, which comes from inspection. And leaving its state when it enters into other things, it then returns and contemplates again with the part of itself that was left behind. But that which stays entirely within itself does this less. Therefore the virtuous man has already been reasoned out, and shows what is in himself to others; but toward himself, he is vision. For he is already toward the One, and toward the quiet, not only of external things, but also toward himself, and all things within.

THAT truly all things, both those that truly exist, come from contemplation and are contemplation—and the things produced from them are objects of contemplation, being themselves contemplations; some to sense, some to knowledge or opinion. And actions have their end in knowledge; and desire is for knowledge; and generations are from contemplation, ending in a form and another object of contemplation. And altogether, being imitations of each of the makers, they produce objects of contemplation and forms. And the produced substances, being imitations of beings, show that the makers make the end—not the makings, nor the actions, but the result—so that it may be contemplated. And the thoughts before it wish to see; and even earlier the senses, whose end is knowledge. And even before these, nature produces the object of contemplation within itself, and the reason, producing another reason. This is clear somewhere, since it is also clear that it is necessary among the first things to be in contemplation. And all other things desire this, which is the end for all and the beginning. Since even when animals give birth, the reasons <note>original: "logoi"</note> within them move them; and this is an activity of contemplation, a labor pain <note>original: "odis," referring to the pangs of childbirth as a creative urge</note>, the making of many forms and many objects of contemplation, to fill all things with reasons, and as it were, always to contemplate. For to make something be is to make a form; and this is to fill all things with contemplation. And errors, both in things generated and in things done, are the result of those contemplating wandering away from the object of contemplation. And the bad craftsman is like one who produces ugly forms.

<meta>The catchword at the bottom "τα ὄντω" refers to the next page's opening Greek text: "the beings."</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that every action in the universe—from human virtue to the reproduction of animals—is actually a "weakened" form of contemplation. He suggests that all of creation is an attempt by the Soul and Nature to express and behold the internal truths they possess.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 348 concerning the hierarchy of contemplation (theoria). Plotinus is moving from the way Nature contemplates to how the Soul and the Intellect (Nous) engage in the same process, emphasizing that the higher one ascends, the more the observer and the observed become one and the same.</meta>

### BOOK EIGHT. ###

And lovers, too, when they see, and through their senses seek to reach the inner beauty. <note>Original Greek: καὶ οἱ ἐρῶντες δὲ ἰδόντων... This sentence concludes the previous thought that even physical attraction is a form of searching for a deeper "vision" or contemplation.</note>

THESE things, then, are so. But when contemplation <note>Greek: *theoria*</note> raises itself from nature to the soul, and from the soul into the intellect, the acts of contemplation become increasingly intimate and unified with those who contemplate. In the case of a virtuous soul, the things known tend toward the same point as the subject <note>The "subject" here refers to the person thinking or perceiving.</note>, since they are striving toward the intellect. In this state, it is clear that both the knower and the known have become one, not merely through a close familiarity—as happens in the most excellent souls—but rather through their very essence, and because in that realm, being and thinking are the same. For there, it is no longer one thing and then another; if it were, there would need to be yet another third thing in which they were not distinct. Therefore, in the Intellect, both must truly be one. This is a "living contemplation," and not a mere "object of contemplation" <note>Latin: *contemplamen*; Greek: *theorema*</note> existing in something else. For that which exists in another living thing is not alive of itself. If, therefore, there is to be an object of contemplation and a thought that is also truly alive, it must not be merely a "vegetative" life, or a "sensory" life, or even the general life of the soul. These are indeed forms of intelligence in their own way: one is vegetative intelligence, another sensory, and another belongs to the soul. But how are they intelligences? Because they are rational principles <note>Latin: *rationes*; Greek: *logoi*</note>. Indeed, every life is a kind of intelligence, though one may be dimmer than another, just as life itself varies in clarity. The clearest and most powerful life is the "First Life," which is also the "First Intellect." Thus, the primary intelligence is the primary life; the second life is the second intelligence; and the final, lowest life is the final intelligence. Therefore, every life of this kind is also an intelligence. Men might perhaps speak of differences in life, but they often fail to speak of differences in intelligence; they say some things have intelligence and others have none at all, because they do not inquire into what life actually is. But we must point out again that our argument shows all things to be forms of contemplation. If, then, the truest life is life according to intelligence, and this is the same as the truest intelligence, then the truest intelligence lives. Thus, contemplation and its object are a living thing and a life, and these two are together as one. How, then, is this "one" also "many"? Perhaps because it does not contemplate the absolute One. For even when it looks at the One, it does not look at it as a pure unity; otherwise, it would not become an Intellect. Instead, having begun as a unity, it does not remain as it began, but secretly becomes multiple, as if it were pregnant. It unfolds itself, wishing to possess all things—though perhaps it would have been better for it not to have desired this. For by doing so, it became a "second" thing. It is as if a circle had unfolded itself to become a shape, a plane, a circumference, a center, and various lines—some above and some below. The source from which it began is better, while the results are lesser. For the source was not the same as that which proceeded from it and toward which it moved.

<column-break/>

Finally, lovers themselves are chief among those who are occupied with beholding, and they hurry more intensely toward the outward form.

<margin>
VII.
In true knowledge, the knower and the known are the same, or become the same. Likewise, the first form is the same as life and first intelligence; therefore, these proceed through all things equally. Likewise, the intellect is necessarily uniform and yet contains all forms.
</margin>

Regarding these matters, let it be spoken of in this way. But when contemplation raises itself from nature to the soul, and from the soul into the mind, the contemplations always become more proper and familiar, becoming united with the contemplators. In a soul perfected through virtue, the things that are known are reduced into the same subject, insofar as they hasten toward the intellect itself. Certainly, in this very intellect, both are now one—not through an acquired familiarity, as usually happens in a most excellent soul, but rather through essence, and because in that state, to be and to perceive are the same. For there, it is no longer that this is one thing and that is another; otherwise, there will again be something else in which there is no longer a "this" and a "that." Therefore, it is necessary that in this state, both are truly one. That is a living contemplation, not merely a thought-object in another. For what exists in another living thing is not living through itself. If, therefore, any object of contemplation or thought is to live, it must be a life that is not merely vegetative, nor sensory, nor any other animal life (for in a sense there are other intelligences), but this one is vegetative intelligence, that one sensory, and finally another is animal. In what way, then, are they intelligences? Because they are clearly rational principles <note>Latin: *rationes*</note>, and all life is a certain intelligence, but one is thinner than another, just as life is. That which is clearer and more valid is the "First Life," and the "First Intellect" is one. Therefore, the first intelligence is also the first life, and the second life is the second intelligence; finally, the last life is the lowest intelligence. Thus, every life of this genus is also judged to be an intelligence. But men might perhaps speak of differences in life, yet they do not speak of differences in intelligence; instead, they say some are intelligences and others are entirely not intelligences, since they do not seek to know what life itself is. But this must also be signified: that our discourse again shows, as if by some chance, that all things exist as contemplations. If, therefore, the truest life is life according to intelligence itself, and this is the same as the truest intelligence, then surely the truest intelligence lives. And thus contemplation and such an object of contemplation is living and is life, and these two are at once one. One being, therefore, is these two. By what reasoning, then, is this "one" also "many"? Perhaps because it does not contemplate the One as such. For even when it looks at the One, it does not behold it as a unity, otherwise it would not become an intellect. But beginning as one, it does not remain as it began, but in a hidden way it becomes multiple, as if already pregnant, and it unfolds itself wishing to possess all things. For this, it might have been better not to have wished for that. From this, it turned out to be a "second" thing; not otherwise than a circle unfolding itself becomes a shape, a plane, a circumference, a center, and lines—some indeed above, others below. The origin from which it proceeds is better; the rest are indeed worse. For that from which the procession begins was not such as that from which, and into which, it proceeds. Nor again is that...

<sig>G</sig>
<meta>catchword: than (Latin: quàm)</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that all life—from plants to the highest Mind—is a form of "thinking" or "contemplation." He explains that in the highest Intellect, the thinker and the thought are no longer separate but become a single, living reality that "unfolds" into the complexity of the universe.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 355, where Plotinus explored how contemplation (theoria) moves from the physical world of nature into the higher realm of the Soul and the Intellect. Here, he argues that while the Intellect contains all things in a unified way, it still contains a form of multiplicity (the thinker and the thought), which implies there must be an even higher, simpler principle: The One.</meta>

->PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III.<-

<margin>A</margin> ...from that very source, and toward that which was of the same nature as the source from which the progression first began. In another sense, this "mind" or Intellect is not the mind of any single individual, but is the totality of Mind. Being the whole, it belongs to all things. Therefore, it is necessary that the Intellect be all things, and that every part of it also possesses this quality: that each part is the whole and is all things. <note>Plotinus is describing a holographic-like reality where the "Intellect" (Nous) contains every idea simultaneously; the part contains the whole.</note> If this were not so, it would contain some part that is not intellect, and it would be composed of things that lack intelligence. It would then be a fortuitous <margin>B</margin> heap, a mere pile of things waiting for some external help to actually become an "intellect." For this reason, it is also infinite; if anything flows from it internally, it is not diminished, because that which comes from it is also "all things." Likewise, the source from which it proceeds remains whole, because it was not a composition made of separate parts.

<margin>
VIII.
In the first intellect there is a multitude, even if it is all things: but the principle of all is not all things, but is above all things.
</margin>

<margin>C</margin> THIS Intellect, therefore, exists in such a state, and for that reason, it is not the "First." Instead, there must be something superior to it. This is why our previous discourse led us upward: because multiplicity is always posterior to unity. The Intellect is a "number" <note>In Platonic philosophy, "number" implies a collection or a plurality, even if highly organized.</note>; but the principle of number is unity, specifically the kind of unity that is the source of such a number. This Intellect is both the "thinker" and the "object of thought" <note>Latin: *intellectus* and *intelligibile*; Greek: *nous* and *noeton*.</note> at the same time; thus, it is simultaneously two things. If it is two, we must find something that exists prior to these two. But what should we call this? Is it simply the Intellect? <margin>D</margin> No, for every intellect is joined to an object of thought; unless that object is present, there can be no intellect. If, then, it is not the intellect, but escapes this duality of thinker and thought, it follows that what is prior to these two must be superior to the Intellect. But what prevents this "First" from being simply the "object of thought" alone? The same reason: the object of thought is always joined to the intellect that thinks it. If, therefore, it is neither <margin>E</margin> the intellect nor the object of thought, what can it be? It is surely that from which the intellect—and the object of thought along with the intellect—arises. What, then, is this source, and how shall we conceive of it? For it must either be something that thinks, or something that does not think. If it thinks, it will be an intellect. If it does not think, it will be ignorant of itself, and it will seem to be nothing of great dignity. Even if we say that this source is "the Good" itself and "the most Simple," we are not <margin>F</margin> bringing forth something clear and easy to see, even if it is the truth, so long as we have no firm ground upon which to fix our mental intuition while we speak of it. Furthermore, since the knowledge of other things occurs through the intellect and by means of the intellect, how can this source—which exceeds the very nature of intellect—be perceived by a single, sudden grasp of the mind? We shall answer this by saying that it is perceived by something within us that is as similar to it as possible. For there is something of it within us; or rather, there is nowhere that it is not, for those who are capable of participating in it. Indeed, wherever you place something capable of receiving it, you will carry something away from it—just as if a voice were to fill a desert, or a desert where people were present. In such a case, wherever you place your ears, you will hear the whole voice, and yet, in another sense, not the whole of it. What is it, then, that we shall receive by placing our intellect near—

<column-break/>

...from which and into which, such as that from which alone it began. And in another way, the Intellect is not the intellect of someone, but is all. Being all, it is of all things. It must therefore be all things and of all things, and its part must also have all and be all. Otherwise, it will have some part which is not intellect; and it will be composed of non-intellects, and will be a sort of gathered heap, waiting to become intellect from all its parts. Therefore it is infinite in this way: and if something comes from it, it is not lessened, because that which is from it is also all things; nor is that from which it comes lessened, because it was not a synthesis of parts.

This [Intellect] then is such, and therefore it is not the first. But there must be that which is "Beyond" <note>Greek: *epekeina*. This refers to Plato's famous description of the Good being "beyond being" in the *Republic*.</note> it, for the sake of which the rational principles of sense-perception exist. These are a multitude that has been given being, and this is a number. But the principle of number, and of such a number, is the truly One. And there was the Intellect: it is also the object of thought simultaneously, so that it is two together. If there are two, one must take that which is before the two. What then? Is it the Intellect alone? But to every intellect is yoked the object of thought. If the object of thought is not yoked to it, there will be no intellect. If it is not intellect, but escapes the two, that which is prior to these two must indeed be beyond intellect. What then prevents it from being the object of thought itself? The fact that the object of thought is also yoked to the intellect. If it is neither intellect nor the object of thought, we shall say it is that from which the intellect and the object of thought with it come. What then is this, and how shall we imagine it? For again, it will either be thinking or not thinking. If thinking, it is an intellect; if not thinking, it will be ignorant even of itself. Thus, what would be so majestic about it? For even if we were to say it is the Good and that it is simple, we would obviously not be speaking the truth clearly and plainly as long as we do not have something upon which to lean the mind while we speak. Moreover, since knowledge of other things comes through the intellect and to the intellect—those things being able to know some intellect—this thing which transcends the nature of intellect, by what sudden intuition could it be captured? To this we must show how it is possible, saying it is by the likeness of it within us. For there is something even in us of it; or rather, there is nowhere it is not, for those who can participate in it. For by placing anything whatever that is able to have it anywhere, you have it from there—just as if a voice occupied a desert, or even with the desert, you placed men in any part of the desert and their ears; you will carry away the voice in its entirety, and yet again not in its entirety. What then is it that we shall carry away, having placed our intellect near—

<meta>Catchword: adhiben- (Latin: "applying" or "bringing to bear")</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Intellect (Nous) is a unified plurality containing all ideas, but because it contains both the thinker and the thought, it requires a higher, perfectly simple source known as The One or The Good. He explains that we can only grasp this ultimate principle through a "likeness" of it that exists within our own souls.</summary>
<keywords>Intellect, Nous, The One, The Good, contemplation, plurality, unity, simplicity, metaphysics, Neoplatonism</keywords>

--- Page 475 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the "Intellect" (Nous) and its relationship to the "One." Having established that the Intellect is a unified "all," he now demonstrates why there must be a simpler, prior source that is not part of the multitude it creates.</meta>

->BOOK EIGHT.<-

<margin>A</margin> ...do we receive it? Perhaps it is necessary for the mind to turn backwards, as it were, and—since it has a face on both sides—to leave itself behind. If it wishes to see the Good itself, it must take care not to be entirely "intellect," <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous). For Plotinus, the Intellect is the realm of divine thought, but even it is too complex to be the absolute Source.</note> nor to be all those things that are understood. For it is itself the "First Life," an activity that moves through all things—a traversal, I say, not one that moves from day to day, but one that has always completed its course. If, therefore, it is both life and a traversal, it contains all things exactly, and not in confusion. Otherwise, <margin>B</margin> if it held them indistinctly, it would hold them imperfectly. It must, then, depend on another which is no longer involved in the "traversal," but is the Principle of the traversal: the Principle of Life, the Principle of Mind, and of all things. For the Principle is not "all things," but rather all things come from the Principle. The Principle itself is neither all things nor any one of the things, so that it may generate all things. It is not a multitude, but the Principle of multitude. For that which is generated <margin>C</margin> is always less simple than that which generates it. Therefore, if this [the One] generated the Mind, it must necessarily be simpler than the Mind. If anyone should think that the Good itself is both the "One" and "All Things," then it would either be each thing individually or all of them together. If it were all things accumulated together, it would be posterior to all things. For if it existed before all things, then all things would be one set of entities, and the Good would be something else besides them. But if the Good and "all things" existed at the same time, it would not be a beginning. Yet it must be the Principle <margin>D</margin> and exist before all things, so that all things may exist after it. If it were said to be each thing individually, then every thing would be identical to every other thing, and all would be the same at once with no distinction. Thus, the Principle is none of these things, but rather is above all things.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...by applying [it] do we receive it? Perhaps indeed the intellect must turn itself as if from behind, and since it has a face on both sides, to leave itself behind; and if it is to look upon the Good itself, it must take care not to be entirely "intellect," nor to be all those things which are understood. For it is itself the First Life, which indeed is an act in a certain "discursion" <note>original: "discursione" / "διεξόδῳ". This refers to the way thought moves through a sequence of ideas rather than being perfectly still.</note> through all things: a discursion, I say, not one that runs about daily, but one which has always filled up its course. If therefore it is life and discursion, and possesses <margin>B</margin> all things—not confusedly, indeed, but most exactly—otherwise if it held them indistinctly, it would hold them also imperfectly: it is necessary that it depend on another, which indeed is no longer occupied in discursion, but is the Principle of discursion: the Principle of life, the Principle of mind, and of all things. For the Principle is not all things, but all things rather are from the Principle: but it itself is neither all things, nor any thing of all, so that it may generate all things, nor is it a multitude, but the Principle of multitude. For by that which is generated, <margin>C</margin> that which generates is everywhere simpler. Therefore if this [the One] generated the mind, it is necessarily simpler than the mind. If anyone however should think that the Good itself is the "One" and "all things," it will either be all things according to each of all things singly, or all things collectively. Because if all things are accumulated together, it will be later than all things. For if it existed before all things, all things indeed will be one thing, but it itself will be another thing besides the whole. But if it itself and all things are together at once, it will not be the beginning. It is necessary, however, for it to be the principle, <margin>D</margin> and before all things, so that all things also may be after it. But if it be said to be singularly according to each one of all, first indeed any thing will be the same as any other thing, then all things will be together at once, and there would never be any distinction. And so also it itself is nothing of all, but rather above all things.

<margin>
IX.
The Principle of the universe is the "One" itself, which is neither moved, nor divided, nor multiplied, even when the multitude of things proceeds from it.
</margin>

### WHAT THEN IS IT? Truly, it is the power of all things;
without which neither the rest would exist, nor would the Intellect exist, which is the first and total life. For that which exists above life is the cause of life. <margin>E</margin> The activity of life, which is "all things," is not the First Principle itself, but is poured forth from the Principle as if from a fountain. Think of a fountain <note>original: "πηγή" (pege). Plotinus uses the fountain and the tree as his primary metaphors for how the Source creates without losing its own substance.</note> that has no other source, but gives itself entirely to the rivers, yet is not exhausted by any of those rivers, but remains quietly in itself. The rivers that flow from it, before they flow their separate ways, remain for a while together, and already know, as it were, into which channels their small streams are about to flow. Or think of the life of a giant tree <margin>F</margin> passing through the whole, while the Principle remains, not divided throughout the tree, but settled as if in the root. This indeed provides the whole and manifold life to the tree; but the Principle itself remains, in no way multiplied, but as the Principle of the manifold life. Nor is it a wonder that it is so. Perhaps it is more a wonder how a multitude of life can come from that which is not a multitude, and how it could not have been a multitude unless there was first that which is no multitude at all. For the Principle is in no way divided into the whole; otherwise, <margin>G</margin> if it were divided, the whole would immediately be lost. Nor would the whole ever have been made, unless the Principle remained in itself, being entirely different from the whole.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the ultimate Source (the One) must be simpler than the Intellect and Life that proceed from it. Using the metaphors of a fountain and a tree root, he explains how the One remains unified and undiminished even while generating the vast complexity of the universe.</summary>
<keywords>The One, Intellect, Principle, Source, Fountain Metaphor, Tree Metaphor, Simplicity, Multitude, Plotinus, Enneads</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous section where Plotinus describes the Mind (Intellect) turning back toward its source. It transitions from discussing the nature of the Intellect as a "totality" to the necessity of a "One" that exists above this totality.</meta>

->### PLOTINUS: ENNEAD III.<-

<margin>A</margin> ...from which at once and into which it was such, as that itself from which the progression merely begins. And in another way, the Mind <note>original: "mens" / "νοῦς" (nous). In Neoplatonism, this is the second level of reality, the realm of pure thought and Forms.</note> is not the mind of any one individual, but is all Mind. Being the whole, it is also the mind of all things. It is necessary, therefore, for the Intellect to hold all things and to be the existence of all things, and to have its parts in such a way that each part is the whole and is all things. If this were not so, it would have some part which is not "intellect"; it would be heaped together from things that are not intellect, and it would be a kind of <margin>B</margin> accidental pile, waiting for assistance from all sides in order to turn into a Mind. For this reason, it is also infinite in this way: if anything flows from it within, it is not diminished, because that which comes from it is also "all things," and the source from which it comes is also within, since it was not a composition made of several parts.

<margin>
VIII.
In the first intellect there is a multitude, and it is all things; but the principle of all things is not all things, but is above all things.
</margin>

<margin>C</margin> THIS, then, is how the Intellect exists, and therefore it is not the "First." Instead, there must be something higher than it, for the sake of which our previous discourse was held. This is because a multitude is always posterior to the "One." Here, the Intellect is a number; but the principle of number is unity, and such a number is a principle because it is "One" in this way. Here, truly, are both the Intellect and the <term>Intelligible</term> <note>The "Intelligible" (noeton) refers to the objects of thought—the Platonic Forms—which exist within the Mind.</note> together; thus, it is two things at once. But if it is two, we must grasp something prior to these two. But what should we call this? Is it perhaps "Intellect" alone? <margin>D</margin> But to every intellect, the "Intelligible" is joined as its mate; and unless there is a mate there, there will not even be an Intellect. If, therefore, it is not an intellect, but has escaped these two, it follows that what is prior to these two is higher than the Intellect. But what prevents this "First" from being the "Intelligible" alone? Clearly the same reason: for the Intelligible also always has the Intellect joined to it. If, then, it is neither the Intellect <margin>E</margin> nor the Intelligible, what will it be? It is certainly that from which the Intellect comes, and with the Intellect, the Intelligible. What, then, is this, and how shall we imagine it? For it will either be something that thinks, or something that does not think. If it thinks, it will be an Intellect; if it does not think, it will even be ignorant of itself, and will seem to be nothing venerable. For if we say this is the "Good" itself and the most simple thing, we do not thereby bring forth something manifest and clear; <margin>F</margin> although it is true, we have nothing upon which to fix the gaze of our thought while we speak of it. Furthermore, since the knowledge of other things occurs through the Intellect and by the Intellect in those who can know something by thinking, how can this "First"—which surpasses the nature of the Intellect—be perceived by any sudden, collective intuition? We shall respond to this: that it is perceived by something in us that is as similar to it as possible. For there is something of it in us; or rather, there is nowhere that it is not, for those who have the capacity to participate in it. Truly, wherever you apply something that is able to receive it, you will carry something away from there—just as if a voice were to occupy a desert, or people within a desert. For then, in whatever part you place your ears, you will drink in the whole voice, and yet again, not the whole of it. What, then, is it that we receive when we apply the intellect <note>The catchword at the bottom of the page "adhiben-" (applying) leads into the next page's discussion of how the human mind reaches toward the One.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...from which and into which, like that from which it only [comes], and in another way the Mind, not of some one thing, but also the whole. Being the whole, it is also of all things. Through itself, being all things and of all things, its very part must have the whole, and be all things: otherwise, some part would be outside the Mind: and it would be composed of those things, and would be a kind of gathered heap, waiting to become Mind from all things. Therefore it is also infinite <margin>B</margin> in this way: and if anything is from it, it is not diminished, because that which is from it is also all things, nor is that from which it comes [diminished], because it was not a synthesis of parts.

THIS [the Mind] then is the whole, therefore not the first: but there must be that which is beyond it, <margin>C</margin> for the sake of which also the previous arguments [were made], first, because a multitude is later than a one, and this is a number. But the principle of number and of such a thing is the truly One, and it is Mind and Intelligible together, so that it is two together: but if two, one must take that which is before the two. What then, is it Mind alone? But to every [mind] the Intelligible is joined. If then the Intelligible must not be joined, [that] will not be Mind. Or it will not be Mind, but will escape the two, [so] the <margin>D</margin> first of these two must be beyond Mind. What then prevents it from being the Intelligible itself? Or because also the Intelligible is joined to something. If then it were neither Mind nor Intelligible, from which we say the Mind and the Intelligible with it [come]. What then is this, and of what kind shall we imagine it? For again, it will either be thinking or something unthinking; if thinking, it is Mind; if unthinking, it will be ignorant even of itself. So what is venerable [about it]? For even if we say it is the Good, and that it is <margin>E</margin> most simple, we say something clear and plain [and] the truth, saying [it] as long as we do not have [something] upon which to lean in thought while we speak. For even of knowledge itself, through the Mind of other things being known and by the Mind, those being able to know by the intelligible, this [First] having transcended the nature of the Mind, by what collective intuition could it be caught? Toward which one must signal, as it is possible by the [thing] in us <margin>F</margin> similar [to it]. For there is something even in us of it, or there is not [a place] where it is not, to those still able to participate in it. For having placed [it] everywhere, whatever is able to have [it], you have from there as if a voice, occupying a desert, or even with the desert, and having placed men in whatever [part of] the desert, [their] ears [would] hear the voice entirely, and yet not entirely. What then is it that we will bring, having placed the Mind [near], that which is before the Mind? Or by the Mind in us, approaching—

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Divine Intellect, though a totality of all things, is a "multitude" and thus requires a simpler, prior "One" as its source. He uses the analogy of a voice in a desert to explain how this transcendent Principle is omnipresent and accessible to the human soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the Intellect (Mind) perceives its source. The Greek text ends with the middle of a word ("-menos"), likely "dechomenos" (receiving), which corresponds to the Latin "accipimus" (we receive). This indicates a direct continuation from the bottom of the previous page.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

...receiving it? Or perhaps the **Mind** <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous). The second level of reality in Neoplatonism, representing the realm of pure thought and the Forms.</note> must, as it were, turn back toward what is behind it; and as if letting itself go, since it has a double-faced nature, it must look upon that [One]. If it wishes to see the One, it must not be entirely Mind. For it is itself the **first life**, being an activity in the **discursion** <note>original: "διεξόδῳ" (diexodo). The process by which the One’s unity unfolds into the multiplicity of the world.</note> of all things—a discursion not in the sense of passing through things in time, but as having already passed through them. If, therefore, it is life and discursion, and contains all things precisely—not in a confused heap, for then it would be imperfect and unformed—it must necessarily depend upon something else which is no longer in discursion, but is the **principle** <note>original: "ἀρχὴ" (archē). The starting point or source of all things.</note> of discursion: the principle of life, the principle of mind, and of all things. For the principle is not all things, but all things come from the principle. The principle itself is no longer "all things," nor any one of all things, so that all things might be generated; and so that it might not be a multitude, but rather the principle of multitude. For that which is generated is always simpler than its generator; therefore, if this [the One] generated the Mind, it must be simpler than the Mind. If anyone should think the One itself is all things—either all things taken individually or all things taken together—then if it were all things gathered together, it would be posterior to all things. If it existed before all things, then all things would be one thing, and the One would be another thing distinct from all. But if the One and all things existed at the same time, the One would not be a beginning. Yet it must be a beginning, and exist before all things, so that all things may exist after it. If it were each thing individually, then first, any one thing would be the same as any other; and second, all things would be together at once with nothing hidden outside them, yet it would not be "before" all things.

---

WHAT then is it? It is the **power of all things**; without which, all things would not exist. Neither would there be Mind, which is the whole of the first life. For that which exists above life is the cause of life. The activity of life, which is all things, is not the first principle; rather, it flows out from the principle like a **fountain**. Imagine a fountain that has no other beginning, but gives itself to all rivers, yet is not exhausted by the rivers, but remains quietly itself. The rivers that flow from it, before they flow their separate ways, remain for a while together, already knowing, as it were, where their streams will eventually flow. Or imagine the life of a **great tree** passing through the whole, while the principle remains—not divided throughout the whole tree, but fixed as if in the **root**. This root provides the entire manifold life to the tree, but remains itself not manifold, but the principle of that manifold life. And this is no wonder. Or rather, it is a wonder how the multitude of life comes from what is not a multitude, and could not be a multitude unless there was something before the multitude that is not a multitude at all. For the principle is not divided into the whole; for if it were divided, the whole would be destroyed, nor would it ever have been...

<column-break/>

...receiving it by applying [the mind]? Perhaps truly the **intellect** ought to turn itself as if from behind, and since it has a face on both sides, leave itself behind. If it is to look upon the Good itself, it must take care not to be entirely intellect, nor to be all those things which are understood. For the intellect is itself the **first life**, which is indeed an act in a certain discursion through all things: a discursion, I say, not one that runs daily, but one that has always filled the discursion. If therefore it is life and discursion, and holds all things—not confusedly, but most exactly (otherwise, if it held them indistinctly, it would hold them imperfectly)—it must necessarily depend upon another, which is no longer involved in discursion, but is the **beginning** of discursion: the beginning of life, the beginning of mind, and of all things. For the beginning is not all things, but rather all things are from the beginning. The beginning itself is neither all things, nor any one of all things, so that it may generate all things; nor is it a multitude, but the principle of multitude. For that which is generated is everywhere simpler than that which generates. Therefore, if this [the One] generated the mind, it is necessarily simpler than the mind. If anyone should think that the Good itself is the One and all things, it will either be all things according to each of all things individually, or all things collectively. But if all things are accumulated together, the One would be later than all things. For if it existed before all things, then all things would be one set of things, and the One itself would be another thing besides all. But if the One and all things are together at once, it will not be the beginning. Yet it must be the beginning and before all things, so that all things may be after it. If it were said that the One is individually each of all things, then first, anything would be the same as any other, then all things would be together at once, and there would never be any distinction. Thus, the One is nothing of all things, but rather **above all things**.

<margin>
IX.
The principle of the universe is the One itself, which is above being, which is neither moved, nor divided, nor multiplied in any way, since the multitude of things proceeds from it.
</margin>

->WHAT then is it? Truly the power of all things:<-
which indeed, if it were not, neither would the rest exist. For neither would there be the intellect, which is the first and entire life. For that which stands above life is the cause of life. The act of life, which is all things, is not the first itself, but is poured out from the principle like a **fountain**. Think of a fountain having no other principle, giving itself entirely to the rivers, yet not exhausted by any rivers, but remaining quietly in itself. The rivers flowing from it, before one flows here and another there, still remain as one, and as if already knowing where the rivulets are to flow from them. Or think of the life of a **huge tree**, propagating itself through the whole tree, while the principle remains, not divided through the whole, but established as if in the **root**. This root indeed provides the whole and manifold life to the tree; but it remains not at all multiplied, but the principle of the manifold life. Nor is it a marvel that it is so. Perhaps it is even to be wondered at how the multitude of life is from non-multitude, and could not have been a multitude unless there were that which is no multitude before the multitude. For the principle is by no means divided into the whole; otherwise, if it were divided, the whole would be immediately lost; nor would it ever have been made, unless the principle remains in itself, and is different from this whole.

<meta>Catchword: [Ancient Greek] ...made, unless the principle remains in itself, being different [from the others].</meta>

<summary>Plotinus explains that the "One" (the Source) must be simpler than the "Mind" and "Life" that flow from it. He uses the famous metaphors of a fountain and a tree root to show how the One provides existence to all things while remaining unmoved and undiminished.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the second and first hypostases (levels of reality) in Plotinian thought. The previous page established that the Intellect must be preceded by a simpler Principle (the One). This page argues that the Intellect contains all things in a unified multiplicity, while the One remains entirely simple and above all thought.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS BOOK III.

<column-break/>

A ...from which and into which it was of such a kind, as that source from which only the progression begins. And in another way, the **Intellect** <note>original Latin: "mens"; Greek: "νοῦς" (nous). The divine mind or second level of reality.</note> is not the mind of any single thing, but of all things. Being all things, it also belongs to all things. It is necessary, therefore, for your intellect to possess all things, and for the part of all existing things to be such that every individual part is the whole, and is all things; otherwise, it would have some part which is not intellect. It would then be built up from things that are not intellect, and it would be a sort of accidental **heap** <note>original Latin: "aceruus"; Greek: "σωρός" (soros). A collection of parts without an organic, internal unity.</note>, waiting for assistance from all things so that it might become an intellect. For this reason, it is also infinite; and if anything flows from it within, it is not diminished, because that which comes from it is also "all things," as is that from which it proceeds internally, since it was not a composition made of many parts.

<margin>VIII. In the first intellect there is multitude, even if it contains all things; but the principle of all is not all things, but is above all things.</margin>

C VIII. THIS [the Intellect], therefore, exists as such, and for that reason is not the first thing; rather, there must be something higher than it, for whose sake our previous discourse was held. This is because **multitude** <note>original: "multitudo/πλῆθος" (plēthos). The state of being many rather than one.</note> is always posterior to the **One** <note>original: "vno/ἕν" (hen).</note>. The Intellect is a number; but the principle of number is unity, and the principle of such a number is that which is truly "One." Here, indeed, both the Intellect and the **Intelligible** <note>original: "intelligibile/νοητὸν" (noeton). The object of thought; the Forms.</note> exist together; thus they are two at once. If there are two, it is necessary to grasp something prior to these two. But what must we say this is? Is it merely the Intellect? But to every intellect, an intelligible is joined; and unless the counterpart is there, there will be no intellect.

D If, then, it is not even the Intellect, but has escaped these two, it follows that what is prior to these two must be higher than the Intellect. But what prevents this from being the Intelligible alone? Clearly, because the Intelligible also always has a counterpart in the Intellect. If, therefore, it is neither Intellect 

E nor Intelligible, what will it be? Surely that from which the Intellect comes, and together with the Intellect, the Intelligible. What then is this, and how shall we conceive it? For it will either be something thinking, or not thinking. If it is thinking, it will be an Intellect; if it is not thinking, it will be ignorant of itself, and will seem to be nothing venerable. For even if we say this is the **Good** <note>original: "bonum/ἀγαθὸν" (agathon). The ultimate goal and source of all existence.</note> and the most simple, we do not thereby bring forth something manifest and clear, 

F although it is true, as long as we have no place to fix the intuition of our thought while we speak of it. Furthermore, since knowledge of other things occurs through the Intellect and by means of the Intellect—among those, namely, who are able to know something by thinking—how shall this, which exceeds the nature of the Intellect, be perceived by a single, collected intuition? We shall answer these things by saying it is through something in us that is as similar to it as possible. For there is something of it in us; or rather, there is no place among existing things where it is not, for those who have the faculty of participating in it. 

G Indeed, wherever you apply something that can receive it, you will report something from there; just as if a voice were to occupy a certain desert, or along with the desert, also men. Then, in whatever part you place your ears, you will drink in the whole voice, and yet again, not the whole. What then is it that we shall receive, having applied the intellect...

<column-break/>

...from which and into which, such as that from which alone [it starts]. And in another way, the **Intellect** <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous).</note> is not the mind of any one thing, but also of all. Being all, it is of all things. It is necessary, therefore, for it to be the same things and of all things, and for its part to possess everything and all things; otherwise, it will have some part which is [not] intellect. It will then be composed of things which are [not], and it will be a sort of gathered **heap** <note>original: "σωρός" (soros).</note>, waiting to become intellect from all things. Therefore, this is also infinite; and if anything comes from it, it is not diminished, because that which is from it is also all things, nor is that from which it comes hesitant, because it was not a composition of parts.

THIS, then, is of such a kind, which is why it is not first; but there must be that which is **beyond it** <note>original: "ἐπέκεινα" (epekeina). A famous Platonic term for the One being "beyond being."</note>, for the sake of which our words were placed. First, because multitude is made essential [within it], and this is a number. But the principle of number and of the first is the truly existing One, and that from which the intellect [comes]. And the Intelligible is together [with it], so that they are two together. If there are two, one must take that which is before the two. What then? Is it the Intellect alone? But to every intellect the Intelligible is yoked. If, then, the Intelligible must not be yoked, it [the First] cannot be Intellect. If it is not even Intellect, but escapes the two, that which is prior to these two must be beyond Intellect. What then prevents it from being the Intelligible itself? It is because the Intelligible is also yoked to the Intellect. If, then, it be neither Intellect nor Intelligible, we shall say it is that from which the Intellect and the Intelligible with it [come]. What then is this, and what kind of thing shall we imagine it to be? For again, it will either be thinking or unthinking. If thinking, it is Intellect; if unthinking, it will be ignorant even of itself. Thus, [how can it be] something venerable? For even if we say it is the **Good** <note>original: "ἀγαθὸν" (agathon).</note> and that it is most simple, we will clearly be speaking the truth, yet we will not be speaking clearly, as long as we have nothing upon which to rest our thought while we speak. For even knowledge itself occurs through the Intellect of other things, and by the Intellect, for those able to know intelligibly; but this, having surpassed the nature of the Intellect, by what sudden intuition could it be grasped? To this we must signal how it is possible, by the "similar within us," as we shall say. For there is something even in us of it, or rather, there is nowhere where it is not, for those who can partake of it. For by placing yourself everywhere, wherever there is that which is able to possess it, you have it from there; just as if a voice occupied a desert, or even with the desert, men; and placing your ear in any part of the desert, you receive the voice as a whole, and yet not as a whole. What then is it that we shall receive, having brought the intellect to it?

<summary>This page discusses the nature of the Intellect (Nous) as a unified "all" that contains the Forms, and argues that it must originate from a higher, absolutely simple source called the One or the Good. Plotinus explains that while the Intellect is a multitude (thinker and thought), the One is beyond this duality and can only be sensed through a "similar" spark within the human soul.</summary>

The previous page discussed how the Intellect contains all things in a unified multiplicity; here, the author explains why the source of that multiplicity must itself be perfectly simple and prior to all things.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

<column-break/>

...or perhaps by means of the **intellect** <note>original Greek: "νοῦς" (nous); Latin: "intellectus." In this philosophy, the divine Mind that contains all forms of reality.</note> it is necessary to turn back, as if from behind. Since it has a face on both sides, one should leave oneself behind if one wishes to see that which is the **Good** <note>The "Good" is another name for "the One," the ultimate source of everything.</note> itself. One must take care not to be entirely "intellect," nor to be all those things that are understood. For it [the Intellect] is itself the **First Life** <note>original Greek: "ζωὴ πρώτη" (zōē prōtē).</note>, which is indeed an activity in a kind of progression through all things; a progression, I say, not one that wanders day by day, but one which has always filled that progression. 

If, therefore, it is life and progression, and possesses B all things—not confusedly, but most precisely—then otherwise, if it possessed them indistinctly, it would possess them imperfectly. It must therefore depend on another, which is no longer involved in progression, but is the **principle of progression** <note>original: "principium discursionis." The starting point from which all diversity flows.</note>: the principle of life, the principle of mind, and of all things. For the principle is not all things, but rather all things come from the principle. The principle itself is neither all things, nor any one of all things, so that it may generate all things; nor is it a multitude, but rather the principle of multitude. For that which is generated C is everywhere simpler than that which generates it. Therefore, if this [the Intellect] was generated by Mind, it is necessarily simpler than Mind. 

If anyone should think the Good itself is both "the One" and "all things," it would be all things either according to each individual thing specifically, or all things taken together. But if it were all things accumulated together, it would be posterior to all things. For if it existed before all things, then "all things" would be one thing, and "the One" itself would be something else besides them. If, however, it and all things existed simultaneously, it would not be D a beginning. Yet it must be the principle, and exist before all things, so that all things may exist after it. But if it were said to be each individual thing specifically, then first, any one thing would be the same as any other; and second, all things would be together without any distinction. Thus, it is none of all things, but rather **above all things** <note>original Greek: "πρὸ τῶν πάντων" (pro tōn pantōn); Latin: "super omnia." The One is transcendent and exists before/beyond the physical and mental world.</note>.

-> WHAT then is it? Truly, it is the power of all things. <-

<margin>
IX.
*The principle of the universe is the One itself, which is neither moved, nor divided, nor multiplied in any way, since the multitude of things proceeds from it.*
</margin>

If this power did not exist, neither would anything else. Nor would there be Intellect, which is the first and total life. For that which exists above life is the cause of life. E The activity of life, which is all things, is not itself the "First," but is poured out from the principle as if from a **fountain** <note>This is Plotinus's famous "emanation" metaphor: reality flows out of the One like water from a spring that never runs dry.</note>. Imagine a fountain that has no other source, but gives itself entirely to all rivers, yet is never exhausted by those rivers, but remains quietly in itself. The rivers flowing from it, before they flow their separate ways, still remain together for a time, already knowing, as it were, where their streams are about to flow. 

F Or imagine the life of a vast tree passing through the whole, while the principle remains not divided throughout the tree, but established as if in the **root** <note>original: "radice." Just as a root provides the "hidden" power that becomes branches and leaves, the One is the hidden power of the universe.</note>. This root provides the entire and manifold life to the tree, yet it remains itself, not multiplied in any way, but the principle of that manifold life. It is no wonder that it is so. Rather, perhaps it is a wonder how the multitude of life comes from that which is not a multitude, and how it could not have been a multitude unless that which is no multitude existed before the multitude. For the principle is by no means divided into the whole; G otherwise, if it were divided, the whole would immediately perish. Nor would anything ever have been made, unless the principle remained in itself, being entirely distinct from this whole.

<sig>G 2</sig>

<summary>Plotinus explains that the ultimate source of reality (the One) must be absolutely simple and distinct from the multiplicity of the world and the mind. He uses the famous metaphors of a fountain and a root to show how a single, unchanging source can generate a vast, complex universe without being diminished.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's argument that the ultimate source of reality—the "One"—must be absolutely simple and distinct from the "Intellect" (the divine Mind). Having previously established that the Intellect contains all forms of reality, Plotinus now explains why the source of that Intellect cannot itself be an intellect or any specific "thing."</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III.

<page-num>352</page-num>

<column-break/>

**A** Therefore, the ascent everywhere leads back to the **one**, and in each thing there is a specific "one" to which it is reduced; and this whole universe is reduced to the "one" that exists before it—not the simple "one," until one reaches the **absolute One** <note>original Latin: "simpliciter unum." In Neoplatonic philosophy, this is the First Principle from which all existence flows.</note>. This, however, is not referred further to anything else. Thus, if you take the "one" of a tree (that is, its enduring principle), or the "one" of an animal, or the "one" of the soul, and additionally take the "one" of the universe, you will everywhere be grasping the most powerful and venerable aspect of that thing. But if you take the "one" of those things which truly *are*—that is, the principle, the fountain, and the power—will we then lack faith and suspect that nothing exists? Certainly, it is none of those things of which it is the principle; it is such that **B** nothing can be predicated of it: not being, not essence, not life, for the reason that it is above all these things. But if you set aside "being" and grasp it in that way, you will immediately be struck with awe; and directing yourself toward it, reaching it, and resting in its very seat, you may now behold it with a most powerful and simple gaze. Having beheld it, you will sense its greatness through those things which come after it and exist because of it.

<margin>
**X.**
The **Intellect** is inferior to the **Good**; thus, through the former we conjecture the Good, just as through this physical world we conjecture the Intellect.
</margin>

**C** FURTHERMORE, consider it in this way: since the **intellect** <note>original Greek: "νοῦς" (nous); Latin: "intellectus." The divine Mind.</note> is a kind of vision—a seeing sight—it is therefore a certain potentiality that has already proceeded into action. There will thus be in it one thing as **matter** <note>original Latin: "materia"; Greek: "ὕλη" (hyle).</note> and another as **form** <note>original Latin: "forma"; Greek: "εἶδος" (eidos).</note>, just as actual vision is composed of both. The matter consists of the **intelligibles** <note>the objects of thought; the Forms.</note>; for indeed, actual vision has a twofold nature. Before it saw, it was one thing. **D** Thus, the one became two, and the two became one. For physical vision, fulfillment and a kind of perfection <unclear>comes forth</unclear> from the sensible object; but for the vision of the mind, the **Good** <note>original Latin: "bonum"; Greek: "ἀγαθόν" (agathon).</note> is that which fills it. For if the Intellect were the Good itself, what would it need to see or to do at all? For other things have their action around the Good and because of the Good; but the Good itself lacks nothing at all; therefore, nothing will belong to it except itself. When, therefore, you pronounce "the Good," add nothing further in your thought. **E** For if you add anything, you will immediately show that the thing to which you added it is, by its nature, needy. Therefore, you must not even add "intelligence," lest you add something alien and make it two things: namely, an intellect and the Good. The Intellect needs the Good, but the Good does not need the Intellect. Thus, the mind following the Good becomes **"Good-formed"** <note>original Latin: "boniformis"; Greek: "ἀγαθοειδὴς" (agathoeidēs). Shaped by and reflecting the nature of the Good.</note> and is perfected by it. This is because the form which is in the mind proceeds from the Good and makes it "Good-formed." Whatever trace of the Good itself is seen in the mind, one should think of the **archetype** <note>the original pattern or source</note> as being like that, estimating its truth through the trace impressed upon the mind. **F** This trace, therefore, is impressed upon the Intellect, through which it might see and possess. Consequently, in the Intellect there is **desire** <note>original Latin: "appetitio"; Greek: "ἔφεσις" (ephesis). A reaching out or longing for the source.</note>; it is always desiring and always attaining. But the Good itself desires nothing. For what should it desire? Nor does it attain anything, for it never desired. Therefore, it is not the Intellect; for in the Intellect there is desire and a certain application toward its own form. The Intellect is indeed beautiful, **G** and the most beautiful of all things, situated in pure light and a similar splendor, encompassing the nature of all beings. Of this Intellect, our world here is but a shadow and an image; but that higher world is situated in all clarity...

<column-break/>

**A** For this reason, the leading up everywhere is toward the **one**, and in each case, there is a certain "one" to which one leads; and this whole universe is led to that which is before it—not the simply "one," until one comes to the **simply One**. This, however, is no longer led to another. But if one takes the "one" of a plant (the remaining principle), or the "one" of an animal, or the "one" of the soul, or the "one" of the universe, one takes in each case that which is most powerful and most honorable. **B** But if one takes the "one" of those things which truly *are* as the principle, the fountain, and the power, shall we be skeptical, or assume it is nothing? Indeed, it is nothing of those things of which it is the principle; it is such, however, that nothing can be predicated of it—not being, not essence, not life—because it is above all these things. But if you take away "being" and grasp it, you will have wonder. And casting yourself toward it, and happening to rest within it, you will understand more by that **direct encounter** <note>original Greek: "προσβολῇ" (probolē). A sudden intuitive strike or contact.</note>. **C** Beholding its greatness, you see it through those things that exist after it and because of it.

**C (continued)** AND also in this way: since the mind is a certain vision, and a seeing vision, it must be a power that has come into activity. It will therefore have both **matter** and **form**, just as actual sight does. For the **intelligibles** are its matter. Since actual sight also has a double nature: before seeing, it was one; **D** but the one became as if it were two, and the two became one. For sight, fulfillment comes from the sensible object, and a kind of perfection; but for the sight of the mind, the **Good** is that which fills it. For if it were itself the Good, why would it need to see or act at all? For other things have their activity around the Good and because of the Good; but the Good needs nothing. Therefore, nothing will be for it, except itself. When you begin with the **E** Good, think of nothing more. For if you add anything, you will make that which you added it to become deficient. Therefore, do not even add "thinking," so that you do not make it something else—namely, Mind and Good. For the Mind needs the Good, but the Good does not need the Mind. Hence, when the Mind attains the Good, it becomes **"Good-like"** and is perfected by it. The form upon it comes from the Good, making it Good-like. **F** Such as the **trace** of the Good that is seen in it, such must one think the archetype to be, intuiting its truth from the trace placed upon the Mind. That trace of it which is upon the Mind, it gave to the Mind for seeing and possessing. Thus, in the Mind there is **longing**, and it is always longing and always attaining. But the Good does not long, for what would it long for? Nor is it Mind, for longing is in the latter, as is the understanding of its own **G** form. While the Mind is beautiful, and the most beautiful of all, situated in pure light and pure radiance, and encompassing the nature of beings—of which this beautiful world is a shadow and an image—that world lies in all splendor...

<summary>Plotinus distinguishes the ultimate source, the "One" or "Good," from the "Intellect," arguing that the One is beyond being and thought, while the Intellect is a secondary power that depends on the Good for its perfection and form.</summary>

It includes both the original text of Plotinus (in Greek and Latin translation) and the start of Marsilio Ficino’s famous commentary, where he harmonizes different Platonic traditions.</meta>

<page-num>353</page-num>
<header>BOOK NINE.</header>

<note>The following section is a translation of the original Greek text by Plotinus.</note>

...where nothing is void of intellect, nor dark, nor lacking a share in the life of one living blessedly. Awe would seize anyone who sees this world and enters into it, becoming one with it—just as one who looks up at the sky and sees the brightness of the stars reflects upon and seeks their creator. So too, one who has beheld and observed the intelligible world <note>The "intelligible world" refers to the realm of pure thought and perfect Forms, which Neoplatonists believed was the blueprint for our physical world.</note> and wondered at it, must seek its creator as well. Who is it, then, who established such a realm? Where or how did he beget such a child—the Intellect, a beautiful and pure son, born from himself and filled by him? Certainly, it is not the Intellect itself, for it is the "son" or the "fullness," but rather that which exists before the fullness. For after him comes the Intellect, or the "fullness," which required nourishment and reached satisfaction, and thus achieved thought. This Intellect is near to that which lacks nothing and has no need of thinking; but the "son" possesses true fullness and thought because he possesses them as the primary recipient. But that which is above them neither needs nor possesses; otherwise, it would actually be the Intellect itself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...where nothing is void of intellect, nothing is dark, nothing is immoderate, but it leads a blessed life in itself. If anyone gazes upon this, he will immediately be struck with amazement: especially if, as is fitting, he works his way into it and comes under its law. Truly, just as one who looks more closely at the heavens and contemplates the splendor of the stars more intensely immediately thinks of and seeks the author of the world; so it is necessary for him who contemplates, perceives, and admires the intelligible world to diligently inquire after its maker <margin>B</margin>: who he may be, who begot such an intelligible world; or where, or how he begot such a son—the Intellect, a pure and beautiful boy, a son, I say, made full by the father. Now indeed, that highest father is neither the intellect, nor the son or boy, but is superior to both intellect and boy. For after him come the intellect and the child, needing nourishment and intelligence: he who is closest to that which lacks nothing, and who himself needs no intelligence. But the son <margin>C</margin> possesses true fullness and intelligence, because he possesses them from the first. But that which is superior neither needs nor possesses; otherwise, it would not be the Good itself.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON
## BOOK IX OF THE THIRD ENNEAD CONCERNING
## EIGHT CONSIDERATIONS,
->COMMENTARY.<-

### SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

->First proposition: that the author of the world is the first intellect,<-
->the son of the Good itself.<-

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'N' featuring a seated figure surrounded by floral patterns.</image-desc>
NINE considerations primarily appear in this book. The first is about the author of the world: where, if one follows the path of Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus was a later Neoplatonist who developed a more complex hierarchy of divine beings than Plotinus.</note> from afar, he will explain that saying of the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the universe.</note> regarding the craftsman of the world: namely, that as many "ideas" as the Intellect perceives in the living being itself, so many species the craftsman of the world thought to arrange in the world. He will explain it thus: that there are at least three divine substances between the first principle (that is, the Good itself) and the world. The first of these, according to its form, is an essence participating in the Good, and moreover the cause of life and intellect. The second, according to its form, is life, which participates in essence; it is the formal cause of the intellect. The third, finally, through its form is the intellect, participating in life, and the cause of the physical world. He will name the first Caelus <note>Uranus/Sky</note>, the second Saturn, and the third Jupiter. He will consider Caelus as much superior to Saturn, and Saturn to Jupiter, as essence is superior to life, and life to intellect. For essence is superior to life insofar as it spreads itself more widely; and life, because of a similar breadth, is superior to mind. He will say, therefore, that the formal intellect, Jupiter, is the immediate maker of the world, having within himself the intellectual ideas of worldly things. He received these ideas from the vital intellect, namely Saturn, in whom the ideas are equally intellectual and intelligible; Saturn, in turn, has them from the essential intellect, namely Caelus, in whom the ideas are purely intelligible. This is how he will interpret the *Timaeus*: The providence of Jupiter devised to create as many species in the world as he observed the Saturnian intellect contemplating as ideas in the "living being itself"—that is, in Caelus, who is the cause of essence and life. In Plotinus, however, there are not three substances, but only one substance that is named the first essence, the first life, and the first intellect. For the first life is nothing other than the most inward and perpetual vigor and act of the first essence and form, which is the most effective of all in acting. The first intellect is also a certain reflection of that first life back upon itself, standing most powerfully with itself. Therefore, Plotinus calls that substance the "first intelligible" insofar as it is living and fertile, and can conceive the intellect within itself, and move the conception, and form it inwardly. He likewise calls this substance "intellect" regarding its vital action arising from itself and reflected back into itself. He calls it "thought" in some way, because he establishes that what it sees within, it distributes without. Accordingly, he thinks that in the order of things, motion arises before division, and that a completely immobile intellect—immobile in the sense of a flowing motion—cannot be propagated into many indivisible intellects; however, the genus of the soul, being mobile by its own nature, can be multiplied into many souls. And since this genus participates in intelligence, the intellect is propagated into many participating intellects insofar as the genus of the soul is propagated into many species of souls. He also believes that the intellect, the maker of the world, generates the soul—both the world-soul itself, the other common souls of the spheres and stars, and finally the particular souls of demons and men. And since distribution belongs primarily to the genus of soul as something mobile and multipliable, he wishes that intellect...
