<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Ennead V.1. Ficino is explaining how the "builder of the world" (the Divine Intellect) organizes the universe through the World Soul and how individual human souls can ascend back to this divine source.</meta>

<page-num>354</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...the builder of the world, through that World Soul first created, and through the common souls that are its colleagues, carried out the distributions of worldly living beings through their various levels.

## Second Proposition: How the soul can gather itself into its own intellect, and through this intellect be shaped by the divine. There are also three other propositions in this chapter: two concerning the soul, and one concerning God.

*Thus far the first consideration, which declared the Intellect to be the maker of the world. The second consideration, however, treats how the soul can transfer itself into this universal Intellect. Namely, just as the soul gathers its multiple senses into the single sense of imagination, so it may gather its widely diverse imaginations into one common rule of reason. Then, it may reduce the various wanderings of our reason to a stable standard of intelligence. Thus, the soul may be formed entirely by its own intellect according to its strength, through which it will then be formed by the universal Intellect, the builder of the whole world. Moreover, this can happen in the stages of life, since it is the same in the stages of knowledge themselves. Geometry consists of a thousand propositions, and the later is deduced from the prior by necessity; therefore, the following ones are grasped by the preceding ones, and all are contained in the first. Our soul, indeed, by its rational faculty, transferring itself from potentiality into act <note>In Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, "potentiality" is the capacity to become something, while "act" (or "actuality") is the fulfillment or operation of that capacity.</note> and back again, if it possesses the whole of geometry, can indeed have all its propositions in a certain potential state and habit while it holds any one of them in act. Meanwhile, even our intellect, in any proposition considered according to act, considers and possesses all of them through that same act. We must strive, therefore, that our rational faculty conforms itself to the intellect as much as possible. In that state, it may behold all subsequent notions in the first notion, by the same act with which it beholds the first. In the third consideration, Plotinus thinks that the World Soul—because it has once and most powerfully embraced the whole animal form of life within itself, and from there has occupied the whole body and place within—cannot change its form of life within itself, nor exchange bodies outside itself. He thinks the same holds true for the souls of the spheres and the stars, and all celestial souls, since from the beginning they were firmly allotted a universal providence. But particular souls, which have obtained a particular mode of providence—such as those of many spirits <note>Original: "daemonum." In this context, "daemons" refers to intermediary spirits or guardian beings, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note> and of humans—fill up that perpetual providence of the higher beings through a certain succession. And insofar as they change from one form of life to another within themselves, they change their bodies and locations accordingly. Hence they seem to approach a body and a place, but with the change having first occurred within themselves. In contrast, the body of the world seems to approach the World Soul itself. For while the Soul remains firmly in its own state, this body, being so affected from the beginning, is then vivified by it—just as the transparent region of the air is always illuminated by the Sun. Moreover, particular souls are said to "descend" sometimes from the World Soul; for from the universal providence and form of life (which they sometimes possess together with the World Soul), they slide down into their own, for they did not possess it firmly. In the fourth consideration, he divides our soul into three forms: the intellectual, the rational, and the irrational. He thinks that the soul is sometimes transferred entirely to its intellectual form, and then it dwells with the divine intellect; sometimes it descends from there into itself, that is, into the rational form proper to this soul; and sometimes it descends from here into a form worse than reason. From this, an "image" <note>The "simulacrum" or phantom of the soul that interacts with the physical body.</note> of itself seems to be communicated to the body. To this life, indeed, the last "image" of all is subject—that is, matter—which the soul, through its vegetative power, shapes with a corporeal quality and a certain figure due to its proximity. Then, soon after, through this affection, it is naturally drawn like bait to vivify this body, which is now disposed in a certain way. In the fifth consideration, you will note this: Just as in a circle there is a point in itself which is the center, and a point in the whole circumference and every part of it (proceeding from that which is in itself, or rather as if it were the thing itself or its propagation). Just as there is a unity in every number and every part of it, flowing from a certain unity outside the number, conceived simply in itself. So, in the entire essence of things, there is a certain unity which is the foundation of essence and the preservation of each thing, proceeding from the Divine Unity. This Divine Unity remains "beyond-being" <note>Original: "superessentiam." This refers to the Neoplatonic concept of the One being above even the category of "Existence."</note> in itself, and thus fills all things, insofar as by its presence everywhere it procreates from itself a certain unity in every created thing—a beyond-being producer and preserver of every essence. Now, because this unity is more excellent than essence, we conjecture that wherever it is, it is created and preserved by the presence of the Divine Unity.*

### Concerning our intellect also, how it is always in act.

The sixth consideration is about the soul together with the mind, in this manner: The transparent (that is, translucent) nature of the eye is made chiefly from the solar nature, and for that reason it naturally hungers for light and is easily filled by the light of the sun. Similarly, the transparent nature in the heavens proceeds from a certain celestial light, preceding the transparent according to the order of the universe, and emanating from the intellectual light. And immediately, while the producer emanates the transparent and fills the product, the heaven becomes like a celestial eye of the soul, providing for all things through this transparency and light together. In the same way, the Divine Mind generates the rational soul by its own light, as if it were transparent matter under that light, and fills it with perpetual light. By this light, the soul always understands both itself as illuminated by the Mind, and the Mind as always illuminating. Moreover, our intellect—the "head" of the soul—does this perpetually. But the rational faculty relates to this intellect as sight relates to light; it does not always understand, but only sometimes understands rationally. When, therefore, a human understands themselves through reason, if they understand perfectly, they recognize meanwhile that they are a thinking being. Therefore, they also recognize they are intellectual, and that they possess a nature that understands in this way. This very "intellectuality" (if I may call it that) is a certain intelligence, placed not so much in manifest motion as in a state hidden from us. Indeed, through rational intelligence, the contemplator understands that before "intellectuality" in themselves, there is life and essence, to which intellectuality itself later arrives as an "act"—an act, I say, born from a certain fruitfulness of essence and life. Hence it is necessary that this essence and life themselves be a certain more eminent intelligence in themselves. Plotinus proves here that the soul, from its new understanding of itself, possesses a prior eternal understanding of itself, which is a fruitful essence and life. Therefore, the soul has within itself stable "intelligibles" <note>Objects of pure thought or Forms.</note> understood there in perpetual act; an image of this intelligence is the "discourse of reason" when it reaches the summit, from which it is also named "intelligence." We confirm the same thing in another way: There are three things in the order of reality reaching our knowledge: a certain singular thing (that is, *this* man), the species shared by individuals (that is, *man*), and also the Idea of man above the individuals. Since these three differ, being disposed by a certain essential order from the prior to the posterior, the powers...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus. In the preceding section, Ficino discussed how the soul gathers its various faculties to ascend toward the divine. Here, he distinguishes between the different levels of human cognition—imagination, reason, and intellect—and begins a deep theological discussion on the nature of God (the "First Principle") as being beyond motion, rest, and even thought itself.</meta>

<page-num>353</page-num>
<header>ON BOOK IX, ENNEAD III</header>

...those who know these things properly also distinguish them from one another in a similar way: the **imagination** indicates the singular <note>original: "singulare"; referring to a specific, individual object</note>, whereas **reason** collects and distinguishes the common species <note>original: "speciem"; the general category or concept of a thing</note> from those individuals, and the **intellect** recognizes the **Idea** <note>In Platonic thought, an "Idea" or "Form" is the perfect, eternal blueprint of a thing that exists in the divine mind</note>. Since the Idea differs further from the species (outside of which it exists) than the species differs from the individual (in which it is preserved), the intellect is therefore further removed from reason than reason is from imagination. Nevertheless, the intellect dwells within the soul: otherwise, the soul could not divine that Ideas exist through reason, unless reason performed this task through a power implanted in us by the intellect. And because reason resolves individual things into the universal, and the body into the incorporeal, without the help of our imagination—indeed, even against its will, for imagination pulls us back toward the opposite—therefore the intellect, without the movement or argument of reason, always gazes upon the Ideas. I say "always," for if it does not reach them through imagination and new argumentation, it either never reaches them at all, or it possesses them forever. Justly so, since the soul is the middle point between eternity and time (for its essence is fixed and precedes the motion that depends on it). It is consistent that within its fixed essence, by that very sign by which it precedes motion, there exists a power and action that is entirely immobile and steadfastly gazing. Indeed, since this gaze turns from a stable essence and power toward an entirely stable Idea, it claims stability for itself on both sides. Therefore, just as a mobile imagination is suited to the soul because it exists beneath eternity, so an immovably acting intellect belongs to it because it exists above time. The act of the intellect is entirely immobile; the act of the imagination is entirely mobile; and finally, the act of reason is a mixture of both. The soul could not be a fitting midpoint for the universe unless it possessed these three within itself.

### How God is above motion, and rest, and cognition. Also concerning that which is in act, and that which is in potentiality.

The seventh consideration proves that in the first principle of all things <note>God</note> there is no motion—not even the flowing kind, nor even the metaphorical kind, which is an act tending toward something else. For that which is utterly the first and the ultimate does not tend toward anything else. It also proves that there is no "state" there—that is, the rest <note>original: "quies"</note> toward which motion tends, which is the opposite of motion. Truly, He does not rest in another thing (as one who does not move toward another), nor does He properly "rest" in Himself, for He is simplicity itself. In Him, no such distinction can fall by which a resting thing is usually distinguished from its rest, or from the seat in which it rests. Now, motion derives its force from a "state" <note>original: "statu"; a condition of stability</note> while it maintains its course from the stability of a moving power, but a state derives from **unity**. For to "stand" is nothing other than to preserve one's own unity. Therefore, Unity itself precedes both motion and the state of rest. Consequently, it also precedes the act of intelligence, which is a certain motion from the *potentiality* of understanding toward the *truth* that can be understood, as if toward a good. In every being that understands, even if it understands itself, such a distinction is observed; but in the First, there is no absolute distinction. Finally, the principle of existence is one thing, and the principle of intelligence is quite another: for not everything that exists understands. Existence will be granted to the First Principle; but if "intelligence" were added to Him, a composition would be created, and it would imply that existence itself was not sufficient for its own perfection, since it would have needed intelligence through which to strive for progress. In the eighth consideration, you will note that he opposes the condition of *formal act* and *formable potentiality* <note>term: "act" and "potentiality"; Aristotelian terms where "act" is the finished perfection of a thing, and "potentiality" is the capacity to become something else</note>: so much so that potentiality receives the act, but the act, by the very reason that it is act, does not receive potentiality. Where there is act alone, as in the First, the thing is eternal, because no potentiality for another form lies hidden there. Likewise, where the entire formable potentiality has been transformed into the nature of the form—so that the form there can in no way be pulled back toward the nature of potentiality—that thing is also eternal. This is especially true because there, potentiality possesses the total act as much as it can and desires to have; such are the intellectual essences and the celestial fire. Fire beneath the heavens, among the lower things, is more perfect insofar as it is most greatly "in act": which is apparent from the efficacy of its form, and from its perpetual motion, and because it does not tolerate being mixed. But because it has matter beneath its act, and is not satisfied by it, it is not eternal. In the ninth consideration, remember that intelligence itself is not the **Good** itself <note>The "Good" is Plotinus's term for the highest principle, the One</note> in a simple sense, the first and last; otherwise, it would be sought simply for its own sake. But as it is, it is chosen under a certain condition. For you choose to know only if you know well and happily, and if it will be of benefit to you as a good. Likewise, the Good itself does not have "recognition" of itself: both because this recognition is one thing and the Good itself is another, and because if it is sufficient to itself before recognition, recognition should not be added; if it were not sufficient, it would not be the Good itself. But in what way...

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD III,
## BOOK IX.
### PLOTINUS
#### ENNEAD THE THIRD,
##### BOOK IX.

->Various Considerations.<-
->On different considerations pertaining to the author of the world, and to the Good itself.<-

---

<margin>
1
The maker of the world is the first intellect, contemplating the ideas within himself, and contains a single consideration.
</margin>

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial M featuring architectural scrollwork and a seated figure.</image-desc>
THE MIND <note>original: "MENS"; here referring to the Divine Intellect or *Nous*</note> (as it is written in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s famous dialogue on the creation of the universe</note>) gazes upon the ideas implanted in that which is living <note>original: "in eo quod viuens est"; referring to the "Living-Being-Itself," the perfect archetype of all life</note>. From this, the craftsman of the world is said to have intended to include in this world those things which the mind contemplates in that which is a living thing or animal. Does he not say, then, that the species <note>The eternal Forms or blueprints of things</note> already exist above the mind, and that the mind looks upon them as they already exist? 
<margin>B</margin>
In the first place, therefore, we must ask about that which is called "the living thing" or "animal-itself": is it perhaps not the intellect, but something different from the intellect? For that which contemplates is the intellect. We shall therefore call the living thing itself not the intellect, but rather the "intelligible" <note>original: "intelligibile"; the object of thought as opposed to the thinking subject</note>, and we shall say that the intellect possesses what it perceives outside of itself. Consequently, it will possess certain images, rather than the true things themselves—if indeed the true things exist in that other place. For he says that truth is also there, namely in being itself, where each thing itself reigns supreme. 
<margin>C</margin>
But perhaps, although each is different, they are not separated from one another, but only insofar as one is different from the other. Furthermore, nothing prevents both from existing as one, at least as far as what is being said is concerned, and being divided only through the understanding: since it alone holds itself as being, and that part is indeed intelligible, while the other part is also the one that understands. 
<margin>D</margin>
For where it is said that the intellect beholds the ideas, it does not mean that it gazes at them entirely in something else, but that it possesses the intelligible within itself. Or perhaps nothing prevents that intellect, while remaining in itself, from being a certain act flowing from that which gazes upon it? And while it gazes upon it, it as it were becomes that thing, and exists as the intellect of that thing, insofar as it understands it. And while it understands it, the intellect itself and the intelligible are otherwise, because it imitates it? 
<margin>E</margin>
This, therefore, is what he thinks out: to make the four kinds of animals in this world according to what he sees there. However, Plato seems there to introduce the one who thinks things out in a certain hidden way as if different from those other two: but to others, it will seem that these three exist as one: the living thing itself, the intellect, and the one who thinks. Or perhaps, as in many cases, he proposes it one way, but another understands that there are three? Now two have been spoken of: but what is the third?

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial O featuring architectural scrollwork and a central figure.</image-desc>
THOSE species which he says the craftsman sees existing as ideas, in that which is the "living-being-itself." Then the creator, he says, thought out those things which the mind sees in that which is the living being, so that this universe might have them. Was he saying, then, that the forms already existed before the mind, and that the mind understands them as they exist? First, then, we must investigate that thing—I mean the "living being"—to see if it is not the mind, but something other than the mind. For that which contemplates is the mind: therefore, we shall say the living being itself is not the mind, but the intelligible. And we shall say that the mind has the things it sees outside of itself. It would then have images, and not the true things, if the true things are there. For he says that truth also is there in being, where each thing is truly itself. Or perhaps they are each different, yet not separate from each other, but only in that they are distinct. Then nothing prevents them, so far as the words go, from being both, yet divided by thought: if indeed it is only as being, one part being the intelligible and the other being the mind. For it does not see, as he says, clearly in another, but in itself, by having the intelligible in itself. Or as for the intelligible, nothing prevents it from also being a mind in a state of rest and silence and stillness, while the nature of the mind—the one seeing that mind within itself—is a certain activity <note>original: "energeian"; the active operation or power</note> from that one, which sees it. And seeing it, it is as if it becomes that mind in that moment, because it understands it. And understanding that, it is also itself mind and intelligible in another way, by having imitated it. This, then, is the thinking power which makes the four kinds of living things in this world based on what it sees there. It seems, however, that the one who thinks is presented secretly <insert>*</insert> as being different from those other two. But to others it will seem that these three are one: the living being itself, the mind, and the thinking power. Or as if proposing it in one way among many, he understands it in another way to be three. And two have been mentioned: but the third, what is it?

Plotinus questions whether these are separate entities or different ways of describing a single, unified divine reality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Living-Being-Itself" and the creative process of the universe. In the previous page, the author explored whether the "Maker" of the world (the Demiurge) is the same as the Intellect or if it follows a higher archetype. Here, the focus shifts to how the One produces the many and how the Soul interacts with the body.</meta>

### BOOK NINE.

#### BOOK NINE.

That which he thought out <note>original: "ὃ διενοήθη"; referring to the divine deliberation of the Creator</note>, having inspected the sights placed by the intellect within the living being, was to work, to make, and to distribute them. Or perhaps it is possible that in one way the intellect is the distributor, and in another way the mind is not the distributor. For if the things being divided remain with the mind itself, then it is the divider; but if the mind itself remains undivided, and the things that come from it are divided—namely, the souls—then it is the Soul that acts as the distributor into many souls. For this reason, he <note>Plato</note> says that the partition belongs to a third <note>original: "τὸ τρίτον"; likely referring to the World Soul as the third hypostasis after the One and the Intellect</note> rank, and in this third rank, "he thought out" <note>original: "διενοήθη"</note>; for this "thought" is not the work of the Intellect, but the task of the Soul, which possesses a divisible activity within a divisible nature.

For just as a single, whole science is divided into individual theorems or notions, yet is not cut or pulled apart into separate pieces—since each part contains the whole in potentiality, where the beginning and the end are the same—so must one prepare oneself to see that the principles inherent within it are both the ends and the whole. All things are ultimately brought back to the best part of nature. For when each thing escapes into this, it dwells there: specifically, in that best part of itself, and once it has entered there, it immediately touches that [higher reality]. The universal soul was never "made" anywhere, nor did it "proceed" out, for there was nowhere for it to go; rather, the body, being close to it, was made to participate in it. Therefore, the soul is not in the body, nor did Plato say so anywhere; rather, the body has been brought into the soul. But where do the other souls come from? They come from the [Universal] Soul itself. They also have a place to which they descend and pass through, and from which they return. The Soul of the whole always dwells in the higher region, where the nature of the soul is naturally meant to be. But that which lies beneath the universe is given life by its proximity, just as a transparent body is illuminated when placed under the Sun. The individual soul is indeed illuminated when it flees to the higher realm, for there it encounters Being itself; but when it slips toward the lower realm, it falls into non-being. It does this when it descends into itself. Desiring to receive itself from on high, it creates that which follows after it: its own "phantom" <note>original: "simulachrum" or "εἴδωλον"; a shadow or reflection of the true self</note>, which we call non-being. It is as if the soul slips through a void and becomes indeterminate there. The phantom of this phantom is indefinite and utterly dark. For it is completely devoid of any rational or intellectual nature, and is furthest removed from Being itself. Meanwhile, the soul dwells in its own home as if in a middle ground; but looking again at the lower things, as if with a second glance, it forms the phantom, and delighted by this task, it enters into it.

How then does a multitude proceed from the One? Because the One is everywhere. There is nowhere it is not. It therefore fills all things. Thus, there are many things; or rather, all things already exist. If it were only "everywhere," it would be all things themselves. But since it is also "nowhere" <note>The paradox of the One: it is present to all things as their source, but is not any of them, remaining transcendent</note>, all things come into being through it because it is everywhere, but they are different from it because it is nowhere. Why then is it not only everywhere, but also somewhere? Rather, it is already all things and all species. All things: but since it is also nowhere, they become diverse from it, precisely because it is everywhere and nowhere.

<column-break/>

That which he deliberated, having inspected the sights seen by the intellect and placed in the living thing itself, was to work, to make, and to distribute. Or perhaps it is possible that in one way the intellect is the distributor, while in another way the mind is not. For in the way that those things which are divided proceed from the mind itself, it is the divider; but in the way that it remains undivided, while the things from it are divided—namely, the souls—the soul itself is the distributor into many souls. For this reason, he says that partition belongs to a certain third part <margin>II. Contains three considerations about the soul: how it ascends to God, and how it descends to the body.</margin>, and in the third rank, the duty of thought is assigned. But thought is not the duty of the mind, but the task of the soul, which has a divisible action in a divisible nature.

ACCORDINGLY, just as a certain whole science is distributed into individual propositions or notions, yet is not cut or distracted into segregated portions, but each part holds the whole in potentiality—where the beginning and the end are the same—so indeed one ought to compare oneself, so that the principles and ends implanted in oneself are wholes. And finally, all things are reduced to the best part of nature. For when anyone has escaped into this, they now dwell there: namely, by this very "best part" of themselves, and when they have worked their way into it, they immediately touch that also. The universal soul was not made anywhere, nor did it proceed: for there was nowhere it could proceed. Instead, the body made next to it participated in it. Therefore, the soul is not in the body; nor did Plato say this anywhere. Rather, the body is carried in the soul. But from where do the other souls come? They come from the Soul itself. Moreover, they have a place to which they descend and pass through, and they have a place from which they return. The Soul of the whole always dwells in the higher region, where the nature of the soul itself is meant to reside. But that which is subject to the whole is vivified by its proximity, just as a transparent body is illuminated when subject to the Sun. The individual soul is indeed illuminated when it takes refuge in the higher realm, for there it meets Being itself; but when it falls to the lower, it slips into non-being. It does this when it descends into itself. For, affecting to receive itself from the height into itself, it now makes that which follows after it: namely, its own "image" <note>original: "simulachrum"</note>, which we also call non-being. It falls, as it were, through the void and becomes indeterminate there. And the image of this image is indefinite and completely dark. For it is entirely devoid of every rational and intellectual nature, and is most distantly removed from Being itself. Meanwhile, it dwells in its domestic seat as if through a middle ground; but looking out again at the lower things, as if by a second cast of the eyes, it forms the image, and delighted by this office, it enters into it.

<margin>
III. Contains five considerations about God: how He is above all and in all; and about the intellect always in act, and that God is above the intellect.
</margin>

IN what way, therefore, does the multitude proceed from the One? Because the One is everywhere. Nor is there any place where it is not. Therefore it fills all things. Now, therefore, there are many things. For if it were only everywhere, it would be all things themselves. But since it is also nowhere, all things are indeed made through it, because it is everywhere; but they are different from it, because it is nowhere. Why then is it not only everywhere, but—

<summary>This page discusses the hierarchy of the Mind, the Soul, and the One, explaining that while the Intellect remains undivided, the Soul acts as a distributor of life into the material world. It introduces the famous Neoplatonic concept that the body exists within the soul rather than the soul being trapped in the body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the metaphysical investigation from the previous section regarding the nature of the "One" (the First Principle) and how it relates to the "Intellect" (Nous) and the "Soul" (Psyche). Plotinus is exploring the hierarchy of reality, specifically arguing that the highest principle, the Good, must be simpler than the act of thinking itself.</meta>

# PLOTINUS: ENNEADS, BOOK III.

<margin>A</margin> ...besides, is it nowhere? Truly, because it must be one in this way through all things. Therefore, it is necessary for it to fill and create all things, yet not be these things which it creates. Furthermore, the soul itself ought to be like sight, while the mind <note>original: "mentem" / "νοῦν"; the Intellect or Divine Mind, the second level of reality in Plotinian philosophy</note> is that which is visible to it. Sight, I say, is indeterminate before it sees; yet it is born to see and understand, being such that it serves as matter for the mind. When we understand ourselves, we look upon an understanding nature; otherwise, we would be lying about intelligence.

<margin>B</margin> If therefore we understand, and we understand ourselves, we certainly understand a nature that is intellectually existent. Therefore, before this intelligence, there is another intelligence which is, as it were, quiet: for there is an understanding of essence and an understanding of life. Thus, before this [intellect], there is another essence and life. These things, then, are known as acts. But if the intellects themselves are acts, consisting of themselves in the act of understanding, then we ourselves truly possess the intelligible <note>original: "intelligibile" / "νοητὸν"; the realm of pure forms or ideas that can be grasped by the mind</note> within us.

<margin>C</margin> The understanding of ourselves carries an image. The first principle of all is the power of motion and rest; therefore, it exists above these. That which is second <note>The Intellect</note> rests around it and is moved. Understanding belongs to this second level. For being one thing, it directs its intelligence toward another; but that First Principle does not possess intelligence in that way. For that which is understanding is already twofold—it is both the thinker and the thought—and it understands itself.

<margin>D</margin> On that account, it is also lacking, because it does not have its own good in its substance, but in the act of understanding. That which comes from potentiality <term>potentia: the capacity to become something</term> into act <term>actus: the state of being fully realized or functional</term> matches that which is in act; it is always the same, as long as it exists. Therefore, it is likewise perfect. Such a thing also applies to bodies, like fire, yet it cannot exist forever because it is joined with matter. But that which is pure act, and is not a composite, exists forever.

<margin>E</margin> That which is in act can also be in potentiality according to something else; but not even the gods on high, who look upon the beings, are the First itself. The mind is the beings, where there is both motion and rest. Now, the First itself is not occupied with anything else, but all other things remain resting around it and are moved. For motion is a desire, but that First Principle desires nothing. For what would the highest desire? Will it then not even understand itself?

<margin>F</margin> Perhaps in the sense that it possesses itself, it is said to understand in every way. Perhaps even more so, it is said to understand not because it possesses itself as something, but because it looks toward the First. But this is the first action, and intelligence itself. If therefore this is first, no other must be prior. That which provides this intelligence exists above it; therefore, intelligence follows after that. For intelligence is not the first thing to be venerated.

<column-break/>

<margin>α</margin> <note>The Greek text in this column runs parallel to the Latin translation provided in the first column.</note> Is it about these things, or nowhere? Because it must be so that the One is through everything. It must fill and make all things, but not be all the things it makes. The soul itself must be like sight, and the mind must be visible to it; it is indefinite before seeing, but born to think. If we think of ourselves, we clearly see a thinking nature...

<margin>β</margin> ...Therefore, before this thinking, there is another thinking, a quiet one. Thinking is of essence and of life. So before this life and essence, there is another life. All these are activities. If the intellects are activities according to thinking themselves in this way, then we truly possess the intelligible.

<margin>γ</margin> Their thinking carries the image. The First is the power of motion and rest, and is beyond them. The second stands and moves around that, and the mind is around the second. Being something else, it has its thinking toward another. But that [the First] does not have thinking. The thinking mind is double; it thinks itself and is incomplete, because it has its well-being in thinking rather than in its own underlying substance... <margin>* if so.</margin>

<margin>δ</margin> ...In every activity, that which goes from potentiality to activity is the same as long as it exists, so it is perfect, and this exists in bodies, like fire. But it cannot always be, because it is with matter. But that which is uncompounded and is in activity, is always. Further, the same thing being in activity can be in potentiality according to something else...

<margin>ε</margin> ...but the gods are not the First, being upon those things. The mind is the beings, and there is motion and rest there. For the First itself is nothing [of these], but the others, resting around it, stand and are moved. For motion is desire, but it desires nothing. For what would the highest have to reach for? Not even itself?

<margin>ζ</margin> Or in the way it has itself, it is said to think at all? Or by having itself, it is not said to think, but by looking toward the First. Further, it is the first activity, and it is thinking itself. If then this is first, no other must be before it. That which provides this is beyond it; so, thinking is second after that. For thinking is not the first thing to be revered—not all thinking, but that of the Good. Therefore, the Good is beyond thinking. But will it [the Good] not follow itself? What then? Is following itself a property of being good? If it is a being, then thinking is about the following of the Good. But if the following makes it so, the Good would not be about this.

***

Therefore, not just any intelligence is to be venerated, but only the understanding of the good: thus, the good itself is above intelligence. Will it then not even notice itself? What then? Is it good before it notices itself? Or is it not yet good? For if it is good, then the good itself already exists before awareness; but if awareness makes it good, it is not the good itself before this; therefore...

# MARSILIO FICINO'S
## COMMENTARY ON THE FIRST AND SECOND BOOKS OF THE FOURTH ENNEAD, ON THE SOUL.

### SUMMARY OF THE BOOKS.

->The first intellect is the first essence, from which and in which other<-
->intellects always exist. Likewise, how the soul is<-
->indivisible and divisible at the same time.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial "Q" featuring classical scrollwork, foliage, and a grotesque mask at the bottom.</image-desc>SINCE we have discussed elsewhere at greater length the things Plotinus treats here concerning the soul—especially in the first, third, and seventh books of our *Theology* <note>Referring to Ficino's own work, *Platonic Theology*</note>—we will touch upon them here only briefly. **Generation** <note>The process of physical birth and coming-into-being</note> always strives toward **Being**: first toward bare existence, then toward living existence, after this toward what is called sensory existence, and finally toward intellectual existence as the highest point, where the intellectual soul descends into a partnership with the body. This is the order of essence or being acquired in the stages of generation. Above this order stands the order of essence in the eternal ranks of the universe, in which the **Intellect** itself holds the highest place as the absolute principle. From this, the "animal intellect" <note>The soul that animates a body</note> descending in generation holds the highest place in the whole order of generation as its goal—not made simply by generation, but adapted to the body to fulfill the providence of the whole. 

However, the pure Intellect is whole everywhere. Within it exist souls, not only through **Ideas** <note>The divine archetypes or patterns of things</note> but also through their own (so to speak) intellectual existences, according to their own specific intellectual faculty, even while they are in the body. Just as lines drawn from a center to a circumference do not depart from the center even when they touch the circumference, and as rays do not leave the sun while they touch the earth; and just as the lines and rays projecting outward are distant from one another in space, yet are together in the principle itself—so souls among us, though distant according to their bodies, are all together there according to the intellect in the **Divine Mind**. I say "according to their intellects," differing from one another there just as the ends of lines and rays are different from each other even where they touch the center and the sun. 

From this, Plotinus wishes it to be concluded that the intellect of a prophet or a detached person, even if he seems to be only in the East, may nevertheless perceive what is happening in the West, and may perform something miraculous in one place from another, and secretly move others by his thought and affection. This is because all intellects are in one another and are everywhere, since they are always in the simple Divine Mind, which is always present everywhere in its entirety. By this presence, God perceives prayers, and humans may converse most intimately with God. He also holds that intellects of this kind are the "familiar <term>daemons</term>" <note>In the Greek sense of 'daimon,' a guiding spirit or higher self, not an evil demon</note> of men, assigned to each individual as constant leaders. For perhaps external spirits cannot be so closely applied to individual men. 

He judges that when Plato says in the *Timaeus* that the soul is composed of a certain "indivisible essence" and also a "divisible" one regarding bodies, he meant by the "first essence" the intellectual power of the soul, which never declines toward bodies. The "second" is that nature of the soul which adapts itself entirely to the body, yet is still called "indivisible." For even when the soul is joined to the body, no matter how far the limbs are distant from each other, the soul is not distant from itself; indeed, it is the same and whole in every limb. He says both these faculties of the soul exist in our soul as well as in the **Soul of the World**. 

Furthermore, when he says the intellect of both the world and of man is present to all members of its body, and that the Divine Intellect is present to all parts of the world, why is it not said to be divided by the body like the soul? Because any intellect, by its presence, contributes nothing to the body except through the soul; thus it seems to be "present to" rather than "inside" it. Moreover, the intellect is equally present in any portion of the body, so it appears completely undivided. The soul, however, exercises one power and action in this limb and another in that one, distributing life, sense, and motion through various degrees to the members of its body, and thus it seems in a way divided in the body. 

In the second book here on the soul, you will note that <term>Entelechy</term> <note>Aristotle's term for the 'actuality' or 'perfection' of a thing; that which makes a body alive</note> of Aristotle—by which the soul is called the "act and perfection of the body"—can be understood even in Aristotle to mean not only a form and soul inseparable from the body, but also one that is separable. Furthermore, you should consider that what is properly "divided" is divided in substance; but what is "moved" can be moved properly according to its accidents, qualities, and modes, while the substance remains. Therefore, substance is affected and harmed by division rather than by motion. Since in the descent of things, Good begins from the highest and Evil from the lowest, we rightly find as we descend that a thing is properly "movable" before it is properly "divisible." Therefore, beneath the Divine Intellect—which is both entirely indivisible and immovable—we find the **Soul**, which is indeed indivisible, though properly movable; then the corporeal form and quality, which is movable and divided everywhere. Finally, the **Body**, which is the origin of this division and is moved by something else, being itself inert.

<summary>Ficino explains the hierarchy of reality, arguing that the Human Soul acts as a bridge between the indivisible Divine Intellect and the divisible physical body, remaining whole even when operating in different limbs.</summary>

furthermore, is it nowhere else? Truly, because it is necessary for the One to be above all things. For this reason, it must fill and create all things, and yet it is not all these things that it creates. Then indeed, the soul itself must be as a power of sight, while the intellect <term>Intellect (Nous)</term> <note>In Plotinian thought, the Intellect is the first emanation from the One, containing the forms of all things.</note> must be what is visible to it. I say it is a sight that is indeterminate before it sees, yet born to see and understand, being such that it serves as matter <note>Original: "materia." Here, it means the receptive potentiality that becomes "informed" by higher truth.</note> for the intellect. When we understand ourselves, we behold an intelligent nature; otherwise, we would be lying about what intelligence is. 
<margin>B</margin>
If then we understand, and we understand ourselves, we surely understand a nature that is intellectual by its own existence. Wherefore, before this active understanding, there is another understanding that is, as it were, quiet. For there is an intellection of essence and an intellection of life; therefore, before this there is another essence and life. These things, then, are known by however many acts there are. 
<margin>C</margin>
But if the intellects themselves are acts, thus standing firm in the understanding of themselves, let us truly possess the intelligible within us. Our own act of understanding, however, carries only an image of this. The first principle of all is the power of motion and of rest; therefore, it exists above these. But that which is second rests around it and is moved toward it. For the intellect belongs to the second rank. For existing as one thing, it directs its intelligence toward another; but that 
<margin>D</margin>
First has no intelligence. For that which is understanding is already twofold <note>Thinking requires a subject who thinks and an object being thought—a duality the One transcends.</note> and understands itself; and for this reason, it is also needy, since it possesses its own good not in its substance, but in the act of understanding. That which comes from potentiality into act corresponds with that which is already in act; this is always the same as long as it exists. Therefore, it is likewise perfect. Such a quality also belongs to bodies, like fire, yet it cannot exist forever because it is joined with matter. But that which is purely an act, and is not a composite, exists forever. Now, that which is in act can also be 
<margin>E</margin>
in potentiality according to something else; but not even the gods in the heights, though leaning toward the beings, are the First itself. The intellect, however, is the beings, where there is both motion and rest. Now, the First itself is not occupied with anything else, but all other things remain resting or moving around it. For motion is a desire, but that First desires nothing. For what could the "Highest" desire? Will it then not even understand itself? Perhaps in the way that it 
<margin>F</margin>
possesses itself, it is said to understand in a general sense. Or perhaps rather, it is said to understand not because it possesses itself, but because it looks up to the First <note>Plotinus describes how the Intellect looks back at the One from which it originated.</note>. This is the first action and intelligence itself. If, therefore, this is first, there must be none prior to it. That which provides this, therefore, exists above it; consequently, intelligence follows after that. For intelligence is not the first thing to be revered.

Neither, then, is every intelligence to be revered, but only the understanding of the Good; thus, the Good is above intelligence. Will it then not even notice itself? What then? Is the Good something before it notices itself? Or is it not yet the Good? For if it is the Good, it is already the Good before the notice; but if the notice makes it the Good, then the Good is not before it. Wherefore—

<column-break/>

...and not also near this, and nowhere? Because it is necessary for the One to be before all things. It must therefore fill itself and make all things, but not be all the things it makes. The soul, in turn, must be like a sight, and the intellect must be the visible thing for it. It is indeterminate before seeing, naturally suited for thinking. When we think of the intellect, we clearly see its thinking nature, or we would be lying about thinking. If then we think, and think of ourselves, we think of a nature that is intellectual. Therefore, before this thinking, there is another thinking, as it were, quiet; for thinking is of essence and thinking is of life. So before this life and essence, there is another essence and life. These then it saw, as many as are activities. If the intellects are the activities according to the act of thinking 
<margin>* those who exist</margin>
thus themselves, then we are truly the <note>original: "οἱ ὄντως" — the truly existing beings</note> intelligible thing. But their thinking carries the image. The first, on the one hand, is the power of motion and of extension, so that it is beyond these. The second, on the one hand, stands and is moved around that, and the intellect is around the second. For being one thing, it has its thinking toward another; but the [First] does not have thinking. For the thinking thing is double, and it thinks itself, and it is lacking, because it has its "well-being" in thinking, not in its foundation. To every act, for everything that goes from power into act, it is the same always, as long as it exists. So also perfection belongs to bodies, such as fire, but it cannot always be, because it is with matter. But whatever is incorporeal in activity, exists always. It is the same thing being an activity, and being in power according to another thing; but the gods, falling upon those things before them, are not the First. The intellect is the beings, and there is motion among these, and rest. For the First itself is about nothing, but other things, resting around it, stand and are moved. For motion is desire; but the [First] desires nothing. For what would the highest then [desire], if it does not even think of itself? Or is it in the way it possesses itself that it is also said to think at all? Or is it said to think not by possessing itself, but by looking toward the First? This is the first activity, and thinking itself. If then this is first, there must be none prior. That which provides this, then, is beyond this; so that thinking is second after that. For thinking is not the first thing to be revered. Therefore, not all [thinking], but only that of the Good; therefore, the Good is beyond thinking. But it will not follow itself. What then? Is the following itself the same as being the Good? Or if—? For if it already exists, the Good is already before the following. But if the following makes it, the Good would not be before this.

Therefore, [does it] not even [perceive] itself? What then? Before it follows [itself], is it not the Good? Or was it already being, before it followed itself? For if it exists before following, it is already the Good itself; but if the following makes it, it would not be the Good before the following.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON
## THE FIRST AND SECOND BOOKS
### OF THE FOURTH ENNEAD, ON THE SOUL,
### A COMMENTARY.
### SUMMARY OF THE BOOKS.

->The first Intellect is the first essence, from which and in which<-
->other intellects always exist. Likewise, how the soul is<-
->indivisible and divisible at the same time.<-

<image-desc>A large ornate woodcut initial Q decorated with floral scrolls and leafy patterns.</image-desc>
SINCE the things Plotinus discusses here concerning the soul, we have treated more extensively elsewhere, especially in the first, third, and seventh books of our *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his major work, *Platonic Theology*, where he argues for the immortality of the soul.</note>, we will touch upon them briefly here. Generation <note>The process of coming into being or being born into the physical world.</note> always strives toward being: first indeed toward bare being, then toward living being, after these toward that which is called sensory being, and finally toward intellectual being as the highest, where the intellectual soul descends into commerce with the body. Such indeed is the order of essence or of being acquired in the stages of generation. Above this order stands the order of essence in the eternal stages of the universe, in which the Intellect itself holds the highest place as a principle; from which the animal intellect, descending in generation, holds the highest place in the whole order of generation as its end—not indeed made simply by generation, but adapted to the body to fulfill the providence of the whole. 

However, the Intellect itself is entirely everywhere: and in it there are not only souls through their Ideas <note>The perfect, eternal archetypes in the Mind of God.</note>, but even through their own (so to speak) intellectual existences, according to their own intellectual faculty, even while they are in the body. Just as lines produced from the center to the circumference do not depart from the center while they touch the circumference, and as rays do not leave the sun while they touch earthly things; and just as lines and rays projecting outward are distant from each other in place, yet in the principle itself are in the same place: so our souls, though distant in location according to their bodies, are all in the same place according to the intellect in the divine mind. I say "according to their intellects," where they differ among themselves just as the ends of lines and rays are different from one another, even where they touch the center and the sun. 

From this Plotinus concludes that the intellect of a prophet and of a detached man, even if it seems to be only in the East, nevertheless looks forward to what is happening in the West, and from one certain place performs something miraculous in another, and moves others secretly by its thought and affection: because, clearly, all intellects are in one another and everywhere, since they are always in the simple divine mind, which is entirely present everywhere. By this very presence, God perceives prayers, and men talk most familiarly with God. He also wants such intellects to be the familiar spirits <term>Daemons</term> <note>Original: "demones." In Platonic thought, these are mediating spirits or higher aspects of the soul, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note> of men, and diligent guides assigned to each individual. For perhaps external spirits cannot be so closely applied to individual men. 

He believes that Plato, when he says in the *Timaeus* that the soul is composed of a certain indivisible essence and also a divisible one around bodies, understood the first essence to be the intellectual power of the soul, never declining toward bodies: but the second to be that nature which fully adapts itself to the body, which nonetheless is called indivisible; because the soul joined to the body, however much the members of the body are distant from each other, is not distant from itself, since it is entirely the same in any member. Such is the state of both faculties of the soul, both in our soul and also in the soul of the world. 

Furthermore, when he says that the intellect of both the world and of man is present to all the members of its body, and likewise that the divine intellect is present to all parts of the world, why is it not at least said to be divided through the body like the soul? Because, clearly, any intellect by its presence contributes nothing to the body except through the soul, so that it appears to be *near* rather than *in* it. Moreover, the intellect relates equally to any portion of the body, so that it appears entirely undivided; but the soul exercises one power and action in this member and another in that, and adapts life, sense, and motion through various degrees to the members of its body, and thus appears somewhat divided in the body. 

In the second book on the soul here, you will note that Aristotelian <term>Entelechy</term> <note>Original: "Entelechiam." Aristotle's term for the "actuality" or "perfection" of a body; that which makes it a living thing.</note>, by which the soul is called the act and perfection of the body, can be understood even in Aristotle not only as a form and soul inseparable from the body, but also as one that is separable from the body. Therefore, you will consider that what is properly divided is divided in substance; but what is moved can indeed be properly moved according to its accidents, qualities, and modes, while meanwhile the substance remains; and therefore substance is reached and harmed by division rather than by motion. When indeed in the very descent of things, good starts from the highest and evil from the least, we rightly find in descending a thing that is properly movable before we find one that is properly divisible. Therefore, beneath the divine intellect, which is both entirely indivisible and immovable, we find the soul, which is indeed indivisible, though properly movable; then the corporeal form and quality, which is everywhere movable and divided. Finally, the body, which is the origin of this division, and being inert, is moved from elsewhere.

<meta>This page continues the transition into the Fourth Ennead, which focuses on the Soul (Anima). It begins with Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on the divisibility of the soul and its relation to the body, followed by a table of contents for the nine books of the Fourth Ennead, and finally the opening of the first book.</meta>

<page-num>360</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS ENNEAD 4</header>

When we say that the soul is divisible, we do not speak in the proper sense, as we do regarding a body or even a quality. Instead, we speak improperly, understanding that the soul is not actually cut into sections according to the divisions of a body (like a quality might be), but rather that it is accommodated to a moving, divided body through its own powers. It distributes its acts and gifts to different members in different ways. You will note, meanwhile, that the bodily mass and form, which are by their very nature entirely capable of being scattered, could not be held together—either in ourselves or in the world—in any other way than by the soul, which is not divided in the same way, but remains whole in every part. Likewise, the World Soul, insofar as it contains a multitude of powers and forms within itself, is in a certain way moved and accommodated to give life to the body of the world. It is accommodated, I say, by the divine Mind itself, which is entirely immobile, yet holds a multitude of forms within itself, although these forms do not differ there as much as they differ in the soul. Likewise, insofar as unity reigns first in the divine Mind and then in the World Soul, and a surpassing simplicity flourishes there, everything is governed wisely by a certain intellectual reason. Conclude here five grades of things: 1. The Good itself, which is only One in itself. 2. The divine Mind, which is "One-Many." 3. The Soul, whether of the world or our own, which is "One-and-Many" in itself. 4. Quality of the bodily form, which is "Many-in-itself-and-One." 5. The mass of the body itself, which is no longer considered one according to itself, but many. The remaining matters are explained in the *Theology* <note>Ficino likely refers to his own work, *Platonic Theology*.</note> (as we have said).

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD FOUR,
### BOOK I.

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD FOUR,
### BOOK I.

->ON THE ESSENCE OF THE SOUL, IN BRIEF.<-
<note>Original: "ΠΕΡΙ οὐσίας Ψυχῆς" / "De essentia animæ summatim"</note>

<margin>
The first Intellect is the first essence, from which and in which other intellects always exist. Also, how the soul is simultaneously undivided and divided.
</margin>
In the intelligible world <note>The "intelligible world" refers to the realm of pure being and thought, higher than the physical world.</note> true essence reigns, the most excellent part of which is the intellect. Souls are also present there, for they came from that place into this world. That world indeed holds souls without bodies; this world, however, holds them already implanted in bodies and divided by those bodies. In that realm, certainly, every intellect exists together, neither discrete nor divided; likewise, all souls are together in one world, and they suffer no distances from any intervals of space. Therefore, the intellect is always indistinct and undivided, but the soul lives there as something indistinct and undivided, yet it possesses a nature capable of being divided.

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the original Greek text of the passage translated above.</note>
In the intelligible world is true essence. Mind is the best part of it; but souls are also there. For from there they come even into this world. Furthermore, that world possesses souls as incorporeal; but here, how they come to be in bodies and are divided by the bodies. There, all things are together and not discrete, nor divided; all souls are together in one world, not in spatial distance. Mind, therefore, is always undistinguished and not divided; and the soul is there undistinguished and undivided, but it has a nature to be divided.

<page-num>361</page-num>
<header>BOOK TWO.</header>
<columns>2</columns>
<sig>H</sig>

For its division is to stand apart from that higher realm and to come to exist within bodies. It is therefore reasonably said to be "divisible around bodies," because it stands apart in this way and has been partitioned. How then is it also "indivisible"? Either the whole soul departed, or there is something of it that has not come down, which by its nature cannot be divided. Therefore, being "from the indivisible and the divisible around bodies" is the same as saying it exists both "above" and "below," and is suspended from that higher realm while flowing down as far as these things here, much like a line extending from a center point. Having arrived here, it sees with a part, yet even with that part it preserves the nature of the whole. For even here it is not merely divisible, but also indivisible. For that which is divided within it is divided in an indivisible manner. For by giving itself to the whole body and not being partitioned, it has been divided by the fact that it is a whole in the whole and present in every part.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
For its partition is to be absent and distant from that higher place, and to be joined to bodies; for this reason, it is said not without cause to be divisible around bodies. For it is so absent and distant that it admits some degree of partition. In a certain way, therefore, it is also indivisible. For it does not depart from there entirely, but something of it remains above which does not come down to lower things, the nature of which can undergo no partition. What is said, therefore, in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue describing the creation of the soul from a mixture of "Same" and "Different."</note>—that the soul is composed of a certain indivisible essence and a certain essence divisible around bodies—is the same as saying that the soul consists of a certain essence, partly remaining among the higher things and partly turning toward the lower, which simultaneously hangs from the former and meanwhile propagates itself even to these latter things, not unlike a line stretched out from a center. Having proceeded to these lower things with this additional part, it clearly preserves the nature of the whole: for even here it is not only partible, but also indivisible.
<margin>B</margin>

<column-break/>

Indeed, that which is said to be divided into parts within the soul is, in a certain manner, divided in an undivided way. For by pouring itself through the whole body, and not being divided by the fact that it is a whole through the whole, it is meanwhile said to be divided because it is within the whole.

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD IV,
### BOOK II.

# P L O T I N U S
## THE FOURTH ENNEAD,
### BOOK II.

#### On the essence of the Soul, which ought to be read regarding all accounts of the Soul.
#### On the essence of the soul.

---

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative ornamental initial 'T' featuring a scene within an architectural frame, depicting what appears to be figures and classical scrollwork.</image-desc>
When seeking what the essence of the soul might be, we have shown that it is not a body at all, nor is it a harmony among incorporeal things. Likewise, we have suspected the truth regarding what is said of "entelechy" <note>Aristotle’s term for the "actualization" or "perfection" of a body; Plotinus argues the soul is more than just a function of the body.</note> and similar theories which we have addressed concerning the essence of the soul. Nevertheless, let us again consider by what path we must proceed, if we are to see what the soul truly is. For some things are primarily divisible and by their own nature scattered; these are the things in which no part is the same as another part, nor the same as the whole, and where the part must be less than the entire whole. These are the sensible magnitudes, such as any body, which exists in a space, not remaining in one point but scattered through space.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>*Correction: Is identical with.*</margin>
\* It is the same, neither with another part, nor with the whole: but their part must be less than the entire whole. These are the sensible magnitudes.

<column-break/>

<margin>*It is necessary that the soul be intermediate between the divisible intellect and the corporeal, and likewise the quality of the body. Also that the soul be whole in any part of the body. Again regarding the grades of the universe.*</margin>
<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative ornamental initial 'S' depicting a figure seated at a desk or table, entwined with lush vine-like scrolling foliage.</image-desc>
IF you ask what the essence of the soul is, we have shown that it is neither a body, nor again a harmony in incorporeal things; likewise, we have passed over what is said of "entelechy"—that is, a certain act and perfection of the body—as being (as the words sound) not at all true, nor declaring what the soul itself is.

<margin>B</margin>
Furthermore, if we assert that it belongs to the intelligible nature and divine lot, we perhaps bring something manifest concerning its essence into the open; yet it is worth the effort to proceed further. Now, therefore, since a distribution has been made between the sensible and intelligible nature, and the soul itself has been placed in the intelligible world, let us in the present moment investigate the property of this nature in another way. We say, therefore, that some things are primarily divisible, and by their very nature subject to dissipation: such things are those in which no part is the same as either another part or the whole, and in which the part is necessarily smaller than the entire whole. Such indeed are sensible magnitudes.

<summary>This page marks the beginning of Book II of the Fourth Ennead, where Plotinus explores the soul's "middle" nature—existing as both an indivisible divine spark and a force divided among physical bodies. He refutes the idea of the soul as a mere physical harmony or bodily function (entelechy), instead defining it as an intelligible, divine substance.</summary>

### PLOTINUS ENNEAD IV.

...and masses, each of which occupies its own space, and it is impossible for the same thing to exist simultaneously in multiple places. But there is, in turn, another essence opposed to this, which is in no way subject to division, being without parts and therefore indivisible. This essence admits no spatial distance even in our imagination; it does not require a place, nor does it reside in other things either by its parts or as a whole. Rather, it supports all things at once—not so that it is held up by them, but because other things are neither able nor willing to exist apart from it. This essence always remains the same. It is the common foundation of all things that follow in sequence, much like the center point of a circle from which all lines drawn to the circumference are continuous; nevertheless, the center itself is allowed to rest within itself. These lines have their birth and existence from it and share in that point, which is an indivisible principle for all of them. They move outward, yet are not disconnected from their source.

Since this is the primary indivisible thing, and chief in the order of <term>intelligibles</term> <note>Intelligibles are realities that can only be grasped by the mind, like mathematical truths or divine ideas, rather than the physical senses.</note> and beings, there is also that which is entirely divisible in the order of <term>sensibles</term> <note>Sensibles are physical objects perceived through sight, touch, etc.</note>. Above the sensible realm, yet near and within it, is another nature. This nature is divisible, though not primarily like bodies are; rather, it becomes divisible within these bodies. Thus, when bodies are cut, the <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; here meaning the 'form' or 'forming principle' (eidos) that gives an object its specific character.</note> within them is also cut, yet it remains in some way whole in each of the divided parts. I mean the same form now becomes many, each of which is entirely separate from the other, since the form has become completely divisible—such as colors and all qualities, or any shape that can exist as a whole in many distant things at once, where no part experiences the same thing that another part experiences. Therefore, this must be considered entirely indivisible in its own right.

Furthermore, beyond that entirely indivisible nature, there is another essence born from it. It holds an indivisible duty from that source, but by a certain progression it hastens toward another nature and ends up in the middle of both: between the first, indivisible nature, and the nature that is divisible around bodies and inherent in them. It does not behave exactly like color or every quality, which fills many places at once while remaining somewhat the same in many bodily masses; for the quality that lies in one part is entirely separate from the quality in another part, just as one mass is distant from another. And although a magnitude may be one, what is called "the same" in individual parts has no shared connection for mutual feeling; for this "same" thing is actually one thing here and another there. For this "sameness" is a mere <term>affection</term> <note>A property or "passion" of a thing, rather than its core essence.</note>, and not the essence itself. But that which we say exists in this nature by virtue of the indivisible essence, and which proceeds from it, is indeed an essence, and it is joined to bodies. It happens that this nature is also divided around them—yet it does not suffer this division until it gives itself to the bodies. Therefore, when it is present in bodies, even if it is present in the largest and most widely spread out mass, it adapts itself to the whole as one...

<column-break/>

**A** ...and masses, each of which has its own place; and it is not possible for the same thing to be in many places at once. But there is another essence, fixed in this way, in no way admitting division, partless and indivisible. It admits no distances, not even in thought, nor does it require a place, nor does it come to be in any of the things that exist, neither by parts nor as a whole, but as if riding upon all existing things together. Not so that it **B** is established by them, but because other things cannot exist without it; nor do they wish to. It is an essence always <margin>*towards itself</margin> <note>The Greek marginalia "*κατὰ αὐτῆ" is likely a correction for the main text, emphasizing the self-contained nature of the essence.</note> having itself, common to all things that follow, like a center in a circle from which all lines extending to the circumference are hung, allowing it to remain in itself. They possess their spread and being from it, and they participate in the point, and the indivisible is their principle. They proceed, however, while remaining attached to it **C** there. That, then, is the primarily indivisible. In the realm of intelligibles and among leading beings, there is again in each thing that which is entirely divisible in the realm of sensibles. Like sensible things, there is another nature near and in them. It is divisible, though not primarily like bodies; but it becomes divisible by being in bodies. So that when bodies are divided, the form in them is also divided, yet **D** it is whole in each of the divided parts, the same thing becoming many. Each of these is entirely distant from the other, since it becomes entirely divisible; such as colors and all qualities. And every shape which can be whole in many distant things at once, having no part that experiences the same thing as another part. Therefore, it is not entirely indivisible, but must be placed there. And again, besides **E** that entirely indivisible nature, there is another essence from it, having the indivisible from that one; but proceeding from it and hastening toward the other nature, it stood in the middle of both. The indivisible and primary, and that which is divisible around bodies and on bodies. Not in the way that color and every quality is the same in many bodily masses in many places; but the **F** mass is distant from mass. And even in magnitude, it is not one, but what is the same in each part has no community of shared feeling; because the "same" is one thing here and another there. For "the same" is an affection, not an essence. But we say that in this nature there is an essence proceeding from the indivisible, which is an essence and is near **G** to bodies. It happens to be divided around them, and it suffers this even before giving itself to bodies. In whatever bodies it may be, even if it is in the largest and most widely distant, it gives itself to the whole, not standing apart...
