## BOOK TWO.

...it does not cease to be one. It is not one in the same way as a body, for a body is a single continuum where each part is distinct; one part is here, <margin>quality</margin> and another is elsewhere. <note>original: "ποιότης" (quality). Plotinus is distinguishing the soul from physical properties like color or heat.</note> Nor is it one like a single quality is one. Indeed, this nature is both divisible and indivisible at the same time—this is what we call the soul. It is not a single continuum with one part here and another there; rather, it is divisible because it is present in every part of the living being in which it resides, and it is indivisible because it is entirely present in every part, and it is not merely a portion of itself. Whoever perceives this—observing the magnitude and power of the soul—will realize how divine and wonderful a thing it is, belonging to those natures that surpass material things. Though it possesses a kind of magnitude, it is present to every physical magnitude; and while existing here, <margin>*in essence</margin> it is also there; not as something else, but as the very same thing. Thus it is both divided and not divided. Or rather, it is not divided, nor has it ever become divided. For it remains whole within itself. It is said to be divided regarding bodies because bodies, through their own divisibility, are unable to receive it indivisibly. Therefore, the division is an experience belonging to the bodies, not to the soul itself.

<margin>* the nature of the soul</margin> THAT it was necessary for the nature of the soul to be such, and that nothing else could be the soul—neither a purely indivisible thing nor a purely divisible one, but necessarily both in this manner—can be made clear from the following. If it were like bodies, having one part and then another, then if one part of the body suffered an experience, the other part would not feel what the suffering part felt. Instead, the soul in the finger, for instance, would be like a separate soul existing within itself and would feel the experience there alone. In such a case, there would be many souls governing each of us. Indeed, this universe would not be ruled by one soul, but by countless souls separate from one another. For "continuity" <note>The physical connection of body parts.</note> is useless unless it leads to a single point of unity. We must not accept the explanation given by those who deceive themselves, saying that sensations reach the <term>ruling faculty</term> <note>original: "ἡγεμονικόν" (hegemonikon). This was the Stoic term for the "command center" of the soul, often thought to be in the heart or brain.</note> by a gradual transmission. First, to speak of a "ruling part" of the soul is a claim made without investigation. For how would they divide it? How can they say one part is this and another is that? How will they distinguish the ruling part from the rest—by what measure of size or what difference in quality—when the soul is a single and continuous mass? Furthermore, will only the ruling part perceive, or will the other parts feel as well? If only the ruling part perceives, it will only do so if the sensation occurs in the specific place where that ruling part is located. But if the sensation falls upon another part of the soul not naturally suited for feeling, that part will not transmit the same experience to the ruling part, and no sensation will occur at all. Even if the experience reaches the ruling part, it will strike only one portion of it; thus, while that portion feels, the rest will not. This would be pointless, or else there would be countless and dissimilar perceptions of the same sensation. One might say, "I am the first to feel it," while another says, "I have now felt the experience of another..."

<column-break/>

...for it does not cease to be. Nor is it one in the way a body is one; for a body is one through a certain continuation, but its parts are distinct from one another and are arranged in different places. Nor, again, is it one in the way a quality is one. Truly, this nature—at once divisible and indivisible—which we call the soul, is not one as a continuum is, having one part and then another. Rather, it is divisible because it communicates itself to all the parts of that in which it resides. It is indivisible, however, because it is whole in all parts and is whole in any given portion. Whoever looks into this more clearly, and rightly considers the magnitude and power of the soul, will understand how divine and how wonderful a treasure the soul is, an extraordinary nature above all other treasures. For though it lacks physical bulk, it is present to the whole of magnitude; and existing in one place, it exists there again—not as something else, but as the very same thing. Thus it is both divided into parts and yet not divided; or rather, it is neither divided nor does it become divided. For it remains whole within itself, but it is said to be divided in relation to bodies, because bodies cannot receive it indivisibly due to their own divisibility. From this it follows that partition is not an experience of the soul, but of bodies.

<margin>The preceding points are confirmed. How sensation, experience, and judgment occur.</margin> THAT it is necessary for the nature of the soul to be such, and that nothing else besides this can be the soul, but that it is necessary for the soul to exist neither as purely indivisible nor purely divisible, but rather as both in this manner, can be made manifest to us through these points. To begin with, if it were like bodies, having one part and then another, then if one part suffered an experience, the other part would by no means receive a sensation of the suffering. Instead, that soul, such as the one in the finger, would be like a separate soul existing in itself and would feel the experience there. There would also be many souls governing each of us. Furthermore, this universe would be ruled not by one soul, but rather by various and innumerable souls. For whatever one might argue concerning "continuity," it is seen to be in vain unless it absolutely leads back and is reduced to a single unity. We must not admit what many say, deceiving themselves: namely, that the senses reach the <term>principal part</term> <note>Latin: "principale." This is Ficino's translation of the Greek "hegemonikon," referring to the mind or ruling faculty.</note> of the soul step by step through a continuous succession. First of all, to speak of a "principal part" of the soul is proposed without due consideration. For in what way will they divide it? How will they affirm that this is one thing and that is another, and how will they designate one part as "principal" above all? By what rule of quantity will they discern the two, or what difference will they mark, where there is only one quality and a continuous mass? Furthermore, will only the principal part feel, or will the other parts feel as well? If they say only the principal part feels, it will only do so if the sensible experience occurs in the principal part's own specific seat. But if it falls upon another part of the soul that lacks sensation, such a part will not transmit the same experience to the principal part, and no sensation will be produced at all. Then, if the experience reaches the principal part, it will fall upon a portion of it, and therefore while that portion feels, the rest will by no means feel. Otherwise, it would be superfluous, or there would certainly be many and innumerable perceptions of the senses, and they would be dissimilar. In one place it would be said, "I am the first to suffer"; in another, "I have now felt the experience of another..."

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul must be simultaneously divisible and indivisible to allow for unified sensory perception across the entire body. He refutes the idea that sensations are simply passed along like a relay to a "ruling part," insisting instead that the soul is present as a whole in every part of the body.</summary>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

<columns>
...and masses, each of which occupies its own proper place; it is impossible for the same material thing to exist in multiple places at the same time. But there is another kind of essence <note>Latin: *essentia*; Greek: *οὐσία*. In this context, it refers to "being" or "fundamental reality."</note> opposite to this, which is in no way subject to division. It is without parts, and therefore indivisible. It does not admit any extension, even in thought. It has no need of a physical location, nor does it dwell within other things as a set of parts or as a physical whole. Rather, it broods over all things simultaneously—not so that it may be supported by them, but because all other things are neither able nor willing to exist apart from it. This essence remains always the same. It is the firm foundation for all things that follow in order, much like the center point in a circle. All the lines drawn from the center to the circumference are connected to it, yet they allow the center itself to remain at rest within itself. These lines derive their generation and their being from that point; they participate in the point, for the indivisible principle is their source. Yet, they proceed outward without being cut off from that source. 

Since this first thing is indivisible and holds the primary rank among "intelligible beings" <note>The "intelligible" world refers to the realm of pure thought and spirit, as opposed to the "sensible" world of the five senses.</note>, and since the material world is entirely divisible, there is another nature between the two. It is near the intelligible realm and exists within it, yet it is also divisible—not primarily divisible like bodies are, but it becomes divisible within those bodies. Consequently, when bodies are cut or divided, the "form" <note>Latin: *species*; Greek: *εἶδος*. Here, the specific organizing principle or shape of a thing.</note> within them is also divided. Yet, in a certain way, the whole remains present in each of the divided parts. This same form becomes many, and each part is distinct from the others, for the form has become entirely divisible. Such are colors and all qualities, and every shape that can exist as a whole in many separate places at once, where no part experiences what another part suffers. For this reason, we must categorize such things as being entirely divisible. 

Furthermore, beyond that completely indivisible nature, there is another essence that arises from it. It holds an indivisible duty granted by its source, but through a certain progression, it hastens toward the other nature. It ends up in the middle of both: between the indivisible, primary nature and the divisible nature that is inherent in bodies. This middle nature does not behave exactly like a color or a quality. While a quality fills many masses of bodies at once, existing as the same thing in many places, the quality that lies in one part is entirely separate from the quality in another part, just as one mass is distant from another mass. And though a magnitude may be one, that which is called "the same" in each individual part has no shared connection of "common feeling" <note>Latin: *communionem ad compatiendum*; Greek: *ὁμοπάθεια* (homopatheia). This is a technical term for the "sympathy" or shared sensation between parts of a living organism.</note>. In those cases, the "same" thing is actually one thing and then another. For that kind of "sameness" is a mere property, not an essence in itself. But that which we say exists in this middle nature—the one that proceeds from the indivisible essence—is itself an essence. It joins with bodies and it happens to be divided by them, yet it does not suffer this division until it has already given itself over to the bodies. Therefore, when it is present in bodies—even if it is present in a massive and widely extended body—it remains one as it accommodates itself to the whole.

<column-break/>

...and the masses, each of which has its own place; and it is not possible for the same thing to be in more than one place at the same time. But there is another being, which is entirely opposite to this essence: it does not admit division; it is partless and indivisible. It admits no extension, not even in the mind's eye. It has no need of a "where" <note>Greek: *ποῦ* (pou). A category of location.</note>, nor does it come to be in any existing thing, whether by parts or as a whole. Rather, it is mounted upon all beings together—not so that <margin>* in the same way</margin> it may be established within them, but because other things cannot exist without it. Nor do they wish to. This essence <margin>according to</margin> is always the same, the common ground of all things that follow it, like a center in a circle from which all the lines around the circumference are hung. These lines allow the center to remain by itself, for they have their existence and being from it; they participate in the point, and their principle is that which is indivisible. They have come forth from it by attaching themselves to it. Thus, while that which is primarily indivisible belongs to the intelligible beings and is their principle, and while those things in the sensible world are divisible in this way, there is another nature that is near the intelligible but not the same as it. It is divisible, but not primarily so like bodies; it becomes divisible only when it enters bodies. So, when bodies are divided, the form within them is also divided, yet it remains a whole in each of the divided parts, becoming many of the same thing. Each of these parts is entirely separate from the others, since the form has become completely divisible; such are colors and all qualities. Every shape likewise, which cannot be a whole in many separate places at once, nor has even a part of itself that experiences what another part suffers—therefore, this must be placed in the category of the entirely divisible. But on the other hand, next to that entirely indivisible nature, there is another essence coming from it, possessing indivisibility from its source. But proceeding from that source toward the "other nature," it has taken its place in the middle of both: between the indivisible and primary nature, and the nature which is divisible in and around bodies. It does not exist in the same way as color or quality, which is the same in many places across many bodily masses; for that which is in each mass is separate. Even if there is a single magnitude, the "same" thing in each part has no communion of shared feeling: because that "sameness" is one thing here and another there. For such sameness is a property (*pathēma*), not an essence (*ousia*) itself. But that which we say is of this middle nature—derived from the indivisible essence—is itself an essence, and it enters into bodies. It happens to be divided around them, but it does not suffer this until it gives itself to the bodies. In whatever bodies it enters, even if it is divided across a vast distance, it does not depart from itself in the whole...

<summary>Plotinus defines the Soul as a "middle nature" that bridges the gap between the indivisible, spiritual world (the Intellect) and the divisible, material world (bodies). He uses the metaphor of a circle's center and its radii to explain how the Soul remains unified while extending into the multiplicity of the physical world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s discussion of the soul’s unique position between the physical and the spiritual. It explores how the soul can be "one" and "many" at the same time, refuting the idea that it is simply a physical substance or a single point within the body.</meta>

### BOOK TWO.

<columns>
...it does not cease to be one. But it is not one in the same way as a body. For a body is one by being continuous, yet each of its parts is distinct, 
<margin>* But it is as a quality</margin>
one part here and another there, or in different positions.* It is also one as a quality; but the nature that is at once divisible and indivisible—which we indeed say is the soul—is not one in the sense of a continuous thing having one part here and another there. Rather, it is divisible because it exists in all parts of the body in which it resides, but it is indivisible because it is whole in all parts and whole in any part of it. And whoever sees this, seeing the magnitude of the power of the soul, will perceive how divine and wondrous a thing its nature is, and that it belongs to those natures that are above material things. Although it possesses no physical size, it is present in every magnitude; it is both here 
<margin>* But it is</margin>
and there, and yet again *it is not there; not as another thing, but as the very same thing. Thus, it is divided and not divided within itself. Or rather, it is not divided within itself, nor has it become divided. For it remains whole within itself. It is only said to be divided among bodies according to the bodies’ own division, as they are capable of receiving it only in an indivisible way; thus, the division is an experience <note>Greek: *pathemata*. Refers to something that happens to a thing, a "passive experience" or "affection."</note> of the bodies, not of the soul.

<margin>* The nature of the soul</margin>
That it was necessary for the nature of the soul *to be of such a kind, and that it is impossible for a soul to be anything other than this—either only divisible, or not only divisible, but necessarily both a pattern of what is generated—is clear from the following. For if it were like bodies, having one part here and another there, <gloss>then</gloss> if one part were to experience something, the other part would not come to a sensation of that experience. Rather, that soul, such as the one in the finger, would be like a different soul existing by itself, sensing the experience there. In short, there would be many souls governing each of us; and indeed, this universe would not be ruled by one soul, but by an infinite number of souls separate from one another. For if a continuous thing does not result in a single unity, it is in vain. We must also address what people say to deceive themselves: that the senses travel to a "ruling part" <note>Greek: *hegemonikon*. The Stoic term for the commanding part of the soul, often thought to be located in the heart or brain.</note> by a process of transmission. First of all, to speak of a "ruling part" of the soul is said without examination. For how will they divide it, and say one part is this and another part is that? By what quantity or measure of mass will they distinguish each, or by what difference of quality, when it is a single and continuous mass? And will only the ruling part perceive, or will the other parts also have sensation? If only the ruling part perceives, then if a sensation falls upon it while it is established in some specific place, it will perceive; but if the sensation falls upon another part of the soul designed to sense, that part will not transmit the same experience to the ruling part, and there will be no sensation at all. And if a sensation should fall upon the ruling part itself, it will fall upon one specific part of it, and while that part perceives, the rest will not. For it would be in vain, or there would be many and infinite sensations. And they would not all be alike; rather, one would say, "I felt it first," and another, "the other..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...nature <note>The Latin text here picks up the end of the word *naturam* from the previous page: *-rum*.</note> it does not cease to be. Nor is it one in the same way a body is one: for a body is one by a certain continuity, but the parts are truly distinct from one another and are arranged in different places. Nor, again, is it one in the way a single quality is one. Truly, this nature which is at once divisible and indivisible—which we say is the soul—is not one like a continuous thing that has one part here and another there, but it is indeed divisible because <margin>B</margin> it communicates itself to all parts of that in which it resides. It is indivisible, however, because it is whole in all parts and whole in any portion of it. Whoever looks upon this more clearly, and rightly considers the magnitude and power of the soul, will understand how divine and how wondrous a treasure the soul is, and that its nature exists above all other treasures. For since it is free from physical magnitude, it is present to the whole of magnitude; and though existing in one place, it is again not existing there—not as something else, but as the very same thing. So it is both divided into parts and yet not divided; or rather, <margin>C</margin> it is neither divided nor does it become divided. For it remains whole within itself, but it is said to be divided around bodies, since bodies cannot receive it in an indivisible way due to their own divisibility. Thus it happens that the partition is not an experience of the soul, but of the bodies.

<margin>D</margin> That it must be that the nature of the soul is such, and that there cannot be a soul besides this, but that it is necessary for the soul to exist as neither only indivisible nor only divisible, but rather that it must be both in this manner, can be made manifest to us through these points. In the first place, if it were such as <margin>Arguments confirming what was said above. Also, how sensation, experience, and judgment occur.</margin> bodies are, having one part here and another there, then if one part were to suffer, the other part would not at all arrive at a sensation of the suffering part. Instead, that soul, such as that which is in the finger, would be like another soul existing in itself and would feel the suffering there. There would also be many souls governing any one of us. Furthermore, this universe would not be ruled by one certain soul, but rather by diverse and innumerable souls acting among themselves. For what someone might claim regarding <margin>E</margin> continuity is seen to be empty unless it leads back and is reduced to a unity. For we must not admit what many say, deceiving themselves: that the senses arrive at the "ruling part" <note>Latin: *principale*; Greek: *hegemonikon*.</note> of the soul by a certain step-by-step continued succession. First of all, to speak of a "principal part" of the soul is proposed without consideration. For in what way will they divide it? How will they affirm this is one thing and that is another? And how will they designate one part as more "principal" than another? By what rule of quantity will they discern each, or by what difference will they mark it, where there is both one quality and a continuous mass? Furthermore, will only the principal part sense, <margin>F</margin> or will the other parts sense as well? If they say "only," then it will only sense if the sensible experience meets the principal part located in its own proper seat. But if the sensation falls upon another part of the soul that lacks sensation, that part will not translate the same experience to the principal part, nor will a sense-perception be produced at all. Then truly, if the experience reaches the principal part, it will fall either upon a part of it, <margin>G</margin> and thus, with that part sensing, the rest will not sense at all; otherwise, it would be superfluous, or certainly there would be many and innumerable perceptions of the senses, and dissimilar ones at that. For in one place it would be said, as it were, "I am the first to suffer," and in another, "I have now felt that another..."

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul is a unique entity that is simultaneously divisible and indivisible, allowing it to be present as a whole throughout the entire body. He refutes the idea that the soul is a physical substance divided into parts, as this would make unified sensation and consciousness impossible.</summary>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK IV.

<margin>A</margin>
...of the previous affection <note>original Latin: *passione*; refers to a sensory experience or "suffering" an external stimulus.</note>, and where exactly the affection was inflicted, any sense-perception will be ignorant except for the first; or perhaps every part of the soul will be equally deceived, thinking that the affection occurred wherever that part itself is located. But if it is not only the principal part <term>principal part: the *hegemonikon* or "ruling" center of the soul</term> that feels, but every other part as well, then why should this part be the principal one, and that one not at all? And why must the sensation travel to that principal part? Furthermore, how can the things that flow together from many senses—such as from the ears and the eyes—recognize a single thing? 
<margin>B</margin>
However, if the soul existed as strictly one, as something entirely indivisible and consisting as a unity within itself, having escaped the nature of multitude and division entirely, then surely no body grasped by the soul would be animated as a whole. Instead, the soul, stabilizing itself as if around a center point, would leave the remaining mass of the body entirely lifeless. It is necessary, therefore, that the soul be both one and many, and divisible and indivisible at the same time; 
<margin>C</margin>
nor should we doubt it, as if it were impossible for one and the same thing to be present in many places at once. For unless we admit this, the nature that contains and governs all things—which indeed embraces everything at once and leads them with wisdom—will exist nowhere. Being a multitude, since beings are many, yet also being one, so that there is one thing that contains them; surely through its "one-multiple" aspect it supplies life to all parts, while through its "one-indivisible" aspect it leads them wisely. But in those things where wisdom is not present, this "one" mimics the principal part. This is what is divinely, though 
<margin>D</margin>
obscurely, stated by Plato in this manner: "The Architect of the world, out of the indivisible essence which is always in the same state, and the essence which becomes divisible around bodies, mixed a third type of essence from both." <note>A reference to Plato's *Timaeus* 35a, describing the creation of the Soul.</note> Thus, the soul is one and many in this way; the forms <note>Platonic "forms" or "ideals" that give shape to matter.</note> that are in bodies are many and one at the same time; bodies, however, are only many; and finally, that which is supreme is only one.

<column-break/>

...of the affection <note>original Greek: *pathema*</note>; and where the affection occurred, each part would be ignorant, except for the first. Or each part of the soul will be deceived, imagining that it happened wherever that part is. But if not only the ruling part <note>original Greek: *hegemonikon*</note> but any part whatever shall perceive, why should one be the ruling part and another not? Or why must the sensation go to that one? And how shall the things from many senses, such as ears and eyes, know any one thing? But if, on the other hand, the soul were entirely one, as something indivisible—if it were entirely one in itself and entirely escaped the nature of multitude and division—then no whole body grasped by the soul would be animated; but as if standing itself around a center, it would leave all the bulk of the living being lifeless. It is necessary then, in this way, for the soul to be both many and divided, and also undivided; and not to distrust that it is impossible for the same thing to be in many places. For if we do not accept this, the nature which holds together and manages all things would be nothing; that which holds all things together at once and leads them with prudence <note>original Greek: *phronesis*</note>. It will be a multitude, since beings are many; but one, so that it may be that which contains them. By its "one-multitude," it provides life to all the parts; by its "one-undivided," it leads them prudently. And in those things which have no prudence, this mimics the ruling part. This then is what was divinely spoken: from the indivisible and always unchanging essence, and the divisible essence that comes to be around bodies, He mixed a third kind of essence from both. Therefore, the soul is one and many in this way; the forms in bodies are many and one; but bodies are only many; and that which is highest is only one.

### MARSILIO FICINO'S COMMENTARY ON THE FIRST BOOK CONCERNING THE DOUBTS OF THE SOUL.
### SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.
->That our souls differ from the World Soul, and are not derived from it.<-

The first book on the doubts of the soul contains seven principal questions. The **first** asks whether our souls are from the World Soul <note>The *Anima Mundi*, a soul that animates the entire universe in Neoplatonic thought.</note>, either as parts of it or as something produced by it. The **second**, in what way the soul is introduced into the body—namely, by what property, in what different order, and by what law of justice. The **third**, whether the soul living outside the body uses a certain discourse of reason. The **fourth**, in what way something in the soul is said to be indivisible and divisible at the same time. The **fifth**, whether the soul is in a place in some way, and under what condition it is in the body. The **sixth**, where the soul is when it is separate from the body. The **seventh**, whether souls separated from here remember human affairs, and generally concerning memory and reminiscence. Perhaps someone will suspect that our souls are certain parts of the World Soul, and will assert this from three sayings of Plato. First, indeed, what he seems to suggest in the *Philebus*: just as our bodies are parts of the world's body, so also our souls are parts of its soul. Next, also what he seems to believe in the *Republic*, the *Phaedrus*, and the *Timaeus* alike: that our souls follow the circuit of the whole world, and from there receive their characters and fortunes. Finally, what he says in the *Phaedrus*: that our soul also has care for all that is inanimate. This common care, however, seems to belong only to the soul of the world. Moreover, it seems likely that humans born within the world obtain life from the world, and have certain portions of the total life. Indeed, I have removed this suspicion to the best of my ability in my *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his own work, *Platonic Theology*.</note>, where I argue against Averroes <note>Averroes was a medieval Islamic philosopher who famously argued that all humans share a single, universal intellect.</note>. And here, to similarly root out the same idea, let us first argue with Plato in this way. Form is more excellent...

# ON BOOK III. ENNEAD IV.

...than matter, and the whole than its parts: therefore, if a material whole is granted, a formal whole <term>formal whole: a totality defined by its organizing principle or essence, rather than just its physical components</term> is also granted. Likewise, if a whole is made of parts, then a whole is also made of wholes. For since the universe is constructed by the highest reason and in the best possible way, whatever true reason concludes to be the best state of affairs already exists in the universe; for it is from the universe that reason draws such conjectures. A material whole is exemplified by a piece of wood: for even if it is multiplied into parts by physical division, it is not multiplied into distinct forms. A formal whole is exemplified by a tree: for it is divided into many forms that are clearly different from one another <note>e.g., roots, bark, leaves, and fruit all share the "tree" form but have distinct sub-forms</note>. In this formal whole, there is also a true material whole: for because it is distinguished into different particular forms, it is also in some way distinguished into different matters, specifically by their own differing forms. Since, therefore, the world is the most absolute whole, it is certainly a formal whole, and a whole made of wholes. However, it will not be a whole made of wholes unless there are many things in it that are not only different in form, as in a tree, but also distinct according to their existence and separated by their actions: like singers in a choir, where each one both harmonizes with the others in a common duty toward the same goal, and meanwhile remains individual, existing by his own right. Not only does the perfection of this world demand it be a true whole made of truly whole things, but the imitation of the archetypal model <term>exemplary imitation: the Neoplatonic idea that our physical world copies an ideal, divine "Intellectual World"</term> requires it: for that higher whole is also composed of wholes. There, in each thing, all things exist in different ways; but in this world, the condition of this work—subject to dimension, place, motion, and time—further introduces a local separation of things. Finally, where the parts are themselves "perfections," the whole is more perfect. Those parts are perfections which have their own existence and their own duty. Thus, the whole is more "formal" where the parts are more formal. These parts are more formal when they are more distinguished by the forms and extensions of their own substance and actions. To make the whole truly one, the order of all things—proceeding equally from the One and directed toward the One—is surely sufficient. From these points, it appears improbable that this world-machine possesses only a single soul; rather, it is more probable that many souls are present, and many living beings besides the World Soul and the world-animal. Indeed, we conjecture that there is a proper substance of our soul in us, different from the World Soul itself, from the fact that our mind possesses its own free and voluntary motion of judgment. We have dealt with this matter sufficiently when discussing free will in our *Theology* <note>original: *Theologia*; referring to Ficino's own work, *Platonic Theology*</note>. Otherwise, if the soul were merely a part of the whole, it would be suddenly swept away by the impulse of the whole; it would not be capable of rational discourse or counsel, nor could it err, since the World Soul cannot err. Plato undoubtedly posits free will in us in the tenth book of the *Republic*, in the *Timaeus*, and the *Phaedrus* <note>The OCR reads "Thimæo atq; Timæo," likely a typo for *Phaedrus* or *Philebus*</note>, and Aristotle confirms it everywhere. To posit that our souls are parts of the World Soul is nothing other than saying that your soul is the entire World Soul, and mine likewise. For that soul cannot be divided into various portions, but is entirely indivisible and exactly the same everywhere at once. But since my soul and yours now completely disagree in actions, opinions, affections, and habits, they cannot exist as the same soul and the same mind. Furthermore, if my mind is in any way a part of the World Soul, it does not have its own existence, nor does it have its own action. Therefore, it does not reflect upon itself, nor can it perceive itself; moreover, as a very narrow part, it would not be able to embrace the whole world in thought, nor traverse it, nor think anything beyond this world and its soul. Consider the human body: it is not some continuous portion of the cosmic machine, but is set apart according to its own shape and motion. Since the soul is more excellent than the body and is the origin of this shape and motion, it is certainly not a continuous portion of the World Soul, but possesses its own substance. Furthermore, it was not made by the soul of the cosmic body: for what that soul makes, it makes with a mobile property; and therefore it makes that essence changeable, so that it cannot touch anything immutable. Our mind, however, resolves motion into stillness and subjects mobile things to the immobile. Finally, since our mind is a certain intellectual essence, it is properly produced by the Simple Intellect itself, from which the World Soul is also born (which is itself a kind of "animal" intellect). From this it follows that our soul, like the World Soul, can become capable of understanding and rise to those eternal things which are above the world; however, the remaining souls, other than the intellectual ones, can either arise from or depend upon the World Soul.

->On the double soul, and that our souls are not parts of the world soul.<-

In the second chapter, you will note that any imperfect thing in any genus <term>genus: a class or category of being</term> must be reduced to something perfect placed within that same genus, through which it may be reduced to something perfect above that genus. Therefore, the soul lacking reason, being imperfect—which is both a part of a composite and bound to bodily instruments—must be reduced to the rational and intellectual soul, which is independent and exists perpetually within itself. This must be done both in us and in the demons, the stars, the spheres, and the world. This opinion agrees strongly with the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle</term>, who rightly place two movers in the heavens: one of which is joined to the mobile body as its form and is a "mobile mover"; the other, however, is a mover that is in a way separate, immutable, and the first principle and end of motion. Accordingly, certain illegitimate Platonists, who said that human souls are parts of the World Soul, meanwhile confessed that the World Soul itself is an indivisible, eternal, one, simple substance, entirely present everywhere. Consequently, they added that any human soul is conformable to the World Soul, touching the same things and all things at once that the World Soul touches. Given these points, they cannot cut the World Soul into our souls as a magnitude is divided into small parts or a number into units. For in that way, what is called the "soul of the whole" would perish by such a division, nor would it remain one. Furthermore, they cannot divide it into these souls in the way that the heat of the whole body seems divided into the parts of heat in the limbs; for they maintain that the soul is a substance in the body that is not extended <note>i.e., it has no physical length or width</note>. Yet heat itself is not properly cut, but rather the dimension in which the heat exists; therefore, the heat of any limb is the common heat in a part of the body, rather than a "part" of heat. Nevertheless, it undergoes division by accident in a way, insofar as it is spread equally through the extension of the body; the soul, however, is not like this. For without any extension or dimension of its own, it is present to dimensions so that it may perfectly connect all divisible and distant things into one. Nor can they, again, distribute the World Soul into our souls as a whole science is distributed into its various notions. For if there is no "whole science" besides the notions, then there will never be one common soul; if there is one soul besides them, it will not be suited to the world, but transcendent. Finally, they will claim that our souls are called parts of the World Soul just as if someone were to say that our soul in the hand or foot is a part of our whole soul. Thus, in dividing, they divide nothing, and they completely misuse the word "division." For one and the same soul is present to every limb, entirely and simultaneously everywhere, possessing all its animal powers everywhere, although it exercises different actions through different limbs as if through instruments; the "passions" <note>sensations or things experienced by the body</note> are indeed in the limbs.

He reconciles this Platonic view with Aristotelian physics by distinguishing between movers that are joined to bodies and those that remain separate and immutable.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the individuality of the human soul. Building on the previous argument that the universe is a "whole made of wholes," Ficino now addresses the psychological and theological reasons why each human must possess a distinct, individual soul rather than merely sharing in a single "World Soul" or universal intellect.</meta>

# COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO

The judge of sensory experiences <note>original: "sensibilium passionum"</note> is ultimately one, presenting a single judgment by comparing diverse things, sometimes through imagination and sometimes through reason; this, I say, occurs within us. However, it cannot happen in entirely the same way in the world at large. If one were to imagine that there is only a single soul for all individual things, different men could indeed experience different things—just as currently different organs <note>original: "instrumenta"</note> within each of us experience different things—but in the end, a single judgment would be applied, resulting in the same opinion and the same understanding. For these judgments belong to a judge who is free from the experience itself—provided that he is a true judge of experiences and things. Therefore, the judge stands within himself, in a sense segregated from those who are experiencing, and is thus unique and not made diverse by the various instruments used. But in truth, since there are contrary judgments among men, it follows that there are distinct understandings and distinct substances of souls. This is because the rational duty is performed not through external instruments, but through the innermost faculty of the soul's substance.

### Many intellectual souls exist besides the world soul, which are distinguished from one another not by internal boundaries, but by internal ones.

In the third chapter and thereafter, I confirm again that it is impossible for there to be only one soul in the world, as follows. The highest providence of the whole, aiming for the greatest beauty of the universe consisting in order, decreed that there would be various kinds of things and, again, innumerable individuals. Among these, as if across great distances, he willed that there be different species in every genus, loving above all else a wealth of species as things that are quite perfect. If, in the lower categories, the soul has arranged order as much as possible across the levels of species, why would it not strive for an equal abundance in the nature and genus of the soul itself? Why would it not arrange a similar order of levels through different species of souls? This is especially true since the nature of the soul itself—because of its condition, which is in a way composite, mobile, and adapted to bodies—is capable of being multiplied and propagated through bodies. Furthermore, the nature of the mind <note>original: "mentis"</note> itself, which does not exclude a certain composition but rather includes one, is able to be derived into many minds. Regarding the marvelous number of minds, enough has been said in the first parts of my *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his major work, *Platonic Theology on the Immortality of the Soul*</note>, through which the number of souls is also confirmed. Finally, only the first principle of the universe itself remains one because of the supreme simplicity of the First; but the rest are divided into various species of intelligence and modes of understanding that pertain most greatly to the common good of the whole. However, the nature of the soul cannot hold the first or second rank in the order of things, but necessarily the third, as our *Theology* sufficiently proves. Therefore, it is not forced to be one, nor should it be, nor finally can it be.

Furthermore, since Plato asserts that the World Soul is always in a body and always leads the same life, while our souls are sometimes separated from bodies and, when separated, subsist in a different state and live in a condition different from one another, and according to their own choices obtain different bodies again, and finally live dissimilarly by their own will, and after death obtain different levels of living according to the diversity of their lives—which Platonist could possibly suspect the soul to be only one? 

Indeed, if anyone should ever suspect, in the manner of Averroes <note>Averroes (1126–1198) was an Islamic philosopher who famously argued that all humans share a single, universal "active intellect." Ficino strongly opposed this "Monopsychism."</note>, that there is a single intellect in all men, we would certainly not raise doubts against him in the same way we do regarding the soul. We would not primarily object by asking how one intellect could be in the body and another outside the body, or how entirely similar intellects could exist in such different bodies, as we were just saying about the soul. For souls, as they incline toward bodies, differ not only by their internal differences but also through various actions concerning various bodies and through the diversity of the bodies themselves. But if we are to prove that intellects (which are more separate than souls) differ from each other even when they perform their own actions without bodily instruments, we will not fly to the variety of bodies or such actions. Instead, we will look to the different species of intelligence and the widely varying modes of understanding, as well as the understandings and habits that are at odds with each other at the same time, which could not exist simultaneously in a single intellect. Just as in the first Intellect we assign differences between its many notions only from the internal diversity of their formal properties, so when we are about to assign the differences between other intellects, we shall bring them forth from their innermost properties. 

For it is fitting that there should be many species of minds and intelligence, if the nature of bodies—which is far inferior to minds—is so rich that there are many species of metals, more of plants, and the most of animals. From this it appears that there are very many of both demons and minds, whatever their nature may be. Furthermore, it is not fitting to distribute the nature of the soul itself (which is of an indivisible substance and perpetually subsists in itself) into many souls and then merge many into one again, just as we divide a large amount of water into parts and سپس blend them back into the same whole. Nor should we derive many from one soul in the same way we distribute the single light of the sun into many homes through windows, only to have it resolved back into the same light shortly after. For visible light depends entirely on its source in the manner of an "accident" <term>accident: a philosophical term for a quality that does not exist on its own but must belong to a substance, like the color of an apple</term>, and does not retain its own subsistence. But the genus of intelligible and intellectual light is far different from this; it is not an accident, but a most absolute substance. 

Therefore, if it has different levels within itself, it does not receive them from the outside like accidental forms, but from within. According to its different properties, it admits many "subsistences" (so to speak) and preserves them in the same genus, distinct by species and free from confusion. In this category of intellectual substance and light, you shall place the rational souls. You will recognize how they differ from one another, and that they are never confused into one in the manner of cheaper liquids. You must recognize that such souls are to the life of the world what certain traces of life are in animals born from plants. For they run through the life of the universe by their action, and transcend it by their affection. Do not imagine that they differ in no way from the World Soul, as if they were certain offshoots of it through the body of the world; nor that my soul differs from yours only because the bodies through which the propagation was made differ from each other; nor that both differ from the World Soul only as a root or the first plant differs from its offshoots. If that were so, the intellectual soul of Socrates himself would have to be resolved into the World Soul after death (as some imagine), and while it would lose its own existence, it would cease to be entirely when it approached "perfect being." 

But intellectual nature does not allow this. It does not need external boundaries for its distinction, like liquids and light, but being more exact, it is distributed into its own species and existing boundaries by its internal nature. It has been sufficiently proven in my *Theology* that the rational soul, insofar as it is intellectual, is more perfect the further it separates itself from the body—more perfect, I say, in relation to its own substance and its peculiar property. Since it is most greatly separated from the body at death, then it is truly necessary that the substance of this soul be perfect. Thus, let no one imagine that individual minds are at any time merged into one or suddenly destroyed.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus' Enneads. Having established that individual souls are distinct, Ficino now explores the metaphysical mechanism of this distinction, arguing that souls are separated by their essential nature (their "Ideas" in the Divine Mind) rather than by physical or accidental circumstances.</meta>

<header>ON BOOK III [OF THE ENNEADS], BOOK IV</header>

### Intellectual souls are distinguished from each other not by accidental traits, but by their own essential ones: and how many souls are said to be one, and from one.

Since the first intellect and the first essence are one and the same, it is right that all intellects are true essences. Therefore, they are distributed among themselves by true differences—that is, not by "accidents" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a non-essential quality, like being tall or sitting down, which can change without changing what a thing is.</note> or by boundaries taken from the outside (like parts of a continuous object or material shapes), but they are distinguished by the unique and innermost differences and limits according to the dignity of their own self-subsisting essences. For one thing is more truly distinguished from another if it differs by its formal property <note>The "formal property" is the internal blueprint or "recipe" of what a thing is.</note> than if it is divided by matter, accident, or location. 

Therefore, any intellect possesses its own essence and being in a certain innermost identity and—if I may put it this way—"otherness." I say "identity" insofar as it is a most simple form, never falling away from its simplicity; and "otherness" again, insofar as such a form is distinguished by its very self from every other thing and every other intellect. If it is distinguished primarily and of itself, it remains forever distinct and far from confusion. Imagine in the Divine Mind a "Great Soul"—that is, the general Idea of intellectual souls—in which the specific kinds of souls are also conceived. That Idea is a certain intellect there, and these specific kinds are also certain intellects there. 

However, these "Ideal" intellects are distinguished among themselves there not by having different existences (for there is only one substance so far), but by a certain rational principle and formal property. If such essential properties are thought of as proceeding outward, they suddenly become more distinct; they are then distinguished by their existences. For they are so effective on the inside that they produce on the outside not something accidental, but substance itself—diverse substances formed according to the diversity of their rational principles. 

Such substances, emerging closest to the first Intellect, exist primarily as intellectual beings. But because they themselves are also very effective at internal conception, each one expresses in itself a certain property—moving from the intellectual level to the "animating" <note>The "animal" or animating level refers to the soul's power to give life to a body.</note> level—and is more distinctly divided into many. Just as a ray flashes out from a spark, or as a complex spoken word is produced from the simpler, innermost thought of the imagination, so do many souls (both of the world and of others) proceed outward from the one Ideal Soul. Although these are different substances, they are nonetheless one among themselves in three main ways: first, because they are all under the same Idea; second, because they are not separated by places or times; and third, because through their intellectual "peaks," each is formed by one and the same Divine Intellect and they all perpetually meet in that same Intellect. I will set aside for now the fact that they all naturally contribute to the same end of universal providence.

### How every rational soul is all things, and how the species of rational souls differ among themselves.

The highest principle of all, because of its supreme simplicity, is above all things; yet because of its power, it immediately brings all things into being. Therefore, the Intellect—which is its "son"—is the "First All," and thus it is everything perfectly. Consequently, every Idea within it is all Ideas. The soul, therefore, proceeding naturally and most closely from its own Idea, draws all things into itself; thus, every intellectual soul is a universe. 

I confirm this whole point again: the first and simplest thing in any category contains everything within that category. Since the first Intellect is the "first form," it is rightly both uniform and "omni-form" (all-formed). Thus, every rational soul, insofar as it is intellectual, is not only a most simple form but is also all-formed—it is all things in "actuality," just as the Intellect itself is all things in actuality. 

However, insofar as the soul becomes not so much intellectual as "animating," it retains the same function by which it is still all things; but retaining it less perfectly, it is now a universe in "potentiality." This is fitting, for when God placed the soul in the middle of things, He tempered it out of everything. 

He tempered the different species of souls in such a way that the Soul of the World (the universal life of the world) would always be turned toward the universal Intellect, and do so universally and most attentively. From this, it follows that it always carries out the universal providence of the whole, and does so with miraculous power and ease—since all power comes from on high. 

The remaining heavenly souls after this one would also turn toward the universal Intellect, yet not so universally nor with equal attention; therefore, they perform a providence that is neither as universal nor as powerful. Finally, the souls lower than these were so constituted that they might sometimes turn themselves toward the universal Intellect—and then do so more or less universally or attentively; thus at times they concur more with universal providence, and at other times less, and with less power. 

Likewise, they sometimes bend themselves not so much toward the universal Intellect as toward their own individual intellect, and then they exist less perfectly. Sometimes they turn toward reason, where they are even less perfect; and sometimes they fall very much toward the imagination and become the most degraded. In short: when the rational soul unfolds the universe within itself, it is admitted into the universal providence of the World Soul; but when it gradually falls from its universal duty and directs itself to a partial duty, it undergoes a particular care, puts on its own body more fully, and labors more.

### Doubts are answered, and it is proven that rational souls are not from the world soul.

Plato, intending to prove in the *Philebus* that the world is an animated being, says: "From where would our body—which is composed of parts of the elements—get a soul, unless the world—which is composed of the whole elements—possessed a soul?" That is to say, the Intellect (the builder of the world) was not so unwise as to give a soul to us but not to the world—especially since the World Soul, through its universal influence, was to prepare the "seminal matter" of living things to receive their own souls from wherever they might come. 

Therefore, our body has an intellectual soul from no other source than the world does—namely, from the same builder of the world. It also has a sensory soul, largely from our intellectual soul, with the World Soul contributing to this from the start. We also maintain that rational souls do not come *from* the World Soul, but from the same Author from whom it came, and that they are constituted from similar "genera" (kinds). These souls are not the World Soul, nor its parts, nor its powers, but are arranged by God in different species and grades. This is why Plato introduces these souls as falling into bodies and wandering, and then leaving them—something that cannot happen to the World Soul. 

He says in the *Phaedrus* that whenever a particular soul (which is also the universe in potential) turns itself toward the universal form through actual thinking and loving outside this body, it too is admitted to the universal providence of the world, being endowed from the beginning with a celestial body. Indeed, even in a decaying body, the contemplative philosopher and the statesman experience this as much as they are able. Therefore, wherever Plato seems to imply that souls follow the celestial motion, he adds there and elsewhere that they are also able *not* to follow it. It has also been proven,

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Enneads. Having previously discussed the distinction between individual souls, Ficino now delves into the specific ways souls differ from one another and provides a metaphysical argument for their immortality based on their "simple" or non-composite nature.</meta>

->COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO<-

[It is possible] through prudence, art, and character to resist the influences of the heavens. From this it appears that if there is any life in us that follows at the heels of the body—and through this serves fate—this life can depend on the soul of the world’s body. However, that soul in us which resists bodily incitements and worldly impulses descends from a higher place than the world. And yet, if we are born within the world, we nevertheless have a superior soul from elsewhere, which even measures the world. For even a fetus in the womb receives another soul besides the mother’s soul, and it possesses a soul from a source other than the mother.

### *How souls differ, and how they are immortal while remaining in their*
### *own proper form, and how the soul of the world, present everywhere,*
### *leads all things to life.*

In the eighth chapter, you will consider these points first: in order for our souls to agree so closely with one another and with the soul of the world—to the point that they are often affected by a similar instinct, and an impulse flows easily from some into others, and particular souls are secretly moved by the universal soul—it is not at all necessary that our souls be the offspring of the world soul. For this consensus and "shared feeling" <note>original: "compassionem"</note> is sufficiently explained by the common origin of both the worldly soul and other souls from the same divine Mind, the same general "Idea" <note>The "Idea" refers to the perfect, eternal blueprint of the Soul existing in the mind of God.</note> of souls, and a similar process of emergence. Accordingly, there are four chief differences among human souls: 

They differ, first, when counted according to the differences of bodies, when they seem to have more or less excited movements according to the differences of blood, bile, and spirit <note>This refers to the "humoral theory" of medicine, where personality was thought to be shaped by bodily fluids.</note>. They are said to differ, second, from a preceding life: if it be true that this soul is now more ready for action and that one for contemplation, because this one led a very busy life before birth, while that one led an entirely contemplative one. Third, the Platonists think they differ in some way by their natural "species" from the beginning: even if human souls fall under the same immediate "genus," they differ among themselves by certain species—even by the smallest possible differences—by which they are distributed from a highest grade through a second, third, or fourth. Finally, they think souls differ because any rational soul, though it is a "universe" in itself, can nevertheless affect itself in different ways through a certain free movement; thus one soul turns itself to the contemplative life, another to the active, and another to the life of pleasure. And among those who betake themselves to contemplation, some choose this form of contemplation, and others choose that one above the rest; and whatever they have chosen, they soon put on as if it were their nature. 

Although every soul is "all things," this kind of equality does not make souls equal to each other without any distinction. For in the first Mind, there is a common and "ideal" principle <note>original: "ratio"</note> of souls—not merely an individual one, but a very general one—possessing various grades of ideal souls within itself, whose number is followed by an equal number of souls and a similar order. And just as in the divine Mind this specific Idea is "all things" in one way, and that Idea is "all things" in another, so this soul is "all things" differently than that soul, and uses its universe differently. 

Furthermore, it is agreeable to reason that things composed of the four elements can be resolved back into pure elements; and if the lesser elements cannot exist entirely apart from the more excellent ones, at least the more excellent can exist somewhere apart from the lesser in their own purity. Similarly, a thing composed of matter and form—as if from twin elements—can be resolved in a way into pure matter, or be reduced entirely to some form that is pure in itself. This form would exist through itself and in itself without matter, even though matter cannot exist far from all form. Just as a formal element (as I said) exists far from a material one, though the reverse does not happen, intellectual souls are numbered among this kind of "form." 

Such a form is a "simple essence," <note>A "simple" essence is one that is not made of parts; because it has no parts, it cannot be broken or "dissolved," making it immortal.</note> possessing its own being through itself and in itself; in this essence, its "being" is the same as its "essential unity." The essence of composite things, however, is the opposite: in them, the essence and the "being" (which consists of a multitude of parts) are one thing, while "unity" is another. Unity, as unity, does not admit a multitude, and "being" there follows the union, which unity precedes. From this you may understand that the form of the soul itself—whose being is the same as its essential unity—is entirely indissoluble, just as unity is indissoluble. Especially since, if being is everywhere in things through "form," it follows that a simple form subsisting in itself continues its own being in itself forever. 

Moreover, if a simple form not mixed with matter were to be lost, it would be reduced to nothing; if it were to be generated, it would be generated from nothing—but physical reason itself does not allow this. Therefore, the soul is eternal. Above all, if it must be fashioned from something, yet cannot be from any material thing, God its author would be forced to procreate it from his own substance; hence he would be forced to be changeable, especially if he should ever do what he had not done before. Plotinus signifies these things to assert that the soul is eternal; to what extent these things should be affirmed, enough has been said in our *Theology* <note>Ficino refers here to his own major work, *Platonic Theology on the Immortality of Souls*.</note>. 

Among these points, note that each of these forms is a certain numerical "one" in itself, distinct from others not by accident, but by itself. I say "by itself" because souls do not receive their number from the number of bodies or of bodily qualities—as if the one soul of the world were propagated into many through the different conditions of bodies. Now, indeed, any soul subsists through itself as always "one" in number, just as it has its "being" in its essence, and its being is the same as its unity. Therefore, just as the essence of the soul is eternal (as something simple and consisting in itself), so also is every singular "being" of that soul, since its being is only in its own essence. Likewise, just as being is eternal, so also is every numerical unity, since there "to be" is the same as "to be some one thing." For a simple essence remaining in itself is distinguished not by external things, but by internal ones. Thus, no one is permitted to dream that our souls, once their personal properties are dismissed, lose their unity, unless they were to draw this unity from the soul [of the world] as from a perpetual fountain of generation. 

Therefore, the soul—as something far more excellent—always retains within itself its own numerical unity, not only a "species" unity <note>Species unity means being the same "kind" (like all humans being one species); numerical unity means being a unique, individual "self."</note>. Indeed, just as composite things which are dissolved return as exactly the same in species when similar times return, so the soul—changing its form within itself in a way, yet being more excellent than the body—returns at some time to the same number, the same body, and the same person. 

After this, where it is asked how a simple and intellectual form (whether the world soul or our own) is sometimes called "infinite," the answer is: not because it can be divided into infinity, but because it flourishes without end, and can act everywhere and always. Thus, the soul of the world is neither divided into infinite souls, nor stretched out in the manner of a bodily quality (as far as the mass of the world extends), but remains unique; and no matter how much any part of the body can receive from it, the soul itself gives life everywhere as a whole. Our souls also do not become as many in number as...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on the fourth book of Plotinus's fourth Ennead. Ficino is exploring the relationship between the universal Soul of the World and individual souls, specifically how the soul remains unified even when present in a divided, physical body.</meta>

->ON THE FOURTH BOOK OF THE FOURTH ENNEAD<-

[Souls are not] in bodily portions and qualities; thus they are not stretched out into a physical mass, nor are they extended across matter in the manner of whiteness. Instead, there are as many souls as there are inner properties, and however much mass is prepared for their influx, they form it into a certain indivisible whole that is everywhere complete and possesses perpetual vigor. Nor is our soul cut into many souls, whether because of different limbs or even if some limb is amputated. In the same way, the Soul of the World is neither divided within itself nor does it become many souls just because the parts of the world are divided among themselves. For this Soul remains one; no matter how much a living part of the world is separated, the Soul is still present as a whole in both parts simultaneously. It is also in the middle <note>In Neoplatonic cosmology, the "middle" often refers to the mediation between the spiritual and material realms.</note> because of the continuity of primary matter—or rather, because of the "fifth essence" <note>original: "essentiæ quintæ," referring to Aether, the celestial element</note>, which is the proper vessel for the soul. 

Among these points, if it seems to anyone that Plotinus—regarding plants and animals born from putrefaction <note>The ancient belief in "spontaneous generation," where life was thought to arise from decaying matter.</note>—posits no soul other than the World Soul, be careful not to concede that easily. For he himself seems to refute this in the book *On the Immortality of the Soul*. You will say, therefore, that the Soul of the World is indeed present to all such things, and is not forced to become many souls because of multiple sections and living beings. Yet, in the meantime, this is not the *only* life they have, even though the World Soul generates lives and souls within them. Indeed, if these souls are said by certain Platonists (and by Plotinus himself in some places) to be eternal according to their own proper substances, then they are not born for the first time from the Soul of the World; rather, they are infused into those things generated by the World Soul's universal instinct. 

One might also say that every life is indeed perpetual, but that souls—if there are any such souls that lack their own motion—subsist after death not so much in themselves as in the "common life" <note>The shared, universal source of all life.</note>. However, those souls which produce their own motions, especially if they are free motions, also preserve their own proper form through themselves perpetually. Always remember that, besides the specific lives of living creatures, there lies beneath all things a common vegetative power from the Soul of the World, flourishing everywhere throughout the "World Tree." This power prepares matter for individual souls, preserves them for a certain time, and unites all living things into one. The Pythagoreans—according to Sextus Empiricus <note>original: "Sexto Pyrrhonio"</note>—say that this is a spirit infused into all things in the manner of a soul, which unites human beings with other living creatures, and unites those who are already reconciled with the divine powers <note>original: "numinibus"</note> elsewhere. While this common power is already flourishing, the rational soul is added to us at the stage of the fetus. Under this common light, the soul then diffuses the light of its own peculiar life into the body; at death, it withdraws its own life into itself, just as the Soul of the World preserves its own common life.

## In how many ways the soul is introduced into the body, what the nature of the World Soul is, how it makes the world and its dimensions, and how it is everywhere.

In the ninth chapter of the book, where the second question begins regarding how the soul is introduced <note>original: "insinuatur," literally "folded into"</note> into the body, you will notice that this happens primarily in two ways. For it comes into the body either from an incorporeal state or from another body. This second branch of the division is again divided into four parts: namely, it passes either from a liquid body into a liquid one, or from a liquid to a solid, or from a solid to another solid, or from a solid back into a liquid. Here you will note that if, according to Plotinus's opinion, the soul can ever strip off every body, it can be imagined that it will live forever outside the body. Plato signifies this in the *Phaedo*, and Porphyry and Iamblichus suspect it as well. If, however, as Proclus says, it is always in some body, then eternal successions of bodies can consequently be imagined. 

But so that you may understand how your soul—or rather, how the Soul of the World is first introduced into its body—consider the intellectual power in the Soul of the World at its highest point as a rational light, its power in the middle as a splendor, and its vegetative power at the bottom as heat. Furthermore, consider two things regarding its essence. First, insofar as it is something other than those three powers; second, insofar as it is already marked by those three. Now, at the moment it is "something else," it is in a way obscure, shapeless, and cold. Obscure, as it does not yet have the light of intelligence; shapeless, as it does not yet possess the splendor of reason; and cold, as it has not yet attained the warmth of the vegetative nature. 

Imagine, then, that from this needy essence proceeds the primary matter of the world, which is utterly needy, entirely dark, shapeless, and cold. But meanwhile, from the essence insofar as it is marked by those three powers, contemplate the matter of the world proceeding to be immediately adorned: through intelligence, it is adorned with forms that are entirely permanent; through reason, with forms that move with stability; and finally, through the vegetative power, with forms that move changeably. This happens in such a way that those things proceeding from intelligence and reason flow out as naturally as those things born from the vegetative nature. Yet the Soul of the World, thus endowed, in forming the world, does not look toward a moving and, as it were, "generatable" nature or reason as its chief model (as the *Timaeus* suggests)—if indeed the reason is mobile—but rather toward an intellectual Form that is devoid of all generation, whether it be the intelligence of a living being or the Primary Intelligence <note>Refers to the "Nous" or Divine Mind in Neoplatonism.</note>. 

Consider again that the soul, insofar as it is mobile internally, naturally strives to move externally to that same extent. From this striving, matter—having just been born—is immediately stretched out far and wide, so that from the soul's motion flashing outward, the dimension of matter arose, along with the motion of the world. Thus, place and time are born from this simultaneously. Place, which the soul inhabits by "vegetating" <note>In this context, "vegetating" means giving life, growth, and physical existence.</note>; and time, by which it moves that place (that is, the body) through that same life-giving process. In the intellectual Model, a certain dimension of both the world and worldly things was first destined ideally. Toward this destination, such a formal efficacy for motion arose in the vegetative nature that it provides for the world a quantity and size equal to what was prefigured in the Idea of the Mind. 

The soul, through its essence, can be present as a whole to every part of so large a world simultaneously; for this world was made only as large as the soul proceeded in its making. The soul itself is neither a dimension nor a quality extended by dimension; rather, it is something indivisible. It is not like a point marking the end of a dimension somewhere within it, but is something released from it, consisting in itself, outside the entire category of quantity, in a category that is more than substance. It towers over the entire physical mass by the vastest interval of nature and power. Therefore, by this very indivisibility of itself, it possesses the entire mass from every side, yet it is not possessed by the mass.

## How the Soul of the World acts within itself, and thus naturally gives birth to the world, which is as multi-formed as the soul itself.

The tenth chapter teaches that just as the upper air is subject to light, and light is subject to the Sun—yet they are always together from eternity—so the Soul of the World is always subject to the Divine Intellect, and the Intellect to the Good. Likewise, the world always buds naturally from the "seminal" power of its soul, just as any living thing grows from its seed. For they obtain that kind of power from that source. Since the particular nature in any living thing does not require deliberation or any machines for motion and generation, much less does universal nature require them. Nature does and moves all things with a wonderful ease...
