<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, specifically exploring the World Soul's relationship with the material realm and the descent of individual souls into bodies. Ficino uses classical mythology (Dionysus, Osiris, Apollo) to explain Neoplatonic concepts of unity and fragmentation.</meta>

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

Since the entire mass of the world and its form depend upon the World Soul, nothing can anywhere resist it. This is especially true because all things follow a sequence depending on it, so that when the agents are first struck by even the lightest nod <note>original: "nutu," implying a divine command or impulse</note>, everything is soon moved and led toward the action and goal of the **first mover**. Accordingly, things that do not live act only outwardly and on external matter, while they remain inert within themselves. But things that live also act within themselves, and they act perpetually. Therefore, the Soul—especially the World Soul—is the principle of living; it acts always and most powerfully within itself, insofar as its intelligence forms its own **reason** on one hand, and its own **nature** on the other. Indeed, reason naturally runs through its own thoughts, and it swells and delights in the <term>seminal reasons <note>original: "rationes rerum feminales," the formative blueprints or "seeds" of all things, even divine bodies, contained within the Soul.</note></term> of all things. From this innermost rational movement through these seeds of things, a rational form of the world is born, which is similarly all-formed—a form, I say, that is as similar as possible to the Soul itself. For if the generating forces that follow strive to produce things like themselves, then this most immediate creator of the world generates a world as similar to itself as possible.

->On the descent of the soul, Dionysus, Jove, the cycles of lives,<-
->the order of the world, and the harmony of the universe.<-

Here, Plotinus calls Nature itself—that is, the vegetative power of the World Soul—**Dionysus**. The "limbs" of Dionysus are the seminal reasons of things within Nature itself. When these "limbs" proceed into matter through generation, they appear more divided among themselves, torn apart by the **Titans** (that is, the <term>demons <note>In this context, "demons" or "daemons" are not evil spirits but intermediary spiritual beings who preside over the material world.</note></term> appointed over birth). This is like the limbs of **Osiris** (that is, life-giving providence) being torn apart by **Typhon** (the leader of the material demons). 

The souls, therefore, living in a certain divine world, at some point looked out through their *imagination* (which was the lowest part of them) and saw the forms lying in the matter of the world. These forms are images of Dionysus and his limbs in matter, as if in a mirror. They perhaps looked at them by directing a straight affection toward nature, and then turning their gaze toward matter. Wherever the imagination turns itself, the reason immediately turns away from the intellect to follow it—and both do so not just by looking, but by **loving**. Love of this kind was the principle of the soul's descent, and even of its remaining there after the fall, because this material province requires the constant attention of our reason. Meanwhile, however, the **intellect**, which is not touched by such an affection, keeps itself unmoved in the higher world. 

The kindness of **Jove** <note>Jupiter/Zeus, representing divine order</note> established that the cycles of time in this laborious life would be short, while in the life among the higher beings they would be long, and longest of all among the supreme beings. Our souls eventually return to the level of the World Soul, where they contemplate its public providence and imitate the ease of its governance regarding their own bodies and provinces. Furthermore, the Soul of the World, like a worldly **Apollo**, sings in nature and strikes his **lyre** in the heavens. In nature, the unfolding and revolution of all reasons at appointed times is a universal harmony composed of many songs and melodies. Similarly, in the heavens, the perpetual arrangement of the stars and their motions is the "Apollonian sound," established for the perpetual concord of that song. If anyone could perceive the continuous arrangement of that song, they would immediately behold the celestial sounds and (to speak properly) almost "hear" them. 

Furthermore, our souls—performing their progressions in their descent, in this earthly dwelling, and in their ascent like a rhythmic dance—adapt themselves to the worldly song and sound. Since they proceed from the same father as the World Soul, are its sisters, and inhabit its province, they naturally dance to its song and sound. They are not forced into this, but do so willingly; they naturally and gladly emulate the worldly order. From this, it follows that one can guess human progressions through celestial movements—if not everywhere as causes, then at least as certain signs. This is because the form of universal nature and the heavens contains, by a certain exemplary reason, whatever is done within the world, whether by nature itself, by individual souls, or from anywhere else. 

Souls sometimes inhabit a celestial body, sometimes a pure celestial state, and sometimes a state below the heavens. Insofar as the soul puts on a different internal habit, it also puts on a different external figure. Thus, it sometimes enters a "heavenly man," sometimes an "airy" one, and other times an "earthly" one. Again, depending on how much it degenerates, it becomes either a divine man, a human man, or a "beastly" one. Indeed, this is how we usually clarify the words of **Plotinus**: for it is not accepted by the Platonists—nor should it have been granted by Plotinus himself—that a rational soul actually becomes the form of an ox's or a pig's body. He had proposed that the change began from the *imagination*, which cannot change the species of the soul's essence. 

It is accepted that there are as many intellects in the human species as there are souls. However, the idea that our intellect remains happy among divine things while our rational power, cast down to earth, is most miserable, does not seem entirely different from the view of **Iamblichus**. Yet it was rejected by **Porphyry**, the disciple of Plotinus, and condemned by **Proclus**. Proclus said that the power of the most blessed mind with God is so great that it would meanwhile retain the power closest to it (the reason), provided the mind itself did not decline; thus, in this life, we would not sin. Nor does it seem logical that the stomach would be very weak as long as the liver remained very strong. 

Porphyry adds that the fall of the soul began not from imagination or nature, but from the **intellect**. For higher things are not dragged down by lower things; rather, that higher power acts according to the measure of its own virtue. Thus, the "intention" of acting is sometimes relaxed in the intellect, and to that extent, the act of the lower power (imagination and nature) is intensified, since the soul cannot be idle in every part. Conversely, the acts of the lower parts are relaxed when the act of the higher parts is intensified. But where Porphyry says the intellect acts "according to the measure of its own virtue," he should be corrected: when the intellect is blessed with God, it acts not so much by its own virtue as by the **divine virtue**, under whose form it now acts. Therefore, one must believe that a soul once made blessed in this way will never depart from there. Let others look to the rest; for us, it is enough to have recounted these things, preferring to approve what our **Theologians** <note>Ficino often uses "Theologians" to refer to Christian authorities, harmonizing them with Platonism.</note> have most strongly confirmed.

---

->The law, judgment, and justice of the universe lead souls from within,<-
->both by choice and by necessity, to their own end.<-

Just as someone offering lettuce allures a goose through its external senses, or a **Magician** allures the internal sense through things friendly to that sense, the soul is moved willingly, just like that goose. In the same way, divine providence draws every will and every affection of the soul toward a fitting end. This happens through a certain affection already conceived in the soul according to its actions and choices, by which it is carried—both willingly and vehemently—toward its just end and competent lot, as if snatched away by a secret magic. For God moves the soul...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains the World Soul’s role as a creative force (Dionysus) and a source of cosmic harmony (Apollo). He discusses the soul's descent into the body through "love" and imagination, while debating with Neoplatonists like Porphyry and Proclus on whether the highest part of the soul remains divine during earthly life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, Book 3, and transitions into the beginning of Book 4. The discussion focuses on the moral mechanics of the soul's movement (judgment and justice) and the metaphysical architecture connecting the material world to the divine, specifically through the myth of Prometheus.</meta>

...not only more interior than art, but even more so than nature; and it acts at certain times just as nature is accustomed to do. Therefore, souls acting of their own accord from the beginning—and having become such by so acting—finally reach their decreed lot justly at the times established by God, not only by their own will but also by the necessity of an internal law. In the universe, this law is judgment and justice. The Law exists in the divine mind, being the very arrangement of all things; Judgment exists in the mind of the **World Soul** <note>The "anima mundi," the vital spirit that animates the entire physical universe.</note>, decreeing individual things according to the pattern of the divine law; and Justice exists in the will of that same soul, willing and executing individual things exactly as they have been judged. Therefore, it transfers impure souls downward, as their own impurity inclines them there—just as universal nature moves heavy things toward the center by their own weight. Conversely, it transfers pure souls upward through their purity, tending in the same direction, just as nature moves light things upward by their own lightness. With this brief summary, one may interpret what Orpheus sings in three hymns concerning the law, judgment, and justice of God, and what Plato, imitating Orpheus in the fourth book of the *Laws*, defines regarding divine law and judgment.

->On the connection of this world to the higher world, and on Prometheus and the speaking statues.<-

The worldly spheres possess innermost souls and, from these, especially their own vital gifts. Through these souls and through their vital endowments, they receive certain intellectual gifts as if through intermediaries, following from the individual intellects that guide their souls. Furthermore, through these, they obtain several divine gifts from the very **Ideas** <note>The eternal, perfect archetypes of all things in the Divine Mind.</note> of the divine mind, to which (as Plotinus and Iamblichus believe) the intellects are inseparably joined. Thus, it is not that the divine world has been "sent" here, but rather that it is entirely infused into this world from every side. Following this, you may observe a certain natural providence reigning in the vital part of the World Soul under the name of **Prometheus**. From "mud"—that is, primary matter—he shapes "statues"—that is, natural things. He is partly bound to this craftsmanship and partly free from it, and here there is no place for **Epimetheus**—that is, for rashness or afterthought. Likewise, in natural things, there are not only vital powers but also certain intellectual and divine endowments, and all the gods contribute something of themselves to this craftsmanship; I mean this craftsmanship not only of the universe as a whole, but of each individual thing. 

Amidst these points, Plotinus alludes to the "voice of the clay-born" by mentioning the <term>magi <note>Specifically referring to the practitioners of "theurgy" or ritual magic in late antiquity.</note></term>, especially those who constructed "speaking statues." In these, it was not properly the souls of the statues or the stars that spoke, but **daemons** <note>original: "daemones." In Neoplatonism, these are intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil, who bridge the gap between gods and humans.</note> led by the same star under whose dominion the statues were fashioned. I also believe that in the case of that son of the King who spoke on the day he was born—as **Aly** <note>Likely Haly Abenragel, a famous 11th-century Arab astrologer often cited by Ficino.</note> testifies, claiming he was present—it was not the conjunction of the four planets meeting in his horoscope that formed the words, nor did the infant’s soul produce the words and the prophecy concerning the calamity of his father's kingdom that followed shortly after. Rather, I believe a daemon spoke through him—a Mercurial daemon, I say. For in the eighth degree of the horoscope in Libra, which is the <term>term <note>In astrology, "terms" are specific subdivisions of zodiac signs ruled by different planets.</note></term> of Mercury, Mercury himself is said to have been in conjunction with Venus, Jupiter, and Mars. But it is not permitted to digress further at present; indeed, I cannot continue to maintain the pace of explaining the books as I have from the beginning. If we were to pursue similarly long arguments and commentaries arranged separately from Plotinus’s own chapters, the interpretation would become confused and the work would grow to an immense size. We have wandered enough; we have said enough already. It will be sufficient from now on to intersperse brief annotations among Plotinus's chapters, as we did with Theophrastus.

## FOURTH ENNEAD,
### BOOK III.
### First on the doubts concerning the soul.
<note>Greek title: ΠΕΡΙ Ψυχῆς ἀποριῶν πρῶτον.</note>

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'P' (from the Greek Pi) showing a scholar at a desk.</image-desc>
Whether it is necessary to bring those who are in doubt regarding the soul into a state of clarity, or whether we should find profit in the very doubts themselves—namely, to know what is truly problematic in them—it would be right to undertake this study. For about what subject could one more reasonably spend a great deal of time speaking and investigating than this one? This is true for many other reasons, and also because it provides knowledge of two things: those things of which the soul is the principle, and those things from which the soul itself originates. Thus, we shall obey the command of the God who exhorted us to: "Know thyself," by making an examination of this matter.

<column-break/>

<margin>How necessary the consideration of the soul is, and how some suspect that we live only by the life of the world.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'I' (Latinized from the Greek) depicting a traveler in a landscape.</image-desc>
IT IS WORTHWHILE to consider whether all doubts concerning the soul ought to be resolved, or whether we should instead place our profit in the doubts themselves. Truly, there is no matter about which we ought to investigate and treat more diligently and at greater length than the soul. This is so for many reasons, but especially because it leads to the knowledge of both: namely, those things of which the soul is the principle, and those things from which it is made. Thus we shall obey God who commands: "Know thyself."

# PLOTINUS: ENNEAD IV.

Moreover, as we desire to examine and discover all other things, we should rightly investigate first of all what this investigator within us actually is. This is especially true since we long to reach that very thing which is lovely and pleasant in the spectacles of contemplation. For in the universal Intellect <note>original Latin: *intellectu*; Greek: *νῷ* (nous)</note> itself, this principle is twofold. Therefore, ->A<- it is reasonable that in particular intellects, this one is more in one way, and that one is rather in another. 

Furthermore, we must consider how the "receptors" of the Gods <note>The physical or spiritual vehicles that allow divine presence to manifest.</note> are formed; ->B<- but we shall investigate that more opportunely after we have asked how the soul exists in the body. Now, however, let us return again to those who say that our souls also come from the Soul of the Universe itself. ->C<- For perhaps they will object to us, saying it is not a sufficient argument against our souls being parts of that Soul, even if we grant that our souls proceed only as far as the World Soul pours itself out, or that our souls are said to possess very similar intellectual gifts. They will say that parts are usually of the same form as the whole. 

Furthermore, they will bring forward ->D<- Plato himself as supporting this opinion, where, proving that the world is animated <note>Possessing a soul or life-force.</note>, he says: "Just as our body is a part of the universal body, so also is our soul a part of the soul of the whole." Likewise, it is said and clearly shown that we follow the rotation of the entire world, and from there we receive our character and fortunes; and again, being born within the world, we deservedly receive our containing soul from the world itself. 

Moreover, just as every part of us receives from our soul, so we, in a similar way—since we are parts of the whole—receive from the Soul of the Whole as parts. Finally, regarding what is written—that "every soul has care for all that is inanimate"—this signifies exactly the same thing: as if, besides the World Soul, nothing of the soul is left anywhere else. For it is the World Soul that takes care of everything inanimate.

<margin>II. The soul cannot be divided into multiple parts like bodies, or numerical dimensions, or the qualities of bodies.</margin>

To these things, therefore, it must first be said that those who posit that souls are of the same form ->E<- because they are allowed to touch upon the same things—while meanwhile admitting the same common genus—secretly bring it about that other souls are not parts of the one. Instead, they would more probably infer that it is one and the same, and that any soul exists as a whole. But by making it "one," they reduce it to something else. 

This would no longer belong to this or that, but would exist as belonging to nothing—neither to the world nor to any other—and yet it would perform whatever is judged to be the work of the life of the world and of any animated being. For it seems right ->F<- that not every soul belongs to something, since it is an essence <note>original: *essentia*; Greek: *οὐσία* (ousia). Plotinus argues that the soul’s primary nature is a being in its own right, not just a property of a body.</note>; rather, there exists a soul that belongs to nothing at all. But those souls which are said to belong to something become so occasionally by "accident"—that is, they happen to belong to something.

Perhaps, however, it is necessary to understand more clearly in these matters how "part" is spoken of. One ought to set aside the manner of parts appearing in bodies—whether the body is uniform or irregular—noting only this: ->G<- when a part is named in bodies of similar parts, it is a part according to mass/bulk, not according to species <note>original Latin: *speciem*; Greek: *εἶδος* (eidos). This distinguishes between a physical piece of a thing (mass) and the "type" or "essence" of a thing (form).</note>, just as we can judge in the case of whiteness. For the whiteness which is in a portion of milk is not a "part" of the whiteness which is in the whole...

<column-break/>

Seeking other things and wishing to find them, we would rightly seek what the seeking principle within us is, <margin>* Most precious</margin> striving to grasp that which is most *lovable among sights. For indeed, in the total Intellect, there is a duality; thus it is reasonable that in particular cases, one part is more this way, and the other that way. 

As for how the receptions of the gods occur, this must be considered; but let us do so then, when we seek how the soul comes to be in a body. But now let us return again to those who say that our souls are not [distinct] from the Soul of the All. For they will perhaps say it is sufficient that our souls reach as far as the Soul of the All reaches; and they will not [accept] that even if we grant they are similarly intellectual, they are not a portion of it. For they say that parts are of the same species <note>original: *ὁμοειδῆ* (homoeidē)</note> as their wholes. 

And they will also cite Plato as holding this opinion when he says the All is animated: that just as our body is a part of the body of the All, so also is our soul a part of the Soul of the All. They also cite that we follow the revolution of the All—which is both said and clearly demonstrated—and that we receive our characters and fortunes from there, and that being born within it and from the environment that surrounds us, we receive our soul. 

Just as each part of us receives from our soul, so we, by the same reasoning, being parts of the whole, participate in the whole soul as parts. And the saying that "every soul takes care of all that is inanimate" means the same thing, for nothing else is left outside of soul after the Soul of the All. For it is that Soul which places the whole inanimate world under its care.

TO these things, first that must be said: by positing that souls are of the same species, and by granting that they touch upon the same things, and by giving them the same common genus, they [the opponents] exclude them from being a "part." Rather, they might more justly say that the soul is the same and one, and whole in each [individual]. But by making it one, they attach it to something else. 

This would no longer be here [in the individual], but being that thing itself—whether of the world or of something else—it does itself what the body or any animated thing does. For it is correct that not every soul belongs to something, being an essence <note>original: *οὐσία* (ousia)</note>; but there is a soul that does not belong to anything at all, while those that belong to something do so by accident. 

Perhaps it is necessary to grasp more clearly how "part" is said in such things. We must leave aside the sense of "part" as it applies to bodies, whether the body is of the same kind or different kinds. Let it be noted only that in the case of things with similar parts, when a part is spoken of, the part is such according to bulk/mass, and not according to form <note>original: *εἶδος* (eidos)</note>; for example, whiteness. For the whiteness in a portion of milk is not a part of the total...

<summary>Plotinus investigates the relationship between individual human souls and the World Soul, addressing arguments (often attributed to Plato) that individual souls are merely "parts" of a larger whole. He begins to refute this by distinguishing between physical parts (like pieces of a body) and metaphysical unity (where essence is not divided by mass).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether the individual human soul is a "part" of the Soul of the Universe. Having previously established that individual souls and the World Soul share a common origin, Plotinus now uses various analogies—whiteness, numbers, geometry, and the structure of knowledge—to define exactly what kind of "part" the soul might be.</meta>

### BOOK THREE.

Of the whiteness of milk, whiteness is a portion, but it is not a "part" of whiteness itself. For whiteness as a quality is entirely without magnitude <note>original Greek: *ἀμεγέθες* (amegethes); Latin: *magnitudine carens*</note>, even if it is associated with a quantity of matter. And let that be the case. But when we speak of a "part" in things that are not physical bodies, we either mean it as we do in numbers—as when two is said to be a part of ten (let this be understood as referring to pure numbers)—or as a part of a circle or a line is spoken of, or as a specific theorem or notion is called a part of a science <note>original Greek: *ἐπιστήμης* (epistēmēs); Latin: *scientiæ*. In this context, "science" refers to a complete body of organized knowledge, like geometry or music.</note>.

<margin>A</margin> In the case of units <margin>B</margin> and geometric figures, it is necessary—just as it is with physical bodies—that the whole itself is diminished by the division into parts, and that each individual part is smaller than the whole. Since these things have quantity and possess their very being in that quantity, they are not the same quantity as the whole; thus, they necessarily become "greater" and "smaller." 

Under this condition, a "part" certainly cannot be spoken of in relation to the soul. For the quantity in the soul is not such that the whole is like a "ten" and the part is like a single unit. If it were, many other absurdities would follow; <margin>C</margin> for surely ten units are not a single unified thing. Furthermore, either each of those units would be a soul, or the soul itself would be composed of a collection of soulless parts.

In addition to this, it is granted that a "part" of the whole soul must be "uniform" <note>original Latin: *uniformis*; Greek: *ὁμοειδὲς* (homoeides). This means the part has the same nature and essence as the whole.</note> in its existence. Yet in a continuous thing, it is not necessary for the part to be of the same nature as the whole, such as the parts of a circle or a triangle. Or, at the very least, not all the small portions are similar in those things where one can take a part, such as triangles within triangles; rather, in these cases, a great variety of changes occur. <margin>D</margin> But philosophers agree that the soul is uniform.

Likewise, in a line, a part is still a line, but here it also differs in magnitude. But in the soul, if the difference between the partial soul and the total soul were taken to be a difference in magnitude, the soul would be a specific quantity and a body. It would be receiving its very identity as a soul from "how much" it is. But it is granted that all souls are similar and are wholes in themselves.

It is clear, moreover, that the soul is not divided in the way magnitudes are divided, nor would those thinkers even <margin>E</margin> admit that the whole is cut into parts; otherwise, they would utterly destroy the whole itself. And if there were an all-encompassing soul from the beginning, it would then be a name only—just as if one were to distribute wine into many cups and then call the wine in a single cup a "part" of the whole wine.

But could "part" be used for the soul in the same way a single theorem is called a part of a whole science? The science itself remains a whole nonetheless. <margin>F</margin> In this case, each part has the whole science within it potentially; yet the science itself remains a whole all the while. If this is how the relationship between the universal soul and the others is understood, then the universal soul—of which the others are parts—would not be the soul of any specific thing, but would exist by itself. Therefore, it would not even be the Soul of the World; rather, it too would be one of those souls placed in the category of "parts." All these souls would then be parts of a single soul, existing as entirely uniform. But how is it that this one is the soul of the world, <margin>G</margin> while that one is the soul of a part of the world?

<column-break/>

<margin>III. That is to say, imagining that there is only one single soul in all men and the world, just as we say there is one single human soul in all the members of one man.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the relationship between the individual soul and the universal soul. Here, Plotinus argues that the soul remains a unified whole even when it appears to be distributed across different bodily organs or individual beings.</meta>

### PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK IV.

[The soul] of the soul which is in the whole living being. But this argument either results in no soul being outside the body, or all souls being not in the body, but rather that the soul which is called the "Soul of the World" <note>original Latin: *mundi anima*; Greek: *ἡ τοῦ παντὸς* (hē tou pantos)</note> exists outside the body of the world. This is indeed a matter worthy of consideration, but for the present we must proceed by way of an image. For if the Soul of the Whole provides itself to all particular living things, and thus each is called a "part" of the soul—for if it were divided, it could by no means provide itself to each one—then surely it will be the same whole everywhere, being one and the same in many things at once.

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, it would by no means be maintained that one soul is a "whole" while another is a "part," especially in those things where the same power is present. Even where there are different tasks for different parts, such as for the eyes and the ears, we should not say that one part of the soul is present in the eye and another in the ears (for such division belongs to other things). Rather, it is entirely the same soul, although a different power exercises itself in each. For all powers are in both, but because the instruments <note>original: *instrumenta* / *ὄργανα* (organa) — referring here to the physical sense organs</note> are different, we must think that the perceptions that occur are also different.

<margin>C</margin> Nevertheless, all these powers belong to the forms, and that which is capable of being shaped is reduced entirely into form, being molded through all things. This is also evident from the fact that it is necessary for all things to finally come together into a unity. By the nature of the instruments through which this is achieved, it is clear that they cannot receive all things at once. While the sensations produced in the instruments are different, the judgment comes from one and the same thing, acting as a judge for me, noticing both what is said and what is done alike. Indeed, that which is "one" is said to be everywhere, even in those actions that do not differ.

<margin>D</margin> But if only the senses were present there, it would not be possible for each of them to understand, but rather "she" <note>The soul is traditionally referred to as "she" in both Latin (*anima*) and Greek (*psyche*).</note> understands through them. If, however, there is a distinct intelligence, then surely each resides within itself. But when the soul is rational, and is called rational as a whole, then what is called a "part" is not a part of a whole, but rather will be entirely the same as it.

#### VIII. The previous points are confirmed, and it is taught how distinction occurs in the Intellect, and how it should occur in the soul, and how some imagine souls are distinguished for a time and then merged again.

<margin>E</margin> What then should be said if the soul is indeed one in this way, when someone asks us: first, doubting how it is possible for one thing to be in all things at the same time; and then, when the soul is in the body, how is another part of it outside the body? For perhaps it follows that the soul is always in a body, especially the Soul of the Universe. For it is not said to leave the body as ours is—though some say that while this body is indeed left behind, the soul will not be entirely outside of body. But if it were entirely outside the body, how could it be that this one leaves and that one never does, since it is the same soul?

<margin>F</margin> Within the Intellect <term>Intellect: (Latin *intellectus*, Greek *nous*) The second hypostasis in Plotinus's philosophy, representing the realm of pure, eternal thought and divine forms</term> itself—which is distinguished within itself by "otherness" <note>original: *alteritate* / *ἑτερότητι* (heterotēti)</note>, especially among its parts, yet they always exist together since the essence itself is indivisible—no such doubt will ever arise. But in the soul, which is said to be "partible" <term>partible: capable of being divided or distributed, though in the soul's case, it is a division of function rather than physical mass</term> around bodies, this claim that all souls are one involves us in many doubts. This is unless one establishes that the One remains in itself, not falling into the body at all. Then one might say that all souls, both the Soul of the Whole and the others, exist together up to a certain point, and are "one" because they do not belong to any specific thing.

<margin>G</margin> But while they are suspended from their own boundaries and together conspiring toward the things above, they meanwhile direct and extend themselves here and there like light— <note>original Greek: *ταῖς αὐτῶν ἐξηρτημένας καὶ συνώσας ἀλλήλαις* (hanging from their sources and joined to one another)</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...a part in the whole living being. But the argument either makes no soul to be outside of body, or all not in body, but outside the body of the world, of that which is called the "All." This must be examined; but now, as one might say, the image must be investigated. For if the soul of the All provides itself to all living things in part, and thus each is a part, if it were divided, it would not provide itself to each. But it is the same everywhere, being the whole, one and the same being in many things at once.

<margin>B</margin> This would no longer allow one to be the whole and another the part; and especially in those things where the same power is present. Since even for those things which have a different function, such as the eyes and ears, it must not be said that one part of the soul sees and another is present in the ears (for it is the nature of other things to be divided thus), but the same soul is present, though a different power acts in each.

<margin>C</margin> But there are those things in which all [powers] are present in both ways; but because the organs are different, the perceptions become different. All powers, however, belong to the forms, and everything that can be shaped is brought into form. This is also shown by the necessity that all things go toward a unity. But of the organs through which this happens, not all can receive all things; and while the experiences are different for the organs, that which judges is the same. Just as

<margin>D</margin> a judge observes both the words being spoken and the deeds being done. But because it is everywhere, it is spoken of in the different functions, as in the senses. Therefore, each of them does not think, but she thinks with that [power]. If the thought is her own, each is by herself whenever the soul is rational, and is called rational as a whole, and what is called a "part" is the same, and the whole will not be a part.

<margin>E</margin> WHAT then must be said if it is thus one, whenever someone seeks to know from this: first, wondering if it is possible to be thus in all things at once. Then, when it is in a body, is it also not in a body? For perhaps it will follow that it is always in a body, and especially the soul of the All. For it is not said to leave the body as ours is; and yet some say that this [body] will be left behind, but it will not be altogether outside of body. But if it is altogether outside of body, how does one leave and the other not, since it is the same?

<margin>F</margin> In the case of the Intellect, which is separated from itself by otherness and has parts, especially from one another, yet they are always together (for the essence itself would be indivisible), no such difficulty would hold. But in the case of the soul, which is said to be divisible among bodies, this saying that all are one would have many difficulties; unless someone

<margin>G</margin> were to establish the one by itself, not falling into the body; then from that one, all souls. Both the soul of the whole and the others up to a certain point; as if joined together or being one, by not belonging to any one thing, and how they apply themselves to their own affairs, here and there, like light.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul remains a unified whole even when acting through different bodily organs (like eyes or ears) or inhabiting different beings. He distinguishes the soul's "partible" nature in bodies from the pure, indivisible unity of the Intellect (Nous).</summary>

### BOOK THE THIRD.

<margin>* The Great [Soul]</margin> [The soul] which is indeed already distributed on earth through various dwellings <note>original Latin: *per domicilia*; the text refers to individual bodies as "dwellings" for the soul</note>, yet it is nonetheless not separated from itself, but remains one. The Soul of the Universe always stands above <note>original Latin: *supereminere*; Greek: *ὑπερέχειν* (hyperechein)</note>, because it never experiences a descent or a falling away into lower things, nor does it turn back toward the things that follow it. Our souls, however, are less excellent because a specific part in the world has been assigned to them, and they bend toward lower things, for they stand in need of care and anxiety due to the nature of the body. Now, the Soul of the World, through its lowest part, <margin>* Turning toward the body</margin> is similar to the soul of a massive tree <margin>* The Great [Soul]</margin> which governs the plant without labor or worry. <margin>* Soul of the Whole</margin> But the lowest part of our soul is like tiny creatures <note>original: *vermes* (worms) or *εὐλαὶ* (maggots/larvae)</note> that arise in a rotting part of a plant. For this is how the animated body exists within the universe. But the other soul, which is of the same form as the highest part of the Soul of the Whole, behaves as if a gardener were to apply himself to the care of those creatures born in the plant, or were anxiously concerned with cultivating the plant itself. Or perhaps, one might say that a healthy person, moving among other healthy people, is occupied with those things he chooses to enjoy, whether in action or in contemplation; but a sick person, occupied with caring for his body, is said to be "at the body’s mercy" and to have become a mere possession of the body.

<column-break/>

<margin>V. How human intellects flow from the divine intellect, distinct among themselves, yet remaining so, and how they conceive of animal natures.</margin> <margin>A</margin> BUT by what further reason is this soul yours, this one his, and that one another's? Or perhaps this one belongs to the soul’s infinite part <note>original: *secundum ipsius infinitum*</note>, but that one does not? But in this way, Socrates will exist only when the soul of Socrates itself is in a body; and he will perish when he is most fully in the highest state. <margin>B</margin> But surely none of the things that truly *are* <note>original: *entium* / *ὄντων* (beings/existences)</note> ever perish. Since even there <note>referring to the intelligible realm</note> the Intellects <term>Nous (Divine Mind)</term> do not perish, because they are not cut into one by a bodily condition. Rather, each remains in its own "otherness," preserving that same thing which constitutes its being. <margin>C</margin> In this way, therefore, souls are suspended from that place, existing according to each Intellect and being certain "reasons" <note>original: *rationes* / *λόγοι* (logoi)—the formative principles</note> of those Intellects, more unfolded than they are, as if they had progressed from a small point to a great expanse. <margin>D</margin> For while they preserve both the "Same" and the "Other," each remains one, and yet all are one together. Indeed, it has already been said, as far as the summary of the argument goes, that all souls are derived from one; I mean that many come from one in the same manner as with the Intellect: divided in the same order, and yet also not divided. <margin>E</margin> For that soul which remains is the single "reason" of the mind, and from it come the partial and immaterial "reasons," just as in the realm above.

<margin>VI. On the differences of souls, insofar as they turn more or less toward the intellect, both universal and particular, and as part of the universe.</margin> <margin>F</margin> BUT why is it that the Soul of the World, which is said to be of the same form as the others, created the world, but the soul of an individual did not? Especially since each soul contains all things within itself? It has already been said that it is possible to be in many things at once; but now this must be further explained. For perhaps we must see how the same thing in different places acts or suffers <note>original: *agit, aut patitur*—the philosophical distinction between doing and being acted upon</note> partly this and partly that. <margin>G</margin> Perhaps it is enough to consider this very point: in what way and for what reason that one created the world, while the others created only a part...

### PLOTINUS' ENNEADS. IV.

...govern the world. Perhaps it should not seem surprising that among humans endowed with the same knowledge, some rule over many things while others rule over few. Someone might ask why this is the case. One might answer that there is also a great difference among souls, insofar as one [the World Soul] has not departed from the whole, but resting there, has contained the body around itself; whereas other souls have obtained their lots gradually, after the body was already made and after their sister soul—the World Soul—already held dominance, as if that soul had already prepared dwellings <note>original Latin: *domicilia*; Greek: *οἰκήσεις* (oikēseis). This refers to the physical bodies the souls inhabit.</note> for them. Nor is another <margin>B</margin> difference lacking, through which this soul looks toward the universal Intellect, while others look rather to particular intellects—that is, each to its own. 

Perhaps these individual souls could also have made the whole; but since the World Soul has already done so, the faculty is no longer given to them, after that first soul laid the foundations. In the same way, anyone would wonder if perhaps any other soul had built the world first. But it is better to say that the chief power and craftsmanship belong to the principal soul because it adheres more closely to the things above. For a greater power arises in souls that lean more attentively toward those higher realms. Preserving themselves in safety upon that foundation, they act more easily; for it is the mark of a greater power not to be affected by the things it creates, but rather that its power remains from on high. Therefore, remaining within itself, it creates the things that follow as others approach; but those other souls which have approached or proceeded forth seem to have descended into the deep. Perhaps because there is much in them that is drawn downward, it has dragged them along too, so that they already seem to have descended even through their thoughts. 

What is said in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the creation of the universe.</note> about the second and third order of souls must be explained as some souls adhering closer to the things above, while others depart further, just as happens among us. For not every soul relates to the higher things in the same way, but some are united to the higher, others approach through their own desire, and finally, others achieve this less because they do not use the same strengths. But some use the first power, others the second, and finally others the third, even though every soul possesses all the powers.

<margin>VII. Responses to doubts proving that our souls are not [merely] from the Soul of the World.</margin>

Let this be said of these matters for now. As for what is said in the *Philebus* <note>Another dialogue by Plato discussing pleasure and the good.</note> which induces a suspicion that perhaps all souls are parts of the World Soul, it does not mean what some people think, but rather what was most useful for his argument then: namely, that the world is animate. For striving to prove this, Plato says it is absurd to say the heavens are inanimate when we, who have a body that is part of the world’s body, have a soul. For how could a part have a soul if the whole were inanimate? 

Plato’s opinion is most clear in the *Timaeus*, where, after the Soul of the World is made, the other souls are subsequently born in the same mixing bowl <note>original Latin: *patera*; Greek: *κρατῆρος* (kratēros). This refers to the vessel where the Demiurge mixes the soul-stuff.</note> in which the World Soul was mixed, and are conformable to it; but he assigns the difference between them through second and third degrees. And as for what is said in the *Phaedrus*, that "every soul has care of all that is inanimate," what is so strange? For what else governs, forms, orders, and creates the nature of the body except the soul? Nor should it be said that while this soul can do so naturally, that one cannot at all. Hence he adds: "The soul being perfect, then," namely that of the universe, "soaring on high, does not submerge itself, but (so to speak)..."

<column-break/>

...govern the world; it is not at all wonderful that those possessing the knowledge before them should rule, some over more things, others over fewer. But why is this? someone might say. There is indeed a difference between souls, or rather, insofar as one has not departed from the whole, but held there as much of the body as was around it. But the others, once the body already existed, received their lots by the grace of their sister soul, as if she had prepared dwellings for them. And it is also possible to see the whole through those souls, while others look more toward their own particular parts. 

Perhaps these souls too would have made the whole; but since one had already made it, it was no longer possible for them, that first one having already received the task. The same cause would have applied if any other had been the first to take hold. But it is better to say that power is greater for those leaning toward the things above. For by keeping themselves stationed in safety, they act. For it is of a greater power not to suffer from the things one makes; and the power from above remains. Remaining, therefore, in itself, it makes the things that follow; but these others have suffered. They fell into the depth, or much of them being dragged down, it pulled them along with their thoughts to be in the lower realm. 

The mention of second and third orders must be understood as being near or further away; just as among us, it does not belong to all souls similarly to be near the things there, but some are in heaven, while others strive toward it by being near. To those for whom this is gentle, it is because they act in their powers or in themselves. But some act by the first power, others by the one after that, and others by the third, though all possess all the powers.

These things were so; but what was said in the *Philebus* provides a suspicion that the other souls are parts of the whole. But the argument does not mean this, as someone might think, but rather what is always useful to him: that the heaven is animate. He establishes this by saying it is absurd to call the heaven inanimate when we, who have a part of the body of the whole, have a soul. For how would the part have it if the whole were inanimate? 

His opinion is most clear in the *Timaeus*. After the soul of the whole is made, he later makes the others: mixing them from the same bowl from which the soul of the whole came, making them of the same kind, even the others. And he teaches the difference by second and third ranks. As for the passage in the *Phaedrus*, "every soul takes care of all that is inanimate," what would it be that governs the nature of the body, and either molds, or arranges, or makes it? The soul. And it is not that one is naturally able to do this and the other is not. "The perfect soul, then," he says, "that of the whole, traveling on high, governs"—but as if...

### BOOK THE THIRD.

...poured out into the world, it acts. And if any soul is complete <note>original Greek: αὐτελεία (auteleia)</note>, it governs in this way. But the soul that has overflowed—as it is said—acts differently from those perfect ones: for to follow the revolution of the universe, and to be carried along from that source, and to be affected by it, would be no sign that our individual parts belong to the whole. For the soul is capable of being defined by many things—by the nature of places, of waters, of air, and the dwellings of various cities, and the temperaments <note>original Greek: κράσεις (kraseis). In ancient medicine, this refers to the "mixing" of bodily fluids that determines a person's character.</note> of bodies. What then? We said that while being in the whole, we possess something of the universal Soul, and we conceded that we are affected by the revolution of the heavens: but we set another soul against these influences, and one that is shown to be distinct precisely by its resistance to them. Concerning the idea that we are born within the world, we say as we do of mothers: that the fetus has one soul, but there is another soul—the one that entered from outside—which existed before the mother.

<column-break/>

That which floats above acts upon the world, and whichever soul is perfect will dispense its power similarly. Moreover, where he introduces the soul with broken wings <note>A famous metaphor from Plato's "Phaedrus" describing the soul's descent into a physical body.</note> as if it were falling, he clearly asserts that a soul of this kind is different from the World Soul. Therefore, the argument brought forward—that souls follow the circuit of the universe, and derive their characters from it, and suffer because of it—by no means signifies that our souls are merely parts of the whole. For the soul can repel many things threatening from the heavens due to the nature of places, waters, and air: the dwelling also <margin>VIII. How souls differ: and how they remain immortal in their own form: and how the World Soul contributes to the life of all.</margin> and urban customs, and the temperaments of bodies, resist celestial influences. And if we have said that we, enclosed in the universe, have something of life from the World Soul, and suffer from the celestial circuit, we have nevertheless introduced, on the other hand, another soul resisting all these things, and clearly showing itself to be distinct by that very resistance. To that which is said, that we were born within the world, we respond similarly: that in the mother’s womb the fetus has a different soul than the maternal soul—namely, the soul that enters from elsewhere.

AND these matters, then, may be considered resolved by us for the present. Furthermore, the fact that souls feel sympathy <note>original Latin: compatiantur; Greek: συμπαθεῖς (sympatheis). This refers to a "shared feeling" or resonance between souls.</note> with one another ought not to hinder our reasoning: for since they all flow from the same source as the World Soul, they naturally feel sympathy for each other. Now it has been said that the soul is both one and many. It has been said concerning the difference of the part to the whole, and finally concerning the difference between souls: and now let it be said summarily. We say, therefore, that besides bodily differences, souls differ among themselves, especially in character, and in the duties of thought, and even from the habits of a previous life. For it is written by Plato in the *Republic* <note>Referring to the "Myth of Er" in Book X of Plato's Republic, which describes how souls choose their next lives.</note> that subsequent lives are chosen by souls according to their preceding lives. If anyone, however, considers the nature of the soul itself entirely, here too the author placed differences, where he arranged second and third degrees of souls. Furthermore, it has been said that all souls contain all things, but each soul is defined by what is active within it: this means, some are united in action, others in knowledge, and others in desire. They differ, moreover, because they look upon different things, and what they look upon, they become. A full and perfect office belongs to souls, yet not the same to all; rather, they are situated as if their entire coordination were a varied arrangement. For there is one universal Reason <note>original Latin: ratio vniuerſa; Greek: λόγος (logos)</note>, manifold and varied, like a multiform living creature. If this is so, and there is a coordination, and beings are not entirely separated from one another, nor is anything found to be made by chance in the order of beings—not even in physical bodies—it follows that there is a certain sequential number to them. For beings must exist together, and the intelligible things themselves <note>The "intelligibilia" or "Forms" in the divine mind.</note> must be the same, and each must be numerically one: for in this way "this specific thing" can be said of each. In the realm of bodies, individual things naturally flow and change, as they only receive a form from the outside; there, existence according to "species" is perpetual only through an imitation of true beings. But among true beings, which are not made of parts, existence itself consists in being numerically one; this exists from the beginning, and does not become what it was not, nor will that which is, ever cease to be.

He uses the analogy of a fetus having a soul separate from its mother to illustrate how the human soul enters the body from an external, higher source.</summary>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

...govern the world. Perhaps it should seem no wonder that among people endowed with the same knowledge, some rule over many things and others over few. Someone might perhaps ask why the matter stands thus. One might also respond that there is a greater difference among souls: specifically, that one soul did not depart from the whole, but resting there, it contained the body around itself; while other souls, once the body was already made and after their sister-soul <note>The "sister-soul" refers to the World Soul, which Plotinus views as a sibling to individual souls, both originating from the same source.</note> had already arisen and was dominant, gradually obtained their lots, as if the first had already prepared dwellings for them. Nor is another difference lacking, by which this one soul looks upon the universal Intellect <note>original Latin: *universum intellectum*; Greek: *τὸν ὅλον νοῦν* (ton holon noun)</note>, while others look rather to particular intellects—that is, each to its own. Perhaps these others could also have made the whole; but since that first one has already done so, no further capacity is granted to them after the first has laid the foundations. But anyone might doubt in the same way if, by chance, any other soul had built it first. However, it is better to say that the primary power and craftsmanship belong to the principal soul for this reason: that it adheres more closely to the things above. For a greater power arises in those souls that lean more attentively toward that place. For by preserving themselves in that secure foundation, they act most easily; for it is the mark of a greater power not to suffer from the things it makes, and that power remains from on high. Remaining therefore in itself, it acts consequently upon other things as they approach; but the others that have approached or proceeded forth seem to have descended into the depths. Perhaps because there is a great draw of the gods <note>original Latin: *deorum tractum*; Greek: *καθελκυσθέν* (kathelkysthen - "dragged down")</note> in them, it has drawn them down as well, so much so that they seem to have already descended even through their thoughts. What is said in the *Timaeus* regarding the second and third order of souls must be explained thus: some adhere closer to the things above, while others depart further, just as happens among us. For not every soul stands in the same relation to the higher things, but some are united to the superiors, others approach closer to the lower, and finally, others achieve this less insofar as they do not use the same strengths. But these use the first power, those the second, and those finally the third, though each soul possesses all the powers.

<margin>
VII.
Responses to doubts proving that our souls are not parts of the World Soul.
</margin>

Let this be said of these matters so far. However, what is said in the *Philebus* <note>Plato’s dialogue *Philebus* discusses the nature of pleasure and the good, and includes a section on the soul of the cosmos.</note> induces a suspicion that perhaps all souls are parts of the World Soul; but that passage does not mean what some might think, but rather what was most useful for the argument then: namely, that the world is animate. For in striving to prove this, he says it is absurd to say the heavens are inanimate when we, who have a body that is part of the world's body, have a soul. For how could a part have a soul if the whole were inanimate? But Plato’s opinion is most clear in the *Timaeus*: where, after the World Soul has already been made, the others thereafter arise in the same mixing bowl <note>original Latin: *patera*; Greek: *κρατῆρος* (kratēros). This refers to the vessel where the Demiurge mixes the ingredients of the soul.</note> in which that first soul was mixed, and they are made conformable to it; but he assigns their difference through second and third degrees. And as for what is said in the *Phaedrus*, that every soul has care for all that is inanimate: what wonder is there? For what else governs, forms, orders, and makes the nature of the body, if not the soul? Nor should it be said that while one can naturally do this, the other cannot at all. Whence he adds: "The soul being perfect, therefore,"—meaning that of the universe—"carried on high, does not become immersed, but (as I might say)"

<column-break/>

...administer in the world. Or is it no wonder that those who possess the same knowledge, some rule more, others fewer? But why this is so, someone might be able to say. But one might say there is a difference of souls, or rather in that one did not depart from the whole, but stayed there and held the body around it. But the others, already being there, we have received our portions as from a sister soul, as if she had prepared dwellings for them. It is also possible to see one soul looking toward the whole Intellect, and others more toward their own individual parts. Perhaps they too could have made the whole; but since she has made it, it is no longer possible for them as well, she having begun first. But someone will again raise the same doubt if any other soul had begun first. It is better to say it is because of being more dependent on the things above. For in those leaning toward that place, the power is greater. For they preserve themselves, and they act upon a secure foundation. For it belongs to a greater power not to be affected by what it makes; and the power is from above, and it remains. Remaining therefore in itself, it makes what follows; but those themselves who have wandered have departed into the depth. Or, much of them being dragged down, it dragged them down even in their thoughts, to be in the lower realm. For the "second" and "third" must be understood to be said of the "near" and the "farther"; just as among us, the relation to those things there does not belong to all souls alike, but some are united, and some come near in their desire, and some have less of them, insofar as they act with their powers or by themselves. But some act with the first power, others with the next, others with the third, though all possess all the powers.

THESE things then are in this way; but what was said in the *Philebus* provides a suspicion that the others are parts of the soul of the whole; but the argument does not wish this, as someone might think, but rather what was useful to him then, that the heaven is also animate. This he confirms, saying that it is absurd to say the heaven is inanimate, when we, who have a part of the body of the whole, have a soul. For how could the part have it if the whole were inanimate? He makes his opinion most clear in the *Timaeus*. For after the soul of the whole has come into being, he later makes the others: mixing them in the same bowl from which the soul of the whole came, making them of the same kind, and the others too. And he gives the difference as second and third. And as for that in the *Phaedrus*, that every soul cares for all that is inanimate, what else would it be that administers the nature of the body, and either molds, or orders, or makes it? It is soul. And one has this by nature in power, and another does not. Therefore, he says, the perfect soul, that of the whole, traveling on high, also administers; but as if...

### THIRD BOOK

->**THE THIRD BOOK OF THE FOURTH ENNEAD**<-

The Soul that hovers above acts upon the world, and whatever is perfect will dispense its influence in a similar way. Furthermore, where he <note>Referring to Plato in the *Phaedrus*, 246c</note> introduces the soul as if falling with broken wings, he clearly asserts that such a soul is different from the World Soul. Therefore, regarding the argument that souls follow the circuit of the universe, derive their character from it, and suffer because of it: this in no way signifies that our souls are merely parts of the whole. For a soul is capable of repelling many things that threaten from the heavens—influences arising from the nature of locations, waters, and the air. One's dwelling <note>original Latin: *habitatio*; Greek: *οἰκήσεις* (oikēseis)</note> and urban habits, as well as the physical temperaments of bodies, can also resist these celestial influences. And if we say that we, being enclosed within the universe, possess some life from the World Soul and suffer from the celestial circuit, we nonetheless introduce another soul on the opposite side that resists all these things; by this very resistance, it clearly shows itself to be different. To the point made that we are born within the world, we respond similarly: in the mother’s womb, the fetus has a different soul from the mother’s soul—specifically, a soul that enters from elsewhere.

<column-break/>

<margin>
VIII.
How souls differ; how they are immortal, remaining in their own form; and how the World Soul contributes to the life of all things.
</margin>

And these matters may be considered resolved for now. Furthermore, the fact that souls feel sympathy with one another should not hinder our reasoning. For since all souls flow from the same source—the same one from which the World Soul proceeds—they naturally feel sympathy for each other. Now, it has already been said that the soul is both one and many. We have also spoken of the difference between the part and the whole, and finally, of the difference between souls themselves; let us now speak of this summarily. We say, therefore, that beyond bodily differences, souls differ among themselves—most especially in their character and in the duties of their thought—partly due to the different ways they conducted their previous lives. For in the *Republic*, it is reported by Plato <note>Refers to the Myth of Er in Book X of Plato’s *Republic*</note> that souls choose their subsequent lives based on their preceding ones. However, if one considers the nature of the soul itself in general, he also placed differences there, where he arranged second and third degrees of rank. Furthermore, it has been said that all souls are "all things," but each soul is defined by what it actively exercises within itself. This means that one soul is unified in action, another in knowledge, and another in appetite <note>The three basic functions of the soul in Neoplatonism: *praxis* (action), *gnōsis* (knowledge), and *orexis* (desire/appetite)</note>. Moreover, they differ because different souls look upon different things, and the things they look upon, they both are and become. A full and perfect duty is appropriate to souls, yet not the same duty to all; rather, they relate to each other as if the entire coordination of them were said to be varied. For there is one universal Reason-Principle <note>original Greek: *logos*</note> that is manifold and varied, like a living creature that is both animated and multiform. If this is so, and there is a coordination, then beings are neither entirely separated from one another, nor is anything found to be made at random anywhere in the order of beings—not even in physical bodies. Therefore, it follows that there is a certain sequential Number. For it is necessary that beings consist of this, and that the intelligible things <note>term: *intelligibilia* — the eternal realities or "Forms" that can only be grasped by the mind, not the senses</note> remain the same, each being "one in number"; for in this way, each is called "this specific thing." Whereas in the realm of bodies, individual things naturally flow and change—since they receive their form as something added from the outside—existence according to "Form" <note>original Latin: *speciem*; Greek: *εἴδους* (eidous)</note> is found here to be perpetual through a certain imitation of true beings. But among true beings, which are not made of parts, existence itself consists in being "one in number." This exists from the very beginning; it does not become what it was not before, nor will that which is ever cease to be.

<meta>catchword: one in number</meta>

He explains that while all souls share a common source, they differ based on their previous lives, their chosen focus (action, knowledge, or desire), and their rank within the cosmic order.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's discussion from the previous section regarding whether individual souls are distinct from the World Soul. It transitions from the unity of the soul's power to the specific mechanisms of how a soul enters or "falls" into a physical body.</meta>

**PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.**

**A** Since, if there is anything that the soul itself produces, it certainly will not produce it from matter. If this is so, it must also add something essential from its own being. For this reason, there will be a change in the soul regarding that very action, depending on whether it now produces more or less. Furthermore, it may be asked why it acts now, and not always in the same manner. Indeed, that which is produced will not be eternal if it admits to "more" or "less." Yet the soul is established as such a thing. How then will it be infinite if it is held stable? Perhaps it is infinite in power, since its power itself is infinite—not **B** as something to be divided into infinity, since even God is not limited. Thus it is with souls: for no soul is what it is by an external limit, as if it were of a certain size, but it exists as much as it wills; nor is it ever led to step outside of itself. Rather, it flows through the whole, which is so prepared by its own nature that the soul runs through bodies into bodies. Yet it is not distracted from itself, since it is present in the finger of the hand and in the foot at the same time. So it is in the universe: into whatever it runs, it is in various parts, just as in the parts of a **C** plant. Even if a part is cut off, the soul remains in the original plant and also in that which has been separated from it. For the body of the universe is one, and the soul is, as it were, everywhere in that one. However, in a decaying animal, if many animals should arise from it, the soul of the whole animal is no longer in that body <note>Plotinus refers to the ancient theory of spontaneous generation, where life was thought to emerge from rotting matter.</note>; for the body no longer has its own proper receptacle for it, yet the soul has not perished. But those things which, through decay, are fit for the generation of animals, receive a soul, some from **D** these sources and some from those; since the soul itself is never absent. When one thing is able to receive it and another is not, the living things thus produced do not force there to be many souls: for they depend on the one, insofar as that soul remains one. Just as in ourselves, when certain parts are cut away and others grow in their place, the soul is absent from the former but applies itself to the latter, insofar as it remains one. In the universe, however, the soul always remains one. Among the things in the universe, **E** some retain life, while others do not, even though the same powers of the soul itself persist meanwhile.

<margin>
IX
The second question: In how many ways the soul is introduced into the body; what the nature of the World Soul is; how it creates the world and its dimensions; and how it is present everywhere.

WE MUST furthermore inquire how the soul is introduced into the body: for this seems no less worthy of wonder and investigation. There are two ways through which the soul enters the body: one occurs when a soul already joined to a body **F** changes either from one solid body to another, or from an aerial or fiery body into an earthly one <note>This refers to the concept of metempsychosis or the transmigration of souls between different types of physical forms.</note>. Many do not call this a "change of bodies" because the source of this introduction is hidden. The other mode is that by which the soul falls from the incorporeal into any body whatsoever: this is indeed the first commerce of the soul with the body. It is worthwhile to consider first this "fall," and what passion occurs when the soul—hitherto living entirely pure and apart from the body—first takes upon itself the nature of a body. Perhaps it is proper **G** to begin from the Soul of the All; indeed, it is necessary to pursue the truth regarding it. Since, if it produces these things, it will not be from matter. If it is by its own being, it must add something essential from itself. Thus there will be a change in that very thing, in producing more or less. And why now, and not always so, if that which is produced is not eternal, being "more" or "less"? The soul is said to be rational. How then will it be infinite if it stands still? Either it is infinite in power, because the power is infinite. Not as if it were to be divided into infinity, since even God is not bounded. And these souls are such that each is what it is not by a foreign limit, such as being "so much"; rather, the soul itself is as much as it wills. And it does not ever happen that it proceeds outside of itself, but it reaches everywhere, as is its nature, to run upon and into bodies. And it remains distinct. It is from itself even when it is in the finger and in the foot as one. So indeed in the universe, into whatever it may reach in one part or another, as in a plant. And if a part is cut off, it exists both in the original plant and in the part cut from it. For if the body of the universe is one, it is as if the soul is everywhere in one. But if all things are life, and many animals come from it, that soul is no longer the soul of the whole animal in the body. For the body has it, but it does not have the body's soul. For those parts died. But those things from the decay, being fit for the life of a living being, have a soul from this or that, nothing being given where it was not. They are present by being able to receive it, or not being able to receive it. And the things that thus become ensouled do not make many souls. For they depend on one, which remains one, just as in us. When some parts are cut and others grow in their stead, the soul departs from some and approaches others, as long as the one soul remains. In the universe, the one always remains. Of the things within it, some it possesses, and some it sets aside, while the same soul-powers remain.

BUT how the soul comes to be in the body must be sought, both the manner and the how. For this is no less worthy of wonder and investigation. Since there is a twofold manner of the soul’s entry into the body. For one soul comes to be in a body, being already in a body, either by changing bodies or by coming from an airy body into an earthly one. This they call "re-embodiment," because it is unclear from where the entry comes. The other is from the incorporeal into any body: which would be the first communion of the soul with the body. It would be right to examine this, what the passion produced then is, when the soul, being entirely pure of body, first takes on the nature of a body. Regarding the soul of the whole, one might perhaps start from here, or rather it happens to be necessary. ### THIRD BOOK.

**A** This universe is animated; indeed, a body could never have existed as a substantial reality <note>original: *ὑποστατικὸν* (hypostatikon)</note> if the soul were entirely absent, nor could matter have ever existed in an unorganized state. It is possible, however, to distinguish these things from one another in our words and thoughts; for we may analyze every composite thing through reason and intellect, even though the truth of the matter is as follows: if there were no body, the soul would not proceed forth, since there is no other place where it is naturally meant to be. But if it is to proceed, it will create a place for itself, and thus it generates a body. **B** When the soul’s stability is strengthened by its very own state of rest—much like a great light shining out—a shadow results at the very furthest edges of its fire. When the soul perceives this shadow, it gives it form, since the soul itself already exists as a reality. For it was not right for anything near the soul to be devoid of reason <note>original: *λόγος* (logos)</note>. Therefore, in that which was produced next, something faint and obscure was received, which is also called "shadow-like." Thus, the world was made like a beautiful **C** and many-colored building; it is not cut off from its maker, nor again is the maker mixed into it, but the whole world is deemed worthy of care and attention in every way. For the world, it is beneficial to exist within beauty, to participate in it as much as it is able; for the creator, remaining unmixed, this process is harmless. For the creator presides while remaining in the heights. Indeed, the world is animated in such a way that it does not so much possess a soul, as it is possessed by it: it is mastered rather than mastering, held rather than holding. For it lies **D** within the soul that supports it, and no part of it is without a share of that soul. Just as a net in the waters is soaked through with life, yet it is not able to make the water its own; rather, as the sea is already extended, the net extends along with it as far as it can. For each part of the net cannot be anywhere other than where it is placed. But the Soul is so great and vast by nature because it is not limited by a physical size. Thus, it can embrace the entire body in one and the same power, and **E** wherever the body extends, the soul is there. And if the body did not exist, the soul would have no need to occupy space. For the soul is whatever it is within itself. The universe is only as large as the soul occupies; the world is defined by how far the soul proceeds, for the soul is its preserver. The shadow is as large as the reason <note>original: *λόγος* (logos)</note> that hangs from the soul. And the reason was such that it produced a magnitude as great as the Form <note>original: *εἶδος* (eidos)</note> itself wished to create.

**F** When we have considered these things, we must return again to that which is always true: we must take all existing things together—such as the air, the light, the sun, or the moon. Consider the sun and its light again as all one, yet having an order of first, second, and third parts. Here, one must consider the soul as always stable. Then there are the primary things, and those that follow, like the furthest reaches of fire extending outward—the first extreme being thought of as the shadow of the fire. **G** Then, this shadow is illuminated at the same time, so that a Form is, as it were, imposed upon that which was applied, which at first was entirely obscure, and it clothes it. It was organized according to the reason and power of the soul, which possesses within itself a power that extends through the whole.

PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

<margin>A</margin>
Since the soul creates things, it certainly does not create them out of matter <note>original: *ex materia*</note>. If this is the case, it must add something essential from its own self. For this reason, if the soul were to do more or less at different times, there would be a change within the soul itself. Furthermore, one might ask: why does it act now, and not always in the same way? Indeed, that which has been created will not be eternal if it admits to being "more" or "less." But the soul is established as something of such a nature. How, then, will it be infinite if it is fixed? Perhaps it is infinite in power <note>original Latin: *potentia*; Greek: *δυνάμει* (dynamei)</note>, because the power itself is infinite, not in the sense that it is to be divided infinitely, since even 
<margin>B</margin>
God is not limited. This is also how it stands with souls: no soul is what it is by an external limit, as if it were a certain size. Rather, it exists to whatever extent it wills. It is never led to go outside of itself; instead, it flows through the whole of that which is naturally fitted to it, so that it runs through bodies and into bodies. Yet, it is not pulled apart from itself when it is present in the finger of a hand and in the foot at the same time. This is exactly how it is in the universe: into whatever part it runs, it is like the various parts 
<margin>C</margin>
of a plant. If a certain part is cut off, the soul remains in the original plant and also in that which has been separated from it. For the body of the universe is one, and the soul is everywhere within it as if in a single entity. If many animals arise from a decaying organism <note>original: *putrefacto*</note>, the soul of the whole animal is no longer in that body, for that body no longer possesses its own proper vessel for the soul; nor, however, has the soul perished. But those things which, through decay, are made fit for the generation of animals, receive a soul—partly from these 
<margin>D</margin>
sources and partly from those. This is because the soul itself is never absent, although one thing may be able to receive it while another cannot. Those things which become living in this way do not force there to be "more" souls; for they depend on the one soul, insofar as it remains one. Just as in us, when certain parts are cut away and others sprout in their place, the soul is absent from the former but applies itself to the latter, insofar as it remains one. In the universe, however, the soul always remains one. As for the things in the universe, some retain life and others do not, yet all the while the same powers of the soul itself persist.
