<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Soul’s relationship to the physical world, moving from the general animation of the universe to the specific ways the Soul imitates higher "reasons" to form matter, and how humans can use this principle to connect with the divine.</meta>

### PLOTINUS ENNEAD IV.

<column-break/>

...should adorn it: Just as the **formative principles** <note>original Latin: *rationes*; Greek: *logoi*. These are the active, creative blueprints that translate divine ideas into physical reality.</note> in seeds shape and form living creatures like certain "little worlds." Whatever the soul touches is perfected in this way, according to the natural state of the soul’s essence. She does this not by some added opinion, nor by waiting for counsel or deliberation; for if she did, she would be acting not by nature, but by an acquired **art**. For art itself is secondary to the soul and merely imitates her, producing shadowy and weak imitations—mere playthings of little value—using many mechanical devices to fashion these images. 

But the Soul, through the power of her own essence, is so much the mistress of bodies that they are made and disposed exactly as she leads them; indeed, even those things formed from the beginning cannot resist her will. In subsequent things, however, because of mutual obstacles everywhere, the matter is often so hindered that it does not receive its own proper form—that which the formative principle, hiding in a small seed, intended. 

But in the higher realm, where the whole form is produced by the soul and the things produced maintain their order, that which is created emerges beautiful, without labor or hindrance. Within the soul herself are established some shrines for the Gods, some dwellings for men, and other things accommodated to others. For what else ought to be produced by the soul, except those things which she has the power to make? Just as it is the property of fire to make things hot, and of something else to make things cold, the work of the soul is partly directed from herself into another thing, and partly remains within herself. 

In inanimate things, that which comes from them lies as if asleep within them; but that which tends toward another can and does strive to make that other similar to itself, as much as the other is capable of being affected. Now, this is common to all things: to strive toward a likeness of themselves in their actions. But the work of the soul is something "awake" and effective, both in what stays within her and what tends toward another. She makes other things live—whatever does not live by itself—and she gives them a life like the one she herself lives. Thus, living in **Reason**, she imparts Reason to the body as an image of her own Reason. For the amount of life she imparts to the body is an image of life, and at the same time she imparts the bodily forms of which she possesses the formative principles. She possesses the principles of the Gods and of all things; therefore, this world also possesses all things.

<margin>XI. Magic <note>Plotinus is referring to "theurgy," the practice of drawing divine influence into the physical world.</note> draws its power specifically from the soul of the world, and through this, from the higher gods to the mundane gods.</margin>

AND so it seems to me that the ancient sages, who desired the gods to be present with them, built temples and statues by looking toward the nature of the universe. They perceived that the nature of the Soul is everywhere "easy to lead" <note>original Greek: *εὐάγωγον* (euagōgon). This suggests the soul is naturally inclined to flow into prepared vessels.</note> and prone to be captured, if one fashions something that can easily be affected by her and receive a portion of her. Now, that which is most easily affected is that which is in any way fit for imitation, like a mirror capable of catching a certain appearance. 

For the nature of the universe fashions all things with a wonderful artistry in imitation of those things whose formative principles it possesses within itself. And since everything is made in this way, surely the **reason** within matter—which was formed according to a higher reason above matter—is joined to that God according to whom it was generated, and toward whom the soul looked when she possessed it.

<column-break/>

...to adorn, just as the formative principles <note>logoi</note> in seeds shape and form living creatures like certain "little worlds." Whatever touches the soul is made according to the essence of the soul’s nature. She acts not by an external opinion, nor by a will that waits for contemplation. If she did, she would be acting not by nature, but by an acquired art. For art is posterior to her and imitates her, making dim and weak imitations—playthings of a sort, not worth much—using many devices for the sake of an image <margin>* images</margin>. 

But the soul, by the power of her essence, is mistress of bodies, so that they come into being and exist just as she leads them; they cannot resist her will from the beginning. In later things, however, which hinder one another, they are often deprived of attaining their own form, even though the Reason <note>logos</note> intends it. 

But there, as the whole form is produced by her and the things produced have their order at once, that which is produced is beautiful, arising without toil or hindrance. Within it are the statues of gods, the dwellings of men, and other things for others. For what must come from the soul, except those things which she has the power to make? It is the property of fire to make things hot, and of another thing to make things cold. Of the soul, one part is from herself into another, and another is within herself. In soulless things, that which comes from them is as if sleeping and lying within them; but that which goes into another makes it like itself, according to its ability to be affected. 

This is common to all: to lead everything into a likeness of itself. The work of the soul is something "awake," both within itself and toward another. She makes other things live—those that do not live of themselves—giving them a life like her own. Living, then, in Reason, she gives Reason to the body as an image of what she holds. For the life she gives the body is an image of life, and she gives the forms of bodies of which she holds the formative principles. She holds those of the gods and of all things; therefore, the world holds all things.

AND it seems to me that the ancient sages, who wished for the gods to be present to them by making temples and statues, looked toward the nature of the whole and took into their minds that the nature of the soul is everywhere "easy to lead." It would be easiest of all to receive her if one were to construct something sympathetic to her, capable of receiving a portion of her. 

Everything is sympathetic that imitates her in any way, like a mirror capable of snatching a certain form. For the nature of the whole, having made all things with good craft in imitation of the Reasons she held, and since each thing was made as a "reason in matter" formed according to the Reason prior to matter, she joined it to that god according to whom it was made, and toward whom the soul looked and held.

<summary>Plotinus explains that the World Soul creates the physical universe effortlessly through internal "formative principles" (logoi), much like a seed grows into a plant. He also provides a philosophical justification for religious statues, arguing that physical objects can "capture" divine presence if they are crafted to imitatively resonate with the Soul.</summary>

# BOOK THREE.

...to do so. Accordingly, it was not possible for anything here to be void of divinity, nor again was it possible for that higher nature to descend into these lower things. For that higher state is the **Intellect** <note>original Greek: *nous*; Latin: *mens*. In Neoplatonic thought, the Intellect is the first emanation of the Divine, containing the eternal "blueprints" of all things.</note> itself, like a divine sun that serves as the model for our reasoning. Immediately following this is the **Soul**, which remains suspended from the Intellect as it stays in its place. The Soul provides her own boundaries to this sun, acting as a medium through which subsequent things are brought back to the higher realm. She becomes an interpreter, both of the things brought from there to here, and of those returning from here to there, insofar as they return to the Intellect through the Soul. For nothing is entirely separated from anything else, yet things are distinct by a certain difference and mixture; everything exists in itself, without being confined to a physical place, yet they all breathe together, remaining both united and distinct. They are still **Gods** <note>original: *theoi*. Plotinus often refers to the stars and the higher aspects of the Soul as "gods" because they never lose their connection to the divine source.</note>, because they never depart from those higher things, and the Soul is suspended from them from the beginning. However, as the Soul diffuses herself down to this realm, she seems in a sense to depart. In this way, because they look toward the Intellect, they are called divine—the Soul herself never looking toward anything else but that higher realm.

<column-break/>

...to do so. Accordingly, it was neither possible for anything here to be void of divinity, nor again for that divine nature to descend into these lower things. For that higher state is the Intellect itself, like a divine sun that serves as the model for our reasoning. Immediately following this is the Soul, which remains suspended from the Intellect as it stays in its place. The Soul provides her own boundaries to this sun, acting as a medium through which subsequent things are brought back to the higher realm. She becomes an interpreter, both of the things brought from there to here, and of those returning from here to there, insofar as they return to the Intellect through the Soul. For nothing is entirely separated from anything else, yet they are separated by a certain difference and mixture; everything exists in itself, without being confined to a physical place, yet they all breathe together, remaining both united and distinct. They are still Gods, because they never depart from those higher things, and the Soul is suspended from them from the beginning. However, as the Soul diffuses herself down to this realm, she seems in a sense to depart. In this way, because they look toward the Intellect, they are called divine—the Soul herself never looking toward anything else but that higher realm.

<margin>XII. On the difference in the descent of souls; on the mercy of Jove toward souls; on the harmony of the world.</margin>
But the **souls of men**, catching sight of their own reflections as if in the **mirror of Dionysus** <note>original: *Dionysio in speculo*. This refers to an Orphic myth where the young god Dionysus is distracted by a mirror, symbolizing the soul becoming fascinated by its own reflection in matter and thus "descending" into a body.</note>, rushed down from above. Yet, they were not cut off from their own source or from the Intellect. They did not descend *with* the Intellect, but they reached as far as the earth, even while their "head" remained fixed above the heavens. It happened, however, that they wandered further because their middle power was forced to care for these lower things, since the realm into which they descended required great care and cultivation. **Jupiter** <note>original: *Iupiter* (Latin) / *Zeus* (Greek). In this context, the king of the gods represents the providential governing power of the universe.</note> the father, taking pity on their struggles, made the bonds by which they suffer mortal and dissolvable. He granted them rests at certain intervals of time, providing freedom from their bodies so that they too might occasionally be where the **Soul of the World** is—she who is never turned toward these lower anxieties. For what the universe already possesses is sufficient for itself and will continue to be so, according to the eternal principles that exist within time. Everything is brought into a single harmony through the measured cycles of defined lives, where these lower things are aligned with the higher according to a single, ordered Reason—including the descents and ascents of souls and all other things. This is further proven by the harmony of souls with the order of the universe; they do not merely depend on it, but accommodate themselves to it in their descent, creating a single concord with the revolution of the world. Thus, their fortunes, lives, and choices are signified by the patterns of the **stars**. It has been said that the universe produces one harmonious sound—a cosmic music—which the ancients designed, albeit obscurely, through musical consonances. This would not be so unless the world acted and was acted upon in each detail according to these revolutions and orders, through the various paths that souls travel—now in that realm, now in this...

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

...indeed in heaven, but at other times turned toward lower things. Every **Intellect** <note>original Greek: *nous*. In Neoplatonic philosophy, the Intellect is the realm of pure, eternal thought and the source of all Forms or blueprints for reality.</note> is always in the highest realms, nor does it ever fall from its seat; rather, remaining firmly in the heights, it sends something down through the soul to these things here. The Soul, indeed, is more closely affected by the **Form** <note>original Latin: *speciem*; the ideal essence of a thing.</note> flourishing there and hands it on to the things following it—sometimes in the same condition, other times differently—maintaining a wandering variety within a certain order. It does not always descend in equal measure, but sometimes more and sometimes less, even if they return to the same genus. Accordingly, each soul falls to its prepared place based on the likeness of its own disposition. For insofar as it has already become similar to this or that thing there, it is then carried into a human, or into this brute animal, and another into something else.

<margin>
XIII
The divine law implanted in souls leads them out both voluntarily and by necessity to the limits suitable to their disposition.
</margin>

### XIII

Regarding what is said of the inevitable law and divine judgment, it exists in nature as a governing and commanding force, so that each thing proceeds in order toward that for which each image was made, according to its prior choice and primary disposition. And that entire type of soul is congruent and close to that for which it conceived an affection within itself; it looks toward that which it then sends where it is necessary and introduces it—not that it must go into a body right then, or into a specific body, but when the prescribed limit is at hand, the souls descend as if of their own accord to where they must and enter. For each has its own "appointed day." When this day finally looms, as if a herald were calling, they slip down and enter the body suitable for them. They behave almost as if they were moved and carried by the powerful forces and attractions of **Magi** <note>Plotinus uses the analogy of magic to describe "sympathy," the natural pull or attraction between the soul and the physical world that operates without conscious effort.</note>. Furthermore, they are like the management of a whole living creature, moving at certain times and producing things like hair, beards, or horns; or like the impulses and vigors toward certain things at specific times, or flowers in plants which never sprouted before—all distributed according to certain ordered rules. Souls proceed neither entirely of their own will nor by compulsion. For they are not said to choose "voluntarily" in the sense of a calculated decision, but rather to leap forward by nature—much like how we are provoked to physical desires or to certain honorable actions by instinct rather than by rational counsel. Yet, such a fate is always present in such a person; likewise, this moment for one and that moment for another occurs as decreed by fate. Consequently, the Intellect above the world is fated to remain there constantly, while also sending something down; then, individual souls, subject to the common law, are sent forth step by step. For a common rule is implanted in each, and the law does not receive the power to fulfill its duty from the outside, but is given on the condition that those who use it carry it around with them. Then, when the time looms which the law itself decreed, it is carried out by those who have the law within them, so that they themselves fulfill the law; for it drives them around and, because it is founded in them, it executes its decrees more powerfully, as if weighing them down with its own weight, while both by zeal...

<column-break/>

...indeed in heaven, but others toward these parts of the whole, being turned; every Intellect is always in eternity, and would never become outside of its own things, but fixed entirely on high, it sends things here through the soul. The soul, from its proximity, is disposed rather according to the Form from there, which it gives to the things after it—sometimes consistently, sometimes differently, prevailing in order through the majority. It descends, not always in equal measure, but sometimes more, sometimes less, though it remains at the same height of itself. Each soul descends into a **fortress** <note>original Greek: *eryma*. This term implies the body is a sort of enclosure or defensive work for the soul.</note> according to the likeness of its disposition. For whatever it has become like there, it is carried toward: one into a human, another into another animal.

That which is inescapable, and **Justice** <note>original Greek: *Dike*. In this context, Justice refers to the cosmic balance that ensures everything ends up where it belongs.</note>, which prevails in nature so that each goes in order—as each is a becoming-image of choice and archetypal disposition. And every form of the soul is similar to that toward which it holds a disposition from itself; and that which sends and introduces it; and both when it should come into the body, and into this specific one; but also at the time it goes into it, it descends as if spontaneously and enters where it must. And one time for one, another for another. When this arrives, as if a herald were calling, they descend and enter the fitting body—as if with a forceful body—just as things happen to each by the powers of the magi and certain strong attractions, to be moved and carried. Just as in each individual, the administration of life is completed; in each time there are movements and growth, such as the growing of beards and the nature of horns. And now toward these impulses and passions, not being present before. And concerning the management of trees, which happen by fixed laws. They go when each is sent. There is a voluntary element, not as if choosing beforehand, but as leaping by nature, or toward the natural deadlines of marriage, or toward certain beautiful actions, not moved by calculation, but always what is fated to such a kind, and to such a person now, and to another later. And the Intellect from the world, by fate, has its remaining there, as much as it also sends. And it subordinates the individual to the universal law, and it is sent. For the universal is situated in each. And the law does not have strength for its completion from outside, but is given to be in those using it, and they carry it around; and time will bring it, and what it wants to happen happens then, by those having it themselves; so that they themselves complete it, since they carry it and have power, because it is established in them as a cause, as if weighing upon them, and zeal...

<meta>catchword: stimu-</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that the descent of the soul into a body is a natural fulfillment of divine law and cosmic order, comparing the process to biological growth or the pull of magical sympathy rather than a conscious choice or a random event. He emphasizes that the "law" governing the soul's fate is internal, carried within the soul itself until the "appointed day" for its incarnation arrives.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the soul's journey. # BOOK THREE <note>original: LIBER TERTIVS. Although the header says Book Three, this text corresponds to what is now known as Plotinus's Ennead IV, Book 3.</note>

...falling into, from which it is possible to go there, or what you are to them, as if he sounds a call to come.

THESE THINGS HAVING HAPPENED, the world, possessing many lights and being illuminated by souls, is adorned according to the prior things <note>The "prior things" are the higher, intelligible realities or Forms.</note>, bringing one world after another from those gods and from other minds that provide souls. It is likely that the myth hints at such a thing when it says that after Prometheus fashioned a certain woman, the other gods also adorned her—mixing earth with water, giving her a human voice, making her form like the goddesses, and Aphrodite and the Graces giving her something, and each one another gift. They named her Pandora <note>Pandora translates to "All-Gifted."</note> because of the gift, for all had given something to this creature, which was made by a certain "forethought" <note>original Greek: *prometheia*, a pun on the name Prometheus.</note>. But if Prometheus refuses her gift, what could it signify except that the choice of the Intelligible <note>The realm of pure thought and spirit.</note> is better? The creator is bound because he somehow touches what he has made; and the bond is from without, and the release is by Heracles, because there is a power in him through which he can be released. However one may judge these myths, they clearly show the gifts coming into the world from above and agree with what has been said.

SOULS GO FORTH, looking out from the Intelligible, first into heaven, and having taken a body there, they pass through it into more earthy bodies, as far as they extend in length. Some pass from heaven into lower bodies, and others move from one body to another—those whose power was not strong enough to lift them from there are weighed down by forgetfulness and carry much with them, by which they are burdened. They become different either through the variations of the bodies into which they are entered, or by fortunes, or by their upbringings; or they bring the difference from within themselves, or through all or some of these things. And some fall entirely under the fate of this place, while others are sometimes under fate and sometimes their own masters. As many as are necessary, they allow to be endured; but they are able to keep their own works as their own, living according to another legislation of all existing things, giving themselves to another law. This law is woven from all the reasons and causes here, and from the movements of souls and the laws from above, harmonizing with those, taking its beginnings from there, and making the consequences follow them—keeping unshaken whatever can save itself according to the state of those higher things. But the other things it leads around as nature dictates, so that the cause is in those who descend, in that they are placed here in one way, and there in another.

<column-break/>

...a stimulus; it strikes from within, [urging the soul] to proceed thither, where the innermost law dictates it should especially go.

<margin>
XIV.
On the connection of this world through the higher one, and the gifts of the gods descending into the worldly work.
</margin>

SINCE these things are so, this world, having many lights and illustrated by souls, is adorned into the prior states through other prior worlds; or, having one ornament from one source and another from another, it receives them both from those gods and from other minds handing down souls. It is likely that something of this sort is indicated by the fable which says: After Prometheus had fashioned a woman, the other gods also adorned her. To this end, it is handed down there that earth was mixed with water, and a human voice was added to that figure. Furthermore, representing the appearance of goddesses, Venus <note>Aphrodite</note> and the Graces bestowed something, each giving a different gift, and she received the name Pandora from the gift and from all the givers. For everyone gave some gift to this fashioned thing—a thing, I say, already formed by a certain providence <note>original Latin: *prouidentia*, translating the Greek *prometheia*.</note>. But as for Prometheus giving her no gift, what else does it signify but that the acceptance and choice of the intelligible gift is superior? Moreover, that creator is bound because he seems in a certain way to touch his own work: but a bond of this kind is from the outside, and is loosened by Hercules: because in him there is a faculty through which he is even, in a way, made free. But let anyone take this as they please. Let it be certain, however, that by these things the gifts coming from above into the world are shown. Therefore, they seem to harmonize with those things which were said in the preceding parts.

<margin>
XV.
On the departure of souls, transmigration, differences, fate, free choice, providence: and how they connect the order to themselves like a very broad fate and free choice alike.
</margin>

SOULS PROCEED, turning away from the intelligible world, first into heaven, and there receiving a body, they glide through it into more earthly bodies, as far as they progress forward. And some indeed pass from heaven into lower bodies and vice versa, while others pass from some into others: because the faculty to lift themselves from here is not available to them due to weight and forgetfulness, dragging much with them, by which weight they are cast down through lower things. Moreover, souls become different among themselves either because of the diversity of the bodies into which they are insinuated, or else because of fortunes, or again educations, or besides they carry a difference from within themselves, and they differ entirely either through all these things or through some of them.

Accordingly, some succumb entirely to the fate dominating here, while others partly yield to fate and partly live by their own right. There are also those who concede that as many things as are necessary must be endured;

yet they are able to reserve as their own whatever belongs to their own duty, living namely according to another certain constitution of laws embracing all beings at once, and committing themselves to another rule. This web is woven from all the reasons and causes that are here, likewise from the movements of souls and the laws depending from there, being clearly consonant with those, and taking its beginnings from there, and weaving all consequences with them:

then indeed keeping all those things unshaken, which can keep themselves according to the habit of those higher things. But the other things it leads around according as their own nature carries them, so much so that the cause is in those descending, because they are so disposed that some are placed here, and in such a way, while others are placed there, and situated differently.

<summary>Plotinus uses the myth of Pandora and Prometheus to explain how the physical world is "gifted" its beauty and life by higher divine realms, while describing the soul's descent into matter as a process influenced by both universal fate and individual choice.</summary>

<meta>The previous page concluded a mythological allegory involving Prometheus and Pandora, illustrating how the soul is "adorned" with gifts as it descends from the divine realm. This page transitions into a philosophical defense of divine providence and the specific mechanics of how the soul moves from the intelligible world into the physical heavens.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

<column-break/>

<margin>
XVI.
Since the super-celestial and even the celestial world is most perfectly ordered, it is necessarily and divinely so even in the sublunary <note>The "sublunary" realm refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, everything "below the moon," which was traditionally seen as a place of change and decay compared to the eternal heavens.</note> realm. Since things lower than man are ordered, then much more so are human affairs. Therefore, individual things are justly dispensed to men by divine power.
</margin>

**PUNISHMENTS** which are justly inflicted upon the wicked must therefore be attributed to the universal Order, which leads all things toward what is fitting. Moreover, whatever happens to good people contrary to what seems just—such as penalties, poverty, or diseases—perhaps occurs because of the offenses of a prior life. <note>Plotinus, following Plato, believed in the reincarnation of the soul; thus, present suffering might be "karmic" retribution for past actions.</note> For these things are woven together and even foretold, so that they too are seen to occur according to Reason <note>original: *rationem*, translating the Greek *logos*, the rational principle governing the universe.</note>. But do these things not occur according to natural reasons, and should they not be placed among those things primarily intended, but rather as consequences of them? For example, if a house falls and someone underneath is killed, whoever they may be; or if two things move in a certain order, or even if one thing is struck and broken or ruined. Perhaps this very thing which is called "unjust" is neither an evil to the sufferer, nor is it unhelpful to the sequence of the Whole; and perhaps it is not even truly unjust, since individual things are dispensed justly based on what preceded them. For we must not think that some things have an order among themselves while others deflect from it into mere whim and license. For if all things must occur according to natural causes and consequences, and according to one Reason and one Order, we must surely believe that even the smallest things are coordinated and woven into the pattern. Therefore, that which is inflicted by one upon another as an injustice is indeed an injustice for the one who does it, and he is not free from blame; yet, being coordinated within the universe, it is not unjust within the context of the Whole, nor is it even unjustly inflicted upon the sufferer, but rather it was fitting. And if the one who suffers is good, the end of these sufferings eventually turns toward the good. Certainly, we must believe that this common order of the universe is not devoid of divinity and justice, but renders what is fitting to each according to an most exact reason—though it keeps the causes hidden within itself, and thereby provides an occasion for complaint to those who are ignorant.

<margin>
XVII.
Just as the highest part of the air is first of all ignited by the lowest part of the fire, so the heaven is the highest earthly body and the last, and is less animated by the soul, which is the last of the divine things. Likewise, the Good itself is like a center; the Intellect is the light flashing and remaining there; the Soul is the light setting itself apart from the light. The body, which is opaque by itself, is illuminated by the soul; but the soul in another thus illuminates as one, not without care beneath the heaven.
</margin>

**WHY** souls descend from the intelligible world <note>The realm of pure Being and Thought, above the physical world.</note> into the heavens first can be conjectured from these points. For if the heaven is the most excellent thing in the realm of the senses, it is rightly the closest to the last of the intelligible things. Therefore, the celestial things are the first to be animated and receive from there, as they are much better suited for receiving. But the earthly body is the last, and can participate less in the soul and less naturally, as it is the furthest removed from incorporeal nature. Truly, all souls illuminate the heaven, and give, as it were, the greatest and first part of themselves to the celestial sphere, while other things are illuminated by the subsequent parts. But those souls that descend further illuminate another thing below, and in a different way; it is not advantageous for them to have fallen so far. There is, indeed, something like a center, and next to this a circle flashing from it; and beyond these another circle, light from light. Beyond these, there is no longer a circle of light, but something now in need of foreign light, due to a lack of its own light. Let this be a "rhombus" <note>original: *rhombus*. In ancient astronomy/philosophy, this can refer to a spinning top or a geometric shape representing the motion of the planetary spheres.</note>, or rather a sphere of such a kind, which receives from the third level to which it is closest, and shines by its proximity. Thus, a vast, permanent light illuminates, and a splendor proceeds from it according to Reason; and the other things shine together, partly remaining, and partly moving further away...

<column-break/>

The errors that occur, falling upon the wicked with justice, should be attributed to the Order, so that it may lead to what is necessary even there. But as for all the things that happen to the good outside of justice, such as punishments, or poverty, or diseases: must we say they happen because of a previous sin? For these things are interwoven and signified there beforehand, so that they too happen according to Reason. Or are these things not even a natural Reason? Rather, they are not among the primary things, but following those—such as when a building falls, and whoever happens to be under it dies, whoever he may be; or if two people are moving and one is struck and wounded, or suffers something. Or is this "injustice" of each event useful to the sufferer for the weaving together of the whole? Or is it not even unjust, but a justification based on things that happened before? One should not think that some things are coordinated, while others are loosened into free-will. For if things happen according to causes and natural consequences, and one Reason and one Order, we must believe that even the smallest things are coordinated and woven together. The injustice, then, from one to another, is an injustice to the one who did it, and the doer is not released from the cause, but it is coordinated in the Whole. It is not unjust in that context, nor for the sufferer; but it had to be so. And if the sufferer is good, the end of these things leads to good. One must believe the things of the Whole are not godless, nor unjust, but exact in the rendering of what is fitting. But the causes are hidden, and to those who do not know, they provide reasons for blame.

THAT the souls go from the intelligible into the region of the heaven first, one might reason from the primary things. For if the heaven is the best in the sensible place, it would be adjacent to the last of the intelligibles; therefore, souls take these things first, or participate in them, as they are more suitable to participate. But the earthy is the last, and is naturally less able to participate in soul, being far from the incorporeal nature. All souls indeed shine upon the heaven, and give, as it were, the great part of themselves and the first part to that, while the other things are illuminated together by the latter parts. But the souls that go down further, illuminate another thing below, and it is not better for them as they proceed far. For there is something like a center, and upon this a circle shining from it; and upon these another, light from light. But outside of these, there is no longer another circle of light, but one needing internal light of its own, through the lack of the borrowed beam; within is a certain "rhombus" <note>original Greek: *rhombos*.</note>, or rather such a sphere as is carried from the third level. This is adjacent, insofar as it is well-lit by that. The great light, indeed, remains and shines out, and the beam from it reaches out according to Reason; and the other things shine together, some remaining, and some moving further...

<meta>catchword: ἐπί- (upon/towards)</meta>

<summary>Plotinus discusses divine providence, arguing that all suffering and "accidents" are part of a rational cosmic order, potentially linked to past lives. He then uses a metaphor of concentric circles of light to explain how the soul emanates from the divine center to illuminate the heavens and, eventually, the darker material world.</summary>

### BOOK THREE

...they are turned away by the illumination of the subject. Then, since those things which are illuminated require great care—just as pilots on storm-tossed ships focus more intensely on steering the vessels, and forgetting themselves, they hardly notice they are in such danger that they might sink along with the shipwreck—so also such souls depart from themselves as much as possible; then they are held more tightly, bound by the chains of enchantment, specifically devoted to the care of nature. <note>Plotinus uses the metaphor of a ship's captain to explain how the soul becomes "lost" in the physical world; it becomes so focused on managing the "ship" (the body) that it forgets its own divine origin.</note> But if every animal were like the universe—having a perfect and sufficient body, established beyond the dangers of passions—surely the soul which is said to be present in the body would not truly be present there as a prisoner, but would provide life to it while remaining entirely in the high places <note>original: *in excelsis*, referring to the eternal, unchanging realm of the stars and the divine.</note>.

<margin>
XVIII
According to Plotinus and Iamblichus, souls are sometimes outside of any body, and then the rational power is so effective and unhindered that it understands everything the intellect brings to it without time, or in the briefest moment. Likewise, souls conversing with each other in the heavens do so without speech, as if understanding through mutual signs; but in bodies, souls and spirits <note>original: *daemones*, which in Neoplatonism refers to intermediaries between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note> form voices.
</margin>

**AFTER THIS**, we must ask whether the soul uses the discourse of reason <note>original: *λογισμῷ* / *discursu rationis*—this refers to step-by-step logical thinking.</note> before it descends into the body and after its departure. Perhaps rational discourse occurs only while it inhabits the body, since it is placed in uncertainty and is anxious with cares, and as if already weakened. For needing the discourse of reason to achieve sufficiency in life and truth happens because of a certain deficiency of the mind; just as the consultation of reason happens in the arts when craftsmen are in doubt, as if falling short of perfection. But where no difficulty or defect is opposed, the art immediately prevails and acts. <note>This is a key Platonic idea: "Reasoning" is a step-by-step process used when we don't already "know" or "see" the truth. A perfect mind just "sees" the truth instantly without needing to think it through.</note> But if souls live there without reasoning, how can they still be called "rational"? Perhaps someone might answer that they are called rational because they *can* consider things rightly if ever it should be necessary. But one must understand reasoning in this way: if one takes reasoning to be a stable disposition and action, always flowing from the intellect and existing in the souls, and like a certain radiance from there, then indeed souls there will use a certain discourse of reason. However, I do not think they use voices there, as long as they inhabit the purely intelligible place.

<column-break/>

When they have bodies in the heavens, they do not use speeches there such as they are accustomed to use among us due to need or ambiguity; and since they do each thing there according to a certain order and according to nature, they rightly neither command anything nor consult. But they know each other's thoughts through a reciprocal notion of consciousness, since even here we perceive many things in those who are silent by a glance alone. There, however, every body is pure, and every inhabitant is like a whole eye. <note>In the celestial realm, Plotinus suggests there is no privacy or deception; because bodies there are "transparent" or "pure," souls see each other's thoughts directly.</note> Nothing there is hidden, nothing is feigned, but before you have said anything to another, the other understands. However, it is not absurd for spirits and souls dwelling in the air to use voices, for such are those animals.

<margin>
XIX
The sensual life is blended from properties that are both individual and shared (divisible). It is called "divisible" regarding the body because it accommodates itself to its individual parts. It is also called "indivisible" because it is present as a whole in each part. But reason and mind are called "impartible" <note>meaning "incapable of being divided into parts."</note> simply because they do not use a bodily instrument and are therefore separate.
</margin>

**WHETHER** "impartible" and "partible" are said to be in the soul according to the same thing, as if these two were blended together; or rather, whether it is called impartible for one reason and partible for another, as if different parts were arranged in succession, just as we are accustomed to call this the "rational" part and that the "irrational" part. This will be manifest to us after we have explained what we mean most especially by each term. In the first place, "impartible" in Plato is taken simply; but "partible" is not taken simply, but regarding the soul.

<summary>This page explores how the soul's reliance on logical reasoning is a sign of its descent and "weakening" compared to its state in the divine realm, where it perceives truth directly and communicates without speech. It also begins a technical analysis of the soul as being simultaneously divisible (in the body) and indivisible (in its essence).</summary>

### PLOTINUS’ ENNEADS, BOOK IV

[A] He <note>Referring to Plato, specifically his dialogue *Timaeus*.</note> says that the soul becomes **divisible** around bodies, yet it was not inherently made to be so. Indeed, it is proper to consider the nature of the body—specifically, what kind of life it requires from the soul, and why it is necessary for the soul's power to be present everywhere throughout the body, and to be entirely present in every part. Every **sensory** <note>original: *sensuale*; Greek: *αἰσθητικόν* (aisthētikon)</note> part must, if it is to perceive through the whole, have already reached a state of being divided throughout the whole in some way. While it exists everywhere, it is not wrongly said to be "divided"; however, because it appears as a whole everywhere, it is not said to be "entirely divided," but rather to **become divisible** around bodies. [B] But if someone should say that the soul is not divided in the other senses, but only in the sense of touch, the response must be that it is also divided in the others: for if the body is what receives the sensation, it must be divided, though perhaps less so than in touch. Furthermore, the vegetative and growth-giving power of the soul is distributed in a similar way; just as if **concupiscence** <note>The faculty of desire or appetite.</note> flourishes around the liver, and **anger** <note>original: *iracundia*; Greek: *θυμὸς* (thymos)</note> around the heart, the logic remains much the same in these cases. But perhaps the soul does not receive these things in that mixture, or perhaps they arise in another way from certain things received there. However, **reason** and **intellect** do not hand themselves over to the body. [C] For their work is not perfected through the instrument of the body; indeed, the body would be a hindrance if anyone were to use it during meditations. Therefore, whether the **impartible** <note>Indivisible or unable to be split into parts.</note> and the **partible** <note>Divisible or split into parts.</note> are different from each other, they do not appear to be fused into one, but are like a whole made of parts, each part remaining pure and separate in its power. If, however, that which becomes divisible around bodies also possesses an indivisible quality from a higher [D] power, then this same thing can be both indivisible and divisible at once—as if it were a blend of its own self and a certain virtue coming into it from above.

<margin>
XX
The soul is not in the body as if in a location or a vessel, nor as a part within a whole, nor as a quality in a subject, nor as a form in matter; rather, the body is in the soul, as if in a life-giving, encompassing, moving, and stabilizing force.
</margin>

[E] It remains for us to explain whether these and other parts of the soul are located in a "place," or if some are not in a place at all while others are, and where and how, or if no part at all is in a place. For if we do not assign a specific place to each part of the soul—that is, placing something somewhere—we shall judge it to be no more inside the body than outside it, and thus we would leave the body within the soul. Nor would we be able to explain how those works are performed which are carried out through bodily instruments. On the other hand, if we describe a location for some parts of the soul but not for others, then those for which we have not described a location will seem not to be placed within us at all, so that we would not seem to believe that our whole soul is [F] within us. In general, however, we must not place any part of the soul, nor the whole soul, in the body as if in a location. For a "place" is something that encompasses and contains bodies. And where each divided thing lies, it lies in such a way that the whole cannot be in any single part. But the soul is not a body; it is that which encompasses rather than that which is encompassed. Nor is it in the body as if in a vessel; for if it were, the body would be left soulless, whether the vessel or the location contained the soul—unless perhaps the soul [G] transmitted something of itself into the vessel, and thus as much as the vessel participated in, that much would have been taken away from the soul. But a "place" in the primary sense of the word is something incorporeal, not a body.

<column-break/>

[A] He says it becomes **divided** around bodies, and that this has occurred. But we must look at the nature of the body to see how it needs life and what kind of soul it requires; and that the soul must be present everywhere in the body and present to it as a whole. For everything that is **sensory**, if it is to perceive through the whole, must arrive at a state of being divided; for being everywhere, it might be said to be divided, but appearing as a whole everywhere, it would [B] not be said to be completely divided; but it becomes divided in the body. And if someone should say that in the other senses it is not divided, but only in touch, it must be said that it is also in the others: since it is the body that participates, it must be divided within, though somewhat less than in touch. And clearly the natural and growth-producing part of it is the same: desire is around the liver, and anger is around the heart, and the same logic applies to these. But perhaps it receives these in that mixture. Or perhaps in another way, or these arise from some things received there. [C] But **reason** and **intellect** no longer give these things to the body, for their work is not fulfilled through the instrument of the body: for this would be a hindrance, if someone were to use it in his reflections. Therefore, each is different, the **undivided** and the **divided**: and they are not as if mixed into one, but as a whole from parts, each being pure, and separate in power. If, however, that which becomes divided around bodies has its undivided nature from that higher power, this same thing could [D] be both undivided and divided; as if mixed from itself and from the power coming into it from above.

[E] It is proper to investigate whether these and the other so-called parts of the soul are in a place, or whether these are not in a place at all, and others are in a place, and how, or if none are at all. For if we do not assign some place to each part of the soul, placing nothing anywhere, or rather having made them more inside the body or outside it, we shall make it soulless; and we will be at a loss to say how the works through the bodily instruments should happen. Or if we give some a place and others not: those to which we do not give a place, we shall seem not to make them in us, so that not all of our soul would be in us. In general, then, one must not say that any [F] of the parts of the soul, nor the whole soul, is in the body as in a place. For place is encompassing, and encompassing of a body, and where each thing is divided, it is there; so that it is not a whole in any part. But the soul is not a body: and it is not encompassed, but rather encompassing. Nor is it as if in a vessel, for the body would become soulless, whether it encompasses as a vessel or as a place; [G] unless perhaps having handed over something, as much as was gathered around itself, and that which the vessel participated in. This would be lost to it. But "place" in the proper sense is something incorporeal and not a body.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul is not "in" the body like an object in a box, but rather the body is "in" the soul; he explains how the soul's higher functions remain independent of physical organs.</summary>

# BOOK THREE.

<column-break/>

**A** Therefore, why would the soul need a place? Furthermore, the body approaches the soul not through itself, but through its own limit <note>Plotinus is arguing against the Aristotelian idea that everything must be "in a place." He suggests the soul, being incorporeal, does not occupy space the way physical objects do.</note>. Many other objections could be raised against those who place the soul in the body as if in a location: for a "place" would always have to be carried along with the thing located within it. And it would remain to be asked what it is that carries the place itself along with it. Moreover, if a place is defined as a certain interval <note>original: *interuallum*; Greek: *διάστημα* (diastēma). Here meaning spatial distance or a "void" occupied by matter.</note>, the soul would be even less likely to be in the body as in a place. For an interval, **B** or space, must necessarily be empty; but the body is not empty, though perhaps that "emptiness" is said to be the thing in which the body exists. Therefore, the body would be in the empty space. Again, the soul is not in the body as if in a substrate <note>original: *subiecto*; Greek: *ὑποκειμένῳ* (hypokeimenō). In ancient logic, a "substrate" is the underlying thing that possesses qualities, like a piece of wax being the substrate for the color red.</note>. For that which is in a substrate is merely a "passion" or quality of the thing in which it resides—like color or shape—whereas the soul is something separable. Nor is it like a part in a whole, for the soul is not a part of the body. If someone should say the soul is like a part in the whole living being, the same doubt **C** will press upon us when we ask how it is in that whole. For it is not in the body like wine in a vessel, nor is it like the vessel itself; nor is it in the body in the way that something remains in itself; but it is even like the "whole" existing in the "parts." Indeed, it is ridiculous to call the soul the "whole" and the body the "parts." Furthermore, it is not like a form in matter <note>original: *species in materia*; Greek: *εἶδος ἐν ὕλῃ* (eidos en hylē)</note>, for a form is inseparable from its matter. And whereas the form arrives after the matter already exists, the soul actually produces the form within the matter, being itself something different from that **D** form. But if they say the soul is not a "produced" form but a "separated" one, it will not yet be clear by what condition this form is in the body; and the soul would thus be entirely separate. 

But if these things are so, why is it said by everyone that the soul is "in the body"? Indeed, since the soul is not visible but the body is, when we see the body and realize it is alive because it moves and feels, we say—not without reason—that the body "has" a soul. **E** Consequently, we think the soul is in the body. However, if the soul could be seen and felt, existing as something full of life, surrounding the body on all sides with life, and extending itself equally to the furthest extremities, we would never admit that the soul is in the body. Instead, we would say that the less important thing exists within the more important—the contained within the container, and the flowing body within that which does not flow.

<margin>
XXI.
The soul is not properly "in" the body, but is present as a pilot to a ship or as a power in a vessel.
</margin>

### WHAT then shall we say if someone asks
**F** how the soul is present to the body, without offering any explanation himself? Also, if he asks whether the whole soul is present at once, or if different parts are present in different ways? Since none of the previously mentioned ways of "being in something" have yet been proven to fit the soul’s relationship to the body, we must consider the saying that the soul is in the body like a "pilot in a ship" <note>This famous metaphor suggests that the soul controls and directs the body without being physically "mixed" with it, allowing for the soul's immortality and independence.</note>. This is a good way of speaking insofar as it regards the soul's ability to be **G** separated from the body; however, it does not perfectly explain the mode of union we are seeking. For if the soul is taken to be like a sailor, the pilot would be there only by "accident" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a non-essential property. Plotinus means the soul wouldn't be truly unified with the life of the body.</note>. If he is there as a pilot only, he is present in the whole ship just as the soul is in the whole body. But is it...

<column-break/>

<summary>Plotinus critiques various theories of how the soul resides in the body, rejecting the ideas that it is like a physical location, a quality (like color), or a part of a whole. He concludes that the soul is the "container" of the body rather than vice versa, introducing the "pilot in a ship" analogy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation into the union of the soul and the body. Having dismissed the idea of the soul being "contained" by the body like water in a jar, Plotinus now explores more sophisticated metaphors: the craftsman's skill in his tools, the pilot in a ship, and finally, the famous analogy of light in the air.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD IV.

**PAGE 388**

<columns>2</columns>

Should it be said this way? Just as art exists within its tools—for example, in a rudder, as if the rudder were itself alive—so that the skill of steering is within it, moving it with technical precision. But there is a difference here, since art of that kind depends on something outside of it. If, therefore, following that model of the pilot, we place the soul within the body as if it were a natural tool—insinuating itself into the rudder—for the soul moves the body in whatever way it pleases, will we have gained anything more toward our inquiry? Or will we again wonder how it exists within this tool? For even if this mode is different from the others, we still desire to find a clearer explanation and draw closer to the truth.

<margin>
XXII.
The soul is present to the body in a separable way, just as light is present to the air. The body is in the soul, just as air is in light. Mind and reason are not present to the body, because they do not communicate with it in action. The senses and the vegetative power are present because they act through the body, and the body requires them; however, they do not depend on the body for their existence.
</margin>

But should we not rather say that the soul is in the body in the same way that fire (that is, light) is in the air? For while light is present in the air, it is also not present: it is present through the whole, yet mixes with nothing. It remains itself while the air flows past it. And when the air moves outside the space where the light is, it leaves immediately, retaining nothing of the light; yet as long as it is under the light, it is illuminated. For this reason, one might correctly say here that the air is in the light, rather than the light being in the air. This is why Plato, in describing the generation of the universe, did not want to say that the soul was placed in the body, but rather that the body was placed within the soul. He says that there is a part of the soul in which the body exists, and another part in which there is no body—namely, those powers of the soul which the body does not need at all. The same reasoning applies to other souls as well. Truly, we must think that the other powers of the soul are not present to the body, but those which it needs are present—and present in such a way that they are situated neither in the parts nor in the whole body. For the power of sensing is present to the whole sensing being; but for the sake of performing specific actions, different powers are assigned to different parts. I speak of it in this manner:

<note>original Greek: "ἱδρυθέντα γὰρ μέρεσιν αὐτῇ..." This passage reinforces that the soul's power is not "fixed" or "seated" in physical parts as if it were a physical substance, but is present to the whole being for the purpose of perception.</note>

*Every power of the soul is whole in every part of the body, just like the soul itself. But it is said to act there where its tool serves it: and primarily there where the tool has its beginning. Thus, the act of sensing and moving is attributed to the head, from which the nerves—the tools of sense and motion—derive. Likewise, the act of anger is centered around the heart, where its tool, the "fiery blood," is located. Nutrition is centered around the liver, where the "airy blood" <note>In ancient physiology, different types of blood or "spirits" (pneuma) were thought to facilitate different bodily functions.</note> is its tool. The act of reason, although it has no physical communion with the body, is in a way attributed to the head, because the act of imagination is close to reason and shares in its nature.*

When the living body is illuminated by the soul, we say that different parts of the body receive this illumination differently, each according to the tool's fitness for a specific task. Thus, we name the power in the eyes "vision," in the ears "hearing," in the tongue "tasting," and in the nostrils "smelling." We are accustomed to placing the power of "touch" in the whole body, for the entire body seems to serve as the soul’s tool for this perception. Furthermore, since the tools of touch are primarily in the nerves which possess the power for the animal's movement, and this power adapts itself there—and since the nerves originate from the brain—thinkers have placed the beginning of sensation and impulse, and indeed the beginning of the entire living creature, in this place <note>original: "ἀρχὴν" (archē) - meaning a starting point, principle, or source of authority</note>, deriving it from there to other parts where the tools have their origins...

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the original Greek text corresponding to the Latin translation provided in the first column.</note>

...should we say it this way? Just as art is in tools, as in a rudder, as if the rudder were ensouled, so that the movement is within it technically and skillfully. But now it differs, because art is from the outside. If therefore, according to the example of the pilot, we place the soul itself in the rudder, to be in the body as in a natural tool: for it moves it thus in whatever it wishes to do. Would anything more be gained for us toward what is sought, or will we again be at a loss as to how it is in the tool? And what other way is there than the previous ones? But we still desire to find it, and to come closer.

Should we then say that when the soul is present to the body, it is present to it as fire is present to the air? For this too, being present, is both present and not present; and it is not mixed, but stays itself, while the air flows by. And when it gets outside that in which the light is, it goes away having nothing; but as long as it is under the light, it is illuminated. So it is correct even here to say that the air is in the light, rather than the light in the air. This is why Plato also beautifully placed the soul in the body throughout the whole, but rather the body in the soul. And he says there is a certain part of the soul in which the body is, and a part where the body is not, clearly regarding those powers which the body does not need from the soul. And indeed, the same account would apply to other souls. Of the other powers, one should not even say there is a presence of the soul to the body; but those which it needs, these are present—and present not being established in parts of it, but as a whole; and for sensation, the sensing power is present to the whole sensing thing; but for activities, one to one part, another to another. I speak thus.

->Chapter XXIII.<-

The body being illuminated by the ensouled principle from the soul, different parts partake of it differently. And according to the fitness of the tool for the work, the appropriate power is assigned to the work. In this it is said that the power in the eyes is the visual; that in the ears is the auditory, and the gustatory in the tongue, and smell in the nostrils; but the tactile is present in all. For toward this perception, the whole body is present as a tool to the soul. Since the tactile organs are primarily in the nerves, which indeed have the power for the movement of the living being, they received this opinion there. Since the nerves receive from the brain the beginning of sensation and impulse, they placed the principle <note>archē</note> and generally that of the whole living being there...

<summary>Plotinus utilizes the analogy of light in air to explain how the soul illuminates the body without being confined by it, concluding that the body is in the soul rather than the soul in the body. He details how specific soul-powers (like sight or hearing) relate to physical organs and identifies the brain as the functional center for sensation and movement.</summary>

### BOOK THREE.

<page-num>389</page-num>

<columns>2</columns>

...having placed that which will use it <note>original: παρεῖναι τὸ χρησόμενον τιθέμενοι</note>. It would have been better to place the principle of that power’s operation there: for where the instrument was to be moved, there the power of the craftsman had to be established, as if in a state of necessity, in proportion to the instrument's weight. Or rather, the power itself is everywhere, for power is active everywhere. But the beginning of the action is there, at the starting point of the instrument. Since the power of sensing and the power of impulse—belonging to the sensory and <term>imaginative nature</term> <note>original: φανταστικῆς / imaginale; the faculty that creates mental images</note>—held reason above itself as if neighboring the lower parts, reason itself was placed by the ancients at the summit of the whole living being, in the head. This was not because reason is "in" the brain, but because it is in the sensory organ which is reasonably situated in the brain. 

<margin>A</margin> For it was necessary to assign the sensory part to the body, and specifically to that member most capable of receiving such activity. But reason, which in no way communicates with the body, had to communicate entirely with that which is the "form" of the soul—that is, the soul which is capable of obeying the perceptions received from reason. For the sensory faculty is a kind of judge, and the imaginative faculty is like a form of intellect. 

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, impulse and pursuit follow imagination and reason. There, then, is the seat of the <term>rational faculty</term> <note>original: τὸ λογιζόμενον</note>, not as if in a physical place, but because the sensory part there enjoys its influence. How the power of sensing is located there, and other powers similarly, has already been stated. 

<margin>C</margin> Accordingly, since the <term>vegetative nature</term> <note>the faculty responsible for growth and nutrition</note> and the powers of growth and nutrition are nowhere absent from the body, and since they nourish by means of the blood, and the nutritive blood is in the veins, and the origin of the veins and blood is in the liver—where this power is rooted—it is not without reason that the part of the soul responsible for <term>desire</term> <note>original: τὸ ἐπιθυμητικὸν / concupiscens; the part of the soul that yearns for physical needs</note> was placed here by the ancients. 

<margin>D</margin> For that which generates, nourishes, and grows must necessarily also desire these things. But since thin, light, sharp, and pure blood is the instrument suited for anger, the source of this—namely, from where such blood flows during the heat of passion—is the heart itself, which has been designated as the dwelling place of <term>spiritedness</term> <note>original: θυμῷ / iracundiæ; the part of the soul associated with courage and anger</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Having considered these things, we must ask where the soul is after it has been separated from the body. Certainly, it will not be here in the physical world; for there is nothing here to receive it in any way. Nor can it linger in that which is not naturally suited to hold it, unless it retains something of itself that draws the "loving soul" <note>a soul still attached to material things</note> toward it. 

<margin>B</margin> But the soul exists in that place where it can naturally be and become. Since there are many such places, the difference must arise both from the soul's own disposition and from that justice and judgment which rules over all things. For no one shall ever escape what they deserve to suffer for unjust actions. For the <term>divine law</term> <note>original: Lex divina</note> is inevitable, containing within itself the power to execute whatever has been judged. The one who suffers is carried along...

<sig>K 3</sig>

---

-> Since the soul is an incorporeal substance, existing in itself, it is not determined to any place except by its inclination and action regarding it. Therefore, once released from the earthly body, if it retains no such inclination, it is nowhere on earth, and yet everywhere—unless perhaps it is in a higher sphere through an inclination toward it. But if it still retains an inclination toward earthly things, it revolves around them with a "spiritual body" <note>an intermediate, airy body between the physical and the purely intellectual</note>, in which it also suffers bodily things. Furthermore, just as among astrologers some fulfill their fate even when unwilling, while in ignorance they choose something through which they secretly fall into fate; so all souls fulfill the divine law in themselves by choosing something, from which they fall into the hidden sentence of the divine law. <-

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD IV.

...to what you ought to suffer you are ignorant, driven by an unstable motion and wandering everywhere in your errors: but finally, as if exhausted by those things it resisted, the soul falls into a place suitable for it, entering into a voluntary suffering through a certain voluntary motion. <note>Plotinus suggests that while the soul's "fall" into a body seems accidental or forced, it actually follows a natural law where the soul "chooses" its destiny based on its own character.</note> It is decreed in the law both how much and how long it ought to suffer: and finally, there occurs both the remission of punishment and the power to escape from those places, and this is achieved by a certain power of the harmony that contains all things. Therefore, souls that inhabit a body also possess the capacity to suffer bodily torments. 

<sig>B</sig> But souls that are pure, and draw nothing of the corporeal with them in any way, are by no means confined by any corporeal situation. If, therefore, they are not designated to anything of this kind—for they do not have a body in any way—they are undoubtedly there where essence and <term>Being</term> <note>original: *ens* / *ὂν*; the fundamental reality of things</note> itself and the Divine consist in God. Here, I say, such a soul will dwell together with these and in this very reality. But if you still ask *where* this is, you must similarly ask where those divine things are. In searching for that, do not seek with your eyes, nor as if you were looking for physical bodies. <sig>C</sig>

<margin>
XXV
In the <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: *intellectu* / *νοῦς*; the divine mind or second principle of reality</note> there is no memory, because nothing new happens there or comes from the outside that needs to be preserved and recalled. Nor does any change from potentiality to action take place there; instead, the duty of recollection belongs to the soul.
</margin>

IT IS WORTHWHILE to investigate memory in a similar way: whether souls, when they have departed from these earthly places, remember; whether some indeed remember while others do not; and again, whether they have a memory of all things or rather of only some; and furthermore, whether they always remember, or perhaps only for a time close to their departure. But if we are to inquire correctly about this matter, we must first determine what this very thing is that remembers.

<sig>D</sig> I do not mean what memory itself is, but in what part of our nature it is most naturally found. For what memory is has been discussed elsewhere and is often repeated; but it must be explained more carefully what part of our nature is designed for memory. If the entire faculty of memory is something "adventitious"—that is, something added on by learning or by being acted upon—then surely <term>reminiscence</term> <note>the act of recalling or recollecting</note> is not suited to things that are free from suffering and not subject to time. Therefore, memory must not be attributed to God, nor to Being, nor to the Intellect. For nothing "happens" to them, nor does time exist around Being; rather, <term>Eternity</term> <note>original: *æuum* / *αἰών*; a state of timelessness, unlike the passing time of the physical world</note> does. In that realm, there is no "before" or "after," but it is always as it is, remaining in the same state and admitting no change at all. How could that which is always in the same and similar state use memory? It does not hold one disposition after another, nor does it gain one thought after a previous one, so that it might remain in one state while remembering a previous one.

<sig>F</sig> But what prevents this Intellect from knowing the changes of other things—such as the cycles of the world—while remaining unchanged itself? Perhaps it is because it would then understand one thing as "prior" and another as "posterior," following the changes of the moving object. Furthermore, remembering is something different from pure understanding; one should not say that the Intellect "remembers" its own thoughts. For its thoughts did not "pass away" so that it must hold onto them to prevent them from leaving; otherwise, it would fear that its very essence might depart from itself.

<sig>G</sig> But we should also not say that the soul remembers in the same way we speak of it remembering things that are innate to it. While the soul is here on earth, it possesses those innate truths, yet it does not always act according to them, especially since it is so far removed...

<column-break/>

<sig>A</sig> ...ignorant of what it was fitting to suffer: wandering everywhere in its errors with an unstable motion. But at the end, as if exhausted by the things it resisted, it fell into the place fitting for it, with a voluntary motion, having the involuntary in its suffering. <note>Greek: "τὸ ἀκούσιον εἰς τὸ παθεῖν ἔχων" — implying that while the fall is voluntary, the resulting suffering feels involuntary to the soul.</note> It is stated in the law how much and for how long one must suffer; and again, the relief from punishment and the power of flight from those places concur together, by the power of harmony which holds <sig>B</sig> all things together. Thus, they are held by the body, and they receive bodily punishments. But as for souls that are pure, or those that do not drag any part of the body along with them, they must of necessity not exist in a body. If, then, they are nowhere in a body, or if they have no body at all, their essence is there where Being is, and the Divine, and with God. There, indeed, with them and in such a state, the soul will be. But if you still seek "where," you must seek those things; but do not seek with the eyes of the flesh, nor as if seeking living bodies.

AND CONCERNING memory, it is equally worthy to ask whether it belongs to the souls themselves when they have gone out of these places: whether to some and not to others, and whether they remember all things or some. And if they remember always, or for some time close to their departure. But if we are going to make our inquiry correctly concerning these things, we must grasp what that which remembers actually is. <sig>D</sig> I mean, not what memory is, but in which of existing things it is naturally constituted. For what memory is has been said in other places and is frequently talked about; but we must more accurately grasp what it is that is naturally suited for memory. If the faculty of memory is a remnant of some learning or experience, then remembering would not belong to those beings that are "impassible" <note>unaffected by external stimuli or suffering</note>, as time does not exist for them. Memory does not belong to God, nor to Being, nor to the Intellect. For nothing happens to them, nor is there time; instead, there is Eternity around Being. And since how it is, is how it follows; it is always as it is in the same state, not receiving any variation. How could there be memory in that which is in the same and similar state? It does not have even a trace of other states which it had before, nor does it change from one thought to another, so that one remains while it remembers another which it had before. <sig>F</sig> But what prevents it from knowing the changes of other things without changing itself, such as the periods of the universe? Or is it because it will think of one thing as prior and another as later, following the changes of things that turn? But remembering is something other than thinking. Should we say it thinks of these things or remembers them? For either the thoughts came so that it might hold them lest they depart, or it would fear for its own essence, lest it depart from it. <sig>G</sig> Therefore, one should not say that memory exists even in the soul in the same way as we say memory is of those things which it has as innate; but since it is here, it has them not according to themselves, and especially being far from those things...

<summary>Plotinus discusses the soul's transition after death, arguing that pure souls return to a divine, timeless state. He begins a technical inquiry into memory, concluding that the Divine Intellect has no need for memory because it exists in an eternal "now" without change or the passage of time.</summary>
