### BOOK THE THIRD.

-> **COLUMN 1** <-

...was heard. The ancients seem to have defined "memory" and "recollection" as the act of already operating through those activities which the soul possessed. Thus, this is a different species of memory. For this reason, time does not necessarily accompany this kind of memory; but perhaps we treat these matters too casually and not with enough critical examination. For perhaps someone might wonder whether such "recollection" and "memory" do not belong to that [higher] soul, but to another dimmer one, or to the <term>composite being</term> <note>original: *synamphoteron* / *συναμφοτέρῳ*; the union of soul and body</note>, the living creature. And if it belongs to another soul, when and how did it receive what it records? Or if it belongs to the living creature, in what way does it do so? Therefore, we must seek what it is within us that possesses memory, just as we sought from the beginning: if it is the soul that remembers, what power or part is it? If it is the living creature—as it seems to everyone that the one who perceives is the animal—then in what manner does it occur? And what exactly should we call the "living creature"? Furthermore, must we assume that the same thing that perceives sensations also grasps intellectual concepts, or is it one thing for the former and another for the latter?

If the living creature is the composite of both soul and body, it must be of such a nature in its actual perception because it is a "sensing" thing; for this reason, it is called a "common" or "shared" activity, much like drilling or weaving. In this analogy, the soul acts as the craftsman, while the body serves as the instrument during the act of perceiving. While the body suffers and serves, the soul receives the impression of the body's own formation, or that which occurs through the body; or at least the soul produces a judgment from the body's affection. Indeed, sensation might be called a common work; but memory would not necessarily be a shared or common thing, since the soul has already received the "impression" <note>original: *typos* / *τύπον*; a stamp or mental image</note> and either preserves it or casts it away—unless one were to argue that remembering is also common because of the temperaments of bodies, as we are made either more or less "memorable" or "forgetful" by them. However, one might say the body acts as a hindrance, or that the body's state is a barrier to memory, while the act of remembering remains nonetheless the soul's own. As for the learning of disciplines, how could that be "common" rather than the soul itself remembering? If the living creature is a composite in such a way that it is a third thing arising from the two, it would be absurd to say the "animal" is neither body nor soul. For if both change, the animal is something different. Nor again is it a mixture such that the soul is in the animal only potentially; for even in that state, remembering would nonetheless belong to the soul—just as in a mixture of honey and wine, if it still tastes sweet, that sweetness comes from the honey. What if the soul itself remembers, but does so by being in the body, and thus is not "pure" but—as if on a tablet—can be imprinted with the forms of things perceived by the senses, the body providing a sort of seat for receiving them so they do not simply flow away? But first, these forms are not physical magnitudes; nor are they like seal-impressions, nor are sensations "stamps," because there is neither a physical pushing nor...

<column-break/>

-> **COLUMN 2** <-

...proceeding from it. The Ancients seem to have called the act of operating already according to those things which one held, "memory" and "recollection," and therefore this is a certain second species of memory. Wherefore time is least suited to this memory; but perhaps regarding these things, we conduct ourselves not so much with consideration as with ease and lightness. For perhaps someone will doubt whether memory and recollection of this kind belong not to that [higher] soul, but to another viler one, or even to this composite animal. Furthermore, if it belongs to another soul, he will wonder when and how it received the things it records; if it belongs to the animal, he will doubt similarly. For which reason it must be investigated what in us is most primarily endowed with memory, which we were also seeking from the beginning: and whether the soul records—and if so, what power or part of the soul—or whether the animal itself uses memory. Just as it appeared to some that it is the sensing thing itself, it must be asked: what is the manner, or what is to be said regarding the animal itself? Likewise, whether the same thing perceives sensibles, intelligibles, and anything else, or whether one thing perceives these and another perceives those.

<margin>
26. The animal is a certain unity, I do not say a unity made from the transformation of both parts into a third thing, but from the transfusion of the soul. To this one common thing belongs the effect of growing and vegetating. But stability belongs properly to the soul, not to the unstable body, which is the occasion of forgetting: for many things are preserved through memory, and are suggested, which were never perceived with the body.
</margin>

If therefore the animal is both together, in the senses according to the act, it is necessary that it also be something of this kind: wherefore it is called "common," just as weaving and drilling are: so that according to the craftsman the soul acts in sensing, but according to the instrument the body conducts itself. While the body indeed suffers and serves, the soul receives the formation of the body itself, or that which is made through the body: or at least the judgment, which it performs from the body's suffering. Where certainly sensation would be called a common action, but memory would not be forced to be so conjoined: since the soul has already received the figure, and either guards it or has cast it away, unless perhaps someone conjectures that memory is also a certain common thing, from the fact that by certain complexions of bodies we are accustomed to become sometimes mindful, sometimes forgetful. But it can indeed be said that the body either hinders or does not hinder the effect of recollection, but nevertheless the function of memory itself is proper to the soul. Now truly, as for the remembering of disciplines, how shall it be said not to belong to the soul, but rather to the conjoined composite? If however the animal is both together in such a way that a certain other thing comes forth from both, first indeed it will be absurd to say the animal is neither body nor soul. For the animal is not a certain diverse thing through the permutation of both, nor again so mixed that the soul is in the animal only by a certain power; and yet, even under this condition, remembering will nonetheless belong to the soul. Just as in a certain tempering made of wine and honey, if any sweetness remains and charms the taste, it has that very thing from the honey. What then? If the soul itself remembers, but from the fact that it is in the body, and therefore it is not pure, on the contrary, it can imprint and as if stabilize a seat in the body for capturing and preserving forms. But first indeed, figures of this kind are not magnitudes: then they are neither like seal-ring impressions, nor reverberations or certain figurations: since there is neither an impulse there, nor does it happen...

### PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK IV.

...just as is accustomed to happen in wax, but rather in another mode, such as that of intellection <note>the act of the mind understanding something</note>, even in things that are sensed. But in the act of understanding, what sort of "impulse" or "impression" could be spoken of? Or what need is there for a body, or even a bodily quality, through which the act of understanding might be completed? Furthermore, it is necessary for the soul to remember its own movements: such as the things it has desired, and those it has achieved, or those it failed to achieve. Nor does it reach all the way to the body when something is proposed to us as desirable. For in what way could it reach the body, when those things did not originate from the body? Or by what reason will the soul remember together with the body that which the nature of the body is in no way able to know? 

Indeed, it must be said that certain things end in the soul itself, namely whatever things come through the body; but certain things belong to the soul alone, if indeed it is necessary that the soul itself be something, and that a certain nature and work of its own exist. If, moreover, this desire is its own, and the memory of that desire is its own, then why should we also remember the attainment and the empty wish? For indeed, the soul’s own nature is not numbered among the class of things that "flow" <note>Plotinus contrasts the stable soul with the physical body, which is in a constant state of change or "flux"</note>. Unless it were so, we would grant the soul neither consensus, nor consequence, nor conspiracy <note>original: *conspiratio*; here meaning a "breathing together" or harmony of parts</note>, nor a kind of self-consciousness. For if the soul does not possess these things by its own nature, it certainly will not acquire them in the body. But surely it has certain actions, the execution of which requires the instruments of the body, and it brings the powers for these with it; it even brings the actions of certain powers with it. 

As far as memory is concerned, the body is an impediment; since even now, forgetfulness occurs from the joining of certain things to us. But in the removal and a certain purification of these things, memory often emerges within us. While the soul is alone, if a mobile and flowing bodily nature were to be added, it would necessarily bring about not the cause of memory, but of oblivion: wherefore this might even be estimated to be the <term>River Lethe</term> <note>In Greek mythology, the river of forgetfulness in the underworld</note>. Memory, therefore, belongs to the soul.

THAT BOTH souls are eternal, and after death there can be reason among the gods, and meanwhile an irrational part, which is its <term>Idol</term> <note>original: *eidolon*; a lower reflection or shadow</note> among men; and that this remembers things done in this life, mostly its own passions, and less of the things pertaining to the rational soul. Likewise in a human being—I do not say one who is temperate, but one who is continent or incontinent—both souls migrate together and are mindful of human affairs: more easily indeed as long as they live in an <term>aerial body</term> <note>A subtle, non-physical envelope believed to surround the soul after death</note>, but more difficultly if they should at some time receive an earthly body. It would perhaps be more probable to say that one soul is within us. And from this, the vital force, or the life-giving act flowing into this body, is called as if it were a second soul. This is said to be made from the "Life of the All" because it flows from our soul under the power of the universal life.

<margin>
XXVII.
A poetic-like opinion that there are twin souls in man, differing in substance from each other. The rational soul from the maker of the world himself, but the irrational from the life of the world.
</margin>

HOWEVER, it must be asked to which soul the condition of memory belongs. For one part of the soul is called more divine, according to which we exist; but the other depends on the whole [universe]. Perhaps it must be said that memory belongs to both, but one memory is private and the other is common. And when both are joined, all memories exist together; but if they are separated, provided that both exist and remain, the one soul preserves its own things for a longer time, but those which pertain to our [earthly] side for a shorter time. This is what is called the <term>Idol</term>. We must think, as I believe, that the <term>Image of Hercules</term> <note>Plotinus uses the example of Hercules from the Odyssey: his "shade" is in Hades, but his true self is on Olympus</note> in the underworld remembers all that was done in life, for his life was mostly this. But the others...

Or why is there a need for a body, or a bodily quality, with which it occurs? But indeed, it is necessary for the soul to have memory of its own movements: such as what it desired and what it did not enjoy, and how the desired thing came into the body. <margin>B</margin> For how will the body speak of things that did not come into it? Or how will the soul remember with the body that which the body is not by nature able to know at all? But it must be said that some things end in the soul, as many as come through the body; but others belong to the soul alone, if the soul is indeed something, and has a certain nature and work of its own. And if it has desire and memory of the desire: then surely also of the attainment or the failure. Since its nature is not among those things that flow. For if this were not so, we would give it neither consciousness nor <margin>C</margin> the power to follow along; nor any preservation of thoughts, nor understanding. For if it did not have these in its own nature, it would not obtain them in the body. But it holds certain activities, for the completion of which it needs organs. Of some things it brings the powers; of others, it even brings the activities. But as for memory, it finds the body to be an obstacle. Since even now, forgetfulness comes from certain distractions; but by <margin>D</margin> removal and purification, memory often resurfaces. But while it is alone, the nature of the body, being moved and flowing, must necessarily be the cause of forgetfulness, but not of memory. Wherefore this may be understood as the River of Forgetfulness; this experience is within the soul.

For one will not say that one thing indeed enjoys, while another remembers those things which the other enjoyed. The power of desiring, therefore, having at some time obtained 
<margin>D</margin>
delights, if ever the desired object meets it again, is moved again through memory. For why is it moved neither by any other object, nor otherwise than thus? What therefore prevents us from attributing to it the sense of such things also? And similarly, we might attribute desire to the sensual part, and so through all things similarly, so that each is named according to that which prevails? Or do we perhaps attribute sense to individuals differently? Just as vision indeed saw, but not the nature of desiring itself. But this was incited by the sense, as if a certain translation followed,
<margin>E</margin>
not indeed so that this part says what the sense is like entirely, but that it suffers without its own observation. By the same reasoning in those things which look toward anger: vision indeed saw the injurer, but the spiritedness was irritated; just as if, with the shepherd seeing a wolf threatening the flocks, the dog is irritated—not having looked itself, but provoked by a certain impulse or noise. For indeed the nature of desiring once possessed, and
<margin>F</margin>
retains the mark engrafted in itself of that which was done, not as memory, but as a certain affection and passion. But it is another thing which observes the consequence of the one possessing, and possesses within itself the memory of the thing done. Indeed, the proof of this is that the memory often does not know what the power of desiring participated in, although they still reside in this very part.

->SHALL WE THEREFORE dedicate memory<-
to the sensory virtue? And will the same thing be capable of sensing for us which is also capable of memory? But if the image of the soul also remembers, as we were saying,
<margin>G</margin>
 the sensory part in us will be double; and if the sensory part is not the rememberer, but any other thing is, then that other thing will at least be twofold in its remembering. Furthermore, if the sensory part also pertains to retaining disciplines,

<summary>Plotinus distinguishes between the emotional impulses of the lower soul (like a dog reacting to a shepherd’s alarm) and the actual faculty of memory, which he begins to locate in the "inner sense" or imagination. He uses the figure of Hercules to illustrate how a soul can have different sets of memories depending on its state of purification from the body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of memory. In the previous section, Plotinus explored whether the soul or the combined entity of soul and body is responsible for remembering. He concluded that memory is a power of the soul, but one that can be hindered by the physical form.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

<margin>A</margin>
...will also perceive the thoughts themselves, or rather will something else pertain to each? Should we then, by establishing a common "perceiver," grant memory of both to this? Indeed, if the perceiver of sensible things and intelligible things <note>sensible things are those perceived by the five senses; intelligible things are concepts or truths understood by the mind</note> were one and the same, then something might be said for this view. But if it is divided in two, there will nonetheless be two distinct things. If we attribute both functions to each part of the soul, four powers would result. Generally, however, what necessity compels us to remember with the same power by which we perceive, and to perform both with the same faculty? Or that we should remember thoughts with the same thing by which we think?
<margin>B</margin>
After all, the same people are not equally powerful in thinking and in retaining things in memory. Those who are equally strong in sense-perception are not equally strong in memory; some have very sharp senses but lack memory, while others excel in memory even though they are not particularly acute in their perceptions. But again, if each faculty is different, it will also be necessary for there to be something else that remembers what the senses had previously perceived; and that thing must also perceive what it will have to remember. 
<margin>C</margin>
Perhaps, however, nothing will prevent the act of perceiving from appearing as a certain act of imagining <note>original: *imaginandi*. Plotinus suggests that for a sensation to be remembered, it must first be transformed into a mental image</note> to the power of memory. Memory and preservation belong to the "imaginal" nature, which is a different faculty. For this imagination is where perception ends; and when the external sensation ceases, the "vision" of it remains here. If, therefore, the imagination of the absent object resides within this faculty, it certainly possesses memory. If it remains only for a short time, it has a brief memory; but if it is preserved for a long time, these people excel more in memory. This is because this power is more robust and is not easily overturned or forced to lose its memorial marks. Memory, therefore, belongs to the imaginal power, and it is the memory of such things as these.
<margin>D</margin>
We shall say that souls differ in their ability to remember either because of the varying strengths of that power, or because of the frequency of their actions, or their lack of use, or because of bodily temperaments <note>original: *complexiones*. This refers to the balance of the four humors/elements in the body, which was thought to affect mental clarity</note> which are either present or absent, and which—when changed—change the memory, or conversely, or even disturb it. But these matters must be discussed elsewhere.

> *There are in us two imaginations: one in the irrational life, the other in the rational soul. The former is the peak of the senses, while the latter is the lowest point of thoughts. They are contiguous, and conscious awareness <note>original: *animadversio*</note> pertains to both. Therefore, just as we often see things but do not notice that we see them unless the sensory imagination attends to it and the vision itself is reflected in it, so we neither understand nor think with awareness unless such actions somehow touch the imagination continuous with them and are reflected in it as if in a mirror. Both the acts of the senses and the lower imagination reach this higher imagination, and it is in this very place that rational memory is located.*

---

<margin>Chapter XXX</margin>
**BUT** what shall we say of remembering thoughts? Does the imagination preserve these too? Indeed, if imagination followed every act of intellect, perhaps with this imagination remaining like a sort of "image" of the thought, there would indeed be a memory of the thing known. If not, another explanation must be sought. Perhaps, however, memory will be the transition and reception into the imagination, with reason accompanying the intelligence itself. For the very notion of intelligence—or, if I may put it this way, the *intelligible object* <note>original: *intelligimen*. Ficino’s Latin rendering of the Greek *noēma*, the content of a thought</note>—is indivisible and has not yet, as it were, come forth, but remains hidden within. But reason, unfolding and leading out from that very notion of intelligence into the imaginal power, has demonstrated that which is called the intelligible object as if in a mirror; and thus its awareness and permanence...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...let the perceiving part be for thoughts, or rather let there be something else for each. If we then set the perceiver as common, shall we give it memory of both? But if the perceiver of both the sensible and the intelligible is one and the same, then perhaps something is being said. But if it is divided in two, there will nonetheless be two. And if we give both to each part of the soul, there will be four. Generally, what necessity is there that we must remember thoughts with the power by which we perceive?
<margin>B</margin>
Since it is not the same people who are best at thinking and at remembering; and those using perception equally do not remember equally. Some are well-endowed with perception, but others are more "memory-inclined" <note>original: *mnēmonikoi*</note> without having used their perception sharply. But again, if each must be different, then something else must remember what the sense perceived before,
<margin>C</margin>
and that which is to remember must also perceive. Or perhaps nothing prevents the sensation from appearing as a kind of "appearance" <note>original: *phantasma*</note> to the one who remembers; and that memory and retention belong to the imaginative faculty <note>original: *phantastikon*</note>, which is something else. For this is where perception ends; and when it is no longer there, the vision is present to this faculty. If, then, the imagination of the thing is present in this, it already remembers. If it stays for a little while, the memory is small; but if it stays for a long time, they are more "memory-inclined" because this power is stronger, so that it is not easily changed and the memory does not slip away. Memory, then, belongs to the imaginative faculty. And let the remembering of such things be so.
<margin>D</margin>
We shall say that souls have different memories in this way, either because the powers themselves are different, or because of their actions, or because of bodily temperaments <note>original: *kraseis*</note> being present or not, or undergoing alteration or not, or even being in a state of turmoil. But these things are for elsewhere.

---

**BUT** as for thoughts: does the imaginative faculty handle these as well? If an imagination follows every act of intellect, perhaps with this imagination—being a sort of image of the thought—remaining, there would be memory of the thing known. If not, something else must be sought. Perhaps memory is the reception into the imaginative faculty by the reason <note>original: *logos*</note> that follows the thought. For the thought <note>original: *noēma*</note> is indivisible. And having not yet, as it were, come outside, it remains hidden within. But the reason, unfolding it and leading it from each thought into the imaginative faculty, shows the thought as if in a mirror; and the conscious grasping <note>original: *antilēpsis*</note> of it is thus, and its staying...

<summary>This page discusses the mechanics of memory, arguing that it resides in the imaginative faculty rather than the senses or the pure intellect. Plotinus explains that for a thought or sensation to be consciously remembered, it must be reflected into the imagination like an image in a mirror.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the dual nature of the soul and how memory functions within it. Plotinus is exploring the relationship between pure intellectual thought and the conscious awareness of that thought, as well as how the "higher" and "lower" aspects of the human soul interact to form a single experience of memory.</meta>

# BOOK THREE.

...and memory. Therefore, since the soul is always moved toward intelligence, whenever this process results in success for us, awareness <note>original: *animadversio*; the conscious "noticing" of a thought</note> arises. For understanding is one thing, and the awareness of that understanding is another. We are, in fact, always understanding, but we do not always notice it. This happens because the faculty that receives these impressions receives not only thoughts, but also sensations from the outside, and it does so interchangeably.

---

->*If our two souls were separated in space, they would have two distinct imaginations and memories. However, as long as they are together, the lower soul yields to the superior one in the formation of the body, just as a smaller light yields to a larger one. Therefore, there are not two separate animals here, because the superior soul acts as the form of the inferior, and the latter acts naturally in the body under the superior's form and activity. Furthermore, although imagination is naturally capable of memory in both souls, when one imagines more frequently and more strongly, the other either remains idle or acts so weakly—just as sight often "sees" nothing when the imagination is working intently on something else. It is fitting and natural that the lower imagination yields to the higher. This higher imagination, because it comprehends both the marks of intellectual things and the forms of sensible things, shows that the living being in us is one; and when it departs the body, if it has subjected the other soul to itself through training, it commits vices to oblivion and retains more honorable things. Chapter XXXI.*<-

<margin>A</margin> BUT if memory belongs to the imagination, and both parts of the soul are said to remember, then there will be two distinct powers of imagining. Certainly, if the souls were separated from each other, they would each have their own. But since they exist together within us, how can they have two, and in which of them is the memory-impression made? If it were made in both, there would always be double imaginations. We should not say that one holds the memory of intellectual truths and the other the memory of sensory things; for if that were the case, there would be <margin>B</margin> two entirely different animals with nothing in common. If, therefore, the impression is made in both, what is the difference? Furthermore, what prevents us from recognizing this duality? Perhaps it is because when one agrees or harmonizes with the other—since the imaginations are not separate—the expression of the more powerful soul prevails, and a single "phantasm" <note>original: *phantasma*; a mental image or appearance</note> is produced. In this state, the second follows like a shadow, and the smaller light yields to the greater. But when there is conflict and <margin>C</margin> discord, the other soul shines forth on its own. However, the duality of the souls usually remains hidden from us because they have merged into one, with the one soul overshadowing the other. Thus, when the higher soul shines out, it sees all things; and as it "exits" <note>referring to the soul's detachment from the body or its upward movement in contemplation</note>, it carries some things with it while leaving others behind with the lower soul. Just as when we have spent time with low-born companions and then move into the company of more excellent people, we retain <margin>D</margin> very little memory of those former associates, but much more of those who are better and follow after.

---

->*In both souls after death, the memory of human affairs remains: but in the lower soul, it remains with agitation, especially when it has not entirely obeyed the superior soul. In the superior soul, however, it remains without agitation, especially when it has held such matters in low esteem. Likewise, in the "airy" body <note>the *spiritus* or subtle body believed to clothe the soul after death</note> we remember many more mortal things; in the celestial body, fewer; and outside the heavens, very few indeed. Remembering fewer things in that state does not result from a weakness of memory, but from a focused attention on better things, neglecting the worse, except insofar as the worse are seen through the better. Chapter XXXII.*<-

<margin>A</margin> WHAT then shall we say of friends, children, and spouses? What of one's country, and other such things that a good man might be expected to remember honorably? Perhaps the "image" of the soul <note>the lower, more worldly part of the soul</note> remembers each of these with a certain agitation; but the higher soul will retain the memory of these without any such disturbance. For agitation was perhaps present in the lower part from the very beginning; and even certain refined affections in the higher soul...

<column-break/>

<summary>Plotinus discusses the dual nature of memory, explaining that while both the higher and lower souls possess the faculty of imagination, they typically function as one, with the higher soul's light overshadowing the lower's. He also addresses how memory changes after death as the soul moves away from earthly concerns toward pure intellect.</summary>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD IV.

...as far as it has had commerce with the other. It is fitting, however, for the lower soul to desire to remember the duties of the better soul, especially when the lower soul is itself modest; for it can become better from the beginning and make progress by being educated under the better soul. The higher soul, however, ought to gladly commit to oblivion <note>original: *oblivioni*; forgetfulness or the act of letting go of memories</note> the trifles of the lower soul. It can also happen that, while one soul is virtuous, the other—which is by nature inferior—is restrained by the force of the better one. Indeed, to the extent that the soul strives toward the higher realms, 
<margin>B</margin>
more of these earthly things are committed to oblivion by it as well, unless perhaps its entire life here was of such a quality that it committed only the best things to memory. For even in this life, it is noble to separate oneself from human pursuits, and this is the duty of absolute virtue; therefore, it is necessarily right to set aside the memory of such things. Consequently, if someone were to say that a virtuous soul is "forgetful," they would be speaking correctly in this sense: for it flees from the many, and reduces the multitude into one, 
<margin>C</margin>
leaving behind that which is entirely infinite and uncertain. In this way, it does not live with the many, but regarding these things as trivial, it dwells within itself, retaining only a few things, and even those with difficulty. For even while it dwells here, whenever it strives to raise itself to the higher realms, it leaves all other things behind. When it finally arrives at that highest peak, it recalls few of these things; though when it is in the heavens, it retains more. Now, that famous Hercules, in his manly courage, will boast in the heavens of his deeds; 
<margin>D</margin>
but the higher Hercules <note>Plotinus is referencing the passage in Homer's Odyssey where the "shade" of Hercules is in the underworld while the true Hercules is among the gods; here he uses it to distinguish between the active/emotional self and the intellectual self</note> will value such things little, having already departed to a more majestic place and been received into the intelligible world itself. Indeed, being superior to the earthly Hercules, he has strenuously practiced the more sacred contests of the wise and has completed them in abundance.

<column-break/>

<note>The following column is a Greek transcription of the same text translated above. Plotinus argues that the "good soul" becomes forgetful of earthly multiplicity as it focuses on the "One."</note>

...virtuous, insofar as it shared something with the other. It is fitting for the lower to desire the objects of the other's affection, for the sake of memory, especially when it is itself well-bred. For one might become better from the start through the education provided by the superior. But the higher soul should gladly welcome forgetfulness of the things from the lower. For even if one soul is virtuous, the other might be inferior by nature, held back by the other by force. The more it hastens toward the heights, the more it forgets, unless its entire life here was such that its memories were only of the better things. Since even here, it is a fine thing to stand apart from human strivings, it is a necessity that one also stands apart from the memories of them. Thus, if one calls the good soul "forgetful," one would be speaking correctly in that way. For it flees from the many, and brings the many together into one, letting go of the infinite. For in this way it does not live with the many, but with things that are light and through itself. Since even here, whenever it wishes to be "there" [in the divine realm], as far as it is able here, it lets go of all other things. Few things then are recalled; though if it be in heaven, more. And if that Hercules boasts of his deeds, the other Hercules—considering even these things small, having been transferred to a holier place and having come to be in the intelligible—is even stronger than Hercules in those labors which the wise endure.

# PLOTINUS
# ENNEAD IV,
## BOOK IV.

->On the Doubts of the Soul, the Second [Part].<-

->MARSILIO FICINO.<-

<image-desc>A large decorative floriated initial 'A' featuring a figure in a landscape with trees and clouds.</image-desc>
**THE SOUL**, once stripped of every body (even the celestial one) and then formed by the divine mind, most intently beholds all divine things simultaneously without discursive reasoning <note>original: *sine discursu*; meaning without the step-by-step process of logical deduction, but rather through immediate intuition</note>. Therefore, it is said not to remember human affairs—not because it is ignorant of lower things, since it contemplates all the causes of lower things and possesses itself most perfectly, but because it most negligibly recalls the smallest things when it is most intent upon the greatest. Furthermore, it does not recall them through a wandering and changeable manner, as human memory is accustomed to do. Instead, it contemplates whatever it knows through both intellect and reason in a single intuition without movement, because it beholds them through the single form of God. Nevertheless, through the very series of Ideas—which have steps distinguished from one another not by time, but by order—it discerns that some things are prior to others in that realm. As for the fact that someone among us, when thinking most intently on one thing, cannot meanwhile think clearly on another, this happens both from the weakness of our power and because we do not think of the principle <note>term: *principium*; the fundamental source or "starting point" of all things</note> of others. But in that higher state, the power is both most strong and contemplates the principles of all things; therefore, in those principles, it sees all things at once, especially since it is now entirely separated from motion and time. Finally, after the soul has been formed by the divine mind and the Ideas, it reaches the "One" itself, which is superior to the mind and the Ideas, and yet from there it still beholds all things. For the power of the One itself, when it is first perceived in another (that is, in the mind or the soul), is derived into a plurality. Cap. I.

Plotinus uses the dual nature of Hercules to illustrate the difference between the active human identity and the pure intellectual soul.</summary>

# BOOK FOUR.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'T' featuring a seated figure in classical robes within a landscape with a tree.</image-desc>
What then will the soul say, and of what things will it hold a memory in the intelligible realm <note>original Greek: *noētō*; the realm of pure forms and divine intellect</note>, once it has entered into that essence? It is perhaps a logical consequence to say that it contemplates those things among which it exists, and acts upon them; otherwise, it would not truly be there. Of the things here, however, it would remember nothing—such as the fact that it practiced philosophy, or that even while it was here, it looked toward those higher things. But if it were the case that when one applies the mind intensely to something, they cannot do or think of anything else, then that which was previously thought is not contained within that act of intellection. Rather, one might speak of it later if the occasion arises. Since that realm is unchanging, a soul that exists purely in the intelligible world would not have a memory of the things that once happened to it here. Furthermore, if, as it seems, all intellection <note>the act of pure mental understanding</note> is outside of time and exists in eternity <note>original Greek: *aiōni*</note>, then it is impossible for memory to exist there, since the things there do not exist in time. This applies not only to earthly things, but to any concept of years or duration. Everything there is present, for there is neither an exit from one state nor a transition from one thing to another. How then can there be a division from the eternal down into the lower world, or from below up toward the universal and the high? For if that which is "above" is not a personal action of mine or of a being, then why will you, the soul, be there? Or is it better to say that this mental application happens all at once to all things? Is the whole of intellection like a single vision, or like many things together? For since the sights there are diverse, the intellection must also be diverse and multifaceted, occurring all at once—much like how the senses perceive many things in a face simultaneously, where the eye sees the nose, the eyes, and the other features at once. But when one divides and unfolds something, is it not already divided by the mind? Such a thing is more like a fixed foundation. What is called "first" and "last" exists in the species/forms, but not by temporal distance. This order is like that of a plant, which begins at the roots and goes to the top; to the observer, the "before" and "after" are seen together as a single whole. But when one looks at the One, if it possesses the many and the all, how does it hold one thing first and others in sequence? Perhaps that single power was so unified that it was also many in another sense, and not everything follows a single thought. For the activities there are according to their types, yet always standing in full power. You, however, are among those things that come to be. For that which is the One, being perfect, could receive the nature of the many within itself, even though they did not exist previously.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'A' featuring architectural ruins and a standing human figure.</image-desc>

<margin>A</margin>
The **SOUL** therefore, having set out for the divine world and being established in that essence, what will it say? Or what memories will it preserve? Perhaps it follows that it contemplates the things in which it exists and acts upon them; otherwise, it would not be there.
<margin>B</margin>
Would it then in no way remember the things that are here? For instance, that it practiced philosophy, or that while living here it looked up toward those higher things? Perhaps if it is impossible for someone to act on or complete anything else while they are most intensely understanding something, then that act of intellection does not include a process by which one recognizes they have understood. Rather, it happens that someone speaks of it afterward, which signifies that they have already changed. Thus, it will not be permitted for one who purely enjoys the intelligible world to recall the memory of things that once
<margin>C</margin>
happened to them here. Furthermore, if as it appears, all intelligence is void of time—since the things there do not dwell in time but consist in eternity—it is impossible for memory to exist there, not only of our affairs but of any others. For everything is present, since there is neither discourse <note>logical progression from one thought to the next</note> nor a change that passes from one thing to another.
<margin>D</margin>
What then? Will there be no division from above to below, or from the infinite to the universal and the celestial? That which is said to be "above" is not there as a separate act in an intellect that holds all things simultaneously; but why will it not be so in a soul existing there? What prevents this intuition from being gathered as a whole, while simultaneously observing things that are similarly gathered together? Does it happen then as if it were a single intuition, or as if all the intellections of many things occurred at once? Since the spectacle itself there is varied, it follows that the intellection also becomes varied and manifold at once.
<margin>E</margin>
These are many intellections, like many senses directed toward a single face, where the eye perceives the nose, the eyes, and the other parts of the face all at once. But when the mind divides and unfolds one thing, what shall we say? Perhaps that division exists in the intellect, and such a thing is more of a support and a foundation there.
<margin>F</margin>
That which is called "prior" and "posterior" exists in the species <note>original: *speciebus*; the Forms or Types</note> not through temporal distance. For the intelligence of the prior and the posterior does not happen in time, but rather by a certain order. It is like the order of a tree, starting from the roots and reaching the top; to the beholder, the "before" and "after" are held only in order, since he perceives the entire plant at once. But when he looks into the One, if it holds many and all things, in what way does it hold one thing first and another thereafter? Perhaps the power itself, which is one, was one in such a way that it was also many in another; nor was everything according to a single intellection <note>original: *intellectionem*; a single act of the mind</note>.

---

For the intellections there do not relate to a single thing, yet they remain perpetually through the total power existing there, so that they are made many in others. For that One, although it is not itself the "many," can receive the nature of many things within itself that did not previously exist.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the soul’s state after death, specifically whether a soul that has ascended to the divine realm retains a sense of individual identity or memory of its earthly life.</meta>

# PLOTINUS' ENNEADS. BOOK 4.

*The soul, while within this body, as long as it is focused on other things, does not know itself in the meantime, because its power here is weak. Furthermore, what is thought by the soul is not the soul's own starting point. However, when it contemplates the divine world—insofar as it has been strengthened and beholds its own origins—it thoroughly recognizes itself, its own state, and its own actions. The soul in this body is mostly turned toward the imagination, and through this, toward sensible things <note>objects perceived by the five senses</note>. But after death, if it lives in an "airy" body, it finally turns entirely toward reason. Through this reason, it turns toward its own intellect, which always contains all things, and for a time it dwells in a state of temporal transition. In a "celestial" body, however, reason is made into a kind of intellect—both its own and the universal intellect—and it reduces its previous transitions almost to a single intuition. Here, then, and insofar as it recalls the forms <note>the eternal blueprints of reality</note> innate to itself, it recognizes itself; and insofar as it recognizes itself, it recognizes the forms in turn, for the soul itself is those very forms. Finally, the soul outside the heavens is shaped by the divine mind and its ideas, just as the body is shaped by the soul and its powers, or as heated iron is shaped by fire. It sees, therefore, and acts through the ideas of the divine mind as if through the powers of its own form. Therefore, through a stable act and by knowing its own origins there, it certainly recognizes itself.*

<margin>A</margin> But let these matters be as they are. Does the soul return to a memory of itself? Perhaps it remembers neither itself, nor that it is the very person who is contemplating—such as Socrates, or some other—nor even that it is a mind or a soul. For in what way would anyone be mindful of these things? Since even here, when one contemplates—especially with the greatest intensity—one does not then turn back toward oneself through the intellect, but rather possesses oneself <note>original Latin: *habet quidem seipsam*; meaning the self is present but not an object of study</note>. The act of the soul is directed toward this or that object, offering itself as a kind of "matter" to be <margin>B</margin> shaped according to what is being beheld. In that moment, the soul exists only in potentiality, for it is only "something" in act when it is not thinking of anything else; or perhaps, if it were only itself, it would certainly be empty of all things when it understands nothing. But if the soul is of such a nature that it is all things, then when it understands itself, it understands all things at once. For this reason, once it is so established and gazes upon itself—beholding itself in action—it holds all things included within itself. By a certain gaze into all things, it likewise holds itself included. But if it acts in this way, it <margin>C</margin> changes its intellections <note>acts of understanding</note>, which is something we denied in the higher realms. Should we then say that in the Intellect itself, this state remains always the same? But in the soul—positioned as it is at the very edge of the intelligible world <note>the realm of pure thought</note>—this change can occur, especially when it is permitted to recall itself to lower things. For if something is produced around that which is permanent, it must have a certain change relative to the permanent thing, since it does not remain equally permanent. But perhaps one should not say that a change occurs there <margin>D</margin> when the soul turns from its own affairs toward itself, and from itself back again. For the soul is all things, and according to both states—remaining in the intelligible world through another soul—it experiences that which is called "one thing and then another" in relation to itself and to those things which are founded within it. Or certainly, living purely in the intelligible world, the soul also possesses stability. For the soul is whatever it is; since even when it is in that world, it must necessarily reach union with the Intellect, provided <margin>E</margin> it has turned toward it. For having turned, it suffers nothing in between. Proceeding into the Intellect, it is tempered with it, and having been tempered, it is soon united. Yet it is by no means dissolved by this; rather, the two are both one and two. Being in this state, the soul will not be changed at all, but will direct itself unchangeably toward understanding, possessing at the same time a consciousness or "con-sent" <note>original Latin: *consensum*; a shared feeling or internal agreement</note> of itself, as one that has now been made one and the same with the intelligible world.

<column-break/>

But let these matters be as they are. Does every soul have a memory of itself within itself? And is it not the one who is contemplating—such as Socrates—or the fact that it is a mind or a soul? How indeed should anyone remember these things? Just as when one contemplates here, and most clearly, one does not then turn toward oneself in the act of thinking, but possesses oneself. The activity is directed toward that object and the other, as if the soul provides itself as the matter, being given form according to the thing seen. At that time, the soul itself is in potentiality. What was it, and what is it in actuality, when it thinks of nothing? Or if it is empty of all things when it thinks of nothing? But if the soul is all things—of such a kind as to be these things—whenever it thinks of itself, it thinks of all things together. So, by such an impulse toward itself, seeing itself in actuality, it holds all things encompassed within. By its impulse toward all things, it holds itself encompassed. But if it acts thus, it changes its thoughts, which is what we later decided was not appropriate for them. Or must it be said that for the Mind, the state remains the same; but for the soul, since it has come to be at the limits of the intelligible, this change is possible, since it can also move inward? For if something happens around that which stays, it must have a variation toward that which stays, not staying in the same way. Or should we say that no change occurs even when it turns from its own things to itself, and when it turns from itself to other things? For it is all things. And both exist in another soul being in the intelligible; it has "this and that" toward itself, and the things within itself. Or, being purely in the intelligible, it also has the unchangeable. For the soul is what it is. Since even when it is in that place, it is necessary to come to the Mind as it is, if indeed it has turned. For having turned, it has nothing in between. Having come into the Mind, it is harmonized, and having been harmonized, it is not at all destroyed, but both are one and two. Being thus, it would not change, but would hold its thoughts unshakeably, having at the same time the "con-sciousness" <note>original Greek: *synaisthēsin*; a joint perception or self-awareness</note> of itself, as if having become the same as the intelligible.

---

*The soul, established outside the heavens in the divine world, is said to be "one" because it acts only through the intellect. It finally descends into a celestial body when it unfolds its own multiplicity within itself, acting now through the intellect, reason, and imagination. Then it also remembers itself and its affairs in much the same way as it was accustomed to do among humans—namely, through the movement of reason (however swift it may be there) and through the formations of the imagination,*

# BOOK FOUR.

Indeed, it matters a great deal what kind of things the mind thinks of with affection: for when it thinks by bringing forth into action its own forms that lie hidden within itself, it certainly becomes those very things which it thinks, and subsequently obtains a place and condition suitable for them.

->Chapter III.<-

---

Departing from that place <note>the divine realm</note>, and not enduring to remain in the "One" but embracing its own individual nature, and wishing to be something else, and as it were leaning forward, it takes up a memory of itself, so it seems. Now, memory of the things from that higher place holds the soul back so that it does not fall; but memory of things here below brings it down to this place. Yet memory in the heavens keeps it there. And in short, whatever the soul remembers, that is what it is and what it becomes. For remembering must be either an act of understanding, or of imagining. Moreover, this imagination does not consist in **having** something, but in what it sees or how it is disposed: and if it sees sensible things <note>physical objects perceived by the senses</note>, then to the extent that it sees the forms of them, it possesses that depth. For although it possesses all things in a secondary condition, yet not even so does it become all things perfectly: and since it participates in both [higher and lower], and is not situated in only one, it is carried toward both.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>But having gone out from there, as if no longer subsisting as a single unit but loving its own specific character and affecting to be something other, just as if flashing out and now leaning forward more steeply, it assumes, as it seems, a memory of itself. Truly, if the memory is of higher things, it still holds the soul back from falling further; but if it is a recollection of our earthly affairs, it precipitates the soul toward our world, whereas with a celestial remembrance it stops its step in heaven. In general, however, of whatever it remembers, that very thing it is and becomes: <margin>B</margin>for to remember is either to understand or to imagine. Moreover, this very imagination does not consist in the fact that it possesses something, but that it sees and is disposed in such a way, and is itself of such a kind. But if it discerns sensible things, insofar as it looks upon them, to that extent it also possesses depth. For since it possesses all things in a certain secondary condition, it is not even so perfectly all things: and since it is of the borderland of things, and placed as if on a boundary, it is certainly transferred into both.

---

->Chapter IIII.<-

> *The soul, contemplating the ideas of the divine mind in the super-celestial world, discerns the **Good** itself like a sun through the mind itself, as if through a luminous transparent medium. And while it sees itself through its own principles, it certainly both knows itself to be intelligent and recognizes itself entirely. But through the very same act and by the same divine power, it glimpses its own proper natural action: therefore, it is not properly said to "notice" its own act and its prior life, because it does not use the wandering discourse of reason or imagination, in which usual recollection and notice reside. But as soon as it comes from there into heaven, and afterward into the air, it exercises these two. Truly, in general, the forms of things in the cognitive power of the soul are not certain "accidents" lying next to the soul like letters on a tablet, but are <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>Latin: rationes seminales; the inner blueprints or vital powers that direct the development of a being</note>, properties, and essential powers, just as the seminal reasons of limbs and bodily qualities are in the vegetative power, and as the properties of a whole plant are in the seed. The soul, therefore, is always all these things, but at one time rather in a kind of potentiality, and at another time more in act. Moreover, the soul is more truly the divine things themselves if it acts upon them through the intellect alone, than if it should meanwhile notice that very thing through the discourse of reason or the fictions of imagination; for these things will distract it.*

---

There, therefore, it also sees the **Good** through the intellect. For it is not barred from that [Good] so as to not pass through to it; since the thing in between is not a body that would act as an obstacle. And yet, even when bodies are in between, the arrival from the first things to the last three is possible in many ways. But if it should give itself to the things below, in proportion to its memory and imagination, it has what it desired. Therefore, memory receives memory; or only in the case where <margin>B</margin> it is not of the better things. One must not be disposed without hope according to present sufferings or sights; it might even happen that one does not follow what they have, and yet they have it more strongly within themselves than if they knew it. For if one knows it, perhaps they have it as if it were something else, they being someone else themselves; but not knowing that they have it, they risk being the very thing they have. This is a condition that, when it falls upon the soul, makes it more so. But if, having arrived at that place there, it brings back memories in whatever way <margin>C</margin> it also had them there in potentiality; then it is the activity of those things which makes the memory appear. For those forms were not like shapes lying there (lest perhaps what happens be absurd), but the power was such that it was afterward released into action.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>The soul, therefore, in the intelligible world <note>the realm of pure thought and forms</note> also sees the **Good** itself through the intellect: for the intellect does not hinder it from running all the way to the [Good] itself; because that which is in the middle is not a body, such that it would be able to hinder it on this account: although even a medium in bodies often allows a descent from the first things to the last. Consequently, if the soul gives itself to inferior things, according to the very proportion of its memory and imagination, it immediately carries back what it affected: for this reason, even memory, <margin>B</margin> when it is of the best things, is not the best state. One ought to receive "memory" not only in the sense that someone perceives themselves remembering; but also in the sense that they are presently affected according to the likeness of prior affections and thoughts: for it can happen that one who does not notice they have something, has it more strongly within them than if they recognized it. For if they recognize it, perhaps they will have it as if it were some other thing, they themselves existing as something else. But he who does not <margin>C</margin> consider that he has it, seems to be that very thing which he has: which affection indeed affects the soul more vehemently and inclines it further. But if, having already departed from that divine region, it brings back memories in any way, the power itself had memory in itself there too, but the act of those higher things somehow obscured the memory. For it must not be said that there were figures lying there; but there was a potentiality to be sent forth into act later.

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

When, therefore, that activity which is accustomed to flourish around intelligible things <term>intelligibilia: realities known by the mind rather than the senses</term> ceases, the soul then recognizes those things which it had known before it was in that higher place.

*The soul in this life can know divine things, not through the imagination, nor even through reason taking its principles from the imagination, but through the intellect and through reason taking its principles from the intellect. When the soul rises through reason into the mind as if into a mirror—even though memory, as commonly defined, involves the imagination—nevertheless, a certain kind of memory also exists within the reason and the intellect. In the soul above the heavens, the customary act of intelligence takes the place of reason and imagination; but in the heavens, a use of this kind arises again, through which it remembers in a quasi-human way the human life and human affairs it once knew: for it looks back upon these things from above the heavens in a certain more eminent manner. Souls therefore recognize one another in the heavens, especially friends and those formerly known, both through the very movements and vivid affections of their souls, and through the bodies they may have there, which possess a similar form, though made of a liquid matter <note>original: "materia liquida"; refers to a subtle, ethereal substance</note> that is far more yielding to the soul as a shaper than earthly matter is now to the soul's affections. Furthermore, even if the bodies there are spherical, they will still be signs and indicators to distinguish different souls, whether in their shape, as we have said, or in their size, quality, motion, gesture, nod, or light—just as happens in the eyes through the affections of the soul, or in various clouds with different shapes and colors. There are those who believe that the heavenly inhabitants produce voices among themselves, for the heavens themselves are capable of sounding; at the very least, they will talk to each other with mutual nods. Indeed, they remember divine things in the heavens more than human ones. But those who have fallen into the air remember the opposite. They can, however, both when they are in heaven and when in the air, remain at a certain stage for many ages because their motion is naturally free, and from there they may return to the heights. Finally, what prevents one from always remaining in the higher realms through a most excellent choice? Nothing, according to Porphyry, Iamblichus, and Julian <note>Famous Neoplatonic philosophers who followed Plotinus's teachings</note>.*

->Chapter V.<-

<margin>A</margin> WHAT then? Does that same power of remembering bring those things back to action for us now? Perhaps if it is not the same power that brings them back, it is performed by a memory we have not seen. But if it represents the same things, it does this by the same means by which we saw them there: for it is this [the intellect] which is awakened in us whenever we are incited toward those higher things, and it is this very thing which sees what has been discussed. For it is not necessary for the soul to demonstrate those things by using a kind of likeness or imaginary condition, nor to take principles for reasoning from elsewhere. Instead, it is possible for one who is still here to speak of intelligible things (as they say) by the very fact that he possesses the power to look up at them. <margin>B</margin> For we must contemplate the things that are there by awakening the same faculty that must be awakened there; just as if someone, ascending a very high watchtower <note>original: "speculam... eminentissimam"</note>, should look out with his eyes upon those things which no one else can see who has not ascended with him. <margin>C</margin> Since, therefore, it appears from reason that memory takes its beginning from the heaven, when the soul has already left the higher region, it is no wonder if, having set out from there into the heaven and residing there, it receives the memory of many things that happen among us, such as have been described. It recognizes many souls known before, since it is necessary for them to have bodies around them in similar shapes. But even if they change their shapes and become spherical, they will seem to recognize each other through the very characters and manners <note>original: "mores modosque"</note> proper to each; for this is neither absurd nor surprising. <margin>D</margin> Grant indeed that they have cast away all passions, yet nothing prevents them from retaining their characters. If it is also permitted for them to converse, they will also recognize each other in this way. But when they fall from the intelligible world, in what condition do they find themselves? Perhaps they will stir up memory again, though less so than those souls concerned with the same things; for they will have other things to remember, and then a longer time will bring about a complete forgetfulness of many things. <margin>E</margin> But if, having already slipped into the sensible world, they fall here into "generation" <note>the cycle of birth and physical existence</note>, what time will be given to memory? Perhaps it is not necessary to be cast down into the full depth. For it is possible for souls, having been moved and having progressed to a certain distance, to stop their feet; nor does anything prevent them

When the activity in the intelligible realm ceases, the soul sees what it saw before, before it was already there having seen them.

<margin>A</margin> What then? Does this same power now bring those things into activity, according to the act of remembering? Or if we did not see by the same memory, but if we saw by the same power both here and there, then that part is awakened in those by whom it is awakened, and this is the seeing part concerning the things mentioned. Or is it not like a representation through those who use images? Or not even by a syllogism that has taken its principles from elsewhere, but it is possible to speak of intelligible things even while being here, for that which has the power <margin>B</margin> to contemplate the things there is the same. For one must see the things there by awakening the same faculty, just as one must awaken it there: as if someone, bringing himself to an eye upon some high watchtower, should see things that those who have not ascended in order with him cannot see. If, therefore, memory is said to appear to begin from the heaven, now that the <margin>C</margin> soul has left the places there, and we agree that it acquires a body in the heaven, it is nothing wonderful if it has memory of many things here, of the kind that has been said, and will recognize many of those known before, since it is necessary for them to have bodies about them, if not in similar shapes. And if they should change their shapes, making them spherical, would they not recognize each other through their characters and the individuality of their manners? This is not out of place. <margin>D</margin> For let them have put away their passions, but nothing prevents their characters from remaining. And if they were able to converse, they would recognize each other in this way too. But whenever they descend somehow from the intelligible, will they stir up memory? They will do so less than those others concerning the same things, for they will have other things to remember, and a longer time will have produced a complete forgetfulness of many things. But if <margin>E</margin> having turned toward the sensible world, they fall into generation here: what kind of time will there be for remembering? Or is it not necessary to fall into every depth? # BOOK FOUR.

<margin>A</margin> ...to emerge, and to return back again before they are cast down into the lowest place of generation <note>original Greek: ἐκδῦναι (ekdynai). This refers to the soul's "stripping off" its divine nature as it descends into a physical body</note>.

<margin>A</margin> One might say that souls which transition and change do indeed remember; for memory is of things that have happened and passed away. But for those souls that remain in the same state, what could they possibly remember? Our inquiry seeks to understand if the highest souls—those of the celestial bodies, and specifically the Sun and the Moon—possess memory. It even goes so far as to question the Soul of the Universe, and will even venture to investigate whether memory exists within <term>Jupiter: representing the cosmic intellect or the governing principle of the world</term> himself. In seeking these answers, we must consider their thoughts and their reasonings, if indeed they have any. For if they neither search for anything nor face any doubts—since they lack nothing and do not need to learn things they previously did not know—then what kind of logical deductions, arguments, or reflections could they possibly have? Nor would they need to anxiously devise plans <margin>C</margin> or "machines" to manage human and earthly affairs; for the superior beings govern the universe in a different, more magnificent way.

*For the souls that guide the heavenly bodies, the service of memory is not necessary for their knowledge, their life, or their movement. Divine things are sufficient for them, seen with a gaze that is never interrupted. While they may perceive that they are seeing, they have no need to remind themselves that they "have seen," because for them there is no "having seen" in the past—there is only a "seeing" that never stops. Therefore, a memory does not need to be resumed or recalled. Their life is always the same, and the movement of their celestial bodies is perpetual and continuous; thus, for each of them, it is always a single movement, even if it appears multiple or changing to us. Even changeable things benefit from this unchanging gaze. Just as someone watching a person walk in a straight line for a certain amount of time sees them in different positions, yet the act of looking remains one continuous, unchanged progression. If that observer judges that the person "is here," "was there," and "will be there," these changes do not happen within the vision itself, even if they are judged to happen within the spectacle being watched.*

<margin>A</margin> What then? Do they remember that they saw God? Or do they rather see Him always? For as long as they see Him, they do not say they "have seen" Him; otherwise, they would be like those who have ceased to see. And what of the fact that they circled the earth yesterday or last year? Or that they lived yesterday and have lived for a long time? They live forever, and "forever" is always the same. What we call "yesterday" or "last year" in their movement is like someone who takes a single step and divides that one motion into many parts, imagining many movements where there is only one. Here, the movement is a single whole. <margin>B</margin> For us on Earth, time is measured as many days because the nights break them up. But where there is only one continuous day, how could there be "many"? Therefore, there is no "last year." But someone might object: "It is not one interval, but one after another; one part of the <term>Zodiac: the belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs</term> and then another." Why, then, would the celestial soul not say, "I have passed this part, and now I occupy another"? <margin>C</margin> Furthermore, if they look down upon human affairs, how could they not see human changes—that some people are new, and others have passed? If this is so, they must see that some existed before others, and they must observe different affairs, which would suggest they possess memory.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...to emerge, and from there to return again before they are plunged into the lowest place of generation.

*The service of a preserving memory is only necessary where something can pass away and then return, or pass away in turn. Therefore, memory does not seem necessary for celestial souls; for they do not scurry about to find or acquire anything new.*

### Chapter VI.

<margin>A</margin> Anyone can easily assert that souls which are in flux and various states of change use memory; for memory belongs to things that have been done or have passed away. But as for souls that rest entirely in the same state, what things would they remember? Human reason asks if memory exists in the souls of all the stars, but especially in the Sun and the Moon. <margin>B</margin> From there, by a similar condition, it transfers the question to the Soul of the Universe, and finally dares to place a "busy" memory even within Jupiter himself. In asking these things, one must further consider their thoughts and reasonings—if there are any—and what kind they might be. Indeed, if they require nothing and doubt nothing (for they lack nothing), and they do not learn what they previously did not know, what kind of reasonings, logical connections, or inventions would exist in them? They would not need to consult anxiously about "machines" <margin>C</margin> with which to arrange human and earthly things; for there is another way in which the higher beings munificently dispense all things.

### Chapter VII.

<margin>A</margin> What then? Do they not remember having seen God? Or do they rather see Him always? As long as they do not *not* see Him, it is not possible for them to say they "have seen" Him; otherwise, they would be in the condition of those who have at some point stopped seeing. What then? Do they not even record that they circled the earth yesterday or in a previous year? Or that they lived yesterday and have lived for a long time? Rather, they live always. <margin>B</margin> That which is always the same is always one. As for what is said regarding "yesterday" or "last year" in terms of motion, it is just as if someone perceived the impulse and movement made by a single foot as being many parts; he himself imagines the one movement to be many different ones. For here, the movement is one, but for us, it is measured as many, and as different days because the nights fall between them. But there, since it is a single day, how can there be many? Therefore, there is no "previous year." But someone will object that the interval is not one, but one after another; and that there is one portion of the zodiac and then another. Why, then, should the celestial soul not say, "I have already passed this part, <margin>C</margin> and now I occupy another"? Furthermore, if they look forward at human things, how would they not also see human mutations—that there are different people now? And if so, that others existed before them, and different business occurred, from which it would seem that they do possess memory.
