# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

The soul of any star, while contemplating the <term>Ideas: the eternal, perfect forms or blueprints of all things in the divine mind</term> and the principles of all things, always maintains within itself a certain knowledge of the universe—whether you wish to call this knowledge "intellectual" or "rational." Meanwhile, through its celestial body, it perceives physical things. However, because it perceives even the smallest details, it does not notice them through the <term>imagination: the faculty that processes and stores sensory images</term>, and therefore does not place them in memory. This is partly because it already understands all these things on a higher level, partly because these details are of no importance to it, and also because it has perceived all things for so long that nothing strikes it as new enough to move the senses. Nevertheless, it does notice through the imagination that it perceives those specific particulars which are especially necessary to the whole, such as the stars, the celestial bodies, and the elements. Indeed, since the purpose of these heavenly souls is not merely to be moved by this or that part, or for a certain time, but to contemplate and to move simply and eternally—and since their motion is perfect at every moment—these souls are certain that the prescribed order of the universe will undoubtedly unfold. Therefore, no care touches them regarding any specific place, time, or motion, nor regarding any changeable thing. Thus, even when they perceive such things, they are not forced to apply their imagination or attention to them. Note that the circular motion of the heavens is neither an "alteration" (because it does not change its form) nor is it "local" (because it does not change its place <note>Plotinus views circular motion as a soul staying in its own "place" even while rotating</note>); rather, it is a <term>vital motion: an act and evidence of the internal life of the soul itself</term>. For to act within oneself and to be moved from one's innermost depths is characteristic of living things. The motion of the celestial bodies is like the pulse or the movement of the heart in animals, or like the process of nutrition in plants.

->Chapter VIII.<-

---

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>Perhaps it is not necessary to commit to memory everything one looks at, or to use the imagination to collect those things that happen purely by chance. Likewise, for those in whose souls a more certain intelligence and knowledge of things resides, if such things are offered to the senses, it is not necessary for them to abandon their intellectual knowledge to stare at a particular, sensible object—unless someone is managing something by the work itself; for even if a thing is particular, it is nonetheless included primarily within the very notion of the whole.
<margin>B</margin>I say this regarding any particular thing in this way: To begin with, it is not necessary for a person to store within themselves everything they see. For when it makes no difference, or is of no importance to the person, then the sense alone experiences the movement of the differences of the things seen without our choice; the soul, meanwhile, does not receive this into itself. Indeed, the soul has no need for these differences of visible things, nor will they contribute to any other necessity or utility.
<margin>C</margin>Now, when someone acts entirely toward themselves or toward certain other things, they do not retain the memory of such past things, since they do not even perceive the sensation of present things. Furthermore, it is not necessary for things that happen entirely by chance to be placed in the imagination; or if they are placed there, it is not in such a way that they are guarded and observed. Anyone will be able to perceive that the image of such a thing does not bring about "consent" <note>original Latin: "consensum"; Greek: "synaisthēsin." This refers to the soul's conscious acknowledgement or "feeling-with" a sensation</note>, provided they understand what is being said in this manner:
<margin>D</margin>If our primary goal was never to divide this part of the air and then that part while we are moving through space, or rather to simply pass through it, we would certainly never think about observing this while walking. Since it was not specifically decreed by us to complete exactly a certain path—but we were allowed to run through the air—we would never care which stadium of the earth we were in, or how much space we had already traveled.
<margin>E</margin>Moreover, if we were required to move, but not specifically for a certain time—only to move—and if we were not accustomed to relating any other action to time, we would certainly never devise one time after another in our memory. This is most evident from the fact that when thought possesses within itself the whole of what is being done, and trusts that it will be carried out exactly as it is, it no longer applies itself to the individual things that happen.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>Or is it not necessary, whether one contemplates things to put them in memory, or whether they occur in the imagination as accidental consequences of passive experiences? For those whose <term>intellection: the act of pure thought</term> and knowledge is clearer, if these things should happen to be perceived by the senses, it is not necessary to let go of their knowledge of them to focus the mind on the particular sensible thing—unless one were managing a specific task where the particular is contained within the whole knowledge.
<margin>B</margin>I speak of each thing in this way: First, that it is not necessary for one to lay up for oneself the things one sees. For when there is no difference, or when none of them matter at all, the sense will be moved by the variation of the things seen without an act of will. The sense alone experiences this, while the soul does not receive it into the interior; for there is no need of it, nor is the difference itself going to be of use for anything else.
<margin>C</margin>When the activity of the soul is directed toward itself or toward other things, or even entirely elsewhere, there is no necessity of memory for such things that have passed, since it does not even know the sensation of present things. Nor is it necessary that things happening by accident should be placed in the imagination. Even if they were, they are not kept or observed; rather, even the "imprint" <note>original: "typos" (τύπος). This refers to the physical or mental stamp left by a sensation</note> of such a thing only gives a simple awareness.
<margin>D</margin>One might learn this if they take what is said in this way: I say it thus—if it were never our primary purpose to cut this air and then that air by moving according to place, or even more to pass through it, there would be no observation of it, nor any thought of it while walking. Since if it were not a primary goal to complete this specific part of the road, but rather to make one's passage through the air, it would not matter to us in which <term>stadium: a unit of distance, roughly 600 feet</term> of the earth we are, or how much we have completed.
<margin>E</margin>And even if it were necessary to move, not for a certain amount of time, but only to move, and if one did not perceive any other action as "time," we would not create in memory one time after another. For we know that because the mind holds the whole of what is being done and trusts in it, it will certainly be done in that way.

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the Greek column is "οὐκ" (not), matching the beginning of the next section of text.</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that celestial souls do not need to remember mundane details because they possess constant, holistic knowledge and their movements are expressions of internal life rather than reactions to external changes. He uses the analogy of a person walking through air to show that we only remember details when we specifically intend to measure them.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Enneads, celestial souls, vital motion, memory, imagination, sense perception, stadium, time, intellect</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of celestial consciousness, moving from the general principle that the stars do not need memory for their repetitive, perfect motions to the specific nature of Jupiter (the World-Soul or Demiurge) as a cosmic governor who acts through eternal "Intellect" rather than human-like recollection.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR

<column-break/>

Furthermore, if someone always performs the same action, they would surely observe the individual parts of their work in vain. If, therefore, the stars perform their own duties as they are carried along, and do not move simply to pass through the spaces they cross—and if their task is neither to look at what they pass nor even to "pass" it in a human sense—then the transition itself is merely accidental to them, while they are meanwhile occupied with greater things. Finally, they always run through the same paths in a similar tenor; among them, time is certainly not calculated by any distinct measure. Even if it were distinguished, it would not be necessary to retain a memory of the places they pass or the times, especially since they possess the same life throughout, revolving perpetually around the same point. Thus, their motion appears not so much **local** <note>original Latin: *localis*; referring to physical displacement from one point to another</note> as **vital** <note>original Latin: *vitalis*; motion that is an expression of internal life and energy</note>. Indeed, a living being acts upon itself in a state of rest regarding external things, but in motion through the life that is wakeful within itself. 

Accordingly, if one were to say the movement of the heavens is like a **dance** <note>original Greek: *choreia*; a circular, rhythmic choral dance</note>: if the dance were one that eventually stops, the entire progression of the movement would be "perfect" only when continued from start to finish. However, each individual part would be imperfect. But if it is compared to a dance that is eternal, it is always perfect. And if it is always perfect, it has no "future" time in which it will eventually become perfect, nor any "place" to reach. For this reason, it has no such appetite or desire, and therefore it is not measured by temporal or local conditions; thus, no memory of these things occurs.

Furthermore, our reasoning will be even more confirmed by the fact that they lead a blessed life, gazing upon life within their own souls. By the very harmony of their souls with the One, and by the light shining from them into the whole heaven—much like strings on a **lyre** moved in unison, which wondrously sound a melody in a certain natural harmony—the whole heaven is revolved. Its parts move toward the whole; the whole itself is moved in one way, and the parts in another, though all toward the same purpose. For their positions differ, yet the life of all is even more unified and similar.

***

-> Jupiter, the ruler of the world, sees and brings about infinite things through a single, simple, and all-encompassing form of his own, which is infinite in power and the creator of infinite effects. He does this not by two separate acts, but by the same act through which he sees, he also creates, and vice versa. It would be absurd to say that he gathers his knowledge of things from the things themselves; for he creates things through a knowledge that precedes them. Nor could he comprehend infinite things if he had to "hunt" for knowledge from each individual thing. As it is, he perceives infinite things through his one form, no differently than if the sun, through its one light, were to produce innumerable shimmering rays from itself. **Chapter IX.** <-

Now Jupiter, who adorns, moderates, and arranges all things, possessing always a **kingly soul** and a **kingly mind** <note>original Greek: *psychēn basilikēn kai basilikon noun*; terms used to describe the governing intelligence of the cosmos</note>, and possessing providence <note>the divine plan</note> for how each thing should be made, as well as command over those things that are made: he likewise arranges individual things according to a certain order. Furthermore, unfolding many circuits and bringing many already begun to their conclusion, why should he not have memory in all these things? That is, would he not remember how many and what kind of revolutions have already been completed, and again, how they should be made in the future—devising, conjecturing, and thinking them out? In this way, he would be the most mindful of all, especially as he is the wisest architect. 

As far as the memory of the revolutions itself is concerned...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s discussion of divine governance. Having previously established that stars move by a "vital" rather than "local" impulse, he now addresses the "Orderer" (Jupiter) to explain why the governing power of the universe does not require human-like deliberation or memory, as its knowledge is an eternal, unified state of life.</meta>

## PLOTINUS: ENNEAD IV

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> This itself brings about much doubt: namely, what the total number of actions is, and whether that number can be grasped. For if the number were finite, it would grant a temporal beginning to the universe; but if it is infinite, the Ruler would not know how many his own works are—unless, perhaps, it is said that he always exists in a single state of knowledge and life, and thus the infinite exists there, and the One consists there. This is not through a knowledge that falls upon him from the outside, but through the thing itself consisting in him. Indeed, since the infinite itself always remains as a whole, it is rather <margin>B</margin> accompanied and observed not by some newly arrived notion: for just as he knows the infinite nature of his own life, so also he knows his action, which is diffused through the infinite universe, precisely because it is directed toward the universe.

*The order of the universe, which unfolds gradually in matter, is at once whole and unchangeable in both "Jupiters": both in the first, who is the pure Intellect and the separate Artificer of the world; and in the second Jupiter, who is the intellectual Soul, the conjoined leader of the world. Neither Jupiter, therefore, runs through thoughts in an ambiguous way regarding things to be done: especially because the Soul, with a certain eternal intuition, looks up to the order of the universe in the first Jupiter, and possesses all the firm, underlying matter of the world. He agitates it from within, turning all things most easily from the single life of himself as if from a single hinge, so that rightfully nothing resists his action, and no ambiguity occurs.*

->Chapter X.<-

<margin>A</margin> The **Adorner** <note>original Latin: *exornator*; Greek: *kosmōn*. This refers to the principle that brings beauty and order (cosmos) to the world.</note> is twofold: for we call one the Artificer; but the other the Soul of the universe. And when we name **Jupiter** <note>The Roman name for the Greek god Zeus, used here as a philosophical placeholder for the highest governing principles.</note>, we sometimes understand the Artificer of the world, and sometimes the Leader of the whole world. Truly, we must separate far from the Architect of the whole any sense of "before" and "after," attributing to him a single, unchangeable life that is devoid of time. But the life of the world, which naturally possesses this quality of leadership within itself, still seems to require <margin>B</margin> an inquiry and a rational account: does it not also have its life in **ratiocination** <note>original: *ratiocinatio*; sequential, step-by-step logical reasoning, which Plotinus argues is a "lower" form of thought than direct intuition.</note>, and in seeking out what is the best thing to be done? But already that which must be done has been found and ordered—not indeed by these things which are being ordered (for those things being ordered are the things that are generated), but rather it is Order itself that performs these things. This Order is the action of the Soul, which depends on a permanent Wisdom, of which the Order thriving in the Soul is an image. And since that Wisdom is not changed, it is necessary that this <margin>C</margin> Soul is also not changed. For it does not look toward that Wisdom at one time and then not look at another; otherwise, if it were to stop, it would immediately fall into doubt. But indeed, the Soul is one, and its work is one. For that which holds the dignity of a single Leader is always superior; it is not sometimes superior and sometimes overcome. From where, then, would a multiplicity arise there, such that a struggle or doubt might be born? Now, indeed, a single Governor <margin>D</margin> always desires the same thing. For what would be the cause for him to desire one thing and then another, such that he would be compelled to doubt, distracted by many things? Furthermore, even if the single existing Soul of the world were to change in some way, it would still not doubt. For it is not because the world has many parts and many oppositions between parts that the Soul would doubt how to arrange them. For it does not begin from the lowest things, nor from the parts, but beginning from the first principles—and following a path entirely removed from impediments starting from the first—it diffuses itself and adorns all things. For this very reason, it dominates and overcomes, because it remains the same in the same work and toward the same end. But if it were to wish for one thing and then another, from where would it desire that other thing?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> And this by itself would have much difficulty: what the number might be, and if he would know it. For if it were limited, it would give a beginning in time to the whole; but if it were infinite, he would not know how many his own works are, or that he stands always in knowledge and in one life, for he is infinite. And it is not as if knowledge were from the outside, but by the work itself, always preserving that which stands in the infinite; or rather by a knowledge that follows and is contemplated, not one that is imported. For as he knows his own infinite life, so also he knows the activity directed toward the whole as one, whenever he possesses the whole.

<margin>A</margin> But since the **Ordering Principle** <note>original Greek: *to kosmon*</note> is twofold: one we call the **Demiurge** <note>original: *demiourgon*; the "Craftsman" or "Creator" of the physical world.</note>, and the other the Soul of the universe; and in saying "Zeus," sometimes we are carried toward the Demiurge, and sometimes toward the Leader of the universe. In the case of the Demiurge, one must remove from him the "forward" and "backward," giving to him one unchanging and timeless life. But as for the life in the world which has the leadership within it, a rational account is still sought. Does it not also have its living in the act of reasoning, and in seeking what it ought to do? For already those things which must be and the things ordered have been linked and arranged. For the things ordered <margin>B</margin> are the things that come to be; but that which makes them is the Order. And this is an activity of the Soul linked to an equal and mid-point wisdom, of which the order in itself is an image. And if that wisdom is unchanging, it is necessary that this also does not change. For it does not look there at one time, and at another time not look; for if it were to fail, it would be at a <margin>C</margin> loss. For the Soul is one, and so is the work. For that which leads is always in control, and not at one time controlling and at another time controlled. For from where would many things come, so as to produce a battle or a difficulty? And that which administers always wills the same thing. For why would it want one thing and then another, so as to be at a loss among many things? And yet even if it were to change anywhere, it would not be at a loss. For it is not because the whole now has many <margin>D</margin> parts, and the parts themselves have oppositions, that it would therefore be at a loss as to how to arrange them. For it does not start from the last things, nor from the parts, but from the first things; and having received from the first, it goes through all things and adorns them by an unimpeded path. And indeed, because it dominates, that which remains as the works of one [always], it also dominates by that same means. But if it should want something else, from where would that "else" come?

**English Vocabulary for Indexing:**
**Plotinus:** The 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism.
**Enneads:** The collected writings of Plotinus, edited by his student Porphyry.
**World-Artificer:** (Latin: *mundi artifex*; Greek: *demiourgos*) The divine mind that shapes the cosmos.
**Soul of the World:** (Latin: *anima mundi*; Greek: *psyche*) The principle of life and order that animates the physical universe.
**Jupiter:** (Greek: *Zeus*) A divine name used to represent either the supreme Intellect or the World-Soul.
**Ratiocination:** (Latin: *ratiocinatio*) Discursive reasoning, which Plotinus distinguishes from divine, intuitive knowledge.

Plotinus distinguishes between the transcendent Artificer (Intellect) and the immanent World-Soul, both of which maintain the universe's infinite complexity as a single, harmonious work.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the World Soul's governance. The previous page established that the universe's order is not a result of a struggle or new decisions, but an eternal state. Here, Plotinus (via Ficino's translation) argues that Nature acts from within, unlike a doctor who acts from without, and thus requires no deliberation or memory.</meta>

### BOOK FOUR.

<margin>α' <note>original Greek: "then it will be at a loss as to what it must do; and its work will grow weak..."</note></margin> then it will be at a loss as to what it must do; and its work will grow weak if it is divided into doubt in its actions, not being equal to its reasoning.

<column-break/>

**A** Then, being thus affected, it will doubt what is better to be done, and so its duty in acting will be weakened, if indeed by its reasoning it is pulled apart into the uncertainty of action.

---

*By the same proportion that the individual natures of individual parts in any living being depend on a single common nature of the whole living being, so do all the natures of worldly things depend on one common nature of the whole world. Therefore, just as the nature of any living thing—containing within itself the natural **seminal reasons** <note>seminal reasons (rationes seminales): the internal blueprint or "seeds" of logic that guide natural development</note> of its parts and natural effects—neither labors, nor deliberates in acting, nor is changed while it produces diverse things (especially since it acts from the innermost parts, and does not begin its work from many parts as it were, but derives everything from one single pivot of all things): so neither does the nature of the world deliberate in its work, or labor, or change. For it stands toward its work just as we were saying a particular nature stands toward its own, and even much more excellently; especially because it is the instrument of eternal and infinite wisdom, guided always toward the same things in turn, and with the same tenor, presiding over all matter.* Chapter XI.

---

<column-break/>

FOR the administration <note>original: "διοίκησις"</note> is just as in a single living thing: one part is from the external parts, and another is from the inside and from the principle. Just as a doctor, beginning from the outside and proceeding part by part, often walks in doubt and deliberates; but Nature, since it leads from the inner principle, is without the consideration of deliberation. And because everyone thinks the administration and the administrator—if he is to lead—must be like a doctor, they fail to see that he is like Nature; or rather, that simplicity is much greater there, insofar as all things are included within as parts of a single living being. For one nature rules all the other natures; and the rest follow, being hung from it and depending on it, or as it were growing out of it, like the natures of branches from the nature of the whole plant. What reasoning then, or what counting, or what memory is needed, when wisdom <note>original: "φρονήσεως"</note> is always present, acting and ruling, and the administration is always according to the same things? Nor indeed, because the things that happen are varied and different, must the maker follow the changes that occur and be led by them. For the things that happen are varied only insofar as the making remains the same. For many things happen naturally in each single living thing, and not all at once: the different ages, the growths at certain times, such as horns, beards, and breasts; the increases and peaks; the births of others, while some "reasons" fall away and others are substituted. It is clear that in the living thing generated from there, the same and entire "reason" exists; and indeed it is worthwhile to be persuaded that this same wisdom is universal—like a wisdom standing within the world—many and varied things coming from it as if from a single, greatest living being. It does not become varied through the multitude of works, but is one reason and all things at once. For if it were not these things, it would not be that wisdom, but rather the wisdom of later things and of parts.

<column-break/>

**A** FOR the governance of the world <note>original: "gubernatio mundi"</note> is like that of a single animal, but this very governance of the animal partly manages from the outside and through the parts, but partly rules from the inside and from the principle. A doctor indeed, beginning from the outside and proceeding through the parts, often walks in doubt and deliberates. But Nature, since it leads from the innermost principle, does not need deliberation. It is necessary, however, that the governance and the governor of the whole world in its dispensing should **B** proceed not in the manner of a doctor, but of nature. Indeed, simplicity is much more preserved there, the more all things are understood there to be within, like the members of a single animal. For one nature encompasses all natures, and the rest follow, depending on it and proceeding from it, and thus as it were sprouting forth, just as the natures of branches sprout from the nature of the entire tree itself. What reasoning then, or numbering, or memory? Since wisdom is always present and acts and dominates, and always governs with the **C** same tenor. For we must not think that because the things that are made are varied and diverse, the maker also has communion with those changes of the things that are made. For insofar as the things that are made are varied, the maker himself remains in the same tenor. For there are many things which are produced naturally even in each of the animals, and not all at once. Indeed, there are different ages and certain sproutings at fixed times, such as **D** horns, beards, and breasts; likewise certain increases and the flowers of age; again, the prescribed propagation of offspring by which others are generated, while the prior seminal reasons in the meantime by no means fail, but others are generated besides. This indeed is evident from the fact that in the animal generated from it, the same seminal reason is preserved entirely. Now truly it is worthwhile to assert that the same wisdom flourishes here, and that this is the universal wisdom, like the standing wisdom of the world: much and varied indeed, and again the simple wisdom of the one greatest animal of all, **E** which indeed does not turn out varied from the very multitude of works, but is one reason and all things at once; otherwise, unless it be all things, it will not be that wisdom itself, but rather a certain wisdom of later things and of parts.

---

*Thought running through many things in succession in an orderly way is a certain motion lacking absolute knowledge, and because of its want, it seeks perfect truth and wisdom; therefore, in such a discourse, neither deliberation nor choice belongs to the mind or the soul that rules the world. For it possesses from eternity a state full of wisdom, and an entire fullness both of ideas and of **seminal reasons**. By this fullness, it anticipates future things in the present, and discerns in what ways they will be, of which it is itself the maker, alone dominating all its matter, and not subject to impediments. Therefore, it is neither anxious, nor doubtful, nor searching, but by its own all-forming nature, it conforms the universe to itself. Since by this very nature it is intelligence and will, it deservedly treats the matters of the world not by counsel, but is strengthened by wisdom naturally, and also by a voluntary craftsmanship.*
->Chapter XII.<-

<summary>Plotinus explains that the universe is governed by an internal, natural wisdom rather than external deliberation. He compares this to a plant growing or an animal maturing, where a single "seminal reason" directs complex changes without the need for conscious "planning" or memory.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion on whether the World Soul governs through a process of deliberation or memory, Plotinus now argues that true Wisdom is a stable state that does not require the "work" of thinking things through step-by-step, as humans do.</meta>

### PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK IV.

<margin>A</margin> But perhaps someone will say that a work of this kind is the task of nature; but since wisdom exists in the universe, they will think that discursive reasoning and memory must also necessarily exist. However, this is the view of men who place wisdom in "not-yet-knowing," and who think that seeking wisdom is the same as actually being wise. For what else is discursive reasoning <note>original: "rationis quoq; discursiones" / "λογισμοὺς". This refers to step-by-step logical thought rather than instant intuition.</note> than the desire to find wisdom, and a true reason that truly possesses the mind? <margin>B</margin> For he who reasons is like a person playing the lute specifically for the sake of the playing, or someone practicing to gain a habit, or a student learning for the sake of knowledge. For the reasoner seeks to learn that which the person who already possesses it has as wisdom; therefore, wisdom exists in a certain fixed and stable state. The reasoner himself bears witness to this: for as soon as he finds what he desired, he stops reasoning, and rests, having been placed within wisdom itself. <margin>C</margin> If, therefore, we believe the leader of the world to be in the position of a student, we will surely attribute to him discursive reasonings, doubts, and memory—comparing, as it were, past things with the present and the future. But if we instead think of him as one who knows within a fixed state that possesses its own boundary, we will rightly judge that wisdom belongs to him instead. Furthermore, if he knows future things—for it would be absurd to deny that—why should he not also hold how those future things will be? <margin>D</margin> But if he already knows how future things will be, what further need is there to investigate by reason, or to compare the past with the present? Again, the knowledge of future things, if it is granted to be present in him, will certainly not be like the knowledge found in prophets, but like that of the creators themselves who know for certain that it will be so. This is the way of those who have authority over all things, for whom nothing is hesitant, nothing happens by chance or ambiguity, and whose judgment, once settled, remains forever at rest. <margin>E</margin> Therefore, the wisdom regarding the future is the same there as the wisdom regarding the present, according to its stable state. But this is far removed from the investigation of reason; nor will he strive to know the future things which he himself is going to do, nor will he not know how to act, nor will he act by looking at something else, but he will act upon whatever happens by chance: but that would be nothing other than acting by luck. Therefore, the reason by which he acts remains; and if the reason by which he acts remains, he certainly will not act otherwise than he designs, because the model <note>original: "exemplar" / "παράδειγμα". In Neoplatonism, this is the ideal form or blueprint of the universe.</note> exists within him. Thus, he will always act by one tenor and by the same reason. <margin>F</margin> For he will not act one way now and another way in the future; otherwise, what would prevent him from wandering far from his purpose? But if he were to hold himself differently at different times, he would not possess this difference from himself, but insofar as he served the **seminal reasons** <term>seminal reasons: the internal biological and logical blueprints (rationes seminales) that guide the development of the natural world</term>; but these depend on the creator. Therefore, the craftsmanship follows the very series of those reasons. Thus the creator is in no way forced to wander, or to doubt, or to labor in his affairs, as some have thought, believing the governance of all things to be a laborious task. <margin>G</margin> Truly, to labor in arranging a work seems to be nothing other than handling foreign materials—that is, materials over which one has very little mastery. But when someone masters the work and commands it alone, what else could he need but himself and his own will? That is his own wisdom: for in such a being...

<column-break/>

BUT perhaps someone might say that such a work belongs to nature; but since wisdom is in the whole, it is necessary that there also be reasonings and memories. But wisdom for men consists in "not-yet-having wisdom," and they have considered the seeking of wisdom to be the same as being wise. For what else could reasoning be, than the longing to find wisdom, and a true logic, and one that hits upon the existing mind? For the one who reasons is like a person playing the lute for the sake of the music, or one practicing to gain a habit, and generally like a student seeking knowledge. For the one who reasons seeks to learn that which the person who is already wise possesses: so that wisdom exists in a state of standing still. And the one who has reasoned also bears witness to this. For when he finds what he must, he has ceased reasoning, and rests as if he has come into the state of being wise. If, then, we place the leader of the whole among the students, we must assign to him reasonings and memories: memories that compare the things that have gone before with things present and future. But if his state is that of one who knows within a fixed boundary, we must consider that he possesses wisdom. And one might say that if he knows the things that are to come—for to say he does not know them is absurd—why must he not also know how they will be? And if he knows how they will be, what further need is there for reasoning, and for comparing past things to present ones? And if the knowledge of future things is granted to be present in him, such knowledge would not be like that which is present in prophets, but like that of the very ones who will act, being persuaded that it will be. And this is the same as the power that is mistress over all, for whom nothing is doubtful, nor is anything misunderstood. For those whose opinion is once fixed, it remains in this way. Therefore, the wisdom of future things is the same as that concerning present things, according to the state of standing still. This is outside of reasoning; but if he did not know the future things which he himself will do, neither would he know how to act, nor towards what he should look to act, but he would act upon what occurs to him. But this is the same as acting at random. Therefore, the way he acts will remain; but if the way he acts remains, he will not act otherwise than as he has the model <note>original: "παράδειγμα"</note> within himself; he will act in a single way, and in the same way, for he will not act one way now and another later, or what would prevent him from failing? And if the thing being made is different, it is different not in itself, but in the reasons that drive it. For it is from the creator. So that the logic follows the things in succession. Thus, the creator is in no way forced to wander, nor to be at a loss, nor to have troubles as some have thought it to be difficult, or the management of the whole. For to have troubles, <unclear>it seems</unclear>, is to set one's hand to foreign works: and this means those things which one does not control. But those things which one controls and rules alone, what would such a one need, except himself and his own will? And this is his own wisdom; for to such a one...

<meta>Catchword: of such a kind,</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that the divine governor of the world does not "think" or "deliberate" like humans do, because true wisdom is a perfect, effortless state of knowing rather than a process of solving problems.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion where the author established that the divine governor of the world does not need to "think" or "remember" in the human sense, this page delves into the specific hierarchy between the Divine Mind, the Soul, and Nature.</meta>

### BOOK FOUR.

<note>original Greek: "πειστῶ, ἡ βούλησις, Φρόνησις..." / original Latin: "hunc ita se habentẽ voluntas est sapientia."</note> <margin>A</margin> For such a being, will is wisdom. Therefore, nothing is lacking for its crafting, since wisdom is not something added from the outside <note>original: "adventitia". This refers to knowledge gained through experience or external senses, which a divine being would not need.</note>, but is the being itself. He uses nothing external; he uses neither discursive reasoning nor memory, for these things are external additions.

*The Divine Mind imprints the forms of its Ideas with its seal upon the World Soul so powerfully that it shapes not only the highest part of the Soul—which is the intelligence—but also its middle part—the imagination—and even into its lowest part, which is nature. These forms, or "seminal reasons" <term>seminales rationes: the internal blueprints or life-forces that direct the growth of living things</term> within nature, are the final traces of the divine. Thus, they lack conscious thought, though they do not lack life. They act upon matter much like fire or similar elements, and they do so with craftsmanship, because they are the living expressions of a divine intelligence—the very words of that intelligence speaking. While Nature acts upon matter, it is said to "suffer" or receive its direction not from matter, but from the Soul. The Soul, in turn, does not "suffer" from the Mind so much as it directs itself toward it.*

->Chapter XIII.<-

<margin>A</margin> BUT how does this kind of wisdom differ from nature? Clearly, in this: that wisdom is the first principle, while nature is the last. For nature is an image of wisdom. Since it is the lowest part of the Soul, it possesses the final "reason" or blueprint shining down from above. It is as if a deep piece of wax were pressed so hard that the shape passed through to the other side; on the top surface, the figure is clear and distinct, but on the bottom <margin>B</margin> surface, there is only a faint trace. This is why nature knows nothing, but only acts: it passes on what it has to the next thing in line without any choice or deliberation, bestowing it upon the physical and material subject. Its action is of that kind alone. In the same way, a hot object provides its own form to the thing next to it, making it hot. For this reason, nature does not possess "imagination" <note>original: "phantasia". In this context, Plotinus means nature lacks a conscious mental "image" of what it is doing.</note>. Intelligence is superior to imagination, but imagination stands in the middle between the natural form and intelligence. For nature has no awareness or <margin>C</margin> understanding of anything, whereas imagination has a conscious grasp of things from the outside; it allows the one imagining to know what it is experiencing. This very offspring and action depends upon the agent itself. Thus, the Mind possesses these things; the Soul of the whole has always received them and continues to receive them, and for the Soul, this receiving is its very life. That which appears and shines within the Soul is always the recognition of its own intelligent understanding. But that which flashes from the Soul onto the surface of matter is nature, where beings end—or rather, nature precedes that which appears <margin>D</margin> physically. These are the final things of the intelligible order, for after these come only the imitations of beings. While nature acts upon matter, it is simultaneously receiving its influence from elsewhere. The Soul, being superior to nature and closest to it, does not "suffer" or receive influence while it acts; finally, the Mind, standing high above, does not act directly upon bodies or matter.

*Universal Nature—that is, the vivifying power of the World Soul, which is full of all "seeds"—is present in all bodies generated from it. It is not present like a quality that is mixed in and becomes part of the body (like heat in the air), but rather as an act of the Soul that remains somewhat separate, yet present in its separateness, just as light is present in the air. Nature stands in relation to the Soul as light does to the sun; but the material form stands in relation to nature as heat stands to the light from which it was generated in matter.*

->Chapter XIV.<-

<margin>A</margin> ACCORDINGLY, regarding the bodies that are said to be born from nature: the elements themselves are these very bodies. But as for animals and plants, do they relate to nature in such a way that they have nature "lying beside" them within themselves, just as air has light? When the light goes away, the air retains none of it; the light exists separately, and the air remains separately, as if no mixing had occurred. Or is it rather like what usually happens with fire and an object that has been heated? For...

<column-break/>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

<margin>A</margin> When fire departs from a place, some heat remains behind; this heat is something different from the active heat within the fire itself, becoming instead an impression <note>Latin: *passio*; Greek: *πάθος*. In this context, it refers to a quality received by an object rather than an active force.</note> left upon the object that was heated. In the same way, we must consider the form that Nature provides to a shaped object to be a different kind of species than Nature itself. It remains for us to ask whether there is something else acting as a middle ground between the shaped object and Nature itself. For enough has already been said regarding the primary difference between Nature and that Wisdom which we have placed within the world.
<margin>B</margin>

> *The internal action of the World Soul is not carried out gradually over time; rather, it is fulfilled all at once in a single moment. Its external action, however—which is a certain procession of power from the Soul into the world—and the very activity of the world itself, is carried out through the succession of time. Therefore, the Soul's own proper action is not in time, but rather it generates time within matter. Chapter XV.*

<margin>A</margin> A doubt may easily arise concerning everything we have just said. If Eternity is associated with the Mind <note>Latin: *mens*; Greek: *νοῦς*. Often translated as the "Intellect," the second level of reality in Plotinus’s system.</note>, and Time is associated with the Soul (since we have said that the nature of time is occupied with the action of the Soul and depends upon it), how can it be that while time is divided and possesses a "past," the action of the Soul is not similarly divided? And would this not create a memory within the World Soul as it turns back toward that past? Furthermore, we ought to place "identity" <note>unfailing sameness</note> within eternity and "diversity" or "otherness" within time; otherwise, eternity and time will be the same thing, provided we remove change from the actions of the Soul. 

Perhaps we should say that while our individual souls admit change—and thus experience both "otherness" and "need" as if they were in time—the Soul of the All <term>World Soul: the cosmic force that animates the universe</term> generates time without being "in" time itself? But even if we grant that it is not in time, what causes it to generate time rather than eternity? Perhaps it is because the things it generates are not everlasting but are gripped by time. For even the souls themselves are not in time, but rather their impressions and their works are. Souls are everlasting; time comes after them. That which is in time is "less" than time, for as the ancient authorities say, whatever is in time must be contained by time, just as a thing is contained by its location or its number.
<margin>B</margin>
<margin>C</margin>

> *The forms of things which are separated by space in matter are separated in the World Soul only by formal difference. Likewise, things that are "before" and "after" one another in time within matter are distinguished in the Soul only by a certain order, in which some things give way to others rather than following them in a sequence. For the Soul, through its all-forming essence, is a specific and firm order—both the model and the executor of the future universal order. So far as it is within itself, it could produce all things at once, if only matter were capable of receiving all things at once. This Soul is said to "move" toward the Good because it turns toward it by desiring it through the mediation of the Mind; the Mind, however, is said to "rest" in the Good because it requires no mediator. The world, meanwhile, revolves in time around the Soul—or rather, within the Soul. Plotinus, in his book On Time, if he does not place time and motion in the higher World Soul, he certainly places them in its lower part—that is, in the "trace" of the higher soul which is Nature. This is not because it acquires or loses forms, but because certain forms within it emerge into "waking" at appointed times, as if from sleep. Chapter XV.*

<margin>A</margin> Furthermore, if a "this after that" or a "before and after" of its works is designated within the Soul, and if the Soul acts in time, it also nods toward the future. If this is so, it also looks back toward the past. But perhaps this "before" and "past" exists only in the things being made; in the Soul itself, they do not exist at all, but all the blueprints <term>rationes: (Greek: logoi) the formative principles or "seeds" of reality</term> exist simultaneously, as we have said. These are not simultaneous in the works produced in time, just as they are not simultaneous in space; yet, in the blueprints, they are together in "place," just as hands and feet are together in a seed. But in the things revealed to the senses...
<margin>B</margin>

<column-break/>

<note>The following Greek text is the original source for the Latin translation provided in the first column.</note>

...once [the fire] has departed, a certain heat remains, a second kind inside compared to the one outside. For it is not together with the fire, but an affection of the thing heated. For regarding the form which shines forth through its own particularity, one must posit a different species from nature itself. If there is something else besides this which is, as it were, between this and nature itself, it must be sought. What the difference is between nature and the aforementioned wisdom in the whole, has been stated.
<margin>B</margin>

THAT is a difficulty, like all the things just mentioned: if eternity is around the Mind, and time is around the Soul (for we say that time has its existence in the activity of the Soul), why is it not of that [Mind]? And how, when time is partitioned and has a "past," will that activity not also be partitioned? And by turning toward the past, will it not create memory in the Soul of the All? For again, they place identity in eternity, and otherness in time. Or eternity and time are the same, if we give the power of changing to the activities of the Soul. Is it then that our souls admit change—being of a certain kind as if in time—while the Soul of the All generates time, but is not itself in time? But let it be not in time. What is it that acts, generating time for itself, but not eternity? Is it because the things it generates are not eternal, but encompassed by time? Since not even souls are in time, but rather their passions and their works. For souls are eternal, and time is later; and that which is in time is less than time. For things in time must be encompassed by time, just as he says of things in place and in number.
<margin>C</margin>

BUT if there was in it "this after that," a "before" and "after" of the things produced; and if it produces in time, it also [looks] toward the future. And if this is so, also toward the past. Or, the "before" and the "past" are in the things produced; but in the Soul itself, nothing is past, but all the formative principles <note>Greek: *λόγοι* (logoi)</note> are together, as has been said. If they are in the things produced, they are not "together," since they are not even in the same place; yet in the principles, they are together, just as hands and feet are together in the principle [seed]; but in the things of sense...

### FOURTH BOOK.

These things are arranged separately in space; and if in the seed-state <note>Latin: *seminario*; Greek: *σπερματικῷ*. This refers to the formative principles or "rational seeds" that contain the potential for all things.</note> they are said to be separated by some other reason, they are therefore also called "prior" by another reason. Certainly, what is said to be "separate" will be judged to be separate by a certain otherness; but as for what is called "prior," in what way is it so? Unless the Orderer <note>Greek: *epistatēs*; Latin: *ordinator*. The governing intelligence that organizes the cosmos.</note> himself commands it so: for in commanding, he will declare this very thing, namely, "let this be after that." For why would all things not exist simultaneously? But surely, if the Orderer were one thing and the Order <note>Greek: *taxis*; Latin: *ordo*</note> another, the matter would be conducted as if by speaking. If, however, the presiding commander exists as the Primary Order itself, he no longer speaks, but only acts, making "this after that." For if he were to speak, he would speak while looking at an order; therefore, there would be something else besides the order. By what reasoning, then, is he the same as the order? Because the Orderer is not matter and species <note>form</note> together, but only the species itself; and the power and the second activity after the Intellect <note>Latin: *mens*; Greek: *νοῦς*</note> will be the Soul. As for what is said—"this after that"—this happens to the works themselves because they are not able to possess all things at once. For such a Soul is a venerable thing, being like a circle most perfectly fitted to a center, expanded immediately after the center, an interval without distance. For in this way individual things are arranged, as if someone placed the Good itself as the center: and applied the Intellect as an immobile circle, but added the Soul as a moving circle, moved—I say—by desire <note>Latin: *appetitus*; Greek: *ἐφέσει*. This refers to the natural inclination or longing of the Soul toward the higher Good.</note>. For the Intellect immediately and suddenly possesses and grasps the Good; but the Soul desires that which is even above being. But the sphere of the world, possessing a Soul that desires under that condition by which it is naturally able to desire, is moved. For it is so arranged by nature that the body is naturally able to desire that very thing which is outside it: this consists in pouring itself around it and running around it on all sides, by which it is made to move in a circle.

<column-break/>

In the World Soul, there is no ambiguous deliberation or temporal wandering <note>Latin: *discursio*. Discursive thought involves moving step-by-step from one idea to another.</note>, because what is best within it always rules over its other powers from eternity. However, such wandering exists in our soul, because now one of our many parts and powers rules, and now another. Likewise, it is because we are ignorant, and also because we lack many things, and finally because many passions <note>emotions or external influences</note> strike us from external things. Our rational power, even if it is not blind, is nevertheless weak by nature and is sometimes overcome by the irrational power: both because the rational is quiet while the irrational is turbulent, and because the former is single while the latter is manifold. The worst man is similar to the worst form of popular government <note>democracy, in the ancient sense of "mob rule"</note>; the less evil man to a less evil popular government. The good man is like the government of the best <note>aristocracy</note>, and the best man is like a kingdom; perhaps someone might say the worst man is like a tyrant.

---

### Chapter XVII.

But in what way are those understandings which belong to the soul itself, and its reasons, not also like this in us? Instead, here the "later" exists according to time, and questions arise here. Is it because there are many things in us that dominate and move, and no single thing commands? Or is it also because one thing after another occurs for use and for the present, not defined in itself, but always pertaining to one external thing after another? Therefore, there is also a different counsel, which is present to us according to the opportunity of the time, when necessity demands it. Furthermore, now this and now that happens from the outside: indeed, from the fact that many things dominate within us, it is necessary that many imaginations also occur—both foreign and new, some regarding one thing and some another. From this, some things become an impediment to others in the execution of movement and action. For when the power of desiring is moved, an imagination of this kind arises in us, which—like a certain sense—announces and brings news of the passion: requiring, namely, that...

# PLOTINUS’ ENNEADS IV.

<margin>A</margin> ...the soul complies with desire, and provides for its wishes. Then, indeed, a soul so affected is necessarily dragged into controversy, whether it complies and suggests, or resists. Yet even the force of anger, which incites one to repel an injury, brings the same upon us whenever it is stirred up. Consequently, the needs and passions of the body introduce various opinions to us. Furthermore, there is an ignorance of good things and a failure to find that which might define judgment, where the soul is pulled hither and thither. From the mixture of these things, other results <margin>B</margin> pertain to the same end, even if that which is best in us thinks differently than the common deficiency and the diversity of opinions. From that which is best, however, right reason <note>Greek: *orthos logos*</note> is brought down into our common nature; it degenerates for this very reason, that it becomes weak within the mixture itself, although by its own nature it is not weak. But just as in a great crowd of an assembly or among counselors, the best man does not persuade by his excellence in speaking, but rather the worse men prevail by their <margin>C</margin> very number of disturbers and shouters. He, however, sits quietly, unable to obtain anything, as one who is overcome by the tumult of the worse sort. For there is in any of the worst men a certain "common part," and a man is heaped together from all these after the manner of a most wretched government. In the middle sort of man, however, it is as in a city where someone rules somewhat better, where there is surely a certain popular government <note>original: *popularis gubernatio*; Greek: *dēmokratia*</note> not entirely <margin>D</margin> devoid of obedience. But in the better man, the form of life is very similar to an aristocratic government <note>original: *optimatum gubernatio*; Greek: *aristokratia*</note>; for now that which is called "common" in the man flees away and obeys the better parts. Finally, in the best man, even separating himself from the common part, there is one prince <note>original: *unus princeps*; Greek: *to archon*</note>, from whom order is extended to the other parts. It is as if there were a double city in us, one of which is superior, while the other is inferior, adorned after the likeness of the superior. Now, it has been said that in the Soul of the universe, one and the same principle always commands in like manner. But in others, the matter stands differently, and the causes of this have been assigned; but enough concerning these things.

Just as light shines from the Sun, inseparable from it—which is not a proper quality of the air, but rather heat is generated from the light as a proper quality of the air—so from our soul shines a life-giving act. This is not a proper quality of the body, but it generates something vital in the body, which becomes the body's own. The Soul indeed is substance and life; that inseparable act of its own is something substantial and life-giving. The quality attributed to the body from this is something accidental, and as it were, vital. This act we call the "idol" <note>original: *idolum*; Greek: *eidolon*. In Neoplatonism, this refers to a reflection or lower manifestation of a higher reality.</note> of the soul, in which there is sensation and a vegetative nature. This quality we name the "image" and "shadow" <note>original: *vmbram*; Greek: *skian*</note> of the soul. From this and the body, the composite being is formed, in which there are bodily pleasures and pains; the sensations of these passions reach the "idol" of the soul, but the passions themselves do not. The previous comparison would be more fitting if we compared the "idol" of the soul (not separated from the soul) to the visual ray not separated from the eye. If this ray should ever proceed from a reddened eye, it will produce a redness in the eye for the observer; you might say the shadow of the soul resulting in the body is similar to this.

->Chapter XVIII.<-

<margin>A</margin> IT REMAINS to investigate whether the body has something in itself, and thus lives by the presence of the soul so that it possesses something of its own, or whether whatever it has is Nature itself <note>Plotinus often uses "Nature" to refer to the lowest, formative power of the Soul.</note>; and whether that is what communicates itself to the body—namely, Nature alone. Perhaps, however, the body itself in which the soul and nature exist ought not to be such as that which is entirely inanimate, or like illuminated air, but rather like heated air. Thus, indeed, the bodies of animals and plants have as it were a shadow of the soul in themselves. Therefore, <margin>B</margin> bodily pains and pleasures are centered around such a body. To us, however, the pain of such a body...

<column-break/>

...the desired thing follows by choice, but that which follows by necessity is like an outflow, and it is greater or that which becomes the primary cause. Or anger, calling one to defense, does such things when moved; and the needs or passions of the body do some things and believe others. Ignorance of the good, and not having what it might say to the whole that is chosen, and from the mixture of these things, other results arise. But even if the best itself thinks other things, there is common perplexity and differing opinion. From the best part, right reason is given to the common whole; by being weak in the mixture, or by its own nature, it is weak. But it is as in the great noise of an assembly: the best of the counselors speaks but does not prevail, while the worse among the noisy and shouting ones do. He sits in silence, unable to do anything, defeated by the noise of the worse sort. And indeed, in the most base man, the "common" is like a man made of all things according to a base constitution. In the middle man, it is as in a city where something better might prevail over a democratic constitution, perhaps not an unmixed one. In the better man, the form of life is aristocratic, for he is already fleeing what is "common" in the human being and giving way to the better parts. But if it is in the best man who separates himself, there is the ruling principle. Or with this man, order is sent to the other parts; as if there were a double city, one above and the other from the things below, ordered according to the one above. But that in the Soul of the All, there is the "well" and "the same" and "likewise"; while in others it is otherwise, and for what reasons, has been said. These things then were in this way.

Just as the radiance from the sun is suspended from it, not being an affection of the air, but heat produced from it in the air is an affection proper to the air; so also the vital power from the soul shines out into the body. It is not, then, an affection proper to the body, but a certain trace of the soul produced in the body. For the soul is substance and life, but its inseparable activity is something substantial and vital. That which is given by it to the body is a certain accident and, as it were, vital. This we call the "idol" of the soul, in which are sensation and the vegetative nature. This quality we call an "idol" and a "shadow"; and from this and the body comes the living being, in which are bodily pleasures and pains, whose passions come upon the idol and the soul, but the passions themselves by no means [affect the higher soul]. The image would be more proper if we took the "idol" of the soul as not being cut off from the soul, like the visual ray not being cut off from the eye. Or if someone, coming from a red eye, should color the thing seen with the color of redness, to which the shadow of the soul in the body is similar.

<margin>A</margin> CONCERNING whether the body has anything in itself, and lives while the soul is present because it already has something of its own; or whether that which it has is Nature, and this is what is mixed with the body—either Nature, or even the body itself in which there is both soul and nature—and it must be such a thing, like that which is soulless, and like illuminated air, but rather like heated air. And the body of the animal, and that of the plant also, are such as having a shadow of the soul. And <margin>B</margin> to feel pain and to feel pleasure are things of the body—pleasures concerning such a body. To us, the pain of this...

<summary>Plotinus discusses the internal hierarchy of the human soul using political metaphors, comparing the virtuous man to a well-governed city and the conflicted man to a noisy assembly. He also uses an analogy of light and heat to explain how the soul projects a "shadow" of life into the body without losing its own substance.</summary>

# BOOK FOUR.

...and such pleasure comes to a passionless knowledge—I mean for us in the secondary soul—inasmuch as it is present in a body that is not alien, but our own. For this reason <margin>*it is a care to us as being our own</margin> it is a care to us as being our own. For even if we are "ourselves"—since we are pure then—the body is nevertheless suspended and hung from us. We are defined by the ruling part of the soul, but this body is also ours in another way. Therefore, we care for it when it is pleased or in pain, and we do so more the weaker we are, and the less we separate ourselves from it. But we must consider what is most precious in us, and where we place "the human," and how we sink into it. For such passions must not be said to belong to the soul entirely, but to a body of this sort, or to the composite of both. For when a thing is one, it is self-sufficient; for example, if a body were alone and inanimate, what could it suffer? If it were divided, the suffering would not belong to the body itself so much as to the union within it. The soul alone <margin>B</margin> suffers no division or passion; and being so disposed, it escapes this entirely. But whenever two things strive to be one, and use an external union, they naturally experience the beginning of pain because they are not permitted to remain one. I say "two," not <margin>D</margin> as if two bodies were merging into one—for their nature is one—but when a different nature seeks to commune with another nature of a different kind, and when the inferior receives something from the superior, and yet cannot truly grasp it, but only its trace. Thus the whole is two, yet becomes one, turning into a middle state between what it was before and what it cannot attain, being now placed in difficulty. Since an unhappy and unstable commerce exists, it is always <margin>E</margin> pulled in different directions: it is revolved up and down in turn, and when it sinks to lower things, it announces its own torment, but when it inclines somewhat higher, it stirs a desire for communion.

---

## Chapter XIX.

THIS is what is meant by the terms pleasure <margin>A</margin> and pain. Pain is the perception of a withdrawal <note>Greek: *apagōgē*; Latin: *dissolutio*</note> from the body, when it is deprived of the image of the soul; whereas pleasure is the perception of life, when the image of the soul is once again harmonized within the body. In the body, then, is the passion; but the knowledge belongs to the sensory soul, which, through its proximity, feels the passion and announces that which the senses eventually terminate in. The former [the body] indeed...

<column-break/>

...is called pleasure; it arrives at a state of knowledge free from passion. <margin>A</margin> To us, I say—that is, to the second soul—as if such a body were not foreign to us, but our own; therefore, it is a concern to us as if it were our own. For we are not the body itself, nor are we entirely separated from it, but it depends upon us and is attached to us. We are judged by that which is the principal part <note>original: *principale*; Greek: *hēgemonikon*, the ruling part of the soul</note>, yet this body is also ours in another sense. For this reason, whether afflicted by pain or soothed by pleasure, we have a care for <margin>B</margin> such a body; and the weaker we are, the more diligently we care for it and the more accurately we cherish it, precisely because we do not separate ourselves from it. But this very thing which is most excellent in us, by which we are also human, we submerge, as it were, into such a body. Surely it must not be thought that passions of this kind belong entirely to the soul, but rather to such a body and to something common and joined together. For when something is only one thing, it is, as it were, <margin>C</margin> sufficient to itself. For example, if the body were alone and inanimate, what would it suffer? For if it were divided, such a passion would pertain not so much to the body itself as to the union that is within it. Moreover, the soul alone suffers no division or passion; and being in this state, it escapes this whole condition. But in truth, as often as two things strive to be one, and thus employ a foreign union, they undoubtedly often undergo the beginning of pain from the fact that they are not permitted to remain one. I say "two," not <margin>D</margin> as if two bodies were to come together into one—for there is one nature in these—but when a different nature attempts to enter into commerce with a nature of another kind. And what is worse, it receives something from the better nature, yet it cannot receive the thing itself, but only its trace <note>original: *vestigium*; refers to the soul's "reflection" or "imprint" in the material body</note>. And so that whole is two, and becomes one, emerging as a middle ground between that which it was before and that which it cannot now reach, placed in difficulty, since an unhappy and unstable commerce will be within it, always <margin>E</margin> distracted in different directions. For it is revolved upwards and downwards in turn, and when it falls to lower things, it announces its own torment, and when it inclines somewhat higher, it excites a desire for communion.

---

> *Destructive passion [pain] or restorative pleasure does not occur in the sense and the soul, but in the body through the presence of the soul, which is already vitally affected. In the sense and the soul, however, there occurs a perception of that passion, which itself does not suffer. The soul is bound to the body by two "knots," as it were: one indeed turns toward the soul, that is, its life-giving act shining toward the body; the other indeed declines toward the body, that is, the vital quality itself infused into the body through this act. Therefore, the body thus affected and thus bound to the soul belongs to the soul and becomes "ours." We therefore care for it, and when a motion occurs that is either destructive or restorative, perceiving this passion with our sense, we are inclined either to avoid it or to pursue it. If the destructive passion occurred in the sensing soul itself, the sense and judgment would be hindered, and it would not discern in which member the passion was chiefly located. For the soul is indivisible and is simultaneously whole in every part. Therefore, if the soul itself suffered, the passion would occupy the entire soul everywhere.*

## Chapter XIX.

THAT, therefore, is what is handed down concerning the nature of pleasure <margin>A</margin> and pain, where it is said that pain is a certain perception of dissolution, namely when the body is stripped of the image of the soul; while pleasure is a perception in the living being where the image of the soul is restored in the body. In the body there is passion, but the knowledge is in the sensory soul—namely by its proximity feeling the passion and announcing to it the end result of the senses. That [the body] indeed is tormented...

Plotinus and his commentator explain that the body becomes "ours" through a vital link or "knot" of life-giving energy, making the soul's care for the body a consequence of this intimate connection.</summary>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD IV.

torture, I say—that is, having suffered—as in a cutting. When a body is cut, the division pertains to its physical mass; but the affliction pertains to the mass not simply as a matter of size, but as a mass of a certain quality. The same must be said of inflammation. The soul, however, perceives this as if by noticing through a contiguous <term>vicinity</term><note>Latin: *vicinitatem*. Plotinus argues the soul is "near" the body but not "mixed" with it like two liquids.</note>. The whole soul perceives the passion arising there, while the soul itself does not suffer at all. <margin>A</margin> For perceiving as a whole, it announces that the passion is located where the blow or the pain occurs. <margin>B</margin> But if the soul itself suffered, since it is present as a whole throughout the entire body, it would neither say nor report where the passion was primarily inflicted; rather, the whole soul would suffer the pain, and it would be distressed by pain deep within and on all sides. It would not indicate or declare a specific location for the suffering; instead, wherever the soul is, there it would say the pain is. And the soul is everywhere. But now the opposite happens: for the finger hurts, and the person hurts because of that very thing, since it is the person's finger that is distressed. We say the person feels pain in the finger, just as a person is called "gray-eyed" because of the gray color in the eye. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, that which suffers is indeed tortured, unless one perhaps includes "torture" under a single definition along with the sensation that immediately follows it. Defining it this way clearly signifies that pain is, in a sense, pain that does not escape the notice of the senses. Nevertheless, it must in no way be said that the sensation itself *is* the pain, but rather that it is the perception of pain. For knowledge must surely be free from the passion <note>original: *passio*. Here meaning an external force acting upon a subject.</note> itself, so that it may both know clearly and report sincerely. <margin>D</margin> For a messenger caught up in the suffering, while occupied by that suffering, either reports nothing at all or does not arrive as a messenger of health.

*Just as in a light body there is a stimulus to rise, in a root toward moisture, or in a leaf toward heat; so in a body already vitally affected by the soul, certain natural inducements arise: for lack, toward fulfillment; for fullness, toward evacuation; for excessive alteration, toward its opposite. Meanwhile, the vegetative nature, which generated and preserves the vital affection in the body, labors while it strives and acts more intensely to preserve or restore the natural disposition of the body. By this very effort, that desire which was beginning in such a body is said to grow into "nature." But while this nature acts more stubbornly, the perception of the passion reaches the senses, and from there reaches the imagination and judgment.*

<margin>A</margin>
### CHAPTER XX.
IT follows, moreover, that the principle of bodily desires arises from that which is "common," and from such a certain bodily nature. For the beginning of desiring and pursuing something more intensely should not be attributed to the body regardless of its condition. Nor should it be thought that the soul itself affects [desires] salty or sweet things, but rather that which is the body. The body strives not only to *be* a body, but it claims more movements for itself than the soul does, and because of such a claim, it is compelled to be moved in many directions. Therefore, being affected in one way, it desires salty things; in another way, sweet things. Likewise, it desires to be moistened or warmed—none of which would be its concern if it existed alone. <margin>B</margin> Just as in the previous case, knowledge was born from pain, and the soul—striving to lead the body away from the passion inflicting it—turned to flight (which also served as a warning, because it first endured the passion while the body itself, in its own contraction, was in a sense fleeing); <margin>C</margin> so here also a certain sense learns, as does the soul which is nearby, which we certainly call "nature," which grants a trace of life to the body. Therefore, nature reports the desire when it is already grown, as if the end of the desire were in...

<column-break/>

...I say "was pained" to mean it "suffered" that thing; as for example in a cut when the body is being cut, the division is according to the mass, but the recovery is also according to the mass—the fact that it is not only a mass, but a mass of such a kind. But the soul is not inflamed there. The soul perceives by receiving what follows, as if in itself. The whole soul perceives the passion there, without itself suffering. <margin>A</margin> For perceiving as a whole, it says the passion is there, where the blow or the pain is. <margin>B</margin> If the soul itself also suffered, being whole in the entire body, it would not have said or signaled that it was "there," but the whole soul would have suffered the pain again, pained as a whole. And it would not have said or signaled that it was "there," but would have said it was in the place of the suffering, which is everywhere. But now the finger is pained, and the man is pained, because the finger belongs to the man. The man is said to be pained in the finger, just as the "blue-eyed man" is named from the blue in the eye. <margin>C</margin> That thing which has suffered is therefore pained, unless one includes the "being pained" with the sensation that follows. Including it, this clearly signifies that pain is such that the sensation does not miss the pain. But while it is sensation itself, it must not be called painful, but a knowledge of pain. And being knowledge, it must be impassive, <margin>D</margin> so that it may know and report soundly. For a messenger who has suffered, limping from the passion, either does not report, or is not a sound messenger.

->Cap. XX.<-

AND the principle of bodily desires, being thus "common" <note>Greek: *koinon*. Referring to the "composite" of soul and body acting together.</note> and belonging to such a nature of the body, follows. For it is still to the body being in a certain state, of whatever kind, that the beginning of appetite and eagerness belongs, rather than to the soul itself seeking salty or sweet things. But it is the body that desires not only to be a body, but it has acquired more movements, and because of this acquisition, it has been forced to turn toward many things. Thus, being in one state it seeks salty things, in another sweet things, and to be moistened and warmed, none of which would matter to it if it were alone. And just as there, knowledge arose from pain, and the soul, wishing to lead [the body] away from the thing causing the passion, produced flight—and the part that first suffered taught this, fleeing itself in its contraction—so also here, the sensation learns, and the soul which is near, which we call "nature," gives the trace [of life]. Nature [reports] the stammering desire, being the end of...
