-># BOOK FOUR.<-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...already begun from such a body. Sensation, however, leads to <term>imagination</term><note>Greek: *phantasia*. In this context, it refers to the mental image or representation of a physical need.</note>, through which the soul—to which the pursuit belongs—either follows and provides for the need, or resists and abstains. The soul does not necessarily consent either to the one initiating the <term>desire</term><note>Latin: *concupiscientia*; Greek: *epithymia*. A strong physical longing or appetite.</note> or to that which is desired after such an initiation. But why do we posit two desires, rather than simply saying it is the body of a certain kind that feels the appetite? Surely, if <term>Nature</term><note>Greek: *Physis*. Here, the life-force or biological organizing principle of the body.</note> is one thing and the body already formed by Nature is another—for Nature exists before such a body is produced, since she herself makes the body by shaping and forming it—it is necessary that neither the soul itself initiates the desire, but rather it is the body of a certain kind that both suffers certain things and, when in pain, seeks their opposites. It seeks delight to remedy weariness, and fullness to remedy lack. It is necessary for Nature, acting like a <term>mother</term><note>Plotinus often uses familial metaphors to describe how higher principles care for lower ones without being corrupted by them.</note> who guesses the wishes of a suffering child, to try to direct and recall the body to herself. Seeking remedies for these weaknesses, Nature—through this inquiry—is joined with the sufferer's desire, and thus this affection penetrates from the body to the soul. For this reason, someone might say that the body of a certain kind desires by its own nature, perhaps regarding the impulse toward the haste of appetite; but Nature desires for the sake of something else and because of something else, while the soul is like a separate entity that either obeys or, more often, opposes it.

<column-break/>

*The impulse to desire bodily pleasures does not arise in the soul's own power of desiring, but in the specific body—that is, the body vitally affected by the soul. We conclude this for five reasons: First, because since there is both lack and suffering in such a body, it is only right that appetites are stirred here. Second, because as the body differs according to age, health, habit, place, and time, different appetites creep in; however, the power of desiring that remains in the soul does not change. Third, because sometimes there is a stimulus in the body for something toward which the power of desiring does not immediately direct itself. Fourth, even if the soul should soon attend to it, the mind does not always admit or allow it. Fifth, a stimulus often arises in a corrupted body for something least agreeable to nature—such as the urge to eat ashes—which Nature, the regulator of the body’s condition, does not accept or adapt to the body or herself. Finally, the power of desiring implanted in the soul (or its image) is neither filled, nor emptied, nor altered in any way; it is the body that changes. Therefore, appetites for such things are stirred from the body, not from the soul.*

### Chapter XXI.

<margin>A</margin> That it is the body of a certain kind in which the principle of appetite arises is further testified by the different ages of life: for the bodily appetites of children are different from those of adolescents, and different again from those of grown men. The same is true for those in good or ill health, while the power of desiring itself remains the same throughout. It is clear, therefore, that it is a bodily thing—I mean the body of a specific state—which, while it is changed in many ways, similarly incites many different appetites. The same is shown by the fact that not every desire is stirred at once in all such impulses, even though the bodily agitation often lasts until the end. Furthermore, even before reason deliberates on the matter, the soul often does not wish to eat or drink, even while a vehement desire impels it toward these things, insofar as that desire exists in such a body. Moreover, Nature herself often does not accept or wish to bring into her "seat" that which the body is urged toward, as if such a pleasure did not suit Nature's requirements; it is as if it were for Nature herself to determine what is consistent with nature and what is not. But if someone should object to the previous point, saying that it is enough for the body to simply be different at different times...

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS, BOOK IV.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...relates to that which, while another part is suffering, this very power has different <term>desires</term><note>Latin: *cupiditates*; Greek: *epithymia*. Here referring to specific physical cravings.</note> for the sake of another, since it is not itself the part to which the need is necessarily suggested. For it does not belong to the power of desire itself to be nourished, or warmed, or moistened, or changed, or relieved by evacuation, or refilled by satiety; rather, all these things belong to the specific <term>body</term><note>Latin: *tale corpus*; Greek: *ekeina panta*. The physical structure that experiences biological lack or excess.</note>.

The Earth, since it generates animals and is a necessary and by no means contemptible member of the world-animal, is an <term>intellectual and divine animal</term><note>A core Neoplatonic concept: the Earth is not a dead rock but a living being with its own higher intelligence.</note>, and possesses sensation. For in its soul, the judicial power flourishes, which, joined to its own body, perceives and judges the experiences of that body—and that is what it means to sense. Although Plotinus and many others attribute a specific soul to each of the elements, someone might perhaps say, not absurdly, that the celestial spheres possess souls distinct among themselves because they are both immutable and remain distinct within themselves. The elements, however—because they were established for the sake of the composite whole, are changed within themselves, are confused with one another, and are reduced into a single globe, bound together in one form by harmonious proportions—might possess a single soul for all of them. This soul would be accommodated to the one complexity of their matter, just as there are four <term>personae</term><note>Latin: *personis*. Here meaning "masks" or "roles," referring to the four humors or elements acting as different characters of a single underlying nature.</note> of the humors; it would flourish most in air and fire, and through these, simultaneously in water and earth. By the power of this soul, even those composite things might carry back vital force. In these, portions of the elements are bound to the whole by a similar proportion: in the earth and water are manifest animals, while in the air are <term>daemons</term><note>Latin: *daemones*. In the Platonic sense, these are intermediary spirits, not "demons" in the modern evil sense, inhabiting the subtler elements like air.</note> having similarly connected bodies, though they are thin and hidden from us.

### CHAPTER XXII.

<margin>A</margin> Is it not also the case in plants that there is one thing which is, as it were, properly implanted in their bodies, and another which supplies it? That which in us is called the power of <term>desire</term>, in them is called the <term>vegetative power</term><note>Latin: *vegetalis*; Greek: *phytikon*. The lowest level of soul responsible for growth and nutrition.</note>. Perhaps this power exists in the Earth because there is a soul within it, while in plants, it is that which proceeds from this power. One might opportunely ask first: what sort of soul is in the Earth? Does it shine into the Earth like a certain radiance from the universal sphere itself (which Plato seems to be the only one to animate primarily)? 
<margin>B</margin> Or rather, should it be said that Plato attributes to the Earth its own soul, where he again says that the Earth is the first and oldest of all the gods who are enclosed within the heavens? For in what way could the Earth be judged a goddess unless she possessed a soul? Hence it happens that it is difficult to find by what reason this matter stands, and a greater—or certainly no less—ambiguity arises from Plato's words. But surely, first of all, how 
<margin>C</margin> can we investigate an opinion consistent with reason? In the first place, who could conjecture that the Earth has a vegetative soul through those things which are born from it? If many animals also seem to be generated from the Earth, what prevents us from judging it to be an animal? Since it is such a vast animal, and not a small portion of the world, why should we not also say that it possesses a <term>Mind</term><note>Latin: *Mens*; Greek: *Nous*. The higher, intuitive intellect.</note> and is thus a God? Now indeed, if we say that any star is an animal, what prevents us from confessing that the Earth too is an animal, since it is a part of the whole animal? 
<margin>D</margin> For it must not be thought that it is held together from the outside by a foreign soul, while having no soul within, as if it alone were unable to have its own soul. For why should fiery bodies be able to, but a terrestrial one cannot? Truly both are bodies; and there [in the stars] there are no veins, nerves, flesh, blood, or humor, even though the Earth is furnished with a much greater variety and is constituted from all bodies. If anyone objects that it is unfit for motion, 
<margin>E</margin> one could say this only because it does not move from its own place. Someone will also ask how the Earth can sense; and we will similarly ask how the stars can sense. Now, sensing does not belong to the flesh alone, nor should it be attributed at all to...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...[the soul] speaks regarding that which another has suffered, that she herself has different desires for the sake of another; since it is not even the thing itself that is preferred. For that which is to the <term>appetitive part</term><note>original: "τῷ ἐπιθυμητικῷ" (*to epithymetiko*). The part of the soul driven by physical needs.</note>—nourishment, heat, moisture, neither movement nor a settled state, nor a filling—but all those things belong to the [body].

<margin>A</margin> Regarding plants, is that which is as it were implanted in their bodies one thing, and that which provides for them another? That which is the appetitive in us, is the vegetative in them. Or is it not that the soul is in the Earth itself, while that which is in plants comes from it? But one might ask first what soul is in the Earth? Does it shine from the sphere, or does it alone seem to be primarily animated, 
<margin>B</margin> as Plato says, like an illumination into the Earth? Or again, when he calls it the first and oldest of the gods within the heavens, what kind of soul does he give it, such as he gives to the stars? For how could it be a god if it did not have that [soul]? So it happens that it is difficult to find out how the matter stands, and a greater difficulty, or no less a one, arises from what Plato has said. But first, how would it be 
<margin>C</margin> reasonable for the matter to stand? That the Earth has a vegetative soul, one might infer from the things growing out of it. And if many animals are seen to be produced from the Earth, why not say again that it is an animal? Being so great an animal, and not a small part of the universe, why should one not say it also has Mind, and thus is a god? If indeed each of the stars [is an animal], why not also the Earth, being a part of the universal animal? 
<margin>D</margin> For it must not be said to be held together from the outside by a foreign soul, while not having one within, as if it were not able to have its own from itself. For why can fiery things do so, but the earthy cannot? For each is a body; and there [in the stars] there are no fibers, nor flesh, nor blood, nor moisture; yet the Earth is more various, and made of all bodies. 
<margin>E</margin> And if someone should say it is hard to move because it does not move from its place, how then does it perceive? And how do the stars? For indeed, perceiving does not belong to flesh, nor to the body at all...

# BOOK FOUR.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> One should not give a body to the soul simply so that the soul may sense, but rather the soul should be granted to the body so that the body might be preserved and kept safe. Truly, since the soul possesses a judicial power, it also has the faculty through which, while it looks toward the body, it is able to judge the <term>passions</term><note>Latin: *passio*; Greek: *pathēma*. In this context, it refers to external impressions or physical changes felt by the body.</note> of that body. What, then, are the passions of the Earth? And what are their judgments? Furthermore, plants, insofar as they are a part of the Earth, do not sense. Of what things, then, are there 
<margin>B</margin> senses? And through what means do they occur? Or perhaps one should not dare to assert that senses occur without physical instruments? Likewise, for what use does the sensation of the Earth lead? For it is not for the sake of <term>cognition</term><note>Knowledge or understanding.</note>: for perhaps the knowledge that consists in wisdom is sufficient for those beings to whom no utility will come from the act of sensing. Or perhaps someone might not grant this? For there is, besides utility, a certain knowledge in the things that are sensed that is not foreign to the <term>Muses</term><note>The Greek goddesses of inspiration; here referring to the aesthetic or harmonious appreciation of the cosmos.</note>, such as the spectacle of the Sun, the other stars, the heaven, and the earth; for to behold these things is delightful in itself.
<margin>C</margin> This, therefore, must be considered in what follows. For the present, we must again investigate whether senses exist in the Earth, which animals possess the power to sense, and by what reason that occurs. Perhaps it is first necessary to resume the points of doubt and understand collectively whether sensation can be effected without physical instruments, and whether the senses were established for the sake of utility, even if something else results from them besides mere use.

> *To sense is not simply to know sensible things, but to know through passions or certain impressions made either by the things to be sensed near the soul, or by the soul concerning them. The soul, when separated from every body, just as it lives in itself, so it is turned toward itself through the forms implanted in it; from divine things, it knows divine things. Through these, as if through principles, it also comprehends <term>sensible things</term><note>Objects perceived by the physical senses.</note>, yet this is not "sensing." For it cannot sense bodily things then, because it has no proportion with them through which any impression or expression might occur between itself and them. But when it is joined to a body, it uses <term>spirit</term><note>Latin: *spiritus*. In Neoplatonism, this is a thin, subtle "aetherial" body that acts as a bridge between the immaterial soul and the heavy physical flesh.</note> as a certain middle instrument between itself and external things, creating a proportion between both. In this spirit, the qualities or passions coming from outside emerge into a pure and spiritual form close to the soul, so that through this, the soul excites the forms of sensible things lying hidden within itself. Indeed, this excitation is what it means to sense. We declare this whole matter more diligently in the book of <term>Theophrastus</term><note>A successor to Aristotle who wrote on the soul.</note> on the soul, together with <term>Priscianus</term> and <term>Iamblichus</term>.*

### Chapter XXIII.

<margin>A</margin> It must therefore be asserted that sensation concerning sensible things is a perception in the soul or the animal; a perception, I say, in a power adhering to the bodies, perceiving quality, and in some way shaping the form of those things for itself. If this is so, does the soul alone, remaining in itself, apprehend sensible things, or does it do so with something else? If it lives alone and in itself, in what way will it be able to do so? For while it is in itself, it perceives in a similar way those things which are in itself, and uses only
<margin>B</margin> <term>intelligence</term><note>Intellect or higher thought (*noēsis*).</note>. But if it then perceives other things as well, it must have already possessed these, either having been made similar to them, or meeting with something that was at some time made very similar. Indeed, for it to be made similar to these things while remaining in itself is impossible. For under what condition could a "point" become similar to a "line"? Since not even an <term>intelligible line</term><note>The perfect, mathematical idea of a line in the mind/intellect.</note> is able to fit a sensible line, nor can an intelligible fire or man fit a sensible fire or man. 
Indeed, not even the nature itself which generates a man is able to 
<margin>C</margin> concur in identity with the man who is generated. Now truly, if the soul, living with itself, could behold the sensible, it would soon be directed from there into the knowledge of the <term>intelligible</term><note>The realm of Ideas or Forms, accessible only by the mind.</note>, with the sensible escaping it, because the soul obviously has nothing with which to receive it. For even when the soul looks at something visible from a distance, although it comes into the soul mostly as a "form," nevertheless that which begins within the soul or the indivisible part ends in—

PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...discerning the underlying color and shape, insofar as it is present there. Therefore, it is not enough for only these two things to be present—the external object and the soul—for in that case, no <term>passion</term><note>Latin: *passio*; Greek: *pathēma*. In this context, it refers to a physical impression or a "suffering" of an external influence by a sense organ.</note> would occur here. Instead, there must be a third thing that is the "sufferer": that which will receive the form. It is necessary, then, for this third thing to coincide with the sensible object in a certain communion of passion and in a single matter; this thing must undergo the impression, while the other [the soul] recognizes the passion. Such a passion must be created so that it preserves something <margin>B</margin> of the acting agent, yet is not identical to it. Truly, that which suffers acts as a kind of medium between the author of the passion and the soul, holding a passion that is halfway between the sensible and the <term>intelligible</term><note>The realm of pure thought or ideas, as opposed to the physical world of the senses.</note>. This medium reconciles the extremes to one another with a fitting proportion, acting simultaneously as a receiver and a messenger: since it can conveniently be made similar to both. For since it is an instrument of some kind of knowledge, it must be identical neither to the <margin>C</margin> knower nor to the thing being known, but must easily become similar to both: to the external object because it undergoes an impression, and to the internal power because such a passion is a kind of <term>species</term><note>In Scholastic and Neoplatonic thought, a "species" is the form or "likeness" of an object that travels to the mind.</note> or form. Therefore, if we speak correctly, the senses must occur through bodily instruments: for this follows from what we have said, that if the soul were entirely outside the body, it would perceive nothing sensible. The instrument must necessarily be either the whole body, or some member determined for a specific task, as we see happen in touch and sight. Then, <margin>D</margin> indeed, anyone will easily see that the instruments of craftsmen are mediums between those who judge and the things being judged, signaling to the judge the property of the underlying things. For a <term>ruler</term><note>Latin: *regula*; Greek: *kanon*. A straight-edge used for measurement.</note> adapted to straightness—both the straightness that is in the mind and that which is in the wood—when placed in the middle, gives the craftsman the ability to judge the work. It would be a matter for another dispute to inquire whether it is necessary for the instrument to be directly joined to that which is to be judged, or <margin>E</margin> whether sensation occurs through some medium distant from the thing to be felt: for instance, if fire is far from the flesh, with the medium suffering nothing; or as if there were a vacuum between the sight and the color, could the object be seen if the instrument of power were present? However, it is certain that sensation belongs to the soul living specifically in the body, and it is fulfilled through the body.

*Since sensation necessarily follows when the soul is joined to the body, the souls of the stellar spheres of the world sense. The world senses through one part of itself another part in turn; likewise, through the whole, it senses the parts. Furthermore, it senses the condition of the whole through a kind of self-consensus: through its widest sphere, as if through an eye, all things within are connected. For if you, through your eye—because it is animated, transparent, and bright—see so many things, and through its ray proceeding toward the heavens you look up at the celestial bodies, why should the world not see all things through its living, clear, and bright celestial eye, diffusing its rays to all things?*

### Chapter XXIII.

BUT we must investigate whether sensation was granted by nature for the sake of utility alone. Certainly, if sensation is not at all fitting for the soul while it lives alone, but the senses are employed only in conjunction with the body, then surely it is for the sake of the body itself that the senses come forth, and for the sake of the body's fellowship that sensation was given. Either it follows from some necessity—that whatever the body suffers, provided it is a vehement passion, passes through to the soul—or it was provided as a means of caution, so that it might be guarded against before the passion becomes so strong that it destroys the body, or before that which inflicts the passion draws too near. If this is so, the senses were given for the sake of use: for even if for...

<column-break/>

...the underlying color and shape, insofar as it sees it there. Therefore, it is not necessary for only these two things to exist, the external object and the soul, for then it would not even suffer; but there must be a "sufferer," a third thing. And this is that which will receive the form. It must therefore be "sympathetic" and of like-passion, as if of one matter: and while the one part suffers, the other knows, and the passion becomes such that it preserves something of the maker, yet is not the same thing. But since it is between the maker and the soul, it holds the passion as something situated between the sensible and the intelligible: a proportionate medium, joining the extremes to each other in some way: being both receptive and reporting at the same time: fit to be made like to each. For being an instrument of some knowledge, it must be neither the same as the knower nor the same as the known: but fit to be made like to each: to the outer by suffering, and to the inner, because its passion becomes a form. If then we speak soundly, the senses occur through bodily instruments. For this also follows: that if the soul were to be entirely outside the body, it would perceive nothing sensible. The instrument must be either the entire body, or a certain part set aside for a specific work, as in the case of touch and sight. And one might see that even manufactured instruments become mediums between the judges and the things being judged, reporting to the judge the quality of the underlying things. For the ruler, having joined the straightness in the soul with that in the wood, being placed in the middle, gave the craftsman the power to judge the artifact. But whether it is necessary to join the thing being judged to the instrument, or through some medium standing far off from the sensible—as if fire were far from the flesh, the medium suffering nothing; or as if there were a vacuum between the sight and the color, would it be possible to see if the instrument were present in power?—that is for another discussion. But that sensation belongs to the soul in a body and through a body is clear.

### Chapter XXIII.

AS TO whether sensation is for utility alone, we must consider it thus: if the soul were alone, sensation would not occur; but with a body, the senses exist, and would be for the sake of the body, from which the senses also arise, and were given because of the body's fellowship. Either they follow out of necessity, because the body suffers and the passion, being greater, reaches as far as the soul; or it has been contrived so that one might be on guard either before the acting agent becomes greater so as to destroy, or before it comes near. If this is so, the senses would be for the sake of utility. For even if for...

BOOK FOUR

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Knowledge and notice are granted to those who do not already possess cognition; they are given to the ignorant due to misfortune, and to the forgetful so that they might eventually remember. Therefore, to a being who neither lacks anything nor forgets, such senses would certainly not be attributed. But if this is the case, we must consider not only the Earth, but all the stars, and especially the whole heaven and the world <note>original: "mundus"; Greek: "kosmos"</note>. For the parts of the world which act upon other parts—and which are subject to <term>passion</term><note>In this philosophical context, "passion" (Latin: *passio*; Greek: *pathos*) does not mean emotion, but the state of being acted upon or receiving a physical impression from an external source.</note>—sensation will be appropriate according to our current reasoning. 

<margin>B</margin> But for the "All" <note>The universe as a single, unified organism.</note> toward itself, what kind of sensation could exist, since it is everywhere free from passion in relation to itself? For if it is necessary that the instrument of the one sensing be one thing, and the object being sensed be something else besides that instrument, and the universe is both the "All" and the "Whole," then surely there will not be within it one part through which sensation is produced and another through which it is perceived. 

Rather, we must grant it a certain "self-awareness" <note>original: "consenfum"; Greek: "fynaiſthefin" (sunaisthesis). A joint-perception or internal consciousness of one's own state.</note> of itself, just as we have a certain self-awareness within ourselves. But as for a sensation that is always directed toward <margin>C</margin> an external "other," we should not grant this. For even we, when we perceive something within our own body that is outside its natural habit, are actually perceiving something coming from the outside. 

Yet, just as in ourselves there is not only the apprehension of external things, but also of one part toward another, what prevents the world from looking through the region of the "fixed stars" <note>The "inerratic" or unwandering sphere of the stars.</note> toward the region of the "planets" <note>The "erratic" or wandering stars.</note>, and through this to look upon the Earth and the things upon it? If these parts have <margin>D</margin> different experiences than others, nothing prevents them from having different senses. 

Furthermore, the vision of the sphere of fixed stars is not only for its own sake, but this very region acts as an eye, reporting what it sees to the Soul of the All. For even if it does not admit other passions, what prevents it from seeing like an eye, since it is a luminous and animated thing? 

But here Plato <note>Referring to Plato's *Timaeus*, where he argues the world-animal does not need eyes because there is nothing outside it to see.</note> will seem to stand in the way, saying the heaven does not need eyes. It is true that nothing was left outside the world to be seen, and thus <margin>E</margin> it did not need eyes for that purpose; nevertheless, inside there is much to be seen, and nothing prevents the world from seeing itself. 

And if someone should object that such sensation is useless because it is vain for a being to see itself: let us say that while the world was not primarily designed by some creator specifically for the sake of seeing in this manner, because its nature is so arranged, this ability necessarily follows. Therefore, nothing prevents it from seeing through a body that is, by its nature, transparent.

---

The world was not constituted for the sake of living in this way by some principal design, but because its nature is so arranged, this also necessarily follows: therefore, nothing will prevent it from seeing through such a transparent body.

*The souls of the spheres and the stars, and the Soul of the World, see and hear humans; but meanwhile, they do not at all perceive that they are perceiving such things, because the imagination (to which such observation belongs) is always most intensely focused on forming within itself the marks of the divine Intelligences. And even if they do perhaps not notice that they are perceiving us, they nevertheless grant favors to those who pray, through some kind of sense and a hidden consensus of nature. This is the opinion of Plotinus among the objections arising from a faulty text. Perhaps someone will say that the imaginations of the celestial souls are so effective that they derive the marks of the <term>intelligibles</term><note>Non-physical truths or ideas accessible only to the mind.</note> into <term>sensibles</term><note>Physical things accessible to the senses.</note>, and thus they perceive internally in a certain way, or are able to imagine both sensible and intelligible things simultaneously in certain wonderful ways.*

Perhaps it is not enough for the instrument to be present through which action occurs for seeing and sensing to happen; rather, the soul must be so disposed that it somehow "nods toward" <note>original: "annuat"; Greek: "neuein". An inclination or focusing of the soul's attention.</note> the sensible objects. 

<margin>A</margin> For it is proper to the soul itself to always be in the presence of the intelligibles; and even if it were possible for it to perceive, it would not be proper for it to do so while it is intent upon the intelligibles themselves, just as we, when we are more intensely focused on understanding...

PLOTINUS ENNEAD IV.

<margin>A</margin> ...the underlying color and shape, discerning the extent of what is there. Therefore, it is not enough for only these two to be present—namely, the external object and the soul—for in that case no <term>passion</term><note>original: "passio"; in ancient philosophy, this refers to the state of being acted upon or receiving an impression, rather than an emotion.</note> would occur. Instead, there must be a third thing that undergoes the experience: that which will receive the form. It is necessary, then, for this third thing to come together with the sensible object in a shared experience and within a single matter. This part must suffer the impression, while the other part—the soul—recognizes the experience. The resulting impression must be of such a kind that it preserves something of the agent that produced it, yet is not identical to it.

<margin>B</margin> Indeed, that which suffers the impression acts as a sort of middle ground between the author of the impression and the soul. It holds a "middle experience" between the sensible and the intelligible. This medium reconciles the two extremes through a fitting proportion; it is both a receiver and a messenger, being conveniently able to resemble both sides. Since it is an instrument of a certain kind of knowledge, it must be identical neither to the one who knows nor to the thing being known. Instead, it must easily become like both: like the external object because it is acted upon, and like the internal power because that very impression becomes a kind of <term>species</term><note>original: "species"; here meaning a mental form or "image" that the mind can grasp.</note>. Therefore, if we speak correctly, senses must be produced through bodily instruments. This follows from what we have said: if the soul were entirely outside the body, it would perceive nothing of the sensible world. The instrument must necessarily be either the whole body or some member determined for a specific task, as we see happening in the cases of touch and sight.

<margin>C</margin> Furthermore, anyone can easily see that the tools of craftsmen act as mediums between those who judge and the things being judged, signaling the properties of the underlying materials to the judge. For a ruler <note>original: "regula"</note>, being adapted to the concept of "straightness" both in the mind and in the wood, and being placed rightly in the middle, gives the craftsman the ability to judge the work. It would be a matter for a different discussion to inquire whether the thing to be judged must be in direct contact with the instrument, or whether sensation can occur through a medium from a distance. For instance, if fire is far from the <margin>D</margin> flesh, can it be felt if the medium between them is not affected? Or, if there were a vacuum between the sight and the color, could the object be seen? However, it is established that sensation belongs to the soul only while it lives in a body and is fulfilled through the body.

*Since sensation necessarily follows when a soul is joined to a body, the souls of the spheres and the stars of the universe also possess sensation. The world senses through one part of itself acting upon another part; likewise, it senses the parts through the whole. Furthermore, it senses the condition of the whole through a kind of internal "self-consent" <note>original: "consenfu"; referring to the Greek "sympatheia" or "sunaisthesis," the shared feeling of a single organism.</note>. It looks upon all things within itself chiefly through the widest sphere, as if through an eye. For if you see so many things through your own eye—because it is animated, transparent, and bright—and you look up at the heavens through its ray reaching toward the celestial realm, why should the world not see all things through its own living, clear, and bright celestial eye, which spreads its rays throughout all things?*

<column-break/>

### Chapter XXIV.

We must now investigate whether the senses were granted by nature for the sake of utility alone. Certainly, if sensation is not at all appropriate for the soul when it lives alone, but senses are employed only in conjunction with the body, then they must exist because of the body itself. It is from the body that the senses arise, and <margin>B</margin> for the sake of the body's fellowship that sensation was given. Perhaps it follows from some necessity: whatever the body suffers—provided the impression is strong—passes through to the soul. Or perhaps it was a provision of foresight, so that the soul might be warned before a passion grows strong enough to destroy it, or before the thing bringing the harm comes too near. If this is so, the senses were given for the sake of use.

#### BOOK FOUR.

<margin>A</margin> Senses are granted for the sake of obtaining knowledge, not to one who already possesses full cognition, but to one who is ignorant due to some misfortune or is forgetful, so that they might eventually remember. Therefore, to a being who neither lacks anything nor forgets, senses would by no means be attributed. But if this is the case, we must consider not only the earth, but all the stars, and especially the whole of heaven and the world. For while the parts may interact with other parts—and thus "suffer" or receive impressions—giving rise to sensation according to our current reasoning, how could the <term>Whole</term><note>The "Whole" refers to the Universe or the World Soul as a single, complete entity.</note> have sensation toward itself? 

<margin>B</margin> How can it sense itself when it is everywhere free from <term>passion</term><note>original: "passio"; here meaning the state of being changed or acted upon by an external force.</note> in relation to itself? Indeed, if it is necessary for there to be one thing that is the instrument of the feeler and another thing, distinct from the instrument, which is felt, and yet the Universe is a single totality, then surely there will not be within it one thing *through which* sensation is produced and another thing *which* is perceived by that sense. 

<margin>C</margin> Nevertheless, we must grant it a certain "self-awareness" of itself, just as we possess a certain self-awareness within ourselves. But we should not grant it a sense that is always directed toward something else. For even when we perceive something specific within our own bodies that differs from our usual natural state, we are then touching upon something that has arrived from the outside. 

<margin>D</margin> Yet, just as in us there is not only the apprehension of external things but also the awareness of one part toward another, what prevents the world from gazing upon the "wandering" region through the "fixed" region, and through this, looking down upon the earth and observing what is upon it? <note>original: "inerraticam regionem erraticam"; The "inerratic" refers to the sphere of fixed stars, while the "erratic" refers to the planets or "wandering stars."</note> If these celestial bodies have experiences that differ from other types of impressions, nothing prevents them from also having different types of senses. Furthermore, the vision of the fixed region is not only for itself, but this very region acts like an eye, reporting what it sees to the Soul of the Whole. 

<margin>E</margin> For even if it does not admit other external impressions, what stands in the way of it seeing like an eye, since it is a luminous and animated thing? But here Plato seems to object, saying that "the heaven has no need of eyes." <note>A reference to Plato’s *Timaeus*, where he argues the universe is a perfect sphere and needs no organs for external perception.</note> Yet even if nothing is left outside to be seen—and therefore it did not require eyes of that kind—nonetheless, there is that which may be seen within, and nothing prevents it from seeing itself. If someone objects that it is not useful to have a sense because it is vain to look at oneself: even if the world was not originally designed with the purpose of living in this way, but was so composed by nature, this self-perception would follow of necessity. Therefore, nothing prevents it from seeing through a body of such transparency.

<column-break/>

> *The souls of the spheres and stars, as well as the Soul of the World, see and hear human things; but meanwhile, they do not "notice" that they are sensing in this way. This is because the imagination, to which such notice belongs, is always most intent on forming within itself the marks of the divine intellects. And even if they perhaps do not notice that they are sensing, they still grant benefits to those who pray, through a certain sense and a secret "natural consensus" or harmony of nature. This is the opinion of Plotinus, found among the objections arising from a faulty text. Perhaps someone might say that the imaginations of the celestial souls are so effective that they derive the marks of the intelligible world into sensible things, and thus they sense inwardly in a way, or are able to imagine both sensible and intelligible things simultaneously in certain wonderful modes.*

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

<margin>A</margin>
While we apply ourselves to one thing, other visions and senses remain hidden in the meantime; and generally, if we focus diligently on one object, others are concealed. Moreover, if the soul should strive to grasp one part of itself with another part—as if it were looking closely at itself—this would be superfluous even in us. Unless such an act were done for some specific purpose, it would be in vain. Furthermore, to look at something else as if it were beautiful is the mark of one who is affected by an external impression and is in a state of need. As for smell, hearing, and the taste of liquids, one might posit that these are certain distractions and pathways of the soul tending toward the exterior world, whereas the sun and other stars might see and hear only by <term>accident</term><note>In philosophical terms, an "accident" is a property that a thing happens to have, but which is not essential to its nature.</note>. But if one posits that they turn toward both, the position is not absurd. Truly, if they do turn toward us, they would also remember human affairs; for it would perhaps be absurd if they did not remember those whom they diligently benefit. Otherwise, if they are not mindful, how shall they bestow their benefits?

*The spheres of the world and the stars possess senses and they hear our prayers. Celestial beings possess sight, though it differs in kind from our sight; yet it agrees in its general nature, being a nature that is divine, transparent, and luminous. They are also said to possess hearing, but of a kind far different from our hearing, because, in the manner of those who listen and grant requests, they often fulfill the prayers of those making vows. Among all parts of the world, like the members of a single living animal, there is said to be a certain communion, or contact, or continuity, or union, for which there appear to be five foundations:* 

*First is the single matter of all things everywhere. Second is the harmony of qualities: for just as the elements, though discordant, are in harmony through certain qualities shared between neighbors, so too all levels of things—whether composed of elements or not—though differing among themselves, touch one another through reciprocal boundaries. Third is the single <term>spirit</term><note>original: "spiritus"; referring to the "pneuma" or life-breath that permeates the Stoic and Neoplatonic universe.</note> everywhere: for just as the heaven is one spirit in the heights, so within the heaven a single spirit—either entirely celestial or very similar to the heaven—is infused into all things. By this spirit, all things are governed from heaven, and the World Soul is joined even to the lower bodies through the spirit, and all living things grow together through it; understand this spirit to be similar to our own. Fourth is the single generative nature nourishing all things, bound to subsequent things through the spirit. Fifth is the World Soul, everywhere one, connected to the spirit and other things by nature. Therefore, through this union consisting of five foundations, every most vehement movement reaches the celestial beings (such as the movements of those making vows), or reaches those making vows from the celestial beings—especially if not only the World Soul, but also all the divine souls are present everywhere, although they may declare their actions more clearly in some places than others. This is what Plotinus, Porphyry, and Iamblichus seem to intend. Moreover, the first God himself, most powerful of all and widest in command, is most present to each individual. The soul of the earth exercises all senses through the spirit there, which is as if celestial and illuminated by the rays of the celestial beings, subject to its own nature and governing earthly things; furthermore, it hears prayers.*

<margin>B</margin>
They also know our vows, as if through a certain contact and a fixed, tempered relationship of all things everywhere; and by this same reasoning, they produce their effects. Furthermore, in the works of the <term>magicians</term><note>original: "magorum"; Plotinus often discusses the efficacy of "natural magic" which works through cosmic sympathy rather than supernatural intervention.</note>, the whole operation is carried out through things that are contiguous. These things consist of certain powers that follow one another by a certain mutual <term>sympathy</term><note>original: "compassione" / "sympathia"; the concept that all parts of the universe "feel" together as one organism.</note>. If this is so, why should we not say that the earth also perceives? But what senses shall we attribute to it? First, why not touch? Whether from part to part, with the sensation being transmitted to the governing center, or whether it feels the fire and other elements as a whole. For even if the earthly body is unsuited for movement, it is not entirely immobile. It will perceive not the smallest things, but the great. But why will it perceive these? Perhaps because it is necessary that, since the soul is present here, the greatest movements do not go unnoticed. Indeed, nothing prevents the earth from having sensation for this reason: so that it may well-arrange human affairs, insofar as human duties pertain to the earth itself. It will arrange them well <margin>C</margin> as if by a certain sympathy or consensus. Nor does anything prevent it from hearing those who pray and nodding to their prayers, yet not in the same condition as we are accustomed to. It might use other senses toward itself and other things, as if regarding odors and tastes known to others. Perhaps it uses the smell of liquids

If this is so, why shall we not also grant that the earth perceives? But what kind of sensation? Why not first touch? Either by a part being sent back to another part to the governing center of sensation, or the whole perceiving the fire or the other elements? Because it is necessary, since there is a soul, that the greatest movements do not go unnoticed. # BOOK FOUR.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...construction and even to the care of its own body. However, we must not demand the same kinds of instruments that exist in us. For these are not the same in all animals; for example, ears are not present in all, and yet those that lack ears nonetheless perceive sounds. But regarding sight: if it requires light, in what way will it belong to the earth? For even if eyes are not to be required, light still ought not to be lacking. But if, after it has been granted that a <term>vegetative nature</term><note>The "vegetative soul" is the lowest level of soul in Neoplatonism, responsible for growth, nutrition, and reproduction.</note> is present, it must consequently be granted that this very nature is like a certain <term>spirit</term><note>original: "pneuma" / "spiritus". In this context, it refers to a subtle material substance that acts as a vehicle for the soul's powers.</note>, and therefore that it primarily exists in this way—why then should we doubt that it is also a transparent thing, since it is spirit? Rather, it must be confessed that because it is spirit, it is transparent; and since it is illuminated by the celestial circle, it is transparent in <term>actuality</term><note>In Aristotelian and Neoplatonic terms, something is "in act" when it is currently manifesting its potential.</note>. Wherefore, it should be thought neither absurd nor impossible for the soul of the earth to see. One ought to remember, truly, that this is not the soul of some cheap or base body, and therefore it possesses intellect and is a goddess:

->*for it is altogether necessary that the soul itself always exist as good.*<-

*It appears that the earth possesses a soul from the fact that plants and stones grow; indeed, they do so as long as they remain rooted in the earth, but otherwise they do not. Just as teeth, nails, and hair grow in an animal, the effect of the <term>genital power</term><note>The power of generation or reproduction.</note> appears in plants clinging to the earth. This power itself seems to have no independent existence in them, for otherwise, even when torn away, they would grow together by their own power. Therefore, this vegetative power is not so much their own as it is common—that is, shared in the soul of the earth. Likewise, the masculine and feminine powers (that is, of generating and conceiving), which are separate in animals, are joined together in plants within the same plant body. This is solely because the nature of the plant is so grafted into the common nature, just as the body of the plant is grafted into the common body. The masculine and feminine forces pertaining to nature are joined in the universal nature, although they are separate in others. Just as sight, where it is perfect, has a keen power joined with the illuminating light, so too does the intellect. Thus Orpheus calls the mundane nature "Jove" both male and female; and Mercury <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> does the same. For this reason, they call the soul of the air Jupiter and Juno. They call the soul of the earth not only Ceres and Vesta, but also Pluto joined with Proserpina. Nature joined both sexes in the tree because the tree cannot move toward another for the sake of mating, although elsewhere one sex may prevail; in those cases, it is necessary for the plants to be brought near to one another.* Chapter XXVII.

---

<margin>within itself the same [power]</margin>
If, therefore, the Earth grants the "soul-power" to plants, does it provide the power itself, or does it keep the power within itself and grant only a "trace" of it to the plants? If the latter, then the plant would be affected in the same way as flesh is when animated. By this condition, if plants have a generative quality, they have drawn it from there. When it is said that the Earth provides to the body of the plant that which is better, it is by this that the plant is distinguished from that which has been cut off; for the cut branch is no longer a plant, but merely wood. But what does the soul attribute to the body of the earth itself? <margin>B</margin> Truly, one must not think that a terrestrial body cut off from the whole is the same as that which is continuous with the whole. This is demonstrated by stones themselves, which grow as long as they are rooted in the earth, but if they are dug up, they no longer increase. Therefore, one must think that each part has a certain "trace" within itself. But above this, the universal vegetative power spreads itself, which is no longer the property of this or that part, but of the whole earth. Then there is the nature of its <margin>C</margin> sensory power, which is no longer mixed with the body, but "sits upon" it. Furthermore, there is another soul and mind, which people call Vesta and Ceres—those people who, relying on divine oracle and genius, prophesy these very things.

---

*The vegetative and generative nature of the soul imprints a certain vital trace upon the composition of the <term>humors</term><note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) believed to control health and temperament.</note>, from which the body becomes vitally affected. In a body thus affected, there exist the "passions" of the animal and the principles of bodily disturbances. In the whole body, there is physical pleasure, and in the liver especially, the principle of desire and pain. In the <term>precordia</term><note>The region around the heart and diaphragm.</note> is the primary seat of anger, for there nutrition and generation flourish, but here is the fiery vigor. The movements of anger start either from the outside or the inside. Anger comes from the outside when it is brought into the body from without...*

PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

<margin>A</margin> From passion to the first motion of sense, a fiery vigor burns, moving the imagination, and through this, it provokes reason. Internally, anger occurs when reason or imagination, thinking upon an injury, stirs up the burning fluid. Furthermore, lust has a physical leaning in the body, and sometimes it is stirred up from the body itself, as if swollen with seeds; at other times, it arises from the first sight of an object, which excites the body and moves the imagination or even reason; and sometimes it comes from the imagination or reason itself dwelling upon a pleasure, which then moves the body. Moreover, the powers of desiring and being angry are like siblings; for those prone to lust are also more inclined toward anger, and vice versa—which is why the poets did not without reason join Mars with Venus.

### Chapter XXVIII.

Let these things be said regarding these matters for now. We must now return to where we left off and inquire into the <term>irascible faculty</term><note>The "irascible faculty" (Latin: *irascendi virtus*; Greek: *thymoeidēs*) refers to the part of the soul responsible for spirit, courage, and anger.</note> itself. Just as we placed the origin of desires, pains, and pleasures—I do not mean those of the senses, but the passions—in a body already affected in a certain way (that is, as a living thing), should we also place the beginning of anger there? And should we locate all anger in the whole of such a body, or rather in a specific part of the body, such as the heart or the bile, as if they were not lacking in life? <margin>B</margin> Likewise, is it something else that grants this "trace of the soul," or is this spiritedness a single thing that does not depend on the other faculties of anger or feeling? In that case, the <term>vegetative power</term><note>The basic level of soul responsible for growth and nutrition.</note> itself, present in the whole body, imprints a trace upon the whole body; thus, feeling pain and pleasure happens to the whole, and the principle of seeking fullness is found throughout. Regarding the lust of Venus, nothing is strictly defined: but let it be centered around the members suited to that function. <margin>C</margin> Let the location of the liver be the principle of desiring, since the vegetative power acts there most strongly; for it provides the liver and the whole body with the trace of the soul. Let it be there, I say, because the action begins there. But it is asked concerning anger: what is it, and what kind of soul is it? Does it imprint a trace upon the heart, or is it something else that brings motion into the heart to complete the common effect? Or does it provide not just a trace, but the very "boiling over" itself? <margin>D</margin> First, therefore, it seems we must investigate what this power of anger actually is. It is clear that we are accustomed to being angry not only for those things which the body suffers, but also for those things which our dear ones suffer, and altogether for the sake of those things we think are inflicted unworthily upon us or ours. Therefore, in anger itself, there seems to be a need for sense and a certain intelligence. Thus, looking at these things, one might think that anger takes its origin not from the vegetative power, but from some other source. <margin>E</margin> Yet when a tendency toward anger follows certain physical states—when those boiling with blood and bile are more prone to anger, while those who have colder bile or blood are slower to it—one sees the physical connection. Likewise, brute animals, beyond their physical compositions, burst into anger simply because someone appears likely to hurt them. Again, through these things, one will easily refer the impulse of anger primarily to a bodily quality and that which constitutes the animal's physical makeup. <margin>F</margin> And when the same men are more prone to anger when they are sick than when they are healthy, and similarly when they are fasting rather than full, it is clear that anger, or the principle of anger, pertains to a body affected in a certain way, and that the bile or blood, as if "animated," excites these impulses. ## BOOK FOUR.

<margin>A</margin> ...immediately the blood or the bile is moved, and once the sense is excited, the <term>imagination</term><note>Original Greek: *phantasia*. In Neoplatonic thought, this is the "mirror" of the soul where sensory data and thoughts meet.</note> also awakens. This imagination, once roused, calls upon the soul—which is in communication with such a body—to attack the very thing that caused the distress. It is also evident that the soul, using its higher reason, is moved when it perceives an injury has been committed, even if the body’s state does not immediately push it toward a "burning" heat. It is as if this spiritedness was naturally designed to immediately attack a declared enemy and <margin>B</margin> to fight like a fellow soldier at the command of reason. Therefore, there is something in us that is usually provoked without reason, which then, through the imagination, calls reason to join its cause. There is also that which begins with reason and ends in that which naturally "boils over" <note>This refers to the "irascible" part of the soul, associated with the heart and heat.</note>. Furthermore, the spark of both anger and desire seems to sprout from the <term>vegetative and generative nature</term><note>The lowest level of the soul's functions, responsible for growth and reproduction, shared by humans, animals, and plants.</note> itself; for this nature has so affected the body that it perceives things as pleasant or painful. It has <margin>C</margin> also infused the body with bitter bile, and has impressed a "trace" upon the soul so affected. When this trace exists in such a state regarding painful things, it is irritated into anger; and since it was poorly affected from the start, it strives to corrupt other things and make them similar to itself. That this is a trace of the soul is proven by the fact that those who desire bodily pleasures less and neglect the body are less easily provoked to anger and are less carried away by <margin>D</margin> irrational passion. Truly, it should not seem strange that trees do not have anger, even though they possess a vegetative nature, since they have neither blood nor bile. Where these are present, a "boiling" arises even without conscious sensation, like a kind of offense. But when sensation is added, an impulse immediately rises to fight off what has caused the offense. But if the irrational part of the soul is divided into the power of desire and the power of anger, and the former is vegetative, while the power of anger is <margin>E</margin> its "trace" residing around the blood or bile (or both), then the division would not be correctly made by opposing them; for one of these is prior and the other is posterior. Perhaps, however, nothing prevents both from being posterior, and the division is such that two things are born from the same source: for this is a division of appetites (based on the way they desire), and not of the essence from which such things come. That essence, in itself, is not an appetite, but perhaps it perfects the appetite by <margin>F</margin> joining its own action to it. Finally, it is not absurd to say that the trace of the soul that falls into spiritedness is located in the <term>precordia</term><note>The region around the heart and diaphragm, traditionally seen as the seat of courage and emotion.</note>; for one should not think the soul is properly located here, but rather that the source of this specific kind of blood is here.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the blood or the bile is moved suddenly, and once the sense is excited, the imagination also awakens: which, having been awakened, may provoke the soul—sharing as it does with such a body—to invade that very thing which brought the trouble. It is further established that the soul, using reason from above, is then moved when an injury is seen to be inflicted, even if the affection of the body does not then drive it toward a glow, as if this spiritedness were naturally established for the sake of immediately invading a declared enemy, and <margin>B</margin> fighting like a fellow soldier under the command of reason. There is, therefore, in us that which is accustomed to being provoked without reason, and once provoked, then calls reason to the same through the imagination. There is also that which begins from reason and ends in that which naturally glows. Accordingly, the fuel for both anger and desire seems to sprout from the vegetative and generative nature itself: since this very nature has so affected the body that it perceives things as pleasant and troublesome. Likewise, <margin>C</margin> it has infused bitter bile, and thus has impressed a "trace" upon the affected soul. Indeed, when the soul is in such a state concerning troublesome things, it is irritated to anger; and since it was poorly affected from the beginning, it also strives to deprave other things and, as it were, make them similar to itself. That this trace of the soul is related in essence to the other trace can be proven to us by this argument: that those who desire bodily delights less and neglect the body are less provoked to anger and are less carried away by <margin>D</margin> irrational passion. Truly, it should not seem a wonder that trees do not have anger, although they have a vegetative nature, since they have neither blood nor bile: for where these are present, even without sensation, a "boiling" merely arises, and as it were, a certain offense. But when sensation arrives, an impetus now rises up to fight off that which has offended. But if the irrational part of the soul is divided into the virtue of desiring and the virtue of anger, and the former is vegetative: while the power of anger is <margin>E</margin> its trace around the blood or bile, or both, the division will not be correctly made from the opposite side: since one of these is prior, and the other is truly posterior. But perhaps nothing prevents both from being posterior, and the division being of such a kind of two things born from the same source: for it is a division of things that desire in the respect that they are desiring things, but not of the essence from whence such things have come. Truly, that essence according to itself is not an appetite, but perhaps it is that which perfects the appetite—namely, by <margin>F</margin> joining to it the action proceeding from the appetite. Finally, it is not absurd to say that the trace of the soul falling into spiritedness is situated in the region of the heart: for one must not think that the soul is properly here, but that the source of such a blood is here.

> *In the animated body, there is not only the soul and the continuous life-giving act of the soul—just as light shines from a luminous body into its own body—but there is also a certain vital trace, like heat beneath the light. I call this heat the "natural spirit" and the "spirit fit for movement," which can remain for a short time in the body after the departure of the soul and produce a certain movement. No life-giving force perishes, but does this vital trace? Truly, the natural heat there ceases to be in a short time, because the natural spirit is quickly dissolved. The vital and animal spirit, however, can survive longer and follow the soul, being held by the soul as if by a curd, serving as a kind of ferment for gathering the airy body after death and affecting it vitally. But if you think there is something in this vital trace besides heat and spirit, which relates to the soul and its light not as heat, but as the splendor resulting from the light of the soul, that indeed does not perish, but accompanies the light of the departing soul. He believes that light depends in no way upon the illuminated object, but only upon the luminous source, and that it always follows it together with the splendor resulting in whatever way. Does he touch upon the opinion that says the powers and, as it were, the little flowers of all colors are in the light?*

### Cap. XXVIII.

<margin>A</margin> Let this be enough said on these matters for now. We must now return to where we left off and inquire about the power of anger itself: whether we should place the origin of anger in the body when it is affected in a certain way (that is, as if "vivified"), just as we placed the source of desires, pains, and pleasures (I mean passions, not just sensations) in such a body? And should we place all anger in such a body as a whole, or rather in a specific part <margin>B</margin> of the body, such as the heart or the bile, when affected in this way, rather than in things lacking life? Furthermore, is there something else that provides the <term>soul-trace</term><note>Original Latin: *animale vestigium*; Greek: *ichnos*. This is the "shadow" or impression the higher soul leaves upon the physical body to give it life.</note>? Or is this spiritedness a single thing that does not depend on other powers of anger or sensation? In the former case, the <term>vegetative power</term><note>The lowest level of the soul, responsible for growth and basic life functions.</note>, being present in the whole body, impresses a trace upon the whole; thus, feeling pain or pleasure happens to the whole, and the drive for physical satisfaction is found in the whole. Regarding the <margin>C</margin> desire for sexual union, nothing is strictly defined, but let us say it concerns the parts designed for such a function. Let the area of the liver be the principle of desire, since the vegetative power acts there most intensely; this power provides the soul-trace to the liver and the whole body. I say it is there, because that is where the action begins. But concerning anger, we ask: what is it, what kind of soul is involved, and is a trace impressed by it around the heart, or is it something else that provides movement to the common parts of the body? Or perhaps it does not provide a trace, but rather the "boiling over" of anger itself. First, then, we must investigate <margin>D</margin> what this power of anger actually is. It is clear that we usually become angry not only because of what the body suffers, but also because of what people dear to us suffer, and generally because of things we think are unjustly inflicted upon us or our kin. Therefore, in the act of being angry, there seems to be a need for sensation and a kind of intelligence. Likewise, even brute animals break into anger simply because someone appears likely to hurt them, based solely on their bodily composition. Again, through these observations, one might easily refer the impulse of anger primarily to a bodily quality and to that which maintains the animal's constitution. <margin>F</margin> And since the same people are more prone to anger when they are sick than when they are healthy, and likewise when they are hungry rather than full, it is clear that anger, or the principle of anger, belongs to the body when it is affected in a certain way, and that the bile or blood, as if "animated," excites these impulses. For instance, in a heart so disposed, or in bile, or in a dead body? # BOOK FOUR.

Immediately the blood or the bile is moved; once a sensation occurs, the <term>imagination</term><note>Original: phantasia / imaginatio. The faculty that forms mental images from sensory input.</note> is awakened. The soul, which shares in a body of this kind, is thus disposed and sees the pain even without acting. From this same source, the soul itself, which uses <term>reason</term><note>Original: logismos / ratio.</note>, is moved when an injury appears. Even if the body is not yet ready to burn with rage, the soul—since it is naturally inclined to fight against what is shown to be an enemy—makes the body its ally. Thus, there is that which is stirred up irrationally, where the imagination drags reason along with it; and there is that which starts from reason and ends in that which is naturally inclined to be angry. Both anger and desire seem to sprout from the <term>vegetative and generative nature</term><note>The "lowest" part of the soul responsible for basic biological functions like growth and reproduction.</note>; for this nature has so affected the body that it perceives both the pleasant and the painful. It has also infused the bitter bile, and impressed a "trace" upon the soul so affected. When this trace exists in such a state, it is irritated to anger by painful things; and because it is ill-affected from the start, it seeks to corrupt other things and make them like itself. That this trace of the soul is related in essence to the other trace is proven by this: those who desire bodily pleasures less and neglect the body are less provoked to anger and are less carried away by irrational passion. We should not wonder that trees do not have anger, even though they have a vegetative nature, for they possess neither blood nor bile. Where these are present without sensation, only a "boiling" or a kind of irritation would occur; but once sensation is added, an impulse arises to drive out what has caused the offense. But if the irrational part of the soul is divided into the <term>desiring</term><note>Original: epithymetikon / concupiscendi.</note> and <term>spirited</term><note>Original: thymoeides / irascendi.</note> powers—where the former is vegetative and the spirited is a trace of it involving blood or bile—then the division is not strictly between opposites. For one of these is prior and the other is posterior. Perhaps nothing prevents both from being posterior, and the division being of two things born from the same source: for this is a division of "appetites" insofar as they are appetites, not of the "essence" from which they came. That essence in itself is not an appetite, but perhaps it perfects the appetite by joining to itself the action coming from the appetite. Finally, it is not absurd to say that the trace of the soul falling into animosity is located in the <term>precordia</term><note>The region of the chest around the heart.</note>; for we should not think the soul is strictly there, but rather the source of the specific blood that produces such effects.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Suddenly the blood or the bile moves, and as the sensation is excited, the imagination also awakens. Once awakened, it provokes the soul communicating with such a body to attack the very person who brought the distress. It is also clear that the soul, using reason from above, is moved when an injury is seen to have been inflicted, even if the body's affection does not immediately push it to a "white heat," as if this animosity were naturally designed to immediately attack a declared enemy and <margin>B</margin> fight like a fellow soldier at the command of reason. There is, therefore, something in us that is usually provoked without reason, and once provoked, then calls reason to the same cause through the imagination. There is also that which begins from reason and ends in that which naturally burns with rage. Furthermore, the fuel for both anger and desire seems to sprout from the vegetative and generative nature itself. For this nature has so affected the body that it catches hold of things pleasant and troublesome; likewise, <margin>C</margin> it has infused bitter bile, and thus impressed a trace upon the affected soul. Because this trace is in such a state regarding troublesome things, it is irritated to anger; and since it is ill-affected from the beginning, it strives to deprave other things and make them, as it were, similar to itself. That this trace of the soul is a relative of the other trace in essence can be proven by this: those who seek bodily delights less and neglect the body are less provoked to anger and are less carried away by <margin>D</margin> irrational passion. It should not seem strange that trees do not have anger, although they have a vegetative nature, since they have neither blood nor bile. For where these are present, only a "heat" arises without sensation, like a certain offense. But when sensation arrives, an impulse now rises up to conquer what has offended. Truly, if the irrational part of the soul is divided into the power of desiring and the power of anger, and the former is vegetative while the power of anger is <margin>E</margin> its trace involving blood or bile (or both), the division will not be correctly made from opposite sides. This is because one of these is prior and the other is posterior. Perhaps, indeed, nothing prevents both from being posterior, and the division being of two things born from the same source. For it is a division of "appetites" in the sense that they are appetites, not of the essence from which such things came. That essence, according to itself, is not an appetite, but perhaps it is the "perfecter" of the appetite, specifically by <margin>F</margin> joining to itself the action proceeding from the appetite. Finally, it is not absurd to say the trace of the soul that falls into animosity is located in the precordia; for we should not think the soul is strictly here, but rather the source of such a kind of blood.

---

*In an animated body, there is not only the soul and the continuous life-giving act of the soul (just as light shines from a luminous source into its body), but there is also a certain vital trace, like heat existing under the light. I call this heat the natural spirit and the tool for movement, which can remain in the body for a short time after the soul's departure and produce a certain movement. No life-giving power perishes, but does this vital trace perish? Certainly, the natural heat ceases to be there shortly after, and the natural spirit is quickly dissolved. However, the vital and animal spirit can survive longer and follow the soul, held by the soul like a "curd" <note>Original: coagulo. A metaphor for the soul gathering its lower faculties together.</note>, intending to gather and vitally affect the "aerial body" <note>A Neoplatonic concept of a subtle body that the soul inhabits after leaving the physical one.</note> after death. But if you think there is something in this vital trace beyond heat and spirit—something that relates to the soul and its light not as heat, but as the splendor resulting from the soul's light—that indeed does not perish, but accompanies the light of the departing soul. He believes that light depends in no way on the illuminated thing, but only on the luminous source, and that it always follows it together with whatever splendor results. Does he touch upon the opinion that says the powers and, as it were, the "little flowers" of all colors are in the light?*

<sig>X</sig>
