### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

...neither to perish, but rather to lie hidden, and to appear again. Likewise, those lights which seem to be extinguished are not actually destroyed; instead, they retreat into the clear, luminous air and into its hidden depths. Finally, whatever belongs to the lower life within us follows our superior soul and does not perish. A <term>vital trace</term><note>Latin: vestigium vitale. This refers to a lingering imprint or "shadow" of the soul's presence that remains in the body for a short time after death.</note> is preserved in the body by the soul—either by the body's own soul or the <term>universal soul</term><note>The Anima Mundi, or World Soul, which Plotinus believes animates the entire cosmos.</note>—at least for a time after its own soul has deserted it.

<margin>Chapter XXIX.</margin>
<margin>A</margin> BUT if the animated body is not like an illuminated object, but rather like a body that has been heated, why then does the body possess nothing vital after the departure of the soul? Perhaps indeed it does, but only for a short time; for it quickly vanishes, just as heat is quickly extinguished in objects when they are removed from the fire. <margin>B</margin> Proof of this is found in the fact that even in the bodies of the dead, hair continues to grow and nails increase in length. Furthermore, many animals continue to move for a long time after they have been cut into pieces; this perhaps happens because some life still remains. Even if this lingering life accompanies the departing soul, that fact would not be enough to prove to us that the two are not distinct. For when the sun departs, not only does the continuous light—which depends directly upon the sun—depart with it, but the <margin>C</margin> splendor that depends on that light (which is reflected in nearby objects and is different from the light itself) also departs. But does it depart with the sun, or is it immediately extinguished?

This must be investigated both in the case of such light and in the life infused into the body, which we consider to be the body’s own. It is certainly clear that absolutely no light remains in objects that were once illuminated. But the question is: does it flow back to its source, or is it destroyed? <margin>D</margin> How could it simply cease to exist if it was previously "something"? And what, in general, was it? Someone might think that light is a property of the bodies from which it originates, much like what we call "color." Since these bodies themselves are perishable, when they are destroyed, their luminous color is also lost. Therefore, no one asks where the color of a fire goes once the fire is extinguished, just as no one asks where its shape goes. <margin>E</margin> Or is shape perhaps merely a certain "arrangement"—like the contracting or stretching of a hand—whereas color is not like that, but more like sweetness? For what prevents sweetness from surviving after a sweet body is destroyed, or a scent from surviving once a fragrant body is ruined? They might remain in some other body, yet remain unperceived because the participating bodies are not of a nature to convey those qualities to our senses. In the same way, what prevents light from remaining after its original source-bodies are destroyed? Could it be that no light is reflected to our eyes from elsewhere, as it used to be? <margin>F</margin> Unless, perhaps, someone says they see with their mind that even those things called "qualities" do not exist without their subjects. But if we admit that, we would also have to admit that qualities are incorruptible; that they are not generated within the physical makeup of subjects, nor do the <term>rational principles</term><note>Latin: rationes; Greek: logoi. In Neoplatonism, these are the formative "blueprints" or spiritual seeds that give shape and quality to matter.</note> within seeds produce colors. It would be like the varied feathers of birds we see: the colors would be already inherent but scattered, and then gathered into one. Perhaps the principles produce the colors, but additionally use the colors that already fill the air. For these qualities may exist in the air, though not in the same way they appear to us when they are generated in physical bodies. But let this particular doubt rest here for now. If, while the bodies remain, the light depends on them and is not separated, what prevents the light from moving along with the body as it moves?
<margin>G</margin>

<column-break/>

HOW then, if the body is like something heated rather than something illuminated, does it possess nothing vital after the soul leaves—or does it possess it for a short time? It fades away quickly, just as in the case of things that have been heated when they are moved away from the fire. Evidence for this is found in hair growing on dead bodies and nails increasing; also, animals that have been divided continue to move for a long time. This is perhaps because of something dwelling within; and even if it departs along with the soul, this is evidence that it is not a different thing. For when the sun departs, not only does the immediate light that is hung from it depart, but also that which was previously seen as an external reflection in nearby things—being different from the former—departs and is destroyed along with it. This sort of thing must be investigated regarding light, and also regarding the life in the body, which we indeed say is the body’s own. It is clear that nothing of the light is left in illuminated things; but the argument seeks to know whether it changes back into that which made it, or if it simply ceases to be. For how can it simply not be, since it is something incorporeal? But what was it at all? One might say it is the "color" (as it is called) of the bodies from which the light comes. But since the bodies were perishable, it is not there when they change; and no one asks where the color of the fire goes when it is destroyed, just as they don't ask about its shape. Either shape is a certain relation, like the contraction or extension of the hand, but color is not like that—rather, it is like sweetness. For what prevents sweetness from not having perished when the sweet body is destroyed, or the fragrance of the fragrant thing, and instead appearing in another body? They might not be perceptible because the bodies that received them are not such as to bring the qualities occurring in them back to the senses. In this way, the light of destroyed bodies might remain; or, due to the lack of resistance from all sides, does it not remain? Unless someone should say that one sees by convention, and that the so-called qualities are not in the underlying subjects. But if this is so, we shall make the qualities that come to be in the constitutions of bodies incorruptible; and not even the <term>formative principles</term><note>Greek: logoi. The internal reasons or blueprints that govern the development of living things.</note> in the seeds would produce the colors—as if one were to say, regarding the iridescent birds, that they merely collect already existing colors. Or perhaps they do produce them, but also use those colors already present in the air which is full of such things. For those things which come to be are in the air, just as they appear when they have been "cooked" in the bodies. But let this puzzle lie here; if the bodies remain, and if the light is joined to them and not cut off, what prevents the light from moving along with the body when it is moved...

<summary>Plotinus discusses whether life and qualities like light and color are inherent to the body or merely reflections of the soul, using the growth of hair and nails after death as evidence for a lingering "vital trace." He questions whether these qualities return to their source or vanish entirely when the physical body is destroyed.</summary>

### BOOK FOUR.

...then that which hangs most closely; and if anything depends on that which is near, although it is not seen when it departs, just as it does not appear when it approaches. But regarding the soul, it will be discussed elsewhere, whether following things always accompany the preceding ones, and whether they always follow in that same connection. Or do individual things perhaps exist in themselves, even if they are deserted by those that came before, and are they able to persist in themselves? Or rather, is no part of the soul divided at all, but instead all souls are one and many at the same time, and by what particular 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> reason? But what shall we say of that <term>trace of the soul</term><note>Latin: vestigio... animae; Greek: ἴχνος τῆς ψυχῆς. This refers to the "shadow" or "residue" of life that remains in a physical body after the higher soul has departed.</note>, which is now impressed upon the body as if it were its own? Perhaps if this very thing is the soul, it will follow the principle of the preceding soul, provided it is not at all separated from the soul's own logic. But if it is like the specific life of the body, the condition here will be the same as that which was doubted a little while ago regarding the image of light. For it must be considered whether life can exist without the soul: <margin>B</margin> unless perhaps that can happen insofar as a certain soul stands by, acting upon something else.

***

THUS FAR in the commentaries of Eustochius <note>Eustochius was a student of Plotinus who prepared an edition of his works separate from Porphyry's more famous Enneads.</note> ends the second book on the soul, and here begins the third. In the commentaries of Porphyry, however, the things that follow are joined to the seventh book.

<column-break/>

THUS FAR in the commentaries of Eustochius the second on the soul, and here begins the third: but in the commentaries of Porphyry the things which follow are joined to the seventh.

***

> The stars possess sight and hearing, but they do not require memory; moreover, they hear prayers. Just as someone who opportunely exposes his body to the light of the Sun is naturally warmed by it, so one who applies his mind and spirit through a vow to the influences of the higher powers reports a natural influx of benefits from those things which are present everywhere. Some ancients worshipped the stars besides the Sun, but many, especially the Platonists and that kind of philosopher, worshipped only the Sun among the heavenly bodies. Julian <note>The Emperor Julian, known as "the Apostate," who attempted to revive polytheism.</note> and Iamblichus composed an oration to the Sun. Plato called the Sun the visible son and image of the highest God. Socrates, saluting the rising sun, often experienced an <term>ecstasy</term><note>A state of being "outside oneself" or in a trance-like spiritual union.</note>. The Pythagoreans sang hymns with the lyre to the rising Sun. As for the worship of the Sun, let those men see to it: certainly God placed his tabernacle in the Sun <note>A reference to Psalm 19:4.</note>. Chapter XXX.

***

NOW since we have established that memory in the stars is superfluous, but we have granted them senses—not only sight, but also hearing—and furthermore we have conceded that they hear prayers directed to the Sun (and as some others do to other stars), we must now investigate. For people believe that they will obtain many things from the stars through prayers, and indeed so easily that the stars act as patrons not only for just duties, but often even for unjust ones. When I say that such doubts arise, we must consider them diligently at present. 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> For these matters contain within themselves the greatest and most famous doubts, especially among those who are deeply troubled that the gods are considered helpers and authors of wicked works—both of other crimes and even of love and <term>incontinent union</term><note>Latin: incontinentisque concubitus. Plotinus is addressing the common belief that planetary "gods" like Venus or Mars could be invoked to aid in illicit sexual affairs or adultery.</note>. Therefore, both for the sake of these things, and especially for the sake of their memory (about which we spoke at the beginning), it seems necessary to investigate. <margin>B</margin> For it is clear that if they indeed do what we pray for, and do not do it immediately, but in the future, and often after a long time, they must preserve human prayers in their memory. <margin>C</margin> But our previous reasoning did not grant this at all; rather, as far as benefits bestowed upon men were concerned, it seemed to be such as if they were said to be granted by Ceres and Vesta—that is, the Earth <note>Plotinus uses the Roman names Ceres (Demeter) and Vesta (Hestia) to symbolize the natural, non-conscious giving of the Earth.</note>—unless someone should say that benefits are conferred upon men from the earth alone. Therefore, we must attempt to demonstrate both: in what way we attribute the function of memory to them (insofar as it pertains to us, not as it seems to others who do not forbid giving memory to the stars), and what should be said about <margin>D</margin> those things which seem to be done wrongly by them. This is indeed the duty of philosophy.

<summary>This page discusses the residual "trace" of life in the body after death and begins an investigation into whether stars (as divine beings) possess memory and hearing. Plotinus explores the ethical dilemma of how stars could "hear" and "grant" prayers for both good and evil deeds if they do not possess human-like memory or morality.</summary>

# PLOTINUS' ENNEADS, BOOK IV.

<margin>A</margin> ...we must consider, specifically, if there is any way to resolve the doubts that arise among men against the celestial God <note>original: "coelestem Deũ"; Plotinus refers here to the divine nature of the stars and the heavens.</note>: likewise against the entire universe, toward which such accusations also tend, as if it were the cause of injustices. This is necessary if we are to give any credit to those who think that even the entire heaven can be swayed to one's will by human audacity and art, as if by certain magic spells. We must furthermore inquire about demons, in what <margin>B</margin> way they are said to provide such services—unless, perhaps, from the very resolution of the previous points, you also receive the solution to these.

*Actions are indeed either natural or artificial. Natural actions are either of the whole universe toward its parts, or of the parts toward the universe, or of the parts toward one another in turn. Artificial actions either end in a work constructed by art, such as statuary resulting in a statue, or they serve the work of nature, such as medicine, agriculture, or magic—with which oratory persuasion and the allurements of poetry and music have a certain similarity. The actions of the celestial bodies upon lower things occur not only through heat and other qualities similar to the elements, but through certain powers far different from known qualities. For the differences in our characters, talents, professions, and fortunes—whether they are caused or portended by the heavens—cannot be attributed to differences in celestial qualities similar to the elements. Nor do the celestial bodies act upon us individually by counsel and choice; otherwise, their minds would always be anxious, and they would be daily ministers of evil. Ch. XXXI.*

<margin>A</margin> IT IS WORTHWHILE to consider generally all actions and passions <note>In a philosophical sense, "passions" (passiones) refers to things acted upon or experienced, rather than just emotions.</note> that occur in the universe, whether they are perfected by nature or by art. We should affirm that those which occur by nature happen partly from the whole itself toward its parts, partly from the parts toward the whole, and finally, partly from the parts themselves toward other parts. Furthermore, those things performed by art are done in two primary ways: for either art gives the beginning to a work and thus also imposes an artistic end upon the work, or it uses natural forces in addition to complete the actions <margin>B</margin> and passions of natural works. Truly, I call the "actions of the universe" those by which the whole circuit of the world acts upon itself or upon its parts. For while it revolves, it both disposes itself in a certain fixed condition and composes its parts with itself—the parts, I say, which are both in the circuit itself and those which are distributed from there onto the earth. Likewise, the actions and passions of the parts toward other parts are manifest to almost everyone: namely, those of the Sun toward other things regarding relationships and effects, and <margin>C</margin> also upon earthly things. Again, those things which are acted upon in the other elements, both by the Sun itself and by the others; moreover, the mutual actions and passions of those things on the earth and in the other elements, which it seems must be considered individually. Next, the arts that construct buildings and fabricate other handiwork end in such a result. Medicine, however, and agriculture and others of that same kind are ministers of nature; they suggest <margin>D</margin> assistance to the works of nature so that they may be carried out naturally. It is also useful to consider oratory and music, and whatever charms the soul with a certain pleasure; these differ among themselves primarily in that they lead either to the better or to the worse. Among these, we must inquire into how many arts there are and what power they have, and if possible, we must treat in all of them that which will be conducive to our present purpose, seeking the causes in these as far as possible. It is established beyond doubt that the circuit of the world <margin>E</margin> acts, first by disposing itself in different ways, and then also upon the things it contains within itself, and without controversy governing all earthly things—not only the constitutions of bodies, but also the dispositions of souls, and each individual thing...

<column-break/>

<note>This right-hand column contains the original Greek text corresponding to the Latin translation provided on the left.</note>

To investigate is another defense: as many things as pertain to the gods in heaven and indeed concerning the whole universe, so that this kind of cause reaches even to this. If those are to be believed who say that they even influence the entire heaven itself by sorceries <note>Greek: γοητείαις (goeteiais); magic or witchcraft.</note>, through the daring and art of mortals. And the discourse will also seek concerning demons, how they are said to perform such services—unless, through the preceding points, the solution for these things also might be grasped.

TAKING A GENERAL VIEW, then, we must grasp all the actings and the undergoings as many as happen in the whole world, both those called "by nature" and those that happen "by art." And of those by nature, we must say some happen from the whole to the parts, and from the parts to the whole, or from parts to parts. Those happening by art either end in the artful objects themselves just as they began, or they use natural powers for the movements and experiences of natural works. I speak of those in the whole, because the entire revolution acts upon itself and upon its parts. Moving in itself, it disposes itself in some way, as well as its parts: both the parts in the revolution itself, and as many as it gives to those upon the earth. The experiences of parts toward parts are somehow clear to everyone: the relations and actings of the sun toward the other things, and toward those upon the earth; and the things in the other elements by it and by the others, and those on the earth. And of those in the others, concerning which each must be examined. The arts, on the one hand, such as building and other crafts, end in this. But medicine and agriculture and such like are subservient, and bring aid to the things of nature so that they may be according to nature. But rhetoric and music and every <term>soul-leading</term> <note>Greek: ψυχαγωγίαν (psychagogian); the art of leading or persuading souls through enchantment or speech.</note> act by altering, leading either toward the better or toward the worse. Among these we must seek how many arts there are and what power they have; and if indeed it is possible, we must busy ourselves in all these things with what is useful for our present need, and the "why" as far as possible. That the revolution acts is certain, being itself first disposed in various ways, and the things within it—unquestionably earthly things—and not only the bodies, but also the dispositions of the soul and each of the parts...

<meta>catchword: cale-</meta>

<summary>Plotinus explores the interconnectedness of the cosmos, distinguishing between natural actions and artificial interventions like medicine, rhetoric, and magic. He argues that the celestial bodies influence both physical health and the disposition of the human soul through universal harmony rather than personal deliberation.</summary>
<keywords>celestial influence, natural vs artificial, magic, rhetoric, psychagogia, universal harmony, astrology, Plotinus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter 31 of Plotinus’s fourth Ennead, Book 4. Having previously addressed the soul’s relationship to the universe and the possibility of magic, Plotinus now investigates the specific mechanism by which celestial bodies (the stars and planets) influence earthly life, arguing against both simple physical causation and divine meddling in human vice.</meta>

# FOURTH BOOK.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...of the celestial things upon the earthly and all subsequent things. Whether these lower things in turn act upon the superior ones, we shall investigate in what follows. But for the present, allowing those things to remain as they appear to be—since they are approved by all or most—we must strive to bring forward only what relies on reason, tracing the manner of their effect from the beginning. For we must not say that only hot and cold, and other such things called the "primary qualities of the elements," or those resulting from their mixture, are able to act. <margin>B</margin> Nor, again, should it be thought that the sun does everything through heat, and some other celestial body performs all things through cold. For what could be cold in the heaven and in an igneous body <note>original: "igneo corpore"; Plotinus refers to the ancient view that the heavens are composed of fire or a radiant "aether."</note>, where there is no moisture in the fire? Added to this is the fact that, by this reasoning, we can by no means grasp the difference in celestial natures and actions. Now, many things happen because of these [celestial bodies] which cannot be referred to any such physical quality as a cause. If someone should attribute differences in character to these powers <margin>C</margin> based on certain constitutions of the bodies—such as an excess of cold or heat—how could he also reduce envies, rivalries, and deceits to these same things? Furthermore, even if these physical qualities were effective, how could they relate to fortunes, whether worse or better, riches, poverty, the nobility of ancestors, one's own generosity, or found treasures? For anyone can enumerate countless things which are far removed from the effectiveness of a physical <margin>D</margin> quality coming from the elements into the bodies and souls of living beings. Yet, individual things that happen to individual lower beings must not be attributed to the counsel and choice of the stars, nor to the judgment or consultations of the universe. For it is a wicked thing to say <note>original: "Nefas enim dictu est"</note> that the gods above plot against men, so that some become thieves, others kidnap free men into slavery, dig through walls as burglars, or commit sacrilege; or that others again are illiberal and cowardly, and <margin>E</margin> effeminate in their actions and passions, or most devoted to shameful habits. For to commit and plot such things is not only beneath the gods, but not even the work of moderately honest men. Perhaps, indeed, it is not even in the nature of anyone to perpetrate such things, from which no benefit would meanwhile come to them.

<column-break/>

For to commit and plot such things is not only beneath the gods, but not even the work of moderately honest men. Perhaps, indeed, it is not even in the nature of anyone to perpetrate such things, from which no benefit would meanwhile come to them.

> *The heavens act upon all these lower things, not by some choice that selects to act in such or such a way; nor only through physical qualities—namely by heating, moistening, thinning, or the opposite—but through certain natural powers of the vegetative soul <note>The "vegetative soul" or anima vegetalis refers to the most basic level of life force responsible for growth and nutrition.</note>, similar to certain powers halfway between deliberate counsel and physical qualities, just as our soul daily restores the humors and limbs of the body, and their shapes and qualities. Since the world is one living being <note>original: "vnum animal"; the concept of the Anima Mundi or World Soul.</note>, all physical things are parts of the world in two ways: first, because individual bodies are certain portions of the universal body; second, because in any body there is both the soul of the world itself and a certain specific power and effectiveness of this soul distributed to that body. Therefore, insofar as individual physical things are members of the world as a living being, they easily experience influence both from the whole and from one another; for even those things which seem distant from each other in space are close, due to the miraculous communion of a single nature.*

### Chapter XXXII.

<margin>A</margin> Since, therefore, we attribute those things which come from heaven into us and other animals—and whatever earthly things exist—neither to physical causes nor to deliberations, what probable cause remains for us? In the first place, this universe must be considered to be a single living being <term>animal: in this context, "animal" means a living, ensouled entity (from the Latin "anima")</term> containing all living beings within itself, having one soul diffusing itself through each of its parts, insofar as any part is a part of it; and every [thing] is a part of it...

<summary>Plotinus argues that celestial influence on Earth cannot be explained by simple heat and cold or by the gods making deliberate choices to cause human vice; instead, it results from the interconnectedness of the "World Soul." He defines the universe as a single living organism where all parts are linked by a shared life force.</summary>

->### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.<-

<page-num>426</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> ...is contained in the order of sensible things: and certainly, as far as the body is concerned, it is entirely a part; and in so far as it participates in the world soul, it is for that reason considered a part of the world. Now, truly, those things which participate only in this [world] soul are parts in every respect; but those which possess another soul in addition <note>Referring to the individual rational soul of humans, which Plotinus argues is distinct from the general soul of the material universe.</note> do not, for this very reason, exist entirely as parts. Nevertheless, they are still affected by other things, in so far as they possess something of the universe, and they are affected accordingly in harmony with those things they possess. Truly, this <margin>B</margin> universe, because it is one, and a single living being <note>original: "vnum animal." Plotinus follows the Platonic tradition of viewing the entire cosmos as a singular, living organism.</note>, shares a common feeling <term>sympathy|The Stoic and Neoplatonic concept that all parts of the universe are interconnected and vibrate in harmony with one another.</term> with itself throughout: and that which seems to be remote within it is also near. This is just as in any single living creature, where the nails, horns, fingers, and any other parts are not positioned next to each other, but are separated by some distance in between; yet when one part is affected, another part that is not nearby feels nothing [directly]. For where things that are similar to one another are not connected directly, but are separated by other things in between, they nevertheless share a common feeling through that very similarity; and it is necessary that the effect of a thing not adjacent reaches even to that which is placed far off. But in this universe, which is both a living being and gathers everything into one, nothing is so remote in location that it is not considered "near" because of the very nature of the single organism, which shares a common feeling with itself everywhere. Therefore, that which has a similarity toward the thing acting upon it receives an experience <margin>D</margin> that is not foreign; but if the agent is dissimilar, it receives a foreign and troublesome experience. Nor, indeed, should it be wondered at that in a single living being, a harmful action might pass from one part to another, since even in ourselves and our own actions, one part is harmed by another; for instance, bile and anger, as it seems, press upon and sting something else. So, truly, in the universe there is something similar in proportion to spiritedness and bile, and other things similar to other parts. Furthermore, even among plants, some are hindrances to others, even to the point of destroying them. But this world is not only a single living being, but is also seen as many. For this reason, in so far as each thing is one with the universe, it is preserved by this very fact; but in so far as many things collide with one another, it is harmed here and there by what is different. In this way, one thing certainly harms another for its own use, and uses another for nourishment, since they are at once related and yet different. Indeed, every thing naturally looks out for itself: it takes into itself as much as is compatible with the other, and destroys as much as is foreign out of love for itself. Furthermore, while each thing performs its own work, it meanwhile <margin>F</margin> benefits that which is able to opportunely admit some of its works into itself. But that which cannot sustain the power of the work is either destroyed or affected by harm; just as things suddenly dry up when fire passes by, or as smaller animals are snatched away or trampled by the path of larger ones. Truly, the generation and corruption of all these things, and their change for better or worse, completes the life of that one world-animal, which remains unhindered and in its natural state. For it was not possible for individual things to exist as if they were alone, or as if they were ends in themselves, looking only to themselves since they are parts; rather, they had to look toward that [the whole] as an end, of which they are parts. Likewise, since they had to be different, it is right that individuals in one <margin>G</margin> life...

<column-break/>

...is, in the whole sensible world, partly the body as it is affected, and in so far as it shares in the soul of the whole, it has its nature from there. But those things that participate in only a small part of this soul are parts from that source. However, as many things as also come from another soul <note>original: "ἄλλης" (allēs). Plotinus distinguishes between the lower soul that animates the body and the higher, individual rational soul.</note> are not parts in that respect, because that soul is itself. But they are affected nonetheless by other things, in so far as they have something [of the whole], and according to what they have. For the whole is indeed <margin>* and life</margin> in sympathy with itself. And because it is a living being, the distant is near, just as in the case of individual things—a nail, a horn, or a finger, or something else not placed in sequence: but through the intervening space, when one part is affected, that which is not near does not [necessarily] suffer. For either similar things lie in sequence, or they are separated by other things in between, yet by their similarity they share a common feeling, so that what is done by the non-adjacent part must necessarily arrive at the distant one. And since they are living beings, and in the whole, even in a distant place so as not to be near, they are in sympathy by the life of the one through nature. That which has a similarity toward the acting thing, therefore, has an experience that is not foreign; but if it is dissimilar to the acting thing, the experience is foreign. And it is not by nature that the sufferer holds it. It is not to be wondered at that harmful things pass from one to another in one living being, since even in our own activities, one part might harm another part, as bile and anger, it seems, press and sting another part. And indeed in the universe there is something analogous to anger and bile, and one thing to another: even in plants, one thing is a hindrance to another, so that they even wither away. And this [world] is not only one living being, but is seen as many. So, in so far as each is one, it is saved by the whole: but in so far as they are many coming together against one another, it has harmed in many ways by the difference. And toward its own need, one thing has harmed another, or even made it food, being at once related and different. And each thing striving for itself according to nature, takes into itself as much as is its own in the other: and as much as becomes foreign, it vanishes out of favor to itself. It is the work of each to do its own; that which is pursued to enjoy some of its own works, it has benefited; but that which is impossible to endure the impulse of the work, it either destroys or harms: just as things that might be scorched when fire passes by, or smaller animals might be swept away by the run of larger ones, or even trampled. But of all these things, the generation and corruption, and the change toward the worse or better, completes the life of that one living being, which is unhindered and according to nature. Since it was not possible for each thing to be as if they were the only things, nor for the end to be toward themselves, and to look [only at themselves], being parts, but toward that of which they are also different parts. Not all their things are in one life...

He justifies the existence of harm and conflict between individual parts as natural results of their diversity within the unified life of the whole.</summary>

Having established that the universe is a single living organism (the "macrocosm") bound by sympathy, Plotinus now explores how the motions of the stars and the "World Soul" create a harmonious, choreographed reality, much like a complex dance.</meta>

### BOOK FOUR. ###

<page-num>437</page-num>

<note>original Greek: "ζωῆ ὄντα ἀεὶ ἔχειν..."</note> From life apprehended, they ought not to have possessed the same things entirely and specifically among themselves perpetually; nor could it happen that anything remained thoroughly in the same way forever, provided that the universe was meant to endure by having its stability within motion.

---

*The whole world is a single living being <note>original: "animal vnum"</note> dancing with musical reason, and by dancing, consequently varying all things together with itself. The Soul of the World possesses within its intelligence, thought, imagination, and nature all the revolutions of the world, described as if present and future according to their musical proportions. Likewise, it has designated all events that either necessarily accompany the revolutions in the heavens or follow them in any way beneath the heavens. Toward such a musical designation, as if toward a song and a harmony of sounds, the revolutions in the world follow through affection like the gestures of one dancing with art. The dancer himself looks primarily at the music inherent within him; then, through this, at the revolutions of the worldly members; thirdly, through these, he foresees in a way what follows from them, or at least what is signified by them. A wise man, like a musician, can also foresee what kind of events follow the revolutions of the world everywhere, just as one sees what gestures of the limbs follow specific parts of a sound—except where either the matter is unsuitable and does not entirely yield to the higher powers, or where a less weak part suffers beyond measure. Similarly, human will can choose not to follow the course of heaven, and conversely, human weakness can suffer from it beyond measure. Finally, just as in a choral dance <note>original: "chorea"</note> certain passions of the limbs or other things occur beyond the artistic gestures, so too do similar things occur from the sacred dance <note>original: "tripudio"</note> of the world. Chapter XXXIII.*

<note>original Greek: "ΤΗΣ δὴ φορᾶς..."</note> Since the movement does not occur at random, but is carried out with reason as a living being, it was necessary for there to be a certain harmony between the agent and the patient, and a certain order arranging them in themselves and toward each other. Thus, according to any disposition of the movement, another and different disposition must again occur for those subject to this movement, as if they were performing a single dance in a widely varied choral performance. In our own dances, who can explain—since they are manifest—the things that happen externally in harmony with the dance in each individual motion, with those things that contribute to the chorus changing in different ways: namely the flutes, the songs, and other connected things? But no one can similarly grasp and explain the parts of the one who performs the dance according to every necessary figure, while the body is guided and bent by a certain reason in following the movement. In this, one part is pressed and held back, another is relaxed, one labors, while another receives a certain rest in a different configuration. Meanwhile, the intention of the dancer looks toward something else, while the rest of the parts suffer as a consequence of the dance, ministering to the dancing, and together they perfectly complete the whole. Thus, one skilled in dancing will be able to assign how, in such a configuration, this limb of the body is raised higher, while that one is contracted, that one is hidden, and another meanwhile is pressed to the ground, while the dancer himself does not deliberate that this be done in any other way, but maintains this necessary disposition in the dance of the whole body itself, for this part performing the chorus. By the same reasoning, it must be thought that the heavenly bodies do whatever they do, and signify most things; indeed, that the whole world lives out its entire life, moving its vast parts within itself and always transforming them. The dispositions of the parts, both toward each other and toward the whole, and their different positions, provide the other things following them, as if a single living being were moved. Thus they hold themselves according to such dispositions, positions, and figures: in such a way according to such things, as if they are not the authors of the things being figured, but the "Figurator" <note>The World Soul or the organizing principle of the cosmos.</note>; nor again does the Figurator himself, doing one thing, produce another. For he does not act upon something else, but it must be considered that he himself is all those things which come to be.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Since the revolution of the world has nothing fortuitous in itself, but is performed with a certain reason looking toward a living being, it was necessary for there to be a certain concord of the agent to the patient, and a certain order arranging things within themselves and toward one another: so that according to any state of the revolution, a different disposition must again occur for those things subject to this revolution, as if they were performing a single dance <note>original: "tripudium"</note> in a greatly varied choral procession <note>original: "chorea"</note>. In our own dances, anyone can explain <margin>B</margin> those manifest things which happen externally in agreement with the dance, as the things that lead the chorus—namely the flutes and songs and other joined elements—change differently in each specific motion. But not everyone can similarly grasp and declare the parts of the one who performs the dance according to every necessary figure, while the body is followed and bent by a certain reason in the pursuit: in which indeed one part is pressed and restrained, another relaxed, another indeed <margin>C</margin> labors, and another receives a certain breathing-space in a different configuration. The purpose of the dancer meanwhile looks at something else, while the remaining parts suffer as a consequence of the dance, and serve the dancing, and together they perfectly complete the whole. Therefore, one skilled in dancing will be able to assign how, in such a configuration, that limb of the body is raised higher, that one is contracted, that one is hidden, while another meanwhile is pressed to the ground, while the dancer himself does not <margin>D</margin> deliberate that this be done otherwise, but in the dance of the whole body itself he holds this necessary disposition for this part performing the chorus. By the same reasoning, it must be thought that the celestial beings do whatever they do, and signify many things: indeed, that the whole world lives its entire life, moving vast parts within itself, and always transfiguring them. The dispositions of the parts, both toward each other and toward the whole, and their different positions, offer the other things consequent to them, as if <margin>E</margin> a single animal were moved, holding themselves according to such dispositions and positions and figures: thus indeed according to such things, as if they are not the authors of the things that are shaped, but the Shaper; nor again does the Shaper himself, doing one thing, do another. For he does not act upon another, but it must be thought that he himself is all those things which are done.

He argues that the cosmos acts as a single living organism where every part's motion, while appearing independent, is actually a necessary component of a grand, rational "musical" design.</summary>

<header>PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.</header>

<margin>A</margin>In that realm there are the figures; here, however, are the consequences of the figures, like necessary experiences affecting a living being moved in such a way. And again, concerning a being so composed and consisting by nature, it both acts and suffers according to the necessary conditions within itself.

Our body, as a part of the world, follows the fated circuit of the universe. The soul, although it complies with the body, is nonetheless able through greatness of spirit to think little of the body’s passions, and to avoid or lighten them through art. In the various spheres and parts of the world, and in the stars, there are naturally various powers <note>original: "virtutes". In this context, these are "virtues" or inherent "powers" of celestial bodies</note>. There are also fixed powers in the different configurations <note>original: "figuris". In astrology, these are the 'aspects' or geometric relationships between stars</note> formed by the stars in relation to each other. Furthermore, different powers arise in succession from the changing figures that occur between the stars due to their perpetual variety of motion. Following these powers of both nature and figure, those things that happen under the Moon <note>The "sublunary" realm: the Earth and its atmosphere, where things are subject to change and decay</note> occur partly by necessity, like those who are caught up by the hand of a dancer, and partly as a more free harmony, like those who move, sing, and dance willingly to a melody and a dance. Indeed, the celestial figures signify these lower things, but their natures, together with the figures, bring them about according to the disposition of the matter. Yet figures signify many things that are produced not from the heavens, but from elsewhere. 

### Chapter XXXIV. ###

<margin>A</margin>We must further judge that when we allow only that part of ourselves which is a piece of the universal body to be influenced by the universe, and do not consider our entire being to belong to it, we then suffer only moderately from it. This is like the most prudent servants: by yielding some things to their masters while wishing to remain their own masters in others, they receive more moderate commands for this very reason, as they are neither mere slaves nor entirely independent. <margin>B</margin>The difference in configurations <note>The "shapes" or geometric patterns stars make in the sky</note> necessarily occurred as it does now because the stars run, and they do not run at equal speeds. Therefore, since they move with reason <note>original: "ratione" / "λόγῳ"</note> and result in the different states of a living being, and since the events among us sympathize with them, it is reasonable to ask whether we should assert that these events follow them in harmony, or whether the figures themselves have the power to produce effects; and whether it is the figures simply, or rather the figures *of these specific things*. For the same <margin>C</margin>configuration does not bring about the same meaning or effect when applied to different things, since each thing seems to have a different nature in its own right. Perhaps it will be correctly said that the configuration of *these* things produces *these* results, and that the configuration of *others*—even if it is the same figure—produces *something else*. But if this is so, we will no longer give authority to the figures, but rather to the things <margin>D</margin>themselves that are configured, or to both together—namely, to the same natures having acquired a different state. We will even grant different things to the same nature solely because of a difference in location. But what shall we grant? Affects or significations? Perhaps both specifically belong to the combination—that is, to the configuration of these things—resulting in both effects and significations in many cases, but elsewhere in significations alone. This reasoning, therefore, grants powers to the figures and powers to the things configured. For in those who dance and play in a troupe, both the hands and the other members have a certain power, and the changing <margin>E</margin>figures of the dance also have power. In the third place are the consequences: both the parts of those taking part in the dance, and the things from which they are made or which come from them—such as things rubbed together by touch, and the nerves and veins reacting in sympathy.

*The Soul of the World, having contemplated this entire universe from eternity in the series of Ideas, chose the entire course of the world once and for all with a single common choice, approving that it should be so. Meanwhile, its "vegetative nature"—which is its subordinate image—carries out the entire course of the world without choice. Likewise, the individual souls of the spheres and stars relate to God and the world in a similar way: they agree so thoroughly with the Soul of the World in both will and nature that all their actions in the world can rightly be called the action of the World Soul. Therefore, all bodily things are parts of the world's living being...*

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin>There the figures, here the consequences to the figures; necessary affections, as if the living being moved in such a way must be; and again concerning what is composed and standing together by nature, both suffering and acting upon itself by necessity.

When we give over a part of ourselves to suffering—only as much as belongs to that body of ours—without thinking the whole belongs to it, we suffer moderately from it. Just as wise servants yield something to their masters but remain their own in other things, they obtain more moderate orders from the master because they are not slaves, nor entirely another's. <margin>Β</margin> The difference in the configurations of those things that run, since they are not of equal speed, had to happen as it does now. Since they are moved by reason and result in different relations and a living being, and since things here among us sympathize with what happens there, it is reasonable to seek which follows which. We must say these things harmonize with those, or that the figures have the powers of the things done. Or the figures simply, <margin>C</margin> or the figures of these things. For the same configuration on one thing, and again on others, does not work the same sign or effect. Since each thing even by itself seems to have a different nature, or it is correct to say the configuration of these things is this and such a disposition, while that of others—being the same in configuration—is another. <margin>D</margin> But if this is so, we will no longer give power to the figures, but to the things configured, or to both: to those things that have taken on a different relation, but also to the same thing differently because of a different place. But are these effects or signs? Or both to the combination—to the configuration of these things? Both effects and signs in many cases; elsewhere, signs alone. The argument, then, gives powers to the figures <margin>E</margin> and powers to the things configured. For in a dancer, each hand and the other members have a certain power, and the figures of the dance also have much power. Third are the consequences: the parts of those taken into the dance, and the things from which they arise—for example, the parts of the hand pressed together, and the nerves and veins reacting in sympathy.

He argues that while our bodies are subject to these cosmic "scripts," our souls can maintain a degree of independence through wisdom and virtue.</summary>

# BOOK FOUR.

...but natural actions are the movements of this living being: all the revolutions of the world are its gestures and, as it were, its speeches. Nothing in it, or from it, happens by chance; for everything is referred to the seminal reasons <note>original: "seminales rationes"—the formative, "seed-like" principles that govern the development of natural things</note> implanted in it, or even higher to the exemplary <note>original: "exemplares"—the ideal forms in the divine mind</note> ones. Therefore, individual things either proceed in order or are immediately brought back into order. The Sun, the heart of the world, possesses and brings much more natural life than the other parts of the world. In it, some have placed the soul of the world itself, diffused through its rays everywhere. All the powers of natural things are first in the seminal reasons of the common nature. From here they are soon transferred into the spheres of the world and their figures, which are as revolving as they are firm. From here they move into the species of natural things, in which then lie hidden wonderful powers above the elements, and from the figures of heaven themselves into lower figures, powers also wonderfully manifest. Even the figures of our own bodies have certain specific powers of attracting or deterring, from which it appears that a specific power can exist in shapes no less than in colors. Chapter XXXV.

<insert>A</insert> HOW then are these powers in them? For it must be said again more clearly what a triangle <note>In astrology, a "trine" or triangular aspect between stars is considered harmonious</note> is, and why one triangle differs from another, or what it does to another, and according to what it works, and for what purpose? Since we have attributed these actions neither to their bodies nor to their choices <note>original: "προαιρέσεσιν" (proairesesin)—deliberate moral choices</note>, not to their bodies because the things that happen are not merely bodily effects, <insert>B</insert> nor to their choices, because it would be absurd for a god to do shameful things by choice. We must remember what we proposed: that the world is one living being <note>original: "ζῶον εὐ" (zoon hen)—the "One Animal" or "Universal Living Being"</note>, and being such, it is necessarily in sympathy with itself. <insert>C</insert> And indeed, the progression of its life is according to reason, entirely in harmony with itself. Nothing is random in this life, but there is one harmony and order. If its movements are according to reason, and each thing according to number, and the parts of the living being are like a choir, then both must be confessed: that the activity belongs to the whole, and the shapes formed within it, and the parts being shaped, and the things that follow them, all belong to it. <insert>D</insert> In this way, the whole lives in this manner, and its powers contribute to this, just as <margin>* traces</margin> those who possess *traces were made by the one who creates according to reason. The shapes are like a language, or the extensions of life, and the rhythm and habits of life. These are the rational principles, while the distinct and shaped parts are something else. There are other powers of the living being apart from choice, which act as parts of the living being. For the function of choice is outside them, or rather it contributes to this nature. For there is one choice of the one living being, but its other powers directed toward itself are many. However many choices there are in it, they tend toward the same point as the one choice of the whole. <insert>E</insert> For the desire of one part is for another. One part wishes to take from another because it is in need; even a kind of natural anger arises against another when it is harmed. Then there is growth from another, and generation into another of the parts. But the whole, even in these things, does not do them for these reasons, but seeks the Good itself; or rather, it looks toward it. This, then, is what the right choice seeks, which is above the passions, and it conspires with this same goal. For even among those who serve others, many of their works look toward the commands given by the master. <insert>F</insert> But the appetite for the good looks toward the same thing as the master himself. If, therefore, the Sun and the other stars do anything to things here, one must think that the Sun himself is looking upward; for on this one account...

<column-break/>

<insert>A</insert> IN what way then do these powers behave? For it must be explained more clearly again, what difference a triangle compared to a triangle has, or what this one has or does toward that one, and according to what it does this, and how far, since we have attributed actions neither to the bodies nor to the counsels <note>original: "consilijs"—intentions or plans</note> of the heavenly beings. Not to their bodies, because it appeared that what happens are not merely bodily effects; not to their counsels, because it would be a sin to say the gods do shameful things by design. <insert>B</insert> To this question, we must remember that we previously proposed that the world is one living being, and since it is such, it must necessarily be in sympathy with itself. Likewise, its life's course is driven according to a reason that is entirely consistent with itself. Again, in that life there is nothing fortuitous, but one concord and order. Furthermore, all configurations happen according to reason, and each according to certain numbers. The parts of the worldly animal are, without a doubt, like those performing a choral dance <insert>C</insert>—certain acts of the world itself—both the figures that are made in it and its figured parts, as well as the things that follow them. And so, in this way, the universe lives and contributes its powers to this very end, just as they were made to be by the one who effects all things through rational principles. <insert>D</insert> It must be considered, moreover, that the figures are like rational principles or forms, or the intervals of the animal itself, its rhythmic modes, and the habits and gestures of the animal perfected by reason. Those things which are distant and shaped are other members. Furthermore, there are other powers of the living being separate from choice, acting as parts of the living being itself. For the task of choice is added there as if from the outside, and does not lead to the nature of this living being. For there is one institution of choice for the one animal, but its other powers toward itself are many. <insert>E</insert> However many choices are in it, they tend to the same place where the one of the whole tends. For the appetite in those things which are in it is of some toward others. For they strive to receive something from others—that is, one part wanting another because it is in need. Even a certain natural anger rises against another when something is hurt. Then, indeed, growth happens from another, and generation from one part into another. But the whole itself, even in these matters, acts in this way, but it seeks the Good itself, or rather, it looks up to it. <insert>F</insert> This, therefore, is also what the right option—which precedes the passions—longs for, and it conspires with this very thing. For even in those who serve others, many works respect the master’s commands; but the appetite for the good looks in the same way as the master himself looks. If, therefore, the Sun and the other stars act upon these things, it must be thought that the Sun himself looks toward the things above; for in this one case, for the sake of example, it is said of the others...

# PLOTINUS: ENNEAD IV.

...think of it this way. Meanwhile, earthly things truly grow warm under the influence of the heavens on this 
<margin>A</margin>
condition: if anything follows by a certain transmission of the soul, as far as it is possible. For the <term>natural soul</term> <note>original: "anima naturalis"—the lower aspect of the soul responsible for physical growth and instinct</note> is abundant there. Similarly, the rest of the celestial bodies act upon these things, as if by shining their power upon them, offering it without conscious choice. All things, being made as a single entity shaped in this way, exhibit one disposition after another, to the point that the very figures themselves possess power. For according to how a thing is disposed in one way or another, it acts differently or is acted upon differently; and we must believe that something is brought about through these very shapes. For 
<margin>B</margin>
one thing occurs for these people, and another for those; since we may observe even in our own affairs that figures possess powers in themselves. Why is it that some figures are terrifying to those who see them, even when those who are frightened have suffered nothing from them before, while other figures do not terrify at all? Likewise, these figures terrify some people, while those figures terrify others. Perhaps it is because such figures act upon one who is predisposed to be affected, while others act upon another, being unable to act upon that which is not naturally exposed to this passion. Furthermore, a sight shaped in one way draws the gaze to itself, while shaped in another way, it does not draw the same gaze. And indeed, if someone should say that it is beauty that provokes this, we shall object: why does this particular beauty allure this man, while that beauty allures another, unless the difference of figures possesses a power within itself? By what reason shall we admit that colors have power and produce effects, yet not confess that figures do the same? For it is altogether absurd to say that something is established in the order of 
<margin>D</margin>
things, yet possesses no capability; for being itself is such that it naturally acts upon something or is acted upon. And certainly, to some things we must attribute acting alone, but to others both. There are also powers in subjects beyond their figures; in lower things, there are many powers which neither heat nor cold provides. Instead, these are substances endowed with differing qualities, shaped by <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>original: "rationibus"—the formative principles that guide natural development</note> in their species, and already participating in the power of nature itself—such as the natures of stones and the effects of herbs, which demonstrate many wonders to us.

*Just as our vegetative life imparts itself to individual members, though differently to each, and inserts wonderful powers into different joints; so, much more excellently, the one <term>World Soul</term> <note>original: "vna mundi anima"—the vital spirit connecting all parts of the universe</note> animates the various parts of the world. Being herself full of innumerable and wondrous virtues, as if pregnant and swelling, she overflows into the whole: filling individual parts, but especially the higher members of the world, with marvelous powers everywhere. Elemental forces cannot emulate these in any way, nor can we easily describe them. Such powers are like the specific offspring of the World Soul diffused through the members of the universal body, which the prayers of suppliants and the works of magicians can sometimes reconcile to themselves and, as it were, graft into place through a certain application.*

->Chapter XXXVI.<-

<margin>A</margin>
TRULY, this whole universe is filled with the greatest variety: all formative principles are within it, as are innumerable and varied powers. Just as they say of man, that the eye contains one power within itself, while the bones contain another, and different parts contain different things. For the bone of the hand has this power, but the bone in the foot possesses a different one, and no part at all is entirely destitute of power, although every part does not have the same one—though this is hidden from us unless someone has perhaps investigated such things diligently. Thus certainly, and 
<margin>B</margin>
much more so, is the case in the world; indeed, these things of ours are <term>vestiges</term> <note>original: "vestigia"—shadowy traces or echoes of higher realities</note> of those. It is therefore consistent that the inexplicable exists in the world and...

<column-break/>

...must be assumed. For they are influenced by them, just as heating on earth is caused by something, so it is with the gift of the soul, as much as is in it, since there is much <term>natural soul</term>. And another thing likewise, such as shining forth, gives power from itself without choice. And things that are thus shaped become such as to give one disposition after another, so that the shapes also have powers. 
<margin>B</margin>
For to be this way or that is one thing, and to be another way is another; and through these shaped things, something comes to be. For as this thing is one way, and another is different for different people, since even the shapes themselves are powers, one might see this again in things here. For why are some shapes fearful to those who see them, though the frightened have never suffered anything, while others seen are not in fear? Or why do these shapes affect some, and those affect others? Is it because the shapes work upon a certain type of person, but upon another they do not, or are they unable to act upon that which is not 
<margin>C</margin>
naturally disposed to it? Thus, one thing delights and moves the sight, while another does not, or does not move the same person. For if someone should say beauty is the mover, why did this beauty move one person and that move another, unless the difference in shape possessed the power? For why shall we say that colors have power and act, but we shall not say the shapes do? Since it is entirely absurd for something to be among existing things, yet not have the power to do or 
<margin>D</margin>
suffer. And to some things belong the power to act, and to others, both. And in the underlying subjects there are powers even apart from the shapes; and in the things among us there are many which neither heat nor cold provides, but which come to be with different qualities, and are given form by formative principles, and partake in the power of nature, such as the natures of stones and the activities of herbs, which provide many wonders.

->Chapter XXXVI.<-

For the whole is <term>most variegated</term> <note>original: "ΠΟΙΚΙΛΩΤΑΤΟΝ"—extremely diverse or multi-colored in its complexity</note>, and all formative principles are in it, and powers infinite and varied. # BOOK FOUR.

<margin>A</margin> He also described a wondrous variety of powers, especially regarding celestial natures and their progressions. For it was not fitting for the universe to be constructed like an inanimate building—even if it were a vast and complex one—made from a certain number of stones or woods or any other materials one might choose to arrange for the ornament of the world. Rather, the universe itself is everywhere wakeful and everywhere living, although it lives in different ways in different places. Nothing can exist that is not also contained within it.
<margin>B</margin> Therefore, the following doubt is resolved: how can there be anything inanimate within a being that is entirely animated? Current reasoning dictates that one thing lives in one way, and another in another, within the whole. We, however, tend to say that something is not "living" if we do not see it moving perceptibly on its own. Yet, even such things possess a hidden life. That which clearly lives is composed of things that live secretly, which nonetheless provide marvelous powers to the living animal for its life. For it would be impossible for a human to be moved to so many 
<margin>C</margin> and such great actions if the powers by which he is moved were entirely inanimate. Again, it is impossible for the whole to live in such a way unless the individual parts within it live their own lives, even if <term>conscious choice</term> <note>original: "electio" / "proairesis"—the capacity for deliberate, rational decision-making</note> is not present in them. For in its activity, the part does not require choice, insofar as natural action is "older" <note>i.e., more fundamental or primary in the hierarchy of existence</note> than choice; thus, it often follows the powers of its parts.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Toward a wondrous variety of powers, especially in celestial natures and progressions. <margin>B</margin> For this reason, that doubt is resolved by which it is asked how anything inanimate can exist in a being that is thoroughly animated. > *Just as our members, both internal and external, have powers for action and movement from our soul, so do all the members of the world from the World Soul itself. Likewise, that a small fire acts from so far away, and so easily consumes all things into itself, and that it shines—it has these from the soul; indeed, individual things have from the soul the fact that they generate something. And the very order of movements and forms is governed by the soul, as is the connection of opposites, and the movement of the celestial machine, so vast, into which the <term>generative soul</term> is especially propagated as if nearest to the soul: through this into fire, through this into air, through this into the rest. Yet this generative life of the world does not act by a kind of practical choice, nor by a conscious observation of its own action upon these things; rather, it acts as naturally as the Sun and fire: indeed, as the <term>vegetative soul</term> acts in us. Natural action is older than practical choice, although the contemplative and universal choice of the celestial mind itself is older than natural action.*

Nothing in the universe is rejected or destitute.

which have no <term>choice</term> <note>Latin: "electionem"; Greek: "proairesis" — the capacity for rational, conscious decision-making.</note>: furthermore, the power of nature is not turned into its own act by the mere transmission of its vigor, even if something of the soul itself is brought into effect by causes. For animals are born from animals without choice playing a part in the meantime; nor is the parent diminished in the process, nor is he then "converted" into the act: otherwise, choice itself would be the origin of generation, or else it would not be the effective cause. If a certain animal does not have choice, much less will it have the capacity to turn back into itself while acting.

*The intellectual soul of the world and of every sphere and star has a <term>vegetative life</term> <note>Latin: "vegetalem vitam". This is the lowest level of soul-power, responsible for growth, nutrition, and reproduction, operating automatically like a plant.</note> infused into its body. Through this life, things are generated naturally rather than by choice; subsequent things are moved, and benefits are bestowed upon those capable of receiving them. Whatever flows out from this kind of life is vital and beneficial; but in some places it turns out to be harmful, either because the <term>matter</term> <note>Latin: "materia"; Greek: "hyle". Our own vegetative life is very much in conformity with the life mentioned above; likewise, our <term>spirit</term> <note>Latin: "spiritus". This is the "pneumatic" or airy body that bridges the gap between the immortal soul and the physical flesh.</note> is penetrated by its rays, both hidden and manifest. It becomes even more closely related when we are strongly affected toward that life, desiring a corresponding benefit from it, and thus transferring our spirit into its rays through love—especially if we employ song and light, and a scent agreeable to the deity, such as the hymns Orpheus consecrated to the worldly deities. Likewise, the scent of frankincense burned for the Heavens; glowing saffron for the Ether; aromatics for the Stars; frankincense and manna for the Sun; aromatics for the Moon and Nature; storax for Saturn and Jupiter; myrrh for Neptune; and frankincense for Mercury. For the spirit, made more kindred to the deity through affection, song, scent, and light, draws a more abundant influx from there.*

### Chapter XXXVIII.

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, whatever things are done by the universe without any mover are produced by its "other life" <note>This refers to the non-rational, automatic life of the World Soul.</note>, and indeed everything that proceeds from it; but whatever things happen by the moving of another—such as by prayers, whether simple or composed with the art of singing—these must be referred not to any of the higher beings at random, but to the nature of that which is being acted upon. Now, those things which contribute as useful for life and other uses are considered attributed to their gift. This gift is poured out from a larger part into another smaller part. <margin>B</margin> As for what is said to be harmful coming from them into the generations of animals, it must be considered as such because the subject is unable to receive what is healthy. For what is made is not made simply, but in a certain way and under a certain condition. Then, indeed, it is necessary that what suffers and will suffer must have a certain and fixed subject nature. Many things are also produced by the mixtures themselves, with each contributing something prosperous to life in their midst. <margin>C</margin> Something will also happen to someone even if things useful by their own nature are not contributing. Yet the common order of all things does not provide to each everywhere what he desires. We also add many things to what is given. Finally, all things are woven together into one, and they produce a wonderful harmony; even some things come from others, though they proceed from contraries. For all are members of a single living being. <margin>D</margin> And if any of the things that are made falls short of the best, as if not formed all the way to the end, surely it is not that matter has triumphed, but like a noble thing degenerating and deprived of its nobility, it slides into foulness. For this reason, some things are produced by the higher powers, some are brought into the midst by the subject nature, and finally others are added by the things themselves.

*Above the vegetative life of the world, which is called both "nature" and the "nursery of natural things," there is an intelligence ordering everything more widely than nature does. From the intention of the nursery, things are born from it; it makes them be born beautiful and for motion: furthermore, they proceed in a certain accustomed and merely natural tenor toward their own progress. Therefore, that deformed and weak things happen due to a certain material necessity, and some things are destroyed by others, and are hindered from completing their accustomed order, and from growing, and from fulfilling their time, and in turn propagating others by their own seed: all this, I say...*

<column-break/>

...possessing [no choice], nor of the one who transmits the power through the gift, and if some part of the soul should come from them, it would not be according to life from life, nor by the making of choice: nor again by being diminished, nor again by following itself. For choice must either be present, if it has it, or it would not be the maker; but if an animal does not have choice, even more so it does not follow [itself].

SINCE indeed from itself, with nothing moving it, it happens from its other life, or generally whatever is from it; but whatever is by the moving of another, such as by prayers, either simple or sung by art, these must not be led to each of those [higher beings], but to the nature of that which is being acted upon. It is necessary indeed that those things which contribute to life, or some other need, be referred to the gift, going from a larger part to a smaller. Whenever something difficult is said to come from them into the generations of animals, it is because the underlying subject cannot receive the benefit. For the thing becoming does not become simply, but into a "this" and "in this way." And indeed both that which suffers and that which will suffer, someone says, has a certain subject and quality; and many things also the mixtures produce, each giving what is useful for living. And it might happen even to those not contributing, who are useful by nature. But the arrangement of the whole gives to each what he wants. We ourselves add many things to the things given. Yet all things are nonetheless woven into one, and have a wondrous harmony, and some things from others, and even from contraries, for all things are of one. And if something of the things becoming is of a lesser quality compared to the better, not having been formed into an <term>ideal form</term> <note>Greek: "eidopoiēthen"; literally "given an eidos" or form. When matter resists the form, the result is "foulness" or deformity.</note> to the end, because matter was not mastered: as if falling short of the noble, or being deprived, it falls into ugliness. So that some things are made by those [higher beings], some are brought in by the underlying nature, and some are added by the things themselves.

<summary>Plotinus and his commentator Ficino explain that the universe functions as a single living organism where the "vegetative" World Soul influences all life automatically. They describe how ritual elements like specific incenses and hymns can align the human spirit with these celestial energies, while attributing earthly "evil" or deformity to the resistance of matter rather than divine intent.</summary>
