BOOK FOUR.

...then it arises from no intention of nature. Therefore, such a <term>contingent</term> <note>Latin: "contingens" — an event that happens by chance or is not strictly necessary.</note> thing cannot be ordered by the intention of nature, since it is hostile to its order. Yet it must be ordered, for all things are reduced under one principle into a single unity. Therefore, through an intelligence superior to nature, accidents of this kind are recalled into order: through that same intelligence, the movements and effects of free will are also disposed in order according to their merits. Our prayers are anticipated, as <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who emphasized the importance of ritual and theurgy in reaching the divine.</note> says, and fulfilled, while we meanwhile operate freely; neither is the divine will changed, nor is the order of things disturbed. Therefore, the arrangement of things is broader in the mind than in nature itself: in the mind, I say, not only the primary Mind, but also in the souls of the world and the heavens.

Indeed, Plato in the *Statesman* names the disposition of things in the primary mind the "Law of Saturn." He calls the same thing in the soul’s intellect the "Law of Jupiter" in the *Statesman* and the *Laws*. Finally, in nature, he calls it the "Fatal Law" in the *Statesman* and the *Timaeus*. But because this law proceeds everywhere with inevitable firmness, he names it the "Law of Adrasteia" in the *Phaedrus*. Furthermore, because he preserves the free efficacy of souls alongside the law, he says in the *Laws* that the principle of actions exists in the souls, but the limit or result exists in the law. In the *Phaedrus* and *Timaeus*, he always introduces the edict of the law with a certain condition, in this manner: "If the soul shall have performed such things, let it receive such things in return." 

Now, when he says in the *Timaeus* that souls did not hear the laws of fate before they were joined to <term>vehicles</term> <note>Latin: "vehiculis"; Greek: "ochemata" — the "astral bodies" or subtle envelopes that carry the soul down into the physical body.</note>, he declares that souls are free in themselves, but fate pertains to bodies. Indeed, fatal necessity pertains not only to the physical body, but also to the bodily life. Such a life, lying hidden in the mundane and celestial body, diffuses its power to lower things not by free choice, but by fatal necessity; this power shines forth as beneficial even from Mars, or Saturn, and similar stars. However, it can be rendered more harmful, not otherwise than one who casts gathered rays of the Sun from a concave mirror onto an object and burns it. For if someone should force ten powers of Saturn—which are necessary and scattered throughout the world and ourselves—into a single point in ten joined materials, he will destroy that person (who clearly cannot tolerate it) against whom he has gathered it; meanwhile, Saturn is innocent. 

Venus has inserted various properties of fertility and reconciliation into various things throughout the world. Therefore, if a person chooses all materials capable of such powers, and employs them gathered into one while Venus is reigning, he kindles immoderate loves between this person and that, yet Venus is not sinning. Similarly, one may accumulate the gifts of Jupiter on others, while the "Jovian animal" meanwhile takes no notice. Indeed, we call the body of a star a "Jovian animal," or "Saturnian," or "Venereal," as it is alive with vegetal power; Pythagoras devised such bodies when he said that the invoked Gods flow into us, compelled by a certain necessity.

Chapter XXXIX.

---

Since, therefore, all things are always ordered together and contribute toward one, it is no wonder that individual things are signified by certain signs. But meanwhile, virtue serves no one; yet its duties are woven together with the common order of things. Since the things that are here depend from there—namely, from those things in this universe which are more divine—this universe participates in those things. Therefore, the things that happen in the world do not occur according to <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>Latin: "rationes seminales"; Greek: "logoi spermatikoi" — the formative "blueprints" or "seeds" within nature that guide growth and development.</note> alone, but according to other <term>broader reasons</term> <note>Latin: "rationes ampliores". Higher intellectual principles that encompass more than just biological growth.</note> which comprehend in themselves powers far prior to the seminal reasons. 

For there is nothing in the seminal reasons of those things which happen anywhere outside the seminal reasons themselves; nor again of those things which are judged to be contributed to the world from <term>matter</term> <note>Latin: "materia"; Greek: "hyle". Neoplatonists viewed matter as a potential source of disorder or "leakage" in the divine plan.</note> itself; nor even of those things which are brought upon one another by created things. Rather, the reason of the whole is similar to the reason of one adorning a city and establishing laws, and certainly knowing what the citizens are going to do and for what reasons they will act, and disposing individual institutes toward all these things, and connecting all their passions and actions to the laws. 

Furthermore, the merits of individual actions receive rewards and punishments everywhere, while all things meanwhile proceed as if spontaneously into a common harmony. Signification indeed happens in nature, not primarily for the sake of this—that a sign should be made—but because things are so disposed and born that some things are signified by others. For whatever is here is, in a certain way, one among themselves and belongs to the One. Thus, one thing is known by another: the cause by the effect, the consequent by the antecedent, and the composite by either of its parts; for one thing produces the other simultaneously. If these things are indeed said correctly, those doubts will be resolved: and especially that one which warned that we should be careful <margin>*of evils</margin> lest we were forced to admit that the Gods do evil. To this person, [we say that these things happen] not by choices, but by natural necessities.

It explains that "evil" planetary influences are not the fault of the stars but result from how their power is concentrated or received by matter and human choice.</summary>

### PLOTINUS ENNEADS BOOK IV.

Whatever proceeds from that higher realm does so as if parts <margin>A</margin>
are transferred into other parts, following the life
of the One. Secondly, many things are added to the things
that are made from the very things themselves. Thirdly, those things
which are given from above are not evil individually
within the givers, but in the mixing, something else
occurs. Fourthly, life is given and judged not for the
sake of any individual part, but for the sake of the whole.
Fifthly, the underlying nature receives one thing,
but suffers another; nor can it always be overcome by
the gift itself, or retain that gift's own power.

<column-break/>

Whatever comes from there, as parts to parts, follows
the life of the One: and by the addition of many things from
themselves to the things being made: and because the things
given by each, though not evil in themselves, become something
else in the mixing; and because life is not for the sake of the
individual, but for the sake of the whole: and because the underlying
nature, having received one thing, experiences another,
and is not even able to master what was given.
<note>This is the Greek version of the five points listed above, emphasizing that "evil" is a byproduct of the material world's inability to perfectly hold divine gifts.</note>

---

Every member of a living creature has the power to attract its own proper portion of nourishment: the heart attracts aromas, the liver attracts sweets, the veins attract blood, the arteries attract the spirit, and the testicles attract the seed. There are also medicines which draw out certain <term>humors</term> <note>In ancient medicine, humors were the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and temperament.</note> and seem to seek out specific limbs. The condition of the **World Animal** <note>Latin: "animalis mundani" — the Neoplatonic concept that the entire universe is a single, living organism with its own soul.</note> is the same: in it, various passions are dispersed which can snatch this or that thing to themselves if they are brought near to it as a single unit. For men can be secretly ensnared by their own lures, horses by theirs, and other men similarly by their own specific means—just as they are openly enticed by the delights of beautiful forms and music. Finally, just as it is openly observed that a magnet attracts iron, or amber attracts stalks, so the diligent and fortunate seeker will find an essence for attracting all things.

For within the individual members of the World Animal, there is an innate power of "curdling" or binding, connecting all things into one living being. This happens moderately by its own nature, but immoderately whenever these forces are gathered from everywhere and transferred into something specific—meanwhile, the world itself neither suffers nor sins. There are also different powers in this living being, separated by nature, which are frequently joined by a **Magus** <note>A practitioner of "natural magic," which involves using the hidden properties of plants, stones, and stars to achieve effects.</note> and cast into this or that member to act more violently or to destroy; yet in these things (as I said) the world does not sin. Plotinus names four things in which a marvelous power resides: the occult qualities of species, figures (shapes), harmonies, and vows. Indeed, those qualities are certain offshoots of powers lying hidden in the world, and lower figures and harmonies often reflect the figures and harmonies of the heavens. 

A vow (or prayer) is a certain vehement movement of our soul toward the divinity we implore. If you throw the finest powder of crushed sulfur toward a fire, the fire will immediately attach itself to this powder in a long, drawn-out flame. Similarly, he who implores a star at the opportune time, being prepared for that star, projects his own spirit into the rays of the star—both those that are manifest and those that are hidden—which are diffused and divided everywhere; through these rays, he claims for himself the vital gifts of the star. Finally, just as all the fixed stars are connected to the firmament, so the lives of all stars and worldly divinities are connected to the **World Life**, to which our own life is also connected. Thus, it is no wonder that the vehement movements of our soul, poured out through the common life flourishing everywhere, are extended even to the worldly divinities, and in turn, the movements of these divinities are brought down to us through that same life. **Chapter 40.**

---

But by what reasoning shall we say **MAGICAL** attractions <margin>A</margin>
occur? Surely from a certain consensus of things in
their suffering, and by a certain law of nature which
creates concord between similar things and discord
between dissimilar things; likewise from the variety of
many powers contributing to one living being. For
without anyone's mechanical interference, many things
are attracted by a kind of magical rite: the true power
of magic is the **Love** in the universe, and conversely,
**Strife**. And the first sorcerer (if I may say so) and <margin>B</margin>
enchanter is the world itself. Men, observing this, 
use its "philters" <note>Love potions or charms.</note> and sorceries upon one another. Indeed,
because most things are naturally able to love one another
easily, and they bring about a reciprocal love between
things, the efficacy of the art of love was born, using
certain philters and fascinations. They apply natures
to be touched, reconciling one to another and possessing 
an innate love; thus they join one soul to another,
just as those who join together plants that were distant. 
Furthermore, they use figures possessing certain powers; <margin>C</margin>
by shaping themselves in a certain proper way, they
secretly snatch powers to themselves, and they do this
more easily because they are within the One, and they
draw things into the One. For if one were imagined to 
be shaped this way *outside* the world, he would neither
attract anything, nor lead anything away with lures
or melodies, nor entangle things in bonds. But as it is,
since he does not snatch things to an alien place,
he gains the power to snatch; he certainly knows by
what condition one thing in the same living being is 
drawn to another. For there is an innate power of <margin>D</margin>
transferring within charms and songs, and in a certain
kind of sound and figure...

<column-break/>

And what of sorceries? They occur through sympathy
and the natural harmony of likes and opposition
of unlikes; and through the variety of the many powers
contributing to one living being. For without anyone
devising it, many other things are drawn and enchanted;
and the true magic is the Love in the universe, and again
Strife. And the first sorcerer and the pharmacist is this
[universe]; men, having understood this, use its drugs
and sorceries upon one another. For because they are
naturally inclined to love, and the things loved are
drawn to one another, an erotic strength has arisen
through the art of sorcery, by those who apply other
natures to others through touch, certain attractions
having an indwelling love, and they join one soul
to another, just as if they fastened distant plants
to one another. And they also use figures that have
powers. And by figuring themselves thus, they bring
down powers upon themselves silently... not being
outside, they draw them... by attractions or bonds.
But now, because it does not lead things as if elsewhere,
it has power: knowing how that which is in the living
being is led toward another. It is natural also in
incantations by the melody and by such a sound,
and by the figure...

<summary>This page explains the mechanism of "Natural Magic" as the result of cosmic sympathy within the "World Animal," where the Magus uses harmonies, shapes, and the universal forces of Love and Strife to connect parts of the world.</summary>

### BOOK FOUR.

...in the manner of one acting: for such things <margin>A</margin> possess a certain marvelous attraction, such as mournful voices, specific accents, and pitiful gestures. But how is the soul drawn in? For it is neither the faculty of choice nor reason, but rather the **irrational soul** <note>In Neoplatonic thought, the 'irrational soul' is the part of us governed by emotions and instincts, which is susceptible to sensory charms.</note> that is soothed by music. No one wonders at these kinds of charms that occupy souls, even though people are often enchanted by them without the musicians intending it. Furthermore, one should by no means think that the power inherent in prayers reaches its fulfillment through the conscious deliberation of the one who hears them. For those who are <margin>B</margin> enticed by songs are not soothed in that way. Nor, when a serpent charms a man, does the one being charmed understand or feel it happening; rather, having already suffered the effect, he realizes he has been affected. The **leading faculty** <note>original: "principale" / "ἡγεμονικόν" (hegemonikon) - the ruling part of the soul.</note> of the soul itself cannot be affected in this way. But for the one who has offered a prayer, something reaches them from that source, or perhaps shifts toward something else.

<column-break/>

...of the agent itself: for such things have a certain power to attract, like wailing voices and accents, and miserable appearances. Indeed, the soul is drawn, but by what means? For neither choice nor reason, but the irrational soul is softened by music. And no one marvels at such "poisonings" <note>original: "veneficia" - refers here to charms or magical enchantments rather than literal poison.</note> occupying the soul, although they are accustomed to being charmed even if it is not requested from the musicians. One must also not think that the power placed in prayers reaches its end through a listening council: for those who are drawn <margin>B</margin> by songs are not soothed in that way. Nor, when any serpent fascinates a man, does the one who is fascinated understand this itself, nor does he feel it, but having already suffered it, he notices he has suffered; yet the governing part of the soul cannot suffer in this way. To the one for whom a vow has been established, something comes to him from that, or conversely to another.

---

*Just as in any perfect animal there is a texture of nerves and veins, so in the animal of the world there is a weaving together of natures and lives. Therefore, just as the movement and suffering of a foot in us pertains to the neck, and that of the neck to the foot, so also in this world-animal the movements of lower things proceed to the higher, and vice versa, and similarly from equals to equals. Every healthy movement comes indeed from on high, provided that as it comes, it is received in such a way, and is able to be received. Nor does the distance of place prevent movements from proceeding back and forth on both sides, where beyond the common texture, the lower thing has a kindred property with the higher, whether acquired or natural: just as the movement of a nerve in a lyre reaches another nerve, distant indeed, but similarly tuned. Chapter XLI.*

---

The Sun or any other star does not "hear" the prayer. The power of the prayer is fulfilled through a certain **sympathy** <note>original: "συμπαθὴς" (sympathēs) - a natural resonance between parts of a whole.</note> of one part suffering with another; just as in a stretched string, when the bottom part is moved, the top also experiences the movement. Often, when another string is struck, another string feels a kind of sensation according to their concord, because they are tuned to one and the same harmony. And if the movement is transferred from one lyre to another, this must also be thought to proceed from a certain sympathetic agreement. Therefore, in the universe, there is one harmony, even if it is composed of opposites; for it is also composed of similar and all kindred things, even those which are contrary. Accordingly, whatever things harm men—such as angry spiritedness together with bile—they proceed in this way not as if they were intended to harm men. It is as if someone, taking fire from a fire, harmed something else; the one who devised the fire did not intend it to proceed to that harm. Perhaps, however, the one receiving it acts because he hands over something transferred from one thing to another. Furthermore, the proceeding fire acts where it cannot be received by the subject into which it is transferred.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> The SUN or any other star by no means notices this. The power of a vow consists in a certain agreement of part to part in "co-suffering" <note>original: "compatiendi" - to feel or vibrate in unison.</note>: just as happens in a certain stretched string, where when the lowest part is moved, the highest is soon moved as well. Often also, when some other string is struck, another trembles as if it feels it through concord. And this happens most of all because they are tuned to the exact same resonance. If the movement is also <margin>B</margin> transferred from one lyre to another, that too must be thought to proceed from a certain sympathetic agreement. Therefore, in the universe, there is one **harmony** <term>harmony: the Neoplatonic idea that the universe functions like a musical instrument where every part affects the others through resonance.</term>, although it may be from opposites. For it is also from similar things and all kindred things, even those which are contrary. Therefore, whatever things harm men—such as wrathful anger along with bile—they occurred in that way not as if to harm men: just as if someone, seizing fire from a fire, should harm another thing, he by no means plotted <margin>C</margin> for the fire to proceed there. But perhaps that receiver acts from the fact that he hands over something as if transferred from one thing to another. Moreover, the proceeding fire does this when it cannot be captured by the subject into which it is transferred.

---

*Many Magi <note>Ancient practitioners of magic and astrology.</note> of old, lovers of the present life and desirous of bodily goods, devised bodily sacrifices and vows agreeable to the living bodies of the stars and the living body of the world, so that they might obtain what they desired from there. They seem to have accustomed the people to these same bodily sacrifices dedicated to the stars. Some therefore doubted whether stars have need of sense, imagination, memory, or choice for this very work, so that they might fulfill such vows. Plotinus responds that it is not necessary: for from the living bodies of the world, vital vigor is derived by its own nature into others. This vigor flows more abundantly into the spirits and souls of bodies when they are more fitly exposed to drinking it in through vows and other suitable means, specifically by a natural and proper influx, even if choice is not present. But Plotinus places the intellectual souls of the stars and spheres above their living bodies, as if segregated from the body, to which no passion or movement continued through bodily natures reaches; therefore, such goods are not drawn from there by a quasi-magical attraction. Porphyry and Iamblichus <note>Successors to Plotinus in the Neoplatonic tradition.</note> assert the same: who together with Plotinus place will and choice in those beings. Choice, I say, not persuaded by lower things, but constituting from itself from eternity to imitate the highest God, and to provide for all following things, to hear the prayers of suppliants who imitate the intellectual governors of the world with an intellectual life. In bodily sacrifices and vows, men report that they receive such goods by being directed to the bodies of the world, even being enslaved to the body; but more divine goods are received through a segregated worship, by a divine man from the divine governors of the world. Porphyry and Iamblichus add that these also bring back certain corporal and external goods beyond the intellectual ones.*

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK IV.

*By the service of the intermediary deities <note>original: "numinum mediorum" — spirits or daemons existing between gods and humans.</note> who obey the higher gods, and through their protection, one can often avoid imminent evils. The astrologer Abraham adds that religious souls, through their devotion to God (who is higher than the heavens), acquire a power by which they may increase fated goods and diminish evils. The Platonists propose pure intellects as the world-rulers for intellectual souls; for these, they propose the Divine Intellect, and for that, its father, the Good itself. They establish physical sacrifices for the worldly gods, but for the higher ones, they dedicate a secluded holiness—first, the most secluded of all. This is confirmed by Apollonius of Tyana <note>original: "Apollonius Theaneus" — a famous 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker.</note>. They choose adoration for the higher beings above all others, and finally, a consecrated adoration for the Supreme Being, for from there greater goods are returned. You may read most extensively about these matters in the works of Iamblichus and Porphyry, which we have recently translated.*

### Chapter XLII.

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, there will be no need for memory in the stars for the sake of hearing a vow (the reason we have discussed these things), nor for senses to announce the vows there. One should not think the stars nod to prayers in the way some believe, as if they were deliberating; rather, something is accomplished simultaneously with the prayer itself, and even without a prayer from them, by the logic that they are parts of one and the same whole. Indeed, there are many powers even without conscious choice, and they proceed into effect both without planning and through art—just as in any single animal, where one part
<margin>B</margin> receives something from another, and is preserved or harmed by it because they are naturally established that way. For this reason, the arts of both physicians and enchanters <note>original: "incantantium" — those who use charms or spells.</note> compel one thing to impart something of its virtue to another. Similarly, the universe spontaneously pours out its gifts from itself to its parts, and when another part attracts it, the universe sends down something inherent in its parts to that specific section, drawn there by the same natural vigor—especially since the one who desires it is not a stranger to the whole. If, however, the one who prays is evil, it is no
<margin>C</margin> wonder that he obtains his request, for even the wicked draw water from rivers. Furthermore, that which bestows the gift is unaware of what it bestows; it merely bestows. Meanwhile, however, the gift itself is connected with the nature of the universe. Therefore, if anyone receives from those things that are laid out for all, it is not necessary that punishment follow him by a mandatory law. We must not, then, grant that the universe "suffers" or is affected in a human sense. Perhaps, indeed,
<margin>D</margin> we should say its ruling part <note>original: "principale" / Greek: "ἡγεμονικόν" (hegemonikon) — the governing faculty.</note> exists entirely free from passion <note>original: "passio" — here meaning 'being acted upon' or 'emotional suffering'.</note>. While passions are brought upon its parts, the passion remains in those parts; but since nothing happens to the whole contrary to nature, the whole itself remains without passion. Even if passions seem to befit the stars insofar as they are parts, the stars themselves remain free of passion, both because choices exist in them without passions, and because their bodies and natures are far from harm. Furthermore, even if they transmit something through their soul to
<margin>E</margin> lower things, the soul is not diminished in the meantime, and their bodies remain the same. If anything flows away from them, it slips away without the senses noticing, and if anything is added to them, it flows in secretly in the same way.

<column-break/>

SO THAT there is no need for memory in the stars (the reason for which we have treated these things), nor for senses to be sent up for their consent to prayers in that manner which some imagine as a matter of choice. Instead, we must grant that something happens alongside a prayer, and even without a prayer, things come from them because they are parts and are one. Many powers exist even without choice, both without contrivance and with art, as in a single living creature where one part benefits or is harmed by another because of how it is naturally constituted. The arts of physicians and charmers compel one thing to provide something of its power to another. Likewise, the whole gives to its parts, both from itself and when another part draws from it, because it is situated in a part of itself and shares the same nature, as the petitioner is not something foreign. If the petitioner is bad, one should not marvel, for the wicked also draw from rivers. The giver does not know what it gives, but only gives. Nevertheless, it is organized and given by the nature of the whole. So if someone takes from what is laid out for everyone, it must follow him by the necessary law of the whole. It is wrong to say the whole "suffers" <note>Greek: "πάσχειν" (paschein) — to be acted upon or to experience emotion.</note>; rather, its ruling part must be granted to be entirely impassive, and though passions occur in its parts, the passion reaches them, but because nothing of it is contrary to its nature, that which happens remains impassive in relation to the whole. Since the stars are parts, they are impassive in themselves, because their choices are without passion, and their bodies and natures exist without harm. Even if they give something through the soul, they do not diminish the soul itself; their bodies remain the same, and if anything flows out imperceptibly, it is replaced by a secret flowing in.

---

*Magical fascination relies on natural forces of both celestial and lower things, namely objects and words. It therefore touches our spirit most closely, and through this, it affects not only the humors but also the irrational life that depends on the world itself. However, it cannot reach the rational soul, which is superior to the physical nature and life of the world and depends solely on the divine mind, except insofar as the soul consents to the lower life.*

### Chapter XLIII.

If one person dresses in a garment of amber and another in straw, the amber will attract the straw. In this way, the Magi have investigated many hidden things, not only natural objects but also words which, pouring out their power from a distance, are able to pull. They also use many things that can be pulled by these means; applying these things secretly to a man or a woman, they draw the woman to the man. They also apply things that can separate them—just as sailors, by suspending iron, vibrate it with a magnet so that it is drawn toward the North Star <note>original: "Vrsam" — literally 'The Bear' (Ursa Major/Minor).</note>, and conversely, when they are failing, they release such a pull with garlic <note>Ancient natural history claimed that garlic could neutralize the power of a magnet.</note>. But it is not expedient to tell in what position of the stars they use something more opportunely for these things, what images they fashion, or what materials they melt together; nor by what...

<summary>This page explains that the universe and stars respond to prayer and magic not through conscious choice or emotion, but through a natural, systemic resonance like the parts of a single living body. It also introduces the concept of magic as the manipulation of natural "sympathies" between objects, which can affect the body and irrational soul but not the higher rational mind.</summary>

# BOOK FOUR.

...by which incantations they might secretly allure. While Mercury <note>The god of communication and intellect, associated here with the planet Mercury.</note> excels in words, and Phoebus <note>Apollo, the sun god, associated here with music and the planet Sun.</note> in songs, Mercury joined with Phoebus excels in incantations. However, where and by what reasoning Mercury is joined to the Sun, and how, relying on the influence of the stars, he provides power to songs—likewise, by what disposition he provides harmful or beneficial incantations—the law of justice forbids me to teach. 

Perhaps, however, just as other mixtures of materials and qualities acquire new power, so certain joinings of words—both those conceived within the soul and those uttered outside the soul—attain a marvelous power while still "living," as it were. This occurs either from the present position of the stars, or from the man's own nativity <note>His birth chart or horoscope.</note>, or even from a certain singular power of the soul itself. This power is so strong that in the effect of the words, their very joining and progression toward an object acts as a direction and application of an internal virtue to something external—just as the finger of a pregnant woman, marked by a strong craving, leaves a sign of the desired object upon her cheek <note>A reference to the "maternal impression" theory, where a mother's intense thoughts could physically mark her child.</note>. 

The vigor of an incantation proceeds toward a distant thing by a certain movement, propagated not only through the air (which is similar to it, like ripples in water once struck), but also through the rays of the spirit <note>original: "spiritus" — in this context, the vital, subtle substance that connects the physical body to the soul.</note> of the one performing the incantation, which a powerful imagination and emotion hurl to a great distance. For the nature of these "rays" proceeds suddenly into the distance, carrying with them the powers of the one who ejected them. Indeed, all things beneath the Moon imitate the stars by emitting their own natural powers and "vapors" outward like rays. By these, they frequently affect even distant objects for better or worse, according to their nature. This happens more easily because every individual thing is a limb of the same "World Animal" <note>original: "animalis mundani" — the Stoic and Neoplatonic idea that the entire universe is a single, living, interconnected organism.</note>. This is evidenced by scents, which are perceived from a great distance and for a long time by dogs and bees. 

I will pass over how much power demons <note>original: "dæmones" — intermediary spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note> apply to poisonings and magical works, which Plato surely confirms in his *Symposium*. A diligent practitioner and Magus can win these over by soothing them, just as a lowly mime or a musician boy might ensnare a noble King, or as certain beasts sometimes fascinate a man. For as a beast relates to a man, or a boy to a man, so does a Magus relate to those lower demons who are close to us. 

Perhaps this is the point of the saying by Albumasar <note>A famous 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note> and other astrologers: that prayers have the greatest power when the Head of the Dragon <note>original: "caput Draconis" — the North Node of the Moon, considered an auspicious point in traditional astrology.</note> holds the Midheaven, and Jupiter is either in it or looking upon it; and when the Moon is either joined with Jupiter or, proceeding from him, pursues a meeting with the Lord of the Ascendant; or when the Lord of the Ascendant seeks a meeting with Jupiter and an aspect with the Head of the Dragon. For they think that such a star provides efficacy and prosperity to our spirit and vows for the sake of alluring the demons subject to Jupiter and the "Head"; provided that many things from the entire genus of sensible things (which are compatible both with this demon and his particular star) are joined to these celestial influences—things which are both laborious to investigate and dangerous to observe. 

A natural philosopher will more safely suppose that, through the benefit of Jupiter, the spirit of a man who is then vehemently desiring celestial goods is exposed to a more generous drinking-in of those goods. However, to move malignant spirits from their place and to fulfill "divination through the dead" <note>original: "diuinationemq; per mortuos" — necromancy.</note>, Ptolemy thinks in his *Tetrabiblos* <note>original: "quadripartito" — Ptolemy's foundational text on astrology.</note> that celestial harmony is needed when the Moon is the mistress of the work and inhabits the houses of Jupiter, namely Sagittarius or Pisces. 

These things are said in reference to that point by Plotinus: where he says that a Magus, in a way, ensnares demons and drives them into parts through the universe, and easily moves lower things through higher things. I, however, suspect that perhaps crafty demons only pretend to be allured or expelled by certain magical machines. For Porphyry and Iamblichus say that through God specifically, and through good angels, we have command over the lowest spirits, who otherwise are accustomed to deceive and harm us frequently. And since they are touched by "perturbation" <note>original: "perturbatione" — emotional agitation or irrationality.</note> (which Plotinus also affirms), Plotinus, along with Porphyry and Iamblichus, rightly condemns that superstition which seeks to flatter deceptive and perturbed demons with exquisite allurements. 

By what reasoning we are able to pluck vital breaths from the "Body of the World" (which is alive everywhere) and from the living stars and other parts of the world—in the natural manner of farmers and doctors—we have sufficiently discussed in the third book of our *On Life* <note>original: "De Vita" — Ficino’s famous work on health and astral magic.</note>. Finally, the Platonists think that the most intense adoration is the most effective of all sacrifices, especially if it is directed toward the higher intellects of the world (namely the angels), and most of all if it is directed to the higher God. But they hold that nothing is obtained from these beings through some "natural" or "celestial" favor—whose movement does not reach that far—but rather through a certain elevation and union of the mind with them. 

As for what we omitted in the previous sections regarding the power of imagination, fascinations, and Magic, we treat those more extensively in our *Theology*, our *Book on Love*, and the third book of *On Life*.

### Chapter XLIII.

<margin>A</margin> NO man of character—how can he be affected by sorcery and drugs? The soul is unaffected by sorcery in its essence, and its rational part could not suffer, nor would its opinions change. But insofar as there is an irrational part of the Whole <note>The "Whole" refers to the World Soul/Animal.</note> within him, he might suffer through this. Rather, this part itself might suffer entirely; but he will not suffer "loves" from drugs, if indeed "to love" implies the assent of the other soul to the passion of another. Just as the irrational part suffers from incantations, so he himself—by chanting and counter-chanting—will dissolve those powers. But death or disease, or whatever is physical, might be suffered from such things. For a part of the whole might suffer from another part or from the whole itself, though the man himself remains unharmed. That it does not happen immediately, but later, is not strange to nature. Demons are not unaffected, nor is their irrational part. It is not absurd to attribute memory and sensation to them.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> IT seems we must ASK how a virtuous man can avoid being subject to magical machines and drugs. Perhaps he cannot be ensnared through the soul itself, nor does the rational power suffer, so as to be changed in its opinion. However, as much of the "irrational" from the universe as is in him, he can suffer through this. Indeed, this irrational part itself is what properly suffers. But he does not suffer this only when someone is ensnared by loves from potions; for love itself thrives and burns only if the other soul consents to the passion of the <margin>B</margin> second soul. Just as the irrational part undergoes passion from the songs of those performing incantations, so the chanter himself, in turn, as a "counter-chanter," dissolves the forces there. Consequently, he will undoubtedly suffer death from these things, or lingering illnesses, or any physical detriments. For a part of the universe is easily affected by another part, or by the whole itself, while the person himself, remaining in control of his own right, lives unharmed. That he does not suffer the passion <margin>C</margin> immediately, but after a certain time, is not foreign to the order of nature. Even the demons themselves are not free from passions in their irrational part. Furthermore, to attribute memory and senses to them will not be absurd.

# PLOTINUS' ENNEADS. BOOK IV.

...then truly they are naturally soothed and led down, and they hear those calling. I mean Daemons <note>original: 'Dæmones' — in Neoplatonism, these are intermediary spirits that inhabit the space between gods and the material world.</note> among others closer to human affairs, who are affected by us more because they are nearer. For whatever has some kinship to another is sometimes ensnared by the other. For that to which it is so related, it captures and draws away as if by a magical rite: but only that which looks only at itself cannot be entangled or seized. Therefore, every action and all active life is ensnared and drawn; for it is carried toward those things which provoke and soothe. Hence that poetic line: *For the people of great-hearted Erechtheus is most beautiful in countenance.* <note>Plotinus is quoting Plato’s 'Alcibiades I', which refers to a Homeric-style description of the Athenian people. He uses it to illustrate how even "noble" political crowds can be seduced by outward beauty and rhetoric.</note> But what is one thought to suffer that is related to another in a certain way? Truly, he is as if drawn not by the arts of mages, but by the art of nature, which is wonderfully seductive, reconciling and joining one thing with another very strongly, not indeed by location, but by using love-charms <note>original: 'philtris' — philtres or potions. Here used metaphorically for the natural attractions (like gravity or instinct) that bind the universe together.</note> from the beginning.

<column-break/>

<note>This column contains the original Greek text of the section above. Plotinus wrote in Greek; the Latin on the left is a parallel translation by Marsilio Ficino.</note>
...and they are naturally enchanted and led, and they hear the causes of the calls from those who are nearer to this place, and insofar as they are toward this place. For everything that is directed toward another is enchanted by another. For that toward which it is directed, that thing enchants and leads it: only that which is directed toward itself is unenchanted. Therefore, every action is enchanted, as is the whole life of the man of action. For he is moved toward those things which soothe him. Whence also the "beautiful countenance of the people of great-hearted Erechtheus." For what does he suffer in being directed toward another? He is drawn not by the arts of mages, but by the deceptions and joinings of nature, which connects one thing to another, not by locations on earth, but by the charms she has given.

---

->*The contemplative life is free; the active life is a servant of actions, things, and fortune; the voluptuous life is a slave to the body. Chapter 44.*<-

*Since the mind has the innate forms of things to be contemplated, and is itself the forms, it rightly dwells free within itself insofar as it moves with native pleasure in contemplating these things. But he who curiously cultivates the body and external things serves the body, men, and fortune. Action and passion are opposed to each other. Therefore, every movement of ours which has its incitement from bodily and human passion is a certain passion and servitude. Finally, nature itself and the life of the world, like a sorceress <note>original: 'maga' — Plotinus views the material world as a realm of "magic" because it uses the "bait" of pleasure to distract the soul.</note>, everywhere fashions images of the good, the true, and the beautiful, like baits with which it deceives souls devoted to this world through pleasure, greed, and empty glory, and holds and draws them like slaves.*

---

<margin>A</margin> Only contemplation remains, therefore, which cannot be drawn away by magical rite: for no one is attracted to himself. For he exists as one, and he himself is that very spectacle which he beholds, and reason is not seduced: but what must be done rightly, he does, and he lives his own life and performs his own work. In the active life, however, the soul does not do what is its own, nor does reason provide the beginning, but the start there is handed over by the irrational part, and the rules of acting are proposed by passion. In the appetite for procreation <margin>B</margin> and the care for children, the attraction is clearly visible; and similarly in all things that allure those desiring with a certain sweetness. Actions also—both those moved through anger without reason, and those incited by desire—as well as the greed for civil government and the zeal for commanding, signify that the desire for dominating, having been incited in us, now incites us. Then truly, the studies of commanding tending especially toward this, that no injuries be brought upon us by others, take their origin from fear; but those tending <margin>C</margin> toward us gaining more than others are led by desire. Finally, those things which serve necessity and utility, attempting to fill the indigence of nature, clearly show the force of nature itself reconciling us entirely to the zeal for living. If someone should object that actions concerning noble things are not drawn away by magical rite, or else that the contemplation of beautiful things is also drawn away by such a condition: it must be answered that if someone follows noble actions as necessary, <margin>D</margin> looking clearly at something else truly beautiful, he is by no means ensnared by magical modes. For he knows necessity, and looks neither at what is in our actions, nor is he directed to other things of this life: unless perhaps through a part of himself...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <note>This column contains the Greek text corresponding to Chapter 44 above.</note>
Only contemplation remains unenchanted, because no one is enchanted toward himself. For he is one, and he himself is the thing contemplated, and his reason is not led astray: but he does what he must, and performs his own life and work. In the other case, he does not do what is his own; reason does not provide the impulse, but the beginning comes from the irrational part, and the premises are set by passion. For the care of children and the zeal for marriage have a clear pull: <margin>B</margin> just as all things that allure toward men, becoming sweet to the desires. Actions moved through anger are moved irrationally; those of desire likewise. Political states and the reach for offices have as their challenger the love of rule within us. And those things done for the sake of not suffering have their beginning in fear; those for the sake of having more, in desire. <margin>C</margin> Those done for the sake of necessities, seeking to fulfill the lack of nature, clearly hold the violence of nature, reconciling us to life. But if someone says that the actions of noble things are unenchanted, or that the contemplation of beautiful things is enchanted, it must be said: if he performs even those called noble actions as necessities, having something else that is truly beautiful <margin>D</margin> in view, he is not enchanted. For he knows necessity, and does not look toward the things here, nor is his life directed toward another thing, but [directed] by the part of nature toward...

# BOOK FOUR.

<margin>A</margin> ...the irrational part is led by a certain force of human nature and by a natural familiarity <note>original: 'οἰκειώσει' / 'naturali familiaritate' — a Stoic and Neoplatonic term for the innate attraction or kinship a being feels toward its own kind or toward life itself.</note> that reconciles us with either the life of others or our own. In this way, one might be said to be entangled. For perhaps it is reasonable that the rational soul does not lead itself out of life because of a certain necessity with life that is most proper to us, by which we are deeply occupied. But if a man devoted to active affairs becomes content with the beauty of such things and chooses those actions, he is already deceived. He has been ensnared by the "footprints of beauty" <note>original: 'ἴχνεσι τοῦ καλοῦ' / 'pulchri vestigijs' — Plotinus argues that physical beauty is merely a faint trace or "footprint" of the true, Divine Beauty.</note> <margin>B</margin> as if by a beneficial gift; thus, he zealously pursues the beauty inherent in lower things. For truly, all preoccupation with that which is merely a likeness of the truth, and every attraction toward it, is a certain "seizure of the mind" by things that snatch the deceived person toward themselves. Indeed, the magical enchantment of nature <note>original: 'φύσεως γοητεία' / 'naturæ magica' — Plotinus views the natural, material world as a sort of "sorceress" that bewitches the soul through the senses.</note> performs this. To follow what is not the Good as if it were the Good—while being lured by its appearance and rushing forward with irrational impulse—is a passion of the mind, being drawn secretly to where it did not wish <margin>C</margin> to go. What else shall we call this but a certain magical enchantment? Therefore, he alone is least snatched by such sorceries who, though drawn by other parts of himself, affirms that none of these things which seem good to the world are actually good. He relies only on what he himself knows, being neither deceived nor a mere follower, but a possessor of the truth. Such a man is never drawn away.

---

->*Man does not only act and suffer many things by fate as a certain part of the world, but he also possesses a proper substance by nature: partly related to higher things and partly to lower things. By free movement, he can moreover take on an affection and a habit that is congruent with either the higher or the lower.*<-

->*Such a habit finally becomes like a second nature to the soul, by whose instinct—under divine judgment—he is carried into a lot and a place fitting for either the heavenly or the earthly.*<-

### Chapter XLV.

---

<margin>A</margin> FROM all that has been said, it is manifest that whatever is contained within the universe is endowed with a specific nature and disposition; according to these, it contributes to the whole, acting and suffering <note>In philosophy, "suffering" (πάσχει / pati) refers to being acted upon or receiving an influence, rather than just physical pain.</note> accordingly. Just as in any living animal, every single part has its own nature and condition, so it contributes to the whole and serves it, being valued by its specific order and use. Furthermore, it gives something of itself and receives from others according to the capacity of its nature. There is, as it were, a certain <margin>B</margin> consensus <note>original: 'συναίσθησίς' / 'consensus' — a "sympathy" or "shared feeling" that binds the parts of the universe together like the organs of a body.</note> of the whole toward the whole. If any part were itself an animal, it would certainly perform the works of an animal, which are different from the works of a mere part. Hence, it is also clear what our own condition is: namely, how we also perform some function in the universe. We do not only do and suffer those things which a body does to a body, but we also bring another nature of our own into the midst. We are coupled through the kinship implanted within us to those kinships existing outside of us. Indeed, <margin>C</margin> we are shaped by our souls and our dispositions. Rather, we are contiguous both with the things placed closely beneath us in the daemonic realm <note>original: 'δαιμονίῳ τόπῳ' / 'loco dæmonico' — the sublunary realm or the intermediate space between the earthly and the purely divine, inhabited by spirits (daemons).</note> and with the higher things. And since we are thus disposed, it cannot be hidden what sort of beings we are. Therefore, we do not all offer the same things, nor do we receive the same. For that which we do not possess, how could we provide it to others as a good? And again, nature in no way...

He describes the universe as a single living organism where every part—including humans—acts and is acted upon according to its natural kinship with either higher divine or lower "daemonic" realms.</summary>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK 4

<margin>A</margin>
...if we are capable of the good, in what way shall we receive something good? Each person, by applying their own depravity, is discovered for who they truly are; according to their own nature, they are driven toward what they possess, both here in this life and after departing for another place, drawn by a certain natural attraction <note>original: 'tractu naturæ' / 'φύσεως ὁλκαῖς' — a Stoic and Neoplatonic concept of "cosmic sympathy" or magnetic-like pull where like is drawn to like.</note> to that which is similar. However, the upright man receives, gives, and is exchanged by a different logic, as each individual is moved to their proper place by certain natural "cords" <note>original: 'quasi funibus' / 'ἐκ μηρίνθων' — Plotinus uses the image of puppet strings or cosmic cords to show how the soul is tethered to the universal order.</note> or pulls.

<margin>B</margin>
This entire universe possesses such a marvelous power and order that all things are dispensed justly through a silent and hidden command, following a path under divine judgment. No one is permitted to escape the sentence of this judgment. No wicked person understands this, but is merely carried along, unaware, into that part of the universe where it is most fitting for them to be transferred. But the good man both knows this and approaches his destination willingly; even before he departs, he foresees where he must necessarily dwell after his passing, and he lives in good hope that he will one day dwell with the gods themselves.

<margin>C</margin>
In a small animal, the changes of the parts are likewise small and the harmonies are slight; the parts themselves are not independent living beings, except perhaps briefly in some cases. But in that Great Animal <note>Plotinus refers to the 'World-Soul' or the Universe itself as a single, living organism.</note> in which the distances are so vast, and every part undergoes its own inclination and change, and which contains many individual living beings within it, it is necessary that the movements and transfers be greater. Indeed, we see the sun, the moon, and all the stars being moved in a certain fixed order and changing their positions.

<margin>D</margin>
Therefore, it is not contrary to reason that souls are also moved from one place to another, not always maintaining the same character, but eventually ordered and arranged in a fitting proportion that agrees with their inner dispositions. For some souls obtain a rank like that of the "head," while others are like the "feet"—a rank that is appropriate to the whole universe. For the universe itself contains differences between the better and the worse.

<margin>E</margin>
If any soul chooses neither the better things found here nor is stained by the worse, it is moved to another place, eventually reaching that pure realm it had chosen. The punishments of souls are like the treatment of sick parts of a body: where some are bound with bandages, others are cut away or purged, and others have their qualities altered so that the whole may be healthy, with each part rightly arranged where it is most useful. For the health of the whole <term>Universal Health: the Neoplatonic idea that cosmic justice is not about revenge, but about maintaining the 'health' or harmony of the world-organism.</term> is the primary concern: this part is bound, that one has its qualities changed, and another is expelled from here as if it were languishing, and translated to a place where it may languish the least.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...being receptive to the good, we receive something of the good. Each person, having joined themselves to their own wickedness, is known for who they are; according to their own nature, they are pushed toward that which they hold, both here and then after departing from here, into another place by the "pulls of nature." But for the good man, whether in his takings, his givings, or his relocations, it is different: as if being moved by certain "strings" of nature <note>original: 'μηρίνθων' — literally "fine cords" or "fishing lines," suggesting a subtle but unbreakable connection to the Divine.</note>.

<margin>B</margin>
This universe possesses such a wonder of power and order, with all things happening by a noiseless path and by Justice <note>original: 'δίκη' (Dike) — the personification of Justice and the natural order of the universe.</note>, which no one can escape. The base man perceives nothing of this, but is led without knowing where he must be carried in the whole. But the good man both knows, and goes where he must. He knows even before departing where it is necessary for him to go and dwell, and he is of good hope, as he will be with the gods.

<margin>C</margin>
For in a small animal, the changes of the parts are minor, as are the shared sensations. In such an animal, the parts are not themselves living beings, except perhaps for a short time in some. But in that Being in which the dimensions are so great, and each thing within it has its own leaning, and there are many living beings within, it is likely that the movements and relocations are greater. We see indeed the sun, and the moon, and the other stars, relocated and moved in a set order.

<margin>D</margin>
It is therefore not unreasonable that souls too are relocated, not always preserving the same character, but being stationed in proportion to what they have experienced. They form a rank, like that of a "head." Some, as it were, take a place in harmony with the whole. For the whole itself has differences, toward the better and the worse. If a soul chooses neither the better state found here, nor participates in the worse, it is changed to another and pure place, receiving that which it had left behind.

<margin>E</margin>
And the punishments are like those of diseased parts: for some, the application of medicines; for others, removals or even alterations, so that the whole might be healthy, each part being disposed as it should. The healthiness of the whole comes from being altered, or from a part being removed from here because it is sick in this place, and being placed where it will not be sick.

# ENNEAD FOUR,
# BOOK FIVE.

->On the third set of difficulties regarding the soul, or on vision.<-

To sense is to perceive individual corporeal things through corporeal instruments. In sensory perception, we observe that the qualities or actions of external bodies reach all the way to the soul, or around the soul in some way; likewise, at times, the power and action of the soul extend themselves toward corporeal things. This could certainly happen in no way unless the soul possessed a certain proportion <note>original: 'proportionem' — a mathematical or harmonic relationship that allows two different things to interact.</note> to these things. Yet the soul does not have this relationship unless it forms a manifest body—and especially a "spirit" <note>original: 'spiritum' / 'πνεῦμα' (pneuma) — in ancient philosophy, this is a fine, airy substance that acts as a bridge or "vehicle" between the immaterial soul and the heavy physical body.</note>—in its own way through its vegetative power. In this way, the soul conforms itself so that its power and action may extend toward external things through its own body, as if through an instrument; and the movements of external things, by coming to this body, seem in some way to have reached the soul. Finally, for sight to perceive the object to be seen, there is no need for a physical medium outside the body to act as a necessary aid for seeing. For sight and the eye are, by their own nature, sufficiently prepared to be occupied with light, and light in turn with sight. If the intervening body is opaque, it hinders the process; but if it is transparent, it only has the property of not obstructing vision as an opaque body usually does; therefore, sight will perhaps occur even without this medium.
->Chapter I.<-

<margin>A</margin>

But since sensing is the perception <margin>truly</margin> of sensible objects only, how can the soul, having become joined to these sensible things, create a certain communion of knowledge or experience with them through things similar to itself? Therefore, even if it acts through instruments that are naturally grown together or continuous with it, it must approach the sensible objects themselves in a way that allows a certain "sympathy" <note>original: 'homopatheia' / 'ὁμοπαθείας' — the Stoic and Neoplatonic idea that all parts of the universe are "in sympathy" and can feel or react to one another instantly.</note> <margin>B</margin> to arise toward them. If, therefore, knowledge of things occurs through a certain contact, one might not question this regarding the senses that work by touch; but regarding vision, and later regarding hearing, there is more doubt. Specifically, concerning sight: must there be some body between the vision and the color? Or <margin>C</margin> perhaps that intervening body is there only by coincidence, and contributes nothing to the act of seeing for those who see? Yet if bodies are dense, like earthy things, they

# ENNEAD FOUR

### ON THE COSMIC ORDER AND THE DESTINY OF SOULS

If we are not capable of receiving the good, in what way shall we receive anything good? Therefore, each person, by applying their own wickedness, is recognized for who they are; according to their own nature, they are driven into that which they possess—both while here and after departing from here to another place—drawn by a certain attraction of nature toward what is similar to themselves. But the upright man receives, gives, and is changed by another principle, with each individual being moved to where they belong by the appropriate tracks of nature,
<margin>A</margin> as if by certain ropes <note>original: 'funibus' / 'μηρίνθων' — Plotinus uses the image of cords or strings to describe the invisible gravitational or sympathetic "pull" that draws a soul toward its appropriate place in the cosmic order.</note>. This universe possesses such a wonderful power and order that, by a certain silent and hidden command and
<margin>B</margin> path, all things are dispensed justly under divine judgment. No one at all is permitted to escape the sentence of this judgment. Indeed, no wicked man understands this, but is instead carried—clueless as he is—into that part of the universe where it is most fitting for him to be transferred. But the good man both knows this and approaches where he must; even before he arrives, he perceives where he must necessarily dwell after his arrival, and he lives in good hope that he will one day
<margin>C</margin> dwell with the gods themselves. In a small animal, the changes of parts are small and the shared sensations are slight, nor are the parts themselves independent animals, except perhaps in some cases for a short time. But in that "Animal" <note>original: 'animali' / 'ζώῳ' — Here, Plotinus refers to the "World Animal" or the Universe as a single living organism, a central concept in Neoplatonism where the cosmos has its own soul and body.</note> in which there are such vast intervals, and where everything undergoes its own inclination and change, and in which many living beings exist, it is necessary that the movements and transfers be greater. We see, surely, that the sun, moon, and all the stars are transferred in a fixed order and change their positions. Therefore, it is not inconsistent with reason that souls also are moved from one place to another, not
<margin>D</margin> always preserving the same character, but finally ordered and arranged in a fitting proportion as suits their dispositions. This happens while some, as it were, occupy the place of the head, and others the feet—a place, I say, that is fitting for the whole. For the whole also has differences between the better and the worse. If any soul chooses neither the better that is here, nor is stained by the worse, it is changed to another place, having at last
<margin>E</margin> attained that pure state which it had chosen. The punishments of souls are such as those of sick parts of a body: where some are bound with poultices, others are cut <note>original: 'circunciduntur' / 'ἐξαιρέσεις' — This refers to surgical "excision" or cutting away of diseased tissue to save the whole body.</note>, or purged, and others are changed in their qualities so that the whole may be healthy, with each part rightly disposed where it is useful. For the health of the whole is looked to above all; thus one part is bound, another is changed in its qualities, and another is expelled from here as if it were languishing, and moved to a place where it will languish the least.

<column-break/>

If you are not receptive to the good, you will not bring any good upon yourself. But each person, having attached themselves to their own wickedness, is known for who they are and is pushed according to their own nature toward what they hold, both here and when departing from here, by the pulls of nature toward another place. For the
<margin>A</margin> good man, the takings, the givings, and the relocations are different; just as if they were moved by certain cords of nature. Thus, this whole universe possesses a wonderful power and order, where all things that happen follow a silent path and
<margin>B</margin> just outcomes, which no one can escape. The base man understands nothing of this, but is led without knowing where he must be carried in the whole. But the good man both knows and goes where he must; he knows before he departs where necessity requires him to live when he has gone. And he is 
<margin>C</margin> of good hope, as he will be with the gods. For in a small living being, the changes and shared perceptions of the parts are small. And it is not possible for the parts in it to be living beings themselves, except perhaps briefly in some cases. But in a Being where the distances are so great, and where each thing in it has its own relaxation <note>original: 'χάλασιν' — A loosening or yielding, perhaps referring to the flexibility or individual movement of parts within the cosmic structure.</note> or where there are many living beings, the movements and migrations must be greater. We see the sun and the moon and the other stars being moved in order and changing their positions. It is not, therefore, irrational that 
<margin>D</margin> souls also are moved, not always keeping the same character, but being ordered in proportion to what they have experienced. This creates an order, such as that of a head, while others take up what is harmonious for the whole. For the whole itself has differences, such as the better and the worse. If a soul chooses neither the better things here nor the worse... <unclear>--</unclear> it is transferred to another place and changes to a pure state, having taken the place 
<margin>E</margin> which it chose. Punishments are like those of diseased parts; for some, there are medicines for rot, for others, removals or alterations, so that the whole may be healthy when each part is fitted where it should be. The health of the whole is maintained by the alteration of some parts and the removal of another from here—as it is sick here—and placing it where it will not be sick.

*TO SENSE is to perceive individual bodies through bodily instruments. He is specifically addressing the Aristotelian and Stoic theories of the "medium" (like air or water) and whether it must be physically altered for us to see, or if vision is a more direct "sympathetic" connection within a living universe.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD IV.

...hinder vision more, whereas the thinner the media are, the more easily we see through them. Someone might say these media contribute to seeing, or if they do not contribute, at least they do not stand in the way of vision. Yet another might say they are indeed obstacles. But we must ask whether the intervening body first receives an "affection" <note>original: 'passionem' / 'πάθος' — in this context, a physical change or impression made upon a substance</note> and is, as it were, formed by it. <margin>B</margin> Someone might offer this sign: that if someone is before our face or looking toward a color, they see it, but that very thing would by no means reach us unless a certain affection had been imprinted on the medium. But perhaps it is not necessary for the medium to be affected while that which is naturally exposed to such affection—namely, the eye—is affected. Or, if the medium is affected then, it is affected in some other way; for even the rod between the numbing fish called the Torpedo <note>original: 'Narcem' / 'νάρκης' — the electric ray fish, famous in antiquity for its ability to numb a fisherman's hand even through a wooden rod or net</note> and the hand is not affected in the same way the hand itself is; although here too, unless the rod and the line or hair were situated in the middle, the hand would not be affected at all. <margin>C</margin> Perhaps this too is to be doubted: for if the fisherman is inside the nets, he is said to be affected and numbed. It seems, however, that this discourse moves toward those things called "sympathies" <note>original: 'compassiones' / 'συμπαθείας' — the idea that parts of the universe respond to one another naturally because they belong to one living whole</note>: namely, if this thing is naturally able to be affected by that thing in turn because it has a certain similarity to it, it is not because the medium between them is affected (if the medium were dissimilar); or certainly the medium will not be affected in the same way. If this is so, the thing naturally subject to the affection will be affected much more where there is no medium, even if the medium were of such a kind as to be affected itself.

---

Between the sight and the visible object, light is necessary by itself, whether it be a common external light or one's own, either from the eye or from the nature of a very bright object. A body, however, is not so necessary as a medium between these. Vision occurs primarily because either a visual ray proceeds from the eye to the visible object, or something proceeds from the already luminous visible object to the sight, or both happen at once; and altogether because both the eye and the visible object are so disposed in the living nature of the world that they have a property highly conformed to each other, through which they are easily moved by each other, and act or are affected mutually. Therefore, a body is not necessary by itself to sustain and carry the ray flashing out from the eye, which naturally flows forward in a straight line without a support; nor to carry light in this way, whether it be the light of the object or an external one; nor even to complete the sympathy between the visible and the sight, for they are sufficiently exposed to each other's influence by themselves. Finally, it is not necessary for the intervening air to be colored and shaped by the object in the manner of wax, through which the sight might then be similarly affected; otherwise, to see, one would not need to turn the eye toward the distant object itself. For it would be enough for the eye to be touched by the part of the air contiguous to us that had already been "formed." In every way, the spiritual flows <note>original: 'spiritales fluxus' — the transmission of visual data</note> of the species of visible things would reach the eye through light without any affection of the air.

->Chapter II.<-

**I**f therefore vision happens in such a way that the light of the sight itself is joined with the intervening light as far as the sensible object, this medium must be light, and this supposition requires that medium. But if the underlying colored body affects and changes the medium in some way, what prevents such a change from reaching the eye immediately, even if no medium intervened? Since now, of necessity, that which intervenes is changed before the eye is changed, simply because it intervenes. <margin>B</margin> Furthermore, those who say we see through a certain effusion <note>original: 'effusionem' — the "extramission" theory where the eye sends out light to "touch" objects</note> of the sight itself are led by no reason to assert a medium, unless perhaps they fear lest the ray itself should fall; but the ray has the nature of light, and light is rightly diffused. Those, however, who assign a certain "resistance" as the cause of vision will certainly need a medium. But the supporters of "images" <note>original: 'simulachrorum' / 'εἰδώλων' — the Epicurean theory that thin films or skins of atoms peel off objects and travel to the eye</note>, who affirm that they pass through a vacuum, clear a small space so that they are not prevented from arriving. <margin>C</margin> Wherefore, if they are hindered much less where there is no medium, they will certainly not bring the present supposition into controversy.

<column-break/>

...prevents seeing. The thinner the media always are, the more we see: someone might again suggest the media are helpers to seeing; or if helpers, they are not hindrances—though another might say they are hindrances. But [we must see] if the affection is first received by the medium and is thus shaped. A sign of this is that if someone were in front of us or looking at the color, they also see it, even if an affection had not occurred in the medium which would then reach us. <margin>B</margin> Or it is not necessary for the medium to be affected if the eye, which is naturally fit to be affected, is affected; or if it is affected, it is affected differently. For the rod between the torpedo fish and the hand does not suffer what the hand suffers, and yet there, if the rod and the hair were not in the middle, the hand would not suffer. Or this itself one might dispute. For even if the hunter were inside the nets, he is said to be affected by the <margin>C</margin> numbness. But indeed the argument risks moving toward the so-called sympathies. If this is naturally fit to be affected by that through sympathy, by having a certain similarity to it, the medium, being dissimilar, would not suffer the same thing that the other would suffer; much more so if there were nothing in between, the thing naturally fit to suffer would suffer, even if the medium were discarded as being able to suffer something itself.

->Chapter II.<-

**I**f therefore vision is most of all like the light of the sight joining with the intervening light as far as the sensible object, then the medium must be light; or this is the hypothesis of the medium of the sensible things. But if the underlying body produces a turning <note>original: 'τροπὴν' — a change or transformation</note> while separated, what prevents the turning from going straight to the eye, with nothing in between? <margin>B</margin> But if now, of necessity, when it exists, that which lies before the eyes is turned in some way, and those who send out their sights would not be able to follow, unless they feared lest the ray should fall; but it is of light, and light travels in a straight path. Those who claim "resistance" <note>original: 'ἔνστασιν' — a Stoic concept of the air being under tension</note> is the cause would definitely need the intervening things. But those who say the images are carried and pass through the vacuum seek a space so they are not hindered. <margin>C</margin> So if it will not be hindered even more when nothing is in between, they do not dispute the hypothesis.

<summary>Plotinus argues that a physical medium like air is not strictly necessary for vision, proposing instead that sight relies on light and a "sympathy" between the eye and the object. He critiques various theories of vision, including those involving physical impressions in the air or the movement of images through a vacuum.</summary>
