<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation from page 442 regarding whether vision requires a physical medium (like air) to be "affected" or changed. He is weighing the Stoic idea of a physical "tension" in the air against his own theory of universal "sympathy," where the unity of the world-soul allows for perception at a distance without the intervening space needing to act as a physical bridge.</meta>

# FIFTH BOOK. 443

<margin>A</margin> Moreover, those who say that seeing occurs through sympathy <note>original: 'συμπαθείᾳ' — a shared resonance between parts of a living whole</note> would say that we see less clearly if something comes between us and the object, because this intervening thing would hinder or impede the sight, making the sympathy faint. Indeed, it is more consistent to say that the intervening space—even if it is of a related nature or is affected in the same way—necessarily makes the sympathy weaker. If a continuous body were burned deep inside by the application of fire, the part deep within would be less affected than the part where the fire was first applied. <margin>B</margin> But if the sympathy belongs to the parts of a single living being, would it be felt less because there is something in between? Or would the affection <note>original: 'πάθος' — a physical change or impression</note> not be less, but rather be as measured as nature intended, with the intervening space merely preventing it from being too intense? This assumes the medium is not of such a kind as to be entirely unaffected; for if the entire living being is sympathetic, we feel the affection because we are within that one unity. <margin>C</margin> Why then should there not be a requirement for continuity when perception happens at a distance? What is the role of the medium in this continuity? Is it because the living being must be continuous? But is the affection and the accidental property also continuous, or shall we say everything is affected by everything else? If one thing is affected by this, and another by that, or if they are not affected in the same way, then a medium would not be needed everywhere. <margin>D</margin> If someone says a medium is required for vision, what reason should they give? For it does not appear that something proceeding through the air everywhere causes the air to be affected; rather, it seems only to "divide" the air. For example, if a stone falls from above, what else happens? Does the air not simply give way? <margin>E</margin> It is not reasonable to say the stone is pushed by the air swirling around it, since the stone has its own natural downward motion. Similarly, fire moves upward—not because of the air swirling around it, but because it darts upward. Indeed, fire outruns the swirling motion of the air by its own rapid movement. If someone says the air is pushed quickly because of the speed of the object, this would only be an accidental effect, not the cause of the motion itself. Even with wood, the impulse is upward as it grows, without being pushed. <margin>F</margin> And when we move, we cut the air; it is not the swirling air that pushes us. The air behind us simply follows and fills the vacuum we create. If air allows for such distance between its parts during the movement of bodies without being otherwise affected, what prevents it from allowing the forms <note>original: 'εἴδεσιν' — the "shapes" or "images" that objects transmit to the eye</note> to pass through for the purpose of sight? <margin>G</margin> If these forms do not even arrive as a kind of "flow," what necessity is there for the air to be affected? And why must the affection reach us only because the air was affected first? For if our sensation resulted from the air being affected first, we would not see by looking at the visible object itself; rather, we would receive the sensation from the part of the air immediately adjacent to us, just as happens with heating. In that case, it is not the distant fire that seems to heat us, but the adjacent air that has been heated. That, however, is a matter of touch. But vision is not touch; therefore, the sensible object does not produce vision by being placed directly against the eye.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Furthermore, those who assert that vision occurs by a certain sympathy will say that we see less if some medium intervenes, because this will prohibit and impede it, rendering the sympathy weaker by its imperfection. Indeed, by consistent reasoning, we can say that the medium itself—even if it is related and also capable of being affected—nevertheless makes that sympathy more feeble. For if a continuous body is burned in its depths by the approach of fire, <margin>B</margin> the part placed in the depths will nevertheless be less affected than the upper part where the fire approached. But if the parts of a single animal are mutually sympathetic, will they be affected less because there is something in between? Perhaps they will be affected less; that is, the affection will turn out to be moderate, just as nature willed. This is because the interposed medium inhibits an excess of affection, unless perhaps it is of such a nature that the medium cannot be affected by it at all. <margin>C</margin> Moreover, if the whole is sympathetic because it is one single animal, and we are affected because we are in that one and belong to that one, why should there not be a requirement of continuity when something positioned far away is perceived? Perhaps continuity and the medium itself must be present somewhere because the animal must be continuous, but the affection is only an "accident" <note>original: 'per accidens' — a secondary property rather than the essence</note> of that continuity. Otherwise, we would have to admit that everything is affected by everything. <margin>D</margin> Then truly, if this thing is affected by this, and another by that, and they do not suffer the same thing, there will not be a need for a medium everywhere. If someone says that a medium is needed at least in vision, he ought to assign a reason; since it does not appear everywhere that what proceeds through the air brings an affection upon the air, but only divides it. Just as when a stone falls from above, nothing else seems to happen to the air except that it does not support the falling stone. <margin>E</margin> Nor is it likely that the stone falls because of a certain swirling intake of the surrounding air, since its descent is natural to it. Similarly, fire would also ascend by a similar intake of air, which is an absurd thing to say. For fire, by the velocity of its own motion, outruns the air that follows it. If anyone should say that the intake of air is itself accelerated by that velocity, this will nevertheless happen accidentally, and not properly "upward," since even from wood an impulse is made toward the heights, with nothing pushing them as they grow. <margin>F</margin> Even we, as we walk, divide the air; the swirling of the surrounding air does not push us then, but the following air merely fills the space that we leave empty. If, therefore, the air admits a distance between its parts through the motion of such bodies without suffering anything else, what prevents it from granting a passage to the "species" <note>original: 'speciebus' — the Latin translation of 'forms' (eidola), the visual images of things</note> for the sake of sight, even without such distance? <margin>G</margin> But if the species do not even arrive as a kind of "flow," what necessity compels the air to be affected? And why must the affection reach all the way to us because the air was affected beforehand? For if the sense were produced because the air was affected beforehand, we certainly would not perceive the visible thing by looking at the object itself, but we would report a sensation from the part of the air closest to us, just as happens in heating. In that case, it is not the distant fire, but the closest heated air that seems to heat us. But this affection belongs to touch, whereas in vision there is no touch; therefore, a sensible thing placed against the eyes does not produce vision.

<summary>Plotinus argues that vision is a result of universal sympathy rather than a physical chain reaction in the air. He uses the examples of falling stones and rising fire to show that the air is a passive medium that is "divided" by motion rather than a necessary transmitter of physical changes.</summary>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD IV.

But the medium must be illuminated, perhaps <margin>A</margin> because the air is dark. And if it were not obscure, perhaps it would not need light. For that which is dark, since it hinders vision, must be overcome by light. Perhaps, indeed, it is for this very reason that an object placed too close to the eye is not seen at all, because it brings with it a certain shadow, both of itself and of the air.

Between the sight and the visible object, the intervening air is not strictly necessary for this purpose: namely, that the form of the object should be imprinted successively through the parts of the air until it is finally imprinted on the eye. The first reason for this was assigned a little earlier. Two more follow, one of which is as follows: When we see a tiny flame <note>original: 'igniculum'</note> from a very great distance in the deep night, we must not think the form is imprinted step-by-step through continuous parts of the air. For it could not do this unless it also illuminated those same parts, yet it does not illuminate them; otherwise, we would see many other things along this straight line of sight. The second reason is this: If the air were painted by the person being seen in its own way—that is, a corporeal way—it would follow that the tiny part of the air closest and equal to the pupil would show the eye only that tiny fragment of the whole person that it carries; yet we see the whole object in any small portion of the air. Finally, the air "suffers" <note>In ancient philosophy, to "suffer" (pati) means to undergo a physical change or impression.</note> nothing from that species <note>original: 'specie' — here meaning the visible form or image of an object.</note> if any is sent from the object, just as it does not suffer from the light itself through which it is sent—from the light, I say, in its capacity as light. For in this way, it is present and gone in a moment, it does not remain once the illuminator is withdrawn, and it is a whole everywhere. From this, it appears that light does not become a proper quality of the air, nor is it truly corporeal. Therefore, this incorporeal thing does not proceed from a body so much as from the unity of the world. For even when you see a spark at a very great distance, you hear the tiny sound of a locust; and certain animals hear even the smallest things; likewise, bees and ants smell honey from very far away; even shellfish taste things at a distance; and the torpedo fish <note>The electric ray (Torpedo marmorata), famous in the ancient world for its ability to numb a fisherman through a wooden rod or spear without direct contact.</note> often numbs you through a long rod as if by touching you. It must not be thought—especially in the cases above—that the longest distance is physically broken and materially affected by even the smallest object; rather, something "spiritual" <note>original: 'spiritale' — meaning an immaterial or life-force influence rather than a ghostly one.</note> intervenes in a way, which acts through such a long distance upon the sense. That is, it is a specific "act" proceeding from the very species of the thing to be sensed. From the species, I say, not so much because it is in matter, but because it depends on a spiritual and living Idea. I also say it is a specific and spiritual "act," whether it happens here within us in the instrument of sense (as in touch and taste), or outside us in the air (as in sight, hearing, and smell), or even if it proceeds from the sight to the object. For in all things to be sensed, an "act" exists everywhere, even amidst the material "suffering" caused by the object in the air regarding the lower senses. It happens, therefore, at the right time by a certain power of the common life, by whose benefit all things are bound together so easily by distant things; thus the sense is moved, and a body of like form suffers from a like form at a distance. This is also apparent in magic, and how celestial bodies and many other things impart their powers to the most remote things. Finally, the common life of the world so tempers this sense with this sensible object that, when the sensible object acts, the sense is moved and acts—just as when a string is moved on a lyre, another tuned to it is immediately moved; and when you shout, a wall thus exposed echoes. We deal with these matters more diligently in our commentaries on Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus was Aristotle's successor; Plotinus's translator, Marsilio Ficino, is likely referring here to his own scholarly work connecting these traditions.</note>.

->Cap. III.<-

<margin>A</margin> But the greatest argument—that the forms of sensible things are not seen because the air has already received their species through continuous transmission—is that fire, stars, and their forms are seen under the cover of dark night. No one could claim that the species are impressed in the dark air and thus continued all the way to the eye; otherwise, it would not be dark where the fire handed over its species by illuminating it. Also, when fire is seen from watchtowers and torches—and from towers that provide signals for ships—even under deep darkness that hides the stars and fire and entirely blocks their light. If anyone should say that the fire also passes through these places, they would clearly be contradicting their own senses; for even the smallest things in the air would have to be seen in the meantime, not just the fire. If, therefore, with darkness in between preventing it, we nonetheless <margin>B</margin> see clearly what is beyond the darkness, we would discern it much better where there is no medium at all. But here someone might perhaps persist, asserting that where there <margin>C</margin> is no medium, nothing is seen—not indeed because a medium is properly lacking, but because the "animal sympathy" <note>The concept that the cosmos is a single 'animal' or living organism (Anima Mundi), where parts resonate with each other regardless of physical distance.</note> toward these very things would be entirely removed, as would the consensus of the parts among themselves within that which is a single consistent whole. For it seems that sense occurs in whatever way it does because this universal living being is everywhere "sympathetic" with itself. For if it were not so, how could one thing receive power from others, even the most remote? This, therefore, is worthy of consideration: If there were another world, and another—

<column-break/>

—but the medium must be illuminated because the air is dark. If it were not dark, perhaps light would not have been necessary, for darkness is a hindrance to seeing, which must be overcome by light. Perhaps also an object brought too close to the eye is not seen because it brings the shadow of the air and its own shadow with it.

<margin>A</margin> The greatest testimony that one does not see the sensible form and its shapes through the air being "affected"—as if by a hand-off <note>original: 'διαδόσει' — a transmission or succession.</note>—is that at night in the dark, fire and stars and their shapes are seen. For surely no one says that the forms, coming into the darkness, are thus joined, or else it would not be dark. Where fire has shone, there was its form; since even when there is much darkness and the stars are hidden, and fire and the light from them does not shine out, <margin>B</margin> the fire is seen from beacon-fires and from the towers signaling to ships. And if someone were to say the fire passes through the places, contradicting the senses, then the faint sight in the air, being squeezed <unclear>by those perceptions</unclear> of it, ought to be <margin>C</margin> clear. If what is beyond is seen while darkness is in the middle, much more would it be seen if there were nothing [in the middle]; rather, those things would act upon themselves. It is not because there is nothing in between that one will not see, but because the "sympathy" in the living being toward them is taken away, and the [relationship] of the parts toward one another for the sake of well-being. For it seems that sensing is somehow like this: because the living being, the "All," is sympathetic to itself. If it were not this, how would one part share in the power of another, especially one that is far away? This must indeed be examined: if there were another world and another—

<summary>Plotinus argues that vision is not a physical process of "stamping" an image through the air like wax, but rather a "spiritual act" made possible by the universal sympathy of the world-soul. He uses examples like night vision and the numbing touch of the torpedo fish to prove that perception can bypass or transcend the physical medium.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 444, where Plotinus challenges the idea that vision requires the physical air to be "stamped" with an image. He is moving toward a theory of universal "sympathy," where all parts of the living cosmos are interconnected.</meta>

# BOOK FIVE.

<margin>*</margin> If there were a living creature <note>original: ζῷον / animal</note> that had no connection to our own world, and there were a sense of sight on the "back" of the heavens, would such a sight see another world across that moderate distance? Or would there rather be no shared interaction <note>original: commercium</note> of acting or being acted upon between this world and that one? But this shall be treated in the following sections. For now, one might bring forward this additional evidence to prove that vision does not happen because the medium "suffers" <note>In ancient philosophy, "suffering" or "passion" refers to a physical change or impression made upon a substance.</note> a change. Truly, if the <margin>*</margin> air were to suffer, it would necessarily suffer in a bodily way; that is, it would be like a shape being imprinted in wax. If so, a specific part of the visible object would be shaped in a specific part of the air. Therefore, the part of the air touching the eye would only be as large as the pupil, and it would receive and pass on only that specific fragment of the visible object. Yet, in reality, the whole object is seen. Furthermore, all those who are in the air—whether looking straight ahead or from an angle, or even standing behind one another—see the object, provided they do not physically block each other. From this, it is clear that every tiny particle of the air contains the whole, like a face being looked upon. This does not happen through the conditions of a bodily "suffering," but rather according to <margin>*</margin> higher, vital, and psychic powers, and the necessities of a single living being that feels in sympathy with itself everywhere.

<column-break/>

---

> *If a medium is necessary between the sight and the visible object, it is not a physical body, but rather light—whether it is native to the eye or the object, or from an external source. Moreover, what contributes to seeing is not a "suffering" of the medium and the eye, but a certain action and light. The author touches upon three opinions regarding vision here: First, that the soul propagates itself through visual rays just as through hairs or hands, thus touching the sensible object without reflection. Second, that the soul does not propagate itself through the rays, but extends them like rods toward the object, which then reverberate back to the soul. Third, that light is shaped by the object, and this "shaped" light reaches the eyes. He plays with the first, mocks the second, and rejects the third. His goal throughout is to show that there is such a conformity of sympathy between the sight and the visible object that they move and act upon each other sufficiently, even if no physical change occurs in the medium. Just as the medium does not "suffer" when one string vibrates and another begins to tremble, or when one man yawns and another follows, or when a close friend imagines something and the other friend occasionally imagines the same thing.*

### Chapter IV.

<margin>* light</margin>
BUT how does the light that is connected to our vision relate to the light near the eye, and even to the light near the sensible object? Perhaps it does not actually need the air as a medium, unless one argues that light cannot be spoken of without air; in that case, the air is only a medium by accident. Light itself is a medium that "suffers" the least, and there is no need for physical "suffering" here at all, but perhaps only for a medium. If light is not a body, there is no need for a bodily medium. Yet someone might say that an external light and medium are not needed for <margin>* that which follows</margin> simple vision itself, but only for seeing things at a distance. Whether light can exist without air or not, we shall investigate in what follows. For now, let us first examine this: If this light connected to the sight is "animated" <note>original: ἔμψυχον / animatum; meaning it possesses the quality of soul/life</note> and the soul is carried through it and flourishes in it—just as it does in the innermost parts of the body—then in perceiving an object (which is what seeing is), the soul would have no need for a medium of light. Instead, seeing would be like touch, for the power of seeing would perceive within the light while the medium itself undergoes no physical change. Rather, the sight itself is carried there. One must then ask: must the sight travel there because of the distance, or because there is a <margin>* body</margin> body within that distance? If it is because there is a body in the way, then if that obstacle were removed, one would see clearly. But if it were said that it is simply because of the distance, one would have to assume that the nature of the visible object itself is idle and does nothing at all. But this is impossible.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of sense-perception, specifically addressing why a physical medium like air is not the primary cause of sight. Plotinus is arguing against the idea that the air must be physically "altered" (suffering a change) before the soul can perceive an object.</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

<margin>A</margin>For touch does not merely report that something is near or that it is being touched; rather, it reports the differences of the tangible object itself as it "suffers" <note>original Latin: passus / Greek: πάσχουσα. In ancient philosophy, "suffering" refers to being acted upon or undergoing a physical change.</note> from it. Indeed, unless something stood in the way, touch might even perceive things from a distance. For we and the intermediate air perceive fire at the same time, without waiting for the air to be heated first. In fact, a solid body is heated more quickly than the air is; therefore, the body grows hot *through* the air rather than *because* of the air. If, then, the visible object has the power to act, and the sense of sight has the power to be acted upon—<margin>B</margin>or however sight operates—why should it require another medium to act upon? To require a medium would be nothing other than requiring an obstacle. Furthermore, when the light of the sun arrives, it is not necessary for the air to be illuminated first and then us; rather, we are illuminated at the same time. Often, even while the light is still elsewhere, it happens that we see it, as if the air were not affected at all; this occurs when the medium has undergone no change, and the light has not yet reached the point where the sight must connect with it. Indeed, <margin>C</margin>under the opposite supposition, it would be difficult to assign a cause for how and why we see the stars and fire at night. But if the soul remains within itself and requires light as if it were a staff <note>original Greek: βακτηρίας. Plotinus refers to a Stoic theory where light acts like a walking stick, physically connecting the eye to the object.</note> through which it reaches out, the perception would have to be a violent one, resulting from a kind of reverberation of the extended light. In that case, the sensible color—insofar as it is color—would have to possess the power of reflecting, for that is how touches are produced through a medium. <margin>D</margin>Furthermore, the object was once near with no medium intervening. If it later makes cognition possible through a medium, it would be as if by a kind of memory or rather by a logical argument, but that is not what happens now. Truly, if the light approaching the sensible object must be "affected," and if that affection must سپس proceed through a continuous hand-off all the way to the sight, we fall back into the same supposition that claimed the medium is first changed and affected by the sensible object—an idea we have argued against elsewhere.

<column-break/>

For touch does not merely say that something is near or touches it, but it reports the differences of the tangible things by being affected, and if nothing were in the way, it would perceive even far-off things. For at the same time both the air in between and we ourselves feel the fire, not waiting for that air to be heated; for the solid body is heated more than the air. Thus, it is through the air rather than because of it. If the one has the power to act, and the other to be acted upon, or however sight works, why does it need another medium in which it has the power to act? This would be to need an obstacle. Since even when light is present, it is not the sun first, then the air, and then us; but at the same time we see the light as it comes near, often while it is still elsewhere, so that the air does not "suffer" for us to see, the medium being something that has not been affected; and the light has not yet come to that point where the sight must join it. Since also to see the stars at night, or fire at all, would be difficult to explain by this hypothesis. But if the soul remains in itself, and needs light like a staff to reach out, the perception would have to be violent and resistant, and the sensible color <gloss>* or color itself, stamping its own form</gloss> would have to be the thing itself. For that is how touches work through a medium. Then, also, it was previously near when nothing was in between. Thus, if touching through a medium later produces knowledge, it is like memory, or even more like a syllogism. But now it is not so; but if the light near the sensible object must be affected, then pass it on until the sight, the same hypothesis arises as the one that changes the medium first from the sensible object, which has already been questioned in other places.

***

*If any material "passion" <note>The term "passion" (passio) here refers to a physical impression or state of being acted upon by an external force.</note> is brought from the things perceived into the medium, it is because it is too different from the incorporeal nature of the sense; therefore, it often confuses the sense by its vehemence and is never suited to be the cause of perceiving, unless something spiritual <note>original Latin: spiritale. This refers to "spiritus," a subtle substance mediating between soul and body.</note> arises either in the medium or at least in the instrument of the sense. This spiritual element suited to the sense also appears in the voice. For the fact that the whole voice is perceived everywhere by many people at the same moment signifies that it is something spiritual. A thing of this kind is not generated by a bodily cause regarding any sense, but the very life of the world <note>The "World Soul" or "Anima Mundi."</note> procreates it in a subject that is then opportunely disposed. Moreover, this is so related to the sense that as soon as it flourishes in action around the sense, the sense itself—the act of it—is awakened toward it at the same time. Just as harmony is especially friendly to some men, and one person excites others to song and dance. That this sense acts immediately upon the action of this sensible object is achieved by the same life of the world everywhere, tempering this most especially with that and moving them together: just as the imagination is moved by the motion of a certain humor, and vice versa. Likewise, the humors are variously moved and affected by the various motions and phases of the Moon; flame is moved by the movement of sulfur; and where you direct your right eye, the left is also directed.*

***

### Chapter V.

<margin>*</margin> HOWEVER, regarding the sense of hearing, must we grant that the air is first moved, and then the air closest to the air first making the sound, and so on, with the air being affected step-by-step in the same way until it reaches the hearing? Or rather, in these cases, is the medium affected only "by accident" <note>original: secundum accidens. Meaning the air's involvement is a side effect, not the primary mechanism of perception.</note> because it happens to be in the middle? If the medium were removed, and a sound were made once by two bodies striking each other, would the sense of it be immediately excited in us?
Regarding sound, as when two bodies strike together,

<column-break/>

CONCERNING hearing, must we grant this: that the air suffers the first motion, then the air adjacent to the one making the noise, by the air suffering the same thing as far as the ear, and thus it arrives at perception? Or is it by accident that the things in between are present in the middle? If the things in between were removed, and the sound occurred once, would the perception immediately meet us?

He uses the examples of light and heat to show that we perceive things simultaneously with the medium, rather than because the medium is affected first.</summary>

# BOOK FIVE.

<margin>voice/sound</margin>
Perhaps there is indeed a need for the air to be struck at the beginning, but as for what follows next, the **medium** behaves in a different way. Here, the air seems to be the "master" of sound; for it seems that no sound could occur from the collision of bodies unless the air, struck by their swift meeting and driven out, handed over such a pulse to the succeeding air all the way to the ears and the sense of hearing. But if air is the master of sound, and sound is simply the pulse of this moved air, we must ask: on what basis are the differences between voices and sounds determined? For bronze struck against bronze sounds one way, but struck against something else it sounds another, and different bodies colliding produce different results. Yet the air is one, and the pulse within it is the same. Therefore, these differences are not determined solely by the "large" or "small" scale of the strike. If it were asserted that the authority over voice and sound belongs to the air—because a strike brought upon the air produces sound—one must respond that this is not caused by the air simply being air. For a resonance occurs when the air takes on the status of a **solid body** before it is dispersed, remaining, as it were, something solid. Therefore, the objects that strike one another are sufficient here, and we must say that the collision and the pulse are themselves the sound reaching the sense. An argument for this view is found in the sounds produced inside the bodies of animals, not in the air, but by one part of the animal striking another: such as the flexing of bones, or their mutual grinding where no air intervenes, as well as certain breakages and cuttings.
<margin>transfer</margin>
But let this be the inquiry concerning these matters, a question similar to the one regarding sight mentioned above. Indeed, concerning both that and this, it must be said that the power of perceiving consists in a certain **shared feeling** <note>original Greek: συναισθήσεώς / Latin: compassione. This does not mean "pity," but "feeling together"—a resonance between the observer and the object.</note> and a mutual agreement of things, as if they were all persisting within a single living being.

*Light depends not on the object illuminated, but on the source of illumination. Similarly, all life depends not on the thing animated, but on the soul, as its own proper activity <note>original: actus</note>, and it is guided by it even if every external support is removed. The primary body is celestial fire; the primary quality of this is light. Therefore, it is so perfect that it exists by way of an activity rather than as a passive quality. Indeed, this activity is so effective that it extends through all things without being severed from its own source. This kind of "color" is also called fire, which, being diffused everywhere, awakens the dormant colors of all things and surrounds them. Furthermore, in whatever body beneath the heavens a certain fiery vigor similar to the celestial prevails, light shines out from it like a familiar color. In the presence of the Sun, light heats the air. This heating indeed requires both—namely, the presence of the Sun and the air. But this heating is a fitting medium between light and heat. Certainly, heat can remain in the air even without the presence of light. Therefore, light can exist in the Sun without air, but the heat left behind by light does not remain in the air for long, because it is foreign to it; light, however, is always around the Sun because it is its own property. For what is one's own is inseparable. Certainly, light is the property of something, not of the **transparent** <note>original: diaphani. Plotinus argues that air/water are just "windows" and do not actually "own" the light they pass.</note> which is dark by itself; therefore, it belongs to the Sun itself and the solar body. And rightly so: just as there is one kind of form in the order of things that exists in itself, and another supported by something else, so too activity is twofold: one belongs only to the acting form, while the other lies upon the recipient. We have said elsewhere that light does not become a property of the transparent medium, because it is neither taken up gradually, nor retained, nor is it stained or moved along with it, nor do lights mix with one another; therefore, they are not mingled with other qualities. That they do not mix is apparent from the fact that if a single body is placed opposite three lights, three shadows result on the opposite side, because the three lights there remain distinct. Furthermore, if a huge board with a hole in the middle is placed opposite three candles, three lights leap out on the other side: one straight ahead, and the other two from the sides, intersecting one another without being confused. Similarly, minds and souls joined together are not at all confused. Light is rightly neither captured by a subject nor mixed with anything, because all light is an image of the celestial light; and that celestial light is the activity of the celestial soul. Just as a word is emitted from the soul as an activity of the imagination reaching outward—in which there are three things: air, motion, and meaning—so from the intellectual light of the celestial soul, a most effective activity is poured through all things, in which there are three things: light, heat, and a **hidden power** <note>original: vis occulta. This refers to the Neoplatonic idea of "sympathy," where things affect each other through non-obvious, spiritual connections.</note>. Light reaches some places where heat does not, and vice versa. But the hidden power in this activity, which is its greatest part, passes through all things and performs wonders, not by heating formally or by illuminating openly, but by bestowing specialized virtues.*

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

#### COLUMN 1

...becomes entirely a vacuum. Indeed, air is now <margin>A</margin> illuminated **by accident**, because it happens to be the medium situated in between. Or perhaps other things are affected because the air itself is **affected** <note>original: "patientem", referring to the air being the recipient of an action</note>, and the very nature of light exists because of the air, of which it is a certain **affection** <note>original: "passio", a state of being acted upon</note>? If it were an affection of the air, light would surely not exist unless the "affected" air also existed. But light does not belong to the air itself primarily, nor by virtue of it being air. For every fiery and brilliant body has its own splendid color, as do certain stones; <margin>B</margin> but what about that which flows from the possessing body into another? If this "flow" were nothing else—that is, if it were merely a **quality**—then since every quality must exist in a subject, we would have to look for light within the body it inhabits. But if light is an **activity** <note>original: "actus", translating the Greek "energeia"</note> proceeding from another, why—if the underlying body were removed and we imagined a vacuum—would it not exist and extend even further? Since it is intense and upright, what prevents it from passing through even if it is not "carried" by anything and <margin>C</margin> is not blocked anywhere? If light were the kind of thing that "falls," it would be carried along on its own accord. Neither the air nor any illuminated thing is what draws this light from the illuminator or compels it to come forth. Light is not an **accident** <note>a secondary property</note> such that it must be entirely in another, or a certain affection of another, requiring something to be affected. Otherwise, when the source of illumination departs, the light would have to remain in the illuminated object. But in fact, the light leaves; therefore, perhaps it moves forward? To where, then? Does it only require space? <margin>D</margin> Otherwise, the body of the Sun would lose its own activity which depends upon it. That activity is light. If this is so, then light will not "belong" to any subject. It is an activity flashing out from a certain source, yet not passing into a subject [as a permanent property]; but if a subject happens to be present, it will be affected by it. Truly, just as **life**—which is an activity—is the activity of the **soul**, such that an underlying body (if present) is affected by it, yet even if the body is not present, that activity remains; so <margin>E</margin> nothing seems to prevent light from behaving the same way, since it is a certain activity of a luminous body. For it is not the darkness of the air that generates light, nor does light produced by the earth’s darkness mixed with impurity create light; that would be like saying something becomes sweet just because it is mixed with something bitter. Therefore, if someone says light is a **transformation** or affection of the air, they must also say the air itself is changed by this transformation, and its dark condition <margin>F</margin> is no longer dark. But in fact, the air remains exactly as it is, as if it has suffered nothing. Yet every affection must belong to the thing that is affected. Light, therefore, is not a "color" of the air, but subsists in itself; the air is merely present alongside it. And let this be enough on that matter.

<column-break/>

#### COLUMN 2

...being a vacuum. And now by accident, because <margin>A</margin> everything is illuminated. But if because the air itself is affected, other things are affected too, and the existence of light depends on the air—for it would be an **affection** <note>original: "pathēma"</note> of it—then the affection would not exist if there were no subject to be affected. First of all, light does not belong to the air primarily, nor as air. For every fiery and bright body, and even such stones, have a luminous color. But regarding that which goes out from the possessor of such color into another—would that not exist if the air were not there? If it were only a **quality**, and a quality of something, then since all quality is in a subject, it would be necessary <margin>B</margin> to seek the light in the body it inhabits. But if it is an **activity** <note>original: "energeia"</note> from another, why—if there were no body following in succession but instead a vacuum in between (if that were possible)—would it not exist and reach to the beyond? For it is un-strained. Why would it not pass through even if it were not "riding" on a medium? If it were the sort of thing that "falls," would it not be carried along? For neither the air, nor the illuminated thing at all, <margin>C</margin> is that which draws light from the illuminator or forces it to approach. Since it is not an accident—so as to be primarily in another—nor an affection of another, there is no need for a subject to be affected. Otherwise, it would have to remain after the illuminator had left. But now it departs, so it might as well move forward. Where to, then? Does it only need a place? Or will it exist as the activity of the sun’s body, depending on the sun? <margin>D</margin> That is what light is. If so, light will not belong to a subject. It is an activity from a certain source, but not *into* a subject; however, the subject would be affected if it were present. Even when the body is not present, the activity exists. What prevents light from being this way, if it is an activity of the luminous source? For neither <margin>E</margin> does the darkness of the air now generate light, nor does the air mixed with earth create a dark and impure light. That would be like saying the sweet exists because it was mixed with the bitter. If anyone calls light a **turning** <note>original: "tropē", a change in state</note> of the air, one must say that the air itself must be turned by that turning; and its darkness, having been altered, would no longer be darkness. But now the air remains as it is, as if <margin>F</margin> having suffered nothing. But an affection must belong to that which is affected. Therefore, light is not a color of the air, but exists by itself. The air is merely present. Let this be investigated thus far.

***

*Just as other bodies always cast something out from themselves—namely vapor, or a power, or an image—so the stellar body and its like emit their own activity. And because it is emitted effectively, such an activity is light even at a distance, reaching external things while meanwhile not leaving its own source. Between the light that is entirely internal to the luminous body, and the heat that has already become internal to the air, light is partly internal to the shining source and partly proceeds outward; it is carried not like a spoken word between thought and its construction. At the same moment light penetrates a soft transparent medium, it also strikes through even the hardest. It is therefore incorporeal, for the hardness of a body does not resist it. Nevertheless, because it is a real thing, we should not attribute the "affections" of a body to it—that is, we should not say it approaches, recedes, flows back, flows through, contracts, or dilates. Rather, we should say that wherever a transparent medium is exposed to a luminous source, light exists there immediately and acts there; otherwise, it does not exist.*

<summary>This page explores the metaphysics of light, arguing that light is an "activity" (energeia) of a source like the sun rather than a physical change or "affection" of the air. Plotinus concludes that light is incorporeal because it can pass through hard transparent solids without being blocked by their physical density.</summary>

# BOOK FIVE

...to stand, there not to act. Nor, however, does it simply cease to be as long as the body is luminous. Similar to light is the radial activity <note>original: "actus", translating the Greek "energeia", meaning the outward operation or "working" of a thing's nature</note> of a sight directed into a mirror. <margin>A</margin>
We must ask whether light, upon the departure of that which illuminates, immediately vanishes: or rather returns back into the source. For perhaps from this we might also gain something for our present purpose: if indeed, in going back inside to where it came from, it has what it received as its own, one might perhaps say it perishes. But if it is an activity <note>original: "energeia"</note> not flowing out from a source—otherwise it would flow around and be possessed within, even more than what came from the agent—it will surely not be destroyed, <margin>B</margin> insofar as that which illuminates remains in its own substance. But when that source is moved, this light also exists in another place: not as if some reflux or transflux were occurring, but because that activity exists, and it reaches as far as nothing stands in the way of its being present. Since even if the distance were much greater than that of the Sun from us now, the light of the Sun would fill that whole space, provided no one prohibited it, nor any obstacle hindered it anywhere. There is, however, one activity in the luminous body, which is like the very life of the <margin>C</margin> luminous body, and as it were a principle and source of activity. There is also another activity beyond the limits of the luminous body, which is the image of the interior one, a second activity not at all separated from the first. Truly, every existing thing has an activity, which is a certain likeness of itself: so that while the thing itself exists, the activity exists: and while the thing remains, the activity proceeds to the remote: partly indeed further, and partly shorter, and some activities are weak and thin, and some even hidden: but of some things, the activities are greater, <margin>D</margin> and are poured out far away. And when they proceed to remote things, they must be thought to exist where the agent and the power are, and again where the activity runs. Hence we see in animals whose eyes naturally shine, light flashing out from the eyes: in animals also which possess fire gathered within, when they open their senses, light shines out in the darkness: and when they close themselves, nothing of light is left outside. This light indeed does not entirely vanish, but either is indeed, or is not <margin>E</margin> outside. What then, does it return into the animal itself? Or rather, must it be said not to be outside? Since neither did the fire proceed to external things, but insinuates itself into the internal parts. Did light itself then insinuate itself? Perhaps not, but only that fire. When, however, that which illuminates hides itself, another body now stands in the way, so that it does not act toward external things. Therefore, the light itself flowing from bodies is a certain activity of a luminous body proceeding to external things: but the light <margin>F</margin> altogether inherent in such bodies, which are indeed primarily luminous, is essence <note>original: "ousia"</note> according to the form <note>original: "speciem" / "eidos", the ideal blueprint of a thing</note> of a primarily luminous body. When, however, such a luminous body is mixed together with matter, it displays color: but activity alone does not display color, but as it were a certain coloration, inasmuch as it belongs to another, and is continually hanging from it; indeed, what is absent from that source is moreover absent from its activity. Then indeed it is necessary to judge light entirely incorporeal, although it is an activity of a body. Therefore not properly...

## PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

<margin>A</margin>...becomes entirely empty. Which indeed is now illuminated by accident, arising from the fact that this intermediate body happens to intervene. Or perhaps, because the air itself is affected <note>original Latin: "patientem"; Greek: "paschonta"—referring to a substance undergoing a change or receiving an influence</note>, other things are also affected, and the nature of light exists because of the air itself, of which it is a certain affection? And since it is an affection of the air, it would surely not exist unless the affected air also existed. But indeed, light does not belong to the air itself primarily, nor by the reason that it is air. For there is also a splendid color belonging to every fiery and shining body, and to <margin>B</margin> similar gemstones: but this very thing which flows from that source possessing such a color into another thing—will it now exist? If this other thing were not there at all: certainly if it is only a quality, and a quality of something, since every quality is in a subject <note>original: "subiecto"; the underlying substance that supports properties</note>, it is necessary to seek light in that body in which it resides. But if light is an activity <note>original Latin: "actus"; Greek: "energeia"</note> from another, why—if the body beneath it were absent and a vacuum were imagined—would it not exist and even extend itself further upward? For since it is intense and upright, what prevents it from <margin>C</margin> passing through even if it is carried by nothing and blocked nowhere? But if it is of such a nature as to fall, it will be carried down of its own accord: for neither air, nor anything illuminated, will be what draws this from the illuminant and compels it to go forward. Since it is not even an accident <note>a non-essential property</note>, such that it must be entirely in another, or a certain affection of another, so that there must be something to undergo the effect: otherwise, it would be necessary for the light to remain in the illuminated thing when the source of illumination departs. <margin>D</margin> But now it departs: and so perhaps it moves forward. To where, then? Or perhaps there must only be a place? Otherwise, the body of the Sun will lose its own activity which depends upon it. And that activity is light. If this is so, light will not belong to anything. It is indeed an activity flashing forth from a certain subject, yet not passing into a subject: but the subject, if it happens to be present, will undergo something beneath it. Certainly, just as <margin>E</margin> life, which is also an activity, is an activity of the soul, under which something like a body, if present, is affected—and even when the body is not present, such an activity exists—so nothing seems to prevent light from behaving in the same way, if indeed it is a certain activity of a luminous body. For it is not the darkness of the air that now generates light, nor does the darkness itself, mixed with the earth and entirely impure, procreate light: for that would be <margin>F</margin> just as if one were to say something becomes sweet simply by being mixed with the bitter. Furthermore, if anyone should say that light is a transformation and affection of the air, he must further say that the air itself ought to be affected differently in this transmutation, and its dark condition, having been changed into something else, would no longer be dark. But now the air remains as it is, as something which has in truth suffered nothing. Yet every affection must belong to that which is affected. Therefore, light is not a color of the air, but consists in itself; the air merely stands by it. And let this much be said concerning this matter.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...being a vacuum, and now it is by accident, because it is present to the illuminated thing. But if because of the air being affected, other things are also affected, and the existence of light is because of the air: for it is an affection to it, so the affection would not exist if the affected thing were not present. First of all, it does not belong to it primarily, nor insofar as it is air. For there is also a luminous <margin>B</margin> color in every body, fiery and bright, and indeed in such stones: but as for that which goes into another thing from that which has such a color, would it exist if that other were not there? But if it is a quality only, and a quality of something, if it is in a subject as every quality is, it is necessary to seek light in the body in which it will be. But if it is an activity <note>original Greek: "energeia"</note> from another, why, if there is no body in succession, but as it were a vacuum in between—if such a thing were possible—will it not exist and reach to the beyond? For being <margin>C</margin> intent, it will also pass through by itself, not being carried. But if it were of the nature to fall, it would be carried down. For it is not the air, nor the illuminated thing at all, that will be: but that which is drawn by the illuminant and forced to come forward. Since it is not an accident, so as to be entirely in another: or an affection of another, so that there must be something affected, or it would have to remain when the source has gone. But now it departs, so it would also go away. Where then? <margin>D</margin> Or must there only be a place? Or will the body of the sun lose its activity, the one from itself—namely, the light? If this is so, not even the light will belong to anything. But it is an activity from a certain subject, but not into a subject: or the subject would be affected if it were present. And even when not present it exists, so what would prevent this from being the case with light? <margin>E</margin> If indeed the luminous were a certain activity. For even now the darkness of the air does not beget light, nor does light mixed with the earth make it dark and truly impure. So that it is similar to saying that the sweet exists if it were mixed with the bitter. But if someone were to say that light is a <margin>F</margin> turning <note>original: "tropē"; a change or conversion</note> of the air, it must be said that the air itself ought to be turned by the turning: or its darkness, having been altered, would not be dark. But now the air remains as it is, as if having undergone nothing. But the affection must belong to that to which it is an affection; therefore it is not even a color of it, but belongs to itself by itself. But the air is present, and as for this, let it have been examined thus far.

---

-> Just as other bodies always project something out of themselves, namely vapor, or power, or an image, so the sidereal body <note>the body of the stars or heavens</note> and its like emit their own activity outward. And because it acts effectively, such an activity is light at a distance, touching external things while meanwhile not leaving its own source. Between the light that is entirely internal to the luminous body, and the heat that has already become internal to the air, there is a light that is partly internal to the shining thing and partly proceeding outside, almost like speech <note>original: "sermo"</note> between thought and the finished work. In the same moment that light penetrates a soft transparent medium, it strikes through even the hardest transparent thing. It is therefore incorporeal, as the hardness of a body does not resist it. Nevertheless, because it is celestial, a naturally earthy obstacle—even if it is less hard—does not admit the light. Since therefore it is incorporeal, we ought not to attribute to it the passions of a body—that is, to approach, to recede, to flow back, to flow through, to be contracted, or to be dilated—but rather, where a transparent medium is exposed in the presence of a shining thing, light immediately exists there and acts there; otherwise, it does not exist. <-

He concludes that light is incorporeal because it can penetrate solid transparent objects and exists immediately whenever a medium is present.</summary>

BOOK FIVE.

...to stand, there not to act. Nor, however, does it simply cease to exist as long as the body is luminous. It is similar to the light of a radial activity of sight <note>original: "radialis actus spectaculi"; referring to the ancient theory of "extramission," where the eye sends out rays to perceive objects</note> directed into a mirror. Likewise, the vital activity of the soul is directed into the body. Every vital activity is immortal. And that activity which is extended from our soul into the body accompanies the soul perpetually. And that which flows into the body from the soul of the world <note>The *Anima Mundi*, a concept in Neoplatonism where the entire universe is envisioned as a single living being with a soul</note> follows this soul also constantly.

# Chapter VII.

<margin>A</margin> IT MUST BE ASKED whether light, when the illuminating source departs, immediately vanishes, or if it instead returns to its source. For perhaps from this inquiry we might also make progress regarding the subject we have proposed. Truly, if light is so fixed in the illuminated body that it has already become its own property, one might perhaps say it perishes. But if it is an activity <note>original Greek: "energeia"; Latin: "actus"</note> that does not flow out from its source—otherwise it would flow around and be possessed within—it exists even more than just <margin>B</margin> to the extent that the thing which illuminates remains in its own substance. But when that source is moved, this light also springs forth in another place: not as if some back-flow or trans-flow occurs, but because that activity exists and is present only so far as nothing stands in its way. For even if the distance were far greater than that which now exists between us and the Sun, the light of the Sun would fill that entire space, provided there was no prohibition or obstacle anywhere impeding it. There is, however, one activity in the luminous source, which is like the abundant life <margin>C</margin> of the luminous body, and a kind of principle of acting outward. There is also a second activity beyond the boundaries of the luminous body, which is the image of the internal one, and this second activity is never separated from the first. Indeed, every existing thing has an activity which is like its own likeness: so that while the thing itself exists, the activity exists; and while the source remains, the activity reaches out to distant things—partly further, partly shorter; some are weak and faint, others are even joyful; but the activities of some things are greater <margin>D</margin> and are poured out from afar. And when they proceed to remote things, they must be considered to exist where the acting and powerful source is, and again, to where the activity runs. Accordingly, we see in animals whose eyes naturally shine that light flashes out from the eyes; also in those animals that possess a fire collected within, when they open themselves, light shines out into the darkness; and when they close themselves, no light is left outside. This light does not entirely perish, but either is or is not <margin>E</margin> external. What then? Does it return into the animal itself? Or is it rather to be said that it is simply not outside? Since the fire did not proceed to the external parts, but has hidden itself within. Has the light itself then hidden itself? Perhaps not, but rather only that fire. When that which illuminates hides itself, another body now stands in the way, so that the light does not act toward the outside. Therefore, the light emanating from bodies is a certain activity of the luminous body proceeding outward. But the light <margin>F</margin> entirely innate in such bodies—those which are primarily of such a nature—is the essence <note>original Greek: "ousia"; Latin: "essentia"</note> according to the form <note>The "form" (eidos/species) is the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is</note> of a primarily luminous body. When such a body is mixed together with matter, it produces color; but the activity alone does not produce color, but a kind of coloration, insofar as it belongs to another and flows continuously from it. From which, indeed, whatever is absent, it is also absent from its activity. Furthermore, one must certainly judge light to be incorporeal, even though it is an activity of a body. PLOTINUS, ENNEADS, BOOK IV.

<margin>A</margin> ...becomes entirely empty. For indeed, it is now illuminated by accident <note>In philosophy, "by accident" means a property that isn't essential to a thing's nature, like the color of a shirt.</note>, because this intermediary body happens to intervene. Or perhaps, because the air itself is affected, other things are affected too, and the nature of light exists because of the air itself, of which it is a certain affection? And since it is its affection, surely it would not exist unless the affected air also existed. But light does not belong to the air itself primarily, nor by the logic of it being air. For there is also a brilliant color belonging to every fiery and shining body, and to similar stones. But this very thing <margin>B</margin> which flows from that which possesses such color into another—what will it be? If it were not something else: certainly if it is merely a quality, and a quality of something, since every quality is in a subject, it is necessary to seek light in that body in which it exists. If, however, light is an activity <note>original: "actus"; Greek "energeia"</note> from another source, why then, if the underlying body were absent and a vacuum were imagined, would it not exist and extend even to what is beyond? For since it is intent and upright, what prevents it from passing through even if carried by nothing and not <margin>C</margin> blocked anywhere? But if it is such that it "falls," it will be carried along of its own accord; for neither the air nor anything illuminated will be what draws this from the illuminator and compels it to go forward. Since it is not even an accident, such that it is entirely in another, or some affection of another, so that there must be something that is affected. Otherwise, it would be necessary that when the thing that illuminates departs, the light would remain in the thing illuminated. But in fact, it goes away; and so, perhaps it moves forward. Where, <margin>D</margin> then? Does it perhaps require space alone? Otherwise, the body of the Sun will lose its own activity which depends on it. And that is light. If this is so, light will not belong to anyone. It is indeed an activity flashing out from a certain subject, yet not passing into a subject; but if a subject happens to be present, it will undergo something beneath it. Truly, just as life—which is also an activity—is an activity of the soul, beneath which even something like a body, if present, is affected; and even when the body is not present, such an activity exists; so nothing seems to prevent <margin>E</margin> light from behaving in this way, if indeed it is a certain activity of a luminous body. For it is not the darkness of the air itself that now produces light, nor does the darkness mixed with the earth—which is entirely impure—generate light. For that would be just as if someone said something would become sweet if only it were mixed with something bitter. Therefore, if anyone should say light is a transformation and an affection of the air, he must further say that the air itself ought to be affected differently in this transformation, and its dark condition, having now been changed into something else, would no longer be dark. But in fact, the air remains as it is, as if it has truly <margin>F</margin> suffered nothing. Yet every affection must belong to that which is affected. Therefore, light is not the color of the air, but it exists in itself; the air, however, is merely present. And let this much be said on this matter.

<column-break/>

...of a vacuum being [present], and now by accident, because it is present to the thing being illuminated. But if, because the air itself is affected, other things [are affected], and the subsistence of light is due to the air—for it would be an affection of it—then the affection would not exist if the thing affected did not exist. First, it does not belong to it [the air] primarily, nor insofar as it is air. For there is also a brilliant color of every fiery body, and indeed of such stones. But that which goes from the thing having color into another—would that exist if the other did not? If it were only a quality, and a quality of something, and every quality exists in a substrate, it would be necessary to seek light in whatever body it is in. But if it is an activity from another, why—if there is no body in sequence but only a vacuum between, if that were possible—would it not exist and reach to the beyond? For being intense, why should it not pass through without being carried? But if it were such as to "fall," it would be carried down. For it is not the air, nor the illuminated thing at all, that draws it from the illuminator and forces it to go forward. Since it is not an accident, so as to be entirely in another, nor an affection of another, so that there must be a recipient; otherwise, it would have to remain when the source departs. But now it goes away, so it would also come. To where? Does it only need a place? Or does the body of the sun lose its own activity, the one from itself? For that is light. If this is so, light will not belong to anyone. It is an activity from a certain substrate, but not into a substrate. Yet the substrate would be affected if it were present. And even if it is not present, it is [an activity]. What prevents this from being the case with light, if light is a certain activity? For the darkness of the air does not now generate light, nor does [the air] being mixed with earth produce a dark and truly impure [light]. So that it would be like saying that sweetness exists if it were mixed with bitterness. But if someone should call light a "turning" <note>Greek: "tropē"; a change or conversion</note> of the air, it must be said that it would be necessary for the air itself to be turned by this turning, and for its darkness to become not-dark, having been altered. But now the air remains as it is, as if it has suffered nothing. And the affection must belong to that which is affected; therefore, it is not its [the air's] color. But it is itself by itself. *Just as other bodies always project something out of themselves—namely vapor, or power, or an image—so the celestial body and its like emit their own activity; and because it is effective, such an activity at a distance is light, reaching indeed external things, while meanwhile not leaving its own source. Between the light that is entirely internal to the luminous body, and the heat that is now made internal to the air, light is partly internal to the shining thing and partly proceeding outside, much like speech between thought and the finished product <note>original: "sermo inter cogitationem atq; fabricam"; comparing the expression of light to how spoken words bridge internal thought and external physical creation</note>. In the moment light penetrates the soft transparent medium <note>original: "diaphanum"; a medium like air or water</note>, at the same moment it pierces even the hardest transparent medium. It is therefore incorporeal <note>original: "Incorporeum"; lacking physical body or matter</note>, which the hardness of a body does not resist. Nevertheless, because it is celestial, the earthly obstacle of nature—even if it is less hard—does not receive light. Since therefore it is incorporeal, we ought not to attribute the affections of a body to it—that is, to approach, to recede, to flow back, to flow through, to be contracted, or to be dilated. But rather, where a transparent medium is exposed in the presence of a shining thing, light immediately exists there and acts there; if not, it does not exist.*

He concludes that light exists instantly in any suitable medium without being "carried" like a physical object.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul’s relationship to the body, specifically investigating whether the life force "departs" or simply ceases to be present when the body dies. It concludes Chapter 7 and begins Chapter 8 of the fourth Ennead.</meta>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS. BOOK IV.

<margin>A</margin> Concerning this, it is said that it specifically either approaches or departs; but these things behave differently there, for the very substance of the soul is like an activity <note>original Latin: "actus", Greek: "energeia"; in Neoplatonism, this refers to the outward expression or "actualization" of a being's power</note>. Indeed, we must also call the image in a mirror an "activity" of that which is seen in the mirror, acting upon that which is capable of being affected. In this case, nothing actually flows out; rather, if the object is present, the image appears there too. It is like the image of a color formed in a certain way. And if the object departs, the transparent body no longer holds what it previously held when the spectacle itself was acting upon the mirror. Accordingly, regarding the soul <margin>B</margin> as well, insofar as it is the activity of a prior soul, as long as the prior soul remains, the accompanying activity also remains. But if there is a power that is not an activity of the soul itself, but derived from an activity—such as the life we have called "proper to the body"—does it behave like light that has been let into bodies? Perhaps we might say this light resides there because that which creates color is mixed with it. But what of the life proper to the body? Perhaps the body retains this while another soul, so to speak, stands by; for nothing can be entirely devoid of soul. When, therefore, the body perishes and it is no longer sufficient for it, either the life it supplied until now or even that which stands by, in what way does life still remain? What then? Has it perished? Perhaps even this has not perished; for this too is a kind of image of an illumination. It must only be said that it is no longer there.

*Since the world is a universal and sensible body, nothing sensible can truly be placed outside the world. If you were to imagine a body outside that communicates in no way with the world, it would not be perceived by the world's senses; but if it communicates in any way, it is no longer outside, but inside. Just as when a toe is hurting, the groin immediately suffers with it—and these parts more than the knees, though they are further away—it happens because they are in the same animal and are especially similar in nature to one another. Similarly, the stomach suffers when the brain is affected, and vice versa. By the same logic, the fact that senses even at a great distance respond to the slightest movements of their sensible objects, even if the medium between them does not suffer, is caused by this single, continuous nature of the world. Just as the continuity of a very long and tight string causes the highest part to vibrate immediately when even the lowest part is struck. From this it also happens that we imagine series of events hanging from the heavens and still to come, or more often imitate them by some hidden instinct, and sometimes anticipate a friend coming toward us by a certain hidden sense before he arrives.*

### Cap. VIII.

<margin>A</margin> If a body were outside the heavens, and an eye from this world were directed toward it, with nothing preventing it from seeing, it is doubtful whether it could see that body, since it would share no "sympathy" <note>original: "passionis communione" / "sympathes"; the Greek idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected and "feel" together</note> with it. For as it stands, a communion of feeling exists in things because of the single nature of the one Living Being <note>The "World Animal" or "Soul of the World"</note> common to all everywhere. Perhaps, if sympathy regarding sensory objects and the senses themselves is judged to belong to the nature of one Living Being, then this world would not see that body at all, unless perhaps that external body were said to be a member <margin>B</margin> of this living being of ours. If it were its member, perhaps it would see it. But if it were not a member, yet were a colored body and had other qualities like those in this world, and were therefore similar in form to the sensory instrument of this world, one might think it could be seen. But not even so, if the supposition is correct: unless one seeks to remove the supposition itself by asserting it would be quite absurd if the sight did not plainly behold a present color, and similarly if the other senses did not act toward the objects present to them. We, however, shall say whence this absurdity appears to us: perhaps because here, being both in one and of one...

<column-break/>

...it has truly departed, nor has it "presence": but these things exist in another way, and its existence is to him as an activity. Since also the image in the mirror must be called an activity of the one who is seen, acting upon that which is able to be affected, not flowing out but if it is present, that image also appears there. And it exists in this way as an image of color, shaped in this manner. And if it departs, the transparent no longer holds what it held before, when the object seen provided the power to act upon it. But also regarding the soul, insofar as it is an activity of another prior soul, while the prior remains, the subsequent activity also remains. But since it may not be an activity, but from an activity—of the kind we called the life already internal to the body—is it like the light already mixed with bodies, or here where things are mixed with that which produces color? But regarding the life of the body, what of it? Or it holds another soul which has been prepared. When, therefore, the body is destroyed, it cannot be devoid of soul. But when the body is perishing, and the gift no longer suffices for it, if something lies near, how then does it still live, or remain? Or no, did this perish, or not even this?
> For this too is an image of an out-shining: it is just no longer there.

If there were a body outside of the heaven, and some sight were directed from somewhere with nothing hindering the seeing, would it not behold it, not being in sympathy with that, if sympathy now is due to the nature of the one living being? Or if sympathy is due to the one living being, both the things perceiving and the things perceived and the senses. Thus it would not, unless this body were an external part of this living being. If it were, perhaps it would. If however it were not a part, but a colored body, and having the other qualities, such as that which is here similar in kind to the organ. Or not even so. If the hypothesis is not so. Unless someone, by this very thing, should try to take away the hypothesis. Saying it is absurd, if the sight will not see color, it being present. And the other senses, the sensible things being present to them, will not act toward them. But from where does this absurdity appear, we shall say? Either because being here in one, and...

<summary>Plotinus explores the soul's presence in the body using the analogy of a mirror reflection and cosmic sympathy, arguing that sensation depends on the interconnected nature of the "World Animal." He questions whether a body outside our universe could be perceived if it does not share in this universal living connection.</summary>
