<meta>This page continues the investigation into the unity of the soul and the universe, specifically addressing how individual experiences and perceptions are linked to the "World Animal" or the universal living being. It moves into Chapter 8 of the fourth Ennead (though the header incorrectly reads 'Book Five' in this edition).</meta>

### BOOK FIVE.

<column-break/>

As we now exist as part of the one, we do and suffer these things; this we must consider, whether it is from that [source]. And if indeed it has been shown sufficiently, it has been proven. But if not, it must be shown through other arguments. That the Living Being <note>original Greek: "zoon"; Plotinus views the entire universe as a single, living organism</note> is sympathetic <note>original Greek: "sympathes"; the Neoplatonic concept of "cosmic sympathy," where parts of the universe react to one another like parts of a single body</note> to itself is clear. And if it is one Living Being, it feels desire. So also the parts belong to one Living Being. But if someone should say it is through similarity—but the apprehension is according to the Living Being, and the sense-perception, because the same thing participates in the like. For the organ <note>The physical sense organ, like the eye or ear</note> is like itself. Thus sense-perception will be an apprehension of the soul through organs similar to the objects perceived. If, then, being a Living Being, it perceives not only those things within itself, but also things similar to those within itself, it will indeed perceive insofar as it is a Living Being. However, the objects perceived will not be the same as the soul, but similar to the things within it; or even the objects perceived are perceived as similar because the soul itself has made them similar. Thus, it would not be that which it has made. Therefore, if the soul there is the creator, then this soul is also different. And the things hypothesized to be similar there have nothing to do with it. But indeed, the absurdity shows the contradiction in the hypothesis, as it is the cause of it. For it would call it simultaneously soul and not-soul, kindred and not-kindred, similar and dissimilar. Therefore, they hold contradictions within the hypothesis itself; it could not even be a hypothesis. For it places the soul in a place, so that it places everything in everything—both another and not another, both nothing and not nothing, both perfect and imperfect. Therefore, the hypothesis must be abandoned, as it is not possible to seek what follows from it, because it destroys the very thing hypothesized within itself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Existing now as part of the one, we do these things and suffer them. Therefore, this must be considered: whether besides this, another [reason] must be brought forward. If this satisfies us, it is already demonstrated; if not, it must be demonstrated again through other things. Therefore, that the animal <note>original Latin: "animal"; translating the Greek "zoon," referring to the ensouled universe</note> is one animal is now sufficient, and all things will be parts of the one; and insofar as they are parts of one living thing, they will agree with one another. But if someone should assert <margin>B</margin> that this body perceives the world here only because of a certain similarity, yet that very perception will be according to the nature of the animal and sense, since it possesses that same similarity: for its instrument is similar to it. Wherefore sense-perception will be the soul's apprehension through instruments similar to the things to be perceived. If, therefore, being an animal, it perceives not only those things which are in itself, but also those similar to its own, it will certainly perceive by the reason that it is an animal. But the things to be perceived <margin>C</margin> will be perceived not insofar as they are its own, but insofar as they are similar. But perhaps instead, the things to be perceived are to be perceived thus because of similarity, because that same soul rendered them similar, so that they might be familiar. Wherefore, if the author there becomes a soul entirely diverse, certainly those things which are imagined there to be similar have no relation to it; for the absurdity in the hypothesis declares a repugnancy, as if this very thing were the cause of the absurdity: namely, it says <margin>D</margin> it is simultaneously soul and not soul, kindred and not kindred, similar and dissimilar. For this reason, since it includes contradictions within itself, the hypothesis is not to be judged as correct. For it posits the universal and not the universal, and something else and not something else; likewise nothing and not-nothing, specifically outside itself; and finally, perfect and imperfect at the same time. Therefore, such a hypothesis is to be rejected, because it is not permitted to seek a consequence from it, because that very thing which is hypothesized within itself is destroyed and perishes through it.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the universe is a single "Living Being" bound by cosmic sympathy, meaning individual perceptions are actually the soul's apprehension of itself or its likeness. He rejects hypotheses that treat the soul as a localized object, as this leads to logical contradictions where the soul is defined as both itself and its opposite.</summary>

# OF PLOTINUS
## THE FOURTH ENNEAD,
### BOOK VI.

# PLOTINUS
## THE FOURTH ENNEAD,
### BOOK SIX.
#### ON sense-perception and memory.
#### On sense & memory.

---

> The forms of sensible things are not imprinted upon the soul. Our Boethius <note>The Roman philosopher Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), author of *The Consolation of Philosophy*. The translator, likely Marsilio Ficino, is citing him as an authority who agrees with Plotinus.</note> in his *Consolation* proves that forms from sensible objects are not imprinted on the soul like a seal in wax; we also discuss this in our *Theology* and in the commentaries on Thrasybulus <note>original: "Thrapsi"; likely referring to Porphyry's treatise *To Thrasybulus on How the Soul is Animated*.</note>. Plotinus thinks that if a form were thus imprinted on the soul, it would take on the nature of the sensible object itself; thus, if the form of the heavens were imprinted on the sight, five absurdities would follow. First, it would not be necessary to direct the eye toward the sky any longer. Second, we would not measure how far the sky is from the eye; indeed, we would not even think it was distant. Third, the sky would not appear wider than the eye. Fourth, we would not see the sky itself, but perhaps only this form of the sky within us. Fifth, we would not be able to discern an object placed so closely upon the sense.
->Chapter I.<-

---

<margin>A</margin> If we say that perceptions are not produced like certain formations or imprints in the soul, we will consequently say that memory is not the preservation of teachings and perceptions—as if some shape were kept in the mind—since it was not even received from the outside in that way before. Therefore, both belong to the same argument. <margin>B</margin> For one must either say that forms are created in the mind and these same forms are preserved, if indeed you remember; or if you deny either one, you ought not to admit the other either. We, therefore, who grant neither, are compelled to investigate what the manner of each is: since we say neither that the shape of a sensible thing is created in the mind and shapes it, nor do we admit that memory is the custody of a shape that was once imprinted and remains. <margin>C</margin> But if we contemplate what happens in the most piercing of senses <note>Referring to sight, which Neoplatonists considered the most divine and clear sense.</note>, perhaps we will find what we seek in the other senses as well, by transferring the same principle to them. It is established everywhere that when we see something, we look there and reach out with our sight to where the visible object itself is placed in view, as if the perception occurs there, and the soul looks outward. This indeed (as I believe) indicates that no form has been or is being made in the soul; nor does the soul see because it admits an imprint, such as wax receives from a seal. <margin>D</margin> For there would be no need to look further outside if it already possessed the form of the thing to be seen within itself, and if it perceived for this very reason—that the form had entered into it. Furthermore, when the mind applies a distance to the thing it sees, and perceives how far away it sees it, this sufficiently indicates that it does not have within itself what it gazes upon; otherwise, since it would be at no distance from it, it would not see it as if it were positioned far away. Likewise, it could not judge through a form received inside, when however, not turning away from itself <note>original Greek: ἀφ’ αὑτῆς, ὡς πόῤῥω; "from itself, as if far off."</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> If we do not say that perceptions are imprints or seals occurring in the soul, then we shall not, in a consistent and following manner, say that memories are the retentions of learnings and perceptions—as if a type <note>original: "typos"; a physical mark or impression</note> remained in the soul which did not exist at the time of its origin. <margin>B</margin> Therefore, by the same logic, both would either be produced in the soul and remain there, if memory exists, or by not granting one of them, one must not grant the other either. But since we say neither occurs, we must necessarily seek the manner of each: since we say neither that the type from the sensible object is produced in the soul and stamps it, nor do we say that memory is the staying of that type. <margin>C</margin> But if we should observe what happens in the case of the most vivid perception, perhaps by transferring the same to the other senses, we might find what is sought. It is clear that, however we receive perception of anything through sight, we look there where the sight is, as if we are shooting out <note>original: βάλλουμεν (ballomen); Plotinus uses the metaphor of "striking" or "darting" the gaze toward the object.</note>, where the act of seeing is positioned in a straight line. Thus, it is clear the apprehension <note>original: ἀντιλήψεως (antilepseos)</note> occurs there, with the soul looking toward the outside, <margin>D</margin> since I believe no type is produced within it. Or if it saw by receiving a seal, just as wax does not see the ring, it would have no need to look outside, already having within itself the form of the thing seen; for by that which entered there, the type would be seen. But indeed, by adding a distance to the vision, and stating how great the view is, the soul shows how it... <note>The Greek text ends mid-sentence at the bottom of the column.</note>

<summary>Plotinus argues that perception and memory are active powers of the soul rather than passive "imprints" like wax. He contends that if the soul merely looked at internal images, we would lose the ability to perceive distance and the external reality of the world.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, perception, memory, soul, wax seal metaphor, optics, Neoplatonism, Boethius, epistemology</keywords>

--- Page 603 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument from the beginning of Book VI, where Plotinus challenges the Stoic and Aristotelian notions of perception. He argues that if the soul were merely a passive receiver of "imprints," we would be trapped within our own minds, seeing only "shadows" of reality rather than the objects themselves. This page transitions from visual perception to hearing and finally to the nature of the intellect.</meta>

BOOK SIX. 453

In what way, then, could it say how great a thing is, or that it is large, such as the heavens? For that which has the power [to see] could say it. But this is the greatest problem of all: if we were to receive imprints <note>original: "τύπως" (typos); refers to a physical impression like a seal in wax.</note> of the things we see, it would no longer be possible to look at the very things we see, but only the images and *shadows* <margin>* shadows</margin> of those visions. Thus, the things themselves would be one thing, and the things seen by us would be another. In short, as it is said, it is as if one were to look at the visible object by placing it directly upon the pupil. Yet everything must be seen in this way. One must much more transfer this principle to the soul. For if we were to place the imprint of the visible object within the soul, that upon which the seal has been impressed would perhaps not be seen. For then two things would come to be: the one seeing, and that which is seen. Therefore, the seeing subject must be distinct, situated elsewhere from the imprint, and not within that in which the imprint resides. It is necessary, therefore, for the one seeing to be situated [apart], and for the objects not to be placed directly upon the soul, so that vision may occur.

---

If it does not happen in this way, what is the manner of it? Or does the soul speak of things which it does not possess? For this is the nature of a power: not to be acted upon, but to be capable, and to work upon that for which it was appointed. For in this way, I think, there is a release for the soul regarding both the visible and the audible. It is not that they are both imprints, but rather that they are not imprints; they are not passions <note>original: "πάθεσιν" (pathesin); in this context, it refers to being "acted upon" or passive reception.</note>, but activities directed toward those things they are naturally suited for. But we, being distrustful, think that each power cannot know its object unless it is struck by it. We are persuaded that we undergo something rather than knowing that which is near; that which is given to us to master, we allow ourselves to be mastered by. In the same way, we must consider what happens in the case of hearing. The imprint is in the air, a certain stroke that is articulated, like letters being written in the air by the one who produced the voice. But the power and essence of the soul reads these imprints written in the air as they come near, where they are naturally suited to be seen. In matters of taste and smell, some things are passions, but the senses themselves are judgments of them; they are knowledges of the passions, distinct from the passions themselves. But the knowledge of intelligible things is much more impassive <note>original: "ἀπαθής" (apathês); without being physically affected.</note> and without imprint. These releases occur from within, as if by falling into them, whereas external things are contemplated from without; and those [intelligible things] are more truly activities, and more sovereign, belonging to the soul itself, and it is the soul's nature to act upon each. Just as the soul itself sees two things and as another, so too with the intellect; both are two in one, and yet in others.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> How great an external thing may be, or even that it exists at all as a quantity—such as how great the heavens are—cannot be understood if the form received within is not also of that size. But what is the greatest point of all: if we were to receive the figures of those things we see internally, it would not be permitted to perceive the very things we look at, but only their images and shadows. Thus it would happen that some things exist in reality, but others appear to us. In short, regarding what is said: <margin>B</margin> the soul being moved [by an object] can be much more applied to the soul itself. For if we were to place the figure of a visible thing in the soul, that spectacle by which it was marked would not be seen at all. For it is necessary that these be two distinct things: that which sees, and that which is seen. Therefore, it is necessary that that which sees the figure be positioned elsewhere, and not within the thing itself. Wherefore it is necessary that vision is not of an imposed object, but rather of one not imposed, if vision is to truly occur.

---

->To sense is not to be acted upon by sensible things, but to act upon them. Chapter 11.<-

> The Soul, because it is incomparably more excellent than sensible things and does not communicate with them in matter or nature, never receives forms from them. Since in the act of sensing it must judge correctly, and being "acted upon" <note>original: "passio"</note> confuses judgment, the soul suffers nothing from its objects. If any physical affection happens, it reaches the body and the spirit <note>term: "spiritus" (a subtle substance connecting soul and body)</note>; when this spirit is struck or affected by external things, the soul, being present, immediately perceives such affections. To perceive this is not to be passive, but rather to act—that is, to animate the spirit in a new way and to bring forth the innate forms of sensible things (as Iamblichus says <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized the soul's active role in perception.</note>). Intelligence is much further removed from being acted upon than sense is, for it possesses internal forms and does not turn toward the outside.

---

<margin>A</margin> IF, therefore, sense-perception does not happen in that way, it remains to inquire how it does happen. Does the soul perhaps speak of things which it does not possess? Certainly. For this is the property of a power: not to be acted upon by something, but to be strong and to execute its own proper work. Thus, I believe, the visible and the audible are discerned; not indeed as if both were certain figures, but rather if they are not figures, nor any "passions" <note>passive states</note>, but actions concerning that which they are naturally instituted to do. We, however, doubting that any power can know its object unless it is struck by it, act as if the soul must be passive to the object; whereas by the gift of nature, the soul ought to overcome its objects, not be overcome by them. <margin>B</margin> By the same reasoning, we must judge concerning hearing: a figure is made in the air, as it were a certain pulse distinctly articulated, like letters written there by the one who uttered the voice. But the power and essence of the soul, as if reading the figures written in the air, approaches them where they have naturally proceeded to be perceived. <margin>C</margin> Furthermore, regarding taste and smell, some things are passions, but others are the cognitions of those passions—namely, the senses and judgments of passions—which certainly differ from the passions themselves. But the cognition of intelligible things is much more free from passion and formation. For these, conversely, proceed as if from the innermost part, while sensible things are reached from the outside; therefore the former are more truly actions, and sovereign actions at that. <margin>D</margin> For they belong to the soul itself, and the soul itself performs each of these. But whether the soul sees itself as two things, and as if another; and whether the intellect is as one, and both are two-in-one, must be disputed elsewhere.

<summary>Plotinus argues that sense-perception is an active judgment of the soul rather than a passive physical imprint. He suggests that if the mind were merely a "wax tablet," we would only ever see internal images and never the external reality itself.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, sense-perception, active soul, Iamblichus, intellect, optics, hearing, passive vs active mind</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 453 regarding the nature of perception and the soul. ### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV. ###
### Remembering and recollecting is not the conservation and repetition of the forms of things once impressed upon the soul. Chapter III. ###

*When they say the soul, as a medium between incorporeal and corporeal things, has the <term>forms</term> <note>original: "formas"; the essential patterns or blueprints of reality.</note> of both in itself, we do not understand these forms as <term>accidents</term> <note>original: "accidentia"; in ancient philosophy, these are qualities that can change or be added without changing the essential nature of a thing.</note> lying in the soul, like letters on a tablet, whether they were inscribed or were innate. For the soul, being of a divine nature, neither undergoes new physical impressions, nor does it hold the <term>reasons</term> <note>original: "rationes" / "λόγοι"; the formative principles of things.</note> of things which it has possessed from the beginning in a way so different from its own nature that they could be called accidents. Rather, as we have said elsewhere, just as there are natural powers within the soul—the intellect, reason, imagination, sensation, and vegetative powers—so too does it possess the reasons of things to be known as essential powers, just as it possesses the <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>original: "seminales rationes"; the biological blueprints for the growth of limbs and organs.</note> of the limbs. When, therefore, the soul meditates upon something, it draws itself out from its natural virtue into a natural act concerning that very thing. But if it meditates more attentively and for a longer time upon the same thing, it conforms itself more powerfully to it, and that is what it means to remember; and from this, it also recollects more easily.*

---

<margin>A</margin>
**AFTER** these things, we must speak of memory. And before all else, it is not to be wondered at—or rather, it is indeed wondrous, yet not unbelievable—that we attribute such a power to the soul: namely, that while it receives nothing into itself, it nevertheless notices those things which it has not "received" in a physical sense. For the nature of the soul is the <term>reason</term> <note>original: "ratio" / "λόγος"; here meaning the ordering principle or account.</note> of all things: I mean the final reason of the <term>intelligible</term> <note>The realm of pure thought and forms, as opposed to the physical world.</note> beings and of the things that exist there, but the first reason of the things in the sensible universe. For this reason, it inclines toward both: by the higher things, it is well-affected and brought back to life; but by the lower things, 
<margin>B</margin>
it is deceived by a certain similarity and slides down as if it were charmed. Therefore, being situated in the middle, it naturally perceives both. It is said to "understand" the higher things when it is called back into memory, if anything from that realm had previously shone upon it. It knows these things because, in a certain way, it *is* these very things; for it does not know them by placing them within itself as if in a seat, but by possessing and contemplating them in a certain way. And from the fact that the soul is these things in a more obscure way, it emerges more clearly from a sort of obscure habit as if awakened, and passes from potentiality into act. Similarly, it makes <term>sensible things</term> <note>Physical objects perceived by the senses.</note> shine forth by fitting them to itself, and places them before its eyes; since the power of the soul was already prepared for this, and was "in labor" with them. When, therefore, it is strengthened toward any of those things which are presented to it, it is affected by that thing for a long time as if it were present, and the more it is strengthened, the longer it remains. This is why children are said to have better memories, because they do not quickly 
<margin>D</margin>
cease their focus, but keep the thing itself before their eyes for a long time; for they are not yet distracted by many things, but apply themselves vehemently to a few. But those whose thought and power are turned toward many things, they merely run through them and stay nowhere. Furthermore, if the <term>forms</term> <note>original: "formae" / "τύποι"; imprints or shapes.</note> of things remained physically impressed in the soul, a multitude of things would not diminish memory. Moreover, if these forms were "residing" there, we would have no need of consideration in order to recollect; nor, when we had previously forgotten, would we need to recollect ourselves shortly afterward, 
<margin>E</margin>
if the figures were still remaining there. Furthermore, the very exercises that help us to recall and resume a memory declare that what is acquired through this process is nothing other than a certain strengthening and vigor of the soul. This is just like the exercises of the hands or feet used to perform certain tasks more easily; the ability does not "sit" in the hands or feet, but these limbs are made more ready through a certain continuous habit. Furthermore, why is it that when you have heard something only once or twice, you do not remember it, but when you have heard it many times, you hold what you previously did not, 
<margin>F</margin>

<column-break/>

**NOW** that these things have been said, we must speak next of memory. If it seems to all to be more remote, as something to wonder at—or rather, a thing to be wondered at, yet not incredible—we should not deny such a power to the soul, that it creates a perception of those things which it has not received into itself. For the <term>reason</term> <note>original: "λόγος" (logos).</note> is the principle of all things. It is the last reason of the intelligible beings, and in the intelligible realm is the reason of nature; but it is the first reason of the things in the entire sensible world. Therefore, it holds toward both. By the former, it is well-affected and its fire is rekindled by them; by the latter, it is deceived by a likeness, and descends as if under a spell. Being in the middle, it perceives both. And it is said to "intellect" the former when it has come into memory, if it should somehow happen to be with them. It knows them because it is these things in a certain way. For it knows, not by establishing them within itself, but by the way it possesses them and sees them. And it *is* these things more obscurely; and from that obscurity, it becomes more active by being, as it were, awakened. And it makes these things shine out from itself. It works so that they are before its eyes, being ready, and as it were previously "in labor" with them and with its powers. Whenever, then, it is strengthened toward any of the things that have appeared, it arrives at it for a long time as if it were present. And the more it is strengthened, the more it is always so. This is why children are said to remember more, because they do not move away, but [the things] are before their eyes, as they do not yet look toward a multitude, but toward a few things. But where the mind and power are upon many things, they are as if by a side-by-side comparison and do not remain. But if the imprints remained, the multitude of them would not have created a loss or a weakening of memory. Furthermore, if the imprints remained, there would be no need to search in order to be reminded. Nor would it be necessary, after having forgotten before, to be reminded later of what was lying there. And the practices aimed at recovery show that what occurs is a strengthening of the soul. Just as the exercises of hands or feet for the sake of doing things easily, which things do not lie in the hands or feet, but toward which they have been made ready by continuity. For why is it that having heard once or twice one does not remember, but when one hears many times, one holds what one previously did not...

<meta>catchword: many</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that memory is not the storage of physical imprints in the soul, but rather an active strengthening of the soul's inherent power to perceive and relate to both the intellectual and physical worlds.</summary>
<keywords>memory, soul, imprints, intellect, habits, recollection, Plotinus, Enneads, perception, education of children</keywords>

Plotinus is arguing that memory is an active power (dynamis) of the soul rather than a passive storage of physical "imprints" (typoi) on a material substance. He uses the analogy of a wax tablet to critique the common but, in his view, mistaken materialist understanding of the mind.</meta>

# BOOK SIX. #

...much later in time one already remembers. For it is not by having stated the parts earlier that one ought to remember the local details. But this happens as if suddenly, from some later hearing or study. These things bear witness to a provocation of the power <note>original: δυνάμεως; the inherent capacity or potentiality of the soul</note> by which we remember the soul, as having been strengthened, either simply or for this specific purpose. For when memory is present to us only for those things we have studied. But those things which many have taken up not to use from a customary delivery, they already make easy recollections of the other things being said, or memory itself might be blamed, or that the power is strengthened. For if the imprints <margin>*</margin> remained, they would testify to weakness rather than power. For that which is more easily imprinted is easier for the one suffering it. And since the imprint is a <term>passion</term> <note>original: πάθος; in ancient philosophy, a "passion" is not an emotion, but a state of being "passive" or "acted upon" by an external force.</note>, that which has suffered more is that which remembers more. But then the opposite seems to happen, in no way now towards exercise, it makes the one about to be exercised susceptible to passion, since even in the case of the senses, it is the weak part that sees, such as the eye, but rather the one who has more power for activity. Wherefore also the aged are weaker in their senses, or likewise in their memories. Therefore, both sensation and memory are a certain strength. Furthermore, if there are no imprints of the senses, how is it possible for memories to be holdings of things not made one's own, nor by being shown. But if it is a certain power and preparation for readiness, where things are held together, but later we come to the sensation of them. Or because of the powers, as we said in the case of <term>habit</term> <note>original: ἕξεως; a stable disposition or state of being</note>, for we see this also in other powers, where powers are added to perform something. And some things happen immediately, while others happen by working to perceive themselves; they mostly come from being mindful and often quick-witted themselves, because the same power holds both. Just as the same person is not both a boxer and a runner. For different ideas prevail. And what then prevented the one having an excess of soul from reading the things lying there, not flowing in this way, and by suffering and having the passion to possess inability? For it is of the soul's lack of magnitude <note>original: ἀμέγεθες; the soul has no physical size or dimensions</note>, and of the soul in general, it witnesses that it is a power. And generally, all things concerning the soul are marvelous, being in another way than men have supposed from not examining them. Or as ready-at-hand attacks occur to them from sensible things, deceiving through similarities. For as if letters were written in tablets or books, so they are disposed concerning the senses and memory. And placing it upon the body, they see that impossibilities happen to their hypothesis, since it is incorporeal.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...then after a long time you now hold it. For this does not happen because you received the parts of the figure first, for you would also remember these, but this is achieved suddenly, as if from a final hearing or meditation performing it. These things surely testify that the power of the soul is provoked, through which we recollect, and by which it is as if strengthened, either simply or toward something: But then when memory supplies to us not only those things we have meditated upon, but also suggests or returns many things, having been accustomed by certain signs <margin>B</margin>, where from the resumption of one thing, many other things are also more easily resumed, what other cause of memory of this kind can one bring, other than that the power of the soul itself has now been strengthened? Indeed, the forms of things remaining in the soul would indicate weakness rather than power. For that which is marked with the most forms was made so by yielding: And since the impression of a figure is a certain passion, it follows that what has suffered most is also most <margin>C</margin> mindful, but the contrary of this clearly happens. For nowhere does exercise for a certain work render that which is exercised more subject to passion: since also in the senses, it is not that which is weak that discerns, such as the eye, but that in which a more abundant power for acting is present. Therefore the elderly are both weaker in their senses and similarly in their memory. Therefore, sensation and memory are a certain vigor and value. Accordingly, since sensations are not certain impressions of figures in the soul, in what way <margin>D</margin> can memory be the conservation of those things which were not even deposited with it from the beginning? But if memory is a certain faculty and preparation for readiness, why do we not resume the same things simultaneously and suddenly, but in succession? Because, clearly, it is necessary to apply the power itself and to intend it. For we see this happen in other powers also, which are indeed prepared to perform what they can: and they expedite their duty partly suddenly, partly truly if they have first collected themselves. <margin>E</margin> For the most part, the same people do not seem to be both sharp-sighted and mindful, since the power of each is not the same: just as the boxer and the runner are not the same. For some ideas dominate in one, others in another. Although nothing prevents a man having certain excesses of soul from reading as if things were placed there, nor that a man flowing in this part should not be exposed to passion: finally, because it is established that the soul is not subject to magnitude, it shows entirely that whatever is in the soul is not a passion, but an efficacy: <margin>F</margin> and entirely whatever things are around the soul, in a certain marvelous way, they behave differently than men suspect, who have never diligently investigated such things: and otherwise than the clear approaches from those things which are sensed passing to them signify, deceiving by a certain similarity. Whence, just as letters are inscribed in certain tablets or books, they think similarly about the senses and memory. And truly those who are so affected, whether they place the soul in a body, or <margin>G</margin> incorporeal, they are entirely ignorant of how many absurdities follow from that hypothesis.

<summary>Plotinus argues that memory is an active power of the soul rather than a passive storage of physical imprints, noting that if memory were merely a "passion" or impression, the weakest minds would be the most mindful. He refutes the materialist analogy of the soul as a wax tablet, asserting its incorporeal and energetic nature.</summary>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEAD IV, BOOK VII.

## PLOTINUS’S FOURTH ENNEAD, BOOK VII.

### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL.

### On the immortality of the soul.

> Each one of us is entirely immortal, if indeed the soul itself is immortal. Chapter 1.

<image-desc>Decorative initial A with floral patterns.</image-desc>
The soul relates to the body in two ways: partly as a substantial <term>form</term> <note>original: species; in this context, the organizing principle or "blueprint" of a thing</note> to matter, since through its presence a certain temperate mixture of fluids and vital spirit is born in the body; and partly as a user to an instrument, in so far as it moves the body according to its will. Thus, it is separable from the body, and in a certain sense, already separated.

---

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'W' (V) showing a landscape scene with classical figures.</image-desc>
WHETHER each of us is indeed immortal, or perishes entirely, or whether one part is fleeting while another is perpetual—namely, that part which is our true self—one may learn by contemplating the order of nature in this manner.

<margin>B</margin>
Man is certainly not a simple thing, but possesses a soul and a body, whether the body is joined to us as an instrument or by some other condition. It must be proposed and granted as a starting point that the nature and essence of each are clearly distinct. As for the body, since it is itself a composite thing, reason demonstrates that it cannot remain forever, and the senses perceive it being utterly dissolved and dissipated. For whatever elements are within it return to their own place, and one thing destroys another, changing it into something else and perishing; especially when the soul—which

<margin>C</margin>
is accustomed to reconcile <note>original: conciliare; the Greek uses 'philia' (friendship), implying the soul is the unifying force that prevents the physical parts from flying apart.</note> these elements—is no longer present in the physical masses. Yet, even if any body were left alone, it is still not entirely a single unit, since it can still be dissolved into <term>form</term> and <term>matter</term> <note>the fundamental components of all physical objects in Aristotelian and Neoplatonic thought</note>, from which even simple bodies must necessarily be composed. Furthermore, since all bodies necessarily possess magnitude, they consequently perish when reduced to their smallest parts. Therefore, if the body is a part of us, we are not immortal in every respect; but if it is our instrument,

<margin>D</margin>
it must be that it was granted to us for a certain time, being such by nature. The principal part, however—the man himself—will be to the body either as the form is to the matter (if the body stands to the form as matter does), or he will be like one using the body as a kind of instrument. In either case, it is the soul that is chiefly the man himself.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' (Ε) showing figures in a landscape, one possibly holding a staff.</image-desc>
If each of us is immortal, or if the whole perishes, or if some parts of him go off into scattering and destruction while others remain forever—which are the man himself—one might learn by looking at it according to nature. Now, one would say that man is not something simple, but that there is in him a soul. He also has a body, whether it is our instrument or attached in some other way, but let them be distinguished in this way. One must establish the nature and essence of each. The body is itself a composite thing <gloss>for indeed</gloss> <note>original: καὶ γὰρ</note> both by reason it is able to remain or by sense one sees it, being dissolved and melting away, and receiving all kinds of destruction. Each of the elements moves toward its own place, destroying every other thing, and changing into another and perishing. And this is especially true when the soul, which creates friendship <note>original: ἡ ψυχὴ ἡ φιλία; the soul acting as the unifying 'love' or bond of the body</note>, is not present in the masses. Even if each thing were made to be alone, it is not immune to receiving dissolution into form and matter, from which even the simple bodies must have their compositions. And furthermore, having magnitude since they are bodies, they are cut and crushed into nothingness, and in this way are subject to destruction. So that if this is a part of us, we are not entirely immortal; but if it is an instrument, it had to be given for a certain time, being such by nature. But the most sovereign part and the man himself would be either as form is to matter, or as this is to the body. If indeed the body is to the form as matter is. Or according to the one using it, as if toward an instrument. In either way, the soul is the man himself.

-> THAT <- <note>This is the "catchword," a print convention where the first word of the next page is printed at the bottom of the current one to ensure the pages are bound in the correct order.</note>

<summary>Plotinus begins his argument for the immortality of the soul by distinguishing the composite, destructible nature of the physical body from the soul, which acts as either the organizing 'form' or the 'user' of the body.</summary>
<keywords>immortality, soul, body, form and matter, instrument, dissolution, dualism, Plotinus, Enneads</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the immortality of the soul from the previous page. Here, the author (Plotinus, with commentary by Marsilio Ficino) begins a systematic refutation of the idea that the soul could be a physical body or a material mixture of elements.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN.

> No body, by virtue of being a body, possesses its own innate life; however, the soul does. Therefore, the soul is not a body, nor does it arise from a body or bodies, since it is more excellent in its nature. Chapter II.
>
> The body is, by its own nature, dissoluble; the soul, by its own nature, binds the body together and reconciles opposites while mixing them according to a certain reason. Therefore, it is neither dissoluble nor a body, nor is it conceived from a specific mixture of bodies; rather, on the contrary, the ordered principle of mixture in bodies proceeds from the soul. We shall be very brief in this book, for we have written at great length on these same matters in the Theology. <note>original: "Theologia"; refers to Ficino's own work, *Platonic Theology on the Immortality of the Soul*.</note>

---

<margin>A</margin>
WHAT nature, then, does this thing we call the soul have? For if it is a body, it would be similarly subject to being broken down, for a body must be a composite. But if it is not a body, but of another nature, we must examine that nature in the same way, or in another. First, however, we must examine into what kind of body those who call the soul a body intend to dissolve it.
<margin>The Soul itself.</margin>
For since life belongs to the soul by necessity, it is necessary that if the soul were a body—whether composed of two or more bodies—
<margin>B</margin>
either both of them, or each one, must have an innate life. Either one would have it and the other not, or neither would have it. If indeed life were present in the body itself, this very thing would be the soul—what would a body be that has life from itself? For fire, air, water, and earth are soulless <note>original: ἄψυχα (*apsycha*)</note> by themselves; and whatever of these has a soul present in it uses a life brought in from the outside. But there are no other bodies besides these.
<margin>C</margin>
To those who believe the elements of these are other bodies, those have been said to be either bodies or souls. But if they have life—even if not one of them has life individually—it is absurd to say that their coming together has created life. If each one were to have life, one would be enough. Indeed, it is even more impossible for a heap of bodies to produce life, and for things lacking intellect to generate intellect. And surely, these things do not become natures by being mixed in just any way; there must, therefore, be something that orders them and is the cause of the
<margin>D</margin>
mixture. So this would have the status of the soul. Or perhaps because it is a composite? But the soul could not even be the <term>disposition</term> <note>original: ἕξις (*hexis*); the state or "holding together" of a thing</note> of soft bodies, if there is a soul existing in the whole; since if a <term>rational principle</term> <note>original: λόγος (*logos*)</note> approaching matter makes a body, where would that principle come from if not from a soul?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
WHAT nature, then, should we say this very thing possesses, which we call by the name of "soul"? Certainly, if it is a body, it is altogether dissoluble. For every body is a composite. But if it is not a body, but of a different nature, it is necessary to investigate this nature as well, either in the same or another manner. To begin, we must ask into what body we ought to resolve this body which they call "soul." Since life is everywhere necessarily in the soul, it follows that if that body which is imagined to be the soul is composed of two or more bodies, then either both or all together, or even individually in some way, must possess an innate life; or this one indeed has life, but that one by no means has it, or neither has it. If, therefore, life is in only one, that one alone will be the soul. But what kind of body is this, which possesses life from itself? Surely fire, air, water, and earth by their own nature lack a soul, and in whichever of these a soul is present, it uses a life that is foreign to it. But besides these, there are no other
<margin>B</margin>
bodies. Moreover, whoever has introduced certain other elements besides these as other bodies, nevertheless did not call them souls, nor did they attribute life to them. But if anyone says that while none of them possess life, the meeting of all has constituted life, he speaks absurdly. Likewise, if each one has life, one is already sufficient. It is altogether impossible for a confluence of bodies to create life, or for things which lack
<margin>C</margin>
intellect to create intellect. And yet, they will not say that these mixed in any way whatever produce either intellect or even the soul. It is necessary, therefore, that there be something that orders and is the cause of the mixture. This, therefore, will rather hold the authority and rank of the soul. Now, not only will there be no composite body, but there will not even be a simple body in the order of things, unless there is a soul in the universe: for if a <term>seminal reason</term> <note>original: *ratio seminalis*; the formative power that organizes matter</note> approaching matter makes a body, that reason itself cannot proceed from anywhere other than the soul.

---

> Every body causes a distance between its parts, so that when one part suffers, the others do not immediately suffer with it. But through the soul itself, the living body behaves so that at the movement and suffering of one part, all are immediately moved together. Therefore, the soul is neither a body, nor a form spread out through the body. Chapter III.
> 
> It is not a dense body, otherwise it would not easily penetrate the whole. It is not a fluid body, otherwise it would not contain a very fluid body. It is not a form imprinted on the body, otherwise it would not easily dominate the body to give it life, move it, and contain it; rather, it depends on a more excellent form remaining in itself and pouring life through the body. And this more excellent form will be the soul itself: which, since it is indivisible and whole everywhere, and outside the genus of contrary qualities, easily reconciles opposites among themselves and connects things that are spread out and dissipable into a single unit.

---

<margin>A</margin>
BUT if someone should say not this, but that atoms or certain indivisible bodies coming together produce the soul by their union, he will certainly be refuted by the very consensus of suffering <note>original: ὁμοπαθεία (*homopatheia*); the ability of a whole organism to feel as one</note> and the bond of nature; for a single thing that feels together is not made through the whole from bodies that do not feel, nor do they admit any union.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
BUT if someone should say not this, but that atoms or certain indivisible bodies coming together produce the soul by their union, he will certainly be refuted by the very consensus of suffering and the bond of nature; for a single thing that feels together is not made through the whole from bodies that do not feel, nor do they admit any union: but the soul itself

<sig>Q</sig>
<meta>catchwords: The soul indeed, the soul</meta>

<summary>This page argues that the soul cannot be a material body or a mixture of physical elements because matter itself is lifeless and requires an external organizing principle (soul) to possess life and unity. It highlights the "consensus of suffering," where a living being reacts as a single whole, as proof that the soul is an indivisible, non-corporeal entity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's argument against materialist definitions of the soul. Having previously argued that the soul cannot be a simple body, he now refutes the idea that it is a "spirit" or a specific material mixture, a view held by the Stoics and Epicureans.</meta>

PLOTINUS ENNEAD IV.
# 458

it is entirely sympathetic with itself. Furthermore, from indivisible parts neither a body nor a magnitude can be formed. <note>Plotinus is arguing against atomism; if the soul were made of indivisible points, it could never form a three-dimensional object.</note> Moreover, if someone brings a simple body into the discussion, certainly, as far as its material aspect is concerned, one cannot say it has life of itself; for matter is devoid of quality. <note>In Platonic philosophy, "prime matter" is a blank slate without any characteristics like "hot" or "alive" until a Form acts upon it.</note> Instead, one should say that it is the form within it that brings life. If he says this form is the essence, then clearly not both, but one of these will be the soul: which indeed no longer exists as a body. For this is not also made of matter; otherwise, we would be forced to resolve it in the same way again. <margin>B</margin> But if he suggests that such a form is not an essence but a certain "affection" or state of matter, he must explain to us where this state and life descended into the matter from. For matter does not form itself, nor does it provide a soul for itself. Therefore, there must be something that supplies this life, whether it is supplied to matter itself or to any body: supplied, I say, by something existing outside and superior to all corporeal nature. <margin>C</margin> Furthermore, there will be no body at all unless the power of the soul exists: for the nature of the body is always flowing and in motion, and the universe would quickly perish if all things were bodies, even if someone applied the name "soul" to one of those bodies. For in this way, the soul would suffer exactly the same things as other bodies, since the same matter is in all things; indeed, nothing would be created anywhere, but all things would remain in matter where the shaper of matter himself is absent. <margin>D</margin> Perhaps even matter itself would not exist at all. This universe would be dissolved if one entrusted its safety to the connection of the body, attributing to this connection the very order of the soul—that is, using the name only—to a certain air and spirit that is completely dissipatable and possesses no union from itself. For since all bodies are divisible, if someone entrusted this universe to some body, he would be forced to admit that it is mindless and agitated far too randomly. What order can there be in <margin>E</margin> spirit—like a wind seeking order only from the soul—or what reason, or what intellect? But if the soul is present, all these things immediately serve it for the constitution of the world and the rest of living creatures, while one power leads everything toward the whole; but if the soul were absent from here, these remaining things would not only lack order but would not even be able to exist at all.

<column-break/>

it is entirely sympathetic. Out of indivisibles, no body or magnitude could ever arise. And indeed, if a body is simple, they will either say that the part which is material does not have life from itself—for matter is without quality—or that it has life by being fixed as a form. If they say this form is the essence, then one of these two will be the soul: which indeed would no longer be a body. For this is not also made of matter. Or again, we shall analyze it in the same way. But if they say it is an affection of matter and not an essence, they must tell us from where the affection and life have come into the matter. For matter does not shape itself, nor does it put a soul into itself. There must therefore be something that is the provider of life. Whether the provision is to matter, or to any of the bodies, it must be something outside and beyond all bodily nature. Since there would not even be a body if a soul-power were not present. For the body flows, and its nature is movement, and it would perish as quickly as possible if all things were bodies; even if someone gave the name "soul" to one of them. For it would suffer in the same way as the other bodies, since there is one matter for them all. Or rather, nothing would even be created, but all things would stop at matter, since there is nothing to shape it. Perhaps even matter itself would not exist at all: and this whole universe will be dissolved, if one trusts its cohesion to a body, giving it the rank of soul in name only—to air and a most dissipatable spirit, which does not even have unity from itself. For how, if all things have become bodies, can one who perceives it make this universe stay together with any duration and movement? For what order is there in a spirit that itself needs order from a soul, or what reason, or what intellect? But if the soul is present, all these things serve it for the composition of the world and of each living being, with one power from another contributing to the whole: but if this soul is not present in the whole, these things would be nothing, let alone in order.

---

<margin>Chapter IIII.</margin>
> *The Stoics and Epicureans suspected that the soul was a spirit, that is, a very subtle body: The former [Stoics] thought it was more fiery, the latter [Epicureans] more airy: and both named the soul not just any spirit, but one affected by a certain specific property.* <note>The Stoics believed the soul was "pneuma," a mixture of air and fire.</note>

> *This very specific property, which is in a way incorporeal and more excellent than the body, is not generated by the body but by a completely incorporeal substance, which should rather be judged as the soul: Which, since it is equally disposed to both producing and governing the opposite qualities and motions in the body, is rightly neither a specific body nor corporeal, nor does it depend on any body or bodies.*

The very defenders of corporeal nature are
<margin>A</margin> compelled by the truth to confess and testify that a certain form of things pertaining to the soul must precede bodies and be more excellent than all bodies, when they bring forward a spirit capable of intelligence and an "intellectual fire" <note>original: "ignem intellectualem"; a Stoic term for the divine active principle.</note> as if the highest level of nature itself could not exist in the order of things without fire and spirit...

<meta>catchword: ana- (Greek: ἀνά)</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul cannot be a material body or "spirit" (as the Stoics and Epicureans claimed) because matter is inherently passive and quality-less. He concludes that an incorporeal soul must exist to provide life, form, and order to the otherwise "flowing" and "dissipatable" material world.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Enneads, Stoicism, Epicureanism, pneuma, incorporeal soul, materialist philosophy, Marsilio Ficino, metaphysics of life</keywords>

--- Page 609 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s critique of the Stoic and materialist view that the soul is a physical "spirit" or "breath" (pneuma). On the previous page, he argued that matter itself is lifeless and requires an external form to animate it. Here, he examines the Stoic claim that the soul is "spirit in a certain state."</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN
## 459

<column-break/>

...to be, and seeking a place to be established, when it should rather seek what established the bodies: as if, because of these things, it were not established by the powers of the soul. But if they place life and the soul in nothing other than the breath <note>original: *pneuma*; the Stoics believed the soul was a physical "breath" or "spirit" pervading the body</note>, what is that famous phrase of theirs, <margin>B</margin> "disposed in a certain way," to which they are forced to flee when they are compelled to propose that bodies have some other active nature? If not every breath is a soul—since there are countless soulless breaths—they will say the soul is "breath disposed in a certain way." We shall ask them whether this "disposition" and this relationship is one of the things that exists, or nothing at all. If it is nothing, then there would only be breath. The phrase "disposed in a certain way" would then be a mere name for them. From this it would follow that they admit nothing exists except matter: and that "soul" and "God" and all such things are just names, while in reality only body exists. But if that "disposition" is something that exists, and something other than the underlying subject and matter—something which is in matter, yet is itself immaterial <note>original: *aylon*; not made of physical matter</note> because it is not again composed of matter—then it would be a certain rational principle <note>original: *logos*</note> and not a body, but a different nature entirely. Furthermore, from the following it appears no less impossible for the soul to be a body of any kind. For a body is either hot, or cold, or hard, or soft, or moist, or solid; or black or white, and all the other qualities that exist in different bodies. And if it were only hot, it would only heat; if only cold, it would only cool; if light, it would make things light and raise them up; if heavy, it would make them heavy; if black, it would blacken; and if white, it would whiten. For it is not the nature of fire to cool, nor of a cold thing to heat. But the soul produces different effects in different animals, and <margin>E</margin> produces opposites even in the same animal: partly solidifying, partly melting; making some parts dense, others thin, black, white, light, or heavy; even though, if it acted according to the quality of a body, it ought to produce only one thing and one color. But now it brings many things at once.

*The soul produces motions and effects of all forms, as much by its vegetative power through seminal reasons <note>original: *rationes seminales*; these are the formative "blueprints" or "seeds" of logic that guide the growth of a living being</note> as by choice. And it increases the body in a certain order to a certain limit, while remaining the same itself meanwhile. Likewise, the whole soul is in any portion of the soul, whether an imagined part or a true portion of the body. And the entire power of the soul is preserved in every drop of seed.*

*These functions, however, cannot belong to a physical mass or bodily quality. Therefore, the soul is non-physical.* <margin>Chapter V.</margin>

<margin>A</margin> Regarding motions: how could they claim there are different motions rather than just one, since every single body has only one motion? If they refer the causes of motions partly to choices and partly to seminal reasons, they will be speaking correctly. But choice is not a property of a body, nor are rational principles—especially since they are different, while the body here is one and simple. Nor can a body be capable of such a rational principle <margin>B</margin> at all, except insofar as it is granted to it by that which makes it hot or cold. As for growing at specific times and to a certain limit, by what power will this be appropriate for the body? For it is natural for a body to *be* increased, but not to *do* the increasing, except perhaps insofar as it takes on bulk from matter...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...might be able, and naturally demands a certain place where it may be established, when it would be more fitting to seek the place where bodies are situated: since indeed these must really be situated by the very powers of the soul. Accordingly, if they say that life and the soul are nothing other than a spirit <note>original: *spiritus*; breath or wind</note> like a wind, they must be asked what they mean by that common saying of theirs: "the soul is a spirit <margin>B</margin> disposed in a certain way." For they are accustomed to flee to this whenever they are forced to introduce another nature effective beyond bodies. If, therefore, not every spirit is a soul—since there are innumerable soulless spirits—but only a spirit disposed in a certain way, we will ask whether that which is called "disposed in a certain way" and such a habit is a real thing, or nothing. For if it is no thing, certainly only the spirit will exist. That which is added, "disposed," will be a name only. From this it will happen that they concede nothing exists besides matter: and they would confess that the soul and God and all <margin>C</margin> similar things are only names, but in reality only body exists. But if that habit is a certain thing, and something other than the subject and matter—which is indeed in matter, but is nevertheless immaterial, because it is not again composed of matter—certainly it will not be a body, but entirely another nature and a certain rational principle. Furthermore, it will appear no less from these things that the soul cannot be a body: for it would be either hot or cold, or hard or soft, <margin>D</margin> or compact or fluid and loose: likewise either black or white, and similarly for the other qualities of bodies. And indeed, if it is only hot, it only heats; if cold, it only cools; if light, it only raises up and makes things light wherever it is present: and if heavy, it makes them heavy and weighed down. Similarly, black produces black things and white properly produces white. For it is not the nature of fire to cool, nor of a cold thing to heat. But the soul both produces different things in different animals, and <margin>E</margin> produces contraries in the same one: partly compacting, and partly flowing and liquefying: likewise it makes some things dense, others thin, white, black, light, and heavy alike: even though not one through another, but only one...

<margin>A</margin> Concerning MOTION, however: in what way will they be able to assert not just one, but different motions, when there is only one motion for each single body? But if they refer the causes of motions partly to choices, and partly to seminal reasons, they will indeed assert this correctly. But choice is not proper to a body, nor are rational principles—especially when they are different, while the body here is one and simple—nor can a body be entirely capable of <margin>B</margin> such a principle, except as much as is granted to it by that which makes it hot or cold. But to increase at certain times and to a certain limit—by what power will that befit the body? To which indeed it naturally befits to *be* increased, but to increase [others] not at all, except perhaps as much as in bulk...

<meta>Catchword: bulk</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK IV.
## 458

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...it is entirely sympathetic to itself. Furthermore, from indivisibles <note>original: *individuis*; referring to atoms or points</note> neither body nor magnitude can be created. Besides, if one brings a simple body into the discussion, certainly, insofaras it is material, one will not say it has life from itself, for matter is devoid of quality. Rather, one will say that what takes the place of form <note>original: *forma*; the "blueprint" or organizing principle</note> provides the life. If, then, one says this form is the essence, certainly not both, but one of these will be the soul: which indeed no longer exists as a body. For this is not also made of matter; otherwise, we would be forced to resolve it in the same way again. But if one suggests <margin>B</margin> that such a form is not an essence, but a certain "passion" <note>original: *passio*; an accidental quality or state</note> of matter, it remains for them to assign to us from where this passion and life descended into matter. For matter does not form itself, nor does it provide itself with soul; it is necessary, therefore, that there be something which supplies this life, whether life is supplied to matter itself or to any of the bodies: supplied, I say, by something existing outside and superior to every corporeal nature. Now indeed, <margin>C</margin> there will be no body at all unless the power of the soul exists; for the nature of the body is always in flux and in motion, and the universe would quickly perish if all things were merely bodies, even if someone applied the name of "soul" to one of those bodies. For in that case, the soul would suffer exactly the same as other bodies, since the same matter is in all of them; or rather, nothing would ever be created anywhere, but all things would remain in matter, where the shaper of matter himself was not present. Perhaps indeed <margin>D</margin> matter itself would not even exist at all. This universe would also dissolve if one committed its safety to a physical connection of the body, attributing the order of the soul to it—that is, using names only—as if it were some air or spirit <note>original: *pneuma*</note> that is entirely dissipable and has no internal union from itself. For since all bodies are divisible, if anyone commits this universe to any body, he will be forced to confess that it is a mad whole and is driven too much by chance. What order can there be in <margin>E</margin> spirit, as if it were a mere wind seeking order from the soul—what reason, or what intellect? But if the soul is present, all these things immediately serve it for the constitution of the world and of the remaining living creatures, while one power leads another from every side toward the whole. But if the soul is absent from here, these remaining things would not only lack order, but they would not be able to exist at all.

<column-break/>

...it is sympathetic to itself. From indivisibles, neither a body nor a magnitude could arise. And indeed, if it were some simple part of a body, that which is material does not have life from itself, as they say, for matter is without quality; but that which is fixed according to form <note>original: *eidos*</note> has life. If, then, they say this form is the essence, and that one of these is the body and the other is the soul, then the soul would no longer be a body. For it would be made of matter and this [form]. Or again, we shall analyze it in the same way. If they say it is a "passion" of matter but not an essence, they must say from where the passion and life have come into the matter. For either matter forms itself, or it will not join the soul to itself. There must, therefore, be something that is the provider of life. Whether the provision is to the matter or to any of the bodies, it must be outside and beyond all corporeal nature. Furthermore, there would not even be a body if the soulish power <note>original: *psychikēs dynameōs*</note> were not present. For it flows, and its nature is motion, by which it would disappear as quickly as possible if all things were bodies—even if the name of "soul" were placed upon one of them. For it would suffer the same things as the other bodies, since there is one matter for them; or rather, nothing would even be created, but all things would remain as matter if there were no one to form it. Perhaps indeed matter itself would not even exist at all. This universe would be dissolved if anyone trusted its continuity to a body, which gives it order only in name—to air and spirit <note>original: *pneuma*</note> that scatters downward, and which has no unity from itself. For since all bodies are divisible, if one trusts this universe to them, the motion would be unstable and would make this whole world perish in time. For what order is in a spirit that itself requires order from a soul—what ratio <note>original: *logos*</note> or intellect <note>original: *nous*</note>? But when the soul is present, all these things follow it into the constitution of the world and life for each thing, while one power after another contributes to the whole. But if this is not present in the whole, these things would be nothing, let alone being without order.

---

*The <term>Stoics</term> and <term>Epicureans</term> suspected that the soul was a spirit, that is, a most subtle body: the former thought it was rather fiery, the latter more airy; and both named the soul not just any spirit, but one affected by a certain specific property. Chapter 4.*

*This very specific property, which is in a way incorporeal and more excellent than the body, is not generated by the body, but by a completely incorporeal substance, which will rather be judged to be the soul. Since this substance is equally capable of producing and governing the opposite qualities and motions in the body, it is rightly neither a certain body nor corporeal, nor does it depend on a certain body or bodies.*

---

Even the proponents of corporeal nature, driven by the truth, confess and testify that a certain form of things pertaining to the soul must precede bodies, being more excellent than all bodies, when they bring forward a spirit capable of intelligence and an intellectual fire—as if the highest grade of nature itself could not exist in the order of things without fire and spirit...

<column-break/>

They testify, being led by the truth, that there must be something before the bodies, a better form of soul, since they posit the spirit <note>original: *pneuma*</note> and a certain intellectual fire, as if it were made of fire and spirit... [text cuts off]

<summary>Plotinus argues that life and order cannot originate from matter or physical "spirit" (pneuma) because body is inherently unstable and qualityless. He concludes that an incorporeal soul must exist as a prior organizing principle to provide life and unity to the physical world.</summary>

# BOOK SEVEN.
## 459

<note>original: "εἶναι, τόπον δὲ ζητήσειε..." / "possit, & locum quendam..."</note> ...it might exist, and might naturally require a certain place where it may be established; however, it would be more fitting to seek where bodies might be placed, since these bodies must in truth be placed by the very powers of the soul. Furthermore, if they say that life and the soul are nothing other than a "spirit" <note>original: *spiritus* or *pneuma*; in this context, it refers to a physical gas or breath-like substance, not a ghostly entity</note>—like a wind—one must ask them what they mean by that common saying of theirs: "the soul is a spirit in a certain state." For they are accustomed to flee to this definition whenever they are compelled to introduce an effective nature other than bodies. <margin>B</margin> If, therefore, not every spirit is a soul (since there are countless inanimate spirits), but only a spirit in a certain state, we shall ask whether this "certain state" and such a disposition is a real thing, or nothing at all. For if it is nothing, then certainly only the spirit exists. The addition of "in a state" would be a name only. From this it follows that they would be forced to concede that nothing exists except matter, and they would have to confess that the soul, God, and all such things are merely names, <margin>C</margin> while in reality only body exists. But if that "state" or disposition is a real thing, and something other than the subject and the matter—something which is indeed in matter, but is nevertheless immaterial because it is not itself composed of matter—then certainly it will not be a body, but a completely different nature and a certain "reason" <note>original: *ratio* or *logos*; a formative principle or blueprint</note>. Furthermore, it will appear no less from the following that the soul cannot be a body: for if it were, it would be either hot or cold, hard or soft, <margin>D</margin> compact or fluid and loose; likewise either black or white, and so on for all the other qualities of bodies. And indeed, if it is only hot, it only heats; if cold, it only cools; if light, it only lifts and makes things light wherever it is present; and if heavy, it weights things down and makes them heavy. Similarly, a black thing produces blackness, and a white thing produces whiteness. For it is not the nature of fire to cool, nor of a cold thing to heat. But the soul produces different things in different animals, <margin>E</margin> and in the same animal it produces opposites: in part contracting, in part pouring out and liquefying. Likewise, it makes some things dense and others thin, white, black, light, and heavy; yet it does not do one thing through one quality and another through another, but it ought to do only one thing according to the single quality and color of its body. As it is, however, it brings about many things at once.

> *The soul produces movements and effects of all forms, as much by its vegetative power through seminal reasons as by choice. And the body remains in a certain order and at a certain boundary, while the soul itself remains the same meanwhile. Likewise, the whole soul is in any part, whether it be a supposed portion of the soul or a true portion of the body. And the whole power of the soul is preserved in any drop of seed.* <note>original: *rationes seminales*; the formative principles or "blueprints" inherent in nature that guide the growth of living things</note>

> *These duties, however, cannot pertain to corporeal mass or quality. Therefore, the soul is incorporeal. Chapter V.*

<margin>A</margin> MOTIONS, moreover, in what way can they claim there are many different ones rather than just one, when there is only one motion for any single body? But if they refer the causes of motions partly to "choices" and partly to "seminal reasons," they would be asserting this correctly. But choice is not a property of the body, nor are reasons—especially since they are different, while the body here is one and simple; nor can a body be capable of such "reason" at all, except insofar as it is granted <margin>B</margin> by that which makes it hot or cold. To increase at certain times and to a certain limit—by what power would this be suited to a body? To such a body it would naturally be suited to be increased, but by no means to *cause* the increase, except perhaps insofaras it consists of mass...
