<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s argument against the idea that the soul is a physical body. Having previously argued that life cannot arise from mere matter, he now explores the logical contradictions that arise if we imagine the soul grows, divides, or changes like a physical substance. This is part of his broader proof for the immortality and immateriality of the soul.</meta>

### PLOTINUS ENNEADS BOOK IV.
### 460

<margin>A</margin>
...is taken up alongside the matter, acting as a servant to that which achieves growth through it. For if the soul, being itself a body, causes growth, it is necessary that the soul itself must also grow in equal measure—evidently through the addition of a similar body—if it is to become as large as the thing it is growing. In that case, the part being added will either be a soul, <margin>B</margin> or an inanimate <note>original: *inanimatum*; soulless</note> body. If it is a soul, we must ask from where and how it enters, and under what conditions it is added. But if that which is added is inanimate, how will it become "ensouled," how will it agree with the soul that preceded it, how will they become one, and how will it share in the same opinions as the original soul? Would this new "soul-part" not rather be like a stranger, ignorant of what the other knows? This is just as our physical bulk <note>original: *moles* or *onkos*; referring to the physical mass of the body</note> suffers: part of it flows away, and part flows in, so that nothing in us remains exactly the same. How then will there be memory in us, or the recognition of our own experiences, if we never use the same <margin>C</margin> soul? Furthermore, if the soul is a body, its nature would be to be distributed into many parts, none of which is the same as the whole. If the soul were a certain magnitude, and if it became even slightly smaller it would no longer be a soul, then surely—just like any quantity—it would be changed from its prior essence by the removal of any part. However, if something that possesses magnitude and bulk were to be diminished in size but remain the same in its quality, it would prove that in the respect that it is a body and a <margin>D</margin> quantity, it has become something else, but through its quality (which is different from its quantity), it is able to preserve its identity. What then will they say, those who think the soul is a body? Will they admit that every part of the soul in a living body is a soul just as the whole is? And again, that a part of every part is a soul? If they admit this, then magnitude would contribute nothing to the soul's essence—even though it ought to contribute, if the soul were a quantity. Yet the whole of the soul would be present everywhere; <margin>E</margin> this is something that cannot happen to a body, namely, that the same whole is simultaneously in many places, and that a part is exactly the same as the whole. But if they deny that every part is a soul, then according to them, the soul would be composed of inanimate, soulless things. Furthermore, if the magnitude of each soul were fixed, it would no longer be a soul if it were stretched in either direction, toward the greater or the smaller. Therefore, when twin offspring are <margin>F</margin> created from a single act of union and a single seed, or as in other animals where even more are conceived from the seed being distributed into many parts—where each part is a whole—why does this occurrence not warn those who wish to learn? Here, the part is the same as the whole. This fact itself shows that the soul in its essence transcends being a quantity of any bulk, and it must be entirely removed from the concept of quantity. For only in this way can it remain the same when any amount of quantity is taken away, as it has no need for quantity or bulk, <margin>G</margin> since its essence is entirely something else. The soul, therefore, is devoid of quantity, and its formative principles <note>original: *rationes* or *logoi*; the organizing patterns of life</note> are likewise without quantity.

<column-break/>

mass, serving that which works through it to produce growth. For it is necessary, if the soul—being a body—grows, that it also increases itself, clearly by the addition of a similar body, if it is to reach an equality with that which is being grown by it. And that which is added will either be soul, or an inanimate body. And if it is soul, from where and how does it enter, and to what is it being added? But if that which is added is inanimate, how will this be ensouled, and how will it be of one mind with the soul that was there before? How will it become one, and share in the same opinions as the former soul? Rather, would it not be like a foreign soul, existing in ignorance of what the other knows? It would be just like the rest of our physical mass: some of it flows out, and some flows in, and nothing is ever the same. How then do we have memories? How do we have recognition of what belongs to us, if we never employ the same soul? Moreover, if it is a body, the nature of a body is to be divided into many parts, and each of the parts is not the same as the whole. If the soul is not a soul unless it is of a certain magnitude, then if it becomes smaller, it will not be a soul. Just as with any quantity, it is changed from its previous being by subtraction. But if something having magnitude is diminished in its mass, yet remains the same in its quality, then insofar as it is a body and a quantity, it is different; but by its quality, which is other than quantity, it is able to preserve its identity. What then will they say, those who say the soul is a body? First, regarding each part of the soul in the same body: is each part a soul of the same kind as the whole? and again, a part of a part? If so, then magnitude contributed nothing to its essence. And yet magnitude was supposed to be a requirement for it to exist. But also, the whole would be in many places, which is impossible for a body—to be the same whole in many parts, and for the part to exist as the whole. But if they say each of the parts is not a soul, then for them, the soul will consist of soulless things. Furthermore, if the magnitude of each soul were defined, it would not be a soul if it were changed in either direction, toward the smaller or the larger. Therefore, when twins are born from one union and one seed, or indeed as in other animals where many are born and the seed is divided into many places—if each part is a whole, how does this not teach those who wish to learn that where the part is the same as the whole, this thing has, in its own essence, transcended being a quantity? It must of necessity be shown to be without quantity. For in this way it would remain the same even if the quantity were stolen away, since it has no concern for quantity and bulk, as its essence is something other. The soul, therefore, is without quantity, as are its formative principles.

<meta>catchword: Necesse (It is necessary)</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul cannot be a physical body because a body is constantly losing and gaining matter (flux), which would make memory and personal identity impossible. He further demonstrates that since a soul can be "whole" in different parts (as seen in twins or animal reproduction), it must be an immaterial essence rather than a physical quantity.</summary>

### BOOK SEVEN
### 461

->It is necessary that diverse things flowing in through the various senses be reduced to an internal, single, and indivisible sense that compares them all with one another.<-
->Chapter VI.<-

Unless they are finally gathered into something indivisible, they cannot be compared by a judgment that is entirely the same. That they are gathered there is apparent because they are gathered in a similar way in the pupil of the eye. This internal sense can neither be divided according to the division of the things perceived, nor can it be equal to them in size, nor can it be fluid <note>original: *humidus*; referring to a moist or liquid consistency</note>, otherwise memory would cease; nor can it be hard, for then the ability to learn <note>original: *docilitas*; literally "teachability" or the capacity to be shaped by new information</note> would perish. And if it were entirely physical, the forms of things would get in each other's way and become confused.

---

<margin>* the same</margin>
**THAT** if the soul were a body, there would be no perceiving, no thinking, no knowing, nor virtue, nor anything noble, is clear from what follows. If it is to perceive anything, it must be a single thing itself, and perceive everything with that same self. This is true whether many things enter through many sense organs, or many qualities are perceived around a single thing, or a complex thing like a face is perceived through one organ. For it is not as if one thing perceives the nose and another the eyes; rather, the same thing perceives all at once. And if one thing comes through the eyes and another through hearing, there must be a single point where both arrive. Otherwise, how could there be a judgment that these are different, unless the perceptions of the senses come together into the same place? Therefore, this must be like a center point, and the senses from all sides must lead to this like lines converging from the circumference of a circle; such a thing is that which truly perceives. But if this "center" were divided, as if the senses were spread across the two ends of a line or converged at a point and then separated again, each part would have its own separate perception. It would be as if I perceived one thing and you perceived another. If the object perceived is a face, it must be gathered into a single point, as is apparent. (Indeed, they are even gathered within the pupils themselves.) Otherwise, how could we see such large objects? It is even more 
<margin>* around that which goes to the ruling part, such as around thoughts</margin>
necessary for them to reach the <term>ruling part</term> <note>original: *hegemonikon*; the central command center of the soul in Greek philosophy</note>, as if around thoughts, and this must be indivisible. For if this part had magnitude <note>physical size</note>, it would be divided along with the object perceived. Thus, one part of the soul would perceive one part of the object, and no part of us would perceive the whole as a whole. But the whole is perceived as one. How then could it be divided? For if it were divided, the soul could not be matched exactly as equal to equal, because our ruling part is not equal in size to every object perceived. Into how many parts would the division occur? Would it be cut into as many parts as the incoming perception is divided into? And would each part of the soul perceive that part? Or would some parts be without perception? But that is impossible. If every part perceives the whole, and since magnitude is infinitely divisible, then infinite perceptions would happen for every single object. It would be as if there were infinite images of the same thing in our ruling part, or as if the perceiver were a body. Perception would happen in no other way than by images being pressed into wax by rings, whether the perceptions are pressed into blood or into air. And if they were in fluid bodies—which would seem likely—the images would be confused as if in water, and there would be no memory. But if the shapes remained, it would not be possible—

<column-break/>

**THAT** if the soul is a body, we will not be granted the ability to feel, nor to understand, nor to know, nor will virtue or anything excellent exist within us, as will appear from these points: for if anything is to perceive, it must be one and the same thing, and perceive everything through that one and the same center. And if many things enter through many instruments of the senses, or if there are many qualities centered on one object, or even if something varied like a face is seen through a single sense, it is not as if one part sees the nose and another
**B** sees the eyes; rather, the same thing sees all at once. And if one thing enters through the eyes and another through hearing, there must be one point to which both arrive; otherwise the mind could not judge the difference between them, unless the intentions of the senses and the sensible objects flowed equally into one. It is necessary, therefore, that this be like a center, and the individual senses from every side be stretched toward it, no differently than lines are drawn from a circumference to a center, and that such a force, encompassing all things, 
**C** is truly a single thing. For if it were something divisible, and the intentions of the senses reached toward the two extremes of a line, or if they ran together into one and the same place as a middle point, or if there were one thing here and another there, then one part would only have the sensation of one thing; it would be as if I were to feel one thing, and you to feel another, even if the spectacle were a single face; rather, they must be gathered into one. This is apparent: for they are gathered even in the pupils, otherwise the largest
**D** things could not be seen through them. Therefore, those things that reach the ruling part of the soul itself are much more like indivisible notions; and for that reason, that part will also be indivisible. Otherwise, if it had magnitude, it would be divided along with the sensible object. Thus, one part would perceive one part, and nothing in us would perceive the whole. But yet, that whole is one thing: for in what way can it be divided? For if it were divided, it could not be fitted exactly as an equal to an equal: because our ruling part
**E** cannot be equal in size to every thing that is to be felt. Into how many parts, then, will the division be made? Will it be cut into as many as the incoming sensible object is distributed into by number? And will every tiny part of the soul perceive the same thing? Or perhaps the tiny parts will lack sensation? But truly, that cannot happen. If, however, every part perceives the whole, and since magnitude can be divided into infinity, then surely innumerable sensations will occur around each single sensible object in each person, as if there were innumerable images of the same thing in our ruling part.
**F** Furthermore, if that which perceives is a body, perception will occur in no other way than if images are pressed into wax by a ring, whether the sensible things are pressed into blood or into some kind of air. And if it were as if in fluid bodies—which is probable—the images would certainly be confused as if in water, and there will be no memory at all. But if the figures remain, it will not be allowed—

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul must be an indivisible, non-physical entity because physical bodies cannot unify different sensory inputs (like sight and sound) into a single coherent judgment. He uses the analogy of a circle's center and the wax-seal to demonstrate why a material soul would result in fragmented or lost perceptions.</summary>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK IV.
### 462

...others would be formed there while the former remained, and thus there would be no new sensations; or if new ones were made, the earlier ones would be immediately destroyed, and therefore memory would cease. If, however, we are able to remember, and to perceive one thing after another without the former sensations hindering us, it is impossible for the soul to be a body. <note>original Greek: ἐμποδιζόντων τῶν πρώτων, ἀδύνατον τὴν ψυχὴν σῶμα εἶναι; "If the first things do not hinder, it is impossible for the soul to be a body."</note>

*The principal sense, as the judge of experiences, immediately perceives the sufferings of any limb; it discerns distinctly in which small part of the limb they are, and immediately moves the eyes and hands there. It would not be able to do this, however, unless it were entirely present everywhere. Therefore, it is not corporeal.*

->Chapter VII.<-

<margin>A</margin> THE SAME can also be shown from pain and the sensation of pain, as when someone is said to have a pain in their finger. In that case, the pain is indeed in the finger, but they will admit that the sensation of the pain occurs around the soul's governing part <term>hegemonikon</term> <note>The ruling or "principal" part of the soul in Neoplatonic and Stoic thought.</note>. While a certain part of the "animated spirit" <term>pneuma</term> <note>A subtle, breath-like substance thought to carry sensations through the body.</note> suffers, the governing part perceives it, and the whole soul then suffers the same thing in a certain way. How, then, does this happen? They will answer, I suppose, by a sort of "successive transmission," where the animal spirit around the finger suffers first, and from there the experience is transmitted <margin>B</margin> to the adjacent part, and then again to another, until it reaches the governing part. It is necessary, therefore, if the first part felt the pain, that there be a second sensation for the second part—if indeed sensation is amplified through a succession—and a third sensation for the third part that suffers. This would result in many, even countless sensations for a single pain, and the governing part would finally feel only its own experience. In truth, each individual act of sensing would not perceive the suffering of the finger, but only the sensation that <margin>C</margin> follows just after the finger. For instance, the palm of the hand nearest the finger would perceive the experience immediately following the finger; a more remote part would perceive a more remote experience, and many pains would occur. Then, certainly, the governing part would feel not the experience pressing upon the finger, but its own experience; it would render judgment on this alone, dismissing all others, remaining entirely ignorant that the finger is in pain. If, therefore, the sensation of such an experience cannot happen by succession, and because a body is a mass <note>original: *moles*; a physical bulk or weight</note> it does not have the capacity for one part to perceive what another part suffers—for in any magnitude, this part is one thing and that part is another—it must be that the perceiving subject is such that it is everywhere the same as itself. To achieve this belongs to another order of things rather than to the body. <note>original Greek: οἷον πανταχοῦ αὐτὸ ἑαυτῷ, τὸ αὐτὸ εἶναι... "being everywhere the same with itself... this belongs to another of the things that exist rather than to body."</note>

*Intelligence frequently reaches and penetrates incorporeal things and separates forms from bodies. It therefore acts without the body; thus, the intellect is not corporeal. Since the indivisible can only be reached by the indivisible, the intellect that reaches individual things is itself indivisible; and where it joins itself to separate things, it is separate from the body; and when it separates things that are joined, it most clearly proves itself to be separate.*

->Chapter VIII.<-

<margin>A</margin> FURTHERMORE, we must demonstrate that if the soul were a body in any way, it would be unable to think. Truly, if sensing is the soul perceiving sensible things by using the body, then thinking cannot be grasping things through the body; otherwise, thinking and sensing would be the same thing. If, therefore, thinking is grasping things without the body, it is much more necessary that the thing which is to think should not be a body itself. Moreover, if sensation is of sensible things, then intellection is of intelligible things. Even if they do not admit this entirely, there will still be [intellections] of intelligible things <margin>B</margin>

<column-break/>

...others would be indicated while those earlier ones were held, so that there would be other sensations; or if others were produced, those earlier ones would perish, so that there would be no remembering. But if there is remembering, and perceiving one thing after another without the former ones hindering, it is impossible for the soul to be a body.

->Chapter VII.<-

<margin>A</margin> ONE MIGHT see this same thing again from the experience of pain and the sensation of pain. When a man is said to have a pain in his finger, the pain is indeed in the finger, but they will clearly agree that the sensation of the pain occurs in the governing part. But while the part in pain is the spirit <term>pneuma</term>, the governing part perceives it, and the whole soul suffers the same. How then does this happen? They will say it is by "transmission," the soul-spirit around the finger suffering first and passing it to the next part, and this to another, until it arrives at the governing part. It is necessary then, if the first part felt the pain, that the second sensation be different, if the <margin>B</margin> sensation is by transmission. And for the third, another. Many sensations, even infinite ones, would arise concerning a single pain. And from all these, the last—the governing part—would perceive its own sensation, not that of the finger. This would be true of each of those parts: <margin>C</margin> not the pain in the finger, but the one next to the finger would be felt, and then the third would feel that the part next to it was sensing. There would be many pains, and the governing part would not perceive the pain in the finger, but the one close to itself. And it would know only this, letting the others go, not knowing that <margin>D</margin> the finger is in pain. If, then, sensation of this kind cannot occur by transmission, nor can the bulk of a body know that another part has suffered (for in every magnitude one part is different from another), one must say that the perceiving subject is such that it is everywhere the same with itself. This belongs to some other kind of being than body.

->Chapter VIII.<-

<margin>A</margin> THAT it is not possible for the soul to think if it were a body of any kind must be shown from these points. For if sensing is the soul perceiving sensible things by using the body, thinking cannot be grasping through a body, or it will be the same as sensing. If, then, thinking is perceiving without a body, much more must the thinking subject itself not be a body. <margin>B</margin> Further, if sensation is of sensible things, and intellection is of intelligible things—even if they do not wish it, there will at least be intellections of intelligible things...

<meta>The catchword at the bottom "τῶν" (of the) indicates the first word of the next page in the Greek text.</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul must be incorporeal because physical matter cannot explain the unity of sensation or the process of thought. He uses the example of pain in a finger to show that if the soul were physical, sensation would be a series of disconnected "relays" rather than a single, immediate experience.</summary>

# BOOK SEVEN.
### 463

...whose thoughts and apprehensions of things without magnitude <note>original Greek: ἀμεγεθῶν (amegethon); referring to things that do not take up physical space, such as abstract concepts or mathematical points.</note> occur within us. In what way, then, if the intellect were a physical magnitude, would it understand that which is free from magnitude? And how could a divisible nature apprehend that which is indivisible? 

<margin>The divisible</margin> Perhaps it does so by some indivisible part of itself? If that is the case, then that which understands is not a body at all. For there is no need for the whole body to reach out and touch the object; it is enough for one single part to do so. If, therefore, they concede—which is true—that the primary acts of the intellect are concerned with things entirely absolute from the body (that is, the "abstracted" essence of each thing, as it is called), it is necessary <margin>B</margin> that the thinking nature also understands only insofar as it is, or becomes, free from the body. 

If, however, they say that these thoughts are concerned with forms attached to matter, they must still admit that these forms are only understood when they are separated from bodies—that is, by the intellect performing the separation. For when the mind separates them, the "Man himself," or the "Circle," "Triangle," "Line," and "Point" themselves <note>Plotinus is referring to the "Platonic Forms" or "Ideas"—the perfect, non-physical versions of objects that the mind perceives through reason rather than the physical senses.</note> do not exist alongside this flesh or with matter at all. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, it is necessary for the soul also to withdraw itself from the body in this state of contemplation. It follows then that the soul itself cannot be a body. Certainly, "the Beautiful" itself and "the Just" itself are exempt from all magnitude, and likewise the understanding of them. Therefore, as these things approach us, they will be received by an indivisible part of the soul and will remain situated in that very indivisibility. Finally, if the soul were a body, I do not see how temperance and justice could be its virtues, since these virtues preserve the soul only insofar as they are grasped by it.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> 
---
->*Corporeal essence, being imperfect, depends on the perfect incorporeal essence, which, since it first exists and lives from itself, always exists and lives; in this category the soul is contained. Chapter IX.*<-

->*Because the soul is the last in the order of divine things, it seems to enter into commerce with perishable things, whereby its best state is interrupted. But because it is included in the category of divine things, it constantly preserves its nature, but can be recalled to its original dignity.*<-
---

<margin>A</margin> IT IS altogether necessary that there be another nature besides bodies, which possesses being from itself. This is that which is judged to be "truly being," which neither comes into existence nor perishes. Otherwise, all other things would slip away and could not be born again if such a nature ever perished; for it is this nature that provides safety <note>In this philosophical context, "salvation" or "safety" (salutem/soterian) refers to the preservation of existence and order.</note> to all these things, and even to the universe itself, which is preserved and adorned through the soul. 

For the soul is the principle of motion, providing movement to other things while moving itself. <margin>B</margin> It provides life to the animated body, yet it possesses life from itself, never to lose it, since it holds it by its own nature. For not all things use a life that is borrowed from elsewhere—otherwise, there would be an infinite progression <note>The "infinite regress" argument: if everything got its life from something else, you would never find the original source. There must be a "Prime Mover" or primary source of life.</note>. Rather, there must exist some nature that is "primarily living," which must be incorruptible and immortal, as it is the principle of life for all others. Truly, in this rank, everything divine and blessed must stand, living and existing from itself—primarily existing and primarily living—without any change in its essence, neither beginning nor ending. 

For from where could it be born, or into what could it be resolved? If the true name of "Being" <term>essentis</term> <note>Latin: *essentis*; referring to the quality of having true, unchanging existence.</note> belongs to it, it must not be at one time and not at another. Just as the color white is white in itself, and is not white at one time and then...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul cannot be physical because it perceives non-physical truths like Justice and Beauty. He posits the necessity of an incorporeal, self-existent "primary life" that sustains the universe and the soul's own immortality.</summary>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD IV.
### 464

...not whiteness. If, however, whiteness itself were <margin>A</margin> Being itself, then surely it would exist alongside that which is white and would exist forever. But as it stands, it only possesses the quality of being white. But that to which Being itself is present from itself and is primarily Being, undoubtedly exists forever. This, therefore, which is primarily Being and eternally Being, ought not to be devoid of life like a stone or a piece of wood: rather, it must be living, and enjoy a pure life—at least for as long as it remains itself. But that part of it which is mixed with a lower nature <note>The "lower nature" refers to the physical body and the material world.</note> suffers an impediment toward reaching the highest things; yet it does not lose its own nature, <margin>B</margin> but rather resumes its ancient state whenever it returns to the heights.

There are two gifts of the divine minds. One is the clarity of the intellect, which discerns all things; the other is the best habit of life. A soul follows these gifts most closely when it separates itself from every bodily stain and returns into itself. From this, it appears that the soul is related by nature to the divine minds.

### Chapter X.

There are two arguments for divinity among us. One is prophecy; the other is the demonstration of miraculous works. Whoever has brought back these divine gifts seems to have claimed them for themselves by this one duty alone: that they have recalled the soul from the body back to itself. From this, it is clear that the soul's nature is inherently joined with divinity.

<margin>A</margin> **THAT THE SOUL** is kin to the more divine and eternal nature is evident from the fact that it is not a body, as has been demonstrated to us; it has neither figure, nor color, nor mass, nor any quality that is graspable in any physical way. Furthermore, the same can be shown through these points. Since it is agreed among us that every divine and truly existing being enjoys a good and wise life, we must next consider our own soul, and what its nature is most of all. Let us take a soul that has not yet conceived irrational desires <margin>B</margin> and angers within a body, nor admitted other disturbances; but rather one which has expelled all these things, and has no commerce with the body, except what the highest necessity compels. Such a soul will undoubtedly reveal to us that vices and evils are mere additions to the soul, thrown upon us from the outside. Indeed, in a soul already purified, the highest things are found to be present—namely wisdom and the rest of the virtues—as if they were its own family. If, therefore, the soul is such a thing whenever it returns into itself, what is there to hinder it from being in the same rank as that nature which we confess to be entirely divine and eternal? For wisdom and true virtue, being divine things, cannot ever exist in any base or mortal nature; rather, it is necessary that such a thing be divine, since it is a partaker <margin>C</margin> of divine things through a certain kinship and a <term>communion of substance</term> <note>original Latin: "communionemque substantiae"; original Greek: "homoousion" (consubstantial). This implies the soul is made of the same "stuff" as the divine.</note>. Therefore, whoever among us is so affected, seems to differ only by a small degree from the heavenly beings according to the soul; <margin>D</margin> yielding only in this, that he is currently in a body. For this reason, if all men, or at least many, were endowed with such souls, no one would be so incredulous as to ever doubt that the nature of our soul is entirely immortal. But now, since men see the soul in most people defiled by many vices, they naturally judge it to be neither a divine thing nor immortal. However, one ought to consider the nature of each thing by looking at it in its pure state. For that which is added <margin>E</margin> always tends to hinder the knowledge of that to which it was added. Consider it, then, by stripping away the additions; or rather, let him who strips them away look at himself, and he will easily believe himself to be immortal:

<column-break/>

...not whiteness. If whiteness itself were Being, it would <margin>A</margin> exist alongside Being and be eternal. But it only possesses whiteness. To whatever Being is present—present from itself and as primary Being—it will exist forever. For that which is primarily Being and eternally Being must not be a dead thing like a stone or wood, but must be alive. And it must enjoy a pure life, so long as it remains alone. But that which is mixed with the inferior possesses an obstacle toward the best things, though it does not entirely lose its own nature; <margin>B</margin> it recovers its ancient state when it runs back to the same heights.

<margin>A</margin> **THAT** the soul is kin to the more divine and eternal nature is made clear by the fact that it was shown not to be a body, and it has no form, nor shape, nor color. This can be shown from the senses, but also from the things following from them. Since we agree that everything divine and truly existing truly enjoys a life that is good and wise, let us look after this at what the nature of our soul is. Let us take a soul, not the one in <margin>B</margin> the body that has taken on irrational desires and angers and received other passions, but the one that has shaken these off, and as far as possible has no communion with the body. This soul makes it clear that evils are additions to the soul, and come from elsewhere; but when it is purified, the best things—wisdom and the other virtues—belong to it as its own. If, then, the soul is such a thing when it <margin>C</margin> withdraws into itself, how can it not belong to that nature which we say is that of all the divine and eternal? For wisdom and true virtue, being divine, would not arise in any base and mortal thing. But it is necessary that such a thing be divine, as it is full of divine things through kinship and being <term>of the same substance</term> <note>original Greek: ὁμοούσιον (homoousion). A pivotal term in Greek philosophy and theology meaning "of one essence."</note>. Therefore, whoever of our race is thus, would differ but little <margin>D</margin> in his soul from the beings above. For he remains less only insofar as he is in a body. Therefore, if every human was such, or a multitude possessed such souls, no one would be so unbelieving as not to believe that the soul itself is entirely immortal. But now, seeing the soul in most people is defiled in many places, they do not think of it as a divine or immortal thing. But one must consider the <margin>E</margin> nature of each thing by looking at it in its purity. Since that which is added is always an obstacle to the knowledge of that to which it was added, look then by stripping it away; or rather, let the one who strips it away see himself. And he will believe himself to be immortal.

<meta>catchword: That (ὅτι)</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul is essentially divine and immortal because its core nature—when stripped of bodily desires and vices—is defined by wisdom and virtue. He suggests that if we perceive the soul as mortal, it is only because we are distracted by the "additions" of the physical body.</summary>

# BOOK SEVEN.
### 469

...namely, when it beholds itself in the **intelligible world** <note>The "intelligible world" (cosmos noetos) is the realm of pure thought and forms, beyond the physical senses.</note> and has come to dwell in that pure place. For it will perceive the Intellect seeing not any sensible thing, nor any of these mortal objects, but by an eternal power it rightly considers the eternal: and it sees all things in the intelligible world, and perceives itself to have become intelligible and radiant—illuminated by the truth that flashes from the **Good** <note>The "Good" is the ultimate principle in Neoplatonism, the source of all being and truth.</note>, which bathes all intelligible things in the light of truth. Indeed, at such a moment, the soul might well feel that the famous saying applies to it: <margin>B</margin> "Greetings! I am now to you an immortal God," <note>original: "χαίρετε, ἐγὼ δ’ ὑμῖν θεὸς ἄμβροτος" – A quote from the philosopher Empedocles, claiming his divine nature.</note> having ascended to the divine and leaning entirely toward the divine likeness. If, then, purification itself causes the soul to know the highest things, then the sciences hidden within will surely shine forth—those which are truly sciences. For the soul does not run outside itself to observe temperance and justice; rather, it gazes upon them within itself, in the contemplation of its own being and in the recognition of what it was before. It sees them like divine images established within itself, which were previously covered with the rust of time; <margin>C</margin> it now wipes them clean, just as if **gold** were endowed with a soul. If such gold were covered in earth, it would not recognize itself as gold because it could not see its own nature; but once it shakes off the earth and sees its own purity, it would marvel at itself and realize it has no need for external beauty, considering it best to simply remain within its own nature.

*An animated body possesses the ability to be moved, in a sense, from within itself by the benefit of the soul. Therefore, the soul possesses this same power to the highest degree; thus, it also possesses life from itself. Consequently, it does not depend on the body for its life; therefore, it always lives, even when separated from the body.*

### Chapter XI.

*It appears that the soul moves and lives from itself and in itself, even without the support of the body—especially when it moves against the body's inclinations and transfers itself to incorporeal things. If any accidental trace of life is impressed upon the body, it must be traced back to the substantial life of the soul existing in itself, just as the heat or paleness of a cloud is traced back to light. But just as light is related to the sun, so the soul is related to the Mind.*

<margin>A</margin> No one of sound mind, therefore, having looked upon such a thing, will doubt that the soul is immortal, since life resides in it from itself and cannot perish. For how could it perish, since life is not something "added on" <term>adventitious</term> <note>Something "adventitious" is a property added from the outside, like the heat in a pot of water, rather than an essential part of the thing itself.</note>? Nor is it like heat is to fire. I do not say this because I think heat is "added" to fire, but because heat resides not in the fire itself, but in the **matter** of the fire. For this reason, fire is dissolved <note>When the material conditions change, fire goes out.</note>; but the soul does not "have" life in the sense that there is a underlying matter and life arrives to turn that matter into a soul. <margin>B</margin> Either **essence** itself is life, and such an essence lives from itself—which is exactly what we call the soul, and which they will admit is immortal—or they must break it down like a composite thing until they reach something immortal that moves itself (which it is a sacrilege to suggest could die). Or, if they say that life is merely an "affection" <note>An "affection" or "accident" is a temporary state, like being happy or being hot.</note> added to matter, they will eventually be forced to admit that the source from which such an affection was given to matter is itself immortal, since it cannot receive the opposite of what it brings. <margin>C</margin> In truth, there is one nature that is alive in its very **activity** <note>original: "ἐνεργείᾳ" (energeia) – the state of being in active operation.</note>.

*Our soul, imitating the Soul of the World in its motion and its understanding of things, is eternal, just as that World-Soul is—especially because, while recalling itself to its own depths to understand things, it declares that it possesses the absolute forms of things born within it. Chapter XII.*

*Finally, since the soul is a simple form, indivisible, not bound to matter, it can neither be dissolved, nor divided, nor destroyed.*

<margin>A</margin> Furthermore, if one were to say that every soul is perishable, then all things should have perished long ago.

<column-break/>

...namely, when it beholds itself in the **intelligible world** and has come to dwell in that pure place. It will perceive the **Intellect** seeing not any sensible thing, nor any of these mortal objects, but by an eternal power it rightly considers the eternal: and it sees all things in the intelligible world, and perceives itself to have become intelligible and radiant—illuminated by the truth that flashes from the **Good**, which bathes all intelligible things in the light of truth. Indeed, at such a moment, the soul might well feel that the famous saying applies to it: <margin>B</margin> "Farewell! I am now to you an immortal God," having ascended to the divine and leaning entirely toward the divine likeness. If, then, purification itself causes the soul to know the highest things, then the sciences hidden within will surely shine forth—those which are truly sciences. For the soul does not run outside itself to observe temperance and justice; rather, it gazes upon them within itself, in the contemplation of its own being and in the recognition of what it was before. It sees them like divine images established within itself, which were previously covered with the rust of time; <margin>C</margin> it now wipes them clean, just as if **gold** were endowed with a soul. If such gold were covered in earth, it would not recognize itself as gold because it could not see its own nature; but once it shakes off the earth and sees its own purity, it would marvel at itself and realize it has no need for external beauty, considering it best to simply remain within its own nature.

*An animated body possesses the ability to be moved, in a sense, from within itself by the benefit of the soul. Therefore, the soul possesses this same power to the highest degree; thus, it also possesses life from itself. Consequently, it does not depend on the body for its life; therefore, it always lives, even when separated from the body.*

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the immortality of the soul, specifically addressing the differences between the Universal Soul and the individual human soul. It explores why a divine soul would descend into a mortal body.</meta>

# PLOTINUS' ENNEADS BOOK IV

<margin>A</margin> If, then, someone were to say that one soul is perishable while another is not—as if the soul of the universe were immortal but ours were mortal—the reason for this distinction must be explained. Truly, both are the principle of motion, and both live from themselves; both reach toward the same heights with the same understanding, contemplating things in the heavens and those beyond the heavens, searching out everything that exists according to its essence, and finally proceeding all the way to the highest principle of all things. Furthermore, <margin>B</margin> because the soul discovers by itself, from its own internal notions, what each thing is—namely through the gift of **reminiscence** <term>reminiscence: The Platonic concept (anamnesis) that the soul does not "learn" new things but remembers truths it knew in the divine realm before birth.</term>—it is clear that the soul lives before the body. Using eternal knowledge, the soul itself must also be eternal. To this it may be added that everything dissolvable, since it receives its being through composition, can naturally be dissolved by the same condition through which it was composed. But the soul is a single and simple act, a nature consisting in the very act of living; therefore, it cannot perish by this means. But could it perhaps perish <margin>C</margin> by being divided into parts and scattered? No, for as has been demonstrated, the soul is neither a physical mass nor a quantity. Could it perhaps be destroyed by being changed and—as is commonly said—altered? But while alteration may destroy a thing, it only removes the **form** <note>In Greek philosophy, "form" (eidos) is the essential nature or "blueprint" of a thing, while "matter" is the physical stuff it is made of.</note> from the remaining matter. This is an experience belonging to composite things. If, therefore, the soul cannot be corrupted in any of these ways, it must necessarily be incorruptible.

---

->*Our soul, although it belongs to the class of divine things, nevertheless because it holds the lowest rank in that class, deservedly descends into the body—and indeed into a perishable one—destined to return again to the divine rank.* Chapter XIII.<-

The nature of the **Intellect** <term>Intellect: In Neoplatonism, the 'Nous' or Divine Mind, the second highest level of reality, containing the eternal archetypes of all things.</term> is far different from the body, for it acts within itself, fleeing from corporeal things. Therefore, pure Intellect and bodies are natures that have both an intellectual part and an "animal" or "soul-driven" part—that is, a part inclined toward shaping bodies to match themselves. There are three ranks in these: in celestial souls, the intellectual part surpasses the animal; in our souls, the reverse is true; in **daemonic** <note>Not "demons" in the modern sense, but "daemons" (daimones)—intermediary spirits or guardians that exist between gods and humans.</note> souls, they are held in balance. It is no wonder, then, that our soul, though divine, descends into a mortal body, since it descends within itself to the third level—that is, beneath the Intellect, through reason and imagination, down to the **vegetative power** <note>The lowest function of the soul, responsible for basic life processes like growth and nutrition.</note>.

<margin>A</margin> Since, therefore, the intelligible itself is separate, for what reason does the soul proceed into the body? Because insofar as the Intellect alone is free from suffering <note>original: "passionis expers" / "ἀπαθὴς" – Meaning the Intellect is not affected or changed by external physical influences.</note> in the rank of intelligible things, having only an intellectual life, it always remains there. For there is no impulse or appetite within it. But that which employs appetite—following closely after that Intellect—is carried further forward, as it were, by the addition of appetite. Longing to adorn the world according to the pattern of those things it knew in the Intellect, and as if pregnant and <margin>B</margin> in labor from them, it strives to create, and finally it fabricates. Thus, by this zeal, the soul draws itself toward the sensible world and governs it; and while it holds the rudders together with the common soul of all things, its companion, it presides over the governed thing from the outside, as if living in the common governance of the whole. But when it desires to govern a specific part, it then governs alone. Being infused into that in which it lives, it does not become entirely or wholly a part of the body, but meanwhile possesses something outside the body; therefore, <margin>C</margin> its intellect is not subject to suffering. But the soul lives sometimes in the body and sometimes outside the body. Indeed, it begins with a certain impulse from the first things, and having progressed to the third things, it descends to ours by a certain act of the intellect; while the intellect itself remains in itself, meanwhile...

<column-break/>

If one soul is immortal and the other not—for example, if the soul of the universe is immortal but ours is not—the cause must be told to them. For each is a principle of motion, and each lives from itself. Both touch upon the same things with the same understanding, contemplating both the things in heaven and the things beyond heaven, and seeking every essence according to its essence, and ascending as far as the first principle. Indeed, the understanding that comes from itself, from the visions within it, and the understanding of each thing that arises from **reminiscence** <note>original: "ἐξ ἀναμνήσεως" – Plotinus uses the Platonic term for the soul's innate memory of the divine.</note>, grants it existence before the body. Since it employs eternal sciences, it must also be eternal. Everything that is dissolved has received a composition; it is the nature of such a thing to be dissolved in the same way it was put together. But the soul is a single and simple activity, its nature being in the act of living; therefore, it will not be destroyed in this way. But will it perhaps perish by being divided or cut into small pieces? But as was shown, the soul was not any kind of physical mass; nor will it come to destruction by being altered. For alteration, while destroying, takes away the form but leaves the matter. This is the experience of a composite. If, therefore, it is not possible to be destroyed according to any of these ways, it is a necessity that it be incorruptible.

---

->Chapter XIII.<-

How then, since the intelligible is separate, does the soul come into the body? Because as much as the Intellect is alone impassive among the intelligibles, having only an intellectual life, it always remains there. And life exists there without impulse or appetite. But that which in turn takes on appetite—being next in order after that Intellect—is carried, as it were, further and further by the addition of appetite. Desiring to order the world according to the things it saw, and being, as it were, pregnant from them and <margin>B</margin> in labor to give birth, it hastens to make and create. And by this zeal, it is stretched toward the sensible world. Together with the whole soul of all things, it oversees the governed world from the outside and cares for the whole. But having wished to govern a part, it becomes solitary. Yet it does not belong to that in which it is. It does not become entirely or wholly the body's, but holds something outside the body. For this reason, its intellect is not impassive <note>The Greek text here asks if the soul is affected by passion/suffering while its intellect remains unaffected.</note>, but the soul itself is? It is sometimes in the body and <margin>C</margin> sometimes outside the body. Having started from the first things and proceeded to the third things—namely to these here—it does so by the activity of the Intellect, which remains in the same place, and through the soul, which fills all things with beauty.

<summary>This page argues for the soul's immortality based on its simplicity, its ability to remember eternal truths (reminiscence), and its role as the principle of life. It also explains the "descent" of the soul into the body as a creative impulse to order the physical world according to divine patterns.</summary>
<keywords>immortality of the soul, reminiscence, Plotinus, Intellect, Anima Mundi, corruption, composition, sensible world, divine rank</keywords>

### BOOK SEVEN

<margin>(On immortality)</margin> Adorned with immortality, *through the immortal.* Since he himself is also ever-existing, he disposes all things through an unceasing activity. <note>original Greek: ἐξακοσμηθεὶς ἀθανάτῳ... "adorned with the immortal... through an unceasing energy."</note>
A: The immortal orderer, through an immortal soul: since he himself also exists forever, he dispenses all things through an unceasing act.

---

->Every soul possesses its own immortal life. Chapter XIV.<-

*Whatever life shines forth from our soul into our body accompanies the soul as it departs from here. But that vital spark which had been impressed from heaven into the fetus is preserved by heaven; our soul, if it departs from here impure, revolves around this with love, whereas a pure soul leaves it behind.*

<margin>On animals</margin> CONCERNING the soul of other animals. <margin>*beasts</margin> For as many of them as have fallen and reached even the bodies of *beasts, these too must necessarily be immortal. But if there is some other species of soul, it must depend on nothing else but the living nature; for it is itself the cause of life for the animals. Similarly, the soul of plants must also be held in this way. For all have proceeded from the same principle, B possessing their own life. They too are incorporeal, indivisible, and essential. But if it is necessary for the human soul, which is tripartite <term>tripartite: Referring to the Platonic division of the soul into three parts: the rational (reason), the spirited (emotion), and the appetitive (desire).</term> in its composite state, to be dissolved, we shall say that those souls which depart pure will put away that which was added to them in their birth <note>original: "prosplaston" / "προσπλαστὸν", referring to the "accretions" or "layers" the soul picks up as it descends into the material world.</note>; but others will wipe away such a conjoined stain through long cycles of time. We shall say that even that which is discarded, though it be the inferior part, is not itself lost, as long as that from which it draws its origin remains. For nothing of that which is considered to be "being" is ever destroyed.

<column-break/>

A: INQUIRY is further made concerning the soul of the remaining animals. And surely, whichever among them are such that, degenerating from higher states, they have fallen even into the bodies of brutes, these also are necessarily immortal. But if there is some other species of soul, it is necessary that this also depends on nothing else than the living nature, since it is itself the cause of life for the animals. Similarly, one must hold that the soul of plants is also such. For all have proceeded from the same principle, B possessing their own life, and these also are incorporeal, indivisible, and essences. But if it were necessary for the human soul, which exists as tripartite, to be dissolved in its composite state, we shall say that those souls which depart pure will dismiss that which had been joined to them in generation; while others will wipe away such a conjoined stain through long courses of time. We shall say that even that which is discarded, though it be the inferior part, is not itself lost, as long as that from which it draws its origin exists. For nothing of that which is considered "being" is ever destroyed.

<column-break/>

->The souls of the deceased remember our affairs, they feel, care for us, and do both harm and good. Chapter XV.<-

*As long as they have a body of any kind—whether airy or ethereal—they also have their own senses. But if they strip off every body, they are judged to use a certain excellence of intelligence for discerning individual things in place of senses. For imagination, especially when perfected, takes the place of sense, and reason drives imagination and sense, while the intellect directs reason and its consequences in a more excellent way.*

A: Those things which needed to be said to those who require demonstration have been said; but those things which are appropriately said to those who need a faith mixed with sensory perception must be selected from the history which abounds in such matters: especially from those things which the gods have commanded through oracles, ordering that the indignation of souls who were once wronged be appeased, and that due honors be returned to the deceased, as if they were aware of such things, just as all people observe toward the departed. B: Furthermore, many souls, which once lived a human life, after being separated from the body have not ceased to bestow benefits upon the human race; indeed, through prophecies and oracles, they both assist us in other matters and demonstrate through themselves that the souls of others have not been extinguished.

<column-break/>

A: THOSE things have been said thus far which were to be said to those who demand demonstration; but those things which might be opportunely said to those who rather require a certain faith permitted by the senses must be chosen from history, which is abundant in such matters: especially from those things which the gods have commanded by oracles, ordering the indignation of souls who were once affected by injury to be appeased, and merited honors to be returned to the deceased, as if they were perceiving such things, just as everyone observes B toward the deceased. Furthermore, many souls, which once lived a human life, then segregated from the body, did not cease to affect the human race with benefits: which indeed, through prophecies and oracles, both confer other things upon us and also demonstrate through themselves that the souls of others are not extinct.

<column-break/>

*Magnanimous Lawrence <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492), the de facto ruler of the Florentine Republic and a great patron of the translator, Marsilio Ficino.</note>, you desire at last a brief summary of this long dispute—a dispute, I say, concerning immortality, which in Theology and in the present work has now been drawn out at length. Our friend Bernardo also desired the same when, as the orator of the Venetian senate here, he heard us disputing most extensively on this matter. I speak of Bernardo Bembo <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519), a Venetian diplomat and humanist, father of the famous Pietro Bembo.</note>, a man of prime learning, a patron of scholars, and my brother in star and spirit. For you, therefore, and for him alike, this summary shall be divided into four chapters: first, that the soul can rule over falling things and resist bodily impulses; second, that it frequently thinks of many things separated from bodies, whether it touches things separated in themselves or prepares itself; third, that it naturally desires eternal things and, through confidence in the eternal, often neglects temporal things; fourth, that it worships the eternal God for the sake of everlasting life. Finally, all natural religion is the firmest foundation of immortality for man.*

<meta>This page transitions from the general discussion of the soul's immortality in Book VII to the specific problem of why a divine soul would choose to inhabit a material body. This begins Book VIII of the Fourth Ennead, one of Plotinus’s most influential writings on the mystical experience and the "descent" of the soul.</meta>

P L O T I N U S
ENNEAD FOUR,
BOOK VIII.

# ON the descent of the Soul into bodies.
## Concerning the soul’s descent into bodies.

*Our intellectual souls descend into the body through a life-giving nature joined to their intelligence, which naturally adopts the body like flame adopts sulfur; similarly, the intellectual souls of the celestial bodies are coupled to their own bodies by such a medium.*

---

<margin>Chap. I.</margin>

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'V' featuring a bearded figure (possibly a philosopher) seated at a desk with an open book, within an architectural interior.</image-desc>
**G**OD willed that there should be certain intellectual living beings—according to the pattern of His own intellect—in every sphere of the world, both in heaven and below heaven. And lest these intellects should be dragged into bodies as if by force, it seems He arranged for them to be willingly adopted by bodies through an animal nature—that is, a vegetative nature born with them like a plant.

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' with a human profile and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>
**O**FTEN indeed, having been awakened from the body to myself, and being placed outside of other things but received within myself, I behold a wonderful beauty. Then, above all, I am confident that I belong to a more excellent portion; for then I lead the best life and harmonize with the divine, in which state, being established, I reach that activity through which I set myself above every other thing known to the mind <note>original Latin: *intelligibile*; Greek: *νοητὸν* — that which is perceived by the intellect rather than the senses</note>.

<margin>B</margin>
But after this rest in the divine, having slipped down from the Mind into the process of reasoning <term>reasoning: Latin *ratiocinationem*; Greek *λογισμὸν*. In Neoplatonism, this is a lower, step-by-step form of thinking compared to the direct, instant intuition of the higher Mind.</term>, I am indeed uncertain by what means I now descend, and how it is that my soul has ever entered into the body, being such as it appeared by itself, even though it lives in a body.

<margin>C</margin>
Heraclitus, then, urges us to inquire diligently into this, and he himself posits certain necessary successions from contraries to contraries, and speaks of a "path from above to the lowest depths." In this change, there seems to be a certain rest, as if it were an intolerable exhaustion to labor and serve perpetually in the same things. But in discussing these matters, he seems to wander through certain likenesses <note>original Latin: *similitudines*; Greek: *εἰκάζειν* — metaphors or riddles</note> as if inventing them, neglecting to reveal his meaning to us, so that perhaps we must seek in him again, just as he himself found by seeking.

<margin>D</margin>
Moreover, Empedocles, having said that a law exists decreeing that souls who have sinned fall to these our regions, and that he himself, as an exile from God, came here trusting in "furious discord" and to serve it, has (as I think) discussed only as much as Pythagoras and his followers signified through certain veils <note>original Latin: *inuolucra*; Greek: *ᾐνίττοντο* — riddles or allegories</note> both regarding this and many other things.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Π' (Pi) depicting a winged putto or angel holding a staff within a landscape.</image-desc>
**O**FTEN awakened into myself from the body, and becoming outside of other things, but inside myself, I see a marvelous beauty, and I believe then most of all that I belong to the better part, and I act out the best life, having become one with the divine; and being established in it, I come into that activity, having established myself above all other intellectual things. After this stay in the divine, descending from Mind to reasoning, I am at a loss as to how I ever now descend, and how ever my soul has come to be inside the body, being such a thing as it appeared when by itself, even though it is in a body. Heraclitus, who urges us to seek this, positing necessary exchanges from contraries, and speaking of a way "up and down," says that "in changing it finds rest," and that it is "toil to labor at the same things and be ruled." He gives us the task of making comparisons, having neglected to make his meaning clear to us, as if it were necessary perhaps to seek from him, just as he himself found by seeking. Empedocles, too, said it is a law for souls who sin to fall here, and he himself, becoming a fugitive from God, comes trusting in "mad strife." He provides as much as I think Pythagoras and those after him used to hint at in riddles, both about this and about many other things.

<summary>Plotinus begins his famous treatise on the soul's descent, opening with a personal account of a mystical ascent to the divine before questioning why such a sublime soul would ever inhabit a physical body. He reviews the cryptic explanations of earlier philosophers like Heraclitus, Empedocles, and Pythagoras regarding this "fall."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the start of Book VIII, where Plotinus explores the paradox of why a divine soul descends into a material body. Here, he examines the apparent contradictions in Plato's dialogues—where the body is sometimes a "prison" and other times a necessary part of a "blessed" universe—and begins to reconcile these views through the lens of later Neoplatonic and Christian thinkers.</meta>

BOOK EIGHT.

<column-break/>

But here too, because of the poetic style, he has become somewhat obscure. There remains for us the divine Plato, who handed down many and excellent things concerning the soul, and in his books discussed much regarding its arrival among our affairs, so that we might hope to receive something clear from him. What, then, does this philosopher say? Certainly, he does not seem to say the same thing everywhere, such that one might easily perceive his meaning. In principle, he everywhere despises the entire sensible world and condemns the soul's commerce with the body, <margin>A</margin> asserting that it is enclosed here in chains and buried in the body. Likewise, he honors that secret oracle <note>original Greek: "λόγον μέγαν" (the great word); Latin: "arcanum illud oraculum" — likely referring to the Orphic tradition.</note> which teaches that the soul is situated here in a kind of custody or prison. Again, the cave in Plato, just like the grotto in Empedocles, signifies for us (as I believe) this universe. <margin>B</margin> There he also says that the release from chains and the ascent from the cave is the soul’s progression toward the intelligible. Furthermore, in the *Phaedrus*, he considers the loss of its wings <note>original Greek: "πτεροῤῥύησιν" — literally "the shedding of feathers."</note> to be the cause of its departure to these lower regions. There, certain circuits drag the soul, once it has set out for that higher place, back again to these things of ours. Other souls are sent down here by divine judgments, as well as by lots, <margin>C</margin> Fortune, and Necessity. In short, in all these instances, he seems to find fault with the soul's arrival in the body. But in the *Timaeus*, when disputing about this universe, he both praises the world and calls the god blessed. He says the soul was handed over to this world by the good Craftsman <note>original Greek: "δημιουργῷ" — the Demiurge or divine architect.</note> specifically so that the world could become intellectual. For while this world ought to have been intellectual, the mundane body was unable to achieve intellect without a soul. Therefore, for this reason, the soul of the whole was infused by God into the universe, <margin>D</margin> and the souls of each of us were infused similarly for the final perfection of the whole world. For it was necessary that as many kinds of living beings as there are in the intelligible world, just as many and similar kinds should be contained in the sensible world.

<column-break/>

*The union of the soul with the body, even if it is according to a certain nature of the soul and for the perfection of the universe, nevertheless harms our souls for two reasons: because it hinders intelligence in a certain way, and because it fills the soul with disturbances; however, these impediments do not happen to celestial souls.* <margin>Chap. II.</margin>

Since, through the generative nature, the union with the body is natural to the soul, the celestial souls—which use only this power—abide in a natural and happy condition toward the body. For since their bodies are neither to be dissolved, nor subject to external passions, nor in need of anything, they are easily ruled and moved by the mere generative power of their soul. Nor do these things hinder their contemplation and tranquility. But for our souls, it happens in the opposite way and for the contrary reason; yet a return to the higher realms is granted, if indeed a conversion to the higher realms occurs at some point. Porphyry <note>A third-century Neoplatonist and student of Plotinus.</note> says that the soul slides toward lower things when the mind, like a field already corrupted, which for many years produced wheat, finally yields tares <note>original Latin: "lolium" — a common weed in grain fields, referencing the biblical parable of the wheat and the tares.</note> instead of wheat; that is, having been accustomed to producing intellectual notions, it now bears imaginary ones. Then, he says, the vegetative act sprouts from the roots of the soul like a bud, through which the soul, now stretched out into the body, glues itself to the body. Porphyry here makes the fall of souls similar to the fall of the demons introduced by the Hebrews, resulting from a vice of the intellect or the will, from which followed a mad concupiscence. Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian theologian.</note> also says this when discussing demons; he seems to place demons among the animals there, just as Basil and many Greek theologians thought. But if that saying of Damascene <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century church father.</note> is true—that only the lowest angels fell and became animals—then the Platonic fall of souls will be very similar to the demons falling according to the Hebrews and Christians. Furthermore, when you read in Plotinus and Proclus that particular souls undergo particular turns, sometimes to higher and sometimes to lower things, do not understand that your soul will change into infinite bodies. For the mutations of a single soul are finite and few in a "Great Year" of the world, <note>A cycle of time after which the celestial bodies return to the same relative positions.</note> and in the following year, as they say, the same things are thoroughly rewoven. Moreover, it is not necessary for every soul to put on every species, nor for any soul to ascend or descend in the same way. For (to speak in a Platonic manner) there are certain differences among the souls of men that are in some way specific, just as in the stars, which appear similar to the sight. Our souls differ among themselves not as a pear differs from a peach, but as one pear differs from another. Therefore, there are determined progresses for each according to its nature. The more excellent souls, therefore, ascend higher or descend less; the worse ones, by way of...

<sig>R</sig>
via <note>catchword: "via" (way)</note>

<summary>This page analyzes Plato's diverse views on the soul's descent—contrasting the 'prison' of the body with the 'perfection' of the Timaeus—and compares these ideas to Porphyry's theories and Christian demonology.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the soul's descent into the physical world. On the previous page, he began comparing the "dark" view of the body as a prison (found in the Phaedo) with the "bright" view of the universe as a divine masterpiece (found in the Timaeus).</meta>

# PLOTINUS: ENNEAD IV.

...in turn. I speak of human souls, and that they descend only into human bodies; for in this way we admire the Platonic opinion, which will be even more moderate if it is taken from the Hebrews <note>Ficino likely refers to the Kabbalistic concept of "Gilgul," suggesting that a soul only undergoes three incarnations before its final fate is sealed.</note>, who think the soul enters a human only three times, and finally will be either miserable or blessed forever.

***

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, while we investigate our own soul according to the teachings of Plato, it necessarily happens that we must simultaneously examine the soul in its entirety: by what law of nature it was so established that it would have commerce with the body. Likewise, we must consider the nature of the world—what kind of world we should assert this to be, in which the soul is placed to manage bodily things, whether by its own will, by necessity, or by some other condition. We must also ask whether the maker of these things acted rightly or otherwise, and whether he acts more excellently than our own souls. Our souls perhaps had to penetrate into inferior bodies to govern them from within <margin>B</margin> if they were to overcome and contain them; for every individual body tends to dissipate and return to its own place, though in the universe as a whole, all things are naturally situated in their proper seats. Furthermore, our bodies require an intense and anxious providence <note>term: "providence" (Latin: *providentia*); here meaning the care and foresight required to maintain a physical form.</note>, as they are subject to many external influences and are always in need of many things. Being placed in the greatest difficulty and danger, <margin>C</margin> they require every possible protection. But the body of the world, since it is perfect, full, and self-sufficient, never suffering anything contrary to its nature, is governed as if by a short and easy command. Just as the soul is naturally disposed to will, so the world-body always remains, neither incited by desires nor affected by any disturbances; for nothing leaves it, and nothing enters it from the outside. Therefore, Plato says that our soul too, whenever it lives with that perfect World Soul, <margin>D</margin> will itself also be perfect, lifting itself through the heights and governing the whole world. For when the soul is not absent from that higher place, nor entirely immersed in bodies, nor belonging to any single part, then it too acts as a colleague of the World Soul, ruling the universe with equal ease. It is not an evil for the soul to provide the power of existence and well-being to a body; for not every providence <margin>E</margin> involved in managing inferior things prevents the provider from remaining in the best state. Indeed, there is a double providence in the universe: common and specific. Common providence, by a command free from anxiety and with royal authority, arranges all things. But specific providence, through a kind of "manual labor" <note>original Latin: "manuaria" / Greek: "αὐτεργῷ"; Ficino uses this to distinguish between the effortless "royal" command of the universe and the "hands-on" struggle of the individual soul in a body.</note>, as it were, fills and contaminates the craftsman with the conditions of the work itself. But when the divine soul is said to always govern the whole heaven in the way I mentioned—towering above what is inferior while infusing its ultimate power into it—no one can accuse God of having placed the soul of the whole in a wretched state. <margin>F</margin> Now, this soul is never deprived of its natural duty; it has possessed this state from eternity and will always hold it. This cannot be against its nature, since it is always present to the soul and never had a beginning. He says the souls of the stars also relate to their bodies in the same way as the soul of the whole world; for he places the bodies of these stars within the circuits of the soul, where he preserves a fitting happiness for them. <margin>G</margin> For since there are two things on account of which the commerce of the soul with the body is primarily blamed... <meta>catchword: ...blamed</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> So it happens to us, when seeking to learn from Plato about our own soul, that we are forced to touch upon the question of the soul in general: how it is its nature to commune with a body, and concerning the nature of the world, what sort of thing it should be considered. In what way the soul dwells there—whether by necessity or some other way—and concerning the Creator, whether he acted rightly, or like our own souls. <margin>B</margin> For perhaps our souls had to manage bodies because they were inferior; by entering into them, they might have the power to master them, even though the body is weak and tends to drift toward its own place. For in the Whole, all things lie in their proper place according to nature. Our bodies require a great and troublesome providence, <margin>C</margin> because many foreign things fall upon them, and they are always in need, and in many difficulties they require help. But the World, being perfect and self-sufficient, having nothing in it contrary to its nature, needs only a brief command, and just as the soul naturally <margin>D</margin> wills, so the world always is. It is neither moved by desire nor by suffering. For nothing leaves it, nor does anything come to it. Therefore, he says that our soul, if it were to be with the perfect soul, would be most perfect itself, soaring on high and governing the whole world. For so long as it does not depart into the interior of bodies, nor belong to any one thing, then it too joins in the governance of the Whole with ease. For it is not an evil thing for the soul to provide existence and well-being to a body; for <margin>E</margin> not all providence for the inferior requires the provider to leave the best state. Providence is twofold: the general providence for the Whole, which orders all things with a royal and effortless supervision; and the specific providence, which by a kind of "self-working" creation, connects the doer to the thing done, filling the craftsman with the nature of the work. As for the divine soul, which is said to always govern the whole heaven in this manner—remaining above in the better part, while sending its furthest power into the lower—God could not be blamed for placing the soul of the Whole in an inferior thing. <margin>F</margin> Nor is that soul ever deprived of its natural state, for it has held this from eternity and will hold it forever; it cannot be against its nature, for it has existed perpetually and never began. He says the souls of the stars relate to the body in the same way as the soul of the whole; for he sets their bodies into the revolutions of the soul. Thus, he preserves for them a fitting happiness. <margin>G</margin> For there are two things because of which the soul's relationship to the body is troubled... <meta>catchword: ...and</meta>

<summary>Plotinus distinguishes between the "World Soul," which governs the universe effortlessly and with royal authority, and individual human souls, which become "contaminated" by the manual labor of caring for flawed, individual bodies.</summary>
<keywords>World Soul, Providence, Plato, Hebrew tradition, transmigration, stars, physical body, divinity, Neoplatonism</keywords>
