# BOOK EIGHT.

<note>This page contains a parallel layout: the left column provides the original Greek text of Plotinus (Ennead IV.8.2–3), and the right column provides the Latin translation and commentary by the Renaissance philosopher Marsilio Ficino.</note>

<column-break/>

communion: <note>original Greek: "κοινωνία" (koinōnia)</note> that the hindrance to thoughts occurs, and that it fills the soul with pleasures, desires, and pains. Neither of these inconveniences happens to a soul that has not plunged into the interior of the body. Nor does it belong to any [body], nor is it implanted in it, but such a thing belongs to the soul itself, so as not to need anything or be lacking in anything. Thus, the soul is not filled with desires or fears. For there is
<margin>B</margin> no danger that it will ever expect such a thing regarding the body. Nor does any distraction produce a downward inclination, leading it away from the better and blessed vision; rather, it is always with those divine things, ordering this universe with effortless power.

### Chapter III.

<margin>A</margin> But concerning the human soul, which is said to suffer and be miserable when in the body, existing in troubles, desires, fears, and other evils—for whom the body is a bond <note>original Greek: "δεσμός" (desmos)</note> and a tomb <note>original Greek: "τάφος" (taphos). This refers to the Orphic/Platonic pun "sōma sēma" (the body is a tomb).</note>, and the world for it is a hole and a cave—this has a certain meaning and the cause is told. Since every intellect
<margin>B</margin> is in the place of intelligence, whole and universal, which we call the "intellectual world," there are also the intellectual powers and individual intellects contained within it. For if there were not just one intellect, but one and many, there must also be many souls and one Soul. For from the one, the many differ.
<margin>C</margin> Just as from one genus there are species, some better and some worse; and some more intellectual, and others less so in their activity. For there in the Mind, one part is the Intellect, containing the others in power, like a "great animal" <note>original Greek: "ζῶον μέγα" (zōon mega); a reference to the universe as a living being in Plato’s Timaeus.</note>. Others are each in activity what the other contained in power, just as if there were a "living city" encompassing other living beings; while the soul of the city would be more perfect and powerful, nothing would prevent the other souls from being of the same nature. Or just as from a universal fire, one part might be a great fire and others small fires. Indeed, all is fire, or rather, it comes from that source from which the essence of the whole fire comes.
<margin>D</margin> Now, the work of the more rational soul is to understand, yet not to understand alone. For how then would it differ from the Intellect? For having added something else to its being intellectual, according to which it obtained its own substance, it did not remain as pure Intellect. It also has a work, just as everything that exists among the Intelligibles. Looking toward what is before it, it understands; but looking toward itself, it preserves itself. And that which comes after it, toward which it is directed, it orders and beautifies.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> is accustomed to happen, both because intelligence is hindered, and because the soul is overwhelmed by pleasures, lusts, and pains. Truly, neither disadvantage befalls the soul, provided it has not entirely immersed itself in the inner recesses of the body, nor become the property of any body, nor emerged from one. Instead, the body is for the soul such that it lacks nothing and suffers no defect anywhere; therefore, it does not infect the soul with lusts and fears. For nothing troublesome, no danger
<margin>B</margin> occurring to such a body, is to be feared by the soul. Nor does any distraction at all, declining toward lower things, twist the soul away from sublime and blessed contemplation. Rather, a soul of this kind always dwells upon divine things, while meanwhile managing the universe with a power that is by no means anxious or laborious.

***

->*Since every nature except the first most simple one is infinitely multipliable, therefore in the intellectual genus there are many intellects; in the animal genus there are many souls; in the order of souls there are many intellectual ones, such as the celestial, the demonic, and our own.*<-

->Chapter III.<-

->*Our souls, besides the intellect which is always active in the intelligible world, possess reason, imagination, sense, and vegetative power, which powers must certainly be used in their proper duties at some time. These they use in the body; therefore, it is consistent that they should descend into bodies at some time.*<-

***

### Chapter III.

<margin>A</margin> But at present our discourse is concerning our soul, which is said to suffer all evils in the body and to lead a miserable life, oppressed by pains, desires, fears, and other evils; for whom the body is a chain and a tomb, and for whom the world is a hole and a grotto. This opinion concerning the soul, though feeling differently about both, does not disagree with the truth, since the reason for descending is not the same in both cases. In the beginning, since every intellect
<margin>B</margin> is in the place of intelligence itself, whole and entire—which we consider a certain intellectual world—likewise, since intellectual powers and individual intellects are contained in the same place (for there is not one solitary intellect, but one and many), it was certainly necessary that there be many souls and one Soul, and many differing from one another from the one. Just as species come from one genus, some indeed better, others truly worse; and some more intellectual, others less so in actual practice. For there in the Mind, one thing is the Intellect
<margin>C</margin> containing all other things in power, like a vast living creature; but others are each one thing in act, which the other contains in power. It is as if some city were alive, encompassing other living things; the common soul of the city itself would be more perfect and powerful, yet nothing would prevent the other souls of the cities from being of the same nature. Or just as if from a universal fire, one part were a great fire, and others small. For the essence itself of all fire is clearly that of the universe; or rather,
<margin>D</margin> it is that from which the essence of all fire comes. Now, the work of the soul which is more rational is certainly to understand, yet not to understand alone—otherwise, I do not see how it would differ from the Intellect. But besides being intellectual, by assuming something further according to which it obtains its own nature, it does not remain as pure Intellect. Moreover, it has a work, since whatever is numbered in the order of beings has its own proper work. Now, the soul, looking up to that which is above itself, understands; but looking back into itself, it truly preserves itself.

<note>The Latin text ends mid-sentence ("preserves itself"), mirroring the Greek on the left.</note>

<summary>Plotinus explores the nature of the soul's descent, contrasting the "suffering" individual soul trapped in the body (the "cave") with the universal Soul that governs the world without effort. He explains that individual souls are like species of a single genus or sparks of a single fire, possessing both a divine intellectual capacity and a practical role in ordering the physical world.</summary>

# PLOTINUS: ENNEAD IV.

But truly, turning now toward that which is lower, the soul adorns, governs, and rules it. It certainly could not have been that all things would simply stand still in the **intelligible world** <note>The "intelligible world" (Latin: *mundus intelligibilis*) is the realm of pure thought and divine forms, which Plotinus considers the true reality.</note>; for since one thing could be produced after another, it was necessary for a sequence to arise, even if each successive thing was continually lesser, so long as the higher realm remained stable.

The divine Intellect has impressed upon our own intellect every possible form of the universe; this "all-form" shines forth into our **reason** <note>Latin: *rationem*</note>. When reason turns itself completely toward this divine light and carries the imagination along with it, it remains in the same state as the **World Soul** <note>The World Soul is the third principle in Plotinus's trinity, acting as the bridge between the divine Intellect and the material universe.</note>.

That is, the soul enjoys a similar contemplation of divine things; while it inhabits the heavens, it directs its gaze and its love toward the universal governance of the world. But when reason—together with the imagination—neglects the universal form of the world to gaze too intently upon some **particular** <note>Latin: *particularem*</note> thing, and loves it with a burning passion, the soul’s nature becomes narrowed. It then takes on a narrow body subject to suffering. From this point, it is troubled and vexed by innumerable cares.

<margin>Chapter IIII.</margin>

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, individual souls must use their intellectual appetite to turn back toward their Creator. Yet they also possess the power to manage the things that come after them, much like light which is suspended from the Sun above, but meanwhile extends itself to the things below without "envy" or loss. I say these souls must be preserved unharmed and uninjured, so long as they live their life together with the **Universal Soul** in the intelligible world. In the heavens, they govern together with the whole Soul as if they were colleagues. 
<margin>B</margin> Just as various kings might gather with the High King of all to organize the kingdom, these souls do not need to descend from their "royal seats"—they remain in the same state as the King himself. However, when souls move away from the "Whole" to become a "part," acting as if they were their own masters—as if tired of being with another—each individual soul withdraws into its own private concern. When a soul does this for too long, fleeing the Whole and separating itself through a certain discrepancy, it no longer looks toward the intelligible. Having become a mere part, 
<margin>C</margin> it is left alone and, as if destitute, it becomes weak and distracted by many affairs. By being tied to a part and segregated from the Whole, it enslaves itself to a single thing, fleeing all else. Turning toward that one thing, it is buffeted by the entirety of the physical world. Thus, it falls away from the Whole and manages its specific circumstances with anxiety, focusing on and 
<margin>D</margin> tending to external things. It does not just stand beside the body; it enters deep within it. This is why it is said that the soul’s **wings are shed** <note>This is a reference to Plato’s *Phaedrus*, where the soul is described as losing its wings and falling to earth.</note> or broken, and it is chained in a body, after wandering far from that unharmed and innocent state of governing a better province—the state that once flourished within the Universal Soul. But what existed before this was altogether better for the soul as it sought refuge in the divine. Therefore, the soul is "bound" once it has fallen from the heights; it is tied with "fetters" and uses its senses to act, because it is prevented from the beginning from using its 
<margin>E</margin> **Intellect** <note>Latin: *mente*; Greek: *nous*</note>. It is even said to be "buried" and "hidden in a cave." <note>A reference to Plato’s famous Allegory of the Cave.</note> But when it turns back toward intelligence, it is judged to be released from its chains and to ascend higher; this begins when it starts to contemplate true beings through the gift of **reminiscence** <note>Latin: *reminiscentiæ*; the Platonic idea that true knowledge is the soul remembering its divine origins.</note>. Nevertheless, it always retains something that remains above. Therefore, souls necessarily experience both lives in turn: both that higher life and the lower life, led alternately.

<column-break/>

...but toward that which is after it, which it [the soul] adorns and administers and rules. For it was not possible for all things to stand still in the intelligible [realm], as it was possible for one thing after another to be generated in sequence: something lesser, yet necessary to exist, if indeed that which is before it also exists.

As for the individual souls, they use an intellectual desire for a "turning back" toward that from which they were born, while also having power over the things here—just like light, which is hung from the sun above but provides an ungrudging supply to what comes after it. In this way, they remain unharmed while staying with the Whole in the intelligible realm, and they help govern the heavens along with the Whole. They are like fellow-rulers joined with the King of all, helping him to administer, yet they do not descend from the royal places themselves. For they are together in the same place. But when they change from the Whole to being a "part" and belonging to themselves—as if tired of being with another—each one withdraws into its own. When a soul does this for a long time, fleeing the All and standing apart by distinction, and no longer looking toward the intelligible, it becomes a part, isolated and weak. It becomes a "busybody" <note>original Greek: "πολυπραγμονεῖ" (polypragmonei); meaning to meddle in many affairs or be over-active in the material world.</note> and looks toward the part, and by its separation from the Whole, it attaches to one thing. Fleeing all else, it comes and turns toward that one thing, being buffeted by the whole and all things; it stands apart from the Whole and administers the particular through its surroundings. It is already touching and tending to things from the outside, present in the body and sinking deep into it. Hence, it happens to "shed its wings" (as is said) and to be in the "bonds" of the body, having missed the chance to govern the higher realm without harm, which was its state with the Universal Soul. Its state before this was altogether better when it ran back [to the divine]. The soul is caught, having fallen and being in "bonds," acting through the senses because it is hindered from acting according to the Intellect at the start; it is said to be "buried" and to be in a "cave." But turning toward thought, it is released from its bonds and ascends, when it takes its starting point from **reminiscence** <note>original Greek: "ἀναμνήσεως" (anamnēseōs)</note> to behold the things that truly are. For it always has something that transcends in us. Souls, therefore, become **living a double life** <note>original Greek: "ἀμφίβιοι" (amphibioi); Plotinus uses this term to describe the soul's ability to live in both the divine and physical worlds.</note> by necessity, living the life there and the life here in turn.

<meta>catchword: & di</meta>

<summary>This page explains the "fall" of the soul, describing how it moves from a state of universal governance alongside the World Soul to a state of being "chained" and "buried" in a physical body after becoming too focused on particular, material things. It highlights the soul's dual nature, being "amphibious" between the divine and physical realms.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul's descent from the divine realm into the material world. While the previous page focused on the soul's loss of the "universal" view, this page explains how the theories of ancient philosophers like Plato, Empedocles, and Heraclitus actually agree on why this descent happens—viewing it as both a natural necessity and a form of divine justice.</meta>

# BOOK NINE.

Those indeed spend more time in the higher life who are able to be more present with the **Mind** <note>original: "νῷ" (nō) – the divine Intellect or Nous, the highest level of reality for Neoplatonists</note>; while those spend more time here below whose nature or fortunes were the opposite. Plato subtly indicates this when he divides the origins of souls from the "second mixing bowl" <note>original: "κρατῆρος" (kratēros) – a reference to Plato’s *Timaeus*, where the Creator mixes the substance of souls</note> or makes them into parts. For he says it is then necessary for them to fall into **generation** <note>The process of being born into a physical, changing body</note>, since they have become such parts. But where he says that God "sows" the souls, we must understand this in the same way as when he introduces God speaking as if delivering a public speech. For the things that exist in the common nature of the universe, this very method of treatment lays bare through reason, setting in order things that are always coming into being and always existing.

The descent of souls into the decay of generation, and their descent for the perfection of the universe, does not disagree with the concepts of **judgment, punishment, and the cave** <note>Plato’s Allegory of the Cave, representing our physical world as a place of shadows and imprisonment</note>. Furthermore, necessity and spontaneous motion are not at odds, since necessity carries within itself the voluntary. Moreover, what is said about the soul being in "evil" while it is in the body does not conflict with **Empedocles's** <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who described the soul as an exile from the gods</note> idea of flight and wandering from God, nor that the soul has sinned and thus follows a judicial penalty. Nor does it conflict with **Heraclitus's** <note>A philosopher who viewed the world in a state of constant flux</note> idea of "rest in flight," nor with the descent being entirely voluntary and yet also involuntary. For whatever falls toward a worse state does not arrive there by choice, yet because it moves by its own impulse and suffers the worse things, it is said to receive the penalty it deserves for what it did. For these things to be suffered and done is necessary by a law of eternal, everlasting nature. If someone should say that the soul descends for the use of something else—namely, sent by the higher power itself—they will be seen to disagree neither with the truth nor with themselves. For from whatever principle each thing is led, it is referred back to that same principle, even if there are many middle stages. Since sin is twofold—one being the cause of the descent itself, and the other being the wrongs committed while in this state of life—the first is the very thing the soul suffered in descending. In this lower state, the penalty is to enter other bodies, and this happens more quickly or slowly according to a judgment of worthiness; this divine decree is signified by the name of "Judgment." A more immoderate form of wickedness is judged worthy of a greater punishment, namely under the supervision of **punishing demons** <note>original: "δαιμόνων" (daimonōn) – in this context, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but spiritual overseers or administrative spirits of justice</note>. Thus, although the soul is something divine and originates from the higher regions, it is nevertheless immersed in the body. And since it is a "lesser god" <note>The individual soul as a secondary divine power</note>, it enters by a certain voluntary inclination and by the cause of power...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Those indeed lead the higher life for a longer time who are able to dwell more with the Mind; but they lead the lower life longer if the opposite happens to them, whether by nature or by fortune. Plato, secretly signifying these things when he divides the origins of souls from the fruitful mixing bowl and makes them into parts, then also says it will be necessary to glide down into generation once they have been made into such parts. When he says that God "sows" the souls, we must understand it just as when he introduces God himself speaking and, as it were, <margin>B</margin> delivering a sermon. For the very things that exist in the common nature of reality are produced by this condition of treatment, declaring in a succeeding order the things that always happen in this way and consist in this way.

### *The sayings of Empedocles, Heraclitus, and Plato concerning the descent of the soul agree. Chapter V.*

---

> *Since the soul is divine, it often turns toward divine things in this falling region. And because it is the "last" of the divine things, it comes into the body through a natural instinct and affection; therefore, it comes by a natural will, and moreover, it comes by a certain choice and necessity. For by divine law it is necessary that souls which are so affected should choose to descend in that very footprint. They come of their own accord, as if toward a good, yet in the meantime, they fall into evil unintentionally. That souls come here pertains to the order of the universe, to the exercise of the soul's lower powers, and to the experience of evil. Souls that sin lightly are punished by a change from a more fortunate person to one less fortunate or unhappy. But those who sin more seriously are even vexed by demons, which **Hermes Trismegistus, Orpheus, and Iamblichus** <note>A group of mystical and Neoplatonic authorities whose works were often read alongside Plotinus</note> confirm. Just as a man terrifies a boy with a fierce expression or a mask, a "scarecrow of the age," so do the influences of Saturn and Mars—through the movements of black or yellow bile—vex the soul's images. Certain "Saturnine" and "Martial" demons, with their horrendous imaginings, toss the imaginations of the sinning souls about miserably, just like masked faces; they can even afflict them through the movements of the **humors** <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to control health and temperament</note>.*

---

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, there is no disagreement between the idea that souls are carried into generation for the perfection of the universe, and the idea that they descend under a sentence of punishment and into a "cave." Again, necessity and spontaneous motion are compatible, since necessity includes the voluntary. Furthermore, the claim that the soul is in "evil" while in the body is not contradicted by Empedocles’s "flight and wandering from God," nor by the idea that the soul has sinned and must face a judicial penalty. Nor is it at odds with Heraclitus’s "rest in flight," <margin>B</margin> nor the condition of the descent being both voluntary and involuntary. For whatever falls to a worse state does not do so willingly, yet by moving of its own motion and meanwhile suffering worse things, it is said to receive its merits for what it has done. Indeed, suffering and doing these things is necessary by the eternal law of nature. If someone should say that it happens for the use of another—namely, the soul descending from the higher power itself—and that it is sent by God, he will be judged to disagree neither <margin>C</margin> with the truth nor with himself. For from whatever principle individual things are led, they are referred back to that same principle, even if there are many intermediate steps. Since sin is twofold—the first being in the very cause of descending, and the second being the wrongs committed during this state of life—the first is this very suffering of the descent. In this state, the lesser penalty is to enter other bodies, and this is judged to happen more quickly according to one's dignity; this, being done by divine institution, is signified by the <margin>D</margin> name of "Judgment." A more immoderate species of wickedness is weighed as worthy of greater punishment, namely through a certain prefecture of punishing demons. Thus, although the soul is a certain divine thing, and arises from the superior regions, it is nevertheless immersed in the body. And since it is a "later god" <note>A divine being that comes after the higher Intellect</note>, it enters by a certain voluntary inclination and by the cause of power...

<summary>This page argues that the "descent" of the soul into a body is a harmonious concept across Greek philosophy, representing a mix of natural necessity, divine order, and individual moral consequence. It introduces the idea that the physical body and planetary influences (like Saturn and Mars) can act as tools of divine justice or purification.</summary>
<keywords>descent of the soul, Plato's Timaeus, Empedocles, Heraclitus, divine justice, demons, planetary influence, generation, necessity vs. free will</keywords>

--- Page 626 ---
<meta>This page continues the exploration of the soul’s descent. The previous page discussed how the soul’s transition into a body can be seen as a "fall" or "punishment" in Platonic terms. This page shifts the focus to a more positive Neoplatonic view: that the soul descends not just out of weakness, but as a natural expression of its creative power—a process of "overflowing" from the divine realm to bring order to the physical world.</meta>

# PLOTINUS' ENNEADS, BOOK IV.

...for the sake of adorning <note>original: "exornandi" – refers to the soul's role in bringing beauty and order to the physical world</note>, it descends here in this way: and if it should flee <margin>A</margin> quickly from here, it is judged to have suffered no detriment to its disposition for this reason above all—that it has arrived at the knowledge of evil, and has learned the nature of evil itself. Likewise, it has brought its own powers into the light, and has made manifest its works and achievements. Indeed, if all these things were to remain forever at rest in an incorporeal state, they would be in vain; they would never proceed into their own **actuality** <note>original: "actum" – the realization or expression of a potential power</note>, and they would remain hidden even from the soul that possesses them, never shining forth or proceeding into effect. For everywhere, action reveals the **potential** <note>original: "potentiam" – the latent power within a being</note> that would otherwise be entirely hidden <margin>B</margin> and obscure—indeed, it would not truly exist at all. For now, everyone admires the internal qualities of a thing because of the variety of its external features, guessing at what the inner nature must be like by observing these very diverse and beautiful things that proceed from within.

*The Soul enters the body not only through a certain weakness in being unable to remain longer among divine things, but also by the power of a fertile nature burgeoning into a sprout: for the bodily form is the offspring of the fertile soul.* Chapter V

*By a similar fertility, the first Good overflows into the all-forming Mind: this in turn overflows into the similar soul of the world: and this into the similarly all-forming world. Likewise, all causes flow into their effects everywhere. Finally, imitating the providence of higher beings, the soul transfers itself to lower things through a certain zeal for providing care.*

<margin>*</margin> If, therefore, it is necessary that the **One** <note>The ultimate, indivisible source of all existence in Plotinus’ philosophy</note> should not exist alone—otherwise all things would be hidden, having no form of their own, and no being at all would exist if the One remained only within itself—then a multitude of these beings must be born from the One. This can only happen if successive things proceed from it, which are then allotted their place in the order of souls. It is likewise necessary <margin>B</margin> that souls themselves should not only exist, but that their effects should also be clearly visible. For it is inherent in every nature to produce something following itself, and to unfold it into the light, just as a plant grows from an **indivisible seed** <note>original: "semine... indiuisibili" – likely referring to the *logos spermatikos*, the formative principle that contains the plan for a living thing</note>, proceeding from a beginning toward a sensory end. While the preceding thing always remains in its own seat, that which follows is procreated from an ineffable power, as much as exists in those higher things. It was not fitting for this power to remain sterile, as if restrained from generating by envy; rather, it must always proceed until all things have advanced to the farthest limit possible. This is because of the cause of inexhaustible virtue, which pours out its <margin>C</margin> gifts through all things and does not allow any place to be devoid of itself. For there is nothing that prevents each thing from participating in the Good, as far as its own nature is capable of receiving it. Whether the nature of **matter** <note>The physical substance of the universe, often seen as the furthest point from the divine light</note> existed forever, it was impossible for it—being present—not to participate in that which supplies the Good abundantly to all, as much as each can take. Or, if the origin of matter followed necessarily from preceding causes, even then it was not right for it to be deprived of these gifts due to its own inherent weakness <margin>D</margin>—the weakness it possesses before the gift is thought to descend upon it from above. For the giver remains within itself, yet gives existence and form as if freely. Therefore, the demonstration of those things which are best in the **intelligible world** <note>The realm of pure thought and divine forms</note> is primarily found in what is most beautiful in the **sensible world** <note>The world we can perceive with our senses</note>; it is a declaration of both their power and their goodness. Indeed, all things are thus always connected, both those judged to be intelligible and those judged to be sensible. The former exist <margin>E</margin> through themselves, while the latter always receive their being through participation in the former, imitating the intelligible nature to the best of their ability.

<column-break/>

...to adorn it <note>original: "αὐτὴν κοσμήσει" (autēn kosmēsei)</note>, it comes thus. And if it <margin>A</margin> flees quickly, it has suffered no harm. It has taken knowledge of evil, and known the nature of vice; it has led its powers into the manifest, showing both works and deeds. For these things, while resting in the incorporeal, would have been in vain, never going into activity. And the soul itself would not have known what it possessed, if they were not revealed, nor ever going forth; for everywhere, activity <margin>B</margin> shows the potential, which would otherwise be hidden and obscured—as if not existing, or never having been. For each person wonders at the inner things because of the variety of the outer. It is as if one sees these polished works and wonders at the craft.

---

If, then, it is necessary not only for the One to be—for then all things would be hidden, having their form only in that One—nor should the multitude of beings exist only in that One. Nor should there be a multitude of beings born from the One, unless those things taking the second path after them should also exist, which have been allotted the rank of the soul. In the same way, it was not necessary for souls alone to exist, without those things which are made manifest through them being shown. Just as it is inherent in every nature <margin>C</margin> to produce what comes after it, and to unfold from a seed, from an **indivisible principle** <note>original: "ἀμεροῦς ἀρχῆς" (amerous archēs)</note>, toward that which is perceived by the senses. While the prior thing always remains in its own seat, that which follows is produced by an unspeakable power—as much as is in those things—it was not necessary to stop as if circumscribed by envy, but to always proceed, until all things have come to the final limit of possibility, by the cause of a boundless power sending its gifts from itself unto all, and not being able to allow anything to be without a share of itself. For indeed, what could prevent anything from having a share <margin>D</margin> of the nature of the Good, as much as each is able to participate? Whether the nature of matter is eternal, it was not possible for it not to participate in that which supplies the Good to all according to their power; or if its generation followed from necessity from the causes before it, not even so was it right for it to be weak before grace <note>original: "χάριτος" (charitos) – here meaning a divine gift or favor</note> came to it, and its existence as well, as if given by grace. The demonstration of the best things in the intelligible is the most beautiful thing in the sensible, a sign of their power and goodness. And all things are held together forever: those which exist intelligibly and those which exist sensibly. The former <margin>E</margin> exist by themselves, while the latter receive their existence forever by participation, imitating the intelligible nature as far as they are able.

<summary>Plotinus explains that the soul's descent into the material world is not a mistake but a necessary expression of divine "fertility," where the Good must overflow into all levels of existence. He argues that the physical world serves as a beautiful reflection and proof of the power and goodness of the divine realm.</summary>
<keywords>Soul, The One, Mind, Intellect, Matter, Emanation, Divine Fertility, Participation, Intelligible World, Sensible World, Potentiality and Actuality</keywords>

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on why the soul descends into the material world. While earlier sections framed this as a potential "fall," this text emphasizes the soul’s role as a mediator—a bridge between the eternal divine realm and the temporary physical world.</meta>

# BOOK NINE.

*Just as air is the medium between fire and water—being like fire on one side and like water on the other, and moving toward both in turn—so the soul stands between things that are divine and things that are perishable.*
->Chapter VII.<-

All bodies bestow something of themselves upon lower things, yet celestial bodies <note>original: "caelestia" — refers to the stars and planets, which Neoplatonists believed were inhabited by superior souls</note> receive nothing in return from those that follow them. In contrast, the elemental bodies receive something back in exchange for what they give. Similarly, the celestial souls, while providing for lower things, are in no way tainted by them. However, certain demonic souls <note>original: "Daemonicae" — in this context, "daemons" are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense</note> and our own souls, while they bring bodies to completion, are in a way tainted by them. This happens because of a more "curious" or intensive providence <note>original: "curiosiorem providentiam" — a detailed or meddling oversight</note> over a harsher province; yet the very malice of this place reminds the soul of the happiness of the higher world and warns it to desire that world more vehemently.

---

Since this nature is twofold—one part being intelligible <note>the realm of pure thought</note> and the other sensible <note>the realm of the physical senses</note>—it is better for the soul to exist within the intelligible realm. However, by its very nature, it is necessary for the soul to also participate in sensible things. The soul should not be angry with itself for not being entirely among the highest things, for it holds a middle rank among all beings, possessing a divine portion. Although it sits at the very edge of the intelligible realm, bordering the sensible world, it naturally bestows something of itself upon the physical world and, in turn, receives something from it. This happens unless the soul governs while keeping its own integrity safe; but if it enters too deeply into the internal affairs of the lower nature with too much desire and passion, it no longer remains "entirely with the Entirety" <note>original: "μεθ’ ὅλης" — referring to the World Soul or the divine unity</note>. Nevertheless, it is possible for the soul to rise up again, bringing back the experience of what it has seen and suffered here, from which it learns how blessed the habitation among the higher beings truly is. By the comparison of opposites, it perceives the better things more clearly. For the knowledge of the good becomes more piercing through the experience of evil, especially where the power of judgment is too weak to obtain knowledge of evil without direct experience. Just as a certain intellectual discourse is a descent to the ultimate and the worse—for the soul cannot move higher, but must act out of itself and, being unable to remain still within itself, must proceed by the necessity of nature and law as far as the soul—this is its limit. On this condition, it hands down its influence to what follows and then runs back again. Thus is the action of the soul: both toward what follows by governing the body, and toward what precedes by contemplating true beings. In many souls, this is fulfilled through a certain cycle of time, and finally a turning back from the worse toward the better occurs. But for the Soul of the Universe, it is certainly fitting that it never be occupied with a "worse" work, nor undergo evils, but rather look upon the things that follow from the vantage of high contemplation, while always leaning upon the higher things. Indeed, both can be fulfilled in her at once—she is the master of both tasks, receiving from above while supplying the lower parts; for being a soul, it is impossible for her not to propagate herself toward both.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Since nature is twofold—the one part intelligible and the other sensible—it is better for the soul to live in the intelligible itself. However, it is necessary, since it is endowed with such a nature, that it also participates in the sensible nature. Nor should it take it poorly if it is not entirely the "best," <margin>B</margin> since it holds a middle order in the universe. It is a partaker of a divine lot, yet placed in the final degree of the intelligible nature, as if related to the sensible nature. It is naturally established so that it exhibits something of its own to this world and also receives something from here, unless it governs while its own integrity is preserved. But if it enters the internal parts of the lower nature with too much affection and zeal, it does not remain as a whole soul with the whole <note>referring to the universal soul or divine unity</note>. <margin>C</margin> Nevertheless, it can in turn rise up from here, bringing back a mastery of those things which it learned and suffered here; from this, it learns how blessed the habitation among those above is, and as if by the comparison of opposites, it perceives the better things more clearly. For the knowledge of the good comes forth more clearly from the experience of evil, especially where the judgment is too weak to follow science without the experience of evil. <margin>D</margin> Just as a certain intellectual discourse is a descent to the last and worse things—for it does not progress higher, but is necessary that, acting out of itself and not being able to rest in itself, it proceeds by the necessity of nature and law as far as the soul—here is its boundary. On this condition, it hands itself over to those things that follow and then runs back again. So also is the action of the soul, both toward things that follow by governing the body, and toward things that precede by contemplating those very beings. <margin>E</margin> This is fulfilled in most souls by a certain alternation of times, and finally a turning from the worse to the better happens. But to the soul which is called the "Soul of the Universe," it is undoubtedly fitting that it is never occupied by a worse work, nor undergoes evils, but rather looks forward to what follows with an exalted contemplation, while meanwhile always leaning upon higher things. Indeed, both can be fulfilled in her at once, as she is capable of both duties—receiving from above and supplying to the lower. For it cannot happen, since it is a soul, that it would not propagate itself toward both.

---

*Since our soul has powers and acts similar to the celestial souls, it is probable that at least our intellect, like theirs, is always active regarding divine things, just as the vegetative nature in us is constantly occupied with bodily things.*
->Chapter VIII.<-

But just as our vegetative actions are hidden from us, so also our intellectual actions are for the most part concealed. No movement made in the vegetative part by the sense of desire is evident to us unless it reaches the imagination, and through the imagination, reaches the reason. Similarly, the act of the intelligence does not reveal itself unless it occasionally shines into the "vacant" reason <note>original: "rationem vacantem" — a mind clear of other distractions</note>, and through this is transferred to a similarly vacant imagination, where awareness usually occurs. The celestial souls rule the bodies obedient to them with ease, through both natural instinct and the mere nod of the mind. Our souls, however, occupy both the imagination and the reason with the body, demanding that kind of providence. Therefore, it is divinely ordained that eventually, departing from here, they return to the heavens.

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS, BOOK IV.

<margin>A</margin> **THEREFORE**, if it is appropriate, contrary to the opinion of others, to openly declare what clearly seems true to me: our soul also does not enter the body in its entirety. Rather, there is always something of it remaining in the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The realm of pure thought and eternal forms, as opposed to the physical world.</note>, while another part exists in the <term>sensible world</term> <note>The world perceived by the five senses.</note>. If this lower part should prevail—or rather, if it is overcome and disturbed by the body—it does not allow us to perceive those things which the highest part of the soul contemplates. For that which is understood only descends into our conscious awareness when it reaches a certain point of <margin>B</margin> perception through its descent. For we do not acknowledge everything that occurs in any given part of the soul until it reaches the soul as a whole. For example, a desire that thrives in the very nature of desiring <note>original: "concupiscendi natura" / "ἐπιθυμητικῷ"</note> is only known by us when we notice it through a certain inner power of sensing, or thinking, or both. For every soul has something lower directed toward the body, and something higher directed toward the <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "mentem" / "νοῦν" — the divine Mind.</note>. The Soul of the Universe <note>The "World Soul" that animates the entire cosmos.</note> governs the whole body of the universe through its lower <margin>C</margin> part; it does this without labor, because it far surpasses the body. This is because it does not rule through <term>discursive reasoning</term> <note>The step-by-step logic humans use to solve problems.</note>, as happens with us, but rather by its very intellect—just as an art does not usually need to deliberate while it works. Thus, the World Soul adorns the whole universe through its lowest part. However, particular and "partial" souls <note>Individual human souls.</note> also have a superior part, but they are too occupied by sense-perception and by the many things they perceive that occur against nature. These things afflict and <margin>D</margin> disturb them on every side. This is because the part they care for is merely a fragment of the whole—a part that is needy and deficient, surrounded by many alien and adverse forces. The soul also affects many things and is ensnared by many allurements, and is even deceived by pleasure itself. But the higher part of the soul is struck by no new or fleeting delight and always leads a similar, eternal life.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **AND** if one must dare to speak more clearly what appears to be the case, despite the opinions of others: not even our own soul has sunk entirely into the body, but there is always a part of it in the intelligible realm. But if the part in the sensible realm dominates—or rather, if it is dominated and thrown into turmoil—it does not allow us to have a perception of the things that the upper part of the soul beholds. For that which is grasped by the intellect only comes to us when it reaches the level of sense-perception as it descends. For <margin>B</margin> we do not know everything that happens in every part of the soul until it arrives at the whole soul. For instance, even a desire, while remaining in the "desiring faculty," is only known to us when we perceive it with the internal power of sensation, or the power of thought, or both. For every soul has something directed downward toward the body, and something directed upward toward the Intellect. And the Whole Soul [of the universe] <margin>C</margin> adorns the whole body of the universe with its own part, presiding over it without effort. This is because it does not act from a process of reasoning as we do, but by Intellect, just as <term>Art</term> <note>original: "τέχνη" — Greek for craft or skill; Plotinus argues that perfect skill acts instinctively rather than through agonizing choices.</note> does not need to deliberate. But individual souls, being parts, also have their own superior part. However, they are preoccupied with sense-perception and with the apprehension of many things that occur contrary to nature, which cause pain and turmoil. This is because the part they care for is incomplete and <margin>D</margin> has many foreign elements surrounding it. The soul is also drawn toward the things it desires, and is deceived by pleasure. But there is a part of the soul that remains untouched by these untimely pleasures, and its way of life remains always the same.

He explains that we are often unaware of this divine connection because our lower consciousness is distracted by the physical sensations and troubles of the body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the nature of the soul. On the previous page, we saw how the soul acts as a link between the divine realm and the physical body. Now, Plotinus moves into a deeper metaphysical question: whether all individual souls (yours, mine, and the stars') are actually just one single, unified Soul.</meta>

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD IV,
### BOOK IX.

->Whether all souls are one.<-

*Plotinus’s opinion is that the world has one soul unique to itself, and that all living beings have their own individual souls. Chapter 1.*

*Unless the world possessed a single soul, it would not be a truly unified and perfect composite, nor would the other souls within the world maintain an orderly arrangement or easily harmonize with one another. Likewise, if we did not possess our own distinct souls, every feeling, suffering, or action of one animal would immediately affect all others and the entire universe. Plotinus, intending to exercise his intellect regarding the theory that posits a single soul in all things, weighs the arguments back and forth, while moving toward a different conclusion.*

<margin>A</margin>
Just as we say that each individual soul is one because it is present as a whole everywhere throughout the body, and it is truly one in this manner—not having one part here and another part there in the body—and just as the <term>sensory soul</term> <note>original: "αἰσθητική" / "sensualis" — the faculty of the soul responsible for processing physical sensations.</note> is present in those parts that feel, and the <term>vegetative soul</term> <note>original: "φυτικοῖς" / "plantis" — the part of the soul responsible for growth and nutrition.</note> is <margin>B</margin> present as a whole everywhere in every part; so too, are my soul and your soul one? Are all souls, in the end, one? And in the universe, are they all one—not as if the soul were distributed like a physical mass, but by being the same everywhere? For why should the soul in me be one, but the soul in the universe not be one? For there is no physical mass there, nor a body, just as there is none in my soul. If indeed my soul and yours come from the soul of the entire universe, and that soul is one, then these individual souls must also be one. <margin>C</margin> Furthermore, if both the soul of the universe and my own soul come from a single [higher] soul, then again, all are one. We must ask, then, what exactly this "one" soul is. But first, we must investigate whether it is even correct to say that all souls are one in the same way that an individual’s soul is one. For it seems absurd <note>Plotinus often uses the "reductio ad absurdum" method, showing where a theory leads to impossible conclusions.</note> if my soul and that of any other person were one and the same. For if they were one, it would follow that when I perceive something, another person would necessarily perceive it too; when I am good, that person would be good; when I feel a desire, they would feel it. In short, we would all share the same experiences <margin>D</margin> with one another and with the whole universe, so that whatever I suffer, the entire universe would feel it with me. Moreover, if the soul is entirely one, how can one part be rational and another irrational? How can one be in animals and another in plants? Yet, on the other hand, if we do not posit a single soul, the universe will not be a unified whole, and no single <term>principle</term> <note>original: "ἀρχὴ" / "principium" — the starting point or fundamental source of all things.</note> of souls will ever be found.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
SHALL WE SAY, just as we say that each individual soul is one because it is present as a whole everywhere in the body, and is truly one in this way—not having one part here and another there in the body—and just as the sensory soul exists in those parts that sense, and the soul is <margin>B</margin> whole everywhere in every part of plants similarly: so too are my soul and yours one soul? And finally, are all souls one? Is that which is in all things in the universe one, not as if distributed through a mass, but possessing the same identity everywhere? For why should my soul be one, but the soul in the world not be one? For there is no mass there, nor a body, just as there is not in mine. Indeed, if both my soul and yours are from the soul of the entire world, and that soul is one, then these must also be <margin>C</margin> one. If, however, both the soul of the world and my soul are from a single soul, then again all are one. We must ask, therefore, which soul this "one" is most of all. But first we must investigate whether it is rightly said that all souls are one, just as each person's soul is one. For it is absurd for my soul and the soul of anyone else to be one. For if it were one, it would certainly be necessary that when I sense something, another also senses it; and when I live well, another lives well; and when I desire, another desires. And entirely, our passions would agree between us and with the whole, so that even when I suffer, <margin>D</margin> the universe would feel it with me. But in what way, if the soul is entirely one, is one part rational and another irrational? Likewise, why is one in animals and another in plants? But again, unless we posit one soul, neither will the universe be one, nor will one principle of souls be found.

<summary>Plotinus introduces the philosophical paradox of the "Unity of Souls," questioning whether all individual human, animal, and cosmic souls are actually a single entity, while acknowledging the logical difficulties this poses for individual identity and experience.</summary>

# PLOTINUS ON THE ENNEADS, BOOK IV

<page-num>476</page-num>

<margin>A</margin>ACCORDINGLY, if it is proper to speak more clearly than the opinion of others has dared—and this is certainly how it appears to me—not even our own soul has descended in its entirety into the body. Rather, there is always something of it that remains in the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>original: "mundo intelligibilis" / "τῷ νοητῷ" — the eternal realm of pure thought and divine forms, as opposed to the physical world.</note>, while another part resides in the <term>sensible world</term> <note>original: "mundo sensibili" / "τῷ αἰσθητῷ" — the world of physical matter perceived by the five senses.</note>. If this lower part is dominated, or rather, if it is overpowered and thrown into turmoil, it does not allow us to perceive the things that the highest part of the soul contemplates. For that which is understood only descends into us when it reaches a certain point of perception through its descent.

<margin>B</margin>Indeed, we do not recognize everything that happens around any given part of the soul until it reaches the soul as a whole. For instance, a desire flourishing in the very <term>appetitive nature</term> <note>original: "concupiscendi natura" / "ἐπιθυμητικῷ" — the faculty of the soul responsible for basic drives and physical wants.</note> is only then recognized by us when we notice it through a certain internal power of sensing or thinking, or perhaps through both.

<margin>C</margin>For every soul has something lower directed toward the body, and something higher directed toward the <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "mentem" / "νοῦν" — the divine, universal mind that contains all truths.</note>. The <term>World Soul</term> <note>original: "tota anima" / "ἡ μὲν ὅλη" — the soul that animates and governs the entire universe.</note> governs the whole through that part of itself directed toward the body, and it does so without labor, because it remains high above. It does not act through a sequence of reasoning, as is the case with us, but rather by intellect itself, much as an art does not usually need to deliberate. This World Soul adorns the whole universe through its lowest part; however, individual and partial souls also have something that remains high above, yet they are too occupied by sensation and the perception of many things that occur contrary to nature, which cause them distress and disturb them on all sides.

<margin>D</margin>This is because the part they care for is a specific part of the world—one that is needy and deficient, and surrounded by many foreign and adverse things. It seeks many objects, is entangled in many charms, and is deceived by pleasure itself. But that which is higher in the soul is touched by no new or passing delight, and it always leads the same [divine] life.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>AND if one must dare to state the truth more clearly, contrary to the opinion of others: not all of our soul, nor even the soul of the universe, has sunk. Instead, there is always something of it in the <term>intelligible realm</term> <note>original: "τῷ νοητῷ" — the realm of Ideas or divine truths.</note>. But as for the part in the <term>sensible realm</term>, if it is mastered—or rather, if it is mastered by being thrown into confusion—it does not permit us to have a perception of those things which the upper part of the soul beholds. For that which is thought only comes to us when it arrives at the level of perception through its descent.

<margin>B</margin>For we do not know everything that happens in any part of the soul until it comes to the soul as a whole. For example, desire, while staying in the <term>desiring faculty</term>, is known to us only when it is communicated to the internal power of sensation, or to the power of thought, or to both.

<margin>C</margin>Every soul has something that looks downward toward the body and something that looks upward toward the <term>Intellect</term>. The Soul of the All governs the whole body of the universe through its lower part; it does this effortlessly because it remains superior. It does not govern by a process of reasoning as we do, but as an art might, ordering the lower world through its lower part. But the souls that have become partial, belonging to a part of the world, also have a superior part; yet they are distracted by sensation and by the grasping of many things that are contrary to nature, which bring pain and turmoil.

<margin>D</margin>From this, they must care for a part that is incomplete and surrounded by many external things; they long for many things and take pleasure in them, and this pleasure is a deception. But there is also that part of the soul which is without such pleasure, and its way of life remains always the same.

# OF PLOTINUS
## THE FOURTH ENNEAD,
### TREATISE IX.

# OF PLOTINUS
## OF THE FOURTH ENNEAD,
### BOOK IX.

->Whether all souls are one soul.<-

->Whether all souls are one soul.<-

> *Plotinus’s opinion is that the world has one soul proper to itself, and that all living creatures have their own proper souls. Chapter 1.*
> 
> *Unless the world had one soul, it would not be a perfect composite and truly one, nor would the remaining souls in the world easily fit into an order among themselves. Likewise, unless we had our own individual souls, the feelings, sufferings, and actions of one living creature would immediately belong to all others and to the universe. Plotinus, about to exercise his intellect regarding the opinion that posits a single soul in all things, plays back and forth with the idea while meanwhile striving toward another conclusion.*

---

<margin>A</margin> <image-desc>Decorative initial A featuring a woman and two children.</image-desc> Is it not just as we say the soul of each individual is one, because it is whole throughout the entire body, and is truly "one" in this manner—not having one part of itself here and another there in the body? Just as in the sensing parts it is the <term>sensitive soul</term> <note>original: "αἰσθητική" / "sensualis" — the faculty of the soul that processes physical sensations from the eyes, ears, etc.</note>, and in plants it is also whole throughout every part, so too are my soul and your soul one? Are all souls one? And in the universe, is the soul that is in all things one—not as if it were divided up by its <term>bulk</term> <note>original: "ὄγκῳ" / "molem" — physical mass or volume; Plotinus argues the soul is non-physical and therefore doesn't take up space.</note>, 
<margin>B</margin> but being the same everywhere? For why is the soul in me one, but the soul in the universe not one? For there is no physical bulk there, nor is it a body, just as it is not in my own soul. If, then, both my soul and yours come from the soul of the universe, and that soul is one, then these individual souls must also be one. Or if both the soul of the universe and my own soul come from <term>one soul</term> 
<margin>C</margin> <note>original: "ψυχῆς μιᾶς" / "ex vna [anima]" — the "Soul-itself" or the hypostasis of Soul that exists before individual souls.</note>, then again all souls are one. We must ask, then, what this "one soul" is; but first we must ask if it is correctly said that "all souls are one," in the same way that each person’s soul is one. For it seems absurd if my soul and the soul of anyone else were one. If they were, then when I sense something, another person would also have to sense it; when I am good, that person would be good; when I have a desire, they would desire. In short, we would all share the same <term>passions</term> <note>original: "ὁμοπαθεῖν" / "passionibus conuenire" — to suffer or feel the same thing at the same time.</note> with one another and with the whole universe, 
<margin>D</margin> so that when I suffer, the whole universe would feel it with me. And how, if there is entirely only one soul, is one part rational while another is irrational? Or how is one in animals and another in plants? But on the other hand, unless we posit that they are one, the universe will not be a single unity, nor will a single <term>principle</term> <note>original: "ἀρχὴ" / "principium" — the starting point or source from which everything else flows.</note> of souls be found.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative initial V showing a scholar seated at a desk reading/writing.</image-desc> Is it not just as we say the soul of each individual is one, because it is whole throughout the entire body, and is truly one in this way—neither is one part of it here and another there in the body? Whether in those things that sense, it is thus the sensitive soul, or in plants, it is whole everywhere in any part similarly: so too both my soul and yours are one soul, and finally all are one soul? And in the universe, is that which is in all things one, not as if distributed through a mass, but having the same thing everywhere? For why is my soul indeed one, but that which is in the world not one? For there is no bulk there, nor body, just as there is none in mine. Truly, if both my soul and yours are from the soul of the whole world itself, and that soul is one, it is necessary that these also be one. If, however, both the soul of the world and mine are from one soul, again they are all one. We must inquire, therefore, which soul this "one" primarily is. But first it must be investigated whether it is rightly said that all souls are one, just as each person's soul is one: for it is absurd for my soul and the soul of anyone else to be one. For if it were one, it would certainly be necessary that when I sense, another also senses; and when I live well, another lives well; and when I desire, another desires. And altogether we would agree in our passions both among ourselves and with the whole itself, to such an extent that when I suffer, the universe feels it with me. But in what way, if the soul is entirely one, is one part rational and another irrational? Likewise, one in animals and another in plants? But again, unless we posit one, neither will the universe be one, nor will one principle of souls be found.

<summary>Plotinus investigates the paradox of the "One and the Many" as it applies to souls, questioning how individual human souls can be distinct if they all originate from a single universal Soul. He weighs the logical necessity of a unified World-Soul against the everyday reality of individual experience and different levels of life (rational, animal, and vegetative).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation of whether all souls are essentially one. While the previous page established the theoretical framework for soul-unity, this page addresses common-sense objections—such as why we don't feel each other's pain—by using the analogy of a single body and the vastness of large creatures.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

*Plotinus, about to concede that souls are indeed distinct, does not easily yield to the previously stated reasoning—namely, that the suffering of one evil person is immediately transferred to another and to the whole universe.*

<margin>Chapter II.</margin>

*He would prefer to say that the bodies of animals, which are neither continuous with each other nor with the whole, require distinct souls. Likewise, when the animal power is gathered entirely into one, the soul itself—holding the highest rank in the animal genus—will by no means suffer in itself the passions and defects appearing in individual animals.*

<margin>A</margin>

**To begin with**, if my soul and another’s are one, it does not immediately follow that both together are the same thing. For the same thing existing in one person and another will not have the same <term>passions</term> <note>original: "passiones" / "πάθη" — in this context, "passions" refers to anything the soul undergoes or experiences from the outside, like sensations or emotions.</note> in both. It is like a man who is the same in me when I move, and in you when you do not: in me he moves because I move, but in you, who are not moving, he will be at rest. It is neither absurd nor contrary to common opinion that what is in me and you is the same thing. Nor

<margin>B</margin>

is it necessary that when I feel something, another person must have that exact same feeling. Even in the same body, one hand does not feel the sensation of the other; rather, it is the soul which is in the whole that feels it. If you were meant to know my sensation, our two bodies would have to be fused into one. Only thus, joined together, would each feel the same thing. It is worth remembering that many things often escape the notice of the whole, even those things occurring in one and the same body—and this happens more often the larger the body is, just as it is said to happen in larger **whales**

<margin>C</margin>

and similar beasts. In these creatures, when a part suffers, no sensation reaches the whole because the movement is so small. Therefore, it is not necessary that because one part suffers, a clear sensation must immediately reach the whole and all its parts. That there is a "shared feeling" <note>original: "compati" / "συμπάσχειν" — literally "to suffer with" or "sympathy" in the physiological sense.</note> is not absurd and should not be denied, but it is not necessary for a distinct sensory impression to be formed. Consequently, that the same soul should have **virtue** in me but

<margin>D</margin>

**vice** in another is not surprising, since it is not impossible for the same thing to be moved in one place and remain at rest in another. For we do not say the soul is "one" in such a way as to be entirely devoid of any plurality; that superior nature indeed claims such unity for itself. Rather, we say the soul is both one and many at once, participating both in that nature which becomes divisible around bodies and in that which remains indivisible—from which it follows that the soul is one. Just as the sensation that

<margin>E</margin>

occurs in a part of me does not necessarily occupy the whole, yet what happens to the <term>principal part</term> <note>original: "principali" / "κυριώτερον" — the 'Hegemonikon' or ruling faculty of the soul, often associated with the heart or brain.</note> is spread in some way to the parts; so too, things that come from the universe to the individual happen more clearly, since individual things "suffer with" the whole. However, whether the things that happen to us immediately affect the whole remains hidden from us.

<column-break/>

**First of all**, it is not the case that if my soul and another's are one, then the combination of both is already a single entity; even if the same thing is in different bodies, it will not have the same experiences in each. Just as the "humanity" in me moves when I move, but does not move in you if you are still; for while it moves in me, it will be at rest in you. It is not strange, nor contrary to expectation, for the same thing to be in both me and you. Nor is it necessary that if I am perceiving, another person must perceive the same experience. For even in a single body, one hand does not perceive the suffering of the other hand, but the soul in the whole does. If it were required for you to know my experience, you and I would have to be a single, joined body. For only thus, being joined, would each perceive the same thing. But one should consider that many things escape the whole, even things happening in one and the same body. And this is especially true the greater the size of the body, as is said of the great whales. In their case, if some suffering occurs in a part, no sensation reaches the whole because of the smallness of the movement. So it is not necessary, through a clear impression, for the sensation to reach the whole and every part when one part suffers. But to have a shared feeling is not absurd; what is unknown is whether a sensory impression must necessarily be formed. Thus, even if there is vice in me and not in another, it is not strange. Just as it is not strange for the same thing to be moving in one place and standing still in another. For we do not call the soul "one" as if it were truly without any plurality. That kind of unity must be granted to the higher nature <note>The "higher nature" refers to the One or the Intellect, which are more unified than the soul.</note>. But we do say it is a plurality, and that it participates in the nature that is divided among bodies, and also in the indivisible nature. Thus, it is once again one. And just as in my case, a suffering that happens in a part is not necessarily mixed into the whole, but what happens in the ruling part brings something to the parts; so the things from the 

---

whole to each individual are much clearer, as they "suffer with" the whole in many ways. But whether our individual experiences contribute to the whole is unclear.

*Our Plotinus is still playing with these ideas.*

<margin>Chapter III.</margin>

*Truly, just as the mutual love of men signifies a union of souls, so does their perpetual and dire hatred signify a diversity. For one man does not differ less from another man, or any animal from another animal, than fire differs from water; therefore, they are not one. As for "magical rapture" <note>The "magical rapture" or attraction refers to the Neoplatonic idea of "sympathy," where things in the universe can be influenced at a distance because they are part of the same cosmic soul.</note>, it is for the most part a fabrication, and we have explained its causes in previous sections. Elsewhere we have said that the **formal reason** of any thing is multipliable into many essences, with the exception of the First Cause. Therefore, just as the formal reason of a body, of a quality, or of nature is distinct across many bodies, natures, and qualities, so too are there many souls and intellects. Furthermore, if the soul is more excellent and formal than a quality, then surely by Divine Providence it is established that there are many grades of souls, formally distinct from one another—not just like this heat differs from that heat because of the object it is in, but as heat differs from cold, or dryness from moisture. Plotinus himself hints at this at the end of the chapter, where he says that intellects are many, and that the judicial senses themselves exist simultaneously with the intellects—that is, with the intellectual souls. He signifies that this discussion suggests there is one soul in all bodies, not a rational one, but a **vegetative** soul <note>original: "vegetalem" — the lowest level of soul responsible for growth and nutrition, shared by plants, animals, and the physical world.</note> participating in a certain confused sensation; nevertheless, any rational soul can form its own life apart from the irrational, provided it is not formed by the Soul of the World.*

# BOOK NINE.

<margin>A</margin> **Indeed, reason dictates** that we are affected by mutual experiences <note>original: "sympathein" / "mutuis passionibus"</note> from opposite sides; we are touched by the sight of another’s pain, we are moved to compassion, and we are naturally drawn toward love. It is certainly worth considering whether this mutual love arises among us for this very reason. Furthermore, if certain incantations and magical arts <note>original: "magiae"</note> can draw multiple people into one, or strike a common feeling into those who are far away, it seems this can only be achieved through the existence of a single soul. Even a word spoken in a low voice 
<margin>B</margin> can affect someone far off and compel them to hear, even across a vast distance. From these things, we can understand the unity of all things, as if they were breathing together through one soul. But in what way is the soul one, if one part is rational, another irrational, and another vegetative? Perhaps that which is indivisible in the soul must be assigned to the rational power, which is not distributed within bodies, while that which is distributed around bodies is also a single thing belonging to it, but 
<margin>C</margin> divided throughout the flesh. This part, which provides sensation everywhere, must be considered a different power of the soul. Finally, there is the power that shapes and creates bodies <note>The "plastic" or "formative" power</note>. Yet the soul is no less "one" simply because it possesses many powers. For even in a seed there are many powers, yet the seed is one, and from this one thing, many things become one. But why are all these powers not present everywhere? Even in the soul, which is said to be one in any given person, sensation is not the same in all parts, and 
<margin>D</margin> reason is not in the whole body, and the vegetative power is present in parts where sensation is absent. Yet they all run back together into a single unity. If the power of nutrition comes from the whole soul, why does the body not also receive its power of nutrition from our specific soul? Because that which is nourished is a part of the universe, which is perceived through a certain passive condition. True sensation, however, is a judging faculty combined with intellect; it did not need to form that which is already being formed by the universe. For it would have formed it, had it not been necessary for it to be counted as part of this forming Whole.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **These things have been said** so that no one should wonder at this reduction to a single unity. But the logic of the argument requires us to ask: in what way is it one? Are all souls one because they proceed from one, or are they all essentially one? And if they come from one, is that soul divided, or does it remain whole while nonetheless producing many souls from itself? And how could an essence <note>original: "ousia" / "essentia"</note> remain while producing many from itself? Let us say, then, having first invoked divine help, that 
<margin>B</margin> one soul must necessarily exist first, if indeed there are to be many souls, and that the many must proceed from this one. Now, if this one were a body, it would necessarily be divided to become many, and would become a completely different essence, even if composed of similar parts. All these parts would be of the same kind, carrying the same form as the whole, but differing in their mass. If this were so according to the underlying masses...
