### PLOTINUS' ENNEAD IV.

...if they possess [this quality] so as to be souls, then they are different from one another; but if they possess it according to their form, then souls are one in species. This, however, means that one and the same soul exists in many bodies. And before this one soul is implanted in the many, there is another soul existing [independently] of the many, upon which the one that is in the many depends, like an image <note>original: "simulachrum"</note> cast in various places from a single thing that exists in one place—just as if many wax impressions were made from a single seal. In that way, the soul would be distributed 
<margin>B</margin> into many signs. But if the matter stands according to the second way, the soul is indeed something incorporeal; and if it were a kind of "passion" or attribute, it would be no wonder that a single quality, derived from a single source, could exist in many. And if the soul were judged to be a combination of both [the corporeal and incorporeal], it would still be no wonder. But as it stands, we consider the soul to be both incorporeal and an essence <note>original: "essentiam" / "ousian"</note>.

---

->*Although souls are distinct from one another through their essences, they are nevertheless all one soul in three ways.*<-

<margin>Chapter V.</margin>

->*First, because a single general Idea <note>The archetypal Form of "Soul" in the intelligible world.</note> of souls presides over them all, and the whole of it is present in each one. Second, because every soul is an entirely <term>omniform</term> <note>The Neoplatonic concept that each soul contains the potential for all forms within itself.</note> form, and therefore every soul embraces all other souls. Yet this soul differs from that one because they are omniform under different modes of activity and specific properties, just as geometric propositions <note>Theorems of geometry exist together in the mind; one may be focused on, but the others are implicitly present.</note> agree with and differ from one another. Third, because they can all be at the same point, just as lights and the images of colors can exist together without confusion. We have sufficiently proved in our "Theology" <note>A reference to Marsilio Ficino’s own work, "Platonic Theology."</note> that there is not just one single soul or mind in all individuals. Therefore, let this be your conclusion: beware of suspecting that Plotinus does not distinguish between the essences of souls; for that would contradict all his books and even the conclusion of this one. Indeed, he wrote a specific dispute in this Ennead against those who believe the soul is only one. But remember that Plotinus everywhere attempts to reduce all things, as much as possible, to a certain unity, while meanwhile preserving the property of their nature. I say "to a certain unity"—that is, to a communion of feeling, action, and passion, so that a concordant harmony is preserved in the universe, and the transmission of virtue and action may occur mutually and easily through each part. This could not happen unless individual souls, though their distinction of essence is preserved, were contained and governed by one, almost as all the virtues of the limbs are governed by the virtue of the heart, or as the nerves are by the neck. He therefore brings forward many signs of such a union, which he confirms as being most valid. He even seems to grant that they can appear to have such vigor that they might lead one to suspect not only such a union, but an even greater one. It is as if he were saying: if anyone could suspect a union of essence through these signs—though I do not approve of that—much more can we, through the same signs, assert a union of feeling, action, consensus, and compassion among souls.*<-

---

IN WHAT WAY then is there one <margin>A</margin> essence in many? Either it is one whole in all of them, or many souls come from one whole while that one remains. That first one, then, is the one; but the many are referred to this as the one, which gives itself to the multitude and yet does not give itself. For it is sufficient for it to exhibit itself to all, and nevertheless remain one. It can be in all things at once, and is not entirely severed from any one thing. Thus, it is preserved in the many. Nor should anyone distrust this; for knowledge <note>original: "scientia" / "episteme"</note> is also a whole, as are its parts, such that the whole remains <margin>B</margin> and the parts come from it. Likewise, a seed is a whole and the parts come from it into which it can naturally be divided, and each part is a whole, and the whole remains nowhere diminished. Matter, however, provides the occasion for division; yet all things are one. But in the case of knowledge, someone might say the part is not the whole; yet here too, that which is brought forward according to use and necessity is a part in "actuality" <note>The specific piece of knowledge currently being used.</note>, and is placed before others. Nevertheless, the remaining parts follow through a certain latent power <margin>C</margin> and are all present in that part. Perhaps it is on this condition that it is called "the whole": the part is there as if in actuality, but all are there together. Therefore, whatever you wish to approach and carry out is ready at hand. Within the part itself, that which we call "prepared" is present, but it exists in potentiality...

<column-break/>

...underlying [subjects], so that while they are souls, they are different from one another. But if they are so according to form, then they are one soul in species. This consists in the fact that one and the same soul exists in many bodies. And regarding this one soul in many, there would be another soul not in many, from which the one in the many [derives], like an image <note>original: "eidolon"</note> carried about in many places, coming from the one; just as if many pieces of wax, having taken the same impression from one seal-ring, were carried away. In that way, the soul would be escaped into many points. Or, in the other way, the soul would be incorporeal. And if it were a passion <note>An attribute or state of being.</note>, it would be nothing marvelous for one quality, produced from one source, to be in many things. And if the soul were judged according to the combination of both, it would be nothing marvelous. But now we posit it to be both incorporeal and an essence <note>original: "ousian"</note>.

HOW then is essence one in many? Either the one is a whole in all, or the many come from a whole and a one, while that one remains. That one is indeed the one; but the many [are related] to it as the one, which gives itself to the multitude, and yet remains sufficient to provide itself to all and remain one. For it is able to be in all at once and is not cut off from each one entirely; it is the same in many. Let no one be distrustful. For knowledge <note>original: "episteme"</note> is a whole, and its parts are such that the whole remains, and the parts come from it. And the seed is a whole, and the parts come from it into which it is naturally divided, each being a whole. And the whole remains; the whole is not diminished. Matter divided it, and all was one. But if in knowledge someone says the part is not the whole: even there, that which is brought to hand and used is a part in activity <note>original: "energeia"</note>, and is ordered in its place. Nevertheless, the others follow, being latent in power <note>original: "dynamei"</note>. And all things are in the part. And perhaps in this way it is called the "whole." The part is there as if all were in activity together. Each thing is therefore ready, whichever you wish to bring to hand. But if the "ready" is in the part, so that it does not remain...

<margin>A</margin>
...is judged, insofar as it coheres to the whole. Nor should it be thought that this notion, which we call a part of science, is void of other notions; otherwise it would not be a truly skillful notion, nor one proper to science, but just as if a child were perhaps speaking by chance. If, therefore, it is suited to science, it possesses all things in potentiality. Thus, when a man of knowledge applies himself more intensely to these things, having first established one specific point, he then produces the rest by a kind of logical consequence. Hence, the Geometer 
<margin>B</margin>
declares in the very process of analysis <note>original: "resolutione"</note> that each single thing encompasses all the preceding steps through which the analysis is conducted, and also encompasses the consequences that are deduced from it in a certain order. But these things are not believed because of our human weakness, and they are obscured by the weight of the body; however, in that divine realm, all things are clear, and every single thing is transparent.

->CONCERNING the three primary <term>hypostases</term> <note>The foundational "substances" or levels of reality in Neoplatonism: The One, the Divine Mind (Intellect), and the World Soul.</note>, which have the nature of a principle.<-

But as soon as the soul applies itself to living and acting under its own form—namely, through rational discourse—it then gradually falls into the discourse of the imagination, and into sensory and vegetative action, so that it now lives as if under a bodily form.*

<margin>Chapter I.</margin>

<margin>From this it finally happens that the soul thinks of itself as corporeal, and, distrusting its own divinity, it never seeks nor venerates divine things.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the opening of Ennead V, Book 1, titled "On the Three Principal Hypostases." In the previous pages, the text established the metaphysical hierarchy, and here it begins to address the human soul's descent and its need to remember its divine origin.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEAD V.

<column-break/>

...to be of their own power. <margin>A</margin> After they began to delight in this liberty or license <note>Plotinus uses the term *tolma* in Greek, often translated as "audacity" or "rashness," to describe the soul's initial turn away from the Divine.</note>, relying heavily upon their own power of moving themselves, and entering upon a contrary path, they moved further and further away until they became entirely ignorant that they themselves originated from that divine source. They are like children immediately separated from their parents at birth and raised far away for a long time, so that they know neither themselves nor their parents. <margin>B</margin> Since, therefore, they see neither their father nor themselves, and because of this ignorance of their own lineage they hold themselves in low esteem, honoring other things and admiring whatever they encounter more than themselves—and thus hanging in a state of stupor and wonderment toward these external things—they have surely cast themselves as far away as possible, and have separated themselves from their father and from their own nature, while they hold in low regard those things from which they have too much turned away. For this reason, an extreme ignorance of divinity seems to happen to the soul as a result of honoring inferior things and despising itself. <margin>C</margin> For as soon as the soul pursues and admires something else, it simultaneously confesses that by admiring and pursuing this thing, it is itself inferior. When the soul considers itself inferior to things that are born and perish, and thus thinks of itself as something most abject and the most fleeting of all things it honors, it deservedly can conceive in its mind neither the nature nor the power of God. Therefore, we must address a twofold discourse to those who are so affected, if indeed we are to turn them back toward the opposites and primary things, and finally lead them back to the supreme One and the First. <margin>D</margin> What, then, is this twofold discourse? One is that which demonstrates for what cause the soul now honors these inferior things, a matter we have run through extensively elsewhere; the other is that which teaches and reminds the soul of how noble a lineage it was born from, and with how much dignity it is endowed. This second discourse is certainly prior to the first, and once clarified, it will clarify the first as well, which is precisely what must now be discussed. For this topic seems to approach most closely the nature of what we seek, and it is appropriately placed before the other. For that which seeks is the soul, and it must certainly know what it itself is while it searches within itself, so that it may first learn whether it has the power to investigate such things, and whether it possesses the eye with which it can see clearly, and whether it is at all appropriate to investigate these matters. For if they are foreign to us, why should we investigate them? But if they are kindred, it is fitting and profitable to search, and the soul may eventually find them.

---
->*How great the dignity of the world-soul is, he shows by the fact that unless she herself were in the world, the world would be nothing other than a mass of unformed matter.*<-
---

## Chapter II.

---
->*The Soul generates the forms of things, rouses the motions and actions of all, implants life in all, and is present as a whole everywhere, ruling by her nod; and so she relates to the world’s body upon entering it, just as the rising sun relates to the dark air. Our own souls have similar powers and almost the same dignity, especially if, purged of bodily filth, the soul returns into herself.*<-
---

<margin>A</margin> EVERY soul ought first of all to consider that the soul herself produced all living beings by breathing life into them: she made, I say, all living things which the earth nourishes, and those which the sea, those which are in the air, and the divine stars in the heaven. The Soul adorned the sun, and the Soul adorned this vast heaven, and leads it in perpetual order, being herself a certain nature distinct from these things which she adorns, which she moves, and to which she suggests life. Therefore, she must necessarily be more excellent than all these; for while these things are born...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...and be persuaded that they are of themselves. But when they appeared to have taken pleasure in moving much from themselves, running in the opposite direction and making a great distance <note>original: "ὑπόστασιν", here implying a distance in existence or standing</note>, they became ignorant even that they themselves were from that source. Just like children snatched away from their fathers at birth, and raised far off for a long time, they are ignorant of both themselves and their fathers. <margin>B</margin> Therefore, since they no longer see him, nor themselves, having dishonored themselves through ignorance of their lineage, and having honored other things, and marveling at everything else more than themselves—and having been struck with awe and admiration for these things, and being dependent on them—they broke themselves off as far as possible from those things from which they turned away in dishonor. So it happens that the honor of these things here, and the dishonor of themselves, is the cause of that complete ignorance. <margin>C</margin> For at the same time, something else is pursued and admired. And the one who admires and pursues confesses that they are worse. Setting itself as worse than things that are becoming and perishing, and supposing itself to be the most dishonored and most mortal of all things it honors, it could neither cast into its heart the nature of God, nor His power. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, there is a twofold argument for those so disposed, if indeed one is to turn them back to the opposites and the first things, and lead them as far as the highest and the One and the First. What then is each? One shows the cause of those things now honored by the soul, which we have also gone through at length elsewhere. The other is that which teaches and reminds the soul what its lineage and worth are. This is prior to the former, and when clarified, it will reveal the other. We must speak of these things now. For that which is sought will be near, and it is useful for that purpose. For the seeker is the soul. And that which is known is for her, so that she may learn before all things if she has the power to seek such things, and if she has the organ, as it were, to see, and if it is fitting to seek. For if they are alien, what is the need? But if they are kindred, it is fitting and she is able to find them.

<margin>A</margin> EVERY soul, then, must first reflect on this: <note>original: "ΕΝΘΥΜΕΙΣΘΩ", a command to contemplate or take to heart.</note> that she herself made all living things, breathing life into them—those which the earth nourishes, those in the sea, those in the air, and the divine stars in heaven. She herself made the sun; she herself made the greatest heaven and adorned it. She herself leads it around in order, being a nature different from those things she adorns, and those she moves, and those she makes live. And this must be more honorable. For while these things are becoming...

He argues that to return to God, the Soul must first recognize its own dignity as the creator and animator of the physical universe.</summary>

# BOOK ONE.

...and they perish whenever the soul leaves them, or it supplies life; but the soul itself exists forever, because it does not abandon itself. As to the manner in which life is supplied, whether to the whole universe or to individual things, let it be reckoned in this way. Let another soul contemplate the Great Soul—a soul that has attained no small dignity for such contemplation, having been freed from deception and the enchantments that have bewitched others, and settled in a state of perfect stillness. Let everything be quiet for it: not only the surrounding body and the storms of the body’s sensations, but also all that surrounds it. Let the earth be still, the sea still, the air still, and even the heavens themselves in their better state. Let the soul conceive of the Great Soul flowing into this stillness from every side, as if being poured in and entering from all directions, illuminating it. Just as the rays of the sun strike a dark cloud and make it shine, giving it a golden appearance, so the Soul, entering the body of the heaven, gave it life and gave it immortality. It roused that which was lying dormant. And the heaven, moved with an eternal motion under the guidance of a wise soul, became a blessed living being. It acquired its dignity once the soul moved in to inhabit it; whereas before the soul, it was a dead body—earth and water, or rather the darkness of matter and "non-being." It was that which "the gods hate," as <term>the poet</term> <note>original: ποιητής (*poiētēs*), referring to Homer; the phrase "hateful to the gods" describes the void or the underworld</note> says. The power and nature of the soul would become even clearer if one considers here how it encompasses and leads the heaven by its own will. For to this entire vast magnitude, however great it is, the soul gave itself. Every span, whether great or small, is ensouled. But while one part of the body is in one place and another is elsewhere—some being opposite and others held in various distances from each other—the soul is not like that. It does not give life by being carved up into little pieces for each part of the body; rather, all things live by the whole soul. It is present everywhere in its entirety, made like the Father who generated it, both in its unity and in its universality. And although the heaven is many things and varied in different places, it is one by the power of the soul, and it is a God. Because of the soul, this world is a God. The sun is also a God because it is ensouled, as are the other stars. And we ourselves, if we have anything of value, have it because of this; for "corpses are more fit to be thrown out than dung." <note>A famous quote from the philosopher Heraclitus, emphasizing that the body without the soul is worthless matter.</note> Since the soul is the cause for the gods being gods, it is necessary that the soul itself be a God older than them. Our own soul is of the same kind. And whenever you examine it, having stripped away its additions and looking at it in its pure state, you will find that very same precious thing which the soul was. It is more precious than anything bodily. For without the soul, all things are just earth. Even if there is fire, what would its burning heat be without soul? And whatever is composed of these elements, even if you add water and air, they are nothing without soul. But if the body becomes a thing to be pursued because it is ensouled, why do you neglect yourself and pursue something else? While you admire the soul in another, admire yourself.

<column-break/>

**A** ...when the soul supplies life, and they die when it leaves: but the soul itself remains forever, because it never deserts itself. What the manner of supplying life may be, both to the universe and to individual living things, should be considered in this way. Let another soul therefore consider the Great Soul, having attained a dignity in contemplation that is not small—having been freed, clearly, from deception and from all those things which are accustomed to fascinate other souls. Thus, let it be settled in a most quiet state. Let not only the body that surrounds it and the storm of the body be still, but let whatever surrounds it from the outside also be at rest on every side. Let the earth be still, and the sea, and the air, and the heaven. Let the soul then imagine a soul flowing from the outside into such a silent mass, poured deeply within and penetrating all things, illuminating them no differently than the rays of the sun are accustomed to light up dark gloom, and often make clouds look golden in appearance. So it was that the soul, entering the celestial body, **C** gave it life and gave it immortality, and immediately roused the dormant mass. But by this perpetual motion, driven by the guidance of a wise soul, it was made a blessed animal; and the whole heaven attained its dignity as soon as the soul inhabited it, whereas previously it was a body void of life, namely earth and water—or rather the darkness of matter, and non-being, and that which (as he says) the gods hold in hatred. But the force and nature of the soul will become clearer and more visible if one observes in these things how **D** it embraces and leads the heaven by its own will. For to this entire mass, as great as it is, it gave itself. Thus this whole interval, both great and small, is animated, whereas one part of the body is situated in one place and another in another. And this part is disposed in one way, while that is disposed differently; some are placed opposite, while others are connected and hanging from one another. But the soul is not so. For it does not introduce life individually by being divided into parts and particles; rather, it vivifies all things as a whole, and it is present everywhere in its entirety, **E** made similar to the Father, both according to His unity and according to a certain amplitude through all things. And truly, the heaven, although it is manifold and different parts are in different places, is nevertheless one by the power of the soul itself. Now, because of the soul, this world is a God: the Sun also is a God because it is ensouled, and all the stars likewise. We also, whatever excellence we have, we have only because of this. For those deprived of soul are said to be more abject than dung. It is necessary that the soul itself, since **F** it is the cause for the gods being gods, exists as a God more ancient than they. Our soul is also conformable to this. Therefore, if ever you consider it without its attachments, looking at it in its pure state, you will surely find that same thing which is the venerable soul, far more precious than any body. For without the soul, perhaps all things are merely earth. And if fire were present, what would its burning vehemence be? And whatever things might be composed of these: even if you added water and air to them, you would still not have found **G** anything venerable. But if the body becomes worthy of pursuit because it is animated, why, I ask, do you dismiss yourself—that is, your own mind—and pursue anything else? But come, having admired the soul itself in another, admire yourself.

PLOTINUS’ ENNEADS, BOOK V.

*Our rational faculty, being mobile and shifting from rest to action and back again, depends on our own intellect which is always stably active; and this intellect, as the property of the particular soul, depends on the common intellect which exists simply in itself.*

->### Chapter III.<-

*Our intellect relates to reason, and the common intellect relates to ours, as light relates to air, or form to matter. But while reason is formed daily by our intellect, our own intellect is always formed and always illuminated by the common intellect. We can, therefore, conjecture the excellence of the common intellect from the very preeminence of the soul's own intellect.*

---

<margin>A</margin> Since the soul is such a venerable and divine thing, trust now that by using such a vehicle you will approach God; by this very path, ascend to Him. You will not have to wander far, nor are there many intermediate stages. Take, therefore, that which is more divine than this divine thing—I mean the soul’s proximity to the world above, after which the soul is the closest neighbor and from which it originates. For although the soul is as great a thing as reason demonstrates, it is nevertheless an <term>image</term> <note>original: imago / εἴκων (eikōn)</note> of <margin>B</margin> the Intellect itself. Just as a word in speech is an expression of the <term>word</term> <note>original: verbum / λόγος (logos); here meaning the inner thought or formative principle</note> dwelling in the soul, so the soul itself is the "word" of the Intellect. It is the total activity and life which the Intellect produces to sustain another existence—just as one kind of heat resides in fire itself, while another kind is the heat which fire provides to something else. However, one must understand that in the higher realm, the soul does not merely flow out, but partly remains within the Intellect while partly following after it. Therefore, since the soul originates from the Intellect, it exists as something intellectual; the intellect of the soul itself is occupied in discursive reasoning. Its perfection comes in turn from the Intellect, as if from a father <margin>C</margin> and a nourisher; for the Intellect produced the soul as something not entirely perfect when compared with itself. Thus, this substance is derived from Mind, and reason is its activity—a kind of intellectual "word"—so long as Mind is perceived by it. For when the soul gazes upon Mind, it possesses within itself and as its own the things it understands and acts upon. Only these should be called the soul's true actions: those which are intellectual and internal. Those actions which are inferior come from elsewhere and are merely <margin>D</margin> affections of such a soul. The Intellect, therefore, makes the soul even more divine, both because it is its father and because it is always present. No medium intervenes between them except the fact that they are distinct from one another; they are joined such that the soul follows and receives, while the Intellect acts as the <term>form</term> <note>original: species / εἶδος (eidos)</note>. Indeed, even the "matter" of the Intellect itself is beautiful, since it is something intellectual and simple. How great the Intellect must be is evident even from this: it is more excellent than the soul, which is itself an exceedingly excellent thing.

<column-break/>

Since the soul is truly so precious and divine, trust that you may reach the Divine through such a nature; with such a cause, ascend to Him. Surely you will not cast yourself far, nor are the intermediaries many. Take, therefore, the more divine part of the soul, its neighborhood to that which is above it, after which and from which the soul exists. For as great a thing as the <term>reason</term> <note>original: λόγος (logos)</note> has shown the soul to be, it is yet an image. Just as the word in utterance is an image of the word in the soul, so the soul is the word of the Intellect. It is its activity, the life it sends out into another subsistence; just as in fire, there is the innate heat and the heat which it gives to others. But we must take the activity there not as flowing out, but as the one part remaining within and the other part subsisting separately. Since it is from the Intellect, it is intellectual. And its intellect is found in its reasonings. Its perfection comes from the Intellect again, like a father who has nourished a child whom he begot as imperfect compared to himself. This subsistence comes from the Mind, and its activity is the "word" seen within it. For when it looks into the Mind, it holds within it as its own what it thinks and acts upon. These alone should be called the activities of the soul: those which are intellectual and from within. What is lower comes from without, and these are the passions of such a soul. The Mind, then, makes the soul still more divine, both by being its father and by being present to it. For nothing is between them except their being different, as that which follows and receives, and that which is the <term>form</term> <note>original: εἶδος (eidos)</note>. But even the "matter" of the Mind is beautiful, being of the nature of mind and simple. What the Mind is, is clear from this: it is superior to the soul, which is such a great thing.

---

*Since the world is from the divine intellect, it is surely all within it. And because that intellect is being, life, and intellect in the most perfect way, therefore whatever is worldly within it is perfect, and is being, life, and intellect.*

->### Chapter IIII.<-

*Parts of time pertaining to worldly things refer to the whole of time, which exists passively in the world; and this time which is actively in the soul refers to the eternity of the divine mind itself. Within the mind, however, the act of understanding and the thing understood differ from one another by a certain formal reason. Likewise, that which understands and that which is understood agree only in substance. There, the act of understanding is metaphorically called "being moved," while the thing understood is like "moving and standing still." Since that intellect is both all-formed and contains within itself some difference and a kind of composition, it must rightly be directed toward something higher and most simple.*

---

Furthermore, someone might be able to know this same truth if they admire this sensible world, looking upon its magnitude, its beauty, and the order of its eternal motion; likewise the gods within it, some of whom are visible and others hidden; the <term>daemons</term> <note>original: dæmones; intermediary spirits, not "demons" in the modern sense</note> also, and animals, and finally all plants. Then, moving toward the very origin of the world—

<column-break/>

One may also see this from the following: if anyone admires this sensible world, looking at its magnitude and beauty and the order of its everlasting motion, and the gods in it—some visible and others invisible—and the daemons and animals and all plants, let him then ascend to the source of it all—

He suggests that the beauty and order of the physical world serve as a starting point for contemplating the even greater excellence of the intellectual realm.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the three primary levels of reality. Having discussed the Soul in the previous section, he now leads the reader upward into the realm of the "Intellect" (the second hypostasis), using the metaphor of the Golden Age of Saturn to describe a state of eternal, perfect thought.</meta>

### BOOK ONE.

<margin>A</margin> Let the soul ascend further toward the very principle and exemplar of this world, into the truer world itself. There, let it behold all intelligible things—not as external objects, but as eternal realities dwelling within the soul's own intelligence and life. Presiding over all these is the pure, untainted Intellect and an inestimable wisdom. This is truly the "Golden Life" <note>A reference to the mythical Golden Age ruled by the god Saturn (Greek: Cronos).</note> under Saturn; for Saturn himself is the Intellect, utterly immaculate. He encompasses within himself all immortal beings: every intellect, every god, every soul, all <margin>B</margin> existing in total stability. For why should that which is in a perfect state seek to change? Where would it travel, when it already possesses everything within itself? It does not even require growth, being already most perfect. Therefore, everything within it is also perfect, so that the whole may be entirely complete, containing nothing that is not perfect, and nothing within itself that it does not actively think. Yet it thinks not by seeking through inquiry, but by possessing. Its blessedness is not something acquired from the outside; rather, all things exist within its <term>Eternity</term> <note>original: æuo / αἰών (aiōn). Distinct from "time," eternity is a simultaneous "now."</note>, of which <margin>C</margin> Time is merely an imitation—Time, which circles around the Soul, letting some things pass by while reaching for others. Indeed, things around the Soul are always changing: at one moment there is Socrates, at another a horse; always one specific thing among the many that exist. But the Intellect is all things at once. It holds all things together, standing forever in the same state. It simply "is," and its "is" is forever present; there is no "future" for it, for it is already everything it could ever be. Nor does it have a "past," for nothing there has passed away. <margin>D</margin> Instead, all things consist in a permanent "now," being eternally the same, content with their present condition. Thus, each of these beings is both Intellect and Being. Taken together, the whole is the sum of all Intellect and all Being. It is "Intellect" because it thinks, thereby claiming Being for itself; it is "Being" because it is thought, and by being thought, it provides both thinking and existence to the Intellect. However, the cause of this thinking is something else, which is also the cause of Being itself. <margin>E</margin> Therefore, there is another cause for both of them at once <note>This refers to "The One," the highest principle above the Intellect.</note>. For these two—Intellect and Being—exist together and never desert one another. Though they are two, this "one" is simultaneously Intellect and Being, the thinker and the thing thought: Intellect in its act of thinking, and Being in its state of being thought. For the act of thinking could not exist unless there were—so to speak—<term>Difference</term> <note>original: alteritas / ἑτερότης (heterotēs)</note> and <term>Identity</term> <note>original: identitas / ταὐτότης (tautotēs)</note>. Therefore, the primary realities are Intellect, Being, Difference, and Identity. One must also include **Motion** and **Rest**. <margin>F</margin> **Motion** is present if it thinks, and **Rest** so that it remains the same; **Difference** allows for a thinker and an object of thought. Otherwise, if you remove this distinction, the reality becomes a single, silent unity. Those things which think and are thought must be

<column-break/>

distinct from one another, yet also the same, insofar as they exist in the same reality and share a common nature. Indeed, difference itself is "otherness." As these elements become many, they produce number and quantity; and finally, the specific quality of each of these produces its unique property, from which, as if from first principles, all other things proceed.

->**Chapter V.**<-

->*The Pythagoreans imagine that in a kind of procession from the "One" itself, the "Two" (the Dyad) arises, and within the limit of the "Two," the "Three" (the Triad) emerges, and so on in succession. The Platonists hold a similar judgment regarding the first essence.*<-

Because this essence exists most perfectly, it lives with a vital internal motion. Since progression is the opposite of regression or reaching a limit—originating from elsewhere—it receives from above the power to return, or to reach its limit...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s explanation of the relationship between the Soul and the higher Intellect. Having previously described the Intellect as a realm of perfect, eternal stability (the "Golden Age"), Plotinus now explains how the Soul serves as an "image" or "word" of that Intellect, and how the beauty of the physical world points us back toward this divine source.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

*Our rational faculty—because it is changeable and moves from rest into action and back again—depends on our own intellect, which is always stably active. This intellect of ours, being particular to the individual soul, depends in turn on the Universal Intellect, which subsists simply in itself. ->Chapter III.<-*

*Our intellect relates to reason, and the Universal Intellect relates to ours, just as light relates to the air that it forms into matter. While our reason is formed daily by our intellect, our own intellect is always formed and illuminated by the Universal Intellect. We can therefore estimate the excellence of the Universal Intellect by looking at the high standing of the soul's own intellect.*

<margin>A</margin>
Since the soul is such a venerable and divine thing, trust that you may reach God by using it as your vehicle. Ascend to Him through this very path. You will not have to wander far; nor are there many steps in between. Take hold of that which is most divine in the soul—namely, its closeness to the realm above, which stands next to the soul and from which the soul originates. For even if the soul is as great a thing as reason has shown it to be, it is nonetheless an image of the Intellect itself: just as a spoken word is an expression of the word existing in the mind. Thus, 
<margin>B</margin>
the soul is the "word" (the outward expression) of the Mind. It is entirely an activity and a life which the Mind produces to exist in another level of reality; just as there is one kind of heat that stays within a fire, and another kind of heat that the fire gives off to something else. In that higher realm, we must understand this power not as something merely flowing away, but as something that partly remains within its source and partly follows from it. Because the soul comes from the Intellect, it is intellectual in its nature, and its own intellect is expressed through discursive reasoning <note>original: discursione / λογισμοῖς (logismois). This refers to step-by-step logical thinking, which Plotinus distinguishes from the immediate, non-linear intuition of the higher Intellect.</note>. Its perfection, in turn, comes from the Intellect, as if from a father 
<margin>C</margin>
and a sustainer; for the Intellect produced the soul, though the soul was not initially perfect when compared to its source. Therefore, the soul’s very substance comes from the Mind, and its activity becomes rational—a kind of "intellectual word"—whenever it gazes upon the Mind. For when it looks into the Mind, it possesses within itself the things it understands and does; these alone deserve to be called the true, domestic, and intellectual actions of the soul. Those actions which are inferior come from elsewhere and are merely "passions" <note>original: passiones / πάθη (pathē). In this context, "passions" are things the soul undergoes or suffers due to external influence, rather than actions it initiates from its own divine essence.</note> of such a soul. 
<margin>D</margin>
The Intellect, therefore, makes the soul even more divine, both because it is its father and because it is always present. Nothing stands between them except the fact that they are distinct from one another—the soul follows and receives, while the Intellect acts as the Form. Even the "matter" of the Intellect is beautiful, being something intellectual and simple. How great the Intellect is can be seen by this: it is superior even to the soul, which is already a thing of such excellence.

---

*Since the world comes from the divine Intellect, the whole world is certainly contained within it. And since that Intellect is Being, Life, and Understanding in the most perfect way, everything in this world that exists within it is also perfect, and is itself Being, Life, and Understanding. Chapter IV.*

*The parts of time belonging to worldly things relate to the whole of time, which exists passively in the world. This time in the soul is active, and it relates to the eternity of the divine Mind itself. Yet within that Mind, the acts of "understanding" and "being understood" differ from each other by a certain formal reason. Likewise, that which understands and that which is understood are the same only in substance. There, "understanding" is metaphorically called "movement," while "being understood" is like "moving" and "standing still." Since that Intellect is "all-formed" (containing all forms) and possesses internal difference and a kind of composition, it must be guided toward something even higher and most simple <note>This refers to "The One," the absolute first principle in Plotinus's philosophy, which is even simpler and higher than the Intellect.</note>.*

<margin>A</margin>
Furthermore, one may recognize this truth through the following: if someone admires this sensible world—beholding its magnitude, its beauty, and the order of its eternal motion—and also the gods within it (some visible <note>The stars and planets, which Neoplatonists considered divine bodies.</note> and some hidden), as well as the spirits, animals, and all plants, let them then ascend to the archetype <note>original: archétypon / ἀρχέτυπον. The original "blueprint" or ideal model of the world.</note> of this world...

<column-break/>

Thus, since these things of the soul are divine, and having trusted that you may travel by such a means, ascend to that higher principle with such a cause. You will certainly not be cast far away. There are not many things in between. Take, then, that which is more divine in the soul because of its neighborliness to that which is after it and from which the soul comes. For as great a thing as reason has shown the soul to be, it is an image. Like a word in speech is to the word in the soul, so the soul itself is the word of the Mind. And all its activity and the life that overflows into another subsistence is like the heat that stays with the fire and the heat that the fire provides to others. But one must understand it there not as flowing out, but as the substance itself remaining while it provides for another. It exists from the Mind and is therefore intellectual. And its Mind is in its reasonings. Its perfection comes from the Mind again, as from a father who nourished it, whom the Mind generated as not perfect compared to itself. This subsistence exists from the Mind, and its activity is a word, with the Mind being seen by it. For when it looks into the Mind, it has within it its own domestic things. And these alone should be called the activities of the soul—those which are intellectual and from within. But the inferior things come from elsewhere. And these are the passions of such a soul. The Mind, therefore, makes it even more divine, both by being its father and by being present. For nothing is between them except being different, as one follows and the other is received. But the Mind is as the form, and its matter is beautiful, being mind-like and simple. What the Mind is, is clear from this: it is better than the soul, which is of such a nature.

---

One may also see it from these things: if someone admires this sensible world, looking at its magnitude, its beauty, and the order of its eternal motion. And the gods in it, some visible and some being hidden. And the spirits, and the animals, and all the plants, let them go to the archetype...

He argues that the beauty and order of the physical world serve as a starting point for the mind to ascend back to these higher, eternal realities.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the hierarchy of being, moving from the Soul to the Intellect (the Divine Mind). It explores the "Great Kinds" of being—Identity, Alterity, Motion, and Rest—which allow the Intellect to be a unified yet diverse reality.</meta>

# BOOK ONE.

<margin>A</margin> Let the soul ascend further toward its own principle and model, to a truer world. There, let it behold all intelligible things, and within itself, things that are eternal, existing in its own understanding and life. Above all these, there presides an intellect that is purely untainted, an immeasurable wisdom, and truly the "Golden Life" under Saturn <note>The Neoplatonists identified the god Saturn (Cronus) with the Intellect (*Nous*) because they interpreted his name as meaning "Pure Mind."</note>. For Saturn himself is the perfectly immaculate Intellect. It encompasses within itself all immortal things: every intellect, every god, every soul, and all these 
<margin>B</margin> things exist there in total stability. Why would it seek to change when it is in a state of well-being? To what place would it move, since it possesses everything within itself? Nor does it seek any increase, being most perfect. Therefore, all things within it are perfect, so that it may be perfect in every way, containing nothing that is not of that nature. It holds nothing in itself that it does not understand—and it understands not by searching, but by possessing. Its happiness is not something acquired from outside; rather, all things exist within eternity. 

<margin>C</margin> This is the true eternity, which Time imitates as it revolves around the soul, letting some things pass and reaching for others. For things around the soul are always changing—now it is Socrates, now a horse, or any other individual being. But the Intellect is all things. It holds all things together, stable in the same place. It simply *is*, and its "is" is forever; there is no future for it, for it already is everything it can be. Nor does it have a past, for nothing there has passed away; 
<margin>D</margin> all things remain in the present, being always the same, content with their current state.

Thus, each of these is both Intellect and Being. The whole is the total Intellect and the total of Being. It is "Intellect" <note>original Greek: *nous*</note> because it thinks, and thus claims Being for itself; it is "Being" <note>original Greek: *on*</note> because it is thought, and this very fact of being thought provides the Intellect with the act of thinking and of existing. But the cause of thinking is something else, which is also the cause of Being for the existent. 
<margin>E</margin> Therefore, there is another cause for both of them together. For they exist together and never desert one another. But though they are two, this "One" is simultaneously Intellect and Being—both the thinker and the thing thought. It is "Intellect" insofar as it thinks, and "Being" insofar as it is thought. For the act of thinking could not exist unless there were—if I may put it this way—"Alterity" <note>original: *alteritas*, meaning difference or otherness</note> and "Identity" <note>original: *identitas*, meaning sameness</note>. 

Therefore, the primary things are Intellect, Being, Alterity, and Identity. One must also add "Motion" and "Rest" <note>These five categories—Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Difference—are known as the "Great Kinds" from Plato's *Sophist*.</note>: 
<margin>F</margin> Motion, because it thinks; Rest, so that it remains the same. One needs Alterity so that there may be a thinker and a thing thought; otherwise, if you remove this diversity, it becomes a single thing and falls entirely silent. Those who think and those who are thought must be different from one another, but also the same, insofar as they exist in the same place and share something in common. Yet, the difference itself is "Alterity." As these become many, they create number and quantity, and the specific property of each produces "Quality." From these, as if from first principles, all other things proceed.

<column-break/>

*The Pythagoreans imagine that in a kind of procession from the One itself, the "Binary" <note>the Dyad or the number two</note> arises, and within the limit of the Binary, the "Ternary" <note>the Triad or the number three</note> emerges, and so on in order. Platonists judge similarly regarding the First Essence.*

### Chapter V.

*Because this Essence is most perfect, and thus lives in a similar way, it proceeds inward with a certain vital motion. But since progression is the opposite of return or reaching a limit—coming, of course, from elsewhere—it receives from above the power to return...*

PLOTINUS, ENNEADS BOOK V.

...be limited: just as the heaven derives its motion from the soul, but its circular motion from the intellect, or perhaps a soul already guided by intellect. That vital act is limited in the intellect, which is most clear and contains all forms; it receives its vigor from a divine source, just as the eye has a natural blink to look, but becomes truly seeing and formed by the power of light. Finally, since in the first Intellect—which understands itself—the <term>Formal Reason<note>original: "ratio formalis"; the underlying blueprint or logical structure of a thing.</note></term> of the thinker is, as it were, proceeding and capable of being formed, while the reason of the Intellect is like that which limits and forms. Therefore, because these are opposed to one another, there exists a certain number there—not an accidental number, but one that is entirely essential. There is also a number of <term>Ideas<note>In Neoplatonism, "Ideas" or "Forms" are the eternal, perfect patterns of all things that exist in the Divine Mind.</note></term> within that formal reason that differ from one another, provided that through them the forms of things that actually differ from each other are understood and created. Thus, an Intellect so manifold depends entirely on a principle that is absolutely simple.

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, this God became manifold in this soul when joined with things of this kind, unless perhaps the soul wishes to depart from here. Approaching Him and becoming, as it were, one with Him, the soul asks: Who, then, is he who fathered this Intellect? Who is this simple being who exists before such a multitude? Who is the author of its existence and its manifold nature? Who procreates <term>Number<note>original: "numerus"; here meaning the structured multiplicity of the universe, not just arithmetic.</note></term>? For number is not the first thing. Before <term>Duality<note>original: "duitas" or "dyad"; the first step away from unity toward multiplicity.</note></term> is the One itself. Duality is second; having been made by the One, it has the One as its definer. By its own nature, however, duality is something indefinite. But when it is <margin>B</margin> defined, it is already number—number as an essence. For the soul, too, is a number. The primary natures are not physical masses, nor are they any kind of magnitude. For these heavy things, which the senses consider to be "beings," are later developments. Even in seeds, it is not the moisture itself that is esteemed, but that which is not visible to the senses: that is number and reason. What is called "number" and "duality" in that higher realm are Intellect and certain reasons. But duality is indefinite when considered as a subject; the number which arises from it and the One is already a species—as if the essence of the Intellect itself were formed through the species made within it. It is formed in one way by the One itself, and in another way by itself, like a vision that is now actually seeing. For intelligence is a seeing vision, and both are one.

*The Supreme God, without any movement of will, generates the divine Intellect as his "word," differing from the Father by a certain "otherness." The Intellect, similarly immobile, generates its own "word," which is the Soul of the World.*

->Chapter VI.<-

*If the first principle were in any way changeable, it would change all things entirely. Likewise, if it were imagined to generate the substance of the Mind through motion as a medium, it would ultimately generate a motion without motion—an accident so imperfect that it would be the most imperfect of all accidents, since it could never possess its own parts simultaneously. Therefore, reason dictates that this most perfect substance is generated by God without such an accident. Since agents act partly by nature and partly by will, and in the first Agent every faculty of acting is contained, and those things which are divided in subsequent things are thus united in the first end: surely God creates things by will and by nature equally. In Him, nature and will are the same. From Him, therefore, without Him being changed by will or nature, the Intellect flashes forth like light; and when it first flashes forth, leaning toward the Father by a certain natural instinct, it is filled with the splendor of Ideas. Thus, the Intellect emerges from this source absolutely formed. Similarly, the Soul of the World relates to the divine Intellect. You will note that prayer will be most effective when the soul, recalling itself entirely to its own intellect, offers itself alone to God alone, burning with love for that one vision.*

<margin>A</margin> How, then, does it see? And what does it see? And how did it exist at all and proceed from that One, so that it might see? For now, the soul grasps the necessity through which these things happen. But it longs to understand again that which has been spoken of even among the ancient sages: in what way, from the One existing as such—as we say the One exists—did every single thing gain its substance? Whether it be the multitude, or duality, or number? And why did that One not remain within itself, but rather such a great multitude flowed out from there, as is seen in... B

<column-break/>

This God is manifold upon the soul, and is present to it if the soul is joined to Him and does not wish to stand apart. Approaching Him and becoming, as it were, one, the soul seeks: Who, then, is the one who generated this? He who is simple, the cause before such a multitude, the cause of both being and being many, he who makes Number. For the first is not number. Before Duality is the One. Second is duality, and having come from the One, it has the One as its limit; but duality is indefinite of itself. When it is limited, it is already number. Number as essence. The soul is also number. For the primary things are not bulks, nor magnitudes. These coarse things are later, which the senses think are beings. Even in seeds, it is not the liquid that is precious, but that which is not seen; this is number and reason. What is called number and duality there are Reasons and Intellect. But duality is indefinite, taken as the substrate. The number from it and the One is each a species; as if [the Intellect] were shaped by the species produced in it. It is shaped in one way by the One, and in another by itself, like a vision in its actual exercise. For intellection is a seeing vision, both are one.

How then does it see? And what? And how did it come to be and come from that One, that it might see? Now, the soul holds the necessity of these things being so; but it yearns for this much-discussed question, even among the ancient philosophers: how from the One, being such as we say the One is, did anything at all—whether a multitude, a duality, or a number—gain its existence? Why did that One not remain by itself, but instead this multitude flowed out, which is seen in...

# BOOK ONE

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> In the order of things, we believe we must trace it back to that First Principle. We should speak of it in this way: calling upon God himself—not with a spoken prayer that reaches the ears, but with the soul stretching itself out in prayer toward Him. For we are able to pray in this manner only when we approach <term>the alone to the Alone<note>original: "soli accedamus ad solum" / "μόνους πρὸς μόνον"; a famous phrase in Plotinus describing the mystical union of the individual soul with the solitary One.</term>. Therefore, the person contemplating God must rest quietly within the inner sanctuary—as if in a temple—remaining within himself, tranquil and existing beyond all things. There, he should behold the statues that stand, as it were, outside the sanctuary, or rather, behold that first statue which shines forth in a way <margin>B</margin> that can be naturally perceived. Concerning everything that moves, there must be something toward which it moves. If there were nothing of that kind, we would certainly not claim it moves at all. But if something is produced after the First Cause, it must necessarily be produced while that Cause is always turned toward itself. Let us now set aside any notion of <term>temporal generation<note>original: "generatio temporalis"; the idea that these things happened at a specific point in time. Plotinus argues this is an eternal, timeless process.</note></term>, for we are currently speaking of eternal things. Even if we use the word "generation" while speaking, <margin>C</margin> we do so only to bring forward the logic of cause and order. Therefore, what is born from that source must be born without the higher being being stirred or changed. Otherwise, if something were generated because the First moved, then that which is born would be the third thing after it, not the second. For this reason, since the First is utterly immovable, it is necessary that if a second thing is born after it, it must exist without the First giving a nod of assent, or decreeing it by will, or being moved in any way. How, then, should we conceive of this <margin>D</margin> stability? Think of it as a <term>radiance<note>original: "perilampsis" / "perilumen"; a light that shines out from a center.</note></term> shed all around, depending on the First while the First remains in deep stillness—just like the brilliance surrounding the sun, which constantly flows from it while the sun itself stays the same. Indeed, all things, as long as they persist in their nature, necessarily produce an outward reality from their own present essence and power; this reality depends on them and is an <margin>E</margin> image, a kind of likeness of the original power from which it flowed. Fire, for instance, emits heat; snow does not keep its cold only within itself, but provides it to others; this is especially proven by things that are fragrant. For as long as they exist, something is breathed out from them to those nearby. Furthermore, all things that are already perfect will generate something. That which is always perfect always generates, and generates something eternal—though that which is born is lesser than the one who fathered it. <margin>F</margin> What then should be said of the Most Perfect? Does nothing go forth from Him? Or rather, do the greatest things after Him proceed from Him? The greatest thing after Him is the <term>Intellect<note>original: "mens" / "nous"; the Divine Mind or second level of reality.</note></term>, which is second. For the Intellect looks upon the One and needs only the One; but the First has no need of the Intellect. It is necessary that what is born from that which is better than mind must itself be a mind. The Intellect is the best of all things that are born, because everything else comes after it. In the same way, <margin>G</margin> the Soul is a certain "word" and activity of the Intellect, just as the Intellect is the "word" of God. But the "word" of the Soul is obscured. To the extent that the Soul is an image of the Intellect, it must look toward the Intellect; in the same way, the Intellect—being the image of God—looks up to God.

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

...so that it becomes the Intellect: indeed, it sees God not as if separated from itself, but because it exists after Him, and nothing is in between, just as nothing is between the soul and the mind. Everything that is generated desires its generator and finds contentment in following it, especially when the generator and the generated are alone together. But where that which generated is the best of all, the generated necessarily clings to it so closely that it seems separated only by a certain <term>otherness<note>original: "alteritate" / "ἑτερότητι"; the first distinction or "twoness" that allows the Intellect to look back at the One.</note></term> (if I may put it that way).

---

->*Just as the intellectual soul depends on the pure intellect, which is not the soul itself: so too this intellect flows from the Good itself, which is not intellect, but transcends it. Chapter VII.*<-

This Intellect first flows from the Father as a living essence, but soon, by naturally looking back there, it turns into Intellect. For Intellect is that very substantial vision resulting from a natural gaze or attraction. Its father is the <term>Simple One<note>original: "simpliciter vnum"; the ultimate, indivisible source of all reality in Neoplatonism.</note></term>. Here, however, is the essential or vital One, where there appears to be a <term>dyad<note>original: "binarius"; the number two, representing the first step toward multiplicity.</note></term>, but with the addition of attraction, it becomes a <term>triad<note>original: "ternarius"; the number three.</note></term>. In the triad, there is even and odd and every number. Similarly, through this gaze or attraction, once it becomes a triad, all numbers are produced at once. For by looking fixedly and by being naturally drawn and strengthened by the Father, it is confirmed and grasps its own living essence, in which the fertile, mothering power of all essences flourishes. Thus, it derives itself into the forms of all things within itself, while unfolding its own power by understanding it. It is therefore "all-formed," and all things are nurtured by the Father; since He is defined by no form of things, He rightly does not act (which would be wrong to say) or rather acts upon all things equally, while from His single existence above all things He generates one all-formed being. This is the one born of <term>Saturn<note>original: "Saturno genitus"; referring to the myth of Cronus. Neoplatonists interpreted Cronus as "Koros-Nous" or "Sated Intellect," which contains all ideas within itself.</note></term>, and called Saturn, swallowing his own offspring—that is, those separated from <term>Rhea<note>original: "à Rhea"; identifying Rhea with the flow of Nature and Matter.</note></term>. This son, <term>Jupiter<note>original: "Iupiter" / "Ζεύς"; representing the World Soul (Psyche) which brings the internal ideas of the Intellect into the physical world.</note></term>, the soul of the world, generates sons—that is, forms in nature—and through her finally produces them into matter.

<margin>A</margin>
We say that the Intellect is the <term>image<note>original: "IMAGINEM" / "ΕΙΚΟ'ΝΑ"; a reflection or likeness that is lesser than the original but shares its nature.</note></term> of that One. For we must explain more clearly: first, that which is generated must be of such a kind as to preserve many traits of its generator, and bear such a likeness to it as light does to the sun. Yet the generator is not the mind. How then does it generate the mind? Simply because the generated thing, by a certain <term>turning back<note>original: "conuersione" / "ἐπιςροφῇ"; the process where the emanation looks back at its source to gain form and intelligence.</note></term>, looks toward the generator; and this vision itself is the Intellect. For that which perceives another is either sense or <margin>B</margin> intellect. Sense is usually compared to a line, while what remains in the process of knowing is compared to a circle. But such a circle is, as it were, divisible, whereas the One is not so. Perhaps here also is the One, but the One as the <term>power of all things<note>original: "potestas omniū" / "δύναμις πάντων"; the One contains the potential for everything without being any one thing.</note></term>. Therefore, the intelligence beholds these things as if they were divided from that very power; otherwise, it would not be intellect at all. Since even <margin>C</margin> by itself it already possesses, as it were, a self-awareness of its own power, noticing how much it is worth, and in this its essence consists. Therefore, by itself, it also defines its own being for itself by a certain power received entirely from the One. Here, indeed, it is observed that essence is like a single part of those things which belong to the One and come from it, being strengthened by it, and being perfected into essence by and from that same source. It sees itself from that source as something divisible coming from the impartible; it sees itself living, and understanding, and absolutely everything—since that One is <margin>D</margin> nothing of all things. For this reason, all things are made by the One, because it is not circumscribed by any single form. For that is only the One, while the Intellect and the order of things flow in sequence; for which reason these are essences. For they are already determined, and each one already possesses a kind of form. But Being itself is not like some...

# BOOK ONE.

<margin>A</margin> [The Intellect] is not to be considered as something indefinite, but rather as something fixed by a certain boundary and stability. In the realm of intelligible things, stability is defined by determination and form, through which these things receive their very substance. This Intellect, therefore, which is worthy of being called the "purest mind," must be judged to have been born from no other source than the first principle. Once it was brought into being, it generated all existing things along with itself: the entire beauty of the <term>Ideas<note>original: "idearum" / "ἰδεῶν"; the eternal archetypes or patterns of all things in the mind of God.</note></term> and all the intelligible gods. We must further understand that this Intellect is
<margin>B</margin> full of all the things it has produced. It is as if it immediately absorbs its offspring, containing all things within itself, so that they do not fall into <term>matter<note>original: "materiam" / "ὕλην"; in Neoplatonism, matter is the lowest level of reality, representing a lack of form and light.</note></term>, nor are they "nourished at the breast of Rhea." This is how the ancient mysteries and myths concerning the gods hint at these truths: they depict Saturn as the wisest God, born before Jupiter, who holds back within himself the things he generates. In this way, he remains full and pure within the fullness of the intellect. After this, they say that Jupiter—already existing as a boy, that is, pure and vigorous and already "saturated"—was generated. For the Intellect generates the Soul, since the Intellect is perfect. Indeed, because it is perfect, it had to generate, for such a great power could not remain sterile.
<margin>C</margin> But here, too, that which is begotten could not be better than its begetter. Since it was lesser, it had to be an image of the begetter, and likewise indefinite in itself, but given definition and form by its source. This offspring of the mind is a certain <term>Reason<note>original: "ratio" / "λόγος" (Logos); the principle of order and logic that proceeds from the Mind to organize the world.</note></term>, whose substance consists in the act of thinking. This is the activity that 
<margin>D</margin> revolves around the Intellect; it is the light of the Intellect and a "footprint" that always depends upon it. On one side, it is joined to the Intellect, and thus it is filled, enjoying it, participating in it, and understanding it. But on the other side, it reaches down toward the things that come after it—or rather, it generates them. These subsequent things must necessarily be inferior to the Soul, and we shall speak of them later. This is the extent to which divine things proceed.

---

> *From the words of Plato’s Parmenides, it is proven that the Good itself, and the simply One, is superior to Being itself and to the Intellect (which is "one-many" and seeks the Good). Likewise, it is shown that the divine Intellect is superior to the World Soul, because the Soul is "one and many" in a more divided sense, and exists as an intellect only through participation.* ->Chapter VIII.<-

### Chapter VIII.

<margin>A</margin> For this reason, in Plato’s works, all things are arranged in a threefold order around the "King of all." He says that the first things are around the first, the second things around the second, and the third things around the third. He also speaks of a "Father of the cause," calling the cause "Intellect." For in Plato, the <term>Artificer<note>original: "artifex" / "δημιουργὸς" (Demiurge); the divine craftsman who shapes the universe based on eternal patterns.</note></term> of the world is the Intellect, and he says this Intellect creates the Soul in that famous "mixing bowl." Since the Intellect is the cause, he calls the <term>Good<note>original: "bonum" / "ἀγαθὸν"; the ultimate source of reality, above even being and thought.</note></term> its Father, as it is 
<margin>B</margin> superior to both intellect and essence. Often, Plato calls "Being" and "Intellect" the "Idea." Therefore, in Plato, we can recognize that from the Good itself comes the Mind and the Idea, and from the Mind comes the Soul. These teachings are not new or recently invented; they were spoken of long ago, though perhaps not as fully explained. Our current discourses are, as it were, interpreters of those ancient ones. We can prove these opinions are ancient by the testimony of Plato's own writings. Even Parmenides, before Plato, touched upon this view insofar as he reduced "Being" and "Intellect" to the same thing. He did not place Being among sensible things, saying that "to think 

<column-break/>

<margin>C</margin> and to be are the same."

### Chapter IX. Anaxagoras, Heraclitus, Empedocles, and Aristotle agree with Plato that the first principle of all things is one and most simple.

*For the fact that all things in the world, though diverse, conspire in order toward one form of the whole, one end, and one effect, comes from the fact that all things exist and are led by the One; all things imitate and desire the One. If you could propose one principle, and another equal principle were also placed as a "first" of all things, then the positioning of this second one would be superfluous. This principle would also be called a principle only by chance, since no reason could be assigned why this second one should also be a principle, or why the first one was positioned. It is not because it is necessary, nor because one is from the other, nor because both are from a certain third thing. A multitude that is not from the One is entirely accidental, reckless, divided, and impossible.*

ANAXAGORAS, when he introduces a Mind that is pure and free from mixture, also proposes the first as simple and the One as separate; however, he omitted a detailed discussion due to his antiquity. Heraclitus, moreover, knew the eternal Intelligible One, for he said that bodies are always becoming and flowing. Furthermore, in the system of Empedocles, Discord indeed divides, but in Concord itself the One is signified. He also held this to be incorporeal, while the elements take the place of matter. Aristotle later says that the **B** first itself is indeed "intelligible" and "separate"; but when he asserts that it "thinks itself," he conversely makes it not the "first." Truly, when he also produces many other intelligibles in the world—as many in number as there are spheres in the heaven, so that each mover moves an individual sphere—he arranges these intelligibles differently than Plato does. Since he lacks a probable reason, he resorts to necessity. Someone might insist, asking if this is said with right reason: saying it is more reasonable **C** that all spheres and the orders of things, contributing together to one coordination, look toward one and the same first principle. One might also ask whether the many intelligibles in Aristotle’s view come from one first principle, or if there are many principles among the intelligible things? And if all things are from one, they will be compared by a certain fitting proportion, just as the spheres in sensible things are related to one another: one indeed encompassing another, and one finally containing the rest from the outside as the ruler. **D** Therefore, the first there will comprehend the rest, and there will be an "intelligible world." Then, just as the spheres here are not empty—the first indeed being full of stars, and each following sphere possessing individual stars—so also there, those movers will have many things within themselves, and all things there will be more real than the celestial ones. But if each is a principle in the number of intelligibles, then these principles will certainly exist merely by chance. And it could be asked: for what reason

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, it is necessary to believe that things are as follows: that the One is beyond being, as our argument intended to show (as far as such things can be demonstrated); and that next in order is Being and Intellect; and in the third place is the nature of the Soul. Just as these three exist in nature, we must believe that these three also exist within us. I mean, however, not in things perceived by the senses—for these three of which we speak are separate—but they are outside the realm of the senses, and in the same <margin>B</margin> way that those [cosmic principles] are outside the entire heaven, so too are these within man. For instance, Plato speaks of the "inner man" <note>original: "τὸν εἴσω ἄνθρωπον" (ton eisô anthrôpon); a concept from Plato's *Republic* referring to the rational soul.</note>. Our soul is therefore something divine, and of a different nature, just as the entire nature of the Soul is. It is perfect when it possesses intellect; one part of this intellect is engaged in reasoning, while the other provides the power to reason. This reasoning part of the soul requires no <margin>C</margin> physical organ for its process of reasoning. Rather, it maintains its activity within itself in a pure state, so that it might be possible to reason purely. If someone were to place this part—separated and unmixed with the body—in that first "intelligible" <note>the realm of pure thought/ideas</note> rank of things, they would not be mistaken. For we should not seek a place to put it, but rather we must place such a power outside of all place. Only in this way can it be "by itself," "outside," and "immaterial," <margin>D</margin> when it is alone and has nothing from the nature of the body. For this reason, Plato says in the *Timaeus* that the Creator wrapped the soul of the universe around the world from the outside, hinting at that part of the soul which remains in the intelligible realm. Regarding our own souls, he speaks cryptically, saying the soul is hidden in the "heights of the head." Moreover, his command to "separate" the soul in the *Phaedo* refers to a separation of nature, not of physical place. But he warns that the mind should not agree with the body, nor be distracted by imaginary things, but should strive to lead the lower form of the soul upward <margin>E</margin> toward the higher things, along with that part of itself which is situated here—that part which alone is the craftsman and shaper of the body and is constantly occupied with such work.

<margin>A</margin> NOW indeed it has been demonstrated that it is necessary for the One to be above being, just as reason desired to show—at least as much as can be shown concerning such matters: and that after the One itself there is Being and Intellect: and finally in the third place, the nature of the soul. Just as these three are in nature itself, as we have said, so also must it be thought that these exist in us. I say this, however, not regarding the things offered to the senses. For these <margin>B</margin> things of which we speak at present are separate; they are regarding things that exceed the powers of the senses and are outside them, and in the same way "outside" as those things in the universal order of nature are entirely outside the heaven. Thus there are three certain things in man—in man, I say, whom Plato calls the "inner man." Therefore, our soul is moreover a certain divine thing, and of another nature, such as is the universal nature of the soul. It is perfect when it has a mind, but one part of the mind is occupied in reasoning, while the other supplies the power of reasoning. <margin>C</margin> This virtue of reasoning in the soul requires no physical instrument at all for its own discourse, but keeps its action in a certain pure degree, so that it may also reason purely. If anyone locates this, separated and not mixed with the body, in that first intelligible rank of things, he will by no means go astray. For we must not seek a place where we may put it, but <margin>D</margin> such a power must be established outside of all place. For only thus can it have what is said to "exist through itself," and to act both from the outside and above matter, when it is alone, having nothing at all from the corporeal nature. For this reason, Plato says in the *Timaeus* that God poured the soul of the world even outside the world, showing the power of the soul remaining in the intelligible itself. Concerning our soul also, he says in the *Phaedrus*, that it now hides <margin>E</margin> its head within the heaven, and now raises its head outside the heaven. And yet when, especially in the *Phaedo* and *Theaetetus*, he commands the soul to be separated from the body, he does not prescribe it to be segregated by place—for that which is so separated is naturally disjoined—but he warns that the mind should not assent to the body, nor be alienated from the mind by imaginary things, and should try if by any means it is able to lead the species of the soul subject to it upward to higher things along with itself: that part which is placed here, which indeed is alone the maker and shaper of the body, and continually applies itself to this very thing.

> *It appears that the substance of the reasoning soul is separable from the body, since it is able to reason even without a bodily instrument. <margin>A</margin> NOW it has already been demonstrated that the One must exist above Being, just as our previous reasoning sought to show—at least as much as can be proven about such lofty matters. We have also shown that after the One comes Being and Intellect, and in the third place, the nature of the Soul. Just as these three principles exist in nature, we must believe that these same three exist within ourselves. By this, I do not mean within the things offered to our senses.
