If someone were to place this power—separated, unmixed with the body, and in that first "intelligible" rank of things—they would not be in error. For we should not seek a "place" where we may put it; <margin>D</margin> rather, such a power must be established outside of all place. Only in this way can it be said to exist by itself, and to act both from the outside and above matter, when it is alone and possesses nothing from the nature of the body. For this reason, Plato says in the *Timaeus* that God wrapped the soul of the world even around the outside of the world, showing the power of the soul remains in the intelligible realm. Regarding our own soul, he says in the *Phaedrus* that it sometimes hides its head within the heavens and sometimes raises its head above the heavens. And when, especially in the *Phaedo* and *Theaetetus*, he commands us to separate the soul from the body, <margin>E</margin> he is not commanding a separation of location (for that which is so separated is already naturally distinct), but he warns that the soul should not "nod" <note>original: "νεύσει," referring to the soul's inclination or leaning toward the material world</note> toward the body, nor consent to the imagination, nor be alienated from the Mind because of its commerce with the body. Instead, the soul should strive, if it is able, to lead that lower part of itself back up to the higher things—that part which is situated here below, which alone is the craftsman and shaper of the body, and which is constantly occupied with that very task.

<margin>A</margin> NOW truly it has been demonstrated that it is necessary for the One to be above being, such as reason desired to demonstrate, as much as can be demonstrated about such things: that after the One itself is being and intellect: and finally in the third place the nature of the soul. <meta>This page continues Plotinus’s explanation of the hierarchical structure of reality—moving from the One to the Intellect and finally to the Soul—and begins to explain why human consciousness often fails to perceive these higher divine activities within itself.</meta>

->PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.<-

*Just as in the universe the One itself is superior to the Intellect, and the Intellect is superior to the Soul, so in our own soul the unity of the soul is more eminent than its mind, and the mind is higher than its reason. Chapter XI.*

*We have sufficiently established in the Theology and in the first books of Plotinus that the One itself is placed before Being, and Being before the Soul. Likewise, we have shown that souls, like lines, have their own unity—a kind of mark by which they are able to touch the unity of the universe, God, as if reaching for a center. Furthermore, we have shown that the common notions of things, the arts, and stable rules are always present in our minds, through which we can reason about similar things at our own discretion.*

<margin>A</margin>Therefore, when the soul deliberates about what is just and beautiful, and inquires whether this thing is just or whether that thing is beautiful, it is necessary that there be some stable "Just" and a similar stable "Beautiful" from which the soul's reasoning might draw its starting point. Otherwise, it would never be able to move through a line of thought. And if the soul sometimes moves through these thoughts and at other times does not, it must be that while the soul is the nature that moves through them, there is also an <term>Intellect</term><note>Latin: "mens"; Greek: "νοῦς" (nous). The faculty of direct, non-discursive spiritual insight</note> within us that always possesses the Just and the Beautiful. Furthermore, the principle and cause of the Intellect—God—must be present. He is in no way divisible but remains entirely consistent; I do not mean He remains in a physical place, but rather He remains in Himself. Meanwhile, He is also observed in many things—in each of those things capable of receiving Him as something different from themselves, just as a center exists in itself. For every point on a circle has its own mark in the center, and the lines bring their own specific point to it. For by such a <margin>B</margin>divine element among those things within us, we also touch, meet, and are joined to the divine. We lean <margin>C</margin>and are fixed there to the extent that we direct our focus toward that place.

*And if our intellect is always active concerning divine things, we nevertheless do not notice it; because reason and imagination are distracted toward the opposites of divine things and toward variety. Chapter XII.*

<margin>A</margin>Moreover, why is it that despite possessing such great powers, we do not notice that we have them, but for the most part remain idle and apart from such actions? There are many who never act concerning these things at all. Yet those higher principles certainly persist in their own actions: the Intellect, and that which is above the Intellect, is always within itself. Likewise, the soul has a power that is either immobile or perpetually in motion. However, not everything in the soul is immediately felt; it only reaches <margin>B</margin>into us when it proceeds as far as the faculty of sensation. But when any active power in us does not transmit its action into the very faculty of sensing, that kind of action has not yet propagated itself through the whole soul. For this reason, we do not yet recognize it, since we identify as who we are alongside our sensing faculty; we are not merely a part of the soul, but rather the whole soul. Indeed, every animated thing within us performs its own function by itself as long as it lives; but <margin>C</margin>it only happens that we recognize it when there is a mutual transmission and perception arises from it. Therefore, if we are to perceive the things thus present to us, we must turn our very power of perception inward and take care that it focuses entirely there. It is just as if someone, wishing to hear one voice above all others, might separate themselves from other sounds and direct their ears with the greatest attention toward the best of all voices as it approaches. So too here, we must dismiss all the noises of the senses that interrupt and call to the soul, except for what necessity compels, and turn the perceiving power toward...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>Since the soul is that which reasons about just and beautiful things, and seeks through reasoning whether this is just and whether that is beautiful, it is necessary that there be something standing firm—the Just—from which reasoning also occurs in the soul; otherwise, how would it reason? And if it reasons at one time and not at another, there must be a soul that reasons, but an Intellect within us that always possesses the Just. There must also be the principle and cause of the Intellect, which is God. He is not divided, but remains there; and not remaining in a place, He is again seen in many things, according to each of those capable of receiving Him, just as a center is in itself. And each of the things in the circle has a point in the center. And the lines offer their own point toward this. <margin>B</margin>For by such a thing among the parts in us, we touch and are with [the divine], and are suspended from it. We run together there, whenever we incline toward that place.

How then, having such great things, do we not <margin>A</margin>perceive them, but for the most part are idle in such activities? And some people never act in them at all. Yet those things are always in their own activities—the Intellect and that which is before the Intellect are always in themselves. And the soul is thus always in motion, yet standing still. For not everything in the soul is already an object of sense; but it comes into us when it goes into sensation. But whenever each active thing does not share with the perceiving faculty, it has not yet <margin>B</margin>gone through the whole soul. Therefore, we do not yet know it, because we are with the sensing faculty, and we are not a part of the soul, but the whole soul. And for each of the psychic living things, it is always active by itself according to its own nature. But knowing occurs when there is a sharing and a perception. Therefore, if there is to be a perception of the things that are truly present, one must turn the faculty of perception inward, and there make <margin>C</margin>it hold its attention. Just as if someone wants to hear desired voices, they stand away from other voices and rouse the ear toward the better of the sounds, whenever that thing approaches; so also here, one must let go of the sensory hearings, except insofar as necessity requires, and the whole... of the soul...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the hierarchy of being, transitioning from the introductory metaphysical definitions of the previous page into a specific exploration of the "Trinity of Principles" found in Platonic, Zoroastrian, and Christian thought, ultimately leading into Book II of the Fifth Ennead.</meta>

<page-num>493</page-num>
<header>BOOK TWO.</header>

To notice higher things, one must keep the power <note>The power of the soul or mind.</note> entirely pure and solitary, ready to hear the voices from above. <note>original: "εἰς τὸ ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι δυνάμιν φυλάττειν καθαρὰν καὶ ἔρημον, ἀκούειν φθόγγων τῶν ἄνω."</note>

<column-break/>

To be more fit for noticing higher things, one must preserve the soul entirely pure, and most ready for hearing supernal voices.

---

This trinity of principles, which is most especially Platonic and Zoroastrian, is confirmed by the Trinity of the Christians. For the Father’s fecundity includes the Good itself; the intellectual emanation of the Son includes the Intellect; and the procession of the Spirit through the mode of will and, as it were, vital motion, includes the Soul. Furthermore, the Good itself reflects the firmament through the fecundity of the stars; Saturn, removed and foreign from generation, reflects the Intellect; Jupiter, favoring generation, reflects the Soul; and Mars, discordant and now combative, reflects the world. Again, the Sun represents the Good; Mercury, closest to the Sun in its path, represents the Intellect; Venus, desiring procreation, represents the Soul; and the Moon, now varied and changeable within itself, represents this world. Likewise, Fire represents the Good; clear and serene Air represents the Intellect; Water, supplying moisture for generation, represents the Soul; and Earth, now a mixture of all things, represents the world. Finally, and individually: the fruitful essence of anything is the Good; the firm virtue of essence is the Intellect; and inclination, motion, and action are the Soul. In summary, regarding the soul: fruitful memory is the Good; the discourse of reason is the Intellect; and imagination and affect are the Soul. Nothing, therefore, is more certain than this trinity of principles, because nothing is confirmed by greater or more numerous testimonies; the universe rightly represents the image of its own principles.

## ENNEAD FIVE.
### BOOK II.

->On the generation and order of those things which come after the first.<-
->On the generation and order of those things which come after the first.<-

Just as the unit <note>The number one.</note> is the principle of numbers but is not itself a number, and a point is the principle of a continuum but is not itself continuous, and light is the principle of color and colors but is not itself color or colors: so the Good itself, the principle of beings, is not some being, or the beings themselves: therefore it is neither life nor intellect.

->Chapter I.<-

For it does not produce these things one after another because it contains them all within itself beforehand, as if pregnant—as do the intellect, the soul, and nature—but it creates simply by being supereminent, just as the unit, the point (or center), and light do. Moreover, that which is procreated most closely from the Good itself, insofar as it exists immediately while the Good remains still, is made into Being; insofar as it suddenly inclines naturally and is, as it were, moved toward the Good, it becomes a living thing; and insofar as it is soon strengthened from that source and turns back into itself as if in a circle, it emerges as the <term>Intellect</term><note>Latin: "intellectus"; Greek: "nous." The realm of pure, eternal forms.</note>. Similarly, from the Intellect remaining still, the intellectual soul exists; but from this soul—not remaining still, but distracted from the intellect and the intelligible realm by the power of discourse toward things of imagination and sense—its image flows into act. This image is, namely, a certain life devoid of reason, endowed with sense and vegetative power. Among these, that which follows persists as long as that which is superior stands. Our soul, in the same body and at the same time, acts as a plant in those members where it only provides growth; it acts as a brute in those instruments where it only feels; it acts as a man while reasoning; and it acts as a <term>daemon</term><note>A guiding spirit or divine intermediary.</note> or as God when it understands. Again, the same man at different times, though under a human persona, exercises various behaviors of this kind. In the human species also, some lead a life like plants, others like brutes, others like men, and some like gods or daemons. Therefore, whoever says that our souls—which have already taken on the habit of this or that life—will soon return into a man of the air or the earth to live in a similar way, will hold a more probable opinion than those who would too freely transform the human species into brutes or plants. For such a transformation is both impossible according to nature and superfluous according to justice.

<meta>This page continues the metaphysical exploration of the "Trinity of Principles." Having previously identified the three primary levels of reality—the Good (the One), the Intellect, and the Soul—Plotinus now explains the specific mechanics of "emanation": how the perfect, solitary One can produce the plurality of the universe without losing its own unity.</meta>

PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

<margin>A</margin>In what way, then, from one simple thing—in which no variety appears, nor any duality or form of any kind—does a multitude proceed? Perhaps it is because nothing was in it that all things are from it; and so that Being itself might exist, the One itself is not "Being," but rather Being is its progeny, its first-born. Truly, since the One is perfect—seeking nothing, possessing nothing, and needing nothing—it has, as it were, overflowed <note>original: "exuberauit" / "ὑπερερρύη" - Plotinus uses the metaphor of a fountain that is so full it must spill over.</note>. This very exuberance of the One has produced another thing. That which was made then turned back toward the One and was filled; it became such that it looked into itself, and thus the Intellect <note>The Divine Mind or *Nous*.</note> came forth. Indeed, its state of rest toward that first Being produced "Being" itself, while its gaze toward itself produced the Intellect. Therefore, when it dwells upon itself in order to know, it becomes simultaneously Intellect and Being. In this way, Being, just as the One did, produces similar things according to its great power of outpouring; and this produced form is also its own, just as the Intellect previously came forth from the One.

<margin>C</margin>And here, from the essence of Intellect, the act is the Soul, which is made while the Intellect remains unchanged; for even the superior Intellect was produced while the One remained unchanged. The Soul, however, does not produce while remaining still, but through its motion it produces an image. Looking back toward the source from which it flowed, the Soul is filled; but as it goes forward into a different and opposite motion, it produces its own image, which is sensation in animals and the generative nature in plants. Yet nothing is severed or divided from its superior.

<margin>D</margin>For this reason, the soul of a human also seems to reach all the way down to the plants. Indeed, it proceeds to that point in a certain way, because that which is in plants belongs to the soul; yet the soul is not entirely in the plants. Rather, it is present in them because it has progressed to that lower level, creating another substance by its procession and its "care for the inferior" <note>original: "curaq; deterioris" / "τῷ ἐπιθυμεῖν τε χείρονος" - implying the soul's desire to organize and animate even the lowest forms of life.</note>. Because that which is above the Soul is dependent on the Intellect, it allows the Intellect to remain at rest within itself.

---

*The individual intellects of men are in command: from these flow the powers of the soul in descending grades, among which the subsequent is always preserved in the antecedent, much like splendor in a ray, a ray in light, and light in the nature of the Sun. Chapter II.*

*And yet the Intellect, from which all powers of the soul flow in order, in one way is, and in another way is not, all things. Finally, all the souls and their powers, since they are neither extended nor circumscribed by certain limits of place, are easily everywhere.*

<margin>A</margin>## THE PROCESSION
therefore happens from the beginning to the end, and meanwhile each thing is always permitted to retain its own seat; but that which is produced is assigned another rank, and a lower one at that. Nevertheless, each thing eventually becomes the same as that which it follows, so long as it continues to follow it. Therefore, when the soul is inserted into a plant, there is a certain part in the plant that is, as it were, the most rash and senseless part, having wandered that far down. <margin>B</margin>But when it is inserted into a beast, then the power of sensation has dominated and led it; but when it enters a human, then either the motion in the rational nature prevails entirely, or there is a certain procession from the Intellect—seeing as the soul has its own mind and a will from itself for understanding, or for moving entirely. Now, in turn,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>How then from a simple One, in which no variety appears in the same, nor any duality of any kind? Is it because nothing was in it, that for this reason all things are from it, and so that Being might exist? For this reason it is not Being, but the father of Being. And this is, as it were, the first birth: for being perfect by seeking nothing, having nothing, and needing nothing, it has, as it were, overflowed, and its super-fullness has made another. That which was born turned back to it and was filled, and it came to be looking toward it; and this is the Intellect. And its state of rest toward that one produced Being, but its gaze toward it produced Intellect. Since, therefore, it stood toward it so that it might see, it became at once Intellect and Being. Being thus, just as that one, it produces similar things, having poured forth much power. And this is also a form of it, just as the One before it poured itself forth. And this activity from the essence is the Soul, this having come to be while the former remained. For even the Intellect came to be while that which was before it remained. But the Soul does not produce while remaining, but having been moved, it generated an image. There, looking toward that from which it came to be, it is filled; but going forth into another and opposite motion, it generates an image of itself: sensation and nature which is in plants. But nothing is detached from that which is before it, nor cut off. Therefore the human soul also seems to reach as far as plants. For in a certain way it reaches them, because that which is in plants belongs to it. The whole soul is not in them, but it is in the plants by coming to be in them, because it has gone over so far into the lower, making another subsistence by its procession and by its desire for the inferior; since that which is before this, being dependent, permits the Intellect to remain in itself.

<margin>A</margin>## IT PROCEEDS
therefore from the beginning to the last, each always being left in its own seat. But the thing being generated takes another rank, the lower one. Each thing, however, becomes the same as that which it follows, so long as it follows it. When, therefore, a soul comes to be in a plant, the part in the plant is another part, the most daring and most foolish, having proceeded as far as that. But when it is in an irrational animal, the power of sensing having prevailed, it led it. But when it is in a human, either the motion is entirely in the rational, or it is by the Intellect, as the soul has its own intellect and from itself a will of thinking or moving entirely. ### BOOK TWO.

<margin>A</margin> If one cuts off the offshoots or certain upper branches of a plant, where does the soul that was within them depart, or from where does it come? For it is not separated from its source by physical space; therefore, it remains one with its original principle. If you cut or burn the root itself, where is that vital force which once flourished in the root? It does not depart to another physical location, but remains within the soul. It does not go to a different place, but stays in the same realm. We say it exists in another if it "runs back" <note>original: "recurrerit" / "ἀναδράμοι" - Plotinus uses this term to describe the soul's ascent or return to its higher source.</note> to its origin; if it does not, it remains in another vegetative <term>vegetalis: the lowest level of the soul responsible for growth and nutrition</term> power, for the soul is not squeezed into a narrow space.

<column-break/>

<margin>B</margin> If it runs back, it will reside in a higher power. But where is that higher power? It is in the one above that again, and so on, all the way up to the Mind <note>original: "mentem" / "νοῦς" - The Divine Intellect, the second of the Three Primary Hypostases.</note>. This is not a matter of physical location, for none of these higher principles were ever in a "place." The Intellect, above all, is not to be situated in any physical spot; therefore, neither is the nature of the soul itself. It is nowhere in terms of physical space. Yet, precisely because it is "nowhere," it is in this way "everywhere."

<margin>C</margin> If the soul, having progressed toward the sublime, comes to a halt before it fully reaches the supreme height, it leads a "middle life" and rests in that part of itself. All these things are both "that" [the source] and "not that." They are "that" because they proceed from it; they are "not that" because the source remains within itself while giving these things existence.

<margin>D</margin> In the universe, therefore, there is something like a single, immense life stretched out into a great length, where each subsequent part is distinct, yet the whole is continuous with itself. Each part differs from the others by its own specific quality, and the preceding part is not destroyed in that which follows it.

->What then of the soul inserted into plants? Does it produce nothing lower? Perhaps it produces only within that in which it exists. But truly, we must consider by what condition this happens, taking our beginning from another point.<-

-> CONCERNING the knowing substances, and that which is beyond. <note>original Greek: "ΠΕΡΙ τῶν γνωστικῶν ὑποστάσεων, καὶ τοῦ ἐπέκεινα." / Latin: "De substantiis cognoscentibus, & de illo quod superius est." This refers to the levels of reality that possess knowledge and the "One" which is beyond them.</note> <-

---

*That which has known itself is not necessarily forced to be so simple that there is no difference at all within it—which would be the "One" itself. Rather, it must be so simple that the whole is contained within any part of it, and its action is completed in a single moment. Such is the nature of the Intellect.* <margin>Chapter I.</margin>

---

*When we say that the Intellect knows itself, we do not divide it into two parts, where one only knows and the other is only known; otherwise, it would not be a single thing knowing itself, but rather one thing knowing another. Instead, we mean that the knowing subject encompasses itself along with the object known. It belongs to the senses only to know things outside the soul; to the imagination, however, to know things within the soul (that is, the actions of the senses); to reason, furthermore, to investigate itself; and finally, to the Intellect to know itself. Through a perfect participation in this, even reason sometimes comes to know itself.*

---

<margin>A</margin><image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'O' with a landscape scene featuring figures and trees.</image-desc>IT IS WORTHWHILE to investigate whether that which understands itself must be complex within itself, so that by contemplating the other things within it with one of its parts, it is judged to understand itself in that way—as if, were it entirely simple, it could not turn back upon itself and know itself. Or is it possible that even what is not composite might understand <margin>B</margin> itself? To begin with, if it is said that something can know itself because it is composite, and thus knows the rest through one of its parts (as if we were to recognize our own form and the rest of our bodily nature through the sense of sight), it does not follow at all that it truly knows itself. For in such a case, the whole will not be the thing known, unless that which understands also understands <margin>C</margin> itself along with the other things joined to it. Otherwise, the goal we seek will not be achieved—namely, that the same thing perceives itself—but rather that one part perceives another. Therefore, we must assert that even the simple itself perceives itself; and we must investigate how this happens, if indeed it is possible. Otherwise, we must abandon the opinion that anything can truly know itself. Yet to cast away such an opinion is not at all easy, since many <margin>D</margin> absurdities would seem to follow. For if we do not grant this power to the soul, it might not seem entirely absurd; but to deny it to the nature of the Mind <term>mentis / νοῦ: the Divine Intellect, the second of the Three Primary Hypostases</term> is surely the most absurd of all—if, I say, it has knowledge of other things but lacks knowledge and science of its very self. And
<meta>catchword: exce</meta>

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'A' with intricate scrollwork and floral motifs.</image-desc>IS IT THEN necessary for the Intellect to be complex in order to know itself? Should it use one of its parts to view the others, so that it can be said to "know itself"? Could a being that is entirely simple not turn back toward itself and achieve self-contemplation? Or is it possible for something that is not composite to have knowledge of itself? If we maintain the idea that it knows itself by using one part to perceive the rest—much like we use our senses to perceive our own physical form and the nature of our bodies—this would not be true self-knowledge. In such a system, the whole is not actually known, for the part that does the knowing remains unknown. If the subject knows only the other parts and not itself, we haven't found a thing that "knows itself," but rather one thing that knows another. We must, therefore, assume that even a simple being can have self-perception, and we must examine how this is possible. If we cannot explain it, we might have to give up the idea that anything can truly know itself. However, abandoning this idea is difficult, as it leads to many absurdities. While it might not seem too strange to deny this power to the Soul, it is completely absurd to deny it to the nature of the Intellect. It would be paradoxical if the Intellect had knowledge of everything else but remained without knowledge and science of itself. And...

He suggests that true self-knowledge requires a form of "simplicity" where the subject and object of thought are identical.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into how the soul and the intellect achieve self-knowledge. # BOOK THREE.
### 497

<margin>A</margin> ...the perception of external things belongs to the senses, but the intellect will grasp things within the mind <note>original Greek: "ἐν νῷ" (en nō)</note>. And if you wish, this includes thought and opinion. Whether the intellect had knowledge of these things or not, it is necessary to investigate. Certainly, the intellect will know whatever things are intelligible. Will it, therefore, know only those things, or also itself, which knows these things? And will it always know itself, namely because it knows it knows these things? But who it is that knows, it will not grasp; rather, perhaps it will grasp that it knows its own contents. <margin>B</margin> But who it is while it perceives, it will not perceive. Or will it rather know both its own contents and itself? Likewise, we must consider in what manner and to what extent this occurs.

---

*The rational power, which is always engaged in discursive reasoning <note>Discursive reasoning (discurrendo) refers to the step-by-step movement of the mind from one thought to another, unlike the immediate "intuition" of the higher Intellect.</note>, is the intermediary between the imagination and the intellect. It admits certain forms into itself from both sides; it composes and divides them, and it adapts the forms newly arriving from the imagination to the ancient forms existing in the mind, or from the mind; and in this adaptation, it is rendered "intellectual." Chapter II.*

*Hence, two intellects appear in us: namely, the permanent one and the discursive one, which follows through the process of reasoning.*

<margin>A</margin> FIRST, therefore, we must inquire concerning the soul: whether knowledge of itself should be attributed to it, and what it is within it that knows, and in what way. We judge the sensory power <note>original Latin: "sensualem virtutem"</note> of the soul, by its very condition, to be concerned only with external things. For even if those things that happen within the body are perceived, such perception belongs to those things that are outside the sense-power; for it then feels the passions that occur within the body beneath it. There is, moreover, in the soul a power of reasoning <note>original Greek: "τὸ δὲ δι’ ὧν αὐτὴ λογιζόμενον" / Latin: "virtus ratiocinandi"</note> which judges the mental images <margin>B</margin> arising from the senses, joining them together and also dividing them. It even gazes upon the "figures" <note>original Greek: "τύπους" (typous) — often translated as "impressions" or "imprints" left on the mind.</note> of those things that descend from the higher intellect, and it possesses the exact same power concerning them. It also takes on understanding, as it weighs and adapts new and recently arriving figures to the ancient ones; in which matter we believe the "reminiscence" of the soul to consist. And indeed, the intellect of the soul stands here by its own power. We must ask, therefore, whether this power of reasoning <margin>C</margin> turns toward itself and knows itself, or whether this should instead be referred to the higher intellect. For if we attribute knowledge of itself to this part of the soul, we shall confess this very part to be the "mind"; and we shall be compelled to seek how it differs most especially from the superior mind. But if we do not attribute it, then reason will lead us to that higher mind, and we will consider what it means to know oneself. But if we attribute that task to this lower power as well, we shall again investigate how the superior and inferior intellects differ <margin>D</margin> in knowing themselves. Truly, if they do not differ at all, then this intellect of ours is "pure" <note>original Latin: "purus" — meaning identical to the highest intellectual principle.</note>. But as for the soul's very power of discursive reasoning, does it also turn into itself? Or rather, does it not turn, but instead possesses knowledge of the forms which it obtains from both sides? And indeed, we must first ask in what way it obtains knowledge of this kind.

---

*Reason, upon the report of the senses and imagination, judges that Socrates is approaching: if it adds that he is "good, just, and wise," it weighs these things and defines them by the rules of goodness, justice, and wisdom—which first shine in the mind, and from there reflect a faint light <note>original Latin: "subrutilant" — literally "to glow somewhat redly" or to shimmer from beneath.</note> upon the reason as it concerns itself with such matters. Chapter III.*

*Since it is the property of reason to act in motion, and motion tends toward "the other," reason quite naturally occupies itself with other things rather than with itself; therefore, it is not its property to know itself. Many place three essences in the heavens, namely...*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the perception of external things belongs to the senses, the perception of internal things the intellect will have; and moreover, if you wish, thought and opinion. Whether the intellect had knowledge of these things or not, it is useful to investigate. Certainly, the intellect itself will know whatever things are intelligible. Does it then know those only, or also itself, who knows these very things? And will it know itself only in this way—namely, because it knows that it knows these things? But who it is that meanwhile knows these things, it will not grasp; <margin>B</margin> but perhaps it will comprehend that it knows its own contents. But who it is while it perceives, will it not perceive? Or will it rather know both its own and itself? Likewise, we must consider in what manner and to what extent this occurs.

---

*The rational power, which is always engaged in discursive reasoning, is the intermediary between the imagination and the intellect. It admits certain forms into itself from both sides; it composes and divides them, and it adapts the forms newly arriving from the imagination to the ancient forms existing in the mind, or from the mind; and in this adaptation, it is rendered "intellectual." Chapter II.*

*Hence, two intellects appear in us: namely, the permanent one and the discursive one, which follows through the process of reasoning.*

FIRST, therefore, we must inquire concerning the soul: whether knowledge of itself should be attributed to it, what it is within it that knows, and by what logic. We judge the sensory power, by its very condition, to be concerned only with external things. For even if those things that happen within the body are perceived, such perception belongs to those things that are outside the sense-power; for it then feels the passions that occur within the body beneath it. There is, moreover, in the soul a power of reasoning concerning the imaginations <margin>B</margin> falling from the sense, judging them, joining them together, and also dividing them. It even gazes upon, as it were, the figures of those things that descend from the intellect, and it possesses the exact same power concerning them. It also takes on understanding, inasmuch as it weighs and adapts new and recently arriving figures to the ancient ones; in which matter we believe the "reminiscence" of the soul to consist. And indeed, the intellect of the soul stands here by its own power. We must ask, therefore, whether this power of reasoning <margin>C</margin> turns toward itself and knows itself, or whether this should instead be referred to the intellect. For if we attribute knowledge of itself to this part of the soul, we shall confess this very part to be the "mind"; and we shall be compelled to seek how it differs most especially from the superior mind. But if we do not attribute it, then reason will lead us to that mind, and we will consider what it means to know oneself. But if we attribute that task to this lower power as well, we shall again investigate how the superior and inferior <margin>D</margin> intellects differ in knowing themselves. Truly, if they do not differ at all, then this intellect of ours is "pure." But as for the soul's very power of discursive reasoning, does it also turn into itself? Or rather, does it not turn, but instead possesses knowledge of the forms which it obtains from both sides? And indeed, we must first ask in what way it obtains knowledge of this kind.

---

*Reason, upon the report of the senses and imagination, judges that Socrates is approaching: if it adds that he is "good, just, and wise," it weighs these things and defines them by the rules of goodness, justice, and wisdom—which first shine in the mind, and from there reflect a faint light upon the reason as it concerns itself with such matters. Chapter III.*

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

*...in the body, matter and form, and beyond this the soul of the heaven itself, and matter always being subject to its own form—this is a part of the soul. Similarly, there are three essences regarding our soul: namely the soul itself, which some call the irrational substance, and the rational substance, which is perpetually clinging to the mind, like a heaven perpetually joined to the celestial soul. Plotinus here seems to touch upon this union. And yet, such a union seems to have been devised by Theophrastus, Themistius, and Averroes <note>These are historical commentators on Aristotle: Theophrastus was Aristotle’s successor; Themistius was a 4th-century politician and philosopher; Averroes was a 12th-century Islamic philosopher famous for his "Unity of the Intellect" theory.</note>. We can also interpret Plotinus in a more Platonic manner, saying that he denies the intellect is a part of the soul because it is not a part—that is, a power of this substance which is called 'soul.' For it is called 'soul' insofar as it pertains to discourse <note>original Latin: "discursum." This refers to "discursive reasoning," or thinking things through step-by-step, rather than knowing them all at once.</note>, whether it discourses through universals or particulars. But the intellect is the substance itself, to which the power called 'soul' is joined. Now, even the substance itself is named 'soul' according to its discursive power, and it is named 'intellect' according to its rational substance itself. For understanding is the same thing as the substance, yet it is not the same as discursive reasoning; therefore, it always understands equally, but it does not always reason equally.*

---

<margin>A</margin>
SENSE perception indeed saw a man and handed over his image to the power of thought. But what does this power say? Perhaps it does not yet say anything, but only knows him and so rests—unless perhaps it runs through the question within itself: "Who is this?" If it has encountered him before, it might say of him now, using memory, that it is Socrates. If it further unfolds and explains the form, it is now dividing what the imagination handed over.

<margin>B</margin>
But if it says further whether he is "good," it speaks such a thing based on what it knew through the senses. But that which it says *concerning* these things, it already has from itself; for it possesses the rule of the good within itself. But in what way does it have the "good" within itself? Insofar as it is (if I may say so) "good-formed" <note>original Latin: "boniformis." This means the soul is naturally shaped or patterned after the Good.</note>, and it has already been strengthened toward perceiving such a thing, with the mind/intellect shining upon it from above. For this constitutes the pure part of the soul, and it receives the tracks <note>original Latin: "vestigia" / original Greek: "ἴχνη" (ichnē). Often translated as "traces" or "footprints" of the divine in the human mind.</note> imprinted by the mind.

<margin>C</margin>
But why is this itself not the "intellect"? Why is it "soul" that remains after starting from the power of sense? Because the soul must be engaged in a certain discourse of reason. All these things are the duties of a discursive power. But why do we not, by attributing the task of self-knowledge to this part, bring an end to the inquiry? Because we have granted it the task of considering external things, while it is further distracted by many worries; but we judge it the property of the mind/intellect to contemplate itself and the things intimate to itself.

<margin>D</margin>
If anyone should say: "What prevents that worried part from sometimes noticing its own affairs through some other power of the soul?"—he certainly does not require the power of thinking and reasoning itself, but he is now accepting a pure intellect. What, therefore, prevents there being a pure intellect in the soul? We shall say that nothing prevents it. Furthermore, shall we claim that a pure intellect is "something of the soul"? Surely we will not say it belongs *to* the soul, but we will confess it to be *our* intellect. It is something else beyond the nature of thinking itself, placed above it, yet still ours, even if we 

<margin>E</margin>
do not count it among the parts of the soul. Perhaps we will affirm it is "ours," and then again "not ours." For this reason, we use it, and again we do not use it—but we are always using thought. Therefore, it is "ours" while we use it, but "not ours" when we do not use it. But what is it to "use the intellect"? Is it perhaps that we, having become that intellect, now speak as it does, or at least speak according to it?

<margin>F</margin>
For we are not the Intellect itself. Rather, we are "according to it," namely when the primary power of discourse receives it. For we also perceive through the senses, and we ourselves are the ones perceiving. Is it therefore...

<column-break/>

For sense saw a man, and gave the type to the thought. And she, what did she say? Or she will say nothing yet, but only knew and stood still. Unless perhaps she should reason with herself who this is, if she has met him before, and says, using memory, "Socrates." But if she should also unfold the form, she divides what the imagination gave. And if she should say if he is good, she has spoken from what she knew through sense. But what she said upon those things she would already have from herself, having the rule <note>original Greek: "κανόνα" (kanona)</note> of the good by her side. How does she have the good by her side? Either she is "good-formed," and was strengthened for the perception of such a thing. Because the Intellect shines upon her. For this is the pure part of the soul. And she receives the imprinted traces. Why then is this not Intellect, but what remains is soul, starting from the sensory? Because it is characteristic of the soul to be in reasonings. And all these things are works of the reasoning power. But why do we not attribute the study of ourselves to this part, and be done with it? Or because we assigned it to look at things outside and to be meddlesome. But of Intellect we deem it to belong, to look at its own things and the things in itself. But if one should say, what hinders this from looking at its own things by another power, as in the thinking power, he does not seek the reasoning power, but takes pure Intellect. What then hinders pure Intellect from being in the soul? We shall say nothing. But is it then to be called "of the soul"? But we shall not say "of the soul." We shall say it is "our Intellect." Being another thing from the thinking power, and having stepped upon it. Nevertheless it is ours, even if we do not count it among the parts of the soul. Or it is ours, and not ours. Wherefore we also use it, and do not use it. But we always use thought; and it is ours when we use it, but when we do not use it, it is not ours. What then is "I use it"? Is it that I myself become that thing and speak as that thing, or according to that thing? For we are not [Intellect]. According to that thing then, with the reasoning power receiving it first. ...in which we think in this way, and we reason in this way—not that the power of reasoning is itself making a calculation, but that we perceive the thoughts within our reasoning power. For as "we" are the ones thinking, we possess the activities of the mind as things truly coming from above, just as we possess the things of the senses from below. For we exist as the sovereign part of the soul, a middle ground between a double power: the lower and the better. The lower power is sensation, while the better is the intellect. Now, sensation seems to be granted as always being ours, for we are always sensing; but the status of the intellect is disputed. This is either because we do not always use it, or because it is "separate." It is separate in the sense that it does not lean down toward us, but rather we lean toward it, looking upward. Sensation is our messenger, but the intellect is our king.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Perhaps we ourselves are the ones who range through things by reason, and do we ourselves also understand the notions of intelligence gleaming within our very thought? For this is what we ourselves are. The actions of the mind are above us in this way, just as the private things of the senses are below us. And we are this very thing proper to the soul—and as far as pertains to it, the principal part—a medium between two powers: namely, the lower and the better, that is, between sensation and intellect. We seem to grant that sensation is always
<margin>B</margin> ours, for we are always sensing; but regarding the intellect, the matter is ambiguous: both because we do not always use it, and because it is separate. It is separate, I say, because it does not bow down to us, but rather we look upward toward it. Sensation, finally, is our messenger; but that [the intellect] is our king.

*The rational power by which we exist uses the intellect in two ways: namely, through participation and through form; and in both ways, it knows itself.*
-> Chapter IV. <-

*Through participation, insofar as it receives forms, notions, and rules daily from the intellect, where, as if from an effect through its own actions, it knows both its own powers and its essence; through these powers, it recognizes its essence and that it always depends upon and is illuminated by the mind. Through form, however, when after frequent use of such reception it thoroughly puts on the mind as matter puts on form, it acts under the very activity of the mind—just as matter, after it has frequently received heat from a fire, finally undergoes the flame. Then at last, the reason perfectly knows itself together with the mind as if from a cause. The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note> named the reason the "possible intellect" and the mind the "active intellect."*

Thus, that which knows itself now exists as double.

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

<margin>A</margin> ...and we in turn of that <note>the intellect</note>, shall we then finally perceive the intellect and ourselves? Perhaps it is rather necessary in this way: if we are to perceive what is most powerful in the intellect, namely, that it knows itself. For then a person becomes that very intellect when, letting go of their other parts, they look upon this very thing with this very thing—and with it, they also see themselves, just as the intellect itself contemplates itself.

---

### *In that which is higher than the rational power—that is, the moving intelligence—the intellect, the one who understands, and the object of understanding are the same in reality; therefore it always understands itself.*

->Chapter V.<-

---

Above the sense which only looks outward, there is the internal imagination looking inward; above this, which observes things coming from the outside, <term>reason</term> <note>Latin: ratio; Greek: λόγος</note> stands forth, which moreover manages internal matters; above this again, which finally returns to itself to be recognized from other known things, is the <term>intellect</term> <note>Latin: intellectus; Greek: νοῦς</note> beginning in turn from itself. While it looks at itself, it beholds all things—I do not mean the mere figures of things, but the things themselves—so that it may be the truest knowledge. If by touching itself it touches all things, then it surely is all things; and by the very same act by which it looks at itself, it also beholds all things, and at the same time and in the same way, it recognizes that it knows both itself and all things. But more properly, the first and divine intellect neither turns to understand anything other than itself, nor does it possess an accidental intelligence; rather, its essence is absolutely living and understanding. By this very essential and vital intelligence, it enjoys itself, meanwhile comprehending itself as existing, living, understanding, entirely uniform, and yet containing all forms.

<margin>A</margin> DOES the intellect, then, look at one part of itself with another part? But in that case, one part will be the one seeing, and the other will be the one seen. This, however, is not a single thing knowing "itself." What then? If the whole is such that it is composed of similar parts, so that the seer does not differ from the seen, then the seer, seeing that part of itself as being the same as itself, meanwhile also sees itself. For there, the seer does not differ at all from the seen. But first, indeed,
<margin>B</margin> it would be absurd to divide the intellect in this way: for how would the division be made? For it is not to be divided by some chance or at random. Then indeed, who is it that divides? Perhaps the one who puts himself in the order of seeing, or rather the one who is in the order of being seen? Furthermore, how will that seer know himself while, according to the act of seeing itself, he places himself in the rank of that which is seen? For the act of seeing does not exist within the object seen. Or will the
<margin>C</margin> one knowing consider himself as the seen rather than as the seer? Therefore, he will notice neither the whole nor all of himself. For he knows what is seen here, but he does not know the seer, and thus he will behold not himself, but another. But will he perhaps add the seer as well to himself, so that he may perfectly comprehend himself? But if he embraces the seer, he simultaneously embraces the things seen. If, therefore, in the very act of looking, the things looked upon are contained,
<margin>D</margin> the question is whether the figures of things are contained, or the things themselves. If only the figures, the things themselves are not possessed; but if the things themselves are possessed, certainly the one who looks at them does not have them from having divided himself, but he was—even before he divided himself—both the contemplator and the possessor. If the matter stands thus, the contemplation must be the same as the thing contemplated (if I may put it that way), and the intellect must similarly be the same as the <term>intelligible</term> <note>the object of thought; Latin: intelligibile; Greek: νοητόν</note>. Otherwise, if it were not the same, there would be no true contemplation. For he who is said to possess beings will instead have a figure of them, undoubtedly differing from the beings themselves,
<margin>E</margin> which is certainly not the truth. For the truth <note>Latin: veritas; Greek: ἀλήθεια</note> ought not to be of something else, but what it says, this it must also be. Thus, therefore, the intellect, the intelligible, and being are one; and this is the first being, and the first intellect possessing all beings—or rather, he is the same...

<column-break/>

...and we of them, in this way we are known to the intellect and to itself, or it is necessary in this way, if we are to know what that "self in itself" ever is. It is indeed the one who, having known himself, has become [intellect], when, letting go of other things, he sees the [intellect] in that place, and then he sees; and with himself he sees himself, just as the intellect sees itself.

---

<margin>A</margin> Does it then look at one part of itself with another part? But in this way, one part will be seeing and the other seen. But this is surely not "itself by itself." If the whole is such that it is composed of similar parts, so that the seer differs in no way from the seen, then having seen that part which is himself, he would see the same thing in himself. For the seer differs in no way from the seen. Or first,
<margin>B</margin> the division is absurd for it. For how can there even be parts? For if it were by chance... And who is the one dividing? The one who has ranked himself in the act of contemplating, or the one in the act of being contemplated? Then how will the contemplator know himself, having ranked himself in the thing contemplated according to the act of contemplating? For the act of contemplating is not in the thing contemplated. Or having known himself as the thing contemplated, but not as the
<margin>C</margin> contemplator, he will think. So he will not know all of himself, nor himself as a whole. For what he saw, he saw as contemplated, but not as contemplating; and thus he will have seen another, and not himself. Or will he add to himself also the one who has contemplated, so that he has perfectly thought himself? But if also the one who has contemplated, he also at the same time has the things seen; if the things contemplated exist in the contemplation, if they are mere images of them, he does not have the things themselves. But if he should have the things themselves, he does not have them by seeing them through
<margin>D</margin> dividing himself. But he [has them] going before he divided himself, both contemplating and having. If indeed in this way, through contemplation, he is the same as the thing contemplated, then the intellect is the same as the intelligible. For indeed, if it were not the same, there will be no truth. For the one having beings will have an image, something different from the beings, which is not truth. Therefore, the truth must not be of another, but what it says, this it also must be. Thus, then, the intellect, and the intelligible, and
<margin>E</margin> being are one. And this is the first being. and indeed the first intellect, having beings; or rather the same...

# BOOK THREE.

...the ideas. But if the act of understanding and the object of understanding are one, in what way, because of this, will the thinker understand itself? For the act of understanding will either encompass the object of understanding, or it will be identical to it; yet it is not yet clear how the intellect plainly knows itself. Furthermore, if the act of understanding and the object of understanding are the same—for the object of understanding is a kind of <term>act</term> <note>Latin: actus; Greek: ἐνέργεια (energeia). In this context, it refers to reality in its fully realized, active state rather than just a potential.</note>: since the object of understanding is not merely a potentiality, nor is it devoid of life, nor is "living" there something added from the outside, nor is the act of understanding in a different subject like a stone or some lifeless thing—then the object of understanding is the primary essence. If, therefore, I say that there is an "act" there, and it is the first act, then surely that act of understanding is the best, and it is (so to speak) an essential understanding. For the truest understanding is of this kind: it is first, existing in the highest degree, and therefore the primary <term>Intellect</term> <note>Latin: intellectus; Greek: νοῦς (nous). This represents the divine, cosmic Mind.</note> will be these things. For this Intellect is neither in a state of potentiality, nor is it one thing while its understanding is another; otherwise, its very essence would again be in a state of potentiality. Therefore, if it is an act and its essence is that act, it will be considered one and the same as its act. Since "being" itself and the "object of understanding" are one act, all things will be one together: the Intellect, the act of understanding, and the object being understood. If, then, its act of understanding is the object of understanding itself, and it is itself that very object, then it surely understands itself. For it will understand through that very act of understanding, which is what it itself is; and it will understand the object of understanding, which is also what it itself is. From both sides, therefore, it will understand itself entirely: both insofar as it is the act of understanding, and insofar as it is the object of understanding, which it understands through this very act of understanding that is itself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the beings of the ideas. But if the act of understanding and the object of understanding are one, in what way will the thinker understand itself? For the act of understanding will either encompass the object of understanding, or it will be identical with it; it will not yet be clear that the intellect knows itself clearly. However, if the act of understanding and the object of understanding are the same—for the object of understanding is a certain act: since the object of understanding is not just a potentiality, nor is it without life, nor is living there something <margin>B</margin> added, nor is understanding in a different subject like a stone or something lacking life, and the object of understanding is the primary essence. If, then, I say that there is an act there, and it is the first act, surely that act of understanding is the best, and it is (so to speak) an essential understanding. Indeed, the truest understanding is of this kind: it is first, and existing in a primary way; therefore, the first intellect will be these things. For this intellect is not in potentiality, nor is it one thing itself while the understanding is another; otherwise, <margin>C</margin> its essential nature would again be in a potential state. For this reason, if it is an act and its essence is an act, it will be judged to be one and the same as the act. Since "being" and "the object of understanding" are one act, all things will be one at once: the intellect, the understanding, and the object of understanding. If, therefore, its understanding is the object of understanding itself, and it itself is the object of understanding, surely it will understand itself. For it will understand through the understanding itself, which it is, and it will understand the object of understanding, <margin>D</margin> which it also is. From both sides, then, it will understand itself completely: both insofar as it is the understanding, and insofar as it is the object of understanding, which it understands through this understanding that is itself.

---

<margin>Chapter VI.</margin>
*Since the Intellect itself remains within itself, and is not inclined toward other things by either action or emotion, it rightly acts upon itself by understanding itself. The Soul, however, being affected in the opposite way, behaves differently regarding knowledge.*

---

*In the entire order of knowledge, the senses hold the lowest step, but the Intellect holds the highest. Therefore, while the senses hold a straight line in knowing, only by touching other things, the Intellect rightly acts in a completely circular way, by contemplating itself deeply within its own being: reason, however, is mostly oblique. The forms of things that are in the mind are entirely essential. Those that are impressed upon the reason from eternity are "as if" essential; those which daily reflect from the mind into the reason are even less essential; finally, those that overflow into the reason from the imagination are not essential at all. The Soul, therefore, only truly knows itself when it fits the lower forms to the higher forms.*

---

<margin>A</margin> REASON, therefore, has demonstrated that there must be something that understands itself properly and principally; however, it understands itself differently when it is in the soul than when it is more fundamentally in the mind. The Soul indeed knows itself as being "of another"; but the Mind knows that it is itself, and what kind of thing it is, and who it is, and this indeed by its own nature, namely, by being turned toward itself. For in seeing the "beings" <note>The eternal Forms or Ideas</note>, it sees itself; and in seeing, it is in act, and it itself is the act. For the Intellect and the act of understanding are the same, and it beholds the whole of itself with its whole self; it does not <margin>B</margin> discern one part with another part. Has reason then demonstrated such a thing as would have a credible action? Truly, it has a necessity, but it does not have a "credibility" derived from persuasion. For necessity dwells in the Mind, but persuasion is found in the Soul. We seek, as it seems, to bring back persuasion rather than to perceive the truth with a pure Mind. And yet, as long as we remained in the higher regions and were content in that state, we then understood,

Perhaps in this way it is rather necessary: if indeed we are to perceive what is most powerful in the intellect, namely, to know itself. ### In that which is superior to the rational power—that is, the "mobile" or changing intelligence—the intellect, the thinker, and the object of thought are in reality the same; therefore it always understands itself. Chapter V.

Above the sense which only looks at things, there is the internal imagination looking inward; above this, which advances toward external things, stands reason, which further arranges internal matters; above this again, which returns from other known things to finally recognize itself, is the <term>intellect</term> <note>Latin: "intellectus"; Greek: "nous". The highest level of divine mind.</note> which in turn begins from itself. While it inspects itself, it gazes upon all things—not, I say, the outward appearance of things, but the things themselves, so that there may be the truest knowledge. If, by touching itself, it reaches all things, then it surely is all things: by the very same act with which it gazes upon itself, it also gazes upon all things; by the same act, it also recognizes at once that it knows itself and all things. But truly the first and divine intellect neither turns to understand anything other than itself, nor does it have an accidental intelligence. Rather, its essence is absolutely living and thinking; by this very essential and vital intelligence, it enjoys itself, meanwhile comprehending itself as existing, living, thinking, entirely uniform, and yet containing all forms.

<margin>A</margin> Does the intellect then behold one part of itself with another part? But in this way, one part will be the one seeing, and the other will be the one seen. However, this is not a single thing knowing itself. What then? If the whole were such that it was composed of identical parts, so that the seer did not differ from the seen: then the seer, seeing that part of itself which is the same as itself, would meanwhile also see itself. For the seer there differs in nothing from the seen. But first, it would be absurd to divide the intellect in this way: for 
<margin>B</margin> how shall the division be made? For it is not to be divided by some chance or at random. Then, truly, who is the one who divides? Is it perhaps the one who places himself in the order of seeing, or rather the one in the order of being seen? Furthermore, how will that seer know himself, while according to the act of seeing itself, he constitutes himself in the rank of that which is seen? For the act of seeing does not exist within the object seen. Or will the one knowing himself consider himself rather as the seen than 
<margin>C</margin> as the seer? Therefore, he will notice neither the whole nor all of himself. For he knows the one who is seen here, but he does not know the seer, and thus he will behold not himself, but another instead. But will he perhaps join to himself the seer as well, so that he may perfectly comprehend himself? But if he embraces the seer, he simultaneously embraces the things seen. If, therefore, in the very act of perception the perceived things are contained, the question arises whether the figures of things, or the things themselves, are contained. If only figures, the things themselves are not 
<margin>D</margin> possessed; but if these things are possessed, certainly the one who perceives them does not have them because he divided himself: but he was, even before he divided himself, both the contemplator and the possessor. If the matter stands thus, it is necessary that contemplation be the same as the thing contemplated (so to speak), and similarly the intellect be the same as the <term>intelligible</term> <note>Latin: "intelligibili"; Greek: "noēton". The pure object of thought.</note>; otherwise, if it were not the same, there will be no true contemplation. For he who is said to possess beings will have a figure of them, undoubtedly differing from them, 
<margin>E</margin> which indeed is not the truth. For the truth ought not to be of another thing, but what it says, this it must also be. Thus, therefore, the intellect, the object of thought, and being are one; and this is the first thing, and the first intellect possessing beings: or rather, it is itself those beings.

and we of that, thus we shall know the mind and ourselves, or it is necessary thus, if we are to know what that which is in the mind is to itself. It is indeed the mind itself having become so, when leaving other things aside, it looks at this by this; and by itself it looks at itself, just as the mind sees itself.

<margin>A</margin> Does it then look at one part of itself with another part of itself? But in this way, one will be the seer and the other the seen. That, again, would not be knowing itself, unless it were all such a thing as to be composed of like parts, so that the seer differs in nothing from the seen. So that seeing that part, being itself, it would see itself as the same. For the seeing differs in nothing from the seen. Or first, the division 
<margin>B</margin> is absurd for it. For how indeed will you divide it? Not by chance. And who is the one who divides? The one who has ranked himself in contemplating, or the one in being contemplated? Then how will the contemplator know himself, having ranked himself in the contemplated according to the act of contemplating? For the act of contemplating is not in the contemplated. The knowledge of himself is not in the contemplated, but he will think not as the contemplator. So he will not know all, nor the whole of himself. For what he saw was the contemplated, but 
<margin>C</margin> he did not know the contemplator, and thus he will have seen another and not himself. Or will he add to it also the one who has contemplated, so that he has thought himself perfectly? But if also the one who has contemplated, then at the same time also the things seen. If the things contemplated exist in the contemplation, if they are impressions of them, it does not have the things themselves. But if it should have the things themselves, it does not have them by having divided itself. But it was, before dividing itself, both contemplating and having. If indeed 
<margin>D</margin> it is necessary for the contemplation to be the same as the contemplated, then the mind must be the same as the object of thought. For if it is not the same, there will be no truth. For the one who has beings will have an impression, different from the beings, which is not truth. Therefore, the truth must not be of another, but what it says, this it also is. Therefore, where there is mind, there is also the object of thought and 
<margin>E</margin> being. And this is the first being. And indeed, the first mind, having the beings; or rather, it is the same

<margin>A</margin> ...the beings of the ideas. But if the act of understanding <note>Greek: "noesis"; Latin: "intelligentia"</note> and the object of understanding <note>Greek: "noeton"; Latin: "intelligibile"</note> are one, in what way does the one who understands understand himself? For the act of understanding will, as it were, embrace the object, or it will be the same as it; yet it is not yet clear how the intellect clearly knows itself. However, if the understanding and the object are the same—for the object itself is a kind of act—for it is certainly not merely a potentiality, nor is it devoid of life, nor is its life something added from the outside. <margin>B</margin> Nor is its understanding in some different subject, like a stone or something lifeless; rather, the object of understanding is the primary essence. If, therefore, there is an act there, and it is the first act, then surely that act of understanding is the best, and it is an essential understanding <note>Understanding that constitutes the very "being" or essence of the thing.</note>. Indeed, such a thing is the truest understanding; and being first, and existing in a primary way, it will be the primary intellect. For this intellect is neither in potentiality, nor is it one thing while its understanding is another; otherwise, its essential nature would again be merely a potentiality. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, if it is an act and its essence is that act, it will be considered one and the same as the act. Since being itself and the object of understanding are one with the act, all things will be one and the same: the <term>intellect</term> <note>The thinker.</note>, the <term>intellection</term> <note>The act of thinking.</note>, and the <term>intelligible</term> <note>The thing thought of.</note>. If, then, its intellection is the object of its thought, and it is itself that object, then surely it will understand itself. For it will understand by means of that very intellection which it is itself, and it will understand the object which it also is. <margin>D</margin> From both sides, therefore, it will understand itself entirely: both insofar as it is the intellection, and insofar as it is the object of thought, which it understands through this intellection which is itself.

->*The Intellect itself, while remaining in itself, is inclined toward other things neither by action nor effect; rightly it acts upon itself by understanding itself. The Soul, however, being affected in the opposite way, holds the opposite position regarding knowledge. Chapter VI.*<-

> *In the whole order of cognition, sense-perception <note>Latin: "sensus"</note> holds the lowest rank, while the intellect <note>Latin: "intellectus"</note> holds the highest. Since sense-perception follows a straight line in knowing, only touching upon external things, the intellect rightly acts in a circle, contemplating itself and its own depths entirely. Reason <note>Latin: "ratio"; the discursive logic of the human mind.</note>, however, is mostly oblique. The Forms of things that are in the mind are entirely essential. Those which are impressed upon reason from eternity are quasi-essential; those which daily result in reason from the mind are even less essential; finally, those which overflow into reason from the imagination are not essential at all. Therefore, the Soul only then knows itself when it aligns its lower forms with its superior forms.*

<margin>A</margin> REASON, therefore, has demonstrated that there must be something that understands itself properly and principally. However, it understands itself in one way when it exists in the soul, and in another, more primary way when it is in the mind. The Soul, indeed, knows itself as belonging to another <note>The Soul recognizes it is a "child" or image of the higher Intellect.</note>; but the Mind knows that it is itself, what kind of thing it is, and who it is, and it knows this by its own nature, being turned toward itself. For in seeing the "beings" <note>The Forms or Ideas.</note>, it sees itself; and in seeing, it is in act, and it is itself that act. For Intellect and intellection are the same, and it perceives itself as a whole with its whole self, <margin>B</margin> not discerning one part with another part. Has reason then demonstrated such a thing as having a "believable" action? Certainly, it has a necessity, but it does not have a "belief" derived from persuasion. For necessity resides in the mind, while persuasion is found in the soul. We seek, it seems, to bring back persuasion rather than to behold the truth with a pure mind. * And yet, as long as we remained in that supernal region, and were content in that state, we then understood; <margin>* to us</margin> <margin>the [others] with them, in which nature we were joined, and we thought,</margin> the very nature of the mind was sufficient for us to have these things from that source,

...and gathering all things into one, we were contemplating. For it was the Intellect <note>Greek: *Noûs*; the divine realm of pure thought.</note> that was then understanding, and speaking concerning itself; the Soul <note>Greek: *Psychē*.</note>, meanwhile, remained at rest, properly yielding to the action and duty of the mind. But since we have come to this point, we desire to induce a persuasion in the soul, as if wishing to contemplate the archetype in an image. Perhaps, therefore, it is necessary to instruct our soul as to the primary way the intellect beholds itself: to teach, I say, this very <margin>A</margin> nature of the soul, which is intellectual in a certain way, by positioning it as a thinking thing, and by that very name secretly signifying that it is a certain intellect, or a certain power through the intellect, and that it obtains its very function from the intellect. It is fitting for this soul to know that it also recognizes whatever it sees, and knows what it says. And if the soul itself were that which it speaks, it would surely know itself in this way. But since these things are present to it, or at least come to it from above—from that source upon which the soul itself depends—it is surely fitting <margin>C</margin> for this soul also, since it is a certain <term>reason</term> <note>Latin: *ratio*; Greek: *logos*. In this context, it refers to the formative principle or "echo" of the higher Intellect within the soul.</note> of the Intellect and receives related things, to harmonize these with the "traces" impressed upon itself, and thus at last to perceive itself. Let it therefore transfer the image into the true intellect, which is surely the same as those things which are truly understood, and which truly and primarily exist: since it is certain that such an intellect cannot exist outside of itself. Therefore, if indeed it is in itself and with itself, and is that very thing which it is, it exists entirely as intellect. For a Mind can <margin>D</margin> never be mindless <note>original: "amens". A play on words in Latin: *mens* (mind) cannot be *a-mens* (without mind/insane).</note>; it is rightfully necessary that knowledge of itself be present in it: especially since it remains in itself, and its work and essence are nothing other than simply being intellect. For this intellect is not engaged in an outward action, where, looking at external things through its function, it might have a specific knowledge devoted to external things while distracted and separated from itself. Nor is it necessary, if it were perhaps situated in action, for it to perceive itself; but for that to which no action <margin>E</margin> looms—for there is no passion <note>Latin: *affectus*; Greek: *pathos*. In Neoplatonism, the pure Mind is "impassible," meaning it is not affected or changed by external stimuli.</note> in the pure mind, provided every hindrance is entirely absent—its conversion toward itself is entirely direct. This shows that its knowledge of itself is not only probable, but necessary. Otherwise, what would its life be, when it is entirely free from outward action and is placed wholly in the mind?
