### Since the Intellect does not turn toward things below it, and is a form entirely in act, and therefore cannot be idle from action, it always acts concerning itself and God. Chapter VII.

> Where it is turned toward itself, it knows itself through form, but God through effect. Where it is turned toward God, it sees God as if through form, but itself through the cause. While the vegetative power acts only concerning lower things, and the rational power acts concerning lower things, higher things, and itself, the intellect deservedly acts concerning itself and what is superior to it. Those things which proceed from the intellect are made while it remains in itself and acts with itself; but those which come from the soul are, in a certain way, moved. But because the soul is the progeny of the divine intelligence, it either turns toward the divine intelligences where it contemplates, or it is occupied with the rules and laws which are the images of those intelligences where it governs, or it occupies itself with corporeal forms, which are shadows of the intelligences, where it builds and wanders among the senses.

**B**UT we might assert that the intellect, in that state, understands God. If anyone confesses that the intellect then understands God, they will be compelled by this very condition to grant immediately that it also knows itself. For it will recognize whatever it has from God, both what He has given and what He can give. And learning these things...

<column-break/>

...and gathering all things into one, we were seeing. And it was the thinker, speaking about itself. The soul, however, kept quiet, yielding to the activity of the intellect. But since we have come to be here, seeking the experiences within itself and in the soul to happen, as if wishing to see the archetype in an image. Perhaps, therefore, it is necessary to teach our soul how the intellect ever beholds itself, and to teach <margin>B</margin> that part of the soul which is intellectual in some way, by positing it as discursive, and by the name signifying that it is some intellect, or a power through the intellect, and that it derives its strength from the intellect. It is proper, then, for this to know that it also recognizes whatever it sees, and knows what it says. And if it were the things it says, it would know itself in this way. But since the things which are its own come to it from there, from where it also happens to depend, being as it is the <term>reason</term> <note>original: *logos*. The mediating principle between the high Intellect and the lower soul.</note> of that intellect and receiving together with it. And fitting itself to the traces within it, it thus knows itself. Let us transfer the image to the true intellect, which is the same as the true objects of thought, and which are primary and exist. And because it is not possible for this intellect to be outside of itself. So if it is in itself, and with itself, and is this very thing which is intellect. But a mind could never be [mindless]. It is necessary that the knowledge of itself [exists] with it. And no longer would the work and the essence be in another, but in the intellect alone. For if it were practical looking <note>Focused on "doing" things in the physical world.</note> toward the outside with the practical [power], and not remaining in itself, there would be knowledge of the external things, but [self-knowledge] would either be absent or not necessary. If it were entirely practical, it would [not] know itself. But where there is no practical [aim]—for there is no desire in the pure intellect—but rather an excellence toward itself in all things, it indicates not only a likelihood of its [knowledge] of itself, but also its necessity. For what would its life be, being released from action, and being in the intellect?

BOOK THREE.

<margin>A</margin> ...recognizing it, and in this way it will know itself. For it is one of those things given; or rather, it is itself all the things that have been given. If, therefore, it knows that source, and perceives the powers within itself, it will also know itself, having come from that source and received what it is capable of holding from there. But if it is unable to perceive that light clearly—because perhaps the act of seeing is itself the same as the object being seen—it is precisely in this respect that it lacks the vision and knowledge of itself, if seeing consists in being the same as the thing seen. <margin>B</margin> For what else should we grant it? By Jove, "quiet" <note>Greek: *hēsychia*; a state of stillness or rest.</note>. But the quiet of the mind is not a departure from the mind; rather, the quiet of the mind is its own activity, a leisure that is an action free from other things. For even in other things that possess "quiet" or "leisure" from external tasks, their own proper activity remains—especially for those whose being is not merely a potentiality, but an actual activity. Where "to be" is "to act," and there is nothing else toward which that action is directed, it must surely <margin>C</margin> be directed toward itself. Therefore, in thinking itself, it dwells with itself and directs its action toward itself. Indeed, if anything else depends upon it, it depends precisely because it turns toward itself and rests within itself. For it must first stand firm in itself before it can act upon another, or before something else can proceed from it as its likeness. This is just like fire: it must first be fire in itself and possess the action of fire before it <margin>D</margin> can leave its trace or impression upon something else. Now, the Intellect is an activity within itself; the Soul, however, insofar as it turns toward the Intellect, dwells as if "inside." But insofar as it departs from the Mind, it stretches out toward external things. From one side, it turns out like that from which it came; from the other side, even if it proceeds into a state of dissimilarity, it still seems to retain a certain likeness, whether it acts or creates. Even while acting, it continues to contemplate; and when it creates, it produces "forms," like certain thoughts derived from the primary ones. Thus, <margin>E</margin> all things are traces of thought and the Intellect, proceeding by degrees according to the first model, and imitating it according to their strength—the closer things imitating it more, and the furthest things preserving only a faint image.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...recognizing [it], by this reasoning it will also know itself: for it is itself one of the things that have been given; or rather, it exists as all the things that have been given. If, therefore, it knows that source, perceiving its own powers, it will also recognize itself as having been made from there, and receiving from that source what it is capable of. But if it cannot see that source clearly—since perhaps the very thing that is said "to see" becomes the very thing that "is seen"—it is for this reason above all that the vision and knowledge of itself will remain; for if seeing <margin>B</margin> is this very thing: to be the same as what is seen. For what else should we attribute to it? By Jove, "rest" [quiet]. But the rest of the mind is not an alienation from the mind; rather, the rest of the mind is its own action, a leisure from all other things. Since for all other things to which rest and leisure from others are given, a proper action remains—especially for those whose "being" is not in a certain potentiality, but in act. Where "to be" is "act," and nothing remains toward which such an act is directed, it surely <margin>C</margin> rests upon itself. Therefore, in understanding itself, it lives with itself and directs its action toward itself. And if anything else depends upon it, it depends because it turns toward itself and rests in itself. For it must first consist in itself, then act upon another besides, or something else must proceed from there made in its likeness. Just as it is fitting for <margin>D</margin> fire to first be fire within itself and have the action of fire, so that it may finally be able to print its trace upon another. Now, the Intellect is an act within itself; the soul, however, insofar as it turns toward the intellect, as it were, dwells within. But insofar as it goes out from the mind, it is extended to external things. Therefore, from one side it turns out similar to that from whence it comes; from the other side, although it may proceed somewhat dissimilar, it nevertheless seems to retain a certain likeness there too, whether it acts or makes. Indeed, even while it acts, it meanwhile contemplates; and when it makes, it then effects "forms," like certain intelligences derived in a long order from the first <margin>E</margin> intelligences. So much so that all things are traces of intelligence and intellect according to the first exemplar, proceeding by degrees and imitating that according to their powers—the closer ones more so, and the last ones displaying a certain small image.

<margin>Chapter VIII.</margin>
> Since the soul extends itself outward through growth, sensation, and imagination, but only through certain "intellectual sparks" <note>Latin: *scintillas*; a common mystical term for the highest part of the soul that remains in contact with the divine.</note> becomes capable of reflecting back into itself, it is established that the Intellect itself is a light perpetually reflected into itself by itself.

> If you press the corner of your eye lightly with a finger, an internal light will immediately flash to itself. It would do this much more easily and abundantly if you had as much light in your eye as the animals that see at night. The Intellect relates to itself in a similar way. Forms in matter are so united with matter that they perform one work and one action; much more are the "seed-reasons" <note>Latin: *seminales rationes*; the formative principles that govern growth in nature.</note> of forms united in nature; and much more still are the intelligible reasons in the Intellect united to the Intellect, like rays to light, through which the Intellect and the Soul discern sensible things more piercingly than through the senses. Now indeed, both Avicenna <note>A 11th-century Persian philosopher whose work on the soul influenced Western thought.</note> and Henry the Great <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a major Scholastic philosopher known as *Doctor Solemnis*.</note>, the teacher of Scotus <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), one of the most important philosopher-theologians of the High Middle Ages.</note> and a Platonist by nature, believe that the intellectual forms in the intellect or the soul—whether innate to the former or acquired by the latter—exist not so much as "characters" or "stamps," but as a certain natural "habit" <note>Latin: *habitus*; a settled disposition or capacity.</note>, by which the mind easily turns itself to this or that.

### PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK V

<margin>B</margin>The formative power <term>logos: the rational, creative principle</term> implanted in seeds is not the same as the seeds themselves. For these powers are invisible by nature, and even more so are the principles from which they come. Indeed, the nature of these principles and the nature of those things which possess them is the same: just as the reason-principle <note>original: "ratio"</note> exists within the seed, so too the soul itself possesses these principles. But the soul does not look upon what it possesses, for it did not generate them itself; rather, the soul is itself an image <note>original: "simulachrum"</note>, and its seminal reasons are images as well.

That source from which they come is clear and true, existing in the highest degree; from there, it belongs to itself and lives for itself. But unless it becomes part of another and exists within another, it does not even remain. For it is characteristic of an image that, since it belongs to another, it must exist within another—unless perhaps it remains connected to its source. For this reason, it does not look upon itself, because it does not possess sufficient light; and even if it does look, since it has been made perfect within something else, it looks upon that other thing and not upon itself. But none of these limitations exist in that higher realm; there, the vision and the object of vision are one and the same. The visible object is of the same nature as the vision, and the vision is of the same nature as the visible object. Who, then, can say what it is truly like? Surely, it is the one who sees.

<margin>D</margin>And it is the Intellect <term>Nous: the divine Mind or pure thought</term> that sees. For even among us, when vision is light—or rather, when it is joined with light—it sees light, for it sees colors. But in that higher realm, it does not see through another medium, but through itself, because it does not look outward. Therefore, one light beholds another light, not through an intermediary. Light, therefore, beholds another light; thus, it beholds itself. This light, shining into the soul, has illuminated the mind; this means making it "intellectual," <note>original: "intellectualem efficere"</note> and this is to be within itself just as the sublime light above is. If, then, you consider the trace <note>original: "vestigium"</note> of light impressed upon the soul, and realize that the heavenly light is even more beautiful, greater, and clearer, you will have come closer to the nature of the Intellect and the Intelligible. For this light, poured into the soul, provides it with a clearer life—a life, I say, that is not a generator of offspring. On the contrary, it turns the mind back into itself and does not permit it to be scattered, but causes it to love the radiance implanted within the mind. Nor does it bring a life of the senses. For the senses look outward and do not grasp things with certainty. But he who drinks from that light, the fountain of truths, sees visible things more clearly, though in an opposite way. It remains, then, for the trace of the mind's life to take on the character of intellectual life. For there, the true things themselves reside.

<margin>F</margin>Yet the life and activity in the mind is the primary light, first shining upon itself—a splendor constantly flashing toward itself, both shining and being illuminated at once. This is truly the "intelligible" <note>the object of thought</note> thinking the "intellect" <note>the subject of thought</note>, perfected in itself, needing nothing else to see, but self-sufficient for the act of beholding. For what it sees is the very thing it is. Among us, it is almost the same, so that our knowledge of it is achieved through it; otherwise, how could we say anything about it? Just as that higher reality is such that it can grasp itself most clearly, so we, through it, are similarly empowered.

<margin>G</margin>Now, it is established through such arguments that we may lift our minds toward that reality—the mind, I say, asserting that it is an image of that source, and that its life is an image and likeness of that higher life. And when it thinks, it takes on the form of that Intellect and of God.

<column-break/>

The principle in the seeds that does these things is not the seeds themselves. For these too are invisible by nature, and even more so are those higher things. The nature of those higher things and of the things that possess them is the same, such as the reason-principle <note>original: "logos"</note> in the seed and the soul which possesses these. But the soul does not see what it possesses, for it did not generate them. Rather, it is itself an image <note>original: "eidolon"</note>, and the reason-principles are too. But where they come from is the manifest, the true, and the first. From there, it exists for itself and lives for itself. <margin>C</margin> But if it does not become another and exist in another, it does not even remain. For it is proper to an image, being of another, to come to be in another, unless it is suspended from that source. Therefore, it does not see, as it does not have sufficient light. And even if it should see, having been perfected in another, it sees that other and not itself. But in that realm, there is no such thing; rather, the vision and the visible are together. And this visible is as the vision, and the vision as the visible. Who, then, shall say what it is like? He who has seen it.

<margin>E</margin>The Intellect <note>original: "Nous"</note> sees. For even here, vision being light—or rather, being united with light—sees light. For it sees colors. But there, it does not see through another, but through itself, because it does not look outside. By another light, therefore, it sees another light, not through an intermediary. Light, then, sees another light; thus, it sees itself. This light, shining in the soul, illuminated it; and this is to make it intellectual. This light is likewise in itself, the light above. Just as there is a certain trace of the light that comes to be in the soul, so that light itself is even more beautiful and greater and more manifest, being near to the nature of the intelligibles. And it <margin>* near to the nature * * and intelligibles . and itself * * or it shone * * it gave life to the soul, a more manifest life. But not the generative life. For on the contrary, it turned the soul toward itself and did not allow it to be scattered, but made it love its own radiance. This light does not bring the life of the senses, for that looks outward and perceives more superficially. But he who receives that light of the truths sees the objects of vision more clearly. But in the opposite way. It is illuminated, an intellectual life having been received, a trace of the life there.</margin>

For there are the true things. The life and activity in the Intellect is the primary light, shining primarily for itself, a radiance toward itself, shining and being shone upon at once—the truly intelligible, both thinking and being thought, and seen by itself. It does not need another in order to see; it is self-sufficient for seeing. For that which it sees is itself, the thing being known. And that very thing is in us, so that our knowledge of it occurs through itself. From where else would we be able to speak about it? It is such that it can apprehend itself more clearly, and we can do so through it. Through these reasonings, it is necessary that our soul also raise itself to it, having established itself as an image of that source. For its life is a reflection <note>original: "indalma"</note> and likeness of that life. And whenever it thinks, it becomes godlike and intellect-like.

### BOOK THREE

And if one demands of oneself what kind of thing the Intellect <term>Nous: the divine Mind or pure intuitive thought</term> is, that is the perfect state. And how does one know about oneself when first becoming that very Intellect, or when the soul has yielded its activity to the Intellect, of which things it held the memory within itself? These things, having been shown to itself, as if through an image of such magnitude as it sees preserved in some way that Intellect—by means of a more accurate similarity to it—insofar as a part of the soul is saved to reach similarity with the Intellect.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It is established again that if anyone should wish to know what sort of thing that perfect Intellect is, which primarily comprehends itself, it is necessary in the first place to lead the soul back into the Mind, or at least to grant its own activity to the Mind—the activity, I say, which occupies itself with those things whose memory it retains within itself. To the soul indeed possessing these things and being so affected, it is possible to demonstrate itself; for it may be able to gaze upon that Intellect through itself as if through an image <note>original: "imaginem"</note>, primarily because of the life of the soul, which reflects that Intellect with a certain more expressive similarity: insofar as you may see that a certain part of the soul can recall itself to the likeness of the Mind.

<margin>B</margin> **SOUL** therefore, as it seems, and that which is most divine in the soul, one must contemplate if one is primarily to know what it is. Perhaps indeed you will achieve this by this condition: if first you separate the body from the human, and especially from yourself; then the soul that forms it; and especially sense, desire, and anger, and other trifles of this sort, as they decline too much toward the mortal. Nor is there any place for this, for there is no place for the Mind. Wherefore the light of the Sun is indeed in the air. ### In the first intellect all things are forms: both identical according to essence, and distinct by formal reason. Chapter 4.

*The forms of things, since they are primary there, are therefore also perfect, and in a perfect manner. Thus they exist essentially: yet they differ from the intellect by a certain reason. For that is the one intellect: but these forms are many. They differ among themselves by formal reason: especially since the intellect only inspects them; and by inspecting, it understands them distinctly, all things being even further different among themselves, that is, in reality, place, and time. Understanding, like vision, is a certain effort and apprehension and discernment: which three things are also proper to light and fire. Therefore, insofar as the intellect is turned toward itself by understanding, it exercises these three toward itself, and declares itself to be entirely manifold: for if there were no difference at all in it, or if none could be, there would be nothing there to strive for or toward which to strive: nor would there be need for application or effort. There will be nothing for it to apprehend, nor anything to be comprehended, nor need for apprehension, or any sort of union, or an embrace of itself: there will be no place for discernment. Thus far the Platonists. Christians, however, prove that the first intellect does not have such a multitude of forms, because through its one form and one act it contains all great things, insofar as it relates itself in various ways to all things as something that can be participated in, disposing the multitude not within itself, but outside.* <note>This italicized summary, likely by the translator Marsilio Ficino, contrasts Plotinus's philosophy with Christian theology regarding whether God contains many "ideas" or is purely simple.</note>

<margin>A</margin> Regarding these matters, let it be spoken thus. If, however, the forms <note>original: "species" / "εἴδη"</note> are not only made in the mind—otherwise these would not be our last forms, but there they would be the first forms, that is, the efficient ones, and therefore primary—then it is certainly necessary both that the forms be made there and that the maker exist there as well, and that both exist as one: otherwise, that intellect will again need something else. What then? Will that which is higher again be in need? Certainly not: for this very thing which is in need is the intellect. But does that supernal thing see itself? Not at all. For it does not need vision. But this will be treated in <margin>B</margin> what follows. For the present, let us treat again of the same matter. For the subject now being discussed must not be undervalued. It must be asserted again, therefore, that this intellect needs to see itself in this very way, or rather, that it possesses this very thing continuously. Thus, first from this it follows that it is manifold: then that it belongs to another: then necessarily that it is capable of seeing, of that seeing, I say, <margin>C</margin> of which it is also said to be: furthermore, that its very essence is vision. For if it were something else, vision would have to exist separately: but if it is not something else, the vision will be empty. It is necessary, therefore, that there be more than one thing there, so that vision may exist, and that the vision itself meet with the visible: and that which is seen by itself must be a certain multitude, and not entirely one. For that which is purely one has nothing upon which to act, but existing alone and singular, it rests entirely. For by whatever reason it might act, there is one thing and another. Indeed, if there were not <margin>D</margin> one thing and another there, what would it do? Or where would it proceed? For this reason, whatever acts must either act concerning some other thing, or be itself manifold: if it is to act upon anything within itself. But if it does not proceed into another, it will come to rest. When, however, it completely rests, it will understand nothing at all. For this reason, it is necessary for the one who understands, while understanding, to be involved in at least two things: and that either one of the two be external, or both be in the same thing, and that intellection always be involved in a certain (so to speak) otherness, and again in a certain identity.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Let them take the opinion-forming power; then, from this let them ascend. But if not even this, let them take sense-perception more clearly bringing the forms: sense-perception, I say, already in itself with those things it is able to do, and already being among the forms. But if someone wishes, descending, let them go toward the producing power, even unto those things which it makes. Then from there let them ascend from the last forms back to the last: or rather, toward the first.

---

<margin>A</margin> These things, then, are so. But if only the things made [were there], they would indeed be the last; but there the first things are the makers, whence also they are first. It was necessary then for the maker and the thing made to be together. Otherwise, there will again be need of another. What then? Is there not again something beyond this? Or is the intellect that which is in need? Does it not see itself? Or what would it need of vision? But this hereafter. Now we speak again. For the investigation is not about <margin>B</margin> chance things. It must be said again that this intellect has need of seeing itself. Rather, it has the seeing of itself; first, then, that it is many. Then, also that it belongs to another, and by necessity is capable of seeing, and seeing that [higher thing]. For its essence is vision. For if there is <margin>C</margin> some other thing, there is vision. But if it is not, it is nothing. It is necessary then for there to be more than one, so that there may be vision. And vision coincides with the visible. And that which is seen by itself is a certain multitude in everything. For it does not have that which is in all, upon what will it act? But being alone and solitary, it will stand in this way. For where it acts, there is one thing and another. If there were not another, what would it do? Or where would it reach out? Wherefore that which acts <margin>D</margin> must act within itself. But if it does not proceed toward something else, it will stand. But when it is in every state of rest, it will not think. Therefore, because the intellect, when it thinks, is in two things: and either one is outside, or both are in the same, and thought is always in otherness, and necessarily in identity.

<summary>Plotinus explains that the Divine Intellect (Nous) must be manifold because the act of thinking requires a distinction between the thinker and the object of thought. He argues that while the Absolute "One" is beyond vision and thought, the Intellect is a unity-in-multiplicity that contains the archetypal forms of all things.</summary>

### BOOK THREE.

Likewise, those things which are properly and primarily understood relate to the mind as being simultaneously the same and yet different. Furthermore, any object of the intellect brings with it a certain identity and alterity <note>Identity and Alterity (difference) are two of the 'Great Kinds' from Plato’s *Sophist*, used here to explain how the mind distinguishes between ideas.</note>; otherwise, what would it understand unless it contained one thing and another within itself? For if each thing is a certain "reason" <term>ratio: the Greek 'logos', meaning both a rational principle and a definition</term>, then it is surely already many. 
<margin>
* variegated 
* a variegated eye, 
* or variegated 
* colors.
</margin>
Therefore, the mind perceives itself as a kind of variegated eye, or something marked with various colors. For if it were to apply itself to something entirely one and indivisible <term>impartibili: that which cannot be divided into parts</term>, it would be void of speech and reason. 
<margin>B</margin> For what could it say or weigh concerning this very thing? And yet, if it were necessary for that indivisible thing to affirm itself as entirely indivisible, it would first have to enumerate those things which it is not. Therefore, in this way, it would happen that it is many so that it might also be one. 

Furthermore, when the mind says of itself, "I am this," it puts forth this "this" either as something other than itself—and thus it lies—or as something accidental to itself, and thus it judges itself to be many. Or perhaps it will say, "I am, I say, I am; I, I say, I." What then? Either only two things will be here (and thus it will say of itself "I" and "this"), or it must be something multiform. Now it will discern these things as different, and by what reason they are different. Thus, number is already here, and many other things occur. It is therefore necessary for the thinking subject to receive one thing and another; 
<margin>C</margin> and that which is understood, being distinguished within itself by intelligence, must be diverse. Otherwise, there will be no intelligence of it, but only a "touch" <term>tactus: a mystical contact or intuition that precedes formal logic</term> and a kind of strike, such that it can neither be spoken of nor speak. It would "pre-understand" (if I may say so) without the intellect; 
<margin>D</margin> for since the intellect is not yet born, he who touches there does not yet understand.

But it is necessary that the thinking subject does not remain simple, especially when it understands itself entirely. For it divides itself, even if someone were to say that intelligence is silence. Furthermore, that which is entirely simple does not need the varied care through which it might apprehend itself. 
<margin>E</margin> For what will it apprehend, even when it has understood itself? 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <note>original: "Item quæ propriè præcipuéq; intelliguntur..." This begins the Latin translation of the Greek text in the left column.</note> Likewise, those things which are properly and primarily understood relate to the mind as being simultaneously the same and yet different. Furthermore, any object of the intellect brings with it a certain identity and alterity <note>original: "identitatem alteritatemq;"</note> with itself; otherwise, what would it understand unless it contained one thing and another within itself? For if each thing becomes a certain "reason" <term>ratio</term>, then it is surely already many. Therefore, the mind perceives itself as a kind of variegated eye, or something marked with various colors. For if it were to apply itself to something entirely one and indivisible, it will be void of speech and reason. 

<margin>B</margin> For what could it say or weigh concerning this very thing? And yet, if it were necessary for that indivisible thing to affirm itself as entirely indivisible, it would first have to count those things which it is not. Therefore, in this way, it would happen that it is many so that it might also be one. Furthermore, when the mind says of itself, "I am this," it puts forth this "this" either as something other than itself—and thus it lies—or as something accidental to itself, and thus it judges itself to be many. Or perhaps it will say, "I am, I say, I am; I, I say, I." 

<margin>C</margin> What then? Either only two things will be here (and thus it will say of itself "I" and "this"), or it must be something multiform. Now it will discern these things as different, and by what reason they are different. Thus, number is already here, and many other things occur. It is therefore necessary for the thinking subject to receive one thing and another; and that which is understood, being distinguished within itself by intelligence, must be diverse in itself. Otherwise, there will be no intelligence of it, but only a touch and a kind of strike, such that it can neither be spoken of nor speak. 

<margin>D</margin> And without intellect (as it were), it pre-understands; for since the intellect is not yet born, he who touches there does not yet understand. But it is necessary that the thinking subject does not remain simple, especially when it understands itself entirely. For it divides itself, even if someone were to say that intelligence is silence. Furthermore, that which is entirely simple does not need the varied care through which it might apprehend itself. 

<margin>E</margin> For what will it apprehend, if ever it has understood itself? For before it uses the mind to understand itself, it exists entirely as that which it is within itself. Finally, knowledge itself seems to be a certain desire, and like a discovery accompanying a search. Therefore, that which has no difference within itself toward itself rests everywhere, and investigates nothing about itself. But that which explains and unfolds itself is surely manifold in itself.

---

-> Since in the first intellect there is a number of many things absolutely different from one another, it is necessary that above this there be another principle, simply one, that is, thoroughly most simple. Chapter XI. <-

---

Unless in the first essence, life and intelligence differed from each other by some reason, these three things—being, living, and understanding—which are so different, would not easily dwell in the order of things. For being <term>esse</term> is the most common of all, while understanding is the least common, and living is in the middle. 

The intellect itself is nothing other than a kind of sight directed toward its first light, just as the bodily sight is directed toward its own. No matter the perfection by which the bodily sight is increased, it will always be inferior to the light. Similarly, the most perfect intellect is seen to be second to its light—that is, truth and the Good itself. 

Essence, being the most common of all, proceeds immediately from Unity after simplicity itself. Beyond the simple reason of essence, it carries a kind of image of that Unity, which differs in some way from the essence. Likewise, by the help of this image, it is turned back toward the One and the Good themselves, not first by an intellectual instinct, but rather by a natural and vital one. Before this act of turning <term>conuersionis: 'conversion', the Platonic return of the effect to its cause</term>, it was both essence and image; in the act of turning itself, it appears as "living"; after this, it appears as "understanding," while thus turned it receives a gift from the Good itself. 

And since the Good itself is above all things, holding itself equally toward all, it does not receive one thing from there, but all things equally, especially since the intellect is the nearest receptacle. It thus becomes a form that contains all forms <note>original: "forma omniformis"</note>, having the ideal forms of things absolutely distinct from one another; from this, a far greater distinction proceeds after it. In the same moment, it is made multiform and an intellect. Finally, since the intellect carries with it a multitude of things absolutely different, it deservedly depends on a certain superior, most simple principle.

<summary>This page argues that the Divine Intellect must contain multiplicity (identity and difference) because the act of self-knowledge requires a subject and an object. It establishes a hierarchy where the "One" (the Good) precedes the Intellect, which is a triad of Being, Life, and Mind.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "One" (the ultimate, simple source of all existence) and the "Intellect" (the second stage of reality). Here, Plotinus explains how the Intellect, in attempting to understand the absolute simplicity of the One, necessarily becomes complex and "manifold."</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD V.

<margin>A</margin> This intellect, therefore, becomes manifold whenever it strives to understand the one above it. For then, as it reaches toward that One, while it endeavors to apply itself to it as if it were simple, it immediately slips away from that very simplicity, always receiving something else within itself that has been multiplied. For this reason, it indeed began from there not as an intellect, but as a gaze <note>original: "aspectus"; in Greek, "opsis"—referring to a raw capacity for vision before it has an object to look at.</note> not yet seeing. However, it proceeded from there because in the meantime it had multiplied what it carried back within itself; thus, it <margin>B</margin> desired indeterminately, having within itself something like an image of the One. But finally, proceeding from there, it carried back something else, which it then rendered as many within itself. Now, indeed, it possesses within itself a certain form of that vision; otherwise, it would never be prepared to receive this very thing. Thus, therefore, from <margin>C</margin> the One, it has now emerged as many. And so, as an intellect, it now observes itself, and only then has it become a gaze that finally sees. Moreover, it is then truly an intellect when it possesses [its object] and holds it as an intellect does. Before these things, it was only desire and an unformed gaze. This intellect, then, directed itself toward that One; having attained it, it emerged as an intellect, and it is always affected and fashioned by its essence. Likewise, the intellect and intellection <term>intellection: the act of the mind thinking or understanding</term> exist after it has understood, but previously there was no intellection, since it did not have an intelligible object; nor was it yet an intellect, since it did not yet understand anything. But that which stands above these things <margin>D</margin> is their principle; it is not, I say, a principle implanted within them. For the very principle from which these things are made is not in them at all, but the elements from which they are composed are within them. That from which each thing is made is not one of those individual things, but is foreign to them all. It is not, therefore, one thing among all, but before all things; and therefore also before the mind, for all things are within the mind. Therefore, for this reason also, it is above the mind. Furthermore, if all things that exist after it have the order of "the all," then in this way too it is superior to all; surely it is necessary that it be none of those things to which it is superior. Therefore, you shall not call it "Mind," nor even "the Good" itself, if perhaps "the Good" signifies one thing among all; but if it signifies that which is above all things, then it may be called so. For which reason, if the intellect becomes manifold insofar as it becomes an intellect, and if intellection itself—even if it proceeds from the One—nevertheless multiplies as if by approaching it, it must be that 
anything that is intellect will also be a multitude.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Therefore also this mind, being manifold, wishes to contemplate that which is beyond. If indeed it wishes to reach that as it goes forth, it always receives something else within itself that is being divided. <note>The Greek text here is fragmentary in the original transcription, but refers to the mind's attempt to grasp the One.</note> So it set out toward it as a mind, but as a gaze not yet seeing. But having [an object], it was itself multiplied. It desired indeterminately, having <margin>B</margin> in itself a certain image. It went forth as another thing, having made that thing many within itself; and again it has a stamp of the vision, or it would not have been able to receive it within itself. Thus indeed from the One it became [many]. And thus as knowing [itself] it [saw]. And then it became a seeing gaze. [It is] now a mind <margin>C</margin> when it holds [the object], and holds it as a mind. At that time, it was desire only, and an unformed gaze. This mind, then, reached toward that One; but having received it, it became a mind. And it is always becoming in that state: both mind, and essence, and intellection, when it understood. For before that, intellection did not exist, as it did not have the intelligible. Nor was it a mind, when it did not yet [understand]. But before these things is the principle of these, not being <margin>D</margin> [inherent] in them. For that from which [a thing comes] is not in [the result], but rather that out of which [it is made]. But that from which each thing is, is not one [of them], but different from all. That therefore is not all things, but before all things. So that it is also before mind; for mind would be all things, [and the One is] for this reason before mind. And if those things after it have the order of all things, and these are all things—since it is before the things that exist—it cannot be all things, nor would you call it Mind itself. Nor <margin>E</margin> [would you call it] the Good, if that means one of all things. <unclear>*</unclear> If it is the Good [as being before all things], then it is so. But if not this, then if it is called that which is before all things, it is not even mind, because [it is simple]. And if the act of thinking itself, as if by accident, should proceed from it, it produces a multitude. [The One] is entirely simple and first of all, beyond being a mind. For if it thinks, it will not be beyond mind, but it will be [mind]. But [as it is], it will be mind, and it will be a multitude.

## He argues against those who, in the first principle of things, place one essence but many acts that are 
## absolutely distinct.
### Chapter XII.

For either essence and act <term>essence and act: 'Essentia' is what a thing is; 'Actus' is what a thing does or its state of being in operation.</term> differ between themselves, or they do not. If they differ, the essence is in itself imperfect, needing to be perfected through act; if they differ in no way, then just as the act is manifold—because it is clearly absolutely manifold—so too is the essence manifold. This argument of Plotinus does not pertain at all to the divine Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the prominent Scholastic philosopher. The commentator is defending Aquinas against Plotinus's logic.</note> who distinguishes the Trinity by relations. As to whether it touches Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), another major Scholastic who proposed a 'formal distinction' between God's essence and His attributes.</note>, let his followers see to it and respond; for I hope they will respond most excellently. Above all multitude, there is necessarily a "One," and above any "one thing" is that which is simply One. Since, therefore, essence and intelligence are "some one thing"—that is, one essence, one life, one intelligence—for this reason Plotinus places before them the most absolutely One, which procreates all things not by any intermediary act or affection, but by the very power of its most absolute simplicity. Plotinus denies of God every number that multiplies nature and declares it to be composite. Relati... <note>original: "Relati" — catchword for the next page's first word, "Relations."</note>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of the "One" (the ultimate source) and how it relates to the "Many" (the created world and the divine Mind). The text contrasts Christian theology regarding the Trinity with the Neoplatonic views of Plotinus and Proclus, specifically focusing on how "number" and "multitude" are applied to the divine.</meta>

# BOOK THREE.

However, the number found among Christians does not do this at all: it certainly denies every number that can exist in created beings and that can be defined. The number placed in the divine unity by Christians is not of that kind; it is neither a number of essences, nor of forms or qualities or similar things. Even if you say it is a number "of persons," you say so by divine authority, but you will not be able to fully explain what you mean. Similarly, if you say "of properties," and the one who says it is distinguished by "relation," he himself will admit that he does not grasp that mystery. Likewise, he who says they differ absolutely will fear to define it. Finally, the mystery of the divinity must be believed. This is also what Nicholas the Greek <note>original: "Nicolaus Graecus"; likely Nicholas of Methone, a 12th-century bishop known for his refutation of Proclus's "Elements of Theology."</note> the philosopher strenuously defended against Proclus.

<margin>A</margin> And what prevents it from being a multitude in this way, so long as the essence is one? For multitude is not a composition, but rather its activities <note>original: "energeiai"</note> are the multitude for it. But if the activities are not essences, but come from power into activity, it is truly but incomplete in essence before it acts. But if essence itself is activity, and activity itself is the multitude, then the essence is as great as the multitude. This we concede to the Mind <note>original: "nous"</note>, to which we also attribute the act of thinking itself. But we do not attribute this to the Principle of all things. For I do not ask about the "well-being" of the many, from which the "much" comes. For in the case of a child's number, the "one" is first. But they say this about number: for the things that follow are compositions. But in the case of beings, it is already a necessity that there is something "well" here from which the many come. Otherwise, the <margin>C</margin> <gloss>*</gloss> many will be torn apart from each other, coming from here and there into a composition by some chance. But those things that exist simply come from the One. They will say that the activities remain, and they will perceive them as substances <term>original: "hypostaseis"; the underlying reality or individual substance</term>. Being substances, they will exist alongside that from which they come. While that remains simple, that which comes from it becomes a multitude of itself and depends on it. <margin>D</margin> For if that One acted in some way and they subsisted from it, then there would be a multitude there too. But if these are the first activities making the second, and if that which is before the activities remains in itself, then to the other thing constituted from the activities, the whole number of activities is granted; for it is one thing, and the activities from it are another. Because it did not act itself. Otherwise, the <margin>E</margin> first activity will not be the Mind. For it is not as if it first desired to become Mind, then Mind was born, with the desire coming between it and the Mind that was generated. Nor did it desire at all. For in that way it would be incomplete. And the desire would not have what it desired. Nor did it have part of the thing and not the other. Nor did it reach out, nor was there extension. But rather, as it were, it stood after it, and while that remained in its own character, it did not subsist. Nor indeed so that something else <meta>pos:</meta> since there is nothing anywhere to which its subsistence might turn, while that remains in its own state,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But perhaps someone will object: what prevents that itself from being a multitude, provided it remains one essence? For multitude does not introduce composition to this. For certain activities <note>original: "actus"; translating the Greek "energeiai," referring to the internal "doings" of a being</note> of it are the multitude. But it is answered thus: If his activities are not essences, but come from a certain power into act, it will not be a multitude, but it will nonetheless be something incomplete, as far as essence is concerned, before it acts. But if its essence is activity, <margin>B</margin> and activity is truly multitude, then its essence will be as manifold as its activity. This, however, we grant to the Mind, to which we attribute knowledge of itself, but by no means to the Principle of all things <note>The "Principle" is the One, which must be simpler than the Mind</note>. For it is necessary that before a multitude there is a "One," from which the multitude proceeds, for before every number is the One. But some may object here that it is so in number: since those things that follow the one are certain compositions, but in the order of things it does not seem necessary for a One to exist from which the many proceed. But we will answer them thus: If the One does not preside over the order of things, the many would be dispersed among themselves, and one thing from here and another from there would perhaps run together into a mass by chance. Therefore they assert that from one intellect, simple in itself, many activities proceed. Nevertheless, they will affirm that that which exists before these activities is simple: then they will recognize that the always-existing activities are certain substances, or certain "suppositions" <term>original: "supposita"; a technical term for individual substances or persons</term>. Since they are certain <margin>D</margin> suppositions, they will certainly be different from that from which they proceed: while that remains simple, that which proceeds from it turns into a certain multitude in itself and depends on that. But if, by that One acting in some way, activities of this kind subsist from it, there too a multitude will occur: but if these are the first activities constituting a second thing, nothing prevents that which is higher than these activities from consisting in itself, and secondly, to that which flows next from it and is composed of activities, <margin>E</margin> the number of activities is assigned: for it is one thing itself, and the activities from it are another, because they proceed without it acting: otherwise the intellect will not be the first action. For the One itself did not first desire the mind to be made, and then the mind was made, as if such an affection intervened as a medium between the creator itself and the mind born from it. For there is no affection there. For in that way, he who desired would be incomplete, and his zeal would not yet have what <margin>F</margin> he desired: nor again is he partly in possession of his prayer and partly not... <meta>flectat</meta> ...turning his affection. But indeed, if something remained after it, it is necessary that something else from there...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the nature of the first principle, contrasting the "One" (the Absolute) with the "Intellect" (the second principle). It explores the idea that the source of all things must be simpler and higher than the mind itself.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

<margin>A</margin>...it subsists, that it rests entirely within itself. Otherwise, before it is moved, it will be moved, and before it thinks, it will think; or at least its first act will be imperfect, being merely a kind of impulse toward something. But to what could it be carried in this way? Or what could it have recently attained? Now, indeed, according to reason, it is more permissible to assert that a certain act flows forth from that abiding one, just as light flows from the sun—namely, the intellect <note>original: "intellectum"; in Plotinus, this refers to the 'Nous' or Divine Mind, the first emanation from the One.</note> and the whole intelligible nature. But the One itself, resting at the highest peak of the intelligible world, reigns there, <margin>B</margin> not separating from itself what shines forth from it. Or we shall place one light upon another light, which, by always remaining, shines upon the intelligible realm. For that which shines from it is neither separated from it, nor again is it the same, nor is it of such a kind that it is not essence—or like something blind—but indeed it sees and knows itself, and it is the first knower. But the One, just as it is above the intellect, so also it is above knowledge. <margin>C</margin> And just as it needs nothing, so it also does not need knowledge; rather, knowledge itself is placed in the second nature. For knowledge is a certain "one thing," but the One is the "One itself," not "some one thing." For if it were some one thing, it would no longer be the One itself; for "itself" stands above that which is called "something."

<column-break/>

<note>The Greek text in this column mirrors the Latin translation provided above, discussing the stillness of the One and the flow of the Intellect (Nous) as light from the sun. It emphasizes that the first principle is "beyond knowledge" (epekeina gnoseos).</note>

->Intelligence is not to be added to the Good itself, which indeed cannot be understood by any created intellect, however high. Chapter XIII.<-

The logic of the Good itself and of intelligence is so different, as we have said, that the former is the most universal, and the latter least so: the former desires nothing, while the latter desires the Good. Likewise, the opposite of intelligence is folly, while the opposite of the Good is evil: folly and evil are entirely the same, therefore intelligence and the Good are not the same. When, therefore, you add intelligence to the Good itself, you see it as another and different thing, and you judge the Good thus far as needy and, as it were, composite. This paradox—namely, that the first principle is above essence, life, and intelligence—is asserted to be confessed by Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-6th century Christian theologian and philosopher who adapted Neoplatonic thought into Christianity; he is cited here to bridge Plotinus with Christian mysticism.</note>, who adds, moreover, that the One enjoys itself in a certain way more than intellectual, which he calls "super-intellectual" <note>original: "superintellectualem"</note>. Likewise, it "pre-understands" in some ineffable way beyond and above the intellect, as if it enjoys itself through touch rather than vision. For intelligence is a kind of vision; it does not speak of itself, but exists simply as what it is. If by any condition one could proceed by degrees of intelligence to the Good itself, let there not be imagined an intellect that lacks intelligence—not an intelligence that is an act of the intellect regarding the Good—but rather the Good itself toward which intelligence tends. Or perhaps it is the very light that intelligence seeks, in which a perfected intelligence finds its end; a light not in this [intellect], but residing in itself. This clarity is not properly "seeing," nor is it deprived of the good of vision like something blind; just as vision itself does not properly "see," yet is not blind. Truly, the clarity itself, which is the cause of all vision, is much more remote from the privation of sight than sight itself is. Nor is that clarity determined to the genus of intellection. For that which is above all things as the cause of all things is defined by none of the number of all things. Therefore, it is not defined by essence, life, or intelligence, nor by intellectual or intelligible clarity, but by clarity itself, simply existing through itself in itself, as the cause of every act of clarity. It is imagined as a power according to an effective potential, the act of powers and the maker of acts. Even if the soul has no hands or feet, yet because it does not need them and has a more eminent power to generate them, it is not called maimed or crippled. By similar reason, reason is not called blind even if it has no eyes, nor is the mind irrational if it never reasons: for it possesses in a higher way what reason seeks through time. Nor is God "unmindful" <note>original: "amens"; literally "without mind" or "mad."</note> if He has no mind: for He is that whole which the mind strives to possess, or rather, to become.

---

<margin>A</margin> WHEREFORE it is truly ineffable. For whatever you might say, you would be saying something particular. But that which is above all things and above the most venerable Mind, being separated from all, has no other true name, nor is it any of all things. And it has no name at all, because nothing can be said of it: but we, as far as we can, attempt to signify something about it to ourselves. Furthermore, when we are in doubt, saying, "Thus it does not feel itself, thus <margin>B</margin> it does not notice itself, thus it knows nothing at all of what it is," then indeed it is right to consider that whenever we say such things, we are being twisted back toward the opposites. For we do as much as is in us...

It concludes by addressing the difficulty of using human language to describe a principle that transcends self-awareness and knowledge.</note>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the "One"—the absolute source of all existence—and why it must be beyond even the act of thinking or "Intellect." It explores the paradox that to think of oneself implies a division between the thinker and the thought, which cannot exist in a perfectly simple first principle.</meta>

### BOOK THREE.

<margin>A</margin> ...being itself is a "many," whenever we bring it forward to be known and attribute cognition to it. For when we grant it intelligence, we make it so that it requires intelligence. And if intelligence exists together with it, it will be superfluous for it to apply intelligence to itself. For intelligence seems entirely to be a certain <term>consensus<note>original Greek: "sinaisthēsis"; a shared perception or self-awareness that implies multiple parts sensing each other as a whole.</note></term> of the whole, where many things concur into one, whenever something understands itself—which is indeed the proper and primary form of intelligence. Each individual thing is merely what it is, <margin>B</margin> and seeks nothing. But if intelligence is extended toward external things, it will be deficient, and not a primary intelligence. That which is entirely simple and truly self-sufficient needs nothing. However, that which is self-sufficient only in a secondary way, being in need of itself, certainly requires the intelligence of itself. Indeed, that which is deficient in relation to itself makes itself sufficient by means of the whole, having obtained sufficiency from all its parts, dwelling with itself and turning toward itself through the act of understanding. For even <margin>C</margin> consensus is the sensation of something that is "many," as the name itself testifies. Then intelligence, since it is prior, reflects the thinker—inasmuch as he is a "many"—back into himself. For if he should say only this: "I am truly a being," he says this as if he were discovering himself, and he says it fittingly; for "being" is a "many." For even when he tends toward something simple and says "I am being," he does not attain either himself or "being" and "truth." For <margin>D</margin> he does not say "being" as if he were naming a stone—when he speaks truly—but he pronounces many things in a single word. For this "to be," which is truly "to be," is not called so as if it held merely a trace of being (which would not even be "being"), and therefore it ought to be spoken of as a kind of image compared to its archetype; it undoubtedly embraces many things within itself. What then? Shall not each of these be understood? Truly, if you wish to take it as separate and alone, you will not understand it, but you will have said something else besides: it "has being." If this is the case, if anything is the simplest of all things, it does not have intelligence of itself; for if it should have it, it would also in some way and in some place have "being." Therefore, it does not understand itself, nor is there any intelligence of it anywhere.

<column-break/>

> Since the intellect does not exclude multiplicity (which the One itself does exclude), and therefore the One itself is more eminent than the intellect by being simpler, it follows that we are by no means able to apprehend and explain the One through the intellect.
->Chapter XIV.<-
> Nevertheless, we speak of it—as <term>Parmenides<note>An ancient Greek philosopher who argued that reality is a single, unchanging, and indivisible "One."</note></term> and <term>Dionysius<note>Likely referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist who used "negative theology" to describe God by what He is not.</note></term> say—through negations and relations. For we possess it in a certain way, insofar as we possess a certain unity as the "head" of our mind, a character of the divine unity; by this we then touch the divine unity, when we have been formed by our mind, and through this divine mind we are alienated from ourselves and made into prophets.

---

<margin>A</margin> In what way, then, do we speak of it? Certainly, we say something *about* it, yet we by no means speak *it* itself. We have neither cognition nor intelligence of it. But in what manner do we speak of it, if we do not possess it? Because even if we do not possess it by cognition, we do not for that reason possess it in no way at all; rather, we possess it in such a way that we can say something about it, while we are by no means able to fully express it. For we are accustomed to pronounce what it is *not*; but what it *is*, we <margin>B</margin> never say. For this reason, we are accustomed to make words about it from the things that come after it; yet nothing prohibits us from possessing it, even if we are unable to explain it.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's argument from the previous section, emphasizing that the "One" (the First Principle) does not need to think or have self-awareness because it is already perfect and complete. It explores the relationship between the source (the One) and its first product (the Intellect/Mind).</meta>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEAD V.

<margin>A</margin>If it subsists, it must rest entirely within itself; otherwise, it would be moved before it moves, and think before it thinks, or at least its first act would be imperfect—being merely a sort of impulse. But toward what could it be carried in this way? Or what could it hope to attain? Rather, it is more in accordance with reason to assert that a certain activity flows from that standing source, just as light flows from the sun. This flow is the <term>Intellect<note>original: "intellectum"; in Neoplatonism, the Intellect is the first radiation from the One, containing all the forms of things that can be known.</note></term> and the whole <margin>B</margin> world of things that can be known. The One itself remains at the highest peak of the intelligible world, reigning there, not separating from itself that which shines forth from it. Or we might imagine light upon light, which shines while always remaining in the realm of the knowable. For that which shines from the One is neither separated from it, nor is it the same as it; nor is it of such a nature as to lack essence, like something blind. Rather, it sees and knows itself, and is the primary <margin>C</margin> knower. But the One, just as it is above Intellect, is also above knowledge. Since it lacks nothing, it has no need of knowledge; rather, knowledge itself is placed in the second level of nature. For knowledge is a "certain one thing," but the One is "the One itself," not just "a certain one thing." For if it were "a certain one thing," it would no longer be the absolute One. For that which is called "itself" stands above—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>If it subsists, it leads a quiet life in itself. Otherwise, it is moved before it is moved, and thinks before it thinks. Or, its first state will still be imperfect, being only an impulse toward something. But if we speak according to reason, we shall say that activity flows from it, as if from the sun. A certain light, then, we may think of <margin>B</margin> as the whole intelligible nature, while the One stays standing upon the intelligible world, reigning over it, not pushing out from itself that which shines, but allowing another light to be from itself. This light shines while the One remains in the intelligible. And since it is from the One, it is not separated from it; yet again, it is not the same as it. It is not such a thing as to be without essence, nor is it blind; rather, it sees and knows itself, and is the primary <margin>C</margin> knower. But that which is "beyond Intellect" is also beyond knowledge. It needs nothing, and thus it does not even need to know. Rather, "to know" exists in the secondary nature. For knowing is "a something," but the One is the thing itself, not "a certain something." If it were "a certain something," it would not be the One itself; for the "itself" is added to the "something."
->this is what is called something.<-

#### Intelligence is not to be added to the Good itself, which can be understood by no created intellect, however high. Chapter XIII.

*The nature of the Good itself and of intelligence are so different, as we have said, that the former is the most universal and desires nothing, while the latter desires the Good. Likewise, the opposite of intelligence is madness, but the opposite of the Good is evil; yet since madness and evil are essentially the same, it follows that intelligence and the Good are not the same. Therefore, when you add intelligence to the Good, you seem to see another and different thing, judging the Good to be lacking and a sort of composite. This paradox—that the first principle is above essence, life, and intelligence—is offered by Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century Christian philosopher who used Plotinus's logic to describe God as "super-essential" and beyond all names.</note>, who adds further that the One enjoys itself in a way that is "more than intellectual," which we call "super-intellectual." He also says that it "pre-knows" in an ineffable way beyond and above intellect, as if it enjoys itself through touch rather than vision. For intelligence is a kind of vision, and it does not exist by saying something about itself, but simply by being what it is. If by some condition one could proceed through the levels of intelligence to the Good itself, one should not imagine an intellect that needs intelligence, nor intelligence which is the act of the intellect regarding the Good, but rather the Good itself toward which intelligence turns. Or perhaps it is the light itself that intelligence seeks, in which a perfected intelligence finds its limit—a light that exists not in the intelligence, but in itself. This clarity is not "seeing" in the proper sense, nor is it blind like one deprived of the good of vision; just as vision itself does not "see" properly, yet is not blind. Truly, the clarity that is the cause of all vision is much further removed from the privation of sight than sight itself is. Nor is this clarity determined by the genus of intellection. For that which is above all and the cause of all is not defined by any of the things it causes. It is not defined by essence, life, or intelligence, nor by intellectual clarity, but by clarity itself existing simply through itself and in itself, the cause of every act of clarity. It is a singular power, an effective act of powers, the maker of acts. Even if the Soul has no hands or feet, yet because it does not need them and has a more eminent power that generates them, it is said to be neither maimed nor lame. By similar reasoning, reason is not blind even if it has no eyes, and the mind is not irrational even if it never reasons; for it possesses in an instant what reason seeks over time. Nor is God "mindless" even if He has no mind: for He is everything that the mind strives to have—or rather, to become.*

### WHEREFORE it is truly ineffable.

<margin>A</margin>Whatever you say of it, you will be speaking of "something" specific. But that which is above all things and above the most venerable Mind, being set apart from all things, has no true name, nor is it any of those things. Indeed, there is no name for it at all, because nothing can be said of it. We only attempt to signify something about it to ourselves as best we can. Yet when we are in doubt, saying that it does not perceive itself, or that it does not take notice of itself, or <margin>B</margin> that it does not know what it is at all, we must consider that whenever we say such things, we are being pulled toward the opposites. For we are doing as much as we can—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>THEREFORE it is truly ineffable <note>original Greek: "arrēton"; meaning that which cannot be spoken or expressed in words.</note>. For whatever you say, you will be naming "something." But that which is beyond all things, beyond even the most holy Mind, is separated among all things; it has no other true name. It is not even among all the things that have a name, because nothing can be said of it. But as far as it is possible for us to signify it, we attempt to speak of it. But when we are at a loss, [saying it has] no sensation in itself, and <margin>B</margin> does not follow itself, nor know itself... then we must remember that in saying these things, we are being turned to the opposites. For much—

# BOOK THREE.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...[If we grant it knowledge], we make Being itself a multiplicity; for as we introduce the One as something to be known, and attribute knowledge to it, we imply that it requires an act of understanding. And if understanding were to coexist with it, then it would be unnecessary for it to apply intelligence to itself. For intelligence <note>original: "νοεῖν" (Greek) / "intelligentia" (Latin)</note> seems to be a kind of collective awareness <note>original: "συναίσθησις" (Greek) / "consensus" (Latin); the idea that consciousness is a "feeling together" of many parts.</note> of a whole, where many parts come together into one, such as when something understands itself—which is the primary and proper form of intelligence. Each thing is simply what it is, <margin>B</margin> and it seeks nothing further. But if intelligence is directed toward external things, it will be deficient, and it will not be the primary form of intelligence. That which is entirely <term>simple<note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "simple" means "without parts" or "not composed of anything else." It is the highest state of being.</term> and truly self-sufficient needs nothing. But that which is self-sufficient only in a secondary way <note>referring to the Intellect, which comes after the One</note>, needing itself, surely requires an understanding of itself. That which is deficient in relation to itself achieves self-sufficiency through the whole; by gathering sufficiency from all its parts, it lives with itself and turns toward itself through the act of understanding. For indeed, collective awareness <margin>C</margin> is the perception of something that is made of many parts, as the name itself testifies. Furthermore, because intelligence is prior [to the things it knows], it clearly reflects the one who understands—who is a multiplicity—back into himself. Even if such a being says only this, "I am Being," it says it as one who has made a discovery, and it speaks reasonably, for <term>Being<note>original: "ὄν" (Greek) / "ens" (Latin). In this system, "Being" implies the world of forms and ideas, which is "many," unlike the "One" which is above Being.</note></term> is many. For when it directs itself toward the simple and says, "I am Being," it fails to reach either itself or Being. It does not speak of Being as if it were a stone <margin>D</margin> when it speaks truly, but rather utters many things in a single word.
For this "to be," which is truly being, is not called such as if it were a mere footprint of Being; rather, because it is an image that clings to the archetype, it must contain many things within itself. What then? Shall each of these parts not be understood? Certainly, if you wish to grasp each part as isolated and alone, you will not understand it; rather, you will have said that it merely "is." If this is how it stands, if there is something that is the most simple of all things, it does not possess an understanding of itself. For if it did, it would have to "be" in a certain way and in a certain place. Therefore, it neither understands itself, nor is there any intelligence of it anywhere.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...[If we grant it knowledge], we make Being itself a multiplicity; for while we introduce it as something to be known and attribute knowledge to it, we make it so that it lacks understanding. For if understanding were to coexist with it, it would be superfluous for it to apply intelligence to itself. For intelligence seems to be a certain consensus of a whole, where many things concur in one, as when something understands itself—which is the proper and chief form of <margin>B</margin> intelligence. But anything that is truly one is what it is, and seeks nothing further. But if intelligence is stretched out toward external things, it will be in need, and will not be the primary intelligence. That which is entirely simple and truly self-sufficient needs nothing; but that which is self-sufficient in the second degree, yet lacking of itself, this undoubtedly needs intelligence of itself. But that which is lacking toward itself makes itself sufficient by its whole; having obtained sufficiency from all its parts, it dwells with itself and turns into itself by understanding. Since indeed <margin>C</margin> collective awareness is the sensing of something consisting of many parts, which the name itself also testifies. Then intelligence, since it is prior, reflects the one understanding (who is a multiplicity) back into himself. For even if he says only this: "I am surely Being," he says this as one who has found it, and says it fittingly; for Being is many. For even when he tends toward something simple and says "I am Being," he does not reach either himself or Being and truth. For he does not speak of Being as if it were a stone <margin>D</term> when he speaks truly, but pronounces many things in a single statement. For this "to be," which is truly to be, is not called such as if it possessed a mere footprint of Being, nor is it [simply] Being; and therefore it ought to be called a kind of image related to the pattern, which undoubtedly embraces many things in itself. What then? Shall each of those things be understood in no way? Truly, if you wish to receive it set apart and alone, you will not understand it, but you will have said that it furthermore "has being." If this is the case, if there is something most simple of all, it has no intelligence of itself; for if it should have it, it would also have to "be" in some manner and some place. Therefore, it neither understands itself, nor is there any intelligence of it anywhere.

> Since the intellect does not exclude multiplicity (which the One itself does exclude), and therefore the One itself is more eminent than the intellect because it is simpler, it follows that we are by no means able to grasp or explain the One through the intellect.
->Chapter 14.<-

> Nevertheless, we speak of it, as Parmenides <note>A Greek philosopher who argued that reality is a single, unchanging "One."</note> and Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist who used "negative theology" to describe God by what He is NOT.</note> say, through negations and relations. For we possess it in a certain way, insofar as we have a certain unity as the head of our mind, in the character of the divine unity; by this we then touch the divine unity, when we are formed by our mind, and through this divine mind we are alienated from ourselves, and having now been made prophets.

---

<margin>A</margin>
HOW then do we speak of it?
Certainly, we say something *about* it, yet we do not say *it* itself. We have neither knowledge nor intelligence of it. How then do we speak of it, if we do not possess it? Is it because, even if we do not possess it by knowledge, we do not for that reason lack it entirely? Rather, we possess it in such a way that we are able to speak about it, but are by no means able to speak it forth <note>original: "eloqui" (Latin); to fully express its essence in words.</note>. For we are accustomed to pronounce what it is not; but what it is, <margin>B</margin> we are accustomed to do [only] regarding it. Yet nothing prevents us from possessing it, even though we are not able to explain it.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
IN what way then do we speak of it?
Truly we say something about it, yet we do not say the thing itself; we have neither knowledge nor intelligence of it. But in what way do we speak of it, if we do not have it? Because even if we do not have it by knowledge, we do not therefore have it in no way at all: but we have it thus, so that we can indeed speak of it, but are by no means able to fully express it. For we are accustomed to pronounce what it is not; but what it may be <margin>B</margin> we are accustomed to do in relation to it: yet nothing prohibits us from having it, although we are not able to explain it.

### PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK V.

should it subsist, it must rest entirely within itself. Otherwise, if it were moved before it began to move, or if it thought before it began to think, its very first act would be imperfect; for it would be nothing more than a mere impulse. But toward what could it possibly be carried? Or what could it have recently sought to attain? Indeed, it is more in accordance with reason to assert that a certain activity flows forth from that abiding source—just as light flows from the sun—namely, the **Intellect** <note>original: "intellectum" / "νοῦς" (Greek); in Neoplatonism, this is the second "hypostasis" or level of reality, representing the Divine Mind containing all forms.</note> and the entire nature of the intelligible world. The principle itself, however, remains at the very summit of the intelligible world, reigning there in stillness. It does not separate itself from the radiance that shines from it; or should we perhaps place one light above another light, which shines while staying forever within the intelligible? For that which shines out from it is neither severed from it, nor is it the same as it. Furthermore, it is not of such a kind that it lacks essence, nor is it a blind thing; rather, it sees and knows itself, and it is the primary "knower." But just as the first principle is beyond intellect, so too is it beyond knowledge. Just as it needs nothing, so it does not even need knowledge; instead, knowledge is situated in the second nature. For knowledge is a "certain thing," but the first principle is the **One itself**, not a "certain one." For if it were a "certain one," it would no longer be the One itself. For that which is called "itself" stands above that which is called "something."
