<margin>A</margin> ...it should subsist, it leads a life of quiet within itself. If there is no motion before motion, and no thought before thought, its first act would be incomplete, being only an impulse. Toward what, then, does it happen to rush? Rather, let us follow reason and state that an activity flows from it <margin>B</margin> like light from the sun—this is how we shall understand the entire intelligible nature. He himself stands at the summit of the intelligible, reigning over it, not casting out from himself that which has appeared, nor shall we make it another light beside him. But he shines while remaining in the intelligible. For it is not cut off from him, nor again is it the same as he. Nor is it such as to be without essence, nor like a blind thing, but seeing and knowing itself. And it is the primary knower. <margin>C</margin> But just as he is beyond intellect, so he is beyond knowledge. He has no need of anything, not even knowledge, which is a way for someone to know. Instead, knowing is in the second nature. For [knowledge] is a "this" and a knowing. But that which is the thing itself, and not a "this," would not be that which is "this" before the "this." For whenever there is a "this," it follows after.

## Intelligence is not to be added to the Good itself, since it can be understood by any created intellect, however high. Chapter XIII.

*The nature of the Good itself and of intelligence are so different, as we have said, that the former is most universal, while the latter is not at all; the former desires nothing, while the latter desires the Good. Likewise, the opposite of intelligence is madness, while the opposite of the Good is evil. Furthermore, madness and evil are essentially the same thing; therefore, intelligence and the Good are not the same. When, therefore, you attribute intelligence to the Good itself, you seem to be adding a second and different thing, judging the Good to be needy and as if it were a composite. This paradox—namely, that the first principle is above essence, life, and intelligence—is frequently asserted by **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A 5th-6th century Christian theologian who adapted Plotinus's ideas into "apophatic" or negative theology, where God is described by what He is NOT.</note>, who adds moreover that the principle enjoys itself in a certain "more-than-intellectual" way, which he calls "super-intellectual." Likewise, it "pre-understands" in an ineffable manner beyond and above the intellect, as if it enjoys itself through contact rather than through vision. For intelligence is a kind of vision; the principle does not act by saying something about itself, but simply by existing as that which it is. If, by proceeding through the steps of intelligence, one cannot reach the Good itself, one should not imagine an intellect that lacks intelligence, nor an intelligence that is merely the act of that intellect toward the Good. Rather, imagine the Good itself toward which intelligence tends—perhaps the light itself which intelligence seeks and in which a perfected intelligence finds its end—a light, indeed, not existing in this world, but within itself. This clarity is not "seeing" in the strict sense, nor is it "blind" as if deprived of the good of vision; just as vision itself neither "sees" in the strict sense nor is it blind. For the clarity that is the cause of all vision is much further removed from the privation of sight than sight itself is. Nor is this clarity determined by the category of intellection. For that which is the cause of all things is above all things, and cannot be defined by anything from the number of all things. Therefore, it is not defined by essence, life, or intelligence, nor by intellectual clarity, but by that clarity itself existing simply by itself in itself, the cause of the act of every power. It is imagined, however, as the effective power of powers, the creator of acts. Even if the Soul lacks hands and feet, yet because it does not need them and possesses the generative power of these things in a more eminent way, it is not called "maimed" or "lame." By similar reasoning, reason is not "blind" even if it has no eyes, nor is the mind "irrational" even if it never reasons; for it possesses in a single whole what reason seeks through time. Nor is God "insane" <note>original: "amens"</note> even if He has no mind; for He is that very thing which the mind tries to possess, or rather, to become.*

---

FOR WHICH REASON it is truly ineffable <note>original: "ἄῤῥητον" (Greek); literally "unspeakable," a core concept in Neoplatonism meaning that the One cannot be captured by language.</note>. For whatever you might say, you will be saying "something." But that which is above all things and above the most venerable Mind, being set apart from all, has no other true name, nor is it any of all things. Absolutely no name belongs to it, because nothing can be said of it; but we, as far as we are able, try to signify something about it to ourselves. However, when we are thus in doubt, saying for example, "thus it does not feel itself," or "thus it does not take notice of itself," or "thus it does not know what it is at all," we must certainly consider that whenever we say such things, we are being pulled toward the opposites. For we do as much as we can...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> THEREFORE it is truly ineffable; for whatever you say, you will say "something." But that which is beyond all, and beyond the most venerable intellect, is the only truth among all things, not being a name for it but something else; it has no name among all things, because nothing is according to it. But as it is possible for us to signify it, we attempt to speak of it. <margin>B</margin> When we are at a loss, [asking if there is] perception in himself, or if he does not follow himself, or does not know himself... but it is necessary to keep in mind that in saying these things, we drag ourselves toward the opposites. ### BOOK THREE <note>original: "LIBER TERTIVS"; likely referring to the third book within the Fifth Ennead in this specific edition's arrangement.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> If we suggest that the One possesses knowledge, and in making it a knower we grant it the act of knowing, we actually make it deficient in its act of thinking. For if thought were inherent to it, thinking would be a superfluous addition. Indeed, thought seems generally to be a sort of shared consciousness <note>original: "consensus" / "συναίσθησις" (synaisthesis); a "joint-perception" or "feeling-together" that implies multiple parts awareness of each other.</note> of a whole, occurring when many parts come together into one, or when something thinks itself—which is the primary and proper form of thinking. But each thing, in itself, is simply what it is <margin>B</margin> and seeks nothing. If, however, thought is directed toward external things, it is needy and is not the primary form of thought. But that which is entirely simple and truly self-sufficient requires nothing. That which is "secondarily" self-sufficient, yet lacks itself, is the thing that needs to think itself. This thing, being deficient in relation to itself, is rendered self-sufficient by the whole; having acquired sufficiency from all its parts, it dwells with itself and turns toward itself in thought. For even <margin>C</margin> "shared consciousness" is the perception of many things, as the name itself testifies. Since Intellect is prior, it reflects the thinker back into himself as a "multitude." Even if it were to say only "I am Being," it says this as one who has discovered it, and says it appropriately, for Being is a multitude. For when it aims at something simple and says "I am Being," it does not reach itself, or Being, or the Truth. For it does not say "Being" as if it were a stone <note>i.e., a simple, inanimate object without internal complexity</note> when it speaks truly, but expresses many things in a single word. This "Being," which is "truly being," is not merely a trace of the "One," which <margin>D</margin> is not even "Being." Therefore, it must be described as an image compared to a model; it undoubtedly encompasses many things within itself. What then? Will each of these things not be understood? Certainly, if you wish to grasp a thing as isolated and alone, you will not understand it; for Being itself is a multitude in itself. And if you should say anything else besides this, it still possesses Being. If this is the case—if there is something that is the most simple of all things—it does not possess a thought of itself. For if it did, it would also have to "be" in some specific way and in some specific place. Therefore, it neither thinks, nor is there any thought of it to be found anywhere.

---

> Since the intellect does not exclude the multitude which the "One" itself excludes, and because the "One" is more eminent than the intellect by virtue of its simplicity, it follows that we are entirely unable to grasp or explain it through the intellect.
->Chapter XIV<-
> Nevertheless, we speak about it, as Parmenides and Dionysius <note>Referring to the Greek philosopher Parmenides and the Christian mystic Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, both of whom argued that God/The One can only be described by what He is NOT (apophatic theology).</note> say, through negations and relations. We possess it in a certain way, insofar as we have a certain unity as the "head" of our mind—a character of the divine unity—by which we touch the divine unity when we are formed by our mind, and through this divine mind we are drawn out of ourselves and become like prophets.

---

<margin>A</margin> In what way, then, do we speak of it? Certainly, we say something *about* it, yet we do not speak the thing itself. We have neither knowledge nor intellectual grasp of it. But how can we speak of it if we do not possess it? Even if we do not possess it through knowledge, it does not mean we do not possess it at all. We possess it in such a way that we can speak *about* it, even if we are entirely unable to express the thing itself. We are accustomed to naming what it is not, but not what it is. Therefore, we usually speak of it from things that come after it. Yet nothing prevents us from "having" it, even if we cannot explain it.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the ultimate principle (the One) cannot think because thought requires a division between the thinker and the object of thought. He explains that we can only describe the One through "negations"—stating what it is not—rather than through direct definition.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the "One," the ultimate source in Plotinus's system, and how it gives rise to the "Intellect" (the realm of forms and thought) without losing its own absolute simplicity. # PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

<margin>A</margin> Truly, just as those who are divinely inspired and possessed <note>original: "divinitus afflantur, atq; rapiuntur" / "ἐνθουσιῶντες καὶ κάτοχοι" (enthousiantes kai katokhoi); refers to a state of being filled with a god or "taken over" by a higher power.</note> perceive that they have something greater within themselves, even if they do not know exactly what it is—and from those very movements that stir them, they speak and receive a certain sense of the power that moves them, being distinct from the mover—so we also seem to stand in relation to that ultimate Source. Whenever we possess a <term>pure mind</term><note>The "pure mind" or "pure intellect" refers to the state of the soul when it has stripped away worldly distractions to mirror the divine Intellect.</note> and rely on it to speak as an oracle, we recognize that this is the internal intellect which is the author of essence and other things of the same rank. Yet, we also realize that the Source is not these things at all, but something more excellent than what we call <term>Being</term><note>original: "ens" / "ὄν" (on); the realm of things that "are," which for Neoplatonists is the world of forms, not the material world.</note>, and fuller and greater than this very thing we name "Being." For that which is above is superior to speech, reason, mind, and sense; it provides these things, yet it is not these things itself.
<margin>B</margin>

->The thinking Being itself is born from the One, just as the light nearest the Sun comes from the inner light of the Sun. Chapter XV.<-

*But just as from a nature that has neither eyes nor feet, eyes and feet are nonetheless generated through a higher power, so from the One itself—which possesses no specific form of essence, life, mind, or intelligence—these things arise by way of eminence. But how does the "many" come immediately from the "most simple"? Because that which is created by Unity itself is indeed something, yet it is not Unity itself. Therefore, that Unity <note>Referring to the first emanation, the Intellect.</note> is a certain multitude; it is both a single thing, yet less "one" than the Source itself, and therefore manifold. It possesses something of the Source, yet by declining from it, it now turns out to be multiple. Whatever exists after the "First" is in some way composite, and it receives its being and is preserved in it both by the unity of its parts and by their mutual union. The "First" itself is rightly Unity itself, for the definition of Unity and the definition of Being are not the same. To Unity, "multitude" is opposed; to Being, "non-being" is opposed. Nor is the definition of Being superior to Unity; otherwise, Unity would be multiple by participating in Being. Conversely, the definition of Being does not exist through itself without Unity; otherwise, Being would not become "one." Unity is therefore superior to Being; indeed, it is (if I may say so) supremacy and primality itself, since the definition of Unity and Simplicity is the same. The simpler things are in any genus, the more "prior" they are, and vice versa. However, the multitude born closest to Unity is equally the first of all and the "all-formed" multitude, most unified with itself; therefore, in any one of its forms, all the other forms of the same kind are somehow comprehended. Thus, the divine mind is "one-all" <note>original: "vnum omnia"; the concept that in the Intellect, every part contains the whole.</note>. The soul born from this is not so much "one-all" as it is "one-many." Plotinus does not entirely deny that "all things" are in the First, but they are not distinct there by absolute definitions. However, in the "Second" (the Intellect), he places the distinction of forms which differ from each other by absolute definitions.*

<margin>A</margin> BUT in what way does it provide such things? Is it by possessing them, or rather by not possessing them? But if it does not have them, how can it provide them? If it does have them, then it is not simple. If, therefore, it handed these things down without having them, how did the multitude flow from it? One might perhaps grant that a "simple one" flows from it, though it is still asked how even that comes from what is entirely One. Yet, one may say that it flows from it just as brilliance shines out from a light. But how the "many" <margin>B</margin> come from it is a further question. Certainly, that which is made by the Source ought not to be the same as the Source. If it is not the same, and certainly not better—for what is better than the One, or entirely superior?—then it must be inferior to it, which means it is more needy. But what is more needy than the One, except that which is "not-one"? This, therefore, is already many, yet it desires the One: it is thus "one-many." For the One itself preserves everything that is not one, and everything is whatever it is through the One. For unless it becomes "one," even if made of many parts, no one can call it a "being"—even though one could call each part what it is individually. Because each thing becomes "one," it becomes in some way the same in itself. But that which does not have "many" within itself is not "one" by participation in the One, but exists as the One itself and is not derived from another. It is clear that this is the very thing from which the others have their unity, some more closely, others more remotely. But that which is closest to it <margin>C</margin> becomes most "the same" in itself—

<column-break/>

But just as those who are divinely inspired and become possessed—to this extent they know they have something greater in themselves, even if they do not know what it is—from the things by which they are moved, they also speak, and from these they receive a certain perception of the mover, since the movers are different from them. So we too are in danger of being in relation to that Source, whenever we possess a pure intellect. Using this as an oracle <note>original: "ὡς ἦτός" (hos etos); likely a corruption or variant of "ὡς ἦτορ" (heart) or "χρησμῳδός" (prophetic), here translated following the Latin sense of 'vaticinamur'.</note>, we find that there is an inner mind, which provides essence and the other things that belong to this rank. But the Source itself is not these things, but something better than this which we call Being. Indeed, it is more and greater than what we call Being, because it provides these things while being better than speech, mind, and sense, and not being these things itself.

BUT how did it provide them? By having them, or by not having them? But if it does not have them, how did it provide them? If it provides them by having them, it is not simple; if by not having them, how did the multitude come from it? For if a simple thing came from it, one might perhaps give a reason, even if one were to ask how it came from the entirely One. But nonetheless, one can speak of it as the radiance that comes out from a light. But how many, or these things? That which comes from that Source was destined—if not the same—certainly not to be better; for nothing is better than the One. If it is not better, it is worse; if worse, it is not-one, and therefore many. Yet it nonetheless desires the One, and so it is "many-one." For how is everything that is not-one preserved? It is what it is by not failing to become one. Even if it were from many parts, one could not yet call it a "being" [unless it were one]. And one can say each thing is what it is by the fact that each of them is said to be, and is yet itself. For that which does not have "many" in itself is not "one" by participation in the One, but is the One itself, not through another, but because it is this. Wherefore also the other things [get their unity], some near and some far.

It clarifies that while the One is the source of all Being, it is itself "beyond Being" and beyond human categories like speech or reason.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "One" as the absolute source. The previous page established that the source of all things is superior to the Mind and Being itself. This page explores how the One, through its "overflowing" power, gives rise to multiplicity without being diminished, and how everything that follows it participates in unity.</meta>

<page-num>511</page-num>
<header>BOOK THREE <note>In this edition, "Book Three" refers to the specific grouping of Plotinus's treatises within the Enneads, likely the third book of the Fifth Ennead.</note></header>

Since the self-same exists, and that which follows it, it is clear that its multitude is itself everywhere. For even though it is a multitude, it nonetheless exists in the same thing. One cannot distinguish them, because all things are together. Since each of the things arising from it participates in life, they are many. For it is impossible to show that it is all things in itself. But that Source itself is not these things, because it is a great principle <note>original: "μεγάλη ἀρχή" (megalē archē); the foundational starting point or source of all reality.</note>. For a principle is not all things, but truly one. But that which follows the principle—the One as it were running over—becomes all things by participating in the One. And whatever belongs to it, is again both all things and not. What then are "all things"? Those things of which it is the principle. But how is that the principle of all things? Is it because as a cause it preserves them, making each of them to be one? Or is it because it brought them into existence? How so? By having them before they were? But it has been said that in this way there will be a multitude. But does it hold them such that they are not yet distinguished? Those things in the second rank <note>Refers to the "Intellect" or "Nous," which is the first emanation from the One.</note> were distinguished by <term>Reason</term><note>original: "λόγῳ" (logō); here referring to the formative principle or rational structure of reality.</note>. For it is already an activity. But the Source is the power of all things. But what is the manner of this power? For that which is called power in the sense of <term>matter</term><note>original: "ὕλη" (hyle); the passive substrate that receives form.</note> is so because it receives; for it is passive. But the Source is the opposite, characterized by acting. How then does it act upon what it does not have? For it does not act by chance. Even if one does not think it acts by planning, it acts nonetheless. It has been said that if anything comes from the One, it is something other than it. Being other, it is not one. For if it were, it would be that Source. If it is not one, it is necessarily two, and already a multitude. For it already contains the "other" and the "same," and quality, and the rest. And that the One is not that thing has been demonstrated. But that it is a multitude, and a multitude of the kind seen in what follows it, is worth investigating; and the necessity of what follows it must also be sought.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> And that it exists after itself is evident because the multitude of this is a certain unity everywhere. For although it is a multitude, it nonetheless exists in the same, nor is it possible to distinguish them, since all things exist together. Furthermore, any one of those things which come from it, insofar as it participates in life, is "one-many" <note>original: "vnum multa"; the Neoplatonic concept that individual beings are a composite of unity and multiplicity.</note>. For it cannot show itself as "one-all." But the Source from which this arises is "one-all," because it is derived from a great principle. For its principle is itself in reality and truly one.

<margin>B</margin> But that which follows from the principle, because the One is in a way pregnant and overflowing, becomes all things, but meanwhile it is a participant in the One; and whatever is in it is, in turn, all things and one. Which "all things" then? Namely, all things of which that is the principle. But how is that the principle of all things? Is it from the fact that the One itself preserves them, specifically while it brings it about that each of them is one? Or is it also because it procreated them? But how? Is it from the fact that it possessed them

<margin>C</margin> beforehand? Truly it has already been said that it would thus be many; but indeed, it holds all things as if they were not yet distinguished from one another. But those things which are in the second rank are distinguished by reason; for they are now perceived in <term>actuality</term><note>original: "actu"; in contrast to "potency" (potentia), this refers to things fully realized and distinct.</note>. But the Source is the power <note>original: "potestas" / "δύναμις" (dynamis); the potential or capacity that precedes actualized being.</note> of all things. But what is the mode of this power? For it is not said to be "in power" in the way that matter is, because matter receives; for that which receives is passive, and thus power stands in the opposite relation to that which is efficient. In what way, then, does it make what it does not have?

<margin>D</margin> For it must not be thought to have acted by chance, nor even by reflecting within its mind on what was to be done, as if it then acted in that way. It has therefore already been said that if anything flows from the One, it is something other than it; and being other, it is not the One. For that was the Source itself. If, however, it is not one, then it is two, and necessarily now many; for it now possesses within itself the "other" and the "same," and quality, and the rest. And that which depends on it is not the One itself which pertains to the higher realm, as has perhaps already been demonstrated. But whether it is a multitude, and a multitude such as is beheld in the following rank, is still to be doubted; and the necessity by which the following rank proceeds from it must be further investigated.

---

*The more excellent a cause is, the more things it produces. The First, therefore, effects all things; likewise, in any genus, the first is the simplest. The First of all things is thus so simple that it is not a certain simple thing, but simplicity itself.*

### Chapter XVI.

*Likewise, just as the nature that generates the body is not the body, so the intellect, the father of the soul, is not the soul; so the Good, the father of the intellect itself, is not the intellect, nor the intelligible world, but something simpler and more sublime, and similarly higher than Being. For the properties of Being are rest and motion; but to be moved is desired not simply, but toward the Good; to stand still also is desired not simply, but in the Good. In Being itself, therefore, rest, motion, life, and intelligence are not the Good itself, but something "good-formed" <note>original: "boniforme"; having the shape or character of the Good without being the Good itself.</note>, insofar as they turn toward the Good itself and are filled by it: and in that same Good they find their greatest rest.*

---

That it is necessary for something to exist after the First has been said elsewhere; and generally that it is a power, and an inestimable power. And this must be believed from all other things, since there is nothing, even among the lowest things, which does not have the power of generating. At present, it must be said that among those things which are begotten, the process does not lie toward the higher, but toward the lower; and that indeed in such a way that one proceeds step by step into a greater multitude. Therefore, the principle of each thing is everywhere...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> IT IS NECESSARY indeed that something exist after the First, as we have said elsewhere, and that it is entirely a power—an inestimable power, I say. I assert this from all other things, since there is nothing, even among the lowest, which does not have the power of generating. <margin>B</margin> In the present, it must be said that among those things which are begotten, the path does not lie toward higher things, but toward lower; and this is so in such a way that one proceeds gradually into a greater multitude, and therefore the principle of individual things is everywhere...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the "One"—the absolute, simple source of all reality. Having previously discussed how the One precedes the "Intellect" (the realm of thought and forms), Plotinus here examines how multiplicity arises from this singular simplicity and why the Intellect must look back toward the Good to find its perfection.</meta>

<page-num>514</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK V.</header>

<margin>A</margin> It is more simple, and it remains the same in itself while a progression into many things is granted. For this reason, that which produced the sensible world is not the sensible world itself, but exists as the <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus" (Latin) / "νοῦς" (Greek); the second hypostasis in Plotinus's system, representing the realm of pure thought and the Platonic Forms.</note> and the intelligible world. Therefore, in the same way, that which is superior to the intelligible world and is its origin is neither Intellect nor the world to be understood, but is simpler than the Intellect and simpler than the intelligible world. For a "many" does not come from a "many," but this "many" proceeds from that which is not many. If that origin were also many, it would certainly not be the principle, but would require some other thing superior to it. Therefore, all things must be gathered back to that which is truly One, beyond all number and any kind of simplicity—if indeed it is truly simple—and in that place we must finally come to a rest. <margin>B</margin> Furthermore, we must consider by what reasoning that which was made by the One is now a manifold <term>Reason</term> <note>original: "ratio" (Latin) / "λόγος" (Greek); here meaning the formative principle or the unfolding rational plan of the universe.</note> and encompasses all things, while the One itself is not a "Reason." If it is not a "Reason," under what condition does a "Reason" come from "Non-Reason"? And in what way does that which is <term>good-formed</term> <note>original: "boniforme"; having the shape, quality, or character of the Good.</note> proceed from the Good, or what does it possess from the Good that it should be called "good-formed"? <margin>C</margin> Is it perhaps judged to have a certain good-form because it possesses a certain stable state according to the same things and remains in a similar way? But what do these things contribute toward the Good? Indeed, we are accustomed to require such a habit—staying according to the same things and in a similar way—only when goods are present. And we desire that thing first, from which one should never depart, because it is Good; but if it were not good, it would be better to depart from it. <margin>D</margin> Must we then desire that as our good: namely, to live always in the same way by staying willingly in the Good itself? If, therefore, this is what the mind most desires—to live in such a way—then it surely requires nothing further. It is established that this habit of always staying the same is sought because the things present are sufficient. But with all things now present to this Mind, living is to be sought as the highest goal; present in such a way, I say, that they are not different from the Mind itself. <margin>E</margin> If, therefore, all life is present to it—a life, I say, that is vigorous and clear, all soul now perfected in this, and the universal mind—then nothing of either life or intelligence is lacking to it. It is therefore self-sufficient and desires nothing further. But if it requires nothing, it already possesses within itself what it would otherwise seek. It has, therefore, the Good within itself—a good, I say, such as we have called life and mind, or some other thing happening to these. <margin>F</margin> Truly, if this were the Good itself, nothing would be superior to these things. But if the Good itself is above these, then life turning toward it and leaning entirely upon it—possessing its substance from it and stretching itself entirely toward it—will surely find its good there; for that is its principle. It is necessary, therefore, that the Good be more excellent than life and mind. For only in this way will life, vigorous in mind, turn toward it, as it is a certain imitation of that which exists in the Good, according to which it lives and follows it. Its intelligence will also turn toward it as a certain imitation of that which exists in the Good, whatever that Good itself may finally be.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It is simpler than the Intellect itself. Therefore, that which made the sensible world would not be the sensible world itself, but mind and an intelligible world. And the first thing of this, which generated it, is a still newer intelligible world, yet it is simpler than mind and simpler than the intelligible world. For the "many" does not come from the "many," but the "many" follows in succession from the "not-many." For if the origin were itself many, it would not be the principle, but something else would be before it. It is necessary, therefore, to come together into the truly One, outside of all multitude and that simplicity which is according to itself—if indeed it is truly simple. But how is the thing generated from it a "many Reason" and all things? Or rather, what I mean is clearly the "Reason." But if the Source is not "Reason," how then does "Reason" come from "Non-Reason"? And how does that which is "good-formed" come from the Good? For what does it have from the Good that it is called "good-formed"? Is it because it has that which is according to the same things and in the same way? And what are these things in relation to the Good? For we seek that "same way" because of the Good; or rather, we seek that which it will not be necessary to depart from because it is Good. But if not, it is better to depart. Is it therefore living in the same way, remaining in that which is free of stain voluntarily? If this living were not desirable, then clearly it would seek nothing. It seems, therefore, that what it seeks is this "same way," because the things present seem sufficient; but with all things already present to it, life is the thing to be sought. And let them be present, being other things that it possesses, if indeed all life is there—life that is clear and entirely perfect—and in it is mind and soul and every mind, and nothing of life or mind is distant from it. It is therefore self-sufficient and seeks nothing. But if it seeks nothing, it has in itself what it would have sought if it were not present. It has, therefore, the Good in itself. Or what is it that exists, which we might say life and mind need? Or some other thing that happens in addition to these? But if this is the Good, nothing would be beyond these. But if the Good is beyond them, then clearly that which is toward it—clinging entirely to it, having its existence from it, and living toward it—is the good. For that is its principle. It was necessary, therefore, for that Source to be better than life and mind. For in this way, the life in it will turn toward the Source, being a certain imitation of that which is in the Source, by which it thus lives. And the mind in it is a certain imitation of that which is in the Source, because this thing is such as it is in the Source.

---

*Neither is essence perfect, unless in life; nor is life perfect, unless in intellect; nor is intellect perfect, unless it depends on the multitude of all these things: namely, from the Good itself.* Chapter XVII.

*The Intellect, therefore, requires many things so that it may be absolute; and where it is absolute, it is manifold. Therefore, it depends on a superior thing that—*

He explains that life and mind find their perfection only by turning back toward and imitating this absolute, self-sufficient principle.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "One" (the Good) as the ultimate source. The previous page established that the One is simpler than the Intellect and the origin of all multiplicity. Here, the author describes the practical experience of reaching this source through a "sudden light" and the stripping away of mental distractions, moving from rational discourse to direct intuition.</meta>

### BOOK THREE.

[...something] sufficient in itself, and most simple. Nor is being simply desired, but well-being; nor is living in any way desired, but well-being; nor understanding in any way, but well, and of good things, and in such a way as will be profitable to you. Nor do we desire truth simply: for we do not desire a true fever, but the true good. Therefore, the Good itself is the end <note>The "end" here means the ultimate purpose or goal (Latin: *finis*; Greek: *telos*).</note> and the principle of all things. The end of our life is to see the Good itself through itself: but because this is most stable and most simple, we do not reach it by the discourse of reason, nor by the action of the intelligence composing or discerning, but by a certain sudden and simple intuition. 

The sign of this enjoyment for us is when, beyond the usual and by no customary machinery of the mind, a light suddenly flows into us—that is, a joyful clarity, which is a certain splendor of the clarity subsisting in itself, which is God himself. It flows in, moreover, when, devoted to Him by His grace, we take away all things—that is, inclinations toward all things from the appetite, images from the phantasy <note>Phantasy refers to the faculty of the mind that deals with sensory images and imagination.</note>, discourses from the reason, intellectual species <note>The "species" are the mental forms or concepts used in abstract thought.</note>, and compositions and distinctions from the intellect. Concerning these things enough has been said by Plato and by us in the great letter of Plato <note>Referring to the *Seventh Letter* of Plato, a key text for Neoplatonists regarding the sudden nature of spiritual insight.</note>.

What, then, is better than the most prudent life—one that is without stumbling and without sin—and better than a Mind possessing all things, and better than all life and every Mind? If we say it is the power that made these things, and consider how it made them, and if nothing better appears to us, our reasoning will not proceed to another thing but will stop right there. 

But one must ascend, for many other reasons, and because self-sufficiency exists outside of all these things. For each of these things, clearly, is not the "One" itself; for in that each thing is what it is, it partakes of the One by having a share in it. It is not the "One" itself, just as that which a thing partakes in is not the thing itself; rather, the One is the cause of being for all things and of all things together. But if it makes each thing to be, and if by the presence of the One the multitude itself becomes self-sufficient, and if it is clearly the creator of essence and self-sufficiency, then that principle itself cannot be "essence," but must be beyond it, and beyond self-sufficiency. 

Is it enough, then, to say these things and be done, or is the soul still in labor, even more so than before? Perhaps, then, it is necessary for the soul now to give birth, having rushed toward the One and being filled with the pains of labor which it keeps hidden. But perhaps we might find some charm <note>original: "ἐπῳδὴν" (Greek); a "healing song" or incantation used as a metaphor for a philosophical argument that calms the soul.</note> from outside to soothe the labor—perhaps even from what has already been said, if one were to chant it often. What then is this other, new charm? It runs over all the truths we partake in, yet it still escapes anyone who wishes to speak of it or think of it. Since the mind, in order to say anything, must grasp one thing after another, it involves a transition; but in every transition there is some kind of discourse. Yet it is enough to touch it intellectually. And when one touches it, while the contact lasts, one is neither able to say anything nor has the leisure to speak; only later does one reason about it. One must believe they have seen it then, when the soul suddenly receives light. For this light is from Him and is Him. And then one must believe He is present, just as when some other god, called to someone's house, comes and illuminates it—for if he had not come, he would not have brought light. So too the soul is without light and without God until it is illuminated. But once illuminated, it has what it sought. And this is the true end for the soul: to touch that light...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> WHAT, then, is better than the wisest life, which cannot fall or err? What is better than the intellect embracing all things? And what is better than the whole of life and the whole of mind? If we answer that it is better which made these things, and how it made them, and if nothing superior to this presents itself to us, the discourse of our reason will not proceed to anything else, but will revolve in that same place. 

Nevertheless, we must progress higher, both for many other reasons and also because the self-sufficiency <margin>B</margin> gathered from all these things depends on something external, where surely each thing is in itself unworthy <note>Or "incomplete" in its own isolated nature.</note>; and also because each thing is a participant in the same One, and partakes of the One, as if it were not the One itself. What then is that thing in which this partakes? That which indeed causes this to be, and at the same time causes all things to be. But if it causes each thing to be, and if the presence of the One makes the multitude of this speaker <note>Likely referring to the soul or the rational principle that gives "voice" to variety.</note> become sufficient, then it is clearly the origin of all essence and sufficiency: itself not being essence, I say, but <margin>C</margin> superior even to this sufficiency. 

Tell me, then, do these things satisfy us, and is it permitted now to put an end to our questions? Or rather, is our soul still vexed as if in labor? And certainly it is now more vehemently spurred on. Perhaps, therefore, it is necessary now to prepare our soul, more ardently stirred toward the One itself, and shaken by the many pains of one in labor. However, it is better to help with certain "magical songs," as it were, if in some way we may find a chant helpful to this birth. Perhaps, indeed, from those things which have been said, if one should <margin>D</margin> chant them often, we shall finally achieve it. 

But what other song is there that is, as it were, new? Truly, the song itself, surpassing all the truths in which we ourselves participate, flees immediately if anyone wishes to speak or think it: for it is necessary for thought, in order to say something, to assume one thing and then another; whereby it certainly turns in a kind of discourse. But in that which is entirely simple, there can be no <margin>E</margin> discourse; it is enough, however, to touch it in a certain intellectual way. And it is necessary for the one touching it, while they touch it, to be entirely unable to speak anything, nor to have the leisure for speaking, but later to reason about it. 

One must believe, truly, that we have finally seen it when the soul has suddenly received light. For this light, I say, flows from the Good itself; this light is the Good itself. Then certainly we must believe it is present to us, just as when another God, at someone's invocation, enters a house and illuminates it entirely; otherwise, unless he entered, he would not illuminate it. So also the soul is empty of light, and empty of God; but when illuminated, it already has everything the mind sought. This, certainly, this is the true end for the soul: namely, to receive its light, and to see the One through the One itself, not through any other...

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD V.

->Column 1 (Translated from Latin)<-

...more simple, and remaining the same in itself, while it is given forth in a <margin>A</margin> progression into many things. Therefore, that which procreated the sensible world is not the sensible world, but is the intellect and the intelligible world <note>The "intelligible world" refers to the realm of pure thought or forms, as opposed to the "sensible world" we perceive with our senses.</note>; and so likewise, that which is superior to the intelligible world and its origin is neither intellect nor the world of thought, but is simpler than the intellect, and simpler than the intelligible world. For many does not come from many, but this "many" proceeds from that which is not many. For if that source were also many, it would surely not be the principle <note>original: *principium*; the first cause or starting point.</note>, but something else would be superior to it. All things must therefore be gathered into that which is truly One, beyond all number and any [degree of] simplicity: if indeed it truly be simple, and in it at last we must come to a halt. We must consider further by what reasoning that which was made by it is already <margin>B</margin> a "many" and an all-encompassing reason <note>original: *ratio*; in this context, it refers to the Greek *Logos*, the ordering principle of the universe.</note>, while that source is not reason. But if it is not reason, by what condition is reason from non-reason? And in what way does the "good-formed" <note>original: *boniforme*; having the shape or nature of the Good.</note> proceed from the Good, or what of it does it possess to be called good-formed? Is it then thought to have a certain <margin>C</margin> good-form because it has a certain stability according to the same things, and is in a similar condition? But what do these things contribute to the Good? Since we are accustomed to demand such a habit <note>Here, "habit" refers to a stable state of being or character.</note> according to the same and similarly-disposed things only when the "goods" are present; and we first desire that from which we should never depart, because it is good: but if it were not good, it would be better to depart from there. <margin>D</margin> Should we then desire it as the good, namely to live always in the same way, spontaneously remaining in the Good itself? If therefore this is most to be desired by the mind, namely to live thus, it surely requires nothing further, and it is certain that the habit of always being in a similar state is sought because present things are sufficient. But with all things now present to this mind, living is to be sought as the highest good: so present, I say, that they are not different from it. <margin>E</margin> If therefore all life is present to this—a life that is vigorous and clear—then all soul and the universal mind is now perfect in this, and nothing is lacking to it of life or intelligence. It is therefore self-sufficient, and desires nothing further. But if it requires nothing, it already possesses within itself what it would otherwise seek. It has therefore the Good in itself—a good of such a sort as we have called life and mind, or something else belonging to these. But if this be the Good itself, surely nothing will be <margin>F</margin> superior to these: but if the Good itself is above these, then life verging toward it and leaning entirely upon it, possessing its substance from there, and directing itself entirely toward it, will be good for this; for that is its principle. It is necessary, therefore, that it [the One] be more excellent than life and mind: for only thus will life, vigorous with mind, turn toward it, as a kind of imitation of what exists in that [the One], according to which it lives and follows. And the intelligence of this will turn as a kind of imitation of that which exists in that, whatever this itself may finally be.

<column-break/>

->Column 2 (Translated from Greek)<-

...more simple and the same. Therefore, in creating the <margin>A</margin> sensible world, it would not be the sensible world itself, but Intellect and the intelligible world. And that which generated this and is its leader is neither Intellect nor the intelligible world, but is one and more simple, and higher than the intelligible world. For the "many" does not come from the "many," but the "many" comes from that which is not many. For if that were many, it would not be the beginning, but something else would be before it. One must therefore collect all things into the truly One, outside of all plurality and all simplicity <note>Plotinus uses "simplicity" here to mean that the One is even more basic than our concept of "simple."</note>, if it is truly simple. But how is that which is produced from it a "many" and a "total reason" <note>original: *logos*.</note>, while that [the source] is clearly not reason? And if it is not reason, how does reason come from non-reason? and how does the "good-like" come from the Good? For what does it possess <margin>B</margin> that it is called good-like? Is it because it possesses the "always the same and in the same way"? And what do these have to do with the Good? For we seek the "same way" because of <margin>C</margin> the Good, or rather that from which one must not depart, because it is good. But if it were not, it would be better to depart. Is it then living in the same way, remaining [there] voluntarily? If this life is not to be loved, clearly it seeks nothing. It seems then that <margin>D</margin> this "same way" is sought because present things seem [sufficient]. But with all things already present to it, life is to be loved. and indeed let them be present, not as others to it; if indeed all life is there, and life is clear and all perfect, in it is Soul and all Intellect, and nothing of life or mind is absent from it. It is therefore self-sufficient in itself, and seeks nothing. But if it seeks nothing, it has in itself what it would seek if it were not present. It has the Good in itself. Or what is it that exists, which we must call life and mind? Or some other attribute <margin>E</margin> of these? But if this is the Good, then nothing would be beyond these. But if the Good is beyond them, then clearly life depends on that, having its existence from that, and living toward that. For that is its principle. Therefore, that [the One] is better than life and mind. For [mind] will turn toward that, and the life in it is a certain imitation of what is in that, <margin>F</margin> according to which it lives. And the mind in this is a certain imitation of what is in that, whatever this may be.

*Neither essence is perfect, except in life; nor life perfect except in intellect; nor intellect perfect except in the very multitude of all those things depending, namely from the Good itself. Chapter XVII.*

*Intellect therefore needs many things to be absolute: and where it is absolute, it is multiple. Therefore it depends on a superior which...*

It defines the Intellect's perfection as a state of self-sufficiency that nevertheless imitates and depends upon the superior, non-multiple Good.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the nature of the "One." The previous text explored how the Good is the primary cause. ### BOOK THREE.

...sufficient in itself, and most simple. For we do not desire "to be" in a simple sense, but to "be well"; not just to live in any way, but to live well; not to understand in any manner, but to understand well and to understand good things, so that it may be of benefit to you. We do not even wish for "truth" in a simple sense; for we do not desire a "true fever," but a "true good." Therefore, the Good itself is the end and the principle of all things. The end of our life is to see the Good itself through itself. But because this [the Good] is most stable and most simple, we do not reach it through the wandering path of reason <note>original: *rationis discursu*; this refers to "discursive reasoning," the step-by-step logic we use to move from one idea to another.</note>, nor by the action of the intelligence putting things together or taking them apart, but by a certain sudden and simple intuition. For us, the sign of this enjoyment is when, beyond our usual state and without any of the customary workings of our cleverness, a light suddenly flows into us. This is a joyful clarity, a certain radiance of the clarity that exists within itself, which is God himself. It flows in when, devoted to Him, by His grace we remove everything—that is, we strip away the inclinations toward all things from our desires, images from our imagination, reasonings from our logic, and intellectual forms, compositions, and distinctions from our intellect. Both Plato and we have said enough about these matters in Plato's great epistle <note>This likely refers to Plato's *Seventh Letter*, where he discusses the "sudden light" of philosophical understanding.</note>.

---

<column-break/>

->Column 1 (Translated from Greek)<-

<margin>A</margin>
What then is better than a life most wise, unerring, and without sin? What is better than a mind that possesses all things, or than all life and every mind? If we say it is that which made these things, and ask how it made them, and if nothing better appears to us, our reasoning will not go further but will stop right there. But we must ascend, both for many other reasons and because for this [the mind], self-sufficiency <note>original: *to autarkes*; the state of needing nothing else.</note> is something brought in from the outside.

<margin>B</margin>
For each of these things is clearly lacking the One; it possesses the likeness of the One and participates in the One, but it is not the One itself. What then is that which participates, which makes it both to exist and to be all things at once? If it makes each thing to exist, and if by the presence of the One the multitude becomes self-sufficient, then it is clearly the creator of being and self-sufficiency. That source itself would not be "being," but beyond being, and beyond self-sufficiency.

<margin>C</margin>
Is it enough, then, to say these things and be done? Or is the soul still in labor? Indeed, it is in labor even more. Perhaps it must now give birth, having rushed toward the One, filled with the pains of labor. But let us try to find a "spell" to chant against this pain, perhaps from the words already spoken, if one were to chant them often. Let it be so. What other new spell is there? For though it runs over all truths, even the truths we participate in, it still escapes the man who wishes to speak of it through thought.

<margin>D</margin>
For thought, in order to persuade, must take up one thing after another. This is a journey through steps <note>original: *diexodos*; a discursive path or "way through."</note>. But in things that are absolutely simple, there is no such journey. It is enough to touch it with the mind. But once having touched it, while one is touching it, one is completely unable to speak, nor has one the leisure to say anything. Only later can one reason about it. One must believe they have seen it then, when the soul suddenly receives light.

<margin>E</margin>
For this light is from Him and is Him. And then one must believe He is present, when, like another god, He comes into the house of someone who called Him and brings illumination. If He had not come, He would not have illuminated. Thus the soul is unlit and without God when He is absent; but once illuminated, it possesses what it sought. And this is the true end for the soul: to touch that light, and to see Him by that very light—not by the light of another, but by the light through which it sees.

<column-break/>

->Column 2 (Translated from Latin)<-

<margin>A</margin>
What indeed is better than a life most wise, which cannot slip and cannot err? What is better than an intellect embracing all things? And what is better than the whole of the mind? If we answer that it is that which made these things, and how it made them, and if nothing more excellent than itself occurs to us, the wandering of our reason will not proceed elsewhere, but will turn back upon itself. Nevertheless, we must progress higher, both for many other reasons and also because the self-sufficiency of the mind <margin>B</margin> is accumulated from external sources. There, every individual thing is in itself needy; for each participates in the same One, and it participates in the One because it is not the One itself. What then is that in which this participates? It is surely that which makes this to be, and to be all things at once. But if it makes each thing to exist, and by the presence of the One this speaking multitude becomes sufficient, then it is clearly the origin of all essence and sufficiency. I say it is not essence itself, but is even above essence and sufficiency.

<margin>C</margin>
Tell me, are these things enough for us, and may we now put an end to our questions? Or rather, is our mind still troubled, as if in the pains of childbirth? And certainly now it is more vehemently driven. Perhaps, therefore, we must prepare our mind to be more ardently moved toward Him, agitated by the many pains of labor. Nevertheless, it is better to help it with certain "songs of the magi" <note>original: *magorum carminibus*; here used metaphorically to mean philosophical incantations or persuasive truths.</note>, if in some way we might find a chant that assists this birth. Perhaps from these things that have been said, if one were to chant them <margin>D</margin> frequently, we shall finally attain it. But what other "new song" is there? Indeed, the song itself, overstepping all the truths in which we participate, flees immediately if anyone wishes to speak or think of it. For it is necessary for thought, in order to say something, to take up one thing and then another in the meantime; thus it is occupied in a certain "wandering" <note>original: *discursione*; discursive logic.</note>. But in that which is entirely simple, there can be <margin>E</margin> no wandering. It is enough, however, to touch it in a certain intellectual way. And it is necessary that the one touching it, while he touches it, is entirely unable to speak anything, nor has he the leisure for speaking, but only later can he reason about it. But we must believe we have finally seen it when the soul has suddenly received light. For this light—I say, this light—flows from the Good itself, and it is the Good itself. Then certainly we must believe it is present to us, when, like another God entering a house at someone's invocation, He illuminates it thoroughly. Otherwise, if He has not entered, He does not illuminate. Thus, the soul is empty of light and empty of God; but when illuminated, it already possesses entirely what it sought with its mind. This, certainly, is the true end for the soul: to receive His light, and to perceive Him by Himself, not by another's light.

The author describes the transition from logical reasoning to a "sudden illumination" that allows the soul to experience God directly.</summary>

<margin>A</margin>
...more simple, and the same remaining in itself, while a progression into many is produced. For this reason, that which created the sensible world <note>The physical world we perceive with our senses.</note> is not the sensible world itself, but is the intellect and the intelligible world <note>The "intelligible world" refers to the realm of pure ideas and forms that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses.</note>. Therefore, similarly, that which is superior to the intelligible world and is its origin is neither intellect nor the intelligible world, but something simpler than intellect, and simpler than the intelligible world. For "many" does not arise from "many," but this "many" proceeds from "not-many." If that source were also many, it surely would not be the principle, but something else would be superior to it.
<margin>B</margin>
Therefore, all things must be gathered toward that which is truly the One, outside all number and any kind of simplicity—if indeed it is truly simple, and in it at last our upward climb must be halted. Furthermore, we must consider by what reasoning that which was made by the One is already a "manifold rational principle" <note>original: *ratio multa*; in Neoplatonism, this refers to the complex logic or "Logos" that structures reality.</note> and indeed "every rational principle," while the One itself is not a rational principle. But if it is not a rational principle, under what condition does a rational principle arise from that which is not? And in what way does the "good-form" <note>original: *boniforme*; a technical term for things that share the quality or "shape" of the Good.</note> proceed from the Good, or by having what quality of the Good is it called "good-form"?
<margin>C</margin>
Is it then thought to have a certain "good-form" for the reason that it has a stable state, remaining the same and behaving in a similar way? But what do these things contribute to the Good? For we are only accustomed to require such a habit—staying the same and behaving similarly—when good things are present; and we first desire that from which we must never depart because it is good; but if it were not good, it would be better to depart from it.
<margin>D</margin>
Must we therefore desire to live always in the same way—voluntarily remaining in the Good itself—as if that were the good? If, therefore, this is what is most to be desired for the mind—namely, to live thus—it surely requires nothing further; and it is certain that this habit of always behaving similarly is sought because the present things are sufficient. But with all things now present to this mind, living is to be sought as the highest goal; present in such a way, I say, that they are not different from it.
<margin>E</margin>
If, therefore, every life is present to this—a life, I say, vigorous and clear—now every soul and the universal mind is perfected in this, and nothing is lacking to it, either of life or of intelligence. It is therefore self-sufficient, and desires nothing further. But if it requires nothing, it already possesses within itself what it would otherwise seek if it were not present. It has, therefore, the Good within itself—the Good, I say, either of such a kind as we have called life and mind, or something else belonging to these.
<margin>F</margin>
But if this [life and mind] were the Good itself, surely nothing would be superior to these; but if the Good itself is above these, then surely for the mind the Good will be something else, and the mind will be entirely leaning upon it, possessing its substance from there, and directing itself entirely toward it: for that is its principle. It is necessary, therefore, that the Good be more excellent than life and mind; for only thus will life, vigorous in the mind, be turned back toward it, as it is a certain imitation of that which exists in the One, according to which it lives and follows. And the intelligence of this mind will be turned back as a certain imitation of that which exists in the One, whatever this One finally may be.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...simpler, the same. Therefore, that which made the sensible world would not be the sensible world itself, but intellect and the intelligible world. And that which is prior to this, its genuine source, whether it is intellect or an intelligible world, is simpler than intellect and simpler than the intelligible world. For "many" does not come from "many," but the "many" comes from the "not-many." For if that itself were many, it would not be the principle, but another would be before it. All must stand or fall by the One which truly exists, outside all plurality and any simplicity whatsoever, if indeed it is truly simple. But how is that which is generated from it "manifold logos" <note>original: *λόγος*; the Greek term for the rational plan or word, here translated as "reason" in the Latin column.</note> and "all"?
<margin>B</margin>
It is clear then that it [the product] is logos. But if it were not this, how would logos not come from logos? And how does the "good-form" come from the Good? For having what quality is it called "good-form"? Is it by having that which is according to the same and in the same way? And what do these have to do with the Good?
<margin>C</margin>
For we seek that "same way" when things are good, or rather that from which it will not be necessary to depart because it is good. Otherwise, it is better to depart. Is it then to live in the same way, remaining in oneself voluntarily? If then one were to take away life from this, clearly it seeks it thus. It seems then that this "same way" is to live,
<margin>D</margin>
because present things seem [sufficient]. But with all things already present to this, life is beloved. And indeed, let them be present as things other than itself. But if all life is ordered [within it], and life is manifest and all-perfect, in which is the soul and every mind, and nothing is lacking to it of life or of the substance of mind, it is self-sufficient and seeks nothing. But if it seeks nothing, it has in itself what it would seek if it were not present.
<margin>E</margin>
It has, therefore, the Good in itself. Or what is it that exists, which we called life and mind? Or is it something else accidental to them? But if this is the Good, nothing would be beyond these. But if that [the One] is the Good, it is clear that [the intellect] is suspended from it, and having its existence from it, and living toward it. For that is its principle.
<margin>F</margin>
It is clear, then, that the One is better than life and mind. For thus [the intellect] will turn toward it, and the life in it is a certain imitation of that which is in the One, by which it naturally lives. And the mind in this is a certain imitation of that which is in the One, whatever this One may finally be.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical ascent toward the "One" or the "Good." The previous page established that the source of all complexity must itself be simple and beyond the "manifold rational principles" of the intellect. We are now exploring the experiential aspect of reaching this source, which Plotinus and Ficino describe as a sudden illumination rather than a step-by-step logical process.</meta>

<page-num>513</page-num>

...sufficient in itself, and most simple. For it is not simply "to be" that we desire, but "to be well"; not to live in any way whatsoever, but to live well; not to understand in any fashion, but to understand well, and to understand good things, and in such a way that it will be of benefit to you. Nor do we desire the "truth" simply—for we do not desire a "true fever"—but rather the "true good." Therefore, the Good itself is the end <note>The ultimate goal or purpose (*finis*).</note> and the principle of all things. The end of our life is to see the Good itself through its own light. But since this is the most stable and most simple of things, we do not reach it through the discourse of reason, nor by the action of the intelligence as it assembles or distinguishes things, but by a certain sudden and simple intuition. For us, the sign of this enjoyment is when, beyond our usual state and through no accustomed mechanical trick of the mind, a light suddenly flows into us. This is a joyful clarity, which is a certain splendor of the clarity consisting in itself, which is God himself. Moreover, it flows in when we are devoted to him and, by his grace, we remove all things—that is, the inclinations toward all things from our appetite, the images from our imagination, the arguments from our reason, and the intellectual forms, compositions, and distinctions from our intellect. Both Plato and we have said enough regarding these matters in our commentary on Plato’s great epistle <note>original: *magna Platonis epistola*; likely referring to Plato's Seventh Letter, which describes the "spark" of divinity that lights up the soul.</note>.

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>A</margin> What then is better than a most prudent life, which is without stumbling and without sin? What is better than an intellect that possesses all things, and better than all life and every intellect? If we should speak of that which made these things, and how it made them, and if nothing better should appear to us, then our reasoning would not proceed to another thing, but would stand still there. But indeed, one must ascend through many other things, and because this self-sufficiency <note>original: *αὔταρκες* (autarkes); the quality of needing nothing external.</note> is outside of all things. For each of them is clearly lacking, or because each participates in the One because it has shared in its own single part.
<margin>B</margin> It is not the One itself, no. What then is the One that things participate in, which makes it both to "be" and to be "all things together," but does not make it to be each thing individually? And by the presence of the One, its multitude becomes self-sufficient. This One is clearly the maker of essence and self-sufficiency, while it is not itself essence, but is beyond essence, and beyond self-sufficiency. Is it enough, then, to say these things and be released? Or is the soul still in labor, and even more so?
<margin>C</margin> Perhaps then the soul must now give birth, having rushed toward it and been filled with the pangs of labor. Nevertheless, let us sing again <note>original: *ἐπάσειν*; to sing an incantation or a healing song.</note> if from somewhere we might find a light to serve as a charm for the labor. Perhaps even from the things already said, the soul might be calmed if one sings to it often. What then is this other, as if new, charm? For it must be placed above all truths, and the truths we share in; yet one must flee to it if one 
<margin>D</margin> wishes to speak or to think. For it is necessary for the thought, in order to say something, to take one thing and then another. For in this way there is a path through it; but in that which is simple, there are no paths through it. But it is enough to touch it intellectually, and for the one who touches it, in the moment he touches, to be able to say neither everything nor nothing. He cannot, nor does he have the leisure to speak. Only later can he reason about it. But then one must believe they have seen it, when the soul suddenly receives light.
<margin>E</margin> For this very light is from him and is him. And then one must believe he is present, just as when some other god, being called to someone's house, enters and illuminates it—whereas if he had not come, he would not have illuminated it. Thus, the soul is unilluminated and without God in that state. But when illuminated, it has what it sought. and this is the true end for the soul: to touch that light.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> What indeed is better than a most wise life, which cannot fall and cannot err? What is better than an intellect embracing all things? And what is better than all life and all mind? If we answer that that which made these things is better, and however it made them, and if nothing more excellent than itself occurs to us, the discourse of our reason will not proceed to another thing, but will revolve in the same place. Nevertheless, we must progress higher, both for many other reasons, and also because the sufficiency accumulated for this intellect from all things
<margin>B</margin> hangs from the outside, where surely each thing is in itself needy; and also because each thing is a participant of that same One, and participates in the One, inasmuch as it is not the One itself. What then is that of which this is a participant? Which indeed brings it about that this thing "is," and at the same time is "all things." But if it makes it so that each thing exists, and by the presence of the One this multitude of the one speaking emerges as self-sufficient, then it is clearly the origin of all essence and sufficiency; it is, I say, 
<margin>C</margin> not existing as essence, but even higher than this sufficiency itself. Tell me, do these things satisfy us, or are we further vexed? And certainly now the soul is more vehemently stimulated. Perhaps, therefore, it is necessary now to prepare our soul, more ardently excited toward it, and agitated by the many pains as if of one in labor. Nevertheless, it is better to help with certain songs, as if they were the songs of mages, if in some way we might
<margin>D</margin> find a song contributing to this birth. Perhaps indeed from these things which have been said, if one sings them often, we will finally achieve it. But what is this other, as if new, song? Truly the song itself, overstepping all the truths of which we ourselves are participants, flees immediately if anyone wishes to describe or think of it: since it is necessary for thought, in order to say anything, to take up one thing and then another in the meantime: where surely it is occupied in a certain discourse. But in that which is entirely simple, 
<margin>E</margin> there can be no discourse: it is enough, however, to reach it in a certain intellectual way. And it is necessary for the one reaching it, while he reaches it, to be entirely unable to speak anything, nor to have the leisure for speaking, but later to reason about it. But we must believe that we have then finally seen it, when the soul has suddenly received light. For this, I say, this light flows from the Good itself; this is the Good itself. Then certainly we must think it is present to us, just as when some other God, having been invoked into some

house, enters and thoroughly illuminates it; otherwise, unless he has entered, he does not illuminate. Thus, therefore, the soul is empty of light, and empty of God; but when illuminated, she already has everything she sought with her mind. This surely, this is the true end for the soul, namely, to receive his light, and to see him through himself, not by another's [light]...

<meta>This page concludes the final thoughts of the previous book and begins Book 4 of the Fifth Ennead. The text continues the discussion of the "One"—the ultimate, simple source of all existence. In the opening fragment, Plotinus emphasizes that we do not see the source through an external light, but through the light of the source itself. To find it, one must strip away all external things.</meta>

<page-num>516</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.</header>

...to behold, I say, by that light, but to see by the very light itself, which it also looks upon. <note>Plotinus uses the analogy of the sun: just as we see the sun by its own light rather than by some secondary light, we perceive the ultimate Source (the One) through its own direct presence in our minds.</note> For that by which one is illuminated is the very thing we must see. For we are not accustomed to looking at the Sun through some other light. But if you ask by what means you might achieve this: take away everything entirely from the middle. <note>original: "omnia prorsus à medio tolle" / "ἄφελε πάντα". This is a famous Neoplatonic instruction: to find the ultimate truth, one must strip away all distractions, thoughts, and material concerns.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...and to behold it by itself. Not by another light, but by itself, through which it also sees. For that by which it was illuminated is that which must be beheld. For neither is the sun seen through another light. How then might this happen? Take away everything.

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD FIVE,
### BOOK IV.

->How that which follows the First is from the First, and concerning the One.<-
->How that which is after the first is made by the first, and concerning the One.<-

<margin>The things in the universe, though diverse among themselves, would not have harmony, order, or union with one another unless they all proceeded from the One. Chapter I.</margin>

*This ultimate principle is not "this" thing or "that" thing, but is simply the One itself. Because of its supreme simplicity, it is the first, the most self-sufficient, and the most powerful. It is the very power of all things, while other things are merely "potential" for acting; the more powerful they are, the more they can do. From this it appears that this Power itself makes all things, holds the widest possible dominion over everything everywhere, and is most present to all things.*

---

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a scholar or philosopher seated in a study with a globe and books, gesturing with his hand as if in discourse.</image-desc>
**Whatever** exists besides the First must necessarily depend on that First itself, and indeed either directly or at least through certain intermediaries; and there is an order of things that are second and third. In this order, certainly, that which is second is led back to the first, and that which is third is led back to the second.

<margin>B</margin>
For it is necessary that something be above all things, and that this thing be entirely simple and different from all things that follow it, existing in itself, not mixed with those things that come after it, and yet, in another way, most easily present to the others. This must truly be "the One," <term>The One (Greek: to Hen)</term> <note>In Plotinus's philosophy, the One is the supreme, totally simple source of all reality, beyond even being or intellect.</note> not in the sense that it is first one thing and then also "one," for in that case "one" would be falsely predicated of it. Furthermore, neither speech <note>or "rational discourse" (ratio/logos)</note> nor any science at all can reach it: for which reason it is also judged to be "above essence" or "beyond being." <note>original: "ἐπέκεινα... οὐσίας" (epekeina ousias). A key phrase from Plato’s Republic, suggesting the ultimate principle is higher than existence itself.</note>

<margin>C</margin>
Unless it were entirely simple, removed from every conjunction and composition, and truly One, it could not be the principle <note>The source or starting point (principium/archē).</note>; for it is only because of its supreme simplicity that it can be the most self-sufficient and the first of all things. For that which is not first needs that which is before it; and that which is not simple needs those simple parts within itself so that it may be constituted from them. Now, that which is judged to be such a principle must be only one and unique. For if another thing were said to be of this kind, both would be entirely one:

<sig>1</sig>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring a seated figure holding a book, possibly a muse or an allegorical representation of wisdom.</image-desc>
**If anything** exists after the first, it is necessary that it be from that one: either directly, or through intermediaries: and its being is directed toward that first through the things in between: and there is an order, of second and third things. The second are referred back to the first, and the third back to the second.

<margin>B</margin>
For there must be something before all things that is simple, and different from all things after it. Existing by itself, not mixed with the things from it. And yet, in another way, it is able to be present to the others, being truly one. It is not some other thing and then "one," in which case it would be false to say it is "one." Neither is there speech, nor knowledge of it. It is indeed said to be "beyond being."

<margin>C</margin>
For if it were not simple, outside of every foundation and every composition, and truly one, it would not be a principle. It is most self-sufficient by being simple, and the first of all. For that which is not first is in need of what is before it. And that which is not simple is in need of the simple elements within it, so that it may be formed from them. Such a thing, then, must only be one. For if there were another such thing, both would not be [distinct]. For we do not say they are like two bodies:
