</margin>
Either the First is not a body, or nothing is a simple body; for every body is generated, and thus is not a principle. But the principle is unbegotten. Since it is not corporeal, but truly One, that must be the First. If, therefore, there is something else after the First, it can no longer be simple. Therefore, it will be "one-many" <note>original: "ἓν πολλά" - a core Neoplatonic concept where the Intellect contains the diversity of all Forms while remaining a single entity.</note>. From where, then, do these things come? From the First. For it is not by chance. Nor, again, if that is the principle of all things. How, then, are they from the First? If the First is perfect, and the most perfect of all, and the primary power, it must be the most powerful of all existing things. And other powers must imitate that one as far as they are able. Moreover, when any of these other things reach perfection, we see that they generate and do not endure to remain within themselves, but produce something else. Not only 
<margin>* that</margin> * that which possesses choice, but also those things which act by nature without choice; even inanimate things share themselves as far as they are able—as fire heats and snow cools. And drugs, too, work upon something else. All these things, in short, imitate the principle according to their power, tending toward eternity and goodness. How then could the most perfect and the first Good stand still within itself? As if the power of all things were grudging to itself or were weak. And how, then, would it be the principle? Something must be generated from it, which will also exist. And of the other things, they must have their subsistence from it. For it is necessary that they come from it. For this reason, that which is generated is more honorable <note>original: "τιμιώτερον" - meaning higher in the ontological hierarchy or more "precious" in a spiritual sense.</note>, and that which is generated must be most honorable, and being second to that [the First], it must be better than all others.

IF, therefore, that which generates were the Intellect itself, then that which is generated would necessarily be inferior to the Intellect, yet very near to it and similar. But since that which generates is beyond Intellect, that which is first generated must necessarily be Intellect. But why is it not Intellect, or rather, why is its activity not thought? Thought is seeing the intelligible, and being turned toward this, and being, as it were, perfected by it,
<margin>...ora ...us,</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> We add, that the First itself is either the one or a body: indeed, no body is simple. Likewise, every body is "becoming" <note>original: "fit" / "γινόμενόν" - implying it is a process or effect, not an eternal cause.</note>, and therefore it cannot be the principle, seeing as the principle is unbegotten. Since, therefore, the principle cannot be corporeal, but is truly one and unique, it clearly exists as the first. If anything else exists besides the first, it will by no means be simple: it will therefore be "one-many." From where, then, does this depend? Surely it depends on the first. For such things
<margin>B</margin> do not happen or coincide by some fortuitous chance; nor, if it were so, would that be the principle of all things. In what way, then, does every other thing come from the first? Surely if the first is perfect and the most perfect of all, and the first power, it must be the most powerful of all things, and other powers must, as much as they can, imitate that one according to their strength. Whatever among other things arrives at its own perfection, we have found, already generates something, and is unable to rest 
<margin>C</margin> sterile within itself, but makes something else from itself. Nor have we found this only in those things which act by a certain choice, but truly also in whatever things are born and beget without choice: even that which lacks a soul <note>original: "caret anima" - inanimate objects.</note> hands down something of its own to others as far as it is able. Thus fire heats, and thus snow likewise cools. Drugs and medicines also act upon another thing toward the likeness of their own nature. Thus all things, finally, imitate the first principle in order to fulfill eternity and goodness. 
<margin>D</margin> Since, therefore, nature is arranged in this way, by what reasoning is it to be believed that the most perfect and first Good of all would, as if through envy, keep itself only within itself? Or perhaps that it could not propagate itself, though it is truly considered the power of all things. Finally, if nothing proceeds from it, it cannot be the principle. For which reason, it is necessary that something be made by it, if indeed anything exists besides itself, and that something be made by those things which are made by it. That certain things are most proximate to it, this necessity demonstrates: then truly it is necessary that that which begets the rest be the most excellent of those that follow. Furthermore, that which is generated most closely from there, and holds the second place, is more excellent than the others.

### *The Intellect depends upon the intelligible almost as sight depends on the visible, therefore it is not the First. Chapter II.*

<note>This chapter heading and the following commentary by Marsilio Ficino explain the core Neoplatonic hierarchy: The One (First) -> Intellect (Nous/Second) -> Soul (Third). The Intellect is "second" because it requires an object—the Intelligible—to think about, whereas the One is beyond even thought.</note>

He touches here upon a double intelligible: one joined with the intellect, and the other truly higher. Consider the eye of an animal that sees by itself day and night; the substance of the eye is very lucid, and the power of seeing depends upon it, which in itself is indeed formless, but is formed by the lucid substance joined to itself. Imagine such an intellect as being also first, even where it beholds itself, just as if a very bright eye, pressed in a certain way by a finger, should gaze upon itself. Now indeed, in the first intellect, its own substantial unity is its own intelligible, from which the power of understanding depends, being turned toward it and formed by it. Such a power, together with its conversion, is an "indefinite duality" <note>original: "indefinita duitas" / "ἀόριστος δυάς" - a Pythagorean and Platonic term for the "Two" or "Otherness" that arises from the "One" before it is defined into specific Forms.</note>: but it becomes the intellect in act and the all-formed Idea when defined by its own intelligible. Hence it is also turned through its own unity toward the simply One: which is also called the "more excellent intelligible." This, Plotinus does not here entirely deprive of knowledge, but only of intellectual knowledge <note>Ficino clarifies that while the One cannot be "thought" in the human or intellectual way (which requires a subject and an object), it possesses a higher form of supra-intellectual awareness.</note>.

---

<margin>A</margin> IF, therefore, that which generates were itself the intellect, it would surely be necessary that what is first begotten from there be inferior to the intellect, yet closer and more similar to it. But since that which first begets is higher than the intellect, for that reason that which is first begotten is necessarily the intellect. But why is that first begetter not the intellect? Because the very action of the intellect is intelligence; intelligence, I say, looking at the intelligible and turned toward it, and as it were defined and completed by it,
<sig>*</sig>

<summary>Plotinus argues that the "One" must be the source of all things because its absolute perfection and power naturally overflow to create reality, much like fire emits heat. This emanation begins with the Intellect, which is "second" to the One because it involves the duality of a thinker looking at a thought.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s explanation of how the One (the First Principle) generates the Intellect (Nous). The previous page established that the First is perfect and must "overflow." This page describes the nature of that overflow using the "double activity" theory and the metaphor of fire and heat.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

<margin>A</margin>
By its very nature, it is indefinite, much like sight, but it is defined by the Intelligible <note>The "Intelligible" here refers to the object of thought, which for the Intellect is its source, the One.</note>. Therefore, as it has been handed down, from the <term>indefinite duality</term> <note>original: "indefinite duitate" / Greek "ἀορίστου δυάδος." In Neoplatonism, this refers to a raw, unshaped potentiality that must be "limited" by the One to become the Intellect.</note> and the One, the forms and numbers are born. This is the Intellect; thus, it is not simple, but multiple, displaying a certain composition—though an intelligible one—and already beholding many things. Now, it is itself both an intelligible object and a thinking subject; therefore, it is already two. There is also something else beyond this, which is the Intelligible itself. But in what way does this Intellect depend upon the Intelligible?

<margin>B</margin>
Certainly, the Intelligible, abiding in itself, is not in need, as is usually the case with that which sees and understands. I say "in need" because that which understands is needy in relation to the Intelligible it contemplates. That source, resting in itself, is not as if it were void of perception; rather, all things belong to it, are in it, and are with it, for it is entirely master of its own self-distinction. Likewise, life is in itself, and all things are in it, and its observation of itself is its very existence, persisting in a perpetual state with a kind of self-awareness and self-consent—an intelligence of a different sort than the intelligence of the Intellect itself.

<margin>C</margin>
Therefore, if something is produced while that source remains in itself, it is generated precisely when that source most truly exists as what it is. Thus, while that source remains in its own state, that which arises is generated from it; it is born, I say, while the source remains. Since, therefore, the Intelligible remains, that which is produced becomes intelligence. Furthermore, since it is intelligence and understands that from which it was generated (for it has nothing else), it surely becomes the Intellect—a kind of second intelligible, and such as that source exists, a certain imitation and image of it.

<margin>D</margin>
But how can this be while that source remains? There is, indeed, one <term>activity</term> <note>original: "actus" / Greek "ἐνέργεια" (energeia). Plotinus distinguishes between what a thing *is* and what a thing *does* as a result of its existence.</note> of essence, and another activity that depends upon the essence of each thing. The activity that belongs to the essence is that which makes the thing what it is. The activity that flows from the essence is that which necessarily follows from it, yet is different from the source from which it flowed. For example, in fire: there is one heat that fulfills the essence of the fire, but another heat that proceeds from it, while the fire meanwhile exercises the heat inherent in its essence, insofar as it remains fire.

<margin>E</margin>
So, therefore, it is there [in the higher realm] and much more so: while that source remains in its own state, from the perfection inherent in itself and its accompanying internal activity, a generated activity goes forth, taking on a subsistence of its own, as it is born from a mighty power—indeed, from the greatest of all powers—into being and essence.

<margin>F</margin>
It has proceeded forth. For that source is higher than essence, and is the power of all things. This [the Intellect], however, is already "all things." But if this is all things, then surely that source is above all things; therefore, it stands even above essence. And yet, if I say this [Intellect] is all things, and the One exists before all things, not admitting a condition equal with all, for this reason also it is necessary that it be superior to essence—that is, superior to Mind. Something, therefore, is more ancient than the Intellect.

<margin>G</margin>
For Being itself is not something dead; it is not as if it were deprived of life and intelligence. Therefore, Intellect and Being are the same. For the Intellect does not relate to the things it understands in the same way that the senses relate to sensible objects (as if the objects preceded the sense); rather, the Intellect itself is the very things themselves.

<column-break/>

...and being perfected, it is indefinite like sight, but is defined by the Intelligible. Therefore, it is said that from the indefinite dyad and the One come the forms and the numbers. For this is the Intellect. Therefore, it is not simple, but many, appearing as a composition of intelligible things, seeing many things. Now, it is itself an intelligible object, but also a thinking subject: two already. And there is still another, that which is the Intelligible after it <note>This refers to the One as the primary object of the Intellect's gaze.</note>. But how does this Intellect come from the Intelligible? The Intelligible remains by itself and is not in need, like that which sees and understands. That which understands was called "needy" in relation to that [the One]. It is not like a sensible thing. Rather, these things are in it, and it is with itself, and it has grasped everything in itself, by its own life. And all things are in it, and its understanding of itself is within itself. It exists, as it were, in a self-consciousness, and in an eternal consciousness, and in a thinking that is different from the [ordinary] thinking of the Intellect. If, then, while it remains, something comes from it, it comes from it when that source is most truly what it is. While it remains in its own character, that which is produced is generated; it is born while the source remains. Since, then, that source was the Intelligible, that which is produced becomes "thinking." Being "thinking," and thinking of that from which it was born (for it has nothing else), it becomes Intellect. It is another kind of intelligible, like that source, and is an imitation and an image of it. But how is it born while the source remains? There is an activity. One belongs to the essence, and another is from the essence of each thing. The one of essence is the very activity of the thing itself. The one from that essence is that which must follow necessarily in every case, being different from it. As in the case of fire: there is a certain heat that completes the essence, and another which is already produced from it, while that source acts upon the heat innate to its essence by remaining fire. And it is the same there [in the divine realm]. And much earlier, while it remains in its own character, from its own perfection and its inherent activity, the generated activity takes on a reality (hypostasis), since it comes from a great power—indeed, the greatest of all—it came into being and essence. For that source was "beyond essence." And that source is the power of all things, while this [Intellect] is already all these things. But if all things are "fire," that source is beyond all things. Therefore, it is beyond essence. And if it is all things, but the One is before all things, or the One holds itself apart from all, then in this way too it is beyond essence. And this [the product] is Intellect. Therefore, the source is beyond Intellect. For Being is not dead, nor is it without life or thinking. Intellect and Being are the same. For the Intellect is not of things [external to it], as sense perception is of sensible things, but the Intellect itself is the things...

<summary>Plotinus explains the emergence of the Intellect from the One, using the "double activity" theory: just as fire has internal heat (its essence) and radiates external heat (its effect), the One remains unchanged while its perfection overflows to create the Intellect.</summary>

If indeed it does not acquire the forms of things through the act of understanding—for from where would it acquire them?—but rather they emerge together with the things themselves, and are one and the same with them; and conversely, the intelligible things themselves are not at all without their own "matter," which is to say, the intellect itself. <note>This introductory snippet emphasizes the Neoplatonic doctrine that in the divine mind, the "Thought" and the "Thing Thought" are identical, not separate as they are in human perception.</note>

If indeed it does not draw the species of things into itself through the act of understanding. For from where would it draw them? But rather, it comes forth together with the things themselves, and is one and the same with them and one; and conversely, the intelligible things themselves are not entirely without their "matter"—that is, the intellect.

## ENNEAD FIVE.
### BOOK V.

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD FIVE,
### BOOK FIVE.

#### That the intelligibles are not outside the intellect; also concerning the Good itself.
#### That the things known by the mind are not outside the mind: likewise concerning the Good itself.

> Just as sense-perception, which is the lowest form of knowledge, looks only at outward things: so the intellect, which is the highest knowledge, looks only at inward things.
> -> Cap. I. <-

*Just as in sense-perception there are only the images of things that are felt, so in the intellect are the things themselves which it understands. Otherwise, if it were to receive images from the things it understands, it would neither equal those things—since knowledge produced through images is far inferior to the things themselves—nor would it be certain that it possessed a pure judgment of the things. For images, when transferred into the nature of the receiver, do not bring the pure nature of the object. Positioned above discursive reasoning <note>Discursive reasoning (ratio discurrens) is the step-by-step logic humans use; Plotinus argues the Divine Intellect knows everything instantly and simultaneously.</note>, the intellect, acting with stability, holds its objects present at its own will. Thus, it possesses within itself not only certain principles of arts and things, but also whatever necessarily follows from those principles. You must not think that the intelligibles themselves are merely propositions or like certain utterances, but rather as essential reasons and forms. Nor are they separate spectacles, but forms within one immaterial form; just as all sensible forms exist in the same unformed matter, so the intelligible forms are much more united with the intellect than sensible forms are with matter, or celestial things with the substance of the heavens. We shall discuss more extensively in 'Theology' how the forms of things are naturally infused into our souls.*

---

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial T containing an illustration of a man standing outdoors within a hilly landscape.</image-desc> Regarding the intellect—the true and real intellect—would anyone say that it could ever be deceived or hold opinions that do not reflect reality? By no means. For how would it be "intellect" if it were subject to the errors of the senses? It must, therefore, always know, and never be subject to forgetting. Its knowledge is not like that of one who imagines or is in doubt; nor is it borrowed from another, as if by hearing. <margin>B</margin> Nor, then, does it arrive at knowledge through demonstration. For even if one were to say that some things are acquired through demonstration, nonetheless something must be self-evident to it from the start, and as the <term>Logos</term> <note>original: "λόγος" / "ratio." In this context, it refers to the rational order or the "Word" that structures reality.</note> says, all things. For how could one distinguish between what is self-evident and what is not? But if one grants that something is self-evident, from where will they say the clarity of these things is present to it? And from where does it gain the conviction that it is so?

It must be asked, in what way one can distinguish which things are known to it naturally and which are sought after? Likewise, for those who concede that some things are known to the mind through itself, from where will they say the certainty of these things is present to the mind? From where can a mind of this kind clearly believe from this,

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative initial A containing an illustration of a landscape with trees and distant hills.</image-desc> Do we think there will be anyone who considers the true and truly existing intellect to be capable of lying at any time, or of holding opinions about things that do not truly exist? Certainly no one. For by what reasoning would that be an intellect if it were at any time (so to speak) out of its mind? <note>original: "dementiret." The Latin text makes a pun on "mens" (mind) and "dementiret" (to be out of one's mind/to act without intellect).</note> It is necessary, therefore, for it to always know, and that nothing remains hidden from it as if it were forgetful. Truly, knowledge exists in it not as if it were imagining or doubting, nor as if it were borrowing from another. Therefore, it ought not to weigh things as if through some demonstration. For even if one were to concede that it compares some things through demonstration, that same person will not deny that, in the meantime, something is known to the intellect through itself—even though true reason dictates that all things are perceived by it through its own nature. Plotinus asserts that the Intellect is incapable of error or forgetting because its knowledge is self-evident and identical with its own being.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous section regarding the relationship between the Intellect (the divine mind) and the Intelligibles (the Platonic Forms or objects of thought). Plotinus is examining the skepticism inherent in sensory knowledge to prove that true knowledge must be internal to the mind.</meta>

<page-num>520</page-num>
-> # PLOTINUS: ENNEAD V <-
-> ### BOOK V: That the Intelligibles are not outside the Intellect; also concerning the Good itself. <-

<margin>A</margin> ...why it should be so? Because even regarding those things offered to the senses, whose reliability seems most certain, we often doubt whether their apparent nature exists in the underlying objects themselves, or merely in our own sensations. In such cases, the judgment of the mind, or at least of discursive thought, is required.
<margin>B</margin> For even if it were granted that the natures of things perceived are present in the objects themselves, that which is known through the senses is merely an image of the thing; the sense does not grasp the thing itself, for the object remains outside. But if the Intellect, in the act of knowing, knows the "intelligibles" <note>The *intelligibles* (noeta) are the eternal truths or Forms that the mind contemplates.</note> as being something other than and existing outside of itself, how can it truly encounter them? For it is possible that it might not encounter them at all, and thus it might happen that it does not know them; or perhaps it only knows them at the moment it happens upon them, and thus it would not possess knowledge eternally.
<margin>C</margin> Furthermore, if some were to say that these intelligibles are "conjoined" to the intellect, we must still ask what this "conjunction" implies. Moreover, the thoughts themselves would be mere figures or shapes. If this were so, they would be impressions brought in from the outside, like strokes or blows. In what way would the intellect be shaped? What would be the specific form of such things? Ultimately, "intelligence" would be a perception of external things, just like sense-perception. How, then, would these two differ? Perhaps only in that the intellect perceives smaller, more subtle things?
<margin>D</margin> Likewise, how will the intellect recognize that it has truly perceived anything? How can it judge that "this is good," or "beautiful," or "just"? For each of these would be distinct from itself, and the principles of judgment by which it might trust its own findings would not be within it; rather, these principles too would be outside, and the truth would reside there. Again, the intelligibles themselves either lack sense, life, and intellect, or they possess intellect. If they possess intellect, then both—the mind and the object—exist together in the same place, and the Truth exists here; this would be the primary Intellect. But even then, we must ask: under what condition does Truth exist here? Are the "intelligible" and the "intellect" two distinct things in the same place, or is it some other way?
<margin>E</margin> But if the intelligibles lack intellect and life, what are they? They are certainly not mere propositions, nor rules <note>original: "regulae" / "ἀξιώματα", often referring to logical axioms.</note> which are called "axioms," nor are they like spoken words. For if they were such, they would merely say something about other things, but would not be the things themselves;
<margin>F</margin> as if they were to say "that which is just is beautiful," while "Justice" and "Beauty" were something else entirely. But if they say these intelligibles are "simple" things—Justice itself and Beauty itself—then first of all, the intelligible would not be a single unity, nor would it exist in a unity; instead, each would be segregated from the others. We would then have to ask where they are positioned in their separation. Next, how would the intellect, in its "running around" <note>original: "circumcurrens" / "περιθέων", implying the mind moving from one external object to another.</note>, find or discover them? How would it remain among them? How would it persist in the same state? Furthermore, what form or shape would they have? Unless, perhaps, they are like golden statues or images composed of some other material by a sculptor or painter. But if this were the case, the mind beholding such things would simply be another form of sense-perception. Therefore, by what reasoning among these...

<column-break/>

...would it provide? Since even in the case of sense-perception, which seems to have the most vivid reliability, it is doubted whether the apparent reality exists in the underlying objects or in the sensations <note>original: "πάθεσιν" (pathesin), meaning the passive impressions or affections of the soul.</note>; and there is a need for the Intellect or for Thought to be the judge. For even if it is granted that the sensible things—which the sense-perception apprehends—exist in the underlying objects,
<margin>*</margin> that which is known through sense is an image of the thing, and the sense does not grasp the thing itself. For that remains outside. Now, if the Intellect, in knowing, and in knowing the intelligibles, were to know them as being different from itself, how would it meet with them? For it is possible for it not to meet them, so it is possible for it not to know them, or to know them only when it has met them. And it will not always possess knowledge. But if they say they are "joined together," what is this "being joined"? And then the thoughts will be impressions <note>original: "τύποι" (typoi), literally types or stamps.</note>. If they are impressions, they are both brought-in and are "blows." How will it be impressed, or what is the form of such things? And the act of thinking will be of something outside, just like sense-perception. And it will differ only in apprehending smaller things. How will it even know that it truly apprehended anything? How will it know that this is "good," or "beautiful," or "just"? For each of these is something other than itself, and the principles of judgment, in which it
<margin>D</margin> will trust, are not in it. But these too are outside, and the Truth is there. Then, either those things are without sensation and devoid of life and intellect, or they have intellect. And if it has intellect, both are here—both of them. And Truth is here. And this is the primary Intellect. And regarding this, we shall seek how the Truth here stands, and the intelligible and the intellect: if they are in the same and together, yet two and different, or how? But if they are without life. For what are they—propositions, or axioms, or "things said" <note>original: "λεκτὰ" (lekta), a Stoic term for the meanings of sentences.</note>? For already these would be said about other things. And they would not be the beings themselves. For example, "the just is beautiful," while the Just and the Beautiful are something else. But if they say they are simple, Justice apart and Beauty apart: first, the intelligible will not be any one thing, but each will be hidden away. And where and according to what are they standing apart? And how will the
<margin>F</margin> Intellect meet them while running around? And how will it stay? Or if it is in the same, how does it stay? And what form or impression will it have at all, if they are not like statues set within, made of gold or some other thing by some molder or painter? But if this is so, the Intellect beholding them will be sense-perception. Why, then, is the one...

<meta>catchword: hoc</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that if the objects of thought (intelligibles) were outside the mind (Intellect), knowledge would be as uncertain and indirect as sense-perception. He concludes that for true, certain knowledge to exist, the mind and the things it knows must be identical and internal to one another.</summary>

--- Page 689 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 520 regarding whether the objects of thought (the Intelligibles) exist outside or inside the Divine Mind (the Intellect). Plotinus argues that if they were outside, the mind could never possess certain truth, only "images" of it.</meta>

<page-num>521</page-num>
<header>BOOK FIVE</header>

...[is one thing] justice for all, and that [is] something else? But this is the most important point of all: for if we were to grant as much as possible that these objects exist outside of us, and that the mind contemplates them as being so situated, it must necessarily follow that the mind does not possess the truth itself, and is deceived in everything it contemplates. For in that case, those external things would be the true ones. The mind, therefore, would contemplate them without possessing them, receiving only images of them in such a form of knowledge. If, therefore, it does not possess the true reality, but only receives certain images of the truth within itself, it will possess falsehoods and nothing of the truth. If it knows that it possesses falsehoods, it will admit it is devoid of truth. But if it is ignorant of even this, and thinks it possesses the truth when it does not, the falsehood within it becomes doubled, distancing it far from the truth. This is why, I believe, there is no truth in the senses, but only opinion <note>original Greek: *doxa*</note>, because in the act of receiving, the sense-perception accepts something different from what the object truly is; that which it receives is derived from an external thing that remains distinct. If, then, truth is not in the mind, such a mind is no longer truth, nor is it truly a mind, nor is it a mind at all; indeed, truth will not exist anywhere else either.

---

### The objects of the intellect are not images of things or mere imaginings, but exist as the true things themselves: since even the objects of the senses are real things in their own way.
->Chapter II.<-

> *For just as the intellect is more excellent and truer than the senses, so the objects of the intellect are more excellent and truer than the objects of the senses, as Timaeus <note>A reference to the character in Plato’s dialogue, the *Timaeus*, who discusses the nature of the physical and intellectual worlds.</note> says. Furthermore, the "intelligibles" <note>The eternal truths or Forms that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses.</note> exist within the very essence of the intellect, since the intellect does not seek them through outward reasoning, nor does it wander outside itself, but turns inward and gazes steadily as if possessing them: it penetrates and defines the very substance of each thing. Indeed, through mere images, it could truly grasp nothing other than qualities and external appearances.*

---

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, we must no longer seek the intelligibles outside, nor say that they are merely "types" or impressions of beings within the mind. To do so would deprive the mind of truth, creating an ignorance of the intelligibles and rendering them non-existent; furthermore, it would destroy the intellect itself. Rather, if we are to introduce both knowledge and truth, and preserve the reality of beings, we must also preserve knowledge—specifically the knowledge of *what* each thing is, rather than merely *what kind* of thing it is. We should not hold merely a trace or an image <margin>B</margin> of the thing, but rather possess the things themselves, living with them and being blended with them—with that which is true and holy in all things. For in this way, the mind would truly know, and would know with certainty; it would neither forget nor wander about searching, for the truth would be within it. It would be the stable foundation for all beings, and it would live and think. All these qualities must belong to the most blessed nature. <margin>C</margin> Otherwise, where would there be anything honorable or venerable? For indeed, there is no need for demonstration or external proof that this is so. For the mind itself is thus, and is clear to itself. And that which is before it is likewise clear to it. Or what could come after it... <note>The text breaks here in the Greek but continues in the Latin below.</note> Then truly, by this reasoning, it will not lack anything. For the intellect itself is that which is entirely in this state: it is thoroughly manifest to itself. And if anything exists before it, it is similarly understood that the mind originates from that; likewise, if anything comes after it,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...this indeed is justice, while that other thing is instead something else? Finally, this is the most powerful argument of all: namely, if someone were to admit entirely that these things exist externally, and that the mind contemplates them as being so situated, it necessarily follows that the mind does not possess the truth of these things, but is deceived and lies to itself in the contemplation of each one. For the external things will be the true ones; the mind will therefore look out at them and will not have them, but will possess only their images in that kind of cognition. Since, therefore, it does not have the <margin>B</margin> truth itself, but holds only certain images of the truth within itself, it will certainly not accumulate truths, but will instead bring back falsehoods. If, therefore, it knows that it has only falsehoods, it will undoubtedly confess that it is devoid of truth; but if it is ignorant of even this, and—though it is not a participant in the truth—it nevertheless thinks itself to be in possession of the truth, it is now deceived by a double lie, and will stand at a very great distance from the truth. For this reason (as I judge), there is no truth in the senses, but only opinion: since the <margin>C</margin> condition of the sense consists in "receiving." Hence, "opinion"—called *doxa* in Greek—takes its name from "receiving" <note>Ficino provides a folk etymology linking *doxa* (opinion) to the verb *dechesthai* (to receive/accept).</note>. Therefore, it receives something other than itself, since that thing from which it possesses what it received is something else entirely. If, therefore, truth is not in the mind, such a mind will be neither truth, nor truly a mind, nor a mind at all; indeed, truth will not live anywhere else either.

<margin>A</margin> THEREFORE, it is not proper to search for the "intelligibles" outside the intellect, nor to confess that only the "figures" of things exist in the mind. To do so would deprive it of truth, while we concede both that the mind does not know the intelligibles themselves and that the very things offered to be understood do not exist in the order of reality; in this way, we would remove the mind itself from existence. But it is necessary to attribute all things to the true mind, if only it is proper to introduce knowledge and truth, to preserve the beings themselves, and that notice by which *what* each thing is <margin>B</margin> becomes known. We must not be satisfied with that notice which merely apprehends *what kind* a thing is—which happens when we have only a likeness and a trace of the thing to be known, but do not hold the thing itself, nor live together with it, nor harmonize with it as one. For by that [higher] reasoning, the mind will know, and will know in reality; nothing will be hidden from it, nor will it ever forget, nor wander about investigating here and there. <margin>C</margin> Instead, truth will be in it, as the seat of all things; it will live and it will understand. All these things must surely belong to the most blessed nature; otherwise, where would there be anything to be honored and venerated?

<sig>X 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: est</meta>

<summary>In this passage from Ennead V.5, Plotinus argues that true knowledge cannot come from external objects, as that would only provide the mind with "images" or "opinions." Instead, the "intelligibles" (true realities) must exist within the Divine Intellect itself, ensuring that truth is internal, stable, and identical with the mind's own essence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the nature of the Intellect and the "One." Having argued that the mind must contain the truth rather than just images of it, he now transitions to describing the hierarchy of divinity using the metaphors of light and ancient kings.</meta>

<page-num>322</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.</header>

Because the Intellect is this very thing itself, no one is more worthy of belief to it than itself; and indeed, it has clearly discovered that Truth is right there and truly exists. Therefore, in reality, Truth itself dwells there, not harmonizing with anyone else, but with itself; it says nothing outside of itself, and it simply exists—and what it is, it also speaks. Who then could refute it? And from where would they bring the refutation? For any argument brought forth would only lead back to the same point as the previous arguer. And even if a different argument is brought in, it will still relate back to the first proposer’s premise and will be entirely one. For nothing can be found that is truer than the truth.

---

*Just as the innermost light of the sun pours out a brilliance around itself, filled with innumerable rays and powers, so the Principle <note>The "One," or the ultimate source of all existence.</note> procreates within itself the all-forming Intellect, and this Intellect, in turn, produces the all-forming Soul.* Chapter III.

---

The ancients named that first Principle "Uranus" <note>The Greek god of the Sky, here representing the One.</note>, they called the Intellect "Saturn" <note>Cronus, the father of the gods.</note>, and finally called the Soul "Jupiter" <note>Zeus, the ruler of the world.</note>. All intellectual souls are able, through their own intellect, to ascend at times to the Divine Intellect. They can and indeed must move toward their own unity, and then through the Divine Intellect, eventually progress toward the Principle.

<margin>A</margin>
Therefore, this one nature of the Intellect is all existing things: it is Truth, and it is a certain great God—or rather, not just any God, but the whole of God. It is not unworthy of itself to think that it is all these things. This nature, then, is God; I say the "Second God" <note>In Neoplatonism, the Intellect is the first emanation from the One, making it the "Second" in the hierarchy.</note>, presenting itself to those who search before they can gaze upon that higher One. For that superior One sits more eminently upon this beautiful throne of the Intellect, which hangs from Him. For it was not fitting for Him to walk upon an inanimate chariot, nor even to meet us by proceeding immediately through the soul; rather, an inestimable beauty must shine forth wonderfully before His sight, just as 
<margin>B</margin>
is arranged before the arrival of a great king. For nature is so ordered that to those progressing toward Him, the lesser things occur first, and then the greater and more excellent things gradually offer themselves to those proceeding further. Those who stand around the king are more "regal" than the rest, and others follow in a similar order. After all these, the great King himself suddenly shines forth. The others, the 
<margin>C</margin>
supplicants, venerate the King himself—at least those who did not turn back before reaching the end, as those often do who think that the things shining forth before the king are enough to satisfy them. In that realm, then, another King rules, and those who appear before Him are surely different from Him. However, that celestial King does not rule over them as if they were strangers, but possesses a most just and natural command. He possesses a true kingdom, for He Himself is the King of Truth and by His own nature 
<margin>D</margin>
is the lord of His entire offspring and the divine assembly. He is certainly the King of a king and of kings <note>original Latin: *rex certè regis atque regum*</note>. Indeed, Jupiter imitated Him in this way as well: he did not rest entirely in the contemplation of his father, but proceeded further to his grandfather, reaching toward the grandfather's own act (if I may put it this way) into the very subsistence of essence.

---

*The Principle of all things, which because of its inestimable simplicity and eminence is called "The One," contains no estimable number within itself, nor does it agree with things in any specific quality.* Chapter IV.

---

For if there were any condition common to this Principle and any other thing, two absurdities would follow. First, that this Principle would be formed from a common...

<column-break/>

...because he is himself, and no one is more trustworthy to him than himself concerning himself; and because the truth is there, and truly exists. Thus, the actual truth is not in agreement with another, but with itself; it says nothing beside itself, but it is. And what it is, it also says. Who then could refute this? And from where would he bring the refutation? For the refutation being brought is the same as the thing shown, and once brought, it brings nothing else, just as all things were from the beginning; and you will find nothing truer than the truth.

One nature, therefore, is for us this Intellect: all beings and the truth. It is a certain great God. Or rather, not just a "certain" god, but all of God, worthy to be these things. This nature is God, a "Second God," manifesting himself before one sees that Higher One. For He sits above and is established upon a beautiful base, as it were, and the Intellect is suspended from Him. For it was necessary that He, in His walking, should not step upon something inanimate, nor even upon a soul immediately, but that there should be an unimaginable beauty before Him—just as before a great king, those in the processions are the lesser ones, then always the greater and more majestic follow them. And those already around the king are more kingly. And those after him are honored. But above all, the Great King himself suddenly manifests, and they pray and prostrate, at least those who did not leave before seeing him, being satisfied by the things seen before the king. There, then, the King is another, and those going before him are different from him. But the King there does not rule over foreigners. Instead, he has the most just and natural kingdom, the true kingdom, being the King of Truth. And being by nature the Lord of this whole collective offspring and divine system. He is the King of a king and of kings, and might more justly be called the Father of the gods. Jupiter imitated him in this too, not being satisfied with the contemplation of his own father, but reaching toward the one before his father—as it were, reaching through the activity toward the subsistence of essence.

<summary>Plotinus describes the hierarchy of the divine, using the Intellect as a "Second God" and a "King of Truth" that leads the soul toward the ultimate "One." He uses Greek mythology (Uranus, Saturn, Jupiter) to illustrate these levels of reality and emphasizes that the highest Principle is entirely simple and beyond comparison.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the hierarchy of being, moving from the Intellect (the realm of Forms) to the ultimate "One." It draws specifically on Plotinus’s Ennead V, Book 5, exploring how the One is the source of all number and existence but remains distinct from them.</meta>

# BOOK FIVE

...composed by its own condition and a certain property of its own. According to this, the common nature itself, being simpler and more universal, will be superior to the thing itself. Furthermore, it does not possess within itself an "essential number" <note>An "essential number" refers to the Ideal Forms or the divine ideas within the Intellect, which are distinct from the numbers used in counting.</note>—the kind Plotinus imagines in the primary essence—namely, a multitude of formal principles <note>Latin: *rationum formalium*</note> that are absolutely distinct from one another even without an act of intelligence. Nor does it have within itself a number categorized under quantity: for number pertaining to quantity, which consists of units, is reduced back to the One itself, the proper principle of quantity, which is higher than any number. Similarly, he reduces the number of essential forms to the "essential one," and finally, this is reduced to the "simply One."

---

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
That we must therefore make the ascent to the One, and truly the One, and not like other things that are "one"—things which, while being many in themselves, are one only by participating in the One. <note>original Greek: "μετοχῇ ἑνὸς ἓν" (one by participation in the one)</note> We must grasp that which is not one by participation, nor that which is "more one than many." We have said that the intelligible world <note>The realm of pure thought and reality, above the physical world.</note> and Being are more "one" than other things, and nothing is closer to the One than they are. We have spoken of that which is purely Being. But now, let us attempt to behold, if it is at all possible, what the purely One is—that which is truly One and not one by virtue of another.

<margin>B</margin>
It is necessary, therefore, in this place, to draw ourselves toward the One and add nothing further to it. We must stand completely still within it, fearing to step away from it in the slightest degree—not even toward the "one," <note>Meaning a single unit among others.</note> but toward the absolute, lest we find ourselves with two.

<margin>* In those things you have two.</margin>
For in those things you have two.* Therefore, where there is not the One, but both [the One and another], these are posterior <note>Coming after or lower in the hierarchy.</note> to the One. For the One does not endure being with another. One is the One, and it cannot be counted along with any other quantity. Otherwise, it would be counted entirely as a part. For the One is the measure itself, not the thing measured. It is not equal to others such that it might be categorized with them. If it were, there would be something common to it and the things counted with it. And that common thing would be prior to the One, yet nothing can be prior to it.

<margin>* Nor is there any number according to it.</margin>
* Indeed, there is no number whatsoever according to it. Nor is that number which follows it—the number of quantity—prior to it. For the essential number <note>The number that grants being to things through thought.</note> is that which always provides being through the act of thinking. But quantitative numbers are those that involve a quantity with others, or exist because they are not with others. If number exists there, it is because it is in those things.

<margin>D</margin>
Reminding us of their origin, the nature found in the first numbers—facing toward the truly One—does not consume the One, nor does it fragment its substance. But even when the "dyad" <note>The number two; the first departure from unity.</note> is produced, the "monad" <note>The number one; the unit.</note> still exists before the dyad. And it is not the case that each unit within the dyad is that primary Monad. For why would one be it more than the other? If, then, neither of them is that Monad, then that Monad is something else. And it remains as it is. How then are those other units different? And how is the dyad a "one," and is it the same "one" that is preserved in each contained unit, or must we say they participate in the first One? We must say they are other things which participate, and the dyad itself participates in the One, though not in the same way.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
**E**nough has now been said: we must finally ascend to the One itself, which is truly One, not one like other things which, though they are many in themselves, are yet one by participation in the One. For we must accept the One itself, which is not one by participation, but rather more than many. It has also been said that the intelligible world and the intellect are "more one" than all other things, and nothing is closer to the One than this; nonetheless,

<margin>B</margin>
this does not exist as the pure One. At present, we desire to contemplate—if in any way we are able—what that pure One itself is: since it is One not according to another, but according to itself. It is worthwhile, therefore, to transfer ourselves from everywhere toward the One itself: and to add nothing further to it, but to rest entirely within it, taking great care that we do not depart from it by even the smallest distance, and thus slip from the One into

<margin>C</margin>
the two. If you do not take care, you will immediately bring back two, and you will not have the One itself in the two; for both are posterior to the One. For the One does not tolerate being counted together with any other thing—whether with any single thing or with any quantity—nor does it allow itself to be numbered at all: for it is the measure itself, by no means the measured. Nor is it equal to any others, so as to agree with them in some category; otherwise, there will be something common in it, as well as in those things which are counted together with

<margin>D</margin>
it, and yet that common thing would be superior to the One, even though nothing can be superior. Consequently, neither "essential number" nor the number posterior to it pertaining to quantity can be predicated of the One. Not the essential number, I say, which through that which is called "to think" always manifests "to be"; nor that which looks to quantity, which embraces it along with others; nor even if it does not coincide with other kinds, since this is number itself.

<margin>E</margin>
Since even the nature inherent in quantitative number—imitating the nature bestowed upon the prior numbers and looking toward the truly One—undoubtedly, by likewise looking toward the One, claims the principle of numbers as its own substance. It neither destroys it nor divides it; rather, even when the dyad has arisen, the unity itself still exists before the dyad, and neither of the two units included in the dyad, nor either one of them, is that unity itself. For why should the dyad be unity itself? Or why should one unit of the dyad be unity itself rather than the other, if it were unity itself? If, therefore, neither both together nor either one alone is unity itself, certainly the unity which is the origin of the whole number is different from all these, and truly remaining in a certain way, it also seems not to remain. In what way, then, are those other units different from it? And in what way is the duality in some sense one? And is it the same "one" that is preserved in each encompassed unit? Perhaps it must be said that both units are participants in the primary unity, but are different from that in which they participate; and that the duality, insofar as it is a certain "one," is a participant in unity itself, though not in the same way everywhere.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the One. Having established that the "simply One" is higher than "essential number" or the Forms, Plotinus now explores how the One remains unchanged while generating the plurality of the universe, using the relationship between units and numbers as an analogy.</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, an army and a house are not "one" in the same way; and these are compared to a continuous thing <note>A "continuum" refers to a physical object where parts are joined together, like a piece of wood, as opposed to an army, which is a collection of separate people.</note> by a different logic, both in terms of their existence as one and their quantity as one. Is it not true, then, that the units found in a group of five relate to "the one" differently than those in a group of ten? But is the "one" itself found in the five exactly the <margin>B</margin> same as the "one" found in the ten? Perhaps if a whole small ship is compared to another whole large ship—or a city to a city, or an army to an army—the "one" in these will also be the same. Yet, if it is not the same in the former case, it cannot be in the latter either. If any doubts remain concerning these matters, they will be resolved in what follows.

*Being, essence, and existence proceed from the One itself; even the Greek names for these things declare this, following the very nature of the reality. Chapter [6].*

*One might think of "being" <note>Latin: ens</note> as a kind of composite or a pair, in which there is both "essence" and "to be," and that which is called "to be" is named as the act of essence. Being, therefore, having been born from the One, possesses essence as a kind of shadow of the One, while its "to be" is like the One’s image. Since the One itself is superior to being, it spreads its power more widely than the specific properties of being; thus it happens that even matter—which is not called "being" because of its extreme lack of forms—is nonetheless called "one." For matter is no less a "single thing" in the world despite its lack of shape. It also happens that any "privation" <note>A lack or absence of a quality.</note> is called "one" no less than a "habit" <note>A possessed quality or state of being.</note> is; yet a privation is judged to be less of a "being" than a habit is. But we have discussed these things elsewhere.*

<margin>C</margin> But we must return to our first point: you were asserting that the One itself always remains the same, even though all other things flow forth from it. In the case of numbers, while the "one" remains stable, "number" is created according to it by the action of something else. But in that which is "above essence," the One itself remains stable to a much greater degree. While it remains, it does not require another to make "beings" according to its pattern; for the One is sufficient by itself to produce beings. 

Just as in numbers, the character of the "unit"—the principle of numbers—is preserved in every number, whether in the first or second degree (for no subsequent number fails to participate in the unit), so too in the order of things: every subsequent thing has something of the First within it, like a "form" of that First. In numbers, participation in the unit produces quantity. Here, however, the trace of the One establishes the very "essence" <note>Latin: essentia</note> of things, so much so that "to be" is itself a trace of the One. 

From this, the word *Ine* <note>original Greek: εἶναι (einai), meaning "to be"</note>—which is the name declaring *usia* <note>original Greek: οὐσία (ousia), meaning "essence" or "substance"</note>—might be said to derive from the word *en* <note>original Greek: ἕν (hen), meaning "one"</note>; if one says this, perhaps they will not wander far from the truth. Truly, that which is called *on* <note>original Greek: ὄν (on), meaning "being"</note> is the first thing shining forth from the One. As if not wishing to stray far, it did not want to proceed further, but turned back toward the interior and stayed there; it was there that essence was made, and the essence of all things exists. Whoever pronounces these words, as if straining in the sound, contains himself; and thus was born *on en* <note>Being-One</note>, declaring by its very pronunciation that it flows from the One. <margin>D</margin> Indeed, the word *on* <note>Being</note>, when spoken this way, signifies that origin as much as it can. In this way, what was made into *usia* (essence) and *ine* (to be) imitate their author to the best of their power, flowing from his virtue. 

The Mind, noticing these things and led by the spectacle itself, having imitated what it knew, suddenly brought forth these voices: *on* (being), *ine* (to be), *usia* (essence), and *estia* <note>A play on words: "Hestia" is the goddess of the hearth/stability, but sounds like "ousia" (essence).</note>. For these sounds attempt to express the substance of the generated thing, with the speaker striving toward that goal, imitating as much as possible the origin of being itself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Since an army is not "one" in the same way a house is; and furthermore, in relation to a continuum, a thing is "one" according to its existence and "one" according to its quantity. Are the units in a five or a ten different, while the "one" in the five is the same as the "one" in the ten? Or if we compare one whole ship to another, or great things like a city to a city, or <margin>B</margin> an army to an army? The same applies here. If there are any difficulties regarding these things, they will be addressed later.

<margin>C</margin> But we must go back to that point: they say the First remains the same, and from it other things are born. In the case of numbers, while the "one" remains and another makes the number, the number is created according to it. But in that which truly exists among beings, the One remains even more so. While it remains, it does not make other things according to itself; rather, it is sufficient for beings to be born from it. Just as <margin>B</margin> <note>Note: The Greek margin letters restart or overlap in the source.</note> in the case of numbers, the primary qualities of the unit are in all things in a first and second degree, and each subsequent part participates in it equally, so too here: each thing after the First has something of that First, like a form of it within itself. And there, participation creates quantity; but here, the trace of the One established their "essence" <note>Greek: ousia</note> for them. So that "to be" <note>Greek: einai</note> is a trace of the One. 

And "to be," the name that reveals essence, could be said to have come from "the one" <note>Greek: hen</note>; perhaps this would hit upon the truth. For that which is called "being" <note>Greek: on</note> is the first thing from the One, as if it had stepped forward only a little and did not wish to go any further, but turned back toward the inside and stood still. It became "essence" <note>Greek: ousia</note> and is the essence of all things. When one speaks this, and holds himself in the very sound of the voice, <margin>D</margin> the "one" is suggested, showing it is from the One. And "being" signifies the speaker as much as possible. Thus, that which is created—essence and to be—imitate the One, having flowed from its power. The soul, seeing this and moved by the sight, imitating what she knows, broke out into the voice "being," "to be," "essence," and "the hearth" <note>Greek: Hestia</note>. For since the sounds were meant to reveal the underlying reality, the speaker was in labor to bring them forth, mimicking as best as possible the knowledge of being.

<summary>Plotinus explores how the "One" serves as the source of all existence and essence without being diminished itself. He uses linguistic wordplay to argue that the Greek words for "being" and "essence" are phonetically derived from the word for "one," reflecting their metaphysical origin.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the One (the Absolute). The previous page explored how units relate to numbers; this page moves into the "ineffability" of the One—the idea that it is so simple and primordial that it cannot be described by any name or category, including "being" or "essence."</meta>

# BOOK FIVE.

*Since by saying "species" <note>Original Latin: *speciem*; Greek: *εἴδους*. In this philosophical context, "species" or "form" refers to the defining characteristics or the Platonic "Form" of a thing.</note> or "essence," you conceive and define something with the intellect, know that it is not the principle of things: for that cannot be comprehended in any way. Chapter VI.*

*"The One itself" or "Unity" is a name invented by the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed numbers were the ultimate reality.</note> so that they might designate the simplicity and excellence of the principle of things as much as possible. They denied all multitude, composition, and determination from it, while affirming nothing in the meantime; they also confirmed this by the name of "Apollo." Just as the genus of sensible things has a proportion with the senses, so the intelligible genus <note>The "intelligible genus" refers to the realm of ideas or forms that can only be understood by the mind, not the eyes.</note> has a proportion with the intellect. Therefore, the principle of things, having no proportion with the intellect, excels the intelligible genus; thus, it is higher than being.*

---

<columns>

<margin>A</margin> But let these things be said as one wishes. Since the essence that is generated is a form—for one could not say that anything else is born from that source—and since it is not just some form, but every form, such that it leaves nothing else behind, it is necessary that the source itself be formless. If it is formless, it is not essence; for "essence" must be a "this something" <note>Original Greek: *τόδε τι*. This refers to a specific, identifiable individual thing.</note>. But "this something" is already defined. One <margin>B</margin> cannot grasp the One as "this something," for then it would no longer be the principle, but only that which you called "this something." If, therefore, all things are in that which is generated, what will you say the principle is among the things in it? Since it is none of these things, it can only be said to be "beyond all things." These things are beings, and Being itself; therefore, the principle is beyond being. * For "beyond <margin>* beyond being * or "truly being," or it says "this." Or the "what it was." Nor a name</margin> being" does not mean "this." It does not establish a "what." It does not even <margin>C</margin> speak a name for it. It only conveys "not this." But by doing so, it in no way encompasses it; for it is ridiculous to seek to encompass that immense nature. For he who wishes to do this moves himself away from it, and by whatever means he prepares himself, he only follows a footprint. But just as one wishing to see the intelligible nature will behold what is beyond the sensible world by having no mental image of the sensible, so also he who wishes to behold what is beyond the intelligible will behold it by <margin>D</margin> letting go of the entire intelligible realm. He learns that it exists through "this," but what kind of thing it is, he learns by letting go. This "what kind" would signify "not what kind," for there is no "what kind" for that which has no "what" <note>Original Greek: *τὶ*. This is a play on Aristotelian categories: if a thing has no substance or "whatness," it cannot have qualities or "whyness."</note>. But we, in our own labor pains, are at a loss as to what we should say. And we speak about that which is unutterable and we give it names, wishing to signify it to ourselves as best we can. Perhaps even the name "the One" contains <margin>E</margin> a removal <note>Original Greek: *ἄρσιν*. A technical term for "negation" or "lifting away" attributes.</note> of the many. Hence the Pythagoreans symbolically signaled this to one another by the name "Apollo," signifying the negation of the many <note>Original: *Ἀπόλλωνα*. A traditional Neo-Platonic etymology: *a-* (not) + *pollon* (many).</note>. But if "the One"—the name and the thing signified—were a positive statement, it would become more obscure than if one had not spoken a name for it at all. For perhaps this name was spoken so that the seeker, starting from it because it is the <margin>* most of all</margin> most indicative of simplicity, might end by denying even this, on the grounds that while it was given as well as the giver could, it is not actually worthy to represent that nature.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But let these things be accepted as each person pleases. When, however, essence is a generated form—for no one would call anything else that is born from that source anything but form—let it be, I say, not just a certain form, but every form, so that nothing of form is left over; it is then necessary that the One itself have no form. Since it is foreign to form, it cannot even be essence: for it is necessary that essence be "this something." That, however, is already determined, but it is not permitted to think of the One <margin>B</margin> as "this something." Otherwise, it would no longer be the principle, but only that which you were calling "this something." If, therefore, all things are in that which is generated from it, you will say that none of those things within it are truly the author of all. And since it is none of these things at all, it can only be said to be that which exists above these. These, however, are beings and Being itself: therefore, that is higher than being. Now indeed, that which is higher than being does not say "this something": for it does not posit anything, nor <margin>C</margin> does it speak its name, but it brings only this: "not this." But in doing so, it never comprehends it: for it is ridiculous to strive to embrace that immense nature. Whoever strives for that removes himself very far from even the smallest footprint of it. Indeed, just as one desiring to know the intelligible nature will then finally know what is above the sensible genus when he holds no image at all of a sensible thing; so <margin>D</margin> also he who desires to contemplate the nature superior to the intelligible nature will contemplate it, provided he dismisses everything intelligible. By this, I say, he learns that it exists, but entirely dismissing what kind of thing it is. This very word that is called "what kind" signifies in truth "not what kind." For to that which the "what" <note>Original: *quid*. The essence or substance of a thing.</note> we are accustomed to say does not belong, neither does that which we are accustomed to call "what kind" <note>Original: *quale*. The quality of a thing.</note> fit. But we, laboring as if in the anxieties of one giving birth, do not know what is most fitting to <margin>E</margin> say. And about that which cannot be spoken, we speak and give names, striving to signify something to ourselves as best we can. Perhaps even this name which is called "the One" signifies, through a certain respect to the many, a negation and an elevation. Wherefore the Pythagoreans also named it "Apollo" among themselves with a more secret signification: namely, by the negation of the many. But if this name "the One" in its signification posits and affirms something, then the name and the thing named will be more obscure than if one had not mentioned its name at all. For perhaps the name was spoken so that the seeker, beginning from that which can most of all signify simplicity, may finally reach the point of denying even this, as if it were imposed only as well as the namer was able; yet even this is not worthy to signify that nature.

</columns>

<summary>This page argues that the ultimate Principle (the One) must be formless and beyond "being" or "essence" because it precedes all definitions. Plotinus explains that names like "the One" or the Pythagorean "Apollo" are merely useful negations to help the mind move beyond the many toward the absolute simplicity of the source.</summary>

<keywords>The One, Essence, Being, Formless, Pythagoreanism, Apollo, Negation, Simplicity, Plotinus, Intelligible World</keywords>

--- Page 694 ---
<meta>This page continues the exploration of the "One" or the "First Principle." Having established in the previous page that the source of all things must be "formless" and beyond "essence" (as it precedes the categories of being), Plotinus now uses the famous analogy of light to explain how the human mind can perceive this ultimate reality through intuition rather than logic or the senses.</meta>

# PLOTINUS: ENNEADS, BOOK V

<columns>

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, that <note>The "One" or the "First Principle."</note> cannot be reached by the ear, nor can it be understood by one who merely hears of it; but if it is to be revealed to anyone, it happens to the one who is looking. Yet, if the observer tries to look upon it as a specific "form" <note>Original Latin: *speciem*; Greek: *εἴδους*. In Platonic thought, a "Form" is the perfect blueprint of a thing. The One is above even these perfect blueprints.</note>, they will not see it as such.

Just as by light itself the eye is made sharp and colors become visible—in which the eye sees the light, even if it does not see the light as an object in itself—so too by the First Principle, the mind <note>Original Latin: *mens*; Greek: *νοῦς* (Intellect). For Plotinus, this is the highest part of the soul.</note> is able to understand, and truths become intelligible. In these truths, the mind perceives the light of the principle itself; however, it cannot perceive that light as a separate thing existing within itself.

<margin>Chapter VII.</margin>

THEREFORE, there are two ways of seeing in practice, just as occurs with the physical eye. Truly, one kind of sight for the eye is the object itself—that is, the form of the sensible thing. But the other kind is that by which it sees that form. This "seeing-power" is also sensible to the eye, yet it is certainly different from the form of the object. It is the cause through which the form is perceived, existing within the form and seen along with it. Because of this, it is not then perceived very clearly, <margin>B</margin> since the eye directs itself more intently toward the thing being illuminated. 

But when there is nothing else besides the light itself, the eye perceives it with a sudden and total intuition, even though it still feels the light as something attached to another thing. However, if the light were alone and joined to nothing at all, the senses would not be able to grasp it; for the light of the sun, dwelling in the sun itself, would perhaps escape our senses unless the solid mass of the sun were placed beneath it. If someone were to say that the whole sun is light, perhaps that would serve as an explanation of what we are saying: <margin>C</margin> for light would exist in no other form of the things that are seen, and perhaps it would be visible only as something bright; for other visible things are not solely made of light. 

By the same logic, the vision of the mind also sees through another light those things illuminated by that First Nature, and in them, it truly sees that light. Nevertheless, by turning itself more greedily toward the nature of the illuminated things, it sees the light within them less clearly. But if the mind lets go of the objects it sees and gazes intently at the light through which it sees, <margin>D</margin> it will then fully perceive the light itself and the source of that light. 

But since the mind must not look at such light as something external, let us return to the example of the eye, which sometimes does not see an external or foreign light, but before seeing external light, perceives a certain light of its own. This light shines more brilliantly in its own private and pure seat, <margin>E</margin> or at night in the darkness, it sees a certain ray springing forth from itself. Or, when it wishes to see nothing of other things, it closes itself behind the covering of the eyelids and meanwhile produces light from within. Or, when someone presses the corners of their eyelids and sees the light that was hidden inside, then truly, by not seeing, it sees—and then it sees most of all. For it sees light itself. The other things it had seen before were indeed bright, but they were not light itself. 

In this way, the mind, separating itself from other things and drawing back into its interior, seeing nothing else, perceives the light immediately—not as one thing within another, but light itself <margin>F</margin> according to itself alone, pure, flashing out from itself by its own power.

<column-break/>

Because that is not something to be heard, nor can it be understood by the hearer in that way. But if it is to be seen by anyone, it is by vision; yet if the one seeing seeks to see a "form," they will not perceive it even then.

<margin>Chapter VII.</margin>

<margin>A</margin> Or rather, since actual seeing is twofold, as it is with the eye: one type of vision for it is the form, the sensible object. The other is that through which it sees the form, which is itself also sensible to it, though it is different from the form. It is the cause for the form's existence, observed in the form and upon the form. Therefore, it does not give a clear perception of itself, <margin>B</margin> because the eye is focused on the illuminated object. But when there is nothing else besides it, it is seen by a sudden assault of intuition. And then it was seen, resting upon another. But if it becomes alone, not directed toward another, the sense cannot grasp it in the same way. For even the light of the sun, being in itself, would perhaps have escaped the senses if a more solid mass did not lie beneath it. If someone should say the sun is all light, this would be for the sake of making clear what is said. <margin>C</margin> for it will be in none of the other things seen. And it is visible only as light, while other things are visible insofar as they are luminous. 

In this way then, the vision of the mind also sees for itself, through another light, the things illuminated by that first nature, and in those things it sees. Looking indeed toward the nature of the things it has grasped, it sees the light less. But if it should let go of the things seen, and look toward that through which it saw, <margin>D</margin> it would see the light and the source of the light. Since it must not see such a thing as if it were outside, one must return again to the eye. Sometimes the eye does not see an external light, nor perceive one that is foreign, but before the external, it gazes upon something of its own, even more glistening, in a momentary flash. <margin>E</margin> Or as in the case of those in the dark, light springs forth from within themselves; or when one, wishing to see nothing of other things, wraps the nature of the eyelids around themselves, the light nevertheless is carried around within. Or if one, by pressing the eye, sees the light held within it. Then indeed, while not seeing, one sees. And most of all then one sees. For one sees light. The other things were light-like, but they were not light. 

So indeed, the mind too, having covered itself from other things and having withdrawn into the interior, seeing nothing, will behold not one light in another; <margin>F</margin> but it will behold the light itself by itself alone, pure, appearing suddenly upon itself.

</columns>

<summary>Plotinus uses the analogy of physical sight and the sun to explain how the human mind perceives the "One." Just as we usually see illuminated objects rather than light itself, we must look past "forms" and "truths" to see the pure, internal light of the First Principle.</summary>
