<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "One" (or the First Principle) from the previous section. While the earlier text established that the source of all things is formless and beyond essence, Plotinus now describes the "arrival" of this principle—not as a physical movement, but as a spiritual realization within the soul and intellect.</meta>

# BOOK FIVE

*Expel three things from the soul: motion, multiplicity, and determination—that is, the state by which the soul devotes itself to some specific thing, whether for thinking or for desiring. Chapter VIII.*

*Immediately the soul—a faculty closest to the immovable, simple, and absolute principle—is filled with a new light from that same source; soon it perceives itself to be wonderfully more beautiful than usual. It truly gazes upon this light of new beauty as something innermost; then it realizes that this very light comes to it from the principle, where it also recognizes the light as something outermost.*

---

<margin>A</margin>
As for that light, one might eventually wonder where it shone from: from the outside or from within? And when it has departed, one might say, "It was within me," and then again, "No, it was not within." But truly, one should not search for where it comes from, for there is no "where" or "source-point" <note>original: "unde". Plotinus is emphasizing that the First Principle does not occupy a physical location.</note> here. For it does not arrive here, nor does it depart from here to go elsewhere; rather, it either appears to us or does not appear. Therefore, one should not chase after it, but rather remain in stillness until it appears, preparing oneself to be a spectator, <margin>B</margin> just as the eye waits for the rising of the sun—which, as the poets say, reveals itself to our sight by rising from the horizon and the Ocean. But this One—the one the sun merely imitates—from where will it shine from above? Or what will it transcend to glow clearly for us? Indeed, it will illuminate the mind <term>Intellect (Nous)</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, the "Intellect" or "Mind" is the first emanation from the One and contains all true forms of reality.</note> that looks up toward it. Thus, the intellect will steady itself for the vision, gazing at nothing other than Beauty itself, turning its whole self toward it and giving itself entirely. <margin>C</margin> Standing firm and as if filled with vigor, the intellect first looks back at itself, now made more beautiful and glowing, because it is now close to the Highest. 

God, however, does not "arrive" as one might perhaps have expected; rather, He comes as if not coming. He appears not by arriving, but as being present before and above all things, even before the intellect approached. It is actually the intellect that "arrives" and "departs." It departs when it does not know where it ought to remain, or where He <margin>D</margin> stays; for in truth, He remains in nothing. If the intellect could also be "nowhere"—and I do not mean just in a physical place, for the intellect itself is not in space, but entirely "nowhere"—it would undoubtedly behold Him always. It would not be "beholding" Him as an object, but by being in Him; and not even then as two separate things. But now, because it is intellect, it sees when it sees by that which is not intellect within itself <note>Plotinus suggests that to perceive the One, the mind must go beyond its usual "thinking" mode and enter a state of pure intuition.</note>. And truly it is a wonder how He is present without arriving, and how <margin>E</margin> while He exists, He is nowhere, yet because of that very fact He is everywhere. This state of affairs is naturally a cause for wonder; but for the one who has known the reality itself, it would be more wonderful if the opposite were said. Indeed, it cannot be otherwise, so that one might wonder even more vehemently; for so it is.

<column-break/>

---

*Since all things depend on God, but He depends on no one: therefore all things are in Him, but He is in no one; He contains all things, but is not contained. Chapter IX.*

*Because He is contained by no one, He is nowhere; but because He contains all things, He is present to all. Thus the body of the world is in the World-Soul, the Soul is in the Mind, and the Mind is in the Good; but not the other way around. Therefore, just as the soul is present as a whole to every individual part of the body as something free, so the Good, being absolute from all limits, is present to all things. Truly, whatever does not depend for its existence on a specific subject or place, nor on a certain nature, is everywhere and nowhere—just like the soul, the mind, and God.*

---

<margin>A</margin>
Whatever is made by another is either in its author, or in something else, if indeed anything remains besides the author. For since it is made by another and requires another for its placement, it surely requires another everywhere; therefore it rests in another.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
Whatever is made by another is either in its author, or in something else, if indeed anything exists besides the author. For since it is made by another and requires another for its birth, it surely requires another everywhere; therefore it rests in another.

<summary>This page describes the mystical experience of the Mind (Intellect) perceiving the "One" as an internal and external light. Plotinus explains that the First Principle (God) is omnipresent yet nowhere in space, existing as the source in which all other things rest.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "One" (or the First Principle) and its relationship to the hierarchy of existence. Having previously established that this principle appears as a light within the soul, Plotinus now explains the logic of its omnipresence: how the higher contains the lower, culminating in a source that is "everywhere because it is nowhere."</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

<margin>A</margin> Thus, nature is so arranged that the last things are everywhere contained within the second-to-last; and these, in turn, are similarly contained in those prior to them, and one thing always within another, until the highest point is reached. But the highest principle, since nothing stands further above it, cannot be within anything else. Since it is not in another, while all other things are in those prior to them, it follows that this principle encompasses all remaining things. Encompassing them, it is not scattered into them, and it possesses them without being possessed by them. And certainly, since it possesses <margin>B</margin> but is not possessed, there is no place where it is not: for if it were not present, it would not possess. Conversely, if it is not possessed, it is not "present" in a restricted sense. It is therefore present and yet not present; indeed, insofar as it is not grasped, it is not present at all; but insofar as it is free from everything, it is nowhere prohibited from being present. For if it were restricted, it would surely be defined by something else, and the things following after it would be left without a share of it. God himself would rule only up to that point, and nothing more would be <margin>C</margin> in him, nor would he stand within himself, but would instead serve the things that follow. Therefore, whatever things are in something else are properly there, belonging to the jurisdiction of that thing. But whatever things are not properly in a specific "somewhere" are of such a nature that there is nowhere they are not. For if something is not *here*, another place surely encompasses it, and it exists in some other place as if in a location; therefore, it would be false to say it is not "somewhere." If, then, it is true that it is not "somewhere," and false that it is "somewhere" (lest it be in another), it is certainly absent from nowhere. <margin>D</margin> If it is absent from nothing, yet does not exist in a specific "somewhere," it will be everywhere within itself. For one part of it will not be here while another is there, nor will the whole be only there; rather, it will be everywhere as a whole. Since no single thing possesses it "somewhere," nor does any thing lack it, it is held in such a way that it is actually the one doing the holding. Come now and consider this world: if no other world exists that is superior to it, it is not in a world, nor is it in a place. For what place could exist before the world came to be? But the parts of the <margin>E</margin> world are gathered into it and located within it. The Soul, however, is not in the world, but rather the world is in the Soul; for the body is not the "place" for the soul, but the Soul is in the Mind <note>original: "mente". Here referring to the *Nous* or Divine Intellect, the second hypostasis in Plotinian thought.</note>, and the body is in the Soul. Finally, the Mind consists in another <note>The One</note>, which does not depend on anything else in which it might be compelled to rest. It rests properly in nothing, and for this reason, it is said to be "nowhere." Where then are other things? Without doubt, they are in it. Thus, it is neither absent from others, nor poured out into them, nor is there anything that "has" it; rather, it contains all things. For this reason, it is judged to be the "Good" of all things: because all things exist through it and are drawn toward it. One thing is related to it in one way, another in another; therefore, some things are better than others, because some are closer to it than others.

<column-break/>

<note>This column translates the original Greek text provided in the source.</note>

It is natural then that the last things are in the things before them, and those in the first things, and those in the things before them, and one thing in another, up to the first principle. But the principle, having nothing before it, has nothing else to be in. Since it has nothing to be in, and other things are in those before them, it has encompassed all other things, being the one that encompasses. It is not scattered into them, and it possesses them without being possessed. Possessing them and not being possessed, it is what it is not <note>meaning it is not any of the specific things it contains</note>. If it were not, it would not possess. But if it is not possessed, it is not. Thus it both is and is not. By not being contained, it is not; but by being free from all things, it is nowhere prevented from being. For if it were prevented, it would be limited by another. Then the things following would have no share of it. And God would only reach to this point. If he were confined to himself, he would be a slave to what comes after him. The things that are in a being are there where they are; but those that are not, there is nowhere they are not. For if it were not here, it would clearly be elsewhere. If it were held here, it would be in another, so it is false to say it is "here" and not in anything else. It is absent from nothing. If it is absent from nothing, either being all things, it is everywhere, or it is in itself. For in this way, one part is here and another there. Yet it is here as a whole. So it is everywhere as a whole. No single thing possesses it, nor does any thing not possess it. It is held by whatever it may be. Look at the world: since it is in no other world, it is carried along. It is not in a world itself. Nor is it in a place. For what place is there before a world exists? But the parts are placed in it and are in that world. The soul is not in that world, but the world is in the soul. Nor is the soul a place for the body, but the soul is in the Mind. If you see where it is, it is nowhere. Are the other things not in it? They are suspended from it, because it is in them. It is not in them as if they held it, but it holds all things. Therefore, in this way, it is the Good of all things, because all things exist and are suspended from it, each in its own way. Therefore, some are better than others, because some exist more than others.

---

*Complex things are resolved into simple things; many simple things into one most simple thing; and this into simplicity itself. And you, if you ever grasp it, will not receive any part of it; for it has no parts, nor is it a "whole" in the sense of having a structure, otherwise you would be equal to it.* <margin>Chapter X.</margin>

You will grasp it, though not in every aspect, but rather through a certain quality and power of it; nevertheless, you will perceive it through a universal and most simple act, regardless of how much or in what capacity you are to perceive it. For God occurs as a whole all at once, and if you use any composition <note>any logical complexity or division</note> in your perception, you will separate yourself entirely from his simplicity.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the "One," the absolute first principle of reality. # BOOK FIVE.

<column-break/>

**A** Truly, I pray you, do not look upon God <note>original: "Deum" / "αὐτὸ" (it/him). Plotinus refers to 'The One,' but the Latin translator uses 'God'</note> through other things; otherwise, know that you will find not God, but only His footprint. Instead, consider within yourself what this most excellent thing might be: that which is permitted to be perceived as existing only in itself, pure, and mixed with nothing—that in which all things certainly participate, yet nothing possesses. Surely nothing else can be such a thing, and it is undoubtedly necessary for something of this kind to exist. Who, then, could grasp His entire power all at once? For if one were to grasp it all at once, how **B** would he be judged to differ from Him? Does he then receive it only in part? Yet, by gazing upon Him, you will behold Him in a single, total, and unique stroke; however, you will not be able to describe the whole to yourself. Otherwise, you would be an intellect that understands, provided you have attained anything at all; but God will immediately escape you—or rather, you will escape God. However, when you look, behold the whole; and as soon as you have understood Him, whatever you preserve of Him in your memory, **C** remember that it is the Good itself. For He is the cause of a wise and intellectual life, since He is the very power from which life and intellect are born; indeed, He is the author of essence and being, because He is the One itself. For He is simple, and He is the first, because He is the beginning. From Him, all things flow forth; from Him, the first movement arises, yet it is not in Him. From Him also comes stability, since He Himself lacks nothing. For He neither moves nor rests, since He has nothing in which to **D** rest or in which to revolve. For around what, or toward what most of all, or in what specifically would He either move or rest? For He is the first. But neither can He be defined, for otherwise, by whom could He be defined? Nor, again, is He "infinite" in the way an immense mass is usually imagined. Then, where must He go? If it were said He goes forth, would it be so that He might bring back something from there—He who lacks absolutely nothing? But the power itself possesses infinity; for He is not infinite in any other way, nor does He ever change His state, nor will He ever fail; since whatever things do not fail have this very quality specifically from Him.

<column-break/>

**A** TRULY, this infinite is called so because it is no more than one, and does not have anything toward which any part of its own might be bounded. Because it is one, it is neither measured nor does it proceed into number; therefore, it is bounded neither toward anything else nor toward itself, for in that way it would surely be two. Nor, again, does it have a shape, since it has neither parts nor a form. Do not, therefore, search for this with mortal eyes, as though it were the sort of thing **B** that reason proves. Do not think, I say, that this can be known in the same way someone might expect who thinks everything is a sensible object <note>meaning something perceived by the five senses</note>; for in doing so, he removes that which is the greatest of all. For those things that someone might perhaps think exist most truly, these most truly do not exist. But that which is great in quantity...

### The first principle, because of its inestimable simplicity and the excellence by which it is called the One, is limited neither from without nor from within. Chapter XI.

> *It neither rests nor moves, nor does it have shape or form: it is infinite in power, not in quantity. They are deceived who think that bodies, because of their size, are the most real and the greatest things; for because of that same size, one might say they are infinitely divisible, and neither this part nor that is the whole itself. One might also say they are infinitely small: this part is small, and that part is small. Therefore, a physical body is not itself "infinitely," and it is infinitely small. Finally, we distrust the truth of things that are separate from matter because of our too much commerce with the material world; souls in this body dream, but outside they wake.*

Plotinus explains that while bodies are "large" in size but small in true being, the One is "infinite" not in size, but in its inexhaustible capacity to generate existence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s argument regarding the primacy of the One (the Good). On the previous page, he established that the One is the source of all essence and life, transcending even the Intellect. Here, he cautions against the error of thinking that because the One is "simple," it is somehow "less" than the complex things it creates.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

<margin>B</margin>
...it is less [than what follows]? On the contrary: that which is first is the principle of being, and is more masterful than essence itself. Therefore, we must shift our opinion to the opposite view, otherwise we shall be left destitute of God. We would be like those who, during the solemn celebration of festivals, gluttonously fill their bellies with feasts which are forbidden for those about to enter the presence of the gods to even taste. Such people think the nourishment of the belly is more certain than the actual contemplation of God, in whose honor the festival is held; thus, they depart without sharing in the sacred rites. Indeed, in such mysteries, because God is not seen with the physical eye, he is thought not to exist by those who believe only that which is tasted by the flesh and seen with the eyes is certain. It is as if a man slept through his entire life and believed that only the things seen in dreams were truly certain. If someone were to wake them, they would have no faith in the things perceived with open eyes, and would immediately fall back to sleep.

*Just as the intellect is different from the senses, so too are intelligible things different from sensible ones. You do not deny that voices exist simply because you cannot see them. Therefore, do not deny that separate realities exist just because you cannot grasp them with your senses or a sense-based intelligence. Finally, know that the Good itself exists even above the intellect and the intelligible world.*

### Cap. XII.

*All things always desire the Good in every way; however, not all things desire the Beautiful, nor do they do so always or in every way. For this reason, in further judgment, the Good itself is considered more excellent than Beauty. Thus, beauty is secondary to the Good, just as the love of beauty is an added thing that falls upon us after our natural appetite for the Good. While supreme beauty exists in the first rank of forms—where the Intellect and the Intelligible reside in their most perfect and all-encompassing shape—the Good itself is rightly judged to be higher than Beauty, and similarly more exalted than both the intellect and the intelligible.*

<margin>A</margin>
**I**t is worthwhile to prepare oneself to perceive each thing using the specific faculty by which that thing ought to be perceived. For some things are perceived by the eyes, others by the ears, and others by different means. One must believe that the mind <note>The term "Mind" or "Intellect" (Latin: *Mens* / Greek: *Nous*) refers to the highest part of the human soul that can grasp divine truths.</note> perceives things beyond the others. One must not think that "understanding" is the same as hearing or seeing—as if one were to command the ears to see, and then deny that voices exist simply because they cannot be seen. 

<margin>B</margin>
Therefore, we must consider that such people have forgotten that which they have desired and yearned for from the beginning until this day. For all things seek that Good by a necessity of nature, as if they were divining <note>original: "vaticinentur." This suggests a prophetic or intuitive "gut feeling" that all living things have about their source.</note> that they cannot exist without it. Furthermore, the knowledge of Beauty itself only comes to souls that are already awake and conscious. It arrives accompanied by amazement and a stirring related to love. But the Good itself—because it has been present from the beginning as an innate appetite—is present even to those who sleep. It never overwhelms those who look upon it with amazement, because it is always there and requires no specific act of memory to be recognized. 

<margin>C</margin>
Yet, it does not occur to those who are noticing it, precisely because it is also present to those who are asleep. The love of Beauty, however, when it first offers itself, brings "labor pains" <note>original: "molestias" / "ὠδῖνας". Plotinus uses the metaphor of birth-pangs to describe the soul's intense struggle and effort when it encounters divine beauty.</note>, because one must seek beauty through conscious knowledge. But since such love is secondary and belongs to those who already possess understanding, it clearly indicates that Beauty itself is secondary. The appetite for the Good, being more ancient and requiring no senses, testifies that the Good itself is more ancient and higher than Beauty. Add to this that everyone believes they have enough once they have attained the Good, as if they have finally reached the end of their journey; but Beauty...

<column-break/>

<margin>B</margin>
...is it more? No, the first is the principle of being, and more masterful than essence itself. Thus, the opinion that it is "more" is correct. Otherwise, you will be left behind, destitute, like those at festivals who stuff themselves and are not permitted to reach the gods within. Thinking that the things they see are more vivid than the vision of God (which is the proper order of things), they do not participate in the sacred rites there. For in these rites, God is not seen, and is thus disbelieved by those who think only that which they see with the flesh is real. It is as if people slept through life and thought their dreams were vivid and real; if one were to wake them, they would distrust what they saw with open eyes and fall back asleep.

<margin>A</margin>
**O**ne must look with the faculty by which each thing is meant to be judged. Some things with the eyes, others with the ears, and so on. One must see other things with the Mind. One should not think that "intellection" is hearing or seeing, as if one were to order the ears to see, and say that sounds do not exist because they are not seen. 

<margin>B</margin>
One must realize that they have forgotten that which they have desired from the beginning until now, and which they still reach for. For all things reach for That, and exist for That, by a necessity of nature, as if sensing by a divine intuition <term>Hypomanteuomena: a quiet, prophetic intuition or "guessing" by the soul</term> that they cannot exist without it. Beauty is perceived by those who are already knowing and awake; it brings wonder and the stirring of love. But the Good, since it has long been present as a natural desire, is present even to the sleeping. It never strikes those who see it with wonder, for it is always there. No "remembrance" is ever needed for it. 

<margin>C</margin>
They do not see it because it is present even to those who sleep. But the love of Beauty, when it is present, brings birth-pangs. For those who see it must yearn for it. This love comes second, to those who already understand, which shows that Beauty is a lesser, secondary thing. But the desire for the Good is more ancient and requires no conscious perception, which tells us that the Good is more ancient and perhaps prior to Beauty. All men think that if they get the Good, it is enough for them, for they have reached the end.

<summary>Plotinus distinguishes between the Good and Beauty, arguing that while Beauty requires conscious effort and "awakening" to appreciate, the Good is a fundamental, innate drive present in all things, even those who are "asleep" to spiritual reality.</summary>

# BOOK FIVE.

But the beautiful is such that when everyone sees it appearing, they think it is beautiful for itself, but not necessarily for them—just as is the case with the beauty of this world. For to the one who possesses it, it is enough to be beautiful and to seem beautiful to others, even if they are not truly so. But the Good—men do not wish to possess it merely in opinion <note>original: δόξῃ (doxē) - meaning reputation or appearance</note>. For they strive most of all for the first principle. And they contend for it, and they are drawn away from it by the beautiful, as if it were something that had come into being for itself just as they had. It is as if someone coming after a king should wish to reach the same level of dignity as the person who immediately follows the king, on the grounds that they both originated from the same source as that person. Such a man is ignorant of how he himself is suspended from the king, and yet that other person is also suspended from him. But the reason for this is not the same cause; it is because both participate in the same things. Or rather, the "well-being" of both comes first, and that even for the king, the Good itself is primary, though he requires beauty. But the beautiful requires that Good. And there [in the Good], everything is mild, and gentle, and more delicate. And even if someone were to leave it behind—
<margin>* present</margin>
even if it were *present to him. But the beautiful possesses a sense of awe, and astonishment, and a certain pleasure mixed with pain. For it even draws away those who do not know the Good, just as a beloved child is drawn away from a father. For the beautiful is younger. But the Good is older—
<margin>* or older, either in time, but in truth. * or because it possesses</margin>
not *older in time, but in truth. * Or because it possesses its power prior to all else. For it possesses all power. But that which comes after it does not possess all power, but only as much as exists after it and comes from it. Thus, the Good is the master of even this power. It has no need of those things that are generated from it; instead, it lets go of everything that has been brought into being as a whole and entirely, because it has no need of anything. But it remains the same as it was—
<margin>* or it will participate before this came to be, since it was already about to * happen</margin>

For even if it were possible for something else to be generated from it, it would not have envied it; however, there is nothing else for it to become. For there is nothing that has not already come into being, since all things are in the process of becoming. But the Good itself is not directed toward all things, for then it would have need of them, having transcended—

<column-break/>

**A** But the beautiful, indeed, not all think will satisfy them sufficiently. Furthermore, some, even when beauty is present, think little of it: likewise, they judge that what is beautiful is beautiful for itself rather than for them, just as they believe this beauty of ours belongs specifically to the one who possesses it. Then, indeed, it seems enough for most people if they *appear* beautiful, even if they are not so at all; but the Good they desire to possess not just in opinion, but in reality. For all men—
**B** what is first of all—strive to acquire it for themselves above all else. What shall we say to this? That souls contend together with the beautiful, as if with a certain zeal for victory? As if beauty itself were made from elsewhere, just as they themselves were made from elsewhere. It is as if someone following after a king should strive to equal the dignity of someone else who immediately follows the king; namely, one who depends on one and the same source as he does, being ignorant, of course, that he also depends on the king, but that the other precedes him. The cause of the error is this:
**C** that both are participants in the same thing, and one thing is prior to both. It is established, moreover, that the Good itself has no need of the beautiful, but the beautiful needs the Good. Accordingly, the Good itself is gentle, mild, calm, and delicate, and just as one is accustomed to being when meeting a friend. But the beautiful either renders the soul stunned <note>Plotinus describes the experience of Beauty as a "shock" or "trauma" to the soul compared to the quiet peace of the Good.</note>, or it stirs it up and mingles pleasure with pain. Finally, it is often accustomed to turning incautious souls away from the Good, just as a beloved often separates a lover from his father. For the beautiful
**D** is younger, but the Good is more ancient—not indeed in time, but in truth—which indeed also possesses a prior power. For it possesses all power; but that which is after it does not possess all, but only so much as is after it and from it. Therefore, that Father is also the master of this power, in no way needing those things which are generated from him, but dismissing the whole and the entire thing which is generated; since it needs this under no condition at all, but
**E** exists as the very same thing that it was before it generated this from itself. And indeed, it would be of no interest to him if this had not been generated; since even if something else could have been generated from him besides, he would not envy it the gift of being. But now, nothing further can be produced; for nothing remains which has not already been procreated, since all things have already been made. But God himself does not exist as "all things," for then he would need all things; rather, surpassing all, he was able to constitute all things, and to permit all things to be themselves, he himself being pre-eminent over all.

*All beings, being more or less good among themselves, end in some being that is maximally good; this is finally resolved into the Good itself—that is, goodness simply in itself, which is superior to being.*

->*Cap. XIII.*<-

When you name this very thing <note>referring to "The Good" or "The One"</note>, do not think of two things—that is, some "thing" together with "goodness." Otherwise, the principle of things will be a composite, and it will not be absolute goodness, but only a certain goodness, and as if it were a participant in the good. It would then be referred back to a higher Good, which is not good by participation. Of essence, life, and mind, it can sometimes be said they are evil, or at least not good, or certainly more or less good. But such things cannot be said of that which is simply Goodness itself. Therefore, the logic of Goodness itself is both different and simpler, and therefore prior to the logic of essence, life, and mind. Do not, therefore, imagine God to be a composite at first; for otherwise, the principle of things will be a composite, and he will be good not formally, but by a certain participation in a higher and simpler good. Finally, the Good itself, which is sought by all essences, lives, and minds, and which perfects and produces them, must not be said to possess essence, life, or mind in the strict sense—just as we do not say the sun possesses those things in itself which it causes in the elements, namely heat of that kind, and growth, and generation, and similar forms and figures. <note>Plotinus uses the sun analogy to explain how the One creates things like "life" without being "alive" in a biological or limited sense; it is the source of life, which is a higher state.</note>

<summary>This page distinguishes between the Beautiful and the Good, arguing that while beauty can be a distracting or overwhelming "younger" reflection, the Good is the "older," self-sufficient, and simple source of all existence. Plotinus emphasizes that the ultimate Principle (the One/the Good) must be absolutely simple and not a composite of different qualities.</summary>

--- Page 700 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s metaphysical exploration of the First Principle, which he calls "The Good" (or "The One"). On the previous page, he distinguished the Good from the Beautiful, arguing that while beauty is desirable, the Good is an absolute necessity. Here, he moves into "negative theology," arguing that the First Principle must be entirely simple and devoid of any attributes—even the attribute of "being good"—to truly be the source of all things.</meta>

# PLOTINUS: ENNEAD V.

<margin>A</margin> Since God <note>The Latin translator uses "Deus" (God) for Plotinus's "The One" or "The Good," reflecting a common Renaissance attempt to harmonize Neoplatonism with Christian theology.</note> is truly the Good itself, and not merely "a good thing," he must possess nothing at all within himself, since he does not even "possess" the Good. For if he possessed something, he would possess either a good or something not good. But in that which is properly, primarily, and chiefly the Good, there can be nothing "not good," nor can the Good itself "have" the Good <note>Plotinus argues that the First Principle does not "have" properties; it *is* reality itself. To "have" something implies a separation between the owner and the property, which would break the absolute unity of the One.</note>. Therefore, if it possesses neither the "not good" nor "the good," it possesses absolutely nothing. And if it possesses nothing, it is alone, set apart from all things.

<margin>B</margin> If, therefore, other things are either good (yet are not the Good itself) or perhaps are not good, and the First Principle possesses neither of these states, then surely by possessing nothing, it is the Good itself. If anyone adds anything to it—whether essence, or mind, or beauty—they certainly take away from it by that very addition. By stripping away everything and affirming nothing about it, and not speaking falsely as if there were something within it, one correctly allows it to be called only "that which is." One testifies nothing of those things which are not present in it.

<margin>C</margin> In this matter, many are accustomed to err. Since they do not know how to praise someone, they actually detract from the glory of the person they wish to honor by adding things to them that are lesser than their true dignity, being ignorant of how to apply true praise to the persons being honored. For this reason, we must be especially careful not to add anything of the later and lesser things. We must strictly observe that this God, who transcends all these things, is their cause, yet he is none of them himself.

<margin>D</margin> Now, the nature of the Good is not to be all things, nor even any one of all things. Truly, if it were any one of all things, it would be under one and the same category as everything else. But if it were under the same category as the others, it would differ from them only by its own specific trait—that is, by a distinction and an addition. It would then be two things and no longer "one." One of those two would be "not good" (the part it shares with everything else), and the other would be "good." It would thus be a mixture of the good and the not-good,

<margin>E</margin> and therefore, it would be neither purely nor primarily the Good. That which is primarily the Good would be that from which this composite thing participates to become good. This composite would be good through a certain participation; but that in which it participates is nothing among all things. Therefore, the Good itself is nothing among all things. But if this "goodness" is within it—since it is the difference through which this composite is made good—it is necessary that this thing depends on another which is entirely simple and is the Good alone.

<margin>F</margin> This composite, being manifold, depends on that which is only the Good. Therefore, it is established that what exists primarily, and is the Good itself, is above all beings, is the Good alone, and possesses nothing in itself. It is entirely unmixed with anything, transcends all things, and is the cause of all things. For beauty does not come from evil, nor do beings come from evil, nor even from things that are indifferent. For the maker is better than the effect, since the maker is more perfect.

<column-break/>

Since he is the Good itself and not just "a good thing," he must not have anything in himself, since he does not even have "the good." For what he has, he has either as a good or a non-good. But in the Good, the truly and primarily Good, there is no "non-good." Nor does the Good have "the good." If, therefore, he has neither the non-good nor the good, he has nothing. If he has nothing, he is alone and solitary from others. If, then, other things are either good (and not the Good itself) or not good, and he has neither of these, by having nothing <margin>likewise</margin> he is the Good. If anyone adds anything to him—either essence <note>original: οὐσίαν (ousian)</note>, or mind <note>original: νοῦν (noun)</note>, or beauty—one takes away his being the Good by that addition.

By taking all things away and saying nothing about him—not even speaking falsely as if there were something in him—allow "he is" <note>original: τὸ ἐσίν (to estin)</note> to stand. Do not testify to anything not present. Just as those who give praise without knowledge diminish the reputation of those they praise by adding things lesser than their worth—because they are at a loss to speak the truth about the subjects—so we should add nothing of the later and lesser things. Instead, we should see him as transcending these, being their cause but not being these things himself. 

For the nature of the Good is not to be all things, nor any one of all things. For it would then be under one and the same category as all. Being under the same as all, it would differ only by its own peculiarity, by a distinction and an addition. It would then be two, not one. One part would be "not good" (the common part), and the other "good." It would be a mixture of good and not-good. It would not be purely good, nor primarily. That would be primarily good which, by participation beyond the common part, became good. By participation, it is a cause of good; but that which it participated in is nothing among all things. Therefore, the Good is nothing among all things. 

But if this "good" is in him—for it is the difference by which this composite is good—it must be from another. But that other is itself simple and only good. Therefore, that from which it comes is much more "only good." <margin>distinction</margin> Thus it has been shown to us that the primary Good is beyond all beings, and is only good, having nothing in himself, but unmixed with all and above all, and the cause of all. For beauty is not from evil, nor are beings, nor from indifferent things. For the maker is better than the thing made, for it is more perfect.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the First Principle (the Good) must be absolutely simple and transcend all categories, including essence and mind. He claims that adding any attributes to the Good actually diminishes it, as the source must be more perfect and simple than the things it produces.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Enneads, Neoplatonism, The Good, The One, negative theology, transcendence, causality, simplicity, participation</keywords>

<meta>Continuing from page 532, Plotinus remains focused on the absolute simplicity of the First Principle (the One). Having previously established that the One does not "possess" properties like goodness but *is* the Good, he now investigates whether the One possesses "thought" or "intellect." This page begins Book VI of the Fifth Ennead, where he argues that even the act of thinking implies a division between the thinker and the thought, which the One must transcend.</meta>

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD FIVE,
### BOOK SIX.

CONCERNING the fact that that which is beyond being does not think; and what is the primary thinking being, and what is the secondary.

->That that which is above being does not think: and what is thinking in the first degree, and what is thinking in the second degree.<-

---

<margin>Chapter 1.</margin>
*The Intellect is both united with the object of thought and yet distinct from it.*

*If the intellect knows external things by being affected from the outside, the difference between the intellect and the intelligible <term>intelligible: the object or concept that is being thought about</term> is manifest; the intellect takes on a foreign form, yet meanwhile, through this form, the intellect is united with the intelligible. But if it understands itself, the essence of the thinker and the thought is the same. Nevertheless, the relationship between one and the other is opposite; therefore they are formally distinct. Furthermore, the nature of the intelligible itself is superior to the nature of the thinker: just as the nature of light, or of a transparent medium, or of a purer light compared to a less pure one. For the relationship of the intellect to the intelligible, when it understands itself, is like a certain incipient light striving to receive the absolute light, to which it may be made equal according to its strength.*

<note>The decorative initial T in the Greek and D in the Latin both depict scholarly figures, reflecting the intellectual rigor of the "Enneads."</note>One kind of thinking is of another thing, and the other is of <margin>* oneself</margin> * oneself. The latter more successfully avoids being two; but the second kind mentioned also desires this, though it is less able to achieve it. For it holds what it sees within itself, yet that thing is still something other. Indeed, it is separated in essence. But being present with it, it sees itself; thus both together become a single being. Therefore, it understands more fully because it possesses the object. And it thinks in the primary sense, because the act of thinking requires there to be something like two. For if it were not one, the thinking would be one thing and the object of thought another. Thus it would not be thinking in the primary sense. Because by receiving its thought from another, it would be the primary thinker [only in a secondary way]. Because what it thinks, it does not possess as itself. Thus it is not itself. Or if it does possess it as itself so that it may properly think, the two will be well-placed. It is necessary, therefore, for both to be one. If, then, it is one, and yet not also two, then it does not possess thought. Consequently, it will not even be an intellect. It is necessary, then, for whatever thinks to be both simple and not simple. One might better grasp such a thing by ascending from the soul. For here it is easy to divide. And it is easier to see the duality if one makes the light twofold, the soul being according to the less pure, and the intelligible of the soul being according to the

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> INTELLIGENCE is twofold. For either it understands something else, or it understands itself: a process which indeed avoids that diversity through which some things are understood as two. But that which understands another also wishes to avoid diversity, but it is less capable of it: <margin>B</margin> it holds indeed with itself what it sees, but it is distinct from itself. But that which understands itself is not separated in essence from that which is understood, but coexisting with it, it gazes upon itself: and so both existing at once are made one. Indeed, it understands more truly because it possesses what it understands. And it understands in the first degree, because it is necessary for the thinker himself to exist as both one and two. For if it were not one, and therefore the thinker were one thing and the object understood were another, it would not be the primary thinker for both. For by understanding another, it will not be the primary thinker <margin>C</margin>, since it does not possess what it understands as something of its own, and therefore it does not possess it as itself. Or certainly, if it possesses it as itself so that it may understand principally, these two will be one. It is necessary, therefore, for both to exist as one; if, however, it is not one, but again is two, it certainly will not have that which it understands: for which reason it will not even be a thinker. It is necessary, therefore, that whatever understands be simple, and at the same time not simple. Furthermore, if anyone should ascend upward from the soul, he will more clearly comprehend that what understands is of such a kind. For here it is easy to divide, and therefore one may more easily perceive the duality. # PLOTINUS ENNEAD V.

...of the same more purely: then let it make itself, as it sees, an equal light to the light seen, since it no longer has a difference to separate them, it will assert that these two are one, which indeed becomes thinking <note>Latin: *intelligens*; Greek: *νοῶν*</note> because it exists as two: but it is now seeing because it is now one: thus he will grasp the intellect as thus intelligible <term>intelligible: that which can be known or understood by the mind, as opposed to being perceived by the senses</term>. Wherefore we indeed by our reason have made one out of two: but that, on the contrary, exists as two out of one, because, of course, it understands by making itself two: or rather, because it understands while existing as two: because it is one, it is able to understand.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...more purely, then it will make the seer equal to the seen light, having no longer any difference to distinguish them; it will no longer be two. It is thinking, because it is two; but seeing, already one; thus it will grasp both the thinker and the object of thought. We then, in our reasoning, have made one out of two. But conversely, from one it becomes two, because it thinks by making itself two. Rather, because it thinks, it is two, and because it is itself one. <note>original Greek: καθαρώτερον, εἶτα ποιήσει καὶ τὸ ὁρῶν ἴσον εἶναι φῶς τῶ ὁρωμένω...</note>

->*The Intellect understanding itself has multiplicity within itself. Chapter II.*<-

*Every intellect is in some way intelligible, yet not every intelligible is necessarily an intellect. Therefore, the principle of the intelligible itself is different, more common, and prior to the principle of the intellect. Thus, the intellect that understands itself has different principles within it. Moreover, since in the very order of beings, essence is prior even in time <note>The translator uses "time" here to mean logical or ontological priority in the chain of existence</note> to intelligence, it is rightly prior at least in origin in the first being. Therefore, essence itself, in its first sign of origin, according to itself, is not yet thinking, nor actually intelligible, unless the faculty of understanding arises within it; which faculty does not become actually thinking unless it is joined with the intelligible. Conclude: if the essence of being does not need intelligence for its own perfection of existence, for it precedes it, much less does that which is superior to being need it. But superior is that in which there is nothing prior and posterior: nor a duality of principles, such as we find in being and intellect.*

---

<margin>A</margin> **IF** therefore one thing is the first thinking being, and another is thinking in a different way, surely that which is superior to the first thinking being does not think: for it would need to be an intellect in order to think: but if it were an intellect, it would need to have an intelligible, and if it were the first thinking being, it would have the intelligible within itself: however, it is not necessary that whatever is intelligible contains an intellect within itself and thinks: for then it would not only be intelligible, but also thinking.

<margin>B</margin> And since it would then be two, it would certainly not be the first. Now indeed, the intellect which possesses the intelligible could never stand firm if there were not an essence of that which is purely intelligible, which will be intelligible to the intellect. But according to itself, it will be neither thinking nor properly intelligible: for what is called intelligible is judged intelligible to another: and yet the intellect also has its power through which intelligence strives, empty, unless it has received and grasped that intelligible which it understands. For it does not have intelligence without the intelligible: then, therefore, it is perfect, when it already possesses it.

<margin>C</margin> But it is necessary that before it understands, it has a perfect essence within itself. Therefore, that from which it exists as perfect according to essence is the very thing before intelligence: wherefore this has no need of intelligence, since it exists sufficiently before it; thus it does not think. There is therefore something supreme which does not think: there is moreover that which thinks primarily: and finally, there is that which has a certain secondary intelligence. Furthermore, if that first principle of all things should think, something would already be present to it: it would not, therefore, be the first, but the second: and not one, but already many, and indeed as many as it understands: even if it only understands itself, it would again turn out to be many.

<column-break/>

If indeed one is the primary thinker, and the other thinks in another way, that which is beyond the primary thinker would not think, for it must already be an intellect to think. But being an intellect, it must have an object of thought. And if it thinks primarily, it has the object of thought in itself. But being an object of thought, it is not necessary also to think; for if it did, it would have the object of thought in itself or think. For it would be not only an object of thought, but also a thinker. Having been sent <unclear>illegible or corrupted text in Greek</unclear>, it will not be two, which is how he who has the object of thought would not exist unless there were a purely intelligible essence. This, to the thinker, will be an object of thought, but in itself, it will be properly neither thinking nor an object of thought, for the object of thought is for another. And the mind, applying itself to thinking, has something new by taking and seizing the object of thought which it thinks. For it has its thinking by the object of thought. It is not perfect until it has it. But it was necessary before thinking to be perfect in itself in essence. Therefore, that to which perfection belongs before thinking will exist. It has no need of thinking, for it is self-sufficient in itself. Therefore it will not think. Thus, one thing does not think; another thinks primarily; another thinks secondarily. Furthermore, if the first thinks, something belongs to it. Therefore it is not first, but second. And not one, but already many; even as many as it shall think. For even if it thinks only <margin>* itself</margin> itself, it will be many.

<meta>Continuing from the discussion in Book Six regarding the absolute simplicity of the First Principle (the One). The text is exploring how the Intellect, which contains multiplicity, must proceed from a single, simple source.</meta>

# BOOK SIX.

...necessarily it exists after the One itself, and is a participant in the One. These Platonic views do not oppose Christian theologians, among whom the first principle does not possess multiple forms by understanding many things—in whatever way it may understand—but rather, by inspecting itself in a single act through its own one form, it beholds all things. This is because it considers its own most simple form as something to be imitated differently and in various ways by others. Furthermore, the divine Trinity (as Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-6th century Christian theologian and philosopher who merged Neoplatonism with Christian doctrine</note> confirms and Gregory Nazianzen <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and influential theologian on the nature of the Trinity</note> asserts) is the same there as unity itself: just as light and heat are two distinct things under the heavens, but in the sun <note>original: "in caelo" (in the heaven/sky)</note> they are one. Indeed, even progression and rest are different here; but there, rest is found in progression, and progression in rest. Thus, in the divine nature, by reason of its infinity, motion concurs with stillness. For if you imagine an infinite velocity of motion, you resolve it into stillness; indeed, even infinite slowness and velocity, when they end in stillness, meet as one with each other. For infinite power, suddenly uniting all things to itself, unites them within itself and with each other. It is no wonder then that in Dionysius and Nazianzen, that which is unity in the divine nature is also the existence of the Trinity itself, and vice versa. For the infinity of power there and its propagation drives an internal and equal movement into the Trinity (as they say) while meanwhile preserving unity. Therefore, the Trinity there is not like a certain multitude that participates in unity (which would then need to be referred to a higher unity); for this is unity itself. If there is indeed any distinction in divine things, it is conducted through a certain relation—as most Christians agree—because a relation usually brings the smallest possible difference and composes nothing <note>Theologians argued that the Father, Son, and Spirit are distinguished only by their relations to each other, not by having different "parts" or "substances"</note>. The followers of Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus, a major High Medieval scholastic philosopher</note> add that the only kind of multitude unworthy of God is that which causes composition through potentiality and act. But there, the multitude—whether of persons or of ideas—is not considered in that way; instead, all things are like acts that compose nothing and do not emerge from potentiality, but are rather like rays of light entirely internal and perpetual to the light itself, into which the light simply propagates itself.

<columns>2</columns>
<note>The Greek text provided is the source for the Latin translation in the adjacent column. It is from Plotinus, Ennead V.3.12, arguing that the First Principle must be simple and prior to all "many."</note>
If they say that nothing prevents the same thing from being many, it will not be as a subject, so that there are many without there being one. But from which it was, or entirely as one. And then let it be numbered first of the others, which must be taken alone by itself. But if it were together with the others, it is necessary that, having taken it together with the others—yet it being different from the others—one should leave it as it is with the others. But one must seek the subject of the others, no longer with the others, but by itself. For that which is the same in others would be similar to it. But it would not be this very thing; rather, it must be alone, if it is to be seen in the others as well. Unless someone were to say that its being consists in existing with the others. Then it will not be simple. But that which is composed of many, which are not simple, will not be it. For to each simple thing it is signified to be, and not as an extension of some simple one, under itself; that which is composed of many, where none of them can have an existence by itself, nor can it provide itself to be with others by not being at all—how then could there be a composite of all, if it were made of things that do not exist? If not of non-beings, but yet of things that do not exist [as simple]. If then there is something that is many, there must be a "One" before the many. If then the thinking thing is a certain multitude, and because of the multitude, thinking is not there. For it is the first. In the things that follow, therefore, there will be thinking itself and the intellect.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> MOREOVER, if someone objects that nothing prevents this first principle from being both itself and many, we shall respond that it is necessary for a single subject to be common to these many. For many things can neither exist nor form a unity unless there is a "one" from which or in which they exist; or at least unless there is an absolute "one," and that first one stands outside of number while the rest are numbered among themselves. This "one" must be understood as existing solely in itself. <margin>B</margin> But if it were together with others, it would be necessary for this "one"—taken together with others, yet differing from the rest—to be allowed to join the assembly of others. However, one should investigate the subject of all things no further in company with the rest, but rather according to itself. For that which is the same in others will indeed be similar to this, yet it will not be this very thing; rather, it must be alone, if it is to be grasped in the others. <margin>C</margin> Unless perhaps someone should say that its very existence is nothing other than having substance together with others. But if that were so, it would never be simple, and therefore there would never be anything anywhere composed of many. For since it cannot be simple, it will not have substance; and since a composite is judged to be made of many, if there is nowhere anything simple, then the composite itself will not exist. For since each thing cannot be simple, and no simple thing supports it with its own foundation, that which is said to be constituted of many—where surely none of them can have substance according to itself, nor can it offer itself to the commerce of anything else—<margin>D</margin> because it does not exist at all: since these things are so, how could anything be composed of all things? Such a thing would be fashioned from those things which do not exist—I do not say things that are not "something," but things that do not exist at all. For this reason, if anything is "many," there must be a "One" before the many. If, therefore, that which is intelligent is a certain multitude, it is necessary that where there is no multitude, there is also no intelligence; and that is the First itself. In those things that follow it, therefore, there will be intelligence and intellect.

<meta>Continuing from the discussion of absolute simplicity in the First Principle. This page focuses on why the "Good" (the One) is superior to the "Intellect" (the second principle), using analogies of light and celestial bodies to explain the hierarchy of existence.</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

...one should not imagine a composite there, nor add "intelligence" to the "goodness" in such a way that it is distinct, even if it is the goodness itself. Therefore, as long as you consider the intellect (as Plotinus does) to be like the Sun—in which intelligence relates to its nature just as light relates to the substance of the Sun (which is far prior and different from the light)—for that long you must deny that the highest God is "intellect." Rather, think of God as light alone, not existing in any nature other than itself, but remaining within itself. Nothing anywhere can be hidden from this light, since all things exist and are made manifest through it everywhere. Nevertheless, you must affirm that the highest God is not any "intellect" understood by you.

<margin>A</margin> THEREFORE, if the Good itself must be simple and in need of nothing, it will in no way require intelligence. Moreover, that which is not necessary to it will certainly not be present in it, since absolutely nothing is "added" to it. Thus, no intelligence whatsoever is within it, just as nothing else is. Furthermore, the intellect is one thing, and the Good itself is another. For the intellect becomes "good-form" <note>original: "boniformis", meaning taking on the shape or quality of the Good</note> by the very fact that it understands the Good.

<margin>B</margin> Likewise, just as among two things where there is "one" and "another," it is necessary for the "one" to be primary, but that "one" must exist as itself alone, above the "one" that is coupled with another. So too, it is necessary that where something "one" is joined with another—approaching simplicity in a certain way—that the simple itself must stand above this, having nothing in itself of those things which exist in the coupled version. For from where would "the other" come to be in "the one" unless that from which the "other" is made already existed separately? For that which is simple cannot be made by another; but that which is manifold, or at least double, must necessarily be referred back to another. Now, one may compare the first (the Good) to light, the second (the Intellect) to the Sun, and the third (the Soul) to the Moon, which draws its light from the Sun. For the Soul possesses an adventitious <note>meaning "coming from outside" or "borrowed"</note> intellect which colors it, making it intellectual. The Intellect, however, possesses its own intellectual light within itself; it is not only light, but its very essence exists as something luminous. But that which pours out this light is not something else existing within itself along with the light; it is simple light itself, providing the Intellect with the power to shine forth. For the source is not the same as that which exists in another. For that which lies in another is different from that which is entirely through itself and freed from all others.

<column-break/>

FURTHERMORE, if the Good is simple and without need, it would not even need to think. That which it does not need should not be present with it; indeed, thinking is not present with it at all. And if nothing is present, then nothing else is either. The Intellect is different from the Good. For the Intellect is "good-like" by thinking of the Good. Moreover, as in the case of two things where there is "one" and "another," the "one" coupled with the "other" can exist; but the "one" by itself must exist before the "one" with the "other." In that which exists with the "other," the underlying part is simple; the simple must exist as simple in itself, having nothing in itself of the things found in the one coupled with the other. For from where else would the "other" have come, if not from that which previously existed separately, from which the "other" arises? For the simple cannot come from another. But the manifold, or the "two," must exist because of a cause prior to itself. And one should not compare them poorly: the first to light, the next to the Sun, and the third to the Moon, as receiving its light from the Sun. For the Soul has a borrowed intellect, coloring itself to be intellectual. But the Intellect has its own light in itself—it is not just light, but is something enlightened in its own essence. But that which provides this light is not something else; it is simple Light, providing power to the Intellect, by being what it is. Why then would it need anything? For it is the very thing which is "in the other." For that which is in the other is the same as that which exists as itself by itself.

---

*If you imagine that "understanding oneself" is like "returning to oneself," and like gathering an innate multitude into oneself, you will find that such an action does not fit the most simple principle of all things.*

->Chapter V.<-

*If you think that "to understand" in any way is a certain striving that desires the Good itself—or like a vision seeking light—do not think that such intelligence applies to that which is considered the Good itself and infinite Light itself. For in the Good there is no appetite for the good, nor is there a vision in the light that needs to crave light. Just as numbers are referred to their Unity (which is prior to the parts), and continuous things to their higher Continuity, so essences are referred to a substantial Unity higher than essence itself. If this Unity is more eminent than essence, it certainly surpasses that intelligence which is the "act" of essence. But if you call that existence of the Good and infinite light "Intelligence" in a better sense—as if it were the "cause" of intelligence existing in itself, containing everything that is desired by thinking beings—perhaps by calling it so you will not go astray.*

---

<margin>A</margin> FURTHERMORE, that which is manifold in itself will rightly seek itself, and will desire to "breathe together" <note>original: "conspirare", meaning to harmonize or act in unison</note> with itself and perceive itself mutually from all sides. But that which is entirely One, where shall it turn to find itself? Where will it catch itself? Where will it have need of an internal sense of itself? For that very thing is better than any "breathing together" of sense and any intelligence. For intelligence is not the first thing. Indeed, it does not hold the first rank, whether regarding "being" simply, or regarding "being" that is to be venerated; rather, it occupies the second place.

<column-break/>

STILL, the manifold would seek itself, and would wish to incline toward itself and be self-aware. But that which is entirely One, where shall it go toward itself? Where would it need self-awareness? But it is the same as self-awareness, yet superior to all thought. For thinking is not the first thing, neither in being, nor in being honorable, but is second.

# BOOK SIX.

<margin>A</margin> [The Intellect] was born after the Good itself existed; and once it arose in essence, it immediately stirred it toward the Good. This essence, having been stirred, then proceeded toward it and knew it. This is precisely what it means to understand: to be moved toward the Good out of a desire for it. Indeed, desire produced the act of understanding and remains its constant companion. For vision consists of a certain appetite <note>original: "appetitu", referring to the soul's natural reaching out</note> of sight itself, which draws it toward seeing. For this reason, it is not necessary for the Good itself to understand either itself or anything else. For there is nothing else <margin>B</margin> besides itself that is "good" for it. Even when anything else besides the Good itself understands itself, it understands precisely because it is (as I might say) "good-form" <note>original: "boniforme"; having the shape or quality of the Good</note> and possesses a certain likeness to the Good <margin>* desire</margin>. It understands itself as something good and as something that has become desirable to itself, as if it had now obtained an image of the Good. If it should always hold itself in this way, it will always produce the same result. Furthermore, in its knowledge of itself, it perhaps knows that Good by a certain chance. For it knows itself while looking up toward the Good; for it understands itself as it is acting, and the action of all things is directed toward the Good.

---

>*Since all powers desire first acts—that is, forms—as if they were something good, and since first acts desire second acts—that is, actions—in the same way, the sought-after Principle of all things is rightly called "Act," being superior to any specific form or action.*

->Chapter VI.<-

This infinite act, although it is not properly said to "act" or to "have action" in return, is nevertheless the source from which all things are moved, and the point toward which all things act. Do not call this act "intellect" or "intelligence" in the way Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and founder of Neoplatonism</note> defines them everywhere. For in his view, within the intellect (or the "First") the thinking nature is one thing, and the act of thinking is another; likewise, essence, life, and intelligence are distinct there. Furthermore, the different "ideas" of things are formally distinct from each other by reason, and similarly distinct from the intelligence through which the mind itself understands them. Both Platonists and Christians believe such distinctions do not apply to the Supreme Being. Finally, that Supreme Being does not understand himself in order to join himself to himself as if he were divided; nor does he understand other things to profit from that knowledge. For a thing is joined to something better than itself through knowledge—that is, the enjoyment of it—and the Supreme Being enjoys himself in a better way than through mere knowing. Those who enjoy God do so through a unity that is superior to the intellect, as Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th to early 6th century</note> asserts.

---

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> IF these things are said correctly, intelligence has no place in the Good itself; for the Good must be something different for the one who is thinking. Therefore, the Good itself is entirely free from action. What need is there for "Act" to act? For no act entirely possesses another act within it. If we apply something further to other acts that are directed toward something else, we certainly must not add anything more to the first of all acts, toward which all remaining acts are directed. Instead, we must allow that which is to simply exist. Therefore, such <margin>B</margin> an act cannot be "intelligence," for it has nothing to understand. It is the First. Furthermore, "intelligence" does not think; rather, that which *possesses* intelligence thinks. Thus, two things arise again within the thinker; but that First is in no way two. Moreover, one might recognize this even more clearly by considering how, in the universe, the thinking subject more clearly encompasses this dual nature <margin>* I say, this one.</margin>. We say that beings themselves as beings, and each individual thing, and those things which truly exist, are in the "intelligible world." This is not only because those things always remain the same in their essence <margin>C</margin>, while those offered to the senses are in a continuous flux—for perhaps even in the realm of the senses there are some things that remain—but rather because they possess the perfection of being within themselves. For it is necessary that what is first called "essence" <note>original: "ousia", the fundamental nature or substance of a thing</note> should not be a mere shadow of being, but should possess being in its fullness. Being is full when it receives the form of thinking and living. Therefore, at the same time...

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the relationship between the "One" (the First Principle) and the "Intellect." The previous page argued that the Good/the One does not need to think because it is the source of all things; here, Plotinus explains why the act of "knowing" implies a duality that cannot exist in the absolute simplicity of the One.</meta>

In Being, these things exist: understanding, living, and being. If, therefore, Being exists, consequently the Intellect exists; and conversely, if the Intellect exists, Being also exists. In that realm, understanding exists simultaneously with being. From this, it follows that intelligence is already a "many" and not a "one." It is necessary, therefore, that in the One itself—which is not of such a nature—there is no intelligence. Indeed, by examining each individual thing in the intelligible world, a double notion occurs everywhere: for instance, the intelligence of "man" and "man" himself; likewise, the intelligence of "horse" and "horse" himself; and again, the intelligence of "justice" and "justice" itself. All things, therefore, are double. There, the "one" is "two"; and there, in turn, the "two" return into a "one." But the First itself is neither any of these things individually, nor is it made from all these things that are double, nor is it double at all. How two arise from one is discussed elsewhere. But since the First stands above essence <note>original: "essentiam"; Plotinus means the One is beyond Being</note>, it is rightly judged to be above intelligence. Thus, it is not absurdly stated if one says that the First does not know itself. For since it is entirely "one," it has nothing at all within itself to learn; nor is it necessary for it to know other things. For it is something better and greater than those things—to know them would be to reach for something lesser—since it is itself the "Good" of all others. Rather, it grants to others that they might attain it within that same place where they are able.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Understanding, living, and being are in Being. If, therefore, there is Intellect, there is also Being. And understanding exists together with being. Intelligence is therefore many and not one. It is necessary, then, that for that which is not "this," there is also no intelligence. And looking at each thing individually, there is the perception and thought of "horse," and "horse" itself; and the thought of "justice," and "justice" itself. All things, therefore, are double, and the one is two. And again, the two come into one. But <margin>B</margin> [the One] is none of these things, nor is it each of them. It is not from all things which are two, nor is it two at all. How the two come from the one is dealt with in other places. But being beyond essence, it is also beyond understanding. It is therefore not strange if it does not know itself; for if it did, it would have something within itself as a learner. But neither is it necessary for it to know other things. For it is something better and greater than knowing them; it grants them the ability to know themselves. Being the <margin>C</margin> [Good] of other things, it is rather in the same [source] according to which each thing is able to touch it.

## ENNEAD FIVE,
### BOOK SEVEN.

### ON WHETHER THERE ARE ALSO IDEAS OF INDIVIDUAL THINGS.
-> Whether there are Ideas for specific individuals. <-

*As many humans as are born in the Great Year of the world <note>The "Great Year" or Platonic Year is a cycle of roughly 25,800 years after which the celestial bodies return to the same positions</note>, there are just as many seminal principles of humans in universal nature, and nearly as many ideas of humans in the divine mind.
Chapter I.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring a seated figure amidst classical architectural elements and foliage.</image-desc>
EVERY rational soul also naturally contains within itself a certain number of <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>original: "rationes seminales"; these are the formative, biological, and spiritual blueprints that guide the development of living things</note> from which it is destined to produce various lives. But just as when we say all heavenly things are in the earth, and conversely all earthly things are in heaven, we understand all things according to the nature of the place—that is, in heaven according to a heavenly reason, and in the earth according to an earthly quality—so when we hear that our soul is "all things," we must understand this according to the property of a human and rational soul. Therefore, your soul will never produce the lives and shapes proper to brute animals, but always human ones; although they may be somewhat similar to brutes, and sometimes even to spirits. Thus, your soul can produce only a few changes of life in the Great Year of the world, especially since it leads a very short life on earth, but a very long one above the earth. In the following Great Year, there is no change of lives, but the <term>resurrection</term> <note>original: "resurrectio"; in this Neoplatonic context, Ficino uses this term to describe the cyclical return or "recurrence" of the same individual in a new cosmic cycle</note> of the exact same humans. Meanwhile, humans differ among themselves, not only by matter, but also by their own proper forms and figures, and various modes of birth. Since formal and ordered difference is produced neither by matter nor by chance, it depends on certain formal reasons which exist both in nature and in the universal mind, and these are not finite in number. For finite forms are born in the Great Year of the world, and in the following year the same ones return, because the same causes evidently return. But in what way are there more things in matter than in the soul, and in the soul more than in the mind? Truly, it is because certain things in matter differ by number—either through a defect of form occurring in matter in one place while the form is more perfect elsewhere, or through the division of quantity. Truly formal differences are equal to the seminal reasons. Moreover, such reasons are more numerous in the soul than the "Ideas" are in the mind; because in the nature of the soul, there is always an absolute distinction of reasons...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the absolute "One" is beyond thought and being because thinking requires a distinction between the thinker and the object of thought. He also explores whether individual humans have unique "Ideas" in the divine mind, linking human diversity to the cyclical return of the Great Year.</summary>

<keywords>The One, Intellect, Duality, Great Year, Seminal Reasons, Individuality, Platonic Ideas, Recurrence</keywords>
