# BOOK SEVEN.

The mind, however, possesses a smaller number of ideas that are absolutely different from one another. For the mind can refer the same idea to various things through an act of intellect and will—referring it, I mean, outward in different ways as something that can be imitated. From this relationship, many things proceed, while the idea itself remains undivided.

***

The two main columns of text begin with large woodcut decorative initials. The Greek initial (representing the letter 'Ε') features a portrait of a man in classical dress within a circular frame, possibly a philosopher. The Latin initial 'N' is an ornate floriated woodcut. Marginal letters A, B, C, D, and E are printed in the gutter between the columns to mark sections of the text.

<margin>A</margin> Is there an idea for each individual? <note>original: "ἰδέα" / "idea"</note> Perhaps, if I and each person can be traced back to the intelligible realm, then the origin of each is also there. If Socrates always exists, and the soul of Socrates is Socrates himself, then he will exist there as well, just as the soul exists as an individual. That is what is said of that realm. <margin>B</margin> But if he does not always exist as Socrates, but his soul becomes different at different times—for example, if it was once Pythagoras or someone else—then individuals would no longer exist there. However, if the soul of each person contains the <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>original: "λόγους" / "rationes"; these are the formative, rational blueprints that govern the development of living things</note> of all those whom it passes through, then once again, all are present there. For we say that the world contains these reasons, and each soul contains them too. <margin>C</margin> If, therefore, the world contains reasons not only for "humanity" in general, but also for individual animals, then the soul must also contain them. This number of reasons would be infinite, unless the cycle repeats in fixed periods. In this way, infinity is actually finite, once these things return to the same state. <margin>D</margin> Furthermore, if the things that come into being are more numerous than the patterns <note>original: "παραδειγμάτων" / "exemplaria"; the "blueprints" or "Forms" in Plato's philosophy</note>, why is it necessary for there to be reasons and patterns for all things that occur in a single cycle? For one "human" would seem to suffice for all humans, just as a fixed number of souls suffice for an infinite number of humans. <margin>E</margin> But it is not possible for different things to have the same reason. For one "human" is not sufficient as a pattern for many humans who differ from one another—not only in their matter, I mean, but by countless specific differences. They are not like images of Socrates compared to their original; rather, their different compositions must proceed from different rational principles. The entire cosmic cycle contains all these reasons; and then, the same things are regenerated again according to the same reasons. We should not fear an infinite multitude in the intelligible world; for all is contained in an indivisible state, and it proceeds, as it were, whenever it acts.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Is there also an idea of each individual? Perhaps if I and each person are brought back to the intelligible order, there too is the principle of each. Perhaps also, if Socrates always exists, and the soul of Socrates is Socrates himself, then he will exist there as an individual soul, just as Socrates and any individual is there. But if Socrates does not always exist, but his soul becomes something else at another time—so that the soul which is now Socrates was previously Pythagoras or someone else, <margin>B</margin> and will be someone else in the future—then each of those who are here is no longer also there. Nevertheless, if the soul of each person possesses the seminal reasons of all the things it carries out and fulfills, then they are all there once more. For we admit that as many reasons as the world possesses, it also possesses as many individual souls. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, if the world encompasses the reasons not only of "man" but also of individual animals, the soul also contains the reasons of individuals. Consequently, an infinite number of reasons would follow, unless restoration to the same state occurs in certain cycles of time. Thus, that infinity will finally be made finite when the same things are returned to the world. <margin>D</margin> Moreover, if the things that are made are altogether more numerous than the pattern, why is it necessary for the reasons and patterns of all things that occur in one revolution of the world to exist? For one "human" seems to suffice for all humans, just as a specific number of souls suffice for fashioning innumerable humans. But indeed, there cannot be one reason for things that are different, nor does one "human" suffice as a pattern for many humans who differ from one another—I mean, not only in their matter, but also differing by very many specific differences. <margin>E</margin> For these things do not relate like images of Socrates to their pattern, but it is necessary that a different result proceeds from different reasons. The entire cosmic revolution encompasses all reasons; and the same things are regenerated again through those same reasons. Nor should it be suspected that an infinite multitude follows from this in the intelligible world: for the entire multitude is there as a whole, and from there, individuals come forth when it acts.

***

-> *Every soul, individual by nature, contains within itself the seminal reasons of all things that are to be generated from it, being distinct from one another by formal differences.* <-
-> Chapter II. <-

*These things can be distinguished in this way, even if they are commonly calculated under the same species. A specific distinction of forms of this kind is prescribed even in the very intention of universal nature: because the order, beauty, and good of the universe consist in such a distinction. Matter, however, brings no specific variety of forms, but rather a defect of form. Furthermore, quantity, by its division in homogeneous things, produces number in some places, but never variety. Finally, in one "year of the world," whatever heterogeneous things are generated in the natural order are formally dissimilar to each other, and therefore are produced through different reasons; but in the following cycle, all those same things are recreated through the same reasons under the same causes.*

***

<margin>A</margin> But if the mixtures of the rational principles of male and female produce different offspring, there will no longer be a specific reason for each one generated. And either of the parents, such as the male, will not produce through different reasons, but through one...

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

<margin>A</margin>
...at least of himself, or perhaps of his father. But perhaps nothing prevents these differences from being produced through different <term>reason-principles</term> <note>original: "rationes" / "λόγους"; the formative blueprints within Nature</note>, because they all possess them, though some are more ready at certain times than others. But what of it when different children are born from the same parents? Perhaps it is because the dominance and excess [of the parental principles] is not always equal. Let us consider if the difference exists not only in appearance, but if sometimes the male principle dominates, and sometimes the <margin>B</margin> female. Or perhaps each parent contributes an equal part, yet the whole is handed over and is naturally implanted, but it dominates one part of the matter or the other. But in what way are those conceived in different places judged to be different? Does matter itself bring about the difference by being overcome in different ways? If that were so, all offspring except one would be "contrary to nature." But if variety itself is everywhere a beautiful thing, it is right that one single <term>species</term> <note>original: "species" / "εἶδος"</note> does not exist everywhere. Yet that which comes from matter must be attributed to deformity alone. <margin>C</margin> Certainly, in the "Artificer" <note>the divine power that shapes the world</note> who is the cause of things, the perfected reason-principles are hidden, yet they are handed over in their entirety. But even if the principles are different, must there be as many of them as there are things born in one single revolution of the world? For it is possible that even if the same principles are applied, different external outcomes may appear. Indeed, this is granted even where the principles are handed over in full. The question is whether this also happens when the same principles dominate. Is it therefore necessary for there to be just as many principles? For a result that is exactly the same can only be repeated in another revolution of the world; in this current revolution, however, nothing is exactly the same.

***

*Since Nature acts through its essence—unlike art, which acts through something added to essence—it rightly contains the variety of things to be generated within its essential principles. Therefore, the entire arrangement of individual things to be lived out in the "Year of the World" was designated from the beginning in the mind of the World-Maker, in the mind of the World-Soul, and in its nature. Chapter IV.*

***

*Many believe that the "Great Year of the World" is fulfilled when all celestial bodies return to exactly the same position and relationship to each other that they have today. Some measure this span as thirty-six thousand solar years, others as thirty-nine thousand; others measure and think of it differently.*

***

<margin>A</margin>
But how shall we say there are different principles in the case of many twins? And if one considers other animals, especially those that conceive many offspring in a single act of mating, what shall we say? Shall we perhaps judge there to be only one principle there, where the offspring differ very little from one another? But if that is so, there will no longer be as many principles as there are individuals. Should we not rather think that there are as many principles as there are individuals that are different—different, I mean, not <margin>B</margin> because they fall short of the species itself? But what prevents us from assigning different principles even to offspring that differ very little, if indeed any things are ever born completely identical? For a craftsman, even when making identical things, nevertheless allows that which is called "the same" to receive a certain rational difference, according to which he makes it diverse, applying something different to that which is the same. But in Nature, where the diversity of things comes not from varied reasoning but only from various principles, the diversity must be linked to the form. We, however, are unable to discern the difference. Certainly, if any element of chance were admitted into the generation of things, another reason...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...at least of himself, or of his father. Or nothing prevents the differences from arising because he possesses all [the principles], but different ones are always more ready to hand. When different children come from the same parents, it is perhaps because of an unequal mastery. But there, the difference is not just in appearance; sometimes it is according to the male, and <margin>B</margin> sometimes according to the female, or according to an equal part given by each. But the whole is given and is present within. It dominates either one part of the matter or the other. How are those in another place different? Does matter have the difference, being differently mastered? If so, all but one would be against nature. But if difference is everywhere a beautiful thing, the form does not have one single state. Rather, it is to the "ugly" <note>the chaotic or unformed</note> alone that we must attribute what comes from matter. And there, in the <margin>C</margin> hidden reason-principles, though they are given as a whole, they are distinct. But let the principles be different. Is it necessary that they be as many as the things born in one period? It is possible that from the same given principles, different things appear. Or let it be granted that they are given as wholes. The question is: if the same principles master the matter, must they be the same? Or is it that the "same" can only be said to occur in another period, while in this period nothing is said to be the same?

***

<margin>A</margin>
How then in the case of many twins shall we say the principles are different? And if one goes to other animals, especially those that produce many offspring, where they are indistinguishable, is there one principle? But if so, it does not hold that there are as many principles as there are individuals. Or is it that there are as many as there are different individuals—different, I mean, not by failing to reach the form? What prevents us, even if they are indistinguishable (if any are indeed completely so), from there being different principles? For just as the craftsman makes even things that are <margin>B</margin> indistinguishable, he must nevertheless take "the same" with a rational difference according to which he will make another, adding something different to the same thing. But in Nature, where the other is not made by a process of reasoning but by principles alone, the difference must be joined to the form. Even if we are unable to grasp the differences. Or if the production has anything of the "at random" or "any which way," then another reason...

<header>BOOK EIGHT.</header>

<margin>A</margin> But if the number of things that exist is measured, their quantity will be determined by the unfolding and spreading out of all the <term>reason-principles</term> <note>original: "λόγων" / "rationes"; the formative blueprints or "seeds" of reality</note>. Thus, when all these things reach their end, another beginning starts again. For the scale of the world, and all that it must pass through in its own life, is established from the beginning in that which possesses the principles. Does this also apply to other animals where many are produced from a single birth—shall we assign as many principles? <column-break/> <margin>A</margin> But if the number of each thing produced is defined by measure, then certainly the quantity and multitude will be determined by the very unfolding and explanation of all the principles; so much so that when all have reached their end, another beginning is woven anew. For how great the world ought to be, and how many things must be transacted in its life, has been settled from the beginning in the one who contains the reasons of all things. <margin>B</margin> Perhaps we should not fear that an infinite multitude occurs in the seeds and principles because the soul encompasses all things. Nor will a countless crowd occur in the intellect or the soul: for all the reason-principles there return again by a certain rotation, appearing readily at their appointed times.

### BOOK VIII.

->ON INTELLIGIBLE BEAUTY.<-
-><note>original: "ΠΕΡΙ τοῦ νοητοῦ κάλλους" / "De intelligibili pulchritudine"</note><-

---

->*That beauty is natural in the human intellect is apparent because it makes raw matter beautiful. Chapter I.*<-

> *Nor does the mind produce this effect solely by imitating external natural works; it also employs internal reason-principles, specifically when it corrects the defects of nature. From this we conclude that form and beauty are more excellent in the mind than in any work of art. Add that they are more powerful, since in the work they are scattered, but in the mind they are entirely united.*

<margin>A</margin> <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' (translated from the Greek 'E') depicting a philosopher with a companion pointing towards a celestial or terrestrial globe.</image-desc>SINCE we say that the soul which has come to exist in the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>the realm of pure thought and perfect Forms, above the physical world</note>, and which has understood the beauty of the true Mind, can also grasp the Father of this mind and that which lies beyond it, let us try to see and express to ourselves—as far as such things can be spoken—how one might behold the beauty of the Mind and of that higher world. <column-break/> <margin>A</margin> <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' (translated from the Latin 'Q') showing a seated scholar reading or writing in a study, with a large bird (possibly an owl) perched nearby.</image-desc>SINCE we admit that the mind which contemplates the intelligible world, and gazes upon the beauty of true intellect, can at some time notice even the Father of this superior mind: come now, let us strive with all our strength to see, and to express to ourselves as much as such things can be explained, by what specific means we may be able to perceive the beauty of the mind and of that world. <margin>B</margin> Imagine, therefore, two stone masses placed near each other: let one be unshaped and void of any artistic touch, but let the other be already refined by art into a statue, whether of a god or a human. If it is a god, let it be a statue of some Grace or a Muse; if it is human, let it not be of any particular man, but rather of one whom art has assembled from all beautiful features.

<meta>The previous page concluded a discussion on the origin of individual differences and the role of "reason-principles" in the unfolding of the world. This page transitions into Ennead V, Book 8, where Plotinus investigates the nature of beauty, specifically arguing that beauty is an internal "form" or "idea" rather than a physical quality of matter itself.</meta>

<header>PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS. V.</header>

<margin>A</margin>A stone, therefore, which has been arranged by art into the beauty of a form, will immediately appear beautiful—but not because it is a stone. Otherwise, any other mass of rock would be similarly shapely. It is beautiful, then, because of the form which art has applied to it. This form was not in the material itself; rather, it existed in the mind of the one who conceived it before it ever entered the stone. It existed in the craftsman, not by virtue of his having eyes and hands, but because he was endowed with art. <margin>B</margin>Therefore, this beauty was much more excellent within the art itself. For the form that exists in the art does not itself enter the stone; rather, it remains there, while another, lesser version of it proceeds from it. This produced form does not remain pure within itself, nor is it exactly as the craftsman desired, but only as far as the material obeyed the art. If, however, art makes that which it is and possesses, and it makes something beautiful according to the <term>reason-principle</term> <note>original: "ratio" / "λόγος"; the guiding internal blueprint</note> by which it acts, then surely the art itself is more truly beautiful, possessing the beauty of art which is greater and more excellent than anything that proceeds outward. For as much as a form, in proceeding into matter, is extended, so much is it weakened compared to that which remains in the One. For whatever undergoes distance in itself departs from itself: if it is strength, it weakens in strength; if heat, in heat; if power, in power; and if beauty, it diminishes in beauty. Now, primarily, every creator must be more excellent than the thing created; for it is not "un-musicality" that makes a musician, but music, and the music that exists above the senses produces the music found in sensible sound. <margin>D</margin>If anyone despises the arts because they produce by imitating nature, it must be answered, first, that natures also imitate other things. Furthermore, one must realize that arts do not simply imitate what is seen with the eyes, but they go back to the very reason-principles from which nature itself consists and acts. Moreover, the arts create many things from themselves and add something where a thing is lacking in perfection, since they possess beauty within themselves. <margin>E</margin>Finally, <note>Phidias was the most famous sculptor of Classical Greece, known for his massive statue of Zeus at Olympia.</note> Phidias himself was able to fashion a Jupiter, imitating no spectacle visible to the senses, but imagining how Jupiter himself would appear if he ever wished to reveal himself to our eyes.

->*Beauty in a natural work is a certain form, not impressed upon matter in just any way, but impressed by nature itself when nature dominates the matter in an excellent manner.*<-

### Chapter II.

->*For this work is not beautiful because of its matter or size: otherwise, whatever was more material or larger would be more beautiful. Rather, it is beautiful by the reason of a certain more excellent form, which has become almost immaterial. Hence it happens that a form first captures you as something beautiful when it has entered the sight and become spiritual; and most of all when it is deeply contemplated. Finally, beauty in character and learning, which is entirely immaterial, captures us with love. This immaterial beauty in nature is far more wonderful than natural beauty. For nature does not work with an external habit, nor labor from the outside like art, but dominating from within by its very essence, it exhibits the beauty of matter with wonderful ease.*<-

<margin>A</margin>BUT for the present, let us set aside the arts. Let us consider those things whose works they are said to imitate: things produced naturally beautiful, namely rational animals and all irrational ones, especially those among them that are more perfectly finished; where the shaper and maker of them, having dominated the matter, has applied the form he desired. What, then, is beauty in these things? For it is not the blood and the menses, but the color and the figure, which are distinct from these; or it is nothing, or something without figure and discordant, or like that which contains something simple, like matter.

<column-break/>

It would appear then, that the stone brought by art into the beauty of form is beautiful <unclear>but not</unclear> <note>original: "ἀλλ' οὐ"</note> because it is a stone; for if that were so, the other stone would be equally beautiful. But it is beautiful because of the form which the art added. The material did not have all this form, but it was in the mind of the one who thought it, even before it came into the stone. It was in the creator, not insofar as he had eyes and hands, but because he participated in art. Therefore, this beauty was in the art, and it was much better there. For the beauty in the art did not go into the stone, but stayed there; while another, lesser beauty came from it. And even this did not remain pure in itself, nor as the artist wanted, but only as much as the stone yielded to the art. If art makes what it is and has—and it makes something beautiful according to the <term>reason-principle</term> <note>original: "λόγος"; the rational structure of a being</note> by which it acts—then it is more greatly and truly beautiful, having the beauty of art. For the principle is greater and more beautiful than what is in the external object; for as much as it is extended into the matter, it is that much weaker than that which stays in the One. For every extension moves away from itself: whether it be strength, it is in strength; or heat, in heat; or power in general, in power; or beauty, in beauty. And the primary creator must always, in himself, be better than the thing made. For it is not a lack of music that makes a musician, but music; and the music beyond the senses makes the music in the senses. If anyone dishonors the arts because they make things by imitating nature, first we must say that natures also imitate other things. Then, one must know that they do not simply imitate what is seen, but they run back to the reason-principles from which nature comes. Then also, they make many things on their own; they add where something is missing, as they possess beauty. Since Phidias made his Zeus not from anything sensed, but by grasping what Zeus would be like if he chose to appear through our eyes.

But let us leave the arts aside. Let us look at those things whose works the arts are said to imitate: those things called beautiful by nature—rational animals and all irrational ones—and especially those where a creator has succeeded, prevailing over the matter and providing the form he wished. What is the beauty in these? For it is certainly not the blood and the fluids; but a color different from these, and a shape; or nothing, or something shapeless, like a simple container of matter.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of beauty from the previous page, moving from the example of a sculpted stone to the archetype of beauty in living forms like Helen of Troy or the goddess Aphrodite. It argues that physical beauty is merely a reflection of an internal, non-material Form or "reason-principle."</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT. 543

From what source did the beauty of Helen shine forth, for whom such a great struggle was stirred up? Or from where did all those forms similar to Aphrodite in beauty illuminate the world? Indeed, from where did the form of Aphrodite herself arise? Or if any human is entirely beautiful, or a god—whether among those who come into our sight, or those who do not—they nevertheless possess a conspicuous beauty within themselves. Is it not, therefore, that this "form" is everywhere, descending into that which is born from the one who creates it, just as it was said in the case of the arts, that beauty proceeds into the artworks <margin>A</margin> from the arts? What then? Are the works indeed beautiful, and is the <term>reason-principle</term> <note>original: "λόγος" / "ratio"; the internal blueprint or formative power</note> within the matter itself? But the reason-principle which is not in the matter, but in the agent—the primary and immaterial one—is it not beauty itself? For it is reduced into a unity. However, if the <margin>B</margin> physical mass <note>original: "ὄγκος" / "moles"</note> were beautiful simply by virtue of being a mass, it would certainly follow that the active reason-principle, because it is not a mass, would not be beautiful. But if the same form, whether it be in a small or a large mass, similarly moves and affects the soul of the one beholding it by its own power, then certainly beauty is not to be attributed to the magnitude of the mass. <margin>C</margin> This is further evidenced by the following argument: as long as the form is outside the soul, we do not yet perceive it, nor are we moved; but when it is conceived within the soul, it affects us. Yet it is only the form of things that flows in through the eyes; otherwise, the most expansive things could not penetrate through the narrowest opening. Magnitude is also contracted, not as a great physical mass, but rather as a "great" form. <margin>D</margin> Furthermore, the cause of the beautiful effect must itself be either ugly, indifferent, or beautiful. If it were ugly, it certainly would not produce its opposite; if indifferent, why would it produce something beautiful rather than ugly? But truly, Nature, the artisan of such beautiful things, is much earlier and more greatly beautiful. We, however, because we are accustomed to seeing nothing of the interior and are entirely ignorant of internal things, naturally pursue the external, unaware that what moves us lies hidden within—just as if someone, seeing his own <margin>E</margin> image and not knowing where it came from, were to pursue that very image. That there is something else which attracts those who pursue it, and that beauty does not consist in magnitude, is testified to us by the beauty inherent in disciplines, in duties, and altogether in the soul. There, beauty truly flourishes more when you contemplate wisdom in a soul and, having contemplated it, you are delighted and love it, not looking at the face of the body— <margin>F</margin> which perhaps might not be shapely—but setting aside the entire form of the body, you pursue its internal beauty. But if that soul does not yet move you to call it beautiful, nor do you delight in yourself as beautiful <margin>* look at himself</margin> after looking within, then you would search for that beauty in vain while in such a state. For you would be searching with something impure and shameful; therefore, words about such matters are not addressed to everyone. But if you have seen yourself as beautiful, then remember beauty itself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> From what source arose the beauty of Helen, for whom such a great contest was raised? From where did other forms similar to Aphrodite shine forth? And yet, from where did the very form of Aphrodite arise? Or if any of men is beautiful from the start, or a God; whether of those who come into our sight, or of those who do not come, they have nonetheless in themselves a conspicuous beauty. Is it not therefore this form everywhere, descending into that which is born from that which generates, just as was said in the arts, <margin>B</margin> that beauty proceeds into the craftwork from the arts. What then? Are the works indeed beautiful, and is the reason-principle in the matter itself? But the reason-principle which is not in matter, but in the agent, the first and free from matter, is it not beauty? Rather, these very things are reduced into one. Furthermore, if the mass, by the reason that it is mass, were beautiful, it would certainly follow that the active reason-principle itself, since it is not mass, would not be beautiful. But if, whether in a small or in some large mass, <margin>C</margin> the same form moves and affects the soul of the beholder similarly by its power, certainly beauty is not to be attributed to the magnitude of the mass. From this again a proof is taken for the same point: since as long as the form is outside the mind, we do not perceive it, nor are we moved from there; but when it is already conceived by the mind, it affects us. But the very form of things flows in only through the eyes; otherwise, the largest things could not penetrate through the narrowest paths. Magnitude is also contracted, not as a great mass, but rather as a great form. <margin>D</margin> Moreover, it is necessary that the cause of the beautiful effect itself be either deformed, or indifferent, or beautiful. If it were deformed, it certainly would not effect the opposite; if indifferent, why would it make something beautiful rather than deformed? But surely nature, the artisan of things so beautiful, is much earlier and more greatly beautiful. We, however, since we are accustomed to inspect nothing intimate, and are utterly ignorant of intimate things, doubtless follow the extrinsic, not knowing meanwhile that what moves us lies hidden within, just as if someone, seeing his own <margin>E</margin> image and ignorant of where it came from, should follow it. That there is something else which attracts those who follow, and that beauty does not consist in magnitude, is witnessed for us by the beauty which is in disciplines and duties, and altogether in the soul: where certainly beauty flourishes more in truth, when, namely, you contemplate wisdom in some soul, and having contemplated it, you are delighted and you love, not then beholding the face of the <margin>F</margin> body—which perhaps may not be shapely—but with the whole form of the body disregarded, following the intimate beauty. But if that soul does not yet move you so that you call it beautiful, nor looking at your own interior will you be delighted with yourself as beautiful. Therefore, affected in this way, you will seek the true and intimate beauty in vain: for you will seek it not with something pure, but with something shameful; therefore, words about such things are not held for everyone. But if you also have inspected yourself as beautiful, from here now remember beauty itself.

He uses the examples of Helen and Aphrodite to show that true beauty is perceived internally, independent of physical size or material bulk.</summary>

It follows the previous page’s argument that beauty is not found in physical size or matter, but in the internal form that gives matter its shape.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS V. PAGE 544

Indeed, the soul seeks in vain to know what beauty itself is if it has not made itself most beautiful through such a conversion. But if it has made itself so, then by gazing upon its own beauty, it will find the higher beauty sufficient. Through its own <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectum" / "νοῦς"; the higher, intuitive mind in Neoplatonic thought</note>, now purified like a piece of gold taken from a larger mass, it sees the divine intellect as the total, pure gold; it will contemplate it in its sincerity, for it is not to be sought in any other way. Finally, the primary beauty is the primary fullness of intelligence. The gods, who are purely intellectual, are beautiful and are gods through their participation in that beauty. By this same participation, the celestial gods—that is, all the worldly gods—are also gods. These celestial gods know divine things through a direct gaze, while they look upon and govern human things through a downward turn. Finally, the purely intellectual gods who dwell in the intellectual heaven are said not to govern (at least in their capacity of being there), but to contemplate. Whatever exists in that intellectual heaven is likewise an "intellectual heaven"; for there, all things are present.

<margin>A</margin> There is, therefore, a <term>reason-principle</term> <note>original: "ratio" / "λόγος"; a formative, rational power that bridges the spiritual and physical</note> of beauty in nature which is the archetype of the beauty appearing in the body. However, the archetype of natural beauty is a more beautiful reason-principle in the soul, from which the beauty of nature flows. This shines more clearly in a virtuous soul, already advancing through beauty itself, adorning the soul and providing light from a greater light, which is also the primary beauty. Thus existing in the soul, it leads one to reason out what 
<margin>B</margin> the higher reason-principle of beauty must be—a beauty that no longer comes to be in another or lies within another, but remains within itself. Therefore, it is not even a "reason," but the author of the first reason. For while the first reason is a certain beauty in the soul as if in matter, the author itself is the Intellect, which is always Intellect and never ceases to be so, since intellect does not come to it from elsewhere. But what image of this Intellect shall we take? For whatever is sought from elsewhere will undoubtedly be sought from something
<margin>C</margin> inferior. An image of the Intellect must therefore be sought from the Intellect itself, so that we do not speak of it through an image, but rather take a piece of gold as a sign of the whole mass of gold. And unless the gold we take is already pure, let us purify it either by action or by speech, demonstrating that what we have taken is not the whole mass of gold, but merely a certain piece of gold from the bulk. Thus, from this intellect which is within us, now purified, let us ascend higher to the Intellect itself. 
<margin>D</margin> And if it pleases, let us proceed from the gods themselves, looking at what kind of intellect exists in them. For all gods are beautiful, lovely, venerable, and endowed with an inestimable grace. But what is it that makes the gods such? It is surely Intellect; I mean the Intellect acting most powerfully within them so that they are seen as they are. It is not because their bodies are beautiful; for even those who have bodies do not possess their godhood in this fact, but they too are gods according to the mind. 
<margin>E</margin> Nor are they judged beautiful gods because beautiful bodies are present to them. For they are not wise at one time and unwise at another, but they are perpetually wise with a mind that is tranquil, stable, and pure. They understand all things and know not merely human things, but their own—that is, divine things—and whatever the Intellect itself perceives. Among the gods, those who inhabit the heaven possess an abundance of leisure and contemplate continually, but as if from a distance, looking with an "uplifted neck" at what is in the first heaven itself. 
<margin>F</margin> Those, however, who are in that first heaven, and those who have obtained a dwelling there, contemplate while inhabiting that entire heaven. For all things there are heaven; there the earth is heaven; the sea, animals, plants, and men are the heaven. In short, whatever belongs to that heaven is heavenly. The gods dwelling there do not look down upon men or anything else that is there, for the very reason that they are of the divine number; for they traverse that whole region and encompass the place while remaining at rest.

<column-break/>

THERE IS, therefore, even in Nature a reason-principle of beauty, which is the archetype of that in the body. But that which is in Nature is a more beautiful one in the soul, from which comes that in 
Nature. It is more distinct in the soul that hastens toward being and is already <gloss>becoming good</gloss> beauty. For having adorned the soul and provided light from a greater light, which is the First Beauty, it causes the soul to reason—being such a soul itself—as to what the one before it is like, which no longer "comes to be" in another, nor is in another, but in itself. Therefore it is not even a reason-principle, but the maker of the first reason-principle, which is a beauty whose matter is the soul. But the Intellect is the creator, being always Intellect and being the whole, because it is not something added to it. What image, then, could one take of it? For any image will be from something inferior. Rather, one must seek Intellect from Intellect. Thus, one should not seek it through an image, but as with all gold, one must take some gold as a sample. And if the piece taken is not pure, one must purify it, either by deed or by word, showing that this thing is gold, but not the whole of it—only that which is in the mass. So also here, we must purify from the intellect within us. And if you wish, start from the gods and see what the intellect in them is like. For all gods are majestic and beautiful, and their beauty is overwhelming. But what is it through which they are such? Is it not Intellect? And it is because Intellect is active within them that they are seen as such. For it is not because their bodies are beautiful. For those that have bodies, it is not this that makes them gods; rather, <gloss>they are gods by having intellect</gloss>. And the gods are beautiful. Or do they perhaps think at some times and <gloss>not think</gloss> at others? No, they always think with a mind that is free from passion, standing firm and pure. They know all things and recognize <gloss>not human things</gloss>, but their own divine things, and as many things as Intellect sees. Of the gods, those in the heaven, having leisure, always contemplate. They see, as if from afar, with their own "head" <note>this refers to the "summit" or highest part of the soul</note> the things in the heaven above them. But those in that higher heaven, as many as have their dwelling upon it or in it, inhabit the whole of that heaven. For everything there is heaven; the earth is heaven, and the sea, and animals, and plants, and men. Everything is heavenly in that heaven. And the gods in it do not disregard men, nor anything else there, because they are of that place; they traverse that whole land <gloss>and the manner of it</gloss>, resting.

# BOOK EIGHT.

->Above the physical heaven, in the incorporeal heaven, there are two kinds of gods: the <term>intelligible</term> <note>original: "intelligibiles"; refers to the highest realm of pure Being or the Ideas themselves</note> and the <term>intellectual</term> <note>original: "intellectuales"; refers to the active, thinking Mind (Nous) that contemplates those Ideas</note>. The former are the Ideas themselves, while the latter are the intellects made blessed by the eternal contemplation of those Ideas. Chapter III: I.<-

*The divine intellect flows into the Ideas in such a way that it is preserved entirely in each one, yet with a different property in each. We should not say that the Ideas are "in" the intellect so much as that the intellect itself exists as those very Ideas—manifesting in many forms from its own uniform self in a marvelous way. If the physical heaven similarly projects itself into the stars, then in any single star, the whole heaven is present, along with all the stars, but with a distinct quality. Therefore, what Anaxagoras <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher famous for the theory that "everything is in everything"</note> said—that "everything is in everything"—applies not just to the world below the heavens (where unity is minimal), but even more so to the world above the heavens (where unity is greatest), and in a sense to the heavenly world (where unity is middling). Where Plotinus proves that the contemplators of divine things will never depart from there, take note of what Porphyry and Iamblichus <note>Neoplatonic philosophers who followed Plotinus</note> touched upon: that our souls can also reach a similar state of bliss. "He who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved forever." "Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord; they will praise you forever and ever."* <note>Quotes from the Psalms, used here to relate Platonic philosophy to sacred scripture</note>

---

**A** This is the goal of what is taught by Plato in the *Phaedrus*: that those above lead an easy life, and that Truth itself is their parent and nurse, both their essence and their food. Likewise, they see all things—not those subject to <term>generation</term> <note>original: "genesis" / "generationi"; the process of birth, change, and decay in the physical world</note>, but those that exist in true essence. They also see themselves in others. For there, all things are transparent; nothing is dark or resistant. Every being is visible to every other, internally and through all things. For

**B** light meets light everywhere. Each person has all things within themselves and again sees all things in another. Thus, all things are everywhere. Everything there is "everything." Each thing is the "universe." There, an immense splendor shines. For every part there is great, since even the small there is great. There, the sun is all the stars, and each star is similarly the sun and all the stars. One quality stands out in each, yet all are seen in every one.

**C** Movement there is undoubtedly pure; for a mover distinct from the movement does not confuse the proceeding motion. <margin>It mingles its own property with that which it moves, yet remains distinct from it.</margin> Rest there is also undisturbed by any change, for it is not mixed with an unstable nature. Furthermore, Beauty itself is "beauty," because it does not simply reside *in* something beautiful. Everyone remains as if on their own ground, not on a foreign floor; for the foundation of each is the very thing that each is. And it joins with them as they rise, so to speak, back to the eternal source from which they come. The being is not one thing and its place another; for the <term>subject</term> <note>The underlying substance or "matter" of the mind</note> is intellect,

**D** and the thing itself is intellect. It is as if someone were to imagine this visible and bright heaven, through its own light, budding and growing together into stars. In physical things, one part does not emerge from every other part; each part is only itself. But there, every part emerges from the whole, and each part exists simultaneously as the whole. It appears as a part, but it is perceived as the whole by one who sees sharply—as if someone had the sight attributed to <term>Lynceus</term> <note>A hero from Greek mythology famous for his keen sight, said to be able to see through trees, rocks, and the ground</note>, who was said

<margin>It was said that Lynceus could see even the things inside the earth.</margin>

to penetrate the depths of the earth with the rays of his eyes. I believe this myth signifies the keenness of the eyes of those above. Furthermore, we must consider that those who see these things are never exhausted by seeing, nor are they ever led by any satiety to stop their contemplation.

**E** For there was no emptiness in them that, once filled and satisfied, would bring an end to their gazing. Nor is one thing different from another in such a way that one part of them would be displeased by what belongs to another. Moreover, all things there are untamable and tireless. What is called "insatiable" there is called so because its fullness never causes one to look down upon the one who fills it; for by seeing, one sees more steadily, and

<margin>Fullness does not make one despise the act of creation because of being satisfied. For seeing, he sees the more.</margin>

Likewise, they see all things—not those subject to generation, but those that exist in essence. They also see themselves in others. For there, all things are transparent. Nothing is dark, nothing resistant, but everyone there is visible to everyone, internally and through all things.

**B** For light meets light everywhere. Each person has all things within themselves and again sees all things in another. Thus, all things are everywhere. Everything there is "everything." Each thing there is the "universe." There, an immense splendor shines. For every part there is great, since even the small there is great. There, the sun and all the stars are present. Each star is the sun, and all the stars are similarly suns. One quality stands out in each, yet all are seen in every one.

**C** Movement there is undoubtedly pure; for a mover distinct from the movement does not confuse the proceeding motion. Everyone remains as if on their own ground, not on a foreign floor; for the foundation of each is the very thing that each is. <meta>This page continues Plotinus’s description of the Intelligible Realm (the world of pure Thought and Being). The previous page established that in this divine realm, all things are transparent to one another and exist in a state of perfect unity. Here, Plotinus argues that this state is not reached through effort or reasoning, but is the very "Life" and "Wisdom" of the divine Intellect itself.</meta>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK V.

<page-num>546</page-num>

...perfecting its own infinite self and following its own nature as its guide, just as the things seen <note>The "things seen" refer to the Ideas or Forms within the Divine Mind.</note> do. Now truly, the life of no one there is laborious, for when life is pure, and because it lives in the best possible way, why should it labor? 

Life in that realm is Wisdom—a wisdom not acquired through step-by-step arguments, because it has always been whole and entire, lacking in no part that would require a search or investigation. Rather, it is the primary Wisdom, not depending on any other wisdom; in that place, essence <note>original: "essentia"; the fundamental "is-ness" or being of a thing.</note> itself is Wisdom. It is not as if the Intellect exists first and then later becomes wise. 

<margin>A</margin> For this reason, there is no greater wisdom. Indeed, in that realm, the knowledge of the Mind itself is its own companion, because they sprout forth together. Just as they say in a kind of imitation <note>Plotinus often uses traditional mythology as a metaphor for philosophical truths.</note> that Judgment and Justice are the companions of Jupiter <note>original: "Iouis"; here referring to the Demiurge or the ruling principle of the universe.</note> himself. For all things of this kind exist there as if they were statues—or rather, as living archetypes <note>The "original models" from which everything in our world is copied.</note> that are visible everywhere from within themselves and in themselves, so that the sight of them is a spectacle for those who are more than happy spectators. 

<margin>B</margin> One may consider the magnitude and power of this Wisdom most clearly from this: that it possesses all things with itself and has created all beings. For all things that truly exist have followed Wisdom; they all consist through it and have arisen together with it, and both are one. In short, the essence there is Wisdom. 

<margin>C</margin> We, however, have not yet arrived at this understanding, because we think that "sciences" are merely a collection of theories, rules, and a flow of propositions—a view that should not even be applied to our own human sciences. If anyone doubts this regarding our sciences, let us set that aside for now. But it seems worthwhile to begin again from here and discuss that Science which Plato <note>A reference to Plato’s *Phaedrus* 247d, describing the soul's journey to the "Plain of Truth."</note> looked up to as reigning there, when he said: "That Science is not one thing in one person and another in another." 

<margin>D</margin> How it truly is, he seems to have left for us to investigate and find out, provided we claim to be worthy of such a title.

<column-break/>

...gazing upon its own infinite self and the things seen, it follows its own nature. And that life has no weariness, whenever it is pure. For that which lives [there], why should it grow weary? That life is Wisdom; a wisdom not reached by calculations <note>original: "λογισμοῖς" (logismois); discursive reasoning or step-by-step logic.</note>, because it is always complete, lacking nothing that would require a search. But it is the first, not from another. And that essence is Wisdom. It is not that he [the Intellect] is one thing, and then wise. 

Because of this, nothing is greater. And Self-Knowledge sits beside the Intellect, by being innate to it. Just as they say in imitation that Justice sits beside Zeus. All such things are there, like statues seen from within themselves. So that it is a sight for happy spectators. One may see the greatness of Wisdom by its power, seeing that it has all things with it and has made all things. And all things followed it. And Wisdom itself is the beings. And it grew together with it. And both are one. And the essence there is Wisdom. 

But we have not come to an understanding of this, because we have considered sciences to be a collection of theorems. But this is not even true in the sciences here. If anyone disputes these things, let us leave them for the present. But concerning that Science, did not Plato see it? That Science is not one thing in another. How it is, for one seeking and being trustworthy—if indeed we say we are worthy of such a sign—perhaps it is best to make the beginning from here.

---

->**Since art imitates nature, and nature imitates God, and since art acts through a certain wisdom, while God acts through Wisdom itself simply, it follows that nature acts through a certain wisdom implanted in it. Chapter IV.**<-

> *If all things recover their essence through Wisdom, it follows that primary Wisdom is primary Essence. The industry of acquired wisdom, which is human art, depends on the wisdom innate to us and imitates the wisdom of nature. Truly, these three wisdoms, because they exist in another, must be referred back to the primary Wisdom, which exists in itself—where, clearly, wisdom is essence itself. The wisdom of human art is heaped up from many acts of meditation and speech; but the wisdom naturally implanted in us, and the wisdom of nature itself and of God, is a single form presenting itself as all-formed, or a single face, not like a single speech or argument. For before the "one" that is heaped up from many, there is a "one" that unfolds itself into many, and before that is the "Simply One."*

---

<margin>A</margin> **Whatever** things are made by either art or nature are made by a certain wisdom, and wisdom leads the action everywhere. If a "wisdom" is created anywhere, let it be the arts of that kind. But the craftsman himself is, in turn, referred back to natural wisdom, according to which the art and every work is performed. I say "according to which" because it is no longer gathered from theories, but is entirely one thing; not composed from many into one, but rather resolving itself from one into many. 

<margin>B</margin> If anyone, therefore, posits that this Wisdom is primary, it will be sufficient; for since it is not from another, it will not even be in another. But if he says that "reason" <note>original: "rationem"; here meaning the formative principle or *Logos*.</note> is in nature, and that the principle of this is nature, we shall ask from where nature has this reason.

<column-break/>

**ALL** things that come to be, whether by art or by nature, are made by a certain wisdom. And wisdom leads the making everywhere. But if indeed someone makes this wisdom itself, let them be the arts of such a kind. But the craftsman again goes back to natural wisdom, according to which he has come to be. Not a wisdom composed of theorems, but a whole; not the one gathered from many into one, but rather the one analyzed into a multitude from one. 

If indeed someone will place this as the first wisdom, it is sufficient; for it is no longer from another, nor is it in another. But if he says that "reason" [the formative principle] belongs to nature, and the beginning of this is nature, we shall ask from where nature has it.

<summary>Plotinus explores the nature of Divine Wisdom, arguing that it is not a collection of facts or logic but is identical to Being itself. He asserts that all creation, whether through human art or natural processes, is a physical unfolding of this unified, non-discursive primary Wisdom.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s discussion of the relationship between Mind, Wisdom, and Being. Having previously argued that divine life is not a struggle but a state of "Wisdom," Plotinus now explains that this Wisdom is not a set of logical arguments or sentences, but is identical to the very "Forms" or "Ideas" that make up reality. He famously uses the example of Egyptian hieroglyphs to illustrate how divine knowledge is a single, unified "image" rather than a series of words.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

<page-num>547</page-num>

But if wisdom is said to be held from another, we shall ask again about that other; and if it possesses it from itself, we shall rest there. Thus, if they turn to the Mind itself, we must investigate there whether the Mind generated Wisdom. If they admit this, from where did it come? If it conceived Wisdom from itself, it could not have done so unless the Mind itself were Wisdom. True wisdom, therefore, is essence <note>original: "essentia" / "ousia"; the fundamental "being" or "is-ness" of a thing.</note>, and true essence, in turn, is wisdom; the very dignity of essence is claimed by wisdom. 

<margin>B</margin> For it is certain that true essence comes from wisdom. Therefore, whatever beings do not possess wisdom—insofar as they were made through a certain wisdom—are indeed beings; but insofar as they do not possess wisdom within themselves, they are not true beings. No one, then, should think that in the intelligible world <note>The realm of divine, perfect reality beyond the physical world.</note>, either the gods themselves or the other "more-than-happy" inhabitants gaze upon certain rules of propositions <note>Logical sentences or "if-then" statements.</note>; rather, all the things said to be there offer themselves to those who behold them as beautiful models <note>original: "exemplaria"; Greek "agalmata" (statues/images).</note> and spectacles, such as one might imagine existing in the soul of a wise man. I do not mean painted images, but existing realities; for this reason, the ancients called the Ideas "beings" and "essences."

---

> *The Egyptian priests, to signify divine mysteries, did not use small characters of letters, but whole figures of herbs, trees, and animals; because clearly, God has knowledge of things not as a complex thinking-out of a matter, but as a simple and firm form of the thing. Chapter VI.*
>
> *The thinking-out of time in your mind is complex and shifting, saying for instance that time is swift, and by a certain revolution joins the beginning back to the end; it teaches prudence, brings forth things, and takes them away. But the Egyptian grasps this whole movement in a single figure, painting a winged serpent gripping its tail with its mouth <note>The Ouroboros, a symbol of eternity and the cyclical nature of time.</note>, and other such figures which Horus describes.*

---

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> The sages of the Egyptians seem to me—whether by a certain perfected wisdom or a natural instinct of the mind—when they decided to signify the mysteries of wisdom to us, not to have used the figures of letters which signify the step-by-step movements of speech <note>original: "sermonis discursiones"; discursive or linear logic where one thought follows another.</note> and certain propositions, nor figures imitating the sounds and pronunciations of rules. Instead, they drew individual images of individual things, and by painting them in their temples, they signified the "discourse" of the thing itself. 

<margin>B</margin> For every image is a kind of knowledge and wisdom, a model or subject, a whole spectacle gathered into one; it is not a complex thought or a plan. Afterwards, from that image-model or total wisdom, a likeness is made in something else, now unfolded and speaking in a kind of step-by-step discourse, finding the reasons why things are so established. When the arrangement of things is so well-ordered, it moves one to wonder. 

<margin>C</margin> Hence, he says that whoever considers how Wisdom itself, having no causes for its own essence, yet provides itself to those things made according to it, will wonder at it. This very thing that can be called the arrangement of things—which is hardly made manifest through investigation—must exist in the intelligible world before all investigation and argument. But let us now take up one great example which is consistent with all things.

<sig>Z 4</sig>

<summary>Plotinus argues that divine Wisdom is identical to Being and consists of unified "Forms" rather than discursive logic. He cites Egyptian hieroglyphs as a metaphor for how the Divine Mind perceives the entire essence of a thing instantly and as a whole, rather than through linear reasoning.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s argument from Chapter 6, where he established that divine Wisdom is not a collection of logical propositions but a unified, living reality. Here, in Chapter 7, he moves to the act of creation, arguing that the "Divine Craftsman" does not plan the world step-by-step like a human builder, but rather projects it effortlessly from his own nature.</meta>

->### PLOTINUS: ENNEAD V.###<-
->#### God’s Knowledge is Not Like Reasoning or Planning, but Rather a Natural Disposition. Chapter VII.####<-

*For He does not first establish a principle and then gather a conclusion through intermediate steps, nor, having set an end goal, does He consequently choose the ways and means to achieve that end, acting only after deliberation. Rather, because He is already so disposed in all things by His own nature, He acts naturally in this way: just as a seed, being multifaceted in its potential, generates a multifaceted offspring. But that all-encompassing nature of God is His very intellect, marked by all the Ideas—not like a tablet marked with figures, but like the heavens filled with stars, which are themselves the heavens. He acts with the greatest ease because He acts by His very nature, and He Himself is the universe. Our soul acts in a nearly similar way when it recalls itself to its all-encompassing state.*

---

<margin>A</margin> Should we really think that this universe—which is admitted to come from another and to exist as it does—was composed by its maker in such a way that he first thought out the "Earth" within himself, deciding it ought to rest in the center? And then the water following the earth, and the other elements in order up to the sky? And then all the animals, with the specific forms and numbers of living things they now possess, and the arrangement of both their internal organs and their external parts and limbs?

<margin>B</margin> Did he then, having arranged these things within himself, set about the actual work of arranging them in reality? Certainly, such deliberation could not have existed in Him. For where would such a thought occur to one who had never yet seen such things? Nor could He have fabricated the world by receiving instructions from another, as our craftsmen do today, using hands and tools—for hands and feet are later additions to the story of creation. It remains, then, that all things exist within "Another" <note>This "Other" refers to the Divine Intellect or the World of Ideas.</note>, and since nothing stands in the way, by the very proximity of Being itself to that "other," its image and likeness flash forth suddenly, whether from itself alone or through the ministry of the Soul.

<margin>C</margin> For it matters nothing for the present discussion whether it happened through a specific Soul; the point is that all these things flowed from there, and they are more beautiful there than they are here. For here they are mixed, but there they are pure. This universe, proceeding from that source, is encompassed by "Forms" <note>original: "speciebus" / "eide"; the perfect blueprints or patterns of things.</note> from beginning to end. First, matter is shaped by the forms of the elements, to which other forms are added, and still others upon those, so that it is difficult to find the underlying matter hidden beneath so many layers of form.

<margin>D</margin> Since matter itself possesses a kind of ultimate form, it can easily take on every other form. But that Craftsman, who holds the pattern of the work as a "Form," produces all forms, and does so without difficulty or any violence, because the acting power there is the entire universe, both essence and form.

<margin>E</margin> For this reason, the fabrication was easy and without labor, and the creation of the whole existed just as the Craftsman himself is the whole. There was, therefore, no impediment, and even now He rules freely in the act of creating. And although some things here may hinder others, nothing can obstruct the fabrication of the universe itself, for it stands as a unified whole. I believe that if we were the primary patterns of things—the essences and forms themselves—and if the very form that creates here were our own essence, our "fabrication" would rule without effort. Even though man, as he is now produced, creates a form distinct from himself, he does so because he has become a specific man and ceased to be the "Universe." But when he ceases to be merely a man, as Plato says, "he soars aloft and governs the whole world." <note>A reference to Plato's *Phaedrus* (246c), suggesting that the soul finds its true power when it identifies with the universal rather than the individual.</note> For having become part of the whole, he creates the whole. But let us return to our purpose.

<column-break/>

Since we admit that this universe comes from another and is of such a kind, should we think that its creator, having conceived of "Earth" within himself, then decided it should stand in the center? And then water, and this upon the earth, and the rest in order up to the heavens? And then all the animals, and the forms each now possesses, and the internal organs for each, and the external parts? And then, having arranged each thing within himself, he set his hand to the work? But how is such a conception possible? For where did it come from to one who had never seen it? Nor was it possible to work by receiving it from another, as craftsmen now do, using hands and instruments. For hands and feet come later. It remains, therefore, that the causes exist in another, and with nothing in between, by the communion of that which is in Being with the "other," an image and likeness of that source suddenly appears, either directly or through the service of a soul. It makes no difference for now whether it is through a soul, but all these things flow out from there. They are more beautiful there; for things here are imitated. And those things are not imitated, but they are begun from the beginning to the end in forms. First, matter is given the forms of the elements, then other forms upon these, and then others again. Hence it is hard to find matter, hidden as it is under many forms. Since it too is a final form, it places every form and all forms. For the pattern was there with him. And it was done silently, because the whole is the maker, both essence and form. Therefore the creation is effortless and without distraction. And being the whole, how could anything hinder it since it is the very thing that creates? It prevails even now; and though other things hinder each other, nothing hinders the whole. For it remains as the whole. It seems to me that if we were the archetypal essence and perceptions, and the form that makes were our essence, our creation would prevail without labor. Even though man is now a small, different form, for he is a "becoming" man, yet when he ceases to be merely a man, he "walks on high," as they say, and "administers the whole world." For having become part of the whole, he makes the whole. But for the sake of the argument...

<meta>The catchword "poter-" at the bottom of the Latin column likely leads to "poterit" or "potest" on the next page, continuing the discussion of the soul's power.</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that the creation of the universe is not a result of "planning" or "deliberation" by a craftsman-god, but is an effortless, natural projection of the Divine Intellect's own nature. He posits that if humans could transcend their individual identity and reconnect with the "Universal Soul," they too would share in this effortless governance of reality.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Chapter 7 and begins Chapter 8 of Plotinus’s "On Intellectual Beauty." It continues the argument that the Divine Mind (the Nous) does not function through step-by-step logic but possesses all truth simultaneously as a unified whole. It transitions into a discussion of why the physical world, as an image of this Divine Mind, possesses beauty.</meta>

### BOOK EIGHT.

If one were to state the cause for why the earth is in the middle, why it is round, and why the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>original: "ὁ λοξὸς", the diagonal path of the sun</note> is arranged as it is, it should not be said that it is so because it was "decided" to be that way. Rather, it is because it exists in that specific state; and because it exists so, it is well-ordered. It is like the conclusion of a <term>syllogism</term> <note>a form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note>: the conclusion does not follow by a secondary thought or effort, but is inherent in the premises themselves. For all these things—reasoning, demonstration, and proof—come later. Since the Divine Mind exists exactly as it is, all these things are as they are, because one must not seek a cause for a first principle <note>original: "ἀρχῆς"</note>, especially a perfect principle that is identical to its own end. That which is both beginning and end is the whole together, lacking nothing.

<margin>Note this</margin>
What is "The Beautiful" is therefore primary. It is a whole, and a whole in every part, so that no part of beauty is left lacking. How then? Shall we call it "The Beautiful"? Or is it that which is the whole itself, while the thing that possesses only a part, or nothing of it, is not? If we do not call that primary reality "beautiful," what else could we call so? For that which is before it does not even wish to be beautiful. That which first comes into our sight, because it is a "form" <note>original: "εἴδει"</note> and a vision of the Mind, is lovable to behold. This is what Plato <term>*</term> <note>Referring to the *Timaeus* 37c</note> wished to reveal when he described the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>The "Craftsman" or Creator of the universe in Platonic thought</note> as accepting the finished work as something more vivid and present to us. Because he wished to praise it, he showed that the beauty of the "Exemplar" <note>The perfect model or Idea</note> and the Idea is good. For whenever someone admires a thing made after another, their admiration is directed toward that original according to which it was made. If the observer does not realize what they are experiencing, it is no wonder. Even lovers, and generally those who admire the beauty here on earth, are often ignorant that they do so because of the heavenly beauty. That they are being led back to the Exemplar is made clear by the words Plato uses next. For he said that the Creator was "delighted" <note>original: "ἠγάσθη"</note> and wished to make the work even more like its model, demonstrating what the beauty of the Exemplar is like. He shows that the created thing is beautiful because it is an image of that higher reality. For if that "Ultra-Beautiful" reality, with its unimaginable beauty, did not exist, what could be more beautiful than this visible world? Therefore, those who find fault with this world are not acting rightly—unless their complaint is simply that this world is not that higher world.

<column-break/>

A. You could indeed provide a reason why the earth is placed in the center, why it is round, and why the <term>oblique circle</term> <note>the sun's path</note> was established in a certain region. However, in the divine mind, it was not "deliberated" because it "ought to be so." Rather, because it exists in the way it does, these things are consequently well-arranged. It is as if, before an argument runs through its causes, the conclusion itself stood firm without any premises. For there, nothing depends on a sequence of consequences, and nothing becomes certain through reflection; rather, the whole stands firm before any sequence or reflection. For all these things—reason, demonstration, and faith—are B. secondary. By the very fact that the "principle" exists, all these things are naturally present and so disposed. Now, as for the saying that the causes of a principle are not to be sought, it is rightly said, especially concerning such a principle that is perfect, and which is the same as its "end." Because the beginning and the end are the same, this universe is a simultaneous whole, failing in no part.

*Since beauty itself is a certain multiform shape suited to the sight, the first principle is rightly superior to beauty.*

### Chapter VIII.

*The divine mind is the first whole, and therefore a whole in every one of its parts. It is also the first beauty, and therefore the total beauty in every part. There are three most beautiful things beneath the Good itself: the divine mind, the soul of the world, and the body of the world; just as in the heavens we see the Sun, Jupiter, and Venus. Those captured by Venus <note>physical beauty</note> do not know what they are suffering, because they do not realize they admire the lower beauty for the sake of the higher.*

A. THIS, therefore, is primarily beautiful: it is a whole; it is a whole everywhere, so that there is no defect of beauty even in any part. What, then, is to be said of beauty itself? Certainly not anything that is not the whole itself, but either has only a part or has nothing of it. Truly, if that is not beauty itself, what else could it be? For that which is before it does not seek to be beautiful. For that which first comes into view, B. because it is a "Species" <note>or Form</note> and a spectacle of the Mind, is lovable and pleasant to the sight. Therefore, Plato, wishing to signify this to us, introduces the Architect of the world approving of his finished work. He moves toward something more manifest to our minds, wishing to show through this that the beauty of the exemplar and the Idea is lovable. For whenever anyone admires a work made according to another model, C. they admire the model itself most of all. Nor should it seem strange if, in the meantime, they are ignorant of what they are experiencing. For lovers, and indeed everyone who admires this beauty of ours, are unaware that they are so affected because of the supernal <note>heavenly or higher</note> beauty; and truly, they are affected because of it. That Plato refers back to the divine exemplar when he says the Architect of the world loved his work is shown by his being delighted by the spectacle itself, where he D. adds: "He was indeed delighted by his workmanship, and even more, he wished to make it similar to the exemplar itself." By this very statement, he demonstrates the quality of the beauty of the exemplar, because he says this work is beautiful from that one, because it is its image. Indeed, unless that were wonderfully beautiful, possessing an inestimable beauty, what could be more beautiful than this universe manifest to our eyes? Therefore, those who disparage the beauty of this world do not think correctly, unless perhaps in disparaging it they mean this: that this world is not the higher one.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the beauty and order of the physical world are direct reflections of a "Divine Mind" (Nous) where all truths exist simultaneously without the need for logical reasoning or deliberation. He uses Plato's creation story to explain that our love for physical beauty is actually a subconscious recognition of the perfect "Exemplar" or Idea from which the world was modeled.</summary>
