<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s "Ennead V," specifically Book 8, "On Intellectual Beauty," Chapter 9. It provides a famous visualization exercise to help the reader transition from perceiving the physical world to understanding the unified, non-spatial nature of the Divine Mind (Nous).</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK V.

When you have received this whole variety of worldly forms <note>original: "formarum mundanarum"</note> all at once, immediately preserve those forms but strip away their local dimensions <note>the physical space they occupy</note>. You then possess the Soul of the World, in which all forms exist within every other form. Then, once the motions are held in a steady state, you possess the Divine Mind <note>original: "mentem iam diuinam"</note>, where every idea contains all others. Finally, once the diversity of things is resolved into a single light, you have reached the First Principle <note>The One</note>. ->Chapter IX.<-

---

>*The corporeal world is not truly great, because it depends everywhere on small things. The incorporeal world is the whole. For it may be called infinite in this sense: in one idea, all others are present; and when all these are accounted for, they are present again in every other idea, and so on. Since the first essence and beauty are the same, it follows that as much as something participates in beauty, it also participates in essence, and vice versa. Likewise, since the first essence is simply Form <note>original: "species"</note> itself, it is certainly by participation in Form that all things have their existence.*

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, let us take this world of ours in thought, holding it in such a way that each part remains what it is, but they all exist within one another. Let us imagine, I say, all things gathered together into one as much as possible, so that whatever individual thing first presents itself to the eyes—for example, if it were an outer sphere—there immediately follows the sight of the Sun, and at the same time the image of the other stars, and within it are seen the earth, the sea, and all living creatures, as if in a <margin>B</margin> certain sphere that is transparent everywhere. In fact, it would be possible to see everything within each thing. Let there be, therefore, in the soul a certain luminous imagination <note>a mental visualization</note> of a sphere, containing all things in itself, whether they are in motion or at rest—or rather, some moving and others stable. While keeping this in your mind, imagine another sphere besides it, but remove its mass; take away its location as well, and at the same time, completely expel every imagination of matter from yourself. Do not, however, imagine this second one as merely a smaller version of the first in terms of its mass. <margin>C</margin> Then, calling upon the God himself who made it—of whom you now hold an image—pray humbly that He may come. He will come suddenly, bringing His own world and His own beauty <note>original: "ornatumq;"</note> with Him, along with all the gods who are within Him. He will come as one who is also all, and each god will meet you, carrying all the others together with himself, coming together into one. There, truly, all the gods are different in their specific powers, but by that one manifold power, they are all one God; or rather, one God is all of them. <margin>D</margin> For that one God does not fail so that all those others may be born. They are all together at once, and yet each is again separate from the other in a state that is in no way distant, showing no form that is subject to the senses. Otherwise, one would be in one place and another elsewhere, and each would not exist as a whole within himself. Nor, again, does any of those beings have parts different from other parts or from themselves. Nor, again, is each thing there a whole power that is divided and only as large <margin>E</margin> as the number of measured parts. Rather, it is the whole, a total power proceeding to infinity, and infinite in its virtue. Indeed, that world is so vast that even its parts turn out to be infinite. For where can anything be said to exist that the Divine has not already reached? This physical world is also great, and all powers are present within it at once; but it would be even greater, and of a size that could not be explained, if there were no small power of the body within it. <margin>F</margin> And if anyone speaks of the great forces of fire and the other elements <note>original: "corporū"</note>, they nonetheless consist of an infinity of true power; but through ignorance of that power, they seem merely to be something and to act by destroying, crushing, and serving the generation of living creatures.

<column-break/>

Therefore, let us take this world <note>Greek: "ΤΟΥΤΟΝ τοίνυν τὸν κόσμον"</note>, with each of its parts remaining what it is, and grasp it in the mind as all things together into one, as much as possible. Thus, when any one part appears, such as the outer sphere, there follows immediately the mental image of the sun and the other stars together, and the earth and the sea, and all living things are seen, as if upon a transparent sphere; and indeed, all things might be seen within it. Let there be then in the soul a certain luminous imagination of a sphere, having all things in itself, whether moving or standing still, or some moving and some standing still. Guarding this, take another in yourself, but strip away the mass. Take away also the places and the phantom of matter within you. And do not try to grasp it as another sphere that is simply smaller in mass. Call upon the God who made it—of whom you have the phantom—and pray for Him to come. And He may come, bringing His own world, with all the gods in it, being one and all, and each one being all, coming together into one. And in their powers they are different, but in that one manifold power they are all one; or rather, the one is all. For the One does not fail so that those others may come to be. They are all together, yet each is separate again, in a state without distance, having no nature that is perceptible to the senses. For if they did, one would be here and another there, and each would not be all in himself, nor would he have parts. But he possesses them in relation to others, or to himself. Nor is each whole a power that is divided, being only as great as its measured parts. But the whole is the whole, a power going toward infinity and capable of infinity. And that world is so great that its parts have also become infinite. For where can one say it does not reach? This world here is also great, and all the powers in it are great. But it would be greater, and so great it could not be described, if some small power of body did not accompany it. And yet one might say the powers of fire and the other bodies are great. But they appear and exist by a true infinite power; yet they destroy and crush and serve the generation of living things. But these things destroy because they themselves...

<meta>catchword: But these things indeed destroy, because they themselves [interimunt, quoniã ipsâ qu / int]</meta>

<summary>Plotinus describes a visualization exercise where the reader imagines the entire physical universe inside a transparent sphere, then strips away its physical mass and spatial dimensions to perceive the Intelligible World, where all things exist simultaneously as a unified, infinite whole in the Divine Mind.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Plotinus’s "Ennead V," Book 8 (titled "On Intellectual Beauty"). The previous page concluded with a mental exercise to strip away physical dimensions to reach the Divine Mind. This page explores the identity of Being and Beauty and describes the celestial procession of souls led by Jupiter toward the intelligible realm.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

<column-break/>

**A** Things in this world perish and are generated in turn, precisely because they are subject to "becoming" <note>original: "generantur"</note>. But the power that flourishes there <note>in the Intelligible Realm</note> possesses only "to be," and only "to be beautiful." For where could anything be beautiful if it were deprived of Being itself? Or where could Essence exist if it lacked the presence of Beauty? For when beauty is removed, essence is taken away. Therefore, "to be" itself is desirable because "to be" and "to be beautiful" are the same; and conversely, "to be beautiful" is lovable because it is also "to be." 

**B** Whether one is the cause of the other is not worth investigating, since their nature is one and the same. This false essence of bodies <note>the material world</note> requires an external image of beauty to appear beautiful and to be anything at all. It exists only insofar as it participates in the beauty consisting of the Form <note>original: "specie"</note> itself; and the more of that Form it receives, the more perfect it is. For thus a beautiful essence is more its own, and it is itself, finally, beauty.

---

->Together with Jupiter—that is, the Soul of the World—all celestial, demonic, and already-purified human souls enjoy the entire divine world.<-
->**Chapter X.**<-

Even if there, individuals contemplate all the Ideas, one soul nourishes itself more attentively and greedily on certain ones, to which it primarily relates the others. Beauty itself is most present there as that universal splendor shining from the entire series of Ideas, like a constellation of stars. All the power of the Intellect <note>original: "intelligentia"</note>, unless an ardent love is added, perhaps only reaches the point of seeing that beauty as something external. But when love approaches, it carries the contemplator into that beauty, and vice versa—until the lover-contemplator sees themselves as beautiful, or rather, has become beauty itself. Plotinus agrees with what Plato says: that philosophers alone walk with Jupiter, sent by Jupiter. For while other men are dedicated to specific things, the philosopher alone embraces the whole, and the Soul of the Whole is Jupiter.

---

For the **A** reasons mentioned above, Jupiter himself—though the oldest of the other gods whom he leads—goes first to contemplate the intelligible world. The other gods, spirits <note>original: "daemones"</note>, and souls who are able to see these things follow him. That divine world shines out to them from a certain hidden and high place; rising from the heights, it illuminates all the divinities, filling each with light. Then, it rouses the **B** lower souls toward it, who then turn back toward it, unable to look directly as if at the Sun. Some perceive it clearly, raised up by it and easily enduring its gaze; others are troubled, however far they are distant from its nature. While all who are able see it individually, they all look up at it and what belongs to it. Yet, no one brings back exactly the same vision; <margin>and this each one...</margin> but while they gaze attentively, one sees the shining fountain and nature of **C** Justice itself; <margin>just as men [possess]...</margin> another gazes abundantly upon Temperance—not the kind that humans possess when they have it. For our temperance only imitates that one in a faint way. That divine Temperance, diffusing itself through everything and around all its greatness, is discerned last, and only by those who have already seen many clear visions. Thus, the gods see both individually and all together; and the souls who see all things there also see, and from all those things they **D** become such that they themselves contain everything from beginning to end. They dwell there, and as much as there is within them that belongs to that place dwells there as well, whenever they are not at all separated from it. These things, then, Jupiter himself sees, and whoever among us loves these things along with Jupiter.

<column-break/>

<summary>Plotinus argues that in the divine realm, Being and Beauty are identical, and describes a Platonic procession where Jupiter (the World Soul) leads other souls to contemplate the Intelligible Ideas like Justice and Temperance.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Jupiter, Plato, Beauty, Essence, Contemplation, Soul of the World, Intellect, Justice, Temperance, Forms, Enneads</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the translation of Marsilio Ficino’s Latin version of Plotinus’s Ennead V, Book 8 (On Intellectual Beauty). The previous page discussed how celestial souls follow Jupiter (the World Soul) to contemplate the Intelligible Realm. This page describes the transformative nature of that contemplation, where the observer and the observed become one.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEAD V.

<margin>A</margin> ...happily contemplates, and contemplates the final universal beauty of all things shining forth from everything, and whatever is a participant in that beauty. For all things there are radiant, and they illuminate those spectators with splendor, so that they themselves also <margin>B</margin> become entirely beautiful: just as often happens to those who climb very high mountains, where the earth has a golden <note>original: "flavum" — literally yellow or golden-blonde, here referring to a divine radiance</note> color: for they are immediately stained by that color, becoming like the land to which they have ascended. But in the divine world, that flourishing color is beauty itself, or rather, whatever is there is entirely color and beauty to the core. <margin>C</margin> For beauty does not exist there as something else flourishing merely on the surface: but among those who do not look up at the whole, only that which glitters on the surface is judged and named beauty. But those who are entirely filled as if drenched with pure nectar, when beauty has poured itself through the whole soul, do not merely become spectators. For here <margin>D</margin> the spectator is on the outside, and there the spectacle is likewise outside: but he who perceives keenly has the thing perceived within himself. And yet, even having it, he often does not know he has it: for he who looks upon it as something external, looks upon it as something visible, and because he has decided to see it this way. But whatever someone contemplates as something to be watched, he sees on the outside. But it is worthwhile to transfer the divine spectacle into oneself and to look upon it as entirely one, and to behold it as if it were one’s very self: just as if someone were possessed by a God, whether Apollo or a Muse, he might now bring it about within himself, if indeed he were able to behold the God within himself.

### Three stages in divine contemplation, and three preparations for it. Chapter XI.

*One who is to enjoy God must first conform himself through a common notion and faith in God into a certain divine likeness: then strive toward God with the whole intention of thought: thirdly, love God alone with a whole burning will. To him who is thus affected, God flows in, appearing like a light present everywhere. Then indeed the soul, occupied by God, as long as it is not yet fully joined to God, feels itself inspired from above and filled. But when it is more closely joined, it looks up at God himself as the one inspiring, and now considers by what means He flows in. Finally, when it is inwardly united to God, it no longer speaks of "occupied" or "occupying" and considers it from that condition: but rather by a simple act contemplates something as one. Nor does it properly contemplate, or hear, or know by similar thought: rather, through a certain universal, intimate, and hidden sense, it enjoys itself and God together as one, and then finally realizes that it is at its very best. This consciousness of self is not a separate perception, but is almost the same as this very optimal health.*

IF, HOWEVER, one of us is unable to see himself, having been entirely seized by that God, let him bring forth into view a vision or spectacle; he brings forth himself indeed, and sees an image of himself that has been made more beautiful. But letting go of the image, however beautiful, and conspiring together into one, and separating nothing further, he exists as one together with all things along with that God, who flows in silently and quietly: furthermore, he is with Him as much as he can and wills. But if he should return to being "two," and meanwhile be pure, he subsequently dwells next to Him, so that he can be present again in that manner whenever he turns back to Him. In that very conversion, he reports this gain: namely, when he first approaches it, he feels himself as long as he is "other": but when he has penetrated to the innermost parts, he possesses the whole, and having left sense behind, fearing lest he become "other," he exists there as one: and if he desires to discern anything as "other," he is outside.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the wealth being seen; over all is a whole beauty, or that which shares in beauty there. For all things there are radiant, and they become full <margin>B</margin> so as to become beautiful themselves, just as often people ascending high places, where the earth has a golden color, <margin>C</margin> are filled with that hue, having become like the ground upon which they stand. But there, the blooming color is beauty. Or rather, every color is beauty from the depths. For beauty is not something else flourishing on the surface: but to those who do not see the whole, <margin>D</margin> only the outward appearance is named. But to those who are as if made drunk and filled with nectar, as beauty has gone through the whole soul, <gloss>*</gloss> they do not merely become spectators; for the thing being seen is no longer outside, but the one who sees keenly has the thing seen in himself, and having it, he often does not know he has it, and looks at it as something outside because he sees it as something visible. And he wishes to see it thus. But whatever someone sees as a spectacle, he sees outside. But it is necessary to transfer it into oneself, and to see it as one, and to see oneself, as if one were possessed by a God, seized by Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> or by some Muse, making the vision of the God in himself, if he had the power to see the God in himself.

IF ANY of us, being unable to see himself, being seized by that God, brings the vision into his sight, he brings himself, and sees his own image made beautiful. But letting go of the image, though it be beautiful, he comes into himself, and no longer being divided, he is one with all things together with that God, who is present without sound, and is still with him as much as he is able and willing. But if he should turn back into being two, if he is pure, he is next to Him, so that he may be present <gloss>*</gloss> in that way again, if he should turn back to himself. And in this turning, he has this gain: at first, he feels himself as long as he is "other": but running into the interior, he has the whole, and leaving sense behind, in fear of being "other," he is there, and desiring to see as something "other," he is outside.

# BOOK EIGHT.

...he makes it his own. But it is necessary for the soul, when contemplating, to remain in <margin>A</margin> that form, and thereafter to seek to know it—as if asking what kind of thing it is and into what it gives itself. Having thus learned, and trusting in it as a now-blessed thing, the soul should enter within, or rather give itself to the interior, and rejoice in seeing it, now becoming a spectacle for another who beholds it. <note>Plotinus describes a mystical state where the person looking and the thing seen become one; the soul becomes the very "beauty" it was seeking.</note> Such a one comes from that place shining with divine thoughts. <margin>B</margin> How then shall anyone be in beauty without seeing it? If he sees it as something "other," he is not yet in beauty. But by becoming it, he is most truly in beauty. If, therefore, vision is of something external, there ought not to be "vision" there—or if there is, it must be identical with the thing seen. This state is like a self-consciousness or a shared sensing of oneself, which is cautious lest, by wanting to perceive too much as a separate sensation, it should depart from itself. <margin>C</margin> We must not overlook the fact that the sensations of evils carry greater "strikes" <note>original: "pulsationes" — meaning a physical or sensory impact</note>, while the cognitions of good things are quieter, for they are mixed with the strike. Disease <margin>C</margin> strikes and excites more vehemently; but health, dwelling quietly with us, provides a clearer knowledge of itself. Truly, it sits silently and tranquil as something familiar to us; it breathes together as one. But disease has nothing domestic about it; it is entirely alien. <margin>D</margin> For this reason, it falls upon us more manifest because it meets us as something greatly different. Those things, however, which are ours and which are ourselves, are within us even without a manifest sensation. Being in this state, we are most known to ourselves of all things: because we have made the knowledge of ourselves and our very selves into one. Therefore, in the divine world, when we use our minds to know in the highest degree, we seem in a way to be "ignorant," because we are waiting for the "passion" of the sense <note>That is, we are used to "knowledge" feeling like a sharp external impact; divine knowledge is so natural it feels like silence.</note>, which certainly says it has seen nothing. For it did not see; nor can the sense ever see such things.

<column-break/>

...puts himself outside. But it is necessary for the soul, <margin>A</margin> about to perceive a divinity of this kind, to hold a certain form <note>term: "form" (Latin: figura) — here meaning an internal disposition or spiritual shape that mirrors the divine</note> of it, and so to persevere while it strives to know it clearly. Thus, recognizing what kind of thing it is entering, and being certain that it enters a most blessed state, it should finally immerse itself entirely, until it passes from being a spectator to being the very specimen of that which it has beheld—shining forth from there, overflowing with divine notions. <margin>B</margin> But how can anyone be in beauty itself unless he sees it? Certainly, if he sees it as something "other," he will not yet be in beauty; but if he has been made into beauty itself, he will be in beauty in the highest degree. If, therefore, vision is directed toward an external thing, it is not expedient for "vision" to be there—or if it is, it must be one and the same as that which is seen. This is like a certain conscience of oneself; a consensus of one being careful lest, by wishing to feel more intensely, he should depart from himself. We must not hide the fact that the senses of evils <margin>C</margin> have greater "pulsations," but cognitions have smaller ones, as they are shaken out by the force of those pulsations. For disease pulsates and excites more vehemently; but health, dwelling more quietly with us, exhibits a plainer notice of itself, sitting silently and tranquil as something familiar to us; it conspires into one. But disease has nothing domestic; it is utterly alien, and therefore it happens more manifestly because it meets us as something most diverse. Those things which are ours, and those things <margin>D</margin> which are ourselves, are in us even without a manifest sense. In this way, we are the most known of all things to ourselves, since we have made the knowledge of ourselves and our very selves one. Therefore, in the divine world, when we use our minds to know most fully, we seem in a some way to be "ignorant," because we lack the "passion" of the sense; which sense truly says it has seen nothing: for it did not see, nor can it ever see such things.

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK V.

...brothers remaining with the father. But here, one might not say in vain that he has come from the father: for there is another world proceeding from him, which has been made beautiful, just like an image of Beauty itself. For it would be a violation of divine law <note>original: "nefas"</note> for an image of Beauty itself and of true Being not to be beautiful. It therefore imitates its archetype in every way. Indeed, it possesses life and the gift of essence as a kind of imitation; it possesses beauty insofar as it proceeds from there; it also possesses eternal existence as an image of that eternity. Otherwise, how could it at one time display his image and at another time not? For an image of this kind was not made by human craft. Every image that exists by nature lasts as long as its archetype remains. <margin>B</margin> For this reason, those do not perceive correctly who believe this world will perish while the divine remains, or who think the world was born in such a way that its creator at some point "took counsel" on the fabrication of the world. These people neither wish to understand, nor do they know, what the nature of such a creation is: that as long as that divine world shines, this world flashes forth from it, and will never fail; rather, since that world exists, the rest exists as well. That world was always, and will be. For our part, we may meanwhile use these names <note>referring to temporal terms like "always" or "will be"</note> because we are compelled by the necessity of signifying something. <margin>C</margin>

->*The Divine Intellect, who is also called Saturn, castrates Uranus <note>original: "Cælium"</note>, that is, the Good itself. Chapter XIII.*<-

*For the Intellect divides the uniform gift of the father into many forms within itself; but it remains in itself without motion, and is separated from any commerce with the body. For it granted the worldly distribution, motions, and generations to Jupiter—that is, to the Soul of the world—whose generative nature is called Venus. The beauty of the corporeal world is a kind of shadow compared to the beauty of the incorporeal world itself. There, again, the beauty of the worldly soul is a kind of image compared to the wondrous beauty of the first intelligence. This, finally, is the splendor of the first light overflowing outward.*

<margin>A</margin> **GOD**, therefore, that Saturn who is fabled to be "bound" <note>In myth, Saturn/Kronos was bound in chains by Jupiter; Plotinus interprets this as the Intellect being "bound" or fixed in its own unchanging perfection.</note>, is so described because he perseveres within himself always in the same state. He is also said to have granted the empire of this world to his son Jupiter; for it was not fitting for him, in dismissing that empire, to pursue a younger and later sovereignty, since he already embraces the fullness of all beautiful things. Saturn, I say, having set these aside, established his own father Uranus <note>original: "Cælium"</note> within himself, and raised himself up to that height. He established, in turn, those things which follow after, having already taken their beginning from his son who came after him. Thus he holds the middle ground between both, <margin>B</margin> partly because he separates himself from the Father by a certain "otherness," and partly because he abstains from lower things by rising into the sublime; while he is fabled to be held by bonds from lower cares, he certainly holds the middle rank between a Father who is greater and a son who is lesser. But because Uranus, the progenitor of Saturn and Jupiter, is far too great to be called "beauty," for this reason Saturn—that is, the Intellect—<margin>C</margin> is the first to stand forth as beautiful, even though the Soul is also beautiful. Yet Intellect is more beautiful than the Soul, because the Soul is a mere trace of it; by this very fact, the Soul is naturally beautiful, but it is even more beautiful when it gazes upon the Intellect. If the Soul of the universe, therefore (to use words that are perhaps more familiar), is itself the beautiful Venus, what then is the Intellect? For if the Soul and Venus have this beauty from themselves, how great must the Intellect be? But if they have it from another, from whom primarily does the Soul have its beauty, both that which comes to it from without and that which is naturally implanted in its essence? Indeed, whenever we ourselves are beautiful,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...and the brothers who remained with the father. He says it is not in vain to say that he came from the father. For there is indeed another world that has become beautiful, as an image of beauty. For it is not lawful for an image of the beautiful not to be beautiful, nor for it to lack essence. It imitates the archetype in every way. For it has life, and it has the quality of essence as an imitation, and it has beauty as coming from there. It also has its "always" as an image; otherwise, at one time it would have the image, and at another <margin>B</margin> not. This image is not made by art; every image exists by nature as long as the archetype remains. Therefore, those who destroy it are not correct, while the Intelligible remains, and they think of its creation as if the maker at some time decided to make it. For they do not wish to understand what kind of making this is, nor do they know that as much as that world shines out, the other things shine out from it; but because that exists, these things also exist. It always was and will be, but we must use these names out of the necessity <margin>C</margin> of signifying something.

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, the god who is bound in the same state, and who conceded to his son to rule over these things of the universe. For it was not fitting for him <margin><unclear>*</unclear></margin> in any way, having left the rule there, to follow a rule younger and later than himself, since he has a fullness <note>original: "κόρον" (koron) - a pun on "fullness/satiety" and "son/youth"</note> of beautiful things. Having left these, he established his father in himself. And reaching up to what is above, he also established, on the other hand, the things beginning from his son to be after him. So that he becomes the middle of both, by the "otherness" of the cut from above, <margin>B</margin> and by the bond that holds him from the things after him towards the bottom, being between a better father and a lesser son. But since his father is greater than can be called beauty, he himself remained the first beautiful one. Even though the soul is also beautiful. But he is more beautiful than her, for she is a trace of him, and she is beautiful by nature, <margin>C</margin> but more beautiful when she looks there. If then the soul of the universe—so that we may speak in a more familiar way—is itself the beautiful Venus, what is that Intellect? For if she has beauty from herself, how great would that be? But if from another, from whom does the soul have both its acquired and its natural beauty?

Because we have become masters of our own rights <note>original: "nostri iuris facti simus"</note>, we are also beautiful; but we are ugly when we are cast down into an inferior nature. Because we have become masters of ourselves, we are beautiful; but we are ugly when we are plunged into an inferior nature. Yet when we recognize ourselves, we are beautiful; but we are ugly when we are ignorant. There, then, beauty shines; from there, beauty flashes forth. But are these things sufficient so far to clearly understand the divine world? Or rather, must we travel another path again toward that same place in this way?

->ON the intellect, and the ideas, and being.<-
->On the intellect and ideas and being.<-

> *The mind that contemplates divine things is already in its homeland. Active and pleasure-seeking men are exiles; but active men return to their homeland more easily than those devoted to pleasure.* <br/> *Chapter I.*

---

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter Π (Pi) set in a square frame containing a detailed landscape with a river, bridge, and classical-style buildings.</image-desc>
SINCE all men from the beginning of their birth use the senses before the intellect <note>original: "noû"</note>, and of necessity they first encounter things perceived by the senses, some indeed, remaining here, pass their lives thinking these things are the first and the last; and taking what is painful among them to be evil, and what is pleasant to be good, they consider this to be enough. Thus they spend their lives pursuing the one and avoiding the other. And those among them who claim a degree of reason for themselves have established this as wisdom—just like heavy birds who, having taken much from the earth and being weighed down, are unable to fly high, even though they received wings from nature. Others, however, are raised up a little from the things below, moved by a better part of the soul. But being unable to see the world above, as they have no other place to stand, they are carried back down—along with the name of virtue—to actions and the choice of things below, from which they first attempted to raise themselves. But there is a third kind of divine men, who, by a greater power and sharpness of sight, have seen the splendor above with a keen vision <note>original: "oxyderkias"</note>. They are raised up there as if above the clouds and the mist of this world, and they remain there, looking down on everything here, delighted by that place, which is true and their proper home, just like a man who has arrived in a well-governed homeland after a long wandering.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial letter Q set in a square frame containing a landscape with trees and a building in the background. The tail of the Q is stylistically integrated into the lower border of the image.</image-desc>
SINCE all men, as soon as they are born, use the senses before the mind, and necessarily first encounter things belonging to the senses and apply their affection to them, some indeed, continuing in that same state, pass their lives this way: thinking these are both the first and the last things, and judging that which is troublesome in them to be evil, but that which is <margin>B</margin> pleasant to be good. And so they finally think they have done enough if they pursue pleasant things throughout their whole life and reject the opposite. Consequently, those among them who claim some degree of reason for themselves judge this to be wisdom. They are affected in the same way as heavy birds: who, after they have snatched many things from the earth and are weighed down by that weight, are unable to fly through the heights beyond, even though they received wings from nature. Others, however, are raised up somewhat from <margin>C</margin> lower things; their own better nature of the soul calls them back from pleasure to what is honorable. But because they are unable to gaze upon the world above, and therefore have nothing else upon which they may rest, they are carried away—along with the very name of virtue—toward actions and the choices of inferior things, from which they first attempted to raise themselves. Finally, there is a third kind of men, which is divine: in this class are those who, relying on both a greater power and a sharpness of sight, look keenly toward the light above. Having perceived it, they raise themselves completely toward it, <margin>D</margin> transcending the lower mists and darkness. And having transcended them, they remain there, utterly despising all these earthly things, and are delighted by the higher region as their true and proper home, no differently than a traveler restored to his lawful homeland after long wanderings.

<summary>Plotinus introduces Ennead V, Book 9 by categorizing humanity into three spiritual types based on whether they are ruled by the senses, worldly virtue, or divine intellect. He uses the metaphor of "heavy birds" to describe those who possess the potential for flight (the soul's wings) but are weighed down by material desires.</summary>

<margin>A</margin>...brothers remaining with their father. But here, he would not have said in vain that he came from the father: for there is another world from him, which was made beautiful, like an image of the Beautiful itself. For it is not right that an image of the Beautiful itself and of Essence should not be beautiful; therefore, it imitates the archetype in every way. For it has life and a gift of essence as a kind of imitation; it also has beauty insofar as it proceeds from there; it also has the quality of existing forever, as 
<margin>B</margin>an image of that eternity. Otherwise, how could it at one time display an image of that and at another time not? For an image of this kind was not made by human art. Every image consisting of nature exists as long as the archetype remains. For this reason, those who think this world will perish while the divine remains do not judge rightly, and they believe it was created in such a way as if its author at some time deliberated on the construction of the world. 
<margin>C</margin>These people certainly neither wish to understand nor do they know what the manner of this kind of influence is: that as far as that divine world shines, so far does this world flash forth from there, and it will never fail, but exists as long as that one exists, and the rest exist besides. Moreover, that world always was, and will be. Meanwhile, we may use these names, being compelled by the desire to signify something.

### The Divine Intellect, who is also named Saturn, castrates Coelus <note>Uranus</note>, that is, the Good itself. Chapter XIII.

->*For he divides within himself the uniform gift of the father into many forms; yet he remains in himself without motion, and separated from the commerce*<-
->*of the body: for he granted the worldly administration of motion and generations to Jupiter, that is, the World Soul, whose*<-
->*generative nature is called Venus. The beauty of the corporeal world is a certain shadow compared to the beauty*<-
->*of the incorporeal world itself. There again, the beauty of the worldly soul is a certain image compared to the marvelous beauty*<-
->*of the first intelligence. This, finally, is the splendor of the first light overflowing outward.*<-

<margin>A</margin>Therefore, that god is Saturn, who is imagined as being bound, because he remains always in the same state within himself. He is also said to have granted the empire of this world to his son Jupiter; for it was not fitting for him, in letting go of that empire, to pursue a younger and later princedom, since he embraces the fullness of all beautiful things. Saturn, I say, having set these aside, established his father Coelus <note>original: "Cælium"</note> within himself, and raised himself up even to that height. 
<margin>B</margin>Again, he established the things that follow after from the son, having now found a beginning after himself. Thus he holds a middle place between both, partly because he cuts away with a certain paternal "otherness," and partly because he abstains from lower things, rising into the sublime, while he is imagined to be held by bonds from lower care, certainly obtaining the middle grade between the greater father and the lesser son. 
<margin>C</margin>But since Coelus, the progenitor of Saturn and Jupiter, is much greater than can be called "beauty," for that reason Saturn—that is, the Intellect—is the first to exist as beautiful, although the soul is also beautiful. Yet he is more beautiful than her, because she is a trace of him, and by this very fact she exists naturally beautiful, but more beautiful when she looks toward him. If, therefore, the soul of the universe (to use more familiar words at times) and Venus herself is beautiful, what sort of thing is that Intellect? For if the soul and Venus have this from themselves, how great is he? But if from another, from whom especially does the soul have beauty, both that which comes to her and that which is naturally implanted in her essence? Truly, as often as we are beautiful,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...and the brothers who remained there with the father. <note>original: "καὶ οἱ μείναντες αὐτοῦ τῷ πατρὶ ἀδελφοὶ"</note> But he says he did not come here from the father in vain, for here indeed is another world born beautiful, as an image to the Beautiful. <note>original: "εἰκόνα καλῷ"</note> For it is not lawful that an image of the Beautiful should not be beautiful, neither in beauty nor in essence. It imitates the archetype in every way. For it also has life, and that of essence, as an imitation. And it has beauty as if from there. And it has the "always" as an image. Or will it at one time have an image, and at another not? This would be an image made by art. But every image by nature exists as long as the archetype remains. Therefore, those who say it perishes while the intelligible remains are not correct. Some say it was created as if the maker at some time deliberated to make it. For what the manner of such making is, they have not wished to inquire. Or they will know that as much as that one shines, the others also shine: but it is from there, or it is the same things. For we must use these names, the necessity being the desire to signify.

<margin>A</margin>The god, therefore, who is bound to remain in the same way, <note>Saturn/Kronos</note> and who yielded to his son to rule over the universe. For it was not necessary for him to change, having left the principles there, to share in a younger and later one. Having a fullness <note>original: "κόρον," a pun on Kronos/Saturn</note> of beautiful things. Having left these, he established his father in himself, and reached toward the eternal. He established again the things that are later, having received them from the son, to be after him. So that he becomes between both,
<margin>B</margin>by the first cutting of the nature of the eternal, and by holding up the things after him toward the lower bond, being in the middle of a better father and a lesser son. But since the father is greater to him than according to beauty, thus he himself first remained beautiful. And the soul also being beautiful, but the beauty of this one is still more beautiful, for it is a trace 
<margin>C</margin>of him. And this is: beautiful by nature, but more beautiful when she looks there. If then the soul of the universe—that we may speak more familiarly—is herself Venus and beautiful, what is that one? For if it is from herself, how great would that be? But if from another, how and from what does the soul have both the derived and the innate beauty in her essence?

Since it is also true that when we are beautiful, we are so by being our own; but we are ugly when we transition into another nature <note>original: "physis"</note>. ## THE FIFTH ENNEAD,
### BOOK IX.

->CONCERNING <gloss>1</gloss> the Intellect, the Ideas, and Being.<-
->Concerning the intellect & ideas & being.<-

> *The soul that contemplates divine things is already in its homeland. Men of action and those of pleasure are exiles: but the active return home more easily than the pleasure-seekers.*

->Chapter I.<-

<margin>A</margin> <image-desc>Decorative drop cap P (originally Pi) featuring a figure sitting beneath a tree in a pastoral landscape.</image-desc> ALL men, from the moment they are born, use their senses before their intellect <note>original: "nous"</note>. Since they necessarily encounter and apply themselves to sensible things first, some remain there and live their lives thinking these are the first and final things. Regarding the pain and pleasure found in them, they suppose that the former is evil and the latter is good, and they believe this is sufficient. They pass their lives chasing the one and managing the other. Those among them who claim to possess reason consider this to be wisdom. They are like heavy birds: having taken many things from the earth and being weighed down, they are unable to fly high, even though they received wings from nature. Others are raised up slightly from <margin>B</margin> lower things, as the better nature of their soul calls them away from pleasure toward what is honorable. Yet, because they are unable to look upon what is above, and having no other place where they may rest, they are carried back—along with the name of virtue—to the actions and choices of lower things, from which they first attempted to lift themselves. But there is a third kind of divine men, who, by a greater power and sharpness of sight, see the radiance above with a keen vision. They are lifted up there, as if above the clouds <margin>C</margin> and the mist of this world, and they remain there. They look down upon all things here with contempt, delighted by the higher region as by a true and familiar home, just like a man who, after long wandering, is finally restored to his own law-abiding fatherland.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <image-desc>Decorative drop cap B (originally Q) featuring two figures, likely philosophers or teachers, in conversation within an outdoor setting with buildings in the background.</image-desc> BECAUSE all men, immediately upon being born, use sense before intellect, and necessarily first encounter things that pertain to the senses and apply their affection to them, some indeed persist in that same habit and live their lives in this way. They think these things are both the first and the last; they judge what is troublesome in them to be evil and what is <margin>B</margin> pleasant to be good. And so they finally think enough has been done for themselves if they pursue pleasant things through their whole life and reject the opposites. Accordingly, whoever among them claims some share of reason for themselves judges this to be wisdom. They are affected exactly like heavy birds, which, when they have seized many things from the earth by whose weight they are burdened, cannot fly further through the heights, although they have received wings from nature. Others truly are elevated somewhat from <margin>C</margin> inferior things, whom the better nature of the soul itself calls back from pleasure to what is honest. But since they cannot gaze upon the supernal, and therefore have nothing else where they may rest, they are carried over—along with the very name of virtue—to actions and the choice of inferior things, from which they were attempting to raise themselves from the beginning. Finally, there is a third kind of divine men, in which are those who, relying on both greater power and clear-sightedness of the eyes, look sharply up at the supernal light. To that <margin>D</margin> perceived light they raise themselves entirely, transcending the lower clouds and darkness; and when they have transcended, they remain there, utterly despising all these lower things. They are delighted by the supernal region as if it were their true and own home, no differently than a traveler restored at last to his legitimate fatherland after long wanderings.

PLOTINUS: ENNEADS, BOOK V.

> *That which is primarily beautiful is beautiful through itself, in its entirety, and forever. ->Chapter II.<-*
> 
> *Therefore, beauty is not primary in the body. For the body is not beautiful through its whole self, but through its form, and thus it is changeable; nor is beauty primary in the soul. For the soul becomes beautiful through a changeable participation in the intellect. Rather, primary beauty is in the intellect—or better, primary beauty is a certain radiance and figure of the Good. Plotinus often touches upon the mysteries of the Apostles John and Paul; however, he seems not so much to have been moved by this mystery of the Trinity as to have scrutinized it and imitated it to the best of his ability.* <note>The translator, likely Marsilio Ficino, is drawing parallels between Plotinus's Neoplatonic hierarchy (The One, Intellect, Soul) and the Christian Trinity.</note>

<margin>A</margin>WHAT then is this region? And in what way can someone ascend to it? Surely he can ascend there who is drawn by nature especially to love beauty, and who is born a true philosopher. Such a man, like a lover, is distressed by a kind of labor of "giving birth" <note>original: "partus labore" / "ὠδίνων"; a Platonic metaphor for the soul's desire to create or reach truth</note> concerning beauty itself; yet he is not content with the beauty of the body, but flees from it toward the beauty of the soul—namely, virtues, sciences, duties, and laws. And from there he <margin>B</margin> again ascends to the cause of those beautiful things which are in the soul: and if anything still higher exists, he proceeds until he finally reaches the First, which is beautiful by itself. Indeed, reaching this, he ceases to be distressed, but certainly not before then. But in what way will he ascend there, and from where will such a faculty be granted? And what reason specifically will lead this love, as if by the hand, to the end? Perhaps such a reason is that the beauty instilled in bodies is external to the bodies themselves. For these forms of bodies are in them <margin>C</margin> as if in matter. The subject is therefore changed, and from beautiful it becomes ugly; from this, reason concludes that the body is beautiful only through a certain participation. What then is it that makes the body beautiful? In one way, the presence of beauty makes it beautiful; in another way, the soul which fashioned it and, by so fashioning it, applied such a form to the body. What then? Is the soul by its very nature beauty itself? Not at all: otherwise one soul would not be wise and beautiful, while another <margin>D</margin> is foolish and ugly. Therefore, beauty comes to the soul through wisdom. But who is it primarily who grants wisdom to the soul? This is necessarily the Intellect <note>original: "intellectus" / "νοῦς"; the divine Mind containing the Ideas</note>: an Intellect, I say, which is not sometimes an intellect and sometimes devoid of intelligence, but rather the true Intellect, which for this reason is beautiful of itself. But should we rest here as if at the first stage? Or rather, must we proceed even above the mind? Indeed, the mind itself meets us as we proceed upward before the very first principle of all, placed as if in the vestibule of the Good itself, announcing and signifying all things within itself, like a certain figure of the Good distributed into a multitude, while the Good itself consists entirely in unity.

<column-break/>

WHAT then is this place? And how might someone arrive at it? One might arrive who is a lover, and truly has the disposition of a philosopher, always laboring with the "birth-pangs" of love for the beautiful, not enduring the beauty in the body, but as if fleeing from there to the beauties of the Soul—virtues and knowledge, and practices and laws. Again he ascends to the cause of the beauties in the Soul, and again from that to what is above it, until he comes to that which is First, which is beautiful of itself. Having arrived there, he ceases his labor. We must consider how he will perceive it, and from where his power comes, and what discourse will guide this love? Perhaps this: this beauty upon bodies is something brought into the bodies. For these are shapes of bodies, as if upon matter. But the substrate changes, and from beautiful becomes ugly. Reason therefore says the body participates in beauty. What then is it that made the body beautiful? In one sense, the presence of beauty, but in another, the Soul. For the Soul fashioned it and placed such a shape upon it. What then? Is the Soul beautiful from itself? Or not? Or would it be that one soul is wise and beautiful, but another foolish and ugly. Therefore beauty in the Soul comes by wisdom <note>original: "phronēsis"</note>, and is it not the one who gives wisdom to the soul, the Intellect <note>original: "nous"</note>, that is beautiful? Is the Intellect sometimes intellect and sometimes thoughtless? No, it is true Intellect; therefore it is beautiful of itself. And before staying here as if at the first, must one go even beyond? The Intellect stands before the primary Soul as if before us, just as in the vestibule of the Good, reporting what is in it. It is like a type or image of that Good, appearing in a multitude while the Good remains entirely in unity.

> *If the soul were by its own nature intellectual, then all souls would be equally intellectual: since they are not so, it is right that the soul, even the first soul, becomes intellectual through a certain participation in a higher intellect.*

<margin>A</margin> WE must indeed consider this nature of the mind, which reason indicates to be true being and true essence, asserting first of all—though proceeding by another path—that it is necessary for there to be such an essence and mind. But perhaps it may seem ridiculous to investigate whether Intellect exists in the order of things. Perhaps also some...

WE MUST examine this nature, which our discourse claims to be true and real essence, persuading those who are being confirmed by going another way, that it is necessary for such a thing to exist. Perhaps indeed it is ridiculous to seek if Intellect is among the things that exist, but perhaps...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the hierarchy of existence. BOOK NINE.
Aa 3

...and they might dispute about this, or rather, they might be ignorant of what we mean: that there is something inseparable from existence, and yet distinct, which constitutes the very nature of the **Forms** <note>original: "εἰδῶν" / "specierum"; in Neoplatonism, these are the perfect, eternal blueprints of all things</note>. This is the subject we have set out to discuss. We see, then, that all things said to exist are composite, and none of them is simple. This applies both to the things produced by art and those constituted by nature. For man-made objects consist of bronze, or wood, or stone; and yet these materials are not brought to completion until each specific art—one producing a statue, another a couch, and another a house—works upon them by imposing the **Form** that it possesses within itself. Furthermore, even those things constituted by nature—especially those called "highly composite" or "mixtures"—can be analyzed back into the Form implanted in all composite things. For example, we analyze a human being into soul and body, and the body into the four elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note>. When you find that each of these is composed of **Matter** and that which gives it shape—for the matter of the elements is formless in itself—you will then ask from where the Form of matter comes. You will also inquire about the soul: is it already a simple thing, or is there something within it acting as matter and something else acting as form? Namely, the **Intellect** <note>original: "νοῦς" / "intellectus"</note> that resides within it. One part of the soul is like the shape within the bronze; the other is like the craftsman who created the shape in the bronze. If one transfers these same observations to the entire universe, they will eventually ascend to the Intellect, recognizing it as the true maker and creator of the whole. One will then say that the underlying Matter, upon receiving Forms, became fire, water, air, and earth; and that these Forms proceed from another source—which is the Soul. The Soul, in turn, provides the Form to the four members of the universe. Moreover, the Intellect itself supplies the Soul with its **rational principles** <note>original: "λόγων" / "rationes"; the formative "blueprints" or logical structures of reality</note>, just as the arts themselves provide the souls of craftsmen with the principles for their work. Thus, one aspect of the Intellect is like the Form of the soul—the Intellect according to its shape—while the other is that which provides the shape, much like the sculptor who possesses all the qualities he bestows upon the statue. And what the Intellect gives to the Soul is very close to the truth, whereas what the body receives are merely images and imitations.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...they might dispute regarding this, and rather about the thing itself: whether the Intellect is such as we have described it. And whether there is some "Separate Intellect" that constitutes true being, and in which the nature of the Forms resides—which is the matter we have decided to dispute at present. Therefore, we perceive that all things said to exist are composite, and none of them is simple.

<margin>B</margin> ...before each art acts—this one producing a statue, that one a couch, and another a house. It acts, I say, by applying its own Form to the matter.

<margin>C</margin> ...for the matter of the elements is in itself formless. You will ask from where the Form of matter originates, and you will also ask concerning the soul, whether it is already simple, or if there is rather something in it that acts as matter and something else as form: specifically the Intellect which is in it.

<margin>D</margin> ...affirming that the underlying matter, receiving Forms from there, turned out to be partly fire, and partly water, air, or earth. These Forms certainly proceed from another source, which is the Soul. And the Soul, in turn, hands down the Form to the four members of the universe.

<margin>E</margin> ...just as the arts themselves show the rational principles to the souls of the craftsmen for the purpose of acting. Accordingly, one Intellect is like the Form of the soul, while the other provides the Form to the soul, just as the craftsman provides the Form to the statue. In this Intellect are present all the things which it bestows. And those things which it bestows upon the soul are closest to the truth; but those which the body receives are already mere images and certain imitations.

> *Above the souls, which proceed from potentiality into the act of understanding, and undergo some passion, and have commerce with the inferior, is the Intellect itself—always understanding in act, free from passion, and separated from the companionship of the body. ->Chapter IV.<-*

> *Since changeability happens to things because of matter, surely if there were not certain things separated from matter, the consequent order and perpetual succession of similar things could not be preserved in the transmutation of things.*

<margin>A</margin> BUT why, after you have reached as far as the Soul, can you not rest in it as the primary principle, but are forced to proceed further? Because, first of all, the Intellect itself is something else and something better than the Soul. And that which is better exists prior by nature. For the Soul does not generate the Intellect when it has become perfected, as many people think. For if something exists in **potentiality** <note>having the capacity to become something, but not yet being it</note>, from where will it ever become **actualized** <note>the state of being fully realized or active</note>, unless there is some cause present to lead it into act? For if it happened by chance...

<summary>Plotinus argues that everything in the physical and spiritual world is a composite of matter and form, leading to the conclusion that a "Separate Intellect" must exist as the ultimate source of all structural principles (Forms). He explains that the Soul is moved from a state of potentiality to actual understanding by this higher Intellect, which is always fully realized and distinct from physical matter.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that the Soul cannot be the ultimate reality because it changes and learns. Plotinus is now transitioning from the Soul to the "Intellect" (Nous), which he argues is the realm of eternal, unchanging truth where the "thinker" and the "thought" are one and the same.</meta>

<header>PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.</header>

<margin>A</margin>...it might proceed from a certain state into an act <note>original: "actum" / "ἐνέργειαν"; in philosophy, "act" refers to something being fully realized or active, rather than just having the potential to exist</note>, it could happen that it might never progress into that act at all. For this reason, it is necessary that the first things consist in act; they are not lacking, but are perfect. Those things which are imperfect must be posterior to the perfect ones, being brought to completion by those that generated them—much like a father, by a certain right and law, brings to completion those things which he generated as imperfect from the beginning. Now, that which has been generated must first relate to its maker as if it were matter, and then afterwards receive its form. Accordingly, if <margin>B</margin> the soul admits any passion <note>original: "passionem" / "ἐμπαθές"; here meaning "affection" or "the capacity to be changed by outside forces"</note> within itself, there must necessarily exist something entirely removed from all passion. Otherwise, all things would slip away and decay over time. Therefore, there must be something higher than the soul. Furthermore, if the soul exists within the world, and there must also be something outside the world, then for this reason too it is necessary that something exists above the soul. For if that which is in the world is the same as that which is in body and matter, then nothing remains the same if only such a thing exists. Wherefore <margin>C</margin> man and the rest of the creatures would not exist forever. The "seed-like reasons" <note>original: "Seminariæ rationes" / "λόγοι"; the formative principles or "blueprints" that govern growth in the natural world</note> would neither be eternal nor remain the same. Therefore, one can understand from these many points we have discussed that the Mind <note>original: "mentem" / "νοῦν"</note> must exist above the soul.

->*The Intellect is perfect in its nature and always understands by itself, because it understands from itself—namely, by being turned toward itself. Again, it is such because by its very essence it is these very beings which it understands.*<-

### Chapter V.

*The perfect Intellect, being a perfect essence, has perfect beings as its objects. The matter of these beings is not found in the first principle of things, nor again in the world, where matter is the lowest point and form is not pure form. For since it exists in another, it depends on another. Therefore, there is a multitude of perfect beings within the Intellect as it understands itself; especially because every multitude of things outside of it proceeds from this internal intelligence. It does not create them nor accompany them, but they follow it, just as words follow a speaker or offspring follow a parent. The power of generating and of understanding, which are distinct in the soul, are the same in the Mind. By understanding, therefore, it generates—indeed, it does so by its very nature of existing—just as fire generates by heating, the sun by shining, and the soul by living. Finally, the reasons of things, which in the soul are destined to become changeable, are not safe from all mutation by themselves unless they are led back to the firm Ideas of the Intellect.*

# THE INTELLECT
<margin>A</margin> however, we must grasp (if we are to use its true name) not as an intellect in potentiality <note>something that *could* think but isn't currently</note>, nor as something progressing from a state of thoughtlessness into a mind. Otherwise, we would be forced to investigate yet another higher principle. Rather, it is proper to accept the Intellect as existing in perpetual act, which thus always exists as Intellect. If such an Intellect does not possess an "adventitious" <note>external or added-on</note> intelligence, then whatever it understands, it understands entirely from itself; and if it possesses anything, it <margin>B</margin> possesses it from itself. If it understands from itself and out of itself, it must truly be these very things which it understands. For if its essence were one thing, and the things it understands were another, then its essence would be void of intellectual power; it would no longer be in act, but only in potentiality. Therefore, it is not proper to separate one from the other, even though we are accustomed, led by our experience with worldly things, to separate them in our thoughts. <margin>C</margin> What then does it do, and what does it understand, so that we may posit that it *is* the things it understands? Clearly, since it is Intellect and Being, it understands and gives existence to beings in a true mode of existence: it is, therefore, those beings. For it will either understand them as existing elsewhere, or in itself as being itself. Elsewhere is impossible. For where would that be? It understands itself, therefore, and entirely within itself. For it does not understand these things as being in the objects of the senses (as many people think). For no primary thing is of the kind found in sensory objects. For what is in those objects is like a form in matter, a mere image of the being itself; a spec-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...it is possible for it not to come into act; so that the first things must be placed in act, and be without need, and be perfect. But the imperfect things are posterior to the perfect ones. They are brought to completion by those that generated them, just as fathers bring to completion that which they generated as imperfect in the beginning. And there is matter for the first maker; then again, it is modeled by a reflection. <margin>B</margin> But if there must be something subject to affection, there must also be that which is impassible <note>incapable of suffering or change</note>. Otherwise, all things are destroyed by time. There must be something before the Soul. And if the Soul is in the world, there must be something outside of the world. And in this way, there must be something before the Soul. For if that which is in the world is that which is in body and matter, nothing remains the same; so that man and all the eternal reasons would not be the same. And that <margin>C</margin> there must now be something before the soul, one might observe from these and many other arguments.

IT IS NECESSARY to receive the Mind, if we are to be true to the name, not as that which is in potentiality, nor that which has come into mind from thoughtlessness. For then we would again seek another before it. But we must take that which is in act and is always Mind. If not, from where does it have the power of thought? Since it has it from itself, then if it possesses anything, it has it from itself. And if it understands from and by itself, it is itself the things it understands. For if <margin>B</margin> its essence is one thing, and that which it understands is different from it, its essence will be without thought. And it would be in potentiality again, rather than in act. They must not be separated, then, neither one from the other. But it is our habit, from the things around us, to separate those things in our concepts. What then does it act upon, and what does it think, so that we may set those things down as being itself? <margin>C</margin> Or is it clear that being Mind, it truly thinks the things that are and gives them substance. Therefore, it is the things that are. For it will either think them elsewhere, or in itself as being itself. From elsewhere, then, is impossible. For where? For it is the beginning. Or are they in the objects of sense, as some think? For each primary thing is not the sensory object. For the form in them is truly an image upon matter, and...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Intellect (Mind) must exist above the Soul as a realm of pure activity and perfection, where the act of thinking and the objects of thought are identical. He asserts that if the Intellect were separate from the truths it contemplates, it would be imperfect and dependent on something else.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the "Intellect" (Nous), moving from the Soul's activity to the higher realm of pure thought. Plotinus is arguing that for the physical world to exist, there must be a prior, perfect "blueprint" or "Intellect" that contains all the forms of things. He is addressing the relationship between the craftsman (the Intellect) and the creation (the world).</meta>

<page-num>559</page-num>
<header>BOOK NINE.</header>

Everything that exists within another also depends upon another, is referred back to that other, and is an image of it. Furthermore, if it is necessary for the Intellect <note>original: "intellectum" / "νοῦν"; the higher realm of pure, eternal thought</note> to be the architect of this entire universe, then surely this architect does not look toward things that do not yet exist in order to create the world. Therefore, before the world existed, those things must have existed—not as mere figures impressed by others, but as the primary models, the first things, and the very essence of the mind.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Everything that lies in another also depends on another, is referred to that thing, and is its image. Moreover, if it is necessary that the Intellect be the craftsman of this universe, this craftsman certainly will not think of things that exist in that which does not yet exist, in order to make it. Therefore, before the world, those things must exist—not as figures impressed from elsewhere, but as certain primary patterns, first things, and the essence of the mind.

<margin>B</margin> If some were to say that the "seminal reasons" <note>original: "rationes seminales" / "λόγοι σπερματικοί"; the life-giving principles or "blueprints" that guide the growth and form of living things</note> are sufficient for this, they will undoubtedly be speaking of eternal reasons. And if they are eternal and far removed from all "passion" <note>capacity to be changed or affected</note>, they must exist in the Mind, and indeed in such a Mind that exists prior to habit, nature, and the soul. For these latter things exist in a certain state of potentiality and consist within the power of that Mind. Therefore, the Intellect is Being itself in the true mode of existing; it does not understand things that are elsewhere. For these things are neither before it nor after it. Rather, the Mind is like the first legislator—or rather, it is the law itself of "being."

<margin>C</margin> Therefore, it was rightly said: "to think and to be are the same thing." <note>original: "τὸ γὰρ αὐτὸ νοεῖν ἐστι καὶ εἶναι"; a famous fragment from the philosopher Parmenides, asserting that reality and thought are identical at the highest level</note> Likewise, the knowledge of things that are without matter is the same as the thing itself. Again, I have investigated myself as one of the things that "are"; the acts of recollection bear witness to this. For none of the things that truly "are" exist outside of the Mind, nor are they in a physical place. Instead, they remain forever firm within themselves; for this reason, they are judged to "be" in the true sense. Otherwise, if they were born and died, they would only possess a borrowed existence, and they would no longer be Being itself. Rather, it would be that "being" itself belongs to those things that are perceived by the senses, which exist only by a certain "participation" <note>the Platonic idea that physical things only "share in" or "copy" the reality of a higher Form</note> in what is called "being."

<margin>D</margin> This is because the underlying nature of matter receives its form from elsewhere—just as bronze receives its form from the art of the sculptor, and wood from the art of the carpenter—while the "art" enters into such materials by means of an image. But the art itself, meanwhile, remains outside the matter in that same state, and holds within itself the true statue and the true bed.

<margin>E</margin> Thus, this entire universe in the realm of bodies, being a participant only in images, clearly testifies that the "beings" themselves are different from the bodies. For those things are unchangeable, while these bodies are changed; those things stand firm within themselves, needing no place; for they are not extended in any size or magnitude, but have an intellectual substance that is self-sufficient. For the nature of bodies always requires some other protector to be preserved. But since the Intellect, by its wonderful nature, sustains and preserves those things which by their own nature fall away, it is rightly not forced to seek a place where it itself might be founded.

---

-> *Ideas in the intellect are properly certain powers of it, through which it is defined in one way or another.* <-
-> Chapter VI. <-

Since the faculty of understanding and generating is the same there, the Ideas there do not only behave like various notions, but also like many "seminal powers" in the soul. From one perspective they are called "models" (archetypes), and from another, they are the principles of things, being both "reasons" and "species" <note>the formal definitions or "types" of things</note> in both cases. Consequently, purely material qualities—such as heat, cold, and the like—cannot have a mutual union without confusion. For they either remain separate, or if they are mixed, one confuses the others, or all are confused by each other, so that something else results from the whole. Qualities that are less material, such as tastes, can be united, as in the previous case but with less confusion. Smells, as if they were still less material, are united in the same medium while remaining different, and one confuses the other somewhat less, though it still confuses it. Different voices are united even more in a medium, and are less confused, because they are less material. But the species <note>qualities or "looks"</note> of colors, even contrary ones, because they are immaterial, are united in the same point, and exist there most distinctly without any mutual confusion. From this it is concluded...

<summary>This page argues that the Intellect (Nous) is the eternal realm of true Being, containing the perfect "Forms" or "Ideas" that act as the blueprints for the physical world. Plotinus explains that while material qualities like heat and cold conflict when mixed, immaterial ideas and perceptions can coexist perfectly within the Mind.</summary>
