<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 559 regarding the nature of the Intellect (Nous). Having established that the Intellect must contain the primary models of all things, Plotinus now explores how these "Forms" can exist together simultaneously without becoming a jumbled mess, using analogies from biology and the arts.</meta>

<page-num>560</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.</header>

*the union of forms without confusion—that is, they are joined and yet distinct—exists in the soul through a certain immaterial power, and much more so in the mind which is even further separated from matter. For as the withdrawal from matter gradually increases, the union of the forms grows, as does their distinction; it follows that in the mind, they are most united and, at the same time, most distinct.*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> The Intellect <note>original: "intellectus" / "νοῦς"; the divine realm of pure thought</note> therefore becomes its very essence, and it holds all things in itself—not as if it were a physical place, but as if it were holding itself, being one with them. All things there exist together at once, but are nonetheless distinguished from one another. Just as the soul holds many different sciences <note>original: "scientias" / "ἐπιστήμας"; here meaning branches of knowledge or skills</note> at once, it holds nothing in a confused state; rather, each science performs its duty when the situation requires it, without dragging the others along with it. Every notion acts purely, free from the other internal notions. So, then, even more so, the <margin>B</margin> Intellect is all things at once, and yet not at once, because each thing there is its own distinct power. The whole Intellect contains all things just as a "genus" contains its "species," or as a whole contains its parts. Furthermore, the very powers of seeds <note>original: "seminum" / "σπερμάτων"</note> reflect an image of what I was just saying. For in the whole seed, all things are undivided, and the "reasons" <note>original: "rationes" / "λόγοι"; the formative blueprints of life</note> are contained there as if collected in a single center. Yet, the seminal reason for the eyes is one thing, and that of the hands is another, <margin>C</margin> which is made clear by the fact that different parts are generated from them. Thus, the powers implanted in seeds have this quality: each one is a single, whole blueprint, necessarily encompassing the parts within itself. Now, that which is corporeal in the seed has matter (such as the moisture), but the "reason" itself is a form <note>original: "species" / "εἶδος"</note> throughout. This reason is the same as the power of the soul that generates; this soul is itself an image of a higher, better soul. Some call this "nature" <margin>D</margin> when it is implanted in seeds. Starting from the things that are superior to it—just as light comes from fire—it transforms and shapes matter, not by pushing it with force or by using those famous "levers" <note>a critique of mechanical explanations of nature</note>, but by applying the seminal reasons.

---

*The notions of physical things recently acquired or produced in the soul are not the physical things themselves. However, the absolute "intelligible" notions that come into the rational power from the Intellect are, in a way, the intelligible things themselves. Chapter V.*

---

*Because the Intellect is the innermost part of the soul, being both its own and common to all: in what is "its own," the notion and the "intelligibles" <note>the objects of pure thought</note> are more the same; in what is "common," they are most the same. The Intellect (as Plotinus often says) exists within as a form, while the common Intellect is present to the soul as an agent. Since the intelligible thing stands in relation to the act of understanding almost like a motor, and therefore precedes it in some way, we should not say that the Intellect becomes the intelligible after it has understood them, but rather the reverse—especially since, otherwise, understanding would exist by mere chance and would be like mere fictions.*

---

<margin>A</margin> ACCORDINGLY, the sciences that exist in the rational soul and pertain to sensible <note>physical/perceivable</note> things—if indeed our knowledge of these things should be called "science," since it is more fitting to call them "opinions"—being later than the things themselves, are merely images of them. But those sciences which look toward things to be understood (the "intelligibles"), which are truly sciences, come from the Intellect into the rational soul and understand nothing of the physical world. Insofar as they are sciences, they are the very things they understand; they possess the intelligible and the <margin>B</margin> understanding from within. This is because the Intellect is within, which is itself those first things, dwelling with them and existing as an "act." It does not direct its gaze as if it did not already possess them, nor does it acquire anything by searching or running through a sequence of thoughts.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Let the Intellect, then, be the things that exist. It is with them, not as if holding them in a place, but as holding itself, being one with them. All things are together there, and yet no less distinct. For even the soul, having many sciences in itself, does not have them in a state of confusion. Each one performs its own work when necessary, without pulling the others along. Nor does each individual part act purely unless it is set apart from the inner notions. Thus, and much more <margin>B</margin> so, the Intellect is all things at once, and again not at once; because each is a specific power. The whole Intellect encompasses all like a genus encompasses species, and like a whole encompasses parts. Even the powers of seeds carry the likeness of what has been said. For in the whole, all things are undistinguished, and the "reasons" are as if in one center. And just as the "reason" of the eye is different from the "reason" of the hands, the difference <margin>C</margin> will be known by the different sense-perceptible result. The powers in seeds, therefore, are each a single whole "reason," along with the parts contained within it. The bodily part contains matter, like the moisture, but the reason itself is the whole form. And the "reason" being the same, it is the generative soul, which is an image of another, better soul. Some call this "nature" <margin>D</margin> when it is in seeds. Starting from there, from the things before it—just as light from fire—it turned and shaped the matter. It did not push it, nor did it use the much-talked-about "levers," but rather gave of its "reasons."

---

<margin>A</margin> The sciences in the rational soul that deal with sensible things—if indeed one should call these "sciences," for the name "opinion" is more suitable for them—being later than the things themselves, are images of them. But of the "intelligibles," those which are truly sciences, having come from the Intellect into the rational soul, they clearly understand nothing of the sensible world. Insofar as they are sciences, they are each of the things they understand. They have the intelligible and the understanding from within. Because the Intellect is within, which is those very primary things, being present with them <margin>B</margin> and existing as an "activity" <note>original: "ἐνέργεια"; active existence/reality</note>. It does not acquire them as if it did not have them, nor does it look around for them, nor does it travel through them.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Divine Intellect contains all primary Forms (archetypes) simultaneously and perfectly, comparing this to how a seed contains the blueprint for an entire organism or how a mind holds multiple branches of knowledge without mixing them up.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 560 concerning how the Divine Intellect (Nous) contains all Forms or Ideas. Plotinus is arguing that the Intellect does not "look out" at things to understand them, but rather that the Intellect and the objects of its thought are one and the same essence.</meta>

<page-num>561</page-num>
<header>BOOK NINE.</header>

...these things were not separated <note>original: "ἐπεκεχωρισμένα"; referring to thoughts being distinct but not divided</note> as if they were acquired from the outside (for those are merely passions of the soul), but rather it held all things together within itself, being all things at once. Intellection <note>original: "νόησις" / "noesis"; the act of pure spiritual thought</note> exists in the subsistence of each thing. For when it thought of God, it became God; if it thought of motion, it became motion. Therefore, if one says that "ideas are thoughts," it is not correct to mean that once the Intellect thought of something, that thing then came into existence or stood toward it; for before this act of thinking, the object of thought must already exist. Otherwise, how would the Intellect even come to think of it? For it certainly did not happen upon it by chance, nor did it strike upon it at random.

<margin>* thus</margin>
If then intellection is * such a thing, then that Form <note>original: "εἶδος" / "eidos"; the perfect blueprint or "Idea" of a thing</note> is not merely potential, but is this very Idea itself. What then is it? How is it that the intellectual essence is not different from each individual Idea? Rather, each Idea is itself an intellect. And while the Intellect as a whole comprises all the Forms, each individual Form is its own individual intellect. It is like a whole science <note>original: "ἐπιστήμη"; a body of knowledge</note> which contains all its various theorems. Each part of the whole is not separated by space, but each part potentially possesses the whole. Thus, the Intellect exists within itself. And if it remains in its own stillness, it possesses an eternal fullness. If we were to imagine the Intellect existed before the things that are, we would have to say the Intellect, after finding and thinking them, then finished and gave birth to them. But it is necessary to conceive of "Being" <note>original: "τὸ ὂν"; the state of existing</note> as existing alongside it. Here, stillness is found in the thinking of things that exist. The activity of thoughts is directed toward those things that are. Just as fire already contains the activity of fire, so the Intellect, being in that which exists, has its activity within itself. Being is also activity. Or rather, both are one. Therefore, Being and Intellect are a single nature; and thus, the things that exist are one. The activity of Being and the Intellect are the same. These thoughts are the Form, the shape of Being, and its activity—though they are conceived of as separate by us, where one thing seems to come before another. For it is our own dividing mind that separates them; but that Mind which is undivided and does not separate is Being itself and all things.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...through those things which it did not previously have ready at hand: for such conditions seem rather to belong to the soul. Instead, the Intellect rests deeply within itself, existing as all things at once, not using intelligence to bring individual things into existence within itself. For it did not become God only after it understood God; nor did it become motion only after it understood motion. Therefore, what is commonly said—that "Ideas are intellections"—if it is meant that after it understood a thing, that thing was made or existed, it is <margin>B</margin> not said correctly. For that which is understood must exist before this act of understanding. Otherwise, by what means would it proceed to the understanding itself? For it did not fall upon it by chance, nor did it struggle toward it in vain or at random.

---

-> *The Intellect, taken in an absolute sense, is all the Ideas. But any specific Idea is not the Intellect in an absolute sense, but an intellect of that specific kind. Likewise, any Idea differs from the Intellect only by a certain intellectual reason. Ideas, however, differ among themselves by the nature of the thing and their formal reason. Chapter VIII.* <-

-> *For it is more correct to say: the Idea of a man is intellect, and the Idea of a horse is intellect, rather than saying the Idea of a man is the Idea of a horse; although under the act of each individual Idea, the others exist potentially or by a certain consequence, just as propositions arranged in order in geometry relate to geometry as a whole and to each other. Furthermore, since Being naturally precedes the Intellect in order, a necessary distinction of Being into its own modes of existing precedes the use of intelligence: a distinction which neither the Platonists nor the Christians willingly admit in the first principle of things. Just as we consider there the nature of Being and common intelligence, so in any Idea we find a specific nature of Being and a specific intelligence. These are like two things—not like matter and heat, or transparency and light—but like heat and "to be hot," or light and "to shine," both of which are acts, and therefore are one in reality. Even though intelligence is the innermost act of Being, both are nonetheless activity.* <-

---

<margin>A</margin> Since, therefore, that which is understood is something internal, this internal thing is itself one, both the species and the Idea. What then is this? Truly, it is the Intellect and the intellectual essence, and any Idea is not different from the Intellect; rather, each is an intellect. Indeed, the common Intellect itself is all the species together, while each species is an individual intellect. It is like how a whole science is the sum of all its observations and notions; and <margin>B</margin> every notion is a part of the whole, not divided by location, but each one having its power within the whole. This Intellect, therefore, exists in itself, resting in the same state with itself, an eternal fullness of all things. If, however, the Intellect were thought to be prior to Being itself, one would have to say that the Intellect, by acting and thinking, generates and perfects the things that exist. But since it is necessary to conceive of Being as prior to Intellect, one must confess that the things that exist are primarily within intelligence, and that the act and the intelligence <margin>C</margin> are added to the beings themselves—just as the act of fire is added to fire that already exists—so that the things that exist, and Being itself, are acts. Therefore, there is one act for both; indeed, both are one. Therefore, Being itself and the Intellect are one nature; on account of which the things that exist, the act of Being, and the Intellect are one. And such intellections are the species, the form, and the acts of Being. However, when these are divided <margin>D</margin> by us, some things are thought of as being before others: for it is our dividing intellect that is different, but that undivided and least-dividing thing is Being itself and all things.

---

-> *If the mind arranges forms in the world through natural intelligence, it embraces those same forms within itself in a certain natural way. Chapter IX.* <-

-> *Just as the essence of the soul has its powers flowing from it, just as the generative nature contains the seminal reasons of the limbs; just as the species...* <-

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Divine Intellect and the objects of its thought (the Forms or Ideas) are identical, existing as an eternal, simultaneous fullness rather than being created through a sequence of thought.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the Divine Intellect. On the previous page, he established that the Intellect and its objects of thought are identical. Here, he moves to explain how the various "Ideas" or "Forms" (the perfect blueprints of reality) exist within this single Mind without losing their individual identities, and what specifically has a corresponding Idea in the divine realm versus what is merely a flaw of the physical world.</meta>

<page-num>562</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.</header>
<columns>2</columns>

...fire possesses light, heat, dryness, and lightness, and rarity; and in this way, Ideas generally agree with one another and yet differ in their being. For to be is for Ideas to differ by their formal definition <note>original: "ratione formali"; the essential nature that makes a thing what it is</note>, lest a confusion of forms and order arise in things, or happen by chance, or occur from various agents meeting by accident. But if God acts with free will—as we prove in Theology—after the manner of an architect and a geometer, He must possess the Ideas of things.

<margin>A</margin> BUT what are those things in that one Mind there, which we ourselves partition when we think? For it is necessary to bring those things forth while they are at rest, and to speak of them as if from a single science remaining in unity, and thus to look more clearly at the things within. Since, therefore, this world is a living being <note>original: "animal" / "ζῶον"; in Platonic thought, the universe is seen as a giant, living, breathing organism</note> embracing all living things, and it receives its existence and its specific nature from another; and since that source from which it comes is traced back to the Mind, it is necessary that the universal archetype of the whole first exist in the Mind. Thus, this world of the intellect is itself the "intelligible world," of which Plato says in the *Timaeus*: <margin>B</margin> "the intellect understands the Ideas within that which is the Living Being." For just as when a seminal reason <note>original: "ratio seminaria" / "λόγος σπερματικός"; the formative power or "DNA-like" principle that directs growth</note> is present—which is itself a kind of living power—and there is underlying matter ready to receive that seminal reason, a living thing must necessarily be generated. In the same way, since an intellectual nature exists that is possessed of omnipotence, and nothing hinders it (because nothing stands as a medium between this nature and the receiver), it is necessary that the one be adorned and the other be the adorner. But that which is adorned already has its form divided: here a man, <margin>C</margin> there a sun. The Adorner, by contrast, possesses all things together in a single unity.

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the Greek parallel of the preceding Latin text.</note>

What then are the things in the One, which we, when thinking, define? For one must bring them forth while they are at rest. For example, from a science that exists in unity, one sees the things within it. Since this world is a living being encompassing all living beings, and its existence and its being of such a kind comes from another, and that source leads back to the Mind, it is necessary that every archetype be in that Mind, and that the world of the Mind be the "intelligible world," which Plato says is the Living Being. For just as there is a certain vital reason, and matter has received that seminal reason, a living being must arise; in the same way, the intellectual nature being all-powerful, and with nothing separating it or standing between it and that which is capable of receiving it, it is necessary that the one be beautified and the other be the beautifier. That which is beautified has its form partitioned: in one place a man, in another a sun. But that which is in the One possesses all things.

---

->*Every idea is commonly and similarly a living intellectual essence, a species, and an act. They differ only by their other properties.*<-

### Chapter X.

->*All formal things in the world—including motions, actions, and their effects—follow a certain natural and special order and have their own Ideas there. Defects of forms and of natural progressions, however, have no Ideas; they occur by chance and are understood through the Ideas of the formal things.*<-

<margin>A</margin> WHATEVER things, therefore, exist in the sensible world as "species" <note>specific types of things, like "human" or "horse"</note> proceed from there; other things do not. For this reason, nothing that is "against nature" <note>original: "praeter naturam"; things like diseases or monstrosities</note> is found there. Just as nothing "against art" exists within the arts, neither is there any "lameness" in the seeds. For a lame condition of the feet occurs during the process of birth, when the seminal reason does not fully prevail; the loss of the form happens by accident and chance. However, qualities that are in harmony with nature— <margin>B</margin> quantities, numbers, magnitudes, habits, developments, actions, and natural passions, as well as motions and states (both in universal and particular conditions)—are among the number of things that exist there and proceed from there. Instead of time, eternity reigns there; but instead of place, one thing is found within another there through a certain intellectual reason. Since all things are together there, whatever you take from among them is essence; it is an intellectual nature and possesses life. Thus, <margin>C</margin> "Same" and "Different," "Motion" and "Rest," the "Moving" and the "Consistent," "Essence," and "Quality" are all there, and all are entirely essence. For each thing exists not merely potentially, but as an act; for this reason, quality is not separated from each essence. But we must consider whether only those things contained in the sensible world are there, or if things dealt with by the arts are also there. For evil is not there, nor does it come from there. Evil...

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the Greek parallel of the preceding Latin text.</note>

Whatever things exist as forms in the sensible world come from there; whatever do not, are not there. Therefore, of the things against nature, none are there. Just as in the arts there is no lack of art. Nor is there lameness in the seeds. Lameness of the feet happens already in the generation, from the failure of the reason to master the matter, or from a stroke of chance against the form. But harmonious qualities, and quantities, numbers, and origins, and relations, and actions and passions according to nature, and motions and rests, both universal and partial, are among the things there. Instead of time, there is eternity. Place there is intellectual: "one thing in another." Since all things are together, whatever you may take of them is essence, and intellectual, and each possesses life. And "Same" and "Other," and "Motion" and "Rest," both moving and standing, both essence and quality. And all is essence. For what each has in activity, that each thing appears to be as a being. So that quality is not separated from each essence. Are then only the things in the sensible world there, or are there more? But first, we must consider the arts. For there is nothing of evil. For what evil...

<meta>catchword: evil... (Latin: malum...)</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that the physical world is a reflection of a perfect "Intelligible World" or Divine Mind, which contains the archetypes of all natural things. He distinguishes between natural forms, which have divine Ideas, and defects or evils, which result from the failure of those forms to manifest perfectly in matter.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the "Intelligible World"—the realm of pure thought and perfect Forms. Having established that the Divine Mind (Intellect) contains the blueprints for all reality, he now asks: which human activities and "arts" have a divine counterpart? He distinguishes between arts that merely copy the physical world (like painting) and those that deal with mathematical or moral principles (like music or justice), which are more closely linked to the divine.</meta>

<page-num>563</page-num>
<header>BOOK NINE</header>

<note>original Greek: "ἐνταῦθα, ἐξ ἐνδείας..."</note> ...here, evil arises from need, deprivation, and deficiency; it is a certain condition of unfortunate matter <term>matter: in Neoplatonism, matter is seen as the "lowest" level of existence, often associated with lack or "non-being"</term> that fails to achieve form, and of that which seems to become similar to matter.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Here, evil happens from need, deprivation, and deficiency. Evil is indeed a certain suffering of unfortunate matter that does not follow a form at all; and likewise of that which seems to escape being similar to matter.

---

*Artistic works that are made only by a certain imitation of natural things and motions, or even those that proceed naturally from a talented mind, do not have their own Ideas in the divine realm. Chapter XI.*

*But they are partly reduced to the Ideas of natural things themselves, and partly to the reasons of things—numbers, measurements, and modes—that are innate to the rational soul and depend on similar Ideas. Philosophical contemplation of things has Divine Wisdom as its Idea; providence, whether governing privately or publicly, looks to Divine Providence, time, and eternity as its Idea.*

<margin>A</margin> BUT to come now to the arts and crafts: those arts which are imitative, such as painting, sculpture, dance, and the gesturing of hands <note>original: "gesticulatio manuum"; likely referring to pantomime or theatrical gesture</note>, since they are organized and exist here in the physical world and use a sensible example—imitating shapes and movements—and transfer the harmonies they see to their own work, they do not seem rightly able to be traced back to the divine realm, except through the human reason itself. If, however, anyone should consider the habit that stems from the harmony inherent in animals, and looks at it across all animals generally, <margin>B</margin> it would certainly be a part of that faculty which also looks upon the divine world and contemplates the concord of all things. Furthermore, all music occupied with consonance and the numbers of melodies—to the extent that it contemplates certain intelligible ratios of numbers and harmony—is in the same state as that Reason which possesses the intelligible number and harmony within itself. <margin>C</margin> Whatever arts produce sensible objects, such as the architect and the carpenter—insofar as they use proportions and measurements—seem to have their beginning from there and possess something of that divine wisdom. But when they mix the rules of measurement with sensible matter, they do not depend entirely on the divine, except perhaps insofar as they exist within the human mind. Furthermore, neither agriculture, which brings help to physical plants, nor medicine, which cares for human health, nor that which provides strength and a firm condition of the body to men, belong there in their entirety. <margin>D</margin> For another power and health flourishes there, through which all living beings have sufficient stability. Furthermore, the art of oratory, the command of an army, and the discipline of household and public affairs—whenever they observe the "Honest" <term>the Honest: Latin "honestum," referring to moral beauty or virtue</term> itself in their actions and consider a celestial honesty—they surely have a share in knowledge from that Science which flourishes there. Then, indeed, geometry, pertaining as it does to intelligible things, must be placed there. Wisdom also, which concerns Being itself through the most exalted things, is likewise there. And so much for the arts and the duties of the arts.

---

*In the Idea of the rational and intellectual man itself, every artistic faculty and whatever proceeds from talent is contained in summary. Chapter XII.*

*All formal differences between individuals that do not happen by chance from the diversity of matter or locations have Ideas there—but rather by a certain virtue than by their own specific act; that is, insofar as various and singular modes of forms, destined to sprout at some time, are contained in the species themselves, of which there are properly and principally Ideas.*

<margin>A</margin> NOW indeed, if there is an Idea of Man there, there is also an Idea of the Rational Man, and similarly of the Skilled Man. There are, moreover, arts there which are conceived and born by the Mind as offspring. It must also be said that the species of universals exist there—not of Socrates, for instance, but rather of "Man." Although regarding Man, we must especially consider whether there might also be a singular Idea there...

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence with the catchword "tius" (likely from "potius"), to be continued on the next page.</meta>

<summary>Plotinus discusses whether human arts have divine origins, concluding that while imitative arts like painting are earthly, arts based on math and virtue (like music, geometry, and ethics) reflect divine "Ideas." He begins to argue that the Idea of Man includes all human potential and skills, though he distinguishes between universal "Man" and specific individuals.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the "Intelligible World"—the realm of pure thought and perfect Forms. Having previously discussed the arts, he now turns to individual physical differences and whether the soul and its virtues exist as primary "Ideas" rather than mere reflections.</meta>

<page-num>564</page-num>

-> # PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK V <-

<margin>A</margin>
I say "singular" or "individual" because one person is not the same as another, nor do they possess the same individual traits. One person, for instance, is snub-nosed <note>original: "simus"</note>, while another is aquiline <note>original: "aquilinus"; meaning hook-nosed like an eagle's beak</note>. Such properties should be placed within the "form" of man, acting as certain differences of forms, just as different species are differences within the category of "animal." However, if these traits arise from matter—meaning one person is aquiline because of certain material conditions and another is different for another reason—then we must conclude that some differences (like certain colors) consist in the rational "form" <term>Form: In Platonic thought, the "Form" or "Idea" is the perfect, eternal blueprint of a thing</term>, while others happen due to the diversity of matter and physical location.

*Every material thing stands in relation to its own Idea, just as a painted image relates to a living being. Chapter II.*

*Souls, minds, and their perfected virtues exist outside of mere "Ideas" as true things, just as the Idea itself does. They are not named the same way by chance (equivocally), but because they share the same essential nature (univocally). They do not differ as a painted man differs from a living one, but rather as a boy differs from a man.*

<margin>A</margin>
It remains for us to investigate whether only those things contained in the sensible order <term>sensible order: the physical world we can perceive with our five senses</term> exist in the divine realm. We must ask: just as "this human" here is one thing and the "Human-itself" is another, is there likewise a "Soul-itself" there that is different from "this soul"? And similarly, is "this mind" different from "Mind-itself"? First, we must say that not everything here should be considered a mere "copy" of a divine model. The soul is not just a shadow of a "Soul-itself," though one soul may excel another in dignity. The soul exists here, <margin>B</margin> but perhaps it is not "the Soul-itself" simply by virtue of being "here" in a body. Since every soul is a true reality, there must also be a certain Justice and Temperance in the souls dwelling here, as well as true knowledge. These are not just images or likenesses of the divine versions—as if they were merely wandering in a physical place—but are those very same divine realities existing here in a different way. For those divine things are not restricted to a specific location. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, wherever the soul emerges from the body, those virtues are there as well. While the sensible world is confined to one place, the intelligible world <term>intelligible world: the higher realm of pure intellect and reality</term> is everywhere. Whatever a soul of such quality possesses here, it possesses again there. Consequently, if we understand "things in the sensible world" to mean everything in the visible category, then not only do those things exist in the divine realm, but many more exist there besides. However, if we define "things in the world" to include the soul and everything within the soul, then indeed, all things that are there are also here.

*Many things, such as decay or accidents, happen without following an Idea and are deformed; this is because the vegetative part of the soul—the lowest of divine things—cannot entirely overcome matter. Chapter XIV.*

*Things that happen by chance or without a certain order directed toward an end do not have Ideas. The highest Ideas contain the ingenious and necessary arts. The soul itself is the Idea of the soul; closest to this is the soul formed by pure intellect. Further away is the same soul when it takes upon itself the universal providence of the world. Furthest of all is the same soul when it is dedicated to the providence of a specific, particular thing.*

<margin>A</margin>
Should we therefore believe that this nature, which contains all things in the "intelligible" or "intellectual" category, is the First Principle itself? But how could that be? For the true Principle <term>The One: The ultimate, simple source of all existence in Plotinus's philosophy</term> must be entirely one and simple, whereas in the fullness of beings, there is necessarily a multitude. But again, how does such a nature and "fullness" exist alongside the One? How did this multitude flow from the One? Under what conditions did all these things arise? And why did the Intellect become these things, and from where did it come? Truly, these matters must be discussed elsewhere, starting from a different beginning.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
Regarding the individual: it is not the same as the general, but for example, one is snub-nosed and another is hook-nosed. We must also place snub-nosedness as a difference within the human "form," just as there are differences in the category of animal. Other differences arise from matter, such that one person is this way and another that way. Regarding differences of colors: some we must say exist in the rational "form," while others are produced by matter and the differences of physical locations.

<margin>A</margin>
It remains to speak on whether only the things in the world are there. Or if, just as there is the "Human-itself" other than the human, there is also a "Soul-itself" other than the soul. It must be said that the causes there are not like images that only have one impression. The soul here is an image, but the "Soul-itself" is also there. <margin>B</margin> There is a difference, even if it exists here. Perhaps it exists as the "Soul-itself." Since each soul truly exists, there is also Justice, Temperance, and true knowledge in our souls—not just images or likenesses of those things as if in a sensible place, but those very things existing here in another manner. For those things are not limited in space. Therefore, wherever the soul rises out of the body, those things are there as well. <margin>C</margin> For while the sensible world is in a single place, the intelligible world is everywhere. Whatever the soul alone possesses here, it also has there. So, if we take "things in the sensible world" to mean visible things, then not only are the sensible things there, but more. But if "the things in the world" include the soul and the things in the soul, then all things that are there are also here.

<margin>A</margin>
Should we then set this nature, which encompasses all things in the intelligible realm, as the Principle? And how? Since the One is truly one and simple, and is everything that exists, yet there is a multitude among beings. How then is there the One, and how is there a multitude, and how are all these things? And why are they these things, and from where? We must speak of this, starting from another principle—

<meta>The text cuts off here, continuing the inquiry into the nature of the "One" and the "Many" on the following page.</meta>

<summary>This page explores whether individual human traits and virtues like Justice have divine blueprints (Ideas). Plotinus concludes that while some physical differences come from matter, the soul and its virtues are real divine entities present within us, and he begins to question how the many things in the universe emerge from the "One" source.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the specific inquiry into the origin of physical traits and shifts to a broader metaphysical question: whether "lowly" or "vile" things like mud and decay have divine archetypes. It also includes the formal table of contents for the Sixth Ennead as compiled by the translator, Marsilio Ficino.</meta>

<page-num>565</page-num>

<header>BOOK NINE.</header>

Regarding things that arise from decay <note>original: "ἐκ σήψεως"</note> and things that are difficult, we must ask whether there is a Form <term>Form: In Platonic philosophy, an "Idea" or "Form" is the perfect, eternal blueprint of a thing existing in the divine mind</term> for evil, or for filth and mud. We should say that insofar as things are brought forth from the First Principle, they are all excellent. In those Forms where these lowly things do not exist, they do not derive from the Mind <term>Mind: Often called "Nous," the divine intellect</term>. Rather, the Soul receives certain things from the Mind, but also admits much from Matter <note>original: "παρὰ ὕλης"</note>, which is where these [vile] things occur. But these matters will be explained more clearly when we return to that core problem: how a multitude flows from the One. As for composite things that exist by chance, they too are linked to the Mind. However, those things in the sensible world that come together on their own are not contained within the Forms; specifically, those things arising from the decay of the soul, perhaps because the soul is unable to produce anything else at that moment. Otherwise, it would have produced something according to nature. At any rate, it produces what it can. Concerning the arts, we must ask if they are contained within the nature of man; all arts are referred back to what is natural to man. But before all else, we must consider the universal soul, or rather the life within the Mind before it became a soul, so that the soul may come into being; for that life is what we call the soul itself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> When it is asked whether there is a Form [Species] there even for those things which arise from putrefaction <note>original: "putrefactione"</note>, and for things that are difficult and quite troublesome—likewise for filth and mud—it must be said: whatever the Mind leads forth from the First Principle, all those things are the best, and these [vile] things are certainly not present in those Forms. The Mind does not receive such things; rather, the Soul receives many things from the Mind, but additionally admits many things from Matter, which is where these defects occur. But these things will be explained more clearly if we return to that doubt <margin>B</margin> by which it is asked: how does the multitude flow forth from the One? Now, it is clear that those composite things which occur randomly and in vain are not governed by the Mind, but rather clash together by their own momentum in this category of sensible things; they are not contained within the Forms themselves. Furthermore, those things which arise through putrefaction happen by a certain chance of the soul, which is perhaps then unable to do otherwise; otherwise, it would have undoubtedly produced something <margin>C</margin> contained within the higher nature of man. All things are referred back to those which are natural to the human race. But the universal is prior to all others, and the Soul itself is prior to the universal—or rather, it is the life in the Mind before it emerged as a soul, so that this soul might be formed from it, and that we might happen to call that [higher life] the Soul especially.

# PLOTINUS
## THE SIXTH ENNEAD.
### BOOK I.

# PLOTINUS
## THE SIXTH ENNEAD.
### BOOK I.

->Concerning the Genera of Being.<-
->On the types of existence.<-

<margin>Chapter I.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring foliage and a stylized human face at the bottom.</image-desc>
It is a very <margin>A</margin> old question: exactly how many and of what kind are the things said "to be"? Some indeed said that Being <term>Being: The fundamental state of existence or "what is."</term> is only one; others said there are many, but a limited number; others finally said they are infinite. Each of these groups brought forward different arguments, whether they posited one, a finite number, or an infinite number. <margin>B</margin> Since such opinions have already been sufficiently examined by later thinkers, we must set them aside for the present. We should consider only the opinion of those who, having discussed the older views, established certain fixed "genera" <term>Genera: The primary classes or categories under which all things can be organized.</term> of things. These thinkers did not accept only one, because they saw that there are many things even in the realm of the mind <note>original Latin: "rebus intelligendis" — things understood by the intellect rather than the senses.</note>; nor, on the other hand, did they want to admit an infinite number, because that would be impossible and there would be no science at all. Reducing the finite <margin>C</margin> count to a specific number, they could not correctly call these "elements"—since elements would comprise many underlying things—so they instead called them "genera." Some said there are ten, others fewer. Perhaps there would even be some who would suggest more to us. There is also a difference in how they view these genera: some wanted the genera to be "principles" <term>Principles: The starting points or fundamental causes of reality.</term>; others held that the things themselves are identical to their genus. To begin, it seems we should take up the opinion of those who partitioned all things <margin>D</margin> into ten. We must investigate whether they mean there are ten genera that share the common name of "Being," or ten "predicaments" <term>Predicaments: Also known as Categories, these are the different ways we can describe or classify a subject (such as its quality, quantity, or location).</term>. For they themselves admit that Being is not "univocal" <note>original Latin: "vniuocum" — meaning the word "being" does not have exactly the same meaning when applied to a substance as it does to a quality.</note> in all things, and they are right to admit it. Nay, rather, this should be asked first: are those ten categories found in the same way in the intelligible world as in the world of the senses, or are some found in one and not the other? Conversely, no one would surely say that they are found in both in the same way. It <meta>catchword: seems</meta> seems necessary to investigate which of the ten numbers best fit the nature of the mind <meta>catchword: In those things which pertain to the intellect</meta>

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Π' featuring leafy vines and a bird perched on a branch.</image-desc>
Concerning beings—how many and of what kind they are—there are old accounts, such as those already mentioned. Some said they are one, others not one. Some said they are many, others infinite. Some spoke of the "Good," others of finite things, and these same thinkers, having spoken of many things, left their opinions to be examined by those who came after them. We should set these aside and examine those who, having scrutinized the earlier views, established things within fixed limits. These later thinkers saw that there are many things even among the intelligible <term>Intelligible: Things that can only be grasped by the mind, such as mathematical truths or divine ideas, as opposed to "sensible" things seen with the eyes.</term>, and they saw that if things were infinite, there could be no science. They reduced the finite things to a number, though they did not correctly call them "elements," but instead named them certain "genera." Some said ten, some fewer; there might even be some who say more. There is also a difference among these genera: some consider the genera to be principles, while others consider them to be the beings themselves. First, then, we must take up the division of beings into ten, examining whether they consider there to be ten genera which happen to share the common name of "Being"—that is, ten categories. For even they do not say this name is "synonymous" <note>original Greek: "συνώνυμον" — used here in the Aristotelian sense where a name is applied to different things but with different definitions, like "being" applied to a person versus "being" applied to the color red.</note>, and they say so correctly. Rather, that should be asked first: whether the ten are found similarly in the intelligible and in the sensible, or if some are in one and some are not. Or indeed, once again, it must be examined which of the... <meta>catchword: the</meta>

<summary>This page introduces Plotinus's critique of the categories of existence, specifically targeting Aristotle's ten categories. He questions whether these categories can apply equally to both the divine/intelligible realm and the physical/sensible world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "Genera of Being" from the previous page. Plotinus is specifically scrutinizing whether a single category of "Substance" can bridge the gap between the divine, intellectual world and the physical, sensory world. He is engaging deeply with Aristotle’s "Categories," questioning if the Aristotelian system (the Peripatetics) is sufficient for describing true reality.</meta>

# BOOK THE FIRST.

And must the things that exist "there" <note>Referring to the intelligible or divine realm of Forms.</note> be gathered under the same genus as these things of ours here, or is "essence" <note>original: οὐσία (ousia) / essentia. This is the fundamental "whatness" of a thing.</note> spoken of equivocally—meaning the name is the same but the nature is different—in both the higher and lower realms? Truly, if it is equivocal, then there are many genera; but if it is used univocally <note>meaning the word has the exact same definition in both cases</note>, it is immediately absurd that "essence" should signify the same thing in those beings which exist primarily and those which exist only secondarily. For there cannot be one common genus among things where one is "prior" and the other is "posterior." They <note>likely referring to the Aristotelians</note> do not speak of things belonging to the intellect according to this division. Therefore, they did not intend to divide all things that exist into categories, but rather they left out the things that "most truly" exist.

### It is not easily granted that incorporeal and corporeal things, as well as form, matter, the composite, and the singular and universal, should meet in one single genus of substance. Chapter II.

We must ask again: should these be considered "genera"? And how can "substance" <term>Substance: The Greek word 'ousia' refers to that which exists in its own right, not as a quality of something else.</term> be a single genus? For it seems we must begin entirely with this. It has already been stated that it is impossible for one genus of substance to be common to both the intelligible nature and the sensible nature. For if it were, there would be something else even "above" both the intelligible and sensible substance that is predicated of both—a thing which would be neither a body nor incorporeal. Otherwise, <margin>B</margin> if that genus were a body, it would follow that the incorporeal thing beneath it would be called a body; if it were incorporeal, it would follow that the body beneath it would be called incorporeal. Furthermore, regarding the things we call "substances" here in our world, we must ask: what exactly is common to matter, form, and the "composite" <note>The physical object made of both matter and form.</note>? For they say all these are substances, yet they are not "equally" substances. Since <margin>C</margin> form is called substance more so than matter—and rightly so—though others might perhaps say that matter is more truly substance. Moreover, what will the so-called "primary substances" have in common with "secondary substances"? <note>In Aristotelian logic, a 'primary substance' is an individual man, while a 'secondary substance' is the species 'Man'.</note> For secondary substances have their very name as substances from the primary ones. In short, it is not possible to explain what "substance" is according to their system. Even if someone assigns us a "property" of substance <note>a unique characteristic</note>, they have not yet explained what substance itself is; perhaps the idea that "one and the same thing, while remaining numerically one, can receive contrary qualities in turn" <note>e.g., a person being first cold, then warm</note> seems to apply to all substances.

### Regarding what the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching.</note> call substances, it is more probable that they are arranged in a single series depending sequentially on one source, rather than sharing in the same nature. Chapter III.

<margin>* grouping together</margin>
But should we say there is one single "category" <note>original: κατηγορία (kategoria)</note> under which we might *group together intelligible substance, matter, form, and the composite? It would be just as if someone spoke of the "lineage of the Herculidae" <note>The descendants of the hero Hercules.</note> as one single thing; not because there is one common nature shared by all of them, but because they all descend from one ancestor. For in that case, that ancestor is "substance" in the first degree, while the others are substances in a second degree or to a lesser extent. But what prevents everything from being <margin>B</margin> one single category? Indeed, what prevents all other things said "to be" from deriving their being from substance? Or is it perhaps that the "rest" are merely "affections" <note>properties or modifications</note> of substance itself, while the substances themselves are arranged one after another in a specific order?

<sig>Bb 2</sig>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> And must the things that are there be gathered under the same genus as these things of ours, or is that which is there, and that which is here, called essence <note>original: essentia</note> equivocally? But if it is equivocal, there are many genera; if, however, it is univocal, it is immediately absurd that essence should signify the same thing both in those things which exist primarily and in those which exist later. Especially since there is not one common genus among them, where one is indeed prior and another is posterior; they do not speak of things pertaining to the intellect <margin>B</margin> according to a division. Therefore, they did not wish to divide absolutely all things that exist, but rather they left out the things that exist most of all.

<margin>A</margin> It must be asked again: should these be considered genera, and how is substance one genus? For it seems we must start entirely from this. It has indeed been said that it is impossible for one genus of substance to be common to the intelligible and the sensible nature. For thus there will also be some other thing above the intelligible and sensible substance, predicated commonly of both, which would be neither body nor <margin>B</margin> incorporeal. Otherwise, if that genus were a body, it would follow that what is called incorporeal under it is a body; or if it were incorporeal, it would follow again that what is called a body under it is incorporeal. Furthermore, in those things which are called substances by us here, it must be asked: what indeed is common to matter and form and the composite? For they say all these are substances, yet they are not equally substances; since <margin>C</margin> form is called substance more than matter, and rightly so—although others might perhaps say that matter is more truly substance. Furthermore, what commonality will the substances called "primary" have with "secondary" substances? Since secondary substances have it from the primary ones that they are called substances. Indeed, it is not possible to explain among them what substance actually is. For even if someone assigns to us a property of substance, he has not yet touched upon what it is; and perhaps that "one and the same thing numerically can receive contraries in turn" seems to fit all substances.

<margin>A</margin> But should we say there is one single predicament <term>predicament: an older term for "category," referring to how we classify types of existence.</term> under which we may commonly encompass intelligible substance, and form, and matter, and the composite? Just as if someone said the lineage of the Herculidae <note>original: Herculidum genus</note> was one single thing, not as if there were something common to all, but as if they descend from one. For that first one is substance in the first degree; and the rest in a second degree, and to a lesser extent. But what prevents absolutely all things from being <margin>B</margin> one predicament? Indeed, what prevents all the rest of the things which are said "to be" from being from substance? Or perhaps the rest are certain "passions" <note>passive qualities or experiences</note> of substance itself, and the substances themselves are arranged one after another in a certain order?

<sig>Bb 2</sig>

<summary>Plotinus questions whether Aristotle's category of "Substance" can truly apply to both the divine intellectual realm and the physical world. He argues that things existing in different degrees of reality (prior and posterior) cannot share a single common genus.</summary>
<keywords>substance, essence, intelligible realm, sensible realm, matter, form, Peripatetics, categories, Herculidae, primary substance, secondary substance</keywords>

--- Page 738 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "Genera of Being." Plotinus has been questioning whether "Substance" can be a single category that covers both the divine and the physical. He now transitions into a critique of the second Aristotelian category: Quantity.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin>
But indeed, we cannot stop at this level of substance, nor can we take it as the most primary thing so that we might derive other substances from it. Therefore, let all things called "substances" be considered related to one another, having something distinct from the other genera <note>The 'genera' are the highest categories of being, such as Substance, Quantity, and Quality.</note>. What then is the meaning of these terms: the "whatness" and "the thing which is," and "subject" versus "not a subject"? <note>Plotinus is using Aristotelian terminology here: a "subject" is that in which qualities (like colors) exist.</note> And what does it mean to not be in another thing as a subject, and that the thing itself is not part of something else—the way whiteness is a quality of a body, or quantity is a property of an essence? Likewise, is time a property of motion, and is motion a property of the thing being moved?

<margin>B</margin>
Yet "secondary substance" <note>original: substantia secunda / δευτέρα οὐσία. In Aristotle’s system, this refers to species and genera (like 'Human' or 'Animal'), whereas 'primary substance' is an individual person.</note> is predicated of another thing. But perhaps this is said of another in a different way than other things are; namely, as a genus, which exists as a kind of part within a thing and belongs to the substance of that in which it exists. Whiteness, however, is predicated of another because it "lies within" it. But someone might call these traits unique to substance compared to other categories, and thus gather them into one and call them "substances."

<margin>C</margin>
However, one cannot rightly call this a single "genus," nor does it truly declare the notion and nature of substance. But let these matters end here; let us proceed to the nature of quantity.

---

*Number, continuum, place, and time—which the Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were the followers of Aristotle, named for the covered walkways (peripatoi) where they studied.</note> place in a single genus of quantity—do not seem to have one nature equally common to all. Rather, they can be arranged in a common series, reduced back to a "primary quantity." Chapter IV.*

---

*Number alone seems to be "quantity" in itself, and quantity itself; in this, unity defines the next unity. Compared to number, dimension is weighed for how great it is; and in relation to dimension, place and body are considered.*

<margin>A</margin>
They <note>The Aristotelians</note> certainly call Number the primary quantity, along with all continuous magnitudes, place, and time. Whatever else they call "quantities," they refer back to these. Thus, they say motion is a quantity because the time in which it occurs is a quantity—though perhaps it should be the other way around, since time receives its continuity from motion. Now, if they say that a "continuum" <note>A continuous thing, like a line, where the parts touch at a common boundary.</note> is a quantity simply because it is continuous, it would follow that what is "discrete" <note>Separate parts, like a pile of stones or a number.</note> is not a quantity. But if a continuum is a quantity only by accident <note>A philosophical term meaning a non-essential property.</note>, what common element is there in both that makes them "quantities"?

<margin>B</margin>
In numbers, it is common that they are quantities. Although it is clear enough that they are called quantities, it is not yet clear what specific nature makes them so. However, a line, a surface, and a body are not called quantities in that same way; they are called "magnitudes." They only come to be called quantities when they are reduced to a number—for instance, when something is measured as being "two cubits" or "three cubits" long. Even a natural body becomes a quantity when it is measured; and place is a quantity only by accident, not by its very nature as place.

<margin>C</margin>
We must not accept "accidental quantity," but that which is quantity by its very self—namely, quantity itself. For we should not admit "three oxen" as a quantity, but rather the number itself which is in them. "Three oxen" involves two categories <note>Substance (oxen) and Quantity (three).</note>. In the same way, a surface involves two categories: the surface itself and its quantity.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
But in this way, we are not yet able to permit a single substance, nor to grasp the most primary thing, so that we might understand the others from it. All things called substances are indeed related, having something apart from the other genera. What then is the "what" and the "this," the "subject" <note>original: ὑποκείμενον (hypokeimenon)</note> and that which is not "in" a subject, nor being in another as if in a subject? Nor is it that which belongs to another, like white is a quality of a body, or quantity belongs to an essence, or time

<margin>B</margin>
belongs to motion, and motion to the thing moved. But secondary substance <note>original: δευτέρα οὐσία</note> is said of another in a different way. But here, the genus exists as a part. Whiteness is in another, because it exists within it. But these things one might call "properties" in relation to others, and so one might collect them into one and call them substances.

<margin>C</margin>
But one would not call this a "genus." Nor does it reveal the concept and nature of substance. Let these things rest here. Let us go toward the nature of quantity <note>original: ποσόν (poson)</note>.

---

<margin>A</margin>
Number <note>original: ἀριθμός (arithmos)</note> is the first quantity, and every continuous magnitude, and time. They refer other things to these when they call them "quantities." They say motion is a quantity because of time, but perhaps again the continuous nature of time comes from motion. If the continuum is a quantity insofar as it is continuous, then the discrete would not be a quantity. But if it is quantity by accident, what is common to both

<margin>B</margin>
in their being quantities? For in numbers, let it be granted that they are quantities. And even in this case, being quantities belongs to them, but it has not yet been shown what that nature is by which they are so called. But line, surface, and body are said to be magnitudes <note>original: μεγέθη (megethē)</note>, but they are not called quantities. They only take on the name of quantity when they are brought under a number, such as "two cubits" or "three cubits." Even the physical body, when measured, becomes a quantity. And place is a quantity by accident, not in itself.

<margin>C</margin>
One must not take the accidental quantity, but that which is quantity in itself, such as "quantity-ness" <note>original: ποσότης (posotēs)</note>. We do not say "three oxen" is a quantity, but the number in them. For "three oxen" is two categories. Likewise, a line of a certain size is two categories, and a surface of a certain size is two, and quantity itself is...

<summary>Plotinus critiques the Aristotelian category of Quantity, arguing that Number is the only true form of quantity. He suggests that magnitudes like lines, surfaces, and time are only called "quantities" when we apply numbers to measure them.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's critical examination of the Aristotelian categories. ->### BOOK ONE.<-

ποσόν: <note>original: "ποσόν" (poson). This is the Greek term for the category of Quantity.</note> and the surface itself, insofar as it is quantity. Having been delimited, for instance, by three lines or four, it is said to be a quantity. What then? Shall we say only numbers are quantity? But if indeed we mean numbers by themselves, as many as are so called, [they are substances]. And especially, by being according to themselves; but those numbers in the things that participate in them, according to which we count—not units, but ten horses and ten oxen—firstly, it will seem absurd if those [abstract numbers] are substances, that these should not also be; and secondly, if they measure the subjects and exist within them, but do not exist outside them while they measure, just as rules and measures do. But if, while existing in themselves, they are taken for measuring and are not in the subjects, then either those subjects are quantities without participating in quantity, or [the number] itself is that by which they are quantity. For they are measures; but why are the measures quantities, or why is quantity itself a measure? Is it because, being among existing things, even if they fit none of the others, they will be this thing which they are called? And they will be placed in the so-called "quantity." For their unit defines them; the "one" moves on and adds another. And number, as it were, indicates and measures the multitude, the soul making use of it. But it does not measure "what" a thing is; for it does not say "one, two" of whatever opposites there may be, but only when a thing has a certain disposition. For example, not "heat" or "beauty," but only what pertains to quantity. Therefore, whether number is viewed in itself or in those things participating in it, it is the number itself by which the participants [are measured]. Or would a "three-cubit" thing become a quantity? <margin>*is it?</margin> No, but rather "the three." In this way, magnitudes are also quantity. Is it perhaps because magnitudes are near to quantities, and because of this proximity we call them quantities, or do we call them so by the primary "quantity"? But we call something "large" just as we call it "many" when it participates in a number. And "small" because it participates in few. But "the large" itself and "the small" are not considered to be quantities, but <term>relatives</term> <note>original: "πρὸς τί" (pros ti). Plotinus follows Aristotle here, noting that 'large' and 'small' describe a relationship between things, not an absolute amount.</note>. Nevertheless, they are called relatives insofar as they seem to be quantities. But we must consider this more accurately: is it that number alone is a distinct kind of character, while others are different? Therefore, it is not primarily a genus, but a single category gathering things that are close to those that are primary, and those that are secondary. But we must investigate how numbers that exist in themselves are substances, or if they too are a quantity. Whichever way it is, they would not have anything common with these others, except perhaps in name only.

As for speech, time, and motion, how do they stand? But first, regarding speech, if you please.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...is quantity: but why indeed does the surface itself become quantity? For this reason, when it has already been delimited, as if by three or four lines, it is judged to be quantity. What then? Shall we assert that only numbers are quantity itself? Indeed, if we admit numbers existing separately by themselves, these are certainly judged to be <term>substances</term> <note>original: "substantiæ" / οὐσίαι.</note>; especially because they exist according to themselves. If, however, we take numbers which are in their <margin>B</margin> participants, according to which we count—not indeed units, but ten horses and ten oxen—firstly, it will seem absurd if the former are substances, that these should not also be substances. Next, it is again absurd if, while measuring subjects, they exist within them and do not exist outside them while they measure, in the same way that certain rules and measures do when they seem to measure. But if, while existing meanwhile in themselves, they are taken up for measuring and are not as if adhering somewhere in the subjects, then surely <margin>C</margin> those things which are subjects are not quantities, since they do not participate in quantity through themselves. But why is it [number] itself considered to be quantity? For they are measures. But why are measures quantities, or why is quantity itself a measure? Is it perhaps because, existing in the order of things, even if they are adapted to no other nature, they will still be this very thing which they are called? And they shall be placed in that which is called quantity. For the unit itself of these defines the "one": then it confers itself to another, and number designates how many <margin>D</margin> things are there, and the soul using number measures the multitude itself. While it measures, therefore, it does not measure what each thing is; for it says "one" and "two," whatever those things may be, even if they are opposites. Nor again does it measure what kind of affection each thing has: such as whether it be hot or beautiful, but only insofar as it properly pertains to quantity. Therefore, whether number is assumed according to itself or in participating things, it is not the participants that are quantity, but <margin>E</margin> the number itself. Neither, therefore, will a "three-cubit" length be quantity, but rather "the three" itself will be this. If this is so, why indeed are magnitudes also called quantities? Is it perhaps because they are close to quantity itself, and we call those things quantities in which quantity is present? Although we do not weigh them by that primary quantity. But we call something "large" as if it participates in a large number; and "small" because it participates in a small number. Nevertheless, "large" itself and "small" are not judged <margin>F</margin> to be quantities properly, but relatives. However, these things must be considered more diligently. Therefore, there will not be one genus and another, number alone [being quantity]; while these other things are quantity in a secondary way. Thus, it is not primarily one genus, but one <term>category</term> <note>original: "praedicamentum" / κατηγορία.</note> gathering together things that are somehow near to each other, both those which are in the first place and those in the second. But we must investigate how numbers that exist according to themselves are substances: or whether they too are a certain quantity. But whichever way they are, they will have nothing in common with these others, except perhaps in name only.

*Quantity itself is that which is not quantity through something else, but through which other things become quantities. Therefore, speech, motion, and time, since they do not have this function, are not quantity, nor do they include quantity in their formal definition, although they become participants in quantity.*

He concludes that quantity might not be a single unified genus but a category covering both primary mathematical units and secondary physical magnitudes.</summary>

### PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin> For it is indeed measured. But while speech, as it exists, has a certain magnitude, it is not a "quantity" <note>original: "quantum" / "ποσόν" (poson)</note> insofar as it is speech; for it possesses the power of signifying, just as a name or a verb does. Its matter is the air, just as air is the matter of the name and the verb from which speech is composed. <margin>B</margin> But it is rather the "striking" <note>original: "verberatio" / "πληγὴ" (plēgē). Plotinus refers to the physical impact of breath upon the air that creates sound.</note> itself that is speech—not simply any striking, but a certain formation acting as a shape. It is, therefore, an action—specifically, a signifying action. One might more correctly assert that such a motion and striking is an "action"; but if it is held in the opposite way, one would call it a "passion" <note>The category of "Passion" or "Being Acted Upon" (Paschein).</note>. Or one might say it is the action of one thing and the passion of another; or an action directed toward a subject, and a passion existing within a subject. However, if voice is to be understood not according to the striking but according to the air, then there will be two categories here and not one, with the signifying striking bringing together and co-signifying that category. <margin>C</margin> After these matters, we must ask about Time: if it is understood as that which measures, we must ask what is to be thought of as the "measurer." For it seems either the soul or the moment <note>original: "momentum" / "νοῦ" (the Greek text here is slightly unclear but the Latin suggests a 'moment' or 'instant').</note> measures here. But if Time is taken as the thing being measured, let it be "quantity" itself, properly speaking—as in the length of a year—but insofar as it is Time, it is a different kind of nature. For that which is "so much" is something else while being "so much"; for Time is not merely quantity. Quantity, however, even if it does not touch upon anything else, is principally quantity by the very fact that it simply is. If anyone asserts that whatever participates in quantity is properly a "quantity," it follows immediately that substance and quantity are the exact same thing. Furthermore, when it is said that "equal" and "unequal" are properties of quantity, this must be understood as applying to quantity itself, not to the things that participate in it, unless by chance they are those things themselves: just as the "three-cubit length" is one genus, but it is one specific thing and one specific category.

> He says that in some things which are spoken of relatively to each other, something else occurs between them besides the subjects themselves—namely, a certain motion, as between the knower and the known, or the agent and the patient. But in many other cases, nothing seems to occur or exist beyond the subjects except for our own thought comparing them, such as "similar to similar" or "equal to equal." Finally, he does not believe that these various types of relatives, nor "relatives" simply stated, fit into a single nature.

After these things, we must consider the category of Relation <note>original: "relatio" / "πρός τι" (pros ti), meaning 'toward something'.</note>: whether any generic communion occurs within it, or if it is reduced to a unity by some other means. And regarding this, we must first ask whether relation itself is a proper "subsistence" <note>An independently existing reality.</note> or merely a certain "habitude" <note>A relative disposition or state of being.</note>, such as "right" and "left," or "double" and "half." Perhaps in some cases it is a subsistence, as in those things I just mentioned; but in the things I mentioned first, it may not exist at all, or rather, it may exist nowhere. For what truly exists in "double" and "half"? Or in "greater" and "lesser"? Again, what of "habit," "disposition," "reclining," "sitting," "standing"? Or even "father" and "son," "master" and "slave"? Or again, "similar" and "dissimilar"?

...similar, equal, unequal, and again, the active and the passive, and the measure and the measured, and knowledge and sensation. For knowledge is directed toward the <term>knowable</term><note>original: "ἐπιστητὸν" (epistēton) / "scibile". This refers to the object of intellectual understanding.</note>, and sensation toward the <term>sensible</term><note>original: "αἰσθητὸν" (aisthēton). This refers to things perceived by the physical senses.</note>. For knowledge may have, in relation to the knowable, a certain individual existence in act directed toward the form of the thing to be known; and sensation, likewise, toward the sensible. Furthermore, that which is called active stands in a certain way toward the passive, and can produce a single work. <margin>B</margin> And the measure performs a measurement in relation to the measured. But what effect does a "similar" thing have upon another "similar" thing? Does it perhaps have nothing that is *produced* then, but rather something that already *exists*—namely, an identity in quality? Yet, apart from the quality residing in each, it adds nothing; likewise with equal things. For identity in the <term>quantity</term><note>original: "quanto" / "ποσῷ" (posō). In Aristotelian logic, equality is a property of quantity.</note> precedes the mutual relation. And what else is a relation <note>original: "habitudo" / "σχέσις" (skhesis)</note> except the judgment of our own mind? That is, while we compare <margin>C</margin> things that exist in themselves as they are, we say: "this one and that one have the same magnitude and the same quality"; likewise, "this one fathered that one," or "this one excels that one." What does "sitting" or "standing" have, other than the person sitting or standing? A "habit" <note>original: "Habitus" / "ἕξις" (hexis). A stable disposition or state of being.</note>, which is spoken of according to that which one "has," seems rather to signify the "having" itself; but a habit spoken of according to that which is "held" <note>Plotinus is playing on the Greek word "echo" (to have/hold), which is the root of "hexis" (habit/state).</note> should rather be called a "quality." The same logic applies to "disposition." <margin>D</margin> What, then, will these things be, besides those which are referred to one another? What are they beyond a certain comparison made by our intelligence? Furthermore, when the "surpassing" is referred to the "surpassed," the former is a magnitude of such-and-such size, and the latter is of such-and-size. This is one thing, and that is another; but the comparison is within us, not in them. Likewise, where the "right" is superior to the "left," and "front" to "back," perhaps these consist in a certain position, insofar as one is here and the other is there. We have devised "right" and "left," but in the things themselves, there is nothing. Likewise, what is called "earlier" and "later" are actually two different times; but the naming of them as "earlier" and "later" is placed in our own judgment.
