PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin> If a relation looks toward a quality, let it have a mutual union; and in all those things which we say are "relative" <note>original: "ad aliquid" / "πρὸς τί" (pros ti). This is the standard Aristotelian term for the category of Relation.</note>, let there exist a certain mutual <term>disposition</term><note>original: "habitudo" / "σχέσις" (skhesis). This refers to the way two things stand in regard to one another.</note> beyond the subjects themselves—a disposition which we perceive as already existing. Similarly, let knowledge be related to the object of knowledge. Indeed, in this matter, it is even more manifest that there is a certain <term>existence</term><note>original: "subsistentiam" / "ὑπόστασιν" (hypostasin). In Neoplatonism, this refers to the underlying reality or "standing-into-being" of a thing.</note> arising from the relation. If these things are so, we should no longer ask whether a relation <margin>B</margin> exists in such things or not. Instead, we must concede that among such things, in some cases—as long as the subjects remain in themselves as they were, even if they are separated in the meantime—the relation itself persists. In other cases, the relation is born only when the subjects come together. In still others, even while the subjects remain, the relation either ceases entirely or becomes something else—as happens with "right" and "left," or "nearness." It is from these latter cases that the suspicion primarily arose that nothing real exists in such relations. <margin>C</margin> Having conceded this, we must investigate what is the same in all of them, and whether there is something common there, acting as a genus rather than just an accident. Then, after something identical is found in them, we must search out what kind of existence it has. 

Now, we must speak of the "relative"—that which is named "toward something." This is not used simply when something is said to "belong" to another—as a certain disposition of the soul or body, or in the way the soul is "of" someone or "in" something. Rather, those things are properly called relative whose very <margin>D</margin> existence is born from nothing else than the relationship. I call this "existence" not that which belongs to the subjects, but that which is properly called "relative." For example, the "double" gives a relative existence to the "half." This existence does not belong to the two-cubit length itself, nor to the number two, nor to the one-cubit length, nor to the number one; but these things existing, it follows immediately from their relationship that—beyond the fact that one is "two" and the other "one"—the "two" is said to be and is "double," and the "one" in turn becomes and is said to be "half." Both, therefore, flow together from themselves to be something else: "double" and "half." These are made in reference to each other, and their being is nothing other than "being toward each other." To be "double" exists in the act of exceeding the "half," and to be "half" exists in the act of being exceeded. Because of this, one of them is not prior and the other posterior; rather, both exist simultaneously. Furthermore, one might ask whether other relatives follow this rule, or if some do not exist simultaneously—as happens with a father and a son, and similar cases. For when the father has died, the son remains; and when a brother dies, a brother remains, since even so we say this or that person is similar to the deceased.

---

> *A common description of relation is the mutual disposition of two things. But this is so different among various relatives that it is not <term>univocal</term><note>Having a single, consistent meaning across all instances.</note>. Between some relatives, there is a certain action along with the disposition, as between a parent and a child; in other cases, there is none, as between similar or equal things. Chapter VIII.*

---

<margin>A</margin> BUT we have digressed somewhat toward these matters; from there we must primarily ask for what reason these things behave so differently. But now, this very phrase "to be toward one another" ought to declare what common existence it possesses. Certainly, that common element cannot be a body. It follows then...

<column-break/>

...the "being-toward" is in the same [category] as the "toward something," and in all things that we call "relative," there is a relation toward one another. We can observe this in ourselves, as knowledge is related to the thing known. This makes the existence <note>original: "ὑποστάσεως" (hypostaseōs)</note> that comes from the relation even clearer. One should stop asking if a relation <note>original: "σχέσις" (skhesis)</note> exists. Let us note that among such things, in some, as long as the subjects remain as they were, the relation exists even if they are separate. In others, it arises when they come together. In still others, even while they remain, the relation either entirely changes or becomes something else—as with "on the right" and "near." From these cases, the idea mostly arose that there is nothing real in such things. Having noted this, one must seek if there is something identical in all of them, and if it is as a genus and not just an accident. Once the identical thing is found, we must see what kind of existence it has. 

The "relative" <note>original: "τὸ πρός τι" (to pros ti)</note> is not simply said to be "of another," such as a state of soul or body, or as the soul is "of this person" or "in another." Rather, it applies to those things whose existence <note>original: "ὑπόστασις" (hypostasis)</note> appears from nowhere else than the relationship. By existence, I do not mean that of the subjects, but the existence called "relative." For example, the "double" gives no existence to the "half," nor to the "two-cubits," or to "two" in general; since they are "one-cubit" or "one" in general. But when these exist, according to their own being—one being this and the other that—it happens that one is called and is "double," and the other becomes "half." Thus, both together generated the being of "double" and "half," which was born from their relationship to each other. And their being is nothing else than "being for each other." For the double, it is in exceeding the half; for the half, it is in being exceeded. So, it is not that one is prior and the other posterior, but they exist together. Whether they also remain together [is a question], as in the case of father and son; when the father is gone, the son exists. And to a brother, a brother remains. For we even say that the survivor is similar to the deceased.

---

BUT we have digressed into these things. From there we must seek why it is so in these cases. But this "being," this "toward each other," must show what common [nature] or existence all these have. For it is clear that this common thing would not be a body. It remains then that it is not a body; and the consequence...

<summary>Plotinus argues that relations (like "double" or "half") possess a real existence (hypostasis) that is distinct from the objects themselves, yet exists only in their mutual relationship. He notes that while some relations require the physical presence of both subjects, others (like family ties or similarity) can persist even after one subject has perished.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's dense metaphysical investigation into the "Category of Relation." Having established that some relations persist even when subjects are separated, he now questions whether "relationship" (skhesis) refers to a single type of reality or if we use the same word for very different things—such as the relationship between a father and son versus the relationship between "large" and "small."</meta>

# BOOK ONE

...if indeed it is, it must be incorporeal: and this [relation] exists either in the subjects themselves or outside them. 
<margin>A</margin> And if the <term>disposition</term> <note>original: "habitudo" / "σχέσις" (skhesis). In this context, it refers to the specific way two things are related or "held" together.</note> is the same in both subjects, we should call it <term>synonymous</term> <gloss>◯</gloss> <note>meaning the term "relation" applies to both in the exact same sense</note>. If not, but rather one thing is related in one way and another in a different way, it must be judged <term>homonymous</term> <note>meaning the word "relation" is used for both, but their actual natures differ</note>. For it does not follow that just because something is called a "disposition," it immediately possesses the same essence. Should we therefore divide these dispositions in this way? That is to say, some have a "latent" relationship—as if they were lying still and merely existing together—while others <margin>B</margin> always possess a relationship combined with potentiality and action. In the latter case, they might have a prepared potentiality beforehand, which then attains <term>actual existence</term> <note>original: "subsistentiam" / "ὑπόστασιν" (hypostasin)</note> through their meeting. Or should we say, in short, that some relations "produce" something while others simply "exist"? And does that which merely exists only provide a name to the other, while that which "produces" actually hands over reality to the other? Such is the case with a father and a son, or an agent and a patient. For these possess a certain <margin>C</margin> life and action. Should we then distinguish the types of relationship in this way? I mean, we should divide them not as if they shared something common with slight differences, but as if the relationship in each case were an entirely different nature—which we ought to call homonymous. We might name the relation that "produces" as "action and passion," as if both were a single motion. But for the other type, we might posit something that does not "act" itself, but is a cause within both subjects, such as <margin>D</margin> "equality," which makes things equal. For it is by <term>Equality</term> that things become equal, just as by a certain "identity" things become the same. However, when we speak of "large" and "small," the former is so called by the presence of Greatness, and the latter by the presence of Smallness. But when one thing is judged "larger" and another "smaller," it is considered so in respect to those participating in those qualities: the "larger" being that in which Greatness is already manifest in act, and the "smaller" being that where Smallness is manifest.

---

->Relation is something non-corporeal and a certain ratio, which consists either in action—as between the mover and the moved—or in species—as when one is more beautiful than another—or in the privation of species—as when one is uglier than another. Chapter IX.<-

->*Sometimes relations are in the same species, such as things that are similar and equal; sometimes they are in opposite species, such as things that are dissimilar and unequal. It is difficult to place such diverse ratios in the same category, along with their habits and privations, and both abstract and concrete forms.*<-

---

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, it is worthwhile in those cases we previously discussed—such as "acting" and "knowledge"—to posit a certain and effective relationship, as well as an "act," and within that act, a <term>reason</term> <note>original: "rationem" / "λόγον" (logon)</note>. In other cases, however, we should assert a certain "participation" in a species or a ratio. Indeed, if all existing things had to be mere bodies, it would be proper to say that these relationships which are called "relative to one another" are nothing at all. But if <margin>B</margin> we grant the primary province of Being to incorporeal things and to "ratios," and if we assert that relationships are themselves certain ratios and participations in the <term>Forms</term> <note>original: "specierum" / "εἰδῶν" (eidon). These are the eternal archetypes in Plotinus's philosophy.</note>, then it is reasonable to assign causes in this way: the cause of a thing being "double" is the "Double itself," which makes it so; and conversely, the cause of something becoming "half" is the "Half itself." Now, some of these things belong to the same species, while others belong to opposite species. Thus, it happens that at the same moment, the "Double itself" falls upon one thing, while the "Half" falls upon the other; <margin>C</margin> Greatness falls upon one, and Smallness upon the other. Or rather, both qualities are in each—namely, likeness and unlikeness, and again, "sameness" and "otherness." For this reason, the same thing is everywhere both "similar" and "dissimilar" at the same time, as well as "the same" and "different."

<column-break/>

<summary>Plotinus explores whether "Relation" is a single category or if active relations (like fatherhood) differ fundamentally from comparative relations (like size). He concludes that relations are incorporeal "ratios" or "reasons" derived from the participation of objects in eternal Forms like Equality or Greatness.</summary>

<keywords>Relation, Category, Incorporeal, Forms, Participation, Equality, Logic, Metaphysics, Plotinus, Action and Passion</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation into the categories of reality, specifically moving from the "Category of Relation" into a critique of how we define "Quality." Plotinus is contrasting the Peripatetic (Aristotelian) view of categories with his own Neoplatonic framework, questioning whether disparate things like "beauty," "habit," and "shape" can truly belong to the same logical family.</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEADS. BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin> What then if one thing is ugly, but another even uglier? Are they called so by participation in the same <term>Form</term> <note>original: "specie" / "εἴδους" (eidos). In this context, it refers to the intelligible pattern or "blueprint" that gives a thing its nature.</note>? Perhaps it should be said that if they are ugly, they are entirely equal to one another in the total absence of Form. But if one is more ugly and another less, we must say this occurs because the one who is less ugly participates in a Form that slightly overcomes its matter, while the more ugly one exists where the Form overcomes the matter even less. <margin>B</margin> Or perhaps they should be judged by a certain <term>privation</term> <note>The lack or absence of a quality that should naturally be present.</note>, if one wishes to compare them to each other, just as if the Form were actually present in them. 

Furthermore, sense perception is a kind of Form resulting from both [the perceiver and the object], and knowledge likewise is a Form resulting from both. <margin>B</margin> A <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitus" / "ἕξις" (hexis). A stable, long-term state or disposition, like knowing a language or having a virtuous character.</note> toward that which is held is a certain activity that contains it, like a kind of production. Moreover, measurement—which is the action of the measurer toward the measured—is a certain <term>ratio</term> <note>original: "ratio" / "λόγῳ" (logō). Can mean reason, proportion, or structural principle.</note>. If, therefore, one places the "disposition" of relatives itself as a kind of form under a general classification, it would not be out of place to call them one genus; <margin>C</margin> and everywhere their existence would be as a kind of ratio. 

But if these ratios are opposed and have the differences we have mentioned, perhaps they cannot be a single genus, but they might all be reduced to a certain similarity and a single <term>category</term> <note>original: "praedicamentum" / "κατηγορίαν". One of the fundamental ways of classifying existence.</note>. Yet, even if the things mentioned could be reduced to one thing, not everything placed under that same category by the [Peripatetics] can be gathered into a single genus. For they even group the negations of things together with the things themselves; <margin>D</margin> for example, they categorize "the double" and "that which is called double" [the thing itself] together. But how can the nature of a thing and the negation of that same thing be collected into one and the same genus? "Double" and "not-double," "relative" and "not-relative"—it is as if someone were to establish "animal" as a genus and then dare to place "non-animal" in that same category. Likewise, how can the concept of "double" and a specific "double thing" be counted in the same group, or "whiteness" and "a white object," since the two cannot be the same?

---

->*Having set down the description of quality according to the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>, namely: quality is that by which something is named "of a certain sort" [qualitative]: they ask whether all qualities so called are contained under one certain genus in a univocal way. Chapter X.*<-

->*Nor can we easily explain what that thing is in itself by which other things are named "qualitative." We cannot define it by power and impotence; likewise, we call something "qualitative" equally by a habit or a privation, and thus similarly through opposites.*<-

---

<margin>A</margin> **AFTER THIS**, it is fitting to consider Quality, from which someone is rightly named "of a certain sort." And first, we must investigate what Quality itself is, which makes other things qualitative. Does it exist as one and the same thing through a common definition that then displays different species, or are qualities so diverse among themselves that they cannot belong to a single genus? 

Indeed, what can be common between a "habit" and a "disposition," an "active quality," a "figure," and a "form"? What shall I say of "thick" and "thin," of "fat" and <margin>B</margin> "lean"? If we say that the common element is "potentiality" <note>original: "potentiam" / "δύναμιν" (dynamis). The capacity to act or be acted upon.</note>, which might apply to habits, dispositions, and natural powers (by which a thing is able to do whatever it can), then "impotence" [lack of power] will no longer fit in this genus. 

Furthermore, in what way is a "figure" <note>The external shape or outline of an object.</note> or the "form" around any given thing a "power"? Moreover, if this were so, being as being would have no power, but only when a "quality" is added to it: yet the very activities of essences [are themselves powers]...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Or is it not that, if one is ugly and another uglier, they are so by the same participation? Or if they are entirely ugly, it is an equality in unworthiness. But if it is "more" in one and "less" in another, it is by a participation in the Form in a certain way; the one who is less ugly has the Form prevailing more. The more ugly one has the Form prevailing less. Or it is by the privation of Form, by having a comparison to it, as if the Form were something that should be there. 

Sense perception is a Form from both [subject and object], and knowledge likewise is from both. <margin>B</margin> The habit is such that the thing held is held together by a certain activity, like a kind of making. The activity toward things that measure, in relation to the measured, is a kind of ratio. If someone should arrange the dispositions of relatives as certain Forms into one genus, their existence would be like a certain ratio. 

But if the ratios are opposite and have the differences spoken of, perhaps <margin>C</margin> it would not be a genus, but would be reduced to a certain similarity and one category. But even if the things mentioned could be reduced to one, they are not worthy to be a genus—those things placed under the category by them. For they even bring the negations of things into that which they reduce, and the things named after them. For instance, "the double" and "the thing that is double." How then can a thing and its negation be in one <margin>D</margin> genus? For example, "the double" and "the not-double"; and "relative" and "that which is about it"; as if one were to set "animal" as a genus and place "not-animal" there. And "the double" and "the double thing," just as "whiteness" and "the white thing," which are not the same.

<margin>A</margin> **QUALITY** itself, from which the so-called "qualitative" person or thing comes, must first be grasped: what is it that, by becoming present, makes something qualitative? And is it one and the same according to a common principle, providing Forms to differences, or are qualities so many that there is no genus? What then is common to habit, and disposition, and passive quality, and figure, and form? And of thinness <margin>B</margin> and color? For if the common thing is "power," if it fits habits, and dispositions, and natural powers, according to which that which is ultimate can do what it can, then it will no longer fit "impotence." Then figure and form—how is each of these a power? Then if being, as being, has no power at all, but only when quality comes to it, then the activities [of being would be qualities]...

<summary>Plotinus explores the definition of "Quality," questioning whether it can be treated as a single category that includes everything from physical shapes to mental habits and even their negations.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Enneads, Quality, Category, Form, Habit, Potentiality, Aristotle, Metaphysics, Logic</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's rigorous examination of the category of "Quality" (poiotēs). Having previously discussed how things participate in Forms, he now debates whether qualities are identical to the "powers" or "activities" of an object, or if they are something added to the essence later. He is specifically wrestling with Aristotelian definitions to see if they hold up under Neoplatonic scrutiny.</meta>

# BOOK ONE

<column-break/>

Whatever activities of an agent are most primary, acting by themselves, and are the very signatures of what they are <note>original: "σημάνσεων ὅ εἰσιν" (sēmanseōn ho eisin). These are the defining characteristics or "signs" of a thing’s true nature.</note>, to what kind of "quality" would they belong? But rather, are they qualities according to those powers that follow upon the essences themselves? For example, the boxing skill of a body is not judged as the man himself, but rather as the rational power: which faculty is therefore not a quality, but rather something that one has acquired through industry <note>Referring to "virtue" or "excellence" (aretē) which is earned through practice rather than being an innate biological function.</note>. For this reason, the "rational power" is called a quality **homonymously** <note>original: "ὁμώνυμον" (homōnymon). This means the same word is used for different things. Here, Plotinus argues that "rationality" as a defining trait of humans is one thing, but "rationality" as a quality or skill is another.</note>. Quality would therefore be a certain power added to the essence, coming after the definition of the essence itself, through which things are then named as being "of a certain sort." But the differences through which essences differ from one another are called qualities only by homonymy: for these are rather activities and <term>logoi</term> <note>original: "λόγοι" (logoi). The structural principles or "inner reasons" that give a thing its shape and function.</note>, or certain parts of logoi, which nevertheless declare the substance of the thing itself, even if they seem to speak of the essence as being "of a certain sort."

But those things which are principally judged as qualities, through which we are made to be "of a certain sort"—and which we also call "powers" in a common sense—will perhaps be certain logoi, and like forms. In the soul, these are beauty or ugliness; and in the body likewise. But in what way will all qualities be powers? Grant that beauty and health are properly qualities: but truly, how are ugliness, disease, infirmity, and impotence qualities? Is it because according to these also some are named as being "of a certain sort"? 

But what prevents those who are called "of a certain sort" from being named not by a single definition, but by homonymy? And they should not be called "of a certain sort" only in the four ways <note>Referring to Aristotle’s four types of Quality: 1. Habits/Dispositions, 2. Natural Capabilities/Incapacities, 3. Affective Qualities, 4. Shape/Form.</note>, but even in each of the four ways, they might be named at least doubly. Perhaps, indeed, quality is not judged according to the motion of acting or suffering itself. Therefore, that which can act is considered and spoken of in one way, but that which is being acted upon in another. Then again, they are accustomed to call health, disposition, <term>habit</term> <note>original: "ἕξιν" (hexin) / "habitum". A stable, long-term state of being.</note>, and similarly disease—likewise strength and debility—a quality. 

But if this is so, "power" itself will no longer be the common element in such things; rather, it will be necessary to track down some other common thing. Nor again will it be permitted to name all qualities equally as "logoi." For in what way will disease, which is a confirmed habit, be any kind of "logos"? Shall we then name those affections which consist in species and powers as qualities? But the opposite <term>privations</term> <note>original: "στερήσεις" (sterēseis) / "priuationes". The absence or lack of a natural quality, like blindness being the privation of sight.</note> would then not be part of the same genus. Instead, we shall always say they are one something, like a single <term>predicament</term> <note>original: "κατηγορίαν" (katēgorian) / "prædicamentum". A logical category.</note>: just as we call knowledge a certain species and power, but ignorance a privation and impotence. 

Or perhaps even impotence and infirmity are a kind of form? And thus both disease and vice can do and perform many things, but they do them badly. But since these are nothing other than to "fall away from the goal," in what way are they rightly named "powers"? Perhaps because each of them acts its own part, not looking toward what is right. Nor indeed would it do anything which it could not do at all. Beauty certainly has the force of something; does a triangle then? Or perhaps in judging quality one ought not to look even to power, but rather to that which is disposed or affected in some way? Wherefore quality is to be weighed according to certain quasi-forms and characters:

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Those which are primarily acts, acting through themselves, and the acts of their own powers, insofar as they are what they are, will belong to "qualities" in this way. Truly, quality should be considered according to those powers which follow after essences, as the faculty of a boxer is judged not as a man as a man, but the rational power itself: which faculty is therefore not a quality, but rather that which someone has acquired through industry. For which reason rational power is called a quality <term>equivocally</term> <note>original: "æquiuocè" (aequivocē). The Latin equivalent of homonymously.</note>. 

<margin>B</margin> Quality will therefore be a certain force added to the essence after the definition of the essence itself, through which things are then named as "of a certain sort." Differences through which essences differ among themselves are called qualities equivocally: which are rather acts and reasons, or some parts of reasons, nevertheless declaring the substance of the thing itself, even if they seem to speak of the essence as being "of a certain sort." 

<margin>C</margin> At those, which are principally judged as qualities, through which we are made "of a certain sort," and which we also call powers in a common notion, will perhaps be certain reasons, and like forms, whether regarding the soul or the body—such as a certain beauty or ugliness. But in what way will all qualities be powers? Grant that beauty and health are properly qualities: but truly, how are ugliness, disease, infirmity, and impotence qualities? Is it because according to these also some are named as "of a certain sort"? 

<margin>D</margin> But what prevents those who are called "of a certain sort" from being named not by a single reason, but equivocally? Nor should they be called "of a certain sort" only in four ways, but even in each of the four ways, they might be named at least doubly. Perhaps, indeed, quality is not judged according to the motion of acting or suffering itself. Therefore, that which can act is considered and spoken of in one way, but that which is suffering in another: but then they are accustomed to call health, disposition, habit, and similarly disease—likewise strength and debility—to be a quality. 

<margin>E</margin> But if it is so, "power" itself will no longer be the common element in such things, but it will be necessary to track down some other common thing: nor again will it be permitted to name all qualities equally as "reasons." For in what way will disease, which is confirmed by habit, be any "reason"? Shall we then name those affections, which consist in species and powers, as qualities? 

<margin>F</margin> Opposed privations, therefore, are not of one genus, but we shall always say they are one something, like one predicament: just as we call knowledge a certain species and power, but ignorance a privation and impotence. Or perhaps impotence and infirmity are also a kind of form? And thus both disease and depravity can do and perform many things, but badly. But since these are nothing other than to fall away from the intention of the goal, in what way are they rightly named "powers"? Perhaps because each of them acts its own part, not looking toward the right itself. Nor indeed would it do anything which it could not do at all. Beauty certainly has the force of something; does a triangle then? Or perhaps in judging quality one ought not to look even to power, but rather to that which is disposed or affected in some way? Wherefore quality is to be weighed according to certain quasi-forms and characters:

<summary>This page explores whether "Quality" can be defined as a "power" (potential). Plotinus concludes that while positive traits like health seem like powers, negative ones like disease are "privations," suggesting that "Form" or "disposition" is a better common denominator for the category of quality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's inquiry into the category of Quality. Having established that some "qualities" are actually essential activities of a substance, he now examines the boundary between an essence and its subsequent qualities, and critiques the traditional Aristotelian (Peripatetic) classification of qualities into habits, dispositions, and powers.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin>...and in its order, that which is common to all is itself a certain form and species, lying within the essence indeed, but coming after the essence. But again, we must investigate how it relates to **powers** <note>original: "potentiæ" / "δυνάμεις" (dynameis). In Greek philosophy, a 'power' is the inherent capacity of a thing to act or be acted upon.</note>. Perhaps even he who is a boxer by nature holds this very trait because he is affected in a certain way; and similarly for one who is born with an incapacity for something. In general, quality is a certain character, or a seal and a mark <note>original: "signaculum, atq; nota" / "χαρακτὴρ" (charaktēr). Plotinus uses the metaphor of a stamp or seal on wax to describe how qualities "mark" a substance without being the substance itself.</note>, which pertains least of all to the essence. 

<margin>B</margin>However, regarding that which seems to contribute to the essence at one time, and yet at another appears as something external to the essence—such as heat, whiteness, or any color—the situation is this: that which contributes to the essence is one thing, being as it were an **activity of the essence** <note>original: "actus essentiæ" / "ἐνέργεια" (energeia). An 'activity' is the essence in motion or expression, rather than an accidental trait.</note>; but that which does not contribute occupies a second place, arising from the essence, yet existing as something else in another thing, like an image or likeness of it. 

Furthermore, if a quality is judged according to its formation, mark, and rational principle, how do those things that signify **incapacity and ugliness** belong to the category of quality? 

<margin>C</margin>Perhaps one must respond that such things are certain **imperfect rational principles** <note>original: "rationes imperfectas" / "λόγους ἀτελεῖς" (logous ateleis). Plotinus often views "evil" or "ugliness" not as a positive force, but as a lack of completion or a failing of the organizing principle.</note>, as is clear in the case of the ugly. But how is there a "rational principle" in a disease? Perhaps in this case we even posit a principle of health, but one that has been moved out of its proper state; or perhaps not all these things should be placed within the category of rational principles. It is sufficient, however, to identify a certain common condition based on affection and disposition that comes upon the subject from outside the essence, so that it becomes a quality of that subject. 

A triangle, however, is called a quality of that in which it exists; not indeed the "Triangle Itself" in a simple sense, but the triangle that is in this particular thing, and insofar as it informs it. Human nature perhaps forms the essence, or rather, it provides the very essence.

---

### Having admitted the description of the Peripatetics, it is most difficult to correctly divide those things called qualities among themselves, or to see if it is possible, by dividing them, to collect them under the same genus with a single definition. Chapter XI. <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle, who defined "Quality" in four specific categories: habit/disposition, power/incapacity, affective quality, and shape/form. Plotinus is testing this Aristotelian framework.</note>

---

<margin>A</margin>BUT if these things are so, why then are there several species of quality? And why is **habit** <note>original: "habitus" / "ἕξεις" (hexeis). A stable, long-lasting state, like knowledge or virtue.</note> one thing, and **disposition** <note>original: "dispositio" / "διαθέσεις" (diatheseis). A temporary or easily changed state, like a passing mood or a slight chill.</note> another? For the difference of a quality does not consist in its lasting or not lasting; it is enough that there is a certain affection, no matter how it stands, to render something "of a certain sort" [a quality]. The function of "lasting" is added from the outside—unless, perhaps, someone were to say that dispositions are merely like imperfect forms, while habits are perfect forms. 

<margin>B</margin>But if they are imperfect, they are not yet qualities; if they are already qualities, the function of "lasting" is merely a condition added from the outside. 

In what way do **natural powers** <note>original: "naturales potentię" / "φυσικαὶ δυνάμεις" (physikai dynameis).</note> provide another species? For if qualities exist according to the very fact that they are powers, then surely the condition of "power" does not apply to all of them, as has been said. But if we say a man is a "boxer by nature" because he is disposed or affected in a certain way, the addition of the word "power" achieves nothing further, since power is already contained within the habits themselves. 

<margin>C</margin>Furthermore, why should he who is a boxer by natural power differ from he who has become a boxer through science? Perhaps insofar as they are "of a certain sort," these are not differences of the quality itself. If this man has acquired it through industry, and that man by nature, the difference comes from the outside. But regarding the species of boxing itself, how do they differ? Moreover, if some qualities proceed from an **affection** <note>original: "passione" / "πάθους" (pathous). In this context, 'passion' means being 'acted upon' or undergoing a change, like turning red from embarrassment.</note> and others do not, do they have a difference from this? For they are not...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...and the form upon the essence, after the [essence]. But again, how are the powers, or how is [the one who is] a boxer, [so called] by being disposed in a certain way? And [the one who is] incapable toward something. And in general, the quality is a character, not essential. But what is the same...

<margin>B</margin>...both to contribute to essence and to [be] in part, such as heat and whiteness and generally [color]. That which [belongs] to the essence is another thing, such as an activity; but that which does not contribute to this is like an activity in another thing, an image of it and a likeness. But if [quality is judged] according to formation and character and rational principle, how [do] those [things] according to incapacity and the ugly [have] a rational principle? 

<margin>C</margin>One must say [they are] incomplete [principles], such as in the ugly and [the diseased]. How is there a rational principle? Or do these also [possess] the rational principle of health, but [moved] out of its state? Or is it not [well] to put all things in a rational principle? It seems that a common [condition] beyond the "how" and [the affection] is to be outside of the essence. And the subject [exists] after the essence; quality [is] for the subject. But the triangle [is] a quality, not in itself, but the triangle in this. And according to... [it] formed. But also humanity formed, or [rather] it essentialized.
...being in a certain way, and after the essence. The Triangle of it, however, in which it exists, is called a quality; if this man indeed acquired it by industry, it is a difference. But truly according to the [species] itself... if some indeed proceed from a certain passion, but others by no means, how do they have a difference? Nor indeed... <note>The Greek transcription here is fragmentary, mirroring the damaged or abbreviated state of the source text, but it follows the same philosophical argument as the Latin on the left.</note>

---

<margin>A</margin>BUT if these things are so, why [are there] more [species] of quality, both habits and dispositions? For the difference of quality is not [in] the permanent and the not [permanent]. But the disposition is sufficient, however it may be, for providing the "of what sort." The [permanence] is from the outside; unless one says that the dispositions are only imperfect, like forms, and the habits are perfect. 

<margin>B</margin>But if they are imperfect, [they are] not yet [qualities]; but if they are already qualities, the permanence is an addition. And natural powers, how [are they] another [species]? For if [they are] qualities according to the powers, the [nature] of power will not fit all, as has been said. If we call the [one who is] by nature a boxer "of a certain sort" by being [disposed], the power added does nothing. 

<margin>C</margin>Since also in the habits [there are] powers. Then why will the [one] according to power differ from the [one according to] science? Or if it makes [him so], but the [other is] disposed, these are [not] of the quality. If one [learned] by practice, but the other [is so] by nature. But the difference is from the outside. And according to the species of boxing, how [do they differ]? Or [if] some [arise] from passion, but others not. For either [there is] a difference...

<summary>Plotinus examines the Aristotelian categories of quality, questioning whether traits like "habit" or "natural power" are truly distinct types of quality or just external descriptions of how a quality is held. He argues that qualities are "marks" or "images" that follow the essence of a thing rather than being the essence itself.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's dense metaphysical investigation into the "Categories." Having previously questioned what constitutes a "quality," he now examines whether physical properties (like roughness or density) and psychic attributes (like virtues) belong to the same class of being, ultimately challenging the standard Aristotelian (Peripatetic) definitions.</meta>

# BOOK ONE.

<margin>A</margin> Whence quality arises: I mean quality in regards to its variations and differences. One might also ask whether some qualities arise from **passion** <note>original: "πάθους" (pathos) / "passione". In ancient philosophy, 'passion' refers to being acted upon or undergoing a change, rather than just emotion.</note>, some in one way and others in another, and yet not in the same way. How can they exist within the same **species** <note>original: "εἴδει" (eidei) / "specie". This refers to the specific 'type' or 'form' that defines a group of things.</note>? If some are defined by having been acted upon, and others by the act of doing, they would only be called "qualities" **homonymously** <note>original: "ὁμωνύμως" (homōnymōs) / "æquivocè". This means they share a name but have different underlying definitions.</note>. Furthermore, what does "form" mean in relation to each thing? For if each thing is defined by its form, it is "qualified" insofar as it has that form. <margin>B</margin> But if "beautiful" or "ugly" is spoken of after the underlying form, it might have some rational basis. However, **rough and smooth** <note>original: "τραχὺ καὶ λεῖον" / "asperum & lene"</note>, or **rare and dense** <note>original: "ἀραιὸν καὶ τὸ πυκνὸν" / "rarum atq; densum". 'Rare' here means thin or porous.</note>, would not be correctly called qualities. For "thin" and "thick" are judged by the distance or proximity of parts to one another. Roughness is simply an unevenness of position, just as smoothness is a total evenness. <margin>C</margin> Even if quality arises from these, nothing prevents them from being judged as such. Finally, if the condition of **light and heavy** <note>original: "κῦφον καὶ βαρὺ" / "leuis & grauis"</note> is understood, it will show us where these ought to be placed. One might find an equivocal nature regarding "lightness"; unless perhaps lightness is measured by a certain release or by a sensation of "more or less" in the body—in which case **leanness and thinness** <note>original: "ἰσχνὸν καὶ τὸ λεπτόν" / "macilentū & tenue"</note> are found, which are numbered in a different species altogether.

---

<margin>A</margin> Whence quality arises: as much, I say, as pertains to the transformation and discrepancy of quality. One may ask besides, even if those things which happen from **passion** arise partly in this way and partly otherwise, how they can be placed in the same **species**. And if it is said that some are qualities by being acted upon, and others by acting upon passion, they will be called qualities equivocally. Furthermore, what is the meaning of that which is said concerning the **form** of each thing? For if it is said by the same logic that each thing is a species, that pertains very little to quality; <margin>B</margin> but if each thing, after the species of the subject itself, is called beautiful or ugly, that being called a "quality" can have some logic. But then rough and smooth, rare and dense, are not rightly named qualities. For "rare," "dense," "smoothness," and "roughness" are not judged because of certain distances between parts or a certain proximity; nor do these everywhere arise from an inequality or equality of position. <margin>C</margin> But if they also arise from these, nothing shall prohibit them from being judged as qualities. If, lastly, the condition of light and heavy themselves be known, it will now be clear to us where these are most especially to be placed. It is permitted, furthermore, to find an equivocal nature regarding the "light"; unless perhaps a thing is weighed as "light" by a certain liberation and by the sensation of "more or less" itself: in which order **leanness and thinness** are also found, which are certainly numbered in another species beyond the four.

<column-break/>

->It is not permitted to divide qualities in the Peripatetic manner; nor is it right to place qualities of the body, soul, and mind under the same genus.<-
->Chapter XII.<-

---

<margin>A</margin> But if one does not think quality should be divided in this way, by what reason could it be divided? We must consider, therefore, whether it is proper to assert that some qualities belong to the body and others to the soul. Then, should we divide the qualities of the body according to the distribution of the senses, so that some pertain to sight, others to hearing, or to taste, and others to smell or touch? But how shall we divide the qualities of the soul? Perhaps by the powers of **desire, anger, and deliberation** <note>original: "θυμητικὰς... λογιστικῇ" / "concupiscendi, irascendi, consultandi". This is the classic Platonic tripartite division of the soul into the appetitive, the spirited, and the rational.</note>? <margin>B</margin> Or by the differences of the actions which are performed according to them, since these are the producers of those actions? Or shall we divide them according to what is useful and harmful? And again, into "benefits" and "damages"? Should we similarly divide bodily qualities by the fact that they produce differences, or according to utility and harm? For such differences are proper to quality. For either utility and harm seem to happen from quality and the "qualified" thing, or we must investigate another way and manner still. <margin>C</margin> We must investigate how it is possible that he who is "qualified" according to a quality exists properly in that very quality. For there is not one single genus for both. Likewise, if a **pugilist** <note>original: "pugil". Plotinus often uses the boxer/athlete as an example of a "qualified" person—someone possessing a specific skill or power.</note> is in the order of quality, how is he not also in the same order as an **effector**? And if so, should we move the "efficient" to the order of **relation** <note>original: "πρὸς τί" / "relationis". In Aristotelian categories, "Relation" is separate from "Quality." Plotinus is asking if being a 'doer' is a quality or a relationship to the thing being done.</note>, and not again the "patient" itself, if this or that patient is contained in the order of quality? And perhaps it is better to place the effector here, if the effector is judged according to a **power**. Now, power is a quality; but if power itself is according to essence, whatever that power may be, even then it is not referred to anything, nor...

<sig>Cc</sig>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation into the categories of being, specifically examining whether "efficiency" (the power to act) is a quality or a relation, and whether qualities in the physical world are the same as those in the divine realm. It transitions into a critique of the Aristotelian category of "When" (Time).</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin>
...is also reduced to the order of quality. For the "efficient" <note>original: "efficiens" / "τὸ ποιοῦν". In this context, it refers to a thing's capacity to produce an effect or act upon something else.</note> itself does not behave in the same way as the "greater." For the "greater" has its existence, insofar as it is greater, in relation to that which is perceived to be "lesser"; but the "efficient" is judged as such because it is already of a certain **quality**. Perhaps, then, insofar as it is of a certain quality, it is placed in the order of quality; but insofar as it has power over another, and is therefore called "effective," it is rightly numbered among the **relatives** <note>original: "relatiua" / "πρός τι". This is the category of things that exist only in reference to something else, like 'double' or 'larger'.</note>.

<margin>B</margin>
Why, then, is the **boxer** <note>original: "pugil" / "πύκτικὸς"</note> not also counted among relatives? And likewise the skill of the boxer? For the faculty of the boxer is entirely referred to something else; for there is no consideration of it that is not related to another. Now, we must consider, and perhaps say, the same regarding other arts, or certainly most of them: insofar as they dispose and affect the soul, they exist as qualities; but insofar as they effect something, they are considered "effectors," and by this very fact are referred to something else and placed in the order of relatives—since they are also referred to something else in another way, insofar as they are called **habits** <note>original: "habitus" / "ἕξεις". A 'habit' in ancient philosophy is a stable, acquired disposition or skill.</note>.

<margin>C</margin>
But is there not some other subsistence according to that which is called "effective," since the effective is effective for no other reason than because it is of a certain quality? For perhaps someone, in the case of animate things—especially those using **deliberation** <note>original: "consilio" / "προαίρεσιν". Referring to conscious choice or intent.</note>—might grant that because it leans toward acting, there is a subsistence even according to the condition of effective virtue. But in inanimate forces, which we have called qualities, what is this "effective" itself? Perhaps when

<margin>D</margin>
it encounters something else of such a kind, it receives from it, and becomes a participant in its own function. But if the same thing acts upon another and also undergoes an action, how does the "effective" itself properly subsist any longer? For even the "greater," which perhaps in itself is three cubits long, is accustomed to become "greater" or "lesser" only in its encounter with another. But someone will say that the greater and lesser come to be by a certain participation in **magnitude** and **smallness**. Perhaps also that which undergoes and acts at the same time has a certain participation 

<margin>E</margin>
in both the "effective" and the "passive." It seems we must also ask here whether qualities which are in this world are numbered under the same genus as those in the **divine world** <note>original: "mundo diuino" / "ἐκεῖ". Plotinus frequently contrasts 'here' (the physical world) with 'there' (the intelligible or divine world).</note>. This might be said against those who place such things there as well. Or perhaps we should ask similarly even if one does not admit the existence of **Forms** <note>original: "species" / "εἴδη"</note>? Surely if one meanwhile admits the **Intellect** <note>original: "intellectum" / "νοῦν"</note> and grants that some habit exists within it, it will be asked whether some common **wisdom** exists there. But if that wisdom is related **equivocally** <note>original: "æquivocè" / "ὁμώνυμος". Meaning they share a name but have different natures.</note> to ours, it is rightly not numbered among such qualities; but if it is related **univocally** <note>original: "vniuocè" / "συνωνύμως". Meaning they share the same essential definition.</note>, then the very notion of quality will be common to ours and theirs—unless someone affirms that all things there are **essences** <note>original: "essentias" / "οὐσίας"</note>, and therefore grants that intelligence itself is similarly an essence. Indeed, a question of this kind can be raised concerning the other categories: whether what is here and what is there are different in genus, or rather both are placed in the same genus.

<column-break/>

...still a certain quality. For if it is like the "greater," it is the "efficient." For the "greater" has its existence as greater in relation to the "lesser." But the "productive" exists by being already of a certain quality. But perhaps according to being of a certain quality, it is a quality; but in that it has power toward another, being called "productive," it is a **relative**. Why then is the **boxer** a relative, and boxing itself? For boxing is entirely in relation to another. For every theory of it is nothing if not in relation to another. And regarding the other arts, or most of them, it must be considered. And it should perhaps be said: insofar as they dispose the soul, they are qualities; but insofar as they produce, they are "productive." And according to this, they are in relation to another. For it is also in another way a relative, according to which they are called **habits**. Is there then some other subsistence for the "productive," since it is productive not otherwise than by being of a certain quality? Perhaps then someone, in the case of animate things, and even more so in those having **choice**, by the inclination toward producing, might say there is a subsistence also according to the productive. But in the case of inanimate powers, which we called qualities, what is the productive? When it meets another, it enjoys and changes from that which it has. But if the same thing both acts upon another and is acted upon, how is it still the "productive"? For there is something—the "greater" being three cubits in itself—which becomes both greater and lesser in the encounter with another. But someone will say, the greater and the lesser exist by participation in magnitude and smallness. Or also it will be by participation productively and passively. It must be sought both there and here, whether the qualities here and those there fall under one genus. And this, if indeed some place them there. Or even if one does not wish for **Forms**, but speaking of **Intellect**, speaks of it as a **habit**. Or is there something common between that habit and this one? For **wisdom** is conceded. But if it is **equivocal** to the one here, it is clearly not numbered with it. But if **univocally**, there will be a common "quality" existing there as well. Unless one were to say all things there are **essences**. And thus also **intellection**. But as to the commonality, let it be toward other categories. Or if the "double" exists there also. Or if both fall under one.

---

->That which is named among the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> as the **category of "When"** <note>original: "prædicamentum quando" / "κατηγορία τοῦ ποτὲ"</note>—that is, "yesterday," "tomorrow," and similar terms—should properly be understood as **time**, or a part of time, in its formal definition. Chapter XIII.<-

If therefore it signifies nothing else, they ought not to place "when" itself in one category and "time" in another; but if it signifies something besides time, this will no longer be one single category, but one assembled from many.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's critique of Aristotle’s categories. Having previously discussed "Quality" and "Relative" (as seen on the previous page), he now shifts focus to the categories of "When" (Time) and "Where" (Place), arguing that these are not independent categories but are instead sub-types of "Quantity" or "Relation."</meta>

# BOOK ONE.

Regarding **When** <note>original: "ΠΕΡΙ͂ τοῦ ποτὲ" / "peri tou pote". This refers to Aristotle’s category of time or "Sometime."</note>, we must investigate it in this way: if "yesterday," "tomorrow," "last year," and such parts of time are considered, why are they not in the same category as time itself? For these are also "in time," just as the "now," the "has been," and the "will be" are. And if they are parts of time, it is surely right that they be ranked within time. Furthermore, time is said to belong to the category of **Quantity** <note>original: "τοῦ ποσοῦ". Plotinus argues that if time is a quantity, "When" doesn't need its own separate category.</note>; so why is another category necessary? If they should say that only time itself is the "now" and the "is," while "yesterday" and "last year" are things placed under the "now"—for these must be subjected to the "now"—yet the "now" is the only true time. But "When" is also time. First, if "When" is time, it is time. Then, if "yesterday" is past time, one might ask what it is. If the "past" is one thing and "time" is another, then there would be two categories, and it would not be a simple thing. But if they say "When" is not time, but rather "being in time," this "being in time" refers to the thing itself—for instance, if one says "Socrates existed last year." In that case, Socrates would be outside the category, and it is not what they are defining. But Socrates or the action would not be entirely time itself, but only in a part of time. If they say it is a "part of time," and they claim it is not simply time but a past part of time, they are making things more complex. For the "part," or being "in a part," is relative to something else, and the "past" is something inherent in them. Or it is the same as the "now," which was time itself. But if they say the difference is that the "now" is indefinite, while "yesterday" and "last year" are definite, we must first ask where we shall rank the "now." Secondly, "yesterday" is also defined. So "yesterday" is defined time. This is how one is "in time." Thus, if time is quantity, each of these will be a defined **quantity** <note>original: "ποσὸν".</note>. But if when they say "yesterday," we mean that "this thing happened in a specific past time," they are bringing even more elements into the discussion. Finally, if it is necessary to establish other categories because one thing is in another, as is the case here with being "in time," we shall find many other categories based on one thing being in another. This will be stated more clearly in what follows, regarding "Where."

---

->*It is superfluous to introduce a new category simply because something is said to be somewhere; for this "Where" is properly defined as "Place." If something else is considered as added to this, it does not bring a new category, but rather some Relation or Substance. Chapter 14.*<-

---

Regarding **Where** <note>original: "ΤΟ’ δὲ ποῦ" / "To de pou". Aristotle’s category of Place.</note>, it is not just "in the Lyceum" or "in the Academy." If the Academy and the Lyceum are entirely places, then it is as if one says, "He is in the Lyceum" or "in the Academy."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> CONCERNING that category which they name **Sometime** <note>original: "aliquando"</note>, or **When** <note>original: "quando"</note>, it must be considered next. Surely if "yesterday," "tomorrow," "last year," or "long ago" and such are parts of time, what prevents these from being in the same category in which Time is? Since "it was," "it is," and "it will be" are species of time, they are not wrongly placed in the same category as time; and time is said to be in the genus of **Quantity**. <margin>B</margin> For what reason, then, is a new category needed? If they say that these are not only time—namely "it was" and "it will be"—and likewise "yesterday" and "long ago" (which are placed under "it was," for such things must be subjected to the term "it was"); if, I say, they claim this is not only time, but "at some time" <note>original: "aliquando"</note> time, the response is immediate. First, if "at some time" is time, it is certainly also time. Secondly, if "yesterday" is past time, it will be something composite: <margin>C</margin> provided that the "past" itself is one thing, and "time" is another. Therefore, there would be two categories here, not a single simple one. But if they say that "When" is not time itself but being "in time," and if this "in time" signifies the thing itself—as if one says, "Socrates existed long ago"—certainly Socrates will be outside the category, and they will not be describing a single thing. But what will Socrates, or the action, be most essentially in this time? Perhaps a part of time? But if they speak of a "part of time," <margin>D</margin> and by that reasoning they consider it not simply time, or a part of it, but specifically a "past part of time," they create a multiplicity: for they take the "part" insofar as it is a part, which is a **Relative** <note>original: "ad aliquid". Things that exist in relation to others.</note>. And the "past" itself will be something added by them, or the same as what is called "it was," which is a species of time. But if they say the difference is that "it was" is indefinite, while "yesterday" and "last year" are definite, we first place "it was" somewhere; then "yesterday" will be judged as "it was" now made definite. From this it follows that "yesterday" is a definite time. But this is a **Quantity** <note>original: "quantitas"</note> of time, or a certain "how much" of time. Therefore, if time is established in the order of Quantity, any of these will be a definite quantity. And if, whenever they say "yesterday," we understand it to mean that something was done in a specific past time, they will bring even more things together at once. Finally, if it is necessary to introduce other categories because one thing is, or happens, in another—as occurs in the present case regarding being or happening "in time"—we shall find many other categories under the same condition, because one thing exists in another in various ways. But this will be more clearly discussed in the following, where we dispute the category of "Where."

---

<margin>E</margin> THOSE WHO treat the category they name **Where** <note>original: "vbi"</note> are accustomed to say: "Where" indeed means the Academy and the Lyceum are places entirely,

He specifically analyzes time-based terms like "yesterday" and "last year" to show they are merely specific measurements of time.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 379, where Plotinus critiqued the category of "When" (Time). Here, he concludes his critique of the category of "Where" (Place) before moving to Chapter 11, which examines the category of "Doing" (Action).</meta>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS. BOOK VI.

...and parts of place, just as up, down, and "here" are species <note>original: "species" / "εἴδη". In logic, species are the specific types that fall under a broader genus.</note> of place, or parts. However, the difference is that some are more clearly defined than others. If, therefore, up, down, and the center are places—just as the region of Delphi <note>Delphi was considered the "omphalos" or navel/center of the world in Greek tradition.</note> is a center, and near the center are Attica <note>The region surrounding Athens.</note>, the Lyceum <note>The grove and gymnasium in Athens where Aristotle taught.</note>, and other regions—why is it necessary to seek anything further beyond "place," especially since we say that each of these signifies a place individually?
<margin>A</margin>But if we say "one thing is in another" when we say "where," we are not stating a single or simple thing. Furthermore, if every time we affirm that "this is here," we are not stating a simple fact but creating a certain relationship—both of this thing within that thing, and of the thing being received to the thing that receives it—why do we not place this
<margin>B</margin>very thing in the category of **Relatives**? <note>original: "relatiuorum" / "πρός τι". Plotinus suggests that "being in a place" is just a relationship between an object and its location, not a separate category of being.</note> For indeed, from the relationship of each to the other, something is generated. Likewise, it makes no difference if, while living in Athens, you say "I am here," or "I am in Athens." But this very word "here," since it is a demonstrative sign, they will admit signifies a place; and therefore, they will confess that the phrase "he is in Athens" also designates a
<margin>C</margin>place. For this reason, "at Athens" properly belongs to the category of place itself. Again, if "at Athens" is the same as "being in the city of Athens," then surely beyond place, the "being" itself is also predicated. Yet this was not appropriate, just as it is not right to assign "it is a quality" as the genus of **Quality**; rather, only "quality" itself should be assigned. To this it may be added that if it is necessary to bring in a different category for what is said to be "in time" or "in place," apart from time and place themselves, why does not that which is "in a vessel" <note>original: "in vase" / "ἐν ἀγγείῳ". Plotinus uses the example of a jar or container to show the absurdity of creating infinite categories for "containment."</note> induce another category? Or that which is "in matter," another?
<margin>D</margin>Again, another for what is "in a subject"? Likewise, should there be another category for what is "a part in a whole," or "the whole in its parts," "the genus in its species," or "the species in its genus"? In this way, we would end up counting even more categories than we already have.

---

### Activity, Action, or Motion might perhaps more rightly be established as a category than "Doing." Chapter XI.

<margin>A</margin>In that category which they call **Doing** <note>original: "facere" / "ποιεῖν". This is one of Aristotle's ten categories, often translated as Action.</note>, one may consider the following. It is taught, indeed, that after **Substance**, those things which surround substance must be placed, just as quantity and number are. Therefore, quantity is asserted by them to be a different genus. Likewise, because **Quality** exists around substance, "the qualified" is placed as another genus. Thus, since **Action** <note>original: "effectio" / "ποίησις"</note> is also around the same substance, they think that this "doing" is itself another genus. Should we therefore establish "doing" itself, or rather "action" from which the "doing" proceeds?
<margin>B</margin>Just as Quality must be established, from which "the qualified" likewise arises. Or rather, should "action," "doing," and "the doer"—or "doing" and "action"—be gathered into one? Now, "doing" designates the agent <note>The one performing the act.</note> more so, while "action" does not. And yet, "doing" clearly signifies being occupied in a certain activity; but that is to exist in a state of **Activity** <note>original: "actus" / "ἐνέργεια". This is a central Platonic and Aristotelian concept meaning "actuality" or "activity."</note>. From this it follows that **Activity** should rather be the category.
<margin>C</margin>Indeed, this activity is affirmed to be observed around the essence, just as quality is there; and this activity in turn moves around the essence like **Motion**. And surely, motion exists as one certain genus of things. For why is quality one thing around the essence, and quantity similarly one thing? Or relation, because of a certain habit of one thing toward another? Why should motion, which is similarly around the essence, not similarly become one genus?

<column-break/>

...and parts of place, just as up and down here are species or parts. They differ, however, in that some are more defined. If, then, up and down and the center are places—as Delphi is the center, and those things near the center, such as the Athenians, the Lyceum, and the others—what further do you think we are seeking beyond "place," especially when we say that each of these signifies place? And if "one thing in another" is said when we speak, we are not speaking of a simple thing. Furthermore, if we say "the thing here," we produce a certain relationship of this in that, and of the receiver toward that which it received. Why then is this not among the "Relatives," if it was generated from the relationship of each toward the other? Whether there is a difference between "here" and "at Athens"—but they will say "here" is demonstrative and signifies place, and "at Athens" as well, so that "at Athens" is in a place. If "in Athens" also signifies "is," then "at Athens" signifies both the place and the "is" beforehand. But it should not. Just as the genus of "quality" is not "it is a quality," but only "quality." In addition to what has been said, if "in time" is something else, both "in time" and "in place," why will "in a vessel" not make another category? And "in matter" another, and "in a subject" another? And "part in a whole" or "the whole in parts," and "genus in species," and "species in genus"—or in this way, our categories will be more numerous.

---

In what is called "Doing," one might investigate these things. For it is said that since, after substance, those things around substance must follow—as quantity and number—they call "the quantified" its own genus. And quality being around it, "the qualified" is another genus. So also, action being present, "doing" is another genus. Is it then "doing," or "action" from which "doing" comes? Just as quality is that from which "the qualified" comes. Or is action, doing, and the doer—or doing and action—to be taken as one? "Doing" rather manifests the "doer," but "action" does not. Is "doing" not simply appearing to be in something, namely, in "activity"? So that "activity" is rather the category. Or it is said to be observed around the essence, as quality is there. And activity itself is around the essence just like "motion." And motion is a motion of beings. For why is quality something around the essence, and quantity something? And relatives because of the relationship of one to another? But motion, being around the essence, shall it not be one genus, though motion is a genus?

<summary>Plotinus argues that the category of "Where" is not a separate genus but belongs to "Place" or "Relative," and suggests that the category of "Doing" should be replaced by "Activity" or "Motion."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section where Plotinus critiqued the categories of "Where" and "When." Here, he transitions to Chapter 16, focusing on the category of "Doing" (Action) and specifically examining the relationship between "Activity" and "Motion."</meta>

# BOOK ONE.

-> Perhaps activity should more correctly be established as a category: and under it, one type of activity being perfect, such as habit and form; and the other imperfect, such as motion toward habit and form. Chapter 16. <-

-> Motion is not called an "imperfect activity" <note>original: "imperfectus actus" / "ἀτελὴς ἐνέργεια". This is a famous Aristotelian definition that Plotinus is examining and refining.</note> by its own nature: for at the very moment it begins, it is already activity and motion; rather, it is called so because of something else to be perfected after the motion. Just as an act and often a change occur in a single moment, so motion beginning in a moment is already simply motion: but it involves time insofar as it also involves quantity. <-

***

<margin>A</margin> BUT IF ANYONE should object that motion is an imperfect activity, nothing would yet seem to prevent us from placing activity <note>original: "actum" / "ενέργειαν". In this context, "activity" refers to the actualization of a potential.</note> in the primary position, and motion as a species <note>A sub-type or category.</note> of it, subjecting motion to activity as something imperfect. In this way, we would predicate "activity" of motion, while adding "imperfect" as a specific difference. For motion is called "imperfect" not because it is not an activity—for it is entirely an activity—but because it involves a certain repeated succession. This is not so that the motion itself
<margin>B</margin> might eventually arrive at being an activity (for it already exists as an activity), but so that it might produce something else which is beyond the motion itself. In that case, it is not the motion itself that is then perfected, but rather the thing toward which the mover intended his mind. For example, walking was "walking" right from the very start. But if it were necessary to cross a certain distance <note>original: "statum" / "στάδιον". A stadium was a Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet.</note>, and that distance had not yet been crossed, surely this deficiency belongs neither to the walking nor to the motion itself, but rather to that "specific amount" of walking. Walking, however, was walking in whatever amount it occurred; and
<margin>C</margin> thus it was already motion. Indeed, he who is moving has already moved, and he who cuts has already cut. <note>Plotinus is arguing that motion is "complete" at every moment of its existence; you don't need to finish a journey for the "act of walking" to have been real.</note> And just as that which is called "activity" does not require time, neither does motion—except for a motion specifically extended to a certain point. If an activity occurs in an instant, surely motion does as well, insofar as it is motion simply and entirely. But if they say that motion must occur in time because it possesses continuity, the answer is that vision, too, when uninterrupted, has continuity and yet acts in time.
<margin>D</margin> An argument for this is also provided by the faculty of proportion: which teaches that one can always take one part after another from any motion, and that there is no "first" moment of time in which it began, nor is there a first starting point of the movement. Instead, it is always possible to divide a motion further back, so that it turns out that a motion just recently begun has already proceeded from an infinite time, and the motion itself is similarly infinite as far as its beginning is concerned. <note>This refers to the paradox of the continuum: if motion and time are infinitely divisible, you can never find a "first" indivisible unit of start-time.</note> This happens because
<margin>E</margin> they separate "activity" from "motion." They claim activity happens in an instant <note>original: "non tempore" / "ἀχρόνῳ" (timelessly).</note>, but they admit that motion requires time. I say "motion" not just as a specific amount, but they claim the very nature of motion is necessarily a quantity. And yet, they themselves admit that being a "certain amount" belongs to motion only by accident <note>A philosophical term meaning a non-essential property; for example, being "two miles long" is accidental to the nature of "walking" itself.</note>—as when a motion lasts a day or any other length of time. Just as activity occurs in an instant, nothing prevents motion from also having begun in an instant; time then accrues to the motion because the motion turned out to be of a certain duration.
<margin>F</margin> Since even "changes" are conceded to occur in an instant—as it is often said that a change is partly completed all at once, and partly not. If change can happen in an instant, why not motion? We have taken "change" <note>original: "mutatio" / "μεταβολή".</note> here not in the sense of a completed shift, for it did not require that specific kind of change which consists properly in a state of having already been changed.

<sig>Cc 3</sig>

<column-break/>

partly not. If change can happen in an instant, why not motion? We have taken "change" here not in the sense of a completed shift, for it did not require that specific kind of change which consists properly in a state of having already been changed.

<summary>Plotinus argues that motion (kinesis) should be classified as a type of activity (energeia). He disputes the traditional view that motion is inherently imperfect or defined by time, suggesting instead that motion is a complete activity at every moment it exists.</summary>
