# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

*It would be more probable to place action and passion under motion as a genus <note>A "genus" is a general category or class that contains more specific "species."</note>, rather than treating these two as additional independent categories. To be a "relative" is not simply to belong to something or to lean toward something, but for its very essence to consist of a mere relationship.*

### Chapter XVII.

<margin>A</margin> BUT IF ANYONE should claim that neither activity nor motion are categories in themselves, but should instead be reckoned in the category of relatives—on the grounds that an act is the activity of a certain active power, and motion is the movement of a certain motive power—we must explain how this "motive" quality arises. Relatives are always generated by the relationship itself, and not merely by the fact that they are spoken of in reference to another. However, when there is a certain underlying reality <note>original: "subsistentia" / "ὑπόστασις" (hypostasis). This refers to the actual, independent existence of a thing before it is compared to something else.</note>, even if it belongs to another or is directed toward another, it nonetheless possesses its own nature prior to that relationship. <margin>B</margin> In this case, activity, motion, and even a "habit" <note>original: "habitus" / "ἕξις" (hexis). In philosophy, a "habit" is a stable quality or disposition a person possesses, like knowledge or a virtue.</note>, though existing in relation to something else, do not lose that internal capacity by which they exist and are understood in themselves before the relationship is considered. Otherwise, everything would be reduced to a relative. For everything has some kind of relationship to something else, which is even true of the soul. Now, why should this "production" or the act of "doing" itself not be placed in the number of relatives? For it will certainly be either a motion or an activity. If, however, <margin>C</margin> they place the "effect" in the order of relatives, but make the "doing" itself a single category, what prevents them from also referring "motion" to something else, while asserting that "being moved" is a single category? And yet, they are permitted to divide "being moved" into two main species: namely, "doing" and "suffering" <note>original: "facere atq; pati" / "ποιεῖν καὶ πάσχειν". In ancient logic, "action" and "passion" (being acted upon).</note>, though they do not claim that "doing" is a genus, nor that "suffering" is a genus.

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the translation of the parallel Greek text for Chapter 17.</note>

If anyone should say that neither activity <note>original: "ἐνέργειαν"</note> nor motion <note>original: "κίνησιν"</note> is a genus in itself, but should be reduced to relatives because activity is the activity of an acting subject and power is the power of a moving subject, it must be said that relatives have their origin in a relation. But when they are only said to be in respect to another, and there is a certain subsistence <note>actual existence</note>, even if it belongs to another and is toward another, it has its nature before the relation. This applies to activity and motion. Even a "habit" <note>disposition</note>, being something else, is not deprived of being understood in itself before it is a relative. Otherwise, everything will be a relative, for everything has some relation to something else—even the soul. Why should "production" and "doing" not be reduced to relatives? For it will be either motion or activity. If they reduce "production" to a relative but make "doing" a genus, why not also reduce motion to a relative and make "being moved" a genus? They will divide "being moved" into two, into "doing" and "suffering," but they do not say "doing" is a genus, nor "suffering."

***

*Motion itself requires time, not so much to simply exist, but to have duration. Likewise, not every action is referred to a "passion" (being acted upon), such as walking or thinking. Furthermore, motion, action, passion, sense-perception, and intellection—beyond the fact that they are the acts of someone and are directed toward something—exist absolutely as something in themselves.*

### Chapter XVIII.

<margin>A</margin> FURTHERMORE, WE MUST CONSIDER whether it is correct to say that within the act of "doing," some things are activities <note>original: "actus" / "ἐνεργείας"</note> while others are motions; and that activities are completed all at once, whereas motions are of such a nature as "cutting" <note>original: "diuidere" / "τέμνειν". Plotinus is distinguishing between a complete act (like seeing) and a process that takes time to finish (like cutting a piece of wood).</note>. For cutting unfolds in time. Or will they perhaps say that all activities are motions, or at least accompanied by motion? Likewise, will they refer all "production" to "passion" <note>the state of being acted upon</note>, or will they claim some are absolute, such as walking and speaking? Again, <margin>B</margin> will they name all impulses directed toward a passion as "motions," while calling absolute ones simply "activities"? Or perhaps place both in both? Now, walking itself, which is something absolute, they will easily call a "motion"; but thinking <note>original: "intelligere" / "νοεῖν"</note>, to which no passive subject responds, they will (I believe) call an "activity" or "action." Otherwise, thinking and walking would not be "doing" something. But if these are not in <margin>C</margin> the category of "doing," where should they be placed? Perhaps they will refer "thinking" to the "thought-object" <note>original: "intelligibile" / "νοητὸν"</note>, just as they refer "intellection" to it. For they refer "sense-perception" to the "sensible object"—so why not also refer the act of "sensing" to the sensible object? And yet, sense-perception, which is indeed referred to another, does have a relationship to it; but meanwhile, it nonetheless possesses something beyond that relationship: namely, the fact that it is a certain activity or a passion. If, therefore, passion exists beyond the fact that it belongs to someone or is produced by someone, it is...
<meta>The text cuts off here with the catchword "a," continuing the sentence on the next page.</meta>

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the translation of the parallel Greek text for Chapter 18.</note>

It must be considered whether they are right to call some things "activities" and others "motions," saying activities are those that happen all at once, and motions are like "cutting." But one should not use "cutting" as the only example. Either all are motions, or they involve motion. And do they refer all "production" to "suffering," or are some absolute, like walking and speaking? And if those involving suffering are all motions, and the absolute ones are activities, or both in each? For walking, being an absolute act, they might call a motion; but thinking, which has no passive object, they would call an activity—otherwise thinking and walking are not "doing." But if these are not in "doing," where are they? Perhaps they will place "thinking" in relation to the "thought-object," just as they do with "intellection." And also "sense-perception" in relation to the "sensible object." But if sense-perception is toward the sensible object, why is the act of "sensing" not also toward the sensible object? Indeed, sense-perception, which is toward another, has its relation to that object, but it has something besides the relation: namely, being an activity or a suffering. If then suffering, besides being of something or by something, is something...

He argues that activities like walking or thinking have an internal reality that exists before they are ever put into relationship with an object.</summary>

# BOOK ONE.

For walking, while it also possesses the quality of "belonging to something"—specifically belonging to the feet and being performed by someone—nevertheless possesses the internal character of being a motion. If this is so, then thought as well, besides its relationship to an object, has the intrinsic quality of being either a motion or an activity <note>Original: "energeia" / "actus". Plotinus is distinguishing between an "act" that achieves a result and "activity" which is the functioning of a faculty like the mind.</note>.

---

-> *We shall probably establish motion as a genus <note>A "genus" is a broad classification that contains sub-categories or species.</note>: which we will divide into motion arising from within and motion occurring from without. Chapter XIX.* <-

-> *The first we shall call "action," whether it remains within or goes out into another. The second we shall call "passion": whether one thinks these motions (action and passion) differ in reality or only in definition.* <-

---

<margin>A</margin> After these things, we must consider whether some activities seem to be "imperfect" unless they have taken up time, so that they coincide with motions—such as "to live" and "life." For "living" for each person seems to consist in a perfected time. Even happiness <note>Original: "eudaimonia." For the Greeks, this was not a fleeting emotion but a lifelong state of flourishing.</note> is considered by some to be an activity that does not exist in an indivisible moment, but is thought to be a kind of motion. From this, it must be said that both are motions, and that motion itself exists as a single genus. <margin>B</margin> This can be seen as a genus existing in itself beyond the category of "Quantity" (which is in substance) and beyond "Quality"; thus, motion is a single thing concerning substance. If you like, you may divide this common motion into two "movings": some of which appear to pertain to the body, and others to the soul. Or, some are in the power of the moving things themselves, while others come into them from elsewhere, under the influence of other things. Or, some come properly from the things themselves, and others from foreign sources. <margin>C</margin> Then, those that come from the things themselves are "actions," whether they pass into other things or are self-contained. Those that depend on other things are "passions" <note>Original: "passiones" / "pathē." In this context, "passion" means the state of being affected or acted upon by an external force.</note>, even though motions that pass into other things seem to be the same as those said to depend on others. For "division," whether considered in the one who divides or in the thing being divided, is one act; but "to divide" is different from "to be divided." Perhaps, however, the division itself is not one and the same when it is inflicted by the divider and received by the divided. Rather, "to divide" and "to be divided" are nothing other than one motion succeeding another in the divided thing <margin>D</margin> as a result of such an action. Or perhaps the difference is not measured by the "being divided" itself, but by something else resulting from the motion, such as "feeling pain"; for in this, "suffering" consists. What, then, should be said when nothing feels pain? What else, except that the act of the agent exists in the patient, taking the place of pain or passion? For it happens that what is called "doing something" is of this nature; thus, "doing" <margin>E</margin> appears to be twofold: one type not in another thing, and the other situated in another. It should not be further divided as if "doing" and "suffering" were two different things; rather, the very fact of "doing in another" provides the occasion for two things to appear here, one of which is "doing" and the other, conversely, is "suffering." For example, the task of "writing," although it is received in another [the tablet], does not bring about a corresponding "passion" in the tablet, because it produces nothing else in the writing besides the act of the writer itself—which is quite different from "feeling pain." If someone says it brings about something else, such as the state of "having been written," he does not thereby introduce a "passion" into the discussion.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the Aristotelian categories of "Action" (doing) and "Passion" (being acted upon). Plotinus is exploring whether these are two distinct categories or simply different ways of looking at a single "Motion." He uses the example of walking and the sensation of pain to distinguish between an act that has an external effect and one that remains internal to the actor.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin> And yet in the act of walking itself, although the ground is beneath us and is trodden upon by our steps, one would not add here that the ground has "suffered" anything from it. But when someone walks upon the body of a living creature, a "passion" <note>The term "passion" (Latin: *passio*; Greek: *pathos*) in this philosophical context does not mean emotion, but rather the state of being acted upon or undergoing a change caused by an external force.</note> is immediately perceived, since one calculates the pain arising from it—considering the pain, I say, and not the walking itself; otherwise, one would have considered the walking a "passion" even in the previous case of the ground. Thus, in all things, we must say that "acting" is one specific type of thing, along with that which is <margin>B</margin> said to "suffer" and its opposite. However, what is said to "suffer" is the result that occurred later; it is not strictly the "opposite" in the same way that "to be burned" is the opposite of "to burn." Rather, "passion" and "suffering" are terms used when something recoils back upon the thing itself from the single event of burning and being burned—whether that result be pain <margin>C</margin> or something else, such as a kind of consumption. What then? If someone performs this very act so as to inflict pain, does not one person act while the other suffers? And from a single activity, are not two things accomplished, where one performs and the other undergoes? Perhaps, however, in the action itself, the intention of inflicting pain is no longer counted; rather, the person does something else, through which they affect the other with pain. This single and identical act, happening within the one who is to feel pain, causes that person to additionally "be affected by pain." What then should be said of that act? That it is a single thing even before it inflicts pain? Or even where no pain is inflicted, is there not a "passion" in that very thing upon which the act is directed? Such as in hearing? But perhaps hearing itself is not a "passion," nor is any sensation a "passion" at all. But to be weighed down by pain is to be placed in a state of "passion," which effect should not be judged as the "opposite" of the action.

---

->*Some actions are not accompanied by "passion" (being acted upon), such as understanding and sensation; some are accompanied by it internally, such as things that rub against each other in turn, or when a heating object is mutually cooled by the cold one; some are accompanied by it externally. And this happens in two ways: either a manifest passion accompanies the action from the outside, as with one who cuts; or it is hidden, as with one who walks; or even most hidden, as when the body is moved and formed by the soul. Chapter XX.*<-

---

<margin>A</margin> BUT let it be, if you like, that they are not opposites; nevertheless, since "suffering" is something other than "doing," it is not placed in the same genus <note>A "genus" is a broad category of being in Aristotle’s system of logic.</note> as the "action." Or perhaps, if both are motions, they are in the same genus, just as "alteration" <note>The term "alteration" (*alteratio*) refers specifically to a change in quality, such as turning from cold to hot.</note> itself is a motion according to quality. Is it therefore the case that when alteration proceeds from a quality, there is "action" and "doing" there, while the quality itself remains free from "passion"? Or perhaps if it is removed from "passion," it is occupied only with "doing." But <margin>B</margin> if it suffers while acting upon another—as in mutual striking—it no longer just "does"; or rather, does anything prevent it from suffering while it acts? If, therefore, "suffering" involves something like being worn down, why is it judged more as "doing" than "suffering"? Is it because it is worn down in turn while it rubs, and thus suffers? Shall we then say that because it is mutually moved, there are two motions occurring around it? But how could there be two? Is there then only one? But in what way is the same motion both "action" and "passion" at the same time? In this view, it would be called "action" insofar as it emanates from one thing, and "passion" insofar as it flows from there into another, while remaining a single motion. Shall we then say the motion is something else? And in what way will that motion, which is itself an "alteration," dispose or affect the sufferer, while the agent itself does not suffer from the other in the same respect?

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> And in the case of walking, even if the ground is underlying, it does not claim to have suffered. But when one walks upon the body of a living thing, the "suffering" is the pain that follows, since one reasons that the walking [caused it], or one would have perceived it even before. For in all cases, regarding the "doing," one must speak of it as one thing along with what is called "suffering," the [later] cause <margin>Β</margin> or the opposite. For example, "to be burned" is the opposite of "to burn." But that which arises from the single event of "burning" or "being burned"—the thing happening to it—is either pain or something else, like wasting away. What then if someone works this very thing so as to cause distress? Does not one person "do" and the other "suffer," and from one activity come the two? Does one "do" and the other "suffer"? Or in that activity, is the "doing of distress" the same as the [feeling] of <margin>C</margin> distress? Rather, he does something else through which the other feels distress. This, happening in the one who will feel distress, being one and the same, has made "feeling distress" something else. What then is that one thing that happens even before it causes distress? Or is it that where distress is not produced at all, is there a "passion" in that into which it is brought, such as "to hear," or is hearing a "passion"? Or is sensation in general a passion? But to feel distress is to be found in "passion," which is not the opposite of "doing."

<margin>Α</margin> BUT let it not be an opposite; yet being different from "doing," it is not in the same genus as the "action." Or are both a "motion," in the same genus, as "alteration" is a motion according to quality? Is it then that when alteration comes from the quality, it is "action" and "doing," while the quality is unaffected, or even being unaffected it remains in the "doing"? But if, * while acting upon another, <margin>Β</margin> such as * striking, it also suffers, it no longer only "does," or does nothing prevent one who "does" from also "suffering"? If then, according to the "suffering" itself, such as "rubbing," why should it be "doing" rather than "suffering"? Is it because it is rubbed in return and suffers? Is it then that because it is moved in return, we shall say there are two motions about it? And how two? Is there then one? And how is the same thing "doing" and "suffering"? In this way, "doing" is what comes from another, and "suffering" is what goes into another. And it is the same. But do we say it is different? And how will the "alteration"—that is, the motion—affect the sufferer in some different way, while the one "doing" is unaffected by that?

# BOOK ONE.

For how would it suffer that which it performs in another? Does the fact that the motion is in another not mean that the "passion" <note>original: "πάσχειν" (paschein) / "passio"; in this context, it refers to the state of being the recipient of an action.</note> is that which the subject undergoes according to the actor? But if the formative principle <note>original: "ὁ λόγος" (ho logos)</note> is what whitens, and the swan is what is whitened—that is, the swan coming into being—shall we say the swan "suffers" as it passes into its essence? And if, after it has come into being, it should be whitened further; or if one thing increases and another is increased, does the thing being increased "suffer," or is "passion" only found in qualitative change? But if one thing makes something beautiful, and another thing is beautified, does the thing being beautified "suffer"? If, in the act of beautifying, one thing becomes worse or is obscured—as happens with tin <note>original: "καττίτερος" (kattiteros)</note>—while the bronze <note>original: "χαλκὸς" (chalkos)</note> becomes better, shall we say the bronze "suffers" while the tin "acts"? And how shall we say the student "suffers" when the activity of the teacher passes into him? How could this be a "passion" if it is a single internal act? Perhaps it is not a passion in itself, but the one who possesses it is "the sufferer," in that "suffering" is understood as something belonging to someone. For it is not because the learner has done nothing himself that he is said to "suffer." For learning is not like being hit or struck, since it consists in a kind of apprehension or discernment; just as seeing is not the same as being struck.

---

**B**Y what notion, then, do we recognize "passion"? Is it by the activity that comes from another? If the one who received the activity made it his own by taking it up. But look whether it is not an activity at all, but only a "passion." Or is it not so, even if the thing becomes better, while the activity itself is in a worse state? Or if someone should act through vice and rule over another intemperately, does anything prevent the action from being base and the passion from being honorable? By what, then, shall we distinguish them? Shall we define "acting" as an act proceeding from oneself into another, and "suffering" as an effect resulting in one thing from another? What then if an act proceeds from a thing but does not pass into another, such as the act of thinking or opining? What if someone grows hot from within himself, whether from intense thought or rather from anger sparked by an internal opinion, without anyone from the outside provoking him? Perhaps "acting" is simply a certain impulse bursting forth from the thing itself, whether it remains within or acts upon another. Is every desire and appetite <note>original: "ὄρεξις" (orexis)</note> then such a thing? Perhaps if the appetite is incited by the desirable object, it is a passion, even if one does not specify who incited it, but only that it was awakened following that object. This appetite is no different than if one were pushed or even cast down by an impulse. Should we then divide appetites, saying that some are actions...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> For in what way would it suffer that which it does in another? Is it not this very fact—namely, that the motion is in another—that is the cause of it being a "passion" for us? Which passion certainly had not existed in the effector. But if this thing makes another white, as the formative principle <note>original: "seminaria Cygni ratio"; the "seed-like reason" or internal blueprint of the swan.</note> of the Swan does, and this other thing is made white—namely, the emerging Swan—shall we say the Swan "suffers" while it is proceeding into its essence? But if, afterwards, having been born, it is made white; likewise, if this thing increases and that thing is <margin>B</margin> increased, shall we grow accustomed to saying the increased thing "suffers"? Or shall we rather place "passion" in the quality itself? Furthermore, if this thing makes something beautiful, and this other becomes beautiful, shall we meanwhile confess that what is made beautiful "suffers"? If, therefore, that which renders a thing beautiful meanwhile becomes worse or is darkened—like tin—while the other turns out better—like bronze <note>This refers to the ancient process of alloying or coating metals where one substance might lose its luster to improve the other.</note>—shall we say the bronze "suffers" and the tin "acts"? Finally, how shall we say the learner "suffers"? Namely, by the very <margin>C</margin> act of the effector now proceeding into him. But truly, how will this be a "passion" when it is a single act? Perhaps it is not a passion in itself; but he who possesses it is "the sufferer"; since the "suffering" itself is accepted just as if it were something belonging to someone. For he is not said to "suffer" from the fact that the learner has done nothing himself. For to learn is not like being hit or struck; since it consists in a certain apprehension and discernment; just as seeing is not the same as being struck.

---

->*We can define both action and passion through a certain motion or act. But that indeed is said to "act" whose motion takes its beginning from itself, whether something happens in another from this or nothing happens. That, however, is said to "suffer" whose motion only falls upon it from elsewhere, whether it goes toward the worse or toward the better. Likewise, whether it falls from a separate agent, like a beating, or from a joined one, like an alteration in the body from an opinion or an affection of its own soul, and those affections incited from without. Chapter XXI.*<-

---

<margin>A</margin> **B**Y what notion, therefore, shall we properly designate "suffering" itself? We certainly shall not discern it by a certain act because it depends on another; if indeed he who has received the act has claimed it for himself as if it were his own. But is it not where no act occurs, but only a passion? What then if that which is said to "suffer" becomes better, but the act itself is in a worse state? Or if someone acts through depravity and rules over another intemperately? Does anything perhaps prevent the action from being <margin>B</margin> depraved, and the passion from being honest? By what, then, shall we most powerfully distinguish them? Shall we define "doing" itself through a certain act passing from any given thing into another? And "suffering" through an effect resulting in another from elsewhere? What then shall we say? If it stands forth from any given thing, but by no means passes into another? Such is certainly the act of understanding and opining. What likewise? When someone grows hot immediately from himself? Whether that happens from a vehement <margin>C</margin> thought, or rather anger, which his own opinion has raised when no one at all was provoking him from anywhere. Perhaps "doing" itself is—whether it remains in itself or acts upon another—a certain impulse bursting forth from the thing itself. Is desire, therefore, and every appetite <term>Appetitus: a reaching out or inclination toward an object.</term> a certain something? Perhaps if the appetite is incited by the desirable object, it is a certain passion, even if no one has added by whom it is incited, but only this: that it was excited after that object. This appetite, therefore, is no different than if someone were pushed, or even as if headlong from an impulse. Should we then divide appetites, saying that some are actions...

<summary>Plotinus explores the definitions of "Action" and "Passion," arguing that they are often two sides of a single motion. He challenges the idea that "suffering" (being acted upon) is always a passive or negative state, using examples like learning, the whitening of a swan, and the interaction of metals.</summary>

->Chapter XXII.<-

> *The same motion can be called "action" if it is referred to the agent, and "passion" if it is referred to the patient. When we speak strictly, we distinguish it from "effecting": saying that after an action, no separate work created by it remains, such as usually exists and remains through the process of effecting.*

<margin>A</margin> Perhaps, then, suffering occurs because something has motion within itself—I mean the motion of alteration—through which it is altered in some way. Acting, however, is either having an absolute motion within and from oneself, or putting forth a motion from oneself that passes into another, and which begins from the very thing said to "act." Yet motion is in both; but the difference distinguishing acting and suffering <margin>B</margin> is this: acting preserves the act itself, in that the acting is free of passion; suffering consists in being affected differently than before, while the very essence of the sufferer acquires nothing pertaining to its essence, but meanwhile suffers something else when some essence is generated. Therefore, the same thing is "acting" in one relation, and "suffering" in another. For in one respect it is considered acting, since the motion is the same; but in another respect it is suffering, because it is now being affected in this way. Both, therefore, seem to refer to something else <note>original: "ad aliquid referri" / "πρός τι" (pros ti). This refers to the Aristotelian category of Relation.</note>, insofar as the condition of acting relates to the property of suffering. Namely, <margin>C</margin> the same thing is acting in one regard, but suffering in another; and both are certainly considered not so much in themselves as together with the actor and the sufferer, where the former moves and the latter is moved, and both are two distinct categories. And here the former hands over motion, and the latter in turn receives motion; therefore, giving and receiving and relation occur there. Or certainly, if the one who receives possesses it—as one is said to possess a color—why should he not also be said to possess motion? Now <margin>D</margin> even absolute motion, such as walking, possesses "a walk," and thinking possesses "thought." Consequently, it is worth considering whether providing <note>original: "prouidere" / "προνοεῖν" (pronoein). Acting with foresight or "Providence."</note> is acting, and conversely, being governed by providence is suffering; for it is toward another and about another...

<column-break/>

->Chapter XXII.<-

Does suffering then occur because of the motion of alteration, according to which one is altered in whatever way? Acting, however, is either having the absolute motion within oneself, or a motion ending in another from oneself, starting from the one said to act. And motion is in both. The difference that divides acting and suffering is this: acting, insofar as it is acting, is kept free of passion. But suffering is in the change to being otherwise than one was before, with the essence of the sufferer receiving nothing toward its essence, but being something else while the sufferer is becoming some essence. Therefore, the same thing is "acting" in one relation, and "suffering" in another. For considered from this side, it will be acting, since the motion is the same; but from that side, it is suffering, because it is disposed in this way, so that both are "relative," insofar as acting is to suffering. If on this side it is the same acting, but on that side it is suffering. And each is considered not by itself, but with the actor and the sufferer. One moves, and the other is moved, and each is two categories. And one gives motion to this one, and this one receives; there is receiving and giving. And it is a relation, or if the receiver has it, just as one is said to have color, why does he not have motion? And absolute motion, such as walking, has "walking." And it has "thought." One must consider then if providing is acting, and being provided for is suffering. For it is toward another, and...

<summary>Plotinus explores the Aristotelian categories of Action and Passion, arguing that they are two ways of viewing a single motion—acting is the motion viewed from the source, while passion is the motion viewed from the recipient. He also distinguishes between changes that degrade a thing and those that contribute to its "essence" or completion, such as a statue being formed from bronze.</summary>

# BOOK ONE.

...providence <note>original: "ἡ πρόνοια" (hē pronoia). The divine foresight or care for the universe.</note>. But if providing is a form of doing, then even if the thinking is directed at something else, either that object is acted upon, or the thinking itself is a doing. For it is not directed into the thinker, but about the objects themselves. This is "making" <note>original: "ποίησις" (poiēsis). The act of creating or producing something external.</note> in the broad sense. Or must we say that every activity is a making? Or that "doing" something can happen by accident? For instance, if someone walking leaves footprints, we say they have "made" them, but this arises from their being something else or acting by accident, because they were not looking toward this result. We even say inanimate things "do" things—for example, that fire heats, or that a medicine "worked." But enough on these matters.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It seems to stem from providence. But perhaps providing is not "making," even if the understanding is about something else; nor is being ruled by providence a "suffering." Perhaps not even understanding is a "making." For the mind does not transfer itself into the object it understands; rather, it is about the object. Therefore, it is entirely an effect. One need not assert that all actions are "makings," or that they "do" anything. It is possible for a "making" to exist there by accident. What then should be said? <margin>B</margin> If someone walking should leave footprints, will we not admit they have made something? But indeed, because that person is becoming, acting, or deciding something, it follows by a certain contingency that they "make," and the action is by accident, since the mind was not at all attending to this result. After all, we even say that inanimate things "do" things, such as fire heating, or a medicine having produced an effect. But enough on these.

->The Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, who taught while walking in the Lyceum.</note> cannot assign a sufficient reason why wearing clothes creates a new category <note>original: "predicamentum." One of the ten fundamental classes of being defined by Aristotle.</note>, while possessing qualities in oneself, or possessing money, does not create a new category. Likewise, "wearing clothes" and "being armed" signify not one, but two different categories.<-

### Chapter XXIII.

---

<margin>A</margin> IT REMAINS to dispute concerning the category they call "Having" <note>original: "τὸ ἔχειν" (to echein) / "Habere".</note>. Surely, if they say "to have" is meant in many ways, what prevents all modes of having from being reduced into this one category? In this way, "how much" (Quantity) would be reduced here, because it "has" magnitude. Likewise, "what kind" (Quality) would be referred here because it "has" color. Again, it would be open to similar things: because a father "has" a son, and a son "has" a father; and <margin>B</margin> in short, all possessions and furniture that are "had." If they say that other things which are possessed remain in their own categories, but armor, shoes, and clothes belong in this specific category of "Having," first someone might ask: why so? And why does "having" these things create one distinct category, <margin>C</margin> while burning them, or cutting them, or hiding them, or throwing them away, does not create another category or categories? If they respond that a category is formed because these things are "around the body," it follows that if a garment is placed on a couch, another category is formed there, and another again if someone is entirely covered by a cloak. But if they assert the category is formed according to the specific act of containing and having, then surely all other things called "having" must necessarily be referred here under the same condition. All those things must be reduced to the "state" <note>original: "ἕξιν" (hexin) / "habitum". A disposition or condition of having.</note> itself, wherever that state may be. For it will make no difference what it is that is being had. Therefore, if in describing such a category one should not say "to have quality" (because quality is already discussed in its own place), nor "to have quantity" (because quantity already obtained its place), nor "to have parts" (because that was described under Substance), why then is it permitted to say "to have armor," when the "Substance" <note>original: "οὐσία" (ousia). The fundamental being or "thingness" of an object.</note> has already been defined, under which genus armor properly belongs? For shoes, clothes, and armor are all substances. Furthermore, how is this a "simple" thing belonging to only one category when we say "this man has armor"? For that signifies what is meant by "to be armed" or "being in a state of armor."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> IT REMAINS to dispute about the category they call "Having." Certainly, if they say that "having" is used in many ways, what prevents all modes of having from being equally brought into this category? Wherefore even "how much" itself will easily be reduced to this, since it "has" magnitude; likewise "what kind" will be referred to the same, because it "has" color. Again, let it be open to similar things: because a father has a son, and a son has a father; and <margin>B</margin> briefly, all possessions and furniture which are had. If they should say that all other things which are had are in those [other] categories of theirs, but armor and shoes and clothes are in this proper category of "Having," first someone will ask for what cause it is so. Then, why does "having" these things produce one other category, while <margin>C</margin> burning them, or dividing them, or hiding them, or casting them away, does not again make another category or others? If they answer that a category is made because they are wrapped around the body, it will follow that if ever a garment is placed on a bed, another category is made from that, and another again if someone were entirely covered by a garment. But if they assert that the category itself is made according to the act of containing and having itself, then surely all other things which are named according to this "having" must be referred here by the same necessity, and all those things must be reduced to "habit" <note>original: "habitum." Here meaning a state of being or "having" something, rather than a repetitive behavior.</note> wherever that habit may be. For it will matter nothing what it is that is had. Therefore, if in describing a category of this kind, one is not to say "having a quality" (since quality itself has already been mentioned in its place), nor "having a quantity" (since quantity has already obtained its place before), nor "having parts" (because that was properly described under Substance), why then is it permitted to say "having armor," when the substance has already been defined, in whose genus armor is properly contained? For shoes, clothes, and armor are substances. Moreover, in what way is this something "simple" and of only one category, when we say "this man has armor"? For that signifies what is said by "to be armed" or "to be in armor."

<summary>Plotinus concludes his discussion on action and providence, then critiques Aristotle's tenth category, "Having" (Habere). <meta>This page continues Plotinus's systematic critique of the categories of being. # PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS. BOOK VI.

Next, does this category of "Having" <note>original: "habendi praedicamentum". In Aristotle’s system, this refers to the state of possessing something, like wearing shoes or being armed.</note> <margin>A</margin> apply only to a living being, or also if a statue possesses the same things? For a living being seems to "have" in a different way than a statue, and perhaps this is an equivocal <note>original: "æquivoca". This means the same word is used for two very different concepts, like a "bank" of a river versus a "bank" for money.</note> condition. For when we say of both that "the living man stands" and "the statue of the man stands," we do not mean that they "stand" in the same sense. Finally, for a category that consists of so few instances and such minimal differences, what logical reason allows it to be made into a distinct category?

->*To be placed in this or that way, in such a figure or place, does not seem to introduce a new category beyond place, action, passion, or relation.*<-

### Chapter XXIII.

Finally, there follows that category <margin>A</margin> which they name "Position" <note>original: "poni vel in situ". This is the tenth Aristotelian category, referring to the physical arrangement of parts, like "sitting" or "lying down."</note> or "to be in a certain state." This also consists of very few examples and minimal differences, where people usually speak of "leaning back," "reclining," or "sitting." However, they want this to be a new category not simply because of being placed, but because of the specific mode of being placed—for instance, when it is said that someone is "positioned in such a shape." Here, the "shape" is one thing, but the "position" or the "act of being placed" signifies something else. Truly, since <margin>B</margin> this signifies being in a certain shape or place—and shape and place have already been categorized elsewhere—why is it necessary to pile two categories into one? Furthermore, if the word "sitting" signifies an act or an action, it should be placed in the genus of Actions; but if it signifies a passion <note>original: "passio". In this context, a passion is something happening to a subject, a being-acted-upon.</note>, it belongs in the genus of Passions. Next, what else does "being suspended" signify other than "being placed upward"? Just as its opposite signifies "being placed downward," and another signifies "being placed in the middle." Furthermore, since "reclining" has been placed in the genus of Relations, why should "being placed upward" not also be there? For since "the right side" is there, then "this thing on the right" and "that thing on the left" are also there. But enough has been argued regarding these matters.

->*Four categories should not be established under a single genus, as many of the Stoics and Cynics have done. Thus far, he has played against the ten categories of Aristotle and Archytas, perhaps for the sake of exercising his intellect. Hereafter, however, he acts more severely against those who placed Matter in the position of a Principle, and then grouped it in the same genus as those things that followed it.*<-

### Chapter XXIV.

After these things, we must speak against those <margin>A</margin> who introduce four categories <note>The Stoics. Unlike Aristotle’s ten, the Stoic school reduced everything to four: Substance, Quality, Disposition, and Relative Disposition.</note>, dividing reality into four: Subjects, Qualities, Dispositions, and Relative Dispositions. They attribute a certain "common something" to all of them, as they embrace everything within a single genus. Against them, one can bring many arguments, especially against their claim that one common genus fits all. Indeed, it was introduced by them quite thoughtlessly and without reason <margin>B</margin> when they call this "something" <note>original: "hoc aliquid" (Latin) or "to ti" (Greek). This is the Stoic "Supreme Genus," the most general category possible.</note>. It cannot be applied to both incorporeal things and bodies at the same time; nor have they left behind any differences by which they can distinguish this "something." And yet, this "something" is either a Being or it is not. If it is said to be a Being, it is just one among many species; but if it is not a Being, it follows that Being would be Non-Being, and many other things would follow from that genus. Therefore, let us dismiss these matters for the present and consider the division itself. To begin with, <margin>C</margin> by placing "Subjects" in the first rank, and placing Matter there before all other things, they act quite absurdly by counting the very thing they believe to be a "Principle" in the same order as those things which were placed after their own Principle.

<column-break/>

Next, does this apply only to living things <margin>A</margin> or to that which possesses these things? For each seems different, and perhaps they are named homonymously <note>original: "ὁμωνύμως" (homōnymōs). Things that share a name but have different definitions.</note>. For though "standing" is used for both, it is not the same thing. Furthermore, how is it reasonable to have another category for such few things?

Regarding "Position," it involves few things and <margin>A</margin> is distinguished by up and down—such as "sitting" and "lying." We speak of these, but in what way are they "positioned"? Even in such a shape. While "shape" is one thing, "downward" signifies something else, or else it is a combination of two categories already mentioned: shape and "a certain way." If "sitting" signifies an activity, <margin>B</margin> it must be placed among activities. If a passion, then among the things that are or are suffering. "To be suspended" or "to recline," just as "to lie downward" or "to be raised up," belong to place. Or again, the act of reclining is in the "Where," and the person reclining is there. Since "the right" is there, the "man on the right" and the "man on the left" are also there. Therefore, these things are sufficient.

Against those who set down four categories, <margin>A</margin> dividing them fourfold into Subjects, Qualities, Dispositions, and Relative Dispositions, and who set a "common something" over them as if embracing all things in one genus: one could say many things regarding this "common something" that happens to be in a genus over all. For just as with their own principles, it is irrational to call it "something" (like fire) <note>original: "τὶ πῦρ" (ti pyr). The Stoics believed the universe was composed of a creative fire.</note>, applying it to both incorporeal and corporeal things. They have not left behind differences by which they will separate this "something." And this "something" is either Being or Non-Being. If it is not Being, then one of the species is gone. If it is Non-Being, then Being is Non-Being and ten thousand other things. We must leave these for now and consider the division itself. For by placing "Subjects" <margin>C</margin> first, and then Matter, and then ordering the others, they rank the very thing that seemed to them to be the "First Principle" along with the things that come after their principle.

<summary>Plotinus concludes his critique of Aristotle's categories of "Having" and "Position," arguing they are redundant, before beginning a critique of the Stoic system of four categories (Substance, Quality, Disposition, Relation) and their overarching concept of "Something."</summary>

# BOOK ONE.

<margin>A</margin> First of all, they <note>Plotinus is referring to the Stoic philosophers here.</note> bring together prior things with posterior things into a single category, even though it is impossible for the prior and the posterior to exist within the same genus. For in those cases where there is a "prior" and a "posterior," the posterior certainly derives its very existence from the prior. However, in things that fall under the same genus, every member has an equality of being in relation to that genus. For a genus must be that which is predicated of species in answer to the question "what is it?" Since they themselves

<margin>B</margin> would admit, I believe, that all other things derive their essence from matter. Furthermore, when they introduce a single "subject" <note>original: "subiectum". In this context, it refers to the underlying material or substance that supports all properties.</note> in their counting, they are not really enumerating the things themselves, but are searching for the principles of things. There is a great difference between speaking of the principles of things and the things themselves. But if they wish matter alone to be "being," and all other things to be merely "passions" or affections of matter, then it was certainly not appropriate to place one genus over both "being" itself and these other things. It would perhaps have been better

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> if they had first established matter as "essence," and the remaining things as "passions" of that essence, perhaps dividing them later. Finally, it is absurd for them to say that some things are "subjects" and others are "the rest," since the subject is one and has no internal difference—unless perhaps it could be divided like a physical mass into parts. However, they do not even allow it to be divided,

<margin>B</margin> because they believe that substance is continuous. Therefore, they would have spoken better if they had not introduced "subjects" to us in the plural, but rather a single "subject."

->It is a sacrilege to establish matter—which is formless in itself and can only receive form from another source—as the primary principle of all things. Chapter XXVI.<-

>Especially because all things desire "act" <note>original: "actum". In philosophy, "act" or "actuality" refers to the fulfillment or reality of a thing, as opposed to its mere potential.</note> as a good: and by "act," I mean both form and action. Therefore, the highest and simplest act itself, in which there is no material "potency" <note>original: "potentiae". Potentiality or the capacity to become something else.</note>, is the ultimate end and the first principle. I say "act" is even superior to "form." For all things desire some act beyond mere form. It is ridiculous that, after they have placed simple matter in the position of a first principle, they add that matter is continuous and extended. For such a thing would no longer be simple, but would be mixed with quantity and quality. Finally, whatever consists of many parts, since it becomes "one" only by participation, depends on something that is "one" in itself, and therefore is entirely indivisible.

<margin>A</margin> Above all else, it seems most absurd to place matter, which exists only in "potency" <note>original: "in potentia" / "δυνάμει". Matter is seen as having the potential to become something, but no reality of its own.</note>, before all other things, rather than preferring "act" <note>original: "actum" / "ἐνέργειαν". Actual reality or activity.</note> itself over potency. For it is impossible for that which is in potency to ever come forward into act if that which is in potency holds the rank of the first principle in the order of things. For that which is only in potency will never lead itself toward something better; rather, there must be something existing in "act" before it. If that is so, then potency is no longer the principle. Or, if they say they exist simultaneously, they are placing the principles of things in a sort of random chance.

<margin>B</margin> Likewise, if they place them together, why do they not prefer the "act"? Why is this—meaning matter—judged to be "being" rather than the other? But if they assert that "act" is posterior to matter, one must ask under what conditions that could happen. For matter certainly does not generate "form" <note>original: "speciem" / "εἶδος". The internal logic or shape that makes a thing what it is.</note>, because the formless does not generate the beautiful, nor does that which is only in potency generate that which is in act. If act had ever existed there, the subject would no longer be "simple" matter. Furthermore, for them, God is also composed of matter and form. Here we must certainly ask: from where does His form come? But if God exists even without matter, since He is a certain "Reason" <note>original: "ratio" / "λόγῳ". Referring to the Logos or Divine Intellect.</note> possessing the property of a first principle,

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin> ...for surely the efficient principle is incorporeal <note>original: "incorporeus". Plotinus argues against the Stoic view that the active principle (God/Logos) is a physical body.</note>. But if he [the active principle] has an essence composed without matter, yet is still considered a body, it follows that they <note>The Stoic philosophers.</note> must introduce another kind of matter that is suitable for God. Furthermore, how can matter be a principle when it is itself a body? For it is impossible for a body not to be a "many" [a composite]. Indeed, every body is composed of matter and quality. But if this "body" they speak of is of a different nature, they are using the word "body" equivocally <note>original: "equiuocè". Meaning they are using the same word for two entirely different concepts.</note> when they apply it to matter. However, if they say the common property of a body is three-dimensional extension, they are certainly describing a "mathematical body."

<margin>B</margin> Truly, if they join this triple dimension with a certain "resistance" <note>original: "resistentia"; Greek: "ἀντιτυπίας" (antitypia). This refers to the physical solidity or "impenetrability" that distinguishes a physical object from a mere geometric shape.</note> to fulfill the definition of a body, they are no longer describing a single, simple thing. Furthermore, this property of resisting is a certain "quality," or something arising from a quality; and so it must be asked: from where does this resistance come? From where does the triple extension come? What forced it to extend? For matter is not contained within the very definition of three-dimensional

<margin>C</margin> dimension, nor, conversely, is three-dimensional extension found in the definition of matter. Therefore, since matter thus participates in magnitude, it is no longer "simple" <note>In Neoplatonism, the "First Principle" must be absolutely simple and undivided.</note>. Furthermore, from where does its unity come? For this underlying subject is not unity itself, but exists only through a participation in unity. It was worth considering that "mass" [bulk] cannot be placed before all things; rather, something separated from mass must be placed first, which is the One itself. And it is fitting that, starting from the One, we descend into the "many," and beginning from that which is segregated from magnitude, we arrive at magnitudes. Indeed,

<margin>D</margin> there cannot be a "many" unless there is a "One"; nor can magnitude exist unless there is something free from magnitude. Since magnitude is "one," it is not because it is the One itself, but because it participates in the One through a certain "meeting" <note>original: "congressionem". A coming together of different elements.</note> or conjunction. It is therefore necessary that that which is primarily and essentially the One exists before that which becomes "one" through a meeting, or even by contingency <note>original: "contingentiam". Something that happens to be true but isn't necessarily true by its own nature.</note>. Otherwise, how can a "fitting" union be produced? And what is the condition of this meeting? If they had asked this, perhaps they would have found the One itself, which is not "one" by chance. I say "by contingency" referring to that which does not possess unity in its own nature, but happens to be one because of something else.

->**Chapter XXVII.** If primary matter is subject to all things, both to moving causes and to forms, it cannot be the principle of things.<-

> *Neither does matter, formless in itself, give birth to forms, nor can any form lying within matter exist on its own, because it can never stand by itself; nor is their principle a certain form mixed with matter, for otherwise matter would not be limited. It is necessary that the most efficient mover be at last free from material impediments. If anyone should imagine that matter is the principle of forms, he will deny that it is a subject <note>A "subject" (hypokeimenon) is that which underlies properties; if matter "creates" forms, it is no longer the passive recipient.</note>, and will instead affirm that all forms exist through the very essence of matter. He would end up claiming that whatever truly exists in the world is matter, and the things produced are merely "imaginings." But in truth, since a form cannot naturally be produced from formless matter, much less can life—which is a more excellent form—be produced; and least of all can the Mind [Intellect], the most excellent form, come from it. Finally, the life-giving principle is something that does not "sprout" from matter, even though it is infused into matter. The principle of this life itself far transcends matter.*

It was right, moreover, to observe the principle of all things in a most venerable seat, and in no way to affirm as a "principle" that which is formless, liable to passion <note>original: "obnoxium passioni". In ancient philosophy, "passion" refers to being acted upon or changed by external forces.</note>, lacking life, deprived of mind, dark, and undefined, and then to ascribe to it the status of Essence itself. Indeed, God himself is introduced by them [the Stoics] only for the sake of a certain outward decorum, even though they possess...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...God would be incorporeal, as would the active cause. But if he [the cause] is himself the cause of composite matter, insofar as he is a body, they will have to introduce another matter for God. Then, how is matter a principle, being a body? For it is either a body, or it is not—and every body is composed of matter and quality. Or if this body is called so in another way, they use the name "body" equivocally for matter. But if they mean "body" as the common three-dimensional extension, they are speaking of a mathematical body.

<margin>B</margin> If they add resistance to the three-dimensional, they are not speaking of a single thing. Then, of what sort is this resistance? Is it a quality? And where does the resistance come from? How is it triply extended? Or who divided it? For matter is not in the triply extended, nor is the triply extended in matter. The triply extended is a participation in matter.

<margin>C</margin> But if it participates in magnitude, it would no longer be simple. Then, from where does the "union" come? For it is not union itself, but a participation in unity. It was necessary to reason that mass cannot exist before all things, but rather the "massless" and the One. And from the One, everything is spread out into the many. And from that which lacks magnitude, one arrives at magnitudes. For it is not possible for there to be a "many" without the One. Nor can there be magnitude without that which lacks magnitude. If magnitude were "one," it would be so not by being the One itself, but by participating in it.

<margin>D</margin> ...by a certain "meeting" [conjunction]. It must be that that which is primarily and properly [the One] exists before that which is so by meeting. How does this meeting occur? One might seek the cause of this meeting; for perhaps they would have always found the One which does not exist by contingency. I say "by contingency" that which is not the One itself, but receives it from another.

->**Chapter XXVII.**<-

It was necessary, moreover, to maintain the place of all things in that which is honorable, and not to refer Essence to that which is formless, nor to that which is passive, nor to that which is without a share of life, nor to that which is without intellect, or dark, or indefinite. It seems God is introduced by them only for the sake of propriety...

<summary>Plotinus argues against the Stoic belief that matter or a corporeal God could be the primary principle of the universe, asserting instead that the "One"—which is simple, massless, and incorporeal—must precede all physical magnitude and complexity.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: In the previous page, Plotinus began his critique of the Stoic categories, specifically attacking the idea that the primary principle of the universe could be a physical body or prime matter. He continues here by examining the relationship between the "underlying subject" (matter) and the active forces that shape it.</meta>

# BOOK ONE

<margin>A</margin> ...deriving its essence from matter, being both composite and subsequent—indeed, really existing as matter itself in a certain state. Therefore, if matter is the underlying subject <note>original: "subiectum"; Greek: "ὑποκείμενον" (hypokeimenon). This refers to the "stuff" that remains constant while qualities change.</note>, it is necessary that there be something else outside of it which, by acting upon it, employs it as something subjected to the functions delivered by that agent. But if the one who is said to be the driver of matter is himself within matter as a subject along with it, he will no longer employ matter as something subjected. Indeed, he cannot himself be a subject along with the matter; <margin>B</margin> otherwise, to what will these things be subjected, if there is no longer anyone present to make them subjects? For all things would have already been consumed into this very thing which is called the subject. Truly, the "subject" necessarily relates to something else—not indeed to what is within itself, but rather to that which is set out to act upon it. Surely the subject is exposed to that which is not the subject; and if this is so, it is exposed to something external. Therefore, this point seems to have been overlooked by them <note>The Stoics, whom Plotinus is critiquing.</note>. Furthermore, if <margin>C</margin> they have no need of anything external, but the subject itself is able to become all things—as if it were variously shaped in the manner of a dancer <note>original: "tripudio"; Greek: "ὀρχήσεως" (orchesis). Plotinus uses the dancer as an analogy for how a single thing can take on many forms through its own internal activity.</note> who transforms himself into almost all figures—then certainly it will no longer be a subject, but rather this very thing will be all things. For just as the dancer himself is not "subject" to his figures (since his gestures are a kind of activity <note>original: "enérgeia".</note> of his own form), so too that which they call matter will not be a subject to all things if all things come from it. Indeed, there would not even be "other things" at all, <margin>D</margin> since the remaining things are nothing other than matter itself in a certain state—just as the dancer, in the dance itself, existing in a certain state, is himself all the figures. But if there are no "other things," then matter itself will not be a subject at all; nor will it be the matter of things, but only matter. Therefore, it would not even be matter in the true sense, for matter is seen to refer to something else. That which refers to something else looks toward another thing and is spoken of in the same category, like "the double" in relation to "the half." Nor is essence <note>original: "essentia"; Greek: "οὐσία" (ousia).</note> defined by being a "double." How can being <margin>E</margin> relate to non-being, except perhaps by accident? But that which exists as being in itself, even matter itself, will be referred to as being. For if it is a certain "potentiality" for what is to come, but that future thing is not an essence, then matter itself is not an essence either. Because of this, it happens to them <note>The Stoic philosophers.</note> that while they blame those who create essences out of non-essences, they themselves meanwhile make a non-essence out of essence. For the world, insofar as it is the world, will not be an essence according to them. It is an impious thing to say that matter, which is the <margin>F</margin> subject, is essence, while bodies are not rather essences. It is much more absurd that the world itself does not exist as an essence, but only something which is a part of it is essence. And further, to say that a living being does not have its substance from the soul, but from matter alone, and that the soul itself is a certain "passion" or affection of matter, and subsequent to matter! From whom, then, did matter receive the power to be animated? And from where does the substance of the soul itself come? Likewise, how does matter subsist and take <margin>G</margin> form? Truly, when these very things become bodies, the soul is something other than they are. For even if the species <note>original: "species"; Greek: "εἶδος" (eidos), meaning the 'form' or 'defining characteristic'.</note> arrived from somewhere other than the soul, they would in no way be anything but inanimate bodies. <insert>+If something forms matter and procreates the soul, it follows that before the soul was procreated, there was already a procreating soul.</insert>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...deriving its essence from matter, being both composite and subsequent—indeed, really existing as matter itself in a certain state. Therefore, if matter is the subject, it is necessary that there be something else outside of it which, by acting upon it, employs it as something subjected to the functions delivered by that agent. But if the one who is said to be the driver of matter is himself within matter as a subject along with it, he will no longer employ matter as something subjected. Indeed, he cannot himself be a subject along with the matter; <margin>B</margin> otherwise, to what will these things be subjected, if there is no longer anyone present to make them subjects? For all things would have already been consumed into this very thing which is called the subject. Truly, the subject necessarily relates to something else—not indeed to what is within itself, but rather to that which is set out to act upon it. Surely the subject is exposed to that which is not the subject; and if this is so, it is exposed to something external. Therefore, this point seems to have been overlooked. Furthermore, if <margin>C</margin> they have no need of anything external, but the subject itself is able to become all things—as if it were variously shaped in the manner of one who transforms himself into almost all figures through dance—then certainly it will no longer be a subject, but rather this very thing will be all things. For just as the dancer himself is not subject to his figures (since his gestures are a kind of form of his figures), so too that which they call matter will not be a subject to all things if all things come from it. Indeed, there would not even be other things at all, <margin>D</margin> since the remaining things are nothing other than matter itself in a certain state—just as the dancer in the dance itself, existing in a certain state, is himself all the figures. But if there are no other things, then matter itself will not be a subject at all; nor will it be the matter of things, but only matter. Therefore, it would not even be matter: for matter is seen to refer to something else. And that which refers to something else looks toward another thing and is spoken of in the same category, like the double in relation to the half. Nor is essence defined by being a double. But how <margin>E</margin> can being relate to non-being, except perhaps by accident? But that which exists as being in itself, even matter itself, will be referred to as being. For if it is a certain potentiality for what is to come, but that future thing is not an essence, then matter itself is not an essence either. Because of this, it happens to them that while they blame those who create essences out of non-essences, they themselves meanwhile make a non-essence out of essence. For the world, insofar as it is the world, will not be an essence according to them. It is an impious thing to say that matter, which is the <margin>F</margin> subject, is essence, while bodies are not rather essences. It is much more absurd that the world itself does not exist as an essence, but only something which is a part of it is essence. And further, to say that a living being does not have its substance from the soul, but from matter alone, and that the soul itself is a certain passion of matter, and subsequent to matter. From whom, then, did matter receive the power to be animated? And from where does the substance of the soul itself come? Likewise, how does matter subsist and take <margin>G</margin> form? For even if the species arrived from somewhere other than the soul, the bodies would in no way be anything but inanimate. If something forms matter and procreates the soul, it follows that before the soul was procreated, there was already a procreating soul.

<summary>Plotinus critiques the Stoic view of matter, arguing that if matter is the primary substance and the soul is merely a "state" of matter, then the soul loses its status as an active principle. He uses the analogy of a dancer to show that matter cannot be both the unchanging subject and the source of its own dynamic activity.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Plotinus’s critique of Stoic philosophy, specifically their belief that matter is the most real substance because it persists through change. Plotinus argues that being "persistent" does not make matter "real" or "superior" to Mind.</meta>

-># PLOTINUS, ENNEADS, BOOK VI<-

*Matter, the more it remains the same beneath the shifting of forms, the more it is subject to change. For this reason, it is the lowest of all things. If the Mind were lower than matter, it could neither transcend matter nor perfectly grasp material things.*

### Chapter XXVIII.

<margin>A</margin> However, since there are many things openly contradicting this opinion which could easily be brought forward, we should be content with what has already been said, lest we find it disgraceful to struggle too stubbornly against such obvious errors. It will be enough to have shown who they are that affirm "non-being" <note>Plotinus considers matter "non-being" because it has no qualities of its own.</note> as the highest form of Being <note>original: "ens"</note>, and how they do not hesitate to place that which is weak at the very beginning of all things. The cause of such a great error arose because they followed the senses as their leader <margin>B</margin>, placing too much faith in them when establishing principles and other doctrines. Because they thought that only bodies were true things, and feared the mutual change of bodies into one another, they naturally thought that what remains beneath those changes is "being" itself. This is as if someone thought that a place was more of a "being" than the bodies within it, simply because the place is not destroyed. And although this matter remains with them, they should not have judged that everything which remains is "being" in any sense. Rather, they should have first considered <margin>C</margin> what the qualities of true Being are, through which the ability to remain always present might also exist. For even if a shadow remains, continually accompanying something else that is in constant flux, the shadow will not be more of a "being" than that which it follows. Yet even the sensible world, along with many other things in number, will surely seem a greater "being" (judging it as a whole) than any single thing contained within it. But if that whole substrate <note>original: "subiectum"; the underlying "stuff" or matter.</note> is "non-being," how can that specific thing be "being"? Truly, the most amazing thing <margin>D</margin> seems to be that those who grant the senses total authority over all things have not also affirmed that Being itself can be grasped by the senses. But they also incorrectly attribute "solidity" or "resistance" to Being, for that is merely a quality. If they say they perceive this with the mind, it would be an absurd mind that places matter before itself and gives the true duty of existing not to itself, but to matter. Since, therefore, the Mind is not "being" according to them, by what condition will it have credibility, when it speaks and judges everywhere concerning things more excellent than itself, even though it has no kinship with them? But concerning this nature and the substrates, enough has been discussed elsewhere.

<column-break/>

But indeed, since many things are said against this hypothesis, let us cease, lest it be strange to contend so zealously against such a manifest difficulty. It is sufficient to show how they established non-being as the most real Being, and placed the later as the first. The cause was that their sensation became their leader and was trusted for the establishing of principles and other things. For thinking that bodies were the beings, and then fearing their change into one another, they thought that which remains under them was Being. It is as if someone thought the place was more real than the bodies, thinking that place is not destroyed. And since it remains for them, they ought not to think that Being is just anything that remains. Rather, they should see what must be present to that which is truly Being, by which it will also share in remaining forever. For if a shadow remains forever while many other things pass by in multitude, it would be more of a "being." Or rather, how is that which is altered anything other than that? And the sensible thing, with many others in multitude, would be more of a "being." Or rather, not the things in that. But if the whole depth is that "non-being," how is it sensed? Most wonderful of all is that they trust sensation for each thing... <unclear>fragments</unclear> ...by not trusting sensation... <unclear>fragments</unclear> ...it is necessary to be Being. For if rightly the same thing... quality... <unclear>fragments</unclear> ...taking the essence, this mind is absurd, which ranks itself under matter and has given Being to matter. Not even the mind being for them, how could it be trusted, concerning the things more authoritative than itself... <unclear>fragments</unclear> ...and being in no way related to them. But about this nature and the substrates, it has been discussed sufficiently in other places.

---

*They had established four categories <note>original: "prædicamenta"</note>: first, the substrate (subject); second, the quality; third, the disposition (a thing in a certain state); and fourth, the relative disposition (a thing in a certain state relative to something else).*

### Chapter XXIX.

*This very thing which is added, called "quality," if it is something simple—as it ought to be—and if it makes its own category, then it must be incorporeal, which is exactly what they do not want. But if "quality" signifies something composite, the division is empty, for it would be dividing into a "substrate" and then again into a "substrate with quality." In general, when they say "quality" and "disposition," they either add nothing beyond matter existing in such a state, or they do add something. If they add nothing, there will really be only one category. If they add something, they never explain what this addition is when questioned. Nor do they ever distinguish between "matter with a quality" and "matter in a certain disposition," even though they intend to create multiple categories by this distinction. Finally, if there is nothing in nature except matter in a certain state, the Mind itself will be material, and will be able to judge neither matter nor separate things with ease.*

<margin>A</margin> THOSE things which are called "qualities" among them must be something other than the substrates themselves—a point they themselves admit, otherwise they would never have listed them as the second category. If, therefore, they are different, it is necessary that they be simple. If they are simple, they are by no means composite. If they are not composite, they do not have matter (for that is the reason they are "qualities"). If, finally, they are this, they must exist as incorporeal and effective things.

<column-break/>

But "qualities" for them must be different from the substrates, and they say they are. For they would not have counted them as second. If therefore they are different, they must also be simple. If they are <unclear>fragments</unclear> ...fire... they are not composite. If this is so, they do not have matter. Or if not <unclear>fragments</unclear> ...they are incorporeal and <unclear>fragments</unclear>...

<summary>Plotinus critiques the Stoic belief that matter is the ultimate reality, arguing that if matter is the only 'being,' then Mind and qualities would be reduced to mere states of matter, which contradicts the logic of their own categories.</summary>
