<meta>Continuity: This page continues Plotinus’s critique of the Stoic categories of existence. Having previously argued against the primacy of matter, he now examines the Stoic definitions of "Quality" and "Disposition," arguing that these categories are logically inconsistent and fail to account for the true nature of Being.</meta>

# BOOK ONE.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> For among those thinkers <note>The Stoics.</note>, matter is set forth as the subject intended to receive various "passions" <note>In this context, "passions" refers to being acted upon or undergoing change.</note>. But if they say that "qualities" themselves are composite, their division of things into "simple" and "composite" becomes first of all absurd, for they are dividing things as opposites and yet piling them both into a single genus. Secondly, this division is incorrect because it places one thing within another species: as if someone, when dividing the branches of knowledge, were to assert that one branch is "grammar," while the other is "grammar plus something extra."

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, if they claim that these qualities are themselves matter in a certain state, then the <term>seminal reasons<note>Original Latin: *seminales rationes*. These are the formative, "seeding" principles that the Stoics believed organized matter into specific shapes and types.</note></term> would be material according to them. These principles would not merely be placed in matter to produce a composite thing, but before the composite is even made by them, they would already consist of matter and form. Thus, these principles would be neither "forms" themselves, nor truly "reasons." If they object and say that these "reasons" are nothing other than matter itself existing in a certain way, they must admit that "qualities" are simply matter in a certain state, and

<margin>C</margin> they would then have to be placed in the fourth category <note>The Stoic category of relative disposition.</note>. But if they introduce some other relationship, we must ask: what is the difference? Is this "being in a certain state" actually a kind of <term>subsistence<note>Original Latin: *subsistentia*. This refers to something having its own independent reality.</note></term> at this level? And if it is not a subsistence, why list it as a genus or a species? For one cannot list under the same heading one thing that is a "being" and another that is a "non-being." Moreover, what is this thing that is said to be "matter in a certain state"?

<margin>D</margin> It must be judged as either "being" or "non-being." If it is "being," then it is entirely incorporeal; but if it is "non-being," it is spoken of in vain, and only matter truly exists. In that case, "quality" exists as nothing at all, and neither does this "being in a certain state." Indeed, such a thing might seem to be even more of a "non-being" than quality itself. As for the fourth category mentioned, it seems even less like a "being." Therefore, only matter would be "being." Who, then, says this? Certainly not matter itself—unless matter were actually "Mind" existing in a certain state.

<margin>E</margin> However, this phrase "existing in a certain state" is an empty addition. It is matter, then, that says these things and understands them. Truly, if matter spoke such sane and sensible things, it would be a miracle to see how it understands and performs the duties of a soul, despite having neither mind nor soul. But if it speaks foolishly, asserting that it is what it neither is nor can be, to whom should we attribute this foolishness? Surely to no one but matter itself, if only it could speak. But as it is, matter does not speak; rather, the person who says such things speaks thus because they have drunk too deeply from matter. They are entirely surrendered to it, even if they possess a soul. Such a person speaks out of ignorance of their own self and of the power that is capable of expressing the truth about such things.

<column-break/>

->They do not correctly distinguish between "quality" and "being in a certain state." For quality is actually matter in a certain state, and conversely, being in a certain state is simply matter with a quality. Furthermore, "being in a certain state" cannot be a unique genus, nor can anything that exists besides "qualified matter" be called by this name of "disposition."<-

->### Chapter XXX.<-

<margin>A</margin> Regarding those things which are said "to be in a certain state" <note>The Stoic category of disposition.</note>, it is perhaps absurd to place them in the third rank, or in whatever order they might hold. Since everything that is said to exist in relation to matter is in a "certain state," there must be differences in the natures of these states. Or they must introduce some other way in which matter itself is affected.

<sig>Dd 3</sig>

<summary>Plotinus critiques the Stoic categories, specifically arguing that if "quality" and "disposition" are merely states of matter, then the Stoics are effectively claiming that only matter is real and mind/soul are illusions. He mocks the idea of "talking matter" and asserts that such materialistic philosophies arise from a soul that has become too attached to physical things.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Plotinus’s critique of the Stoic categories of existence. Having previously argued against the primacy of matter, he now examines the Stoic definitions of "Quality" and "Disposition," arguing that these categories are logically inconsistent and fail to account for the true nature of Being.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK VI.

*The more matter remains stable under the changing of forms, the more it is acted upon. Therefore, it is considered the most receptive. If the Mind were posterior to matter, it could neither transcend matter nor even comprehend material things.*

### Chapter XXVIII.

<margin>A</margin> But since there are many points openly repugnant to this opinion which could easily be brought forward, we ought to be content with what has already been said; otherwise, it might be disgraceful for us to struggle too stubbornly against such obvious errors. It shall suffice to have shown who they are <note>Plotinus is referring to the Stoics, who held a materialist view of the universe.</note> and in what manner they affirm and establish "non-being" <note>original: *non ens*</note> as the highest form of "being," and do not hesitate to place that which is weak as the primary principle. <margin>B</margin> The cause of such a great error arose because they followed the senses as their guide, placing too much faith in them for establishing principles and other matters. Indeed, since they thought that only bodies were true things, and they feared the mutual change of bodies into one another, they naturally thought that what remains beneath those changes is "being" itself. It is just as if someone thought that "place" was more of a "being" than the "bodies" within it, imagining that place is never destroyed. <margin>C</margin> And although this matter remains among them, they should not have judged that which simply remains in any way at all to be "being" itself; rather, they should have first considered what the qualities of true "being" are, which, when present, allow the faculty of remaining forever to exist simultaneously. Now, even if a shadow remains, continually following something else that is constantly changed, the shadow will not be more real than that object. And yet, the sensible object itself, along with many others in number, will seem more worthy of being judged as "being"—since it is a whole—than any one thing contained within it. But if that whole substrate <note>The underlying material "stuff."</note> is "non-being," how can the individual thing be "being"? <margin>D</margin> Most wonderful of all, it seems, is that those who granted the senses authority over everything did not also affirm that "being" itself could be comprehended by the senses. Yet they do not even correctly attribute solidity or resistance to it, for that is a certain quality. But if they say they perceive it with the mind, this mind will be absurd, for it has placed matter above itself, giving the true office of existence not to itself, but to matter.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> For although there are many things contrary to this hypothesis, we should stop, lest it be strange to contend too much against what is manifest. It is shown that "non-being" is presented as "being" in the highest degree, putting the posterior first; the cause is the senses acting as a leader and being trusted for the establishment of other principles. <margin>B</margin> For having thought that bodies are beings, and then fearing their change into one another, they thought that what remains under them is Being. Just as if someone thought that place is the bodies, because the manner of it does not perish, and these remain in themselves. But one ought to consider that which is stable as Being. One's whole vision should be directed toward the Idea itself. <margin>C</margin> But to those who have the faculty of remaining always. But a shadow following that which is altered is not more real than it. The sensible, with many other true things, would rather be "being." Or if there is a whole in that. But if the whole substrate is "non-being," how can that be? Most wonderful of all is that which is observed by each sense. * Not by the sense, or by itself. For they do not even correctly give it resistance, for that is a quality. And if they say <margin>D</margin> it participates, this mind is absurd, imagining it in itself, or giving "being" to it rather than holding it in itself. Therefore, the mind would not be trustworthy to them concerning its own more sovereign parts, for it would be in no way related to them. But it would belong to this nature and to the substrates and in other things.

Since, therefore, the mind among them is not "being," what condition will have authority when it speaks and judges everywhere concerning those things which are more excellent than itself, yet has no kinship with them? But concerning this nature of substrates, enough has been disputed elsewhere.

---

*They established four categories: first the Subject, second the Quality, third the State, and fourth the Relative State.*

### Chapter XXIX.

*This very thing which is added, called "quality," if it is something simple as it ought to be, makes an incorporeal category separately—which they themselves admit—otherwise it would never be placed between the matter which is the subject, and again the quality in the subject. And entirely when they say "quality" and "a certain state," they add nothing besides matter being in such a state, or they do add something: if they add nothing, there is in truth only a single category, which, when asked what it is, they never explain. Nor do they ever discern between matter and matter in a certain state, by which distinction they would make several categories. Finally, if there is nothing besides matter in such a state, the mind itself will be material, and will be able to explain neither matter nor separate things.*

<margin>A</margin> Those things which are called "qualities" <term>Qualities<note>In Stoic physics, qualities are "pneumatic" (breath-like) tensions that give matter its specific characteristics.</note></term> among them must be something other than the subjects themselves, which they themselves admit; otherwise they would never have listed them as if they were productive. If, therefore, they are different, it is necessary that they also be simple. If they are simple, they are by no means composite. If this is so, they do not have matter, by reason of which they are "qualities." If, finally, this is the case, they must exist as incorporeal and effective principles.

<column-break/>

But the qualities for them are other than the subjects, as they say. They will count them as if they were fertile. If they are different, it is clear they are also simple. If they were fire, it would be different; if this, they would not even have matter. If they were fire <note>The Stoics often associated qualities with the element of fire or "pneuma."</note>, they would have to be incorporeal.

<summary>Plotinus critiques the Stoic materialist worldview, arguing that prioritizing matter over the Intellect is logically flawed. He further demonstrates that the Stoic category of "Quality" must be incorporeal, contradicting their core belief that only bodies exist.</summary>

# BOOK ONE.

For among them <note>The Stoics</note>, matter is set forth as the substrate intended to receive "passions" <note>original: *passiones*, referring to external influences or changes undergone by an object</note>. But if they say that these qualities themselves are "compounds" <note>things made of both matter and form</note>, first of all, their method of division is absurd, for it separates simple things and compound things as opposites and yet heaps them together into a single genus. Furthermore, this division is not correct because it places one of the species within the other; it is as if someone, when dividing the category of "knowledge," were to assert that one part is "grammar" and the other part is "grammar plus something else." But if they say that these qualities are "material matter" <note>matter already possessing some quality</note>, then first of all, their "seminal reasons" <term>Seminal Reasons (logoi): the formative principles that the Stoics believed shaped matter from within</term> would be material. These principles would not merely be placed within matter to create a compound, but would themselves consist of matter and form before the compound is even made by them. Therefore, these principles would be neither the forms themselves nor the "reasons" at all. However, if they were to object that these "reasons" are nothing other than matter itself existing in a certain state, then they must admit that qualities are merely "dispositions" <term>dispositions (πῶς ἔχοντα): the fourth Stoic category, describing the accidental state or 'how' a thing is situated</term>, and thus they ought to be placed in the fourth genus of their system. But if they introduce some other relationship, we must ask: what is the difference? Is this "being in a certain state" a kind of underlying substance in this rank? Yet, unless there is a substance there too, is he not simply listing something as a single genus or species? For one cannot count "being" and "non-being" under the same category. Furthermore, what is this thing in matter that is said to be "in a certain state"? It must be judged as either being or non-being. If it is being, it is entirely incorporeal; but if it is non-being, the term is used in vain, and there is only matter, while the "quality" itself does not exist at all—nor even that which is called a "disposition." For such a thing would seem much more like non-being to anyone. Finally, that which is numbered as the fourth category seems even less to be a "being." Therefore, only matter is being. Who then says this? Not matter itself, unless perhaps matter is "mind" existing in a certain state; though even this phrase "in a certain state" is a hollow addition. Thus, it is matter that says these things and perceives them. And indeed, if it spoke with sanity and wisdom, it would be a wonder how it could understand and perform the duties of a soul, since it possesses neither mind nor soul. If it asserts what it is not and cannot be, to whom should we most rightly attribute this folly? Surely to no one but matter itself, if only it could speak. But as it is, matter does not speak; rather, he who speaks such things says them because he is already drawing deeply from matter, being entirely addicted to it even if he possesses a soul. He speaks thus out of ignorance of himself and of the power that is able to express the truth about such matters.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> For among them <note>the Stoics</note>, matter is set forth to receive "passions." But if they say that these qualities themselves are "compounds," first of all, the division will be absurd, as it divides simple and compound things as opposites and yet accumulates them into one genus. <margin>B</margin> Secondly, it is also incorrect for this very reason: it places one of the species within the other, just as if someone dividing "science" were to assert that one part is grammar, and the other part is grammar plus something extra. Truly, if he says that these qualities are "material matter," then first, their seminal reasons would be material; and they would not merely be placed in matter to create a compound, but would consist of matter and form before the compound is even made by them. Therefore, they would be neither the forms themselves nor the "reasons." But if they object that these reasons are nothing other than matter itself in a certain state, they will clearly admit that qualities are "dispositions" <margin>C</margin> and must be placed in the fourth genus. But if they introduce some other habit or state, it must be asked: what is the difference? Specifically, is this "being in a certain state" a kind of substance at this level? Although, unless there is a substance there, is he not listing something as a genus or species? For one cannot count "being" and "non-being" under the same heading. Moreover, what is this that is said to be "in a certain state" in matter? <margin>D</margin> For it is judged to be either being or non-being. If it is being, it is entirely incorporeal; but if it is non-being, it is said in vain, and there is only matter. The "quality" itself exists as nothing at all, nor even that which is usually called "being in a certain state." For that could seem much more like non-being to someone. Finally, that which is numbered as the fourth category seems even less to be a "being." Therefore, only matter is being. Who then says this? <margin>E</margin> Not matter itself, unless perhaps it is mind existing in a certain state; yet even this "being in a certain state" is a hollow addition. Therefore, matter says these things and perceives them. And surely if it spoke things that were right and healthy, it would be a marvel how it could understand and perform the duties of the soul when it has neither mind nor soul. If it asserts what it is not and cannot be, to whom is it most fitting to attribute this foolishness? Truly to no one but itself, if only it could speak. But as it is, it does not speak, and he who speaks such things says them because he is already drinking deeply from matter, being totally devoted to it even if he has a soul. Thus he speaks from an ignorance of himself and of the power which can express the truth about such things.

<column-break/>

->They do not correctly distinguish between "quality" and "disposition" <note>how a thing is disposed</note>. For a quality is truly matter in a certain state, and conversely, a "disposition" is matter possessing a quality. Furthermore, "disposition" cannot be a single genus, nor can anything that exists beyond "qualified matter" be named by this term "disposition."<-

### Chapter XXX.

<margin>A</margin> In the matter of things that are said to be "disposed in a certain way," it is perhaps absurd to place them in the third rank, or to say they hold any particular order, since everything regarding matter is "disposed" in some way. But they will introduce a difference among these dispositions, or say that matter itself is disposed in another way...

<summary>Plotinus critiques the Stoic categories, specifically arguing that their definitions of "Quality" and "Disposition" are logically circular and reduce all existence to mere matter. He contends that if qualities are just states of matter, then matter itself would have to possess a mind to understand or define its own existence, which is a philosophical absurdity.</summary>

### PLOTINUS: ENNEADS, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin> ...to be affected in some way or another, while other things are said to be affected in a different way, based on how they are positioned. Furthermore, they claim that qualities themselves are somehow related to matter, but those things specifically called "dispositions" <note>original: *quodammodo se habentia*; the Stoic category of things in a certain state</note> are concerned with the qualities themselves. But since these qualities are nothing at all unless matter is affected in some way, those things which are said to be "in a certain state" among the Stoics are revolved back into matter and will be concerned with matter. Moreover, in what way can that which is said to "be in a certain state" be a single thing, when there is such great difference in such things?

<margin>B</margin> For how can "three cubits long" and "white" be reduced into one category, when the former is a quantity and the latter is a quality? Likewise, how can "at some time" <note>time</note> and "somewhere" <note>place</note> be the same? Again, how is it possible for these to be "states of being" at all—namely, what is called "yesterday" or "long ago," or "in the Lyceum" and "in the Academy"? <note>The Lyceum and the Academy were the famous schools of Aristotle and Plato in Athens.</note>

<margin>C</margin> How can it be that time itself is also a "state of being"? For neither time itself, nor the things in time, nor place, nor the things in place can be that same thing. Furthermore, that which is said "to do" <note>action</note> cannot be that which is named as "being in a certain state" or "being affected"; for the one acting is not himself a "state of being," but rather "acting in some way," or simply "acting." 

<margin>D</margin> And the one who "suffers" <note>passion/undergoing action</note> is not properly a "state of being," but rather "suffering in a certain way," or simply suffering in this way or that. Perhaps what is called "being in a certain state" will agree with what is usually called "position" <note>original: *situm*; the category of posture or arrangement</note>; and perhaps also with that which is called "having" <note>original: *habere*; the category of possession</note>. Yet, in this very act of "having," it is not properly the "state of being" itself, but rather the act of having. Therefore, unless they had established the genus of relation <term>Relation (πρός τι): the Stoic category describing how one thing is positioned relative to another</term> together with the others as one, there would be another reason for those seeking whether such a "habit" <note>original: *habitus*</note> provides any true substance, since they do not provide it anywhere else.

<margin>E</margin> Finally, what shall we say to the fact that they place a newly arriving thing <note>an accidental property</note> in the same genus as things that existed before? It is absurd to couple a thing that is adventitious <note>secondary or added later</note> together with prior things in the same category. For "one" and "two" must exist first so that "half" and "double" <note>which are relations</note> can also exist. As for the rest, whoever else has positioned things or the principles of things differently—whether infinite or finite, whether corporeal or incorporeal, or perhaps both together—it is permitted for us to inquire into each one separately, taking up in addition what was treated by the ancients against such opinions.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...matter in this way and that. But it is otherwise in the things that possess it, and regarding qualities, which are held around the matter; but those things that are specifically "in a certain state" <note>original: *pōs echonta*</note> are around these things. But there is nothing of the qualities themselves. Or, if they are things of matter being in a certain state, then "being in a certain state" runs back to the matter itself, and will be the matter. How then, in "being in a certain state," can there be one thing...

<margin>B</margin> ...when there is such difference in them? For how can "a cubit long" and "white" be one, when one is a quantity and the other is a quality? How indeed can "at some time" and "somewhere"? And how, in general, are "yesterday" or "last year" states of being? Or "in the Lyceum" and "in the Academy"? And how is time a state of being, or the things in time itself? Moreover, things in place,

<margin>C</margin> and place itself. But "acting" <unclear>is not</unclear> a state of being; for the one acting is not a state of being, but rather <unclear>acting in a certain way</unclear>, or not being at all, but only a quality. And the one suffering <unclear>is not</unclear> a state of being, but rather suffering in a certain way, or simply suffering thus. Perhaps not only <unclear>is this different</unclear>, but also "being in a certain state" relates to "position" and "having." Regarding "having," it is not a state of being but a "haver" <note>one who possesses</note>. If they did not place "relation" <note>original: *pros ti*</note> easily with the others, there would be another argument. But if...

<margin>D</margin> ...of them, if they give any substance to the relations, though they give it in many places. Since it is <unclear>absurd</unclear> for a thing that comes upon another to be in the same <unclear>category</unclear> as those which <unclear>existed</unclear> before, and to arrange the newly-arriving thing into a principle and nature with the things that were prior. For it is necessary for "one" and "two" to be first, so that "half" and "double" can exist. Concerning those who have otherwise placed the things that are, or the principles of things, whether infinite or finite, whether bodies or incorporeal,

<summary>Plotinus critiques the Stoic category of "disposition" (being in a certain state), arguing that it is a logical dumping ground that incorrectly groups unrelated concepts like time, place, and quantity. He asserts that basic qualities and numbers must logically exist before the complex relations and states that the Stoics try to prioritize.</summary>

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD SIX
### BOOK II

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD SIX
### BOOK II

-> ON THE GENERA OF BEING, SECOND PART. <-
-> On the genera of being. <-

> We consider only that to be true being, with which the opposite of being is not mixed—that is, a lack or privation of existence.
-> Chapter I. <-

*It is necessary, therefore, that this being be complete in its own nature and remain so forever. It is not fitting to place false being in the same genus as true being, just as one would not place the image of Socrates with Socrates himself. Plotinus will proceed to discuss the genera of beings in the Platonic manner. You will now receive from your Marsilio <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the translator and philosopher who led the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note> a very brief interpretation of these matters, O Magnanimous Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, the ruler of Florence and Ficino’s patron.</note>. For you have heard at times, and perhaps will someday read, your and my friend Pierleone <note>Pierleone Leoni, a famous physician and scholar in the Medici circle.</note> treating such mysteries with a certain divine instinct, as is his custom in other things.*

---

<margin>Since</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring two classical figures in discussion.</image-desc>
Since we have already examined the so-called ten genera <note>original: *δέκα γενῶν*; referring to Aristotle's ten categories of reality (Substance, Quantity, Quality, etc.).</note>, and have also spoken about those who reduce all things to a single genus, or who place all four categories under the "One" as if they were species, it follows that we should state what our own view on these matters appears to be, as we attempt to trace our opinions back to the doctrine of Plato. If it were not necessary to establish <term>Being</term> <note>original: *τὸ ὂν*; the fundamental reality or existence of things.</note> as a category, there would be no need to search for whether there is one genus for all things, or if there are genera not under one, or if there are principles. But since the <term>principles</term> <note>original: *ἀρχὰς*; the first causes or fundamental origins of the universe.</note> and the genera must be established as the same, we must ask: are the genera and the principles identical? Or are all the principles also genera, while the genera are not necessarily principles? Or is it the other way around? Or, in both cases, are some principles also genera, and some genera also principles? Or in one case, are all of them also the other, while in the other case, only some are? Since we do not define "Being" in the way [the others] do—for reasons explained in Plato and elsewhere—it becomes necessary to examine these things a second time, bringing into the open what number of genera we propose and how. Since, therefore, we are inquiring about Being itself or about beings, it is first necessary to distinguish among these: what we call Being itself, about which our inquiry may be conducted rightly, and what seems to others to be Being, but which we call <term>Becoming</term> <note>original: *γινόμενον*; the realm of physical change and growth, which Plotinus views as less real than the eternal world of ideas.</note>—which is never truly "Being." We must understand these as distinct from one another, not as if they were a single genus divided into parts. One should not think that Plato categorized them in that way.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' showing a scholar seated at a desk or lectern.</image-desc>
After we have considered the ten genera, and spoken then of those who embrace all things under one certain genus as if they were four species: it remains now that we explain our own opinion on these things, attempting clearly to lead our opinion back to the judgment of Plato. If, therefore, it had been necessary to propose only one Being, there would be no need to inquire whether there is one genus in all things: or whether, again, the genera are not reduced to one: and whether they should be called "principles": nor, again, whether the principles should also be proposed as genera: nor, conversely, whether the genera themselves are the same as the principles: nor whether all principles are indeed also genera, but the genera are not equally principles, or vice versa: or rather whether in both there are some which are principles and genera at the same time, and some also which are genera and principles at the same time: or perhaps in some cases all are both one and the other, while in others only some are both. Since, however, we do not propose Being as one, and the reason for this opinion has been assigned by Plato and especially his followers, it is perhaps necessary to consider these things also—firstly, what number [of genera] we should propose, and how we should bring them into the open. Since, therefore, we are investigating Being itself or beings, it is necessary in the first place to distinguish these things internally: namely, what we may call Being itself, about which we are presently conducting a proper consideration, and what may seem to be Being to others, which we nevertheless call not that which ever *is*, but rather that which *becomes*. It is, however, worthwhile to understand these as distinct from one another, not as if there were one single genus divided within itself. For it is not right to think that Plato distributed them in such a way.

## ENNEAD VI
### BOOK II

<margin>A</margin>
For it would be ridiculous to join being itself into a single category with non-being; it would be as if someone were to place Socrates himself and a mere image of him under the same heading. Indeed, to make a division in this very matter is nothing other than to separate and arrange them apart, and to declare that what merely *appears* to be being is actually non-being, while meanwhile demonstrating that something else exists as truly real being. Moreover, he <note>Referring to Plato, specifically in the *Sophist*.</note> who always joined "always" to being, showed that being must be of such a nature that it never lies or fails in the very nature of being. Therefore, speaking of this being, we shall treat it as if it were not a single, simple unity. Then, if it seems appropriate, we shall further offer something regarding generation, that which is generated, and the sensible world.

<margin>B</margin>
*The first Being is indeed one, but in a certain manner it consists of many things, which are both principles <term>principia: the fundamental origins or starting points of reality</term> and genera <term>genera: the primary "kinds" or categories of existence</term>, because the nature of being itself is, as it were, composed of them. They are genera because each of them contains under itself many things in gradual stages, as well as individuals. Nor are these confused into a single mass: for each preserves its own identity there. In that realm, being itself should be called a genus, yet it is not divided like a genus into species, nor is it predicated of its subordinates in the manner of a typical genus.*

<margin>C</margin>
Since, therefore, we say it is not a single unity, the consequence is to assert either a specific number or an infinite one. For in what way can we say it is "not one," unless we say it is at once one and many—a kind of varied unity comprehending many things within itself? It is necessary, then, that this which is "one" in such a way is either one in genus, while its species are the individual beings (by which it would surely be many and one at the same time); or that there are more genera than one, yet in such a way that they are all under one; or that there are indeed several genera, not one under another, but each containing the things that fall under it—whether these be narrower genera or species placed beneath them—so that all lead back into a single nature, and the substance <note>original: *substantia*; here referring to the essential reality of the higher realm.</note> of the intelligible world, which we call Being, consists of them all. If this is indeed the case, it follows that these are not only genera, but also the principles of being itself: they are genera because beneath them are other narrower genera, followed by species and individuals; and they are principles because being is made of many parts, and the whole itself exists out of these. However, if there were several parts from which the whole consists, which when running together produced the entire universe but had nothing else beneath them, they would be principles, but by no means genera; just as if one were to compose a sensible object from the four elements—namely fire and the rest. For these would be principles, but <margin>D</margin> never genera, unless perhaps one used the term "genus" in an ambiguous sense. Therefore, when we say that these principles are also genera, we must ask: do we call them genera in such a way that we take each of them together with the things that follow them and mix everything together, producing a whole by making a blending of all things with one another? But in that case, the individual things would exist there only in potentiality, not in actuality, and each thing would not be pure. Perhaps, then, we shall set aside the genera but mix the individuals. <margin>E</margin> What then will be the genera in themselves? Will they also exist in themselves and be pure? And will the mixed things not destroy them, and in what way? But concerning these things we shall speak in what follows. Now, however, after we have admitted that there are certain genera, and moreover principles of essence itself, and that in another sense certain compositions of principles exist there, we must first say toward what those genera—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
For it is laughable <note>original: *γελοῖον* (geloion)</note> to place non-beings under the same heading as being. It is as if one were to place Socrates and his image under the same category. To divide in this way within "that which is" means to separate and set apart; they showed that one thing is being, and said that another is not being. In this way, someone adding the word "always" to being <note>Referring to the Platonic definition of Being as that which "always is."</note> assumed that non-being is the opposite of being, as the nature of being is that which never admits of falsehood. We shall therefore look into such a being. Later, if it seems good, we shall also speak about generation and that which is becoming, and the world according to its parts.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
Since, then, we say it is not one, do we mean a certain number or the infinite? For how can we say "not one" unless we mean one and many? It is like something variegated, having many things within one. It is necessary, therefore, that this state of being is either one in genus, and the beings are its species—in which it is many and one—or there are more genera than one. And either all things are under one, or there are more genera, not under another, but each encompassing those things under it; whether these be smaller living things <note>original: *ζῶων* (zōōn); Plotinus often uses the term "living beings" to describe the vibrant, active Forms in the Intelligible World.</note>, or species, or individuals under places, until all come together into one nature. And from all these, the intelligible world, which we call Being, is a composed substance. If this is so, then these are not only genera, but also at the same time the principles and hypostases <note>original: *ὑποστάσεις* (hypostaseis); fundamental underlying realities.</note> of being. They are genera because under them are other smaller genera and species after them and individuals; they are principles because in this way Being is composed of many, and out of these things it consists. If, however, there were many parts from which the whole was made, but there were nothing under them, they would be principles, but not genera. For example, if someone made a sensible object out of the four elements—fire and such things—these would be principles but not genera, unless one used the name "genus" equivocally. Saying, then, that these are both certain genera and principles, are they genera in the sense that we mix the things under them together, and from all of them we complete the whole, making a certain mixture of all, but each would be there in potentiality and not in actuality? Or will each thing itself be pure? We shall leave aside the genera but mix the individual things. What then are the genera by themselves? Or will those also be by themselves and pure? Will the things that are mixed not destroy them, and how? But these things are for later. Now, since we have granted that there are genera, and furthermore principles of essence, and in another way principles and compositions, we must first say towards what things we say—

Plotinus (and Ficino) distinguishes true Being from its mere images and debates whether the fundamental principles of reality are "pure" or "mixed."</summary>

<header>BOOK TWO</header>

<note>original: "καὶ πῶς διίστωμεν... / & quomodo inter se partiamur..." This section continues Chapter 2 of Plotinus’s Ennead VI.2, questioning how we distinguish species without losing their unity.</note>

<margin>A</margin>
And how can we distinguish these things from one another, and not bring them under a single heading as if they had come together by mere chance to produce some effect? Certainly, it would be much more reasonable for them to be brought under a single unity. Indeed, if it were possible for all things to be species of <term>Being: "ens" or "on," the fundamental reality of things that truly exist</term> itself, and for each subsequent thing to follow in order with nothing left outside, then perhaps such an arrangement would be permitted. But since such a position utterly destroys these very things—for then the species would no longer be species, nor would many things be gathered into one—but rather

<column-break/>

<margin>B</margin>
all things would be entirely one, so that one thing would not be outside another, where all things belong to that one. For in what way could the One have become many, so as even to generate species, unless there were something else besides it? For the One does not exist as a "many" in itself, unless one were to divide it like a <term>magnitude: a physical or mathematical quantity that can be sliced into parts</term>. But even in that case, there would be something else doing the dividing. If it were divided either by itself or by another, even before it was divided, it would already be divided, or else it would be indivisible. For this reason and many others, we must be careful not to establish a single <term>genus: a general category under which specific types (species) are organized</term>, especially because it is impossible to call whatever you perceive either "Being" or "Essence." For it frequently happens that something can only be called "being" or "essence" <term>by accident: "per accidens," meaning a quality that isn't essential to the thing's nature, like a man being "tan" or "musical"</term>, as if one were to call a substance "white." For in that case, one is not declaring that the thing which is white is white in its very essence.

---

->*The many things that exist in the first Being, because they do not meet there by chance, are necessarily from the One. Conversely, since the primary genera of things are distinct from one another there, they cannot be reduced internally to a single genus that is predicated of them in the manner of a genus. Rather, they are reduced to a single unity—not so much as a cause, but as a nature—which is not so much composed of them as it consists of them, propagating itself within them and preserving itself entirely in each of the differing parts. We reduce this single nature, because it is not simply "one" but "one being," to the "One" itself that stands simply outside as its cause.*<-
<note>This italicized section is Marsilio Ficino’s "Argumentum" or summary, explaining that while Plotinus seeks unity, he distinguishes between a "genus" (which defines what a thing is) and a "source" (the One) which is beyond definition.</note>

### Chapter III.

<margin>A</margin>
We say, therefore, that there are many things, and that they are not many by some accidental chance. Are they not, then, from the One? Certainly, if they depend on the One, it is not from some "one" that is predicated of them in their actual being; therefore, nothing prevents each thing, though it is not the same form as another, from existing as a genus on its own. Does this One, then, exist as a cause outside the emerging genera, while not being predicated of the others in terms of their "whatness" <note>original: "τῷ τί ἐστι / in eo quod quid est" — the essential definition of a thing.</note>? Perhaps it is indeed outside. For the <term>Good: "to eu," often used by Plotinus as a synonym for the One</term>

<column-break/>

<margin>B</margin>
itself stands above, since it is by no means counted among the genera. If, through it, other things exist which are counted together and distinguished among themselves equally for the purpose of being genera, in what way is that [the One] not counted together with them? But surely we are now seeking "beings" <note>original: "ὄντα / entia"</note>, not that which stands above. Let this, then, be the case. But what shall we say of that which is counted among them? Regarding this, one might wonder: under what condition is it numbered together with its own

<margin>C</margin>
effects? If those higher things and the others were numbered together under one single genus, it would be an error. But if it is numbered together with those things of which it is the cause—as if it were itself the genus and the rest followed from it—and if the things that follow are different from it, and it is not predicated of them as a genus, nor spoken of in some other way, then it is necessary that they too are genera, having other things beneath themselves. For if you produce <term>walking: "incedendo," used here as a logical example</term> by your act of walking, walking is not "under" you as if you were its genus. And unless there were something higher than walking, acting as the genus of walking itself, there would still be some things beneath it, and walking itself would exist as a genus in the order of things.

<summary>Plotinus argues that "Being" cannot be a single, all-encompassing genus like those in Aristotle's logic, because the ultimate source (the One) remains distinct from and above its effects. He uses the analogy of a person and the act of walking to show that a cause is not the same as a taxonomic category.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, metaphysics, Genus and Species, The One, Being, accidental properties, causality, Platonic categories, Marsilio Ficino</keywords>

Perhaps, however, it should not be said at all <margin>A</margin>
that the One is the cause of the others, but rather
that the others are like parts and elements of it, and
all things together are a single nature, distributed by
our own thoughts. That "One," however, because of
its marvelous power, is a "One" over all things, 
appearing as many and becoming many—as if it were 
set in motion, and a power of an amplifiable and
multipliable nature brought it about that the one 
should no longer be one. We, however, producing 
certain portions of it, as it were, set them down <margin>B</margin>
individually as if each were a single thing, giving
them the name of a *genus*, clearly being ignorant 
that we have not glimpsed the whole at once. Instead,
producing them according to parts and individually, 
we gather them together again; clearly, we are unable 
to hold them back for long, as they meanwhile 
hasten back toward themselves. Therefore, we 
release them again into the whole, and allow them 
to become one—or rather, to *be* one. But perhaps 
these things will finally become clearer when those <margin>C</margin> 
very things are first recognized, and we have 
learned how many *genera* <note>original: "γένη" (genē) - the primary categories or "kinds" of being</note> there are. For in this way, 
how they relate to one another will be more 
clearly declared. Since, however, when dealing with 
such matters, it is necessary not only to introduce 
negations, but also to penetrate into the very 
notion and understanding of those things under 
discussion—come now, let us proceed in this way.

->*Since the mind and soul are separate from matter and quantity, and for that reason are simple and indivisible, it is difficult to see how unity there possesses a distinct multitude within itself.* Chapter IV.<-

->*Union, or rather unity, in bodies follows after the actual composition of many parts, and is, as it were, a kind of end-point of generation. Therefore, it deservedly depends on a certain unity which exists before the multitude, and which is the principle of generation. Such is the unity in the soul and mind; it is not made from many things, but is the source of many. From this it proceeds from a unity that has no such mixed multitude within itself.*<-

<margin>A</margin> If we were eager to learn what, and of what 
sort, the nature of the body is in this whole 
order of things, would we not first consider it in 
some of its parts? For example, in a stone, 
thinking that there is one thing which is the 
subject <note>original: "ὑποκείμενον" (hypokeimenon) - the underlying "stuff" or substrate</note>, another which is the magnitude, and 
finally another which is the quality, such as color—
and similarly in any other body? And from there we 
would immediately say that in the nature of the 
body, one thing is like the <term>substance: the essential reality or "being" of a thing</term>, 
another like the quantity, and another like the 
quality. To be sure, all exist at once, but by a 
certain reason they are distributed into a <margin>B</margin> 
triad of numbers, and it would be established 
that these three are one body. If motion were also 
present, implanted in the substance, we would count 
this too with the others; these four would indeed 
exist as one body, so that the body, which is one, 
is composed of and depends upon all these 
toward the nature of itself and its unity. In almost 
the same way, since this discourse concerns 
intelligible substance and its *genera* and 
principles, it is proper to consider such things by <margin>C</margin> 
taking away the "generation" <note>original: "γένεσιν" (genesin) - the process of coming-into-being in the physical world</note> that belongs 
to bodies, and even removing the thought that 
proceeds from the senses, and moreover setting 
aside physical bulks. For in this way, it will be 
possible to grasp that which is spoken of 
separately, and those things which are distinct 
among themselves, as a certain intelligible 
substance, and as a thing that truly *is*, and is 
more truly one. In this, indeed, wonder arises: 
in what way can that which is so "one" be at once 
one and many? In bodies, certainly, it is 
conceded without controversy that the same 
thing is at once one and many. For the same 
thing is also divided infinitely, and color there 
is one thing...

<column-break/>

In general, perhaps, it should not be said that 
the One is the cause, but rather that these are 
like parts of it and elements of it, and all are 
one nature, divided by our own thoughts. 
And it, by a marvelous power, not being 
among all things, appears as many, and 
becomes many when it is moved; and the 
manifold nature of its power makes it so 
that it is not one. And we, as if carrying 
portions of it around within ourselves, speak 
of each of these as if it were a *genus*, 
ignoring that we have not seen the whole 
all at once, but rather by parts. Then, we 
join them back together, as we are not 
able to hold them for a long time as they 
separate back toward themselves. Therefore, 
we let them go back into the whole and 
permit them to become one—or rather, to 
be one. But perhaps these things will be 
clearer if we take up the *genera*, once 
they have been recognized. For in this 
way, the "how" will be clear. But since 
one must not only speak through 
negations, but also go into the concept 
and understanding of the things being 
discussed, we must act in this way.

->*How the mind and soul, being separate from matter and quantity, and therefore being simple and indivisible, makes it hard to distinguish how unity there has a divided multitude in itself.* Chapter IV.<-

->*Union or unity in bodies follows after the composition of many things, and is like an end of generation; so it reasonably depends on a certain unity which is before the multitude and is the beginning of generation. Such is the unity in the soul and mind, not having been made from many, but being a fountain of many. From there it proceeds from the unity, which has no such mixed multitude in itself.*<-

<margin>A</margin> If one wished to see the nature of the

the substance, <margin>B</margin> another is the quantity, another

And if motion were also innate in its

<margin>C</margin> those things which stand apart

<summary>Plotinus discusses how the "One" (the ultimate reality) can appear as many categories or parts due to the limitations of human thought, using an analogy of a stone's properties (substance, size, color) to explain how the Mind and Soul contain multiplicity within a simple, indivisible unity.</summary>

SECOND BOOK.

<margin>A</margin> The form is also different, for in that realm these things are separated. But if someone should take a single soul—one that is indivisible, without magnitude, and as simple as it appears at the first glance of thought—how could they ever hope to find that same soul to be multiple? This is especially true if they have reached the conclusion that a living being is divided into body and soul, where the body is easily seen to be <margin>B</margin> multiform, composite, and varied, while they hoped to find the soul to be something simple and to rest there, as if having reached the very end of their journey and a final principle. Therefore, let us take this soul—since it was set apart for us in the intelligible world <note>original Greek: "νοητῷ τόπῳ" (noētō topō); Latin: "intelligibili mundo" — the realm of pure thought and reality, distinct from the physical world</note> just as the body was previously introduced from the sensible world—and let us consider how this "One" is "Many," and how the "Many" are "One." I do not mean a "One" composed of many parts, but rather a single nature that is itself many. For if this is understood and clearly seen, we said that the truth concerning the kinds of being <note>original: "γενῶν" (genōn) / "generum" — the primary categories of existence</note> reigning in true reality will also become clear.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> The figure is different; for there, these things are separated. If, however, someone takes a soul as one, indivisible, and segregated from magnitude—likewise most simple, as it will appear at the first glance of thought—how can one hope to find that same soul to be manifold again? Especially when he has judged that he would finally reach this as the simplest point when the living being is divided into body and soul, and it is easily established that the body is <margin>B</margin> multiform, composite, and varied. But meanwhile, anyone hoped to find the soul to be most simple, and to rest there, as if he had already reached a certain boundary of the progression. Therefore, when we have brought this soul forward as something taken from the intelligible world, just as we had previously introduced the body from the sensible world, come, let us now consider how that "One" is "Many," and how the <margin>C</margin> "Many" are "One." Not, I say, a "One" as if composed of many, but as a certain single nature which is itself many. For we said that if this itself is perceived and clearly seen, the truth of the kinds reigning in being itself will be further clarified for us.

<margin>A</margin> FIRST, it must be considered—since the bodies of animals and plants in particular are so constituted that each of them is "many," whether in colors, shapes, diversity of size, or the species of their parts, and because one thing is in one place and another elsewhere—that all these things proceed from a "One." This "One" is either something entirely one, or it exists in the condition of an entire "One-Universe," or it is something that is more "one" than that <margin>B</margin> which proceeds from it, so much so that it also exists as "being" more than that which proceeds from it. For the further one departs from the "One," the further one departs from "Being." Therefore, since the constitution of bodies comes from a "One," yet not proximately from that which is entirely "One" (or the "One" itself, otherwise it would not create such a distant multitude), it remains that this very composition of bodies is fashioned by a certain "One-Multitude." That which makes bodies is the soul; therefore, this is a <margin>C</margin> certain "One-Multitude." But what is the primary multitude in the soul? Surely it is the "seminal reasons" of the things that are produced from it. Is the soul itself one thing, then, and the reasons another? On the contrary, the soul itself is Reason <note>original: "λόγος" (logos) / "ratio" — both "reason" and "formative principle"</note> and the head of all reasons: and its acts, according to its essence as an agent, are the reasons themselves. Its essence is the very power of these seminal reasons. For this reason, this "One" is thus "Many," and it is found to be so through the things it does to others. But what if it does nothing, but someone considers it as performing no action at all, having progressed into that very part of the soul which does nothing? Will he not find many powers here as well? For anyone would easily admit that the soul *is*; but would he affirm that its "being" is exactly the same as saying a stone *is*?

<summary>Plotinus explores how the Soul, while appearing simple and indivisible, contains a "One-Multitude" of formative principles (seminal reasons) that generate the diversity of the physical world. He argues that the Soul is a bridge between the absolute Unity of the higher realm and the fragmented multiplicity of material bodies.</summary>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

Certainly not in that way. Now, even regarding a stone itself <margin>A</margin>, the "being" of a stone is not "being" in a simple sense, but rather the "being of a stone." So too here, for the soul, its "being" includes both existence and "being a soul." But is one thing "to be" and another thing the remainder which completes the essence <term>essence: "essentia" or "ousia," the fundamental nature or "what-it-is-ness" of a thing</term> of the soul? And is one part "being," while the difference makes it "soul"? Perhaps the soul is indeed a certain being, yet not in the way a "white man" is <note>where "white" is an accidental quality added to "man"</note>, but in the way "man" is by his essence alone. This is the same as saying it does not hold what it has from outside its essence. <margin>B</margin>

---

*Essence and life in the soul are indeed one in reality, but they differ in reason: for the soul belongs to all things through essence, yet differs from them through life. Life there—that is, animal life—does not come to the essence from the outside, but from the essence itself; therefore, life flourishes hidden within the very power of essence, and essence is more clearly unfolded in the very act of life.*

### Chapter VI.

BUT does it not have something outside <margin>A</margin> its essence, so that it is partly according to "being" and partly according to "being such-and-such"? But if it is according to a "being such-and-such," and this "suchness" comes from the outside, then surely the whole, insofar as it is soul, will not be essence. Rather, it would be essence according to some part, and therefore essence would be a part of it, but not the whole essence. Furthermore, what will its "being" be without the others? A stone? Or rather, must this "being" of its exist within "being" itself, like a fountain and a principle? Indeed, all things exist as many as <margin>B</margin> it itself exists; therefore, life also exists, and both exist together as one—namely, being and life. Is it then one in the way a single definition is? Truly the subject is one, yet one in such a way that it is again two, or even more—as many as the soul is in its primary state. Either, then, it is essence and life, or it has life. But if it has life, it follows that what has it is not life in itself, and conversely that life is not in essence. But if one does not have the other, it must be said that both <margin>C</margin> are one, or one and many, and as many as appear within the one. And it is one to itself, and many again toward others: then indeed it exists as one in itself, yet meanwhile, as if by its own motion, it makes itself many. Yet the whole is one, but as if striving to look upon itself, it becomes many—not unlike how Being itself seems not to subsist remaining unique, inasmuch as it can do all things, as many as it is. Now, contemplation <note>original Greek: "theoria"; Latin: "contemplatio" — the intellectual "seeing" or activity of the mind</note> itself is the cause for it appearing as many, so that it may understand. If it appeared as one, it would not yet seem to have understood, but would still be that very thing itself.

---

*In the first intellect there is being, motion, and rest, like three kinds of things: there they are one by nature, differing among themselves by verbal reasoning.*

### Chapter VII.

Just as the great diversity of limbs in an animal declares some difference of formative principles <term>formative principles: "rationes seminales" (seminal reasons), the internal "blueprints" or powers that guide the development of a living thing</term> in the seed, so in the archetypal world, Being and Life—that is, motion and rest—differ from one another in some way. It is clear to us that in the corporeal world these three are most separated. However, there [in the intelligible realm], life is a certain inward, perpetual motion of Being itself—an act of Being, Being fully matured. And Being itself is essentially life, and conversely, it is vitally Being. Finally, since rest is opposed to motion, we gather that there, rest is not motion, nor is the other entirely the same as Being.

WHAT then are they, and how many, which are <margin>A</margin> seen within? Truly, since we have found essence in the soul along with life, and essence itself is common in every soul, and life is also common—yet life is again in the Mind <note>original: "mens" / "nous"</note>—surely by introducing Mind additionally along with its life, we shall establish a certain single genus, namely...

<column-break/>

But nonetheless, even there <note>in the intelligible realm</note>, regarding the stone, the "being" of the stone is to be a stone, but it is the "being of a stone." And here also in the soul, along with "being," there is "being a soul." Is it then that "to be" is one thing, and the rest which completes the essence of the soul is another, and "being" is one part, while the difference makes it "soul"? Or is the soul a certain "being," not indeed in the way a "white man" is, but like a certain essence alone, by being itself, and by not having from the outside that which it holds?

---

BUT does it not have the things of its essence from the outside, so that it is according to "being" on the one hand, and according to "being such-and-such" on the other? But if it is according to "being such-and-such" and the "suchness" is from the outside, then the whole, insofar as it is soul, [is not essence], but according to what part of itself? Nothing else than that the whole is essence. Then what will its "being" be when stripped of the others? A stone? Or must its "being" be in "being," like a fountain and a principle—or rather all things, as many as it is—and must life also be "being," and the two together be one, namely "being" and "life." Is it then one in the way a single definition is, or is the underlying subject one, yet one in such a way as to be two or even more—as many as the soul is primarily. Either it is essence and life, or it has life. But if it has it, that which has it is not itself in life. Or if it is in life, it is not in essence. But if one does not have the other, it must be said that both are one. Or that the one is the many. And as many as appear in the one. And in itself. But how are the others many? "Being" on the one hand, but making itself many in its, as it were, motion. And the whole is one. And as if attempting to contemplate itself, it becomes many. For just as "Being" does not endure being only one, but is all things because it remains [what it is]; therefore contemplation is the cause of it appearing as many, or of it thinking. For if it appeared as one, it has not yet thought, but was already that thing.

---

WHICH ones then are they, and how many are those seen within? Since indeed we have found in the soul essence along with life, in that essence is common to every soul; and life is also common, and life is also in Mind. By introducing both Mind and its life, we shall establish as a certain genus that which is common to all life, namely motion...

### BOOK TWO.
Ee

<note>original: "Cap. VIII."</note>

...essence and motion, existing in the primary living being <term>primary living being: 'proton zoon,' referring to the Intelligible World or the Divine Mind which contains the archetypes of all things</term>, we shall now establish as two distinct things. For even if they are one, thought distinguishes them by finding one to be not the same as the other; otherwise, it would be unable to separate them. Observe this even more clearly in other things, where motion or life is separated from "being" itself—if not in true Being, then at least in the shadow of being and in that which is called "being" only by name. For just as many things are missing in a portrait of a man, and especially the most important thing, which is life, so too in the things of the senses, their "being" is a shadow of true Being. It lacks that which is most vital in being: the life that exists in the original archetype. But from this, we have the means to distinguish "living" from "being," and "being" from "living." Truly, there are many species of Being. Indeed, motion is to be placed under Being—not as something added to Being, but as something existing alongside Being. For motion is found within it, not as if it were lying in a subject <note>In Aristotelian logic, a "subject" is a thing to which qualities are added; Plotinus argues here that motion is not just a quality of Being, but essential to it</note>. For motion is the very activity of Being, and neither exists without the other, except perhaps in our thought. And these two natures are one; for Being is not merely a potentiality, but an actual activity. Even if you take each separately, motion will still appear in Being, and Being in motion. It is as if in a single entity, each part held the other while remaining distinct. Nevertheless, thought declares them to be two, and each as a double thing. When motion appears around Being, it does not distract from its nature; rather, it is present there because Being is perfect, and such a nature always persists in this order of motion. Certainly, if someone did not introduce "rest" here, they would be more absurd than one who did not admit motion. For the notion and understanding of rest seems more suited to Being than the notion of motion. For there, that which is famously said to "remain the same, in the same way, and with one reason" flourishes. Let rest also be one genus, in a way different from motion, since it can even be seen as its opposite. That it is also different from Being can be clear from many things: especially since if it were identical with Being, then motion would not be identical with Being—and yet motion is a certain life of Being, an act both of essence and of "to be" itself. But just as we separated motion from it, as both the same as it and not the same, and spoke of both as two and yet as one; in the same way, we may separate rest from it, and yet not separate it: separating it with the mind only so far as it may be arranged as another genus in the order of things. Otherwise, if we were to join rest and Being together entirely, saying they differ in no way, and similarly if we were to merge Being and motion into one, we would by the same logic join rest and motion together through Being as a middle term—from which it would follow that motion and rest were entirely one and the same.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...motion common in all life: yet we shall establish essence and the first motion, which is also the first life, as two genera. For even if they are one, it will be permitted to separate them by the intellect, finding that which is one to be not one; otherwise, separation would not be possible. See this also more clearly in other things: that motion or life is secret from "being" itself: and if less so in true Being itself, then at least in the "shadow" of being, and in that which is called "being" equivocally. Just as in a man’s image <margin>B</margin> many things are lacking, especially that which is most powerful, namely life: so also in the things that are perceived by the senses, their "being" is a shadow of Being itself: inasmuch as it lacks that which is most vital in being, which is found in the principal form and the exemplary life of things. Do we not therefore find it proven from this, how one may separate "to be" from that which is "to live," and conversely, "to live" from "to be" in a similar way? Of Being itself, there are indeed many species: there is also a genus. But motion is to be placed neither under being nor in being, <margin>C</margin> but together with being: since it is found in it, yet not as if lying in a subject. For it is the very act of Being, and neither is without the other, unless perhaps by a certain thought. Yet these two natures here are one: for Being itself is not in potentiality, but in act. And if you take each separately, even then motion will be seen to be in Being, and Being in motion: just as in one being, each taken separately possesses the other. However, thought dictates that they are two things, and each is like a species and each <margin>D</margin> is double. But when motion appears around Being, it does not pull apart its nature; rather, because it is perfect, it is present there, and such a nature always persists in this same order of motion. Surely, if one does not introduce "rest" <note>original: "statum," referring to the state of being at rest or stability</note> here, he will be more absurd than he who did not apply motion. For the notion and understanding of rest seems more accommodated to Being than the notion of motion. For there, that which is usually said to "remain always according to the same things, in the same way, and by one reason" is in force. <margin>E</margin> Let rest now also be one genus, in a way diverse from motion: since it can even be seen as its contrary. That it is also different from Being can be clear from many things: and especially because if it were the same as Being, then motion would by no means be Being: since motion is a certain life of it, and an act of both essence and Being itself. But <margin>F</margin> truly, just as we separated motion from it, as being the same as it and again not the same, and spoke of both as two, and again as one, by the same condition one may segregate rest from it, and again not segregate it: namely, by separating it through the intellect, insofar as it is arranged as another genus in the order of things: otherwise, if we were to couple rest and Being entirely into one, saying they differ in no way: and similarly if we were to melt Being together with motion into one, we would surely by the same reason join rest and motion through Being itself as a middle term into the same thing: from which it would happen that motion and rest would be entirely one.

---

*Forms separated from matter are either intellects, or they are in the intellect; and there they are not according to accident, but according to an intellectual and equally intelligible essence.*

*Thus the first intellect conceives within itself five genera of things: namely Being, Motion, Rest, the Same, and the Other. In this intel—*

<summary>Plotinus explores the primary "Great Genera"—Being, Motion, and Rest—arguing that while they are unified in the Divine Intellect, they are intellectually distinct. He explains that life and motion are not mere accidents of Being but are its very activity, and that stability (Rest) is equally essential to the perfection of true Essence.</summary>

<header>PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.</header>

...essence and intelligence differ from one another in a certain way; otherwise, if intelligence proceeded from the order of things born from it, essence would also proceed. In that realm, therefore, the act of thinking—acting as a kind of primary motion—rests upon essence or Being as if upon a hinge. It rests there, I say, in two ways: for it both leaps forth from it and faithfully recoils back into it. In that place, Being is essentially intelligence, and in turn, intelligence exists as intellectual Being. Consequently, intelligence both begins from a certain state—that is, the firm vigor of the mind—and tends toward a state—that is, the "Idea," its internal boundary. Furthermore, besides Being, Motion, and Rest <note>original: "statum," literally a standing still or stability</note>, there is also Otherness <note>original: "alteritas," the principle of difference</note> there, insofar as these are distinguished from one another by some reason, and again Sameness <note>original: "identitas"</note>, insofar as they are all within the same nature. Yet truly, these following four are not called "species" of Being, but rather certain companion acts of Being itself. Finally, those five are called the primary "genera" of beings, and whatever exists is reduced to one of them; all of them together are included in every single thing, and in this respect, they can also be called the principles of all things.

---

<margin>A</margin> BUT it is necessary to establish these three, since the intellect understands each of them separately: but it understands and establishes them simultaneously, provided they have been understood. For those things whose being is tied to matter, their being is not found within the intellect; otherwise, they would be separated from matter. But those things which are separated from matter—if they are understood—that very act of being understood is their actual being. Come then, contemplate the pure intellect, and look deep into it, not fixing your gaze on the outside, but looking entirely within.

<margin>B</margin> Behold, you now see Essence there as a Vestal deity <note>original: "Vestale numen," referring to Hestia, the goddess of the hearth, symbolizing the stable, central essence of the Divine Mind</note> and as a foundation; you also discern there an ever-vigilant and inextinguishable light. You notice, moreover, how the intellect both rests within itself and rightly discerns and distinguishes the things that exist together. You observe, furthermore, a permanent life; you recognize an intelligence that does not act regarding the future, but rather focuses itself on the present—or rather, it possesses and always now holds the present.

<margin>C</margin> In that realm, certainly, the "now" itself is and is forever. There, the thinking subject does not look out toward anything external, but looks into what is within itself. Therefore, by the very reason that it understands, there is activity and motion; but by the reason that it observes itself, Essence and Being flourish there. For it understands as a thing that exists, and it understands itself as existing; and that very thing upon which it relies, or toward which it strives, exists as Being. Indeed, the act directed toward itself is not the essence; but that upon which it exerts itself and upon which it depends is judged to be Being. Neither the perfection itself, but rather the thing perceived, should be called Being.

<margin>D</margin> Furthermore, these things possess being because that on which it depends and toward which it tends is Being. But since it does not exist merely in potential, but exists in act, it joins those two into one again; it does not divide them, but makes itself into that other thing, and in turn, that other thing into itself. Now, Being itself is the firmest of all things, in which all other things are founded, and what it possesses, it does not hold as something foreign, but possesses from itself within itself.

<margin>E</margin> There is also a state in which intelligence terminates, not as a beginning state, and from which it breaks out, not as a breaking state. For it is not motion from motion, nor into motion. Furthermore, the Idea indeed consists in Rest <note>original: "statu"</note>, since it is the limit of the intellect; but the intellect itself is Motion. For this reason, all things seem to be one: Motion, Rest, and those things which exist commonly throughout the whole, which are the "genera." Every subsequent thing is a certain being, a certain rest, and a certain motion. Anyone who has contemplated these three—namely, while inspecting Essence and seeing Being in that which is within itself, and seeing in the others a kind of motion within it by his own motion, and rest by his rest, fitting these to those—mixes these very things as if they were fused into one. He does not pull them apart, but after a slight distinction is made, he immediately reaches the level from which his gaze rightly discerns Being, Rest, and Motion: these three, and each one as an individual.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> BUT one must establish these three, if one understands each separately. But at the same time, one understands and establishes them if they are understood. For those things to which being belongs with matter, their being is not in the mind, for then they would be immaterial. But those things which are immaterial, if they are understood, then their very being is that they are understood. See then the Intellect, and see it pure, and look upon it intently, not looking from the outside <margin>B</margin> but within it... You see Essence <note>original: "οὐσίας" (ousias), transcribed in OCR as "ἡσίας"</note> there, and how much light it has, never sleeping. And how it stands in itself, and how it is distinguished while being together. And a life that remains, and a thought not acting toward the future, but what is already being is "now." Rather, it is "already," and "always already." And it is always already present. And as one thinking in himself, and not looking outside, nor outside in the act of thinking, there is either activity or motion. But that which looks into itself is Rest and Being. For it thinks because it is being, and because it thinks being. <margin>Γ</margin> It thinks itself. And that upon which it rests is Being. For the activity directed toward itself is not Essence <note>original: "οὐσία"</note>. But that from which it is and toward which it is, is Being. For the thing seen is Being, not the sight itself. And sight itself has being, because it is from being and is activity; being not in potentiality, it joins the two together again, and does not separate them, but makes itself that thing, and that thing itself. Being is the most stable of all things, and that upon which other things rest, by having what it has, as it is said. and it does not have it as something brought in from the outside, but it is from itself and in itself. And there is that in which thinking ends, <margin>Δ</margin> a rest not departing from itself, and from which it started, a rest not departing. For it is not motion from motion, for it is already intellection. Furthermore, the Idea is in rest, being the limit of the mind. But the mind itself is motion. So that in all things there is motion and rest. And these are the genera existing through all things. And each of the subsequent things is a certain being, and a certain rest, and a certain motion. Someone seeing these things, becoming part of the nature of Being, sees Being with the being that is in himself. And seeing the others with the others, he sees <margin>E</margin> the law in himself, by his own motion. And rest by rest. And fitting these to those, which are together and as if mixed, he mingles and distinguishes them, standing for a little while. And having distinguished them, he enters into rest, and motion, and these three, and each one.
