<header>SECOND BOOK.</header>

<margin>A</margin>
If someone contemplates these things in this way, does he not judge them to be diverse from one another in some manner, and distinguish them by the principle of Otherness? And does he not notice this very "Otherness" <note>original: "alteritatem"</note> within Being itself? He sets down three things, certainly, and each one as a unit. Then, seeing all these together again in one and within the one, and looking at them all as directed toward the one, he recognizes an Identity <note>original: "identitatem," the quality of being the same</note> already made—or rather, already existing. Is it not therefore necessary, besides those three [Being, Motion, and Rest], to add these two: namely, Sameness and Otherness? Therefore, it follows that all things are governed by five genera. These genera pass down their own qualities to the things that follow them, from which both "sameness" and "diversity" proceed; for indeed, every subsequent thing is "the same" as some things and "different" from others. For they place the concepts of "The Same" and "The Different"—simply and without any additions—within the order of the genera. Furthermore, these are the primary genera because we can predicate nothing of them in terms of their "Whatness" <note>original: "quid est," the essential definition</note>. It is true that one can predicate "Being" of them, for they are beings; but "Being" is not predicated of them as a genus. For "Being" is not predicated of Essence in such a way that Essence itself is said to be a specific type of Being. Nor, again, is it predicated that way of Motion or Rest; for these are not "species" <note>sub-categories</note> of Being. For some beings are like species of Being itself, while others are participants in it. Again, Being should not be called a participant in these as if they were its own genera; for they do not transcend Being, nor are they prior to it.

<column-break/>

If someone contemplates these things in this way, does he not judge them to be diverse from one another in some manner, and distinguish them by the principle of Otherness? And does he not notice this very "Otherness" <note>original: "alteritatem"</note> within Being itself? He sets down three things, certainly, and each one as a unit. Then, seeing all these together again in one and within the one, and looking at them all as directed toward the one, he recognizes an Identity <note>original: "identitatem"</note> already made—or rather, already existing. Is it not therefore necessary, besides those three, to add these two: namely, Sameness and Otherness? Therefore, it follows that all things are governed by five genera. These genera pass down their own qualities to the things that follow them, from which both "sameness" and "diversity" proceed; for indeed, every subsequent thing is "the same" as some things and "different" from others. For they place the concepts of "The Same" and "The Different"—simply and without any additions—within the order of the genera. Furthermore, these are the primary genera because we can predicate nothing of them in terms of their essential definition. It is true that one can predicate "Being" of them, for they are beings; but "Being" is not predicated of them as a genus. For "Being" is not predicated of Essence in such a way that Essence itself is said to be a specific type of Being. Nor, again, is it predicated that way of Motion or Rest; for these are not species of Being. For some beings are like species of Being itself, while others are participants in it. Again, Being should not be called a participant in these as if they were its own genera; for they do not transcend Being, nor are they prior to it.

### The One itself, simply as it is, which is superior to Being, is not predicated as a genus of any things or beings. Chapter IX.

*Because of its utterly indivisible simplicity, the One admits no differences within itself; it allows no divisions, additions, or compositions through which a genus is usually branched out into species. Likewise, the "One" that exists within Being cannot be predicated as a Peripatetic genus <note>Referring to the followers of Aristotle, who defined a "genus" as a category that applies equally to all its members</note> in a single, uniform way. For in the order of things, Being and the One are spoken of in different ways, some more and some less, some prior and some posterior. Finally, just as in the Moon, that which looks upward toward the sun is simply bright, while that which looks downward is both bright and not-bright at the same time; so too Being, depending on the "One" itself, insofar as it naturally inclines toward the One, is rightly Being as a total unity or a unified thing. But that which follows after this within Being is "One-Being" equally as much as it is "Many-Beings." The former, being entirely one or unified since it is indivisible, is not a genus; the latter, which follows it, does not introduce a new genus beyond those five already mentioned.*

---

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>A</margin>
That these are the primary genera, someone might assert through these arguments and perhaps through others. But how can it be made probable that these alone exist, and no others besides? For why is "The One" not a genus? Why not "Quantity"? Why not "Quality" as well? Or "Relation" and the rest that others <note>A reference to Aristotle’s ten categories</note> have enumerated? As far as "The One" is concerned, if it is taken as that which is entirely One, to which nothing else is added—not soul, not intellect, nor anything else—it will be predicated of nothing; therefore, it will not be a genus. But if we take the "One" that is attached to Being, in which we call it the "One-Being," this itself will not be the primary One. Furthermore, since it never admits any differences within itself, how could it produce species? And if it does not produce species, it cannot be a genus. Indeed, how could you divide it? You would make many things by dividing. Therefore, the One would then become "Many," and if it wished to be a genus, it would destroy its own nature. Added to this is the fact that if you divide it into species, you must add something to it; otherwise there would be no differences in the One, just as there are differences in Essence. The Mind
certainly admits the differences of Being; but how could it

<header>PLOTINUS, ENNEADS VI.</header>

In their reading, his essence and intelligence differ in a certain way; otherwise, in the order of things born from there, as far as essence proceeds, intelligence would also proceed. In that realm, therefore, the act of understanding, like an **internal motion**, rests upon its essence—being—as if on a hinge. It rests there, I say, in two ways: for from there it both continually leaps forth and leaps back. Being there is essentially intelligence, and in turn, intelligence exists intellectually as being. Intelligence both begins from a certain state—that is, the firm vigor of the mind—and tends toward a state—that is, the Idea as its boundary. Therefore, besides being, motion, and rest, there is also otherness <note>original: "alteritas"</note> insofar as these are distinguished from one another by reason, and again identity <note>original: "identitas"</note> insofar as all things are in the same nature. But then, the four things following there are not species of being, but rather certain acts that accompany being itself. Finally, those five are called the **genera of beings** <note>These are the "Five Great Genera" derived from Plato’s *Sophist*: Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Otherness.</note>, and whatever exists is reduced to one of them; all of them together are included in any given thing, and for this reason, they can also be called the principles of things.

---

<margin>A</margin> MOREOVER, it is necessary to establish these three, since the intellect understands each of them separately; yet it understands and establishes them simultaneously, provided they have been understood. For those things whose being is joined with matter, their being is not "to be in the intellect," otherwise they would be segregated from matter. But for those things which are separated from matter, if they are understood, that very understanding is their very being. Come then, contemplate the pure intellect, and look deeply into it—fixing your gaze not on the external, but entirely on the internal. Behold, you are now intuiting 
<margin>B</margin> essence there like a Vestal deity <note>original: "Vestale numen." Ficino uses the image of Vesta, the Roman goddess of the hearth and eternal fire, to represent the stable, central, and sacred nature of Essence.</note> and a foundation; you perceive there a wakeful and inextinguishable light. You notice, moreover, the manner in which the intellect both rests in itself and rightly discerns and distinguishes those things which are together. You further observe a permanent life; you recognize an intelligence that is not acting regarding the future, but rather intending itself toward the present—or rather, possessing it and always already holding it. There, certainly, the "present" is itself and is always; and there, the one who understands does not look at anything external, but looks within himself. 
<margin>C</margin> In what way, therefore, does it understand? There, the act is also motion. But in the way it observes itself, essence and being flourish there; for it understands as an existing thing, and understands itself as existing. And that very thing upon which (or into which) it rests exists as being. Truly, the act directed toward itself is not the essence; rather, that upon which it rests and from which it depends is judged to be being. Neither the act of perceiving itself, but rather the thing perceived, must be called being. 
<margin>D</margin> This [perception] further possesses "to be," since both that from which it hangs and that toward which it tends is being. But since it is not merely in potentiality, but exists in act, it joins those two into one again; it does not separate them, but makes itself into that other, and in turn, makes that other into itself. 
<margin>E</margin> Now, being itself is the firmest of all things, in which all other things are founded, and what it possesses, it possesses not as something foreign, but from itself within itself. It is also that in which intelligence ends—a state <note>original: "status," meaning a condition of rest or stability.</note> that does not begin—and from which it breaks out—a state that does not break out. For it is not a motion from motion, nor into motion. Furthermore, the **Idea** indeed consists in a state of rest, since it is the limit of the intellect; the intellect, however, is the motion of the Idea itself. Therefore, all things seem to be one: both motion and rest; and those which exist commonly throughout the whole are the genera. Each of the subsequent things is a certain being, a certain rest, and a certain motion. Someone having contemplated these three—namely, while he looks at beings—intuits being through that being which is within himself. And by other things, he similarly perceives others: either the motion in that [higher being] by a certain motion of his own, or rest by rest, adapting these to those, or mixing these very things as if they were confused, not separating them, but after some distinction, he immediately reaches the level from which his intuition rightly discerns being, rest, and motion—these three, and each individual thing.

<column-break/>

BUT it is necessary to consider these three things, if the intellect understands each separately. But simultaneously it understands and establishes them, if they have been understood. For those things whose being is with matter, the being of these is not in the intellect. But if they are immaterial, those things which are immaterial, if they are understood, their very being is that [understanding]. See the pure intellect and looking into it, gazing intently, not having seen through other things. You see then the light of essence in it, sleepless. And how it stands and how it is distinguished while being together. And life remaining and intelligence not as an activity toward the future, but rather toward the "now"—or rather, it is already and always already. And always present, and how it understands in itself and not outside. Not in the act of understanding is the activity and the motion; but in the act toward itself, the essence and the being. For it understands as existing, and understands itself as being. And that on which it is supported is being. The activity toward itself is not essence. But that toward which it leans is being. For the thing seen is being, not the act of seeing. And it itself also has "to be," because it is from it and toward it. And being in activity, not in potentiality, it joins those two, and does not separate them, but makes itself that, and that itself. Being is the most stable thing. And that around which other things [exist], which it possesses. And it has it not as something brought in, but from itself and in itself. It is also that in which the act of thinking ends—a rest not having started—and from which it has set out—a rest not having set out. For motion from motion is not into motion. Furthermore, the Idea is rest, the limit of the intellect. And the intellect of it is the motion. So that in one are all: motion and rest, and being through all, they are the genera. And each of the later things is a certain being, and a certain rest, and a certain motion. And someone having seen these things, having become in that standing part of nature, and by the being in himself [sees] being. And by the others seeing the others, by the motion in himself [seeing] the motion, and the rest by the rest. And applying these to those, becoming together, and as if having mixed them confusedly, and distinguishing them, as if having stopped and waited a little and distinguished them, he saw being, and rest, and motion, these three and each.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 602 regarding the "Five Great Genera" of the intelligible realm—Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Otherness—and begins Chapter IX, which argues why the "One" is superior to these categories and cannot be considered a "genus" or classification itself.</meta>

603
<header>BOOK TWO</header>

<margin>A</margin> <note>original: "ἆρ᾽ ἔχ᾽ ἕτερα ἀλλήλων..."</note> Does someone contemplating these things not consider them in some way diverse among themselves, and distinguish them by their otherness? And does he not notice this very otherness within being? He establishes three things, clearly: Being, Motion, and Rest, and each one is a "one." Then, looking at them again as a whole and within a unity, and bringing all things back to one—looking at them as the same—he recognizes that identity <note>The quality of being the same as itself.</note> has been established, or rather, already exists. Is it not necessary, then, to add these two—Identity and Otherness <margin>B</margin>—to those first three? Consequently, it follows that there are five primary genera <term>genera</term><note>The "Five Great Genera" or highest categories of reality according to Plato’s Sophist, which Plotinus adopts here.</note> for all things. These genera then pass down their own characteristics to the things that follow them, from which both "sameness" and "difference" arise. For every subsequent thing is "the same" as itself and "different" from something else. Indeed, they place Identity and Otherness simply, without any addition (which usually happens when we speak of "something" being the same or "somewhat" different), in the order of the primary genera. Furthermore, these are the *first* genera because we can predicate <note>To "predicate" means to state or assert a quality about a subject.</note> nothing of them in terms of their "whatness" <margin>C</margin> (their essential definition). It is true we can say they "are" (predicating "being" of them), for they are indeed beings; but "being" is not predicated of them as if it were their genus. For "being" is not spoken of in relation to essence in a way that makes essence merely a type of being. Nor is it spoken of in this way regarding motion or rest, for these are not merely species <note>Sub-categories.</note> of being.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> For some beings are like species of being itself, while others are beings by "participation" <note>A Platonic concept where things have a quality because they "share in" a higher Form.</note>. Again, Being should not be called a "participant" in these categories as if they were its own genera; for these things do not transcend Being, nor are they prior to it.

---

# ->The One itself, which is simply above being, is not predicated of any genus or being as a genus. Chapter IX.<-

Because of its utterly indivisible simplicity, the One admits no differences within itself. It accepts no divisions, additions, or compositions—the very tools by which a genus is usually divided into species. Likewise, the "One" that exists within Being cannot be predicated of the genera or beings in the way a Peripatetic <note>Followers of Aristotle; Plotinus is contrasting his view with Aristotelian logic.</note> genus is used. In the order of things, one thing is considered "being" and "one" differently from another, in greater or lesser degrees, and as prior or posterior. Finally, just as the part of the Moon facing upward is simply bright, while the part facing downward is both bright and not-bright; so too Being, depending on the "One itself," is entirely unified insofar as it naturally tends toward the One. But what follows after this in Being is "one" and "many" at the same time. The first—utterly one or unified—is indivisible and is not a genus. The second, which follows it, does not introduce any new genus beyond the primary ones already discussed.

<margin>A</margin> <note>original: "Α’ ΛΛ᾽ ὅτι μὲν ταῦτα γένη πρῶτα..."</note> One might assert that these are the primary genera based on these arguments, and perhaps others; but by what reasoning can we be sure that these are the *only* ones, and there are no others besides them? Why not include the "One"? Why not "Quantity"? Why not "Quality"? Or "Relation" and the rest which other philosophers <note>Likely referring to Aristotle’s ten categories.</note> have enumerated? As far as the "One" is concerned, if we mean the "absolute One" to which nothing else is added—neither soul, nor intellect, nor <margin>B</margin> anything else—it cannot be predicated of anything; therefore, it cannot be a genus. But if we mean the "one" that is present in being (which we call "one-being"), this is not the "Primary One." Furthermore, since it never admits any differences within itself, how could it produce species? And if it does not produce species, it cannot be a genus. Now, how could you even divide it? By dividing, you would create many things. Therefore, the One would become many, and if it <margin>C</margin> tried to be a genus, it would lose its own nature. Added to this, if you were to divide it into species, you would have to add something else; otherwise, there would be no differences in the "one," just as there are differences in "essence." How could the Intellect admit such a thing? Likewise, wherever there is a difference...

<meta>This page continues the logical investigation into whether "The One" (the Absolute) can be categorized as a "genus" or whether it stands entirely outside the system of classification. Plotinus is currently refuting the idea that Unity and Being are simply the same thing or that they exist on the same level of reality.</meta>

<header>PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.</header>

<margin>A</margin> By proposing two distinct things <note>namely, Being and Unity</note>, you effectively destroy the nature of the One; for wherever the addition of unity occurs, it inevitably obscures what was there before. But if someone should say that the "one" found in being, and the "one" found in motion and the rest, is a common trait, and should reduce that "one" and "being" into the same thing—just as he did not allow "being" to exist as a genus of the others because they were not identical to being itself, but were called beings in a different way—likewise, the "one" itself will not be common among them. Rather, one thing will be "one" in a primary sense, and another in a different way.

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, if he should say that the One is not a genus for all things, but something existing in itself like the others, and if he wishes "being" and "the one" to be the same, then since "being" has already been numbered among the genera, he is now merely introducing a different name. But if he says the "one" itself is something else, he is certainly describing each as having a specific nature; if he adds something to it, he introduces "a certain one," but if he adds nothing, he simply brings back that which is predicated of nothing at all.

<margin>C</margin> If he again introduces the "one" as coming together with "being," we shall respond as we said before: that this does not exist as the "primary one." But what prevents this from being the "primary," setting aside, of course, that which is absolutely and strictly One? For we call "being" that which comes after the One, and we affirm that it is "primary being." Perhaps it is forbidden to say this because that which exists above "being" should not be called "being" at all; otherwise, this "primary being" would not be judged as such. Yet, that which is placed above this "one" <note>referring to being</note> actually exists as the One.

<margin>D</margin> Moreover, if the "one" is separated from "being" by the intellect, it admits no differences. Therefore, the "one" which is placed within "being"—whether it is a consequence of being or of all things—will certainly be posterior <note>Logically "after" or dependent upon.</note> to them. A genus <term>genus</term><note>A general category or class under which species are grouped.</note>, however, must be prior. Whether it concurs with being or with others, the response is the same: a genus ought not to be simultaneous, or if it is prior, it will certainly be a principle of that thing alone; but if it is a principle of that thing, it is not also its genus. And if it is not a genus of that thing, it is not a genus of others either; otherwise, it would be necessary for "being" to likewise be the genus of everything else.

<margin>E</margin> In general, the "one" in being seems to approach the nature of the One and, as it were, to coincide with being. Since being itself, which tends toward the one, is "one being," that which comes after it is "being," which can indeed also be many. In this case, since that [primary One] remains one and does not wish to be divided, it certainly does not allow itself to become a genus.

---

### The Absolute One is not predicated as a genus of anything—neither of the genera themselves, nor of any Ideas. Chapter X.

> *For any genus and any Idea is necessarily a "one something" that participates in "multiplicity." That primary One and these others are named "one" equivocally <note>Using the same word to mean different things.</note> and through a vastly different logic; multiplicity is predicated of genera and Ideas no less than unity is. Furthermore, a genus admits variety within itself, which the Absolute One does not. Since it is simply One, it is not a "one genus." Additionally, the "one" is present in all beings commonly, but it does not exist as a genus for that reason—just as the unit is not the genus of numbers, nor the point the genus of lines, nor the simple part the genus of composites. Finally, that which comes together with essence, if considered without being, is not divided by any differences into "this one" or "that one"; division occurs by reason of being and within being. This [being], therefore, remains the genus, whatever kind of genus it may be.*

<margin>A</margin> **IN WHAT** way, then, is each of those things which are proper to being "one"? Perhaps it is because it is a "certain one," but not the One itself. For that which is "a certain one" is already many; but each species <term>species</term><note>A specific type or sub-category within a genus.</note> is "one" in an equivocal sense, for a species is a multiplicity. Therefore, the "one" in this context is like an army or a choir; the Absolute One is not in these, and thus the One is not a common genus. Nor can the One itself be considered as identical to being, nor to those things which are properly something—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <note>original: "Δύο τιθείς, ἀναιρεῖς τὸ ἕν..."</note> By positing two, you destroy the One; for if the addition of the unit is around everything, it will make the prior thing disappear. If someone were to say that the "one" on being, and the "one" on motion and the others is common, and if he brings being and the one to the same thing, then in the same way that "being" did not make a genus of the others because they were not beings but beings in another way, so too the common element will not exist among them. Rather, one is primary, and the others are in another way.

<margin>B</margin> If he says it is not common to all, but something in itself like the others, and being and the one are the same to him, then since being is already numbered among the genera, he is merely introducing a name. But if he says each is different, he must say what their nature is. If he adds something, he says something. But if nothing, he again says that which is predicated of one—he says it again.

<margin>C</margin> If the one comes together with being, we said that he does not speak primarily. But what prevents that which was mentioned from being primarily that which is entirely One, and we call the thing before that "being," and "primary being"? Either that which is before it is being, or if he says so, he would not say it... <note>The Greek text here is truncated in the original transcription.</note>

<margin>D</margin> Regarding this, if the thing before it, then being separated in thought from being, it has no differences. Then to being, if it is a consequence of it, and of the others, and of those things later, but the genus is prior. Or is it simultaneous and of all? But the genus is either simultaneous or prior, a certain principle and itself alone? But if it is the same, is it a genus to itself? If not to itself, then not to the others. Or would it be necessary again that "being" be the genus of other beings.

<margin>E</margin> For in general, the one seems different from being. And as if falling together with being; of being, one part is being toward that [the One], and the other is being after that, which can also be many. But the same thing, even if it wishes to be divided, would not even wish to be a genus.

---

<margin>A</margin> How then is each of the real beings "one"? Or by having the "one" it is "one." For what a thing is is already many. But each of the species is "one" equivocally. For the species is a multiplicity. Just as "one" is here, like an army or a choir; therefore that "one" there is not in types. So that where it is common, it contemplates the one with being, and to the things which are in whatever way...

<summary>Plotinus argues that "The One" cannot be a genus because it is logically prior to all categories and lacks the internal differences required for a classification. He distinguishes between the Absolute One and the "oneness" found in individual things like an army or a species, which are actually composed of many parts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s dialectical exploration of the "One" and "Being." Having previously argued that the One cannot be reduced to Being, he now examines whether the One can be classified as a "genus"—a general category or class that contains species—and concludes that the One transcends such logical structures.</meta>

605
<header>SECOND BOOK.</header>

<margin>A</margin> That which is simply the One itself is not a genus. For every genus is such that while it is predicated of its members, its opposites <note>original: "opposita," referring to contrary qualities</note> are not also predicated of them. However, regarding whatever part of the universal whole that "the one" is affirmed, opposites are also affirmed. Therefore, whatever the "one" is affirmed of as a genus, it must be judged as not being a genus. For this reason, it cannot truly be called a genus even in relation to the primary genera.

<margin>B</margin> Since "one being" <note>original: "vnum ens"</note> is no more "one" than it is "many," and since none of the other genera are "one" in such a way that they are not also many, the "one" cannot be predicated of these later things—which are entirely many—as a genus. In short, no genus is a total "one" in itself. Therefore, if the One were a genus, it would immediately cease to be "one." For the One itself is not a number, but it would become a number if it were a genus.

<margin>C</margin> Furthermore, it would be a specific "one" within a number; for if it were a "one" by genus, it would not be the "one" in a primary or foundational sense. Just as in the study of numbers, "one" is not called a genus of the numbers, but is said to be present within them <note>as the building block of all numbers</note> without being a genus, so too even if the One is present in beings, it does not mean it is the genus of Being itself, nor of other things, nor of all things combined. Just as a simple principle <note>original: "simplex principium"</note> can be the origin of a thing that is not at all simple, yet it is not the genus of that thing (otherwise that which is not simple would also be simple),

<margin>D</margin> so must it be said of the One: if it holds the place of a principle, it cannot be the genus of those things that follow it. Thus, it will neither be the genus of Being nor of other things. But if it were a genus at all, it would only be the genus of those things which are individually called "one," as if one were to think that "oneness" could be separated from "essence" <note>original: "essentia"</note>. Thus, it would only belong to some things. For just as Being is not the genus of all things, but only of the species that are specifically named "beings,"

<margin>E</margin> so too would the One be a genus only of those species that are specifically called "ones." What difference, then, would there be between one thing and another insofar as they are "one," just as there is a difference between one being and another? If "the one" is divided simultaneously with Being and Essence, and if Being exists as a genus because it is divided and considered the same across many things, why should the One not also exist as a genus, since it appears to be as numerous as the essences and is divided equally?

<margin>F</margin> But truly, it is not necessary that if something is present in many things, it must be a genus, either of those things it inhabits or of any others. Nor is it necessary that if something is common, it must be a genus. For instance, a point <note>original: "punctum"</note> which is present in lines is not a genus of those lines, nor a genus at all. Furthermore, as we said, the "one" in numbers is not the genus of numbers or of anything else.

<column-break/>

For it is necessary that what is common and single among many things—if it is to be a genus—must admit its own specific differences <note>original: "differentias," the traits that divide a genus into species</note>, and thus create species, and be predicated in the category of "what it is" <note>original: "in eo quod quid est," the essential definition</note>. But what are the differences of the One itself? What kind of species does it produce? If it were said to produce the same species as Being, then it would certainly be the same as Being; therefore, the name alone would be different, and "Being" itself would be judged sufficient.

---

### and by prior and posterior. Chapter XI.

Again, the definition <note>original: "ratio"</note> of the One and the definition of Being are not entirely the same between themselves. For an army is no less a "being" than a house is, nor a house less than a continuous object; yet an army is "less one." The definition of the One and the Good is the same, and insofar as...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the relationship between "the One," "Being," and "the Good." Having established that the One is not a mere category or genus, he now explores how different levels of reality (from physical objects like ships to the human soul) participate in unity and how this unity is synonymous with their goodness or perfection.</meta>

PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK VI.

whatever is a participant in the One is to that extent also a participant in the Good, and vice versa. It has been said elsewhere that the One is a different, higher state of existence, and for that reason, "well-being" is sought by things beyond mere "being." Indeed, the Good of each individual thing consists in its union—that is, those things that are joined to one another—and that the whole should be united to its related principle. Thus, all things come together, both those that are more closely related and those that are less so, finding reconciliation.

---

<margin>A</margin> It is worth the effort to consider how unity exists in Being, and in what way the so-called "partition" <note>original: "partitio," referring to the logical division of a whole into parts or a genus into species</note> occurs; and overall, what kind of partition of the genera there is, and whether both partitions are the same or different. First, we must think about how anything at all is said to be "one" and how it exists as such; then, whether we speak in the same way regarding "One Being," and how it is spoken of in that context. <margin>B</margin> Now, the "One" that is attributed to all things is not the same. For it does not hold the same status in sensible things <note>objects perceived by the senses</note> as it does in those things perceived only by the intellect; but neither does "Being" hold the same status among them, nor does it exist in the same way among sensible things themselves. For the "one" in a choir is not the same as the "one" in an army, a ship, or a house; nor, again, is it the same in these as it is in a continuous object. Nevertheless, all these things imitate the same One, some from further away and others more closely; and in the Mind <note>original: "mente," referring to the *Nous* or Divine Intellect</note>, it is undoubtedly more true. <margin>C</margin> For the soul is one; and the Mind is much more one, just as Being is one. Therefore, when we speak of any being of its own, do we likewise speak of it as "one"? And as it possesses Being, does it also possess unity? Or rather, does that happen by accident? Does it not exist as "one" simply because it is a "being"? For it is possible that something which is no less a "being" is nevertheless "less one." An army or a choir is no less a "being" than a house is, yet it is "less one." <margin>D</margin> It appears, therefore, that the "one" in anything looks toward the Good itself—being "more one"—and as much as it attains the Good, so much does it also possess unity. Its degree of "more or less" depends on this very unity. For everything does not wish simply to exist, but to exist with the Good. For this reason, even things that are not "one" strive as much as they can to become "one"; and things that consist by nature affect that very nature by coming together into the same thing, namely, while they desire to be united to themselves. For individual things do not hasten to become separate from one another, but hasten toward one another and toward themselves. Indeed, all souls wish to pass into "one," provided their own essence is preserved. <margin>E</margin> And certainly, in the universe, the One reigns on both sides. For the One is both that from which all things depend and that toward which all things tend. For they begin from the One and hasten toward the One; for in this very thing consists the Good of all things; and thus, in the order of things, each thing exists. And after it exists, it would not persist unless it hastened toward the One, nor can it restrain itself from hurrying toward this point. Those things, therefore, that are led by nature behave in this way; and those treated by art behave so. Every Art <term>Ars (Techne): In this context, any skilled craft or systematic knowledge</term> rightly disposes each thing toward this very goal, as much as the art itself can and as much as the individual parts are able; <margin>F</margin> and Being itself achieves this most of all. Indeed, some things are only called what they are called, just as when we say "one [man]," we say it while looking toward "two" <note>treating unity as a count or number</note>. But if we call something "one" in another way, we are speaking of something added to it. But in Being itself, we say that this whole is "One Being," and we judge it as "one," clearly demonstrating its greatest proximity to the Good.

<column-break/>

We must investigate how, in Being, there is the so-called partition, and the mind as a whole; and whether each is the same or different. Thus, how in general each is said to be "one," whether in the same way as we say "one" in the "One Being," as it is said there. Now, the "One" is not the same in all things. For it is not the same in sensible things as in intelligible things. But neither is "Being" the same in sensible things compared to one another. For the unity in a choir and an army, and a ship and a house, is different; and again, it is different in types and in the continuous. But all things strive to imitate the same thing, though some attain it from afar, and others more so. For there is already a truer unity in the Mind. For the soul is one, and even more so is the Mind and Being. Do we then, in each thing, call "Being" itself "one," and as it has Being, so does it have unity? Or does this happen by accident, the "one" being something added? But if it were no less a "being," yet "less one"—for an army or a choir is no less [a being] than a house. But clearly, each is "one." It seems, then, that the "one" in each thing looks toward the Good, being "more one" according to how much Good it has, and to that extent it is "one." And the "more or less" of unity is in this. For to be <unclear>one</unclear> is desired with the Good, and according to this is the Good. Because of this, that which is not "one" hastens as much as it can to become "one"; and things that are by nature, that very nature hastens toward unity, wishing to be in themselves. For they do not hasten away from each other, but each into the other and toward themselves. And all souls wish to be "one" again, while remaining within their own essence. And on both sides there is the "One." For it is that from which they come, and that toward which they tend. For they come from the One and hasten toward the One. For in this way the Good exists in all things. For they would not endure unless they were oriented toward it, having the same Being. Some things are by nature, others by art; and each art brings each thing toward this [unity], as much as it can and as it is able. And Being itself would most of all achieve this. For it is near to that from which other things are called. For example, "man." For if we say "one," we speak in relation to "two." But if we say something else is "one," we speak of it as something added. But in the case of Being, we speak of the whole Being. And we judge it as "one," showing its greatest communion <note>original: "συνουσίαν," meaning fellowship or association</note> with the Good.

For it is closest to the One. For this reason, if we ever say "this one," we say it looking toward "two." But if we call something "one" in another way, we are speaking of something added. But in Being itself, we say that this whole is "One Being," and we judge it as "one," showing its greatest proximity to the Good.

<summary>Plotinus argues that unity and goodness are inseparable, explaining that every being—from a choir to the Divine Mind—strives for the "One" to achieve its natural perfection and goodness. He distinguishes between mathematical unity (counting) and the essential unity that defines the existence and value of all things.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s metaphysical inquiry into the nature of the "One" and how it relates to the primary categories of existence. # BOOK TWO

It results, therefore, that the One is in itself as both principle and end, yet not in the same way, but rather otherwise. For this reason, within this "one" itself, there is both a "prior" and a "posterior." What then of this "one" itself within it? Is it not considered similarly and as common to all parts? Perhaps even in lines, the point is common, yet it is not the genus <note>A "genus" in this philosophical context refers to a broad category or class that contains species; Plotinus is arguing that unity is a shared attribute rather than a classifying category.</note> of lines. And in numbers, the "one" is perhaps common, yet it is not a genus. <margin>B</margin> For the "one" which exists in itself is not the same as the "one" which exists in unity, or in the number two, or in the other numbers. Furthermore, even in Being, nothing prevents some things from being primary and others following after; some being simple, and others composite. Yet, if the "one" were the same in those things which properly belong to Being, because no difference is present in it—and therefore it produces no species—it follows that it cannot be a genus.

<column-break/>

---

> ## The Good of even inanimate things, of discrete things, and of numbers, consists in a certain union: likewise each of the five genera is both one in itself, and not torn apart in those things that participate in it. Chapter XII.

<margin>A</margin> Let these matters be so; but in what way is there "good" in numbers, in the sense that each individual number is "one," since they are inanimate <note>soul-less or lacking life</note>? Perhaps this unity is common in other things as well which lack a soul. If anyone should object that numbers do not exist at all, we shall answer that we have set out to speak of "beings" insofar as each thing is "one." But if they ask how a geometric point participates in the Good, we must ask in turn whether the point receives it according to itself or not. And if it does receive it so, and they grant it is inanimate, we shall say they are asking the same thing they asked regarding other such things. <margin>B</margin> If, however, they take the point in relation to other things—for instance, in a circle—we shall answer that whatever is the "good" of the circle is also the good for the point, and that the point itself desires this and tends toward it through the circle. 

But in what way are these "genera"? Are they perhaps each divided? Or is the whole existing in each of those things of which it is the <margin>C</margin> genus? And how is it still "one"? Perhaps it is one in genus, as a whole existing in many parts. Is it then only in those things which participate in it? Perhaps not only in them, but also according to itself, and in those which participate. But perhaps this will be clearer in what follows.

---

> ## Motion, rest, identity, and alterity are the primary genera of things along with Being, since they exist as certain primary and intimate acts of Being itself; but number resulting from there is posterior, and also posterior is magnitude; therefore these two are not primary genera. Chapter XIII.

<margin>A</margin> We must investigate at present why "quantity" is not also numbered among the primary genera, and likewise "quality." But surely quantity is not primary along with the others, because those others exist simultaneously with Being. For Motion exists together with Being—with Being, I say, existing in act—and motion is its very activity, since it is also its life. Rest <note>also translated as "stability" or "stasis"</note> likewise conspires together in that very essence; or rather, the very "to be" is present with them, <margin>B</margin> by which I mean both with "alterity" <note>the state of being different</note> and "identity" <note>the state of being the same</note>, so that these are also seen together. But number is posterior <note>later in the logical order of creation</note> to them and to itself; and the very fact that it is "posterior" it receives from the "prior." And they exist in sequence within one another, and the posterior things are within the primary ones. Wherefore among the primary...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the categories of existence, specifically critiquing Aristotle's categories from a Neoplatonic perspective. Following the previous discussion on the "One," Plotinus now examines whether Quantity (Number and Magnitude) and Quality can be considered "primary genera" or if they are derived from more fundamental principles like Being, Motion, and Rest.</meta>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK VI

...they will not be numbered at all. But it must be asked <margin>A</margin> whether number itself is a genus <note>In ancient logic, a "genus" is a broad category that can be divided into species. Plotinus is questioning if "Number" is a fundamental building block of reality or just a description.</note> at all. For magnitude <note>original Latin: *magnitudo*; Greek: *megethos*. This refers to geometric size or extension.</note> is even more "posterior" <note>In Neoplatonism, "posterior" means something is lower in the hierarchy of reality and derived from something more "prior" or fundamental.</note> than number, as well as being composite. For in magnitude, there is both number and the line, which are two distinct things; there is also the plane, and thus there are three. If, therefore, continuous magnitude derives its very nature as a "quantum" <note>A "quantum" refers to an amount or "how-much-ness."</note> from number, and if number itself is not a genus, in what way can magnitude be a genus? Furthermore, among magnitudes there is also a <margin>B</margin> "prior" and a "posterior." But if the quality of being a "quantum" is common to both number and magnitude, we must consider what exactly this "quantum" is; and once we have found it, we must place it as a posterior genus, and by no means among the primary genera. And if it is a genus but not among the primary ones, we must track down which of the primary genera it should be reduced to, or to which of those things that relate to the primaries. It has been found <margin>C</margin> perhaps that the nature of the "how much" designates a certain quantity, and measures the quantity of each thing, and is itself a certain "quantum." But if this "quantum" is common to both number and magnitude, then either number is primary and magnitude is derived from it, or number is entirely involved in a certain mixture of motion and rest, while magnitude <margin>D</margin> is a kind of motion, or at least depends on motion—insofar as motion proceeds into the indefinite, while rest, by halting what proceeds, produces unity <note>original: *monada*, the "monad" or "the one."</note>. But concerning the generation of number and magnitude—or rather, the underlying substance <note>original: *hypostasis*.</note> and the concept of each—it seems we should consider these in what follows. For perhaps number is indeed placed among the primary genera, while magnitude is a later composite; number belongs to stable things, while magnitude is involved in motion. But we shall speak of these things in the following sections.

*Quality is not among the primary things of reality: since quality is posterior to essence <note>original: *essentia*; Greek: *ousia*. Often translated as "Substance" or "Being."</note> itself, appearing as an "accident" <note>An "accident" is a property that a thing has but which is not essential to its being what it is (e.g., a man being tan is an accident; a man being rational is essential).</note> to that which subsists absolutely. The primary genera, however, accompany that essence as its innermost acts. Within the essences of natural things, there are certain natural and intimate properties similar to qualities—such as heat in the essence of fire, or the rational faculty in man—which are in truth "essential" rather than merely qualities. But those things which do not spring from a specific essence, but happen to it from elsewhere—such as whiteness in a man—these are truly qualities and "passions" <note>A "passion" (Greek: *pathos*) in this sense is something that happens to a thing or a state it enters into.</note>.*

### Chapter XIV.

<margin>A</margin> Why is Quality not among the primary genera? Surely because this, too, is posterior and is born after essence. It is necessary for the primary essence to possess these subsequent genera for itself, yet it is neither constituted by them nor completed through them; otherwise, essence would be posterior to quality and quantity. In composite essences <note>Things in the physical world made of many parts.</note>, which consist of many things and in which numbers and qualities exist, these qualities produce their diversity <margin>B</margin>, and it happens that they are qualities of those essences; one may perceive a certain commonality in them. But in the primary genera, it is not fitting to create a division of things that are not simple and are composite, but rather from those things that complete the essence—and I do not mean a "certain" essence. For it is perhaps not absurd that a "certain" essence be completed by a quality, provided that the essence exists before the quality <margin>C</margin> and the "suchness" <note>A literal translation of *qualitas* or *poiotēs*.</note> happens to it from the outside. But the primary Essence itself must possess whatever it has as essential characteristics. Although in other cases we have judged that those things which complete an essence...

<column-break/>

...would not be counted. But it must be asked <margin>A</margin> if, in general, magnitude is even more posterior. For number is in the line, and the line is a composite. The plane makes three. If then there are two things, and the plane makes three; if indeed <margin>B</margin> the "how much" is held by the continuous through number, and number is not a genus, how can magnitude be? And there is also among magnitudes a prior and a posterior. But if the "how much" is common to all, we must grasp what it is. And <margin>C</margin> having found it, we must place it as a later genus, not among the primary ones. If the genus is not among the primary ones, to which of the primaries should it be led back, or to those leading to the primaries? It is clear perhaps that the nature of the "how much" is to measure the quantity of each. If this is so, or if the "how much" is common to number and magnitude, then number is primary and magnitude is from it; or entirely, number is in a mixture of motion and rest, while magnitude is a certain motion, or from motion; for while motion proceeds toward the indefinite, rest, in the halting of that which proceeds, makes the monad <note>The unit of one.</note>. But concerning the generation of number and magnitude, or rather the "subsistence" <margin>D</margin> <note>original: *hypostasis*.</note> concerning them, we must investigate. For perhaps number is among the primary genera, but magnitude is in the composition. And number belongs to the standing; magnitude is in motion. But these things we shall say later.

### CONCERNING QUALITY.

WHY IS IT NOT <margin>A</margin> among the primaries? Is it because this too is later, and after substance? For substance must have the primaries following it. But it should not be from these, nor be completed through these. For then it would be later than quality and quantity. Therefore, in composite substances, and those from many things, there are both numbers and qualities, and these produce differences <margin>B</margin> in them, and they are qualities of them. A certain commonality will be observed in them. In the primary genera, one should not make a division from things that are not simple and are composite, but from those things that complete the substance. For as for substance, that a "certain substance" is completed even from quality is perhaps nothing strange. Substance already being there before the quality, <margin>C</margin> the "such-a-kind" comes from outside; but substance itself must have whatever forms it has. And yet in other places we said that those things which are "completing" of the substance...

<summary>Plotinus argues that Quantity (Number/Magnitude) and Quality are not primary categories of reality because they are derived from more fundamental principles like Being and Motion. He distinguishes between essential properties that define a thing's nature and "accidental" qualities that are merely external additions.</summary>

# SECOND BOOK

<margin>A</margin>
...are called "qualities" equivocally <note>original Greek: ὁμωνύμως (*homonymos*). This means they share the same name ("quality") but have different fundamental natures.</note>. Those which come from the outside, following after the essence, are truly qualities; however, those that exist within the essences themselves are the "acts" or "activities" of those essences. On the other hand, those which follow after the essences are then considered "passions" <note>original Latin: *passiones*; Greek: *pathe*. In this philosophical context, a "passion" is anything that happens to a thing or any property it "undergoes," rather than something it does or is.</note>. But now we say that those things which relate to a specific essence do not entirely "complete" the essence itself. For they are not added to a human being, insofar as he is a human, to form his essence; rather, the essence exists from above before reaching the "differentia" <note>The specific trait that distinguishes a species from its broader group, such as "rationality" distinguishing humans from other animals.</note>, just as the "animal" already exists before one descends to the specific property of being "rational."
<margin>B</margin>

---

*Just as fire is not first fire, and then afterwards its light, heat, dryness, and lightness; rather, these four exist simultaneously with the essence of fire as properties and accompanying acts of its actual existence. In the same way, the being's internal motion, rest, identity, and alterity relate to Being itself. Chapter XV.*

<margin>A</margin>
In what way, then, do the four genera <note>Plotinus is discussing the primary categories of the Intelligible World: Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness (Identity), and Alterity (Difference).</note> complete the essence, while not yet creating a "specific kind" of essence? For they do not yet produce a particular essence. It has already been stated that Being itself is primary. It is also well-established that Motion is not a different Being, nor is Rest, nor again is Identity or Alterity. Furthermore, it is perhaps manifest that this Motion does not bring "quality" into that realm; yet, if explained, it will become even more manifest.
<margin>B</margin>
For if Motion is the "act" of essence, and Being itself is an "act"—and all primary things are, in general, acts—then Motion is rightly not an "accident" <note>A non-essential property that can change without the thing losing its identity.</note> there. Rather, since it is an act of Being truly existing in actuality, it should certainly not be said to "complete" the essence as an addition, but is instead the essence itself. Therefore, it does not arrive as something secondary, nor does it take the place of a "quality," but is established in an order of simultaneous companionship. For it is not the case that Being exists first and then afterwards moves. Nor
<margin>C</margin>
should it be said that Being exists first and then afterwards stands still. For Rest (or "Status") is not a "passion" there. Moreover, Identity and Alterity are not posterior, because that Being did not become "many" at a later time; rather, it was already this very thing—a "one-many" <note>A core Neoplatonic concept where the Intelligible realm is simultaneously a unified whole and a collection of distinct forms.</note>. If it is many, then Alterity (Difference) was there. But if from the beginning the many are one, then Identity (Sameness) is also there simultaneously. And these indeed suffice for essence. But when there is to be a progression from there to lower things, then other things arise which no longer "make" essence, but rather make the "quality of essence" and the "quantity of essence," and such types of genera are formed, but they are not the primary ones.

---

*Relation, place, "where," "when," time, position, habit, and action along with passion are neither primary genera, nor equal to them. For they are adventitious (external) and signify composition and deficiency. Chapter XVI.*

<margin>A</margin>
Consequently, since "Relation" is like a certain accidental offshoot, how could it be ranked among the primary things? For relation is of one thing to another; it is not a state regarding itself, but always toward something else. Furthermore, that which is usually numbered among the categories as "where" and "when" is even further removed from the primaries. For "where" seems to signify one thing in another, and therefore involves two things. It might be a genus of a sort, but it is not a single, primary thing; nor is there "place" in that higher realm. We are currently speaking of things as they truly exist. One must consider whether
<margin>B</margin>
"time" is there—but in truth, time is not there. If time were a measure, and not just a measure simply but a measure of motion, it would be two things and a composite whole, and posterior to motion. Therefore, time does not exist in the same equal distribution as motion. That which...

He contrasts these with secondary categories like Time, Place, and Relation, which he deems "posterior" and inapplicable to the primary level of reality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the "Categories of Being." Having established the five primary genera (Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Difference), he is now explaining why other significant concepts like "Action," "Passion," "Possession," and even "The Good" and "Beauty" are not considered primary genera in the same way.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin>Furthermore, what is said to "act" and to "undergo" <note>original Latin: *facere atq; pati*; Greek: *poiein kai paschein*. These are two of Aristotle's ten categories which Plotinus is here reducing to Motion.</note> is involved in motion. Therefore, if acting and undergoing exist there [in the intelligible realm], since acting and undergoing are two distinct things, neither will be a simple thing, and thus neither will be a primary genus. Indeed, even what they call "having" <note>The category of "Possession" or "State."</note> involves two things within itself. Likewise, what they call "position" or "lying" <note>The category of *Situs* or *Keisthai*.</note> in a certain way—one thing in another—comprehends three things.

### *The Good is not among the primary genera. For if it signifies the First Good, it is above the genera; if it signifies the goodness in things, it is posterior to the genera. Whatever things are called "good" are not so by a single generic nature, but because they belong to the First Good and incline toward it; and "good" in the primary Being is its life and its motion toward the First Good. Chapter XVII.*

<margin>A</margin>Moreover, why should Beauty, the Good, the virtues, knowledge, and intellect not also be numbered among the primary genera? Truly, if we take the "Good" itself to be that which we usually call the Nature of the Good—about which nothing can be properly predicated <note>Plotinus believes the absolute "One" or "Good" is beyond language and description.</note>, even though we speak of it as best we can because we are unable to explain it otherwise—it certainly cannot be called a genus of anything. For it is not predicated of any other things; otherwise, each of those things of which it was predicated <margin>B</margin> would be that very thing which was predicated. Furthermore, that Good is not within essence, but above essence <note>original Latin: *super essentiam*; Greek: *epekeina tes ousias*. A famous Platonic phrase meaning the ultimate principle transcends being itself.</note>. But if the "good" here is taken as a "quality," it must be said that quality is not among the primary things at all. What then? Is the nature of Being itself not a good? Certainly it is a good, but in a different way, and not in the same way as the First Good. And thus it is good not as a quality, but as a thing possessing the Good within itself. But we have said that other genera consist within the nature of Being itself, and for this reason—because each of them is something common <margin>C</margin> and is seen in many things—it has been established that they are genera. If, therefore, the "good" is also seen in every part of essence or being, or at least in most parts there, what prevents it from being a genus and placed in the order of the primary things? But this seems to be prevented because it is not the same in all parts, but is arranged in a first, second, and then a third and posterior order. For indeed, anything there is called "good" either because one thing comes from <margin>D</margin> another (the posterior from the prior, and so on), or because all things depend on one superior thing, while different things participate in it differently according to their own nature. If someone should wish to place it as a genus, it will be a "posterior" genus; for it is posterior to essence. And yet, this "being good" is something that belongs to that essence, even if it is always present with it. Those other things [the five genera], however, were said to belong to Being itself by the very reason that it is Being, and they contribute to its essence <margin>E</margin>. From here, one ascends to that which is above Being, since Being and Essence cannot be "not many," but it is necessary for these to have those numbered genera within themselves, and for the "One" to be "Many." Nevertheless, if we wished to say that the "good" here is the "One," we should not fear to assert that its "act" <note>original Latin: *actus*; Greek: *energeia*. The active expression or "shining out" of a thing's nature.</note> tends by nature toward the One itself; to affirm that its being is good, so that it becomes "good-formed" <note>original Latin: *boniforme*; Greek: *agathoiedes*. Having the form or character of the Good.</note> from that source, that goodness will surely be an act. And that act is its life; and that is motion, which is already numbered as one certain thing among the genera.

### *Beauty, knowledge, intellect, and virtue do not bring new genera there, but are reduced to those five primary ones in some way. Chapter XVIII.*

<margin>A</margin>When we speak of Beauty: if the first, supereminent Beauty itself is intended, we shall give the same or very similar answers [as we did for the Good],

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...to act and to undergo are not [primary categories]. If all things are there [in the intelligible realm], and acting is there similarly to undergoing, neither is simple. Nor is "possession" simple, as it involves two things; and "position" involves one thing in another, so it involves three.

<margin>A</margin>But why are Beauty and the Good not numbered among the primary [genera]? Regarding the Good: if it is the First—that which we call the nature of the Good, of which nothing is predicated, though we speak of it as we do because we have no other way—it is not a genus of anything. For it is not spoken of in relation to other things; or if it were, then each thing it was spoken of would be that very Good. And <margin>B</margin> that Good is not Essence, but is [above it]. But if it is like a "quality," then "quality" as a whole is not among the primary things. Is the nature of Being not good? It is, but not as the First. And not in that way, as the First. And not as a quality, but as having [the Good] in itself. But we said there are genera in [Being] because they are common, and seen in many things. If, then, the <margin>C</margin> Good is seen in each part of Essence or Being, or in most parts, why is it not among the primary things? Because it is not the same in all parts, but exists primarily, secondarily, and in a following order; one thing alongside another, the posterior after the prior. Or because all things come from the One, but each receives it differently according to its own nature. If one wants to call it a genus, it is a posterior one. For it is posterior to Essence; and it is a "certain kind" of <margin>D</margin> good, even if it is always present. Those other things [the five genera] belong to Being insofar as it is Being, and belong to its Essence. From there, one ascends to what is beyond Being. Since Being and Essence cannot be anything but "many," it is necessary to have these numbered genera. If we were trying to speak of the Good as the "One" in Being, we should not hesitate to say that its activity <note>original Greek: *energeia*.</note> is its nature toward the One; its being is "good" <margin>E</margin> so that it may be "good-shaped" from that source. That goodness would be an activity toward the Good. Let that be its life; and that is Motion, which is already one of the genera.

<summary>Plotinus argues that "The Good" and "Beauty" are not primary categories (genera) of Being because they either transcend Being entirely (as the One) or are qualities that things possess by moving toward the One. He maintains that concepts like Action and Passion are actually subsets of the primary genus of Motion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the "Primary Genera" of the intelligible world. Having excluded "The Good" as being above all categories, he now examines why Beauty, Intellect, and the Virtues (like Justice) are also not primary genera, but rather manifestations or activities of the five primary ones: Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Difference.</meta>

# BOOK TWO <note>original: LIBER SECVNDVS. In this edition, this refers to the second tractate of the Sixth Ennead, which focuses on the "Kinds of Being."</note>

<note>The following is the translation of the Greek column, which covers the conclusion of Chapter 18 and the start of Chapter 19.</note>

...to the arguments concerning the Good. But if Beauty is like a brilliance shining upon the Idea <note>or "Form"</note>, it follows that it is not the same in all things, and that this "shining" is something that comes afterward. If, however, Beauty is nothing other than Essence itself, then it has already been discussed under the category of Essence. But if Beauty is defined in relation to us who behold it, by the fact that it produces a certain state in us, then this "acting" is a form of Motion. And if that activity is directed toward that higher realm, it is also Motion. Knowledge, too, is a "self-motion," for the Intellect is a Being that acts—it is an activity, not a mere habit or state. Thus, knowledge also falls under the category of Motion. If, however, it is regarded as a fixed state, it falls under Rest—or perhaps under both. If it falls under both, it is a "mixture." Since a mixture is something that comes later <margin>*or "an entity of the mind"</margin> than its components, and since the Intellect is the being that understands, it is not a single primary genus. True Intellect is that which exists along with all things, and is indeed already all existing things. But "Being" alone, taken in its simplest form, is merely an element of it. Justice, Temperance, and virtue in general are all specific activities of the Intellect; therefore, they are not primary categories, but are posterior to the genus and are classified as species.

### Chapter XIX.
->He raises many doubts here; he defines almost nothing.<- <note>This is a characteristic Renaissance-era summary of Plotinus's difficult dialectical method.</note>

Since these four <note>Plotinus often oscillates between four and five primary genera: Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Difference.</note> are the primary genera, does each one produce its own species independently? For example, would Being be divided within itself, separate from the others, or not? Since one must take "differences" from outside a genus, are these beings "differences," or not? If they are differences, where do they come from? If they come from non-beings, that is impossible; if they come from beings, and there are only three other genera remaining, then they must clearly come from those. Thus, species are produced through the combination and simultaneous occurrence of these genera. But in this "breathing together" <note>original: ἐπιπνοίᾳ; literally "inspiration" or "confluence"</note>, the result is a composite of all of them. How then do other things remain "after" that which is composed of all? And how does the Intellect, which is already all things, create species? How does Motion create species of motion, or Rest create species of rest, and so on? Moreover, one must be careful that each genus does not disappear into its species, nor that it be spoken of as a mere empty abstraction. Rather, it must exist both in the species and in itself; it exists both as a mixture and as something pure and unmixed, lest it lose its own nature by contributing to the essence of another. These matters must be investigated. Since we have said that the Intellect is each thing that consists of all beings, and we have placed "Being" and "Essence" above all species and parts as the Intellect, we are saying that the "actual" Intellect comes later. We shall make this inquiry useful for our search, using these points as models to lead us into a true knowledge of what is being discussed.

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the translation of the Latin column, which parallels the Greek text above.</note>

<margin>A</margin> ...to the answers we have already given concerning the Good. If, however, Beauty is understood as some splendor reflecting in the Idea, the objection will be raised that it is not the same in all things. Likewise, such a "glow" would be a posterior thing. But if it is asserted that Beauty is nothing other than Essence itself, then it is already accounted for within Essence. Truly, if Beauty is assumed in relation to us who look upon it—because it affects us with a certain condition—it will be established that this very act of "effecting" is Motion. 
<margin>B</margin> And if that act is directed toward that higher realm, it will similarly be Motion. Science <note>or "Knowledge"</note> is also a motion; for it is the very "looking" of a being, and it is not a habit, but an act. For this reason, it will likewise be contained under Motion. But if its power is contained under Rest, or even under both, then if it is under both, it will be something mixed; and a mixture arrives later. Now, the Intellect is Being itself understanding itself, and it is composed of all things, not just one thing from the genera. Indeed, the true Intellect is Being together with all things; it is already all beings. But Being, 
<margin>C</margin> if it is taken as something solitary and bare, is assumed as a genus, and the Intellect is an element of it. Justice, 

temperance, and virtue in general are all certain acts of the Intellect. For this reason, they are not placed among the first principles, but are posterior to the genus, and are designated as species.

<margin>A</margin> IT REMAINS to inquire, since these four genera are the primary ones, whether any of these genera procreates species—as if Being were divided in itself separately from the others. Perhaps not in that way, since one must receive "differences" from outside the genus, and though those are differences *of* being insofar as it is being, the differences are not the same thing as the genus itself. From where then will it have them? Surely not from things that are not beings. If they come from beings, and there are only 
<margin>B</margin> three other genera remaining, it will obviously receive them from these; and with these added, preserved, and produced together. But these things, once constituted together, seem to have already completed that which is "made of all." How then do others remain after that which is from all? And how do the genera, since they are all beings, make species? Likewise, how does Motion produce species of motion? And Rest itself and others similarly? This must be observed in the first place: that each thing is not lost in its species, nor is it considered only in them. Rather, let it be 
<margin>C</margin> in them and in itself at the same time—both mixed and again pure and unmixed—lest if it should contribute to essence in another way, it might lose itself. Concerning these things, therefore, it is right to consider. Since we have said that the Intellect is that which consists of all beings, and we have placed Being itself and Essence as being above all species and parts, yet not yet being the Intellect <note>i.e., Being is the raw material, Intellect is Being in action</note>, we have rightly 
<margin>D</margin> brought this into doubt as a useful inquiry. For by using this very thing as a kind of model, we shall penetrate more effectively into the knowledge of the things we are treating.

The divine Intellect stands in relation to the Ideas just as Geometry stands to its own propositions. For that Intellect is both...
