<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the nature of the Intellect and how it relates to the "Primary Genera" (Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Difference). Having previously established that the Intellect is a composite of these genera, Plotinus now investigates how a single, universal Intellect can contain multiple individual "Intellects" or Ideas without losing its unity.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK VI.

This very thing exists in itself in **actuality** <note>original: *in actu*. Plotinus uses "act" to mean something fully realized or functioning, as opposed to "potentiality."</note>, and it possesses the **Ideas** in two ways: simultaneously all together there in actuality, and yet each one there in **potentiality** <note>original: *in potentia*</note>, soon to be distinguished from one another. In turn, each individual Idea is what it is by its own specific quality in actuality; however, in potentiality, it is the whole itself. Furthermore, that which is "above" in that realm is the **genus** <note>the general category or "family"</note> and the cause of what follows. Therefore, in the sense that it is a genus, it is in potentiality; but in the sense that it is a cause, it is again in actuality.

<margin>A</margin> Let us then consider the **Intellect** <note>the Divine Mind or *Nous*</note> itself as being in such a state that it touches none of those things which exist in part, nor does it act specifically upon any one thing (lest it become merely a *particular* intellect). Instead, let it be like **Knowledge** before it is divided into specific branches, or like a specific branch of knowledge that stands above the individual parts contained within it. Universal knowledge is none of the individual parts, but it is the power of them all; yet each part is its own specific thing in actuality, while being all parts in potentiality. The same condition applies to the Intellect when it is considered universally. <margin>B</margin> Now, those things which are in the "species" <note>individual forms</note> are placed within the whole according to potentiality; and having obtained their specific form, they are the whole itself in potentiality. For the "Universal" is predicated of them, yet it is not merely a piece of the universal; it must remain whole and simple within itself. Thus, in one sense, it is right to say the Universal Intellect is above all things that exist individually in actuality, <margin>C</margin> while in another sense, the individual intellects relate to it differently. These individual ones, though they are partial, are filled with all things; and the Intellect existing in all things supplies something to each, being their potentiality. It contains them in their universal forms, and they in turn hold the common Intellect within their particularities—just as a specific branch of knowledge contains "Knowledge" itself. Furthermore, the "Great Intellect" exists in itself, and again the individual ones exist in themselves; <margin>D</margin> those which are partial are encompassed in that whole, and the whole in turn is present in the particulars. Each exists both in itself and in another, and that whole exists in itself and in them. Likewise, all are in the whole—in that whole, I say, existing in itself—and they exist there in potentiality (specifically in the one which is all things together in actuality). Each individual is also a potentiality on its own. Again, they are in actuality what they are, but they are also the whole in potentiality. For insofar as they are in that genus, it is clear they are that genus in potentiality. That genus, in the sense that it is a genus, is the potentiality of all the species under it; it is not any one of them in actuality, but <meta>catchword: all</meta> all are present secretly and in quiet. But in the sense that it is that which exists in actuality before the species, it is the act... they do not exist only individually. It is necessary, if they are to be in actuality, that the act itself depending on that [genus] be the cause of this very thing.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <note>This column translates the Greek text, which mirrors the preceding Latin discussion of the Universal Intellect and its parts.</note> We took it, then, that the [Intellect] is not merely grasping things in part. Or rather, so that it does not become a specific intellect, it is **Knowledge** prior to the specific forms. And that which is in Knowledge, concerning the parts within it, is nothing of the part; but it is the power of all. In actuality it is that [the whole], and in potentiality it is the parts. And in the case of the universal, it is the same: in the species, they lie in the whole in potentiality. <margin>B</margin> Having taken their place in the species, they are the whole in potentiality. For the "all" is predicated of them. Not as a part of the all... for the "one" must remain undefiled in itself. Thus, in one way, the entire Intellect exists as something beyond the individual ones. In another way, each part is filled from all, and the Intellect in all is the provider for the individuals, <margin>C</margin> and it is [the potentiality] of them, and it has them in their universalities. And those in turn [hold] certain universals in their parts. Just as a specific science [holds] Science. And the "Great One" exists by itself, and each exists in themselves, and they are in [the whole]. And he himself is in the part as the whole. And the whole is in the part. Each is in itself and in another, and that one is in himself and in them. <margin>D</margin> And all are in [that one], while he exists in himself. In potentiality... in actuality. In the whole... For insofar as they are distinguished, they are that thing in actuality. But insofar as they are in that [genus], they are that in potentiality. Insofar as it is a genus, it is the power of all the species. And it is none of those in actuality, which are themselves quiet. But insofar as it is that which is before the actuality of the individuals... but if they are to be in actuality, as a form from it... to become the causal activity.

***

### CHAPTER XXI.
*The first Intellect, while discerning all things within itself by the act of understanding, reveals **Number** there; it declares **Magnitude** through its immense size, and opens up **Quality** through the clarity of its intelligence.*

Therefore, qualities and shapes are visible there, and through **Alterity** <note>the principle of "Difference"</note> itself, the differences of all qualities and shapes are seen; through **Identity** <note>the principle of "Sameness"</note>, their communion is also seen. Since the Intellect contains all things according to its own nature—and this nature is a living and intellectual **Essence**—it is right that the things understood within it are not mere figments, but are entirely intellectual beings in their own right. Finally, just as the movement of birth <note>original: *generationis motus*</note> relates to the power of nature to create life, so does the process of reasoning relate to the Intellect. For the movement of birth strives to generate limbs one by one, which are all present together at once in the power [of the seed]; similarly, the process of reasoning seeks out beings which are always all present together in the mind, without the need for reasoning. Just as perpetual searching is the sign of a reason that does not yet possess its object, so is it the nature of the Mind to "search" by way of a proof, even while already possessing all things.

<summary>This page explores the relationship between the Universal Intellect and individual intellects (or Ideas), using the analogy of Knowledge to explain how a whole can contain its parts. It also introduces Chapter 21, explaining how Number, Magnitude, and Quality arise in the intelligible world through the primary genera of Sameness and Difference.</summary>

# BOOK THE SECOND.

<margin>
...standing together, and in their own properties, just as you are. Chapter 20.
</margin>
How then, while remaining itself within the **Reason** <note>original: *logos*; here meaning the governing principle or formative power</note>, does it produce the individual parts? How is it the same? How do the things mentioned follow from those four [genera]? I see, therefore, in this great mind something impossible for a talkative mind, but possible for a **many-minded** mind. All things are in the mind, both as a whole and in part. But it is a specific mind, in such a way that all things arising from it are within it. It certainly possesses **number** in the forms <note>original: *ideois*</note> it sees and provides; in it are many, and all are **powers**, wonderful powers—not weak, but because they are pure, they are greatest and, as it were, vigorous and truly powers. It holds them to a certain point, for they are infinite. And infinity is greatness. To that greatness, along with the beauty of its essence and the splendor and light around it—seeing them as being in the mind—notice how even "quality" already begins to bloom there. Furthermore, along with the continuity of its activity, you see a "magnitude" shining forth to your sight, resting in a most quiet seat. But where there are one and two, and magnitude appears as a third, so too does all "quantity." When quantity and quality are beheld there, and both flow into one and become as if joined, you rightly see "figure" <note>geometric shape</note> there. Because "Otherness" <note>one of the primary genera</note> falls upon them and divides both quantity and quality, the differences of shapes and other qualities arise. Then "Sameness" <note>another primary genus</note>, acting in harmony, introduces equality, while "Otherness" introduces inequality in quantity, in number, and in magnitude. From these come circles and squares, and figures composed of unequal parts, and numbers both similar and dissimilar, odd and even. For where there is intellectual life and activity that never fails in any part, it rightly leaves out nothing of what we now find, leaving no intellectual work behind. Instead, it contains all things in its own power, possessing them as its essence, in the way a mind possesses. A mind possesses by way of **intellection** <note>original: *noēsei*; the act of thinking</note>, but an intellection that does not wander or move from step to step. It has omitted none of those things which are "reasons," but is like one single **Reason**—huge, perfect, and containing all reasons. It proceeds from its first principles in order—or rather, it is always already perfect, so that it is never true to say the mind "goes through" a process. For all things are there together. Whatever one might perceive in nature through reasoning, one will find those same things existing in the mind without the need for reasoning. Thus, one might think that **Being** itself made the mind reason in such a way—just as happens with the "reasons" that produce living animals. For just as the sharpest mind would reason in the best possible way, so all things exist in the "reasons" that precede all reasoning. What then should we expect to find in those higher forms, which precede both nature and the "reasons" implanted in nature? For in those higher forms, essence is nothing other than **Intellect**. Being and Intellect are not something added to them from the outside; rather, the thing itself exists in the best possible state, since all things there exist according to the mind's will, and that Being is what the Intellect wills.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> In what way, therefore, does the **Intellect** <note>original: *intellectus*</note> itself, while remaining one, by its own nature <note>original: *ratione*</note> bring about the things that exist in part? This is indeed the same as asking how from those four [genera] the things that are spoken of are subsequently produced. Come now, contemplate this great and altogether inestimable mind—not a "wordy" mind, but a **many-minded** <note>original: *multimente*; many-layered or containing many thoughts at once</note> one, understanding many things: which is indeed Mind through all things, and the whole Mind. Not just in part, <margin>B</margin> nor just a certain mind. Contemplate, I say, how all things are within it from itself. It certainly possesses **number** in those things which it beholds; it is one and many—"many," I mean, in the sense of numerous powers, and wonderful powers, in no part weak. Rather, because they are pure, they are greatest, vigorous to the highest degree, and truly powers, not merely powerful up to a certain limit. They are therefore infinite, and infinity itself, and depth of magnitude. This greatness, <margin>C</margin> together with the beauty of essence and its own splendor and light—which are in the mind—when you behold these, you also perceive the "quality" already blossoming there. Furthermore, along with the continuity of action, you behold "magnitude" flashing before your sight, situated in a most quiet seat. But since there is one and two, and likewise three, magnitude occurs as a third, and similarly all "quantity." Likewise, when quantity and quality are inspected there, and both flow into one and, as it were, become one, you rightly behold "figure" <note>shape</note> there again. Because "Otherness" itself falls upon them from within and divides both quantity and quality, the differences of figures and other qualities arise. Then indeed "Sameness," harmonizing there, introduces equality; but "Otherness" introduces inequality in <margin>E</margin> quantity, in number, and in magnitude, from which arise circles and squares and figures composed of unequals; likewise numbers, similar and dissimilar, and odd and even. Since there is intellectual life and activity there, never failing in any part, it rightly leaves nothing outside itself of those things which we now find. It leaves no work that is intellectual, I say, but contains all things by its own power, possessing these very things as its essence, and in that way which a mind possesses. But the Mind possesses through **intellection**, an intellection, I say, that does not wander <note>original: *non discurrente*; Plotinus argues that the Divine Mind knows everything instantly and simultaneously, unlike human logic which moves from A to B</note>. Now indeed, nothing has been omitted <margin>F</margin> of those things which are "reasons" <note>original: *rationes*; the formative principles of things</note>, but it is like one single reason: vast, perfect, containing all reasons, proceeding from its first principles in order—or rather, it is always already perfect, so that it is never true there that the mind "wanders" through a process. Truly, however <margin>G</margin> many things one might perceive existing in nature through argumentation, one will find those same things existing in the mind without the need for argumentation. Thus, one might consider that Being itself makes the mind argue in such a way—as also happens in the "reasons" that procreate animals. For just as the sharpest intellect will argue in the best possible way, so all things hold themselves in the "reasons" that precede all argumentation. What then must be thought to exist in those higher forms, which precede both nature itself and all the reasons implanted in nature? For in those forms, essence is nothing other than intellect; neither Being nor Intellect is adventitious <note>added from outside</note> to them. The thing itself easily holds itself in the best way, if all things are there according to the mind and according to its will, and that Being is what the Intellect wills.

### PLOTINUS: ENNEAD VI.

...and exists. Therefore, it is true and primary. For if it depended on another being, that being would rather be the Intellect. Since, therefore, all shapes and every quality appear in Being itself—for it is not merely a single quality that exists there, nor could it be, where **Difference** <term>Difference (heterotes): One of the five primary categories, allowing for the distinction between different forms</term> exists; rather, they are many and yet one, for **Identity** <term>Identity (tautotes): The principle that allows a thing to be itself and remain unified</term> is also there, by which Being itself becomes one and many. This is so from the very beginning, such that in all species there is similarly one and many: different magnitudes, different shapes, and different qualities. Nor was it possible or fitting for anything to be omitted there; for the universe is perfect there, otherwise it would not be a universe at all. Since, I say, life converges there in each thing—or rather, it exists everywhere simultaneously—it is no wonder that all things have necessarily come forth living and, in a sense, as "animals" <note>original: *animalia*; here meaning "living beings" in the broadest sense, including stars and formal principles</note>. For bodies were not lacking, as matter and quality were present. And since all things have already been made forever and remain, and are encompassed in eternity by their very being, and each thing is this very thing that it is individually, yet they are simultaneously together in the One—certainly, this very harmony and constitution of all things existing in the One is the **Intellect**. It possesses beings within itself as a living entity, exhibiting itself to that which proceeds from it as something to be seen; therefore, it is rightly called the **Intelligible** <note>original: *intelligibile*; the object of thought which the mind contemplates</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Which also exist, wherefore it is also true and primary. For if it were another, that would be the Intellect. Since all shapes of all things are placed in Being, and quality simply... for one could not say that the nature of the One is single, but one and many, where Identity was. Being is both one and many, and from the beginning. Just as in all forms, the one is similar... many, different magnitudes, and different shapes. <margin>B</margin> And different qualities. For it was not right for the Intellect to have omitted anything. Perfect is the whole. Or it would not be a whole. And since life is present, or rather preserved everywhere, by necessity living beings were produced. And bodies were there, since matter and quality were there. Since they are those things which are always and remain, and in Being are gathered, each is separate in what it is, <margin>C</margin> but together again they are in the One. The "weaving together" and "composition" of all existing things is the Intellect, which, having beings in itself, is a living whole. And it is the "Living-Itself" <note>original: *autozoon*; the Platonic Form of the Living Being</note>. By having itself to be seen by that which comes from it, it becomes the Intelligible, and allows itself to be rightly named.

->*The primary essence, living of itself, is called the 'Living-Itself' and the 'Animal-Itself': its act, reflected back into itself, is called the*<-
->*Intellect, which in this living substance of its own fashions as many ideas as there are species to be manufactured in the world. Chapter XI.*<-

*Sensation in itself only feels, but in the imagination, it perceives additionally that it feels. Similarly, imagination*
*imagines in itself; in reason, it perceives itself imagining. Reason argues in itself; in the intellect, it notices its own arguing.*
*Our intellect understands in itself; in the divine intellect, it notices its own understanding. The divine intellect, in its living essence,*
*finds and discovers all things. This essence is living, being both uniform and all-formed at once; therefore, this world is*
*understood and generated. Truly, the forms of things are multiplied there only as far as the ultimate species; in the world*
*of the soul, they are born more multiplied, and most of all in the 'generative nature,' which is the last part of this soul.* <margin>Plotinus</margin>
*Indeed, this Intellect calls these 'ideas,' but it names the general idea of souls sometimes 'Intellect' and sometimes 'Soul,'* <margin>ideas</margin>
*insofar as it looks upward or downward; similarly, it considers our soul worthy of a triple name for a triple reason.*

<margin>A</margin> PLATO, therefore, signified this with these words, though they are obscure: the Intellect, seeing the **ideas** existing in the "universal living being," beholds what kind and how many they are. For even the Soul, coming after the Intellect, possesses things in itself insofar as it is a soul, yet it looks up more effectively at what is above it. And our intellect, similarly holding things within itself, nevertheless contemplates more perfectly in that which is superior to it; for in itself it only looks, but in the superior, it additionally looks at its own looking. <margin>B</margin> Certainly, this Intellect, which we say contemplates the ideas, is not at all separated from its own superior; existing from it—inasmuch as it is many arising from the One—and having the nature of **Difference** as its companion, it becomes one and many. Since, therefore, it is one and many, it is so by a certain necessity. In the same way, the Intellect acts and is acted upon in turn. It is not permitted there to find any one thing numerically, such as is called an "individual" <note>original: *individuum*; an indivisible unit</note>. For whatever you take there will be found to be a **species**; for it is without matter. Therefore, Plato, hinting at this, says that the essence is "torn apart" or "divided" <note>original: *discerpi*; referring to the division of the World-Soul in the Timaeus</note> as it is led through infinites. For insofar as it...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> And having seen, therefore, in Plato, that the Intellect sees the ideas existing in the perfect Living Being, what kind and how many they are. Since also the soul of the intellect, insofar as it is a soul, has these things in itself, yet it sees better in the one above it. And our intellect, having things in itself, sees better [in the superior]; and in itself, it also sees that it sees. This Intellect <margin>B</margin> which we say sees, not being departed from the same, being from it, as being many from one through the nature of "The Other" <note>original: *thaterou*; the principle of Otherness</note> being present with it, becomes one and many. Being one and many intellects... because of the many, it is an intellect of such necessity. In general, it is not possible to take the "One in number" or the "atom" [individual]. Whatever you take is a form. For it is always without matter. Therefore, Plato, hinting at this, says that all [essence] is divided into fragments through the... for as far as it goes into another form, as if from... <gloss>Plato, involving this in obscure words, says: essence—just as from a genus one proceeds into another species.</gloss>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the Intellect’s internal structure, specifically addressing how the "Infinite" relates to the division of Being into specific forms (species) and the subsequent generation of the Soul.</meta>

# BOOK THE THIRD.

<column-break/>

**[615]**

<margin>A</margin> Infinity has not yet occurred. For that which proceeds in this manner is bounded by the generated **species** <term>species (eidos): Here referring to the specific "Forms" or "Types" that define individual things</term>; however, the final species, which is not further divided into other species, is more "infinite." And this is what is said by Plato: it is necessary for one who has now come close to individual things to grant them to infinity and let them go. <note>original: "infinitati concedere atque dimittere" — a reference to Plato's *Philebus* 16c, suggesting that once you reach the most specific level of a thing, you encounter the infinite variety of individuals.</note> But these individuals, insofar as they exist in themselves, are certainly infinite; <margin>B</margin> yet insofar as they are encompassed by a certain **One**, they come together into a specific number of species.

The **Intellect** <term>Intellect (Nous): The realm of pure thought and the Forms</term>, therefore, possesses that which comes after itself: the **Soul** <term>Soul (Psyche): The level of reality that mediates between the Intellect and the physical world</term>. Thus it happens that the Soul also exists within a certain number, reaching down to its very last part. This last part of the Soul is now entirely infinite. Indeed, such an Intellect exists as a "part"—even though it possesses all things and is itself the "all"—and those things which are its parts exist as parts of it while it exists in **actuality** <note>original: "actu" / "ἐνεργείᾳ" — meaning they are fully realized and active, not just potential.</note>. The Soul, however, is a "part of a part," but as if depending upon it in actuality. <margin>C</margin> For when the Intellect acts within itself, these very acts are the other intellects; but when it acts out of itself, as if externally, the Soul emerges.

Furthermore, when the Soul acts as a **genus** or a **species** <term>genus/species: Logical categories used here to describe the hierarchy of the Universal Soul and individual souls</term>, other souls exist as its species, and these have a double action. Specifically, the act directed toward what is above is the Intellect; but the act inclined toward what is lower manifests other powers according to **reason** <term>reason (ratio/logos): The organizing principle that shapes the material world</term>. Finally, the last vigor already touches and gives form to matter. <margin>D</margin> Yet, that which is lowest in the Soul does not prevent the rest of the universe from standing in a higher rank.

Perhaps even that which is called the lowest part of the Soul is an image of itself, not severed from it, but rather like the images appearing in mirrors—which remain as long as the primary **archetype** <note>original: "principale exemplar" — the original form that a reflection or copy is based upon</note> stands outside. But it is worthwhile to consider how such a thing is said to be "outside." Truly, up until that which is closest to the image of the Soul, the **intelligible world** <term>intelligible world (mundus intelligibilis): The divine realm of the Forms, accessible only to the mind</term> is entirely perfect, constituted from all intelligible things. <margin>E</margin> This world here below is a certain living imitation of that world, just as a certain likeness appears in a painting or in water—namely, a likeness of that which is seen to exist above the water and the painting.

<column-break/>

---

Therefore, the imitation in a painting or in water is not an imitation of both at once, but only of the one which was formed by the other. Thus, the image of the intelligible world possesses certain likenesses—not indeed of the **Creator** <note>original: "effectoris" — the "maker" or "producer," often associated with the Demiurge in Platonic thought</note> himself, but rather of those things which are contained within the Creator. Among these are both "Man" and every other "Animal." To be sure, both this world and the Creator are "living animals," but in different ways; and both consist within the intelligible world.

<summary>This page marks the beginning of Plotinus's investigation into the categories of the physical (sensible) world, questioning whether the same metaphysical categories used for the divine realm apply to the material world. He concludes that while we use the same terms, the physical world is merely an "image" of the true reality and requires its own distinct classification system.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation into how we categorize reality. Having discussed the "Greatest Kinds" of the spiritual or "Intelligible" realm on the previous pages, he now turns to the physical world. He argues that the Soul does not belong to the physical categories because it originates in the higher realm.</meta>

The nature of the Soul, existing in that intelligible realm <note>The "intelligible realm" refers to the world of pure Being and Intellect, contrasted with the physical "sensible" world.</note>, will neither fit nor be silent within the essences spoken of here; it must be set apart—even if with difficulty—from the business of this world. It is as if someone wishing to organize the citizens of a city according to their wealth, or their honors, or their trades, were to leave out the visiting foreigners as a separate group. Regarding the passions of animals, as many as happen to the Soul either with the body or because of the body, these must be examined later to see how they should be arranged when we investigate the things of this world.

<margin>
*and indeed
*for even
</margin>

And first, we must consider what is called essence <note>original: "οὐσίας" (ousias) / "essentia." This refers to 'Substance' or the fundamental 'Being' of a thing.</note>, granting that the nature regarding bodies is called essence equivocally <note>original: "ὁμωνύμως" (homonymos). Plotinus argues that a physical 'substance' is not the same kind of 'substance' as a spiritual one; they only share the name.</note>, or is not essence at all, because the definition of things that are "in flux" fits it; instead, it should properly be called "becoming" <note>original: "γένεσιν" (genesin). In Platonic thought, the physical world is always 'becoming' (changing), whereas the spiritual world 'is' (eternal).</note>. Then, of this "becoming," some things are of one sort, and others of another sort. And bodies should be gathered into one group—the simple, the compound, and their accidents or consequences—dividing all these from one another. We might say one part is matter, and the other is the form <note>original: "εἶδος" (eidos). The 'form' is the internal blueprint or shaping principle of a physical object.</note> upon it. Should each be treated separately as a genus, or both under one, since they are "essence" only in name, or rather "becoming"? But what is common to both matter and form? And how can matter be a genus? Or of what things? In what difference of matter, and in what place, should that which is composed of both be ranked? If that which consists of both is the bodily essence, yet neither of those two is a body, how could they be placed in one and the same rank with the composite? And how can the elements be ranked together with what comes after them? If we begin from bodies, we would be starting from syllables <note>A metaphor: studying the physical world first is like trying to understand a language by looking at syllables before knowing the letters (the higher principles).</note>, which is not a proper analogy. Even if the division is not made according to their own nature, we might say that in place of "Being" which is there, we have "Matter" here; and in place of the "Movement" which is there, we have "Form" here, as if it were a certain vital perfection of matter. Of matter, there is an escape from essence, and the "Same" and the "Other," of which there is much difference and greater unlikeness here. Or rather, matter does not have it so, and it receives form not as its own life or activity, but as a presence from elsewhere. Then, form there is activity and movement, but here, movement is something else and an accident. Form here is rather its "stasis" <note>original: "στάσις" (stasis). A state of standing still or fixedness.</note> and a kind of quiet; for it defines that which is itself indefinite. The "Same" there and the "Other" there exist because they are one and the same; but here, "other" is by participation, and how it is different. *For even the same and the other, if they were as they are there, would be something in the later things.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But the very nature of the soul, consisting in that intelligible world, does not belong in the same order with that which is here called essence: therefore it must be set apart—though the task be difficult—set apart nonetheless from the present condition of discussion which we are currently conducting: just as if someone wishing to arrange the citizens of some city according to their taxes, and honors, and trades, should leave the foreigners and newcomers separated from the citizens. Regarding the passions, however, as many as happen to the soul together with the body or because of the body, only then shall we discuss how they are to be arranged, after we have disputed concerning those things which are properly contained in this world.

---

->*In the intelligible world he posits true essence; in this one, however, the apparent, and a flowing in place of essence. Also, he refutes those who do not correctly arrange the categories here, though he does not yet arrange them himself. Chapter II.*<-

<margin>A</margin> In the beginning, it seems we must act concerning that which is called essence, and it must be granted first of all that this corporeal nature is called essence equivocally <note>original: "æquiuocè." Using the same word for two different things.</note>, or that it should by no means be called essence, because the notion of flowing things fits it, but properly it should be called "generation" or "becoming." Furthermore, regarding "becoming," it seems it should be said that some things are of this sort, and others of that sort. And bodies indeed are to be piled into one, <margin>B</margin> both the simple and the composite, and their accidents and consequences, meanwhile dividing these among themselves: or it may seem to someone that this is indeed matter, and that is species <note>original: "speciem" / "form." The shape or defining quality.</note> within matter, and each should be treated separately as a genus, or both should be joined into one, as if both were called essence or substance equivocally, or properly "becoming." But what indeed is common to matter and form at the same time? And how can matter be a genus? Of what things? <margin>C</margin> Since it is also a wonder what the difference of matter might be. Furthermore, in what place especially ought we to station that which is composed of both? If that which consists of both is a corporeal substance, yet neither of the two is a body, in what way should these two be placed in one and the same rank along with the composite? And in what way can those things which are the elements of a thing be established together with it in the same place? <margin>D</margin> If someone says we ought to begin from bodies, he advises just as if he had commanded that in discussing words one must begin from syllables. But what prevents us—if it is not permitted to divide according to the same nature—from dividing these at least according to a certain analogy and proportion, so that in place of being itself existing there, we place matter here? And for the movement of that being, we place form here as a certain life and perfection of matter? Then, for that which there is the "Same" and "Status," here we place a certain condition of matter not departing from itself: furthermore, in the place of "Alterity" <note>original: "alteritatis" / "otherness." One of the five Platonic categories.</note> itself, we place the <margin>E</margin> greatest diversity and dissimilarity of these things, surpassing opposites. But certainly matter does not have it so, nor does it receive form as its own life or act, but form enters from elsewhere, and is not anything belonging to matter. Furthermore, "Species" <note>Form</note> there is indeed activity and motion. Here, however, motion is something else and an accident: but form is rather its status and a kind of rest; for it defines that which is according to itself infinite. Furthermore, the "Same" itself and the "Other" itself are there for this reason: because one exists there as the "Same" itself and one as the "Other" itself: but here, "other" is said by participation, and in relation to something else, and something "same" and something "other," nor as it is there is it so in the later things...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the categories of the sensible (physical) world. Having previously established that the Soul belongs to a higher, intelligible realm, he now attempts to classify the components of physical reality, such as matter, form, and the objects created from their combination.</meta>

PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.

is said, but similarly as something same and something other. How can stability <note>original: "status"</note> be assigned to matter, which is pulled apart into all magnitudes, receives its shapes from external things, and is not sufficient on its own to generate other things along with them? It is therefore proper to set aside this division.

*Whatever things are properly in the sensible world <note>The "sensible world" refers to the physical universe perceived by the senses.</note> seem likely to be referred to five genera <note>“Genera” (plural of genus) here means the highest, most general categories of being.</note>. Let the first be substance; the second, the accident that is in substance; the third, the accident in which substance is; the fourth, relation. In the first genus, matter, form, and the composite are gathered; in the second, quantity and figure; in the third, place and time; in the fourth, action and passion; in the fifth, as many other things as signify in any way.*

->Chapter III.<-

## <margin>A</margin> HOW then shall we distinguish?
First, it may be done in this way: surely one thing is matter, another is form, and another is the mixture of both; then there are the remaining things concerning these. Of those things concerning them, some are only predicated <note>A "predicate" is a term used to describe a subject, like saying a rose "is red."</note> of them, while others are furthermore contingencies <note>original: "contingentia" / "accidētiūm." These are "accidents"—properties like color or size that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist.</note>. Moreover, of these contingencies or accidents, some exist within these substances, while in others, these substances conversely exist. Furthermore, some of these are actions, others are passions <note>In ancient philosophy, a "passion" (passio) is not an emotion, but the state of being acted upon by an external force.</note>, and others finally are consequences. It is also <margin>B</margin> permitted to say that matter is something common, and exists in all substances; yet it is not a genus, since it has no differences—unless perhaps one identifies its difference by the fact that this matter takes on a fiery form, while that matter takes on an airy form. But if someone thinks it is sufficient for matter to be <margin>C</margin> a genus because it is something common to all things that can be made of matter, or perhaps because matter itself stands in relation to many specific matters as a whole to its parts, it would be a genus in a way different from the usual sense. And this one thing will be an element, if indeed an element can also be a genus. Furthermore, if the "species" <note>original: "species." Here meaning the specific form that defines a thing.</note> is added to it—as being around matter or in matter—it will be separated from other species by this condition, yet it will not encompass every essential species. But if we call "species" that <margin>D</margin> very thing which is the producer of essence, and the essential logic <note>original: "rationalem" / "logos." The underlying principle or blueprint of a thing.</note> according to the form, we shall still remain in ambiguity. For we have not yet declared how essence <note>original: "essentia" / "substantia." The core reality of an object.</note> is to be understood. Accordingly, if only the composite of both is affirmed to be substance, those two (matter and form) will not be substances at all. But if both this composite and those two are substances together, it remains to investigate what is common to all of them. But those things that are only <margin>E</margin> called predicates will perhaps be in the order of relation, such as being a "cause" or being an "element." However, among those things which are accidents in them, one is "how much" (quantity), another is "what kind" (quality), which are properly in the substances themselves. There are also certain things in which those substances themselves exist, such as place and time; furthermore, their actions and passions behave like motions; then there are the consequences, such as place and time. Place is for the composites, while time is for... Consequently, we might find three primary things that concur into one common category, namely "substance," though here the word is used equivocally <note>original: "æquiuocè." This means the word "substance" has a different meaning when applied to a physical object than when applied to a divine or mental reality.</note>. After these follow the others in order: relation, quantity, quality, in time, in place, motion, place, time—although once place and time are accepted, it is superfluous to bring in again "what is in time" and "what is in place." Therefore, it will be possible to make five categories, if indeed the first three are counted as one. But if those three do not unite into one, they will be arranged thus: matter, species, composite, relation, ...

<column-break/>

## <margin>A</margin> HOW then do we speak?
We must certainly try: that one thing is matter, another is form, and another is from both, and other things are around these. Of the things around these, some are only predicates, others are accidents; of the accidents, some are for those things, others are in those things. Some are their activities, others are passions, others are consequences. Matter is common and in <margin>B</margin> all substances, yet it is not a genus, because it has no differences; unless one takes the differences according to this matter having the form of fire, and that having the form of air. Nor would it be sufficient for it to be a genus that it is common to all things in which it is the substrate, or as a whole to parts, but a genus in another way; which would be an element <margin>C</margin>, if it were possible for it to be a genus in that way. And as for form, when it is added as being according to matter or in matter, it is separated from the other forms, or rather it encompasses every essential form. But if we call "form" that which is productive of essence and the essential principle according to form, we have <margin>D</margin> not yet said what essence is, or how it is grasped. As for the composite of both, if that alone is substance, then those (matter and form) are not substances; but if both those and this are, we must look for what is common. Those that are only predicates might be placed in the category of "toward something" (relation), such as being a cause or being an element. Of the accidents, one is being "how much" (quantity), another is being "of a certain kind" (quality), which are in them. Others are those things in which they are, <margin>E</margin> such as place and time. The activities and the passions are like motions. The consequences are as place and time. Place belongs to the composites; time belongs to motion. And as for the first things, could we find some common name for them here, like "substance" used equivocally? Then the others in order: relation, quantity, quality, in time, in place, motion. But since place and time are taken, "in place" and "in time" are redundant. So there are five, if the first three are in one. But if not, the five would be in one: matter, form, the composite, relation, ...

<summary>Plotinus attempts to organize the physical world into five categories: substance (composed of matter and form), quality, quantity, relation, and motion, while noting the instability of matter.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the categories of the sensible world, specifically focusing on the definition of "substance" (ousia) in the physical realm. Having previously listed the five genera, he now examines what unites matter, form, and the composite object as "substances."</meta>

# BOOK THREE.

Quality, motion. Or perhaps these will be encompassed by relation <note>original: "relatione" / "πρός τι"</note>, for relation encompasses more broadly. Rather, it is more containing.

---

It is the property of corporeal substance to be the underlying support <note>term: "subjectaculum" — a foundation or "seat" that holds other qualities.</note> of accidents; but it is itself leaned upon by nothing as an accident, but exists in its own right. This property, which belongs to substance alone, is common to three substances: namely matter, form, and the composite.

->Chapter IV.<-

<margin>A</margin> What then is the same in these three, and what is it that makes these "substance"? Is there something in the definitions placed beneath the others? Indeed, while matter is a foundation and a seat, so too is form with matter—placed beneath as a foundation for the composite, or at least for all those things that follow the composite, such as quantity, quality, and motion. But perhaps substance is this very thing: because that which is said to be substance is not "of another"? For whiteness and blackness belong to another; namely, to the thing whitened or blackened. The "double" also <margin>B</margin> belongs to another. I do not mean here the double of a half, but wood that is double; and a father is a father of another. Knowledge belongs to another—the one in whom it exists. Again, place is the limit of another. And time is the measure of another. But fire does not belong to another. Nor does wood, insofar as it is wood, belong to another; nor does a man belong to another. Likewise Socrates, or any <margin>C</margin> composite substance at all. But what about the form <note>original: "εἶδος"</note> which exists according to the essence—is it "of another"? Since it is a "passion" <note>term: "passio" — here meaning an attribute or something that happens to a thing, rather than its core being.</note> of another, or rather the form of matter. But the combination of both is a part. And the form of a man and the man himself are the same. Matter also is a part of the whole. Is it "of another" as a part of the whole, or not as if that other exists independently, of which matter itself is said to be? Whiteness, however, is of another in the very way it is defined. Therefore, that which is "of another" while being something else itself <margin>* of another</margin>, is not substance. Substance, therefore, is that which is certainly what it is, existing of itself. Or certainly, if it is said to be a part of something, it is a completing part of a composite. Each part exists of itself; but toward the composite, it is said to belong to it in another way. Or certainly, by the reason that it is a part, it is said to be "of another"; but by its own nature, in its being what it is, it is not said to be "of another." Being a "subject" <note>term: "subiectum" — the underlying reality that supports qualities like color or size.</note> seems to be <margin>D</margin> common to matter, to form, and to the composite. But matter is a subject for form in one way, while form is a subject for "passions" in another way, and the composite in another way still. 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> What indeed is common in those three? Or what is it that makes them essence or substance <note>original: "essentia siue substantia"</note>? I mean substance of the kind that can exist in lower things. Is any of these a substance because it becomes a certain foundation and support for others? But matter seems to be the support and seat of form, while form does not seem to be a seat in the same way; <margin>B</margin> for which reason form would not be in the genus of substance. The composite also is surely a foundation and seat for many other things; and so the form, together with the matter, will be subjected to the composites—or rather to all things that follow the composite, such as quantity, quality, and motion. But perhaps that which is substance is this very thing because the thing itself which is spoken of is not "of another"? For whiteness and blackness belong to another—namely, the whitened or blackened thing. The "double" also <margin>C</margin> belongs to another. I do not mean for now the double of a half, but wood that is double; and a father, insofar as he is a father, is of another. Likewise, knowledge is of that in which it exists. Again, place is the limit of another. And time is the measure of another. But fire is not of another, nor is wood, insofar as it is wood, of another. Similarly, neither man, nor Socrates, nor any composite substance at all. And yet, neither is the form, which is according to essence, "of another," because it is a "passion" of nothing. For it is not <margin>D</margin> the "passion" of matter, although it is a part of the composite. Indeed, the form of a man and the man are the same. Matter also is a part of the whole, and it is "of another" insofar as it is of the whole—not as if that other exists as a separate thing of which matter is spoken; but whiteness, in the very way it is spoken of, is "of another." Therefore, that which exists as "of another" and is spoken of as such, is not substance. Substance, therefore, is that which is certainly this very thing that it is, existing of itself. Or certainly, if it is said to be a part of something, <margin>E</margin> it completes the composite itself, while each part or both exist of themselves, but toward the composite they are said to be "of it" in some other way. Or certainly, by the reason that it is a part, it is said to be "of another"; but by its nature, in being that which it is, it is spoken of as itself. However, to be a "subject" seems to be common to matter, form, and the composite. But matter is subject to form in one way, while form is subject to passions in another. 

---

And the composite in another way still. Or rather, matter is not even a subject for form. For form is the perfection <note>original: "perfectio"</note> of matter, both as it is matter and as it is in potential. Nor again does the form exist in this matter as in a subject; for where one thing together with another makes one single thing, the one will not be "in" the other as an accident. Instead, both matter and form together are the subjects for another—just as "man" and "a certain man" are subjected to "passive affections" <note>original: "passio" — used here to mean external influences or changes.</note>, and they precede actions and their consequences. It will seem, therefore, that substance is that from which other things come, and because of which other things exist, and that which is the center around which "suffering" <note>original: "pati" — to be acted upon.</note> happens and from which "acting" <note>original: "agere" — to perform an action.</note> proceeds.

<summary>Plotinus explores the definition of substance, arguing that while matter, form, and composite objects all serve as foundations for qualities (accidents), their true nature as substance lies in the fact that they exist "of themselves" rather than being attributes of something else.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation of the definition of "substance" (ousia) from the previous page. Plotinus is specifically looking at the traditional Aristotelian definition—that a substance is not "in a subject"—and testing whether this definition holds for both the physical and the higher, spiritual realms.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

->It is the property of substance alone that it does not exist anywhere as if in a subject <note>term: "subject" (Latin: subiectum, Greek: hypokeimenon) — In logic, the "subject" is the underlying thing that possesses qualities. For example, in the phrase "the apple is red," the apple is the subject and "red" is a quality existing "in" it.</note>, nor is it predicated of any external subject. Likewise, when we name things in the incorporeal realm using terms proper to corporeal types, we do not do so according to the same logic and nature, but attribute them through comparison and similarity.<-

->Chapter V.<-

<margin>A</margin> These things <note>original: "ACCIPIENDA verò sunt hæc"</note> must be understood regarding that substance which is said to exist "here" <note>note: "Here" refers to the physical, sensible world as opposed to the "There" of the higher, intellectual realm.</note>. If these properties also happen to fit the higher substance, they perhaps agree through a certain analogy or an equivocal naming. Now, that which is called "primary" is so named through a certain comparison to those things which follow it. For it is not named "primary" in an absolute sense, but rather in relation to those things that are lowest; indeed, those things that follow immediately are similarly called "primary" relative to those that follow them in turn.

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, what is called a "subject" behaves differently here and there; indeed, it is doubted whether there is "passion" <note>term: "passion" — Here meaning the state of being acted upon or undergoing change (the opposite of action).</note> there, and if there is, "undergoing" <note>original: "pati" / "πάσχειν"</note> is certainly something different there than it is here.

<margin>C</margin> It also seems to be common to every substance not to be in a subject—provided that "being in a subject" is defined as that which is not a part of that in which it exists, and does not combine with it to produce a single whole. For that which contributes with something else to the composition of a substance cannot be in it as if in a subject. Therefore, neither does form seem to be in matter as if in a subject, nor is "man" in Socrates, since he is a part of Socrates.

<margin>D</margin> Therefore, that which is not in a subject is judged to be substance. But if we say that substance itself is that which is neither in a subject nor said of a subject, we must add "of a subject" meaning "as of something else." In this way, in the description of substance where we add that substance is not predicated of another, "man" is also included when predicated of a particular man. For when I predicate "man" of Socrates, I do not speak as if I were calling "wood white," but as if I were calling "white, white." For when I say Socrates is a man, I am confessing that a certain man is a man, and I predicate "man" of the very man who is in Socrates. This is the same as if we said Socrates is Socrates, or just as if we were to predicate "such an animal" of a "rational animal."

<margin>E</margin> But if someone should object that "not being in a subject" is not unique to substance—arguing that "differences" <note>note: A "difference" is a defining characteristic, such as "two-footed" for a human.</note> are among the number of things not in a subject—that person should consider from which part of essence they took that which is called "two-footed" <note>original: "bipes" / "δίπουν"</note>. He will certainly admit that this is not in a subject, provided he takes "two-footed" as being the essence itself. But if he understands it as "two-footedness" [the quality], he will surely say it is not a substance but a quality, and therefore that which is called two-footed will then be in a subject.

<margin>F</margin> Furthermore, neither time nor place seems to be in a subject. But if the "measure of motion" regarding time is taken according to a subject <note>note: The Latin text here is slightly garbled in the OCR; the sense follows the Greek "measure in the thing measured."</note>, and motion is understood in that which is moved, the measure will be in the thing measuring. Place, on the other hand, since it is the limit of the containing...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> These things must be heard <note>original: "ἌΚΟΥΣΤΈΟΝ ΔῈ ταῦτα"</note> regarding the substance that is said to be "here" in this world. If in any way it happens to apply to that substance "there," it is perhaps by analogy or by a shared name. And "primary" is spoken of in relation to the things that come after it. For it is not simply primary to those things, as if they were the extremes, but in relation to those things and those beyond. That which is the subject <note>original: "ὑποκείμενον"</note> is one way here and another there, which is also disputed. Or if it is there, then
<margin>B</margin> undergoing <note>original: "πάσχειν"</note> is also something else. And not being in a subject is common to all substance—if "being in a subject" means not existing as a part of that in which it is, or not being something that results from a combination with that in which it is. That which contributes to the essence of what it is, even if it is in something, is not "in a subject." Thus, neither is form in matter as in a subject, nor is "man" in Socrates, being a part of
<margin>C</margin> Socrates. Therefore, that which is not in a subject is substance. But if we say it is neither in a subject nor "of subjects," we must add "as of another." For if "man" is spoken of in relation to individuals, that "man" is included in the definition. It is not predicated as being "of another." For when I predicate "man" of Socrates, I speak in this
<margin>D</margin> way: not as "the wood is white," but as "white is white." For in calling Socrates "man," I am calling that specific man "man." Thus, of the "man in Socrates," one predicates "man," which is in Socrates, just as one predicates "this particular thing" of "rational animal." But if someone says that not being in a subject is not a unique property of substance—for how is "differentia" <note>note: The Greek "φορὰν" (motion/carrying) here is likely a scribal error for "διαφορὰν" (difference), matching the Latin "differentia."</note> itself not among those things in a subject?—one takes "two-footed" as a part of substance and says it is not
<margin>E</margin> in a subject. For if he does not take "two-footed" as that which is this particular substance, but calls "two-footedness" a substance, he is actually naming a quality; thus "two-footed" is in a subject. Furthermore, neither is time in a subject, nor is place. But if "measure" is taken as the measure of motion and the measure is in the thing measured, then the
<margin>F</margin> measure is in the motion, and the measure is as if in a subject. And the motion is in the thing being moved. But if "that which measures" is taken, how will the measure be of the measure? Or how will place be the limit of the container? Not as something measured itself in the container, but...

<summary>Plotinus explores the definition of "substance" (ousia), examining the rule that a substance cannot be "in a subject." He argues that defining characteristics (like being "two-footed") are parts of a substance’s essence rather than accidental qualities, distinguishing the physical world from the higher intellectual realm.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's inquiry into the nature of substance (ousia). Having previously discussed how substance is defined by not being in a subject, he now examines whether "Being" (existence) means the same thing for a physical object as it does for a quality like "whiteness."</meta>

# BOOK THREE.

<columns>2</columns>

...of those things. And concerning the nature of essence, about which our discussion revolves entirely, such a substance is to be understood either according to one of these aspects, or several, or all that have been mentioned—since these apply to the matter, the form, and the combination of both.

<column-break/>

A similarly, it will be from the same containing principle. But conversely, the matter stands regarding this essence, about which we are presently disputing; concerning which it seems probable that one accepts such a substance either according to one of those things which have been said, or several, or all of them: seeing as the things mentioned are applicable to matter, form, and the composite <note>term: "composite" (Latin: composito, Greek: synamphoteros) — In Aristotelian and Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to a physical object made of both matter (the "stuff") and form (the "identity" or "pattern").</note>.

---

->Being is predicated of incorporeal and corporeal substance, as well as of accidents, not according to the same definition, but according to a different one, though through a certain similarity. Chapter VI.<-

->Corporeal substance, when compared to incorporeal substance, does not have being from itself, but from the latter; yet when compared to its own accidents, it possesses being in itself, and primarily and simply. Accidents, however, obtain their being through substance, and thus have being only in a secondary and relative way. There is, however, a kind of reciprocity here: for while the accident has its simple existence through the substance, the substance also acquires the state of "being such-and-such" through its accidents.<-

---

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>*</margin> But if someone should say that while these things have been considered regarding essence or substance, what it actually *is* has not been stated, perhaps they require us to look further into this sensible world. Yet this very thing "is," and its "being" cannot be directly seen. What then? Shall I say fire and water are substances? Does each become a substance because it is visible? Not at all. Or is it because they possess matter? Not even because of that. But is it because they have form? <margin>* the</margin> Not for that reason alone; nor even because they are a composite of both. By what then are they called substances? Clearly by the very fact of their "being." Yet quantity "is" and quality "is" as well. We shall perhaps say that this "is" is said of them equivocally <note>term: "equivocally" — When one word is used for two different things that don't share the same nature. For example, "bank" of a river and "bank" for money. Plotinus is asking if "being" means the same thing for a rock as it does for the color "red."</note>. But what then is this "is" in fire and earth and such things? And what is the difference between this "is" and the "is" that belongs to other things? <margin>C</margin> Perhaps the answer is that the former signifies "being simply" or "being in the primary sense," while the latter signifies "being white." What then? Is the "being" added to the white the same as that to which nothing is added? Not at all. One exists as being in the first degree, the other exists through participation <note>term: "participation" — The idea that physical qualities are just shadows or "participants" in a higher, perfect Reality or Form.</note> and in a second degree. For adding "white" to "being" has made "white being," and adding "being" to "white" has made "a white that is." Thus, the white is an accident to the "being," <margin>* to</margin> and "being" is an accident to the white. And we do not speak of this as we might of a "Socrates who is white" or "the whiteness of Socrates." <margin>* of it</margin> For in both cases, Socrates is the same. But perhaps "white" is not the same. For when it is said "the white is Socrates," Socrates is included in the white. But in the phrase "Socrates is white," the white is purely accidental. And here, "white being" has the white as an accident. But where it is said "the white is a being," the white has "being" included within it. And generally, the white has its being because it exists around and within "being"; it receives its existence from that. But "Being" exists as being from itself. From the white, it becomes white—not because "being" is in the white, but conversely, because the nature is in it. Since that "being" which is in the sensible world does not exist by itself, it must be said that it has its being from "Truly Existing Being." And from "Truly Existing Whiteness," it has its being white.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> If someone says these things have been considered regarding essence or substance, but what it actually is has not been stated, perhaps they further demand to inspect this sensible thing. Yet this very thing "is," and its "being" cannot be inspected. What then? Is not fire and water a substance? Does each become a substance because they are seen? By no means. Is it perhaps because they have matter? Not even for that. But is it because they have form? <margin>B</margin> Not for this cause; nor even because a composite is there. By what then are they called substances? Clearly by "being" itself. But quantity also "is" and quality "is." We shall perhaps say that this "is" is said of those and these equivocally. But then it will be asked: what is this "is" in fire and earth and others of this kind? And what is the difference between this "is" and that "is" which belongs to others? <margin>C</margin> It will perhaps be answered that they differ because this "is" signifies "being simply" and "being" in a simple sense, while the other signifies "being white." What then? Is the very being that belongs to the white the same as that to which nothing is joined? By no means. But this exists as being in the first degree, while the other exists according to participation and in a second degree. For "white" joined to "being" has rendered "being white," and "being" joined to "white" has made "white being." Therefore, white is an accident to "being," <margin>D</margin> and "being" in turn is an accident to the white. Nor do we speak as someone might perhaps say: namely, "white Socrates" and "Socrates white." For in both, Socrates himself is the same; but perhaps "white" is not similarly the same. For where it is said "the white is Socrates," Socrates is included in the white; but where it is said "Socrates is white," the white is purely contingent. And in these matters of which we treat, "white being" has white as an accident. But where it is said "white is being," <margin>E</margin> the white itself has being included in a certain way. And overall, white has being because it revolves around being and exists in being; from that, therefore, it receives being. "Being," however, exists as being from itself. From the white, it becomes white—not because being is in the white, but on the contrary, because the nature is in it; it does not become being from itself. Therefore, it must be said that it has its "being white" according to a certain participation in the "White" existing there. And in turn...

<meta>catchword: And in turn... (Latin: ip- / ipfius)</meta>

<summary>Plotinus distinguishes between the "Being" of a substance (like Socrates or fire) and the "Being" of a quality or accident (like the color white). He argues that physical substances and their qualities only "exist" by participating in a higher, truer level of Reality.</summary>
<keywords>substance, essence, being, accident, participation, Socrates, matter and form, Plotinus, Enneads</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the categories of Being. Having previously established that "Being" applies differently to incorporeal things (like the soul) and corporeal things (like physical bodies), he now moves to Chapter VII to discuss the hierarchy within physical objects themselves—specifically matter, form, and the combination of the two.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. BOOK VI. <note>original Greek: "ἐκεῖ ὄντος ἔχοντος τὸ εἶναι" — "While Being is there, it possesses existence."</note>

...itself possesses being by participation in that Being which reigns there <note>Plotinus is referring to the "Intellectual Realm," the higher reality that grants existence to our physical world.</note>.

*Both matter and material form depend on a separate cause, and the form is more similar to that cause than the matter is. Therefore, form is Being, Essence, and Substance to a greater degree than matter. Chapter VII.*

Therefore, neither <term>Being</term> <note>Latin: ens; Greek: on — the state of existing.</note>, nor <term>Essence</term> <note>Latin: essentia; Greek: ousia — what a thing truly is in its core.</note>, nor <term>Substance</term> is predicated of matter and form together as if they belonged to a single "genus" or category. Instead, they are related by analogy—that is, they share a proportional relationship and can be compared. Furthermore, "essence" applies even less to <term>accidents</term> <note>Non-essential qualities like color or size that can change without changing what the thing is.</note> than to substances. For the components of substance—namely matter, form, and the <term>composite</term> <note>The physical object made of both matter and form.</note>—exist by their own right under a certain common condition. But accidents are enslaved to substances. Finally, matter depends from above upon Being, yet it is the least "ideal" or perfect thing; form, however, depends on that which is conceived as the most ideal possible.

---

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>A</margin> But if someone should say that all things existing here in matter have their existence from matter itself, we must ask where matter itself gets its "Being" and its existence. We have stated elsewhere that matter is not the primary principle in the order of things. If it is argued that other things cannot exist unless they are within matter, we will admit that this is true for "sensible" or physical things. But regarding matter itself, which exists before these things, there is nothing to prevent it from being secondary to all the things that exist "there" <note>In the higher, divine realm of Ideas.</note>. This is because matter possesses an obscure kind of existence, 
<margin>B</margin> and possesses less "being" than the things that are within it. For these things are certain <term>Ratios</term> <note>Latin: rationes; Greek: logoi — the organizing principles or "blueprints" of nature.</note> and exist more fully from the nature of Being itself. Matter, however, is entirely devoid of reason; it is a certain shadow of reason, and a "falling away" from reason. But if someone argues that matter provides existence to the things within it—just as the person Socrates provides existence to the "whiteness" found in Socrates—we must reply that it is the "Greater Being" that provides a "lesser existence" to the "Lesser Being." That which is 
<margin>C</margin> "Lesser Being" can never grant anything to a "Greater Being." Now, if the <term>Form</term> <note>The internal pattern or identity of an object.</note> is more of a "Being" than matter is, then "Being" itself is no longer predicated of both as something they have in common. Nor will "Essence" be a single category that contains matter, form, and the composite beneath it. Instead, they will share many things in common (as we have said for a long time), yet their actual "Being" will be different. For when a "Greater Being" approaches a "Lesser Being," it is prior in rank, 
<margin>D</margin> but it is lower in the degree of its essence <note>Meaning it becomes limited or diluted by entering into the physical world.</note>. Therefore, unless form and matter—and again, matter, form, and the composite—are "Essence" in equal measure, then Essence will never be a common genus for them. However, it will relate to those things that come after it as something they have in common, in the sense that they possess their own specific identities. Just as in the order of life, one form of life is weak, while another is more effective; and similarly 
<margin>E</margin> among images, one is a faint sketch, while another is a more perfect representation. If someone measures "Being" by a very small degree of existence, but ignores the greater "Being" found in other things, then "Being" will once again seem common. But we must be careful not to do this. For each thing is a distinct whole, and that which is faint and obscure is not a "common" denominator. Just as in Life, there is no single thing common to vegetative life, sensory life, and intellectual life. Thus, "Being" here is one thing in matter and another 
<margin>F</margin> in form; and both of these depend on a single source, which flows into them in different ways. It is not only true that where a second thing comes from a first, and a third from a second, the first is "more" of that thing and the later ones are worse and "less." Even if both depend on the same source, one may still see a similar succession. The potter’s clay, when more thoroughly baked by the fire, becomes a vessel or a tile; but there will also be...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> If anyone should say that all things upon it [matter] hold their being from matter, we shall demand to know from where matter gets its being and its existence. That matter is not the first principle has been said elsewhere. If it is said that things would not consist of anything if they were not upon matter, we shall say that this applies to sensible things. But concerning those things, nothing prevents matter from being posterior to all of them, to all the things "there" <note>The Greek term "ekeī" (there) always refers to the higher intelligible realm in Plotinus.</note>, 
<margin>B</margin> having a dimmer and lesser existence than the things upon it. To the extent that those things are "Reasons" (Logoi) and come more from Being, matter is entirely "unreasonable" (alogos)—a shadow of Reason and a falling away from Reason. If someone says that matter gives being to the things upon it, just as Socrates gives being to the white upon him, it must be said that the "More Being" might give a "Lesser Being" to the "Lesser Being." 
<margin>C</margin> But the "Lesser Being" could not give to the "More Being." If the Form is more of a "Being" than the matter, then "Being" is no longer common to both. Nor could "Essence" be a genus having under it matter, form, and the composite. Rather, many things will be common to them, as we are saying. However, the "Being" is different. When a "More Being" approaches a "Lesser," it is first in order, 
<margin>D</margin> but posterior in Essence. Thus, if Form is not equal to matter, and to the Form, and to the composite, then "Essence" would not be common as a genus. It will, however, hold toward the things after it a commonality, as those things possess their own essence. Just as of Life, one kind is dim, while another is an *Activity* [energeia]; and of images, one is a sketch, while the other is 
<margin>E</margin> a more finished work. If someone measures "Being" by the dim part, while the part that exceeds in other things is left out, then "Being" will again be common. But perhaps one should not do this. For each is a whole, but as a common thing the "dim" part does not encompass life—there would be nothing common in vegetative, sensory, and intellectual life. And so here, Being is one thing in matter and another 
<margin>F</margin> in the composite, flowing from one source in different ways. For it is not only that if the second comes from the first and the third from the second, the first is "more" and the following is worse and "less." But even if both come from the same source, one can see this—that which is more between the fire [and the clay], like a tile, while the...

<summary>Plotinus argues that "Being" is not a uniform category; instead, Form is more "real" than matter. He describes matter as a "shadow of reason" (skia logou) that receives a diminished existence from higher principles rather than providing existence to them.</summary>
<keywords>Being, Matter, Form, Essence, Substance, Hierarchy of Reality, Logic, Neoplatonism, Reason (Logos)</keywords>
