<meta>This page continues the discussion of whether physical (sensible) things can truly be called "substances." In the previous section, the author established that "Being" applies differently to the physical and spiritual worlds. Now, he addresses whether a physical object—like a stone or a plant—is a single substance or merely a collection of qualities like color and size.</meta>

### BOOK THREE.

...so that it does not become pottery. Matter and form are affected by the same thing. But there is a difference even in those.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Fired, so much so that it by no means becomes a vessel or a tile. <note>original: "vas vel tegula"</note> Perhaps, indeed, matter and form are not from the same source. For there is a difference even in those.

---

->*When we speak of <term>sensible substance</term> <note>Physical reality perceivable by the senses.</note>, it is better to accept the <term>composite</term> <note>The object as a whole, made of both matter and form.</note> rather than the matter or the form alone. Moreover, it is a general property of composite substance to be the underlying "subject" of things, and not to exist inside other subjects. Chapter VIII.*<-

->*Incorporeal substance is pure substance because it does not depend on <term>accidents</term> <note>Changing qualities like color, weight, or temperature.</note>; corporeal substance, however, is not pure substance, since it is composed of at least certain internal and specific accidents; otherwise, it would not be the sensible, physical substance we are currently seeking.*<-

---

But perhaps it is appropriate to omit for now the division into <term>elements</term> <note>The basic building blocks like earth, air, fire, and water.</note>, especially when we are discussing sensible substance, which should be understood through the senses rather than through abstract reasoning; nor should we focus on what it is composed of. For those components are either not substances themselves, or at least they are not "sensible" substances. It seems worthwhile to grasp in one general category that which is common to stone, earth, water, and further to those things composed of them—namely plants and animals— <margin>*</margin> insofar as they are perceivable by the senses. In this way, neither matter nor form will be overlooked by us in the meantime; for sensible substance contains both within itself. For fire and earth and the elements between them are both matter and form; but <term>composites</term> are already many substances gathered into one. Yet, it is common to all these things that they are distinguished from others by their own nature. For these are the "subjects" for everything else; they do not exist inside a subject, nor are they considered to belong to another’s authority. And in general, all the things we have described as specific to "substance" rightly apply to this. Furthermore, if sensible substance cannot exist without magnitude <note>size or volume</note> and quality, how shall we separate the <term>accidents</term> from it? If we set aside size, shape, color, dryness, and wetness, what else can we claim it to be? For these qualities are, in a way, what make these substances what they are. Truly, there is something around which these things converge, which together ensure that what was merely "substance" becomes "such a substance." Thus, fire will not be entirely substance, but some part of it will be judged to be substance. And what would this be? Perhaps it is the matter. Is sensible substance, then, a "congeries" <note>a heap or collection</note> of qualities and matter? And are all these things, mixed together in one matter, the substance? Each one of them taken separately would be either a quality or a quantity, or many qualities. Then, whatever is among these such that, if it were missing, it would leave the essence incomplete, exists as a part of that essence. But whatever happens to an essence that is already complete occupies another specific rank, and is not included in that mixture which creates the stated essence. Nor indeed am I saying at this moment that such a thing, while it is there with the others, is the essence or substance—specifically while it completes a single mass of a certain size and kind. But where it does not complete such a thing, it is instead a quality. Rather, I am saying that not even there is each thing a substance; but the whole, gathered from all of them, is the substance. Nor should it be taken poorly if we compose sensible substance out of things that are not themselves substances; for that whole is not "true substance" or essence, but rather it imitates true essence.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> BUT perhaps it is fitting to omit now the division into elements, especially where we dispute concerning sensible substance, which it is more appropriate to accept by sense than by reason, and not to add those things from which it is composed. For those are not substances, or certainly not sensible substances. It seems a work of value to comprehend in one certain genus that which is common to stone, to earth, and to water, and moreover to those things which are composed of these: <margin>B</margin> namely plants and animals, insofar as they are sensible. For in this way neither matter nor form will be passed over by us in the meantime; for sensible substance has these within itself. For fire and earth and their intermediates are both matter and form; but composites are already many substances reconciled into one. Yet it is common to all these that very thing by which they are separated from others. For these <margin>C</margin> are the subjects for the rest, and they are not in a subject, nor are they judged to be under the right of another. And altogether, whatever things we have narrated as proper to substance rightly fit this. Furthermore, if sensible substance is not without magnitude and quality, in what way shall we segregate the accidents from it? For separating these—magnitude, figure, color, dryness, moisture—what further shall we pose it to be? For these substances are like certain kinds of substances. But certainly there is something around which <margin>D</margin> these very things concur, which together effect that what was only substance turns out to be "such a substance." And so fire will not be entirely substance, but something of it, like a part, will be judged to be substance. But what will this be? Perhaps indeed it is matter. Is sensible substance, therefore, a certain collection of qualities and matter? And all these things mixed together in one matter are substance. But each one taken separately from there will be one thing a quality, another thing a quantity, or many <margin>E</margin> qualities. Then indeed, that which among these is so held that, if ever it should be missing, it leaves the essence imperfect, exists as a part of this essence. But that which happens to an essence already absolute obtains another certain proper order, and is not included in that mixture which makes this said essence. Nor indeed do I say in the present that such a thing, while it is there together with the rest, is the essence or substance—specifically while <margin>F</margin> it completes one mass so great and such as it is. But where it does not complete something of that kind, it is rather a quality. But I say that not even there is whatever exists a substance: but the whole, gathered from all, is the substance. Nor must it be borne heavily if we compose sensible substance out of non-substances: for not even that whole is true substance and essence, but rather it imitates true essence.

<summary>Plotinus explores whether physical objects are "true" substances or just collections of matter and qualities (like color and size), concluding that the physical world is merely an imitation of a higher, truer reality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the end of Chapter VIII regarding the nature of substance. Having distinguished between the true Being of the intellectual realm and the "becoming" of the physical world, Plotinus now begins Chapter IX, which focuses on how to categorize and divide physical (sensible) substances.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

These things indeed, without the other qualities placed around them, possess being in themselves, so that other things arise from them because they truly and completely exist. In this physical world, however, even that which is laid down as a foundation is sterile; it is not even sufficient to truly be "being," let alone to allow other things to derive their existence from it. Instead, it is a kind of shadow, and upon that shadow, there is a kind of painting—not true being, but entirely an appearance. <note>original: "phantasia"</note>

---

->*Species under the genus of substance are to be numbered either by the distinction of bodies among themselves—such as simple or animate ones—or by their forms. However, one should not say that the "primary substance" is this specific man, while the "secondary substance" is the concept of man in general.* Chapter IX.<-

---

*A species is more universal than an individual, and therefore it is simpler; thus, it is prior in nature. For this reason, its essence is also prior. For "this man"—that is, a man of a certain kind and in a certain matter—exists later by a kind of participation in the specific nature of "man" itself, which first exists more perfectly in itself and then imparts itself to others.*

<column-break/>

<note>This column contains the Greek translation of the preceding Latin text.</note>

Whichever of these, without the other things lying around it, possesses "being," and has other things arising from it because of its true existence; but here [in the sensible world], that which is cast underneath is solid, yet not sufficient to be "being," because those other things do not come from it. Rather, it is a shadow, and it exists upon a shadow; it is not "being," but an image and an appearance. <note>original: "φαντασία καὶ τὸ φαινόμενον"</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> THUS FAR we have spoken of that which is called substance among sensible things, treating it as a single genus. But what specific species of it can one most effectively bring forward? And how shall one divide them? Surely this entire universe must be posited as a body; within it, some parts are more material, while others are <term>organic</term> <note>From the Greek 'organon,' meaning an instrument; these are bodies equipped with specialized parts for life functions.</note>, meaning they are endowed with various instruments. The material parts are those such as fire, earth, water, and air. The organic parts are the bodies of plants and animals, which are distinguished from one another by their forms. Next, <margin>B</margin> one may categorize the species of earth and the other elements; and among organic bodies, one may properly divide the bodies of plants and animals by their forms, or even distinguish them by the fact that some are earth-dwelling and made of earth, while others belong similarly to any of the other elements. Or perhaps bodies are divided as some being light, others heavy, and others intermediate: some consisting in the middle of the world, others poured around it from above, and others occupying the middle region. And in each of these, the bodies are already distinguished by their shapes, so that some are the bodies <margin>C</margin> of celestial animals, and others belong to the remaining elements. One might first divide them into the four elements as species, then mix them with each other in another way, thus creating their differences according to location, forms, and mixtures—such as those things commonly called "fiery" or "earthy" because a particular element is abundant or dominant there.

As for the claim that some substances are "primary" and others "secondary"—as if "this fire" were primary and "fire itself" were secondary—one must realize that while they differ in the sense that one is individual and the other universal, <margin>D</margin> they do not admit any actual difference in their "substance." For even in the category of quality, there is "white" in general and "this white"; likewise, there is "grammar" in general <margin>E</margin> and a specific instance of "grammar." Furthermore, what does "grammar" in general lack when compared to a specific instance of grammar, or science in general when compared to a specific science? For grammar itself is not "posterior" to a specific instance of grammar; rather, because grammar itself exists, this grammar in you also exists. Indeed, the grammar in you is a "certain" grammar only because it is in you; in itself, it is the same as universal grammar. Likewise, Socrates did not give the quality of "being a man" to that which was not a man; rather, the "Man" <note>The universal form or essence of humanity.</note> gave that quality to Socrates. For a specific Socrates is a "certain man" through participation in "Man." Furthermore, what is Socrates other than "a man of a certain sort"?

<column-break/>

<note>This column contains the Greek translation of the preceding Latin text.</note>

<margin>A</margin> AND concerning the so-called substance in the sensible world, as a single genus, it has been discussed in this way. But what species of it would one divide? And how would he divide them? Should the whole be posited as "body," and of these, some as more material and others as organic? Material, such as fire, earth, water, and air; organic, the bodies of plants and animals, having their variations according to their forms. Then again, <margin>B</margin> taking the other elements and the organic bodies, dividing the forms in them and the bodies of plants—either as being of the earth or existing in each element—some in it, or of which it is the body; or some light, some heavy, and some in the middle. Some stand in the middle, some encompass, and some <margin>C</margin> are in between. In each of these they are distinguished by shapes, as there are bodies of celestial animals, and others according to the rest. Or as he signifies the four; then the things of these are prepared to be woven together. Or I think their differences are according to places and forms and mixtures, such as fiery or earthy, by the prevailing and dominating element.

As for the saying that there are "primary" and "secondary" substances, such as <margin>D</margin> [this] fire and Fire itself: one must think they differ in another way—that one is particular and the other universal—but not by a difference of substance. For even in quality, there is "white" in common, and a certain "grammar" and Grammar. Then, what does Grammar have less than a certain grammar? And science in general compared to a certain science? For Grammar is not <margin>E</margin> posterior to a certain grammar; rather, because Grammar exists, it is in you, since a certain one of the things in you is in you. But it itself is the same as the universal. Socrates himself did not give to that which was not a man the "being a man," but the Man gave it to Socrates. For Socrates participates in the Man. Then, what else is Socrates but "a man of a certain sort"? And what else is "a certain sort"?

<meta>catchword: But this itself which is called "such," what...</meta>

<summary>Plotinus explores the classification of physical substances, distinguishing between simple elements (material) and complex living beings (organic). He argues against Aristotle's view of "primary substance," asserting that universal forms are naturally prior to individual instances.</summary>

But if it is said that it contributes because "man" is only the species, while a specific man is the species within matter, it would follow that this man is "less" of a man for that reason; for the rational principle <note>original: "logos"—the formative, organizing principle of a thing</note> itself becomes degraded when it exists in matter. But if "man" is not defined by the species alone, but also exists in matter, what will he lack compared to the species of man existing in some specific matter, since that very rational principle belongs to this individual existing in matter?

Likewise, that which is more general is prior by nature; therefore, the species is prior to the individual. What is prior by nature is also "prior" in a simple, absolute sense. In what way, then, would the species be "lesser"? Nevertheless, the singular individual is better known to us, and therefore seems "prior" to us; however, this creates no actual difference in the reality of the things themselves. Finally, if this is how things stand, there will not be a single definition of substance: for the definition of the primary thing is not the same as that which is only "secondarily" such, nor are such different levels of reality easily gathered under one single genus.
*The same reasoning applies to that which is primarily such, and to that which follows.*

And indeed, it is from the senses themselves that men have received their conviction that such things even exist. But if the possible combinations of matter seem infinite, it is permitted to distinguish them according to the species of animals: for example, the "species of man" as it exists in a body. For this specific type of form is itself a quality of the body, and it is not absurd to divide things by their qualities.

But if it is objected that we previously categorized some things as "simple" and others as "composite"—as if the composite and the simple were opposites—we will remind the reader that we said some things are more "material" while others are more "organic," <note>original: "organica"—complex structures like living bodies</note> rather than simply setting composites in the middle. Indeed, one can assert a diversity between the simple and the composite, not as equal opposites, but by following the first division: either by starting with the simple bodies and mixing them, or by introducing a difference from some other underlying principle...

...leads toward it being more of a substance. But if man is not according to the species alone, but is also in matter, what will he have less than the species of man existing in some matter, since that very principle belongs to this one existing in some matter?

Likewise, that which is more general is prior by nature, and therefore the species is prior to the individual. What is prior by nature is also simply prior. In what way, then, will it be "less"? Nevertheless, the singular individual is better known to us, and therefore prior to us; but this makes no difference in the reality of things. Finally, if the matter stands thus, there will not be one definition of substance: for it is not the same as that which is "secondarily" such; nor are such things gathered under one genus.

WE CAN ALSO divide in this way: namely, by the hot together with the dry; likewise by the dry together with the cold; again by the cold and the moist together, or in whatever combination one chooses to make. Then, from these, one can create a composition or a mixture, and either remain here, resting in the composite, or divide according to the earthy and those dwelling on the earth, or according to the forms and differences of animals—not indeed by dividing the animals themselves, but by partitioning according to their bodies as if they were certain instruments.

Nor indeed is a difference introduced according to forms inappropriate: since a division according to their qualities is not absurd—as if one spoke of heat, cold, and such things. But if someone objects that bodies are formed rather according to these, we shall certainly respond that they are also formed according to mixtures, colors, and shapes. For since the discussion concerns sensible substance, a distinction will not be absurd if such substance is distinguished through differences pertaining to the senses.

For this does not exist as "Being" simply, but the whole of it is "sensible being": indeed, we have even said that its apparent substance is a certain conflux of things pertaining to sense. And indeed, concerning such things, men have received their certainty of their existence from the senses themselves. But if an infinite composition occurs to us, it is permitted to distinguish according to the species of animals: such as the species of "man" existing in a body: for such a species is this very quality of the body. Nor is it absurd to divide by qualities.

But if it is objected to us here that in previous sections we placed some things as simple and others as composite, as if we were dividing the composite and the simple as opposites: we will remind them that we said there that some are more material, and others more organic rather, not bringing the composite into the middle. Indeed, one can assert a diversity between the simple and the composite, not by an equal opposition, but according to the first division, mixing them from the starting point of the simple bodies themselves, or from some other underlying principle...

->In the genus of quantity, there is properly number and continuity, or dimension: the rest are in another genus.<-
->Chapter XI.<-

*Time, in the respect that it is a measure and a measurer, and place, in the respect that it is a container, are considered in relation; Great and Small are considered in quantity, while beauty is in quality; but greater and smaller and more beautiful are considered among relatives.*

AS FAR as it pertains to quantity and the quantitative, it has often been said that it must be placed in number and magnitude, insofar as each thing is properly just "so much," which indeed consists in the number of bodily things and in a certain space of the subject. For we are not presently disputing about quantity separated from matter, but about this very quantity which makes it so that a piece of wood is three cubits long <note>original: "tricubitum"—a cubit was a standard ancient measurement, roughly the length of a forearm.</note>; similarly about the number five <note>original: "quinario"</note> which is in five horses. We have said before that only number and magnitude are properly "quantities"; place and time are by no means counted in the reasoning of quantity. Rather, time, because it is considered the measure of motion, is placed in the order of relations; place also, since it properly has the function of being the grasper of a body <note>original: "corporis... comprehensor"</note>, is judged in a certain habit and relation. Since motion is also continuous, it is nonetheless not established in the genus of quantity. Why indeed are "Great" and "Small" not placed in quantity? For that which is great is great by a certain quantity; yet this magnitude itself is not placed in relation, but "greater" and "lesser" are rightly thought to belong to relation. For they are spoken of in respect to something else, just like "double" and "half." Why then is a mountain often called "small," while a grain of millet is often called "large"? Perhaps when we call a mountain small, we wish "small" to be understood there as "smaller." For if even among those who treat these matters it is conceded that a mountain is called small insofar as it is compared with things of the same kind—that is, with mountains—it is rightly also conceded that "small" there is taken for "smaller." Now indeed, a large millet seed is not judged as simply large, but as a properly large grain of millet. This, however, is the same as if it were only said to be compared with things of the same kind, compared to which it can certainly by natural reasoning be called larger. Then, why should not beauty also be placed in relation? But it will be answered that this by no means happens, because beauty, however it is taken according to itself, is a quality; but "more beautiful" is among the number of those things which are referred to something else. Although even that which is called beautiful can sometimes seem ugly if it is compared, such as human beauty compared with the beauty of the gods. Hence that saying <note>Plotinus is referencing Heraclitus (Fragment 82).</note>, "The most beautiful of monkeys will be ugly if compared with another kind." Certainly it will be said that this thing is considered very beautiful according to itself, but judged as either more beautiful or uglier against another. Therefore, in this genus also, something is "great" in itself, endowed with magnitude itself, but toward another it is not great; otherwise, if it were not fitting to speak thus, we would be forced to deny that anything is beautiful, for the reason that something else...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...of composites, or by places or forms, it makes some heavenly and others earthly. And regarding sensible substance or generation, <unclear>these things are sufficient</unclear>.

<margin>A</margin> REGARDING quantity and the quantitative <note>original: "ποσοῦ καὶ ποσότητος" (posou kai posotētos)</note>, let it be said to be placed in magnitude and number, each being that which is in the number of things in matter, the substrate. For regarding the separated [quantity], that is the argument. But that which makes a thing three cubits long, or the number five in horses, it has been said often, that only these should be called quantities; but time should not be conceived according to quantity. <margin>B</margin> For time, because it is the measure of motion, must be granted to be a relative. And place, as a container, is also in a state of relation. And being moved, since motion is continuous, is also not placed there [in quantity]. But great and small, why are they not with quantity? For by what is the great great? Magnitude is not among the relatives. But the "greater" and the "lesser" are among relatives, for they are toward another, like the double. Why then a small mountain, <margin>C</margin> and a large [grain of millet]? Or first, is it because it is said instead of "smaller"? For if it is agreed by them that it is said in relation to things of the same kind, it is agreed that it is called "smaller." And the "large" [grain of millet] is not simply called large, but a large grain of millet. This is the same as saying it would be called larger by nature compared to things of the same kind. Next, why would beauty not also be called [a relative]? <margin>D</margin> But we say, beauty is [a quality] according to itself, but "more beautiful" is among the relatives. And yet if something is beautiful, it might appear ugly compared to another. For example, human beauty compared to the gods. Heraclitus says that the [most beautiful] of monkeys is ugly compared to another genus. It is beautiful in itself, but toward another it is less [beautiful], or the opposite. And here then, [the great] is very much with magnitude in itself. But toward [another] it is not placed. Or one must do away with beauty, because...

...the more beautiful it may appear to us: but we should not deny this. Therefore, we should not deny that something is "great" just because something else is greater than it: since there would be nothing "greater" at all unless there were also the "great"; just as there would be no "more beautiful" unless there were also the "beautiful."

*Extension and contraction are contraries. If a number is extended, it becomes "many"; if it is contracted, it becomes "few." Similarly, dimension becomes "small" through contraction, but "large" through extension. Therefore, few and many are contraries, just as small and large are. Chapter XII.*

*Just as there is a certain fixed definition of the beautiful, so there is of the hot and the great. Then, indeed, there is an opposition of place that is properly relative, such as between "above" and "below." Finally, speech is considered in the category of quantity only by accident, but it is essentially found in the category of motion.*

---

WE MUST THEREFORE ADMIT that <note>original: "ΑΠΟΛΕΙΠΤΕΟΝ" / "PERMITTENDVM"</note> contrariety exists within the category of quantity. For our very thoughts admit to this opposition when we speak of "large" and "small," which produce contrary images in our minds, just as when we speak of "many" and "few." Indeed, similar things must be said about "few" and "many." For we might say there are "many" people in a house, yet there are "more" elsewhere; and "few" in a theater, meaning "fewer" than usual. In general, to say "many" is to describe a large multitude in number. But how can multitude be counted among relative things? This is the same as saying that multitude is the extension and propagation of number, while its contrary is contraction. The same occurs in our notion of the continuous, where the mind extends the continuous. Quantity seems to arise when a point progresses forward. But if this progress stops quickly, the result is "few" or "small"; if the progression does not end quickly, it becomes "many" or "large." What then is the boundary or definition? What is the boundary of the "beautiful" or the "hot"? In the order of heat, there is also the "hotter," yet "hotter" is a relative term, while "hot" is simply a quality. In general, just as there is a definition for the beautiful, so there must be one for the great, which, when perceived, makes a thing great, just as the definition of beauty makes a thing beautiful. Thus, there is contrariety in quantity according to these principles. Regarding place, there is no longer any true contrariety, as it is not strictly in the category of quantity; even if place were a quantity, "up" would not be the contrary of anything unless there were a "down" in the universe as a whole. In specific parts, "up" and "down" mean nothing other than "higher" and "lower," similar to "right" and "left," which are relative terms. Syllables and speech also happen to be quantities, falling under that category because sound is a quantity; however, sound is a type of motion. Therefore, speech should be reduced to the category of motion, just as action is.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> WE MUST ADMIT therefore that contrariety exists regarding quantity. For our thoughts themselves admit to this opposition when we speak of "large" and "small," which bring to mind contrary imaginations, just as when we say "many" and "few." For similar things happen with "few" and "many." Many are said to be at home, and yet under this name "many," we understand that there are "more" [elsewhere]. But this very thing called "more" <margin>B</margin> refers to something else: often they even say there are "few" in the theater, meaning there are "fewer" than expected. It is worthwhile, whenever we say "many," to understand it as a very large multitude in number. But in what way will multitude be counted among relative things? This is the same as saying that multitude is the extension and propagation of number, of which the contrary is contraction. The same happens <margin>C</margin> in the very notion of the continuous, when the mind draws out the continuous in length. For quantity seems to arise when the unit and the point move forward. But if both quickly stop their step, that becomes "few" and this becomes "small"; but if the progression in moving forward does not quickly cease, that certainly becomes "many" and this becomes "large." What then is the limit or definition? But what is the limit of the beautiful? What of the hot? And yet in the order of heat, there is the "hotter"; but <margin>D</margin> "hotter" is indeed referred to something else, while "hot" exists simply as a quality. Entirely, however, it is fitting that there be a certain definition of the great, just as there is of the beautiful; which, once perceived, renders a thing "great," just as the definition of beauty itself renders a thing "beautiful." Therefore, there is contrariety regarding quantity according to these points. For regarding place, there is no longer any such contrariety, because it is not properly in the category of quantity: since even if place were in the <margin>E</margin> category of quantity, that which is called "up" would not yet be a contrary to anything, unless there were that which is "down" in the universe. In the parts of the universe, however, that which is called "up" or "down" signifies nothing other than "higher" and "lower"; and that is similar to what is called "right" and "left." These, however, are numbered in the category of relation. Indeed, it happens that syllables and speech are quantities and are subject to quantity. For voice will be forced to be a quantity; but it is itself a certain motion. To motion, ->therefore, just as action, it seems<- ->entirely to be reduced.<-

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's analysis of the category of "Quantity" from Ennead VI, Book 1. Following the discussion on "great" and "small" as relative or absolute terms, he now moves to classify the sub-types of quantity: the "discrete" (numbers) and the "continuous" (geometry/magnitude).</meta>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEAD VI.

*One genus of quantity is common to both numbers and continuous magnitudes; likewise, number is a single genus for all specific numbers, and continuity is a general genus for all continuous things. The species of numbers are identified by the difference between even and odd; the species of continuous things are identified by the differences between the line, the surface, and the solid; and so forth in order. Chapter XIII.*

<margin>A</margin> It has already been stated that the **continuous** <note>Continuous quantity refers to things that are infinitely divisible, like a line or time.</note> is correctly distinguished from the **discrete** <note>Discrete quantity refers to distinct units, like the number of people in a room.</note> by whether they are defined by a common or a proper limit. Next, we must say that in the case of number, the distinction is made through the properties of "odd" and "even." Similarly, if there are further differences within each of these, or perhaps if such a distinction must be granted to things that already possess number, one must assert that these differences belong to numbers composed of units <margin>B</margin> <note>original: "monadicorum numerorum"</note>, but not at all to numbers existing in sensible <note>Physical or "sensible" things are those we can perceive with our senses.</note> objects. If, however, some reasoning were to separate the numbers existing in sensible objects, nothing would prevent us from understanding the same differences in them as well. But how is the continuous distinguished? Surely, if we say that this is a line, that is a plane, and that other is a solid; or if we say this pertains to one dimension, that to two, and that to three, we will seem not to be dividing it into species, but merely counting them out. <margin>C</margin> For in numbers taken this way according to "prior" and "posterior," a common element acting as a genus is not found; nor will there be anything common in the first, second, and third levels of growth. But perhaps they are common insofar as they are "quantities," and there is an equality among them. One is not "more" of a quantity and another "less," even though some possess dimensions in more directions and others in fewer. <margin>D</margin> In numbers, therefore, insofar as they are all numbers, there can be something common. For perhaps it is not the "one" that produces the "two," nor the "two" that produces the "three," but some identical thing that generates all of them. But if these numbers are not "made" but simply "exist," and we only imagine them as being made, then let the smaller number be prior and the larger be posterior; nevertheless, insofar as they are numbers, let them all be reduced to one genus. <margin>E</margin> For this reason, it is appropriate to apply the condition of numbers to the order of magnitudes. It will be possible to distinguish between the line, the plane, and the solid (which is also called a "body") because, while they are all magnitudes, they differ in species. If it is necessary to divide each of these, we shall divide the line into the straight, the circular, and the spiral; the plane into rectilinear and circular figures; and finally, the solid into solid figures—namely, the sphere and figures with straight lines for sides. These again, in the manner of geometers, we shall divide into triangles and quadrangles, and these again into others, considering the conditions under which they are formed.

*Straightness or curvature applied to a line signifies a property of it and does not imply a composite nature; likewise, these are to be placed in the category of quantity, rather than quality. Chapter XIV.*

*When you say a triangle consists of three lines arranged in a certain way, you mean they are bounded by one another in a specific limit; but a limit and a determination of this kind seem to belong to the genus of quantity rather than quality.*

<margin>A</margin> ACCORDINGLY, what shall we say a straight line is? Is it not a magnitude? Perhaps someone might call "straightness" a certain "quality" of magnitude. What—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It has been well said that the continuous is separated from the discrete by the common and proper limit. From this point forward, we say that number is divided by the "even." And again, if there are certain differences in each of these, either they must be accepted by those things which already have number, or these must be placed as differences of monadic numbers <note>Greek: "monadikos" - relating to units or "monads."</note>, but least of all for those in sensible things. But if some logic separates <margin>B</margin> the numbers in sensible things, nothing prevents us from perceiving the same differences in them too. But how is the continuous divided? If one is a line, another a surface, and another a solid? Or if one is in one dimension, another in two, and another in three? This will seem not like a division into species, but merely a list. For always in numbers taken according to the "prior" <margin>C</margin> and the "posterior," there is no common genus among them. Nor will there be anything common in the first, second, and third increase of dimensions. But perhaps it is insofar as "being quantity" is present in them. And in this, one is not "more" quantity or "less," even if some have more dimensions and others fewer. In the case of numbers, then, insofar as they are all numbers, the commonality would exist. <margin>D</margin> For it is not the "one" that produces the "two," nor the "two" the "three," but the same [principle] produces the same. If they are not "becoming" but simply "are," and we only think of them as becoming, then let the smaller be prior and the larger posterior. But insofar as they are numbers, they all fall under one. Thus, for magnitudes as well, we should adopt the same rule as for numbers. We shall distinguish from each other the line, the <margin>E</margin> surface, and the solid—which indeed he [Aristotle] called "body"—by the fact that these magnitudes exist in this specific way. If it is necessary to divide each of these: the line into straight, curved, and spiral; the surface into rectilinear and curved figures; and the solid into solid shapes, like the sphere or those with rectilinear sides. And these again, as the geometers do, into triangles and quadrilaterals; and we must examine these and others in the same way.

<margin>A</margin> What then should we say a straight line is? Is it a magnitude? Or would someone say that "straight" is a "quality" of magnitude?

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Category of Quantity" from Plotinus’s Enneads. Having previously explored the definitions of discrete and continuous quantities, the text now examines whether the specific shapes of things (like a "straight" line or a "triangle") belong to the category of Quantity or the category of Quality.</meta>

# BOOK THREE.

What prevents there being a "difference" <note>In Aristotelian logic, a "difference" is the specific characteristic that distinguishes one species from another within a genus.</note> in a line? Straightness belongs to nothing else but a line. Since we also bring in differences of substance based on quality, even if a line is "straight," it is still a quantity with a difference, not a composite thing. For the straight line derives from the straightness of the line. But if it were a composite, it would be as if it were joined with its own proper difference. Why is a triangle, which consists of three lines, categorized under quantity? Perhaps because it is not simply three lines, but three lines held in a certain relation. A quadrilateral is four lines held so. If a line is straight in this way, it is a quantity; for if we call a straight line only a quantity, what prevents us from saying that a bounded line is not just a quantity, but the limit of a line, marked by a point? The same applies to other things. Therefore, a bounded plane is also a quantity. Since they provide limits, they are all the more within quantity. If, then, a bounded plane is a quantity, then a square, a polygon, a hexagon, and all figures are within quantity. If we say a triangle is of a "certain kind" <note>original Greek: "poion" (ποῖον), meaning qualitative.</note> or we place a square under "quality," nothing prevents us from placing the same thing in multiple categories. Insofar as it is a magnitude—and a magnitude of such a kind—it is in Quantity. Insofar as it provides a certain form, it is in Quality. Or perhaps the very form of the triangle is its "shape," and nothing prevents a sphere from being called a "quality." Yet geometry does not proceed in the same way. It would then follow that geometry is concerned not with magnitudes but with qualities. But that does not seem right; this study is understood to be about magnitudes. The differences between magnitudes do not take away their nature as magnitudes, just as the differences between substances do not stop substances from being substances. Furthermore, every plane is bounded; it is impossible for a plane to be infinite. Moreover, just as when I take a quality regarding a substance, I call it an "essential quality," so much more when I take shapes, I am taking a difference of quantity. It follows that if we do not take these as differences of magnitudes, to what shall we assign them? If they are differences of magnitudes, then the magnitudes arising from these differences must be arranged into species by their differences.

Just as when I take a quality in relation to a substance, I call it an essential quality: so, and much more so, when I take figures, I am taking a difference of quantity. Finally, unless we take these as differences of magnitudes, to what specifically shall we judge them to belong? For if they are differences of magnitudes, then surely different magnitudes constituted from these differences ought to be placed within their own species.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <unclear>Question.</unclear> What, therefore, prevents such a difference from existing, by which a line is defined? For straightness is not said to belong to anything other than a line: since we often derive the differences of substances from quality. If, therefore, a straight line is a certain quantity together with a difference, the straight line is not for this reason a composite of "straightness" and "line"; but if it is something composite, it is certainly so as if with its own proper difference.

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, why should a triangle, properly constituted of three lines, not be in the category of quantity? And yet a square is said to be four lines arranged in such a way; indeed, a straight line has within itself both quantity and a certain "mode" of quantity. For if we say a straight line is not only "how much" <note>original Latin: "quantum," the root of Quantity.</note> something is, what prevents us from calling a limited line something more than just "how much"?

<margin>C</margin> But indeed, the limit of a line is a point, and that does not exist in another category. For which reason a bounded plane is also properly a quantity: since lines, which exist much more clearly in the category of quantity, provide the boundaries. If, therefore, a bounded plane is in the category of quantity—and that includes the triangle, the quadrangle, or even a figure composed of many angles—certainly all figures are numbered in the category of quantity.

<margin>D</margin> But if, because we say a triangle is of a "certain kind" <note>original Latin: "qualem," the root of Quality.</note> and a quadrangle is of a "certain kind," we should therefore place them in the category of quality, nothing will stand in the way of us placing the same thing in several categories. For insofar as it is a magnitude—and a magnitude of such a kind—it is in the category of quantity; but insofar as it exhibits a certain form, it is in the category of quality. Perhaps even the triangle itself is such a form.

<margin>E</margin> What, then, will forbid us from calling a sphere a "quality" as well? If anyone proceeds in the same manner, he will concede that geometry is concerned not with magnitudes, but with qualities. But this does not seem admissible: for this very study is judged to be concerned with magnitudes. The differences of magnitudes do not take away the fact that they are magnitudes: just as no differences of substances result in substances no longer being substances. Furthermore, every plane is bounded: for it is not possible for a plane to be somewhat infinite; likewise

---

### Equality and inequality belong only to the category of quantity: while similarity and dissimilarity belong properly to the category of quality. Chapter XV.

In a certain way, we also say that figures are similar to each other not so much by quality as by some other condition. Substance, insofar as it is thought of as corporeal and sensible <note>Meaning something that can be perceived by the senses, like a physical object.</note>, is a certain gathering of substance along with accidents. Consider man in four stages: first in the **Idea** of the mind; second in the **seminal reason** <note>The "logoi spermatikoi," or the formative principles that guide the growth of a soul into a body.</note> of the soul; third in this body of ours; and fourth, finally, in a painting. By as much as the fourth is inferior to the third, so the third is to the second, and the second again to the first.

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS. BOOK VI.
<columns>2</columns>

<margin>A</margin> Furthermore, in what way is it a property of quantity that it is usually called "equal" and "unequal"? For even triangles are said to be "similar." <note>original Latin: "similes". In geometry, similar triangles have the same shape but different sizes.</note> Or are magnitudes also rightly called "similar"? And if something is called "similar," it does not prevent "similar" and "dissimilar" from being found within the genus of quantity. For perhaps here, in the order of magnitudes, that which is named "similar" behaves differently, and not in the same way as in the genus of quality. Moreover, if he <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, whose "Categories" Plotinus is critiquing.</note> said "equal" and "unequal" are properties of quantity, he did not therefore forbid "similar" from being predicated of certain things. But if he should say that "similar" and "dissimilar" are properties *only* of quality, then we must speak otherwise, as we said before regarding this very thing in quantity. But if that which is called "similar" is the same thing, it is profitable for us to consider in this genus as well other properties of both genera—both quantity and quality. <margin>B</margin> Or perhaps it must be said that "similar" itself is also spoken of in the genus of quantity, insofar as there are differences within it; but it is proper to arrange them together generally, and to join the differences that complete the essence <note>original: "essentiam".</note> with that very thing of which they are differences: especially when the difference or substance of that thing alone is to be joined with that whose nature it completes, and not at all in another thing. <margin>C</margin> But that whose substance this least completes must be taken only in itself. Now, I say "to complete the substance" not simply as substance, but as being "of such a kind." <note>original: "eius modi". This refers to the specific qualities that define a thing's nature.</note> Where, surely, this very thing which is called "of such a kind" does not admit a substantial addition. <margin>D</margin> Indeed, it is worthwhile to notice that we rightly call triangles and quadrangles "equal," as well as figures in any species, whether flat or solid. Therefore, "equal" and "unequal" must be placed without controversy in the genus of quantity as its property. <margin>E</margin> But whether "similar" and "dissimilar" occur only in the genus of quality is something to be considered. Regarding "quality" itself, it was said in the preceding parts that matter, together with other things, and something mixed with quality, produces the "completion of the sensible substance" <note>The physical reality we perceive with our senses.</note>; and that this substance, which among us is called "substance," appears to be that which is gathered from many things—not "this specific thing" properly, but rather a "quality." It also seems that the rational principle <note>original: "ratio", Greek: "logos" (λόγος). The underlying formative blueprint of a thing.</note> itself, as if of fire itself, signifies "this specific thing" more; but this form signifies "this specific thing" more than the rational principle does. <margin>F</margin> However, that which is produced therefrom in the nature of the body, since it is an image <note>original: "simulachrum".</note> of the rational principle, is rather "of a certain quality": just as if this Socrates whom we see were the man himself, but nevertheless his image in a painting, <unclear>consisting</unclear> only of colors and pigments, were called "Socrates."

->So indeed, since<-
->the rational principle is that according to which Socrates exists, we nevertheless call this man who is seen "Socrates": yet we ought to call the colors and figures of this appearing Socrates<-
->certain imitations of those things<-
->which consist in the rational principle itself: and judge that this rational principle<-
->furthermore suffers the same<-

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> But how is "equal" a property of quantity? For triangles are called "similar." Or are they called magnitudes? And does the "similarity" spoken of take away from "similar" and "dissimilar" being in Quality? For perhaps here, among magnitudes, "similar" is used differently, and not as it is in Quality. It is not as if, by saying "equal" and "unequal" are properties, he prevented the predication of "similar" to some <unclear>proportionally</unclear>. But if he said <margin>Β</margin> [similar] or "dissimilar" belong to Quality, we must speak otherwise, as we did regarding Quantity. But if the <unclear>same thing</unclear> is meant in these cases, we must examine the properties of each genus, both Quantity and Quality. Or it must be said that differences are also spoken of in Quantity, insofar as there are differences in it. Generally, one must arrange together the completing differences with that of which they are differences. And especially when the difference is alone, and if the difference is in another <margin>C</margin> it completes the essence <note>original: "ousia" (οὐσία).</note>, but in another it does not, or does not complete it, they must be arranged together. But that which does not complete [the essence] must be taken by itself. By "completing the essence," I do not mean essence simply, but that which is "of such a kind," <note>original: "toiande" (τοιάνδε).</note> which does not admit an essential addition. And that too must be signaled, that "equal" is said of triangles and quadrangles, and of shapes, both plane and solid. Let "equal" <margin>D</margin> and "unequal" be established as properties of Quantity. But as for "dissimilar," we must examine if it belongs to Quality. Regarding Quality, it was said that when mixed with Quality and other things, it works the completion of the sensible essence. And that the so-called "essence" is in danger of being this thing composed of many, and somehow is "quality" rather [than essence]. And the rational principle <note>original: "logos" (λόγος).</note> signifies the "what it is" more clearly. But as it is formed <margin>Ε</margin>, it is rather "quality." And the rational principle of the sensible thing is not its [true] being. But that which is finished in the nature of the body, being an image of the rational principle, is rather "a certain quality," just as if Socrates himself being the man, the <unclear>visible</unclear> Socrates, his image in a painting made of colors and pigments, were called "Socrates." [The visible Socrates] is from these things, and the rational principle being that according to which he is Socrates, we call [the image] Socrates, but the colors and shapes are imitations of those things in the rational principle. And this <margin>F</margin> rational principle, in relation to the truest [principle] of Man, is judged to have suffered the same thing. Regarding these things, then, let it be so.

<page-num>631</page-num>
# BOOK THREE.

> Incorporeal substance is truly called "this something" <note>original Latin: "hoc aliquid"; Greek: "tode ti". This refers to an individual, primary reality.</note>: whereas corporeal substance is called "such a something." An "accident," however, is called "of such a sort" or "of that kind." Likewise, the qualities of the soul, insofar as it is occupied with seeking or handling matter, are counted in the class of qualities joined to bodies; but those qualities which are more eminent are counted in the class of separate qualities.
> ## Chapter XVI.
> Likewise, qualities in the power of the soul are numbered among the "joined" class as seeds, even though they are not in matter but in the separable soul. We place the substance of the soul itself not in this class, but in the class of separate essence.

<margin>A</margin> When we consider each of these things separately—those which relate to what we call "essence"—we find a quality existing in them. We should not signify this as "this something" [an individual entity], nor should we signify quantity or movement as "this something." Rather, these things signify a character, or what is usually called "of such a kind" or "of what sort." For example, we might speak of the "beautiful" or the "ugly" as they appear in a body. <margin>B</margin> The term "beautiful" is used equivocally <note>original Greek: "homōnymon". This means the word is the same, but the definition or reality behind it differs depending on the context.</note> when applied to things here among us and to things separated from matter.

For this reason, "quality" is also an equivocal term, just as "black" and "white" differ in different contexts. But what about that which consists in the "seed" <note>Plotinus uses the concept of "seminal reasons" (logoi) to explain how the blueprint of a thing exists before it is physically formed.</note> and in its defining ratio? Is it the same as what appears to us, or is it equivocal? Should it be numbered among the separate things, or among these lower things? And what of the "ugly" in the soul? Is it attributed to these same categories? It is already clear that the <margin>C</margin> "beautiful" is different in each case.

But again, a doubt arises: does virtue consist within the soul according to its own "quality," or should it be computed among these qualities of our world? Truly, we ought to place some virtues in this lower rank of quality, and others in that superior quality. <margin>D</margin> One might even doubt concerning the arts—which are certain rational principles <note>original: "rationes"; Greek: "logoi".</note>—whether they should be placed in the genus of our worldly qualities. For even if these principles are said to be "in matter," the soul serves as their "matter" [or foundation].

Yet when these arts are combined with physical matter, they seem to be situated here in our world—for instance, the music played on a lute. Such music is concerned with strings, and the song is a part of the art in a certain way, being a sound perceptible to the senses. Unless, perhaps, one were to call these "activities" rather than "parts" of the art; nevertheless, they are activities perceived by the senses. For even the beauty found in a body is itself incorporeal, yet because it is perceptible, we attribute it to those things <margin>E</margin> that concern the body and belong to the body.

It is proper to establish two types of Geometry and two types of Arithmetic. Some types "bend down" toward this world and are established in this lower genus of quality; others, however, which are the meditations of the soul itself, are to be traced back to the Intelligible realm. Indeed, Plato says that Music and Astronomy behave in this same way. Therefore, the arts that deal with bodies—using physical instruments and the senses—even though they are "affections" <note>The state of being influenced or acted upon.</note> of the soul, we rightly number among our worldly qualities, because <margin>F</margin> they belong to a soul that is already declining toward lower things.

Furthermore, nothing prevents us from placing the active virtues in this same place—those which act in such a way that they perform only "civic" duties <note>referring to the "political virtues" mentioned by Plato and Aristotle, which govern social conduct but are lower than contemplative wisdom.</note>. These virtues do not separate the soul from this world to lead it to the heights, but rather place their perfection in the fulfillment of human duties. They do not choose such honorable business as a mere necessity, but establish these tasks as their primary concern. For this reason, the "beauty" found in the power of the seed, and even more so the "black" and "white" found there, seem to be counted among the lower qualities.

What then? Shall we judge the soul in which such principles exist to be in the same order of essence as the things in our world? But indeed, not even these things are bodies...

<column-break/>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

...[we] said: but since the formative principles <note>original Latin: "rationes"; Greek: "logoi". In Plotinian philosophy, these are the rational, shaping forces that translate higher forms into the material world.</note> concern the body and the affections of bodies, we have therefore placed them in this category of quality. Since we have affirmed that sensible substance <note>The physical world known through the senses.</note> is something gathered from all the aforementioned things, we shall in no way place "incorporeal substance" within it. Although all the qualities of the soul are incorporeal, because there are certain passions <note>original: "passiones"; Greek: "pathē". These are not just emotions, but states of "undergoing" or being affected by external physical things.</note> in it that incline toward lower things, we have numbered them among these [corporeal qualities], as well as the formative principles that belong to a particular soul. For we attribute "passion" to the soul in a two-fold way: both regarding that which it concerns, and that in which it exists. This is indeed not a corporeal quality, but it exists in relation to the body. Yet we do not assign the soul itself to this [lower] essence, since we have already granted its affection and its state toward the body to the genus of quality; but we have restored the soul itself—considered without such an affection and seminal reason <note>original: "seminariāque ratione". The internal blueprint or "seed" that directs the development of a living thing.</note>—to that very place from which it originates, leaving behind no essence that is in any way "intelligible" <note>Belonging to the higher realm of pure thought rather than the physical world.</note> in this lower genus.

->He questions by what method the genus of quality is rightly divided through its differences into its species, but in this chapter he defines almost nothing. Chapter XVII.<-

<margin>A</margin> If, therefore, it seems so, the genus of quality must be divided into qualities of the soul and of the body. If someone wishes for all souls to exist in the higher realms, and likewise their own proper qualities, it will at least be permitted to divide the lower qualities according to the distribution of the senses: namely, assigning some to the eyes, others to the ears, and likewise through touch, taste, and smell. Similarly, if there are differences within these: distributing colors to the sight, voices to the hearing, and others to the other senses. Voices, insofar as they are of a certain quality, can be divided into sweet, harsh, or smooth. But since we divide the differences concerning substance by qualities, and to these we also assign acts and actions—whether beautiful or shameful, and suchlike—for we rarely or never divide quantity through differences that constitute species, but rather we are accustomed to divide even quantity by its own qualities, <margin>B</margin> it can be doubted in what way anyone might divide quality itself. For what differences will one chiefly use in dividing, and from what genus will one derive these? For it seems absurd to divide quality itself by another quality; it would be just as if someone were to say that the differences of a substance are themselves substances. By what, then, will one divide white and black? By what will one divide colors from flavors and the qualities of touch? If we assign the differences of these qualities through the various instruments of the senses, the difference will not be in the subjects themselves. Furthermore, we must ask how we discern the difference of qualities belonging to the same sense. If a diversity is assigned based on the fact that 

<column-break/>

this [quality] concentrates the sight, while that one disperses it; <note>Plotinus is referencing an ancient theory (found in Plato's Timaeus) that certain colors or tastes physically "contract" or "dilate" the sensory organs.</note> yet something else disperses the tongue, and another concentrates it. First of all, it will be doubted regarding these very [qualities] whether they are certain concentrations and dispersions; then, by what those things which differ in this way might be assigned. If anyone brings forward such things, or asserts that he has brought them into the open...

# THIRD BOOK

...[if they] are able, and it is not unreasonable to divide them by what they are able to do. Perhaps this should be argued: that those things which are not seen—such as the sciences—ought to be divided by their specific capacities <note>original Greek: "dynameis"; Latin: "vires". These are the inherent powers or functions of a thing.</note>. But as for these things that are apparent to the senses, why should they be divided by what they do? Truly, when we distribute the sciences according to what they can achieve, and arrange them entirely by the various powers of the soul—as if their diversity consists in what they produce—we can meanwhile

<column-break/>

grasp their differences through reason. We do this not only by looking at what subjects they deal with, but by inspecting their internal principles <note>original Greek: "logoi"; Latin: "rationes". These are the rational blueprints or "formative principles" that define a thing's essence.</note>. Is it perhaps that we can easily distinguish the arts by their specific principles and notions? But in what way are we able to similarly divide the qualities implanted in bodies? And yet, even in the higher nature [of the soul], one might ask how those principles themselves are distinguished from one another. For it is obvious that white differs from black, but we are seeking to find exactly *by what* it differs.

---

->*Sensible species <note>The outward appearances of things that we perceive with our senses.</note> of things are distinguished from one another by differences—internal ones especially, but in a certain way also by external ones. However, the differences themselves are not distinguished by other "differences," but by themselves. Chapter XVIII.*<-

->*Qualities are discerned among themselves not by other qualities, but either entirely by themselves or by certain modes of their existence.*<-

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, all these matters that have just come into doubt for us clearly show that we must seek the "differences" of other things so that we may discern each thing from the others. However, to demand "differences of differences" is something we neither can nor should do by any logic. For it is impossible to investigate the substances of substances, the quantities of quantities, the qualities of qualities, or the differences of differences. Instead,

<column-break/>

<margin>B</margin> it is necessary, wherever possible, to divide things by what is external, or by their active condition, or by other such traits. But where these are not available, the distinction is made as one might distinguish green from pale. But since they say that a distinction is also made between white and black, what shall we say? Truly, the senses or the intellect <note>The higher mind or intuitive understanding.</note> declare this difference to us, even if they do not provide a formal reason. The senses do this because <margin>C</margin> it is not their job to bring forth a reason, but only to provide us with the indicators of difference. The intellect, however, can discern through its own simple intuition <note>original Latin: "intuitu". A direct, immediate "seeing" of the mind.</note>. For the intellect does not use formal reasoning everywhere so as to say of everything: "this is that." There is surely a certain "otherness" <note>original Greek: "heterotēs"; Latin: "alteritas". A fundamental philosophical category meaning the state of being different or "other."</note> in the very movements of intelligence that divides one thing from another, without that otherness itself needing a further "otherness" to define it.

One might then ask whether all qualities are "differences" or not; yet it does not seem so. For whiteness, and colors in general, and things pertaining to touch and taste, can become the differences of <margin>D</margin> other things, even though they exist as species in their own right. But what of grammar and music? Perhaps they can be differences because one makes the soul "grammatical" and the other "musical," especially if these traits are present by nature, so that they become specific differences <note>A "specific difference" is the essential characteristic that defines a species within a genus (e.g., "rationality" is the specific difference that distinguishes humans from other animals).</note>. Furthermore, one must consider whether a difference is drawn from the same genus <note>A general category or family of things.</note> or from another. If it is from the same genus, we must say that the difference is of the same kind as the things it distinguishes—just as qualities are the differences of qualities. For virtue and vice are perhaps related in this way: the former is a certain kind of habit <note>original Latin: "habitus"; Greek: "hexis". A stable internal disposition or state of being.</note>, and the latter is another kind. Therefore, since habits are certain qualities, the differences here will be qualities—unless someone were to say...

He concludes that qualities like virtue or artistic skill can serve as the "specific differences" that define the state of a soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's dense metaphysical investigation into "Quality." Having previously discussed how we distinguish sciences, he now moves to the logic of "difference"—the specific trait that distinguishes one thing from another—and whether that difference is itself a quality or something else entirely.</meta>

<header>PLOTINUS, ENNEADS VI.</header>

**Left Column**

<margin>A</margin> A state <note>original: "habitum"; Greek: "hexis". A stable disposition or condition of a thing.</note> indeed is not a quality without a difference, but the difference itself properly constitutes the quality. However, if "sweet" is useful to us and "bitter" is harmful, and they are distinguished in this convenient way, they will be distributed by a certain relationship <note>original: "habitudo". A relative state or connection.</note> rather than by quality. But what if "sweet" is said to be "thick," while "harsh" is said to be "thin"? Perhaps this "thickness" does not explain what sweetness is, but rather signifies the means by which sweetness is produced; and the same reasoning applies to the harsh. 
<margin>B</margin> Therefore, we must consider whether it is universally true that the difference of a quality is not itself a quality, just as the substance of a substance is not a substance, nor the quantity of a quantity a quantity. Tell me, do five differ from three by "two"? On the contrary, five exceeds three by two, but they do not differ by "two" in any way. 
<margin>C</margin> For in what way are they separated from three by "two," since "two" is also contained within the three? Furthermore, neither does motion differ from motion by "motion," nor is any other thing distinguished from another in such a manner. But as far as virtue and vice are concerned, the whole of one must be opposed to the whole of the other as something diverse, and thus they are distinguished from each other by their own selves. If someone divides qualities within the same genus—namely, the "qualified"—and not from another genus, by granting that this one is concerned with pleasures while another is concerned with anger, and thus admits they are correctly distinguished, it will follow that the differences themselves are not qualities.

<column-break/>

**Right Column**

<margin>A</margin> If a habit or state <note>original Greek: "hexis".</note> does not always belong to the difference, but the difference itself is the quality; yet if "sweet" is beneficial and "bitter" is harmful, it divides them by relation rather than quality. And what if the sweet is "thick" and the harsh is "thin"? Perhaps one does not call the sweet "thick," but rather that by which the sweetness exists; the same logic applies to the harsh, so that 
<margin>B</margin> everywhere the quality of a quality is not a quality, nor the difference of a substance a substance. Does quantity differ from quantity, or five from three? It exceeds by two, but we do not say it "differs" by two. In what way does it differ by two, when two is also in three? Would motion differ from motion by motion? And so one might find it with all other things. But in the case of virtue and vice, the whole must be taken against the whole, and thus they will differ by themselves. 
<margin>C</margin> But if one divides the "qualified" either into other things or within itself, such as that which concerns pleasures or that which concerns anger, or that which concerns the gathering of fruit, and so on for each thing, it is clear that these are differences that are not themselves qualities.

---

->*In the category of quality, quality itself is primarily placed, such as beauty; then the thing that is "of such a quality," according to the reason why it is so affected, such as "beautiful." Third, the movement of a quality, such as what is called by the adverb "beautifully." However, negations of qualities or the movement toward them are not placed in this category.* Chapter XIX.<-

---

**Left Column**

<margin>A</margin> Furthermore, those things which are named "qualified" <note>original: "quales". Things possessing a quality, like a "white object."</note> through their qualities should be arranged under the genus of quality, insofar as the quality is present in them. Yet we ought not to employ them as if they were their own distinct category, lest two categories appear to exist; instead, we must refer ourselves back from the objects to that very thing from which they get their names. Now, regarding what is commonly called "not-white": if it signifies another color, it belongs to the genus of quality. But if it is merely a negation denying the things themselves, 
<margin>B</margin> or a kind of enumeration, it is nothing other than a voice, or a name, or a statement, which also seems to be a certain kind of thing, and itself similarly so. And if it is a voice, it will be a certain motion; but if it is a name or a statement, it will lean toward "relation," insofar as these have the power of signifying. But if such an enumeration is not only of things according to their genus, but it is also necessary that both what is said and what is signified should individually signify a certain genus, we shall certainly say that some words only posit the things themselves by declaring them, while others remove the things from the midst. Yet perhaps it is better not to number the negations of things in the same genus with the things themselves, especially since we do not count certain affirmations—such as a composition—among them. 
<margin>C</margin> But what shall we say of privations? <note>original: "stereseis". The absence of a quality that should naturally be there, like blindness.</note> Surely, the qualities of which they are privations are qualities themselves; and being clothed or naked is neither properly "qualified,"

<column-break/>

**Right Column**

<margin>A</margin> Under quality, one must also arrange, as is fitting, those things called "qualified" according to the qualities themselves, insofar as the quality is about them. But we should not treat them as if they were two separate categories. Instead, one should reduce them to that from which they are named. "Not-white," if it signifies another color, belongs to quality. If it is only a negation of things, or a listing, 
<margin>B</margin> it would be nothing but a voice, or a name, or a statement, even if the statement itself is a "thing." And if it is a voice, it is a motion; if a name or statement, it is a relation, insofar as it signifies. But if the listing is not only of things according to genus, but it is also necessary that the words and the things they signify each signify a certain genus, we would say that some words only show the things themselves, while others negate them. And it is perhaps better not to count the negations among them, 
<margin>C</margin> just as we do not count the affirmations or the composite. But what of privations? Those qualities for which there are senses are qualities, and the privations are themselves qualities, such as being toothless or blind. For he who is naked or clothed is neither properly "qualified," but rather it is spoken of as a state—let us avoid using too many categories. Furthermore, if those things of which privations are spoken, such as being toothless or blind; but truly it is not [a quality], but is rather said to be in a certain way... <note>original: "sef-". The text is cut off and likely continues as "se habere" (to have itself/to be in a state).</note>

<summary>Plotinus explores the logic of categories, arguing that "differences" (like the "two" that separates five from three) are not themselves qualities or quantities, but inherent distinctions. He also discusses how negations (like "not-white") and privations (like "blindness") should be classified, suggesting they are often linguistic markers or relations rather than independent qualities.</summary>
