# BOOK THREE.

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, it is situated in a certain relationship looking toward something else. Proactively, an **affection** <note>original: "passio" / "πάθος" (pathos). In this context, it refers to a state of being acted upon or undergoing a change.</note> which is still in the act of being undergone is not a **quality**, but a kind of **motion** <note>original: "motio" / "κίνησις" (kinesis). A process of change rather than a finished state.</note>. However, that which is said to result from someone having already undergone it, and who now possesses a permanent affection, is rightly judged to be a quality. But if one no longer possesses the active affection, yet is still said to have "undergone" it, they are properly considered to have been "moved." <margin>B</margin> This is the same as saying: "this person was in motion." One must conceive of motion itself with the element of time removed; for the present moment <note>original: "momentum praesens" / "τὸ νῦν" (to nyn).</note> should not be added to this definition. Furthermore, regarding common expressions like "beautifully" or "well," and other such terms, it is proper to reduce them into a single notion of their genus.

It is worth considering whether we should refer "blushing" <note>original: "rubere" / "ἐρυθριᾶν" (erythrian).</note> to the genus of quality. To be "red" or "reddening" is perhaps different: for the act of "becoming red" is not rightly reduced to that genus. Indeed, one who "becomes red" is undergoing an affection or is entirely in motion. But if they are no longer "becoming red" but already *are* red, why are they not "qualified" <note>original: "qualis" / "ποιός" (poios). Possessing a specific quality.</note>? It is not merely a matter of time. Therefore, when we call someone "red" or "reddened," we are describing their quality. Otherwise, we would think that only stable **habits** <note>original: "habitus" / "ἕξεις" (hexis). Permanent states of being.</note> are qualities, and that **dispositions** <note>original: "dispositiones" / "διαθέσεσιν" (diatheses). More temporary or changeable states.</note> are not. Thus, a "hot" person is a quality in this sense, not the person who is currently being heated; similarly, a "sickly" person is properly qualified, not one who is merely falling into sickness.

---

> We ought not define only those qualities as **contraries** which are most distant from each other by the space of intermediate qualities; but simply those which, while being in the same genus of quality, have no mutual likeness in their species and produce opposite effects upon us. **Chapter XX.**

> By this reasoning, **health** and **disease**, between which there is no middle ground, are contraries. Where a middle quality is composed of extremes, it cannot be contrary to the extremes—such as "greenness" <note>original: "uiredo". Considered a mixture of other colors.</note>. But where it is not composed of them, it can be—as with **moral virtue**. Where a quality consists in a certain indivisible proportion, it does not admit of "more" or "less," such as **harmony**, **temperance**, **justice**, or **health**; where it has a wide range of degrees, it does admit them, such as **heat** and **cold**.

---

<margin>A</margin> It must be observed whether perhaps every quality has another quality as its contrary. Certainly, regarding **virtue** and **vice**, a middle quality seems to be contrary to the extremes; however, regarding **colors**, the intermediate ones do not seem to be contrary in this way. If it is said that this happens because middle colors are certain mixtures of the extremes, then it would not be right to divide the middle and the extremes against each other. Instead, one should divide the genus of color into **white** and **black**, <margin>B</margin> and consider the others to be more complex compositions of these, or distinguish them such that we oppose one specific quality found in the middle states (if it is established that such exists by composition). 

But if they say that middle states are not contrary to the extremes because things that are contraries not only differ from each other but differ "to the greatest degree," we will object to this: that very idea of "differing to the greatest degree" is derived from the fact that <margin>C</margin> certain intermediates have already been positioned between them. For if someone defines the greatest difference as a disposition: and if they say the cause is that "grey" <note>original: "fuscum" / "φαιὸν" (phaion).</note> is closer to white than black is, our very senses report this to us. The same logic applies to **flavors**, just as with **hot** and **cold**, and the fact that the "neither" is the middle of both. Truly, we have found that we are accustomed to thinking this way, and anyone might perhaps grant us these points. But white and yellow, and whatever else is set against another...

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin> They seem to differ among themselves; and since they are different, they are like **contraries** <note>original: "contraria" / "ἐναντία" (enantia). In logic, these are extremes within the same class, such as black and white.</note>. For it is not strictly because something exists between them that they are contraries; rather, their own specific opposition to each other is how they should be judged. Indeed, nothing intervenes as a middle ground between **health** and **disease**, yet they are nonetheless contraries to one another. Is it perhaps that they are judged as contraries because the states resulting from either differ to the greatest degree? But how <margin>B</margin> can one claim the "greatest distance" there, where there are no smaller intermediate steps anywhere? It is not possible, therefore, to affirm a "greatest distance" regarding health and disease. From this it is clear that the very thing called a "contrary" must be defined by something else rather than by a measure of space. Furthermore, if it were determined by a "great deal" of distance, we would have to ask whether this "great deal" is understood as the opposite of "a little," or simply as "much" in an absolute sense. If <margin>C</margin> it is understood in the first way, then things lacking a middle ground would immediately escape the definition of contrariety. But if in the second way, while it is easily granted to any nature to be "much distant" from another, and yet no measure is given to calculate that distance, we must consider entirely how a contrary thing is to be weighed. Is it not true, then, that things which have a certain similarity—I do not mean only according to their genus, nor even entirely because they are mixed with other forms in greater or <margin>D</margin> lesser amounts—is it not true that these should be denied the status of contraries? Certainly, those things in which nothing is identical according to their **species** <note>original: "species" / "εἶδος" (eidos). The specific form or definition of a thing.</note> are rightly judged to be contraries; but we must add that they must be within the same genus of quality. Hence we may surely assert that even those contraries we encounter without any middle ground possess nothing that contributes to a similarity; for there are no other things there which, by leaning toward either extreme, would have or provide a mutual similarity. But if this is the case, those colors which share a certain community are not contraries at all. Yet nothing prevents us from saying that not everything is contrary to everything else, but one thing is contrary to another; and the same applies to tastes. But let us end the doubt regarding these matters here. It is further asked whether a **quality** admits of "more and less." And indeed, it is granted that those things which participate in qualities <note>i.e., physical objects or people</note> can participate more or less. But whether **Health** itself and **Justice** admit of these degrees is a matter of debate. If each of these has its own "latitude" <note>original: "latitudinem." A range of variation within a definition.</note>, then it must be granted that **habits** <note>original: "habitus" / "ἕξεις" (hexeis). Stable, acquired dispositions of the soul or body.</note> of this kind admit degrees; but if they have no latitude, but each possesses its whole essence in a certain fixed state, then surely it admits neither more nor less.

<note>The following section transitions from the discussion of Quality to the discussion of Motion.</note>

*We more probably posit **motion** as a genus rather than **transformation**, because transformation changes the nature of a thing and brings something else into the medium. **Motion**, however, signifies both this and, besides this, signifies progression while the prior nature is preserved in the meantime. Chapter XXI.*

---

### Whether we ought to assert that **motion** is a **genus** or not
<margin>A</margin> can be contemplated in this way: certainly, it can be a genus under this condition. First, if it is not appropriate to reduce motion into any other genus; second, if nothing higher is predicated of motion in terms of "what it is"; furthermore, if it produces species by receiving many differences. Tell me, then, into what genus would you most especially be able to reduce motion? For it is neither **substance**, nor is it a **quality** of those things which possess motion

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> ...to be different from each other. And being different, they are contraries. But regarding the "being in the middle," the beauty of these things, or their contrariety—take health, for example: nothing falls in between, yet they are called <note>The Greek text here parallels the Latin discussion of health and disease lacking a middle ground.</note> ...because the things arising from each have the greatest change. And how is there a "greatest" among those where there are fewer intermediates? It is not possible in the case of <margin>Β</margin> health and disease to speak of a "greatest" [distance]. But rather, that which is contrary must also owe something to the "more." But if the "much" is compared as "more" against "less," those things without a middle will escape the definition. But if it is simply conceded that each is naturally "much" distant, but not measured by the "more," we must <margin>C</margin> examine how it is a contrary. Is it not that they have a certain similarity—I mean in genus—but are not at all mixed with each other's forms, whether in more or less... but those in which nothing is the same according to their being? They would be defined in the genus by sensation; for if those contraries without a middle have no similarity, as there are no other things of the sort that change and share similarity with each other... or if there is a commonality in colors, but not in some of them. But nothing prevents not everything, but <margin>D</margin> one thing being thus contrary to another. And similarly in these matters, these things have been thus doubted. And if the "more" is seen in those participating in the quality, but [does it exist] in Health itself and Justice, or not? If each of these itself has "latitude," one must say they are habits; but there, each possesses the whole and does not have the "more."

---

### CONCERNING MOTION, whether it is a genus
<margin>Α</margin> ...one might consider it thus. First, if it is proper to lead it back to a genus. Then, if anything from above is predicated of it in its "whatness" <note>original: "τί ἐστι" (ti esti). The essence or definition of a thing.</note>. If, taking many differences, it [divides] into species. Into what genus could one lead it back? It is not substance, nor a quality of those possessing it...

# BOOK THREE.

**Column 1**

<margin>A</margin> For if [motion is divided] into **acting** and **being acted upon**, then there are many motions. But if it is placed in "being acted upon" because there are many motions, then you will be performing **actions**; yet by acting, you are also being acted upon, and so we return to the same point. If, on the other hand, motion is correctly placed under **Relation** <note>original: "πρὸς τί" (pros ti) / "relatio". This is the category of things that exist only in reference to something else.</note>, because motion belongs to something and does not exist by itself, then consider this: **Quality** would also be in Relation. For quality belongs to something and exists in something. The same applies to **Quantity**. If it is argued that those are specific types of beings even if they belong to something—insofar as one is a quality and the other a quantity—that has already been addressed. In the same way, even though motion belongs to something, it is still something in itself before it belongs to that thing. That which it is "in itself" must be grasped. For generally, a relative term is not defined by what it is, but by its relationship to another; it is a "promise" or a connection that generates a naming, where nothing else exists except the relationship by which it is described. For example, "the double" is called "double" by being compared to "the half," receiving its birth and its definition from that comparison. Nothing of it is conceived

<margin>C</margin> <margin>* concerning this</margin> beyond this * except for being compared to another; its very being is its being-said. What then is this thing [motion], which exists as something else while also being something in its own right—so that it may also belong to another—just as quality and quantity already exist [before they are attributed]? Or rather, we should first grasp that nothing is predicated of it as a higher **genus** <note>A "genus" is a broad category. Plotinus is asking if "Motion" is the top-level category or if "Change" is higher.</note>. But if someone says that **Change** is the genus of Motion, we must ask first if "Change" is said of all things, or if by calling it a genus, one makes it something different from those categories

<margin>D</margin> previously mentioned. It would then be clear in what species one should place motion. And then, one would place something else in opposition to motion—perhaps **Generation** <note>original: "γένεσις" (genesis) / "generatio". This refers to the process of "coming into being" or birth.</note>—calling that a "change" as well, but not a "motion." Why is generation not a motion? If it is because the thing being generated does not yet exist, and motion cannot exist around that which is not, then generation would clearly still be a "change." But if generation is nothing other than **Alteration** <note>original: "ἀλλοίωσις" (alloiosis). A change in quality, like turning from cold to hot.</note> and **Growth**, and since it is certain things that are altered

<margin>E</margin> and grown that constitute generation, then this view takes the things *before* the generation to be the generation itself. But one must grasp generation among these as a different species. For "to become" or "generation" consists in being altered through a state of passion—for example, becoming hot or becoming white. For when these things happen, the "absolute generation" <note>Generation "simpliciter" or "absolute" refers to the creation of a whole new substance (like a child being born) rather than just a part of it changing (like a child getting a tan).</note> has not yet

<margin>* from which something becomes</margin> occurred. * But rather, something "is becoming" something else; and this is to have been altered in some way. But when an animal or a plant is formed, when it takes on a specific **Form**, one might say that the change occurring fits better under the category of species, or perhaps motion:

<margin>F</margin> because "Change" signifies one thing being substituted for another, while "Motion" possesses a departure from one's own state, just as in **Local Motion** <note>Moving from one place to another.</note>.

...whether it is altered, generation and "to be born" consist [in this], such as those things which are already made, yet we do not yet say they are "becoming" then; we shall respond that this was the case. But then at last generation happens, when clearly a certain Form is received there. Accordingly, someone could argue it would be more fitting to place this under "change" rather than... the condition of change has something else, while the nature of motion has a certain transition from its own place, just like local motion.

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

<margin>A</margin> ...nor can you even reduce it to **action**: for in **passion** there are many motions: nor again to passion, because many motions are actions. It is more probable that actions and passions are brought back to motion, but neither is it correctly reduced to **relation**, because motion is not of itself, nor in itself, but rather belongs to something and is in something. For in that case, **quality** would also be placed in relation: for quality is of something and in something, and **quantity** in the same way. If to

<margin>B</margin> this it is responded, that those things are properly certain "beings" even if they belong to something—insofar as this one is quality and that one is quantity—by that same reasoning, although motion belongs to something, it is something before it belongs to something; deservedly this very thing which it is, in a certain way in itself, must be properly grasped by us. But generally, the **relative** must be properly placed as this: not that it is first what it is and then also belongs to another, but that it is generated in the very relationship itself, with no

<margin>C</margin> other thing existing there besides the relationship, insofar as it is named. Just as the "double" or "quadruple" is named, receiving its birth and substance in the very comparison to the "half"; and before this, nothing at all is thought of it, and it only obtains its name and being in comparison to the other. What then is this? That which, being of another, is nevertheless something itself so that it may also be of another: just like quality, and quantity, and **Essence** <note>original: "essentia" / "οὐσία" (ousia). The fundamental substance or "whatness" of a thing.</note>. But it is perhaps better first to

<margin>D</margin> assert that nothing is predicated of it as a genus. But if anyone objects that **change** exists before **motion**, firstly they would either be saying the same thing entirely, or by calling that a "genus" they would be making a certain other genus exist besides those ten **categories** <note>Referring to Aristotle's ten categories: Substance, Quantity, Quality, Relation, Place, Time, Position, State, Action, and Passion.</note>. Then, without controversy, they would place motion in a certain species, and setting something else in opposition, they would oppose it to motion—and perhaps they would say that "generation" is also a change,

<margin>E</margin> but by no means a motion. What then prevents generation from being a motion? For if it is said that this is prevented because that which is being born does not yet exist—and motion cannot be about **non-being**—we will say it follows from this that generation is not even a change. But if it is argued for the same reason that generation is nothing other than an **alteration** or a certain permutation and a certain **growth**, because the generation of things occurs which are permuted or altered and in some way grown: certainly, whoever says these things brings into focus the things that *precede* the generation. But it is necessary to accept generation among these as a different species: for it does not consist in the fact that something is passively heated or whitened in a certain way. For it can happen that "absolute generation" was not there. And if you ask about this thing which we say is altered—either it becomes an animal, or a plant, or similar—when clearly a certain **Form** is received there. Accordingly, someone could argue it would be more fitting to place **change** rather than **motion** in the species, because the condition of change signifies something else happening in place of another; whereas the nature of motion has a certain transition from its own state, just like local motion.

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.

If anyone should find that less than satisfactory, at least the act of learning itself, or the plucking of a lyre, or indeed any movement arising from a habit <note>original: "habitu" / "ἕξεως" — a stable disposition or skill</note> would be of this kind. Therefore, change itself—or transformation, since it is a certain kind of motion—which sets something outside of its previous state, would rather be a species of motion.

<margin>A</margin> BUT let this be the notion of transformation or alteration, insofar as it follows another motion: what then must we say motion itself is? Let motion be—to speak of this summarily by way of a figure—the exit from potency <note>original: "potentia" / "δυνάμεως" — the capacity or potential to be something</note> into that which is said to be "possible." For when something exists in potency, through which it may proceed into some form—just as a statue exists in potency [within the unworked stone]—and again, when there is something in potency by which it may escape into act, such as the power of walking; when that former thing proceeds into a statue, the process itself is the motion. And when the power of walking executes the act of walking, the progression itself is the motion: <margin>B</margin> likewise, jumping is the same in one who is able to jump, when they are actually jumping. Yet, in one kind of motion, namely that which leads to a statue, the form produced is something other than the motion itself; but in another, such as jumping, the act of jumping itself is a simple form of the jumping-potency, and it leaves nothing behind itself after the motion has ceased. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, if someone were to call motion a "waking" or "aroused" form, opposed to other forms that are, so to speak, dormant—insofar as some things are at rest while others are by no means so—and if they called it the cause for other forms when something is produced after it, they would not be far from the mark. Furthermore, if someone were to call this motion of which we currently speak the "life of bodies," they would not seem to be far from the truth. <margin>D</margin> For we ought to call this motion "equivocal" <note>having the same name but a different nature</note> compared to the motions of the mind and the soul. Thus, one will persuade themselves that motion is a "genus" <note>a primary category of being</note> no less because of this: that it is neither easy, nor perhaps even possible, to encompass it in a single definition. But how then is motion a "form" when it slides toward the worse, or when the motion is entirely passive? <margin>E</margin> Perhaps this is much like how heating under the sun increases some things while it diminishes others; the motion itself is something common and the same in both, but it receives a difference according to the subjects in which it appears. But from this, it seems to follow that sickness and recovery would be the same. Yet, insofar as they are motions, they do seem to be the same, but how they differ will be treated in what follows, when we discuss alteration—namely, what it is that remains the same in all motions: it is manifold, and stands in the same way as

<column-break/>

If someone does not wish to accept this, but rather [the motion] of learning, or lyre-playing, or generally any movement from a habit, it would be a "form" of motion rather than a motion that displaces something from its state.

<margin>A</margin> BUT let the concept of alteration be the same, according to its following upon motion. Must we say motion is something else? Let motion be, to speak in outline, the exit from potency into that which is called "power" <note>original: "δυνάσει" — here referring to the realization of a capacity</note>. For since one thing is in potency because it might come into a form, such as a statue in potency, and another because it might come into activity, such as the power of walking; when the one proceeds toward the statue,
<margin>B</margin> the progression is motion. And the act of walking in the power of walking is itself motion. So too is dancing in those who are able to dance, when they are dancing. And in the case of the motion toward the statue, that which the motion worked upon is a different form. But in the case of jumping, which is from the "out-standing" of the potency, nothing remains after it when the motion has ceased. So if one were to say that motion is a kind of "waking" form,
<margin>C</margin> compared to other forms that stand still—in that some are at rest, while it is the cause for other forms when something comes into being after it—one would not be mistaken. And if one were to call it the "life of bodies," they would grasp the same thing. For now, we must call motion "equivocal" to the motions of the mind and the soul. If indeed it is a genus, one might be persuaded of this by the very fact that it is difficult or impossible to define it.
<margin>D</margin> How then is it a form when the motion is toward the worse, or when the motion is passive? It is like how heating from the sun increases some things, but leads others to the opposite. Either motion is something common, or it is the same in both subjects but possesses a difference in its "out-standing" <note>original: "ἐκστάσαν" — the way it departs from a state</note>. Are healing and sickening therefore the same? Insofar as they are motion, they are the same, but in what will they differ? Either
<margin>E</margin> by their subjects, or by something else. But we shall look into these things when we consider alteration. For now, we must observe what is the same in every motion. If it were a single genus, or if it were said in many ways, it would stand just as "Being" does. Let us consider...

# BOOK THREE.

<columns>

<margin>A</margin> Regarding the difficulty <note>original: "ἀπορίαν" / "aporia" — a philosophical puzzle or state of being at a loss</note> of how we ought to classify motions: all those that lead toward a natural state, or act within those things that are according to nature, should be considered as species of motion, as has been said. However, those transitions that lead to something contrary to nature should be categorized by analogy to the states they lead toward. But what is the common element found in alteration, growth, and generation <note>The three classical types of change: qualitative, quantitative, and substantial</note>, as well as in their opposites? And what is common to change of place, insofar as all these are motions? <margin>B</margin> Perhaps it is the fact that each thing is not in the same state or position in which it was previously. It does not rest, nor is it in total stillness. Rather, insofar as motion is present, it always maintains a direction toward something else. The "other" means it never stays in the same state. Indeed, motion would be dissolved if it did not constantly involve something else. Therefore, there is a quality of "otherness" <note>original: "ἑτερότης" / "heterotes" — the state of being different or "other"</note>; if a thing is in the state it has become, it does not remain in that "otherness," but "otherness" is always occurring. <margin>C</margin> This is why time is also always "other," because motion produces it. For motion that is measured—or rather, motion that does not stay still but is seen as something being carried along—is what creates time. The common feature of all motion is the progression and leading out from potency <note>original: "δυνάμεως" / "dynamis" — the capacity or potential to be</note> into the potential—that is, into actuality <note>original: "ἐνέργειαν" / "energeia" — activity or actualized existence</note>. For everything that is moved, according to whatever kind of motion, exists first in a state of being able to act or be acted upon, and then becomes that thing in the process of being moved.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Regarding the point that was especially doubted just now, it seems necessary to say that perhaps all motions which lead a thing toward its nature, or at least act in those things which are according to nature, should rightly be placed as species, as was stated; whereas the transition to something contrary to nature should be accommodated by a certain analogical proportion to the things toward which they lead. But what is common to alteration, growth, <margin>B</margin> and generation, and their opposites? And again, in change of place, insofar as all these are motions? Truly, for all things that are motions, this seems most common: that each thing which is moved is not afterwards in the same state as it was before, nor does it rest, nor does it remain idle at all. Rather, insofar as motion is present, it is always led toward something else, and always has "otherness" as its companion, for the reason <margin>C</margin> that it never remains in the same state. Otherwise, motion would be immediately destroyed if it ever ceased for one thing after another to succeed it. Therefore, otherness is in motion, not because something exists through a completed act and is now at rest in another state, but in such a way that a perpetual otherness is driven forward. From this it follows that time is also always "other," since motion procreates it. For motion, not resting but being continually measured by its flowing, produces time, which indeed runs along with motion itself, as if carried by the very thing that runs. Finally, common to all motions is a certain process and leading out from potency, and from that which is possible, into act. For whatever is moved, by whatever motion it is carried, proceeds into motion because a certain potency precedes it for doing or for suffering <note>original: "patiendum" — being acted upon</note> something.

</columns>

---

->*Motion is like a certain stimulus <note>original: "stimulus"</note> tending toward various acts, modes, habits, and various forms, through which variety things attain a likeness of life. The motile power, like life itself, is invisible. Motion, though invisible in itself, is perceived through this variety. Truly, motion depends on the mover and ends in the mobile thing, like a breath of the mover. From this, the differences of motions are to be understood from both sides.*<-

->Chap. XXIII.<-

---

<margin>A</margin> THERE is also the motion that deals with sensible things <note>Things perceived by the senses, like heat or physical movement</note>, which is a certain stimulus or impetus tending from one thing to another, exciting and impelling the participant of the motion so that it does not grow sluggish, nor remain in the same state; so that through such a restlessness, and a sort of distracted concern for many things, it might attain a certain image of life. Nor should it be thought that the things being moved are the motion itself. For the feet are not the walking; rather, walking is <margin>B</margin> a certain act from potency involving the feet. Since potency is not visible, it is necessary that we see only the feet in action—not the feet simply, as if they were resting, but the feet now together with something else, which is indeed invisible. Because it is together with something else, it is seen "by accident" <note>An "accidental" property is one that isn't essential to a thing's definition but is true of it in a specific moment</note>, insofar as we see the feet occupying one place after another, and not resting anywhere. Furthermore, we are accustomed to notice alteration from the fact that a thing is being altered, because the same quality is no longer sensed there. <margin>C</margin> In which thing, then, is the motion when one thing moves another? And when it proceeds from an infused potency into act, is it in the mover? But if that is so, how will that which is moved and acted upon become a participant? Is it then rather in that which is moved? But if so, why does it not remain there once it has proceeded? Surely, motion must neither be severed from the mover, nor reside solely within it, but must emanate from itself and into the other.

<summary>Plotinus explores the essence of motion as a perpetual "otherness" and a transition from potentiality to actuality. He distinguishes between the physical organs of motion (like feet) and the invisible act of motion itself (walking), suggesting motion provides a "likeness of life" to the material world.</summary>

nor is it separated from the mover in any other thing: rather, it flows from this into that like a breath and a blast <note>original Latin: "spiritum afflatumq;"—referring to a physical or spiritual 'current' of force</note> flowing into another. Therefore, when the power of moving is progressive, it as it were propels and forces a constant change of place: but when the power is heating, it heats immediately, and the motion there is <term>alteration</term> <note>qualitative change, such as a change in color or temperature</note>. But where the faculty itself, having found matter and occupying it, builds it into a natural state, it is to be called <term>growth</term>; but when another power takes something away, <term>decrease</term> occurs, namely in that which is capable of being diminished. Accordingly, where the generative power acts, <term>generation</term> <note>the process of a thing coming into existence</note> occurs: but when this power is least effective, and that which can destroy prevails, <term>destruction</term> <note>original: "deſtructio"—the passing away or corruption of a thing</note> follows: I do not mean destruction in that which has already been made and completed, but in that which is still in the process of becoming. Similarly, <term>recovery of health</term> occurs where the power capable of creating health acts and dominates; <term>illness</term>, however, happens when the contrary power does the opposite. Wherefore it follows that motion must be considered not only in terms of those things in which it occurs, but also in terms of those things from which it arises, and through which it is transmitted: and that for the motion itself, a motion of such a kind and quality exists in such things.

*Local motions seem to differ among themselves, either by the opposite boundaries they seek, such as ascent, descent, and return; or by the shape of their progression, such as straight and circular. Chapter 24.*

<margin>A</margin> BUT regarding local motion, how the difference is taken is ambiguous, if moving upward is the opposite of moving downward, and circular motion is opposite to straight motion: just as if something were thrown over one's head or beneath one's feet. For the impulsive power is the same: unless one were to say there is one power that pushes upward and another that pushes downward, and that the motion of one tending upward is different from the motion of one falling to lower parts, especially if something moves so naturally: for here <term>lightness</term> occurs, while there <term>gravity</term> <note>or "heaviness"</note> occurs: yet the common and identical element in these is being carried to a proper place. Here, therefore, it appears that the difference of motions is taken according to external factors: surely in circular and straight motion, if someone were to move the same thing now straight and now circularly, how could the motion be different? Or perhaps the difference will be taken according to the shape of the progression itself? Unless perhaps someone should contend that circular motion is a mixture, as if it were not entirely... But finally, one local motion seems to be in itself, [taking] differences only through external—

*Composition and separation are motions differing from all other motions, and even from qualities. Yet, local motion and alteration occur around composition and separation; as do generation and passing away; and condensation and its opposites. Chapter 25*

<margin>A</margin> FURTHERMORE, it must be considered how <term>composition</term> <note>original: "concretio" / "σύγκρισις"—the joining of parts</note> and <term>separation</term> <note>original: "discretio" / "διάκρισις"—the dividing of parts</note> behave. Are they other motions besides those we recounted above—I mean generation and corruption, growth and decrease, local motion, and alteration? Or perhaps it is necessary to reduce them to these motions in some way? Or rather to assert that some of these motions are certain compositions and separations? If, therefore, composition consists in this, that one thing approaches and nears another, and again separation in this, that those which have neared then recede from there, they will be called local motions, while namely there occurs—

<column-break/>

nor to be cut off from those things, [but flows] from that into this, like a breath <note>original Greek: "πνοὴν" / "pnoen"</note> into another. Nor if the power of moving is progressive <note>original: "βαδισικὴ" / "badistike"—literally 'walking' or 'advancing'</note>, it would have made another but always goes away. When it is heating, it heats, and when [the power] having taken matter builds it into a nature, [it is] growth. But when another power takes away from that which is capable of suffering removal, it is decrease. <margin>B</margin> When the generative nature acts, it is <term>generation</term>; when it is powerless, and the power capable of destroying [prevails], it is <term>destruction</term> <note>original: "φθορά" / "phthora"—decay or corruption</note>. Not the [destruction] in that which has already happened, but in that which is passing away. And <term>healing</term> occurs according to the power capable of producing health, when it acts... healing. But [illness occurs] when the contrary power does the opposite. So that it happens [that we consider motion] not only in those things [where it occurs], but also according to those things from which [it starts], and those things through which it is transmitted... the peculiarity of the motion, of what kind <margin>C</margin> and quality it is in such things.

<margin>A</margin> REGARDING local motion, for which being carried downward is the opposite of being carried upward, and moving in a straight line [is the opposite of circular], how is the difference [taken]? ...thrown over the head or under the feet. The impulsive power is one. Unless someone says there is one [power] pushing upward and another [downward], and [the motion] is different toward the upward carrying, or especially if it moves naturally, if one were <term>lightness</term> and the other <margin>B</margin> <term>heaviness</term>. But the common and identical thing is the being carried to the proper place. Here it is likely that the difference occurs according to external things. In circular and straight [motion], if indeed they were to run both in a straight line and in a circle, how is it other, unless according to the shape of the path? Unless someone [considers] the circular to be mixed, as if it will not be motion entirely... but it seems to be altogether one [kind of motion], <margin>C</margin> taking differences from external things... for motion is made, as a thing not entirely... taking differences only through external—

<margin>A</margin> COMPOSITION and SEPARATION, how do they stand? Are they other motions than those... generation and destruction, growth and decrease, change of place, and alteration? Or should they be reduced to these, or should some of these be placed as compositions and separations? If indeed this is what they have: composition is the approach of one thing to another, and [separation] is the joining and again the receding, backward, they would be called local motions. Two things move toward one, or recede from one another—either motion toward one, or recession from one—

# BOOK THREE.

> *The species of motions are more probably distinguished by internal differences rather than external ones. That is to say, by the moving forces—whether they be inanimate, or animate, and likewise whether they are animated in this way or that: and again, whether they occur by the impulse of nature, or of art, or of deliberate counsel.*

### Chapter XXVI.

**WE MUST CONSIDER** these matters, or rather investigate them now. Returning to those things which are already called motions—for instance, in the case of <term>local motion</term> <note>original Greek: τοπικὴ κίνησις (topikē kinēsis)—movement from one place to another</note>, if the distinction is not merely made by movement upward or downward, or by straight and circular lines (as was doubted above), perhaps it should be distinguished by the motion of animate and inanimate things. For the motion of these things is not similar to one another. And again, these may be divided into walking, swimming, and flying. Or 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> if those things which are moved are said to obtain a certain <term>blending</term> <note>original: "commistionem quandam"—the mixing of two things into one</note> and a certain temperament and constitution into a single unit—I mean that constitution which exists in the very act of being formed, not in a fixed state after something has already been established—then indeed one might be able to reduce these to one of the motions already described. For <term>local motion</term> <note>change of place</note> will be the starting point there; but besides this motion, something else would occur there. <margin>B</margin> Just as anyone easily finds that local motion is the principle of <term>growth</term>, but that a specific motion of quality soon follows. So, in this case also, a certain local motion begins, but there follows—not necessarily—either <term>composition</term> <note>original Greek: σύγκρισις (sygkrisis)—the gathering together of parts</note> or <term>separation</term> <note>original Greek: διάκρισις (diakrisis)—the breaking apart of parts</note>. But when those things which meet one another embrace each other, composition occurs; conversely, separation follows. Often, <margin>C</margin> where separation occurs, local motion also follows, or happens at the same time. This is because a certain other <term>affection</term> <note>a "passion" or change in state</note> is understood concerning those things which are being discerned, not only in the sense that they change their place; and in composition, a certain other affection and constitution follows that is distinct from the local motion. Should we, therefore, place these motions in a category of their own? Or is it right to reduce <term>alteration</term> <note>change in quality, like color or heat</note> to these? For that which has become dense has already been altered. But that is the same as saying it has been <margin>D</margin> "composed" or gathered together. That which has become rare is also understood to be altered; but this is the same as considering it to be "separated." Furthermore, when one thing is mixed with water, each becomes something other than what it was before. That is a kind of composition which has produced an alteration. Or perhaps it must be said here also that compositions and separations precede certain alterations, but the alterations themselves differ from the compositions and separations. For <margin>E</term> other alterations are not of this kind, nor is <term>rarefaction</term> <note>becoming less dense</note> and <term>condensation</term> <note>becoming more dense</note> themselves simply a composition and separation, nor do they consist entirely of these; otherwise, one would immediately have to admit the existence of a <term>vacuum</term> <note>empty space</note> in nature. Now truly, under what condition would anyone concede that blackness and whiteness consist of composition and separation? If someone were to doubt this, they would be forced to utterly uproot all colors, and perhaps many qualities—indeed, all of them. For if someone contends that every alteration (which we say is a certain change in quality) is actually just composition and separation, then certainly what happens there is in no way a "quality," but only things placed either near each other or apart. Furthermore, in what way can teaching and learning be a form of "composition"?

For the way these things move—walking, swimming, flying—is not similar to one another. Or

also through a natural or less-than-natural impulse. For perhaps one might divide motion in this way according to each specific kind. In this way, the differences between motions would not be taken from the outside. Perhaps the motions themselves are the causes of these differences, yet they do not exist without them; indeed, nature itself seems to be the principle of these motions and of their external differences. Perhaps it is also possible to divide motion so that one part occurs by **nature**, another by **art**, and another by **choice**. By nature, for example, we see growth and decay; by art, we see the building of houses or ships; and by choice, we see contemplation, learning, political governance, and in general, all speaking and acting. Finally, regarding growth, <term>alteration</term> <note>original: "alterat." or "alteratio"—a change in quality rather than size or place</note>, and generation, one may distinguish them either by a natural or non-natural mode, or by the variety of the subjects involved.

*Stability exists in eternal things, where there is no motion; but rest exists in temporal things—namely, the cessation of some motion, or a motion that is extremely slow.*

### Chapter XXVII.

*Since rest is a certain privation, it is not a "genus" (category) unto itself. Motion, however, is not the privation of rest, but is an effective act that removes something and brings something else. Stability in eternal things is not a privation of motion, even if stability is found there when motion ceases, or if those things are naturally suited for motion. Motion has two opposites: the start and the end. Motion seeks its own boundaries and rest, especially if rest is considered the point from which the motion has already departed.*

<margin>A</margin> **REGARDING** "stability" <note>original: "status"—the state of being at a standstill, usually applied to the divine realm</note>, which is the opposite of motion, or regarding "rest" <note>original: "quies"—the temporary cessation of movement in the physical world</note>, what ought to be said? Should this also be established as a single <term>genus</term> <note>a primary category of being</note>? Or should it rather be reduced to one of the categories we have already discussed? Perhaps it is better to grant "stability" itself to divine things, and here investigate "rest." Concerning this rest, we must first investigate what it is: if it is found to be exactly the same as stability, it would not <margin>B</margin> seem right to seek it here, since here in the physical world nothing remains completely still, but that which seems to remain still is actually carried along by a slower motion. But if we say that rest is something other than stability—because stability concerns a thing that is entirely immovable, whereas rest concerns a thing that is standing still but is naturally suited for motion even when it is not moving—this must be distinguished as follows: <margin>C</margin> Certainly, if "becoming restful" is assumed here, the act of resting is said to be a motion that has not yet ceased, but is imminent. But if we assume that rest exists in something that is no longer moved, we must surely ask whether anything among us is entirely unmoved. If it is impossible for something to be agitated by all motions at once, but it must be that it is not moved by certain motions (so that we may at least be able to say that this thing which is moved exists), <margin>D</margin> what else should be said of that which does not move in space, but is at peace as far as this particular motion is concerned, except that it "does not move"? Thus, rest will be a negation of motion. And that which is of such a kind is not properly counted as a category. A thing rests not according to any motion other than local motion. Rest, therefore, signifies only the <term>privation</term> <note>original: "privatio"—the absence of a quality that would normally be there</note> of this. If someone asks why we do not also call motion the privation of stability or rest, we shall answer that motion arrives bringing something with it; it exists as an active thing, shaking the subject, and creating and destroying many things. Rest only signifies not having motion. But why not in the things themselves—

...and both by nature and against nature, in whatever way one might divide each species. Regarding the difference of motions, or their quality, it is established; and those [differences] would not exist without them. By art: building, shipbuilding. <margin>B</margin> And generally speaking: acting. Concerning growth, alteration, and generation, whether according to nature, or generally in the subjects themselves.

Should it be placed as a single genus, or to what genus should it be brought back? It is perhaps better to seek stability among the eternal beings, and rest here [in the physical world]. Regarding this rest, we must first seek what it is, and if it appears the same as stability, one would not seek it here, where nothing <margin>B</margin> is [totally still], but that which appears to be so is using a slow motion. If we say rest is different, stating that stability is about the completely [immobile], while rest is the state of a thing standing still that is naturally suited to move when it is not moving: "becoming restful" might be said of "resting" while it has not yet stopped, but is present. If <margin>C</margin> it is no longer about the thing moved, we must first [ask] if anything is not moved here. Since it is not possible to be moved by all motions, it is necessary not to be moved by some motions, so that it may be said that this thing which is moved exists. What else is the thing not moving in place, [specifically] in this motion, except that it does not move? Therefore rest will be a negation: "it does not move." And that which is [a negation] is not in a genus. It rests according to no other <margin>D</margin> [motion] than this [local] motion, which is a privation. Nor does one then speak of an "abstraction." If [someone asks] why we do not call motion a negation of stability, we will say that motion comes bringing something, it is something else active and, as it were, [shaking] the subject, and working a thousand things, and destroying. He also classifies motions by their origin: nature, art, or deliberate human choice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of stability and motion, specifically addressing whether "rest" can be considered a distinct category or merely the absence of movement. It concludes the discussion on the Aristotelian categories (Predicaments) of acting, being acted upon, and relation.</meta>

BOOK THREE.

<margin>A</margin> We have previously spoken of whether we should call stability a negation of motion, or if stability is the removal of motion—not that stability comes into being only when motion has ceased, but rather that it exists alongside it. Nor is it stability there <note>The "there" usually refers to the Intelligible realm in Neoplatonic thought, where motion and stability coexist eternally.</note> simply because something naturally suited for motion is not moving at a certain time. Rather, in the sense that stability has encompassed the intelligible, it stands firm; yet insofar as it also possesses motion, it will be moved forever. For this reason, it both consists in stability and moves with motion. But bodily nature, on the other hand, moves by motion and <margin>B</margin> rests when motion is absent, being clearly deprived of its required movement. Furthermore, we must see what stability itself is. For example, when one passes from sickness to health, they are said to recover. What kind of species of "rest" or "quiet" shall we oppose to this process of recovery? If we mean the state from which one departs, that is sickness, not stability. If we mean the state toward which one arrives, that is health, which is not the same as stability. If anyone claims that health or sickness is a kind of stability, they would be asserting that health and sickness are species of stability—which is absurd. But if one admits that stability is merely a property that happens to belong to health, then health itself would not be health until the stability arrived. But regarding these matters, let each person judge as they see fit.

<column-break/>

...we assert that stability is a privation of motion. Because it is not right to call stability a "privation" <note>original: "priuationem"</note> of motion; for it is not when motion ceases that stability itself comes into being; rather, while motion exists, stability is present. Nor is stability there simply because that which was born for motion is not moving at some time. But by the reason that stability there encompasses the intelligible itself, it remains: but where it is moved, it will be moved forever; wherefore it both consists in stability and is moved by motion. But bodily nature is moved by motion, and in the absence of motion it rests, being clearly deprived of its required motion. Furthermore, we must see what stability itself is: likewise, when someone arrives from sickness to health, they recover. What kind of species of rest, then, shall we oppose to this recovery? For if it is the state from which one recedes, that is sickness, not stability; but if it is the state to which one approaches, that is health, which indeed is not the same as stability. If anyone, however, says that health or sickness is a certain stability, he will surely concede that health and sickness are species of stability: which is judged to be absurd. But if he should properly confess that stability happens to belong to health, health before stability will not be health. But concerning these things, let each speak according to his own judgment.

## EPILOGUE OF THE CATEGORIES.

We have said in the preceding sections that **acting** and **being acted upon** <note>original: "facere atque pati"</note> are to be called motions. Some motions are absolute, while others are partly actions and partly passions. Furthermore, it was said regarding the other so-called categories <note>original: "genera" or "kinds"</note> that they ought to be referred to these classifications of ours. It was also said concerning **relation** <note>original: "relatione" / "πρὸς τι"</note>, namely that it is the disposition of one thing toward another, and that both occur simultaneously. Finally, it was said regarding relation that when the disposition itself produces the substance, that which is referred—not by the reason of being a substance—is a relative; but rather as some part, such as a hand, or a head, or a cause, or a principle, or an element. It is also possible to divide relations in the manner of the ancients <note>Plotinus often references "the ancients," usually meaning Plato, Aristotle, and the Pythagoreans.</note>, so that some are as if they were productive, others as if they were measures; some are concerned with excess and defect, and others finally are distinguished by similarities and differences. But let these things already said concerning the categories suffice.

### BOOK FOUR.

-> THAT BEING, ONE AND THE SAME, IS SIMULTANEOUSLY WHOLE EVERYWHERE. <-

-> That being is one and the same, and is simultaneously whole everywhere. <-

---

> *Since the soul possesses no physical quantity, nor is it merely a property of a physical body, the question arises: how is it spread through a large space? Does it exist by itself before the body, or is it extended along with the body and through the body as far as the body goes?*

---

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' depicting a seated scholar or philosopher holding a book, representing the beginning of the Latin text.</image-desc>Is the soul present everywhere in the universe because the body of the universe is so vast? Does the soul, which has a nature that is divided among bodies, exist everywhere of its own accord? Is it not "pulled" or stretched out by the body, but rather, does the body find the soul already present everywhere? Indeed, wherever the body is placed, it finds the soul already existing there, even before that part of the body was positioned in a specific part of the universe. Thus, the entire body of the universe is placed within a soul that already exists. But if the soul was already so "diffused" before the body arrived—filling the entire interval of the universe—what prevents us from saying the soul has a physical size? Furthermore, how could it be in the universe before the universe was created, if the universe did not yet exist?

<margin>B</margin>
On the other hand, how can one admit that the soul—which is said to be indivisible and lacking in physical magnitude—is everywhere, when it has no size at all? Even if one says it is extended along with the body, since the soul itself is not a body, we cannot avoid the problem by saying it has magnitude "by accident" <note>original: "secundum accidens"; this refers to a property that is not part of the essential nature of a thing but happens to belong to it because of its circumstances.</note>. One might still rightly ask how something can become "large" even by accident.

<margin>C</margin>
The soul is not like a <term>quality</term> <note>In Greek philosophy, a "quality" (like sweetness or color) depends entirely on the object it resides in.</note>, such as sweetness or color, which is spread through the whole body. These qualities are merely "passions" <note>original: "passiones," translating the Greek "pathe," meaning things that happen to or affect a body.</note> of bodies. It is not surprising that a body, being affected, possesses such a quality throughout its whole self, as the quality has no independent existence; it exists only as "something of the body" and is known only within the body. Therefore, the quality is necessarily as large as the body itself.

<margin>D</margin>
Furthermore, the whiteness in one part of a body does not share a single existence with the whiteness in another part. In a white object, the whiteness in this part is the same in *species* <note>meaning they are the same "kind" of white.</note> as the whiteness in that part, but it is not *numerically* the same. <note>Numerical identity means being the exact same individual thing, not just a similar type.</note>

<margin>E</margin>
But in the case of the soul, the same soul—numerically identical—is in the foot and in the hand. Our perceptions and feelings demonstrate this.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Α' (Alpha) mirroring the Latin column, depicting a seated scholar.</image-desc>Is the soul present because the whole of it is in the body's quantity? Or because its nature is such that it is divided among bodies, and yet is everywhere of its own accord? It is not as if it were <margin>B</margin> dragged along, but rather the body is found worthy of it; it was everywhere about the body. Wherever the body is placed, there it finds the soul already existing. It does not need to be placed in a part of the whole, for the whole body is placed in a soul that is already there. If it were so vast before the body came, filling the entire interval, how could it not have size? How could it be in the universe before the universe was born, when the universe did not yet exist?

<margin>C</margin>
How can that which is said to be indivisible and without size be everywhere, having no magnitude? How could one accept this? Even if it were said to extend with the body, not being a body itself, this does not <margin>D</margin> solve the difficulty. One might still ask without logic how it is made large by accident. For it is not like sweetness or color which is throughout the whole body—for the soul is not like that. For those are "passions" of bodies, and it is natural for the whole affected body to have the passion; it does not exist by itself, but is of the body and known there. Therefore, of necessity, it is as large as the body. One white part is affected the same as another, yet the white is the same in species in another part, but it is not the same numerically.

<margin>E</margin>
But in the soul, the same thing is numerically present in the foot and the hand, as our perceptions show. And yet, while in the soul it is the same, in the body it is divided.

<summary>Plotinus begins an investigation into how the soul can be present throughout the entire body without having physical size or being "stretched." He argues that the body exists within the soul rather than the soul being contained by the body, distinguishing the soul's presence from physical qualities like color.</summary>
<keywords>soul, body, omnipresence, magnitude, indivisibility, quality, numerical identity, Plotinus, Neoplatonism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the opening of the Fourth Book of the Sixth Ennead. The previous page ended with a question about whether the soul, being non-physical, can be said to have a location or if it is the body that exists within the soul. Here, Plotinus begins to resolve the paradox of how a single, undivided "Being" can be present in many places at once.</meta>

# FOURTH BOOK.

<margin>
Summary of Chapter 1:
Whether the whole is in the body or is contained within all of it. It is not that they are held by the body to be in it, but that they have a memory of the sizeless being everywhere. This might be said of everything. It happens that the body is in it, so that it is found in no other part. How the numbers show what quality is contemplated.
</margin>

Regarding the soul, the same question arises: is it divided or not? It is said to be divided in this way: because it is everywhere. Let us speak of these things again from the beginning, seeking to find a clear and acceptable way to explain how the soul—being <term>incorporeal</term><note>Non-physical; having no material body.</note> and lacking <term>magnitude</term><note>Physical size or volume.</note>—is able to extend into a wide space, whether we speak of it being before bodies or within bodies. Perhaps if it becomes clear that this is possible even before bodies exist, it will be easy to accept that such a thing occurs within bodies as well. <sig>A</sig>

There is, indeed, a certain "True Whole." There is also an image of that whole, which is the nature of this visible world. That which is truly the Whole exists in nothing at all, for there is nothing prior to it. But that which comes after it must necessarily be within the Whole, if indeed it is to exist. It depends primarily upon that Whole and cannot remain or move without it. For even if one were to place such a thing in a "place," one must not think of place as the boundary of a surrounding body, nor as a hollow interval of space that existed previously as a vacuum. Rather, let one think of it as resting upon and being supported by that which is everywhere. <sig>D</sig> Because that Being contains it, and because of the limitations of our language, let the mind grasp what is meant even if the words are imperfect. This is said for another reason: that the first Being, the Whole, does not seek a place, nor is it in anything at all. For the Whole can never be separated from itself; rather, it fills itself and is equal to itself.

<margin>* Furthermore, that Whole is itself</margin>
\* And either that Whole is itself—for it is the Whole itself—or, if something else is established within the Whole, it participates in it, encounters it, and gains strength from it. It does not divide the Whole, but finds the whole of it within itself, approaching it without the Whole ever leaving itself. For it is impossible for <term>Being</term> to exist in <term>non-being</term>; but if non-being exists within Being, it does not encounter it merely in part. It must not be torn away from itself. When we say it is "everywhere," we mean it exists in Being, and thus in itself. It is not surprising if that which is everywhere is in Being and in itself. For "everywhere" now exists in the One. But we, having assumed that "Being" is the same as the <term>sensible world</term><note>The physical world we perceive with our five senses.</note>, also assume that "everywhere" refers to this physical space. Thinking the sensible world is "great," we wonder how that higher Nature extends through something so large. But in truth, this physical world which is called "great" is actually small; while that which is thought to be "small" <note>The Intelligible Realm or the Soul</note> is actually great. For the whole of that realm is present in every part.

<column-break/>

[The following text continues from the previous page's Latin translation] ...it is said to be; but in the soul the same is true, though not divided. However, it is said to be divided because it pours itself out everywhere. Let us speak of these things again from the beginning, investigating if there is any way it can be made clearly manifest to us how the soul, since it is non-physical and lacks physical size, can be propagated across so many things, whether it extends before bodies or within bodies. For perhaps if it is established that this can happen even before bodies, it will be very easy to admit such a thing also within bodies. <sig>B</sig>

---

*The Intelligible World—that is, the first Being—is true, universal, and great, because it is all beings, and it is a whole in every part of itself, and it is not contained in the universe. And when it is said to be "everywhere," it is itself the very thing called "everywhere." The sensible world, however, is truly small, because "everywhere" in it consists of small parts. Moreover, it exists in the higher world not as if in a containing place, nor as if in some empty interval, but as if in that which is the cause, preserver, stabilizer, mover, and embracer. This world touches that whole world through every part of itself; therefore, it does not move in a straight line to find it, but revolves around that which is found everywhere in the same place. Chapter II.* <sig>C</sig>

---

There is indeed a certain true Universe; there is also an image of that true Universe, namely the visible nature of this world. That which is truly the Universe exists in no place at all; for no being exists before it. But that which exists after it must now necessarily be in the Universe, if anything is to exist in the future—especially since it depends on that Universe and cannot remain or move without it. For if anyone places this within that, not understanding "place" as the limit of a containing body, or as some interval that was previously like a vacuum and still exists, but rather asserts that this is founded and rests in that—in that, I say, which exists everywhere and completely embraces it—whoever places it so, let them set aside the name of "place" and grasp with their thought what is being said. This, however, is said for another reason: because that first Universe does not seek a place, nor does it rest in anything at all. Since it is entirely the Universe on every side, it cannot be that it is somehow lacking to itself, but it fills itself and is equal to itself. Nor is there anything else that is the Universe, for it exists as the Universe itself entirely. Truly, if anything is founded in the Universe, being something else besides it, it participates in it and harmonizes with it. Likewise, it is strengthened by it, not by dividing it, but by finding <sig>E</sig> it within itself. It approaches the Universe while the Universe is not placed outside itself. For it is impossible for Being to be in non-being; but if non-being is in Being, it does not fall upon it as a whole. For it could not be distracted or plucked away from itself. But that which is said—that the Universe is "everywhere"—must be understood as existing in Being itself, and thus in itself. Nor is it a wonder if that which is called "everywhere" is in Being and in itself. For now "everywhere" would be in the One. But we, thinking that Being itself is this sensible world, consequently think that "everywhere" is here. Likewise, thinking this sensible world is great, we rightly wonder how...

---

...that nature extends through this thing that is so great. But in reality, this which is called "great" is small; and that which is thought small is great; since that whole is present through every part of the universe...

<summary>Plotinus explores the metaphysical puzzle of how the non-physical Soul and "True Being" can be present everywhere in the physical world without being physically divided. He concludes that the physical world exists within the Intelligible World, rather than the other way around.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Enneads, Intelligible World, Sensible World, Omnipresence, Soul, Being, Metaphysics, Place vs Space</keywords>
