<meta>This page continues the discussion from the beginning of Ennead VI, Book 4, where Plotinus investigates how the "True Being" or the Intelligible World can be present everywhere without being divided. The previous page established that the physical world exists within the "Whole," rather than the other way around.</meta>

PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

<column-break/>

...pours itself out into each individual thing; indeed, this universe, approaching that <term>Whole</term><note>The 'Whole' refers to the Intelligible World or True Being, which is the source of all reality.</note> from every side with its own parts, finds it everywhere as a whole, and undoubtedly larger than itself. Therefore, as if it would receive nothing more through further extension—for in that way it might seem to escape even outside the universe—it rightly wished to revolve within its own bounds. Since it could neither comprehend the Whole nor push itself entirely inside it, it considered itself satisfied if it could obtain a place and order where it might remain close to that which is present, and yet again, not present. For the Whole exists within itself, even if something else wishes to be near it. The body of the universe, turning toward it, finds the Whole everywhere, so that it has no need to go further, but finds it better to revolve in the same place, as if this space in which it turns were truly the Whole. There, certainly, it enjoys that Whole in every one of its parts. For if the Whole were in a specific location, the universe would have to travel toward it in a straight line and touch one part of it with another part; it would then necessarily be sometimes far and sometimes near. But since it is neither far nor near, the Whole must be present in its entirety, provided it is present at all. And indeed, it is present as a whole to each of those things to which it is near and not distant—that is, to those capable of properly receiving it.

---

### The intelligible world, by the excellence of its power, spreads its forces through all parts of the world: and is present to each, while remaining transcendent. Chapter III.

*Just as it communicates its powers to all things capable of participating, so it is present through its powers; and where there are more powers, it is more clearly present; where all are present, it is most clearly seen. It does not become the specific <term>form</term><note>The 'form' (species) here refers to the essential nature or blueprint of a thing.</note> of any one thing, nor is it circumscribed by a specific place; otherwise, it would no longer be the universe, nor would it be present to all in common. A body is divided not by its essence, but by its quantity; therefore, when a division is made, even if the same quantity does not remain, the same essence remains. But since unity, life, and the primary mind constitute a nature devoid of quantity, if it were divided according to its nature, the division would not change the essence itself.*

<margin>A</margin> **S**hall we say then that the <term>Whole</term><note>original: "ipsum" / Greek: "αὐτὸ" — referring to the One or the Intelligible Reality.</note> itself is present? Or does it remain within itself, while its powers are spread from it through all things, and thus it is thought to be everywhere? For some teach that <term>souls</term><note>original: "animas" / Greek: "ψυχὰς"</note> are like certain rays cast out from there, so that the source itself rests within itself, while the souls sent out from it become one animal after another. But truly, for those to whom a single part of it is granted—because they cannot preserve its entire nature within themselves—it is said to be present in such a way that its power is present. Yet it is not as if the source itself is not present at all. For even then, it is by no means severed from that power which it gave to the thing; rather, the recipient was only able to grasp so much from the whole that was present. 

<margin>B</margin> But where all powers are communicated, the source itself is most clearly present, yet in such a way that it remains simultaneously separate. For if it became a mere <term>form</term><note>original: "species" / Greek: "εἶδος"</note> of this material thing, it could neither be the "Whole" nor could it exist everywhere remaining within itself; instead, it would exist only accidentally and belong to another. But since it belongs to no one, even to those who wish it to be theirs, it draws near to everyone who desires it according to their capacity; yet it does not become theirs, but is present through their desire for it. 

<margin>C</margin> Therefore, it is not surprising that it is thus in all things, since again it is in nothing in such a way as to become part of them. For this reason, it is perhaps not absurd to say that the soul, in an accidental way, suffers alongside the body; yet the soul itself is said to be within itself, belonging neither to matter nor to the body.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It reaches out—or rather, the universe approaches it from every side with its parts—and finds it whole and greater than itself. Thus, as if seeking to receive something more than the whole, it would find itself outside the whole. It was content to revolve around it, unable to grasp it or enter into it; it was satisfied to have a place and an order for itself. It exists in itself, even if something else should desire it.

<margin>B</margin> Where the body of the universe meets it, it finds it as a whole. Thus, it has no need to pursue what is further away, but circles within itself. Since it is the Whole, it partakes of it as a whole in every part. For if that reality were in a place, the universe would have to be far from it or move toward it, touching one part of itself to another part of that.

<margin>C</margin> If there is no "far" or "near," it must be present as a whole if it is present at all, and it is entirely there for those who are neither far nor near, but are able to receive it.

---

<margin>A</margin> Shall we then say that it is present itself, remaining in itself, while its powers go out to all things, and thus it is said to be everywhere? For some say that souls are this way: that the source is established, while those souls sent out become the different living beings. Or is it that in some, where the "One" is present, it preserves the nature that is in it...

<margin>B</margin> ...there its power is provided. Yet not so that the source is not entirely present in that place; it is not cut off from its power which it gave to the thing. Rather, the thing was able to take as much as it could, while the whole was present. There all its powers are clearly present, yet it remains separate. For if it became a form, it would cease to be the whole or to be in itself. 

<margin>C</margin> Now it is everywhere, and yet it is accidental. To whoever is of the Mind—to the one who wishes it to be—it draws near as it is able, as the one who desires it...

<summary>Plotinus explains that the Intelligible World (True Being) is omnipresent not by being divided into parts, but by being present as a whole to anything capable of receiving its power. He argues that while physical bodies are limited by space and quantity, the soul and the Intelligible realm are non-spatial and remain transcendent even while they are "present" to the material world.</summary>

<keywords>Plotinus, Enneads, metaphysics, Intelligible World, soul, omnipresence, transcendence, power, form, being, Greek philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 821 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into Ennead VI, Book 4. Plotinus is exploring the paradox of how a non-physical reality (like the Soul or the Divine Mind) can be present to every part of the physical world as a whole without being divided into pieces.</meta>

BOOK FOUR.

<column-break/>

...but that [soul] longing for it, and another for another, it is not at all strange that it is thus in all things. Furthermore, in whichever of these it exists in such a way as to belong to them, one might say it occurs by accident—<margin>becoming</margin> running alongside the body toward the soul. It would perhaps be absurd if the soul were said to exist by itself, <margin>becoming</margin> without matter or body. Yet the whole body, in every part of itself, is as it were illuminated by it. It is worth wondering if it, not being in a "where" <note>Greek: *pou*, meaning a specific location</note>, is present to everything that is in a "where." For the opposite would be strange—and impossible besides being strange and absurd—either if it had a house of its own in some other place, or if it were present to each thing individually in the way we usually speak of presence. But now the argument says that it is necessary for it, not having been allotted a place to which it is present, to be present as a whole to that to which it is present, just as it is present as a whole to each thing; otherwise one part of it would be here and another there, and so it would be divisible and a body. For how else could it have parts? Would you divide it by life? But if the whole is life, the part will not be life. Or will it be either nothing, or one part in one thing and another in another? But it would be another of them. But if it were Being itself, the part would not be Being if the whole were the Being. Why then might one not also say that the body is divided? Even the parts have a body; if they are beings, then the division is not of the body, but of a <margin>D</margin> body of such a size. And each body was called such by its <term>form</term><note>The 'form' or 'species' is the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is, regardless of its size.</note> according to whatever size it might be.

HOW then is it right to speak of being and identity, and many souls? If being is everywhere one, and not as if merely uniform, and there is one mind and one soul, even though one is the soul of the whole and others are the rest, these things seem to contradict what has been said; and what has been said, even if it carries necessity, does not bring persuasion, since the mind thinks it incredible for the <margin>B</margin> soul to be one and the same everywhere. Perhaps it is better to divide the whole in such a way as to diminish nothing from that from which the division is made, or rather to generate from it—to use better names—so that the one remains, while the things produced like parts are souls now filling all things. But if that being rests <margin>on its own</margin> within itself, because it seems a paradox for a whole to be everywhere at once, the same reasoning will apply to souls. <margin>And to those things which are said</margin> For they will be heard as being whole within the whole bodies in which they are said to be. But they will either be divided, or if they remain whole, they will give their power to the body. Regarding which powers, the same difficulty will arise: whether the power is whole everywhere, or if some part of the soul is in the body, or if it is only a power...

<insert>
and the same ambiguity will arise concerning the soul, whether the power itself is everywhere as a whole. Furthermore, one member of the body will have the soul, while another will have only the power. But first it must be investigated in what way...
</insert>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But every body throughout its whole self is, as it were, illuminated by the soul. Nothing, indeed, should seem surprising if that divine whole, since it is not itself in a place, is present to everything that is in a place. On the contrary, it would be both wonderful and moreover impossible if that whole, having a place of its own, were present to something in a place, or if it were present at all, and were present in the way we currently describe presence. But now reason dictates it to be necessary that the thing itself, since it has no place, be present as a whole to whatever it is present; and since it is present to the universe, it is so present that it is present as a whole to individual things. Otherwise, one part of it would be here and another there, so that it would be both divisible and a body. Now indeed, one may ask how you divide it. Will you divide life? But where you have divided it, if the whole was life, the part will not be life. But will you divide the intellect, so that this part is in one thing, and that in another? Truly, neither of them will be an intellect. Will you then divide its very being? But truly, the part will not be being in this way, if the whole was being. What then? If someone objects that a divided body also has parts which are themselves still bodies: but certainly the partition was not of the "body" [as an abstract form], but rather of "so much" of a body. And each individual body is made and described by its <term>species</term><note>original: "specie", referring to the formal cause or 'form' that defines a thing's nature.</note> insofar as it exists as a body. But this, especially regarding species, does not properly have a certain quantity, nor even quantity in any way whatsoever.

---

->*One primary essence, that is, the divine mind, is everywhere as a whole; similarly, the one soul of the world: nor does the multitude of mundane parts prevent it from being one and whole everywhere: nor does the unity of the primary mind and soul prevent there being many other minds and souls besides.*<-

->Chap. IV.<-

->*Neither through the many members of the same body is the soul forced to be multiple and divisible: nor through many bodies do souls become many: for there are both minds and souls differing among themselves in their own properties within themselves, even before bodies: and they are joined to one another by a certain natural kinship and communion of duty, and meanwhile distinguished by the otherness of the property of essence, not by location.*<-

---

**MOREOVER**, in what way is it right to speak of being and essence, and many minds, and many souls? If being is one everywhere, and not one as if merely of some uniform shape: likewise if there is one mind, if there is one soul: even though we have accepted that there is one soul of the universe, and others which are the rest. For these things seem to contradict what has already been said: and what has been said, if they perhaps carry some necessity, yet they do not bring persuasion, since the mind thinks it incredible that <margin>B</margin> one thing should thus be the same whole everywhere. Perhaps, therefore, it is better to divide that one whole, yet in such a way that the thing itself from which the division is made is not diminished at all: or rather from that, to speak more correctly, to generate certain things, and to allow that whole indeed to remain within itself: but to think that those things which are brought forth as if they were parts are the souls now filling all things. But if that being rests within itself for this reason—specifically because it seems incredible for one whole to be everywhere at once—the <margin>C</margin> same reasoning will similarly doubt concerning souls. For these, in which bodies they are said to be whole in the whole, will no longer be so: but they will either be divided, or if they remain whole: they will rest specifically in a certain part of the body, and from there diffuse their powers through the limbs: and now the same [doubt] also concerning powers...

<summary>Plotinus argues that spiritual realities like the Soul and Being are not divisible like physical matter; if life were cut in half, the result would not be two half-lives, but a loss of the essence of life itself. Consequently, these higher realities must be present as a complete whole to every part of the universe they inhabit.</summary>

--- Page 822 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration in Ennead VI, Book 4 (and moving into Book 5), concerning how the One and the Many coexist. The previous page discussed how the Soul is present to the body without being confined by space; this page extends that logic to the plurality of individual souls within the single Universal Soul.</meta>

<page-num>648</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.</header>

<margin>A</margin>Since we have established the higher principles, there are many souls, many minds, and many beings besides the One. Now indeed, those things which flow from the prior causes—provided they are not physical magnitudes but rather numbers <note>Plotinus distinguishes between "magnitude" (physical size) and "number" (metaphysical multiplicity)</note>—will similarly raise the question of how they fill the universe. Therefore, nothing clearly discovered by us regarding the multitude flowing out in this way helps to explain the doubt. For we even concede that Being itself is "many" <margin>B</margin> by a certain otherness <note>Original Latin: *alteritas*; Greek: *heterotes*. This refers to the concept that things are distinct not by location, but by being "other" than one another</note>, but not by location. For all Being exists together at once, even though it is multiple; indeed, as Parmenides says, "being draws near to being," and the universe exists as a whole together. Furthermore, the Intellect is multiple through otherness, not by location, but the whole of it exists at once. Do souls not also behave this way? Perhaps souls do as well. For even that which is called "divisible" regarding bodies is considered to be "indivisible" again according to its own nature. <margin>C</margin> Bodies, of course, possess magnitude because the nature of the soul itself is present to them; or rather, when bodies come into existence there, and insofar as they are extended in every part, that nature of the soul itself appears, which is occupied with bodies; thus, it happens that the soul is thought to be divisible in relation to them. For it is clearly evident to us that the soul is not distributed into parts along with the parts of the body, but is present as a whole everywhere, because its nature is found to be truly one and indivisible. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, the fact that the soul is "one" does not prevent there being "many" souls; just as the fact that Being is "one" does not prohibit the existence of many beings, nor does multitude there conflict with the One. Nor is it necessary to fill bodies with life through a kind of "multitude" [of pieces]; nor because of the physical magnitude of the body should one think that a multitude of souls is created. Instead, many souls and the One soul exist even before bodies. <margin>E</margin> For in that very Whole, many already consist—not merely in potentiality, but each one already in actuality. For that one whole soul does not prevent many from existing within itself; and the many, in turn, do not hinder the one. For they are distant from one another while remaining not distant, and they are present to each other without being foreign. They are not separated from one another by any boundaries, just as many sciences gathered in one mind are not separated; but the one mind is such that it contains all of them within itself. Such is the nature of this Infinite.

---

>*The Soul of the world, like the Mind, is indivisible and yet a universe; therefore, it is present as a whole everywhere in the world. Chapter VI.*
*Since the soul does not have physical quantity, it is not smaller or larger in quantity than the world, but in virtue/power, which the world receives in its entirety. The same soul suffices for a larger body as well as a smaller one because of the greatness of its power.*

---

<margin>A</margin>ACCORDINGLY, the greatness of this nature is not to be judged according to physical mass <note>Original Latin: *moles*; Greek: *onkos*. Plotinus warns against thinking of "greatness" as physical size</note>; for mass is a small thing that falls toward nothingness if one takes anything away from it. But from that higher nature, it is not right to subtract, nor if you were to subtract from it, would it fail in any way. But if it never fails, there is no fear that it might ever be absent from anything. For how could it be absent from anything, since it suffers no defect, but is an eternal nature that does not flow? Otherwise, if it flowed, it would proceed only as far as it was able to flow. <margin>B</margin> But since it does not flow at all—for it has no place to flow into—it already completely encompasses the whole. Or rather, it is itself the "Whole," and is something greater than can be measured by the magnitude of a physical nature. For it is rightly judged that a small thing is granted to this physical universe, namely, as much as the universe is able to bear of that higher nature. It is best, however, neither to call that higher universe "lesser," nor to place it as lesser according to mass...

### *Questions concerning the world soul and our own. Chapter VI.*

> *He asks thus: If the soul has such a magnitude of power as we were just saying, why does it not also provide life to any body placed near it? He responds that it can, provided that the body "approaches" it—that is, through a formable conformity <note>The body must be "tuned" or structurally ready to receive the soul's influence.</note>. Likewise, he doubts thus: If the soul of the world occupies the whole, does a body animated by its own private soul have both its own soul and the common one at the same time? And he raises a sub-doubt by asking how these two souls differ there. He responds that they differ by "adjunctions" <note>Original Latin: *adiunctiones*. This suggests that while the essence of "Soul" is the same, they differ based on what they are attached to or their specific functions.</note>, because although both are soul, yet this one is a soul of one kind, and that one of another kind. Then he confirms that the soul of the world can be the same whole in distant bodies, because even in us, our soul is the same whole in the foot and the hand at once. And he adds that different senses and passions <note>Here "passions" refers to "undergoing" a sensation or an external effect.</note> do not prevent there being one soul in a human and one in the world: for clearly in any human there is one judge, and so it is in the soul of the world. Then he asks, since there are two souls in us, one common and one private, why does our soul not perceive the judgment of the world soul? He responds: Because from that judgment no shared feeling <note>Original Latin: *compassio*. In this philosophical context, it means "co-feeling" or a shared sensory experience.</note> results in us. Furthermore, the power of the soul that judges does not always notice that it is judging, nor does every power in the same soul communicate its judgment to another. Therefore, it is no wonder if the power of our soul does not sense the judgment of the common soul, nor does that soul communicate its own to ours. But the Reason in us notices the judgments of the lower powers within us, and the Reason in the common soul similarly notices the judgments of its own powers. Our Reason is indeed occupied and distracted by sensible things, but the Reason of the common soul is collected around intelligible things. Therefore, since they are turned toward opposites, judgment is not easily communicated from one to the other. I pass over for now how, through the common soul, a certain communion of life, consent, and shared feeling exists among us, as well as with worldly and celestial things; in this union consists the power of attraction and magic. You must take care not to think that Plotinus posits only one single soul for all things. For this is everywhere repugnant to his thought.*

Why then does another body not come to it? Or rather, it must be that if it were able to approach, that which has approached and received it, possesses it. What then? Otherwise, how is it the same soul in the foot and the hand? And the soul in this part of the universe, and the same in that part? If the senses are different, and the incidents that befall them are different, one must say they are distinct; but that which is produced is one thing, and that which judges is another. But the one who judges is the same judge, though existing in different passions. And yet it is not the sufferer who is the cause. Rather, it is the nature of this particular body. It is as if one of us judges both the pleasure in the finger and the pain in the head. Why then does the one soul not perceive the judgment of the other? Perhaps because it is a judgment, not a passion. Furthermore, the power that judged does not say "I have judged," but it merely judged. For even among us, the sight does not tell the hearing, even though both have judged; rather, the Reason presiding over both knows it. But this Reason is different from both of them. Often Reason has seen the judgment in another part and had a shared understanding of another's passion. We have spoken of this in other places as well.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 649, where Plotinus argued that the "greatness" of the soul is a matter of power rather than physical size. Having established that the soul is not a physical substance, he now uses mathematical and physical analogies—such as centers, hands, and light—to explain how a single, indivisible entity can be present throughout a large, divided body without itself becoming divided.</meta>

PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK VI.

The multitude of numbers proceeding from the one, and the lines flowing from a center, do not prevent either the one or the single center from being indivisible and unique. Similarly, the soul is not forced to become divisible or multiple because of those members or bodies it inhabits. Rather, just as the governing force is entirely present in any part of a weight, and the same light is everywhere in any part of the air, so too is the soul.

### Chapter VII.

<margin>A</margin> BUT let us speak again of how the same thing is present through all things. This is similar to asking under what condition each of the many sensible things <note>Sensible things: objects that can be perceived by the five senses.</note>, which are arranged scattered in every direction, participates in the same nature. Truly, it is established that it is a sacrilege to divide that "One" into many on account of the multitude of things; rather, it is more fitting to rightly gather the many divided things into the One—which indeed does not "come" to these things. But because these things are scattered, they compel us to imagine that the "One" is also somehow dissected according to them—as if someone thought that that which surpasses and contains a thing must be divided into equal parts along with that which is contained. And yet, a hand can contain a whole body and a piece of wood many cubits long, or anything else. In such a case, the power itself that contains it is active everywhere in that which is held; nevertheless, it is not divided into equal parts along with the object held by the hand—even though it appears that the power is circumscribed <note>original: *circumscriptam*; limited within a boundary</note> only as far as the hand reaches. But the hand meanwhile is defined by its own particular size, not by the size of the body which is suspended and held. Moreover, if you were to add another length to the suspended body, and the hand were able to support it, the governing power itself would rule that too, without being cut into as many parts as the body has. What then? If someone imagined the physical <term>bulk</term> <note>Bulk (Latin: *moles*): The physical mass or volume of an object, which Plotinus distinguishes from spiritual power.</note> of the hand to be secretly snatched away, but left there meanwhile the same power which previously supported the weight and was formerly in the hand, would not that same <term>indivisible</term> <note>Indivisible (Latin: *impartibilis*): Having no parts; something that cannot be split or shared out like physical matter.</note> power be similarly in the whole weight through every part? Furthermore, if you fixed a certain tiny and bright little body as a center somewhere, and placed around it a larger spherical and transparent body, so that the light of the innermost little body shone through the whole surrounding mass (where there is no earth from elsewhere to block it), would we not say that the innermost light, while suffering nothing itself, remains and has proceeded through the whole external mass? And the light visible there in the small body has from that point completely grasped the whole that stands around it. But since that light did not exist because of the physical mass of that center—for it did not possess light insofar as it was a body, but insofar as it was a *luminous* body, by virtue of another incorporeal power—tell me then: if someone removed the mass of that body but preserved the power of the light there, would you say the light was still properly in any one place? Would it not rather be equally both inside and throughout the whole exterior sphere? No longer would you fix your thought on where it was previously placed, nor would you say further from where or where the light is; but you would be uncertain and altogether full of wonder about this: for you would see the same light simultaneously both here and there through the globe. Indeed, you can say the same concerning the sun: from where exactly the light most powerfully illuminates the whole air, namely when you direct your sight to the body of the sun, and simultaneously you look around at that same light everywhere and not divided. This is testified by the fact that certain "shadow-cuts" <note>original: *decisiones*; perhaps referring to shadows or the way light is blocked</note> are made from the light: which surely do not return light elsewhere than from the region where the light had flowed out, and they neither cut nor diminish the light.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> BUT let us say again how the same is the same <note>The Greek text here is slightly repetitive or corrupted in the source transcription.</note>, the one among the many sensible things, not being without a share though situated in many places. For either that [One], from what has been said, must be divided into the many, or the many divided things must be led back into the one; and that [One] has not come again, but because these things are scattered...

<margin>B</margin> ...it seems to us <note>The Greek text here is fragmented.</note> that according to these things that [One] is also divided. Just as if someone were to divide that which holds and contains along with that which is held, and to some extent it holds the whole body, or a piece of wood many cubits long, and the holder is over the whole. Or is it divided into parts equal to that which is held in the hand? It appears so, and the power seems to be circumscribed to that extent. But nevertheless, the hand is limited by its own quantity, not by that of the...

<margin>C</margin> ...one and held body. Even if you were to add to the held body another whole length which the hand could carry, the power would also [hold] that, without being divided into as many parts as the body has. What then if someone were to suppose the physical bulk of the hand to be removed, but were to preserve the same power which previously supported it—that which was before in the hand?

<margin>D</margin> Would it not itself be entirely indivisible in all things in the same way according to every part? And if you were to make a certain small bulk like a center, and placed around it a larger spherical transparent body, so that the light within appeared in everything that contained it, not having come to it from anywhere else outside. Would that interior body suffer anything in its bulk? No, but remaining, it has...

<margin>E</margin> ...gone out into the exterior bulk, and the light seen in the small bulk has occupied the outside? Since therefore the light was not in that small thing because of its being a body—for it held the light not as a body, but as a luminous body by another power, different from the physical. Come...

<margin>F</margin> ...suppose one were to take away the bulk of the body, but keep the power of the light. Would the light still be anywhere? Or would it be equally throughout the whole exterior sphere? And you would no longer fix your thought on where it was previously situated. You would not seek from where or where; but concerning these things you would be in wonder. At the same time, looking at the spherical body, you would see the light itself thus. Since also in the case of the sun, you have [a point] from where the light shines throughout all the air, as you look at the whole body of the sun, and the light...

<margin>G</margin> ...likewise you see the light everywhere. Or is it divided? Clearly the "cuttings" <note>The Greek *apotomai* corresponds to the Latin *decisiones*, referring to the way shadows or obstructions seem to "cut" the light without actually dividing the source.</note> on that side... [show it] to have come from there, or show it to be, nor [to be] divided.

<column-break/>

And indeed, everywhere, if it were power alone—or if the sun were said to exist without a body—and were to provide light, it would not have begun <margin>here</margin> *here. Nor, again, could you say from where it came; rather, the light would immediately be everywhere, being the same in itself, not having begun, nor having a beginning from any specific place.

# THUS, since light is of the body, <margin>from where</margin> *one can state the cause of where it has come from—that is, the body in which it exists. But since the soul is immaterial, it requires no body; it exists prior to the nature of every body, established within itself. Or rather, needing no nature of such a kind, for that which has such a nature has no beginning from which it set out, neither from some place, nor by being in some body. How then could one part of its nature be here, and another there? For then it would already have a "from where" it set out. Or one must say that it "becomes" part of something, as if it were shared by the whole power <note>The "whole power" refers to the complete, undivided essence of the soul or the divine.</note>; it is shared by the whole, not followed by anything else, nor divided. For while a body possesses something, its "suffering" <note>In ancient philosophy, "suffering" or "passion" refers to being acted upon or undergoing a change, rather than feeling pain.</note> might occur by accident. In this <margin>divisible</margin> state, it would be called "passive" and "divisible." Since it is something of the body, it is like an affection or a form. *But that which belongs to no body, but instead wants the body to belong to it, must necessarily neither suffer the other affections of the body, nor be able to be divided in any way. For division is primarily an affection of the body, and it is by being a body that the body is divisible; where it is not a body, it is indivisible. For how could one divide that which has no magnitude? Nor does it come from that which has magnitude; that which possesses magnitude participates in the soul in an unmixed way. Or, if it were divided, it would participate in it by being divided, or it would increase in magnitude again. Therefore, when you speak of it being in many things, you are not saying it has become many; rather, you are attributing the affection of the many to that one thing, seeing it in many things at once. *That which is in them must be understood as not having become part of each of them, nor of the whole. *But that it is itself, and <margin>that which is in them / but it is itself</margin> being itself, it does not depart from itself. Nor, again, is it such a thing as the sensible universe <note>The "sensible universe" is the physical world we can see and touch.</note>, nor even any part of the universe; for it is not a quantity at all. How then could it be a quantity? To a body, it is "so much"; but to that which is not a body, but of another nature, one must say it should not be attached in any way. <margin>wherever / neither of such / stretching / the whole</margin> *Wherever it must be, it "becomes" so. Everywhere it then "becomes," or in the way that it is "here" and "there." For already, many times...

<column-break/>

A But if the sun itself were a certain power alone, separated from the body, and poured out light, it would not start from here or from any specific place at all, nor would you indicate from where it is sent: but it would be light everywhere, existing as one and the same, neither starting nor having a beginning from anywhere.

*Since the soul is prior to every corporeal thing, it rightly depends on nothing: therefore it requires no place, and is bound to none. Thus it relates itself indifferently and equally to every place: and for that reason, it is both everywhere in common and nowhere, unless a particular soul, through its own affection, occasionally applies itself to something specific. Chapter VIII.*

A **TRULY**, since light is something belonging to a body, you can easily say where it came from: since you are able to indicate where that body is located. But if something is devoid of matter and does not require a body—since it is naturally prior to every body and founded in itself, or rather, not requiring any such foundation—I say that this nature, being so endowed, has no beginning from which it might start, nor does it live within any place, nor exist as part of any B body. In what way then will you be able to say that "this part of it is here" and "that part of it is there"? For in that case, it would have a starting point and would exist under the law of another <note>original: "alieni iuris" - a legal term meaning "under the power of another," used here to mean being subject to physical constraints.</note>. It remains, therefore, to assert that if anything receives it, it receives that whole thing by the power of the whole. Nor does that thing, on that account, become either something else or something divisible. For it is proper for that which possesses a body—though often by accident—to C truly be "acted upon" <note>original: "pati" - to undergo change or influence.</note>. And for this very reason, it can be judged passive and divisible: since it is something of a body, either as an affection or as a species <note>original: "species" - the formal essence or "blueprint" of a thing.</note>. But that which belongs to no body, but exists entirely so that the body affects to be its own, it is necessary that it neither admits any other bodily affections into itself, nor, most importantly, can it be divided in any way. For division is an affection of the body, and primarily so insofar as it is a body. If, therefore, it is divisible insofar as it is a body, then clearly insofar as it is not a body, it exists as D entirely indivisible. For by what condition will you divide that which has no magnitude? If, therefore, that which has magnitude also participates in it in its own way, that which has no magnitude perceives it as undivided; otherwise, it would again possess magnitude. Therefore, when you say it is "one in many," you do not say it has become many, but rather you will see the affection of the many surrounding that one subject in many things simultaneously. But that "one in them" is to be understood in such a way that it has become neither one of them individually, nor all of them together; rather, it remains in its own right <note>original: "sui iuris" - independent or self-governing.</note> and exists as itself. And while it exists as itself, it is never lacking to itself, nor does it admit any defect. Nor, again, should it be thought that it is exactly as large as the sensible universe, let alone only as large as some part of the universe; for it is not "how much" in any way at all.

*In what way, therefore, will it be properly "so much" or "this much"? For such measurement belongs to the body; but to that which is not a body, but endowed with another nature, such measurement is in no way to be applied, since it is not even such a thing. Therefore, it is not to be placed anywhere: nor is it "here" and "there" in such a way, otherwise often...*

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul, like light from an immaterial source, is indivisible and not confined to a specific location. He explains that because the soul is "prior" to the body, it does not "suffer" the physical limitations of division or magnitude that material objects do.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into how the One or the Soul can be present in many things simultaneously without being divided into parts. It transitions into Chapter IX of the sixth Ennead, focusing on the "Anima Mundi" (World Soul) and its relationship to the physical universe.</meta>

PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

If, therefore, division according to location is appropriate—where one part of a thing is here and another part is there—it follows that for that which does not belong in a "somewhere," partition is in no way fitting. <note>Plotinus is arguing that because the Soul is immaterial and not bound by physical space, it cannot be "cut up" like physical matter.</note> For this reason, it is necessary that the thing remains indivisible within itself, even though many things may strive for it or even attain it. If, then, many things desire it, it is clear they seek the whole itself; thus, if they are able to attain it, they attain the whole as much as their strength allows. Wherefore, those things that participate in it must participate in such a way as if they do *not* participate, since it has emerged as the private property of none. For in this way, it remains a whole in itself, and simultaneously remains and occurs as a whole in those things in which it is perceived. Otherwise, unless it remains there as a whole, it would not be the thing itself, nor would the things themselves participate in the very thing they desire, but rather in something else which they did not seek at all.

---

*The primary Soul, while showing itself as a whole to many parts of the world, is neither multiplied into many souls—for these would differ in no way from one another—nor into parts, for it is indivisible; and otherwise, where its guidance recedes, it would fail, being utterly weakened. Chapter IX.*

*It fits its powers to the members of the world; but these powers are so essential and proper to it that they cannot be separated from it. Therefore, it is everywhere whole. Moreover, even if it only imparts images of its powers to the world, it is itself present as a whole, ruling its images everywhere. Finally, just as in ourselves, so in the world: unless the same life flourished everywhere, there would not be such a wonderful agreement <term>consensus</term> and shared feeling <term>compassio</term> of the parts among themselves and toward the whole. Whatever I say of the World Soul, understand it similarly of the Divine Intellect.* <note>Marsilio Ficino, the likely translator of this Latin edition, uses "Divine Intellect" to refer to the second hypostasis in Plotinus's system, the "Nous."</note>

---

THEREFORE, IF that one common thing were so divided into parts among many that any part were like the whole itself, it follows that there would be many "first principles," and each one would be a "first." Furthermore, by what means would these many first principles be distinguished, so that they are not all one and the same? For they will not be separated by their bodies; for it is impossible that they be the "species" <note>In this context, "species" refers to the outward form or appearance of a thing.</note> of bodies, since these too are similar to that first principle from which they flow. But if those things called "parts" in many things are actually of that common power, then firstly, each will no longer be a whole; secondly, in what way did they proceed from there as divided things, leaving the whole behind? For if they leave it, it is clear they must have left it somewhere while they proceeded elsewhere. Likewise, [one must ask] whether those powers which have been made here in this sensible place are still in that source or not. For if they are not there, it is absurd that the source should become common and weak—deprived, evidently, of the powers it previously held. It is again an absurd impossibility for powers to be severed from their essences. But if they are both in the source and elsewhere, they will be here either as wholes or as parts. If as parts, then those left behind there will surely be parts; but if as wholes, either the same ones that are there are also here, in no way divided—and thus the same thing will again be everywhere, in no way divided—or these powers are that whole which has now become many individually, of which any one would be a whole, and the powers would be similar to each other. And so, along with any essence, the power itself will be only one, namely accompanying the essence; the rest will be only powers. And yet it is impossible for either an essence to exist without power, or a power to exist without essence. For power there is substance and essence, or something even greater than essence. But if there are certain other powers here, as if smaller and thin, which flow from there—as if light from light, or a glow from a bright source—and certain essences are joined to such powers, lest perhaps a power exist apart from an essence: surely even in powers of this kind, which are entirely similar to one another, it is necessary that either the same be everywhere...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...it would be. If, therefore, division according to place [applies]... <margin>A</margin> ...the thing [being] here, and the [thing being] there, how could it have that which is after it? <note>This right-hand column contains the original Greek text from which the Latin on the left was translated.</note> Thus, it must be that it is under itself, in some way... those things striving for it. If indeed many things strive for it, clearly they strive for the whole... even if it is able to participate, it may participate in the whole again as much as it is able to participate. It is necessary for those participating in it to have it thus... as not having participated, and it being nothing of its own. For in this way it remains whole in itself, even if it is seen in those things... for if it were not whole, it would not be itself. And again, the participation would be of something else, and not of that which was desired...

<margin>A</margin> FOR indeed, if the part that has come to be in the whole were each itself, just as the first thing which has remained always each, there would be many first things, and each would be first. Then, what would separate these many firsts, as if all things were in one thing together? For surely not their bodies. For either of the bodies... it is not possible to see: for they are certain things, if indeed they are similar to that first thing from which [they come]. But if indeed... <margin>B</margin> those very things called parts in those things... first, is each still a whole? then, how did they come out, being cut off and left behind? For if they left it, clearly they left something... whether those powers are still in it which have been generated here in the sensible world, or... it is absurd for that to be diminished or to have become powerless, deprived of the powers which it previously had... and it is impossible to see the powers as being cut off from the essences. <margin>C</margin> If they are in [the source] and elsewhere, either as wholes or parts... they will be, but if as parts, those parts there also... if as wholes, either the same as there, and in... [not] divided. Or again * if the same is... which having been divided or become many... as many as the powers, and similar to one another, so that... each of the essence, or the power which... <margin>D</margin> is, or preserving the essence. But if others... only. And yet it is not possible, just as an essence without power, so a power without essence. For power there is the substance, the essence, greater than... but then, as lesser and faint powers from that one * as if light from light. Faint... and more visible and to be saved in these powers, lest power come to be without essence. First, indeed, even in such powers, it is necessary that they be altogether of the same kind as one another... or the same...

<summary>Plotinus explores the metaphysical paradox of how a single, indivisible "First Principle" or Soul can be present in many physical things without being divided itself. He concludes that the Soul is present as a whole everywhere, acting as a unifying force (Anima Mundi) that allows the universe to function as a single, sympathetic organism.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 652 regarding the nature of the Soul and its presence in the physical world. Plotinus is exploring the relationship between the "archetype" (the original spiritual form) and its "image" (the physical manifestation), specifically whether the Soul must be present in its entirety within the body or if it can be divided.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR.

...to be allowed to exist, or if not everywhere, then not everywhere at once as the same whole or divided? For example, in one and the same body—if it is in it, why is it not in the whole? If it is divided for each thing to infinity, and yet is the same whole, it becomes powerless through that division. Then, if different powers are in different parts, it will leave behind no shared consciousness <note>Greek: *synaisthēsin*; the capacity for the whole body to feel a single sensation</note>. Furthermore, if it is like a reflection <note>Greek: *indalma*</note> of something, like a weaker light being sent out, or if it is the thing itself, and generally everything that derives its existence from another as its image, it is not possible to exist if the source of that existence is cut off. If these powers that come from the source are cut off, they no longer belong to it. But if they belong both to the power and the source from which they arose, then the source must be there at the same time; thus, the whole will again be everywhere at once, or it will be a divided whole.

*Every intellectual soul is a distinct image and power of the first intellect, which is immovable in its essence, because true essence exists only from that which is immovable. Similarly, the rays of the sun would remain firm if the sun itself remained: everywhere there are things and powers so deeply dependent on the mind, or the primary soul, just like a reflection in a mirror. Therefore, the primary mind is everywhere, as is the primary soul. Furthermore, here and above and below, you will often note through Plotinus's words that there are many substances of minds and souls always distinct among themselves, although the union between them is wonderful. Chapter X.*

**IF SOMEONE** should object that it is not necessary for an image to depend continuously on its archetype for its survival, arguing that an image can exist even when the model from which it came is absent; or that heat remains in a warmed object even after the fire has been removed: first, as far as it pertains to the archetype and the image, we respond. If someone brings up a statue of Phidias <note>A famous ancient Greek sculptor</note> or a painting, we say that the archetype itself did not make the image, but rather the painter or sculptor produced it; and yet, the work is not an image of the creator themselves. Even if a painter chose to paint himself, it is not the painter's body or the form that the painting imitates that is doing the painting; nor should we think it is the painter, but rather a certain arrangement <margin>* of the colors</margin> of the colors that creates such an image. But the likeness of an image is not properly understood in that way; it is more like the images found in water, mirrors, or shadows. In those cases, a likeness properly exists because of the prior thing and is produced <margin>* it is made from it</margin> from it; it cannot exist separately once it is cut off from its source. In this way, indeed, we should correctly think that the weaker powers are produced by the more excellent and superior ones. Furthermore, regarding the objection about fire, we respond that heat is not the "image" of fire, unless one argues that fire is actually present within the heat. For if one affirms that, the heat is not being separated from the fire; and indeed, even if not suddenly, the warmed body eventually <margin>* it cools</margin> cools after the fire has departed. But if some should say that these powers infused into the universe from the intelligible world <note>The realm of pure thought and forms, as opposed to the physical world</note> are eventually extinguished, they would first have to conclude that only one thing is immortal, and they would judge souls and the intellect to be mortal. Moreover, they would be wrongly suggesting that things made from an immovable essence can simply "flow away," even though if the sun were fixed in place, it would pour the same light into the same locations. If someone objects that it is not the exact same light, they might easily persuade themselves that the body of the sun itself is continually flowing away. But the fact that the things of that world are immortal has been confirmed elsewhere through many arguments.

<column-break/>

...to be present in, or if not everywhere simply, at least passim <note>here and there</note> the same whole and not divided, as if in one certain and the same body. If however this is so, why not in the whole universe besides? But if it happens that anything can be divided infinitely, it will no longer consist of the whole itself, but through partition it will turn into some potentiality. Next, since one power exists in different parts and another in others, no mutual communion of sensing will be left. Finally, if it is like the image of another or like a weaker light separated from that from which it comes, it is no longer; and everything that depends on another in this way, so as to be its image, cannot exist without it: rightly, then, these powers proceeding from that source cannot exist where they are separated from it. But if this is the case, wherever these are, there at the same time is that from which they are generated. For which reason, that whole will again be everywhere at once, in no way divided.

If someone should object that it is not necessary for an image to depend continuously on its exemplar, finding that an image remains even when the example from which it stood has been removed; likewise that heat remains in a warmed thing when the fire is absent: first indeed, as far as the exemplar and the image are concerned, we respond. If someone brings up an image made by a painter, the exemplar itself did not make the image, but the painter rather produced it, and yet it is not an image of the painter himself: even if someone chose to paint himself: for it is not the body of the painter, nor the form which the painting there imitates, that properly paints: nor should we think the painter, but such a certain arrangement of colors makes such an image. But neither is the likeness and production of an image properly introduced here: such as is rather in water, mirrors, and shadows. Where truly a certain likeness properly underlies the prior thing, and is made by it: nor can it exist separately when it is properly made from it. In this way, indeed, they will rightly think that the weaker powers are also made from the more excellent and superior ones. Furthermore, to that which was objected regarding fire, we respond that heat is not the image of fire, unless one perhaps says that fire is also in the heat. For if he affirmed that, he would not separate the heat from the fire: now truly, even if not suddenly, yet a little later the heated body cools, the fire having departed from there. But if any should say that these powers infused into this universe from the intelligible world are extinguished: first indeed, they will think that only one thing is immortal. They will judge souls and the intellect to be mortal. Moreover, they will not rightly concede that things made from an immovable essence flow: although if the sun itself were imagined to be fixed, it would pour the same light into the same places. But if someone objects that it does not pour exactly the same light, he can easily persuade himself from this very thing that the body of the sun continually flows. But that those things from the [intelligible] world are immortal has been confirmed elsewhere from many arguments.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Soul’s omnipresence. Having previously established that the Soul is not divided like a physical body, Plotinus now explores how the "Intelligible" (the realm of pure thought and being) can be present everywhere at once without being diluted, using the analogy of light and sound.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

<page-num>654</page-num>

*Our whole soul is present with all its powers in every individual member of the body, even though different members receive different powers or receive them in varying degrees. Similarly, the Soul of the World and the Divine Mind relate to the various parts of the universe. Chapter XI.*

*Physical things are often separated from one another by external boundaries. However, incorporeal things <note>Non-physical realities like thoughts, souls, or mathematical truths</note>, although they are not separated by external boundaries, are distinguished by their internal properties. In this way, ideas are distinguished from other ideas in the mind, one science from another, the intellectual soul from the mind, minds from other minds, and souls from other souls. It is not easy for one body to merge with another body, but it is easy for a body to be joined to a soul; it is easier still for a soul to join a soul, and easiest of all for minds to join with minds. Indeed, the union of the mind with light is easier than the union of light with a transparent object. This latter union is easier than that of one quality with another or with a body; and if that is easy, it is far easier than the interaction of physical bodies with one another.*

---

<margin>A</margin> MOREOVER, if the intelligible universe <note>The "intelligible" refers to the realm of pure Being and Mind, which Plotinus views as the true reality behind the physical world</note> itself is everywhere as a whole, why do not all things receive that whole intelligible reality? Furthermore, how is it that in the intelligible order one thing is first, another second, and others follow in sequence? Truly, those things that are better prepared to receive it are judged to be more "present" to it. Indeed, one must judge that Being itself exists everywhere by its very nature, never failing itself; but whatever is capable of being present to it becomes present, and it is present to it only as far as that thing is able—not in a spatial sense, but in the way a transparent body is present to light. For in a murky or opaque body, we must assume the participation happens differently. <margin>B</margin> Furthermore, when first, second, and third ranks are arranged there, it is not by steps of physical space, but by order, power, and gradual differences. For nothing prevents things that differ from being in the same place at once—just as the soul, the intellect, and all the sciences (both greater and lesser) exist together. For instance, regarding an apple: the eye sees the color, while the sense of smell perceives the sweetness of the odor. <margin>C</margin> Likewise, another sense there perceives another quality, where nonetheless all these qualities exist together and are not actually separated from one another. But then, will that intelligible realm be entirely varied and manifold? Certainly it is varied, yet in such a way that it remains simple—the "One-Many." For Reason <note>Latin: *Ratio*; Greek: *Logos*</note> is both one and many at the same time. Furthermore, all Being is one; for that which becomes "other" has this within itself, and otherness itself is a part of it. For otherness does not belong to non-being. <margin>D</margin> Being itself consists in such a way that the One is not separated from it; for wherever Being is, its Unity is also present to it, and the One-Being in turn consists within itself. For it is possible for that which is distinguished in some rational way to nonetheless exist and be present simultaneously. However, sensible things <note>Physical things perceived by the senses</note> are present to intelligible things in one way (whichever are present and to whatever they approach), while intelligible things are present to one another in another way. For a body approaches the soul in one way, while knowledge clings to that same soul in another. Indeed, one science exists together with another science in that same way. But a body approaches another body in a manner quite different from these.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> BUT why, if the whole is everywhere, do not all things participate in the Intelligible? Is it because the "first" is there, but the rest to a lesser degree? We should not think it is the Intelligible that is absent, but rather that the recipient receives it according to its own aptitude. Being is everywhere present to Being, never failing itself. But that which is capable of being present is present to it; it is present to it in whatever degree it is able. <margin>B</margin> For it is present just as light is to the air, though to air that is clouded, the participation is different. And the first, second, or third ranks are by order, power, or difference, not by locations. For nothing prevents different things from being together, such as the soul and the mind, and the sciences, both greater and lesser; since even in the same object, the eye sees color, while the sense of smell perceives the scent, and another sense perceives other things. <margin>C</margin> They are not all apart, but exist together. Is that realm then varied and many? Or is the varied also simple? And are the many also one? For the Reason-Principle <note>Greek: *Logos*</note> is one and many. And so is Being. For it is other to itself. * Or rather, its "otherness" exists within it, since it does not belong to non-being. Being exists by not being divided. And so Being is already present. And the same exists in the One, being in itself. It is possible to be present without being separate, * just as sensible things <margin>D</margin> are present to the Intelligible, in whatever way they are present. Or they are present in one way, and the Intelligible things are present to each other in another. For a body is in the soul in one way, and science is in the soul in another. Or one science will be in another science in the same place. And a body is near another body in a way different from these.

---

*Just as many ears hear the same voice undivided, but sounding as a whole everywhere: so many bodies throughout the world receive life as a whole everywhere at once from the soul, and many members in us receive life similarly from our soul. Chapter [XII].*

*To say that the bodies of the world are first fit to receive something vital from the Soul of the World does not prevent them from having their own souls in the meantime, because prepared bodies receive these, and the souls in turn vivify the bodies. The "World of Life" mentioned here signifies the gathering and mutual communion of all intellectual souls into one. Any intellectual soul is always, according to its whole substance, simultaneously in the World of Life and in the corporeal world, although it does not exercise all its powers here. And because it always exists excellently as a whole there, and because it exists here and there simultaneously by its essence: therefore, it is not the soul that seems to approach the body, but the body that approaches the soul, specifically through a certain suitability and formative property toward it.*

---

<margin>A</margin> OFTEN a voice sounds through the air, and a speech is contained within that voice. A present ear receives and perceives it, especially in a quiet region. And if another ear is placed in another part of that same region, the voice and the speech reach it similarly; but in truth, the ear reaches toward the speech and the voice.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> JUST as when a voice exists in the air, often there is also a word <note>Greek: *logos*</note> within that voice. The ear receives it and perceives it, and if you were to place it anywhere in silence and stillness, the word or the voice would come to it. Or rather, the ear comes toward the...

# FOURTH BOOK

And many eyes look toward the same object, and everyone is filled with the sight; and that which lies in a distinct spectacle—where one is an eye, and another looks on—is what provides the soul with its vital power. <note>original: "πικρὴ" — The OCR here likely misreads the Greek for 'bitter' or 'sharp', but in the context of Plotinus, he is discussing the "sting" or "impact" of perception on the soul.</note> And it is one thing and another from the same source. And the voice is everywhere in the air, a single thing distributed. But it is entirely whole everywhere. And as for sight: if the air, having been affected, should hold the form, it holds it undivided. For wherever the sight is placed, it holds the form there. But while common opinion concedes this, they do not concede it for the Soul, namely that participation in the one comes from that same one. But in the case of the voice, it is more evident: how the whole form is in the entire air. For otherwise, not everyone would hear the same thing unless the spoken word <term>Logos</term> <note>Logos here refers to the rational content or 'meaning' behind the spoken sound</note> were whole in every place, and every hearing received the whole equally. If, however, even here the whole voice were not spread through the whole air—such that one part of it were with one part of the air and another with another—why should we disbelieve that the Soul is not laid down as one thing being divided, but is present everywhere as itself? For it is present everywhere as a whole, or else it is divided. If it were in bodies like tastes, it would have an analogy to the voice already in the air... <note>Plotinus argues that the Soul doesn't get "cut up" when it enters different bodies, just as a voice doesn't get cut up when many people hear it.</note>

<margin>*whole</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Many eyes also are directed toward the same spectacle, from which all are filled with the vision; although that spectacle is located in a certain place of its own. Truly, a diverse perception occurs there, because this is an ear, but that is an eye. By a similar reasoning, whatever is able to receive the soul receives it, and one after another receives from the same source. Moreover, the voice is everywhere through the air, one and not divided, but whole everywhere. Furthermore, if the air, as if receiving the form of the thing to be seen, <margin>B</margin> possesses it similarly undivided: for wherever sight is applied, it receives the form there. But not every opinion admits this. Therefore, let it be said so that it may be confirmed that participation in many is fulfilled from one and the same. But in the case of the voice, what we seek is more manifest: namely, that in a certain total air, and in any part of it, the form is whole. For not everyone would hear the same thing unless the speech expressed through the voice existed entirely everywhere, and every hearing drew in the whole similarly. <margin>C</margin> Accordingly, if the whole voice is not so extended through the whole air that this part of it is joined with this part of the air, and that part is distributed with another, why should it now be less believed that the one soul is indeed infused in all things, yet not extended with the extension of things, nor divided with the division of things, but wherever it is present, it is present as a whole, and is in any part of the universe without being distributed into parts? Now, when it is poured through bodies, in whatever way it approaches, it has a certain proportional likeness with that voice which is already expressed through the air. <margin>D</margin> While it stands above bodies, it seems to have a certain likeness with the one who speaks. Even though it is insinuated into the body, it does not even then cease to hold the role of the speaker, who surely both possesses the voice and hands it over. But as far as the voice is concerned, this is well known to those to whom it was introduced for explanation, for it has some likeness. <margin>E</margin> However, as far as the soul is concerned, being of a different nature, it must be understood in such a way that there is not one soul in bodies and another in itself; rather, the whole appears both in itself and again in many. And yet, another thing meanwhile approaches to receive the soul; and this itself also receives from the hidden source, which certainly also existed in others. For the matter was not so prepared that a part of the soul placed here would approach it; <margin>F</margin> but this very thing which is said to approach was in the universe, namely in itself, and it exists in itself, although it may seem to descend here. For in what way would it come? If therefore it did not "approach" in a physical sense, but the soul now appeared as present—nor was it present in such a way that it waited for something that would participate in it—it is clear that the soul, existing in itself, is also present to the body. But if, existing in itself, it is present to this body, then this body has rightly "approached" it. If this be so, it follows that since this body was outside that which so exists, it has approached that very thing which so exists, and has been received into the world of life. <margin>G</margin> But the world of life <note>The "World of Life" or *Mundus Vitae* is Ficino's Latin term for the Intelligible realm where all life originates</note> itself consists in itself, and is thus whole in itself, so that it is not distributed into any mass of its own. For there is no mass <note>Mass or *moles* refers to physical, bulky matter that takes up space</note> there. Indeed, even that which has moved there did not move into a mass. It has therefore become a participant of it, not indeed of some part, but of the whole. And if anything should ever ascend to such a world, it will similarly become a participant of the whole. Wherefore, if it be said that the Soul is in these things, it similarly consists as a whole in any part of the universe. Therefore, the same soul is one in number everywhere, not divided, but entirely whole and present.

<summary>Plotinus explains that the Soul is present in the physical world without being divided, using the analogy of a voice that can be heard in its entirety by many people simultaneously. He concludes that the physical body "approaches" the Soul, rather than the Soul moving into or being cut up by the body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of how the Soul and the "Intelligible" (the realm of pure thought and being) exist within the physical world. ### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

*Our soul is present as a whole and with all its powers to any limb, although different limbs receive different powers from it, some more and some less: the Soul of the World and the Divine Mind relate to the parts of the world in a similar way. Chapter XI.*

*Bodily things are often distant from one another by their external boundaries: but incorporeal things, although they are not distant by external boundaries, are distinguished by their innermost properties: thus ideas are distinguished from ideas in the mind, sciences from sciences in the intellectual soul, the mind from the soul, minds from minds, and souls from souls. It is not easy for a body to join with another body, but it is easy for a body to join with a soul; it is easier for a soul to join with a soul, and easiest of all for minds to join with the Mind. Indeed, union with light is easier than the union of light with a transparent object. And this is easier than the union of a quality with a quality or with a body: and that is easier than the physical interaction between bodies.*

---

MOREOVER, if the <term>Intelligible</term> <note>The "Intelligible" refers to the realm of pure reality, forms, and thought, which Plotinus believes is more real than the physical world.</note> universe itself is everywhere a whole, why do not all things receive the whole of that Intelligible? Likewise, how in the Intelligible order is one thing first, another second, and others following in sequence? But surely those things that are more "ready" to receive it are judged to be more present to it: indeed, one must judge that Being itself exists everywhere by its very nature, never failing itself. Whatever is capable of being present becomes present to it, and to the extent that it has the power, it is present to it—not by location, but in the way a transparent body is present to light. For in a turbid or opaque body, we must think the participation happens differently. Furthermore, when first, second, and third things are arranged there, it is not by steps of location, but they must be assigned according to order, power, and gradual differences. For nothing prevents things that differ from being together at the same time: just as the soul contains the intellect, all sciences, both greater and lesser. For even regarding an apple, the eye sees the color, while the sense of smell perceives the sweetness of the odor: and another sense perceives another quality in the same place, where all are nevertheless together and not actually separated from each other. But will not that Intelligible then be entirely varied and manifold? Surely it is varied, but in such a way that it is also simple, and "one-many." For it is <term>Reason</term> <note>original: "Ratio" / "Logos" — the organizing principle of the universe.</note> which is at once one and very many. Then truly every being is one: for the fact that it becomes "other" it has from itself, and that very "otherness" is something belonging to it. For it does not belong to non-being, and Being itself consists in such a way that the "One" is not disjoined from it; namely, wherever there is Being, its "One" is present to it; and the "One Being" in turn consists in itself. For it is possible that what is distinguished by some reason may yet exist and be present simultaneously. However, sensible things are present to Intelligible things in one way—whichever are present and to which they approach—and Intelligible things are present to one another in another way. For a body approaches a soul in one way, but knowledge clings to that same soul in another. And knowledge is present to knowledge in the same way, existing simultaneously. But a body approaches another body in a different way than these.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But why, if the whole is everywhere, did not all things receive a share of the Intelligible? Or is it that one thing is first there, and another is after it? We must consider that presence is based on the fitness of the receiver. And Being is everywhere as Being, not deserting itself, but that which is able to be present is present to it as far as it is able, according to its own nature.
<margin>B</margin> It is present as light is to a transparent medium; but to that which is clouded, the participation is different. And the first, second, and third ranks are by order and power and differences, not by places. For nothing prevents different things from being together, such as the soul and the mind, and all those things beneath them. Since even in the same object, the eye sees color, the smell perceives the scent, and another sense perceives another quality,
<margin>C</margin> not as if all were separated. But that [the Intelligible] is varied, yet it is varied and simple, and the "many" are in it. For it is one <term>Logos</term> and many. And Being is one. For where it is "other" than itself, * there otherness itself is. For it is not of non-being. And where Being is, it is with the One, not separated. And wherever Being may be, there also is the same One. And the One Being is again by itself. It is possible to be present without being apart * in a different way than sensible things are present to Intelligible things, as many of them as are present. And to others
<margin>D</margin> who are there, the Intelligible things are present to themselves in another way: since a body is in a soul in one way, and knowledge is in a soul in another: and knowledge is to knowledge in the same way * but these things are in a body in yet another way.

---

*Just as many ears hear the same voice, not divided, but sounding as a whole everywhere: so many bodies of the world everywhere receive the life of the World Soul as a whole simultaneously, and many members in us similarly receive life from our soul. Chapter XII.*

*To say that the bodies of the world, when they are first fit to receive something vital from the World Soul, do not in the meantime have their own souls from afar, because they receive these as they are prepared, and the souls in turn vivify those bodies. The "World of Life" named here signifies the gathering and mutual communion of all intellectual souls into one. Any intellectual soul is always according to its whole substance in the World of Life and in the corporeal world simultaneously, although it exercises its powers here. And because it always exists excellently as a whole even then: and since it exists through its essence here and there simultaneously: therefore it does not seem to approach the body, but the body seems to approach it, namely by a certain accommodation and formable property toward the soul.*

---
