<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 652 regarding the nature of the Intelligible and how the Soul participates in the physical world. Plotinus is moving into a famous series of analogies—sight and sound—to explain how a single, indivisible unity (the Soul) can be present in many different things simultaneously without being divided into parts.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR.

And many eyes look toward the same sight, and everyone participates in the same viewing; and if the sight is situated in a specific spot, wherever an eye is, it sees it, provided it is something capable of having a soul. But it is one thing and another from the same source. Therefore, the voice is everywhere in the air—the one voice is not divided, but is one whole everywhere. Or consider sight: if the air, being affected, should hold the form, it holds it in an undivided way. For wherever sight is placed, it takes the form there. Indeed, every opinion concedes this. But in truth, it is not even for that reason, but because the sharing comes from the same source. This is even more evident in the case of the voice: the whole <term>Form</term> <note>original: "εἶδός" (eidos). In Neoplatonism, "Form" refers to the essential nature or "blueprint" of a thing that exists in the divine mind.</note> is in the whole air. For everyone hears the same thing, not in different places, since the spoken word is a whole. And every hearing receives the whole similarly. But if even here the whole voice is not stretched out through the whole air so that one part of it is in one part of the air and another part is elsewhere, but rather it is poured out—<gloss>how then</gloss> could it be divided? Why should we disbelieve that the soul, without being divided, is shared? But is it present everywhere, as it was before? Furthermore, is the whole of it everywhere, or is it divided? Or, having come into bodies, does it become analogous to the voice already in the air? The voice remains a voice concerning bodies, and for the one about to speak, the voice comes to be in the body; or as if exhausted, the things according to the speaker are whoever is speaking. And it holds the voice, if it gives it; some things in this voice might have it in one way, but how they relate to one another does not even have a similarity in some respects. But concerning the soul, being of the other nature, or receiving it as if it were of itself, one part is in the body, and the other is in itself; but it is a whole in itself. Or it is imagined in many again. Or another thing came to those receiving a soul. Hidden again, or by having that which was one in others. Or it preceded so that a part of it, lying here, came to there; but that which is said to "come" is in everything, in itself, in itself; and it seems to have come here. For how could it have <margin>or not</margin> come, <insert>or</insert> not come, to that which was already present, <insert>or</insert> being present or by waiting for that which would receive it? It shows that as much as comes from itself is present to the form; and as much as is of itself is present to this; it came to itself. If this is so, being outside of that which truly exists, it came to that which truly exists, and it came to be in the world of life. And the world of life exists in itself. For everything that is in itself is not intercepted into its own mass. For there is no mass there. That which has come there has not come into a mass. It has shared in it, then, not as a part of a whole. But even if another should come into such a <margin>* whole</margin> world, it will share in the * whole of it; similarly, then, if that is said to be in these as a whole, it will be in each and every one, and thus everywhere the same, one in number, not divided, but existing as a whole.

<column-break/>

A Many eyes are also directed toward the same spectacle, by which all are filled with the vision: although that spectacle is situated in its own particular place. A different perception happens there, because this is an ear, while that is an eye. By a similar reasoning, whatever can receive the soul receives it, and one thing after another receives from the same source. Moreover, the voice is everywhere through the air; it is one, not divided, but everywhere a whole. Furthermore, if the air, as if experiencing the thing to be seen, receives the form, B it holds it similarly undivided: for wherever sight is applied, it receives the form there. But not every opinion admits this. Therefore, let it be said so that it may be confirmed that participation in many is fulfilled by one and the same thing. But in the voice, what we seek is more manifest: namely, that in the whole of the air, and in any part of it, the species is whole. For not everyone hears the same thing unless the speech expressed through the voice existed entirely everywhere, and every sense of hearing C drew it in similarly as a whole. Therefore, if the whole voice is not spread through the whole air in such a way that this part of it is joined with this part of the air, while that part is distributed with another, why then should it be less believable that one soul is infused in all things? It is indeed infused, yet it is not extended by the extension of things, nor divided by the division of things; but wherever it is present, it is present as a whole, and it exists in any part of the universe without being distributed into parts. Now indeed, when it is poured through bodies, in whatever way it D approaches, it has a certain proportional similarity with that voice which is already expressed through the air. While it stands above bodies, it seems to have a certain similarity with a speaker and also with that which is called. Although it is introduced into the body, it does not even thus cease to hold the role of the speaker: who surely, while speaking, both has the voice and transmits it. But as far as the voice is concerned, it is not entirely the same as those things for the sake of which it was introduced to explain to us, yet it has some similarity. As far as E pertains to the soul, as something of a different nature, it must be understood in such a way that there is not one soul in bodies and another rather in itself: but the whole appears both in itself and in many again. And yet again, something else meanwhile approaches to receive the soul: which itself also receives from a hidden source, which certainly existed in others as well. For the matter is not prepared such that a part of the soul placed here would approach this; but this very thing which F is said to "approach" was in the universe, namely in itself, and it exists in itself: although it seems to descend here. For in what way would it come? If therefore it did not approach, the soul appeared as now present, yet not so present that it waited for something to participate in it. It is clear, of course, that the soul, existing in itself, is also present to the body; but if, existing in itself, it is present to this, it has rightly approached itself. If this is so, it follows that since this was outside that which thus exists, it approached that very thing which so G exists, being received into the world of life itself. The world of life itself consists in itself, and thus the universe is in itself, such that it is not distributed into any mass of its own. For there is no mass there. Now indeed, even that which betook itself there did not betake itself into a mass. It turned out to be a participant of it, then—not of some part, but of the whole. And if anything else should ascend to a world of this kind, it will similarly turn out to be a participant of the whole. Wherefore, if that is said to be in these, it similarly consists as a whole in any part of the universe. Therefore, the same thing, one in number, is present everywhere, not divided, but entirely whole.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of how the spiritual realm—the "world of life" and intellect—interacts with the physical world of space and matter. Having used the analogies of light and sound on the previous page to show how one thing can be in many places, he now turns to a more logical, geometric argument about why the Soul cannot have "size" or "extension" like a physical body does.</meta>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK VI.

*What is the extension of quantity in the corporeal <note>Meaning "physical" or "body-like."</note> world, is power and abundance in the world of life. And when we say life is "here" and "there," we must not imagine any local or physical condition; rather, whatever is anywhere, we must find it present there as a whole and entire. For through that indivisible vigor—acting like a kind of glue—all things scattered throughout the world are held together. Such a vigor, which commands all things, is not some tiny point; for life itself is no less than the whole.*

->Chapter XIII.<-

<margin>A</margin> Where, then, does this extension come from, which spreads through the whole heaven and all living creatures? Surely that world of life is not itself extended. Our senses—upon which we rely and which make us slow to believe these arguments—tell us that a thing is "here" or "there." But Reason dictates that this very "here and there" does not mean that divine nature is stretched out across space. Instead, it means that whatever is extended in space participates in that sublime nature, even though the nature itself suffers no distance or separation within itself. <margin>B</margin> If something participates in something else, it is clear that it does not participate in itself; otherwise, it would not be a "participant," but would be the thing itself. Therefore, a body that participates in something must not be participating in another body, for it already possesses a bodily nature. Thus, a body will not participate in "Body," nor will magnitude <note>Magnitude refers to size or physical volume.</note> participate in "Magnitude," for it already has it. Furthermore, if something that is already large receives an addition of magnitude, it does not truly "participate" in magnitude for that reason; <margin>C</margin> for a <term>two-cubit</term> <note>A cubit was an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.</note> object does not become a three-cubit object by Magnitude itself growing, but rather the subject, possessing one quantity, then takes on another; otherwise, the number two would simply become the number three. If, therefore, that which is dispersed and extended into a mass of quantity participates in some other kind of thing, that thing which it participates in must be neither dispersed nor extended, nor possess any quantity at all. For this reason, that which must be present as a whole everywhere must be present in an indivisible way. <margin>D</margin> Nor is it "indivisible" in the sense of being "small" (like a tiny particle). For if it were small, it would still be divisible and would not fit the whole universe. Nor, as a physical mass grows, would this nature be able to spread itself throughout; nor is it like a mathematical point. A mass is not a single point, but contains infinite points. Therefore, if the soul were like a point, there would have to be infinite souls to fill the mass. Thus, the mass does not have the soul as a continuous physical part, but possesses it entirely through every one of its parts.

---

*Besides the one and primary World Soul, there must be individual souls that are more excellent, distinguished from one another not by external or local boundaries, but by their own internal properties. Chapter XIV. These we call "lives," acting as colleagues working together with the Mind—the queen and leader of the World Soul. They are more united with each other at the "top," where through their intellectual nature they rest upon the intelligible world <note>The realm of pure thought and forms, above the physical world.</note> as divine things, like lines meeting at a center. However, they become more distinct from one another as they unfold their reason; and soon, through the vegetative power <note>The "vegetative" power is the lowest level of soul, responsible for basic growth and life.</note> that governs them, they take on different bodies in this world of life—which is always everywhere as a whole with all its souls—receiving them in various ways; just as various bodies are perceived daily by the World Soul, and as different limbs, powers, and actions are perceived by any individual soul according to its differences.*

<margin>A</margin> But if the same soul is vigorous everywhere, how is there an individual soul for each person? And why is this soul good, while that one is evil? Perhaps it is because each soul is sufficient unto itself, yet also contains all souls and all intellects. For in that realm, there is the "One" which is also infinite, where all things exist together; and yet it holds each thing distinctly, but not separated apart—otherwise, how could it be infinite? Or one might say it this way: that nature possesses all things at once—every life, every soul, every m... <meta>Catchword: mind,</meta>

<column-break/>

From where, then, does extension come—that which is in the heavens and in living things? Or is it not extended? Or is it that by paying attention to the senses, we disbelieve those who say it is "here" and "there"? But Reason says it is not extended "here" and "there," but rather that everything extended participates in it, while it remains without interval <note>original: "ἀδιάστατός" (adiastatos). In Neoplatonism, this refers to being non-spatial or without physical dimensions.</note>. If, then, something participates in something, it is clear that in changing toward it, it has partaken; but the extended thing itself does not partake of something in the way of becoming it. For it already has it. Body will not partake of Body. Nor, then, will magnitude partake of magnitude. For it already has it. Or if it should take on magnitude in addition to what it has, that magnitude would be what it partakes in. For either a two-cubit thing becomes three, but the underlying subject having one, now has another. Otherwise, two would be three. If then that which is dissolved and extended into such a size becomes another thing, or entirely of another kind, it is necessary that what it partakes in is neither divided nor extended nor entirely a "quantity" of any sort. It is necessary, therefore, that the thing partaken in itself is present everywhere indivisibly. But if it were indivisible in the sense of being "small," it would be no less divisible. And it would not fit all things. Or if, as something grows, the same thing stays—but if it is there as a point? If so, the mass would be a point; but there are infinite points in it. So it would not be that all things are points, even if they were to exist. And so they would not be touching. If then the mass holds it as a whole, it will hold it according to all its parts.

IS IT THEN the case that if each soul is its own, how is one good and another evil? It is because in each it holds all souls, and intellects, and it is One and infinite itself at once. And it holds each as distinct, yet not distinguished separately. For how would it be infinite? Or as it might be said, it holds all life together, and all soul, and all intellect.

He explains that individual souls are both unified in the divine intellect and distinct in their earthly expression.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the Soul and Intellect—the higher realities—relate to the physical world. The previous page established that the Soul is not "spread out" like a physical object but is present everywhere as a whole. This page moves into the nature of human identity: whether we are our physical bodies or our eternal souls.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR.

<margin>A</margin> Every one of these things is distinguished by its own specific boundaries. For this reason, that higher realm must possess not just one life, but an infinite life, and yet a life that is truly one. <note>original: "ἄπειρον... ζωὴν" / "vitam infinitam"</note> It is "one" because it has gathered all lives together into a single point, starting from the One and remaining where it began—or rather, it has always existed in this way. In that realm, nothing is "becoming" or being made; everything already is. <margin>B</margin> Nothing there is divided, though it may appear divided to those who receive it. What exists there is that which has been from the very beginning. However, that which is "becoming" <note>Referring to the physical world of change.</note> draws near to that higher realm, appears to be connected to it, and depends upon it.

But what about us? Who are we ourselves? Are we that eternal reality, or are we the thing that "draws near" and is created in time? Before this physical birth took place, we existed there as different kinds of human beings—as <margin>C</margin> pure souls and as Intellect <note>original: "νοῦς" / "intellectus" - the divine, intuitive part of the mind.</note> connected to the whole of essence. We were parts of the Intelligible world <note>The realm of perfect Forms or Ideas.</note>, not walled off or cut away, but belonging to the whole. Even now, we are not truly cut off. But now, a "second man" has approached that eternal human being, wanting to be something else. Finding us (for we were not outside the universe), this new self has wrapped itself around us and attached itself to that original human which each of us truly was then. <margin>D</margin> It is as if there were one single voice and one single speech, and different people from different places turned their ears to hear and receive it. Each person's hearing becomes an "active" event, because the voice is present and acting upon them. Thus, we have become a "composite" of both. We are no longer just that original being we were before; we are also this second self we have added, while the original part remains quiet, present in a different way.

<column-break/>

> *If the entire world of life—that is, the assembly of intellectual souls—breathes together with the Primary Mind and the Primary Soul, and is always a whole and indivisible everywhere, it follows that it does not approach bodies by moving through space, but through a certain effect. Likewise, bodies do not approach it except through a certain readiness to be formed. It is much like fire approaching nearby sulfur, or light reaching a transparent object. Chapter XV.*
> *Bodies affected in certain ways receive vital powers from the Soul of the World. Our own nature, having been prepared in this way and having obtained such powers, is further exposed to this world. Thus, the rational soul, which is more specifically our own, inspires a specific life into us. In this life, disturbances arise which did not exist in the rational soul before, and do not primarily belong to it.*

---

<margin>A</margin> **B**ut in what way did this "access" occur? Or why do we say it "approached"? It is because there was a "suitability" <note>original: "ἐπιτηδειότης" / "aptitudo" - a Neoplatonic concept where matter must be "ready" or "tuned" to receive a higher form.</note> present in the body, and so it received that to which it was exposed. The body was disposed to receive a soul, but it does not receive the *entire* soul; even though the whole soul is present, it is not "present" to the body in its entirety. Just as other animals and plants only take in as much as they are able to receive. Consider the sound of a voice carrying a message: <margin>B</margin> some listeners perceive the meaning of the speech along with the sound, while others perceive only the sound and the vibration of the air. 

When life is produced, the soul that is present to the body comes from the true Being of souls, through which it is linked to the whole of Reality. Since the body is neither a void nor entirely without a share of soul (for it previously lay in a state that was not entirely soulless), it becomes even more connected as it draws near through this "suitability." It is no longer just a body, but a living body, <margin>C</margin> and by this "neighborhood" it enjoys a certain trace of the soul. It does not take a "piece" of the soul, but rather a certain power or influence flows from the soul into it.

<summary>Plotinus explains that humans have a dual nature: an eternal, "pure soul" that exists in the divine realm, and a temporal "added" self that joins with the physical body when it becomes "suitable" to receive life. He uses the analogy of many people hearing one voice to show how the soul can be both one and many.</summary>
<keywords>human identity, dual nature, suitability, emanation, Intelligible world, Soul of the World, rational soul, Neoplatonism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the human self, exploring how the higher, eternal soul interacts with the physical body. It addresses the tension between our rational mind and our bodily desires, using the metaphor of a city council versus a rowdy mob.</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

A certain warming or illumination <note>original: "calefactio... illustratio" / "θερμασίᾳ... ἔλλαμψις"</note> arises within the body, giving birth to desires, pleasures, and pains. This body of the animal, once formed, was not something foreign to the soul. The soul, for its part, remained quiet and divine, according to its own nature and habit, staying centered within itself. However, the body—troubled by its own inherent weakness, fluctuating by its nature, and buffeted by external blows—first raised a clamor that reached the common life of the animal and passed its disturbance into the whole. It is like when a senate <note>original: "senatu" / "ἐκκλησίᾳ δημογερόντων"</note> is sitting and deliberating in a quiet state of mind, but an unruly mob, driven by hunger or other complaints, suddenly throws the entire assembly into a chaotic uproar.

<margin>B</margin>
Whenever reason <note>original: "ratio" / "λόγος"</note> from a wise ruler reaches such people while they are quiet, the crowd is brought into a certain order, and the "worse" element in the city does not prevail. Otherwise, the worse part wins out because the "better" element is inactive—specifically when the rowdy mob is unable to receive the guidance from above. This is what constitutes the wickedness of a city or an assembly.

<margin>C</margin>
This is also the depravity of a human being: having within themselves a "mob" of pleasures, lusts, and fears that overpower the rest. This happens when a person gives in to such a "people" within themselves. But another type of person reduces this crowd to slavery and flees back to that higher self they once were, living according to that nature; they are truly themselves, while treating the body as something foreign and different, granting it only what is necessary.

<margin>D</margin>
Nor is there a lack of those who live a life that is sometimes one way and sometimes another—a mixture of their own good and evil traits.

*When we hear that our soul "descends" or "ascends," we should not think of it as literally changing places. To "descend" means to breathe life into the body and to be affected by it; to "ascend" is the opposite: to neither breathe life into it nor be affected by it. Chapter XV.*

Our soul is always the "Universal" <note>The totality of all things in the divine mind.</note> through its intellectual power, but it is sometimes the Universal and sometimes a part of the universe through its rational, imaginative, and vegetative powers—much like the moon waxes and wanes. When the soul is not yet affected by this particular body, it dwells upon the whole form of the world, much like the World Soul, through reason and imagination; it moves through the expansion of the "seeds" of life as much as it can. In this state, our soul is universal in its current action, but particular only in its potential. However, it becomes a "part" of the universe when it turns its own affection toward this specific body. In that state, it is particular in its current action, but universal in its potential. Therefore, when the soul becomes universal, it does not stop being particular, for these individual traits are held within its universal state. Understand the "Idol of the Soul" <note>original: "Idolum animæ" / "εἴδωλον" – a lower reflection or shadow of the soul that animates the physical body.</note> as the vital breath surrounding the body. This breath in us is twofold: one part comes from our own soul, and the other from the Soul of the World. Our own part cannot be separated from our soul, though it may become inactive; however, the part belonging to the World Soul can be separated from our soul.

<margin>A</margin>
But if that higher nature cannot become evil, and if this is how the soul comes to be present in the body, the next question is: what is this "descent," and what is the "ascent" that is restored in certain cycles of time? What are the judgments and the just punishments of souls? And finally, what are these "infusions" into the bodies of other animals? We have received these teachings from the ancient philosophers who spoke best about the soul. Certainly, we must try to show that our present discourse is either in harmony with them or at least not in disagreement. Since it has already been established that "participating" in that nature does not mean the soul leaves itself to descend here, but rather that this lower nature exists within the soul, we can see that when they say the soul "comes," they mean the nature of the body comes to be there, participating in life and soul. In short, this "coming" is not to be understood in terms of physical space, but rather as the condition of this kind of communion.

<column-break/>

But it is as if a certain warming or illumination, a birth of desires and pleasures and pains, has sprouted within it. For the body of the generated animal was not something alien. The soul from God <note>original: "ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ ψυχὴ"</note> remained quiet, standing within itself according to its own character. But the body, troubled by its own weakness and its own flowing nature, and struck by external blows, first cried out to the common part of the living thing. It gave all the disturbance to the reason, just as if an unruly mob in need of food, or complaining of other sufferings, should throw into unseemly turmoil a whole assembly of elder statesmen <note>original: "δημογερόντων"</note> sitting in quiet meditation. When, therefore, such people are kept quiet by the wise person, or when reason comes to them to arrange the multitude into a moderate order, then the "worse" part does not prevail. But if not, the worse part prevails, the "better" part keeping quiet because it was not able to overcome the "mass" <note>original: "ὄγκον"</note> of the turmoil from above. And this is the vice of a city and an assembly. Likewise, the vice in a human being is when they have a "mob" within them of pleasures and desires and fears that have conquered the soul. The person then becomes what is generated by this mixture. But if a person enslaves the crowd and runs back to that which they once were, they live as that higher self; they are that self, giving to the body only what they give to it as something different from themselves. Another person lives sometimes this way and sometimes that: a mixture of good and evil.

<margin>A</margin>
But if that higher nature would never become evil, and if this is the way the soul relates to bodies—by being present—what then is the "descent" or the "return" in cycles, or the judgments, or the transitions into the bodies of other animals for judgment? For we have received these things from the ancients who philosophized best about the soul, and it is proper for the mind to try to align our present argument with theirs. Since, therefore, "participating" in that nature meant that the soul did not come here by departing from itself, but rather that the things here came to be in that soul and shared in it, it is clear that when they say it "comes," they mean the nature of the body comes to be there, sharing in life and soul. In general, "coming" is not about location, but is the manner of this kind of communion.

<summary>Plotinus explains that the soul does not "move" into the body but remains divine while the body "approaches" it; he uses the metaphor of a senate and a mob to describe the struggle between reason and desire.</summary>
<keywords>descent of the soul, world soul, reason vs desire, senate analogy, nature of evil, reincarnation, vital breath, idol of the soul</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the soul's relationship with the physical realm, moving from the metaphor of the "unruly mob" of the body to the philosophical mechanics of how the soul "descends" and "ascends." It focuses on the distinction between the soul's universal nature and its localized, "partial" experience when tied to a body.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR.

Therefore, "descending" means the soul comes to be within a body—as we say, the soul gives something of itself to the body so that it might come to life—while "departing" means the body no longer shares in the soul at all. There is a certain order to this communion, a trust given to the parts of the universe... <note>The Greek text is slightly fragmented here</note> it often gives of itself to the lowest form of the intelligible realm, since it is near in power, even if within shorter intervals of nature according to this law. Such a communion is considered an evil, and the separation from it a good. Why? Because <margin>or not this</margin> even if it were not strictly necessary, the soul becomes in some way "partial" <note>original: "μερική" / "particularis" - meaning limited to one part rather than being universal</note> instead of universal. Its activity is no longer directed toward the Whole, even though the soul itself belongs to the Whole. It is like a scientist who possesses an entire field of knowledge but chooses to work only on one specific theorem. The "good" for that scientist is not to act through a single part of their science, but through the entire knowledge they possess. Now, since the soul belongs to the entire intelligible world, even if it hides its "part" within the Whole, it eventually leaps out from the Whole into a part, as if acting only as a portion of itself. It is like fire: though it has the power to burn everything, it might be forced to burn only a small thing, even though it possesses its full power. For the soul is entirely separate when it is itself; or rather, it becomes "each individual thing" when it is distinguished or when its activity becomes localized. It is a portion of the Whole. Indeed, the Whole is also there, but in another way—if one looks closely—it is entirely present, as the part exists potentially within it. To be "in Hades" <note>Hades, the Greek underworld, was etymologically linked by philosophers to the "unseen" (a-ides)</note> if it means to be in the "unseen," is to be separate from the body. But if Hades refers to a lower place, why is that surprising? For even now, wherever our body is, the soul is said to be there too. But what happens when the body no longer exists? If the phantom-image <note>original: "εἴδωλον" / "simulachrum"</note> is not torn away, why shouldn't the soul be where its phantom is? But if philosophy should completely release the soul, the phantom-image alone goes to the "worse place," while the soul itself lives purely in the intelligible world, with nothing of its essence hanging onto the image. Thus, the phantom-image is produced from such a state. But when the soul shines, as it were, back upon itself through a turning away from other things, it is drawn back into the Whole. It does not exist then as a localized activity, yet it has not perished. But enough on these matters; let us return to the argument we began at the start.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> For this reason, we must say that the soul "descends" when it is introduced into the body—just as we said it is "infused" into the body. This means the soul grants something of itself to the body, yet in such a way that the soul does not truly become a property of the body. To "depart" from the body, then, is simply for the body to no longer participate in the soul. Furthermore, one must consider that the law of the universe assigns an order to this kind of communion. Such a "marriage" is an evil, while "divorce" is a good. But why is this so? Because even if the soul did not properly belong to this specific body, yet when it is said to become "of this body" in <margin>B</margin> whatever way, it somehow turns from a universal being into a particular one. Its activity is no longer directed toward the whole, even though the soul is itself part of the whole. This is similar to what happens to a person who possesses a complete branch of knowledge <margin>C</margin> but acts only according to one single concept. The "good" of that scientist was to act through the entire knowledge they possess, not through a single part of it. Now, when the soul itself belonged to the entire intelligible world and hid its individual part within that whole, it eventually broke forth from the whole into a part: for that into which it drove itself was a mere part. It is as <margin>D</margin> if fire, capable of burning the whole, is compelled to scorch only a small thing, though it still possesses its full power. Each individual soul, when it is entirely segregated from this world, is not properly just "each individual soul"; but when it is separated—not by location, but by its activity—and becomes something singular, it is then a portion and no longer the universal, even though in another sense it remains as the universal. When it properly presides over nothing, it is entirely universal: for then it must be judged as a "part" only in potential. Accordingly, when they say the soul "goes to the underworld" <note>original: "ad inferos" / "εἰς ᾅδου"</note>, if they mean the name "underworld" to signify something hidden or unseen, then "going to the underworld" is nothing other than being apart. But if they use this name to designate a "worse place," why should we wonder? For even now, the soul is said to be in the same place where our body is. But when the body no longer exists, what does it mean for the soul to be in the underworld? Perhaps, if the phantom-image <note>original: "simulachrum" / "εἴδωλον"</note> of the soul is not entirely torn away, why should we not think the soul is where its phantom is? But if philosophy should dissolve the bond entirely, the phantom-image alone goes to the worse place; the soul itself lives most purely in the intelligible world, with nothing of itself then being left behind or led out. And so it is regarding the phantom-image that is produced from such a state. But when the soul shines as if within itself, by a certain leaning toward those things which are foreign to this world, it is then contracted back to the Whole; it does not exist as a localized activity, nor has it perished. But concerning these things, let what has been said suffice; let us resume the discussion proposed at the beginning.

<summary>Plotinus explains that the soul's "descent" into the body is a shift from universal, total activity to limited, "partial" activity, likening it to a scientist focusing on only one theorem. He clarifies that "going to Hades" means the soul becomes "unseen" or separate, though a "phantom" of the soul may linger in the physical realm until philosophy achieves a total release.</summary>

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD SIX,
## BOOK V.
### CONCERNING THE FACT THAT BEING, WHILE REMAINING ONE AND THE SAME, IS SIMULTANEOUSLY EVERYWHERE AS A WHOLE.

->That being, existing as one and the same, is simultaneously everywhere as a whole.<-

*A natural judgment that cannot be deceived declares that the one God is everywhere as a whole. Likewise, the natural desire that recalls all things to the one good testifies that the universal nature of beings depends on the one simple source and possesses mutual union through it. Now, the first receptacle of that one good is Being itself, which is one together with it and is simultaneously everywhere as a whole. Chapter I.*

***

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'V' within a square woodcut illustration depicting a seated figure in a pastoral landscape with mountains in the background.</image-desc>
That a certain thing is one and the same in number, yet simultaneously everywhere as a whole, is indicated by the common conception of the human mind. This occurs when all people, moved by a certain natural instinct, cry out that God is within each of us, so that there is one and the same God in all. And if one does not strictly inquire of them the manner of this presence, nor strive to dismantle that opinion through logic, they will undoubtedly confirm it. Having devised this from their own deep thought, they will find complete rest in it. <margin>B</margin> In this matter, they strive for the one and the same with equal zeal, and would not want to be separated from this union in any way. Now, this principle is the firmest of all, sounding in our souls by a natural spirit; it is not, I say, concluded from individual observations, but comes into our minds before all things are arranged individually—even before that principle which teaches that "all things desire the good." <margin>C</margin> For this principle is true if all things naturally hasten toward the One <note>original: "unum" / "ἓν" (Hen) – referring to the ultimate source of reality in Neoplatonism</note>, are in some way one, and if the One itself exists as the target toward which their desire is directed. Indeed, if this One, proceeding into another part as far as it is possible to proceed, can both appear as "many" and yet remain in some way "one." <margin>D</margin> The ancient and primary nature, and the desire for the good—which indeed exists of itself—truly leads back into unity. In this, the whole of nature strives toward itself. For this is the "good" for this one nature: to exist as itself and to be itself; and this is to be One. <margin>E</margin> In this way, the "good" is very rightly called "one’s own" or "domestic" <note>original: "domesticum" / "οἰκεῖον" (oikeion) – meaning something that belongs naturally to one's own house or essence</note>; therefore, it is not to be sought outside. Truly, where would it be for someone who has fallen away from Being, either here or there? Or in what way could he find it in non-being? But certainly, it must be sought within Being itself, and not in such a way that it is non-being. If, however, that Good is Being and is within Being, it is surely within itself in every instance. Therefore, we are not distant from Being, but are in it; nor, again, is that One distant from us. All beings, therefore, are one.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'O' within a square woodcut illustration depicting a figure seated in a natural landscape.</image-desc>
That which is one and the same in number
is everywhere simultaneously as a whole,
the common conception says it is so,
when all, being moved
naturally, say that the God in
each of us is one
<margin>B</margin>
and the same. And if someone should try to examine the manner [of this], not investigating by logic how it might be so, the conception would be set into action in this way, and would find rest. Coming again to the one, they would wish for it and it alone, rather than to be separated from unity. And this is the most certain principle of all, which is like our souls: it does not come from a summary of particulars, but has been felt before all particulars, <margin>C</margin> and before that principle which states that all things desire the good. For it would be true that if these things are the same, they would be one in him, and then there would be desire. For that which proceeds to the other side as far as it is possible to proceed, appears as many, and yet all the ancient nature and the desire for the good leads toward it, into the truly One. And toward this, <margin>D</margin> all nature [strives] toward itself. For this is what exists for this one nature: its own being. And this is: to be one. Whence also the good may be rightly called "one's own." Therefore one must not seek it outside. For where would it be, for one who has fallen away? Or how would someone find it in non-being? <margin>E</margin> But clearly it is in being. And it is not non-being. But if it is in being, it would also be in the same way in each thing. We have not, therefore, departed from it, but we are in it. Nor is it far from us; thus are all beings.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the unity of Being from the previous chapter. While the previous section established that God or the "One" is present everywhere based on human intuition, this page shifts to a rigorous philosophical defense. It explains why we often fail to grasp this unity (because we mistakenly apply the logic of physical bodies to spiritual realities) and distinguishes between the "sensible world" of change and the "intelligible world" of eternal Being.</meta>

# BOOK FIVE.

### The sensible world <note>The physical world perceived through the five senses.</note> is dispersed primarily in three ways: by spatial extension and division; by temporal succession; and by the mutual opposition of qualities. However, the intelligible world <note>The realm of pure thought, Ideas, and divine reality.</note>—that is, the first fullness of Ideas—admits no such division. Likewise, the world of life—that is, the assembly of intellectual souls wonderfully joined with the first Mind and its Ideas—is also undivided.

->Chapter II.<-

But lest you suspect, because of the union so frequently celebrated here and above and below by Plotinus, that neither minds nor souls are many in number, pay attention to what I say. For here he says that all beings are "one," though it is certain they are not one by a single individual essence. Rather, he says they are one because they originate from the One, and they flow toward the One by a certain unity of natural desire. Likewise, he says this because all separate things which he calls "beings" exist within one another, with no spatial boundaries preventing them. Furthermore, the lower ranks of beings perform their primary actions under a higher form and activity. He understands the union of rational souls with the Universal Soul in a similar way. Also, in the book *On Numbers*, he says that all beings are one—not one like a single numerical unit, but one like a single number made of many, such as a thousand. This is what he means when he says all souls are one. Finally, one must contemplate the wonderfully united world of life, not through reasoning that argues from the corporeal world, but through the intellect—which is most unified within us—beginning from the very substance of the thing itself. For whatever exists in 그 world must be judged as substantial.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But when human reason and the condition of our discourse attempt to discuss what has been proposed here for examination, it is not a single, unified thing, but something divided. It takes the nature of bodies <note>Physical matter.</note> as the basis for its inquiry. Taking its principles from there, it divides the reality, judging essence to be of that same divided nature, and thus distrusts its unity. This is because its investigation did not begin from the proper principles. <margin>B</margin> For us, however, in a discussion concerning the One and the whole of Being, we must adopt principles proper to establishing faith <note>Here meaning philosophical certainty or conviction.</note> in the matter. These are the intelligible principles of intelligible things, which are strictly joined to true essence.

First, therefore, we must consider the nature of this universe. It is surely placed in a state of perpetual change, is transformed in every way, and is distributed through every space of location. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, it should not be called "essence" <note>Stable, true being.</note> but rather "becoming" <note>original: *generatio* / *genesis*; the state of constantly changing or coming-into-being.</note>. But Being itself is always undivided, remaining exactly the same and in the same state, neither rising nor passing away. It has no receptacle, no place, and no seat. It does not depart from one place, nor does it enter into another, but remains within itself. Therefore, when someone discusses corporeal nature, they will rightly argue from that nature itself and from those qualities properly attributed to it, weaving together suitable arguments through appropriate comparisons.

<margin>D</margin> Conversely, when someone discusses the intelligible reality, if they have grasped the nature of the essence being dealt with, they will have correctly constructed the principles of the discussion from that source. They will not secretly stray into a different nature, as if forgetting their own purpose, but will instead think through the matter based on the reality itself. Everywhere, this principle—"what a thing is"—is judged to be the chief principle of understanding and debate. Thus it is often said that for those who have correctly defined a thing, many of its accidental properties <note>Characteristics that are not part of a thing's essential nature.</note> are easily perceived. Therefore, in these matters where the whole consists everywhere in "what it is," one must intend toward this much more, look toward this, and refer all things to this.

<column-break/>

### If the intelligible world and the world of life admit no division within themselves regarding place, time, or opposition, and do not depend on any subject or location, then by right, the whole is always everywhere.

->Chapter III.<-

The entire corporeal world necessarily requires the "mode of life" everywhere; therefore, it possesses that life everywhere. But for life to be present everywhere in the body, it is not forced to become thin or divided, which are the sufferings of a physical body. Therefore, it is present to each thing almost entirely, like life or light, and it must not be thought of as spatially segregated from anything. For if it were, it would be reduced to a narrow place.

<sig>K k</sig>

<summary>This page explains that human reason often fails to understand the unity of God and Being because it mistakenly applies the rules of physical matter (which is divided by space and time) to spiritual realities. Plotinus argues that true Being is undivided and present everywhere simultaneously, much like how light or life inhabits a space without being "cut up."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of the "Intelligible" realm—the world of pure ideas and divine reality—arguing that because this realm is not physical, it does not obey the laws of space and can be "everywhere" without being divided into parts.</meta>

<page-num>662</page-num>

**PLOTINUS ENNEADS BOOK VI.**

<margin>A</margin> If, therefore, this very intelligible <note>Intelligible: Reality that can be grasped by the mind or intellect rather than the physical senses.</note> truly exists as being, it always holds itself in the same way and never departs from itself. No process of "becoming" <note>Generation or change.</note> falls upon it, and it is enclosed by no place. It is necessary that this being, being so constituted, always dwells within itself and is never distant from itself; one part of it is not here while another is there. Nothing flows out from it, for otherwise it would exist in different places at different times, and would be entirely within something else and no longer within itself, <margin>B</margin> nor would it be secure from change. For it would undergo change if it were situated in another. But if it consists in a nature that does not undergo change, it does not rest in another. If, then, it is not distant from itself and not divided, and if it is present in many things at once without any kind of transformation, it must surely exist as one whole and yet be the same everywhere. It admits the very quality of which it is said: to exist in many things. But this is the same as saying that while existing in itself, it is again not in itself. <margin>C</margin> It remains for us to say, therefore, that while that being is in nothing, other things participate in it—namely, whatever things are able to approach it, and to the extent that they are able. It is necessary, therefore, either to do away with those initial assumptions and principles and admit no such nature at all, or certainly—if this is impossible and such a nature and essence necessarily exists—to concede entirely what we established at the beginning: namely, that it is one and numerically undivided, existing as a complete whole, and is removed from nothing of the remaining things that exist besides <margin>D</margin> itself. Yet, it is not compelled to be spread out in any way in order to be present to all things; nor again is it present only in such a way that portions flow out from it. Nor, again, does it remain a whole in itself while some other thing created by it leaves it and thus proceeds everywhere into other things. Otherwise, that which is made by it would certainly be something else, and it would be located elsewhere. And if it were then separated from its own effects, it would possess its own distinct place. <margin>E</margin> We may again argue regarding those things which flow from it in this way: either each of them exists as the whole itself, or only as a certain part. But if it is a part, it will not preserve the nature of the whole, as has been said. But if each is a whole, we must either divide each into as many parts as there are things in which it remains—and thus it is already divided—or we must confess that the same whole can be everywhere at once. And so the reasoning is derived from the thing itself and from its very essence; it admits nothing foreign, nor does it take anything from a different nature.

->The common opinion of all, and reason itself, dictates that each of the Gods exists everywhere at once. But although God occupies the whole space at once, He is not forced to be thinned out or divided; otherwise, He would be corporeal <note>Physical or having a body.</note> and would perish through weakness. Therefore, the same God is whole everywhere. The power of no God suffers any defect; therefore, He is lacking nowhere. Therefore, God is an infinite power. The more excellent a natural power is, the wider the province it occupies. The power of each God is more excellent than the most excellent power of nature. The power of the First God is immeasurable. Finally, whatever comes after God cannot be moved or preserved without the presence of God.<-

### Chapter IV.

<margin>A</margin> CONSIDER, if you please, this God, whom we do not say is here in one place and not there in another, but whom we confess is equally everywhere. It is surely well-established among all who think anything of the gods—not only concerning this God, but all the gods—that they are present everywhere, and reason itself concludes this to be so. If, therefore, God is everywhere, it is impossible that He should be divided everywhere; otherwise, He Himself would not be everywhere, but each part of Him would be arranged such that this part was in this place, and that part was in that place. And yet...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <note>This column contains the original Greek text corresponding to the Latin on the left.</note> If indeed this is truly being, and is in the same state, and does not depart from itself, and if no generation occurs around it, nor is it said to be in a place, it is necessary that it, being so, is always with itself and never stands apart from itself. Neither is one part of it here and another there, nor does anything proceed out of it. For it would already be in one thing and another, and generally in something, and not in itself, nor unaffected. <margin>B</margin> For that which is in another, if it is to be unaffected, will not be apart from itself, nor divided, nor changing one single change, but would be in many at once, being one whole together with itself, the same everywhere to itself; that which is in many is that which exists in itself, not being in itself. It remains, then, to say that <margin>C</note> it is in nothing, but the other things participate in it, as many as are able to be present to it, and in as much as they are able. It is necessary then either to take away those hypotheses or principles, or to say that there is no such nature. Or if this is not impossible and such a nature and essence exists of necessity, then we must accept what was said from the beginning: that which is numerically the same, not divided, but being a whole, does not fall away from any of the other things besides itself. Nor in the... <margin>D</margin> so that certain parts from it come to be near it. Nor again does it remain a whole in itself, while something else having come from it leaves it, so that it is in many other things, and that thing stays in another, while the thing from it is elsewhere. And it would already be distant from the things that come from it. And it will be somewhere again if each is a whole or a part. If a part, it will no longer save the nature of the whole, which was indeed <margin>E</margin> said. If each is a whole, we will either divide each into equal numbers to that in which it is, or we will concede the same whole to be everywhere through itself. This very reasoning is from the thing and the essence, and has not drawn anything foreign from the other nature.

---

<margin>A</margin> See now, if you will, even this god, who we say is not in one place and not in another, for he is over all things; among all who have a conception of gods, they say not only about that one, but about all, that they are everywhere. And reason also stands this way. If then he is everywhere, it is not possible for him to be divided. For he would no longer be everywhere himself, but each part of him would be one here and another there.

<summary>This page argues for the omnipresence of the Divine and "Being," explaining that spiritual reality is not subject to physical division or spatial limitations. Plotinus asserts that the First God and the intelligible realm are present everywhere as a complete whole, rather than being spread out in pieces.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section (Ennead VI, Book 4) into Book 5, further exploring how the "Intelligible" (the divine realm of pure thought) can be present everywhere as a single, undivided whole. The translator/commentator provides a bridge explaining the relationship between ideas and their source.</meta>

<page-num>663</page-num>
<header>BOOK FIVE.</header>

<margin>A</margin>
Perhaps it will not be as if it were divided. For if a <term>magnitude</term><note>In this context, magnitude refers to physical size or a spatial quantity.</note> is split into many parts, the original whole is destroyed, and the parts together no longer constitute that specific whole. Furthermore, it would then be a physical body. If these things are impossible, the seemingly incredible truth is revealed once more: in all perceived nature, we must consider God to be simultaneously and everywhere the same indivisible whole. Again, if we say that nature is infinite—for we would not concede that it is limited—<margin>B</margin> why should it be infinite, if not because it never fails or runs out? But if it were to fail, it certainly could not be present to every individual thing. For if it could not be present, it would surely be lacking, and there would be some place where it does not exist. Now, if we say that something else exists after "the One" <note>The "One" is the ultimate, simple source of all reality in Plotinus’s philosophy.</note>, it must nonetheless exist together with it. That which follows the One must revolve around it and strive toward it; it is a sort of offspring of the One, remaining connected to it. <margin>C</margin> Thus, whatever participates in that which follows the One also participates in the One itself. Consequently, since there are many things in the <term>intelligible world</term><note>The "intelligible world" (mundus intelligibilis) is the realm of pure reality, ideas, and intellect, existing beyond physical space.</note>—first, second, and third ranks—and all follow like the center of a single sphere, they are not separated by any gaps. Rather, they are all present together there; wherever the third things are, the second and first are equally present.

---

> *The author often takes the "intelligible world" to mean the primary being and the intellect, in which the ideas of things reside like a common center. Often he also takes it as I have said, but by joining to those ideas—as centers—immaterial forms that depend on them like lines. These forms are one when they are joined there at the center, but as they are produced from there, they become many. This entire assembly of the intelligible world is more of a "one" than the assembly of material forms joined to matter, which is called the "sensible world" <note>The physical world we perceive with our senses.</note>. This intelligible world is more unified because immaterial forms are more closely and firmly attached to their ideas, and through those ideas to the Intellect, than material forms are to their own beginnings, and through them to matter. Likewise, because that world is a unity of the highest form, whereas this physical world is a unity of the lowest matter; furthermore, because in this physical world, union is hindered by the spatial distance of parts, the conflict of qualities, and the constant change of time. In the intelligible world, however, these obstacles do not exist. This same intelligible world is compared to a vast sphere, within whose circuit other circuits are contained, and to whose center the centers of immaterial forms are reduced—as if smaller spheres were contained within a primary form, just as smaller spheres are in a larger one. Such a union does not prevent the distinction of essences, just as the union of forms in matter does not, nor does the connection of lines to their points and center, nor the gathering of spheres within a sphere.*

### Chapter V.

<margin>A</margin>
As is often said for the sake of clarity: just as many lines proceed from a single center, so do the <term>intelligibles</term> proceed from a single source. This metaphor helps lead the mind to understand how a multitude can be generated. It is worthwhile, while keeping this image in mind, to first accept that all those things said to be many in that realm exist simultaneously. We must then add that even in a circle, one can take the lines as distinct, even though they are not entirely separate; <margin>B</margin> for the surface is one. But where there is no physical surface or spatial interval, but instead entirely "non-distant" powers and essences, all things are reasonably thought of as centers joined to one another in a single center. In this state, the lines themselves are let go, and only the ends of the lines touching the center are preserved—where, indeed, all are one. Again, if you join lines to these points, they will hang from their own specific centers which they left behind. Nevertheless, each center will be in no way separated from the one primary center; they are together with it while remaining individual, as many as the lines for which they serve as boundaries. Therefore, as many...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...as there are, the One would no longer be one, just as if a certain magnitude were divided into many: for thus it would be scattered, and all the parts would no longer exist as that other whole. To this is added that God, being in such a state, would also be a body. But if these things cannot happen, we again find that which seemed incredible to be certain: namely, that in all of human nature, it is believed that God is simultaneously everywhere. From this it is established that a certain undivided "one" is everywhere simultaneously as a whole. Again, if <margin>B</margin> we say that nature is infinite—for we would not concede that it is limited—why especially infinite, except because it fails nowhere? But if it fails, it certainly does not remain present to each thing. For if it could not be present, it would surely fail, and there would be something where it was not. Now indeed, even if we say something else exists after the One, it must again be together with it; and that which is after it must revolve around it, strive toward it, <margin>C</margin> and be its offspring connected to it, so that what participates in that which is after it, also participates in it. Accordingly, since in the intelligible world there are many things—first, second, and third grades—and all following things are fixed as if to the center of a single sphere, they are not separated from one another by any intervals, but all are there together. Therefore, wherever the third things are, the second and first are present there equally. But let us explain this matter more clearly in what follows.

<margin>A</margin>
What is often said—that just as many lines proceed connected from a certain single center, similarly the intelligibles proceed from a single source—conveniently attempts to bring an understanding of the multitude produced there. It is worthwhile, while observing this, to first understand that all things said to be produced as "many" there exist simultaneously. One must add again that in a circle, it is permitted to take lines that are not entirely distinct in themselves as if they were distinct; for the surface is one. <margin>B</margin> But where there is no interval according to a surface, but entirely non-distant powers and essences, all things are not without reason conceived of in the manner of centers, joined to one another in a certain single center. There, indeed, the lines themselves may be dismissed, and only the ends of the lines touching the center are preserved, where all are truly one. On the other hand, if you join lines to the points, they will be suspended from their own centers, which each left behind. Nevertheless, each center will be at the same time in no way separated from the one primary center, so that while they are together with it, they are also meanwhile individual, and as many as the lines for which they had granted that they should exist as boundaries. Therefore, as many...

<meta>catchword: individual (singula)</meta>

<summary>This page discusses how the divine reality (the Intelligible World) remains a single, undivided whole even while being present everywhere and producing a multitude of forms. Plotinus uses the geometric metaphor of a circle's center and its radiating lines to explain how the "Many" remain unified within the "One."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 663, where the author argued that the divine or "intelligible" nature is present everywhere as a whole. Here, Plotinus employs geometric analogies (circles and lines) to explain how the One can appear as many without losing its unity, and transitions into a discussion on the soul's relationship to universal Being.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

[Left Column]
There, the lines touch the center itself, and they seem to be as many points as there are lines. But in reality, that One appears to be all things simultaneously. Therefore, if we admit that all <term>intelligible things</term><note>original: "intelligibilia" — these are realities that exist in the realm of pure thought, such as the "Forms" or "Ideas," which are more real than physical objects.</note> are like many centers—centers, I say, reduced to a single center and completely joined—they appear to be many only because of the lines. These lines do not create the centers but merely reveal them. Certainly, these lines will now help us to show a certain 
<margin>B</margin> proportion in themselves toward that intelligible nature which, by touching them, appears to be many and present everywhere.

*If you consider all and each of the individual ideas in the first Mind, you will soon recognize in any single idea the entire fullness of ideas: yet the distinct property of that specific idea is preserved. Likewise, if you see many bodies belonging to an intellectual soul, that soul is one in many; but in the case of the intelligible world, many things are rather in one, or around the one.*

<margin>A</margin> Since the <term>intelligibles</term> are many beings, they are simultaneously one. Conversely, since they are one, they are also many due to their infinite nature. They are many in one, one in many, and all things together. Indeed, all things there act toward the whole along with the whole; and again, they act toward the part along with the whole itself. Yet the part receives into itself the primary action as if it were a part, and the whole then follows. This is just as if a "man himself" <note>This refers to the "Ideal Man" or the universal concept of humanity.</note> were to come into a specific man; he would become a certain man, while still existing as "Man." The man who exists in matter is made into many of the same men by the one Man who exists after the Idea; thus, one and the same thing, like a **seal**, is impressed upon many. But the Man himself, and each thing in itself, and the entire universe itself, is not in the many in that way; rather, the many are in it, or rather, they are around it. For whiteness is present everywhere in one way, but the soul of each individual is in every part of the body as the same thing in another way; and thus we must judge that Being itself is everywhere.

*Our soul understands the fullness of ideas—namely, by being turned toward its own intellect—yet it does not do so through mere images of things. Therefore, the soul itself is the universe through the intellect. Thus, in the universal form of things, all are in some way one, even though each is distinct by its own property; however, insofar as they are separated from the intellect, they are disjoined from one another.*

->Chapter VII.<-

*In these two books, Plotinus does not intend to prove that there can be only one soul, but that there is one soul which is present everywhere, despite the size or multitude of bodies. He argues that it is not necessary to place many souls in different worlds, as if one common soul were not sufficient to be everywhere and to rule. If many souls are posited, they are posited for the same reason rather than because of the insufficiency of that one; and these many are one with that soul, namely in power. Likewise, they act under its common power and are reduced to a common Idea of the soul. Also, any soul contains within itself all the seeds of things, just like the Soul of the World. When it turns into itself, it unfolds itself into ideas, which are equal to it; it governs equally with it, and contemplates all things equally with the common mind. Such a soul becomes one in the lights of all the stars and in the light of the sun, where all things are everywhere, and all have equal power to understand, though the rest act by the power of the Sun. An example is found in the five senses, which are one, first in a single <term>common sense</term><note>The "common sense" (sensus communis) was a theorized internal faculty that combined the inputs from the five individual senses into a single perception.</note> and directed toward one thing. Second, because in withdrawing from the body, each of them feels in common. Third, let us imagine that sight, in the common sense, perceives not only visible things, but soon the other sensible things as well. Likewise, hearing would first perceive its own objects, then others; and so with the rest. Then each would be one with the others and with all; yet they would still remain distinct. This is because each can reflect upon its own objects as before, and although it pours itself through all things, it begins from its own specific starting point and finally returns to the same. Know that after this book and the book "Whether all souls are one soul," Plotinus composed three books on "Doubts of the Soul," where he explains this number of souls.*

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, that which is ours is also brought back to Being itself, to which we ourselves are brought back; we ascend to it, and we exist from it from the beginning. We understand those things not through their images, nor through any figures that we might possess. But if we understand them, and yet not through images or figures, it follows that we understand them by being those things ourselves. If, therefore, we are partakers of true knowledge...

<column-break/>

[Right Column]
<margin>Α</margin> ...the lines touch, so many the points appear to be. But those things are one. If then we also compare all the intelligible things to many centers <margin>original: "νοητὰ" (noēta) - things understood by the mind</margin> being referred back to one center, they appear as many because of the lines; it is not that the lines generated them, but rather the lines show them to us for the present purpose, as an analogy for those things which the 
<margin>Β</margin> nature touches, and thus appears to be many and in many places.

<margin>Α</margin> Since the intelligibles are many, yet being one, they are many by their infinite nature. They are in one and one over many, and all things are together. For indeed, the activity is toward the whole along with the whole. Again, the part along with the whole receives the first activity as a part, and then as the whole. For example, if "Man" coming to a certain man, should become a certain man. 
<margin>Β</margin> Therefore, the man who is in the one [material] world, by the Man who exists after the Idea, made the same men; and there is the One truly in the many, because it is as if the same thing is being **sealed** in many. But each thing is itself by itself, and the whole is all, and it is not in many, but the many are in it. Or rather, they are around it. For whiteness is present in one way, 
<margin>C</margin> and each soul is in every part of itself as the same; and in this way, Being is everywhere.

<margin>Α</margin> That which is ours is also brought back to Being, and we ascend toward that, having our beginning from it. And we perceive those things, not as images of them, nor having types of them, but by being those things. If, therefore, we participate in true knowledge, we are those things. Not receiving...

It emphasizes that human knowledge of divine truths occurs because the soul "becomes" or is fundamentally united with those truths, rather than just observing images of them.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the "intelligible world"—the realm of pure thought and Forms. Following the previous page’s geometric metaphors, Plotinus now discusses how individual souls and the "Forms" (the perfect blueprints of reality) are unified in the Divine Mind, and how these Forms interact with physical matter.</meta>

# BOOK FIVE.

<column-break/>

[Left Column]
It is not that those things <note>The "Forms" or "Ideas," the eternal templates of all things.</note> are in us, but rather that we exist in them. Since not only we are those things, but other beings are those things as well, we are certainly all those things together. Therefore, existing as one with all things, we are those things; thus, we are all one. When we look outward, or away from that source upon which we depend, we are ignorant of our unity—just as many faces might be turned outward in a circle, yet they all share a single <margin>A</margin> head at the center. But if one were able to turn back—either by one’s own nature or by the lucky pull of <term>Minerva</term><note>The goddess of wisdom; here representing the sudden spark of intellectual insight.</note>—one would see God, oneself, and the whole. One will see this whole at first not as a separate "everything," but rather, having no place to stand and define its limits, one will stop trying to mark oneself off from the rest of Being. One will then arrive at the whole without moving anywhere, but by remaining in that very place where the <margin>B</margin> whole itself is established.

<column-break/>

[Right Column]
**A** Indeed, those things are not in us, but we rather exist in them. Since it is not only we who are those things, but other things are also those things, we are surely all those things. Existing simultaneously with all, we are those things: and so, we all are one. When we look outward, and do not direct our gaze toward that from which we are suspended, we naturally fail to notice that we are one: just as if many faces in a circle were connected by a single <margin>B</margin> crown or a single innermost root. If someone could be reflected back to the innermost parts, either by his own nature or by Minerva turning him back, he would see himself now to be God and the universe. I say he would look upon himself at first not as the entire universe, but then, having no place where he might fix his step to determine himself, or define how far he himself extends, he would soon cease to circumscribe himself and separate himself from the universal being. Thus, he would arrive at the universe itself from every side, yet in such a way that he would proceed nowhere, but would remain in the same place where the whole consists.

---

->*The divine Mind acts upon matter through its Ideas, not from the outside in the manner of human art, but from within in the manner of artistic nature: it is not separated from matter by location—otherwise it would be assigned a specific place—nor is it mixed with matter, otherwise it would not rule over it. Chapter VIII.*<-
->*The Idea of fire is everywhere, ready to generate fire: it is not divided, lest it perish; it is not extended, lest it become corporeal; it is not multiplied in number, lest it become innumerable: one is sufficient; one is whole everywhere.*<-

---

<column-break/>

[Left Column]
I think indeed that if anyone were to examine **A** the <term>participation</term><note>original: "metaleptis" — the way physical objects "take part" in or mirror their eternal Forms.</note> of matter in the Forms, they would more easily come to believe what is being said, and would no longer doubt it as if it were impossible. For I think it is both reasonable and necessary that the Forms are not placed separately, with matter located far off, and an <term>illumination</term><note>original: "ellampsis" — a metaphor for how a higher reality projects its image onto a lower one, like a light casting a shadow.</note> comes into matter from somewhere far away. For otherwise, what is said would be empty. For that term "far off" in these matters, and "separated," is difficult to **B** explain. And the most difficult thing is what is said of "participation," though it might be stated very simply, being familiar through examples. But we speak of "illumination" sometimes so that we may speak as we do regarding the illuminations of sensible things. But since the things in matter are images, and the Forms hold the rank of archetypes, and the nature of illumination is such that it keeps the thing illuminated separate, we **C** speak in this way. But now, speaking more accurately, we must not pose it so, as if the Form were in a separate place, and then the Ideas were seen in matter as if in water; rather, matter must be thought of as touching the Idea from every side, and yet again not touching it. By being near, matter holds all the Forms according to its capacity, with nothing in between; the Idea does not go through or run over it, but **D** remains in itself. If, then, the Idea of fire is not in matter—taking matter here as that which underlies the elements—then the "rational principle" <note>original: "logos"</note> takes hold, and the ideal Fire itself [acts upon] the matter...

<column-break/>

[Right Column]
**I BELIEVE** indeed that whoever considers under what condition matter in a certain way receives the species <note>The Latin "species" corresponds to the Greek "eide" (Forms/Ideas).</note>, will more easily grant what is said at present; nor will he further deny it as impossible, or again doubt anything. For I think it probable and necessary that nature is not so disposed that the species are placed separately here, while matter is located separately there, and some illumination from elsewhere above comes into the matter. **B** For it is to be feared lest this should perhaps be ridiculous to say: namely, what would that very thing be which is said to be "far off" and "separate"? Furthermore, would it not then be difficult to explain, and full of ambiguity, what we just touched upon regarding the condition of participation? But if that is ever said, it is brought forward far too easily and promptly, since one arrives at knowledge of it through examples. However, if ever we introduce a certain "illumination" into the discussion, **C** we do not wish it to be said as we see distant things illuminated by other distant things in matters manifest to the senses. But since those things which are in matter are certain images, and the species themselves hold the order of the first patterns, these seem to flash out from those; and we use the name "illumination" in these cases because that which illuminates is by no means mixed with that which is illuminated. But now, speaking more exactly, we must not arrange these things so that the species itself is in a place apart, and then, as if in water, the brightness of the Idea is seen in matter; but matter **D** must be thought to touch the Idea from all sides, and yet again by no means to touch it; and thus to carry away something from the species according to its whole self, with proximity contributing to this, insofar as it can receive it with absolutely no medium intervening: nor again does the Idea run through the whole of matter or is it spread over it, but rather remains in itself. For if the Idea of fire itself does not lie in the matter—and we now take matter as that which is subject to the elements—the ideal fire itself surely [reaches] the matter...

It further explains that "participation" of matter in these Forms is not a physical mixing or a distant projection, but a direct, non-spatial contact where the Form remains unchanged while matter reflects its image.</summary>
