<meta>This page continues Plotinus's argument regarding the relationship between the "One" (the source of all being) and the "Many" (the material world). Having previously discussed how we exist within the intelligible realm, he now explains how a single "Idea" or "Form" can manifest in many different material objects without being divided itself, using fire and the "World Soul" as his primary examples.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS BOOK VI.

<column-break/>

[Left Column - Translated from Latin]

The Form does not inhabit matter directly; rather, it remains superior and exhibits the "shape" of fire through the entirety of the ignited matter. Let us assume, however, that material fire was first created as a vast mass. This same reasoning applies to the other elements. If, therefore, the <term>Ideal Fire</term><note>The "Form" or eternal, perfect blueprint of fire that exists in the divine mind, as opposed to a physical, flickering flame.</note> itself is seen in all things, providing an image of itself, it does not provide it as if it were separated by location—like the light visible to our eyes. Otherwise, this whole fire would already be somewhere in the presence of the senses, if indeed it were many parts. Certainly, it provides images of itself while its own "Idea" remains uncircumscribed by any location; instead, the Idea generates locations out of itself. Otherwise, if it were made of multiple parts, it would have to flee from itself so that, in becoming many, it could participate in itself multiple times. Now, since the Idea itself cannot be cut or divided, it offers nothing of its own substance to the matter. Yet, although it is one, it is not powerless to form that which is not part of its own unity. Nor is it compelled to be present in the universe in such a way that it forms one part of the world with one of its parts and another with another; rather, it forms every part and the whole with its entire self. It would be ridiculous to suggest many "Ideas" of fire just so that each individual fire could be formed by its own Idea—this one by that one, and that one by another. If that were so, the Ideas would be infinite. Furthermore, how would you conveniently divide the things that are created, if fire is one and continuous? Then, if we add more fire to this matter, increasing its size, we must admit that according to that portion of matter, the exact same Idea produced the same effects; for no one would say there was a different Idea in that place.

->The single machine of the world was both crafted by a single Mind and is animated by a single Soul, present as a whole everywhere at once.<-

->Chapter IX.<-

> *Just as within one sphere there are many other spheres—united with it yet distinct—so too are there many souls within the one Soul. The <term>World Soul</term><note>The "Anima Mundi," the universal spirit that Neoplatonists believed organized and gave life to the entire physical universe.</note> is not like a single point made of many parts; it is preeminent. Therefore, it does not have a fixed position in terms of physical dimensions. Nor is it one made of many, but rather a unity that unfolds a multitude within itself. Thus, it can be present to many things and bodies simultaneously as a whole, and it is not separated from anything by location, since it is more eminent than such things. It generates both unity and place. Finally, since it is not supported by the machine of the world, but rather supports the world itself, it rightly flourishes as a whole everywhere; and similarly, the Intellect is the maker of the world.*

<margin>A</margin> Accordingly, if one conceptually leads all the created elements into a single circular figure, one certainly should not say that many authors produced the sphere (as if one were distributed here and another there to create their respective parts). Instead, one must say that there is a single cause of the construction that completes it with its entire self, not crafting one thing with one part of itself and another thing with another. Otherwise, there would again be many creators, unless you trace the entire construction back to a single indivisible whole. Indeed, the creator of the whole sphere must be a single impartible being—not in such a way that the creator is poured out into the sphere, but such that the whole sphere hangs suspended from and clings to the creator. Therefore, one life possesses the same sphere, and the sphere is located within one life. Thus, all things that are in the sphere are reduced to a single life, and so all souls are, in a certain way, one. Yet the Soul is one in such a way that it is also infinite. For this reason, some have said that the Soul is a "Number," while others have taught that "Number" itself increases the nature of the soul. They perhaps thought this because the soul is never absent from anything, but stands out in all things, while remaining that very thing which it is. <note>The final Greek fragment at the bottom of the Latin column translates to: "likely imagining it in this way, that it fails nothing."</note>

<column-break/>

[Right Column - Translated from Greek]

<margin>A</margin> The Idea is not itself born into the matter; it provides the form throughout the entire matter that has been set on fire. Let us suppose that the first fire produced was a great mass. The same logic suffices for the other so-called elements. If, then, the fire in that realm—the Idea—is seen in all things, providing an image to itself and to all <margin>B</margin> things (for indeed, all fire would then be in perception, either as a whole or as many parts of itself), its Idea exists* <gloss>in a placeless state; it generated place for itself.</gloss> For it would have been necessary for that which became many to flee from itself, or to be truly many, participating in the same thing many times. And the Idea did not need anything from the matter for itself; instead, it is without relation <margin>C</margin> and has become indivisibly in the whole. It does not shape with one part of itself while being absent from another, nor is it present to the whole in such a way that one part of it shapes one thing and another part shapes another. Rather, it is the whole in every single thing. For it is ridiculous to introduce many Ideas of fire so that each fire might be shaped by a separate Idea. For then the Ideas would be infinite. Furthermore, how would you divide the things being produced, since fire is a single continuous thing? And if we were to add more fire to this matter, making it larger, we must say that even in that part of the matter, the same Idea has worked the same things; for it is certainly not by another Idea.

<margin>A</margin> And therefore, if these elements, having already been produced, are brought by reason into a single spherical shape, one must not say that many makers produce the sphere, with one being cut off from another to make a specific part. Rather, there is one cause of the making, creating with its whole self. It does not make one thing with one part and another with another. For if it were so, then <margin>B</margin> there would be many makers, unless you refer the whole to one indivisible being. Rather, the maker of the sphere would be one indivisible thing; the maker is not poured out into the sphere, but the whole sphere is suspended from the maker. Life, therefore, being one, possesses the sphere as the same; the sphere itself is placed in one life. And thus all things in the sphere belong to one life. And all souls, therefore, are one, insofar as it is one and yet infinite; for which reason some <margin>C</margin> called it a "Number," while others said that Number itself increases its nature. They perhaps imagined it in this way, because it fails nothing.

<summary>Plotinus explains that the "Forms" (Ideas) of physical elements and the World Soul are indivisible unities that govern the material world without being fragmented by space or matter. He argues that the entire universe is supported by a single, all-present life and intellect rather than a collection of separate parts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's metaphysical inquiry into how the "One" (the ultimate source of all existence) can be present everywhere without being divided. The previous page used the example of the "Form of Fire" to show how a single ideal can manifest in many physical places; this page expands that logic to the World Soul and the Divine Intellect.</meta>

# BOOK FIVE.

<column-break/>

If the cosmos were even larger, the power of the One would not fail to reach every part of it. Indeed, it would be more accurate to say that the power exists within the whole. We should understand "increasing" <note>original Greek: *auxon*</note> not in the literal sense of physical growth, but as meaning that the One is never absent from any place, insofar as its nature is a unity that cannot be divided into parts like a physical object. For while other things may touch the One or participate in it as a mental image, that which is truly One is not a collection of many parts—if it were, the whole would perish if any part were removed. Nor is it confined by boundaries; if it were, it would either be smaller than the things it inhabits, or it would be torn apart in its desire to reach everything. If it were divided, it would not be present as a whole to all things, but only as parts of itself to parts of them. As the saying goes, "they would not know where in the world it is," <note>original: *vbinam gentium sit*—a classical idiom used here to describe the confusion of those who seek the source of being in physical space rather than in the spiritual realm.</note> because it would be unable to reach a state of unity, being severed from itself. If this "One" is truly what we call <term>Essence</term><note>Ousia; the fundamental reality or "beingness" of a thing.</note>, then it must appear to possess a nature opposite to that of a multitude. This multitude is not something the One adopts from the outside; rather, the One possesses this power within itself and from itself, being truly the <term>Good</term>. In the One, "being" includes both infinity and multitude. Because it is of such a nature, it appears everywhere as a whole, possessing a single internal logic <note>original: *logos*</note>, containing itself, and being the very thing that is contained. Those things that are contained by it are not scattered far and wide, but exist within it everywhere. Thus, it is the other things that are divided by location. For one must see that things in space depend on the One, even if they do not know it, so that they may be established. Once established, the One does not leave its own "seat" within itself. If that seat were moved, those things would immediately perish, for their foundation would be removed. Yet the One is not so foolish as to depart from itself and risk dissolution; while it is preserved entirely within itself, it does not recklessly commit itself to an unfaithful place—for it is the place that needs the One to be preserved, not the other way around.

---

->*These three principles of things are everywhere: the Good itself, the Divine Intellect (which is Beauty itself), and finally the Life of the World. These draw all things to themselves through hidden paths, gathering them into one through the desire for goodness, beauty, and life.*<-

### Chapter X.

*Supernal goodness, intelligence, and life are present everywhere in their entirety, and they suffice for all things because they remain in themselves, bound to nothing. Furthermore, just as many eyes enjoy the single light of the Sun throughout different places, so all intellectual souls possess the one light of the First Intelligence. This light is present everywhere and is never divided, and within it, all souls are one. Similarly, all souls feed upon the one Good, which is nowhere absent; indeed, they breathe a single life that flourishes everywhere. Truly, there would be no union of things in a world full of physical distance and discord unless that higher world and its inhabitants possessed a miraculous unity. In this chapter and many others, it is revealed that these inhabitants differ from one another in their essences.*

<summary>Plotinus argues that the One, the Divine Intellect, and the World Soul are omnipresent foundations of reality that do not divide themselves among physical objects, but rather contain all physical objects within themselves.</summary>
<keywords>The One, World Soul, Divine Intellect, omnipresence, metaphysics, Neoplatonism, unity, essence, the Good</keywords>

--- Page 844 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of the One and the Divine Intellect. Having previously argued that the source of all being is not divided by space, Plotinus now uses the metaphor of light and the experience of beauty to explain how many individual souls can "participate" in a single, undivided reality.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS BOOK VI.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It remains, therefore, within itself, excelling in wisdom, and never clings to other things. But all other things depend continuously upon it, so that wherever it may be, they find it through their own desire. And here is that love <note>original: *amor*; Greek: *eros*</note> which is said to lead many to spend the night at the doors of the beloved. I speak of a love that is always standing on the outside, desiring the beautiful, and which thinks itself satisfied if it can only catch a glimpse of it whenever possible. For even the lover of that higher realm does not possess beauty itself, but participates in it through a certain proximity. But beauty itself
<margin>B</margin> remains within itself, and many are the lovers of this one thing. They love the whole, and when they possess it according to their strength, they possess the whole—for that which is loved is itself the whole. What, then, prevents this from being sufficient for all, while it remains within itself? Indeed, it is for this very reason that it satisfies everyone: because it remains, and it is beautiful for this reason—that it is present as a whole to all. Now, intelligence <term>Intelligentia</term><note>Plotinus uses this to refer to *Nous*, the Divine Mind or Intellect, which is the second level of reality below the One.</note> itself is present as a whole to all, which is why it is a "common intelligence." It is not as if this specific intelligence exists here
<margin>C</margin> and another exists there. For it would be a ridiculous thing if it required a specific location. Certainly, intelligence does not distribute itself in the way that whiteness <note>A reference to "accidents" in Aristotelian logic, where a property like color exists only within a physical body.</note> does. For it is not the function of a body to understand; rather, if we truly participate in intelligence, we necessarily converge into something that is one and the same, existing as a whole within itself. We do not receive it in such a way that we take certain portions of it; nor, again,
<margin>D</margin> is it divided so that I have the whole and you have the whole, separated one from the other. This is imitated by assemblies and gatherings of those seeking truth, as if they converge into a single intelligence, even though each person on their own is incapable of wisdom. But when they cast themselves together in that gathering, in a true union for the purpose of understanding, they bring together and generate intelligence, and they find it. For what can prevent the intellect from being present in one person and another at the same time?
<margin>E</margin> But truly, although others who are intelligent may join with us in the same pursuit, they do not appear to join us simultaneously. It is just as if someone were touching the same object with many fingers at once, and yet imagined they were touching different things; or if someone were to strike the same string on a lyre without seeing that they were striking it. Yet we ought to consider how we reach the Good <term>Bonum</term><note>The ultimate principle in Neoplatonism, also called "The One."</note> in our souls. For I do not reach one "Good" and you another; we reach the same one.
<margin>F</margin> Nor, again, do we reach the same thing in such a way that one part flows into me and another into you—as if the source were located somewhere high above and its gifts descended down to us. On the contrary, the Giver itself must be entirely present to those who receive, so that they truly receive from that source; and the one who gives does not give from things that are foreign, but from his own. For the intellectual gift is not performed in the manner of a transmission <note>original: *transmissio*; Plotinus argues that spiritual "giving" doesn't deplete the source, unlike passing a physical object.</note>; since even

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It remains, therefore, in itself, acting with temperance <note>original: *sophronoun*</note>; it would not come to be in another. But those other things, as many as are directed toward it, are raised up as if by a longing <note>asterisk in text</note>. This is the "love at the door," always present and desiring the prizes of beauty, and loving in such a way as it is able to participate. Since even the spectator who receives beauty is affected in this way by touching it. But it remains in itself,
<margin>B</margin> and the lovers of the One are many. Having seen the whole, they possess it in this way, whenever they possess it. For the whole is that which remains. How then is that not sufficient for all, remaining as it does? Since it suffices for this very reason: that it remains. It is beautiful because it is whole to all. For indeed, the whole is for all. Therefore, they have it from the source, and not one part here and another there. For it is a ridiculous thing to think that thinking <note>original: *phronein*</note> needs a place to stand and does not
<margin>C</margin> stand still, like whiteness. For is thinking the work of a body? But rather, as being participants, we share in thinking in that same whole which is with itself. We do not take it as if we were taking parts of it. Nor is it divided if I have the whole and you have the whole, each snatched from the other; it remains. Since every assembly and meeting of those going toward thinking shows this. Each one separately would be weak, but contributing to one in the gathering—to that which is truly understanding—the whole
<margin>D</margin> has generated at the door. For what indeed prevents the mind from being separated in another way, so as to be Intellect away from each other? But rather being together. They do not seem to be together, just as if someone were touching the same thing with many fingers, but thought they were touching many different things. Or as the strings of a lyre to one not seeing. And so it is in souls. We touch the good; it is necessary to realize that I do not touch one thing while you touch another. But rather
<margin>E</margin> the same thing. It is not that the same thing comes as a flowing stream, some parts here and some to you. For the source must be above, and the things with it must be present to the ones who receive it. So that they may receive, and the Giver gives what it gives, not as something foreign, but how? As itself. Since even a procession or a gift in the case of bodies is one thing, but in the case of things that permeate through
<margin>F</margin> places, the gift is different. For the gift and the making are toward itself. Even the physical part of the universe acts upon itself. And nothing comes into it from the outside. If nothing comes from the outside or from nature, such as light, in a thing that is without distance from itself, how could it come from elsewhere? Therefore, being in the same place, we both see and touch the Good, being together with those primary intelligible things. And the world there is much more one than this one.

a message or a report is performed; since even the very similar is attributed to different people at the same time, and the effect is carried to the same point. Furthermore, the body of the universe acts and suffers within itself, and nothing from the outside comes to it. If, therefore, nothing from the outside falls into the body itself—which nevertheless flees from itself as if through a sieve—then surely in a reality that suffers no distance, in what way could it be in an external place? Wherefore, existing in the same thing, we both see and touch the Good itself: existing together, I say, reaching it with our intelligible parts. And truly, the world there is much more one than the world here.

# BOOK FIVE <note>Original: LIBER QVINTVS. While the header indicates Book 5, the content corresponds to what modern scholars categorize as Ennead VI, Treatise 4: "On the Presence of Being, One and the Same, Everywhere as a Whole."</note>

<language>Translated from Ancient Greek</language>
There would be two sensible worlds, divided in the same way. And the intelligible sphere, if it were "one" in the same way as this world, would either be distinct from it, or the concept becomes even more ridiculous. For if the rational principle <note>original: *logos*</note> necessarily requires physical mass <note>original: *ogkos*</note> in this world, then the intelligible sphere—which needs no such thing—would be forced to stretch itself out and depart from its own nature. What, then, is the obstacle to everything becoming one? Does one thing push another away to make room for itself? We do not see this happening with lessons, theorems, or sciences, which are all contained within the soul without being crowded for space. But one might say this is impossible for true beings; I respond that it would only be impossible if true beings were physical masses.

<column-break/>

<language>Translated from Latin</language>
<margin>A</margin> There will be two sensible worlds, divided in a similar fashion, and the intelligible sphere itself will be sensible, provided it is not "one" in a different way than our world is. Therefore, it would either excel in its unity, or certainly be more ridiculous: for if a certain mass is necessarily suited to this sphere, then that intelligible sphere, truly not needing extension, would stretch itself out and depart from itself. Finally, what obstacle is there in that realm to prevent all things from yielding into one? Does one place repel another, as if we did not see that every doctrine and contemplation, and all sciences whatsoever, are not at all crowded within the soul? If anyone should object that this union cannot happen in true essences, I will respond that it could by no means happen if true essences existed as physical bulks <note>original: *moles*</note>.

-> The divine mind—just as through its indivisible eternity, which is the cause of time, it equals and surpasses all time—so through its indivisible essence and infinite power, it occupies and exceeds all space; for it creates and preserves space and all that is within it everywhere. Chapter 45. <-

-> For just as the whole of time relates to its own indivisible state <note>the "eternal now"</note>, so the whole of physical dimension relates to the excellent power of the indivisible substance: for there is an immensity there of both perseverance and power, and here in the physical world is a certain image of both those gifts. <-

<language>Translated from Latin and Ancient Greek</language>
<margin>A</margin> **BUT** <note>original: Greek *ALLA*; Latin *CÆTERVM*</note> in what way does that which has no dimension in itself touch the entire physical body, which is endowed with such great magnitude? And why is it not scattered by such a propagation, since it is one and the same thing extending through all things? This is a doubt we have often raised, for we are eager to finally put an end to this uncertainty. It has been demonstrated often that it is so, but it is worthwhile to offer further persuasion. Indeed, that very nature <note>the Divine Nature</note> has contributed not a little—in fact, it has contributed the most—to our persuasion. 
<margin>B</margin> For we must realize that this nature is not like a huge stone <note>original: *saxum*; Greek: *lithos*</note> situated in a specific place: which, where it is situated, occupies as much space as it is large, and is unable to cross those same limits. Such a stone has a fixed measure of quantity and a power that is circumscribed within its stony nature. 
<margin>C</margin> But because that divine nature is the *primary* nature, it is neither measured nor determined by how large it "ought" to be. Rather, it is the nature by which all other things are measured. It is a universal power that is not "this much" or "that much" in size. For this reason, it is not in time, but exists outside of all time. While time is continually scattered through intervals, eternity remains in itself in the same state; it contains and surpasses time, and exists more amply than time through its everlasting power, even though time seems to spread out into many things. 
<margin>D</margin> It is as if a line seemed to proceed into the infinite, yet was always tied to a single point <note>original: *signum*; Greek: *semeion*</note> and ran around it; wherever the line runs, that point is seen within it. The point itself does not run, but the line revolves around it. If, therefore, time has a certain proportional relationship to that which remains the same in essence, then that divine nature is infinite—not only because it is everlasting, but also because of the magnitude of its infinite power. It is necessary, therefore, to return to this infinity of power...

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

...to perceive a certain nature running alongside and equally: one that is raised up in parallel and depends upon that higher source, while another power moves through time in sync with that steady, enduring force. And truly, that power is all the more vast because it ensures the entire universe is expanded to its own magnitude, as much as its strength allows. What, then, is this thing that partakes in this nature as far as it is able? While this nature is present everywhere in its entirety, it is not perceived as a whole in every individual thing due to the weakness of the recipient <note>original: *infirmitate subiecti* - literally "the weakness of the subject," referring to the limited capacity of physical matter to hold divine perfection</note>. It is present within the universe, but not in the way a physical triangle is—which is somehow the same form repeated in many separate instances—but rather like the *immaterial* Triangle itself, upon which all physical triangles depend. But why is the physical triangle not everywhere, if the immaterial one flourishes everywhere? Because not all matter is made a participant; it has something else within it as well. For not everything is immediately suited to every form; first, it applies to the primary categories <term>genera prima - the "Great Kinds" of Being (Being, Rest, Motion, Sameness, and Difference) defined by Plato</term>, and then through these to the rest. The higher nature was equally present to the whole.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> The nature that gives, being caused by that one, and stretching out equally with it, is a power that approaches. That higher one makes things more numerous in proportion to how far they are extended. What is it that partakes of this universal as much as it can? That which is present, in which the power of the subject exists through the whole. <margin>B</margin> It is present in this way, as the material triangle is many in number but the same form; or rather, as that from which the things in matter derive. Why then is the immaterial triangle everywhere? Because all matter participates, yet each piece of matter has something different toward the whole. It does not go to all things immediately, but to the first things, then to others. The whole is present.

---

->*Life in the world is twofold, namely intellectual and animal: it is also entirely free from all physical mass, possessed of such infinite efficacy that it occupies all parts of the world-machine equally, remaining itself whole and indivisible.*<-

### Chapter XII.

->*Your soul also, although it is attached to your body through lower powers, would nevertheless exist through the intellect, and as a "middle" through reason. When, therefore, reason turns both itself and the lower powers toward the intellect, it becomes the whole universe. Then you do not fall away from that life of the universe reigning everywhere, because you yourself are made almost similar to it. Everywhere there are also all the gods, the rulers of souls and cities, directing all things to the First.*<-

---

BUT how is it present? Truly, as a single life. For life in a living creature does not extend only to a certain boundary beyond which it cannot progress; rather, it pours itself through the entire being. If anyone should ask again how, they must remember that the power of life itself does not have a specific "size"; indeed, if you were to divide it infinitely in thought, you would always encounter that same, fundamentally infinite power. For life itself does not possess matter, which would cause it to fail or shrink from a large mass into a small one. If, therefore, you grasp the infinity perpetually flourishing within it—a nature untiring and utterly unconquered, never failing within itself, like a life overflowing—do you think there is anywhere you could look or fix your mind where you would not find it? Quite the opposite: you will not pass beyond it by moving forward, nor will you stop at some small stage as if it had nothing more to give because it was gradually running out. But if you are able to join with it—or rather, if you stand within the whole and seek nothing beyond it—only then will you grasp its presence everywhere. Otherwise, if you cannot or refuse to do this, you will immediately fall away into something else, slipping from what is present, and failing to notice it because you are looking elsewhere. But if you seek nothing beyond, how will you emerge in such a state? Truly, by having approached the whole, rather than remaining in a part of it. You must not even say, "I am only this much." For when you speak of "this much" <note>original: *tantum* - referring to a specific quantity or limit</note>, you have left the whole behind. You have become the whole, even though you were already the whole before. But because something else was added to you besides and after the whole...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> How then is it present? As life is in a living thing up to a certain point. Then it cannot reach further, but is everywhere. Again, how? By remembering that power has no size. But if you divide it infinitely in your mind, it always has the same infinite power within. <margin>B</margin> For life is not in matter, such that it fails into a small space along with the mass of matter. If you take the ever-flowing infinity in it, untiring and unwearied, it nowhere fails within itself, like a life boiling over. Do you think you can go anywhere or turn to anything where you will not find it? It would not happen to you, for you cannot go beyond it. You will not stop at a small part, as if it failed to give because it was running out bit by bit. <margin>C</margin> If you go toward something else, you will fall away while it is still present, but by looking at that other thing. But if you seek nothing else, how will you experience this? By approaching the whole and not staying in a part of it, nor saying "this is who I am, I am this much." For by letting go of "this much," you become the whole, and yet you were already the whole before. But because something else was added to you after the whole...

<summary>Plotinus explains that the Divine Life is an infinite power without physical size, present everywhere as a complete whole rather than divided into parts. He argues that a person "becomes" the entire universe by turning their reason toward the intellect and letting go of their identification with limited, individual boundaries.</summary>

# BOOK FIVE. 671

...you became smaller by such an addition. <margin>A</margin> For your addition was not from the whole; you can never add anything to that. Rather, your addition was from that which is "not-the-whole." But when someone becomes a particular thing and comes from "not-being," he is not the Whole. But when you let go of "not-being," you then increase yourself by letting go of other things. The Whole is present to you when you let go of the rest. While you are with other things, it does not shine upon you; it did not "arrive" in order to be present. Rather, it was you who departed when it seemed absent. Even if you departed, you did not leave it behind, for it is present everywhere; nor did you go anywhere else. Instead, while still being present, you simply turned yourself toward the opposite things. <margin>B</margin> For in the same way, the other gods, though they are present to many, often appear to only one, because that one alone is able to look upon them. But while these gods, in all their various forms, are present everywhere and turn cities toward better things, the cities themselves are ultimately turned toward that supreme being. To Him the whole earth and the whole heaven are turned; they remain everywhere near Him and in Him, <margin>C</margin> having from Him their existence and the things that truly exist, being connected to Him all the way down to soul and life, and united in one through His infinite magnitude.

<column-break/>

...you became smaller by an addition of this kind. For your addition was not from the universe: for you can never add anything to that; but rather it was from that which is not the universe. Indeed, whoever becomes a specific "someone," and does so from "not-being," is at that moment least of all the universe. But he truly exists as the universe when he has completely dismissed "not-being." You increase yourself, therefore, when you dismiss other things; then the universe is present to you when you dismiss the rest. But while you are together with the rest, it does not shine for you. When it does shine, it does not "approach" to be present; rather, you had departed from it when it was not there. If you had departed, it was not from the One—for that is present everywhere—nor did you go off to any other place; rather, even while you were present, you turned yourself away toward the opposites. By the same logic, the other gods may be equally present with many people, yet they appear to only one: because he alone of all of them is able to look up at them. But these gods of every kind, being present everywhere, turn cities toward better things; and the cities are finally turned toward that celestial being. To Him the whole earth is turned, and finally the heavens, remaining everywhere in His power and in Him. From Him, moreover, those things which truly are have their very being, being utterly annexed to Him even down to soul and life. And even that which I just called "being" <note>original: *ens* - existence or being</note> joins together into the One by means of His infinite magnitude.

### BOOK SIX.
### ON NUMBERS.
->On numbers.<-

> *If the Good itself is the One, and they are the same, then multiplicity rightly departs further from the One and from union, and thus becomes worse. Therefore, if a multiplicity is imagined to be either infinite or in any way devoid of unity, it will be evil itself. Chapter I.*
> *Any separate form and the "Idea" of anything is most unified with itself, since its essence is simple and individual. A natural form <note>meaning a physical or biological form in the material world</note> is less unified with itself because it is extended through the parts of a body, even as long as it keeps its continuity: therefore it is less good. A discrete multiplicity <note>a collection of separate things</note> that happens through the breaking of continuity has the least unity: therefore it is an evil. That which is imagined to preserve no union at all is called the greatest evil.*

672 PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.

<columns>2</columns>

For is there evil in magnitude? Surely, if it could feel, evil would be apparent in it. For that thing would feel that it has already wandered far from itself. Truly, each thing seeks not another, but itself. But the progression toward external things is either in vain or certainly forced. Each thing truly exists most of all, not when it becomes many or great, but when it belongs to itself; and it belongs to itself when it looks only toward itself. <margin>B</margin> But that which desires to become great in this way ignores what is truly great <note>original: "magnum" / "μέγα". In Neoplatonism, "Magnitude" often refers to physical extension or bulk, which Plotinus contrasts with the spiritual "greatness" of unity.</note>, and it hurries to where it should not, but breaks out toward the exterior. To turn toward oneself, however, is to remain continually within. This is especially evidenced by that which is produced by magnitude. For if it is pulled outward, so that each of its parts exists separately, they will indeed be individual parts, but not properly that which it was from the beginning. But if it is to be itself, all parts must turn toward the one, so that it exists when it is in some way one, not when it is great. Therefore, because of magnitude itself, and insofar as it is in it, it is lost to itself. But insofar as it possesses unity, it also possesses itself. Nevertheless, the universe is great and beautiful; but it is beautiful precisely because it has not been allowed to escape entirely into infinity, but is held together by unity. Now, it is beautiful not indeed by magnitude itself, but rather by beauty; therefore, it required beauty precisely because it was made great. For if this were destitute of beauty itself, insofar as it is great, it would be foul; and thus this very magnitude needs ornament. Therefore, that which is great, if it is more [of itself], is also more foul <note>The Latin text here suggests that without the limiting power of beauty/unity, larger size only leads to greater ugliness or lack of form.</note>.

---

*If an infinite multitude is imagined, it will not properly be a number. For the number of beings in the incorporeal world is fixed, and from there it is limited in the corporeal world; nor does the numbering mind actually create or increase the numbers that it gathers, but they are naturally limited on both sides within it. <margin>Chapter II.</margin>*

<margin>A</margin> ## WHAT THEN should be said of that which is called the number of infinity? But first we must ask how it can be a number if it is infinite. For the things subject to the senses are not infinite. Therefore, neither is the number which is in them infinite. Furthermore, neither does the one who counts enumerate infinity itself; but although he computes double and triple, and thereafter similarly multiples, he certainly defines these. And if he takes the multiplication toward the future or the past, he seems meanwhile to define these as well. <margin>B</margin> Should we then say that number is not simply infinite, but only in such a way that it is always permitted to add to it? But surely the authority for generating numbers does not reside in the one who counts; rather, the numbers were already determined and existed entirely. Now, in the intelligible world, just as beings are determined, so too is a definite number designated by the number of beings. But we, just as we make a "man" many by often applying to him both "beauty" and other things of that kind, so along with any image, <margin>C</margin> we also conceive an image of number. And just as we multiply a city that does not exist, so we are accustomed to multiply numbers, as if we were counting in time; using these numbers which we possess, we translate them into times, while the numbers themselves remain within us.

<column-break/>

The danger in magnitude, or its weakness, is that which has become a certain thing and departs from itself, or would feel [this departure] if it were sentient. For each thing seeks not another, but itself. The outward journey is either in vain or forced. A thing is more truly itself not when it becomes many or great, but when it is with itself. And it is with itself when it is inclined toward itself. The desire for magnitude belongs to one who is ignorant of what is truly great, and who hastens where he should not, namely toward the outside. But turning toward oneself is to stay within. Evidence for this is that which becomes great; if it is pulled apart so that each of the parts exists, those things will be individual parts, but not the original whole. But if it is to be itself, all parts must be directed toward the one, so that it is a whole when it is unmixed with magnitude. For it is through magnitude that it perishes from itself, but by the one, it possesses itself. The universe is indeed great and beautiful, but it is such because it was prevented from fleeing into infinity, and was encompassed by the one. It is beautiful not by magnitude, but by beauty. It stood in need of beauty because it became great. Since, if it were left desolate of beauty, as far as it was great, it would appear ugly. So magnitude is the matter of beauty. Therefore, that which is great is more in need of order; rather, magnitude itself is more ugly.

---

## WHAT THEN about the so-called number of infinity? But first, how is it a number, if sensible things are not infinite? So there is no infinite number in them, because the one counting does not count infinity, but even if he makes things double or multiple, he defines them. And if he takes things toward the future or the past, he likewise defines them. Is it then not simply infinite, but so that it is always possible to take more? Or is the power of generating not in the one who counts, but rather is already limited? And in the intelligible world <note>original: "νοητῷ" (noētō). The realm of pure thought or divine intellect in Greek philosophy.</note>, just as beings are, so there is a limited number as great as the beings. But we, when we make "many" of "man" by applying to him often "the beautiful" and other things, so with each image, we also conceive an image of number. And as the multiplication of a city is a mental projection, so in the same way we make numbers multiple and count them in relation to times, using the numbers we have; we apply them to times, while they remain within us.

<summary>Plotinus argues that physical size (magnitude) is a form of dispersion that leads away from the self, while beauty and true existence are found in unity. He then begins an inquiry into whether number can be infinite, concluding that in the divine mind, numbers are fixed and finite, though humans can count toward infinity in time.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book VI, Treatise 6 of Plotinus's Enneads, specifically focusing on the nature of number, multiplicity, and infinity. # BOOK SIX.

->*The intelligible world <note>The realm of pure ideas and divine intellect, as opposed to the physical world.</note>, since it proceeded from unity itself into a multitude of ideas, is not the Good itself; yet multiplicity there is not an evil, because it is overcome by the One. For there is one common and indivisible nature of all ideas, and every idea is united with all. Chapter III.*<-

*Infinity itself has no actual being of its own; otherwise, it would be counted among the category of beings, and being designated there, it would therefore be defined. For this reason, it would no longer actually be infinity; nevertheless, something that always sets a limit lies hidden under an infinite term. Therefore, if you ever remove all forms—as if they were terms and boundaries—from the middle, that which remains in the imagination is called infinity. If you grasp this, you are already defining it; if you define it, you do not grasp infinity. Finally, if you run through all types of opposites at will, you will assign neither of the opposites separately to infinity, otherwise you will have soon defined it for yourself: and again, you will be able to call either of the opposites in it by the negation of the other.*

---

<margin>A</margin> But the infinite—how does it exist, being infinite? Is it because it exists already in number and deficiency? But first, among those things which truly exist by nature, how can multiplicity <note>original: "πλῆθος" (plethos) / "multitudo". A key term for the "Many" that emerges from the "One."</note> be an evil? Is it because in the immaterial realm, multiplicity is prevented from being truly multiple, because it is truly one? And because of this, it is diminished in relation to the One, because it possesses multiplicity. And as far as it looks toward the One, and does not possess that nature, but has stepped out from it, it is diminished. But by the power of the One, it possesses something venerable, and the multiplicity has turned back toward the One, or remained there.

But how does infinity exist? For it must either be defined among the things that exist, or if it is not defined, it is not among the things that exist. But perhaps it is among things that are coming into being, as is the case with time; or if someone wishes, let it be infinite. For either there is a limit, or the infinite is defined. For there is something else between the limit and the infinite, which receives the nature of a boundary. But the infinite itself flees the idea of a limit, yet it is captured like an image when encompassed from the outside. It does not flee into another place from one place; for it does not even have a place. But when a place is established by another, it is then that it must be placed. Or some other of the things said of it from itself belongs to it. So that it might be moved. But it stands still in itself, becoming later in that which is produced. But it seems that the motion of infinity itself is spoken of as being outside, because it does not remain. From which it has its exterior, as if being suspended in the same place, or as if each thing is hovering and the power is the same—both indeed, as they are judged in the same way, both that which is suspended and that which declines. What then would someone think of it? Perhaps by separating the form from it in thought. What then will he think? Perhaps opposites at the same time, and not opposites. For he will think both large and small. For it becomes both. And standing and moving, for these things happen; but concerning the process of becoming, it is clear that neither is defined. But if you do not define it, insofar as it is infinite, and these things are infinitely and indefinitely there, both would certainly appear.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> BUT how did this infinite exist, since it is infinite? For that which has come to exist is already encompassed by number: but first it must be investigated, if multiplicity is truly placed in the order of true beings, how multiplicity might be an evil. But truly, multiplicity there is united, nor is it permitted to escape entirely into a multitude, since there multiplicity is one being: and yet for this very reason it degenerates from the One, and yields to it, because it has multiplicity, and as far as it looks toward the One, it falls into a lower state. And since it does not have the nature of the One, but has fallen away from it, it deservedly undergoes a defect: but by the virtue of the One itself, it has something to be honored within it, namely that the multiplicity has been converted toward the One, and has stood firm.
<margin>B</margin> But how can infinity itself be there? For if it has being, it is already defined in the order of beings: or certainly, unless it were defined, it is not to be placed in the category of beings, but perhaps
<margin>C</margin> it will seem to be counted in the order of those things which are becoming, just as happens in time. Perhaps also even if it is defined, because of this very thing it is also infinite: for not the boundary, but the infinite is determined: nor is any other thing placed between the infinite and the boundary, which might take on the nature of a boundary. This infinite indeed flees the very idea of a boundary, but is grasped as if surrounded from the outside: but it flees not into another place from another, for it does not have any place: but when it is grasped,
<margin>D</margin> then for the first time a place has existed. For which reason it is not to be thought that motion, which is attributed to infinity in speech, is a place, nor that any other of those things which are usually named happens to it from itself. Therefore it is never moved, but neither again does it remain. For where would it remain, since this very thing which is called "where" arises later?
<margin>E</margin> It seems, however, that motion is attributed to infinity because it does not stand still. Is it then so that it is suspended on high in the same place, revolving itself? Or is it rather both raised up there and tossed about even to this point? In no way. For both of these are judged in relation to the same place, both that which is raised up without declining belongs to the same place, and also that which declines. What then will someone think infinity to be? Surely he will think of it then, when the intellect has separated the form <note>original: "speciem" / "εἶδος". The specific defining characteristics of a thing.</note>. What then will he understand? Perhaps opposites at the same time, and not opposites: for he will understand the large there and the small: for it becomes both; the standing, clearly, and the moved, for these things happen there: but before they happen, it is certain that it is neither of those things determinately, otherwise you would have already limited it. If therefore that nature is infinite, and these things which I just mentioned are there infinitely and indeterminately, so they both clearly appear there...

<summary>Plotinus explores the metaphysical status of the "infinite," arguing that in the divine realm of Ideas, multiplicity is redeemed by its orientation toward the One. He explains that infinity is what remains when Form is mentally stripped away, existing as a state of indeterminate potentiality before it is captured by a boundary.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation in Ennead VI, Treatise 6, "On Numbers." Having previously discussed the nature of the "One" and the "Infinite," Plotinus now examines whether numbers exist as independent realities in the Divine Mind (the Intelligible World) or if they are merely concepts created when the human soul counts objects.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK VI.

...they will flee. But if you approach that place and do not apply any limit with which you might catch it, it will immediately slip away from you, and you will find nothing there; otherwise, you have already defined it. Indeed, if you encounter it as one, it suddenly appears as many. But if you say it is many, you will again be lying: for where each thing is not one, then all things are not even many. And this is the very nature of infinity <note>original: "infinitatis" / "ἀπειρία". Plotinus is describing the "Indefinite Dyad," a state of pure potentiality before it is limited by form.</note>: so that according to one mental image it is motion, but insofar as the imagination has reached it, it is rest. Now, the very fact that you cannot look upon it by itself is a kind of motion and a falling away from the Mind. But because it cannot flee, but is held together from the outside—so much so that it is not permitted to cross the boundaries—it must be judged as a kind of rest. From this it appears that one may affirm not only motion there, but rest.

---

->*A question: Do unity and numbers in the intelligible world <note>The "intelligible world" (mundus intelligibilis) refers to the realm of pure Ideas or Forms, the highest level of reality accessible to the intellect rather than the senses.</note> have their own distinct logic from other Ideas? And if so, do they precede the Ideas and exist in their own right, or do they follow as attendants? It is unlikely they are created by the counting mind.* Chapter IV.<-

<margin>A</margin> Next, we must consider the condition in which numbers exist in the intelligible world. Are they, perhaps, implanted in the other species <note>The "Forms" or "Species" (eide) of things like Justice, Beauty, or Man.</note>, or are they rather always following them? For instance, after "Being" <note>original: "ens" / "ὂν". The fundamental existence of all things.</note> is established as the first thing there, we then think of unity. Then, since motion and rest follow from Being, we recognize three things, and so on through each of the others, we recognize any number. Or perhaps it is not so, but a certain unity is born with each thing? Or is there unity in the first principle, and in that which comes after it, duality—clearly a specific order? Or is the number as great as the multitude of each thing—for instance, if there are ten, then there is a "decad" (the number ten itself)? Or perhaps it is not so, but number is conceived in itself? And if so, we must investigate whether it is the first of all things or the last. Now Plato <note>Refers to Plato's *Timaeus* (39b), where he suggests humans learned to count by observing the cycle of days and nights.</note> said that men learned number from the very variation of days and nights, and thus he attributed the knowledge of number to the variation of things. He might, therefore, confess that the things to be numbered first create number because of their diversity; thus, number itself consists in a certain "discourse" <note>original: "discursu" / "μεταβάσει". The step-by-step movement of the mind from one thought to another.</note> of the soul when it runs from one thing to another. In this view, number is created when the soul counts. This happens when the soul, running through the things themselves, asserts within itself that this is one thing and that is another; for as long as it thinks of one and the same thing, it asserts nothing other than that specific "one." However, when Plato says that "Essence" <note>original: "essentia" / "οὐσία". The true substance or reality of a thing.</note> exists in true number, and number in essence, he is again accepting a certain subsistence of number in itself. He would not affirm that number is born only in the counting soul; rather, he would say that the notion of number is recalled in the soul from the very variety and distraction found in sensible things.

---

->*A refutation of those who say that unity and number are not real things, but are merely names for when things are called "one" individually, and then "one" again, and that this repetition is called "number."* Chapter V.<-

From this opinion, we have no logic to discern the different types of numbers, nor to reduce any number to a single principle of numbers; indeed, number itself would be thought of as less than even an "accident" <note>A philosophical term for a non-essential quality, like being "tall" or "red."</note>. When we predicate "one" of a man, the "one" is something other than the man; for the "one" itself does not have the multitude opposed to it, and it is predicated commonly of all things beyond just man. It is, therefore, more common, simpler, and prior to all things; it is even prior to "Being" itself for a similar reason: especially because "one" is predicable not only of Being, but of anything whatsoever—whether you think of something higher or lower than Being, or even something opposed to Being. Since, therefore, beings are referred back to Being itself, but numbers are referred back to a "One" that is higher than Being, numbers rightly seem to be prior to beings.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> And if you approach [the infinite] without casting your thought like a net, it will escape you; for if you have defined it, you have already limited it. But if you approach it as one, it will appear as many; and if you say "many," you will again be lying. For since each part is not one, then the whole is not many. This nature itself is a movement according to another of the mental images. But insofar as <margin>B</margin> the imagination has approached it, it is a state of rest. And because the soul cannot see it through its own power, it is a movement and a slipping away from the Mind. But the fact that it cannot run away, but is held from the outside and in a circle, and is not permitted to advance further, would be rest. Thus, it is permitted to say it is not only in motion [but also in rest].

---

<margin>A</margin> We must consider the numbers, how they exist in the intelligible realm. Are they things that come upon the other Forms, or do they always accompany them? For example, since Being is such that it is first, we have conceived of the "Monad" <note>original: "μονάδα". The Unity or the number One.</note>. Then, since movement and rest arise from it, there are now three. And so it is for each of the others. Or is it not so, but a single monad was born with each? Or since the first is a monad, and that which is after it is order, is it a "Dyad" <note>The number two.</note>? Or is it as great as the multitude of each—for instance, if ten, a decad? Or not so, but number was conceived by itself? And if so, is it prior to the others or posterior? Now, Plato says the concept of number came to men through the variation of days and nights, attributing the concept to the difference between things. <margin>C</margin> Perhaps he would say that the things to be numbered, through a certain difference, first produce number. And he might say that number itself is constituted in the transition of the soul as it moves through one thing after another. And then number is created by the soul. This is when the soul itself goes through and says to itself "another." But as for the "other," so long as it thinks of something as the "same" and not "other" after it, it is saying "one." But when he says that in the <margin>D</margin> true number, there is also number in essence, he would again be saying that number has a certain subsistence in itself. Even if it does not subsist in the soul that is counting, the concept of numbers is stirred up within the soul by the variation concerning sensible things.

<summary>Plotinus explores whether numbers are objective realities that exist within the divine essence (Forms) or if they are merely mental constructs used by the soul to track variety. He concludes that unity and number are fundamental principles that precede even "Being" itself.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 674 regarding the metaphysical status of numbers. Plotinus is exploring whether numbers are merely mental constructs used for counting or if they possess a "subsistence" (independent existence) in the realm of Ideas. This section specifically addresses the "Decade" (the number ten) and the "Tetrad" (the number four) as ontological realities.</meta>

# BOOK SIX.

Therefore, when we say "ten men," the decade <note>original: "decas" / "δεκάς". A term referring to the number ten treated as a single collective unit or essence.</note> itself is neither the men themselves, nor does it belong to them as a mere accident <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing has (like being tan or tall) which does not change its fundamental nature.</note>; otherwise, it would not be able to measure other things equally. Instead, it exists in itself first, before it is found in the things that are counted as ten. Finally, if some should say that "the One" itself is joined with beings—whether as an accident or as an element—it still follows that it exists in its own right before it either happens to all things in common or is added as an element.

---

What then is this nature itself? Is it an accompaniment, a sort of observation made upon each essence? For example, "man," and "one man," and "being," and "one being"—do these individual intelligible things <note>The "intelligibles" are the eternal, non-physical realities or Forms in Plotinus's system.</note> result in the whole of number? But how can "two" (the dyad) and "three" (the triad) exist there, and how are all things measured according to "the one"? And how would such a number be gathered back into a single unit? Or will there simply be a multitude of units? There is a "one" in which you are placed, besides the "Simple One." Unless, perhaps, someone says that the "dyad" remains that specific thing, or rather, it is something observed in the thing that possesses two powers joined together, like a composite made into one. Or perhaps it is as the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed that numbers were the fundamental building blocks of the universe.</note> seemed to say when they spoke of number by way of analogy.

<margin>Justice</margin>
For instance, they called "justice" the number four <note>original: "quaternarium" / "τετράδα". The Pythagoreans associated the number four with justice because it is the first square number (2x2), representing perfect balance or "evenness."</note>, and other things by other numbers. In that way, rather than focusing on the multitude of the thing being one, they joined the number to it as a single quantity—like a decade—even though we do not usually treat "the ten" in this way. Instead, when we gather things that are distant from one another, we call them "ten." Perhaps we say "ten" in that case, but when one thing is made out of many, we call it a "decade." The same logic applies in the intelligible world. But if this is so, will number have any real existence <note>original: "subsistentia" / "ὑπόστασις". A core philosophical term for "real being" or "underlying reality."</note> if it is only observed in objects?

Yet someone might say: what prevents whiteness, even if only observed in objects, from having its own existence within those objects? Since motion is observed in being, there was a subsistence of motion in whatever amount of being there was. But number does not seem to behave like motion; rather, because motion is a specific "one thing," it is said to be observed in itself.

If such a subsistence exists, it allows number to be a quantity, but it makes it more of a contingent property <note>original: "contingens" / "συμβεβηκός". Often translated as "accident."</note>. And yet, it is not entirely contingent. For a contingency to exist, it must exist *before* it happens to anything; and though it may be inseparable, it must still be something of its own nature, just as "whiteness" is a nature in itself before it is predicated <note>"Predicated" means to assert or declare something about a subject (e.g., in "the ball is white," whiteness is predicated of the ball).</note> of another thing.

<margin>* For it shall now be predicated</margin>
* Now, that which is to be predicated must already exist. So, if "one" is around each thing, "man" is not the same as "one man." Rather, the "one" is something different from "man," and this "one" is common to all things and exists in each of the others. Therefore, the "one" must exist before "man" and each of the others, so that both "man" and each of the others may happen to be "one" individually. This must also be true before motion—if indeed motion is one—and before being, so that being itself might also be "one." I am speaking here not of that "One" which we say is above being <note>Plotinus distinguishes between "The One" (the absolute Source of all) and the mathematical "one" that defines the unity of a single object.</note>, but of this "one" which is predicated of each species.

<margin>* The decade in each.</margin>
* Therefore, the decade itself exists before the things of which "decade" is predicated. This is the Decade-in-Itself. For the decade will not be the thing in which it is observed.

<margin>* Now then</margin>
* But was it then born together with and does it exist together with...

<column-break/>

->A<- What then is the nature of number itself? Is it something following after, seen as if within any essence, like "man" and "one man"? Likewise, "being" and "one being"? And do all intelligible things thus result in the whole of number when taken individually? Truly, if things were so, how would "two-ness" (the dyad) or "three-ness" (the triad) exist there, and how are all things measured according to the one? In what way will a number of this kind be gathered into a single thing?

->B<- For in that case, there will be a certain multitude of units, but no number will be reduced into a unity, except for the "one" which is simply "one" itself. This is unless someone perhaps says that the "dyad" is that thing, or rather that which is considered in it, which has two implicit powers like something composed into a unity—or perhaps like the numbers the Pythagoreans introduced. They certainly seem to describe numbers according to an analogy (that is, a certain proportion), just as they called "justice" the number four, and similarly other things by other numbers.

->C<- By that condition of the thing itself which exists, one might join unity and number to a multitude, so that the "one" is like a decade, even if we do not usually define "the ten" in that way. We are accustomed to saying "ten" when we gather things that are distant from each other. But perhaps we say "ten" in that manner, but when a single thing is made from many, we call it a "decade"—for the same reason it is used there. However, if that is how it happens, will there be any further subsistence of number, since it is only considered within things?

->D<- Someone will perhaps respond that nothing stands in the way, and that since whiteness is only considered in things, the subsistence of whiteness itself is rightly weighed within the things themselves. After all, since motion is considered within being, it follows that there is some subsistence of motion existing within being itself. But truly, number does not seem to behave in the same way as motion; rather, motion is said to be a "one thing" considered in itself.

->E<- Furthermore, that kind of subsistence makes it so that number is not an essence, but rather a contingency—though not entirely a contingency. For a contingency must exist before it happens to something; and even if it is inseparable, it must still be something, possessing a certain nature of its own (like whiteness), and it must be predicated of another while already existing in itself, which then becomes something to be predicated of another.

->F<- For this reason, if "one" is around anything, and "man" is not the same as "one man," but "one" is something other than "man"—and if "one" is common to all things and exists in this way in any of the remaining things—then certainly "one" will be prior to "man" and to any of the rest. Thus, "man" and any of the others can attain being "one" individually. Therefore, it is also prior to motion (if indeed motion is one) and prior to being similarly, so that being itself may be able to be "one." I say this, however, not of that "One" which we judge to be above

---

being, but of this "one" which is predicated of any species. Therefore, the decade itself exists before that of which "decade" is predicated, and this very thing is the Decade itself; for it is not the thing itself, nor is it in the thing in which the decade is observed, that the decade itself will be. Is it then born together with beings, and is it altogether with them...?

<summary>Plotinus argues that numbers like the "Decade" (ten) or "Tetrad" (four) are not just labels we give to groups of objects, but are independent realities (Forms) that exist in the divine Mind before they are applied to physical things. He distinguishes between the absolute "One" and the "unity" that makes an individual thing what it is.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of whether numbers like "the One" or "the Decade" (ten) exist as independent, eternal realities (Forms) or if they are merely attributes of physical things. Plotinus is moving into the relationship between Intellect and the objects of its thought.</meta>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK VI.

...this very "one" itself? But if it is innate [to the thing], or merely like an "accident" <note>In ancient philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change without changing the thing's essence, like being tan or healthy.</note>—just as health is to a man—then health must first be something in its own right, and similarly for that "one." And if someone should say that "the one" is an element of some composite thing, the One itself must first exist as "one-in-itself" so that it can then be combined with something else. Next, if it must first be mixed with another thing that has become "one" because of it, it follows that the result is falsely called "one," because it has actually become two [the thing plus the "one" added to it]. But in the case of the decade <note>original: "decade" / "δεκάδα" — the number ten treated as a single essence or Form.</note>, how does that work? For why would the "one" have need of a decade, if the decade is created by such great power? But if the One shapes the decade like matter, and the presence of the decade makes it both "ten" and "a decade," then the decade must first exist in itself as nothing other than the decade, purely and singularly.

*The species <note>original: "species" / "ειδῶν" — the eternal Forms or Ideas.</note> of things in the primary essence precede the understanding of them by a certain order. Just as objects exist before those who observe them. Therefore, if anyone says that these species are procreated there by the act of intelligence, he must also concede that they are "posterior" [later in time or logic], which is absurd.*

->Chapter VI.<-

*To understand a certain species there—such as justice, rest, motion, and the others—is nothing other than to declare or define that species. Unless this definition is somehow distinct from the thing itself, it is not a true definition. In short, every species there is a property and an act existing and shining with its own vigor. This "flashing out" [emicatio] depends on that source, and within itself it differs by a certain reason; that is its very intelligence.*

<margin>A</margin> But if, beyond the things themselves, "the One" itself and "the Decade" itself exist—and then the intelligible things exist—apart from the fact that they exist as what they are, some are units, while others are dyads [twos] and triads [threes]; what then will be their nature? And how are they constituted? We must consider that their generation is fulfilled by a certain rational order. First, then, we must generally consider that the essence of the species [the Forms] does not come into existence because a thinker first understood each individual thing, and then the act of thinking produced their substance. <margin>B</margin> For it is not because the Intellect knew what justice was that justice arose. Nor because it thought what motion was did motion arise. If that were so, this very act of thinking would have to be "posterior" [later] than the thing being thought—just as the thought of justice would be later than justice itself. And yet, conversely, the act of thinking is prior to that which is produced by thinking, if indeed the thing exists for the very reason that it was thought. <margin>D</margin> But if justice is entirely the same thing as such a thought, it would be absurd for justice to be nothing other than a description of itself. For what else is it to have "understood" justice or motion than to have grasped a description of what each is? This would be like grasping the logic [ratio] of things that do not even exist, which is impossible. Therefore, if someone argues that in things separated from matter, knowledge and the thing known are the same, that statement must be understood with a condition: he must not assert that the knowledge is the thing itself, nor that the logic contemplating the thing is the thing being contemplated. <margin>E</margin> But rather, the thing itself, when separated from matter, is an "intelligible" and exists as intelligence. I do not mean the intelligence that acts as a "reason" for the thing, or a mere gaze directed at it, but that the thing itself in the intelligible world is intellect and knowledge. For knowledge there does not simply turn toward the thing to understand...

<column-break/>

...as it is. But if it was born together with it, as <margin>A</margin> a world like health is to a man, * grant that it is health itself, and the ones that are like elements; suppose the one, it must first be one and according to itself <margin>B</margin> in order to be with another. Then if it must be first, not in another that has become one through it, that [result] would be falsely called one, making itself two. In the case of the decade, how? For what need does * that [One] have of the decade, if it is a decade through such great power? But if it will form it like matter, and the presence of the decade makes it ten and a decade? It is necessary that before the decade exists in itself, it is nothing other than the decade alone.

<margin>A</margin> But if, on the other hand, before the things themselves there is the One itself and the decade itself, and since things are what they are after being, some are monads [units], others are dyads, and others are triads, what would their nature be? And how is it composed? We must think that their birth is made of certain things whose essence and each of the species we must grasp: that it exists not because someone thought of it <margin>B</margin> or had understood it, and then the thought itself provided their species. For it was not because he knew what justice is that it came to be. Nor because he thought of motion did motion subsist. For in that way the thought would have to be either later than the thing thought, later than justice itself, or justice itself. And again, motion would be prior to the thought of its subsistence, if it came to be for someone. But if such a thought is the same as justice, <margin>D</margin> first it is absurd that justice is nothing other than its own definition. For what is it to think of justice, or motion, or to grasp what it is? It is the same as taking the account [logos] of a thing that does not subsist, which is impossible. But if one says that in the case of things without matter, knowledge is the same as the thing, it must be said in this way: that knowledge is the thing, or that the account [logos] which will be contemplated is the thing itself. <margin>E</margin> But conversely, the thing itself being without matter is something intelligible; not as if it were a "reason" for the thing, or an approach to it, but the very being existing in the intelligible world—what else is it but intellect and knowledge? For knowledge itself again [turns] toward...

<summary>Plotinus argues that metaphysical "Numbers" and "Forms" (like Justice or the Decade) exist as independent realities prior to being thought of or applied to physical objects. He concludes that in the divine mind, the object of thought and the act of thinking are identical, rather than one creating the other.</summary>
