<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous chapter regarding how the Forms (Species) exist within the Divine Intellect. It transitions from discussing the nature of numbers and knowledge to the concept of the "All-Form" or the "Universal Living Being" which contains all things in a state of perfect unity.</meta>

# BOOK SIX. 677
Ll i

<margin>A</margin> The thing itself in that realm <note>The "intelligible world," the realm of eternal truths.</note> ensures that knowledge is not distinct from the object of knowledge, as is the case with the knowledge of material things. This is what it means to produce true knowledge: not to present an image of the thing, but the thing itself. <margin>A</margin> Therefore, the understanding of movement did not create the movement itself; rather, movement itself created the understanding. For this reason, it conceived of itself as both movement and understanding. For movement in that realm is the understanding of that Being, and is movement itself because it is primary. For there is nothing else before it. <margin>B</margin> It is also movement in reality because it does not happen to something else <note>It is not an "accident" or a secondary property of another object.</note>, but is the actual activity of the existing thing. For this reason, it is also essence, which seems to differ from Being itself only by a certain way of thinking. Then there is a certain understanding of Justice, which is like a disposition or state of that mind—or rather, a kind of activity whose face is so truly beautiful that neither the Morning Star <note>original: "Lucifer"</note> nor the Evening Star <note>original: "Hesperus"</note>, nor anything else among sensible things, shines so brightly. <margin>C</margin> It is like an intellectual statue, standing out from itself and

<column-break/>

The thing itself in that realm causes that knowledge to not be so different from the thing itself, as knowledge of a material thing usually is. This is to produce true knowledge: to not bring an image of the thing, but the thing itself. <margin>A</margin> Therefore, the understanding of movement did not create movement itself, but movement rather created the understanding; wherefore it conceived of itself as movement and understanding. For movement there is the understanding of that being, and it is movement itself, because it is first. For there is no other before <margin>B</margin> it. It is also truly movement, since it does not belong to another, but is the act of the existing thing which is there considered to be moved in some way. Therefore, it is also essence, which seems to differ from Being itself by a certain mental conception. Then truly there is a certain understanding of justice, like a disposition and affection of that mind, or rather a certain act of such a kind, whose face is truly beautiful, so that neither the Morning Star nor the <margin>C</margin> Evening Star, nor anything else of those things which are sensed, shines so much. It is like an intellectual statue, standing out from itself and 

->shining in itself, or rather, consisting in itself.<-

---

->*If you were to subtract extended matter from the corporeal world, but preserve the various forms of things in one living form of the world, you would see one "all-form," where all forms in each part are most united and yet most distinct, all things living in one living being. Chapter VII.*<-

### Chapter VII.

->*The universe is therefore of this kind, both in its nature and in the intellectual soul, and also in the intellect, in which the species reside. So that things are truly distinct and truly understood before the contrivance of intelligence, they are thus distinct in act, though united in nature, just as in fire there is light, shimmering, and heat: for all species there are acts.*<-

---

<margin>* Living Being</margin>
**Universally** one must contemplate those things in one nature, and as all having one nature and embracing them from all sides. There, it is not as it is in the sensible region where each thing is separate: the sun in one place, and elsewhere another thing. But all are together in one. Since this is the nature of the Mind, the Soul also imitates it. And that which is called Nature <note>The formative power that creates the physical world.</note>, through which and under which each individual thing is generated, is different in different places, while she herself remains together in herself. Though all things are together, each is again separate. But that Intellect which possesses them sees those things within, which are in essence and being; not merely looking at them, but possessing them, and not separating each one. For the individual things are already and always distinct within it. Among those who admire these things too much, we gain their trust by pointing to the things that participate in them. We are accustomed to judge the magnitude and beauty of that world from the love the soul has for it. And also from the love of those things that strive toward the soul because of such a nature, and from the fact that through the soul they attain some likeness to that higher realm. Now, it is a sacrilege to deny that a beautiful living being exists, unless that Living Being <note>original: "animal" / "ζῶον"</note> itself has a certain wonderful and inestimable beauty. That universal Living Being is surely absolute, consisting of all living things—or rather, containing all living things in itself—being one and at the same time as many as all things are. Just as this universe of ours is one, and is all that is visible, embracing all things that are in the visible region.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **To contemplate** those things, it is necessary to look at them entirely in one nature, and as one nature possessing all things everywhere and embracing them from all sides. There, certainly not as it happens in the sensible region where each thing is separate—in one place the sun, in another the moon, and elsewhere something else—but all things are together in one: for this is the nature of the mind itself. Since even the soul imitates the mind in this way: and that which is called nature, according to which and under which individual things <margin>B</margin> are generated, is in one place one thing and in another another, while that nature remains together in itself. Although all things are together, each is again separate. But he who possesses the intellect sees those things which are within in the mind and essence, not indeed looking at them, but rather having them, nor again separating each one. For the individual things are always already distinct in it. Therefore, among those who admire these things excessively, we gain trust from those things which participate in them: we are accustomed to guess and affirm the magnitude of that world and its beauty from the love of the soul itself for it. Furthermore, from the love of those things which strive toward the soul, on account of a certain nature of this kind, and also from the fact that through it they follow some likeness to that world. Now truly it is a crime to confess that some beautiful animal exists, unless the Living Being <note>The "Animal-itself" or the Form of Living Being.</note> itself has a wonderful and inestimable beauty. That universal Living Being is surely perfect, made of all living beings, or rather containing all living beings in itself, and being one and at the same time as many as all things are: just as this universe of ours is one, and is all that is visible, embracing all things that are in the visible region.

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS, BOOK VI.

*True essence is a certain power beyond material bulk, grounded in itself, a self-living intellect. It is called the "intellectual animal," wherein all numbers exist before the act of the mind and even...* <note>The "intellectual animal" refers to the *Animal-Itself*, the divine blueprint of all living things.</note>

### Chapter VIII.

<margin>A</margin> Since, therefore, the Living Being is primary, and for that reason the self-existent Living Being is the Intellect, it constitutes true essence. It possesses all living things and holds every number—Justice itself, Beauty itself, and others of that kind. For we speak of "Man-Himself" there in one way, "Number-Itself" in another, and "Justice-Itself" in another. It is certainly worth considering how each of these relates to the others, or what each is, as far as such things can be discovered. To begin, it is proper to set aside all sensation and to contemplate the Intellect with the Intellect itself. We must observe, furthermore, that within us, life and intellect do not consist of physical bulk, but in a certain power devoid of bulk. True essence is released from physical mass and similar things; it is a power grounded in itself. It is not something thin or weak, but is the most intellectual and vital of all things. Nothing can be more intellectual, more vital, or (if I may say so) more essential than this. Thus, whatever reaches this reality attains these same qualities in a way. To the degree that one reaches it step by step, one attains it: whoever touches it more closely brings back things more intimate; whoever is more distant brings back things more remote. Accordingly, if "being" is something to be desired, then that which is "more being" is more greatly to be desired. Similarly, if intelligence simply is to be chosen, then that which is "most intellect" is most especially to be chosen; and by these same degrees, life also is to be sought. Therefore, if "Being itself" is to be taken first (since it is the first), "Intellect" second, and the "Living Being" third—for this third seems to already embrace all things. Intellect, however, holds the second place, for it is the "activity" of essence. Certainly, Number itself is not thought to exist after the Living Being; for already Number must be established after the Intellect. For...

*Just as the One precedes Being, so Number, existing within Being itself, precedes specific beings—that is, the particular Ideas. Through the number that is counted within beings, there exists a Number residing in its own source: which is surely the cause that allows it to be derived into various beings and species.*

### Chapter IX.

*Through Number itself, which is an essential power and a certain distinguishing act of Being, it is defined—in one of the stages—that many beings flow forth from the One. Again, it determines how many and in what orders they are distributed. But that Number is folded within beings, yet unfolded among them: this is "substantial number." The number used in common counting is merely an image of this higher Number. Beings are grounded in Number, Number in Being, and Being in the One, so that it might not be immediately scattered.* <note>Plotinus uses "substantial number" to mean the divine logic that gives structure to reality, as opposed to simple arithmetic.</note>

<margin>A</margin> It remains, therefore, to investigate whether Essence, by some partition of itself, produced Number, or whether Number instead partitioned Essence. Did Essence, Movement, Stability, Sameness, and Difference generate Number, or did Number generate them? The starting point of our consideration will be this: Is it possible for Number to exist in itself, or must we see "two" only in two things and "three" only in three things, and similarly consider the "One" as something inserted into numbers? For if Number could exist in itself, apart from the things being numbered, it could surely exist before Beings. Can Number, then, exist even before Being? But perhaps it is better for the present to concede that Being precedes Number, and that Number proceeds from Being.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Since, therefore, the Living Being—and because of this, the self-existent Life—is also truly Intellect, we say that it contains all living things within it. And Justice, and Beauty, and all such things. Thus, we speak of "Man-Himself" and "Number-Himself." We must consider how each of these is a Being, so far as it is possible to see into this genus. We must leave behind all sense-perception... <note>The Greek text here mirrors the Latin precisely, though the transcription is fragmented.</note>

<margin>B</margin> ...and we must contemplate it, for life and intellect are not in bulk, but in power. True essence is lacking in nothing, being a power established in itself. It is not a fleeting thing, but the most intellectual of all, than which nothing is more vital, more essential...

<margin>C</margin> ...near to the nearer, and far from the farther. If being is not desired, that which is most "being" is most... and intellect is above all thinking... and similarly, if Being is first, then we must take Being, then Intellect, then the Living Being; for this seems to contain all.

<margin>D</margin> ...indeed, that which is before it in the Living Being, or in the Intellect. For before it is Essence in...

...and before itself was the One, and the Two was before the Mind; Being is One.

### Chapter IX.

<margin>A</margin> It remains then to consider whether Essence generated Number... or if Number generated Essence. And if Essence, Movement, Stability, Sameness, and Difference [generated] Number itself... The beginning of the inquiry: Is it possible for Number to exist by itself, or must "three" be seen in three things?

<margin>B</margin> ...and indeed the One, which is in numbers. For if they [numbers] can exist apart from the things numbered, they could exist before Beings. Is Number before Beings? Or is this [Being] first? And before the numbered...

<meta>The catchword "considering, and we must grant number comes from being" indicates the argument will continue to prioritize the unity of Being over the plurality of Number in the following section.</meta>

He explores the hierarchy of reality, questioning whether the concept of Number creates the diversity of things or if Number arises from the nature of Being itself.</summary>

# BOOK SIX.

<page-num>679</page-num>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But if Being is one, and two beings are two beings, the One will precede the Being. <note>original Greek: "τὸ ἓν" (to hen) and "τὸ ὂν" (to on). Plotinus is playing on the linguistic and metaphysical link between "The One" (the source) and "Being" (existence).</note> And as for the number of beings, from where does it arise? Is it from a concept in the mind and an act of perception, or does it come from actual substance? We must consider it in this way: when someone thinks of a man as being one, and a beautiful thing as one, he surely thinks of the "one" after the fact in each case. And so too when he thinks of a horse and a dog; here the "two" clearly comes later in his mind. <margin>B</margin> But if one were to generate a man, and generate a horse and a dog, or bring forth those existing in oneself—not just by chance, but producing and bringing them forth—would you not say that one must go to one, and then move on to another one, and so make two, and then another one? Or rather, even before the beings were made, were they already numbered? Was it clear how many there ought to be, specifically how many it was necessary to be? Therefore, all number existed before the beings themselves. But if it preceded the beings, then number was not the beings; instead, it was already in Being, though it was not yet the number of that specific being, for that Being was still one. <margin>D</margin> But the power of number itself, having its own substance, divided Being into many parts, and, as it were, pushed it to give birth to a multitude. Thus, either essence itself or activity will be number, and the Living Being itself and the Intellect will be number. Perhaps, then, Being is "united number," while beings are "unfolded number." <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "νῦς" (nous). In Neoplatonism, this is the Divine Mind or the second principle of reality.</note> is number moving within itself, and the Living Being is the number that encompasses all. Since Being is born from the One as it existed in that source, <margin>as it was in the Idea</margin> it must itself be a number. For this reason, they <note>Referring to the Pythagoreans or Plato.</note> were accustomed to call the Forms both "unities" and "numbers." This is "essential number." But the other, called "monadic number," <note>Monadic number refers to the abstract numbers we use for counting (1, 2, 3), which Plotinus considers a mere image of the divine, essential numbers.</note> is an image of this. Essential number is seen in the Forms and creates them; it also exists first in Being itself, flourishes together with Being, and precedes the specific beings. In this number, beings have their foundation, their source, their root, and their principle. For the "one" is the principle of <margin>F</margin> Being itself, and in this "one" Being exists; otherwise, it would be immediately scattered. Yet the "one" is not grounded in Being; for then the "one" would already be a "one" before it attained unity, just as something attaining the <margin>E</margin> "decad" <note>A "decad" is the number ten. Plotinus uses it to show that the concept of "Ten-ness" must exist before ten individual items can be grouped together.</note> would be a decad before it actually reached the number ten.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But if Being is one, Being exists, and two beings are similarly two beings, the "one" indeed precedes, and number likewise precedes the beings. Does this precedence occur by a certain notion and perception? Indeed, it occurs by substance. It should be considered thus: when someone understands an existing man as one, and a beautiful thing similarly as one, then he considers the "one" itself as somehow posterior in each. Even more, when he considers a horse and a dog, then and there he clearly notices the "two" as posterior. <margin>B</margin> But if you were to generate a man, and generate a horse and a dog, or bring forth those existing in yourself—not merely as it happens that you generate and produce—would you not say that you must go to one, and then pass to another one, and thus make two, and together with yourself make another also? Now, not even beings, when they are made, are counted after the fact; rather, it was already established how many ought to be made, namely how many it was most fitting to produce. Therefore, all number preceded the beings. But if it preceded the beings, then number was surely not the beings; instead, it was already in Being, yet it was not the number of Being itself, for as yet Being was one. <margin>D</margin> But the very power of number subsisting divided Being into many, and as it were impelled it toward the bringing forth of a multitude: for truly, either the very essence or the act is number, and the Living Being itself and the Intellect are number. Perhaps, then, Being is "unified number," while beings are "unfolded number." Intellect, however, is number acting within itself, and the <term>Living Being</term> <note>original: "animal" / "ζῷον". This refers to the Intelligible Living Being, the cosmic blueprint containing all species.</note> is the number that comprehends all. Since Being is generated from the One as it was in it, <margin>E</margin> it must itself be number in this way. For this reason, they were accustomed to call the species (Forms) both "unities" and "numbers"; and this is "essential number." The other, which is called "monadic"—that is, gathered from certain units—is a kind of image of that. Essential number is partly seen in the species and creates them together; partly, and more primarily, it flourishes in Being itself, exists together with Being, and precedes the beings. In this number, the beings have their firmament, their source, their root, and their principle. For the <margin>F</margin> "one" itself is the principle of Being itself, and in this is Being; otherwise, it would be immediately dissipated. Yet the "one" is not founded in Being; otherwise, it would already be "one" before it attained the "one"; and that which attained the decad would become a decad before it actually reached the decad itself.

---

-> *The nature of the first Being, since it follows the One, is necessarily manifold in its first origin—that is, it is numerical. Through these numbers, it relates to the beings (that is, the Ideas) in much the same way as many teachers say that matter relates to the forms—through the "inchoate forms" generated within it.* <-

---

-> ### Chapter X. <-

That numbers exist before beings is clear, because if number followed after the beings were already established, the numerical distinction and order of beings would happen by mere chance. Furthermore, just as all things that are "beings-through-another" refer back to "Being-in-itself," so whatever is "one-through-another" is reduced to "One-in-itself." But "One-in-itself" cannot be subordinate to Being; otherwise, it would necessarily be manifold—that is, a composite of the nature of Being plus an added property. Therefore, it would not be simply "One-in-itself." Being is therefore subordinate to the One, and similarly, beings are arranged under number; for even above the number which exists in beings, there stands "Number-in-itself," existing before the beings. Finally, in the formal reason of each species, unity and number are necessarily included. I say unity, because in its first sign, a species is indistinct from itself and equally distinct from everything else through unity; and I say number, because a species has a common nature within itself joined with a specific property. From this we clearly learn that unity and number precede all species of things, since the formal reasons of all things consist in unity and number.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's metaphysical investigation into whether Number is a primary reality or merely a human concept used for counting. Having previously established that Number exists within "Being," he now explores how Number acts as a "prefiguration" or blueprint for all existing things.</meta>

### PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.

<page-num>680</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, Being, when it consists in a multitude, becomes **number**; this happens when it is stirred and rises up as something manifold. In a certain sense, it served as a preparation and a prefiguration for existing things, where units seem to hold a place already prepared for the things that are to be established within them. And yet, even now, someone might say: "I certainly desire a great quantity of gold," or perhaps a multitude of other possessions.

<margin>B</margin> Gold, to be sure, is a single kind of thing. But such a person does not wish to make the gold into a number; rather, they wish to make the gold *conform* to a number. Since they already possess the concept of number in their mind, they strive to apply this to the gold, so that the gold happens to become "this much." 

However, if existing things preceded Number, and Number was only observed in them later—moving only as the counting mind moves whenever the things to be counted are multiplied—then the fact that there are as many things as there are now would be a mere matter of chance. There would be no pre-determined plan for why there are exactly as many things as exist. If, therefore, there is a specific total, it is certainly not by chance. **Number**, as that which precedes them, is the cause of their being exactly that many. That is to say: because Number already exists, the things that are created fall under its conditions and become "so many." Thus, every single thing participates in the **One** so that it may exist as an individual. 

<margin>D</margin> Furthermore, Being comes from Being, just as Being is Being from itself; likewise, the One is the One from itself. But if those things which are individually "one" are also many things together, the "one" that is in them is like a **trinity** <note>original Latin: "trinitas"; Greek: "τριὰς" (trias). Here, Plotinus refers to the abstract number three or "three-ness," rather than the theological Trinity.</note> being one, and all beings are "one" in this way. This is not like the "one" that is weighed as a single unit, but rather like how a **thousand** is called "one," or any other number is considered a single total.

<margin>E</margin> Now, consider someone who calculates already-made things and says there are a thousand of them. He does not mean that the things are a thousand or ten thousand by their own nature, as if they were calling out their own names. It is not as if the things themselves display their numbers the way they show their colors. Rather, he judges them so because his own thought dictates the total to him. For if his thought did not dictate it, he would not know how great the multitude was. 

How then does he speak? Surely as one who knows how to count. But he knows this only if he knows Number itself. And he can only know it if Number exists as a reality. Indeed, it would be absurd—even impossible—to suggest that the divine Nature <note>The "Intelligible World" or the realm of the Forms.</note> is ignorant of its own quantity. 

<margin>F</margin> Therefore, if someone speaks of "good things," they either mean things that are good in themselves, or they are predicated "Goodness" of them as an **accident** <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that a thing has, but which is not essential to its basic nature (e.g., a shirt being blue).</note> of those things. If he means the first, he is introducing a **Primary Substance**. But if he refers to things to which "goodness" happens to belong, there must exist a Nature of the Good itself, so that it can also belong to other things. Either the Cause itself, which produces goodness in another, must exist, or the Good itself must exist in its own nature, having generated that which is good.

<margin>G</margin> There is a similar condition in the order of existing things. Whoever speaks of a number, such as a **Decad** <note>term: Decad (Greek: "δεκάδα"). For Neoplatonists, the number ten was the "perfect number" representing the completion of all things.</note>, either names the Decad as something that subsists by itself, or, if he introduces things that happen to be ten, he is forced in turn to place the Decad itself within its own realm, existing as nothing other than the Decad. It is necessary, therefore, if one speaks of beings as a "decad," that either the beings themselves *are* the Decad, or there is another Decad standing above them, which is truly nothing other than the Decad itself.

<margin>H</margin> Generally, whatever is predicated of something else either comes to it from another source or is an act of that thing. And when a quality is such that it is not sometimes present and sometimes absent, but is always with the thing—if that thing is **Essence**, then...

<column-break/>

<note>The Greek text in the right column follows the same argument as the Latin translation above, discussing "arithmos" (number) as a prefiguration ("protypōsis") of beings. It emphasizes that the mind knows quantity only because "Number" exists as a formal reality.</note>

<summary>Plotinus argues that Number is a primary, metaphysical reality (a "substance") that exists before physical objects. He uses the example of the "Decad" (ten) to show that for ten things to exist, the concept of "Ten-ness" must be an objective blueprint in the divine Mind.</summary>

# BOOK SIX.

<page-num>681</page-num>
<sig>q</sig>

<margin>A</margin>...that "One" itself is more truly that [source], or essence itself. But if one could see, it is not even among the things that are. And if that thing <note>original: "πρᾶγμα" (pragma) — referring to the fundamental reality or 'thing' under discussion</note> were able to be thought of without its activity, it would exist simultaneously; nonetheless, in our conception, the activity is placed later. But if it could not be thought of without it—as a human cannot be thought of without the "one," or at least as something later than it—but rather <margin>B</margin> coexisting with it, or prior to it, so that the thing exists because of the "one." We, however, say that the "one" and Number are prior.

*Whatever being you perceive, whether it is sensible <note>perceived by the senses</note> or in any way intelligible, or even an "Idea" <note>a perfect Platonic Form</note>, the "one" is predicated of it individually. Therefore, since the "one" is found commonly in all individual things, it is added to nothing from the outside; indeed, even above the "one" which is in "another" (that is, in Being) and in its opposite (that is, in the multitude of beings), the One surely exists by itself, separate from the "other" and the multitude.*

->Chapter XI.<-

Neither indeed do we speak here properly of the One itself <note>The Absolute One or the Good</note>, which is higher than the First Being, but of the "one" which, naturally flourishing within the First Being, reigns in its own order before the multitude of beings and Ideas. In this "one," all unities exist, and from them come certain Numbers that precede the Ideas and are equally predicable of those Ideas. Indeed, this very "one" of Being exists as those same unities. The nature of Being, therefore—fertile with these unities as if with seeds—now brings forth the Ideas. Subsequently, it composes them into smaller or larger Numbers. Similarly, those things which are born inferior to the Ideas follow this rule; for unless the fertility of Being proceeded by certain proportions of numbers—both within itself and outward—nothing would ever be born, or all things would happen by chance and without order. 

But so that you may understand whose authority Plotinus uses regarding numbers and unity, listen: **Pythagoras** <note>The famous Greek mathematician and philosopher (6th century BCE)</note> says that number is the extension and the act of the "seminal reasons" <term>seminal reasons: "logoi spermatikoi," the rational blueprints or "seeds" that determine how a thing grows and develops</term> reigning within unity. Likewise, he says number is the first thing consisting in the divine mind, from which and by which all things are composed, and they remain distributed among each other in a certain indissoluble order. **Hippasus the Pythagorean** says: "Number is the first exemplar <note>model or pattern</note> of the world's manufacture, and the judicial instrument of the world-maker." **Philolaus** <note>A student of the Pythagorean school</note> says: "Number is a certain commanding and self-begotten eternal container of the world's endurance." They say **Pythagoras** held that: "Unity is that very thing through which any of the beings is called 'one,' and unity is itself the lowest part of number and parts, from which, as if from an eternal nursery and root, ratios and proportions proceed infinitely in both directions: here by multiplying, and there by dividing." Likewise, unity is the "Species of species," containing within itself all numbers and the ratios of numbers.

<margin>A</margin> But if someone should say that the "Decad" <note>the number ten</note> is nothing other than ten units: if he concedes that the unit exists, why would he admit one unit exists but deny the existence of the ten? For on the same grounds that the single unit has its substance <note>Greek: "hypostasis"</note>, so do the others. For if every thing makes use of it upon one of the beings, the single unit would not be in that which is applied to each of the others, but if indeed it is common for each of the others to be "one," then the "one" is common. That "one" is a single nature predicated of many, which we said must exist by itself even before it is observed in the many. But when a unit is observed in this thing, and again in another, if that [unity] also exists, then not only a single unit will be judged to subsist, and thus there will truly be a Number of units. 

But if someone thinks that only that "first" unit subsists—either coexisting with that which is "most Being," or with that <margin>C</margin> which is "most One"—if it coexists with the "most Being," then certainly the other units will be called units "equivocally" <note>sharing a name but having a different definition</note>; nor will they be established in the same rank as the first. Or else, Number will be gathered from dissimilar units, and there will be certain differences between the units themselves, insofar as they are units. But if someone says that unit is coupled to the "most One," why would that which is "most One" need this unit in order to be "one"? If, therefore, these things are impossible, it is necessary for the "One" to exist: which <margin>D</margin> indeed is nothing other than the "naked One," segregated by its own essence from anything else; whatever "one," therefore, exists there without that which is called "one," why should not another "one" also subsist there? And...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...itself, nor is it more that [thing] than it is essence. If anyone does not concede that it is essence, at least he will concede it is "being" in a certain order of things. And yet, even if that thing can be understood without its activity, it nonetheless exists together with it, although by a certain thought process among us, it is judged to be later than it. But if it cannot be thought of without it—just as a human cannot be thought of without that which makes him "one"—surely it is either not later than it, but coexisting, or it is even prior to <margin>B</margin> it, so that the thing exists through it: we, however, confess that the "One" is prior, and Number similarly.

<margin>A</margin> Perhaps someone will say that the Decad, that is, the ten, is nothing other than so many units. But if he has conceded that the unit exists, why then will he admit that there is one unit, but deny those ten? For just as that single unit is granted to have substance, why not the others? For it is not necessary to join that single unity to a specific one of the beings; otherwise, in this way, none of the others would be "one" anymore. Rather, if it is necessary for any of the rest to be "one," certainly the "one" is common to all. <margin>B</margin> That, however, is a single nature predicated of many, which we said must exist by itself even before it is in the many. But when unity is in this thing, and again is seen in another, if that also exists, not only a single unity will be judged to subsist, and so there will be some Number of units. 

But if someone should think that only that which is placed first subsists: then either it is coexisting with that which is "most Being," or with that <margin>C</margin> which is entirely "most One." If it is with "most Being," certainly the remaining units will be so called equivocally: nor will they be placed in the same order as the first: or surely Number will be gathered from dissimilar units, and there will be certain differences of the units themselves, even in how they are units. But if someone says that it is coupled to the "most One," why then does that which is "most One" need this unit, so that it may be "one"? If therefore these are impossible, it is necessary that the "One" exists: which <margin>D</margin> indeed is nothing other than the "naked One," segregated by its own essence from anything else; whatever "one," therefore, exists there without that which is called "one," why should not another "one" also subsist there? # PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. BOOK VI.

...each separately are many units, and also a "many-one"? <note>Plotinus is exploring the relationship between the many individual units and the single collective number they form.</note> If nature then generates in sequence—or rather, has already generated, or at least has not ceased within one of those things which it generated—it has therefore made the "one" into a kind of continuum. Indeed, where nature circumscribes it and immediately halts its step in its progress, it procreates smaller numbers. However, if it proceeds further, not into foreign things but within its own proper movements, it establishes larger numbers. Thus, it accommodates specific multitudes and every kind of being to specific numbers, as one who rightly understands that unless each thing fits with a specific number, it would either not exist at all or become something erratic, lacking proportion or reason <term>reason|ratio; in this context, the mathematical and logical order that governs the universe</term>.

->It is questioned whether that which is called "the one" is a thing existing in itself, or rather a mere mental conception. Chapter XII.<-

---

*There is, however, a substantial true notion of the "one" implanted in the mind, by which we judge this to be more "one," and that in turn not to be "one" at all.*

<margin>A</margin> If anyone should deny that the "One" and Unity themselves exist, asserting that the "one" is nowhere to be found except as "some one thing," and therefore claiming that what we call "the one" is merely a certain mental state <term>mental state|affectio animae; literally an "affection of the soul," suggesting that unity is just a feeling or a way we perceive things rather than a reality</term> regarding any being: first, what would stop them from saying that "Being" itself is also just a mental state, and that "Being" does not exist at all? But if they affirm that "Being" exists because it strikes the mind and brings forth an image of existence, then we see that the mind is similarly struck every day by the "One," and the image of it enters our consciousness. Furthermore, we must ask whether we perceive this mental state or notion of the mind as a "one" or as a multitude. Indeed, even when we say something is "not one," we do not derive the concept of "not one" from the object itself; rather, we say there is no "one" in that thing. Therefore, we must already possess the concept of the "one" within ourselves.

<margin>C</margin> This concept is certainly in the soul without being called "some one thing"; although someone might object that we hold the "one" as an intelligence or a kind of figure received from external things, like a concept formed by the mind from the thing itself. For those who introduce such concepts and place Number and the "One" in that category would assert that these are their forms of existence—if indeed such things have any existence at all. One might opportunely argue against them regarding such matters: specifically, if they say that such a mental state or notion is produced in us as something secondary to the things themselves, such as when we use terms like "this," "something," "a crowd," "a festival," "an army," or "a multitude."

<margin>D</margin> For just as a "multitude" <note>original: "multitudo" / "πλῆθος" (plethos)</note> exists as nothing apart from those things which are called "many," and again a "festival" is nothing apart from people gathered together and enjoying sacred rites; so too they would assert that the "one" is nothing apart from the "one thing"—even though you can see that we are affirming the "one" itself when we think of something alone and separated from others. They will, moreover, bring forward many other things of the same kind, such as "right" and "up," and their opposites. For what will "right" be (to speak according to their opinion) pertaining to actual existence, except merely that this person stands or sits in that particular place? Likewise, in that which is called "up," they will judge the same to occur: namely,

...each separately, many units, and the "ones" are one? Or if it were to have happened in sequence, or again not having come to generate, or having stood according to what it generated as if making a continuous one, having circumscribed it entirely, it generated number more quickly in its progress, or if not upon other things, but within the movements themselves number subsists. And thus to apply numbers to the multitudes of beings. If indeed, as if not upon each, each number. Or they would not even exist; it would be a deviation, but some irrational stopping-out.

<margin>A</margin> But if one were to say that both the "one" and the "monad" <term>monad|μονάδα; the fundamental, indivisible unit in Pythagorean and Platonic thought</term> can be held, for there is no "one" which is not: but a state of the soul toward each thing; first, what prevents one from saying that "Being" is also a state of the soul, and that "Being" is nothing at all? But if it is when this and a multitude, and Being regarding that which is, the soul being pricked, and receiving Being, and indeed we see this in it.

We speak of the "one" in itself. Therefore we have the "one" within. And if someone says "this one thing," we still have the "one," having come to take some notion, and we think of some concept from the thing, from the concepts proposed among them, such as placing numbers and the "one" among them, for they would place such things, if indeed they were among the things that are. Against whom it should be spoken concerning them.

<margin>C</margin> But not even if they should say such a thing as having become later than the things, a mental state or notion, such as "this" and "something," or "a crowd," "a festival," or "an army," and "multitude."

<margin>D</margin> For just as the multitude is nothing apart from the things called "many," nor is the festival anything apart from those gathered or celebrating for that purpose; so the "one" is nothing only something separate and removed from others when we think of it, when we say "one." And there are other such things as "right," and the opposites to these. For what is there toward existence in "on the right," except that someone stands here, or sits? Likewise in "above."

->When a man is called one, "man" is one thing, and "the one"—by participation in which he becomes one man—is another.<-
->Chapter XIII.<-

For "one" is predicated of a "non-man" just as much as it is of a "man," and a "man" is a certain multitude in the same way that he is also "one." The "one" itself, when predicated of a man, is not merely a negative term—as if it only meant "this man and not another." For once you have perceived that this man is truly one, you immediately judge that there is no other man there who is also himself "one" within himself. Furthermore, the nature of the "one" itself is so firm that its opposite—that is, multitude—can neither exist nor be understood without the "one." Indeed, all things, whatever they are, consist by virtue of their union. It is as if the "one" itself exists most purely through itself and is the supreme principle of all things. Without participation in this "one," no thought arises or remains within us. Likewise, through participation in unity, even a discrete multitude becomes "one certain thing," and a continuous thing becomes even more "one," while an indivisible thing is "one" in the highest degree. Certainly, the "one" itself possesses its own proper existence. Furthermore, the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, who studied while walking in the Lyceum.</note> confirm that the "one" signifies something that is entirely undivided within itself and without internal distance, and that it is an affirmative concept, not a negative one. For they say the opposite of this meaning is something divided within itself; in such division, multitude occurs along with privation. This is because a prior essence ends there, and also because when multitude occurs, we speak negatively, saying "neither is this that, nor is that this." Since the meaning opposite to "one" is negative, it follows that the meaning of "one" is affirmative. Finally, the "one" is so affirmative that it actually establishes the existence of multitude, but not vice versa. And as **Avicenna** <note>original: "Auicenna"; an 11th-century Persian philosopher. His presence in this text indicates that this is a Renaissance edition where the translator (likely Marsilio Ficino) has blended Plotinus's Greek text with later Medieval scholastic insights.</note> proves in his *Metaphysics*, the "One" is perceived and conceived by the intellect before "the many," even though the imagination might perhaps experience it differently.

<margin>* thought</margin>
As for the idea that the notion of the "one" arises from the subject—being attached to the subject, such as the man perceived by the senses, or any other animal, or even a stone—how could it be considered reasonable to say that? For the man who is seen is one thing, but the "one" is another, and they are by no means the same. Otherwise, the intellect would never predicate "one" of a "non-man." Furthermore, just as in the case of "the right side" and similar things, where the mind is not moved at random, but seeing a different position, it says "here" or "there"; so too in this matter, when it has inspected something, it pronounces it "one." For this is not a hollow feeling, nor does it affirm the "one" in a vacuum. <margin>* for it is not hollow</margin> And it should not be thought that it considers the "one" only because this thing is alone and nothing else; for in the very act of saying "nothing else," it is meanwhile calling that "else" a "one." Furthermore, this very thing which is called "other" or "different" occurs later. For unless the mind leaned upon the "one," it would say neither "other" nor "different." Likewise, when it pronounces that which is called "only" or "alone," it then says "one alone." Therefore, it speaks of the "one" before it speaks of "alone." Add to this that the speaker himself, before he speaks of another, exists as "one"; and that very thing of which he speaks, before he says or understands anything about it, is similarly "one." For it is either one, or more than one (and thus many). And if it be many, it is necessary that the "one" precedes it; since even when one says "multitude," one is pronouncing "more than one." And when one says an "army" is many, one understands many armed men organized into a "one." Truly, the mind’s thought...

Since the man who is discerned is one thing, and the "one" itself is another, they are in no way the same. Otherwise, the power of thought would never predicate "one" of a "non-man." Furthermore, just as regarding the "right side" and such things, the thought is not moved blindly, but seeing a <margin>B</margin> different position, it says it is "here" or "there"; so too in this matter, when it has looked upon something, it announces it as "one." For this experience is not some empty passion, nor does it apply the "one" to nothingness. Nor should it be thought that it weighs the "one" for the reason that this is "only this" and nothing else; for in that very thing which it says—"nothing else"—it is meanwhile calling the "else" a "one." Then, this very thing which is called "other" and "different" falls into place later. For unless <margin>C</margin> thought strove toward the "one," it would say neither "other" nor "different." Likewise, when it pronounces that which is named "alone," it says "one alone." Wherefore it says "one" before "alone." To this is added that the speaker himself, before he speaks of another, exists as a "one," and that very thing about which he speaks, before he says or understands anything about it, is similarly "one." # PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>A</margin> ...is not deceived or mistaken concerning the One: just as in a house we encounter a certain unity made of many stones, yet it is more truly "one" in a house than in an army. If, therefore, "one" is found more in a continuous thing, and even more so in a thing that is entirely indivisible, it is clearly established that this occurs because the "one" itself is a certain nature and possesses subsistence <term>subsistence|subsistentia; a term for independent, objective reality</term>. For it is in no way possible for "more" or "less" to exist in things that do not exist at all. 

<margin>B</margin> But just as when we predicate something of each sensible thing, and also of the substance of intelligible things, we predicate it more principally of the intelligibles—placing this very thing which is spoken of more principally in the order of beings, and just as "being" exists more in substance than in other categories: so too we consider the "one" to exist more truly and principally, observing it as differing according to degree in sensibles, and as being "one" in every way in the intelligibles, so that ultimately all things are referred back to the One itself. 

<margin>C</margin> Moreover, just as essence and "being" are not something sensible but intelligible, even though the sensible participates in them: so too the "one" is considered in the sensible through a certain participation, yet it is truly intelligible. The mind perceives it in an intelligible fashion, and in perceiving it, it understands through one thing another which it does not see. It therefore knew it beforehand <note>Plotinus often argues that the soul has an innate, "pre-knowledge" of the One and the Good</note>; and if it knew it beforehand, then this is an existing thing, which is the same as that which is called existing. 

<margin>D</margin> Furthermore, when one says "one something," one says "one" again, just as when one says "a certain two" or "a certain many." If, therefore, it is not permitted to understand anything without "one" or "two" or some other number, it is not permitted to say that that thing does not exist, without which we are unable to understand or say anything. For it is impossible to deny the existence of that without which we can neither speak nor understand anything; rather, that which is everywhere necessary for the generation of all intelligence and speech must precede speech and intelligence. For in this way it seems able to be taken up for the generation of these things. 

<margin>E</margin> But if it also necessarily contributes to the subsistence of any essence—for there is no being which is not also "one"—then surely it stands even before essence and generates essence. For this reason, it is customary to say "one being" <note>original: "vnum ens"</note>, but not "being" and then "one"; for in that which is "being," there also exists "one," and therefore "many." Conversely, "being" does not exist in the "one" in a similar way, unless perhaps the very nature of its generation made it so. 

<margin>F</margin> Accordingly, what is commonly said as "this" <note>original Latin: "hoc", Greek: "τόδε"</note> in demonstrating a thing is not in vain: for in place of the name of the thing itself, it speaks of a demonstrated subsistence and a certain presence, whether it manifests essence or any other of the things that exist. Thus, what is commonly called "this" signifies nothing empty to us, nor is it merely an affection of thought regarding a non-existent thing, but it places the subject matter before us, just as if it were uttering the proper name of someone.

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> ...is not deceived concerning the One, just as in the case of a house, the "one" is something made of many stones, yet the "one" is more present in the house than in an army. And if the "one" is more present in the continuous, and even more in the indivisible, it is clear that the One is of a nature that truly exists. For it is not possible for "the more" to exist among things that do not exist. But just as we predicate of each of the sensible things, 

<margin>Β</margin> and also predicate of the intelligibles, we apply the category more principally to the intelligibles, placing "the more" and "the more principal" among the things that truly are, and "being" is more in substance itself than in the other genera. So also the "one" is more and more principally found in the intelligibles than the sensibles, though it differs by degree; and looking at the intelligibles, we consider it to be "one" in every way, and we must say that all things depend upon the One. And just as 

<margin>C</margin> essence and being are intelligible and not sensible, even if the sensible partakes of them, so too with the One. While it is observed in the sensible according to a certain participation, it is an intelligible thing, and the intellect grasps it in an intelligible way. Thus, it perceives one thing through another, even what it does not see. It knew it beforehand, therefore. And if it knew it beforehand, then it is an existing thing, just as "being" is. And when it says "one" of something, it says "one" again, just as it does with "two" or with "many." If it is entirely 

<margin>D</margin> impossible to think without the "one" or the "two" or some number, how is it possible for that which is necessary for all thought to not exist? For if it does not exist, one can neither think nor say anything. It is impossible to say it does not exist; rather, it is a necessity everywhere, so that before the generation of any thought or speech, it must pre-exist as the source of speech and thought. For thus it is taken up for the generation of these things. And if it also contributes to 

<margin>E</margin> the subsistence of each essence—for nothing is a "being" if it is not "one"—it must exist before essence and generate essence. For this reason one says "one being," and not "being" then "one." For in being, there is the "one" and also the "many," but in the "one," being is not present in the same way, unless the One produced it by giving itself to the generation of being. And this term "this," in demonstrating something, is not empty. For it points to a subsistence, 

<margin>F</margin> and signifies its name and its presence, whether it be essence or something else among beings. Thus the "this" signifies something to us and is not empty; it is not merely a state of the mind directed at nothing, but it refers to a subject thing, just as if one were speaking the proper name of something.

---

*One should not think that what is called "the One" signifies only a certain relation: for it does not define "being one" except through its own property. And because a mass, through accidental division, becomes two instead of one, it ceases to be one, yet it does not cease to be a mass or heat—as if unity were something else there besides the mass, or the heat, and similar things.*

# BOOK SIX.

M m

...indeed essential in incorporeal <note>original: "incorporeis"</note> things, but in corporeal things it is accidental. Even in these physical things, unity is something incorporeal rather than material. Thus, by the presence of unity as a certain nature, any given thing becomes "one," just as by the presence of a quality, a thing becomes "such-and-such." Similarly, the fact that two things exist is not properly caused by their being near each other; for sometimes separation or division can also lead to the same result. Rather, it is the participation in duality <note>original: "duitas"</note>, which is itself a species <term>species|a specific "form" or "kind" in Platonic philosophy</term> in its own right, just like quality or quantity. Indeed, it is even more of a species than the continuous quantities measured by number. Therefore, there are six grades of numbers placed in order: the first is in the First Being above the Ideas; the second is innate to the Ideas; the third is in incorporeal substances; the fourth is in powers of that kind; the fifth is in aptly connected bodies; and the sixth is in bodies that are, as it were, torn apart.

---

<margin>* That he speaks irrationally. <note>original: "ὅτι μὲν ἀλόγως λέγοι"</note></margin>
<margin>* And that... <note>original: "ὅτι δὲ"</note></margin>
<margin>A</margin> But against those things which are said by some who place the "one" in a certain relation, one can probably respond that the "one" itself is not the sort of thing where, when something else undergoes a change, it loses its own nature without having undergone any change itself. Instead, it is necessary that if a thing falls away from being "one," it must suffer a certain deprivation of unity—namely, by being divided into two or more parts. <margin>B</margin> If, therefore, the same mass is divided into two, it is not destroyed in the process insofar as it is a mass. It is clearly evident that, besides the underlying subject <term>subject|subiectum; the underlying matter or substance</term>, there was a "one" present in it which it has now cast off, the division having destroyed that unity. Now, since this unity is present at one time and departs at another, what prevents us from calculating it within the order of beings, wherever it may be? <margin>C</margin> Let us say that it "happens" to things as an accident, but that it exists in itself whenever it appears in both sensible <note>physical things perceived by the senses</note> and intelligible things. In lower things, it arrives like an accident; but in itself, it is considered to exist within the intelligibles, and primarily in the first of them, since the "one" exists first, and then "being" exists. But if someone objects that the "one" itself suffers nothing—claiming that when another thing is added to it, it is no longer one but "two"—they would be speaking incorrectly. For the "one" itself did not become "two," nor did the thing to which something was added, nor the thing that was added; rather, each remains "one" just as it was. "Two" is predicated <note>stated or attributed</note> of both together, while "one" remains separately in each. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, "two" does not consist by its own nature in a mere relationship or disposition <note>original: "habitudo"</note>, and the same is true of duality. However, if that which occurs during a meeting or gathering—and the fact of being in that gathering—is the same as "making two," then perhaps such a relation is "two" and "duality." But as it stands, duality appears again in the opposite experience: for when a single thing is divided, it becomes two. Therefore, "two" is neither a gathering nor a separation, such that it would be merely a relationship. <margin>E</margin> The same logic applies to every number. For when a relationship is the thing that generates something, it is impossible for the opposite relationship to generate the exact same thing. Does this mean that the relationship itself is the thing? Or is it not the primary cause? Surely the cause by which something is "one" is the presence of unity; similarly, that which makes things "two" is the presence of duality, just as whiteness makes a thing white, beauty makes it beautiful, and justice makes it just. Otherwise, one would have to say these things do not exist either, and we would have to assign relationships as the causes in these cases as well: claiming a man is "just" only because of a certain relationship to this or that. Or that a thing is "beautiful" only because we are affected a certain way, even though there is nothing in the subject itself to affect us, nor any added quality that meets our gaze as "the beautiful." Therefore, when you see a "one" and call it "one,"

<column-break/>

you are identifying something real within it.

# PLOTINUS ENNEADS. BOOK VI.

...altogether, it is both "great" and "beautiful," and is affected in many other such ways. Just as, therefore, "great" and "Greatness" exist in that realm, along with "sweet" and "bitter" and other qualities, why should the "One" not also be there? For we must not think that while every quality—whatever it may be—truly exists, quantity does not exist in the very order of beings. Nor should we think that only continuous quantity <term>continuous quantity|Magnitude like length or volume that can be divided infinitely</term> exists, while discrete quantity <term>discrete quantity|Number, or things that can be counted individually</term> does not—especially since continuous quantity uses the discrete as a measure. Therefore, just as something is "great" by the presence of Greatness, so too is a thing "one" by the presence of Unity itself, and "two" by the presence of Duality, and so on. If anyone were to inquire more curiously by what specific condition things participate in unity and number, such an inquiry would be a common one, investigated along with the participation of other species <term>species|In Platonic philosophy, this refers to the "Forms" or "Ideas" that define the essence of things</term>. Finally, it must be judged that the number ten <note>original: "denarium"</note> is considered differently in discrete things (where it exists within them), differently in continuous things, and differently again in so many great powers gathered into one. And finally, it is different in the intelligibles <term>intelligibles|Realities that can only be grasped by the mind, not the senses</term> themselves, which are easily reached from there. Furthermore, the truest numbers are there—not those seen in other things, but those existing in themselves, like the "Ten-itself"; I do not mean the "ten" of certain intelligible things, but simply "Ten" as an Idea.

*That divine world is a perfect living being <note>original: "animal"; in this context, it refers to a 'living being' or 'ensouled entity'</note> precisely because it already possesses the entire number of living beings; it has the number of living beings because it possesses the entire universal number itself simply. There, therefore, number itself precedes both all living beings and the perfection of that world.*

### Chapter XV.

For it produces all-formed Ideas within itself by its own specific motion—a numbered motion, I say—otherwise it would not generate. Truly, Being itself conceives beings within itself, merely by multiplying itself into them. But since it multiplies into itself only by the power of number, the number of Being rightfully precedes it there, just as the One is higher than Being. In the manner of the Moon, which looks up to the Sun with uniform light from above, but spreads diverse light below, Being first affects the "Simple One" itself with its own unity as if at its summit, but then, with number soon following, it brings forth species and forms <note>original: "rosas speciesq;" — 'rosas' is likely an OCR error for 'formas' (forms)</note>.

<margin>A</margin>
BUT let us speak again from the beginning after these things already said: that whole and true Being is at once Being itself, Intellect, and the Absolute Living Being, and at the same time all living beings together. This worldly, sensible living being <note>the physical universe</note> imitates the unity of that Divine Being with its own unity as far as its powers allow. "As far as its powers allow," I say, because the nature of this sensible world has departed from that One, since it had to be sensible <term>sensible|Something that can be perceived by the five senses</term>. Furthermore, it is necessary that that celestial realm be the universal number; for if the number were not perfect, it could suffer the lack of some number, and unless the universal number of living beings were in it, it would not be a completely absolute living being.

<margin>B</margin>
Therefore, number exists before every living being, and before the universal living being. Surely "Man" exists in the intelligible world, as do other living beings insofar as they are living beings; and again, insofar as that world is the universal living being. For even the "man" among us is a part of the universe, and by that reasoning, a living being is the universe. Similarly, every individual living being that is there exists within the Living Being.

<margin>C</margin>
In the Intellect, however, insofar as it is intellect, all individual intellects exist as parts, of which there is also a number. Therefore, number is not first in the mind. Insofar as it is in the mind, it is considered a total, just as there are so many acts of the mind there;

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...altogether, it is both "great" and "beautiful," and thousands of other things which one might say are all in it; just as "Greatness" is in it, and "sweet" and "bitter," and other qualities, why not also the "One"? Or should every quality exist, whatever it may be, but quantity <note>original: "ποσότης"</note> not exist among beings? Or should continuous quantity exist, but discrete not? Especially since the continuous uses the discrete as a measure.

<margin>B</margin>
Is it not, then, that something is "great" by the presence of Greatness, "one" by the presence of Unity, and "two" by Duality? And other things likewise. And if someone asks how it participates, the reasoning is common to all the species being sought. One must say that in discrete things, one sees the "Ten" existing in one way, while in continuous things in another, and in powers in another,

<margin>C</margin>
and in those things which have already ascended <note>to the intelligible realm</note> in another way. Furthermore, these truest numbers are not seen in other things, but are self-sufficient, such as the "Ten"—not a "ten" of some intelligible things, but the "Ten-itself."

---

<margin>A</margin>
AGAIN, let us speak from the beginning of these things: that whole Being was Being, and Intellect, and the Perfect Living Being, all living beings together; which this universe here has imitated as much as it was able <gloss>in the way it is possible for it to [imitate] that same [unity]</gloss>. For the nature of the sensible fled from the One, since it was intended to be sensible. But it must be the whole [number]; for if it were not,

<margin>B</margin>
it would be lacking in some number. And the number <gloss>of the living being</gloss> would be in it, so that it would not be [imperfect]. Therefore, number is before everything, even before the Perfect Living Being. "Man," therefore, is in the intelligible, and other living beings insofar as they are living beings, and insofar as that realm is the Perfect Living Being. For also

<margin>C</margin>
he himself, and each thing insofar as it is a living being there, is within the Living Being there. In the Intellect, insofar as it is intellect, they are all as parts, each individually. And number also <gloss>belongs to the mind</gloss> insofar as number is first in the mind. And again, as many as are the activities of the mind. And as the mind...

<summary>Plotinus explores the metaphysical reality of numbers, arguing that concepts like "Unity" and "the number Ten" exist as primary Ideas in the divine realm before they manifest in physical objects. He describes the Intelligible World as a "Perfect Living Being" that contains the blueprint for all life and all numbers.</summary>

# BOOK SEVEN.
<note>While the header reads "Book Seven," this text corresponds to the Sixth Ennead in the standard arrangement of Plotinus's works.</note>

<columns>2</columns>

Just as the justice of the mind exists there <note>In the intelligible realm of divine thought.</note>, along with temperance and the other virtues, so too does knowledge and everything that a possessing intellect is truly considered to be. But if knowledge is in it, what prevents knowledge from existing in something else rather than in itself? It is certainly prevented because, in that realm, the knower, the known, and knowledge itself exist simultaneously as one and the same; and so it is with the other virtues. For this reason, each thing exists there primarily. Justice is not an "accident" <term>accident|A property that a thing happens to have, but which isn't essential to its nature (e.g., a shirt being blue)</term> there, although for the soul—insofar as it is a soul—justice is an
<margin>B</margin>
accident. For in the soul, these virtues seem to exist as potential; they only become actual when the soul rises toward the Intellect and dwells with it. Beyond this, Being itself already exists, and Number exists within it, through which it generates all beings. This Being is moved according to number; thus, it places numbers before the existence of beings and fits them to that existence. Just as the "One" of Being itself is set over it, joining Being to the "First" <note>The "First" refers to the One, the ultimate source of everything in Neoplatonism.</note>, numbers do not join other things to the First. For it is sufficient that Being itself is
<margin>C</margin>
entirely annexed to the One. However, Being, as it becomes Number, reconciles all other beings to itself. For it is divided not insofar as it exists as one, but as its own unity remains. Once divided by its own nature into as many parts as it willed, it perceived exactly into how many it should be divided, and thus generated Number existing within itself. For it was divided by the powers of number, and it generated as many things as Number itself contained. Therefore, Number itself is the first and true principle and fountain of existence for all
<margin>D</margin>
beings. For this reason, in this physical world, the generation of individual things is driven by certain numbers; if a different number is applied, either something else is born, or nothing is generated at all. These are the "primary numbers" which act as the objects of counting <note>original: "numerabiles"</note>. Those numbers found in other things have a dual nature: because they come from the primary numbers, they are countable; but because they exist beyond them and act according to them, they measure other things, counting both numbers and countable objects. For by what power could people say "ten," unless they had numbers existing within themselves?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
Just as Justice and Temperance are in the mind there, so too are the other virtues and knowledge, and everything that an intellect possesses is truly judged to be Intellect. If knowledge is in it, what prevents knowledge from being in another rather than in itself? It is certainly prohibited, because there the knower, the known, and the knowledge are one and the same, and the others likewise. Therefore, each thing exists there in a primary way; justice is not an "accident" there, although it is an accident to the soul, insofar as it is a soul. These things seem to be in the soul as potential, but they are in "act" <term>act|The full realization or expression of a thing's potential</term> when it looks toward the Intellect. After Being, or rather being Being itself, and in the number with which all beings exist, it moves according to number. <margin>* Noted beforehand</margin> Having noted beforehand the numbers of their existence, just as the One itself joins Being to the First. Numbers there do not join other things to the First, for Being itself, joined to the One, is sufficient. But Being, having become number, joins beings to itself. For it is divided, not insofar as it is one, but Being itself remains, being separated by its own nature as much as it willed; it saw into how many it generated number. Therefore, beings are in it, for it moved through the powers of number. Or, it generated as many things as Number was. Number is the principle and source of existence for all beings, the first and true number. Therefore, here too, the generation for each thing is with numbers. And if one takes another number, either something else happens, or nothing happens. And there are primary numbers, as countable things. But those in other things already have both: from these, they are countable, but according to these, they measure other things, counting the numbers or the countable things. For with what would they say "ten," if not by the numbers within them?

---

->*When you count men who happen to be running by, you create a new number within yourself in the category of quantity. But when you consider ten men arranged together in a chorus, besides your own counting, there is a "ten" arranged within them in the category of quantity; however, the number of parts in any natural thing is essential, and is naturally placed in the category of substance.*<-

### Chapter XVI.

->*Essential number is also in the soul, which is harmonically constituted by its own nature from many parts; essential number is in the divine mind, both in the fixed series of Ideas arranged among themselves, and in the parts within any given Idea, and finally, there is Number itself simply existing above the Ideas.*<-

---

<columns>2</columns>

Someone will perhaps ask us next in this manner: "Where do you place these numbers that you call primary and true? In what category of things do you rank them?" To everyone, they clearly seem to belong to the category of Quantity. You yourselves made mention of quantity earlier, judging that just as there is "continuous quantity" <term>continuous quantity|Magnitudes like lines or surfaces that aren't broken into parts</term>, so also "discrete quantity" <note>original: "discretam quantitatem" - things that can be counted, like individual apples</note> should be placed in the very order of beings. But then you assert that these numbers are the very essence of the first beings, or
<margin>B</margin>
even above them, and you say there are other numbers besides those used for counting. Please explain to us, then, how you arrange these things: for many doubts arise from this opinion. Even the "One" that exists in sensible things <term>sensible things|Physical objects we can perceive with our five senses</term> comes into dispute: is it a "quantum" <note>original: "quantum" - a thing of a certain size or amount</note>, or is it rather that if "one" is taken many times, it becomes a quantum? If it is taken alone, is it not a quantum at all, but rather the beginning of quantity?

<column-break/>

These ones whom we call the first true numbers, <margin>* where would someone say</margin> where would someone say they are seen, and in what class of beings? For in Quantity, they seem to be according to everyone. And you made mention of quantities in the previous parts, being worthy to place them equally in the continuous and the discrete among beings. But again you say that they are the first beings, or they are numbers, and again you say there are other numbers besides those being counted. How then do you arrange these? Tell us. <margin>* a difficulty</margin> For it has many *difficulties. Since even the "one" in sensible things—is it a certain quantity? Or is it that "one" is often a quantity, but the "one" alone is not a quantity, but the start of quantity?

<summary>Plotinus argues that Number is not just a way of counting, but a fundamental "fountain of existence" that allows Being to divide into many individual entities. He distinguishes between "essential number," which defines what a thing is, and "accidental number," which we use when counting external objects.</summary>
