# PLOTINUS: ENNEAD VI.

<columns>

<margin>A</margin> Again, where is the beginning <note>original Latin: *principium*; Greek: *archē*</note> of quantity? Is it something innate to a thing or something external? It is only right that you expect us to explain all these matters. We must, therefore, treat these subjects by perhaps beginning from this point:
When exactly? Well, first we must examine this within "sensible" <term>sensible|Things that can be perceived by the five senses, as opposed to "intelligible" things known by the mind</term> matter. When, I say, you take one thing along with another and say "two"—such as a dog and a man, or even two men—or when you count many, such as ten, and speak of a "decad" <note>A group of ten</note> of men, this number is not a "substance" <term>substance|The essential reality or "thingness" of an object</term>,
<margin>B</margin> nor does it exist within these sensible things as an inherent quality; rather, it is purely quantity. Now, when you divide this group by units of one, making each part of this ten a single unit, you are creating the principle of quantity. For "one" is missing from the number itself; it is not the "One-in-itself."
However, when you say that "Man" himself is a certain number within his own nature—such as a "dyad" <note>A group of two; original Latin: *binarium*</note>, consisting of "animal" and "rational"—you are no longer observing things in the same way. In the first case, as you move through and count, you are creating a "how much" (a quantity).
<margin>C</margin> But in the second case, by what reasoning are they "two," and each "one"? If each unit completes the "essence" <term>essence|The fundamental nature of a thing that makes it what it is</term>, and there is a "unity" in both, then you are speaking of a different kind of number—one that is essential. This "two-ness" is not something that happens later, nor does it merely signify a quantity outside the thing itself; rather, it exists within the essence and contains the very nature of the thing. You do not create this number by the act of counting as you track things that exist on their own; these numbers are not produced by your act of enumeration.
<margin>D</margin> For what is added to one man's essence when he is counted alongside someone else? There is no inherent "unity" there like there is in a choir. That "ten" of men can only exist within you, the person doing the counting. In the ten people themselves whom you count, if they are not joined together into one by any specific order, they cannot even be called a "decad." You are the one making them "ten" by counting them and assigning the value of "ten" to them. But in a choir or an army, there is something real outside of yourself, beyond the number that exists in your mind.
<margin>E</margin> But in what way does it exist in you? Perhaps the number itself, implanted in you before the act of counting, exists in a different state. The number we use for counting results from what appears externally compared to the number within you; it is an act either of those external things, or according to them, while you simultaneously count and produce the number. In this very act, you bring the existence of quantity into being, just as in the act of walking you bring the existence of a certain motion into being. In what way, then, does the number implanted in us exist differently?
<margin>F</margin> It is surely the number of our own essence, which Plato says participates in number and harmony; and again, he says that number and harmony exist. Thus, some say that the soul is neither a body nor a magnitude, and therefore the soul is a number. If it is an essence, then the number of a body is an essence in the way a body is, but the number of the soul is a certain essence in the way souls are. Now, in the deep intelligible world <note>The realm of pure thought and Forms</note>, if the "Living Being-in-itself" is several things—such as a certain "Trinity" <note>original: *trinitas*; here referring to a grouping of three essential Forms</note>—this very Trinity which is in the Living Being exists essentially.
<margin>G</margin> But a Trinity that is not yet part of a living being, but is simply "Three-ness" within "Being" itself, is the principle of essence. If, however, in that realm you count "Living Being" and "Beautiful," each is surely one; but you conceive the number within yourself, creating quantity and "two-ness." Yet, if you say that "Virtue" consists of four parts, it is certainly a "Quaternary" <note>A group of four</note>...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> And where is the beginning of these things that are related to us? You have a right to ask. We must speak, then, beginning from here. First, we must make our argument regarding sensible things. Whenever you take one thing alongside another and say "two"—as with a dog and a man, or two men, or more, such as a "decad" of men—the number
<margin>B</margin> exists in this way among sensible things. But how is number "quantitative"? It is purely quantity, divided by one. When you make the "ten" into individual "ones," you are making a beginning. For one of the ten is not "The One" in itself. When you call "Man" himself, in his own right, a certain number—such as a "dyad," being "animal" and "rational"—the method here is not the same. In one way,
<margin>C</margin> as you count, you create a quantity; but in the sense that the subjects are "two" and each is "one," they fulfill the essence. This unity is a "number without matter" and is essential. This "dyad" is not secondary, nor is it merely a quantity from outside the thing; it is that which holds together the nature of the thing. You do not create this number; you are observing things that exist by themselves.
<margin>D</margin> For what could be added to one man by being counted with another? There is no inherent "oneness" there as there is in a choir. Rather, the "ten" of men has its existence only in you, the one counting. Among the ten who are not arranged into a single unit, there is no "decad"; you are the one who makes them "ten" by counting them, rendering the "ten" as a quantity. But in a choir
<margin>E</margin> or an army, there is something else. How is the number in you? Perhaps the number dwelling within is different. The number that appears from the outside, relative to the one in you, is an activity either of those things or according to them. While you count and generate the number, you bring the existence of quantity into being through that activity, just as walking creates a movement. How, then, is the number within us? Is it the number of our essence? Plato says it
<margin>F</margin> participates in harmony. Some say it is neither a body nor a magnitude, and therefore the soul is a number, provided it is an essence. The number of a body is an essence as a body is; the number of the soul consists of essences as souls are. And indeed, in the realm of the truly existing, if the "Living Being" there is several things, this "Trinity" is essential within that Living Being. But the Trinity that is not yet a living being, but is simply "Three-ness" in Being, is a beginning of essence. If number is "Living Being" or "Beautiful,"
<margin>G</margin> each is one. But you generate the number, and you act to create quantity and "two-ness." If you say "Virtue" is four things, then it is a "Quaternary"...

</columns>

<summary>Plotinus distinguishes between numbers used for counting physical objects (quantitative number), which exist only in the mind of the counter, and numbers that define the essential structure of a being (substantial number), such as the dual nature of "Man" as animal and rational.</summary>

# BOOK SEVEN.

<columns>

...the parts of virtue contributing to the one: and you might call this unity a "four" <note>original Greek: *tetrada*; a group of four</note>, as if it were a certain underlying subject: and you would then apply the "four" that is within you to it.

But as for what is called "infinite number," how can this be? For rational principles <note>original Greek: *logoi*</note> provide a limit for it; or rather, they do so correctly, for if it is to be a number, it must have a limit, since the "infinite" is at odds with the nature of number. Why then do we say that number is infinite? Is it not in the same way we speak of an "infinite line"? We speak of an infinite line not because such a thing actually exists, but because it is possible to conceive of something greater than any given magnitude—as if there were an "Idea" of every possible size. Let this also be the case with number. For once its size is known, it is possible in the mind to double it and join it to the previous amount. For how could you join a mere thought or mental image <note>original Greek: *phantasma*</note> that exists only in you to the things within the divine realm? 

Or shall we say that an "infinite line" exists among the "intelligible" <term>intelligible|The realm of pure thought and Forms, accessible to the mind rather than the senses</term> things? For what size would the line be in that realm? But if it does not possess quantity, it would be infinite in number. Or perhaps "the infinite" has another meaning there, as something always sought after. But how is it infinite in the "rational principle" <note>original Greek: *logos*</note> of the "Line-itself"? For it is not a limited thing that is being thought of as a limit. What, then, is the line in that realm? It is something that exists after number, for the "One" is seen within it. For from the one, it proceeds toward one: a single dimension. But it does not have a measure of quantity for that dimension. Where, then, does it exist? It exists only in the "Intellect" <note>original Greek: *noesei*</note> as something that defines. Or it is a real thing, yet an intellectual one; for all things there are intellectual. But how is it a "thing"? Truly, this is the case for planes, solids, and all geometric shapes. For we do not merely invent these shapes ourselves; this is proven by the shape of the universe which existed before us, and all other natural shapes assigned to physical bodies. These shapes must necessarily exist in the divine realm without physical "shaping," as the "Primary Shapes." For while they are forms in other things, there they exist in their own right, and are not extended into space. For things that are extended are dependent on others. Thus, the shape exists as a unity within Being, but the distinction between shapes was made either within the "Living Being" <note>original Greek: *zoon*; referring to the Divine Mind as a living totality</note> or even before it.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...parts of virtue contributing to the one: and it is permitted to call that unity a "four" <note>original Latin: *quaternarium*</note>, as if it were some underlying subject: and you indeed accommodate that "four" which is within you to it.

---

->Bodies are indeed resolved into dimensions, and these into numbers. Therefore, in the first archetype, numbers precede dimensions, and dimensions precede bodies.<-
->Chapter XVII.<-

---

Certainly, before the natural body, there is the "Body-itself" in its simplest form: therefore, the principles of this "Body-itself" exist before the principles of the physical body. Thus, dimensions (which are the boundaries of a body) and numbers (which are the measures of dimensions) are conceived before the specific principles of natural things. For this reason, they are known even without sensible matter. A body, truly, is not a body specifically because of its matter or its quality, but because of its quantity; for unless quantity is added, both matter and quality are incorporeal.

Therefore, since numbers are the principles of quantity, they are likely called the "beginings of bodies" by the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed that number was the fundamental substance of the universe</note>. For they possess the character of principles: since they are established by the first and smallest differences, and they proceed immediately from the simplest unity. Indeed, this unity, which surpasses any fixed position, precedes the "point" <note>original Latin: *punctum*</note> which has a position. Furthermore, the "super-essential unity" precedes every "essence" <term>essence|The fundamental nature or 'being' of a thing</term> designated by a specific type.

Certainly, there are "Ideas" of shapes in the divine realm, through which shapes are given to the spheres of the world and to every specific species. In that realm, however, a dimension or shape is terminated by nothing other than a certain definition of the intelligence. A line is called "infinite" there in its rational principle <note>original Latin: *ratione*</note> because the principle of the "Ideal Line" has no limit of quantity; otherwise, it would not fit equally with all lines, whether larger or smaller.

The "First Essence" is considered primarily as living, and then it is recognized as intellectual. But since it is primarily intellectual, it is simultaneously defined as a "living intellectual being" or an "intellectual animal." Numbers and shapes are first folded up within it, and then they are unfolded equally with that intellectual living being.

<margin>A</margin> IT REMAINS to explain under what condition a number may be called "infinite." For these rational principles <note>original Latin: *rationes*</note> apply a limit to number, and perhaps quite rightly, if it is to be a number at all; for the infinite is the opposite of number. Why then do we often speak of an infinite number? Perhaps it is in the same way we speak of an infinite line. We speak of an infinite line not because such a thing exists, but because even the greatest line <margin>B</margin> can be considered as a number. For after we have learned how great a number is, we may double it in our minds, though not by actually joining this number to that one. For in what way could you join a notion or imagination that exists only in you with things that exist externally? 

Otherwise, we might say there is an infinite line in the "intelligible" region: for how great would the line be that was there? But if there is no such quantity there, the infinity will be in the number. But truly, "the infinite" is said there by another <margin>C</margin> reasoning, not as something that cannot be crossed. In what way, then, is it infinite? Perhaps because in the rational principle of the line itself, no limit is added by the intelligence. What, then, and where is the line in that realm? It is surely something posterior to number, for "the one" is seen within it: since it both begins from the one and is produced into a single dimension. But the quantity of the dimension has no limit. Where then is it? It exists only in the intelligence as a "definer." Or it is the thing <margin>D</margin> itself, but an intellectual one. For all things are there in such a way that they are intellectual, and that is how the thing itself behaves. 

And truly, concerning the plane, the solid, and all shapes, it is pre-ordained there where and how they are arranged. For we do not create shapes simply by thinking of them. This is surely witnessed by the shape of the world itself, which precedes us, and the other natural shapes assigned to things that consist of nature. These must necessarily exist before bodies, as "un-shapable" or "primary shapes" in that realm. For they are not merely forms lying in other things, but they exist in their own right, and therefore they do not require physical extension; for things that are extended are dependent on others. Therefore, there is one shape everywhere in "Being," but the distinction between shapes was made either in the "living being" <note>The Divine Intellect</note> itself, or before that living being.

It transitions from discussing the shapes of elements (like the pyramid of fire) to the nature of life and beauty in the realm of the Forms.</meta>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEAD VI.

<columns>

<margin>A</margin> I say, however, that each thing was distinct, not because it was stretched out into a physical mass, but because its own figure <note>original: *figura*; the geometric shape or Form</note> was distributed to each living thing. Consequently, for the bodies existing there <note>In the intelligible realm of the Forms</note>, their own appropriate figures are assigned—such as that pyramid, if you like, for fire. For this reason, even this world of ours strives to imitate those forms, although it is entirely unable to do so because of the nature of matter. Furthermore, other figures exist both here and there according to a certain analogy and proportion. But do these exist in the living being insofar as it is a living or breathing thing? <margin>B</margin> Or are figures first in the Intellect? Certainly, they are in the living being. Therefore, if the living being were to encompass the Intellect, they would exist first in the living being; but if, on the contrary, the Intellect is prior, they are first in the mind by order of rank. Indeed, even if souls are within that utterly absolute living being, the Intellect is still prior. But what shall we say to that Platonic saying? "The Intellect beholds," he says, "as many as are in the universal living being," <note>A reference to Plato's *Timaeus* 39e</note> and those things which follow there. If, therefore, the Intellect beholds that, it seems to be posterior—unless perhaps this very thing which is said, "it beholds," was so placed by Plato so that it might subsist in the very perfection and nature of the living being itself. For he who perceives and that which is seen are not different, but all things are one; the entities themselves possess a bare sphere, but the living being itself possesses the sphere of the living creature.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> I say that it has been distinguished, not because it was divided into parts, but because each was divided in relation to that other; and to the bodies there, their appropriate shapes were given, such as the pyramid to fire. Thus, this world desires to imitate those things, even though it is not able. And there are other things here analogous to those there. But are they not in the living being according to the things of the Intellect? For indeed, they are in the living being, for the living being contains the Intellect. <margin>B</margin> Is it primarily in the Intellect? If it is the Intellect, it is according to the things in the Intellect; but if it is in the living being so that it contains all, then the Intellect is prior. But he says the Intellect is in the "completely perfect living being" <term>perfect living being|The *Pan-zoon*, the divine archetype of all life</term>, if it is not possible that "seeing" is spoken of in this way, as an underlying reality being produced. For they are not different things. Or even the thinking itself possesses the bare sphere, but the living being possesses the sphere of the living.

<column-break/>

->The number of things that differ from one another in form is determined in the incorporeal world by a certain number in the divine world; nevertheless, it is called infinite there, just as any Idea is: because it possesses the fullness of its whole nature, and is not bounded from the outside. Chapter XVIII.<-

---

>*The beauty of the first essence is living by its own nature: its intelligence is always turned toward itself, the Good. Furthermore, every intellect and mind truly contemplating that intellectual life is transformed into it by a soul that is equally intellectual and vital, and by the immediate arrival of love. The first being suffers, as it were, from the opposite: for it is the cause of the whole being, and is every being in an eminent way, nor is it perceived by non-being; since it is through itself, it is deservedly always, and most fully. Moreover, it hangs from the Good itself, while it even precedes life. For this reason, living and understanding are to be desired by us, so that we may also have the fullest being—so that we may have the good being. Finally, the Principle is that which is sufficient unto itself. The soul indeed is sufficient for itself for movement; the intellect for its very being; but the Good itself for the good, and for all things. Therefore, three principles are seen.*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ACCORDINGLY, every number there is definite: we, however, imagine a number greater than any given number, and thus the infinite occurs in our counting. But there, once a number is understood, it is not possible to understand a larger number; for it already exists, nor is any left out, nor will any be left hereafter, so that another might be added to it. It is therefore right to call the number there "infinite," because it has not been measured. For by whom could it be measured? But that which is, exists as a whole, existing as one and all at once, and not grasped by any limit, <margin>B</margin> but it is that which is, subsisting by itself and for itself. For absolutely none of the entities is circumscribed by a boundary: for that which is prevented from falling into infinity and stands in need of a limit is judged to be bounded and measured. But those things there are themselves the "Measures" of all things, wherefore all things there are beautiful. For insofar as the living being itself is, it exists as something beautiful, endowed with the best life, in which nothing of life is lacking at all, nor does it have a life mixed <margin>C</margin> with death. For nothing there is mortal, nothing is dying. Nor again is the life of the living being itself thin or weak, but first and most certain, having the full vigor of life, like a primary light, from which the souls also live there; and those souls which come down here, lead from there. But it also knows for what purpose it lives, and toward what it lives, and from what it lives.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> BUT indeed, the number there is definite; but we imagine more than the limit, and thus the infinite. For of those things, it is not possible to think of more than the thinking; for it is. And that which was taken is a certain thing. And that which remains is taken and added to it. But it is not itself measured, because it is not measured by anything. But that which is, is all. Being one and together, and not encompassed by a limit, but being what it is. For of the things that are, none is bounded at all. <margin>B</margin> But it is the limited and measured that is prevented from running into infinity and is in need. But those things are all measures; therefore all are beautiful. And indeed, insofar as it is a living being, it is beautiful, having life, and not one life is mixed with death. For nothing is mortal or dying. <margin>C</margin> Nor is the life in the living being itself diminished, but is most manifest and clear, like the first light, from which the souls both there and those that are divided here live. And it knows why it lives, and for what it lives...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the "universal living being" or the Divine Intellect. Having previously discussed how geometric forms exist within this Intellect, Plotinus now moves toward the relationship between Being, Life, and Wisdom, arguing that in the higher realm, these three are inseparable and all-encompassing.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN [of the Sixth Ennead]

<columns>

<margin>* or the whole mind</margin>
From which it lives and toward which it lives. But the Wisdom of all * and
<margin>* itself</margin>
the Intellect of all, existing within the essences and living together with them, having blended itself more excellently and having mixed in Wisdom, provides a more venerable beauty to that very thing. Since even here [in our world] a wise life is truly something venerable and beautiful, even if it is seen only dimly. But there, it is seen purely. For it gives to the viewer the vision and the power to live more fully; and to see while living more wakefully, and to become the very thing which one sees. For here, our focus is often directed toward inanimate things. And even when it is directed toward living creatures, it is the non-living part of them that is presented to us first. The life within them is always mixed with something else. But there, all things are living, and they are entirely alive and pure. Even if you take something as if it were not a living thing, its own life flashes forth from within it. The essence in those things is provided to them as something unmoving toward change, granting them life and wisdom. If, then, one has contemplated the wisdom and knowledge in them, they would laugh at all of the lower nature, which only pretends to have a dignity of its own. For from this higher source, life remains, and intellect remains; for all beings stand within eternity. Nothing departs from it, nor does anything turn or move it. For either everything else is after it, or nothing can touch it. But if there were something else, <margin>* by this</margin> it would be *by this* higher source. And if there were something contrary, this Being would be unaffected by that contrary, because of what it is in itself; the contrary would not have made it to be what it is. Rather, there would be some other common thing before it, or that Being would exist within it. In this way, Parmenides <margin>* and not through the absence of another, is it unaffected.</margin> would be right in calling it "Being," *and not through the absence of another is it unaffected, but simply because it is Being. For it is only through itself that it possesses its existence. How then could someone take "Being" away from it, or anything else, as many things as are <margin>* entirely</margin> *entirely in activity, and as many as come from it? As long as it exists, it provides. It exists always, so those things exist as well. And it is so great in power and beauty that it draws <margin>* wishing</margin> *wishing even all things to be hung upon it, having a trace of it from it, so that they love it. And after this, they seek the Good. For "to be" for those things is as it is to us. Nor does this whole world even live and think, so that it might desire what every soul and every intellect desires, which is "to be"; and Being is self-sufficient unto itself.

<column-break/>

A Indeed, from the source which it lives, it lives again toward the same: But the very wisdom of all things and the universal intellect standing by, and co-existing, and existing together, makes it better as if colored, and by mixing in wisdom, it makes its beauty more venerable and more charming. Since even here, a wise life is in truth the beautiful and venerable itself among us—though it is seen only dimly by us—there, however, it is purely discerned. For it grants to the viewer the vision itself, and at the same time the power by which one may live more [fully]; B and living more effectively, one may perceive even through sharpness, and become that very thing which one sees. Among us, indeed, the gaze is very often turned toward inanimate things; and even when it is turned toward animals, then that which is non-living in them is what first occurs to us; and the life which lies hidden within is already mixed. There, however, all things are living and animal-like, and all are pure living things. And if you take anything there as if it were not a living animal, soon that thing also brings its own life into the light for you. If finally someone has contemplated the essence diffusing itself in them, and providing to them a life that is entirely immobile <note>original: *immobilem*; meaning unchanging and eternal</note>, and again prudence and the wisdom and knowledge proper to them, he will immediately mock this entire lower nature, because it claims for itself an essence by common judgment. For from that essence, life remains near it, and intellect remains; for beings consist in eternity. Nothing departs from there, nothing turns, nothing moves it. D For there is no being beyond it which might touch it; and if there were something, it would undoubtedly be beneath it; and if there were something contrary to it, it would still be very little affected by that contrary. But this Being itself would by no means have made it "Being," but rather another common thing above it, and that would be Being itself. For this reason, Parmenides correctly, when he had called Being "One," added that it was unaffected <note>original: *impassibile*; meaning it cannot be acted upon or changed by external forces</note>, not for any other reason, but simply because it is Being itself. F For this alone possesses "being" from itself. In what way, therefore, could someone take "being" from it, or anything else of those things which it truly is in activity, and as many as it possesses from itself? For as far as it exists, it suggests its own things to itself. But it exists always, therefore those things are also always. It is indeed so great in power and beauty, that it allures toward itself and seizes all things hanging entirely from it, and those things think they have done well for themselves if they follow even its trace—which surely after this they seek as the Good.

---

For Being itself, as far as it regards us, is before the Good. Finally, this whole world, toward this very thing so that it may be, affects life and wisdom: and every soul and every intellect desires this very thing which it is—to exist: but "to be" itself is sufficient for itself.

<summary>Plotinus describes the intelligible realm as a place of pure, vibrant life where "Being," "Wisdom," and "Intellect" are one, contrasting this with our physical world where life is mixed with non-living matter. He invokes Parmenides to argue that true Being is self-sufficient, eternal, and the source of all beauty and desire.</summary>

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD SIX, BOOK SEVEN

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD SIX,
## BOOK VII.

->How the multitude of Ideas came into existence, and concerning the Good.<-

->In what way the multitude of Ideas stood forth, and concerning the Good itself.<-

> *God, providing for the living being, did not think in this way: first, that a living being placed among opposites might suffer; second, he created senses so that it might be careful; and third, the instruments of the senses. Rather, by a single stroke of intelligence and an instant of power, all things were arranged in order within the Divine Living Being itself.* Chapter I.

> *For perfect intelligence and virtue, wonderfully preceding motion, sense, and sensible things, neither starts from the world of the senses, nor is it led from one thing to another in order like some moving object as if by steps; it possesses all things at once. The Idea of each thing, however composite or distracted by motions it may be, is simple in God, possessing all those things at once which, in our world, unfold over time.*

---

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing a figure of a man, possibly a representation of a deity or philosopher, standing in a landscape.</image-desc>

<margin>A</margin>When God himself, or at least some God, sent souls down into the realm of generation <note>original: *generationem*, the physical world where things are born and die</note>, he fashioned light-bearing eyes in the face, and applied other instruments to the remaining senses. He did this foreseeing that a living creature could only be preserved if it could see and hear things ahead of time, and finally touch them; thus it might flee some things and pursue others.
<margin>B</margin>But from where did God foresee these things? For we must not think that some living beings were first made by him which, lacking senses, suddenly perished; and that God, being warned by this, then granted these tools in the future so that humans and other animals, equally fortified, might avoid destruction. Perhaps, however, someone will assert that God knew beforehand that the living being would exist among heat and cold, and the other sufferings of bodies. Therefore, knowing these things, so that the bodies of living beings would not be easily destroyed, he attributed sense and instruments through which the sense might be used more conveniently.
<margin>C</margin>But we must ask next whether he joined instruments to souls that already possessed these powers, or whether he gave both. If he also handed over the senses, then the souls were not sensory <note>original: *sensuales*, capable of feeling or perceiving</note> beforehand, even though they already existed then. But if they already had them when the souls were made, and were made to come into generation, then it is certainly innate to them to enter into the physical world.
<margin>D</margin>From which it will seem to follow that it is contrary to nature to depart from generation and live in the intelligible world <note>the realm of pure thought and Forms</note>. Therefore, they seem to have been made to belong to another's jurisdiction, and to live in evil; and providence schemes so that they may be kept in evil. Yet the reasoning of God would be this way, and reasoning would exist in God entirely. From which it must be asked: what are the principles of such discursive thought? For if it comes from other reasonings, one must eventually reach something—or at least some things—existing before reasoning. These
principles are either sense, or rather intellect. But sense had not yet arisen,

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' containing a figure of a person seated on the ground.</image-desc>

<margin>A</margin>Sending them into generation, he—or some god—placed light-bearing eyes in the face for the souls, and the other organs of the senses for each of the senses, foreseeing that they might be saved if they could see and hear beforehand. And by touching, they might flee or pursue.
<margin>B</margin>But from where did he know these things? For surely it was not that other beings had been made before, and then, because of the absence of senses, they perished; and he later gave these things so that the other animals might have sensation and guard themselves against suffering. Or did he know the causes—that the living being would be in heat and cold and other bodily affections—and fearing these things, lest the bodies of the animals be destroyed, did he give them sensation?
<margin>C</margin>And the organs through which the senses would act? Did he give the organs to souls already containing the powers, or both? But if he also gave the senses, the souls were not sensory before. And they would not have had them when they became souls, if they were to go into generation; for it would be innate for them to go into generation.
<margin>D</margin>It would be contrary to nature, then, to be away from generation and to be in the intelligible. And they have been made so that they belong to others. To be in evil they would be. And providence is so that they might be saved * <note>Greek text adds: "in the beautiful"</note> and this is the reasoning of god and reasoning in general. But it must be asked what these reasonings are. For if they are from other reasonings, it is necessary to arrive at something before reasonings. What then are the principles? For they are either sensation or intellect.

...but if there is sense-perception, then there must be Intellect. But if the <term>propositions</term><note>original: "προτάσεις" (protaseis). In logic, these are the premises of an argument.</note> are Intellect, and the conclusion is scientific knowledge, then nothing sensible was planned. For it is not the case that the starting point depends on the intelligible, while the final wealth of results arrives at the non-intelligible. How then can this disposition and thought reach toward sensible things? Furthermore, the providence <note>original: "πρόνοια" (pronoia). Divine care or "thinking ahead."</note> of any animal, or of the whole universe, did not arise from <term>reasoning</term><note>original: "λογισμοῦ" (logismou). Discursive reasoning or "thinking things through" step-by-step.</note>. For reasoning exists not at all there. It is only called "reasoning" to indicate that all things are as they would be if a wise man—who might himself only become wise later—had foreseen them. <margin>* in the latter things</margin> For <margin>Because in those things that have come to be</margin> * reasoning occurs in things that have already come to be; it is useful because of a lack of the power that precedes reasoning. And "foresight" is only necessary because the power in the one who foresees is not so great that he would not need foresight. For foresight exists so that *this* thing might happen and not *that*. But he who foresees is, in a way, afraid that things might not turn out so. And it is not only this. Foresight and reasoning seek one thing in preference to another, but when only one of the two is present, why would one reason? How then does the "Only" and "One" and "Absolutely Simple" admit a perception of "this" so that "that" does not happen? It was as if "this" would happen if "that" did not; and "this" appeared useful, and "this" became the means of salvation. If he had thought this way, then he would have foreseen, and he would have reasoned beforehand. And indeed, what was said from the beginning—that he gave the senses and powers for this reason—remains a most difficult question: how this gift was given. And it is a matter of report. But if a simple activity is not assigned to each thing, and it is not lawful for God to have anything that is not a whole and a totality, <margin>* but because</margin> * then he must consider that in which none of his own attributes are missing. Therefore, he must be present even to the future as if it were already here. That which is "later" in that future is already present there, but it becomes "later" when it happens in another thing. If, therefore, the future is already present, it must be present as something fore-thought into the "later." This means that nothing is seen by anyone at that time. But in reality, since nothing is lacking, all things were already there, and were always there, and were in such a way that one could say "this" comes after "that." For as it unfolds and, as it were, spreads out from there, "this" is shown after "that." But where it is necessary for all to be together, "this" is the whole, and the whole is that which possesses its own cause within itself.

<column-break/>

A Intellect. But if Intellect consists of certain propositions, and the conclusion is scientific knowledge, it follows that no deliberation concerning any sensible thing occurred then. For the beginning does not depend on the intelligible while the end descends into something not-intelligible. Then indeed, how did it happen that such a <term>habit</term><note>original: "habitum," a settled disposition or state of mind.</note> and thought occurred before the sensible world? Wherefore, the providence of no animal, nor of this world in general, occurred from a certain <term>discursive reasoning</term><note>original: "rationis discursione." Step-by-step movement of the mind from one thought to another.</note>. B Providence: since there is no reasoning at all in God. However, a certain "rational counsel" in God is sometimes named, so that it might best be indicated that individual things were established by him just as a wise man would do through counsel in later affairs. Then indeed, it is called "foresight" in God, because he disposed things just as a wise man would have provided for later things. For in those things which are by no means done before reasoning, reasoning is useful on account of the weakness of that power which precedes the act of reasoning. C Foresight also contributes, because the one who foresees did not have the faculty through which he would not need foresight. For foresight tends toward this: that *this* should happen, but not *that*; where there is a certain fear lest something foreign should occur. But where not "this or that" is imminent, but only "this" is present, there is no foresight. Furthermore, reasoning is accustomed to seek or assume *this* instead of *that*. But where only the one is present, D what need is there for reasoning? How then does that which is alone, and one, and altogether simple in itself, admit a revolution within itself of this kind: in which "this" something is established lest perhaps "that" should happen? In which it might be said, "unless this is done, that would happen." In which, again, it might be added, "this has now appeared useful, and if this is done, it will preserve the effect." For if it were so thought by God, he would have foreseen; and therefore he would have reasoned beforehand. E And yet what was said just now from the beginning—that he seems to have given senses and powers for this very reason—although this giving, whether it happens and how it happens, undergoes the greatest doubt. Nevertheless, if it is necessary for any action there to be free from defect, and it is not lawful for anything to be with God that is not a whole and universal, surely it is necessary that in each one of those things which are God's own, all things are contained. F Wherefore, since even the future itself is already present there, there is nothing in him that is "later." But what is already present there becomes "later" in another. If therefore the future is already present, it must be present as if fore-known in the later: that is, so that it then needs nothing from anything else: that is, so that nothing is lacking at all. All things, therefore, were already; and they were always; and they were so, that it was permitted to say "later" that this is after that. Namely, when what is there is unfolded and spread out, then "this" appears after "that." But by the reason that it exists together with itself, "this" and "that" no longer occur, but rather "this whole"—that is, possessing the cause also within itself.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Divine Intellect does not use step-by-step reasoning or "planning" to create the world, as these imply a lack of power or a fear of failure; instead, all causes and effects exist simultaneously and perfectly within the One.</summary>

--- Page 870 ---
<meta>This page continues the exploration of the Divine Intellect (Nous). Having previously established that the Intellect does not "plan" like a human builder, Plotinus now explains that in the higher realm, the essence of a thing and the reason for its existence are one and the same.</meta>

->PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.<-

->*Two things are usually asked about any given matter: what the thing is, and for what reason it exists. The first is explained by definition; the second is shown by identifying the efficient and final causes. In the divine realm, these two are joined together.*<-

---

->### Chapter II.<-

Sense-perception seeks neither of these; <term>reason</term><note>Latin: *ratio*; Greek: *logos*. Here referring to discursive, step-by-step human thought.</note> seeks both separately; but the <term>Intellect</term><note>Latin: *intellectus*; Greek: *nous*. The highest level of reality in Neoplatonism, representing pure, intuitive thought.</note> possesses them both at once. In the Intellect, reason achieves both simultaneously: for as soon as it defines what the nature of a thing is, it immediately grasps through that definition its <term>efficient cause</term><note>The force that brings something into being.</note> and its <term>final cause</term><note>The purpose or goal for which a thing exists.</note>. Conversely, as soon as it knows a cause of this kind, it comprehends the very nature of the thing. Furthermore, in any living being—whether the world itself or any individual creature—these elements are so woven together and emerge so entirely at once that whenever any part is observed, its cause is immediately visible. This union of essence and cause is even greater in the divine world, where every <term>Idea</term><note>Latin: *idea*; Greek: *eidos*. The eternal, perfect blueprints of things.</note> is connected to all others. Each Idea exists as itself while simultaneously holding within it the "reason why" for its own being. Finally, consider fire: whatever it does or undergoes, it receives its cause from elsewhere. However, the fact that it is what it is—namely a body that is hot, dry, and bright—it does not receive from elsewhere. Rather, because it is fire, these qualities emerge together and reciprocally. In this way, "what" is in its nature and "for what reason" it is so are not separated at all. Such forms and definitions are called "necessary and eternal" by the Platonists.

<margin>A</margin> From this, one can perceive the nature of the Mind no less than—and indeed even more than—the things we see with our eyes; yet not in such a way that we see the full magnitude of the Mind. Now, we say that the Mind possesses within itself "what" each thing is, but by no means the "reason why." Or, if we do grant it that, it will not hold the one separately from the other. Let us consider "Man," or perhaps "the Eye" if it happens to be there, existing as a sort of image and a spectacle, or a part of a spectacle.
<margin>B</margin> Such a thing is "Man" in that higher realm, and the "reason why" is also Man. For if there is to be an intellectual Man and an intellectual Eye there, the "reason why" must be contained within that intellectual condition. Otherwise, it would not be there at all, unless it contained within itself the very thing called the "reason why." Among us, however, just as the parts of the body are somewhat separated from one another, so too is the "reason why" separated from the "what it is."
<margin>C</margin> But there, all things are in one. For this reason, the thing itself and the "reason why" the thing is so are entirely identical. Often, even in the realm of bodies, the thing itself and the "reason why" pertaining to the same thing are exactly the same—as in the case of an eclipse of the Sun or Moon <note>In ancient logic, the definition of an eclipse (the Earth's shadow falling on the moon) is also the "reason why" the eclipse happens.</note>. What, then, prevents each thing from being both the "what" and the "reason why"? Indeed, the "reason why" is the very essence of each thing; it is, in fact, necessary.
<margin>D</margin> Thus, it turns out correctly for those who attempt to grasp what each thing is in this way. For what each thing is, it exists for that very reason. I do not mean this simply because the <term>Form</term><note>Latin: *species*; Greek: *eidos*.</note> is the cause of being for each thing—though that is certainly true—but because if you unfold any Form within itself, you will immediately find the "reason why" inside it. For whatever receives an ineffective and empty essence and life does not possess the "reason why" within itself. But that which is both a Form and a property of the Mind—how could it receive the "reason why" from elsewhere? If someone says it is received separately, they ignore that the Mind is this very Form. Therefore, if the Mind must have these things without defect, the "reason why" cannot be missing from them in any way. It holds within itself the reason why the individual things within it are as they are, which is the very same Mind existing. This is true both in total and in part, so that nothing requires a "reason why" after the fact; instead, it is made and simultaneously holds within itself the cause of its own substance. Since it was not generated by chance, it omitted nothing at all pertaining to the logic of why it came to be.

<column-break/>

Therefore, even here, if one does not learn the nature of the Mind, we see even more clearly that which is "the what" of it. For we grant that the Mind provides the "that it is," but not yet the "why," or if we do, not separately. Let us look at "Horse" or "Eye," if it happens to be there, like a statue—that which is "Man" there, since it is an intellectual thing. Both "Man" and "Eye" must exist there, and be intellectual, or they would not be there at all, unless the "reason why" was interwoven. For here each of the parts is separate, and the "why" is also separate. But there, in all things, the thing and the "reason why" are the same. And even here, sometimes the thing and the "reason why" are the same, such as "What is an eclipse?" So what prevents each thing from being its own "why," and this being the case for other essences? It is better to say that the "what it is" and the "why it is" coincide. For what a thing is, it is for that reason. I do not mean just that the Form is the cause of being—though that is true—but if you look at the Form itself toward itself, you will see the "why" in it. For that which has life, has the "why" entirely within. Being a Form and Mind, from where else would it take its "why"? If one says from Mind, or separately, then Mind is that very thing. It must not have these things lacking, nor the "why" lacking. It has the "why," and thus each of the things in it must be itself; so that it needs nothing else for the "why," but has been brought forth together, and has in itself the cause of its own existence. Having been brought forth, it would have nothing left out of the reason...

<summary>Plotinus argues that in the Divine Intellect, a thing's essence (what it is) and its purpose (why it is) are identical and inseparable. Unlike human reasoning, which figures out the "why" after the "what," divine thought possesses both simultaneously as a single, perfect reality.</summary>

# BOOK SEVEN.

<margin>It is explained that both are missing.</margin>

<margin>Both at once. In that very thing it does not grasp in the invisible members the mind itself, that which is born, which is natural; it refers thus far: from where things come.</margin>

Why <note>original: "διὰ τί"</note> things are as they are is not a separate question for the Intellect; rather, possessing everything, it also possesses the excellence <note>original: "τὸ καλῶς"</note> which belongs to the cause. And so, to those things that participate in it, it grants their nature in such a way that they also possess their own "reason why." Or rather, just as in this universe—which is composed of many parts—all things are connected to one another, so too in the whole would be the "why" of each thing, just as in any individual object a part is seen in relation to the whole. If things were produced one after another, then the causes and the effects would be separate; but in the divine realm, all things exist toward the whole individually, and each towards itself. Therefore, if the <term>co-existence</term><note>Latin: *consistentia*; Greek: *sunupostasis*. The state of existing together as a unified whole.</note> of all things is simultaneous and not by chance, and they are in no way detached, they must contain their effects and causes within themselves. Each thing is such that it is, as it were, a cause without a cause. If they do not have a cause for their being, but are self-sufficient and isolated from external causes, then they must contain their own cause within themselves. Furthermore, if nothing there is by chance, but many things exist in each, then because each thing is all that it possesses, you could say "why" each thing is. The "why" was already present and existed there. It is not just a "why," but a "that" <note>original: "ὅτι"</note>, or rather both. For everything that is perfect must rule. Since a thought is not like an imperfect <term>generation</term><note>Latin: *genitura*; Greek: *ginomena*. Something that is in the process of becoming or being born, rather than being eternally complete.</note>, if it is perfect, one cannot say where it is lacking. 
<margin>† Since all things that have [this]</margin>
The "why" is <note>original: "διὰ τί"</note> present in what is present. 
<margin>† where it is present</margin>
Since it is present, you can say "why" it is present. Therefore, in the very substance of a thought or an action, the "why" is contained. For example, the <term>Ideal Man</term><note>The perfect, eternal form of humanity in the Intellect.</note> appears as a whole, bringing himself along with him. And having all things together from the beginning, he is stable as a whole. If he were not present as a whole, but something were to be added to him, that would belong to the realm of "becoming." But he always is, and so he is present. The man who is "becoming" in our world, however, is <term>generable</term><note>Subject to birth, change, and decay.</note>.

<column-break/>

But possessing the whole, the Intellect possesses at the same time the reason "why" it is made so well, which belongs to the cause. Furthermore, to those things that participate in it, it passes on nature in such a way that they also obtain the "reason why" they received it. Therefore, just as in this world—composed of many parts—all things are connected to each other, and within the very fact that they exist in it, the "why" is included, so each thing exists just as in any body a part is seen to relate to the whole. In that realm, it is certainly not a case where one thing comes first, followed by another; rather, they mutually contain the cause and the effect at the same time. Thus, it is much more necessary there that all things relate to the whole individually, and each thing to itself. For this reason, if the consistency of all things is simultaneous and not random, and if they must not be separated in any way, then surely effects contain their causes within themselves. Each thing is such that it has a cause, as it were, without an external cause. If they do not have an external cause for existing, but are self-sufficient in themselves, even if they are solitary as far as the fellowship of causes is concerned, they certainly have the cause within themselves. Moreover, if nothing there is by chance, but many things are in each, and each thing is everything it possesses, you will certainly be able to explain the "why" of each. The "why" was leading, then, and was present there simultaneously—not as a "why" properly speaking, but as a "what" existing entirely. Indeed, both are one. Surely, if the intellectual concept of the mind itself, insofar as it is mind, were like some imperfect generation, it would suffer from some excess or lack. If, then, the concept is perfect, it cannot be pointed out where it fails; nor can a reason be brought for why this or that is not present. Since it is present, you can affirm the "why" it is present. In the substance itself, therefore, the "why" is contained. In any notion or action of the mind, the whole occurs at once, as in the case of the Ideal Man: the whole man shines forth at once, bringing himself with the notion, and possessing from the beginning all things that he has. Thus, he is placed there as a whole, ready at hand. Now, unless he were whole, and something else had to be added, that would belong rather to the realm of "becoming." But that Ideal Man always exists; therefore he is whole. The man who is "made" here, however, is undoubtedly subject to generation.

Someone might ask here what prevents the Intellect from having consulted with itself beforehand. But it must be said that it is entirely fertile according to its own nature. Therefore, nothing is to be taken away and nothing added. However, because of our <term>supposition</term><note>A logical starting point used for the sake of argument.</note>, it is imagined to deliberate and reason. For we have supposed that things are being "made." Let us grant, then, that there is will and reasoning for the sake of showing things as if they were always being made, and as if the Intellect reasons from a source. For if there were reasoning in what exists eternally, 
<margin>* it had been forgotten,</margin>

Someone here will ask: what prevents the Intellect from having consulted beforehand? But it must be said that the Intellect is inwardly fertile; therefore, nothing is to be taken away and nothing added. Nevertheless, because of the very hypothesis <note>The idea that the world was "created" at a point in time.</note>, it is imagined to consult and argue. But from the fact that it has been demonstrated that they exist always, such argumentation is removed. For argumentation does not apply to that which always exists; for this condition would belong to one who had forgotten how he acted before. # PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin> In the same way, the matter itself stands. Things are truly beautiful if they are present together with their cause; for even now, a thing is beautiful because it possesses all its own parts. This is because the <term>Form</term><note>Latin: *species*; Greek: *eidos*. In Platonic thought, this is the ideal "blueprint" or eternal essence of a thing.</note> itself is that which possesses all things, especially if it occupies matter; it occupies it if it leaves nothing unformed. Indeed, it would leave it unformed if any form were missing, such as an eye or any other part. For this reason, when you assign a cause, you name all the parts. Why, then, are there eyes? So that all parts may be present. Again, why the nose? So that every single part may be present. <margin>B</margin> Now, if you argue that these things are granted for the sake of "preservation," you are bringing in a certain guardian of <term>Essence</term><note>Latin: *essentia*; Greek: *ousia*. The core reality or "being" of a thing.</note> existing within that essence itself; and you will judge that this contributes to its being. Thus, even before this, the essence existed: and so the cause is a part of the essence. And even if it were something else, this very thing which is its essence still exists. Therefore, all things harmonize among themselves, and the essence is whole, perfect, and universal. This very fact—that it fares well—exists together with the cause and is within the cause. And so, essence, the "what-it-is," and the "reason-why" are proven to be one and the same. <margin>C</margin> If, therefore, this condition is included in the Form itself (such as the Human Form), so that there is a "sensible man" <note>A human being as perceived through the five senses, rather than the pure "ideal" man of the mind.</note>, and he is sensible in a certain way by an eternal necessity and perfection of the <term>Intellect</term><note>Latin: *mens*; Greek: *nous*. The realm of pure thought and divine reality.</note>; if that Intellect is perfect, it embraces the causes within itself, so that we may observe afterwards that the matter is rightly disposed. For there, the cause is one with the essence, completing the essence. There, man is not merely <margin>D</margin> an "intellectual" being who later, when sent into the world of becoming <note>The physical world where things are born, change, and die.</note>, has the power of sensation added to him. If, I say, the matter stands thus, one wonders what prevents that Intellect from inclining toward these lower things. For what is this very thing called "sensible"? Is it perhaps that which is able at some point to grasp sensible things? If so, would that not be absurd? For there, something sensitive would exist from eternity, but here it would finally be fulfilled; and the "falling away" of that power would only be completed here, when the soul has already become worse.

*Each thing naturally possesses its very being from its own internal specific form. Therefore, he who defines the good as that which is joined from soul and body does not yet assign the formal reason by which this very thing exists.*

---

### Cap. IIII.
### Chapter IV.

<margin>A</margin> **R**eturning again to unravel this doubt: we must take up from the beginning what "Man" is. And perhaps it is better to first explain what this living man here is; lest, perhaps not yet fully knowing what is here, we investigate that higher Man too curiously as if we already held this one. For perhaps it may seem to some that our man here and that one there are the same. Let the beginning of our consideration be taken chiefly from this point. We must certainly ask: is this <margin>B</margin> man of ours a certain <term>Reason</term><note>Latin: *ratio*; Greek: *logos*. Here meaning a formative principle or "logic" that defines a being.</note> differing from the soul that makes this man, supplying him with life and the discourse of reason? Or rather, is the soul itself—such a soul, I mean—the man? Or finally, is man the soul using a certain kind of body? But if man is a "rational animal," and an animal is that which is composed of soul and body, this definitive reason for man will not be the same as the soul. Yet if the "reason of man" consists of a <margin>C</margin> rational soul and a body, how will it be an eternal substance? For the reason of such a man only comes into being when the soul and body meet: surely such a reason...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But if they are indeed beautiful, they possess the same quality together with their cause, since even now and the same thing; for the form is all things, and it holds the whole. It holds it, unless it leaves it unformed. It would be lacking in form, for instance, if an eye were missing. When you assign the cause, you speak of all things. Why eyes? So that all things may be there. And why the <margin>B</margin> nose? So that all things may be there, for all things must be. But if you speak for the sake of preservation, you place the preservation of the essence within itself, and that which contributes to being; then you will find being within the essence itself. So that even before this, essence was, and thus the cause is a part of the essence. And this is another thing. And being for the essence is the cause of this for each other. And the whole essence is everything, and the "well-being" is with the cause and in the cause. And the essence, and the "what it was to be," and the "wherefore" are entirely one and the same. If, then, in the form—for example, the human form—such a disposition exists, to be a sensible man, <margin>C</margin> and what kind he is, by eternal necessity and the perfection of the Intellect; which, if it is perfect, possesses the causes within itself. So that we see afterwards that it is rightly disposed; for there, the "one" is the completion of the essence. And man there is not only Intellect, but also a certain sensitive part, when he is sent into generation. But if it is so, what hinders <margin>D</margin> even that Intellect from being inclined toward the things here? For what would be "sensible"? Or "sensible" of sensible things. How is it not absurd there, that the power is there, but the activity is here, whenever the soul becomes worse?

---

### Cap. IIII.
### Chapter IV.

<margin>A</margin> **A**gain, therefore, we must take up from above this problem: what man is. Perhaps it would be better, before that one there, to examine the one here, lest perhaps not knowing perfectly the one here while thinking we have him, we seek the one there. For it might seem to some that he is the same. The beginning of the inquiry is from here: is this man a certain "reason" of the soul, different from the one <margin>B</margin> making this man and providing the power of reasoning? Or is such a soul the man? Or is it the soul making use of such a body? If man is a rational animal, and an animal is that which is from soul and body, then the "reason" itself would not be the same as the soul. But if the "reason" is truly from a rational soul and a body for the sensible world, <margin>C</margin> is this itself an eternal substance? For then the reason of such a man comes into being when the soul comes together.

He then begins an inquiry into the definition of "Man," questioning whether man is the soul, the body, or a composite of both.</summary>

->**Man is an intellectual and rational soul, at once both soul and sense. And this condition of the human soul is expressed exactly according to the character of our Idea. Chapter V.**<-

> *Which Idea indeed is the "first man"; but the soul, being as I have said, is the "second man"; and the "third man" is as if no longer man, but an animal composed of our body together with a certain life infused into it by the preceding soul, in which sense-perception is more effective, while in the [physical] animal sense is more dull—yet it is a certain human affection, which declares that this life of the animal does not only hope in the soul, but also depends upon our own, just as our soul always depends upon and acts from the divine.*

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the "Form of Man" from page 696. Plotinus is moving from the abstract definition of "Man" in the Divine Intellect to the practical application of how the soul manifests as "Man" across different levels of reality—intellectual, rational, and sensory.</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin> ...a lesser man, who nevertheless possesses form, and <term>Reasons</term><note>Latin: *rationes*; Greek: *logoi*. These are the formative principles or blueprints that shape matter.</note>, or habits, as well as affections and powers, though they are weak and obscure. Indeed, all things here are obscure, because this is not the primary man. Furthermore, the species of the senses are different, as are the senses themselves; for even if they appear sharp, they are nonetheless dull and mere images when compared to the higher senses. However, the man presiding over this one exists as a more divine soul, possessing a better "man" and far clearer senses. Perhaps it is this man whom Plato defines. <margin>B</margin> He adds to the definition, however, "the soul using a body," because the soul which is defined as "man" hovers over that soul which directly uses the body. For the more divine soul uses the body only in a secondary way. For when that which has been made has already emerged as a sensory being, this higher soul follows, providing a more complete life—or rather, it does not merely follow, but employs it, as it were. For it does not stand apart from the intelligible world, but by constantly touching it, it holds the lower soul suspended from itself, mixing itself with Reason according to Reason. Therefore, this man, though obscure in himself, becomes more radiant through such illumination.

---

->*Our soul possesses sense so fundamentally that it always uses a sense of some kind. Chapter VI.*<-

> *For even outside the earthly body, it perceives in the air through an aerial body, and in the heavens through a celestial body—perceiving things here in a direct way, but there perceiving celestial things. Indeed, even beyond the heavens, by a certain sense of imagination, it transforms the very concepts of the intellect into imaginable forms. Each of us has three men: the ideal, the rational, and the sensory, which are connected in a descending order. But different people among us live according to different ones of these three, as they live one life or another. And insofar as they change their forms of living, they also change their own <term>daemons</term><note>Latin: *daemonas*. In Neoplatonism, a "daemon" is a guiding spirit or a higher level of the self that leads the soul toward its next stage of existence.</note>, the leaders of their present life. At last, those who live an intellectual life most fully, having obtained a more sublime daemon, even achieve God as their leader through it. After this, Plotinus speaks after the Egyptian fashion regarding the transmigration of the irrational soul, and even the transition of such a soul into the very nature of a beast; which he himself does not entirely affirm, nor do other Platonists approve, and so we shall omit it here.*

---

<margin>A</margin> But in what way is the faculty of sensing present in that more excellent soul? Truly, that power of sensing belongs properly to those things which are there called "sensibles"; and thus, there is sense there, just as there are sensibles. Wherefore, in this way, it perceives the sensory harmony by that higher sense; while, evidently, the sensory man is contained by and perceives through sense, and fits what follows all the way to the end to the harmony flourishing there. Furthermore, this fire here corresponds with that fire there, which the soul perceived by its own particular sense—a sense, I say, having a certain proportion suitable to the nature of that fire. <margin>B</margin> For if these bodies were there, the soul would also sense and notice them there. But in fact, the man living there is a soul of such a kind as is capable of apprehending these things; whence the later man, being a certain imitation of that one, also possesses <term>Reasons</term> by a certain imitation. And the man who is in the Mind <note>Latin: *in mente*; Greek: *en noi*. Referring to the Divine Intellect.</note> offers a man preceding all men, who indeed shines upon the second man; and the second man likewise refines the third. In a certain way, the last man has all the others, not by being made into them, but rather by lying adjacent to them. <margin>C</margin> Our man here acts toward the ultimate end; but to this man, something shines forth from the one preceding him; and to that one, in turn, an act is suggested by the third, higher man. Thus, each person is defined according to the level at which they act, although everyone possesses all levels, and yet, in another sense, does not possess them. But after this third life is separated from the body, and likewise the third man, if the soul immediately preceding follows him—that is, a follower not at all segregated from the higher realms—then <margin>D</margin>
<meta>The catchword "ubicumque est vltima" suggests the next page begins with "wherever the last is, the preceding also..."</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> <note>original: "πλὼ μορφὼ ἔχει..."</note> ...it has form and the reasons, or dispositions and powers, which are dim, as it is not primarily existent. And indeed, there are other senses of other forms, which are clear, but these are dimmer compared to the forms and images. But the one presiding over it is of a soul already more divine, having a better man and clearer senses. <margin>B</margin> Plato, defining this, added "using a body," because it stays upon the soul that first uses the body. For once that which is generated becomes sensory, this soul follows with a clearer life—or rather, it does not follow, but has attached it to itself. For it does not depart from the Intelligible, but having touched it most closely, it holds the lower soul suspended from it, mixing itself with Reason. <margin>C</margin> Whence this man, although dim, becomes clearer by that illumination.

---

<margin>Α</margin> How then is the sensory power in the better soul? The sensory power is of those things which are sensibles there; for there are sensibles there. Therefore, it also perceives in this way the sensory harmony, and by the sense of the sensory man, it fits the sensory things which reach the lowest level to the harmony there. <margin>Β</margin> Just as fire here is fitted to the fire there, for there was a sense of that fire in the soul, analogous to the nature of things there. For if there were bodies there, there would be senses and apprehensions of them in the soul. And the man there is such a soul, capable of sensing these. Whence the later man, the imitation, has the reasons in imitation. And the man in the Intellect is the man before all men. This one shines upon the second, and that one upon the third. And the last one has the others in a way <margin>C</margin>, being adjacent to them. And the one of us acts toward the last; and to him comes something from the one before him; and to that one, the activity comes from the third. For each is that according to which he acts. Although he has all and does not have them. But with the separation from the body of such a life, and of the third man, if the second follows, being inseparable from the things above, that one is already... <margin>D</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the human soul, which contains all "Reasons" or formative principles, manifests in different physical forms. It explores the transition from human to animal existence and the role of the World Soul in preparing matter for life.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN.

...to be. But when it is transferred into the body of a beast, it may seem a wonder how that which is the very <term>Reason</term><note>Greek: *logos*; Latin: *ratio*. The divine blueprint or formative principle that defines a thing's essence.</note> of a man is transferred there as well. In truth, the soul was already all things; it simply acts according to a different principle at different times. Insofar as it remains pure and not yet corrupted, it wills to be man, and it exists as man. For that is the better state, and the soul acts according to what is better. It also produces higher <term>Daimons</term><note>Greek: *daimones*. In Neoplatonism, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits or higher states of being between humans and gods.</note>, yet these are of the same kind as the soul that acts as a man. Indeed, that which precedes the human soul is more "daimonic"—or rather, it is a God. For a daimon attached to God is a kind of imitation of God, just as the man here is suspended from the Man there in the divine realm. For the one to whom man is immediately joined is not called "God" in the highest sense. There is a difference between souls, even if they belong to the same rank. We must speak of the "species of daimons," those whom Plato calls daimons. But when the soul follows a path and chooses the nature of a beast, then the "seminal reason" <term>Seminal Reason</term><note>Latin: *ratio seminalis*. A latent 'seed-principle' within the soul that allows it to take on different biological forms depending on its moral state.</note> of that animal—which was already present within the soul even when it acted as a man—exhibits itself. For the soul possesses this lower principle, though such an activity is judged to be a degradation.

<column-break/>

### Chapter VII.

<margin>### Chapter VII.</margin>
BUT if the soul, having already been corrupted and made worse, fashions a beast-like nature, it does not mean that from the beginning it was destined to create an ox or a horse. In that case, the seminal reason of the horse and the horse itself would be contrary to nature. Rather, they are something "lesser," but not truly against nature. In a way, that horse or dog was present from the beginning; if the soul's power is sufficient, it creates what is better; if not, it creates whatever it can. The soul is, as it were, already committed to action, much like craftsmen who, though they know how to manufacture many kinds of objects, ultimately produce what they are assigned to do, or what the material—by its own readiness—demands. What is to stop the power of the <term>World Soul</term><note>Greek: *tēs tou pantos psychēs*; Latin: *animæ mundi*. The universal soul that animates the entire physical cosmos.</note>, since it contains every "Reason," from pre-figuring the matter? This happens even before the individual life-powers come from the specific soul; this pre-figuration acts like "rays of light" running ahead into the matter. Then, the individual soul follows these traces to complete the work, articulating each part and limb. Any given soul becomes what it has fallen into by shaping itself, just as a dancer in a play or a pageant adapts himself to the specific role and gestures commanded of him. But we have been led to this point by following the sequence of the argument. Our original purpose was to inquire how the faculty of sensation exists in Man, and how that divine part of us does not stoop toward the cycle of birth and death. It now appears to us, and reason has demonstrated, that the divine does not look toward these lower things, but rather these things strive toward the divine, hanging and depending upon it.

---

->*Plotinus argues that the Idea of "Man" cannot be mixed with the Idea of "Horse." Furthermore, he maintains that our Intellect remains perpetually in the divine realm, while our Reason is governed directly by that Intellect. Thus, the divine nature of our soul is never truly cast down into lower things; instead, lower things are lost in the higher. Consequently, the human species is never truly transformed into a horse's species. You should note that in our body, beyond the general "vital trace" impressed by the World Soul, there is a specific vital trace impressed by our own individual soul. This soul is distinct from the World Soul and is changed by its own internal state rather than external forces. From this, it follows that the soul never entirely sheds its own proper species through such a change. Finally, the soul is said to use "senses" even in the divine world, because it perceives bodily things, though it views them as if from a high watchtower.*<-
