...to have powers toward those things. Moreover, these sensible things are joined with this physical man, but those intelligible things are joined with that divine Man. For those things are also sensible in a certain way; we have named them so because they are "bodies" in the divine sense, but they are perceived differently than these of ours. It was established, furthermore, that this sense [on earth] is dimmer than that perception [in the divine], which we called "sense" only because it perceives bodies, but we granted it to be far more clear. And for this reason, we also said that this earthly man is "sensual": since he apprehends in a worse way and worse things—namely, only the images of those higher things. Thus, it may rightly be said that these earthly senses are obscure intelligences, while those divine intelligences are very clear senses.

->*The first Intellect, with an overflowing fecundity of light, naturally pours itself forth inwardly into as many powers as possible. From this intellectual and natural propagation, the natural forms of things go forth like lights.*<-

## Chapter VIII.

In that divine realm, then, a horse is not "thought up" so that a horse might be made here. Otherwise, these things here would be the cause of those things there, and the horse would be known to us before it was known there. Furthermore, the multitude of forms there seems to be enumerable only insofar as Being, which exists after the <term>One</term><note>The Absolute, the first principle of all reality in Neoplatonism, from which all things emanate.</note>, always appears as a manifold Plenitude; indeed, every primary thing there is equally full of all things.

<margin>A</margin> **B**UT let the faculty of sensing be as it is. But in what way does that "Whole Horse," or any animal there, not look toward these creatures of ours? For if that Intellect had "found" the notion of a horse just so a horse could be generated here, then (though it is impossible to understand how) it would have first willed the horse and then thought about how to make it. But the intellection of "horse" must have already existed if it willed to make the horse. Therefore, it is not that the Intellect "thought it out" as a plan, but rather it is clear that the "unbegotten" horse existed before the horse that was to exist here.

<margin>B</margin> If, then, the horse existed before its generation on earth, and it was not thought of by the Intellect merely so that it might be born here, then surely the Intellect—which possesses the Horse there—did not look toward these things of ours, but held the horse within itself. It did not have the horse and other things in order to produce these physical versions; rather, those things existed in their own right, and these earthly versions necessarily followed from them. For it was not possible for the divine power to stop only at those divine forms and proceed no further.

<margin>C</margin> For who could have restrained that power, which is capable of both remaining within itself and proceeding outward? But one might ask: why are these [irrational] animals there at all? What place do they have in God? We can accept that rational beings are there; but what honor is there in such a multitude of irrational creatures? Indeed, it seems to introduce something base. Yet it is clear that Being itself, while one, must also be many, since it follows after that which is entirely One. Otherwise, it would not be the "second" stage after the One, but would be the One itself.

<margin>D</margin> But since it comes after the One, it cannot remain perfectly single, but must fall short of that unity. Since the One is altogether the best, it was necessary for Being to be "more" than one, for multitude is a sign of falling away from absolute unity. But what prevents Being from stopping at the number two (the <term>Dyad</term><note>The principle of "twoness" or the first step into plurality.</note>)? Because each part of a pair is such that it cannot be entirely one. It is necessary for "one and another" to exist as a pair, and then for each of those to be multiplied in the same way.

<margin>E</margin> Accordingly, in the first "twoness" or <term>Binarius</term><note>Latin: *binarius*; Greek: *duas*. The principle of duality.</note> there is both motion and rest. There is also Intellect, and there is Life—I mean a perfect Intellect and a perfect Life. Therefore, the Intellect is not just one single mind, but the "Total Intellect," containing all individual intellects within it, multiplied to the extent that...

<column-break/>

...having the powers toward those things. Those [divine] things use these sensible things, through the relationship to those. For those are in a way sensible, or we named them so because they are bodies, but in a different way than these. He says that this sense here is dimmer than the perception there—which we call "sense" because it was of bodies—yet [that one] is more vivid. But the sensing part of this [earthly man] became a perceiver of lesser things, of the images of those. So that

<margin>B</margin> these senses are obscure intellections, while the intellections there are vivid senses.

<margin>A</margin> BUT as for the sensing part, or how the Horse in general and each of the animals exists there: does it look toward the things here? If it held a thought in its mind so that a horse might come to be here, then Being [the Intellect] was wishing to make a horse. But it is already clear that the thought of the horse existed before it wished to make it. So that

<margin>B</margin> it did not think in order to produce. Rather, the horse existed before it was generated, before the one that was to follow. If, then, it existed before the generation, it was not thought of so that it might be generated; nor did it have the horse within itself by looking at the things here. Rather, it [the Intellect] was the one who held the horse there. It did not hold the form of those and other things so it could make these; rather, those were the primary things, and these followed those. For the power was not such that it stopped at the

<margin>C</margin> divine things; for who would have stopped the power, which is both staying and capable [of proceeding]? But how are these animals there? Are these in God? For the rational ones are there; but this great multitude [of beasts], what is honorable about it? Or is it the opposite? Because Being must be many, being after the "entirely One." Otherwise it would not be after that, but would be it. Being after that—

<margin>D</margin> it did not exist above that [the One]. It falls short. Since the One is best, it was necessary for there to be "more" [than one], for multitude is in deficiency. Why then does it not stop at being a Dyad? Because each of the things in the Dyad was not entirely one. But all had to obtain being. And of those, again, there was motion

<margin>E</margin> in the Dyad, and rest. There was also Intellect, and Life, and perfect Intellect, and perfect Life. It was not as one Intellect, but as all. And each individual intellect, having such a...

# BOOK SEVEN.
Nn 3

...to all, and more, and holding as one following soul, but as all and more... possessing the power for producing each individual soul. And it was a complete living being <note>Greek: *zoon panteles*; the "Universal Animal" or the sum total of all life within the Divine Mind</note>. It did not contain man alone within it, for otherwise only man would be here on earth.

---

But someone asks: if we exclude the "honorable" animals, how then were the lesser and the irrational ones there in the divine? Clearly, the "complete" must include even the irrational. If the rational is honorable, and the intellectual is honorable, then the "unintelligent" would be its opposite. Yet how can anything be unintelligent or irrational there, since it exists within the very source of all things? But before we speak further on these matters, let us understand that the man here on earth is a reflection of that Man there. Just as other animals here are reflections of those there, but we must understand the heavenly ones in a much greater sense. Perhaps there is no "reasoning" there in the way we know it; for while man is "rational" here, there he exists in a state *before* the need for logical discourse. Why then does man reason here, while other animals do not? Is it because the Intellect is different there for man than for other animals, and thus the resulting "reasoning" here is also different? For in a way, even in other animals on earth, we see many works of thought. Why then is the term "rational" not applied to them? And why are even men not equal to one another in their thinking? It is because of the way they deliberate. Since there are many lives (as motions) and many thoughts, they did not all have to be the same. Rather, there are different lives and different thoughts, and these differences are more or less luminous and clear. Those closest to the First Principle are the "first" differences, followed by the second and third. Therefore, among these divine thoughts, some are gods, while others belong to a second genus—which contains what we call "rationality" here. Next follows the nature we call "irrational." But there, even that which we call irrational was a form of Reason <term>Logos</term><note>In Neoplatonism, *Logos* is the formative principle that flows from the Intellect to shape the world; even a "lower" animal is shaped by a divine "reasoning" or "code."</note>. And it was eternal, because the mind that understands a "horse" is Intellect, and the thought of a "horse" is itself Intellect. If it were only a thought, it would be strange; for nothing would prevent the thought itself from being merely an image of a sensible thing. But in that realm, the thought and the thing are the same...

<column-break/>

...all acts, indeed even more abundant. That Intellect certainly lives not as a single soul, but as the sum of all souls, possessing an even more abundant power for procreating individual souls. It is a universal living being, not containing man alone within itself; otherwise, only man would exist here in the physical world.

### *Since in the first Being the "first number" is the origin of things, it is right that the entire count of things exists there. Likewise, since it is the first Form, it is right that the forms there differ by degrees, just like species. Again, in the perfect life and intellect, every "Idea" of a thing—even of those which do not have life here—is a certain life and intelligence. Chapter IX.*

Similarly, the forms of metals—which do not shine by their own power here—all shine within their own planets with a variety of light. The forms of animals that we consider "ugly" are beautiful in the heavens. Life there, and its wonderfully effective intellect, moves within itself as much as possible; by this movement, it pours itself out as if dividing itself, yet this is not a material division of a solid thing, but a formal one. It distinguishes itself through many degrees of forms. Just as the progression of the physical world moves from the broad to the narrow, so the Divine proceeds into more specific ideas of "lesser" things. But since all Ideas there arise from one individual life and intelligence, all are contained within each other: just as in any single star there are also the powers of the other stars, insofar as all things in heaven agree in the same light of the Sun, even though each star displays its own unique appearance and primary effect. In the same way, every Idea brings forth its own nature while still containing all the others within itself.

---

<margin>A</margin> But truly, someone will say, let those animals there be primarily the ones to be "honored": but in what way can the "viler" or "irrational" ones exist there? These are surely judged lowly here because they are deprived of reason; we usually think an animal is worthy of honor because of its "rational virtue." And if a thing is honored because of its intellectual nature, it should rightly be despised if that nature is absent. <margin>B</margin> However, it is difficult to say how anything there can be lacking mind or reason, since the source in which each thing exists is Reason itself and the "First Intellect." Now, therefore, before we address these specific points, let us agree on this: the man living here on earth is not the same as that "Ideal Man" there. Similarly, the animals there do not exist as they do here; they are to be understood at a much more excellent degree. Furthermore, nothing strictly "rational" <note>original: "rationale"</note> exists there in our sense. Here, perhaps, <margin>C</margin> someone might use reason to discourse and move from one thought to another; but there, an "act" flourishes that is superior to logical reasoning. But why does man here reason, while the animals do not? Surely because the Intellect is different for man than for other animals, and therefore the "reasoning" we see here is also different. Indeed, other animals do show many signs of "thoughtful duties." Why then are they not called "equally rational"? To that, one must ask in turn: why are not even men themselves equal to one another in their reasoning? <margin>D</margin> It is worthwhile to consider that there are many "lives" (acting as motions) and many "intelligences." It was not necessary for these to be identical to one another; rather, there are different lives and different intelligences. These differences are more or less "luminous" and clear. That which is closest to the first principles is designated by the "first" differences, while that which is second is designated by the second...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Ennead VI, Book 7, where Plotinus explores how diversity exists within the Divine Intellect. He is addressing the question of how "lesser" or "irrational" features of animals—like claws, teeth, or horns—can have a perfect, intellectual archetype in the divine realm.</meta>

# PLOTINUS: ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin> In what way is this [the Idea] an act of intelligence, while the thing itself is deprived of intellect? Otherwise, the Mind itself would be making itself mindless. But indeed, the thing there <note>referring to the intelligible realm or the World of Forms</note> is not lacking in intellect, but is an intellect of a specific kind. For it is also a life of a specific kind. For just as any life is not lacking in the function by which it becomes life, so too such an intellect is not far from the similar function by which it becomes an intellect. For the intellect corresponding to each individual animal flourishing there is not deprived of the quality that makes it an intellect—both of the whole and, for example, of man. Indeed, whatever part you take, that part is itself all things there, but perhaps in a different way. For in actuality it is a specific part, but meanwhile it has the power of all things. We, however, perceive in individual things only that which exists in actuality. That which exists in actuality is the "ultimate" form: so that the ultimate of this particular intellect is a "horse." Where the intellect reaches its limit, the "horse" arises, always proceeding into a lesser life; and where it reaches a lower limit, a lower animal arises. For those powers, while they unfold, continuously leave behind what is above. <margin>C</margin> They proceed, always letting something go, and in that letting go, they always provide other and different things. And because of the deficiency <note>Greek: *endeia*</note> of the animal now appearing, they devise something to be added from that which suffers from the defect: for example, since there is no longer a sufficiency for life, the claw and the beak appeared, and horns and teeth appeared. Therefore, wherever the Mind itself, descending, receives itself back from above into the sufficiency of its own nature and emerges, it finds within itself the remedy for that deficiency.

> *The primary Life and Intelligence, and the most perfect Living Being, contains all possible grades and species of life, intelligence, and animals that can be conceived.*

### Chapter X.

Since the first multiplication <note>the transition from the Absolute One into the Many Ideas</note> occurs there, it is right that the "Better" is multiplied into species; these are both united in an extraordinary way and yet distinct. In dark matter, the forms of things are hardly united and are confused among themselves; but in the primary Form <note>the Divine Mind</note>, they are at once most effective and most clear. All the forms of things are said to have sent their own properties into one common nature, and the universe there occurs equally as "uniform" and "omni-form" <note>having one shape and every shape at once</note>.

<margin>A</margin> BUT in what way is there any deficiency there? Why are there horns there? Are they for the sake of defense? Truly, such things exist there for the sake of self-sufficiency and perfection, as part of the Living Being itself. For it was necessary for the Living Being to be perfect, just as Mind is perfect and Life is perfect. Therefore, if not this, then that must exist. And the difference itself arises because one thing is made for another, so that from all things comes the most perfect Living Being, the most perfect Mind, the most perfect Life; and each individual part is also perfect as an individual. Then truly, even if it consists of many things, it must again be <margin>B</margin> one, and vice versa. Otherwise, it is impossible for it to be made of many parts while those many parts remain the same as one another; otherwise, the One would have existed as self-sufficient by itself. It is necessary, therefore, to consist of things that always differ in species, just as every composite does—yet in such a way that individuals are properly preserved, as are the Forms and the Patterns <term>rationes <gloss>the Greek *logoi* or organizing principles</gloss></term>. For the Forms, such as the Form of Man, must display as many differences as they consist of; although there is a single thing in all of them, where there are <margin>C</margin> certain things better and others worse relative to each other, like the eye and the finger. Yet they are members of one and the same body, any of which is "worse" than the whole. But it is undoubtedly better that the matter stands thus: for the Pattern <note>*Ratio*/*Logos*</note> is a living being, and that which is not entirely the same as the living being is something else. Virtue also has something in common within you, and the beauty of all things is found where that which is common is equally common.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...to the thing, how the one is thought, the thing is un-thought. For in this way the mind would make itself mindless, but it is not mindless, but a mind of such a kind... in life and... for as any life is not separated from its function, since neither is the mind according to its definition separated from it, by being the mind of all things and of man. For each part is itself... <margin>B</margin> it appears, but perhaps otherwise, in actuality... but it is able to receive these... according to each thing in actuality, and that in actuality... so that this is the last, a horse... and where it stopped proceeding, always into a lesser life... being another lower stop... <margin>C</margin> for the powers, leaving behind... always proceeding... and to appear other things. But through the deficiency <note>Greek: *endeia*</note>... to the appearing thing, failing, to add another. As for example, since there is no longer... for life, there appeared a claw and the hooked [beak]... or the jagged tooth, or the nature of a horn. The claw descended. In this way again... the restorations of nature not to see in the failing thing a remedy for the labor.

<margin>A</margin> BUT how is there deficiency <note>Greek: *endeia*</note> there? How [are there horns] there? How do they defend? Or for the sake of self-sufficiency and the perfect. For as a living being, it was necessary to be perfect... as a mind it is perfect, and as a life it is perfect... if not this, then this. And the difference... one and another, so that from all things the most perfect living being and the perfect mind, and the perfect life [arise]. Each as an individual is perfect. And although it is from many, it is itself, or hearing well... <margin>B</margin> to remain, but of all the same... it was one. It is necessary therefore from others always... [in] species just as every composite, and each is preserved, such as the forms and the patterns <note>Greek: *logoi*</note>... for the forms, such as of man, from as many differences. And for the one in all and the better... in the place of each other, eye and finger... but of one. and the whole... but better... and in the patterns, a living being, and another <margin>C</margin> not the same as the living being. And virtue is the common... and the whole is beautiful, *indifferently*... being common.

<summary>Plotinus argues that all physical traits, even "inferior" ones like claws or horns, have a perfect intellectual origin within the Divine Mind to ensure the "Universal Living Being" is complete. He explains that diversity and hierarchy among species are necessary for the perfection of the whole.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of Ennead VI, Book 7, where Plotinus discusses how the Intelligible Realm (the World of Forms) contains the archetypes of all things found in the physical world, including plants and inanimate elements like earth and fire.</meta>

<page-num>705</page-num>
<header>BOOK SEVEN</header>

*If, just as the physical heavens contain the forms of lower and even lowly animals in a noble manner: so too the intellectual heaven of the whole world possesses the forms of the entire world in a certain more excellent way than the celestial.* Chapter XI.

Whatever order and form exists anywhere has been impressed by the first mind and wisdom, which contains the same more expressively within itself. In that realm, the Ideas <note>In Platonic philosophy, Ideas or Forms are the perfect, eternal archetypes of all things.</note> of those things that possess a more manifest life along with formal order are more expressive. Finally, those things which also possess intelligence are the most expressive of all. Nevertheless, all species in the world, along with their formal function and motion, also possess something vital and intellectual, so that it is not wrongly thought that they all exist in that higher realm. All material forms are generated most directly from their own "seminal reasons" <note>Latin: *seminarijs rationibus*. These are the formative principles or "seeds" of logic that guide the growth of physical things.</note> living within the life of the world; these, in turn, derive a truer life from the Ideas of those same forms living in the divine mind. In all the elements, many living things are generated in conformity with that element, clearly through the presence of the soul, which is certainly present—perhaps as a single soul within the four elements—implanted in these spheres like fluids. It remains always in the elements even when they are changed, just as light remains while the air flutters by. Note that intellectual souls are present in bodies not as if they were enslaved to them, but as the creators of the bodily species.

<columns>2</columns>

It is said that the heavens appear to contain many things, so as not to dishonor the nature of all living things; since here too the whole contains all things. From where, then, does it receive them? <margin>* by reason</margin> It holds all things that are here, insofar as they are made by reason, or according to others. But when it holds fire and water, it also holds plants. How then are plants there? And how is fire? And how is earth? Is it because they live there, or are they like dead things, so that not everything there lives? Or are there many things there, and we have harmonized these plants with reason? Since even a plant here is a reason <note>Greek: *logos*. In this context, it refers to a formative principle or "blueprint."</note> residing in life. If, indeed, the material reason—that according to which a plant is a plant—is a certain kind of life and a certain kind of soul, and the reason is one, is there not a "first plant" in that primary nature, or rather something before it, from which these plants here arise, while that one remains there? And these many here arise from that one by necessity. If this is so, it is clear how that first thing must live, and be the Plant itself. From that one, these here come in a second and third degree, and live according to its traces. But how is there earth? And what is the "being" of earth? Or what is the earth there that possesses life? Or rather, how is this earth here? For these things exist. In what way does being belong to this earth? There must be some form and reason here. In the case of the plant, the reason of the plant lived. Is it not then the case that in this earth, the reason of the earth itself lives? <margin>* becoming<br/>* seen<br/>* natural<br/>through shaping</margin> We see the things that are most "earth-like" *becoming* and being molded within it; we see the *nature* of the earth *here*. We see the growth and shaping of certain stones and the formations of mountains rising up within, which we must believe happen by some indwelling, living, and shaping reason. For the "form" of the earth is what produces it, just like the so-called "nature" in trees. The so-called earth is analogous to the wood of the tree. A stone cut away from the earth is like a branch cut from a tree. When it is not yet cut, but still attached—like a branch not yet cut from a living plant—the indwelling nature of the earth is creating it. If we look for life flourishing in reason, we will easily be persuaded that the earth there is living much earlier, and that the *irrational* <margin>* irrational</margin> life of the earth is the "Earth-itself," the primary earth, from which this earth here proceeds. And if fire is also a certain reason in matter, and other such things, then fire does not arise by chance...

Just as fire is a certain reason in matter, and so on.

<column-break/>

It is furthermore handed down that heaven does not refuse the form of all animals, many of which are observed: since this universe also possesses all things. But from where does it receive them? Did it receive everything it has from above? Certainly it has from there whatever things are made by reason and are judged to exist according to species. But since it has fire, it also has water, and has plants; in what way are plants there? And how does fire live there? How does the earth live as well? For either these things live there, or they lie as if dead: to the point that not everything there would live. Or are these things also there in their entirety? Plants can easily be accommodated to reason itself: since even among us, a plant is a certain reason consisting in life. If indeed the material reason of a plant, according to which it is a plant, is a certain life and a certain soul, and the reason itself is one thing, is this not itself the "first plant"? Certainly not: but before this is the first plant, from which this one is born. For that one is a single thing: while these are necessarily many from the one. If therefore it is necessary for that one to live much earlier, and for that itself to be the Plant: then these things here are from it, hanging in a certain second and third degree, and living according to its traces. But how does earth exist there? What is the "being" of the earth itself? And what is the earth there that has life? Perhaps it is better first to investigate what this lowest earth is, that is, what its being consists of. There must be some form and reason in it here. Certainly, as far as the plant is concerned, the reason of the plant lives even among us. Does the reason of the earth itself live in this earth as well? Perhaps if we take those things which are most earthly, born and produced in the earth, we will find in these also the nature of the earth itself. It must be thought, therefore, that the increments and concretions of stones, and of mountains rising and coalescing, are undoubtedly formations made from within by a certain animal-like <note>Latin: *animali*. Meaning "endowed with anima/soul" or "living."</note> reason, fabricating and shaping them from the inside. And this is the "species" of the earth which produces the earth, just as that which is called "nature" behaves in trees. The thing commonly called earth is similar by a certain proportion to the wood of a tree: yet a stone cut out is like something truncated from a tree. When the rock does not suffer that, but is still annexed, like a branch not yet pruned from a living tree, we find the nature implanted in the earth as the fabricator, being a certain life flourishing in reason. We will more easily believe from this that the celestial earth is living much earlier, and that the rational life of the earth is the earth itself—the primary earth—from which this earth also proceeds; and likewise, fire is not born by chance or accident.

***

<summary>Plotinus argues that everything in the physical world, including plants and seemingly inanimate elements like earth and stones, originates from living "Reasons" and "Ideas" in the divine Mind. He uses the growth of stones within the earth as evidence of an indwelling, creative life force similar to the nature found in trees.</summary>

<margin>A</margin> For from where does it come? Surely not from a certain collision (as one might suppose); for when fire is already present in the universe, friction occurs between bodies, and where bodies are rubbed together, they already possess fire. Nor again does matter possess fire potentially in such a way that fire is produced by matter itself. If, then, the matter is disposed in this way, and there must be something that acts as a forming principle <note>original: "velut formans"</note> according to reason <term>ratio (Greek: logos) — the organizing principle or "blueprint" of a thing</term>, what then will this be? Surely it is the soul, which is capable of producing fire; that is to say, it is a kind of life and reason, yet in such a way that both are one and the same. <margin>B</margin> For this reason, Plato says that there is a soul in each of these elements, not otherwise than as the producer of this fire manifest to the senses. Therefore, that which produces fire from that higher realm is a certain fiery life—truly a more authentic fire. The higher fire, then, since it is more truly fire, is more fully engaged in life; therefore, fire itself lives. The same reasoning seems to apply to the others: namely, water and air. <margin>C</margin> But why are these not also seen to be animate <note>having a soul or being "alive"</note> just as the earth is? Surely it is established that these also exist within the Universe as a Living Being, and exist as parts of that animal. Yet life does not appear in them, just as it does not appear [on the surface of] the earth. But one may argue that the earth is animate from those things which are born within it; similarly, one may conjecture the same regarding fire. For even in fire, living creatures are generated. <note>Plotinus refers to the ancient belief that certain animals, like the salamander, were born in fire.</note> But this is even more manifest in water; and there are also certain living compositions of the air. <margin>D</margin> Yet individual flames of fire, which occur daily and are soon extinguished, pass away while the soul remains vigorous in the whole. And since this fire has not obtained a permanent mass, it naturally does not reveal an indwelling soul. It is similar with air and water: for if they cohered naturally into a more constant substance, they would demonstrate an infused soul; but because they were required to be diffused, they do not easily reveal the soul's presence. And yet these elements seem to behave just like the fluids of a living body, such as blood. For flesh reveals that it possesses a soul, but flesh is congealed from blood. <margin>E</margin> Blood, however, because it does not exhibit sensation, does not seem to have a soul, although it is necessary for the soul to be in the blood as well. Yet this does not appear because nothing violent happens to it; rather, it is most ready to easily depart from the infused soul. This is how one should judge the situation in the three elements. For whatever animals are composed more from congealed air have a nature such that they perceive without suffering <note>original: "sine passione"</note>.

Just as the air wears away <note>original: "terit"</note> the light, which is fixed and permanent, as long as that light remains; so the soul is present everywhere in the sphere of air, and again it is not present; and it is the same in the other elements.

*In the first life, the maker of all things, all things are alive: and since that life is the first form, on account of its wondrous efficacy it is entirely capable of propagation; all things living there are formally distinguished. Moreover, that form is almost everything in this way: just as the nature of the Sun contains all the powers of the stars, and its light contains all rays and colors, and the vegetative life contains the members that are to be born from it through formative principles <term>rationes seminariae — "seed-like reasons" or biological blueprints</term>.*

### Chapter XII.

<margin>A</margin> BUT again we shall speak thus: surely since we concede that this world is fashioned according to the exemplar <note>The Intelligible Realm, which serves as the perfect model for the physical world.</note> of that higher world, it is necessary that the Universe as a Living Being <note>Greek: "pan zoon"</note> exists much earlier in that realm, and if its being exists as something entirely perfect, then all things must be there. Now truly, the heaven there is a living being, and is not vacant of those stars which are beheld in this heaven; and the very "being" of the heaven consists in this. It is also clear that the earth there is not vacant, but...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> From where then? Not from friction as one might suppose; for friction occurs when fire is already in the universe, when the bodies being rubbed together already possess a body. If matter is thus potential, so as to be affected, then according to reason there must be a producer, like light; what would this be? Surely the soul, being able to produce fire; this is life and reason, both being one and the same. <margin>B</margin> Wherefore Plato also says there is a soul in each of these, not otherwise than as the maker of the sensible fire. Therefore, the fire from there is also a certain fiery life, a truer fire. And the fire beyond, being more fire, is also more in life. Therefore fire itself lives. And the same argument applies to the others, water and air. <margin>C</margin> But why are these not animate like the earth? That these also are in the Universe as a Living Being is clear, and that they are parts of a living being. But life does not appear in them, just as it does not on earth. But one may conclude that there is life there also from the things produced in it. For living things are produced even in fire. In water it is more manifest. And there are also aerial constitutions of living things. <margin>D</margin> But each fire that is produced, being quickly extinguished, passes by the soul in the whole. It does not have a mass that remains, so as to show the soul in itself, just as with water likewise. But if it were congealed in some way according to nature, it would seem to have it; but because it had to be poured out, it does not. It is likely similar to the fluids in us, like blood, whereas flesh seems to have it. Flesh is like earth, and blood is like water; and blood, not providing sensation, does not seem to have life. <margin>E</margin> And by necessity <insert>*</insert> it is there also, since even that which is no longer becoming is without violence, but is ready to stand apart from the inherent soul. One must think the same of the souls of the elements, since even those animals which are more from congealed air have the quality of not perceiving through suffering, just as the air is to the light...

<margin>A</margin> BUT again we say this: since we hold that world to be as a kind of archetype of this whole world, it is necessary that the "All-Living Being" <note>The Intelligible Universe</note> be there also; and if its being is perfect, the "All" must be there. And indeed the heaven there is a living thing, and not empty of the stars which are here called the heaven. And the being of heaven is there. It is clear that the earth also is not empty...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the four elements (fire, air, water, earth) are alive and possess souls because they are physical manifestations of perfect, living archetypes in the Intelligible Realm. He compares the presence of soul in these elements to the presence of life in bodily fluids like blood, which support life even if they do not show sensation.</summary>

<column-break/>

**A** There [in the divine realm], life is far more vivid and full of vitality; it contains all living beings within it. Whatever is called a "walking" or "terrestrial" animal here on earth, and even the plants rooted in the ground, exist there as well. There is a sea there, and every form of water exists in a state of life—a flowing stream that never runs dry. All the creatures of the water are there too. The nature of the air is also a part of that world, containing "aerial" living beings that perfectly correspond to that celestial air. For if the realm itself is alive, how could the things within it not be living? Indeed, the situation there is the same as it is here. What, then, prevents every animal from being there by necessity? Just as each of the great parts of the universe exists there, so too must the nature of the creatures living within them exist there, in whatever way is appropriate to that realm. Just as the heavens are there, they possess all the celestial animals within them. They could not fail to be present; otherwise, the heavens themselves would not exist. Therefore, anyone who asks where those animals come from is really asking where the heavens themselves come from. This is the same as asking where "animal" comes from, which is the same as asking where life itself comes from—and all life, and all soul, and the universal mind <term>νοῦς (nous) — the divine Intellect or "universal mind" that contains the blueprints of all things</term>. In that place, there is no poverty <margin>* or lack</margin> or deficiency; instead, all things are filled with life and, so to speak, are boiling over with it. Their "outflow" (if I may call it that) comes from a single source, not as if from a single wind or a single breath of heat, but as if there were one single Quality that possessed and preserved all qualities within itself: the sweetness of honey combined with the fragrance of flowers, the vigor of wine, the strength of every juice, the sight of every color, and everything the sense of touch perceives. Let there also be every sound, every melody, and every rhythm.

> *The primary life and mind, because it is the first of all forms, is therefore the most simple <note>original: "simplicissima"</note> of all and as uniform as possible; yet, because it is the beginning of all things, it is also "all-formed" <note>containing every possible shape and essence</note>.* ->Chapter XIII.<-
> *That Form is every form in its most perfect state, acting as a pure formal act. It is, therefore, every activity, since it is the first and most effective movement and act, bringing forth all activities within itself. Furthermore, because it is a "multiplicity-in-unity," it contains all its parts within any one of its parts. Every movement necessarily involves a certain variety—moving from one thing to another, or being between two things—but in the physical body, movement requires space and time. In the soul, besides variety, it requires only time. But in the Mind <note>original: "in mente"</note>, it preserves variety alone without the need for time, due to the wonderful power of its virtue and action. The variety in the primary motion, life, and mind is an "all-encompassing variety," just as all life and action exist there. Truly, just as every ray flows from the vast circle of the Sun into a point <note>original: "conum"</note>, and in its preceding width embraces all the powers of the Sun, but in the point produces one specific effect and accomplishes various things with various strikes; so from the first Intellect, every intellectual act proceeds inward. Where it begins, it embraces all Ideas, but each one concludes in a single, specific Idea, like the tip of a cone. For every Idea is both distinct from others and yet connected to them all.*

**A** For there, the Intellect <note>original: "intellectus"</note> is not something entirely simple, nor is the soul that hangs from it entirely simple; rather, all things are far more varied, even insofar as they are "simple"—that is, insofar as they are not compounded of parts, insofar as they are Principles, and insofar as they exist as pure acts. For that which is indicated there as the "last" thing—an act that is, as it were, already coming to an end—is indeed simple; but that which is considered the "first," its very act is the sum of all acts. The movement of the Intellect <margin>* where the soul comes from</margin> also moves in the same way, always according to the same and similar patterns. However, it is not just one thing in one specific part, but rather all things. For that which is "in a part" is not just one thing, but is itself infinitely divisible. We can say that from a certain source such a process occurs and is directed toward something, as if toward an ultimate end. But what of the middle ground? Is it like a line, or like a body made of uniform parts without variety? But what dignity would there be in that? If it has no variation, and is merely the result of everything, it would be nothing but a single straight line or a body of uniform and unvarying parts. But what beauty or greatness would there be in that? If it possesses no diversity,

He argues that this divine Mind is a unified source that simultaneously contains all the diversity of the universe without being divided into physical parts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the Intelligible World, specifically focusing on the relationship between the divine Mind (Intellect), life, and the concept of "otherness" or diversity. It explains how the Mind must be active and "move" through different ideas to truly be considered alive and thinking.</meta>

<page-num>706</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS' ENNEADS, BOOK VI.</header>

If some otherness stirs it <note>the divine Mind or Intellect</note> to life, then it will surely be an activity. For a mere state of being of that kind would not differ from a total absence of activity. Moreover, even if there is motion of this sort, life will not exist in every possible way, but only in one single manner. However, it is necessary for everything there to live, and to live from every side, so that nothing is present that does not possess life. It is necessary, therefore, for it to be moved toward all things—or rather, to have already been moved toward all things. 

Furthermore, if that which is entirely simple is moved, it possesses only that motion: and either it remains the same, and thus does not proceed or advance toward anything; or if it does proceed and advance, it has already become something else. For this reason, it has become two. If this "other" is the same as the "first," it remains one and has not proceeded. But if it is truly other, then it has certainly proceeded with "otherness" <term>alteritas — the principle of difference that allows for more than one thing to exist</term>, and has made a third thing out of the "same" and the "other" combined. 

Now, since what has been made is formed from both the same and the other, it rightly possesses a nature by which it is simultaneously the same and the other. I say "other," not merely as a single thing, but as a total and complete otherness; for even what is "the same" within it is a universal sameness. Therefore, since it is entirely the same and entirely other in a simple sense, nothing of those things called "others" is left out by it. It thus possesses a nature by which it is distributed throughout universal otherness. 

If, then, all "others" were above it, it could be acted upon by them; but if they are not, then this Intellect has generated all things—or rather, it has already existed as all things. For this reason, beings cannot exist unless the Mind has performed its work; and I mean working upon one thing after another continually, and as if wandering through every possible condition of wandering. I say "wandering" <note>original: *peruagata*; Plotinus uses the concept of the Mind "wandering" or "traveling" through the forms to describe the process of thought</note> within itself, just as the true Intellect is born to wander within itself. It is born to wander through essences, while those essences coincide equally with its own turnings. 

Yet everywhere, the Intellect itself exists; therefore, it carries out a **stable wandering**. This wandering of the Mind takes place within the field of truth itself, from which it never departs. It occupies the whole, since it has created for itself a place for its own motion; and yet that place is identical with the Mind itself, for which it is the place. Furthermore, this "field" is varied, so that the Mind can run through it; for unless it were varied and universal throughout, the Mind would come to rest wherever it was not varied. And if it rests, it does not think; thus, if it has stopped, it has not thought. If it does not think, it does not truly exist. Therefore, it is Thought <term>intelligentia — the act of thinking or Intellection</term>. 

The universal motion there fills the entire essence; and the whole essence, being total Thought, encompasses all life, always moving from one thing to another. This is especially true since that which is "the same" within it is also "other," so that to one who is perpetually dividing it, one thing and then another will always be encountered. Every progression there is carried out through life and through all living beings. Just as one traveling on the earth encounters earthly things everywhere, though they are earthly in different ways, so it is there: the life through which one proceeds is the same;

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <note>original Greek: μὴ δή τις ἐξεγείρει αὐτὸ εἰς τὸ ζῆν... — "Unless someone stirs it to life..."</note> If someone does not stir it to life, there would be no activity. And if it were a state of rest, it would not differ from a lack of activity. Even if such a motion exists, it would not be in all ways, but only in one. But everything there must live, and live from every side, so that nothing is not living. It must therefore be moved toward all things, or rather, have been moved. If a simple thing moves, it has only that motion. Either it is the same, or there is a progression.

<margin>B</margin> <note>original Greek: ἢ ἡ’ ῥ’ πρόβῃ ἄλλο μενον ὥστε δύο... — "...or if it progresses, it becomes another, so that there are two..."</note> Or if it progresses, it becomes another, resulting in two. If it were the same as that, it would remain one and not progress. If it is other, it progresses with otherness and makes a third thing from the same and the other. Being made from the same and the other, it has the nature of both same and other. 

<margin>C</margin> <note>original Greek: ἐστὶν ὅ, ἡ ἀπολείποι ζώντων ἑτέρων... — "...is there anything left of other living things?..."</note> It is not something that would leave out other living things. It has a nature that is made "other" in every way. If there were other things above it, it would be affected by them. But if not, then it generated all things, or rather, it *was* all things. Therefore, things do not exist without its activity. It acts upon one thing after another, as if wandering a "wandering" within itself.

<margin>D</margin> <note>original Greek: αὑτῷ ὁ ἀληθινὸς πέφυκε πλανᾶσθαι... — "...the true [Mind] is born to wander in itself..."</note> The true Mind is born to wander in itself. It is born to wander in essences, coordinating the essences with its own wanderings. It is everywhere. Thus it has a stable wandering. This is its wandering in the field of truth, which it does not leave. It possesses the whole, having made for its motion a kind of place. 

<margin>E</margin> <note>original Greek: ἀεὶ ποικίλον, καθόσον μὴ ποικίλον ἕστηκεν... — "...always varied, and where it is not varied, it stands still..."</note> But the place and the Mind are the same. It is diverse and varied so that it may pass through it. If it were not always varied, it would stand still where it is not varied. If it stands still, it does not think. So if it has stood still, it has not thought. If it does not think, it does not exist. It is therefore thought. It fills the whole essence. 

<margin>F</margin> <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ καὶ τὸ διὰ γῆς ἰόντι... — "...just as for one going through the earth..."</note> And the whole essence is thought, encompassing all life, always one thing after another. Because the "same" is also "other," one who divides it always finds the "other." All progression is through life and living beings, just as for one going through the earth, all things are earth, even if the earth has differences. And there, the life through which the progression happens is the same.

---

Yet, because it is in a certain sense always "other" things, the same thing is not always encountered. It carries out an identical traversal through things that are not similarly the same. For while the Mind itself changes through distinction, that very condition of "wandering" is preserved in the same way and according to the same rules among the diverse things. For unless the pattern of wandering in the same way and according to the same rules existed, at least among varied things, it would surely become entirely sluggish. From this, it follows that what is said to be "in act" <note>active/actualized</note> and the activity itself is nowhere, yet it is both other and diverse things itself; for which reason, it is all things. And if it is indeed itself...

<note>original Greek: εἰ μὴ, ἐκ αὐτῆς...</note> If the Mind were not itself, if it were not all itself, if it were not all things because it is the "All." But if it is one, because it does not contribute to the whole, then it is that very thing itself; because it is not something else, so that by being something else it might also contribute to the whole. But if it is not something else, but rather the same as another, it will diminish its own essence, or rather the nature it provides to the completion of the whole.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Otherwise, it would not even be itself. However, if it is all things within itself, then certainly it is also the "All," because it contains everything. Nothing is found there <note>in the Intelligible world</note> that does not contribute to the whole: nor is any part of it ever so separate that it is not also something else: so that by existing as something distinct, this very thing also serves the common good. For unless it stood out as something different, but remained completely identical, it would diminish the essence of the whole; for in that case, it would not contribute its own specific nature to the common harmony and perfection of the whole.

->*Everywhere in the world, even in its smallest parts, there is an ordered distinction achieved through Forms. This kind of formal and ordered variety does not happen by chance, nor does it arise from dark matter; rather, it depends upon the One, because it leads back to the One. This is expressed by a similar variety of Forms flourishing both in the life of the world and in the Mind.*<-

### Chapter XIV.

->*But both Mind and Soul are each a certain "one" in themselves—not indeed composed of many parts, but displaying a multiplicity within, directed not toward external things but toward the innermost depths, moving and revolving as if around a center. They bring the wider circles of more universal forms into smaller ones, finally refining themselves into the most specific individual types.*<-

---

<margin>A</margin> <note>original Greek: ΕΣΤΙ δὲ καὶ παραδείγμασι...</note> We can also understand what the Intellect is like by using intellectual examples. It cannot endure being a mere unit, as if it were entirely devoid of any "otherness." For what "reason" <term>Logos — the ordering principle of reality</term> would one wish to take as an example? Since it is by nature a living thing. If it were merely one thing and not diverse within itself, it would no longer be a "Reason-principle." That which is produced would merely be matter for the Reason, unless the Reason-principles themselves were all things. Just as the Reason-principle, falling everywhere into matter, leaves no part of it untouched, so it is with a face. A face is not just one solid mass; it consists of a nose and eyes. And the nose is not just one thing inside; it has various parts. For if it were simply one thing, it would be nothing but a lump. So it is in the Mind: it is infinite, because it is both one and many. It is not "one and many" like a single house <note>made of separate bricks</note>, but like a Reason-principle containing many things within itself. It is like a single shape or outline,
<column-break/>
<margin>A</margin> WE ARE further able to know the nature of the Intellect by using examples from the realm of the mind: we can see how it cannot bear to be a mere unit, entirely stripped of all diversity. We may, if we like, bring forward as an example the "Reason-principle" of either a plant or an animal. For if this principle were just one single thing without any variation, it would not even be a "Reason" at all. Furthermore, what is produced from it would be nothing but matter; unless, of course, the Reason-principle itself is all things, for the specific purpose of falling upon matter everywhere
<margin>B</margin> and permitting no part of that matter to remain the same <note>undifferentiated</note>. Just as a face is not merely one single mass, but possesses nostrils and eyes. And the nostrils do not contain just one single thing within them, but one part and then another, if indeed they are to be nostrils. Truly, if a nose were only one simple thing, it would be nothing more than a lump. And so it is in the Mind: it is "infinite" <note>in potential and variety</note>, because both the Mind itself and everything within it is at once one and many. The Intellect is not "one and many" in the way a house is, but rather like
<margin>C</margin> a Reason-principle that contains very many things within itself. In the single "figure" of the Mind, as if within a certain boundary, it holds boundaries and circuits within, and internal configurations, powers, and acts of understanding. It possesses a distinction that is not stretched out in a straight line, but is always propagated toward the innermost center. It is as if, within a "Universal Animal," the natures of vast numbers of animals were contained, and these in turn were derived into smaller animals and led down to lesser powers, until the process finally stops at an individual species. Yet, even there, the distinction of things is not a confusion of parts, even though they all breathe together in a marvelous unity. Now, truly, this "breathing together" <term>conspiratio — the Greek 'sympnoia', meaning a harmonious agreement of parts</term>
<margin>D</margin> is itself that "Friendship" <term>Philia — the cosmic force of attraction and harmony</term> which is said to exist throughout the universe—though not exactly the kind of friendship that appears in this physical world. For this worldly friendship merely imitates the higher one, being a harmony flowing from things that are

---

->*separate and discordant. But true Friendship is that where all things are one, so much so that they are never separated from one another. The author asserts that being separated or distant is something that happens only here in the physical heavens.*<-

### Since the first Intellect is the first Life, only the intellectual life is true life. Chap. XV.

*The first Essence, having been turned toward the Good itself through a vital act, becomes "good-form" <term>boniformis — shaped by the Good</term>. Because its own form is capable of being multiplied, it derives the single gift of the Good into many forms within itself, specifically by the power of God. One might imagine the first Mind as countless faces, distinct from one another, woven together in order within a sphere, shining with intense light and life.*

*If you preserve the distinct forms of these "faces" while removing physical distance from them, and imagine their activity reflecting back into a circle, you will soon understand the first Intellect—especially if you yourself first become such a person, and then look within yourself.*

<summary>This page uses analogies like the human face and the structure of organisms to explain how the Divine Mind (Intellect) contains infinite variety and "Friendship" (harmony) without losing its fundamental unity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the Divine Mind (the Intellect) from page 707. Having established that the Mind must contain diversity to be complete, Plotinus now explains how this diversity arises from the absolute unity of "the Good" and why the Mind represents the highest form of life we can contemplate before reaching the absolute Source.</meta>

<page-num>708</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.</header>

<margin>A</margin>If anyone, therefore, were to look upon this very life—so abundant, so universal, so primary, and so unified—a life beyond any possible estimation, he would rejoice in it and utterly despise every other kind of life. For all other inferior lives are but shadows: lives that are meager, dim, base, and impure, contaminating the pure lives they touch. As soon as you look upon these lower lives, you no longer see the pure ones, nor do you truly live according to those higher states in which nothing exists that does not live. In those higher realms, everything lives purely, admitting no evil. For evils reign only here in our world, since here <margin>B</margin> there is only a mere trace of life. Here, there is nothing of the Mind <note>Latin: *mens*; Greek: *νοῦς* (Nous)</note> except a footprint; but there, the primary model flourishes, which Plato calls "Good-form" <note>Greek: *ἀγαθοειδές* (agathoeides), meaning "having the form or nature of the Good"</note> because it possesses the Good within its species, that is, its forms. Truly, the Good itself is one thing, but here the "good person" is one who possesses life through contemplation. Such a person contemplates "Good-formed" sights which he prepared for himself the moment he first gazed upon the nature of the Good itself. The Good flowed into the Mind, not exactly as it existed there at the source, but in the manner the Mind was able to receive it. <margin>C</margin> For that Source is the Principle itself, and in the Mind, the Good is derived from it; the Mind, which is the maker of all these things, holds its office by the gift of the Source. It was not right for the Mind, while gazing upon the Source, to understand nothing, nor again to see only sights within the Source; otherwise, the Mind itself would never have generated those sights. Therefore, the Mind received from the Source the power to give birth, through which it is filled to the depths with its own offspring. <margin>D</margin> The Source, of course, bestowed these things without possessing them within itself in a fragmented way. From that absolute One, many things fell to the Mind: for the Mind, since it could not properly hold the raw power it received, broke it into fragments. It caused the One to become many, so that it might at least be able to carry it piece by piece. Whatever the Mind generated, it generated from the power of the Good; and that which was born is "Good-form." The Mind itself is good—a varied and diverse good constituted from these "Good-forms." <margin>E</margin> Therefore, if one compares the Mind to a living, diverse sphere, or if one imagines a spectacle composed of many faces looking out from every side, shining everywhere with living countenances—or perhaps if one thinks of all pure souls running together into the same point, lacking nothing but possessing all their desires—and furthermore, the universal Mind sitting upon the very peaks of those souls, so that the whole region shines with a golden light—if someone imagines the Intellect in this way, he sees it as an observer from the outside. But it is worthwhile for a person first to become the Intellect itself within himself, and then to behold the spectacle he has become.

*The first Essence, as soon as it came into being, was turned from the Good back toward itself, not so much by a specific method as by a vital instinct; just as a plant turns toward the Sun or toward moisture; for this act follows the other in order. Chapter XVI.*

*But when, directed toward the Good, it was filled there by a certain ray that was both shining and warm, it immediately conceived all things within itself like colors; and having turned back to perceive its own conceptions, it became the Intellect. Finally, it produces colors and brings them into harmony with one another. Meanwhile, the Intellect is not itself a color, but something superior; thus the Good creates both the things to be understood and the understanding, joining them together while remaining more eminent than both.*

It is not profitable, however, to linger forever in this great beauty. For the soul must proceed from here, lifting itself more eagerly to the heights, and leaving behind this heaven...

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the original Greek text corresponding to the Latin above.</note>

If anyone sees this abundant life, the primary and the one, beyond which one cannot ascend, all other life is then darkness. The other lives below are dim, incomplete, and they defile the pure ones with stains. If one looks at those subsequent lives, one no longer sees them all living together, for in the higher realm there is nothing that does not live, and live purely, containing no evil. There <note>in our world</note> is only a footprint of life and a footprint of Mind. But there is the archetype, which he <note>Plato</note> calls "Good-form," because it holds the Good within its forms. For the Good itself is the Source, but the Mind is good through the contemplation of the Good; the things contemplated are "Good-formed," which it acquired when it contemplated the nature of the Good. This came into it, not as it was there, but as the Mind itself was able to hold it. For that is the beginning, and in this <note>the Mind</note> is the Good, and this maker of things looks toward that Source; for it did not see the things actually in the Source. Nor again, while looking, did it fail to receive life from it, <margin>*</margin> filling itself with connections. Because it could not hold what it did not have, but from the One it took a power that it could hold, <margin>*</margin> it strained to have many things. It made many things so that it might hold the power part by part. What it gave birth to was a good from that power; it was "Good-form." And the Mind itself is a good made of "Good-forms," a variegated good. Wherefore, if someone imagines the Mind as a living, variegated sphere, or as a form shining with living faces, or imagines all pure souls running to the same point, not lacking but possessing all things, and the whole Mind established at their very peaks, <margin>*</margin> as a place of light and unshadowed radiance—to one imagining it thus, being somewhat outside and seeing it as something else, it is necessary to become that very thing and make the vision one with himself.

One must not always remain in such beauty, but must pass beyond it, growing toward the things above and leaving behind the things of this world.

<summary>Plotinus describes the Divine Mind as a "living sphere" of many forms that originates from the absolute unity of the Good. He explains that the Mind fragments this original power into many parts so it can be understood and contemplated, eventually urging the seeker to move beyond even this beauty toward the Source itself.</summary>

Plotinus is describing the process by which the Mind, initially a simple "movement" toward the Source, becomes filled with the diversity of all "Forms" or "Species" of existence.</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>And the movement...</margin>
...of the heavens, but rather, transcending from there, should wonder at who its progenitor is and how he begot it. Each form, therefore, is a distinct type. Being "good-formed" <note>Greek: *ἀγαθοειδές* (agathoeides); having the nature or quality of the Good</note>, this epithet is common to all these things. Thus, it possesses Being in all things; it also possesses life in each. Each possesses a common life that exists in all. Perhaps it also possesses other things. But insofar as they are good, and because they are good, what would this contribute to our inquiry? Perhaps it is better to begin from within: whether, when it looked toward the Good, it conceived that which was in the Source as many. And in that state where it itself conceived itself as many, it lived within itself. In its presence, was thinking not yet whole? Or was it Mind already while looking there, yet looking without understanding? Or should we say it had never yet seen? Rather, it lived toward it and depended upon it, and was turned toward it. <margin>* And the movement...</margin> * But this movement itself, having been filled by moving there and around that Source, fulfilled itself. And it was no longer merely a movement, but a movement satisfied and full. Next, all things came into being. Or perhaps it then knew itself in its own self-awareness, and was already Mind. Having been filled, it possessed that which it would see. And it sees these things by the light of the one who gave them. For indeed, while receiving, it is not only said to be the cause of essence, but also the cause of vision. And how can that be? Just as the sun is the cause for sensible things to be seen and for their generation, it is also in some way the cause of sight. Whether that sight is the eye or the things that come to be, so indeed the nature of the Good is the cause of essence and of Mind, and it is a Light according to reason. That light there is seen by the Mind, or rather, the things that are are seen in that light, or within the Mind. But being the cause of things that are, he shines within his own light, providing for both the things that are and for the Mind. Thus, while being filled, it was not yet becoming; but having been filled, it was. And at once it was completed and it saw. But the Mind within it was that which existed before being filled. And it was another beginning, as if from the outside, which filled it, from which it was, as it were, formed while being filled.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...if he should let that go, he should also let the other go; not only from this, but rather transcending it, he should immediately wonder who the father of that one might be, and by what logic he begot him. Everything, therefore, existing there is a certain species and, as it were, a definite figure. And since that is "good-formed" <note>Latin: *boniforme*; essentially the same as the Greek *agathoeides*</note> because of a certain common quality shining everywhere in all things, it possesses all good-formed things. It therefore possesses Being in all; it possesses life in each <margin>B</margin> individual; it has a common life implanted in all; perhaps it has other things as well. But what is that thing because of which they are primarily "good," insofar as they are judged to be good? Toward this contemplation, it will perhaps be most helpful to begin from this point. Did it, therefore, when it looked upon the Good, understand that one thing as if it were many? And since the intellect itself existed as one being, did it understand that as many—understanding it within itself more partially because it could not understand <margin>C</margin> the whole at once? But it was not yet the Intellect while it first looked up at that Source. But did it look forward without an intellect? Truly, we must think that it had not yet even "seen" it. For it was indeed living toward it, and depended entirely upon it, and was totally turned toward it. This movement, then, was fulfilled when it was first carried there and was thoroughly occupied around it; it filled the thing itself, and it was no longer merely movement, but a movement now saturated and full. Soon, Being itself became all things, and it recognized this by noticing itself. <margin>D</margin> and now it emerged as the Intellect, imbued so that it might possess what it could inspect. But inspecting these things with a certain light received from the very same source from which it received the forms themselves. For this reason, that supreme God <note>Referring to the "One" or "the Good"</note> is handed down as not only the author of essence but also the cause of essence being seen. Just as the sun is the cause for things that are perceived by the senses so that they may exist and be seen, and at the same time is the cause of vision, although in the meantime he himself is neither vision <margin>E</margin> nor the things that are to be seen; so also the nature of the Good itself is undoubtedly the cause of essence and of mind. It is also a light in a certain proportion of analogy, by which these visible things and sight reflect that essence and intellect; yet it is not the beings themselves,

<column-break/>

nor even the intellect, but the cause of both, and it provides the mind with the understanding of things by its own light diffused over beings and the mind. Having been filled, therefore, it has now been made; but it had been filled, and at once it was perfected, and it saw. Its beginning, however, was that which preceded its filling. Its other principle is, as it were, external, which filled it, and by which it was, as it were, formed while it was being filled.

---

### Whatever things exist, as soon as and as long as they exist, naturally act toward the Good: from which we argue that the primary essence naturally acts toward the primary Good. The Good itself, therefore, is superior to essence and its act, and to life and intellect. It is not, therefore, to be called "being," "living," "acting," or "understanding" in a literal sense. Chapter XVII.

*Neither should it be thought that the Good contains within itself, in a literal sense, those forms which it grants to the Intellect, just as unity is not "full" of numbers, nor is a point full of dimensions, nor does the light thriving in the center of the Sun contain within itself those specific rays which, by its own power, flash forth innumerably from the Sun's circumference, ending as they move away from the sphere. Furthermore, just as the light poured out through such rays does not, while full, sustain within itself those specific qualities of things which it generates among us through various strikes of the rays, so neither does the Mind, although it is "all-form" <note>Latin: *omniformis*; containing all possible forms</note> in itself, possess the material forms which it produces. Then, indeed, the first life arises as a kind of indeterminate and unformed act of essence; which, certainly directed toward the One itself, claims for itself from that Source the "ideal boundaries" <note>The fixed patterns or Forms</note>, and many of them at that, because its condition is already subject to number and inclined toward proceeding outward. In that same moment, life becomes perfected, which is also when it emerges as the Intellect. Finally, just as the intellect relates to the soul, so the Good relates to the intellect. Wherefore, just as the intellect forms reason in the soul, and is itself separate from rational discourse, so the Good, impressing species upon the intellect, is segregated from those species in a way that is beyond our reach.*

<margin>A</margin>But in what way are these things in the intellect, and in what way do they exist as the intellect itself, since they were not in the one who fills it, nor were they previously in that which is being filled? For when it was not yet imbued <note>Latin: *imbutus*; the state of the Intellect before it is "filled" with the Forms by looking back at the Source</note>, it did not possess them at all. But perhaps it is not necessary that what someone grants, they must have within themselves; rather, in matters of this kind, it is necessary to consider that the one who hands it over is greater, while that which is handed over is less than the giver. For such is the nature of generation in the very order of beings. First, it is necessary that what exists be in actuality <term>actu; the state of being fully realized or active</term>; whereas subsequent things exist in potentiality <term>potentia; the capacity to become something or receive form</term> relative to what is higher.

<margin>B</margin>Indeed, that which is first is superior to those things that follow it. And the giver, by the same logic, is superior to the gift bestowed, for the giver is more excellent. If, therefore, something is prior in actuality, it is superior in actuality; and for this reason, life is also superior. If, then, life is in this [the Intellect], surely the one who gave it granted life indeed, but is himself judged to be better and more honorable than life. Thus, he possessed life, yet did not require a diverse provider; and life itself exists as a certain trace <note>Latin: *vestigium*; a footprint or reflection</note> of the giver, not as the life of that giver himself. <margin>C</margin>To be sure, when this life first looked toward its provider, it was still indefinite <note>Greek: *aoristos*; lacking boundaries or specific form</note>; but after it looked there, it was immediately determined by that which has no limit. For immediately, by looking toward a single thing, it is determined by this very act, and it brings back within itself a limit, a boundary, and a species <term>species/eidos; the specific "Form" or "Idea" that makes a thing what it is</term>. This species lies within the thing that has been formed; however, the former <note>the One</note> is utterly formless. Nevertheless, the limit itself is not applied there as if added from the outside, in the same way that <margin>D</margin>a limit of magnitude is usually placed around something; rather, it is the limit of that entire life, which exists as something multiple and infinite, inasmuch as it had already flowed forth from such a nature. And yet, it was life, though not yet the life of *this* specific thing; otherwise, it would have already been determined as if it were already an individual. Nevertheless, it was determined. It was therefore determined as the "many" of a certain "one"; and each of the many is also determined. And because of the abundant condition of life, many things are determined; <margin>E</margin>and again, because of the limit itself, they are also one. What, therefore, is the "one" that has been determined? Truly, it is the Intellect. For a determined life is the Intellect. And what of the fact that it is said to be "many" determined things? These are clearly many intellects. All things, therefore, are intellect, and this is indeed the whole Intellect; but these individual things are specific intellects. But does the whole Intellect itself, embracing each one, contain each as if it were the same? By no means; otherwise it would <margin>F</margin>contain only a single thing. If, therefore, there are many, it is necessary that they differ among themselves. Again, we must ask how each one differs. Perhaps, indeed, in the very fact that it has become "one," it takes on a difference. For the whole and any individual intellect are not the same. Therefore, life in that realm is all power, and the vision that shines from there is the power of all things. But the Intellect that is born there appears as all these things. Finally, another [the One] sits above them, not so that it may be founded in them, but to give the form of the primary forms, while remaining far removed from form itself. And so, the Intellect relates to the soul almost as an infused light, just as the One relates to the Intellect; for when the Intellect determines the soul, it makes it rational, by offering a trace of what it possesses. Therefore, the Intellect is also a trace of that higher Source. Since the Intellect is a form existing in a certain differentiation and consisting of a multitude, the One exists outside of form and species, for in this way it gives form to the rest of the species.
