### Whatever was first produced by the Good itself is entirely good: but in it, essence is a kind of beginning of birth, of a good work. Life is truly the youth of the Good; intelligence and the Forms are the Ideal Good in its maturity.

### Chapter XVIII.

### Every good thing is good for this reason: since it comes from the Good itself, it possesses something of that Good within itself—though it remains indescribable—which is common to all things. Just as the movement of the tongue, the hands, and the feet are all called "coordinated" because they receive a similar order from the same musical principle, so too is the common nature of the Good far more internal to the mind than the order of music is to the limbs.

<margin><note>Greek original: "ἢ καλὰ"</note> or beautiful things</margin>
But in what way are the things in the Intellect "good-like" <term>agathoiedes; having the form or quality of the Good</term>? Is it because each is a Form? Or because each is beautiful? Or for some other reason? Indeed, if everything that comes from the Good bears a trace and a stamp of that source—just as what comes from fire bears the trace of fire, and what comes from something sweet bears the trace of sweetness—then life and intellect come to us from that Source. For the Intellect arose from an activity depending on the Good, and the Intellect exists because of it. Likewise, the beauty of the Forms descends from there. Therefore, everything will be "good-like"—life, intellect, and the Ideas.

<margin>B</margin>
Furthermore, in what way are the things in the mind primarily "good-like"? Is it by the same logic that each is a Form? Or because they are each beautiful? Or because of something else? If, in truth, whatever proceeds from the Good possesses its trace and shape—or because it descends from it, just as that which is born of fire has the trace of fire, and what comes from sweetness has the impression of sweetness—then life and intellect proceed into the mind from that Good. For from a certain activity hanging upon the Good, it came to exist, and the Intellect exists because of that Good. Likewise, the beauty of the species descends; all things will surely be "good-like": life, intellect, and the Idea.

<margin><note>Greek original: "ὡς ἐς ἄλλο"</note> as into another</margin>
But what is this common element? It is not enough to say that they simply "come from" the Good for there to be something identical in all of them; there must be a common quality within the things themselves. For it is possible for the same source to produce different effects, or for a gift given in the same way to turn out differently among those who receive it. 

<margin>C</margin>
But what is this common element? For it is not enough that they are "from it" for something to be the same in all of them; that common element must actually exist within them. For it can happen that the same source does not produce the same result, or that what is given in the same way becomes different in the recipients. This is because the recipient into which the gift of the Good is translated is the first activity, while the thing itself is what is granted to that first activity. What results in these things is already something else; or perhaps nothing prevents everything from being "good-like" in its own way, yet more so in one respect than another. What then is this quality by which a thing is primarily judged "good-like"? But perhaps it is better to investigate this first: is life itself the Good?

<margin>D</margin>
Specifically, is it the Good by the very fact that it is life, even if it is considered purely and stripped of everything else? Or is it rather the life that is properly from the Good? And does being "from the Good" mean nothing other than being such a life? Again, then, what is such a life? Is it the life of the Good? But truly, it does not belong to the Good properly, but comes from it. Yet if that life contains this very thing which comes from the Good, and is itself "True Life," and nothing flowing from the Good can be called "vile," then surely it must be judged as good by the same reasoning that it is life.

<margin><note>Greek original: "ἢ ἀγαθὸν"</note> or good</margin>
Does it follow that in the first and true Intellect we must concede it is good, and that every Form is good and "good-like"? If this is the case, perhaps each of these possesses some specific good, whether common or distinct, or perhaps one has it primarily and the other in a secondary degree. For when we accept each thing as already having something of the good in its essence, then each thing is good because of that. It is established that life is a good, not simply as life, but because it is True Life from the Source; and Intellect is similarly good because it is true and born from there. Surely, some part of that same Source must be found in them. 

<margin>E</margin>
For when the same thing is predicated of different objects <note>i.e., when we call many different things "good"</note>, there must be something shared.

<sig>Oo 2</sig>

<summary>This page discusses how all higher realities like Life and Intellect are "good-like" because they carry a trace of their source, the Absolute Good. Plotinus uses the analogy of music to explain how a single principle can coordinate different parts of a whole, giving them a common quality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of the Good (the One). On page 711, the text explored how the Intellect and Life derive their value from the Good. Here, Plotinus asks whether "the Good" is a category that applies to things like life and intelligence in the same way, or if it is something entirely unique that gives them their value from above.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS VI. 712

Nothing prevents the Good from being present in the essence of those things, yet at the same time, it can be grasped separately by reason: just as the quality of "animal" is present in both man and horse, or "heat" is in both water and fire. But in those instances, it acts as a genus <note>In logic, a "genus" is a broad category that contains species. Plotinus is testing if "the Good" is just a category like "animal."</note>, whereas here, it is as if one thing is primarily good, and the other only secondarily so. Are life, intellect, and the rest then called "good" individually in a univocal sense <note>original: "univoce"; meaning the word has exactly the same definition in every case</note>, or equivocally <note>original: "aequivoce"; meaning the word is the same but the meanings are unrelated</note>, or rather by a certain analogy? Does the Good exist within their essence? Or is each thing a "good" as a whole? Not according to a single good. How then? Perhaps as parts? But the Good itself is indivisible. Perhaps the Good is one thing, and it relates to them in this way: the first act is the Good, and that which is determined within it exists as a good; thus, they are both good. And that first act is good because it was made by the Good itself; the second is good because it is an adornment <note>original: "ornamentum"</note> from it; and the third, because it is considered both together. All these things, therefore, come from the same source; and nothing is the same, just as if a voice and a walking gait <note>Plotinus uses the metaphor of a single person producing different things—a voice and a walk—which are both "well-ordered" because they come from the same person.</note>, or something else, were to come from the same source, and all were correctly composed. Perhaps in these cases all things are said to be similarly well-disposed because order and number are present in all of them. But what is common in those higher things? Someone might say that in these lower things, each thing achieves being "correct" from the outside, since the things that order deals with are different; but in the higher realm, the things are themselves good individually. But why? For we must not trust only in the fact that these things are good because they are there and are at rest. It must certainly be granted that these things, being from the Good, are very precious; but the soul does not desire them for themselves; it seeks the reason why they are considered good.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Nothing prevents the "being" from being in their essence, yet it is possible to grasp it separately by reason: just as "animal" is in man and horse, and heat in water and fire—the one being primary, the other secondary. Are they then called "good" individually in the same way, or does each have a different meaning? Does the Good dwell within their essence, or is each one a "good" as a whole? Or according to a... <margin>B</margin> ...good. How then? Perhaps as parts? But the Good is indivisible. Perhaps it is one itself: and in this way, the first activity <note>original Greek: "energeia"; the active expression of a thing's nature</note> is the Good, and that which is defined is the Good, and the combination of both. One is good because it was produced by the Good, the other because it is a beauty from it, and the third because it is both. All these are from the same source and are now the same, just as if from the same source came a voice and a gait, and other things that are all well-composed. <margin>C</margin> Or is it here that order and rhythm reside? But someone might say that here, the whole is "well" from the outside, the things being different, and there is order; but there, they are the same, yet distinct. Or is it that we trust in those things because they are there? We must grant that they are from the Good and are precious, but the reasoning seeks to grasp from where they derive their "goodness."

### Chapter XIX.

---

<margin>A</margin> Shall we then assign the power of judgment to desire and the soul? And placing complete trust in its feeling, shall we judge that what is desirable to it is the good, without investigating why it is desired? Shall we explain what each of these things is through demonstrations, yet leave the very definition of the Good to desire? However, many absurdities arise from this. First, the Good would be something that belongs to something else <note>In other words, the Good would only exist because someone wants it, rather than being a thing on its own.</note>; second, since there are many things desired, how shall we judge if one is better than another among the things sought? How can we judge which is better by the feeling of the desirer alone? But perhaps we will not even know what is "better" if we are ignorant of the Good. Should we instead think of the Good according to the virtue of each thing? In this way, we would reduce it to a form and a rational principle—which is a step in the right direction. But once we have finally reached that point, what shall we answer if we must investigate by what reason these things themselves are good? In lower things, it seems we might easily recognize such a nature, even if they are not very pure. But in the higher realm, it is not primary; but where there is no evil, and the things themselves are better in themselves...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Shall we then leave the power of judgment to the impulse <note>original: "ephesis"; the natural reaching-out or desire of the soul</note> and the soul? And is it safe to trust its feeling, that what it desires is the good? Shall we not ask why it desires? Or shall we bring demonstrations for everything else, but leave the Good itself to the impulse? But many absurd things appear. First, the Good becomes one of the things related to something else; then, since the things desired are many... <margin>B</margin> ...others. How could we judge by the impulse what is better? Perhaps we will not know the better if we are ignorant of the Good. But shall we speak of it according to the virtue of each thing? In this way, we will lead it back to a form and a rational principle, and we proceed correctly. But having gone there, and seeking how these are good, we will meet... <margin>C</margin> ...we might know them, as they have a certain purity. But from there, it is not primary, by comparison to the worse; but where there is no evil, and things are better in themselves, we will be at a loss... by a certain comparison to worse things, they exist; we will involve them in doubts.

<summary>Plotinus discusses whether "the Good" is a category that encompasses life and intellect, concluding that their goodness is derived from their source (the One) rather than being an inherent property like a genus. He also argues that the Good cannot be defined simply as "what we desire," as desire is a secondary effect of goodness, not its cause.</summary>

Following the previous discussion on how the Good (the One) relates to the many forms of the Intellect, Plotinus now examines why we seek the "reason why" (the cause) and whether the Intellect itself can be considered the ultimate Good.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN

<margin>* Anticipating <note>original: Φθάνοντος</note></margin>
<margin>* and yet <note>original: κὴ μὴν</note></margin>
Since reason seeks the "reason why," and these things are good in themselves, it wonders about the "why" that follows. Just as if we were to say that God is the cause: if reason does *not reach* there, the same difficulty remains. * And yet, we must speak by another path so that what we expect might become manifest.

<margin>* we shall be saved <note>original: σωσόμεθα</note></margin>
<margin>* the preference <note>original: ἡ προτίμησις</note></margin>
**SINCE** we currently distrust our desires regarding what the nature or quality of God is, it is necessary to turn to judgments and the oppositions of things: such as order and disorder, the symmetrical and the asymmetrical, health and disease, form and formlessness, essence and corruption—in short, consistency and disappearance. For regarding these, who would doubt that the first members of each pair belong to the species of the "good"? If this is so, then their productive causes must necessarily be placed in the portion of the good; and so too must virtue, intellect, life, and the soul. If a life is wise, it is of the form of the good. And that which a wise life desires is also good. Why then should we not say that we *will find* the good in the intellect? For soul and life are its traces. Thus the soul desires it, and then judges, and desires the intellect; having judged that justice is better than injustice, and each form of virtue better than the form of vice, the *preference* for these is the same as the choice for them. But if it only desired the intellect, perhaps more argument would be needed to show that the intellect is not the ultimate end; for not all things desire the intellect, but all things desire the good. And of those things that do not possess intellect, not all seek to acquire it. But those that do have intellect do not stop there, but seek the good further—and they seek the intellect through reasoning, but the good is desired even before reason. And if they desire life, and to be and to act always, it is not insofar as they are "intellect" that this is desirable, but insofar as it is "good." For life itself is good, and it is directed toward the good.
<meta>catchword: ri.</meta>

<column-break/>

Since the present reason investigates the "reason why" <note>original: "propter quid," translating the Greek "dioti"</note>, and these things are good in themselves, it is for this reason that it doubts: for there, this very thing which is called the "reason why" is the same as that which is called the "essence" <note>original: "quid est"</note>. Because even if we bring forward another cause for this, namely God himself, since reason has not yet reached that far, a similar ambiguity remains. But finally, we must attempt to withdraw our step from here, striving to see if some more manifest thing might occur to us by proceeding along another path.

---

*To those seeking what the Good itself is, the intellect appears clearly to us as a good: because through it we truly judge concerning good and evil things; and order, the species of things, and life proceed from the intellect. Furthermore, the mature life which the soul desires is the intellect. Nevertheless, the intellect is not the Good itself. For not all things desire the intellect. Indeed, souls desire the good earlier and more frequently than they desire intelligence, and they do not rest in the latter, but in the former. They desire to be, to live, and to act—not under the rationale of being, living, acting, or understanding—but under the rationale of the Good. Therefore, the Good is distinct from all these, and is higher than them.*

### Chapter XX.

**SINCE** we therefore currently distrust our affections <note>original: "affectibus," referring to internal feelings or desires</note> as far as confirming what each thing is and of what quality, is it not perhaps worthwhile to arrive at certain other judgments, and to approach the oppositions of things, such as order and the absence of order? The tempered and the uncomposed, health and infirmity, form and formlessness, essence and corruption, consistency and evanescence. For regarding the first of these in any pair <note>original: "coniugationem"</note>, who would doubt that they should be reckoned within the species of the good? If this is the case, it is necessary to count their productive causes in the lot of the good as well: and thus virtue, intellect, life, and the wise soul are turned toward the rank of the good, and for that reason, those things which a wise life desires are placed there as well. Why then should one not say that we should stop our progress at the mind <note>original: "mente," translating the Greek "nous"</note>, and assert that it is the Good? For the soul and life are traces of the mind, and the soul affects the mind, and judges according to it. By judging, it brings itself to the mind, judging indeed that justice is better than injustice, and undoubtedly preferring any species of virtue to a species of depravity: and it is established that the soul prefers in honor those things which it judges should be chosen above others. But whether it desires the intellect alone or not requires much discussion, to demonstrate that the intellect is not the supreme and ultimate end: likewise, that not all things desire the intellect, but all things desire the good. Furthermore, from the number of those things which lack intellect, not all desire the possession of the mind; but those that have a mind do not yet rest, but affect a further good. Finally, the intellect is desired from a certain discourse of reason, but the good is desired even before reason. But if they desire life, and to be always, and to act, surely this very thing is not to be sought by the reason that it is "intellect," but by the reason that it is "good"—and it depends on the good and is referred back to the good. For even life is only to be desired in this way.

---

*Life, intelligence, and species are "good-form" <note>original: "boniformia"</note> and are to be desired: because the first is an act concerning the good, the second is an act already determined by the good, and the third is the very term impressed by the good. All these things have a twin light from the Good itself. One is made proper to each thing at its birth, different in different things, like a color; the other is carried over all things as a single common light, shining more gracefully in some places than others. Through the first, things are indeed good, and are desired secretly and gently; through the second, they are better, and are loved openly and ardently.*

### Chapter XXI.

<sig>Oo 3</sig>

<summary>Plotinus argues that while Intellect and Life are inherently good, they are not the "Absolute Good" because the desire for the Good precedes reason and extends to all things, even those without intelligence. He introduces the concept of a "double light" from the Good—one that gives things their nature and another that makes them beautiful and lovable.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Ennead VI, Book 7, where Plotinus explores how the "Good" (the One) imparts its nature to the Intellect and the Soul. The previous page established that while the Intellect contains all forms, it is the Good that makes those forms desirable.</meta>

<page-num>714</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.</header>

<margin>A</margin> What then is it that exists as one and the same in all these things that makes each of them good? Let us therefore venture to assert this: that while there is indeed an Intellect, and that Life is undoubtedly "good-formed" <note>original: "boniformem," from the Greek ἀγαθοειδῆ, meaning having the shape or quality of the Good</note>, these things are sought precisely because they are good-formed. I say they are good-formed because Life is an activity <note>original: "actus"</note> of the Good itself—or rather, an activity depending upon the Good—whereas the Intellect exists as an activity that has already been determined and defined. And these things <margin>B</margin> are surrounded by a certain splendor poured down from above, and for this reason the soul pursues them: because they originate from that source. The soul is affected by them as if they were its own property, yet not as if they were the Good itself. But since they are of the "form of the good," they are not to be despised. For even if something is familiar and one's own, if it is not good, it remains one's own, yet a person may eventually flee from it. Indeed, other things that are far distant and placed lower sometimes draw our desire toward them. However, a vehement love is incited toward these things not when <margin>C</margin> they exist merely as what they are, but when they, existing as they do, receive something else from on high. Just as in bodies, even though light is naturally mixed within them, another light is needed so that the color implanted in them may become clearly visible; so too there is a natural light in the higher things, yet even though they possess much light, they require a certain more excellent light so that they may be discerned both by themselves and by any other.

### Without the miraculous grace of the first good, no things love, nor are they loved. Chapter XXII.

*That which seizes us with love when we look upon beautiful things is neither the matter nor the proportion, but a certain vivid soul reflecting within that proportion. Again, that which captures our goodwill when we contemplate minds and their virtues and duties is a certain intellectual splendor glowing from the divine intellect. Finally, that which contemplates the Intellect and intelligible things, and inflames us with a new kind of love, is a ray flashing from the First Good, intensifying and arousing the will. From that source comes the miraculous grace of the things we contemplate; before this, no grace shines anywhere to be loved, nor is love ever kindled.*

<margin>A</margin> Whenever the soul beholds this light, it is incited toward the divine things that are surrounded by this light; and affecting the light that shines forth in them, the soul rejoices greatly at its arrival. Just as those who see these physical bodies and seem to love them do not love the underlying subjects, but rather the beauty that openly shines forth in the bodies. For each thing exists as what it is in itself; but it becomes desirable when the Good itself "colors" it, so to speak—when it grants abundant graces <note>original: "gratias," meaning charms or divine favors</note> to the things being sought, <margin>B</margin> and pours love into those who desire them. Now, when the soul receives an influx from that source, it is moved, it revels like a Bacchic initiate <note>original: "debacchatur"</note>, and is driven by stings of desire: and thus love flows into it. Before this, the soul is not moved even toward the Mind <note>or Intellect</note>, despite its beauty; for the beauty of the Mind itself is sluggish <note>original: "torpet"</note> until it receives the light of the Good. The soul itself falls back into a listless state and is numb to everything, and even in the presence of the Mind, it seems to slumber. But after <margin>C</margin> the warmth from that source has kindled it, the soul is immediately strengthened and awakened, and it is supported by other powers. And while it is vehemently affected by that which is closest to it, it is meanwhile raised toward something more excellent by a certain reminiscence <note>original: "reminiscentia," the Platonic idea that the soul "remembers" its divine origin</note>. And as long as anything remains of that superior nature present within it, the soul is lifted upward.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> What then is it that is in all these? Let it be ventured: Intellect and that Life are of the form of the Good <note>original: ἀγαθοειδῆ</note>, and these are sought because they are of that form. I say they are so because Life is an activity—or rather, an activity from the source—already defined. <margin>B</margin> It is a splendor <note>original: ἀγλαΐας</note> that the soul pursues from that source, and it is drawn back to those things as if they were its own; yet they are not the Good itself, but of its form. For what is one's own, if it is not good, one flees from it. Even things far off and below can cause movement. Love is not intense <margin>C</margin> merely for what a thing is, but when it receives something else from there. Just as light is mixed in things, yet they need light so the color in them may appear. So too for the things there: though they have light, they need another, better light for them to be seen by themselves or others.

<margin>A</margin> When the soul sees the light, it is moved toward those things, and yearning for the light upon them, it rejoices. Just as with the love of bodies here: the love is not for the substrates, but for the beauty shining upon them. For each thing is what it is in itself, but it becomes desirable when the Good pours itself over it, giving graces <note>original: χάριτας</note>. <margin>B</margin> When the soul receives the outflow from there, it is moved to a Bacchic frenzy <note>original: ἀναβακχεύεται</note> and sent into a sting of desire. Before this, it is not moved even to the Mind, though it is beautiful. For the Mind's beauty is idle <note>original: ἀργὸν</note> before it takes the light of the Good. The soul has fallen away and is cold; even with the Mind present, it sleeps. But when <margin>C</margin> warmth from there comes into it, it is strengthened and wakes, and is winged. While it is excited by what is near, it is lifted higher by memory <note>original: μνήμῃ</note>. It is raised up by what is present from the higher world.

<summary>Plotinus explains that the Intellect and Life are only desirable because they are "colored" by the light and grace of the Good (the One). He uses the analogy of physical light making colors visible to describe how divine grace awakens the soul's love and pulls it back toward its source.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the nature of the Good and Beauty in Ennead VI, Book 7. Building on the previous page's discussion of how the Good imparts "splendor" to forms, Plotinus now argues that beauty is not merely a matter of symmetry or proportion, but rather a "grace" or "light" that shines from the Good through the soul.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN.

<margin>* beloved
* or of the</margin>
<margin>* the substrate <note>original: "τὸ ὑποκείμενον," the underlying matter or subject</note></margin>
It transcends; what is it that can run beyond the Good? For the * substrate is nothing, if it remains in itself; it gazes upon beautiful and venerable things. From above, it seeks all that it might have. For it is as if one approaches a face—beautiful, indeed, but not yet able to move the sight, because the grace that runs over the beauty does not yet shine upon it. Wherefore, here too one must say that beauty is rather that which shines upon the symmetry, than the symmetry itself. And this is the object of love. For why is the light of beauty more present in a living face, while only a trace remains in a dead one, even if the face is not yet decomposed in its flesh and symmetries? And why are the more lifelike statues more beautiful, even if others are more perfectly symmetrical? Why is a living person, though less symmetrical, more beautiful than a beautiful statue? Is it not because that which is desired is more present here? And this is because it has a soul. And this is because it is more "good-formed" <note>original: "ἀγαθοειδέστερον," having the quality of the Good</note>. And this is because it is somehow colored by the light of the Good. And having been so colored, the soul is awakened, and is lightened, and it lightens what it possesses. And as if entirely transformed by that which makes it good, it awakens.

THERE the soul pursues, and it moves the trace of the light which it provides to the mind and which has fallen upon it, so that it must marvel at what kind of power it possesses, drawing the soul toward itself and calling it back from all wandering, so that it might find rest in Him. Not since then has anything been better for it than the All. But if the causes are lesser, how is the best of all beings not the Good? And indeed, if we consider the nature of the Good, it must be something most self-sufficient, and lacking in
<margin>* or first of others</margin>
nothing else whatsoever. What else would you see standing there but this? * Either before all others, or that which was when even evil did not yet exist. But if evils came later, among those things that do not participate in these gifts, or in the lowest things, and if there is nothing beyond evils toward the worse, then evils would stand in opposition to the Good, having no middle ground for their opposition. Therefore the Good—which you cannot praise enough—is either the Good entirely, or if it must exist, it would be this and no other. But if someone were to say it does not exist, then evil would not exist either. Then all things would be indifferent to choice by nature: but this is impossible. The other things they call good are referred to this, but this itself is referred to nothing. It is nothing else that makes it such:

<column-break/>

Lifted up by him who infused love: it transcends the intellect indeed, but it cannot go beyond the Good: since nothing can be higher than the Good. If the soul fixes its gaze upon the mind, it discerns beautiful and venerable things, yet it does not yet possess entirely what it seeks. For it is as if one approaches a beautiful face, yet one that does not yet seize the affection; for it still lacks that decorous grace which is accustomed to shine forth in beauty and allure. Wherefore here too we must consider beauty to be that which shines upon the proportion, rather than the proportion itself; and that this is properly what is lovable. For why does the splendor of beauty appear more in the face of a living person, while in the face of a dead person—even if the form is not yet changed—scarcely a vestige of beauty remains? Why, again, among images, do those which seem more lifelike also appear more beautiful, even though others might be composed with a more exact measure? Why does the form of a living being, even if it is less composed, appear more beautiful than any beauty of a statue? Perhaps because this is truly more to be sought: and that is because it has a soul: and that, again, because the soul is marked with a certain light of the Good itself. From there, colored, it is immediately awakened, and lifted higher as if lighter, and it raises what it possesses, and insofar as it can grasp the Good, it renders it good and awakens it.

->The first principle of things is the same as the Good itself. Chapter XXII.<-

> For nothing is better than the Good itself: nothing is likewise better than the first principle of things. Also, the Good is most self-sufficient through itself: but only the principle can be self-sufficient for itself. Furthermore, evil increases through departure from the principle, but by approach to it, the good is increased. Therefore, the lowest of things is evil itself: and similarly, the first is the Good itself. Finally, since all things seek the Good and profit by participation in it, it is clearly established that all things both exist and are preserved by it, and by its virtue they are moved, and do whatever they do rightly and naturally.

NOR indeed should anyone wonder that that which the soul follows, which infuses light into the mind, and whose trace moves the soul everywhere, has such power, while it clearly draws the soul and mind toward itself and everywhere recalls them from error, so that they may finally rest within it. For if that from which all things come allows nothing to be better than itself, while all other things are less good, it follows that the best of all things is the Good itself. Furthermore, if it is necessary that the nature of the Good be most self-sufficient in itself, and not in need of anything: what other thing would one find to be that Good, except this which is before others that which it exists as, when evil was not yet? But if evils are later, in those things which participate in nothing of the divine gifts and are the lowest, and there is no evil among the higher beings, nor anything worse than evil itself—just as there is nothing better than the Good itself—then certainly evils stand in a contrary way to the First [Principle]: having no middle ground for their contrariety. Therefore, this [the Good] is by no means "nothing." For either there is no Good at all, or if it is necessary for the Good to be, this at least and no other shall it be. If anyone should object that the Good does not exist at all, he will be forced to confess similarly that evil does not exist: whence it would follow that all things are indifferent to choice according to nature: but that is impossible. Other things that are called good are referred to the First, but the First itself is referred to none. Since therefore the Good itself is such, what then does it do?

<summary>Plotinus argues that beauty is not found in symmetry or physical proportions, but in the "grace" or "light" of the Good that animates a being. He identifies the Good as the self-sufficient First Principle of all things, from which all existence and value flow.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the "Good" (the One) following the previous discussion on how beauty is a "grace" or "light" that shines from a source. Plotinus is now transitioning from the experience of beauty to the metaphysical structure of how the Good generates and sustains Mind, Life, and Soul.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

Indeed, He <note>The Good, or the One</note> made Mind, He made Life, He made souls from Mind, and absolutely all other things that participate in reason, mind, or life. Who then could express what kind of or how great a good that is, which is the fountain and principle <note>original: "principium," meaning the source or first cause</note> of these things? But what does He do now? Certainly, He now preserves those things which He made. For He causes both the intelligences everywhere to understand, and living things to live, inspiring Mind, inspiring Life, and inspiring Being <note>original: "esse," or existence</note> at the very least, where life cannot be received.

->*Desirability is not so much the nature of the Good itself as it is a certain condition following from the nature of the Good: therefore, what is the nature and reason of the Good, and do those things which follow the Good do so through pleasure alone, or do they bring back something else from it; and by what certain sign are we able to discern the presence of the true Good. Chapter 24.*<-

<margin>A</margin> **I**t remains to inquire what it primarily works towards us. But we shall speak again concerning the light: what that light is by which the Mind is illuminated, and in which the Soul also participates. But it is better for the present, deferring this for later, to first investigate whether the Good itself is called "Good" because it is to be desired by another: and whether that which is desirable to one is also good for that one: and whether we should assert that the Good itself is that which is to be desired by all. Or rather, should someone judge this to be merely a sign <note>an outward indication rather than the essence</note> of the Good, and that which is desirable ought to possess a nature by which it might justly claim such a title for itself? Furthermore, we must ask: do those who desire it do so by receiving something from it, or simply by rejoicing in it? And if they receive something, what might that be? But if they only rejoice, why is it in this only, and not in something else? Here, indeed, we must also investigate whether the Good is to be weighed by its own proper nature, or by something else? Then truly, is the Good entirely for another's sake, or is the Good also a good to itself? Or rather, is it the case that to whomever it is a good, it is not a good to itself, but necessarily to another? Likewise, for what nature is it primarily a good: for there is some nature for which nothing is good. Nor do I think we should pass over in silence what some stubborn and contentious person might object. "What then, O men," he will say, "do you adorn your cause more gloriously by looking upward at the gods? You call life a good, and Mind a good: although you place the Good itself above these. Tell me, I pray, what is Mind itself as a good? What good does it have when understanding the forms <note>original: "species," the Platonic Ideas</note> themselves, while it contemplates what each thing is?" It may perhaps happen that, deceived by the delight of these things, one calls them good: similarly, one might think life is a good because it is sweet to him. If such a person should happen to be in a state where he is touched by no pleasure, why then would he affirm these things to be good? Or will he perhaps think it is a good simply that he exists? But what fruit will he perceive from being itself? What difference will it make to him to be, or not to be at all, unless one asserts that a certain friendship <note>original: "amicitiam," a natural affinity or self-love</note> toward oneself is the cause of these things? So much so that by this deception, and our natural fear of death, the estimation of things as "goods" is induced in us.

->*The Good is the form for matter, the soul for the body, the intellect for the soul, and the principle of all for the intellect and for all things together. Chapter 25.*<-

Form exhibits act and order to matter as a good; the Soul gives life and motion to the body, virtue to the Soul, and the Principle <note>The One</note> gives vital and intellectual act to the Intellect, and an inestimable light: just as it follows in nature that it illuminates distant things, but also warms those that approach; indeed, just as the center attracts heavy things, so this condition accompanies the nature of the Good, that it draws remote things through desire, but retains and satisfies those that are present.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> * Indeed He made. He made Life, Soul, and the others as many as are of Reason, or Mind, or Soul, which is the fountain and principle of these; how and what kind of good and how great? But what now? Even now He saves those things, and causes them to understand, and the living things to live, breathing in Mind and Life.

<margin>A</margin> And if it is not able to live, to be? Or of what kind. Or again concerning the Light. * What is the Light by which [the Mind] is illuminated, and which the soul receives from it, or leaving this intellectual [matter], let us first consider those things. Whether the Good is something, what it is itself, or is it called good because it belongs to someone, and to another it is good, but to all it is the end <note>original: "τέρμα," the goal or boundary</note>...

<margin>B</margin> ...to be the Good, or did we make its being good a witness of it? But it is necessary for it to have that which is desired by that thing, as if perhaps obtaining such a name. And what do the desiring things receive? Do they desire to rejoice in it? If indeed they receive, what? Or if it is the rejoicing, why this and not another? In which indeed, whether the Good is by its own Mind...

<margin>C</margin> ...or by some other. Or whether the Good is anything other than it is, or the Good is good to itself * or whether it is good to itself. To itself it is not. By necessity, or to what nature is it a good? There is some nature to which nothing is good, and that must not be left out, which perhaps someone who is annoyed might say, as if he said to us: "Why do you deprive us of bodies, [looking] up and down, calling Life and Mind good?"

<margin>D</margin> ...beyond these, what would it be that one calls good? And what does the one who understands the Forms themselves have as a good? Contemplating each one. For being deceived and led by these, he might perhaps say it is good, why would he say they are good? Or to be. For what would he harvest from being? And what would it differ to be or not to be at all?

<margin>E</margin> ...unless someone [claims] friendship toward himself as the cause. So that through this same hidden deception... and the fear of destruction caused the setting of "goods" to be believed.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Good (the One) is the source that generates and sustains Mind, Life, and Soul, asserting that its goodness is an inherent nature rather than a result of being desired by others. He challenges the skeptical view that we only value life and intellect out of a primitive self-preservation or fear of death.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the examination of the nature of the Good, specifically responding to Plato’s "Philebus." It explores the relationship between pleasure, intellect, and the Good, while establishing a hierarchy of being where each level finds its "good" in the level above it (Matter to Form, Body to Soul, Soul to Intellect, Intellect to the One).</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **P**lato, therefore, when he mixed pleasure with the "end" <note>original: "fini" (Latin) / "τῷ τέλει" (Greek); the ultimate goal or purpose of life</note> and did not place the Good itself as something simple or residing in the intellect alone—as is written in the *Philebus*—did so perhaps because he sensed a certain ambiguity. He did not dare to place the Good entirely in pleasure (and rightly so), yet he did not think the intellect, if it were devoid of pleasure, should be judged as the Good itself; for he did not see in such a thing that which incites the affection or desire. Perhaps, however, he did not understand it in quite that way, but rather composed the Good in this manner because he judged that the Good, having such a nature in itself, must necessarily be delightful <note>original: "delectabile"</note> and desirable to the one seeking it, and delightful to the one who has attained it. Therefore, for whom there is no joy, the Good is not present. Thus, if the first seeker finds no gladness, neither is the Good present. Nor did he compose the Good in this way without reason. For he was not investigating the "First Good" <note>The Absolute or the One</note> there, but only the "human good," which belongs entirely to another thing and is itself another thing, since it is deficient and perhaps a composite. For this reason, that which is solitary and alone he judges to have no "good" <note>in the human sense</note>, but rather to exist as the Good by some other condition and a more excellent reason. It is necessary, therefore, that the Good itself be sought, yet it does not become good because it is desired; rather, it becomes desirable because it is good.

<margin>C</margin> Is it not the case, then, that in the final order of things, that which precedes is the "good," and a constant ascent of this kind ensures that what is higher is present to what follows it as its good? This is true provided the ascent never departs from the proportion of analogy, but always proceeds toward greater things. <margin>* ascent</margin> But the ascent will finally stop at that which is supreme, beyond which nothing remains that can be received as higher. This is the First and the truly Good, and the Good that is chiefly greatest, and the cause of goodness for all others. For 
<margin>D</margin> **Matter**, the good is **Form**. Indeed, if matter were to obtain sensation, it would undoubtedly rejoice at the arrival of form. For the **Body**, the good is the **Soul**; for without the soul it would neither exist nor be preserved. For the **Soul**, the good is **Virtue**. Moving higher, the good is the **Intellect**. Finally, for the **Intellect**, the good is that which we are accustomed to call the **First Nature**. It must be considered, moreover, that each of these produces something in those things for which they are the "good." Some provide order and ornament; others provide life; others provide wisdom and the gift of living well.

<column-break/>

->the gift of living well: finally, the Good itself bestows a gift upon the intellect, which we say comes from there into the intellect and turns out to be good, because it is an "act" <note>original: "actus"; the realization of a potential</note> from that source. And because even now what is called "light" is infused from there into this <note>the intellect</note>: exactly what that is, we shall discuss in what follows.<-

*Those things which are endowed with sensation can have this most powerful sign of a present "good": that by this very fact they are steadily delighted, and they most willingly rest in it, and they find themselves better off from it.* Chapter 26.

*Just as concerning things lacking sensation these two things exist—namely, the inclination toward a natural good and its end, and rest in that end and natural state—they are something other than the natural good itself: for they are certain acts of the thing pursuing the good, or concerning the good, or in the good. So in things endowed with sensation, appetite and pleasure are something other than the Good, nor is pleasure itself sufficient. For it is more desirable, when the good is present, to be delighted by what we desire, than to be delighted in a similar way without it.*

<margin>A</margin> <margin>* Or to perceive</margin> **T**HEN truly, that which is able by nature to perceive, when it approaches the Good itself, or if ever the Good approaches it, it is able to know it and to say that it possesses it. But what indeed must be said if it is perhaps deceived? It is necessary, certainly, that there be some similarity, by which...

<summary>Plotinus explores the hierarchy of being, explaining that each level of existence (Matter, Body, Soul, Intellect) finds its "Good" in the level immediately above it, culminating in the "First Nature" or the One. He critiques and refines Plato's view on pleasure, arguing that while the Good is naturally delightful, it is defined by its own nature rather than by the pleasure it provides.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the nature of the "Good" from the perspective of desire and fulfillment. It transitions from a critique of Plato’s "Philebus" to a deeper analysis of why we desire certain things and whether pleasure or "familiarity" defines what is good for us.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

...is deceived. But if it is placed there, that thing by which it was deceived will certainly be its "good"; for when the real thing arrives, it departs from that which had previously misled it. Indeed, the appetite and the internal sting <note>original: "stimulus"; the inner drive or "pang" of desire</note> within each person testify that there is some Good for everyone. In inanimate things, the granting of "good" comes from another source; however, in that which possesses a soul, the appetite itself pursues its own good. Just as bodies naturally lacking life are cared for and tended to by living beings, <margin>B</margin> so living beings provide for themselves according to their powers. 

That someone has finally attained the Good can be believed without doubt when they find themselves in a better state, feeling no regret, but rather filled with satisfaction; they remain in that state and seek nothing else. For this reason, pleasure is not sufficient in itself. For one who is affected by pleasure does not always desire the same thing. Even if they are said to desire pleasure itself, they cannot be proven to seek the same thing consistently, for the object in which they take delight is always changing. <margin>C</margin> It is necessary, therefore, that the Good—which one seeks above all else—be not a mere passion <note>original: "passionem" (Latin) / "πάθος" (Greek); an external impression or emotion one undergoes</note> or a certain affection by which the seeker is inwardly moved. If the Good were merely a feeling, a person could remain "empty" if they judged the feeling itself to be the Good; they would possess only the affection, which someone else might possess even in the absence of the actual Good. 

For this reason, no one would choose to be so affected without actually possessing a good thing, just as no one would choose the joy of having a son if they did not actually have one. Nor do those who desire to fill their bellies choose the delight of eating as a "good" while not actually eating. For even those who indulge in Venus <note>A reference to sexual desire and physical love</note> as if choosing their own good, do not truly enjoy the pleasure unless they are actually possessing or performing the act, rather than merely imagining they possess or perform it.

*Neither appetite nor pleasure makes something good; rather, the nature of the Good itself attracts the appetite from a distance, and soothes it with pleasure from nearby. Similarly, a certain "familiarity" or "belonging" is not the reason something is good for you.*

### Chapter XXVII.

*For not everything that is similar or near to you is desirable or healthy; nor does mere equality satisfy. Rather, the nature of the Good is accompanied by a virtue that meets us as something domestic and our own, even though its nature is superior to ours. Therefore, the Good of each thing exists everywhere, either as a Form <note>original: "species" (Latin) / "εἶδος" (Greek); the organizing principle or "blueprint" of a thing</note> toward a subject, or as a Principle of Form toward a subject.*

<margin>A</margin> But what must happen to each thing so that it possesses what is suitable to it? Surely we shall call it a "Form." For Form is suitable to Matter, and Form—that is, Virtue—is suitable to the Soul. But does this Form become a "good" simply because it is "one's own" <note>original: "propria" (Latin) / "οἰκεῖον" (Greek); the Stoic and Platonic concept of things that belong to one's own nature</note> or familiar? Does appetite lean toward what belongs to it? Perhaps not. For the "similar" is also "one's own"; yet if someone desires and rejoices in something similar, they do not yet necessarily possess the Good. Or, when we have granted that something is Good, shall we not also grant that it is "one's own"? <margin>B</margin> It must be said that the judgment of what is "one's own" must be referred back to that which is more excellent and better, toward which something exists "in potentiality." For since it is in potentiality toward another thing, it undoubtedly lacks that thing. That more excellent thing which it lacks is certainly its Good. 

Matter, indeed, is the most destitute of all things, for which the final and nearest Form is suitable. But beyond matter, one rises step by step to higher things. <margin>C</margin> Accordingly, if a thing is its own good, then its perfection and its Form—or whatever is more excellent than it—is much more its good. This is such a thing by its own nature, and it becomes such for the subject because it brings the Good to it. But why is it the Good itself? Is it because it is most especially its o—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...he is deceived. But if this is so, that thing is his good from which he was deceived. For when that arrives, he departs from that by which he was deceived. And the individual drive and the birth-pang of each person bear witness that there is a good for each. For soulless things, the gift of their good comes from another. But for that which has a soul, the appetite <note>original: "ἔφεσις"; a reaching out or yearning</note> produces the pursuit, just as in the case of bodies born among the dead, <margin>B</margin> the care and guardianship of living things holds them. For the living, there is providence from themselves; in whatever state they may be, they will be better. And this is to have been filled, and to remain so, and not to seek another thing. Therefore, pleasure is not self-sufficient. It is not the same as the Good. For when one has it, they seek the same again, and the object of it is always something else. The Good which one chooses must be an actual being, not just a passing feeling <note>original: "πάθος"</note> in a random person. <margin>C</margin> Thus, the one who thinks pleasure is the Good remains empty, having only the feeling, which is merely a consequence of the Good. Therefore, one would not endure the feeling without having the object—for instance, being pleased that a son is present when he is not, or as if he were present. And those who delight in the physical filling of the body as the Good, as if eating when not eating, or as if using things not holy, or not being with the one they wished, or not acting.

<margin>A</margin> BUT what must happen to each thing for it to have what is its own <note>original: "τὸ οἰκεῖον"</note>? Shall we say it is a certain Form? Form is to matter, and to the soul, virtue is Form. Is it then that because the Form is "one's own," it is a good for that thing, and the appetite is toward what is one's own? For the similar is also one's own. And if one desires and rejoices in the similar, he does not yet have the Good. How shall we say it is "one's own" after having called it "Good"?
<margin>B</margin> One must say that "one's own" is judged by what is better. For it is toward that which is better than itself, toward which it is in potentiality—for that which is in potentiality toward something is in need of it. That which is in need is in need of something better, which is that which it is for itself. Matter is the most needy of all things, and the last Form is that which is close to it. For it [the soul] looks toward the upper things. And if it is indeed its own good, much more is that which is better than itself its good, 
<margin>C</margin> and by its own nature, which also makes it good. Why then is it the Good itself? Is it because it is most "one's own" <note>The Greek text ends here with Latin fragments in the original printing: "bonum? An quoniã sibi est maximè p"</note> good? Or because it is most especially p...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Good is not merely a feeling of pleasure or a sense of "belonging," but is a higher state of being or "Form" that perfects a thing. He uses the example of a father’s joy to show that reality matters more than just the internal sensation of happiness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 718 regarding the nature of the Good as the ultimate object of desire. Plotinus is moving from the internal experience of "familiarity" with the Good toward a metaphysical analysis of Matter (Hyle) and Form (Species), and whether Matter can truly desire the Good.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN

...or not; but rather because everything is a portion of the Good. For this reason, you will find a greater "familiarity" <note>original: "οἰκειώσεις" / "familiaritas"; a Stoic and Neoplatonic term for the sense of belonging or being "at home" with something that suits one's nature</note> toward the Good in those who are sincere and of a better character. Now, it is truly absurd to ask why something, since it is good, should be good to itself—as if it were necessary for it to sing outside of its own nature <note>original: "ἔξω ἃδειν τῆς ἑαυτοῦ φύσεως"; a Greek idiom meaning to be out of tune with oneself or to act contrary to one's essence</note> and not love itself as a good. But we must investigate this in the simplest terms: whether, in a state where there is absolutely no "other," there can be a proper relationship to oneself, and thus be good to itself. 

For the present, if these things have been correctly stated by us, and the gradual ascent reveals the Good established in a certain nature, then it is not our desire that creates the Good; rather, desire arises because the thing is already Good. Furthermore, for those who attain it, a certain pleasure accompanies the possession of the Good. However, even if no pleasure were produced, the Good would still be chosen and must be sought for its own sake.

<column-break/>

*We think of "prime matter" <note>The underlying, formless "stuff" of the universe</note> as a certain formless power, yet one naturally prepared to receive form. In the respect that it is formless, it is evil; nor in that state does it properly desire the good. But in the respect that it is a potentiality prepared for form, it is not evil. And if it were able to desire in any way, it would desire the good—that is, form—driven especially by a hidden hatred for its own deformity.*

### Chapter XXVIII.

*Just as the Good itself is lovable to itself and to all, so if we were to imagine "Evil itself," it would be loved neither by others nor by itself. To each thing, its "good" is its own particular appearance, form, perfection, and activity descending from above. But form and appearance are everywhere opposed to material formlessness. Therefore, the more form is separated from matter, the more it is truly a "species" <note>original: "εἶδος" / "species"; in this context, it means the intelligible "look" or "essence" of a thing</note> and the more it is a Good. Finally, the most separate species of all is the Best. But the Good itself is no longer any single species, nor the good of any one thing, but rather the author of both species and goods alike.*

<margin>* not matter

* or sense</margin>
What follows from the previous arguments must now be considered more fully. If everywhere that which presents itself as a good is a certain "form," and form is the good for matter itself, we must ask: if matter were to become capable of willing, could it will to become form alone? But if it willed this, it would will its own destruction <note>Because matter, by definition, is that which lacks form; if it became pure form, it would cease to be matter</note>. Yet all things seek the Good itself. But perhaps matter does not seek to be form, but simply to "be"; and having attained being, it wishes to cast off its own inherent evil. 

But how can "evil" have a desire for the Good? Truly, we do not actually attribute desire to matter; we only make this supposition for the sake of the argument, ascribing "sense" <note>perception or awareness</note> to it if such a thing could be attributed while it remains matter. And certainly, when form arrives—like a beautiful dream of the good—matter is placed in a better order. If, therefore, matter is evil, how things stand has already been said. But if some other thing—let us call it "wickedness"—were to receive a sense of its own being, would it still look toward the Good as something familiar? Surely it would not be wickedness itself that chose the good, but rather the subject that held evil within itself. If, however, "being" and "evil" were the same thing in that instance, how would it seek the good? Or perhaps, if evil felt its own nature, would it love itself? But how can the unlovable be loved? We have not placed the nature of the Good in that which is merely "one's own" or familiar. Let this be enough said on these matters.

<column-break/>

*But if form is everywhere the Good itself, and as one ascends higher, form is more purely encountered—for the soul is more truly a "form" than the form of a physical body—then within the soul, one part is more...*

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Good is sought because of its intrinsic nature, not because of the pleasure it brings. He explores the paradox of "Matter," which is formless and "evil," suggesting that while matter cannot desire without ceasing to be itself, the arrival of Form acts like a "good dream" that brings order to chaos.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation into the nature of the Good, specifically exploring its relationship to Form (Species) and Intellect, and beginning a critique of the role of pleasure (voluptas) in the definition of the Good.</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin>...more so; and finally, the intellect is more of a form <note>original: "species"; here referring to a Platonic Form or Idea</note> than the soul is. Certainly, the Good itself proceeds by a path directly opposite to that of matter; it belongs especially to that which is purified and far removed from matter, according to each thing's degree of purity. Indeed, the Greatest Good belongs to that from which everything that can be thought of as "matter" is most distantly <margin>B</margin> separated. Furthermore, the nature of the Good itself flees from all matter—or rather, it never approaches it under any condition—and undoubtedly escapes into a nature that is entirely vacant of form, from which the primary form arises. But this will be discussed more thoroughly in the following sections.

*We are usually moved by a more manifest pleasure while we are being restored to a perfect state of body or mind than when we have already achieved that perfect state. From this, it is clear that such pleasure, which is somewhat stinging <note>original: "mordax"; biting or sharp</note>, is not the end or the perfection of nature. Chapter XXIX.*

*In the natural state and perfect condition of life, that moving pleasure ceases, having become a tranquil and (if I may say so) optimal health and natural disposition—more constant, truer, and more desirable than fleeting pleasure. Against those who believe that nothing is good without pleasure, or apart from pleasure, Plotinus asserts that to be, to live, and to understand are goods to be chosen, not only because they commonly happen to involve certain manifest pleasures, but because their opposites are naturally shunned as evils.*

<margin>A</margin>BUT if pleasure does not follow the good, but something else exists before pleasure for the sake of which pleasure usually follows, why would the good not even then be pleasing and lovable? But when we call something "pleasing" and "joyful," we have already spoken of pleasure. But if the good exists while the truth exists, and it is possible for it not to be "delightful," what shall we say? Perhaps if it were so, even in the <margin>B</margin> presence of the good, one who possesses a sense of the good would not recognize it is there. Perhaps also nothing prevents someone from indeed knowing the good, yet not being moved by it once they possess it—which most especially suits a person who is perfectly temperate and in need of nothing. For this reason, a sudden burst of joy <note>original: "exhilaratio"</note> is not appropriate for such a person, not only because the Good is entirely simple, but because only the act of "attaining" (which belongs to one who lacks) is bathed in pleasure. But this will only appear clearly after we have purified all <margin>C</margin> other things and expelled that opposing argument from our minds. This is the argument of the one who doubts what fruit he might receive by possessing a mind aimed at obtaining the Good—perhaps because he is moved by no emotion when he hears these things, because he does not perceive them in reality. Either when he hears the name "Good" he thinks of each of these things individually, or he seeks something perceptible to the senses and places the Good in riches or other things of that kind. <margin>D</margin> Against this person, therefore, it must be said: when he despises these things, he meanwhile confesses that some Good is placed within himself; but when he doubts where it is most powerful and by what reason it is placed there, he then tries to fit these external things to the notion of the Good already implanted within him. For it is impossible for someone who is entirely unskilled and ignorant of this very thing to ever say: "this or that cannot be the Good itself." Perhaps also such a discourse prophesies that the Good itself is above the Mind. Furthermore, if one looking toward the Good itself (or toward what is nearest to it) does not discern it, it is helpful at least to think of the Good from its opposites. Otherwise, he will not even admit that ignorance is an evil, although all men desire to understand and glory in their intelligence. To this, the senses also bear witness, for they naturally strive toward knowledge and a kind of understanding. If, therefore, the intellect is something pure and venerable—and most especially the Primary Intellect—tell me, what would you imagine it values...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...to a greater degree; and the Mind [Intellect] is more than the Soul. The Good proceeds in the way opposite to the soul's opposite <note>meaning Matter</note>. It belongs to that which is, as it were, purified and cut off, according to the power of each, and most of all to that which stays away from matter. And indeed, the nature of the Good, <margin>B</margin> fleeing matter—or rather, never having come near it anywhere—has escaped entirely into a formless nature, from which the first form comes. But about these things, later.

<margin>A</margin>But if pleasure did not follow the Good, and there were something before pleasure because of which pleasure exists, or if by calling it "welcome" we already implied pleasure, yet it existed as a reality, could it be that it is not "welcome"? But if the Good were present to one having a sense of it, <margin>B</margin> would he not know that it is there? Or what prevents him from knowing it but not being moved by it, as if having the thing itself were more important than the lack of it? Therefore, it is not just because it is simple, but because "attaining" belongs to the one in second place, that it is pleasant. But this is clear, and all other things are by necessity. Still, having pushed away that resistant argument—that is, the one who wonders what fruit <margin>C</margin> he would harvest by having a share of the Good, if when he hears these things he is not moved, because he lacks the understanding of them. Either hearing the name or taking each thing for something else, or seeking something perceptible, and placing the Good in money or some such things. To whom it must be said, that when he dishonors these things, he admits there is a Good within him. But being at a loss as to where it is, he fits it to the concept he has. For it is not possible to say that this thing is not "it" <margin>D</margin> if one is inexperienced and has no thought of it. Perhaps he is intuitively sensing that which is above the Mind. Then, if looking toward the Good or what is near it he does not know it, he must go toward a concept of it from its opposites—otherwise he would not even set down ignorance as an evil. And yet everyone wants to think and know, and prides himself on it. The senses also bear witness, wanting to be types of knowledge. If then the mind is something honorable and beautiful, and the first Mind most of all, let one imagine what it would be like to possess...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Good is entirely separate from matter and formless in its origin. He further contends that pleasure is a byproduct of moving toward the Good, not the Good itself, which remains desirable even in a state of tranquil possession where "stinging" pleasure is absent.</summary>

# BOOK SEVEN.

...the one who is also the father. By dishonoring being and living, he bears witness against himself and all his own passions. But if someone is displeased with living because death is mixed in, he is displeased with the mixture, but not with that which truly lives. <note>original Greek: "τὸ ἀληθῶς ζῶ"</note>

<column-break/>

Can he see from the generator and father of the mind? Therefore, he who in words scorns being and living, meanwhile testifies to the contrary, and holds all his feelings to be repugnant to his words. But if someone bears life heavily, he is certainly judged to reject not true life, but rather that life which is mixed with death.

### Chapter XXX.

->The end of the intellectual soul is the unhindered and highest act of intelligence, directed entirely toward the good of the universe.<-

*An act of this kind is happiness <note>original: "beatitudo"</note>, even if no external pleasure is added to it; yet it is not itself devoid of pleasure. For the very unhindered integrity and height of action is pleasure. Then indeed it exists most especially as a simple and single thing: it rejoices deep within itself, having already been formed by a higher light. Truly, just as the summit of light around a concave mirror is now heat, so the summit of being is now life. Similarly, the sense of living, the imagination of sensing, the reasoning of imagining, the intelligence of reasoning, the joy of intelligence, the good of joy: certainly, one ascends gradually to the highest level of the universe, not through division, but through union. Now, just as the elements, by the same thrust of nature, seek and enjoy what is harmonious with themselves; so the mind, by the same act, when it is at its highest, tends toward the ultimate end as the truth, and enjoys it as the good. But we discuss the end, intelligence, and pleasure in the Commentaries on the Philebus <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the relationship between pleasure and wisdom</note>.*

---

<margin>A</margin>
After these things, we must investigate by touching the Good with the mind: whether pleasure <note>original Greek: "ἡδονὴν"; original Latin: "voluptate"</note> ought to be mixed with the Good, otherwise life would be imperfect, even if one contemplates divine things and their principle. Now indeed, where Plato seems to compose the Good from intellect as a subject, and from a certain affection of the soul which follows intelligence, there certainly he asserts that neither the end nor the Good itself is a composite. Rather, in that place, the intellect itself is the Good, while we rejoice in the possession of this Good.
<margin>B</margin>
And this is one opinion concerning the Good. The other opinion or exposition is that which so mixes intellect with pleasure that it places one single thing as a subject arising from both, so that we, acquiring or perceiving such an intellect, already possess the Good: since a thing that is deserted or alone can neither happen, nor if it could, would it be desirable to us as a good.
<margin>*as one completion of nature</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
But it must be asked, under what condition especially is the intellect mixed with pleasure into one common harmony and perfection of nature. It is established beyond doubt that the pleasure of the body cannot be mixed with the mind: nor indeed can any joy of the soul be congruent with the pleasure of the body. But certainly, it is necessary that every action, affection, and life follow and equally accompany the Good, like something poured over it; while an impediment stands in the way of some act naturally striving, and something contrary is mixed in, it does not permit life to exist in its own right. But for another, the very course of action proceeds pure and sincere,
<margin>D</margin>
and life flourishes in a serene affection. For this reason, those who judge such a habit of mind to be the most pleasant and most desirable, meanwhile say that it is mixed with pleasure: and they seem to bring this about through a lack of a proper name, just as those do who transfer other names beloved by us to divine things. Wherefore it is said: "The Intellect is drunk on nectar" <note>A metaphor for the soul's intoxication with divine wisdom</note>. Likewise: "One goes to the banquet and the food." Again, among the poets:
<margin>E</margin>
<margin>*for that which is truly sufficient is there</margin>
"Jupiter himself smiled," and many similar things. For there, in truth, the lot of life is most pleasant and most lovable, and to be desired most of all. And a condition of this kind neither begins at some time, nor is it involved in motion: the cause of which is that it colors itself, illustrates, and clears. On which account Plato applies truth...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
After these things, whether it is necessary for pleasure to be mixed with the good, otherwise life would be imperfect, even if one should contemplate divine things and their principle, we must investigate by reaching for the good with the mind. Now indeed, where Plato seems to compose the good from intellect as if from a subject, and from a certain affection of the soul which follows intelligence, there certainly he asserts that neither the end nor the good itself is a composite, but there the intellect itself is the good, and we rejoice in the possession of this good.
<margin>B</margin>
And this is one opinion concerning the good. The other opinion or exposition is that which so mixes the intellect with pleasure that it posits one thing as a subject from both, so that we, by preparing or seeing such an intellect, now possess the good: since anything deserted and alone can neither happen, nor if it could, would it be sought by us as a good.
<margin>C</margin>
But it must be asked, under what condition especially the intellect is mixed with pleasure into one harmony of nature and a common perfection. It is certain beyond doubt that the pleasure of the body cannot be mixed with the mind: indeed, not even any gladness of the soul is congruent with the pleasure of the body. But truly it is necessary for every action, affection, and life to follow and accompany it equally, as if something poured over it, while an impediment stands in the way of some act naturally striving, and something contrary is mixed in, which indeed does not permit life to exist in its own right. But for some action, the course itself proceeds pure and sincere,
<margin>D</margin>
and life flourishes with a serene affection. For this cause, those who think such a habit of mind is most delightful and most desirable, meanwhile say that it is mixed with pleasure: and they seem to offer this for lack of a proper name, just as those do who also transfer other names loved by us to divine things. Wherefore it is: "The Intellect is drunk on nectar." Likewise: "To the banquet and the food one goes." Again, among the poets:
<margin>E</margin>
"Jupiter himself smiled," and many similar things. For there, in truth, the lot of life is most delightful and most lovable, and to be desired most of all. And a condition of this sort neither happens at some time, nor is it turned in motion: the cause of which is that it colors itself and illustrates and clears. On which account Plato applies truth...
