# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS VI.
### Page 722

<margin>A</margin> ...to the mixture, and he <note>Likely referring to Plato, whom Plotinus often interprets</note> places a moderator over the mixture. He also says that contemplation and beauty in the mixture proceed from there <note>original: "inde," referring to the Good</note> into the beautiful. Therefore, according to this, we take our own parts in this. This is truly what we must love and pursue, insofar as we recall ourselves to the best part within us to the best of our abilities. Therefore, this tempered and beautiful thing, and the form so composed, is clearly the manifest, intellectual, and beautiful life.

*The Good itself, the principle of the universe, not only procreates the mind and the soul, but also by a certain visionary ray—acting as a hook—constantly calls them back to itself: where it turns that ray both in the soul and in the mind, and finally makes it gracious; and this, on both sides, is happiness itself. Chapter XXXI.*

*The soul is lured to the heights not only through a divinely implanted love, but also through reason. Specifically, when it is proved that bodily beauty, standing as it does in deformity and shifting instability, is necessarily imperfect, and therefore originates from the incorporeal. Thus the soul finally recognizes the form of the divine mind.*

<margin>A</margin> Since, therefore, all things have been made beautiful by that which is before all, and everything reflects light from there: the intellect <note>original: "intellectus," corresponding to the Greek "nous"</note> has obtained from there the glow of intellectual action, by which it subsequently illustrated the nature it brought forth; the soul, however, receives power from there for living, with a very great life overflowing into it. Certainly, the intellect was immediately raised toward that and remained there, considering itself satisfied while it stands closer to it; and the soul, having turned toward that, as soon as it recognized and perceived whatever it could, greatly rejoices in the spectacle: and as far as it is capable of seeing, it is immediately struck with awe.

<margin>B</margin> It sees as if struck from there, and having something of that within itself, it perceives it in itself as if conscious of itself. And yet in a way it has already begun to desire with affection, like those who are incited by a certain image of a thing to be loved to long for the sight of the thing itself. Just as among us lovers fashion themselves into the likeness of the beloved, making both their bodies more graceful and their souls more elegant out of zeal for the likeness of the beloved, so that as far as possible they turn out no inferior in temperance and other virtues to the beloved; otherwise they would be utterly despised by beloveds endowed with virtue. Those are from the number of lovers who can eventually enjoy the familiarity of the beloved.

<margin>C</margin> In the same way, the soul also loves the Good itself, but it was provoked to love by that same Good right from the beginning. And indeed, whatever soul has a ready love by no means waits to be recalled to the memory of the Good itself by these things which are beautiful among us: but having love within itself, even if it is ignorant of what it has, it seeks it constantly, and wishing to approach it, it despises all these things of ours. For considering the things that seem beautiful in this world, it rightly despises them, since it sees them lying in flesh and body, polluted by the present subject and place, and dispersed by dimensions; for even if they are called beautiful, they are not themselves truly beautiful.

<margin>D</margin> For it is wrong to think that those things which are truly beautiful <note>original: "quæ reuera pulchra ſunt"</note> would immerse their own natures, such as they are, into the mud of bodies, and defile and destroy themselves. Now, when the soul considers that the things thought beautiful among us are in constant flux, it understands entirely that the light which shines in them originates from elsewhere.

<margin>E</margin> After this, the soul is raised up again, being able at last to attain what it loves, and it does not stop until it reaches it, unless someone perhaps roots out its love. There at last it discerns all things beautiful and truly existing, and being filled with the life of Being itself, it is greatly strengthened. It also becomes truly Being itself, and dwells there truly comprehending, and dwelling nearby, it now clearly feels and perceives.

Symmetry is made in itself, and in the mixture, he says it comes from there <note>original Greek: "ἐκεῖθεν," referring to the source of the Good</note>... like according to its own parts. That which is truly desired by us, to the best of ourselves... [This column mirrors the Latin text but is partially cut off at the right margin.]

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration from page 722, moving from the soul's recognition of divine light into Chapter 32, which examines the nature of the "First Principle" (the Good or the One) as the source of all beauty and form. # BOOK SEVEN.

Whatever exists in the intelligible world <note>The realm of pure thought and perfect Forms, as opposed to the physical world.</note> is a certain form <note>original: "species"</note>; and that world is itself a whole form consisting of forms. Moreover, each individual form is something defined by the intellect. Hence, one is clearly distinguished from another. Again, the universal form, consisting of defined parts, is ultimately defined itself. Likewise, in the multitude of forms, a single splendor of beauty shines forth from that place.

### Chapter XXXII.

*It is necessary, therefore, to go even beyond the defined nature of that world to reach the very immensity of its incomparable power; and from beauty—which is a kind of splendor found in many things, like stars—we must be ignited toward the simple light of the Good itself, as if toward the Sun. Although this Good is no specific form, it is nonetheless the very beauty of beauty. And because goodness and beauty are infinite, they kindle an infinite love in those who approach. From this, we can argue for the eternal happiness of souls.*

---

<margin>Where then is he who made such beauty? <note>original Greek: Ποῦ οὖν ὁ ποιήσας τοῦτο τοιοῦτον κάλλος</note></margin>
Where then does he who made [it] perceive such great beauty, and such great life and intellectual essence? Is the beauty already present in all these varied things? It is indeed beautiful, as far as the vision can grasp it. But when one is already within the beautiful, it is necessary to see from where these things come, and from where they become beautiful. It is necessary that he himself be the one who is none of them; for if he were one of them, he would be merely a part. Or if you become such a form or such a power, all [other] powers and forms would then be held and exist there. But he must be above all powers and above all forms; the principle, however, is the formless <note>original: "aneideon," meaning without a specific shape or limit</note>, not because it lacks form, but because from it every intellectual form comes, and everything that lives comes into being. If everything that was made has a specific form, who then made it? It could not be any of the existing things, and yet it is all of them; none of them, because the things that exist are posterior to him; all of them, because they come from him, and he is able to make all things. Should he have magnitude? He would then be infinite. But if he has magnitude, he would not be one. Magnitude belongs to the things that come after. And it is necessary that the maker of magnitude does not possess magnitude himself. Then he would be a part of essence and a quantity. He would also have something else after himself, namely magnitude. But the truly Great itself is that which nothing can be more powerful than, for by itself nothing is able to be. For to which of his own things would he come as a cause, if he did not possess the same nature? He is the One always and for all things, and he gives measure to them, while he himself is not subject to measure. For how could he measure others if he were himself measured? He is the object of desire, though you cannot grasp his shape or form; from where then does he come as the most beloved? And if love is, it would be a love without limbs <note>original: "ameles," meaning without parts or physical structure</note>. And love is not limited here, because neither is the beloved limited. But that love would be infinite, just as his beauty is of another kind: beauty above beauty. For since he is none of the existing things, how could he be a specific beauty? Since he is lovable, he is surely the author of beauty. He is the power and the flower of all beauty, the beauty-maker who makes beauty: for he generates it, and makes it more beautiful by the abundance of beauty within him. Therefore he is the beginning and the end of beauty. Since he is the beginning of beauty, he makes beautiful that which he is the principle of; but he makes it beautiful not in a specific shape, but in its very existence.

<margin>of beauty <note>original Greek: κάλλους</note></margin>
<margin>of beauty and makes it more beautiful <note>original Greek: κάλλους καὶ κάλλιον ποιεῖ</note></margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> HERE it is now right to ask in this manner: Come, tell me, O Soul, where is he who procreated such immense beauty, who made the first essence? Do you see, O Soul, beauty itself flickering in all these various forms? It is indeed beautiful to dwell there. But it is worthwhile for the mind, already existing within the beautiful, to investigate from where these things come and how they become beautiful. It is certainly necessary that the author of all beautiful things is himself none of them; otherwise, if he were any of them, he would only be a certain part.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, he will be neither a certain form nor a certain power. Nor again is he all the forms and powers that exist and come to be there: rather, he must stand above all powers and forms. The principle itself is therefore devoid of form <note>original: "specie vacans"</note>, not because it lacks form, but rather because he is the one from whom every intellectual form arises. For that which has been made, if it was indeed being made, needed to become something, and therefore it received its own form; but that which was made by no one is surely not a "something" that was made.

<margin>C</margin> This, therefore, is none of the beings, and yet all beings: none, because beings are posterior to him; all, because they are born from him. Since he can make all things, what magnitude could he have within himself? Perhaps he will be immense? Truly, if he is immense, he has no magnitude. For magnitude has a place only in limited things. Now, it is necessary that the maker of magnitude is not a participant in magnitude himself.

<margin>D</margin> Furthermore, even that which is usually called the magnitude of essence is not any kind of quantity. Without doubt, that which comes after him can have magnitude. But his magnitude consists in being more powerful than nothing, and that nothing can be equated with him. For who among his own creatures could be equal to him, since he possesses nothing of the same kind? Moreover, when it is said that God reigns through all ages and everywhere throughout the universe, this signifies neither a measure in God, nor a vast immensity; otherwise, how could he measure anything?

<margin>E</margin> Therefore, it is not fitting to imagine any figure in him. Consequently, that desirable thing, of which you can grasp neither figure nor any form, is to be desired and loved above all else, and the love for it is immense. For this love is not finite, since the beloved itself is not finite; rather, the love of this is infinite. For this reason, his beauty is of another order. It is beauty above beauty. Since he is none of the beings, how can he be any specific beauty? But since he is lovable, he is surely the author of beauty. He is therefore the power and the very flower of universal beauty, producing a beautiful beauty: for he generates it, and by the abundance of his own beauty, he makes the generated beauty more beautiful; for which reason he is the beginning and the end of beauty. And since he is the beginning of beauty, he makes beautiful that for which he is the principle: but he makes it beautiful not in form, but in itself.

# PLOTINUS: ENNEAD VI.

even what is produced there is formless <note>In the sense of being an absolute archetype not yet restricted by physical boundaries.</note>, and in another certain way, it exists within form. For that which exists merely as the "form itself" resides in another; yet, if it were to reside in itself, it would be considered something without form. Therefore, that which participates in beauty is shaped; however, beauty itself is not given a shape.

*The beauty of the Good itself is superior to every universal species <note>The word "species" here refers to the Platonic "Forms" or "Ideas"—the perfect blueprints of reality.</note>: the beauty of the intelligible world is a pure species, since nothing there is formless; nothing is so shaped that it is not itself also a form. The beauty of the lower world is inferior to true species, since it is composed of form joined with formless matter, and even with deformity.*

### Chapter XXXIII.

*That all-form beauty of the divine world, though it is to be admired as much as possible, is nevertheless a defined beauty; therefore, it is not to be loved above all else. Rather, goodness itself is better than "all-form." For even in the divine world, although each thing is a certain form, there is something there compared to another as if it were "matter" <note>Plotinus uses the concept of "Intelligible Matter" to explain how ideas can be distinct from one another within the divine mind.</note>. Thus, both this and that are "something." Beauty in the divine world, acting as the splendor of the Good itself, calls the soul there to the Good through wonder. Similarly, beauty in the soul, as the splendor of intelligence, secretly invites the soul toward the intellect through love. Beauty in the body, like an image of the soul's beauty, encourages us to desire bodily beauty.*

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, when beauty is spoken of, we must flee far away from any such "form" <note>Meaning a limited, defined shape.</note>; we must not place it before our eyes, lest we fall away from the truly beautiful into something that is called beautiful only by a small participation. Indeed, a species that is "unformed" <note>original Latin: *species non formata*; Greek: *amorphon eidos*. This paradox describes the pure essence of a Form before it is limited by a specific instance.</note> is truly beautiful—provided it is a species. And surely, as you progress toward every form by separating it from matter—as if moving toward the "seed-like principles" <term>ratione seminaria</term> <note>The *logoi spermatikoi*, or rational seeds that organize matter according to divine patterns.</note> in which we say one thing differs from another; <margin>B</margin> just as justice and temperance are distinguished from one another because the intellect perceives something unique in each—surely, even if all things there are beautiful, you will find them somewhat diminished because they are designated as something specific. This remains true even if you grasp all things in the intelligible world together; for if you take each thing individually there, you will see it has one intelligible form; if you take them all together, they are like a single form distinguished by variety. Now, if you have proceeded this far, you must consider further <margin>C</margin> what sort of thing that "highest" principle must be: it must be superior in every way to the "all-beautiful" and the variety of distinct forms, yet itself be distinguished by no variety. This is what the soul hungers for, yet the soul can never express why it hungers for such a thing. But Reason dictates that this is what we must truly love; for the nature of the "Best" and "Most Lovable" resides at that level which towers over every species. Therefore, <margin>D</margin> whatever you show to the soul by referring it to a species, the soul always seeks something else beyond it—the thing that gave it form. Reason thus teaches that what possesses form, and even form and species themselves, are something "measured." Such a thing is not the whole, nor is it self-sufficient, nor is it beautiful by its own nature alone, but is a mixture. It is necessary, therefore, that these things be beautiful but measured; while that which is the "Beautiful"—or rather, the **Super-Beautiful** <note>original Latin: *superpulchrum*</note>—is circumscribed by no limit of measure. If it were so, it would be a "shaped" thing; it would be a species. Therefore, that which is primarily lovable and exists as the "First" completely transcends species; and there, the beauty and grace of the Intelligible Good are the nature of the Good itself. The passions of lovers testify to this. For as long as one is occupied only with looking at a physical shape with the eyes, one is not yet seized by love; but as soon as he recalls himself to his soul and conceives the shape within himself—not as something visible or divisible—then love immediately [arises].

<column-break/>

[The soul] is formless, but in another way, having come to be in form. For that which is only "this form" exists in another, but that which exists in itself is formless. Therefore, that which participates in beauty is shaped, namely, beauty [itself].

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, when beauty is spoken of, one must [move] away from such a form. One must [act], lest we fall away [into] those things which are called beautiful by a dim participation. An unformed species is beautiful, if indeed it is a species. [For you], having stripped away every form and those things in reason which we say differ from one another, such as justice and temperance <margin>B</margin> and others, which are beautiful. [The intellect] perceives a certain unique cause, or lesser things, and [takes] as many as are in the Intelligible. Even if one should [take] each thing [singly] in the Intelligible, it would have [a form]. But all things together [are] a variety, still in need, as it were; for [it is necessary to seek] that which is beyond the "all-beautiful" and the multi-faceted. This is what the soul reaches for, and [it] longs for such a thing. But Reason says, <margin>C</margin> truly, those things which appear in the [Good] are its nature, and it is the most lovable. [Reason] brings the soul to the species and shows it. It seeks another thing that gave it form. It says that which has form, and the form itself, are all measured; and this is neither the whole, nor [sufficient] in itself, nor beautiful by itself, but is mixed. Therefore, these things are beautiful, <margin>D</margin> but the Super-Beautiful is not measured, nor is it shaped, nor is it a species. Therefore, the primary and the first [principle] entirely transcends species, and [it] is there, the nature of the Intelligible Good. The passion of [lovers] bears witness to this; for as long as [they] look at the sensible thing, they are not yet [in love]; but when he [conceives] the type in his indivisible soul, then [he loves].

<summary>This page discusses how the ultimate source of reality, the Good, transcends all "Forms" and defined beauty. Plotinus argues that because forms are distinct and "measured," there must be a formless, infinite "Super-Beauty" that serves as their origin and the true object of the soul's desire.</summary>
<keywords>The One, The Good, Forms, Intelligible World, Super-Beautiful, Neoplatonism, Plotinus, Intellectual Beauty, Formless Form, Desire</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical journey of the soul from the previous discussion on the nature of beauty. Having established that beauty originates in the divine realm of "Forms," Plotinus now explains how the soul must transcend even these perfect intellectual forms to reach the "Good" or "The One." This page marks a transition into the mystical climax of the Sixth Ennead, Chapter 33.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN.

<note>original: LIBER SEPTIMVS. In this specific Renaissance edition, this portion of the Enneads is categorized as the seventh book of a series, though it corresponds to Ennead VI.7 in modern scholarly editions.</note>

### Since any beauty, by whomever it is loved, is always sought under the rationale of the Good, it is necessary that the Good itself be the principle of beauty and love. Chapter XXXIII.

> The Good itself, therefore, always and everywhere present, as soon as it has shone upon a soul that is already serene, kindles a wondrous love: namely, when the soul has stripped away all forms and mental concepts—not only those that can be imagined, but even those that are purely intellectual. Then, through the love of the infinite Good, it is miraculously joined as one with that Good, filled with ineffable joy. This is something that can be achieved not only after this present life, but even sometimes during this life.

***

But the soul still seeks to see the beloved, so that what is withering within you <note>Plotinus uses the metaphor of a plant withering without light; the "beloved" here is the divine source that refreshes the soul.</note> may be restored if it should receive <margin>* synthesis</margin> <margin>original: * σύνθεσιν</margin> a new composition. Thus one must pass over to that which is most formless; for the soul would not yearn for that <margin>* that thing</margin> <margin>original: * ἐκεῖνο</margin> [which is already shaped], since what it suffered from the beginning—incited by a dim glow—was a love for a great light. For the trace of the formless is form. To the one who generates the form, the form itself is never the act of generating; rather, when matter approaches, it is the matter that receives it, being by necessity the most distant thing, because matter possesses nothing of the forms of the waters <note>A metaphor for the fluid, changing nature of the material world.</note> from its own nature. Therefore, that which is lovable is not the matter itself, but that which has been given shape through the "Species" <term>Species: The Greek 'eidos,' referring to the perfect, divine blueprints of reality.</term>. But the form upon the matter comes from the soul, and the soul is more truly a "form," and more lovable; yet the Intellect is even more a form, and still more lovable. Beyond this, one must place the first nature, which is without form, as the source of beauty.

The soul is a species, and even more lovable: without doubt, it constitutes the limits of the first form.

***

AND we shall no longer wonder at that which causes such intense longings, if it is entirely removed from all intelligible form. For even the soul, when it receives the love that saves her, sets aside every form she possesses, even any intellectual form that might be within her. For it is impossible for one who holds onto something else or acts upon something else to see that One, or to be harmonized with it. Instead, one must have nothing else at hand—neither evil nor even any other good—so that the soul may receive the "Alone with the Alone" <note>original: "monē monon" (Greek) / "sola solum" (Latin). This is Plotinus’s most famous description of the mystical union between the individual soul and the One.</note>. When the soul happens to reach this, or rather, when the One appears as present (once the soul has turned away from all other present things and prepared herself to be as beautiful as possible, coming into likeness with it), the preparation and the "adorning" are clear to those who prepare themselves. When she sees it suddenly appearing within her—for there is nothing in between—they are no longer two, but both are one. You could not distinguish them as long as it is present. This is imitated by lovers and the beloved in this world who wish to be blended into one. The soul no longer feels the body, nor does it perceive itself to be in the body, nor that it is anything else—not a man, not a living thing, not a being, nor the whole universe. For the sight of these things is "uneven" <margin>* and that [One] and of this [soul]</margin> <margin>original: * κἀκεῖνο καὶ ταύτης</margin> and distracting. Nor does the soul have the leisure for such things when it wishes for this; rather, having sought it out, the soul plunges into it when it is present, and sees that [One] instead of itself. It does not even have the leisure to recognize this event. In this state, it would never exchange its present treasure for any other, not even if someone offered it the whole of heaven; for it knows there is nothing better.

<column-break/>

Yet the soul still desires to look upon the Beloved, so that what withers in the lover may be constantly watered by the sight of the beloved. But if it notices that it must transcend toward something further removed from form, it will desire that even more clearly. For what it has suffered from the beginning is certainly this: it was incited by a certain thin light to a love for a massive light. For the form of any thing is (so to speak) a trace of the formless; she who produces form is not herself the form she produces, I say, when the matter is already near. But matter, by its own spontaneous nature, is necessarily the most remote thing: since it possesses none of even the lowest forms from itself. Therefore, if something is lovable to us, it is not indeed the matter, but that which is shaped by a species: yet species is made in matter by the soul, and the soul is more truly a species and more to be loved. Likewise, the Intellect is more of a species than the soul.

***

SINCE things are so, we shall by no means wonder any further that the thing which incites the sharpest stings of love is removed far from every form, even the intelligible one. Since the soul, when it burns with an ardent love for that [the One], sets aside whatever form it has in itself, even if there be some intellectual form of its own within it. For it cannot be that one who possesses anything else, or acts around something else, should either see that One, or harmonize with it, or be joined to it: but it is necessary to have nothing else of either evil or good ready at hand, so that at some time one may take the "Alone to the Alone." After the soul has successfully attained this, and it has approached her—or rather, being already present, it has recently shone forth, specifically when she has recalled herself from all other present things—preparing herself meanwhile to become most beautiful and to turn out most similar to it. When the soul has thus prepared itself, it will behold God himself suddenly flashing within it: for nothing intervenes between them. Nor are two things discerned there any longer, but both are now one: for as long as it is present, one cannot distinguish them. This is what lovers and those who mutually love in return in our world tend to imitate, who strive to melt together into one. Now, indeed, the soul thus fixed on God no longer feels its own body, nor does it notice itself to be in the body, nor does it pronounce itself to be any other thing—not a man, not an animal, not a being, not the universe. For the prospect of these things is in some way unequal and distracting. Nor does the soul then have such leisure that it might turn its gaze toward them, nor would it wish to have it: but when it has zealously sought him, it involves itself entirely with him as he is present, and sees him now instead of itself, nor is it so at leisure as to acknowledge this happening. In this state, it will exchange the present treasure for no other treasures: not even if someone were to bestow the whole heaven upon it: since it knows that nothing is more excellent.

<summary>Plotinus describes the soul's mystical ascent, explaining that to achieve union with the "Good" (the One), the soul must strip away all material and intellectual forms to become "the alone with the alone." This state is described as a sudden flash of divine light where the boundary between the soul and God vanishes.</summary>

# PLOTINUS' ENNEAD VI.

[perceived], nothing is better: for indeed it cannot ascend any higher. To look at any other thing would be nothing other than to descend, even if those things are lofty and the soul itself is sublime. Then at last the soul attains a judgment that is entirely true: then it thoroughly recognizes that this is the very thing it once sought with all its strength: then without a doubt it asserts that nothing is more excellent. For there is no deception there; otherwise, it would be possible to encounter something truer than truth. Therefore, what the soul says then, it already exists as that thing; it speaks of it later, and it speaks of it in silence. And since it is now affected by a blessed sweetness because it is in the best possible state, it is by no means deceived. <margin>B</margin> For it does not say this as if the body were being tickled <note>original: "corpore titillato" - Plotinus uses this to distinguish deep spiritual joy from mere physical sensation</note>, but having already become that which it was once, when it existed in a state of happiness. Then indeed, it recognizes that all other things in which it used to take delight—when it was pleased by power, wealth, ornaments, beauty, and doctrines—<margin>C</margin> are now utterly to be despised. This, indeed, it could not easily have grasped then, when it had not yet attained better things. Furthermore, it fears no adversity while it is either joined to that One or beholds it. Finally, if it should happen that all other things around the soul were destroyed, it would approve of this, so that it might be alone with the One itself, so far has it now proceeded in a state of prosperous and sweet affection.

The Good itself is so far removed from any suspicion of multiplicity or changeability that the soul is compelled to cast off its "intellectual-ness" <note>original: "illoggentiam" - the state of being a discursive, logical being</note>, which is in some way similar to a manifold and changeable action. Chapter [XXXIV].

---

> *In this enjoyment, God Himself is the light which the soul beholds, and through which it beholds: for he is the light of light itself. But in the intellect, there is first an intuition and a contemplation: the former is direct, carried toward God, and soon becomes a contemplation of its own nature thus formed. In the former, it enjoys God above itself; in the latter, it enjoys itself. For the soul is also a unity superior to the intellect, through which it enjoys God by a certain vision that surpasses understanding.*

INDEED, the soul is then so affected according to its wish that it values the intellect as nothing; and even if it previously admired it, it now values it not at all. For it clearly knows that the intellect is a certain motion, whereas the soul itself does not wish to be moved. And yet it does not even declare that which it perceives to be the intellect, although the soul itself, having now become intellect, beholds it: inasmuch as it is entirely occupied within the intellect and established in the intelligible place. But being placed in it and having the intelligible around it, it surely understands. After it has seen that God, it leaves all things behind: just as if someone, having entered a house richly decorated in various ways, should consider the individual ornaments within and admire them before seeing the master of the house. <margin>B</margin> But after he has looked upon the master, who far surpasses the beauty of those images—seeing as he does not appear as some beautiful image, but as truly beautiful—he therefore admires him beyond measure. Leaving those objects behind, he gazes only on him for the future, and fixing his eyes more intently upon him, he no longer sees the visible object properly through the continuity of the act of seeing, but merges his vision with the visible, so that in that which was previously visible, the <margin>C</margin> vision now becomes the thing itself, while the other spectacles meanwhile escape him. Perhaps these likenesses would preserve the analogy and proportion if the one who met the beholder of the house were not a man, but a God: and this one were not visible to the sight, but one who filled the mind of the beholder from within.

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> ...nor rather by the Good: since even above all other things it stands, even if it were <unclear>k'</unclear>. Then it also has the ability to judge well, and that this is what it desires, and it is possible to grant grace to it: for that which is truly truer than truth, it happens to be that thing, and it speaks later, and speaks in silence, and what the soul has experienced <margin>B</margin> of affections. * But it does not speak of being tickled <note>original: γαργαλιζόμενον - physical titillation or stimulation</note>, but of becoming this, which it once was, but also all the other things which before it took joy in, either in powers, or wealth, or beauty, or knowledge, it speaks of these as being looked down upon, <margin>C</margin> not having met with better things then. [The soul fears] nothing it might suffer while with that one... the other things around itself, which it especially wishes, so that toward that one, it has come into such an experience.

By being so disposed, it somehow despises the act of thinking, which before it had time for, because thinking was a certain motion. But it does not wish to move, and that which it sees through that one, it says is not the intellect, although having become intellect, it beholds. Just as if it were in the intelligible place. But being in itself, or having the intellect around itself, it understands. But when it sees that God, it leaves all behind, <margin>B</margin> just as if someone entering into a house which is beautiful on the outside should behold each of the ornaments or admire them before seeing the master of the house. But seeing him—[who is the source] of the nature of the statues—and truly a sight, leaving those things, he looks only at him. Then looking and not looking away, he no longer beholds a spectacle through continuity, but merges his sight with the object. <margin>C</margin> So that in himself now the visible has become the sight. And all other spectacles are hidden. And perhaps the image would be preserved, if the one appearing to the beholder were not a man, but a certain God, or all of him appearing, but filling the soul...

# BOOK SEVEN.

<margin>\* and he possessed mind.</margin>
51. Or then the Mind <note>Greek: *nous*</note> has one power for thinking, by which it looks at the things within itself; and another power by which it looks at what is beyond it by a certain impulse and reception. By this latter intuition and perception, it formerly saw only, and by seeing, it later possessed intellect, and it exists. <note>original: "καὶ ἔνεστι καὶ ἔστιν"</note> And indeed, that first vision belongs to the sober mind, but this second is the **Mind in love**. When it becomes "foolish," <note>Plotinus uses "foolish" or "insane" here to mean moving beyond the constraints of cold, discursive logic</note> being drunk with nectar, then it becomes a lover, spreading itself out into a state of blissful well-being through its fullness. And <margin>\* he says majesty is the</margin> \* it is better for it to be drunk in this way than to be more "majestic" than such drunkenness. But does the Mind see one thing after another in turn? Not at all; though our teaching discourse introduces it as if it sees in turns so we may learn. But it always possesses its power of thinking. It also possesses a way of "not-thinking," but rather seeing that [Ultimate One] in another way. For while seeing that One, it conceived offspring within itself, and felt them. And as it sees these things now existing within it, it is said to "think." But it looked upon that One by the power through which it was destined to think. The soul, as if confusing and blurring the Mind remaining within her—or rather, her Mind sees first. But the vision also comes to the soul, and the two become one. The Good, having extended itself over them and harmonized with their dual nature, runs toward them and stands over them, giving them a blessed sense and vision. Because it is of such height, it is not in a place, nor in any other thing where things naturally exist—one inside another—for the One is everything in itself. The place of the intelligible is in it, but it is in no other. Therefore, the soul does not move then, because the One does not move; indeed, you are not truly a soul then, because you do not live in the ordinary sense, but rather you are above life. Nor are you "Intellect," because you no longer "think." For one must become like [the One]. And the mind "thinks" that One, in the sense that it does not think in a limited way.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It must be considered, therefore, that the intellect has a twofold power: one for understanding, through which it views its own internal things; the other, however, by which it looks up at higher things by a certain thrust of intuition and perception. Indeed, by this intuition and perception, it previously only saw, and through that seeing, it later received intellect and truly exists. Now, that former vision belongs to the healthy mind, but this latter is the **mind itself in love**. For when it "loses its mind," being deeply drunk with nectar, then it is seized by <margin>B</margin> love, pouring itself out into a blessed affection and sweetness through its satiety. And truly, for this mind, it is better to be occupied by this drunkenness than to live soberly and far removed from such a drink. But does that mind contemplate one thing first and another later? By no means; although for the sake of teaching, our discussion presents it as if it were contemplating things alternately. But the Intellect itself always exercises that act by which it understands in the proper sense; and again, in a proper sense, it does "not understand," <margin>C</margin> but looks upon God by another reason. Truly, while it beheld God, it conceived offspring within itself, and sensed them as they were born; and while it gazes upon these, it is said to "understand." But it looked up at God by that power through which it was afterwards to be an intellect. Hence, the soul, as if confounding and erasing the intellect remaining in it, looks up at God; or rather, the intellect itself looks first, but the vision is also passed on to the soul, and the two there become one. The Good itself, <margin>D</margin> propagating itself through these and applying itself to their constitution, flies over them, and joining the two into one, it hovers over them, granting a happy sense and a blessed contemplation. Furthermore, it raises these things to such a height that they are no longer in a place, nor in any other thing, in whatever condition one thing can be in another. For God himself is not "in" anyone. But the intelligible place is 

---

in him, while he himself exists in nothing at all. For this reason, the soul is not moved then, since he is not moved; therefore, the soul is not properly "soul" then, since it does not properly "live," because he does not properly live, but exceeds the function of living. Neither is it "intellect," since it does not think. For it must be made like [him]; and it "understands" not that one, since it does not even think.

->Chapter XXXVI.<-

> The **ladder** by which one ascends to the Principle has seven steps: first is the **purification** of the soul; second, the **knowledge** of divine works compared individually; third, the **contemplation of the order** by which lower works are led back to higher ones step by step; fourth, a certain **proportional comparison** which, from such order, brings itself to the divine order; fifth, **negation** <note>original: "negatio" - referring to apophatic theology, or defining God by what He is not</note> through which you separate everything you can conceive from the Principle; sixth, **supplicant prayer** to God, so that the Father of the intellectual world may make you an intellectual world in actuality (for this world is that world in potential from the beginning); seventh, so that when you have emerged as an intellectual world yourself, and are further moved by the **love of the Good**, you may be transformed from the intellectual state into the Good which is higher than intellect.

> Since the Good is far superior to the intellect, and therefore the enjoyment of it is not correctly called "intelligence," it seems it should not even be named "knowledge." For it is more natural and more desirable than knowledge. We call it, however, as best we can, sometimes "vision" because of its light and purity, and sometimes "touch" <note>original: "tactum"</note> because of the greatest union. It is also called "taste" because of the sweetness infused deeply into the soul there, nourishing it healthily and transforming it wonderfully for the better.

---

The other things are clear. Much has already been said about these matters; nevertheless, something more must be said now briefly, starting from that point and proceeding through arguments. \* Indeed, the knowledge of the Good itself, <margin>\* For the [knowledge] of the Good</margin> or rather its **touch**, is the greatest thing; and he says it is the "greatest lesson," <note>original: "megiston mathema" - a reference to Plato's *Republic* (505a)</note> or rather, that to see it is the same as the lesson—not that the Good itself is a lesson, but that one must first learn something about it. Therefore, analogies teach us...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> THE OTHER things indeed are clear. Something has also been said about this; nevertheless, something must be added now, beginning from that point and proceeding through arguments. For either the knowledge or the **touch** of the Good itself is undoubtedly something greatest: which study Plato called the "greatest," not indeed calling the Good itself a study, but rather a certain notice that precedes this intuition. Therefore, **analogies** (that is, proportions) teach us this...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the soul's mystical ascent. Having established that the "Good" (the One) is the source of all being, Plotinus now describes the final stages of the journey: how the soul moves beyond mere intellectual understanding into a direct, luminous union where the distinction between the observer and the observed disappears.</meta>

### PLOTINUS: ENNEAD VI.

<columns>
...certain harmonies; likewise negations; again, the knowledge of those things which arise from Him; finally, certain ascents proceeding duly by steps. We reach Him through purifications, prayers, and the worship that adorns the soul, through an ascent to the intelligible world <note>The realm of pure thought and forms, above the physical world</note>, and by persevering there. This occurs while the soul feeds upon the banquets of that world, becoming at once the spectator and the spectacle, both of itself and of others. Having become essence, and intellect, and the universal living being, the soul no longer looks upon the Good from the outside, but having finally become that, it now draws near to the Highest. That Highest is undoubtedly near at hand there, shining from above through the entire intelligible world. There, certainly, having set aside all learning, the soul is led this far and established in beauty; it understands as far as that in which it exists. But then, carried out from there as if by a certain wave of that same intellect, and lifted higher by the intellect itself as it swells and overflows, the soul suddenly perceives, though it knows not how. But this very intuition, filling the eyes with light, does not make them see something else by means of that light; rather, the light itself is the very thing that is seen. For in that state, there is not one thing that is visible and another that is its light, nor is there intellect and the object of intellect; instead, there thrives a law which generates things in succession, while allowing them to remain with itself. Yet that light alone exists, generating the intellect, and it is not extinguished by generating; rather, while the light remains, another thing follows from that which exists. For unless the light stood firm in this way, nothing else would subsist from it.

->Since Plotinus once defined intelligence as a reflexive act of a living essence dependent on the Good,<-
->seeking itself and its cause at once, and living both its own parts and itself by the merit of its cause,<-
->[it follows that] an intelligence of this kind requires aids. CHAPTER XXXVII.<-

Indeed, it seems that just as sight relates to light, so the intellect relates to the light of the Good; nevertheless, the intellect differs much more from the Good than sight does from light. In fact, by a vast height, the intellect seems a transgression of the Good, more so than sight is of light. Since, therefore, the intellect and the Good itself are so distinct, and are thus two natures, you are right when you first speak of the Good, so that you may preserve its simplicity; but when you speak of that which produces [the intellect], do not apply "intelligence" <note>In the sense of discursive or divided thought</note> to it, which indeed follows after essence and life. The Good, however, exceeds both, and is desired solely by reason and the grace of the Good. Nor yet is God without mind <note>The Latin *demens* suggests "mindless" or "insane" in a literal sense, but here means lacking the *nous* that characterizes lower levels of being</note>, for He is present to the mind; <margin>*</margin> nothing is hidden from Him through whom all things are made plain.

<margin>A</margin> WHOEVER, therefore, by their arguments have attributed intelligence <note>The Greek *nóēsis* refers to the act of thinking</note> to the highest principle of all things, have utterly taken away the knowledge of those lesser things which proceed from Him. Although this seems absurd to some—that God should in no way know other things—yet those people, finding nothing more excellent than Him, attributed the knowledge of Himself to Him. They did this as if He would become more venerable by the gift of intelligence, and as if the gift of intelligence were more excellent than the Principle itself, while the Principle simply exists as what it is; as if the Principle does not provide all dignity to intelligence, but receives it instead. Accordingly, it must be asked: from what source does God rather possess His dignity—from intelligence, or from Himself? If He acquires dignity through intelligence, then He certainly does not possess it through Himself, or He is less venerable. But if He possesses His own dignity through Himself, He is certainly perfect before intelligence, and does not become perfect by thinking. And if someone should say that since God is not a potentiality but an act, He must therefore think, we shall immediately distinguish thus: Either His essence is always thinking, or He is only the act of thinking. If His essence is always thinking...

# BOOK SEVEN.

### PAGE 729

<margin>* and by activity <note>original: "καὶ ὑπ' ἐνεργεία"</note></margin>
<margin>* and from itself <note>original: "καὶ ἐξ αὐτοῦ"</note></margin>
By speaking of "activity," they nonetheless speak of two things: essence and thinking. They do not present it as something simple, but they add something else to it, just as one is accustomed to adding "the act of seeing" to the eyes, even if they are not currently looking. * But if they say it is "activity," they mean that activity is also thinking. For wherever there is thinking, they perceive it, and from activity comes motion; and if there is motion, it moves. Where to? * And if that thing is said to be both "essence" and "activity," we must admit that these are many things, and these are different. But the First is simple. We grant "thinking" to that which comes from another, as if it were seeking its own nature and itself, or seeking what produced it. When it has turned toward that source in vision and knowledge, it then rightly becomes a "thinking" thing. But that which is neither produced nor has anything prior to itself, but always is what it is—what cause would it have for thinking? For this reason, Plato rightly says that the Supreme God is above Intellect. For an intellect that thinks of nothing is senseless. To that whose nature it is to think, if it does not perform its act, it is senseless; but to that which has no work to perform, why would anyone assign a "work" to it, and then misuse it by accusing it of not performing that act? It is as if one were to call someone "non-medical" when they have no medical work to do. No task is imposed upon Him to perform. For He is sufficient unto Himself, and one must seek nothing beyond Him, who exists above all things. He is sufficient for Himself and for others, being exactly what He is.

---

*Since essence and reason themselves are something else, and inferior to the reason of the Good, it is not correctly stated that "to be" applies to the Good. And if the Good, because of its supreme simplicity, composes nothing of itself as if speaking inwardly, it is nevertheless not obscure or internal to itself. For He Himself is the origin of certainty and the Father of lights. Chapter XXXVIII.*

---

<margin>* not in itself <note>original: "οὐκ ἀντῷ"</note></margin>
<margin>* nor even adding "itself" to it <note>original: "οὐδὲ τὸ τὸ προστιθέναι αὐτοῦ"</note></margin>
It "is," yet not even the word "is" belongs to it, for neither does this. He is "The Good" itself; it is not according to a certain time, but rather He is what He is. Not as one thing predicated of another, but as signifying what He is. We say "the Good" concerning Him, * speaking of Him. We do not predicate that goodness "belongs" to Him, but that He "is" it. For if we deem it right to say He "is" good, * we are not even adding "itself" to it. We show what we can, while we could take it away entirely so that we do not make Him "one thing and then another." We should not even use the word "is" anymore when we say "the Good." But who will demonstrate a nature that does not sense or know itself? Or will He not know "I am"? But there is no "He is" there; He will not say of the Good "I am." Or again, will He predicate "is" of Himself? But He will only say "the Good" without adding anything. For one might think of the Good as if it were unconditioned, unless it were predicated of something else. But he who thinks of himself as "the Good" will certainly think "I am the Good." If not, he will think of "the Good," but it will not happen that he thinks of himself as being this. It is necessary, then, that thinking exist,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
And for that reason, when they name "activity," they bring forward two things together: essence and intellect. They do not posit it as simple in this way, but they apply something else to it, just as they are accustomed to join "vision according to the act" to the eyes, even if they are always looking. But if they say that God is "in act" because He is activity and thinking, it follows that since He is thinking, He does not think, just as "motion" itself is not moved. <note>Plotinus uses a paradox here: if the Good is the very definition of "Thinking," it cannot "perform" thinking as a separate action, just as "Motion" doesn't have to "move" itself to be motion.</note>
<margin>B</margin>
But here someone will object to us: "Do you not also say that divine essence is activity?" We certainly admit that such things are many and diverse; but the First is entirely simple. We assign thinking to that which depends on another, through which it seeks, as it were, its own essence, itself, and its creator. By beholding that, it preserves itself; and thus, in seeing it, we certainly call it "intellect." But that which is neither made nor has anything else above it, but always exists as that very thing which it is—we do not see what occasion it would have for thinking. Therefore, Plato rightly placed the Supreme God above intellect. For an intellect, unless it thinks, is rightly judged "senseless." In a being whose nature requires thinking, if it does not think, it is justly considered "insane." But for one who has no work, what work can you assign to Him, so that you might then rightly object to the absence of this work, saying He is vacant from work and duty? It is just as if one said God was lacking the office of healing. We assign no work to God, because it is not fitting for God to "do" or "make": for He Himself is sufficient, nor is anything else beyond Him to be sought, as He exists above all things. He is sufficient both for Himself and for others, while He Himself exists as this very thing which He is.

---

<margin>A</margin>
FURTHERMORE, we ought not even predicate the word "is" <note>Latin: *est*</note> of God; for He does not need even this. For neither do we truly predicate of Him "God is good." Rather, that of which "is" is predicated, of that same thing "is good" is predicated. But to God, "is" itself belongs, not as if one thing were predicated of another, but as if it signified this very thing which He is. We speak of "the Good" concerning Him, not assigning something to Him, nor predicating it as if goodness were present in Him, but because He Himself exists as the Good.
<margin>B</margin>
Moreover, since we by no means think that "He is good" should be said of Him—nor that such a phrase as "this" or "that" should be placed before Him—and yet we are unable to express Him: if anyone, by taking everything away, were to be careful lest perhaps we make Him "one thing and another," then He truly does not need even this word "is." Thus we simply pronounce "the Good."
<margin>C</margin>
But who will admit a nature of this kind, neither sensing nor knowing itself in any way? What then? Will He at least know "I am"? But how so, since He "is" not in any categorical sense? Or perhaps He will say "I am good"? But again, He would thus be predicating "is" of Himself. But if He were to pronounce only "the Good," what can anyone say without this word which is called "is," unless perhaps he predicates "good" of something else? But he who knows himself to be good will certainly understand this very thing, namely, "I am good." Otherwise, he will indeed understand "the Good," but he will not achieve the understanding that he himself is this. It is necessary, therefore, if there is a thinking of the Good there, that it be of such a kind...

### PAGE 730

...that it is the good, so that it might understand. But if intelligence itself is the good itself, surely it will not be an intelligence of itself, but of the good; and indeed, it will not be the good itself, but rather the intelligence will be the good itself. If, however, the intelligence of the good is different from the good, it follows that the good already exists before its own intelligence. But if the good itself is by its own nature sufficient before intelligence—and it is certainly sufficient to itself as the good—it will in no way need intelligence of itself; therefore, by the very reason that it is the good, it by no means understands itself.

*In the first principle of things there is neither intelligence of self, nor of others: provided that intelligence is a cognition having certain conditions.*

### Chapter XXXIX.

*The first condition is that, along with stability, it must have something similar to motion. Second, that along with identity, it must have difference. Third, that you must discern by composing at the same time. Fourth, that the nature whose act is intelligence must be, while it is intellect, also the intelligible and the intellection <note>In Plotinian thought, "Nous" (Intellect) involves a triple identity: the thinker, the thought, and the act of thinking.</note>. Fifth, that it must also be "all-formed" <note>containing the forms of all things</note>, if indeed it is to perceive through this intelligence. Plotinus denies a perception of this kind—full of variety—in God <note>The One</note>, but he does not deny a simple certainty and light; likewise, he denies an action and providence that is different from goodness or that declines outward, yet he maintains that all things are produced from there and are providently disposed.*

IF God <note>The One</note> does not understand himself by the reason that he is the good, it may be asked: by what reason then does he? One might answer that nothing else is present to God, but that a simple intuition exists in him toward himself. Yet, since there is not, as it were, any interval there, nor any difference at all toward himself, this very thing which is said to be aimed at himself, or to intuit himself, is nothing other than himself. For this reason, where intellect and essence are, diversity rightly occurs. For it is necessary that when he is about to understand by forming the intellect, he must always admit difference and identity. For he will never discern himself from the "intelligible" <note>the object of thought</note> by some relation of a different nature toward it, nor will he understand all other things if no difference is present. Furthermore, so that all things are there together: even without the reason of diversity, there would not even be two things there. Moreover, if he understands, he will not understand only himself, if he understands at all; for what prevents him from understanding all things? Could it be that he is less able to understand other things than himself? Every being who understands himself becomes, by that fact, not simple; for it is necessary that the intelligence of oneself exists as something different, if one is to be able to understand oneself at all. But we have said that this is not intelligence unless one regards oneself as another. One who understands himself necessarily becomes multiple: the intelligible, the thinking subject, motion, and whatever else is adapted to the mind. Furthermore, as we have said elsewhere, it must be considered at present that any intelligence, if it is to be a true intellection, must be something varied; where, however, there is something entirely simple and the same, like a certain uniform motion—if it behaves just like a "touch"—it possesses no intellectual condition. What then? Will he know neither other things nor himself? And will he thus retain his dignity whole? Other things are certainly posterior to him, and he himself is that very thing which is before them. And the intellection of those things is adventitious <note>added from the outside</note>, and neither always the same, nor of things that remain; and even if he understands permanent things, he nonetheless becomes multiple. For it is not the case that posterior things possess essence alongside intellection, while the speculations of the first principle are merely empty. Accordingly, the rationale of providence is preserved because God himself is the one from whom all things are. But what is referred to him: how will God understand, unless he has understood himself, but instead has persisted so pure in his majesty?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...that I am good <note>original: "ὅτι ἀγαθόν ἐἰμι"</note>. And if thinking <note>original: "νόησις"</note> is the good, it will not be a thinking of itself, but that it is the good; but either the thinking is the good, or the thinking will be the good. Because it is before its own thinking. If the good is self-sufficient without thinking, it is sufficient unto goodness. It would have no need of thinking for itself.

<margin>A</margin> THEREFORE, insofar as it is good, it does not think itself. Nothing else is present to it, but it is for itself toward itself a certain... but without any interval. But the difference... to apply to itself, what would it be but... as it takes on otherness, which as... the intellect again [takes] otherness and sameness... if it shall think. For both itself... <margin>B</margin> by the intelligible, by the otherness toward it... all these things will be present, with no otherness... to be all things. But... then if it shall think, which indeed... itself, if it shall think at all. For why... will it be unable? In general, simply... itself. But how thinking... being other, if at all... <margin>C</margin> We were saying that thinking is this... if it should wish to see, and having thought itself, [it becomes] many: intelligible, thinking, moving, and all other things [pertaining] to the mind. In addition to these, one must also see that which has already been said in other places, that each thinking, if it is to be thinking, must be something varied... simple and the same, entirely as a motion... would be like a touch. It does not have an intellectual [quality]. <margin>D</margin> But it will not even know itself, but... [will it lose its dignity]? Other things are posterior to it... of them which it was. And the [knowledge] of them is acquired... not the same always. And if it has [knowledge] of standing things... it is many. For that which... along with thinking also the essence... the thinkings of these, empty contemplations... and providence [is] enough in being itself... all. But that [which is] toward itself, how, if not... <margin>E</margin> it shall stand in majesty? He was saying then...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into why the First Principle—often called "The One" or "The Good"—transcends both Being (Essence) and Thought (Intelligence). Plotinus argues that while "Intelligence" is the highest form of Being, the source of that Being must be even simpler and more "venerable" than thought itself.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN.

### PAGE 731

...speaking about essence, he says that it either understands, or it is that which is held as venerable. It is as if essence itself thinks, while we hold that which is not understood as venerable; this is because he could not explain it otherwise, considering that which transcends thinking to be even more venerable than that which is simply "venerable" <note>original: "σεμνὸν" (semnon) - meaning august, holy, or venerable. Plotinus is interpreting Plato's use of this word to describe the First Principle.</note>.

AND since it is not necessary for intelligence to be present in him [the First], if it were necessary to attach something to him, one might say he brings what is worthy to these stated things, but not through shared feeling, since he signifies by reason. But it must be by a state [of being], mixed with necessity. Therefore, one must know and understand that all intelligence is *from* something and *of* something. And while intelligence consists of that from which it comes, it has no underlying subject, for it is itself the act of intelligence.
<margin>* adverb</margin> Just as an "action" <note>original: "ἐνέργεια" (energeia)</note> is placed upon it, being its own activity and fulfilling that which was potential, it knows nothing of itself; for it is only that which it is, like a perfection. But then intelligence, existing with essence and giving substance to essence, cannot be in that from which it was made; or if it were, it would have produced nothing. But where the power of knowing is, it arises by itself. <margin>* that which exists together in essence</margin> Its activity is intelligence. <gloss>* that which exists together in essence</gloss> And intelligence is not something different from essence itself. And this Nature <note>The second principle, the Divine Mind or Nous</note> understands itself. It is not something different, except in the way that the thing known and the thing thinking are distinguished by reason, being a plurality, as has often been shown. This itself is the first activity, becoming a foundation like essence, being at once the image of another; it is the image of something so great that it is called essence. But if it were from that source, yet nothing else of that source were in it except that it belonged to it, it would not be a substance in itself. Since this is the first activity and the first intelligence, it would have neither an activity nor an intelligence prior to itself. Therefore, if one passes beyond this essence and intelligence, one will reach essence, but not by thinking. Instead, one will go beyond essence and intelligence to something wonderful, which contains within itself neither essence nor intelligence, but is solitary by itself, needing nothing of those things that come from it. For if an acting being existed before, it would have generated the action. Or if it had already thought, then nothingness would have existed before thinking; for altogether, if intelligence is of the Good, it is lesser than the Good. Thus it would belong to the Good—I say "of the Good," not because the Good does not exist (for let that be granted), but because in the Good itself there would be no intelligence, or the name "the Good" would be one thing, and the intelligence of it would be something lesser than it.

<column-break/>

Plotinus, speaking of essence, says: essence will indeed understand, but the most venerable itself will not exist for that reason. It is as if essence understands, but that which does not understand is able to stand as the most venerable. In these words, Plato says "to exist" or "to consist," because he was otherwise unable to express it. But he [Plato] considered that which transcends intelligence to be truly august and venerable.

*He considers every action to both belong to someone and to be directed toward something else: soon he wishes intelligence to be an action: then he considers essence to be the foundation of action and intelligence. He rightly denies action, intelligence, and essence to the first principle, because it neither underlies an act nor is it turned toward another in any way. If, once Goodness itself is established, you immediately attribute intelligence to it, you must think it either differs not at all or by some degree. If it differs not at all, you name intelligence there in vain; if it differs by some degree, then by mixing it with the supreme Good, you make it a "lesser good." Let Goodness itself, therefore, not be intelligence properly speaking, but let it be the light, certainty, and truth consisting in itself, which is the cause of intelligence: into which the whole effort of intelligence is directed as its highest and most desirable goal. Finally, Goodness is such a great power that intelligence, which exists as its first image, is the first substance.*

### Chapter XL.

<margin>A</margin> ONE WILL BE ABLE TO KNOW that it is not necessary for intelligence to exist around the First Principle, if one has touched upon such a thing. It is better, however, to apply certain persuasions to the higher things, so that we may signify what we wish with words. It is necessary, indeed, to mix logical necessity with probable persuasion. It must first be noticed that all intelligence exists both *from* something and *of* something. And indeed, it adheres to that from which it comes; <margin>B</margin> it has that which it understands as its subject, and it is itself like something inherent, an act of that subject, filling its potential while generating nothing in the meantime. For it belongs only to that of which it is, as if it were a certain perfection. But the intelligence which exists with essence, and through which the subsistence of essence consists, cannot be in that from which it was made: otherwise, if it were in it, it would have generated nothing. But since it is a certain power of generating, it generated within itself, <margin>C</margin> and its action is essence, and it coexists in essence. Nor are intelligence and essence different there: but this nature understands itself, not as something different, except by reason alone; there, that which is understood and that which understands are one, although there is a certain plurality, as has already been frequently demonstrated. Now indeed, this very act is the first action generating substance into essence. And since it is an image of another, it is the image of one so high that it is also essence. But if it were of that [higher source], yet nothing else were in it except that it was of it, it would not be a substance in itself. <margin>D</margin> Since, therefore, this is the first action and the first intelligence, it surely has no action or intelligence above itself. Whoever, therefore, transcends this essence and intellection will proceed beyond essence and intelligence; he will ascend beyond essence and intelligence to something wonderful: which admits within itself neither essence nor any intellection at all: but consists alone and pure in itself, needing nothing of those things which are from it. For <margin>E</margin> an acting being did not first generate action: otherwise, an act would already exist before the act itself arose. Nor did a thinking being generate intelligence: otherwise, it would have understood before intelligence was born. Altogether, indeed, if intelligence is of the Good, it is something lesser than the Good. Therefore, it is not the Good itself. I say "not of the Good itself," not because the Good cannot be understood (for let this be granted for the present), but because in the Good itself there is no intellection: otherwise, the Good itself and that which is lesser than the Good—that is, the intelligence of it—will be one and the same.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the First Principle (the Good) must transcend thought and essence because thinking requires a subject and an object, which implies a division or plurality that cannot exist in a perfectly simple source. He defines Intelligence as the "first image" or "first act" of the Good, which contains plurality and essence, whereas the Good itself is a self-sufficient "light" beyond being.</summary>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

### PAGE 732

If, however, there were something inferior, then intellection and essence would exist together. But if the Good itself is more excellent than intelligence, then both intelligence and the "intelligible" <note>the object of thought</note> will simultaneously be inferior to it; thus, intellection will not exist within the Good. Rather, because intellection is something inferior, and for that reason stands in awe of the majesty of the Good, it surely dwells apart from the Good, leaving the Good to remain free from it, just as it remains free from all other things. Truly, since the Good is pure of intellection, it exists as quite sincerely what it is, hindered by no presence of thought from being entirely one and pure. If <margin>B</margin> someone should imagine this [the Good] as being both a thinker and that which is thought at the same time, combining essence and intelligence as if they were conspiring together, and should strive to depict the Good as thinking itself, such a person would certainly require yet another principle higher than that one. For indeed, the act of intelligence is either the perfection of another subject, or if it is—so to speak—a kind of "co-subsistence" <note>existing together in a single substance</note>, it still has another nature preceding itself, by whose power it rightly possesses the ability to understand. Now, it possesses the capacity to understand precisely because <margin>C</margin> there is something else above it. Furthermore, when it understands itself, it then recognizes, as it were, what it previously brought back from a certain gaze upon another. But as for that which has nothing higher than itself, and in which nothing exists from another—what would it understand? Or in what way would it understand itself? Indeed, if it were to turn toward itself in the act of understanding, what would it be seeking? Or what would it desire? Would it be striving to measure how great its own power is? If so, that power would be outside itself insofar as it understands it. I say this because the power would be one thing while it is being learned, and another thing while it is being spoken. But if it is entirely one, what is there to search for?

->Sight was created and it strives to capture light; light, therefore, has no need of sight. In the same way, neither does the Good have need of<-
->intellect, which is merely an act that by its nature strives only to receive the light of the Good.<-

### Chapter XLI.

> *If you say that the Good itself understands, it either gains nothing by understanding (and thus understands in vain), or if it was the Good beforehand, and its self-understanding contributes to this very fact—that it might count its own internal parts and be reconciled to itself—then a being that is most simple has no need of intelligence. Where you have placed intellect at the highest point in the order of knowledge, you do not add reason, imagination, sense, or the eye, lest you also add darkness alongside the best. Similarly, when you have granted the immense light of the most sufficient Good, which is the goal of intelligence, you ought not to apply these things to it.*

<margin>A</margin> It seems that the gift of understanding was granted to divine natures (though not to the primary ones) for the sake of assistance, added like an eye to those who were, by their own nature, as if blind. If the eye itself were the light, it would in no way need to look upon a being as if it were light. But that which has need, being dark within itself, seeks the light through the eye. If, therefore, the effort of intelligence seeks light, and light does not seek light, then surely the primary nature—since it does not desire light—does not even desire to understand. Therefore, you must not <margin>B</margin> attach intelligence to this principle; for you will gain nothing by it. And if either the soul or the intellect strives to attach it, it is because it itself needs the help of intelligence that it is led to understand. Therefore, the Good neither perceives itself (for it has no need of this), nor is it a duality; rather, if intellection were there, it would be more than two. For the Good is not itself intellection. It would additionally be necessary for a third thing to be present: namely, the object being understood. But if the intellect, the intellection, and the intelligible were exactly the same thing, they would be entirely merged and confounded. And if they were distinguished, so that one thing and another were there, again they could not be the first principle. Therefore, in considering the best nature, it is necessary to set aside all other things entirely.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> If it is inferior, intellection and [essence] will be together. But if intellection is better, the intelligible will be inferior... intellection is not in the Good, but rather inferior... having been deemed worthy of the Good, since that which is pure, just as those things of negation, is pure of intellection and is what it is. To what is it hindered? As if it were not pure and one. <margin>B</margin> Someone who fashions the act of thinking and the object thought together, or joins intellection with essence, then fashions another thing; but this will also require another. Since the activity and the intellection are either the perfection of a subject, or a co-subsistence, or [from another], it too has another nature through which it rightly possesses the act of understanding. For that which has the act of understanding has it because something else is before it. Thus, it turns to itself, as if by an addition, <margin>C</margin> possessing the view of another within itself. But regarding that which is before it, what use is there for intellection, or how would it know itself? For what would it seek? Its power, however great it is, itself... * of them, according to which it understood. I say both that the power was it, and it learned what it learned. But if it is one, what does it seek?

<margin>A</margin> The aid [of intellect] is at risk of being for divine natures—for those natures that follow—as a kind of eye for those that are blind. But if the eye is light itself, it does not need light, being light itself. But if it needs to see, having darkness within itself, it seeks light. Intellection is light. But light does not seek light. The Good itself, not seeking light, will not seek to understand. It is not fitting for it to understand. For what would <margin>B</margin> one add to it by needing it? And so that it may understand, it does not even perceive itself. Nor is it two, but rather more or many... since intellection is [in] it. It must be a third... If on the other hand it is intellect, intellection, and the intelligible, these being joined will vanish into themselves. Because that which is other would again not be that [first principle]. One must therefore [set aside] all other things in this nature...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the First Principle (the Good) transcends thought because thinking implies a lack or a desire for light, whereas the Good is the source of light itself. To attribute intellect to the Good would be to introduce division and duality into a being that must be absolutely simple and unified.</summary>
