<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 732 regarding Ennead VI, specifically focusing on why the supreme principle (the One or the Good) does not possess "Intellect" or "Self-Knowledge" in the way lower beings do. Plotinus is interpreting Plato’s dialogues to establish a hierarchy of existence.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN

<column-break/>

<margin>* For you could not add to it</margin>
...indeed, as it stands in need of no assistance. <margin>*</margin> For you could not add to it—or rather, you would diminish it by the addition—since its nature is without want. To us, indeed, the act of understanding is a beautiful thing, because the soul needs to possess intellect; it is even beautiful for the Intellect itself, because for the Intellect, "being" and "understanding" are the same thing, and its own intellection has brought it into existence. It is therefore advantageous for the Intellect to be joined with understanding, and to always be conscious of itself—to perceive, that is, that the "two" there <note>The thinker and the object being thought of</note> are actually one. But if a thing were strictly One <note>Plotinus's term for the absolute source</note>, it would certainly be sufficient unto itself, and would have no need <margin>B</margin> to receive anything into itself. Now, as for that famous command, "Know thyself," it only applies to those who, because of the "multiplicity" inherent in them, are driven to count their own parts. They must learn how many and what kind of things they possess, for they either do not know their whole selves, or perhaps nothing at all; they do not know what holds the primary place or by what standard they truly exist. But if <margin>C</margin> there is something that is singularly One, it is more excellent than if it "knew" or "understood" or "perceived" itself; for it is not even "itself" to itself <note>The One is so simple it doesn't even have the division of 'self' looking at 'self'.</note>. It introduces nothing into itself, but is undoubtedly sufficient as it is. Therefore, it is not "the Good" for itself, but rather for others. All other things stand in need of it, but it does not need itself; that would be ridiculous, for it would then be "needy" of itself. Nor does it look upon itself; for such an act of looking would require that something be "becoming" or "happening" within it. It seems he [Plotinus] easily grants all these functions to the things that follow after the One, appearing to say that nothing belonging to other things is <margin>D</margin> present in it—just as essence <note>In the sense of 'defined being'</note> is not present in it. Therefore, intellection is not there either; for if essence and intelligence run together, and both are the primary and principal form of understanding, then "Being" and "Thinking" conspire as one. For these reasons, Plato says that neither speech, nor sense-perception, nor scientific knowledge can be had of the First Principle: because, quite clearly, nothing can be predicated of it as if it were an added attribute.

---
->There are three primary principles of things: the Good, the First Mind, and the World Soul. Just as the affections and the individual members of the world should not be placed within the World Soul from which they were born, nor should the shifting discourses and domestic affections of the soul be placed in the Intellect—so, finally, the species of intelligence (which depend properly on the Intellect) must not be attributed to the Good. Chapter 42.<-
---

<margin>A</margin> But truly, when you are in doubt about these matters and ask where these things are best placed—your reason having been drawn toward these heights—reject those very things you consider honorable in secondary beings. Do not apply secondary things to the First, nor third-tier things to the secondary. Rather, place the secondary things "around" the First, and the third-tier things "around" the second. In this way, you will allow each thing to remain as it is in itself, while the following things hang suspended from them, as if spreading out everywhere around them, while those higher things remain stable in themselves. <margin>B</margin> For this reason, it is rightly written by Plato: "All things are around the King of all; all things are for his sake; he is the cause of all beautiful things." When he says "all things," he understands all existing beings. <margin>C</margin> He adds "for his sake" with good reason, because he is the cause of those things that indeed desire him, as one who is different from all things, possessing nothing that belongs to them. Otherwise, he would not be "beyond all things" if any of those things that come after him happened to be in him. If, therefore, the Intellect is counted among the number of "all things," then rightfully, Intellect is not in him. Furthermore, where he calls him the Cause, he means the God of beautiful things...

He interprets Plato's "King of All" as the source around which all other levels of reality—Intellect and Soul—are organized.</summary>

### ON the voluntary and the will of the One.
### ON the liberty & will of the One.

> That which is voluntary in our case is that which we do by our own free and certain will. Free, meaning with no violence <note>no external compulsion</note>. Certain, meaning not falling into error through any ignorance; regarding such things, we are truly masters. Chapter I.

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap V in a square border, showing a figure with a staff in a pastoral landscape with trees.</image-desc>IS IT appropriate to inquire even regarding the Gods whether anything is placed within their free choice <note>original: "arbitrio"</note> or not, or is it rather more fitting to ask such a thing regarding humans on account of our weakness and doubtful capacity? It must be conceded that the Gods can do all things: and that not only is "something" placed within their choice, but everything. Or perhaps should we attribute all power and the free choice of all things to the One alone? Among the others, some things behave in this way, and others in that way: and in some, one might assert that both reasons apply equally. Or rather, should these things also be investigated: we must even dare to inquire into the primary things, and into that which is above all else, to track such a quality. Namely, in what sense we should accept what is commonly said—that things are placed within their choice—even though we concede they can do all things. Furthermore, regarding this "being able" <note>original: "posse", referring to power or potential</note> which we mention, we must rightly consider how it is spoken of, lest perhaps by speaking thus we admit that among the Gods "power" <note>original: "potentia"</note> is one thing and "act" <note>original: "actu"</note> is another: and perhaps we might be conceding an act that is only to be in the future. But these matters should be deferred for later, and first the same must be investigated within ourselves, regarding whom it is usually asked whether anything is placed within our own choice. First, therefore, we must ask what this very thing should be called which is said to be "in us," that is, constituted in our own choice. We must seek what the definition of this faculty is: for in this way it will be known, in a certain sense, whether it [applies] also to the Gods...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap Alpha (Α) in a square border, showing a tall classical tower and buildings in a landscape.</image-desc>IS IT also possible to inquire concerning the gods whether anything is "up to them" <note>original: "ἐπ’ αὐτοῖς", meaning within their power or agency</note>, or does our own human weakness and the uncertainty of our power make us ask this? Should we grant that the gods can do all things? And is it not just "something," but actually "everything" that is up to them? Or should we say <margin>B</margin> that all power and the being "up to itself" of all things belongs to the One more than all? And for the others, some things are one way, some another: and for all, both ways? Or must this too be investigated? We must dare to inquire even of the things above, and the One above all, how we say something is "up to him," even if we grant he can do all things. And yet this "being able," we must see how it is said, lest we should say that one part is "potentiality" and another "actuality." And the act as something to come. <margin>C</margin> But let these things be postponed for the present. First, let us look at ourselves, regarding whom it is customary to inquire whether anything happens to be "up to us": and we must seek what exactly we mean when we say "to be up to us" <note>original: "ἐφ’ ἡμῖν εἶναι"</note>. For such a thing is a certain concept. First, then, how might it be known, if it is also among gods, and among...

...whether it is more fitting to transfer these matters to God himself, or not. **A** Or rather, while it may be fitting, we must nevertheless investigate how something can be said to be "in the power" <note>original: ἐφ' ἡμῖν (eph' hēmin) — a technical term in Greek philosophy for what is within our control or free will</note> of both others and especially the supreme beings. What, then, do we have in mind when we say something is "in our power"? And for what reason do we inquire into this? I believe that when we are tossed about by contrary fortunes, compelled by adverse necessities, and snatched away by the violent attacks of passions that besiege the soul, we begin to think that all **B** these things have mastery over us. Serving them, and being hurried along wherever they lead, we deservedly fall into this controversy, fearing that perhaps we ourselves have no power, and nothing rests in our own authority. We speak as if "in our power" would be that state where, at some time, we are slaves neither to fortunes, nor necessities, nor violent passions, but act by our own will, with nothing in the meantime opposing that will. If this is the case, then the definition of what consists in our "free choice" <note>Latin: arbitrio</note> will be of this sort: **C** namely, that which serves the will, and exists (or does not exist) only insofar as we ourselves will it. Now, that is "voluntary" <note>Latin: voluntarium</note> which is performed both without violence and with knowledge. But that which is "in us"—that is, in our power—is that which we ourselves are the masters of performing. Yet these two often coincide, even though their definitions differ. Sometimes, however, they seem to disagree: for instance, if someone has the power and authority to kill a man, yet it is not "voluntary" for him after he has done it, **D** if he did not know that the man he killed was his father. Perhaps, however, this very thing called "voluntary" will never be at odds with the will of one who possesses true "free choice." It is certainly necessary that the knowledge of what is called "voluntary" be held not only regarding individual circumstances, but entirely and simply. Tell me, why should it be judged an involuntary homicide if one is ignorant that the man was a father or a friend, yet if one is ignorant that killing is wrong, it is not also judged involuntary? But if it is argued that such a homicide is not considered involuntary because one *ought* to have learned this, certainly it is not "voluntary" to be ignorant of what one ought to have learned, or even of that which prevents one from learning.

<note>This right-hand column continues the same argument, mirroring the Greek text on the left.</note>

**A** ...it is more fitting to transfer these things to God himself, or not. Or rather, it may be proper, but it must be investigated how something is placed in their choice, both in others and in the supreme beings. What indeed do we think when we say something is in our power? For what reason do we ask this? **B** Tossed by contrary fortunes (as I believe), and driven by adverse necessities, and snatched by the violent incursions of perturbations <note>passions or emotions</note> occupying the mind, we have surely thought that all these things now have command over us. Serving them, and precipitated wherever they pull, we have rightly fallen into this controversy, fearing that perhaps we are not in our own power, and nothing consists in our authority. It is as if this would be in our power: that which, at some point serving neither fortunes, nor necessities, nor violent perturbations, we might both act by will, and nothing meanwhile opposes the will. If this is so, the logic of that which consists in our power will be of this kind: **C** namely, that it serves the will, and to that extent either is or is not, insofar as we ourselves will. Now truly, the voluntary is that which is performed both without violence and with knowledge; but "in us"—that is, in our power—is that for which we ourselves are the masters of the acting. And yet both of these often concur, although their logic is different; sometimes they truly seem to disagree. Just as if someone had the mastery and authority to slay a man, and yet it was not voluntary for him after he did it, **D** if he did not know that the one he killed was his father. Perhaps indeed this very thing which is called voluntary will never be discordant from the power of him who has true choice. It is certainly necessary that knowledge of this which is called voluntary be had not only concerning particulars, but altogether and simply. Tell me, why if he is ignorant that he is a father or friend, is the homicide judged involuntary? But if he is ignorant that homicide is not fitting, should it not also be deemed involuntary? But if it is said that this homicide is not considered involuntary because he ought to have learned this, surely it is not voluntary to be ignorant of what he ought to have learned, or even that which prohibits him from learning.

> *We do not act as if truly free or masters of our action insofar as we act according to a movement of the soul incited through the senses and the affections of the senses by external bodies, or even by our own body. Now, with the movement thus incited, reason either does nothing, or is led by the movement, or leads. In the first and second degree we are slaves of the body and of fortune; in the third, however, we seem to govern the body and similar things with a certain authority, yet we obey and live for others, indulge necessity, and do not live with that tranquility which we wish. Therefore, we are not altogether free and masters.*

BUT we must investigate this: what exactly is that which is referred to us as being "in our power," and to what faculty should we specifically attribute it? Should we give it to impulse <note>Latin: impetus</note> and some kind of appetite <note>desire</note>, such as that which is done through anger or lust? Or should we attribute it to the reasoning <note>Latin: ratiocinationi</note> regarding what is beneficial, joined with appetite, whether something is done or not done? But if we attribute it to anger and lust—which children and beasts also have—what shall we say is "in their power"? And what of those who are mad, or out of their minds, or affected by drugs, or occupied by sudden hallucinations over which they are not masters? But if we grant it to reasoning joined with appetite, we must ask if this applies even when the reasoning is mistaken.

**A** IT REMAINS to investigate this very thing: that which is referred to us as being in us, to what should we most especially attribute it? Truly, if we attribute it to anger and concupiscence, we shall be forced to admit, consequently, that children **B** also, and beasts, and those who are raging and entirely alienated in mind—likewise those irritated by poisons and occupied by incident imaginations—have the gift of "free choice," even though they cannot be masters of those things we have related. # PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin> Is it the case that this power belongs even to a reasoning that goes astray, or rather only to right reason and right desire? Furthermore, someone might ask here whether reasoning produces desire, or vice versa, whether desire produces reasoning. For if desires are according to nature, we may distinguish them thus: if they belong to the animal—that is, the composite of body and soul—then the soul will surely follow the necessity of nature. But if they belong to the soul alone, many things which are now said to consist "within us" <note>original: "ἐφ’ ἡμῖν" (eph' hēmin) — a technical term for what is in our power or under our control</note> will be seen to occur outside of its control. Moreover, a certain bare reasoning often precedes our feelings; likewise, the imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note> itself can be compelling, and desire draws us where necessity demands—in what way, then, are we masters in these matters? Again, how are we masters of that by which we are led? For that which <margin>B</margin> is in want, desiring of necessity to be filled, is clearly not the master of that toward which it is entirely drawn. Finally, how can there be any "free choice" <note>original: "arbitrium"</note> in that which depends on another, and has its beginning in something else? And from that source, whatever it may be, the effect is produced. <margin>C</margin> Certainly, it lives according to that source, and it lives in such a way as it was formed; otherwise, if this were said to have free choice, then even inanimate things would be granted the same. For even fire acts just as it was generated.

<margin>D</margin> But if it is said that there is a difference because the animal and the soul know what they are doing, we must distinguish further: if they know it through sensation, what condition is added here to achieve the result that they act by free choice? For sensation, being merely perceptive, does not make one the master of the action. But if it is said that something is done freely by some other knowledge beyond sensation, it will further be asked whether that knowledge is merely of what is being done—in which case it would be proved that here, too, one only "knows," but is led by another to the act. But if, besides desire, reason or a certain knowledge acts and dominates, we must investigate to what it primarily refers, and generally where and how this happens. And if reason itself produces another desire, we must understand how it does so. But if someone "calls upon reason" within themselves by calming desire, and places free choice in this state, then surely it will not reside in action, but in stillness; for whatever is involved in acting—even if reason prevails—has a certain mixed quality and does not possess that pure function of choice by which it could be judged to be truly "within us."

> *Just as there are two degrees of servitude, so there are two of liberty; however, there is one that is a middle ground between the two. Chapter I.*
> *A slave is one who follows imagination alone, incited by our body or by external bodies, whose reason also entirely indulges this imagination. Free, in the first sense, is the one who lives content with the mind alone, having entirely neglected all other things. Free, in the second sense, is the one who, if he does anything further, chooses only those things from contemplation according to the laws, and refers the things to be done to that example. He seems to be a mixture of a certain liberty and servitude; he subjects his reason to right reason, but chooses the active life (otherwise an honorable one) as an end.*

<margin>A</margin> We must, therefore, consider these things diligently. For now we are approaching that which seemed to be asked concerning the Gods: specifically, when we referred this very thing which is "within us"—that is, free choice—primarily to the Will; then we placed this in Reason; and after this, in Right Reason. Perhaps it is fitting to add: in Right Reason, I say, which includes knowledge <note>original: "scientiam"</note>. For if someone acts having formed a right opinion, he does not yet seem to have an indisputable free choice unless <margin>B</margin> he knows *why* he has such a right opinion; rather, he might seem to have happened upon what is appropriate through a certain imagination. Indeed, since we do not grant that the imagination is entirely placed within our choice, we rightly...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...to reasoning, or to right reasoning, or to desire. And yet here also someone might ask whether reasoning works upon desire, or desire upon reasoning. For if the desires are according to nature, on the one hand as the animal and the composite, then the soul would follow the necessity of nature. But if they belong to the soul alone, many of the things now said to be "up to us" would then come from elsewhere. <margin>B</margin> Furthermore, what is bare reason before the passions, or what is the imagination that compels, or what is the desire, toward which nature has come—how are we sovereign in these? Or sovereign at all, over that by which we are led? For that which is in need, desiring fulfillment, is led by that toward which it is entirely drawn. How could that which is "up to it" reside in itself, when it is with another? For how it is, and from where it has become what it is, and how it lives, <margin>C</margin> is how it has been fashioned. Or should the soul of the animal have what is "up to itself" in this way? Or would it belong to all things, even fire, just as it was generated? But if it is because the animal and the soul perceive what it does—if it is sensation, what is the addition toward it being "up to itself"? For sensation has not "made" the thing that works, or not alone. But if it is knowledge—if it will only know, then it does not follow that it is "up to it" just because it knows. Something else is that which leads. But if, besides desire, knowledge <margin>D</margin> produces and masters, one must ask toward what this is directed. And generally where this happens. But if one produces another desire, how? Or indeed, if one stops the desire and it is at rest in us, it will not be in the act, but will be the "up to us" elsewhere; since everything in action, even if reason masters it, is something mixed and cannot have the "up to us" in a pure way.

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, these things must be considered. For we are already becoming close in our argument to what we brought up concerning the gods; having first placed what is "up to us" in the will, then in reason, then in right reason, and perhaps we should add "with knowledge." For it is not the case that if someone held a right opinion, or acted on it, he would perhaps have an indisputable "voluntary" act, if he did not know *why* it was right, but was led <margin>B</margin> toward what is necessary by some imagination. Since we say that imagination is not "up to us."

Plotinus distinguishes between acting by mere imagination or sensation, which he deems a form of servitude, and acting from pure contemplation or intellect.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of free will, specifically distinguishing between actions driven by bodily impulses (imagination) and those governed by the higher Intellect (Mind).</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

<column-break/>

Those who act upon these [bodily impressions], how could we ever place them in the category of self-authority <note>original: "αὐτεξούσιον" (autexousion) — a Greek term for being the master of one's own power</note>? For we define imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note>—specifically that which is properly called imagination—as that which is stirred up by the affections of the body. For the emptying of food or drink, or the fullness of it, shapes the imagination in different ways; and someone full of reproductive seed will imagine things differently than one who is exhausted. In short, according to the various qualities of the humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) thought to determine health and temperament</note> in the body, quite diverse imaginations are incited.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, those who act through such imaginations, we do not place at the starting point of free action. For this reason, even when the wicked do many things according to these imaginations, we will not grant them free authority over their actions, nor will we call their deeds voluntary. But to the one who acts through the mind, free from all the passions of the body, we will undoubtedly grant free choice. Thus, we reduce this very power of free action back to a most beautiful principle, referring it primarily to the activity of the mind. Furthermore, we shall confess that the propositions and deliberations that proceed from there, as well as the desires <note>original: "appetitiones"</note> stirred up by intelligence, are truly free. We shall also say that the gods, who live in this manner—whoever lives by the mind and by a desire that follows the mind—possess this kind of liberty.

->*Since the nature of liberty consists in a certain free motion, and all things are turned toward what is willed and what is good, the intellect proceeds with a free and voluntary motion when it moves toward its own true good by acting and governing.*<-

---
### Chapter IV.
---

<margin>C</margin> Furthermore, if the intellect understands, wills, chooses, and acts according to its own nature, it is not said to be compelled for that reason, because this very thing is primarily voluntary for it. It is not led to this by anything external; nor should intellectual action be said to "serve" its intellectual nature. For there, the action is the nature itself, and it is not compelled by the Good, which is entirely internal to it. Since this very thing called "existing by one's own right" is to be willed by reason and by the grace of the Good, the intellect—which is closest to the Supreme Good—is most of all in possession of its own right.

<margin>A</margin> **HOWEVER**, someone might inquire from this point: in what way can that which is produced by desire be free? For desire leads toward something external and possesses a sense of lack. For that which desires is being "led," even if it is led toward the Good. Furthermore, we must doubt the mind in the same way: if it acts according to what it is and how it was naturally designed, can it simultaneously be said to possess liberty and the principle of acting within itself, when it is not in its power *not* to act?

Moreover, it is worth questioning: <margin>B</margin> among those to whom action does not belong, is "free choice" properly considered to exist? And for those to whom action does belong, necessity is often introduced from the outside; for they do not act entirely at random or without any purpose. But in what way will liberty be preserved for those who serve their own nature?

On the contrary, one might object: How can that which is not forced to follow another be said to serve? In what way can something be "coerced" while it is being carried toward the Good, <margin>C</margin> since the desire itself is voluntary if it recognizes that it is proceeding toward the Good? For the "involuntary" is a certain abduction away from the Good itself. Something is said to be "coerced" and "compelled by violence" when it is carried toward that which is not its own good. That thing properly "serves" which does not have the authority to proceed toward the Good, but is led away from its own goods by some more powerful force standing over it, serving that force in the meantime. For this reason, servitude is condemned—not indeed where someone lacks the license to go toward evil, but where they are unable to reach their own good, being dragged meanwhile toward the good of another.

<sig>Qq 3</sig>

<summary>Plotinus argues that true free will exists only in the Intellect (Mind), whereas actions driven by bodily "imaginations" or humors are a form of servitude. He clarifies that acting according to one's own nature toward the Good is the highest form of liberty, not a form of compulsion.</summary>
<keywords>free will, self-authority, imagination, phantasia, intellect, bodily humors, voluntary action, the Good, servitude vs. liberty</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of free will, shifting from the human soul's impulses to the absolute freedom of the "Simple Nature" (the Intellect) and how virtue interacts with external circumstances.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

...to serve its own nature. That makes it a duality: both that which serves and that to which it serves. But a simple nature, being a single act—not having one part in potentiality <note>The state of being able to become something</note> and another in actuality <note>The state of actually being that thing</note>—why should it not be free? Indeed, it is not even proper to say it is "born" to operate in this way: for we should not even say that the "operating" within it is one thing and its essence is another, since there, "to be" and "to act" are the same. If, therefore, it does not exist or act for the sake of another, nor is it contained in another, what prevents it from living freely? And even if it is not fitting to say "it is within its own power" in the same way we say it of others, nevertheless there is something greater here than what is meant by "being in itself." For it is considered to be in itself because it is not in another, nor is any other the master of its action; nor, again, is anyone the master of its essence, since it is the principle <note>original: "principium" / "ἀρχή" (archē) — the starting point or first cause</note>. And although the Intellect has another principle above it, it does not have that principle outside of itself, but rather in the Good itself. And if the Intellect's "good" is according to that, then much more does this "being in itself" and "liberty" belong to it from that source, since everyone seeks liberty and "being in themselves" for the sake of the Good. If, then, it acts according to the Good, it possesses even more of what is called "being in itself" and "free choice." For it already holds what is looked for in itself; it is "in itself" precisely because it is directed toward itself. This is indeed better for it—to be in itself—since it is directed toward the Good.

->### Chapter V.<-

*The Intellect lives free in the act of contemplation, and by a free decree it determines to refer its public actions to that contemplation.*
*It knows, moreover, that many inconveniences—which it would less prefer—will often come to its people, to the body, and even to the soul; it applies opportune remedies to these according to its strength. All this internal disposition in the mind remains voluntary; however, the actions that follow daily, occurring to remedy involuntary inconveniences, are not so much free as they are dependent on the circumstance.*

<margin>A</margin> Is liberty and free choice, then, placed only in the pure and thinking Intellect? Or is it also in the soul that operates according to the Intellect and acts according to virtue? Now, if we attribute this to the one who acts, perhaps it should not be attributed to the "confection" <note>The final result or completion of a deed</note>. For we are not masters of the outcome. But if we designate it as the ability to compose one's duties honorably, it might be said rightly. But how can that be "in our power"? As if it were said: because war is raging, we exercise the duty of courage.

<margin>B</margin> I ask, then: an action performed at that time—how can we judge it to be "in our power" then, since if the battle had not surrounded us, we would not have been given the chance to use such an action? The same applies to all other actions composed by virtue: virtue itself is always compelled by whatever happens to do either this or that. Indeed, if someone gave virtue the choice of whether it would prefer for disasters to happen to us—such as imminent wars—so that it might demonstrate the duties of courage; or for injuries to be committed so that it might define what is just and resolve lawsuits; or for poverty to press down so that it might show the gifts of liberality. Or, instead, if all things were properly at peace, would it choose to remain quiet? It would undoubtedly choose a vacation from such actions, with no one needing its care.

<margin>C</margin> Just as if some lawful physician, such as Hippocrates <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine"</note>, were to hope that no one should need his medicines. If, therefore, virtue consists of these actions...

<column-break/>

...itself by nature, making two. Both that for which it is, and the nature itself being simple and in act. How then is it free, or would it not even be said to "act," the act being one thing and the essence another, if indeed "to be" and "to act" are the same? If it is not through another, nor in another, how is it not free? Even if it were not fitting to say "it is up to itself," which is said of others,

<margin>B</margin> yet the "up to itself" here is greater, because it is "up to itself" by not being up to another. Nor is another the master of its activity. Nor indeed of its essence, since it is the principle. And if it has another principle, it is not outside itself, but in the Good. And if it is according to the Good, much more is it "up to itself" and free. For freedom and being "up to one's self" are for the sake of the Good. If then it acts according to the Good, it would possess the "up to itself" more;

<margin>C</margin> for it is looking toward itself. And the activity, in as much as it is toward itself, is what is better for it. And its being is "up to itself," if indeed it is toward itself.

<margin>A</margin> Is the "up to us" and the "up to itself" only in the Mind when it is thinking? Or also in the pure Mind? Or also in the soul acting according to the Mind, and practicing virtue? As for the deed performed, if we attribute the "up to us" to it, perhaps it could not be so in relation to life. For we are not masters of the result. But that the "doing well" and the "doing these things" belongs to the virtues, perhaps that would be said correctly.

<margin>B</margin> How is it "up to us," for example, if because there is war, we act bravely? I speak of the activity that happens when it is engineered by war; for if it were not for this activity being done, it would not exist, and so it is for all other actions according to virtue; virtue being forced by what falls upon it to do this or that.

<margin>C</margin> For if someone should give virtue a choice of what it wants: that there should be war so that it might be brave, and that there should be injustice so that it might define and set justice in order, and poverty so that it might show forth liberality? Or if it should choose to be at peace if all such things were absent, and nothing were in need of care. Its work would be unneeded. Just as if some doctor, like Hippocrates, were to wish that no one should need his art. If, then, virtue acting in these deeds...

<summary>Plotinus argues that true freedom (self-authority) exists primarily in the Intellect because its existence and its actions are identical and directed toward the Good. He questions whether human virtue is truly "free" since it often depends on external misfortunes (like war or poverty) to manifest its excellence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of free will (the "in-our-power") and its relationship to virtue and the Intellect. Having previously argued that the Intellect is free because its essence and action are one, Plotinus now examines whether human actions performed under necessity or virtue can truly be called "free."</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

If someone is compelled to bring help, how can that act be considered "purely" their own, so that we might judge the matter to rest entirely with them? Shall we then admit that the actions themselves are necessary, but claim that the will and the reason preceding the actions are entirely compelled? But if we do this, placing free choice only in that which precedes the acting, we will certainly be situating liberty outside of the action, and within the authority of virtue. But ->B<- what shall we say of virtue itself, considered according to its habit <note>original: "habit" / "ἕξις" (hexis) — a stable disposition or state of character</note> and disposition? Shall we say it comes to the aid of a weary soul to organize its disturbances and desires? In what way, then, do we say that being good is "in our power" and that virtue serves no master—or is it only for those who have willed and chosen it? Perhaps it is because virtue, when present, provides liberty and the gift of that which is said to be "in us," and no longer allows us to serve those things we served before. If, then, virtue is like a second intellect <note>Plotinus often describes virtue as a process of making the soul like the Divine Intellect (Nous)</note>, and a habit transforming the soul into mind, then this very thing which is said to be "in us" does not incline toward actions, but returns to the mind, freed from actions.

<column-break/>

->A<- If someone is compelled to bring help, in what way does they possess that gift purely, so that we may judge the matter to consist entirely in them? Shall we then confess that the actions are indeed necessary, but assert that the will and the reason preceding the actions are entirely compelled? And if it is so, that we place free choice only in that which precedes the acting, we will certainly place liberty outside the action, and judge it to consist in the authority of virtue. But ->B<- what indeed shall we say concerning virtue itself, considered according to habit and disposition? Does it not approach the soul when it is weak, to heal and compose the disturbances of the appetite? By what reason, then, do we say that "the good" consists in our own authority, and that virtue serves no master? Perhaps we shall judge that it consists in those of us who are willing and choosing. Perhaps also because virtue, standing by, prepares liberty and the gift which is said to be "in us," and does not permit us to serve any longer those things we served before. If, therefore, virtue is like another intellect, and a habit transforming the soul into mind: again, this very thing which is said to be "in us"

*is said not to decline toward actions, but to betake itself to the mind, which is unencumbered by actions.*
*The intellect, content with contemplation alone, must be thought to live for itself as a free being; truly also, reason—having conceived through virtue from the intellect—dwells free within itself, insofar as it does not establish the outcome of things and actions as its goal, but rather internal honesty and contemplation.*

### Chapter VI.

*The primary Intellect lives most freely, where to live is to understand. It understands exactly as it wills; indeed, will and intelligence are scarcely distinguished there. For they are almost the same act. That which inclines toward the good is called "will"; that which attains the good is named "intelligence": just as a ray in its course is related to the light in its perfected reflection. If the greatest good is the most voluntary, then he lives most greatly as he wills and is free, who spends his life in the good itself.*

->A<- BUT by what reason did we previously refer this gift to the will, saying that what is "in us" is that which occurs according to our will? Truly, the answer must be that it was also added there: "or would not occur." Therefore, if this is correctly said at present, and those things entirely agree with these, we shall assert that the mind and virtue are the masters, and that it is proper to refer "what is in us" and "liberty" to them. Since these two are by no means subservient, it must be thought that the mind ->B<- indeed sits within itself, while virtue wills to rest within itself, presiding over the soul so that it may be good; and up to this point, virtue itself remains free, and the soul is made free by it. But when necessary passions and actions occur, virtue applies itself to governing them, though it does not wish for these things to happen; nevertheless, even in these matters it preserves the free choice <note>original: "arbitrium" / "αὐτεξούσιον" (autexousion)</note> which is in itself, provided that it refers the care of these things back to itself. For the thing itself does not follow as if it wished entirely to save one in danger; rather, if ->C<- it judges it best to provide this, it does so; otherwise it casts it aside, and commands that money, and children, and country, and life itself be thrown away: establishing for itself as a goal not the safety of lower things, but its own internal beauty. From this it appears that liberty, and what is "in us" among things to be done, is referred neither to the effect of the actions, nor to the external action, but entirely to the internal act, and to the intelligence and contemplation of virtue itself. ->D<- This virtue ought to be thought of as a certain mind; not by counting along with it the disturbances reduced into slavery by reason or tempered by it. Speaking of these, Plato <note>A reference to Plato's *Republic* or *Laws* regarding the training of the spirited and appetitive parts of the soul</note> says that by a certain manner of caring for the body, these things are accustomed to be corrected and directed by use and exercise. From this, therefore, it is more clearly established that liberty belongs to the thing itself which is void of...

<summary>Plotinus argues that true freedom and "what is in our power" do not reside in outward actions—which are often compelled by necessity—but in the internal contemplation of virtue and the Intellect. He concludes that virtue makes the soul free by redirecting it away from external pressures and toward its own internal beauty and reason.</summary>

# PLOTINUS: ENNEAD VI.

...pertain to matter: and that which <margin>A</margin> is in us is reduced to this: and this will itself is the master, and consists in itself. Now indeed, if it prescribes anything regarding external things, it usually prescribes it led by a certain necessity. Therefore, whatever things are done from this and because of this, they consist in us: and both outside and within itself simultaneously, it is that which it wills and performs, not at all hindered: and this is also the first thing in us. However, the contemplative and primary Intellect <note>original: "Intellectus" / "Νοῦς" (Nous) — the second principle in Plotinus's system, representing divine thought</note> possesses what is called "in itself" in such a way that its work in no way consists in <margin>B</margin> another, but is entirely reflected back upon itself, and its work is itself; and being situated in the good, and not needing anything further, but full, it lives according to its will and desire. For the will itself is intelligence itself, but it is called "will" because it is seen to exist according to the intellect. For that which is called "will" imitates that which is according to the intellect. For the will desires the good. But truly to understand is to be in the good: the intellect, therefore, possesses what the will prepares, or what <margin>C</margin> has already followed by that reason and emerges as intelligence. Wherefore, if we have given to the will of the good itself that which is in us—because it is already situated in that which the will desires to be—why should it not have what is said to be "in itself"? Now indeed, if someone thinks this should pertain to...

> *If the soul through intellectual virtue is at some time free, it follows that the intellect is free in the primary sense. Likewise, it possesses a life that is supremely free and voluntary, since it is as close as possible to the good itself; liberty itself is its merit. Chapter VII.*

> *If slavery and fortune revolve around lower things, but liberty and order pertain to higher things, and as much as a thing is more orderly it is likewise more free, certainly the principle of all things is neither accidental nor compelled, but is the origin of all order and free authority. In which, as in the highest good, the whole voluntary rationale of liberty exists. Where, if only essence and action could be named, you cannot call the action of its essence something else, because there is no distinction there. Therefore, if it exists naturally in a certain way, so also it acts; in turn, it also exists naturally. But we have said enough about these things in our Theology.*

<margin>A</margin> The soul, therefore, through the mind, emerges as free, applying itself to the good without hindrance; and what it does because of this, consists in itself. But the Intellect is free through itself. The nature of the good itself is that which is to be desired by all, and because of which other things have what consists in them—whenever this can follow without hindrance, while that is already possessed. Therefore, that which is the master of all things, which are deemed precious under it, and which sits in the primary seat, toward which others everywhere wish to ascend, and hang from it, and receive strength from it through <margin>B</margin> which they might have the gift of what consists in them—in what way could anyone reduce it to this same condition in which exists properly what is said to consist either in me or in you? Since the intellect itself is seen to be drawn to this condition hardly, and by a certain force: unless perhaps some rash argument thrown in from elsewhere should bring it about that the first nature obtained its state by chance <note>original: "forte" / "τύχη" (tyche) — Plotinus is arguing against the idea that the First Principle is the way it is merely by luck or accident</note>, so that it held itself as it does, and were not the mistress of this itself which it is: since clearly this very thing which it is <margin>C</margin> is not from itself. Therefore, it would have neither liberty, nor that which consists in it: because it would do or not do what it does or does not do, already compelled by necessity. Which argument is surely contradictory and uncertain, and removes from our midst the nature and reason of all that is voluntary and free, and of that which is in us: so much so that these things would be named by us in vain, being voices of things existing nowhere. For the author of that speech

Whatever things [come] from this [are] in our power, both outside and in itself, what it wills and acts upon unhindered, and primarily in our power. But the contemplative <margin>B</margin> [intellect] is primary, thus what is in itself [is so] because [its work is] in no way in another, but is entirely toward itself. And its work is itself, situated in the good, without need and full, [living]. And just as the life according to the will is intelligence. For it was called "will" because it is [according to the intellect]. [The will] desires the good, which is to understand in the good. Therefore, that [intellect] has what the will <margin>C</margin> desires. And that which it has attained is intelligence. If therefore we place the things in our power in the will for the good, and that in which the will desires to be—how could it have what is in itself? It must be greater, unless someone wishes to ascend to this... which is made in itself, more excellent...

<margin>A</margin> The soul, therefore, becomes free, stripping itself for the good without hindrance; and what it does because of this, is in its power. But the Intellect is first, or where the nature of the good is, which is itself in its power; other things have what is in their power whenever they can attain this without hindrance. How then can that which is the master of all, the most honored and in the primary seat, toward which <margin>B</margin> [all things] wish to ascend, and from which it is suspended, and from which it has powers, so that it might have what is in me—how can someone bring this to the condition of "what is in me"? <summary>Plotinus explores the hierarchy of freedom, arguing that while the soul becomes free by aligning with virtue, true liberty resides primarily in the Divine Intellect and the Good. He refutes the idea that the first principle of the universe exists by mere chance, asserting instead that it is the source of all autonomy and order.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation from the previous page (Page 740) regarding whether the concept of "what is in our power" (liberty) can be applied to the First Principle, often called "The Good" or "The One" in Neoplatonic philosophy. Plotinus is arguing against those who suggest that if the Good is "naturally" good, it lacks the freedom to be otherwise.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

<column-break/>

<margin>to take additionally</margin>
<margin>* of himself</margin>
A But if he is to think, it is necessary for him to use this very expression. If he admits that he understands it, he would already be easily refuted concerning the notion of "what is in our power" as applied to us—the very things he said it did not apply to. For the concept of a thing neither disturbs its essence <margin>* or that essence</margin> nor does it encompass that essence by adding something else to it. For it is impossible for a concept to create itself or to bring something into substance. 
B Instead, the concept seeks to contemplate which of the things that exist is clearly distinct from others, and which possesses **self-mastery** <note>original: "αὐτεξούσιον" (autexousion) — the power to act by one's own authority; free will</note>, and which is not subject to another but is itself the master of its own **activity** <note>original: "ἐνεργείας" (energeias) — the actualization or "work" of a being</note>. This quality belongs purely to eternal beings, insofar as they are eternal, and to those who pursue or possess the Good without hindrance. 

Beyond these things is the Good itself; to seek another "good" beyond the Good itself is 
C absurd. Furthermore, it is not correct to say that the Good exists by chance. For chance is not found in many things among those that come after, but in the First, we cannot say it exists by chance, nor that it is the master of its own nature, because it was never "born" or "created" at all. Why then say it "acts as it is"? That is absurd. It is worth noting that a thing is "free" when it acts according to its nature. 
D In this way, that which possesses **monarchy** <note>The "Monarch" here refers to the First Principle or the One, which rules alone</note> does not lose its power simply because it is a monarch; provided it is not hindered by another, it remains <margin>* to be itself</margin> truly itself. It pleases itself, and there is nothing better than it. Otherwise, one would be stripping self-mastery away from that which most perfectly attains the Good. 

If this were absurd, it would be much more absurd to deprive the Good itself of liberty. For the Good, because it remains within itself, does <margin>* or there is no fear in needing</margin> not need to move toward another, while other things move toward it. It needs nothing from anyone. When its very substance is its own **activity** <note>In God/The One, Plotinus argues that "being" and "doing" are the same thing</note>, one is not different from the other. Even in the intellect, this distinction does not happen: the activity is not produced "according to being" any more than 
E being consists "according to activity." Therefore, it is not subject to a condition of acting as its nature dictates. Nor is its activity or its life referred back <margin>* into the essence</margin> to a separate essence. Rather, its essence is, as it were, coinciding with its activity; having been fused into one from eternity, he <margin>* making itself himself</margin> makes himself from both within himself.

---

->### Chapter VIII.<-

A Let us consider whether **self-mastery** belongs to that Principle as an accident. We can think of this by looking at the liberty found in other things and subtracting their opposites. We transfer the concept from lesser things to the First, even if we are unable to fully reach the words that properly describe it. And so, we might say these things about him, although we can find nothing in him—

<column-break/>

A —from which he does not even understand or know in any way what such a voice means. But if he affirms that he knows it, he is easily refuted by the logic of that which is "in us" agreeing with those things to which he said it could not be applied. For the notion of a thing does not disturb the essence, nor does it increase it by assuming another thing. For nothing can act through itself to bring something into substance or existence; rather, the notion attempts to meditate on what among various things serves others, and what possesses liberty. Liberty means not being subjected to others in acting, but being the master of one's own action. This role belongs purely to eternal things, and to those specifically as they are eternal; and to all who possess or pursue the Good without impediment. 

Therefore, it is absurd to say that the Good itself desires some other good beyond itself. Furthermore, it is in no way correct to say that the Good exists by a kind of "fortune" or "chance." 
C For chance occurs in many posterior things; but it is not right to assert that the First exists according to fortune. Nor, on the other hand, can we say it is not the master of its own generation, since it could never have been "generated" (created) at all. Moreover, when someone denies that the First is free because it only acts as it naturally is, it is absurd to think something is "free" only when it acts or operates against its nature. 
D Truly, that which exists in a single way is not deprived of liberty for that reason—provided this "uniqueness" does not come from being hindered by another, but from being properly itself. Thus it pleases itself; it is not permitted, nor is it desirable, for anything to be more excellent than it. Otherwise, one could claim that the being which most possesses the Good is deprived of liberty. 

If that were absurd, it would be much more absurd to deprive the Good itself of liberty. For the Good remains in itself and never needs to move toward another; 
E rather, other things are moved toward it, and it does not need anything under any condition. Finally, since its "substance" is its "activity"—for these are not two different things—and since this distinction does not even exist in the divine intellect, the activity is not produced "according to being" any more than being consists "according to activity." Therefore, it is not subject to the condition of operating only as it is "naturally" designed. Nor will its activity and life be referred back to some prior essence; rather, the essence there is, as it were, breathing together with the activity, and as if forged into one from eternity, it produces the same result from both. This belongs to no one else and exists only of itself.

---
> We should not attribute liberty or any other venerable quality to God in the same way we do to subsequent things, but in an ineffable way. The condition where something exists and acts as it is naturally designed belongs properly to things subject to time; for eternal things, we use this term by a kind of "extension," and for the Primary Essence, by a kind of "misuse" of language. For it is properly said to exist from itself, having no beginning. Chance is so remote from the First that it is scarcely found even in the lowest things ordered by the First.

---

A Let us think of the role of liberty as belonging to him, not as an accident, but by taking the instances of liberty attributed to others and subtracting their opposites. We contemplate the Principle in himself and toward himself, transferring concepts from the lesser to the higher, because we cannot fully grasp the words that befit him. And so, it happens that we speak of him in this way, even if we can find nothing—

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's dense metaphysical investigation into the nature of the "First Principle" (the One or the Good). The previous page established that the One is the source of all things and is not subject to external mastery. Here, Plotinus refines the argument to explain why the One cannot be said to exist "by chance" or "accidentally," as it is the very foundation of necessity itself.</meta>

# THE ENNEADS OF PLOTINUS, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin> ...that we may speak correctly, not only in preaching about Him, but in not even properly accommodating Him to any form of reasoning. For all things, both beautiful and venerable, are **posterior** <note>original: "posteriora" — things that come after or are secondary in rank</note> to Him. For He is the principle <note>original: "principium" / "ἀρχή" (archē) — the first cause or origin of all things</note> of all these, although in another way He is not a principle, since we separate all things from Him. Therefore, we should set aside from Him what is usually called "free will in acting" or what is said to "consist in itself," as if it were something secondary. For that seems to signify an action tending toward something else: tending, 
<margin>B</margin> I say, without impediment. Thus, while there are other things that strive without impediment toward the same goal, we must not refer the First Himself to any goal at all. For He is this very thing that exists even before all things, since we even separate from Him this which is called "being" <note>original: "eſſe" / "είναι" (einai)</note>; therefore, we rightly deny "being" to Him in the way it applies to existing things. Furthermore, we shall not say that He exists in the way that things are naturally ordained, for this too is secondary. And if we speak of higher things, we certainly speak of those which come from
<margin>C</margin> another. Therefore, "essence" <note>original: "eſſentia" / "ουσίας" (ousias)</note> is spoken of first because it was born from Him. But if nature is occupied with subjects in time, we certainly shall not say of that essence itself that it was "born" to be a certain way; nor indeed should it be said that essence does not exist from itself, for in that way we would take away "being" itself. And surely it would not be said to exist from itself if it received its being from elsewhere. Should we then say of the highest principle of things that it **happened** to exist in this way? Certainly, we must not say it "happened." 
<margin>D</margin> For it did not "happen" to Him, nor did it occur by chance in relation to another. For contingency <note>original: "contingentia" — the quality of being accidental or not necessary</note> has a place among many things: where some things exist, and this or that happens to them. By what "luck" then could the First Himself have occurred? For where did He come from, that we should need to ask how He came, or what fortune led or established Him? For there was no fortune, nor was there any kind of accidental chance. Chance 
happens in relation to another, and is accustomed to occur in things that are produced.

> *One may not imagine that it occurred by chance that this very thing, which is now the principle of all things, became the principle; as if it could have happened that the principle was something else or was differently affected. CHAPTER IX.*

> *For there is only one reason for the principle: namely, its very supremacy, which we can also call **infinity**, which imposes firmness and necessity upon those things that are closest to it. Deservedly, it does not exist by chance, but by necessity—or rather, it is **necessity itself**. And since it is the First and the Good itself, it is necessity by its own accord. It could not have existed in just any way; nor on the other hand was it "obliged" to be, nor is it determined as this or that, but it is more than necessity, existing equally and spontaneously as that very thing which it is.*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...to say, not that it is said of him, but not even 
strictly. For all things and the 
venerable things are later than him. For he is the 
principle of these, in a different way than a principle, 
having set aside <gloss>* to take additionally</gloss> 
the things from him as later, and even <gloss>* of himself</gloss> 
for it already speaks of activity toward another, 
unhindered, and other things being those 
that [strive] toward the same goal absolutely. But it is necessary to refer the First to nothing 
<margin>B</margin> at all. For he is what he is even before them. Since 
even this which is called "being," 
we remove from him. So that <gloss>* also the things before</gloss> 
we rightly deny being in 
any way. For it is necessary that [he be] as he is by nature 
and by <term>r</term> <note>Likely an abbreviation for "ratio" or "reason"</note>, and if it were said, it would be said of 
the things from him; so that 
the essence is because it was born from him. <gloss>* if nature</gloss> 
is in time, that nature of essence 
is not from itself, it must be said to be. For both 
<margin>C</margin> we take away the "to be." And the things said to be from itself 
are under another. How then did it happen, or should it 
<gloss>* not</gloss> be said. For as to him, and as to what 
happens to many. When some things are, 
this happens to them. How then did the First 
occur? For he did not "come," so that you might ask how he came, 
or what fortune led him or established him? Since 
not even fortune was, nor chance either. For 
<margin>D</margin> both are in another and in things being made.

---

<margin>A</margin> BUT if anyone, regarding this, accepts 
what is commonly said—that it "happened" or "occurred"— 
one should not dwell upon this name, 
but rather notice what the speaker means to understand. What then 
does it mean? Is it that he, having this nature and 
power, existed as the principle? And if he had had 
some other, he would still have been a principle according to 
what he was, and if by chance he were worse, he would have acted 
according to his own essence. To such a thing it must be said 
that it was not possible, since he was the principle of all, 
that he should be contingent or fortuitous; 
not only that he could not have been worse, but not even 
<margin>B</margin> "good" in any other way, such as being good out of

and therefore, as if he were a certain determined thing—determined, 
I say, because of his singular and unique reason. Yet I do not say 
"determined" and "consisting of a unique reason" as if by 
necessity. For necessity did not yet exist.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the First Principle (the One) cannot exist by chance or contingency, as He is the source of all things, including essence and necessity itself. Because He is "above being," the concepts of accidental birth or forced existence do not apply to Him; He is spontaneously and perfectly what He is.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the First Principle (the One). Having previously established that the One is not subject to external mastery, Plotinus now argues that the One cannot be considered a product of "chance" or "accident." He posits that if the source of all order were itself accidental, then the universe would lack the rational structure we observe.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT. 741

For those things that follow the First Principle <note>original: "principium" / "ἀρχή" (archē) — the source or starting point of all things</note>, necessity holds sway; yet this is not a violence imposed upon them. This First Principle possesses its unique and singular nature from itself. This very thing is what it is, and not another; it is what was expedient, or what ought to be. It did not, therefore, happen by chance <note>original: "contigit" / "συνέβη" (synebe) — to happen, often used for accidental occurrences</note>, but it was necessary <note>original: "oportuit" / "ἔδει" (edei) — it was necessary or fitting</note> that it be so. This very "ought" is said to be the principle of all things that must exist. Therefore, it is by no means the case that the Principle is as it "happened" to be—for it does not exist as if by a stroke of luck—but rather as it was required to be. Indeed, it is not even strictly that which "ought" to be. It is proper to expect other things 
<margin>A</margin>
<margin>* nor what it ought to be</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
to appear as they are at some time, but as for the King himself <note>original: "βασιλεὺς" / "rex" — Plotinus often uses royal imagery for the One</note>, one should contemplate him as he truly is. He will not appear as one who happened to be, but as a true King, a true Principle, and truly the Good. He does not act according to the Good—for then he would seem to follow something else—but he exists fundamentally as the Good itself. Thus, he does not act according to goodness, but is essentially the Good. If, therefore, there is nothing accidental even in "Being" <note>original: "ente" / "ὂν" (on)</note> itself—for any accidental thing would be a "happening" within being—and if being itself did not happen by chance to be as it is, nor did it receive its nature from another, but rather the very nature of being is to exist as being: how could anyone imagine such a condition of "happening" or "chance" in that which stands superior to Being? Especially since the Principle itself generated Being. It did not happen by chance, but exists as the very essence <note>original: "essentia" / "οὐσία" (ousia)</note> of what essence is, and the very 
<margin>* happened</margin>
<margin>* so</margin>
<margin>* so</margin>
<margin>* of being</margin>
<margin>* and whatever</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
<margin>* but he did not provide [this] knowing</margin>
<margin>E</margin>
<margin>F</margin>
<margin>* [The nature] of himself / * properly</margin>
Intellect <note>original: "intellectus" / "νοῦς" (nous)</note> itself. Otherwise, one might similarly say that the Intellect also "happened" to be so, as if the Intellect could have been something other than what its nature is. That which does not transcend its own nature, and never deviates from itself, can easily be called most truly that which it is. What, then, shall he say who transcends even this and beholds the Supreme? Should he say that as he saw Him, so He "happened" to be? Truly, we must say He did not happen to be so, nor in any other way; indeed, we cannot say He "happened" at all. Can we say He is "so" only, and not otherwise? No, for even this word "so" <note>original: "οὕτως" (houtōs) / "ita"</note> cannot be assigned to Him, for that would circumscribe Him and make Him a specific "this." Certainly, the one who beholds Him should not say "He is so" or "He is not so," otherwise you speak of Him as one of the number of existing things to which the term "so" is applied. He is, therefore, something else beyond all things that are said to be "so" or "in this manner." But when you find Him, the Infinite, you will say that all things belong to Him, but as a universal power existing. Indeed, He casts this very thing which He wills into existing things, while He Himself is more excellent than any act of will, and subjects such acts to Himself. Therefore, He did not even will that He should be "so" in a way that He would say it to Himself; nor did anyone else make Him to be as He is.

<column-break/>

Since the principle imposes form, limit, and order on all things, and rational order is the opposite of fortune <note>original: "fortunae" — chance or luck</note>, it follows that if the principle happened upon things by chance, no order would remain anywhere. Because the principle is uniquely firm and remains as that which already exists, it does not acquire its state from elsewhere: for this is its very nature. Nor is any weakness the cause of its inability to have existed otherwise or to have proceeded to another state. For to be and to remain as immense goodness and power is itself the highest liberty and power. **Chapter X.**

<summary>Plotinus argues that the First Principle (the One) cannot be accidental or a product of chance, as it is the very source of necessity and order in the universe. He emphasizes that the One is "beyond Being" and exists as its own supreme freedom, rather than being "so" by happenstance.</summary>

--- Page 920 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 743 regarding the nature of the First Principle (the One). Having previously argued that the One is not subject to "ought" or external standards, Plotinus now addresses the question of "chance" or "accident" (contingency), arguing that the source of all order cannot itself be a product of luck.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin>One may ask the person who says that God "happened" to be this way: under what condition do they think it possible to discover that a "contingency" <note>original: "contingentiam" / "συνέβη" (synebē) — the quality of happening by chance rather than by essence or necessity</note> is false, if indeed it were ever false? In what way might someone take away contingency itself? Yet, if there were some nature that removed contingency from the equation, surely the condition of the "accidental" would not align with that nature. For if you commit to fortune <note>original: "fortunae" — luck or chance personified</note> this very nature—the one that removes the element of chance from all other things—then nowhere would anything exist that did not arise by mere accident.

<margin>B</margin>However, the very principle of all other things removes random contingency from everything, by granting to each one its species, its boundary, and its form. It is not right to ascribe this sequence to fortune anywhere in things so rationally disposed. By assigning a cause to reason here, we think a cause must be provided in this way. Fortune, however, is concerned with things that are neither made from a prior purpose, nor proceed in a consequent order, but rather fall together by chance.

<margin>C</margin>But as for the principle of all reason, order, and limit—how could anyone allow that it stands by some accidental luck? Fortune is certainly the mistress of many things, but she cannot generate intellect, reason, and order. Truly, since fortune appears to be the opposite of reason, she can in no way be the mother of reason. If, therefore, fortune does not generate intellect, she rightly does not generate that which is superior to and better than intellect. She could not have had the source from which to create it, nor did she exist at all, nor is she present in eternal things.

<margin>D</margin>Wherefore, if nothing is above that Principle, and it exists as the first, it is best to stop at that point and say nothing further about it. Instead, one should investigate how the things that follow it were made. But concerning the Principle itself, one should in no way search for how it arose, since in truth it was never "born" <note>original: "natu" / "ἐγένετο" — Plotinus emphasizes that the One is unbegotten and eternal, unlike created things</note>. What then if it was not born, yet is as it is, without being the master of its own essence?

<margin>E</margin>And if it were not the master of its essence, but existed as this very thing it is—not providing existence to itself, but using itself however it may be—then this very thing that it is would exist by necessity, and never otherwise. But surely it is not in this state because it *could not* have been otherwise, but because it is the *best* for it to be exactly as it is. Indeed, proceeding toward the better is not always voluntary for all things; but coming toward the worse can by no means be prohibited by another. Yet, that it has not declined into the worse is due to itself—not because it was restrained, but because it is the very thing that never proceeded in that direction.

<margin>F</margin>Now, the inability to decline toward the worse does not signify any weakness in that which does not decline; rather, it possesses this quality of not going that way from itself and because of itself. And that it is said to never approach anything else, and to have been and to be the power of all power, demonstrates its total authority. For it is understood not to be excluded by necessity, but rather it is the necessity and the law for all other things. Did necessity itself, then, have a source from which it gained its existence? On the contrary, it did not even "come into being" <note>original: "extitit" — appeared or arose</note>, since all other things which are after that first one exist by its order. How then should that which is above existence and subsistence be said to have existed or subsided either by itself or from itself?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>And it is necessary to ask those who say "it happened so": how would they deem "it happened" to be possible? If it turns out so, then how could "it happened" be taken away? If there were a nature that fits "it happened," then if you take away the "happened so," you fall into the idea that things are not from chance. If the very principle of other things turned out to be "as it chanced,"

<margin>B</margin>giving both limit and form, and if it were reasoned to happen according to reason, then it is not by chance, but there is a cause for this. I mean that which is not preceded by purpose, and does not follow in order, but chance occurs in coincidences. How could one attribute the substance of the principle of reason, order, and law to chance? Fortune is mistress of many things, but it is not in the nature of fortune to generate these things; and where she is mistress,

<margin>C</margin>fortune seems to be the opposite of reason. How then could she be the cause? If therefore fortune does not generate intellect, then she does not generate that which is beyond intellect, nor that which is better than intellect. For she had nothing from which she might generate, nor was she herself present at all among eternal things. If then there is nothing above the first, we must not speak about it as we do here <note>original: "ἐνταῦθα" — meaning in the realm of physical/generated things</note>, but rather speak of the things after it—

<margin>D</margin>how they were made. But of the Principle itself, no longer ask "how," for it did not truly "come to be." What then if it did not come to be? Is it somehow as if it is not the master of its own essence? And if it is what it is, not having established its own substance, but using itself as it is, then by necessity it would be what it is. And it could not be otherwise. Not because it "could not," but because the best is thus. To go toward the better is a desire for all, but to go toward the worse—nothing is prohibited by another, but because it did not go there of itself, it did not go;

<margin>E</margin>it was not prevented, but by being itself that which does not go. The impossibility of going toward the worse signifies not a weakness of that which does not go, but that it has its not going from itself and through itself. Its not going elsewhere, and its being nothing else, shows the excellence of its power within itself. It is not grasped by necessity; rather, it is the necessity of all other things.

<margin>F</margin>Did necessity then establish it, or did it not even "come to be," since the other things that exist after it were established by it? Concerning substance then, how could it be said to have been established by itself, or to have been established under itself?

---

*The wonderful order of the universe, perceived by intellectual reason when the eyes of the mind are finally cleansed, reveals that Principle as an incomparable summit: simplicity, power, and goodness. But once the Principle has shone upon you in this way, do not seek to ask what it is or for what reason it is. Chapter XI.*

<summary>Plotinus argues that the First Principle (the One) cannot be a product of chance or "contingency," because it is the source of all order and reason. He concludes that the One exists as it does because it is the "Best," serving as the ultimate law for all other things without being subject to necessity itself.</summary>
