<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of the First Principle (the One or God). Having argued that the One is not subject to chance, Plotinus now explores why human language and spatial imagination fail to describe the source of all existence.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT
### PAGE 745

*For if you try to track down what it is, you will only shrink and squeeze it into the narrow limits of your own understanding, and it will immediately slip away from you. Indeed, when reason finds the principle that exists above essence <note>original: "super essentiam" — refers to the Neoplatonic idea that the ultimate Source is beyond being and definition</note>, it cannot investigate what it is any further; for a question of that kind must end once it reaches essence. Nor is it right to pry into the "why" of the first principle; truly, this line of questioning is resolved back into the principle itself. Finally, since you are going to deny that it has essence—and much more so that it has accidents—how can you possibly claim that "chance" or "luck" is its lot?*

---

<margin>Seeking another principle before it</margin>
BUT that which does not exist as a defined "what," we should either pass over in silence or depart from, leaving our judgment in a state of wonder <note>original: "ἐν ἀπόρῳ" (en aporō) — literally in a state of "no path" or impasse</note>, and seek nothing further. For what could anyone seek when they have nowhere further to go? Every inquiry moves toward a principle and comes to a rest there. Thus, one must realize that every inquiry is either about "what it is," or "what sort of thing it is," or "why it is," or "if it is." We say that "it is" <note>original: "τὸ εἶναι" (to einai)</note> based on the things that come after it. But the question of "why" is a search for yet another principle; and for the principle of all things, there is no prior principle. To ask "what sort" it is, is to ask what "accidents" <note>original: "συμβεβηκέναι" (symbebekenai) — properties that happen to belong to a thing but are not its core nature</note> it has, but nothing "happens" to it. The question of "what it is" actually reveals that we should seek nothing at all concerning it. We can only grasp it by itself, understanding through direct insight that it is impossible to add anything to it. We only seem to fall into this confusion about this divine nature because we start by imagining a space or a place, like a sort of chaos. Having established this space, we then bring this divine nature into the place we have created in our imagination. Introducing it into such an absurd "place," we are then led to ask: "where and how did it come here?" We treat it like an immigrant <note>original: "ἔπηλυν" (epelyn) — a newcomer or stranger</note> and investigate its presence, as if it had been thrown here from some depth or some height. Therefore, it is worthwhile to remove the cause of this confusion by setting aside all concepts of "place" from our vision of God. We should not place Him anywhere—neither as if He were always seated there, nor as if He had arrived there. We must think only of His existence, as the necessity of logic dictates. Place and other categories come later. If place is later than the First, how could you think of it as being "around" Him or containing Him? We cannot say how "great" He is, nor that "greatness" is an accident of His. He has no "quality," no "shape"—not even an intellectual one—nor is He related to anything else. For He exists in Himself before anything else existed. How then can we speak of "how" He is? How can we say anything about Him if all descriptions must be stripped away? It is truer to say He does not "happen" to be this way at all.

<column-break/>

**A** But what should we call this thing which does not properly "subsist" or "exist" in the common way? Truly, we should depart from here in silence with an uncertain mind, seeking nothing further. For what can someone seek when nothing further is open for them to approach? Indeed, every question carries itself toward a principle, and finally rests in such a place. To this is added the fact that every inquiry asks either *what* something is,
**B** *what quality* it has, *why* it is, or *whether* it exists or not. We are accustomed to infer that there is a principle of all things (that "it is") through the things that come from it. But the question of "why" seeks another principle behind it; yet for the principle of the universe, there can be no prior principle. Furthermore, to ask "what quality" <note>original: "quale"</note> it has is nothing other than to ask what "accidents" it has—but nothing at all "happens" to it. The question of "what it is" actually declares
**C** that we should ask nothing about it, except that we might grasp it alone, knowing that it is not permitted to add anything to it. We seem to have thrown this thorn of doubt into our minds regarding this nature because we first assume a region or place, like a chaos; then, having positioned that region, we introduce this nature into a place already fashioned by our imagination or discovered in nature. But when we have introduced it into such a place,
**D** we are naturally led to ask: from where and by what condition did it suddenly come here? Judging it like a stranger <note>original: "advenam" — a newcomer or guest</note>, we ask by what reason it is present, and what its essence is—as if it emerged here from some deep abyss or descended from on high. Therefore, it is worthwhile to remove the occasion for doubt by separating all "place" far from our gaze when directed toward God. We should not place Him in any location, whether as if He were always founded in it,
**E** or as if He had arrived at some time. Instead, it is right to think of Him as existing only as the necessity of reason dictates: that place (like other things) is secondary, the very last of all. Therefore, as we understand this being that thrives wonderfully outside of place, we cannot attach anything further to Him, as if we were surrounding Him with something. We cannot measure how "large" He is, nor can we grant that "size" belongs to Him. Nor, again, will we imagine
**F** what "quality" He has. For there is no "form" around Him—not only no sensible form, but not even an intelligible one. Furthermore, it is not permitted to describe Him as something referred to another thing in any way. For He consists in Himself, and existed before anything else existed.

---

Since this is so, how shall we dare to speak of it, since all other things said of Him are said through negation? Thus, it is not even true to say of Him, "it happened to be so"; but on the contrary, "it did *not* happen to be so" is much truer—since we shouldn't even say that He "happened" in any simple sense at all.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the ultimate Source (the One/God) is beyond "essence," "place," and "chance," warning that human attempts to define God using spatial metaphors or "why" questions are logically flawed. He suggests that we must strip away all qualities and accidents to contemplate the First Principle as it is in itself, prior to all creation.</summary>

--- Page 922 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the First Principle’s "will" and "freedom." On the previous page, the author argued that the One cannot be subject to chance because it is the source of all reason and order. Here, he moves to define the One as the ultimate expression of freedom, transcending even the concept of being "master of oneself," as mastery implies a division between the ruler and the ruled.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI

The Supreme God <note>In Plotinian philosophy, this refers to "The One," the absolute and simple first principle from which all existence flows.</note> is more rightly said to be freedom by his very nature, rather than the master of his nature. For he is not distinguished from his nature in such a way that he should be called the master of his nature in his actions. Instead, he is either the most simple—which is more aptly called freedom—or he is the beginning and the end of all acts and actions. From this, he is named freedom; for a "master" is not so much a master of himself as he is a master of others. The First Essence <note>original: "Essentia prima" — here referring to the level of Divine Intellect or Being that proceeds from the One</note> can, in a certain way, be called the mistress of its own existence through its own action. But the Soul, since it is not essence itself in a simple way, but rather a certain kind of essence, should be called the mistress of its own essence, although in another sense it is the mistress of itself. Finally, the bodily form has no free mastery over itself at all. On the contrary, God—through whom higher things are free—is for those things that follow him both freedom and supreme mastery simultaneously.

->Chapter XII.<-

What then shall we say? Does he not exist as that very thing which he is? And regarding his very being what he is, or his being superior to being itself—is God himself the master of this? Again, the mind not yet persuaded by what has been said remains hesitant. To these things, therefore, we must presently speak in this way: Each of us, according to the body, is indeed far removed from essence; but according to the soul—which is what we most truly are—we are participants in essence, and indeed we are a certain kind of essence. This, however, is like something composed of both "difference" and "essence" <note>Plotinus is referencing the "Five Greatest Kinds" from Plato's Sophist: Being, Sameness, Difference, Motion, and Rest</note> simultaneously. Therefore, we are neither essence in the highest degree, nor essence itself; for which reason we are not the masters of our own essence. For in a certain way, essence is one thing, and we exist as another. We are not the masters of our essence; rather, essence itself is the mistress of us, since it is essence that provides the "difference." But since we are, in a certain way, also that which masters us, we can nonetheless be called the masters of ourselves under this condition. However, that which is entirely what it is—that is, essence itself—is not one thing while its essence is another. Certainly, this very thing which exists is the mastering principle, and it is no longer referred back to another thing either in its reason or its existence as essence. For again, the idea of being "master of oneself" is let go, since that which is first there is reduced to essence itself. Now, that which makes essence free—insofar as its nature is to make things free, and is rightly named the Liberator—whom would it serve? If indeed it is even lawful to speak of it in any way at all. This First is judged free by its own essence; but even essence is free because of him, and is posterior to him. He himself does not "have" essence. If, therefore, there is any action in him, and we place him within that action, he will not for this reason be something other than himself; nor is he any less the master of himself from whom the action is produced, because there the action is not one thing and he himself another. But if we do not grant that action is in him at all, but rather that other things working around him retain their substance, we shall much less confess that there is a master or a ruler there; nor shall we even say he is the master of himself. This is not because anything else dominates God, but because we have already attributed "being master of oneself" to the level of Essence. We have placed the Supreme God in a certain more excellent grade than that of mastering himself. What, then, is more exalted than he who is master of himself? Truly, because in that which is called master of self, essence and action are in some way two things—the action surely provided the rationale for the "master." But since this action is the same as the essence, it resulted in him being a master, and he was called the master of himself. Where, however, they are not two acting as one, but are utterly one—whether he is solely activity, or whether there is no activity there at all—it is not even correctly said that he exists as the master of himself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> What then is that which he is? Since his being is beyond those things, is he perhaps the master of himself? The Soul, not being persuaded by anything, is at an impasse. It must then be said thus: that each of us, according to the body, is far from essence, but according to the soul—which we especially are—we participate in essence, and are a certain essence, as if a certain composite of difference and essence, and not yet essence in the strict sense. <margin>B</margin> Therefore, we are not masters of our own essence, but essence itself is our master, if indeed this is the cause of our being. But since we are in some way that which is the master, in this way we might be called masters of ourselves. But that which is what it is, namely essence itself, or rather where the thing and its essence are not different, there that which exists is the master, and is not referred to another. <margin>C</margin> For either he is master by his own choice, or as essence, that which has made it free—being by nature such as to make things free—would be called the "Freer." To whom would he be a slave? If it is at all permissible to speak of this. He is not free by essence, but essence is free through him, and it is posterior to him, and he does not have essence. <margin>D</margin> If there is an activity in him, and we place him in that activity, he would not for this reason be another from himself, and not the master of himself from whom the activity comes, if the activity and himself are not different. But if we will not grant that activity is in him, but that other things act around him in their own subsistence, even more so we will not grant that there is a "master" or "ruling thing" there. But neither will we say he is master of himself, <margin>E</margin> not because another is master over him, but because we attributed "being master of oneself" to essence. We placed the One in a more honorable rank. What then is more honorable than being master of oneself? Because since essence and activity are two in some way, the activity provided the notion of the master, and the essence was the subject. Because of this, they were distinct. And if he was called master of himself, <margin>F</margin> it was not as two, but as one. For either he is only activity, or not activity at all. Nor is "master" correctly said.

<summary>Plotinus explores the concept of freedom in the Divine, arguing that the "One" (the Supreme God) is beyond the duality of being a "master of oneself" because it is absolute unity. He distinguishes between the limited freedom of humans/souls, who participate in essence, and the absolute freedom of the First Principle, which is the source of all liberation.</summary>
<keywords>The One, Essence, Freedom, Mastery, Neoplatonism, Soul, Activity, Divine Unity, Liberator, Plotinus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's inquiry into whether the "First Principle" (the One or God) possesses free will. The previous page established that God is not a "master" of himself in a way that implies internal division, but rather is freedom itself. Here, Plotinus argues that in the Divine, essence, will, and action are a single, unified reality.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

->In whatever way essence, will, and action can be named in God, they are entirely the same thing. If, therefore, God wills and acts according to what his essence naturally brings forth, conversely his nature is also such as he wills and acts. He is, therefore, what he is not by chance or by fate, but by his own will. Chapter XIII.<-

To that extent, each thing wills itself and exists as its own master, insofar as it is joined with the Good. Therefore, the Good itself exists exactly as it wills and is free; and if it were given the choice of changing, it would never wish to be anything other than what it is. Furthermore, since the wills of all things flow together toward the Good and are united in it, certainly in the Good itself, will is identical to goodness, and it does not wish to be anything other than itself. Now, indeed, it is greatly pleased with what it is, since things possess the ability to be pleased with themselves only through participation in the Good. After this, Plotinus says: If willing and being are the same in the Good, it follows that just as it is in itself naturally, so it wills; and conversely, as it wills, so it naturally exists. Meanwhile, he considers—in the manner of the Christians <note>The translator is likely referring to the concept of the Trinity or the generation of the Word/Son, suggesting a parallel between Plotinus’s "subsistence" and Christian theology.</note>—that God produces a certain subsistence <term>subsistentia: the state of existing as a distinct, self-sustaining reality</term> (so to speak) in himself through an act of will. Elsewhere he also said that God, through intelligence, generated some kind of subsistence in himself. Finally, just as he grants an act of will to the Good itself through a more excellent will, he will undoubtedly grant an act of intelligence through a more excellent intelligence.

...or to have existed: nor does anything happen to it as if it turned out to be what it is by some compelling necessity, precisely because it is specifically what it always willed and continues to will. For in truth, the nature of the Good is its very own will—not indeed in the sense that some portion of it was assigned to it, or that it followed some nature of its own, but rather that it willed itself, since there was nothing else toward which it could instead be drawn. Added to this is the fact that none of the other things includes within its own essence a reason for being pleased with itself: indeed, there can be some things that offend themselves and are displeased with themselves. But in the substance of the Good itself, the choice of itself and its will must undoubtedly be contained; otherwise, nothing anywhere will ever achieve the ability to be pleased with itself—things which, indeed, are usually pleased with themselves either by some participation in or at least a false image of the Good. However, one ought to grant pardon for names <note>Plotinus often warns that human language is inadequate for describing the "One."</note>, if anyone speaking of it is compelled to use less suitable names for the sake of demonstration, which a more exact rule of disputation would not admit. At least, in any less congruous name, phrases such as "as if," "just as," and "as though" should be understood individually. If, therefore, the Good itself exists, and choice and will exist simultaneously with it—for it will not exist without these—it is necessary that this should not be a plurality; indeed, we must reduce will, essence, and the act of willing entirely into one. Since, truly, the act of willing itself comes from it, it is necessary that the act of being should also come to it from itself. For this reason, this line of reasoning finds that it has produced itself. For if the will is from itself, and as if its own work, and this will is the same as its substance, then surely it has brought itself forth into the act of existing. Therefore, it is not that which happened to be, but rather that—

### Confirmation of the previous points. — Chapter XIV.

*Individual things in bodies can indeed have come forth into existence contingently <term>contingenter: by chance or without necessity</term>; in these, essence is especially something added from the outside. But the intellectual soul and any Idea—where the whole is necessary because of its form—this very thing which exists comes forth from its innermost nature, not by chance indeed, but by necessity. Just as they follow that Good from a proximate principle, that Good holds that gift primarily, outside of fate in every Idea; it is the same as substance, or form expressed exactly according to the Idea. It joins these two together: what exists and for what reason it exists. Therefore, if you look diligently into the very disposition of nature on the part of reason, you will find the cause of the parts and of the whole: they hold such a great gift from the principle of things, possessing the same thing. Fortune, truly, is most foreign to that place where the reason and cause for existing are contained within.*

<margin>A</margin> ACCORDINGLY, it is fitting for us to consider the same thing by this reasoning as well. Each of those things which are said to exist is either the same as its own being, or rather something else. Just as this man is one thing, and the very "being" for a man is another; yet this man is a participant in that which is "being a man." But the soul and "being a soul" are the same, if the soul is simple and is not predicated of another. Likewise, the Ideal Man <note>The "Ideal Man" refers to the perfect archetype or "Form" of humanity existing in the Divine Mind (Nous), as opposed to an individual human on earth.</note> itself is the same as "being a man." And this individual man can become a man by a certain fortune, where "being a man" is something different. But that which is "being a man" for the man, or the "beingness" of a man, never happens to occur by fortune. That is, the Ideal Man is from himself. Therefore, if this very thing which is called "being a man" or "the being of a man" is from itself, and this does not exist according to fortune, nor does it happen to be so, then in what way can that which is higher than the Ideal Man, and which generates the Ideal Man himself, and generates that by which all beings are contained—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...not to have been willed, nor did it come to itself as if under necessity to be this which it is, but it is that which it always willed. And truly the nature of the Good is will, not constrained. But in its own nature, it chose itself, because there was nothing else to go toward. If indeed that other thing is this very thing by which each of the other things exists, <margin>B</margin> then it contains the reason of being pleased with itself. But anything else might be displeased with itself. But in that which is primary, it is necessary that choice and will be included, or else it would not be pleased with itself. But even the image of the Good is pleased with itself. One must yield to names <note>original: "τοῖς ὀνόμασιν"</note>, if someone speaks about such things out of necessity for the sake of an action, though we might speak more accurately if we were more precise. <margin>C</margin> Let the "as if" <note>original: "τὸ οἷον"</note> be applied to each term. If therefore as the Good, it is also joined to choice, and without these it will not be, and it is necessary that it not be many, we must lead it into one, toward essence and the act of willing. And since the act of willing is from it, of necessity being must be from itself, so as to have made itself, as it were, to be perceived. If indeed the best will is from <margin>D</margin> it, and this is the same as essence, it is perhaps its own subsistence. It is not what it happened to be, but what it willed.

<margin>A</margin> FURTHERMORE, one must see in this way each of the things said to be. Either it is the same as its being, or different, as a man is one thing and "being a man" is another. For the man participates in "being a man." But the soul and "being a soul" are the same, if the soul is simple and not in another. And the Man-itself and "being a man" are the same. A man might exist by chance, where "being a man" is different. <margin>B</margin> But "being a man" could not occur by chance. For of those things, it is the Man-itself. If indeed "being a man" did not stand by chance, and it is with that which is above the Man-itself, this is "being a man" itself, and is the one through which all beings...

**A** How can it be: especially since its nature is more simple than the nature of being a human, or even the nature of Being itself? <note>Plotinus uses "simple" to mean something that has no parts and cannot be divided.</note> Truly, as one proceeds toward the simple in order, it is not permitted to bring fortune along with it. For this reason, fortune cannot ascend to that which is the simplest of all things. Furthermore, it must be recalled—as has already been stated—that each of those things which truly exist, and which have come into their substance from that divine Nature, possess the cause of their substance (or subsistence) along with their essence.

<margin>B</margin> If there is anything among the things we perceive through the senses that is of such a kind, it is because it depends primarily upon those higher things for its existence. From this, it follows that whoever contemplates any thing afterward can assign a "wherefore" <note>Original: "propter quid," the specific reason or cause for a thing's existence.</note> for the individual parts—either why they exist or why they are as they are. For example: for what purpose is the eye? And for what reason were feet given to certain creatures?

<margin>C</margin> A person should be able to prove the cause by which each part is created for the sake of the individual, and how the parts mutually assist one another in that same design. Why, for instance, are the feet extended in length? Clearly, it is because the foot is of such a kind, and the face is of such a kind; therefore, the feet are also such. In short, the mutual harmony of all the parts is the cause of one another. Likewise, why is this thing as it is? Because this very thing constitutes being a human. Therefore, being and cause are one and the same.

<margin>D</margin> These things have flowed from a single source, not by any use of a discursive process of reasoning, but by providing the "wherefore" and the "being" simultaneously and in their entirety. Therefore, it is called the source of being itself and the source of the reason for being, providing both at once.

<margin>E</margin> However, as for the things that are created, the source from which they come is of a far superior and truer nature, exceeding the things that are made in a way that surpasses all measure. Since, therefore, none of those things that possess causes within themselves are the result of rashness, or chance, or any condition of luck, so it is with the First Principle. From Him come all things: He is the father of reason, and of cause, and of causal essence (if I may put it that way). All these things are far removed from

->mixture with fortune, chance, or luck; for He is the cause of Himself, and exists from Himself,<-
->and is Himself because of Himself. For He is primarily Himself, or super-naturally, and (so to speak)<-

### Confirmation of the preceding. Chapter XV.

If everything is lovable to itself insofar as it participates in the Good, then surely the Good itself is most lovable to itself; and there, the lover and the beloved are the same. It is, therefore, nothing other than that which always loves its own existence. Furthermore, we are placed beyond the reach of contingencies and experience true liberty <term>libertas</term> only when, having set aside all other things, we expose ourselves to the single light of the Good itself which surpasses all intelligence. Therefore, the Good itself is liberty itself, existing beyond fortune. Finally, since reason is the opposite of chance, and the entire reason of the universe proceeded from the Principle, it follows that the Principle is not only beyond chance but even its very existence is above reason.

substance and is considered as a sort of subject: again, from this it has appeared to us that desire and essence are the same. If this is the case, it is established once more that God makes himself, and exists as his own master; he was not made in such a way as any other thing might have willed, but exactly as he himself wills. Hence, when we say that God neither receives anything into himself nor is contained by another, we further separate him by this reasoning from that condition by which he might be said to have turned out a certain way by chance. This is not only because he acts, or renders himself unique, and (if I may say so) preserves himself solitary and pure from all things; but also because if ever we ourselves should inspect such a nature within us, having nothing of other things—those many things which cling to us and through which we usually suffer whatever happens to befall us and live by chance—we shall experience absolute freedom. For all other things that are called "ours" are in servitude, exposed to fortune, and happen to us as if by accident. In this alone <note>Meaning the higher, divine part of the soul.</note> consists the state of being one's own master and being free: namely, through a certain act of light that is "boniform" <note>original: "boniformis"; having the form or nature of the Good</note>, and a Good that surpasses the mind—an act, I say, possessing a power within itself that is not borrowed from outside, which exceeds all understanding. Therefore, when we have ascended to this point and have become that alone, having left all other things far behind, come now, what shall we say of this state? Truly we shall cry out that we are then far superior to liberty and all free will. Who, at that time, could expose us to fortune, or make us subject to randomness or fate? For indeed, we have then become the very "True Life" itself: or are thoroughly established within it, which surely possesses nothing else, but exists entirely as itself alone. Other things indeed, if they are separated from others, cannot suffice for their own being; but the Principle itself exists as that very thing which it is, even if it is set apart. Certainly, the First Substance <note>The primary reality or the One.</note> did not consist in a non-living thing, nor even in a life devoid of reason. For such a life is weak for existing, since it is a dispersion of reason and a certain indefinite nature. But insofar as it proceeds into reason, to that extent it leaves fortune behind; for that which proceeds by reason is in no way involved in fortune. To those proceeding higher, the Principle itself is not encountered as reason, but as something more beautiful than reason; it is so far removed from happening by chance. For it is a certain root of reason by its own nature, and here all things end. It is like the principle and source of some immense tree living by reason, remaining indeed within itself, but handing over being to the tree through the reason received from it.

### Confirmation of the preceding points. Chapter XVI.

> *If God is neither in time nor in place, that which he is cannot be said to be either "at some time" or "somewhere." However, God is not so much "always" as he is Eternity itself; nor does he properly dwell "everywhere," but he is certainly that very thing which we are accustomed to call "everywhere." The Intellect in God is marvelous, superior to the intelligible intellect, so that it effectively generates existence within itself. Similarly, his Will, superior to desiring will, creates existence in the One. Since there is nothing in God besides himself, certainly by thus understanding and willing, he shines forth from himself by his own power, or rather perhaps exists as that which he is according to his own intelligence and will, without any external force being applied. But these points and those that follow, we explain more diligently in our Theology.* <note>Marsilio Ficino, the translator, likely refers here to his own "Platonic Theology."</note>

# BOOK EIGHT. <note>original: "LIBER OCTAVVS"; in the Renaissance editions by Marsilio Ficino, the Enneads were sometimes grouped differently; this section corresponds to Ennead VI, Book 8.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> This did not happen by chance. <note>original: "αδαμῶς συμβέβηκε"</note> For if he is everywhere, then surely as great as he is, so great is he everywhere. Therefore, this very thing called "everywhere" and "in every way" is he himself. He is not contained by "everywhere," but rather he is the "everywhere" itself, and by his being he allows all other things to exist within that "everywhere." He who holds the supreme rank—or rather, who does not merely hold it but *is* the Supreme itself—possesses all things subject to him. He does not "happen" to them, but rather they happen to him, or more accurately, all things <margin>B</margin> look up toward him as they circle around him. But he, as it were, is carried into his own interior, loving himself as a pure light—he himself being the very thing he loves. This means he brings himself into substance <note>original: "ὑπόστασις" / "subsistentiā"</note>, since he is a permanent activity <note>original: "ἐνέργεια μένουσα" / "actus permanens"</note>. That which is most lovable in him exists as a kind of Intellect. But Intellect is his own workmanship; therefore, he is his own workmanship. Since he is the work of no other, it follows that he is the work of himself. Therefore, he is not as he "happened" to be, but as <margin>C</margin> he himself acts. Furthermore, if he exists primarily because he rests upon himself and looks toward himself—and if for him "to be" is the same as "looking toward himself"—then he essentially makes himself. He is not, therefore, as he happened to be, but as he himself wills. Nor is that will a matter of chance, nor did it "just happen" that way. For since his will is for the Best, it is not empty or accidental. That such a "nod" <note>original: "nutus"; a metaphorical divine command or inclination</note> toward himself—which is a kind of action and a resting in himself— <margin>D</margin> causes him to exist as he is, is proven by the opposite case. For if he were to incline or "nod" toward the outside, he would lose what he is. Therefore, his being what he is consists in this action toward himself. But he and his action are one. He therefore provides his own substance, his action being brought forth together with him. If, then, his action was not "made" but always existed as a kind of "awakening" <note>original: "ἐγρήγορσις" / "vigilantiā"</note>, and if the one who is awake is not one thing and the awakening another, then he is a "hyper-intellection" <note>original: "ὑπερνόησις"</note> that is always vibrant. He is exactly as he has "awakened." But this <margin>E</margin> awakening is beyond essence <note>original: "ἐπέκεινα οὐσίας" / "superessentiam"</note>, beyond intellect, and beyond wise life. He himself is these things. He is therefore an activity beyond intellect, wisdom, and life; these things come from him and not from any other. From him and out of him, his own being is produced. He does not exist as he happened to, but precisely as he willed.

<column-break/>

->*Confirmation of the preceding.* **Chapter XVII.**<-

->*In man, nature is one thing, through which he generates his like, while art and providence are another, through which he performs skillful tasks. But in the Craftsman of the world <note>The Demiurge or Divine Intellect.</note>, life, intelligence, and nature are the same. Since, therefore, the provident and skillful arrangement of the world proceeds from there by both an intellectual and natural reason, it is necessary that this exists there as his natural form. If, then, such a form of the world is far removed from chance, how much further from fortune is the principle of that form, which by its own nature and will has separated its "son" <note>Referring to the produced Intellect or the Logos.</note> from fortune. Finally, if the principle were affected by others, it would lose itself. While it looks only to itself, it preserves and acts as itself. Therefore, from himself, that which is, exists.*<-

->*He does not exist by fortune.*<-

<margin>A</margin> **FURTHERMORE**, we prove the same point by this reasoning: we assert that each thing placed in the world, and the whole world itself, exists in such a way as it would have existed if its author had chosen its laws through deliberation. It is as if the world were created according to providence, with a preceding counsel and a certain reasoning that foresaw it. But since all things always are and always become this way, the "reasons" <note>original: "λόγοι" / "rationes"; the formative principles of reality</note> exist in a certain tranquil state of mind...

<margin>A</margin>
...remaining firmly in a truly certain state. Therefore, those things are above providence <note>original: "providentiam"; here meaning the divine administration of the lower world</note>, and above choice and purpose: all things that consist within Being itself always persevere firmly in an intellectual condition. If anyone, therefore, should name such a disposition "providence," let them understand it this way: that there is a firmly permanent Intellect <term>Intellectus (Nous)</term> <note>In Plotinus's philosophy, the Intellect is the first emanation from the One, containing all the eternal Forms or Ideas.</note> over the universe, by which and according to which this whole is constituted. If, then, the Intellect is before all things, and if such an Intellect is the principle, it never exists by mere chance, especially since it is manifold—yet conspiring with itself, and as if joined into one. For that which exists as an ordered multitude, and in which all "reasons" <term>rationes (logoi)</term> <note>The formative principles or blueprints of things.</note> are comprehended throughout the whole into one, must by no means be thought to exist by chance or fortune. Rather, the rashness of fortune is far removed from such a nature; fortune itself, wandering in a certain orbit of unreason, is entirely subordinate to reason. If, however, that which exists before such a thing is the principle of all, it is certainly closest to this state just described. And being so disposed, it is arranged according to that principle, participates in it, and exists as that power and will desire. He, therefore, is God <note>The One</note> who is without distance. One reason for all things, one number. One greater and more powerful than any presiding spirit <note>original: "genio"</note>; nothing is greater than him, nothing is better. He receives neither his being, nor his being "such" (however he may be described), from another. He himself is, therefore, by himself what he is: himself and entirely within himself, so that even in this condition he does not look outward or toward another, but rather focuses entirely toward himself.

->**Confirmation of the points above. Chapter XVIII.**<-

*Nothing may be imagined outside of God. For God is conceived as the immensity of a power beyond-being <note>original: "supereſſentialis poteſtatis"</note>, both a surface that encompasses all and a depth that penetrates the core of all things. The Intellect is compared to it like an inferior circle applying itself to the center of a superior circle, and naturally extending outward from there—just as light poured out through many rays relates to the simple and intimate light of the sun. Since the Intellect is a natural image of the first God, and is entirely and thoroughly the whole Reason, it is certain that the Father of the universal reason, by both nature and will, admits nothing accidental into himself. Finally, since the whole nature of what is expedient and fitting is contained within the Good itself as good things, the Good itself is rightly called Beauty and Grace. It does not exist by chance, but naturally exists through its own natural beauty.*

<margin>A</margin>
Therefore, when you seek, seek nothing outside of God; rather, seek all things that come after God within Him. But let Him be. For that which is "outside" is God himself, the comprehension and measure of all things, or the intimate depth of the universe. But that which occurs outside of God, as if touching him like a circle, and hanging entirely from him, is Reason and Intellect. Indeed, it becomes Intellect insofar as it touches him, and by the manner in which it touches him and depends upon him, since it holds its very existence as Intellect from him. Come, <margin>B</margin> consider a circle touching a center on all sides: therefore, it has its power from the center and is, so to speak, "central" and (if I may say so) "center-formed." Where the lines of the circle converge toward a single center, they make their furthest point—the one nearest the center—to be such as that point toward which they are carried and from which they somehow <margin>C</margin> sprout. This is indeed more excellent than the condition of the lines and the endpoints, which are merely signs of the lines. And yet these are in some way like that center, though obscure and weak, like traces of it—which itself contains and gives birth to both the lines and the points by its own power. These lines...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...standing within the thoughts. So that it is beyond necessity, and beyond choice, always standing intellectually, as many things as are in Being. If anyone names such a disposition "providence," let him <margin>B</margin> think that this Intellect is before these things—the one from whom and according to whom this whole exists. If such an Intellect were not the principle of all, it would not be as it happened to be. Though it is many, it is again in unison, coordinated into one. For it is a coordinated plurality. And all the reasons <term>Logoi</term>, and the powers in the individuality of the whole, are not as they happened to be, or as if by no plan; for they are far from such a nature. In that realm, <margin>C</margin> chance lies in unreason; if it were near reason, it would be close to that which is called the principle. Or that which is so called is disposed according to it, and participates in it. And that power is as it wills. Therefore, the One is without interval; all things are one Reason, one Number. And he who is greater and more powerful. And nothing is greater, nor is anything better. Therefore, he does not have it from another. Nor is his being "of what sort" from another; he himself is therefore <margin>D</margin> himself and toward himself, so that he does not look to the outside, or toward another, but toward himself.

<margin>A</margin>
And you, seeking, seek nothing outside; but all things after him are within, but he himself is the outside; he himself is the encompassing of all things, or the depth within. But the "outside" of him, like a circle touching him and hanging from him and depending entirely on him, is Intellect. Rather, it would be Intellect insofar as it touches him, and by how it touches him, and how it depends. From there <margin>B</margin> it has its being, that it is Intellect. Just as one might think of a circle touching a center; it would be agreed that it has its power from the center, and is, as it were, center-like. Or lines from a circle converging toward the center, they make their end which is toward the center to be such as that toward which they were going, and from which they, as it were, sprouted. These being, as it were, along these lines or their endpoints, are signs <margin>C</margin> of them, and it is, in a way, like that; but more obscure, and like traces of that which is able to produce both the points and the lines...

He emphasizes that everything in the higher realm exists by divine reason rather than random fortune.</summary>

A They have this everywhere: and through the lines, what it is itself appears everywhere, both as if unrolled and again not unrolled. By a similar reasoning, contemplate the Intellect itself and Being itself as generated from that, and as if poured out and unfolded, and suspended from its own intellectual nature: therefore, think of the Intellect as testifying to such a thing, as if it were an Intellect flourishing in the One, which nevertheless is not the Intellect: for it is entirely One. Just as in a circle there is neither center nor any line,
B nor circumference: but it is the father of the circumference and the lines, while it offers its own tracks <note>original: "vestigia"; traces or imprints left by the source.</note>, and by its permanent power produces the lines and the circumference. These are indeed not entirely segregated from it, but are produced from there by a most powerful vigor. So also think of the Supreme God as being as it were the first exemplar of the intellectual power running around it, as if of his own image: God, I say, as if an Intellect flourishing in the One, whose vigor is moved as if in many ways 
C and through many things, and so the Intellect escapes from there: while nevertheless God stands above the mind, and from his own power generates the Intellect. What contingency is there then? What chance? What fortuitous event can happen in such and so great a power, the procreatress of the mind, and truly its effective cause? For such as that which is in the mind is, so almost is that which is in 
D the One thought to be, although it is far more excellent: just as if light, widely diffused, should proceed from one source remaining in itself and being entirely transparent. Where indeed that which is diffused is the image of the other. But that from whence this shines forth is undoubtedly true light: yet the diffused image is not alien and deformed, namely the Intellect itself: which surely admits no fortune, but whatever is individually in it, is a certain reason in itself and a cause: but God is the cause of the cause. Therefore, in a more powerful degree, God exists as the cause, as being the highest cause: a cause, I say, by a much truer 
E reason, embracing in himself at once all the intellectual causes about to sprout from there, and generating his own work not as it happened to occur, but as he himself willed. But the Will was not devoid of reason, nor was it carried along rashly and in vain, nor did it fall out by chance, but rather as it was fitting; since nothing there is rash or vain. Hence Plato called it the "fitting" <note>original: "decens"; translated here as fitting or appropriate.</note> and the "opportune," desiring to signify 
F by any means possible, that God is most remote from fortuitous chance, but that this very thing which he is, is being "fitting" himself. But if this "fitting" thing exists, certainly it does not exist without reason. And if it is opportunity itself, whose property is most dominant in the things that follow, surely much earlier is opportunity present to itself. Therefore, it does not exist as it happened to occur: but this is rather what he himself willed: if indeed he should will "fittingness," and there "fittingness" or the "opportune" is one and the same as the action of the fitting. And the "fitting" is not like a subject <note>original: "subiectum"; a substance that has attributes.</note>, but as the first action, this properly bringing itself into the light, as was fitting. Pardon must be given to our names. For so we must speak of God, since we are not able to speak of him as we would wish.

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS VI.

<page-num>754</page-num>

From the preceding arguments, therefore, if someone is moved toward the highest <margin>A</margin> principle of things, let him receive that very thing; and thus he will perceive it for himself, although he may not be able to express it as much as he might wish. But seeing that principle within himself, having set aside all speech, he will affirm that it exists from itself, so much so that if it possessed an essence <term>essentia - the fundamental nature or "what-ness" of a thing</term>, its essence would serve it, and would, as it were, emanate from it. He, therefore, who has contemplated this will no longer dare to say that it exists by chance, <margin>B</margin> nor will he be able to utter such a thing at all. For if he dared to pronounce it, he would be seized by a sudden stupor. Furthermore, having been raised to this height, he will not be able to assign where that principle is; for it demonstrates itself everywhere equally before the eyes of the soul, and wherever the mind fixes its gaze, it beholds it. Unless perhaps, having dismissed God, the mind looks backward, thinking nothing more of Him; but perhaps it is worthwhile to consider in this way also that ancient mystery involved in obscure words: namely, that God is above essence <note>original: "deum scilicet esse super essentiam"</note>. This is true not only because He generates essence, but also because He serves neither essence nor Himself. His own essence is not His principle; rather, He is the principle of essence. Nor did He make essence for Himself, but having made it, He sent it outside of Himself, seeing as He has no need of being, since He Himself is "to be" <note>Plotinus argues the One doesn't "have" a nature, but is the source of all nature</note>. Therefore, He does not act according to what He is, nor does He "make" that very thing which He is called.

## Confirmation of the above. Chapter XX.

*Since every essence strives with all its strength toward action <term>actus - the state of being active or realized</term> as toward something better and higher, the principle is master of all essence, just as action is far superior to essence. If, therefore, there is being and existing, He certainly declares Himself to exist by reason of being pure action. I say action not contained within an essence, but superior to nature, and thus free. And insofar as He is not preserved from elsewhere, but preserves Himself, He is also said to be of eternal generation. Finally, where acting and existing in any manner are the same, and action is the most excellent thing that can be thought, certainly action can be considered to carry its own existence with it as its companion.*

<margin>A</margin> What then, will someone say? Does it not follow that God existed before He was made? For if He makes Himself, certainly in the sense that He makes Himself, He is said not yet to exist; but in the sense that He is said to "make," He already exists before Himself, since He Himself is that which is said to be made. To this objection it must be answered that God should not be thought of at all as a product, but as a producer, affirming His production to be absolute. Nor is it such that something else is produced from His action; rather, His action performs nothing beyond itself, but all <margin>B</margin> of this exists simply as one. For there are not two things there, but they are entirely one. Nor should we fear to place the primary action without an essence; rather, we must affirm this very thing as the substance <term>substantia - the underlying reality</term>. But if someone posits a substance lacking action, certainly the principle itself will be deficient and will turn out to be imperfect—which is, however, the most perfect of all. And if someone joins action to substance, he will not preserve simple unity. For which reason, if action is more perfect than essence, and the <margin>C</margin> first is the most perfect, then surely the first is itself action. Therefore, God as the agent is already this very thing. Nor is it permitted to say that He existed before He was made, since He was not before He was made, but was already whole by acting. Indeed, He is action not serving essence; this action is purely and entirely free, and thus God exists from Himself. Now, if God were preserved in His being by another, He would not be the first from Himself—

<column-break/>

Let one therefore take from the <unclear>above</unclear> having been moved toward that [principle], he will see it for himself, not as much as he is able to wish, but seeing that [principle], having set aside all [speech] in himself, he will place it with him; that, if it possessed an essence, would be a slave to itself, and as it were, be with itself. But he who sees in silence is driven to speak of how it happens to be. Then <margin>B</margin> we might say, and what it might have <unclear>suddenly about it</unclear>. In this way, it lies before the eyes of the soul, wherever it might look, it sees that [principle] elsewhere... God... considering about it, it is necessary perhaps <unclear>to think of those things beyond essence</unclear>, or in this way to be understood by those before, <note>referring to the "ancient mystery" mentioned in the Latin</note> speaking through riddles, that only He is... <margin>C</margin> but that slavery is not there, nor is his essence a principle for him, but being of essence itself, he also made it for himself, but having made this, he left it outside, as needing nothing of being, he who made... therefore, he does not "make" according to what he is.

<margin>A</margin> What then? Someone might say, if he has made himself, he has come to be; if he makes himself, before he makes, [he is not], but again to make, he already is before that which is made. Against this, we must place him entirely according to the maker, setting the making as absolute, lest another thing be given from the making, but <unclear>being in</unclear> <margin>B</margin> not as an effect, but as the whole of such... not two, but one. For one should not fear to place in the first [principle] that which is without essence; but one must call it the <unclear>hypostasis</unclear> <note>original: "ὑπόστασιν" - fundamental reality</note>. But if anyone thinks of essence without activity, the essence is deficient, and it will be the most perfect of all. But if one should place activity <unclear>within</unclear>, if therefore activity is of essence, it is most perfect; <margin>C</margin> since it is the first, it would be activity. He is already this, and it is as it was necessary to be. For he was not before he was made, but was already whole. Activity is not enslaved <unclear>to essence</unclear>, it is purely free. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the First Principle from page 754, specifically examining how the One can be said to "cause" or "will" itself without being subject to chance or external necessity. If He is rightly said to contain Himself, He must certainly be judged to produce Himself. For if that which contains something according to its nature is the same as that which made it from the beginning, then He is His own cause. If there had been a time from which He began to exist, the term "having made" would be used in its most literal sense. But since He existed even before eternity <note>original: "πρὶν αἰῶνα"</note> as that which He is, this "having made Himself" must be understood as a concurrence <term>concurrence - the simultaneous happening of being and acting</term> between His making and His being. For in that eternal making and, as it were, generation, the source of His being is also the ruler of Himself. If there were a beginning, it would be the ruler of that which is begun. But how can He be a ruler if He has no subject? Is He perhaps a ruler in the sense that there is nothing prior to Him? If there is nothing prior, He is first—not first in a sequence of time, but in authority and purely free power <note>original: "αὐτεξουσίου καθαρῶς"</note>. If He exists there in purity, He cannot receive anything that is not free. Therefore, everything in Him is purely and freely within Himself. What then is He, if not Himself? What could He be that He does not act upon? And what is there that is not His work? For if there were anything in Him that was not His own work, He would not be purely free or all-powerful. He would not be the lord of that thing, and thus not all-powerful, for He would not have the power to act where He was not lord.

<margin>*inactive</margin>
COULD HE have made Himself into something other than what He did make? Or shall we take away His power to do good because He cannot do evil? For power in that realm does not consist in the ability to do opposites, but in a solemn and unshakeable power, which is most truly power when it does not depart from the One. For the ability to do opposites is actually a form of weakness. To remain in the best state is the mark of true power. We must also say that His making and His being are one and the same. For that will is beautiful, and who could turn aside the will of God, since it is the very will of God? But did this will exist before He existed? What shall we say of that will? Did it exist in His substance <note>original: "ὑποστάσα"</note> while He did not yet will? From where would He have such a will? From an essence *not yet acting?

<margin>A</margin>
If He is rightly said to contain Himself, then He must also be judged to produce Himself. For if that which contains a thing according to its nature is the same as that which made it from the beginning, then He is His own author. If there had been a time from which He began to be, this statement that He "made Himself" would be spoken in a very literal sense. But since He existed as God even before eternity itself, the phrase "He made Himself" must be understood primarily in this way:
<margin>B</margin>
that His being is absolutely one with His acting, as if by a kind of eternal generation. Similarly, when God is said to be the "prince of Himself," if there were two distinct things there, the term would be used literally; but if there is only one, He is "prince" there only in the sense that He has no subject beneath Him. But how can He be called prince and lord of Himself when there is no subordinate to whom that lordship refers? Perhaps
<margin>C</margin>
He is considered a ruler in the highest sense, because it is seen that nothing higher exists. If nothing is higher, then He is undoubtedly first—first, I say, not in some order, but by His own authority and by a purely free power. If He is pure, He cannot admit anything that is not free. Therefore, the whole of Him is freely and willingly within Himself. What then is His, that is not Himself? What is there that He does not act upon? What, finally, occurs there that is not His own work? For if anything were in Him that was not His own work, He would by no means be purely free or all-powerful. He would not be lord of that thing, nor all-powerful, since He would not have the power to act where He was not lord.

---

### Confirmation of the preceding. Chapter XXI.

->*The Principle is the most excellent and immeasurable power. Therefore, if anyone imagines that this power could or could have been otherwise, they imagine an impotent being. For just as it is an evil for the Good itself to be changed, so too is it a pitiable impotence for the highest and total power to be able to be changed. Plotinus, in what precedes and in the present, does not deny to God an intellect and a will—specifically a superior intelligible intellect and a desiring will. Accordingly, the will in God is the very nature of God. Therefore, just as God is considered to have come forth from his own nature, so he is considered to have come forth by his own will; for him, to exist and to will are the same. Note: your soul is able to touch something of God, but only by a light shining from above; you, however, must immediately remove whatever else might occur to you.*<-

---

<margin>A</margin>
IT IS ASKED, therefore, whether He could have made Himself other than what He did? However, if we concede that, we would also be denying that He does good, for He certainly does not do evil. Now, power is not understood there as the ability to do opposites; rather, because He enjoys a constant and immutable power, which is the highest power, He never departs from that which is the One. For the ability to do opposites is entirely a sign of weakness;
<margin>B</margin>
it is the mark of the all-powerful to remain in the best. His existence and His making must be simultaneous and singular; for His making is the best. And who could pervert that making, which exists by the will of God and is itself the will of God? But it is asked: does He come to be by the will of a God who does not yet exist? What shall we say again of the will there? Is it the will of one not yet willing within the substance itself? And from where would He have a will? From an essence not yet operating? But the will was in the essence; therefore, nothing there is different from the essence. Otherwise, something would have stood there which was the will, and nothing there would have been "not-willing." God exists as the will itself. Thus, therefore...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the First Principle (the One) is self-caused and entirely free, existing as a perfect unity of being, will, and power. He concludes that divine power consists not in the ability to choose between opposites like good and evil, but in the absolute, immutable necessity of remaining in the best state.</summary>

[...He] was, just as He willed, and in the manner He willed. **Moreover**, regarding the statement that "His will follows His being" <note>original: "voluntatem sequi"</note>, meaning that such a will generated Him, it must be understood that this will generated nothing further in God: for He already was that very thing. Furthermore, regarding the tradition that God contains Himself—if this is said correctly—it must be understood in this way: that all other things are entirely sustained by God. For they exist by a certain participation in God, and all things are led back to Him. He, however, exists from Himself, needing neither connection nor containment, nor participation nor presence. Rather, He is all things to Himself; or rather, He is now nothing to Himself, insofar as He has no need of anything in relation to Himself. But whenever you speak or think of Him, strip away all other things from Him. And when you have stripped away everything and left Him alone, do not seek what more you might add, but rather consider whether there is still something left in your thought that you have not yet sufficiently removed. For it is possible even for you to touch something <note>The "touching" refers to a mystical or intellectual contact with the One that surpasses logical description.</note> about which you can say or assume nothing further. Let that alone stand out from above, that which is truly free: for it does not serve even itself, but is only itself, and truly itself.

<meta>catchword: through another.</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, He was as He willed, and such as He willed. **And** regarding the idea that His will follows Him <note>original Greek: "ὡς ἐβούλετο... ἑπόμενον"</note>, and that such a will produced Him: He produced nothing in Himself. For if we are to speak correctly, we must understand that He contains Himself in this way: that all other things, as many as they are, are contained by Him. They exist through a participation in Him, and their direction is toward Him. But He is already from Himself, not needing any gathering together of parts, but being all things to Himself <margin>B</margin> and yet needing nothing of all things. But whenever you speak of Him or think of Him, let go of all things; having stripped away all, seek Him alone without adding anything. See if you have not yet stripped away something from Him in your thought. For it is possible to touch something <term>touch - "ἐφάψασθαι," a term for non-discursive, direct apprehension of the One</term> such that it is not possible to say or add anything else to it. <margin>C</margin> Rather, it lies alone above all, the free, because it is not even a slave to itself; it is only itself, and truly itself, whereas each of the others is itself and something else besides.

### BOOK IX.

->ON THE GOOD OR THE ONE.<-

---

*Whatever exists besides the First Principle consists of many parts or powers combined into one form of a whole.*
### Chapter I.

To the extent that unity flourishes within the multiplicity of each thing, to that extent its essence persists, which otherwise would be scattered abroad. Unity, therefore, preserves essence; consequently, it also constitutes essence and being. Unity, dominating the multiplicity within itself, neither exists from itself nor produced itself from an opposing multiplicity. Therefore, from unity proceeds every essence that is manifold within itself, while unity remains simply consistent in itself. When you say "one body" and "one soul," or "one coldness," the unity predicated here is not the body itself (otherwise it would not apply to the soul) nor is it coldness (otherwise it would not suit the soul). By a similar discourse, you will find that the One itself is more eminent than any essence; by its power, things become more participatory in essence as they become more unified. Furthermore, the highest perfection of being itself consists in identity with itself, and this identity is founded in unity, just as diversity and motion are founded in number. Unity, therefore, which stands as the cause of being, is superior to being. Accordingly, you may say either that being is the same as unity, or that it is different from it. You will certainly admit that unity is a requirement for identity. Therefore, if you say the former—that being is the same as unity—then this unity certainly stands before being as that through which being is identical. But if you say the latter—that unity is distinct from being—then unity is surely more identical to itself than it is distinct from being, and it will be absolutely first in itself through absolute primality; that is, it is prior to being insofar as it is related to being. Nor is it permitted to say that being is so distinct from unity that it is not one; for if it is said to be distinguished from unity, it must first be identical to itself, and I say it is identical through unity. To this is added that nothing can be thought of as superior to unity. This, then, is Unity itself. Therefore, Unity is not only the first of all things, but also...

unity, by whose reason all other things are everywhere prior. Through this, even being itself is prior to those things that follow it—namely, through the unity joined to itself, and also by that which is higher than itself. Nor is it permitted to say that being, in its first state <note>original: "in primo figno," a technical term referring to the logical priority or the first manifestation of Being</note>, is neither one nor not one. For unless it is one—that is, most simple—it will not yet be in that first state. Therefore, that it exists there, it seems to have through unity. Think of being and the "one" concurring at the same time: being, since it is capable of containing a multitude, does not by its own nature force the "one" to be with it; but the "one" itself compels being to be either unique or united. Rightly, therefore, Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher; Plotinus's translator, Ficino, often cites later authorities to show the continuity of this tradition.</note> says, "The cause and reason of being is unity." And Avicenna and Averroes <note>Famous Persian and Andalusian philosophers; their inclusion shows the translator's attempt to harmonize Greek, Latin, and Arabic thought.</note> confess that the unity of each thing is its own nature.

Then moreover health flourishes, when the body is reconciled into one; then beauty blooms, when the power of the One connects the members; then virtue reigns in the soul, when the mind conspires into one and into one agreement. Yet at the same time assuming the One itself in the man together with the man.

Wherefore those things that have less of being, possess less of the One; but the more they "are," the more they are "one." Now indeed the soul, although she is something other than the One, yet insofar as she is more and more truly, to that extent she possesses more of the One; yet she does not exist as the One itself. For the soul is "one" where the One is, as it were, a contingent attribute. And these two things are the soul and the One, just as there is body and the One.
F

If anyone should object that the soul is not that which is unified: we shall respond, first indeed, that other things likewise exist individually, and at the same time the One exists; nevertheless, [it is] another...

Furthermore, each individual soul exists in itself as a multitude, even if it is not composed of parts. For there are many powers within it: namely, it reasons, it desires, and it perceives or notices; these are certainly connected by a kind of single bond. The soul indeed passes on unity to another thing, since it is itself one; but meanwhile, the soul also receives this unity from another, as if receiving an impression.

*Every essence possesses a natural multitude from the beginning, and yet meanwhile it is a certain "one." In running through things individually, this "being" <note>original: "ens," referring to a thing that exists</note> is one thing, and this "one" is another. For insofar as it is being, it is a certain something; but by the reason that it is one, it cannot be a multitude. For this reason, above individual beings, "Being itself" is the One, nor are they arranged as equals, lest there be two principles of things. Nor is the One subordinate to Being; otherwise, the One would be being and would not participate in unity. Being, therefore, is subordinate to the One especially because the first essence and Mind <note>original: "mens," the Platonic Nous or Divine Intellect</note> is suited for forms, and is therefore posterior to pure simplicity. This pure unity, while it clarifies all things through union in its essence, shows that it has created all essences through unity. Furthermore, we see that the "intelligible" is broader than "being," for we contemplate not only beings and "to be," but also non-beings and "to be." Yet it is not broader than the One; for even when we think of a multitude, we understand it as many instances of "one." If anyone says being is the most widespread, it is indeed indeterminate toward all species; yet meanwhile, it is determinable toward all. But the One itself is determinable toward nothing; therefore, it is the most simple and the first. Likewise, essence, life, and intelligence are three specific parts formally distinct from one another; therefore, perfection itself, before it is divided into three such parts, always remains in itself. This very state of being undivided in itself is the definition of the perfectly One. Therefore, unity is before being, life, and wisdom. Since simple perfection and goodness are the same, it follows that the Good itself is superior to Being. Also, being is either entirely simple or composite. If the first, its essence is unity and simplicity; if the second, the essence of the being is the union of its essential principles; but above the essential and the essential union is simplicity itself: Unity. If this were posterior to being, it would be multiple and not one; and being, in its first state <note>original: "primo sui signo," a logical point of origin</note>, would not be a single thing. Therefore, it would be infinite multitude or nothing. It follows that being, or Being itself, is divisible into parts, whether instant, or subject, and capable of containing multitude. But unity itself admits no such thing. It is therefore diverse and superior. Being is derived by the division of the whole; unity, however, is not diffused by division, but by the repetition of the whole into "this one" and "that one." Likewise, being is divided, but unity, on the contrary, is always multiplied by division. Finally, even the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, who walked while teaching</note> declare this excellence; for they teach that the nature of form and unity is the same, since by whatever reason a thing is a being, by that same reason it is "one." Therefore, since being and the one are the same, the nature of form and unity are rightly the same. They add that the definition of the one and the other is different. If the property of form is to diffuse itself through a formable power, and the property of unity is to be simple and meanwhile to unite other things both inside and out, it is clear that the definition of unity is not only different from form, but also simpler, prior, and pertains more to the height of the Principle.*

<margin>A</margin> IT REMAINS to investigate whether, in any of those things which are individually "one," their own essence is not the same as their unity. In the universal being and essence, however, the essence or "being" and the "one" are entirely the same, so that whoever finds Being itself has also attained the One. Surely, since essence itself is the One—for instance, if essence is Intellect, then the One itself exists as Intellect. I speak of the Intellect which is primarily Being and primarily One. And since it hands down the gift of existing to others, it thus and to that extent also bestows the "one." <margin>B</margin> For what else would anyone say the "one" is, other than being and intellect? For the One itself exists as either the same as being (for "man" and "one man" are the same), or at least in the way that there is a number for anything—as if you spoke of "two"—so "one" is said of a single thing. If, therefore, number is something among beings, then "one" is certainly something among beings; it would then remain to be asked what it is. But if all this is a kind of machination of the mind, as it sets about counting and following things, it follows that the One itself does not truly exist in things. Yet the argument above asserted that whatever loses its "one-ness" simultaneously loses its "being." <margin>C</margin> It is therefore worthy of consideration whether "this being" and "this one" are the same, and similarly whether Being itself and the absolute One are the same; but surely, if the "being" of each thing is a certain multitude, but the "one" itself...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of the One. The previous page established that while a soul or a body can be "one" through participation, they are not Unity itself. This page argues that even the Divine Intellect (the realm of forms and Being) is a "multitude" and therefore cannot be the ultimate First Principle, which must be absolutely simple.</meta>

### BOOK NINE.

<margin>A</margin> It cannot be otherwise; without a doubt, both will be different from each other. A human, therefore, is both an animal and rational, and has many parts, and many things in him are glued together into a certain "one." Therefore, a human is one thing, and the "one" is another. Indeed, a human is divisible, while the "one" is entirely indivisible. Furthermore, the whole of "Being" <note>original: "ens," referring to the totality of all that exists</note>, containing all things within itself, exists even more so as a multitude, and is different from the "one," though it possesses the "one" through participation. Moreover, Being possesses life and mind. For it is wrong <margin>* perhaps</margin> to think of it as void of life. <margin>B</margin> Being, therefore, is also a multitude. But if Being is the Intellect <note>original: "intellectus," the Platonic 'Nous' or Divine Mind</note>, in this way it is again necessarily many, and even more so if it encompasses the Forms <note>original: "species," the eternal blueprints or Ideas of all things</note>. For an Idea is not entirely one, but is rather a certain number, both as an individual Idea and as the whole collection. And it is "one" in the same way the world is one. Generally, the "one" exists as the first; but the Intellect, the Forms, and Being <margin>* the first</margin> cannot be the first things. For every Form consists of many things and is a certain composite, and is therefore posterior. For those things from which each thing is composed are rightly judged to be prior. <margin>C</margin> That the Intellect itself cannot be the "first" will also be clear through these following points. It is necessary for the Intellect to consist in the act of understanding. And certainly, the highest Intellect, which does not look at external things, must necessarily understand what is above it; namely, while it turns toward itself, it returns to <margin>D</margin> the principle. Now, if the Intellect is the same as both that which understands and that which is understood, it is already double. Since it is not simple, it is rightly not the "one." But if <margin>* but what looks toward itself is different</margin> it looks toward something else, it altogether looks up toward what is better and higher. But if it fixes its gaze both on itself and on what is more excellent, in this way too <margin>D</margin> it is seen to hold the second rank. One must indeed assert that the Mind is so affected that it stands by the Good and the First, and looks up to it; furthermore, that it dwells with itself, observing itself, and thus knowing itself to know all things. Therefore, since <margin>E</margin> the Intellect is so varied, it is far from being the "one" itself. For this reason, not even the "one" itself is "all things"; otherwise, it would no longer be one. Nor is it the Intellect. For in that case, it would again be all things, since the Intellect itself is all things. Finally, it must not even be thought of as "Being," for Being itself is simply all things.

<margin>A</margin> [The Greek text mirrors the Latin] A multitude exists. But each would be different.
