And it is with itself, and thinks of itself, and thinks of itself as being all things. It is many, therefore, because of being one, being varied. And <margin>E</margin> it knows that it is all things. For in this way, it would no longer be one, nor one as a single thing. For this is not all things, but the intellect is all things; nor is it Being. For Being is all things.

<column-break/>

->Access to God. Chapter III.<-

> *The soul, even when it draws near to God, suffers from ambiguity. This is because the Intellect is both a "form" and is accustomed to leaning upon forms. God, however, has no form. Furthermore, the soul can only be said to have arrived when it has itself become "god-like"; it then hesitates, wondering whether it has met itself or another. Whoever approaches God—the Supreme Good and the One—let them depart from opposites: that is, from evil, from the lowest things, and from multitude. Let them even transcend the Intellect. For the Intellect is not "Being" in a simple sense, but only "Intellectual Being." God, however, is superior to any being, and even to Being itself. For just as a sensible being is limited by a sensible form, so an intelligible being is bounded by an intelligible form. Finally, Being itself is determined by the very form of Being. But the Principle stands above everything determined. It is not said to "stand," lest it be forced into a state of standing. Nor does it do anything through a relationship to things; rather, things are made by it as if it were not doing them, just as things are changed by the Unchanging.*

---

<margin>F</margin> What, then, is the One itself? And what nature does it have? But truly it is no wonder that it is not easy to describe, since neither Being nor Form can be easily expressed; for our knowledge leans upon forms. But whenever the soul is carried toward something <margin>* there</margin> formless, being unable to grasp it because it is not determined and, as it were, not shaped by any shaping variety, it immediately slips away, fearing lest perhaps it is nothing...

<column-break/>

<margin>F</margin> WHAT, then, is the One itself? And what nature does it have? But truly it is nothing strange that it is not easy to say, since neither Being nor Form can be easily expressed: for our knowledge leans upon forms. But when the mind is carried toward something formless, since it cannot grasp it because it is not determined, nor, as it were, figured by any figuring variety, it immediately slips away from there, fearing lest perhaps it is nothing...

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

[no]thing to bring back from there. For this reason, the soul labors greatly in such matters and often gladly descends from them, falling away from all things until it arrives at something sensible, where it may rest as if on solid ground; just as the sight, often exhausted by discerning small things, gladly turns itself toward larger ones. But when the soul strives to see by itself, seeing only itself because it is fused into one with the object of its vision and is now one with it, it certainly does not think it possesses what it seeks—precisely because it is one with it—since it is not different from that which is understood. It is worthwhile, above all, for one who is to philosophize about the One itself to prepare themselves in this way: since what we seek is the One, the principle of all things and the Good itself and the First, it is right that one should not be remote from those things which are near the First, nor in any way be cast down toward the extremes of all things; but rather, ascending toward the first things, one must lead oneself back to the heights, away from those things which are sensed and are last. Again, it is necessary for the soul to be purged of all wickedness when it desires to approach the Good; furthermore, it must first raise itself to the principle implanted within it and emerge as one from many, if it is to behold the Principle and the One. Therefore, the soul must then become Intellect <note>original: "intellectus"; in Greek, "Nous"—the divine, intuitive mind that contains the eternal Forms</note>, and for that reason commit the entire soul to the Mind and place it deep within, so that the soul, having been awakened, may receive what the Intellect itself sees, and contemplate the One with the Intellect itself. Yet this must be done such that it employs no sense, nor anything proceeding from the senses; but with the pure Mind alone, and with the very "first of the Mind," it should contemplate the Purest One. Whenever, therefore, someone drawn to contemplate it imagines magnitude, or figure, or any mass concerning this nature, the Intellect certainly did not act as a guide for this speculation, since the Intellect by its own nature does not turn toward such things; rather, such an action belongs to the senses and to opinion, which follows the nature of the senses. However, one must receive from the Intellect the report of those things which are within its power. Truly, the Intellect can behold either what is above itself, or its own contents, or what is produced by it. Those things in it are indeed pure; but those things above the Intellect are even purer and simpler, or rather, that which is above the Intellect is. For this reason, that which is above the Intellect is not the Intellect, but exists before the Intellect. For the Intellect is one of the "beings" <note>original: "entium"; items belonging to the realm of true existence</note>; but that One is not a particular thing, but is superior to each one. Nor is it Being; for Being possesses, as it were, the very form of Being. But that One is utterly formless, separated even from intelligible form. For since the nature of the One is the generator of all things, it is rightly none of them; therefore, it exists neither as a "what" <note>a specific substance</note>, nor as a "quality," nor as a "quantity." Furthermore, it is not Intellect, nor Soul; it is not moved, nor is it at rest; it is not in place, nor in time; but it is itself uniform according to itself, or rather, it is formless above every existing form, above motion itself, and above stability. For these things are associated with Being, and they are what make it many. But why is it not necessary for either or both of these to be present...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...has nothing. Wherefore it labors in most things and often descends, falling away from them, until it arrives at some sensation, resting as if on a solid support. Just as the sight, failing at small things, gladly falls upon large ones. But when the soul is by itself, and wishes to see by being alone with it, through being one with it, it thinks it does not yet have <margin>B</margin> what it seeks, because that which is understood is not something different from itself. Nevertheless, it is necessary to act in this way for the one who intends to speak about the One. Since, therefore, the One is what we seek, and we contemplate the principle of all things, we must look from the first things—lest we, being far from the first things, fall into the last of all things—but striving toward the first things from the last sensible things, one must lead oneself back, freed from all vice, <margin>C</margin> and having raised oneself to the Good, one must ascend to the principle within oneself; and from being many, become one, so as to behold it. Thus, one must become Intellect, and having entrusted one's soul to the same, and established it there, so that what that Mind sees, the soul may see while awake; and through this Mind, behold the One. Without employing any sense, nor receiving anything from the senses into the Mind, <margin>D</margin> but with the pure Mind, and with the "first" of the Mind, one must behold the Purest. If, however, when one turns to this vision, one imagines magnitude, or shape, or mass concerning this nature, then the Mind was not the leader of this vision. For the Mind is not of a nature to see such things, but these are the activities of sense and of opinion following sensation. Rather, one must receive from the Mind the promise of what it is able to do. <margin>E</margin> For the Mind is able to see either those things before it, or those things within itself. Pure indeed are the things in it; but even purer and simpler are those before it. Or rather, that which is before it. But that which is before the Mind is not the Mind, but prior to the Mind. For the Mind is one of the things that exist; but that One is not a "thing," but prior to each thing. Nor is it Being, for Being has a certain form of Being. But that One is formless, even of intelligible form. For the <margin>F</margin> nature of the One, which generates all things, is none of them. Therefore, it is neither a "what," nor a "quality," nor a "quantity," nor Mind, nor Soul; neither moving, nor again standing still; not in place, nor in time. But it is itself by itself, of one form, or rather formless, before all form, before motion, and before stability. For these things are about Being, <margin>G</margin> and they are what make it many. Why then is it not at rest, if it does not move? Because for Being, these things—rest and motion—or both, are necessary. For that which is "at rest" is so by virtue of stability...

# BOOK NINE.

<column-break/>

[the One] is called "A" <note>original: "A appellatur"; referring to the Greek letter Alpha, symbolizing the numerical one or the First Principle</note>, and it is not entirely the same as a state; therefore, it happens to it, and it no longer remains a simple unity. But indeed, when we affirm that it is the cause of all things, we do not say this because of something happening to it, but rather something happening to us: namely, because we have something from it, while it remains in itself meanwhile. Therefore, one speaking of God with the most exact reason must say neither "that" nor "this": but we, as if wandering around the outside, attempt to interpret our own affections or passions there as best we can. And sometimes we approach closer to this very thing, but at other times we fall further away in the uncertainty of ambiguity.

<column-break/>

[The One] is the same as the expression of it, so that it will happen to it, and no longer be simple. Since even saying the "cause" is not to predicate an accident of it, but of us—that we hold something from it, while it is in itself. <margin>one must not say 'that' or 'this' if speaking accurately</margin> *One must not say 'that' or 'this' if speaking accurately.* But we, as if running around it from the outside, wish to interpret our own experiences. Sometimes we are near; at other times, we fall away due to the difficulties surrounding it.

### The Approach to God. Chapter 4.

> *The principle of things is entirely incorporeal, immobile, and one. Since we cannot reach it through opposites, we rightly do not reach it through the imagination that devises physical things, nor through mobile reason that always thinks of something changeable, nor through an intelligence that is by its own nature multiple and always meditates on something varied. But we finally reach it through a certain unity of the soul that is higher than the intellect, when we take refuge in it, having been entirely separated from the multitude both internal and external. Then first we have the sign of God, who is always present everywhere, now perfectly present to us—chiefly as a triple, new light, an unaccustomed love, and inestimable joy. Two things contribute to achieving this: teaching, as a way, and the aforementioned separation as a preparation of the mind.*

---

<column-break/>

The difficulty arises most of all because the understanding of that One is not through science <note>original: "episteme"; formal, demonstrative knowledge</note>, nor through intellect, as with other intelligible things, but according to a presence that is greater than science. The soul suffers the loss of being one <margin>some negation of existence</margin> and is not entirely one when it takes in knowledge of things. For science is a form of reason <note>original: "logos"</note>. And reason is many. It therefore passes over the One, falling into number and multitude. It is therefore necessary to run beyond science, and in no way depart from being one, but one must stand away from science and the objects of science and everything else, even from a beautiful sight. For every beautiful thing is posterior to that, and comes from that, just as all daylight comes from the sun. Therefore it is "unspeakable." <note>original: "arrheton"; a key term in mystery religions meaning something that cannot or should not be put into words</note> But the writing says this. Yet we speak and write, sending the soul toward it, and awakening it <margin>from words to the vision</margin> *from words to the Word* <note>original: "logos"</note> *toward the vision.* It is just like showing the road to one who wishes to see something. For teaching is only for the road and the journey. But the vision of it is already the work of the one who has willed to see. If someone has not come to the vision, nor suffered it, nor had in himself a kind of erotic passion from seeing, resting in the loved one, receiving a true light, and illuminating the whole soul by having become nearer, and has yet ascended—but is heavy from behind <margin>not existing alone, things which were obstacles to the vision, and either not yet gathered into one</margin> *not existing alone in things which were obstacles to the vision*, and not only having ascended, but having that which separates him from it, or not yet having been gathered into one. For that One is absent from no one. It is present to all, so as to be present yet not present.

<column-break/>

**C** Doubt and deficiency happen to us concerning the knowledge of God, especially because we know him neither through some science, nor through any intelligence, as we are accustomed to know other things which are called "intelligibles," but through a certain presence better than science. Indeed, the soul escapes far from the one, nor is it entirely one, when it assumes knowledge of something. For science is a certain reason, and reason is many. The One therefore is transcended as the soul falls into **D** number and multitude. Therefore it is necessary to transcend science, nor in any way to deviate anywhere from that which is to be one: but to be called away from science and things to be known and every other beautiful spectacle. For every beautiful thing is both posterior to that and from that, just as every daylight is from the sun. For which reason Plato says the supreme God can neither be written nor spoken of. **E** But we write and speak about him frequently, so that at least in this way we may rouse the mind by our discussions, and direct it toward the divine spectacle, as if showing a certain way to one desiring to see something. Teaching indeed extends its strength as far as the way and the journey: but to see God is now the work of him who has willed to see. He indeed neither arrives at the spectacle, nor beholds the light of it, and therefore is neither affected by it, nor tastes in himself the amatory affection or passion **F** accustomed to proceed from intuition, if ever the lover now rests in the beloved, where surely the true light is received, illuminating the whole soul as it approaches nearer: he, I say, does not attain such things, who strives to ascend there, still weighted down from behind and pulled back by those things which are obstacles to those who would look. Nor does he ascend there alone, but meanwhile draws with him what separates him from it, or rather he is not yet entirely reduced into one. For God is absent from no one anywhere, and in a certain way seems to be absent from all, so that he is present everywhere, and again not present. For

# PLOTINUS’ ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin> [The One] is present only to those who are able to receive it, and who are so prepared as to be in harmony with it. They are able, as it were, to touch it <note>original Latin: "attingere"; Greek: "ψαύειν καὶ θίγειν" (to touch and handle)</note> through a certain internal likeness and an innate power that is related to the gift bestowed from that source. This occurs when the soul is disposed exactly as it was when it first proceeded from the One; thus, it is now able to see, just as God is by nature meant to be seen. <margin>B</margin> I say that he has not yet arrived there who is pulled back by obstacles, or who lingers on the journey, because he lacks the reasoning and the discipline that leads the way and creates faith in divine things. Truly, as far as other obstacles are concerned, each person might rightly blame themselves; for one must strive to be far from all things and to emerge alone. But as for the reasons which a traveler might think are less believable...

## The Approach to God. Chapter V.

*In our Theology <note>A reference to Marsilio Ficino’s own work, "Theologia Platonica" (Platonic Theology)</note>, and in our book "On Love," and in the second book of "Letters," we have more carefully assigned the reasons why one must ascend step by step. We move from corporeal nature—which is subject to dimension, motion, and number—to the soul that is now free. From the mobile and manifold soul, we rise to the Intellect, which is indeed immobile but still the "first many." From the intellect proper to the soul, we move to Intellect itself, and finally from the multiform Intellect to the Simply One. This One is not "one being" <note>original: "ens vnum"</note>, lest it be manifold; for the definition is different. "Being" admits multitude and has "nothingness" as its opposite. But the "One" limits multitude and rejects it as an opposite. It is therefore not "being," but the principle of being—utterly absolute and placed among the absolute forms. For all natural species possess their absolute being in the First. We call it "The One"; we prophesy a simplicity that is entirely indivisible, which exists far more excellently above essence than the unity of numbers or the points of dimensions. Truly, just as discrete being is resolved into something indivisible, so "Being Itself" refers back to the "Simply One."*

<margin>C</margin> **W**HOEVER thinks that things are governed by blind chance and accident, or are contained only by physical causes, is far removed from the concept of God and the One. We do not address our words to such men, but only to those who posit a nature other than bodies and who reach at least as far as the soul. To these people, it is useful to diligently observe the nature of the soul—both how it relates to other things and, most importantly, how it proceeds from the Intellect, receiving from it the reason and virtue it pursues. <margin>D</margin> Beyond these things, it is proper to consider another Intellect beyond the "reasoning intellect" (which is called the "rational" part). One should also consider the movements and arguments of reason as being at a certain distance and in motion; likewise, the sciences are such reasons in the soul, now made manifest because the Intellect—the cause of the sciences—has been infused into the soul. This higher Intellect sees even the "sensible" intellect <note>The aspect of intellect that interacts with the physical world</note>. For one can perceive and notice the Intellect <margin>E</margin> leaning down from above the soul as its father. This is the intelligible world: an intellect entirely at rest—or rather, a certain "quiet motion"—holding all things within itself. It is all things: a multitude that is at once undivided and yet distinct. For its parts are not separated like words in a speech, but are like reasons held together in a single thought; yet, the things in that mind are not confused. <margin>F</margin> Each thing comes forth separately, just as happens in the sciences: even though all knowledge fits together in a single individual, the gathered multitude is at once together. This is the intelligible world.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Rather, it is for those capable of receiving it and who have been prepared so as to fit, touch, and handle it through likeness and power <note>original: "ὁμοιότητι καὶ δυνάμει"</note>, in a way related to that which is in the soul. The soul must be as it was when it came from Him, to see Him as He is naturally visible. He is not yet there, but because of these things, or through a lack of the guiding word <margin>B</margin> provided about Him, he places himself in the opposite state. Let him try to be alone. As for what he lacks in other things, let him think as follows.

<margin>C</margin> Whoever thinks that beings are governed by chance and spontaneity, and by bodily causes, is driven far from the idea of the One. This discourse is not for him, but for those who posit a nature other than bodies and ascend to the soul. For these, it is necessary to understand the nature of the soul and other things, and how it comes from the Intellect. By participating there, it possesses virtue. <margin>D</margin> After this, one must grasp another [intellect] beyond what is called the reasoning part. The extensions and motions of reasoning are the sciences of the soul, made manifest by the fact that the Intellect is the cause in the soul. Now, having seen it as if it were sensible, one must ascend [to] <margin>E</margin> its Father, the intelligible world. One must call it a "restful motion" containing all things in itself. And all things are a multitude, both undivided and again divided. For those things conceived according to the One are not yet divided, nor are the things in it confused. By a "setting forth," each is separate, just as in the sciences all things are in an indivisible state, yet each is separate from the others. This <margin>F</margin> multitude is the intelligible world. It exists in the first. And the word says to itself that these things appeared thus: each one separate...

BOOK NINE.

<margin>prior to the One's being</margin>
<margin>the One is a miracle, which is not being so that it is not being</margin>
...it concludes by necessity that if any reason convinces us that the soul also exists, this is surely more excellent than the soul. Yet it is not the first, for it is neither one nor simple. But the One itself, the principle of all things, is undoubtedly simple.
<margin>A</margin> Therefore, that which is superior to the most excellent of beings—if indeed something must be superior to the Mind, which wishes to be one, yet is not one, but is at least something uniform—must exist.
<margin>B</margin> Since the intellect is not dispersed within itself, but truly conspires with itself, and does not handle itself as a jointed composite because it is as close as possible to the One, even though it seems to venture out <note>original Greek: "ἀποτολμᾷ" (boldly venturing); a Neoplatonic term for the Intellect's "daring" to exist as a separate entity from the One</note> by receding from the One in a certain way. What I say exists above this is a marvelous thing, like a miracle: the One itself, which certainly must not be called "being" <note>original Latin: "ens"; Greek: "ὂν"</note>, lest here too the One be predicated of something else. To this [One] truly no name appropriately fits. But if we are compelled to name it, it is conveniently called "the One" by a common title.
<margin>C</margin> However, it is not so much that it is first one thing, then the One. It is truly difficult to know for this very reason: it becomes known chiefly through its offspring, which is Essence <note>The "offspring" of the One is the realm of Being and Intellect</note>; for the Intellect leads us toward Essence. The nature of the One itself exists such that it is the source of all the best things, and the power that generates beings, remaining within itself, and not becoming diminished by the emanation of generating, nor coming to rest within the things generated.
Indeed, we name that which exists before these things "the One" compelled by a certain necessity, wishing
<margin>D</margin> to designate the first nature of all things among ourselves by a name, leading ourselves toward an indivisible notion, and striving to reduce the soul to a unity. In this, we certainly do not mean "one" and "impartible" in the same way we mean a point <note>original Latin: "signum"; Greek: "σημαῖον"</note> or a

<column-break/>

numerical unit <note>original Latin: "unitatem... numeralem"; Greek: "μονάδα"</note>. For that which is "one" in this [mathematical] way would never exist unless Essence, and that which is before Essence, preceded it. For this reason, we ought not to fix the sharp edge of our thought upon these [mathematical concepts], but we should consider that this unity and "point" represent the One itself through a certain analogical similarity, due to a certain simplicity that is devoid of multitude and division.

->Access to God. Chapter VI.<-

> *By an opposite path, we approach the indivisible in dimensions and numbers, and the indivisible that is the principle of beings. For there [in math], one arrives at something internal and smallest; but here [in God], one arrives at the outermost and most ample: the greatest, I say, in simplicity and power. For it is always simpler than any simplicity you can imagine, and similarly more powerful than any power. Only the One itself can be the principle of the universe; for it alone is entirely self-sufficient. Whatever truly exists besides it is necessarily manifold and suffers at least a fourfold deficiency: since in it, the whole lacks parts; the part lacks another part; the parts also lack the whole; and finally, everything lacks an external composer. Now, it belongs to the Principle to seek nothing, to receive nothing, to lose nothing. Only the One itself has this privilege, otherwise, it certainly would not be the One. When we deny that the One understands, we call it so lest it be termed manifold; we do not deny that it is the wondrous light that creates intelligence. Or if intelligence signifies a light better than intelligence, then it is intelligence, having in itself—indeed, being entirely—whatever is desirable to those who understand. It is not uncertain of itself or of others, but without composition or relation, it shines marvelously to itself and to all others. Finally, as we have said elsewhere, Plotinus thinks no differently than Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century Christian theologian (Pseudo-Dionysius) who synthesized Neoplatonism with Christianity; Ficino often highlights the harmony between them</note> that the Principle is above intelligence, life, and essence.*

<margin>E</margin> In what way, then, do we speak of the One? And by what reasoning can we best accommodate our intellect to it? Truly, we do so if we assert it is the One by a much more excellent reason than when we are accustomed to asserting unity or a point. For here the soul, gradually stripping away magnitude and multitude, finally settles upon the smallest thing; and yet it still resides in something which, although it is indivisible, was nevertheless in a divisible thing, and lay within another.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the "One," the ultimate source of reality in Plotinus's system. Following the previous page's discussion on the One's simplicity, this section focuses on its absolute self-sufficiency and infinite power, distinguishing it from the "Intellect" or "Being."</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI. ###

But the One itself resides neither in another, nor in a divided thing; nor is it "indivisible" in the way that something very small is <note>Plotinus is careful to distinguish the One from a physical atom or a mathematical point</note>. For it is the greatest of all things, not indeed in magnitude, but in power. Therefore, when it is called "indivisible," we mean a power that cannot be divided; for indeed, those things which come after it are judged to be indivisible not according to their mass, but according to their strengths. Furthermore, we must call God infinite, not as if he were some magnitude or a multitude that cannot be crossed, but because his power is such that you cannot comprehend it. For although you may conceive of him as exceeding all your strength—as if he were the Intellect or God—yet he still remains far more excellent. And again, when you lead your thought with the utmost effort toward the One, then too it surpasses this unity you have devised in its simplicity. For you were reducing him to the highest unity of your own intelligence according to your strength; but he surpasses all measure. For he remains within himself, and nothing ever happens to him. 

Moreover, one may nonetheless prove the supreme unity of God through that which is called self-sufficiency. For it is necessary that the highest principle of all things be in no way needy, but the most sufficient of all, and especially content within itself. For whatever is not one, but many, is necessarily needy: since it is not itself "one," it must become one out of many. Therefore its essence needs to become one. But the One itself does not need itself: for it already exists as itself. Furthermore, that which is many within itself needs as many things as it consists of. And any of those things which are in it, since they are not in themselves but together with others, certainly need the others; and therefore, both according to each part and according to the whole, such a thing declares itself to be needy. If, therefore, it is necessary for something to be most self-sufficient, it must also be "one": existing alone in such a way that it is needy neither toward itself nor toward anything else. For it does not seek anything so that it might exist at one time, nor again that it might be well, nor even that it might be founded there: for since it is the cause for others both of being <note>original Latin: "effendi"</note> and of being well, it rightly does not have from others this very fact that it is, and is well. For why would "being well" overflow to it from elsewhere? Therefore, "being well" does not happen to it as an accident: for it itself exists as this very thing. Likewise, there is no "place" for this; for it needs no foundation, as if it could not support itself. For that which must be founded in another is judged to be void of life, a falling mass, unless perhaps it is supported. Other things are stabilized because of him, through whom they both simultaneously existed and obtained the place where they might be arranged in order. But that which seeks a place is undoubtedly needy.

<unclear>
it needs the least; therefore the principle of all things needs absolutely nothing. Now truly, that which is therefore judged needy, because it seeks the principle. But if it seeks the One itself, it will seek to be no longer the One; it will therefore need a destroyer. Nevertheless, it is called unworthy, it is in need of a good state and a savior. Wherefore to the One nothing, neither will therefore of anyone, but it is (as I might say) above the good: and it exists as good not for itself but for others, if only they are able to participate. Nor is there one intelligence within it, lest diversity arise from it. Again, nor is there any motion: for intelligence is posterior to motion. For what will it understand? Perhaps itself? But if it were so, before the understanding...
</unclear>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But that which is in another [is needy]; but the One is not in a divided thing as if it were the smallest part. It is the greatest of all, not in magnitude, but in power, so that those things after it have an indivisible power, and are themselves indivisible. We must also take it to be infinite, not by being inexhaustible in magnitude or number, but by the incomprehensibility of its power. For when you think of it as Intellect or God, it is more. And again,
<margin>B</margin> * even if you make it more in your thought than you imagined God himself to be, it is still more unified than your thought. For it is by itself, and nothing happens to it; it is faithful to its own pure self because it is in itself, where there is no running out. But it is necessary that before all causes, it should be the self-sufficiency of all things and that which all things desire to be. For whatever is many and not one, or becomes one from many, is in need. This essence [needs] to be one. But the One does not need itself; 
<margin>C</margin> it is. And let it not be many. * At least it needs to be one, and each of the things in it, being with the others and not by itself, is in need of the others. Both in each part and in the whole, such a thing goes about in need. If, therefore, something must be most self-sufficient, it must be the One, which is not only [sufficient] by itself, but is not needy toward anything else.
<margin>D</margin> Lest it should not be, or that it should be well, or that it should be established, for it is not the cause for others so that it should receive "well-being" from them; its "well-being" would then be outside itself, or its "well-being" would be by accident. For it itself is not [needy]. And how could there be pleasures for it? It does not need a foundation, nor is it able to carry itself; but that which remains elsewhere is soulless. It is a falling mass unless it be established. But other things are established through it, through which they also subsisted together. And it has that in which they were ordered.
<margin>E</margin> It is needy, and that which seeks the whole. But it is the cause. That which is needy [is so] because of the things after it, but it is without cause to itself. It is the needy of the causeless. But that which is needy, in whatever it has of a principle, is needy. If, then, the One were needy, it would not be the One. Clearly it would be needy by not being one. So it is needy because it is in need of a savior. Thus the Good belongs to the One. Or rather, there is no will in it, but it is "Super-Good" <note>original Greek: "ὑπεράγαθον"</note>. And it is not a good to itself,
<margin>F</margin> but a good to others, if anything is able to participate in it. Nor is there Intellect <note>original Greek: "νόησις" (noesis/thought)</note>, lest there be diversity, nor motion. For before motion and before Intellect [it is]; for what would it even think? Itself? For before thinking...

But indeed, the principle least of all needs those things which follow it: and so the principle of all things needs absolutely nothing. Now truly, that which is in itself the One by which [it is], will seek to be no longer further the One: it will therefore need a destroyer. Nevertheless, it is called unworthy; it is in need of a good state and a savior. For which reason nothing [is added] to the One, nor is there any will of anyone, but it is (so to speak) above the good: and it exists as a good not for itself, but for others, if only they can participate. Nor is there one intellect within, lest there be diversity. Again, there is no motion: for intellect is posterior to motion. For what will it understand? Perhaps itself? <meta>This page continues the discussion of the "One" (God) from Plotinus’s Enneads. Having established that the One is the source of all power and magnitude but remains simple, the text now addresses why the One does not "think" or "know" in the way humans or the Divine Intellect do, as such processes would imply a division between the knower and the known.</meta>

BOOK NINE.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...he would be ignorant and would need intelligence to fully know himself, despite being considered self-sufficient in himself. Therefore, even if he neither recognizes nor understands himself, there is no "ignorance" in him. For ignorance only occurs in relation to another, when one thing does not know another. But that which is solitary neither knows anything, nor has anything to be ignorant of. Rather, being one and (so to speak) most <margin>B</margin> united with itself, it surely does not need an understanding of itself. We must not even apply to it the concept of being "with itself," so that you may preserve its absolute unity. Indeed, we must entirely remove from it intelligence, consciousness, the awareness of its own state, the recognition of itself, and the perception of others. It is proper to think of God not according to the condition of a "thinker," but rather as the very act of intelligence itself <note>Plotinus argues the One is the source of thought, not a being that needs to process thoughts</note>. Yet, this supreme intelligence does not "think" in a human sense; it is the cause of thinking for others. The cause of all things is not the same as the things it causes. Therefore, we should not judge it to be merely the "good" that it provides to others, but rather it is "the Good" in a different sense, vastly more excellent than all other goods.

---

->### The Approach to God. Chapter VII.<-

> And though God is everywhere, he shines most clearly in the highest point of intelligence. To see this light, all forms—not only those we can imagine but even those we can understand—stand in the way like clouds. Therefore, shake all these away from you, so that with a serene mind you may happily perceive the divine light.

<margin>C</margin> If, because God is none of these things, you waver with an indefinite wandering of the mind, then at least fix your mental gaze on these truths, and from them return with your whole mind to God. Yet do not do so as if you were casting your thoughts outward. For God is not placed in some location so as to leave other things behind; rather, wherever there is something capable of touching him, God himself is present—he is only absent to those who cannot reach him. For just as in other matters it is impossible for someone who is thinking of one thing <margin>D</margin> and is totally occupied by it to understand another thing at the same time—but rather it is necessary to apply nothing else to the thing being understood so that it may be the thing understood itself—similarly here, it is impossible for one who holds the image of something else in the soul to understand God while that image is performing its own action. Nor, again, is it possible for a soul occupied and held by other things to be shaped by a contrary image. Just as they say of "matter" <note>original: *materia*. Plotinus references the philosophical concept of "prime matter" which must be formless to receive any shape</note> that it must be void of all qualities if it is to receive the forms of all things, so <margin>E</margin> much more must the soul become formless if it is to be free of every obstacle that might prevent it from being illuminated and filled to its desire by the very first nature of all. If this is so, it is worthwhile for the mind, separated from all external things, to turn itself entirely to the innermost depths and not be called back to anything external. It should ignore all things—first in its disposition, and then even in their forms <note>original: *speciebus*</note>. Ignorant <margin>F</margin> also of itself, it should lean upon the contemplation of the One and cling to it familiarly. And then, having conversed sufficiently with it, it may return as a messenger, if it can, to declare that union to others. In this way, perhaps, even Minos <note>The mythical King of Crete who was said to have received his laws directly from Zeus (Jove) in a cave</note> was once considered a familiar companion of Jove because he relied on such a conversation.

<summary>This page argues that God (the One) transcends thought and self-knowledge because he is the absolute cause of these things. It also provides a mystical guide for the soul to reach God by becoming "formless" and shedding all external images.</summary>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK VI.

...established laws in His likeness <note>Plotinus refers here to the legendary King Minos, who was said to have communed with Zeus to draft laws</note>, being clearly instructed by that divine communion to frame those laws. Perhaps, however, some soul might consider civil occupations less worthy of divine intimacy, if it preferred to remain in the heights. This indeed seems to happen rightly to one who has gazed most deeply. He says, therefore, that God is outside no one, but is within all, even though they do not know it. For they themselves flee outside of God, or rather, outside of themselves. Rightly, therefore, they cannot grasp Him whom they flee. And those who have already lost themselves cannot search for another. But even a son, placed outside himself by some madness, will not recognize his father; yet he who has learned to know himself will also rightly know from whence he comes.

---

->### The Approach to God. Chapter VIII.<-

> *God is like an individual and immobile center of the universe, upon whom and toward whom all things depend. The divine intellect and intellectual souls created from there have their own centers—that is, superior unities of essence. In divine intellects, therefore, beyond such a center, there exists one circle (that is, its own); but in the soul, beyond its own center, there are three circles: intellect, reason, and imagination. The center [of the soul] is always joined to the center of the universe. The intellectual circle perpetually revolves around the same; but the rational and imaginary circle revolves around its own center and the divine center. Sometimes it is, as it were, broken, and turns away at an angle while we lead a life similar to brute beasts, our reason not being turned toward God through the intellect; yet at least secretly we still revolve. It remains that some affection in reason itself may at times recall us to God: to whom we are coupled, because through essential unity we are joined to Him, enjoying Him far more deeply and fully within than is achieved through knowing. It is probable that, being joined by such a coupling, we shall never depart from there. The coupling is most firm when the incorporeal is joined to the incorporeal, provided that the one differed from the other only by formal diversity.*

---

<margin>C</margin>If any soul, therefore, knows itself at some other time, and recognizes that its motion is not straight (unless perhaps when it suffers some fracture), but that its natural motion is like a circular one around something—not something external, but around a center—and that the center is that from which the circle proceeds, it will surely move around that very thing from which it exists. And bringing itself toward that from every side, it will draw itself completely to that point to which it was fitting for all souls to bring themselves. The souls of the Gods are always carried there; and for that reason they are Gods, <margin>D</margin> because they are carried toward that: for God is whatever is joined to Him. But that which stands far off is man—and a "manifold" man and a beast <note>original Latin: "homo multiplex atque brutum." This refers to the human condition of being divided by many desires, unlike the simple unity of the divine</note>. Therefore, is that which is like the center of the soul the very thing we have studiously sought? But indeed, we must consider it to be something else, into which all things, like centers, concur. However, one must remember that the naming of this center and circle is brought in here according to a certain comparative analogy. <margin>E</margin> For the soul is not a circle in the way a geometric figure is, but because within it and around it is the ancient and principal nature. And from such a thing the soul depends, and even more so when the whole soul is separated [from the body]. But now, after some part of us is submerged in the body—just as if someone had his feet in the water, while the rest of his body was above the water—certainly by that very part which is not submerged by the body, being raised higher, we are joined through our center with Him who is, as it were, the center of all things; just as we are often <margin>F</margin> accustomed to fix the centers of many circles to the center of a surrounding and containing sphere. If, therefore, the circles of souls were corporeal circles, they would certainly revolve around a center in a specific location and shared space. But since souls...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <note>The following is a translation of the Greek parallel text</note> Minos, the best of men, as it is said, being mindful of Zeus, made [the laws]... and there is no touch there for the south wind... those laws... or even civil matters are not worthy of him... he wishes to remain above, which happens to the [gazer]... he says the One is in all for those who give themselves to it. They flee to the outside, or rather, outside of themselves. <margin>B</margin> Having lost [themselves], they seek another. But just as a [son] being in madness, did not [recognize his father]... but having learned himself, he will know also [whence he is].

<margin>C</margin> If any soul therefore knows itself [at some] time, and knows that its motion [is not straight], but only when it receives a "break," and its natural motion is like that in a circle around [something]... around a center [and the center is that from which it comes]... it will move around that from which it is. And [it will move], bringing itself toward [the center]... where indeed all [souls] go. And they are carried toward that... and being carried toward it, they are Gods. God is [that which is] <margin>D</margin> joined. But that which stands far off is [the mass of men], and a beast. Therefore, this [center] of the soul, is this the thing sought? And we must [consider] it into which all centers, as it were, [concur]... [by] analogy * the center... For the soul is not a circle in this way * and the [ancient nature] is in it and around it... from such a thing, and even more, because [it is separated]... <margin>E</margin> and now * in part we [are submerged] in the body, as if someone [had his feet]... and in the rest of the body he were above... by that which is not [submerged] by the body, being above... we join according to our own center... with the center of all, just as [we fix the centers] of the greatest circles to the center of the sphere that [contains them]... resting in the center. If indeed [they were] <margin>F</margin> corporeal circles, the psychic circles would be locally [positioned]... and placed toward the center... but since these souls are intelligible...

...are themselves intelligible, and that center is between them, and they revolve around such a center...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the mystical union between the soul and the One (God). Having established that God is the center around which all things revolve, the text now explains how the soul achieves contact with this center—not through physical movement, but through shedding "otherness" and joining the divine choral dance.</meta>

# BOOK NINE.

<note>This section translates the Greek and Latin parallel texts regarding the nature of the soul's union with the Divine.</note>

It must be understood that this union occurs through certain other powers <note>original Greek: δυνάμεσιν (dynameis)</note> by which the intellect is naturally moved toward that which it seeks to understand. This connection is more than a simple meeting; it is a presence characterized by likeness and a kind of identity. The soul is joined to its own kin with nothing separating them. For while physical bodies are prevented from merging with * <margin>other</margin> bodies by their very mass, incorporeal things are not divided by such obstacles. They are not separated by distance or location, but rather by "otherness" <note>The term "otherness" (alteritas) refers to the state of being different or alienated from the divine source</note> and difference. Therefore, when this difference is absent, those things which are no longer "other" are immediately present to one another. Since the Divine admits no "otherness" within itself, it is always present; we, however, are present to it only when we shed our own "otherness." The Divine does not seek us out to revolve around us; rather, we seek it so that we may revolve around it. While we always circle around the same center, we do not always look toward it. We are like a choir of singers who, though they stand in a circle around the <term>coryphaeus</term> <note>The leader or conductor of a Greek chorus</note>, might occasionally be distracted and look away, singing out of tune. But when they turn back toward the leader, they sing beautifully and truly belong to the circle. So it is with us: we always revolve around God, even when we are entirely dissolved * <margin>and even if we shall still be</margin> from the body and no longer know Him through the senses. Yet we do not always look toward Him. Only when we gaze directly into Him do we reach our desired end and find rest; then, we no longer sing out of tune, but truly perform a divine dance around Him.

---

### The Blessedness of the soul contemplating God. Chapter IX.

Just as all good things come from the First Good, so all love, toward whatever good it may be directed, is naturally kindled by that same source. Because our love finds no rest in any finite good, it holds that same Good as its final destination which it also had as its beginning. Just as the appetite is naturally built for the Good, it also demands a natural enjoyment—not merely an imaginary one or one consisting of simple knowledge, but one that truly affects our inner nature. This is evident in the senses and the body, but the natural and essential enjoyment of the First Good ought to be much deeper. It is not reached through simple intellect alone, but through our very nature; this enjoyment penetrates our "marrow" <note>meaning the very core of our being</note> more deeply than the intellect penetrates the senses. Thus, to enjoy God is not so much to *see* Him as it is to *touch* Him—not from the outside, but to glide into Him inwardly, to be divinely affected, and to "become God." Just as one who eats food is eventually transformed by that food (or perhaps vice versa). But, O Plotinus, since you have granted these points, you should also have granted that a soul once translated into God would never depart from Him. And a soul that is naturally fit to be turned toward God by its most intimate act, becoming God-like, is surely not fit to be transferred into the body of a brute animal by its own movement.

<margin>D</margin> **I**n this dance, the soul beholds the * <margin>pure</margin> fountain of life, the fountain of the mind, the principle of Being itself, the cause of the Good, and the root of the soul. These things do not flow out of God in a way that diminishes Him. For God is not a physical mass; if He were, the things generated from Him would be corruptible. In truth, they are eternal because their source remains always the same. He is not divided among them but remains whole even while producing them. Therefore, those things <margin>E</margin> also remain, just as light remains as long as the Sun remains. We are not cut off from Him, nor do we live apart, even though the intervening nature of the body has dragged us toward itself. For we are simultaneously breathed into by Him and preserved; He does not simply give us life and then stand apart, but rather He continually bestows it. As long as He remains what He is, we exist—or rather, we exist to the extent that we turn toward Him. Here, truly, lies our Good; to be far from Him is nothing else than to "be less." Here the soul finds rest; here only...

<column-break/>

<summary>Plotinus and Ficino describe the soul's union with God as a rhythmic dance where "otherness" is shed to achieve a state of "touching" the divine source. Ficino adds a Christian-influenced critique of Plotinus, arguing that a soul capable of such union should never be demoted to an animal form.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul’s ascent to the Divine. Having described the "choral dance" around the center in the previous section, Plotinus now explores the nature of true life in union with God and the distinction between heavenly and earthly love (Venus).</meta>

-># PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.<-

<margin>A</margin> The soul is free from evils once it has hurried back to that place which is free from evils. There, it truly understands and is no longer subject to any sufferings; there alone, it truly happens to live. For what is called "living" here on earth without God is but a trace of life imitating that life which is above. To live in that higher realm is an act of the mind <note>original Latin: "mentis est actus"; Greek: "ενέργεια νοῦ" (energeia nou)</note>. This activity even generates "Gods" while it touches God in a certain hidden and tranquil contact. It generates beauty, it generates justice, and it generates virtue itself. For the soul, pregnant with God, gives birth to these things.

<margin>B</margin> This is the beginning and the end for the soul. It is the beginning because it proceeds from there; it is the end because its Good is located there. Having arrived there, the soul becomes what it truly was. For our life here, in the midst of worldly things, is a kind of fall, an exile, and a "loss of wings" <note>A reference to Plato’s *Phaedrus*, where the soul loses its feathers and falls to earth</note>. That our Good consists in that higher place is indicated by the love which is innate to the soul—just as Love is joined to souls in both writings and myths. Specifically, because the soul is something other than God, and yet originates from Him, it necessarily loves Him. Indeed, when it lives there, it possesses a heavenly love; but here, that love becomes common and vulgar.

<margin>C</margin> For in that higher realm, the Heavenly Venus <note>original: "Cœlestis Venus"; Greek: "Ἀφροδίτη οὐρανία". In Neoplatonism, this represents the higher, intellectual love of the soul for the Divine</note> reigns; but here, Venus becomes vulgar, appearing as if she were (so to speak) adulterated. Every soul is a "Venus," as is hinted at by the stories of the birth of Venus and the Love <note>Eros</note> who was born alongside her. Therefore, the soul in its natural state loves God, desiring to be joined with Him, like a beautiful maiden moved by an honorable love for a noble father.

<margin>D</margin> But after the soul has fallen into the world of generation <note>The physical world of birth and decay</note> and is deceived by various "marriages," it exchanges its divine love for a fleeting one. Then, separated as if from a father, it behaves with unrestrained passion. But eventually, growing to hate these human excesses and purifying itself of them, it returns once more to its father, having attained a blessed state. If anyone is ignorant of this state of affection or passion, let them reflect on it by considering human loves—how great a happiness it is thought to be when one attains what they ardently love. Yet, those things we love here are mortal and harmful; they are mere images, and our love for them eventually turns into its opposite. This is because what we chased was not the truly Beloved, nor was it our Good, nor that which we naturally long for.

<margin>E</margin> In that higher realm, however, the truly Beloved flourishes. There, one may be joined with it, participate in it, and truly possess it, for it is not governed by external flesh. Whoever has known this certainly knows what I am saying: that the soul then leads another life. As it advances, and having now progressed and finally attained God, it clearly recognizes—having been completely affected—that the Giver of true life is present.

<margin>F</margin> And truly, there is no need for anything further there. On the contrary, one must set aside everything else and stand in Him alone, becoming God alone, having utterly cut away the remaining things that cling around us. Therefore, we must hasten to depart from here, grieving that we live partially bound to these things, so that we may embrace ourselves entirely with the whole soul, touching nothing else. In that state of living, one can see both Him and oneself: seeing oneself illuminated, full of intellectual light.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...outside of evils, having run back to the place of... and there it thinks, and... and to truly live is there. For that which is not with God is a trace of life imitating that... life. The activity of the mind. And the activity in the quiet contact with that... the soul is pregnant, being filled with God. And...

<margin>B</margin> ...beginning and end. The beginning, because from there... the good is there. And being there, it becomes... what it was. But the being here in these things... flight, and a loss of wings. It shows that... that place. And the love of the soul... according to which love is also yoked... in writings and in myths, since... from that, and from that it loves, and... there, it has the heavenly love.

<margin>C</margin> ...becomes common. For she is... heavenly. But here she becomes... having been [soiled?], since every soul... it hints at the things of Aphrodite <note>The Greek name for Venus</note>... and the Love born with her... the soul having its nature... God... like a maiden [desiring] beautiful... love. But when it comes into generation...

<margin>D</margin> ...be deceived, having received another mortal... the father is insulted. Having hated... the insults here, having purified... the father again [from] falling, which... the passion is unknown to... let him remember from the loves here... having succeeded. Those things which are most loved... the things loved, mortal and harmful...

<margin>E</margin> ...loves, and it changes because it was... nor our good. But that... which is the true... as the beloved... to be with, having shared in it and... not embracing flesh from the outside... [he who] knows, knows what I say, how the soul... has then. And proceeding, and already...

<margin>F</margin> ...having partaken of Him, so as to know... the provider of true [life] is present... no longer. But everything to the contrary... to put away and to stand in this alone, and... having cut away the rest as much as... to go out not needing... to be indignant at being bound to the other... let us embrace them, with which nothing... with which we do not touch the divine. To see... both Him and oneself, as it is right to see... radiant. Full of intellectual light...

Plotinus argues that true life is found only in union with God, where the soul sheds its worldly attachments to be filled with divine light.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Plotinus’s famous treatise on "The Good or the One" (Ennead VI.9). Having discussed the soul’s preparation, the text now reaches the climax: the mystical union where the soul becomes one with the Divine. It concludes with a personal prayer from the translator, Marsilio Ficino.</meta>

# BOOK NINE.

Light itself, pure, clear, weightless, seen as God—or rather, being God. Having appeared then; but if the soul should again become heavy, it is as if that light fades away.

<margin>* so that</margin>
Why then does it not remain there? Either because it has not yet departed entirely from this world. There is a part of the vision that is poor, as if troubled—not that the body itself is a single disturbance, or that anything seen is a disturbance, but rather the "other thing" <note>likely referring to the lower soul or the discursive mind</note> prevents the vision when the one who has seen tries to explain it. It arises from the signs within the soul, its habits and its faiths. For it is of the soul's reasoning. But to see and to have seen is no longer reason, but something greater than reason, and before reason, and upon reason, through which the seen object exists. Therefore, having seen himself—

<margin>* then the one who saw, shall touch such a thing</margin>
* See then, when he sees the mixture, or rather when he stands with such a self. And he will perceive such a thing, having become simple. Perhaps, however, one should not even say "he will see." Regarding the "thing seen"—if indeed we must speak of these two as separate, the one seeing and the thing seen—they are not two, but both are one. The statement is bold, for then he does not see even while he sees.

<margin>* neither does the one seeing distinguish</margin>
* Neither does the one seeing distinguish, nor does he imagine two. But as if having become another, and not himself. He belongs to that place, and having become part of that—

<margin>* later</margin>
* It is one, just as if one joined a center to a center. For even here, when things come together, they are one. They are two only when they are separated. So also we now speak of "the other." For this reason, the spectacle is extremely difficult to describe. For how could anyone report it as "another," when, while he was seeing it, he did not see it as another, but as entirely one with himself?

<column-break/>

A But truly that light itself is pure, weightless, sublime, then made God—indeed, rather already existing as such—then indeed kindled. But if the burdened soul should slide back down from there, it is as if the light is again extinguished.

### The Enjoyment of God. Chapter X.

> The soul, through a perfect preparation, finally becomes closest to God. From the infinite Good, which possesses an entirely infinite power of attraction, the soul conceives an infinite love toward Him. On both sides, therefore, it is so transformed into God that to those looking on, it no longer appears as a soul, but as God—just as if air were thinned into light, which perhaps already happened to fire from the beginning. Hence that saying of our Paul: *He who adheres to God, becomes one spirit.* <note>Reference to 1 Corinthians 6:17</note> Plotinus indeed conceded that our intellect, once placed in God, is never diverted from there. He also concedes that reason is turned toward the intellect when, having set aside its wandering discourse, the argumentation within it suddenly becomes intuition. He was even going to concede that reason remains there perpetually, especially when completely freed from the body, which he seems to have touched upon here in passing.

B Why then does the soul not remain there? Surely because it has not yet emigrated from here entirely. But there will be a time when a continuity of gazing will be granted, specifically when the body will in no way disturb the vision. However, it is not the part that sees which is properly disturbed, but "something else." Yet even he who was seeing is especially vacant from the vision when he is not vacant from science <note>referring to discursive knowledge or logical proofs</note>, which is occupied with demonstrations, conjectures, and the wandering of reason. But that which is C "to see" and the "seer" himself, is no longer a kind of reason, but something more excellent than reason, and preceding reason. And if in any way it exists in reason, it is there rather as the thing seen. Whoever, therefore, sees himself, certainly while he sees, he inspects himself as being so affected; or rather, he will cling to himself as so disposed, and will perceive himself as such, having now been made entirely simple. Perhaps D one should not even say "to see," but rather "to become" the thing seen itself. Since we must think of these as two things—namely the seer and the seen—they are not both one; although in speech, he <note>Plotinus</note> seems bolder here. Then, surely, he does not properly "see," nor does he distinguish as a "seer," nor does he imagine two things: but the soul, having then become as if another, is no longer itself, nor does it merely bring itself there, but it has given itself to Him, and having become entirely His, it straightway escapes into being one, just as if joining a center to a center. For here, things that run together become one, E but they are two when they are pulled apart from each other. Thus we also now speak of "the other." For this reason, this spectacle is very difficult to put into words. For in what way shall anyone pronounce it as "another," which, while he saw it, he did not see as another, but as inwardly one with himself?

### The Enjoyment of God. Chapter XI.

> By the power of the One itself, union occurs everywhere: for no other reason do similar things unite more easily than because they are "one" in quality. The soul, therefore, is then finally united most closely with the one principle of all things when it most especially becomes "one" within itself. That is achieved when, stripped of the multitude belonging to the imagination, reason, and intelligence, it escapes into its own sole unity, and through this very thing, by means of an amorous affection, it enjoys the divine unity, joining its own center with the center of the universe. Plotinus asserts that a soul so affected has transferred its intellectual form to unity; and again has similarly transferred its rational form to the intellectual. Hence, he was going to concede that the rational should now be held as the intellectual, and that this, like the other, would remain there perpetually: especially since he says the soul, established there in an immobile state, has become as if "stability" itself, and has transcended not only its mobile nature but also the primary essence itself, where it makes an end to its motions and labors. We certainly, O Magnanimous Lorenzo <note>referring to Lorenzo de' Medici, Ficino's patron</note>, now place an end to our labors on Plotinus, God helping us: thus humbly adoring the omnipotent God.

> We give thanks to You, highest God, illuminator of minds and author of all good things, because You have supplied us with Your grace, beyond our merit, to complete so great a work. I pray, most merciful God, for true prosperity for the pious Reader: pour in, moreover, a light by which he may be able to discern true things from false, lest he ever disagree with Your will, either in meditating or in acting.

It concludes with Marsilio Ficino’s formal completion of the translation and a prayer of thanksgiving to God and his patron, Lorenzo de' Medici.</summary>

# PLOTINUS: ENNEADS, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin> This is what the institution of such mysteries indicates when it forbids revealing them to those not yet initiated or purified. Just as it is not lawful to explain it, so it forbids opening the divine to anyone else, except to the one who has had the good fortune to see it. Since, therefore, there were not two, but the seer himself was one with that which was seen—as if it were not a vision in the proper sense, but a union—if anyone who reached it, while being thoroughly blended with it, should perhaps remember it, he will have <margin>B</margin> an image of it within himself. But he himself was one, having no difference within himself toward himself, nor again regarding other things. For nothing was moving within him: neither anger nor the appetite of the soul for anything higher was present—not even reason, nor any intelligence, nor (if it is even lawful to say so) even he himself. But as if snatched away, or completely occupied by God in a safe retreat and a tranquil state, he was now established <margin>C</margin> as utterly immobile, not deviating from his own essence, nor turning back around himself, since he rested completely and had become, as it were, "rest" itself. Now indeed he does not even dwell upon the beautiful, but has already transcended beauty itself. He also surpasses the choir of virtues—just as if someone had entered the <term>adytum<note>The adytum is the innermost, most sacred sanctuary of a temple, where only priests were permitted.</note></term> of a sacred shrine and left behind all the statues arranged in the temple. Upon exiting the sanctuary, those statues are the first things he encounters again <margin>D</margin> after that innermost sight. After this, the interaction is not with the statues or images, but rather with the thing itself which the statues and images represent; these should certainly be judged as secondary sights. But perhaps that "thing" should not be called a sight; rather, it is a different way of seeing. You see, it is a departure from oneself <note>original: "exitus", a "going out" or ecstasy</note>, a spreading out, a miraculous progression, a desire to touch, and <margin>E</margin> finally, stillness. There, every thought strives for union, provided one can look upon what is in the inner sanctuary. But he who looks in any other way carries away nothing. Therefore, the wise ones among the prophets involve such divine things in obscure imitations, showing by what means that God is seen. But the wise <margin>F</margin> priest, explaining the wrapped mystery and entering the sanctuary, attains true contemplation there. If he has not yet entered, then thinking of the sanctuary as something invisible, a fountain, and a principle, he will know it simply as a principle. But having entered there, he sees the principle itself and is joined to it; like perceives like, neglecting none of the divine things that the soul is able to attain. Now indeed, before the vision itself, what remains of the vision—of the Truth that now transcends all—is that which surpasses all things. For the nature of the soul will never reach absolute non-being; but having fallen downward, it falls into evil and thus is judged to rush into non-being. This is not because it plunges into total non-existence, but if it takes the path contrary to this, the soul will not reach another thing, but—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> This is surely what the command of the mysteries intends to show: not to reveal them to the uninitiated. For since the divine is not to be spoken of, it is forbidden to reveal it to others, except to the one who has been fortunate enough to see it. Since then they were not two, but the seer was himself one with the seen—as if not having been seen, but having been united—if one should remember, having been mingled with that, <margin>B</margin> he would have an image within himself. And he was also within himself, having no difference in himself toward himself, nor toward other things. For neither was anything stirred in him—not anger, nor desire for anything else was in him, having ascended. Neither was there any reason or thought. Nor, in short, was he himself, if one must say even this. But as if seized or in a divine frenzy, he came into a quiet, solitary state, <margin>C</margin> unmoved in his essence, nowhere swerving, nor turning about himself, standing entirely still and becoming "standing" itself. Having already transcended the beautiful, even above the gods. Having also bypassed the choir of virtues, just as one who enters into the inner sanctuary <note>original: "adytum"</note> leaves behind the statues in the shrine. These become the first things he meets again upon leaving the sanctuary, after the sight within <margin>D</margin> and the communion there. Not with a statue or image, but with "It." These other things are secondary sights. That [union], perhaps, was not a sight, but another way of seeing: an ecstasy, a simplification, and a giving of oneself. A longing for touch, and stillness. And a thinking-around for fitting [union], if one is to behold what is in the sanctuary. But if one looks otherwise, nothing is present. These things, then, are imitations which the wise among the prophets <margin>E</margin> hint at in riddles, showing how that God is seen. And the sacred priest, understanding the riddles, makes the true sight once he has arrived at the sanctuary. Even if he has not yet arrived, but considers the sanctuary to be some form, and a fountain and source, he will know it as a source, as he sees it. And like [perceives] like, leaving behind nothing of the divine things as much as a soul is able. <margin>F</margin> And before the vision, there meets him what remains of Being. What remains is for one who has surpassed all things, that which is before all. For the nature of the soul will never go into total non-existence. But as for going downward, it will come into evil. And into non-being, the complete non-being there. But running the opposite way, it will come not into another thing...

<summary>This page concludes Plotinus’s description of the soul’s mystical union with 'The One,' using the metaphor of a priest entering a temple's inner sanctuary. It describes 'ecstasy' not as a feeling, but as a literal 'standing outside oneself' where the distinction between the seer and the seen vanishes.</summary>

# BOOK NINE.

<column-break/>

<margin>* He associates with <note>original: πρεσομιλᾶ</note></margin>
himself; and thus, since he is not in another, he is not to be judged as being in nothing at all, but rather as remaining within himself. But to be in oneself alone, and not in <term>Being<note>In Neoplatonism, "Being" refers to the realm of Intellect and forms; God (The One) is considered "Beyond Being."</note></term>, is nothing other than to be in That One. For he himself becomes something that is not <term>essence<note>The fundamental nature or substance of a thing.</note></term>, but is even superior to essence, insofar as he indeed *associates with* that One. If, therefore, anyone should see himself having become this, he will possess himself as an image of that One. And if he should pass beyond himself, as an image led back to its archetype, he will have reached the final goal of his journey. But if at any time he should fall away from this vision, by once again awakening the virtue within him and noticing himself to be <margin>* adorned in every way</margin> thoroughly adorned with these virtues, he will be lifted up again through virtue, proceeding into the <term>Mind<note>The "Nous" or Divine Intellect, the first emanation from the One.</note></term> and through wisdom toward the One itself. This, then, is the life of the gods and of divine and happy men: a release from all other things here below, a life that takes no pleasure in the things of this world—a flight of the alone to the alone.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
himself; and thus, since he is not in another, he must not be judged on that account to be in nothing at all, but rather to consist in himself. But to be in oneself alone, and not in <term>being</term>, is nothing else than to be entirely in God. For he himself becomes someone who is not essence, but is even superior to essence, insofar as he indeed infuses himself entirely into God. If, therefore, anyone should ever see himself having become this, he will certainly possess himself as a kind of image of that One. <margin>B</margin> And if he should pass beyond himself, as an image led back all the way to its exemplar <note>original: exemplar; the perfect original pattern of which the soul is a copy.</note>, he will have finally attained the very end of his journey. But if at any time he should fall away from this contemplation, by once again awakening the virtue implanted within him and noticing himself to be thoroughly adorned, he will be lifted up again to the heights, namely proceeding through virtue into the mind, and through wisdom progressing toward God. This, then, is the life of the gods and of divine and happy men: utterly disregarding human pleasures, and a flight of the alone to the alone <note>original: fuga solius ad solum; one of the most famous phrases in mystical philosophy.</note>.

*This page features a detailed woodcut illustration at its center. Within a highly decorative <term>Mannerist cartouche</term>—an ornamental frame characterized by intricate architectural scrolls, garlands of fruit, and symbolic masks—is an oval medallion. It depicts a woman in classical robes holding a lit oil lamp in one hand and a scepter in the other, representing the illumination of the mind and the authority of truth.*

->Your word is a lamp for my feet<-
<note>original: "LVCERNA PEDIBVS MEIS VERBVM TVVM"; This is a translation of Psalm 119:105. In the context of a philosophical work, it suggests that the "Word" or "Logos" <note>original: 'Verbum'</note> acts as a guiding light for the reader’s intellectual and spiritual path.</note>

<summary>The final page of the work presents a printer’s emblem featuring a biblical motto from the Psalms. The imagery of the lamp and the "Word" symbolizes the enlightenment provided by the philosophical text.</summary>

# The Binding of the Volume

The book is encased in a <term>blind-stamped pigskin binding</term> <note>A technique where metal tools are pressed into damp leather to create impressions without the use of gold or color. Pigskin was a favored material for its durability and its ability to hold fine detail.</note>. The exterior shows signs of its long history, including significant wear and a large dark stain on the lower-left quadrant, likely caused by old water or oil damage.

The decorative scheme consists of concentric rectangular borders. The outer frames are adorned with Renaissance-style "rolls" featuring floral motifs and small medallions containing portrait busts. At the heart of the front cover is a central rectangular panel containing a portrait of **Duke Christoph of Württemberg**. He is shown in full armor, holding a sword across his chest, symbolizing his role as a Christian prince and protector. The year **1568** is stamped in the upper corners of this central panel.

Below the Duke’s image is a five-line inscription identifying the figure:

->BY THE GRACE OF GOD · CHRISTOPHER<-
<note>original: "VON GOTTES GNADEN · CHRISTOPH"</note>
->DUKE · OF · WÜRTTEM-<-
<note>original: "HERTZOG · ZU · WIRTEN-"</note>
->BERG · AND · TECK · COUNT · OF<-
<note>original: "BERG · UND · THECK · GRAVE · ZU"</note>
->MONTBÉLIARD · AT THE AGE OF · 53<-
<note>original: "MUMPELGART · SEINES · ALTERS · LIII ·"; Mumpelgard is the German name for Montbéliard, a county in present-day France that was a territory of the House of Württemberg.</note>
->YEARS<-
<note>original: "IAHR"</note>

This style of decoration is known as a <term>supralibros</term> <note>A mark of ownership or patronage, such as a coat of arms or a portrait, applied to the outside of a book's cover.</note>. Duke Christoph (1515–1568) was a pivotal leader of the Reformation in Germany, and his appearance on this binding suggests the book was produced or bound during the final year of his life, perhaps for a library under his patronage.

<summary>This page describes the ornate 16th-century pigskin binding of the volume, featuring a blind-stamped portrait and the titles of Duke Christoph of Württemberg. The binding identifies the book’s association with the ducal court and the Protestant Reformation in Germany.</summary>
